# Compendium Theologiae Positivae


## 1 Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology

[They] understood [it] as θείων, i.e., concerning the generation, nature, and worship of the gods. Aristotle: "Thales (he says) [held] water to be the principle of nature for moist things. And there are some who think that even the most ancient [thinkers], and those long before the present generation, and the first to theologize, held such opinions about nature; for they made Oceanus and Tethys the fathers of generation, etc." (Metaphys. I, 3.) CICERO: "In the beginning, those who are called theologians count three Joves." (De N. D. III, 21.) EUSEBIUS: "All theology spoken of outside the Church concerning God... is improper." (In Psalm, in collect, nova Montefalc. T. I. p. 313.)

θεολογία is an abstract noun, and, if you look at the grammatical derivation, it descends from the concrete θεολόγος; although, by attending to the logical denomination, the concrete or denominative [form] may have its appellation from the abstract, as from a denominating form. See the blessed Jac. Martini, LL. theol. disp. I. th. 9. p. 3. Now, he is called θεολόγος to whom the λόγος περί τού θεού is adjacent or inherent. Thus the name theologian is accepted in the inscription of the Apocalypse. Thus in Lactantius, *De ira Dei* cap. XI. p. m. 638. and August. L. XVIII. d. C. D. cap. XIV. Tom. VI. Opp. p. m. 620. Conf. the blessed Musaeus, *Introd. in theol.* p. 2. N. Hunnius: "Form is the internal cause, through which a thing is what it is, or which gives being to a thing." (Canones logici. Wittebergae, 1621. p. 176.) Calovius: "As far as the sacred use of the Church (of theology) is concerned, that name is found in the designation of the author of the Apocalypse, who is inscribed as θεολόγος in the title of the book—whether this proceeded from the author himself or not is in doubt; which name the Doctors wish to be assigned peculiarly to John, because he, above others, asserts and confirms the divinity of the Son of God." (Isag. ad ss. th. Ed. 2. 1665. I. 8. sq.) Athanasius: "Thus says also the theologian man: 'In the beginning was the Word.'" (C. gentes or. Opp. ed. Bonutius. I. f. 35.)

Lactantius: "All those who are worshipped as gods were men, and the same were the first and greatest kings; but who is ignorant that they were endowed with divine honors after death, either on account of their virtue, because they had benefited the human race...? Which, when the most ancient writers of Greece, whom they call θεολόγους, as well as the Romans, following and imitating the Greeks, teach." (De ira Dei c. 11.) Augustinus: "During the same interval of time there existed poets who were also called theologians, because they made poems about the gods; but about such gods who, although they were great men, were nevertheless men... Nor could even they themselves abstain from the fabulous disgrace of their gods, Orpheus, Musaeus, Linus. But those theologians worshipped gods, they were not worshipped as gods." (De Civit. D. L. XVIII, 14.)

Thus Augustin. L. VIII. de C. D. cap. 1. p. m. 87.: By the Greek word (theology) we understand to be signified a reason or discourse concerning divinity. For although theology, as to the thing itself, is not only λόγος περί τού θεού, but also άπο τού θεού, χαί πρός τον θεόν, nevertheless the force of the word does not signify all these things equally as it does that one; but the name θεού in composition with the name λόγος denotes the object, just as φύσις, αρετή, άστρα [do] in the compounds φυσιολογία, άρετολογία, αστρολογία. Compare the blessed Jac. Martin. l. c. § 12. 13. 14. p. 3. 4., the blessed Gerh. in Exeg. LL. p. 1., Musaeus in Introd. p. 1. Calovius: "The name of God in this composition of the word properly denotes God, but under some breadth, not only viewed by reason of nature or essence, but also by reason of works, or as divine things are simultaneously connoted." (Isagog. I, 6.) ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

For men are not usually called theologians simply because of any thought or discourse about God or divine things (even if they might perhaps be said ϑεολογεῖν), but rather those who, by virtue of a habit, are able and accustomed to reason or discourse about God. When the doctrine of God, by which God and divine things are proposed and explained, is also called theology in the nominative case, it is a metonymical expression, not a proper one. For the name of the cause is put for the effect. See the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* p. 3; the blessed Koenig, *Compend. theol. pos.* p. 4, § 27.

N. Hunnius: "A habit is a quality acquired by frequent exercises (and such a readiness, by which we easily and promptly perform those things which were previously performed with more difficulty and with trouble), so confirmed that it cannot be removed without the greatest change." (*Canones log.* p. 426 sq.) So that it may be a science, or a habit analogous to science.

However, the knowledge of God that falls to simpler men, unskilled in teaching, is not accustomed to denominate them theologians. Thus, the blessed Theologians of Leipzig, in the *Append. Consil. Dedek.* fol. 137 A, warn that no one is properly called a theologian on account of some knowledge of the Word of God, namely because theology properly so-called, besides apprehensive and judicial cognition, also comprehends the end, which is to instruct, or at least to render one fit to instruct man for the attainment of eternal salvation. Cf. the blessed Meisner, *P. III. Ph. S.* p. 104.

For to the habit of the mind is required τὸ ἀληϑεύειν, i.e., to state the truth about its object, by affirming or denying.

And therefore, in this place, we do not concern ourselves with the diverse kinds of pagan theology, full of lies and impious superstitions: μυϑικόν or fabulous, in which the poets were occupied, and πολιτικόν or civil, in which the priests were occupied.

Indeed, even the φυσικόν or natural, which the philosophers claimed for themselves, although it agrees in name with the natural theology which we praise in the following §, nevertheless, as it is found among the pagan philosophers, it is contaminated by not a few errors and is not entirely worthy of the name of theology.

Whence also Clement of Alexandria calls that which absolutely deserves this name ϑεολογίαν ἀληϑῆ καὶ ὀρϑήν, right and true, *L. V. Strom.* f. m. 569 A, 574 B. By which reasoning, at the same time, the entire ματαιολογία of the heretics is removed. Cf. Gerhard in *Exeg.* § 13, 14, p. 6, 7, and the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* p. 3, 4.

Augustine: "They call the first kind *mythicon*, which poets use most; *physicon*, which philosophers use; *civile*, which peoples use. In the first, which I mentioned, there are many things invented against the dignity and immortal nature of the gods. For in this, one god is born from a head, another from a thigh, another from drops of blood; in this, the gods have stolen, have committed adultery, have served man; finally, in this, all things are attributed to the gods which can fall not only to a man, but even to the most contemptible man... The second kind is that about which philosophers have left many books; in which it is discussed who the gods are, where they are, what kind they are, of what nature, from what time, whether they have existed from eternity, or whether they are from fire, as Heraclitus believes, or from numbers, as Pythagoras, or from atoms, as Epicurus says, and so on; things which ears can bear more easily within the walls of a school than outside in the forum. ... The third kind is that which citizens in cities, especially priests, ought to know and administer. In which it is determined which gods it is fitting for each person to worship publicly, and what rites and sacrifices to perform. ... The first theology is most accommodated to the theater, the second to the world, the third to the city." (*De Civitate Dei*, VI, 5.)

Calovius: "The term theology is used in various ways: 1. άκΰρως and καταχρηστικάς, improperly and abusively, regarding false theology, both that which is occupied with falsely so-called gods, such as the theology of the Gentiles, and that which indeed proposes the true God, but not truly, such as the theology of heretics; 2. κυρίως and γνησίως, properly and truly, regarding true theology, which proposes God as He has revealed Himself... For although the use of the Greek word among the pagans may seem older, it is no more proper than the gods of the Gentiles are proper gods." (Isag. I, 12.)

Quenstedtius: "The distinction of theology into true and false is nominal only and merely or purely equivocal. For false theology, which is also called opinionative, participates in the name of theology only and is called so only καταχρηστικάς, since it should rather be called ματαιολογία and ψευδολογία from 1 Tim. 4:2 and Tit. 1:10, and it is no more theology than a painted horse is a horse." (Th. did.-pol. P. I. c. 1. s. 1. th. 2. f. 3.)

They call it the theology of wayfarers (viatorum) otherwise, inasmuch as they call this life a way, by which one tends toward the goal or the heavenly fatherland. See below at § 5, note b.

For although the most exact knowledge of GOD exists in God Himself, and no less in Christ as man through the communication of divine idioms by virtue of the personal union, and the angels confirmed in good and the blessed humans also know God more perfectly than any of us; yet because the usage of speech does not allow that for this reason either God, or Christ, or the blessed humans, or the angels should be called theologians, it easily appears that this signification is left here, which otherwise obtains when we say "theology of wayfarers" with the addition.

Meanwhile, that knowledge which God has of Himself is called by the authors (looking not so much to the usage of speech as to the force of the meaning according to the reason of the etymology) archetypal theology (αρχέτυπος), since it does not depend on another knowledge of God in another subject, as if from an exemplary cause; rather, that knowledge of God and divine things which angels and humans have by divine benefit—and which is therefore called ectypal (εχτυπος)—imitates it as a form and exemplar, albeit in a lesser degree of perfection (which is not unusual otherwise in ectypes).

Conf. the blessed Mari. 1. c. disp. II. § 23. sqq. pag. 27., the blessed Gerh. in Exeg. § 15. pag. 7., the blessed Himmel. Syntagm. pag. 2. § 10. 11. 12.

But the knowledge of God and divine things which is in Christ according to the human nature through the communication of idioms by virtue of the personal union, since it is the very infinite science which Christ has from eternity according to the divine nature, viewed in relation to God as a certain object, is indeed archetypal theology itself, not another or ectypal, although it does not belong to the human nature subjectively, but communicatively, not of itself, but because of the personal union.

Augustinus: „Mythicon (genus) appellant, quo maxime utuntur poetae, physicon, quo philosophi, civile, quo populi. Primum, quod dixi, in eo sunt multa contra dignitatem et naturam immortalem ficta. In hoc enim est, ut deus alius ex capite, alius ex femore sit, alius ex guttis sanguinis natus; in hoc, ut dii furati sint, ut adulteraverint, ut servierint homini; denique in hoc omnia diis adtribuuntur, quae non modo in hominem, sed etiam quae in contemtissimum hominem cadere possunt. . . Secundum genus est, de quo multos libros philosophi reliquerunt; in quibus est, dii qui sint, ubi, quod genus, quale, a quonam tempore, an a sempiterno fuerint, an ex igne sint, ut credit Heraclitus, an ex numeris, ut Pythagoras, an ex atomis, ut ait Epicurus, sic alia; quae facilius intra parietes in schola, quam extra in foro ferre possunt aures. . . Etsi enim exactissima cognitio DEI in ipso Deo, nec minus in Chiristo homine per communicationem divinorum idiomatum vi unionis personalis locum habeat, angeli quoque in bono confirmati et homines beati Deum perfectius, quam quisquam nostrum, cognoscant; quia tamen usus loquendi non fert, ut propterea vel Deus, vel Christus, vel beati homines, aut angeli theologi dicantur, facile apparet, eam significationem hic relinqui, quae alias obtinet, quando cum addito theologiam viatorum dicimus.

Interim illa cognitio, quam Deus de se ipso habet, ab auctoribus (non tam ad usum loquendi, quam ad vim significandi pro ratione etymi spectantibus) theologia αρχέτυπος dicitur, quippe quae non dependeat ab alia cognitione Dei in subjecto alio, tanquam ab exemplari causa; ipsam potius, tanquam formam et exemplar, licet in minori perfectionis gradu (quod nec alias in ectypis insolens est) imitetur ea cognitio Dei ac rerum divinarum, quam angeli atque homines habent ex divino beneficio quaeque ideo εχτυπος dicitur.

Conf. b. Mari. 1. c. disp. II. § 23. sqq. pag. 27., b. Gerh. in Exeg. § 15. pag. 7., b. Himmel. Syntagm. pag. 2. § 10. 11. 12.

Quae vero in Christo secundum humanam naturam est per communicationem idiomatum ex vi unionis personalis cognitio Dei et rerum divinarum, cum sit ipsa scientia infinita, quam Christus secundum divinam naturam ab aeterno habet, spectata in ordine ad Deum, tanquam certum objectum, utique est ipsa theologia αρχέτυπος, non alia aut έχτυπος-, licet humanae naturae non competat subjective, sed communicative, non ex se, sed propter unionem personalem.


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: However, that habitual knowledge of God which is naturally in the H

However, that habitual knowledge of God which is naturally in the H. C. N. (Human Nature of Christ), just as it is rightly called ectypal, so it is rightly distinguished from the theology of union.

See the blessed J. F. Koenig in Theol. pos. pag. 2. § 15., and especially the blessed Musaeus Introd. Cap. I. § 4. sqq. to the end, pag. 4. to 23.

Quenstedtius: "Archetypal theology is substance and, as to the thing itself, the infinite essence of God; ectypal is a habit and is contained in the genus of quality. Archetypal theology (αρχέτυπος) is the origin and principle of all wisdom; but ectypal (έκτυπος) is its απόρροια καϊ απαύγασμα, a certain emanation and reflection or image... Archetypal theology (αρχέτυπος) is not only in God, but is God Himself, who here is wondrously the object of knowledge (επιστητόν), the knower (επιστήμων), and the knowledge (επιστήμη)." ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

the one who knows, the knowing, and the knowledge—that is, the subject itself which knows, the object itself which is known, and the knowledge itself, or the theological thing, the theologian, and theology. For in God, to be, to know, and to be wise are the same. Since archetypal theology is essential to the divine nature, therefore, just as the essence of God itself is, so this θεοσοφία is common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We prove this thesis from Matt. 11:27 and 1 Cor. 2:10, 11. (L. c. th. 3. 4. f. 5.)

Rudelbach: "I do not know whether anyone has drawn attention to the scriptural basis for this division (into archetypal and ectypal) of this concept of theology. Yet, where else could it be sought than in the words of the Lord in Matt. 11:27: 'No one knows the Son except the Father; and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him,' as well as in the apostolic concept of the ongoing μεταμόρφωσις of all believers, and consequently also of the New Testament teachers, into the image of the Lord, whose glory they behold as in a mirror (κατοπτριζόμενοι, 2 Cor. 3:18)—by which word the Apostle surely did not designate merely a province of the Christian life, but the whole life in Christ, and therefore also the condition of true theology as the pinnacle of the same?" (Zeitschrift. 1848, I, 7.)

There is a peculiar acceptance of the word θεολογία among ecclesiastical writers, by which it denotes a part of sacred doctrine, contrasted with another, which they call οἰκονομία. For by the name of the former is denoted that which concerns the essence, persons, and attributes of God; the latter, however, deals with the incarnation and office of Christ, the Son of God. See Greg. Nazianz. Orat. XXXVIII. on the Nativity of Christ or Theophany; Basil, Ep. CXLI.; Cyril, L. I. in Joh.

Chrysostom: "The former (the first three evangelists) flashed the οἰκονομία, but the latter (John) thundered the θεολογία." (Homil. 106.)

Athanasius: "For the Father of Him (Christ) is God by nature, but ours by grace, and He has become His God by οἰκονομία because He is man." (De hum. nat. suscepta, Opp. I, 468.)

Basil M.: "The Holy Spirit confirms our minds everywhere, lest, while we approach the one, we fall away from the other; that is, lest, while we attend to theology, we despise the dispensation (οἰκονομία) of Christ, and it happens that, while we are unable to attain the sublimity of the divine nature, we fall into impiety." (Epist. 141. Opp. T. II, f. 107.)

Greg. Naz.: "One is the discourse of theology or of nature; another is that of the οἰκονομία."

Hollaz: "In how many senses is the word 'theology' taken? In a fourfold sense: a) most generally, for any doctrine about God, even if it be false or mixed with errors; b) generally, for true theology, whether it be original, or participated, or that of wayfarers, or of the blessed, or natural, or revealed; c) specially, for revealed theology, leading man the wayfarer to eternal salvation; d) most specially, for the doctrine concerning the one and triune God." (Examen th. Prolegom. I. q. 6. p. 3.) §

2. True theology of men in this life, on account of the twofold method of knowing, is twofold: Natural and revealed. The former rests upon the principles or light of nature; the latter upon supernatural manifestation or revelation. Both are concerned with God, not only as He is in Himself, but as the end and the highest good of man.

Hollazius: "By the light of nature are here understood the principles of nature and reason, upon which the natural knowledge of God rests as if upon a ratio cognoscendi (reason for knowing); these have obtained the appellation of light because they are to the intellect a reason for knowing other things, and they stand in relation to it as light, which, when joined to colors, is to the visual power a reason for seeing and knowing colors, stands in relation to the visual power. Wisely says J. Phil. Melanchthon in *Erot. dial.* p. m. 234: as light is established in the eyes for discerning bodies, so the innate notions are light in the mind, by which we are advanced to some knowledge of God." (*Exam. P. I. c. 1. q. 5. p. 188.*)

The distinction of theology into natural and supernatural returns to the same point. We call this latter species supernatural by its origin, and revealed or the theology of revelation by its gracious mode of communication, says the blessed J. Mart. *l. c. Disp. IV. § 3. p. 80.* Moreover, there is a distinction of such a kind here, that among Christians, revealed theology or supernatural theology is called theology absolutely, while natural theology is scarcely called so otherwise than with this addition of its own, natural theology. Cf. the blessed Mus. *Introd. Cap. III. § 1. p. 105.*

For otherwise the word to reveal, in a more general signification, also pertains to natural knowledge, just as the Greek word φανερώσαι is taken in Rom. 1:19. But here revelation is understood in the stricter sense, by which either things occult and hidden, or naturally unknowable, are manifested and as it were uncovered, or are presented to be viewed with the veil removed, to which the Greek word ἀποκαλύπτειν corresponds, Luke 10:22, or a peculiar manifestation of any things whatsoever, even those which can be known by the guidance of the light of nature, made supernaturally by God, is denoted. See the Introd. of the blessed Mus. *Cap. III. § 25. n. 5. p. 155.* and *Tract. de Convers. Disp. VI. Cap. II. § 29. p. 359.* Concerning revealed theology, it will appear more distinctly below.

Concerning natural [theology], it is certain even from this, that no other discipline can claim for itself this distinguished task, and that the perfections of God, if this consideration be absent, cannot be sufficiently explained and known. See the blessed Mus. *Introd. Cap. II. § 1. pag. 23.*

Similarly, the blessed Jacob Martini, concerning the theology of wayfarers, which embraces natural as well as supernatural, says its internal (i.e., intermediate) end is the contemplation of God and divine things and a pious life; but its external and ultimate end is the most blessed eternal conversation with God, *Disp. III. § 37. p. 57.* Cf. *Disp. I. § 80. and 89. p. 18. 20.* §

3. Natural theology is a science, and indeed a practical one, in which occur the end, the subject of operation, and the causes and means, as well as the material and formal object.

N. Hunnius: "Science has cognition for its end. For every science is ἀπρακτος (non-practical)... And thus the whole essence of science consists in this, that it only knows its subject; which being done, it rests entirely, nor does it proceed further (unless perhaps by reason of an accidental and external end)." (*Can. log. p. 5. sq.*) ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

a) For it is an evident habit concerning a necessary object, deducing conclusions from necessary principles. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* Cap. II. § 3. p. 28. Or, as the honorable Jac. Martini speaks, *l. c.* Disp. III. § 47. p. 58: It proceeds from natural principles known in themselves, by the natural light of the intellect: Whence, as he adds *l. c.* § 54. p. 59, certain and true conclusions concerning God and divine things are gathered and established.

That practical sciences exist, Aristotle acknowledged in *Nicom.* I and VI, and *Metaph.* II, as did those who follow him: Ammonius, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Franc. Bonamicus, Antonius Montecatinus, the Conimbricenses, Scherbius, Piccartus, and those whose locations are indicated by the blessed Joh. Conr. Duerrius, *Institut. eth.* p. 2, 3, and *Not. ad Isag. Piccarti*. That theology, however, is a practical science is evident, because all its conclusions, if not formally, are at least virtually practical.

We call those [formally practical] which formally and directly prescribe some operation which (as far as the present is concerned) pertains to the worship of God, and therefore ought to be exercised by man in this life, e.g., God is to be invoked, the neighbor is to be helped in his needs.

We call those [virtually practical] which, while they do not formally prescribe some operation pertaining to the worship of God, nevertheless look toward it and, within the scope of this very science, contribute to inferring formally practical conclusions; just as, for example, these: God is the cause of the goods of which we are in need, and this: The neighbor is loved by God just as much as we are; although they do not formally prescribe some operation to man, they nevertheless contribute to inferring those former formally practical ones which we mentioned; and therefore, since they themselves also exist and are treated for the sake of practice, they are rightly held to be practical. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* Cap. II. § 4. p. 29, and Cap. III. § 4. p. 125.

J. G. Walchius: "In the metaphysics of the Scholastics, *virtualiter* is contrasted with the word *formaliter* and has the meaning that something is said of another not really, in regard to existence and essence, but only by its power; e.g., the King is everywhere in his land, not *formaliter*, as if he were really in all places, but *virtualiter*, because he has his servants everywhere who are there in his stead. We were all previously in Adam, not *formaliter* or really and *actu*, but *virtualiter*, by his power. The theologians make use of these two words when they say that the whole of theology is practical, not *formaliter*, as if there were only such propositions therein that are in and of themselves practical and prescribed something to be done or left undone, but *virtualiter*, because even the theoretical propositions carry with them the power of the practical." (*Philosophisches Lexicon*, sub tit. *Virtualiter*, p. 2737.)

Vid. b. J. F. Koenig in Theol. pos. pag. 2. § 15., inprimis vero b. Musaeum Introd. Cap. I. § 4. sqq. ad finem, pag. 4. ad 23.

Allein, wo könnte er wohl zu suchen sein, als in den Worten des Herrn Matth. 11, 27.: ,Niemand kennet den Sohn, denn nur der Vater; und niemand kennet den Vater, denn nur der Sohn, und wem es der Sohn will offenbaren4, sowie in dem apostolischen Begriffe von der fortgehenden μέταμόρφωαις aller Gläubigen, folglich auch der Neutestamentlichen Lehrer, in das Bild des Herrn, dessen Herrlichkeit sie wie in einem Spiegelbilde schauen (κατοπτριζόμενοι, 2 Cor. 3*, 18.) — durch welches Wort der Apostel doch wahrlich nicht blos eine Provinz des christlichen Lebens, sondern das ganze Leben in Christo, mithin auch die Bedingung der wahren Theologie als der Spitze desselben bezeichnet hat?44 (Zeitschrift. 1848, I, 7.)

2. Theologia vera hominum in hac vita, pro duplici ratione cognoscendi, duplex a est: Naturalis et revelata. Hollazius: „Per lumen naturae heic intelliguntur principia naturae et rationis, quibus notitia Dei naturalis velut rationi cognoscendi innititur; quae luminis appellationem sortita sunt, quod intellectui sunt ratio cognoscendi res alias et ad eum se habent, ut lumen, quod, coloribus conjunctum, potentiae visivae est ratio videndi et cognoscendi colores, ad potentiam visivam se habet. Scite inquit JPhil. I. c. 1. q. 5. p. 188.)

Eodem redit distinctio theologiae in naturalem et supematuralem. Posteriorem hanc speciem supernaturalem ab ortu, et revelatam aut revelationis theologiam a gratioso eommunicationis modo appellitamus, ait b. J. Mart. l. c. Disp. IV. § 3. p. 80. Est autem et hic discrimen ejusmodi, ut inter Christianos theologia revelata aut supernaturalis theologia absolute, naturalis vix aliter, quam cum hoc suo additamento, naturalis theologia dicatur. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. Cap. III. § 1. p. 105.

Alias enim verbum revelare, in generaliori significatione, etiam ad naturalem notitiam pertinet, prout vox Graeca ψανερώσαι accipitur Rom. 1, 19. Sed hic revelatio strictius sic dicta intelligitur, qua vel res occultae et latentes, seu naturaliter non cognoscibiles, manifestantur, et quasi deteguntur, aut sublato velamine conspiciendae praebentur, cui respondet vox Graeca άπηχαλύπτειν, Luc. 10,22., vel rerum quarumvis, etiam quae ductu luminis naturae cognosci possunt, peculiaris manifestatio, supernaturaliter a Deo facta, denotatur. Vid. Introd. b. Mus. Cap. III. § 25. n. 5. p. 155. et Tract. de Convers. Disp. YI. Cap. II. § 29. p. 359. De revelata theologia infra distinctius patebit.

De naturali vel inde hoc certum est, quod nulla alia disciplina sibi hanc insignem operam vendicare potest quodque Dei perfectiones, si haec consideratio absit, explicari satis et cognosci non possunt. Vid. b. Mas. Introd. Cap. II. § 1. pag. 23.

Similiter b. Jacob. Martini de theologia viatorum, qua naturalem pariter et supernaturalem complectitur, finem ejus internum (s. intermedium) dicit esse Dei rerumque divinarum contemplationem et piam vitam; externum vero eumque ultimum, aeternam conversationem beatissimam eum Deo, Disp. III. § 37. p. 57. Conf. Disp. I. § 80. et 89. p. 18. 20.§

3. Theologia naturalis est scientia, a et quidem practica, b in qua occurrunt c finis, subjectum operationis et causae atque media, itemque objectum d materiale ac formale. e

N. Hunnius: „Scientia pro fine habet cognitionem. Omnis quippe scientia est άπρακτος... Totaque adeo essentia scientiae in eo consistit, ut tantum subjectum suum cognoscat; quo facto, tota conquiescit, nec ulterius (nisi forte ratione finis accidentarii et externi) progreditur.“ (Can. log. p. 5. sq.) DB NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

a) Est enim habitus evidens circa objectum necessarium, conclusiones ex principiis necessariis deducens. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. Cap. II. § 3. pag. 28. Seu, ut loquitur h. Jac. Martini 1. c. Disp. III. § 47. p. 58.: Procedit ex principiis naturalibus secundum se notis, naturali intellectus lumine: Unde, quod addit 1. c. § 54. pag. 59., certae et verae conclusiones de Deo et rebus divinis colliguntur et constituuntur. .

Dari scientias practicas, Aristoteles agnovit I. Nicom. I. et VI., Metaph. II., quique eum sequuntur: Amnumius, Alexander Aphrodisaeus, Franc. Bonamicus, Antonius Montecatinus, Conimbricenses, Scherbius, Piccartus, et qui horum loca indicat b. Joh. Conr. Duerrius, Institut, eth. p. 2. 3. et Not. ad Isag. Piccarti. Theologiam autem esse practicam scientiam, constat, quia conclusiones ejus omnes, si non formaliter, saltem virtualiter practicae sunt.

Illas dicimus, quae formaliter ac directe praescribunt operationem aliquam, quae (quantum ad praesens) ad cultum Dei pertinet, ideoque. ab homine in hac vita exerceri debet, v. g. Deus est invocandus, proximus in necessitatibus est adjuvandus.

Has appellamus, quae cum formaliter non praescribant operationem aliquam ad cultum Dei pertinentem, spectant tamen et intra ambitum hujus ipsius scientiae faciunt ad inferendas conclusiones formaliter practicas; prout v. g. haec: Deus est causa bonorum, quibus indigemus, et ista: Proximus a Deo aeque, ac nos, diligitur; licet formaliter non praescribant homini operationem aliquam, faciunt tamen ad priores illas formaliter practicas, quas diximus, inferendas; ideoque cum et ipsae sint ac tractentur praxeos causa, pro practicis recte habentur. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. Cap. II. § 4. p. 29. et Cap. III. § 4. p. 125.

J. G. Walchius: „Virtualiter wird in der Metaphysik der Scholasticorum dem Wort formaliter entgegengesetzt und hat die Bedeutung, dass etwas von dem ändern in Ansehung der Existenz und des Wesens nicht wirklich, sondern nur der Kraft nach gesagt wird; z. E. der König ist allenthalben seines Landes, nicht formaliter, als wäre er wirklich an allen Orten, sondern virtualiter, weil er überall seine Bedienten hat, die statt Seiner da sind. Wir sind alle vorher in Adam gewesen, nicht formaliter oder wirklich u. actu, sondern virtualiter, der Kraft nach. Dieser beiden Wörter bedienen sich die Theologen, wenn sie sagen, die ganze Theologie.sei praktisch nicht formaliter, als wenn darinnen nur solche Sätze wären, die an und für sich praktisch und etwas zu thün oder zu lassen vorschrieben, sondern virtualiter, weil auch die theoretischen Sätze die Kraft der praktischen bei sich haben.“ (Philosophisches Lexicon, sub tit. Virtualiter, p. 2737.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Namely, insofar as it is a practical habit, where first the end occurs, by…

Namely, insofar as it is a practical habit, where first the end occurs, by which the will of the agent is moved to act; then the subject, which is placed under the operation that the practical habit prescribes; furthermore, the efficient cause of the end (if not of the thing, as if to be effected or obtained through operation, yet of the operation by which we attain that thing which contains the highest goodness in itself); also the impulsive cause, moving him who effects or confers the end to effect or confer the end; finally, the means, which, if they do not themselves have the nature of a cause for attaining the end, when it is obtained by the unmerited or gratuitous benefit of another (just as in this place, as we shall soon indicate), are nevertheless

conditions required on the part of the subject. Cf. the Introduction of the blessed Musaeus, pp. 29 sqq. to 44.

The blessed H. Hoepfner, in Disp. II. de Justif. § 25, p. 113, and Disp. XI. § 5, p. 1021, also teaches the distinction of means, some of which precede a thing so as to have the nature of a cause, upon which that thing depends; while others denote a mere precedence of order, and are interposed only between the causes of a thing and the thing itself, by a necessity not of efficiency, but of presence; where he distinguishes between an organic or causal medium, and a medium of the way, which denotes an order of precedence and consequence.

The blessed Balth. Meisner also acknowledges the same in Anthropol. S. Deoc. III. Disp. XXVIII. § 20, e.g., that the sorrow of the sinner has the nature of a medium, not of a merit.

Similarly, he teaches in Consid. theol. Photin. Cap. II. p. 177, that there are conditions which only determine the subject to be saved, but do not contain or express the cause of salvation.

He writes in Anthr. l. c. § 21, that there are conditions which contain the removal of obstacles, not the promotion or causation of the end itself (justification or salvation).

The blessed Gerhard agrees entirely and frequently inculcates the distinction between the condition of the subject and the cause of the effect, Conf. cath. L. II. P. III. art. XXIII. cap. VI. pp. 777, 779.

And the blessed Hoepfner, l. c. Disp. XI. Aph. I. § 6, and § 48 sqq., Aph. II. § 19, pp. 1021, 1022, 1031, 1032, 1047, bids us distinguish between a causal condition and that which is of mere order, or of a sign.

Both Gerhard and Hoepfner, ll. cc., concede that non-causal conditions have some relation to the end, although they do not have a relation as of a cause to its effect.

Namely, insofar as it is a science; where there occur both the thing to be known, or that about which conclusions are inferred; and that from which, being previously known, conclusions are deduced, or that which, being first known, is the reason for knowing the rest. The former is called the material object, the latter the formal. Cf. Introd. of the blessed Musaeus, c. II. § 14, 15, pp. 47, 48.

However, it is evident from what has been said that natural theology is a habit that is entirely practical. For although, just as God can be considered in two ways: 1) in Himself absolutely, 2) in relation to man, as He is his ultimate end and highest good, so natural theology is sometimes said to be twofold on account of this double consideration of God; yet there are not therefore two natural theologies; but there is one natural theology, under which, as one science, both considerations fall; so that it belongs to one and the same science (natural theology) to explain the end (the essence and essential perfections of God) and the means of attaining the end (or that highest good); and it belongs to one and the same science (natural theology) to consider the objective end and the rule of operation concerning the same, which it contains radically and virtually in itself, and to elicit and deliver it from the same once known.

And it must be confessed that the essence and essential perfections of God cannot be so absolutely explained and known without the nature of the highest good being simultaneously explained and known in them, and that natural theology does not satisfy man’s appetite with a bare knowledge of God, but rather kindles in man a greater desire of enjoying Him; which the blessed Musaeus shows at length in Introd. Cap. II. pp. 24, 25, 26. ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

§ 4.

The end toward which natural theology ultimately and of itself tends, and to which it refers everything it delivers, is the ultimate blessedness of man, by which name we embrace God as the objective end, and the attainment and fruition of Him, consisting in the most perfect operation of the intellect and will, as the formal end. Calovius: "The end of natural theology is not, indeed, the preparation of man for receiving supernatural grace, as Alstedius wishes in *Praecognita Theologica*, Book 1, Chapter 15; which end cannot be conceded, except regarding natural theology before the fall; but it is the leading of man to a further investigation of God, which in the state of integrity existed by way of some preparation, [but] in the state after the fall is merely pedagogical, since there is no ίκανότης in us, no preparation on our part for supernatural grace." (*Isag.*, Book I, p. 63 sq.)

The same: "A distinction must be made between grace that is immediately saving and a certain pedagogical grace. We call that [the former] which leads directly to the conversion of souls; [we call] this [the latter] that which leads to the church, to which, having been led, they may, through the proclamation of the Word, enjoy saving grace. We deny the former to the Gentiles, who are destitute of the revelation of the Word of God; but we grant the latter, which also suffices for their άναπολογίαν. Rom. 1:21." (*L. c.*, p. 83.) Reuschius: "The end of natural theology viewed absolutely, intended by God of itself, is blessedness; but the end of theology in fallen and sinful man, intended by God of itself, is pedagogy toward revealed theology. And if this is neglected through the fault of men, the end of natural theology by accident is the inexcusability of men in their own destruction, or the conviction of the same, that they perish by their own fault. Cf. Acts 17:26 sqq.; Rom. 1:19, 20." (*Annotatt. in Baieri Compend.*, p. 23.)

M. Chemnitius shows that God has naturally manifested the knowledge of Himself to the Gentiles: 1. for the sake of external discipline, 2. that God might be sought, 3. that He might render men inexcusable. Cf. *Locc. theol.*, loc. *de Deo*, c. 1, s. 4, fol. 20 sq. For otherwise it is not denied that the end of natural theology is rightly said to be to render man inexcusable, and to lead him gradually to supernatural theology: concerning which see the blessed Himmelius, *Syntagm. Disp.* I, § 20. Indeed, this end was added only after the fall and the corruption of the human race had been introduced and supernatural theology had been communicated for the restoration of men, and thus [it is] by accident, since in the primordial state the Author of the light of nature and of natural theology did not intend this end; but [rather] the one which we indicate in the thesis. See Jac. Martini, *Disp.* II, § 46, 52, 53, p. 32, 33, 34. For natural theology is 1) the most noble of the practical sciences, and therefore treats of the most perfect end, 2) it deals with God as the highest good, and therefore as to be obtained, 3) it deals with man as to be blessed absolutely. But man does not become absolutely blessed except in God. See *Introd. B. Mus.*, Cap. II, § 6, p. 30. Who contains all goodness in Himself and alone can satisfy the appetite. Whence Augustine says: You have made us, O Lord, for Yourself, and...

our heart is restless until it rests in Thee, Lib. I. Confess. Cap. I. Conf. Introd. Mus. l. c. and Jac. Mart. l. c. Disp. II. § 55. sqq. p. 34.

For it is a good proper to man, and therefore to be placed in the operation of the rational soul. See Introd. Mus. Cap. II. § 9. p. 35.

By the act of the intellect we possess God or are joined to Him, attaining the reason of the good which is in God; by the act of the will we enjoy the same or adhere to Him, as our obtained good. B. Mus. l. c. p. 36, 37.

Namely, so that it may satisfy the appetite. And therefore there must be an operation other than that which has a place in this life, where the knowledge of God is imperfect; but the will has a desire for a more perfect conjunction with God; although man cannot distinctly know through the light of nature what the knowledge of God will be like after this life, namely, intuitive and clear. Mus. l. c. p. 37, 38. Jac. Martini Disp. III. § 35, 36, 37. p. 56, 57.

So that both ends, taken together, constitute one complete end. For otherwise we are not blessed through God or in God, unless we possess and enjoy Him by a certain operation. Also, the operation of our soul, whatever it may be, does not make us blessed unless it is occupied with God. Mus. l. c. § 9. p. 34. § 5. ,

The subject of the operation of [natural theology] is man the wayfarer, or one tending toward eternal blessedness. Musaeus: “In natural theology, the subject of the operation is rightly established as man the wayfarer, as is understood from the requirements of the subject of an operation. For in every practical science, it is required for that subject: both that it lacks that perfection which is its end, and that it can become a participant of the same through the principles and means which are prescribed in it. Both of which apply to man the wayfarer, viewed in himself and in his original state. For by the very fact that he is a wayfarer, i.e., established on the way to attaining blessedness, he lacks that perfection which is the end for natural theology, namely, blessedness. Yet he could become a participant of it in his original state through the principles and means which are prescribed in it. In the state of sin, however, man the wayfarer cannot indeed become a participant of blessedness through the principles and means which natural theology prescribes; but this is accidental. For it is accidental that man sinned and through sin fell from his end, for which he was created. Yet by this, even in the state of sin, he does not cease to be the subject of natural theology. For the practical acts which it itself prescribes bind him even now no less than in the state of integrity, although he cannot attain through them the end for the sake of which they exist.” (Introductio in th. Jenae 1678. p. 41 sq.)

Or that which is placed under the operation which natural theology prescribes in respect to attaining blessedness. It is otherwise called the end *cui* (for whom). Mus. l. c. § 10. p. 41. J. Scharffius: “The end *cui* (for whom) is the use of a thing in another, for whom the end is procured; as the end *cui* of medicine is the sick person, for to him the medicinal good is procured. The end *cujus* (of which) is that for the sake of whose acquisition the efficient cause is moved and acts; as health is the end *cujus* in medicine.” (Metaphysica exemplaris. Ed. 5. Witteb. 1649. p. 127.) ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

Latin:

Nempe quatenus est habitus practicus, ubi primum occurrit finis, a quo movetur voluntas agentis ad agendum; deinde subjectum, quod substernitur operationi, quam praescribit habitus practicus; porro causa efficiens finis (si non rei, tanquam per operationem efficiendae aut obtinendae, tamen operationis, qua rem illam, quae bonitatem summam in se continet, adipiscimur); causa quoque impulsiva, movens eum, qui efficit aut confert finem ad efficiendum aut conferendum finem; denique media, quae, si non et ipsa causae rationem ad finem consequendum habent, quando is alterius beneficio indebito seu gratuito obtinetur (quemadmodum h. l., ut mox indicabimus), sunt tamen

conditiones ex parte subjecti requisitae. Conf. Introd. b. Musaei pag. 29. sqq. ad 44.

Distinctionem mediorum, quorum alia antecedant rem, ut causae alicujus rationem habeant, a qua res illa pendeat;,qlia nudum antecessum ordinis notent, et inter causas rei et rem ipsam duntaxat interjecta sint, necessitate non efficientiae, sed praesentiae, tradit etiam b. H. Hoepfnerus Disp. ΙI. de Justif. § 25. p. 113. et Disp. XI. § 5. p. 1021, ubi distinguit inter medium organicum seu causale, et medium viae, quod ordinem antecessus et consequentiae notat.

Eandem etiam agnoscit b. Balth. Meisnerus Anthropol. S. Deoc. III. Disp. XXVIII. § 20., e. g. quod luctus peccatoris habeat rationem medii, non meriti.

Similiter dari conditiones, quae tantum determinqnt subjectum salvandum, non continent vel exprimunt. salutis causam, his verbis docet in Consid. theol. Photin. Cap. II. pag. 177.

Dari conditiones, quae continent remotionem obstaculorum, non promotionem aut causationem ipsius finis (justificationis aut salutis), scribit in Anthr. l. c. § 21.

Et B. Hoepfnerus l. c. Disp. XI. Äph. I. § 6, et § 48. sqq., Aph. II. § 19. p. m. 1021. 1022. 1031. 1032. 1047., inter conditionem causalem, et eam, quae est nudi ordinis, vel signi, distinguere jubet.

Uterque, Gerhardus et Hoepfnerus ll. cc. concedunt, conditiones non causales habere relationem aliquam ad finem; quamvis non habeant relationem velut causae ad causatum suum.

Scilicet quatenus est scientia; ubi occurrunt cum res cognoscenda sive de qua conclusiones inferuntur; tum illud, ex quo prius cognito conclusiones deducuntur, sive quod primo cognitum est ratio cognoscendi caetera. Illud materiale, hoc formale objectum appellatur. Conf. Introd. b. Mus. c. II. § 14. 15. p. 47. 48.

Constat autem ex dictis, theologiam naturalem esse habitum ex toto practicum. Quamvis enim, quemadmodum Deus duobus modis considerari potest 1) in se absolute, 2) in ordine ad hominem, ut est ejus finis ultimus et summum bonum, ita theologia naturalis pro hac duplici Dei consideratione duplex aliquando dicatur: non tamen ideo duae sunt theologiae naturales; sed una est theologia naturalis, sub quam tanquam unam scientiam utraque consideratio cadit; ita ut unius et ejusdem scientiae (theologiae naturalis) sit, explicare finem (Dei essentiam et perfectiones essentiales) et media consequendi finis (seu summi boni illius), unius et ejusdem scientiae (theologiae naturalis) sit considerare finem objectivum et regulam operationis circa eundem, quam radicaliter et virtualiter in se continet, ex eodem cognito eruere et tradere.

Ac fatendum est, quod Dei essentia et perfectiones essentiales non possint ita absolute explicari et cognosci, quin simul in iis ratio summi boni explicetur et cognoscatur, quodque theologia naturalis non satiet hominis appetitum cognitione Dei nuda, sed accendat potius in homine majus desiderium fruendi illius; quod prolixe ostendit b. Musaeus Introd. Cap. II. p. 24. 25. 26. DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

§ 4.

Finis, ad quem ultimo et per se a tendit, et omnia, quae tradit, eo refert theologia naturalis, est ultima hominis beatitudo, b quo nomine Deum, c tanquam finem objectivum, et consecutionem atque fruitionem ejus, in operatione d intellectus et voluntatis perfectissima e consistentem, tanquam finem formalem, complectimur. f Calovius: „Finis theologiae naturalis est non quidem praeparatio hominis ad supematuralem gratiam suscipiendam, uti vult Alstedius in praecognit. theol. libr. cap. 15; qui finis concedi nequit, nisi de theologia naturali ante lapsum; sed manuductio hominis ad ulteriorem Dei indagationem, quae in statu integritatis sese habebat per modum alicujus praeparationis, in statu post lapsum mere est paedagogica, cum nulla in nobis sit ίκανότης, nulla a nobis praeparatio ad supematuralem gratiam.“ (Isag. L. I. p. 63. sq.)

Idem: ,,Distinguendum inter gratiam immediate salutiferam et gratiam quandam paedagogicam. Illam dicimns, quae directe ad conversionem animarum ducit; hanc, quae ducit ad ecclesiam, ad quam perducti, mediante praeconio verbi, salutifera gratia frui possint. Illam gentilibus, verbi Dei revelatione destitutis, denegamus; hanc autem concedimus, quae etiam ad άναπολογίαν eorum sufficit. Rom. 1, 21.“ (L. c. p. 83.) Reuschius: „Finis theologiae naturalis absolute spectatae, a Deo per se intentus* est beatitudo; theologiae vero in homine lapso et peccatore finis, per se intentus a Deo, est paedagogia ad theologiam revelatam. Atque si haec negligatur culpa hominum, finis th. nat. per accidens est inexcusabilitas hominum in pernicie ipsorum seu convictio eorundem, quod sua culpa pereant. Cf. Act. 17,26. sqq. Rom. 1,19.20.“ (Annotatt. in Baieri Compend. p. 23.)

M. Chemnitius ostendit, Deum sui notitiam gentibus naturaliter manifestasse: 1. propter externam disciplinam, 2. ut quaeratur Deus, ut reddat homines inexcusabiles. Cf. Locc. theol. loc. de Deo, c. l. s. 4. fol. 20. sq. Alias enim non negatur, finem theologiae naturalis hunc recte dici, reddere hominem inexcusabilem, eundemque paulatim manuducere ad theologiam supematuralem: de quo vid. b. Himmelius Syntagm. Disp. I. § 20. Nempe hinc finis post lapsum introductamque corruptionem generis humani et hominibus restaurandis communicatam theologiam supematuralem demum accessit, adeoque per accidens, cum in primaevo statu hunc finem non intenderet auctor luminis naturae ac theologiae naturalis; sed eum, quem in thesi indicamus. Vid. Jac. Mari. Disp. II. § 46. 52. 53. p. 32. 33. 34. Est enim theologia naturalis 1) scientiarum practicarum nobilissima, ideoque finem perfectissimum tractat, 2) agit de Deo, ut summo bono, adeoque ut obtinendo, 3) agit de homine, tanquam beando absolute. Homo autem absolute beatus non fit nisi in Deo. Vid. Introd. B. Mus. Cap. II. § 6. p. 30. Qui omnem bonitatem in se continet et solus potest explere appetitum. Unde Augustinus: Fecisti nos, ait, Domine, ad te, etinquie

PRÖLEGOM. CAP. I. tum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te, Lib. I. Confess. Cap. I. Conf. Introd. Mus. l. c. et Jac. Mart. l. c. Disp. II. § 55. sqq. p. 34.

Est enim bonum homini proprium, adeoque in operatione animae rationalis collocandum. Vid. Introd. Mus. Cap. II. § 9. p. 35.

Actu intellectus potimur Deo seu conjungimur ei, attingentes rationem boni, quod in Deo est; actu voluntatis eodem fruimur seu inhaeremus illi, tanquam bono nostro impetrato. B. Mus. l. c. p. 36. 37.

Nempe ut satiare possit appetitum. Ideoque aliam esse oportet operationem, quam quae in hac vita locum habet, ubi cognitio Dei imperfecta est; voluntas vero desiderium habet perfectioris conjunctionis cum Deo; licet, qualis sit futura cognitio Dei post hanc vitam, videlicet intuitiva et clara, non possit homo per lumen naturae distincte cognoscere. Mus. 1. c. p. 37. 38. Jac. Martini Disp. III. § 35. 36. 37. p. 56. 57.

Ita, ut uterque finis, junctim sumti, unum completum finem constituant. Alias enim per Deum aut in Deo non beamur, nisi certa operatione eo potiamur et fruamur. Operatio etiam animae nostrae, qualiscunque sit, beatos nos non efficit, nisi circa Deum versetur. Mus. 1. c. § 9. p. 34.§5. ,

Subjectum operationis a est homo viator b seu ad beatitudinem aeternam tendens. c Musaeus: „In theologia naturali constitui subjectum operationis recte hominem viatorem, ex requisitis subjecti operationis intelligitur. Requiritur enim ad illud in unaquaque scientia practica: cum ut careat ea perfectione, quae ei pro fine est, tum ut ejusdem particeps fieri possit per principia et media, quae in ea praescribuntur. Quod utrumque homini viatori, per se et in suo primaevo statu spectato, convenit. Hoc ipso enim, quod viator h. e. in via ad adipiscendam beatitudinem constitutus est, caret perfectione ea, quae theologiae naturali pro fine est, beatitudine scilicet. Ejus vero particeps fieri poterat in suo statu primaevo per principia et media, quae in ea praescribuntur. In statu peccati autem homo viator beatitudinis quidem per principia et media, quae theologia naturalis praescribit, particeps fleri non potest; sed hoc per accidens est. Per accidens enim est, quod homo peccavit et per peccatum fine suo, ad quem conditus est, excidit. Per hoc tamen jam in statu peccati non desinit esse subjectum theologiae naturalis. Actus practici enim, quos ipsa praescribit, stringunt eum jam quoque non minus, quam in statu integritatis, licet ad finem, cujus gratia sunt, per eos pertingere non possit.“ (Introductio in th. Jenae 1678. p. 41 sq.)

Sive id, quod operationi, quam theologia naturalis, in respectu ad consequendam beatitudinem, praescribit, substernitur. Dicitur alias finis GUI. Mus. l. c. § 10. p. 41.J. Scharffius: „Finis cui est usus rei in alio, cui finis procuratur; ut medicinae finis cui est aegrotus, huic enim procuratur bonum medicinale. Finis cujus est, cujus acquirendi gratia efficiens movetur et agit; ut sanitas est finis cujus in medicina.“ (Metaphysica exemplaris. Ed. 5. Witteb. 1649. p. 127.) DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: He] who is opposed to the *comprehensor*

[He] who is opposed to the *comprehensor*; just as otherwise the state of the way (*status viae*) and the state of the homeland (*status patriae*) are distinguished, from 1 Cor. 9:24ff., where those who live on earth are likened to those running toward the goal, and those who depart this life in blessedness are likened to those who have attained the goal; and 2 Cor. 5:6 and 8, where those who are in this life are said to be away from home (ἐκδημοῦντες) from the Lord, and to be touched by the desire of dwelling with the Lord, where they might be as if dwelling at home (ἐνδημοῦντες). Cf. Phil. 3:12, 13 and Musaeus, *Introd.*, Cap. I, § 8, p. 13. However, we do not call man a sinner in this place, but a traveler (*viator*): because thus far we are dealing with natural theology, precisely and considered in itself, in which respect it prescinds from the state of integrity and corruption. See Musaeus, *Introd.*, Cap. II, § 10, p. 41 And indeed, insofar as he is to be led to blessedness, and thus especially by reason of intellect and will. For in practical sciences, judgment must be rendered concerning the subject of operation from the end. B. Musaeus, *l.c.*, § 30, p. 87. § 6 To the causes of blessedness are referred: 1 The efficient [cause], which is God; 2 The internal impulsive [cause], which is the goodness or gratuitous favor of God. Not nature, or doctrine, or habituation. For by these, after this life, nothing is finally acquired; but then that which corresponds to the previous life, whether spent well or ill, is received. And since blessedness consists in the most perfect knowledge of God, it is certain that no one can confer this upon man except God Himself. B. Musaeus, *l.c.*, § 11, p. 42. Reuschius: “All things besides God are finite, and therefore mutable and inconstant; consequently, their possession and intuition cannot provide perpetual and supreme pleasure, and therefore neither perpetual and supreme felicity nor blessedness. If, therefore, a rational creature wishes to aspire to blessedness, and likewise to perpetual and consummated felicity, it must possess God, i.e., have Him so present and united to itself through immediate operations that it may experience them in itself or have the intuition of God. But no one can bestow the intuition of God except God Himself; whence the causal medium of blessedness and consummated felicity is God.” (*Annotatt. in Baieri Compendium*. Jen. 1757, p. 15.) Not justice, [which is] contradistinguished from goodness. For to man, who 1) depends on God for existing and acting, and 2) whatever good he does, does it out of debt, there is no right toward God, no merit properly and strictly so called. B. Musaeus, *l.c.*, § 12, p. 43 And this is the reason why we made mention only of the internal impulsive causes, not equally of the external. Gerhardus: “That to which the properties of merit do not belong cannot be meritorious. But the properties of merit do not belong to our good works. Therefore, they cannot be meritorious. The assumption is proved in this way. The nature and reason of merit demand these four things:

1. That that work by which we merit be our own. For that which we do not bring forth from the shrine and grove of our own powers, but obtain from the liberality of another, by that we cannot merit his gifts, but we only render due obedience.

2. That it be an undue work. For that which is already owed beforehand does not constrain to new benefits him to whom it is owed...” PROLEGOM. CAP. I. is performed. These are contradictory: to render a work that is owed to someone, and by that very work, which was already owed, to merit something. One must be quite impudent who, as if having earned it, demands a reward for the fact that he has paid what was owed.

3. That it be useful and advantageous to the one to whom it is performed. For if no utility accrues to another from our work, he will never acknowledge it as a merit.

4. That it be equal in both value and dignity to that which is returned for our work. For if there is a certain inequality between labor and wages, between work and reward, then merit *ex condigno* (from worthiness) has no place. A minister, distributing alms in the name of a prince, does not merit anything by that act, because he does not give from his own; he who pays wages to a laborer does not merit anything from him, because he gives nothing except what he owes; he who gives a vial of water to a thirsty king, if he were gifted a city by him, could not be said to have merited such a great gift by his own liberality, since there is no proportion between what was given and what was received.

Now, however, good works 1. are not our works, but God’s, who effectively works in us through His Spirit. It is God who inclines our heart to His testimonies (Ps. 119:36, 37; Phil. 2:13; 1:29; John 15:5; 2 Cor. 3:5). The saints acknowledge this in Isa. 26:12: “Lord, You have wrought all our works in us.” From the fact that God works in us out of mere grace—from good works, I say—is God obligated to us, or are we not much more obligated to God? Rather, let us say with the prophet Hosea 13:9: “Your destruction is from yourself; your salvation is only in God.” Certainly, no one of sound mind would say that it is a sale properly so-called when a certain house is bought by a poor man from a rich man himself for a small price given to him; rather, it is a donation of the house, not indeed immediate, yet mediate. And even if it were granted that a certain purchase, so-called *καταχρηστικώς* (catachrestically), intervenes, it has not yet been proven that the same is the case for eternal life; for it cannot be demonstrated from the Scriptures that it is given to us on account of our works.

2. Our good works are already owed to God beforehand on many counts: by right of creation, preservation, dominion, redemption, sanctification, etc. Indeed, whatever we do is not the whole of what we owe to God, but only a certain part of our duty toward God; therefore, “if we were to do all things that are commanded us, we would still have to say that we are unprofitable servants” (Luke 17:10). Therefore, since our works are already owed to God beforehand, the reward is not returned to them as a debt. If works are owed, the reward is unowed; if the reward is owed, the works are unowed.

3. Our works bring no utility to God. Job 22:2–3: “Can a man be profitable to God? But he who is wise will be profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty (Shaddai, i.e., God, who is sufficient to Himself for all things) that you are justified, and is there any utility to Him that you perfect your ways?” Ps. 50:12: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine and its fullness” (God does not need the sacrifices of His people, therefore neither does He need our other works).

4. There is no equality between our works and eternal life, which is an infinite good. “The sufferings are not worthy (*τα παθήματα οὐκ ἄξια*) of the future glory” (Rom. 8:18); therefore, neither are works worthy.

Perhaps they will object: good works are indeed owed and do not bring any advantage to God, yet they are nonetheless meritorious because God promised to return eternal life on account of the works. But even if it were granted that eternal life is returned on account of works (which itself is a *μέγα λίαν αἴτημα* [a very great begging of the question]), it still could not be said that good works are meritorious of eternal life *ex condigno*, due to the lack of properties that are required for merits properly so-called. To the first man, the possession of eternal life would have been handed over for his holy obedience toward God and for his perseverance in good works; meanwhile, however, if we wish to speak properly and accurately, that obedience of the first man would not have been meritorious of eternal life, since it was already owed beforehand, since no advantage accrued to God from it, and since no proportion intervenes between temporal obedience and eternal blessedness. What presumptuous audacity, therefore, is it to ascribe this to man after the fall—who, though indeed renewed by the Spirit of God, is meanwhile still in part carnal and sold under sin—which would not even belong to him in the state of integrity!

OF THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

The same: "Whatever rewards God renders for good works, He renders out of gratuitous goodness; yet He renders them as a just judge (Heb. 6:10), not because He owes us anything, but because He promised it, and out of truth, which is a part of justice, He performs that which He promised gratuitously. There does not intervene here a certain debt of ours, by which we bind God to us, but a certain debt of God, by which He bound Himself to us by a gratuitous promise." (L. c. § 119.) §

7. The means of attaining blessedness in natural theology are the acts of the mind and will occupied with God, by which God is rightly acknowledged and worshipped. They are called by one name, religion. They are contained in the law of nature or the moral law, and are partly occupied directly and immediately with God, and partly order man directly toward himself or toward his neighbor, yet consequently toward God. We understand means more generally so-called, which are the same as non-causal conditions required on the part of the subject to be blessed, concerning which we spoke in the preceding § 3, note c. However, that is evident in this place from what we said in § 6, that God is moved by His gratuitous favor to bless men, by which very thing a causal or meritorious means on our part is excluded. Nor does natural theology acknowledge an alien merit, which by apprehending it becomes our own. Whence it is necessary that the means which are given here are only conditions, and therefore means in a looser and less properly spoken sense.

Cf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 13. p. 43. 44. For religion cannot be separated from wisdom, nor can wisdom be severed from religion, because it is the same God who must both be understood, which is of wisdom, and honored, which is of religion. But wisdom precedes, religion follows, because it is prior to know God, and consequent to worship Him. See Lactantius, Book IV, on True Wisdom, chap. IV, p. m. 176. Sometimes, however, the very acknowledgment of God is comprehended under the name of divine worship: namely, because the principle of divine worship is to know whom you worship.

Balduinus: "Religion is accepted in two ways: 1. concerning the moral virtue which attributes just and due honor to God; 2. concerning a certain state and condition of the life of many men, who think they worship God by a special mode and rule." (Tract. de cas. consc. p. 143.)

Calovius: "According to the name taken equivocally, religion is distinguished into true and false... False religion is said of any superstitious worship of God, as also of the opinions of heretics concerning God and divine things; in which manner we call the pagan, Mohammedan, papistic, Calvinistic, etc., religion, which come under this name only equivocally." (Isag. I, 280. sqq.)

Vid. Mus. Introd. Gap. II. § 10. p. 41 Et quidem quatenus ad beatitudinem deducendus est, adeoque potissimum ratione intellectus et voluntatis. Quodsi ergo rationalis creatura velit adspirare ad beatitudinem, itemque ad felicitatem perpetuam et consummatam, Deum possidere debet i. e. per operationes immediatas ita sibi praesentem et unitum habere semper, ut illas in se experiatur seu Dei intuitionem habeat. Sed Dei intuitionem nemo largiri potest, nisi Deus ipse; unde medium causale beatitudinis et felicitatis consummatae est Deus.“ (Annotatt. in Baieri Compendium. Jen. 1757. p. 15.) Non justitia, bonitati contradistincta. Homini enim, qui 1) inesse et operari dependet a Deo, et 2) quicquid boni agit, ex debito agit, ad Deum jus nullum, nullum meritum proprie et stricte dictum est. B. Mus. 1. c. § 12. p. 43 Atque haec causa est, quam ob rem causae impulsivae internae tantum, non aeque externae, mentionem fecimus.Gerhardus: ,,Cui non competunt proprietates meriti, illud non potest esse meritorium. Atqui bonis operibus nostris non competunt proprietates meriti. Ergo non possunt esse meritoria. Assumtum probatur hoc modo. Meriti natura ac ratio postulat haec quatuor:

1. Ut opus illud, quo meremur, sit nostrum. Quod enim non afferimus ex nostrarum virium phano ac luco, sed ex alterius liberalitate obtinemus, per illud non possumus dona ejus mereri, sed debitum obsequium tantummodo reddimus.

2. Ut sit opus indebitum. Quod enim jam ante debitum est, illud non constringit ad nova beneficia eum, cui ex debito PROLEGOM. CAP. I. praestatur. Contradictoria haec sunt, opus debitum alicui exhibere, et opere illo,' jam ante debito, aliquid mereri. Admodum impudens sit oportet, qui quasi bene meritus praemium.sibi ob id poscit, quod debita solvit.

3. Ut sit utile atque commodum illi, cui praestatur. Si enim ex opere nostro nulla accedit alteri utilitas, nunquam id pro merito agnoscet.

4. Ut sit et pretio et dignitate aequale illi, quod pro opere nostro redditur. Si enim inaequalitas quaedam est inter laborem et mercedem, inter opus et praemium, tum meritum ex condigno non habet locum. Minister, principis nomine distribuens eleemosynam, non meretur ea re quippiam, quia non dat de suo; qui solvit mercedem laboranti, non meretur quippiam apud eum, quia nihil dat, nisi quod debet; qui regi sitienti dat phialam aquae, si ab eo donaretur civitate, non posset dici liberalitate sua tantum donum meruisse, cum inter datum et acceptum nulla sit proportio.

Jam vero opera bona 1. non sunt nostra, sed Dei, per Spiritum suum in nobis· efficaciter agentis, opera. Deus eßt, qui inclinat cor nostrum ad sua testimonia. Ps. 119, 36. 37. Phil, 2, 13. 1, 29. Joh. 15, 5. 2 Cor. 3, 5. Id sancti agnoscunt Es. 26, 12.: ,Domine, omnia opera nostra tu operatus es in nobis.‘ Ex eo, quod Deus in nobis ex mera gratia operatur, ex bonis, inquam, operibus, an Deus nobis obstrictus, an non multo magis nos Deo? Quin potius dicamus cum propheta Osea 13, 19.: ,Ex nobis perditio nostra, tantummodo in Deo salus nostra.'.. Certe nemo sanae mentis dixerit, eam esse venditionem proprie dictam, quando exiguo pretio ab ipso divite pauperi donato domus quaedam emitur, sed est donatio domus, non quidem immediata, tamen mediata; ac si vel maxime detur intercedere quandam emtionem καταχμηστικώς sic dictam, nondum tamen evictum est, eandem esse rationem vitae aeternae; eam enim propter opera nostra nobis dari ex scripturis demonstrari nequit. . . .

2. Opera nostra bona jam ante multis nominibus Deo sunt debita jure creationis, conservationis, dominii, redemtionis, sanctificationis etc. Imo quicquid agimus, non est totum id, quod Deo debemus, sed nostri erga Deum officii pars duntaxat quaedam; proinde,si vel maxime omnia, quae praecepta nobis sunt, faceremus, tamen dicendum nobis foret, quod simus servi inutiles.· Luc. 17, 10. Ergo cum opera nostra sint jam ante Deo debita, merces non redditur illis ex debito. Si opera sunt debita, merces est indebita; si merces est debita, opera sunt indebita.

3. Opera nostra nullam utilitatem Deo afferunt. Job. 22, 2. 3.: ,Nunquid Deo proderit vir? Sed proderit sibi ipsi intelligens. Nunquid voluntas omnipotentis (Schaddai i. e. Dei ad omnia sibi ipsi sufficientis), quod justificeris, et nunquid utilitas ei, quod perficias vias tuas?' Ps. 50, 12.: ,Si esuriero, non dicam tibi, quia orbis meus est et plenitudo ejus·, (non indiget Deus sacrificiis populi sui, ergo nec aliis operibus nostris). . .

4. Nulla est aequalitas inter opera nostra et vitam aeternam, quae est bonum infinitum. ,Passiones non sunt condignae (τα παθήματα ονκ »ίσι άξια) ad futuram gloriam', Rom. 8, 18.; ergo nec opera sunt condigna.

Excipient fortassis: bona opera esse quidem debita nec Deo afferre quoddam commodum, nihilo tamen minus esse meritoria, quia Deus propter opera vitam aeternam reddere promisit. Sed si vel maxime daretur, vitam aet. propter opera reddi (quod ipsum μένα λίαν αίτημα), nondum tamen posset dici, bona opp. esse vitae aet. ex condigno meritoria, propter defectum proprietatum, quae ad merita proprie sic dicta requiruntur. Primo homini pro sancto erga Deum obsequio et pro perseverantia in opp. bonis vitae aet. possessio esset tradita; interim tamen, si proprie et accurate loqui velimus, illa primi hominis obedientia non fuisset vitae aet. meritoria, cum fuerit jam ante debita, cum nihil commodi ex ea Deo accesserit, cum nulla inter obedientiam temporalem et aeternam beatitudinem proportio intercedat. Quae ergo praesumtuosa audacia est, homini post lapsum, qui renovatus quidem Dei Spiritu, interim tamen ex parte adhuc carnalis est et sub peccatum venumdatus, hoc adscribere, quod ne quidem in statu integritatis ipsi competeret I“

DB NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Idem: „Quaecunque praemia bonis operibus Deus reddit, ex gratuita bonitate reddit; eadem tamen ut justus judex (Ebr. 6, 10.) reddit, non quia nobis quicquam debet, sed quia promisit, et ex veritate, quae est pars justitiae, id, quod gratis promisit, praestat. Non intercedit hic debitum quoddam nostrum, quo Deum nobis obstringimus, sed debitum quoddam Dei, quo sese gratuita promissione nobis obstrinxit.“ (L. c. § 119.) §

7. Media a consequendae beatitudinis in theologia naturali sunt actus mentis et voluntatis circa Deum occupati, quibus recte agnoscitur b et colitur Deus. Dicuntur uno nomine religio. c Continentur lege naturae seu morali, d et partim directe atque immediate e circa Deum occupantur, partim directe hominem ad seipsum, f vel ad proximum, g consequenter tamen ad Deum h ordinant. Intelligimus inedia generalius sic dicta, quae idem sunt, atque conditiones non causales, ex parte subjecti beandi requisitae, de quibus diximus § praecedente 3. nota c. Patet autem illud hoc loco ex eo, quod § 6. diximus, Deum gratuito suo favore moveri ad beandos homines, quo ipso excluditur medium causale seu meritorium a parte nostra. Neque meritum alienum, quod apprehendendo nostrum fiat, theologia naturalis agnoscit. Unde necesse est, media, quae hic dantur, conditiones tantum esse, adeoque media in significatu laxiore et minus proprie dicta.

Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 13. p. 43. 44. Non potest enim religio a sapientia separari, nec sapientia a religione secerni, quia idem Deus est, qui et intelligi debet, quod est sapientiae, et honorari, quod est religionis. Sed sapientia praecedit, religio sequitur, quia prius est, Deum scire, consequens edere. Vid. Lactant. Lib. IV. de Vera sap., cap. IV. p. m. 176. Nonnunquam tamen ipsa agnitio Dei nomine cultus divini comprehenditur: scilicet, quod principium cultus divini est, nosse, quem colas.

Balduinus: „Religio duobus modus accipitur: 1. de virtute morali, quae justum debitumque honorem Deo tribuit; 2. de certo statu et conditione vitae multorum hominum, qui speciali modo ac regula se Deum colere putant.“ (Tract. de cas. consc. p. 143.)

Calovius: „Juxta nomen όμωννμως acceptum distinguitur religio in veram et falsam. . . Falsa religio de quovis Dei cultu superstitioso, ut et haereticis de Deo et rebus divinis opinionibus, dicitur; quo pacto vocamus religionem paganam, mahometanam, papisticam, calvinisticam etc., quae nonnisi aequivoce hoc nomine veniunt.“ (Isag. I, 280. sqq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: H. Kromayerus: "Religion is opposed both by impiety, i.e., contempt of God,…

H. Kromayerus: "Religion is opposed both by impiety, i.e., contempt of God, when one lives even against the dictate of conscience, as if God were not; and by ἐθελοθρησκεία, i.e., elective worship (as θρησκεία τῶν ἀγγέλων, Col. 2:18); and on the other hand by hypocrisy, when that worship is performed indeed with the gestures of the body, but with an alienated mind."

Calovius: "The term 'religion' is used abusively among the Papists when they define it as the state of men who tend toward Christian perfection through the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience (Bellarm. lib. 2, *de monachis*, c. 2). This religion of the Papists, however, is mere superstition." (*Isag.* P. I, p. 278.)

The name of religion is derived from the bond of piety, because God has bound man to Himself and constrained him with piety: because it is necessary that we serve Him as Lord and obey Him as Father. Lactantius, *l. c.*, Chapter XXVII, p. m. 349, 351.

The word 'religion' in a stricter sense denotes either the habit of the will by which we are inclined toward devotion and the honor and worship due to God on account of His excellence; or the very acts of honoring or worshipping God on account of His excellence; and it connotes, on the part of the intellect, the right knowledge of God, and on the part of the will, other virtues (or acts of virtues) which are directed toward the honor and worship of God; in a broader sense, however, it imports the complex of all virtues or acts pertaining to the worship of God. See the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* Chapter II, § 2, p. 25, 27, and in *Refut. Tract. Theol. Pol. de libert. philos.* § 37, p. 19, and § 47, p. 28.

Calovius: "Various reasons for the name (religion) occur, but especially four: 1. Masurius Sabinus in *Comment. de Indigenis*, as reported by A. Gellius, lib. 4, *Noct. Att.*, c. 9, thinks it is said from *relinquendo* (leaving behind). 'Religious,' he says, 'is that which, on account of some sanctity, is removed and set apart from us,' a word derived from *relinquendo*, just as *ceremonia* is from *carendo*. Thus also Macrobius, lib. 3, *Saturnal.*, c. 3, hints that it is called religious, and cites Servius Sulpitius to the same opinion. In this way, temples and shrines are considered to be called religious because, on account of their sanctity, they are to be revered and feared rather than made common; but days are called religious because, for the opposite reason, on account of the direness of the omen, they are to be left alone. — 2. Cicero, lib. 2, *de N. D.*, and Zwingli, lib. *de vera et falsa rel.*, and others derive it from *relegendo* (re-reading/gathering); 'those who prayed and sacrificed all day,' says Cicero, 'so that their children might survive them, were called superstitious, which name later became broader; but those who diligently reviewed and, as it were, re-read all things that pertained to the worship of the gods, were called religious from *relegendo*, just as *eligentes* (choosers) from *eligendo* (choosing) and *intelligentes* (those who understand) from *intelligendo* (understanding).' — 3. Augustine, lib. 10, *de C. D.*, c. 4, hints that it was derived by some from *eligendo* (choosing), because we choose God again through religion. 'He Himself,' he says, 'is the source of our blessedness, He is the end of all desire. Choosing Him, or rather re-choosing Him (*religentes*)—for we had lost Him by neglecting Him—therefore re-choosing Him, from which religion is also said to be named, we tend toward Him by love, so that by arriving we may rest.' — 4. The same Augustine, lib. *de vera rel.*, c. 53, and Jerome in c. 9 of Amos, as also Ambrose, lib. *de virginibus*, and likewise Lactantius, *Institutionibus div.*, lib. 4, c. 18, said it is derived from *religando* (binding back), 'because God has bound man to Himself and constrained him with piety as if with a bond,' as Lactantius says; because 'we are bound and tied to the Lord by religion as if into a bundle,' as Jerome says *l. c.* Which etymology, as it is approved by the principal Latin Fathers and also by Gellius *l. c.*, so it seems most convenient to the nature of the thing no less than to the word itself, since it neatly hints at both the form and the end of religion." (*Isag.* P. I, p. 275 sqq.)

Livy: "No religion is absolved by crime," i.e., no obligation is removed by crime. (*Hist.* lib. 2, c. 32.)

Those things which are appropriate to a rational creature, insofar as it is rational, and therefore pertain to morals or the manner of living, are defined and prescribed; but the opposites, or those things which are inconsistent with it, are prohibited. And that law of God, as the author of nature, is [written] by the finger or in ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

implanted in the very creation of the human soul by a flow: concerning which we shall see more below in its proper place.

Dannhauekus: “The moral law, I. natural and eternal, is the law of nature, not of the universe, by which every creature consists and maintains its order; not common to man and beast, which Ulpian improperly calls the right of nature; but specifically 1. the law of human nature considered in itself, which would obligate man even if solitary, if not to the act, yet to the habit, such as: that God is to be worshipped, parents are to be honored, injury is to be inflicted on no one, promises are to be kept; what you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another; what you wish to be done to you, that you also should wish for another; that αντοφονίαν [self-murder] is illicit. (Otherwise, that which obligates man as a companion in some republic to preserve public peace by special contracts, is gladly called the law of nations; such rights are: not to violate ambassadors, not to use poisoned weapons in war, etc.) 2. Good in itself and consonant with the ideas of divine holiness, so much so that even if it had never been promulgated, it would still seem to obligate by true judgment. Whence it is not because God willed, for example, to prohibit idolatry, but because it is worthy of hatred in itself, that it is a sin; thus we worship God not only because He willed it, but also because He is our God. Thus we owe obedience to God, not only because God commanded it (otherwise we would owe equal obedience to an angel commanding it), but because we are God’s property, consequently obligated by natural law. The first and general precept or work of this law is: good is to be done, evil is to be avoided (which principle is as common as that theoretical one: It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at the same time), to live honestly, to harm no one, to render to each his own. 3. Immutable and eternal; for as it is impossible for the norm of this law, which is the eternal law in the divine mind, to be changed, so it is impossible for its ray to be changed; as the sun is incorruptible, so also is the sun’s ray. The foot, which the right of nature constitutes, is sometimes changed, not the right. If, for example, a creditor forgives what is owed to him, the debtor is no longer bound to pay, not because the law of nature has ceased to command the payment of what I owe, but because what I owed has ceased to be owed. Thus, when God commanded Isaac to be killed (Gen. 22:2), parricide does not thereby become licit, but because it is done by the Lord’s authority, it ceases to be parricide. 4. Σνμφντος [innate] and connate through promulgation inscribed upon the hearts of men by the finger of God... II. Positive moral law is that which depends solely on the will of God, and unless God had so ordained, it would not be held as a sin.” (Hodosoph. phaenom. VI. p. 240, 242.)

M. Chemnitius: “These disputes are agitated by many as philosophical, concerning which Paul said, Col. 2:8: ‘Beware, lest anyone plunder you through philosophy and empty deception.’ But candor must be employed in judging, lest those things which have been rightly and usefully handed down be petulantly disturbed and torn apart in the name of philosophy. Rather, let the causes be considered for which it is useful to observe the consensus of the law of nature with the Decalogue, and let the boundaries be shown within which that comparison ought to contain itself. For if anyone wished to refer that comparison to the end of bending and restricting the interpretation of the Decalogue only to the natural notions of the law, so that he would contend that only those sins which are known by nature are reproved by the law of God, and that the Decalogue is satisfied by whatever obedience reason dictates from the law of nature and can perform, he, because he would be exceeding the true boundaries, would rightly be said to be plundering, Col. 2: 8.

And there is no doubt that Pharisaic corruptions drew their origin from there. For it is a plausible opinion to take the interpretation of the Decalogue from the law of nature.
