And this imagination has fascinated many even in the church, who feigned that the fathers before Moses were saved by the law of nature, etc. Judgment must therefore be applied in the use of the dispute concerning the law of nature.

In the loci, however, the true reason is shown, how the consensus of the laws of nature with the Decalogue can be rightly and usefully sought and considered. And these causes are handed down: Because Paul treats that dispute professedly in Rom. 1 and 2 and tri- PROLEGOM. CAP. I. has given the law of nature most honorable designations. For in Rom. 1:18 he calls it the truth of God; v. 19, the manifestation of God; v. 32, the ordinance of God; Rom. 2:15, the work of the law, written in the hearts at creation itself. And indeed, the designation "law of nature" is taken from there; for he says in v. 14: "Gentiles, who are by nature, do the things of the law." And let us gratefully acknowledge that benefit, that He did not will for the light of the law to be entirely extinguished by the fall; but He willed that certain remnants should survive, so that there might be a political association among men, in which God might gather the church through the voice of the Gospel. And that those remnants are to be highly esteemed, Paul’s words admonish. —

2. This comparison is useful, so that we may learn to love, venerate, and highly esteem moral maxims that agree with the law of nature, wherever they exist and are read among poets, historians, philosophers, legislators, etc. Because they are divine law and the truth of God divinely revealed. Thus, Paul was not afraid in a most serious matter to cite a maxim from Menander, 1 Cor. 15:33: "Evil communications corrupt good manners." —

3. It is also profitable for this, that we should highly esteem the testimony of conscience even in the unregenerate; lest, namely, the accusing thoughts (which Paul calls such in Rom. 2:15), when they are felt, be blunted by this imagination, as if it were some empty fantasy that it is womanish to heed; but let us maintain that it is truly the judgment of God, reproving sins. —

Latin:

H. Kromayerus: „Religioni opponitur tum impietas i. e. contemtus Dei, cum quis etiam contra dictamen conscientiae vivit, ac si Deus non esset; tum έ&ελο&ρησκεία i. e. cultus electitius (ut θρησκεία των αγγέλων, Col. 2, 18.); tum ex parte hypocrisis, quando cultus iste gestibus quidem corporis, sed mente aliena peragitur.“

Calovius: ,,Abusive religio dicitur apud pontificios, cum eam definiunt statum hominum, ad perfectionem Christianam per paupertatis, continentiae et obedientiae vota tendentium (Bellarm. l. 2. de monachis c. 2.). Haec autem pontificiorum religio mera est superstitio.“ (Isag. P. I. p. 278.)

Nomen religionis a vinculo pietatis deductum est, quod hominem sibi Deus religaverit et pietate constrinxerit: quia servire nos ei, ut domino, et obsequi, ut patri, necesse est. Lactantius l. c. Cap. XXVII. p. m. 349. 351.

Denotat autem vox religionis in significatione strictiore vel habitum voluntatis, quo inclinamur ad devotionem et honorem cultumque Deo debitum propter ejus excellentiam; actus ipsos honorandi aut colendi Deum propter excellentiam ejus, et connotat ex parte intellectus agnitionem Dei rectam, ex parte voluntatis virtutes alias (aut actus virtutum), quae (qui) ad Dei honorem cultumque diriguntur; in laxiore vero significatione importat complexum omnium virtutum aut actuum, ad Dei cultum pertinentium. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. Cap. II. § 2. p. 25. 27. et in Refut. Tract. Theol. Pol. de libert. philos. § 37. p. 19. et § 47. p. 28.

Calovius: „Variae occurrunt nominis (religionis) rationes, praecipue autem quatuor: 1. Masurius Sabinus in Comment. de Indigenis, referente A. Gellio l. 4. Noct. Att. c. 9., a relinquendo dictum putat. ,Religiosum“, inquit, ,est, quod propter sanctitatem aliquam remotum ac sepositum a nobis est, verbum a relinquendo ductum, tanquam ceremonia a carendo.4 Sic etiam religiosum dici innuit Macrob. 1. 3. Saturnal. c. 3. et in eandem sententiam adducit Servium Sulpitium. Hoc pacto templa ac delubra religiosa dicta censentur, quod ob sanctitatem reverenda ac reformidanda potius sunt, quam invulganda; dies autem religiosi, quod ex contraria causa propter ominis diritatem relinquendi. — 2. Cicero 1.2. de N. P. et Zwinglius 1. de vera et falsa rei. et alii a relegendo derivant; ,qui tota die', inquit Cicero, »precabantur et immolabant, ut sibi sui liberi superstites essent, superstitiosi sunt appellati, quod nomen patuit postea latius; qui autem omnia, quae ad cultum deorum pertinerent, diligenter retractarent et tanquam relegerent, dicti sunt religiosi a relegendo, ut eligentes ab eligendo et ex intelligendo intelligentes.' — 3. Augustinus l.10. de C. D. c. 4. ab eligendo a quibusdam innuit deductum, quod iterum eligamus Deum per religionem. ,Ipse', inquit, ,est fons nostrae beatitudinis, ipse est omnis appetitionis finis. Hunc eligentes, vel potius religentes (amiseramus enim negligentes), hunc ergo religentes, unde et religio dicta perhibetur, ad eum dilectione tendimus, ut perveniendo quiescamus.' — 4. Idem Augustin. l. de vera rel. c. 53. et Hieron. in c. 9. Amos., ut et Ambros. 1. de virginibus, nec non Lactantius Institutionibus div. 1. 4. c. 18. a religando derivari dixere, ,quod Deus hominem sibi religaverit et pietate quasi vinculo constrinxerit', dicente Lactantio; quod »religione quasi in fascem Domini vincti et religati simus', uti Hieron. ait l. c. Quae etymologia, ut praecipuis latinorum Patrum, nec non Gellio l. c. probata, ita rei naturae non minus, quam ipsi voci videtur convenientissima, quum et formam et finem religionis concinne innuat." (Isag. P. I. p. 275. sqq.)

Livius: „Nullam scelere religionem exsolvi" i. e. scelere nullam obligationem tolli. (Hist. l. 2, c. 32.)

Qua, quae creaturae rationali, quatenus rationalis est, conveniunt, ideoque ad mores seu rationem vivendi attinent, definiuntur et praescribuntur; opposita autem, seu quae illi disconveniunt, prohibentur. Estque lex illa Dei, tanquam auctoris naturae, digito seu in DE NATUEA THEOLOGIAE.

fluxu in ipsa creatione animae hominis implantata: de quo infra suo loco plura videbimus.

Dannhauekus: „Lex moralis I. naturalis ac aeterna, est lex naturae, non universae, qua omnis creatura constat ac ordinem suum tuetur; non communis homini et bestiae, quam improprie jus naturae appellat Ulpianus; sed speciatim 1. lex naturae humanae per se consideratae, quae hominem etiam solitarium obligaret, si non ad actum, tamen ad habitum, ut: Deum esse colendum, honorandos parentes, nemini inferendam injuriam, promissa servanda; quod tibi fleri non vis, alteri ne feceris; quod tibi vis fleri, id et tu alteri velis; αντοφονίαν esse illicitam. (Alias, quae hominem qua socium in aliqua republica ad pacem publicam servandam ex specialibus contractibus obligat, jus gentium appellari gaudet; cujusmodi jura sunt: non violare legatos, non uti in bello armis veneno illitis etc.) 2. Per se bona ac ideae sanctitatis divinae consentanea, adeo ut si vel maxime nunquam lata fuisset, tamen vero judicio videretur obligare. Unde non quia Deus voluit, exempli gratia, prohibere idolatriam, sed quia per se digna odio, peccatum est; sic adoramus Deum non tantum, quia ipse voluit, sed et quia Deus est noster. Ita obedientiam debemus Deo, non solum, quia Deus id jussit (alioquin etiam angelo jubenti parem obedientiam deberemus), sed quia res Dei sumus, consequenter ex naturali jure obligati. Praeceptum sive opus hujus legis primum ac generale est: bonum esse faciendum, malum fugiendum (quod principium tam commune est, quam illud theoricum: Impossibile esse, ut idem simul sit et non sit), honeste vivendum, neminem laedendum, suum cuique tribuendum. 3. Immutabilis et aeterna; quam enim impossibile est, normam hujus legis, quae est lex aeterna in divina mente, mutari, tam impossibile est, ejus radium mutari; ut sol incorruptibilis est, ita etiam solis radius. Pes, quam jus naturae constituit, quandoque mutatur, non jus. Si exempli gratia creditor, quod ei debetur, acceptum ferat, jam solvere debitor non tenetur, non quia jus naturae desierit praecipere solvendum, quod debeo, sed quia, quod debebam, deberi desiit. Ita cum Deus occidi praecepit Isaacum (Gen. 22, 2.), non eo ipso parricidium fit licitum, sed quod Domino auctore fit, parricidium esse desinit. 4. Σνμφντος et connativa per promulgationem inscriptam cordibus hominum digito Dei. . . II. Moralis positiva illa est, quae unice pendet a Dei voluntate, ac nisi Deus ita sanxisset, peccatum non haberetur.“ (Hodosoph. phaenom. VI. p. 240. 242.)

M. Chemnitius: „Exagitantur a multis hae disputationes tanquam philosophicae, de quibus Paulus dixerit, Col. 2, 8.: ,Cavete, ne quis vos depraedetur per philosophiam et inanem deceptionem.* Sed candor adhibendus est in judicando, ne petulanter in nomine philosophiae turbentur et convellantur, quae recte et utiliter tradita suut. Considerentur potius causae, propter quas utile est observare consensum legis naturae cum decalogo, et ostendantur metae, intra quas collatio illa se continere debet. Si quis enim illam collationem eo referre vellet, ut interpretationem decalogi inflecteret et restringeret tantum ad naturales legis notitias, ita ut contenderet, lege Dei argui tantum illa peccata, quae natura nota sunt, et satisfieri decalogo qualicunque obedientia, quam ratio ex lege naturae dictat et praestare potest, is, quia egrederetur veras metas, recte diceretur depraedari, Col. 2, 8.

Et non est dubium, pharisaicas corruptelas inde traxisse originem. Plausibilis enim opinio est, interpretationem decalogi sumere ex lege naturae. Et haec imaginatio multos etiam in ecclesia fascinavit, qui finxerunt, patres ante Mosen salvatos fuisse per legem naturäe etc. Adhibendum igitur est judicium in usu disputationis de lege naturae.

In locis vero ostenditur vera ratio, quomodo recte et utiliter quaeri et considerari possit consensus legum naturae cum decalogo. Et traduntur hae causae: Quia Paulus ex professo illam disputationem tractat Rom. 1. et 2. et tri PROLEGOM. CAP. I. buit legi naturae honestissimas appellationes. Vocat enim Rom. 1, 18. veritatem Dei, v. 19. patefactionem Dei, v. 32. jus Dei, Bom. 2,15. opus legis, scriptum in cordibus in ipsa creatione, Et quidem appellatio legis naturae inde sumpta est; inquit enim v. 14.: ,Gentes natura, quae legis sunt, faciunt.' Et grati agnoscamus illud beneficium, quod non voluerit lucem legis totam exstinctam per lapsum; sed voluit reliquias quasdam superesse, ut possit esse consociatio politica inter homines, in qua Deus per vocem evangelii colligat ecclesiam. Et reliquias illas esse magnifaciendas, monent Pauli vocabula.—

2. Utilis est haec collatio, ut discamus amare, venerari et magnifacere sententias morales congruentes legi naturae, ubicunque extent et legantur apud poetas, historicos, philosophos, legumlatores etc. Quia sunt jus divinum et veritas Dei divinitus patefacta. Ita Paulus non est veritus in gravissima causa ex Menandro citare sententiam 1 Cor. 15, 33.: ,Corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava.' —

3. Prodest etiam ad hoc, ut testimonium conscientiae etiam in non renatis magnifaciamus; ne scilicet cogitationes accusantes (quas Paulus ita vocat Bom. 2,15.), quando sentiuntur, retundantur hac imaginatione, quasi sit inanis quaedam phantasia, quam muliebre sit curare; sed statuamus, esse vere judicium Dei, arguentis peccata. —


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: That by a careful comparison it may be observed in which parts the natural…

4. That by a careful comparison it may be observed in which parts the natural knowledge of the law has been obscured, where the judgment is depraved, and what those things are, whether sins or good works, which, unknown to reason, are shown in the Decalogue. In this way, the comparison of the laws of nature with the Decalogue can be rightly and usefully employed, and indeed in some way the true meaning will thus be illustrated. . .

The second table of the law of nature is posited negatively by the philosophers: "What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another." Christ, however, recites it affirmatively in Matt. 7:12: "Whatever you want men to do to you, do also to them"; and He clearly shows the agreement of this maxim with the Decalogue. For He says: "This is the law and the prophets," namely, in the second table. (Loc. th. P. II. fol. 96. sq.)

Apology of the A. C.: "Human reason naturally understands the law in some way. For it has the same judgment written divinely in the mind. Because the natural law, which agrees with the law of Moses or the Ten Commandments, is innate and written in the hearts of all men, and thus reason can grasp and understand the Ten Commandments to some extent, it wants to imagine that it has enough in the law and that through the law one can obtain forgiveness of sins." (Art. 4. p. 87. sq.) "

Natural law is truly divine law, because it is an ordinance divinely impressed upon nature. If it is now natural law, then it is God’s ordinance, thus planted in nature, and is therefore also divine law." (Art. 23. p. 238.)

Luther: "If the natural law were not written and given by God into the heart, one would have to preach for a long time before the consciences were struck; one would have to preach to a donkey, a horse, an ox, or a dog for a hundred thousand years before they would accept the law, even though they have ears, eyes, and hearts like a human; they can also hear it, but it does not fall into the heart. Why? What is the fault? The soul is not formed and created in such a way that such a thing falls into it. But a human, when the law is held before him, soon says: Yes, it is so, I cannot deny it. One could not persuade him of this so quickly, were it not already written in his heart. Since it is now already in the heart, albeit dark and quite faded, it is awakened again by the Word, so that the heart must indeed confess that it is as the commandments sound, that one should honor, love, and serve one God, because He alone is good and does good, and not only to the pious, but also to the wicked." (Exposition on several chapters of the 2nd Book of Moses. 1525. III, 1575.)

The same: "Why then do we teach and keep the Ten Commandments? Answer: Because the natural laws are nowhere so finely and orderly composed as in Moses. Therefore, one rightly takes the example from Moses."

For example, on the part of the intellect, the acts of meditating upon and knowing the divine essence, attributes, providence, works, and benefits; on the part of the will, the acts of fear, love, trust, hope, patience, etc., to which correspond external acts, by which those internal ones are declared; for example, prayers, the invocation of God, and thanksgiving, performed with sensible signs, whether in a public assembly or privately, hymns, and various celebrations of God, His perfections, and His benefits, etc. For example, internal acts occupied in moderating the affections; acts of cultivating the mind with honest arts and sciences; acts of rightly protecting life, body, reputation, wealth, etc., which are partly internal and partly external. For example, acts of justice, by which to each his own is rendered; acts of liberality, of fortitude for the protection of the fatherland, relatives, etc., which likewise are either elicited in the mind or commanded and external. They also have the character of divine worship, insofar as they are ultimately referred to God as to the end and are done in His obedience, praise, and glory. See regarding all these things the blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 33. sqq. p. 88. 89. § 8.

Regarding the sufficiency, however, of the divine worship which natural theology prescribes in order to attain blessedness after this life, a very great diversity occurs and must be most diligently observed, regarding the different states of man: the original state, or state of integrity, and the state of corruption, or sin. In that former state, man was able, under the guidance of natural theology and through the powers granted to him, to attain to a sufficient knowledge of God and to perform the worship owed to God without defect or sin, and thus in this way to obtain eternal blessedness from God. In this latter state, however, through the very condition of his corrupted nature, he is turned away from God and inclined toward those things which displease God; and since he has God as hostile to him on account of his sins, he nevertheless does not find in natural theology a means by which he might satisfy the offended God and be brought back into favor with Him; indeed, he can neither perfectly know and prescribe to himself those things which otherwise pertain to the worship of God, nor can he perform that worship which he understands by the light of nature to be owed to God. Whence, for the present state, natural theology suffices for salvation for no one among men. Those different states are hitherto presupposed, but they will be more clearly taught in their proper place below in revealed theology.

PROLEGOMENA. CHAPTER I. M. Chemnitius: "What, of what kind, and how great is that 'natural' knowledge, and how far does it progress? — Speaking truly: it is either nothing, or imperfect, or languid. Nothing, because the whole of philosophy knows nothing of the gratuitous promise of the remission of sins; for the Son of God brought that forth from the bosom of the eternal Father and revealed it to the Church. John 1:18, Matthew 11:27, and 1 Corinthians 1:21 and 2:7. — Imperfect, because the nations knew only a small particle of the law. Regarding the interior worship of the first table, reason knows or determines nothing certain; certain philosophers of the nations teach only about some external and civil matters. Meanwhile, they mix in many άτοπα καϊ παράδοξα [absurdities and paradoxes], about which there is not sufficient agreement even among themselves. — Languid, because, even though it is impressed upon human minds that there is a God and that He commands obedience according to the distinction between honorable and base things, yet the assent is not only languid, but is often shaken by horrible doubts. Just as there exists a most beautiful description in the *Tusculans*, where Cicero, disputing about the immortality of the soul, says to Antonius: 'Unroll diligently the book of Plato which is about the soul; there will be nothing more that you could desire. I have done so, by Hercules, said Antonius, and indeed quite often; but I do not know how it is that while I read, I assent, but when I have laid the book aside and have begun to think by myself about the immortality of souls, all that assent slips away.'" (Loc. th. P. I. f. 20.)

For he [man] held God to be propitious and, without difficulty, inclined to confer blessedness upon him at some time. Cf. the blessed Jac. Martini, l. c. Disp. III. § 84 sqq. p. 66 sqq., the blessed Musaeus, Introd. Cap. II. § 13. num. 4. pag. 45.

For although God is most good, He is nevertheless also supremely just and a most grave avenger of sinners who oppose His most holy law, and this by the power of His immutable justice: for which reason, unless the injured divine justice is satisfied, the goodness of God, which does not abolish the justice of God, cannot be so known that from it one can expect the remission of sins and salvation to be conferred upon the sinner. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. peculiaris de Insuff. theolog. nat. ad sal. contra Ed. Herbert, de Cherbury* (which is annexed to the treatise on the eternal decree of election) § 64. p. 36, 37.

But this is the principal thing, in the absence of which no worship pleasing to God can be offered. For it is necessary that the person first please God (and that for the sake of Christ alone), if the works of that person are to please God and be acceptable; these are the words of the *Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord*, Art. IV. p. 700, 701. But how can the human heart also love God, while it feels that He is horribly angry and oppresses us with temporal and eternal calamities? The law, however, always accuses us, always shows that God is angry. Therefore, God is not loved until after we apprehend mercy by faith; only then does He become a lovable object; these are the words of the *Apology of the Augsburg Confession*, pag. 83, 84. cf. p. 66.

And thus it is established that natural theology, which cannot supply that which is primary in the state after the fall, from which worship pleasing to God begins, is not sufficient for salvation. For although natural theology may prescribe repentance to a sinful man, by which he may grieve over his sins: yet this repentance does not extend to all sins, since many are committed by those who are ignorant or negligent, and original sin is not rightly acknowledged by man left to himself and destitute of supernatural revelation. But neither can that sorrow for sins wash away sins, insofar as they imply an offense against God and subject man to the wrath of God and the guilt of eternal punishment, although it does imply a certain retraction of them. See the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. cit.* § 37 sqq. p. 22 sqq. ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

Because of the innate obscurity of the intellect, even in natural matters—concerning which see below in the Book on Original Sin—it is meanwhile worth noting the words by which the blessed G. Mylius shows that natural knowledge (theology) is lame and mutilated, because, he says, it inculcates only one part of heavenly doctrine, and that the smallest, namely the law, and not even this in its entirety, but only half of it, while the knowledge of true divine worship and of evangelical salvation is partly ignored, in both of which the very nucleus of divine knowledge lies hidden. Posit. de Deo, th. 13.

Calovius: “What specifically pertains to the more important heads of this natural theology are the following: 1. Concerning God, as to His nature and attributes, as well as the legal will of God in part and some of His works; but by no means as to the distinct persons of the Godhead or the evangelical will of God and the works of grace, and other divine mysteries which are entirely unknown to reason. 2. Concerning the law of God, as it is held from the law of nature according to the precepts of both tables. To this pertain the laws of Zaleucus, the golden verses of Pythagoras, the moral precepts of Socrates and Plato, the rules of Epictetus, the admonitions of Iamblichus, Simplicius, and other Platonists, as well as the excellent warnings of Aristotle and the Peripatetics, the laws of the Twelve Tables, etc. 3. Concerning sin and the transgression of the law. 4. Concerning the punishment of sin, which the law of nature and the conscience of each person also dictates of its own accord. 5. Concerning the immortality of the soul and life after this life, which we demonstrate from Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus, Phocylides, Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Xenocrates, Epaminondas, Cicero, Plotinus, Iamblichus, etc., in Decad. dissertat. de Pseudo-Theol. Soc. p. 80.” (Isag. L. I. p. 68. sq.)

Latin:

4. Ut exilia collatione observetur, in quibus partibus obscurata sit naturalis notitia legis, ubi judicium depravatum, et quae sint illa, sive peccata sive bona opera, quae ignota rationi in decalogo ostendantur. Hoc modo collatio legum naturae cum decalogo recte et utiliter potest adhiberi et quidem aliquo modo ita illustrabitur vera sententia. . .

Secunda tabula legis naturae a philosophis negative ponitur: Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris. Christus vero affirmative recitat Matth; 7, 12.: ,Quidquid vultis ut faciant homines vobis, et vos facite illis'; et diserte ostendit consensum hujus sententiae cum decalogo. Inquit enim: ,Haec est lex et prophetae', scilicet in secunda tabula.“ (Loc. th. P. II. fol. 96. sq.)

Apologia A. C.: ,,Humana ratio naturaliter intelligit äliquomodo legem. Habet enim idem judicium scriptum divinitus in mente. Dieweil das natürliche Gesetz, welches mit dem Gesetz Mosi oder zehen Geboten übereinstimmt, in aller Menschen Herzen angeboren und geschrieben ist und also die Vernunft etlichermass die zehen Gebot fassen und verstehen kann, will sie wähnen, sie habe genug am Gesetz und durch das Gesetz könne man Vergebung der Sünden erlangen.“ (Art. 4. p. 87. sq.) „

Jus naturale vere est jus divinum, quia est ordinatio divinitus impressa naturae. Ist’s nun natürlich Becht, so ist es Gottes Ordnung, also in der Natur gepflanzt und ist also auch göttlich Becht.“ (Art. 23. p. 238.)

Lutherus: „Wenn das natürliche Gesetz nicht von Gott in das Herz geschrieben und gegeben wäre, so müsste man lange predigen, ehe die Gewissen getroffen würden; man müsste einem Esel, Pferde, Ochsen, Binde hunderttausend Jahre predigen, ehe sie das Gesetz annähmen, wiewohl sie Ohren, Augen und Herze haben, wie ein Mensch; sie können es auch hören, es fällt aber nicht in das Herz. Warum? Was ist der Fehler? Die Seele ist nicht darnach gebildet und geschaffen, dass solches darein falle. Aber ein Mensch, so ihm das Gesetz vorgehalten wird, spricht er bald: Ja, es ist also, ich kann es nicht leugnen. Des könnte man ihn nicht so bald überreden, es wäre denn zuvor in seinem Herzen geschrieben. Weil es nun zuvor im Herzen ist, wiewohl dunkel und ganz verblichen, so wird es mit dem Worte wieder erwecket, dass ja das Herz bekennen muss, es sei also, wie die Gebote lauten, dass man einen Gott ehre, liebe, diene, weil er alleine gut ist und Gutes thut, und nicht allein den Frommen, sondern auch den Bösen.“ (Ausl, über etliche Capp. des 2. B. Mosis. 1525. III, 1575.)

Idem: „Warum lehret und hält man denn die zehen Gebot? Antwort: Darum, dass die natürlichen Gesetze nirgend so fein und ordentlich sind verfasset, als im Mose. Darum nimmt man billig das Exempel von Mose.“

V. g. ex parte intellectus actus meditandi et cognoscendi essentiam, affectiones, providentiam, opera et beneficia divina; ex parte voluntatis actus timoris, dilectionis, fiduciae, spei, patientiae etc., quibus respondent actus externi, per quos interni illi declarantur; v. g. preces, invocatio Dei et gratiarum actio, signis sensibilibus facta, sive in publico coetu, sive privatim, hymni et variae celebrationes Dei, perfectionum et beneficiorum ejus etc. E. gr. actus interni, in moderandis affectibus occupati; actus excolendi animum honestis artibus ac scientiis; actus recte tuendi vitam, corpus, famam, opes etc., qui partim interni, partim externi sunt. V. g. actus justitiae, quibus suum cuique tribuitur, actus liberalitatis, fortitudinis ad tuendam patriam, propinquos etc., qui itidem vel in animo eliciti, vel imperati et externi sunt. Habent etiam rationem cultus divini, quatenus ad Deum, tanquam ad finem, ultimo referuntur et in ejus obsequium, laudem et gloriam fiunt. Vide de his omnibus b. Mus. l. c. § 33. sqq. p. 88. 89.§ 8.

Quoad sufficientiam vero cultus divini, quem theologia naturalis praescribit, in ordine ad beatitudinem post hanc vitam consequendam, maxima occurrit et diligentissime observanda est diversitas, quoad diversos status a hominis, primaevum seu integritatis, et statum corruptionis seu peccati. In illo statu poterat homo, ductu theologiae naturalis et per concessas sibi vires, ad sufficientem Dei cognitionem cultumque Deo debitum, absque defectu seu peccato praestandum, pertingere, adeoque b hoc modo beatitudinem aeternam a Deo impetrare. In hoc posteriore autem statu per ipsius naturae corruptae conditionem a Deo aversus atque ad ea, quae Deo displicent, propensus est; cumque Deum propter peccata sibi infensum c habeat, non tamen invenit in theologia naturali medium, quo Deo laeso satisfacere d et cum eo in gratiam reduci e possit; imo neque, quae alias ad Dei cultum pertinent, perfectef cognoscere sibique praescribere, neque eum cultum, quem Deo deberi vi luminis naturae intelligit, praestare g potest. Unde pro praesenti statu nulli hominum11 sufficit theologia naturalis ad salutem. Status illi diversi hactenus supponuntur, infra autem in theologia revelata suo loco manifestius tradentur.Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. I. 2

PROLEGOM. CAP. I. M. Chemnitius: ,,Quae, qualis et quanta est illa notitia 'naturalis et quousque progreditur? — Vere loquendo: aut nulla, aut imperfecta, aut languida est. Nulla, quia de gratuita promissione remissionis peccatorum nihil novit tota philosophia; illam enim Filius Dei e sinu aeterni patris prolatam revelavit ecclesiae. Jöh. 1, 18. Matth. 11, 27. et 1 Cor. 1, 21. et 2, 7. — Imperfecta, quia gentes aliquam tantum particulam legis noverunt. De interioribus vero cultibus primae tabulae nihil certi vel novit vel statuit ratio; tantum de quibusdam externis et civilibus negotiis docent quidam gentium philosophi. Interea miscent multa άτοπα καϊ παράδοξα, de quibus nec inter ipsos satis convenit. — Languida, quia, etiamsi impressum est humanis mentibus, esse Deum et praecipere obedientiam juxta discrimen honestorum et turpium, tamen assensio non tantum languida est, sed horrendis dubitationibus saepe excutitur. Sicut extat pulcherrima descriptio in Tuscul., ubi Cicero, disputans de immortalitate animae, dicit ad Antonium: ,Evolve diligenter librum Platonis, qui est de anima; amplius quid desideres, nihil erit. Feci, me Hercule, inquit Antonius, et quidem saepius; sed nescio, quomodo, dum lego, assentior, cum posui librum et mecum ipse de immortalitate animarum cogitare coepi, omnis illa assensio elabitur.‘ “ (Loc. th. P. I. f. 20.)

Habebat enim Deum propitium atque ad beatitudinem aliquando sibi conferendam sine difficultate propensum. Conf. b. Jac. Martini 1. c. Disp. III. § 84. sqq. p. 66. sqq., b. Mus. Introd. Cap. II. § 13. num. 4. pag. 45.

Licet enim Deus sit maxime bonus, est tamen etiam summe justus et peccatorum, sanctissimae legi suae adversantium, vindex gravissimus, idque ex vi immutabilis suae justitiae: quam ob rem, nisi laesae justitiae divinae satisfiat, bonitas Dei, quae Dei justitiam non tollit, ita cognosci non potest, ut ab ea expectari queat remissio peccatorum et salus, peccatori conferenda. Conf. b. Musaei Disp. peculiarem de Insuff, theolog. nat. ad sal. contra Ed. Herbert, de Cherbury (quae tractatui de aet. elect. decr. annexa est) § 64. p. 36. 37.

Hoc autem praecipuum est, quo absente, nullus Deo placens cultus exhiberi potest. Neces se est enim, ut persona Deo antea placeat (idque propter solum Christum), si modo personae illius opera Deo placere et accepta esse debent, verba sunt Solidae Deci. Form. Cone. Art. IV. p. 700. 701. Quomodo autem etiam potest humanum cor diligere Deum, dum sentit eum horribiliter irasci et opprimere nos temporalibus et perpetuis calamitatibus? Lex autem semper accusat nos, semper ostendit irasci Deum. Non igitur diligitur Deus, nisi postquam apprehendimus fide misericordiam, tum demum fit objectum amabile, verba sunt Apol. A. C. pag. 83. 84. conf. p. 66.

Atque ita constat, theologiam naturalem, quae non potest suppeditare illud, quod primum est in statu post lapsum, unde incipit cultus Deo placens, non esse sufficientem ad salutem. Quanquam enim theologia naturalis poenitentiam homini peccatori praescribat, qua doleat de peccatis: tamen haec poenitentia neque ad omnia peccata sese extendit, cum multa a nescientibus aut negligentibus committantur, originale vero peccatum ab homine sibi relicto ac relevatione supernaturali destituto non recte agnoscatur. Sed neque dolor ille de peccatis peccata, quatenus offensam Dei important et hominem irae Dei ac reatui poenae aeternae subjiciunt, eluere potest, licet retractationem quandam eorum importet. Vid. b. Musaei Disp. cit. § 37. sqq. p. 22. sqq. DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Ob connatam intellectus, etiam in naturalibus, obscuritatem, de qua infra in L. de Pecc. Orig. Interim notatu digna sunt verba, quibus b. G. Mylius ostendit, notitiam (theologiam) naturalem mancam esse et mutilam, quia, inquit, doctrinae coelestis partem duntaxat unam, eamque minimam, legem nimirum, et ne hanc quidem etiam integram, sed dimidiatam tantummodo inculcat, ignorata partim veri cultus divini, partim evangelicae salutis cognitione, in qua utraque nucleus ipse notitiae divinae inclusus latet. Posit. de Deo, th. 13.

Calovius: „Quod in specie ad capita theologiae istius naturalis potiora, sunt sequentia: 1. De Deo, qua naturam et attributa, nec non voluntatem Dei legalem ex parte et opera nonnulla; minime autem qua personas distinctas deitatis vel voluntatem Dei evangelicam et opera gratiae, aliaque mysteria divina, quae rationi prorsus ignota sunt. 2. De lege Dei, qua eadem e lege naturae habetur secundum praecepta utriusque tabulae. Huc pertinent Zaleuci leges, aurea Pythagorae verba, Socratis, Platonis moralia praecepta, Epicteti regulae, Jamblichi, Simplicii aliorumque Platonicorum, itemque Aristotelis et Peripateticorum monita egregia, leges XII tabularum etc. 3. De peccato et transgressione legis. 4. De poena peccati, quam etiam lex naturae et conscientia cujusque dictat propria. 5. De immortalitate animae et vita post hanc vitam, quam e Zoroastre, Hermete Trismegisto, Phocilide, Pythagora, Socrate, Platone, Xenocrate, Epaminonda, Cicerone, Plotino, Jamblicho etc. ostendimus Decad. dissertat, de Pseudo-Theol. Soc. p. 80.“ (Isag. L. I. p. 68. sq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Because the whole of human nature is corrupted, destitute of the powers it…

Because the whole of human nature is corrupted, destitute of the powers it ought to have, and has become prone to evil. Beautifully again the blessed Mylius, l. c. th. 12: “It tinges and sprinkles the mind with knowledge, but it subdues the disordered motions of the heart too languidly.” Compare with these and the preceding the blessed Jac. Mart. l. c. § 112. 113. p. 73., the blessed J. Mus. l. c. p. 45. 46. and the cited Disp. § 32. 33. p. 18. 19. 20.

Whether he has heard something about supernatural revelation and about Christ the mediator, or not. For by the grace of God and the merit of Christ, no one is saved except he who apprehends by faith the satisfaction performed by Christ for sins and appropriates it to himself, so that it may be presented to the angry God as if it were his own merit. See again the cited Disp. of the blessed Mus. § 101. sqq. p. 6. sqq. and his Dissertation against Steph. Curcellaeus on the question: Whether the Gentiles can attain to eternal salvation without faith in Christ through the extraordinary grace of God, etc.

Calovius: “Not all things that are found in the writings of the Gentiles which are theological are to be referred to natural theology: for some things have proceeded from the abuse of reason and natural principles, such as the various errors and false opinions of the Gentiles (concerning which [we speak] more fully in the theology of the Gentiles); some have proceeded from divine revelation, not indeed made as directly to the Gentiles, but proceeding from the people of God, through report or tradition, because of the conversation and some commerce of the Gentiles with those who were of the people of God. Thus, when the patriarchs lived among the Gentiles, certain traces of the religion revealed by God were left among them; e.g., among the Egyptians and Chaldeans (who were held among the Gentiles as the greatest theologians), some things remained from the instruction of Abraham, whence the theological writings of Trismegistus and others of great authority existed among the Gentiles, in which not a few things analogous to Christian theology concerning God, the Word, the generation of the Son of God, the Most Holy Trinity, etc., are read; which gave the Socinians occasion to cavil at the mysteries of the faith, [claiming] that they were drawn and proceeded from the writings of the Gentiles, when rather the Gentiles received them from the Church.”

PROLEGOM. CHAP. I. Chemnitius: "Does God approve of that knowledge? — You ask: does God wish us to seek and consider these traces of His divinity in our minds and in the whole nature of things?

I answer: Yes; because Paul adorns this consideration with an illustrious title, when he calls it 'the truth of God' (Rom. 1:18), and Christ commands us to consider the birds of the air, likewise the lilies, how they grow (Matt. 6:26, 28), and Solomon in Prov. 6:6 sends the sluggard to the ant. And to this pertains the entire 104th Psalm and the whole of the 45th chapter of Ecclesiasticus.

If only we would diligently unfold the most ample book of nature, then we would experience in reality that it is true what the poet of our age sang: 'And every herb reflects the present God.' If only man, the μικροκόσμος, would also consider himself, then without doubt he would discover illustrious traces of divinity.

But, alas, that which is said in Is. 5:12 comes to pass: 'They do not consider the work of the Lord.'

What, therefore, is the true and pious use of this natural knowledge in the church? It is written in Heb. 11:3 that creation is an image of the invisible things of God; but it is added: by faith. This sentence shows the true use of the traces of divinity in the nature of things. For it affirms that reason cannot truly and usefully know the Maker from the effects, unless faith is added.

Therefore, the beginning is not to be made from natural knowledge; but 1. the mind is to be confirmed from the Word of God and the illustrious testimonies in which God has peculiarly revealed Himself to the human race. Afterward, the consideration of philosophical demonstrations can be usefully added.

2. Natural knowledge ought to be subordinated to divine revelation in the Word; so that, wherever it dissents or conflicts, the natural should yield to the divine; which, even in those things in which they agree, adds strength and certainty to the natural.

3. The consideration is pleasant, from that as it were mere spark of knowledge which remains in nature, how illustrious the knowledge of God would have been in integral nature, how firm the assent, how compliant the obedience conformable to that knowledge; and to what extent all these things have been shaken, indeed almost extinguished in this depravity of nature, cannot be better considered than in these traces, which God willed to remain even for this reason." (Loc. theol. l. de Deo c. I. s. 5. and 6. fol. 21.) §

9. Meanwhile, natural theology, both as to its principles and as to the conclusions which depend upon them, is entirely true and certain, nor does it conflict with true revealed theology, although it must be admitted that, as it is found to exist in men actually after the fall, it is contaminated by various prejudices and errors.

Which is one in itself, nor is it to be thought that it is one thing or another in species on account of the different states of men; although a diversity as to degrees of perfection and imperfection must be admitted. Compare Mus. Introd. Chap. II. § 6. p. 32.

For they depend, as constituting ectypal theology, upon God the author, to whom the false is repugnant. And just as the first principles are of those things which cannot be otherwise and are therefore necessarily true, so it is evident that the conclusions, which have a necessary connection with those principles, are likewise true and certain.

To this the Leipzig theologians refer in App. Consil. Ded. fol. 143, that Paul, when saying in Rom. 1:18 concerning the Gentiles that they hold the truth, etc., refers to natural knowledge, such as it is in itself, as being true science or cognition. ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

Melanchthon: "Just as light is divinely implanted in the eyes, so certain notions are implanted in human minds, by which they recognize and judge most things. Philosophers call this light the knowledge of principles; they call them κοινας έννοιας and προλήψεις.

And the common division is well known. Some are speculative principles, such as the knowledge of numbers, order, the syllogism, and geometric and physical principles. Everyone confesses that these are most certain and are the sources of the greatest utilities in life. For what would life be without numbers, without order? Others are practical principles, such as the entire natural distinction between honorable and base things; likewise, that God must be obeyed.

And indeed, these practical principles ought to be as illustrious and firm to us as the knowledge of numbers; yet, because a certain darkness has entered on account of the fall of origin, and the heart has impulses contrary to the distinction between honorable and base things, therefore men do not assent to these notions as constantly—that God must be obeyed, that adultery is to be avoided, that honorable covenants must be kept—as they do to this notion: Twice four is eight.

The knowledge of the laws remains, but the assent is weak on account of the contumacy of the heart. The knowledge is a testimony that we have originated from God and owe obedience to God, and it accuses disobedience. Indeed, doubt and contumacy are an illustrious sign that the nature of man is not whole; just as death and the infinite calamities of the human race and many prodigious vices signify the same.

Paul explained this in Romans 1 in these words: 'They hold the truth in unrighteousness,' that is, even though a true notion is impressed upon men—that there is one eternal mind, the creator and preserver of things, wise, good, just, etc., and that this God must be obeyed according to the distinction between honorable and base things—yet these true notions are held in unrighteousness, that is, they are held captive; they do not reign, but unrighteousness reigns, fighting against these notions, namely, the aversion of the will from God, contempt of God, trust in one's own powers, and finally various impulses fighting against the light divinely implanted in minds. Therefore, the assent is also weaker, and ' The charioteer is carried by the horses, nor does the chariot heed the reins.'

Therefore, philosophers, when they saw that assent was weak and that men were being swept away by great impulse toward diverse pleasures, asked whether just and unjust things are distinguished by nature or by opinion. To doubt about this matter is base and flagitious, just as if someone were to ask whether twice four is eight by nature or by chance.

The divine light in minds must not be extinguished, but rather stirred up, and the soul must be strengthened so that it may recognize practical principles, embrace them, and determine that they are in truth as certain and firm as speculative ones, indeed, that they are equally the immutable decrees of God. Just as Paul also preaches in Romans 1, saying: 'God has shown it to them'; likewise in Romans 2: 'The work of the law written in their hearts.' He also calls these notions divine law in Romans 1: 'Who, knowing the law of God.' Therefore, the true definition of the law of nature is that the law of nature is the knowledge of the divine law, implanted in the nature of man." (Loci praecipui theologici. Lips. 1552. p. 199—202.)

But it is truly consistent. Nor is there anything but a single truth. Although natural theology does not attain to the objects that are proper to revealed theology, it does not therefore deny or impugn any of them, or establish the opposite, but suspends its judgment as concerning things placed outside its sphere. Indeed, if revelation is added, it is certain that the defect of our natural cognition is supplied by the added, more sublime cognition. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Introduct. P. II. Cap. V. § 7. p. 324. sqq. and § 15. p. 337. 338. and the booklet of the blessed Grauer on the single truth. A fuller collation of true natural theology with revealed theology was presented in the year 1676 under our presidency in an inaugural dissertation by the blessed Heinricus a Lith, a most beloved relative. PROLEGOM. CAP. I.

Gerhard: "In itself and by itself there is no contrariety, no contradiction between philosophy and theology, because those things which theology proposes concerning the highest mysteries of the faith from revelation, sound and sincere philosophy knows are not to be discussed and evaluated from the principles of reason, lest a μετάβασις εις αλλο γένος occur, or the distinct principles of distinct disciplines be confounded. Thus, when theology teaches that Mary gave birth and remained a virgin, sound philosophy does not say that this assertion contradicts its conclusion that it is αδύνατον for a virgin to give birth; because it knows that that conclusion must necessarily be accepted with this limitation: that for a virgin to give birth naturally, and to remain such, is αδύνατον, the contrary of which it does not assert; for it says that it was done by supernatural and divine power that a virgin gave birth. But when some philosophaster wishes his axioms and pronouncements to be so general that even the highest mysteries of the faith are to be judged by them, and thus invades foreign boundaries, then it happens accidentally that what is theologically true is called philosophically false, regard being had, of course, not to the true use of sounder philosophy, but to its most shameful abuse. Thus, justice and the principle of law is everywhere one, in a general concept, to be sure; meanwhile, however, the law of this province is not the same as the law of another province, but every commonwealth lives by its own special laws. So truth is one in a general concept; meanwhile, every discipline has its own axioms, which are not to be dragged into another forum, but left in their own sphere, lest a μετάβασις εις αλλο γένος occur, which sound philosophy itself repudiates." (Exeges. locc. L. de S. S. § 474.)

Latin:

Quia tota natura humana corrupta bonisque, quas habere debebat, viribus destituta et ad malum proclivis facta est. Pulchre iterum b. Mylius l. c. th. 12.: Mentem scientia tingit et aspergit, cordis autem motus inconditos nimis languide subigit. Confer cum his et praecedd. b. Jac. Mart. l. c. § 112. 113. p. 73., b. J. Mus. l. c. p. 45. 46. et Disp. cit. § 32. 33. p. 18. 19. 20.

Sive audiverit aliquid de revelatione supernaturali deque Christo mediatore, sive non. Per gratiam Dei enim et meritum Christi nemo quisquam salvatur, nisi qui praestitam a Christo satisfactionem pro peccatis fide apprehendit sibique appropriat, ut istud Deo irato, quasi suum esset meritum, sistatur. Vid. iterum Disp. cit. b. Mus. § 101. sqq. p. 6. sqq. et Dissert. ejusdem contra Steph. Curcellaeum in quaestione: Utrum gentiles absque fide in Christum per extraordinariam Dei gratiam ad salutem aeternam pertingere possint f etc.

Calovius: ,,Νοn omnia, quae in scriptis gentilium reperiuntur theologica, ad theologiam naturalem referenda sunt: quaedam enim ex abusu rationiS et principiorum naturalium promanarunt, ut sunt varii errores et falsae opiniones gentilium (de quibus in theologia gentilium fusius); quaedam profecta sunt e revelatione divina, non quidem tam directe facta gentilibus, quam e populo Dei profecta, per famam vel traditionem, ob conversationem et commercia nonnulla gentilium cum iis, qui fuere de populo Dei. Sic, cum patriarchae inter gentiles vixere, vestigia quaedam religionis a Deo patefactae inter ipsos relicta fuere, e. g. inter Aegyptios et Chaldaeos (qui inter gentiles pro summis theologis habiti), ex Abrahami institutione nonnulla remansere, unde Trismegisti et aliorum scripta theologica magnae auctoritatis inter gentiles extitere, in quibus non pauca Christianae theologiae analoga de Deo, de verbo, generatione Filii Dei, SS. Trinitate etc. leguntur; quae occasionem dedere Socinianis cavillandi mysteria fidei, quod e gentilium scriptis hausta et profecta sint, cum potius gentiles ea ab ecclesia acceperint.“

Chemnitius: „Approbatne Deus illam notitiam? — Id quaeris: an Deus velit nos vestigia haec divinitatis suae in mentibus nostris et in tota rerum natura quaerere et considerare?

Respondeo: Sic; quia Paulus hanc considerationem illustri titulo ornat, dum appellat,veritatem Dei‘ Rom. 1, 18., et Christus jubet considerare volatilia coeli, item lilia, quomodo crescant, Mtth. 6, 26. 28., Salomon in Prov. 6, 6. remittit pigrum ad fornicam. Et huc pertinet Ps. 104. integer et totum 45. c. Ecclesiastici.

Utinam vero amplissimum naturae librum diligenter evolveremus, tunc re ipsa experiremur, verum esse, quod nostrae aetatis vates cecinit: ,Praesentemque refert quaelibet herba Deum.' Utinam etiam homo μικροκόσμος seipsum consideraret, tunc absque dubio illustria divinitatis vestigia deprehenderet.

Sed fit proh dolor illud, quod Es. 5, 12. dicitur: ,Opus Domini non considerant.'

Quis ergo in ecclesia est verus et pius usus hujus naturalis notitiae? Ebr. 11, 3. scriptum est: Creationem esse simulacrum invisibilium Dei; sed additur: perfidem. Haec sententia ostendit verum usum vestigiorum divinitatis in rerum natura. Affirmat enim, rationem non posse vere et utiliter ex effectibus opificem cognoscere, nisi accedat fides.

Non ergo initium faciendum est a naturali notitia; sed 1. mens confirmanda est ex verbo Dei et illustribus testimoniis, in quibus se Deus generi humano peculiariter patefecit. Postea utiliter potest addi consideratio philosophicarum demonstrationum.

2. Notitia naturalis debet subordinari divinae revelationi in verbo; ita ut, sicubi dissentiat vel pugnet, cedat naturalis divinae; quae etiam in illis, in quibus consentiunt, robur et certitudinem addit naturali.

3. Jucunda est consideratio, ex illa quasi scintilla tantum notitiae, quae reliqua est in natura, quam illustris fuisset notitia Dei in integra natura, quam firmus assensus, quam obsequens obedientia conformis notitiae; et in quantum labefactata, imo paene exstincta sint haec omnia in hac naturae depravatione, non potest melius considerari, quam in his vestigiis, quae etiam propter hanc causam Deus voluit esse reliqua.“ (Loc. theol. l. de Deo c. I. s. 5. et 6. fol. 21.) §

9. Interim theologia naturalis a tum quoad principia sua, tum quoad conclusiones, quae ab illis pendent, vera b omnino ac certa est, neque theologiae revelatae verae c repugnat, licet, prout hominibus post lapsum actu inesse deprehenditur, praejudiciis atque erroribus variis contaminatam esse, fatendum sit. d

Quae in se una, neque propter diversos status hominum ipsa quoque quoad speciem alia atque alia esse putanda est; licet quoad gradus perfectionis et imperfectionis diversitas admittenda sit. Confer Mus. Introd. Cap. II. § 6. p. 32.

Dependent enim, velut constituentes theologiam ectypam, ab auctore Deo, cui falsum repugnat. Et quemadmodum principia prima sunt de his, quae aliter se habere non possunt adeoque necessario vera sunt, ita conclusiones, quarum cum principiis istis necessarius nexus est, similiter veras ac certas esse, constat.

Huc referunt theologi Lipsienses in App. Consil. Ded. fol. 143., quod Paulus Rom. 1, 18. de gentilibus dicens, eos veritatem retinere etc., respiciat ad notitiam naturalem, qualis in se est, quippe vera scientia aut cognitio. DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Melanchthon: „Ut lumen oculis divinitus inditum est, ita sunt quaedam notitiae mentibus humanis inditae, quibus agnoscunt et judicant pleraque. Philosophi hoc lumen vocant notitiam principiorum, vocant κοινας έννοιας et προλήψεις.

Ac vulgaris divisio nota est. Alia esse principia speculabilia, ut notitias numerorum, ordinis, syllogismi, principia geometrica, physica. Haec omnes fatentur esse certissima et fontes maximarum utilitatum in vita. Qualis enim esset vita sine numeris, sine ordine? Alia sunt principia practica, ut totum discrimen naturale honestorum et turpium; item, Deo est obediendnm.

Ac debebant quidem haec practica principia tam illustria nobis esse et firma, quam sunt notitiae numerorum; tamen quia propter labem originis accessit quaedam caligo et cor habet contrarios impetus discrimini honestorum et turpium, ideo homines non tam constanter assentiuntur his notitiis: Deo obediendum est, adulterium est vitandum, honesta pacta sunt servanda; sicut huic notitiae: Bis quatuor sunt octo.

Manet notitia legum, sed assensus est infirmus propter contumaciam cordis. Notitia testimonium est, nos a Deo ortos esse ac Deo obedientiam debere, et accusat inobedientiam. Dubitatio vero et contumacia illustre signum est, naturam hominis non esse integram; sicut idem significant mors et calamitates infinitae humani generis et multa prodigiosa vitia.

Haec Paulus Rom. l. his verbis exposuit: ,Veritatem in injustitia detinent', id est, etsi impressa est hominibus vera notitia: quod sit Deus una quaedam aeterna mens, conditrix et conservatrix rerum, sapiens, bona, justa etc., et quod huic Deo obediendum sit juxta discrimen honestorum et turpium; tamen hae verae notitiae detinentur in injustitia, id est, captivae tenentur, non regnant, sed regnat injustitia, pugnans cum his notitiis, scilicet aversio voluntatis a Deo, contemtus Dei, fiducia propriarum virium, denique varii impetus pugnantes cum lumine divinitus insito mentibus. Ideo et assensus infirmior est, ac, Fertur equis auriga, nec audit currus habenas.'

Ideo philosophi, cum viderent, infirmam assensionem esse et rapi homines magno impetu ad diversas voluptates, quaesiverunt, utrum justa et injusta natura vel opinione discernantur. Qua de re dubitare, turpe et flagitiosum est, perinde ac si quis quaerat, an natura, vel casu bis quatuor sint octo.

Lumen divinum in mentibus non exstinguendum est, sed potius excitandum, et confirmandus animus, ut agnoscat principia practica, eaque amplectatur, et statuat, revera tam certa et firma esse, quam sunt speculabilia, imo pariter esse decreta immutabilia Dei. Sicut et Paulus concionatur Rom. 1., inquiens: ,Deus ipsis ostendit'; item Rom. 2.: ,Opus legis scriptum in mentibus eorum/ Yocat item has notitias jus divinum Rom. 1.: ,Qui cum jus Dei norint/ Est ergo vera definitio legis naturae, legem naturae esse notitiam legis divinae, naturae hominis insitam.“ (Loci praecipui theologici. Lips. 1552. p. 199—202.)

Verum enim vero consonat. Neque est nisi unica veritas. Quanquam autem theologia naturalis non assequitur objecta, quae theologiae revelatae sunt propria; non tamen ideo quicquam eorum negat aut impugnat, seu oppositum statuit, sed judicium suum, tanquam de rebus extra sphaeram suam positis, suspendit. Imo si accesserit revelatio, certum est, naturalis nostrae cognitionis defectum addita cognitione sublimiore suppleri. Conf. b. Musaei Introduct. P. II. Cap. V. § 7. p. 324. sqq. et § 15. p. 337. 338. et libellum b. Graueri de unica veritate. Pleniorem vero collationem verae theologiae naturalis cum revelata a. 1676. sub praesidio nostro exhibuit in Disp. inaug. b. Heinricus a Lith, affinis desideratissimus. PROLEGOM. CAP. I.

Gerhardus: „Per se et in se nulla contrarietas, nulla contradictio inter philosophiam et theologiam, quia quae de summis fidei mysteriis theologia proponit ex revelatione, illa philosophia sanior ac sincera novit non esse discutienda et aestimanda ex principiis rationis, ne fiat μετάβασις εις αλλο γένος, neve confundantur distinctarum disciplinarum principia distincta. Sic quando theologia docet, Mariam peperisse, et virginem mansisse, sanior philosophia non dicit, hoc assertum repugnare suae conclusioni, quod virginem parere sit άόννατον; quia novit, conclusionem illam necessario cum hac limitatione accipiendam, quod virginem naturaliter parere; et talem manere, sit αδύνατον, cujus contrarium non asserit; dicit enim, supernaturali et divina virtute esse factum, ut virgo pareret. Quando vero philosophaster. aliquis sua axiomata et effata vult esse tam generalia, ut ex illis etiam de summis fidei mysteriis sit judicandum, et sic fines alienos invadit, tunc ex accidenti contingit, ut verum theologice falsum dicatur philosophice, respectu scilicet habito non ad verum sanioris philosophiae usum, sed ad turpissimum ejusdem abusum. Sic justitia et juris ratio est ubique una, in conceptu scl. generali, interim tamen jus hujus provinciae non est idem cum jure alterius provinciae, sed quaelibet respublica suis specialibus vivit legibus. Ita veritas est una in conceptu generali, interim quaelibet disciplina sua habet axiomata, quae non sunt trahenda in aliud forum, sed in sua sphaera relinquenda, ne fiat μετάβασις εις άλλο γένος, quam ipsa sanior philosophia repudiat.“ (Exeges. locc. L. de S. S. § 474.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Luther: "Sixth, let us compare this institution (the monastic) also to natural…

Luther: "Sixth, let us compare this institution (the monastic) also to natural reason, that is, to that crude light of nature, which, although it does not attain to the light and works of God by itself, so that in affirmative matters (as they say) its judgment is fallacious, yet in negative matters it is certain. For reason does not grasp what God is, yet it most certainly grasps what God is not. Thus, although it does not see what is right and good before God (namely, faith), it nevertheless knows evidently that infidelity, murder, and disobedience are evil. Christ also uses this when He argues in Luke 11 that every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and Paul, when he says in 1 Cor. 11 that nature itself teaches that a woman should not prophesy with her head uncovered. Therefore, whatever evidently opposes this reason is certain to oppose God much more. For how will that which fights against earthly truth not fight against heavenly truth? In the same way, Christ in John 3 distinguishes truth and argues from both: 'If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?'" (Opp. lat. varii argumenti; Edited by D. H. Schmidt. Frankfurt, 1872. Vol. VI. p. 318. sq. Opp. Hal. Tom. XIX, 1940. Cf. Luther's theological treatise on the question: "Whether the theological proposition, 'The Word became flesh,' is true in philosophy"; which Luther denies when a μετάβασις εις αλλο γένος is committed. See Opp. Hal. T. X, 1396—1402.)

Calovius: "Junius is mistaken, 1) when he assigns principles and common notions to false theology; for these, even if they bring about only an imperfect knowledge and are conjoined with falsity by reason of the subject as the corrupt state of man, are nevertheless not false in themselves, but, truly drawing their origin from God and being inscribed upon nature, they are indeed held back in unrighteousness, yet they contain the truth, Rom. 1:18. He is mistaken, 2) when he constitutes those common principles, which are commonly called κοινάϊ ’έννοιαι, as the root of all false theology, since from the true nothing follows except the true, and false theology has flowed not from the common principles themselves, as such, but from the corruption of them. He is mistaken, 3) when he points to philosophical knowledge of God as false, and asserts that it has arisen from the cultivation of a natural notion; because certain philosophical knowledge about God is also true—indeed, all that which is properly philosophical (for the error of philosophers is not to be attributed to philosophy itself)—and whatever arises from the legitimate cultivation and genuine use of natural knowledge is true, not false, since it is only the abuse of the same that begets false opinions, not the use."

OF THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

The same: "The matter from which [they are derived] are principles known by the light of nature, from which conclusions are deduced according to the measure of human reason. . . The principles indeed remained in a certain way from the prior state (of integrity), but they are common and imperfect; yet these must be distinguished from the adventitious corruption, even if they are not found in the subject after the fall, except with that corruption." (L. c. p. 64. 66.)

Thus, we have removed the ψυχική or natural theology of the Gentile philosophers, along with the other kinds of Gentile theology, as erroneous, note f. to § 1. And that men destitute of true divine revelation have also abused their own reason and have been swept away into various errors regarding the knowledge and worship of God, we are taught by revelation itself, Rom. 1:22 sqq. And hence it is that, since they had not found true revelation, they embraced false revelations rather than none at all. Compare, blessed Himmel, Syntag. Disp. I. § 23. sqq. to 28. § 10. The formal object of natural theology, as a practical science, is its end, and that is objective, or God, insofar as He is known from the light of nature before demonstration, both through knowledge that is innate, or a certain light inborn in the intellect and an instinct of nature, and through that which is acquired, common, or vulgar, from the inspection of creatures.

Or that which is first known in natural theology, and once known, is the reason for knowing the rest; according to those things which we said at § 3, note d. For in any science, the end must be to some extent known beforehand, whereby man is induced to practice or operation, undertaken for its sake. See blessed Musaeus, Introd. Cap. II. § 5. p. 29., § 15. p. 48 For the knowledge of the formal end, if not distinct, is yet confused, and depends on the objective end; and therefore it is not the former, but the latter that is known first. Musaeus, l. c. § 15. p. 48 For insofar as it becomes known from divine revelation, its knowledge pertains not to natural, but to revealed theology. Musaeus, l. c. p. 49 By the appellation of the light of nature, however, we understand in this place those propositions which declare the existence, essence, and essential perfections of God, insofar as they are known either from the principles of nature and reason through discourse, or by the power of the agent intellect and phantasms apprehended from terms, immediately and without discourse. Musaeus, l. c. p. 50. 51. 52 And it is to be noted that the formal object of natural theology is not constituted precisely by the light of nature, but by God known from the light of nature. For the former is not the reason for assenting proper and proximate to natural theology, but is too general and remote. Musaeus, l. c. and § 28. p. 85. 86. J. Gerhard: "Since it is said in Ps. 96:5 that the gods of the Gentiles are demons, and since Christ expressly testifies in John 5:23 that he who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father: it is rightly asked in what sense he says

How can the] Apostle [say] that the Gentiles knew the eternal power and divinity of God from the creation of the world? Rom. 1:20. Resp.: A distinction must be made between the concept of God, drawn by the minds of the heathens from created things, and the application of that concept; the former was legitimate, but the latter was not. For although they discovered from the book of nature the eternal power and divinity and, as Plato speaks, "the eternal mind, the cause of all good in nature," or, as Aristotle says, "some supreme being and the first principle of all motion, the very ἀκίνητον," or, as Cicero speaks, "a preeminent, eternal, and venerable nature": yet they did not rightly apply it to that one Jehovah, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; not to God the Father, from whom the Son is eternally begotten and in time sent, that He might be the mediator and redeemer of the human race; but they attributed it either to irrational animals, serpents, reptiles, etc., Rom. 1:28, or even to the devil himself, Ps. 96:5. And since they devised the form and norm of worshiping God from their own ingenuity, they therefore worshiped the idol of their own heart, and not the true God, which the Apostle expresses thus: "When they knew God, they glorified Him not as God," Rom. 1:21, "they changed the truth of God into a lie," v. 25. (Loc. de natura D. § 14.)

This is called such, not because an actual knowledge of God, or an expressed species, resides in man by nature before the use of reason; but because, once the terms are grasped, it resides in the intellect immediately without discursive reasoning, just as if it had been implanted in him actually with nature itself. Mus. l. c. § 19. p. 52.

This is indeed not an impressed species, existing in the intellect by nature before the use of reason; nor is it a habit properly so called, nor even the mere δύναμις or power of knowing: but something superadded to or innate in the power of knowing. Namely, a certain perfection, by which the intellect is constituted powerful or in a proximate potency to elicit acts of knowing immediately; which, although it is not a habit properly so called, is nevertheless ἀνάλογον (analogous) to a habit; just as the blessed Musaeus taught at length not only in his many manuscript lectures, but also in his Introd. Cap. II. § 19. p. 52 sqq. up to 80, and asserts again in his *Ausführliche Erklärung* p. 150 sqq. But also the blessed Huelsemann in *Praelect. ad Breviar.* Cap. I. p. 1134 expressly confesses that he assents to that opinion which maintains that this natural knowledge is born with man, not by way of a habit, but by a mere power of knowing (he undoubtedly understands a proximate power), and having adduced the passages Rom. 1:19, 20; 2:14, he proves that opinion and concludes that this natural knowledge resides in man by power, not by an infused habit.

Hollazius: "It is certain that the τὸ εἴ ἐστι (that it is) or the true existence of the innate knowledge of God [is established]; but the τὸ τί ἐστι (what it is) or its definitive definition is not so clear. From which it happens that it is defined in various ways even by orthodox theologians. . . . Whatever it is that, according to their mind, can be said to reside in the intellect by nature or to be connate to it, it is necessary that it return to a certain inborn perfection or light of the intellect, aided by which it perceives the truth of common notions about God immediately upon grasping the terms, without discursive reasoning. And in this they almost all agree. . . . Yet we do not deny that the innate knowledge of God is a certain perfection, congenital to man as a wayfarer and analogous to a habit. Which analogy consists in the following: 1. Just as the image of God in the protoplasts was a habit, so the remnants of the same, to which the law of nature pertains, dictating that God must be worshiped, approach in a certain way to his very nature; since homogeneous parts are of the same nature as the whole. 2. Just as a habit is a certain perfection, superadded to nature, facilitating it for operation, so also [is] the knowledge..." ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

is superadded to the cognitive faculty of God, inclining it to apprehend God in whatever way. 3. Just as a habit is difficult to move, so this natural knowledge adheres deeply to the soul, nor can it be entirely eradicated.” (Exam. P. I. c. 1. q. 6. p. 189. sq.)

The same: “The idea representing the essence of God, congenital to the human intellect, is a sweet dream of the Cartesians.” (L. c. p. 195.)

Cicero: “Nor is there any nation so savage, no one of all so brutal, whose mind has not been imbued with the opinion of the gods. Many think wrongly about the gods, for that is usually brought about by vicious custom; yet all judge that there is a divine power and nature. Nor does the conversation of men or consensus bring this about, nor is the opinion confirmed by institutions, nor by laws. But in every matter, the consensus of all nations is to be considered a law of nature.” (Tusc. qq. lib. 1.)

Latin:

Lutherus: „Sexto comparemus institutum istud (monasticum) etiam ad rationem naturalem, h. e., ad crassum illud lumen naturae, quae, tametsi lucem et opera Dei non attingat per sese, ita ut in affirmativis (quod ajunt) fallax sit ejus judicium, in negativis tamen est certum. Non enim capit ratio, quid sit Deus, certissime tamen capit, quid non sit Deus. Ita licet non videat, quid rectum et bonum sit coram Deo (nempe fidem), scit tamen evidenter, infidelitatem, homicidia, inobedientiam esse mala. Qua et Christus utitur, dum disserit Luc. 11., omne regnum in se ipsum divisum desolari, et Paulus, dum dicit 1 Cor. 11., nec naturam docere, ut mulier nudato capite prophetet. Quod ergo huic rationi evidenter adversatur, certum est, et Deo multo magis adversari. Quomodo enim coelesti veritati non pugnabit, quod terrenae veritati pugnat? quo modo et Christus Joh. 3. veritatem distinguit et ex utraque arguit: Si terrena vobis dixi et non creditis, quomodo, si coelestia vobis dixero, credetis?“ (Opp. lat. varii argumenti; Curavit D. H. Schmidt. Francof. 1872. Vol. VI. p. 318. sq. Opp. Hai. Tom. XIX, 1940. Cf. Lutheri Theologische Abhandlung von der Frage: „Ob der theologische Satz: ,Das Wort ward Fleisch*, in der Philosophie wahr sei“; quod Luth. negat, quando committitur μετάβασις εις αλλο γένος. Vid. Opp. Hal. Τ. X, 1396—1402.)

Calovius: „Fallitur Junius, 1) dum falsae theologiae assignat principia et notiones communes; quae, etsi imperfectam tantum notitiam inferant et cum falsitate conjunctae sint ratione subjecti qua corruptum hominis statum, per se tamen falsae non sunt, sed, vere a Deo ortum trahentes et naturae insculptae, detinentur quidem in injustitia, veritatem tamen continent, Rom. 1, 18. Fallitur, 2) dum radicem omnis falsae theologiae principia illa communia, quae κοινάϊ ’έννοιαι vulgo dicuntur, constituat, cum e vero non nisi verum sequatur nec ex ipsis communibus principiis, qua talibus, sed e corruptione eorum profluxerit falsa theologia. Fallitur, 3) dum philosophicam notitiam Dei falsam indigitat, eamque ortam e cultura naturalis notionis, asserit; quia et philosophica quaedam notitia de Deo vera est, imo omnis illa, quae proprie est philosophica (error enim philosophorum non est ipsi tribuendus philosophiae), et quicquid e naturalis notitiae cultura legitima usuque genuino oritur, verum est, non falsum, cum abusus saltem ejusdem gignat falsas opiniones, non usus.“

DB NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Idem: „Materia ex qua sunt principia naturae lumine nota, unde deducuntur conclusiones pro rationis humanae modulo. . . Principia quidem permanserunt quodammodo e priori statu (integritatis), sed ea communia sunt et imperfecta; quae tamen a corruptione adventitia distinguenda, etsi non reperiantur in subjecto post lapsum, nisi cum illa corruptione.“ (L. c. p. 64. 66.)

Sic theologiam ψυσιχψ aut naturalem philosophorum gentilium, una cum caeteris theologiae gentilis generibus, supra removimus, tanquam erroneam, not. f. ad § 1. Et homines vera revelatione divina destitutos, ratione quoque sua abusos atque in errores varios quoad cognitionem cultumque Dei fuisse abreptos, docemur ex ipsa revelatione Rom. 1, 22. sqq. Atque hinc est, quod cum veram revelationem non invenissent, falsas pro veris potius, quam nullas, revelationes amplexi fuerunt. Confer, b. Himmel. Syntag. Disp. I. § 23. sqq. ad 28.§ 10. Objectum formale a theologiae naturalis, tanquam scientiae practicae, finis b est, isque objectivus c seu Deus, quatenus ex lumine naturae d ante demonstrationem, per notitiam cum insitam e seu lucem quandam f intellectui ingenitam et instinctum g naturae, tum ex inspectione creaturarum acquisitam vulgarem seu h communem, cognoscitur. i

Sive id, quod in theologia naturali primo cognoscitur, et cognitum est ratio cognoscendi caetera; juxta ea, quae diximus ad § 3. not. d. In quavis enim scientia finem oportet esse quadantenus praecognitum, unde ad praxin seu operationem, ejus causa suscipiendam, homo inducitur. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. Cap. II. § 5. p. 29., § 15. p. 48 Formalis enim finis cognitio, si non distincta, confusa tamen, pendet a fine obiectivo; neque adeo ille, sed hic primo cognoscitur. Mus. l. c. § 15. p. 48 Nam quatenus ex divina revelatione innotescit, non ad naturalem, sed revelatam theologiam cognitio ejus pertinet. Mus. 1. c. p. 49 Luminis naturae appellatione autem intelligimus h. 1. propositiones, quae Dei existentiam, essentiam et perfectiones essentiales declarant, quatenus vel ex principiis naturae et rationis per discursum, vel virtute intellectus agentis et phantasmatum ex terminis apprehensis per se immediate et citra discursum cognitae sunt. Mus. 1. c. p. 50. 51. 52 Ac notandum est, objectum formale theologiae naturalis non constitui praecise lumen naturae, sed Deum ex lumine naturae cognitum. Illud enim non est ratio assentiendi theologiae naturali propria et proxima, sed nimis generalis et remota. Mus. 1. c. et § 28. p. 85. 86.J. Gerhardus: „Cum Ps. 96, 5. dicatur, gentium deos esse daemonia, cumque diserte testetur Christus Joh. 5, 23., qui non honoret filium, eum nec honorare patrem: merito quaeritur, quo sensu dicat

apostolus, quod gentiles aeternam Dei potentiam ac divinitatem ex creatione mundi cognoverint? Rom. 1, 20. Resp.: Distinguendum est inter conceptum Dei, ex creaturis ab ethnicorum mente haustum, et inter conceptus istius applicationem; ille fuit legitimus, haec vero minime. Quamvis enim aeternam potentiam ac divinitatem et, ut Plato loquitur, ,mentem aeternam, causam omnis boni in natura', vel, ut Aristoteles dicit, ,summum aliquod ens et primum omnis motus principium, ipsum ακίνητον' vel, ut Cicero loquitur, ,praestantem aeternam ac suspiciendam naturam' ex libro naturae deprehenderint: tamen illam non recte applicarunt uni illi Jehovae, qui est Pater, Filius et Spiritus S.; non Deo Patri, a quo Filius ab aeterno progenitus est et in tempore missus, ut esset mediator et redemptor generis humani; sed eam vel animalibus irrationalibus, serpentibus, reptilibus etc. tribuerunt, Rom. 1, 28., vel etiam ipsi diabolo, Ps. 96, 5., et siquidem ex proprio ingenio formam ac normam Deum colendi excogitarunt, ideo cordis sui idolum, non autem verum Deum coluerunt, id quod apostolus sic effert: ,Cum cognovissent Deum, non ut Deum glorificaverunt', Rom. 1, 21., ,veritatem Dei commutarunt in mendacia4, v. 25." (Loc. de natura D. § 14.)

Quae talis dicitur, non quod cognitio Dei actualis, aut species expressa, homini per naturam ante rationis usum insit; sed quia apprehensis terminis statim intellectui citra discursum inest, non secus, ac si cum ipsa natura ei actu implantata esset. Mus. l. c. § 19. p. 52.

Quae quidem non est species impressa, intellectui ante usum rationis per naturam inexistens; neque adeo habitus proprie dictus, neque etiam ipsa nuda δύναμις seu potentia cognoscendi: sed aliud potentiae cognoscendi superadditum aut innatum. Perfectio videlicet aliqua, per quam intellectus potens aut in potentia propinqua ad actus cognoscendi immediate eliciendos constituitur; quae, licet non sit habitus proprie dictus, habitui tamen ανάλογης est; quemadmodum b. Musaeus non solum in collegiis MSS. pluribus, verum etiam in Introd. Cap. II. § 19. p. 52. sqq. usque ad 80. prolixe docuit, et rursus asserit in der Ausführl. Erklärung p. 150. sqq. Sed et b. Huelsemannus in Praelect. ad Breviar. Cap. I. p. 1134. expresse fatetur, se illi sententiae assentiri, quae naturalem illam cognitionem non per modum habitus, sed per nudam potentiam cognoscendi (intelligit autem haud dubie potentiam propinquam) connasci cum homine statuit, adductisque locis Rom. 1, 19. 20. 2, 14. probat sententiam illam, et concludit, cognitionem illam naturalem inesse homini per potentiam, non per infusum habitum.

Hollazius: ,,Constat το εΐ εστι sive existentia vera notitiae de Deo innatae; at το τί εστι sive ejus definitiva ratio non adeo liquida est. Ex quo fit, ut a theologis etiam orthodoxis diversimode definiatur. . . . Quicquid est, quod ex illorum mente intellectui natura inesse sive ei connatum dici possit, necesse est, ut redeat ad ingenitam quandam perfectionem sive lucem intellectus, qua adjutus veritatem communium de Deo notionum apprehensis terminis statim citra discursum perspiciat. Atque in hoc fere conveniunt. . . Non tamen diffitemur, notitiam Dei insitam esse perfectionem quandam, homini viatori congenitam et habitui analogam. Quae analogia consistit in sequentibus: 1. sicut imago Dei in hominibus protoplastis fuit habitus, ita reliquiae ejusdem, ad quas pertinet lex naturae, Deum colendum esse dictitans, ad ipsius naturam quodammodo accedunt; cum partes homogeneae sint ejusdem naturae cum toto. 2. Sicut habitus est quaedam perfectio, superaddita naturae, eam facilitans ad operationem, ita quoque notitia DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Dei naturalis superaddita est facultati cognoscitivae, illam inclinans ad apprehendendum quocunque modo Deum. 3. Sicut habitus est difficulter mobilis, ita profunde inhaeret ista notitia naturalis animae, nec penitus eradicari potest.“ (Exam. P. I. c. 1. q. 6. p. 189. sq.)

Idem: „Idea, essentiam Dei repraesentans, intellectui humano fcongenita, suave est Cartesianorum somnium.“ (L. c. p. 195.)

Cicero: „Neque ulla gens tam fera, nemo omnium tam immanis est, cujus mentem non imbuerit deorum opinio. Multi de diis prava sentiunt, id enim vitioso more effici solet; omnes tamen, esse vim et naturam divinam, arbitrantur. Nec vero id collocutio hominum aut consensus efficit, non institutis opinio est confirmata, nqn legibus. Omni autem in re consensio omnium gentium lex naturae putanda est.“ (Tuse. qq. lib. 1.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: The same: “It is innate in all and, as it were, inscribed upon the mind, that…

The same: “It is innate in all and, as it were, inscribed upon the mind, that there are gods.” (De N. D. lib. 2.)

Hollazius: “Speculative atheists can exist, not by nature, but through the just desertion of God and the blinding of the devil; not through the total eradication of the light of nature as regards the habit, but through its suffocation as regards act and exercise; not through the whole span of life and permanently, but only through a certain paroxysm passing for some time. For the law of nature does not allow that a settled and firm opinion should adhere to anyone that there is no God. For although the mind of an impious man may be lulled as if into a lethargy, so that he does not think about God; yet no one can be found in whom conscience does not eventually vindicate itself and, even in death itself, accuse him of the neglected God.” (Exam. P. I. c. 1. q. 5. p. 194.)

Which is nothing other than an inclination of nature toward God as its end, which determines the intellect, possessing that connate light, as if by an added weight, to grant assent—both to other common notions about God and especially to that which concerns the existence of God—immediately and without discursive reasoning. See Mus. in Introd. p. 78, 79, 80. Detailed Explanation p. 161, 162, 163.

Such as is commonly wont to be in all, even the simpler ones who are not capable of demonstrations, and is acquired either from the testimony of others, e.g., parents, teachers, magistrates, and the people, or from the inspection of creatures, by a consequence indeed, but one that is easy and obvious to any illiterate person. Mus. Introd. 1. c. § 23, 24, p. 81.

Natural theology, therefore, presupposes both of these knowledges; but from them, as from a principle of knowing, it seeks the rule of right operation and draws its conclusions, as a demonstrative habit. Mus. 1. c. § 28, p. 86.

And thus the blessed Himmelius writes in Syntagm. Disp. I. § 19, p. 3: There are two principles of natural theology: the internal, namely, κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι, the ruins or relics of the divine image, and the external, namely, the inspection of creatures. §

11. To the material object pertain a the subject of the operation, b and the end of the causes to be attained, and c the means, indeed in its own way even the end itself, both d formal and e objective, insofar as this is precisely known through demonstration.

By this name are understood the things to be known in natural theology, as a science, which it considers and from which it infers its conclusions for the purpose of explaining their nature and proving their truth, from some antecedent cognition or from certain principles that are better known and prior. Musaeus, loc. cit., § 14, p. 47.
