For this, insofar as it is placed under a certain operation for the sake of attaining an end, falls under the consideration of natural theology as a practical science; although it must be admitted that, in the state of corruption, its full nature and the depravity of that corruption itself are not sufficiently known through the light of nature, at least as much of it as still remains. Musaeus, loc. cit., § 31, p. 87.

For the relation of these to the end is most manifest, and see what we have said in § 6 et seqq. For the cognition of this, if not distinct (which we said at § 4, note e, cannot be investigated by the guidance of the light of nature regarding its specific nature), at least confused, depends upon the objective end and can be sought from it.

Namely, the existence of God, as well as His attributes and essential perfections, can certainly be demonstrated a posteriori from created things, as divine effects, and from a more accurate consideration of them, concerning which the schools of the philosophers treat in various places and may be consulted. Meanwhile, you will see Musaeus, loc. cit., § 26 et seqq., pp. 82 to 86.

Gerhardus: “The book of nature can be posited as twofold for the sake of instruction, internal and external, whence natural knowledge is divided into ἔμφυτον, innate or implanted, and ἐπίκτητον, acquired. Innate knowledge has its origin from κοιναῖς ἐννοίαις, which are certain obscure ruins of the lost divine image, and traces of that lost light which shone in the human mind before the fall, certain little sparks through which a common and anticipated notion—that God exists—is naturally inscribed upon the minds of all men. We therefore refer these to the internal book of nature, to which also belongs the book of συνειδήσεως, the testimony of the internal conscience, which the scholastics call συντήρησιν; for from principles born with us, that practical syllogism arises in the heart of every man: he who leads an impious life will feel the wrath of God the avenger. The reason depends on this, because it is naturally inscribed upon all that God exists, that God is to be worshipped, and that God is the avenger of crimes. The conscience of the impious man subsumes: I have led a flagitious life. Acquired knowledge is gathered from the external book of nature, namely from the contemplation of divine works and effects, by the power of natural discourse by the human mind. For just as from many letters, so from many creatures a certain book is composed, since every creature is nothing but a certain letter written by the finger of God, in which we can read and from that reading know God.” (Exeges. 1. 2. § 60.) The same: “It is useful to have certain demonstrations in view, so that a comparison with revealed knowledge may be instituted:

1. From the order of movers. We perceive by sense that some things in this world are moved; but everything that is moved must be moved by another, since nothing can be simultaneously in act and in potency according to the same thing; but among movers and things moved, there is no process to infinity, because there would be no first mover and consequently nothing else, because secondary movers do not move except by the fact that they are moved by the first. It is therefore necessary to arrive at one first mover, whom we call God. The Philosopher uses this demonstration in books 7 and 8 of the Φυσικὴ ἀκρόασις. — 2. From the series of efficient causes. We find in these sensible things an order of efficient causes, nor yet is it found in them, nor is it possible, for anything to be an efficient cause... ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

of itself, because thus it would be prior to itself, which is impossible. Since, therefore, in causes of this kind there is no infinite regress, from the fact that secondary causes do not act except by the power of the first, it is necessary to posit some first efficient cause, which all call God. Aristot. 2. Metaphys. text. 6. —

3. From the degree and connection of beings. In created things, there is found something more good and less good, something more being and less being. But this cannot have a place in different kinds of goods and beings, except insofar as each of them approaches more or less to some highest good and highest being; there must, therefore, be some best and most noble being, which by common consent we call God. Anselm in Monol. c. 1.

To this also pertains that demonstration: Whatever things exist, they are either all possible, or not. If all are possible, it follows that at some time there was absolutely nothing; for it is possible that what can be, at some time was not; for if it always was, it was not possible, but necessary. But it is absurd in many ways that at some time there was absolutely nothing. Therefore it follows that not all things are possible, but that at the very least there has always been something that was necessary. This, however, either has a cause of its necessity, or it does not. If it has one, we will eventually arrive at something that is necessary of itself; since an infinite regress is impossible. If it is necessary of itself, it does not have a cause of necessity, but rather is the cause of necessity in others; this very thing, however, is the highest being, which we call God. Rich. 1. 1. de Trin. P. I. c. 7. —

4. From operation directed toward an end. We see not only beings endowed with reason, but also those that lack cognition, operating for a certain end, because they always or more frequently operate in the same way and attain their ends through proper means; whence it is clear that they do not act by chance or accident, but from the intention of some intellect directing those operations, which intellect we call God. Aristot. 12. Metaph. t. 52., and from him Thom. P. I. q. 2. art. 3. —

5. From natural inclination. No natural inclination can be in vain. But naturally all men are inclined to believe that there is some governor of this universe, whom they call God; and what is common to all and at all times seems to be natural. Furthermore, in sudden events, the habit and natural inclination of each person is most clearly discerned; but in sudden dangers, all men, when they recognize themselves to be destitute of human aid, by a certain natural instinct turn to higher things; therefore it is naturally implanted in them that there is some highest principle of things and governor of the universe. Savan. de verit. fid. 1. 1. c. 6.

The Apostle, Acts 14:15–17, points out these sources of natural demonstrations, from which it can be demonstrated that God exists: 1. from the production of things, 2. from their conservation, 3. from their governance, 4. from the bestowal of benefits upon the human race, 5. from the condition of the human mind, 6. from political association. Lactantius 1. 1. Div. Instit. c. 2.: "There is no one so unrefined, of such savage manners, who, lifting his eyes to heaven, even if he does not know by whose providence all that is seen is ruled, does not nevertheless understand that there is some [God] 1. from the very magnitude of things, 2. their motion, 3. their arrangement, 4. their constancy, 5. their utility, 6. their fullness, 7. their tempering." (Exeg. 1. 2. de nat. Dei. § 61.) Cf. Bock's Defense of the Christian Religion. Königsberg. 1768. P. I. p. 136. sqq.

Luthardt: " 1. The proofs that arise from reflection upon the world are: a. in reflection upon the being of the world: the cosmological proof, which concludes from the world to the author of the world, according to Rom. 1:19f. ... b. reflection upon the constitution of the world yields the physico-theological or teleological proof, which concludes from the purposiveness of the world to a highest intelligence, Ps. 104:24. ... Connected to this is the historico-theological proof, which concludes from the teleology of history to a highest intellect and a will governing therein according to moral laws. 2. The proofs that arise from man's reflection upon himself are: a. the proof from theoretical PROLEGOM. CAP. I. reason. Its first form is to infer the necessity, and therewith the truth, of the idea of God from the universality of that idea. This argumentum e consensu gentium is found already in Cicero, De Natura Deorum 1, 17; Tusculanae Disputationes 1, 13; and then also in Christian scholarship in Clement of Alexandria, Stromata V, 14; Lactantius, Divinae Institutiones I, 2. The second form is to conclude from the idea within us to its cause outside of us, which has produced it. Descartes, Meditationes III: 'This idea, which is in us, requires God as its cause, and therefore God exists.' The third form is the ontological proof of Anselm, Proslogion 2, which concludes from the content of the idea of God to the existence of God: 'Even the fool is convinced that there is in the intellect something than which nothing greater can be thought. And certainly that than which nothing greater can be thought cannot be in the intellect alone. For if it is even in the intellect alone, it can be thought to be also in reality, which is greater. — Therefore, there undoubtedly exists something than which nothing greater can be thought, both in the intellect and in reality.' ... b. The proof from practical reason infers in its first form, from the fact of the moral law within us, the author of the same outside of us: thus already Melanchthon and Calvin; in the second form, from the collision of the moral law with the drive for happiness, it infers a future reconciliation of both, and thus an absolute Being who reconciles both." (Kompendium der Dogmatik. Third ed. Leipzig, 1868. p. 64 sq. cf. Philippi, Kirchliche Glaubenslehre. II. p. 1 sqq.)

Latin:

Idem: „Omnibus innatum est et animo quasi insculptum, esse deos.“ (De N. D. lib. 2.)

Hollazius: „Possunt dari athei speculative tales, non per naturam, sed per justam Dei desertionem et diaboli excaecationem; non per totalem eradicationem luminis naturae quoad habitum, sed per suffocationem quoad actum et exercitium; non per totum vitae spatium et permanenter, sed tantum per quendam paroxysmum transeuntem ad aliquod tempus. Neque enim lex naturae patitur, ut rata et firma sententia alicui inhaereat, non esse Deum. Quanquam enim mens hominis impii lethargo quasi sopiatur, ut de Deo non cogitet; nullus tamen potest dari, in quo tandem conscientia se non vindicet et vel in ipsa morte neglecti Dei ipsum accuset.“ (Exam. P. I. c. 1. q. 5. p. 194.)

Qui nihil aliud est, quam inclinatio naturae in Deum, tanquam finem suum, quae intellectum, luce illa connata pollentem, velut addito pondere ad assensum, cum aliis communibus de Deo notionibus, tum praecipue illi, quae est de existentia Dei, immediate ac citra discursum, praebendum determinat. Vid. Mus. in Introd. p. 78. 79. 80. Ausführl. Erklärung p. 161. 162. 163.

Qualis vulgo omnibus, etiam simplicioribus, qui demonstrationum capaces non sunt, inesse solet, et vel ex aliorum, v. g. parentum, praeceptorum, magistratus populique, testificatione, vel ex inspectione creaturarum, per consequentiam quidem, sed facilem, et cuivis etiam illiterato obviatn, comparatur. Mus. Introd. 1. c. § 23. 24. p. 81.

Hanc itaque utramque notitiam supponit; inde autem, velut ex principio cognoscendi, regulam rectae operationis petit et suas conclusiones infert theologia naturalis, tanquam habitus demonstrativus. Mus. 1. c. § 28. p. 86.

Et sic b. Himmelius Syntagm. Disp. I. § 19. p. 3. scribit: Naturalis theologias duo sunt principia: internum, videlicet χοίνα'ι swntat, divinae imaginis rudera seu reliquiae, et externum, videlicet inspectio creaturarum.§

11. Ad objectum materiale a pertinent subjectum operationis b et tinis consequendi causae atque c media, imo suo modo etiam tinis ipse, cum formalis, d tum objectivus, quatenus quidem hic exquisite per demonstrationem e cognoscitur.

Quo nomine intelliguntur res cognoscendae in theologia naturali, tanquam scientia, quas considerat et de quibus conclusiones suas ad explicandam earum naturam probandamque veritatem ex aliqua antecedente cognitione aut ex principiis quibusdam notioribus et prioribus infert. Mus. l. c. § 14. p. 47.

Hoc enim, in quantum finis consequendi causa certae operationi substernitur, sub considerationem theologiae naturalis, tanquam scientiae practicae, cadit; licet fatendum sit, in statu corruptionis plenam ejus rationem ipsiusque corruptionis pravitatem per lumen naturae, quantum quidem eius adhuc reliquum est, non satis cognosci. Mus. l. c. § 31. p. 87.

Horum enim habitudo ad finem manifestissima est, et videantur, quae diximus § 6. sqq. Hujus enim cognitio, si non distincta (quam ductu luminis naturae, quoad specificam ejus rationem, investigari non posse, diximus ad § 4. not. e.), saltem confusa a fine objectivo pendet indeque peti potest.

Nempe existentia Dei pariter et attributa ac perfectiones essentiales ejus a posteriori ex rebus creatis, tanquam effectibus divinis, earumque consideratione accuratiore demonstrari utique possunt, de quibus scholae philosophorum passim agunt et consuli possunt. Interim videbis Mus. l. c. § 26. sqq. p. 82. ad 86.

Gerhardus: „Liber naturae docendi causa potest statui duplex, internus et externus, unde notitia naturalis dividitur in έμφυτον, innatam s. insitam, et 'επίκτητου, acquisitam. Notitia insita originem habet ex κοιναϊς ’εννοίαις, quae amissae imaginis divinae sunt obscura quaedam rudera, ac vestigia amissae illius lucis, quae in hominis mente ante lapsum fulgebat, quaedam scintillulae, per quas communis et anticipata notio, quod sit Deus, omnium hominum mentibus naturaliter est insculpta. Eas ergo referimus ad librum naturae internum, ad quem etiam pertinet liber συνειδήσεις, internae conscientiae testimonium, quod scholastici vocant συντήρησιν; nam ex principiis nobiscum natis practicus ille syllogismus in corde cujus vis hominis oritur: qui vitam degit impiam, sentiet Dei vindicis iram. Ratio pendet ex eo, quia omnibus naturaliter insculptum, Deum esse, Deum esse colendum, Deum esse scelerum vindicem. Subsumit conscientia impii: Ego vitam flagi tiosam duxi. Acquisita notitia ex libro naturae externo, videlicet ex contemplatione operum et effectuum divinorum, vi naturalis discursus a mente humana colligitur. Ut enim ex pluribus literis, ita ex pluribus creaturis quasi liber quidam componitur, cum quaelibet creatura non sit nisi quaedam litera digito Dei scripta, in quo legere et ex lectione Deum cognoscere possumus.“ (Exeges. 1. 2. § 60.) Idem: „Prodest, quasdam demonstrationes in conspectu habere, ut collatio cum notitia revelata institui possit:

1. A moventium ordine. Sensu percipimus, aliqua in hoc mundo moveri; omne autem, quod movetur, necesse est ab alio moveri, cum nihil possit esse simul actu et potenftia secundum idem; sed in moventibus ac motis non datur processus in iniinitum, quia non esset aliquod primum movens et per consequens nec aliquid aliud, quia moventia secunda non movent, nisi per hoc, quod sunt a primo mota. Necesse igitur est devenire ad unum primum motorem, quem Deuin vocamus. Hac demonstratione utitur Philosophus lib. 7. et 8. ψνσικ. άκροάσ. —2. Ab efficientium serie. Invenimus, in his sensibilibus esse ordinem causarum efficientium, nec tamen in eis invenitur, nec est possibile, aliquid esse causam efficien DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

tem sui ipsius, quia sic esset prius se ipso, quod est impossibile. Cum ergo in hujusmodi causis non detur processus in infinitum, ex eo, quod secundae causae non agunt, nisi in virtute primae, necesse est dare aliquam primam causam efficientem, quam omnes Deum vocant. Aristot. 2. Metaphys. text. 6. —

3. Ab entium gradu et connexione. In rebus creatis invenitur aliquod magis bonum ac minus bonum, aliquod magis ens ac minus ens. At hoc non potest in diversis bonorum et entium generibus locum habere, nisi prout quodlibet eorum magis vel minus appropinquat alicui summo bono ac summo enti; oportet ergo esse aliquid optimum et nobilissimum ens, quod communi consensu Deum vocamus. Ansh. in monol. c. l.

Huc pertinet etiam ea demonstratio: Quaecunque sunt, ea aut omnia sunt possibilia, aut non. Si omnia sunt possibilia, sequitur, quod quandoque άπλώς nihil fuerit; possibile enim est, quod potest esse et aliquando non fuit; nam si semper fuit, non possibile, sed necessarium fuit. At multis modis absurdum est, aliquando simpliciter nihil fuisse. Ergo sequitur, non omnia esse possibilia, sed ad minimum semper aliquid fuisse, quod fuit necessarium. Hoc autem vel habet necessitatis causam, vel non. Si habet, tandem deveniemus ad aliquid, quod est necessarium per se; cum progressus in infinitum sit impossibilis. Si per se est necessarium, causam necessitatis non habet, sed potius est causa necessitatis in aliis; id ipsum autem est summum ens, quod Deum vocamus. Rich. 1. 1. de trin. P. I. c. 7. —

4. Ex certa propter finem operatione. Videmus non solum entia ratione praedita, sed etiam ea, quae cognitione carent, operari propter certum finem, quia semper aut frequentius eodem modo operantur ac fines suos per debita media consequuntur; unde patet, quod non fortuito ac casu agant, sed ab intentione alicujus intellectus eas dirigentis operationes illae, quem intellectum vocamus Deum. Aristot. 12. metaph. t. 52., et ex eo Thom. P. I. q. 2. art. 3. —

5. Ex naturali inclinatione. Nulla inclinatio naturalis potest esse frustranea. At naturaliter omnes homines inclinantur ad credendum, aliquem esse hujus universi gubernatorem, quem Deum vocant; quod autem omnibus et omni tempore convenit, naturale esse videtur. Praeterea in repentinis cujusque habitus et inclinatio naturalis maxime dignoscitur; at in periculis repentinis omnes homines, ubi se humano auxilio destitutos cognoscunt, naturali quodam instinctu ad superiora convertuntur; ergo naturaliter ipsis insitum, quod sit aliquod summum rerum principium et gubernator universi. Savan. de verit. fid. 1. 1. c. 6.

D. Apost. Act. 14,15—17. monstrat hosce fontes naturalium demonstrationum, ex quibus esse Deum demonstrari possit: 1. a rerum productione, 2. a conservatione, 3. a gubernatione, 4. a beneficiorum in genus humanum collatione, 5. a mentis humanae conditione, 6. a politica consociatione. Lactantius 1. 1. div. Instit. c. 2.: ,Nemo est tam rudis, tam feris moribus, qui, oculos suos in coelum tollens, tametsi nesciat, cujus Dei providentia regatur hoc omne, quod cernitur, non aliquem tamen esse intelligat 1. ex ipsa rerum magnitudine, 2. motu, 3. dispositione, 4. constantia, 5. utilitate, 6. plenitudine, 7. temperatione.“* (Exeg. 1. 2. de nat. Dei. § 61.) Cf. Bock's Vertheidigung der christlichen Religion. Königsberg. 1768. P. I. p. 136. sqq.

Luthardtius: ,,1. Die Beweise, die sich aus der Reflexion auf die Welt ergeben, sind a. bei der Reflexion auf das Sein der Welt: der kosmologische Beweis, der von der Welt auf den Welturheber zurückschliesst nach Rom. 1, 19. f. . . b. die Reflexion auf die Beschaffenheit der Welt ergibt den physiko-theologischen oder teleologischen Beweis, welcher von der Zweckmässigkeit der Welt auf eine höchste Intelligenz schliesst Ps. 104, 24. . . Daran schliesst sich der historico-theologische Beweis, welcher von der Teleologie der Geschichte auf einen höchsten Verstand und einen nach sittlichen Gesetzen waltenden Willen in derselben schliesst. 2. Die Beweise, die sich aus der Beflexion des Menschen auf sich selbst ergeben, sind a. der Beweis aus der theoreti PROLEGOM. CAP. I. sehen Vernunft. Seine erste Form ist, aus der Allgemeinheit der Gottesidee die Nothwendigkeit und damit die Wahrheit derselben zu folgern. Dieses argumentum e consensu gentium hat schon Cicero D. N. D. 1,17. Tuse. I, 13. und dann auch die christliche Wissenschaft bei Clem. Al. Strom. V, 14. Lact. div. instit. I, 2. Die zweite Form, aus der Idee in uns auf ihre Ursache ausser uns, die sie gewirkt hat, zu schliessen. Cartes. Medit. III.: Haec idea, quae in nobis est, requirit deum pro causa, deusque proinde existit. Die dritte Form ist der ontologische Beweis Anselms, Proslog. 2., welcher vom Inhalt der Gottesidee auf die Existenz Gottes schliesst: Convincitur etiam insipiens, esse in intellectu aliquid, quo majus cogitari non potest. Et certe id, quo majus cogitari nequit, non potest esse in intellectu solo. Si enim vel in solo intellectu est, potest cogitari esse et in re, quod majus est. — Existit ergo procul dubio aliquid, quo majus cogitari non valet, et in intellectu et in re. . . b. Der Beweis aus der praktischen Vernunft folgert in seiner ersten Form aus der Thatsache des Sittengesetzes in uns den Urheber desselben ausser uns: so schon Melanchthon und Calvin'; in der zweiten Form aus der Collision des Sittengesetzes mit dem Glückseligkeitstrieb eine künftige Ausgleichüng beider und so denn ein absolutes Wesen, welches beide ausgleicht.“ (Kompend. der Dogm. Dritte Aufl. Leipz. 1868. p. 64. sq. cf. Philippi, Kirchliche Glaubenslehre. II. p. 1. sqq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: C. Hasius: "Theism is that persuasion by which a certain religious relationship…

C. Hasius: "Theism is that persuasion by which a certain religious relationship of man to God is established, as of person to person, and is never mingled with the other. Arbitrary distinction of the Kantian school: Theism is the recognition of God as a free, moral intelligence; Deism only as the primal ground of the universe. — Atheism is that persuasion by which the existence of the divine is denied. — The common definition (of Pantheism) according to Klein and Ammon: Pantheism is the opinion by which it is established that the world is not diverse from the divine, but pertains to the very nature of God (ἓν καὶ πᾶν), or God is confused with the world. a. Material or Ionic Pantheism, by which it is assumed that ὕλη is the infinite essence of God (Hylozoism, Materialism, Naturalism); b. Stoic Pantheism, which teaches that the world is an animal, of which God is the plastic part; c. Realistic or Spinozistic Pantheism, by which it is contended that the single essence of God exerts itself through two infinite attributes, extension and infinite power of thought; d. Idealistic or Fichtean Pantheism, by which it is established that all things that are proceed from an absolute idea; e. Identitalistic or Schellingian Pantheism, by which God, evolving himself from his absolute principle, is said to distinguish nature and spirit; f. Panlogistic or Hegelian Pantheism, by which it is asserted that the highest notion and existence are the same. His (pantheism’s) God is not personal, but the power forming the persons in whom he arrives at the consciousness of himself. A certain freedom and immortality is compatible with him, but not moral freedom nor individual immortality. In its consistent execution, it destroys both religiosity in general, which for it is only a titanic reciprocal relationship, at the deepest level only a self-love of God, not a human love and adoration of the Highest, as well as the need for reconciliation, which for it is only a natural event or a dialectical appearance." (Hutterus redivivus. 11th ed. 1868. p. 107 sqq.)

Ammonius: "It is evident that every pantheism fosters intolerable arrogance, patronizes materialism, removes moral liberty, pollutes the holiness of the divine with the infamy of all crimes, extinguishes all sparks of the love of God in the human mind, and dissolves the very sinews of duty and virtue."

12. There are three parts of natural theology: the first concerning the end, the second concerning the subject of operation, and the third concerning the principles and means. These ought to be arranged according to the analytical method, just as in other practical sciences.

Flacius: "Sciences are usually taught in a threefold order: by synthesis or composition, as they are made; by analysis or resolution, as they are applied to use; and finally by definition and division, as they can be comprehended most briefly and quickly... Theology is most conveniently taught by synthesis, just as Grammar, Dialectic, and Geometry are.

Synthesis is that method or order which begins from the first and simplest elements, principles, or causes, and by composing them, progresses until it finally constructs the whole body and arrives at a certain end or desired goal. Just as grammar, beginning from the elements of letters, by composing them first produces syllables, then from those words, then thirdly sentences, from which fourthly it constructs entire discourses, and finally from there completes full volumes...

Nor is it a wonder that the Holy Scriptures are taught historically, for the method of both is synthetic, and most things in them are historical or deeds performed... Which are most conveniently expounded by synthesis and in their natural order...

The synthetic method of theology (which is most proper to it) begins from God, as the simplest element, the first cause or mover, and by variously composing Him with man, it progresses until it arrives at the ultimate end, i.e., at God Himself, according to that passage in Rom. 11:36: 'From whom, through whom, and to whom are all things'; which is the briefest and synthetic summary of theology... According to this method proceed (as far as the whole body is concerned) Catechisms, Institutions, Loci, and generally most compendia of this doctrine. For it is, as has been said, most convenient for it, for the things that are posterior by nature and also in the present series always arise from, depend upon, and are understood by the prior things.

The analysis of theology regresses from its ultimate end or scope, i.e., from eternal life, through proximate causes and the causes of causes to more remote ones, and finally to the first fountains and thus to God Himself, who is the first and supreme fountain and author of truth, by resolving and investigating everything. By this order, postils and expositions of the Holy Scriptures (which are indeed true and mere expositions of the text and do not degenerate into Institutions) are for the most part treated. For thus entire discourses or writings are resolved...

Although the body of theology cannot be conveniently comprehended and taught by this method, because in it the things that are posterior by nature must be expounded before the prior things; yet, since the knowledge of the former depends upon the exposition of the latter, it will be useful to contemplate this delineation also, because, since it begins from those things which are prior to us or more necessary and better known, we perceive here what are the proximate causes or means for it, through which we might arrive at that about which we are most anxious and are accustomed to inquire, etc...

Furthermore, the definitive method is accustomed to propose the definition first... Which order is more artificial than natural." (

Clavis S. S. P. II, f. 54—59. Cf. Philos. Lexicon by J. G. Walch. Leipz. 1733. See the title Analyt. Methode, Synthet. Meth.: "The analytical method has its surname from the Greek word ἀναλύειν, *resolvere*, whence it is also called in Latin *methodus resolvens*, *resolutiva*... By it one generally understands that order in the knowledge and presentation of truth where one comes from the particular to the general, from the conclusions to the principles, or, as the Peripatetics speak, where one [goes] from...")

proceed from the ultimate ends to the means. . . The synthetic method derives its name from the Greek word συντίθημι, i.e., I compose, whence it is also called in Latin the *methodus compositiva*. . . By this is generally understood that order in the cognition and presentation of truth whereby one proceeds from the general to the particular, or from principles to conclusions and particular truths (from causes to effects). . . Since mathematicians have used it almost exclusively, it has become almost peculiar to mathematics, and has also acquired the name of the mathematical method.” (L. c.) § 13.

Natural theology may be described as a practical science, derived from the principles of nature concerning God, prescribing to man as a wayfarer the worship appropriate to God, and explaining, confirming, and defending it, for the sake of attaining eternal blessedness in God and from God. Conf. Introd. b. Mus. l. c. § 41. p. 103. And thus far concerning natural theology. § 14.

In order to be rightly informed concerning revealed theology, it must above all be certain that a certain supernatural and divine revelation exists. This, however, is evident not only to us, who were born in the church, but also to the Gentiles. For once this is shown, it is then not difficult to conclude that there exists a habit of revealed theology, by which certain men are rendered apt to know those things which have been divinely revealed in such a way that they are able to teach, explain, confirm, and defend them. For not only is divine revelation, made immediately to a few, known to have occurred to them so that others might be instructed through these divinely taught men; but revelation itself also expressly teaches that teachers are given by God for the edification of the saints, Eph. 4:12, and in other places.

Calovius: “If anyone denies that a divine revelation exists, that principle is proven from elsewhere, not only by those reasons by which the truth of principles is usually established, but by far more eminent ones, which are greater than any exception. For once it is proven—if that be denied—that God exists, and that there must exist some reason by which God is worshipped by men, it must be taught: that it cannot be otherwise than that God has revealed that very reason, so that He might be worshipped in a due manner; then, that God has willed that men be brought to the enjoyment of Himself, and therefore the manner by which they might be brought had to be revealed to men; finally, that God has indeed revealed Himself, which must be shown from history, which revelation God willed to be accompanied by miracles and documents, from which we are rendered infallibly certain that it is truly divine.” (Syst. th. Tom. I. Proleg. c. 3. s. 1. p. 268.) ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

For in the first age, revelation, comprised in the Scriptures, became known to us through the guidance of parents or teachers; and in part, that very revelation provided testimony of its own divine origin and generated divine faith. Cf. Musaeus, ch. III, § 2, p. 106. This is what we noted at § 4 from the blessed Himmel: that natural theology itself leads men gradually to supernatural theology, to which he refers the passages Rom. 1:19, 20; Acts 17:27. Therefore, the Gentiles, since they knew through the light of nature that God exists, that the human soul survives after the death of the body, that there are also different states for the good and the evil after death, and that men are indeed most prone to sin and offend God daily, yet do not have from natural theology a means by which they might appease God; they easily came to the thought of believing that God, in His goodness, had shown the way and means of salvation somewhere through a special revelation. It is also established by experience that no nation has remained within natural theology. See the blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., and Part II, Chapter V, Section I, § 15, p.

Latin:

C. Hasius: „Theismus est ea persuasio, qua hominis ad Deum ratio quaedam religiosa statuitur, ut personae ad personam, neque unquam alteri immiscetur. Willkührliche Unterscheidung der Kantischen Schule: Theismus Anerkennung Gottes als freie, moralische Intelligenz, Deismus nur als Urgrund des Weltalls. — Atheismus est ea persuasio, qua numinis existentia negatur. — Die gewöhnliche Bestimmung (des Pantheismus) nach Klein und Ammon: Pantheismus est opinio, qua statuitur, mundum a numine non esse diversum, sed ad ipsam Dei naturam pertinere (h< και παν), sive Deus cum mundo confunditur. a. Pantheismus materialis vel Jonicus, quo νλην essentiam Dei infinitam esse sumitur (Hylozoismus, Materialismus, Naturalismus); b. Pantheismus Stoicus, qui mundum animal esse docet, cujus pars plastica sit Deus; c. Panth. realisticus s. Spinozisticus, quo unicam Dei essentiam duobus attributis infinitis, extensione et vi cogitandi infinita, sese exserere contenditur; d. Panth. idealisticus s. Fichtianus, quo omnia, quae sunt, ab idea absoluta proficisci statuitur; e. Panth. identitalisticus s. Schellingianus, quo Deus ex principio suo absoluto se ipsum evolvens naturam atque spiritum discernere dicitur; f. Panth. panl&gisticus s. Hegelianus, quo summam notionem atque existentiam eandem esse asseritur. Sein (pantheismi) Gott ist nicht persönlich, aber die Personen bildende Macht, in denen er zum Bewusstsein seiner selbst gelangt. Eine gewisse Freiheit undünsterblichkeit ist ihm vereinbar, aber nicht sittliche Freiheit noch individuelle Unsterblichkeit. Er vernichtet in seiner consequenten Durchführung sowohl die Religiosität überhaupt, welche ihm nur ein titanenhaftes Wechselverhältniss, im tiefsten Grunde nur eine Selbstliebe Gottes ist, keine menschliche Liebe und Anbetung des Höchsten, als auch das Bedürfniss der Versöhnung, welche ihm nur Naturereigniss oder dialektischer Schein ist.“ (Hutterus redivivus. 11. Aufl. 1868. p. 107. sqq.)

Ammonius: „Patet, pantheismum quemvis intolerabilem arrogantiam fovere, materialismo patrocinari, libertatem moralem tollere, numinis sanctitatem omnium facinorum infamia polluere, omnes amoris Dei igniculos in mente humana extinguere, et ipsos officii et virtutis nervos resolvere.“

12. Partes theologiae naturalis tres a sunt: Prima de fine, secunda de subjecto operationis, et tertia de principiis ac mediis. Quae juxta methodum analyticam, perinde ut in aliis scientiis practicis, collocari debent.

Flacius: „Solent scientiae potissimum triplici ordine tradi: per synthesin aut compositionem, sicut fiunt; per analysin aut resolutionem, ut ad usum adhibentur; et denique per definitionem, ac divisionem, quomodo brevissime et citissime comprehendi queunt. . . Theologia per synthesin commodissime traditur, sicut et Grammatica, Dialectica, Geometria. . .

Est synthesis ea methodus aut ordo, quae incipit a primis et simplicissimis elementis, principiis aut causis, eaque componendo eo usque progreditur, donec tandem totum corpus extruat et ad certum finem metamve desideratam perveniat. Ut grammatica ab elementis literarum incipiens componendo illa primum efficit syllabas, ex illis deinde voces, inde tertio sententias, ex quibus quarto integras disputationes, ac postremo inde conficit plena volumina...

Nec mirum est, sacras literas historice tradi, nam et methodus utriusque est synthetica et pleraque sunt in eis historica aut res gestae. . . Quae per synthesin commodissime suoque naturali ordine exponuntur. . .

Synthetica theologiae methodus (quae ei maxime propria est) incipit a Deo, tanquam simplicissimo elemento, prima causa aut motore, eumque varie cum homine componendo progreditur, donec ad ultimum finem i. e. ad eundem Deum perveniat juxta illud Rom. 11, 36.: ,Ex quo, per quem et in quem omnia'; quae est brevissima et synthetica theologiae summa. . . Secundum hanc methodum progrediuntur (quod ad totum corpus attinet) Catecheses, Institutiones, Loci et omnino pleraque doctrinae hujus compendia. Est enim ei, ut dictum est, commodissima, nam semper posteriora natura et etiam nunc serie ex prioribus oriuntur, dependent ac intelliguntur. . .

Analysis theologiae ab ultimo ejusyirae aut scopo i. e. a vita aeterna per proximas causas causarumque causas ad remotiores et tandem ad primos fontes atque adeo ad ipsum Deum, qui primus ac supremus veritatis fons auctorque est, omnia resolvendo ac pervestigando regreditur. Per hunc ordinem postilla et expositiones sacrarum literarum (quae quidem verae ac merae expositiones textus sunt et non in Institutiones degenerant) magna ex parte tractantur. Sio enim integrae disputationes aut scripta resolvuntur. . .

Licet autem hac methodo theologiae corpus commode comprehendi ac tradi non possit, quod prius sunt in ea exponenda posteriora natura, quam priora; cum tamen illorum notitia ex horum expositione dependeat, utile fuerit, et hanc delineationem contemplari, quod, cum incipiat ab iis, quae nobis sunt priora seu magis necessaria magisque nota, cernimus hic, quaenam sint ei proximae causae aut media, per quae ad id pervenire queamus, de quo maxime angimur ac quaerere solemus etc. . .

Definitiva porro methodus solet primum definitionem proponere. . . Qui ordo magis artificialis, quam naturalis est.“ (

Clavis S. S. P. II, f. 54—59. Cf. Philos. Lexicon von J. G. Walch. Leipz. 1733. Vid. tit. Analyt. Methode, Synthet. Meth.: „Die analytische Methode hat ihren Beinamen von dem griechischen Wort άναλυε/,ν, resolvere, daher sie auch im Lateinischen methodus resolvens, resolutiva genannt wird. . . Man versteht insgemein dadurch diejenige Ordnung in der Erkenntniss und Vorstellung der Wahrheit, da man von dem Besonderen auf das Allgemeine, von den Schlüssen auf die Principien komme, oder, wie die Peripatetiker reden, da man von

den Endzwecken zu den Mitteln schreite. . . Die synthetische Methode hat ihren Beinamen von dem griechischen Wort σνν-ίΰημι i. e. compono, daher sie auch im Lateinischen methodus compositiva genennet wird. . . Man versteht dadurch insgemein diejenige Ordnung in der Erkenntnissund Vorstellung der Wahrheit, da man von dem Allgemeinen auf das Besondere oder von den Principien auf die Schlüsse und besonderen Wahrheiten (von den Ursachen zu den Wirkungen) komme. . . Da die Mathematiker sich derselben fast allein bedient haben, so ist sie der Mathesis fast wie eigentümlich geworden, hat auch den Namen der mathematischen Methode erlangt.“ (L. c.) § 13.

Describi potest theologia naturalis, quod sit scientia practica, ex principiis naturae de Deo, praescribens homini viatori cultum Deo convenientem, eumque explicans, confirmans ac defendens, consequendae in Deo et a Deo beatitudinis aeternae causa. Conf. Introd. b. Mus. l. c. § 41. p. 103. Et hactenus de theologia naturali. §14.

Ut de theologia revelata recte informemur, ante omnia certum esse debet, dari supernaturalem quandam revelationem a divinam. Hoc autem non nobis tantum, qui in ecclesia nati sumus, b sed etiam gentilibus c constat. Hoc enim ostenso, deinde non difficulter colligitur, dari habitum theologiae revelatae, quo homines quidam apti reddantur ad ea, quae divinitus revelata sunt, ita cognoscenda, ut docere eadem atque explicare, confirmare et defendere possint. Non solum enim revelatio divina, immediate ad paucos facta, ideo illis obtigisse cognoscitur, ut per hos, divinitus instructos, alii erudirentur; verum etiam ipsa revelatio expresse docet, dari a Deo doctores ad instaurationem sanctorum, Ephes. 4, 12. et locis aliis.

Calovius: „Dari revelationem divinam, siquis neget, principium illud aliunde comprobatur, non tantum iis rationibus, quibus alias solet principiorum veritas adstrui, sed longe eminentioribus, quae omni exceptione majores sunt. Evicto enim, si id negetur, quod Deus sit, quodque aliquam oporteat extare rationem, qua Deus ab hominibus colatur, docendum: fleri non posse, quin Deus rationem ipsam patefecerit, ut debito modo coleretur; tum, Deum homines ad sui fruitionem perductos voluisse, ideoque modum etiam, quo perduci queant, revelandum fuisse hominibus; tandem, patefecisse omnino sese Deum, ex historia ostendendum, quam revelationem Deus illis miraculis et documentis stipatam voluit, ex quibus infallibiliter certi reddimur, eam vere divinam esse.“ (Syst. 11. th. Tom. I. Proleg. c. 3. s. 1. p. 268.) DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Partim enim in prima aetate revelatio, scripturis comprehensa, ductu parentum aut praeceptorum nobis innotuit; partim ipsa illa revelatio de divina origine sua testimonium praebuit et fidem divinam ingeneravit. Conf. Mus. c. III. § 2. p. 106. Hoc est, quod ad § 4. annotavimus ex b. Himmelio: ipsam theologiam naturalem manuducere homines paulatim ad supernaturalem, quo is refert loca Rom. 1, 19. 20. Ad. 17, 27. Itaque gentiles, cum per lumen naturae nossent, esse Deum, et animam humanam post mortem corporis superesse, dari quoque status diversos bonorum et malorum post mortem, homines vero ad peccandum maxime propensos esse et quotidie Deum offendere, neque habere ex theologia naturali medium, quo Deum placare possint; facile in eam cogitationem venerunt, ut crederent, Deum pro sua bonitate peculiari revelatione viam et media salutis alicubi ostendisse. Constat etiam per experientiam, quod nulla gens in theologia naturali substiterit. Vid. b. Mus.c. et P. II. Cap. V. Sect. I. § 15. p. 387.PLATO: ,,Νομίζοντες αθάνατον την ψυχήν και δυνατήν πάντα μεν κακά άνεχεσΰαι, πάντα δε άγαΰα, τής άνω όόον άεϊ έξόμε&α και δικαιοσύνην μετά φρονήσεος πάντι τρόπφ έπιτηδενσωμεν, Ινα και ήμΐν αυτδίς φίλοι ώμεν και τοίς ’&εοϊς, αυτού τε μενοντες έν&άδε και επειδάν τα ά&'λα αυτόν κομιζώμεda, ώσπερ οΐ νικεφόροι καί έν&άδε καί εν πάντι τώ αίώνι ευ πράττωμεν. “ (L. 10. de Republ. Gf. Gerhard, loc. de vita aet. § 21.: ,,Immortalem esse animam statuentes, talemque, ut mala possit et bona omnia sustinere, viam semper ad superiora ducentem sequamur, justitiamque cum prudentia omni ratione colamus, ut et nobis ipsis simus et Dei amici, dum hanc ducimus vitam, et postquam virtutis praemia reportaverimus tanquam potiti victoria et triumphantes, et hic et in perpetuum feliciter habeamus.“)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: PLATO: “Believing the soul to be immortal and capable of enduring all evils and…

387. PLATO: “Believing the soul to be immortal and capable of enduring all evils and all goods, we shall always hold to the upward path and practice justice with wisdom in every way, so that we may be friends both to ourselves and to the gods, both while we remain here and when we receive the rewards of virtue, just as victors do, so that we may fare well both here and in all eternity.” (Book 10 of the Republic. Cf. Gerhard, loc. on eternal life, § 21: “Establishing that the soul is immortal, and such that it can endure all evils and all goods, let us always follow the way leading to higher things, and let us cultivate justice with prudence in every way, so that we may be friends to ourselves and to God, while we lead this life, and after we have brought back the rewards of virtue, as those who have attained victory and are triumphant, we may fare happily both here and forever.”) Sallust: “It is certain to me that the life of all mortals is watched over by divine power, and that neither the good nor the evil deed of anyone is held for nothing, but that different rewards follow the good and the bad by nature.” (To Caesar.)

Cicero: “Thus I have persuaded myself, thus I feel: since there is such speed of minds, such memory of the past and foresight of the future, so many arts, so many sciences, so many inventions, that nature which contains these things cannot be mortal; and since the nature of the mind is simple, and has nothing in itself mixed that is disparate or unlike itself, it cannot be divided; and if it cannot be divided, it cannot perish.” (On Old Age.) Ovid: “We always strive for what is forbidden and desire what is denied.” (Amores III, 4, 17.) “ What is permitted is unpleasing; what is not permitted burns more fiercely.” (Ibid. II, 19, 3.) “I see the better things and approve them, I follow the worse.” (Metamorphoses 7, 21.)

Horace: “Drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she will always return.” (Epistles I, 10, 24.) Lycurgus: “Good heavens, how depraved is the nature of man.” (In Stobaeus, Sententiae Sermones II, p. 31.)

PLATO: “The ancients, being better than we and living nearer to the gods, handed down this report.” (Philebus, p. 16.) Cicero: “Antiquity approaches most closely to the gods.”

PROLEGOM. CHAP. I. The same: "If nature had created us such that we could contemplate and perceive her herself, and could complete the course of our life with her as our best guide, there would certainly be no need for anyone to seek reason and learning. As it is, she has given us small sparks, which we quickly extinguish with evil habits and depraved opinions, so that the light of nature nowhere appears. For there are seeds of virtues innate in our minds, which, if they were allowed to mature, nature herself would lead us to a blessed life; but now, as soon as we are brought into the light and received, we are immediately involved in every kind of depravity and in the greatest perversity of opinions, so that we seem to have sucked in error almost with our nurse’s milk." (Tuscul. III, 1.)

The same: "Which of these opinions is true, the gods will see; which is probable, is a great question." (L. c. I, 11.)

The same: "To Socrates, nothing seemed capable of being known. He excepted only one thing: that he knew that he knew nothing, nothing more." (Acad. pr. II, 23, 74.)

Ovid: "Ah! too easy are you, who think that the sad crimes of slaughter can be washed away by river water." (Fast. l. 2. v. 45.)

Cicero: "Whom (i.e., one in whom perfect wisdom will exist) we have indeed seen no one as yet, but by the opinions of the philosophers it is explained what he will be like, if only he should ever exist." (Tusc. II, 22.) §

15. Moreover, it is a habit of the science of revealed theology, if not primarily or in the strict sense so called, at least in a looser meaning, and indeed a practical science.

That revealed theology, speaking properly, is a habit, the theologians of Wittenberg openly declared on the occasion of the Magdeburg controversy between M. Andr. Cramer and his colleagues in the year 1623, stating that they were astonished that this could be called into doubt by anyone. The theologians of Leipzig determined the same in the year 1624, as is found in the Appendix to the Consilia of Dedeb., fol. 136, and they said that if the name of theology is taken for doctrine, this happens by metalepsis.

But many others also have advised that theology, considered essentially, denotes a habit of the mind, and accidentally and relatively, denotes doctrine; namely, because it happens to theology that it is taught and learned. Compare the blessed Musaeus, Introd. P. I. cap. I. § 2. p. 3.

J. Fecht: "That theology is a habit, and indeed a practical one, is evident from Heb. 5:14. For although it treats there of the more perfect knowledge of the word of righteousness (or the Christian doctrine concerning righteousness in Christ Jesus) to be obtained by all Christians; if, however, that is an ἕξις or habit of those having the senses exercised (exercised through frequent reading and meditation of the word, with the help of the Holy Spirit, having the senses of the mind), theology itself will enjoy that title far more, inasmuch as it intends not only to obtain righteousness and salvation for itself, but also to implant them in others. But whoever discerns between good and evil, assuming an accurate knowledge of things (inasmuch as it is not understood by the good and evil alone, the very nature of the words commanding it), no one can doubt that he is practical." (Philocalia S. p. 1.)

Calovius: "The more remote genus is habit, namely, intellectual, and that the principal one; by which we remove as inconvenient genera 1. doctrine, 2. discipline, which two are relative, since theology is something absolute." ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

is, and it happens to it that it is taught or learned; 3. revelation, and 4. the recognition of truth, which are reduced to the category of action, whereas theology belongs to the category of quality; furthermore, the former is the principle of theology, not its genus, while the latter, if understood as a habit, provides nothing but a remote genus. II. The proximate genus is a practical habit, because theology by its nature tends toward practice, and indeed, as it is viewed here, so that man may be led to eternal salvation (John 20:31; Rom. 15:4), nor is anything known in it so that one might rest in that knowledge, but for the sake of practice. . . Whence we exclude 1. a mixed or composite habit: partly theoretical, partly practical, which is an αιδηρόξυλον, since the same habit cannot ultimately subsist in bare knowledge and at the same time by its nature tend toward practice; 2. a middle habit between purely speculative and practical, which, as they are contradictorily opposed to each other, admit no middle ground; 3. the intellect and the dependent use of Ravensperger; because theology is only one discipline, and must be handed down by one method, namely, analytical, not synthetical or both; 4. the science, wisdom, and prudence of some; 5. the science and wisdom of Ant. Walaeus, who joins both genera, because one habit admits only one genus; 6. the science and 7. the wisdom of others; for these habits are theoretical, and are only contradictorily imagined as practical wisdom and science. Theology, however, does not acquiesce in bare knowledge, but tends toward practice, and that by its very nature. Although it comes under the name of wisdom (1 Cor. 2:7; Jas. 3:15), now of intelligence (Col. 1:9), now of science (John 17:3) in the Scriptures, yet these should not be assigned to it in place of a genus, since not all predicates are immediately generic, nor are they to be understood in a common, but in an eminent sense. III. The proximate genus is a practical habit drawn from divine revelation, because it arises from divine revelation, whether immediate or mediate. Others say it is θεόδοτον or divinely given, because it is among the gifts of God, not indeed precisely sanctifying, but ministering (1 Cor. 12:8; Jas. 3:15). Some, acknowledging it to be practical, prefer to define it either as prudence with Keckermann, or as art with Ramus. But prudence is concerned with τὰ ἀνθρώπινα (6 Eth. c. 5); art, however, is an effective habit occupied in external work and leaving behind some ποίημα. Neither expresses the nature of theology. Furthermore, if the name of prudence is to be broadened, we do not deny that this genus is more suitable for others, since theology is a practical habit, just as prudence is also indicated (Prov. 1:2; Ps. 119:104, 130) and the prudence of the children of light, so that it may be distinguished from human prudence (Luke 16:8). (System, locc. th. Proleg. c. 1. s. 1. Tom. I. p. 4. sq.)

Certainly, since it is established that theology is a habit of the mind, it is not without cause that it is investigated to which species it is most correctly referred, so that we may attain the concept of a more proximate genus. Yet among the habits that have been recognized thus far, there is no species to which it is more correctly referred than to science. For it tends by its nature to teach, explain, and confirm the things underlying it as a certain and determined object, and therefore it infers certain conclusions from certain principles, or constructs demonstrations, which is proper to science, and does not fit any other habit equally. See the blessed Musaeus, Introd. Cap. III. § 4. p. 112, 113. The same is aimed at by what our blessed G. Mylius wrote already in the year 1598 in his positions on the Word of God and Sacred Scripture, thesis 1: Just as any science emerges from its own principles through the conclusions of proofs and demonstrations, so theology (as a science) has its own principle in the Christian religion, etc. The same also in a special disputation held in the year 1602 expressly exhibited the method of τῆς θεολογικῆς ἀποδείξεως, and showed that ἀπόδειξις, although it creeps through all kinds of sciences, is nevertheless nowhere held to be more perfect than in theology, in which, because of divine revelation, there is such [greatness].

PROLEGOM. CHAP. I. certainty, such that a greater or equal degree cannot be given. See thesis 45 and following. Therefore, those who acknowledge revealed theology to be a habit of the intellect, and to be a habit of teaching and deducing certain conclusions about a peculiar and determined object, in such a way that the connection of the extremes is necessary, because the conclusions depend upon necessary and certain premises, do not without cause constitute the genus of theology as a science, because the formal reason of science consists in this, that it is a demonstrative habit. Calovius: “It is debated whether the genus of theology ought to be assigned as science properly so called; which we deny:

1. From the definition of science, which is έξις αποδεικτική εξ αναγκαίων, 6 Ethic. c. 3. For theology is not such a demonstrative habit from necessary things. It indeed has its own causes, αποδείξεις, but πνευματικός, and not indeed 'επιστημονικής, as the Apostle teaches in 1 Cor. 2:4; because for these it is required that the affections be proven through their reasons concerning a necessary subject, and indeed principally a priori. But theology neither has a subject of demonstration, but rather of operation, nor does it consist in demonstrating affections, but in handing down the means of salvation, nor does it prove primarily a priori, but a posteriori; indeed, it does not use reason, but divine authority, which is indeed a most efficacious proof, but not a properly called demonstration, nor does it beget science, but requires faith.

### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: From the requirements of science, which are gathered from its definition and…

2. From the requirements of science, which are gathered from its definition and the nature of demonstration: 1) By reason of the subject, which ought to be necessary and universal. 2) By reason of the affections, which ought to properly inhere in the subject and be demonstrated concerning it. 3) By reason of the principles, by which the affections are to be demonstrated a priori from immediate causes or reasons. For these conditions are not given in theology, whose a. object is contingent, namely man as one to be saved; indeed, theology is concerned more with singulars than universals. b. The affections in theology are not handed down as properly belonging to this object, but rather its state is foreknown, and it deals professedly with the means through which the end ought to be introduced. c. Whence neither are the principles of the affections employed; rather, all things are proven from divine revelation, by the sole authority of God speaking, which are either asserted αυτολεξεί in the Scriptures, or are gathered διανοητικώς and by consequence from the Scriptures.

3. From the nature and condition of science, because science is evident and perfect knowledge; which likewise does not entirely fit theology, whose knowledge is rather inevident, since it is concerned not with επιστητά or things knowable, but with τα πιστά or things credible, and thus wills its mysteries to be believed, not known; it commands reason to be captivated in knowing these, not to dominate. Furthermore, the knowledge of theology is imperfect in this life, as the Apostle teaches in 1 Cor. 13:12.

4. From the end of science, because the end of science is theory; but the end of theology is practice.” (Isag. I, 239—241.) N. Hunnius: “Science has knowledge as its end. For every science is άπρακτος. Science is certainly convertible with its end and, as acquired, does not differ from the end; and thus the whole essence of science consists in this, that it only knows its subject, which being done, it rests entirely and does not progress further (unless perhaps by reason of an accidental and external end).” (Canones logici. Witteb. 1621. p. 5. sq.) Calovius: “It must be observed, however, that it is not debated whether theology can be called a science in a looser signification of the word, nor whether theology ought to be called a science rather than an opinion or an imperfect habit on account of its perfection; which Thomas asserts in part I, quaest. I, art. 2. We readily admit both of these; since it is called science by the Holy Spirit in a loose signification in 1 Cor. 12:8, etc., and it is rightly taught by Thomas, as also by Augustine, passim, that it is not only an opinion, but also a science; but in that sense, science cannot be assigned to it in the place of a genus, since that signification is less proper, and not only theology, but also other disciplines, even practical ones, can be named sciences by reason of their perfection, although they are not under the genus of sciences properly so called.” (Syst. Proleg. I, 42.) ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

Rudelbach: "It (theology) is a science mediated by the Spirit of God. That was it, and nothing else, which the theologians of that school held fast to when they further described theology as a *habitus practicus*; they mean by this that this science, like no other, is conditioned by immediate currents of life. . . By the *habitus practicus* (whereby, as far as the point of connection is concerned, they take the side of the Scotists against the Thomists, the latter of whom grasped theology as a partly speculative, partly practical science), they wish to indicate that hidden efficacy of the Spirit which is the *primus et perpetuus motor* of true theology. . . We cannot abandon this determination; it is the living center of our contemplation. Theology is practical through and through, practical in its roots, means, and relations. . . In the narrower sense, the theological disciplines are practical: catechetics, keryktics, liturgics; not as if they alone were to be put into practice, but because they primarily represent the Word in immediate motion." (On the Concept of Theology and that of New Testament Isagogics. cf. *Zeitschrift* 1848. Vol. I. p. 8. sq. 27. sq.)

ANTITHESIS: Luthardt: "Theology is the ecclesiastical science of Christianity. . . In that definition (of the older Lutheran dogmaticians), however, both the immediate relation of theology to salvation and its conception as a personal quality are indeed intended in the best sense of religious earnestness, but are scientifically incorrect. . . Just as jurisprudence is the science of law, in the sense of the state as the seat of law, so theology is the science of Christianity, in the sense of the church as the seat of Christianity." (*Kompend. der Dogm.* 3rd ed. 1868. p. 1. 2. 3.)

Harless: "Christian theology is the scientific knowledge of faith according to its ground and essence." (*Theol. Encyklop. und Method.* Nuremberg, 1837. Section I. § 4. p. 25.)

Kahnis: "Theology is the scientific self-consciousness of the church. It was undoubtedly one-sided when the old dogmaticians considered theology merely (!) as the personal *habitus* of a theologian: as an abstraction borrowed from the *concretum* of a theologian. Rightly, on the other hand, the objective significance of theology as an ecclesiastical or Christian or religious science was asserted by the dogmaticians of the Enlightenment era, just as one does not view jurisprudence, medicine, philology, philosophy, etc., merely as the specific quality of a jurist, physician, etc., but as a substance of knowledge that transcends the individual persons who cherish and cultivate it." (*Die Luth. Dogm.* Second ed. Leipz. 1874. Vol. I. p. 8. sq.)

Indeed, if it is required for a science simply and properly (as is commonly done according to Aristotle) that it construct demonstrations from evident and self-evident principles. For it must be admitted that revealed theology, in the principal chapters of Christian doctrine which are called mysteries, deduces its conclusions from divine revelation alone, which is naturally non-evident. See the blessed Musaeus in *Introd.* 1. c. p. 116. 117.

Meanwhile, it is better, while retaining the name of science, to express in the very generic concept of theology those things which are accommodated to it, not only as a *habitus* of the mind, and a practical one at that, but also as a *habitus* of conclusions, or a demonstrative one, which it shares with other *habitus* of the mind, but for the purpose of designating the concept of a genus that is not more remote, but closer; rather than

so that we may omit those, and bid those who are learning or teaching others to be content with only the name of a habit, or a habit of the mind, or a habit of the practical intellect, or a habit of θεοδίδακτον (none of which expresses the nature of a demonstrative habit). For all conclusions, if not formally, are at least virtually practical. The former formally prescribe something to be done or omitted: e.g., the Triune God is to be adored. The latter, on account of their conjunction with others that are formally practical, infer a formally practical conclusion: e.g., that Christ is true God, from which it is concluded: Therefore, one must believe in Him. Compare the blessed Joh. Olearius, *Univ. theol. prooem.*, pp. 8, 9.

It amounts to the same thing that the blessed Gerhard writes in *exeg. LL. prooem.* § 12, p. 5: "All things that are handed down in theology look toward πρᾶξιν, if not immediately and directly, yet mediately and indirectly." That it is not repugnant to a science to be practical, the blessed J. Martini shows in the same place, Disp. II, § 13 sqq., p. 52 sqq., and Disp. IV, § 22 sqq., p. 86. Compare above, § 3, note b. §

16. The end of revealed theology is twofold: Internal, which consists in the acts of knowing the objects of theology, not in any manner whatsoever, but insofar as they are to be accurately explained, confirmed, and defended for the sake of faith and the salvation of men; and external, which is faith itself and the salvation of men, and whatever things are conjoined with faith.

Calovius: "The ultimate end *secundum quid* [in a certain respect], namely on our part, is eternal salvation, or rather the leading to eternal salvation... The end of Holy Scripture is the same as the end of theology, since both are occupied with the same object; Scripture proposes the articles of faith σποραδικῶς [sporadically] or scattered, while theology explains the same σνστηματικῶς [systematically] and in an orderly fashion... The end of the same is the leading to the enjoyment of God or eternal salvation. And all things that are handed down in theology tend toward this; although some may seem theoretical, they are not proposed in theology under the aspect of theory and mere contemplation, but for the sake of practice; for when the nature of God, an angel, or man is known, it is not done so that we may rest in the knowledge, but rather that knowledge is directed toward practice, so that we may enjoy God, become ἰσάγγελοι [equal to the angels], and aspire to blessedness." (*Isag.* I, 183 sq.)

Quenstedtius: "Absolutely and simply, theology is not necessary, not even to the whole church: for God can inform and convert men immediately, i.e., without the ministry of human theologians; but *ex hypothesi* [by hypothesis], given the will of God. For it has pleased God to deal with us through His Word and its preaching, Rom. 10:14, and the searching [of the Scriptures], John 5:39, and to lead men to salvation by way of doctrine and instruction. (I say notably: without the ministry of human theologians; for 'immediately' can be understood either concerning the ministry of men, or concerning the proclamation of the Word; in the latter sense God never converts anyone immediately, but in the former sense He does so quite often.)" (*Th. did.-pol.* P. I. c. 1. s. 2. q. 2. f. 20 sq.)

Calovius: "This πρᾶξις of leading men to salvation constitutes the theologian, or is his proper function and the office of the theologian himself. Although the theologian is not always occupied in this, that men..." ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

may lead to eternal salvation, yet he must be equipped with that habitus of leading men to salvation, which by its nature tends toward that end. And it is the proper duty of the theologian to act in this way, even if that external end which he intends—eternal salvation—does not follow on the part of the subject, despite the function being administered most holily.” (Isag. I, 190 sq.)

Latin:

2. E requisitis scientiae, quae e definitione ejus et natura demonstrationis colliguntur: 1) Ratione subjecti, quod id debeat necessarium esse et universale. 2) Ratione affectionum, quae proprie inhaerere subjecto et de eo demonstrari debent. 3) Ratione principiorum, quibus a priori ex immediatis causis vel rationibus demonstrandae sunt affectiones. Hae enim conditiones non dajitur in theologia, cujus a. objectum contingens est homo qua salvandus, imo versatur magis theologia circa singularia, quam universalia. b. Affectiones in theologia non traduntur hujus objecti proprie dictae, sed status potius ejus praecognoscitur et de mediis, per quae finis introduci debeat, ex professo agitur, c. Unde nec principia affectionum adhibentur, quin potius omnia e revelatione divina probantur, sola Dei dicentis auctoritate, quae vel αυτολεξεί in scripturis asseruntur, vel διανοητικώς et per consequentiam e scripturis colliguntur.

3. Ex indole et conditione scientiae, quia scientia cognitio est evidens et perfecta; quod itidem theologiae non omnino congruit, cujus cognitio potius inevidens est, cum versetur non circa επιστητά vel scibilia, sed circa τα πιστά seu credibilia, adeoque velit mysteria sua credi, non sciri; jubet rationem in iis cognoscendis captivari, non dominari. Ad haec imperfecta est cognitio theologiae in hac vita, docente apostolo 1 Cor. 13, 12.

4. E fine scientiae, quia scientiae flnis theoria; at theologiae finis est praxis.“ (Isag. I, 239—241.) N. Hunnius: „Scientia pro fine habet cognitionem. Omnis quippe scientia est άπρακτος. Scientia certe cum fine suo convertitur et, ut acquisita, a fine non differt; totaque adeo essentia scientiae in eo consistit, ut tantum subjectum suum cognoscat, quo facto tota quiescit nec ulterius (nisi forte ratione finis accidentarii et externi) progreditur.“ (Canones logici. Witteb. 1621. p. 5. sq.) Calovius: „Observandum autem, non disquiri, utrum theologia scientia dici possit laxiori vocis significatione, nec etiam, an theologia potius scientia ob sui perfectionem, quam opinio aut imperfectus habitus dici debeat; quod asserit Thomas part. I. quaest. Ϊ. art. 2. Utrumque illud facile admittimus,· cum et a Spiritu S. vocetur scientia laxa significatione 1 Cor. 12, 8. etc. et recte a Thema* ut et ab August., passim doceatur, eam non solum opinionem, sed et scientiam esse; sed eo sensu non poterit scientia loco generis ei assignari, cum ista significatio minus propria sit, nec theologia tantum, sed et aliae disciplinae, etiam practicae, ratione perfectionis nominari possint scientiae, licet sub genere scientiarum proprie dictarum non sint.“ (Syst. Proleg. I, 42.) DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Rudelbachius: „Sie (die Theologie) ist eine durch den Geist Gottes vermittelte Wissenschaft. Das war es und nichts Anderes, was die Theologen von jener Richtung festhielten, wenn sie nun ferner die Theologie beschrieben als einen habitus practicus; sie wollen damit sagen, dass diese Wissenschaft, wie keine andere, durch unmittelbare Lebensströmungen bedingt ist. . . Sie wollen mit dem habitus practicus (wodurch sie, was den Anknüpfungspunct betrifft, sich auf die Seite der Scotisten gegen die Thomisten stellen, welche letztere die Theologie als eine theils speculative, theils praktische Wissenschaft fassten) jene verborgene Wirksamkeit des Geistes andeuten, welche der primus et perpetuus motor der wahren Theologie ist. . . Wir können diese Bestimmung nicht aufgeben; sie ist die lebendige Mitte unserer Betrachtung. Praktisch ist die Theologie durch und durch, praktisch durch die Wurzeln, Mittel und Bezüge. . . Im engeren Sinne praktisch sind die theologischen Disciplinen: Katechetik, Keryktik, Liturgik; nicht als ob sie allein ins Werk gesetzt werden sollten, sondern weil sie hauptsächlich das Wort in unmittelbarer Bewegung darstellen.“ (Ueber den Begriff der Theologie und den der Neutestamentlichen Isagogik. cf. Zeitschrift 1848. Vol. I. p. 8. sq. 27. sq.)

ANTITHESIS: Luthardtius: „Die Theologie ist die kirchliche Wissenschaft vom Christenthum. . . In jener Definition (der älteren luth. Dogmatiker) ist aber sowohl die unmittelbare Beziehung der Theologie zur Seligkeit, als auch ihre Fassung als eine persönliche Eigenschaft zwar im besten Sinne des religiösen Ernstes gemeint, aber wissenschaftlich nicht richtig. . . Wie die Jurisprudenz die Wissenschaft vom Recht ist, im Sinne des Staates als der Stätte des Rechts, so die Theologie die Wissenschaft vom Christenthum, im Sinne der Kirche als der Stätte des Christenthums.“ (Kompend. der Dogm. 3. Aufl. 1868. p. 1. 2. 3.)

Harlessius: „Die christliche Theologie ist die wissenschaftliche Erkenntniss des Glaubens nach seinem Grund und Wesen.“ (Theol. Encyklop. und Method. Nürnberg, 1837. Abschnitt I. § 4. p. 25.)

Kahnisius: „Theologie ist das wissenschaftliche Selbstbewusstsein der Kirche. Es war ohne Zweifel einseitig, wenn die alten Dogmatiker die Theologie blos (!) für den persönlichen habitus eines Theologen hielten: für eine aus dem Concretum eines Theologen entlehnte Abstraction. Mit Recht wurde dagegen von den Dogmatikern der Aufklärungszeit die objective Bedeutung der Theologie als kirchlicher oder christlicher oder religiöser Wissenschaft geltend gemacht, wie man auch die Jurisprudenz, Medicin, Philologie, Philosophie u.s.w. nicht blos für die specifische Eigenschaft eines Juristen, Mediciners u. s. w. ansieht, sondern für eine über die einzelnen Personen, die sie hegen und pflegen, übergreifende Wissenssubstanz.“ (Die Luth. Dogm. Zweite Ausg. Leipz. 1874. Band I. p. 8. sq.)

Nempe si ad scientiam simpliciter et proprie requiratur (quod juxta Aristotelem vulgo solet), ut ex principiis evidentibus ac per se notis demonstrationes conficiat. Fatendum enim est, theologiam revelatam in praecipuis doctrinae christianae capitibus, quae mysteria dicuntur, ex sola revelatione divina, quae naturaliter inevidens est, conclusiones suas deducere. Vid. b. Mus. in Introd. 1. c. p. 116. 117.

Interim satius est, retento nomine scientiae, in ipso conceptu generico theologiae ea exprimere, quae ipsi, tanquam habitui, non solum mentis, eique practico, verum et habitui conclusionum, seu demonstrativo, cum aliis habitibus mentis communia, sed ad designandum conceptum generis non remotioris, sed propinquioris, accommodata sunt; quam

ut illa omittantur, ac tantum nomen habitus, aut habitus mentis, aut habitus intellectus practici, aut habitus &εο<τδότυυ (quorum nullum exprimit naturam habitus demonstrativi), discentes docentesve alios contentos esse jubeamus. Conclusiones enim omnes, si non formaliter, saltem virtualiter, practicae sunt. Illae formaliter aliquid agendum aut omittendum praescribunt: v. g. Deus trinunus est adorandus. Hae, ob conjunctionem cum aliis formaliter practicis, inferunt conclusionem formaliter practicam: v. g. Christum esse verum Deum, unde concluditur: E. in illum credendum est. Confer, b. Joh. Olearii Univ. theol. prooem. p. 8. 9.

Eodem redit, quod b. Gerhardus scribit in exeg. LL. prooem. § 12. p. 5.: Omnia, quae in theologia traduntur, ad πραξιν spectant, si non immediate et directe, tamen mediate et indirecte. Quod autem scientiae non repugnet, esse practicam, ostendit b. J. Martini l. c. Disp. II. § 13. sqq. p. 52. sqq. et Disp. IV. § 22. sqq. p. 86. Confer, supra § 3. not. b.§

16. Finis theologiae revelatae a duplex est: Internus, qui consistit in actibus cognoscendi objecta theologiae, non quomodocunque, sed quatenus b accurate explicanda, confirmanda ac defendenda sunt, fidei et salutis hominum causa; et externus, c qui est ipsa fides et salus hominum, quaeque cum fide sunt conjuncta.

Calovius: „Finis ultimus secundum quid, nimirum ex parte nostri, est salus aeterna, vel potius ad salutem aeternam perductio... Qui finis est S. Sacrae, idem finis est theologiae, cum utraque versetur circa idem objectum, scriptura proponat fidei articulos σπομαδικώς vel sparsim, theologia eosdem σνση/μητικώς et ordinate explicet. . . Finis ejusdem est perductio ad Dei fruitionem vel aeternam salutem. Atque huc tendunt omnia, quae in theologia traduntur, quorum licet nonnulla videantur theoretica, non tamen sub ratione theorias et merae contemplationis ergo proponuntur in theologia, sed ob praxin; utpote cum Dei, angeli vel hominis natura cognoscitur, non id fit, ut in cognitione acquiescamus, sed directa potius est cognitio illa ad praxin, ut Deo fruamur, Ισάγγΐ'λοι evadamus et ad beatitudinem adspiremus.“ (Isag. I, 183. sq.)

Quenstedtius: „Absolute et simpliciter theologia non est necessaria, ne quidem toti ecclesiae: potest enim Deus homines immediate h. e, sine ministerio hominum theologorum informare et convertere; sed ex hypothesi, posita sci. Dei voluntate. Placuit enim Deo nobiscum agere per verbum ejusque praedicationem, Rom. 10, 14., et scrutinium, Joh. 5, 39., hominesque perducere ad salutem via doctrinae et institutionis. (Notanter dico: sine ministerio hominum theologorum; το immediate enim intelligi potest vel de ministerio hominum, vel de annuntiatione verbi; hac ratione Deus nullum unquam immediate convertit, sed illa ratione saepius.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. I. c. 1. s. 2. q. 2. f. 20. sq.)

Calovius: „Haec πράξις homines ad salutem perducendi constituit theologum, vel functio ejus propria est et ofiicium ipsius theologi. Quanquam autem theologus non semper in eo occupetur, ut homines DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

ad salutem aeternam perducat, habitu tamen isto instructus sit oportet homines ad salutem perducendi, qui natura sua eo tendit. Estque id agere proprium theologi munus, utut saepe functionem, eandemque sanctissime administratam, non sequatur ex parte subjecti finis ille externus, quem intendit, salus aeterna.“ (Isag. I, 190. sq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Gerhardus: “The intermediate and proximate end is either internal, the…

Gerhardus: “The intermediate and proximate end is either internal, the instruction of men unto eternal salvation, or external, the very attainment of blessedness or eternal life (Luke 1:77; John 5:39; 20:31; Rom. 15:4; 2 Tim. 3:16). Therefore, whatever does not lead or conduce to this end, whether directly or at least indirectly, whether immediately or mediately, does not pertain to theological knowledge. From this it is easily gathered what must be determined concerning certain questions of the scholastics that are more futile than useful, and idle speculations, which the Apostle calls μωρας και απαίδευτους ζητήσεις (2 Tim. 2:23), namely, that they pertain to ματαιολογίαν rather than to θεολογίαν (1 Tim. 1:6).” (Exeges. locc. th. Prooem. § 26.) Meisnerus: “The theologian knows God as the end, since our blessedness is situated in the enjoyment of God; and he knows Him not in order to rest in that knowledge, nor to desire nothing else, but rather so that through that knowledge... both he himself and others who hear him may become partakers of eternal salvation. He who does not always intend this end, nor look to it in all his theory (γνώσει), does not deserve the name of a true theologian.” (Philos. sobr. P. III. s. 5. c. 2. p. 163.) ANTITHESIS:

Luthardtius: “Therefore it (theology) is designated (by the older dogmaticians) as a sapientia eminens practica, and compared to medicine; cf. the dedication of Gerhard’s Meditationes sacrae. This rests upon a confusion of theological science with the ecclesiastical proclamation of salvation. The necessity of theology, as it is already evident from its actual existence, is conditioned by the intellectual need of the Christian, as well as by the practical need of the Church; its possibility is grounded in the relationship of cognition to faith.” (Kompendium etc. p. 3.) Harlessius: “Just as every scientific discipline is a product of a historical development of human cognition, so also the need for theological cognition is not to be derived and understood from the essence of religion in itself, but only from the historical development of the Church, from which scientific theology itself has emerged. The necessity of theological cognition lies, in its potentiality, in the nature of the rational spirit itself, which is compelled not merely to have what it possesses as a given possession, but to posit it at the same time as its own most proper movement and as absolute truth.” (Theologische Encyclopädie. Nürnb. 1837. p. 26 sq.)

As a practical science. For theology reaches these acts in themselves, and the theologian, by virtue of the science existing within him, has them in his power. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Introd. Cap. III. § 6. p. 127, and the blessed Meisner, P. III. Ph. S. p. 112, where, having made a comparison of the theologian with the physician, he says the internal end of theology is the theological healing, or working toward the saving of man; so that the theologian is said to have performed his duty correctly if he has omitted nothing that is in his power to heal and restore men, even though he may not lead all to salvation. That which is outside the power of the theologian is not always reached by the force of the science that is in him, which is evident from experience. Cf. the blessed Meisner, l.c.

§ 17.

The external end is usually distinguished into the ultimate and the intermediate. Furthermore, each is distinguished into objective and formal. The objective is God, infinitely perfect and supremely good. The formal is a certain operation concerning God, by which we possess and enjoy Him as the supreme good. Thus, the objective end is one and the same in both cases. The formal end, however, is one thing if you consider the ultimate, and another if you consider the intermediate. § 18. Indeed, the ultimate formal end consists in the intuitive and clear knowledge of God, and likewise in the most intense love of God, who is intuitively known.

Thus Christ, in Matthew 5:8, about to declare the blessedness of those who are pure in heart, says that they shall see God. And John, in 1 Ep. 3:2, places the future blessedness, which has not yet appeared, in the fact that we shall see God (whose children we are) just as He is. We are said to possess God in this way, as the supreme good, because God is apprehended through that act of the intellect and is rendered intimately present and united to us. See the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* Cap. III. § 11. p. 130. We shall say more below in its proper place. By this God, as our good, being clearly known or apprehended, we cling to Him for His own sake. For it cannot be that the will is not drawn into the supreme love of God when the intellect perfectly knows Him as our supreme good. Musaeus, *l. c.* p. 131. § 19. The intermediate formal end is faith in Christ, as the cause of obtaining grace before God. Furthermore, the love of God, as reconciled to us, pertains to the same; indeed, even other acts by which we are made partakers of divine goodness; and in its own way, the entire holiness of life.

Calovius: "The intermediate end can likewise be distinguished into internal and external. The latter is the faith of men who are to be led to salvation... The internal, however, is any function of theologians that contributes to the faith and salvation of men; especially prayer, the preaching of the divine word, the administration of the sacraments, and the administration of ecclesiastical discipline." (*Isag.* I, 192. sq.) The same: "For the theologian ought not to intend knowledge solely for its own sake, but so that the truth known may be apprehended by a fiducial heart; but true and living is the practice of faith, from which furthermore flows and follows πραξις ενσεβείας as the fruit of true faith." (*L. c.* p. 216. sq.)

Hollazius: "By the intermediate end of theology is understood that means of salvation by which we attain the ultimate end, or eternal blessedness. But we attain it through faith. Therefore...
