Love toward God and neighbor, the holiness of life, and the restoration of the divine image follow faith in Christ in an individual connection, and thus pertain to the consequences of the intermediate end of theology, but they are not causes of attaining eternal blessedness. There are some authors who call the holiness of life the intermediate end of theology concomitant, with Musaeus in *Introd. theol.* p. 135, or the secondary end with Hildebrand in *th. dogm.* p. 21, or the non-causal intermediate end with Baier. We shall not litigate with them, since they confess that they take the end of theology in a broader sense." (*Exam. theologic. acroamat.* Prolegom. c. 1. q. 18. p. 13.)

Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between the practice of faith and the practice of piety. Both practices are given in theology; yet the former, not the latter, is on our part the sole means of either arriving at or being led to salvation; and therefore theology is called practical not on account of the latter, but on account of the former." (*Th. did.-pol.* P. I. c. 1. s. 2. q. 3. f. 25.)

For through this we possess God, as our good, already in this life; insofar as Christ, whose merit we apprehend by faith, becomes our propitiation, Rom. 3:25, so that we may have peace toward God, Rom. 5:1, and the right or inheritance of eternal life, John 3:16. Thus John joins the love of God with the true and saving knowledge of God, 1 Ep. 4:7, 8. And it is certain that by the act of love we already cleave to God in this life, and enjoy Him as our good.

E.g., filial confidence, or the acquiescence of the will in the reconciled God, as the cause of obtaining other goods; so that as children we cry out to God: Abba, Father! Rom. 8:15. Whence also there immediately has place the hope of those goods, spiritual and temporal; just as in the same place, verse 24, we are said to be saved by hope, i.e., to expect salvation firmly by the act of hope; and verse 28, being certainly persuaded, and thus also securely hoping or expecting, that it will be that all things together are for our help for good.

Indeed, theology tends entirely toward the whole holiness of life, and in order to obtain it, it is occupied in delivering and confirming conclusions which lead to it and aim at it as a target; although it is certain that it does not have the nature of a cause in relation to the ultimate end in the same way as faith does, but rather, just as the term "means" is used, so here the term "intermediate end" ought to be taken in a broader signification; for which reason some also use here the term "secondary" or "concomitant" end.

Meanwhile, the blessed J. Foerster in *Probl. th. disp. I.* writes: The architectonic end of theology consists in practice, which practice may be exercised either in faith or in life. Th. 19 and following up to 23. And the blessed Jac. Martini, in the same place § 34, p. 38, says the external end of theology is piety, a true description of which is had in 1 Tim. 1:5: The end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned; and he adds another passage, Heb. 12:14: Without holiness no one will see God.

The blessed Gerhard also in *exegesi prooem.* § 12, p. 5, says that that practice, toward which theology tends as toward an end, consists in doing the will of God, according to the passages of Matthew 7:21, Luke 6:48, John 13:17.

If, therefore, the end of theology is the holiness of life, but one does not stop ultimately in it, but a further end is given, namely eternal salvation; so indeed that, although the holiness of life is not prescribed so that through it, as a cause, we may attain eternal life...

For, if that [theology] is prescribed as pertaining to the way of eternal life, through which one must walk lest we fall from it, why should the holiness of life not rightly be called the intermediate end of theology? If anyone were to call it an intermediate end, with the addition that it is not a causal end (in respect to the ultimate end), we shall not object. §

20. The subject of operation is a) man the sinner, b) insofar as he is to be led to eternal salvation.

c) Gerhard: "Just as in medicine, physiology and pathology are set forth first, which consider the affections of the subject (namely, the human body) with which it is occupied insofar as it is to be healed: so in theology, which is a spiritual medicine, the nature of man, both instituted and destitute, is treated first; afterwards, the means leading to the end of theology (namely, the restoration and salvation of man) are proposed." (Exeges. locc. Prooem. § 28.)

Latin:

Gerhardus: „Intermedius ac proximus finis est vel internus, informatio hominum ad salutem aeternam, vel externus, ipsa beatitudinis sive vitae aeternae consecutio Luc. 1, 77. Joh. 5, 39. 20), ult. Rom. 15, 4. 2 Tim. 3, 16. Quaecunque ergo ad hunc finem non ducunt nec conducunt, sive directe, sive saltem indirecte, sive immediate, sive mediate, ea non pertinent ad theologicam jvüaiv. Ex hoc facile colligitur, quid de quibusdam futilibus magis, quam utilibus scholasticorum quaestionibus et otiosis speculationibus, quas apostolus vocat μωρας και απαίδευτους ζητήσεις 2 Tim. 2, 23., statuendum sit, videl. quod ad ματαιολογίαν potius, quam ad θεολογίαν pertinent. 1 Tim. 1, 6.“ (Exeges. locc. th. Prooem. § 26.) Meisnerus: „Deum cognoscit theologus tanquam finem, siquidem in fruitione Dei sita est nostra beatitudo; et cognoscit ipsum non ideo, ut in i£ta cognitione acquiescat, nec aliud desideret; sed potius, ut per istam cognitionem ... et ipse et alii, qui ipsum audiunt, salutis aeternae participes fiant. Hunc finem qui non semper intendit nec in omni sua theoria (γνώσει) respicit, is veri theologix nomen non meretur.11 (Philos. sobr. P. III. s. 5. c. 2. p. 163.) ANTITHESIS:

Luthardtius: „Darum wird sie (die Theologie) bezeichnet (von den älteren Dogmatikern) als eine sapientia eminens practica, und verglichen mit der medicina; vergl. die Dedication von Gerhardi Meditationes sacrae. Dies beruht auf einer Verwechslung der theologischen Wissenschaft mit der kirchlichen Heilsverkündigung. Die Nothwendigkeit der Theologie, wie sie schon aus ihrer thatsächlichen Existenz erhellt, ist durch das intellectuelle Bedürfniss des Christen, wie durch das praktische der Kirche bedingt; ihre Möglichkeit in dem Verhältniss des Erkennens zum Glauben begründet.“ (Kompendium etc. p. 3.) Harlessius: „Wie jede wissenschaftliche Disciplin Product einer historischen Entwicklung der menschlichen Erkenntniss ist, so ist auch das Bedürfniss der theologischen Erkenntniss nicht aus dem Wesen der Religion an sich, sondern nur aus der historischen Entwicklung der Kirche, aus welcher die wissenschaftliche Theologie selbst hervorgegangen ist, abzuleiten und zu begreifen. Die Nothwendigkeit der theologischen Erkenntniss liegt ihrer Potenz nach in der Natur des vernünftigen Geistes selbst, der, was er besitzt, nicht blos als ein gegebenes Besitzthum zu haben, sondern es als seine nunmehr eigenste Bewegung und als absolute Wahrheit zugleich wieder zu setzen gedrungen ist." (Theologische Encyclopädie. Nürnb. 1837. p. 26. sq.)

Tanquam scientiae practicae. Hos enim actus per se attingit theologia, et theologus vi scientiae sibi inexistentis in potestate sua habet. Conf. b. Musaeus Introd. Cap. III. § 6. p. 127. et b. Meisn. P. III. Ph. S. p. 112., ubi, facta theologi cum medico comparatione, finem internum theologiae dicit esse τυ medicari theologicum, vel operari circa hominem salvandum; ita ut theologus munere suo recte perfunctus dicatur, si, quae in sua potestate sunt, ad sanandos restituendosque homines nihil omiserit, quanquam non omnes ad salutem perducat. Qui est extra potestatem theologi, nec vi scientiae, quae ipsi inest, semper attingitur, quod per experientiam constat. Conf. b. Meisnerum 1. c.

§ 17.

Finis externus distingui solet in ultimwm et intermedium. Uterque porro distinguitur in objectivum et formalem. Objectivus est Deus, infinite perfectus et summe bonus. Formalis est operatio quaedam circa Deum, qua eo velut summo bono potimur et fruimur. Itaque objecti vus finis utrinque unus est. Formalis vero alius est, si ultimum, alius, si intermedium spectes. § 18. Nempe finis formalis ultimus consistit in intuitiva et clara Dei a cognitione, itemque amore b Dei intuitive cogniti intensissimo.

Sic Christus Matth. 5, 8., beatitudinem eorum, qui corde mundi sunt, declaraturus, Deum visuros dicit. Et Johannes 1. Ep. 3, 2. beatitudinem futuram, quae nunc nondum apparuerit, in eo collocat, quod Deum (cujus filii sumus) visuri simus, sicuti est. Dicimur autem hac ratione potiri Deo, tanquam summo bcpo, quia Deus per actum illum intellectus apprehenditur nobisque intime praesens redditur atque unitur. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. Cap. III. § 11. p. 130. Plura dicemus infra suo loco. Quo Deo, tanquam bono nostro, clare cognito seu apprehenso, inhaeremus propter ipsum. Neque enim fieri potest, quin voluntas in summum Dei amorem pertrahatur, quando intellectus eum, tanquam summum bonum nostrum, perfecte cognoscit. Mus. l. c. p. 131.§ 19. Finis formalis intermedius est fides a in Christum, tanquam causam impetrandae gratiae apud Deum. Eodem autem deinde pertinet amor Dei, b tanquam nobis reconciliati; imo et actus c alii, quibus divinae bonitatis participes reddimur; ac suo modo tota vitae sanctimonia. d

Calovius: „Finis intermedius itidem distingui potest in internum et externum. Hic est fides hominum ad salutem perducendorum. . . Internus autem est quaevis functio theologorum faciens ad fidem et salutem hominum; cumprimis vero precatio, verbi divini praedicatio, sacramentorum dispensatio et disciplinae ecclesiasticae administratio.“ (Isag. I, 192. sq.) Idem: „Non enim cognitionem theologus intendere debet unice sui causa, sed ut veritas cognita corde fiduciali apprehendatur; vera autem et viva est praxis fidei, e qua porro emanat et consequitur πραξις ενσεβείας ceu fructus verae fidei.“ (L. c. p. 216. sq.)

Hollazius: „Per finem theologiae intermedium intelligitur illud salutis medium, quo finem ultimum seu aeternam beatitudinem consequimur. Atqui consequimur eam per fidem. Ergo... Dilectio in Deum et proximum, vitae sanctimonia et instauratio imaginis divinae fidem in Christum individuo nexu sequuntur, atque adeo ad consequentia finis intermedii theologiae pertinent, sed non sunt causae consequendae aeternae beatitudinis. Sunt nonnulli auctores, qui sanctitatem vitae vocant theologiae finem intermedium concomitantem cum Musaeo in Introd. theol. p. 135., vel finem secundarium cum Hildebrando in th. dogm. p. 21., vel finem intermedium non causalem cum Baiero. Cum quibus non litigabimus, cum illi fateantur, se finem theologiae in latiori sensu accipere.“ (Exam. theologic. acroamat. Prolegom. c. 1. q. 18. p. 13.)

Quenstedtius: „Distingue inter ττράξιν τής πίστεως s. fidei, et πράξιν τής ενσεβείας s. pietatis. . . Utraque praxis in theologia datur, illa tamen, non haec, a parte nostra est unicum medium vel perveniendi vel perducendi ad salutem; ac proinde theologia non oh hanc, sed propter illam practica dicitur.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. I. c. 1. s. 2. q. 3. f. 25.)

Per hanc enim potimur Deo, tanquam bono nostro, jam in hac vita; quatenus Christus, cujus meritum fide apprehendimus, fit nobis placamentum, Rom. 3, 25., ut pacem habeamus erga Deum, Rom. 5, 1., ac jus seu haereditatem vitae aeternae, Joh. 3, 16. Sic dilectionem Dei cum vera et salutari cognitione Dei conjungit Johannes 1. Ep. 4, 7. 8. Ac certum est, actu amoris jam in hac vita nos inhaerere Deo, ac frui eo, tanquam bono nostro.

V; g. fiducia filialis, seu acquiescentia voluntatis in Deo reconciliato, tanquam causa caeterorum bonorum impetrandorum; ut tanquam filii clamemus ad Deum: Abba, Pateri Rom. 8, 15. Unde statim etiam locum habet spes bonorum illorum, spiritualium ac temporalium; prout 1. c. vers. 24. spe salvi facti dicimur, i. e., salutem actu spei firmo expectare; et vers. 28. certo persuasi, adeoque etiam secure sperantes aut expectantes, fore, ut omnia simul nobis adjumento sint in bonum.

Nempe theologia ad totam vitae sanctimoniam, omnino tendit atque, ut eam obtineat, occupata est in tradendis et confirmandis conclusionibus, quae eo ducunt ac tanquam ad scopum collineant; licet certum sit, eam non aeque, ut fides, rationem causae habere in ordine ad finem ultimum, verum, sicut vocem medii, ita et hic terminum finis intermedii in latiore significatione accipi oportere; quam ob rem etiam aliqui hic terminum finis secundarii aut concomitgntis usurpant.

Interim b. J. Foersterus in Probl, th. disp. I. scribit: Finem theologiae architectonicum consistere in πράξει, quae πραξις vel in fide, vel in vita exerceatur. Th. 19. et sqq. ad 23. Et b. Jac. Martini 1. c. § 34. p. 38. finem externum theologiae dicit esse pietatem, cujus vera descriptio habeatur 1 Tim. 1, 5.: Finis mandati est charitas ex puro corde, scientia bona et fide non fida; additque alterum locum Ebr. 12, 1J+.: Sine sanctimonia nemo videbit Deum.

B. Gerhardus quoque in exegesi prooem. § 12. p. 5. πραξίν illam, ad quam, tanquam ad finem, tendat theologia, consistere dicit in facienda voluntate Dei, juxta LL. Matthaei 7, 21. Duc. 6, 48. Joh. 13, 17.

Quodsi ergo finis theologiae est vitae sanctimonia, in ea autem non subsistitur ultimo, sed datur finis ulterior, nempe salus aeterna; ita quidem, ut, quamvis sanctimonia vitae non praescribatur, ut per eam, tanquam causam, consequamur vitam aeter

nam, praescribatur tamen illa, tanquam ad viam vitae aeternae pertinens, per quam eundum est, ne hac excidamus: quidni sanctimonia vitae finis theologiae intermedius recte dicatur? quem si quis cum addito finem intermedium non causalem (respectu finis ultimi) dixerit, non repugnabimus. §

20. Subjectum operationis a est homo peccator, b quatenus est ad salutem aeternam perducendus.

c Gerhardus: „Quemadmodum in medicina praemittitur φυσιολογία ac 'παθολογία, quae affectiones subjecti (corporis sci. humani), circa quod, quatenus sanandum est, occupatur, considerat: sic in theologia, quae spiritualis est medicina, de natura hominis instituta ac destituta prius agitur, postea med a ad finem theologiae (videl. hominis reparationem ac salutem) ducentia proponuntur.“ (Exeges. locc. Prooem. § 28.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Our theologians, who hold revealed theology to be a practical habit,…

Our theologians, who hold revealed theology to be a practical habit, acknowledge that there is a subject of the operation of revealed theology. And although philosophers otherwise teach that the subject of the operation of habits and practical sciences must bring a certain natural Ικανότητα, or aptitude, to perform the operation that is prescribed; and although they also restrict πραξιν to those things which are ἐφ' ἡμῖν, or in our power, whereas here the practice of faith depends upon the supernatural grace and influx of God, and man is by nature inept for it, like a dead person: yet our theologians think it sufficient in this place that the end is nonetheless to be introduced into man, as the subject, through certain means prescribed here, by the virtue of divine grace, or that he himself is to be led to the end through the means.

See the blessed Gerhard, in Exeg. I. c. § 28. p. 17., the blessed Meisner, Ph. S. P. III. p. 114. 121. Moreover, the subject of operation coincides with the end for whom. See the blessed Musaeus, Introd. 1. c. § 15. p. 136.

Or corrupted by sin or liable to it, such as every man carnally begotten is throughout his whole life after the fall. For we do not take the state of sin so strictly as it is opposed to the state of regeneration; rather, we confess that even the regenerate man continues to need theological practice as long as he is on the way or in this life.

Namely, man the sinner constitutes the material subject of operation; but insofar as he is to be formed and led to salvation, he constitutes the formal subject of operation. Compare the blessed Gerhard, 1. c., the blessed Meisner, Ph. S. P. III. p. 115. §

21. The efficient cause of the ultimate formal end is a) God, b) the Triune c) [God]. Or of that operation by which we perfectly possess and enjoy God Himself, as our highest good. ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

For God alone can endow the human intellect with the light of glory, and thus elevate it to elicit that operation which altogether exceeds the natural power of a finite intellect. Consequently, He alone can perfect the will in such a way that the act of the most intense love of this Good may arise within it. For the bestowal of blessedness is an outward work, common to the three persons. § 22.

The internal impulsive cause is the goodness of God; the external and meritorious cause is the merit of Christ. This is not only because blessedness is not owed to man by divine justice, but especially if you consider the blessedness to be given to a sinner. For since the justice of God, offended by sins, demands satisfaction or punishment from man, the grace or goodness of God does not become the complete principle of our salvation unless the merit by which divine justice is satisfied intervenes. And thus Paul, in Rom. 3:24, joins, in order to the justification of the sinner, the grace of God and the redemption that is in Christ Jesus; and in 1 Tim. 2:4 and 6, when he had said that God wills all men to be saved, he immediately adds the mediator between God and men, who gave himself as a ransom, so that we might be saved. § 23.

But faith in Christ is also rightly reckoned among the causes of salvation. For thus faith, or the believing in Him, is joined to the remaining causes—to the grace or love of God, by which He loved the world, and to His only-begotten Son, insofar as He was given to the world as mediator, expiating the sins of the world by His merit—in John 3:16. And elsewhere we are said to be saved διά της πίστεως, through faith, Eph. 2:8, and to live ἐκ πίστεως, by faith, Rom. 1:17, Gal. 3:11, Heb. 10:38. Moreover, the particles ἐκ and διά have the manifest force of a cause there. Yet it is not considered in itself and absolutely, as it is an act or quality; nor insofar as it is effective through love, but in relation to the object, which is Christ the mediator. But if one must arrive at some certain genus of causes: just as it must be confessed that faith does not relate to salvation and the beatific vision by way of an efficient, material, formal, or final cause, but that its causality consists in this, that while it presents the merit of Christ to God as apprehended by man, by this very act it moves God to confer salvation upon that man out of grace; so faith is rightly referred to the genus of the impulsive cause; and because it moves God not by its own dignity, but by the dignity of the merit of Christ, it can therefore be called a less principal impulsive cause, in distinction to the merit of Christ itself. See the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.*, l. c., § 18, pp. 138, 139.

PROLEGOMENA CHAPTER I. Gerhard: “We also say that faith is a cause of justification, namely, an instrumental one. It is one thing to be justified διὰ τὴν πίστιν, and another to be justified διὰ τῆς πίστεως; the former denotes a meritorious cause, but the latter an instrumental one. We are not justified because of faith, as if it were some merit, but through faith, which apprehends the merit.” (Loc. de justific. § 179.)

Quenstedt: “The moving cause (of predestination) is partly internal and partly external. The internal cause is the purely gratuitous grace of God, excluding altogether every merit of human works, or everything that comes under the name of work or action, whether done through the grace of God or from the powers of nature. For God chose us not according to works, but out of His mere grace. Even faith itself does not belong here, if it is viewed as a condition, more or less worthy, whether in itself or by estimation, added to faith by the will of God; for none of these things enters into the decree of election as a moving or impelling cause for God to make such a decree, but it is to be ascribed to the pure and unmixed grace of God, as Huelsemann teaches in Breviar. c. 15. th. 6.” (Theol. did.-pol. P. III. c. 2. s. 1. th. 10. f. 25.)

Reusch: “The principal impulsive cause is that which, by its own goodness and its own value, moves the efficient cause to act; the less principal, instrumental, or organic cause, however, is that which does so by an alien goodness or one received from elsewhere, and by an alien value.” (Annotatt. in Baieri Compend. p. 771.) §

24. And because faith is conferred upon men only by God, who produces and confirms it through the Word and Sacraments as through organs, therefore these also are rightly numbered among the causes of salvation. For it is not a work of human powers, but is conferred supernaturally upon man, who is by nature inept for believing, as we shall see below. Thus, in James 1:21, the Word of God is called the seed from which believers are born; and therefore, active power and true causality are attributed to it in order to produce faith in men. And baptism, in Titus 3:5, is called the washing of regeneration; namely, because regeneration depends upon it as upon a cause. For because they are causes of faith, which is a cause of salvation, they are rightly considered causes of salvation itself, as the caused effect.

Carpzov: “This must still be added: that the Augsburg Confession treats here (Art. 5) of the Word and Sacraments insofar as they are operative media and act by way of physical operation, since the question in this place is: Whence is faith? and do the Word and Sacraments work it? For besides this mode of operating, another also pertains to the Word and Sacraments, which behaves morally, and consists in the giving, offering, or presentation, conferring, and sealing of the justifying good. For the action of the Word and Sacraments, insofar as they generate, nourish, and excite faith, ought not to be confused with the action of the Word insofar as it concurs proximately to justification. For while in the former action the Word and Sacraments behave as organs both effective of the spiritual powers for believing and excitative of the spiritual motions of faith; in the latter, namely in justification, they are at least datary, collative, and sealing organs of the justifying good, which is the obedience of Christ.” (Isag. in libros symb. Ed. 2. Lips. 1675. p. 251.) ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

25. The object of revealed theology is twofold: material and formal. The material object consists of things revealed, which are known in revealed theology. And to this pertain not only the subject of the operation and the causes and means of attaining the end, but also the end itself, insofar as it is known by the habit of theology.

The formal object, or the principle and reason for knowing, from which the knowledge of the things proposed in revealed theology depends, is divine revelation.

Brochmand: "The object of theology is in one sense adequate, in another proximate, and in another principal. The adequate object of theology is whatever God has seen fit to have written down in His Word. For since the principle of theology is the written Word of God, it cannot be otherwise than that everything which is found handed down and written in the Holy Scriptures must be acknowledged as the object of theology. Therefore, since the Holy Scriptures deal not only with God, with creation, with the original integrity of angels and men, with the fall of angels and men, and with the restoration of men through Christ, but also with the natural knowledge of God, with the love owed to God and neighbor, and with the deeds of many men, both pious and impious, all these things cannot but be the subject of theology, according to the statements in Rom. 15:4 and 2 Tim. 3:16. The proximate object of theology is that which the eye has not seen, the ear has not heard, and which has not entered into the heart of man, but which has been prepared by God for men and revealed through the Holy Spirit (Is. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9, 10). This assertion is confirmed by these testimonies of the Holy Scriptures: John 1:18; Matt. 11:27; 16:17; 1 Cor. 2:7, 8. The principal object of theology is God, insofar as He has manifested Himself in Christ to sinful men for salvation. To this point serve these testimonies: 1 Cor. 2:2; John 5:46; Acts 4:11, 12." (System. univ. th. Ulm, 1664. Artic. I. c. 1. S. 4. f. 2. sq.)

Pfeiffer: "Positive theology is nothing other than the coordination of conclusions concerning faith deduced from the Holy Scriptures rightly understood, or articles of faith solidly proven from the oracles of Holy Scripture; indeed, it is nothing other than Holy Scripture itself reduced to certain topics in a neat order and a clear method; whence there should not be a single member, however small, in that body of doctrine which is not established from the Holy Scriptures properly understood." (Thesaur. hermeneut. p. 5.)

Gerhard: "The sole principle of theology is the Word of God; therefore, whatever is not revealed in the Word of God is not theological." (Loc. de creatione, § 3.)

Latin:

Dari subjectum operationis theologiae revelatae, agnoscunt nostrates theologi, qui theologiam revelatam pro habitu practico habent. Et quamvis alias philosophi doceant, subjectum operationis habituum ac scientiarum practicarum Ικανότητα sive aptitudinem quandam naturalem ad operationem, quae praescribitur, praestandam afferre debere; quamvis etiam ipsam πραξιν restringant ad ea, quae sunt ἐφ’ ἡμῖν, sive in nostra potestate, hic autem praxis fidei a supernaturali Dei gratia et influxu pendeat, et homo ad eam natura ineptus sit, instar mortui: putant tamen nostri, sufficere h. l., quod finis nihilominus in hominem, tanquam subjectum, per certa media hic praescripta, virtute gratiae divinae, est introducendus, aut ipse ad finem per media deducendus est.

Vid. b. Gerhard, in Exeg. I. c. § 28. p. 17., b. Meisn. Ph. S. P. III. p. 114. 121. Coincidit autem subjectum operationis cum fine cui. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. 1. c. § 15. p. 136.

Seu peccato corruptus aut obnoxius, qualis est post lapsum omnis homo carnaliter genitus per omnem vitam. Neque enim statum peccati ita stricte accipimus, prout opponitur statui regenerationis; fatemur potius, hominem etiam regenitum porro indigere praxi theologica, quoadusque in via aut in hac vita est.

Nempe homo peccator subjectum operationis materiale; quatenus autem ad salutem formandus ac perducendus est, subjectum operationis formale constituit. Confer, b. Gerh. 1. c., b. Meisn. Ph. S. P. III. p. 115.§

21. Causa efficiens finis ultimi formalis a Deus b trinunus c est. Seu operationis illius, qua Deo ipso, tanquam summo bono nostro, perfecte potimur et fruimur. DB NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Solus enim Deus potest intellectum humanum lumine gloriae donare, atque ita ad eliciendam illam operationem, quae naturalem vim intellectus finiti prorsus excedit, elevare. Solus etiam proinde voluntatem ita perficere potest, ut actus intensissimi amoris hujus boni in ea oriatur. Est enim collatio beatitudinis opus ad extra, tribus personis commune.§ 22.

Causa impulsiva interna est Dei a bonitas; externa ac meritoria meritum Christi. b Non solum, quod homini ex justitia divina non debetur beatitudo; sed inprimis, si spectes beatitudinem peccatori dandam. Cum enim justitia Dei, peccatis laesa, satisfactionem aut poenam ab homine exigat, gratia seu bonitas Dei non fit principium completum nostrae salutis, nisi intercedente merito, quo satisfiat justitiae divinae. Et sic Paulus Rom. 3, 24. conjungit, in ordine ad justificationem peccatoris, gratiam Dei et redemptionem, quae est in Christo Jesu; et 1 Tim. 2, 4. et 6., cum dixisset: Deum omnes velle salvos fieri, statim addit mediatorem Dei et hominum, qui semetipsum dederit pretium redemptionis, ut possimus salvi fieri.§ 23.

Sed et fides in Christum a causis salutis b recte accensetur. Sic enim reliquis causis, gratiae seu amori Dei, quo mundum dilexit, et filio ejus unigenito, quatenus mundo is datus est, tanquam mediator, expians peccata mundi suo merito, fides sive τύ credere in eum conjungitur Joh. 3, 16. Atque alias dicimur salvari διά της πίστεως, per fidem, Ephes. 2, 8., vivere ix πίστεως, ex fide, Rom. 1, 17. Gal. 3, 11. Ebr. 10, 88. Particulae autem ix et διά vim causae manifestam ibi habent. Non autem in se et absolute spectata, ut est actus vel qualitas; neque quatenus est efficax per dilectionem, sed in ordine ad objectum, quod est Christus mediator. Quodsi ad certum aliquod genus causarum accedendum sit; sicut fatendum est, fidem non habere se ad salutem ac visionem beatificam, per modum causae efficientis, materialis, formalis, aut finalis, causalitatem autem ejus in eo consistere, quod, dum Deo meritum Christi, tanquam ab homine apprehensum, exhibet, hoc ipso Deum movet ad salutem homini illi ex gratia conferendam; ita ad genus causae impulsivae recte refertur fides; et quia non sua, sed meriti Christi dignitate Deum movet, ideo ad differentiam ipsius meriti Christi causa impulsiva minus prrincipalis dici potest. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. l. c. § 18. p. 138. 139.

Gerhardus: „Etiam nos dicimus, fidem esse causam justificationis, puta instrumentalem. Aliud est δια την πίστιν, aliud διά της πίστεως justificari; illud causam meritoriam notat, hoc vero instrumentalem. Non justificamur propter fidem, tanquam meritum aliquod, sed per fidem, quae meritum apprehendit.“ (Loc. de justiflc. § I79.)

Quenstedtius : „Causa movens (praedestinationis) alia interna est, alia externa. Interna est gratia Dei mere gratuita, excludens omne omnino operum humanorum meritum sive omne id, quod nomine operis vel actionis, sive per gratiam Dei, sive ex viribus naturae factae, venit. Elegit enim nos Deus non secundum opera, sed ex mera sua gratia. Etiam fides ipsa huc non pertinet, si spectatur tanquam conditio, magis vel minus digna, sive per se, sive ex aestimio, per voluntatem Dei fidei superaddito; quod nihil horum decretum electionis ingrediatur tanquam causa movens aut impellens Deum ad tale decretum faciendum, sed id purae putae gratiae Dei est adscribendum, ut docet Huelsemannus Breviar. c. 15. th. 6.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. III. c. 2. s. 1. th. 10. f. 25.)

Reuschius: „Causa impulsiva principalis est, quae propria bonitate proprioque valore movet causam efficientem ad agendum; minus autem principalis, instrumentalis seu organica, quae id facit bonitate aliena seu aliunde accepta alienoque valore.“ (Annotatt. in Baieri Compend. p. 771.) §

24. Et quia fides hominibus non nisi a Deo a confertur, qui illam per verbum et sacramenta, tanquam per organa b producit et confirmat: ideo et haec inter causas salutis recte numerantur. c Non enim humanarum virium opus est, sed supernaturaliter confertur homini, natura inepto ad credendum, ut infra videbimus. Sic Jac. 1, 21. verbum Dei dicitur semen, unde nascuntur fideles; adeoque tribuitur ei vis activa et vera causalitas in ordine ad fidem in hominibus producendam. Et baptismus ad Tit. S, 5. dicitur lavacrum regenerationis; scilicet quod regeneratio ab illo, tanquam a causa, pendeat. Quia enim sunt causae fidei, quae est causa salutis, etiam salutis ipsius, tanquam causati, causae recte censentur.

Carpzovius: „Hoc addi adhuc debet, Augustanam Confessionem de verbo et sacramentis hic (art. 5.) agere, prout operantia media sunt et per modum operationis physicae agunt, cum quaestio sit hoc in loco: Unde fides sit? et an verbum et sacramenta eandem operentur? Praeter hunc enim operandi modum verbo et sacramentis alius etiam competit, qui moraliter sese habet, et in datione, porrectione seu oblatione, collatione et obsignatione boni justifici consistit. Neque enim confundi debent actio verbi et sacramentorum, quatenus fidem generant, alunt atque excitant, et actio verbi, prout ad justificationem concurrit proxime. Cum enim in priori actione verbum et sacramenta sese habeant ut organa tum effectiva virium spiritualium ad credendum, tum excitativa motuum spiritualium fidei; in posteriori, scl. in justificatione, organa saltem dativa sunt, collativa et obsignativa boni'justifici, quod est obedientia Christi.“ (Isag. in libros symb. Ed. 2. Lips. 1675. p. 251.) DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

25. Objectum theologiae revelatae duplex est: Materiale et formale. Materiale sunt res a revelatae, quae in theologia revelata cognoscuntur. Atque huc pertinent non tantum subjectum operationis et causae ac media consequendi finis, sed et finis ipse, b quatenus habitu theologiae cognoscitur.

Formale, seu principium et ratio cognoscendi, unde pendet cognitio rerum, quae in theologia revelata proponuntur, est revelatio divina. c

Brochmandus: „Aliud est adaequatum, aliud proximum, aliud pripceps theologiae objectum. Adaequatum theologiae objectum est, quicquid Deus in verbo suo perscribi curavit. Cum enim principium theologiae sit verbum Dei scriptum, fieri non potest, quin omne illud pro objecto theologiae agnoscendum sit, quod in S. S. traditum et perscriptum invenitur. Quocirca cum in S. S. non tantum agatur de Deo, de creatione, de primigenia angelorum et hominum integritate, de lapsu angelorum et hominum, de hominum per Christum restitutione; sed etiam de notitia Dei naturali, de caritate Deo et proximo debita, de rebus gestis plurimorum hominum, piorum et impiorum: non possunt non haec omnia esse subjectum theologiae juxta dicta Rom. 15, 4. 2 Tim. 3, 16. Proximum theologiae objectum est, quod oculus non vidit, auris non audivit, in cor hominis non descendit, a Deo praeparatum hominibus et per Sp. S. revelatum, Es. 64, 4. et 1 Cor. 2, 9. 10. Quae assertio firmatur his Scripturarum sacrarum testimoniis Joh. 1, 18. Matth. 11, 27. 16, 17. 1 Cor. 2, 7. 8. Princeps theologiae objectum est Deus, quatenus se in Christo manifestavit hominibus peccatoribus ad salutem. Huc faciunt haec testimonia 1 Cor. 2, 2. Joh. 5, 46. Act. 4, 11. 12.“ (System.·univ. th. Ulmae. 1664. Artic. I. c. 1. S. 4. f. 2. sq.)

Pfeifferus: „Theologia positiva nil aliud est, quam coordinatio conclusionum de fide e S. S. recte intellecta deductarum sive articulorum fidei e Scripturae S. oraculis solide probatorum, imo nil aliud, quam ipsa Scriptura S. in certos locos concinno ordine et perspicua methodo redacta; unde ne unicum quidem membrum, quantillum etiamf in illo doctrinae corpore esse debet, quod non e S. S. probe intellecta statuminetur.“ (Thesaur. hermeneut. p. 5.)

Gerhardus: „Unicum theologiae principium est verbum Dei; quod ergo in verbo Dei non est revelatum, non est theologicum.“ (Loc. de creatione, § 3.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Calov: "The general object of consideration..

Calov: "The general object of consideration... is said to be things divinely revealed, insofar as they are to be perceived by us for salvation; in which manner the blessed Meisner (P. III. Philos. sobr. s. 1. ethic. p. 174) calls the object 'every divine thing by which man can be led to eternal salvation.' Nor does our same Meisner inappropriately judge that all this can be called by one word, 'religion,' inasmuch as it embraces all things necessary for salvation, to be believed and to be done, and to which all things usually proposed in a system of theology are referred or have a certain respect; so that religion itself constitutes the material of this object, while the formal object is the extent to which we are promoted to salvation through it. In this opinion we also acquiesce, until something more convenient is shown by which the general object can be explained."

The same: "It is necessary to assign an object of theology of such a kind that it respects true blessedness, and it is necessary that those things which do not contribute to this end be removed from theological treatment." (L. c. p. 264.) The same: "The formal reason of the object of theology is not revelation, but revealed things rather constitute the material object, which are viewed in theology under this formal reason, insofar as they respect the ultimate end, eternal salvation." (L. c.) However, those things are called revealed things in this place which have been manifested supernaturally by God, whether or not they could also have been known through the light of nature: as will be evident from what follows.

Otherwise, indeed, the end is the principle of knowing in practical sciences; but the objective and formal end of revealed theology is not so well known that it should not be handed down and taught under another previously known principle of knowing, namely, divine revelation. See the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* l. c. § 24. p. 151, 152. It is otherwise called the primary revealing truth; and by one name, if we speak of theology as it is today, it is understood as the θεόπνευστος Scripture, which testifies of itself through the concurrence of God in the mind of man, and from which all theological conclusions are deduced; which will be taught in the following chapter. §

26. The material object is distinguished into things to be believed and things to be done. Things to be believed are called those which are so subject to faith that they are not formally operations directed by prior practical acts; yet they are to be believed by those who are to attain salvation; e.g., that God loves the human race, that Christ is the Son of God and the Son of Man, etc. By the name of things to be done are understood the very operations of theology prescribed by practical acts, perhaps also habits to be transferred to operation, or to be acquired through operation, if not for the sake of attaining salvation, yet so that we do not fall from salvation; e.g., the actual or habitual apprehension of the merit of Christ, which we call faith, the actual or habitual love by which we love God, Christ, and our neighbor, the hope of eternal life, etc.

Musaeus: "We call things to be believed here, not whatever deserves belief, but those things which are necessary to be believed by those who are to attain salvation; nor do we call things to be done those which for any reason whatsoever are incumbent upon man to do, but those which, if not for the sake of attaining salvation, yet so that we do not fall from salvation, have been instituted and commanded by God to be done. For in divinely inspired Scripture, histories and various matters are found mixed in here and there, which, by the very fact that they are contained in it, are to be believed, but which bear no relation to our salvation. Many things to be done also occur in the Scriptures which likewise are not ordered toward the eternal salvation of man and therefore do not come into the part of the material object of theology." ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

unless perhaps indirectly and accidentally, insofar as they can be referred to man’s salvation in some indirect and accidental way. For in practical sciences, the breadth of the object is to be estimated from the end.” (Introd. in th. Jena 1678, p. 156 sq.)

Rudelbach: “The main thing is that they (the old dogmaticians) hold fast to the fundamental concept of revelation, which, according to our conviction, alone can measure the entire field and assign to every doctrine of faith its place. Christology, the doctrine of Christ’s person and work, nevertheless always remains the decisive center point, for which everything is prepared, and through which everything reaches its goal.” (Zeitschr. 1857, p. 382.) If you look at the force of the words, they can coincide, and sometimes things to be believed and things to be done are really the same. Indeed, things to be done, by the very fact that they are supernaturally revealed, could also rightly be called things to be believed; and conversely, if something is to be believed in such a way that it must be led to operation, or as an operation that ought to be performed by us, it truly pertains to things to be done. See Musaeus, l. c. § 26, p. 156. How, however, they are distinguished here by usage of speech is evident from what follows in the thesis. And for this reason, it is clear that the foundation of that distinction is not the hypothesis that theology is a habit partly theoretical and partly practical; for we said above that things to be believed, although they are not formally πράξεις (actions), are nevertheless treated as the cause of a πράξις (action). § 27.

Things to be believed are otherwise called articles of faith, which in a broader sense are divided 1. into pure and mixed articles of faith, 2. into fundamental and non-fundamental. They are called articles of faith because the faith, or the doctrine of faith, which is to be believed, consists of them as parts cohering in a tight connection; just as the parts of the fingers, fitted to one another and cohering in a tight connection, are called joints (articuli). See Musaeus, Introd. Cap. III. § 30, p. 163. Others call them not so much articles of faith as articles of the doctrine of faith. But it has long since become the case that faith is said to be not only that by which one believes, but also that which is believed, or the doctrine of faith. Reusch: “Articulus properly denotes a part either of a chain or of the human body, insofar as it is connected with other parts.” (Annotatt. in Baieri Compend. p. 39.)

It is certain that the term article of faith has sometimes been accustomed to be taken in a stricter sense; insofar as it precisely denotes mysteries of faith necessary to be believed for salvation, and thus pure articles, and those fundamental ones alone. Thus Luther, Enarrat. in Ps. 45, Tom. III. Jen. lat. fol. 490: “You must first know this,” he says, “that articles of faith are truly sentences concerning such things as the eye has not seen, the ear has not heard, nor have they descended into the heart of man, and are taught and understood only through the Word and the Holy Spirit. And it is the nature of all articles of faith that universal reason abhors them.” Similarly, Conr. Schluesselburg, Lib. II. Theol. Calvin, p. 13, has the customary definition of articles of faith handed down by our theologians thus—

[It] announces: An article of faith is a statement or doctrine not known naturally, but divinely revealed and handed down in the express Word of God, or constructed from it by indubitable consequence, concerning God, His essence, will, Word, and sacraments, and the benefits of God, pertaining to the true worship of God and the salvation of men, to be apprehended by faith. It is also known how the blessed Hunnius, in the Ratisbon Colloquy, sess. XI, p. 351 sqq., contended at length: That all articles of faith whatsoever must necessarily be known and believed by all and each of the Christians. To these respond the things which the blessed Musaeus taught concerning the requirements of an article of faith, strictly so called, in *Quaest. IV. de syncret.* § 13, p. 28, 29. Otherwise, however, the term "article of faith" is frequently accepted, especially today, in a broader signification and admits the division indicated in the thesis, and the blessed Musaeus discoursed at length on this matter in *Introd. C. III. § 30, p. 162 sqq.* Cf. *Ausführl. Erklärung* p. 111 sqq. and *Quaest. IV. de syncret.* in the annotations p.

38. N. Hunnius: "Dogma in this thesis is taken only concerning the doctrine of faith and the Christian religion, and that in the broadest sense, insofar as every doctrine, whether true or divine, or false or heretical, is comprehended under the name of dogma." (*Δίάσκεψις theologica de fundamentali dissensu etc.* Witteb. 1626. § 179.) The same: "Article signifies nothing other than a part of the heavenly doctrine revealed in the prophetic and apostolic Word. But in order that the excessive breadth of this declaration may be restricted in some way, I distinguish historical word from dogmatic, and moral doctrines—or those prescribing what is to be done and what is to be omitted—from dogmas of faith, or those teaching what is to be believed and what is not to be believed (which are properly and primarily accustomed to be called dogmas). And because I am not now concerned with the foundation of piety, but of faith—not of things to be done, but of things to be believed—historical and moral matters must be entirely removed, which never deserve to be called articles of faith." (L. c. § 53, 54.)

Quenstedtius: "The object, about which articles of faith are occupied, are τὰ πιστά, or things to be believed as such... For although faith, viewed generally, is concerned with all things that are contained in the Word of God, whether they be historical, moral, or dogmatic; yet specifically it is concerned with dogmas of faith, or things to be believed as such. This is to be observed, lest anyone fall into the absurdity of the Jesuit Adam Tanner, who asserted in the Ratisbon Colloquy, sess. 11, that everything which is believed or which occurs in the Holy Bible obtains the force of a dogma and is an article of faith, in such a way that he would even ridiculously forge new articles of faith from the incest of Judah and the dog of Tobit wagging its tail. Thus also the history of the tails of Samson’s foxes, of Balaam’s ass, of the years of Methuselah, of the building of the tower of Babel, etc., would have to be numbered among the articles of faith." (*Theol. did.-pol.* P. I. c. 5. s. 1. not. 6. f. 349.) Smalcald Articles: "The Papists allege Augustine and certain Fathers who wrote about purgatory... But this was altogether nothing but the devotion of men, and indeed of one or another, not constituting an article of faith, which belongs to God alone... But we have another rule, namely, that the Word of God shall establish articles of faith and no one else, not even an angel." (P. II. art. 2. p. 303.)

Latin:

Calovius: „Generale objectum vel considerationis. . . dicuntur res divinitus revelatae, quatenus a nobis percipiendae sunt ad salutem; quo pacto b. Meisnerus P. III. Philos. sobr. s. 1. ethic. p. 174. objectum dicit,omnem rem divinam, qua ad salutem aeternam homo perduci potest.* Nec incommode idem Meisnerus noster censet, id omne uno vocabulo vocari posse religionem, utpote quae cuncta ad salutem necessaria, credenda et agenda, complectatur, et ad quam universa in systemate theologiae proponi solita referantur aut quendam respectum habeant; ut ita religio ipsa constituat materiale hujus objecti, formale autem, quatenus per eam ad salutem promovemur. Qua sententia etiam nos acquiescimus, donec commodius quid ostendatur, quo explicari possit generale objectum.“

PROLEjßOM. CAP. I. Idem: „Oportet objectum theologiae ejusmodi assignare, quod respiciat veram beatitudinem, et necessum est, ea, quae ad hunc finem non faciunt, removeri a tractatione theologica.“ (L. c. p. 264.) Idem: „Ratio formalis objecti theologiae non est revelatio, sed res revelatae materiale potius objecti constituunt, quae sub hac formali ratione spectantur in theologia, qua respiciunt finem ultimum, salutem aeternam.“ (L. c.) Dicuntur autem hoc loco res revelatae, quae supernaturaliter a Deo sunt manifestatae, sive per lumen naturae etiam potuerint cognosci, sive non: ut ex seqq. patebit.

Alias quidem finis est principium cognoscendi in scientiis practicis; sed finis theologiae revelatae objectivus pariter et formalis non tam notus est, ut non su6 alia prius cognita ratione cognoscendi, nempe revelatione divina, tradi et doceri debeat. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. l. c. § 24. p. 151. 152. Vocatur alias veritas prima revelans; et uno nomine, si de theologia, qualis hodie est, loquamur, intelligitur Scriptura θεόπνευστος,, quae de se ipsa per Dei concursum in animo hominis testificatur, et unde omnes conclusiones'theologicae deducuntur; quod in seq. cap. docebitur.§

26. Materiale objectum distinguitur a in credenda et agenda. Credenda dicuntur, quae ita subsunt fidei, ut formaliter b non sint operationes praeviis actibus practicis directae; sint autem credenda ab his, qui perventuri sunt ad salutem; v. g. Deum diligere genus humanum, Christum esse filium Dei et filium hominis, etc. Agendorum nomine intelliguntur ipsae operationes theologiae actibus practicis praescriptae, forte etiam habitus ad operationem transferendi, aut per operationem acquirendi, si non consequendae salutis causa, tamen, ne salute excidamus; e. g. apprehensio actualis aut habitualis meriti Christi, quam vocamus fidem, dilectio actualis aut habitualis,. qua Deum, Christum et proximum diligimus, spes vitae aeternae, etc.

Musaeus: „Credenda hic dicimus, non quaecunque merentur fidem, sed quae salutem adepturis creditu necessaria sunt; nec agenda dicimus, quae quacunque de causa homini agenda incumbunt, sed quae, si non consequendae salutis causa, tamen ne salute excidamus, a Deo, ut agantur, instituta ac praecepta sunt. In scriptura enim divinitus inspirata reperiuntur sparsim admixtae historiae et res variae, eo ipso quidem, quod in ea continentur, credendae, sed quae ad nostram salutem nullam important habitudinem. Multa etiam agenda in Scripturis occurrunt, quae itidem ad hominis salutem aeternam non ordinantur et propterea in partem objecti materialis theologiae non veniunt, DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

nisi fortan indirecte et per accidens, in quantum scilicet aliqua ratione indirecta et accidentali ad hominis salutem referri possunt. In scientiis practicis enim latitudo objecti aestimanda est ex flue.“ (Introd. in th. Jenae 1678. p. 156. sq.)

Rudelbachius: ,,Die Hauptsache ist, sie (die alten Dogmatiker) halten den Grundbegriff der Offenbarung fest, welcher, nach unserer Ueberzeugung, allein das ganze Gebiet bemessen und einer jeglichen Glaubenslehre ihren Platz anweisen kann. Die Christologie, die Lehre von Christi Person und Werk, bleibt dennoch immer der durchschlagende Mittelpunct, auf welchen Alles vorbereitet, durch welchen Alles zum Ziele kommt.“ (Zeitschr. 1857. p. 382.) Si vim vocum spectes, possunt convenire, et nonnunquam realiter idem sunt credenda et agenda. Nempe agenda hoc ipso, quod supernaturaliter sunt revelata, recte etiam possent vocari credenda; et contra, si quid credendum sit ita, ut ad operationem sit deducendum, aut tanquam operatio, quae fieri a nobis debeat, revera ad agenda pertinet. Vid. Mus. l. c. § 26. p. 156. Quomodo autem ex usu loquendi hic distinguantur, ex seqq. in thesi patet. Et hac ratione constat, fundamentum distinctionis illius non esse hypothesin illam, quod theologia sit habitus partim theoreticus, partim practicus; nam et credenda, licet formaliter non sint πράξεις, tamen πράξεως causa tractari, supra diximus.§ 27.

Credenda vocantur alias articuli fidei, a qui in latiore b significatione dividuntur 1. in articulos fidei puros et mixtos, 2. in fundamentales et non fundamentales. Articuli fidei dicuntur, quia ex illis, tanquam partibus, arcto nexu cohaerentibus, constat fides seu doctrina fidei, quae credenda est; prout partes digitorum sibi invicem coaptatae et arcto nexu cohaerentes dicuntur articuli. Vid. Mus. Introd. Cap. III. § 30. p. 163. Alii articulos non tam fidei, quam doctrinae fidei appellant. Sed jampridem factum est, ut fides non tantum dicatur ea, qua creditur, verum etiam, quae creditur, seu doctrina fidei.Reuschius: ,,Articulus proprie notat partem vel catenae, vel humani corporis, quatenus cum aliis partibus connectitur.“ (Annotatt. in Baieri Compend. p. 39.)

Certum est, vocem articuli fidei aliquando in strictiore significatione accipi consuevisse; prout praecise denotat mysteria fidei ad salutem creditu necessaria, adeoque articulos puros, eosque fundamentales solos. Sic Lutherus Enarrat, in Ps. 45. Tom. III. Jen. lat. fol. 490.: Vos hoc primum scitote, ait, articulos fidei vere esse sententias de talibus, quae oculus non vidit, auris non audivit, nec descenderunt in cor hominis, et per solum verbum et Spiritum sanctum docentur et intelliguntur. Et est ea natura omnium articulorum fidei, ut universa ratio ab eis abhorreat. Similiter Conr. Schluesselburgius Lib. II. Theol. Calvin, p. 13. usitatam definitionem articulorum fidei a nostris theologis traditam sic habere pro-

nunciat: Articulus fidei est sententia seu doctrina non nota naturaliter, sed divinitus revelata et expresso verbo Dei tradita, vel indubitata consequentia inde extructa, de Deo, de ejus essentia, voluntate, verbo et sacramentis ac beneficiis Dei, ad cultum Dei verum et hominum salutem pertinens, fide apprehendenda. Notum etiam est, quomodo b. Hunnius in Colloquio Ratisb. sess. XI. p. 351. sqq. prolixe contenderit: Omnes omnino articulos fidei omnibus et singulis christianis necessario notos esse et credi debere. Quibus respondent, quae de requisitis articuli fidei, stricte sic dicti, docuit b. Musaeus Quaest. IV. de syncret. § 13. p. 28. 29. Alias autem terminus articuli fidei in latiore significatione praesertim hodie frequenter accipitur ac divisionem in thesi indicatam admittit, eamque in rem prolixe disseruit b. Musaeus Introd. C. III. § 30. p. 162. sqq. Conf. Ausführl. Erklärung p. 111. sqq. et Quaest. IV. de syncret. in annotatt. p.

38. N. Hunnius: ,,Dogma in hac thesi sumitur tantum de doctrina fidei et religionis Christianae, idque in sensu latissimo, prout omnis doctrina, vera pariter sive divina, atque falsa sive haeretica, nomine dogmatis comprehenditur.“ (Δίάσκεψις theologica de fundamentali dissensu etc. Witteb. 1626. § 179.) Idem: ,,Nihil aliud significat articulus, quam partem coelestis doctrinae in verbo prophetico et apostolico revelatae. Ut vero nimia hujus declarationis latitudo quodammodo restringatur, distinguo verbum historicum a dogmatico et doctrinas morales seu praecipientes, quid faciendum, quid omittendum, a dogmatibus fidei sive docentibus, quid credendum, quid non credendum (quae proprie ac primo appellari solent dogmata). Et quia nunc non sum sollicitus de fundamento pietatis, sed fidei, non faciendorum, sed credendorum, prorsus removenda sunt historica et moralia, quae nunquam merentur appellari fidei articuli.“ (L. c. § 53. 54.)

Quenstedtius: „Objectum, circa quod occupantur articuli fidei, sunt τα πίστα s. credenda qua talia. . . Licet enim fides generaliter spectata versetur circa omnia, quae in verbo Dei continentur, sive historica ea sint, site moralia, sive dogmatica; specialiter tamen versatur circa dogmata fidei s. credenda qua talia. Quod observandum, ne quis in Adami Tanneri Jesuitae absurditatem incidat, qui omne, quod creditur sive quod in Bibliis sacris occurrit, vim dogmatis obtinere et articulum fidei esse, in Colloquio Ratisbonensi sess. 11. ita asseruit, ut etiam ex incestu Judae et cane Tobiae caudam movente novos fidei articulos ridicule procuderet. Sic etiam historia de caudis vulpecularum Samsonis, de asina Bileami, de annis Methusalem, de aedificatione turris Babel etc. articulis fidei annumeranda esset.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. not. 6. f. 349.) Articuli Smalcaldici: ,,Pontificii allegant Augustinum et quosdam Patres, qui de purgatorio scripserint. . . At hoc in universum nihil nisi hominum et quidem unius atque alterius devotio fuit, non constituens articulum fidei, id quod solius Dei est. . . Regulam autem aliam habemus, ut videlicet verbum Dei condat articulos fidei et praeterea nemo, ne angelus quidem.“ (P. II. art. 2. p. 303.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Hollazius: "An article of faith is a part of the doctrine revealed in the…

Hollazius: "An article of faith is a part of the doctrine revealed in the written Word of God concerning God and divine things proposed to the sinner to be believed for the sake of being saved." (*Exam. etc.* Proleg. c. 2. q. 12. p. 43.) Quenstedtius: "The generic form of the articles of faith does not consist in conformity with the written revelation of God, but in the relation of the chapters of faith, distinct among themselves, both to each other and, especially, to the whole—namely, to the whole body of heavenly doctrine, whose parts or par-

are particular members. And although they cohere closely among themselves, like the joints in a finger, one is nevertheless placed outside the other.” (L. c. not. 7. f. 349.)

Hollazius: “For a true article of faith it is required: that it be revealed by the written Word of God, that it concern the salvation of man, that it be closely connected with the remaining dogmas of faith, and that it be non-evident. . . (It must be established that certain articles of faith are non-evident by reason of their material and formal object, while others are evident only by reason of their formal object.)” (Examen etc. Proleg. c. 2. q. 14. p. 44.)

The same: “An article of faith is taken either collectively or distributively. Collectively, it denotes an entire head of Christian doctrine; distributively, it designates any assertion or enunciation that constitutes a part of the doctrine. — Proof: Christian doctrine is distributed into heads or theological loci, and the heads are divided into certain theses. Both the heads of the doctrine of faith and the theses of the heads are called articles of faith; e.g., the theological locus concerning Christ is called an article of faith, and this proposition: ‘Christ, according to his flesh, sits at the right hand of God,’ is likewise named an article of faith.” (L. c. q. 13.)

N. Hunnius: “The things that contribute to a building are of three kinds: 1. some that provide the foundation and are not founded; 2. some that both provide the foundation and are founded; 3. some that are founded and do not provide the foundation. Of the first kind is the foundation and those things that essentially enter into it. Of the second are the intermediate walls, which rest upon the lower parts and support the higher ones. Of the third are the summit, the roof, and things pertaining thereto. Since, however, the third order provides the foundation in no way, the second only in part and in a certain respect, and the first absolutely, therefore neither the last nor the middle, but only the first holds the name of foundation, to which the others are ordered, whether this happens immediately or through the mediation of another.” (Διάσκεψις etc. § 13.)

Kromayerus: “Others divide the articles of faith into fundamental, circum-fundamental, and praeter-fundamental. By fundamental, they understand those that enter into the definition of saving faith and touch it more closely; by circum-fundamental, those that are more remotely absent or are elicited through consequences; by praeter-fundamental, they understand matters of indifference or matters of question.” (Scrutinium religionum, p. 447.)

Quenstedtius: “They distinguish the dogmas necessary for salvation into those that precede, constitute, and follow the foundation of faith, or into the antecedents (or presuppositions), the constituents, and the consequents of faith. Dn. D. Calovius approves this distinction in System. Theol. P. I. Gen. cap. 5. sect. 1. p. 776, but in such a way that the antecedents and consequents of faith are not denied to be necessary to be known, much less are they established as things that can be plainly denied or rejected while faith remains intact, at least because they do not enter into the constitution of faith, but precede or follow faith. The antecedents or presuppositions are, to them, those things which do not indeed produce justifying and saving faith itself, nor are they required for it by absolute necessity and immediately, yet they are necessary so that the dogmas that generate and constitute faith may be rightly believed and remain safe and sound, which, if these were not posited, or were ignored, or denied, could not happen. Therefore, they establish, aid, and preserve the foundation of faith, yet they do not primarily generate faith itself. . . Those things that proximately and immediately constitute faith, or the fundamental articles, which. . . intrinsically constitute and are caused by faith, are the heads of Christian doctrine concerning the φιλανθρωπία of God, concerning the merit and universal satisfaction of Christ, and its appropriation made in the individual. . . The consequents of faith are those which, namely, follow the established trust in such a way that, unless they are posited, the trust itself vanishes, such as the eternal duration of God, the executive justice of God, the effective sanctification of God, the communication of idioms and operations in the person of Christ, the kingly office of Christ, the existence of the church, the conversion of man through repentance and the justification of the converted (according to some), the peace and tranquility of conscience, the zeal of piety toward God and of charity toward the neighbor, the efficacy of the Word and sacraments, etc.”

Large Catechism: "In the beginning, our theologians have hitherto divided the faith into twelve articles, although, if all the particulars which Scripture delivers and which are to be referred to faith were comprehended one by one, there are many more articles; but neither can they be expressed with sufficient significance in so few words." (Book of Concord, p. 449.)

Scherzer: "The Scholastics say that the articles of faith have increased as to explicit knowledge; which is the mystery and secret of advancing scholastic theology." (System, th. p. 8.)

Kromayer: "We premise, first, that the articles necessary for salvation to be known are of all times, i.e., that they find a place in the Old and New Testaments, just as the Apostle says in Ephesians 4:5: 'One Lord, one faith' (namely, that which is believed, not that by which it is believed; the objective faith or the doctrine to be believed, not the subjective, which apprehends the merit of Christ and is distinguished from its subjects), 'one baptism, one God and Father of all.' And Acts 13:32: ἡμεῖς ὑμᾶς εὐαγγελιζόμεθα τὴν πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας ἐπαγγελίαν γενομένην, i.e., we announce to you the promise made to the fathers, now actually completed. They differ, to be sure, in ἐπαγγελία and εὐαγγελία, insofar as the latter is taken in the strictest sense, that the former is a proclamation concerning Christ to be exhibited, while the latter is a proclamation concerning Christ already exhibited.

Therefore, the object of both is Christ; the τέλος σκοπιώτατον of Scripture, that is, the end and center toward which all things in the sacred writings converge, and indeed to be apprehended through faith.

Thus the apostolic synod determined in Acts 15:11: 'We believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they [the fathers of the Old Testament] were,' who could not bear the yoke of the law, which was ἀβάστακτον, i.e., impossible to be carried.

Wherefore, when faith is called one and the articles of faith necessary for salvation are said to be of all times, this is to be understood as meaning that they obtained before and after Christ was exhibited, excluding, however, the state of integrity, in which, if man had persisted, he would have been justified and saved not through faith in the merit of Christ, but through obedience to the divine commandments. These things standing: that a dogma which was unknown even to one from that time was not precisely necessary for salvation." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. Prooem. p. 1 sq.) §

28. Articles of faith are called pure which are known solely from divine revelation: such as the article concerning the Most Holy Trinity, the article concerning the incarnation of the Son of God, and others. They are called mixed which consist not only of revelation but also of the light of nature: e.g., the article concerning the existence of God and concerning the divine attributes.

Quenstedt: "There are certain dogmas in the Scriptures which are simply πιστά and can in no way be known by reason, but surpass it by a great distance; there are also certain πιστά κατά τι, or credible in a certain respect, which, even though they are revealed in the Scriptures and necessary to be known, are nevertheless such that reason can also, through its own principles, arrive at some knowledge of them.

Hence arise pure and mixed articles: The former are sought from the Word of God alone and are only believed, such as the article concerning the Trinity, the incarnation, etc. The latter, even if they become known in some way from the light of nature, are nevertheless believed only insofar as they are established by divine revelation; thus, e.g., that God exists, that God has care for all things, that He is powerful, wise, one, good, etc., is both known through evident demonstration and believed on account of divine revelation. Yet all these things, which become known in a certain way by the light of nature, are not believed insofar as they are from the light of nature, but insofar as they are held from divine revelation." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. thes. 1. fol. 350.) ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

Hollazius: "The distinction of the articles of faith into pure and mixed must be understood correctly. For no article of faith, considered formally, insofar as it is an article of faith, is mixed; since all articles of faith depend upon divine revelation and, therefore, with respect to their formal object, are non-evident. However, they are distinguished into pure and mixed with respect to their material object. Namely, those divine matters which are set forth in the articles of faith that are called 'mixed' consist partly of reason and partly of supernatural revelation. They consist, I say, of the principles of reason—though less well, less safely, and less fully—but they are known far better, more certainly, and more fully for the salvation of man from the revealed Word. Add to this that certain circumstances concerning things knowable from both lights belong to mere faith and revelation. Let the creation of this universe, completed within the hexaemeron, be an example. Not without reason does the Apostle say: πίστει νοοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι θεοῦ. Heb. 11:3." (Exam. Proleg. c. 2. q. 17. p. 45.)

Quenstedtius: "The principle of being of the articles of faith is God alone; the principle of knowing is not the authority of the church, nor human reason, but divine revelation made in the Word. Where it must be observed that every article of faith has its own proper and native seat in Holy Scripture, from which it also ought to be judged; e.g., the article concerning creation has its seat in Gen. 1; the article concerning the divinity of the Son of God in the N.T. in John 1; concerning original sin in Rom. 5; concerning the Lord’s Supper in the words of institution in Matt. 26, Mark 14, Luke 22, 1 Cor. 10 and 11; concerning justification in Rom. 3, 4, 5; concerning election in Eph. 1, etc. From these seats, therefore, the articles of faith are rightly judged and explained, as they are the places in which they are treated *ex professo*. Because Papists and Calvinists neglect this, they fall into the greatest difficulties and most serious errors—e.g., the former, when they wish to explain the article of justification from James 2; the latter, when they take their judgment concerning the Lord’s Supper from John 6." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 1. f. 349.)

Latin:

Hollazius: „Articulus fidei est pars doctrinae verbo Dei scripto revelatae de Deo et rebus divinis peccatori salvando ad credendum propositis.“ (Exam. etc. Proleg. c. 2. q. 12. p. 43.) Quenstedtius: „Forma generica articulorum fidei non consistit in conformitate cum revelatione Dei scripta, sed in relatione distinctorum inter se fidei capitum cum ad se invicem, tum, et praecipue, ad totum, sci. ad totum corpus doctrinae coelestis, cujus partes sive par- '

ticularia membra sunt. Et licet arcte inter se cohaereant, ut articuli in digito, unus tamen extra alterum est positus.“ (L. c. not. 7. f. 349.)

Hollazius: ,, Ad verum articulum fidei requiritur: ut verbo Dei scripto sit revelatus, ut salutem hominis respiciat, ut cum reliquis fidei dogmatibus arcte sit connexus, ut sit inevidens. . . (Statuendum est, quosdam articulos fidei esse inevidentes ratione objecti materialis et formalis, quosdam esse evidentes tantum ratione objecti formalis.')“ (Examen etc. Proleg. c. 2. q. 14. p. 44.)

Idem: ,,Articulus fidei accipitur vel collective vel distributive. Collective notat integrum doctrinae Christianae caput; distributive designat quamlibet assertionem s. enuntiationem, quae partem doctrinae constituit. — Probatio: Doctrina christiana distribuitur in capita s. locos theologicos, capita in theses certas dividuntur. Tam capita doctrinae fidei, quam capitum theses appellantur articuli fidei, v. g. locus theologicus de Christo dicitur articulus fidei, et haec propositio: Christus qua carnem sedet ad dextram Dei, itidem nominatur articulus fidei.“ (L. c. q. 13.)

N. Hunnius: ,,Quae ad aedificium concurrunt, sunt triplicia: 1. quaedam fundant et non fundantur, 2. quaedam fundant et fundantur; 3. quaedam fundantur et non fundant. Primi generis est fundamentum et quae illud essentialiter ingrediuntur. Secundi parietes intermedii, qui inferioribus partibus innituntur et superiores portant. Tertii cacumen, tectum atque eo pertinentia. Siquidem vero tertius ordo nullo modo, secundus tantum ex parte et secundum quid, primus absolute fundat; ideo nec ultimus nec medius, sed unice primus fundamenti nomen tenet, ad quem ordinantur reliqui, sive id fiat immediate, sive alio mediante.“ (Διάσκε-ψις etc. § 13.)

Kromayerus: ,,Alii fidei articulos in fundamentales, circumfundamentales et praeterfundamentales dividunt. Per fundamentales eos, qui fidei salvificae definitionem ingrediuntur, eandemque propius attingentes; per circumfundamentales, qui remotius absunt aut per consequentias eliciuntur,· per praeterfundamentales res indifferentes aut res quaestionis intelligunt.“ (Scrutinium religionum, p. 447.)

Quenstedtius: „Distinguunt dogmata ad salutem necessaria in ea, quae fundamentum fidei praecedunt, constituunt, et sequuntur, sive in antecedentia (seu praesupposita), constituentia, et consequentia fidei. Approbat hanc distinctionem Dn. D. Calovius in System. Theol. P. I. Gen. cap. 5. sect. 1. p. 776., sed ita, ut antecedentia et consequentia fidei non negentur scitu necessaria esse, nedum talia statuantur, quae possint salva fide plane negari aut reprobari, saltim quia fidei constitutionem non ingrediuntur, sed antecedunt aut consequuntur fidem. Antecedentia seu praesupposita illis sunt, quae fidem justificam et salvificam ipsam quidem non efficiunt, nec absoluta necessitate et immediate ad eandem requiruntur, necessaria tamen sunt ad id, ut dogmata fidem gignentia et constituentia recte credi et sarta tecta manere queant, quod illis non positis, aut ignoratis, aut negatis, fieri non posset. Fundamentum igitur fldei stabiliunt, juvant, conservant, fidem ipsam tamen primario non generant. . . Fidem proxime et immediate constituentia, sive articuli fundamentales, qui. . . fidem intrinsece constituunt et causantur, sunt capita doctrinae christianae de Dei φιλαν- &ρωπία, de merito et satisfactione Christi universali, ejusque appropriatione in individuo facta. . . Consequentia fidei sunt, quae scil, ita fiduciam constitutam sequuntur, ut, nisi ponantur, ipsa iterum fiducia evanescat, utpote aeterna Dei duratio, justitia Dei executiva, sanctificatio Dei effectiva, idiomatum et operationum in persona Christi communicatio, officium Christi regium, ecclesiae existentia, hominis per poenitentiam conversio et conversorum justificatio (juxta quosdam), pax et tranquillitas conscientiae, studium pietatis erga Deum et caritatis erga proximum, verbi et sacramentorum efficacia etc.“

Catechismus major: „Principio theologi nostri fidem hactenus in duodecim articulos diviserunt, quamquam, si omnes particulae, quas tradit scriptura et ad fidem referendae sunt, sigillatim comprehenderentur, multo plures sunt articuli, sed neque tam paucis verbis satis significanter possunt exprimi.“ (Lib. Cone. p. 449.)

Scherzerus: „Scholastici ajunt, crevisse articulos fidei quoad cognitionem explicitam; quod est mysterium et arcanum provehendi theologiam scholasticam.“ (System, th. p. 8.)

Kromayerus: ,,Praemittimus, l. quod articuli ad salutem cognitu necessarii sint omnium temporum, i. e., quod in V. et N. T. locum inveniant, prout apostolus inquit ad Ephes. 4, 5.: ,Unus Dominus, una fides1 (scl. quae creditur, non qua creditur, objectiva sive doctrina credenda, non subjectiva, quae Christi meritum apprehendit et subjectis suis distinguitur), ,unum baptisma, unusDeus etPater omnium.' Et Act. 13, 32.: ημείς υμάς εναγγελιζόμε-άα την πρός τονς πατέρας επαγγελίαν γενομένην, i. e., nos vobis annunciamus actu completam promissionem patribus factam. Differunt nimirum επαγγελία et ευαγγελίαν, quatenus in significatu strictissimo sumitur, quod illa sit concio de Christo exhib,endo, haec sit concio de Christo exhibito.

Utriusque igitur objectum est Christus; scripturae τέλος σκοπφώτατον, id est, finis et centrum, ad quod in sacris omnia collineant, et quidem per fidem apprehendendus.

Ita synodus apostolica statuit Act. 15, 11.: ,Per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi credimus salvari, quemadmodum et illi, patres sel. V. T., jugum legis άβάστακτον, i. e. portatu impossibile, ferre non poterant.

Quare cum fides una dicitur et articuli fidei ad salutem necessarii omnium temporum, intelligendum hoc est, quod ante et post Christum exhibitum obtinuerint, excluso tamen integritatis statu, in quo si perstitisset homo, non per fidem in Christi meritum, sed per obedientiam mandatorum divinorum justificatus et salvatus fuisset. Stantibus his: quod dogma vel uni ex eo tempore fuit ignoratum, ad salutem praecis e non fuit necessarium.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. Prooem. p. 1. sq.) §

28. Articuli fidei puri dicuntur, qui unice ex revelatione divina cognoscuntur: qualis est articulus de SS. Trinitate, articulus de incarnatione filii Dei, et alii. Mixti dicuntur, qui non solum ex revelatione, verum etiam ex lumine naturae a constant: v. g. articulus de existentia Dei, deque attributis divinis.

Quenstedtius: ,,Dantur quaedam dogmata in Scripturis, quae sunt simpliciter πιστά et nullo modo per rationem cognosci possunt, sed illam longissime superant; sunt etiam quaedam πιστά κατά τι sive credibilia secundum quid, quae, etsi sint in Scripturis revelata et cognitu necessaria, ita tamen se habent, ut et ratio per sua principia possit aliqualiter in eorum cognitionem devenire.

Hinc oriuntur articuli puri et mixti: Illi ex solo Dei Verbo petuntur et tantum creduntur, ut articulus de Trinitate, incarnatione etc. Hi, etiamsi ex lumine naturae aliquo modo innotescant, solum tamen creduntur, quatenus e revelatione divina constant; sic v. g. Deum esse, Deum omnium rerum curam habere, esse potentem, sapientem, unum, bonum etc., et scitur per evidentem demonstrationem et creditur propter divinam revelationem. Haec tamen omnia, quae lumine naturae quodammodo innotescunt, non creduntnr, quatenus e naturae lumine, sed quatenus e divina revelatione habentur.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. thes. 1. fol. 350.) BE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Hollazjius: „Distinctio articulorum fidei in puros et mixtos dextre intelligenda est. Nam nullus articulus fidei formaliter consideratus, quatenus est articulus fidei, mixtus est; siquidem omnes articuli fidei pendentes a divina revelatione adeoque ratione objecti formalis inevidentes sunt. Distinguuntur autem in puros et mixtos ratione objecti materialis. Nempe res illae divinae, quae articulis fidei, quos mixtos vocant, exponuntur, partim ex ratione, partim ex supernaturali revelatione constant. Constant, inquam, ex principiis rationis minus bene minusque tuto et plene, e verbo autem revelato longe melius, certius et plenius innotescunt in salutem hominis. Adjice, quod quaedam circumstantiae circa res ex utroque lumine cognoscibiles merae fidei et revelationis, sint. Exemplo sit creatio hujus universi intra hexaemeron consummata. Haud abs re inquit apostolus: π/στ« νοονμεν, κατψτίσ·&αι , τους αιώνας ρήματι &εον. Hebr. 11, 3.“ (Exam. Proleg. c. 2. q. 17. p. 45.)

Quenstedtius: „Articulorum fidei principium essendi est solus Deus, principium cognoscendi non auctoritas ecclesiae, non humana ratio, sed divina revelatio in verbo facta. Ubi observandum, quemlibet articulum fidei in S. Scriptura habere propriam suam et nativam sedem, ex qua etiam debet judicari, v. g. articulus de creatione sedem habet Gen. 1., articulus de divinitate filii Dei in N.T. Joh. 1., de peccato originis Rom. 5., de Coena Domini in verbis institutionis Matth. 26., Marci 14.', Luc. 22., 1 Cor. 10. et 11., de justificatione Rom. 3., 4., 5., de electione Eph. 1. etc. Ex his ergo sedibus recte judicantur et explicantur articuli fidei, utpote in quibus ex professo tractantur. Quod cum negligant Papistae et Calvinistae, in maximas difficultates et gravissimos errores incidunt, v. g. illi, dum articulum de justificatione ex cap. 2. Jacobi explicatum volunt; hi, dum de coena Domini ex Joh. 6. cap. judicium sumunt.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 1. f. 349.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Brochmandus: "It is not a matter of controversy whether it is in the hand and…

Brochmandus: "It is not a matter of controversy whether it is in the hand and power of the church to establish new articles of faith. For this was not granted even to the apostles themselves, as Christ bears witness, who enjoined the disciples to teach only those things which they had received from Him, Matt. 28:19-20. And we read that the apostles obeyed this admonition, Acts 26:22, 1 Cor. 11:23, 2 Cor. 13:3, 2 Pet. 1:6." (System. Artic. 25. q. 5. Tom. II. f. 236.)

And concerning these it is rightly said that they are not only believed, but also known. However, they are called articles of faith, not insofar as they are known evidently from the principles of the light of nature, but insofar as they are believed, or insofar as they are received by the assent of faith on account of divine revelation. §

29. Fundamental articles of faith are those which import such a relationship to the foundation of faith and salvation that, while that foundation remains, they cannot be ignored or at least denied. The foundation of faith is spoken of in two ways: first, as that thing upon which the faith and salvation of men rests, and it is Christ, insofar as He is the cause of our salvation; second, as the doctrine by which that thing, upon which faith rests, is contained; and it is a complex of several propositions divinely revealed, which import a certain relationship to salvation. Authors call the former the real or substantial foundation, and the latter the dogmatic foundation.

Quenstedtius: "The form is the closest and necessary cohesion of these articles, both among themselves and with the foundation of faith... Hence that trite axiom: Faith is one and copulative, by which it is signified that all fundamental articles of faith are so closely concatenated that he who denies one, denies also the rest." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. thes. 2. fol. 351.)

Hollazius: "Certain fundamental articles of faith are read ῥητῶς, or in express words, in the Holy Scriptures; others are contained in Holy Scripture διανοητικώς and only according to the matter itself, which are perceived from it by manifest and immovable consequence. We read it expressly written that there are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one (1 John 5:7); that Christ is true man (1 Tim. 2:5), that the same is true God (1 John 5:21), the one mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2:5), the only-begotten Son of God (John 1:14); that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father (John 15:26); that all nations are to be baptized (Matt. 28:19).
