By valid consequence we infer that God, one in essence, is three in persons; that God from eternity begat the ὁμοούσιον Son; that Christ is one person consisting of two natures; that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son of God; that infants are to be baptized, etc." (Exam. Proleg. c. 2. q. 22. p. 52. sq.)

Luther: "For where he (the devil) brings it about that one yields to him in one article, he has won, and it is as much as if one had already lost them all and Christ; he can thereafter easily disrupt and take the others as well; for they are all wound and locked together like a golden chain, so that where one link is loosened, the whole chain is loosened and everything falls apart. And there is no article that he cannot overturn if he brings it about that reason interferes and wants to play the clever critic, and then knows how to twist and stretch Scripture nicely so that it rhymes with it; that then enters like a sweet poison. Therefore we also see now, because the devil has once gained room, that he is always introducing one heresy and swarm of sects after another, attacking this article today, another tomorrow, as he is already on the path now through his forerunners, by which he wants to challenge again Christ’s divinity, likewise the resurrection of the dead." (Sermon on the Christian Armor. 1532. IX, 450. sq.)

The same: "It is certain: whoever does not rightly believe one article, or does not want to (after he has been admonished and instructed), certainly believes none with earnestness and true faith. And whoever is so bold that he dares to deny God or call Him a liar in one word, and does so willfully against and beyond that which he has been admonished or instructed about once or twice, he also dares (and certainly does) deny God and call Him a liar in all His words. Therefore it is said: round and pure, believe everything and all, or believe nothing. The Holy Spirit does not allow Himself to be separated or divided, so that He should teach or allow one to believe one piece as true and another as false. Except where there are the weak, who are ready to be instructed and do not stubbornly contradict. Otherwise, where it should hold that it would have to be without harm for everyone if he might deny a vain article, because he held all the others to be right (although in principle such is impossible), then no heretic would ever be condemned, nor could there be any heretic on earth. For all heretics are of this kind, that they first begin with only one article, thereafter they must all follow, and all together be denied: just as a ring, if it gets a crack or a fissure, is no longer of any use at all, and where a bell cracks in one place, it no longer rings at all and is entirely useless." XX, 2216. sq.

The same: "In philosophy, a small error in the beginning is a very great one in the end. Thus, in theology, a small error overturns the entire doctrine. Therefore, doctrine and life must be distinguished as far as possible... For doctrine is like a mathematical point; it cannot, therefore, be divided—that is, it can bear neither subtraction nor addition... Doctrine must therefore be a certain single, perpetual, and round golden circle, in which there is no fissure. If even the smallest one occurs, the circle is no longer whole, etc... If they believed it to be the Word of God, they would not play with it so, but would treat it with the highest honor, and would give it credence without any dispute or doubt, and they would know that one Word of God is all things, and all things are one; likewise, they would know that one article is all, and all are one, and that if one is lost, all are gradually lost. For they cohere and are held together by a certain common bond... Therefore, if you deny God in one article, you have denied Him in all, because God is not divided into many articles, but is all things in each, and one in all articles." (Comment. on the Ep. of St. Paul to the Gal. Ed. Dr. J. C. Irmischer. Vol. II, p. 334 sqq. Cf. Walch, Vol. VIII, 2653–62.)

A foundation is otherwise viewed primarily in architecture and denotes that which is the first of those things that enter into the constitution of a building, such as its parts, and it is the reason and cause why that which it founds—namely, the building—is or can be. Whence, in this place, by analogy, that which is first in saving faith and the salvation of men is called the foundation of faith and salvation, and it is the reason and cause why saving faith and salvation itself of men is or can be. See the blessed Musaeus, Introd. chap. III, § 34, pp. 166, 167.

Quenstedtius: "A threefold foundation of faith is established by the same Dr. Hunnius and others: substantial, organic, and dogmatic... The organic is the Word of God, which, just as it is the seed from which Christians are regenerated (1 Pet. 1:23), so it is also called the foundation, insofar as it is the medium of generating faith and the principle of doctrine, which underlies and is laid beneath faith, and thus the foundation of faith; cf. Eph. 2:20, 21... Whence heresy is not just any error contrary to the Word of God, but one that shakes and overturns the foundation of faith itself, whether it be substantial—the proper object of faith—or organic—the Word of God, the principle and medium of faith—or dogmatic—that very doctrine from which faith is conceived and sustained." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I, c. 5, s. 1, thes. 2, fol. 350 sq.)

Thus, Paul says that the foundation upon which the church, or the assembly of the faithful and those to be saved, insofar as it is such, and thus the saving faith of men, rests, is Jesus Christ, and that no other foundation can be laid besides this (1 Cor. 3:11). However, just as Christ is the cause of our salvation through this, that by His merit, satisfying divine justice, He moves the benevolent will of God to remit our sins and confer eternal salvation; so God Himself is not excluded, but included in the foundation of faith and salvation, as the efficient cause, and His grace or φιλανθρωπία as the internal impulsive cause of the salvation conferred upon us. See the blessed Musaeus, l. c., p. 169.

Thus, in Eph. 2:20, Paul says that the faithful are built upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles, that is, the doctrine preached by them; indeed, with Jesus Christ Himself being the cornerstone, into whom the reason for the foundation ultimately returns. Musaeus, c. l., pp. 171, 172.

For it is not the individual articles, which are called fundamental, viewed separately; but all taken together, that constitute the dogmatic foundation of faith. However, with one or another fundamental article removed, faith itself and salvation fail. Mus. p. 172.

N. Hunnius: “A dogma in theology is a doctrine concerning the Christian faith and religion. Among these dogmata there is an order, such that without some, faith exists, but without others, it does not exist; therefore, I understand the dogmatic foundation to be that part of heavenly doctrine which, when proposed to man, alone generates justifying and saving faith in him, and without which being proposed, saving faith cannot be generated.” (Διάσκεψις. § 95.)

Hollazius: “You say: A single thing has only a single foundation. Therefore, there is not given a double foundation, namely, real and doctrinal. I reply: The substantial and dogmatic foundation of faith and salvation are not two adequately contradistinguished foundations, nor do they differ in reality, but according to our mode of conceiving them on account of their diverse connotations. For Christ is the foundation on the part of the thing; the doctrine concerning Christ is the foundation on the part of our cognition. However, the doctrine concerning Christ is nothing other than Christ known by the intellect and proposed to others for knowing through the written or preached word. Therefore, the dogmatic and substantial foundations do not differ, except as doctrine and the object of doctrine, which, when finally taken together, constitute a foundation that is in reality one, even though our mind conceives it as double.” (Exam. Proleg. c. 2. q. 19. p. 47. sq.)

Latin:

Brochmandus: „Non controvertitur, an in manu et potestate ecclesiae sit condere novos fidei articulos. Nam hoc ne ipsis quidem apostolis concessum fuit, teste Christo, qui discipulis injunxit, ut ea tantum, quae ab ipso acceperant, docerent, Matth. 28, 19. 20. Cui etiam monitioni paruisse apostolos, legimus Act. 26, 22. 1 Cor. 11, 23. 2 Cor. 13, 3. 2 Pet. 1, 6.“ (System. Artic. 25. q. 5. Tom. II. f. 236.)

Ac de his recte dicitur, quod non tantum credantur, verum etiam sciantur. Vocantur autem articuli fidei, non, quatenus evidenter ex principiis luminis naturae sciuntur, sed quatenus creduntur, seu quatenus propter revelationem divinam assensu fidei recipiuntur.§

29. Articuli fidei fundamentales sunt, qui talem habitudinem ad fundamentum fidei et salutis important, ut eo salvo ignorari aut saltem negari non possint. Fundamentum fidei a autem dicitur cum res illa, cui fides et salus hominum innititur, et est Christus, b quatenus est causa nostrae salutis; c tum doctrina, qua res illa, cui fides innititur, continetur; d estque complexus pluri um propositionum e divinitus revelatarum, quae habitudinem quandam ad salutem f important. Illud fundamentum reale sive substantiale, hoc fundamentum dogmaticum auctores appellant. Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. I. 4 PROLEGOM. CAP. I.

Quenstedtius: „Forma est arctissima et necessaria horum articulorum tum inter se, tum cum fundamento fidei cohaesio. . . Hinc tritum Illud axioma: Fides est una copulativa, quo significatur, omnes articulos fidei fundamentales tam arcte esse concatenatos, ut, qui unum neget, neget etiam reliquos.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. thes. 2. fol. 351.)

Hollazius: „Quidam articuli fidei fundamentales ρητως sive disertis verbis in sacris litteris leguntur; quidam διανοητικώς et secundum rem tantum in sacra Scriptura continentur, qui per manifestam et immotam consequentiam ex illa percipiuntur. Expresse scriptum legimus, tres esse, qui testificantur in caelo, Patrem, Yerbum et Spiritum Sanctum, et hos tres esse unum 1 Joh. 5, 7.; Christum verum esse hominem 1 Tim. 2, 5., eundem verum esse Deum 1 Joh. 5, 21., unum mediatorem Dei et hominum 1 Tim. 2, 5., Filium Dei unigenitum Joh. 1, 14.; Spiritum Sanctum a Patre procedere Joh. 15, 26.; omnes gentes esse baptizandas Matth. 28, 19. Per validam consequentiam inferimus, Deum, unum essentia, personis esse trinum, Deum ab aeterno genuisse Filium δμοονσιον, Christum esse unam personam e duabus constantem naturis, Spiritum Sanctum etiam a Filio Dei procedere, infantes esse baptizandos etc.“ (Exam. Proleg. c. 2. q. 22. p. 52. sq.)

Lutherus: „Denn wo er (der Teufel) es dahin bringet, dass man ihm in Einem Artikel einräumet, so hat er gewonnen, und ist ebensoviel, als hätte er sie alle und Christum schon verloren, kann darnach auch wohl andere zerrütten und nehmen; denn sie sind alle in einander gewunden und geschlossen, wie eine güldene Kette, dass, wo man ein Glied auflöset, so ist die ganze Kette aufgelöset und gehet alles von einander. Und ist kein Artikel, den er nicht könne umwerfen, wenn er es dazu bringet, dass die Vernunft drein fället und klügeln will, und weiss darnach die Schrift fein darauf zu drehen und zu dehnen, dass sichs mit ihr reime; das gehet denn ein, wie ein süsses Gift. Darum sehen wir auch jetzt, weil der Teufel einmal Raum gewonnen hat, dass er immer eine Ketzerei und Rottengeschmeiss über das andere einführet, haute diesen, morgen einen andern Artikel angreift, als er bereits jetzt auf der Bahn ist durch seine Vorlauft, dadurch er Christi Gottheit, item die Auferstehung der Todten will wieder anfechten.“ (Predigt v. d. Christi. Rüstung. 1532. IX, 450. sq.)

Idem: „Gewiss ists, wer Einen Artikel nicht recht glaubet oder nicht will (nachdem er vermahnet und unterrichtet ist), der gläubt gewisslich keinen mit Ernst und rechtem Glauben. Und wer so kühne ist, dass er darf Gott leugnen oder Lügen strafen in einem Wort und thut solches muthwilliglich wider und über das, so er eins oder zweimal vermahnet oder unterweiset ist, der darf auch (thuts auch gewisslich) Gott in allen seinen Worten leugnen und lügenstrafen. Darum heissts, rund und rein, ganz und alles gegläubt oder nichts gegläubt. Der Heilige Geist lässt sich nicht trennen noch theilen, dass er ein Stück sollte wahrhaftig, und das andere falsch lehren oder gläuben lassen. Ohn wo Schwache sind, die bereit sind, sich unterrichten zu lassen und nicht halsstarriglich zu widersprechen. Sonst, wo das sollte gelten, dass einem jeden ohne Schaden sein müsste, so er eitlen Artikel möchte leugnen, weil er die ändern alle für recht hielte (wiewohl im Grund solches unmöglich ist), so würde kein Ketzer nimmermehr verdammt, würde auch kein Ketzer sein können auf Erden. Denn alle Ketzer sind dieser Art, dass sie erstlich allein an Einem Artikel aniahen, darnach müssen sie alle hernach, und allesammt verleugnet sein: gleichwie der Ring, so er eine Bersten oder Ritz kriegt, taugt er ganz und gar nicht mehr, und wo die Glocke an einem Orte berstet, klingt sie auch nichts mehr und ist ganz untüchtig.“ XX, 2216. sq.

Idem: ,,Ιη philosophia modicus error in principio in fine est maximus. Sic in theologia modicus error totam doctrinam evertit. Quare longissime discernenda sunt doctrina et vita. . . Est enim doctrina instar mathematici puncti, non potest igitur dividi, hoc est, neque ademtionem neque additionem ferre potest. . . Debet igitur doctrina esse unus quidam perpetuus et rotundus aureus circulus, in quo nulla sit fissura. Ea accedente vel minima circulus non est amplius integer etc. . . Quod si crederent esse verbum Dei, non ita cum eo luderent, sed summo honore afficerent, et sine ulla disputatione et dubitatione fidem ei adhiberent, scirentque unum verbum Dei esse omnia, omnia esse unum, item, scirent unum articulum esse omnes, omnes esse unum, et urio amisso omnes paulatim amitti. Cohaerent enim et quodam communi vinculo continentur. . . Quare si Deum in uno articulo negas, in omnibus negasti, quia Deus non dividitur in multos articulos, sed est omnia in singulis, et unus in omnibus articulis.“ (Comment. in ep. S. Pauli ad Gal. Cur. Dr. J. C. Irmischer. Tom. II. p. 334. sqq. Cfr. Hai. Tom. VIII, 2653—62.)

Fundamentum alias potissimum in architectonicis spectatur et denotat illud, quod primum est ex illis, quae aedificii constitutionem, velut partes ejus, ingrediuntur, estque ratio et Causa, cur illud, quod fundat, nempe aedificium, sit aut esse possit. Unde h. l. χατ αναλογίαν fundamentum fidei et salutis dicitur id, quod in fide salutari hominumque salute primum est, estque ratio et causa, cur fides salvifica et salus ipsa hominum sit aut esse possit. Vid. b. Musaei Introd. cap. III. § 34. pag. 166. 167.

Quenstedtius: „Fundamentum fidei triplex ab eodem D. Hunnio aliisque constituitur: substantiale, organicum, dogmaticum... Organicum est verbum Dei, quod, uti semen est, ex quo regenerantur Christiani 1 Petr. 1, 23., sic fundamentum quoque dicitur, quatenus medium est generandae fidei ac principium doctrinae, quod substat et substernitur fidei, adeoque fundamentum fidei, conf. Ephes. 2, 20. 21... Unde haeresis non est error quivis verbo Dei contrarius, sed fundamentum ipsum fidei labefactans et evertens, sive substantiale, objectum fidei proprium, sive organicum, verbum Dei, principium et medium fidei, sive dogmaticum, ipsam illam doctrinam, ex qua fides concipitur et sustentatur.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. thes. 2. fol. 350. sq.)

Sic Paulus fundamentum, cui ecclesia seu coetus fidelium et salvandorum, quatenus talis, adeoque fides salvifica hominum innitatur, dicit esse Jesum Christum, neque aliud fundamentum, praeter hoc, posse poni, 1 Cor. 3, 11. Quemadmodum autem Christus per hoc est causa salutis nostrae, quod suo merito satisfaciens justitiae divinae benignam Dei voluntatem movet ad remittenda nobis peccata et conferendam salutem aeternam; ita non excluditur, sed includitur in fundamento fidei ac salutis Deus ipse, tanquam causa efficiens, ejusque gratia seu φιλανϋρωτζία, tanquam causa impulsiva interna conferendae nobis salutis. Vid. b. Mus. l. c. p. 169.

Sic Ephes. 2, 20. Paulus dicit, fideles superstructos esse super fundamentum prophetarum et apostolorum, id est, doctrinam ab illis praedicatam; imo angulari lapide existente ipso Jesu Christo, in quem ratio fundamenti ultimo redeat. Musaeus c. l. p. 171. 172.

Neque enim singuli articuli, qui fundamentales vocantur, seorsim spectati; sed omnes conjunetim sumti, fundamentum fidei dogmaticum constituunt. Sublato autem uno alterove articulo fundamentali, fides ipsa et salus deficit. Mus. p. 172.

N. Hunnius: „Dogma in theologia est doctrina circa fldem et religionem Christianam. Inter haec dogmata est ordo, ut sine quibusdam fides existat, sine aliquibus non existat; ideo fundamentum dogmaticum intelligo illam partem coelestis doctrinae, quae sola homini proposita justificam et salviflcam fldem in eo generat et qua non proposita fides salvifica generari non potest.“ (Διάσκεψις. § 95.)

Hollazius: „Dicis: Unius rei unum tantum est fundamentum. E. non datur duplex fundamentum, nempe reale et doctrinale. R. Fundamentum fidei salutisque substantiale et dogmaticum non sunt duo fundamenta adaequate contradistincta, neque differunt secundum rem, sed secundum nostrum concipiendi modum propter diversa connotata. Etenim Christus est fundamentum ex parte rei; doctrina de Christo est fundamentum ex parte nostrae cognitionis. Doctrina autem de Christo nihil est aliud quam Christus intellectu cognitus et aliis ad cognoscendum verbo scripto aut praedicato propositus. Non ergo differunt fundamentum dogmaticum et substantiale, nisi ut doctrina et doctrinae objectum, quae demum junctim sumta constituunt fundamentum reapse unum, quamvis mens nostra illud ut duplex concipiat.“ (Exam. Proleg. c. 2. q. 19. p. 47. sq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Indeed, all articles bear some relation to salvation, although not an entirely…

Indeed, all articles bear some relation to salvation, although not an entirely equal one, as will be evident from what follows. Meanwhile, it is not necessary for an article to be fundamental that its relation to salvation be delivered in the Scriptures under an express necessity of believing it for salvation. For although this sometimes happens, e.g., regarding the article concerning the one only true God and the Son of God sent in the flesh, John 17:3, it is nevertheless sufficient if their relation to salvation is delivered in the Scriptures implicitly and by consequence, when they, although not under an express necessity of believing, are nonetheless proposed in such a way that their necessary connection with the foundation of salvation, Jesus Christ, can be understood from a more thorough consideration of them themselves and concluded by a ready and manifest consequence. B. Musaeus de Syncret. Q. IV. § 15. p. 30. §

30. The fundamental articles of faith are distinguished into primary and secondary. The reason for the distinction is founded upon the unequal relation and necessity of their explicit cognition for generating and sustaining faith. § 31. Those are commonly called primary which, while faith and salvation are preserved, can not only not be denied, but also not be ignored. ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

Quenstedtius: "Nor is the opinion of those to be disapproved... who establish that those articles of faith are simply fundamental, the ignorance of which also damns, which constitute and explain some cause of our salvation, such as: by reason of the principal efficient cause, the article concerning God, One and Triune; by reason of the internal impulsive cause, the article concerning the love of God toward the whole human race fallen into sin; by reason of the meritorious cause, concerning the person, merit, and satisfaction of Christ; by reason of the material cause, the doctrine concerning man as a sinner (the knowledge of sin is necessary not as a cause of faith or a medium by which trust toward God can be excited or eternal salvation procured—for the recognition of a disease is not the cause of health—but as a certain condition or requirement in the subject necessary for being led to salvation); by reason of the instrumental cause on the part of God, concerning the Word of God; on the part of man, concerning faith or the fiduciary apprehension of the merit of Christ; by reason of the formal cause, concerning the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ; finally, by reason of the end, the article of eternal life. So that this may be the dogma of faith necessary for all to believe: God, One in essence and Triune in persons (efficient cause), out of immense love toward the fallen human race (internal impulsive cause), to every sinful man who acknowledges his sins (material cause), through and on account of Christ the Mediator and His merit (meritorious cause), announced in the Word (instrumental cause on the part of God) and apprehended by faith (instrumental cause on the part of man), remits sins and applies the righteousness of Christ (formal cause) and grants eternal life (final cause)." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 10. f. 354.)

Kromayerus: "Those dogmas intrinsically constitute faith which enter into its definition. Now, the definition of saving faith is: that it is a trust by which one believes that God, on account of the merit of His Son, wills to have mercy on him as a sinner, so that he may not be damned, but may attain eternal salvation. It is manifest that those things which do not enter into this definition are either presupposed or follow from it. There are, however, very few things that enter into the definition, idea, and concept of faith, and in them the nucleus and marrow of what must be believed for salvation is contained. The first ingredient is that it must be trust; the second, that God wills to have mercy on the sinner; the third, on account of Christ; the fourth, of the sinner individually; the fifth, that such a man may be saved eternally." (Theol. posit.-pol. P. I. Prooem. p. 4.)

Or, those whose explicit knowledge is necessary in order that saving faith may be generated and exist. B. Murinius on fundamental disagreement § 63. p. 41. 42., b. Musaeus Introd. p. 176. 177.

The reason *a priori* is that the knowledge of them is necessary for apprehending or retaining the real foundation of salvation. For the foundation does not generate faith or cause salvation unless it is known. Mus. l. c. p. 177. § 32.

Primary articles can again be distinguished into others, whose signified matter is of the intrinsic nature of the real foundation: e.g., the article concerning Christ the θεάνθρωπος, likewise the article concerning the merit and satisfaction of Christ for our sins; and others, whose signified matter, although it is not of the intrinsic nature of the real foundation, is nevertheless most closely connected with it, so that, unless it itself is explicitly

known, the rest entering into the constitution of that foundation would not be suitable for generating and sustaining saving faith: e.g., the article concerning God and God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the article concerning the gracious will of God, by which He wills all men to be saved, the article concerning sin, by which we are polluted, rendered hateful to God, and worthy of punishment, the article concerning justification or the remission of sins to be obtained through Christ, and concerning faith, through which the remission of sins is obtained, concerning the blessed life which they are to attain who have departed from this life with God propitious. See Musaeus, loc. cit., p. 173.

Indeed, just as the real or substantial foundation of salvation is Christ, insofar as He is the meritorious cause of obtaining the remission of sins and eternal salvation from God, according to note b. to § 29: so the article concerning Christ the θεάνθρωπος exhibits Him who is the meritorious cause; and the article concerning the satisfaction of Christ for sins exhibits that by which He merits the remission of sins. Therefore, both belong to the nature of the real foundation.

N. Hunnius: "He who professes and teaches that Christ is the foundation of faith does not on that account really posit or constitute Him, nor does he who is ignorant of or denies Him on that account really destroy or overturn Him. He constitutes the foundation notionally who believes and professes that it is truly and really posited." (Διάσκεψις, § 66 sq.)

For to this end, that it may be known that Christ has satisfied for us, it is necessary that it be known that He sustained and performed something which men ought to have sustained or performed, and therefore that He is man; it is also necessary to know that that which He performed or sustained was sufficient, or had value and a sufficient price, and therefore that Christ Himself is God. Whether this, that Christ is θεάνθρωπος, is known directly through preaching, or obliquely, while one judges of the cause from the effect, it is the same; it must certainly be known. See Hunnius, loc. cit., p. 183, § 294.

Dannhauerus: "In the faithful, God-breathed (away with the apocryphal dog of Tobias) [writings], the fundamental part, the preeminently principal, the root of spiritual life and as it were its balsam, is the Christosophic word, radical and final, the cause and source of life simply, absolutely necessary for the being of spiritual life, without which spiritual life cannot exist and eternal life cannot be obtained (just as the fundamental laws of any republic stand and fall with their master), the ignorance of which, not only that which is called κατά διάθεσιν, but also κατ’ ἀπόφασιν, condemns, 2 Thess. 1; and therefore this πιστόν of this kind is neither to be ignored nor denied while salvation is preserved." (Hodos. Phaen. II. p. 667.)

For just as there is a very close connection between the meritorious cause and the efficient cause, which, moved by that merit, bestows the effect; so, if anyone is ignorant that it is God who confers the remission of sins and salvation, he can neither acknowledge Christ as the meritorious cause of salvation. Mus. loc. cit., p. 173, 174. ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

For it is necessary to know the Father, so that He may not be unknown, who offers such ample grace to the human race. If the Father, then also the Son; for he who ignores the Father, ignores also the Son (and he who does not have the Son, does not have the Father either). Furthermore, by the same necessity that the recognition of the Father demands the knowledge of the Son, the same recognition of the Father and the Son who breathes forth [the Spirit] requires the knowledge of the Holy Spirit. B. Hunnius, l. c. § 272, 273, p. 172, 173, and § 427, p. 270. Cf. blessed Musaeus, Q. IV. de syncret. § 9, p. 26. It must be noted, however: it is one thing to consider the mystery of the Trinity formally and distinctly with personal characters, or when the numbering number (numerus numerans) is simply attended to and precisely three persons only, no more and no fewer, are established in the Trinity; and it is another thing to consider it materially or according to the numbered number (numerum numeratum), when the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are believed. See blessed Joh. Meisnerus, Iren. dur. sect. II. § 211 sqq. p. 191. Cf. blessed Huelsemann, Dial. apol. p.

56. Apologia A. C.: “Our adversaries approve the first article of our confession, in which we explain that we believe and teach that there is one divine essence, indivisible, etc., and yet there are three distinct persons of the same divine and coeternal essence, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit... And we constantly affirm that those who think otherwise are outside the church of Christ, are idolaters, and offer insult to God.” (Lib. Conc. Art. I. p. 77.) Gerhardus: “The mystery of the Trinity is necessary to be known and believed by all who are to be saved.” Exegesis: a) We exclude from those to be saved not only the denial of the Trinity, but also the ignorance of it. Certain things revealed in the Word are so constituted that they can be ignored without peril to salvation, although they cannot be denied without the danger of the same; but not only the denial, but also the ignorance of the Trinity is damnable. b) We do not require an equal degree of knowledge from all members of the church, since the light of spiritual knowledge and faith is brighter in some and dimmer in others. c) Nor do we require from those to be saved a perfect and full κατάληψιν (comprehension) and intuitive knowledge of this mystery, since we cannot be advanced to it in this life (Exod. 33:20; 1 Cor. 13:9), in which sense Cyprian, serm. I. de bapt. Christi, rightly pronounces that the Trinity is known to Himself alone. But we assert only this: that for the catholic faith necessary for all who are to be saved, not a confused and implicit, but a distinct and explicit knowledge and confession of the three persons of the Godhead is required. We demonstrate this 1) from the definition delivered in the Scriptures of God. He who does not acknowledge God as He has revealed Himself in His Word, wanders away from the true God; he who ignores or denies the definition of God delivered in the Scriptures, ignores or denies God Himself... 2) From the most intimate and indissoluble union of the persons of the Trinity. Of which persons one is not outside the other; one of them cannot be acknowledged, worshipped, or invoked unless the other is simultaneously acknowledged, worshipped, and invoked... 3) From the express assertion of the Savior, Matt. 11:27: No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal Him. 4) From the description of the Gentiles outside the church. Gentiles could know from the light of nature that there is a God and that He is one, good, just, and the avenger of crimes. But because they could not know the mystery of the Trinity, which is revealed in the Word and in the light of grace alone, through the light of nature, therefore Scripture denies them a saving knowledge of God and attributes to them mere αγνωσίαν (ignorance) with respect to saving knowledge... 5) From the condition of this mystery. If the mystery of the Trinity is ignored or denied, the entire οικονομία (economy) of salvation is ignored or denied. 6) From the testimony of the pious ancients. Athanasius in the creed: “This is the catholic faith, that we worship one God in Trinity and Trinity in unity. Unless one holds this faith whole and inviolate, he cannot be saved.” Gregory Nazianzen at the end of orat. II. de pace: “The Trinity will one day be known to all, to some by illumination, to others by punishment.”

Latin:

Aliquam sane habitudinem ad salutem omnes important, licet non prorsus aequalem, ut ex seqq. patebit. Interim nec necesse est ad articulum fundamentalem, ut habitudo ejus ad salutem sub expressa necessitate credendi ad salutem tradatur in scripturis. Quanquam enim hoc aliquando fiat, v. gr. quoad articulum de uno solo vero Deo deque Filio Dei misso in carnem, Joh. 17, 3.: sufficit tamen etiam, si in scripturis implicite et per consequentiam tradatur habitudo eorum ad salutem, quando illi, licet non sub expressa necessitate credendi, ita nihilominus proponuntur, ut nexus eorum necessarius cum fundamento salutis, Jesu Christo, ex ipsa illorum consideratione penitiore intelligi et per consequentiam pronam ac manifestam concludi possit. B. Musaeus de Syncret. Q. IV. § 15. p. 30.§

30. Articuli fidei fundamentales distinguuntur in primarios et secundarios. Ratio distinctionis fundata est in inaequali habitudine et necessitate cognitionis explicitae eorum ad generandam ac sustentandam fidem. § 31. Primarii vulgo dicuntur, qui a salva fide et salute non solum non negari, sed nec ignorari b possunt. DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Quenstedtius: „Nec improbanda est eorum. . . sententia, qui articulos fidei simpliciter fundamentales, quorum etiam ignoratio damnat, illos esse statuunt, qui causam aliquam nostrae salutis constituunt et explicant, ut sunt: ratione causae efficientis principalis articulus de Deo Uno et Trino; ratione causae impulsivae internae articulus de amore Dei erga totum genus humanum in peccatum prolapsum; ratione causae meritoriae de Christi persona, merito et satisfactione; ratione causae materialis doctrina de homine peccatore (cognitio peccati necessaria est non tamquam causa fidei aut medium, quo fiducia erga Deum excitari aut salus aeterna procurari queat — nec enim agnitio morbi est causa sanitatis —, sed tanquam conditio quaedam seu requisitum in subjecto ad salutem perducendo necessarium); ratione causae Instrumentalis a parte Dei de verbo Dei, a parte hominis de fide sive flduciali meriti Christi apprehensione; ratione causae formalis de remissione peccatorum et imputatione justitiae Christi; denique ratione finis articulus vitae aeternae. Ut ita hoc sit dogma fidei omnibus creditu necessarium: Deus Unus in essentia et Trinus in personis (causa efficiens) ex immenso erga genus humanum lapsum amore (causa impulsiva interna) omni homini peccatori peccata agnoscenti (causa materialis) per et propter Christum mediatorem ejusque meritum (causa meritoria) in verbo annunciatum (causa Instrumentalis aparte Dei) et fide (causa Instrumentalis a parte hominis) apprehensum peccata remittit et justitiam Christi applicat (causa formalis) et vitam aeternam donat (causa finalis).“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 10. f. 354.)

Kromayerus: „Ea dogmata fidem intrinsece constituunt, quae definitionem ejus ingrediuntur. Est autem definitio fidei salvificae: quod sit fiducia, qua quis credit, Deum propter Filii sui meritum sui tamquam peccatoris misereri velle, ne damnetur, sed salutem aeternam consequatur. Quae definitionem hanc non ingrediuntur, ea vel praesupponi vel consequi manifestum est. Sunt autem paucissima, quae fidei definitionem, ideam et conceptum ingrediuntur, et in iis nucleus ac medulla credendorum ad salutem continetur. Primum ingrediens est, quod debeat esse fiducia; alterum, quod Deus peccatoris misereri velit; tertium, propter Christum; quartum, peccatoris in individuo; quintum, ut ejusmodi homo aeternum salvetur.“ (Theol. posit.-pol. P. I. Prooem. p. 4.)

Seu, quorum cognitio explicita necessaria est ad id, ut fides salvifica generetur et sit. B. Murinius de dissensu fundam. § 63. p. 41. 42., b. Musaeus Introd. p. 176. 177.

Batio a priori est, quod ad salutis fundamentum reale apprehendendum aut retinendum cognitio illorum necessaria est. Fundamentum enim non generat fidem, aut causat salutem, nisi cognitum. Mus. l. c. p. 177.§ 32.

Primarii articuli rursus distingui possunt a in alios, quorum res significata est de intrinseca ratione fundamenti realis: e. g. b articulus de Christo $εαν§ρώπφ, c item articulus de Christi merito et satisfactione pro nostris peccatis; et alios, quorum res significata, licet non sit de intrinseca ratione fundamenti realis, tamen cum eo arctissime connexa est, ita ut, nisi ipsa explicite sit

cognita, caetera fundamenti illius constitutionem ingredientia ad generandam et sustentandam fidem salvificam idonea futura non sint: e. g. articulus de Deo d eoque Patre, Filio et Spiritu S., e articulus de gratiosa Dei voluntate, qua vult f omnes homines salvos fieri, articulus de g peccato, quo polluamur, Deo exosi reddamur ac poena digni, articulus de justificatione seu remissione peccatorum per Christum impetranda, h deque fide, per quam impetretur remissio peccatorum, i de vita beata, k quam consecuturi sint, qui Deo propitio ex hac vita discesserunt. Vid. Musaeus 1. c. p. 173.

Nempe sicut fundamentum salutis reale sive substantiale est Christus, quatenus est causa meritoria consequendae a Deo remissionis peccatorum et salutis aeternae, juxta not. b. ad § 29.: ita articulus de Christo $εαν$ρώπω exhibet eum, qui est causa meritoria; et articulus de satisfactione Christi pro peccatis exhibet id, quo is meretur remissionem peccatorum. Utrumque ergo est de ratione fundamenti realis.

N. Hunnius: ,,Qui profitetur ac docet, Christum esse fidei fundamentum, non propterea ipsum realiter ponit aut constituit, vel qui ignorat aut abnegat, non propterea ipsum realiter destruit aut evertit. Notionaliter fundamentum constituit, qui credit, ac profitetur, illud vere et realiter positum esse.“ (Αιάσκεψις, § 66. sq.)

Ad hoc enim, ut cognoscatur, Christum satisfecisse pro nobis, necessarium est, ut sciatur, eum sustinuisse ac praestitisse aliquid, quod homines sustinere aut praestare debuissent, adeoque esse hominem; necessarium quoque est scire, illud, quod praestitit aut sustinuit, fuisse satis, aut habuisse valorem ac pretium sufficiens, adeoque Christum ipsum esse Deum. Sive autem hoc, Christum esse $εάν$ρωπον, cognoscatur directe per praedicationem, sive oblique, dum, ex effectu de causa judicatur, perinde est; cognosci certe debet. Vid. Hunnius l. c. p. 183. § 294.

Dannhauerus: ,,Έν τοις πιστοίς ΰεοπνενστηις (facessat canis Tobiae apocryphus) pars fundamentalis, exochice principalis, vitae spiritualis radix et quasi balsamum est verbum christosophicum, radicale et finale, causa ac fons vitae simpliciter, ad esse vitae spiritualis absolutissime necessarium, quo sine vita spiritualis esse ac aeterna obtineri nequit (nimirum ut leges fundamentales alicujus reipublicae cum domino stantque caduntque suo), cujus ignorantia, non duntaxat ea, quae dicitur κατά όιάΰεσιν, sed et κατ’ άπόφασιν, damnat, 2 Thess. 1.; adeoque hoc hujusmodi πιστόν nec est ignorabile nec negabile salva salute.“ (Hodos. Phaen. II. p. 667.)

Nam sicut inter causam meritoriam et inter causam efficientem, quae merito illius mota, effectum largitur, arctissimus nexus est; ita, si quis ignoret, esse Deum, qui conferat remissionem peccatorum et salutem, is neque Christum pro causa salutis meritoria agnoscere potest. Mus. l. c. p. 173. 174. DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Nosse enim oportet Patrem, ideo ut non sit ignotus, qui gratiam adeo amplam humano generi offert. Si Patrem, ergo et Filium; nam qui ignorat Patrem, ignorat quoque Filium (et qui non habet Filium, is nec Patrem habet). Porro qua necessitate Patris agnitio poscit notitiam Filii, eadem agnitio spirantis Patris et Filii requirit notitiam Spiritus S. B. Hunnius l. c. § 272. 273. p. 172. 173. et § 427. p. 270. Conf. b. Mus. Q. IV. de syncret. § 9. p. 26. Notandum autem: aliud esse, mysterium trinitatis formaliter et distincte cum characteribus personalibus consideratum, seu quando simpliciter' numerus ternarius numerans attenditur et praecise tres tantum personae, nonplures, nec pauciores in Trinitate statuuntur: et aliud, materialiter seu secundum numerum numeratum, cum creditur Pater, Filius et Spiritus S. Vid. b. Joh. Meisnerus Iren. dur. sect. II. § 211. sqq. p. 191. Conf. b. Huelsetn. Dial. apol. p. 56.Apologia A. C.: „Primum articulum confessionis nostrae probant nostri adversarii, in quo exponimus, nos credere et docere, quod sit una essentia divina, individua etc., et tamen tres sint distinctae persönae ejusdem essentiae divinae et coaeternae, Pater, Filius et Spiritus Sanctus. . . Et constanter affirmamus, aliter sentientes extrg ecclesiam Christi et idololatras esse et Deum contumelia afficere.“ (Lib. Conc. Art. I. p, 77.)

Gerhardus: „Mysterium Trinitatis salvandis omnibus scitu ac creditu necessarium est. "Ήκΰεσις: a) Excludimus ab hominibus salvandis non solum Trinitatis negationem, sed etiam ignorationem. Quaedam in verbo revelata ita comparata sunt, ut citra salutis discrimen possint ignorari, quamvis sine ejusdem periculo non possint negari; sed Trinitatis non solum negatio, verum1» etiam ignoratio est damnabilis, b) Non requirimus ab omnibus ecclesiae membris aequalem cognitionis gradum, Cum lux notitiae spiritualis ac fidei in quibusdam sit illustrior, in quibusdam vero obscurior, c) Nec perfectam et plenam hujus mysterii κατάληψιν ac intuitivam notitiam a salvandis requirimus, cum ad eam in hac vita provehi non possumus Exod. 33,20.; 1 Cor. 13, 9., quo sensu Cyprianus serm. I. de bapt. Christi recte pronunciat, quod sibi soli nota sit Trinitas. Sed hoc duntaxat asserimus, quod ad fidem catholicam omnibus salvandis necessariam non confusa et implicita, sed distincta et explicita trium divinitatis personarum cognitio et confessio requiratur. Demonstramus hoc 1) ex tradita in Scripturis Dei definitione. Qui non agnoscit Deum, prout in verbo suo se revelavit, is a vero Deo aberrat; qui definitionem Dei in Scripturis traditam ignorat vel negat, is Deum ipsum ignorat vel negat. . . 2) Ex arctissima et indissolubili personarum Trinitatis unione. Quarum personarum una non est extra aliam, earum una non potest agnosci, coli, invocari, nisi simul agnoscatur, colatur et invocetur etiam altera. . . . 3) Ex diserta Salvatoris asseveratione Matth. 11, 27.: Nemo novit Filium, nisi Pater, nec Patrem quis novit, nisi Filius et cui voluerit Filius revelare. . . 4) Ex gentilium extra ecclesiam descriptione. Gentiles ex naturae lumine cognoscere potuerunt, esse Deum eundemque esse unum, bonum, justum, scelerum vifidicem. Sed quia Trinitatis mysterium in verbo et in solo gratiae lumine patefactum per naturae lumen cognoscere non potuerunt, ideo salutarem Dei agnitionem Scriptura eis derogat ac meram αγνωσίαν respectu ad salvifleam notitiam habito illis tribuit. . . 5) Ex mysterii hujus conditione. Ignorato vel negato Trinitatis mysterio tota salutis οικονομία ignoratur vel negatur. . . 6) Ex piorum veterum testificatione. Athanasius in symb.: ,Fides catholica haec est, ut unum Deum in Trinitate et Trinitatem in unitate veneremur. Hanc fidem nisi quis integram inviolatamque tenuerit, salvus esse non poterit.' Gregorius Nazianzenus sub fine orat. II. de pace: τριάς ττασί ποτέ γνωΰησομένη, τοις μεν τ~ι ελλάμψει, τοϊς δέ κολάσει.“


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Meisnerus: "Number is either numbering or numbered

Meisnerus: "Number is either numbering or numbered. When the question is asked concerning the number of the elect, this can be understood either of the number itself, which they call the numbering [number], namely, how great it is or how many thousands of men are elected; or of the numbered number, or the men numbered, namely, who in particular are elected or which persons they are. The Scholastics call the former the formal number, the latter the material number. By the former it is asked: how many are elected; by the latter, however: who are the elect.

This distinction can be illustrated by a certain example. As, if someone knows that a certain prince supports two hundred courtiers, but is ignorant of who they are: to him the number of courtiers is both certain and uncertain. Certain formally, because he knows how many there are; uncertain materially, because he does not know who they are.

Whence it is clear that the distinction between formal and material number is by no means to be rejected." (Anthropol. d. 18. q. l. n. 1.)

Indeed, that benevolent and gratuitous will of God is the προηγουμένη, or the internal impulsive cause of the remission of sins being obtained for us, with which, therefore, the merit of Christ is most closely connected as the external impulsive cause, which would not even have a place if it were without the former. For if God had not loved men, so as to give His only-begotten Son for their sake, there would be no reason why God should accept the merit of Christ, as something foreign, from us as our own: for this whole matter depends upon the benevolent will of God toward us miserable men, writes the blessed Musaeus, Tract. de Syncret. Q. IV. § 9. p. 26. Moreover, this dogma concerning the universality of divine grace (just as the other concerning the universality of the death of Christ), taken literally and universally, just as it ought by all means to be taken, is simply so necessary for all to believe that no one, by the ordinary and customary way of the Word of God (whatever may be the case regarding the simpler of the faithful, and the special mode of gracious operation by which the Holy Spirit works faith in them), can be certain of himself individually that God wills him to be saved (that Christ died for him), except through those parts of doctrine actually known and believed, as the praised Musaeus expressly taught, l. c. p. 66. § 7. With these, those things which the blessed J. Meisnerus writes in Iren. Dur. S. II. § 228. p. 200 and 201, clearly agree, where, discussing those universal propositions without which, he says, if one were to be without them, no one can certainly know and determine that the benefits obtained by the death of Christ pertain to him. He adds, however, these words: "If, however, I were to concede at all that some man, e.g., Adam and Eve, conceived faith, or could still conceive it, who perhaps never heard anything about the universal benevolence of God or the universal merit of Christ, or because of weakness of intellect, defect of judgment, or for some other reason could not penetrate that far; I nevertheless deny that this can happen if the intellect is imbued with the contrary error of particularity." For the satisfaction of Christ for sins certainly imports a certain relation to sins. See the blessed Musaeus, l. c. p. 27. And unless one knows that men sin, and each one understands in particular that he has sinned, no faith is to be hoped for; these are the words of the blessed Hunnius, l. c. § 340. p. 206. cf. § 454. p. 291. For no one will have thought that he has need of the satisfaction of the Mediator before God who has not thought that he has offended God. For if there were no justification, the merit of Christ would profit us (sinners) nothing. Mus. l. c. And Christ the Mediator stands in relation to the remission of our sins as a meritorious cause to an effect, by meriting that which is to be acquired or has been acquired. However, there is a perpetual connection here between the meritorious cause and the effect, so that if the effect, of which the merit is the cause, is not... ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

be granted: there would be no future meritorious cause, or certainly its endeavor, labor, action, or passion, for meriting the effect, would be a cause undertaken in vain and to no effect. Mus. Introd. p. 173.

Luther: "For in this (article of justification) everything hangs and stands, and it draws all the others along with it, and everything is done for the sake of this one; so that whoever errs in the others certainly does not have this one rightly either, and even if he holds to the others but does not have this one, it is all in vain.

Conversely, this article also has the grace, where one remains with diligence and earnestness, that it does not let one fall into heresy nor run against Christ or His Christendom. For it certainly brings the Holy Spirit with it, who thereby illuminates the heart and keeps it in a right, certain understanding, so that it can give a pure and dry distinction and judge of all other articles of faith and powerfully maintain and defend them.

As one can also well see in the ancient Fathers: where they remained with such articles and founded their doctrine upon them or derived it from them, they remained fine and pure in all points; but where they departed from them and disputed outside of this, they also went astray and stumbled mightily; as has also happened at times to the oldest, Tertullian and Cyprian.

And what is still lacking, not only to the Papists, but to all our sectarians who swarm against Baptism and other articles, but that they have already fallen from this one, have not concerned themselves with it, and have set up other things instead, and thereby lost their understanding, so that they can teach nothing right about this and cannot certainly maintain any article? As one can well see in their books; thereafter they fall from one error into another, until they finally lead themselves and other people into ruin.

For where this knowledge of Christ is gone, there the sun has lost its shine and it is vain darkness, so that one understands nothing more rightly and can defend oneself against no error nor false doctrine of the devil.

And even if one retains the words about faith and Christ (as they remained in the Papacy), yet there is no foundation for any article in the heart, and what remains there is vain foam and uncertain *persuasiones* or conceits, or a painted, colored faith.

As they themselves call their faith *fidem acquisitam et informem*, that is, a loose, rotten, empty thought that does nothing and is good for nothing, neither holds nor fights when it comes to the encounter where it should hold and prove itself.

And indeed, that their boasting of faith and Christ is entirely false and lied, they prove themselves by the deed, that they will not tolerate this article of the knowledge of Christ and right faith, but rage against it with excommunications and murders.

Conversely, where this sun shines and glows in the heart, there is a right, certain understanding of all things, so that one can stand firm and hold to all articles: as, that Christ is true man, born of the Virgin Mary, and also true, almighty God, born of the Father in eternity, Lord over angels and all creatures.

Likewise, he thus believes and teaches rightly of the Holy Spirit, of Baptism, Sacrament, good works, resurrection of the dead, goes thus simply in faith, does not dispute and speculate over God's Word, and stirs up no strife nor doubt.

And where someone comes who attacks one or more of such articles, a Christian can defend himself and beat them back; for he has the right Master (the Holy Spirit), who alone reveals this article from heaven, and is given to all those who hear and accept this Word or sermon of Christ.

Therefore, such a one will not let himself be led into heresy and error; and even if he sometimes fails and stumbles, yet (as long as he does not fall from this) he soon comes back onto the path. For this light the

[He] consumes and drives away the clouds and darkness, and shows him [the way] again and sets him upright. But if he loses this light, then there is no helping him. For where this knowledge is gone, it takes everything with it, and you may thereafter hold and confess all the articles (as the Papists do), but there is no earnestness nor right understanding; rather, it is like groping in the dark, or a blind man hearing talk of colors that he has never seen.” (Exposition of the 14th, 15th, and 16th Chapters of St. John, 1538. VIII, 504—506.)

The same: “For if the article of justification is lost, the entire Christian doctrine is lost at the same time. And as many as there are in the world who do not hold it are either Jews, or Turks, or Papists, or heretics. . . For from it and in it alone does the church come into being and consist.” (Comm. on St. Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians. Ed. Dr. J. C. Irmischer. Vol. I. p. 20. sq. Cf. Hall. VIII, 1552. sq.) The same: “This locus is the head and the cornerstone, which alone begets, nourishes, builds up, preserves, and defends the church of God; and without it, the church of God cannot subsist for one hour.” (Preface of D. M. Luther to the exposition of J. Brentius on the Prophet Amos. See J. Brent. Opp. Vol. IV. p. 1087. Cf. Luther’s Opp. Hall. XIV, 191.)

i) For if there were no faith, the merit of Christ would profit us nothing. Mus. Tr. de syncr. l. c. p. 27. And just as it is necessary to know that Christ by His merit has acquired for all the grace of the remission of sins; so it is necessary to know that the merit of Christ actually profits those who believe for the obtaining of the remission of sins. k) What we said in note h regarding the article of justification pertains here in its own way. For eternal life also relates to Christ and His merit as an effect to a cause, just as justification confers the right to eternal life or the inheritance of it upon men. And if anyone is ignorant that a blessed life is given, which those who depart from this life with God propitious are eventually to attain; he can neither acknowledge Christ as the meritorious cause of our salvation, nor have confidence fixed in Him for obtaining eternal life from God. Mus. in Introd. p. 173.

174. N. Hunnius: “He overturns the foundation who holds the fundamental dogmas, yet denies some doctrine necessarily presupposed by the fundamentals. Examples are Hymenaeus, Alexander, and Philetus, who suffered shipwreck concerning the faith and subverted the faith of some, 1 Tim. 1:19, 20; 2 Tim. 2:17, 18; however much they acknowledged the saving grace of God and the merit of Christ, and professed that men are saved by faith, they nevertheless made shipwreck of the faith by denying the resurrection of the dead.” (Διάσκεψις, § 356.) § 33. Secondary fundamental articles are accustomed to be described as those parts of Christian doctrine which, although they may be ignored without endangering the foundation of salvation, nevertheless cannot be denied without endangering it. Such are the articles concerning the characteristic properties of the divine persons, concerning the personal union viewed distinctly, and the communication of attributes in Christ, concerning original sin, concerning the decree of election—

Latin:

Meisnerus: ,,Numerus est vel numerans vel numeratus. Cum de electorum numero quaeritur, intelligi hoc potest vel de numero ipso, quem numerantem vocant, quantum nimirum sit sive quot hominum milia sint electa; vel de numero numerato seu hominibus numeratis, quinam in specie electi sint vel quae personae. Scholastici numerüm illum formalem, hunc materialem appellitant. Illo quaeritur: quot sint electi; hoc autem: qui sint electi.

Distinctio haec per exemplum quoddam illustrari potest. Ut, si quis scit, principem quendam ducentos ministros aulicos alere, ignorat autem, quinam illi sint: huic numerus aulicorum et certus est et incertus. Certus formaliter, quia novit, quot sint; .incertus materialiter, quia ignorat, qui sint.

Unde patet, quod discrimen inter numerum formalem et materialem minime sit rejiciendum.“ (Anthropol. d. 18. q. l. n. 1.)

Nempe voluntas illa Dei benevola et gratuita est cama προηγουμίνη, sive impidsiva interna impetrandae nobis remissionis peccatorum, cum qua proinde arctissime connectitur meritum Christi, tanquam causa impulsiva externa, quae ne locum quidem haberet, si absque illa esset. Si enim Deus non dilexerit homines, ut propter eos dederit filium suum unigenitum, nulla ratio erit, cur Deus Christi meritum, tanquam alienum, acceptet a nobis tanquam nostrum: hoc enim totum dependet a benevola Dei erga nos miseros homines voluntate, scribit b. Musaeus Tract. de Syncret. Q. IV. § 9. p. 26 Dogma autem hoc de universalitate gratiae divinae (aeque ut alterum de universalitate mortis Christi) ad literam universaliter acceptum, sicut omnino accipi debet, esse simpliciter omnibus ita creditu necessarium, ut nemo per verbum Dei ordinario et consuebo modo (quicquid sit de simplicioribus fidelium, et speciali modo gratiosae operationis, quo Spiritus S. fidem in illis operatur) de se in indimduo certus esse possit, Deum velle se fieri salvum (Christum esse pro se mortuum) nisi per illas doctrinae partes actu cognitas et creditas, expresse docuit laudatus Musaeus l. c. p. 66. § 7 Cum quibus plane consentiunt, quae scribit b. J. Meisnerüs Iren. Dur. S. II. § 228. p. 200. et 201., ubi de propositionibus illis universalibus disserens, absque quibus, ait, si fuerit, nemo certo scire atque statuere potest, beneficia Christi morte parta ad se pertinere. Addit autem et haec verba: Si tamen omnino concesserim, aliquem hominem, v. g. Adamum et Evam, fidem concepisse, aut adhuc concipere posse, qui forte de universali Dei benevolentia, universali Christi merito nunquam quicquam audiverunt, aut ob imbecillitatem intellectus, defectum judicii, vel aliam ob causam eousque penetrare non potuerunt; nego tamen id fieri posse, si intellectus contrario errore particularitatis imbutus sit. Christi satisfactio enim pro peccatis utique relationem quandam importat ad peccata. Vid. b. Mus. 1. c. p. 27 Et nisi quis sciat homines peccare, et quisque in singulari intelligat, se peccasse, nulla est fides speranda, verba sunt b. Hunnii l. c. § 340. p. 206. conf. § 454. p. 291 Nemo enim satisfactione mediatoris apud Deum se opus habere putaverit, qui se offendisse Deum non putaverit. Si enim justificatio nulla esset, Christi meritum nobis (peccatoribus) nihil esset profuturum. Mus. 1. c. Et habet se Christus mediator ad remissionem peccatorum nostrorum, ut causa merjtoria ad effectum, promerendo acquirendum vel acquisitum. Inter causam meritoriam autem et effectum hic perpetuus nexus est, ut si effectus, cujus causa meritum est, non DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

detur: causa meritoria nulla futura, vel certe ejus conatus, labor, actio aut passio, promerendi effectus Causa suscepta, vana et irrita futura sit. Mus. Introd. p. 173.

Lutherus: „Denn in diesem (Artikel von der Rechtfertigung) hanget und stehet es alles und zeucht die ändern alle mit sich und ist Alles um diesen zu thun; dass, wer in den ändern irret, hat gewisslich auch diesen nicht recht, und ob er gleich die ändern hält und diesen nicht hat, ist es doch alles vergeblich.

Wiederum hat auch dieser Artikel die Gnade, wo man mit Fleiss und Ernst dabei bleibet, dass er nicht lässt in Ketzerei fallen noch wider Christum oder seine Christenheit laufen. Denn er bringet gewisslich den Heiligen Geist mit sich, welcher dadurch das Herz erleuchtet und hält in rechtem, gewissen Verstande, dass er kann rein und dürre Unterscheid geben und richten von allen ändern Artikeln des Glaubens und dieselben gewaltiglich erhalten und vertheidigen.

Wie man auch wohl siehet bei den alten Vätern: wo sie bei solchen Artikeln blieben und ihre Lehre darauf gegründet oder daraus geführet, sind sie in allen Stücken fein rein blieben; wo sie aber davon gegangen und ausser diesem disputiret, sind sie auch irre gangen und weidlich gestrauchelt; wie auch den ältesten, Tertulliano und Cypriano, unterweilen geschehen ist.

Und was mangelt noch; nicht allein den Papisten, sondern unsern Rottengeistern allen, so wider die Taufe und andere Artikel schwärmen, denn dass sie schon von diesem gefallen, sich nicht dafür bekümmert und dafür andere Dinge aufgeworfen und damit den Verstand verloren, dass sie hiervon nichts rechts lehren und keinen Artikel gewiss erhalten können? wie man in ihren Büchern wohl sehen kann; darnach von einem Irrthum in den ändern fallen, bis sie zuletzt sich und andere Leute ins Verderben führen.

Denn wo dies Erkenntniss Christi hinweg ist, da hat die Sonne ihren Schein verloren und ist eitel Finsterniss, dass man nichts mehr recht verstehet und kann sich keines Irrthums noch falscher Lehre des Teufels erwehren.

Und ob man wohl die Worte vom Glauben und Christo behält (wie sie im Pabstthum blieben sind), so ist doch kein Grund einiges Artikels im Herzen, und was mehr da bleibet, das ist eitel Schaum und ungewisse persuasiones oder Dünkel, oder ein gemalter, gefärbter Glaube.

Wie sie selbst ihren Glauben nennen fldem acquisitam et informem, das ist, ein loser, fauler, lediger Gedanke, der nichts thut noch taugt, weder hält noch kämpft, wenn es zum Treffen gehet, dass er halten und sich beweisen soll.

Und zwar, dass ihr Rühmen vom Glauben und Christo ganz falsch und erlogen ist, beweisen sie selbst mit der That, dass sie diesen Artikel vom Erkenntniss Christi und rechtem Glauben nicht leiden wollen, sondern dawider toben mit Bannen und Morden.

Wiederum, wo diese Sonne scheinet und leuchtet im Herzen, da ist ein rechter, gewisser Verstand von allen Sachen, dass man kann vest stehen und halten ob allen Artikeln: als, dass Christus wahrhaftiger Mensch ist, geboren von der Jungfrauen Maria, und auch wahrhaftiger, allmächtiger Gott, vom Vater in Ewigkeit geboren, Herr über Engel und alle Creaturen.

Item, also gläubet und lehret er recht von dem Heiligen Geist, von der Taufe, Sacrament, guten Werken, Auferstehung der Todten, gehet also einfältiglich im Glauben, disputiret und klügelt nicht über Gottes Wort und richtet kein Gezänk noch Zweifel an.

Und wo jemand kömmt, der solcher Artikel einen oder mehr anficht, so kann sich ein Christ wehren und dieselben Zurückschlagen; denn er hat den rechten Meister (den Heiligen Geist), welcher allein diesen Artikel vom Himmel offenbaret, und allen denen gegeben wird, so dies Wort oder Predigt von Christo hören und annehmen.

Darum wird sich ein solcher nicht lassen verführen in Ketzerei und Irrthum; und ob er schon etwa fehlet und strauchelt, doch (so er nur hiervon nicht fället) kommt er bald wieder auf die Bahn. Denn dies Licht die

Wolken und Finsterniss verzehret und vertreibet und ihn wieder weiset und aufrichtet. Verleuret er aber dies Licht, so ist ihm nicht zu helfen. Denn wo diese Erkenntniss weg ist, so nimmt sie es alles mit ihr, und magst darnach alle Artikel führen und bekennen (wie denn die Papisten thun), aber es ist kein Ernst noch rechter Verstand; sondern wie man im Finstern tappet und ein Blinder von der Farbe höret reden, die er nie gesehen hat.“ (Auslegung des 14., 15. und 16. Cap. St. Joh. 1538. VIII, 504—506.)

Idem: „Siquidem amisso articulo justificationis amissa est simul tota doctrina Christiana. Et quotquot sunt in mundo, qui eam non tenent, sunt vel Judaei, vel Tureae, vel Papistae, vel haeretici. . . Ex illa enim et in illa sola doctrina fit et consistit ecclesia.“ (Comm. in ep. S. Pauli ad Gal. Cur. Dr. J. C. Irmischer. Tom.I. p. 20. sq. Cfr. Hai. VIII, 1552. sq.) Idem: „Hic locus caput et angularis lapis est, qui solus ecclesiam Dei gignit, nutrit, aedificat, servat, defendit; ac sine eo ecclesia Dei non potest una hora subsistere.“ (Praef. D. M. Lutheri ad exposit. J. Brentii in Proph. Amos. Vid. J. Brent. Opp. Tom. IV. p. 1087. Cfr. Lutheri Opp. Hai. XIV, 191.)

i) Si enim fides non esset, meritum Christi nobis nihil esset profuturum. Mus. Tr. de syncr. l. c. p. 27. Et quemadmodum necesse est scire, Christum suo merito omnibus acquisivisse gratiam remissionis peccatorum; sic necessarium est, scire, meritum Christi actu prodesse ad obtinendam remissionem peccatorum credentibus. k) Pertinent huc suo modo, quae diximus in nota h. de articulo justificationis. Nam et vita aeterna habet se ad Christum ejusque meritum, ut effectus ad causam' quemadmodum justificatio confert jus vitae aeternae aut haereditatem ejus hominibus. Et, si quis ignoret, dari vitam beatam, quam tandem aliquando consecuturi sint, qui Deo propitio ex hac vita discedunt; is nec Christum pro causa salutis nostrae meritoria agnoscere, nec in eo fiduciam impetrandae a Deo vitae aeternae defixam habere potest. Mus. in Introd. p. 173.

174. N. Hunnius: „Fundamentum evertit, qui dogmata fundamentalia tenet, negat tamen doctrinam aliquam fundamentalibus necessario suppositam. Exemplo sunt Hymenaeus, Alexander, Philetus, qui circa fidem facti sunt naufragi et quorundam fidem subverterunt, 1 Tim. 1, 19. 20. 2 Tim. 2, 17. 18.; quantumvis agnoverint gratiam Dei salutiferam et Christi meritum, et professi sunt, homines fide salvari, nihilo minus naufragium fidei fecerunt negando mortuorum resurrectionem.“ (Αιάσκεψις, § 356.) § 33. Articuli fundamentales secundarii describi solent, quod sint partes a doctrinae christianae, quae licet ignorari b possint salvo salutis fundamento; negari tamen c salvo illo non d possunt. Tales sunt articuli de personarum divinarum proprietatibus e characteristieis, de unione personali distincte spectata, et communicatione idiomatum f in Christo, de peccato g originis, de decreto electio-


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: in view of faith] as the final [cause], concerning justification by faith…

in view of faith] as the final [cause], concerning justification by faith alone, with the merit of works excluded, etc., the explicit knowledge of which, although it is not possessed by all simpler believers, yet the denial of it on the part of the denier cannot stand with faith and salvation, unless a vast simplicity and ignorance of the consequence—by which that denial is opposed to the very foundation of faith by consequence—and a mind abhorring the error that is directly opposed to the foundation of faith and prepared to admit a better interpretation, have intervened.

Book of Concord: “As for the condemnations, censures, and rejections of false and impure doctrine, especially in the article concerning the Lord’s Supper, which must be expressly and distinctly set forth in this declaration and thorough exposition of the disputed articles, so that everyone may know how to guard against them, and which for many other reasons can by no means be bypassed: it is likewise not our will and intention that by this the persons who err out of simplicity and do not blaspheme the truth of the divine Word, and much less entire churches within or outside the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation, are meant, but that only the false and seductive doctrines and their obstinate teachers and blasphemers, whom we do not intend to tolerate in our lands, churches, and schools in any way, are properly rejected, since the same are contrary to the expressed Word of God and cannot stand alongside it, so that pious hearts may be warned against them; since we have no doubt at all that many pious, innocent people are to be found even in the churches that have not yet fully agreed with us, who walk in the simplicity of their hearts, do not rightly understand the matter, and take no pleasure at all in the blasphemies against the Holy Supper, as it is held in our churches according to the institution of Christ and is taught unanimously by virtue of the words of His testament, and who, it is hoped, when they are rightly instructed in the doctrine, will, through the guidance of the Holy Spirit, betake themselves and turn to the infallible truth of the divine Word with us and our churches and schools.” (Preface of the Electors, etc., p. 16 sq.)

Apology of the Augsburg Confession: “Although there are also many weak people among these, who build upon the foundation with perishable stubble, that is, certain useless opinions, which, however, because they do not overturn the foundation, are both forgiven them and also corrected. And the writings of the holy fathers testify that they sometimes also built stubble upon the foundation, but which did not overturn their faith.” (Concordia, p. 155 sq.)

Luther: “There is a twofold reason why sins do not harm the saints, and yet strangle the godless. The first is that the saints have faith in Christ... The second reason is that the saints, through faith, are so understanding that they hang solely upon the mercy of God, esteem their works as nothing at all; indeed, they confess from the bottom of their hearts that they are vain, useless works and sins... Do we not see in Augustine many errors which he retracts? All of which would have been damnable to him if he had not been preserved through faith; they are for the most part against the faith; but the confession and the fear of God made them harmless to him. Whoever now followed them would follow them to his own ruin.” ... It “undoubtedly still happens to many pious Christians that they, in a

keep to the simple faith of their hearts, and consider it to be a sacrifice. But because they do not rely upon the sacrifice—nay, they hold that everything they do is sin, and they cling solely to the pure mercy of God—they are preserved so that they do not perish in this error. . . Since we have now recognized the error, it is not fitting that we should continue to err and consider the Mass a sacrifice. For it would be to sin against the entire faith and our own conscience. Here no faith, no confession could excuse it. You cannot say: I want to err in a Christian way. A Christian error happens out of ignorance. . . Those who now know and recognize the error and still cling to it, just as if it were no error, they follow the fathers, but they will not come to them.” (On the Abuse of the Mass. 1522. XIX, 1380—1385.)

Indeed, they are parts and declarations of the primary articles of faith themselves, rather than constituting peculiar, entire, complete, and distinct articles of faith; although in a more general sense they are rightly called articles of faith, insofar as they pertain to faith and cohere with the foundation of faith: e.g., in the article concerning the person of Christ, three parts concerning as many genera of the communication of attributes are contained. See the blessed Musaeus, Tract. de syncret. p. 53, 54. Conf. Ausführl. Erklärung, p. 126, sqq.

Balduinus: “Since the capacity of intellect or the opportunity for learning is not the same for all, a distinction must be made here between the substance of the articles of faith and the disputes arising therefrom, which have been added for the sake of explanation. Every unlearned person ought to and can hold the substance of the articles of faith; but disputes and explanations are not required of everyone. Now, the substance of the articles of faith is that which is signified by the words of the article simply, even if generally and confusedly; as, that God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods, but one God in three persons; if anyone believes this in general, it is sufficient, even if he cannot say in particular what a person is, what the personal properties are, and how these differ among themselves; for these things pertain to the schools of the learned and to a clearer explanation of this article. Thus, it is sufficient for a rude and unlearned man to know that there are two natures in Christ, human and divine, and that the Son of the Most High is called the son of Mary, that the Lord of glory was crucified, etc., all of which Scripture says of Christ in conceived words; even if he does not exactly understand the mystery of the personal union and the communication of attributes, nor perceive what is disputed concerning these; for these things also pertain to the schools of the learned; and so it is with the others.” (Tract. de cas. conscient. L. II. c. 1. cas. 7. p. 62, sq.)

In which respect they are called secondary, and are distinguished from the primary. According to others, they are said to be necessary to be believed, not in themselves, positively and directly (which is the property of primary fundamental articles), but by reason of another, negatively, indirectly. See the blessed Hunnius, De diss. fund. § 63, p. 42, and § 284, p. 178; the blessed Meisner, Iren. Dur. S. II. § 227, p. 199. For which reason they merit and retain the name of fundamental articles.

Quenstedtius: “Some (fundamental articles), although they can be ignored while faith is preserved, nevertheless cannot be denied while the same is preserved, e.g., that God is infinite, immense, immutable, that the name of God, Jehovah, is incommunicable, that the divine persons are distinguished among themselves by certain characteristic properties.” ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

distinct, etc., can be clearly ignored without detriment to faith and loss of salvation, because when these are ignored, trust in God who promises and in Christ who merits remains inviolate, and many simple Christians never consider these and similar things, yet they are not on that account endangered regarding faith and salvation; but if anyone were to deny that God is infinite, immense, and immutable, he, by accusing the Spirit of truth of lying and transforming God into an idol, by robbing Him of the honor due to Him, and thus sinning most gravely against God, would altogether make shipwreck of the faith; as Dr. Nic. Hunnius rightly teaches in the place frequently cited, § 58 sq.” (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 3. fol. 351 sq.)

The same: “There are other articles of faith which are not simply fundamental or the cause of salvation, yet they pertain to the foundation, the denial of which damns and makes one a heretic, such as the dogmas concerning creation, election, the church, the sacraments, etc. Furthermore, there are less principal articles of faith, which are indeed proposed in Scripture to be believed, yet not under necessity for salvation, the denial of which does not strike at some fundamental article of faith by itself, but by some consequence not so evident, and overturns it; and this denial makes one a schismatic, e.g., that sin is not the substance of man, that election is not universal, etc.; and finally, there are innate questions, which are agitated among the learned concerning the more difficult passages of Scripture.” (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 10. not. 1. fol. 355.)

Namely, that the denial of such an article necessarily and always imports an error indirectly opposing the foundation of faith and salvation, and by which, through consequence, that [foundation], or something without which it cannot be safe, is destroyed. B. Musaeus, l. c. p. 177.

For just as the divine persons are constituted in the being of certain persons through certain properties or hypostatic characters, and are distinguished from other persons: so, when the properties are denied, the divine persons are denied to be. Meanwhile, those who have never thought about what a person differs from an essence, in what the personality of the Holy Spirit differs from the personality of the Son or Messiah, or who and what the proper and distinctive character of each is, and about other such consequences, can nevertheless believe in and worship the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as the one true God. B. Huelsem. Dial. Apol. p. 56. and B. J. Meisner. Iren. Dur. p. 191, 192.

For the personal union and the communication of idioms are contained in the person of Christ, the θεάνθρωπος, and His merit necessarily presupposes both. Therefore, he who acknowledges and believes in the person of Christ as θεάνθρωπος, by that very fact, if not explicitly, yet implicitly believes also in the personal union and the communication of idioms. And conversely, he who denies the personal union or the communication of idioms, or confuses the natures or the properties of the natures, he by consequence denies Christ Himself as θεάνθρωπος, and imagines either that He is only God, or only man, or that there are two Christs. See B. Mus. Introd. p. 175, 176.

Latin:

nis intuitu fidei h finalis, de justificatione per solam fidem, excluso operum merito i etc., quorum etsi cognitio explicita non est omnium fidelium simpliciorum, tamen negatio ex parte negantis stare non potest k cum fide et salute, nisi ingens simplicitas et ignorantia consequentiae, per quam negatio illa ipsi fundamento fidei per consequentiam adversatur, et animus ab errore, qui fundamento fidei directe adversatur, abhorrens ac meliorem interpretationem admittere paratus, intercesserit. l

Liber Concordiae: „Was denn die Condemnationes, Aussetzung und Verwerfung falscher und unreiner Lehre, besonders im Artikel von des Herrn Abendmahl betrifft, so in dieser Erklärung und gründlichen Hinlegung der streitigen Artikel ausdrücklich und unterschiedlich gesetzt werden müssen, damit sich männiglich wüsste vor denselbigen zu hüten, und aus vielen ändern Ursachen keineswegs umgangen werden kann: ist gleichergestalt unser Wille und Meinung nicht, dass hiemit die Personen, so aus Einfalt irren und die Wahrheit des göttlichen Worts nicht lästern, vielweniger aber ganze Kirchen inoder ausserhalb des heiligen Reichs deutscher Nation gemeinet, sondern dass allein damit die falschen und verführischen Lehren und derselben halsstarrige Lehrer und Lästerer, die wir in unsern Landen, Kirchen und Schulen keinesweges zu gedulden gedenken, eigentlich verworfen werden, dieweil dieselben dem ausgedrückten Wort Gottes zuwider und neben solchem nicht bestehen können, auf dass fromme Heizen für denselben gewarnet werden möchten, sintemal wir uns ganz und gar keinen Zweifel machen, dass viel frommer, unschuldiger Leute, auch in den Kirchen, die sich bishero mit uns nicht allerdings verglichen, zu finden seind, welche in der Einfalt ihres Herzens wandeln, die Sache nicht recht verstehen und an den Lästerungen wider das heilige Abendmahl, wie solches in unsern Kirchen nach der Stiftung Christi gehalten und vermöge der Wort seines Testaments davon einhelliglich gelehret wird, gar keinen Gefallen tragen, und sich verhoffentlich, wenn sie in der Lehre recht unterrichtet werden, durch Anleitung des Heiligen Geistes zu der unfehlbaren Wahrheit des göttlichen Worts mit uns und unsern Kirchen und Schulen begeben und wenden werden.“ (Praefat. Electorum etc. p. 16. sq.)

Apologia A. C.: „Etsi sunt in his etiam multi imbecilles, qui supra fundamentum aedificant stipulas perituras, hoc est, quasdam inutiles opiniones, quae tamen, quia non evertunt fundamentum, tum condonantur illis, tum etiam emendantur. Ac sanctorum patrum scripta testantur, quod interdum stipulas etiam aedificaverint supra fundamentum, sed quae non everterunt fidem eorum.“ (Cone. p. 155. sq.)

Lutherus: „Es ist zweierlei Ursache, dass die Sünden den Heiligen nicht schaden, und doch die Gottlosen daran erwürgen. Die erste ist, dass die Heiligen haben den Glauben an Christum. . . Die andere Ursache, dass die Heiligen durch den Glauben so verständig sind, dass sie allein an der Barmherzigkeit Gottes hangen, achten ihrer Werke gar nichts, ja sie bekennen aus Grund ihres Herzens, dass es eitel unnütze Werke und Sünden sind. . . Sehen wir nicht in Augustino viel Irrthum, welche er widerruft? die ihm wären alle verdammlich gewesen, wenn er nicht durch den Glauben wäre erhalten worden; sind sie doch des mehreren Theils wider den Glauben; aber das Bekenntniss und die Furcht Gottes hat sie ihm unschädlich gemacht. Wer ihnen nun nachfolgete, der folgete zu seinem Verderben.“ . . Es „geschieht noch ohne Zweifel viel frommen Christen, dass sie in einem

einfältigen Glauben ihres Herzens Messe halten, und achten, es sei ein Opfer. Aber dieweil sie sich auf das Opfer nicht verlassen, ja, sie halten’s davor, dass alles, was sie thun, Sünde sei, und hangen allein an der lautern Barmherzigkeit Gottes, werden sie erhalten, dass sie in diesem Irrthum nicht verderben. . . Dieweil wir nun den Irrthum erkannt haben, so ziemet sichs nicht, dass wir weiter irren und die Messe für ein Opfer halten. Denn es wäre wider den ganzen Glauben und unser eigen Gewissen gesündigt. Hie könnte kein Glaube, kein Bekenntniss entschuldigen. Du kannst nicht sprechen: Ich will christlich irren. Ein christlicher Irrthum geschieht aus Unwissenheit. . . Die nun wissen und erkennen den Irrthum und ihm, gleich als obs kein Irrthum wäre, noch anhangen, die folgen den Vätern nach, aber zu ihnen werden sie nicht kommen.“ (Vom Missbrauch der Messe. 1522. XIX, 1380—1385.)

Nempe sunt partes ac declarationes ipsorum fidei articulorum primariorum potius, quam ut peculiares, integros, completos, et a caeteris distinctos articulos fidei constituant; licet in generaliori significatione articuli fidei recte dicantur, quatenus pertinent ad fidem et cohaerent cum fundamento fidei: v. g. in articulo de persona Christi partes tres de totidem generibus communicationis idiomatum continentur. Vid. b. Musaeus Tract. de syncret. p. 53. 54. Conf. Ausführl. Erklärung, p. 126. sqq.

Balduinus: „Cum non omnium eadem sit ingenii capacitas vel occasio discendi, distinguendum hic est inter substantiam articulorum fidei et inter disputationes inde ortas, quae explicationis causa accesserunt. Substantiam articulorum fidei quilibet idiotarum tenere debet et potest; disputationes vero et explicationes non requiruntur ab omnibus.
