Est autem substantia articulorum fidei id, quod simpliciter, licet generatim et confuse, vocibus articuli significatur; ut, Deum Patrem, Filium et Spiritum S. non esse tres deos, sed unum Deum in tribus personis; si quis hoc credit in genere, satis est, licet in specie dicere non possit, quid persona sit, quae personales proprietates et quomodo hae inter se differant; haec enim ad scholas eruditorum et clariorem hujus articuli explicationem pertinent. Ita satis est pro rudi et imperito homine, scire, duas esse in Christo naturas, humanam et divinam, et Filium Altissimi vocari filium Mariae, Dominum gloriae crucifixum esse etc., quae omnia conceptis verbis Scriptura de Christo dicit; licet mysterium unionis personalis et communicationis idiomatum exacte non intelligat, nec, quae de his disputantur, percipiat; haec enim etiam ad scholas eruditorum pertinent; et sic de caeteris.“ (Tract. de cas. conscient. L. II. c. 1. cas. 7. p. 62. sq.)

Quo respectu dicuntur secundarii, et primariis contradistinguuntur. Juxta alios dicuntur creditu necessarii, non secundum se, positive et directe (quod articulorum fundamentalium primariorum proprium sit), sed ratione alterius, negative, indirecte. Vid. b. Hunnius De diss. fund. § 63. p. 42. et § 284. p. 178., b. Meisn; Iren. Dur. S. II. § 227. p. 199. Qua ratione fundamentalium articulorum nomen merentur et retinent.

Quenstedtius: „Quidam (art. fund.), etsi salva fide possint ignorari, attamen eadem salva negari nequeunt, v. g. Deum infinitum, immensum,' immutabilem esse, nomen Dei Jehovah incommunicabile esse, personas divinas certis proprietatibus characteristicis inter se esse DB NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

distinctas etc., plane ignorari potest citra fldei detrimentum et salutis dispendium, quia his ignoratis fiducia in Deum promittentem et Christum promerentem est inviolata, et multi simplices Christiani haec et similia nunquam considerant, nec tamen propterea de fide et salute periclitantur; verum si quis neget, Deum infinitum, immensum, immutabilem esse, is, Spiritum veritatis mendacii arguendo et Deum transformando in idolum, honorem debitum illi rapiendo, adeoque in Deum gravissime peccando, fldei naufragium omnino faceret; ut recte docet D. Nie. Hunnius loco saepius alleg. § 58. sq.“ (Theol. did.- pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 3. fol. 351. sq.)

Idem: ,,Sunt alii articuli fidei, qui non simpliciter fundamentales seu causa salutis sunt, ad fundamentum tamen pertinent, quorum negatio damnat et haereticum facit, ut sunt dogmata de creatione, electione, ecclesia, sacramentis etc. Sunt porro articuli fldei minus principales, qui quidem ad credendum in Scriptura propositi sunt, non tamen sub necessitate ad salutem, quorum negatio non per se, sed per consequentiam aliquam non adeo evidentem impingit in aliquem fidei articulum fundamentalem, eumque evertit; et haec negatio facit schismaticum, v. g. peccatum non esse hominis substantiam, electionem non esse universalem etc.; et denique sunt quaestiones adnatae, quae inter eruditos de difficilioribus Scripturae locis agitantur.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 10. not. 1. fol. 355.)

Nempe quod negatio hujusmodi articuli necessario et semper importat errorem fundamento fidei et salutis indirecte adversantem, et quo per consequentiam illud, vel aliquid, absque quo id salvum esse non potest, destruitur. B. Musaeus l. c. p. 177.

Quemadmodum enim personae divinae in esse certarum personarum per certas proprietates aut characteres hypostaticos constituuntur, et ab aliis personis distinguuntur: ita, negatis proprietatibus, negantur esse personae divinae. Interim possunt Patrem, Filium et Spiritum S., tanquam unum verum Deum, credere et colere, qui neque cogitarunt, quid differat persona ah essentia? in quo differat personalitas Spiritus Sancti a personalitate Filii seu Messiae? seu quis et qualis sit utriusque character proprius et discretivus? deque aliis hujusmodi consectariis. B. Huelsem. Dial. Apol. p. 56. et b. J. Meisner. Iren. Dur. p. 191. 192.

Unio personalis enim et communicatio idiomatum continetur in Christi persona ΰεανΰρώπω, et ejus meritum praesupponit necessario utramque. Itaque qui personam Christi dzdvftpwnov agnoscit et credit, is eo ipso, si non explicite, implicite tamen etiam unionem personalem et communicationem idiomatum credit. Et ex adverso, qui unionem personalem aut communicationem idiomatum negat, aut naturas vel proprietates naturarum confundit; is per consequentiam ipsum Christum dsavdpuir.ov negat, et vel tantum Deum, vel tantum hominem, vel duos Christos esse fingit. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. p. 175. 176.


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: To be sure, for conceiving trust in Christ, the knowledge of it (original sin)…

To be sure, for conceiving trust in Christ, the knowledge of it (original sin) in the intellect is not simply required; yet it is required for guarding against the contrary opinion, which is the persuasion of innate holiness and the ability to keep the divine commandments, by which if anyone is deceived, he will never arrive at the acknowledgment of sin and salvation. B. Huelsem. Calv. irreconc. p. 475., B. J. Meisn. § 229. p. 201.

For just as it is necessary that the decree and the execution correspond accurately to one another, so if it is denied that the decree of election was made in view of faith in Christ, it will also be denied by consequence that God saves men in time in view of faith in Christ: which the blessed Musaeus shows in his *Tractatus de aeterno electionis decreto*, especially Chapter V, § 119 sqq.

It is certain, however, that simple ignorance of that decree does not stand in the way of the faith of the simpler sort, who can nevertheless embrace the grace of God and the merit and satisfaction of Christ as the cause of salvation, even if they have not thought about the decree of election.

Scripture itself indeed opposes faith and works in justification in such a way that it argues from the position of one to the destruction of the other—for example, from justification by works to the negation of justification by faith (Rom. 3 and 4). Meanwhile, one can believe in Christ and through this faith obtain the remission of sins, who has not thought about justification by faith alone and not by works. Whence also the blessed J. Meisner refers that dogma among those things which become necessary only by accident, lest an opposite error or false opinion enter the intellect, which might weaken or destroy that which has once been rightly established. *L. c.* § 239, p. 205.

k) Namely, he who denies some secondary fundamental article in such a way that he can at the same time see, and does see, that by its denial some primary article of faith—and indeed the very foundation of faith—is overturned by consequence; he not only indirectly, by the force of that negation, opposes the foundation of faith, but now, through the error deduced from that negative, directly destroys the foundation of faith itself, and brings it about that faith cannot be generated or exist in him. See Musaeus, *l. c.*, p. 177.

l) For because the negation of a secondary article does not oppose the foundation of faith except by consequence; and he who embraces that negative out of simplicity does not grasp the consequence: therefore, in such a subject, that negation can coexist with the foundation itself. And because explicit knowledge of the article which is denied is not simply necessary for generating faith and causing salvation; therefore, its negation, proceeding from mere ignorance and simplicity, can coexist with the knowledge of the rest of those things which pertain to the foundation itself, insofar as it is necessary to be known for causing faith and salvation, and thus faith itself and salvation are not necessarily removed and hindered. The blessed Musaeus, *l. c.*, pp. 177, 178.

The blessed Huelsemann agrees in *Calvin. Irreconc.*, p. 432 sqq., where he presents this axiom: Not every dogma, which by its own nature asserts or destroys something necessarily presupposed by faith or consequent to it, effects the same thing in the mind of every man; and while he warns that the question returns to the understanding of consequences, he thinks one must distinguish between the seduced and the teachable, and the seducers and the pertinacious, and he declares this by the example of the article concerning the communication of idioms, etc. The blessed Kromayer follows Huelsemann in *Prooem. theol. pos.-pol.*, p. 4.

Kromayer: "Regarding the evidence of consequences, it must be known beforehand (e.g., if the other party denies that this or that follows from these or those premises) that a distinction must be made between seducers and the seduced, between the pertinacious and the teachable, between false teachers and the heterodox. The seduced and the teachable are to be tolerated and instructed; there is no doubt that the pertinacious and the calumniators of the truth fall from divine grace. For the judgment is more severe for false teachers," ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

which the Savior in Matt. 5:19 threatens only against the heterodox, especially the simple and teachable. . . . Furthermore, one must appeal to the conscience of each person, whether it is tranquil in the denial of that consequence, or otherwise. If it is not tranquil, but fluctuates regarding that denial of the consequence, so that trust in Christ wavers on account of it, such a person, without a doubt, deprives himself of faith and consequently of salvation.” (Theol. posit.-pol. P. I. p. 4.)

Aeg. Hunnius: “There are lighter errors, which strike at less principal articles, which errors the Apostle likens to stubble, burning up in the fire of temptation, yet in such a way that the erring person himself is saved, having retained the foundation of salvation, having grasped the Rock, namely Christ, and so that he suffers the loss of his ‘work’ which he had built upon the foundation. (1 Cor. 3:11–15.) It is another matter if someone should say out of contempt: ‘The foundation of salvation is sufficient for me, and it is enough for me to think rightly in this article,’ and meanwhile refuses to admit better information regarding the rest. Such a person would err indeed regarding lighter articles, but yet not with a simple error, but one joined with contempt for the divine word.” (Colloq. Ratisbonae hab. a. 1601. Lauingae. Sess. 14. p. 433. sq.)

Gerhard: “Before the Scriptures were published, it was not necessary for salvation to believe that there are any divine scriptures. But after they were published, one must distinguish between simple ignorance and stubborn denial. To believe that there are any divine Scriptures is not simply and absolutely necessary for salvation, namely if that proceeds from simple ignorance, because many have been saved who embraced the substantial or fundamental parts of the Christian faith, even though they were ignorant that there were any divine scriptures; but whoever, after the scriptures have been published, wishes to deny stubbornly that there are any divine scriptures, he shall be rendered a heretic and excluded from the possession of salvation.” (Loc. de eccl. §121.)

Hülsemann: “It has long been proven by our side that the Holy Spirit proceeds as much from the Son as from the Father. . . If, however, someone, out of weakness of intellect, does not perceive the force of these consequences and thinks that one must adhere to the bare letter of the saying in John ch. 15, but is otherwise orthodox, we do not take away salvation from him, nor do we judge him to be counted among heretics, neither on account of ignorance of the truth, nor on account of a denial proceeding from mere ignorance, unlike Bellarmine. . . and others who here and there defame the Greek Church with the name of heresy on account of the denied procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son.” (Praelectt. in Form. Conc. Art. 3. s. 1. c. 5. § 10. p. 282.)

Calov: “When one head of faith is denied or overturned, one fundamental dogma, one article from the system of things to be believed, it is heresy materially; if stubbornness is added, it is formal heresy.” (System. VIII. p. 226. sq.)

Kromayer: “What? That any adulterated doctrine outside of and beyond the θεόπνευστον (God-breathed) word, when it is stubbornly defended, can come under the name of heresy taken generically.” (Scrutin. rel. p. 480.)

Luther: “I taught 20 years ago that faith alone without works makes one righteous, as I still do today. But if someone had arisen at that time who had taught that monkery and nunnery should be called idolatry and the Mass the true abomination, I would not have helped to burn such a heretic, yet I would have held that it served him right. And I, an unthinking fool, could not see the consequence that I would have to concede, that if faith alone did it, then monkery and the Mass could not do it. . . . The apostles at Jerusalem (Acts 15:11), together with many thousands of Jews, had been made righteous through faith alone, that is, through the grace of Christ; yet they still had their Nestorios and Eutyches in their skin; they did not see this consequence, that the law of Moses did nothing nor could do anything toward it, but they wanted to give to it also the *idiomata* (properties) which belong only to the Lamb of God, and said (as

(as said above): the heathens could not be saved unless they were circumcised and kept the law of Moses. That was tantamount to denying Christ and His grace, as St. Paul says in Gal. 2:21: "If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died in vain"; and Rom. 11:6: "If it is by grace, then it is no longer by works." But those at Jerusalem say this: It is indeed grace alone, but it must nevertheless [also] be the work; for since grace has not yet done such a thing, the law must do it, as follows. That means, in German, to slap one’s own cheeks and not understand what one is saying. The schools call it (as said): *antecedens concedere, et consequens negare*, or *consequens destruere, antecedens affirmare*, to say Yes and No at the same time regarding the same thing. (On the Councils and the Church. 1539. XVI, 2737. 2740. sq.)

The same: "They do not distinguish between erring and remaining in error. Erring does not harm the Church, but remaining in error, that is impossible; as Christ says in Matt. 24:23, that even the elect would be led into error, if it were possible. For the Church confesses in the Lord’s Prayer that she sins and errs, but everything is forgiven her." (On the Private Mass. 1533. XIX, 1515.) The same: "As St. Augustine says of himself: *Errare potero, haereticus non ero*: I may err, but I will not be a heretic. The reason: Heretics do not merely err, but they refuse to be instructed, they defend their error as right, and they fight against the recognized truth and against their own conscience. Of such, St. Paul says in Tit. 3:10-11: 'A heretic you should avoid, after he has been warned once or twice, and you should know that such a one is perverted and sins *autocatacritos*,' that is, he who willfully and knowingly wants to remain condemned in error. But St. Augustine is glad to confess his error and let himself be told. Therefore, he cannot be a heretic, even if he were to err. Thus do all other saints also, and they gladly give their hay, straw, and wood into the fire, so that they may remain upon the foundation of salvation. As we have also done and still do." (On the Councils and the Church. 1539. XVI, 2664.)

Latin:

Scilicet ad fiduciam in Christum concipiendam non requiritur simpliciter ejus (peccati orig.) in intellectu notitia; requiritur tamen ad praecavendam opinionem contrariam, quae est persuasio connatae sanctitatis et facultatis, divina mandata servandi, qua si quis fallitur, ad agnitionem peccati et salutem nunquam perveniet. B. Huelsem. Calv. irreconc. p. 475., b. J. Meisn. § 229. p. 201.

PKOLEGOM. CAP. I. Prout enim decretum et executionem sibi accurate respondere necesse est, ita si negetur, decretum electionis factum esse intuitu fidei in Christum, per consequentiam etiam negabitur, Deum in tempore salvare homines intuitu fidei in Christum: quod ostendit b. Mus. Tract. de aeterno el. decr., inprimis Cap. V. § 119. sqq.

Certum tamen est, ignorantiam simplicem decreti illius non obstare fidei simpliciorum, qui gratiam Dei et meritum ac satisfactionem Christi nihilominus amplecti possunt, tanquam causam salutis, etsi de decreto electionis non cogitaverint.

Ipsa sane scriptura fidem et opera in justificatione ita opponit, ut. ab unius positione ad alterius destructionem, v. g. a justificatione per opera ad negationem justificationis per fidem, argumentetur Rom. 3. et 4. Interim potest credere in Christum et per hanc fidem consequi remissionem peccatorum, qui de justificatione per solam fidem, et non per opera, non cogitaverit. Unde et b. J. Meisnerus dogma illud inter ea refert, quae ex accidente et ideo tantum necessario fiunt, ne error oppositus aut falsa opinio intellectum subeat, quae id, quod semel recte constitutum est, labefactet aut destruat. L. c. § 239p. 205.

k) Nempe qui articulum aliquem fundamentalem secundarium ita negat, ut simul videre possit et videat, eo negato, per consequentiam everti articulum aliquem fidei primarium ipsumque adeo fundamentum fidei; is non solum indirecte, vi illius negationis, adversatur fundamento fidei, sed jam, per errorem ex illa negativa deductum, directe destruit ipsum fundamentum fidei, et quo minus fides in ipso generari aut esse possit, efficit. Vid. Mus. l. c. p. 177.

l) Quia enim negatio articuli secundarii non adversatur fundamento fidei, nisi per consequentiam; consequentiam autem non capit, qui ex simplicitate negativam illam amplectitur: ideo cum fundamento ipso negatio ista in tali subjecto stare potest. Et quia cognitio expressa articuli, qui negatur, ad generandam fidem et causandam salutem simpliciter necessaria non est; ideo negatio ejus, ex mera ignorantia et simplicitate profecta, stare potest cum cognitione caeterorum, quae ad fundamentum ipsum, in quantum ad causandam fidem et salutem cognitu necessarium est, pertinent, neque adeo fides ipsa et salus necessario tollitur atque impeditur. B. Mus. l. c. p. 177. 178.

Consentit b. Huelsemannus in Calvin. Irreconc. p. 432. sqq., ubi hoc axioma exhibet: Non omne dogma, quod ex sua natura aliquod fidei necessario praesuppositum aut eam consequens astruit vel destruit, idem in hominis cujusque mente illud efficit; dumque ad consequentiarum intelligentiam quaestionem redire monet, distinguendum putat inter seductos ac dociles, et seductores ac pertinaces, idque exemplo articuli de communicatione idiomatum declarat etc. Huelsemannum autem sequitur b. Kromayerus Prooem. theol. pos.-pol. p. 4.

Kromayerus: ,,De consequentiarum evidentia praecognoscendum (v. g. si pars altera neget, positis his vel illis hoc vel illud sequi), quod distinguendum sit inter seducentes et seductos, inter pertinaces et dociles, inter heterodidascalos et heterodoxos. Seducti et dociles tolerandi sunt et informandi; pertinaces et veritatis calumniatores gratia divina excidere, dubium non est. Gravius enim judicium heterodidascalis, DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

quam heterodoxis tantum, simplicibus praesertim et docilibus, Salvator Matth. 5, 19. minatur. . . Deinde provocandum ad cujusque conscientiam, an ea tranquilla sit in consequentiae istius negatione, an secus. Si non est tranquilla, sed circa negationem istam consequentiae fluctuat, ut fiducia in Christum propterea vacillet, is dubio procul fide et consequenter salute se privat.“ (Theol. posit.-pol. P. I. p. 4.)

Aeg. Hunnius: ,,Sunt errores leviores, qui impingunt in articulos minus principales, quos errores apostolus assimulat stipulae, deflagranti igne tentationis, sic tamen, ut ipse errans salvus flat retento fundamento salutis, apprehensa petra, Christo nimirum, et ut operis ‘sui, quod super fundamentum extruxerat, jacturam faciat. (1 Cor. 3, 11—15.) Aliud est, si quis ex contemtu dicat: sufficit mihi fundamentum salutis et satis est mihi, in hoc articulo me recte sentire, ac interim nolit admittere informationem meliorem in reliquis. Talis erraret circa leviores quidem articulos, sed tamen non errore simplici, sed cum contemtu divini verbi conjuncto.“ (Colloq. Ratisbonae hab. a. 1601. Lauingae. Sess. 14. p. 433. sq.)

Gerhardus: „Antequam Scripturae ederentur, non erat necessarium ad salutem, credere, aliquas esse divinas scripturas. Postquam vero editae sunt, distinguendum inter simplicem ignorationem et inter praefractam negationem. Credere, quod sint aliquae divinae Scripturae, non est simpliciter et absolute necessarium ad salutem, nimirum si ex simplici ignoratione illud procedat, quia multi salvati sunt, qui substantialia sive fundamentalia fidei Christianae complexi sunt, licet ignorarent, esse aliquas divinas scripturas; sed qui post editas scripturas pertinaciter negare velit, esse aliquas divinas scripturas, is haereticus reddetur et a salutis possessione excludetur.“ (Loc. de eccl. §121.)

Hueisemannus: „Evictum dudum a nostris (sit), tam a Eilio, quam a Patre procedere Spiritum S. . . Si quis tamen ex imbecillitate intellectus vim harum consequentiarum non sentiat et nudae literae dicti c. 15. Joh. inhaerendum censeat, caetera vero orthodoxus sit, illi neque propter ignorantiam veritatis, neque propter negationem ex nuda ignorantia profectam, aut salutem adimimus aut inter haereticos eum computandum censemus, secus quam Bellarminus. . . aliique passim haereseos nomine ecclesiam Graecam deformantes propter negatam processionem Sp. S. a Filio." (Praelectt. in Form. Cone. Art. 3. s. 1. c. 5. § 10. p. 282.)

Calovius; „Cum unum negatur aut evertitur fidei caput, unum dogma fundamentale, unus articulus e systemate credendorum, haeresis est materialiter; si accedat pertinacia, formalis haeresis est.“ (System. VIII. p. 226. sq.)

Kromayerus: „Quid? quod quaevis adulterina doctrina extra et praeter verbum Gεόπνανπταν, quando pertinaciter defenditur, haereseos nomine γενικώς sumto venire queat.“ (Scrutin. rel. p. 480.)

Lutherus: „Ich habe vor 20 Jahren gelehrt, dass allein der Glaube ohn Werke gerecht mache, wie ich noch immer thue. Wäre aber dazumal einer aufgestanden, der da hätte gelehret, Möncherei und Nonnerei sollt Abgötterei und die Messe der rechte Greuel heissen, hätte ich solchen Ketzer nicht helfen verbrennen, so hätte ichs doch gehalten, ihm wäre recht geschehen. Und ich unbedächtiger Narr konnte nicht sehen die Folge, die ich müsste nachgeben, dass, wo es der Glaube allein thäte, so könnte es die Möncherei und Messe nicht thun. . . . Die Apostel zu Jerusalem (Apost. 15, 11.) sammt vielen tausend Jüden waren durch den Glauben allein gerecht worden, das ist, durch die Gnade Christi; noch hatten sie auch ihre Nestorios und Eutyches in der Haut; sahen diese Folge nicht, dass Mosis Gesetz nichts dazu thäte noch thun könnte, sondern wollten demselben auch geben die idiomata, so allein dem Lamm Gottes zustehen, und sprachen (wie

droben gesagt): die Heiden könnten nicht selig werden, wo sie sich nicht beschnitten und Mosis Gesetz hielten. Das war ebensoviel als Christum verleugnen mit seiner Gnade, wie St. Paulus sagt Gal. 2, 21.: ,Ist aus dem Gesetz Gerechtigkeit, so ist Christus vergeblich gestorben4; und Rom. 11, 6.: ,Ist’s Gnade, so ist’s nicht Werk.4 Aber die zu Jerusalem sagen so: Es ist wohl allein die Gnade, aber es muss gleichwohl [allein] auch das Werk sein; denn weil die Gnade solches noch nicht hat gethan, so muss es das Gesetz thun, wie es folget. Das heisst auf deutsch, sich selbst in die Backen hauen und nicht verstehen, was man redet. Die Schulen nennens (wie gesagt): antecedens concedere, und consequens negare, oder consequens destruere, antecedens affirmare, zugleich Ja und Nein sagen in einerlei Sachen." (Von Conciliis und Kirchen. 1539. XVI, 2737. 2740. sq.)

Idem: ,,Sie unterscheiden nicht, irren und in Irrthum bleiben. Irren schadet der Kirche nichts, aber in Irrthum bleiben, das ist unmöglich; wie Christus spricht Matth. 24, 23., dass auch die Auserwählten in Irrthum geführt würden, wo es möglich wäre. Denn die Kirche bekennet im Vater Unser, dass sie sündige und irre, aber es wird ihr alles vergeben." (V. d. Winkelmesse. 1533. XIX, 1515.) Idem: ,,Wie St. Augustinus von sich spricht: Errare potero, haereticus non ero: Ich mag irren, aber ein Ketzer will ich nicht werden. Ursach: Ketzer irren nicht allein, sondern wollen sich nicht weisen lassen, vertheidigen ihren Irrthum für Recht und streiten wider die erkannte Wahrheit und wider ihr eigen Gewissen. Von solchen sagt St. Paulus Tit. 3, 10. 11.: ,Einen Ketzer sollt du meiden, wenn er eins oder zweier vermahnt ist, und sollt wissen, dass ein solcher verkehret ist und sündiget autocatacritos', das ist, der muthwilliglich und wissentlich will in Irrthum verdammt bleiben. Aber St. Augustinus will seinen Irrthum gern bekennen und ihm sagen lassen. Darum kann er kein Ketzer sein, wenn er gleich irrete. Also thun alle andere Heiligen auch und geben ihr Heu, Stroh und Holz gern von sich ins Feuer, damit sie auf dem Grunde der Seligkeit bleiben. Wie wir auch gethan haben und noch thun." (Von Conciliis und Kirchen. 1539. XVI, 2664.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: The same: "We must indeed confess that the enthusiasts have the Scripture and…

The same: "We must indeed confess that the enthusiasts have the Scripture and God’s Word in other articles, and whoever hears and believes it from them will be saved, even though they are unholy heretics and blasphemers of Christ." (Letter on Re-baptism. 1528. XVII, 2675.) The same: "Where else would one make a distinction as to which is the true Church of Christ and which is the devil’s church, if not by obedience and disobedience toward Christ, especially when the disobedience is publicly recognized and understood, and is wickedly and brazenly excused and claims to be right? For the holy Church sins and stumbles or even errs, as the Lord’s Prayer teaches; but she does not defend or excuse herself, but humbly asks for forgiveness and improves herself as best she can; thus it is forgiven her, so that her sin is no longer reckoned as sin. If I am now not to recognize or distinguish the true Church from the false by obedience and hardened disobedience, then I know nothing more to say of any church." (Letter regarding his book on the Private Mass. XIX, 1579.) § 34.

Non-fundamental articles are called those which, while the foundation of faith remains intact, can not only be ignored, but even denied, or disputed on either side. E.g., concerning sin ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

and the perpetual rejection of certain angels, concerning the immortality of the first man before the fall, concerning the Antichrist, and concerning the origin of the soul through creation or traducianism, etc.

Fechtius: “Articles of faith are either fundamental or non-fundamental. Where it must be observed, however, that this distinction is not of articles properly so called, and thus taken univocally, but rather an equivocal distinction, since non-fundamental articles are called articles of faith only improperly and very remotely.” (Compend., universam th. complexum. Praecognita. C. 1. § 42. p. 29.)

Calvoerius: “One must diligently distinguish between those things which are necessary to be believed by every believer who is to be saved, and those which are necessary for the church for the purity, exposition, and defense of saving doctrine; and the distinction between Christian and catholic articles, and ecclesiastical and theological articles, pertains here.” (Fissurae Sionis. Lips. 1710. p. 1172.)

Quenstedtius: “To the non-fundamental articles, or those which can be both ignored and denied while the foundation of faith remains safe, D. Hunnius (l. c. § 65) refers the dogma concerning the perpetual rejection of certain angels; concerning the immortality of man before the fall; concerning the Antichrist; concerning the irremissibility of the sin against the Holy Spirit; concerning Christian liberty in rites, etc. Whether these are ignored or denied, they bring no harm to faith in themselves, provided they do not remove any cause of faith or fundamental dogma through their denial.” (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 2., f. 350.)

Meanwhile, even in these matters, one must be careful not to sin rashly against divine revelation and God Himself by embracing or professing error; especially, that nothing be established against conscience and with the seduction of others, by which the pillars and truth of one or more fundamental articles of faith might be undermined. For in this way, as if by a mortal sin, the Holy Spirit and faith can be—and are accustomed to be—cast out. To this point tend the things which the blessed J. Meisnerus wrote (l. c. § 242. p. 207).

N. Hunnius: “When in the following this form of speech occurs: ‘this or that dogma can be ignored or denied while the foundation of faith remains safe,’ this is by no means the sense of the phrase, that such a denial or ignorance has a place while faith is safe; since such a denial can be destructive to faith, however much it may not overturn the foundation of faith.” (Διάσκεψις § 353.)

The same: “Faith is removed by doctrine which has the character of moral sin. There is a twofold doctrine salutary to man; one, which is the proximate cause of faith, or which causes a man to trust in God and Christ, and hence certainly expects the remission of sins and eternal salvation; the other, which indeed does not work this trust, but is meanwhile proposed to man by God either to declare the faith or to learn other things necessary to Christianity: he who fails in the former kind of doctrine not only errs dangerously, but also errs concerning faith; he who fails in the latter errs dangerously, yet not concerning the doctrine of faith, but morally, so that nothing is taken away from the trust (by reason of the doctrine from which trust is born) which a man has toward God, yet the wrath of the Lord is provoked. By this reasoning, one who denies the history of Samson, David, etc., or denies that circumcision was a divine institution, etc., by this very act takes nothing away from the foundation of faith or fundamental doctrine, yet he does not err without danger to salvation, because by taking away the praise of truth from God, he offends Him with a mortal sin and thus provokes His wrath against himself, which is joined with the loss of faith and salvation, unless repentance is performed. To this pertains the birth of Christ from a virgin and many other dogmas, the denial of which does not overturn or even deprave the fundamental doctrine of faith, yet it irritates the wrath of God, whence faith falls through the defect of the efficient cause, even while its foundation stands.”

Huelsemannus: "I deny that any approval of a non-true theological dogma is innocent of all guilt; for although not every guilt is lethal or brings about condemnation in the second act, it is nevertheless condemnable in the first act, in which way the Apostle distinguishes the 'condemnable' from that which brings about condemnation in the second act, Rom. 8:1. . . For concerning the quality of a dogma in itself, we have an express commandment in 1 Pet. 4:11, that whoever proposes something to be believed by another is bound to propose the λόγια θεοῦ. . . It follows that, in relation to guilt before God, no proposition of any theological dogma—whether it pertains directly or indirectly to faith and is not true in itself—is a matter of indifference; although in relation to the attainment of supreme glory, it may be innocent in the second act." (Praelect. F. C. p. 950.)

Carpzovius: "The Augsburg Confession does not hold non-fundamental dogmas in low esteem, but says that they are to be pardoned at least in the weak." (Isag. etc. p. 310.)

Dannhauerus: "An article of faith is not. . . every gloss, assertion, or opinion which does not have a certain and clear definition in the Holy Scriptures, such as questions about the time of the creation of the world—whether in spring or autumn?—about the year and day of the birth of Christ; add to this the ἀειπαρθενία even after the birth of the blessed Virgin (which, following the papal doctors, Hornej. disp. 4. de sufficientia Scripturae s. p. 339, concedes to be an article of faith, and the contrary opinion of Helvidius and the Antidicomarianites is undoubtedly rightly condemned as heresy; but Basil in his Homily on the Nativity of Christ removed it from this series, by the very fact that he denied by the contrary opinion that the doctrine of piety was violated and asserted that it did not pertain to the discourse of the mystery); add to this the Psychopannychia*) and other such opinions, in which minds can be exercised, yet they ought not to be prescribed by these as sacraments of the church. You might find a heap of such swellings in scholastic theology, where one milks a he-goat, and another holds a sieve underneath." (Hodos. Phaen. 11. p. 667.)

Buddeus: "Many things are contained in Holy Scripture which, because they have been revealed to us by God, we are also bound to believe, yet they are not necessary for the attainment of salvation. Furthermore, many things are required and are thus necessary so that someone may be a member of a certain particular church, and much more so that he may be able to perform the office of a pastor in it, which, however, are not equally necessary for salvation, and therefore we are not speaking of these." (Institt. theol. dogm. p. 41.) See concerning these the blessed Nic. Hunnius, l. c. § 65. p. 43.

Quenstedtius: "A distinction must be made between fundamental articles of faith, which pertain to saving faith, and articles which are not fundamental, the knowledge of which is also handed down in the Word of God, and these pertain to dogmatic or historical faith. To this class we refer the doctrine concerning the Antichrist because of the prophecies of the Scriptures, which were revealed to us by the Holy Spirit in the prophet Daniel, in St. Paul, and in the Apocalypse of John. However, we do not say that this question concerning the Antichrist is such that its decision is necessary for all Christians to know for salvation, or that ignorance of it is in itself damnable, since in previous centuries there were, and today there are, many Christians, not at all devoted to papistic errors, who are undoubtedly saved without the knowledge of this truth. For many Fathers brought forth differing opinions concerning the Antichrist, because, being further removed from the fulfillment of these prophecies, they indulged more freely in their own opinions or more incautiously seized upon and propagated the uncertain opinions of others." (Theol. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 16. s. 2. f. 1688.)

Huelsemannus: "Just as in other articles of faith those who attempt to overturn the truth of the thing itself are accustomed to make a beginning from the denial..." *) The same Dannhauerus: "Ψυχοπαννυχία is a fable contrary to the Holy Scriptures, in which the martyrs in Rev. 6:10, 11 cry out with a loud voice under the altar." (p. 719.) ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

necessary knowledge of this matter, just as it happens today with the doctrine of the Antichrist. For although we have already explained the mode of necessity in the thesis, namely that it is hypothetical, not absolute; yet, the hypothesis existing—that is, the presence of the Antichrist and the present danger of seduction—the doctrine of distinguishing the Antichrist from true teachers is no less necessary today than the doctrine concerning the malice and snares of the devils. Compare here the serious admonitions of Christ and the apostles regarding the need to beware of the Antichrist’s snares, which cannot be obeyed without a distinct knowledge of the Antichrist: Matt. 7:24; Luke 12:42 sq., 17:35 sqq., 21:8; 2 Thess. 2; 2 Tim. 3:4; 2 Pet. 2; 1 John 2:4; Rev. 11, 12 sqq.

Latin:

Idem: ,,Müssen wir doch bekennen, dass die Schwärmer die Schrift und Gottes Wort haben in andern Artikeln, und wer es von ihnen höret und gläubt, der wird selig, wiewohl sie unheilige Ketzer und Lästerer Christi sind." (Brief von der Wiedertaufe. 1528. XVII, 2675.) Idem: „Wobei wollte man sonst Unterschied nehmen, welches die rechte Kirche Christi, und welche des Teufels Kirche sei, ohne bei dem Gehorsam und Ungehorsam gegen Christum, sonderlich so der Ungehorsam öffentlich erkannt und verstanden, sich frevelich und frechlich entschuldiget und Recht haben will. Denn die heilige Kirche sündiget und strauchelt oder irret auch wohl, wie das Vater-Unser lehret; aber sie vertheidiget noch entschuldiget sich nicht, sondern bittet demüthiglich um Vergebung und bessert sich, wie sie immer kann; so ist’s ihr vergeben, dass alsdenn ihre Sünde nicht mehr Sünde gerechnet wird. Wenn ich nun bei dem Gehorsam und verstockten Ungehorsam nicht soll erkennen noch unterscheiden die rechte Kirche von der falschen, so weiss ich von keiner Kirche mehr zu sagen." (Brief wegen seines Buches v. d. Winkelmesse. XIX, 1579.) § 34.

Articuli non-fundamentales dicuntur, qui salvo fidei fundamento non solum ignorari, verum etiam negari, aut in utramque partem disputari a possunt. E. g. de peccato DE NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

et rejectione perpetua quorundam angelorum, de immortalitate primi hominis ante lapsum, de Antichristo, b de origine animae per creationem vel traducem c etc.

Fechtius: „Articuli fldei sunt vel fundamentales, vel non-fundamentales. Ubi tamen observandum, distinctionem hanc non esse articulorum proprie dictorum, adeoque univoce sumtam, sed potius distinctionem aequivocam, dum articuli non-fundamentales improprie tantum et remotissime articuli fldei vocantur.“ (Compend., universam th. complexum. Praecognita. C. 1. § 42. p. 29.)

Calvoerius: „Diligenter discernendum inter illa, quae sunt necessaria creditu cuivis fideli ac salvando, et illa, quae sunt ecclesiae ad puritatem, ad expositionem, ad defensionem doctrinae salutaris necessaria; et pertinet huc distinctio inter articulos Christianos ac catholicos, et articulos ecclesiasticos ac theologicos.“ (Fissurae Sionis. Lips. 1710. p. 1172.)

Quenstedtius: „Ad articulos non-fundamentales, sive qui salvo fldei fundamento et ignorari et negari possunt, refert D. Hunnius l. c. § 65. dogma de perpetua angelorum quorundam rejectione; de immortalitate hominis ante lapsum; de Antichristo; de irremissibilitate peccati in Spiritum S.; de libertate christiana in ritibus etc. Haec sive ignorentur, sive negentur, per se nihil damni afferunt fldei, siquidem nullam causam fldei aut dogma fundamentale per sui negationem tollunt.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 5. s. 1. th. 2. ,f. 350.)

Interim etiam in his cavendum est, ne errorem amplectendo aut profitendo in revelationem divinam Deumque ipsum temere peccetur; praesertim, ne contra conscientiam et cum seductione aliorum aliquid statuatur, quo labefactentur fulcra et veritas unius aut plurium articulorum fidei fundamentalium. Sic enim, tanquam per peccatum mortale, excuti tamen potest et solet Spiritus S. et fides. Quo tendunt, quae scripsit b. J. Meisnerus l. c. § 242. p. 207.

N. Hunnius: „Quando in sequentibus haec loquendi forma occurret: potest hoc aut illud dogma salvo fldei fundamento ignorari aut negari, minime hunc fore phraseos sensum, quod ista negatio aut ignoratio salva fide locum habeat; cum talis negatio possit fidei esse exitiosa, quantumvis fldei fundamentum non evertat.“ (Αιάσκεψις § 353.)

Idem: „Fides tollitur per doctrinam, quae rationem habet moralis peccati. Duplex est doctrina homini salutaris; una, quae est proxima causa fldei sive quae facit, ut homo confidat in Deum et Christum, atque hinc peccatorum remissionem et salutem aeternam certo expectat; altera, quae quidem hanc fiduciam non operatur, interim homini a Deo proposita est sive ad fidem declarandam, sive ad discendum alia christianismo necessaria: qui deficit in priore doctrinae genere, is non solum periculose, sed etiam circa fidem errat; qui in posteriore, periculose errat, non tamen circa fldei doctrinam, sed moraliter, ita ut nihil decedat fiduciae (ratione doctrinae, unde fiducia nascitur), quam homo habet ad Deum, attamen provocetur ira Domini. Qua ratione negans historiam Simsonis, Davidis etc., negans, circumcisionem fuisse institutum divinum etc., hoc ipso nihil detrahit fldei fundamento seu doctrinae fundamentali, attamen non absque periculo salutis errat, quod Deo veritatis laudem adimendo mortali peccato illum offendat adeoque iram ejus in se provocet, quod cum dispendio fldei et salutis conjunctum est, nisi agatur poenitentia. Huc pertinet Christi nativitas a virgine aliaque dogmata complura, quorum negatio fundamentalem fldei doctrinam non evertit, vel etiam depravat, Dei tamen iram irritat, unde fides cadit per defectum efficientis causae, etiam stante illius fundamento.“ (AcäoK. § 350.) Multa praeterea requiruntur adeoque necessaria sunt, ut aliquis ecclesiae cujusdam particularis membrum esse queat, et multo magis, ut pastoris in ea fungi possit officio, quae tamen non aeque necessaria sunt ad salutem, adeoque de iis nobis sermo non est.“ (Institt. theol. dogm. p. 41.) Vid. de his b. Nic. Hunnius l. c. § 65. p. 43.

Ad hanc classem referimus doctrinam de Antichristo propter vaticinia Scripturarum, quae apud prophetam Danielem, apud S. Paulum et in Apocalypsi Johannis a Spiritu Sancto nobis sunt revelata. Non autem dicimus, quaestionem hanc de Antichristo esse talem, cujus decisio omnibus Christianis ad salutem scitu sit necessaria, vel ignoratio per se damnabilis, cum et superioribus seculis fuerint et hodie sint multi christiani, erroribus papisticis minime dediti, qui absque hujus veritatis notitia sine dubio salvantur. ### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: Nevertheless, just as the threat and signs of the flood, already imminent and…

Nevertheless, just as the threat and signs of the flood, already imminent and actually beginning to pour down, were mocked by the relatives of Noah (Gen. 6:4, 13; Luke 17:27), so also the mutual mockery and caviling of the Papists and Calvinists, who object to one another the deceits of the Antichrist in trivial and false matters, are not undeservedly held to be a mockery of the thing itself, as if one were to call another Polyphemus, Medusa, Charon, or by some other such name, whose subject one does not believe to exist in the nature of things.” (Praelect. ad Breviar. c. 22, p. 1229.)

So indeed thought the blessed Luther, when, even with the urgent and pressing insistence of Dr. Pomeranus (Bugenhagen) that he determine with certainty what finally ought to be established concerning the origin of the soul, he resisted; and although inclining toward the opinion of traducianism, he nevertheless preferred, with Augustine, to think and contend that it should not be held as an article of faith, against the bold dogmatists who are little attentive in these matters, etc., as reported by the blessed Joh. Wigand, who says he remembers his discourse (lib. de neutralibus et mediis, p. 38, 39), and And. Musculus in LL. Comm. ex patribus collectis Lib. I, pag. 89 sqq., where he presents "Extracts from the mouth of Luther in a dissertation held this year, in which he died, 1546."

Wigand himself, l. c. p. 38, after having brought forward the arguments for both sides, concludes: that it is free to leave the whole matter in the middle, and that it is not to be considered heresy to lean toward either this or that opinion.

And within these bounds, besides the blessed Musculus l. c., other authors of the Formula of Concord also remained: the blessed Mart. Chemnitius (LL. Th. P. I. L. de Pecc. orig. Q. IV, p. m. 234 to 256) and the blessed David Chytraeus (Comment. in Apoc. cap. III, p. 91). Cf. Balduin. (Comm. in Ep. ad Tit. c. III, Q. I, p. 1519). Cf. Luther’s "Disputation on the Distinction of the Persons in the Godhead," Thes. 30—34, 41—50. Opp. Hal. Tom. X, 227 sqq.

Reuschius: “It is also easily evident that articles of faith (simply) not fundamental cannot have their basis in a clear testimony of Holy Scripture; for if, this being posited, they were denied, by that very fact the divinity of Holy Scripture would be denied, and the knowledge of the foundation of faith, which becomes known solely from Holy Scripture, would be undermined. They are also called by some 'theological problems,' the number of which is huge and can be increased daily; but their knowledge is useless and disputes about them are vain.” (Annott. etc. p. 62.)

Balduinus: “The theological matters about which they dispute are not of one kind. Some are not of faith, but of question, or do not directly concern an article of faith, but only some circumstance; such is the dispute about the time the world was created; about the destruction of the world, whether it will be according to substance or accident; about the stature of those rising on the last day; about the location of paradise, in which Enoch and Elijah now live, etc. Concerning these and similar questions, because nothing certain has been decided in Scripture, a probable judgment of reason can be admitted without danger; indeed, in these matters many things can be unknown while maintaining the Christian faith, and one may err in some place without any crime of heretical dogma, says Augustine (lib. 2 de pecc. orig. cont. Pelag. et Celest. c. 23).”

Rechenbergius: "Theological problems are questions which occur in almost all articles of theology, whether thetic, polemic, or even exegetical and moral; but since they do not pertain to the substance of the Christian faith and the economy of salvation designated in the Holy Scriptures, they are usually disputed pro and contra in the schools. Because they have not yet been determined by the common consent of the orthodox church, no one, whether they affirm or deny such questions, ought to be besmirched with the stain of heresy. Many such questions occur in the scholastic theology of the Romanists between the Thomists and the Scotists." (Hierolex. sub tit. Probl, p. 1309.)

Huelsemannus: "That the ministerial proximate cause, or the individual writing a certain canonical book, be known by name, and that no error be committed regarding the name, we deny that this is necessary to be believed for salvation. ... Whether Philip or Bartholomew wrote that Gospel which is read under the name of Mark makes no difference to saving faith. ... The θεόπνευστος (divine inspiration) of Holy Scripture is perceived from the internal nature of the things themselves, not from the quality of the speaker." (Anti-Bellarminus. c. 9. § 10. p. 106. sq.) The same: "That this book is of a prophet and not an apostle, and vice versa, and that the authors had this or that name—for example, to be ignorant of or to think that Barnabas, Joseph, or anyone else besides Luke was the writer of the Acts of the Apostles (the certainty of which things or facts the Papists require as necessary to be known and believed, and that it must be drawn from tradition alone)—is not an article of Christian faith, and when it is known, it is not believed by divine faith, but by human faith. ... Some, like Brochmand (art. 2. c. 8. qu. 5.), deny that knowledge of the numerical quantity of the canonical books is necessary for salvation." (Praelectt. in Form. Conc. Art. I. c. 3. § 12. p. 225.)

Quenstedtius: "We deny that the catalog of canonical books is an article of faith, added over and above the rest of the things contained in Scripture. Many have faith and can attain salvation who do not know the number of the canonical books." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 8. f. 135.) § 35. The formal object of theology, which is divine revelation, exercises its function through this, that it affects, strikes, and bends the human will, so that it may command the intellect to give assent.

Reuschius: "The formal object of revealed theology is revelation or Holy Scripture, insofar as by its aid a) dogmas are determined, and β) the knowledge of these is raised to that clarity in which it is living and possesses immovable assent. ... Therefore, he who has investigated the true sense of Holy Scripture through his natural cognitive faculty, and from this has determined the dogmas which explain the kingdom of grace and things connected to it, and has reduced them into a system for further declaration, but has not attained the living knowledge of these dogmas through the supernatural efficacy of Holy Scripture on account of malicious resistance, he has obtained a part of the formal reason in that knowledge which he ought to have of the kingdom of grace and things connected to it through theology—namely, that that knowledge of the kingdom of grace and things connected to it is derived solely from revelation or Holy Scripture; but the other part of that formal reason in this knowledge, namely that it be living, is lacking, and therefore the formal object of theology has place in that man only in part." (Annott. in B. Comp. p. 53. 55.) See above § 25. and note c. ON THE NATURE OF THEOLOGY.

For divine revelation contains these two principles: The first, that whatever God says or reveals is true; the second, that this—or (when we speak of revealed theology and its formal object regarding the present state) whatever is contained in the Holy Scriptures—is what God says. The former principle is evident from the nature and attributes of God known through the light of nature.

The latter is non-evident, and therefore, since the intellect cannot clearly perceive its truth, or the identity of the predicate with the subject, it is necessary that assent be commanded to the intellect by the will, and that the will be enticed or moved by the revelation itself, so that it may determine the intellect to assent. Thus, in Acts 16:14, it is said that the Lord opened the heart of Lydia, that is, that He effectively moved her soul—which is often called by the name of "heart" in the Scriptures—so that she might attend to those things which were spoken by Paul, or that the will itself might apply the intellect to attention and to the rendering of assent. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* c. III. § 39. p. 184.

Meanwhile, theology, formally considered, remains a habit of the intellect. For it does not cease to be a habit of knowing and assenting; however, it connotes or presupposes a certain habit of the will, which the authors of pious affection call [such]. Musaeus, *l. c.* § 42. p. 185. § 36.

And hence it is evident that theology is a habit in its substance supernatural, acquired indeed by our acts, but through the powers of grace and the operation of the Holy Spirit. Or, such as it is and ought to be in itself and by the power of its genuine formal object; or, considered regarding the genuine habit of assenting. For if you look precisely at the habit of apprehending objects already revealed and handing them down to others, in this sense, if the supernatural habit of assenting is absent—as it falls to unregenerate and impious men—then it is theology only equivocally so called. Blessed Musaeus, *l. c.* § 42, 43. p. 189 sqq. Cf. Mr. Dr. Ph. J. Spener, *Tr. Germ.: Die allgemeine Gottes-Gelahrtheit etc.* [The General Theology of God, etc.], P. I. Qu. V. p. 185 sqq., where the consonant passages of many of our theologians are brought forward.

Luther: "One finds more heathen and human conceits than holy, certain doctrine of Scripture in the theologians. How shall we now deal with this? I know no other counsel here than a humble prayer to God that He Himself may give us Doctors of Theology; the Pope, Emperor, and universities may make Doctors of Art, Medicine, Law, and the Sentences; but be assured, no one will make you a Doctor of Holy Scripture except the Holy Spirit alone from heaven, as Christ says in John 6:45: 'They shall all be taught by God Himself.'" (*To the Christian Nobility, etc.*, 1520. X, 383 sq.)

The same: "There is a twofold clarity of Scripture, just as there is a twofold obscurity: one external, placed in the ministry of the Word; the other situated in the knowledge of the heart. If you speak of the internal clarity, no man sees one iota in the Scriptures unless he has the Spirit of God; all have a darkened heart, so that even if they speak and know how to utter all things of Scripture, they nevertheless feel or truly know nothing of these, nor do they believe in God, nor that they are creatures of God, nor anything else, according to that of Psalm 14: 'The fool has said in his heart, God is nothing.' For the Spirit is required to understand the whole of Scripture and any part of it. If you speak of the external [clarity], nothing at all is left obscure or ambiguous, but all things that are in the Scriptures have been brought into the most certain light by the Word and declared to the whole world." (*De servo arbitrio* [On the Bondage of the Will]. A. 1525. *Opp. lat. ad ref. hist. pert. cur. Dr. H. Schmidt.* Vol. VII. p. 127. Cf. Walch, Vol. XVIII, 2071 sq.)

Latin:

Verumtamen ut comminatio et signa diluvii jam imminentis et actu jam depluentis ridebantur tamen ab affinibus Noae, Gen. 6, 4.13. Luc. 17, 27., sic etiam mutuae irrisiones et cavillationes Pontificiorum et Calvinianorum, objicientium sibi invicem Antichristi dolos in rebus ludicris et falsis, non immerito habentur pro derisione rei ipsius, ac si quis alterum Polyphemum, Medusam, Charontem aut alio ejusmodi nomine vocet, cujus subjectum in rerum natura non credit existere.“ (Praelect. ad Breviar. c. 22. p. 1229.)

Ita sane existimavit b. Lutherus, quando etiam urgente et instante D. Pomerano (Bugenhagio), ut determinaret certo, quid tandem de origine animae statuendum esset, reluctatus est; et licet inclinans in sententiam de traduce, tamen cum Augustino maluit sentire et pugnare, non esse pro articulo fidei habendum, contra dogmatistas audace, qui parum in his rebus sint attenti etc., referentibus b. Joh. Wigando, qui se ejus discursus meminisse ait, lib. de neutralibus et mediis p. 38. 39., et And. Musculo in LL. Comm. ex patribus collectis Lib. I. pag. 89. sqq., ubi exhibet Excepta ex ore Lutheri in dissertatione habita hoc anno, quo obiit, 1546.

Ipse autem Wigandus l. c. p. 38., postquam rationes pro utraque parte adduxisset, concludit: liberum esse, totam rem in medio relinquere, nec esse haeresin putandam, vel in hanc, vel illam sententiam deflectere.

Atque intra hos terminos substiterunt praeter b. Musculum l. c. etiam alii auctores Form. Conc.: b. Mart. Chemnitius LL. Th. P. I. L. de Pecc. orig. Q. IV. p. m. 234. ad 256. et b. David Chytraeus Comment. in Apoc. cap. III. p. 91. Conf. Balduin. Comm. in Ep. ad Tit. c. III. Q. I. p. 1519.Cf. Lutheri Disputation von der Unterscheidung der Personen in der Gottheit. Thes. 30—34. 41—50. Opp. Hal. Tom. X, 227. sqq.

Reuschius: ,,Facile patet quoque, quod articuli fidei (simpliciter) non fundamentales in perspicuo sacrae Scripturae testimonio non habere possint sui rationem; nam si, posito hoc, negarentur, eo ipso divinitas sacrae Scripturae negaretur atque cognitio de fidei fundamento, quod ex sacra Scriptura innotescit unice, subrueretur. Vocantur quoque a nonnullis problemata theologica, quorum numerus est ingens atque in dies augeri potest; sed inutilis est eorum cognitio et vanae sunt de iisdem disputationes.“ (Annott. etc. p. 62.)

Balduinus: „Materiae theologicae, de quibus disputant, non sunt unius generis. Quaedam non sunt fldei, sed quaestionis, vel non directe articulum fidei, sed circumstantiam tantum aliquam concernunt; qualis est disputatio de tempore creati mundi; de interitu mundi, num vel secundum substantiam vel accidens futurus sit; de statura resurgentium in novissimo die; de loco paradisi, in quo jam vivunt Enoch et Elias etc. De his et similibus quaestionibus, quia nihil certi in Scriptura decisum est, absque periculo probabile rationis judicium admitti potest; quin et in iis multa ignorari queunt salva fide Christiana, et alicubi errari sine aliquo haeretici dogmatis crimine, inquit Augustinus lib. 2. de pecc. orig. cont. Pelag. et Celest. c. 23.“

Rechenbergius: „Problemata theologica sunt quaestiones, quae in omnibus fere articulis theologiae tum theticae, tum polemicae, tum etiam exegeticae ac moralis occurrunt; sed cum substantiam fldei Christianae et oeconomiae salutis in s. literis designatae non attineant, pro et contra in scholis disputari solent. Quia communi ecclesiae orthodoxae consensu nondum fuerunt determinatae, et nemo, sive tales quaestiones affirmet, sive neget, labe haereseos adspergi debet. Tales in theologia scholastica Romanensium inter Thomistas et Scotistas plurimae occurrunt.“ (Hierolex. sub tit. Probl, p. 1309.)

Huelsemannus: ,,Ut ministerialis causa proxima seu individuum scribens librum quendam canonicum nomine tenus certo agnoscatur, nec in nomine committatur error, id negamus ad salutem esse creditu necessarium. . . Sive Philippus seu Bartholomaeus conscripserit illud evangelium, quod Marci nomine legitur, nihil facit ad fldem salviflcam. ... Ex interna rerum indole, non dicentis qualitate, animadvertitur sacrae Scripturae ΰ-εώτης.“ (Anti-Bellarminus. c. 9. § 10. p. 106. sq.) Idem: ,,Hunc librum esse prophetae et non apostoli et vicissim, et hoc vel illud fuisse auctoribus nomen, v. g. scriptorem Actorum apostolicorum, vel ignorare vel putare Barnabam, Josephum, aut alium quencunque praeter Lucam (cujusmodi rerum sive factorum certitudinem pontificii requirunt, ut scitu et creditu necessariam, eamque ex sola traditione depromendam), non est articulus Christianae fidei, et quando cognoscitur, non creditur divina fide, sed humana. . . Quidam, ut Brochm. art. 2. c. 8. qu. 5., negant, necessariam esse ad salutem notitiam quantitatis numericae librorum canonicorum.“ (Praelectt. in Form. Cone. Art. I. c. 3. § 12. p. 225.)

Quenstedtius: „Negamus, librorum canonicorum catalogum esse articulum fldei, reliquis in Scriptura contentis superadditum. Multi fldem habent et salutem consequi possunt, qui numerum librorum canonicorum non tenqnt.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 8. f. 135.) § 35. Objectum formale theologiae, quod est revelatio a divina, per hoc b exercet munus suum, quod voluntatem humanam c afficit, pulsat et flectit, ut intellectui imperet assensum.

Reuschius: „Objectum formale theologiae revelatae est revelatio seu sacra Scriptura, quatenus ope illius a) dogmata determinantur, atque ß) horum cognitio ad eam claritatem evehitur, in qua est viva atque assensum habet immotum. . . Quapropter, qui, per facultatem cognoscitivam naturalem verum sacrae Scripturae sensum investigavit, hinc dogmata, quae regnum gratiae eidemque connexa explicant, determinavit atque illa, ad ulteriorem declarationem, in systema redegit, sed vivam horum dogmatum cognitionem per efficaciam sacrae Scripturae supernaturalem propter resistentiam malitiosam non est adsecutus, is partem rationis formalis in illa cognitione, quam de regno gratiae eidemque connexis habere debet per theologiam, obtinuit, scil, quod illa cognitio de regno gratiae eidemque connexis ex revelatione seu sacra Scriptura sit unice derivata; altera vero pars illius rationis formalis in hac cognitione, scilicet ut sit viva, deficit, eoque objectum formale theologiae ex parte modo habet locum in illo homine.“ (Annott. in B. Comp. p. 53. 55.) Vid. supra § 25. et not. c. DB NATURA THEOLOGIAE.

Continet enim revelatio divina haec duo principia: Unum, quicquid Deus dicit, seu revelat, id verum, est; alterum, hoc, seu (quando de theologia revelata ejusque objecto formali pro statu praesente loquimur) quicquid in Scripturis s. continetur, Deus dicit Prius principium evidens est ex natura et attributis Dei per lumen naturae cognitis.

Posterius inevidens est, adeoque, cum intellectus non possit veritatem ejus, seu identitatem praedicati cum subjecto, clare perspicere, necesse est, assensum intellectui a voluntate imperari ac propterea voluntatem ab ipsa revelatione allici seu moveri, ut intellectum ad assensum determinet. Sic Act. 16, 14. dicitur, Dominum, aperuisse cor Lydiae, id est, animam, quae cordis nomine in scripturis saepe appellatur, efficaciter movisse, ut attenderet his, quae a Paulo dicebantur, seu ut voluntas ipsa intellectum ad attentionem ac praebendum assensum applicaret. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. c. III. § 39. p. 184.

Interim theologia formaliter spectata manet habitus intellectus. Non enim desinit esse habitus cognoscendi atque assentiendi; connotat autem aut supponit habitum quendam voluntatis, quem piae affectionis auctores vocant. Mus. l. c. § 40. p. 185.§ 36.

Atque hinc constat, theologiam esse habitum in substantia sua a supernaturalem, actibus nostris b quidem, sed per vires gratiae et operationem Spiritus Sancti c acquisitum. d Seu qualis per se et vi genuini objecti sui formalis est et esse debet; vel, quoad habitum assentiendi genuinum spectata. Nam si spectes praecise habitum apprehendendi objecta dudum revelata et apprehensa aliis tradendi, hoc sensu, si absit habitus assentiendi supernaturalis, sicut in homines non renatos atque impios cadit, ita non nisi aequivoce dicta theologia est. B. Mus. l. c. § 42. 43. p. 189. sqq. Conf. Dn. D. Ph. J. Speneri Tr. Germ.: Die allgemeine Gottes-Gelahrtheit etc. P. I. Qu. V. p. 185. sqq., ubi multorum theologorum nostratium loca consona afferuntur.

Lutherus: „Man findet melir heidnische und menschliche Dünkel, denn heilige gewisse Lehre der Schrift in den Theologen. Wie wollen wir ihm nun thun? Ich weiss hie keinen ändern Rath, denn ein demüthiges Gebet zu Gott, dass uns derselbe Doctores Theologiae gebe; Doctores der Kunst, der Arznei, der Rechten, der Sententien mögen der Pabst, Kaiser und Universitäten machen; aber sei nur gewiss, einen Doctor der heiligen Schrift wird dir niemand machen, denn alleine der Heilige Geist vom Himmel, wie Christus saget Joh. 6, 45.: ,Sie müssen alle von Gott selber gelehret sein.'" (An den christl. Adel etc. 1520. X, 383. sq.)

Idem: „Duplex est claritas Scripturae, sicut et duplex obscuritas, una extema in verbi ministerio posita, altera in cordis cognitione sita. Si de interna claritate 'dixeris, nullus homo unum jota in. Scripturis videt, nisi qui spiritum Dei habet, omnes habent obscuratum cor, ita ut, si etiam dicant et norint proferre omnia Scripturae, nihil tamen horum PROLEGOM. CAP. I. sentiant aut vere cognoscant, neque credunt Deum, nec sese esse creaturas Dei, nec quicquam aliud, juxta illud Ps. 14.: ,Dixit insipiens in corde suo, Deus nihil est.· Spiritus enim requiritur ad totam Scripturam et ad quamlibet ejus partem intelligendam. Si de externa dixeris, nihil prorsus relictum est obscurum aut ambiguum, sed omnia sunt per verbum in lucem producta certissimam, et declarata toto orbi, quaecunque sunt in Scripturis.“ (De servo arbitrio. A. 1525. Opp. lat. ad ref. hist. pert. cur. Dr. H. Schmidt. Vol. VII. p. 127. Cf. Hai. Tom. XVIII, 2071. sq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Nature of Theology: The same: "Thus you can conclude for yourself that St

The same: "Thus you can conclude for yourself that St. Matthew here (5:23) is not to be understood as referring to the common works that everyone ought to do toward another out of love, of which he speaks in Matthew 25:35ff., but most especially of the true Christian work: such as teaching rightly, promoting the faith, and instructing, strengthening, and maintaining others in it, by which we testify that we are true Christians. For the others are not as certain, because even false Christians can adorn and cover themselves with great, beautiful works of love. But to teach and confess Christ rightly is not possible without faith. As St. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 12:3: 'No one can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit.' For no false Christian or sectarian spirit can understand this doctrine. How much less will he preach and confess it rightly, even if he takes the words and repeats them, yet does not abide by them nor leave them pure? He always preaches in such a way that one grasps that he does not have it right, yet smears his slaver upon it, thereby taking his honor from Christ and attributing it to himself. Therefore, that is the most certain work of a true Christian alone, when he praises and preaches Christ in such a way that people learn how they are nothing and Christ is everything." (Exposition of the 5th, 6th, and 7th Chapters of Matthew. 1532. VII, 623.)

Musaeus: "He who is born and raised in the church and, as it were, imbibes with his mother's milk the opinion that the book of the Scriptures contains the word divinely revealed and committed to writing by divine inspiration, he certainly believes this on account of the testimony and authority of his parents. In this faith, he can be confirmed by the authority of the church spread far and wide throughout the world and by other signs or motives of credibility, even though he may be a hypocrite and, through malice, may place an obstacle to the grace that would work a certain and divine faith in this matter through the Word itself. Although he may give assent to the Scriptures, albeit only of human faith or opinion, he can furthermore acquire for himself, through human study, the habit of interpreting the Scriptures, of deducing conclusions from them, and of confirming and defending them, and this again with an assent resting upon human authority. Experience also testifies to this. For there are found impious men, and even heretics, who are often more adept at explaining the Scriptures and deducing, confirming, and defending conclusions from them than other orthodox and most pious theologians. This is perhaps the reason why serious authors have ascribed theology simply to natural habits, which also fall to unregenerate men. But this, which we readily acknowledge to be a natural habit, is theology spoken of equivocally, and it is as far removed from theology properly so called as human faith or opinion, conceived in the mind from external motives regarding the truth of divine revelation, is removed from divine faith. For its ultimate reason for assenting is entirely different from the ultimate reason for assenting of theology properly so called. For the ultimate reason for the assent of the latter, as has been said, is the First Truth revealing, as revealing, which, through the revelation related in the Scriptures, elevated by its supernatural concurrence, moves the intellect and the will of itself immediately—the latter to command the intellect to assent, the former to elicit the same within itself—so that the assent rests ultimately in that [First Truth]. But the ultimate reason for the assent of the former, as has just been shown, is human authority, namely that of parents and the church, which generates human faith, or miracles or other motives, which generate opinion; e.g., a hypocrite..."

or a secret heretic, who feigns being a theologian, will indeed assent to this conclusion derived by himself from the Scriptures: "Christ is ὁμοούσιος to God the Father," on account of this: "Christ is the only-begotten Son of God"; but he does not believe it immediately through and because of itself, so that his assent rests ultimately in the authority of the primary truth revealing, but because he sees that it is contained in the Gospel of John. And he believes that those things which are contained in the Gospel of John are true, because from his tender years he was so taught by his parents or instructors, or received from the church that what is contained therein is revealed by God and infallibly true. And in this testimony of parents, instructors, or the church, as in the ultimate reason for assenting, his assent finally rests. But just as that testimony is human, so it can produce nothing but human faith or opinion; and just as the acts of assenting of theology, spoken of in this second sense, resting in this ultimate testimony, are in substance natural and merely opinionative, so theology itself, taken in this way, is a habit in substance natural and merely opinionative.

But theology properly so called, because it rests ultimately in the primary truth revealing, is a habit in substance supernatural and simply certain. For the primary truth revealing, whenever it sustains the office of the ultimate reason for assenting and moves the intellect immediately through itself into its assent, generates an assent in substance supernatural, and that not opinionative, but simply certain, to which it is utterly repugnant that anything false should underlie it. . . Nor can it be acquired through acts other than those into which the primary truth revealing, as revealing, moves the intellect by itself and by its own nature, as its ultimate reason for assenting, namely, through acts in substance supernatural, which, elicited by the primary truth illuminating the intellect through its revelation and drawing the will into consent, leave behind them a disposition inclining toward other similar acts, from the repetition of which is finally generated a habit of the same nature as them, i.e., in substance supernatural. . .

It must be repeated that theology can be taken in a double sense. One, for the habit of declaring, confirming, and defending those things which have been revealed for the sake of our salvation, resting precisely upon the primary truth revealing, as revealing, as the ultimate reason for assenting. The other, for the habit of explaining, confirming, and defending the same things from the Scriptures, yet not resting upon the primary truth revealing, but upon human authority or other motives of credibility generating opinion, as the ultimate reason for assenting.

We grant that theology taken in this latter sense falls even upon unregenerate men. But this, as was shown in the aforementioned place, is theology spoken of equivocally. But we deny and utterly deny that theology taken in the former way falls upon unregenerate men. For it is, as we taught in the same place: a habit in substance supernatural, which therefore finds a place only in the regenerate, nor can it be obtained without the supernatural grace of God and the concurrence with His Word, which elevates it to testify of itself. . .

Therefore, faith can exist in a man without the habit of theology, yet the habit of theology properly so called cannot exist in anyone without the habit of faith." (Introd. in th. P. I. c. 3. §§ 43—45. p. 190—192. 193. 195. sq. 199.)

Understand this today, and according to the common law, or ordinarily. For otherwise we do not deny that the habit of theology can be obtained in an extraordinary way through immediate divine illumination and inspiration, as happened to the prophets and apostles. Blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 43. p. 192. 193., blessed Gerhard, Exeg. prooem. § 17. p. 9.

For which reason some call theology a habit θεόδοτον: which blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 44. p. 169., acknowledges is rightly said in this sense, or having regard to the gracious concurrence or illumination of God, although, taking the word in the Aristotelian sense (to which εὐδαιμονία is called θεόδοτος in I. Nicom. IX. in opposition to those things which are acquired by our study and labor), he has not denied without cause that our theology is θεόδοτον. L. c. p. 194.

Gerhard: "We certainly admit that, if a certain genus from the intellectual habits enumerated by Aristotle is to be attributed to theology, wisdom among all of them approaches most closely to its nature; meanwhile, if it is considered absolutely, it is more correctly defined by a habit ϑεόδοτος [God-given] than by a genus taken from the Aristotelian intellectual habits; since, as Savonarola warns (lib. III. de scient. divis, p. 800), 'it is learned rather by purity of heart, good works, contemplation, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit than by the power of intellect,' which he proves in the same place from John 6:45." (Exeg. loc. prooem. § 10.)

Quenstedt: "The question is not... about the habit ϑεόδοτος by reason of immediate infusion, but by reason of discovery, principle, and object... We distinguish between the assisting grace of the Holy Spirit and the indwelling grace; theology as a habit is conferred not so much by the latter as by the former. For this is a divine information, by which theologians are made, an operation of the grace of the Holy Spirit not precisely indwelling, but rather assisting, which assisting grace even the unregenerate and the impious possess in a certain way. But in those who are theologians both in reality and in name—that is, who are not only instructed by the theological habit as such, but are at the same time reborn, or are faithful and pious—in them, theology is not only from the Holy Spirit, but is also with the Holy Spirit and joined with His gracious indwelling." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 1. s. 2. q. 3. f. 22. sq.)

Deyling: "The habit is called ϑεόδοτος because it contains sanctifying and administrative gifts, which are not to be separated from one another. Both are χαρίσματα and supernatural gifts, the collation and distribution of which is expressly ascribed to God, from whom πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαϑή [every good gift] (James 1:17), or to the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:4; 2 Cor. 3:5)." (Institut. prud. past. prooem. p. 2.)

Successively, indeed, and not without the labor and study of some years. In which sense the blessed Scherzer also says that theology is an acquired habit, because it includes meditation (Ps. 1:2), for which the apparatus of arts and languages is a prerequisite, and prayer (Ps. 119:18). (System. theol. proleg. § 8. p. 3.; cf. the blessed Gerhard in Exeg. l. c. § 17. p. 9.)

Luther: "Concerning that, I will show you a right way to study in theology, which I have practiced; if you hold to the same, you shall be so learned that you yourself could (if there were need) make books as good as the Fathers and Councils. As I (in God) may also presume and boast without pride and lies, that I would not yield much to some of the Fathers when it comes to book-making; of my life, I cannot by far boast the same. And this is the way that the holy King David (without doubt also all the patriarchs and prophets held) teaches in the 119th Psalm; there you will find three rules, abundantly set forth throughout the whole Psalm, and they are called thus: Oratio, Meditatio, Tentatio.

Latin:

Idem: „So kannst du nun selbst schliessen, dass St. Matthäus hier (5, 23.) nicht zu verstehen ist von den gemeinen Werken, die ein jeglicher gegen dem ändern thun soll, aus der Liebe, davon er Matth. 25, 35. ff. redet, sondern allermeist von dem rechten christlichen Werk: als rechtschaffen lehren, den Glauben treiben und darinne unterrichten, stärken und erhalten, damit wir bezeugen, dass wir rechtschaffene Christen sind. Denn die andern sind nicht so gewiss, weil auch wohl falsche Christen sich können schmücken und decken unter grossen, schönen Werken der Liebe. Aber Christum recht lehren und bekennen, ist nicht möglich ohne den Glauben. Wie St. Paulus 1 Cor. 12, 3. sagt: ,Niemand kann Jesum einen Herrn heissen, ohne durch den Heiligen Geist.' Denn kein falscher Christ noch Rottengeist kann diese Lehre verstehen. Wie viel weniger wird er sie recht predigen und bekennen, ob er gleich die Worte mitnimmt und nachredet, aber doch nicht dabei bleibet noch rein lässet? predigt immer also, dass man greift, dass ers nicht recht habe, schmieret doch seinen Geifer daran, dadurch er Christo seine Ehre nimmt und ihm selbst zumisset. Darum ist das allein das gewisseste Werk eines rechten Christen, wenn er Christum so preiset und predigt, dass die Leute solches lernen, wie sie nichts und Christus alles ist.“ (Ausl, des 5. 6. 7. Cap. Matthäi. 1532. VII, 623.)

Musaeus: ,,Qui in ecclesia natus et educatus est et a parentibus cum lacte quasi imbibit opinionem, quod Scripturarum codex contineat verbum divinitus patefactum et ex divina inspiratione in literas relatum, is credit utique hoc propter testimonium et auctoritatem parentum. Qua in fide confirmari potest auctoritate ecclesiae longe lateque per orbem diffusae et signis sive motivis credibilitatis aliis, quamvis hypocrita sit et per malitiam gratiae, hujus rei fidem certam divinamque per verbum ipsum operaturae, obicem ponat. Etsi assensum praebeat Scripturis, licet fidei humanae tantum vel opinionis, potest porro studio humano sibi acquirere habitum Scripturas interpretandi, conclusiones ex illis deducendi, confirmandi ac defendendi, idque rursum cum assensu humana auctoritate nixo. Quod et experientia testatur. Reperiuntur enim homines impii, quin et haeretici, qui in explicandis Scripturis et conclusionibus inde deducendis; confirmandis ac defendendis saepe expeditiores sunt, quam alii orthodoxi ac pientissimi theologi. Quae forsan causa est, cur theologiam simpliciter habitibus naturalibus et qui in homines non renatos etiam cadunt, auctores graves adscripserint. Verum haec, quam habitum naturalem esse ultro agnoscimus, aequivoce dicta theologia est et a theologia proprie dicta tanto distat intervallo, quanto fides humana vel opinio, ex motivis externis de veritate divinae revelationis animo concepta, a fide divina distat. Ejus enim ratio assentiendi ultima plane diversa est a ratione assentiendi ultima theologiae proprie dictae. Hujus enim ratio assentiendi ultima, uti dictum, est prima veritas revelans, ut revelans, quae per relatam in Scripturas revelationem, suo supernaturali concursu elevatam, intellectum et voluntatem per se immediate movet, hanc quidem ad. assensum intellectui imperandum, illum ad eundem in se eliciendum, ita ut assensus ultimo in illa sistat. Illius vero ratio assentiendi ultima, ut modo ostensum, est auctoritas humana, parentum scl. et ecclesiae, quae fidem humanam, vel miracula aut motiva alia, quae opinionem generant; v. g. hypocrita

vel haereticus occultus, qui theologum mentitur, assentietur quidem huic ex Scripturis a se deductae conclusioni: Christus est Deo Patri δμοονσως, propter hanc: Christus est Filius Dei unigenitus; sed non per et propter se immediate creditam, ut in auctoritate primae veritatis revelantis ultimo sistat assensus, sed quod videt, eam in Evangelio Johannis contineri. Quae autem in evangelio Johannis continentur, credit esse vera, quod a teneris ita a parentibus vel praeceptoribus edoctus sit, vel ab ecclesia acceperit, quae in eo continentur, esse a Deo revelata et infallibiliter vera. Atque in hoc parentum, praeceptorum vel ecclesiae testimonio, velut in ratione assentiendi ultima, sistit tandem assensus ipsius. Sicut Autem testimonium illud humanum est, ita non nisi fldem humanam vel opinionem gignere potest; et ut theologiae, in hoc altero sensu dictae, actus assentiendi, in hoc testimonio ultimo sistentes, in substantia naturales et mere opinativi sunt, ita theologia ipsa sic accepta habitus in substantia naturalis et mere opinativus est.

Sed theologia prbprie dicta, quia in prima veritate revelante ultimo sistit, habitus in substantia supernaturalis et simpliciter certus est. Nam prima veritas revelans, quandocunque sustinet munus rationis assentiendi ultimae ac per se immediate intellectum in sui assensum movet, gignit assensum in substantia supematuralem, eumque non opinativum, sed simpliciter certum, cui falsum subesse prorsus repugnat. . . Non autem per actus alios acquiri potest, quam eos, in quos per se et suapte natura movet prima veritas revelans, ut revelans, tamquam ejus ratio assentiendi ultima, nempe per actus in substantia supernaturales, qui, veritate prima intellectum per suam revelationem illuminante voluntatemque in consensum trahente eliciti, relinquunt post se dispositionem ad alios similes actus inclinantem, ex quibus iteratis tandem gignitur habitus ejusdem cum illis naturae h. e. in substantia supernaturalis. . .

Repetendum, theologiam posse accipi in significatu duplici.
