### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Regarding the fallibility of the Roman Pontiff, cf

Regarding the fallibility of the Roman Pontiff, cf. Gerhard, *Confessio catholica*, Lib. I, P. II, c. 2, f. 77–111.

Quenstedtius: "That this principle of the Papists—'Whatever the Roman Pontiff determines, that is infallibly true'—cannot be a first principle is evident from the fact that they attempt to prove it from elsewhere, namely, from Scripture itself, Matt. 16:18, John 21:15, 16, 17... Those who 1. can err in the doctrine of faith and become heretics, 2. have sanctioned many erroneous dogmas *ex cathedra*, and 3. contradict themselves: they cannot be the principle of faith and of theological conclusions." (L. c., f. 51.)

The same: "Nor is human reason, or natural theology, the principle of supernatural things." (L. c., f. 55.)

The same: "Thesis I is proved from the nature of the mysteries of faith... II. From the nature of reason, which is entirely blind in supernatural matters... III. From the silence of Scripture. Nowhere are Christ, the prophets, or the apostles read to have used this principle, nor does Scripture ever remit us to the judgment of reason in defining matters of faith. For thus the Calvinists have hitherto believed with us: 'What is not written is not to be held.' IV. From the examples of the pious, who in matters of faith did not follow the judgment of reason, but believed while it contradicted them in vain, such as Abraham, Rom. 4:18, who, against hope (dictating the barrenness of reason), believed in hope (of God promising) that he would be the father of many nations according to the saying (Gen. 15:5): 'So shall your offspring be.' And not being weakened in faith, he did not consider (οὐ κατενόησε) his own body now dead... Compare the example of Naaman, 2 Kings 5:10, 11, 13; Paul, Gal. 1:15, 16. V. From the examples of those who, having followed the judgment of reason in matters of faith, either erred most gravely or perished most miserably, such as the incredulous captain, 2 Kings 7:12, Nicodemus, John 3:4, 9, Thomas, John 20:25, the Sadducees, Matt. 22:23." (L. c., f. 59.)

The same: "Antithesis I. Of the Scholastics, whose entire theology is nothing other than a mixture of theology and philosophy, or, in the judgment of Erasmus in the *Praise of Folly*, 'a discipline forged from divine utterances and philosophical reasonings, like a biform mixture of the Centaur kind.' For in the highest mysteries of faith, the Scholastics derive their conclusions from logical, physical, and metaphysical principles, while omitting or only lightly touching upon the sayings of Scripture, as we insinuated in Chapter 1, Section 1, Thesis 2, Note 8, page 3. II. Of the Papists and especially the Jesuits, who not rarely prove articles of faith from the principles of reason—see Bellarmine, Book IV *de poenit.* c. 5, Book III *de Eucharistia* c. 22, Book II *de Missa* c. 4, Book IV *de Christi anima* c. 10—and sometimes impugn the same from the principles of reason—see Bellarmine, Book IV *de Monachis* c. 6, Book II *de justific.* c. 7 (where he denies 'the imputation of Christ’s righteousness, insofar as it conflicts with reason'), Book IV *de Eccl.* c. 11. Gregory of Valencia, in Book VIII *de analys. fid. cathol.* c. 6, p. 101, among the documents 'for understanding Scripture and deciding matters of faith,' places this sixth and final point: 'that natural reason also be consulted.' III. Of the Calvinists; for that they preposterously subject the mysteries of faith to the magisterium of reason, or even impugn the same from philosophical principles, can be evidently demonstrated both from their practice and from their words. See Sturm in the *Ambrosian Epistle* to Pappus, p. 5; Nicolaus Taurellus in the dedicatory epistle of *Triumphus*, where he calls philosophy 'the foundation of faith'; Ludovicus Crocius in *Assertion. A. C.*, disputation 1; Conrad Vorstius, *Anti-Pistorian Disputation* XV, where he says, 'the principles of faith are twofold: partly natural, such as sense and reason, and all axioms known by the natural light of reason; partly supernatural,' etc. Goclenius, in *Metaphysical Disputation* XV, thesis 1, writes: 'In the studies of human and heavenly wisdom, I acknowledge the ministry, the magisterium, and a certain judgment and command of dialectic; that is, I establish dialectic as both the minister and mistress, and the judge and queen or regulator of teaching and understanding things both sacred and profane.' Zwingli, in the Marburg Colloquy, made that saying of Averroes and the Socinians his own: 'nothing

ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

that it is to be believed, because it cannot be comprehended by reason, because God does not propose incomprehensible things to us," Philip [Melanchthon] notes in a brief annotation regarding the Marburg Colloquy; see Chytraeus’ *History of the Augsburg Confession*, p. 641. Vedelius says in *Rationalis Theologia*, Book III, ch. 6, pp. 513, 531, etc., "that reason is a norm, not primary, but secondary, to which some degree of perfection may be added." But the principle of nature, which Vedelius—and Massonius with him—make a secondary principle of faith when speaking in theory, they make the primary principle of faith in practice and use, as D. Jacob Martini demonstrates in his treatise *De Principio Fidei*, disputation VII, § 9 ff. Keckermann, in Book I of his *Systema Theologiae*, ch. 4, writes thus: "That God wills to kindle the light of His Holy Spirit in the minds of men through those two clearly divine disciplines, metaphysics and logic, using this as an aid"; he further says: "That He will declare this mystery (of the Most Holy Trinity)." See D. Menzer in his response to the second defense of the Prussian Conversion of Crocius, ch. 2, vol. I of his Works, p. 858 ff. Peter Martyr, in his preface to the Book of Kings, says: "Not so much the divine word, as also the words of nature are to be followed in theology." IV. Of the Socinians, who establish reason as a second principle of theology alongside the Word of God and judge that the Christian religion must be bent to it, as this is their axiom: "Nothing is true in theology which is not approved by reason." Likewise: "Nothing can be believed which cannot be grasped and understood by reason." These are the words of Slichtingius in his *Disputation on the Trinity against Meisner*, p. 125. Compare Smalcius, disp. 4 on justification against Franzius, fol. 137, and disp. 8, f. 421. "Nothing can in any way be true to which reason and common sense are repugnant," says Socinus in *On the Authority of Scripture*, p. 54. Indeed, that blasphemous assault on the Most Holy Trinity and the Incarnation flowed from no other source than the dictate of predominant human reason, which these men—even though they do not wish to appear to do so—far prefer to the dictate of the Holy Spirit speaking in the Holy Scriptures. For thus Osterodus writes in his *German Institution*, ch. 4, p. 31: "If reason expressly demonstrates that the trinity of persons in God is false, who then, among sensible men, would ever let it enter his mind that it is nevertheless true and can be proven from the Word of God." V. Of the Arminians, who allow nothing in religion unless it conforms to reason, and who judge that the judgment concerning the mysteries of faith must be committed—and indeed do commit it—to human reason; see their *Confession*, ch. I, § 16. (L. c. f. 57.)

The same: "A distinction must be made between reason in man before the fall and after the fall. . . Distinguish between reason taken passively as the subject of information, and taken normally as a principle of proof. . . The former is necessary in any knowledge of things, and thus also of divine things, as a *principium quo* (principle by which), for man does not understand except by intellect or reason; the latter, however, is not admitted in the knowledge of divine things as a *principium quod* (principle which). . . Without the use of reason or intellect, no one can be occupied with theology; for theology is not to be proposed to brutes or animals devoid of reason. Therefore, just as a man cannot see without eyes, cannot hear without ears, cannot taste without a tongue, so without reason—without which he is not even a man—he cannot perceive what faith (which Augustine, Sermon 250 de tempore, calls the 'soul of the soul') embraces in its περιφεμεία (circumference). . . Distinguish between organic principles, such as grammar, logic, rhetoric, the study of languages, etc., and philosophical principles strictly so called. The former are to be employed in theology (as aids for acquiring theology), since without them neither the sense or meaning of words can be elicited (which belongs to grammar), nor figures and modes of speech weighed (which belongs to rhetoric), nor connections and consequences perceived, nor discourses instituted (which belongs to logic). Well does D. Balth. Meisner, in his *Disputatio de Calvinismo fugiendo*, thesis 83, say: 'Who among us has ever denied that reason must be used in its own way in theological matters? Do we not use it ourselves as often as we attend to either the propriety of language or the structure of the entire context? Faith comes from hearing, Rom. 10: 18. But for hearing, the use of reason is required, so that voice may be distinguished from voice and some sense perceived. Thus, we do not deny that the use of reason is necessary in confirming, in destroying, and in expounding, because in all things the τρόπος παιδείας (mode of instruction) and the method prescribed in logic must be observed.' — Distinguish between general or transcendent principles of reason, which are verified of every being, and special or particular ones, which are valid only in a certain subject matter, such as physics or mathematics. We admit the former in theology; for they are formed not only with a view to finite nature, but also infinite nature, whence they are also called transcendent. But we deny that the latter can be used as principles of theological conclusions, such that the decision and judgment of these would depend upon them. — Distinguish between theological questions of pure faith and mixed questions (where one term is taken from philosophy and the other from theology). In mixed questions, we concede that special philosophical principles can be used, not indeed for the sake of decision and demonstration, but only for the sake of illustration and secondary proof, where the matter has already been defined by Scripture. — Distinguish between the ministry of reason, when it yields to its mistress or lady like a handmaid (from the ancient comparison of Ambrose, *De Abrahamo*, bk. 2, ch. 10), and the magisterium of reason, when it arrogates to itself judgment concerning things unknown and placed above its grasp. . . Distinguish between reason left to itself, or judging according to its own natural principles, and reason enclosed and chastened within the sphere of the divine Word, or illuminated by Holy Scripture; we do not deny that the latter can judge concerning matters of faith; however, we deny that judgment concerning matters of faith belongs to the former." (L.c., f. 55 sqq.)

Latin:

De pontificis R. fallibilitate cf. Gerhardi Confessio catholica. Lib. I. ΡΓII. c. 2. f. 77—111,

Quenstedtius: „Principium hoc pontificiorum: ,Quicquid Rom. pontifex determinat, illud est infallibiliter verum', primum esse non posse, patet inde, quia aliunde id probare conantur, niin. ex ipsa Scriptura s. Matth. 16, 18. Joh. 21, 15. 16. 17. . . Qui 1. possunt errare in doctrina fidei atque haeretici fleri, 2. multa erronea dogmata de cathedra sanciverunt, et 3. sibi ipsis contradicunt: illi non possunt esse principium fidei et conclusionum theologicarum.“ (L. c. f. 51.)

Idem: „Nec ratio humana seu naturalis theologiae et rerum supernaturalium principium est.“ (L. c. f. 55.)

Idem: ,,Probatur thesis I. ex natura mysteriorum fidei . . II. Ex natura rationis, quae in rebus supematuralibus prorsus coeca est. . . HI. Ex Scripturae Silentio. Nusquam Christus, prophetae, apostoli hoc principio usi leguntur, nec unquam in rebus fidei definiendis ad rationis judicium Scriptura nos remittit. Ita enim hactenus Calviniani nobiscum credidere: ,Non scriptum non esse sentiendum.' IV. Ab exemplis piorum, qui in rebus fidei non sunt secuti rationis judicium, sed, illa frustra contradicente, crediderunt, ut Abraham, Rom. 4, 18., qui, contra spem (rationis orbitatem dictantis) sub spe (Dei promittentis) credidit, se fore patrem multarum gentium juxta dictum (Gen. 16, 5.): Sic erit semen tuum. Ac non infirmatus fide haud consideravit (ον κατενόησέ) suum ipsius corpus jam emortuum... Confer exemplum Naemanis 2 Reg. 5,10.11.13., Pauli Gal. 15,16. V. Ab exemplis eorum, qui rationis judicium in rebus fidei secuti vel errarunt gravissime vel perierunt miserrime, ut incredulus tribunus 2 Reg. 7,12., Nicodemus Joh. 8, 4.9., Thomas Joh. 20, 25., Sadducaei Matth. 22, 23.“ (L. c. f. 59.)

Idem: „Antithesis I. Scholasticorum, quorum tota theologia nihil aliud est, quam theologiae et philosophiae mixtura, sive Erasmi judicio in Encomio Moriae, ,ex divinis eloquiis et philosophicis rationibus tanquam ex Centaurorum genere biformis mixtione quadam conflata disciplina'. In summis enim fidei mysteriis Scholastici ex principiis logicis, physicis ac metaphysicis, praetermissis vel levi manu tactis Scripturae dictis, conclusiones suas accersunt, ut c. 1. s. 1. th. 2. n. 8. p. 3. insinuavimus. II. Pontificiorum ac inprimis Jesuitarum, qui haud raro articulos fidei e rationis principiis probant, v. Bellarm. 1. IV. de poenit. c. 5., 1. III. de Eucharistia c. 22., 1. II. de Missa c. 4„ 1. IV. de Christi anima c. 10., quandoque eosdem ex rationis principiis impugnant, v. Bellarm. 1. IV. de Monachis c. 6., 1. II. de justific. c. 7. (ubi negat,justitiae Christi imputationem, siquidem ea cum ratione pugnet'), lib. IV. de Eccl. c. 11. Gregor, de Valent, lib. VIII. de analys. fld. cathol. c. 6., p. 101. inter documenta,ad Scripturam intelligendam et res fidei decidendas' hoc sexto et ultimo loco ponit, ,ut consulatur etiam ratio naturalis'. III. Calvinianorum; hos enim rationis magisterio mysteria fidei praepostere subjicere, vel etiam e principiis philosophicis eadem impugnare, et ex praxi et ex verbis eorum evidenter demonstrari potest. Vide Sturmium in Epist. Ambrosiana ad Pappum p. 5., Nicol. Taurellum in Epist. dedic. Triumphi, ubi philosophiam,fidei fundamentum' vocat, Ludov. Crocium in Assertion. A. C., disput. 1., Conrad. Vorstium, disput. XV. Anti-Pistoriana, ubi ait, ,fidei principia duplicia esse, partim naturalia, ut sensus et ratio, tum axiomata omnia naturali rationis lumine nota, partim superaaturalia' etc. Goclenius Disput. XV. Metaphys. th. 1. scribit; ,In sapientiae humanae et coelestis studiis dialecticae tum ministerium, tum magisterium, et judicium ac imperium aliquod agnosco, h. e., dialecticam docendi et intelligendi res tam sacras, quam profanas et ministram et magistram, et judicem et reginam seu temperatricem quandam statuo.' Zwinglius in colloq. Marpurg. illud Averrois et Socinianorum suum fecit, ,nihil

DE PKSNCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

esse credendum, quod ratione comprehendi nequeat, quia Deus nobis non proponat incomprehensibilia', referente Philippo in brevi annotat, ad Colloq. Marp., vide Historiam A. C. Chytraei p. 641. Dicit Vedelius in Bation. theol. 1. III. c. 6. p. 513. 531. etc., ,rationem esse normam, non primariam, sed secundariam, cui aliquid perfectionis accedere possit.' Ast principium naturae, quod in theoria loquentes Vedelius et cum ipso Massonius faciunt principium fldei secundarium, illud in praxi et usu faciunt principium fidei primarium, ut demonstrat D. Jacob. Martini in tract. de principio fldei, disput. VII. § 9. sq. Keckermannus lib. I. System. Theol. c. 4. ita scribit: ,Deum lucem Spiritus S. sui per duas illas plane divinas disciplinas, metaphysicam et logicam, in mentibus hominum velle accendere, hoc igitur adminiculo usum'; ait porro: ,Mysterium hoc (SS. Trinitatis) se declaraturum esse.' Vide D. Menzerum in respons. ad defens. secun. Pruten. Convers. Crocii c. 2. tom. I. Opp. p. 858. sqq. Petrus Martyr praefat. super lib. Begum inquit: ,Non tam verbum divinum, quam et verba naturae sequenda esse in theologia.' IV. Socinianorum, qui rationem alterum theologiae principium praeter Dei verbum constituunt et religionem Christianam ad eam inflectendam censent, utpote quorum hoc est axioma: ,Nihil in theologia verum est, quod a ratione non approbatur.' Item: ,Nihil credi potest, quod a ratione capi et intelligi nequeat.' Sunt verba Slichtingii Disput. de Trinit. contra Meisner. p. 125. Confer Smalcium disp. 4. de justific. contra Franzium fol. 137. et disp. 8. f. 421. ,Nullo modo verum esse potest, cui ratio sensusque communis repugnant', inquit Socinus de auctor. Script, p. 54. Sane blasphema illa SS. Trinitatis et Incarnationis oppugnatio ex nullo alio fonte fluxit, quam ex praedominantis rationis humanae dictamine, quod isti homines, tametsi videri nolint, dictamini Spiritus S. in s. literis loquentis longe praeferunt. Sic enim Osterodus Instit. Germ. c. 4. p. 31. scribit: ,Si ratio expresse demonstrat, quod trinitas personarum in Deo falsa sit, qui igitur unquam homini cordato in mentem veniat, quod illa nihilominus vera sit et ex verbo Dei probari queat.' V. Arminianorum, qui nihil, nisi rationi conforme in religione concedunt, rationi humanae judicium de mysteriis fidei committendum censent et committunt, vide Confess. eorum cap. I. §16.“ (L. c. f. 57.)

Idem: ,,Distinguendum inter rationem in homine ante lapsum et post lapsum. . . Dist. inter rationem passive sumptam pro subjecto informationis, et acceptam normaliter pro principio probationis. . . Illa in quavis rerum et sic quoque divinarum cognitione necessaria est ut principium quo, non enim nisi intellectu seu ratione homo intelligit; haec vero in rerum divinarum cognitione ut principium quod non admittitur. .. Sine usu rationis seu intellectus nemo in theologia versari potest; neque enim brutis aut animalibus rationis expertibus proponenda est theologia. Uti itaque homo sine oculis non potest videre, sine auribus non potest audire, sine lingua non potest gustare, ita sine ratione, sine qua ne quidem homo est, non potest percipere, quae fides (quam,animam animae* appellat Augustinus, sermo 250. de tempore) περιφεμεία sua complectitur. . . Dist. inter principia organica, qualia sunt grammatica, logica, rhetorica, studium linguarum etc., et principia philosophica stricte dicta. Illa in theologia adhibenda sunt (utpote adminicula theologiae acquirendae), cum sine illis nec sensus aut significatio vocum erui (quod grammaticae), nec figurae modique loquendi expendi (quod rhetoricae), nec connexiones et consequentiae percipi, nec discursus.institui (quod logicae est) possint. Bene D. Balth. Meisnerus disput. de Calvinismo fugiendo th. 83.: ,Batione suo modo utendum esse in rebus theologicis, quis nostrum umquam negavit? Annon utimur ipsi, quoties vel proprietatem linguae vel structuram totius contextus attendimus? Ex auditu est fides, Rom. 10, 18. Ad auditum vero usus rationis requiritur, ut vox a voce discernatur et aliquis sensus percipiatur. Sic in confirmando, in destruendo, in exponendo rationis PROLEGOM. CAP. II. usum necessarium esse, non imus inficias, quia in omnibus τρόπος παιδείας et modus in logicis praescriptus observari debet.' — Dist, inter principia rationis generalia seu transcendentia, quae de omni ente verificantur, et specialia seu particularia, qUae in certa materia tantum valent, ut physica, mathematica. Illa in theologia admittimus; sunt enim non tantum intuitu finitae, sed etiam infinitae naturae formata, unde et transcendentia vocantur. Haec vero tanquam conclusionum theologicarum principia, ut scil, ex illis harum decisio et dijudicatio dependeat, adhiberi posse negamus. — Dist. inter quaestiones theologicas purae fidei, et mixtas (ubi alter terminus e philosophia, alter e theologia est petitus). In mixtis principia philosophica specialia, non quidem decisionis et demonstrationis, sed tantum illustrationis et secundariae probationis causa, ubi e Scriptura res definita est, adhiberi posse concedimus. — Dist. inter rationis ministerium, cum instar ancillae cedit herae seu dominae (ex antiqua comparatione Ambrosii, 2. de Abrahamo c. 10.), et rationis magisterium, cum sibi judicium arrogat de rebus ignotis et supra captum positis. . . Dist. inter rationem sibi relictam sive juxta principia sua naturalia judicantem, et rationem intra verbi divini orbem conclusam et castigatam sive e s. Scriptura illustratam; hanc de rebus fidei judicare posse, non negamus; illi autem judicium de rebus fidei competere, inficiamur." (L. c. f. 55. sqq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: The same: "It is one thing to peddle reason or the principles of reason in…

The same: "It is one thing to peddle reason or the principles of reason in theological matters theoretically and in words as a principle, and another to use it or the principle of proof practically and in the very act. The former cannot indeed be said of many Scholastics, Jesuits, Calvinists, and Socinians, but the latter is common to all the aforementioned heterodox." (L.c., f. 60.) The same: "Distinguish between explicit and implicit contradiction; the former occurs between two propositions, one of which affirms a thing, while the other denies it; the latter occurs when, in one and the same proposition, the predicate is repugnant to the subject. The former is called contradictory opposition or even explicit contradiction; the latter, contradiction in the adjective or implicit contradiction. The judgment of an explicit contradiction must be sought entirely from the rules of logic regarding connections or, rather, oppositions; but human reason cannot judge concerning an implicit contradiction, since it does not perceive or understand the thing itself."

(L. c. f. 60 sq.) The same: "Rom. 12:1, by λογικήν λατρείαν or rational worship, is not understood a worship which is derived from the judgment of reason or examined by the balance of reason; rather, this λογικός worship is opposed to the αλόγῳ worship of the O.T., where the victims of brute animals were offered to God; but Christians in the N.T. present themselves to God as a living sacrifice, and they offer to God not ζώα άλογα, but their own bodies. (For the apostle explains λογικήν λατρείαν in this place by the offering of our bodies, and that offering is accomplished not by the slaughter of a living animal, but by the mortification and renewal of the old man.)" (L. c. f. 62.) The same: "The adversaries object: 'Religion has many things above reason, but nothing against reason.' Resp. 1: Articles of faith are not in themselves against reason, but only above reason; however, it happens per accidens that they are also against reason, when reason takes upon itself to judge them according to its own principles, and does not follow the light of the Word, but denies and attacks them. 2: Articles of faith are not only above, but also against corrupt and depraved reason, which judges them to be foolishness. Smalzius insists (Disp. IV. contra Franz. p. 137): 'Let someone teach that one sentence of the Holy Scriptures conflicts with reason, and then let reason be silent in the church.' Resp.: No sentence of Holy Scripture conflicts with reason when it keeps itself within its own bounds, but all mysteries of faith, such as the Trinity, the Incarnation, etc., conflict with reason when it exceeds its own bounds." (L. c.)

The same: "They object: 'As a small light is not contrary to a great one, so reason is not contrary to Scripture.' Resp. 1: In itself there is no contrariety here, but per accidens. Reason, keeping itself within its own sphere, is not contrary to Scripture."

contrary, but when it has gone outside and beyond its own sphere and judges the highest mysteries of faith from its own principles. 2 Reason is contrary to Scripture not where it is light, but insofar as it is blind and dark. 3 In great light more things are seen than in lesser, etc. 4 Corrupt reason, or its corrupt use, opposes theology when it measures infinite things by finite ones, or sells as universal axioms those which are not such; for example, when it opposes to creation its own κυρίαν δόξαν: "nothing comes from nothing"; to the mystery of the Trinity: "one cannot be three." For these are not truly universal, since they cannot be verified in all particulars. Thus, "the whole is greater than its part"—namely, naturally—remains true in philosophy; nevertheless, the parts of the blessed and miraculously increased whole can exceed the whole not yet increased, John 6:9, 13. Thus, "the finite is not capable of the infinite"—namely, by physical and mathematical capacity." (L. c. f. 62 sq.) The same: "They object: What is true in theology is not false in philosophy, because truth is one. Resp. 1: Truth is one in a general concept; meanwhile, every discipline has its own axioms, which are not to be dragged into another forum, but left in their own sphere. 2 When theology says: 'A virgin gave birth,' and philosophy says: 'For a virgin to give birth and remain such is αδύνατον,' they do not contradict each other; for theology does not assert that a virgin gives birth and remains such naturally, but says that this was done by supernatural and divine power. — Distinguish between philosophy considered abstractly and by reason of its essence, and philosophy considered concretely and by reason of its existence in a subject corrupted by sin; in the former way, it is by no means opposed to divine truth (for there is no truth given except one, and one that is harmonious by reason of its mutually subordinated objects); in the latter way, however, because of the ignorance of the intellect and the perversion of the will, it is not rarely used preposterously by the philosopher for depravation and empty deception, Col. 2:8." (L. c. f. 63.) The same: "When Vedelius, lib. III. Ration. Theol. c. 6, calls reason 'a secondary norm of faith, to which some degree of perfection might be added,' Dr. Weller rightly responds in Anti-Massonio P. 1. disp. 4. th. 9. p. 107: 1. that it is αώηρόξυλον to be a secondary norm, since a norm or canon, as Varinus defines it, is μέτρον ἀδιάψευστον, πᾶσαν πρόσθεσιν καὶ ἀναίρεσιν μηδαμῶς ἐπιδεχόμενον. And Basil the Great, 1. 1. c. 2. against Eunomius, says: 'That to which something is lacking is an addition, but that' (the gnomon and rule), 'if anything is lacking to them, they cannot even be called by these names appropriately.'" (L. c.) The same: "The Calvinists urge that they understand 'regenerate reason,' or human reason made after spiritual regeneration, as Calvin lib. IV. Institut. c. 17. n. 26., Bucanus loc. 48. q. 68., Grynaeus in Disp. Theol. de hom. ortu p. 515., Massonius part. I. p. 366 The blessed Dannhauer responds in the place cited, p. 58: 'This suggestion would have some merit if reason were found in man pure, without the influx of a still-remaining sinful fountain; but the water is troubled, similar to fresh water, yet suspected of poison, since every figment of the human heart is evil at all times. And was not Sarah regenerate? And yet she laughs at the promise of the Lord, mocks it as a paradox.'" (L. c. f. 63 sq.) Balduinus: "When the regenerate also wish to dispute about matters of faith from the principles of reason, then their reason is called corrupt." (Disp. de 2. c. ep. ad Col. Witteb. 1617. B. 2.) Quenstedtius: "Nor is the consensus of the primitive church or of the fathers of the first centuries after Christ a principle of the Christian faith, whether primary or secondary; nor does it beget divine, but only human and probable faith... This is the true state of the controversy: Whether the consensus of the doctors of the church of the first five centuries after Christ, insofar as it could be shown from their remaining writings today, is to be held as a secondary or subordinate principle of the dogmas of faith, not only regarding the person, but also regarding the matter." (L. c. f. 64.) PROLEGOM. CHAP. II. Chemnitius: "Andradius does us an injury by shouting that we hold the testimonies of antiquity in no regard at all, and that we undermine the approval, faith, and majesty of the Church. . . We confess that we dissent from those who invent opinions that have no testimony from any time in the Church, as Servetus, Campanus, the Anabaptists, and others have done in our time. We also believe that no dogma is to be received in the Church that is new and conflicts with all of antiquity." (Exam. Conc. Trid. De tradit, gen. 6. f. 71.) Quenstedtius: The corollary is proven: From the nullity or non-existence of that consensus. Many writings of the ancient doctors of the Church are ἀνέκδοτα (unpublished); few of those that have been published have reached us; most have perished; many fathers, especially from the most ancient antiquity, wrote little or nothing, and the writings of the fathers that still survive are mutilated, interpolated, and corrupted. Moreover, the consensus of a few fathers is not immediately the consensus of the whole Church. — The adversaries have argued: that the best writings of the fathers were nevertheless preserved by divine providence, while the baser ones perished. But who will guarantee this? Who will prescribe laws to divine providence? Or who will persuade us that in the funeral pyre of a library—whether the Alexandrian, of which Gellius speaks in lib. VI. Noct. Att. c. ult., or the Diocletian, of which Dr. Dannhauer speaks in Christeid. p. 231—only the baser monuments perished, and that those worthy of cedar were snatched from the teeth of fate? Indeed, the blessed Luther rather ascribes it to divine providence in the Preface to the 1st Wittenberg Part, "that no small part of the ecclesiastical writings perished, so that men would not find it necessary to spend the time that should be devoted to the reading and scrutiny of Holy Scripture on the turning of the pages of fathers and councils." — They press the point: that the consensus of the ancient Church can be sufficiently estimated from the ἐκδότοις (published works). I reply: I concede that it can be estimated particularly and probably, but I deny that it can be estimated by divine faith; it can be estimated in those matters where a συμψηφισμός (unanimous vote/agreement) appears, not in others where they themselves take sides; it can be estimated if they have openly, universally, and perseveringly conspired in some tradition of faith. Thus, for example, we have a most beautiful harmony of the ancient doctors regarding the canon of Scripture, if you collect all the testimonies over five or more centuries; but that consensus does not appear in the same way in dogmas. How great is the discrepancy often found in the writings of the fathers, even regarding the sense of Scripture? How great is the hiatus of time? How great are the vacuums of places where nothing was committed to writing? That five-century consensus would address only contemporary controversies, not heresies that arose after five centuries. See D. Dannhauer, Myster. Syncretismi p. 45. sq.

2. From the weakness of error. . .

3. From the multitude of supposititious writings. There is hardly any one of the ancient fathers into whose nest the eggs of others—and those deformed ones—have not been placed. . .

4. From the condition and quality of that consensus. . .

5. From the negation of the required principle." (L. c. f. 66. sq.) Smalcald Articles: "The Papists allege Augustine and certain fathers who wrote about purgatory, and they do not think we understand to what end and why they spoke in such a way. Augustine does not write that there is a purgatory, nor does he have the testimony of Scripture upon which to rely, but he leaves it in doubt whether it exists, and says that his mother requested that a commemoration of her be made at the altar or sacrament. To this end, it was altogether nothing but the devotion of men—and indeed of one or another—not establishing an article of faith, which belongs to God alone. But our Papists cite those opinions of men so that faith may be had in their foul, blasphemous, and cursed trafficking regarding masses for souls in purgatory, or regarding funeral rites and offerings, etc. . . For articles of faith are not to be constructed from the words and deeds of the fathers; otherwise, the food they ate, their manner of dress, their houses, etc., would also become articles of faith, just as they have played games with the relics of the saints. But we have another rule, namely, that the Word of God shall establish articles of faith, and no one else, not even an angel."

Idem: „Aliud est, rationem seu rationis principia in materiis theologicis theoretice et verbis pro principio venditare, et aliud, practice et facto ipso illam seu principium probandi adhibere. Resp. 1.: Veritas est una in conceptu generali, interim quaelibet disciplina sua habet axiomata, quae non sunt trahenda in aliud forum, sed in sua sphaera relinquenda. 2 Quando theologia dicit: Virgo peperit, philosophia: virginem parere et manere talem, est αδύνατον, non contrariantur; theologia enim non asserit, virginem naturaliter parere et manere talem, sed dicit, supernaturali et divina virtute id factum esse. — Dist. inter philosophiam abstracte et ratione suae essentiae consideratam, et philosophiam concrete et ratione existentiae in subjecto per peccatum corrupto spectatam; priori modo veritati divinae nequaquam opponitur (non enim nisi unica et ratione objectorum sibi invicem subordinatorum harmonica datur veritas); posteriori vero modo ob intellectus ignorantiam et voluntatis perversionem non raro ad depravationem et inanem deceptionem a philosopho praepostere adhibetur, Coi. 2, 8.“ (L. c. f. 63.) Quenstedtius: „Nec etiam consensus primitivae ecclesiae aut patrum priorum post Christum saeculorum principium Christianae fidei est, sive primarium, sive secundarium; nec divinam, sed tantum humanam et probabilem fidem gignit. . . Consensui autem paucorum patrum non statim est consensus totius ecclesiae. — Pegerunt adversarii: optima tamen scripta patrum a coelesti pronoea esse servata, viliora tamen periisse. Scripturae lectioni ac scrutinio tempus patrum et conciliorum volutationi impendere necesse haberent.' — Instant: ex ίκδότοις satis aestimari posse ecclesiae antiquae consensum. Resp., posse particulariter et probabiliter aestimari, concedo, nego de fide divina; posse in iis, in quibus συμψηφισμός apparet, non in aliis, ubi ipsimet in partes eunt; posse aestimari, si in aliquam fidei traditionem uno eodemque consensu aperte, universaliter et perseveranter conspirarint. Syncretismi p. 45. sq. 2 Ex erroris imbecillitate. . . 3 Ex scriptorum suppositiorum multitudine. Vix ullus est ex antiquis patribus, in cujus nidum alieni pulli, iique deformes, non sint suppositi. . . 4 Ex consensus illius conditione et qualitate. . . 5 Ex requisitorum principii negatione.“ (L. c. f. 66. sq.) Nostri autem pontificii sententias istas hominum citant, ut fides habeatur tetris, blasphemis et maledictis nundinationibus de missis pro animabus in purgatorio seu de inferiis et oblationibus etc. . . Regulam autem aliam habemus, ut videlicet verbum Dei condat articulos fidei, et praeterea nemo, ne angelus quidem.“


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Quenstedtius: "Antithesis

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, as Bellarmine (lib. II. de Christo c. 2) and Gord. Huntlaeus (Controv. II. c. 28) assert: that the concordant opinion of the fathers is to be held by all as an infallible norm of faith. 2. Of the Crypto-Papists in England, such as the Laudians, who descend from William Laud, the beheaded Bishop of Canterbury." §. Of the Innovators, who, following the lead of Vincent of Lérins, make two principles of theology and of assertions to be believed: one primary, namely Scripture, and the other secondary and subordinate, namely the catholic consensus of the primitive church, and indeed of the first five centuries after Christ." (L. c. f. 65.)

Council of Trent: "The Tridentine synod... perceiving that this truth and discipline are contained in written books and in unwritten traditions, which, having been received by the apostles from the mouth of Christ himself, or from the apostles themselves, by the dictation of the Holy Spirit, have come down even to us, transmitted as it were from hand to hand, following the example of the orthodox fathers, receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and of the New Testament, since one God is the author of both, as well as the traditions themselves, whether they pertain to faith or to morals, as having been dictated either orally by Christ or by the Holy Spirit, and preserved in the Catholic Church by a continuous succession." (Sess. 4. decret. de canon. scripturis. Ed. Smets. p. 14.)

Roman Catechism: "The entire rationale of doctrine, which is to be delivered to the faithful, is contained in the Word of God, which is distributed into Scripture and traditions." (Prooem. q. 12.)

Calixtus: "There are two principles: the authority of the divine law, and then the tradition of the Catholic Church." (De arte nova, p. 49.)

Regarding this, Kahnisius: "When Calixtus spoke of two principles in the Church, Scripture and Tradition, this happened obviously at the expense of the Protestant principle of Scripture and was once again an approach toward the Roman Church." (Der innere Gang des deutschen Protestantismus. 3rd ed. Leipz. 1874. I, 105.)

Theologians of Dorpat: "Accordingly, our Confession contains, besides the articles and dogmas of faith already symbolically developed and fixed, also such elements of the generally Christian and ecclesiastical Credo—we mean the Apostolic Symbol—which are partly still in the process of becoming, and partly have not yet entered, or have only entered in a rudimentary way, into the historical movement of dogma-formation, because the Church has hitherto been prompted to express itself regarding them only from one side, or because they have not yet become the subject of its closer explanation and determination at all." (Gutachten. 1866. p. 12.)

Augustine: "I have learned to defer this honor and fear only to those books of Scripture which are now called canonical, so that I most firmly believe that none of their authors has erred in writing anything; but others I read in such a way that, however much they may excel in holiness and doctrine, I do not think something is true because they thought so, but because they were able to persuade me, either through those canonical authors or by probable reasoning, that it does not deviate from the truth." (Ep. 19. ad Hieron.)

Huelsemannus: "Vincent of Lérins is no authority here, and his rule is foolish: 1. because of the later age, which falls in the middle of the fifth century after Christ; 2. because of the lack of support from other, more ancient fathers, who not only never approved this rule—'Whatever all writers everywhere have written simultaneously, openly, frequently, and constantly, that alone is finally to be held as an article of faith and as true,' etc.—but even openly rejected it, appealing to the open and literal consensus that exists among the prophets and apostles." (Praelect. in Form. Conc. art. 16. s. 6. § 5. p. 876.)

Quenstedtius: "The adversaries urge the promise of Christ in Matthew 28:20: 'I am with you,' etc. But whence will they prove, from that gracious [promise]..." PROLEGOM. CAP. II. divine presence with the Church, which the Savior promised there, has flowed forth, so that, namely, the testimonies of the doctors or fathers of the Church, being in agreement, might obtain the place of a secondary or subordinate principle? . . . It is one thing to be the norm and rule of things to be believed absolutely, and another to be the norm and rule under a certain respect and with certain limits, as it were. Confessions and bodies of doctrine, e.g., the Augsburg Confession, the Corpus Julium, the Prutenicum, the Formula of Concord, etc., are a norm and rule not simply, but under a certain respect—a tessellated, testimonial norm of the public doctrine of certain particular churches; but the principle and norm of that is Holy Scripture, from which the authors of those confessions derived that which they believed ought to be believed and which they wished to be believed in their territories. . . . That which is not αὐτόπιστον [self-evident], which requires the passage of centuries, nor is sufficient of itself, which is not simply necessary, which can be denied to some, etc., cannot properly be called a principle; but all these things belong to this inferior principle, as they call it, or sub-principle. . . . Cf. Huelsemannus, who writes thus: "It is a prejudice that the consensus of the fathers restricts antiquity, universality, and continuity (what has been taught everywhere, always, and by all) as a κριτήριον [criterion] of infallibility to the principal heads of faith, and not to the minute little questions of divine law, nor yet has it determined which and how many in number those questions are upon which, as he says, the foundations of the entire Catholic dogma rest; which determination is everywhere necessary for the application of this rule." (L. c. f. 67 sqq.)

The same: "Finally, neither visions, apparitions, private revelations, nor internal angelic addresses are to be employed in proving the dogmas of faith." (L. c. f. 69.)

The same: "Status of the controversy: The question is whether, besides or outside of Holy Scripture, a norm for either things to be believed or things to be done is to be sought from peculiar enthusiasms and private revelations. — Distinguish between visions and revelations made before the departure of the apostles and those made after their death which reveal new dogmas of faith; our discussion here is not about the former, but about the latter. — Distinguish between the word that is ἄγραφον [unwritten], whether external or internal; the former is boasted of only by the Papists, the latter by both the Papists and the Enthusiasts, as well as the Socinians and some Calvinists. . . . Distinguish between true ἐνθουσιασμόν [enthusiasm] or divine inspiration, and the apparent kind, which again is either feigned or presumed. We are dealing here with the latter kind of enthusiasm, which is ordinarily accustomed to be called by that name, and thus by enthusiasts we understand fanatical men who either feign or presume the inspiration, revelations, and promptings of God, and by calling diabolical, melancholic, or voluntary illusions and imaginations 'divine revelations,' they deceive themselves and others. — Distinguish between the power of God and His will; no one denies that God can give new revelations, but it is doubted whether He wills to do so. — Distinguish between the hidden will of God and His revealed will; the latter is to be judged solely from the written Word of God; concerning the former, because it is hidden, nothing certain can be pronounced." (L. c. f. 70.)

The same: "Distinguish between revelations that concern or impugn an article of faith, and those that concern the state of the Church or the polity, common life, and future events; we repudiate the former, but some maintain that the latter are not indeed to be forced upon anyone with the necessity of believing, yet neither are they to be rashly rejected. B. Balduinus in Comm. in 1 Tim. 4. P. I. q. 1. says: 'We do not doubt that God still sometimes reveals to some people future things that pertain to the state of the Church and the republic, to be announced for the use of men.' Distinguish between the true Samuel and the personated Samuel or his specter; it was not the former, but the latter that appeared to Saul in 1 Sam. 28. For the circumstances of the text show that it was a deception of Satan." (L. c. f. 75.)

Smalc. Art.: "Why many words? Enthusiasm is implanted and infused into Adam and his children from the first fall until the end of the world by the ancient dragon with a certain poison, and it is the mother of all heresies."

and the origin, force, life, and power of the papacy and of Mohammedanism. Wherefore we must steadfastly persevere in this, that God does not wish to deal with us otherwise than through the vocal word and the sacraments, and that whatever is boasted as spirit without the word and sacraments is the devil himself. For God even wished to appear to Moses through the burning bush and the vocal word. And no prophet, whether Elijah or Elisha, received the Spirit without the decalogue or the vocal word. And John the Baptist was neither conceived without the preceding word of Gabriel, nor did he leap in his mother’s womb without the word of Mary. And Peter says (2 Pet. 1:21): “Prophets spoke not by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit,” who were not holy without the external word, nor were they impelled to prophesy by the Holy Spirit as if they were unholy or profane; but they were holy, says Peter (Acts 28:25), when the Holy Spirit spoke through them.” (P. III. art. 8. p. 322. sq.) Concerning the specter of Endor (1 Sam. 28) cf. A. Pfeiffer’s Dubia, vexata S. S. V. T. p. 377—379. — Concerning predictions through the Holy Spirit, through the devil, and from the stars cf. Luther Vol. XIV, 231. sqq. — Concerning appearing dead, astrology, and necromancy, cf. the same Vol. XIX, 1385—96. XI, 1632—35. 436—42. — Concerning enthusiasts cf. the same Vol. I, 2287—92. Quenstedt: “We seek proofs of the orthodox opinion: 1. From the authority of Scripture, which recalls us from all other principles, from revelations and apparitions, to the law and to the testimony (Is. 8:19), to Moses and the prophets (Luke 16:29); Christ commands us to search the Scriptures (John 5:39). And Peter warns that attention must be paid to the prophetic word (2 Pet. 1:19): ‘until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts.’ 2. From the perfection of the sacred writings...

Tridentinum: „Tridentina synodus. . . perspiciens, hanc veritatem et disciplinam contineri in libris scriptis et sine scnpto traditionibus, quae, ab ipsius Christi ore ab apostolis acceptae aut ab ipsis apostolis, Spiritu S. dictante, quasi per manus traditae, ad nos usque pervenerunt, orthodoxorum patrum exempla secuta, omnes libros tam veteris quam novi testamenti, cum utriusque unus Deus sit auctor, necnon traditiones ipsas, tum ad fidem tum ad mores pertinentes, tamquam vel oretenus a Christo vel a Spiritu S. dictatas et continua successione in ecclesia catholica conservatas, pari pietatis affectu et reverentia suscipit et veneratur.“ (Sess. 4. decret. de canon, scripturis. Calixtus: „Duo sunt principia: divinae legis auctoritas, tum deinde ecclesiae catholicae traditio.“ (De arte nova, p. 49.)

Ad hoc Kahnisius: „Wenn Calixtus von zwei Principien in der Kirche sprach, der Schrift und der Tradition, so geschah dies offenbar auf Kosten des protestantischen Schriftprincips und war abermals eine Annäherung an die römische Kirche.“ (Der innere Gang des deutschen Protestantismus. 3. Ausg. Leipz. 1874. I, 105.)

Theologi Dorpatenses: „Demgemäss enthält auch unser Bekenntniss ausser den symbolisch schon entwickelten und flxirten Artikeln und Dogmen des Glaubens auch solche Elemente des allgemein christlichen und kirchlichen Credo, wir meinen des apostolischen Symbolums, die theils noch mitten im Werden begriffen, theils noch gar nicht oder nur ansatzweise in die geschichtliche dogmenbildende Bewegung eingetreten sind, weil über sie sich auszusprechen, die Kirche bisher nur von einer Seite her veranlasst gewesen ist, oder weil sie überhaupt noch nicht Gegenstand ihrer näheren Erklärung und Bestimmung geworden sind.“ (Gutachten. 1866. p. 12.)

Augustinus: „Ego solis iis scripturarum libris, qui jam canonici appellantur, didici hunc honorem timoremque deferre, ut nullum eorum auctorum scribendo aliquid errasse, firmissime credam; alios autem ita lego, ut, quantalibet sanctitate doctrinaque praepolleant, non ideo verum putem, quia ipsi ita senserunt, sed quia mihi vel per illos auctores canonicos, vel probabili ratione, quod a vero non abhorrent, persuadere potuerunt.“ (Ep. 19. ad Hieron.)

Huelsemannus: ,,Vincentius Lerinensis nulla hic auctoritas, et regula ejus stolida est: 1. propter sequiorem aetatem, quae incidit in medium saeculum quintum p. Chr.; 2. propter defectum suffragiorum ab aliis vetustioribus patribus, qui hanc regulam: , Quicquid omnes ubique scriptores simul, aperte, frequenter, constanter scripserunt, id solum demum pro articulo fidei et vero habehdum est' etc., non solum nusquam approbarunt, sed aperte etiam rejecerunt, provocantes ad consensum apertum et literalem, qui est inter prophetas et apostolos.“ (Praelect. in Form. Cone. art. 16. s. 6. § 5. p. 876.)

Quenstedtius: „Urgent adversarii promissionem Christi Matth. 28, 20.: ,Ego vobiscum sum' etc. Sed unde probabunt, ex gratiosa illa PROLEGOM. CAP. Aliud est, esse normam ac regulam credendorum absolute, et aliud, esse normam et regulam sub certo respectu et quibusdam quasi limitibus. Confessiones et doctrinae corpora, v. g. Aug. Conf., Corp. Julium, Prutenicum, Form. Cone, etc., sunt norma et regula non simpliciter, sed sub certo respectu, norma tesseralis, testimonialis doctrinae publicae quarundam ecclesiarum particularium; principium vero et norma istius est s. Scriptura, ex qua confessionum istarum auctores deduxerunt id, quod ipsi credendum esse crediderunt et quod in territoriis suis credi voluerunt. . . ### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: From the certainty of faith, which must be sought solely from the sacred…

3. From the certainty of faith, which must be sought solely from the sacred writings (John 20, end; 2 Tim. 3:15)...

4. From the lack of promise. Nowhere are immediate revelations or visions promised to be expected in our times. In Luke 16:29, the damned rich man is rebuked because he had asked for revelations of the dead for his brothers who were still living.

5. From the diabolical fraud and fallacy in those revelations...

6. From the condition of those revelations; for they are obscure, doubtful, uncertain, suspicious, often absurd, fallacious, dangerous, useless, unnecessary, contrary to the word of God, subject to the deceits and mockeries of Satan, and subject to the judgment of others (1 Cor. 14:29, 32), and therefore cannot be held as a principle of theology and faith.

7. The new-fangled prophets seek their prophecies not so much from a peculiar revelation as through a certain plagiarism from Ezekiel, Daniel, and the Apocalypse.

8. Those angels, whom the adversaries dream of, either announce the same thing in faith that is contained in the word, or something different and other; if the latter, they are not to be heard (Gal. 1:8); if the former, there is no need for their revelation.

9. Through the revelations of the enthusiasts, the order of the ministry, or the order divinely sanctioned in the church between teachers and learners, is overturned.” (L. c. f. 71. sq.) The same: “They object: That many things were truly predicted by their own people through a prophetic Spirit, which the history of our times has confirmed. Resp. 1: It is a begging of the question [petitio principii], and revelations of future events and their predictions are boasted, not proven. 2. A false hypothesis is assumed, that all predictions of future things are prophetic or theopneustos [God-breathed]. But there are many that are also daimonopneustoi [demon-breathed], many natural, many conjectural, many casual, many ambiguous and mere equivocations, such as very many among the Gentiles emanated from the oracles and various seers of the devil, who would also have to be referred to the number of true prophets if an argument were to be drawn from the prediction of certain future things.” (L. c. f. 74. sq.) The same: “They object: The apostle Paul explicitly says in 1 Thess. 5:19, 20, ‘Do not quench the Spirit, and do not despise prophecies.’ Resp.: It is not understood here by ‘Spirit’ as a fanatical spirit, but the motions of the Holy Spirit kindled in the hearts of the faithful, which (like the sacred fire of old) must always be fostered, lest they be extinguished, and must always be anazopyrein [rekindled] (2 Tim. 1:6). Thus, by ‘prophecies’ are not understood enthusiasms, but either objectively the prophetic writings, or instrumentally their explanation and application, whether from a singular gift, of which prophecy there is talk in 1 Cor. 12 and 14, or from a common and ordinary gift.” (L. c. f. 77.) The same: “Antithesis: 1. Of various fanatics, who maintain: ‘The knowledge of God and of all dogmas to be believed is not to be sought from the written word of God, but from a revelation made peculiarly to each one and from an innate light, from raptures, dreams, conversations with angels, from the internal word, from the inspiration (Einsprechen) of the heavenly Father, from the internal information of Christ essentially united with them, from the magisterium of the Holy Spirit speaking and teaching within, a wisdom higher than that which is contained in the sacred Scriptures.’ It is established that very many fanatics, ancient and modern, have been seized by such enthousiasmos; among the ancients can be counted the Montanists, Donatists, Adelphius... The words of the Historia Tripartita are these: ‘At that time the heresy of the Messalians, whom they call euchitas, i.e., pray-ers, arose. They are also called by another name enthousiastai, i.e., inspired and divine. For these await the operation of a certain demon and consider this to be the presence of the Holy Spirit. But those who participate in the complete languor of this matter avoid the operation of their hands as evil, and surrender themselves to sleep and call the phantasies of their dreams prophecies. The leaders of this heresy were Dadoes and Sabbas and Adelphius, Hermas and Symeones and others.’ The more recent enthusiasts are those who... emerged from hell... under the leadership and auspices of Thomas Müntzer, that seditious standard-bearer of the Anabaptists in Thuringia, Caspar von Schwenckfeld in Silesia, Theophrastus Paracelsus in Switzerland, Coppin and Quintin in Picardy, Valentin Weigel in Misnia. All these contended that not only the written word of God, but also revelations, enthusiasms, dreams, and the immediate voice of God must be heard and the government of the church instituted according to them... To these add the Rosicrucians, the new prophets, John Warner, George Richard, the Quakers or Tremblers in England, who also dream of divine raptures and immediate revelations. Thus also Jean de Labadie publicly boasted of heavenly revelations, conversations with the blessed saints, and apparitions of the blessed Virgin Mary made to him during prayer, and his followers; they assert that God deals with the faithful immediately, often without the word, and therefore warn that ‘one must flee to the internal revelations of the Spirit and diligently pay attention.’ Thus also Schurmann, Enkler. p. 80, tries to prove that ‘besides Scripture, there is given even today dogmatic prophecy and internal revelations.’ 2. Of the Papists, whom Dr. Dannhauer, Hodom. Spirit. Pap. phantasm. I. p. 61. sq., shows to admit revelations made to private individuals, e.g., Bridget, Catherine of Siena, among the principles of faith... 3. Of the Socinians. Thus Faustus Socinus against Erasmus John p. 166 thinks that Laelius Socinus... obtained through many prayers from Christ himself the interpretation of those words of Christ in John 8:52: ‘Before Abraham, the father of many nations, is, I am the light of the world,’ and that it was revealed by God himself. Ostorodus, Instit. Germ. c. 1, requires immediate revelations or internal special illumination to understand the prophetic Scriptures and the greatest part of the Apocalypse of John. See Mr. D. Calovius 11. cc. 4. Of certain Calvinists. Thus Andreas Karlstadt made much of private revelations and visions, whom the blessed Luther refuted in the book ‘Against the Celestial Prophets,’ Vol. III. Jena. cf. Sleidan, l. III. p. 61. and l. V. p. 117, where he says: ‘That Karlstadt, of whom we spoke above, dissenting from Luther, having left Wittenberg, was very familiar with those clandestine teachers who feigned visions and conversations with God, as we said before.’ And Huldrych Zwingli, who claimed to have known from a peculiar revelation through the Spirit that the little word ‘is’ in the words of the Supper was placed for ‘signifies.’ Hence D. Dannhauer, Hodom. Spirit. Calv. Phantas. I. §9. p. 59: ‘If you look at the beginnings, Calvinism owes not a little to the fanatical enthusiasm of Karlstadt and Zwingli, although later it seems to have fallen away.’”

F. A. Philippi: "The source from which dogmatics must draw is, therefore, the reason of the dogmatizing subject, enlightened by revelation. However, the individual Christian personality knows that divine revelation, in accordance with its content and purpose, is not given to a single subject alone, but is intended for all of humanity, and that within humanity there exists a community of those in whom this divine purpose of the revelation of salvation in Christ has already actually been realized. Therefore, the dogmatizing subject will feel the need to bring the enlightenment of his reason into connection with the enlightenment of the community of Christ in general, and the agreement of his individual consciousness with the collective Christian consciousness will offer him a confirmation of the truth of the former...

Now, however, in order to correctly carry out the examination of the various church communities and then to be able to decide freely, an infallible rule and standard is required, by which the doctrines of these communities can be measured... This norm will then have to be applied to the doctrine of the universal church as well as to the doctrine of the individual church, in order to impress upon the assumption of its correctness the inviolable seal of unconditional certainty...

We have now recognized a threefold source from which Christian doctrine must draw its material, namely: the enlightened reason of the dogmatizing subject, the doctrine of the church, and the canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testaments... From our entire development thus far, it follows of itself that the doctrine of Scripture will not, as in older dogmatics, appear at the beginning of each article of faith, but at the end, because we do not regard Scripture as the first source, but as the final norm of dogmatic knowledge." (Kirchliche Glaubenslehre. Stuttgart 1854. I, 86–92, 226.)

Luthardt: "Dogmatics is the science of the connection of dogmas, which it must reproduce from the religious faith of the Christian himself... Scripture, as the normative factor of the dogmatic system, gives it its biblical character." (Kompendium der Dogmatik. Leipzig 1868. pp. 5, 23.)

Von Hofmann: "It is a common demand that one should test the doctrine valid in the church by Scripture, but interpret Scripture according to faith. But where do I find the faith according to which I interpret Scripture, if not in myself? For outside of me, it is church doctrine, which wishes to be tested by the Scripture that is to be interpreted. And even if it were the Apostolic Creed, from which people have recently wanted to make a law of scriptural interpretation that is, moreover, incapable of being handled, this too—no matter how old—as a product of church activity, must first be tested again by Scripture, not so much as to whether it is correct in detail, but whether it is truly that sum total of Christianity which our fathers, for their part, also wanted to be known as having been derived from Scripture.

The sum total of divine doctrine, gathered from the clearest passages of Scripture, was for them the faith according to which Scripture should be interpreted. But they thereby only proved that Scripture appeared to them like a collection of laws of faith, which it is not.

F. A. Philippius: „Die Quelle, aus der die Dogmatik zu schöpfen hat, ist also die durch die Offenbarung erleuchtete Vernunft des dogmatisirenden Subjects. Die christliche Einzelpersönliehkeit weiss aber, dass die göttliche Offenbarung ihrem Inhalte und Zwecke entsprechend nicht nur einem einzelnen Subjecte gegeben, sondern für die ganze Menschheit bestimmt ist, sowie dass innerhalb der Menschheit sich eine Gemeinschaft derer vorfindet, an welchen diese göttliche Bestimmung der Heilsoffenbarung in Christo sich schon thatsächlich verwirklicht hat. Daher wird das dogmatisirende Subject das Bedürfniss fühlen, die Erleuchtung seiner Vernunft in Zusammenhang zu bringen mit der Erleuchtung der ChristusGemeinschaft überhaupt, und die Uebereinstimmung seines individuellen Bewusstseins mit dem christlichen Gesammtbewusstsein wird ihm eine Bestätigung der Wahrheit des ersteren bieten...

lfm nun aber die Prüfung der verschiedenen kirchlichen Gemeinschaften richtig vollziehen und sich dann frei entscheiden zu können, bedarf es einer untrüglichen Hegel und Richtschnur, nach welcher die Lehren dieser Gemeinschaften bemessen werden können. . . Dieser Norm wird dann mit der Lehre der Einzelkirche auch die Lehre der Gesammtkirche zu unterwerfen sein, um der Voraussetzung ihrer Richtigkeit das unverbrüchliche Siegel unbedingter Gewissheit aufzuprägen. . .

Wir haben nun als Quelle, aus welcher die christliche Glaubenslehre ihren Stoff zu schöpfen hat, eine dreifache erkannt, nemlich die erleuchtete Vernunft des dogmatisirenden Subjectes, die Lehre der Kirphe und die kanonische Schrift des Alten Und Neuen Testaments. . . . Aus unserer ganzen bisherigen Entwickelung geht von selbst hervor, dass die Schriftlehre bei uns nicht, wie in der älteren Dogmatik, an den jedesmaligen Anfang, sondern an das jedesmalige Ende des dargelegten Glaubensartikels treten wird, weil wir die Schrift nicht als erste Quelle, sondern als letzte Norm der dogmatischen Erkenntniss betrachten.“ (Kirchliche Glaubenslehre. Stuttgart 1854. 1, 86—92.226.)

Luthardtius: „Die Dogmatik ist die Wissenschaft vom Zusammenhang der Dogmen, welche sie aus dem religiösen Glauben des Christen selbst zu reproduciren hat. . . Die Schrift als normativer Factor des dogmatischen Systems gibt demselben seinen biblischen Charakter.“ (Kompendium der Dogmatik. Leipzig 1868. S. 5. 23.)

De Hofmann: „Es ist eine geläufige Forderung, dass man die kirchlich geltende Lehre an der Schrift prüfe, die Schrift aber nach dem Glauben auslege. Wo finde ich aber den Glauben, nach welchem ich die Schrift auslege, wenn nicht in mir? Denn ausser mir ist er kirchliche Lehre, die an der auszulegeuden Schrift geprüft sein will. Und wäre es auch das apostolische Symbolum, aus welchem man neuerdings ein noch dazu keiner Handhabung fähiges Schriftauslegungsgesetz hat machen wollen, es muss auch dieses, gleichviel wie alte, Erzeugniss kirchlicher Thätigkeit erst wieder an der Schrift geprüft werden, nicht sowohl, ob es im Einzelnen richtig, sondern ob es jene Hauptsumme des Christenthums wirklich ist, welche unsere Väter vielmehr auch selbst aus der Schrift entnommen wissen wollten.

Ans den deutlichsten Schriftstellen zusammengebrachte Hauptsumme göttlicher Lehre war ihnen der Glaube, nach welchem die Schrift ausgelegt werden sollte. Aber sie bewiesen damit nur, dass ihnen die Schrift wie eine Sammlung von Glaubensgesetzen erschien, was sie nicht ist.


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Experience also teaches that clear Scripture speaks clearly again only to those…

Experience also teaches that clear Scripture speaks clearly again only to those who desire salvation or are certain of salvation; and regarding the scope of that sum total, there has never been certainty, but rather fruitless strife to this day over the difference between the fundamental and the non-fundamental.

That demand, therefore, points to the necessity of becoming certain of Christianity as we carry it within ourselves as a present reality... That relationship to God, after I have become a partaker of it, has a"

independent existence has begun in me, which does not depend on the Church, nor on the Scripture to which the Church appeals, nor does it have the actual and immediate guarantee of its truth in this or that, but rests in itself and is immediately certain truth, borne and guaranteed by the Spirit of God dwelling within it. Nevertheless, it wants and must, where one wishes to bring it to knowledge and statement (doctrinal presentation), remain purely only itself, unmixed with, undisturbed by, that which lies outside of it, and thus outside of us anywhere. And whether that which lies outside of us stands in an ever so close, in a causal relation to that which is in us, and whether it manifests itself as the same truth beyond doubt: here it is a matter of accomplishing the one immediate task purely for itself, in closed independence. Admittedly, where things go rightly, Scripture and Church will offer exactly the same thing that we raise up within ourselves. But to find it there is a second task after that one." (Der Schriftbeweiss. Nördlingen, 1852. 1st half, pp. 9, 10, 11.) §

2. By the name of Holy Scripture is understood that collection or volume of books which not only treat of sacred matters and tend toward faith and the holiness of life, but have also been recorded by the peculiar operation of the Holy Spirit, which we commonly call the Bible.

Indeed, the term Holy Scripture, by the force of the word and usage of speech, in the nominative case, signifies the writing or rather the books, rather than the sense; although it connotes the sense and mind of God, as that which they exhibit and for the sake of exhibiting which the books were recorded. See the blessed Hutterus in Comp. Q. I. from Chemnitius, Exam. conc. trid., and the blessed Quenstedtius in Not. § 3. p. 5.

Similarly, the blessed Aegidius Hunnius, Disp. I. th. 50: "Holy Scripture is a volume which consists of certain books of the prophets, apostles, and evangelists, which are called biblical and canonical."

In this respect it is called "holy" from its object; which, however, it has in common with other writings, catechetical, homiletical, etc. Thus it is called "holy" from its end; which likewise it has in common with others. This denomination is sought from the efficient cause, and this is the most proper signification of Holy Scripture, as will appear from what follows.

Namely, κατ’ ἐξοχήν; and by the plural name τῶν βιβλίων, which, though many, written at different places and times, appear in one codex; just as otherwise, not only ἡ γραφή (John 2:22), but also αἱ γραφαί (Matt. 21:42), αἱ γραφαὶ ἅγιαι (Rom. 1:2), and ἱερὰ γράμματα (2 Tim. 3:15) are cited.

Although it must be admitted that in the biblical codex, besides the books that proceeded from divine inspiration, others are also contained which are indeed holy in respect to object and end, but were nevertheless recorded by human effort, and that the name of Holy Scripture has been accustomed to be attributed to the whole codex by synecdoche; yet here we retain the special and proper signification.

Reuschius: "By the manner of speaking in the singular, it is hinted that all the particular books of Holy Scripture constitute one whole and have one primary author." (Annotatt. etc. p. 74.) ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

3. The principal efficient cause of Holy Scripture is God, the Triune; by appropriation, however, the Holy Spirit. See Rom. 3:2. Paul calls Scripture λόγια του θεού, the oracles of God, or those that have proceeded from God, and 2 Tim. 3:16, where Scripture is called θεόπνευστος, and by this very fact it is indicated that it depends efficiently upon God.

Gerhard: “Between the word of God and Holy Scripture taken materially, there is no real difference. This is proved 1. from the matter of Scripture... 2. From the ισοδυναμία of the phrases... 3. From the logical rule: An accident does not change the essence of a thing... 4. From the δεικτική particle used by the apostles. Paul says demonstratively regarding Mosaic Scripture and the homogeneous books of the Old and New Testaments: ‘Τοϋτ’ εστι το ρήμα τής πίστεως, which we preach,’ Rom. 10:8; 1 Pet. 1:25.” (Exeges. 1. 1. § 7.)

QUENSTEDTIUS: “That these words (‘πάσα γραφή θεόπνευστος’) are spoken elliptically, no one fails to see, for the link of the substantive verb εστί is missing, as it is very often elsewhere in Holy Scripture; if you insert it, the statement becomes perfect: πάσα γραφή ’εστι θεόπνευστος. The subject is γραφή, Scripture, not just any, but determinately Ιερά, v. 15.” (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 3. f. 100.)

The same: “Although St. Peter does not speak precisely of writing, but of speaking, by which the holy men of God with living voice brought forth the prophecies that had come to them divinely and communicated them to others; yet by λαλιάν both speaking and writing are signified here, and under the former the latter is simultaneously comprehended, see Acts 2:31; 3:24; Rom. 3:19; Jas. 5: 10. For just as the holy men of God spoke while moved and impelled by the Holy Spirit, so also they wrote while moved and impelled by the same. Indeed, προφητεία γραφής, i.e., the prophecy of Scripture or prophetic Scripture, as Erasmus translates v. 20, was formerly brought forth by writing. And thus the holy writers in writing depended no less upon the Holy Spirit than in speaking, and were merely instrumental causes.” (L. c. f. 101. sq.)

For Scripture is an outward work, and the λόγος προφορικός of God, according to the essence, wisdom, and power of the One. Or, by a mode of speaking received in the Scriptures, by which a work is attributed to the Holy Spirit as if it were His own, which is common to the whole Holy Trinity. Thus Peter, 2 Epist. 1:21, says that the prophets in their writings, according to v. 20, spoke φερομένους ύπυ πνεύματος άγιου. And Paul, writing to the Corinthians, 1 Epist. 2:13, says that he speaks in words which the Holy Spirit teaches. Compare 2 Sam. 23:2, where David refers the origin of his Psalms to the Spirit of Jehovah, who spoke in him. §

4. The causality of the principal efficient cause is the very θεοπνευστία, or divine inspiration, that is, an action of such a kind by which God supernaturally communicated to the intellect of the writers not only the concepts of all things to be written, in conformity with the objects, but also the concepts of the words themselves and of all things by which they were to be expressed, and excited their will to the act of writing.

Or the formal reason, by which God is constituted in the actual being of its (Scripture’s) cause and exerted His influence upon it. Indeed, just as in 2 Tim. 3:16, where Scripture is called θεόπνευστος, its dependence upon God as its cause is indicated, so it is simultaneously established that God, through the θεοπνευστία itself, from which Scripture is denominated θεόπνευστος, is constituted in the being of the efficient cause of Scripture. Mus. Introd. P. II. C. II. § 3. p. 245.

Quenstedtius: “Distinguish between divine revelation and inspiration. Revelation, formally and by the force of the word, is the manifestation of unknown and hidden things, and can occur in many and diverse ways, namely, either by external address or by dreams and visions (for ‘to reveal,’ in Greek ἀποκαλύπτειν, is to uncover that which was hidden). Inspiration is an action of the Holy Spirit, by which the actual knowledge of things is supernaturally infused into the created intellect, or it is the internal suggestion or infusion of concepts, whether the things conceived were already known to the writer beforehand or were hidden. The former (revelation) could precede the writing in time; the latter was always joined with the writing and exerted influence upon the writing itself. Meanwhile, I do not deny that θεοπνευστία or divine inspiration can be called revelation in a qualified sense, insofar as it is the manifestation of certain circumstances, as well as the order and manner by which things were to be consigned and written. Sometimes revelation also concurs and coincides with divine inspiration itself, namely, when divine mysteries are inspired by being revealed and revealed by being inspired in the writing itself.” (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. S. 2. q. 8. fol. 98.)

Dannhauerus: “The light of the heavenly way is Holy Scripture, comprised in the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments, θεόπνευστος, i.e., divinely inspired; for πάσα γὰρ γραφὴ (τῶν ἱερῶν γραμμάτων) ἐστὶ (for this must be supplied entirely, lest it be an ἀνακόλουθον) θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος etc. Indeed, the letter of David to Uriah was a γραφή, yet not a γραφὴ of the ἱερὰ γράμματα. — Divinely, I say, inspired by the Father, as the fountain of wisdom, and by the Son, Christ, through the Spirit, the searcher of hearts, by whose ὥρᾳ the holy men of God were moved and spoke. For because the end of Holy Scripture is divine and supernatural, the medium also had to be supernatural, ‘that our faith might not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.’ And therefore Scripture is divine, not because God inscribed everything with His own finger immediately, as He did the Law (which God is said to have written, not only authoritatively and by dictating, but by writing; ‘He wrote on the tables the words of the covenant, the ten commandments,’ Exod. 34:28. Who wrote? The Lord Himself, with whom Moses was for forty days, etc.), but because He inscribed it through divine men and appropriated the Scripture to Himself as His own.

Furthermore, the θεόπνευσις of Holy Scripture is from the Holy Spirit, not only 1. by inspiring, with an external, open command; and that either general: ‘teach all nations’ — therefore also the most remote, to whom the feet of the apostles did not come, and therefore also the most recent, whom the death of the apostles preceded; both had to be assisted by the pen, and that by the necessity of some persons. For although Scripture is an accident of the divine word, yet to that word, which must shine forth into all nations without fear of falsehood, it is essential, just as whiteness is an accident of a wall, but belongs to the essence of a white wall; — or special, made to Isaiah and John twelve times in the Apocalypse (1:11, 19; 2:1, 8, 12, 18; 3:1, 7, 14; 14:13; 19:9; 21:5); where, for the reason that Isaiah had to write, namely, out of a concern for perpetuity; and for which St. John, because he could not teach by living voice while exiled on Patmos: for the same reason the remaining writers understood that the task of writing was given to them, who, if they undertook such a great matter without a divine mandate, bound themselves to the same sin by which a secretary errs who writes a document to subjects without the order of the prince; —

Latin:

Auch lehrt die Erfahrung, dass wieder nur Heilsbegierigen oder Heilsgewissen die deutliche Schrift deutlich redet; und über den Umfang jener Hauptsumme ist nie Sicherheit, wohl aber über den Unterschied von Fundamentalem und Nichtfundamentalem bis auf diesen Tag fruchtloser Streit gewesen.

Auch jene Forderung weis’t demnach atu die Nothwendigkeit hin, sich des Christenthums, wie wir es als gegenwärtigen Thatbestand in uns selbst tragen, zu vergewissern. . . Jenes Verhältniss zu Gott, nachdem ich seiner theilhaftig geworden, hat ein

selbständiges Dasein in mir begonnen, welches nicht von der Kirche abhängt, noch von der Schrift, auf die sich die Kirche beruft, auch nicht an jener oder dieser die eigentliche und nächste Verbürgung seiner Wahrheit hat, sondern in sich selbst ruht und unmittelbar gewisse Wahrheit ist, von dem ihm selbst einwohnenden Geiste Gottes getragen und verbürgt. Dennoch will und muss dasselbe, wo man es sich zur Erkenntniss und Aussage“ (Lehrdarstellung) „bringen lassen will, rein nur es selber bleiben, unvermengt mit dem, ungestört durch das, was ausser ihm, also ausser uns wo irgend gelegen ist. Und ob das ausser uns Gelegene in noch so naher, in ursächlicher Beziehung steht zu dem in uns, und ob es sich als die gleiche Wahrheit unzweifelhaft zu erkennen gibt: hier gilt es, die eine nächste Aufgabe rein für sich, in geschlossener Selbständigkeit zu vollziehen. Freilich werden, wo es recht hergeht, Schrift und Kirche ganz das Gleiche bieten, was wir in uns selbst erheben. Aber es dort aufzufinden, ist eine zweite Aufgabe nach jener.“ (Der Schriftbeweiss. Nördlingen, 1852. 1ste Hälfte, S., 9.10. 11.) §

2. Intelligitur autem nomine Scripturae sacrae complexus ille seu volumen a librorum, qui non tantum res sacras b tractant et ad fidem ac vitae sanctimoniam c tendunt, verum etiam peculiari operatione Spiritus Sancti d consignati sunt, quos vulgo Biblia e appellamus.

Significat utique Scriptura sacra, ex vi vocis et usu loquendi, in casu recto, scripturam seu libros potius, quam sensum; etsi connotet sensum ac mentem Dei, tanquam id, quod exhibent et cujus exhibendi causa consignati sunt libri. Vid. b. Hutterus in Comp. Q. I. ex Chemn. Exam. conc. trid. et b. Oundis. in Not. § 3. p. 5.

Similiter b. Aegid. Hunnius Disp. I. th. 50.: Scriptura sacra volumen est, quod certis prophetarum, apostolorum et evangelistarum libris constat, qui biblici et canonici appellantur.

Qua ratione sacra dicitur ab objecto; quod tamen cum aliis scriptis, catechleticis, homileticis etc. commune habet. Ita sacra dicitur a fine; quod itidem ei cum aliis commune est. Quae denominatio petita est a causa efficiente, et significatio maxime propria est Scripturae s., ut ex seqq. patebit.

Scilicet χατ έξοχψ; et nomine plurali των βιβλίων, qui multi, diversis locis ac temporibus scripti, in uno codice apparent; prout alias, non solum ή γραφή Joh. 2, 22., sed etiam ai γραφώ. Matth. 21, 42., ai γραφώ αγια: Rom. 1, 2., et ιερά γράμματα 2 Tim. 3, 15. citantur.

Quanquam vero fatendum sit, in codice biblico praeter libros ex divina inspiratione profectos etiam alios ex parte objecti et finis quidem sacros, sed tamen humano studio consignatos una contineri et nomen Scripturae sacrae toti codici per synecdochen tribui consuevisse; hic tamen significationem specialem ac propriam retinemus.

Reuschius: „Ratione loquendi in singulari innuitur, quod omnes sacrae Scripturae particulares libri unum constituant totum atque unum habeant auctorem primarium.“ (Annotatt. etc. p. 74.) DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

3. Causa efficiens principalis Scripturae s. Deus a trinunus b est; per appropriationem c autem Spiritus Sanctus. d Vid. Rom. 3, 2. Paulus Scripturam vocat λόγια του θεού, eloquia Dei, seu a Deo profecta, et 2 Tim. 3, 16., ubi Scriptura dicitur θεόπνευστος, et hoc ipso eam a Deo efficienter dependere indicatur.

Gerhardus: „Inter verbum Dei et Scripturam sacram materialiter acceptam non esse reale aliquod discrimen. Probatur hoc 1. ex Scripturae materia. . . 2. Ex phrasium ισοδνναμίφ. . . 3. Ex regula logica: Accidens non mutat rei essentiam... 4. Ex δεικτική particula ab apostolis usurpata. Paulus de Scriptura Mosaica et homogeneis Vet. ac Novi Test, libris δεικτικώς inquit: ,Τοϋτ’ εστι το ρήμα τής πίστεως, quod praedicamus', Rom. 10, 8. 1 Pet. 1, 25.“ (Exeges. 1. 1. § 7.)

QUENSTEDTIUS: ,,’Έλλειπτικώς haec (πάσα γραφή θεόπνευστος') dici, nemo non videt, deest enim, ut alibi in s.
