L. saepissime, vinculum verbi substantivi εστί, quod si interseras, perfectum evadit enunciatum: πάσα γραφή ’εστι θεόπνευστος. Subjectum est γραφή, Scriptura, non quaevis, sed determinate Ιερά, v. 15.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 3. f. 100.)

Idem: „Quamvis s. Petrus non praecise de scriptione, sed de locutione, qua viva voce sancti Dei homines prophetias, quae divinitus sibi contigerant, protulerunt et cum aliis communicarunt, loquatur; per λαλιάν tamen et locutio et scriptio hic significatur et sub illa haec simul comprehenditur, v. Act. 2, 31. 3, 24. Rom. 3, 19. Jac. 5, 10. Uti enim a Spiritu S. acti et impulsi locuti sunt sancti Dei homines, ita etiam ab eodem acti et impulsi scripserunt. Imo προφητεία γραφής, h. e., prophetia Scripturae sive prophetica Scriptura, ut Erasmus vertit v. 20., olim allata est per scriptionem. Atque ita s. scriptores in scribendo non minus, quam in loquendo a Spiritu S. pependerunt et causae mere instrumentales fuerunt.“ (L. c. f. 101. sq.)

Est enim Scriptura opus ad extra, et λόγος προψοραός Dei, secundum essentiam, sapientiam ac potentiam unius. Seu, per modum loquendi Scripturis receptum, quo Spiritui s. velut opus proprium tribuitur, quod toti SS. Trinitati commune est. Sic Petrus 2. Epist. 1, 21. dicit, prophetas in scriptis suis, juxta vers. 20., locutos fuisse, φερομένους ύπυ πνεύματος άγιου. Et Paulus scribens ad Corinthios 1. Epist. 2, 13. dicit, se loqui sermonibus, quos docet Spiritus Sanctus. Confer. 2 Sam. 23, 2, ubi David Psalmorum suorum originem refert ad Spiritum Jehovae, qui locutus sit in ipso.§

4. Causalitas causae efficientis principalis a est ipsa Seoτΐνενστία, seu divina inspiratio, b id est, actio ejusmodi, qua Deus non solum conceptus c rerum scribendarum d omnium, objectis conformes, sed et conceptus verborum ipsorum atque omnium, e quibus illi exprimendi essent, supernaturaliter communicavit intellectui scribentium ac voluntatem eorum ad actum scribendi f excitavit.

Sive ratio formalis, per quam Deus in esse actu causae ejus (Scripturae) constitutus est et influxum suum in illam praebuit. Nempe sicut 2 Tim. 3, 16., ubi Scriptura θεόπνευστος dicitur, dependentia ejus a Deo, tanquam a causa, indicatur, ita simul constat, Deum per θεοπνευστίαν ipsam, a qua Scriptura θεόπνευστος denominatur, in esse causae efficientis Scripturae constitui. Mus. Introd. P. II. C. Π. § 3. p. 245.

Quenstedtius: „Dist. inter divinam revelationem, et inspirationem. Revelatio formaliter et vi vocis est manifestatio rerum ignotarum et occultarum, et potest fleri multis et diversis modis, sci. vel per externum alloquium, vel per somnia et visiones (nam,revelare', graece άποκαλυπτειν, est id, quod occultum erat, retegere). Inspiratio est actio Spiritus 8., qua actualis rerum cognitio intellectui creato supernaturaliter infunditur, seu est interna conceptuum suggestio seu infusio, sive res conceptae jam ante scriptori fuerint cognitae, sive occultae. Illa (revelatio) potuit tempore antecedere scriptionem, haec cum scriptione semper fuit conjuncta et in ipsam scriptionem influebat. Interim non nego, ipsam θεοπνευστίαν sive inspirationem divinam dici posse revelationem secundum quid, quatenus scl. est manifestatio certarum circumstantiarum, item ordinis et modi, quibus res consignandae et scribendae erant. Quandoque etiam revelatio cum ipsa inspiratione divina concurrit atque coincidit, quando sci. divina mysteria revelando inspirantur et inspirando revelantur in ipsa scriptione.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. S. 2. q. 8. fol. 98.)

Dannhauerus: ,,Lux viae coelestis est Scriptura sacra canonicis veteris ac novi testamenti libris comprehensa, θεόπνευστος, h. e., divinitus inspirata; πάσα γάρ γραφή (των ιερών γραμμάτων) εστί (hoc enim omnino supplendum, ne sit ανακόλουθου') θεόπνευστος και ωφέλιμος etc. Equidem epistola Davidis Uriae letifera fuit γραφή, non tamen γραφή Ιερών γραμμάτων. — Divinitus, inquam, inspirata a Patre, ut fonte sapientiae, et Filio Christo, per Spiritum cordis scrutatorem, cujus ώορά acti et moti locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Nam quia finis Scripturae sacrae divinus est et supernaturalis, medium quoque supernaturale esse debuit, ,ut fides nostra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei.1 Ac ideo divina est Scriptura non quod omnem Deus suo digito immediate sicut legem (quam Deus scripsisse perhibetur* non duntaxat aucto ritative et dictando, sed scribendo; ,scripsit in tabulis verba foederis decem', Exod. 84, 28. Quis scripsit? Dominus ipse, cum quo Moses fuit quadraginta dies etc.) exararit, sed quod per viros divinos exarasset ac eorum sibi Scripturam appropriasset tanquam suam.

Caeterum θεόπνενσις Scripturae sacrae est a Sp. S. non solum 1. aspirante, cum jussu exteriori, aperto; eoque vel generali: ,docete omnes gentes*, — ergo et remotissimas, ad quas pes apostolorum non venit, ergo et novissimas, quibus apostolicum alloquium mors apostolorum praevertit; utrisque calamo succurrendum erat, idque necessario aliquo aliquorum. Tametsi enim Scriptura sit accidens verbi divini, tamen ei verbo, quod in omnes gentes inclarescere sine formidine mendacii debet, est essentialis, sicut albedo accidens est parietis, at de essentia parietis albi; — vel speciali, facta ad Esaiam et Johannem duodecies in Apocalypsi (1, 11. 19.; 2, 1. 8. 12. 18.; 3, 1.7. 14.; 14, 13.; 19, 9.; 21, 5.); ubi ex qua causa Esaias scribere debuit, nimirum ex perpetuitatis cura; ex qua d. Johannes, quod exui in Patmo non posset viva voce docere: ex eadem etiam reliqui scriptores sibi scribendi negotium datum esse intellexere, qui, si absque divino mandato rem tantam susceperunt, ejusdem se peccati alligarunt, quo secretarius, injussu principis ad subditos diploma scribens, delinquit; —


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: or most special, joined with obligation, determination, and divine rapture, by…

or most special, joined with obligation, determination, and divine rapture, by which Judas, moved, [felt] the necessity...” ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY. confessed that it was imposed upon him; an occasion arose as a kind of *ίπαναγκές τι* [certain necessity]; see Aeg. Hunnius on the Church, p. 201 sq. —

Then there was the antecedent pedagogy, acting as a directress and a preventer of error, which indeed would have rendered Scripture alone infallible, yet not strictly *θεόπνενστον* [God-breathed]; it would have been joined with the labor and difficulty of the writer, of which the author of Maccabees complains. (2 Macc. 2:27.) For although even the *θεόπνευστοι* [God-breathed ones]* applied scrutiny and study in the exercise of teaching, yet that the writing was done without labor is shown by that cited and swift recitation (Jer. 36:2) from memory of those things which had fallen from the parchment.

Not only 2. by sub-or post-breathing, consequently a testimony by which the pedagogue judges and approves what the disciple has produced by his own effort, for the same reasons we just held; but 3. by breathing in through a most present, concomitant grace; taking care that the writer would not err even in a point, revealing anew things superior to human reason, moderating the consigning to writing of those things which he had received either by sight or hearing ("For," these are the words of Bellarmine, "a letter is called the true letter of a prince which is dictated by the prince, even if he who wrote it knew beforehand what he was going to write; so that is called and is the immediate word of God which is written by the evangelists while God is inspiring and directing, even though they wrote those things which they had seen and heard"), suggesting what had fallen away, guarding against error, with not even the lighter matters excepted,** dictating the most apt words, sanctifying and appropriating them to Himself. — "What is written by the hand of the apostles is written by the hand of God Himself," August. Lib. I. de consens. evang. c. ult. —; but also 4. by breathing again, as often as the oracle of Holy Scripture is sought in due order. As a pneumatic musical organ, as it were, revives, breathes, and sounds as often as it is played with skill: so when Holy Scripture is handled with pious reading, hearing, and meditation, the Holy Spirit, as it were, breathes through it, brings forth divine oracles, and manifests counsels from the inner sanctuary of the divine heart necessary for salvation. And this *θεόπνενσις* [God-breathing] is the soul of Holy Scripture, from which it has its divine being and *αύτόπιστον* [self-evidencing authority], from no other source." (Hodos. phaen. 1. E. p. 18—20.)

Certainly, it is not so much the things, according to their real being (in which respect they are outside the intellect of the writer), as the concepts of the things to be expressed in writing that are inspired into the intellect of the writer. Moreover, we believe that the concepts not only of sublime things, exceeding the grasp of human reason, but also of all other things which Scripture contains, as they are to be committed to letters, were inspired into the sacred writers by God; since *πάσα γραφή* [all Scripture], the iota, Scripture, not just some part of it, is said to be divinely inspired. Inspiration, however, does not import a bare assistance or governance for the sake of preventing errors, but the very communication or suggestion of concepts; just as those things which an amanuensis ought to write are dictated to his pen. See Mus. Introduct. P. II. Cap. II. § 3. n. 4. 5. p. 246. sqq.

Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between bare divine assistance and direction, by which it is only guarded that the sacred writers do not stray from the truth in speaking and writing, and that divine assistance and direction which includes the inspiration and dictation of the Holy Spirit; not the former, but the latter makes Scripture *θεόπνενστον* [God-breathed], and this is what has place here." (L. c. q. 3. f. 98. sq.) *)

1 Pet. 1:10, 11. 2 Tim. 3:14. 1 Cor. 7:15, where the apostle, endowed with the Holy Spirit v. 40, nevertheless denies that that precept of his was expressly handed down by the Lord, but was collected by himself finally through argumentation with the singular assistance of the Holy Spirit, which guards against error. **)

2 Tim. 4:13, where the care for the parchments and membranes shows that the form of the garment is an adiaphoron and that the apostolic membranes are not to be lightly esteemed.

The same: "Distinguish between the infallibility of Holy Scripture and its divinity; the former is from divine assistance, the latter from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Nor can it be said immediately that what is written through the infallible assistance and direction of God is θεόπνευστος or divinely inspired." (L. c. f. 99.)

Augsburg Confession: "Why does Scripture so often forbid the establishing and hearing of traditions? Why does it call them doctrines of demons (1 Tim. 4:1)? Did the Holy Spirit warn of these things in vain?" (p. 66.)

Apology of the A. C.: "Do they think it is in vain that the same thing is repeated so often? Do they suppose that these words escaped the Holy Spirit, who did not notice them?" (p. 107.) "

You have, therefore, reader, our apology, from which you will understand both what the adversaries have judged (for we have reported it in good faith), and that they have condemned several articles against the manifest Scripture of the Holy Spirit." (p. 74.)

Luther: "First, he (David, 2 Sam. 23:2) names the Holy Spirit, to whom he gives everything that the prophets prophesy. And St. Peter looks to this and similar passages in 2 Ep. 1:21: 'For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.' Therefore, one sings in the article of faith (in the Nicene Creed) concerning the Holy Spirit thus: 'who has spoken by the prophets.' Thus, one now gives the whole Holy Scripture to the Holy Spirit... Hear now, whoever has ears to hear! My words are not my words, but, 'whoever hears me, hears God; whoever despises me, despises God' (Luke 10:16). For I see that many of my descendants will not hear my words, to their great harm. Such glory we may not yet claim, nor anyone who is not a prophet. We may do this, insofar as we are also holy and have the Holy Spirit, that we boast of being catechumens and students of the prophets, as those who repeat and preach what we have heard and learned from the prophets and apostles, and are also certain that the prophets taught it. In the Old Testament, these are called the children of the prophets, who set forth nothing of their own nor anything new, as the prophets do, but teach what they have from the prophets... So we have here again two distinct persons, the Father and the Son; thus the Holy Spirit is there without that, who has introduced, made, and spoken such psalms of the Father and the Son with their words. Thus, the distinct Trinity of persons in one inseparable divine essence, and that the Son is man and Messiah, is confessed, just as it is confessed in the last words of David. A carnal heart runs over it or thinks that David made it as a pious man of himself or others, as the blind Jews do: but David will not suffer that one should ascribe the words to him. They are the sweet psalms of Israel (he says), but I did not make them, but the Spirit of the Lord has spoken through me." (Exposition of the Last Words of David. 1543. III, 2797. sq. 2802. sq.)

Quenstedtius: "The original canonical Holy Scripture is of infallible truth and devoid of every error, or, which is the same thing, in the canonical Holy Scripture there is no lie, no falsehood, no error, not even the slightest, whether in matters or in words; but all and singular things that are handed down in it are most true, whether they are dogmatic, moral, historical, chronological, topographical, or onomastic; and no ignorance, lack of thought, or forgetfulness, no lapse of memory can or ought to be attributed to the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit in the recording of the holy letters." (L. c. q. 5. f. 112.)

Formula of Concord: "With our whole heart we receive and embrace the prophetic and apostolic writings of the Old and New Testaments as the most clear and pure fountains of Israel."

Luther: "I faithfully ask and warn every pious Christian that he should not be offended by the simple speech and history that will often meet him; rather, do not doubt that, however poor it may appear, these are the pure words, works, judgments, and history of the high divine majesty and wisdom. For this is the Scripture that makes all the wise and prudent into fools and is open only to the small and simple, as Christ says in Matthew 11:25. Therefore, let go of your conceit and feelings and hold this Scripture to be the highest, noblest sanctuary, the richest mine that can never be fully exhausted, so that you may find the divine wisdom which God here presents so simply and poorly, that He might dampen all pride. Here you will find the swaddling clothes and the manger in which Christ lies, to which the angel also points the shepherds in Luke 2:11. They are poor and meager swaddling clothes, but the treasure, Christ, who lies within, is precious." (Preface to the O.T., 1523. XIV, 2 sq.)

The same: "By this I also wish to have answered those who accuse me of rejecting all the holy teachers of the Church. I do not reject them, but since everyone knows well that they have sometimes erred, as men, I will not give them faith further than insofar as they provide me with proof of their understanding from the Scripture, which has not yet erred. And St. Paul calls me to this in 1 Thessalonians 5:21, where he says: 'Test and prove all doctrine; hold fast to that which is good.' In the same way, St. Augustine writes to St. Jerome: 'I have learned to show such honor only to those books which are called Holy Scripture, that I firmly believe that none of their authors ever erred.'" (Ground and Cause of All Articles Condemned by the Roman Bull, 1520. XV, 1758.)

Quenstedt: "Distinguish between the state of the apostles before they received the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, and their state after the gift of the Holy Spirit was bestowed; in the former, they were subject to errors and labored under ignorance and false apprehension of certain dogmas, see Acts 1:7; Luke 24:25; in the latter, however, they were led by the Holy Spirit into all truth, John 16:13. — Distinguish between the conversation of the apostles and their preaching and writing, or between the infirmities of life and errors of doctrine. In doctrine, the apostles could in no way err after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit; their mind and tongue were as the plectrum or pen of the Holy Spirit Himself, who was giving what they should speak, and speaking in them (Matthew 10:19), and thus leading them into all truth (John 16:13). In life and external conversation, however, they were not entirely ἀναμάρτητοι (sinless), but because of inborn original corruption, they were still subject to infirmities and falls, and sometimes even suffered from human frailty (ἀνθρώπινον), as Theophylact affirms regarding the two brothers in Matthew 20:20. — Distinguish between error in faith and doctrine, and error in some special act, such as the sin of Peter in Galatians 2:11 sq., i.e., a fault not of preaching, but of conversation, as Tertullian says in his book *De Praescriptione*. — Distinguish between error in the theory of faith, in which way no holy writer erred, and error in practice; and thus Peter erred, because his practice and external conversation did not agree with his theory or doctrine and profession of faith." (L. c. q. 5. f. 116.)

Latin:

vel specialissimo, cum obligatione, determinatione ac raptu divino conjuncto, quo motus Judas necessitatem DE PRINCIPIO THEOROGIAE. sibi impositam fassus est; accessit occasio tanquam ίπαναγκές τι; vide Aeg. Hunnium de eccles. p. 201. sq. —

Tum paedagogia antecedanea, directrice et erroris praecautrice, quae quidem solam Scripturam praestitisset infallibilem, nondum tamen proprie θεόπνενστον; conjuncta fuisset cum scribentis molestia et difficultate, de qua conqueritur auctor Maccabaeorum. (2 Macc. 2, 27.) Tametsi enim etiam θεόπνευστοι*) scrutinium adhibuerint ac studio in exercitio docendi, tamen scribendi raptum fuisse sine molestia, ostendit cita illa et expedita recitatio (Jer. 36, 2.) e memoria eorum, quae in charta exciderunt.

Non solum 2. subvel post-spirante per consequens testimonium, quo pacto paedagoga censet et approbat, quae discipulus proprio marte edidit, ob easdem, quas modo habuimus, rationes; sed 3. inspirante per gratiam praesentissimam concomitantem; accurante, ne vel in puncto erraret scriptor, revelante de novo res ratione humana superiores, moderante consignationes eorum, quae vel visu vel auditu accepisset (,Utenim‘, verba sunt Bellarm., ,dicitur vera epistola principis, quae a principe dictatur, etiamsi is, qui eam scripsit, antea sciebat, quae scripturus erat; ita dicitur et est immediatum Dei verbum, quod scriptum est ab evangelistis Deo inspirante et dirigente, licet scripserint ea, quae viderant et audierant‘), suggerente, quae exciderunt, cavente errorem, ne levioribus quidem exceptis, **) dictitante verba aptissima, sanctificante sibique appropriante. — ,Quod manu apostolorum scriptum est, ipsa manu Dei scriptum est‘, August. 1. I. de consens. evang. c. ult. —; sed et 4. respirante, quoties debito ordine oraculum Scripturae sacrae quaeritur. Ut organum musicum pneumaticum quasi reviviscit, spirat, sonat, quoties ex arte pulsatur: ita cum lectione, auditione ac meditatione pia tractatur Scriptura sacra, Spiritus S. per eam respirat quasi, edit oracula divina, consilia ex cordis divini adytis ad salutem necessaria manifestat. Atque haec θεόπνενσις est Scripturae s. anima, a qua habet suum esse divinum ac αύτόπιστον, non aliunde.“ (Hodos. phaen. 1. E. p. 18—20.)

Sane non tam res, secundum suum esse reale (qua ratione sunt extra intellectum scribentis), quam conceptus rerum scripto exprimendarum inspirantur intellectui scriptoris. Non solum autem rerum sublimium, humanae rationis captum excedentium, sed et caeterarum omnium, quas Scriptura continet, tanquam in literas referendarum, conceptus scriptoribus sacris a Deo inspiratos fuisse credimus; cum πάσα γραφή, iota, Scriptura, non aliqua tantum pars ejus, divinitus inspirata dicatur. Inspiratio vero non nudam assistentiam aut gubernationem ad praecavendos errores, verum ipsam conceptuum communicationem aut suggestionem importat; prout amanuensi in calamum dictantur, quae is scribere debeat. Vid. Mus. Introduct. P. II. Cap. Π. § 3. n. .4. 5. p. 246. sqq.

Quenstedius: „Dist. inter assistentiam et directionem divinam nudam, qua tantum cavetur, ne scriptores sacri in loquendo et scribendo a vero aberrent, et inter assistentiam et directionem divinam, quae includit Spiritus S. inspirationem et dictamen; non illa, sed haec Scripturam efficit θεόπνενστον et hic locum habet.“ (L. c. q. 3. f. 98. sq.) *)

1 Pet. l, 10.11. 2 Tim. 3, 14. 1 Cor. 7,15., ubi apostolus Spiritu S. praeditus v. 40., tamen negat, illud suum praeceptum expresse a Domino traditum, sed a se demum cum singulari Spiritus S. assistentia, erroris cautrice, argumentando collectum. **)

2 Tim. 4, 13., ubi pennulae et membranae cura ostendit, vestis formam esse adiaphoram ac membranas apostolicas non esse parvi pendendas.

Idem: ,,Dist. inter s. Scripturae infallibilitatem, et divinitatem; illa ab assistentia divina est, haec ab inspiratione Spiritus S. Nec statim, quod per assistentiam et directionem Dei infallibilem scriptum est, θεόπνευστου seu inspiratum divinitus dici potest.“ (L. c. f. 99.)

Conf. Augustana: ,,Cur toties prohibet Scriptura condere et audire traditiones? Cur vocat eas doctrinas daemoniorum (1 Tim. 4,1.)? Num frustra haec praemonuit Spiritus Sanctus?u (p. 66.)

Apologia A. C.: „Num frustra existimant toties idem repeti? Num arbitrantur, excidisse Spiritui Sancto non animadvertenti has voces?“ (p. 107.) „

Habes igitur, lector, nunc apologiam nostram, ex qua intelliges, et quid adversarii judicaverint (retulimus enim bona fide), et quod articulos aliquot contra manifestam Scripturam Spiritus Sancti damnaverint.“ (p. 74.)

Lutherus: „Erstlich nennet er (David, 2 Sam. 23, 2.) den Heiligen Geist, dem giebt er alles, was die Propheten weissagen. Und auf diesen und dergleichen Spruch siehet St. Petrus 2. Ep. 1, 21.: ,Es ist noch nie keine Weissagung aus menschlichem Willen hervorgebracht, sondern die heiligen Menschen Gottes haben geredet aus Eingebung des Heiligen Geistes.' Daher singt man in dem Artikel des Glaubens, (im Nicänum) von dem Heiligen Geist also: ,der durch die Propheten geredet hat.' Also giebet man nun dem Heiligen Geiste die ganze heilige Schrift. . . Höre nun, wer Ohren hat zu hören! Meine Reden sind nicht meine Reden, sondern, ,wer mich höret, der höret Gott, wer mich verachtet, der verachtet Gott',·Luc. 10, 16. Denn ich sehe, dass meiner Nachkommen viel werden meine Worte nicht hören, zu ihrem grossen Schaden. Solchen Ruhm dürfen wir, noch niemand führen, der nicht ein Prophet ist. Das mögen wir thun, soferne wir auch heilig und den Heiligen Geist haben, dass wir Catechumenos und Schüler der Propheten uns rühmen, als die wir nachsagen und predigen, was wir von den Propheten und Aposteln gehöret und gelernet und auch gewiss sind, dass es die Propheten gelehret haben. Das heissen in dem Alten Testament der Propheten Kinder, die nichts eigenes noch neues setzen, wie die Propheten thun, sondern lehren, das sie von den Propheten haben. ... So haben wir nun hier abermal zwo unterschiedliche Personen, den Vater und den Sohn; so ist der Heilige Geist ohne das da, der solchen Psalmen vom Vater und Sohn mit ihren Worten eingeführet, gemacht und geredet hat. Also ist die unterschiedliche Dreifaltigkeit der Personen in einem unzertrennlichen göttlichen Wesen, und dass der Sohn Mensch und Messias sei, bekennet, gleichwie es in den letzten Worten Davids bekannt ist. Ein fleischlich Herz läuft überhin oder denket, David habe es als ein frommer Mann gemacht von sich selbst oder andern, wie die blinden Juden thun: aber David will es nicht leiden, dass man sollte ihm die Worte zuschreiben. Es sind lustige liebliche Psalmen Israel (spricht er), aber ich habe sie nicht gemacht, sondern der Geist des Herrn hat durch mich geredt.“ (Ausl, der letzten Worte Davids. 1543. III, 2797. sq. 2802. sq.)

Quenstedtius: „S. Scriptura canonica originalis est infallibilis veritatis omnisque erroris expers, sive, quod idem est, in s. Scriptura canonica nullum est mendacium, nulla falsitas, nullus vel minimus error, sive in rebus sive in verbis; sed omnia et singula sunt verissima, quaecunque in illa traduntur, sive dogmatica illa sunt, sive moralia, sive historica, chronologica, topographica, onomastica; nullaque ignorantia, incogitantia auit oblivio, nullus memoriae lapsus Spiritus S. amanuensibus in consignandis s. literis tribui potest aut debet.“ (L. c. q. 5. f. 112.)

Form. Conc.: „Toto pectore prophetica et apostolica scripta V. et N. T. ut limpidissimos purissimosque Israelis fontes recipimus ac amplectimur.“

Lutherus: „Ich bitte und warne treulich einen jeden frommen Christen, dass er sich nicht stosse an der einfältigen Rede und Geschichte, so ihm oft begegnen wird; sondern zweifle nicht daran, wie schlecht es sich immer ansehen lässt, es seien eitel Worte, Werke, Gerichte und Geschichte der hohen göttlichen Majestät und Weisheit. Denn dies ist die Schrift, die alle Weisen und Klugen zu Narren macht und allein den Kleinen und Albernen offen steht, wie Christus sagt Matth. 11, 25. Darum lass deinen Dünkel und Fühlen fahren und halte von dieser Schrift als von dem allerhöchsten, edelsten Heiligthum, als von der allerreichesten Fundgrube, die nimmer ganz ausgegründet werden mag, auf dass du die göttliche Weisheit finden mögest, welche Gott hier so alber und schlecht vorleget, dass er allen Hochmuth dämpfe. Hier wirst du die Windeln und die Krippen finden, da Christus inne liegt, dahin auch der Engel die Hirten weiset Luc. 2,11. Schlecht und geringe Windeln sind es, aber theuer ist der Schatz, Christus, der drinnen liegt.“ (Vorr. auf das A. T. 1523. XIV, 2. sq.)

Idem: „Damit ich auch denen will geantwortet haben, die mir Schuld geben, ich verwerfe alle heilige Lehrer der Kirchen. Ich verwerfe sie nicht, aber dieweil jedermann wohl weiss, dass sie zuweilen geirret haben, als Menschen, will ich ihnen nicht weiter Glauben geben, denn sofern sie mir Beweisung ihres Verstands aus der Schrift thun, die noch nicht geirret hat. Und das heisset mich St. Paulus 1 Thess. 5, 21., da er saget: ,Prüfet und bewähret zuvor alle Lehre; welche gut ist, die behaltet.' Desselben gleichen schreibet St. Augustinus zu St. Hieronymo: ,lch habe erlernet, allein denen Büchern, die die heilige Schrift heissen, die Ehre zu thun, dass ich vestiglich gläube, keiner derselben Beschreiber habe je geirret.'“ (Grund und Ursach aller Artikel, so durch die röm. Bulle verdammt worden. 1520. XV, 1758.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Dist. inter apostolorum statum ante acceptum in die pentecostes Spiritum S., et inter eorum statum post collatum Spiritus S. donum; in illo erroribus erant obnoxii et laborabant quorundam dogmatum ignorantia et falsa apprehensione, vide Act. 1, 7. Luc. 24, 25.; in hoc vero a Spiritu S. in omnem veritatem deducebantur, Joh. 16, 13. — Dist. inter apostolorum conversationem et eorundem praedicationem ac scriptionem, sive inter infirmitates vitae et errores doctrinae. In doctrina nequaquam errare potuerunt apostoli post acceptum Spiritus S. donum; erat mens et lingua eorum quasi plectrum aut calamus ipsius Spiritus S. dantis, quod loquerentur, et loquentis in ipsis Matth. 10, 19., adeoque ducentis eos in omnem veritatem Joh. 16, 13. In vita vero et conversatione externa non fuerunt prorsus αναμάρτητο,, sed propter ingenitam originalem corruptionem infirmitatibus et lapsibus adhuc obnoxii, et interdum etiam άνάρωπινον passi sunt, ut de duobus fratribus Matth. 20, 20. affirmat Theophylactus, — Dist. inter errorem in fide et doctrina, et inter errorem in facto aliquo speciali, quale fuit peccatum Petri Gal. 2, 11. sq., sci. vitium non praedicationis, sed conversationis, ut inquit Tertullianus libro de praescriptione. — Dist. inter errorem in theoria fidei, quo pacto nullus scriptorum s. erravit, et errorem in praxi, et sic erravit Petrus, quia ejus praxis et externa conversatio non congruebat cum theoria sive doctrina et professione fidei.“ (L. c. q. 5. f. 116.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: The same: "Distinguish between those who are introduced by the holy writers…

The same: "Distinguish between those who are introduced by the holy writers speaking from their own impulse, such as Eve (Gen. 4:1), Cain (same chapter, v. 13), Job cursing the day of his birth (c. 3:1), the Jews (John 8:48) affirming of Christ that He has a demon; and those who are introduced speaking from the instinct or inspiration of the Holy Spirit, such as Stephen the protomartyr, John the Baptist, and his father Zacharias, Simeon, the Virgin Mary; not the former, but the latter are to be reckoned among the θεόπνευστοι (God-breathed) writers."

The same: "Distinguish between execrations and blasphemies, e.g., of Job, the Jews, etc., and the historical report and recording of the same; God did not inspire the Jews themselves to proclaim blasphemies, as in John 8:48, nor Job to curse the day of his birth, c. 3:1; but He did inspire His holy amanuenses to write and record them, not for imitation, but for caution and avoidance." (L. c. q. 4. f. 104.)

The same: "Luke indeed says that he 'had followed all things closely' and that through the tradition of those who were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, so that he might thereby also gain some credibility for himself; but when he wrote those things which he had followed, he did not draw them from the report of others or from his own memory, but from the divine inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who directed his mind and pen and suggested to him both the things to be written and the words by which they were to be written." (L. c. q. 4. f. 104.)

Luther: "Because here (1 Cor. 7:12, 13) St. Paul testifies that the Lord does not speak this piece, but he himself, he gives to understand that it is not commanded by God, but is free, to do it otherwise or so. For he distinguishes his words from the word of the Lord, so that the Lord's word shall be a commandment, but his word shall be a counsel." (Exposition of the 7th Chapter of the 1st Epistle of St. Paul to the Corinthians. 1523. VIII, 1109.)

Quenstedtius: "All things that were to be written were suggested to the sacred writers by the Holy Spirit in that very act of writing and, as it were, dictated to their intellect into the pen, so that they might be written with these and no other circumstances, in this and no other manner or order." (L. c. q. 3. f. 98.)

For just as Holy Scripture has from the characters of the words and letters that it is writing: so when the whole Scripture is said, absolutely, simply, and without any restriction, to be θεόπνευστος (according to those things which we indicated in the preceding note), it must be confessed that even the concepts of the words which were expressed by letters were inspired in the sacred writers; which the blessed Musaeus proved at greater length and answered the objections of dissenters in l. c. n. 7. sqq. p. 250. sqq. That he always taught this, he shows most clearly in Tract. quaest. de Syncr. et Script. S. L. I. Q. III. p. 319. sqq. Cf. Ausführl. Erklärung, Q. VI. p. 42. sqq.

Quenstedtius: "Nor does the apostle say: πάντα εν γραφή are θεόπνευστα, but πάσα γραφή θεόπνευστος, to show that not only the things written, but also the writing itself is θεόπνευστος. And whatever is said of the whole Scripture must necessarily be understood also of the words as a not insignificant part of Scripture. For if even a little word were to occur in the Scriptures not suggested or inspired divinely, it could not be called πάσα γραφή θεόπνευστος. If, I say, the words and terms had not been suggested to the holy writers through θεοπνευστία, Holy Scripture could not be called θεόπνευστος, inspired by God, properly, absolutely, and simply, but only improperly, in a certain respect, and at least as regards the concepts of the things signified; just as Scripture translated into another language by human effort cannot be called properly, absolutely, and simply θεόπνευστος, because the formal words themselves of which it consists were not suggested by the Holy Spirit through inspiration, although it may be called θεόπνευστος in a certain respect and with a qualification, namely, as regards the concepts of the things once inspired to the holy writers, which are signified by the words of the version." (L. c. q. 4. f. 107.)

The same: "1 Cor. 2:12, 13. In this place 1. words are distinguished from the things communicated through the words... 2. λόγοι διδακτοί ανθρώπινης σοφίας (words taught by human wisdom) are opposed to λόγοι διδακτοί τοϋ θεού (words taught by God), words which human wisdom teaches, or human words, even those most wisely devised, and words which the Holy Spirit teaches, suggests, and dictates (for the genitive expresses the efficient cause, as in John 6:45: 'They shall all be διδακτοί τοϋ θεοϋ, taught by God'). ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

God, from Isa. 54:13.) Those apostolic λαλίαι [utterances] are removed, but these are truly attributed to Him. For the apostle wishes to say: Just as we have received that wisdom or knowledge of divine mysteries from the Holy Spirit, so also have we been taught by Him the very words with which we express it.” (L. c.)

Luther: “One apex of doctrine is worth more than heaven and earth. Therefore, we do not suffer it to be injured in the least.” (Comm. in Ep. S. Pauli ad Gal. Tom. II. p. 341. Ed. Hai. VIII, 2661.)

The same: “But if they were not such frivolous despisers of Scripture, a clear passage from Scripture ought to move them as much as if the world were full of Scripture; as indeed it is true. For it is so with me, that every single passage makes the world too narrow for me.” (That these words, ‘This is my body,’ still stand firm. 1527. XX, 982.)

The same: “But if we grant that any one epistle of Paul, or any one passage of someone, does not pertain to the universal church, then the entire authority of Paul is evacuated. For the Corinthians will say that those things which he teaches concerning faith to the Romans do not pertain to them. What could be imagined more blasphemous and insane than this insanity? Far be it, far be it, that there should be any apex in the whole of Paul which the entire universal church ought not to imitate and preserve.” (De capt. Babyl. Opp. cur. J. C. Irmischer. Vol. V. p. 27. Ed. Hai. XIX, 21. sq.)

The same: “All confess that which Christ says in John 10: ‘The Scripture cannot be broken,’ and that its authority must be entirely uninjured, to which it is permitted neither to contradict nor to deny it.” (Operat. in Psalmos. Cur. J. C. Irmischer. Vol. III. p. 318. Ed. Hai. IV, 1763.)

The same: “Therefore, when Moses writes that God created heaven and earth and what is therein in six days, let it remain that they were six days, and do not look for a gloss, how six days could be one day. But if you cannot understand how they were six days, then give the Holy Spirit the honor that He is more learned than you. For you ought to deal with Scripture in such a way that you think how God Himself speaks. But because God speaks, it does not befit you to twist His Word out of wantonness wherever you wish, unless necessity compels one to understand a text otherwise than as the words sound; namely, when faith does not suffer such an understanding as the words provide.” (Sermons on the Book of Moses. 1527. III, 23.)

To this pertains what is said in 2 Pet. 1:20-21, that prophetic Scripture (προφητείαν γραφῆς) was not brought about of old by the will of man (those men did not bring forth their prophecies by their own motion and judgment), but that they spoke (having girded themselves for the exercise of the act, both of speaking and of writing) being moved (φερομένους) by the Holy Spirit. For in part, the divine inspiration itself, by which those things that ought to be committed to writing are suggested, implies an influx for the exercise of the act of writing; and in part, it is also certain that the holy writers were stirred to write by an express command of God, e.g., Moses, Deut. 31:19; Isaiah, ch. 8:1, 30:8; Jeremiah, ch. 30:2; John, Apoc. 1:11, 19, 2:1, 8, 12, 18, etc., or that otherwise the occasion and incentives for writing were presented through the peculiar providence of God, by which they were made certain of the will of God. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 8. p. 257. sqq.

Quenstedtius: “Distinguish between a fortuitous and accidental occasion, and an occasion provided by God; the apostles wrote sometimes from an occasion, but not a fortuitous one, but one provided by God. God directed all things so that we might have a complete and perfect canon of faith and life, namely, the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures, so that the Scriptures ought to be attributed to His direction, instinct, and impulse, and not to a fortuitous and accidental occasion.” (L. c. q. 2. f. 62.)

PROLEGOM. CHAP. II. ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, 2. of some Calvinists, 3. of the Socinians, 4. of the Arminians, and finally 5. of the Innovators, all of whom deny that the Holy Spirit revealed, inspired, and dictated those things which could have been known by natural reason and elsewhere, either through personal experience and the ministry of the senses (or of which the writers themselves were eyewitnesses and earwitnesses), and which contribute nothing to salvation and concern the circumstances of a fact or a narrated event, and likewise appear to be of lesser importance; rather, they claim that the Spirit only excited the writers to record these things and simultaneously governed them through a singular assistance and direction, so that they would not admit anything false, indecorous, or incongruous, or suffer anything human in their writing. Thus Bellarmine, in his book *De Verbo Dei*, ch. 15, says: ‘God was present with the prophets in one way, and with the historians in another. To the former, He revealed future things and at the same time stood by them, lest they admit anything false in writing; to the latter, He did not always reveal those things which they were about to write, but merely excited them to write those things which they had either seen or heard, which they remembered, and at the same time He stood by them, lest they write anything false.’ . . .

The words of D. Georg. Calixtus, in Part I of his *Responsio* to the Mainz theologians, thesis 72, are these: ‘Scripture is not called divine because every single thing contained in it must be imputed to a special divine revelation (e.g., concerning the two sons of Abraham, the father of David, the series and succession of the kings of Jerusalem and Samaria, that Herod was king of Judea, Pilate the governor, or what St. Paul writes to Timothy in 2 Tim. 4:13: “The cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, bring when you come”), but because the principal things, or those which Scripture primarily and per se regards and intends—namely, those which concern the redemption and salvation of the human race—are owed to that special divine revelation; whereas in other matters, which are known from elsewhere, whether through experience or through the light of nature, the writers were so governed by divine assistance and the Spirit in recording them that they would write nothing that was not factual, true, decorous, and congruous.’” (L. c. q. 3. fol. 99.)

Latin:

Idem: „Dist. inter illos, qui a s. scriptoribus introducuntur loquentes ex proprio motu, ut Eva Gen, 4, 1., Cain cap. eod. v. 13., Hiob maledicens diem nativitatis suae c. 3, 1., Judaei Joh. 8, 48. de Christo affirmantes, quod daemonium habeat; , et inter illos, qui introducuntur loquentes ex instinctu seu afflatu Spiritus S., ut Stephanus protomartyr, Johannes baptista, ejusque pater Zacharias, Simeon, virgo Maria; non illi, sed hi scriptoribus ι9εοπνενστοις sunt accensendi.“ (L. c. q. 3. fol. 99.) Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. I. 7

Idem: „Dist. inter execrationes et blasphemias, v. g. Jobi, Judaeorum etc., et inter earundem historicam relationem et consignationem; non inspiravit Deus ipsis Judaeis Christum ut daemoniacum proclamantibus blasphemias Joh. 8, 48., nec Jobo execrationem diei nativitatis suae c. 3, 1.; inspiravit vero sanctis amanuensibus suis, ut illas scriberent et consignarent, non ad imitationem, sed ad cautionem et vitationem.“ (L. c. q. 4. f. 104.)

Idem: „Dicit quidem Lucos, ,se omnia penitus assecutum esse, idque per traditionem eorum, qui spectatores et ministri verbi fuerint, ut inde etiam aliquam sibi fidem conciliaret; ast cum illa scriberet, quae assecutus erat, non ex aliorum relatione aut memoria sua ea depromsit, sed e divina Spiritus S. inspiratione, qui mentem et calamum direxit ipsique et res scribendas et verba, quibus eaedem scriberentur, suggessit.“ (L. c. q. 4. f. 104.)

Lutherus: „Weil hier (1 Cor. 7, 12.13.) St. Paulus bezeuget, dies Stück rede nicht der Herr, sondern er, gibt er zu verstehen, dass es nicht von Gott geboten, sondern frei sei, sonst oder so zu thun. Denn er unterscheidet seine Worte von dem Worte des Herrn, dass des Herrn Wort soll Gebot, sein Wort aber soll Rath sein.“ (Ausl. des 7. Cap. der 1. Ep. St. Pauli a. d. Corinther. 1523. VIII, 1109.)

Quenstedtius: „Omnia, quae scribenda erant, a Spiritu S. sacris scriptoribus in actu isto scribendi suggesta et intellectui eorum quasi in calamum dictitata sunt, ut his et non aliis circumstantiis, hoc et non alio modo aut ordine scriberentur.“ (L. c. q. 3. f. 98.)

Quemadmodum enim Scriptura sacra ex vocum et literarum characteribus scriptis habet, quod est scriptura: ita quando Scriptura tota, absolute, simpliciter et absque ulla restrictione θεόπνευστος dicitur (juxta ea, quae in not. praeced. indicavimus), fatendum est, etiaih conceptus vocum, quae literis,exprimerentur, scriptoribus sacris inspiratos fuisse; quod prolixius probavit et ad objectiones dissentientium respondit b. Musaem l. c. n. 7. sqq. p. 250. sqq. Quod autem semper ita docuerit, clarissime ostendit in Tract. quaest. de Syncr. et Script. S. L. I. Q. III. p. 319. sqq. Conf. Ausführl. Erklärung, Q. VI. p. 42. sqq.

Quenstedtius: „Neque dicit apostolus: πάντα εν γραφή sunt θεόπνευστα, sed πάσα γραφή θεόπνευστος, ut ostendat, non modo res scriptas, sed etiam ipsam scriptionem esse θεόπνευστου. Et quicquid de tota Scriptura dicitur, idem etiam de verbis ceu parte Scripturae non postrema, necessario intelligendum est. Si enim vel verbulum in Scripturis occurreret non suggestum vel inspiratum divinitus, πάσα γραφή θεόπνευστος dici non posset. Si, inquam, verba et voces non fuissent s. scriptoribus suggestae per θεοπνευστίαν, Scriptura s. non proprie, non absolute et simpliciter, sed improprie, secundum quid et quoad conceptus rerum significatarum saltem esset dicique posset θεόπνευστος, inspirata a Deo; perinde ut Scriptura humano studio in aliam linguam translata proprie, absolute et simpliciter θεόπνευστος dici non potest, quia ipsa verba formalia, quibus constat, a Spiritu S. per inspirationem suggesta non sunt, licet secundum quid et cum apposito θεόπνευστος dici queat, nempe quoad conceptus rerum scriptoribus s. olim inspiratos, qui verbis versionis significantur.“ (L. c. q. 4. f. 107.)

Idem: „1 Cor. 2, 12. 13. Hoc loco 1. verba a rebus per verba communicatis distinguuntur. . . 2. Opponuntur λόγοι διδακτοί ανθρώπινης σοφίας, et λόγοι διδακτοί τοϋ θεού, verba, quae docet humana sapientia, sive verba humana, etiam sapientissime excogitata, et verba, quae docet, suggerit et dictitat Spiritus S. (Genitivus enim causam efficientem exprimit, ut Joh. 6, 45.: ,Erunt omnes διδακτοί τοϋ θεοϋ, docti a DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

Deo‘, ex Jes. 54, 13.) Illa λα/.φ apostolica removentur, haec vero ipsi tribuuntur. Vult enim dicere apostolus: Sicut a Sp. S. sapientiam illam sive notitiam mysteriorum divinorum accepimus, ita quoque ab eo ipsa verba, quibus eam eloquimur, edocti sumus.“ (L. c.)

Lutherus: ,, Unus apex doctrinae plus valet, quam coelum et terra. Ideo in minimo non patimur eam laedi.“ (Comm. in Ep. S. Pauli ad Gal. Tom. II. p. 341. Ed. Hai. VIII, 2661.)'

Idem: ,,Wenn sie aber nicht so leichtfertige Verächter wären der Schrift, so sollte sie ein klarer Spruch aus der Schrift so viel bewegen, als wäre die Welt voll Schrift; wie es denn wahr ist. Denn mir ist also, dass mir ein jeglicher Spruch die Welt zu enge macht.t( (Dass diese Wort, das ist mein Leib, noch feste stehen. 1527. XX, 982.)

Idem: „Quod si demus unam epistolam aliquam Pauli, aut unum alicujus locum non ad universalem ecclesiam pertinere, jam evacuata est tota Pauli auctoritas. Corinthii enim dicent, ea, quae de fide ad Romanos docet, non ad se pertinere. Quid blasphemius et insanius hac insania fingi possit? Absit, absit, ut ullus apex in toto Paulo sit, quem non debeat imitari et servare tota universalis ecclesia.“ (De capt. Babyl. Opp. cur. J. C. Irmischer. Vol. V. p. 27. Ed. Hai. XIX, 21. sq.)

Idem: „Fatentur omnes, quod Christus Joh. 10. dicit: ,Non potest solvi Scriptura', et ejus auctoritatem prorsus illaesam esse oportere, cui neque liceat contradicere, neque eam negare.“ (Operat, in Psalmos. Cur. J. C. Irmischer. Vol.. III. p. 318. Ed. Hai. IV, 1763.)

Idem: „Darum wenn Moses schreibet, dass Gott in sechs Tagen Himmel und Erde und was darinnen ist, geschaffen habe, so lass es bleiben, dass es sechs Tage gewesen sind, und darfst keine Glosse finden, wie sechs Tage ein Tag gewesen sind. Kannst du es aber nicht vernehmen, wie es sechs Tage sind gewesen, so thue dem Heiligen Geist die Ehre, dass er gelehrter sei, denn du. Denn du sollt also mit der Schrift handeln, dass du denkest, wie es Gott selbst rede. Weil es aber Gott redet, so gebühret dir nicht, sein Wort aus Frevel zu lenken, wo du hin willt, es zwinge denn die Noth, einen Text anders zu verstehen, denn wie die Worte lauten; nämlich, wenn der Glaube solchen Verstand, als die Worte geben, nicht leidet.“ (Predigten über das Buch Mosis. 1527. III, 23.)

Quo pertinet, quod 2 Petr. 1, 20. 21. dicitur, propheticam scripturam (προφητείαν γραφής) non esse allatam olim hominis voluntate (non suo motu et arbitratu protulisse homines illos suas prophetias), sed actos (φερομένους') a Spiritu Sancto locutos fuisse (seque accinxisse ad exercitium actus, ut loquendi, ita et scribendi). Partim enim ipsa inspiratio divina, qua suggeruntur, quae in literas referri debeant, importat influxum ad exercitium actus scriptionis; partim etiam certum est, scriptores sanctos expresso Dei mandato ad scribendum fuisse excitatos, e. gr. Moysen, Deuter. 31, 19., Esaiam, c. 8, 1. 30, 8., Jeremiam, c. 30, 2., Johannem, Apoc. 1, 11. 19. 2, 1. 8. 12. 18. etc., aut alias occasionem et incentiva ad scribendum per peculiarem Dei providentiam fuisse objecta, quibus de Dei voluntate certi redderentur. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 8. p. 257. sqq.

Quenstedtius: „Dist. inter occasionem fortuitam et accidentariam, et inter occasionem a Deo subministratam; scripserunt quandoque apostoli ex occasione, sed non fortuita, sed a Deo subministrata. Deus omnia ita direxit, ut completum perfectumque canonem fidei et vitae haberemus, Scripturas sci. propheticas et apostolicas, ita ut ejusdem directioni, instinctui et impulsui, non vero fortuitae.et accidentali occasioni, Scripturae acceptae ferri debeant.“ (L. c. q. 2. f. 62.)

PROLEGOM. CAP. II. ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: „Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, 2: nonnullorum Calvinianorum, 3. Socinianorum, 4. Arminianorum, denique 5. Novatorum, qui omnes ea, quae naturali ratione et aliunde vel per experientiam propriam et sensuum ministerio cogfiosci potuerunt (vel quorum scriptores ipsi ο,ΰτόπται καί αντηκοοι extiterunt), quaeque nihil ad salutem faciunt et facti vel rei narratae circumstantiam spectant, itemque leviora videntur, non revelasse, inspirasse et dictasse Spiritum S., sed solum ad haec consignanda scriptores excitasse et simul gubernasse per assistentiam et directionem singularem, ne quid falsi, indecori aut incongrui admiscerent, vel aliquid humani in scribendo paterentur. Sic Bellarminus lib. de V. D. c. 15. ait: ,Aliter Deus adfuit prophetis, aliter historicis. Illis revelavit futura et simul astitit, ne aliquid falsi admiscerent in scribendo; his non semper revelavit ea, quae scripturi erant, sed excitavit duntaxat, ut scriberent ea, quae vel viderant, vel audierant, quorum recordabantur, et simul astitit, ne quid falsi scriberent.' . . .

Verba D. Georg. Calixti P. I. Resp. Moguntinis oppositi th. 72. haec sunt: ,Neque Scriptura dicitur divina, quod singula, quae in ea continentur, divinae peculiari revelationi imputari oporteat (v. g. de duob. filiis Abrahami, de patre Davidis, de serie et successione regum Jerosolymae et Samariae, quod Herodes fuerit rex Judaeae, Pilatus praeses, aut quod Timotheo scribit s. Paulus 2 Tim. 4, 13.: Penulam, quam reliqui Troade apud Carpum, adfer, cum venies), sed quod praecipua, sive quae primario et per se respicit ac intendit Scriptura, nempe quae redemptionem et salutem generis humani concernunt, nonnisi divinae illi peculiari revelationi debeantur; in caeteris vero, quae aliunde, sive per experientiam, sive per lumen naturae nota, consignandis divina assistentia et Spiritu ita scriptores sint gubernati, ne quidquam scriberent, quod non esset ex re, vero, decoro, congruo.'“ (L. c. q. 3. fol. 99.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: The same: “Observe that Suarez admits θεοπνευστία (or divine inspiration) of…

The same: “Observe that Suarez admits θεοπνευστία (or divine inspiration) of the very words of Scripture in all things that concern the mysteries of faith and exceed human comprehension; but he admits a special assistance through preservation from all error and falsehood only in those things which are human in themselves and subject to the senses. Bellarmine, in *De Conciliorum Auctoritate*, bk. II, ch. 15, col. 264, writes: ‘The sacred writers did not have to labor much in their books; for it was sufficient if they labored in writing or dictating, if they were issuing prophecies, or at most in recalling to memory what they had seen or heard, and thinking of the words with which to write them, if they were writing histories or epistles or something similar.’ . . . To this also pertain those who attribute the method or arrangement, the ornamentation, ἑρμηνεία, phraseology, and style of Scripture to human ingenuity and industry, and not to the immediate and infallible inspiration of the Holy Spirit, among whom Sebast. Castalio stands out in his second dialogue *De electione*.” (L. c. q. 4. f. 106 sq.)

Calvin: “When David complains there (Ps. 22) that he was prey to his enemies, he designates all his possessions metaphorically under the name of garments, as if he had said in one word that he had been despoiled and stripped by the wicked. While the evangelists neglect this figure, they depart from the native sense.” (Commentary on John, p. 190.)

The same: “When the prophet discourses on the excellence of men, the apostle in Heb. 2 draws it to the humiliation of Christ. . . That which the apostle subsequently treats concerning the brief rejection is not exegetical, but he deflects it to his own purpose, which had been said by David in a different sense. Thus in Eph. 4:8, he does not so much interpret the passage of Psalm 68:19 as he accommodates it by a pious deflection to the person of Christ.” (Opp. Tom. III. p. 24, on Ps. 8.)

Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: Of the Papists, who trifle that the evangelists and apostles did not approach writing by any divine command, but...”

incidentally, from some accidental occasion offered from elsewhere, or compelled by necessity. Likewise: That God neither expressly commanded them to write, nor not to write. That the apostles nowhere testify that they were writing by the Lord’s command.

Thus Bellarmine, Bk. IV, *de V. D.*, ch. 3, col. 169, where he says: "It is false that God commanded the apostles to write; for we read in the end of Matthew the command to preach the Gospel, but that they should write, we nowhere read. Therefore, God neither expressly commanded that they should write, nor that they should not write. Yet we do not deny that, God willing and inspiring, the apostles wrote what they wrote," etc. And ch. 4, § 3, in the second proof, he says: "If it had been the intention of Christ and the apostles to confine and restrict the Word of God to Scripture, especially in a matter of such importance, Christ would have openly commanded it, and the apostles would testify somewhere that they were writing by the Lord’s command, just as they taught in the whole world by the Lord’s command; but we nowhere read this." (L. c. q. 2, f. 94.)

The same: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, such as Albert Pighius, Bk. I, *Hierarch. Eccles.*, ch. 2, saying: 'Matthew and John the evangelists could both lapse in memory and lie,' likewise: 'Who will make us certain that all things they write about Christ are true and certain (especially Mark and Luke), which they had never seen, but believed because others narrated them,' etc.; of Erasmus in his notes on chapters 2 and 27 of Matthew, positing that 'the evangelists did not derive testimonies of this kind from books there, but, trusting their memory, as happens, they lapsed.' ... 3. Of the Socinians, such as Socinus in his booklet on the authority of Scripture, where he writes in ch. 1, p. 15: 'That some things in Scripture appear false in themselves, but which are of little moment'; on page 71 he says: 'It could have happened that the evangelists and apostles erred slightly in some things.' ... 4. Of the Arminians, in the preface to their apology and in the third specimen of errors against the Leiden theologians; Episcopius, *Institut. theolog.*, Bk. IV, s. 1, ch. 4, p. 232, where he asserts: 'That the sacred writers could have lapsed and in fact did lapse in memory in light matters and those not pertaining to salvation,' etc. ... 5. Of the Weigelians, who teach concerning the writers or amanuenses of God, namely the prophets and apostles: 'That they were not immune from all error in dogmatic matters.' See Weigel in *Güldengriff*, p. 57." (L. c. q. 5, f. 114.)

R. F. Grau: "The theologians of the 17th century taught a divine manner and nature of Holy Scripture which, just as it does not agree with its human and historical reality, so also in no way proves itself to be a truly divine manner. The divine in Jesus Christ proves itself to be truly divine precisely by the fact that it enters entirely and completely into human reality—in birth, human growth and development, indeed suffering and dying—even though it had to divest itself of divine appearance and glory. Thus, Holy Scripture, in order to be an infallible and comprehensive source of truth for the Church and its entire development, did not originate in a purely divine way, such that the Holy Spirit, as the sole author, dictated both content and words to the human authors as mere scribes or instruments.

On this basis, the high and divine attributes, such as perfection and sufficiency, clarity, etc., were ascribed to Holy Scripture. This is indeed the doctrine of inspiration of the 17th century. We can, however, only say with the greatest biblical scholar of our time: 'One could not do justice to the questions arising from the nature of the text, nor those from the nature of the language, nor the literary peculiarities of the authors, nor the immediate purposes and the resulting particularities of the individual writings, nor the multiplicity of the modes of teaching, nor the diversity of the historical reports, without coming into contradiction with that dogmatic statement of what divine inspiration of Holy Scripture is: it was compatible, as far as the New Testament writing is concerned, only with a harmony of the Gospels, not..."

but with the Gospels, and only with a collection of proof-texts, but not with the apostolic epistles. A conception of Scripture formed according to it would have only a distant resemblance to its reality.’*). . .

The Godhead did not reveal itself on earth in a human phantom-form, as the Docetists taught. Thus, the human manner, the historical development of the Holy Scriptures, is not a mere appearance, brought about by an external accommodation of the Holy Spirit to the natural manner of the human authors. Here it is necessary to recognize: it is not in spite of the authorship of the Holy Spirit that Scripture has truly originated and come into being in a human and historical way, but precisely through that origin. The Spirit of God, as the one working in the world, is a Spirit of history and development; and as the Spirit of Christ, he is a "Spirit of self-emptying and humility. (!) ...

A retreat to Quenstedt and Calov is no longer possible. . . Holy Scripture is no longer for us a large code of laws sent down from heaven with its individual paragraphs, called proof-texts. For the sake of faith, we must reject such a conception as docetic, and for the sake of science, as contrary to history. Scripture is for us a collection of writings that has come into being through genuine human and historical development, a manner which does not contradict, but alone corresponds to, the Holy Spirit who rules in this development as the Spirit of Jesus Christ, the Son of Man and Son of God. The boundaries of the divine and the human in Scripture cannot be determined mechanically and quantitatively at all, just as little as in the person of Jesus.” (Entwickelungsgeschichte des Neutestamentlichen Schriftthums. Gütersloh 1871. I, 11. 12. 18. sq.)

Kahnisius: "The old-dogmatic inspiration rests on the fundamental thought that Scripture is God’s Word because God the Holy Spirit is its actual author. This, however, he is, insofar as he once gave the holy writers the impulse to write, and then dictated to them both content and words. . .

The untenability of the old-orthodox doctrine of inspiration will leap to the eyes of anyone who only takes the trouble to form a clear picture of it in detail. Are we to think that the Apostle Paul, when he wrote that tender, urbane letter to Philemon, touched by a quiet humor, was only recording what the Holy Spirit dictated to him? Does an inspiration theory that attributes all solecisms and barbarisms of the apostolic writings, all failed constructions of Paul, all inaccurate citations, differences in presentation (and indeed in points where the wording matters, as in the Ten Commandments, the Lord’s Prayer, the words of institution of the Lord’s Supper), borrowings from other writings, purely personal judgments and expressions, etc., to the Holy Spirit, really think worthily of the Holy Spirit? . . .

If we had to assume a human coefficient in prophets and apostles even at the reception of revelation, we could certainly not conceive of conceptual working-through and presentation without the cooperation of human peculiarity, and we could simply point to quite unmistakable facts. This human side emerges even more decisively in poets, lyrical and didactic writers, and historians. Are we to assume that what David felt in his heart, the Holy Spirit dictated in the form of a Psalm? If the Evangelist Luke only wrote down what the Spirit dictated to him: why does he appeal to tradition and research? If Solomon’s Proverbs, as even the stricter side admits, are not *) v. Hofmann, die heilige Schrift neuen Testaments zusammenhaengend untersucht, Noerdlingen 1862. 1. Th. p. 9. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

rest upon revelation, but upon worldly wisdom: what a contradiction lies in the assumption that the Holy Spirit dictated human worldly wisdom! Do these rules, which must be taken *cum grano salis*, not then become laws of the Holy Spirit? And to apply this doctrine of inspiration to a book like Ecclesiastes: what monstrosities arise for us! . . .

Latin:

Idem: „Observa, Suaresium admittere ϋεοττνενστίαν (sive divinam inspirationem) ipsorum verborum Scripturae in omnibus, quae mysteria fidei concernunt et captum humanum excedunt; specialem autem assistentiam per custodiam ab omni errore et falsitate tantum in iis admittere, quae secundum se humana sunt et sensibus subjacent. Bellarminus 1. II. de Cone. Auctor, c. 15. column. 264. scribit: ,Scriptores sacros non debuisse multum laborare in suis libris; satis enim fhisse, si laborarent scribendo vel dictando, si ederent vaticinia, vel ad summum revocando ad memoriam, quae viderant aut audierant, et cogitarent verba, quibus ea scriberent, si scribebant historias vel epistolas vel aliquid simile.4 . . Huc pertinent etiam illi, qui methodum seu dispositionem, exornationem, ερμηνείαν, phrasin et stylum Scripturae humano ingenio atque industriae attribuunt, et non immediatae atque infallibili Spiritus S. inspirationi, quos inter eminet Sebast. Castalio in dialogo 2. de elect.44 (L. c. q. 4. f. 106. sq.)

Calvinus: „Quum illic (Ps. 22.) queratur David, se hostibus praedae fuisse, metaphorice sub nomine vestium sua omnia designat, ac si uno verbo dixisset, spoliatum se ac nudatum ab improbis fuisse. Quam figuram dum negligunt evangelistae, a nativo sensu discedunt." (Commentar, super Joh. p. 190.)

Idem: „Quum de praestantia hominum disserat propheta, apostolus Ebr. 2. ad Christi exinanitionem id trahit. . . Quod de brevi abjectione deinde tractat apostolus, non est exegeticum, sed ad suum institutum deflectit, quod alio sensu a Davide dictum fuerat. Sic Eph. 4, 8. locum Psalmi 68, 19. non tam intrepretatur, quam pia deflectione ad Christi personam adeommodat.44 (Opp. Tom. III. p. 24. ad Ps. 8.)

Quenstedtius: „Antithesis: Pontificiorum, qui nugantur, evangelistas et apostolos nullo divino mandato ad scribendum accessisse, sed

incidenter, ex occasione quadam accidentaria aliunde oblata, aut necessitate coactos. Item: Deum nec mandasse expresse, ut scriberent, nec ut non scriberent. Apostolos nullibi testari, se ex Domini mandato scribere.

Ita Bellarminus 1. IV. de V. D. c. 3. col. 169., ubi ait: ,Falsum est, Deum mandasse apostolis, ut scriberent, legimus enim Matth. ult. mandatum, ut praedicarent evangelium, ut autem scriberent, nusquam legimus. Itaque Deus nec mandavit expresse, ut scriberent, nec ut non scriberent. Nec tamen negamus, quin Deo volente et inspirante apostoli scripserint, quae scripserunt* etc. et c. 4. § 3. secundo prob, inquit: ,Si Christo et apostolis fuisset propositum, V. D. coarctandi et restringendi ad Scripturam, inprimis rem tanti momenti, Christus aperte praecepisset et apostoli alicubi testarentur, se ex Domini mandato scribere, quemadmodum ex Domini mandato in toto orbe docuerunt, at id nusquam legimus.*“ (L. c. q. 2. f. 94.)

Idem: „Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, ut Alberti Piggii 1. 1. Hierarch. Eccles. c. 2. dicentis: ,Matthaeus et Johannes evangelistae potuerunt et labi memoria et mentiri', item: ,Quis certos nos reddet, vera esse et certa, quae scribunt omnia de Christo (praesertim Marcus et Lucas), quae nunquam viderant, sed crediderunt narrantibus aliis etc.*; Erasmi in notis in cc. 2, et 27. Matthaei statuentis, ,ibi evangelistas testimonia hujusmodi non e libris deprompsisse, sed, memoriae fidentes, ita ut fit, lapsos esse.' ... 3. Socinianorum, ut Socini in libello de auctoritate Scripturae, ubi cap. 1. p. 15. scribit: ,Quaedam in Scriptura per se ipsa falsa apparere, sed quae parvi sint momenti* ; pag. 71. ait: ,fleri potuisse, ut evangelistae et apostoli in aliquibus leviter errarint.* ... 4. Arminianorum, in praefatione apologiae suae et in specimine errorum tertio contra Leidenses; Episcopii Institut, theolog. 1. IV. s. 1. c. 4. p. 232, ubi asserit: ,Scriptores s. potuisse labi et reipsa lapsos esse memoria in rebus levibus et nihil ad salutem pertinentibus etc.' . . 5. Weigelianorum, qui de scriptoribus seu amanuensibus Dei, prophetis sci. et apostolis, docent: ,Eos ab omni errore in dogmaticis immunes non fuisse.' Vide Weigelium in Gfiildengriff p. 57.“ (L. c. q. 5.f. 114.)

R. F. Grau: ,,Es haben die Theologen des 17ten Jahrhunderts eine göttliche Art und Natur der heiligen Schrift gelehrt, welche, wie sie nicht mit ihrer menschlichen tind geschichtlichen Wirklichkeit stimmt, so auch keineswegs als eine wahrhaft göttliche Art sich erweis’t. Das Göttliche in Jesu Christo erweis’t sich gerade dadurch als wahrhaft göttlich, dass es ganz und gar in die menschliche Wirklichkeit eingeht, in Geburt, menschliches Wachsthum und Entwickelung, ja Leiden und Sterben, ob es auch der göttlichen Erscheinung und Herrlichkeit sich entäussern musste. So ist nun auch die heilige Schrift, um untrügliche und umfassende Quelle der Wahrheit für die Kirche und ihre gesammte Entwickelung zu sein, nicht auf die pur göttliche Weise entstanden, dass der Heilige Geist, als der alleinige Autor, den menschlichen Verfassern als blossen Schreibern oder Instrumenten so Inhalt wie Worte dictirt habe.

Auf Grund dessen wurden eben die hohen und göttlichen Eigenschaften, als Vollkommenheit und Genügsamkeit, Klarheit u. s. w. der heiligen Schrift zugeschrieben. Dies ist ja die Inspirationslehre des 17. Jahrhunderts. Wir können dagegen nur mit dem grössten Schriftforscher unserer Zeit sagen: ,Weder den aus der Beschaffenheit des Textes, noch den aus der Beschaffenheit der Sprache erwachsenden Fragen, nicht den schriftstellerischen Eigenthümlichkeiten der Verfasser, noch den nächsten Zwecken und den davon stammendem Besonderheiten der einzelnen Schriften, nicht der Mannichfaltigkeit der Lehrweisen, noch der Verschiedenheit der geschichtlichen Berichte konnte man gerecht werden, ohne mit jener dogmatischen Aussage, was es um die göttliche Eingebung der heiligen Schrift sei, in Widerspruch zu kommen: sie vertrug sich, was diei neutestamentliche Schrift anlangt, nur mit einer Evangelienharmonie, nicht

aber mit den Evangelien, und nur mit einer Sammlung von Lehrbeweisstellen, nicht aber mit den apostolischen Briefen. Eine nach ihr gebildete Vorstellung von der Schrift würde mit der Wirklichkeit derselben nur eine entfernte Aehnlichkeit haben.'*). . .

Nicht in einer menschlichen Scheingestalt, wie die Doketen lehrten, hat sich die Gottheit auf Erden offenbart. So ist auch die menschliche Art, die geschichtliche Entwickelung der heiligen Schriften nicht blosser Schein, hervorgerufen durch eine äussere Accommodation des Heiligen Geistes an die natürliche Art der menschlichen Verfasser. Hier gilt es, zu erkennen: nicht trotz der Autorschaft des Heiligen Geistes ist die Schrift wahrhaft menschlich und geschichlich entstanden und geworden, sondern gerade durch jenen Ursprung. Der Geist Gottes ist als der in der Welt wirkende ein Geist der Geschichte und der Entwickelung; und er ist als der Geist Christi «sin Geist der Selbstentäusserung und Demuth. (!) ...

Es ist jetzt kein Rückzug zu Quenstedt und Calov mehr möglich. . . Die heilige Schrift ist uns nicht mehr ein grösser vom Himmel herab gesandter Gesetzescodex mit seinen einzelnen Paragraphen, Beweisstellen genannt. Solche Auffassung müssen wir um des Glaubens willen als doketisch und um der Wissenschaft willen als geschichtswidrig zurückweisen. Die Schrift ist uns eine durch echt menschliche und geschichtliche Entwickelung gewordene Schriftensammlung, welche Art dem in dieser Entwickelung waltenden Heiligen Geiste, als dem Geiste Jesu Christi des Menschenund Gottessohnes, nicht widerspricht, sondern allein entspricht. Die Grenzen des Göttlichen und Menschlichen in der Schrift können überhaupt nicht mechanisch und quantitativ bestimmt werden, so wenig, wie in der Person Jesu.“ (Entwickelungsgeschichte des Neutestamentlichen Schriftthums.“ Gütersloh 1871. I, 11. 12. 18. sq.)

Kahnisius: ,,Die altdogmatische Inspiration ruht auf dem Grundgedanken, dass die Schrift Gottes Wort ist, weil Gott der Heilige Geist ihr eigentlicher Verfasser sei. Dies aber ist er, sofern er einmal den heiligen Schriftstellern den Impuls zum Schreiben gab, dann aber ihnen sowohl Inhalt als Worte dictirte. . .

Die Unhaltbarkeit der altorthodoxen Inspirationslehre wird Jedem in die Augen springen, der sich nur die Mühe gibt, sich einjanschauliches Bild von derselben im Einzelnen zu machen. Soll man sich denken, dass der Apostel Paulus, als er jenen zarten, urbanen, von einem leisen Humor berührten Brief an Philemon schrieb, nur aufzeichnete, was der Heilige Geist ihm dictirte? Denkt eine Inspirationslehre, welche alle Solöcismen und Barbarismen der apostolischen Schriften, alle verfehlten Constructionen des Paulus, alle ungenauen Citate, Differenzen in der Darstellung (und zwar in Puncten, wo auf den Wortlaut etwas ankommt, wie bei den zehn Geboten, dem Vaterunser, den Einsetzungsworten des Abendmahles), Entlehnungen aus anderen Schriften, rein persönliche Urtheile und Ausdrücke u. s. w. dem Heiligen Geiste zuschreibt, wirklich würdig vom Heiligen Geiste? . . .

Mussten wir bei Propheten und Aposteln selbst bei Empfängniss der Offenbarung einen menschlichen Coefficienten annehmen, so konnten wir uns begriffliches Durcharbeiten und Darstellung durchaus nicht ohne Mitwirkung der menschlichen Eigenthümlichkeit denken und durften auf ganz unverkennbare Thatsachen einfach verweisen. Diese menschliche Seite tritt noch viel entschiedener bei Dichtem, lyrischen und didaktischen, und Geschichtsschreibern hervor. Soll man annehmen, dass was David in seinem Herzen empfand, der Heilige Geist in Gestalt eines Psalms dictirt habe? Wenn der Evangelist Lucas nur niederschrieb, was ihm der Geist dictirte: wozu beruft er sich auf Ueberlieferung und Forschung? Wenn Salomo’s Sprüche, wie man doch selbst strengererseits zugibt, nicht ·) v. Hofmann, die heilige Schrift neuen Testaments zusammenhaengend untersucht, Noerdiingen 1862. 1. Th. p. 9. DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

auf Offenbarung ruhen, sondern auf Lebensweisheit: welch ein Widerspruch liegt in der Annahme, dass der Heilige Geist menschliche Lebensweisheit dictirt habe! Werden dann nicht diese sehr cum grano salis zu nehmenden Regeln zu Gesetzen des Heiligen Geistes? Und diese Inspirationslehre auf ein Buch wie Koheleth übertragen: welche Monstrositäten entstehen uns! . . .


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Among these prophetic and apostolic writings, however, there are differences…

Among these prophetic and apostolic writings, however, there are differences both from the standpoint of origin and of content. We cannot equate Deuteronomy with the first four books. Among the prophets, Obadiah and Jonah stand below Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. In the New Testament, the Pastoral Epistles (p. 531) and the Epistle to Philemon step into a second rank.

The word of revelation, which goes forth within the realm of the Old and New Covenants, is only to be understood in the context of the history of the same. And thus, the historical books of the Old and New Covenants enter into their canonical right, but a right of the second degree. Just as their content is the interaction of the divine and the human in the kingdom of God, so too are the holy historians not necessarily men of revelation, but men who stand in the spirit of the kingdom of God. To this category belong, in the Old Testament, the prophetic historical books in the first rank, the hagiographic Ruth, Ezra, and Nehemiah in the second, and the books of Esther and Chronicles in the third rank (p. 285 ff.). In the New Testament, the first three Gospels (p. 406 ff.) fall into this second rank in the first place, and the Acts of the Apostles (p. 518) in the second.

A third class is formed by 'the Old and New Testament hagiographers, whose content is neither revelation nor history of the kingdom, but life in the kingdom of God as it presents itself in the individual.' To this category belong, in the Old Testament, primarily the Psalms (p. 294 ff.), secondarily the Proverbs of Solomon (p. 304), Job (p. 305), and the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and tertiarily the Song of Songs (p. 303), Ecclesiastes (p. 309), and Daniel (p. 369 ff.); in the New Testament, primarily the Epistle to the Hebrews and the 2nd and 3rd Epistles of John, which, in all probability, are not of certain Johannine origin and, moreover, are of a more personal content (p. 546), and secondarily the remaining Catholic Epistles and the Apocalypse (p. 537 ff.).

If, in the first class, the personality is of essential significance, it recedes in the second class, since here everything depends on the objective truth and the spirit of the presentation. However, it lies in the nature of the third class that the subject gains in importance. It is not indifferent whether a Psalm is by David or not, whether the Proverbs are by Solomon or others, whether Daniel is genuine or spurious, etc. But one must be very careful with these writings of the third rank not to place too much weight on authenticity. This attempt to divide Scripture into three classes from the standpoint of inspiration may be deficient: in any case, a distinction of degrees of inspiration is in the sense of Scripture, as it also has significant authorities in its favor in ancient and modern times." (Die lutherische Dogmatik historisch-genetisch dargestellt. First Volume. Leipzig 1861. p. 666. sqq.) The same: "Protestantism stands and falls with the principle of the sole authority of Scripture. This principle, however, is independent of the doctrine of inspiration of the old dogmatics. To take it up again as it was can only happen with a hardening against the truth (!)." (Der innere Gang etc. Ed. 2. p. 241.)

Thomasius: "They (the Holy Scriptures) bear throughout the stamp of the individuality and personal activity of their authors, both in the conception of the thoughts and in the execution and presentation. One only needs to surrender oneself to them without prejudice, and one is immediately convinced that these writings are not 'dictated by the Holy Spirit'." (Christi Person u. Werk. Third Part. First Section. 2nd ed. p. 449 sq.) PROLEGOM. CHAP. II.

Hofmann: "The latter (the New Testament Scripture) testifies not to how the former (the Old Testament Scripture) originated, but to what it is. For when we read in 2 Pet. 1:21 concerning the Old Testament prophets that it was a divine operation, an operation of the Holy Spirit, by virtue of which they spoke; this, according to its immediate wording and context, is not even said of all the individual components of the Old Testament Scripture, let alone of their summary into the unified whole of the same... Jesus does not appeal to anything that was spoken at any time, nor to anything that is merely contained in the Scripture, but to the whole of the Scripture... When, therefore, He cites individual passages of Scripture, be it to point out their fulfillment in His person and history, or to clothe His instructions in them, He does not mean them in their isolation; rather, it is the Scripture as a unified whole which He allows to testify of Himself or to declare the will of God. Likewise, the New Testament writers do not appeal merely to this or that word of Moses or David or Isaiah because these individuals spoke by virtue of the Spirit of God; rather, they introduce the Scripture as speaking, whether they name the one who said this or that, or not... That the Old Testament Scripture is a work of the Holy Spirit, that it is inspired, our doctrine does not mention; but only for the reason that it is established for us once and for all that everything which serves the advancement of sacred history happens by virtue of an operation of the Holy Spirit, who for this purpose dwells within man, determining his natural life in the manner required for the respective purpose of such an operation... Such an operation occurred not only upon those who wrote, but also upon those who compiled the individual components of the Scripture, be it into books or into the whole of the same. According to this, the manifold operation of the Spirit of God, which one gathers together under the one name of inspiration, will have to be described; in such a way, however, that one always keeps in view how the individual was brought forth in each case in its relation to the intended whole through the operation of the Holy Spirit." (Der Schriftbeweis. Nördlingen, 1852. I, 567—573.)

Luthardt: "On the whole, believing theology is still seeking to find a formula in which it might be able to express the 'theanthropic' character of the Scripture... Tholuck and Rothe have demonstrated the untenability of the old doctrine... One must proceed from the necessity and significance of the whole of the Scripture for the Church, and from there derive both the certainty which the Church as a whole initially has of the whole of the Scripture and its individual parts, insofar as they are integral parts of this whole, and also conclude as to the divine operation of its origin, so that the individual is always grasped in relation to the whole, but the psychological state is understood as that of the unity of receptivity and spontaneity. The Scripture is the normative Word of God (for the Church) and contains the saving Word of God (for the individual). Cf. Hofmann, Schriftbew. II, 2, 98—109." (Compendium. Third ed. p. 255.)

Delitzsch: "Theopneustia is also a generic term, which comprises very manifoldly graduated operations of the Spirit, depending on whether the writer relates to the revelation of salvation and the history of salvation productively and continuatively, or reproductively and applicatively. But in both cases, the Divine appears under the affections of the human. In the latter case, errors in the reproduction of the historical and the given are even possible—errors of memory, errors of combination, and in general such errors above which the most spiritual human activity is not absolutely exalted. Whoever [does] that..."

denies [it], knows the historical books of the Old and New Testaments only superficially, and whoever is offended by it sins against the Holy Spirit, whose entirely non-docetic, loving condescension (!) into humanity he should rather admire and praise.” (System of Biblical Psychology. Leipzig, 1855. p. 319. sq.)

Kurtzius: “We assert boldly and with the sure confidence that we are not in the least encroaching upon the divine character of Holy Scripture and history, that the holy men of God in the O. and N. T., whom the Spirit of God impelled to divine works or words, could very well have been caught up in the errors generally prevailing in their time regarding natural scientific knowledge. ... Thus, Moses could also have had many a physically erroneous view regarding the nature of the starry heavens or the interior of the earth when, in the prophetic spirit, he grasped the history of the creation of heaven and earth, without these errors having to be taken from him thereby; for the Mosaic creation account has no physical purpose at all, but merely a religious instruction.” (Bible and Astronomy. Berlin, 1858. p. 8. sq.)

Dieckhoffius: “It will likely have to be conceded that the way in which the inerrancy of the Word of Holy Scripture was conceived in the old orthodox dogmatics is untenable, and that one cannot master negative criticism if one thinks one must hold back from that concession.” (Church Journal of Kliefoth-Mejer. 1858. p. 757.)
