Philippius: “At the same time, one should not from the outset resist the acknowledgment of the possibility that some subordinate differences are actually present, and therefore remain unresolved. For there is indeed here a realm of insignificant contingency, just as the likeness of a portrait is not conditioned by the exactly corresponding length of the nails and hair. How far inspiration has completely overcome human weakness even here seems to us to be determinable only by historical means, not dogmatically. We would therefore at least not wish to say a priori with Calov: Nullus error, vel in leviculis, nullus memoriae lapsus, — ullum locum habere potest in universa Scriptura sacra (No error, not even in trivial matters, no lapse of memory, — can have any place in the entire Holy Scripture). Julius Africanus already expressed something similar in relation to historical-chronological difficulties in the New Testament: το μέντοι εὐαγγέλιον πάντως ἀληθεύει (The Gospel does indeed speak the truth throughout).” (Ecclesiastical Doctrine of Faith. Stuttgart 1854. I, 208. sq.)

Latin:

Unter diesen prophetischen und apostolischen Schriften aber sind sowohl vom Gesichtspuncte des Ursprungs als des Inhaltes aus Unterschiede. Wir können das Deuteronomium nicht den vier ersten Büchern gleichstellen. Unter den Propheten stehen Obadia und Jona unter Jesaia, Jeremia, Ezechiel. Im Neuen Testamente treten die Pastoralbriefe (S. 531) und der Brief an Philemon auf eine zweite Linie.

Das Wort der Offenbarung, welches innerhalb des Reiches alten und neuen Bundes ergeht, ist nur im Zusammenhänge der Geschichte desselben zu verstehen. Und so treten denn die Geschichtsbücher alten und neuen Bundes in ihr kanonisches Recht, aber ein Recht zweiten Grades. Wie der Inhalt derselben das Zusammenwirken des Göttlichen und Menschlichen im Reiche Gottes ist, so sind auch die heiligen Geschichtsschreiber nicht nothwendig Männer der Offenbarung, sondern Männer, die im Geiste des Reiches Gottes stehen. Dahin gehören im Alten Testamente die prophetischen Geschichtsbücher in erster, die hagiographischen Ruth, Esra, Nehemia in zweiter, die Bücher Esther und Chronik in dritter Linie (S. 285 ff.). Im Neuen Testamente fallen in diese zweite Reihe in erster Linie die drei ersten Evangelien (S. 406 ff.), in zweiter die Apostelgeschichte (S. 518).

Eine dritte Classe bilden 'die altund neutestamentlichen Hagiographen, deren Inhalt weder Offenbarung noch Geschichte des Reiches ist, sondern das Leben im Beiche Gottes wie es sich im Einzelnen darstellt. Dahin gehören im Alten Testament in erster Linie die Psalmen (S. 294 ff.), in zweiter die Sprüche Salomo’s (S. 304), Hiob (S. 305) und Klagelieder Jeremias, in dritter das Hohelied (S. 303), Koheleth (S. 309) und Daniel (S. 369 ff.), im Neuen Testamente in erster Linie der Hebräerbrief und der 2. und 3. Brief Johannis, welche bei aller Wahrscheinlichkeit doch nicht sicher johanneischen Ursprungs und überdies mehr persönlichen Inhalts sind (S. 546), in zweiter die übrigen katholischen Briefe und die Apokalypse (S. 537 ff.).

Wenn bei der ersten Classe die Persönlichkeit von wesentlicher Bedeutung ist, so tritt sie dagegen in der zweiten Classe zurück, da hier Alles auf die objective Wahrheit und den Geist der Darstellung ankommt. Es liegt aber in der Natur der dritten Classe, dass das Subject in Bedeutung tritt. Es ist nicht gleichgültig, ob ein Psalm von David ist oder nicht, die Sprüche von Salomo sind oder Anderen, Daniel echt oder unecht u. s. w. Aber man muss sich bei diesen Schriften dritten Ranges wohl hüten, auf Authentie zu viel stellen zu wollen. Mag dieser Versuch vom Standpunkte der Inspiration aus die Schrift in drei Classen zu theilen mangelhaft sein: jedenfalls ist eine Unterscheidung von Graden der Inspiration im Sinne der Schrift, wie sie denn auch in alter und neuer Zeit bedeutende Auctoritäten für sich hat.“ (Die lutherische Dogmatik historisch-genetisch dargestellt. Erster Band. Leipzig 1861. p. 666. sqq.) Idem: „Der Protestantismus steht und fällt mit dem Grundsätze von der alleinigen Auctorität der Schrift. Unabhängig aber ist dieser Grundsatz von der Inspirationslehre der alten Dogmatik. Sie wieder aufzunehmen, wie sie war, kann nur mit Verhärtung gegen die Wahrheit (!) geschehen.“ (Der innere Gang etc. Ed. 2. p. 241.)

Thomasius: „Sie (die heiligen Schriften) tragen durchaus das Gepräge der Individualität und Selbstthätigkeit ihrer Verfasser, sowohl in der Conception der Gedanken, als in der Ausführung und Darstellung. Man darf sich nur unbefangen an sie hingeben, so überzeugt man sich sofort, dass diese Schriften nicht,dictirt sind vom Heiligen Geiste'." (Christi Person u. Werk. Dritter Theil. Erste Abth. 2. Aufl. p. 449. sq.) PROLEGOM. CAP. II.

Hofmannus: „Nicht wie erstere (die alttestamentliche Schrift) entstanden, sondern was es um sie sei, bezeugt die letztere (die neutestamentliche). Denn wenn wir 2 Pet. 1, 21. von den alttestamentlichen Propheten lesen, dass es göttliche Wirkung, Wirkung des Heiligen Geistes gewesen, kraft welcher sie geredet haben; so ist dies seinem nächsten Wortlaute und Zusammenhänge nach nicht einmal von allen einzelnen Bestandteilen der alttestamentlichen Schrift gesagt, geschweige von deren Zusammenfassung in das einheitliche Ganze derselben. . . Nicht auf irgend etwas, das irgend wann geredet worden, noch auf irgend etwas, das in der Schrift nur enthalten ist, sondern auf das Ganze der Schrift beruft sich Jesus. . . Wenn er also einzelne Schriftstellen anführt, sei es um ihre Erfüllung in seiner Person und Geschichte aufzuzeigen, oder um seine Weisungen darein zu kleiden, so meint er sie nicht in ihrer Vereinzelung, sondern die Schrift als einheitliches Ganzes ist es, welche er von sich zeugen oder den Willen Gottes aussagen lässt. Ebenso berufen sich die neutestamentlichen Schriftsteller nicht etwa nur auf dieses oder jenes Wort Mose’s oder David’s oder Jesaja’s, weil diese Einzelnen kraft des Geistes Gottes geredet haben, sondern die Schrift führen sie redend ein, mögen sie den nennen, welcher dies oder jenes gesagt habe, oder nicht. . . Dass die alttestamentliche Schrift ein Werk des Heiligen Geistes, dass sie inspirirt ist, dessen gedenkt unser Lehrsatz nicht; aber nur deshalb nicht, weil für uns ein für alle Mal feststeht, dass alles, was zur Portführung der heiligen Geschichte dient, kraft einer Wirkung des Heiligen Geistes geschieht, welcher hiefür dem Menschen in der Weise, wie es für den jedesmaligen Zweck solcher Wirkung erforderlich ist, hinsichtlich seines Naturlebens bestimmend innewaltet. . . Nicht blos auf die Schreibenden, sondern auch auf diejenigen ist solche Wirkung geschehen, welche die einzelnen Bestandtheile der Schrift zusammenstellten, sei es zu Büchern, sei es zum Ganzen derselben. Darnach wird die mannigfaltige Wirkung des Geistes Gottes, welche man unter dem einen Namen der Inspiration zusammenbegreift, beschrieben sein wollen; so zwar, dass man immer im Auge behält, wie das Einzelne je in seinem Verhältnisse zu dem beabsichtigten Ganzen durch Wirkung des Heiligen Geistes hervorgebracht worden ist.“ (Der Schriftbeweis. Nördlingen, 1852. I, 567—573.)

Luthardtius: „Im Ganzen sucht die gläubige Theologie noch eine Formel zu finden, in welcher sie den,gottmenschlichen' Charakter der Schrift auszusprechen vermöge. . . Tholuck und Rothe haben die Unhaltbarkeit der alten Lehre nachgewiesen. .. Es ist auszugehen von der Nothwendigkeit und Bedeutung des Ganzen der Schrift für die Kirche und von da aus sowohl die Gewissheit abzuleiten, welche zunächst die Kirche als Ganzes von dem Ganzen der Schrift und ihren einzelnen Theilen hat, sofern sie integrirende Theile dieses Ganzen sind, als auch auf die Gotteswirkung ihrer Entstehung zu schliessen, so dass das Einzelne immer in Beziehung zum Ganzen gefasst, der psychologische Zustand aber als der der Einheit von Receptivität und Spontaneität begriffen wird. Die Schrift ist das normirende Wort Gottes (für die Kirche) und enthält das seligmachende Wort Gottes (für die Einzelnen). Vergl. Hofmann, Schriftbew. II, 2, 98—109.“ (Compendium. Dritte Aufl. p. 255.)

Delitzschius: „Auch ist Theopneustia ein Gattungsbegriff, der gar mannigfach abgestufte Geisteswirkungeu unter sich begreift, je nachdem der Schriftsteller sich productiv und continuativ, oder reproductiv und applicativ zur Heilsoffenbarung und Heilsgeschichte verhält. Aber in beiden Fällen erscheint das Göttliche unter den Affectionen des Menschlichen. Im letzteren Falle sind sogar Irrungen in Reproduction des Geschichtlichen und Gegebenen möglich, Gedächtnissfehler, Combinationsfehler, überhaupt solche Fehler, über welche die allergeistlichste menschliche Thätigkeit nicht absolut erhaben ist. Wer das

leugnet, der kennt die altund neutestamentlichen Geschichtsbücher nur oberflächlich, und wer sich daran ärgert, der versündigt sich an dem Heiligen Geiste, dessen ganz und gar nicht doketische liebreiche Herablassung (!) in die Menschlichkeit er vielmehr bewundern und preisen sollte.“ (System der bibl. Psychol. Leipzig, 1855. p. 319. sq.)

Kurtzius: „Wir behaupten kühn und mit der sicheren Zuversicht, dem göttlichen Charakter der heiligen Schrift und Geschichte nicht im mindesten zu nahe zu treten, dass die heiligen Männer Gottes im A. und N. B., welche der Geist Gottes zu göttlichen Werken oder Worten trieb, gar wohl, was naturwissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse betrifft, in den zu ihrer Zeit allgemein herrschenden Irrthümern mitbefangen sein konnten. ... So konnte auch Moses gar manche physikalisch-irrige Ansicht über die Natur des Sternenhimmels oder des Erdinneren haben, als er im prophetischen Geiste die Geschichte der Schöpfung des Himmels und der Erde auffasste, ohne dass ihm diese Irrthümer dadurch hätten benommen werden müssen; denn die mosaische Schöpfungsgeschichte hat eben gar keine physikalische, sondern blos religiöse Belehrung zum Zwecke.“ (Bibel und Astronomie. Berlin, 1858. p. 8. sq.)

Dieckhoffius: ,jEs wird wohl zugestanden werden müssen, dass die Art, wie man die Irrthumslosigkeit des Wortes der heiligen Schrift in der alten orthodoxen Dogmatik gefasst hat, eine unhaltbare ist, und dass man der negativen Kritik nicht mächtig werden kann, wenn man mit jenem Zugeständnisse meint zurückhalten zu müssen.“ (Kirchliche Zeitschrift von Kliefoth-Mejer. 1858. p. 757.)

Philippius: „Dabei hat man sich nicht von vomeherein gegen die Anerkennung der Möglichkeit zu sträuben, dass manche untergeordnete Differenzen wirklich vorhanden seien, und darum ungelöst Zurückbleiben. Denn es gibt ja hier allerdings ein Gebiet der unbedeutenden Zufälligkeit, wie die Aehnlichkeit eines Porträts nicht von der genau entsprechenden Länge der Nägel und Haare bedingt ist. Wie weit die Inspiration auch hier die menschliche Schwachheit völlig überwunden habe, scheint uns nur auf geschichtlichem Wege, nicht dogmatisch bestimmt werden zu können. Wir möchten deshalb wenigstens nicht a priori mit Calov sagen: Nullus error, vel in leviculis, nullus memoriae lapsus, — ullum locum habere potest in universa Scriptura sacra (Kein Irrthum, selbst nicht in geringfügigen Dingen, kein Gedächtnissfehler, — kann in der ganzen heiligen Schrift statt haben). Aehnlich äusserte schon Julius Africanus in Beziehung auf historisch-chronologische Schwierigkeiten im Neuen Testamente: το μέντοι dιηγγέλιον πάντως d/.T/devEi (Das Evangelium redet ja durchweg die Wahrheit).“ (Kirchliche Glaubenslehre. Stuttgart 1854. I, 208. sq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Cf. Rudelbachius: “The doctrine of the inspiration of Holy Scripture, with…

Cf. Rudelbachius: “The doctrine of the inspiration of Holy Scripture, with consideration of the newest investigations thereon by Schleiermacher, Twesten, and Steudel, developed historically-apologetically and dogmatically.” (Journal for the Entire Lutheran Theology and Church. Edited by Dr. A. G. Rudelbach and Dr. H. E. F. Guericke. First Year 1840. First Quarterly Issue, p. 1—59. Second Quarterly Issue, p. 1—66.) §

5. The impulsive cause of Holy Scripture, consigned to writing by divine will, is the internal goodness of God, and the external need of men to be saved. How necessary it is for those who examine and hand down the causes of the divine counsel to acknowledge why God [willed] heavenly doctrine, for some time

through the tradition of the living voice, preserved without the aid of the Scriptures, He willed to be committed to writing. See the blessed Gerhard, *Exeg.*, Book I, § 19, p. 36. Gerhard: “Moses received the command to write only then, when God had written the tables of the Decalogue with His own finger. Exod. 34:27.” (*Exeg.*, Book I, § 16.)

For the communication of Scripture made to men is indeed an unmerited benefit of God. This is what they commonly call the προκαταρκτική [preliminary/antecedent cause]; in which manner our theologians elsewhere call human misery the προκαταρκτική cause of the divine will to send the Son, so that it differs greatly from a meritorious cause. For thus, the indigence of a poor man moves a rich and liberal man to give him alms, yet that poor man does not thereby merit the alms by his indigence.

Namely: 1) with the human race multiplied, 2) and the span of human life shortened, all men could not be instructed face-to-face by the living voice as they once were by the patriarchs, who were instructed by the immediate revelation of God. But also 3) with various corruptions of doctrine having been introduced, and 4) the infirmity of men to be instructed and the weakness of memory supervening, a written letter was not unreasonably desired, so that a revelation might be at hand to which one could securely flee in every case of necessity. And thus it seemed most wise to divine providence that the heads of divine revelations be comprised in writing. Cf. Gerhard, *l.c.*, p. 37.

Chemnitz: “It is worthy of consideration that, since the purity of doctrine was not preserved through traditions and God did not wish to use that method any longer, so that He might repeat, restore, and preserve the purity of that doctrine which had been revealed and handed down to the patriarchs from the beginning of the world through new, constant, and peculiar revelations—it is worthy of observation, I say, what other method He Himself established and showed at the time of Moses, namely, that the purity of heavenly doctrine should be propagated and preserved through writings approved and confirmed by divine authority and testimony, lest, when questions or controversies arose concerning the ancient, genuine, and pure doctrine of the patriarchs, new and peculiar revelations would always have to be sought and expected. That history, indeed, must be diligently considered. For it will usefully illustrate and explain the present controversy concerning Holy Scripture, having shown its first origin. Moreover, the history shows—which is especially to be observed in judgment—that God not only instituted, but by His own deed and example, when He first wrote the words of the Decalogue, dedicated and consecrated that way and method, that the purity of heavenly doctrine be preserved and retained through divinely inspired Scriptures. Thus, the first origin of Holy Scripture will have God Himself as its author.

We speak, however, of divinely inspired Scriptures...

The Jews fable that the book of Genesis was written by Moses before God wrote the words of the Decalogue, because in Exodus 24 there is mention of the book of the covenant before the tables of the Decalogue were brought. But they do not notice that many things are said in sacred history by anticipation or by ὕστερον πρότερον [putting the latter first]; for that book, which is mentioned in Exod. 24, was the book of the Old Testament which God struck with the children of Israel on Mount Sinai, as is manifestly written in Heb. 9. But in Exod. 34, when God wrote the words of the Decalogue on the tables, Moses had not yet written the book of the covenant, but only then did he receive the command to write. There is, therefore, no doubt that what is reported in Exod. 24 concerning the writing and dedication of the book of the covenant was done after those things which are described in Exod. 34, so that God wrote the Decalogue on the tables before Moses wrote his books..., and these things are recited for this purpose, that it may be observed from the divinely inspired Scriptures, which to posterity... ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

God willed that the truth be preserved and exist, [and] that nothing was written before the tables of the Decalogue, inscribed by the fingers of God. For it contributes much to illustrating the dignity and authority of Holy Scripture that God Himself not only instituted and commanded the method of comprehending heavenly doctrine in letters, but that He Himself first initiated, dedicated, and consecrated it with the written words of the Decalogue by His own fingers.

For if the writing of the sacred books had first been begun by men, a prescription of more than two thousand years could have been opposed, when in the better times of the world and among the most excellent patriarchs, the doctrine of the divine word was handed down by living voice without writing. Therefore, God Himself made the beginning of writing with His own fingers, so that He might show how much is to be attributed to this method, so that the purity of doctrine might be preserved for posterity by writings. But that He took stone tables, upon which He wrote the words of the Decalogue, there is another reason, which is explained in 1 Cor. 3.

But lest those things which were either written down by men of God, adorned for this purpose with miracles and divine testimonies, or were approved once written, should be held of lesser or no authority for the confirmation of dogmas and the refutation of corruptions, God did not will to write the whole law Himself, but, having written the words of the Decalogue, He gave a command to Moses that he should write down the rest from His mouth. And so that the people of God might be certain that that Scripture of Moses was not brought forth by human will, but was divinely inspired, God procured authority for the testimony of Moses by very many stupendous miracles, both before the writing, and after, and in the very writing itself. (Exam. conc. Trid. De S. S. f. 8. sq.)

Quenstedtius: “Question 1: Was Holy Scripture necessary? — Status of the controversy: The question is 1. not concerning Holy Scripture considered formally, but viewed materially; 2. not concerning necessity on the part of God, or the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, but concerning the necessity of the church; 3. not concerning necessity in any state of the church whatsoever, but concerning the church today, dilated throughout the whole world, to be preserved until the consummation of the age, destitute of immediate revelations and θεόπνευστοι teachers after the limits of the Scriptures were closed; 4. not concerning absolute necessity, but hypothetical; nor 5. is it asked whether Scripture was not necessary for one or another individual, but whether it was necessary for the whole church.” (L. c. q. 1. f. 89.)

The same: “The Apostles wrote not only to consult the necessity of their own times, but so that they might leave to men of all times a certain and exact norm and rule both of believing and of living, cf. Rom. 15:4. Hence Tertullian against Marcion, ch. 5, says: ‘The apostles wrote to all, while writing to some.’ And Cyril, Prologue in John: ‘Moved by this matter, John thought it right to consult both the present and the future by the writing of this gospel.’” (L. c. q. 2. f. 96.)

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who assert that Holy Scripture is not necessary and that the church can lack that Scripture; thus Gregorius de Valentia in Anal. fid. p. 388, where he says, ‘heavenly doctrine can be preserved more purely by tradition than by Scripture.’ Bellarmine, l. IV de V. Dei c. 4, contends, ‘the church can consist without Scripture, but cannot without tradition.’ Costerus asserts, ‘Christ did not will that He or His church should depend on paper Scriptures, nor commit His mysteries to membranes.’ Petrus a Soto: ‘Let that be established as most certain, that this plan of writing divine words and revelations was devised by God because of human imperfection and infirmity, and is more expedient for the weaker and more imperfect; but for the holier and purer, it is either less necessary or not necessary at all.’ To this points that impious voice of a certain cardinal, reported by Tilenus, part 1, disp. 2, th. 35: ‘It would have been better consulted for the church if no Scripture had ever existed.’...

2. Of the Fanatics, such as the Anabaptists, Schwenkfeldians, and Weigelians, who deny the necessity of Scripture through their hypotheses. For they send men to be informed away from Scripture, as a dead and killing letter, to an internal natural word, to divine revelations, conversations with angels, etc.”

6. The less principal efficient causes of Holy Scripture were holy men, prophets, and apostles. For God did not, as He once did with the Decalogue, reduce the Holy Scripture which we possess into letters with His own fingers, or by immediate operation; rather, He made use of the work of men as amanuenses, who, both in regard to the species and the exercise of the act of writing, depended upon God as the principal cause, who inspired them or supplied the concepts of the things and words to be expressed in writing; although, in regard to the characters of the letters and syllables to be painted with a pen upon parchment or paper, they acted by way of a principal cause by the power of the art of writing, whether natural or conferred once by supernatural influx. See the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* 1. c. and § 9. p. 259., likewise *de Syncr. et Script. S.* p. 322. 325.

Quenstedtius: "Cyprian, *serm. de eleem.*: 'The Holy Spirit was the scribe, the prophets were His pens, to whom the Holy Spirit dictated what was to be written.' Augustine elegantly [states] in *lib. 1. de consensu evang. c. ult.*: 'Whatever the Savior wished us to read concerning His deeds and words, He commanded them (the evangelists and apostles) to write, as if by His own hands.' Therefore, if we wish to speak accurately, God alone is to be called the author of Holy Scripture; the prophets and apostles, however, cannot be called authors, except by a certain catachresis; inasmuch as they were rather the notaries and amanuenses of God the author, and of the Holy Spirit, the arch-scribe, who dictated and inspired the Word." (L. c. s. 1. f. 80. sq.)

Latin:

Cf. Rudelbachius: „Die Lehre von der Inspiration der heiligen Schrift, mit Berücksichtigung der neuesten Untersuchungen darüber von Schleiermacher, Twesten und Steudel, historisch-apologetisch und dogmatisch entwickelt.“ (Zeitschrift für die gesammte lutherische Theologie und Kirche. Herausg. von Dr. A. G. Rudelbach und Dr. H. E. F. Guericke. Erster Jahrg. 1840. Erstes Quartalheft, p. 1—59. Zweites Quartalheft, p. 1—-66.) §

5. Causa impulsiva a consignatae ex voluntate divina Scripturae sacrae interna est bonitas b Dei, externa c hominum salvandorum indigentia. d Quam necesse est agnoscere eos, qui consilii divini causas scrutantur, et tradunt, quam ob rem Deus doctrinam coelestem, aliquamdiu

per vivae vocis traditionem sine Scripturarum adminiculo conservatam, literis mandari voluerit. Vid. b. Gerh. Exeg. L. I. § 19. p. 36. Gerhardus: „Scribendi mandatum tum demum Moses accepit, cum Deus decalogi tabulas suo digito scripsisset. Exod. 34, 27.“ (Exeg. 1. 1. § 16.)

Est enim communicatio Scripturae hominibus facta utique beneficium Dei indebitum. Quam vulgo προχαταρχηχψ vocant; qua ratione alias nostrates voluntatis divinae de mittendo filio causam προχαταρχτιχψ dicunt miseriam humanam, ita ut a causa meritoria valde differat. Sic enim et indigentia pauperis movet hominem divitem ac liberalem ad dandam ei eleemosynam, nec tamen ideo pauper ille sua indigentia meretur eleemosynam.

Scilicet 1) multiplicato genere humano, 2) vitae vero humanae spatio abbreviato, non aeque ut olim a patriarchis, immediata revelatione Dei instructis, viva voce coram instrui poterant omnes homines. Sed et 3) invectis variis doctrinae corruptelis, accedente 4) hominum informandorum infirmitate et memoriae imbecillitate, ut tamen praesto esset revelatio, ad quam in omni necessitatis casu secure confugi posset, litera scripta non abs re desiderabatur. Atque ita divinae providentiae consultissimum visum est, capita divinarum revelationum scripto comprehendi. Conf. Gerh. l. c. p. 37.

Chemnitius: „Dignum est consideratione, cum per traditiones puritas doctrinae non conservaretur et Deus non vellet amplius illa ratione uti, ut erroris corruptelis per novas subinde et peculiares revelationes repeteret, instauraret et conservaret puritatem ejus doctrinae, quae ab initio mundi patriarchis patefacta et tradita fuerat, — dignum, inquam, est observatione, quam aliam rationem tempore Moysis ipse constituerit et ostenderit, ut scilicet scriptis, divina auctoritate et testimonio approbatis et confirmatis, puritas doctrinae coelestis propagaretur et conservaretur, ne quaestionibus aut controversiis de veteri genuina et pura patriarcharum doctrina exortis semper quaerendae et expectandae essent novae et peculiares revelationes. Illa vero historia diligenter consideranda est. Utiliter enim illustrabit et explicabit praesentem controversiam de sacra Scriptura, monstrata prima ejus origine. Ostendit autem historia, quod judicio praecipue est observandum, Deum non tantum instituisse, sed ipsum suo facto et exemplo, cum primus verba decalogi scripsit, dedicasse et consecrasse viam illam et rationem, ut per Scripturas divinitus inspiratas conservetur et retineatur coelestis doctrinae puritas. Ita prima origo sacrae Scripturae Deum ipsum habebit auctorem.

Loquimur autem de Scripturis divinitus inspiratis. . .

Judaei fabulantur, librum Genesis a Mose conscriptum fuisse, priusquam Deus verba decalogi scriberet, propterea quod Exodi 24. iit mentio voluminis foederis ante allatas tabulas decalogi. Sed non animadvertunt, multa per anticipationem seu per ύστερον πρότερον in historia sacra dici; volumen enim illud, cujus mentio fit Exod. 24., fuit liber Veteris Testamenti, quod Deus in monte Sina pepigit cum filiis Israel, sicut manifeste scriptum est Ebr. 9. Sed Exod. 34., cum Deus verba decalogi scriberet in tabulis, Moses nondum scripserat volumen foederis, sed tunc primum accepit mandatum scribendi. Nullum igitur dubium est, quae Exod. 24. de scriptione et dedicatione voluminis foederis referuntur, gesta esse post ea, quae Exod. 34. describuntur, ita ut Deus decalogum prius scripserit in tabulis, quam Moses suos libros conscriberet. . ., et haec eo recitari, ut observetur ex Scripturis divinitus inspiratis, quas ad poste DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

ritatem Deus conservari et extare voluit, nihil scriptum fuisse ante tabulas decalogi Dei digitis conscriptas. Multum enim facit ad dignitatem et auctoritatem sacrae Scripturae illustrandam, quod Deus ipse rationem comprehendendi literis doctrinam coelestem non tantum instituit et mandavit, sed quod illam primus scriptis verbis decalogi suis digitis initiavit, dedicavit et consecravit.

Si enim ab hominibus primum scriptio sacrorum librorum inchoata fuisset, potuisset opponi praescriptio. plus quam bis mille annorum, ubi in melioribus mundi temporibus et inter praestantissimos patriarchas sine scripto viva voce tradita fuit doctrina verbi divini. Deus igitur ipse suis digitis fecit initium scribendi, ut ostenderet, quantum huic rationi, ut doctrinae puritas ad posteritatem scriptis conservetur, tribuendum sit. Quod vero tabulas lapideas sumpsit, in quibus verba decalogi scripsit, alia est ratio, quae explicatur 1 Cor. 3.

Ne vero ea, quae per homines Dei, miraculis et testimoniis divinis ad hoc ornatos, vel conscriberentur, vel conscripta comprobarentur, minoris vel nullius ad confirmationem dogmatum et refutationem corruptelarum auctoritatis haberentur, noluit Deus ipse totam legem conscribere, sed, scriptis verbis decalogi, Mosi mandatum dedit, ut reliqua ex ore ejus conscriberet. Et ut populus Dei certus esset, Scripturam illam Mosis non humana voluntate allatam, sed divinitus inspiratam esse, Deus valde multis stupendis miraculis testimonio Mosis auctoritatem conciliavit et ante scriptionem et post et in ipsa scriptione.“ (Exam. conc. Trid. De S. S. f. 8. sq.)

Quenstedtius: „Quaestio 1.: An s. Scriptura fuerit necessaria? — Status controversiae: Quaestio est 1. non de s. Scriptura formaliter considerata, sed materialiter spectata; 2. non de necessitate ex parte Dei, aut amanuensium Spiritus S., sed de necessitate ecclesiae; 3, non de necessitate in quovis ecclesiae statu, sed de ecclesia hodierna in omnem orbem dilatata, ad consummationem seculi conservanda, revelationibus immediatis et doctoribus $εοπνενστοις destituta post limites Scripturarum clausos; 4. non de necessitate absoluta, sed hypothetica; nec 5. quaeritur, an uni et alteri individuo Scriptura non fuerit necessaria, sed an toti ecclesiae.“ (L. c. q. 1. f. 89.)

Idem: „Apostoli scripserunt non tantum, ut suorum temporum necessitati consulerent, sed ut omnium temporum hominibus relinquerent certam et exactam tum credendi, tum vivendi normam ac regulam, cf. Rom. 15, 4. Hinc Tertullianus contra Marcion. c. 5. ait: ,Ad omnes apostoli scripserunt, dum ad quosdam.4 Et Cyrillus Prolog, in Joh.: ,Hac re commotus Johannes par esse putavit, tam praesentibus, tam futuris hujus evangelii conscriptione consulere.4“ (L. c. q. 2. f. 96.)

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: „Antithesis: 1. M/.noypatpow pontificiorum asserentium, Scripturam sacram non esse necessariam et posse ecclesiam Scriptura illa carere; ita Gregorius de Valentia in Anal. fld. p. 388., ubi ait, , doctrinam coelestem purius conservari posse per traditionem, quam per Scripturam.' Bellarminus 1. IY. de V. Dei c. 4. contendit, ,ecclesiam sine Scriptura consistere posse, sine traditione non posse.' Costerus asserit, »Christum nec ecclesiam suam a chartaceis Scripturis pendere nec membranis mysteria sua committere voluisse.' Petrus a Soto: ,Illud statuatur ut certissimum, quod hoc scribendi verba divina atque revelationes consilium ob imperfectionem et infirmitatem humanam est excogitatum a Deo, atque infirmioribus et imperfectioribus magis expediens; sanctioribus vero et purioribus aut minus aut nullo modo necessarium.' Huc spectat vox impia illa cardinalis cujusdam, relata Tileno parte 1. disp. 2. th. 35.: ,Melius consultum fuisse ecclesiae, si nulla unquam extitisset Scriptura.'..

2. Fanaticorum, ut Anabaptistarum, Schwenkfeldianorum, Weigelianorum, qui per hypotheses suas Scripturae necessitatem negant. Homines enim informandos a Scriptura, ut litera mortua et occidente, ad verbum internum naturale, ad divinas revelationes, angelorum colloquia etc. remittunt."

6. Causa efficiens minus principalis a Scripturae s. fuerunt homines b sancti, c prophetae d et apostoli. e Non enim Deus, sicut olim semel decalogum, ita et Scripturam sacram, quam habemus, suis digitis, seu immediata operatione, in literas redegit; verum opera hominum, tanquam amanuensium, usus fuit, qui quoad speciem pariter et exercitium actus scribendi a Deo inspirante aut conceptus rerum et verborum scripto exprimendos suppeditante, velut a causa principali, dependebant; quamvis ad characteres literarum et syllabarum, calamo in membrana aut charta pingendos, ex vi artis scriptoriae, seu naturalis, seu per supernaturalem influxum semel collatae, ipsi per modum causae principalis sese haberent. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. 1. c. et § 9. p. 259., it. de Syncr. et Script. S. p. 322. 325.

Quenstedtius: „Cyprianus serm. de eleem.: ,Spiritus S. erat scriba, prophetae erant ejus calami, quibus Spiritus S. scribenda dictabat.* Eleganter Augustinus lib. 1. de consensu evang. c. ult.: ,Quicquid Servator de suis factis et dictis nos legere voluit, hoc scribendum illis (evangelistis et apostolis) tanquam suis manibus imperavit.' Solus ergo Deus, si accurate loqui velimus, s. Scripturae auctor dicendus est; prophetae vero et apostoli auctores dici non possunt, nisi per quandam catachresin; utpote qui’ potius Dei auctoris calami et αρχιγράμματος Spiritus S., verbum dictantis et inspirantis, notarii et amanuenses fuerunt.“ (L. c. s. 1. f. 80. sq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Though they were indeed not entirely immune from sin otherwise, they were not…

Though they were indeed not entirely immune from sin otherwise, they were not exposed to the danger of erring in the act of writing, inasmuch as they were then entirely subject to the Holy Spirit, so that they could neither admit a lapse of memory or any other error whatsoever, nor could they wish to deceive. Thus, 2 Pet. 1:21, they are called men of God, i.e., men peculiarly and immediately called and elected by God for this purpose, that they might consign divine revelations to writing. The blessed Gerhard in *Exeg. L. I. § 18. p. 35.*

For also among the Hebrews אִישׁ הָרוּחַ is a man governed by the Spirit of God; although the term is sometimes taken more broadly elsewhere. Quenstedtius: "They were called men of God because of the divine office which they discharged; for the epithet denotes the excellence of the name of God, as in Gen. 23:6 and elsewhere. They are called holy, however, not so much on account of inherent or imputed holiness, as by reason of their singular segregation and peculiar vocation to the prophetic or apostolic office; so that 'holy' here is the same as 'set apart' and 'consecrated to divine use'." (L. c. th. 7. f. 83.)

That is, men consigning Scripture before the incarnation of Christ, the nucleus of which was Christ who was to come. See Heb. 1:1. Cf. Musaeus, l. c. § 4. p. 252.

Luther: "A prophet is named one who has his understanding from God without means, to whom the Holy Spirit puts the word into his mouth. For He is the source, and they have no other master than God, 1 Cor. 14:1, 2. No one can make a prophet through human preaching and teaching, 2 Pet. 1:21, and even if it were..." ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

God’s Word is, and if I preach the Word in the purest way, I still do not make a prophet; I can make a wise and understanding man. As in Matthew chapter 23, verse 34, those are called 'wise' who drew their doctrine from the prophets, for God speaks through people and not without means. But prophets are those who have the doctrine from God without any means." (Exposition on several chapters of the 2nd Book of Moses. 1525. III, 1172.)

By this name are designated not only those whom Christ had chosen in the days of His flesh to teach all nations, and those added after His ascension: Matthias (whose writings, however, we do not possess, although we know he is to be held as an apostle) and Paul; but also apostolic men, next to the apostles in office and dignity, such as Mark and Luke the evangelists, who were to inform the universal church by public writings no less than by the proclamation of their voice. See Musaeus, loc. cit., § 7.

The matter from which the Holy Scriptures are [composed] are words, phrases, and periods, in the Old Testament according to the Hebrew language, in the New Testament according to the Greek language, recorded with a style—that is, a choice and structure of words—varying according to the diverse temperaments, customs, affections, and customary character of speech of the writers.

Or that from which Holy Scripture is composed, and which can be common to Holy Scripture and other writings, as signs of certain things. For otherwise it must be admitted that Scripture is not so much a substance composed of matter and form, as one [thing] through the aggregation of parts. Blessed Gerhard, Exeg. L. I. § 54. p. 73.

Others prefer to say *materiale* rather than *materia*. Words, indeed, viewed absolutely in themselves, can be called the remote matter of Holy Scripture, but the same words, when placed or constructed in context, can be called its proximate matter. See Musaeus, loc. cit., § 10, 11, 12, p. 259 sqq.

And it seems to come to the same thing that blessed Gerhard writes in Exeg. loc. cit. Cap. IV. § 54, p. 73: That the very framework and series of the biblical books can not inconveniently be posited as the matter from which Scripture, formally considered, is [composed]. Cf. his Isag. LL. Disp. IV. § 2, p. 11.

Or regarding the books written before Christ was born, which are signified by the term Old Testament, taken systematically or dogmatically.

Although certain Chaldean [passages] also intervene, e.g., Gen. 31:47, in Jeremiah 10:11, Daniel 2:4 sqq. up to Chapter 8:2, and Ezra 4:8 sqq. up to Chapter 6:18, and from Chapter 7:11 sqq. to 27.

It is evident, however, that God, in employing a certain language, accommodated Himself to the state of the people whom He had hitherto wished to make, as His chosen possession, a participant primarily in gracious revelation; so that, while the free state of the Israelites was in force, God addressed the people in the Hebrew language of the patriarchs, but by similarly addressing those accustomed to the power and language or dialect of the Chaldeans, He condescended to them.

Luther: "The text (Is. 9:6) seems to have been corrupted by the punctuators, who wrote ויקרא instead of the passive ויקרא. For the letters, whether read with points or without points, are the same, and the grammar is perfectly consistent. But the Jews, most pestilential men, often deprave the sentences of the prophets with their points and distinctions, and they wish their points—which are, however, a recent invention—to be of more value than the simple, genuine, and grammatically correct meaning. Why, therefore, do I not concern myself much with those grammatical superstitions, even though the grammar stands on our side, if it is correctly punctuated?" (Enarratio uberior on Isaiah ch. 9. Exegetical Works, ed. Dr. H. Schmidt. Vol. XXIII, p. 410 sq. Cf. Halle Tom. VI, 292.)

The same: "I cannot indeed deny the method of pointing, but I am not pleased with it because of the ambiguity, which renders Scripture uncertain and tears and rends it apart. Munster somewhere cites a rabbi who says: 'Without above and below, the Holy Scripture cannot be understood,' that is, without the superior and inferior points. And that is true among the Hebrews. But they do not show the author of this reading, nor do they bring forward certain arguments why points ought to be added in this manner; nay, they even make an arbitrary usurpation of the points. I believe that one word is to be read and understood differently, as here כז^ה and מטה, but who makes me certain which reading is truer, even though they say it is to be read according to the above and below? In the time of Jerome, the use of points does not seem to have existed yet, but the whole Bible was read without them. However, I do not accept the more recent Hebrews, who take upon themselves the judgment concerning the true sense and understanding of the language, who are nevertheless not friends, but enemies of Scripture. Therefore, I often pronounce against the points, unless the prior sentence agrees with the New Testament. For from the points nothing else is left than mere divinations: whether מטה or מטה is to be read, and so in many other things which are written with the same letters. Therefore, I do not care much for the 'above and below' of the rabbis; it would be better to read Scripture according to the 'within.' And the New Testament provides us with the internal understanding, not the superior or inferior." (Enarratt. in Genesis [Gen. 47:31]. Exegetical Works XI, p. 85. Halle II, 2703 sq.)

Gerhard: The question is: "Whether the vowel points were coeval with the letters in the edition of the Bible, or whether they were added in later times? The former is affirmed... 2. by almost all of our theologians. Chemnitz in Harmon. ch. 51, Flacius part 2, Clav. Script., Hafenreffer in Ezechiel's Temple, etc." (Exeges. 1.1. § 333 sq.)

By this name, taken systematically, are usually designated the books written after the birth of Christ. It pleased God, however, to use the Greek language, which for some centuries had been most customary among the Jews as well as among almost all the nations in which the church was to be planted through apostolic preaching, and even at the very time of the consigning of the New Testament Scripture. And from this συγχαταβάσει (condescension) it also came about that that Greek diction was ἑλληνιστική (Hellenistic), or mixed with Hebraisms. See the blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 11, p. 261. And compare the blessed Scherz, System. L. I. § 14, p. 14. Although we do not therefore say that solecisms and barbarisms are to be attributed to Holy Scripture: which the blessed Musaeus never maintained, who, when he was defending certain learned and well-deserving men in a philological disquisition on the style of the New Testament held in the year 1641—men who, wishing to show the difference between the style of Scripture and other writers famous in the Greek language, had used those terms, following the lead of Jerome among the ancient fathers—against the imputed crime of impiety and blasphemy committed against the Holy Spirit, and therefore [defending] the arguments of the writer CONCERNING THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

he] examined the [work] of a certain person and noted an ασυλλογιστίαν (in the same manner in which the blessed Huelsemannus also believed that the fathers and more recent authors who spoke in this way were to be excused, and he cites the *Disquisitio* of the blessed Musaeus and the *Vindiciae* that followed it, *Praelect. in F. C. art. I. c. III. § 5. p. 222*), he not only never made the opinion itself—that there are truly barbarisms and solecisms in the Scriptures—his own, but he even testified several times in that same disputation and throughout the entire *Vindiciae* that he did not embrace it; in this whole matter, however, he obtained the approval of the blessed Joh. Major, the primary professor of theology at that time, whose congratulatory poem, which is as it were an έπιτομή and άναχεψαλαίωσις of almost everything that is disputed in that *Disquisitio*, still adorns the disputation itself today. And the appendix of the blessed Musaeus to the *Vindiciae* of the *Disquisitio* (pp. 457, 458) deserves to be read, as does his *Tr. de Syncr. et Scr. S. L. I. pp. 319, 320*. For this reason, the blessed Scherzerus also, in his *System. 1. c. p. 14*, although he denies that solecisms importing χαχίαν or foulness, and barbarisms opposed to Greek ίλλψιστιχτ, are to be attributed to Scripture, nevertheless commends the *Disq. de stylo N. T.* of the blessed Musaeus.

Furthermore, regarding what is disputed concerning the Gospel of Matthew and the Epistle to the Hebrews: whether those books were first composed in the Hebrew language, which seemed to be the case to not a few of the fathers: it suffices here that the Greek text of them which survives today, whether it be the original or translated from another language, is truly θεόπνευστος, and therefore rightly enters into the part of the principle of things to be believed as αϋτοπίστου. Cf. Mus. *Introd. l. c. p. 261*.

For the thing itself truly speaks, that the manner of speaking in the Scriptures appears in some places smoother and more submissive, in others more grave and vehement, again in some places more humble and less polished, in others more grand and polished, sometimes purer regarding the usage of a single language, and at other times mixed with the idioms of other languages; and since the primary author of Scripture is one, and the whole of Scripture is θεόπνευστος, it must be confessed that the Holy Spirit Himself, in suggesting the concepts of the words, accommodated Himself to the character and condition of the amanuenses. See Mus. *l. c. § 13. pp. 262, 263*. That this property of style, which some call the external and occidental form of Scripture, is rightly referred to the matter as a material affection, is gathered from what has been said. Cf. Mus. *§ 18. p. 272*.

Latin:

Alias equidem a peccato non plane immunes, non tamen in aetu scribendi periculo errandi expositi, quippe Spiritui 8. tunc plane subjecti, ut nec memoriae lapsum aut alium quemcunque errorem admitterent, nec fallere velle possent. ### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Dannhauerus: "They confirm the θεόπνευστον of the words

Dannhauerus: "They confirm the θεόπνευστον of the words: 1. The divine oracles (Exod. 4:15; Num. 28:12; 2 Sam. 23:2; Is. 51:16; Jer. 1:9; 30:1, 4; Mark 13:11; Luke 1:70; 21:15; Acts 2:4), which assert God to be the author not only of the senses, but also of the prophetic and apostolic mouth, and consequently also of the written letter; nor is there one source for the voice uttered by the mouth and another for the written [word], which clearly attribute Scripture also to God (Exod. 34:27; Jer. 30:2; 36:2; 2 Tim. 3:16) as its author; which deny that Scripture is of Ιδίας έπιλνσεως (2 Pet. 2). The Holy Spirit inspired everything that is not of Ιδίας έπιλνσεως; but the words also are not of Ιδίας έπιλνσεως. Therefore... 2. The difference between the authentic language and a version, which would be nothing. For the sense is the same in both. Imagine that the words were also from man in both cases, and there would be no difference anymore. 3. The property of a uniform style regarding substance in both bodies of the Testament, so that it may appear as one mouth of all the θεοπνευστων; although regarding the accidental conformation of the style, the Holy Spirit, by a singular συγκαταβάσει, lowered Himself to the talents, studies, and nations of the θεοπνευστων; from which it happened that Isaiah (of royal blood) wrote more neatly, Amos more humbly, and Luke, imbued with Greek letters, more elegantly, just as in a musical organ the substance of the song, the harmony, and the tone (Phrygian or Lydian) is one, but the spirit that blows the pipes accommodates itself to some pipes that are sharper and others that are blunter." (*Hodos. Phaen. 1. G. p. 30 sq.*)

Quenstedtius: “Distinguish between the genus of speaking and the phrases, words, and expressions themselves; the sacred writers owed the genus of speaking to daily use and custom, or even to their education, and from this also the diversity of style, especially the prophetic, arises. For according to how they were educated or accustomed to a more sublime or more humble genus of speaking and writing, so the Holy Spirit, wishing to adapt Himself to the character of men and to condescend, used the same, and thus expressed the same things more magnificently through some, and more simply through others; but that the sacred writers employed these and not other words, or equivalent ones, this is solely from divine instinct and inspiration. For the Holy Spirit adapted Himself to the capacity and character of the sacred writers, so that the mysteries might be recorded according to the customary mode of speaking. And thus the Holy Spirit inspired into the amanuenses those words which they would have otherwise used if they had been left to themselves... In a musical instrument, the pipes sound unequally, but they are moved by one musician. Truly, this opinion—that the Holy Spirit accommodated Himself to His instrument and its genius and customary genus of speaking—does not please everyone; they think the cause of the diverse speech is that ‘the Holy Spirit gives to each to speak as He Himself wills’ (Acts 2:4), and that He regarded not so much the faculty of speaking of the authors as the nature of the matters about which He wished them to speak or write. Thus D. Calovius, System. Theol. Tom. I. c. 4. q. 5. p. 574.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 109. sq.)

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of Erasmus in his annotations to chapter 10 of Acts, who asserts that ‘the speech of the apostles is not only unpolished and unrefined, but even imperfect, disordered, and sometimes clearly solecistic.’ 2. Of Beza among the Calvinists, who, while writing an invective against Erasmus (annot. to Acts 10:46), imprudently admits solecisms, saying on p. 329 of the Cambridge edition: ‘I acknowledge the highest simplicity in the apostolic writings; I do not deny hyperbata, anantapodota, and even some solecisms.’ And shortly after: ‘The apostles had most grave reasons why they sometimes thought it necessary to stammer and even to commit solecisms with the common people.’ Hence, regarding Luke 22:20, he denies that in the words of institution το εκχυνόμενον can be referred to τῷ αἵματι without a solecism.” (L. c. q. 6. f. 120.) §

8. The form or formal reason of Holy Scripture is the very concepts of things and words (of which written words are the signs), insofar as they were divinely inspired into the minds of the writers. That, I say, by which Holy Scripture is constituted in its specific being, as if by an *a priori* and proper reason, and is distinguished from any other writing. B. Musaeus, l. c. § 15. p. 265. For this reason, some say that the internal form or the formal of Scripture is the sense. See blessed Quenstedtius [Oundixius] to Comp. Hutt. Q. I. p. 7. For the sense of the words of Scripture is nothing other than the concepts of the mind by which objects are represented to the intellect; and when the things themselves are understood under the name of sense, it is certain that they are viewed not in themselves, but insofar as they are signified by words and concepts. Musaeus, l. c. p. 269. For just as Holy Scripture is constituted in the generic being of Scripture by the sense signified by words, so it is constituted in its specific being, or in the being of Holy Scripture, by the sense as it is θεόπνευστος. And it comes to the same thing, if ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

You may say that the form of Scripture is θεοπνευστία (divine inspiration); provided this is not taken precisely as the action of inspiring (for thus it pertains to the efficient cause, as the blessed Gerhard also observed in *Exeg. L. I. § 305. p. 322*), but terminatively, or as it is terminated in the very concepts of things and words in the intellect of the holy men, which were to be expressed in writing. Whence also the blessed Himmel writes in *Syntagm. Disp. II. § 17* that the internal form of Scripture is θεόπνοια (divine breathing). Compare the blessed Musaeus, *l. c.*, who also on p. 266 shows how the form of Holy Scripture remains one and the same, not only in the αὐτόγραφα (autographs) of the sacred writers, but also in the ἀπόγραφα (apographs) of the scribes, and thus even today; namely, because those ἀπόγραφα codices were prepared in imitation of the original Scripture, either immediately or mediately, whence, although the codices of Scripture have been multiplied as to their external characters, the θεόπνευστοι (divinely inspired) concepts of things and words nevertheless remain the same.

Huelsemann: "Regarding the difference between what is called the material and the formal of the divine word, some twenty years ago, even within the orthodox church, some raised a question based on some poorly understood phrases of the blessed Luther, Brentius, and others. That controversy, however, was decided in the year 1624 by the electoral and ducal theologians and reduced to these terms: 1. A distinction must be made between the material and the formal of the word and of the divine word. The material of the word is the sound produced by the human mouth, articulated and intelligible in common usage, in which sense it is distinguished from the sound of a bell or any other sign introduced by human whim, but which is not brought forth in articulated speech; which difference the apostle shows in 1 Cor. 14:7, 8, 9. The formal of the word in general is a certain determined sense, indicating a singular thing or person, and this is either complex or incomplex, which is treated in logical theorems. The material, however, of the divine word is the intelligible sound concerning divine things brought forth by God mediately or immediately, having divine authority to bind to faith and obedience, which they demonstrate from 1 Thess. 2: 13. And the formal of the divine word is the determination of the divine sense itself, brought forth by an audible sign, concerning a certain thing or person; which is likewise evident from 1 Cor. 14:8, 9, et seq. ... When the term or word 'Holy Scripture' is taken in the concrete, as it is for the most part taken and ought to be taken for the written word, then the formal of the divine word and the formal of the divine Scripture do not differ from one another, i.e., the formal of the spoken word does not differ from the formal of the written word, because that accidental form is not attended to by ecclesiastical writers when they treat of the formal of the substance itself, or the ectypal sense, which God expressed by sound, whether audible or analogous and legible. The reason is that the reader of the Scriptures conceives the words of the writer under this imagination, as if he were hearing the writer sound these forth with a voice, which he sees and reads to signify through characters; and because of this analogy of human apprehension, which occurs through the eyes or through reading, with the apprehension which occurs through the ears, and then because of the analogy of the mode of revelation, which occurs through characters, with the mode which occurs through words and sounds, the Holy Spirit, by a metonymy of the accident for the subject, calls the characters themselves the word of God, and by a metonymy of the container for the contained, calls the subject of inhesion, or the matter in which the characters are written bearing the word of God, the word of God, the covenant of God, etc. ...

Papists, Calvinists, and other sectarians have the true word of God and do not have it. They have it regarding the truth and existence of the object before their eyes and ears, just as the rich man's five brothers are said to have Moses and the prophets in Luke 16: 29. They do not have it regarding the truth of knowing (cognition) or regarding the conformity of their concepts with the mind of God who proposes it. In which sense Chrysostom, Augustine, Luther, Brentius, and others cited by Movius in the *Response to the Triad of Disputations of Mislenta* p. 86 sq. deny that Papists and other heretics have the true word of God, adding the reason, because the truth of the divine word is not..."

consists not in the signs of the words, but in their true understanding. Where it is manifest that by the term 'truth' is not understood the truth of existence, but the relative truth of cognition." (Praelectt. Form. Concord. p. 431 sqq., 433 sqq., 435 sqq.) Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between the grammatical and external sense of the divine word, and the spiritual, internal, and divine sense of the divine word. The former is the formal aspect of the Word of God, insofar as it is a word; the latter, insofar as it is a divine word; the former can be perceived even by any unregenerate person, but the latter is apprehended only by an illuminated intellect." (L. c. s. 1. th. 5. f. 81.) §

9. The object of Holy Scripture, speaking generally, is all sacred things in the commemoration of which Holy Scripture is occupied, but specifically and primarily those things which are in themselves ordained for the salvation of men, and which pertain either to dogmas necessary to be believed or to a life suitable for a man to be saved. It is otherwise called the *materia circa quam* (matter about which). For it is certain that Holy Scripture, recorded in a historical style, contains various things which, although they are not all equally necessary to be known, nevertheless all contribute in their own way to edification and are therefore rightly called the object of Scripture. See Mus. Introd. § 14. p. 264. Thus the blessed Gerhard, Exeg. L. I. § 52. p. 72, calls the Law and the Gospel the primary heads of divine revelation, to which all things that are handed down in the Scriptures can be referred. And in this respect, the object of Scripture and the object of revealed theology coincide; although even those things which are treated in Holy Scripture beyond the primary object pertain in their own way to revealed theology, either for the sake of illustrating the dogmas of faith and morals, or for the sake of the interpretation of Scripture itself. See the blessed Mus. l. c. p. 265. §

8. Forma seu ratio formalis a Scripturae sacrae sunt ipsi conceptus b rerum et verborum (quorum signa sunt verba scripta), quatenus c mentibus scribentium divinitus sunt inspirati. Illud, inquam, per quod Scriptura sacra in esse suo specifico, velut per rationem α prwri et propriam, constituitur, atque ab alia quavis scriptura distinguitur. B. Mus. 1. c. § 15. p. 265. Qua ratione quidam dicunt, formam internam aut formale Scripturae esse sensum. Vid. b. Oundixius ad Comp. Hutt. Q. I. p. 7. Sensus enim verborum Scripturae nihil aliud est, quam conceptus mentis, quibus objecta intellectui repraesentantur, et quando res ipsae sub nomine sensus intelliguntur, certum est, eas non in se, sed prout verbis et conceptibus significantur, spectari. Musaeus l. c. p. 269. Sicut enim Scriptura s. per sensum verbis significatum in esse generico Scripturae, ita per sensum, ut est θεόπνευστος, in esse specifico seu in esse sacrae Scripturae constituitur. Atque eodem redit, si DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

dicas, formam Scripturae esse θεοπνευστίαν; modo haec non accipiatur praecise pro actione inspirandi (sic enim ad causam efficientem, pertinet, quod etiam observavit b. Gerhardus in Exeg. L. I. § 305. p. 322.), sed terminative, seu prout terminatur ad ipsos conceptus rerum et verborum in intellectu hominum sanctorum, qui scripto exprimi debebant. Unde etiam b. Himmelius in Syntagm. Disp. II. § 17. scribit, formam Scripturae internam esse θεόπνοιαν. Conf. b. Mus. 1. c., qui etiam p. 266. ostendit, quomodo non solum in αυτογράφοις scriptorum sacrorum codicibus, verum etiam in άπογράψοις librariorum, adeoque etiam nunc hodie Scripturae sacrae forma una et eadem maneat; scilicet, quod codices illi ά-6γραφ»ι ad imitationem primigeniae Scripturae seu immediate seu mediate sunt concinnati, unde, multiplicatis quoad apices externos codicibus Scripturae, tamen conceptus θεόπνευστοι rerum et verborum iidem supersunt.

Huelsemannus: ,,De differentia ejus, quod materiale et formale verbi divini vocatur, silscitarunt nonnulli ante 20 annos etiam in orthodoxa ecclesia quaestionem ex male intellectis nonnullis bb. Lutheri, Brentii aliorumque phräsibus. Decisa autem est illa controversia anno 1624 a theologis electoralibus et ducalibus et reducta inter hos terminos: 1. Distinguendum esse inter materiale et formale verbi et verbi divini. Materiale verbi est sonus hominis ore prolatus, articulatus et usu vulgari intelligibilis, quo sensu distinguitur a sono campanae, vel alio quovis hominum arbitrio introducto signo, sed quod articulato sermone non profertur; quam differentiam ostendit apostolus 1 Cor. 14, 7. 8. 9. Formale verbi in genere est sensus quidam determinatus, indicans singularem rem vel personam, isque complexus vel incomplexus, de quo in theorematibus logicis agitur. Materiale autem verbi divini est sonus intelligibilis de rebus divinis a Deo mediate vel immediate prolatus, habens auctoritatem divinam obligandi ad fidem et obedientiam, quod demonstrant ex 1 Thess. 2, 13. Et formale verbi divini est ipsius sensus divini, audibili signo prolati, determinatio de certa re vel persona; quod itidem patet ex 1 Cor. 14, 8. 9. et seq. . . Quando terminus vel vocabulum sacrae Scripturae in concreto sumitur, ut plerumque sumitur et sumi debet pro verbo scripto, tunc non differre ab invicem formale verbi divini et formale Scripturae divinae, i. e. non differre formale verbi dicti a formali verbi picti, quia accidentalis illa forma non attenditur a scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, quando agunt de formali ipsius substantiae sive sensus ectypi, quem Deus sono, sive audibili sive analogo et legibili, expressit. Ratio est, quia lector Scripturarum concipit verba scribentis sub hac imaginatione, ac si scribentem audiret ista resonare voce, quae videt et legit ipsum significare per characteres, et propter hanc analogiam apprehensionis humanae, quae fit per oculos sive per lectionem cum apprehensione, quae fit per aures, deinde propter analogiam modi revelationis, qui fit per characteres, cum modo, qui fit per verba et sonos, Spiritus S. per meton. accidentis pro subjecto ipsos characteres vocat verbum Dei, et per meton. continentis pro contento appellat subjectum inhaesionls sive materiam, in qua picti sunt characteres verbum Dei portantes, verbum Dei, foedus Dei etc...

Pontificii, Calviniani et alii sectarii habent verum Dei verbum et non habent. Habent quoad objecti veritatem et existentiam coram oculis et auribus eorum, quemadmodum quinque fratres epulonis dicuntur habere Mosen et prophetas Luc. 16, 29. Non habent quoad veritatem cognoscendi (cognitionis) seu quoad conformitatem conceptuum suorum cum,mente Dei proponentis. Quo sensu Chrysostomus, Augustinus, Lutherus, Brentius aliique a Movio citati in responsione ad Triadem disputationum Mislentae p. 86. sq. negant, pontificios aliosquc haereticos habere verum Dei verbum, addita ratione, quia veritas verbi divini non Baieri Comp.' ed. Walther. I. 8

in signis verborum, sed vero eorum intellectu consistat. Ubi manifestum est, per vocabulum,veritatis4 non intelligi veritatem existendi, sed relativam veritatem cognoscendi.“ (Praelectt. Form. Concord. p. 431. sq. 433. sq. 435.) Quenstedtius: „Dist. inter sensum verbi divini grammaticum et externum, et sensum verbi divini spiritualem, internum et divinum. Ille formale est verbi Dei, quatenus verbum est; hic, quatenus verbum divinum est; ille a quovis etiam irregenito percipi potest, hic vero nonnisi ab intellectu illuminato apprehenditur.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 5. f. 81.) §

9. Objectum Scripturae a generaliter loquendo sunt res sacrae omnes, in quarum commemoratione b occupatur Scriptura s., speciatim vero et primario res illae, quae ad hominum salutem per se ordinantur, et c vel ad dogmata creditu necessaria, vel ad vitam homini salvando convenientem spectant. d Vocatur alias materia circa quam. Certum enim est, Scripturam s. stylo historico consignatam varias res continere, quae, quamvis non aeque omnes sint cognitu necessariae, suo modo tamen omnes faciunt ad aedificationem ideoque objectum Scripturae recte dicuntur. Vid. Mus. Introd. § 14. p. 264. Sic. b. Gerh. Exeg. L. I. § 52. p. 72. legem et eoangelium dicit primaria divinae revelationis capita, ad quas omnia, quae in Scripturis traduntur, revocari possint. Et hac ratione objectum Scripturae et objectum theologiae revelatae coincidunt; quamvis et ea, quae praeter objectum primarium in Scriptura sacra tractantur, suo modo ad theologiam revelatam, vel quoad illustranda fidei ac morum dogmata, vel quoad ipsius Scripturae interpretationem, pertineant. Vid. b. Mus. l. c. p. 265.§


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: The *finis cui* (end for which) of Holy Scripture is, in general, all men…

10. The *finis cui* (end for which) of Holy Scripture is, in general, all men without distinction of ecclesiastical or secular status, as those to be instructed from the Scriptures not only by the works of others but also by their own; specifically, however, those who are or are to be teachers of the church.

Or the subject for whose benefit Holy Scripture is intended. See Mus. § 23. p. 277, 278. Some call it by the name of object, but distinguished from the *materia circa quam*, or with an addition call it the personal object. See the blessed Gerhard, l. c. § 480. p. m. 525.

This will be clearer if one attends to the *finis cujus* (end of which) (of which we shall speak immediately), which pertains to all men by the intention of God. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

Certainly, in the ancient Israelite as well as the primitive Christian church, Scripture was not only read publicly and the people instructed therefrom, but the reading of Scripture was also granted and commended to all indiscriminately, and that by divine command in Deut. 6:6, 7: "These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them." Similarly, in chapter 31:11, 12, where God commands that the whole Scripture then extant be read to the assembled people—men, women, children, and the sojourners who were within the gates of the Israelites. And in Isaiah 34:16, the prophet, addressing the promiscuous multitude, says: "Seek and read from the book of the Lord: not one of these shall be missing," etc. Indeed, David in Ps. 1:2 declares him blessed who is occupied in the meditation of the law, or Holy Scripture, day and night.

In the New Testament, however, Christ in Luke 16:29 and 31 says—not incidentally in a parable, but by the very force of the parable’s scope—that the writings of Moses and the prophets must be thoroughly unfolded and consulted by individual men, and that what is handed down there must be embraced. And in John 5:39, He commends to the Jewish people the searching of the Scriptures, by which the readers themselves might strive to penetrate into the sense of Scripture and to recognize the Messiah by its testimony for the sake of obtaining eternal life (for this is what έρευναν τάς γραφάς means, like those who search into metallic veins or the dens of wild beasts), whether by formal command or at the very least by His own approval. Christians are also praised for being diligent in the study of reading the Scriptures and searching their sense: the Bereans in Acts 17:11 and Timothy, when he was still a youth, indeed a child, in 2 Tim. 3:15.

Quenstedtius: "We do not say that the reading of Scripture is *ἁπλῶς* (absolutely and simply) necessary for every man, such that without it he cannot conceive faith and obtain salvation. For at times there were no Scriptures that could be read, as from the beginning of the world until Moses, when nevertheless there were believers who obtained eternal salvation... But we say that biblical reading is lawful and in a certain way commanded, or even necessary *κατά τι* (by hypothetical necessity), if the lack and *ἀδυναμία* (inability) to read is not insurmountable... For one or the other is simply necessary for the being, so to speak, of a faithful man, that he either read the Word of God himself or hear it read... When we do not forbid private searching of Holy Scripture as a domestic exercise of piety to pious heads of households and their domestics who are able to read, but faithfully commend it, we do not by that very fact permit everyone indiscriminately, learned and unlearned alike, to constitute themselves judges of the Holy Scriptures—that is, that each should interpret the Holy Scriptures according to his own judgment and gather dogmas from them that suit his own sense, as the Jesuit Costerus frames the state of the controversy, *Apolog. II. contra Gomarum*. For this very thing is to be granted to no one, neither learned nor unlearned, neither cleric nor layman, in any way." (*L. c. s. 2. q. 21. f. 313. sq.*)

The same: "Regarding the predicate *ἐρευνᾶτε*, some explain it as an imperative, some as an indicative. Cyril, *lib. III. in Joh. c. 4.*, and with him most Papists and some Calvinists—among whom are Beza, Piscator, Camerarius, Tossanus, and from our own, Brentius, Erasm. Schmidt, and others—maintain that *ἐρευνᾶτε* is spoken not in the mode of commanding, but of indicating, or that it is an indicative and designative of the practice of the Jews, not of their duty; as if the Savior said: 'You search the Scriptures, not indeed impiously, but unskillfully, drowsily, perfunctorily, without fruit; for although they bear witness of Me, you do not wish to come to Me.' They derive the argument from the preceding and following words. Since the other verbs *ἔχετε, πιστεύετε* in the former, and *δοκεῖτε, θέλετε* in the latter, are of the indicative mood, they conclude that this controversial one is of the same. But Athanasius, Augustine, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Luther, and likewise the Genevans in..." in the latest version, and many others, judge that the word ερευνάτε should be understood as an imperative, not as an indicative; to which we also subscribe. . . 8. Even if someone should wish to contend rigorously for the indicative, he must nevertheless admit that the imperative is not to be entirely excluded. 9. Finally, whether it is indicated what the custom of the Jews is, or whether it is commanded what they ought to do, our argument taken from this passage against the Papists nevertheless stands firm, namely: that the diligent and precise investigation of Scripture is not forbidden to the common people, but that all, of whatever order, condition, or age they may be, are to be admitted to, and indeed urged toward, the scrutiny of Scripture." (L. c. f. 317.)

The same: "If, because of the danger of heresies, the laity are to be barred from the reading of the Scriptures, much more so the clergy, bishops, and presbyters, because experience has hitherto proven, and Bellarmine himself admits in Book I, de Rom. Pontif. c. 8. § 8: 'There has scarcely been any heresiarch, or anyone among the heretics of any note, who did not come from the clergy.'" (L. c. q. 21. f. 325.)

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: "The antithesis of the Papists, among whom the power of reading the sacred codes in the vernacular is granted to the clergy, and indeed to them alone (though not to all, nor at all times, as the blessed Meisner observes in *Anti-Lessio*, p. 52), whereas the laity are barred from the reading of the Holy Scriptures in the vernacular language, and it is permitted to only a very few—namely, those who have obtained the faculty to read from a bishop or inquisitor upon the advice of a parish priest or confessor, who read according to the papal sense, and whom they judge will receive no harm from it, along with other annexed precautions. . . Note, however: 1. In the papacy, for the reading of the Bible to be granted to any layman, there is required in general a privilege of bishops and inquisitors, given singularly and specifically in writing, without which it is a crime and a most grave sin if anyone from the common people undertakes the reading of the Bible. 2. In the so-called inquisition of heretical depravity, there is nothing more heretical and capital than the reading of the Bible. And it is established from histories that some were condemned to the stake and dragged to the fire on account of reading Scripture in the vernacular language. Hence Molinaeus says: 'It is a horrible thing that in lands where the inquisition dominates, to possess the Bible in the vernacular language is a crime to be expiated by fire.' And those profane men consume not only men but the sacred codes themselves in the flames; 'if they discover Luther’s German version in anyone’s possession, they take it away and burn it,' says Elias Hasenmueller in his *Jesuit History*, ch. 11. But how many of the laity, hindered by so many difficulties and deterred by so many threats, would dare with impunity to seek permission from those tyrants to read a book so interminably prohibited, so odious, and adjudged to the flames? 3. If there is deep peace from heresies in the church, they can tolerate the laity tasting the Scriptures, but not being satisfied with the whole; they may only sample a little of that part which informs morals and recounts histories. But the part that proposes and explains the mysteries of faith, they wish to be set aside. They therefore permit only the reading of certain biblical books. 4. The decrees command that a layman be permitted only a copy of a version by some Catholic author, who, namely, in his translation has expressed not so much the sources themselves as the sense of the Roman Catholic Church, as Bonfrerius teaches in his *Prologomena to Holy Scripture*, ch. 11, s. 9, p. 37. 5. In free kingdoms and provinces where the inquisition does not have a place, e.g., in Germany, France, Poland, the Papists use this privilege, so that specifically to many or generally to all, 'by word or deed,' as Serarius says, power is granted by the bishops to read vernacular Bibles from the versions of the Papists—as in Germany the versions of Eck and Dietenberger are read with impunity, in France the Louvain French version, etc.—namely, so that those who eagerly hunger for sacred reading may be drawn away from the versions of the 'heretics,' as they call them, from which they fear more for themselves than from those which they themselves have fashioned according to their Latin Vulgate. But where the Pope reigns absolutely, as in Italy, Spain, Sicily, etc., vernacular Bibles are nowhere to be found." (L. c. f. 314 sq.)

The Fourth Rule of the Index of Pius IV (1564): “Since it is manifest from experience that if the Holy Bible be permitted everywhere in the vulgar tongue without distinction, more harm than utility arises therefrom, due to the rashness of men; let the judgment of the bishop or inquisitor be observed in this matter: so that with the counsel of the parish priest or confessor, they may grant the reading of Bibles translated by Catholic authors in the vulgar tongue to those whom they understand can derive not harm, but an increase of faith and piety from such reading; which permission they shall have in writing. But those who presume to read or possess them without such permission, unless they first surrender them to the ordinary, cannot receive absolution of sins. Booksellers, however, who sell Bibles written in the vulgar tongue to one not having the aforementioned permission, or grant them in any other way, shall forfeit the price of the books, to be converted by the bishop to pious uses, and shall be subject to other penalties at the discretion of the same bishop, according to the nature of the offense. Regulars, however, may not read or buy them unless they have permission from their superiors.” (SS. oecum. Concil. Tridentini Canones et decreta. Ed. D. Guil. Smets. Bielefeld 1851. p. 224.)

Latin:

10. Finis cui a Scripturae sacrae sunt in genere quidem homines omnes citra status ecclesiastici et secularis discrimen, b tanquam ex Scripturis erudiendi non aliorum solum, sed et sua c opera; speciatim vero illi, qui ecclesiae doctores d sunt aut futuri sunt.

Sive subjectum, cujus bono destinata est Scriptura sacra. Vid. Mus. § 23. p. 277. 278. Quidam nomine objecti, sed a materia circa quam distincti, appellant, aut cum addito objectum personale vocant. Vid. b Gerh. 1. c. § 480. p. m. 525.

Patebit istud clarius, si attendatur ad finem cujus (de quo statim dicemus), qui ad omnes homines ex intentione Dei pertinet. DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

Certe in veteri pariter Israelitica et primitiva christiana ecclesia non solum Scriptura publice praelecta et populus inde informatus, verum etiam lectio Scripturae omnibus promiscue concessa et commendata fuit, idque ex mandato divino Deut. 6, 6. 7.: Verba ista, quae ego praecipio tibi, acute ingeres filiis tuis ac loqueris de eis. Similiter cap. 31, 11. 12., ubi jubet Deus congregato populo, viris feminisqus et parvulis et peregrinis, qui in portis Israelitarum futuri essent, legere totam, quae tunc extabat, Scripturam. Et Esaiae 34, 16. promiscuam multitudinem alloquens propheta: Quaerite, ait, ex libro Jehovae et legite, unum ex his non defuturum est etc. Imo David Ps. 1, 2. beatum illum praedicat, qui in meditatione legis, seu Scripturae sacrae, occupatur die ac nocte.

In N. T. autem Christus Luc. 16, 29. et 31. non obiter in parabola, sed vi ipsius scopi parabolae a singulis hominibus scripta Mosis et prophetarum omnino evolvenda, consulenda, et quae ibi traduntur, amplectenda esse dicit. Et Joh. 5, 39. scrutinium Scripturarum, quo ipsi lectores in sensum Scripturae et agnoscendum ejus testificatione Messiam, vitae aeternae consequendae causa, penetrare nitantur (hoc enim est έρευναν τάς γραψάς, instar eorum, qui in venas metallicas inquirunt, aut antra ferarum), populo Judaeorum commendat, sive mandato formali, sive approbatione minimum sua. Laudantur etiam christiani, in studio legendarum Scripturarum et scrutandi sensus diligentius versati: Berrhoenses Act. 17, 11. et Timotheus, cum adhuc adolescens, imo puer esset, 2. Ep. 3, 15.

Quenstedtius: ,,Νοη dicimus, cuivis homini Scripturae lectionem άπλώς, absolute et simpliciter esse necessariam, ita ut sine ea fidem concipere et salutem consequi nequeat. Aliquando enim nullae fuerunt Scripturae, quae legi possent, ut ab initio mundi usque ad Mosen, cum tamen essent fideles, qui salutem aeternam consequerentur. . . Sed dicimus, licitam esse et certa ratione mandatam vel etiam necessariam lectionem biblicam κατά τι, necessitate hypothetica, si defectus et αδυναμία legendi non sit insuperabilis. . .
