Scripturae scrutinium ad domesticum pietatis exercitium piis patribus familias eorumque domesticis legere valentibus non interdicimus, sed fideliter commendamus, eo ipso non omnibus passim, doctis pariter et indoctis, permittimus, ut se judices constituant sacr. Literarum, h. e,, ut s. Scripturas pro suo quisque judicio interpretetur atque ex iis, quae suo sensui sapiunt, dogmata colligant, ut Jesuita Costerus statum controversiae format, Apolog. II. contra Gomarum. Hoc ipsum enim nulli, neque docto, neque indocto, neque clerico, neque laico ullo modo concedendum.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 21. f. 313. sq.)

Idem: „Quoad praedicatum rb ερευνάτε quidam per imperativum, quidam per indicativum exponunt. Cyrill. 1. III. in Joh. c. 4. et cum illo plerique pontificii ac nonnulli Calviniani, quos inter Beza, Piscator, Camerarius, Tossanus, ex nostris Brentius, Erasm. Schmidt aliique statuunt, rd ερευνάτε non imperantis, sed indicantis modo dictum esse, sive esse indicativum et designativum praxeos Judaeorum, non officii; q. d. Salvator: ,Vos scrutamini Scripturas non impie quidem, sed imperite, oscitanter, perfunctorie, sine fructu; nam cum de me reddant testimonium, non vultis ad me venire.‘ Argumentum desumunt ex antecedentibus et consequentibus. In illis reliqua verba ίχετε, πιστεύετε, in his δοκεϊτε, ΰέλετε cum sint indicativi modi, inde ejusdem et hoc controversum esse colligunt. Athanasius vero, Augustinus, Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Lutherus, itemque Genuenses in PROLEGOM. CAP. II. postrema versione, aliique plurimi cum imperio, non cum indicio verbum ερευνάτε intelligendum esse censent; quibus nos quoque adstipulamur. . . 8. Si vel maxime quis de indicativo rigorose contendere velit, tamen fateatur oportet, imperativum non esse penitus excludendum. 9. Denique, sive indicetur, quid moris sit Judaeis, sive imperetur, quid facere debeant, nostrum tamen contra pontificios ex hoc loco desumptum argumentum firmum stat, sci. quod nec plebejis Scripturae investigandae σπονδή mt ακρίβεια vetita sit, sed quod omnes, cujuscunque sint ordinis, conditionis sive aetatis, ad Scripturae scrutinium admittendi, quin et instigandi sint."(L. c. f. 317.)

Idem: ,,Si ob haeresium periculum laici sunt arcendi a Scripturarum lectione, multo magis clerici, episcopi et presbyteri, quia experientia hactenus comprobavit et Bellarminus ipse fatetur lib. I. de Rom. Pontif. c. 8. § 8.: ,Vix quemquam fuisse haeresiarcham et inter haereticos paulo celebriorem, qui ex clero non prodierit.'“ (L. c. q. 21. f. 325.)

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: „Antithesis pontificiorum, apud quos clericis et quidem solis (quamvis non omnibus, nec omni tempore, ut observat b. Meisnerus in Anti-Lessio p. 52.) potestas vernacule legendi sacros codices conceditur, laici vero a lectione s. Literarum in lingua vernacula arcentur et nonnisi paucissimis ea permittitur, illis videl., qui ab episcopo aut inquisitore consilio parochi vel confessarii legendi facultatem impetrarunt, qui legunt sensu papali, quosque nullum inde damnum accepturos esse existimant, et quae sunt annexae cautelae aliae. . . Nota vero: 1. in papatu ad lectionem biblicam laico alicui concedendam requiri in genere privilegium episcoporum et inquisitorum singulariter et speciatim in scriptis datum, quo sine nefas sit et piaculum gravissimum, si quis de vulgo lectionem bibliorum aggrediatur. 2. In inquisitione, quam vocant, haereticae pravitatis nihil magis haereticum et capitale esse, quam lectionem biblicam. Et constat ex historiis, quosdam ad rogum esse condemnatos et ad ignem raptos ob Scripturae in vulgari lingua lectionem. Hinc Molinaeus inquit: ,Res horribilis, quod in terris, ubi dominatur inquisitio, habere Biblia in lingua vulgari, sit crimen igne expiandum.' Nec solum homines, sed et ipsos sacros codices flammis consumunt profani illi homines; ,si apud quem Lutheri versionem germanicam deprehendant, eam auferunt et comburunt*, ait Elias Hasenmuellerus in historia Jesuitica c. 11. Quotus quisque vero laicorum tot difficultatibus praepeditus,, tot minis absterritus, impune ausit a tyrannis illis veniam petere, librum tam interminatorie prohibitum, tam odiosum et flammis adjudicatum legendi? 3. Si alta ab haeresibus pax est in ecclesia, pati possunt, laicos Scripturas degustare, at non integris satiari, sed de ea tantum parte, quae mores informat et historias recitat, delibare nonnihil. Quae vero fidei mysteria proponit et explicat, hanc partem seponi volunt. Permittunt ergo tantum certorum librorum biblicorum lectionem. 4. Jubent decreta, ut permittatur laico nonnisi exemplar versionis auctoris cujusdam catholici, qui sci. in translatione sua non tam ipsos fontes, quam sensum ecclesiae romanocatholicae expresserit, docente Bonfrerio in praeloquiis ad s. Scripturam, c. 11. s. 9. p. 37. 5. In liberis regnis et provinciis, in quibus locum non habet inquisitio, v. g. in Germania, Gallia, Polonia, hoc privilegio utuntur pontificii, ut speciatim pluribus vel generatim omnibus, ,verbo aut facto', ut loquitur Serarius, flat potestas ab episcopis legendi vernacula biblia ex versionibus pontificiorum, ut in Germania leguntur Eckii et Dietenbergii versiones impune, in Gallia Lovaniensis versio gallica etc., scl. ut abstrahantur, qui sacrae lectioni avide inhiant, ab haereticorum, ut vocant, versionibus, a quibus magis sibi metuunt, quam ab illis, quas ipsi ad Vulgatam suam latinam exegerunt. Ubi vero papa absolute regnat, ut in Italia, Hispania, Sicilia etc., nuspiam biblia vernacula lingua inveniuntur.“

Quarta regula Indicis Pii IV. (1564): „Cum experimento manifestum sit, si sacra biblia vulgari lingua passim sine discrimine permittantur, plus inde, ob hominum temeritatem, detrimenti, quam utilitatis, oriri; hac in parte judicio episcopi aut inquisitoris stetur: ut cum consilio parochi vel confessarii bibliorum a catholicis auctoribus versorum lectionem in vulgari lingua eis concedere possint, quos intellexerint ex hujusmodi lectione non damnum, sed fidei atque pietatis augmentum capere posse; quam facultatem in scriptis habeant. Qui autem absque tali facultate ea legere seu habere praesumpserint, nisi prius ordinario redditis, peccatorum absolutionem percipere non possunt. Bibliopolae vero, qui praedictam facultatem non habenti biblia idiomate vulgari conscripta vendiderint, vel alio quovis modo concesserint, librorum pretium, in usus pios ab episcopo convertendum, amittant, aliisque poenis pro delicti qualitate ejusdem episcopi arbitrio subjaceant. Regulares vero non nisi facultate a praelatis suis habita ea legere aut emere possunt.“ (SS. oecum. Cohcil. Tridentini Canones et decreta. Ed. D. Guil. Smets. Bielefeldiae 1851. p. 224.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Clement VIII: “It must be noted regarding the above-written fourth rule of the…

Clement VIII: “It must be noted regarding the above-written fourth rule of the Index of Pope Pius IV of happy memory, that by this printing and edition no new power is granted to bishops, or inquisitors, or superiors of regulars to grant license to buy, read, or retain Bibles published in the vulgar tongue; since hitherto, by the mandate and usage of the Holy Roman and Universal Inquisition, the power of granting such licenses to read or retain vulgar Bibles, or other parts of Holy Scripture of both the New and Old Testament published in any vulgar tongue, and furthermore summaries and compendia, even historical ones, of the same Bibles or books of Holy Scripture written in any vulgar idiom, has been taken away from them; which indeed is to be observed inviolably.” (Observatio circa Quartam Regulam. Cf. Index etc. Cologne, at the expense of B. Gualther 1602.) Indeed, they are to be instructed from the Scriptures not only for their own good, but also for the good of others whom they serve. Cf. 2 Tim. 3:16, 17, where Scripture is said to be useful to the man of God for sufficiently instructing him for every work of his office. § 11.

The end of Scripture, and that the ultimate one, is eternal salvation. The intermediate end, with respect to all men, is faith in Christ. With respect to the ministers of the church, the ends of Scripture are specifically the ministerial operations themselves, which depend upon divine revelation. Namely, with respect to us. For others, the absolutely ultimate end, which is also the common end of all things that are done or given by God, is the glory of God. Cf. Gerh. Exeg. § 361, 362. Regarding which, see what we said above concerning the end of revealed theology in Chapter I, § 17 and 18, p. 38, namely, that the ultimate end of theology and the principle of theology are the same. Thus, John in the final verse of his Gospel indicates the intermediate end of Scripture and joins it with the ultimate end, saying: These are written, proximately indeed to this end, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may attain the ultimate end, or eternal life.

for you may have [life] through his name. Furthermore, other acts that are joined with faith are not excluded here, but rather are included in their own way, according to what we said in Chapter I, § 19, p. 38 sqq., concerning the intermediate end of revealed theology. Or all good works, those which Paul enumerates and for which he says Scripture is useful as an end to be attained, namely: for διδασκαλίαν, or the instruction of men in those things which are necessary to be known regarding the articles of faith and the whole Christian doctrine; for ἔλεγχον, the demonstration or refutation of errors conflicting with heavenly truth; furthermore, for ἐπανόρθωσιν, or the correction of disordered morals through rebukes and corrections, by which men may be drawn away from sins; finally, for παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, or exhortation to righteousness, or to a just and holy conversation of life, 2 Tim. 3:16. See Gerh. in Comm. ad h. l., where he also teaches how παράκλησις or consolation, for which, as an end, Scripture is said to have been consigned in Rom. 15:4, is comprehended either under διδασκαλία or under παιδεία. Namely, insofar as it either presents the doctrine of the cross and its origin, and the intention of God who sends it, while at the same time exhibiting testimonies of divine grace under the aspect of divine revelation, or exhorts Christians to patience. And thus it is simultaneously evident that these ends, even if they are not the ends of Scripture considered simply in itself, but rather considered particularly in relation to the ecclesiastical ministry, are nevertheless consequently directed toward faith in Christ, since the ministers of the church, by teaching, refuting, correcting, and instructing others, act so that men may be led to faith in Christ and to the holiness of life that perpetually accompanies it, and once led, may be preserved in these. See Mus. Introd. l. c. § 22. p. 277. §

12. Among the affections of Holy Scripture, its authority or manifest dignity holds the first place, moving the human intellect to assent to its sayings and the will to offer obedience to its commands. For thus it appears how Holy Scripture performs the office of the formal object of revealed theology. Which you might call in Greek αὐθεντίαν, just as among jurists those instruments and writings are called authentic which have certain and just authority, so that they can obligate one to assent or even to obedience. Conf. b. Quenstedtius in not. ad Comp. Hutt. L. I. Q. 1. p. 20. For, according to the usage of speech, one is not said to be in authority or to have authority unless his dignity, by which he merits assent or obedience, is so known that it attracts minds to it. For this reason, some call the authority of Scripture ἀξιοπιστίαν, others αὐτοπιστίαν, that is, authority in speaking or testifying, so that faith may be had. To this corresponds the word ἐξουσία, or power, as of one commanding, or authority in prescribing. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

13. And this authority of Scripture, in itself and absolutely, or as viewed with respect to the thing itself, depends solely upon the author of Scripture, God, and results from His veracity and His supreme and infinite power.

Indeed, authority primarily and per se belongs to the author himself of any saying or writing, e.g., a law, a command, etc., and the remote foundation of authority is the perfection of the author viewed in himself, the proximate [foundation] is his known perfection.

From this, however, or on account of the dependence of the saying or writing upon him who possesses authority, authority also belongs to such a saying or writing itself; and thus the authority of Holy Scripture is founded in its very θεοπνευστία or dependence upon God, as upon the author whose supreme perfection is known to all. See the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* P. II. C. III. § 1. and 4. p. 282. and 288.

Moreover, it does not have authority from a less principal cause, just as other writings do not have it from their amanuenses, but from him who composed them or dictated them to the pen. Musaeus, *l. c.* § 3. p. 289.

And from this it is evident that Holy Scripture does not have authority from the church, since the church was not its author and efficient cause. Musaeus, *l. c.* p. 290.

For just as God, on account of His infinite knowledge and goodness, is supremely truthful in speaking, so that He can neither be deceived nor deceive, whence assent is deservedly to be granted to Him when He speaks: so Holy Scripture, through its dependence upon the truthful God, is likewise worthy of the assent of all men.

For just as God, by right of creation, has supreme dominion over men as His creatures, by virtue of which He can oblige men to render obedience to Him: so Scripture, through the fact that it is the Word of God, is also worthy that all men should render obedience to its precepts. Cf. Musaeus, *l. c.* § 6. p. 289. §

14. As regards us, however, or in order for it to be certain to us that Holy Scripture is worthy of having faith and obedience rendered to it, it is necessary that not only the perfections of God themselves be known, but also the dependence of Scripture upon God, or its θεοπνευστία. Cf. here § 11. note c.

Therefore, this knowledge, although it is not a constitutive part of the authority of Scripture, nor the cause or foundation or part of the foundation of it viewed in itself—that is, of the dignity which the name of authority imports in the nominative case—is nevertheless a necessary condition on the part of men, whose minds must be moved to faith and obedience through the known dignity of Scripture. Musaeus, § 11. p. 292.

15. The authority of Scripture, insofar as it concerns the assent to be granted to its statements, can be considered in two ways: partly, precisely in order to the causing of the assent of things to be believed, through which Scripture possesses the quality of being the principle of knowing and the formal object of faith and of revealed theology; partly, in order to the distinguishing from Scripture itself of other writings and doctrines that treat of matters of faith and morals, which are θεόπνευστα and truthful; in which respect Scripture possesses the quality of being canonical, or of being the norm and rule for discerning the true from the false.

a) And this is that which theologians commonly understand by the name of the authority of Scripture simply, and in the explanation of which they are almost exclusively occupied. And it must also be confessed that this is prior in the order of doctrine to the other, which implies the power of obligating one to render obedience to its commands, since the latter possesses no difficulty once the former has been demonstrated. See Musaeus, loc. cit., § 14, p. 294.

b) For although the authority of Scripture is one and the same, founded in the veracity of God and the dependence of Scripture upon God, through which it is constituted both in the capacity of a formal motive for causing the assent of faith and in the capacity of a norm for examining and judging any other writings and doctrines; yet, just as Scripture is to be employed somewhat differently by way of a formal motive for causing the assent of faith (since the doctrine of Scripture in any language can perform this function), and differently by way of a norm for distinguishing the true from the false (which Scripture performs only in the original text): so the authority of Scripture must deservedly be treated distinctly in regard to both relations. See Musaeus, loc. cit., § 15, p. 295. This you might perhaps call the motive and faith-causing authority. Otherwise, it is called the canonical or normative authority of the true and the false. Compare Musaeus, loc. cit., § 16.

The authority of Scripture, viewed in order to the causing of the assent of faith, requires the knowledge of two complex principles. One is: Whatever Scripture has been recorded by the inspiration of God, that is certainly and infallibly true. The other: Holy Scripture has been recorded by the inspiration of God. The truth of the former principle is almost devoid of doubt. But concerning the latter, one must inquire a little more fully: whether the discourse is about the knowledge of human faith, by which the divine origin of Holy Scripture becomes known, or about the knowledge of divine faith. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

Compare what we said in § 13. For it is naturally and evidently known from the very terms grasped. By this name is understood knowledge of such a kind, the ultimate reason for assenting to which is human testimony, or another probable reason, begetting an opinion, or such that it is judged to be credible that Holy Scripture is not an invention of human genius, but has proceeded from God Himself and is truly divine. That is, concerning knowledge that is simply certain and excludes every fear of the opposite, on account of the absolutely infallible certainty of divine revelation or testimony, upon which it relies as its ultimate reason for assent. §

Latin:

Scripturae tam N., quam V. Testamenti partes, quavis vulgari lingua editas, ac insuper summaria et compendia etiam historica eorundem bibliorum seu librorum s. Scripturae, quocumque vulgari idiomate conscripta; quod quidem ihviolate servandum est.“ (Observatio circa Quartam Regulam. Cf. Index etc. Coloniae sumpt. B. Gualtheri 1602.) Nempe illi non solum suo, sed et aliorum bono, quibus ministrant, ex Scripturis erudiendi sunt. Conf. 2 Tim. 3, 16. 17., ubi Scriptura utilis esse dicitur homini Dei ad opera omnia officii sufficienter instruendo.§ 11.

Respectu ministrorum ecclesiae peculiariter finis Scripturae sunt ipsae operationes ministeriales, ex revelatione divina pendentes. d Scilicet respectu nostri. Aliis finis absolute ultimus, qui et communis omnium, quae a Deo fiunt aut dantur, est gloria Dei. Conf. Gerh. Exeg. § 361. 362. De qua vid., quae supra de fine theologiae revelatae diximus Cap. I. § 17. et 18. p. 38., nempe finis ultimus theologiae et principii theologiae idem est. nam habeatis per nomen ipsius. 12. Inter affectiones Scripturae s. primum a locum obtinet ejus auctoritas b seu dignitas c manifesta, d movens intellectum humanum ad assensum e dictis ejus et voluntatem ad obsequium f ejus mandatis praebendum. Sic enim apparet, quomodo Scriptura s. obeat munus objecti formalis theologiae revelatae. Quam graece αυθεντίαν dixeris, prout apud jurisconsultos authentica instrumenta et scripta dicuntur, quae certam et justam habent auctoritatem, ut ad assensum vel etiam obsequium obligare possint. Conf. b. Oundis. in not. ad Comp. Hutt. L. I. Q. 1. p. 20. Non enim, ex usu loquendi, in auctoritate esse aut auctoritatem habere dicitur, nisi cujus dignitas, qua assensum aut obsequium meretur, ita cognita est, ut animos eo alliciat. Qua ratione auctoritatem Scripturae quidam αξιοπιστίαν, alii αυτοπιστίαν appellant, id est, auctoritatem in dicendo aut testificando, ut habeatur fides. Cui respondet vocabulum έξουσία, seu potestas, velut imperantis, sive auctoritas in praecipiendo. DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

13. Atque haec Scripturae auctoritas, in se et absolute, seu quoad rem a spectata, ab auctore Scripturae, Deo, unice b dependet et ex ejus veracitate c ac potestate d summa et infinita resultat.

Nempe auctoritas primo et per se competit ipsi auctori alicujus dicti aut scripti, v. g. legis, mandati etc., ac fundamentum auctoritatis remotum est perfectio auctoris in se spectata, proximum perfectio ejus cognita.

Inde autem, seu propter dependentiam dicti aut scripti ab eo, qui auctoritate valet, ipsi quoque dicto aut scripto tali competit auctoritas; et sic Scripturae sacrae auctoritas in ipsa #3οπνευ<ττία seu dependentia a Deo, tanquam ab auctore, cujus summa perfectio omnibus cognita est, fundatur. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. P. II. C. III. § 1. et 4. p. 282. et 288.

Non autem a causa minus principali, sicut nec aliae scripturae ab amanuensibus, sed ab eo, qui eas composuit aut in calamum dictitavit, auctoritatem habent. Mus. l. c. § 3. p. 289.

Atque inde patet, quod Scriptura sacra nec ab ecclesia habeat auctoritatem, quippe quae illius auctor et causa efficiens non fuit. Mus. l. c. p. 290.

Sicut enim Deus propter infinitam scientiam ac bonitatem suam summe verax est in dicendo, ut nec falli nec fallere possit, unde illi loquenti merito assensus commodandus est: ita Scriptura sacra per suam a Deo verace dependentiam similiter digna est assensu omnium hominum.

Nam sicut Deus jure creationis supremum in homines, tanquam creaturas, habet dominium, cujus vi homines ad obsequium sibi praebendum obligare potest: ita Scriptura per hoc, quod est Dei verbum, digna quoque est, cuius praeceptis homines omnes obsequium praestent. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 6. p. 289.§

14. Quoad nos autem, seu ut nobis constet, a Scripturam s. dignam esse, cui fides et obsequium praestetur, notas esse oportet non solum ipsas perfectiones Dei, verum etiam Scripturae a Deo dependentiam, seu Seortvevariav. b Conf. h. 1. § 11. not. c.

Itaque haec notitia, licet non sit pars constitutiva auctoritatis Scripturae, neque causa vel fundamentum aut pars fundamenti illius in se spectatae, id est, dignitatis, quam auctoritatis nomen in casu recto importat: conditio tamen est, ex parte hominum, quorum animi per dignitatem Scripturae cognitam ad fidem et obsequium moveri debent, necessaria. Mus. § 11. p. 292.

15. Auctoritas Scripturae, quatenus spectat assensum a dictis ejus praebendum, dupliciter b considerari potest: partim praecise in ordine ad causandum assensum credendorum, per quem Scriptura habet, quod est principium cognoscendi et objectum formale fidei ac theologiae revelatae; c partim in ordine ad dignoscendas ab ipsa Scriptura $εοτίνενστφ et verace scripturas et doctrinas alias, quae de rebus fidei ac morum agunt; qua ratione Scriptura habet, quod est canonica, seu quod est norma ac regula discernendi verum a falso. d

a) Atque haec illa est, quam theologi communiter nomine auctoritatis Scripturae simpliciter intelligunt, in eaque explicanda fere unice occupantur. Ac fatendum est etiam, eandem esse ordine doctrinae priorem, altera, quae importat vim obligandi ad obsequium mandatis ejus praebendum, quippe quae etiam nihil difficultatis habet, ubi illa ostensa fuerit. Vid. Mus. l. c. § 14. p. 294. -

b) Quamvis enim una et eadem sit auctoritas Scripturae, in Dei veracitate ac dependentia Scripturae a Deo fundata, per quam ipsa, cum in ratione motivi formalis ad causandum fidei assensum, tum in ratione normae ad examinandas ac dijudicandas quaslibet scripturas et doctrinas alias, constituitur; sicuti tamen Scriptura paulo aliter adhibenda est per modum motivi formalis ad causandum assensum fidei (quippe quo munere doctrina Scripturae in quavis lingua fungi potest), aliter per modum normae ad dignoscendum verum a falso (quod Scriptura in textu primigenio tantum praestat): ita de auctoritate Scripturae ratione utriusque habitudinis merito distincte agendum est. Vid. Mus. l. c. § 15. p. 295. Quam forte auctoritatem motivam fideique causativam dixeris. Dicitur alias auctoritas canonica seu normativa veri et falsi. Conf. Mus. l. c.§ 16.

Auctoritas Scripturae, in ordine ad causandum fidei assensum spectata, notitiam duorum principiorum complexorum requirit. Unum est: Quaecunque Scriptura Deo inspirante consignata est, illa certo et infallibiliter vera est. Alterum: Scriptura sacra Deo inspirante consignata est. a Prioris principii veritas fere dubio b caret. De posteriore vero paulo plenius dispiciendum est: quatenus vel de notitia fidei humanae, c qua Scripturae sacrae origo divina innotescit, vel de notitia fidei divinae d sermo est. DB PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

Confer., quae § 13. diximus. Est enim naturaliter atque evidenter ex ipsis terminis apprehensis notum. Quo nomine intelligitur notitia ejusmodi, cujus ratio assentiendi ultima est testificatio humana, aut alia ratio probabilis, opinionem gignens, seu ut judicetur, eredibile esse, quod Scriptura sacra non sit humani ingenii inventum, sed a Deo ipso profecta vereque divina. Id est, de cognitione simpliciter certa et formidinem omnem oppositi excludente, ob certitudinem divinae revelationis sive testificationis prorsus infallibilem, qua velut ratione assentiendi ultima nitatur.§


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: The arguments which declare that the divine origin of Scripture is to be…

17. The arguments which declare that the divine origin of Scripture is to be acknowledged by human faith, or is credible, are some internal, or taken from the intrinsic nature and properties of Scripture; others are external, or taken from elsewhere outside of Scripture.

Quenstedtius: "Those who are tempted are not indeed to be held in the same census as infidels, since they still retain a spark of faith like a smoldering wick; yet because they often have no or very little sense of their former knowledge concerning the authority of Scripture, one must deal with them entirely regarding this head, as we observed above from the blessed Hunnius. But the hardened, if they are corrigible and curable, must be constrained by the same arguments as infidels; since those who have never had faith and those who have lost it once received walk here with equal step; if they are incorrigible and incurable, they are to be left to themselves and to divine judgment. . . It is objected: If one believes the divine word properly and principally for its own sake, it is in vain that faith is conciliated to it through other arguments. Resp.: I deny the consequence. For just as formerly, when miracles were still being performed, they were brought forth so that incredulous men might be led to faith, even though it could be believed without them and one was not to believe properly and principally on account of those miracles: so also today, when miracles have ceased to be performed, infidel men are rightly led by the hand to faith through those other arguments, even though it can be believed, and is often believed, without them by the bare preached word." (L. c. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 9. f. 146. sq.)

Dannhauerus: "We fall here into the question: Whence do you know that the Gospel, e.g., of Matthew is Matthew’s? That the Epistle to the Romans is written by St. Paul as θεόπνευστον? — a question, to wit, that ought not to be heard among Christians by right, according to the most grave judgment of Augustine, a man more worthy of a pagan than a Christian, yet extorted by the impudence of adversaries, who capture the incautious in this snare and attempt to shake off their shame, while they themselves know not how to blush; likewise by the temptation of conscience, by which it can happen that one is vexed by this scruple, and by the possible necessity which those outside impose." (Hodos. Phaen. I. p. 20. sq.), Cf. Lutherus Opp. T. XIX, 1238. VI, 2,68. sq.

Huelsemannus: "Just as the ancients, both Jews and Christians, demonstrated from these principles that the one God is the true God, and that the gods of the Gentiles are not true, because they are subject either to composition or fragility or vices and crimes; for their parents, birth, death, parricides, adulteries, etc., are known, as can be seen also from some places of Scripture, Deut. 32, 17. 18. 31. 32. Isa. 40—47. Jer. 10, 3. 4. 5. sq. 11. 12. sq. . .: — so from the same principles it can and must be demonstrated which word is divine."

For although they do not themselves generate the divine faith that is to be yielded to Holy Scripture, they nevertheless provide not a null, but an excellent use, namely, that contempt and rash judgments concerning a doctrine not sufficiently known may be restrained, and that men’s minds, having a certain opinionative or human faith already ingrained in them concerning the divine origin of Scripture, may be prepared and led to read and meditate upon Holy Scripture with zeal and a desire to learn, so that, with obstacles removed, Scripture itself, with the concurrence of God, may further produce the divine faith that is to be yielded to it; as will be evident from what follows. §

18. Internal arguments occur, on the one hand, from the material or the style, and on the other hand, from the formal or the θεόπνευστος (God-breathed) sense and the things signified. See Musaeus, *Introd.* P. II. Chap. V. § I. sqq. p. 305. §

19. To the former class belongs the simplicity of the style, a) joined with a gravity worthy of God alone; b) and the fact that things to be believed and done are not rarely proposed c) expressly under the name of God Himself. Not as if the diction were confused and mixed, without connection and order of words and things (which is entirely false), but because Scripture does not use the allurements of words and the paint of secular eloquence, adapted to captivate minds. Namely, that those things which are to be believed, even if most sublime and difficult, are nevertheless proposed without demonstrations, through bare assertions; and those things which are to be done or omitted, even if they themselves are arduous and burdensome, are nevertheless proposed as if by authority, and by commanding or prohibiting even to all men, including those who have no superior on earth. Musaeus, *l. c.*

Or that such formulas of words occur, by which God is introduced as speaking or testifying that it is He Himself who, through His ministers, e.g., the prophets, declares this or that. For although, insofar as God Himself, just as He joins His power with others, so also joins His power with this part or doctrine of Holy Scripture and works effectively in the human soul, not so much a human faith as a divine one arises; which the blessed Musaeus also acknowledges in *Quaest. de Syncr. et Scr.* L. I. Q. I. § 7. p. 84 and 195. Cf. *Detailed Explanation* [Ausführl. Erklärung] page 40. Yet when the argument is viewed precisely, insofar as it pertains to style and formulas of speaking, it must be admitted that it can happen and often does happen that even false prophets and seducers bring forth such sayings: whence also the blessed Joh. Schroeder in *Opusc. de principio theol.* Sect. I. Q. VII. η. 1. warns that this argument alone ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

to be of those from which, when taken individually, it is not easy to conclude what is plain. And the blessed Joh. Mueller in *Atheis*, dev. P. I. cap. III. num. 3. p. 110, 111, and likewise the blessed Huelsemann in *Comm. ad Jerem.* cap. I. aphor. III. theor. p. 42, agree. Meanwhile, this also remains certain and contributes not a little to rendering the divine origin of the Scriptures credible: that when it cannot be presumed from elsewhere regarding the authors of Scripture (e.g., that they are infamous or suspect persons, or from the underlying subject matter, or from a lack of fulfillment of predictions, etc.) that they spoke falsely or deceitfully; it is indeed entirely consistent that the Scripture, which with such assertion refers to God as its author, is not a human invention, but the true word of God Himself. Cf. Mus. *Introd.* l. c. p. 309. § 20.

To the latter class of internal arguments belong those which are sought from the properties of any writing, if, with natural reason itself as judge, it is to be considered as having been divinely destined for instructing men unto salvation; such as are: a) the truth of the assertions without any admixture of errors, b) holiness, c) perfect sufficiency, excluding all things that are dishonest or indecorous, of those things which are proposed as to be believed or done by those tending toward salvation. See Mus. *Introd.* l. c. § 6, 7, pag. 317, 318. And the blessed Huelsem. *Praei. in F. C.* A. I. c. II. § 4, p. 216, 217.

Indeed, as far as the matter pertains, those things which are proposed by others in such a way that they are referred to the truly divine perfections of the Author of Scripture Himself return to the same point: e.g., to the veracity, holiness, wisdom, and perfectly plain goodness of the Author of Scripture, insofar as these shine forth from Scripture itself; which will not be difficult to see once a comparison has been made.

For just as a true knowledge of God, and of those things which pertain to His worship, is required of men who are to attain eternal salvation: so also, for Scripture or doctrine divinely granted for the salutary instruction of men, the very light of nature requires the truth of dogmas pure from every error. Namely, just as a holy life, or one to be instituted in conformity with divine laws, is required of men to be saved: so it is necessary that Scripture, destined for true religion and the salvation of men, be holy, so that it may deliver those things which pertain to the holiness of life in such a way that it puts forth nothing base or alien to what is honest and decorous. For otherwise, unless all things necessary for men to be saved to believe and to do are delivered in such a Scripture without defect, the Scripture itself will be able to lead no one to salvation.

PROLEGOMENA, CHAPTER II. § 21. The truth of Scripture is proven partly by an induction of all the dogmas which are delivered in it for the sake of salvation, and which can either be known from the very light of nature, or exceed the light of nature, none of which can be convicted of falsehood; partly from the consensus of the books of the Old and New Testaments and all their parts among themselves; and partly by comparing the prophecies of contingent future events—especially such as depend precisely upon the free will of God and men—with the event or fulfillment that corresponds accurately to them. See the blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., § 8, p. 319.

For these things, e.g., concerning God and His essence, attributes, providence, worship, and the life to be rightly ordered according to the will of God, are delivered in the Scriptures not only in complete agreement with right reason, but also more simply, more certainly, and sometimes more perfectly than they could be known by reason left to itself in this corrupt state of nature. Whence it is evident not only that the truth of Scripture regarding these very dogmas is manifest—and indeed such that it argues God, whose perfection immensely surpasses the power of human nature and reason, to be its author—but also an argument arises by which it may be concluded that this Scripture is likewise true and proceeded from God in other matters which it delivers and which exceed the light of nature. Musaeus, loc. cit., § 11, p. 321-322, and § 14, p. 334.

J. G. Hamann: "Reason must content itself with the judgment of that philosopher regarding the writings of Heraclitus: What I understand is excellent; I therefore conclude the same regarding that which I do not understand." (Works, I, 63.)

And of these, some indeed fall under the light of nature according to a certain generic reason, but exceed it according to their specific reason: e.g., concerning the creation of this universe and of the first humans, concerning the state of man both in integrity and in corruption, and concerning the ultimate end or blessedness of man; these not only do not truly oppose the light of nature, but also, when they are known from the revelation contained in the Scriptures, they can be known to perfect our natural cognition and to supply its defect, as if by a certain more sublime cognition being added, under the guidance of the light of nature itself. Whence it may again be concluded that Scripture is not only true in such matters, but also entirely worthy of God as its author, and indeed to be attributed not to men, but to God who reveals. See Musaeus, loc. cit., § 12, p. 324 sqq., and § 15, p. 336 sqq.

Latin:

17. Argumenta, quae divinam Scripturae originem humana fide agnoscendam, seu credibilem, declarant, a alia interna sunt, sive ex intrinseca Scripturae natura ac proprietatibus ejus desumta; alia externa, seu extra Scripturam aliunde desumta.

Quenstedtius: ,,Tentati non quidem eodem cum infidelibus censu habendi sunt, cum scintillam fidei ceu linum fumigans adhuc retineant; quia tamen nullum saepe aut exiguum sensum pristinae cognitionis de auctoritate Scripturae habent, agendum omnino cum illis de hoc capite est, ut supra ex b. Hunnio observavimus. Obdurati vero, si corrigibiles et sanabiles, iisdem argumentis, quibus infideles, constringendi sunt; cum hic pari passu ambulent, qui fidem nunquam habuerunt et qui semel acceptam amiserunt; si fuerint incorrigibiles et insanabiles, sibi et judicio divino relinquendi sunt. . . Objicitur: Si proprie et principaliter verbo divino propter seipsum creditur, frustra ei fides per alia argumenta conciliatur. Resp.: N. V. C. Sicut enim olim, cum miracula adhuc fierent, ideo ea edebantur, ut homines increduli ad fidem perducerentur, etsi etiam sine illis credi poterat nec propter miracula illa proprie et principaliter credendum erat: ita et hodie, cum miracula fleri desierunt, homines infideles recte per argumenta illa caetera ad fidem manuducuntur, utut etiam sine illis verbo nudo praedicato credi possit et saepe credatur.“ (L. c. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 9. f. 146. sq.)

Dannhauerus: ,,Incidimus hic in quaestionem: Unde scis, Evangelium e. g. Matthaei esse Matthaei? epistolam ad Romanos esse d. Pauli ΰεόπνενστον ΰεοττνενστως scriptam? — quaestionem sci. inter Christianos de jure non audiendam, gravissimo Augustini judicio, homine ethnico, quam Christiano digniorem, extortam tamen adversariorum impudentia, incautos hoc laqueo captantium ac ruborem, cum erubescere ipsi nesciant, excutere conantium; conscientiae itidem tentatione, qua fieri potest, ut hoc scrupulo vexetur, ac possibili, quam imponunt ol έξω, necessitate.“ (Hodos. Phaen. I. p. 20. sq.), Cf. Lutherus Opp. T. XIX, 1238. VI, 2,68. sq.

Huelsemannus: „Quemadmodum antiqui, cum Judaei tum Christiani, ex his principiis demonstrarunt, 2?e«m solum esse Deum verum, deos gentilium non esse veros, quia obnoxii §int vel compositioni vel fragilitati vel vitiis et flagitiis; sciri namque ipsorum parentes, ortum, occasum, parricidia, adulteria etc., ut videre est etiam ex aliquot Scripturae locis, Deut. 32, 17. 18. 31. 32. Jes. 40—47. Jerem. 10, 3. 4. 5. sq. 11. 12. sq. . .: — ita ex iisdem principiis demonstrari potest et debet, quodnam verbum sit divinum.“

Quanquam enim divinam fidem Scripturae sacrae praebendam ipsa non gignant, non tamen nullum, sed egregium praebent usum, videlicet ut contemtus et temeraria judicia de doctrina non satis cognita coerceantur, ac potius ingenerata animis hominum opinativa quadam, vel fidei humanae notitia de divina Scripturae origine praeparentur illi atque inducantur ad Scripturam s. cum studio et desiderio discendi legendam ac meditandam, ut, remotis obstaculis, Scriptura ipsa porro cum concursu Dei fidem divinam sibi praebendam producat; prout ex sequentibus patebit.§

18. Interna argumenta alia ex parte materialis seu styli, alia ex parte formalis seu sensus θεόπνευστου et rerum significatarum occurrunt. Vid. Mus. Introd. P. II. Cap. V. S. I. sqq. p. 305. §

19. Ad priorem classem pertinet styli simplicitas, a conjuncta cum gravitate solo Deo digna; b quodque non raro expresse sub ipsius Dei nomine c proponuntur credenda atque agenda. Non, quasi dictio confusa et commixta sit, sine connexione et ordine verborum ac rerum (quod omnino falsum est), sed quia Scriptura non utitur verborum lenociniis et fuco eloquentiae secularis, ad captandos animos accommodato. Scilicet quod quae credenda sunt, etsi maxime sublimia ac difficilia, tamen sme demonstrationibus per nudas assertiones quaeque agenda aut omittenda sunt, etsi et ipsa ardua ac molesta, tamen velut pro auctoritate et hominibus quidem omnibus, etiam illis, qui superiorem m terris neminem habent, praecipiendo aut prohibendo proponuntur. Mus. l. c.

Seu quod tales occurrunt verborum formulae, quibus Deus introducitur loqui aut testificari, seipsum esse, qui per ministros suos, v. g. prophetas, hoc aut illud enuntiet. Quamvis enim, quatenus Deus ipse, sicut cum aliis, ita et cum hac parte seu doctrina Scripturae sacrae virtutem suam conjungens efficaciter in hominis animo operatur, non tam fides humana, quam divina oriatur; quod etiam agnoscit b. Mus. in Quaest. de Syncr. et Scr. L. I. Q. I. § 7. p. 84. et 195. Conf. Ausführl. Erklärung pag. 40. Quando tamen argumentum spectatur praecise, quatenus ad stylum et formulas loquendi pertinet, fatendum est, fieri posse ac solere, ut etiam pseudoprophetae ac, seductores talia dicta proferant: unde et b. Joh. Schroederus in Opusc. de principio theol. Sect. I. Q. VII. η. 1. monet argumentum hoc unum DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

ex illis esse, ex quibus sigillatim sumtis non proclive sit concludere, quod planum est. Et b. Joh. MueUerus Atheis, dev. P. I. cap. III. num. 3. p. 110. 111. itemque b. Huelsemannus in Comm. ad Jerem. cap. I. aphor. III. theor. p. 42. consentiunt. Interim et hoc certum manet et ad credibilem reddendam Scripturarum originem divinam non parum facit, quod, quando de conditoribus Scripturae aliunde (v. g. quod personae infames sint aut suspectae, vel ex materia substrata, vel ex defectu complementi praedictionum etc.) praesumi non potest, quod falso aut fallaciter locuti fuerint; utique vero prorsus consentaneum sit, Scripturam eam, quae cum tanta asseveratione Deum auctorem refert, non esse hominum inventum, sed verum Dei ipsius verbum. Conf. Mus. Introd. l. c. p. 309. § 20.

Ad posteriorem classem internorum argumentorum pertinent ea, quae petuntur a proprietatibus alicujus scripturae, si quam hominibus ad salutem instruendis divinitus destinatam esse, vel ipsa naturali ratione judice existimandum sit, quales a sunt: veritas assertionum sine admixtis erroribus, b sanctitas c perfecta, exclusis omnibus, quae inhonesta aut indecora sunt, sufficientia d eorum, quae tanquam credenda aut agenda tendentibus ad salutem proponuntur. Vid. Mus. Introd. 1. c. § 6. 7. pag. 317. 318. Et b. Huelsem. Praei, in F. C. A. I. c. II. § 4. p. 216. 217.

Eodem vero, quantum ad rem attinet, redeunt, quae ab aliis ita proponuntur, ut referantur ad perfectiones ipsius auctoris Scripturae vere divinas: v. g. ad veracitatem, sanctitatem, sapientium et bonitatem plane perfectam auctoris Seripturae, quatenus hae ex ipsa Scriptura reluceant; quod facta collatione haud difficulter patebit.

Sicut enim ab hominibus ad salutem aeternam perventuris requiritur vera cognitio Dei, et quae ad cultum ejus pertinent: ita ad Scripturam seu doctrinam, hominibus salutariter informandis divinitus concessam, vel ipsum naturae lumen requirit veritatem dogmatum ab omni errore puram. Nempe sicut ab hominibus salvandis requiritur vita sancta, seu legibus divinis conformiter instituenda: ita Scripturam, verae religioni et saluti hominum destinatam, sanctam esse oportet, ut, quae ad sanctitatem vitae pertinent, ita tradat, ne quid turpe aut alienum ab honesto ac decoro ipsa proferat. Alias enim, nisi ea, quae creditu factuque hominibus salvandis sunt necessaria, in tali Scriptura tradantur omnia sine defectu, Scriptura ipsa ad salutem perducere poterit neminem.

21. Veritas Scripturae probatur a partim per inductionem omnium dogmatum, quae salutis causa in ea traduntur et vel ex ipso lumine naturae b cognosci possunt, vel lumen naturae excedunt, c quorum nullum falsitatis convinci potest; partim ex consensu d librorum veteris et novi testamenti omniumque partium inter se; partim collatis vaticiniis rerum futurarum contingentium, talium cumprimis, quae praecise ex Dei et hominum voluntate libera pendent, cum eventu e seu complemento accurate illis respondente. Vid. b. Mus. l. c. § 8. p. 319.

Haec enim, v. g. de Deo ejusque essentia, attributis, providentia, cultu ac vita juxta voluntatem Dei recte instituenda, traduntur in Scripturis non solum rectae rationi per omnia convenienter, verum etiam simplicius, certius et aliquando perfectius, quam pro hoc corrupto naturae statu per rationem sibi relictam cognosci possent. Unde non solum veritas Scripturae quoad haec ipsa dogmata patet, ac talis quidem, quae Deum, cujus perfectio vim naturae et rationis humanae immensum supergreditur, ejus auctorem arguit; verum etiam argumentum nascitur, quo colligatur, Scripturam hanc etiam in aliis, quae tradit quaeque lumen naturae excedunt, itidem veram atque a Deo profectam esse. Musaeus l. c. § 11. p. 321. 322. et § 14. p. 334.

J. Ge. Hamannus: „Die Vernunft muss sich mit dem Urtheile jenes Philosophen über des Heraklitus Schriften begnügen: Was ich versteife, ist vortrefflich; ich schliesse daher ebenso auf dasjenige, was ich nicht verstehe.“ (Werke, I, 63.)

Atque ex his alia quidem cadunt sub lumen naturae secundum genericam quandam rationem, excedunt vero illud secundum suam rationem specificam: v. g. de creatione hujus universi et primorum hominum, de statu hominum cum integritatis, tum corruptionis, de fine ultimo seu beatitudine hominis, quae non tantum lumini naturae revera non adversantur, verum etiam, quando cognita sunt ex revelatione in Scripturis comprehensa, naturalem nostram cognitionem perficere ipsiusque defectum, velut sublimiore quadam cognitione accedente, supplere, ductu luminis naturae ipsius cognosci possunt. Unde rursus colligere licet, non solum Scripturam in talibus esse veram, verum etiam Deo auctore omnino dignam, imo non hominibus, sed Deo revelanti tribuendam. Vide Musaeum l. c. § 12. p. 324. sqq. et § 15. p. 336. sqq.


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Others, however, simply exceed the light of nature

Others, however, simply exceed the light of nature: e.g., concerning the Trinity of the divine persons in one essence, concerning the incarnation and the two natures and the unity of the person of Christ, concerning the redemption of the human race through the passion and death of Christ, concerning justification through faith in Christ, concerning the resurrection of the dead, and concerning the intuitive and beatific vision of God— ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY,

tion of bodies, in which our blessedness is constituted, etc., which, by the very fact that they are commended as mysteries revealed by God for our salvation, deserve to be held as true and certain, not devised by man, but first known and committed to writing by God supernaturally revealing them; and they also argue that Scripture, in its remaining parts, and thus in its entirety, is true and perfect from God. Musaeus, blessed memory, l. c. § 16. p. 338 sqq.

For although these mysteries may seem to involve a contradiction to corrupt reason (that is, reason so following the lead of its own principles that it transfers to divine things, by a μετάβασιν εις άλλο γένος, matters that are not entirely, but perhaps only universally true in the sphere of natural things), it is nevertheless sufficient that a true contradiction (or, that the same thing be simultaneously affirmed and denied of the same thing, in the same respect, and at the same time) cannot be most evidently demonstrated in those mysteries. See Musaeus, blessed memory, l. c. p. 341 sqq.

Indeed, the fact that so many writers, most dissimilar in talent, education, and character, and some even separated by vast intervals of place and time, lacking the opportunity to communicate their thoughts to one another to be committed to writing, yet conspire so remarkably and everywhere in one opinion on a matter so grave and so sublime, concerning the religion and salvation of men, shows the truth of Scripture in such a way that it bids us look at one and the same author of the whole of Scripture, who inspired the concepts to be expressed in writing to each and all of them—in a word, God. Musaeus, l. c. § 16. p. 345.

For those more obscure or difficult passages that occur here and there and seem to conflict with others do not therefore truly conflict with them, but rather have long since been reconciled through the work of more learned interpreters. See Musaeus, l. c. p. 346 sqq.

For future contingencies of such a kind cannot be certainly and infallibly foreknown and predicted except by God, whose knowledge is infinite (as we shall see below in the Book on God); therefore, Holy Scripture, which is full of such prophecies confirmed by their outcome—for example, concerning those things that pertain to the coming of the Messiah and His circumstances, as well as the fates of the Jewish people, etc.—is known to be true in such a way that it must be believed to have proceeded from an omniscient and truthful God. Cf. Musaeus, blessed memory, l. c. § 18. p. 364 sqq. §

22. The holiness of Scripture is established by an induction of all the parts of true religion, by which man is ordered according to the will of God and His eternal law, both directly toward God, toward himself, and toward other men, and which are handed down in Holy Scripture more perfectly than elsewhere. See Musaeus, l. c. § 19. p. 368 sqq. See what we have just said at § 20, note c, and § 21, note b.

And thus it is simultaneously acknowledged that the most holy God is the author of that Scripture.

23. The sufficiency of Holy Scripture for salvation, given the preceding attributes, must certainly be admitted, unless it can be shown that there is something necessary for a man to believe or do for his salvation which is not contained therein. a

Meanwhile, this can be known even from the fact that Holy Scripture shows so clearly and perspicuously the method of reconciling sinful man with God, which no other religion or writing provides. b

And because no human being can know or teach all those things which are necessary for a man to know and do for his salvation, unless God reveals them (for we showed above in Chapter I, § 8, p. 17, that natural theology is insufficient): it further follows that the author of this Scripture, which suffices for salvation, is God. Cf. Musaeus, l. c., § 20, pp. 373 and 377.

For it presents a method of expiating sins through the sacrifice of a mediator, established by God Himself, which is truly admirable; the Gentiles, by ineptly imitating this through their own χαχοζηλίαν, confirm its excellence even while being unaware of it. Cf. Musaeus, l. c., pp. 374, 375, 376. §

24. Among the external arguments by which the divine origin of Scripture is proven, the first to occur is antiquity, a or the fact that Scripture, with respect to the doctrine of faith and morals, partly began with the very origin of the world, b and partly became known to the very first men shortly thereafter; c but with respect to the written words, it precedes the books of all the Gentiles in age. d

This could indeed be referred to the internal signs in its own way, insofar as the duration of a thing differs from the thing itself only in reason; here, however, it is viewed with regard to the time by which the duration of the thing is measured, and which is extrinsic to the duration of the thing itself. See Musaeus, l. c., Sect. II, § 1, p. 378.

If we look at that part of the doctrine which had to be known to man in the state of integrity, concerning God and His worship and concerning living a just and holy life, which was subsequently recorded in the Holy Scriptures. Musaeus, l. c.

Regarding those things which are necessary for a sinful man to know for his reconciliation with God, to which the πρωτευαγγέλων, Gen. 3:15, pertains. See Justin Martyr, Paraenes. ad Gentes, p. m. 18 sqq.; Tertullian, in Apolog., cap. XIX, pp. m. 711, 712; Eusebius, in Prooem. Chron.; Augustine, de C. D., Lib. XVIII, Cap. XXXIV, T. X. Opp., p. m. 233. Cf. Phil. Mornay, de Verit. Rel. Chr., Cap. XXIV, p. m. 405; S. Orosius, de V. R. Chr., L. I, § 15, 16, p. 26 sqq.; J. H. Ursinus, Exerc. de Zoroastre etc., where he also strives to prove that the writer of the very first books was Moses. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

Grotius: "Added to this is the undoubted antiquity of the writings of Moses, with which no other writing can compete; an argument for which is also this: that the Greeks, from whom all learning flowed to other nations, confess that they received their letters from elsewhere—letters which, among them, have neither a different order, nor name, nor even ancient form than the Syriac or Hebrew; just as the most ancient Attic laws, from which the Roman laws were later derived, trace their origin from the laws of Moses." (De Verit. rel. Christ. Ed. Koecheri. L. I. § 15. p. 26. sqq.) §

25; A second argument can be drawn from the men themselves who recorded Holy Scripture, both from their knowledge of the matters to be handed down, and from their sincere zeal for the truth, without any bias of parties or affections; whence it is not difficult to recognize that they are worthy of belief. For, in part, they recount histories of events that were either performed by them, or in their own time, and at which they were present, or even events of earlier times; and by the work itself they show that they were cognizant of all that they recount. In part, they propose dogmas knowable from the light of nature in such a way that you would marvel at the knowledge of them, by which they surpass others. Finally, in part, they expound things that exceed the grasp of reason, where you will perceive—no less, and indeed, if you consider that most of them were unlearned men, rude in letters, arts, and philosophy—that this knowledge is most excellent of all, and you will esteem it as having been bestowed divinely. Cf. Mus. l. c. § 12. p. 383. sqq., H. Grotius de V. R. Chr. L. III. § 5. p. m. 208.

Truly, it is so far from being the case that either fear of danger, or hope of gain or private advantage, could be said to have moved them either to write, or to conceal certain things while writing, or to express them otherwise than the matter itself required, that, on the contrary, the writings themselves testify that they did not learn to flatter others or curry favor, nor to conceal their own faults, nor to avoid hatreds, persecutions, and extreme dangers at the expense of the truth. See the blessed Mus. l. c. p. 387. sqq. and what is adduced from the blessed Aeg. Hunnius’ Tract. de majestate Scripturae, arg. 10. Add H. Grot. l. c. § 6. p. m. 210. Indeed, just as every falsehood proceeds either from ignorance or from an evil will, so knowledge and a zeal for the truth make a writer trustworthy. §

26. Added to this is a third argument taken from miracles, by which the sacred writers show both their own mission and the divine origin of the doctrines proposed by them. By this name are understood works or effects produced beyond the order of the whole created nature, and which can be produced only by divine power.

Regarding the miracles of Moses—that they were performed before the people, were numerous, remarkable, and committed to memory by the clearest testimonies, and finally, that they were truly divine and entirely alien to the deceptions of Satan—see the blessed Aegidius Hunnius, l. c., arg. 13, T. I. Opp., fol. 21, 22, 23. The case is the same for the miracles which the prophets, Christ Himself, and the apostles performed, or which, being divinely produced, demonstrate that their mission and doctrine proceeded from God, a wealth of which the sacred codex itself exhibits. See the same, arg. 14, and compare Musaeus, l. c., § 13, p. 391, sqq. That the miracles of Peter and others at the beginning of the New Testament also became known to the Gentiles, H. Grotius teaches in *de V. R. Chr.*, l. c., § 7, p. 212, 213. Indeed, God, by working miraculously, does not assist seducers in deceiving the minds of men, or in persuading them that they are divinely sent to teach and therefore ought to be heard, but rather assists those whom He Himself has truly sent to propose what is true and salutary. §

27. Fourthly, there follows the concordant and clearly unanimous testimony of the church diffused throughout the world, from the very times of the apostles, concerning the divine origin of the Scriptures. I speak of that assembly which acknowledges the θεοπνευστίαν of Scripture, and which at the same time constitutes the flower of the human race, and in which the fine arts, disciplines, and honest morals flourish more than anywhere else. For it is not credible that such an innumerable multitude of people, dispersed throughout the whole world and excelling others, could have conspired or been able to conspire in such a lie—namely, to hold these books, however much they may be abhorrent to the sense of the flesh and human φιλαυτία, in such high esteem, and to testify as if with one voice that they were written by divine inspiration, if, in fact, each of their authors had composed them by human study and judgment. Compare the blessed J. Schroeder, *de Princ. Theol.*, Cap. I, n. 12 and 14; the blessed Musaeus, l. c., § 4, p. 423, sqq. §

Latin:

Alia vero lumen naturae simpliciter excedunt: v. gr. de trinitate personarum divinarum in una essentia, de incarnatione deque duabus naturis et unitate personae Christi, de redemtione generis humani per Christi passionem et mortem, de justificatione per fidem in Christum, de resurrectione mortuorum, de visione Dei intuitiva et clarificaDE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE,

tione corporum, in quibus beatitudo nostra sit constituta etc., quae hoc ipso, quod tanquam mysteria a Deo ad salutem nostram revelata commendantur, pro veris ac certis, neque ab homine excogitatis, sed Deo supernaturaliter revelante primum cognitis et in literas relatis, haberi merentur et Scripturam etiam in reliquis suis partibus, atque adeo totam, veram et a Deo perfectam esse arguunt. B. Musaeus l. c. § 16. p. 338. sqq.

Nam quamvis haec mysteria rationi corruptae (id est, suorum principiorum ductum ita sequenti, ut per μετάβασιν εις άλλο γένος ad res divinas transferat, quae non omnino, sed forte tantum in sphaera rerum naturalium universaliter vera sunt) contradictionem involvere videri possint, sufficit tamen, contradictionem veram in istis mysteriis (seu, quod idem simul affirmetur et negetur de eodem secundum idem et eodem tempore) evidentissime demonstrari non posse. Vid. b. Mus. l. c. p. 341. sqq.

Sane quod scriptores tam multi, ingenio, educatione, moribus dissimillimi, quidam etiam locorum ac temporum intervallis longissime sejuncti, deficiente occasione communicandi secum invicem animi sensa in literas referenda, tamen in materia tam gravi tamque sublimi, religionem ac salutem hominum attinente, in unam sententiam tam egregie et ubique conspirant, id verita-tem Scripturae sic ostendit, ut simul in unum et eundem totius Scripturae auctorem et conceptus scripto exprimendos singulis atque ommhus illis inspirantem, uno verbo, Deum, spectare juDeat. Musaeus l. c. § 16. p. 345.

Nam quae alicubi occurrunt et cum aliis pugnare videntur loca obscuriora aut difficiliora, non ideo revera cum illis pugnant ac potius pridem, interpretum eruditiorum opera, conciliata fuerunt. Vid. Mus. l. c. p. 346. sqq.

Nam futura contingentia ejusmodi certo et infallibiliter praesciri ac praedici nequeunt, nisi a Deo, cujus scientia infinita est (ut infra in L. de Deo videbimus); itaque Scripturam s., quae plena est talibus vaticiniis eventu comprobatis, v. g. de his, quae adventum Messiae ejusque circumstantias, item fata populi Judaici etc. attinent, ita esse veram cognoscitur, ut a Deo omniscio et verace profectam esse credendum sit. Conf. b. Mus. l. c. § 18. p. 364. sqq.§

22. Sanctitas Scripturae per inductionem omnium verae religionis partium, a quibus homo cum directe ad Deum, tum ad seipsum, tum ad homines alios juxta voluntatem Dei aeternamque ejus legem ordinatur, quaeque in Scriptura sacra perfectius, quam alibi, traduntur, b constat. c Vid. Mus. l. c. § 19. p. 368. sqq. Vid., quae modo diximus ad § 20. not. c. et § 21. not. b.

Atque ita simul agnoscitur, Deum sanctissimum esse ejus Scripturae auctorem.

23. Sufficientia Scripturae sacrae ad salutem, prioribus affectionibus stantibus, utique necessario admittenda est, nisi ostendi possit, aliquid creditu aut factu necessarium esse homini salvando, quod in illa non contineatur. a

Interim vero ea vel exinde cognosci potest, quod rationem reconciliandi hominis peccatoris cum Deo, quam nulla alia religio aut scriptura tradit, Scriptura sacra tam clare et perspicue monstrat. b

Et quia nemo hominum omnia illa, quae homini salvando scitu et factu sunt necessaria, nisi Deo revelante, nosse ac docere potest (nam et theologiam naturalem insufficientem esse, supra ostendimus cap. I. § 8. p. 17.): porro patet, Scripturae hujus, quae sufficit ad salutem, auctorem esse Deum. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 20. p. 373. et 377.

Exhibet enim rationem expiandi peccata per sacrificium mediatoris; a Deo ipso constituti, plane admirandam, quam gentiles per χαχοζηλίαν suam inepte imitantes hoc ipso praestantiam ejus vel imprudentes confirmant. Conf. Mus. 1. c. p. 374. 375. 376.§

24. Inter argumenta externa, quibus Scripturae divina origo probatur, primum occurrit antiquitas, a seu quod Scriptura ratione doctrinae fidei ac morum partim cum ipsa mundi origine b coepit, partim paulo post ipsis primis hominibus innotuit, c ratione vocum scriptarum vero omnium gentilium libros aetate d antecedit.

Quae quidem suo modo ad signa interna referri posset, quatenus duratio rei a re ipsa tantum ratione differt; hic tamen spectatur, habita ratione temporis, quo duratio rei mensuratur, quodque duratio rei ipsi extrinsecum est. Vid. Mus. l. c. Sect. II. § 1. p. 378.

Si spectemus eam doctrinae partem, quae praeciso statu peccati homini cognoscenda erat, de Deo et cultu mus deque vita juste et sancte degenda, quae deinceps relata est in s. Scripturas. Mus. l. c.

Quod attinet ea, quae homini peccatori cum Deo reconciliando sunt cognitu necessaria, quo spectat πρωτευαγγέλων, Gen. 3, 15. Vid. Justin. Martyr. Paraenes. ad Gentes p. m. 18. sqq., Tertullianus in Apolog. cap. XIX. p. m. 711. 712., Eusebius in Prooem. Chron., Augustinus de C. D. Lib. XVIII. Cap. XXXIV. T. X. Opp. p. m. 233. Conf. Phil. Mornaeum de Verit. Rel. Chr. Cap. XXIV. p. m. 405., S. Orotium de V. R. Chr. L. I. § 15. 16. p. 26. sqq., J. H. Ursinum Exerc. de Zoroastre etc., ubi etiam probare nititur, primi omnino libri scriptorem fuisse Mosen. DB PBINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

Gkotius: „Accedit indubitata scriptorum Mosis antiquitas, cui nullum aliud scriptum possit contendere; cuius argumentum et hoc est, quod Graeci, unde omnis ad alias gentes fluxit eruditio, literas se aliunde accepisse fatentur, quae apud ipsos literae et ordinem et nomen et ductum quoque veterem non alium habent, quam Syriacae sive Hebraicae; sicut et antiquissimae leges Atticae, unde et Eomanae postea desumptae sunt, ex legibus Mosis originem ductint.“ (De Verit. rel. Christ. Ed. Koecheri. L. I. § 15. p. 26. sqq.)§

25; Alterum argumentum desumi potest ab ipsorum hominum, qui Scripturam sacram consignarunt, cum notitia rerum tradendarum, a tum studio veritatis sincero, absque ullo partium aut affectuum b studio; unde illos fide dignos esse, haud difficulter agnoscitur. c Partim enim recensent historias rerum a se, vel suo tempore, et quibus ipsi interfuerunt, vel etiam anterioribus temporibus gestarum; omnium autem, quas recensent, sese gnaros fuisse, ipso opere ostendunt; partim dogmata e lumine naturae cognoscibilia sic proponunt, ut illorum cognitionem, qua alios superant, in ipsis mireris; partim denique exponunt, quae rationis captum excedunt, ubi non minus; imo si cogites, plerosque ex illis idiotas ac literarum, artium et sententiarum rudes fuisse, omnium maxime deprehendas ac tanquam divinitus collatam aestimes notitiam plane eximiam. Conf. Mus. 1. c. § 12. p. 383. sqq., H. Grotium de V. R. Chr. L. ΙΠ. § 5. p. m. 208.

Sane tantum abest, ut vel metus periculi, vel spes lucri aut commodi privati illos sive ad scribendum, sive ad quaedam inter scribendum dissimulanda aut aliter, quam res ipsa posceret, efferenda permovisse dici possit, ut potius ex adverso scripta ipsa testentur, quod nec adulari aliis aut gratiam captare, nec naevos suos ipsi dissimulare, neque odia, persecutiones et extrema pericula cum veritatis detrimento declinare didicerint. Vid. b. Mus. 1. c. p. 387. sqq. et quae ex b. Aeg. Hunnii Tract. de majestate Scripturae arg. 10. adducuntur. Adde H. Grot. l. c. § 6. p. m. 210. Nempe sicut omne falsum vel ab ignorantia, vel a mala voluntate proficiscitur, ita notitia et veritatis studium scriptorem άξιόχιστον faciunt.§

26. Accedit tertium argumentum a miraculis a petitum, quibus scriptores sacri et suam missionem b et doctrinas a se propositae originem divinam c ostendunt. Quo nomine intelliguntur opera aut effectus praeter ordinem totius naturae creatae producti, quique non nisi divina virtute produci possunt.

De miraculis Mosis, quod coram populo edita, multa, insignia ac liquidissimis testimoniis memoriae mandata, denique vere divina et a praestigiis satanae alienissima fuerint, vid. b. Aegid. Hunnius l. c. arg. 13. T. I. Opp. fol. 21. 22. 23. Par autem est ratio miraculorum, quae prophetae, Christus ipse et apostoli patrarunt, seu quae divinitus edita ipsorum missionem et doctrinam a Deo profectam ostendunt, quorum copiam ipse sacer codex exhibet. Vid. eund. arg. 14. et conf. Mus. l. c. § 13. p. 391. sqq. Quod autem miracula Petri et aliorum sub initium N. T. etiam gentilibus innotuerint, docet H. Grotius de V. R. Chr. 1. c. § 7. p. 212. 213. Nempe Deus miraculose operando non assistit seductoribus ad fallendos hominum animos, seu ut persuadeantur, eos esse divinitus ad docendum missos ideoque audiendos, sed his, quos tanquam vera et salutaria proposituros ipse revera misit.§

27. Sequitur quarto ecclesiae per orbem terrarum diffusae a jam inde ab apostolorum temporibus concors et plane consentiens testimonium b de origine Scripturarum divina. Coetus, inquam, illius, qui Scripturae θεοπνευστίαν agnoscit, simul autem florem generis humani constituit et in quo bonae artes ac disciplinae honestique mores magis, quam usquam alias, vigent. Neque enim credibile est, tam innumeram per totum orbem dispersam hominum prae aliis praestantium multitudinem in mendacium ejusmodi conspirasse aut conspirare potuisse, ut libros istos, quamlibet a carnis sensu et φιλαυτία humana abhorrentes, tanto in pretio haberent ac velut uno ore testarentur, divino afflatu fuisse scriptos, si tamen eos suus cujusque scriptor humano studio judicioque confecisset. Conf. b. J. Schroederum de Prine. Theol. Cap. I. n. 12. et 14., b. Mus. 1. c. § 4. p. 423. sqq.§


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Fifthly, one must specifically note the more than human constancy and strength…

28. Fifthly, one must specifically note the more than human constancy and strength of the martyrs—of both sexes and of every age and nation, conspicuous also for the praise of their innocence and holiness—in bearing witness to the truth and divine origin of that doctrine, even amidst the most grievous tortures, and in sealing it with their own blood and death. Indeed, these, although they were a part of the church, nevertheless bore a peculiar testimony to Christian doctrine, not merely verbal, but most especially real, provided by the occasion of the mirror of persecutions. Musaeus, l. c., § 5, p. 444, 445. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

For who would believe that so many and such diverse men, endowed with the use of reason and devoted to virtue, having neglected and as it were trampled underfoot all earthly things—honor, riches, family, and life itself—would have fought for the divine origin of that doctrine, not only individually but in throngs, and through the voluntary endurance of the most bitter evils from which they could easily have withdrawn themselves, unless they had been inwardly convinced in their souls by the very power of God that it was such, and had been sustained and confirmed in those evils? B. Mus. l. c. p. 445 sq. Cf. Schroeder l. c. n. 11, Grotius lib. II. de V. R. Chr. § 22. p. m. 196 sqq. § 29.

Added to this, sixth, is the so successful and sudden propagation of Christian doctrine throughout the whole world, and seventh, its admirable preservation amidst so many persecutions. Especially if you weigh those obstacles: partly on the part of those to be converted, who were already at that time entangled in other sacred rites and the cares of earthly things; partly on the part of the doctrine itself, which demands or foretells things that surpass the grasp of reason and are so difficult; partly on the part of the men proposing that doctrine, who were excellent neither in eloquence nor human wisdom, and were rather despised in the world; and finally, partly on the part of the adversaries, who were more powerful and more cunning: all of which seemed destined to hinder that propagation of the doctrine. Whence it is easy to recognize the divine power, which, being superior to all those impediments, took possession of the hearts of men and rendered them certain of the divine origin of that doctrine. Cf. Mus. l. c. § 6. p. 448, 449, Hunnius l. c. argum. 15. p. m. 33 sqq. Augustine: "Whoever still seeks miracles in order to believe is himself a great miracle, since, with the whole world believing, he does not believe." (De C. D. l. 22. c. 8.)

The reason for the preservation of the doctrine is nearly the same as for its propagation, and the divine power and efficacy must be acknowledged, both as regards producing and strengthening faith in the hearts of men, and also as regards restraining and beating back the assaults of so many and such great enemies without human force. Cf. Mus. l. c. § 7. p. 449 sqq., and Hunnius arg. 16. § 30. Nor should the testimonies of the remaining peoples of the earth be neglected, eighth, because, although they were strangers to those sacred things, they nevertheless bore witness—even unwittingly—to the deeds of the people of God and to the doctrine itself.

See what the blessed Hunnius recounts at greater length concerning the Gentiles, l. c. argum. 6. p. 39 sqq., and what the blessed Schroeder presents in his compendium, l. c. n. 15. Concerning the Jews also, the deeds of Christ, which were truly miraculous...

were, acknowledging them (although, with blasphemous audacity, they ascribe them to magic), and the Muhammadans, who celebrate Christ as a prophet sent by God and illustrious for miracles, can be seen to be the same. For it is relevant here that the pagan religion spontaneously failed as soon as human aids were lacking, and that certain dogmas of the Christian religion are read to have been approved by the wise men of the Gentiles themselves; indeed, those things which are found to be more difficult there are nevertheless superior to those things which the pagans hold as peculiar, and no less difficult to believe—nay, for the most part, absurd—and that they themselves imitate the sacred rites of the more ancient and truer religion through a certain κακοζηλία. See Grotius, Book IV, n. 10 and 12, pp. 282, 286; Hoornbeck, *De conversione Indorum et gentilium*.

The Jews, however, can be convinced not only from the Scripture of the Old Testament, which they retain, but also from their own traditions, that the Messiah has come and that he is Jesus of Nazareth, in whom, therefore, one must believe and by whose merit alone salvation is to be obtained. See Grotius, Book III, *De Veritate Religionis Christianae* (entire); Mornay, *De Veritate Religionis Christianae*, Ch. XXIX, XXX, XXXI; Hoornbeck, *Lib. de convertendis Judaeis*.

It is certain, however, that the Muhammadan religion is a certain hodgepodge conflated from diverse religions, which is overturned by itself and, upon comparison with the Christian religion, is forced to lower its banners. See Grotius, Book VI (entire).

Koran: "Remember how, when I spoke with Moses for forty nights, you idolized the calf, which we later forgave you, so that you might be grateful. We also gave the Scripture and the revelation to Moses as your guide. ... The believers, be they Jews, Christians, or Sabaeans (John-Christians), if they only believe in God, in the Last Day, and do what is right, then a reward will one day come to them from their Lord, and neither fear nor sadness will come upon them. ... Once we revealed the Scripture to Moses, let other messengers follow him, equipped Jesus, the son of Mary, with power of conviction, and gave him the Holy Spirit... They say: We want to know nothing until God himself speaks with us or shows us miracles. So spoke others before them already; truly, to those who wanted to believe, we have already given sufficient proofs." (Second Sura, ch.: The Cow.) — "

The Jews devised a ruse, but God outwitted them. For God said: I will let you, Jesus, die and raise you to me and free you from the unbelievers. ... Before God, Jesus is like Adam, whom He created from earth and said: 'Become!' and he became. This truth comes from God; therefore, be no doubter. ... It does not befit a man that God should give him Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood, and that he should then say to the people: Worship me and not God. ... Whoever adopts a religion other than Islam, God will not accept him; he belongs among the lost in that world. ... O you believers, do not be like the unbelievers who say of their brothers who travel about the land or go to war: 'Had they stayed at home with us, they would not have died and would not have been killed': God determined it so, to sadden their hearts." (Sura 3, ch.: The Family of Amram.) — "

Because they did not believe (in Jesus) and uttered great blasphemies against Mary, therefore we have cursed them. Furthermore, they have said: We have killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of God. But they did not kill him and did not crucify him, but rather another who was similar to him. ... God has raised him to Himself; for God is almighty and all-wise. But before their death, all the possessors of the Scripture will believe in him, but on the day of resurrection he will be a witness against them. ... Truly, we ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

have revealed ourselves to you, as we revealed ourselves to Noah and the prophets after him, and as we revealed ourselves to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, and Jacob and the tribes, to Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon. We also gave the Psalms to David. . . Verily, the Messiah Jesus, the son of Mary, is a messenger of God, and his word, which he cast into Mary, and his spirit. Believe, therefore, in God and his messenger, but say nothing of a Trinity. Avoid that, and it will be better for you. There is only one single God. Far be it from him that he should have a son. . . Christ is not too proud to refuse to be a servant of God.” (Sura 4. c.: The Women.) — “

Verily, they are unbelievers who say: God is Christ, the son of Mary. Say to them: Who could prevent God if he wished to destroy Christ, the son of Mary, together with his mother, together with all the inhabitants of the earth?. . . We let Jesus, the son of Mary, follow in the footsteps of the prophets, confirming the Torah which was in their hands, and gave him the Gospel, containing guidance and light, and confirmation of the Torah which was already in their hands, for the God-fearing as guidance and reminder. The possessors of the Gospel shall now judge therein according to the revelations of God; but whoever does not judge according to the revelations of God therein, he belongs to the evildoers. We have now also revealed to you the Book (the Koran) in truth, confirming the earlier scriptures which were in their hands, and appointed it as a guardian over them. Judge you now according to what God has revealed, and do not follow their desires, that you might depart from the truth which has come to you. To every people we give a religion and an open path (religious custom). . . O you Jesus, son of Mary, remember my grace toward you and your mother, I have equipped you with the Holy Spirit, so that you could speak to men already in the cradle, and also when you had grown up. . . You created with my will the shape of a bird out of clay; you breathed into it, and with my will it became a real bird; with my will you healed a man born blind and a leper, and with my will you brought the dead out of their graves.” (Sur. 5.) — “

They do not esteem God as highly as they should, because they say: God has never revealed anything to men. Say: Who then revealed the book which Moses brought to men as light and guidance, which you wrote on parchment, of which you publicly acknowledge some, but conceal the greatest part, and through which you learned what you and your fathers did not know? . . , The Creator of heaven and earth, how should he have a son, since he has no wife? . . . Whom God wishes to guide, he opens his breast for Islam; but whom he wishes to lead into error, his breast he wishes to narrow, as if he were about to climb up to heaven.” (Sur. 6.) — (The Koran. Translated word-for-word from the Arabic etc. by Dr. L. Ullmann. Crefeld 1840.) §

Latin:

28. Speciatim quinto notanda est martyrum a utriusque sexus variaeque aetatis ac gentis innumerabilium, innocentiae quoque et sanctitatis laude conspicuorum, in edendo vel inter gravissimos cruciatus ac suo sanguine et morte obsignando testimonio de doctrinae illius veritate atque origine divina constantia et robur plus quam humanum. b Nempe hi, quamvis pars ecclesiae, peculiare tamen testimonium de doctrina christiana tulerunt, non verbale tantum, sed maxime reale, occasione specmli ex persecutionibus praestita. Mus. l. c. § 5. p. 444. 445. DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

Quis enim crederet, homines istos tam multos tamque varios, rationis usu pollentes ac virtuti deditos, neglectis et velut conculcatis omnibus rebus terrenis, honore, opibus, familia, vita ipsa, singulos non solum, sed agminatim et per voluntariam tolerantiam acerbissimorum malorum, quibus se facile subducere potuissent, pro doctrinae illius divina origine adeo pugnaturos fuisse, nisi eam talem esse intime apud animum per ipsam Dei virtutem convicti et in malis istis sustentati et confirmati fuissent? B. Mus. 1. c. p. 445. sq. Conf. Schroederum l. c. n. 11., Qrotium lib. II. de V. R. Chr. § 22. p. m. 196. sqq.§ 29.

Accedunt sexto doctrinae christianae tam felix et subita per totum terrarum orbem propagatio a et septimo inter tot persecutiones admiranda conservatio. b Praesertim si expendas obstacula illa, cum ex parte luminum convertendorum, jam tunc aliis sacris eurisque terrenarum rerum implicitorum, tum ex parte ipsius doctrinae, rationis captum supergredientia tamque difficilia postulantis aut praenuntiantis, tum ex parte proponentium doctrinam illam hominum, nee facundia, nec sapientia humana excellentium, ac potius in mundo contemtorum, tum denique ex parte adversariarum potentiorum atque callidiorum: quae omnia propagationem illam doctrinae impeditura videbantur.
