Unde facile est agnoscere vim divinam, quae impedimentis illis omnibus superior corda hominum occupaverit ac de divina origine ejus doctrinae certos reddiderit. Conf. Mus. 1. c. § 6. p. 448. 449., Hunnium l. c. argum. 15. p. m. 33. sqq.Augustinus: „Quisquis adhuc prodigia inquirit, ut credat, magnum ipse prodigium est, cum, toto mundo credente, non credat.“ (De C. D. 1. 22. c. 8.)

Eadem prope ratio est conservationis, quae propagationis doctrinae, atque agnoscenda virtus et efficacia divina, cum quoad fidem in cordibus hominum producendam et roborandam, tum etiam quoad coercendos ac retundendos sine vi humana tot ac tantorum hostium insultus. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 7. p. 449. sqq, et Hunnium arg. 16.§ 30. Neque negligenda sunt octavo testimonia reliquorum orbis terrae populorum, quod, quamvis a sacris illis alieni, tamen rebus gestis populi Dei a atque ipsi doctrinae b vel imprudentes perhibuerunt.

Vid., quae de gentilibus prolixius recenset b. Hunmus l. c. argum. 6. p. 39. sqq., quaeque in compendio exhibet b. Schroederus l. c. n. 15. De Judaeis quoque, facta Christi, quae vere miraculosaBaieri Comp. ed. Walther. I. 9

erant, agnoscentibus (quamvis ea, blasphemo ausu, magiae adscribant), et Muhamedanis, Christum tanquam prophetam a Deo missum et miraculis clarum celebrantibus, iidem videri possunt. Huc enim pqrtinet, quod religio pagana sponte defecit, simul ac humana auxilia defuerunt, quodque christianae religionis quaedam dogmata ipsis gentilium sapientibus probata leguntur; ea vero, quae difficiliora illic deprehenduntur, praestant tamen his, quae pagani peculiaria, nec minus difficilia creditu, imo plerumque absurda, habent, quodque sacra religionis antiquioris et verioris ipsi per χαχαζ-ηλίαν quandam imitantur. Vid. Grotius Lib. IV. n. 10. et 12. p. 282. 286., Hoombeckius de conversione Indorum et gentilium.

Judaei vero non solum ex Scriptura V. T., quam retinent, verum etiam traditionibus suis convinci possunt, venisse Messiam eumque esse Jesum Nazarenum, in quem proinde credendum ejusque tantum merito consequenda sit salus. Vid. Grotius Lib. III. de V. R. Chr. integro, Mornaeus de V. R. Chr. Cap. XXIX. XXX. XXXI., Hoornbeck. Lib. de convertendis Judaeis.

Muhamedanam vero religionem constat farraginem quandam esse ex diversis religionibus conflatam, quae per se ipsam evertitur et, facta collatione cum christiana, fasces submittere cogitur. Vid. Grotius Lib. VI. integro.

Koranus: „Denket daran, wie ihr, als ich vierzig Nächte mit Moses mich besprach, das Kalb vergöttert habt, was wir später euch verziehen, damit ihr dankbar werdet. Auch geben wir dem Mose die Schrift und die Offenbarung zu euerer Richtschnur. . ... Die Gläubigen, seien es Juden, Christen oder Sabäer (Johannes-Christen), wenn sie nur glauben an Gott, an den jüngsten Tag und das Rechte thun, so wird einst ihnen Lohn von ihrem Herrn und weder Furcht noch Traurigkeit wird kommen über sie. . . Einst offenbarten wir Mose die Schrift, Messen ihm noch andere Boten folgen, rüsteten Jesus, den Sohn Mirjams, aus mit Ueberzeugungskraft und gaben ihm den heiligen Geist... Sie sagen: Wir wollen nichts wissen, bis Gott selbst mit uns redet, oder die Wunder uns zeiget. So sprachen auch Andere vor ihnen schon; wahrlich denen, welche glauben wollten, haben wir hinlängliche Beweise schon gegeben.“ (Surae secundae c.: Die Kuh.) — „

Die Juden ersannen eine List, allein Gott überlistete sie. Gott sprach nämlich: Ich will dich, Jesus, sterben lassen und dich zu mir erheben und dich von den Ungläubigen befreien. . . Vor Gott ist Jesus dem Adam gleich, den er aus Erde geschaffen und sprach: ,Werde!' und er ward. Diese Wahrheit kommt von Gott; sei daher kein Zweifler. . . Es geziemt dem Menschen nicht, dass Gott ihm sollte Schrift, Weisheit und Prophetenthum geben und darauf zu den Leuten sagen: Betet mich und nicht Gott an. . . Wer eine andere Religion, als den Islam, annimmt, dessen nimmt sich Gott nicht an, der gehört in jener Welt zu den Verlornen. . . O ihr Gläubige, seid nicht wie die Ungläubigen, welche von ihren Brüdern, die im Lande umherreisen oder in den Krieg gehen, sagen: ,Wären sie bei uns zu Hause geblieben, würden sie nicht gestorben und nicht getödtet worden sein': Gott bestimmte es so, um ihr Herz zu betrüben.“ (Surae 3, c.: Die Familie Amrams.) — „

Weil sie nicht (an Jesum) geglaubt und wider die Maria grosse Lästerungen ausgestossen, darum haben wir sie verflucht. Sie haben ferner gesagt: Wir haben den Messias, den Jesus, Sohn der·Maria, den Gesandten Gottes, getöd1tet. Sie haben ihn aber nichf getödtet und nicht gekreuzigt, sondern einen Andern, der ihm ähnlich war. . . Gott hat ihn zu sich erhoben; denn Gott ist allmächtig und allweise. Aber vor ihrem Tode werden die Schriftbesitzer alle an ihn glauben, aber am Auferstehungstage wird er Zeuge gegen sie sein. . , Wahrlich, wir DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

haben uns dir offenbaret, wie wir uns offenbaret haben dem Noah und den Propheten nach ihm, und wie wir uns offenbart haben dem Abraham, Ismael, Isaak und Jacob und den Stämmen, dem Jesus, Hiob, Jonas, Aaron und Salomon. Wir haben auch dem David die Psalmen eingegeben. . . Wahrlich, der Messias Jesus, der Sohn Marias, ist ein Gesandter Gottes, und sein Wort, das er in die Maria übergetragen, und sein Geist. Glaubet daher an Gott und seinen Gesandten, saget aber nichts von einer Dreiheit. Vermeidet das, und es wird besser um euch stehen. Es gibt nur Einen einzigen Gott. Fern von ihm, dass er einen Sohn habe. . . Christus ist nicht stolz, um nicht ein Diener Gottes sein zu wollen.“ (Surae 4. c.: Die Weiber.) — ,»

Wahrlich, das sind Ungläubige, welche sagen: Gott ist Christus, der Sohn Marias. Sage ihnen: Wer könnte es Gott wehren, wenn er den Christus, den Sohn Marias, sammt seiner Mutter, sammt allen Erdbewohnern vertilgen wollte?. . . Wir haben Jesus, den Sohn der Maria, in die Fussstapfen der Propheten folgen lassen, bestätigend die Thora, welche in ihren Händen war, und gaben ihm das Evangelium, enthaltend Leitung und Licht, und Bestätigung der Thora, welche bereits in ihren Händen war, den Gottesfürchtigen zur Leitung und Erinnerung. Die Besitzer des Evangeliums sollen nun nach den Offenbarungen Gottes darin urtheilen; wer aber nicht nach den Offenbarungen Gottes darin urtheilt, der gehört zu den Frevlern. Wir haben nun auch dir das Buch (den Koran) in Wahrheit geoffenbank, die frühem Schriften, welche in ihren Händen, bestätigend, und zum Wächter darüber eingesetzt. Urtheile du nun nach dem, was Gott geoffenbart, und folge durchaus nicht ihrem Verlangen, dass du abgehest von der Wahrheit, welche dir geworden. Einem jeden Volke geben wir eine Religion und einen offenen Weg (religiösen Gebrauch). . . O du Jesus, Sohn der Maria, gedenke meiner Gnade gegen dich und deine Mutter, ich habe dich ausgerüstet mit dem heiligen Geiste, auf dass du schon in der Wiege, und auch als du herangewachsen, zu den Menschen reden könntest. . . Du schufst mit meinem Willen die Gestalt eines Vogels aus Thon; du hauchtest in ihn, und mit meinem Willen ward er ein wirklicher Vogel; mit meinem Willen heiltest du einen Blindgebomen und einen Aussätzigen, und mit meinem Willen brachtest du die Todten aus ihren Gräbern.“ (Sur. 5.) — „

Sie schätzen Gott nicht so hoch, wie sie sollten, weil sie sagen: Gott habe Menschen nie etwas geoffenbart. Sprich: Wer hat denn das Buch geoffenbart. welches Moses als Licht und Leitung den Menschen gebracht, welches ihr auf Pergament geschrieben, wovon ihr Einiges öffentlich bekennet, aber den grössten Theil verheimlichet, und wodurch ihr lerntet, was ihr und eure Väter nicht gewusst? . . , Der Schöpfer des Himmels und der Erde, wie sollte er einen Sohn haben, da er ja keine Frau hat? . . . Wen Gott leiten will, dem öffnet er die Brust, für den Islam; wen er aber in den Irrthum fuhren will, dessen Brust will er so verengen, als wolle er zum Himmei hinaufsteigen.“ (Sur. 6.) — (Der Koran. Aus dem Arabischen wortgetreu übersetzt etc. von Dr. L. Ullmann. Crefeld 1840.) §


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Finally, examples of divine vengeance, manifest and wondrous against the…

31. Finally, examples of divine vengeance, manifest and wondrous against the persecutors and violators of this doctrine, also deserve to be reckoned as a ninth point.

Concerning which see Hunnius, arg. 21; Schroeder, no. 13. For these show that God wills that Scripture itself, as having proceeded from Him, be acknowledged and honored, since He punishes so severely those who act otherwise.

§32.

Divine faith, by which the divine origin of Holy Scripture is acknowledged as to its formal part (that is, its sense or doctrine), is generated at all times by the doctrine of Scripture itself, insofar as it is read with attention or proposed by the voice of a teacher, explained, and perceived by hearing. It does so, indeed, immediately of itself, but by a divine power which it always and indissolubly possesses joined to itself; and thus, with God concurring and exerting this power, it illuminates the intellect of man—or, having excited a holy thought congruent with the object, it inclines it to assent—and it entices and moves his will, so that it may command the intellect to grant assent to the doctrine itself (as contained in the Scriptures) as having proceeded from God; and thus it determines the intellect itself to assent under the aspect of divine revelation. For it is certainly required for the assent of divine faith, which is to be granted to revealed doctrines, that the very revelation of them be believed by divine faith. See Musaeus, *Introd.* P. II. cap. VI. § 2. p. 463 sqq. Namely, the concepts, produced long ago in the intellect of the sacred writers through the act of revelation, exist even today comprehended in the words of Scripture, and through the words of Scripture—whether by the voice of teachers or the reading of the Scriptures—transmitted to our intellect, they are similarly produced in us today, and move the intellect to a supernatural assent of their dependence upon God. See the blessed Musaeus, *l. c.* § 12. p. 468 sqq. Or, it is such that the ultimate reason for the assent of divine faith is the divine revelation itself as comprehended in the Scriptures, in which the assent rests, and is not resolved into another distinct revelation or any further reason for assenting whatsoever. Musaeus, *l. c.* § 2. p. 466. For divine revelation, or Holy Scripture, by itself alone, apart from the supernatural concurrence of God, is not a complete motivating reason for the intellect to grant a supernatural assent to itself or to its dependence upon God. For words, as such, and excluding all supernatural concurrence of God, cannot move the intellect further than to a simple apprehension of the things which they signify; but the things, represented to the intellect by the words of revelation, are in themselves non-evident even when they are apprehended; and although they may possess an outstanding goodness by which they might seem able to draw the will into consent and move it to command the intellect to assent, yet because the will, in relation to spiritual things, is by nature inept and as it were dead, therefore the will, lacking the supernatural concurrence of God, is not moved to command the intellect to assent. Musaeus, *l. c.* § 5. p. 481, 482. Reuschius: “Fechtius... calls the command of the will over the intellect a *οἰηρόξυλον* [wooden-headed/absurd notion] invented by the Scholastics. Generally, it is evident from these that other theologians think that it is repugnant to the nature of the soul for the will to command

ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY. 133 assent to the intellect, for they think experience teaches that assent depends upon the clarity of cognition, which the soul obtains through the cognitive faculty by the power of the characters perceived in objects and the reasons deduced from them. But since the blessed Musaeus was not so unskilled in psychology as to have pronounced that contrary to its principles, when it can be taken with reason, there will undoubtedly be another sense of Musaeus’s words than that which is alleged by the blessed Fechtius and others.” (Annotatt. etc. p. 89.) Cf. Apol. A. C. art. 4. p. 139. Musaeus: "It is well known that the logicians divide the *operationes mentis*, or the operations of the intellect, into the apprehension of simples, the composition and division of simples (i.e., judgment), and discourse. They call it the apprehension of simples when the intellect conceives a simple term, e.g., wood, stone, and affirms or denies nothing about it; to which is also referred the case when the intellect conceives and grasps an entire proposition, but *absque judicio* [without judgment], in such a way that it neither affirms nor denies it, which act of knowing we call the apprehension of simples, also in opposition to judgment. They call composition and division of simples, or judgment, that which occurs when the intellect joins together the simple terms apprehended through the copula 'is' and makes an affirmative or negative proposition out of them, such that it holds the same to be true or false. They call discourse that which occurs when the intellect infers and concludes something else from recognized and accepted principles... What we call by the school term (also known to beginners in logic) the 'apprehension of the simples of the things to be believed'—that is what theologians usually call the knowledge of the literal sense of the doctrine of faith and life." (Detailed Explanation of the Jena Theologians, pp. 344, 350.)

For although the authority of Scripture and its efficacy ought not to be confused, it is nevertheless certain that the latter is conjoined with the former insofar as the concurrence of God, or His power through which Scripture is efficacious, is required in order for the dependence of Scripture upon God to be recognized by the assent of faith. Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, p. 490. Concerning this conjunction of divine virtue with the divine Word, we shall see more below, where we must treat of the efficacy of Scripture. Indeed, otherwise the intellect of man, left to itself, when it fixes its thoughts upon sacred doctrine proposed to it in writing or by word of mouth and known by the force of the words through simple apprehension, and when it employs judgment to inquire into its truth or falsehood (human or divine origin), is rather inept, like a blind man, to judge rightly; nay, it is rather inclined to deny what is affirmed and to affirm what is denied therein: according to 1 Cor. 2:14. Therefore, in order that it may be inclined to judge more rightly and to grant assent, it stands in need of the concurrence of divine virtue. Cf. Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, § 8, pp. 492 ff., 509, 510. For, because spiritual objects are non-evident to us, it is necessary, in order to overcome the perverse judgments that are wont to arise on the part of the intellect and to provide an actual and supernatural assent to sacred doctrine, that the will (which otherwise follows the condition of the naturally corrupt intellect and is dead to spiritual things, or alienated from them, Eph. 2:1; Col. 2:13), being divinely excited, be drawn into consent, and that by its command the intellect be determined to assent (notwithstanding any doubts that may emerge here and there). Cf. Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, § 9, pp. 516 ff.

These things which we have said are proven, 1) from 1 Thess. 2:13, where Paul, cheerful in spirit and giving thanks to God, mentions that his hearers received the λόγον ἀκοῆς, the word of hearing, preached by him with a living voice and perceived by hearing, not as the word of men, but, as it is in truth, as the word of God, and thus acknowledged that that doctrine had proceeded from God; he adds, moreover, that this happened because God ένεργούμενος, effectively worked in them who believe, or because, by concurring supernaturally with the word, He testified that this is His word, and moved their minds to believe it with divine faith, as the word of God.

2) From 1 Cor. 2:4-5, where Paul says: My speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως, in demonstration of the Spirit and of power: that your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. For this is nothing other than that the doctrine delivered by Paul, while it did not move to assent through arguments drawn from human wisdom, nevertheless moved through the power of God and the Holy Spirit conjoined to it, and possessed the force of a most solid demonstration, so that, although it was full of non-evident mysteries, according to v. 7, it nevertheless made known its dependence upon the Holy Spirit, to be believed by divine faith, and effectively moved the minds of those people to the assent of faith. Cf. Musaeus, l. c. § 4, p. 475, 476.

How, moreover, when the Holy Spirit works a certain spiritual light in the intellect through the word, He simultaneously provides some impulse and holy motions in the will, is shown by the example of the converted: the Eunuch, Acts 8:36, 37, Lydia, ch. 16:14, and the hearers of Peter, ch. 2:37, by Musaeus, l. c. § 9, p. 522, 523.

Furthermore, it is to be noted here that by the same arguments by which the hearers were once persuaded to believe the apostolic preaching, we also are persuaded today to believe their writings; for they wrote the same things that they taught, says the blessed Gerhard, T. I. Loci Theologici, de Scriptura Sacra § 31. Indeed, the word of God preached by the apostles by divine inspiration and the Scriptures composed by divine inspiration do not differ, except accidentally, in that the former consists of words spoken aloud, the latter of words committed to writing. But in relation to the intellect of the believing man, the motive force for assent is one and the same for both. Musaeus, l. c. p. 476, § 33.

And this is indeed the sole argument by which divine faith concerning the divine origin of the doctrine contained in the Scriptures is engendered in individual men; although the use of arguments generating human faith perhaps has not been absent. But yet it must be confessed that, in order to convert others, those arguments are to be premised according to the common law; indeed, even in the case of temptation, they are not uselessly employed by the faithful themselves to remove certain difficulties; indeed, according to the condition of those persons, they are in a certain way necessary. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

To be sure, the remaining arguments indeed contribute to moving and persuading, as well as to convincing an adversary, but not to producing the persuasion [of faith], in such a way that they either kindle, foster, or sustain the full assurance of faith, by which, as if by a heavenly ray, all the mists of a soul debating with itself are dissipated. This assurance is a benefit of the Holy Spirit, who, as Augustine says, has a chair in heaven and teaches hearts from within; these are the words of the blessed Schroeder, l. c. no. 16, where he treats of the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit. Cf. the blessed Huelsemann, *Praei. in Form. Conc. Art. I. C. II. § 6. p. 217. 218.* and those whom he orders to be consulted besides Schroeder, the blessed Hunnius, *Comment. in 1 Cor. 2, 1.* and Meisner in the writings against the papists concerning the crime of calumny, Th. 25. 26.

Latin:

31. Denique etiam nono accenseri merentur exempla vindictae divinae a manifesta atque admiranda adversus persecutores et violatores hujus doctrinae. b

De quibus vid. Hunnius arg. 21., Schroederus num. 13. Haec enim ostendunt, Deum Scripturam ipsam, velut a se profectam, agnosci et coli velle, quando in illos, qui secus agunt, tam graviter animadvertit.

Π. §32.

Divinam fidem, qua Scripturae sacrae ex parte formalis (seu sensus aut doctrinae), divina origo a agnoscatur, doctrina ipsa Scripturae omni tempore b gignit, quatenus cum attentione lecta aut voce docentis proposita, explicata et auditu percepta, per se immediate c quidem, sed virtute d divina, quam sibi semper et indissolubiliter conjunctam e habet, adeoqüe, concurrente et virtutem hanc exserente Deo, intellectum quidem hominis illuminat, seu, excitata cogitatione sancta et objecto congrua, in assensum inclinat;f voluntatem vero ejus allicit ac movet, g ut intellectui assensum, sibi ipsi (doctrinae in Scripturis comprehensae) tanquam a Deo profectae praebendum imperet; et sic intellectum ipsum ad assentiendum sub ratione revelationis divinae determinet.h Utique enim ad assensum fidei divinae, doctrinis revelatis praebendum, requiritur, ut ipsa illarum revelatio fide divina credatur. Vid. Mus. Introd. P. II. cap. VI. § 2. p. 463. sqq. Nempe conceptus, per revelationis actum olim in sacrorum scriptorum intellectu producti, verbis Scripturae adhuc hodie comprehensi extant, et per verba Scripturae, sive docentium voce, sive Scripturarum lectione, ad nostrum intellectum transmissa, hodie in nobis similiter producuntur, moventque intellectum in assensum supernaturalem dependentiae suae a Deo. Vid. b. Mus. l. c. § 12. p. 468. sqq. Seu ita, ut ratio assentiendi fidei divinae ultima sit ipsa revelatio divina in Scripturis comprehensa, in qua sistat assensus, neque in aliam revelationem distinctam, aut qualemcunque rationem assentiendi ulteriorem resolvatur. Mus. l. c. § 2. p. 466. Nam revelatio divina, seu Scriptura sacra, per se sola citra supernaturalem Dei concursum, non est completa ratio motiva intellectus in sui, aut suae a Deo dependentiae assensum supernaturalem. Verba enim, ut talia, et praeciso omni concursu Dei supematurali, non possunt intellectum ulterius movere, quam ad simplicem rerum, quas significant, apprehensionem; res autem, verbis revelationis intellectui repraesentatae, etiam tunc, quando apprehenduntur, in se inevidentes sunt; et quamvis sua bonitate insigni polleant, qua voluntatem in consensum trahere et ad imperandum intellectui assensum movere videri possent: quia tamen voluntas, in ordine ad spiritualia, natura inepta ac velut mortua est, ideo voluntas, deficiente supematurali Dei concursu, non movetur ad imperandum intellectui assensum. Mus. l. c. § 5. p. 481. 482..Reuschius: „Fechtius ... imperium voluntatis in intellectum vocat οιόηρόξυλον a Scholasticis confictum. Generatim ex his patet, alios theologos existimare, quod naturae animae repugnet, voluntatem imperare

DE PRINCIPIO THE0LOGIAE. 133 adsensum intellectui, nam adsensüm a cognitionis claritate dependere, quam anima per facultatem cognoscitivam, vi characterum in objectis perceptorum atque rationum ex his deductarum, obtineat, docere putant experientiam. Sed quoniam b. Musaeus psychologiae non adeo imperitus fuit, ut ejus principiis contrarie illum pronuntiasse, cum ratione sumi queat, alius procul dubio sensus erit verborum Musaei, ac a b. Feehtio aliisque perhibetur.“ (Annotatt. etc. p. 89.) Cf. Apol. A. C. art. 4. p. 139. Musaeus: „Es ist. bekannt, dass die logici die operationes mentis oder die Wirkungen des Verstandes abtheilen in apprehensionem simplicium, in compositionem et divisionem simplicium s. judicium, et in discursum. Apprehensionem simplicium nennen sie, wenn der Verstand einen terminum simplicem concipirt, v. g. lignum, lapidem, und davon nichts afflrmirt oder negirt; wohin denn auch gezogen wird, wenn der Verstand eine ganze Proposition concipirt und fasset, aber absque judicio, so, dass er dieselbe weder bejahe, noch verneine, welchen actuni cognoscendi wir apprehensionem simplicem nennen, auch in oppositione ad judicium. Die compositionem et divisionem simplicium oder judicium nennen sie, wenn der Verstand die terminos simplices apprehensos durfeh die copulam,est‘ zusammenfüget und eine affirmativam oder negativam propositionem daraus machet, so dass er dieselbe für recht oder für falsch halte. Discursum nennen sie, wenn der Verstand aus den erkannten und angenommenen principiis etwas anders folgert und schleuset. . . Was wir mit dem (auch tyronibus logices bekannten) Schultermino,apprehensionem simplicem credendorum' nennen, — das pflegen sonst die Theologi cognitionem sensus literalis der Glaubens und Lebenslehre zu nennen.“ (Der Jenaischen Theologen ausführliche Erklärung, p. 344. 350.)

Quamvis enim auctoritas Scripturae et ejus efficacia confundi non debeant, certum tamen est, hanc cum illa eatenus conjungi, quatenus conclarsus Dei, seu potentiae ejus, per quam Scriptura efficax est, in ordine ad dependentiam Scripturae a Deo assensu fidei cognoscendam requiritur. Mus. l. c. p. 490. De hac autem virtutis divinae cum verbo divino conjunctione plura videbimus infra, ubi de efficacia Scripturae agendum erit. Nempe alias intellectus hominis sibi relictus, quando cogitationes suas in doctrinam sacram scripto aut viva voce sibi propositam et vi verborum simplici apprehensione cognitam defigit, adhibitoque judicio de ejus veritate aut falsitate (humana aut divina origine) disquirit; ineptus potius est, instar coeci, ad recte judicandum, imo inclinatus potius ad negandum, quae affirmantur, et affirmandum, quae illic negantur: juxta 1 Cor. 2, 14. Itaque, ut ad rectius judicandum assensumque commodandum inclinetur, divinae virtutis concursu indiget. Conf. Mus. 1. c. § 8. p. 492. sqq. 509. 510. Nam, quia objecta spiritualia nobis inevidentia sunt, ideo ad superanda, quae ex parte intellectus oboriri solent, judicia perversa et actualem eumque supernaturalem assensum doctrinae sacrae praebendum necessarium est, ut voluntas (quae alias conditionem intellectus natura corrupti sequitur et mortua est ad spiritualia, seu ab illis alienata, Ephes. 2, 1. Col 2, 13.), divinitus excitata, in consensum trahatur ejusque imperio intellectus (nihil quicquam obstantibus, quae hinc inde emergunt, dubitationibus) ad assensum determinetur. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 9. p. 516. sqq.

Probantur autem ea, quae diximus, 1) ex 1 Thess. 2, 13., ubi Paulus, hilaris animo et gratias agens Deo, memorat, quod auditores sui λόγον άχιη'ς, sermonem, a se viva voce praedicatum audituque perceptum, acceperint, non ut sermonem hominum, sed, sicut est revera, ut Dei sermonem, adeoque, doctrinam illam esse a Deo profectam, agnoverint; addit autem, id inde factum esse, quod Deus in ipsis, qui credunt, ένεργούμένος, efficaciter operatus fuerit, seu quod, supernaturaliter concurrendo cum verbo, testatus fuerit, hoc esse verbum suum, atque animos eorum ad credendum fide divina illi, tanquam Dei verbo, moverit.

2) ex 1 Cor. 2, 45., ubi Paulus dicit: Sermo meus et praedicatio mea non erat in persuasoriis humanae sapientiae verbis, Sed έν ά-αδέίςεί πνεύμαπος xai δυνάμεως, in ostensione Spiritus et virtutis: ut fides vestra non sit sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei. Hoc enim nihil aliud est, quam quod doctrina a Paulo tradita, cum non moveret ad assensum per argumenta ex sapientia humana depromta, moverit tamen per potentiam Dei et Spiritus S. sibi conjunctam et habuerit vim demonstrationis solidissimae, ita ut, quamvis plena esset mysteriis inevidentibus, juxta v. 7. suam tamen a Spiritu Sancto dependentiam, fide divina credendam, notam faceret et ad fidei assensum efficaciter moveret animos illorum. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 4. p. 475. 476.

Quomodo autem, cum Spiritus S. per verbum ex parte intellectus lucem quandam spiritualem operatur, simul ex parte voluntatis pulsum aliquem et motus sanctos praestet, exemplo conversorum: Eunuchi, Act. 8, 36. 37., Lydiae, cap. 16,14. et auditorum Petri, cap. 2, 37., ostendit Musaeus l. c. § 9. p. 522. 523.

Caeterum et hic notandum est, quod, quibus argumentis olim persuasi fuerunt auditores, ut crederent apostolicae praedicationi, iisdem argumentis etiam hodie persuadeamur, credere ipsorum scriptis; eadem enim, quae docuerunt, scripserunt, ait b. Gerh. T. I. LL. de Script. S. § 31. Nempe verbum Dei ab apostolis ex divina inspiratione praedicatum et Scripturae ex divina inspiratione concinnatae non differunt, nisi accidentaliter, in quantum illud verbis are prolatis, hae verbis scripto consignatis constant. In ordine autem ad intellectum hominis credentis una et eadem utriusque est vis motiva ad assensum. Mus. l. c. p. 476.§ 33.

Atque hoc quidem argumentum unicum a est, quo fides divina de divina origine doctrinae in Scripturis comprehensae singulis hominibus ingeneratur; licet argumentorum fidem humanam gignentium usus fortasse non b intercesserit. Sed tamen fatendum est, in ordine ad convertendos alios de lege communi praemittenda esse argumenta ista, c imo etiam in casu tentationis fidelibus ipsis ad removendas difficultates quasdam ea non inutiliter d adhiberi, imo, pro ratione status illorum, esse quodammodo necessaria. DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

Nempe reliqua, argumenta conducunt quidem, cum ad movendum et suadendum, tum ad convincendum adversarium, sed non ad persuadendum, ita ut vel accendant, vel foveant aut sustineant fidei diam plerophoriam, qua velut coelesti radio omnes nebulae animi secum disceptantis dissipantur. Quae plerophoria est beneficium Spiritus S., qui, ut loquitur Augustinus, cathedram in coelo habet et docet corda intus; verba sunt b. Schroederi l. c. num. 16., ubi agit de Testimonio Spiritus S. interno. Conf. b. Huelsem. Praei, in Form. Cone. Art. I. C. II. § 6. p. 217. 218. et quos ille praeter Schroederum consuli jubet, b. Hunnium Comment. in 1 Cor. 2,1. et Meisnerum in dica pontificiis scripta ob crimen calumniae, Th. 25. 26.


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: From this it is simultaneously evident how the argument taken from the efficacy…

From this it is simultaneously evident how the argument taken from the efficacy of Scripture, according to the diverse acceptance of the term, must now be referred to the class of those things which produce only human faith, and now, in truth, return to this one argument which produces divine faith.

Namely, insofar as we gather from the external and sensible acts of other men—e.g., the confession of the doctrine of faith, a holier life, and martyrdom itself—that these proceed from the very efficacy of Scripture, or that they argue for the efficacy of the doctrine which the Scriptures embrace in rousing, striking, kindling, and soothing souls: thus, in the judgment of the blessed Schroeder, l. c. and no. 9, this argument does not kindle divine faith, namely, before the intrinsic testimony of the Holy Spirit approaches, forming in the mind of individual believers this minor premise and conclusion: "This word contained in these books is such: Therefore it is divine"; these are the words of the blessed Huelsemann, l. c. Cf. the blessed Cundisius, *Not. ad Comp. Hutt. L. I. Q. IV. p. 22. 23.*

But when the efficacy of Scripture is viewed insofar as it exerts itself internally in the hearts of individuals through the spiritual acts of illumination, conversion, etc., then it is nothing other than that very testimony of the Holy Spirit, which He, through His concurrence with that doctrine, produces in the hearts of these men concerning the divine origin of this doctrine and works assent. And thus we said at § 32, note d, that the efficacy of Scripture concurs toward recognizing the dependence of Scripture upon God, which is required for the authority of Scripture. Cf. Musaeus, *Tr. de Syncr. et Scr. S. Q. I. L. de Scr. S. § 8. p. 185. et 196. sqq.* Likewise *Ausführl. Erklärung L. I. Q. V. p. 41. 42.*

Quenstedtius: "1 John 5:6: 'It is the Spirit who bears witness, because the Spirit is truth.' ... That the word 'Spirit' placed in the subject is properly taken for the third person of the Holy Trinity is beyond doubt; for immediately in v. 7, with the same attribution of μαρτυρία, He is called τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα. In the predicate, however, by 'Spirit' we understand metonymically the word of the Holy Spirit, the Gospel concerning Christ, which is the peculiar ἔργον and ὄργανον of the Holy Spirit, whence it is also called the ministry of the Spirit in 2 Cor. 3:6. This very Gospel, therefore, receives attestation concerning its truth from the testimony of the Holy Spirit, which He bears within our hearts. But that testimony (the words are of D. Dorscheus) 'flowing from the Holy Spirit through Scripture, from Scripture, and in Scripture, impressing His divine meanings and thus even insinuating Himself into individual men and creating faith in them concerning the majesty of the divine Scriptures, is by no means private, but is the very public and solemn testimony of divinity, the ordinary principle of attestation, one and the same Spirit in the church.' The Spirit testifies that the doctrine of the Holy Spirit is truth, i.e., most true, when He works internally in the hearts of men through the doctrine revealed by Himself and contained in the Scriptures, striking, drawing, and moving them so that they believe it to have proceeded from God or to be truly divine. Hence in v. 10 John adds: 'He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself.' Cf. 1 Cor. 2:11, 12; John 7:16, 17." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 9. f. 145.)

Andreas Knoesius: "Whoever reads or hears Scripture without morose resistance, and indeed with a mind desirous of truth, experiences this efficacy, which is a 'legitimate condition of the subject' that Christ describes in John 7:17, and which must be carefully noted... Most efficacious movements are excited in the heart, and indeed with a consciousness of their origin, such that a man is aware that he is moved in this way because of this or that divine truth recognized in his conscience. These movements are diverse according to the diversity of the subjects, affections, and other circumstances; sometimes they begin with sorrow, as the 'επανορθώσεις' (corrections) of Holy Scripture demonstrate their power, sometimes with joy, admiration, etc. These movements have a certain character of divinity so evident that for some time objections are almost silenced, nor does anything dare to protest in the mind, and a certain veneration of divine truth is produced in the intellect... Just as God has impressed upon His other works—from the sun down to the most contemptible worm and blade of grass—the traces of His attributes, by which divine works are known and distinguished from human ones without learned demonstration through the mere sense of a perfection greater than what they possess: so it cannot seem absurd to sound reason that we should posit that God willed that that book, which contains His special revelation, be distinguished from human writings in the same way... There is a very great difference between this testimony, which the regenerate experience in the state of grace, and that informative testimony of which we treat here, which pertains also to the ungodly, insofar as through prevenient grace it occasionally exerts itself in them and convinces them of the truth of the Word... Just as he who looks at the sun concludes that it is luminous from the very sense of light slipping into his eyes and affecting them: so the divinity of Holy Scripture is indubitably known from the sense of divinity latent within it; and therefore, he who proves the divinity of Scripture from its own divinity, i.e., from the sense of divinity, does not beg the question any more than he who proves that water is wet from the very sense of wetness, as Fechtius well teaches (Comp. theol. p. 34 sq.)... That objection is of no moment at all, which not only the most learned Michaelis but also the unlearned common people frequently urge, saying: 'I have read the Bible very often, and I have not experienced this efficacy of Scripture: therefore it has none.' For since the efficacy of Holy Scripture is ordered and resistible, as is evident from what has been said, it is wrongly concluded from a lack of personal experience that this most noble affection of Holy Scripture is absent. This consequence is of equal value to [arguing from] a lack of experience, just as in physics the falsity of a proposition could be said to be proven by a failed experiment, before it has been shown that the experiment was instituted exactly according to the rules. For we have long since warned that the legitimate condition of the subject is described by Christ in John 7:17." (Institutt. th. practicae. Stockholm 1768. 4. p. 66—71.)

Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between a circle and an apodictic or demonstrative regress. A circle, properly speaking, is when the proof returns in a circle and we proceed from the unknown to the equally unknown, or when the resolution is not made into something better known and more certain, but into something equally unknown. A demonstrative regress is when we proceed from a confused cognition to a distinct one. When we prove the authority and divinity of Holy Scripture from the intrinsic testimony of the Holy Spirit, and the testimony of the Holy Spirit from Holy Scripture, we do not commit a circle, but it is a demonstrative regress. For they differ as cause and effect; for the Holy Spirit primarily operates and effects such proof and sealing through the Word concerning the Word of God in the heart of the faithful, and this sealing in turn testifies of the Holy Spirit as an effect of its cause. Pesantius writes in Tom. II. fol. 467: 'a circle is committed only when the proof is made of the same thing by the same thing according to the same thing,' which does not happen in this proof of ours. Therefore, wrongly..."

The Papists falsely accuse us, as if we were committing a circle here, while we prove Holy Scripture from the testimony of the Holy Spirit, and the testimony of the Holy Spirit from Holy Scripture. For by this reasoning, there would also be a circle when Moses and the prophets prove Christ, and Christ proves Moses and the prophets, or even when John the Baptist testifies that Christ is the Messiah, and in turn Christ testifies that John the Baptist is a prophet, *Joh. 1; Luc. 7.* (L. c. f. 146.) See the example of Christian Gerson, a convert from Judaism, in Musaeus, *Tr. de Syncr. et Scr. S. Q. II. L. de Scr. § 24. p. 244.*

Musaeus: "Therefore, the testimony of the church is not necessarily required in order for the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit concerning the divine truth of the Scriptures to be able to exert itself in the hearts of men. Many examples of converts prove the same thing. Among others, Christian Gerson, a converted Jew, provides an illustrious example of this matter. In the history of his conversion, he relates that he often wondered what that error could be, so effective as to keep so many myriads of people in the superstition of the Christians. It happened one day that the books of the New Testament were given to him as a pledge by a woman in the vernacular language, and he read them, having taken the opportunity—not because he himself acknowledged any authority of the Christian church or thought there was anything true in them, but only to learn what the errors of the Christians were. However, he says that while reading, his mind was struck in such a way that he began to recognize the divinity and majesty of the books to a certain extent. Excited by a desire to learn, he read them again and compared them with the Scriptures of the Old Testament, and then such a light was kindled in his mind that he acknowledged the authority and divinity of the books with full faith and professed the Christian faith. Here, indeed, that internal testimony of the Holy Spirit exerted itself in the heart of the reader through the Scriptures read in the vernacular language, without any preceding testimony of the church, which he would have acknowledged." (*QQ. theolog. de Syncretismo et S. S. 1679. p. 244.*)

Melchior Adami: "Franciscus Junius († 1602), having been sent to Lyon as a youth, while he was reading Cicero’s books *De Legibus*, a certain man came to him and confirmed with many arguments those words of Epicurus: 'God cares for nothing, neither his own nor another’s.' This poison was so strengthened in him by the authority of the man and the subtlety of his sayings that his mind, clinging to that evil, became calloused. But God miraculously snatched him from that immense abyss of perdition after he had wallowed for more than a year in the most depraved delights. Recalled home by his father, who had learned that his son was imbued with such poison of ἀθεότης, and invited to the reading of the New Testament, he cast off that most pestilential opinion. But it is better to hear him confessing it himself: 'I open the New Testament,' he says, 'divinely offered to me; while I was occupied with other things, that most august first chapter of John the Evangelist and Apostle presents itself to me: *In the beginning was the Word.* I read a part of the chapter, and I am so moved while reading that I suddenly sensed the divinity of the subject matter and the majesty and authority of the writing, far surpassing all the rivers of human eloquence. My body shuddered, my mind was stunned, and it affected me for that whole day in such a way that I seemed uncertain to myself as to who I was. You remembered me, O my Lord God, in your immense mercy, and you received the lost sheep into your flock.' Thus Junius. From that time on, he began to treat all other things coldly, but those things which pertain to piety, fervently." (*Vitae German. theologor. etc. Francof, 1653. II, 194. sq.*)

Latin:

Unde simul patet, quomodo argumentum ab efficacia Scripturae desumtum, pro diversa acceptione vocis, nunc ad classem eorum, quae humanam tantum fidem gignunt, referendum sit, nunc vero ad hoc ipsum unum argumentum, quod fidem divinam gignit, redeat.

Nempe quatenus ex actibus externis et sensibilibus aliorum hominum, v. g. confessionis doctrinae fidei, vitae sanctioris ipsiusque martyrii, colligimus, proficisci illos ab ipsa Scripturae efficacia, seu arguere doctrinae, quam complectuntur Scripturae, in ciendis, percellendis, accendendis et demulcendis animis efficacitatem: sic, judice b. Schroedero l. c. et num. 9., argumentum hoc non accendit fidem divinam, nempe, antequam aecedit intrinsecum Spiritus Sancti testimonium, formans in mente singulorum fidelium hanc minorem et conclusionem: Hoc verbum his libris contentum est tale: Ergo est divinum; quae verba b. Huelsemanni sunt 1. c. Conf. b. Cundis. Not. ad Comp. Hutt. L. I. Q. IV. p. 22. 23.

Quando autem efficacia Scripturae spectatur, quatenus se interius in singulorum cordibus per actus spirituales illuminationis, conversionis etc. exserit; sic nihil aliud est, quam ipsum illud testimonium Spiritus Sancti, quod is per suum cum doctrina illa concursum de doctrinae hujus origine divina in horum hominum cordibus edit et assensum operatur. Et sic efficaciam Scripturae concurrere ad cognoscendam Scripturae a Deo dependentiam, quae ad auctoritatem Scripturae requiritur, diximus ad § 32. not. d. Conf. Mus. Tr. de Syncr. et Scr. S. Q. I. L. de Scr. S. § 8. p. 185. et 196. sqq. Item Ausführl. Erklärung L. I. Q. V. p. 41. 42.

Quenstedtius: „1 Joh. 5, 6.:,Spiritus est, qui testatur, quoniam Spiritus est veritas.' . . Vocem.Spiritus' in subjecto positam proprie sumi pro tertia persona SS. Trinitatis, extra dubium est; statim enim v. 7. cum eadem μαρτυρίας attributione vocatur το άγων πνεύμα. In praedicato vero per Spiritum metonymice intelligimus verbum Spiritus S. Evangelium de Christo, quod est peculiare έργον et δργανον Spiritus S., unde et ministerium Spiritus vocatur 2 Cor. 3, 6. Hoc ipsum itaque evangelium de veritate sua attestationem accipit ex Spiritus S. testimonio, quod is intus in cordibus nostris perhibet. Est autem illud testimonium (verba sunt D. Dorschei), ,a Spiritu S. per Scripturam et ex Scriptura et in Scriptura sensus suos divinos imprimente promanans adeoque sese singulis hominibus etiam insinuans illisque de divinarum Scripturarum majestate fidem faciens, nequaquam privatum, sed est ipsum publicum et solenne divinitatis testimonium, ordinarium testificationis principium, in ecclesia unus idemque Spiritus.* Testatur autem Spiritus, quod doctrina Spiritus S. sit veritas h. e. verissima, quando interius per doctrinam a se patefactam et in Scripturis comprehensam in hominum cordibus operatur, ea pulsat, trahit ac movet, ut, eam a PROLEGOM. CAP. Π. Deo profectam sive vere divinam esse, credant. Hinc v. 10. subjungit Johannes: ,Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet testimonium in seipso.' Cf. 1 Cor. 2, 11. 12. Joh. 7, 16. 17.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 9. f. 145.)

Andreas Knoesius: „Hanc efficaciam experitur, quicunque Scripturam sine repugnantia morosa adeoque cum animo veritatis cupido legit vel audit, quam «conditionem subjecti legitimam Christus Joh. 7, 17. describit, probe notandum. . . Excitantur in corde motus efficacissimi, et quidem cum conscientia originis, ita quidem, ut homo conscius sibi sit, quod propter hanc vel illam veritatem divinam in conscientia agnitam ita moveatur. Diversi sunt hi motus pro diversitate subjectorum, affectuum aliarumque circumstantiarum; interdum initium sumunt a dolore, uti 'επανορθώσεις s. Scripturae vim suam demonstrant, interdum a laetitia, admiratione etc. Hi motus characterem quendam divinitatis habent ita evidentem, ut per aliquod tempus objectiones fere sileant, nec in animo quidquam obstrepere audeat et veneratio quaedam divinae veritatis in mente producatur. . . Quemadmodum Deus caeteris operibus suis,-inde a sole usque ad contemtissimum vermem et gramen, ea impressit attributorum suorum vestigia, quibus opera divina esse cognoscuntur et ab humanis sine docta demonstratione distinguuntur per nudum sensum majoris, quam habent, perfectionis: ita sanae rationi absonum videri non potest, quod Deum voluisse statuamus, ut liber ille, qui specialem ejus revelationem continet, eodem modo a scriptis humanis internoscatur. . . Permagna est differentia inter hoc testimonium, quod regeniti in statu gratiae experiuntur, et informatorium illud, de quo heic agimus, quod impiis quoque competit, quatenus per gratiam praevenientem illud in iis sese subinde exserit eosque de veritate verbi convincit. . . Quemadmodum is, qui solem intuetur, lucidum esse ex ipso sensu lucis in oculos labentis eumque afficientis, colligit: ita ex sensu divinitatis in s. S. latentis divinitas ejus indubie cognoscitur; ideoque qui divinitatem Scripturae ex ipsa ejus divinitate h. e. divinitatis sensu probat, aeque non petit principium, ac ille non petit, qui aquam humidam esse probat ex ipso sensu humiditatis, ut bene docet Fechtius Comp. theol. p. 34. sq. . . Nullius plane momenti est objectio illa, quam non doctissimus solum Michaelis, sed et infleeta plebs saepenumero urget, dicens: ,Biblia persaepe legi, nec expertus sum hanc Scripturae efficaciam: ergo nullam habet.· Quum enim efficacia s. Scripturae sit ordinata et resistibilis, ut ex dictis constat, a defectu experientiae propriae male concluditur, quod nobilissima haec affectio Scripturae s. desit. Aequeparum haec consequentia valet a defectu experientiae, atque in physica ab experimento ^quodam male succedente falsitas propositionis evicta dici potest, antequam ostensum sit, experimentum exacte secundum regulas esse institutum. Etenim dudum monuimus, conditionem subjecti legitimam describi a Christo Joh. 7, 17.“ (Institutt. th. practicae. Holmiae 1768. 4. p. 66—71.)

Quenstedtius: „Dist. inter circulum, et regressum apodicticum seu demonstrativum. Circulus proprie est, quando probatio in orbem redit et ab ignoto ad aeque ignotum progredimur, sive quando resolutio non fit in notius et certius, sed in aeque ignotum. Begressus demonstrativus est, quando a cognitione confusa ad distinctam procedimus. Quando auctoritatem et divinitatem s. Scripturae ex testimonio intrinseco Spiritus S., et ex Scriptura s. testimonium Spiritus S. probamus, non committimus circulum, sed est regressus demonstrativus. Differunt enim tamquam causa et effectus; Spiritus S. enim primario operatur et efficit talem probationem et obsignationem per verbum de verbo Dei in corde fidelium, et haec obsignatio iterum testatur de Spiritu S. tamquam effectus de sua causa. Pesantius in Tom. II. fol. 467. scribit: ,tunc demum committi circulum, quando probatio flt ejusdem ab eodem secundum idem·, quod in hac nostra probatione non fit. Male ergo

nobis affingunt pontificii, . . ac si hic circulum committamus, dum ex testimonio Spiritus S. Scripturam sacram et ex Scriptura s. testimonium Spiritus S. probamus. Hac enim ratione etiam circulus esset, quando Moses et prophetae probant Christum, et Christus Mosen et prophetas, vel etiam, quando Johannes Baptista, Christum Messiam, et rursus Christus, Johannem Baptistam prophetam esse, 'testatur, *Joh. 1. Lue. 7.“ (L. c. f. 146.) Vid. exemplum Christiani Gersmis, ex Judaeo christiani, apud Musaeum Tr. de Syncr. et Scr. S. Q. II. L. de Scr. § 24. p. 244.

Musaeus: „Non ergo ecclesiae testificatio necessario requiritur ad hoc, ut internum Sp. Sancti testimonium de Scripturarum divina veritate in hominum cordibus se exserere possit. Idem evincunt exempla conversorum plurima. Inter alia illustre exemplum hanc in rem praebet Christianus Gerson, Judaeus conversus, qui in historia suae conversionis refert, se saepe miratum esse, quinam ille tam efficax error sit, ut tot myriades hominum in superstitione Christianorum detineat, et contigisse aliquando, ut libri N. T. a foemella in vernaculo idiomate sibi pignori darentur, a se autem, occasione inde sumta, legerentur, non quod Ullam ecclesiae Christianae auctoritatem ipse agnosceret aut aliquid veri iis inesse existimaret, sed tantum, ut, quinam Christianorum errores essent, cognosceret. Inter legendum autem, dicit, esse animum suum percussum, ut librorum divinitatem et majestatem quadantenus agnoscere inciperet, eosque desiderio discendi excitatus iterum legeret et cum Scripturis V. T. conferret, et tum esse in animo suo lucem tantam accensam, ut plena fide librorum auctoritatem et divinitatem agnosceret et fidem Christianam profiteretur. Hic sane testimonium illud internum Sp. Sancti exseruit se in legentis corde per Seripturas lingua vernacula lectas absque ulla praecedente ecclesiae testificatione, quae quidem ab ipso fuisset agnita.“ (QQ. theolog. de Syncretismo et S. S. 1679. p. 244.)

Melchior Adami: ,, Franciscus Junius († 1602.), Lugdunum adolescens missus, cum legeret Tullii de legibus libros, venit ad ipsum homo quidam et illa Epicuri verba: ,Nihil curare Deum nec sui, nec alieni·, multis confirmavit. Hoc venenum ita fuit in ipso corroboratum auctoritate hominis et argutiis dictorum, ut animus ejus in malo isto haerens occalluerit. Ex immani autem isto perditionis barathro mirifice ipsum eripuit Deus, postquam amplius annum perditissimis in deliciis jacuisset. A patre, qui resciverat filium, tali ά&εόττ/τος veneno imbutum, domum revocatus ac ad lectionem N. T. invitatus, pestilentissimam illam sententiam abjecit. Sed praestat audire ipsum de se confitente: ,Novum Testamentum·, inquit, ,divinitus oblatum aperio; aliud agenti exhibet se mihi adspectu primo augustissimum illud caput Johannis evangelistae et apostoli: In principio erat Verbum. Lego partem capitis, et ita commoveor legens, ut repente divinitatem argumenti et scripti majestatem auetoritatemque senserim, longo intervallo omnibus eloquentiae humanae fluminibus praeeuntem. Horrebat corpus, stupebat animus, et totum illum diem sic afficiebat, ut qui essem, ipse mihi incertus viderer esse. Recordatus es mei, Domine Deus mi, pro immensa misericordia tua, ovemque perditam in gregem tuum recepisti.' Haec Junius. Ab eo itaque tempore frigide alia omnia, fervide autem, quae ad pietatem faciunt, cepit tractare.“ (Vitae German, theologor. etc. Francof, 1653. II, 194. sq.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: See what we said in the note to § 17, and compare Gerhard, *L

See what we said in the note to § 17, and compare Gerhard, *L. I. de Scr. S. § 22*, where he warns that those who deny the authority of Scripture should not be told to wait until the Holy Spirit testifies immediately in their hearts concerning the authority of Scripture; but they should be led to the arguments...

ments, both external and internal. Add Munnius, *Treatise on the Majesty of Scripture*, at the beginning. Compare the note at § 17 of this place. Indeed, if the faithful begin to doubt the authority of Scripture during temptations, one must deal with them just as one deals with those who deny it. For doubt is next to denial, as are the words of the blessed Gerhard, *l. c.* § 20. §

34. The authority of Holy Scripture, or its normative authority, which it possesses not only in regard to the sense, but also in regard to the very words divinely inspired, or the original text, in relation to versions likewise consigned by human effort, and other writings and doctrines to be judged—insofar as it is viewed in itself and absolutely—is founded upon the veracity of God who inspires, and upon the dependence of Scripture upon God by reason of the words of the original text. Likewise, in relation to us, or in order that we may believe with divine faith that the books of Scripture, under the idiom in which they are exhibited to us—that is, in the selection, series, and context of words in a certain language—are divinely inspired, and thus possess that normative power or canonical dignity, the testimony of the church alone does not suffice; but here also the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, or His efficacious operation through Scripture itself, must concur.

Concerning which, see § 15 of this place. The word χανόνος, that is, of a norm or rule, which is properly mathematical, but is thence transferred to civil laws, military orders and stations, and also to the scales which merchants use to designate tongues (see the blessed Chemnitz, *Examination of the Council of Trent*, Part I, Section on Canonical Books, p. 81, 82; the blessed Cundisius, *on the Compendium of Hutter*, Book I, Q. III, p. 15, 16), occurs, according to a similar analogy, in the Scriptures themselves to designate a certain rule of faith and Christian actions, so that those things which agree with it may be admitted, while those that disagree may be rejected.

For thus in 2 Cor. 10:13, Paul says that he does not boast except χατά το μέτρον του χανόνος, according to the measure of the rule; and in Gal. 6:16, he prays for and promises peace and mercy to all δσοι τω χανόνι τούτω στοιχ-ήσουσιν, as many as shall walk according to this rule, as if in military order. And the same phrase recurs in Phil. 3:16.

Indeed, the doctrine of Scripture moves one to assent to itself as divine, through the concurrence of God, in whatever language it is proposed, and in whatever words, provided the doctrine itself, as it has been revealed, is sincerely proposed. But in order that the doctrine of faith and morals, which is proposed here or there as divine, may be recalled to the genuine norm, and its orthodoxy or truth, or its heterodoxy or falsehood, may be accurately known, one must have recourse to Scripture, which is infallible in regard to its words, and therefore to Scripture under that idiom where the words themselves ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

were used by divine inspiration, without the intervention of human and fallible judgment. Cf. Mus. l. c. p. 540. For some of those versions are truly liable to errors; and, even if there should occur some that are exactly congruent with the authentic text, they nevertheless depend upon the original text in the matter of certainty and truth; and thus they do not have authority until their agreement with the authentic text has been investigated and known. Mus. l. c. Hence, when our symbolical books are sometimes called by the name of a norm or of normative books, it is not understood as a norm absolutely so called, but *secundum quid* [in a certain respect], or with the addition of a secondary, regulated norm, that is, less properly so called. See the blessed Himmel, in F. C. disp. 1., Grauer, in A. C. P. I. p. 3. and Supplem. C. IV. p. 149.

Carpzovius: "The symbolical books are not written by the impulse of the θεόπνευστος [God-breathed], just as the biblical writers composed their canonical writings, nor by absolute necessity and because of the insufficiency of the biblical canon, as Bellarmine (l. 4. de verbo Dei c. 4.) desires in the biblical books, because a catechism is not contained in them; but they were written for another reason, namely, by a necessity which in the schools is called a necessity of expediency, so that, namely, the contentions of certain minds might be restrained, scandals among the weak might be prevented, and the craftiness and malice of heretics might be recognized... What is composed from Scripture and to and according to it, that is not a principle, but a principled thing [principiatum]. We must indeed confess that the symbolical books also come under the name of a norm in the preface on page 34, and that this name is attributed to the symbolical books of our church. But principle and norm are not taken by the authors of this preface simply and equally as synonyms. For even to that which is a principled thing, something can be directed and judged by convention and therefore merit the name of a norm. And in this way the word 'norm' is taken in this place (in the preface of the Book of Concord, p. 21) and among the writers of the primitive church, e.g., when the ecumenical symbols, and especially the Apostolic (so called *ἐξοικώς* and *ἐξαιρέτως* [outwardly and especially]), are called by the Fathers κανὼν τῆς ἀληθείας ἀκλινής, a canon of truth not in the least wavering (Iren. l. 1. c. 1. § 19.), 'an immovable and irreformable rule of faith' (Tertull.), 'a norm of preaching established in common through all nations' (Ruffin. and Vernant. Honor.), 'a certain rule of faith, through which believers may hold the catholic unity and refute heretical depravity' (Aug. serm. de temp. hom. 181.). And thus also the word 'norm' in the blessed place signifies nothing other than a principle of knowing, from which we are led into the knowledge of some conclusion or question about which there is controversy. Such a principle is also that which depends upon another and has been proven from elsewhere, as Aristotle shows (l. prior. analyt. c. 2. and 8). Therefore, the symbol is not a norm absolutely and simply, but in respect to certain churches, which presuppose its truth and certainty as proven from Scripture... Although it cannot be denied that by this nomenclature or encomium the nature of not only a discretive but also a definitive norm has been attributed to the symbolical books; yet they did this with the greatest discrimination and... held the symbolical books as nothing but secondary norms, after the manner of those postulates which, as they are in need of proof, are nevertheless proven elsewhere and are also admitted in a certain discipline as indubitable." (Isagoge in libros eccles. lutheranarum symbolicos. p. 5. 6. 27. 28.)

The same: "The authors of the Book of Concord do not deny that Scripture alone is the unique norm, to and according to which all dogmas are to be examined and judged, indeed they profess this in so many words..., nor do they deny that in their own way and sense these writings are also a norm... They attribute more to them than a mere manner of testifying... But when the symbolical book is called a norm and a form of doctrine, to and according to which, etc., then PROLEGOM. CAP. II. this is understood only in a qualified sense on account of a certain analogy, namely an external one, consisting in this, that even according to it something may be judged and estimated, although it is not the principle of that which is judged and estimated. And indeed 3. in the instituted question, it is not so much about the truth of the doctrine as about its reception, vigor, and approval in a certain church; whether this dogma, for example, the Flacian dogma concerning original sin, was ever received and approved in the Lutheran church? Whether the doctrine of Flacius agrees with the doctrine handed down and approved in the Lutheran church from the beginning of the Reformation? So that 4. a symbolical book may be called a norm not of faith itself, but of the profession of faith, 5. not of everything, but only regarding certain controversial chapters, and indeed as 6. it persists in certain churches. ... And thus our theologians have detracted nothing from our doctrine by a norm absolutely so called, nor have they equaled the symbolical book to it, but they have attributed to their symbolical book what the nature and reason of symbolical books demand, and they have declined to neither extreme here. To be sure, 1. they wished not only to testify concerning the apprehension of doctrine and faith, and how they publicly taught it as drawn from the Word of God, but also 2. furthermore to set bounds and limits to the lust for speaking and professing in our churches, within which those teaching ought especially to contain themselves, and 3. also to supply and constitute a norm according to which the writings of others could be judged, not whether they are true or false (for this must be judged from Scripture alone), but whether they agree with the doctrine received and handed down in the Lutheran church from the beginning, by which 4. the simple might be protected from the spurious writings of others disturbing the purity of the doctrine once received, and 5. the holy deposit of the pure doctrine of Luther might by this reason be transmitted to late posterity. Cf. p. 638.” (L. c. p. 1143—45.)

G. Walchius: “The primary norm is that which has the force of a norm by itself, that is, by its own proper virtue; the secondary, however, is that which is endowed with the virtue of a norm not by itself, but through the authority of Holy Scripture and its agreement with it, and hence depends upon the primary. ... Others, to whom these distinctions we have just recounted are displeasing, distinguish between a norm of decision and a norm of discretion. The former is that αὐτόπιστον and clearly infallible principle, in whose judgment both dissenting parties ought to acquiesce; the latter, however, or the norm of discretion, does not indeed define the controversial question, yet it distinguishes the orthodox from the heterodox and shows who are addicted to the purer doctrine. ... Wemsdorfius thinks that the symbols can be called a norm of cognition, so that they are some principle by whose benefit we may attain the knowledge of certain truths; but this seems to be referable solely to Scripture as the norm. ... If anyone considers these things, he will easily understand that the symbols are to be called a norm of cognition where cognition is referred not to the truth itself and its foundation, but to the profession. The symbols are a norm of cognition insofar as it is understood from them which dogmas are proper to a certain church. Therefore, when you ask whether this or that dogma is Lutheran, you must know this from the symbols, and then they are the norm of this cognition. But when you ask whether this or that dogma is true or false, that certainly is to be known not from the symbols as a norm, but from Holy Scripture.” (Introd. in libb. eccl. Luth. symb. p. 934—36.)

Latin:

Vid., quae diximus ad § 17. in nota, et conf. Gerh. L. I. de Scr. S. § 22., ubi monet, non esse jubendos eos, qui auctoritatem Scri|)turae negant, ut expectent, donec Spiritus S. in ipsorum cordibus iminediate de Scripturae auctoritate testetur; sed ducendos esse ad argu

PROLEttOM. CAP. II. menta, cum externa, tum interna. Add. Munnius Tr. de Maj. Scr. sub initium. Confer h. 1. § 17. notam. Nempe, si fideles in tentationibus de auctoritate Scripturae dubitare incipiant, perinde cum illis agendum atque cum iis, qui negant. Est enim dubitatio negationi proxima, verba sunt b. Gerh. l. c. § 20.§

34. Auctoritas Scripturae s. canonica, a seu normativa, quam ex parte non solum sensus, sed ipsarum vocum b divinitus inspiratarum, seu textus primigenii, in ordine ad versiones c pariter, humano studio consignatas, et scripta ac doctrinas d alias judicandas habet, prout in se et absolute spectata, e fundatur in Dei inspirantis veracitate, et Scripturae, ratione vocum textus primigenii, a Deo dependentia; ita etiam in ordine ad nos, seu ut fide divina f credamus, Scripturae libros sub eo, quo nobis exhibentur, idiomate, i. e. verborum in certa lingua delectu, serie et contextu, esse divinitus inspiratos, et sic habere vim illam normativam, seu dignitatem canonicam, non sufficit solum ecclesiae testimonium, g verum et hic internum Spiritus S. testimonium, seu operationem, efficacem per ipsam Scripturam, concurrere h oportet.

De qua vide h. 1. § 15. Vox autem χανόνος, id est normae aut regulae, quae proprie mathematica est, inde autem ad leges civiles, ordines ac stationes militares, nec non librarum, quibus mercatores uttintur, lingulas designandas transfertur (vid. b. Chem. Exam. C. Tr. P. I, S. de Libb. Can. p. m. 81. 82., b. Cundis. ad Compend. Hutt. L. I. Q. III. p. 15. 16.), occurrit, juxta similem analogiam, in ipsis Scripturis ad designandam certam regulam fidei et actionum Christianarum, ut, quae illi congruunt, admittantur, discrepantia vero rejiciantur.

Sic enim 2 Cor. 10, 18. Paulus dicit, se non gloriari, nisi χατά το μέτρον του χανόνος, secundum mensuram regulae; et Gal. 6, 16. pacem et misericordiam precatur et pollicetur omnibus, δσοι τω χανόνι τοότω στοίχ-ήαουσιν, quotquot juxta hanc regulam, velut in ordine militari, incedent.
