Nempe doctrina quidem Scripturae movet ad assensum sui, tanquam divinae, per concursum Dei, in quacunque proponatur lingua, et quibuscunque verbis, modo doctrina ipsa, qualis revelata est, sincere proponatur. Ut autem doctrina fidei ac morum, quae hic aut illic tanquam divina proponitur, ad genuinam normam revocetur, atque ejus seu ορθοδοξία aut veritas, seu έτεροδοζία, aut falsitas, accurate cognoscatur, accedendum est ad Scripturam ex parte verborum infallibilem, adeoque ad Scripturam sub eo idiomate, ubi verba ipsa DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

ex divina inspiratione, non intercedente humano ac fallibili judicio, adhibita fuerunt. Conf. Mus. l. c. p. 540. Versionum enim illarum aliquae revera erroribus sunt obnoxiae; et, si maxime occurrant, quae textui authentico sint exacte congruae, tamen in ratione certitudinis ac veritatis a textu primigenio dependent; adeoque auctoritatem non habent, nisi postquam convenientia earum cum textu authentico investigata et cognita est. Mus. l. c. Unde, quando libri nostri symbolici aliquando normae aut normalium librorum appellatione veniunt, non tamen intelligitur norma absolute sic dicta, sed secundum quid, aut cum addito norma secundaria, normata, id est, minus proprie sic dicta. Vid. b. Himmel, in F. C. disp. 1., Grauer, in A. C. P. I. p. 3. et Supplem. C. IV. p. 149.

Carpzovius: ,,Νοη impulsu Θeοπvebστφ scribuntur lib. symb., sicuti biblici scriptores sua canonica scripta confecerunt, neque absoluta, necessitate et propter insufficientiam canonis biblici, prout Bellarmiuus 1. 4. de verbo Dei c. 4. in 11. biblicis desiderat, quod catechesis non habeatur in illis; sed alia de causa scripti fuerunt, per necessitatem sci., iquae in scholis necessitas expedientiae vocatur, ut sci. contentiones nonnullorum ingeniorum compescerentur, scandala apud infirmos praeverterentur et vafrities et malitia haereticorum agnosceretur. . . Quod ex Scriptura et ad ac secundum eam componitur, id non principium est, sed prindpiatum. Fateri equidem oportet nos, libros symbolicos etiam in praefatione pag. 34. sub normae nomine venire atque nomen istud libris symb. ecclesiae nostrae tribui. Verum principium et norma non simpliciter et ex aequo ut synonyma ab auctoribus praefationis hujus accipiuntur. Siquidem etiam ad id, quod prindpiatum est, ex conventione dirigi ac dijudicari aliquid potest et nomen normae propterea mereri. Et taliter vocabulum normae accipitur hoc in loco (in praefat. libri Cone. p. 21.) et apud scriptores primitivae ecclesiae, v. g. quando symbola oecumenica et imprimis apostolicum (ίξοικώς et εξαφέτως ita dictum) vocantur a patribus κανών της αλήθειας άκλινης, , canon veritatis minime versatilis* (Iren. 1. 1. c. 1. § 19.), ,regula fidei immobilis' et 'irreformabilis' ('Tertull.), ,norma praedicationis in commune per omnes gentes constituta* (Kuffln. et Vernant. Honor.), ,certa fidei regula, per quam credentes catholicam teneant unitatem, haereticam convincant pravitatem' (Aug. serm. de temp. hom. 181.). Et sic etiam normae vocabulum b. 1. nil aliud significat, quam principium cognoscendi, ex quo deducimur in cognitionem alicujus conclusionis seu quaestionis, de qua controvertitur. .Quale principium etiam est id, quod ab alio pendet, et aliunde probatum est, uti ostendit Aristoteles 1. prior, analyt. c. 2. et 8. Non ergo absolute et simpliciter norma est symbolum, sed in respectu ad ecclesias certas, quae veritatem et certitudinem ejus ex Scriptura probatam praesupponunt. . . Quamvis vero negari non possit, nomenclatione hac aut encomio non tantum discretivae, sed etiam definitivae normae rationem libris symb. fuisse attributam; tamen cum maximo discrimine id fecerunt et. . . libros symbol. nonnisi pro secundariis normis habuerunt, ad inodum illorum postulatorum, quae uti probationis indiga, ita tamen alibi probata sunt et etiam in disciplina certa ut indubia admittuntur.“ (Isagoge in libros eccles. lutheranarum symbolicos. p. 5. 6. 27. 28.)

Idem: „Non negant auctores libri Concordiae, solam Scripturam esse unicam normam, ad et secundum quam omnia dogmata exigenda et judicanda sint, quin tot verbis profitentur ..., nec tamen inficiantur, suo modo et sensu etiam haec scripta normam esse. . . Plus tribuunt illis, quam nudam testificandi rationem. . . Quando vero 2. liber symb. norma appellatur et forma doctrinae, ad et secundum quam etc., tunc PROLEGOM. CAP. II. id nonnisi secundum quid intelligitur propter analogiam aliquam, sel. externam, in eo consistentem, quod etiam secundum eam aliquid judicetur et aestimetur, licet non sit principium ejus, quod judicatur ac aestimatur. Et quidem 3. in quaestione instituta non tam de veritate doctrinae, quam de ejus receptione, vigore ac approbatione in certa ecclesia; an hoc dogma, v. g., Elacianum de peccato originis in ecclesia lutherana umquam fuerit receptum et approbatum? an doctrina Flaeii cum doctrina ab initio reformationis tradita et approbata in ecclesia lutherana conveniat? Ut ita 4. liber symbolicus norma appelletur non ipsius fidei, sed professionis fldei, 5. non omnis, sed tantum quoad certa capita controversa, et quidem prout 6. illa in certis ecclesiis perennat. ... Atque ita nihil norma absolute ita dicta doctrinae nostrae detraxerunt nostrates, nec eidem librum symbolicum exaequarunt, sed quod symb. libri natura et ratio exigit, suo symbolico quoque libro attribuerunt et ad nullum extremum hic declinarunt. Nimirum 1. non tantum testari voluerunt de apprehensione doctrinae ac fldei, et quomodo eam ex verbo Dei haustam publice docerent, sed et 2. insuper libidini loquendi ac profitendi in nostris ecclesiis terminos ac liipites ponere, inter quos docentes maxime se continere deberent, ac 3. quoque normam suppeditare ac constituere, secundum quam de aliorum scriptis judicari posset, non, an sint vera aut falsa (de hoc enim ex sola Scriptura judicandum), sed an cum doctrina ab initio in ecclesia lutherana recepta et tradita convenirent, quo 4. ab aliorum spuriis scriptis puritatem doctrinae semel receptae turbantibus prohiberentur simplices et 5. sanctum purae doctrinae Lutheri depositum ad seram posteritatem hac ratione transmitteretur. Cf. p. 638.“ (L. c. p. 1143—45.)

G. Walchius: „Norma primaria est, quae per se, id est, sua et propria virtute vim normae habet; secundaria vexo, quae non per se, sed per Scripturae sacrae auctoritatem ac consensum cum ista virtute normae praedita est hineque a primaria dependet. . . Alii, quibus hae distinctiones adhuc a nobis enarratae displicent, distinguunt inter normam decisionis et discretionis. Illa sit principium illud αντόπιστον et plane infallibile, in cujus sententia utraque pars dissentientium adquiescere debeat; haec autem, sive norma discretionis, quaestionem controversam non quidem definiat, discernat tamen orthodoxos ab heterodoxis atque ostendat, quinam puriori doctrinae sint addicti. . . Existimat Wemsdorflus, symbola normam cognitionis dici posse, ita ut sint principium aliquod, cujus beneficio veritatum quarundam cognitionem consequamur; sed hoc'unice ad Scripturam, tanquam normam, referendum esse videtur. . . Quae si quis consideret, facile intelliget, symbola adpellanda esse cognitionis normam, ubi cognitio non ad ipsam veritatem ejusque fundamentum, sed ad professionem referatur. Sunt symbola norma cognitionis, quatenus ex illis intelligatur, quaenam dogmata ecclesiae cujusdam sint propria. Quando igitur quaeris, num hoc illudne dogma sit Lutheranum, hoc cognoscere debes ex symbolis, tumque sunt norma hujus cognitionis. Ubi autem quaeris, num hoc illudne dogma verum an falsum sit, id certe non ex symbolis tanquam norma, sed ex Scriptura sacra cognoscendum est.“ (Introd. in libb. eccl. Luth. symb. p. 934—36.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Hollazius: "G. Mylius in his explanation of the A

Hollazius: "G. Mylius in his explanation of the A. C., p. 2, says: 'Because the A. C. rests upon the most firm foundation of the Holy Scriptures, we can and ought with the best right to call it θεόπνευστον.' D. Hutterus, in his explanation of the 1st article of the Formula of Concord, p. 1, writes: 'We constitute the primary author of the Book of Concord, the κύριον, not any man, whether theologian or politician, but God Himself, the Holy Spirit, the fountain and bestower of every good; so much so that we do not in the least hesitate to call it θεόπνευστον, divinely inspired.' Resp. . . The aforementioned theologians call the symbolical books θεοπνεύστους in a broader sense, mediately. . . 1. by reason of the object. . . 2. by reason of mediate illumination." (Exam. Proleg. II. q. 27. p. 58.) Schelwigius and J. G. Neumann likewise contend that the symbolical books can be called θεοπνεύστους, by right.

ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

with Loescher (see *Unschuld. Nachrr.* 1707, p. 117; 1710, p. 414, 735), Carpzov (Isag. p. 3), and others dissenting. Luther: "The Christian Church has no power to confirm articles of faith or good works, or the Gospels and Holy Scripture, as a judge or overlord; it has never done so, nor will it ever do so. The Christian Church, however, is indeed confirmed by the Gospel and Holy Scripture as by its judge and overlord. The Christian Church confirms the Gospel and Holy Scripture as a subject, showing and confessing them just as a servant shows the colors and coat of arms of his master. For this is certain: whoever does not have the power to promise and give the future and temporal life, he also has no power to establish articles of faith." (*On the Power of the Christian Church*, 1530. XIX, 1191.)

For we have said as much in the note to § 15, note b: that the authority of Scripture is one in reality, which is both the causative of the assent of faith and the normative of doctrine. We confess, however, that this can and ought to be believed by divine faith. Cf. Musaeus, *Introd.* l. c. p. 552. The blessed Musaeus teaches this expressly in *Introd.* P. II. Cap. VII. § 3. p. 533.

Quenstedt: "The authority of Scripture does not depend solely or necessarily upon the testimony of the church, neither by reason of itself—that is, its intrinsic constitution—nor by reason of us—that is, with respect to cognition and manifestation." (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 129.)

The same: "The thesis is proven: 1. From the saying of Christ in John 5:34: 'I do not receive testimony from man.' ... 2. From the testimony of the Samaritans in John 4:42, who said to the woman: 'We no longer believe because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves and know that this is indeed the Savior of the world, Christ.' ... 3. From the nature and condition of Holy Scripture. ... 4. From the nature and condition of the church. ... 5. Finally, from the absurdity. If the authority of the church were the primary motive and means by which the Holy Spirit proved its αὐθεντία [authority], it would follow: 1. that our faith is founded primarily on human testimony and is ultimately resolved into it; 2. either the universal church is understood, and its testimony is not given; or a particular church, and such is insufficient and uncertain; 3. or the authority of the church is the primary motive with respect to the faithful, but they have already received Scripture; or with respect to the unbelievers, but they will not admit the authority of the church any more than that of Scripture." (L. c. f. 132 sqq.)

Chemnitz: "Those divinely inspired writings were, at the time they were written, proposed, delivered, and commended to the church by public testimony, so that the church, employing the greatest care and providence, might preserve them incorrupt and, as it were, hand them down and commend them to posterity. And just as the old church in the time of Moses, Joshua, and the prophets, so also the primitive church in the time of the apostles was able to testify with certainty which writings were divinely inspired. For it knew the authors, whom God had commended to the church by peculiar testimonies; it also knew which were those things that had been written by them, and from those things which it had received by the tradition of the living voice from the apostles, it could judge that those things which were written were that very doctrine which the apostles delivered by living voice. Thus in John 21, the testimony of the apostles and the attestation of the church are joined: 'This is that disciple who wrote these things, and we know that his testimony is true.' Thus Paul marked his genuine epistles with a certain sign, 2 Thess. 3:17-18. Therefore, Scripture has canonical authority principally from the Holy Spirit, by whose impulse and inspiration it was produced; then from the writers, to whom God himself [gave] certain and peculiar [proofs] of truth— PROLEGOM. CAP. II bore witness to it; afterwards, it has authority from the primitive church as from a witness, in whose time those writings were published and approved.

This testimony of the primitive church concerning the divinely inspired writings was later handed down to posterity by perpetual succession and diligently preserved in certain histories of antiquity, so that the subsequent church was the guardian of the primitive church’s testimony concerning Scripture. There is, therefore, a very great difference: 1. between the testimony of the primitive church, which was in the time of the apostles; 2. between the testimony of the church which followed immediately after the times of the apostles, and which had received the testimony of the first church; 3. and between the testimony of the present church concerning Scripture. For if the church, which both exists now and existed before, can show the testimonies of those who had received and known the testimony of the first church concerning the genuine writings, we believe it as a witness proving its statements. However, it does not have the power of establishing or deciding anything concerning the sacred books for which it cannot bring forward certain documents from the testimony of the primitive church.” (Exam. Conc. Trid. Sess. 4. decr. 1. fol. 47.)

Quenstedtius: “If we wish to speak accurately, it is one thing to depend on the church, and another to be known by the benefit of the church or through the church. . . We distinguish between the ancient church. . . and the modern church. . . Even if we were to grant that the church is a necessary means of knowing the authority of Scripture, we would understand this not as the latter, but rather as the former. . . It is one thing for Scripture to be known as divine from the testimony of the church, and another for it to be known from the testimony of the church alone. For experience testifies that very many have been converted by the mere reading of the Holy Scriptures without the proposal and authority of the church. . . D. Dorscheus recounts examples, Theol. Zachar. P. II. 1.1. q. 1. p. 48.” (L. c. f. 130.)

The same: “Aeg. Hunnius well says in the Colloquy of Ratisbon held in the year 1601, sess. 11. p. 247: ‘That the Epistle to the Romans is Paul’s, we have from the testimony of the primitive church; but that it is sacrosanct, canonical, and a rule of faith, that we do not have and derive from the testimony of the church, but from internal κριτήρια.’” (L. c. f. 135.)

Kromayerus: “Between the phrases: to believe *through* the testimony of the church, and to believe *on account of* the testimony of the church (i.e., with divine faith) that this writing is θεόπνευστον, a distinction must be made. We believe that this writing has God as its author not on account of the testimony, but through the testimony of the church.” (Scrutin. rel. p. 14.)

Quenstedtius: “Dreierus objects: Nowhere does it stand written that this or that book is canonical, and that these writings are divine and others are not, and that these writings are integral while those are mutilated: therefore, the testimony of the church is needed for this, because without the Word it cannot be believed. Resp. . . Even if it is not written expressly, yet as to the sense and the fact, it is abundantly contained in Scripture. . . For Holy Scripture is nothing other than those very divine books arranged in order. Who, therefore, would deny that it stands in Scripture which are the divine books? ... That Scripture is not corrupted or mutilated is evident from divine providence and the express assertion of Christ in Matthew 5, even if the testimony of the church does not approach.” (L. c. f. 138.)

The same: “Regarding that statement of Augustine in his book against the Epistle of Manichaeus, ch. 5: ‘I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the church moved me.’ There Augustine 1. explains not the cause of his faith, as he is already a Catholic, but the occasion by which he arrived from Manichaeism to the love of the divine Scriptures. 2. That which Augustine says about the church applies most especially to the primitive church, because the pontifical church has defected from the consensus of the primitive. 3. The prelate of Hippo speaks only of his own person, or of himself as an individual, and does not prescribe a rule for everyone. We do not deny that someone can be led by the authority of the church to believe in Scripture; but that all must be led in this way, this was to be proven. 4. He speaks of himself not as he was then, a Christian and a bishop,”

but such as he had been when he was led from Manichaeism to the orthodox religion, he knew, namely, that he would not have believed ("I would believe," he says, using an African phrase familiar to him, for "I would have believed"), unless he had first been moved by the authority of the church... There are, moreover, various occasions for believing, such as: 1. the report concerning the church and the true religion, 2. the conversation of unbelievers with believers, 3. the authority of parents or others, 4. miracles, 5. the constancy of martyrs, 6. the integrity of life of those who profess Christianity, etc." (L. c. f. 137 sq.) Cf. Luther’s Report to a Good Friend Concerning Both Kinds, 1528. XIX, 1660—1665.) ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: "Antithesis:

1. Of the Papists; where, however, the older ones must be distinguished from the more recent. The former suspend the authority of canonical Scripture more crudely and crassly upon the authority and testimony of the church, and indeed of their own Roman church, even in respect to its own or intrinsic constitution or canonization; so that Scripture is not in itself authentic without the authority of the church. Hence that rash and impious voice of Andradius, *Defens. Concil. Trident.*, lib. fol. 150: 'There is nothing of divinity in Scripture, except insofar as it has received it from the church.' ... The latter [the more recent ones] judge more mildly and cautiously, holding that Scripture is indeed divine in itself and that its authority, as regards the thing and in itself, depends upon God; yet they contend that Scripture does not obtain divine authority in relation to us, except on account of the authority of the church...

S., fontem et largitorem omnis boni; usque adeo, ut 4εόπνενστον, divinitus inspiratum, ipsum appellare minime dubitemus. Resp. . . Memorati theologi libros symb. sensu latiori vocant mediate ΰεοπνεύστονς ... 1. ratione objecti ... 2. ratione mediatae illuminationis." (Exam. Proleg. II. q. 27. p. 58.) Schelwigius et J. G. Neumannus itidem, libros symb. ΰεοπνενστονς vocari posse, contendunt, jure

dissentientibus Loeschero (vid. Unschuld. Nachrr. 1707, p. 117. 1710, p. 414. 735.), Cdrpzovio (Isag. p. 3.), aliis. Lutherus: „Die christliche Kirche hat keine Macht, Artikel des Glaubens oder gute Werke, oder die Evangelia und heilige Schrift zu bestätigen als ein Richter oder Oberherr, hat’s auch noch nie gethan, wird’s auch nimmermehr thun. Die christliche Kirche wird aber wohl wiederum von dem Evangelio und von der heiligen Schrift bestätigt als vom Richter und Oberherrn. Die christliche Kirche bestätigt das Evangelium und heilige Schrift als ein Unterthan, zeigt und bekennet gleichwie ein Knecht seines Herrn Farbe und Wappen. Denn das ist gewiss, wer nicht Macht hat, das künftige und zeitige Leben zu verheissen und zu geben, der hat auch keine Macht, Artikel des Glaubens zu setzen.“ (Artikel von der christlichen Kirchen Gewalt. 1530. XIX, 1191.)

Sic enim diximus ad § 15. nota b., unam a parte rei esse Scripturae auctoritatem, quae et causativa assensus fidei sit, et normativa doctrinae. Posse autem istud ac debere fide divina credi, fatemur. Conf. Mus. Introd. l. c. p. 552. Sic expresse docet b. Musaem Introd. P. II. Cap. VII. § 3. p. 533.

Quenstedtius: ,,Auctoritas Scripturae nec ratione sui, hoc est, intxinsecae constitutionis, nec ratione nostri, hoc est, respectu cognitionis et manifestationis, ab ecclesiae testimonio unice vel necessario dependet.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 129.)

Idem: „Probatur thesis: 1. ex dicto Christi Joh. 5, 34.: ,Ego non ab homine testimonium accipio'. . . 2. Ex testimonio Samaritanorum Joh. 4, 42., qui mulieri dicebant: ,Quia non amplius propter tuam loquelam credimus; ipsi enim audivimus et scimus, quia hic est vere salvator mundi, Christus.' . . 3. Eas natura et conditione s. Scripturae. ... 4. Ex natura et conditione ecclesiae. . . 5. Denique ab incomeniente. Si auctoritas ecclesiae esset praecipuum motivum et medium, quo Sp. S. probaret ejus av-Sfevriav, sequeretur: 1. fidem nostram primo fundari in testimonio humano et ultimo in id resolvi; 2. vel intelligitur ecclesia universalis, et illius testimonium non datur; vel ecclesia particularis, et tale insufficiens est ac incertum; 3. vel auctoritas ecclesiae est praecipuum motivum respectu fidelium, at illi jam receperunt Scripturam; vel respectu infidelium, at illi non magis ecclesiae auctoritatem, quam Scripturae, admittent.“ (L. c. f. 132. sqq.)

Chemnitius: „Scripta illa divinitus inspirata tunc, cum scriberentur, publica testificatione proposita, tradita et commendata sunt ecclesiae, ut ea, adhibita summa cura et providentia, incorrupta conservaret et quasi per manus traderet et commendaret posteritati. Et sicut vetus ecclesia tempore Mosis, Josuae et prophetarum, ita etiam primitiva ecclesia tempore apostolorum certo potuit testificari, quae scripta essent divinitus inspirata. Noverat enim auctores, quos Deus peculiaribus testimoniis ecclesiae commendarat; noverat etiam, quae essent illa, quae ab ipsis scripta erant, et ex iis, quae traditione vivae vocis ab apostolis acceperat, poterat judicare, illa, quae scripta erant, esse illam ipsam doctrinam, quam apostoli viva voce tradebant. Ita Joh. 21. apostoli testimonium et ecclesiae testificatio conjunguntur: ,Hic est discipulus ille, qui scripsit haec, et scimus, quia verum est testimonium ejus.* Ita Paulus certo signo notavit genuinas suas epistolas, 2 Thess. 3, 17. 18. Habet igitur Scriptura canonicam auctoritatem principaliter a Spiritu S., cujus impulsu et inspiratione prodita est; deinde a scriptoribus, quibus Deus ipse certa et peculiaria veriPROLEGOM. CAP. II« tatis testimonia perhibuit; postea a primitiva ecclesia habet auctoritatem ut a teste, cujus tempore scripta illa edita et approbata fuerunt.

Haec vero testificatio primitivae ecclesiae de scriptis divinitus inspiratis postea perpetua successione per manus tradita est posteritati et in certis antiquitatis historiis diligenter conservata, ita ut sequens ecclesia custos esset testificationis primitivae ecclesiae de Scriptura. Maxima igitur est differentia: 1. inter testificationem primitivae ecclesiae, quae fuit tempore apostolorum; 2. inter testificationem ecclesiae, quae proxime post apostolorum tempora secuta est, quaeque primae ecclesiae testificationem acceperat; 3. et inter testimonium praesentis ecclesiae de Scriptura. Quae enim et nunc est et antea fuit ecclesia, si potest ostendere testimonia eorum, qui acceperant et noverant testificationem primae ecclesiae de germanis scriptis, credimus ei ut testi probanti sua dicta. Non autem habet potestatem statuendi aut decernendi aliquid de libris sacris, cujus non possit certa documenta ex testificatione primitivae ecclesiae proferre.“ (Exam. Conc. Trid. Sess. 4. decr. 1. fol. 47.)

Quenstedtius: „Si accurate loqui velimus, aliud est dependere ab ecclesia, et aliud cognosci ecclesiae beneficio sive per ecclesiam. . . Disting. inter ecclesiam antiquam ... et inter ecclesiam hodiernam. . . Si vel maxime concederemus, ecclesiam esse medium cognoscendi auctoritatem Scripturae necessarium, non tamen hanc, sed illam potius intelligeremus. . . Aliud est, Scripturam divinam cognosci ex ecclesiae testimonio, et aliud, eam cognosci ex solo ecclesiae testimonio. Testatur enim experientia, plurimos sola s. Literarum lectione esse conversos sine ecclesiae propositione et auctoritate. . . exempla recenset D. Dorscheus, Theol. Zachar. P. II. 1.1. q. 1. p. 48.“ (L. c. f. 130.)

Idem: „Bene Aeg. Hunnius in Coli. Ratisbon. anno 1601. habito, sess. 11. p. 247. ait: ,Quod epistola ad Romanos sit Pauli, habemus ex ecclesiae primitivae testimonio; quod autem sit sacrosancta, canonica et fidei regula, id non ex testifleatione ecclesiae, sed ex internis κριτήριο ις habemus et desumimus.*“ (L. c. f. 135.)

Kromayerus: „Inter phrases: credere per testimonium ecclesiae, et credere propter testimonium ecclesiae (fide sci. divina), scriptum hoc esse ϋεόπνενστον, distinguendum. Non propter testimonium, sed per testimoninm ecclesiae, scriptum hoc Deum auctorem habere, credimus.“ (Scrutin. rei. p. 14.)

Quenstedtius: „Objicit Dreierus: Nuspiam scriptum extat, quod hic aut ille liber sit canonicus, et quod haec scripta sint divina, alia non, quod haec scripta sint integra, illa vero mutilata: ergo ecclesiae testimonio ad id opus esse, quia sine verbo credi nequit. Besp. . . Utut scriptum id non sit expresse, quoad sensum tamen et factum abunde id in Scriptura habetur. . . Nihil enim aliud est Scriptura sacra, quam illi ipsi divini libri ordine digesti. Quis ergo neget, extare in Scriptura, quinam sint libri divini? ... Non esse autem corruptam aut mutilatam Scripturam, e divina providentia 'et expressa Christi assertione Matth. 5. constat, etiamsi non accedat ecclesiae testificatio.44 (L. c. f. 138.)

Idem: „Ad illud Augustini libr. contra epist. fundamenti c. 5.: ,jTvangelio non crederem, nisi me ecclesiae commoveret auctoritas.' Ibi enim Augustinus 1. non causam suae fldei, ut jam catholicus est, sed occasionem, qua a Manichaeismo ad divinarum Scripturarum amorem pervenerit, explicat. 2. Id, quod de ecclesia dicit Augustinus, in primitivam ecclesiam potissimum quadrat, quia pontificia ecclesia a primitivae consensu defecit. 3. sed qualis fuerat, cum a Manichaeismo ad orthodoxam religionem deduceretur5 se sci. haud crediturum fuisse (,crederem*, dicit phrasi Aphricana, sibi familiari, pro »credidissem‘), nisi primum ecclesiae auctoritate commotus fuisset. . . ### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Of the Innovators, such as D

2. Of the Innovators, such as D. Hornejus, who in *disput. theol. P. I. disp. 2. s. 2. de canon. Script, th. 77. sq. p. 116. et 119.* says: 'The Word of God cannot be known without the testimony of the church, nor can its true books be distinguished from false and supposititious ones.'" (L. c. fol. 131. sq.) For divine faith arises from no other source, whatever the reasons for which the divinity of the Scriptures may be believed, not only as probably true, but even as humanly infallible. Conf. the blessed Huelsemann, *Praelect. ad F.

C. Art. I. C. II. p. 118. § 35.* The Holy Spirit, however, testifies concerning the certain idiom of the books of Scripture, which is to be acknowledged as θεόπνευστον, not excluding, but taking up the testimony of the church—not, however, just any church, but the primitive one—in such a way that the discourse of faith almost returns to this: By whatever idiom Holy Scripture was originally recorded, by that same idiom it was inspired by God Himself for writing, and thus also recorded by divine inspiration. But the Holy Scripture of the O.T. was originally recorded in that Hebrew which has been received into use up to this time, and the Scripture of the N.T. in that Greek which serves our use. Therefore, the Holy Scripture of the O.T. was inspired by God Himself for writing in that Hebrew which has been received into use up to this time, and the Holy Scripture of the N.T. in that Greek which serves our use, and thus it was also recorded by divine inspiration. The major proposition, which [is] of the doctrine itself comprehended in the Scriptures...

is a part, is undoubtedly of divine faith, and through the power of the Holy Spirit, intimately joined to the whole of sacred doctrine, it moves one to the assent of divine faith. The minor proposition, which regards some singular fact, and that a sensible one, distinct from the doctrine of holy Scripture itself, depends upon the testimony of witnesses who are αὐτόπται καὶ αὐτήκοοι, just as is otherwise customary in proving matters of fact and sensible things. Meanwhile, the conclusion does not cease to be of faith, just as otherwise a conclusion that is revealed and to be believed by divine faith follows not only from two revealed premises, but also from one revealed and another metaphysically or morally evident premise. Brentius: "We are not speaking now of that tradition by which the Holy Scriptures, and what is contained in them, have been handed down to us by our ancestors. For we affirm this tradition to be certain, firm, and indubitable." (Prolegom. Apolog. Wirtemberg. Frankfurt, 1556, fol. 141.) Chemnitius: "The second kind of tradition is that the books of holy Scripture have been guarded by the church in an uninterrupted series of times (as Augustine speaks) and in a certain succession of connection, and faithfully transmitted to posterity, and as it were handed to us by hand. Thus Origen says that he learned by παραδόσει (by tradition) that the four gospels are indubitable in the universal church. And Eusebius, disputing about the canonical books, several times uses the words of tradition, that is, of the church testifying concerning the genuine and canonical books of Scripture. And this tradition, by which the books of holy Scripture are placed into our hands, we receive reverently; however, it provides no patronage to the Papists, who fight for dogmas that can be proven by no testimony of Scripture. For the church, by that tradition, confesses that it is bound to the voice of the doctrine sounding in the Scriptures, and by the propagation of that tradition, it has taught that posterity is also bound to Scripture." (Exam. Conc. Trident., fol. 62.)

Gerhardus: "The question is not about historical traditions, by which the primitive church proved the books of these or those authors from the autographs and other reasons sought from the senses, and continued this its sensitive knowledge to succeeding churches. For we concede that these historical traditions, or testimonies of the church, are not all contained universally in holy Scripture; but we deny that they concern the very substance of the revealed word and contain in themselves articles of faith. For although it is an article of faith that πᾶσαν γραφὴν θεόπνευστον, containing in itself revelations immediately inspired by God, is divine and canonical; yet it is not an article of faith, but a historical assertion, when the church in particular testifies that this or that book is of this or that author; e.g., that the Gospel of Matthew is Matthew’s, that the Epistle to the Hebrews is Paul’s." (Conf. cathol., lib. 1, p. 2, c. 5, fol. 126, b.) However, by the name of idiom in this place is understood not only the language itself of a certain nation, distinguished from the languages of other nations; but (as has already been said in the previous § 34) the very choice of words in a certain language, the series, the context, etc., to which corresponds the name of syngramma, which in this matter was used by G. Zeaemannus in his Tract. de Colloq. Ratisb. Cap. IX. or Exegesis of the Question concerning the Canonical Books, pages 91, 108, 112. Whence those who prove from certain assertions of Scripture that the Scripture of the O.T. was first written in Hebrew, and the Scripture of the N.T. was first written in Greek, do not yet prove the original idiom of Scripture; for to a certain idiom or syngramma, more is required.

For the internal illuminating power of Scripture is so joined to the sense in any language whatsoever, that it does not precisely point out the words of the original text as needing to be distinguished from other equivalent words of the same or any other language, text, or version. Indeed, the other criteria which prove the θεοπνευστίαν [divine inspiration] of the doctrine contained in the Scriptures do not pertain at all to the material, or the words of Scripture, but precisely to the formal, or the doctrine; or, when they pertain in their own way to the material—that is, to the words and their context—they indeed confusedly argue that God is the author of the material of Scripture in some idiom, whatever that may be; yet they do not certainly show the specific and determined idiom or writing in which each book of Scripture was originally recorded. There remains, therefore, the testimony of the church, which does not indeed bestow canonical or normative dignity upon the books of Scripture in any certain idiom, nor does it move the soul by its own power to the assent of divine faith, by which the θεοπνευστίαν of such an idiom is believed; but yet, insofar as it historically shows a certain idiom or writing as the original of the books of Scripture—under which it received them as recorded by the writers themselves—and generates moral certainty concerning it, [it is] so joined with that which Scripture itself teaches, and with which the Holy Spirit has intimately joined His power, that it now has a place in the discourse of faith; as is evident from the following argument (in the thesis). Meanwhile, see the blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., § 16, pp. 542, 543, 544. Likewise, Tract. QQ. de Syncret. et Script. S. Q. II. L. I. de Script. § 5, 6, 7, pp. 227, 228, and 273. Detailed Explanation, p. 9 ff. Hollazius: "When it is asked: Was the Gospel of Matthew written first in Greek or in Hebrew? that question is not dogmatic, but historical. For it is a question of fact falling under the senses, concerning which the canonical writers themselves testified to the senses by word of mouth, by the subscription of their hand, by the tradition of the autographs, and by the autographs themselves, which were delivered to the church and preserved in it with the greatest zeal. The witness of this sensible fact is the primitive church, which served under the banner of Christ on earth while the writers were still living in the flesh, and received their αὐτόγραφα [autographs] from their hands; as well as the subsequent church, which flourished in the times immediately following, when the αὐτόγραφα [autographs] of the canonical books were still extant, were handled by the hands and seen by the eyes of readers, and the idiom in which they were recorded was observed. However, the more recent church cannot testify of itself concerning the authority of the holy canonical Scripture; but if it wishes to testify, it is necessary that it recur to the primitive and subsequent church and borrow from it the testimony of the authentic text. Thus, we seek the testimony of the Hebrew idiom in the Old Testament from the Jewish church, and the testimony of the original Greek text in the New Testament from the primitive Christian church. We willingly accept the testimony of the primitive church, but not that alone. We join to it the testimony of Scripture, its long-continued preservation for the salutary use of men, and the quality of its style. — That the Old Testament was recorded in the Hebrew style, we gather from Romans 3:2, where Paul expressly writes that the oracles of God were entrusted to the Jews. From this Pauline utterance we argue: Whatever oracles were entrusted to the Jews, so that through them they might be made wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, those were entrusted to them in the Hebrew idiom. But the oracles of God contained in the sacred code of the O.T., etc. Therefore. The major premise is certain, because by no oracles, by no sayings, can a man or a whole nation be made wise unto salvation, unless the words or oracles are proposed to the man or the nation..."

in a familiar and vernacular idiom, which that nation understands and can therefore apply to its own salutary use. The minor premise is evident from the cited Pauline dictum, Rom. 3:2, compared with the statement of the same apostle in 2 Tim. 3:16. We apply the testimony of Paul to the Greek language of the New Testament, and we conclude with probability: Whatever oracles were entrusted to all nations, so that through them they might be made wise unto salvation through the faith which is in Christ Jesus, those were entrusted to them in the Greek language. But the oracles of Christ and the apostles are contained in the sacred code of the New Testament, etc. Therefore. The connection of the minor premise is shown: Just as God and the prophets entrusted their oracles to the Jews in the language vernacular to them, which all Jews understood, namely Hebrew, so Christ and the apostles entrusted their oracles to all nations, most widely diffused throughout the whole world, in the language most common and known to all nations, namely Greek, so that through it all nations might be made wise unto salvation. Cicero says gravely in his oration for the poet Archias: "Greek is read among almost all nations, while Latin is contained within its own borders, which are indeed small." (Exam. theol. Proleg. c. 3, p. 127 sq.)

2. Novatorum, ut D. Horneji, qui disput. theol. P. I. disp. 2. s. 2. de canon. Script, th. 77. sq. p. 116. et 119. dicit: 'Verbum Dei non posse sine testimonio ecclesiae cognosci aut veros ejus libros a falsis et supposititiis discerni.'“ (L. c. fol. 131. sq.) Fides divina enim aliunde non oritur, quibuscunque etiam de causis divinitas Scripturarum, non solum tanquam probabiliter vera, sed etiam tanquam humanitus infallibilis, credatur. Conf. b. Huehem. Praelect. ad F.

C. Art. I. C. II. p. 118.§ 35. pars est, haud dubie est fidei divinae, et per virtutem Spiritus Sancti, toti doctrinae sacrae intime conjunctam, movet ad assensum fidei divinae. Minor propositio, quae respicit factum aliquod singulare, idque sensibile, ab ipsa doctrina sacrae Scripturae distinctum, ex testificatione testium αντόητον xai αντηχόων f pendet, prout alias in probandis rebus facti et sensibilibus id fieri solet. Nam hanc traditionem affirmamus esse certam, firmam et indubitatam.“ (Prolegom. Apolog. Wirtemberg. Francof. 1556. f. 141.) Chemnitius: „Secundum genus traditionum est, quod libri Scriptuiae sacrae non interrupta serie temporum (sicut Augustinus loquitur) et certa connexionis successione ab ecclesia custoditi et fideliter ad posteros transmissi nobisque quasi per manus traditi sunt. Ita Origenes dicit, se παραόώσει (per traditionem) didicisse, quod quatuor evangelia in universa ecclesia sint indubitata. Et Eusebius, de libris canonicis disputans, aliquoties utitur verbis traditionis, hoc est, ecclesiae testiflcantis de germanis et canonicis Scripturae libris. Et hanc traditionem, qua nobis in manum dantur sacrae Scripturae libri, reverenter accipimus; nihil autem patrocinatur pontificiis, qui pugnant pro d&gmatibus, quae nullo Scripturae testimonio probari possunt. Ecclesia enim illa traditione fatetur, se alligatam esse ad vocem doctrinae sonantis in Scripturis, et propagatione illius traditionis, posteritatem etiam ad Scripturam alligatam esse, docuit.“ (Exam. Cone. Trident, fol. 62.)

Gerhardus: „Non est quaestio de traditionibus historicis, quibus ecclesia primitiva libros biblicorum horum vel illorum auctorum ex autographis et aliis rationibus a sensu petitis probavit et ad ecclesias succedaneas hanc suam sensitivam cognitionem continuavit. Hasce enim historicas traditiones sive ecclesiae testificationes concedimus non contineri universim omnes in Scriptura sacra; sed negamus, eam concernere ipsam verbi revelati substantiam et in se continere articulos fidei. Quamvis enim sit fidei articulus, πάσαν γραφήν Οεόπνενστον, immediate inspiratas a Deo revelationes in se continentem, esse divinam et canonicam; non tamen est fidei articulus, sed historica assertio, cum ecclesia in partipulari testatur, hunc vel illum librum esse hujus vel illius auctoris; v. g. evangelium Matthaei esse Matthaei, epistolam ad Hebraeos esse Pauli.“ (Conf. cathol, lib. 1. p. 2. c. 5. f. 126. b.) Zeaemannus in Tract. de Colloq. Ratisb. Cap. IX. seu Exegesi Quaest. de Libris Can. pag. 91. 108. 112. Unde nondum probant idioma Scripturae primigenium ex ipsa Scriptura,

Interim vid. b. Mus. l. c. §r 6. p. 542. 543. 544. Item Tract. QQ. de Syncret. et Script. S. Q. II. L. I. de Script. § 5. 6. 7. p. 227. 228. et 273. Ausführl. Erklärung p. 9. sqq.Hollazius: „Quando quaeritur: Estne evangelium Matthaei graece, an hebraice, primum scriptum? quaestio illa non dogmatica, sed historica est. Est enim quaestio facti in sensus incurrentis, de quo et scriptores canonici ipsi ore, subscriptione manus et traditione autographorum et ipsa autographa, ecclesiae tradita inque ea summo studio asservata, ad sensum testabantur. ### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: By the designation "primitive church" is understood that church which…

By the designation "primitive church" is understood that church which flourished in those times when the writers of the sacred books lived: namely, regarding the books of the Old Testament, the Jewish church, from Moses to Malachi; regarding the books of the New Testament, however, the Christian church, contemporary with the apostles and their co-workers, to whom the θεόπνευστοι books were delivered by their writers, and which, relying on the testimony of the senses, could equally know and testify which books, in what idiom of language and speech, and with what choice and sequence of words, it had received from the hands of those who had written them. See Musaeus, l.c., p. 545 The church of subsequent times, however, can define nothing in this question of ancient fact unless it relies on the testimony of the primitive church. The same, l.c., p. 551 This argument exists in the blessed Musaeus's Introd. l.c., § 7, p. 554. Cf. Ausführliche Erklärung p. 20, Tr. Quaest. de Syncr. et Scr. S. L. I. Q. II. § 18, p. 237 For to this pertains what we read in 2 Tim. 3:16: πασαν γραφην, that all Scripture is divinely inspired, which is the same as saying that when it was first written, even regarding the idiom itself, or the words of a certain language and their choice, sequence, and context, it proceeded from divine inspiration. Cf. here § 10 and the note. Indeed, that the testimony of the primitive church for recognizing with moral certainty the original idiom of the books of Scripture was not only truly published long ago, but also survives in such a way that it suffices for it even today, although there is no one in the modern church who has seen the πρωτότυπα, is clearly shown by the blessed Musaeus, Introd. p. 545 sqq. and Tr. QQ. de Syncr. et Scr. S. l.c. p. 247 sqq., having brought forward at the same time for this opinion the discourses of the blessed Doctors Martin Chemnitz p. 259, Jacob Andreae p. 263, Aegidius Hunnius p. 266, and G. Zeaemann p. 296 To these many others could be joined, especially those who disputed against the Papists (whose known fraud is that by which they strive to lead us away from the testimony of the primitive church in searching and following these matters); e.g., the blessed Albert Grauer, Disp. Inaug. de Scr. S. contra Costerum, praes. P. Piscator, § 126; the blessed J. Major, Tr. contra Valerianum M. de Regula Cred. Resp. ad quartam Conseq. Cap. 3, § 7, p. 367; the blessed Gerhard, in Exeg. L. I. § 75 sqq.; the blessed Salomon Glassius, in Glaubensgrund Cap. II, p. 38 sqq. and Cap. VII, p. 231. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

P. Haberkorn against Valer. M. Disp. II. Cap. IV. p. 71, 79, 102, 107. Add the blessed Georg Mylius, *Posit. de V. D.* § 70 sqq., Kromayer, *Theol. Prof. Pol.* Art. I. p. 37.

However, it must be admitted that the cited doctors treat in the aforementioned places not only of the secondary authors of the books of Scripture, but also of the idiom, indeed, they treat of it most especially; namely, that the πρωτότυπα and αύτόγραφα of the sacred writers were preserved by the ancient church, and were seen, read, and faithfully transcribed by them: these are the words of the blessed J. Major in the place cited.

Moreover, the blessed Gerhard, as well as Glassius and Haberkorn, urge that statement of Tertullian concerning the authentic letters of the apostles, which were recited in the apostolic churches, preserving the voice of the apostles, etc.

Kromayer also, among the criteria of a canonical book of the N. T., refers in the fourth place to the fact that it must have the testimony of the primitive Christian church, which had seen, read, and known the αύτόγραφα.

Finally, the blessed Dan. Oramerus in *Isag. ad Libb. Prophet, et Apost.* p. 15, where he treats of the distinction of apocryphal books from canonical ones, says: "This entire—N.B.—testification depends upon the first inspection of their autograph, into whose hands it came."

Most manifestly, however, the blessed Zeaemann (in that place which the blessed Musaeus alleges in *Tract. QQ. de Syncret. et Scr. S.* page 226, namely in *Tr. Theol. et Scholast. de Colloq. Batisb.* Cap. IX. or *Exeg. Quaest. de Libb. Can.* p. 91 and 108) refers the historical tradition of the ancient church not only to the question concerning the authors of the sacred books, but also to that which concerns the *syngramma* (as he calls what is otherwise called the *idioma*), and he affirms that the church testifies concerning it as an object of αἴσθησις or sense, and that one must lean upon that testimony.

Tertullian: "Come now, you who would better exercise your curiosity in the business of your salvation, run through the apostolic churches, in which the very chairs of the apostles still preside in their places, in which their authentic letters are recited, sounding the voice and representing the face of each. Is Achaia near to you? You have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi. If you can travel to Asia, you have Ephesus. But if you are near Italy, you have Rome, from whence also authority is available to us." (*De praescriptionibus adv. haeret.*)

For thus, for example, the conclusion of faith is that by which a regenerate man gathers concerning himself individually: "I, through baptism, have been made a son of God and an heir of eternal life."

The premises, however, upon which that conclusion rests, are these: The major premise, indeed, is revealed: "Whoever is baptized, he has been made through baptism a son of God and an heir of eternal life"; which is taught in Galatians 3:27. The minor premise, however, is not revealed, but rests upon the assertion of other trustworthy men, if one was baptized in infancy, or upon the testimony of one's own senses, if one was baptized in adult age; this is: "But I am baptized" (i.e., water was poured upon me in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, which was perceived partly by sight, partly by hearing).

Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* in the place cited, p. 554, 555, who discussed at greater length this method of concluding in *Tract. de Usu princip. Kat. in Theol.* Book II, c. XIII sqq. p. 435 sqq. and *Tr. de Convers.* Disp. IX, p. 569 sqq. §

36. Therefore, the canonical books of the O. T., which the ancient Jewish church received and handed down to the Christian church, are the following:

The five books of Moses, the book of Joshua, Judges, the two of Samuel, the two of Kings, the two of Chronicles, one of Ezra, one of Nehemiah (or the latter Ezra), the book of Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, the four books of the major prophets, which are: Isaiah, Jeremiah (whose also are the Lamentations), Ezekiel, Daniel, the twelve books of the minor prophets, which are: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi: all of which survive uncorrupted in the Church.

For thus they are mentioned by Christ as being undoubtedly found among the Jews, and are divided into Moses and the Prophets (Luke 16:29, 31), and into Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms (Luke 24:44).

With this division, that of the Jews in some measure agrees: into תורה, or the Law; נביאים, or the Prophets (which they further divide into ראשונים, the former, and אחרונים, the latter); and כתובים, the Writings, which are otherwise called ἁγιόγραφα. Although one must be careful, following the example of the more recent Jews, not to attribute an inequality of perfection and dignity to writings that are equally divinely inspired.

See Mr. Frischmuth’s special dissertation on this division of Scripture. Regarding each of these, see the blessed J. Gerhard in *Exegesis*, Book I, Chapter VII, p. 118 ff.; the blessed Michael Walther in *Officina Biblica*; the blessed Daniel Cramer in *Isagoge ad Libros Propheticos et Apostolicos*; and the blessed Laurentius Fabricius in *Partitione Codicis Hebraei*. For the nature of this undertaking does not allow for a more prolix enumeration of these.

That those books survived uncorrupted in the time of Christ cannot be denied; otherwise, He certainly would not have spoken so absolutely: "They have Moses and the Prophets" (Luke 16:29), "Search the Scriptures and they are they which testify of me" (John 5:39-40). Rather, if there had been any corruptions at that time, He would have warned His own.

And although He reproves the blindness and infidelity of the Jews in defending true doctrine and in acknowledging the manifested Messiah, Paul nevertheless attributes to them and proclaims their faithful custody of the sacred code itself, which was deposited with them (Rom. 3:2; 9:4).

Moreover, after those times, with copies of Scripture multiplied among Christians, there was not even any room left for a universal corruption that would extend to all codices, especially if you consider that the providence of God watched over His Word.

Furthermore, the particular corruption of certain codices does not remove the certainty of the θεόπνευστος Scripture. Compare the blessed Glassius, *Philologia Sacra*, Book I, Tract I, § 37.

However, those books which sometimes appear in the biblical codex of the Old Testament besides these are: Judith, Wisdom, Tobit, Ecclesiasticus, Baruch, two (or three) of Maccabees, (the third and fourth of Ezra), the fragments of Esther, of Daniel concerning Susanna, concerning Bel and the Babylonian Dragon, the prayers of Azariah, ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

of the three youths and Manasseh, since they were held neither by the ancient Israelite church, nor by Christ and the apostles, nor by the Christian church that immediately followed as θεόπνευστοι [divinely inspired], nor did they possess canonical authority among them, therefore they ought not to possess it today; but so that they may be distinguished from those canonical books, they are rightly called apocryphal.

Indeed, they are not only seen intermixed with the canonical books in the Vulgate version, but are also read published elsewhere in various versions of different languages, inasmuch as they are not entirely rejected, but are to be read usefully for edification.

For they [the ancients] did not hold any books as canonical except those which were consigned in the language then received by the people of God, offered to the priests, and, with the calling and divine inspiration of the writers being known, and the fact that these books were written by them in this series and context of words, were commended to the church.

Compare Gerh. Exeg. L. I. § 73, 74.

Certainly, nowhere in the New Testament is any one of them cited to prove any head of the doctrine of faith. Compare here § 36, note a. For that [early] church anxiously followed the canon of the Hebrews, and did not dare to add any book to it. Witnesses are Melito of Sardis in Eusebius, Hist. Eccles. Book IV, chap. XXVI; Origen in the same, Book VI, XXV; Eusebius himself, Book III, chap. IX; especially Jerome in the Prologus Galeatus, and many others in Gerh. in Confess. Cath. Book II, art. I, Cap. I, p. 19.

### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Compare his Exeg. L. I

For the fact that they are sometimes called canonical, even by Augustine himself, cannot be taken in the proper and principal signification; but it is said only in that sense, indeed more general and less proper, in which it pleased them to call any book that is to be read usefully in the church by that name.

i.e., hidden, or because their origin from divine inspiration was not established to the church of that time in which they appeared, nor therefore is it established to the church of succeeding centuries.

38. The canonical books of the N. T. are all those which are held in the biblical codex: namely, not only those concerning whose θεοπνευστία [divine inspiration] there was never any doubt, which are: the four Gospels, of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, to the Corin

two to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, the first of Peter and the first of John; but also the remaining writings, concerning whose authors, as well as their divine origin, some formerly entertained doubts, though today no dispute remains: namely, the Epistle to the Hebrews, the second of Peter, the second and third of John, the Epistle of James, the Epistle of Jude, and the Apocalypse of John: all of which also survive uncorrupted. They are therefore called πρωτοκανονικοί, or canonical of the first order. See regarding these the blessed Martin Chemnitz, Part I of the *Examen*, section on the evangelical writings and on the writings and epistles of the apostles; the blessed Gerhard, *Exegesis*, § 243 sqq.; the blessed Walther in *Officium Biblicum*; the blessed Cramer in his *Isagoge*, etc.

It certainly cannot be denied that the ancients so doubted the authors that they simultaneously denied to these books the authority proper to θεόπνευστοι [God-breathed] writings. For thus Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, ch. XXIII, near the end, says of the Epistle of James: Ίστέον, ώς νοθεύεται; which Grynaeus translates: "It must be known that it is adulterine." Valesius, however: "Which some consider spurious and supposititious." And long ago Rufinus: "It must be known that it is not received by some." So that, in the mind of Eusebius, for that epistle to be νοθεύεσθαι is not indeed to be spurious, but to be held as spurious, and therefore not held to be θεόπνευστον. For Christians would not say ώς νοθεύεται concerning a θεόπνευστον writing when only the writer, the amanuensis of God, is unknown or disputed, but the divine origin of the writing itself is certain.

Similarly, Eusebius, Book III, ch. XXV, makes mention of the ἀντιλεγόμενα, or books that are contradicted or called into doubt, and refers to this category the epistle which is called James’s, and that of Jude, and the second of Peter, and likewise the second and third of John.

Indeed, he allows the Apocalypse of John to be reckoned among the νόθοις or spurious books, which some reject, ήν τινες ἀθετοῦσιν, he says. Compare Book VI, ch. XXV.

That this, however, is to be understood not of the whole Christian church, but of certain particular congregations (which had not themselves inspected the autographs offered to them, nor had been sufficiently informed of the origin of those books from elsewhere through certain testimonies), is indicated in the aforementioned places.

Rather, he says expressly in Book II, ch. XXIII, concerning the epistles of James and Jude: "Nevertheless, we have known these also to be read publicly in most churches along with the others." Or, if we prefer to follow Rufinus: "We, however, know that even these are received by almost all churches along with the others." And in Book III, ch. XXV, concerning the Apocalypse of John, after the words cited: "Ετεροι, he says, ἐγκρίνουσι τοῖς ὁμολογουμένοις, others number them among the books approved by the consensus of all."

Chemnitz: "The third question, therefore, is whether those writings, concerning which there was doubt in the most ancient church due to the contradiction of some—because the testimonies of the primitive church did not agree concerning them—whether, I say, the present church can make those writings canonical, catholic, and equal to those which are of the first order. The Papists not only argue that they can do this, but in fact usurp that authority, altogether removing the necessary [authority] of the primitive and most ancient church." ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

the distinction between canonical and apocryphal or ecclesiastical books. But it is most manifest from what we have said that the church in no way possesses that authority; for by the same reasoning, it could either reject canonical books or canonize adulterated ones. For this whole matter (as we have said) depends upon the certain testimonies of that church which existed in the time of the apostles, which the immediately following church received and preserved through certain and trustworthy histories. Where, therefore, the most certain documents of the primitive and most ancient church cannot be brought forward from the testimonies of the ancients, who lived not long after the times of the apostles, that those books which are in controversy were accepted and commended to the church as legitimate and certain without contradiction and doubt, no human decrees are valid.

For how insolent is the audacity to decree thus: although the primitive and the subsequent most ancient church doubted concerning those books because of the contradiction of many ecclesiastics, because there did not exist sufficiently certain and firm testimonies of their authority, yet notwithstanding this, we decree that they must be received as altogether certain and of equal authority with those which have always been judged legitimate!

But by what documents do you prove this decree of yours? Pighius answers: The church has that power, that it can impart to certain writings a canonical authority which they have neither from themselves nor from their authors. Why then do they not impart that authority either to the fables of Aesop or to the true narratives of Lucian? Not that I wish those books, concerning which there is controversy, to be compared to the fables of Aesop (for I attribute to them, with Cyprian and Jerome, the honorable place which they always held in the ancient church), but by an *epagoge eis adynaton* [reduction to the impossible], as the dialecticians speak, I wished to show that in a dispute concerning the books of Scripture, the church does not have that power, that it can make true things out of false writings, false out of true, and certain out of doubtful and uncertain, canonical and legitimate, without any certain and firm documents, which we said above are required for this matter. . .

In this testimony, there is also a different role for that church which existed in those times when those books were first written, and for that church which followed afterward. For the latter only preserves and transmits to posterity the testimony of the first church, but it neither ought to nor can decree anything concerning those books for which it does not have certain documents from the testimony of the first church. . .

The third question is: Which books are in the canon, and which are not in the canon? as Jerome speaks. We are not now speaking of supposititious, adulterated, and false writings, the catalog of which exists in Eusebius and in dist. 15, Can. "Sancta Romana." But the question is concerning those books which exist together in the Vulgate edition of the Bibles, and which are read by the faithful in the churches. Concerning them, the testimony of the ancient church is sought, whether all are of the same certainty and equal authority. It is, however, most certain and manifest that this is the testimony of the ancient church: that of those books, some are in the canon, and some are not in the canon, but are apocryphal. . .

Among the writings of the O.T. that are not in the canon, the book of Wisdom, Sirach, etc., are numbered among the apocrypha. Among the books of the N.T. which in the first and ancient church did not have sufficiently certain, firm, and consenting testimonies of their certainty and authority, the following are recounted: Eusebius, bk. 3, ch. 25: "The writings which are not held as indubitable, but which are contradicted, although they are known to many, are these: the Epistle of James, of Jude, the second of Peter, and the second and third of John; some reject the Apocalypse of John, others adjudge it to the certain and indubitable scriptures.". . "It must not be ignored that some in the Roman church rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, asserting that it is contradicted, as if it were not Paul's.". .

I have noted these testimonies of the ancients so that not only might the catalog of the writings of the N.T. be known which do not have sufficiently certain, firm, and consenting testimonies of their authority, but that especially the reasons might be noted why they were doubted: 1. Because among the ancients, sufficiently certain, firm, and consenting testimonies were not found concerning the attestation of the first apostolic church, that those books were approved by the apostles and commended to the church. 2. Because PROLEGOM. CAP. II. it was not certain from the testimony of the first and ancient church whether those books were written by those under whose names they were published, but they were judged by others to have been published under the names of the apostles. 3. Since some of the most ancient writers attributed some of those books to the apostles, while others contradicted them, that matter, as it was not indubitably certain, was left in doubt.

For this whole dispute depends upon certain, firm, and consenting testimonies of the first and ancient church; where these are lacking, the subsequent church, just as it cannot make true things out of false ones, so neither can it make certain things out of doubtful ones without manifest and firm documents.

Against these such manifest testimonies of antiquity, the Council of Trent in its fourth session decrees as follows: "If anyone shall not receive as sacred and canonical the books entire with all their parts, as they are contained in the old Latin Vulgate edition, let him be anathema."
