Chemnitius: „Tertia igitur quaestio est, an ea scripta, de quibus in antiquissima ecclesia propter quorundam contradictionem dubitatum fuit, ideo quod testificationes primitivae ecclesiae de his non consentirent, an, inquam, praesens ecclesia possit illa scripta facere canonica, catholica et paria illis, quae primi ordinis sunt. Pontificii hon tantum disputant, se hoc posse, sed de facto illam auctoritatem usurpant, in universum tollentes primitivae.et antiquissimae ecclesiae necessariam DB PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

distinctionem inter libros canonicos et apocryphos seu ecclesiasticos. Sed manifestissimum est ex iis, quae diximus, ecclesiam nullo modo habere illam auctoritatem; eadem enim ratione posset etiam vel canonieos libros rejicere, vel adulterinos canonisare. Tota enim haec res (sicut diximus) pendet ex certis testificationibus ejus ecclesiae, quae tempore apostolorum fuit, quas acceptas proxime sequens ecclesia certis et fide dignis historiis conservavit. Ubi igitur non possent proferri certissima documenta primitivae et antiquissimae ecclesiae ex testificationibus veterum, qui non longe post apostolorum tempora vixerunt, libros illos, de quibus controvertitur, fuisse sine contradictione et dubitatione pro legitimis et certis acceptos et commendatos ecclesiae, non valent ulla humana decreta.

Quam insolens enim est audacia, ita statuere: licet primitiva et sequens antiquissima ecclesia de libris illis propter multorum ecclesiasticorum contradictionem dubitarit, ideo quod non satis certa et firma auctoritatis ipsorum testimonia extarent, hoc tamen non obstante decernimus, debere illos pro omnino certis pari auctoritate cum illis, qui legitimi semper judicati sunt, recipi!

Sed quibus documentis hoc vestrum decretum probatis? Respondet Pighius: Ecclesia habet illam potestatem, quod potest scriptis quibusdam impertiri canonicam auctoritatem, quam nec ex Se, nec suis auctoribus habent. Quin igitur impartiantur illam auctoritatem vel fabulis Aesopi vel veris narrationibus Luciani? Non quod libros illos, de quibus controversia est, velim fabulis Aesopi comparari (tribuo enim illis cum Cypriano et Hieronymo honorificum locum, quem in veteri ecclesia semper habuerunt), sed επαγωγή άς αδύνατον, sicut dialectici loquuntur, volui ostendere, in disputatione de libris Scripturae ecclesiam non habere illam potestatem, quod possit ex falsis scriptis facere vera, ex veris falsa, ex dubiis et incertis facere certa, canonica et legitima sine ullis certis et firmis documentis, quae ad hanc rem requiri, supra diximus. . .

In hac testificatione alia etiam est ratio illius ecclesiae, quae fuit illis temporibus, cum libri illi primum scriberentur, et ejus ecclesiae, quae postea secuta est. Illa enim tantum conservat et ad posteros transmittit testificationem primae ecclesiae, non autem vel debet vel potest aliquid de libris illis statuere, cujus non habeat certa documenta ex testificatione primae ecclesiae. . .

Tertia quaestio est: Qui libri sunt in canone, et qui non sunt in canone? sicut Hieronymus loquitur. Non autem de suppositiciis, adulterinis et falsis scriptis nunc loquimur, quorum catalogus extat apud Eusebium, et dist. 15. Can. ,Sancta Romana‘. Sed de illis libris quaestio est, qui simul extant in Vulgata bibliorum editione, quique in ecclesiis a fidelibus leguntur. De illis quaeritur veteris ecclesiae testificatio, an omnes sint ejusdem certitudinis et paris auctoritatis. Est autem certissimum et manifestissimum, veteris ecclesiae hanc esse testificationem, quod ex illis libris quidam sint in canone, quidam non sint in canone, sed sint apocryphi. . .

Ex scriptis V. T. inter apocrypha, quae non sunt in canone, numerantur liber Sapientiae, Syrach etc. Ex libris N. T., qui in prima et veteri ecclesia non habuerunt satis certa, firma et consentientia certitudinis et auctoritatis suae testimonia, hinc recensentur: Eusebius 1. 3. c. 25.: ,Scripta, quae non habentur pro indubitatis, sed quibus contradicitur, licet multis sint cognita, haec sunt: Epistola Jacobi, Judae, posterior Petri et altera cum tertia Johannis; Apocalypsin Johannis quidam reprobant, quidam certis et indubitatis scripturis adjudicant.'.. ,Non est ignorandum, quod quidam in Romana ecclesia epistolam ad Ebr. reprobarunt, asserentes, contradici, quasi non sit Pauli.'..

Haec veterum testimonia ideo annotavi, ut non tantum notus sit catalogus scriptorum N. T., quae non habent satis certa, firma et consentientia auctoritatis suae testimonia, sed ut praecipue notari possint rationes, quare de illis dubitatum fuerit: 1. Quia apud veteres non inventa fuerunt satis certa, firma et consentientia testimonia de testificatione primae apostolicae ecclesiae, quod libri illi essent ab apostolis comprobati et ecclesiae commendati. 2. Quia PROLEGOM. CAP. II. non certo ex testificatione primae et veteris ecclesiae constitit, an ab illis, sub quorum nomine editi sunt, libri illi conscripti essent, sed judicati fuerunt ab aliis sub apostolorum nomine editi. 3. Cum quidam ex vetustissimis aliquos ex illis libris tribuerent apostolis, quidam vero contradicerent, res illa, sicut non erat indubitato certa, relicta fuit in dubio.

Pendet enim tota haec disputatio a certis, firmis et consentientibus primae et veteris ecclesiae testificationibus, quae ubi desunt, sequens ecclesia, sicut non potest ex falsis facere vera, ita nec ex dubiis potest certa facere sine manifestis et firmis documentis.

Contra haec tam manifesta antiquitatis testimonia Tridentinum concilium sessione quarta ita decernit: ,Si quis libros integros cum omnibus suis partibus, prout in veteri Vulgata latina editione habentur, pro sacris et canonicis non susceperit, anathema sitΛ


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: But whence do they prove and confirm this decree of theirs against the…

But whence do they prove and confirm this decree of theirs against the testimonies of antiquity? Do they bring forward certain and manifest documents from the testimonies of the first apostolic and ancient church, that those controversial books have the same certainty and equal authority with the rest, about which there was never any doubt? Nothing of the sort; for they cannot do this. But they seize for themselves this power, that the Pope with his prelates can impart to those books, and perhaps to others as well, a canonical authority which they do not deserve either from themselves or from their authors, and which they did not have in the time of the apostles and the primitive church, as Pighius contends.

Why then do they not openly say what the case is? "Although it cannot be proven that those books were either written or approved by the prophets or apostles, and certainly and constantly received by the first and ancient church; nay, although the contrary is proven by the most manifest testimonies of antiquity more clearly than the midday light: this notwithstanding, we establish and decree that this must be believed as certain, although no suitable documents for this matter are brought forward by us, because (if it pleases the gods) the fullness of this kind of antichristian power is buried in the shrine of the pontifical breast." —

They say anathema to all who do not receive the apocryphal books with the same certainty and authority as the canonical ones. Therefore, Eusebius, Jerome, Origen, Melito, and that entire first apostolic church, from whose testimony those things which we recited above concerning these books are taken, will be anathema. . .

The whole dispute in this question therefore consists in this: whether it is certain and indubitable that those books, about which this controversy is, are Scripture divinely inspired by the prophets and apostles, who divinely possessed that authority either to publish or to approve. All of antiquity answers that it is not certain, but that because of the contradictions of many, it was held in doubt. The Tridentine arrogance, however, threatens anathema unless one receives them with equal, nay, the same certainty and authority as the remaining books, about which there was never any doubt. What wonder is it, therefore, that certain papal parasites have argued that the Pope can establish new articles of faith, when in this place he does not fear to fabricate a new canonical Scripture? So that there may no longer be any doubt who that is, who, sitting in the temple of God, exalts himself above everything that is called God, 2 Thess. 2. —

Are those books, therefore, to be simply rejected and condemned? By no means do we seek this. What use, then, does this dispute have? I answer: that the rule of faith or of sound doctrine in the church may be certain. For the ancients judged that the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas must be confirmed from canonical books alone, as the testimonies alleged above show. The authority of canonical Scripture alone was judged suitable for strengthening those things which come into contention; but the remaining books, which Cyprian calls ecclesiastical and Jerome calls apocryphal, they indeed wished to be read in the church for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of church dogmas. For they did not wish them to be brought forward to confirm the authority of faith from them. And their authority was judged less suitable for strengthening those things which come into contention. Therefore, no dogma should be constructed from those books which does not have certain and manifest foundations and testimonies in other canonical [books].

books. Nothing that is controversial can be proven from those books if there are no other proofs and confirmations in the canonical books. But what is said in those books must be explained and understood according to the analogy of those things which are manifestly handed down in the canonical books. That this is the opinion of antiquity, there is no doubt. But the Council of Trent, for that very necessary and most true reason, infringes upon, subverts, and removes this distinction of the ancient church, because (as my Andradius says) they do not wish to cast themselves into these straits, so that, destitute of all other supports, they might borrow their faith from canonical Scripture alone. For the Tridentine synod says that it makes the apocryphal books canonical for this reason: to show what testimonies and supports it intends to use primarily in confirming dogmas and restoring morals.” (Exam. Conc. Trid. Ed. Genev. f. 48. sq. 50. 51. sq.) Flacius, A. Osiander (d. 1617), Aeg. Hunnius, Hafenreffer, C. Dietericus, F. Balduinus, Th. Thummius, and others teach the same. Cf. “Is he to be declared a heretic or a dangerous false teacher who does not hold and declare all the books found in the collection of the N.T. to be canonical?” See “Lehre und Wehre” II, 204—216.

Therefore, even today they are called apocryphal by some, and more conveniently by others, canonical of the second order or δευτερυχανονιχοί. For they are not hidden when the norm of doctrine is demanded, but they have this authority among Christians, especially our own, commonly today. See Gerh. Exeg. § 242. Gerhard: “We, indeed, cannot yet be persuaded (by them) to reject the authority of this book (the Apocalypse), or to attribute it to Cerinthus, but we establish the Apostle John as its author. . . . Meanwhile, however, since in the primitive church there was for some time doubt among some regarding the author of this book, we therefore refer it to the canonicals of the second order; not indeed detracting from its canonical authority, yet meanwhile not simply and in all respects joining it to the remaining canonical books, about which there was never any doubt; and we demand with the most equitable right that the interpretation of this book be established in such a way that it in no way conflicts with the canonical books of the first order.” (Disputatt. theologic. Jenae, 1655. p. 1015. sq.) See b. Glassius lib. I. Phil. 8. Tract. II. Conf. Buxtorf’s Anticritica and Hottinger’s Thes. Philol. fol. 118. sqq., where it is shown that not even by chance or the injury of time have all modern codices been fundamentally corrupted. § 39.

Furthermore, the efficacy of Holy Scripture pertains secondly to the affections of Scripture, or the fact that it possesses an active supernatural and truly divine power to produce supernatural effects, namely, to convert, regenerate, and renew the minds of men, which, by divine ordination, is intimately and indissolubly united to it—as regards its sense—even outside of use in *actu primo*; and which, upon the addition of the use of reading, hearing, or meditation, exerts itself in *actu secundo*, so that those effects of grace super

natural, inasmuch as they are produced efficiently by God, as the principal cause, and likewise by Scripture itself, as the instrumental efficient cause, simultaneously and jointly, by one undivided influx. Quenstedtius: “Theses; The Word of God, by the very ordination and will of God, possesses—even before and outside of its legitimate use—an intrinsic, divine, and sufficient power and efficacy, indifferent toward all men, for the immediate, true, and proper production of spiritual and divine effects (both gracious and saving, such as regeneration, conversion, illumination, and salvation; and punitive, such as conviction, mortification, damnation, etc.).” (Th. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 16. f. 246.) We have said in note e. to § 32 that this must be joined with the authority of Scripture.

By the name of efficacy (by which, elsewhere, the second act, or actual operation, is designated, just as among the Greeks by the name of ἐνέργεια), we understand in this place the very δύναμις ἐνεργητική, or the effective power for spiritual effects. B. Mus. Introd. P. II. c. VIII. § 2. p. 559. Not a merely objective power, but an effective or productive power of supernatural forces and motions in the intellect and will of man, who is by nature blind and dead to the embracing of spiritual things. Mus. l. c. p. 560. Certainly, it is not to be sought in the cultivation of speech, nor in the gravity of the sentences, nor in the oratorical weight of the arguments, but it is superior to every created and finite power of acting; which, therefore, is not so much natural to Scripture—whether on the part of the words or on the part of the things signified—but is supernatural, or, by divine ordination, intimately conjoined with the nature of Scripture; as is said in the following. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 3. 4. p. 561. 562. Thus also our elders, on the occasion of the Rathmannian controversy, in App. Consil. Ded. Q. VI. § 3. fol. 263. b. 264. a., taught that the power of illuminating and converting belongs to Scripture not by physical necessity, nor in a natural way, but in a supernatural way; and that those theologians who perhaps said that the Word of God has that natural power used that word not in opposition to the ὑπερφυσικόν, but in opposition to the Rathmannian παραστατικόν; meanwhile, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity and strife, one could abstain from that word. Similarly, l. c. § 9. and 10. p. 265. b., they warn concerning the term essential, although it can be said in a sound sense that the power of illuminating pertains to the essence of the Word, insofar as things are otherwise thought to pertain to the essence of a thing not only as constitutive, but also as consecutive and necessarily connected, with the name of essence NB. taken more broadly; yet because this term is ambiguous and liable to calumny, another can be substituted in its place, and it can be said that the power of illuminating, converting, etc., pertains to the total perfection of the Word, because, without indicating this virtue, the Word of God cannot be perfectly described. Conf. p. 225. b. Huelsemannus: “The instruments (the Word of God and the sacraments) exercise virtue, when applied to a suitable subject, by way of an instrumental cause—not indeed physically through the contact of an agent, just as opium, rhubarb, poison, fire, etc., act physically upon suitable subjects; but morally, by illuminating the mind, moving the will, purging the affections, etc., just as Christ, in the raising of Lazarus, by calling and commanding him, is said to have acted not physically, but morally, namely with respect to the passive subject. For thus is the term morally to be accepted here, so that it is opposed not ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY. to hyperphysical contact and motion, but is only contradistinguished from physical motion and contact, which occurs between material things.” (Praelect. in F. C. p. 436. sq.) Quenstedtius: "Rathmann and Movius pretend that the Word of God is merely an instrument and vehicle of the Holy Spirit, and that therefore divine efficacy is not natural or intrinsic to the Word of God itself; but we reply: Strictly speaking, it is not the Word of God itself, but the external ministry of the Word or the external and ministerial economy of the Word that is an instrument or vehicle of the Holy Spirit; the Word itself, however, is spirit and life (John 6:63). Rathmann attempts to prove a representational and separable union of the Holy Spirit and the Word from the German words of the litany: 'Give Your Spirit and power to the Word' (see Rathmann, *contra Dieder*, p. 15, and in the *Erinnerung*, p. 34). But here, too, by the term 'Word,' the ministerial dispensation of the Word or the external preaching of the Word is understood." (L. c. f. 268.) Indeed, that same infinite virtue, which is essentially, in itself, and independently in God, and through which God illuminates and converts men, has been communicated to the Word, and, as communicated to the Word, it must nevertheless be viewed here as divine. Cf. *Jenens. Consil.* loc. cit. pp. 265b, 266b, 267a, and the preceding page 242b, from which the blessed Musaeus reviews certain points in *Introd.* 1. c. Cap. V, p. 566. This assertion is proved from Ephesians 1:19, where that virtue or power, through which God, by means of the Word, illuminates and converts men, is said to be the same as that excellent magnitude of divine power and strength which He exerted in raising Jesus from the dead. And for this reason it is said in Romans 1:16 that the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes—not that the Word of the Gospel itself, in the nominative case and speaking properly, is the power of God itself, which does not really differ from the essence of God (for thus the Gospel would be God Himself); but that it is a powerful organ, by a customary metonymy, concerning which see D. Glassius, *Philol. S. L. V. Tract. I.* p. 25, whom the blessed Dannhauer cites and follows in these words in *Hodos. Chr. Phaen. I.* p. 95. (64.) Indeed, according to Glassius, it is called δΰναμις, i.e., an organ or medium through which God exerts His power in bringing believers to salvation and preserving them. And it comes to the same thing that he teaches in *Gramm. S. Tract I. Can. VII.* p. 395 (27), that in the cited place the abstract is put for the concrete, or the substantive for the adjective with significant emphasis and energy; so that the Gospel is called power, i.e., notably powerful and efficacious for the conversion and salvation of men. Similarly, when Christ says in John 6:63: "My words are Spirit and life," the divine force and efficacy of the divine Word (not only preached, but also written) is indicated, not only in order to signify, but to confer efficiently the gifts of the Holy Spirit and spiritual life. However, the expression is metonymical, not indeed of the signate for the sign, but of the effect for the cause; as our forefathers expressly taught in *App. Consil. Ded.* p. 308b: "It is such (they are speaking of the words of Christ: 'the words that I speak are spirit and life') a metonymical expression; the external and internal Word is called spirit and life because it brings spirit and life with it." And a little later: "If one rightly distinguishes between cause and effect, then the life-giving Word, which is the cause of spiritual life, and the life itself, which is the effect of the life-giving Word, must always be distinguished." Confer the blessed Glassius, *Lib. V. Philol. S. Tr. I. cap. I. n. 1.* p. 3; the blessed Tarnovius on John ch. VI, P. 3, p. 555.

Latin:

Sed unde hoc suum decretum contra antiquitatis testimonia probant et confirmant? Num proferunt certa et manifesta quaedam documenta ex testificationibus primae apostolicae et veteris ecclesiae, quod libri illi controversi eandem certitudinem et parem auctoritatem cum reliquis, de quibus nunquam dubitatum fuit, habeant? Nihil minus; nequ^ enim possunt hoc facere. Sed rapiunt sibi hanc potestatem, quod papa cum suis praelatis possit et illis et forsan aliis etiam libris impertiri canonicam auctoritatem, quam nec ex se, nec ex suis auctoribus merentur et quam tempore apostolorum et primitivae ecclesiae non habuerunt, sicut Pighius contendit.

Quin igitur aperte dicunt, quod res est? Licet probari non possit, libros illos vel a prophetis, vel ab apostolis sive scriptos, sive comprobatos et a prima veterique ecclesia certo et constanter receptos, imo licet contrarium manifestissimis antiquitatis testimoniis meridiana luce clarius probetur: hoc tamen non obstante statuimus et decernimus, certo hoc credendum esse, licet nulla a nobis hujus rei idonea proferantur documenta, quia (si dis placet) plenitudo hujusmodi antichristianae potestatis sepulta est in scrinio pectoris pontificii. —

Dicunt anathema omnibus, qui libros apocryphos non recipiunt eadem certitudine et auctoritate, sicut canonicos. Anathema igitur erit Eusebius, Hieronymus, Origenes, Melito et tota prima apostolica ea ecclesia, ex cujus testificatione illa, quae supra de libris istis recitavimus, accepta sunt. . .

Tota igitur disputatio in hac quaestione consistit: an certum et indubitatum sit, libros illos, de quibus haec controversia est, esse Scripturam divinitus inspiratam a prophetis et apostolis, quae divinitus auctoritatem illam habuerunt vel editam vel approbatam. Tota antiquitas respondet, non esse certum, sed propter multorum contradictiones fuisse dubitatum. Tridentinum vero supercilium anathema minatur, nisi quis illos susceperit pari, imo eadem certitudine et auctoritate, sicut reliquos libros, de quibus nunquam dubitatum fuit. Quid igitur mirum est, quod parasiti quidam pontificii disputarunt, papam posse novos fidei articulos condere, cum hoc loco novam Scripturam canonicam fabricare non vereatur? ut nullum amplius sit dubium, quis sit ille, qui, in templo Dei sedens, super omne, quod Deus dicitur, extollitur, 2 Thess. 2. —

Numquid igitur simpliciter abjiciendi et damnandi sunt libri illi? Nequaquam hoc quaerimus. Quem igitur usum habet haec disputatio? Respondeo: ut regula fidei sive sanae in ecclesia doctrinae certa sit. Ex solis enim libris canonicis auctoritatem ecclesiasticorum dogmatum confirmandam veteres censuerunt, sicut testimonia supra allegata sunt. Solius canonicae Scripturae auctoritas idonea judicata fuit ad roboranda illa, quae in contentionem veniunt; reliquos vero libros, quos Cyprianus ecclesiasticos, Hieronymus apocryphos nominat, legi quidem voluerunt in ecclesia ad aedificationem plebis, non ad, auctoritatem ecclesiarum dogmatum confirmandam. Non enim volueyuiit illos proferri ad auctoritatem ex his fidei confirmandam. Et illorum auctoritas ad roboranda ea, quae ln contentionem veniunt, minus idonea judicata fuit. Nullum igitur dogma ex istis libris exstrui debet, quod non habet certa et manifesta fundamenta et testimonia in aliis canoni

cis libris. Nihil, qnod controversum est, ex istis libris probari potest, si non extent aliae probationes et confirmationes in libris canonicis. Sed quae in illis libris dicuntur, exponenda et intelllgenda sunt juxta analogiam eorum, quae manifeste traduntur in libris canonicis. Hanc esse vetustatis sententiam, nullum est dubium. Sed concilium Tridentinum propter illam ipsam causam necessariam et verissimam hanc veteris ecclesiae distinctionem infringit, subvertit et tollit, quia (sicut Andradius meus inquit) non volunt se in has conjicere angustias, ut omnibus aliis praesidiis destituti a sola canonica Scriptura fidem mutuentur. Inquit enim synodus Tridentina, se ideo ex libris apocryphis facere canonicos, ut ostendat, quibus potissimum testimoniis et praesidiis in confirmandis dogmatibus et instaurandis moribus sit usura.“ (Exam. Conc. Trid. Ed. Genev. f. 48. sq. 50. 51. sq.) Idem docent Flacius, A. Osiander (f 1617), Aeg. Hunnius, Hafenrefferus, C. Dietericus, F. Balduinus, Th. Thummius et a. Cf. „Ist derjenige für einen Ketzer oder gefährlichen Irrlehrer zu erklären, welcher nicht alle in dem Convolut des N.T. befindlichen Bücher für kanonisch hält und erklärt?“ Vid. „Lehre und Wehre“ II, 204—216.

Itaque etiam hodie a quibusdam apocryphi dicuntur, ab aliis commodius canonici secundi ordinis seu δευτερυχανονιχοί. Non enim absconduntur, cum norma doctrinae postulatur, sed auctoritatem hanc inter christianos, praesertim nostros, hodie communiter habent. Vid. Gerh. Exeg. § 242.Gerhardus: „Nos quidem (illis) nondum permoveri possumus, ut libri hujus (Apocalypseos) auctoritatem rejiciamus, vel Cerintho eum attribuamus, sed Johannem apostolum illius auctorem statuimus. . . . Interim tamen, cum in primitiva ecclesia aliquamdiu apud quosdam de hujus libri auctore dubitatum fuerit, ideo ad secundi ordinis canonicos eum referimus; non quidem canonicam auctoritatem ei detrahentes, interim nec reliquis libris canonicis, de quibus nunquam dubitatum fuit, simpliciter et per omnia ipsum conjungentes; et aequissimo jure postulamus, interpretationem hujus libri instituendam esse talem, quae cura primi ordinis canonicis libris nulla ratione pugnet.“ (Disputatt. theologic. Jenae, 1655. p. 1015. sq.) Vid. b. Glassius lib. I. Phil. 8. Tract. II. Conf. Buxborfii Anticriticam et Hottingeri Thes. Philol. fol. 118. sqq., ubi ostenditur, ne casu quidem et injuria temporum codices modernos universos et capitaliter esse corruptos.§ 39.

Ad affectiones Scripturae s. pertinet porro secundo efficacia a ejus, seu quod habet vim aut potentiam activam b supernaturalem c ac vere divinam, d ad producendos supernaturales effectus, scilicet mentes hominum convertendas, regenerandas et e renovandas, ex divina f ordinatione sibi, quoad sensum g spectatae, intime h et indissolubiliter i etiam extra usum actu primo k unitam; quaeque, accedente usu lectionis, auditus aut meditationis, sese actu secundo l exserit, ita ut effectus illi gratiae super

Π. naturales, prout a Deo, tanquam causa principali, sic ab ipsa Scriptura, tanquam a causa efficiente m instrumentali, simul et junctim, uno indiviso influxu n efficienter producantur. Quenstedtius: „Theses; Habet V. D. ex ipsius Dei ordinatione et voluntate etiam ante et extra usum legitimum intrinsecam, divinam et sufficientem, indifferentemque ad omnes homines vim et efficaciam ad spirituales et divinos effectus (cum gratiosos et salviflcos; ut regenerationis, conversionis, illuminationis, salvationis; tum punitorios, ut concussionis, mortificationis, damnationis etc.) immediate, vere ac proprie producendos.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 16. f. 246.)

Quam cum auctoritate Scripturae conjungendam esse, diximus not. e. ad § 32 Intelligimus autem nomine efficaciae (quo alias actus secundus, seu actualis operatio, sicut apud Graecos nomine ένεργείας, designatur) hoc loco ipsam δύναμη ίνερργτικψ, seu potentiam effectricem spiritualium effectuum. B. Mus. Introd. P. II. c. VIII. § 2. p. 559 Non vim mere objectivam, sed effectivam, seu productivam virium ac motuum supernaturalium in intellectu et voluntate hominis, natura coeci et mortui ad spiritualia amplectenda. Mus. l. c. p. 560 Sane nec in sermonis cultu, neque gravitate sententiarum, aut rationum pondere oratorio quaerendam, sed omni vi agendi creata ac finita superiorem, quae proinde non tam Scripturae, seu ex parte vocum, seu ex parte rerum significatarum naturalis est, sed supernaturalis, seu cum natura Scripturae, ex divina ordinatione intime conjuncta; ut in seqq. dicitur. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 3. 4. p. 561. 562 Sic autem etiam majores nostri, occasione controversiae Bathmannianae, in App. Consil. Ded. Q. VI. § 3. fol. 263. b. 264. a. docuerunt, vim illuminandi et convertendi competere Scripturae non ex necessitate physica, nec naturali, sed supernaturali modo, ac theologos, qui forte dixerint, verbum Dei habere vim illam naturalem, usos fuisse voce illa non in oppositione ad υπερφυσικόν, sed in oppositione ad παραστατικόν Rathmannianum; interim cavendae ambiguitatis et litium causa abstineri posse ab illa voce. Similiter l. c. § 9. et 10. p. 265. b. de termino τοδ essentialis monent, quamvis sano sensu dici possit, vim illuminandi pertinere ad essentiam verbi, prout alias non solum constitutiva, sed etiam consecutiva et necessario connexa, ad essentiam alicujus rei pertinere putentur, nomine essentiae NB. latius accepto; quia tamen hic terminus ambiguus et calumniae obnoxius sit, alium in ejus locum substitui ac diei posse, vim illuminandi, convertendi etc. pertinere ad totam perfectionem verbi, quia, non indicata hac virtute, verbum Dei non possit perfecte describi. Conf. p. 225. b. Huelsemannus: „Instrumenta (v. D. et sacr.) virtutem exercent, applicata ad subjectum idoneum, per modum causae Instrumentalis non physice quidem per contactum agentis, sicut opium, rhabarbarum, venenum, ignis etc. physice agunt in subjecta idonea; sed moraliter, illustrando mentem, commovendo voluntatem, purgando affectus etc., quemadmodum Christus in suscitatione Lazari compellando et jubendo eum non physice, sed moraliter dicitur egisse, scilicet respectu subjecti patientis. Sic enim τό moraliter hic accipiendum est, ut opponatur non DB PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE. hyperphysico contactui et motui, sed contradistinguatur tantum motui et contactui physico, qui inter res materiatas versatur.“ (Praelect. in F, C. p. 436. sq.) Quenstedtius: „Praetendunt Rathmannus et Movius, verbum Dei esse solum Άχτ/μα et vehiculum Spiritus S., adeoque ipsi verbo Dei efficaciam divinam non esse naturalem sive intrinsecam; sed resp.: Non tam ipsum Dei verbum accurate loquendo, quam externum verbi ministerium vel externam et ministerialem verbi οικονομίαν esse δχψα vel vehiculum Spiritus S.; ipsum autem verbum est spiritus et vita Joh. 6, 63 Rathmannus παραστατικήν et separabilem Spiritus S. et verbi unionem probare conatur ex verbis germanicis litaniae: ,Deinen Geist und Kraft zum Wort geben*, vid. Rathmann, contra Dieder, p. 15., und in der Erinnerung p. 34 Verum et hic verbi voce ministerialis verbi dispensatio sive externa verbi praedicatio intelligitur.“ (L. c. f. 268.) Nempe eadem illa infinita virtus, quae essentialiter, per se et independenter in Deo est, et per quam Deus homines illuminat et convertit, verbo communicata est, et, tanquam verbo communicata, divina tamen, hic spectari debet. Conf. Jenem. Consil. loc. cit. pag. 265. b. 266. b. 267. a. et p. praeced. 242. b., unde quaedam recenset b. Mus. Introd. 1. c. Cap. V. p. 566 Probatur autem haec assertio ex Ep. ad Ephes. 1, 19., ubi virtus aut potentia illa, per quam Deus, mediante verbo, homines illuminat et convertit, eadem esse dicitur cum excellente illa magnitudine potentiae divinae et robore fortitudinis, quod exseruit, suscitans Jesum ex mortuis. Atque hac ratione dicitur Rom. 1, 16., Evangelium esse potentiam Dei ad salutem omni credenti, non, quod ipsum verbum evangelii in casu recto et proprie loquendo sit ipsa potentia Dei, quae ab essentia Dei realiter non differt (sic enim evangelium esset Deus ipse); sed quod sit organum potens, usitata metonymia, de qua D. Olass. Philol. S. L. V. Tract. I. p. 25., quem his verbis citat et sequitur b. Dannk. in Hodos. Chr. Phaen. I. p. 95. (64.) Nempe juxta Glassium dicitur δΰναμις i. e. organum aut medium, per quod Deus suam potentiam in credentibus ad salutem adducendis et conservandis exserit. Atque eodem redit, quod is in Gramin. 8 Tract I. Can. ΥΠ. p. 395. (27.) docet, poni l. c. abstractum pro concreto, seu substantivum pro adjectivo cum insigni emphasi et energia; ita ut evangelium dicatur potentia, h. e., potens et efficax insigniter ad conversionem et salvationem hominum. Similiter quando Joh. 6, 63 Christus ait: Verba mea sunt Spiritus et vita, utitjue indicatur verbi divini (non solum praedicati, sed et scripti) divina vis et efficacia, seu in ordine non ad significanda tantum, sed Conferenda efficienter dona Spiritus S. et vitam spiritualem. Locutio autem metonymica est, non quidem signati pro signo, sed effectus pro causa; prout expresse majores nostri docuerunt in App. Consil. Ded. pag. 308. b.: Es ist solches (loquuntur de verbis Christi: die Wort, die ich rede, sind Geist und Leben) eine metonymica locutio, das äusserliche und innerliche Wort wird Geist und Leben genennet, weil es Geist und Leben mit sich bringet. Et paulo post: So man causam und effectum billig unterscheidet, so, muss auch das lebendigmachende Wort, welches des geistlichen Lebens causa ist, und das Leben selber, welches des lebendigmachenden Worts effectus ist, jederzeit unterschieden werden. Confer b. Glassium Lib. V. Philol. S. Tr. I. cap. I. n. 1. p. 3. b. Tarnovium in Joh. cap. VI. P. 3. p. 555. ,155


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: b. Th. Thummius in *De Majest

b. Th. Thummius in *De Majest. Chr.* p. 252, and those who follow him, b. A. Prueckner in *Vindic. ad h. l.* p. 624. By this, however, the efficacy or active power of the Word is not denied, but established. For when the Word is called the cause of the gifts of the Spirit and of spiritual life, it is certainly necessary that an active power, as the reason for causing, be attributed to it. Furthermore, this efficacy of the preached and written Word is also proven by the passages Rom. 10:17, where faith is said to be ἐξ ἀκοῆς, that is, perceived from doctrine or hearing (the reason for reading is the same). The particle ἐξ is causal, and argues for a power of causing in that which is heard (or read); and John 17:20, where it is said that men will believe διὰ τοῦ λόγου, through the Word, and thus, by the force of the particle διά, the power of exciting faith is attributed to the λόγος itself, or the Word of God, as preached by the apostles.

Quenstedtius: “The Word of God, considered formally, is not to be numbered among the catalog of creatures, since it is the divine concept or the mind of God, the counsel of God, as it is described in the Holy Scriptures. If you say: The Word of God is either creator or creature; we respond that the opposition is not sufficiently accurate, since it is not necessary that everything which is not the Creator be a creature of God. Creation certainly is not the Creator Himself, nor yet is it a creature, an instance which the Saxon theologians use, p. 238; therefore some say that the Word of God is something of God, as Paul speaks, τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ 1 Cor. 2:11, that it is a certain divine emanation. The divine virtue, communicated to the Word of God, is certainly not a creature,” (L. c. f. 270.)

Concerning these things we shall say more below in the *loci* on regeneration, conversion, and renovation. For the virtue of illuminating is in the Word by the free will of God, *by a voluntary divine ordinance*, as our elders write l. c. p. 264. a., and they repeat and inculcate this; they also prove it from 1 Cor. 1:21: It pleased God (and it was freely established by God), through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.

Certainly, that the Jena theologians admit that this power is not really joined and united to the letters and points of words written on paper, they confess l. c. fol. 200. a., 240. a., 265. a., 270. b. But they teach that it is joined to the sense of Scripture, whether it be in the mind of the apostles, or expressed by them through preaching, or written in a book, or in the mind of the readers, p. 240. a., 267. a., 273. b.

Quenstedtius: “Distinguish between the Word of God materially, for the characters, points, letters, and syllables adhering to paper or parchment, by which the word of salvation is signified, or even for the sound and external voices formed in the air, passing and vanishing (which are rather the *vehicle* of the divine Word, through which it is transferred to the ears and afterwards into the heart of man, than the Word of God itself), but formally, for the divine concept and sense expressed and exhibited by letters and syllables in writing and by voices in preaching. In the former way, it is called the Word of God only improperly and *significatively*, but in this latter way it is *properly* and truly the Word of God, the wisdom of God, the mind of God, the counsel of God. We do not ascribe divine power and efficacy to the former, but to the latter. For we do not posit that a certain divine converting, regenerating, illuminating, etc., power subjectively exists or inheres in the letters, characters, syllables, or voices themselves, as such.” (L. c. q. 16. f. 246.)

Thus, against Rathmann, the blessed Musaeus taught that that divine power is not communicated to Scripture only in use through a mere *presentation* and external... ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

for assistance, as viewed in itself and outside of use, is destitute of the power of illuminating and converting the souls of men, and is ineffective and a dead letter; but Scripture is always effective in itself and possesses the power of illuminating and converting the souls of men, whether it is viewed in use or in itself outside of use. Introd. l. c. § 6. p. 567. and § 7. p. 571.

i) Namely, by virtue of that ordination, indeed freely made but never to be revoked, as the Jena theologians write l. c. p. 264. a.: That, by virtue of a voluntary order made by God Himself, the power of illumination, conversion, and salvation is always and inseparably united with the Word.

k) For although that divine power, which on the part of the thing is the very essence of God, is not communicated to Scripture, which is the λόγος προφορικός of God, in such a way that it inheres in it formally and subjectively (for even the formal element of divine Scripture is the sense of the signs, not that archetype which is immanent to the divine mind, but the έκτυπος, proposed, delineated, and represented through these signs concerning divine things; according to the mind and words of the blessed Huelsemann in Praelect. Form. Concord. Art. VIII. S. I. Part. I. § 3. p. 432.).

For which reason the Jena theologians l. c. diligently and often warned that the same virtue indeed belongs to God and to Scripture, but not in the same way: for to God it belongs essentially, principally, originally, and independently; but to the Word of Scripture it belongs dependently, participatively, or by way of communication (mittheilungsweise), see p. 225. b. 264. b. § 5. 267. a. § 14. 270. b.

Nevertheless, the conjunction of divine virtue with the Word must certainly be acknowledged, concerning which our predecessors may be seen l. c. p. 270. a. 271. a., where they also refer to the words of Luther, Tom. IV. J. L. f. 530. b.: Scripture has an inseparable companion, the Holy Spirit. Likewise the words of the Wittenberg Theologians in the censure of Tr. Movius: The Spirit is always conjoined with the Word, conf. p. 246. b. p. 264. a. 265. b. 266. a., which words the blessed Musaeus also cites Introd. p. 569. 570. and finally p. 577. 578. teaches how the divine power of illuminating and converting the souls of men is conjoined to the sense of Scripture, both outside of the intellect and insofar as it is apprehended by the intellect: namely, in the intellect through its actual conjunction or union with the species of the signified things, impressed and expressed; but to the sense viewed outside of the intellect, it inheres insofar as God by His most free will has so ordained that the Holy Spirit, with His divine power and potency of illuminating and converting the souls of men, is always and everywhere present to the Holy Scripture, even outside of the intellect, and when it is read or proposed by the voice of a teacher, He penetrates to the soul of man at the same time, united everywhere with the species of the signified things, partly impressed, partly expressed, and exerts Himself through them for conversion.

Quenstedtius: “The reason for the sacraments and the Word of God is different, because the nature of the sacraments consists in an action, which cannot exist without use. But the Word of God does not consist essentially in the act of meditation, reading, or preaching, but these things only happen to the Word, which remains forever when these cease. Therefore, it does not hold: The sacraments do not exist outside of use, therefore neither does the Word exist outside of use. For the reason is different.” (L. c. f. 272.)

1) Namely, unless its operation is hindered on the part of man by the security of the flesh or the thorns of pleasures or the cares of this world. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 7. p. 571. 574. and the Predecessors in App. Consil. Ded. p. 228. b., p. 241. a. b.,

p. 265. a., § 7. p. 269. a, b., p. 270. b., 271. a., in which last place the words of the blessed J. Brentius in the *Confessio Wirtembergensis*, chapter on the Gospel, p. 407, are also explained, where he states that the Gospel, when it is contained only in letters or even pronounced by voice, but outside of its legitimate use, is not of itself efficacious: which words the blessed Balduinus (Comm. on 1 Ep. to Thess. c. I. P. II. Q. I. p. 1127) and the blessed Dannhauerus (in *Hodos. Chr.* Ph. I. p. 64. [94.]) report and make their own, namely, that they ought to be understood regarding efficacy viewed in *actu secundo*, which has no place outside the use of hearing, reading, meditation, etc.; add p. 340. a. 350. a. Quenstedtius: "This is the native power and character of the divine Word, that it persuades its truth and never fails to persuade, unless its operation is shaken off and hindered by a voluntary, adventitious contumacy, which is added to the natural repugnance." (L. c. f. 250.)

m) Indeed, our predecessors inculcated this distinction between God and His Word, as principal and instrumental cause, in this matter and in the Rathmannian controversy, so solicitously and frequently that they could not have done so more. See l. c. p. 225. a. end, p. 227. b. beginning, p. 228. a. near the end, § 20. p. 231. b. near the end, § 27. from the *Formula of Concord* p. 236. a. in the middle, p. 240. a. b., p. 242. b. beginning, p. 247. b. in the middle, p. 253. a. beginning and b. middle, p. 254. a. beginning and middle, from the *F. C.* p. 267. b. § 17., p. 343. b. in the middle, p. 344. a. beginning and middle.

Where especially the passages on p. 240 and 343 are to be observed, and most of all the passage on p. 267. § 16., which the blessed Musaeus also mentions (*Introd.* § 9. p. 593), where the distinction between a passive and a cooperative instrument is brought forward, and it is shown that Scripture, although it is rightly distinguished from passive instruments, nevertheless cannot be denied to be an instrument (namely, a cooperative one); with the Symbolic Books themselves leading the way, especially the *Augsburg Confession*, Art. V., cf. l. c. App. *Consil. Dedek.* p. 243. b., § 37. p. 272. a. end.

And this opinion concerning the term "instrument" or "instrumental cause" in this matter—of applying the Word of God appropriately in relation to supernatural effects—the aforementioned doctors never deserted or changed; rather, they repeated and inculcated it whenever the occasion arose; as appears from the blessed J. Gerhard (*Comm. on 1 Ep. Peter* c. 1. v. 23. p. 136): "Regeneration, as the apostle describes it from the instrumental cause, which is the Word of God, etc."; the blessed Himmelus (*Syntag. Disp.* XVIII. p. 20): "The instrumental cause (of repentance) is the Word of God, etc." Cf. his *Colleg. Anal. Libri Conc.* Disp. III. § 43., the blessed Glassius (*Philol. S.* in the place cited above, note a.), the blessed Gothofr. Cundisius, with the blessed Hutterus leading the way in *Comp. L. IX. de Lib. Arb.* Q. XVI. and XXI. p. 662. § 2.: "The Word of God is an *organon* for working (conversion), etc.," and p. 671: "There are two causes of conversion: one the principal efficient, the Holy Spirit; the other the instrumental, the Word of God, which is the *organon* of the Holy Spirit, by which He effects the conversion of man"; the blessed Christ. Chemnitius (*Comm. ad Rom.* 1. v. 16. p. 38 and 43): "The Gospel is δύναμις του θεού, that is, a powerful and efficacious *organum* or instrument, etc."; the blessed J. E. Gerhard (*in Isag. LL.* of his father, L. XVIII. de Poenitentia, th. IX. p. 767): "The *organike* or instrumental cause of repentance is the Word of God, etc."

Latin:

b. Th. Thummium de Majest. Chr. fteavftp. p. 252. et, qui illos sequitur, b. A. Prueeknerum in Vindic. ad h. 1. p. 624. Per hoc autem non negatur, sed adstruitur efficacia sive vis activa verbi. Quando enim verbum causa donorum Spiritus et vitae spiritualis dicitur, utique vim activam, velut rationem causandi, ei tribui necesse est. Caeterum efficaciam hanc verbi praedicati et scripti probant etiam loca Rom. 10, 17., ubi fides dicitur esse έξ άχοής, seu ex doctrina, auditu (par est ratio lectionis) percepta. Particula autem causalis est, et vim causandi in eo, quod auditur (aut legitur), arguit; et Joh. 17, 20., ubi dicuntur homines credituri διά του λόγου, per verbum, adeoque vi particulae διά, ipsi λόγω aut verbo Dei, per apostolos praedicando, tribuitur vis excitandi fidem.

Quenstedtius: „V. D. formaliter consideratum non est creaturarum catalogo accensendum, quum sit conceptus divinus vel mens Dei, consilium Dei, prout in s. L. describitur. Si dicas: V. D. aut creator est, aut creatura; respondemus, oppositionem non esse satis accuratam, quum non necessum sit, ut omne, quod non est creator, sit creatura Dei. Creatio certe non est ipse creator, nec tamen creatura est, qua instantia utuntur decisores Saxon, p. 238.; ideo dicunt nonnulli, v. D. esse aliquid Dei, ut Paulus loquitur, τα τον &t:ov 1 Cor. 2, 11., esse απορροήν quandam divinam. Divina utique virtus, verbo Dei communicata, creatura non est,“ (L. c. f. 270.)

De quibus plura dicemus infra in LL. de regeneratione, conversione et renovatione. Virtus enim illuminandi in verbo est ex libera Dei voluntate, aus freiwilliger göttlicher Ordnung, prout majores nostri scribunt l. c. p. 264. a. idque repetunt et inculcant; probant etiam ex 1 Cor. 1, 21.: Placuit Deo (et libere constitptum est a Deo), per stultitiam praedicationis salvos facere credentes.

Certe quod vis illa non verborum literis et apicibus, in charta scriptis, realiter conjuncta et unita sit, fatentur Jenenses 1. c. fol. 200. a. 240. a. 265. a. 270. b. Sensui autem Scripturae, sive sit in mente apostolorum, sive ab ipsis per praedicationem exprimatur, sive scriptus sit in libro, sive sit in mente legentium, conjunctam esse docent p. 240. a. 267* a. 273. b.

Quenstedtius: „Dist. inter verbum Dei materialiter pro characteribus, apicibus, literis et syllabis in charta sive membrana haerentibus, qhibus verbum salutis signatur, vel etiam pro sono et Vocibus externis in aere formatis, transeuntibus et evanescentibus (quae verbi divini όχημα sive vehiculum potius sunt, per quod illud ad aures et postea in cor hominis transfertur, quam ipsum verbum Dei), sed formaliter pro conceptu et sensu divino literis et syllabis in scriptione et vocibus in praedicatione expresso et exhibito. Isto modo tantum improprie et σημαντικώς dicitur verbum Dei, hoc vero modo κυρίως.et proprie est verbum Dei, sapientia Dei, mens Dei, consilium Dei. Non illis, sed huic vim et efficaciam divinam adscribimus. Neque enim statuimus, ipsis literis, characteribus, syllabis aut vocibus, qua talibus, vim quandam divinam conversivam, regeneratricem, illuminatricem etc. subjective inesse aut inhaerere.“ (L. c. q. 16. f. 246.)

Ita contra Rathmannum docuit b. Musaeus, vim illam divinam communicari Scripturae non demum in usu per nudam παράστασιν et exter DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

nam assistentiam, ita ut in se et extra usum spectata, vi illuminandi convertendique hominum animos destituta, inefficax et litera mortua sit; sed Scripturam in se semper efficacem esse et vi illuminandi convertendique hominum animos pollere, sive ea in usu, sive in se extra usum spectetur. Introd. 1. c. § 6. p. 567. et § 7. p. 571.

i) Nempe vi illius ordinationis, libere quidem factae, sed nunquam revocandae, prout Jenenses 1. c. pag. 264. a. scribunt: Dass, vermöge freiwilliger von Gott selbst gemachter Ordnung, die Kraft der Erleuchtung, Bekehrung und Seligmachung immerdar und unauflöslich mit dem Wort vereinbaret.

k) Quanquam enim vis illa divina, quae ex parte rei est ipsa Dei essentia, Scripturae, quae est λόγος προφορικός Dei, non ita communicetur, ut ei formaliter et subjective insit (nam et formale Scripturae divinae est sensus signorum non αρχέτυπος ille et immanens menti divinae, sed έκτυπος, propositus, delineatus et repraesentatus per haec signa de rebus divinis intelligibüia; juxta mentem et verba b. Huelsemanni in Praelect. Form. Concord. Art. VIII. S. I. Part. I. § 3. pag. 432.).

Quam ob rem Jenenses l. c. diligenter ac saepe monuerunt, eandem quidem virtutem competere Deo et Scripturae, verum non eodem modo: Deo enim eam esse essentialiter, principaliter, originaliter et independenter; verbo Scripturae autem eam competere dependenter, participative aut per communicationem (mittheilungsweise), vid. p. 225. b. 264. b. § 5. 267. a. § 14. 270. b.

Utique tamen agnoscenda est conjunctio virtutis divinae cum verbo, de qua videri possunt antecessores nostri l. c. p. 270. a. 271. a., ubi etiam eo referunt verba Luiheri, Tom. IV. J. L. f. 530. b.: Habet scriptura inseparabilem comitem Spiritum Sanctum. Item verba Theologorum Wittebergensium in censura Tr. Movii: Spiritus semper conjungitur cum verbo, conf. p. 246. b. p. 264. a. 265. b. 266. a., quae verba etiam adducit b. Mus. Introd. p. 569. 570. ac denique p. 577. 578. docet, quomodo vis divina illuminandi et convertendi hominum animos conjuncta sit sensui Scripturae, cum extra intellectum, tum quatenus intellectu apprehensus est: scilicet in intellectu per actualem sui conjunctionem seu unionem cum speciebus rerum significatarum impressis et expressis; extra intellectum autem spectato sensui eam inesse, quatenus Deus liberrima sua voluntate ita ordinaverit, ut Scripturae sacrae, etiam extra intellectum, Spiritus Sanctus sua divina vi et potentia illuminandi convertendique hominum animos semper et ubique adsit et cum eadem lecta, vel docentis voce proposita, simul ad hominis animum penetret, ubique cum speciebus rerum significatarum impressis partim, partim expressis unita, ad conversionem sese per illas exserat.

Quenstedtius: „Diversa est ratio sacramentorum et verbi Dei, quia sacramentorum natura consistit in actione, quae sine usu esse nequit. At verbum Dei non consistit essentialiter in actu meditationis, lectionis aut praedicationis, sed haec tantum accidunt verbo, quod illis desinentibus in aeternum permanet. Non ergo valet: Sacramenta extra usum non sunt, ita nec verbum extra usum est. Diversa enim est ratio.“ (L. c. f. 272.)

1) Nempe nisi ex parte hominem securitate carnis spinisve voluptatum aut curarum hujus seculi ejus operatio impediatur. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 7. p. 571. 574. et Antecessores in App. Consil. Ded. p. 228. b., p. 241. a. b.,

m) Sane discrimen hoc, Dei et verbi ejus, tanquam causae principalis et instrumentalis, in hoc negotio, et controversia Rathmanniana, ita solicite et frequenter inculcarunt antecessores nostri, ut non possent magis. ### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: But if the Saxon theologians, in the German writing published in the year 1629…

But if the Saxon theologians, in the German writing published in the year 1629 on the occasion of the Rathmannian controversy, *von der heiligen Schrift*, p. 141 sqq., did not equally attribute the name and concept of instrument or instrumental cause to the Word of God... ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY. seem to attribute, it must be observed that this is said with respect to passive instruments (which, namely, Kathmann alone acknowledged), which have in themselves no power (mere passive instruments, which have no power in themselves) p. 141., mere passive instruments and άεργα (mere powerless and passive tools) p. 142. 143., such as are commonly called by the name of instruments, from whose rank the Word of God is to be removed (the Word of God is not to be placed in the number of common passive instruments and tools) p. 146., whence, or from the hypothesis that the word "instrument," without an addition, would seem to designate passive instruments, those theologians added that the Word of God, in this stricter sense, is not an instrument, but if it must be called by that name, the word "instrument" must be taken ίν πλάτει, in a broader signification, p. 146.

Namely, so that it does not precisely denote passive instruments, but includes active ones no less.

This very thing the blessed Musaeus also acknowledges and inculcates, when he accurately and solicitously distinguishes between other instruments, which are not joined with the principal cause except in use (and which coincide with those that are called passive), e.g., an axe, a hammer, etc., and others, which have the principal cause always joined to them even outside of use, by supposition and by virtue; and consequently also always have in themselves the power of the principal cause to act (and are active instruments): such as are the members of the human body, e.g., the hand; and he refers Holy Scripture not to the former, but to the latter class of instruments, inasmuch as, just as it always, even outside of use, has the Holy Spirit joined to it by supposition and virtue, so it also has the power of the principal cause to illuminate and convert, always, even outside of use in itself, Introd. 1. c. § 9. p. 588. 589., clearly in the same manner in which his predecessors wrote in the App. Consil. Dedek. p. 224, a.: An axe is an instrument not joined, but separated; not living, but inanimate; nor does it act by an inherent power, but by one impressed from without, whence it is called, by the hypothesis, especially of Rathmann, a passive instrument, although it acts in its own way. On the contrary, however, the hand in an animate body is a joined, living instrument, acting by an inherent and intrinsic force, whence it is called an active and cooperative instrument. Conf. p. 267. b., where the Word of God or Holy Scripture is indeed removed from the class of passive instruments, but is reckoned among the cooperative ones.

Indeed, our other countrymen also, when they dispute against the Schwenkfeldians and similar Enthusiasts, whose frequent objection is (by which they strive to impugn our opinion concerning the efficacy of Scripture) that by this reasoning there is attributed to the Word or Scripture that which is proper to God, they respond by the distinction between the principal and the instrumental cause; that the former is God, the latter the Word of God. See the blessed Conr. Schluesselb. Catal. Haer. Lib. IX. de Stenckfeld. p. 301. sqq., the blessed Theodor. Thumm. in Imp. Weigel. Err. XII. p. 21., the blessed Gerhard in Dispp. Acad. Disp. I. contra Weigel. § 19. p. 827. and very recently the Theologians of Lubeck, Hamburg, and Luneburg in the doctrinal and defensive writing against the Guthmannian patron of revelation P. II.: p. 273. 287. 311. 313. 506. sqq.

But this being admitted, that Scripture is an instrumental cause of spiritual effects, since from the nature of an instrumental cause it seemed to be required and to be declared how Scripture is elevated beyond its native power by the principal cause to produce supernatural effects? The blessed Musaeus taught l. c. § 11. p. 595. sqq., that Holy Scripture is indeed not elevated by the power of the principal cause only in use extrinsically to itself.

not] by a supervening [power] (since it already possesses it intimately conjoined to itself outside of use), but by the fact that the Spirit, by His virtue of illuminating and converting, flows into the illumination and conversion of man simultaneously in act with the Scripture, to which He has long since communicated it, and assists it—for the producing of these effects, which are nobler than its own (the Scripture’s) native and proper virtue (distinct from the virtue of the Holy Spirit)—by the influx of His own nobler (indeed, truly infinite) virtue.

For this reason, the blessed J. Gerh. writes (Tom. VI. L. de Min. Eccl. § 253. p. m. 406): "It pleased God to elevate the external word, as an instrumentally acting cause, to that divine effect of the conversion and salvation of men."

Nor did the blessed Christ. Chemnitius hesitate, in his Disp. de Gratuita Justif. Hom. Pecc. coram Deo, § 18., to defend the same opinion, that God uses the word as an instrumental cause, and that the word, although it does not attain the effect by itself and by its own virtue, is nevertheless elevated by the principal cause beyond its natural virtue to produce it.

Compare, however, with these things which we have said thus far, the blessed Musaeus, *Ausführl. Erklärung*, Lib. I. Q. X. p. 57. sqq. ad 110.

Quenstedtius: "The Word of God, if we wish to speak accurately, is not so much an instrument as a medium, since not every medium is an instrument... The Augsburg Confession indeed uses the word 'instrument' and calls the Word of God an instrument of conversion, but *in a broad sense* and primarily by reason of the material, namely, the external writing, preaching, *economy* or dispensation and ministry, but not properly by reason of the internal virtue of the Holy Spirit communicated to the Word... For the power of God, which is preached concerning the Gospel, is not other than the power of God Himself, but is the very power of God. Who, however, would call this power of God an instrument?" (L. c. f. 270.)

Huelsemannus: "What is the proper and natural and ordinary virtue of the Word of God, as it is God’s, beyond which it must be elevated in the conversion of man? What is natural to the Word of God, what is natural to the sacraments, what is natural to justifying faith, except that which God Himself has implanted in them through supernatural grace? Who has ever heard it said that the media ordained by God for the salvation of men—which Calixtus openly confesses the Word of God to be—must be elevated by God beyond their own proper and natural and ordinary virtue so that they might attain the effect? That the incorruptible seed, the Word of the living and eternal God, must be elevated beyond its own proper and natural virtue? What, finally, is that force and virtue superior to the virtue of the Word of the living and eternal God, to which it must be elevated? Is there given a virtue more virtuous than the virtue of God, a power more powerful than the power of God, by which name the Gospel is called, that it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes?" (Dialys. p. 407.)

The same: "Although a medicinal force is inherent in every Word of God and is never entirely taken away, we nevertheless confess that it is increased by God more or less, or not increased, but left in a state of ordinary efficacy; see Psalm 86:10, Isaiah 5:5 sqq." (Praelect. Form. Conc. p. 440.)

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: I. Of the Schwenkfeldians, Weigelians, Enthusiasts, Anabaptists, and other fanatics, such as Theophrastus Paracelsus, Andreas Osiander, Fabian Teckel and Fanker, Wilhelm Gnapheus, Hermann Rathmann, and Caspar Movius, who all distinguish the Word of God into internal and external, as a genus into two diverse and separable species, separated in act. And to the internal word alone (by which they understand the Son of God Himself, or the Spirit of God coming from heaven and working in the heart of man, or even singular revelations concerning matters of faith)... ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

they understand the divine, immediate, and silent inspirations of the angels) ascribe divine efficacy; but they derogate from the external word, as if it were a human voice, a vanishing sound, and a dead letter, all power and efficacy and divine virtue, or they attribute to it only an objective, significative, and representative virtue, but not an effective one. . .

Rathmann asserts that the divine efficacy is external to the Word of God, separable at any moment, and merely παραστατικήν ("comes from the outside"), and that the Holy Spirit joins Himself with His virtue to the Word ("is added to and joined with") only in the mind, soul, or heart of man, and that only in the legitimate or salutary use. See him in *der Erinnerung* p. 13, 44, 49, where he says: "The axe does not hew, unless the woodcutter first gives the axe power and force; Scripture does not convert, unless the Holy Spirit brings the light of grace and His power to the Scripture.". .

3. Of the Socinians, who also attribute no other efficacy to the written and preached Word than that of signifying. . .

4. Of the Arminians, who, in the inept Bodecher (c. 11, § 4), do not acknowledge any other virtue of the Holy Spirit than that which "consists in the communication of knowable matter and which is communicated to every man.". .

5. Of most Calvinists, who also embrace the distinction between the internal and external Word of God. . . . John Calvin, Inst. IV, c. 14, § 17, says: "It is to be noted that by the external action the minister figures and testifies that God is working within, lest that which God claims for Himself alone be drawn to a mortal man.". .

6. Of certain Papists, who also place the efficacy of the divine Word only in signifying and representing; for thus Bellarmine, distinguishing between external and internal preaching (lib. 1, *de grat. et lib. arbitrio* c. 13, col. 510), says: "The external (preaching) only proposes the object, but does not infuse light into the mind to know it, nor does it inspire the affection to love it.". .

7. Of the Quakers in England. 8. Of Jean de Labadie." (L. c. f. 251—255.)

Zwingli: "Speaking canonically or regularly, we see that among all peoples the external preaching of the apostles and evangelists or bishops preceded faith. Which, however, we attribute solely to the Spirit. For we see, alas! quite many who indeed hear the external preaching of the Gospel, but do not believe, which happens because of a lack of the Spirit. Therefore, wherever prophets or preachers of the Word are sent, it is a sign of the grace of God, which wishes to manifest the knowledge of Himself to His elect. And to whom they are denied, it is a sign of imminent wrath." (*Ad Carolum fidei ratio*, 1530. See *Abgedrungener Unterricht von kirchlicher Vereinigung* by E. S. Cyprian. Tom. II, p. 34.)

Latin:

Quodsi autem theologi Saxonici in scripto Germ., A. 1629. occasione controversiae Rathmannianae edito, von der heiligen Schrift, p. 141. sqq., nomen et conceptum instrumenti aut causae instrumentalis verbo Dei non aeque tri DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE. 150 buere videantur, observandum est, id dici in respectu ad instrumenta (qualia Kathmannus sola agnovit, videlicet) passiva, quae in se nullam wrtutem habent (leidende Instrumenta, die in sich keine Kraft haben) p. 141., Instrumenta mere passiva 'et άεργα (blosse unkräftige und leidende Werkzeuge) p. 142. 143., qualia vulgo nomine instrumentorum appellentur, e quorum censu verbum Dei eximendum sit (das Wort Gottes sei nicht in die Zahl der gemeinen leidenden Instrumente und Werkzeuge zu setzen) p. 146., unde, seu ex hypothesi, quod vox instrumenti, sine addito, designare videretur instrumenta passiva, theologi illi addiderunt, verbum Dei, hoc sensu strictiore, non esse instrumentum, sed si eo nomine appellandum sit, vocem instrumenti ίν πλάτει, in latiore significatu accipi debere, p, 146.

Scilicet ut non praecise passiva instrumenta denotet, sed activa non minus complectatur.

Quod ipsum etiam b. Musaeus agnoscit et inculcat, quando accurate et solicite distinguit inter instrumenta alia, quae cum causa principali conjuncta non sunt, nisi in usu (quaeque coincidunt cum his, quae passiva dicuntur), v. g. securis, malleus etc., et alia, quae causam principalem etiam extra usum sibi semper conjunctam habent supposito et virtute; ac proinde etiam virtutem agendi causae principalis semper in se habent (et sunt instrumenta activa): qualia sint membra corporis humani, v. g. manus; et Scripturam sacram non ad priorem, sed posteriorem classem instrumentorum refert, quippe quae, ut semper, etiam extra usum, Spiritum Sanctum supposita et virtute mbi conjunctum habet, ita habeat etiam ejus, tanquam causae principalis, virtutem illuminandi et convertendi, semper, etiam extra usum in se, Introd. 1. c. § 9. p. 588. 589., plane ad eum modum» quo antecessores ejus in App. Consil. Dedek. p. 224, a. scripserunt: Sectoris est instrumentum non conjunctum, sed separatum; rwn vivum, sed inanime; nec agit virtute insita, sed extrinsecus impressa, unde vocatur ex hypothesi, praesertim Rathmanni, instrumentum passivum, quamvis site modo agat. Contra vero manus in corpore animato est instrumentum conjunctum, vivum, insita et intrinseca vi agens, unde vocatur instrumentum activum et cooperativum. Conf. p. 267. b., ubi verbum Dei seu Scriptura sacra ex passivorum quidem instrumentorum classe eximitur, cooperativis vero accensetur.

Imo vero et alias nostrates, quando adversus Schwenkfeldianos et similes Enthusiastas disputant, quorum frequens objectio est (qua sententiam üostram de efficacia Scripturae impugnare nituntur), tribui hac ratione verbo seu Scripturae illud, quod sit Deo proprium, respondent per distinctionem inter causam principalem et instrumentalem; illam esse Deum, hanc verbum Rei. Vid. b. Conr. Schluesselb. Catal. Haer. Lib. IX. de Stenckfeld. p. 301. sqq. , b. Theodor. Thumrnium in Imp. Weigel. Err. ΧΠ. p, 21., b, Gerji. in Dispp, Acad. Disp. I. contra Weigel. § 19. p. 827. et nuper admodum Theologos Lubec., Hamburg, et Luneb. in der Lehrund Schutzschrifi wider den Guthmannischen Offenbarungs - Patron P. Π.: p. 273. 287. 311. 313. 506. sqq.

Hoc autem admisso, quod Scriptura sit causa Instrumentalis spiritualium effectuum, cum ex natura causae Instrumentalis requiri et declarandum esse videretur, quomodo Scriptura ultra nativam suam virtutem elevetur a causa principali ad producendos supernaturales effectus? docuit b. Musaeus l. c. §11. p. 595. sqq., Scripturam sacram equidem non elevari per virtutem causae principalis demum in usu sibi extrinsecus

supervenientem (cum eam jam extra usum sibi intime conjunctam habeat), sed per hoc, quod Spiritus 8. ma virtute illuminandi et convertendi cum Scriptura, cui eam jam pridem communicavit, in hominis illuminationem et conversionem simul actu influat eamque ad hos, velut sua (scripturae) nativa et propria (a virtute Spiritus Sancti distincta) virtute nobiliores effectus producendos, suae virtutis nobilioris (quippe vere infinitae) influxu adjuvet.

Qua ratione etiam b. J. Gerh. Tom. VI. L. de Min. Eccl. § 253. p. m. 406. scribit: Placuit Deo, ad divinum iMum effectum conversionis et salutis hominum verbum externum, tanquam causam instrumentaliter agentem, evehere.

Nec dubitavit b. Christ. Chemnitius in Disp. de Gratuita Justif. Hom. Pecc. coram Deo, § 18., defendere eandem sententiam, quod Deus utatur verbo, tanquam causa instrumentali, et verbum, licet effectum per se et virtute propria non attingat, tamen ultra suam naturalem virtutem ad eum producendum a causa principali elevetur.

Confer autem cum his, quae hactenus diximus, b. Musaei Ausführl. Erklärung. Lib. I. Q. X. p. 57. sqq. ad 110.

Quenstedtius: „Verbum Dei, si ακριβώς loqui velimus, non tam instrumentum est, quam medium, quum non omne medium instrumentum sit. . . Augustana quidem confessio instrumenti voce utitur verbumque Dei instrumentum conversionis vocat, sed ώ{· kv πλάτη et imprimis ratione materialis, sci; externae scriptionis, praedicationis, οικονομίας seu dispensationis et ministerii, non autem proprie ratione internae virtutis Spiritus S. verbo communicatae... Dei namque potentia, quae de evangelio praedicatur, non est alia ab ipsius Dei potentia, sed ipsa Dei potentia. Quis autem hanc Dei potentiam instrumentum nominaret?“ (L. c. f. 270.)

Huelsemannus: „Quaenam est propria et naturalis et ordinaria virtus verbi Dei, ut Dei est, ultra quam illud oporteat elevari in conversione hominis? Quid est verbo Del, quid est sacramentis, quid est fldei justificanti naturale, nisi quod Deus ipse per supernaturalem gratiam iis indidit? Quis fando unquam audivit, media a Dei parte ordinata ad hominum salutem, quale Calixtus apertis verbis fatetur esse Dei verbum, elevanda esse a Deo ultra propriam et naturalem et ordinariam virtutem suam, ut effectum consequi possint? Semen incorruptibile verbum Dei vivi et permanens in aeternum elevandum esse ultra propriam et naturalem suam virtutem? Idem: „Quamquam omni verbo Dei insit vis medicinalis eaque nunquam plane auferatur, fatemur tamen, eam a Deo augeri magis vel minus, vel non augeri, sed relinqui in statu ordinariae efficaciae, vide Psalm. 86, 10. Jes. 5, 5. sqq.“ (Praelect. Form. Conc. p. 440.)

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: „Antithesis: I. Schwenhfeldianorum, Weigelianorum, Enthusiastarum, Anabaptistarum aliorumque fanaticorum, ut Theophrasti Paracelsi, Andreae Osiandri, Fabiani Teckel et Fankeri, Guilielmi Gnaphaei, Herrn. divinas immediatas et tacitas angelorum inspirationes intelligunt) efficaciam divinam adscribunt; verbo vero externo, ceu voci humanae, sonb evanescenti et literae mortuae omnem vim et efficaciam et vim divinam derogant, vel nonnisi objectivam, significativam et repraesentativam, non autem effectivam virtutem ipsi tribuunt. . .
