### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: n) See Mus. Intr. l. c

n) See Mus. Intr. l. c. § 9, p. 580 sqq. Compare the predecessors in the Appendix. Conf. Dedek. p. 266, where they praise that saying of Movius: The Holy Spirit and the Word of God are two distinct principles of conversion, but in the act of conversion they are joined, and stand as it were for one cause; whence only one, unique, and undivided action of the Word and the Holy Spirit can result. §

40. Furthermore, thirdly, the perfection or sufficiency of Holy Scripture pertains to its affections, through which it can fully and perfectly instruct us concerning all things that are necessary to be believed and done by a man who is to attain salvation. Indeed, it flowed from the fact that Holy Scripture is the primary principle of knowing theology, which therefore must be adequate to all things subject to the habit of theology. And to the same point pertains what [was said] above.

20. And note that we have indicated that the Scripture which has been divinely granted to men for the purpose of instructing them in the true religion unto salvation must be sufficient. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Introduction*, Part II, Chapter V, § 7, pp. 317, 318.

Indeed, in this place, perfection and sufficiency coincide; nor is regard had so much to the number of books, as many as were ever written by holy men, of which some, regarding the names of the authors or titles cited in the surviving books of Scripture, are thought to have perished; but the perfection of the surviving Scripture is viewed in relation to its end, as will be evident from what follows.

Although, even concerning those books which some say are lost, it must be observed that some have not truly perished, but still exist, albeit under other titles; just as, for example, it is probable that the words of Nathan and Gad, cited in 2 Chronicles 29:29, survive under the title of the books of Samuel; likewise the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite and Iddo, 2 Chronicles 9:29; and finally the visions of Iddo (Hozai), 2 Chronicles 33:19, under the name of the books of Kings.

But if some books written by holy men have truly perished, it must be maintained that they were 1) not composed by divine inspiration, but by human effort; 2) historical rather than doctrinal; indeed, even if 3) it were conceded that θεόπνευστους (God-breathed) books had perished, the dogmas themselves nevertheless appear no less correctly and fully handed down in other surviving books; and certainly 4) it must be established that no book which had once entered into the canon or norm by the intention of the Holy Spirit has perished to the detriment of canonical Scripture, or in such a way that it ceased to be an adequate principle and norm of the doctrine of faith and morals.

Cf. the blessed Gerhard, *Confessio Catholica*, Book II, Art. I, Chapter IV, p. 254 sqq., to which respond the things which the blessed Musaeus wrote in the continuation of his introduction, to be published hereafter, ἐὰν ὁ θεὸς θελήσῃ (if God wills), Chapter IX.

Indeed, we have just said that the perfection of Scripture is to be viewed in relation to its end, and this is the constant opinion of our theologians. Now, things are called perfect in relation to an end to which nothing is lacking of those things that are necessary for attaining that end. But the ultimate end of Scripture is our salvation; the intermediate end is faith in Christ, with which the holiness of life is necessarily conjoined, as we said in § 11.

Quenstedtius: "Holy Scripture is called perfect, not with an absolute perfection, comprehending every divine and supernatural thing that can be known; for this does not befit the church militant on this earth, for which Scripture is intended; but with a restricted perfection, or in relation to those things which are necessary for a Christian man to know in order to believe rightly and to live holily and piously in this life. Others call it relative perfection. . . .

We do not say with the Papists that Scripture is perfect implicitly, or that it contains all things necessary for faith as if in the root, in the seed, in a universal principle, or as if in an index, in such a way that it does not itself contain everything, yet shows where or from whom they are to be sought, by making a referral to the church and its traditions, from which the deficiency of those dogmas that are missing might be supplied—which is how they explain the 'containing of all things in the Scriptures' (Bellarmine, *Book 4 on the Word of God*, ch. 10; add Stapleton, *Relectio on the Principles of Faith*, ch. 5, q. 5, art. 1; Cardinal Hosius, Jacobus Davius, Bishop of Évreux, Tanner, etc.).

For in this way, any poor man would be rich implicitly, because he can point out where riches are; and any illiterate person who can point out where an academy is, in which doctors teach, would have to be considered learned; and he would be said to abound in food who shows others a sumptuous table filled with various delicacies. By this very thing, the church is rendered perfect and sufficient for all dogmas of salvation, but Scripture [is rendered insufficient]." ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

most imperfect, inasmuch as it necessarily has to send us from itself to another teacher. To us, Holy Scripture is so perfect and sufficient that it contains within itself, and does not point outside of itself to, whatever is necessary to be known for salvation. A remissive norm is not a norm, but that to which the remission is made. To the Papists, however, Scripture is sufficient for all dogmas of salvation because it teaches that the church is sufficient for all those things, and perfect because it sends us away to the perfection of the church. But it would have been sufficiently so to write only these two words: "Hear the church," or rather, according to the Papist analysis: "Hear the Roman Pontiff." But he is not the one of whom Scripture says: "Hear him." Matt. 17:5. (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 10. f. 147. sq.)

So that another principle, or another partial norm, e.g., unwritten traditions, is not to be joined to it from the side; since all dogmas of faith and morals, without exception, are contained in the Scriptures, some indeed αυτολεξεί, or κατά ῥητόν, according to the letter, explicitly and in so many words, some κατά διάνοιαν, virtually and implicitly, so that from those things which are read expressed, they can be gathered and known by legitimate and easy consequence. Cf. the blessed Gerhard in Exeg. L. I. c. XVIII. § 366. p. m. 385., who also usefully advises this: That which was written exhibited a perfect canon at any time of the church, since divine revelation was perfectly exposed in those books with respect to that time. And thus, when only the Mosaic books existed, Scripture was perfect, namely, having respect to that time of the church when there did not yet exist more revelations which God willed to be committed to writing. L. c. § 366. p. 386.

Quenstedtius: "Some things are contained in the Scriptures expressly, some analogically, some explicitly, some implicitly, some γενικώς, some ειδικώς, some αυτολεξεί, some κατά πράγμα. Whatever things are necessary to be known for salvation are contained in Scripture in one of these ways." (L. c. f. 160.)

Bebelius: "From the things said (Irenaeus l. l. c. 2.) it appears that some things contained in the Apostolic Creed are omitted here, and some things are inserted here which are passed over in silence in the Apostolic one, which Irenaeus would not have done in a place where he deals professedly with creeds, if he had believed that the creed commonly called Apostolic had been prescribed by the apostles as a perfect and perpetual rule and norm of the church. Jodocus Coccius is therefore in vain in thes. cath. de scr. art. 29., when he wishes to prove from this place of Irenaeus that the creed of the Christian faith was written down by the apostles. For either the church did not diligently guard that apostolic tradition, or Irenaeus alleged it in bad faith or at least negligently, nor indeed did he allege it as it exists today, so that, which is safest, it was not fashioned by the apostles in its present form. Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch, wrote three books against the gentile Autolycus: σύμβολον καί αρραβώνα τής αληθείας, as he himself calls it at the end of book 3; yet he nowhere mentions the Apostolic Creed in the series received today, but cites and explains only one or another article piecemeal here and there, so that I doubt that the creed commonly called Apostolic was held at that time as an adequate norm of things to be believed." (Antiquit. eccles. I, 235. sq.)

Gerhardus: "It has not yet been demonstrated beyond doubt whether it (the Apostolic Creed) was brought together and composed by the apostles themselves before they departed into the whole world for the sake of preaching the Gospel, which the greater part of the ancient writers affirms, or whether it was collected by someone else from the sermons and writings of the apostles and approved by the apostles." (Loc. de eccl. § 149.)

Augustine, in a sermon falsely ascribed to him, is said to have written: "What is called symbolum in Greek is named 'collatio' in Latin. Collatio, therefore, because the faith of the catholic law, brought together into one, is gathered into a symbol." PROLEGOM. CHAP. II. brevity, the text of which we shall now state, God willing. Peter said: "I believe in God the Father Almighty"; John said: "Creator of heaven and earth"; James said: "I believe also in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord"; Andrew said: "Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary"; Philip said: "Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried"; Thomas said: "He descended into hell, the third day He rose again from the dead"; Bartholomew said: "He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty"; Matthew said: "From thence He shall come to judge the living and the dead"; James of Alphaeus: "I believe also in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church"; Simon the Zealot: "The communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins"; Jude of James: "The resurrection of the flesh"; Matthias completed: "Life everlasting, Amen." (Opp. ed. Erasm. Vol. V, fol. 280.)

Gerhard: "Nor can it be said that contrary things are merely prohibited from being added, but not those things which are diverse, since a contrary is not properly added to a prior thing, but abolishes and annuls the prior; a diverse thing is properly added, for contraries destroy one another, but diverse things consist together; now, however, God not only forbids His law to be abolished, but also that anything be added to it." (Loc. de S. S. § 48.)

n) Vide Mus. Intr. l. c. § 9. p. 580. sqq. Conf. antecessores in Append. Conf. 40. Nempe hoc loco perfectio et sufficientia coincidunt; nec tam respectus habetur ad numerum librorum, quotquot unquam ab hominibus sanctis scripti fuerunt, ex quibus aliqui, quoad npmina auctorum aut titulorum, in superstitibus libris Scripturae citati, ipsi vero libri periisse putantur; sed spectatur perfectio Scripturae superstitis in ordine ad finem, ut ex seqq. patebit.

Conf. b. Gerh. Conf. Cath. L. Π. Art. I. Cap. IY. p. 254. sqq., quibus respondent, quae b. Mus. scripsit in continuatione introductionis, posthac έάν o θεύς θέλησή edenda, Cap. IX.

Nempe perfectionem Scripturae in ordine ad finem ejus spectandam esse, modo diximus, et constans est nostratium sententia. Dicuntur autem perfecta ad finem, quibus nihil deest eorum, quae ad consequendum finem sunt necessaria. Finis autem Scripturae ultimus est salus nostra; intermedius, fides in Christum, cum qua necessario conjungitur sanctimonia vitae, ut diximus § 11.

Quenstedtius: „Dicitur s. Scriptura perfecta, non perfectione absoluta, omne scibile divinum et supernaturale comprehendente; haec enim ecclesiae in his terris militanti, cui Scriptura destinata est, non competit; sed perfectione restricta, sive in ordine ad ea, quae homini christiano ad recte credendum et sancte ac pie vivendum in hac vita cognitu sünt necessaria. D. c. 10., adde Stapletonus Relect. prine, fidei c. 5. q. 5. art. 1., Cardinal. Hofius, Jacob. Davius, episc. Ebroic., Tannerus etc.

Hoc ipso ecclesia redditur perfecta et sufficiens ad omnia salutis dogmata, Scriptura vero DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

imperfectissima, utpote quae, ut a se ad alium doctorem nos amandet, necesse habet. Nobis s. Ita ut aliud principium, aut norma partialis alia, v. g. traditiones non scriptae, ei a latere non sint jungendae; cum dogmata fidei et morum omnia, nullo excepto, contineantur in Scripturis, aliqua quidem αυτολεξεί, sive χατά βητδν, secundum liter am, explicite et totidem verbis, aliqua χατά διάνοιαν, virtualiter et implicite, ita, ut ex his, quae expressa leguntur, per consequentiam legitimam ac facilem colligi et cognosci possint. Et sic, cum soli libri Mosaiei extarent, pefectam fuisse Scripturam, respeetu scilicet habito ad illud ecclesiae tempus, quo nondum extabant plures revelationes, quas Deus in literas redigi voluerit. L. c. § 366. p. 386.

Quenstedtius: „Quaedam in Scripturis continentur expresse, quaedam analogice, quaedam explicite, quaedam implicite, quaedam γενικώς, quaedam ειδικώς, quaedam αυτολεξεί, quaedam κατά πράγμα. Quaecunque ad salutem scitu necessaria sunt, aliquo horum modorum in Scriptura continentur.“ (L. c. f. 160.)

Bebelius: „Ex dictis (Irenaeil. l. c. 2.) apparet, quaedam in symbolo apostolico contenta hic esse omissa, et quaedam hic inserta, quae in apostolico tacentur, quod non fecisset Irenaeus in loco, ubi ex professo de symbolis agit, si credidisset, symbolum vulgo dictum apostolicum ab apostolis ut perfectam et perpetuam regulam et normam ecclesiae esse praescriptam. Frustraneus igitur est Jodocus Coccius in thes. cath. de scr. art. 29., cum ex hoc Irenaei loco probare vult, symbolum Christianae fidei ab apostolis esse conscriptum. Aut enim ecclesia traditionem illam apostolicam diligenter non custodivit, aut Irenaeus mala fide vel saltem negligenter allegavit, nec enim, ut hodie extat, allegavit, ut, quod tutissimum est, ab apostolis sub hodierna forma non est concinnatum. Theophilus, episcopus Antiochenus, scripsit tres contra Autolycum gentilem libros: σύμβολου καί αρραβώνα τής αλη&είας, ut sub finem lib. 3. ipse vocat; neque tamen uspiam symboli apostolici in recepta hodie serie meminit, sed frustulatim hinc inde tantum unum vel alterum articulum citat et explicat, ut dubitem, symbolum vulgo apostolicum dictum tum quidem temporis pro norma credendorum adaequata fuisse habitum.““ (Antiquit. eccles. I, 235. sq.)

Gerhardus: „Nondum indubitato demonstratum est, an ab ipsis apostolis, antequam in universum orbem praedicandi evangelii causa discederent, comportatum sit ac compositum (symb. apost.), quod major pars veterum scriptorum affirmat, an vero ex concionibus et scriptis apostolorum ab alio quodam collectum sit et ab apostolis comprobatum.“ (Loc. de eccl. § 149.)

Erasm. Tom. V. f. 280.)

Gerhardus: ,,Nec dici potest, contraria saltem prohibita esse, ne addantur, non autem ea, quae diversa sunt, siquidem contrarium proprie non additur priori, sed prius abolet et antiquat; diversum proprie additur, contraria se invicem tollunt, sed diversa simul consistunt; jam vero Deus non solum prohibet, legem suam aboleri, sed etiam ei aliquid addi." (Loc. de S. S. § 48.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Quenstedt: "He does not prohibit additions that proceed from divine will and…

Quenstedt: "He does not prohibit additions that proceed from divine will and authority, but those that proceed from human. For here God sets a law for man, not for Himself." (L. c. f. 184.)

The same: "The dogmas which the Papists say are άγραφη [unwritten] and yet necessary for salvation are these: the invocation of saints; solemn fasting; abstinence from meats; the suffrages of the living for the dead; voluntary vows of chastity and virginity; purgatorial fire; the sacraments of confirmation and extreme unction; the sacrifice of the mass; the celibacy of priests, etc., from the review of Joh. Driedo, *De ecclesiast. Script.*, lib. 4, fol. 282, who also adds there: 'If we despise tradition in these matters, we shall have no shield with which we can defend the doctrine of faith that now exists.' But it is next to insanity to say that the dogmas already named are those very things which Christ had to say and the apostles could not bear, regarding the same passage, John 16:12." (L. c. f. 160.)

The same: "By the name of unwritten traditions, the Papists understand dogmas and decrees necessary for salvation to be believed and done, which indeed proceeded from Christ Himself and the apostles, but which nevertheless nowhere exist as handed down in the books of the Old and New Testaments. These, I say, unwritten traditions [traditiones άγραφους] we reject. Distinguish between the insufficiency of dogmas and the insufficiency of clarity and evidence or express proposition; the Jesuits indeed wish to appear to be adding traditions to Scripture not because of the former, but because of the latter, or to assert their necessity only for better information; but it is a pretext [πρόφασις], not a cause, a cloak, not a true reason... The Papists maintain that many things are lacking in Scripture which are necessary for salvation, as we saw above; therefore they contend that there is need of a supplement and of traditions, which are commonly called the unwritten word... Costerus, *Enchirid.*, c. 1, says: 'Traditions, impressed upon the heart of the Church, surpass in many parts the Scriptures, which the apostles left us on membranes.' Therefore, unwritten traditions in the Roman Church are valued much more highly, and their authority is far greater than that of Scripture. Certainly Baronius, *Annal.*, Vol. I, year 53, no. II, was not afraid to write: 'Traditions excel over the Scriptures, since the Scriptures do not subsist unless they are confirmed by tradition, whereas traditions retain their firmness without the Scriptures.'" (L. c. q. 11, f. 162 sq.)

The same: "Regarding the passage 2 Thess. 2:15: 'Hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by our word or by our epistle,' Paul exhorts the Thessalonians to persevere in all the doctrine handed down by him, whether they had drawn it from his living voice while present or from his writing while absent. Not all the books of the New Testament existed at that time, but who would conclude from this that unwritten dogmas exist in our time?"

Scherzer: "The same canon is perfect without the assumption of any traditions (dogmatic; for concerning historical, exegetical, and ritual matters, insofar as they do not oppose Scripture, there is no dispute) regarding the doctrine of faith and morals. For 1. 'The sacred letters can make one learned,' etc., 2 Tim. 3:15–17. 2. 'These things are written, that you may believe and through faith have eternal life,' John 20:31. I argue: That which makes one perfect is perfect. For a cause cannot be nobler than its effect. Therefore, it does not need unwritten traditions. For either 3. those traditions hand down something different in kind beyond those things which are written regarding faith and morals, or they hand down the same. If the latter, they are not necessary and do not differ from the written Word regarding doctrine. If the former, they are impious and must be rejected under penalty of anathema (whether they are against Scripture or beyond it, as παρά is taken in Rom. 16:17, 1 Cor. 3:11, and the Vulgate itself has in Gal. 1:9: 'Scripture does not suffer addition or diminution.' Deut. 12:31, Rev. 22:18. Therefore, nothing can be added beyond it), Gal. 1:9, nor do they acknowledge θεόπνευστους men as their authors. For they know well that one ought not to be wise υπέρ ὃ γέγραπται, beyond and above that which is written, 1 Cor. 4:6... 4. Christ in Matt. 15:9, 13, expressly rejects human traditions. And 5. Paul says ουδέν έκτος των προφητών in Acts 26:22; just as Peter wished to say ονδέν άτερ γραφών according to Clement of Alexandria, Strom. 1. VI. f. 678. 6. That the faith of those who hand down traditions is not always safe (and therefore not certain) is taught even by the Chiliasm of Papias. And 7. the Papists have not wanted to publish a catalog of their traditions at the Colloquy of Regensburg, Sess. 1, nor have they been able to do so to this day." (

System, th. p. 22, sq.) For it is expressly said in 2 Tim. 3:15 that the sacred letters, which Timothy had known from childhood (and therefore the Scripture of the Old Testament, which alone existed when Timothy was a boy), were able to σοφίσαι him, to make him learned and wise unto salvation, through faith which is in Christ Jesus; where the proportion of Scripture as a perfect principle to its end, common to all members of the church, namely faith and salvation, is most manifest. But if even one of those things which pertain to faith and are necessary to be known for a man to be saved were not contained in the Scriptures, then Scripture, regarding this very dogma omitted by itself, would leave man in ignorance or lead him into error, and would not be able to make him wise unto the attainment of salvation.

The apostle continues in the same place and shows in v. 16 and 17 that Holy Scripture is perfect in relation to the end proper to teachers. For he says that Scripture, just as it is entirely divinely inspired, so also is it entirely—or regarding the complex of the dogmas it contains—useful for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness; and it is useful for accomplishing these things, not in just any way, but so that the man of God, the minister and teacher of the church divinely called, may be άρτιος, perfect (holding all parts of his office, as Estius interprets) for every such good work, and therefore for teaching all things whatsoever are necessary to be believed; for solidly refuting all opposing errors; for persuading the flight of all vices and the cultivation of morals regarding all species of virtues whatsoever; and that he may be ἐξηρτισμένος, absolutely or perfectly instructed and equipped; which could not happen unless Scripture itself contained all these things within itself and sufficiently demonstrated them.

Compare John 20, last verse, where those things which John had written (not only concerning the deeds of Christ, but also concerning his doctrine, person, and office) are said to be written for this reason, or for the sake of this end, that men, having known these things which are written, might believe that Jesus is the Christ,

that Savior of the world and that Son of God, and that believing they might have life through his name. Therefore, it is necessary that Scripture contain and teach, without defect, all things that are necessary to be known for saving faith and for salvation itself.

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who contend that not all things necessary to be believed for salvation are contained in Holy Scripture, and that therefore unwritten traditions, by which the deficiency of Scripture is to be supplied, must be admitted and received ‘with an equal affection of piety’ as Scripture itself. Thus the Council of Trent, Bellarmine, Costerus, Melchior Cano. Likewise, they maintain that ‘no heresy, no error, could ever have been, or can even now be, sufficiently refuted from Scripture alone without the presupposed infallible authority of the church,’ which was the pronouncement of the Jesuits at the Colloquy of Ratisbon. 2. Of the Innovators, who, with Vincent of Lérins, the semi-Pelagian monk, in his Commonitory, ch. 1, say that the canon of the Scriptures is sufficient, ‘yet that there is nonetheless a need at times for tradition or the testimony of the church to be joined to it.’ Thus D. G. Calixtus, Dreier, Horneius. 3. Of the Schwenkfeldians, Anabaptists, and Weigelians, who maintain that the doctrine of salvation is to be learned today not from Scripture alone, but also from private revelations and inspirations which they invent for themselves, and from conversations with angels. 4. Of the Socinians, who assert that only those things are necessary to be known for salvation which are contained in the Scriptures ῥητῶς and in so many words.” (L. c. q. 10. f. 150.) §

41. Finally, in the fourth place, among the affections of Scripture, there is a place for perspicuity, or the fact that those things which are necessary for a man tending toward salvation to believe and to do are proposed in Scripture in words and phrases so clear and received in common usage that any man, skilled in the language and possessing even a mediocre judgment and attending to the words, can attain the true sense of the words, as far as those things are concerned which are necessary for him to know, and can embrace the very heads of doctrine with a simple apprehension of the mind: just as the intellect of man is led by Scripture itself and its supernatural light, or the divine power joined to it, to provide the assent of faith to the word apprehended and the things signified.

For it is required for a principle of knowing and the formal object of any habit that it should lead what is known first into the knowledge of the others which are subject to the habit; according to those things which we said in Chapter I, § 3, note 1, and Chapter II, § 1, note a. Luther: “Thus we say that all spirits are to be tested by the judgment of Scripture in the face of the church, for this must be established among Christians as primary and most firm: that the Holy Scriptures are a spiritual light, far clearer than the sun itself, especially in those things which pertain to salvation or necessity. But, because we are persuaded to the contrary now ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

...long ago, by that pestilential word of the Sophists, that the Scriptures are obscure and ambiguous, we are compelled first to prove that very first principle of ours, by which all other things must be proved, which to the philosophers would seem absurd and impossible to do.” (De serv. arb. diatr. Opp. ed. Schmidt. Vol. VII, 177. Hai. XVIII, 2157.) For we are not looking here at the general object of Scripture in its breadth, but at its special and primary object: concerning which we treated above in § 9. For otherwise, if you were to run through all those things which occur in the Scriptures, it must be admitted that much obscurity will be found, e.g., in onomastics, chronologies, genealogies, prophecies before their fulfillment, etc., but not equally so in the elementary principles of faith. B. Cundisius, Notes on Comp. Hutt. L. I. Q. VII. p. 31. Indeed, the perspicuity of Scripture can be established as threefold: one on the part of the things themselves; another on the part of the words; and a third on the part of supernatural light. But the first (which consists in the evidence of things, or clarity in order to their distinct cognition, either by themselves and from the terms grasped, or because of principles which are known by themselves, and with which they have a necessary connection) is not attended to in this place. For although it has a place in some objects of Scripture which are subject to the light of nature; yet, regarding the mysteries of faith, in the transmission of which Scripture is chiefly occupied, it has no place. But what some of our own have said, that the things of Scripture are not obscure, is to be understood in this way: that those things, although they are in themselves non-evident (just as those same men also said that the things of God are obscure), are nevertheless clearly proposed in Scripture, so that the sense of that expression returns to the perspicuity of the words. Conf. b. Gerhard, Conf. Cath. L. II. Spec. Art. I. Cap. III. p. 210. The third (which in its own way returns to the authority and efficacy of Scripture) is treated toward the end of the §, and will be treated more fully in note m. Meanwhile, concerning the second, or the perspicuity of the words, it is to be noted that it consists in the choice of the words themselves and their congruence with the things signified, and their connection and order among themselves according to the common use of speaking, which therefore the blessed Luther called the external clarity of Scripture. Lib. de Serv. Arb. T. III. Jen. Lat. fol. 169. a. Others call it grammatical perspicuity. See b. Cundisius from b. Hoepfner, notes on Comp. Hutt. Q. VII. p. 30. The blessed Musaeus has discoursed at greater length on that triple perspicuity of Scripture in his unpublished Introduction, Cap. X. Luther: “I certainly confess that there are many places in the Scriptures that are obscure and abstruse, not because of the majesty of the things, but because of ignorance of the vocabulary and grammar, but which do not at all hinder the knowledge of all things in the Scriptures. For what more august can remain hidden in the Scriptures, after the seals have been broken and the stone rolled away from the door of the sepulcher, and that highest mystery has been brought forth: that Christ the Son of God has been made man, that God is triune and one, that Christ has suffered for us and will reign eternally? Are these things not known and sung even at the crossroads? Take Christ out of the Scriptures, what more will you find in them? The things, therefore, contained in the Scriptures are all brought forth, even if some places are still obscure due to unknown words. It is truly foolish and impious to know that the things of Scripture are all placed in the clearest light, and yet, because of a few obscure words, to declare the things themselves to be obscure. If in one place the words are obscure, yet in another they are clear, and the very same thing, most manifestly declared to the whole world, is spoken of in the Scriptures both in clear words and still lies hidden in obscure words.” m PROLEGOM. CAP. II. Now it matters not at all if a thing is in the light, or if some sign of it is in the darkness, since meanwhile many other signs of the same thing are in the light. Who will say that a public fountain is not in the light because those who are in a narrow alley do not see it, when all who are in the marketplace do see it? . . . Therefore, you and all Sophists, come forth and produce some one mystery that is still abstruse in the Scriptures; but that many things remain abstruse to many, this does not happen because of the obscurity of Scripture, but because of the blindness or sloth of those who do not strive to see the most clear truth, just as Paul says concerning the Jews in 2 Cor. 4: A veil remains over their heart, and again: If our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing, whose minds the god of this age has blinded. With the same rashness, one would blame the sun and the bright day who would veil his own eyes, or go from the light into the darkness and hide himself. Let miserable men, therefore, cease to impute the darkness and obscurity of their own hearts to the most clear Scriptures of God with blasphemous perversity. . . . Likewise, your examples, which you append not without suspicion and a sting, do nothing to the point, such as those concerning the distinction of persons, the conglutination of the divine and human nature, and the irremissible sin, the ambiguity of which you say has not yet been resolved. If you understand this concerning the questions of the Sophists agitated about these matters, what has the most innocent Scripture done to you that you should object the abuse of wicked men to its purity? Scripture simply confesses the trinity of God, the humanity of Christ, and the irremissible sin. There is no obscurity or ambiguity here. But in what ways these things exist, Scripture does not say, as you imagine, nor is there a need to know; the Sophists here treat their own dreams—argue against and condemn them, and absolve the Scriptures. But if you understand this concerning the substance of the thing itself, again argue not against the Scriptures, but against the Arians and those to whom the Gospel is veiled, so that they do not see the most clear testimonies concerning the trinity of the divinity and the humanity of Christ through the operation of Satan, their god. And to speak briefly: The clarity of Scripture is twofold, just as its obscurity is twofold: one external, placed in the ministry of the Word; the other situated in the cognition of the heart. If you speak of internal clarity, no man sees one iota in the Scriptures unless he has the Spirit of God; all have a darkened heart, so that even if they say and know how to bring forth all of Scripture, they nevertheless feel or truly know nothing of these things, nor do they believe in God, nor that they themselves are creatures of God, nor anything else, according to that of Ps. 14: The fool has said in his heart, God is nothing. For the Spirit is required to understand the whole of Scripture and any part of it whatsoever. If you speak of external clarity, nothing at all is left obscure or ambiguous, but all things are brought into the most certain light by the Word and declared to the whole world, whatever is in the Scriptures. (De serv. arb. diatr. Opp. Vol. VII, 124—127. Hal. XVIII, 2068—2072.) At least in those places where, as they say, one deals professedly with a certain dogma of faith or morals, or where its seat is contained, so that it is a naked article of faith, there is no precept of life that is not proposed somewhere in Scripture in proper, clear, and perspicuous words. B. Gerh. Conf. Cath. L. II. Art. I. Cap. III. p. 209. For certainly in those things which are openly placed in the Scriptures, all those things are found which contain faith and the morals of living, as Augustine says in Lib. II. de C. D. c. IX., where he also adds: The Holy Spirit has magnificently and wholesomely modified the Holy Scriptures so that He might meet hunger with more open places, but might remove loathing with more obscure ones. For almost nothing is drawn from those obscurities that is not found stated most fully elsewhere. Quenstedtius: “God did not will that all and singular things be set forth in Holy Scripture equally clearly and perspicuously, but that some things be handed down in a more recondite style: 1. so that our diligence in reading the Scriptures might be excited; 2. so that loathing and contempt for divine things might be removed (for it is easy to investigate... Denique quarto inter affectiones Scripturae locum habet a perspicuitas, seu quod ea, quae creditu et factu homini ad salutem tendenti sunt b necessaria, verbis c et phrasibus ita claris et usu loquendi receptis, in Scriptura d proponuntur, ut quilibet homo, e linguae gnarus f et vel mediocri judicio g pollens verbisque h attendens, verum verborum i sensum, quoad ea, quae sibi sunt scitu necessaria, assequi et capita ipsa doctrinae simplici k mentis apprehensione amplecti l possit: prout ad assensum fidei, verbo apprehenso et rebus significatis praebendum, intellectus hominis per Scripturam ipsam ejusque lumen supernaturale, m seu virtutem divinam illi conjunctam perducitur.

Requiritur enim ad principium cognoscendi et objectum formale alicujus habitus, ut ipsum primo cognitum deducat in cognitionem caeterorum, quae habitui subjiciuntur; juxta ea, quae diximus Cap. I. § 3. nota I. et Cap. II. § 1. nota a. Lutherus: „Sic dicimus, Scriptura judice omnes spiritus in facie ecclesiae esse probandos, nam id oportet apud Christianos esse imprimis ratum atque firmissimum, Scripturas sanctas esse lucem spiritualem, ipso sole longe clariorem, praesertim in iis, quae pertinent ad salutem vel necessitatem. Verum, quia in contrarium persuasi sumus jam DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

dudum, pestilenti illo Sophistarum verbo, Scripturas esse obscuras et ambiguas, cogimur primum probare illud ipsum primum principium nostrum, quo omnia alia probanda sunt, quod apud philosophos absurdum et impossibile factu videretur.“ (De serv. arb. diatr. Opp. ed. Schmidt. Vol. VII, 177. Hai. XVIII, 2157.) Non enim hic objectum Scripturae generale in sua latitudine, sed speciale ac primarium, illud spectamus: de quo actum est supra § 9. Alias enim, si ea omnia, quae in Scripturis occurrunt, percurras, fatendum est, multum obscuritatis deprehensum iri, v. g. in onomasticis, chronologicis, genealogicis, vaticiniis ante complementum etc., non autem aeque in elementaribus fidei. B. Cundis. Not. ad Comp. Hutt. L. I. Q. VII. p. 31. Potest equidem perspicuitas Scripturae constitui triplex: una ex parte rerum; altera ex parte verborum; et tertia ex parte luminis supernaturalis. Sed prima (quae consistit in evidentia rerum, seu claritate in ordine ad distinctam earum cognitionem, vel per se et ex apprehensis terminis, vel propter principia, quae per se sunt cognita, et cum quibus illae necessarium nexum habent) hoc loco non attenditur. Quamvis enim in aliquibus Scripturae objectis, quae lumini naturae subjacent, locum habeat; tamen, quoad mysteria fidei, in quibus tradendis Scriptura praecipue occupatur, locum non habet. Quod autem nostratium quidam dixerunt, res Scripturae non esse obscuras, sic intelligendum est, quod res illae, licet in se sint inevidentes (prout etiam isti dixerunt, res Dei esse obscuras), tamen in Scriptura perspicue proponantur, ut locutionis istius sensus ad perspicuitatem verborum redeat. Conf. b. Gerh. Conf. Cath. L. II. Spec. Art. I. Cap. III. p. 210. De tertia (quae suo modo ad auctoritatem et efficaciam Scripturae redit) sub finem § agitur, et in nota m. plenius agetur. Interim de secunda, seu de perspicuitate verborum, notandum est, eam consistere in ipsorum verborum delectu et congruentia cum rebus significatis eorumque inter se connexione et ordine juxta communem usum loquendi, quam proinde b. Lutherus claritatem Scripturae externam vocavit. Lib. de Serv. Arb. T. III. Jen. Lat. fol. 169. a. Alii perspicuitatem grammaticam vocant. Vid. b. Cundisius ex b. Hoepfnero, not. ad Comp. Hutt. Q. VII. p. 30. Pluribus de triplici illa perspicuitate Scripturae disseruit b. Musaeus in Contin. άνεχδότω Introd. Cap. X.Lutherus: „Hoc sane fateor, esse multa loca in Scripturis obscura et abstrusa, non ob majestatem rerum, sed ob ignorantiam vocabulorum et grammaticae, sed quae nihil impediant scientiam omnium rerum in Scripturis. Quid enim potest in Scripturis augustius latere reliquum, postquam fractis signaculis et voluto ab ostio sepulcri lapide illud summum mysterium proditum est, Christum Filium Dei factum hominem esse, Deum trinum et unum, Christum pro nobis passum et regnaturum aeternaliter? Nonne haec etiam in biviis sunt nota et cantata? Tolle Christum e Scripturis, quid amplius in illis invenies? Res igitur in Scripturis contentae omnes sunt proditae, licet quaedam loca adhuc verbis incognitis obscura sint. Stultum est vero et impium scire, res Scripturae esse omnes in luce positas clarissima, et propter pauca verba obscura res obscuras dictare. Si uno loco obscura sunt verba, at alio sunt clara, eadem vero res, manifestissime toti mundo declarata, dicitur in Scripturis tum verbis claris, tum adhuc latet verbis obscuris, m PROLEGOM. GAP. II. jam nihil refert, si res sit in luce, an aliquod ejus signum sit in tenebris, cum interim multa alia ejusdem signa sint in luce. Quis dicet fontem publicum non esse in luce, quod hi, qui iri angiporto sunt, illum non vident, cum omnes, qui sunt in foro, videant? . . . Igitur tu et omnes Sophistae, agite et producite unum aliquod mysterium, quod sit in Scripturis adhuc abstrusum; quod vero multis multa manent abstrusa, non hoc fit Scripturae obscuritate, sed illorum caecitate vel socordia, qui non agunt, ut clarissimam veritatem videant, sicut Paulus de Judaeis dicit 2 Cor. 4.: Velamen manet super cor eorum, et iterum: Si Evangelium nostrum opertum est, in iis qui pereunt opertum est, quorum corda Deus hujus seculi excaecavit. Eadem temeritate solem obscurumque diem culparet, qui ipse sibi oculos velaret, aut a luce in tenebras iret et sese absconderet. Desinant ergo miseri homines, tenebras et obscuritatem cordis sui blasphema perversitate Scripturis Dei clarissimis imputare. . . Sic et exempla tua, quae subjungis non sine suspicione et aculeo, nihil faciunt ad rem, qualia de distinctione personarum, de conglutinatione naturae divinae et humanae, de peccato irremissibili, quorum ambiguitatem dicis nondum esse resectam. Si de Sophistarum quaestionibus circa has res agitatis intelligis, quid tibi fecit innocentissima Scriptura, ut abusum sceleratorum hominum objicias illius puritati? Scriptura simpliciter confitetur trinitatem Dei et humanitatem Christi et peccatum irremissibile. Nihil hic obscuritatis aut ambiguitatis. Quibus vero modis ista habeant, Scriptura non dicit, ut tu fingis, nec opus est nosse, Sophistae hic Sua somnia tractant, illos argue et damna, et Scripturas absolve. Si vero intelligis de ipsa rei substantia, iterum non Scripturas, sed Arianos argue, et eos, quibus opertum est Evangelium, ut clarissima testimonia de divinitatis trinitate et humanitate Christi per operationem satanae dei sui non videant. Et ut breviter dicam: Duplex est claritas Scripturae, sicut et duplex obscuritas, una externa in verbi ministerio posita, altera in cordis cognitione sita. Si de interna claritate dixeris, nullus homo unum jota in Scripturis videt, nisi qui Spiritum Dei habet, omnes habent obscuratum cor,, ita ut, si etiam dicant et norint proferre omnia Scripturae, nihil tamen horum sentiant aut vere cognoscant, neque credunt Deum, nec sese esse creaturas Dei, nec quicquam aliud, juxta illud Ps. 14.: Dixit insipiens in corde suo, Deus nihil est. Spiritus enim requiritur ad totam Scripturam et ad quamlibet ejus partem intelligendam. Si de externa dixeris, nihil prorsus relictum est obscurum aut ambiguum, sed omnia sunt per verbum in lucem producta certissimam, et declarata toto orbi, quaecunque sunt in Scripturis.“ (De serv. arb. diatr. Opp. Vol. VII, 124—127. Hal. XVIII, 2068—2072.) Saltem in iis locis, ubi ex professo, quod ajunt, de certo dogmate fidei aut morum agitur, seu ubi sedes ejus continetur, ita ut nudus sit fidei articulus, nullum, vitae praeceptum, quod non alicubi verbis propriis, claris et perspicuis in Scriptura proponatur. B. Gerh. Conf. Cath. L. II. Art. I. Cap. III. p. 209. Certe enim in iis, quae aperte in scripturis sunt posita, inveniuntur iUa omnia, quae continent fidem moresque vivendi, dicente Augustino Lib. II. de C. D. c. IX., ubi et illud adjicit: Magnifice et salubriter Spiritus Sanctus itu Scripturas sanctas modificavit, ut locis apertioribus fami occurreret, obscurioribus autem fastidia detergeret. Nihil enim fere de ittis obscuritatibus eruitur, quod non plenissime dictum alibi reperiatur.Quenstedtius: „Noluit Deus omnia et singula in S. L. aeque clare et perspicue exponi, sed quaedam stylo magis recondito tradi: 1. ut nostra in legendis Scripturis diligentia excitaretur; 2. ut fastidium et contemtus rerum divinarum amoveretur (facile enim investi DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: things that are common usually become cheap)

things that are common usually become cheap); 3. so that human arrogance and pride might be tamed by labor; 4. so that we might be reminded of our congenital blindness; 5. so that we might approach the reading of Scripture only with reverence, the sanctification of ourselves, and prior prayers; and 6. finally, so that a more vehement desire for the other life and the higher academy might be kindled in us.” (L. c. f. 173.)

Luther: “But if anyone among them attacks you and says: One must have the interpretations of the Fathers, for Scripture is dark—you should answer that it is not true. There is no clearer book written on earth than the Holy Scripture; it is against all other books just as the sun is against all lights. They say such things only so that they may lead us away from Scripture and raise themselves up as masters over us, so that we should believe their dream-preaching. It is a horrible, great disgrace and vice against the Holy Scripture and all Christendom when one says that the Holy Scripture is dark and not so clear that everyone may understand it to teach and prove his faith. Note this well: Would it not be a great shame if I or you were called a Christian and did not know what I believed? But if I know what I believe, then I know what stands in Scripture, because Scripture contains nothing more than Christ and the Christian faith. Therefore, when faith only hears Scripture, it is so clear and bright to it that, without the glosses of any Fathers and teachers, it says: That is right; I believe that too. . . It is indeed true, some passages of Scripture are dark, but in them there is nothing else than exactly what is in other places in the clear, open passages. And heretics come from this, that they grasp the dark passages according to their own understanding and fight with them against the clear passages and the foundation of faith. There, then, the Fathers fought against them through the clear passages, thereby illuminating the dark passages, and proved that exactly that which is said in the dark is also in the light. . . Just be certain, without doubt, that there is nothing brighter than the sun, that is, Scripture; but if a cloud has stepped before it, there is still nothing behind it but that same bright sun. Thus, if there is a dark passage in Scripture, do not doubt, there is certainly the same truth behind it that is clear in another place, and whoever cannot understand the dark, let him stay with the light.” (Exposition of Ps. 37, from the year 1521. V, 456. sqq.)

For not only the regenerate and the faithful, but even the unregenerate and the impious, by the power of the very clarity of the words signifying by design—which applies equally to all readers—can attain knowledge of the sense signified by the words, namely the literal or historical sense; but not the saving or the sense of faith, as will be said shortly. And indeed, the blessed Musaeus taught this in the Disputations on Conversion, held in the year 1647 and following, and later edited again in the year 1658 at Halle in Saxony, Disp. IV. § 27. et seqq., and in the Treatise on Conversion edited at Jena in 1661, Disp. IV. c. II. § 44. sqq. p. 272. sqq., and again in the *Ausführliche Erklärung* [Detailed Explanation], Q. XLIV. p. 342. sqq. to 397. He followed the footsteps of his predecessors, the blessed Doctors Joh. Major and Joh. Gerhard, of whom the former, in the year 1630, in the *Confutatio Judicii a Valeriano M. de Acatholicorum Regula Credendi editi* [Refutation of the Judgment published by Valerianus M. concerning the Rule of Faith of the Non-Catholics], Prop. III. Cap. I. Sect. III. p. 162, expressly disputes the opinion of Valerianus, which grants the true sense of Scripture to no one unless he is meanwhile illuminated and taught by the Holy Spirit; and he himself (J. Major) warns on the contrary that the true and indubitable sense of the Holy Scriptures is either joined with the assent of the heart and the fruit of conversion, or is destitute of it: the latter can happen to infidels, such as the Jews; the former belongs only to the faithful. And he adds notably: Just as

the apostles, adorned with the immediate and extemporaneous gift of many-tonguedness and the Holy Spirit, set forth the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven to various nations, so that they might be understood word-for-word by each individual and received by faith through the working of the Holy Spirit—although there were not lacking those who indeed grasped the sense of the apostolic proclamation, yet, denying assent to the words, they perceived no fruit from it, Acts 13; just as many, of the languages in which God has caused his oracles to exist

Furthermore, § 9, p. 365, he writes: Since these things are so, it should not have been said nakedly and crudely by Valerianus that no one certainly attains the true sense of the sacred writings unless internally illuminated and taught by the Holy Spirit. And § 10: Therefore, applying the critical rod of distinction, let us correct and chastise that proposition in this manner: Every person skilled in the biblical language certainly attains the true sense of the sacred writings, which the meanings of the known words produce, even if he is neither taught nor illuminated internally by the Holy Spirit. Then: No one attains the true sense of the sacred writings in those places which treat of the articles of faith in such a way that he gives assent to the words and takes fruit from them, unless the Holy Spirit moves and illuminates the heart from within.

Blessed Gerhard, however, in the year 1625, in *Exeg. L. I.*, after having distinguished in § 413, p. 447, between the external clarity of Scripture and the internal clarity or illumination to be sought from the Holy Spirit, subsequently responds in § 424, p. 461, to Bellarmine’s objection against the perspicuity of Scripture—which he sought from the necessity of prayers to attain its understanding, as indicated in Ps. 119:18—by means of a distinction between the knowledge of the letter and of the Spirit: namely, that for the literal knowledge of the articles of faith, the external clarity of Scripture suffices, but for spiritual knowledge, the interior illumination of the Holy Spirit, to be obtained through pious prayers, is required.

Indeed, the entire Theological College of Jena, and together with it the Theological Faculty of Wittenberg, in *the Refutation of the Rathmannian Counter-Report*, no. 69, p. 365a, respond affirmatively to the question: "Whether an unconverted Jew, without preceding and accompanying light of grace, can understand the Holy Scripture according to the letter and fathom the literal sense from it?" And having brought forward the examples of Jerome, Graser, and Buxtorf, who consulted Jews in order to attain the true sense of the words of the Old Testament Scripture, they finally add: "It is one thing to understand the words and the significations of the terms and to interpret them correctly; it is another thing to understand the matters themselves, and to rightly grasp, rightly apply, and embrace them in faith. For this, the gracious illumination and assistance of the Holy Spirit is required: but for the investigation, explanation, and understanding of the literal sense, it is not."

And in the following number, 70, p. 365b, after the middle: "If the Counter-Report aims at this, that no unconverted person can attain the right understanding which the words in Scripture carry with them and yield of themselves—that is, the grammatical and literal—unless the Holy Spirit steps in with His light of grace, then we do not hold with the Counter-Report, but remain by our opinion, which we have made earth-and nail-fast (NB.) in the previous entry. For the vocabula, and those who interpret them and equip them for right use, namely the Lexicons, Dictionaries, as also the Grammatical Books in Latin, Greek... ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

prepared in Hebrew, Arabic, and other languages, are *humani ingenii inventa* [inventions of human ingenuity], and belong among the *dona naturae* [gifts of nature], but not among the *dona Spiritus Sancti gratiosa* [gracious gifts of the Holy Spirit]: for He is not appointed (NB.) nor poured out to teach the *praecepta Grammatices* [precepts of grammar], or to teach how to seek the *radices* [roots] among the Hebrews, or to teach how to decline and conjugate, and in *Logicis* [in logic] to construct *enuntiationes* [propositions] and *syllogismos* [syllogisms], but rather that He might propose to us the Articles of Faith from the Scripture and instruct us in the saving truth. Many a man has the right understanding of the words, but he does not have the saving understanding of the mystery, which pertains to faith; therefore, one must also here (NB.) guard against equivocation.

Moreover, one could cite the *dicta óμόψηφα* [unanimous sayings] of the blessed Aeg. Hunnius, Disp. LXIV. Cap. III. § 6, 7, 8, Tom. V. Op. fol. 681; of the blessed Jac. Martini, LL. Th. Disp. XI. § 29 and 30, § 100 et seqq.; of the blessed Conr. Dietericus, in Inst. Catech. de Scr. S. Q. XXX. resp. ad obj. I. pontif. p. m. 45; of the Marburg Theologians and specifically the blessed Joh. Steuber, Disp. VII. de Aug. Conf. art. XVIII. § 56. p. m. 154; furthermore, of the blessed Justus Feuerborn, in AntiOstorodo Disp. II. § 3. p. 17; of the blessed H. Kromayer, Theol. Pos.-Pol. A. I. antith. VI. p. 70.

Thus the blessed Gerhard writes: We by no means affirm that Scripture is clear and perspicuous to everyone; but to those for whom there is no impediment from age, or from ignorance of the language in which they read the Scripture. Exeg. I. c. § 413. p. 447, 448. And the blessed Jac. Martini, l. c. § 99 sqq., warns that the fact that not all understand Scripture arises from the privation of a twofold means, natural and supernatural; among the natural, however, the first is the knowledge of languages.

Indeed, as the blessed Musaeus teaches in the Disputations on Conversion held in the year 1647 sqq., Disp. IV. § 37: For those who are ignorant of the languages in which the Word of God was originally written, namely Hebrew and Greek, or who have not even learned to read, it is sufficient if they believe the dogmas of faith, proposed to them in the vernacular language, to be true, and in that sense in which they are proposed to them, revealed by God in the Holy Scriptures; which assent the Holy Spirit works in them, inasmuch as He is efficacious in the hearts of men through the Word even when preached in the vernacular, and testifies of it that it is the divine Word.

Latin:

gata plerumque vilescunt); 3. ut humana arrogantia atque superbia labore domaretur; 4. ut congenitae coecitatis admoneremur; 5. ut nonnisi cum reverentia, nostri sanctificatione et praeviis precibus ad Scripturae lectionem accederemus, et 6. denique, ut desiderium vehementius alterius vitae et superioris academiae in nobis accenderetur.“ (L. c. f. 173.)

Lutherus: „Wenn euch aber jemand von ihnen antastet und spricht: Man muss der Väter Auslegen haben, die Schrift sei dunkel— sollet ihr antworten, es sei nicht wahr. Es ist auf Erden kein klärer Euch geschrieben, denn die heilige Schrift; die ist gegen alle andere Bücher, gleichwie die Sonne gegen alle Lichter. Sie reden solch Ding nur darum, dass sie uns aus der Schrift führen und sich selbst zu Meistern über uns erheben, dass wir ihren Traumpredigten glauben sollen. Es ist eine greuliche grosse Schmach und Laster wider die heilige Schrift und alle Christenheit, so man sagt, dass die heilige Schrift finster sei, und nicht so klar, dass sie jedermann möge verstehen, seinen Glauben zu lehren und zu beweisen. Das merke dabei: Sollte es nicht grosse Schande sein, dass ich oder du ein Christ genennet wäre, und wüsste nicht, was ich glaubte? Weiss ich aber, was ich glaube, so weiss ich, was in der Schrift steht, weil die Schrift nicht mehr, denn Christum und christlichen Glauben in sich hat. Darum, wenn der Glaube die Schrift nur höret, so ist sie ihm so klar und lichte, dass er ohne aller Väter und Lehrer Glossen spricht: das ist recht; das glaube ich auch. . . Das ist wohl wahr, etliche Sprüche der Schrift sind dunkel, aber in denselben ist nichts anders, denn eben was an ändern Orten in den klaren offenen Sprüchen ist. Und da kommen Ketzer her, dass sie die dunkeln Sprüche fassen nach ihrem eigenen Verstände und fechten damit wider die klaren Sprüche und Grund des Glaubens. Da haben denn die Väter wider sie gestritten durch die klaren Sprüche, damit erleuchtet die dunkeln Sprüche, und bewiesen, dass eben das im Dunkel gesagt sei, das im Lichten. . . Seid nur gewiss, ohne Zweifel, dass nichts helleres ist, denn die Sonne, das ist, die Schrift; ist aber eine Wolke dafür getreten, so ist doch nichts anders dahinten, denn dieselbe helle Sonne. Also, ist ein dunkler Spruch in der Schrift, so zweifelt nur nicht, es ist gewisslich dieselbe Wahrheit dahinten, die am ändern Orte klar ist, und wer das Dunkel nicht verstehen kann, der bleibe bei dem Lichten.“ (Auslegung des 37. Ps. v. J. 1521. V, 456. sqq.)

Non solum enim renati et fideles, verum etiam irregeniti et impii vi ipsius claritatis verborum ex instituto significantium, quae ad omnes lectores aequaliter sese habet, assequi possunt notitiam sensus per verba significati, literalem quidem seu historicam; non autem salutarem seu fidei, ut mox dicetur. Atque ita quidem docuit b. Musaeus in Dispp. de conversione, A. 1647. et seqq. habitis, ac postea A. 1658. Halae Saxonum denuo editio, Disp. IV. § 27. et seqq. et Tract. de Convers. A. 1661. Jenae edito, Disp. IV. c. II. § 44. sqq. p. 272. sqq., rursus in der Ausführl. Erklärung. Q. XLIV. p. 342. sqq. ad 397. Secutus autem est vestigia antecessorum bb. DD. Joh. Majori» et Joh. Gerhardi, quorum ille A. 1630. in Confut. Judicii a Valeriano M. de Acathol. Regula Cred. editi, Prop. III. Cap. I. Sect. III. p. 162. ex professo disputat de sententia Valeriani, quae verum Scripturae sensum nemini concedit, nisi interim illustrato et a Spiritu Sancto edocto; atque ipse (J. Major) ex adverso monet, sensum SS. Litterarum verum et indubium vel esse conjunctum cum assensu cordis et conversionis fructu, vel eodem destitutum: hunc posse contingere infidelibus, utpote Judaeis; illum tantum esse fidelium. Et notanter addit: Quemadinoaum

apostoli, dono πυλυγλωττίας immediato et extemporaneo et Spiritu Sancto ornati, mysteria regni coelorum proposuere variis gentibus, uit a singulis possent verbotenus intelligi et operante Spiritu Sancto fide suscipe, quamvis non defuerint, qui sensum quidem praeconii apostoliei cepere, assensum vero dictis denegantes, fruetum inde percepere mdlum, Act. 13.; sic multi, linguarum, quibus Deus sua oracula extare voluit, gnari, sensum Scripturae in locis plurimis eruunt et percipiunt ex verbis (NB.) verum et genuinum; fructum interim et effectum illuminationis praepediunt improbi et a se repellunt απιστία perditi.

Porro § 9. p. 365. scribit: His ita se habentibus, non tum nude et crude dicendum erat a Valeriano, nullum certo assequi verum sensum sacrarum liter arum, nisi interius illustratum et edoctum a Spiritu Sancto. Et § 10.: Censoriam itaque distinctionis virgulam adhibentes, corrigamus et castigemus propositionem istam in hunc modum: Omnis linguae biblicae gnarus certe assequitur verum sensum sacrarum literarum, quam vocum notarum significata pariunt, quamvis interius a Spiritu Sancto neque edoctus sit neque Illustratus. Deinde: Nemo verum sensum sacrarum literarum in illis locis, quae agunt de articulis fidei, assequitur ita, ut assensum dictis adhibeat et fruetum inde capiat, nisi Spiritu Sancto intus cor movente et illuminante.

B. Gerhardus autem A. 1625. in Exeg. L. I., postquam § 413. p. 447. distinxerat inter claritatem Scripturae externam et claritatem seu illuminationem interiorem, a Spiritu Sancto petendam, ita deinceps § 424. p. 461. ad objectionem Bellarmini contra perspicuitatem Scripturae, quam ex necessitate precum ad intelligentiam ejus consequendam, Ps. 119,18. indicata, petiit, respondet per distinctionem inter notitiam literae et Spiritus: scilicet, quod ad notitiam literalem articulorum fidei sufficiat claritas externa Scripturae ^ ad notitiam vero spiritualem requiratur interior Spiritus Sancti illuminatio per pias preces obtinenda.

Imo vero totum Collegium Theol. Jenense, et una cum eo etiam Facultas Theol. Witteb. in der Widerlegung des Rathraannischen Gegenberichts, num. 69. p. 365. a. ad quaestionem: Ob ein unbekehrter Jude ohne vorhergehendes und herzutretendes Gnaden-Licht könne die heilige Schrift nach dem Buchstaben verstehen, und den sensum literalem daraus ergründen? affirmative respondent cumque exempla Hieronymi, Graseri et Buxtorfii. qui, ut verum sensum verborum Scripturae V. T. assequerentur, Judaeos consuluerunt, adduxissent, denique addunt: Ein ander Ding ist es, sich auf die Wörter und significationes vocum verstehen, und solche recht auslegen: ein anders, sich auf die res verstehen, und selbige recht einnehmen, recht appliciren, im Glauben fassen. Hierzu gehöret des Heiligen Geistes GnadenErleuchtung und Handreichung: aber ad investigationem, explicationem et intellectum sensus literalis non item.

Et num. seq. 70. p. 365. b. post. med.: Will Gegenbericht dahinaus, dass kein Unbekehrter könne den rechten Verstand, welchen die Wörter in der Schrift bei sich haben und von sich geben, id est, grammaticum et literalem, erlangen, es sei denn, dass der Heilige Geist mit seinem Gnaden-Licht herzu trete, so halten wirs nicht mit dem Gegenbericht, sondern bleiben bei unserer Meinung, die wir in voriger Post (NB.) erdund nagelfest gemacht. Denn die vocabula, und welche selbige auslegen, und zum rechten Gebrauch ausrüsten, nämlich die Lexica, Dictionaria, wie auch die Libri Grammatici in Lateinischer, Griechi DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

scher, Hebräischer, Arabischer und andern Sprachen verfertiget, seynd humani ingenii inventa, gehören unter die dona naturae, nicht aber unter die duna Spiritus Sancti gratiosa: denn er nicht darauf bestellet (NB.) noch ausgegossen, dass er die praecepta Grammatices tradire, und lehre bei den Hebräern die radices suchen, oder lehre decliniren und conjugiren, und in Logicis enuntiationes und syllogismos machen, sondern dass er üns die Glaubens-Artikel aus der Schrift proponire und in der seligmachenden Wahrheit instruire. Es hat mancher den rechten Verstand der Worte, aber er hat nicht den seligen Verstand der Geheimniss, der zum Glauben gehöret; darum muss man auch allhier sich (NB.) vor aequivociren vorsehen.

Possent autem praeterea adduci dicta όμόψηφα b. Aeg. Hunnii Disp. LXIV. Cap. III. § 6. 7. 8. Tom. V. Op. fol. 681., b. Jac. Martini LL. Th. Disp. XI. § 29. et 30. § 100. et seqq., b. Conr. Dieterici in Inst. Catech. de Scr. S. Q, XXX. resp. ad obj. I. pontif. p. m. 45., Theologorum Marpurgensium et nominatim b. Joh. Steuberi Disp. VII. de Aug. Conf. art. XVHI. § 56. p. m. 154., porro b. Justi Feuerbornii in AntiOstorodo Disp. H. § 3. p. 17., b. H. Kromayeri Theol. Pos. -Pol. A. I. antith. VI. p. 70.

Sic b. Gerhardus scribit: Nos nequaquam affirmamus, quod Scriptura quibusvis sit dara et perspicua; sed Olis, quibus nullum ah aetate, vel ah ignorantia linguae, in qua Scripturam legunt, est impedimentum. Exeg. 1. c. § 413. p. 447. 448. Et b. Jae. Martini 1. c. § 99. sqq. monet, quocl non omnes Scripturam intelligunt, oriri ex privatione duplicium mediarum, naturalium et supernaturalium; inter naturalia autem primum esse cognitionem linguarum.

Nempe, ut b. Musaeus in Dispp. de Convers. A. 1647. sqq. habitis, Disp. IV. § 37. docet: Illis quidem, qui linquarum, quibus originaliter conscriptum est verbum Dei, Ebraieae scilicet et Graecae, ignari sunt, aut ne legere quidem didicerunt, satis est, si dogmata fidei, in lingua vernacula sibi proposita, credant vera esse, et sensu eo, quo proposita ipsis sunt, a Deo in Scripturis sacris revelata, quem assensum in ipsis Spiritus Sanctus operatur, utpote qui per verbum etiam in vernacula, lingua praedicatum efficax est in cordibus hominum, et de ipso testatur, quod sit divinum verbum.


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: But for those who ought to be (instructed and) converted through the Word of…

But for those who ought to be (instructed and) converted through the Word of God read or preached in those languages in which it was originally written, it is absolutely necessary that they be skilled in those languages, and, if they are not distinctly certain of the sense of every passage of Scripture containing some dogma of faith, they must nevertheless believe that those dogmas which concern the foundation of salvation are each contained in the Holy Scriptures, in such a way that they doubt nothing concerning the sense of those passages (grasped from the words themselves, which signify by institution, through the mediation of the knowledge of that language); for otherwise they could not believe that the dogmas themselves are true, since they are believed to be true for no other reason than that they are revealed by God, or because they are contained in the Scriptures in that sense.

Cf. the predecessors in App. Consil. Dedek. l. c. Luther: "The Sophists have said that Scripture is dark; they have supposed that God's Word is by nature so dark and speaks so strangely. But they do not see that all the deficiency lies in the languages; otherwise, nothing would ever have been spoken more easily than God's Word, if we understood the languages. A Turk must surely speak darkly to me, whom, however, a Turkish child of seven years understands well, the..."

because I do not know the language.” (Letter to the Councilmen of all cities of Germany, that they should establish and maintain Christian schools, in the year 1524. X, 551. sq.) This is what the blessed Gerhard, l. c., requires, namely, an impediment from age, and so that a defect of judgment arising from the reason of age does not occur. But the reason is the same if those who are more advanced in age are children in judgment. Indeed, he who does not attend to the words themselves, but indulges his own prejudices and twists the words of Scripture to them, can err even in clear passages and in investigating the genuine sense; whence the blessed Gerhard in *Conf. Cath.* L. II. A. I. C. III. p. 209. 210. requires that no impediment be placed by a preconceived opinion. Compare the blessed Glassius’ *Glaubens-Grund* Chap. III. p. 103.

Quenstedtius: “To owls and bats the sun itself is dark, and the Word of God is dark to the light-shunning [people] of the Scriptures, as Tertullian sometimes calls heretics. Therefore, obscurity does not inhere in Scripture or biblical discourse in itself, but it is rendered obscure ‘by the fault of men, with the veil of sins clouding the eyes of the heart,’ as Abbot Theodore says in Cassian, *Institutes* L. V. c. 34. But the fault of a person is not to be imputed to a thing good in itself. Rivetus rightly [says in] *comment. in Hos.* c. 14. Tom. II. Opp. p. 811. b.: ‘The Word of God is light, and that clear and perspicuous; but it happens to it as it did to the Word made flesh: The light shone in the darkness, but the darkness did not comprehend it.’ ... The illumination of the Holy Spirit is required, not that which brings light to the Scriptures, but that which makes the eye lucid, by which those things that are contained in the Scriptures ought to be read. Or [we must] distinguish between the native perspicuity of Scripture and that which is relative, or accepted comparatively and in respect to the capacity of the human intellect. However, in describing the perspicuity and facility of Scripture, the relation must be established not to any intellect whatsoever, however affected, even if preoccupied by heresy or errors and blinded by Satan; but to an intellect illuminated by the prevenient grace of the Holy Spirit, accompanying the reading, hearing, or meditation of the divine Word; as the apostle declares in 2 Cor. 2:15 sq., 3:5, and especially 4:3, 4. ... For it is necessary that he who reads the Scriptures should seek understanding from the same Spirit by whom they were inspired, through assiduous prayers.” (L. c. q. 12. f. 171. sq.)

For although not all believers are teachers, nor do all interpret, according to 1 Cor. 12:29, yet theologians have [a source] from which (as from a perspicuous principle) they, being learned, may be apt for teaching and reproving, according to 2 Tim. 3:16, 17; and the rest of the believers also have [a source] where they may find eternal life, the way that leads to life being clearly shown to them by the Scriptures themselves, John 5:39. k)

This is what they otherwise call literal or historical knowledge, and distinguish from saving cognition, which pertains to the second operation of the mind and imports a congruent judgment concerning the sense of the words as truly divine, and therefore an assent that is plainly certain and of divine faith (that the things signified are truly such as they are signified to be by the words). See Musaeus and the other authors cited in note d in their respective places.

l) But that perspicuity of the words of Scripture is proved 1) from the very efficient and final cause of Scripture: namely, that since God, the author of Scripture, caused it to be recorded so that men might be instructed from its reading unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, according to 2 Tim. 3:15, and He Himself, as the artificer of mind and tongue, [knows how] to speak clearly. OF THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

undoubtedly it could, and indeed it must be believed, that He willed with supreme providence that those things which are divine should be free from guile, so that all might understand what He was speaking to all, according to the words of Lactantius, *Div. Inst.*, Book VI, ch. XXI; cf. the blessed Gerhard in *Exeg.*, 1. c., § 415, p. 449; the blessed Olassius, *Glaubens-Grund*, ch. III, pp. 73, 74. And just as the chief virtue of speech destined for the instruction of others is perspicuity, and perspicuous speech ought to be so constituted that you are not only able to understand, but that you are not at all able not to understand, according to that saying of Quintilian, *Inst. Orat.*, Book II, ch. III, so it must be acknowledged that Holy Scripture, which was given by God Himself, the most perfect Being, προς διδασκαλίαν, παιδείαν, etc., possesses in those things which are necessary to be known an absolute perspicuity, which is owed to it by its end.

To this is added 2), that Paul, 1 Cor. 14:8-9, where he most diligently inculcates to the teachers of the Church that they should propose the dogmas of faith in a perspicuous and customary manner of speech, by which they may be easily understood by all, adds this reason: "For," he says, "if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself for the battle? So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue speech that is significant, how shall it be known what is spoken? For ye shall speak into the air." Therefore, unless we say that Scripture speaks not so much for the instruction of men as into the air, and that it behaves like a trumpet giving an uncertain sound, from which no one prepares himself for battle, and that Scripture is therefore in vain (which cannot be said without impiety), it must be confessed that the signification of the words employed in Scripture is known to readers according to the common use of speaking, and that therefore the speech of Scripture is perspicuous. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Dispp. de convers.*, held in the year 1647 et seqq., Disp. IV, § 28.

Furthermore 3), Deut. 30:11 it is said: "This commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven... But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart," i.e., it is consigned in words significant, drawn from common use (and as it were from the mouth of men), so that it can easily be understood (just as the heart, or the mind of man, has otherwise become accustomed to a certain signification of words). For thus in the preceding verses that nearness is explained, that this word is not hidden, so that its understanding must be sought either from heaven or from the abyss, as interpreted by the blessed Kromayer, *Theol. Pos.-Pol.*, Art. I, Thes. 6, p. 67. Whence, although the law, of which God speaks through Moses, and which is the rule of things to be done, constitutes only one part of Scripture, yet because Paul [says] these very things, which were once said by God concerning the law, are θεόπνευστος, he transfers them also to the gospel concerning Christ and the righteousness of faith, Rom. 10:6, 8; it must certainly be confessed that Scripture, regarding the gospel just as much as the law, is clear and perspicuous on the part of the words. Cf. what we shall say in the following note.

Quenstedtius: "Dist. 1. between the epistles of Paul themselves and the mysteries about which Paul writes in his epistles. When Peter says 2 Pet. 3:16, ἐν οἷς ἐστι δυσνόητά τινα, he is not speaking of the epistles of Paul, but of the mysteries and dogmas contained in them. For the relative in Greek is not of the feminine, but of the neuter gender; for he does not say ἐν αἷς, but ἐν οἷς, and therefore τὸ ἐν οἷς is not to be referred to the epistles, but to the things immediately preceding, περὶ τούτων, i.e., to the last things; which construction even Lorinus, Cornelius a Lapide, Estius, and Gagnaeus acknowledge here... Peter therefore wishes to say that Paul wrote in almost all his epistles about those things, namely, about which he himself had written here, i.e., about the final judgment and the destruction of the world... 2. The apostle does not say πολλά, he does not say πάντα, but τινα; not many, nor all, but certain things in those—not epistles, as has been said, but mysteries—are difficult to understand; therefore, from the difficulty of the things, the obscurity of Scripture is wrongly concluded... 3. Indeed, this passage makes..."

for the perspicuity of Scripture; for St. Peter teaches that the epistles of Paul are so treated by the unlearned and unstable (ἀστηρίκτοις) on account of many things hard to be understood (δυσνόητα), that they wickedly twist the words from a sufficiently clear meaning into a sense that is not genuine. He indicates a twofold occasion for this distortion: one is ignorance, the other is instability. Neither is from Scripture, of which both are rather a remedy—a remedy that would be sought in vain from it, unless it were in itself lucid and solid.” (L. c. f. 180 sq.)

The same: “Obj. The passage 1 Cor. 13:12: ‘We see now through a glass, in a riddle.’ ... Resp. 1: Although in this place Scripture is compared to a glass and a riddle, it is not therefore to be called entirely obscure; for what we properly call a glass exhibits a clear, distinct, and express likeness of a thing. ... 2. If any obscurity is noted in the cited passage by the name of a riddle, it is not to be understood in regard to the language, but in regard to the things proposed in the Scriptures, which we are bound to believe, even if we do not yet understand them, though we shall understand them in the other life. 3. The Apostle makes the knowledge through a glass and in a riddle common to all wayfarers, nor does he except himself and the other apostles. For he does not say, ‘You now see,’ but ‘We now see through a glass and in a riddle.’ Cf. 2 Cor. 3: 18. Was Scripture, therefore, obscure even to the Apostle when he wrote these things? ... 4. Knowledge and perception in a riddle and vision through a glass are compared to the beatific vision; that the former is obscure with respect to the latter, we readily grant.” (L. c. f. 180.) m)

Latin:

His vero, qui per verbum Dei in iis linguis, quibus originaliter conscriptum est, lectum aut praedicatum (erudiri et) converti debent, omnino necessarium est, ut linquas istas calleant, et, si non distincte de cujusque loci Scripturae, aliquod dogma fidei continentis, sensu simpliciter sint certi, credant tamen, ea dogmata, quae fundamentum salutis concernunt, singula in Scripturis sacris contineri, ita, ut de locorum illorum sensu (ex verbis ipsis, ex instituto significantibus, mediante notitia ejus linguae, apprehenso) nihil dubitent; alias enim credere non possent, ipsa dogmata esse vera, cum non alia de causa credantur vera esse, quam quia a Deo revelata sunt, seu quia eo sensu in Scripturis continentur.

Conf. antecessores in App. Consil. Dedek. l. c. Lutherus: „Die Sophisten haben gesagt, die Schrift sei finster; haben gemeinet, Gottes Wort sei von Art so finster und rede so seltsam. Gerhard. l. c. requirit, m impedimentum ab aetate, adeoque ne defectus judicii ex ratione aetatis occurrat. Par autem ratio est, si, qui aetate profectiores, judicio pueri sint. Gerhardus in Conf. Cath. L. II. A. I. C. III. p. 209. 210. requirit, ne a praeconcepta opinione objiciatur impedimentum. Confer b. Glassii Glaubens-Grund Cap. III. p. 103.

Quenstedtius: „Noctuis ac vespertilionibus sol ipse obscurus est et verbum Dei lucifugis.Scripturarum, ut haereticos quandoque appellat Tertullianus. Non itaque Scripturae aut orationi biblicae per se inest obscuritas, sed,hominum vitio, velamine peccatorum cordis oculos obnubente, redditur obscura·, ut ait Theodorus abbas apud Cassianum 1. V. institut. c. 34. Vitium autem personae rei per se bonae imputandum non est. Recte Rivetus comment. in Hos. c. 14. Tom. II. Opp. p. 811. b.: ,Verbum Dei est lux, eaque clara et perspicua; sed ei accidit, quod Verbo Filio: Lux in tenebris luxit, sed tenebrae eam non comprehenderunt.· . . Requiritur Spiritus S. illuminatio, non quae lucem inferat Scripturis, sed quae lucidum efficiat oculum, quo legi debent ea, quae in Scripturis continentur. Sive dist. inter evidentiam et perspicuitatem Scripturae nativam et relativam sive comparate et in respectu ad capacitatem humani intellectus acceptam. In describenda autem Scripturae perspicuitate et facilitate relationem oportet institui non ad quemvis intellectum, qualitercunque affectum, etiam praeoccupatum haeresi vel erroribus et a satana excoecatum; sed ad intellectum per praevenientem Spiritus S. gratiam, lectionem, auditionem vel meditationem verbi divini concomitantem, illustratum; ut declarat apostolus 2 Cor. 2, 15. sq., c. 3, 5. et inprimis c. 4, 3. 4. . . Necesse enim est, ut legens Scripturas ab eodem Spiritu, a quo inspiratae sunt, assiduis precibus petat intelligentiam.“ (L. c. q. 12. f. 171. sq.)

Etsi enim non omnes fideles sint doctores, neque omnes interpretentur, juxta 1 Cor. 12, 29., habent tamen et theologi, unde (tanquam ex principio perspicuo) eruditi, ad docendum et redarguendum apti sint, juxta 2 Tim. 3, 16. 17.; habent et caeteri fideles, ubi inveniant vitam aeternam, via, quae ad vitam ducit, sibi perspicue ostensa ab ipsis Scripturis, Joh. 5, 39.k)

Haec est, quam alias notitiam literalem aut historicam dicunt, et distinguunt a cognitione salutari, quae ad secundam mentis operationem pertinet et judicium congruum de sensu verborum tanquam vere divino, adeoque assensum plane certum ac fidei divinae (quod res significatae revera tales sint, quales verbis significantur) importat. Vid. Musaeus et caeteri auctores in not. d. citati suis locis.

l) Probatur autem perspicuitas illa verborum Scripturae 1) ex ipsa causa efficiente et finali Scripturae: quod videlicet, cum Deus, Scripturae auctor, eam consignari fecerit ideo, ut homines ex ejus lectione erudirentur ad salutem per fidem, quae est in Christo Jesu, juxta 2 Tim. 3, 15., ipse vero, tanquam mentis et linguae artifex, diserte loqui DI PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIA!.

haud dubie potuerit, utique etiam credendum sit, eum summa providentia voluisse, fuco carere ea, quae divina sunt, ut omnes inteUigerent, quae omnibus loquebatur, juxta verba Lactantii Lib. VI. Div. Inst. cap. XXI., conf. b. Gerh. inExeg. 1. c. § 415. p. 449., b. Olassii Glaubens-Grund, Cap. III. p. 73. 74.
