II. Instit. Orat. c. Π., ita agnoscendum est, Scripturam sacram, quae προς διδασκαλίαν, παιδείαν etc. a Deo ipso, perfectissimo ente, data est, in bis, quae scitu necessaria sunt, pollere omnino perspicuitate, quae illi ex fine debetur.

Quo accedit 2), quod Paulus 1 Cor. 14, 8. 9., ubi doctoribus ecclesiae diligentissime inculcat, ut fidei dogmata perspicuo et usitato sermonis genere proponant, quo ab omnibus facile intelligi possint, hanc addit rationem: Etenim, inquiens, si incertam vocem tuba dederit, quis apparebitur ad bellum? sic et vos, per linguam nisi significantem sermonem dederitis, quomodo intelligetiir, quod dicitur? Entis enim in aerem loquentes. Itaque, nisi dicamus, Scripturam non tam ad informationem hominum, quam in aerem loqui, et habere se instar tubae, incertam vocem dantis, unde nemo apparetur ad bellum, adeoque frustraneam esse Scripturam (quod citra impietatem dici non potest), fatendum est, vocum in Scriptura adhibitarum significationem lectoribus juxta usum communem loquendi notam, atque adeo sermonem Scripturae esse perspicuum. Conf. b. Mus. Dispp. de convers. A. 1647. seqq. habit., Disp. IV. § 28.

Praeterea 3) Deut. 30, 11. dicitur: Verbum hoc, quod loquor tibi, prope est in ore ac corde tuo, i. e. verbis significantibus ex usu communi (et quasi ex ore hominum) depromptis consignatum est, ita, ut facile possit inteUigi (prout alias cor, seu mens hominis certae significationi vocum assuevit). Sic enim in versiculis antecedentibus ista propinquitas exponitur, quod verbum hoc non sit absconditum, ut ejus intellectus vel ex coelo, vel ex abysso peti debeat, interprete b. Kromayero Theol. P0S.-P0I. Art. I. Thes. 6. pag. 67. Unde, licet lex, de qua Deus per Mosen loquitur, quaeque agendorum regula est, unam saltem Scripturae partem constituat, quia tamen Paulus θεόπνευστος haec ipsa, quae olim de lege a Deo dicta fuerunt, transfert etiam ad evangelium de Christo et justitia fidei, Rom. 10, 6. 8., utique fatendum est; Scripturam, quoad evangelium aeque ac legem, ex parte verborum esse claram et perspicuam. Conf., quae in nota seq. dicemus.

Quenstedtius: „Dist. 1. inter Ipsas epistolas Pauli et mysteria, de qulbns Paulus in epistolis suis scribit. Quando Petrus dicit 2 Pet. 3, 16. i,έν όίς εση όνσνόητά riva*, non loquitur de epistolis Pauli, sed de mysteriis et dogmatibus in illis contentis. Relativum enim in Graeco non feminini, sed neutrius generis est; non enim dicit,έν αϊς*, sed,έν όίς*, adeoque xd έν οίς non ad epistolas, sed ad proxime antecedentia περί τούτων, sci. ad res novissimas, referendum est; quam constructionem etiam Lorinus, Cornei, a Lapide, Estius, Gagnaeus hic agnoscunt, . . . Vult ergo dicere Petrus, Paulum in omnibus fere epistolis scripsisse de istis, nempe de quibus ipse hic scripserat, i. e. de judicio extremo et interitu mundi. . . 2. Non dicit apostolus πολλά, non πάντα, sed nva, non multa, nec omnia, sed quaedam in istis, non epistolis, uti dictum, sed mysteriis esse intellectu difficilia; ex rerum itaque difficultate male concluditur obscuritas Scripturae. . . 3. Imo facit hic locus

pro Scripturae perspicuitate; docet enim s. Petrus, ita tractari epistolas Pauli ab indoctis et instabilibus (’άστηρίκτοις) propter multa mysteria δυσνόητα, ut nefarie ab aperta satis sententia in sensum nön genuinum verba torqueantur. Detorsionis autem duplicem indicat occasionem, una est ignorantia, altera instabilitas. Neutra est a Scriptura, a qua utriusque potius est remedium, quod frustra inde peteretur, nisi esset in se lucida et solida.“ (L. c. f. 180. sq.)

Idem: ,,Obj. locum 1 Cor. 13, 12.: ,Cernimus nunc per speculum, in aenigmate.· . . Resp. 1.: Licet hoc loco Scriptura cum speculo et aenigmate comparetur, non tamen propterea tota obscura est dicenda; nam quod proprie speculum dicimus, claram, distinctam et expressam exhibet rei similitudinem. . . 2. Si quae l. c. nomine aenigmatis notatur obscuritas, illa non intelligenda est ratione sermonis, sed rerum in Scripturis propositarum, quas credere tenemur, licet jam non intelligamus, intellecturi autem in altera vita. 3. Apostolus cognitionem per speculum et in aenigmate omnibus viatoribus communem facit, nec quidem excipit seipsum et alios apostolos. Non enim ait: ,Vos nunc cernitis', sed,nos nunc cernimus per speculum et in aenigmate'. Cf. 2 Cor. 3, 18. Ergone etiam apostolo, cum haec scriberet, obscura erat Scriptura? ... 4. Cognitio et perceptio in aenigmate et visio per speculum comparatur visioni beatificae; illam autem respectu hujus obscuram esse, facile damus.“ (L. c. f. 180.)


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Namely, this is what is meant when, in Ps

Namely, this is what is meant when, in Ps. 19:9, the law of the Lord (by which name is not understood precisely the law specifically so called and contrasted with the gospel, but rather the gospel itself, as is evident from a comparison with Rom. 10:18, and thus the whole doctrine which is treated in Scripture as the primary object and of which there is speech here) is said to enlighten the eyes and make the simple wise. And Ps. 119:105, that the word of God is a lamp to the foot of man and a light to his path, namely, so that he may be prudent and beware of the path of falsehood, according to v. 104. Again, 2 Pet. 1:19, it is said that one must attend to the prophetic word (the prophetic Scripture, according to v. 20) as to a lamp shining (ὡς λύχνῳ φαίνοντι) in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts.

For all things tend to this, that we may understand that Scripture, in those things which must be manifest to man in the state of the way, as they call it, lest he be led into errors and not find salvation, and thus, regarding the doctrine of faith and morals, performs for the intellect (as the eye of the mind) what a lit and shining lamp performs for the traveler and the eyes of his body, so that the right path may be trodden, avoiding deviations and without stumbling. It is necessary, therefore, that Scripture be lucid not only in itself, but also to others; and because for this, that a man may rightly know the way of salvation, two things are required: one, that he may perceive by simple apprehension of the mind those things which are necessary to be known for his salvation; the other, that he may embrace those things once apprehended as true and divinely revealed and grant the assent of faith: so it is necessary that Scripture, which in this matter ought to act as a light and a shining lamp, should provide these two things: one, that it should represent those things which are to be known to the intellect in words that are intentionally significant and perspicuous, so that they may be perceived by simple apprehension of the mind; the other, that when the thing signified is more sublime and the intellect itself is weaker, or plainly corrupted, so that it cannot by its own powers rightly judge of that which is signified by those words, nor itself provide or elicit the assent which it owes, Scripture itself, by its own power as an illuminator, should lead the intellect to it and bestow the faculty of knowing and assenting. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

Quenstedtius: "The Papists object that the Scriptures are sometimes called by the Fathers easy, clear, and open on account of the interpreter, who is easy, clear, and open, and who is always present in the Church. Resp.: In this way, the riddles of the Sphinx could also be called clear and open, because Oedipus was able to solve them. Who does not see that, in this way, it is conceded that Scripture is perspicuous only by accident? Dannhauer well says (l. c.): 'Thus there is no difference between the written oracles of God and those of Delphi, and Scripture will be the Sphinx, the Pope the Oedipus.'" (L. c. f. 183.)

Dannhauerus: "Gretserus says: 'Scripture is a lamp, not because it shines for us of itself, but because, when it is explained by the Church, then at last it shines for us.' He clarifies the matter with an example: 'Metaphysics and mathematics make a man wise and enlighten the eyes; they are a lamp. But where does that shine for men? In the huts and hovels of peasants? Not at all! But in the schools of philosophers and mathematicians; here it shines, here it enlightens, etc.' Thus Gretserus accuses the Holy Spirit of a lie. For He clearly calls it a lamp, not a lantern; a shining lamp, not a latent one; a lamp, not a color or a transparent object that illuminates only when it is illustrated by an adventitious light, having no light of itself. If Scripture is a lamp only when it is illuminated by the Church, then even the air could be called a lamp, or any transparent object whatsoever. Our Aeg. Hunnius, although sophistically treated by Gretserus, said very well: 'By the same reasoning, it could be said that the Arabic language is a light and a lamp to our people, and then interpreted thus: if it is understood by them, it is lucid; thus also the leaves of the Sibyl and the Delphic oracles could be called lamps.' 'Altogether,' the Jesuit retorts, 'whatever illuminates the mind, if it is explained, can be called a lamp or a light.' Nothing, therefore, is any longer obscure in all literature, nay, in the world and beyond; thus the Egyptian darkness would be lamps, and those by which hell is described would be outer lamps. The instance regarding metaphysics and mathematics is inept; for both are of themselves obscure by their own sharpness and do not make light, but receive it from the intellect; Scripture itself testifies the contrary concerning itself." (Hodos. phaen. 1. L. p. 43.)

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: "Antithesis; 1. Of the Papists, and indeed a. of the cruder ones, who contend that the whole of Scripture is so obscure, ambiguous, and flexible in all directions that hardly any sentence can be found in it which cannot be bent into various and contrary senses; or if they sometimes assert it is perspicuous, they understand this on account of an easy, clear, and open interpreter who is always present in the Church. Thus Martin Cromer and the Cologne Jesuits, Ruard Tapper, whose insults and taunts against Scripture are these: 'That Scripture is like a nose of wax (which can be bent into any interpretation); that it is like a sheath which admits any sword; that it is like the leaden rule of Lesbian building; that it is a word abbreviated (since it needs commentaries); a Delphic sword,' etc.

b. Of the milder ones, who indeed confess that many things are handed down perspicuously in the Scriptures, yet assert that not everything, but at least some dogmas of faith necessary for salvation are clearly proposed in them. Thus Bellarmine, Costerus, Becanus, Leonard Marius. Gregor de Valentia (lib. 5. analys. fid. c. 2.) says: 'Scripture is so obscure and difficult to understand even regarding the greatest questions of faith that even well-educated men, not to mention common believers, easily hallucinate in its investigation and wander away from it.' —

2. Of the Enthusiasts and Weigelians, to whom Scripture is double-handed, equivocal, an obscure lamp, a book sealed with seven seals and a sealed riddle, a sheath, not the sword of the Spirit, the killing letter; see Weigel’s Postill. part II. p. 185, Sebastian Franck in the preface to his Paradoxa 280. These are Weigel’s words: 'The Scripture is a two-edged sword; one can use it on both sides, let one be as wrong as he will, yet he can wield the Scripture against his opponent.' — 3. Of the Praeadamites..."

of the founder of the [Pre-Adamite] system, Isaac Peyrère, who says that "many things in the Scriptures are written with such carelessness and such darkness that nothing, for the most part, can be read that is more intricate or more obscure; that God has spoken with men in a perplexed and enigmatic manner, and that the same has been handed down in the writings." See him in *System. theol.*, lib. IV, c. 1, p. 184, and against him, Samuel Maresius in the *Praefat. apolog. pro αὐθεντία Scripturae*, p. 8 sqq. —

4. Of the Arminians, who, on the contrary, contend that Holy Scripture is so clear and perspicuous that there is no need for the illumination of the Holy Spirit and the special light of grace for its saving understanding. See Arnoldus against Tilenus, p. 441, 464. Episcopius, *De perspicuit. Script.*, thes. 8, says: "It is impossible that even any unregenerate person cannot perceive the sense of Scripture." Cf. *Exam. censurae*, c. 1, fol. 35. —

5. Of the Socinians, who also assert that man can "understand Holy Scripture with the help of the intellect alone, without the special and internal grace and illumination of the Holy Spirit, and with profit"; thus Ostorodus, *Instit. Germ.*, c. 1, p. 3 sq., cf. *Catech. Racov.*, p. 224 b. Smalzius against Franz, D. 3, *De persona Christi*, fol. 81, and in his *Refut. lib. de erroribus Arianorum*, fol. 206, attributes "a studiously affected ambiguity" to Christ. Enjedinus, *Explic. locorum*, fol. 136, contends that the entire Gospel of John is obscure; his words in the cited place are these: "If a concise, abrupt, and disjointed discourse, consisting of allegories, is to be called sublimity, I confess that John is sublime." (L. c. f. 173 sq.) §

42. But in order that Scripture may be consulted by men, even by those unskilled in the holy languages, Hebrew and Greek, for the purpose of knowing the doctrine of faith and morals, it is therefore useful that versions of Scripture in any languages should exist and that men should be incited to read them. For they are the end of Scripture; see § 10 and notes a, c. See § 41 and note f. Or translations of the words of Scripture from a less known idiom into another, more known idiom or language, which the Greeks call μετάφραση.

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: "The antithesis of the Papists, who nevertheless do not agree among themselves. For in the beginning they condemned all versions of the Bible, denying altogether that Scripture ought to be translated into vernacular languages, because that would be more pernicious than salutary; thus Petrus Sutor, a Carthusian, in his book *De translat. bibliae*, c. 22, not only disapproves of the 'vernacular and mother' (for so he calls it) 'version of the Bible,' but also promises 'that he will show it to be inept, rash, and dangerous.' ... Andradius, in his *Defensio fidei*, lib. IV, f. 241, says: 'We can now hope for nothing from the Holy Bibles that have been made common and turned into vernacular languages (if they are permitted everywhere) except the destruction of piety, the ruin of religion, and the perdition of faith.' ... 'The Bibles of the Protestants must be purged, not with the pen, but with the pyre,' says Gretser, lib. II, *De libb. prohib.*, c. 10.

Afterward, however, the Papists became milder and denied that their church prohibits vernacular versions, as Bellarmine, lib. II, *De V. D.*, c. 15, according to whom 'the Popes, the authors of the Index of Prohibited Books, do not prohibit the vernacular translations themselves, but only circumscribe the use of them within certain limits.' ... But these two phalanxes of Papists differ more in words than in reality. For 1. both use the same arguments from those... ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

from the inconveniences sought; why, therefore, should we not judge that they conspire in a friendly manner toward the same end?

Latin:

m) Scilicet hoc est, quod Ps. 19, 9. lex Domini (quo nomine non intelligitur praecise lex specialiter sic dicta et evangelio contradistincta, sed una ipsum evangelium, ut patet ex collatione Rom. 10, 18. adeoque tota doctrina, quae in Scriptura, tanquam objectum primariupa, tractatur et de qua hic sermo est) dicitur illuminare oculos, et sapientem efficere simplicem. Et Ps. 119, 105., verbum Dei esse lucernam pedi hominis et lumen semitae ejus, nempe ut prudens sit et caveat sibi a semita mendacii, juxta v. 104. Rursus 2 Petr. 1,19. dicitur, ad sermonem propheticum (Scripturae prophetime, juxta v. 20.) esse attendendum, tanquam ad lucernam lucentem (ώς λύχνψ ψαίνυντι) in obscuro beo, donec dies illucescat, et lucifer exoriatur in cordibus nostris.

Omnia enim eo tendunt, ut intelligamus, Scripturam in his, quae homini in statu viae, quem vocant, manifesta esse debent, ne in errores inductus salutem non inveniat, adeoque, quoad doctrinam fidei et morum, id praestare intellectui (velut oculo mentis), quod lucerna accensa et lucens praestat viatori et oculis corporis ejus ad viam rectam, vitatis deviis ac sine offensione, calcandam. Oportet ergo Scripturam non solum in se, sed et aliis esse lucidam; et quia ad id, ut homo viam salutis recte cognoscat, duo requiruntur: unum, ut, quae sibi ad salutem tendenti sunt cognitu necessaria, simplici apprehensione mentis percipiat, alterum, ut illa apprehensa, tanquam vera ac divinitus revelata, amplectatur et fidei assensum commodet: ita Scripturam, quae in hoc negotio instar luminis ac lucernae lucentis se habere debet, duo haec praestare oportet: unum, ut, quae cognoscenda sunt intellectui, verbis ex instituto significantibus ac perspicuis repraesentet, ut simplici mentis apprehensione percipi possint; alterum, ut, quando res significata sublimior est et intellectus ipse debilior, aut plane corruptus, ita ut non possit suis viribus recte judicare de eo, quod verbis illis significatur, neque assensum, quem debet, ipse praebere aut elicere, Scriptura ipsa, virtute sua, tanquam illuminatrice, intellectum eo perducat et facultatem cognoscendi atque assentiendi largiatur. DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

Quenstedtius: „Objiciunt pontificii, Scripturas aliquando nominari a patribus faciles, claras, apertas ob interpretem, facilem, clarum, apertum, qui semper praesens in ecclesia. Resp.: Sic clara et aperta dici poterunt etiam Sphyngis aenigmata, quia Oedipus ea solvere potuit. Quis non videt, sic, tantum per accidens Scripturam perspicuam esse, concedi? Bene Dannhauerus 1. c.: ,Sic inter oracula Dei scripta et Delphica non est differentia, et Scriptura Sphynx erit, papa Oedipus.'“ (L. c. f. 183.)

Dannhauerus: ,, ,Est‘, inquit Gretserus, ,Scriptura lucerna, non quod per se nobis luceat, sed quia, quando ab ecclesia explicatur, tum demum nobis lucet/ Exemplo rem declarat: ,Metaphysica et mathematica efficiunt hominem sapientem et illuminant oculos, sunt lucerna; atubi illa hominibus lucet? num in casis et tuguriis rusticorum? — Minime gentium! sed in scholis philosophorum et "mathematicorum; hic lucet, hic illuminat etc.' Ita Gretserus mendacii arguit Sp. S. Hic enim clare vocat lucernam, non laternam, lucernam lucentem, non latentem, lucernam, non colorem aut diaphanum, quod adventitio demum lumine illustratura illuminat, per se lucem non habet. Si Scriptura tum demum lucerna est, cum ab ecclesia illuminatur, etiam aer lucerna dici poterit, etiam quodlibet diaphanum. Optime noster Aeg. Hunnius, quamvis sophistice tractatus a Gretsero, ,eadem ratione posset dici, nostris hominibus linguam Arabicam esse lucem et lucernam, idque deinde sic interpretari: si ab illis intelligatur esse lucidam; sic et Sibyllae folia et oracula Delphica lucernas dici posse/ ,Omnino', regerit Jesuita, ,quicquid mentem illuminat, si explicetur, lucerna, lux dici potest.' Nihil igitur amplius in omnibus literis, imo in mundo et extra obscurum est; sic lucernae fuerint tenebrae Aegyptiae et, quibus infernus describitur, exteriores. Instantia de metaphysica et mathematica inepta est; utraque enim per se suo acumine est obscura nec lucem facit, sed accipit ab intellectu; contrarium de se Scriptura ipsa testatur." (Hodos. phaen. 1. L. p.,43.)

ANTITHESIS: Quenstedtius: „Antithesis; 1. ### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: The authors of the latter opinion signify not obscurely that it is permitted to…

2. The authors of the latter opinion signify not obscurely that it is permitted to no one to translate the Holy Bible into vernacular languages, unless it be to one to whom this has been permitted by the Pope; but the Pope grants this to no one, unless he knows him to be so versed that the errors which lie hidden in the Vulgate version are simultaneously poured into the vernacular languages. In different words, therefore, Bellarmine says the same thing as the defenders of the former opinion.

3. Let no one think that the pontiffs and their sycophants decree that it is in itself useful and expedient that Holy Scripture be translated into vulgar languages, if that is understood absolutely, and not comparatively. For if no vulgar translations of the Lutherans or Calvinists existed, they would all with one voice pronounce that it is not expedient for that to be done...

Finally, others of the Papists say that versions and their reading are licit, but that the laity perceive no fruit from them on account of the obscurity of Scripture.” (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. 4. s. 2. q. 22. f. 330. sqq.)

Just as the church was to be planted and preserved throughout all the nations of the world and peoples of any languages. See Matt. 28:19; Mark 16:15; Col. 3: 11.

Namely, that the word of Christ may dwell in them richly (πλουσίως ἐνοικείτω) and that they may be able to teach and admonish one another. Col. 3: 16.

Moreover, the arguments which we brought forward in note c to § 10 also hold in this place. Cf. blessed Musaeus, preface to the Treatise on Conversion, ed. 1660, p. 7 sqq., p. 21 sqq.

Although versions arranged by human effort do not have canonical authority, as do the θεόπνευστοι texts, yet insofar as they are conformed to these, they certainly contribute to attaining faith and the progress of faith, and to excluding opposing errors. §

43. But in order that the true sense of the words of Scripture—especially the literal, which of one place is but one, and then also the mystical, wherever it has a place—may be rightly understood, and that not only the meaning of the clearer passages may be firmly held against the distortions of the heterodox, but also that more difficult passages may be unfolded and understood for the progress of spiritual knowledge, the laws of good interpretation must be observed.

Or the concept of the mind which the author of Scripture intended and wished to signify through the words. For that, speaking absolutely, is called the sense of the words, and that which is to be signified proximately and immediately through the words is said to be intended; if these are taken properly, it is called the proper sense; if they are modified by some trope, it is called the figurative sense. Confer blessed Glassius, Phil. S. L. II. P. I. Tr. II. S. I. p. m. 260 sqq.

For it is customary in every language, in every kind of speech, that an author who speaks not to deceive but to teach or inform others does not intend to signify more than one sense through one and the same set of words placed once in one and the same context. Because, therefore,

since God speaks to men in Scripture in a human manner and by words that signify by design, or are taken from the customary usage of speech, it is rightly believed that even in Scripture the literal sense of a single statement is one, not many. Cf. the blessed Glassius, *Phil. S.*, lib. 1, cap. 1, p. 268 (of the edition in my possession).

The sense that is signified not immediately through the words themselves, but through the things signified by those words, insofar as those things are types, shadows, figures, and signs or symbols of other things. It is otherwise called the spiritual sense. Cf. the blessed Glassius, *l. c.*, Tr. I, S. I, p. 249.

And thus it is also established that the literal sense is prior to the mystical by nature and order, according to the same *l. c.*, Tr. II, S. II, p. 289, who also deserves to be read in the following pages specifically regarding the allegorical, typical, and parabolic sense.

For that twofold sense, literal as well as mystical, is not to be sought and embraced in every single text of Scripture and in every individual passage; see Glassius, *l. c.*, Tr. I, S. I, p. 248. And one must distinguish, for example, between innate allegories, which are expressly delivered in the Scriptures themselves and, strictly speaking, are the mystical sense of Scripture, and inferred allegories, or accommodations of things signified by words to other things devised by interpreters, which, strictly speaking, are not senses intended there by the Holy Spirit. See the same, Tr. II, S. III, art. III, p. 291, 292.

For although even the simplest of men can conceive the true and determinate sense of the words of Scripture—which treat of some dogma *ex professo* and are proposed in a known language—without difficulty, it can nevertheless happen, and often does, that the sense of even clear words is perverted by the frauds of heterodox persons and rendered doubtful by far-fetched arguments (as is manifest from the examples of the words of institution and various passages that prove the deity of Christ). In order to counter this rightly, the laws of good interpretation must be called to one's aid, and thus the true sense, conforming to those laws, must be distinguished from other false and fictitious ones. See what we said at § 41, notes b and d.

And indeed, some passages of Scripture are obscure in themselves and when viewed in isolation; others are obscure in respect to others with which they seem to conflict. Both must be addressed by the benefit of legitimate interpretation. See the blessed Gerhard, *de interpr. Script.*, § 64 sqq.

For our theologians do not establish that the private spirit of any individual is to be followed, but they fully acknowledge the laws of good interpretation, both general ones, which right reason provides as being founded in nature and common to the interpretation of all writings, and special ones, which have been peculiarly observed in Holy Scripture itself. And that the blessed Luther was an observer of both is shown by the blessed Musaeus in the *Praef. Tract. de Convers.*, p. 37 sqq., and *Vindic. Bibl. Germ. Glossat.*, Disp. II, Th. 35, p. 111 sqq. §

44. The laws for interpreting Scripture, regarding the literal sense, generally come down to this: I. That the habit and construction of words and phrases [must be understood] according to the custom of the holy language. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

must be diligently considered; II. that the intention of the speaker is to be investigated from the antecedents and consequents, from the occasion, the scope, the subject matter, and other causes; c concerning which, as well as other more specific rules which they contain under them, more prolix treatment is given in the schools of exegetical theology. d

Thus the blessed Franzius included in two precepts what pertains to the interpretation of Scripture, whom the blessed Glomus follows in *Phil. S. L. II. P. II. S. I.* p. 351 sqq. Namely, that just as every language has its own genius and idioms, so also do the Hebrew and Greek languages; concerning which, the sacred grammar and rhetoric of the blessed Glassius in *Phil. S.* are to be consulted, as well as lexicons, concordances, and the critical observations of learned men. For thus, not only the πολυσημία of words, but also the εμψασις, and not rarely the occasion and means for resolving ἀντιφάσεις, are recognized. This was formerly recognized and taught by Hilary in *Lib. IV. de Trinit.* p. m. 37 and *Lib. IX.* p. m. 116. And among our own, besides Gerhard, Franzius, and Glassius in the aforementioned places, one may also consult Flacius in *Clavis*, Dannhauer in *Hermeneutica s.*, Dan. Oramerus in *Isag. ad Libb. Proph. et Apost.*, Georg. Grossehäyn in *Epitome Hermeneut. s.*, and others. The nature of this undertaking does not permit adding more here. § 45. But especially, in order that the mysteries of faith, delivered in the Scriptures, may be rightly recognized, a it must be observed that b one must persist in the proper and customary signification of words, c as long as no manifest circumstance of the text, or condition of the subject matter, or other urgent reason compels one to descend to an improper signification. d

For this reason, we have thought this rule should be particularly inculcated. This rule is founded upon the natural reason of understanding, by which we are commanded to attend to that sense which all conceive or would conceive according to the common use and signification of words; otherwise, no certainty of our understanding will be given. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Vindic. Bibl. Disp. II. § 35. p. 111, 112.* Although the thing signified may be more remote from the human mind and the condition of other things to which we are accustomed, it must nevertheless be considered that this is proper to mysteries. Add the blessed Musaeus, *Dissert. de S. Coena contra Vorstium § 5. p. 2.* But if the analogy of faith, or clearer parallel passages, or the antecedents and consequents in the context, and the scope of the speaker, or other circumstances most openly contradict the proper signification of the words, or even if, upon admitting the proper signification of some word or phrase, a manifest contradiction clearer than the sun presents itself; then certainly the necessity of departing from the proper signification of the words will be imposed upon the interpreter.

46. Finally, just as theological conclusions, and those things which are to be believed by divine faith, are rightly deduced from Holy Scripture as a perspicuous principle, a so in arguments of this kind, even those whose conclusion is merely b theological, not only are the formal principles of reason c undoubtedly used usefully, d but also the material principles of reason e are rightly employed; f provided that, when they are particular or singular, they are subordinated to a universal theological principle, g and that no universal principles of reason are employed other than those which are of absolute necessity, h so that the opposite implies a manifest contradiction. i

For our theologians never denied this, even though they said they used Scripture alone as their principle, norm, or rule; rather, they asserted it whenever they said they would prove their dogmas from the Scriptures or wished to refer controversial questions to Scripture as the norm.

For to prove is to deduce something from another by consequence, as a conclusion from premises.

However, those things are not so much to be referred to the norm which are formally affirmed or denied in that which is the norm, as those concerning which a doubt has arisen as to whether they agree with what is formally contained therein.

Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Tractatus de usu principiorum rationis*, Book I, near the beginning, and Book II, Chapter XXX; likewise in *Tractatus de Conversione*, Disputation IX, Chapters II and III. Finally, Disputation I against Masenius, in which the concord meditated upon by him is examined, § 29 ff., p. 122 ff.

Latin:

2. Posterioris sententiae auctores haud obscure significant, nemini licere s. biblia in linguas vernaculas vertere, nisi cui hoc a papa permissum sit; ast papa hoc nemini concedit, nisi quem sciat, ita versatum esse, ut errores, qui in vulgata versione latent, simul in vernaculas linguas transfundantur. Diversis ergo verbis.Bellarminus idem dicit, quod prioris sententiae defensores.

Si enim nullae Lutheranorum aut Calvinistarum extarent translationes vulgares, omnes uno ore pronunciarent, non expedire, ut id flat. . .

Alii denique pontificiorum licitas esse ajunt versiones earumque lectionem, sed nullum fructum inde percipere laicos propter Scripturae obscuritatem.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. 4. s. 2. q. 22. f. 330. sqq.)

Prout ecclesia per omnes orbis terrarum nationes et quarumvis linguarum populos plantari et conservari debebat. Vid. Matih. 28,19. Mare. 16, 15. Coi. 8, 11.

Nempe ut verbum Christi in illis habitet abundanter (-λουαίως ένοίχειτω) atque alii alios docere et commonefacere possint. Col. 3, 16.

Quamvis vero versiones humano studio concinnatae non habeant auctoritatem canonicam, quemadmodum textus θεόπνευστοι) quatenus tamen illae his conformes sunt, faciunt utique ad fidem fideique profectum consequendum et excludendos errores oppositos.§

43. Sed ut verus sensus a verborum Scripturae, literalis praecipue, b qui unius loci non nisi unus est, c deinde vero etiam mysticus, d sicubi e is locum habet, recte intelligatur, ac non solum locorum clariorum sententia contra detorsiones heterodoxorum f firmiter teneatur, verum etiam loca difficiliora g ad profectum cognitionis spiritualis evolvi atque intelligi possint, leges bonae interpretationis h observari debent.

Seu conceptus mentis, quem auctor Scripturae per verba intendit et significare voluit. Is enim absolute loquendo sensus verborum, et per verba proxime atque immediate significandus intendi dicitur; quae si proprie accipiantur, sensus proprius, si tropo quodam modificata sint, sensus figuratus dicitur. Confer, b. Glassii Phil. S. L. II. P. I. Tr. Π. S. I. p. m. 260. sqq.

Est enim in omni lingua, in omni locutionis genere id usitatum, ut per una et eadem verba in uno eodemque contextu semel posita non nisi unum sensum significare intendat auctor, qui non ad decipiendos, sed docendos aut informandos alios loquitur. Quia ergoBaieri Comp. ed. Walther. I. 12

Deus in Scriptura ad homines loquitur, modo humano et verbis ex instituto significantibus, seu ex usu loquendi consueto desumtis docendos, recte utique creditur, quod etiam in Scriptura unius dicti sensus literalis unus sit, non plures. Conf. b. Glassii Phil. S. 1. c. p. m. 268.

Qui rwn significatur proxime per ipsa verba, sed per res verbis illis significatas, in quantum illae aliarum rerum typi, umbrae, figurae et signa vel symbola sunt. Dicitur alias sensus spiritualis. Conf. b. Glass. l. c. Tr. I. S. I. p. 249.

Atque ita etiam constat, sensum literalem priorem esse mystico natura et ordine, juxta eundem 1. c. Tr. II. S. II. p. 289., qui etiam in seqq. speciatim de sensu attegorico, typico et parabolico legi meretur.

Non enim in omni omnino Scripturae textu et in singulis locis duplex iste sensus, literalis pariter et mysticus, quaerendus et amplexandus est; vid. Glass. 1. c. Tr. I. S. I. p. 248., ac distinguendae sunt v. g. allegoriae innatae, quae in Scripturis ipsis expresse traduntur ac proprie loquendo sensus mysticus Scripturae sunt, et illatae, sive ab interpretibus excogitatae accommodationes rerum verbis significatarum ad res alias, quae proprie loquendo non sunt sensus a Spiritu Sancto illic intenti. Vid. eund. Tr. II. S. III. art. III. p. 291. 292.

Nam quamvis ex verbis Scripturae, quae de dogmate aliquo ex professo agunt, in lingua nota propositis, homines etiam simplicissimi sensum verum ac determinatum citra difficultatem concipere possint: potest tamen et solet aliquando accidere, ut fraudibus heterodoxorum sensus etiam clarorum verborum pervertatur et conquisitis ratiunculis dubius reddatur (quemadmodum exemplis verborum institutionis et locorum variorum, quae Christi deitatem probant, manifestum est); cui ut recte occurratur, leges bonae interpretationis in subsidium vocari et sic sensus verus, legibus illis conformis, ab aliis falsis fictisque discerni debet. Vide, quae diximus ad § 41. not. b. et d.

Atque aliqua quidem Scripturae loca obscura sunt· per se et seorsim spectata; aliqua in respectu ad alia, cum quibus pugnare videntur. Utrisque occurrendum est beneficio legitimae interpretationis. Vid. b. Gerh. de interpr. Script. § 64. sqq.

Non enim nostrates privatum cujusque spiritum sequendum statuunt, sed omnino agnoscunt leges bonae interpretationis, cum generales, quas recta ratio, tanquam in natura fundatas et interpretationi omnium scriptorum communes, suppeditat; tum speciales, quae in Scriptura sacra ipsa peculiariter animadversae fuerunt. Atque observantem utrarumque fuisse b. Lutherum, ostendit b. Musaeus in Praef. Tract. de Convers. p. 37. sqq. et Vindic. Bibi. Germ. Glossat. Disp. II. Th. 35. p. 111. sqq.§

44. Leges interpretandi Scripturam, quoad sensum literalem, fere huc a redeunt: I. quod vocum phrasiumque habitus et constructio juxta consuetudinem linguae sanctae b DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

diligenter sint consideranda; II. quod ex antecedentibus et consequentibus, ex occasione, scopo, materia et aliis causis intentio loquentis sit investiganda; c de quibus, ut et specialioribus aliis, quas sub se continent, regulis, in scholis theologiae exegeticae d prolixius agitur.

S., lexica quoque atque concordantiae et observationes criticae eruditorum. Sic enim non solum πολυσημία vocum, verum etiam εμψασις, nec raro solvendarum havTio<pavita>v occasio et medium agnoscitur. Hanc olim agnovit et tradidit Hilarius Lib. IV. de Trinit. p. m. 37. et Lib. IX. p. m. 116. Grossehäyn in epitome Hermeneut. s. aliique. Plura hic addere non fert ratio instituti.§ 45. Inprimis vero, ut mysteria fidei, in Scripturis tradita, recte agnoscantur, a observandum est, quod b in propria et usitata verborum significatione sit persistendum, c quamdiu non manifesta circumstantia textus, aut subjectae materiae conditio, aliave urgens ratio ad impropriam significätionem descendere cogit. d

Quapropter hanc regulam peculiariter inculcandam putavimus. Fundatur haec regula in naturali ratione intelligendi, qua jubemur ad eum attendere sensum, quem secundum communem verborum usum et significationem omnes concipiunt aut conciperent; alioqui enim nulla dabitur intelligentiae nostrae certitudo. 46.
