Hoc enim nunquam negarunt nostri, etiamsi se sola Scriptura, tanquam principio, norma aut regula, uti dicerent; sed potius asseruerunt, quoties se sua dogmata ex Scripturis probaturos aut quaestiones controversas ad Scripturam, velut normam, revocari velle, dixerunt.

Probare enim est, per consequentiam aliquid ex alio, velut conclusionem ex praemissis, deducere.

Ad normam autem non tam revocanda veniunt ea, quae in eo, quod norma est, formaliter affirmantur aut negantur; quam ea, de quibus, utrum cum his, quae formaliter illic continentur, conveniant, dubitatio orta est.

Confer b. Musaei Tract. de usu prine. Rat. L. I. sub initium, et Lib. H. Cap. XXX., item in Tr. de Convers. Disp. IX. Cap. II. et III. Denique Disp. I. contra Masenium, qua meditata ab eo concordia examinatur § 29. sqq. p. 122. sqq.


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Or a pure article of faith

Or a pure article of faith. For concerning those things which pertain to mixed articles of faith and, besides revealed theology, are also treated in philosophy from the light of reason, there is less difficulty. See, however, concerning this distinction of theological questions, the blessed Musaeus, *de Usu Principiorum Rationis*, Book I, Chapter VI, § 6, Chapter XIII ff., and Book II, Chapter I.

Or those things which pertain to the form of syllogisms and the disposition of terms in figure and mood, and which pertain to the rules of consequences. See Musaeus, *Tractatus citatus*, Book II, Chapter II.

For although not all theological discourses must be expressly brought forth in syllogistic form; yet, whenever the reason of a serious and solid disputation demands it, that labor is not to be shirked.

Otherwise, however, it suffices to connect such discourses as are reducible to syllogistic form.

By this name are understood propositions known by the light of nature and having metaphysical, physical, or moral evidence; which pertain to the matter of arguments and constitute the major or minor premise. See Musaeus, *loco citato*, Book II, Chapter II.

It follows, indeed, that if these are rightly joined with a theological proposition, the conclusion is not only true and certain, but also one which ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

is a matter of faith; which the blessed Musaeus shows in *Tract. de Convers. Disp. VIII. and IX.* Compare here what we said in note g to § 35. An example which we brought forward in the aforementioned place pertains to this. To which may be joined that one by which a man argues: Every man is seriously loved by God, and has grace and salvation seriously offered to him. I am a man. Therefore, I am seriously loved by God, etc. Add the blessed Musaeus, *Tr. de Convers. p. 593 and 594.*

For example: Whoever has perfections proper to God alone, he is the true God. But Christ has perfections proper to God alone. Therefore, Christ is the true God. The minor premise must be proved from revelation. The major premise is known by the light of nature, but it is of absolute necessity, and it implies a contradiction if you say that someone has perfections which are really identical with the divine essence, and yet does not have the divine essence, or is not the true God. For otherwise, if the principles of reason are applied not absolutely, but in a certain respect, or as universal and necessary only in a certain genus, it easily happens that a conclusion is inferred which is repugnant to mysteries or even primary articles of faith; which is evident from the examples of the Antitrinitarians and others. See the blessed Musaeus, *de Usu Princ. Rat. L. II. Cap. XIV. sqq. p. 451 sqq.*, likewise *Tract. de Convers. Disp. IX. § 30, 31. p. 595, 596.*

Hollazius: "The principles of reason are either organic or philosophical. Organic principles of reason are rightly applied to explaining and confirming the dogmas of faith and morals. From philosophical principles, mixed articles of faith become known to a certain extent. Pure articles of faith, however, are demonstrated and known solely from Holy Scripture as from a domestic, fundamental, and primordial principle. Meanwhile, it is permitted to use absolutely universal philosophical principles in theological discourses, as common, ministerial, and subservient principles for completing a fully expressed syllogism. —

They are called organic principles which pertain to the instrumental disciplines: grammar, rhetoric, and logic. Some philosophical principles are absolutely and unlimitedly universal, which consist in an essential and simply necessary connection of terms, so that they cannot be shaken by any instance, even from Scripture, e.g.: It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at the same time; whatever is, when it is, it is necessary that it be; every spirit is immaterial, etc. Others are limited and universal only in a certain respect, which are indeed true in a certain genus, by hypothesis, or according to the sphere of natural cognition, yet they admit of limitation and can be infringed by some instance, if not taken from nature, certainly taken from Scripture, e.g.: As many as are the persons, so many are the essences; every human individual is a person by itself; everything begotten is numerically distinct in essence from the begetter. —

Without the use of reason, we can neither perceive, nor confirm, nor defend theological dogmas from the sophistries of adversaries. Certainly, God has revealed the wisdom of eternal salvation in His Word not to brutes, but to men using sound reason, and has seriously enjoined upon them by command that they should read, hear, and meditate upon His Word; Deut. 6:6; John 5:39. Therefore, the intellect is required as a receiving subject or an apprehending instrument. For just as without eyes we see nothing, and without ears we hear nothing, so without reason we understand nothing. Meanwhile, however, human reason is not the source or primordial element from which the proper and proximate principles of faith are derived. —

Organic principles are applied as aids for acquiring the theological habit, since without them neither the sense or meaning of words can be elicited (which is the task of grammar), nor the figures and modes of speaking weighed (which is the task of rhetoric), nor connections and consequences perceived, nor discourses formed (which is the task of logic). —

Mixed articles of faith are called those which consist not only of revelation, but also of the light of nature, which PROLEGOM. CAP. II. are primarily and most safely proven from Holy Scripture up to the πληροφορίαν [full assurance] of faith; secondarily and less safely, they are deduced from the principles of reason. Thus, philosophers proceed to prove the existence and attributes of God in metaphysics and pneumatics from the principles of reason. —

Regarding the pure articles of faith, reason left to itself knows nothing; rather, it is blind and dim-sighted toward the mysteries of faith. The Apostle of the Gentiles warns man of this spiritual blindness, 1 Cor. 2:14, saying: "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned."

One must observe here the Apostle’s genuine argument. The former is taken from the congenital corruption of the human intellect after the Fall. Whatever the natural man (not illuminated by the Word of God) does not grasp, but rejects with a certain natural disgust as absurd, that cannot be judged from the principles of reason. But the divine mysteries, etc. Therefore. The latter is sought from the condition of the mysteries. Whatever is not discerned except spiritually (through the light of the Holy Spirit), that is not to be estimated or decided by the judgment of reason. But the mysteries of faith, etc. Therefore. —

That philosophical principles can be rightly applied in theological discourses as ministerial and serving to complete a syllogism is shown by the following theological discourse. If the truth of Christ’s human nature is to be proven against Marcion, the fundamental principle of theological demonstration is drawn from Holy Scripture: Christ has a human body and soul. Matt. 26:27, 28. Luke 24:39. Therefore, Christ is true man. You say: Let the consequence or the connection of the antecedent and the consequent be proven. I prove the consequence by employing a principle of reason: Whoever has a human body and soul, he is true man. Christ has a human body and soul. Therefore, Christ is true man. In this discourse, the truth of the theological conclusion rests upon the minor proposition taken from the revealed Word of God, as the proper, fundamental, and primordial principle of demonstration. The major proposition is an absolutely universal principle of reason and concurs only as a common, secondary, and ministerial principle, flowing in of its own accord and superadded to complete the syllogism and to show the syllogistic δοκιμασίαν [testing]." (Exam. theol. Proleg. III. q. 4. p. 68. sqq.)

Quenstedtius: "In this syllogism: A true man has a soul and body; Christ is a true man: therefore Christ has a soul and body — the major is of evident and necessary reason; the minor is of Scripture; however, it is clear that the subject and predicate of the question are not joined by the power and force of the major, but by the force of the minor, in which is the conjunction of the terms, which are partly the same as the terms of the conclusion even as to the sound itself, and partly the same as to their power and value. For although a man has a soul and body, the Son of God nevertheless did not have a soul and body before He began to be man. Therefore, the cause and principle of the conclusion is properly the minor, which is of Scripture. The major, however, is properly nothing but a declaration of one term, which is predicated in the minor, and thus an instrument and aid for understanding the minor and deducing the conclusion." (Th. did.-pol. P. I. c. 3. s. 2. q. 2. f. 64.)

Hollazius: "Although the mysteries of faith are not contrary to the principles of reason, one must not, however, judge the former by the latter. Medicine and jurisprudence are not contrary to one another; yet a physician does not demonstrate the method of curing a fever from legal proceedings, nor does a jurist seek the method of settling forensic disputes from anatomy. The art of painting and the art of shoemaking do not fight with each other, yet the shoemaker does not go beyond his last. Right reason, keeping itself within the limits of its object, does not contradict the mysteries of faith; but it happens accidentally that corrupt reason, having stepped out of its sphere, becomes enormous and unbridled and struggles against divine revelation. (Socinians object:) 'Every discourse is ultimately resolved into that principle: Impossible

is, that the same thing is and is not at the same time, which is the principle of reason. As, therefore, the final resolution is made into it, so the final judgment is deferred to reason." Resp.: That principle can be considered in two ways: 1. as it is the common foundation of contradiction; 2. as it is appropriated to divine things and restricted to their nature. Although reason may formally pass judgment on the common "foundation of contradiction," nevertheless, the real and normative judgment belongs to Holy Scripture, insofar as that foundation of contradiction is appropriated to divine things. (

Socinians object:) "Evangelical doctors not rarely use the principles of reason in theological syllogisms. Therefore, they cannot accuse the Socinians of an abuse of reason." Resp.: 1. Evangelicals in theological syllogisms use absolutely universal principles of reason; the adversaries use particular principles, or at least those that are limitedly universal and restricted to the sphere of nature or finite being. 2. Evangelicals use the principles of reason not as proper to theology, but as common to many sciences; not as ministerial and, as it were, instrumental, providing aid for understanding and deducing a conclusion; not as primordial, from which the principle of demonstration is to be taken, but as superadded to show the syllogistic δοκιμασίαν (testing).

Latin:

Seu articulus fidei purus. Nam de his, quae ad articulos fidei mixtos attinent ac praeter theologiam revelatam etiam in philosophia ex lumine rationis tractantur, minus est difficultatis. Vide autem de hac distinctione quaestionum theologicarum b. Mus. de Usu Princ. Rat. Lib. I. Cap. VI. § 6., Cap. XIII. sqq. et Lib. II. Cap. I.

Sive quae ad formam syllogismorum pertinent et terminorum dispositionem in figura ac modo, atque regulas consequentiarum attinent. Vid. Mus. Tract. cit. Lib. H. Cap. II.

Quamvis enim non omnes discursus theologici in forma syllogistica expresse proferri debeant; quoties tamen ratio disputationis seriae ac solidae postulat, non est opera ista subterfugienda.

Alias autem sufficit, discursus tales nectere* qui ad formam syllogisticam sunt revocabiles.

Quo nomine intelliguntur propositiones lumine naturae notae atque evidentiam metaphysicam, physicam, aut moralem habentes; quae ad materiam argumentorum spectant et majorem aut minorem ex praemissis constituunt. Vid. Mus. 1. c. L. II. C. II.

Sequitur profecto, si haec cum propositione theologica recte conjungantur, conclusio non solum vera ac certa, verum etiam, quae DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

est de fide; quod ostendit b. Musaeus Tract. de Convers. Disp. VIII. et IX. Confer h. 1., quae diximus in nota g. ad § 35. Pertinet huc exemplum, quod attulimus l. c. Cui jungi potest et istud, quo homo argumentatur: Omnis homo a Deo serio diligitur, et habet oblatam sibi serio gratiam et salutem. Ego sum homo. E. ego a Deo serio diligor etc. Adde b. Mus. Tr. de Convers. p. 593. et 594. V. g.

Quicunque habet perfectiones soli Deo proprias, is est verus Deus. Atqui Christus habet perfectiones soli Deo proprias. E. Christus est verus Deus. Minor ex revelatione probari debet. Major lumine naturae nota est, sed absolutae necessitatis, et contradictionem implicat, si dicas, aliquem habere perfectiones, quae cum essentia divina realiter idem sunt, nec tamen habere essentiam divinam, aut non esse verum Deum. Alias enim, si adhibeantur principia rationis non absolute, sed secundum quid, aut in certo genere universales ac necessariae, facile contingit, ut inferatur conclusio, mysteriis aut articulis fidei etiam primariis repugnans; quod exempljs Antitrinitariorum et aliorum patet. Vid. b. Mus. de Usu Prine. Rat. L. II. Cap. XIV. sqq. p. 451. sqq., item Tract. de Convers. Disp. IX. § 30. 31. p. 595. 596.

Hollazius: ,,Principia rationis vel sunt organica vel philosophica. Organica rationis principia dogmatibus fldei et morum explicandis atque confirmandis recte adhibentur. Ex principiis philosophicis articuli fidei mixti quadantenus innotescunt. Articuli autem fldei puri unice ex sacra Scriptura tanquam ex domestico, fundamentali et primordiali principio demonstrantur et cognoscuntur. Principia interim philosophica absolute universalia discursibus theologicis, velut principia communia, ministerialia et subservientia ad integrandum syllogismum plene expressum, coadhibere licet. —

Principia organica dicuntur, quae ad disciplinas instrumentales, grammaticam, rhetoricam et logicam pertinent. Principia philosophica alia sunt absolute et illimitate universalia, quae constant nexu terminorum essentiali et simpliciter necessario, ut nulla instantia neque ex Scriptura labefactari queant, v. g.: Impossibile est, idem simul esse et non esse; quicquid est, quando est, necesse est esse; omnis spiritus est immaterialis etc. Alia sunt limitate et secundum quid universalia, quae in certo genere, ex hypothesi, aut secundum naturalis cognitionis sphaeram, vera quidem sunt, attamen limitationem admittunt et instantia quadam, si non ex natura, certe ex Scriptura petita infringi possunt, v. g.: Quot sunt personae, tot sunt essentiae; omne individuum humanum per se est persona; omne genitum numerica essentia diversum est a generante. —

Sine usu rationis dogmata theologica neque percipere, neque confirmare, neque a strophis adversariorum vindicare possumus. Certe non brutis, sed hominibus sana ratione utentibus Deus aeternae salutis sapientiam in verbo suo revelavit, et serio iis injunxit mandato, ut verbum suum legerent, audirent, meditarentur; Deut. 6, 6. Joh. 5, 39. Requiritur itaque intellectus ut subjectum recipiens aut instrumentum apprehendens. Sicut enim sine oculis" nihil videmus, sine auribus nihil audimus, ita sine ratione nihil intelligimus. Interim tamen ratio humana non est fons aut primordiale elementum, ex quo propria et proxima fidei principia deriventur. —

Principia organica adhibentur, ut adminicula acquirendi habitus theologici, cum sine illis nec sensus aut significatio vocum erui (quod est grammaticae), nec figurae modique loquendi expendi (quod est rhetoricae), nec connexiones et consequentiae percipi, nec discursus formari (quod est logicae) possint. —

Articuli fidei mixti vocantur, qui non solum ex revelatione, verum etiam ex lumine naturae constant, qui PROLEGOM. CAP. II. primario et tutissime usque ad πληροφορίαν fidei e Scriptura sacra probantur, secundario et minus tuto e principiis rationis deducuntur. Sic, philosophi existentiam et attributa Dei in metaphysica et pneumatica ex principiis rationis probatum eunt. —

De articulis fidei puris nihil novit ratio sibi relicta, sed ad mysteria fidei caecutit et caligat. Cujus caecitatis spiritualis gentium apostolus hominem admonet, 1 Cor. 2, 14. inquiens: ,Animalis homo non suscipit ea, quae (sunt) Spiritus Dei; stultitia enim illi sunt, et non potest scire, quia spiritualiter dijudicantur.*

Observandum heic est genuinum apostoli argumentum. Prius a congenita intellectus humani post lapsum corruptione sumitur. Quidquid homo animalis (e verbo Dei non illuminatus) non capit, sed naturali quodam fastidio tanquam absurdum respuit, illud ex principiis rationis dijudicari nequit. Atqui mysteria divina etc. Ergo. Posterius petitur a conditione mysteriorum. Quaecunque nonnisi spiritualiter (per lumen Spiritus S.) dijudicantur, illa judicio rationis non sunt aestimanda aut decidenda. Atqui mysteria fidei etc. Ergo. —

In discursibus theologicis principia philosophica velut ministerialia et ad integrandum syllogismum subservientia recte applicari posse, ostenditur sequenti discursu theologico. Quodsi veritas humanae Christi naturae contra Marcionem probanda sit, ex s. Scriptura fundamentale demonstrationis theologicae principium depromitur: Christus habet corpus et animam humanam. Matth. 26, 27. 28. Luc. 24, 39. Ergo Christus est verus homo. Dicis: Probetur consequentia sive connexio antecedentis et consequentis. Probo consequentiam adhibito rationis principio: Quicunque habet corpus et animam humanam, ille est verus homo. Christus habet corpus et animam humanam. Ergo Christus est verus homo. In hoc discursu nititur veritas conclusionis theologicae propositione minori e verbo Dei revelato petita, tanquam proprio, fundamentali et primordiali demonstrandi principio. Major propositio est principium rationis absolute universale et concurrit tantum ut principium commune, secundarium et ministeriale, sponte sua affluens et superadditum ad integrandum syllogismum et ostendendam δοκιμασίαν syllogisticam.“ (Exam. theol. Proleg. III. q. 4. p. 68. sqq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,In hoc syllogismo: Verus homo habet animam et corpus; Christus est verus homo: ergo Christus habet animam et corpus, — major est rationis evidentis et necessariae; minor est Scripturae; perspicuum autem est, subjectum et praedicatum quaestionis non jungi potestate et vi majoris, sed vi minoris, in qua est conjunctio terminorum, qui partim quoad sonum ipsum etiam, partim quoad virtutem et valorem saltem iidem sunt cum terminis conclusionis. Nam tametsi homo animam et corpus habeat, Filius Dei tamen animam et corpus non habuit, antequam esse homo inciperet. Causa igitur et principium conclusionis est proprie minor, quae est Scripturae. Major autem proprie nihil est, nisi declaratio termini unius, qui in minore praedicatur, et sic instrumentum et adjumentum intelligendi minorem et deducendi conclusionem.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. I. c. 3. s. 2. νό/j.2. f. 64.)

Hollazius: „Quamvis mysteria fidei non contrarientur principiis rationis, non tamen ex his judicandum est de illis. Medicina et jurisprudentia sibi non contrariantur; neque tamen medicus ex processu juris ostendit methodum curandi febrem, neque JCtus ex anatomia petit modum dirimendi lites forenses. Ars pictoria et sutoria non pugnant inter se, neque tamen sutor ultra crepidam. Ratio recta, continens se intra limites objecti sui, non contradicit mysteriis fidei; per accidens autem fit, ut ratio corrupta, sphaeram suam egressa, enormis et effrenata revelationi divinae obluctetur. (S ociniani objiciunt:),Omnis discursus ultimo resolvitur in illud principium: Impossibile

est, idem simul esse et non esse, quod principium est rationis. Ut itaque ultima in id fit resolutio, ita ultimum rationi defertur judicium.' Resp.: Principium illud duobus modis potest considerari: 1. ut sit commune contradictionis fundamentum; 2. ut approprietur rebus divinis et ad earum naturam coarctetur. Quamvis ratio formale ferat judicium de communi 'contradictionis fundamento: judicium tamen reale et normale competit sacrae Scripturae, quatenus illud contradictionis fundamentum rebus divinis appropriatur. (

Sociniani objiciunt:),Doctores evangelici haud raro utuntur principiis rationis in syllogismis theologicis. Ergo Socinianos abusus rationis non possunt accusare.' Eesp.: 1. Evangelici in syllogismis theologicis utuntur principiis rationis absolute universalibus, adversarii principiis particularibus, aut saltem limitate universalibus et ad sphaeram naturae aut entis finiti adstrictis utuntur. 2. Evangelici utuntur principiis rationis, non ut theologiae propriis, sed multarum scientiarum communibus; non ut ministerialibus et quasi instrumentalibus, adjumentum intelligendi et deducendi conclusionem subministrantibus; non ut primordialibus, a quibus capiendum sit demonstrandi principium, sed, ut superadditis ad ostendendam δοκιμασίαν syllogisticam.


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: Not attending to this, the adversaries stubbornly oppose themselves to the…

Not attending to this, the adversaries stubbornly oppose themselves to the mysteries of faith divinely revealed. For example, they attack the mystery of the Trinity with this philosophical axiom: "As many as are the persons, so many are the essences." They assault the mystery of the incarnation with this principle of reason: "Every intelligent nature that is complete in being is a person." They go about removing the substantial presence of the body of Christ from the sacrament of the Supper with this lemma: "Every natural body is in one determined place." These principles of reason, since they are restricted to the sphere of nature and finite beings, are wrongly peddled as absolutely universal, nor are they applied to matters of pure faith without a μεταβάσει εις άλλο γένος (transition into another genus). Reason is not the leader of theology, but its handmaid. Let the handmaid Hagar serve her mistress, not rule; let her, affecting rule, be cast out of the sacred house." (L. c. p. 71.) §

47. In regulating the doctrine of faith and morals according to the Scriptures, there is no need for a peculiar judge, properly and strictly so-called, who may pass sentence by authority and be visible. Nevertheless, in order that truth and falsehood may be rightly judged, it is necessary, in part, to carefully weigh that which is proposed and comes to be judged, and to form the state of the question sincerely and accurately; and in part, also, to compare the known opinion with the Scriptures in such a way that it may be evident, either by the clear and express words of Scripture, or by necessary consequence deduced from the perspicuous and clear words of Scripture—understood according to the rules of good interpretation and observing also the laws of good consequence—that it is truly contained in the Scriptures, or not contained, or that its opposite is contained. And this judgment, just as it belongs to the doctors and ministers of the church, both individually and gathered in council, so it can also be exercised by other Christians in their own way.

Or, so that Scripture, as a norm, may be rightly applied to the deciding of questions which are disputed in theology, such as those concerning matters necessary to be believed or done. For our theologians, who have said that Scripture is the judge of controversies of faith, have used the word "judge" in an improper sense, for the rule of judging, or for the norm according to which a sentence is to be rendered, just as it is not otherwise unusual for the law to be accepted as the judge. Cf. the blessed Dr. Seb. Niemann, *Disputation for a place in the Theological Faculty on the Judge of Controversies of Faith*, Y. et seq. to XII.

Quenstedtius: "In the strict sense, Holy Scripture cannot be called a judge, but the Holy Spirit is the supreme judge in controversies of faith; Holy Scripture, however, is the voice of the supreme judge, by which his sentence concerning the disputed matter is set forth to the litigating parties. Nothing, however, prevents Scripture from being called a judge when speaking more broadly, since it is the same thing in this place whether you say: 'The Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture and through Scripture is the supreme judge,' or you say: 'Scripture is the supreme judge,' because the Holy Spirit does not pronounce his judgment immediately, but through the Word or through Holy Scripture; in which sense Aristotle said in *Nicomachean Ethics* V, ch. 4: 'To go to the judge is to go to justice. For a judge seems to be nothing other than justice animate.'" (*Theol. did.-pol.* P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 15. fol. 215.)

The same: "The Papists object: When controversies are moved concerning Scripture itself, Holy Scripture cannot be the judge of them, since no one can be a judge of himself and in his own cause, according to that rescript of the Emperors Valens, Gratian, and Valentinian: 'The laws have removed from all the faculty of giving testimony in their own cause.' L. Omnibus. 10. c. de testibus. — Resp.: In a civil court, indeed, no one can sustain the roles of plaintiff, defendant, and judge. But in the divine judgment, God accuses through the Law; He Himself is a competent witness and judge. Christ says in John 8:18: 'I am He who bears witness of Myself.' He had said, however, in verse 14: 'Even if I bear witness of Myself, My testimony is competent.'

2. When controversies are moved concerning Scripture itself, e.g., concerning its authority, canon, or interpretation, either the matter is with infidels outside the Church, or with those who are in the Church; if any infidel stubbornly denies that Scripture is the Word of God: it is certain that Scripture cannot be a competent judge or norm for this controversy, because every dispute must be instituted from principles common to both parties; since, as the philosophers teach: 'It is necessary for those who wish to agree in the conclusion to agree in some principle.' But such a discussion is not about some dogma of faith, but about the very principle of faith, which we suppose as true, known, primary, immutable, and indemonstrable in this assertion of ours, and therefore infidels are to be convinced not by the book of Scripture, but by nature, and are first to be led to Holy Scripture by certain extrinsic motives.

If one disputes with a person who is in the Church concerning the authority of Scripture, he must be convinced from Scripture itself, and this controversy can be judged from Scripture, provided the state of the controversy is correctly set. The same must be said concerning the canon, namely, that it is not so much a dogma of faith as it is a principle of faith, which is necessarily presupposed in eliciting the dogmas of faith. Even in controversies concerning the interpretation of Scripture, it itself ought to enjoy the office of norm and rule. For it is beyond doubt that a metaphrastic interpretation must be tested against the original text. That Scripture itself is the norm of exegetical interpretation is evident from the fact that it must be interpreted by the same Spirit by which it was first dictated. Moreover, it is falsely supposed that Scripture is instituted as the judge of itself. It suffices if it is the judge of us and of our faith, for Scripture does not have need of a judge, but we do." (*L. c.* f. 223.)

The same: "Scripture is not deaf to the hearing of causes, nor mute to the pronouncing of a sentence in the proper sense. Not deaf; for the cause..." ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

in a certain way knows, as is evident from John 7:51. It is not mute (except in the papacy, where it is forbidden to speak in a known tongue); for it speaks, cries out, says, teaches, Mark 15:28; John 19:24; Rom. 3:19; 4:3; 9:27. Cicero indeed, in Book 3 of *De Legibus*, calls law a "mute magistrate," and a magistrate a "speaking law"; in which sense the same can be said of Scripture and pastors; for just as magistrates, if they speak according to the law, are a speaking law, so also pastors, when they speak from Scripture, will be a speaking Scripture. However, the edicts of princes and holy Scripture itself can be called mute until they become known through the voice of a herald, or until they explain their meanings to everyone through reading. But a herald is neither the judge of the edicts nor their interpreter, much less the supreme one." (L. c. f. 224.)

The same: "Distinguish between the forum of the world or the political forum, and the forum of heaven or the ecclesiastical forum. The reasons of the church are not to be demanded according to the arrangement of a political republic. The ecclesiastical ministry is one thing, and political rule and magistracy is another. The church is the invisible and spiritual kingdom of Christ, John 18:36, in which the matter is conducted not with carnal, but with spiritual weapons, 2 Cor. 10:3 sq. In the political forum, it is absurd if someone wishes to be accuser, judge, and witness at the same time, but in God and His word, all these concur." (L. c. f. 235.) The same: "Distinguish between the political rule of the O.T. and the ecclesiastical rule of the N.T.; for there is no transition from the former to the latter; for of a different kingdom there is also a different rule. Therefore, it does not follow: In the O.T. there was one supreme visible political judge: therefore there must also be one ecclesiastical one in the N.T. The nature of the kingdom or the Jewish people in the O.T. and of Christians in the N.T. is different. In the O.T. the rule was priestly, in the N.T. it is a royal priesthood, 1 Pet. 2:9." (L. c. f. 237.)

The same: "The Papists err by a perpetual fallacy of *ignoratio elenchi* (ignoring the point at issue), because they apply what is said about human judgments in the causes and lawsuits of this age to divine judgments in the cause of faith. And they transfer what is said about inferior judges to the supreme judge; but 1. it is the duty of an inferior judge to inspect, examine, and know the reasons and foundations of both contending parties. For because his office is to pronounce according to the laws, he has need of investigation, so that, having inspected the foundations, he may inquire which party of the litigants the laws favor. The supreme judge, with the question nakedly proposed, can answer immediately either affirmatively or negatively without investigation, so as not to undertake the examination of the parties' reasons, since the supreme reason resides in him. 2. Holy Scripture, speaking properly, does not indeed inspect the reasons and foundations of the contending parties, but neither is it itself properly the judge, but rather the voice of the judge; the judge, however, is the Holy Spirit Himself, who speaks infallibly through it, who indeed is so far from being ignorant of the reasons of both contending parties that He has them most clearly perceived from eternity. Even if, therefore, the proposition were true regarding a judge taken from among men, who is involved in ignorance of things, it nevertheless does not touch the Holy Spirit, whom nothing anywhere escapes or passes by. Add 3., that where parties are heard in this way by a judge, it is a matter of fact, not of law." (L. c. f. 225 sq.) ANTITHESIS: Pius IX.: "We, faithfully adhering to the tradition received from the beginning of the Christian faith, for the glory of God our Savior, the exaltation of the Catholic religion, and the salvation of Christian peoples, with the approval of the sacred council, teach and define that it is a divinely revealed dogma: that the Roman Pontiff, when he speaks *ex cathedra*, that is, when in the discharge of the office of pastor and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine regarding faith or morals to be held by the universal Church, by the divine assistance promised to him in blessed Peter, is possessed of that infallibility with which the divine Redeemer willed that His Church should be endowed for defining doctrine regarding faith or morals; and that therefore such definitions of the Roman Pontiff are of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church..."

Latin:

Id quod non attendentes adversarii, mysteriis fidei divinitus patefactis se praefracte opponunt. V. g., mysterium Trinitatis impugnant hoc axiomate philosophico: Quot sunt personae, tot sunt essentiae. Mysterium incarnationis adoriuntur hoc principio rationis: Omnis natura intelligens et in essendo completa est persona. Substantialem corporis Christi praesentiam e sacramento coenae sublatum eunt hoc lemmate: Omne corpus naturale est in uno determinato loco. Quae principia rationis, cum adstricta sint ad naturae et entium finitorum sphaeram, perperam venditantur pro absolute universalibus, neque sine μεταβάσει εις άλλο γένος ad res merae fldei applicantur. Est ratio non dux theologiae, sed pedissequa. Serviat ancilla Hagar dominae, non imperet: imperium affectans aede sacra eliminetur.“ (L. c. p. 71.) §

47. In normanda doctrina fidei et morum juxta Scripturas a non opus est judice peculiari, b proprie et stricte dicto, qui pro auctoritate ferat sententiam c ac visibilis d sit. Ut tamen nihilominus verum et falsum recte e dijudicetur, partim necesse est, id, quod proponitur et dijudicandum venit, solicite expendere ac statum quaestionis sincere et accurate formare, f partim etiam sententiam cognitam ita conferre cum Scripturis, ut vel claris ac disertis verbis Scripturae, vel per necessariam consequentiam, ex perspicuis et claris verbis Scripturae, juxta regulas bonae interpretationis intellectis, observatis etiam legibus bonae consequentiae, deductam, g constet, illam in Scripturis revera contineri, aut non contineri, vel contineri ejus oppositum. Atque hoc quidem judicium sicut doctoribus et ministris ecclesiae, cum singulis/ tum in concilio i congregatis competit, ita et ab aliis christianis k suo modo exerceri potest.

Seu, ut Scriptura, tanquam norma, recte applicetur ad decidendas quaestiones, quae in theologia disputantur, tanquam de rebus creditu vel factu necessariis. Nostrates enim, qui Scripturam dixerunt esse judicem controversiarum fidei, judicis voce usi sunt in significatione impropria, pro ratione judicandi, seu pro norma, juxta quam sententia sit ferenda, prout alias insolens non est, legem pro judice accipi. Conf. b. D. Seb. Niemanni Disp. pro loco in Fac. Theol. de Jud. Controv. fid. Y. sqq. ad XII.

Quenstedtius: ,,In stricta significatione s. Scriptura judex dici, nequit, sed Spiritus S. est supremus judex in controversiis fidei; s. Scriptura vero est vox supremi judicis, qua partibus litigantibus illius de re controversa sententia exponitur. Nihil tamen prohibet, quominus Scriptura latius loquendo dicatur judex, cum idem sit hoc loco, sive dicas: Spiritus S. in Scriptura et per Scripturam loquens est supremus judex, — sive dicas: Scriptura est supremus judex, quia Spiritus S. judicium suum non pronunciat immediate, sed per verbum sive per s. Scripturam; quo sensu dixit Aristoteles V. Nicom. c. 4.: ,Adire ad judicem, est adire ad jus. Judex enim nihil videtur aliud esse, quam jus animatum.'“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 4. s. 2. q. 15. fol. 215.)

Idem: ,,Objiciunt pontificii: Quando de ipsa Scriptura controversiae moventur, illarum non posse esse judicem s. Scripturam, cum nemo judex esse possit sui ipsius et in propria causa, juxta illud Valentis, Gratiani et Valentiniani impp. rescriptum: ,Omnibus in re propria dicendi testimonii facultatem jura submoverunt.* L. Omnibus. 10. c. de testibus. — Resp.: In foro quidem civili iiemo potest actoris, rei et judicis partes sustinere. At in judicio divino Deus accusat per legem, ipse testis et judex est idoneus. Christus ait Joh. 8, 18.: ,Ego is sum, qui testor de me ipso.* Dixerat autem v. 14.: ,Etiamsi ego testor de me ipso, idoneum est testimonium meum.*

2. Quando de ipsa Scriptura controversiae moventur, v. g. de ejus auctoritate, canone aut interpretatione, vel res nobis est cum infidelibus extra ecclesiam, vel cum illis, qui sunt in ecclesia; si quis infidelis praefracte negat, Scripturam esse verbum Dei: certum est, hujus controversiae Scripturam non posse esse idoneum judicem aut normam, quia ex principiisutrique partium communibus omnis institui debet disputatio; siquidem ut philosophi docent: In principio aliquo convenire necesse est, qui in conclusione convenire volunt. At talis disceptatio non est de aliquo dogmate fidei, sed de ipso fidei principio, quod tanquam verum, notum, primum, immutabile et indemonstrabile supponimus in nostra hac assertione adeoque infideles non libro Scripturae, sed naturae sunt convincendi et certis motivis extrinsece primum deducendi ad s. Scripturam.

Si cum illo, qui est in ecclesia, de auctoritate Scripturae disceptatur, is ex ipsa Scriptura convinci debet, haecque controversia ex Scriptura dijudicari potest, modo status controversiae recte ponatur. Idem dicendum de canone, scl. non tam esse dogma fidei, quam principium fidei, quod necessario praesupponitur in dogmatis fidei eruendis. Etiam in controversiis de interpretatione Scripturae ipsa frui debet officio normae ac regulae. Nam metaphrasticam interpretationem ad originalem textum exigendam esse, extra dubium est. Interpretationis autem exegeticae ipsam Scripturam esse normam, patet ex eo, quod eodem Spiritu interpretanda est, quo primum fuit dictata. Supponitur insuper falsum, Scripturam institui judicem sui ipsius. Sufficit, si sit nostri judex et fidei nostrae, nec enim Scriptura opus habet judice, sed nos.“ (L. c. f. 223.)

Idem: ,,Νοη est Scriptura ad auditionem causarum surda, aut ad proprie dictam sententiae dictionem muta. Non surda; causam enim DE PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

quodammodo cognoscit, ut patet ex Joh. 7, 51. Non muta (nisi in papatu, ubi' prohibetur lingua nota loqui); loquitur enim, clamat, dicit, docet, Mare. 15, 28. Joh. 19, 24. Rom. 3, 19. 4, 3. 9, 27. Cicero quidem lib. 3. de legibus appellat legem,magistratum mutum', magistratum autem,legem loquentem4; quo sensu idem dici poterit de Scriptura et pastoribus; uti enim magistratus, si secundum legem loquantur, sunt lex loquens, sic etiam pastores, quando ex Scriptura loquuntur, erunt Scriptura loquens. Edicta autem principum ipsaque s. Scriptura muta dici possunt, donec praeconis voce innotescant, vel per lectionem cuique sensus suos exponant. Praeco autem neque judex est edictorum neque eorum interpres, nedum summus." (L. c. f. 224.)

Idem: „Dist. inter judicium lori seu politicum, et judicium poli seu ecclesiasticum. Non sunt exigendae rationes ecclesiae ad ordinationem reipublicae politicae. Aliud est ecclesiasticum ministerium, et aliud politicum regimen et magisterium. Est ecclesia regnum Christi invisibile et spirituale, Joh. 18, 36., in quo res geritur non corporalibus, sed spiritualibus armis, 2 Cor. 10, 3. sq. In foro politico absurdum est, si quis simul velit esse accusator, judex et testis, sed in Deo ejusque verbo haec omnia concurrunt.44 (L. c. f. 235.) Idem: „Dist. inter regimen V. T. politicum et regimen N. T. ecclesiasticum; ab illo ad hoc n. v. c.; disparis enim regni dispar quoque est regimen. Non ergo sequitur: In V. T. unus fuit visibilis judex politicus supremus: ergo et in N.T. debet esse unus ecclesiasticus. Diversa est ratio regni seu populi Judaici in Y. et Christianorum in N. T. In V. T. regimen erat sacerdotale, in N. T. est regale sacerdotium, 1 Pet. 2, 9." (L. c. f. 237.)

Idem: ,,Fallunt pontificii perpetuo paralogismo ab ignoratione elenchi, quia, quae de judiciis humanis in causis et litibus hujus saeculi dicuntur, accommodant ad judicia divina in causa fldei. Et quae de judicibus inferioribus dicuntur, transferunt ad judicem supremum; ast 1. judicis inferioris est, utriusque controvertentium partis rationes et fundamenta inspicere, examinare et cognoscere. Quia enim ejus munus est, secundum leges pronunciare, ideo opus habet investigatione, ut inspectis fundamentis, litigantium utri parti faveant leges, disquirat. Judex supremus, quaestione nude proposita citra disquisitionem illico respondere potest vel affirmative vel negative, ut rationes partium examinandas non suscipiat, cum penes ipsum sit ratio summa. 2. Scriptura s. proprie loquendo non inspicit quidem rationes et fundamenta controvertentium, sed nec ipsa proprie est judex, sed potius vox judicis, judex vero est ipse Spiritus S., qui infallibiliter per ipsam loquitur, qui vero rationes utriusque controvertentium partium adeo non ignorat, ut vel ab aeterno perspectissimas habeat. Quodsi igitur maxime propositio esset vera de judice ex hominibus assumpto, qui in rerum ignoratione versatur, Spiritum S. tamen, quem nihil uspiam latet, aut praeterit, nihil attingit. Adde 3., quod, ubi partes ita audiuntur a judice, agatur de facto, non de jure." (L. c. f. 225. sq.) ANTITHESIS: Pius IX.: „Nos traditione a fidei christianae exordio perceptae fideliter inhaerendo, ad Dei Salvatoris nostri gloriam, religionis catholicae exaltationem et Christianorum populorum salutem, sacro approbante concilio, docemus et divinitus revelatum dogma esse definimus: Romanum pontificem, cum ex cathedra loquitur, id est, cum omnium christianorum pastoris et doctoris munere fungens pro suprema sua apostolica auctoritate doctrinam de fide vel moribus ab universa ecclesia tenenda definit, per assistentiam divinam, ipsi in beato Petro promissam, ea infallibilitate pollere, qua divinus Redemptor ecclesiam suam in definienda doctrina de fide vel moribus instructam esse voluit; ideoque ejusmodi Romani pontificis definitiones ex sese, non autem ex


### Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or Holy Scripture: by the consent of the Church, are irreformable.” (First Dogmatic Constitution…

by the consent of the Church, are irreformable.” (First Dogmatic Constitution on the Church of Christ, issued in the first session of the Vatican Council, 1870, which begins: “Pastor aeternus.”) Whom they otherwise call an authoritative, likewise decisive, absolute, and principal judge, namely, because by the power of the authority which he possesses, he can oblige litigants to acquiesce in the sentence rendered by him without further inquiry or hesitation. See l. c. § 18., blessed Gerhard, Exeg. L. I. § 452.

For otherwise our theologians admit that the Holy Spirit, especially in those things which are contained in Scripture in clear and express words, and in His own way also regarding those things which are deduced from the Scriptures by consequence, is the judge of controversies, and indeed an authoritative one. Blessed Niemann, l. c. § 20 sqq.

Namely, although He does not force men by external power to acquiesce in His decision, regarding the λόγον τον 'έξω, or so that they do not speak against it by any external act; yet, when the sentence of Scripture, as the divine voice, is open, it is certain that the minds of men are convinced regarding the λόγον τόν έσω, so that, unless their conscience protests, they can object to nothing.

Controversies that pertain to the very dogmas of faith and morals, necessary to be defined and known, could indeed all be judged and ended in this way, provided that when an occasion for controversy arises, pious, truth-loving, and learned minds are brought forward to engage in the dispute.

For thus, with prejudices, party spirit, and depraved affections set aside, and the arguments of both sides weighed according to the norm of Scripture, it would easily appear which opinion is true and which is false, on account of the very perspicuity of Scripture, which treats of these matters by design.

But as for other questions, which can be disputed on either side without prejudice to faith, the judgment and end of these ought not to be equally demanded or expected.

To this it pertains that the ambiguities of words and phrases be diligently unfolded, and that what is conceded or indubitable be separated and removed from what is doubtful and controversial, and that that which remains in question be expressed in proper and most congruent terms and phrases.

Hence, what we said above regarding the interpretation of Scripture and the drawing of conclusions (§ 44 sqq.) recurs here.

For it is their task to rightly divide (όρθοτομεϊν) the word of truth, 2 Tim. 2:15, and to reject profane and vain babblings, and foolish and unlearned questions, v. 16, 23, to be instructed not only for doctrine, but also for reproof (έλεγχον), 2 Tim. 3:16-17, so that they may be able to convince those who contradict (τους αντιλέγοντας έλέγχειν), Tit. 1:9, and to stop the mouths of such (έπιστομίζειν αυτούς), v. 11.

Indeed, the judgment of many gathered in a synod, if they are learned and pious, is not without cause preferred to the judgment of one or another rendering a sentence separately.

And if a universal council could be held, exhibiting the concordant votes of all Christians whatsoever, it would certainly have the greatest weight.

Meanwhile, such councils as we have, just as they do not possess the privilege of infallibility, so they grant a judgment of discretion, not of authoritative decision, just as individual teachers do.

For they cannot oblige the intellect to assent and acquiesce in their decisions, unless they have demonstrated the agreement of their decisions with the Scriptures. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THEOLOGY.

Huelsemannus: "The immediate subject to whom authority has been delegated by the Holy Spirit to judge concerning matters of faith—or, which is the same thing, to expound the judgment already laid down by the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures, through words equivalent or homogeneous to the words of the Holy Spirit or the Scriptures, and to whom infallibility in so judging is promised—is not the doctors of the church alone, whether in or out of a council, nor are they Christians viewed individually, and least of all is it any one doctor, whether Roman, Antiochene, or any other bishop whatsoever. This proposition is to be proven from all those sayings and the definition of the subject of which all those sayings speak, by which the promise of infallibility is made and the faculty of publishing and expounding the judgment of the Holy Spirit is given. For it is most false that any of all those sayings has as its subject (the promise) either one doctor or doctors taken alone together; rather, it has as its object the whole assembly of the faithful, embracing the sheep with the shepherds, Matt. 16:18; 18:20; Eph. 4:11–13; John 14:16; 1 Tim. 3:16, and other places." (Praelect. in F. C. p. 211 sq.)

k) For if they are instructed with the necessary aids for explaining the Holy Scriptures and treating theological controversies, they can judge controversies with sufficient accuracy. To the simpler folk, however, it suffices if, being informed from the clear sayings of Scripture concerning those things which are necessary to be known, they remember that they must beware of all things that differ from them; even though they themselves may not be sufficient for a more accurate examination of controversies. For otherwise, the admonition of Philipp Melanchthon in *Resp. ad Art. Bavar.* (Tom. I. Opp. p. 370) is to be observed: "Let there be such modesty of intellects that they modestly retain honest opinions, and indeed those delivered by God, even if they cannot destroy all the deceits that are constructed against them." Cf. the blessed Chemnitius, *P. III. LL.* p. 82, and *de Fundam. SS. Coenae* c. X. p. 160.

Lutherus: "To recognize and judge over doctrine belongs to all and every Christian, and indeed in such a way that he is cursed who infringes upon this right by a hair's breadth. For Christ Himself has ordained such a right in many invincible sayings, e.g., Matt. 7: 'Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing.' This word He certainly speaks against the teachers to the people, and commands them that they should avoid their false doctrine. But how can they avoid the same without recognizing them? And how recognize them where they do not have the power to judge? Now, however, He not only gives them the power to judge, but also commands it to them; so that this single passage can be enough against all the sayings of popes, all fathers, all councils, and all schools that have ascribed the right to judge and conclude solely to the bishops and clergy, but have robbed the people—that is, the Church, the Queen—of it in a godless and sacrilegious manner...

As everyone believes rightly or wrongly at his own peril, so everyone also has the duty to see to it that he believes rightly; so that even common sense and the necessity of salvation dictate that the judgment over doctrine must necessarily reside with the hearer... (It) is surely not to be denied that the tyranny of this stolen right has lasted for over a thousand years. For already in the Nicene Council, which was yet the best, they began to make laws and to arrogate such a right to themselves. And from that time on it has so taken root that nothing is more common or more firmly established—because it can be proven by the multitude of people and long custom—than this right; so that nowadays there is hardly anyone who does not hold it to be salutary, just, and divine. But here you see that it is pure sacrilege and godlessness against the most manifest and invincible Scripture of God." (*Wider König Heinrichen in England*, 1522. XIX, 424 sqq.) PROLEGOM. CAP. II.

The same: "All the warnings that St. Paul gives in Rom. 16:17, 18; 1 Cor. 10:15; Gal. 1:8, 9; Col. 2:8, and everywhere else, as well as all the sayings of the prophets where they teach that human doctrine is to be avoided, do nothing other than take the right and power to judge all doctrine away from the teachers and impose it upon the hearers with a serious command, under pain of the loss of their souls; so that they not only have the right and power to judge everything that is preached, but are obligated to judge, under penalty of the displeasure of the Divine Majesty." (Ground and Cause from Scripture, that a Christian Assembly or Congregation has the Right and Power to Judge all Doctrine. 1523. X, 1799 sqq.)

Gerhard: "Bellarmino replies: 'Since the people are unlearned, they cannot judge the doctrine of the pastor otherwise than by comparison with the doctrine of their predecessors and ordinary pastors.' Resp.: That this is false is shown by the example of the Bereans, who searched the Scriptures daily, diligently inquiring whether those things which were brought forth by Paul and Barnabas were so, Acts 17:11; they established as the rule of judgment not the doctrine of the ordinary pastors, but the Holy Scriptures, for which name they are commended by the Holy Spirit. That unlearnedness of the people, of which Bellarmino speaks, takes its origin in the papacy from the prohibition of reading the Holy Scripture, for which sacrilege its authors will one day render a grave account. We, however, invert Bellarmino’s argument: If the unlearnedness of the people does not prevent them from being able to compare the doctrine of pastors with the doctrine of predecessors or ordinary pastors, then certainly it will not prevent them from being able to compare the doctrine of pastors with the doctrine of Christ, the prophets, and the apostles, set forth in the Scriptures, and according to this norm to discern the true prophet from the false. But the former is true; therefore, the latter is also. The connection of the major premise is proven because Christ, the prophets, and the apostles can teach as perspicuously, and indeed truly have taught as perspicuously, as ordinary pastors. When Christ, the prophets, and the apostles exercised the ministry of teaching on this earth, they preached not only to the learned but also to the unlearned people, and indeed in such a way that they could understand their doctrine; how, therefore, could the writings of the prophets and the apostles be so obscure and perplexing that the unlearned people cannot judge doctrine from them at all? Certainly, the prophets and apostles wrote not other things, but the same things which they preached by word of mouth. — '

But,' says Bellarmino, 'if the people could judge the doctrine of the pastor by themselves, they would not need preachers.' Resp.: What kind of connection (συνάφεια) is there in this inference? Both are commanded by God: namely, that the people should judge the doctrine of the pastor, which Bellarmino himself previously granted to them in express words, and that nevertheless there should be certain and ordinary ministers in the church, 'for are all teachers?' 1 Cor. 12:29, Eph. 4:11. It is one thing to inquire into the truth of doctrine and to discern heresies from orthodoxy, and false prophets from true teachers, which is a general calling pertaining to all Christians; it is another thing to teach publicly in the church, which is a special calling. We do not make pastors out of the sheep, but we command that they be and remain sheep; meanwhile, we do not want them to be brute sheep, who cannot and ought not to discern between pastors and wolves. The Papists make brute sheep out of their hearers, who without any discretion follow the pastor, even if he should lead them to harmful pastures or even turn into a wolf; they make parrots out of their hearers, hanging on the nod of the prelates, and out of the prelates they make angels, who are clearly infallible and unaccountable (ἀνυπεύθυνοι). . . .

The reason which Bellarmino adds is clearly antichristian: 'When an ordinary pastor (he says) and some other person, who preaches, not being called, teach contrary things, the people ought by all means to follow their own pastor rather than that other one, who is not a pastor, even if it should happen that the pastor were in error.' But it is false that the people ought to follow an ordinary pastor even when he is in error; for this is nothing other than commanding that the sheep follow their pastor even to harmful pastures, that Christians prefer darkness to light, errors to truth, and human constitutions to divine authority. Bellarmino indeed adds, 'it is not credible,'"

That God will permit an ordinary pastor to err in such a way that he deceives the simple people; but it is argued in vain whether it can happen, concerning which it is manifestly certain that it has happened; that ordinary pastors have often erred and deceived the simple people cannot be denied without significant impudence; here, therefore, we press Bellarmine and ask, whether the people ought to follow ordinary pastors even when they are erring? If he were to answer in the affirmative, he will make it manifest that he has sold his services to him who, in 'Si papa' dist. 40, roars thus: 'If the Pope is found unmindful of his own and his brother's salvation, negligent, useless, and remiss in his works, and furthermore silent about the good, which harms himself more, and nevertheless others, and leads innumerable peoples in crowds with him, the first slave of hell, to be beaten with him with many stripes forever: let no mortal presume to rebuke his faults here; because he who is to judge all is to be judged by no one.' (Loc. de minist, eccl. § 88.) § 48.

Holy Scripture can be defined as Scripture, a inspired by b God, c consigned d through the prophets and apostles e partly in the Hebrew, partly in the Greek idiom, f instructing g sinful man concerning all things that are necessary to be believed and done, h so that he may obtain i faith in Christ, and being reconciled to God, may live holily, and at length k obtain eternal life by the benefit of God. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. P. II. Cap. II. § 24. p. 278. See above § 2. note a. p. 92. Nor is it difficult to recognize that the generic concept of Scripture is correctly constituted in this, which is common to holy Scripture and other writings. But if it pleases to substitute the word of God in place of the genus, it must certainly be understood as the external word and the verbal sign. See b. Mus. 1. c. p. 279.

281. What is said here and further pertains to the specific difference, taken from the causes of Scripture; from which first occurs the principal efficient cause, God. See above § 3. Thus is indicated partly the causality of the principal efficient cause, partly the formal cause of Scripture. See § 4. and § 8. Who are the less principal efficient cause. See § 6. They pertain to the matter from which, or to the material of Scripture. See § 7. Who is the end to which of Scripture. See § 10. These are the primary object of Scripture. See § 9. Who is the intermediate end of which. See § 11. k) Who is the ultimate end. See l. c.

Latin:

consensu ecclesiae, irreformabiles esse.“ (Constitutio dogmatica prima de eccles. Christi ed. in sess. i. concilii Vaticani 1870, quae incipit: „Pastor aeternus.“) Quem alias judicem auctoritativum, item decisivum, absolutum, principalem appellant, nempe quod vi auctoritatis, qua pollet, litigantes obligare possit, ut in lata a se sententia citra ulteriorem inquisitionem aut haesitationem acquiescant. Vid. l. c. § 18., b. Gerh. Exeg. L. I. § 452.

Alias enim fatentur nostri, Spiritum Sanctum inprimis in his, quae claris et expressis verbis continentur in Scriptura, suo modo autem etiam quoad ea, quae per consequentiam ex Scripturis deducuntur, esse judicem controversiarum, eumqüe auctoritativum. B. Niemann. l. c. § 20. sqq.

Scilicet quamvis vi externa non cogat homines in sua decisione acquiescere, quoad λόγον τον 'έξω, seu ne quid actu externo obloquantur; tamen, quando aperta est sententia Scripturae, tanquam vocis divinae, certum est, animos hominum, quoad λόγον τόν έσω convinci, ut, nisi reclamante conscientia, nihil excipere possint.

Possent sane controversiae, quae ipsa fidei et morum dogmata, definitu scituque necessaria, attinent, omnes hac ratione dijudicari et finiri, modo exorta controvertendi occasione mentes pias, veritatis amantes atque eruditas afferrent, qui disputaturi sunt.

Sic enim, sepositis praejudiciis studioque partium et pravis affectibus, argumentis vero utriusque partis ad Scripturae normam expensis, facile appareret, quaenam vera, quae falsa sententia sit, propter ipsam Scripturae, de his ex instituto agentis, perspicuitatem.

Quod autem caeteras quaestiones attinet, quae salva fide in utramque partem disputari possunt, harum dijudicatio et finis non aeque postulari aut expectari debet.

Quo pertinet, ut ambiguitates vocabulorum et phrasium diligenter evolvantur et concessa seu indubitata a dubiis et controversis secernantur ac removeantur, id vero, de quo superest quaestio, terminis et phrasibus propriis maximeque congruis exprimatur.

Unde hic recurrunt, quae supra de interpretatione Scripturae et deducendis conclusionibus diximus § 44. sqq.

Eorum enim est, recte secare (όρβ-οτομεϊν) sermonem veritatis, 2 Tim. 2,15. , et profanas vocum inanitates, stultas et ineruditas quaestiones rejicere, v. 16. 23., esse instructos non solum ad doctrinam, sed etiam ad redargutionem (έλεγχον'), 2 Tim. 3, 16. 17., ut possint contradicentes convincere (τους αντιλέγοντας έλέγχειν), Tit. 1, 9-, OS obturare Ulis (έπιστομίζειν αυτούς), V. 11.

Imo judicium plurium in synodo congregatorum, si docti ac pii sint, non sine causa praefertur judicio unius aut alterius, seorsim ferentis sententiam.

Ac si haberi posset concilium universale, omnium omnino christianorum concordia suffragia exhibens, valeret utique plurimum.

Interim qualia habemus concilia, sicut infallibilitatis privilegium non habent, ita aeque ac singuli doctores judicium discretionis, non auctoritativae decisionis largiuntur.

Non enim intellectum ad assentiendum et acquiescendum in suis decisionibus obligare possunt, nisi decisionum suarum cum Scripturis convenientiam demonstraverint. DB PRINCIPIO THEOLOGIAE.

Huelsemannus: „Subjectum immediatum, cui delegata est a Spiritu S. auctoritas judicandi de rebus fidei, seu, quod idem est, exponendi sententiam a Sp. S. in Scripturis jam latam, per verba aequipollentia seu homogenea verbis Spiritus S. vel Scripturarum, et cui promissa est infallibilitas, sic judicandi, non sunt soli doctores ecclesiae, sive in, sive extra concilium, neque sunt christiani seorsim spectati, minime omnium autem unus doctor, sive Romanus, sive Antiochenus, sive quicunque alius episcopus. Quae propositio probanda est ex omnibus illis dictis et definitione subjecti, de quo loquuntur omnia illa dicta, quibus fit promissio infallibilitatis et datur facultas publicandi et exponendi Sp. S. sententiam. Falsissimum est enim, ullum ex omnibus illis dictis habere pro subjecto ώ promissionis vel unum doctorem, vel solos doctores simul sumtos, sed habet pro objecto totum coetum fidelium complectentem oves cum pastoribus, Matth. 16, 18. 18, 20. Eph. 4, 11—13. Joh. 14, 16. 1 Tim. 3, 16. locisque aliis.“ (Praelect. in F. C. p. 211. sq.)

k) Si enim adminiculis ad Scripturas sacras explicandas et controversias theologicas tractandas necessariis instructi sint, possunt satis accurate dijudicare controversias. Simplicioribus vero sufficit, si ex claris Scripturae dictis de his, quae scitu necessaria sunt, informati ea omnia, quae ah illis discrepant, sibi cavenda esse meminerint; quamvis accuratiori examini controversiarum ipsi non sufficiant. Nam et alias observandum est monitum Philippi Mel. in Resp. ad Art. Bavar. Tom. I. Opp. p. 370.: Sit ea modestia ingeniorum, ut honestas sententias, et quidem divinitus traditas, modeste retineant, etiamsi non omnes praestigias, quae contra struuntur, destruere possint. Conf. b. Chemn. P. III. LL. p. 82. et de Fundam. SS. Coenae c. X. p. 160.

Lutherus: „Ueber der Lehre zu erkennen und zu richten, gehöret vor alle und jede Christen, und zwar so, dass der verflucht ist, der solches Recht um ein Härle in kränket. Denn Christus selbst hat solches Recht in unüberwindlichen und vielen Sprüchen angeordnet, z. B. Matth. 7.: ,Sehet euch für vor den falschen Propheten, die in (Schafskleidern zu euch kommen.' Dies Wort sagt er je gewiss wider die Lehrer zum Volk und gebeut ihm, dass es ihre falsche Lehre meiden solle. Wie können sie aber dieselben meiden, ohne sie zu erkennen? und wie erkennen, wo sie nicht Macht haben, zu urtheilen? Nun aber giebt er ihnen nicht allein Macht zu urtheilen, sondern geheut es ihnen auch; dass diese einzige Stelle genug sein kann wider aller Päbste, aller Väter, .aller Concilien, aller Schulen Sprüche, die das Recht zu urtheilen und zu schliessen blos den Bischöfen und Geistlichen zugesprochen, dem Volk aber, das ist, der Kirche, der Königin, es gottloser und kirchenräuberischer Weise geraubet haben. . .

Wie ein jeder auf seine Gefahr recht oder falsch glaubet, so hat auch ein jeder billig dahin zu sorgen, dass er recht glaube; dass auch der gemeine Menschenverstand und die Nothwendigkeit der Seligkeit es giebt, dass das Urtheil über die Lehre nothwendig bei dem Zuhörer sein müsse... (Es) ist wohl nicht zu leugnen, dass dieses geraubten Rechts Tyrannei wohl über tausend Jahr gewährt habe. Denn schon im nicänischen Concilio, welches doch noch das beste war, fingen sie schon an, Gesetze zu machen und sich solches Recht anzumassen. Und von der Zeit an ist es bisher so eingerissen, dass nichts gänger noch fester ist, weil es mit der Menge der Leute und langem Brauch bewiesen werden kann, als dieses Recht; so dass heutiges Tages niemand leicht ist, der es nicht für heilsam, gerecht und göttlich halte. Aber hier siehest du, dass es lauter Kirchenraub und Gottlosigkeit sei wider die offenbarste und unüberwindlichste Schrift Gottes.“ (Wider König Heinrichen in England. 1522. XIX, 424. sqq.) PROLEGOM. GAP. Π.

Idem: „Alle Warnung, die St. Paulus thut Köm. 16, 17. 18. 1 Cor, 10, 15. Gal. 8, 4. 5. Col. 2, 8. und allenthalben, item aller Propheten Sprüche, da sie lehren, Menschenlehre zu meiden, die thun nichts Anderes, denn dass sie das Recht und Macht, alle Lehre zu urtheilen, von den Lehrern nehmen und mit ernstlichem Gebot bei der Seelen Verlust den Zuhörern auflegen; also, dass sie nicht allein Recht und Macht haben, alles, was gepredigt wird, zu urtheilen, sondern sind schuldig, zu urtheilen, bei göttlicher Majestät Ungnaden.“ (Grund und Ursach aus der Schrift, dass eine christliche Versammlung oder Gemeine Recht und Macht habe, alle Lehre zu urtheilen. 1523. X, 1799. sq.)

Gerhardus: „Regerit Bellarminus: ,Populus cum sit rudis, non potest aliter judicare de doctrina pastoris, quam ex collatione cum doctrina praedecessorum et ordinariorum pastorum.4 Resp.: Hoc falsum esse, ostendit exemplum Beroensium, qui quotidie scrutabantur scripturas, sedulo inquirentes, an haec ita se haberent, quae a Paulo et Barnaba proferebantur, Act. 17, 11.; regulam judicii statuebant non doctrinam ordinariorum pastorum, sed Scripturas sacrae, quo nomine a Spiritu Sancto commendantur. Ruditas illa populi, de qua Bellarminus loquitur, in papatu originem ducit ex prohibitione legendi Scripturam sacram, pro quo sacrilegio gravem olim reddent rationem illius auctores. Invertimus autem Bellarmini argumentum: Si ruditas populi non obstat, quominus possit doctrinam pastorum conferre cum doctrina praedecessorum vel ordinariorum pastorum, utique etiam non obstabit, quominus doctrinam pastorum conferre possit cum doctrina Christi, prophetarum et apostolorum, in scripturis proposita, et juxta hanc normam verum prophetam a falso discernere. Sed verum prius; ergo et posterius. Connexio majoris probatur, quia Christus, prophetae et apostoli tam perspicue docere possunt et vere etiam tam perspicue docuerunt, quam ordinarii pastores. Cum Christus, prophetae et apostoli docendi ministerio in his terris fungerentur, non eruditis solum, sed etiam rudi populo praedicarunt, atque eo quidem modo, ut doctrinam ipsorum intelligere possent; quomodo igitur scripta prophetarum et apostolorum adeo essent obscura et perplexa, ut ex illis de doctrina rudis populus judicare omnino nequeat? Certe non alia, sed eadem scripserunt prophetae et apostoli, quae viva voce praedicarunt. — ,

At‘, inquit Bellarminus, ,si populus per se posset judicare de doctrina pastoris, non egeret praedicatoribus.' Resp.: Quae vero in hac illatione συνάφεια? Utrumque a Deo mandatum: ut scilicet populus judicet de doctrina pastoris, quod ipse Bellarminus antea disertis verbis illi concessit, et ut nihilominus sint certi et ordinarii in ecclesia ministri, ,non enim omnes doctores', 1 Cor. 12, 29. Eph. 4, 11. Aliud est, inquirere in veritatem doctrinae et haereses ab orthodoxia, pseudoprophetas a veris doctoribus discernere, quae vocatio generalis est, ad omnes Christianos pertinens; aliud, publice in ecclesia docere, quae est vocatio specialis. Ex ovibus non facimus pastores, sed jubemus, ut sint ac maneant oves; interim nolumus eas esse brutas oves, quae non possint nec debeant discernere inter pastores et lupos. Pontificii ex auditoribus suis faciunt brutas oves, quae sine ulla discretione sequantur pastorem, si vel maxime ad noxia deducat pascua vel etiam in lupum vertatur; faciunt ex auditoribus psittacos a nutu praelatorum pendentes, ex praelatis angelos, qui plane sint infallibiles et άνυπευϋννοι. . . .

Ratio, , quam Bellarminus addit, est plane antichristiana: ,Cum pastor ordinarius (inquit) et aliquis alius, qui praedicat, non vocatus, contraria docent, debet omnino populus pastorem suum potius sequi, quam illum alterum, qui non est pastor, etiamsi forte contingeret, ut pastor erraret.' At falsum est, quod pastorem ordinarium etiam errantem populus sequi debeat; hoc enim nihil aliud est, quam jubere, ut oves etiam ad noxia pascua suum sequantur pastorem, ut tenebras christiani praeferant luci, errores veritati, humanas constitutiones divinae auctoritati. Subjicit quidem Bellarminus, ,non esse credibile,

Deum esse permissurum, ut ordinarius pastor ita erret, ut decipiat simplicem populum'; sed frustra disputatur, an fleri possit, de quo manifeste constat, quod factum sit; ordinarios pastores saepius errasse et simplicem populum decepisse, absque insigni impudentia negari nequit; hic ergo urgemus Bellarminum et quaerimus, an ordinarios pastores etiam errantes populus sequi debeat? si adflrmate responderet, manifestum faciet, se operam venalem locasse ei, qui in,Si papa' dist. 40. sic rugit: ,Si papa, suae et fraternae salutis immemor, negligens deprehenditur, inutilis et remissus in operibus suis, et Insuper a bono taciturnus, quod magis officit sibi, et nihilominus omnibus, innumerabiles populos catervatim secum ducat, primo mancipio gehennae, cum ipso plagis multis in aeternum vapulaturos: hujus culpas istic redarguere praesumat mortalium nullus; quia cunctos ipse judicaturus a nemine est judicandus.'“ (Loc. de minist, eccl. § 88.) § 48.

Definiri a potest Scriptura s., quod sit Scriptura, b Deo c inspirante, d per prophetas et apostolos e partim Ebraeo, partim Graeco idiomate f consignata, hominem peccatorem g de omnibus, quae creditu ac factu necessaria sunt, h instruens, ut fidem i in Christum consequatur, Deoque reconciliatus, sancte vivat, ac tandem k vitam aeternam Dei beneficio consequatur. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. P. II. Cap. II. § 24. p. 278. Vid. supra § 2. not. a. p. 92. Nec difficile est cognoscere, conceptum Scripturae genericum in hoc recte constitui, quod sacrae Scripturae et scripturis aliis commune est. Quod si verbum Dei generis loco substituere placeat, intelligendum certe erit verbum externum et signum verbale. Vid. b. Mus. 1. c. p. 279.

281. Quae hic et porro dicuntur, ad differentiam specificam pertinent, a causis Scripturae desumtam; ex quibus primum occurrit causa efficiens principalis, Deus. Vid. supra § 3. Ita indicatur partim causalitas causae efficientis principalis, partim formalis causa Scripturae. Vid. § 4. et § 8. Qui sunt causa efficiens minus principalis. Vid. § 6. Pertinent ad materiam ex qua, sive ad materiale Scripturae. Vid. § 7. Qui est finis cui Scripturae. Vid. § 10. Sunt haec objectum primarium Scripturae. Vid. § 9. Qui est finis cujus intermedius. Vid. § 11.k) Qui est finis ultimus. Vid. l. c.
