where temptation is also treated 317 OF POSITIVE THEOLOGY PART ONE Chapter I. CONCERNING GOD. § 1. By the name of God, we commonly understand the most excellent being of all, than which nothing better can be or be conceived; or the first being, which is from itself and is the cause of all other beings, and which preserves and governs all things. Quenstedtius: "The definition of the natural knowledge of God is this: Natural knowledge of God is that by which it becomes known to us from the light of nature that there is some supreme Deity, and that the same governs this whole universe and all things created by Him with His wisdom and power." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 6. s. 1. th. 10. f. 366.)

That the subject of God must be treated first in theology is evident from Proleg. Chap. I. § 3. note c. p. 7, 8, compared with § 17. p. 38, and § 39. p. 76. Gerhardus: "Since Holy Scripture is the sole and proper principle of theology, we therefore rightly make our beginning from it. Some think that the explanation of theological topics should begin with the article concerning God, since He is the principle of being and the author of Holy Scripture itself; but in the treatment of disciplines, regard is had not so much to the principle of being as to the principle of knowing, and not so much to the dignity of the subject as to the ease of teaching and perceiving." (Exeges. l. I. § 1.)

Properly, that is to say, when taken. For otherwise the word "God" is taken improperly when it is transferred to creatures more excellent than others, e.g., angels and magistrates, or even to the idols of the Gentiles, which, by the false opinion of men, are held to be gods. See note a. to the following § 3. Quenstedtius: "Whether the name of God is also attributed anywhere in the Scriptures to ministers of the church or priests is doubted. For the affirmative, some bring forward the words of Exod. 4:16: 'You (Moses) shall be to him (Aaron) לֵאלֹהִים, for God.' From which passage they attempt to prove that priests are also called אֱלֹהִים in Holy Scripture, because Moses was a priest. But Moses sustained a double person or a double office, political and ecclesiastical; not by reason of the latter, but by reason of the former is he called Elohim, i.e., just as Aaron was to be the interpreter of Moses, so Moses was to be the judge and prince of Aaron." (L. c. c. 7. s. 1. th. 10. f. 388.)

PART I. CHAP. I.

Indeed, it is established by experience that all men who are wayfarers conceive of God only in relation to created things. See the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.*, Cap. II, § 12, num. II, p. 76. To this pertains the fact that men, especially in calamities, flee to God, and commonly call Him the Best and Greatest; compare Seneca, *de Benef.*, ch. VI and VII; and that they sometimes invoke Him as Judge among themselves and others; and at other times, conscious of their own evil, fear Him as the most holy and most powerful. § 2.

Among the names of God, which occur in many forms in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, that of יהוה stands out as essential and incommunicable. Ten are usually enumerated. Of these, four stand out: אל, אלהים, יהוה, and אדני. See Jerome, *Epist.* CXXXVI to Marcellinus, and the blessed Gerhard, P. I., *Loci de Nat. Dei*, § 21. Gerhard: "Jerome, in his epistle to Marcellus, vol. 3, p. 95, collected ten names of God: 1. אל, 2. אלהים, 3. אדני, 4. יהוה, 5. צבאות, 6. שדי, 7. עליון, 8. יה, 9. אשר אהיה, 10. אהיה. The name Jehovah (for which sometimes in the Scriptures Jehovih is read, Gen. 15:2, etc.) is usually called ἀγράμματον, because it consists of four constituent letters... The Hebrews write that this name is ἀνεκφώνητον, the reason for which Galatinus gives in book II, ch. 1, because it denotes the ineffable essence of God... Nor should this be passed over, which some gather, that this is the proper name of God, because י among the Hebrews serves for the formation of proper names. Thus from עקב, Jacob; from צחק, Isaac, etc... They consider it more subtle, or rather forced, that some write that by י in this name the person of the Father is denoted, by ה the Son, by ו the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, and by the second ה the human nature of the Son, which was assumed into the λόγος and thus raised into the fellowship of the most holy Trinity (on account of the personal union with the λόγος), as Ambrose speaks concerning the resurrection." (*L. de nat. Dei* § 21.)

This is thought to be derived from that passage in Exodus 3:14: אהיה אשר אהיה. I am (will be) who I am (will be). For although it is derived from the verb היה or הוה and the future אהיה, it is not therefore the third person of the future, היה; or יהוה will be, because God speaking to Moses enunciated it in the first person, אהיה, I will be. For both the noun is distinguished in grammar from the verb, and the points of the name Jehovah, by which it is expressed in the Scriptures, are not the points of the verb, but are proper to the noun. Whence it is more correctly said that יהוה is the same as what is enunciated in John in the Apocalypse, ch. 1:4: ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος; so that God or the Messiah is not expressed by this name precisely under the aspect of some future, but rather a Being is denoted that is superior to all differences of time: a Being, I say, that exists in the most perfect manner. Whence Plato likewise and Philo retain the simple name τὸ ὄντος, which Damascenus also uses. By Junius it is called αὐτοόν; by Scaliger, αὐταυτός; by the blessed Walther, αὐταυτώτατος.

For it denotes the essence, not just any essence, but κατ’ ἐξοχήν; or that God is such a being as no other is, or can be; a being that cannot not be. Certainly 1) in the entire Scripture there occurs no passage in which the name יהוה is found attributed to any creature in the nominative case. And when the appearing angel claims this name for himself, the context shows that it is not to be understood as a created angel, but an uncreated one, that is, the Son of God, e.g., Exod. 3:14. Indeed, 2) God Himself claims this name for Himself alone, Exod. 3:14, Num. 6:24, 25, 26, Isaiah 42:8. And 3) elsewhere Scripture attributes it to God as His proper name, Exod. 15:3, Is. 48:2, 54:5. It also 4) sometimes adds an exclusive particle, Ps. 83:19, Is. 37:20. To which is added 5) that all the marks of a proper name belong to this name, e.g., that it lacks the plural number, that it does not admit the demonstrative ה, that it admits no suffixes, that it is never placed in the construct state. And thus taught the blessed Musaeus in his manuscript *Collationes* against the Socinians, Disp. III, Q. II. And likewise in his manuscript *Collationes Quaestionum Illustrium* (the former of which, concerning Syncretism and Holy Scripture, exist in print), on the *Locus* concerning God, Q. II. Quenstedtius: "The name Jehovah is proper and incommunicable to God alone, both grammatically and logically. In the grammatical sense, since the requirements of a proper name belong to it entirely; in the logical sense, because since it is the name of God, it is so proper to God that it belongs to no one else outside of God. Because the name Jehovah is proper to God alone and communicable to no creature, hence we rightly assert the deity of the second and third persons of the Holy Trinity, i.e., of the Son and the Holy Spirit, against the heretics." (L. c. c. 7. s. 2. q. 1. f. 391. sq.) The same: "Those passages in which Jehovah is called the God of gods do not have the word θεόν, but the name Elohim, e.g., El Elohim, Ps. 50:1, which some explain as 'strong God'; others by apposition, so that the two are considered joined names of God; others by construction as Elohei Elohim, 'God of gods,' as in Deut. 10:17, where, however, both words are not taken properly, and indeed the former in an eminent sense and the latter in a subordinate sense, as Socinus wishes (establishing that eminence is denoted, as in that: 'Song of songs,' 'being of beings,' i.e., most eminent); but the former word Elohim is taken properly, the latter improperly. For by the latter Elohim, either the gods of the nations are understood ἀντιφραστικῶς, or metaphorical titular gods, namely, magistrates and judges." (L. c. c. 7. s. 2. q. 3. f. 407.) Luther: "First, I will let that pass regarding the ten names, as it is not new, but St. Jerome also mentions it in his epistle to Marcellus, where he counts them thus: El, Elohim, Elohe, Zebaoth, Eljon, Ehje, Adonai, Ja, Jehovah, Schadai. Others do it differently; I think nothing of it. There are surely more names of God in Scripture than these, such as Ab, Bore, Or, Chai, etc., Father, Creator, Light, Life, Salvation, and the like. And what can be called good or exist that must not be attributed to God beforehand, as He has it in Himself, as Christ says: God alone is good; but we receive from Him everything that we are and have. But now we want to deal with the one name called Jehovah, with which the devil and the Jews practice much sorcery and all kinds of misuse and idolatry. This name Jehovah, according to grammar, comes from the word Haja, or Hava, which means in Latin, *fuit*, in the past, *esse*; in German, *wesen* or *sein*; and the 'J' can be a *nota nominis verbalis*, like Josaphat, Jesaias, Jeremias, and many other names, and it is as much as *ens* in Latin, *on* in Greek. We Germans must say, 'He is,' and thus it becomes a Trigrammaton in Latin, a Digrammaton in Greek..." PART I. CHAP. I. ...hexagrammaton in German, or if we simply take IS, then it is also a trigrammaton. Now, that they pretend the name Jehovah should be unpronounceable, they do not know what they are babbling; if they mean the letters, it cannot be true, for it is called Jehovah. And if it can be written with pens and ink, why should it not also be named with the mouth, which is much better than pens and ink? Or why do they not also call it unwriteable, unreadable, unthinkable? In sum, it is a rotten thing. But if they do it for the sake of honor, then they should also do it with all other names and let them be unpronounceable as well. For it is written: Thou shalt not misuse God’s name; therefore that is also rotten. Scripture nowhere says that any name of God should be unpronounceable; otherwise, all those who misuse God’s name would be innocent, because they could say they were unable to name His name, let alone misuse it. It does indeed say that God’s essence, power, wisdom, goodness, and whatever else one can say of God, is unutterable, immeasurable, infinite, incomprehensible, etc., so that it is not the letters or syllables, but that which is signified by them, that is unutterable. Yes, one would have to speak of the unutterable name of God in this way. For He has His essence from no one, and has neither beginning nor end, but is from eternity, in and of Himself, so that His essence cannot be called "was" or "will be," for He never began, cannot begin to be, has not ceased, and cannot cease to be; but with Him it is pure IS, or essence, that is, Jehovah. Exod. 3:14. When the creature was created, His essence already IS, and whatever is yet to be, He IS already present with His essence. In this way Christ speaks of His divinity, John 8:58: Before Abraham was, I am; He does not say: Then I was, as if He were no longer afterward; but: I am, that is, My essence is eternal, has not been, will not be, but is a pure IS. Therefore, as His Is, Am, or essence is incomprehensible, so it is also unutterable; for no creature can comprehend that which is eternal. Hence the angels are eternally blessed, for they cannot see their fill of, rejoice in, or comprehend the eternal essence of God; and if it were to be comprehended, it could not be eternal, would itself have to have an end or beginning, and could neither give nor sustain an essence for anyone, because it would itself be uncertain of its own essence. Furthermore, His wisdom, power, goodness, etc., are also eternal and incomprehensible, because they must be nothing other than His divine essence itself. Thirdly, which is indeed higher, that in the divine essence there is God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three persons in one, eternal, incomprehensible essence. Yes, to say all such things of God, that might be called an incomprehensible, unutterable name? Who wants to name, think out, pronounce, or write out such a wondrous essence? In this way, perhaps the ancients called the name Jehovah unutterable, because it signifies God’s essence, according to grammar, which (as heard) is a pure IS, from eternity, and is named three persons." (Vom Schem Hamphoras etc. 1543. XX, 2564—66.) The same: "I do not boast that I am a Hebrew, but it is certain that this word אל has an etymological origin from strength, and it signifies God Himself; when it is a name, as here, it is one of the ten names of God. Just as Adonai, Jehovah, and Tetragrammaton are proper names of God, so El is nowhere found in the singular except regarding the true God, as in Psalm 42: My soul thirsts for El, that is, the strong one, and Psalm 50: The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken. But yet, whether you say 'strong' appellatively or 'God,' it seems to signify the proper name of God, and it comes to the same thing. I would prefer, however, that it be explained as God, even though the word 'God' does not express the appellation of strength, for by this word we understand nothing other than the divine itself..."

Lutherus: ,,Erstlich, lass ich das fahren von den zehen Namen, als das nicht neu, sondern auch St. Hieronymus in epistola ad Marcellum anzeucht, da er sie zählet also, El, Elohim, Elohe, Zebaoth, Eljon, Ehje, Adonai, Ja, Jehovah, Schadai. Andere machens anders; ich halte nichts davon. Es sind wohl mehr Gottes Namen in der Schrift denn diese, als, Ab, Bore, Or, Chai etc. Vater, Schöpfer, Licht, Leben, Heil, und dergleichen. Und was kann guts heissen oder sein, das nicht Gott zuvoraus zugeeianet werden muss, als ders in ihm selber hat, wie Christus spricht: Gott ist allein gut; wir aber von ihm alles empfangen, was wir sind und haben. Aber jetzt wollen wir den einen Namen, Jehova genannt, handeln, mit welchem der Teufel und Juden viel Zauberei und allerlei Missbrauch und Abgötterei treiben. Dieser Name Jehova, nach der Grammatica, kommt her von dem Wort Haja, oder Hava, das heisst lateinisch, fuit, in praeterito, esse; deutsch, wesen oder sein; und das 1. kann sein nota nominis verbalis, wie Josaphat, Jesaias, Jeremias, und viel andere Namen, und ist so viel, als im Lateinischen ens, im Griechischen on. Wir Deutschen müssen sprechen, er ists, und wird also Trigrammaton im Latein, Dygrammaton im Grie PART. I. CAP. I. chischen, Hexagrammaton im Deutschen, oder wollen wir schlecht IST nehmen, so ists auch Trigrammaton. Dass sie nun vorgeben, der Name Jehovah solle unaussprechlich sein, wissen sie nicht, was sie lallen; meinen sie die Buchstaben, so kanns nicht wahr sein, denn er heisst Jehova. Und so er kann mit Federn und Tinten geschrieben werden, warum sollte er nicht auch mit dem Munde, der viel besser denn Federn und Tinten ist, genennet werden? Oder warum heissen sie ihn nicht auch unschreiblich, unleserlich, undenkerlich? Summa, es ist faul Ding. Thun sie es aber von Ehren wegen, so sollten sie es auch in allen andern Namen thun, und dieselben auch unaussprechlich sein lassen. Denn es heisst: Du sollt Gottes Namen nicht missbrauchen; darum ist das auch faul. So sagets die Schrift nirgend, dass einiger Gottes Name soll unaussprechlich sein, sonst wären die alle unschuldig, so Gottes Namen missbrauchen, weil sie sagen möchten, sie hätten seinen Namen nicht können nennen, schweige denn missbrauchen. Das sagt sie wohl, Gottes Wesen, Gewalt, Weisheit, Güte, und was man mehr von Gott sagen kann, sei unaussprechlich, unmesslich, unendlich, unbegreiflich etc., dass nicht die Buchstaben oder Sylben, sondern dasjenige, so damit bedeutet wird, unaussprechlich sei. Ja, so müsste man vom unaussprechlichen Namen Gottes reden. Denn er hat sein Wesen von niemand, hat auch keinen Anfang noch Ende, sondern ist von Ewigkeit her, in und von sich selbst, dass also sein Wesen nicht kann heissen, gewest, oder werden, denn er hat nie angefangen, kann auch nicht anfahen zu werden, hat auch nicht aufgehört, kann auch nicht aufhören zu sein; sondern es heisst mit ihm eitel Ist, oder Wesen, das ist, Jehova. 2 Mos. 3, 24. Da die Creatur geschaffen ward, da IST schon sein Wesen, und was noch werden soll, da IST er bereitan mit seinem Wesen. Auf diese Weise redet Christus von seiner Gottheit, Joh. 8, 58.: Ehe denn Abraham ward, bin ich; spricht nicht: Da war ich, als wäre er hernach nicht mehr; sondern: Ich bin, das ist, mein Wesen ist ewig, ist nicht gewest, wird nicht werden, sondern ist ein eitel IST. Darum, wie sein Ist, Bin, oder Wesen unbegreiflich ist, so ists auch unaussprechlich; denn keine Creatur kann begreifen das, so ewig ist. Daher die Engel ewig selig sind, denn sie können sich des ewigen Wesens Gottes nicht satt sehen und freuen, noch begreifen; und wo es zu begreifen wäre, so könnte es nicht ewig sein, müsste selbst auch ein Ende oder Anfang haben, und könnte niemand ein Wesen geben noch erhalten, weil es selbst ungewiss seines Wesens wäre. Weiter, ist seine Weisheit, Macht, Güte etc. auch ewig und unbegreiflich, weil es nichts anders, denn sein göttliches Wesen selbst sein muss. Zum dritten, das wohl höher ist, dass im göttlichen Wesen ist Gott Vater, Sohn, Heiliger Geist, drei Personen in einigem, ewigen, unbegreiflichen Wesen. Ja, solches alles von Gott sagen, das möcht ein unbegreiflicher, unaussprechlicher Namen heissen? Wer will ein solch wunderlich Wesen nennen, ausdenken, aussprechen, ausschreiben? Auf die Weise werden vielleicht die Alten den Namen Jehova unaussprechlich genennet haben? weil er Gottes Wesen, nach der Grammatica, bedeutet, welches (wie gehört) ein eitel IST, von Ewigkeit, und drei Personen genennet wird.“ (Vom Schem Hamphoras etc. 1543. XX, 2564—66.) Idem: ,,Non jacto me Ebraeum, sed certum est hanc vocem אל originem etymologicam habere a fortitudine, et significat Deum ipsum, quando est nomen, ut hic, estque unum de decem Dei nominibus. ### Concerning God: WITH GOD. ... ness, which is above all things

WITH GOD. ... ness, which is above all things. But the Hebrew אל in the singular signifies God in such a way that it simultaneously signifies the etymology of its origin, namely, the strong one. And this strength is not that active strength, concerning which it follows in the word נבויר, but a substantive substance, which is its own nature, firmness or steadfastness, just as a solid, firm stone is spoken of, upon which one leans certainly and safely. Therefore, in our German translation, we have rendered it *Kraft* (strength/power). For that which is not weak and languid in itself, but subsisting in its own solidity and firmness, is called by that word among the Hebrews. And this is properly the signification of this strength. God is that strong one, that is, substantive firmness itself, and invincible and stable solidity.” (Exeget. opp. lat. Erlang. Vol. XXIII, 426. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Jews, who deny that the name Jehovah is proper to God alone, so that they may undermine the argument for the deity of Christ drawn from this name. 2. Of certain Papists, such as Bellarmine, who maintain that the name Jehovah is also attributed to angels. 3. Of some Calvinists, who make the name Jehovah common, but *metonymically*; for although they acknowledge that this name is proper to God, they nevertheless assert that it was attributed elsewhere to those who represented God, as Calvin does, Instit. l. 1. c. 13. § 19. ... 4. Of the Socinians, who maintain that the name Jehovah, when placed simply, is also attributed to creatures. ... Enjedinus flatly denies that “the name Jehovah is proper to God, and contends that it is attributed not only to persons, such as angels, priests, and judges, but also to other created things, such as the Ark of the Covenant, Jerusalem, etc.” Socinus, however, with his followers, indeed concedes that it is a proper name of God, yet in such a way that it also pertains to “angels sustaining the person of Jehovah in some matter.” 5. Of the Arminians and Innovators, of whom the former say in the *Apologia Confessionis*, c. 3, p. 51, that there is nothing more certain or clearer than that the name Jehovah is also attributed to creatures here and there in the Scriptures. ... These latter contend that the name of Jehovah was attributed to angels as legates of God in the Holy Scriptures, such as Calixtus and Dreierus.” (L. c. q. 1. f. 392.)

The same: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Socinians, who a. maintain that the name Elohim is attributed promiscuously to creatures and to God; likewise that the name אלהים is by its nature common and is attributed to God only *κατ’ εξοχήν* (by way of eminence). ... b. Because they utterly deny the mystery of the Trinity, they therefore constantly deny that a certain plurality in the divine essence is inferred by the word Elohim. ... 2. Of the Papists, such as Thomas, Bellarmine, and others. ... 3. Of the Calvinists, such as Calvin, Peter Martyr. ... 4. Of Dr. Calixtus the elder. All of whom agree in this, that the word Elohim is indeed plural in its termination, but singular in its signification, and denotes a single individual, by no means a plurality of persons in the unity of the divine essence.” (L. c. q. 2. f. 399.) §

3. Similarly, the Greek name Θεός, when taken properly, is a name not so much of dignity as of the divine nature. In the Scriptures of the New Testament themselves, it is indeed sometimes used of magistrates (John 10:34; 2 Thess. 2:4), and even of idols (1 Cor. 8:5), but improperly and by a certain *ἀναλογίαν* (analogy), whether true or fictitious, to Him who is truly and properly God. For although the name θεός, by the force of its origin, seems to denominate God from some operation (inasmuch as it is derived either *ἀπὸ τοῦ θεᾶσθαι*, from contemplating... PART I. CHAPTER I.

according to Damascenus, *lib. de orthod. fide* c. 12, or is derived «from θέειν, from running, or because He penetrates, fosters, and preserves all things, or from θεῖν, from placing [which is explained by κατασκευάζειν and ποιεῖν, to prepare and to make, because God is πάντων ποιητής, καὶ τῆς τῶν πάντων κατασκευῆς αἴτιος, i.e., the maker of all things and the cause of the structure of all things]; or from αἴθειν, from burning, because He is as a consuming fire [to vices], Deut. 4:24); yet it must be confessed that, just as upon hearing the abstract noun θεότης we first conceive of the divine nature or essence, so upon hearing the noun θεός we first of all conceive of the suppositum which possesses the divine essence or nature. Thus also the blessed Musaeus taught in *Coll. MS. contra Socin.* l. c. Q. I. And to this point it pertains that Scripture distinguishes between θεόν φύσει, or by nature, and θεοὺς λεγομένους, gods by name (not by reality or nature) such as in 1 Cor. 8:5, Gal. 4:8.

Gerhardus: "It is more correctly said that the Greek θεός and the Latin *Deus* are primitive words, which we also say of the German word 'Gott'." (*Exeg.* l. II. § 11.) Quenstedtius: "The Socinians confuse appellative and common nouns. Not all appellative nouns are common, or apply to many, just as 'sun' and 'light' are appellative nouns, but not common, or do not apply to many." (*L. c. q. 3. f. 405.*) § 4.

That God exists can be proved 1. from the contemplation of this universe, 2. from the testimony of conscience, 3. from the consensus of peoples, both Gentile and Christian. Indeed, among Christians it may seem that it ought to be supposed rather than proved; yet because we must contend not only with atheists, but also at other times, on account of the corruption of nature, with the doubts of our own minds, therefore those things which prove the existence of God are not to be neglected. Cf. the blessed Gerh. *Exeg. L. II. § 58.*

As Paul writes in Rom. 1:20: ἀόρατα τοῦ θεοῦ, the invisible things of God, as of one who exists, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶσθαι. And it is otherwise evident how, when we turn our eyes to this universe, we are immediately led into the knowledge of its cause, and conceive of some first being upon whom it depends for its existence. See the blessed Mus. *Introd. Cap. II. § 22. p. 74., § 24. p. 81. 82., § 25. et 31. p. 82. 83.*, where it is also mentioned how an exquisite and accurate knowledge of the existence of God is demonstrated by arguments drawn from a more exact consideration of this universe, e.g., from movers subordinated among themselves to one …first mover; from causes subordinated among themselves to a first cause; from the governance of this universe to a supreme governor, etc. Thus Paul teaches in Rom. 2:14, 15, that τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου, the work of the law (that is, those notions concerning the distinction between honorable and base things, with a relation to a supreme legislator, or God) is written (as if by the finger of nature or of God) in the hearts not only of Jews, but also of Gentiles, who do not have the written law; their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts mutually accusing one another (so that wicked men

are convicted of their own crimes and denounce divine vengeance upon themselves), or even excusing them (so that the good are encouraged by the rectitude of their good deeds). See the blessed Musaeus, *Introd.* Cap. II. § 22. p. 57, 58, and *Diss. de Insuffic. Lum. Nat. contra Ed. Herb.* § 71, 72, p. 43, 44. And to this point also pertain, in their own way, the things we said above in the Prolegomena, c. I. § 10, concerning the innate knowledge of God. For 1) that men by nature…f God. For the fact that men 1) by nature prescribe to themselves, as if by the authority of another superior, what is to be done and what is to be avoided; and thus 2) if they do anything otherwise, it arises from the fact that they hold the truth, or the true knowledge of things to be done according to the will of the superior, captive (κατέχουσι) in unrighteousness, and hinder it from being able to exert itself toward the honesty of morals and the true worship of God, according to Rom. 1:18; and that 3) after good deeds are performed they rejoice, and after evil ones they tremble, not thinking of human rewards or punishments: all these things argue for an internal and naturally innate sense of the Deity (see Musaeus, *Introd.* l. c. p. 57, 58). Although it should not therefore be said that habitual knowledge is connate to us. For although (writes the blessed Scherzer in *Brev. Huelsem.* Cap. II. p. 85, 86) the passages Rom. 1:19, 20; 2:14 refer this knowledge to φύσις, they do not, however, determine the mode by which it inheres φύσει. Meanwhile, because the cause of condemnation in the cited passages is referred to the abuse of the νοῦς or intellect, Huelsemann judged it more probable that this knowledge is born with man by way of a power (sc. proximate and without the help of a teacher), if the exercise of the intellect is added. Rom. 1 (for so it must undoubtedly be read: not 2), 19, 20, 21, 28, 32; 2:2 sqq. (suppose it should be read 2:14 sqq.). It is added that in the same place, voluntary sloth and unjust detention are opposed to the exercise of the intellect; which habits are not connate, nor opposed to other habits, but to powers, and to the act flowing from them, and thus they manifestly show that this natural knowledge is in man by power, but not by an infused habit. A habit, that is, properly so called. For otherwise we teach with the same mind: by innate knowledge, not actual before the use of reason, but habitual; not ἐνεργείᾳ, by expressed species, but ἐν δυνάμει, by the implantation of an analogous habit. Indeed, if you say that habitual knowledge is simply connate to us, it will certainly be understood as a habit properly so called. But if you say it is analogous, you will indicate that it is not a habit speaking properly, but something similar to a habit. Not only as it pertains to acquired knowledge of the fact that God exists, but also regarding innate knowledge. See Musaeus, l. c. p. 58, 59, 60.

Latin:

DB DEO. tatem, quae est super omnia. Sed Ebraicum אל in singulari sic significat Deum, ut simul significet etymologiam originis, scilicet fortem. Et haec fortitudo non est illa activa, de qua sequitur in voce נבויר, sed substantiva substantia, quae est sua natura, firmitas seu firmitudo, ut lapis solidus firmus dicitur, cui quis certo et tuto innititur. Ideo in translatione nostra germanica reddidimus Kraft. Quod enim in se ipso non est debile et languidum, sed subsistens in sua soliditate et firmitudine, id apud Ebraeos illa voce dicitur. Et haec est proprie hujus fortitudinis significatio. Deus est ille fortis, id est, ipsa substantiva firmitas, et invicta ac stabilis soliditas.“ (Exeget. opp. lat. Erlang. Vol. XXIII, 426. sq.)

### Concerning God: Antithesis

ANTITHESIS.

Gerhard: "Concerning this natural knowledge of God, 1. some err by defect, who deny it entirely, which is done by a. The Neophotinians (whose πρῶτον ψεῦδος and origin of error seems to depend on the fact that they deny that the first man was created for immortality and possessed a certain original righteousness, of which the remnants of the divine image are the natural knowledges). . . Ostorodt, *Inst.* c. 7. p. 10: 'That men know something of God or of the Godhead, they do not have this from nature, nor from the contemplation of creation, but from hearsay, since God has revealed Himself to men from the beginning.' . . b. Flacius, P. I. *Clavis* under the word 'lex' col. 563: 'That there are still any true principles or knowledges of the one God and His government in man ought not to be conceded.' Col. 566: 'Man knows no more of God by nature than a brute.' c. Vorstius in *exeg. apol.* c. 1: 'Innate knowledge is not actual nor habitual, but only potential.' PART I. CAP. I. that is, the power of knowing itself. d. Those also err who rashly and indiscriminately pronounce that it is false and is to be called false if the Gentiles affirm that God is eternal, omnipotent, etc., since the Apostle expressly calls it the truth of God. Rom. 1:18. . .

2. They sin by excess who establish that it [natural knowledge] is sufficient for obtaining salvation, which is done by a. certain of the fathers and scholastics, who assert that men before the law was promulgated by Moses could have been saved and were saved by natural knowledge. (For as Augustine rightly warns, Ep. 49: "By a certain disposition of the mind, the virtues of the heathens delight us, so that we are not willing to condemn them.") Clement of Alexandria, lib. I, Strom.: "Philosophy sometimes justified the Greeks by itself, for there are many ways to salvation." Justin, Apol. 2: "Those who lived μετά λόγον are Christians, even if they were thought to have not known God, such as Socrates and Aristides among the Greeks." Similar things occur in Irenaeus, Tertullian, Epiphanius, Jerome, Chrysostom, etc. But Augustine, stirred by the Pelagian controversy, corrected those things which had been stated inconveniently by the ancients. Acosta teaches that this was the opinion of the scholastics and refutes it. . . b. Certain of the Papists. Andradius in *Defens. Conc. Trid.*, lib. III, p. 292: "True faith and true knowledge of God for righteousness and eternal salvation can be had not only from the sacred scriptures and divine oracles, but also from those things which are subject to the senses.". . Erasmus in the preface to Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*: "They will not find me very opposed in casting my vote, who hope that he [Socrates] leads a quiet life among the blessed above." The same in *Convivium Religiosum*: "When I read such things, I can scarcely restrain myself from saying: Saint Socrates, pray for us." And later: "But I myself often cannot restrain myself from wishing well to the holy soul of Morus and Flaccus.". .

3. Certain of the Calvinists. Zwingli, in his *Exposition of the Christian Faith* written to the King, places "Numa, Aristides, Socrates, etc., among the blessed in heaven," and asserts that God "wrote something of faith with His own hand into the heart of Seneca," from which arose the joke of Vitus Winshemius: "Beware, hearers, of the heaven of the Zwinglians; I would not willingly live in that heaven, for I would fear for myself from the club of Hercules." See also Zwingli’s *Elenchus contra Anabaptistas*, tom. I, opp. fol. 35. The same, tom. I, ep. 1, f. 382: "A heathen, if he fosters a pious mind at home, is a Christian, even if he is ignorant of Christ"; in *De Providentia*, tom. 1, f. 358, he writes of Seneca that "he spoke religiously concerning the creation and preservation of things, and that he had a divine mind." Gualther, his son-in-law, undertook the defense of Zwingli in an apology published in the year 1545, page 52, where he attempts to bolster Zwingli’s opinion with certain arguments. . . 4. The Photinians, although they plainly deny the natural knowledge of God, nevertheless, given their hypotheses, cannot establish otherwise than that the Gentiles, even outside the church, could have had knowledge of God sufficient for salvation. . . The Racovian Catechism, pp. 25, 26, to the question: "What are those things which pertain to the essence of God that are absolutely necessary for salvation?" answers in this way: "They are these: that God is, that He is only one, that He is eternal, that He is perfectly just, perfectly wise, and perfectly powerful." Ostorodus, *Inst.*, c. 3, p. 28: "Besides these, we know nothing else necessary to be known, as far as the essence of God is concerned." But all these things can be drawn from natural knowledge; therefore, according to the hypothesis of the Photinians, the Gentiles could have sought from nature those things which are necessary for salvation. (Exeges. loc. II, § 63, 81.) Luther: "I recall how M. Johannes Wesalia (who was a preacher at Mainz, and previously governed the university at Erfurt with his books, from which I also became a Master there) had to be condemned by those desperate, arrogant murderers, called *haereticae pravitatis inquisitores* (I should say, *inventores*), the Dominican friars, for no other reason than that he would not say: *Credo, Deum esse* [I believe that God exists], but said: *Scio, Deum esse* [I know that God exists]. For all the schools held that *Deum esse* [that God exists] is *per se notum* [known of itself], as St. Paul also says in Romans 1:19."

5. However, in order that what God is, and who He is, may be rightly known, those things which pertain to the divine essence and attributes must first be distinctly viewed and proved from the Scriptures, and then those things which pertain to the divine persons. By the name of the divine essence is understood that which is first conceived in God and by which God is adequately distinguished from all other things, and which, in our mode of conceiving, is the principle and root of all perfections that are attributed to God by way of properties. That is, they are perfections which follow the essence of God, or that which we first conceive in Him, according to our mode of understanding, and are thus attributed to God by way of adjacent forms, although in reality they are not accidents, nor do they differ really from the divine essence. They are, however, distinguished from the divine essence and likewise from one another on account of the infinite perfection of God and the imperfection of our intellect.

Quenstedtius: "Essence, substance, spirit, and consequently the remaining attributes which are attributed to God and creatures alike, are predicated of God and rational creatures not συνωνύμως, univocally, nor ὁμωνύμως, equivocally, but ἀναλόγως, analogically, in such a way that they belong to God πρώτως and absolutely, and to creatures δευτέρως and by dependence; which analogy is properly called that of intrinsic attribution... Things agree univocally, speaking properly and strictly, which have in common both the name and the thing denoted by that name equally, with no inequality intervening due to the dependence of one upon the other. Things agree equivocally which have a common name, but not the thing signified by the name. Things agree analogically which have in common both the name and the thing designated by the name, but unequally, since the name and the thing belong to one πρώτως and absolutely, and to the other δευτέρως and by dependence." (L. c. c. 8. s. 2. q. 1. f. 422. sq.)

The same: "The essence of God is τὸ πᾶν καὶ οὐδέν, all and nothing. It is all, because the perfections of all things are in it, and whatever is, has its essence from it. It is nothing, however, not indeed by defect, as if the divine essence were lacking, but because it exceeds all things that are." (L. c. s. l. f. 409.)

The same: "Because our finite intellect cannot adequately conceive the infinite and most simple essence of God with one adequate concept, it therefore apprehends the same by distinct and inadequate concepts, which inadequately represent the divine essence; which inadequate concepts are called affections and attributes of God; affections, indeed, because they affect and denominate the divine essence; attributes, because they are attributed to the same by our intellect, even if they are distinguished from the divine essence not really, but only by reason." (L. c.)

Chemnitius: "No accident falls into God... This rule exists in Cyril, book 2 of the Treasury, c. 2. And an accident is understood, as Bonaventure explains, as that which can either be lost, or could have come to a substance already existing, or can depart while the substance remains, such as the virtues in the angels, which the devils lost while their substance remained; or it can at least be intended or remitted, or receive change, such as the virtues in regenerate men. Therefore, because Augustine says: 'In God there is nothing mutable or losable,' nothing is said of Him according to accident. The true and simple sense of this rule is, therefore: that God is always like Himself, and is not changed either by time or by our malice. Likewise, that we must argue to God from our virtues and actions, not [by way of accident]..." PART I. CHAP. 1. similar, but from the lesser to the greater. . . Thus, those things which are predicated of God, such as truth, goodness, justice, chastity, mercy, etc., do not inhere in Him as virtues do in angels or men. Thus, when it is said: the love of God, it is not understood as such love as exists in creatures (which is an accident), mutable and losable, but it signifies the essence itself, seriously and ardently loving us. In creatures, the person who has life, wisdom, etc., is one thing, and the life, wisdom, etc., which is in the person is another; but in God, these are not things distinct from the essence itself, but life, wisdom, grace, mercy, goodness, love, etc., are the very substance of God, nor can they be changed in Him, as they can in men. However, it is objected that certain things are said of God temporally. Such as: The Word was made flesh, Creator, a helper in times of need, a refuge made for us. Therefore, these are predicated of God according to accident. Cyril replies in the passage cited above: "By relation to creatures, certain things are said of God temporally, and they are said according to accident, not because anything happens to the substance of God Himself with change, but according to the accident of the creature, in which the change occurs, such as Creator, refuge," etc. In the schools, they say it this way: Nothing temporal is predicated of God by essence or inherence, but by way of cause, as Creator, or by way of union, as The Word was made flesh. And then the change occurs regarding the creature. This rule is not an empty figment of the scholastics, but is taken from manifest passages of Scripture: Num. 23:19; Mal. 3:6; Ps. 102:13; Jas. 1:17; 1 Tim. 6:16; Heb. 13:8. — The true use of this rule must also be learned. For the scholastics, from a perverse understanding of this rule, removed all affections from God, so that they even affirm that that sweetest consolation in Hos. 11:8-9 must be taken according to effect only, not according to affection. "It is indeed true that, because no accident falls into God, commiseration in Him is not such an affection as it is in us; but because His mercy is not distinguished from His essence, it is something much more ardent in God than we can think." (L. th. 1. de Deo. c. 3. f. 28.)

Neophotiniani (quorum κμώτον ψεϋΑος et origo erroris videtur ex eo pendere, quod negant, primum hominem ad immortalitatem esse conditum et justitiam quandam originalem habuisse, cujus divinae imaginis reliquiae sunt notitiae naturales). . . Ostorodns, Inst. c. 7. p. 10.: ,Dass die Menschen von Gott oder von der Gottheit etwas wissen, das haben sie nicht von der Natur, noch aus Betrachtung der Schöpfung, sondern vom Hörensagen, sintemal sich Gott von Anfang den Menschen offenbaret hat.‘ . . b. Flacius P. I. Clavis in voce legis col. 563.: ,Quod aliqua vera principia aut notitiae unius Dei ejusque gubernationis sunt adhuc in homine, concedi non debet.‘ Col. 566.: ,Hominem de Deo natura non plus scire, quam brutum.‘ c. Vorstius in exeg. apol. c. 1.: ,Notitia innata non est actualis nec habitualis, sed tantum potentialis, PART. I. CAP. I. hoc est, ipsa tantum cognoscendi potentia, d. Rom. 1, 18. . . 2. In excessu peccant, qui eam ad salutem consequendam sufficientem esse statuunt, quod faciunt a. quidam ex patribus et scholasticis, qui homines ante promulgatam a Mose legem notitia naturali salvari potuisse et salvatos fuisse asserunt. (Ut enim recte monet Augustinus, ep. 49.: ,Quadam indole animi delectant ethnicorum virtutes, ut non libenter illas damnemus.‘) Clemens Alexandr. lib. I. strom.: ,Per se aliquando Graecos justificabat philosophia, multae enim sunt viae ad salutem.‘ Justin, apol. 2.: ,Qui μετά λόγον vixerunt, Christiani sunt, etiamsi non novisse Deum existimati sunt, quales apud Graecos fuerunt Socrates, Aristides.‘ Similia occurrunt apud Irenaeum, Tertullianum, Epiplianium, Hieronymum, Chrysostomum etc. Sed Augustinus, Pelagiano certamine excitatus, ea, quae incommode a veteribus dicta fuerant, correxit. 1. III. p.

292.: ,Vera fides et vera Dei cognitio ad justitiam et salutem aeternam non ex sacris tantum literis divinisque oraculis, sed ex rebus etiam iis, quae sensibus subjiciuntur, haberi potest.‘ . . Erasmus in praef. super. Tuse. qq. I. opp. fol. 35. Idem tom. Photiniani, licet notitiam Dei naturalem plane negent, salvis tamen suis hypothesibus aliter statuere non possunt, quam, cognitionem Dei ad salutem sufficientem gentiles etiam extra ecclesiam habero potuisse. . . Catech. Racov. p. 25. 26. quaestioni: ,Quaenam sunt, quae ad essentiam Dei pertinent, prorsus ad salutem necessaria?‘ respondet hoc modo: ,Sunt ea, quod Deus sit, quod sit tantum unus, quod aeternus, quod perfecte justus, perfecte sapiens et perfecte potens.‘ Ostorodus Inst. c. 3. p. 28.: ,Praeter haec nihil aliud scimus cognitu necessarium, quantum ad essentiam Dei attinet.‘ Atqui ista omnia ex naturali notitia hauriri possunt, ergo juxta Photinianorum hypothesin gentiles eorum, quae ad salutem sunt necessaria, cognitionem ex natura petere potuerunt.“ (Exeges. loc. II. | 63. 81.) Lutherus: ,,Ich gedenke, wie M.
