Denn alle Schulen liielten, dass Deum esse, per se notum sit, wie St. Paulus Röm. 1, 19. auch sagt.“

5. Ut autem, quid sit Deus, et quis sit, recte cognoscatur, Ideo primum ea, quae ad essentiam a et attributa b divina, deinde illa, quae ad personas c divinas pertinent, distincte d spectari atque ex Scripturis e probari debent. Intelligitur autem nomine essentiae divinae illud, quod primo in Deo concipitur et per quod Deus ab aliis rebus omnibus adaequate distinguitur, quodque nostro modo concipiendi principium, et radix est omnium perfectionum, quae Deo per modum proprietatum tribuuntur. Id est, perfectiones, quae essentiam Dei, seu id, quod in ipso primo concipimus, nostro modo intelligendi consequuntur atque ita Deo per modum formarum adjacentium tribuuntur, licet revera non sint accidentia, neque. ab essentia divina realiter differant. Distinguuntur autem ab essentia divina pariter et inter se propter infinitam Dei perfectionem et intellectus nostri imperfectionem.

Quenstedtius: ,,Essentia, substantia, spiritus et consequenter reliqua attributa, quae Deo et creaturis simul tribuuntur, de Deo et creaturis rationalibus non συνωννμως, univoce, nec όμωννμως, aequivoce, sed άναλόγως, analogice, praedicantur, ita, ut Deo πρώτως et absolute, creaturis όεντίρως et per dependentiam conveniant; quae analogia proprie dicitur attributionis intrinsecae. . . Univoce proprie et stricte loquendo conveniunt, quae et nomen et rem, nomine illo denotatam, communem habent aequaliter, nulla ob dependentiam unius ab altero inaequalitate interveniente. Aequivoce conveniunt, quae nomen habent commune, sed non rem, nomine significatam. Analogice conveniunt, quae et nomen et rem, nomine designatam, communem habent, sed inaequaliter, cum nomen et res alteri πρώτως et absolute, alteri δεντέρως et per dependentiam conveniat.“ (L. c. c. 8. s. 2. q. 1. f. 422. sq.)

Idem: ,,Est essentia Dei το παν καϊ ονδεν, omne et nihil. Omne est, quia omnium rerum perfectiones in ipsa sunt et, quidquid est, ab ipsa essentiam suam habet. Nihil vero est, non quidem defectu, quasi essentia divina deficiat, sed quoniam omnia, quae sunt, excedit.“ (L. c. s. l. f. 409.)

Idem: ,,Quia intellectus noster finitus infinitam et simplicissimam Dei essentiam uno conceptu adaequato adaequate concipere nequit, ideo distinctis et inadaequatis conceptibus, essentiam divinam inadaequate repraesentantibus, eandem apprehendit; qui conceptus inadaequati dicuntur affectiones et attributa Dei; affectiones quidem, quod essentiam divinam afficiant et denominent; attributa, quod ab intellectu nostro eidem attribuantur, etiamsi ab essentia divina non realiter, sed ratione tantum distinguantur.“ (L. c.)

Chemnitius: ״,In Deum non cadit accidens. . Extat haec regula apud Cyrillura, lib. 2. thesauri, c. 2. Et intelligitur accidens, sicut Bonaventura explicat, quod potest vel amitti, vel potuit substantiae prius existenti advenire, vel potest recedere manente substantia, ut virtutes in angelis, quas diaboli amiserunt manente substantia; vel potest saltem intendi remittive, vel mutationem recipere, ut virtutes in hominibus renatis. Quia ergo Augustinus inquit: ,In Deo nihil est mutabile vel amissibile‘, ideo nihil dicitur de eo secundum accidens. Est ergo verus et simplex hujus regulae sensus: Deum semper esse sui similem, non mutari vel tempore, vel nostra malitia. Item, a nostris virtutibus et actionibus argumentandum esse ad Deum non a PART. I. CAP. 1. simili, sed a minori ad majus. . . Ita quae praedicantur de Deo, ut veritas, bonitas, justitia, castitas, misericordia etc., non insunt illi siout virtutes in angelis vel hominibus. Ita cum dicitur: caritas Dei, non intelligitur talis caritas, qualis est in creaturis (quae est accidens), mutabilis et amissibilis, sed significatur essentia serio et ardenter nos diligens. In creaturis aliud est persona, quae habet vitam, sapientiam, et allud est vita, sapientia etc., quae est In persona; in Deo vero non sunt res distinctae ab ipsa essentia, sed vita, sapientia, gratia, misericordia, bonitas, caritas etc. sunt ipsa Dei substantia, nec possunt in eo, nt in hominibus, mutari. Objicitur vero, dici quaedam de Deo temporaliter. Ut: Verbum caro factum est, creator, adjutor in opportunitatibus, refugium factum nobis. Ergo haec praedicantur de Deo secundum accidens. Respondet Cyrillus loco superius allegato: ,Relatione ad creaturas quaedam dicuntur de Deo temporaliter, et dicuntur illa secundum accidens, non quod substantiae ipsius Dei aliquid accidat cum mutatione, sed secundum accidens creaturae, in qua fit mutatio, ut creator, refugium‘ etc. In scholis ita dicunt: Per essentiam vel inhaerentiam nihil praedicatur de Deo temporale, sed per modum causae, ut creator, vel per modum unionis, ut Verbum caro factum est. Et tunc mutatio accidit circa creaturam. Non est inane scholasticorum figmentum haec regula, sed sumta est ex manifestis Scripturae locis: Num. 23, 19. Mal. 3, 6. Ps. 102, 13. Jac. 1, 17. 1 Tim. 6, 16. Hebr. 13, 8. — Discendus quoque est verus usus hujus regulae. Scholastici enim ex pravo hujus regulae intellectu ademerunt Deo omnes affectus, ut etiam dulcissimam illam consolationem Ose. 11, 8. 9. affirment accipiendam esse secundum effectionem tantum, non secundum affectionem. Verum quidem est, quia in Deum non cadit accidens, commiserationem in ipso non esse talem affectum, sicut in nobis est; sed quia misericordia ejus non distinguitur ab essentia ejus, est quiddam multo ardentius in Deo, quam, nos cogitare possumus.“ (L. th. 1. de Deo. c. 3. f. 28.)


### Concerning God: Gerhardus: "If those attributes differed really from the essence of God, then…

Gerhardus: "If those attributes differed really from the essence of God, then God would be composed of essence and accidents, and thus the divine essence would not be supremely one and undivided. . . For God is not good by some other superadded thing, but by Himself, that is, by His essence, and therefore He is goodness itself and the supreme good; He is not powerful by some other accident superadded to the essence, but by Himself, that is, by His essence, and therefore He is omnipotence itself, and thus consequently it must be pronounced concerning the other attributes as well. Hence it has come about that power, goodness, wisdom, etc., are named attributes, but not qualities or accidents. . . Hence the rules: There is nothing in God that is not God Himself. There are no accidents in God. The divine essence identifies to itself all things that are in the divine. This all-encompassing identity of the divine attributes with the divine essence is proven, first, by those sayings in which God is called life itself, light itself, goodness itself, etc. . . Next, this is proven by a comparison of the places of Scripture. Ps. 25:6, the royal prophet prays: 'Remember your mercies, O Lord, and your steadfast loves, for they have been from of old. Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me, for the sake of your goodness, O Lord'; compare this with Isa. 43:25. . . Finally, those sayings which testify to the immutability of the divine essence must be referred here. . . Although, however, those attributes of God are not really distinct in God either among themselves or from the divine essence: nevertheless, the weakness of our intellect requires that we treat of them individually. 'God condescends to us, that we may rise up,' Augustine, *de spec.* c. 112, and since we are men, He speaks to us in a human manner." (Loc. theol. de N. D. §§ 47—51.)

Quenstedtius: "Whatever creatures do and accomplish by diverse and distinct powers and qualities, all of that God does and accomplishes by His essence. We are human by our essence, good and wise by quality, just by one power, and free by another."

etc.; but God is and acts as everything through His essence. Therefore, the consequence does not hold: "Those things whose effects are really diverse, or even contrary, are themselves also really different." (L. c. q. 3. f. 436.) The same: "Hence the theological rule: Divine attributes can be predicated of one another in the abstract, insofar as they are in God, but not insofar as they are in our concepts." (L. c. f. 435.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of Scotus and the Scotists and certain Nominalists, who maintain that being, essence, spirit, etc., are predicated univocally of God and creatures. Thus Scotus, Occam, Gabriel Biel, and others, among whom Slevoytus, Prof. at Jena, professes himself to be, in his academic disputation § 46. p. 66., saying: 'Since, therefore, being is not analogous with respect to inferiors, however analogy may be explained, and indeed not only the name but also the definition of being truly belongs to them, there is no reason why anyone should wish to deny that this being is univocal; we therefore follow the Scotistic school and certain Nominalists.' So much for him.

2. Of certain scholastics and others, who maintain that essence, substance, spirit, etc., are predicated of God and intellectual creatures only όμωνϋμως or equivocally, such as Aureolus, Polanus (asserting that 'spirit is predicated of God, angels, and the souls of men όμωνίφως or equivocally'), Keckermann, Bartholinus (thinking that spirit is said of God equivocally). Thomas attributes the same opinion to Rabbi Moses, namely, that being is predicated of God and creatures equivocally. Dionysius Petavius, vol. V. dogmat. theol. l. c. 6. § 4. 5. p. 40. sq., where he proves at length that to be and to exist truly and properly belongs to God alone. — ... Thomas Part. I. q. 13. art. 5. concludes thus: 'If these things were predicated equivocally of God and creatures, nothing could be known or demonstrated about God from creatures, but one would always fall into the fallacy of equivocation. And this is contrary both to the philosopher, who proves many things demonstratively about God, and also to the apostle, Rom. 1, 17. sq.'

An equivocal concept brings about the following absurdities: 1. Thus creatures would participate in the mere name of being and would in reality be non-entities. But who would assert that God produced mere non-entities? 2. If a creature were a complete non-entity, it could not be referred to God as an effect and a dependent being. 3. Christ, in assuming human nature, would have assumed a non-entity." (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 423. sq.)

G. Thomasius: "These (immanent or essential) properties are therefore distinguished on the one hand from the actual essential determinations (being, consciousness, will) upon which they rest, and no less from the trinitarian relations, which establish personal differences in God. On the other hand, however, those must be separated from them which merely express God's relations to the world. . . Thus, for example, the attributes of omnipotence, omnipresence, omniscience, and punitive justice undoubtedly express God's relations to the world; they cannot be conceived at all without the addition of the concept of the world. If these attributes were now essential properties, then the world would also have to exist in order for God to be. . . That separation is therefore indispensable. . . It is also found among our old teachers, who divide the attributes into immanent or absolute, and transient or relative, . . . only that the correct consequence is not drawn from this correct distinction. . . For Christology, our view is important in so far as, according to this, a relinquishing of relative divine properties can very well be asserted without endangering the essential ones." (Christi Person u. Werk. First Part. Second Ed. Erlangen, 1875. p. 49. sqq.)

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of certain Calvinists, who contend that the attributes of God are non-entities, are improperly attributed to God, and do not truly exist in God, that God in Himself is devoid of idioms, etc.; see PART I. CHAP. I.

Beckmann’s Zerbst Disputation, P. I. p. 272, 294 (who argues: "What one does not have, one cannot give to another; but God does not have attributes; therefore, He cannot give and communicate them to another, namely, to the human nature of Christ"); Masson’s *Anatomia universi triumphi*, Vol. I, p. 330; and Sachs’s disquisition against B. Meisner, who deny that there are or can be idioms of the true name in God, so that they may maintain that no such idiom could have been communicated to the human nature of Christ.

Of the Socinians, who also attribute accidents to God, as Crellius in *De Deo et attributis divinis*, ch. 32, f. 348: "They also deny that the divine properties are, on the part of the thing, God Himself." (L. c. s. 2, q. 2, f. 427.)

Namely, because Scripture presents several who are really distinct among themselves, each of whom conducts himself by way of an intelligent suppositum, and each is taught to possess that essence and the divine properties, as we shall see below. And those things which pertain to the essence and divine attributes are known in a certain way even from the light of nature, apart from the Scriptures; but those things which pertain to the persons can be known only from divine revelation (concerning which more will be said below), and therefore the consideration of the former deservedly precedes the treatment of the latter. For insofar as some of these, as we have just indicated, are known from the principles of reason, their consideration belongs to philosophy or natural theology; here, however, we are treating revealed theology. §

6. The essence of God can be described thus: God is a spiritual being subsisting of Himself; or more briefly: God is an independent spirit. As it is distinguished from the attributes. There is no reason why anyone should demand or expect a definition strictly so-called. For it must be confessed that in this life we do not have the quidditative, proper, and adequate account of the divine essence known and perceived. For we know only in part, according to 1 Cor. 13:12. So also the blessed Musaeus in *Coll. MSto contra Socin.*, Disp. I, Q. V, § 12. Cf. the blessed Hafenreffer, *L. de Deo*, p. 27; the blessed Franz, *Interpr. Script. S. Orae.* CIII, p. 226, 227; likewise *Disp. V. de Sacrif.*, thes. 119; the blessed Quenstedt, *Not. ad Comp. Hutt.*, L. II, Q. II, p. 70, 71.

Hafenreffer: "A perfect and accurate definition of the essence of God cannot be given by man in this life; however, it is easier to explain what God is not than what He is." Damascenus, *De orthodoxa fide*, l. 1, c. 4, after he had demonstrated concerning God that He is not corporeal, finally adds these words: "But this is not the definition of His substance, nor is 'unbegotten,' 'without beginning,' 'unchangeable,' and 'incorruptible,' and whatever else is predicated of God or about God. For these do not signify what He is, but what He is not. But it behooves him who wishes to assign the substance of something to say what it is, not what it is not. But to say what God is according to substance is impossible; it is far more appropriate to make a discourse about God by way of the removal of all things. For He is none of the things that are; not as a non-entity, but as..."

surpassing all beings and being itself above being.” And after a few words: “His infinite divinity is incomprehensible; and this alone of Him is comprehensible: infinity and incomprehensibility. Whatever, however, we say about God through affirmative theology, does not insinuate His nature, but those things which are around the nature. For even if you say He is good, if just, if wise, or whatever else you wish, you do not state the nature of God, but those things which are around the nature, οὐ τὴν φύσιν, ἀλλὰ τὰ περὶ τὴν φύσιν.” (L. th. lib. 1. 1. 1. pag. 27.)

Gerhardus: “Two things are sought in this place: I. Whether God can be defined. ... We answer in the negative. 1. From the defect of genus ... God, as creator, and the creature are separated by an infinite interval, nor is there anything that can be predicated equally of both. ... 2. From perfection. God is the highest being and is mere and purest act. Because He is the highest being, therefore He does not have anything superior; now, truly, whatever is properly defined is defined by something prior. ... 3. From a sufficient enumeration. If God could be properly defined, that would be either an essential or a causal definition. It cannot be essential, because that consists of genus and specific difference. Now, truly, God does not have any univocal genus with the rest of beings, nor is His most simple essence composed of genus and difference. A causal definition likewise cannot exist, because God is the cause of all things; but there is no cause given for God; He is ἀναίτιος, ἄναρχος etc.” (Exeges. loc. 2. § 89.)

Latin:

Gerhardus: ,,Si attributa illa realiter differrent ab essentia Dei, utique Deus ex essentia et accidentibus esset compositus, et sic essentia divina non esset summe una et indivisa. . . Neque enim Deus alio quodam superaddito, sed se ipso, hoc est, sua essentia bonus est ideoque ipsa bonitas et summum bonum; non alio quodam essentiae superaddito accidente potens est, sed se ipso, hoc est, sua essentia potens, ideoque ipsa omnipotentia, et sic consequenter de aliis quoque attributis pronunciandum. Inde factum, ut potentia, bonitas, sapientia etc. nominentur attributa, non autem qualitates vel accidentia. . . Hinc regulae: Nihil est in Deo, quod non sit ipse Deus. Nulla in Deo sunt accidentia. Essentia divina identificat sibi omnia, quae sunt in divinis. Hanc divinorum attributorum cum divina essentia omnimodam identitatem comprobant primo dicta illa, in quibus Deus ipsa vita, ipsa lux, ipsa bonitas etc. appellatur. . . Deinde comprobat hoc locorum Seripturae collatio. Ps. 25, 6. orat propheta regius: ,Reminiscere miserationum tuarum, Domine, et misericordiarum tuarum, quae a seculo sunt. Delicta juventutis meae et ignorantias ne memineris, secundum misericordiam tuam memento mei, propter bonitatem tuam, Domine‘; id conf. cum Es. 43, 25. . . Denique referenda huc sunt dicta, quae de immutabilitate essentiae divinae testantur. . . Quamvis vero attributa illa Dei nec inter se nec ab essentia divina realiter sint in Deo distincta: tamen sigillatim de illis ut agatur, intellectus nostri imbecillitas requirit. ,Condescendit nobis Deus, ut nos consurgamus‘, Augustinus de spec. c. 112., et cum homines simus, humano modo nobis loquitur.“ (Loc. theol. de N. D. §§ 47—51.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Quodcunque creaturae agunt et perficiunt diversis et distinctis virtutibus et qualitatibus, id omne agit et perficit Deus per essentiam. Nos per essentiam nostram sumus homines, per qualitatem boni et sapientes, per unam virtutem justi, per alteram libera

les etc.; sed Deus per essentiam omne est et agit. Non valet ergo consequentia: Quorum effectus realiter diversi, imo contrarii sunt, illa ipsa quoque realiter differunt.“ (L. c. q. 3. f. 436.) Idem: ,,Hinc regula theologica: Attributa divina de se mutuo possunt praedicari in abstracto, quatenus sunt in Deo, non autem quatenus sunt in nostris conceptibus.“ (L. c. f. 435.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Scoti et Scotistarum atque quorundam Nominalium, statuentium, ens, essentiam, spiritum etc. de Deo et creaturis univoce praedicari. Ita Scotus, Occam, Gabriel Biel, et al., quos inter se profitetur Slevoytus, Prof. Jen., disput. academ. § 46. p. 66., inquiens: ,Cum itaque ens respectu inferiorum non sit analogum, quomodocunque etiam analogia explicetur, et vero iis non nomen tantum, sed ratio etiam entis vere competat, nihil est, cur, univocum istud esse, quisquam negare velit; nos inde Scotisticam scholam sequimur et quosdam Nominales.’ Haec ille.

2. Quorundam scholasticorum aliorumque, qui essentiam, substantiam, spiritum etc. de Deo et creaturis intellectualibus nonnisi όμωνϋμως seu aequivoce praedicari statuunt, ut Aureolus, Polanus (asserens, ,spiritum de Deo, angelis et animabus hominum όμωνίφως seu aequivoce praedicari), Keckermannus, Bartholinus (spiritum existimans de Deo aequivoce dici). Eandem sententiam R. Mosi tribuit Thomas, quod sci. ens praedicetur de Deo et creaturis aequivoce. Dionysius Petavius, tom. V. dogmat. theOl. I. c. 6. § 4. 5. p. 40. sq., ubi το vere et proprie esse ac existere soli Deo convenire, prolixe probat. — ... Thomas Part. I. q. 13. art. 5. ita colligit: ,Si aequivoce ista praedicarentur de Deo et creaturis, nihil posset de Deo ex creaturis cognosci, nec demonstrari, sed semper incideret fallacia aequivocationis. Et hoc est tam contra philosophum, qui multa demonstrative de Deo probat, quam etiam contra apostolum, Rom. 1, 17. sq.’

Conceptus aequivocus sequentia infert absurda: 1. Sic creaturae nudum entis nomen participarent et revera essent nonentia. Sed quis Deum nuda producisse nonentia assereret? 2. Si creatura plane nonens esset, ad Deum referri non posset ceu effectus et ens dependens. 3. Christus, assumens naturam humanam, assumsisset nonens.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 423. sq.)

G. Thomasius: ,,Diese (immanenten oder wesentlichen) Eigenschäften unterscheiden sich daher einerseits von den eigentlichen Wesensbestimmtheiten (Sein, Bewusstsein, Wille), auf denen sie ruhen, und nicht minder von den trinitarischen Relationen, welche persönliche Unterschiede in Gott setzen. Andrerseits aber müssen von ihnen diejenigen ausgeschieden werden, welche blos Beziehungen Gottes zur Welt ausdrücken. . . So z.B. drücken die Attribute der Allmacht, Allgegenwart, Allwissenheit, Strafgerechtigkeit ohne Zweifel Beziehungen Gottes zur Welt aus, sie lassen sich ohne Hinzunahme des Weltbegriffs gar nicht vollziehen. Wären nun diese Attribute wesentliche Eigenschaften, so müsste auch die Welt sein, damit Gott sein könne. . . Jene Ausscheidung ist also unerlässlich. . . Sie findet sich auch bei unsern a. D. 1)., welche die attributa in immanentia oder absoluta, und in transeuntia oder relativa eintheilen, . . . nur dass diesem richtigen Unterschied nicht die rechte Folge von ihnen gegeben wird. . . Für die Christologie ist unsere Ansicht in so fern von Wichtigkeit, als hiernach eine Aufgcbung relativer göttlicher Eigenschaften ohne Gefährdung der wesentlichen gar wohl behauptet werden kann.“ (Christi Person u. Werk. Erster Theil. Zweite Aufl. Erlangen, 1875. p. 49. sqq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Quorundam Calvinianorum, qui contendunt, attributa l)ei esse nonentia, improprie Deo tribui, nec vere esse in Deo, Deum in se expertem esse idiomatum etc.; vide PART. I. CAP. I.

Beckmanni disceptationem Servestanam P. I. p. 272. 294. (qni argumentatur: Quod quis non habet, illud alteri dare non potest; sed Deus attributa non habet; ergo alteri, sel. naturae humanae Christi, ea dare et communicare non potest); Massonii anatomiae univers. triumphi· tom. I. p. 330., et Sachsii disquisitionem c. b. Meisnerum, qui negant, esse sive dari in Deo veri nominis idiomata, nt obtineant, humanae Christi naturae nullum ejusmodi idioma potuisse communicari. .

Socinianorum, qui etiam Deo accidentia tribuunt, ut Crellius de Deo et attributis divinis c. 32. f. 348. Negant quoque, proprietates divina» a parte rei esse ipsummet Deum.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 427.)

Nempe quod Scriptura exhibet plures inter se realiter distinctos, quoruta quisque se habet per modum suppositi intelligentis, et quisque essentiam illam ac proprietates divinas Ixabere docetur, quemadmodum infra videbimus. Atque illa quidem, quae ad essentiam et attributa divina pertinent, praeter Scripturas etiam ex lumine naturae quodammodo cognoscuntur; quae vero ad personas pertinent, non nisi ex revelatione divina cognosci possunt (de quo infra dicetur), ideoque illorum consideratio merito antecedit horum tractationem. Quatenus enim aliqua ex his, ut modo indicavimus, ex principiis rationis cognoscuntur, sic eorum consideratio ad philosophiam aut theologiam naturalem pertinet; hic autem revelatam theologiam tractamus.§

6. Essentia Dei a ita deseribi b potest: Deus est ens spirituale c a se,subsistens; d vel brevius: Deus est spiritus independens. Prout attributis contradistinguitur. Definitionem exquisite sic dictam, non est, cur quis postulet et expectet. Fatendum enim est, quod in hac vita essentiae divinae quidditativam, propriam et adaequatam rationem cognitam et perspectam non habeamus. Ex parte enim tantum eognosdmus, juxta 1 Cor. 13,12. Sic etiam b. Musaeus in Coli. MSto contra Socin. Disp. I. Q. V. § 12. Conf. b. Hafenreff. L. de Deo, p. 27., b. Franz. Interpr. Script. S. Orae. CIII. p. 226. 227., item Disp. V. de Sacrif. thes. 119., b. Oundis. Not. ad Comp. Hutt. L. II. Q. II. p. 70. 71.

Hafenrefferus: ,,Perfecta et accurata essentiae Dei definitio in hac quidem vita ab homine dari non potest; facilius autem, quid non sit, quam quid sit Deus, explicatur. Damascenus de orthodox, fid. 1.1. c. 4., posteaquam de Deo, quod non sit corporeus, demonstrasset, tandem haec subjicit: ,Sed non hoc substantiae ejus diffinitionem, ut neque ingenerabile, sine principio, inalterabile et incorruptibile, et quaecunque de Deo vel circa Deum esse praedicantur. Haec enim non ejus quid est significant, sed quid non est. Atqui oportet eum, qui vult alicujus substantiam adsignare, quid est, dicere, non, quid non est. De Deo autem, quid est secundum substantiam, dicere, impossibile, convenienti usque de Deo longe est, per onmium ablationem facere sermonem. Nam nihil eorum, quae sunt, est; non ut non-ens, sed ut

omnia entia supereminens et super ipsum esse ens.‘ Et post pauca: ,Infinita illius divinitas est incomprehensibilis; et hoc solum ejus comprehensibile: infinitas et incomprehensibilitas. Quaecunque autem per theologiam affirmativam de Deo dicimus, non naturam ejus, sed ea,, quae sunt circa naturam, insinuant. Nam etsi bonum, si jüstum, si sapiens, si quid vis aliud dixeris, non naturam dicis Dei, sed ea, quae circa naturam, ον την φϋσιν, άλλα, τα πεμϊ την φνσιν.“ (L. th. lib. 1. 1. 1. pag. 27.)

Gerhardus: ״Duo hoc loco quaeruntur: I. An Deus possit deflniri. . . Respondemus negate. 1. Ex generis defectu. . . Deus, utpote creator, et creatura infinito intervallo inter se distant, neque quicquam est, quod aequaliter de utroque praedicari possit. . . 2. Ex perfectione. Deus est summum ens et est merus ac purissimus actus. Quia est summum ens, ideo non habet aliquod superius; jam vero, quicquid proprie definitur, id per prius definitur. . . 3.Ex sufficienti enumeratione. Si D. proprie definiri posset, illa foret vel essentialis, vel causalis definitio. Essentialis esse nequit, quia illa constat genere et differentia specifica. Jam vero Deus non habet univocum aliquod genus cum reliquis entibus, nec simplicissima ejus essentia ex genere et differentia est composita. Causalis definitio itidem esse nequit, quia D. est omnium rerum causa; sed Dei nulla datur causa, est αναίτιος, άναρχος etc.“ (Exeges. loc. 2. § 89.)


### Concerning God: Dannhauerus: “To be defined otherwise, because He is infinite, and cannot be…

Dannhauerus: “To be defined otherwise, because He is infinite, and cannot be circumscribed by a certain genus and difference, much less represented by a single concept. Every properly spoken genus is multiplied in the plural number with its species and individuals; e.g., Abraham is a man, Isaac is a man, Jacob is a man; therefore, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are three men. But in divine matters, it is not permitted to speak in the same way; it is not permitted to say: The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; therefore, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three Gods.” (Hodosoph. Phaen. III. B. p. 92.)

Which holds the place of a genus or a more common concept. And just as a complete being is immediately distinguished into material and immaterial, or spiritual: so God is rightly considered to be an immaterial or spiritual being. Compare John 4:24, where it is expressly said πνεῦμα ὁ θεός, God (is) Spirit.

Gebhardus: “When we call God a spiritual essence from Exod. 3:14, or Spirit from John 4:24, then the word essence or spirit is not a certain universal νόημα abstracted by the mind from individuals, belonging equally to God and the angels; but it signifies an infinite thing, one in number, truly existing, most simple, common equally to the three persons of the deity, which is predicated neither univocally nor analogically of God and angels or other creatures, but in a purely singular mode, since infinite and finite essence, uncreated spirit and created spirit, differ by more than a whole genus. From this principle, the unity of God or of the divine essence is deduced.” (Exeges. 1. II. § 95.)

Luther: “Who knows what that is, which is called God? It is above body, above spirit, above everything that one can say, hear, and think.” (That these words: This is etc. XX, 1005.) For by this, just as God is adequately distinguished from all other things; so there is nothing that you can conceive in God, as a proper and determined concept, prior to the fact that He is not from another, and thus exists from Himself and necessarily. This, however, is also what Scripture says, that God is the first, Isa. 41:4, 44:6, 48:12. For to be the first is not to acknowledge anything prior, upon which He might depend, or from which He might have His... PART I. CHAP. I.

has being. Therefore, that which is such, certainly subsists of itself. Compare Exodus 3:14, where God says that He is who He is; and thus, just as He attributes to Himself a mode of existing that is entirely peculiar, so He indicates that He does not exist from another, nor in such a way that He could not-be, as any other beings exist; but rather from Himself, and in such a way that His nature and essence involve necessary existence. §

7. Divine attributes are divided into negative and positive. The former are: Unity, simplicity, immutability, infinity, immensity, eternity. To the latter class belong: Life, knowledge, wisdom, holiness, justice, truthfulness, power, goodness, perfection. See their common description in note b to § 5. Namely, that either by the force of the words or by the force of their meaning, they import a certain negation or removal of some imperfection from among those things which occur in creatures. These, with respect to the perfections which we perceive in creatures, are conceived after the manner of those perfections, albeit in a more eminent degree. We shall treat of each of these in its own order.

Hollazius: "There is a certain distinction between divine perfections and properties. Namely, perfections are those attributes which can indeed be communicated to created and finite things in a certain determined measure, but which belong to God alone in every way and in the highest degree, such as: intellect, will, knowledge, wisdom, justice, power, blessedness. I call properties those attributes which are to be ascribed entirely to God alone and in no way fall into any created things. Of these properties, some are natural, equally common to the three persons of the Godhead, namely: independence, absolute eternity, infinity, immensity, immutability; others, however, are personal, inasmuch as by them either the individual persons differ among themselves, or one or another is distinguished from the third, namely: eternal generation and procession, both active and passive." (Exam. th. P. I. c. 1. q. 21. p. 234.)

Quenstedtius: "There are two kinds of these attributes: some describe the divine essence absolutely and in itself without regard to operation, and are called immanent, ανενεργητα or quiescent, which, to wit, are not ordered toward any acts, such as immensity, eternity, spirituality, etc. Some describe the divine essence relatively, by reason of ενέργεια, or operative and exerting themselves outwardly, or which are known to be directed toward certain operations, such as power, knowledge, justice, mercy." (L. c. c. 8. s. 1. th. 4. f. 409.) §

8. Unity belongs to God, both when taken absolutely, which speaks of the undivided essence of God; and exclusively, by which we acknowledge God as the only one, besides whom there is no other God.

And this indeed almost coincides with the simplicity of God, of which we are about to treat. For although every other being is said to be one, in such a way that one and many—as being and beings—are distinguished; yet, because we know God to be not only undivided but also indivisible, we say that He is one absolutely, in such a way that we simultaneously assert Him to be simple.

Quenstedtius: "We are speaking of that unity of God which is drawn from supernatural light alone and becomes known to us through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. Now, this very unity of the divine essence can indeed be conceived by the human intellect, with the Trinity of persons abstracted and only the plurality of gods excluded; but such a concept is not a part of saving faith, which never conceives the unity of the divine essence affirmatively and positively apart from the communion of the divine essence which exists between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, whoever conceives the unity of the divine essence with an abstraction of the three persons, in this concept overlooks and, as it were, ignores the true essence of God, which is nothing other than the one essence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit." (L. c. c. 8. s. 2. q. 4. f. 437. sq.) The same: "Others say that God is one in number, since a singular one is also one in number, not because it contains number, but because it excludes it." (L. c. f. 437.)

The same: "Tertullian, in Book I against Marcion, says: 'If God is not one, He is not.' Athanasius prays against the idols: 'Ή πολυθεότης ἐστὶν ἀνυπόστατος'—'a multitude of gods is the nullity of gods.' To have many gods is the same as if you acknowledged none. In Eph. 2:12, the apostle teaches that the Ephesians, before they had given their name to Christ, were 'ἄθεοι in the world,' however many myriads of gods they worshipped. The sounder of the Gentiles themselves, although very often, carried away by the popular mode of speaking, said 'gods,' yet acknowledged and confessed one only God." (L. c. f. 439.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: ... of the Tritheists, whose ἀρχηγός was John Philoponus, most exercised in the πλοκαῖς and trifles of Aristotle, according to Nicephorus, lib. XVIII. c. 44 and 45, who posited three eternal spirits, differing in essential number." (L. c. f. 438.)

Indeed, unity thus signifies the negation of more than one of the same nature or kind. This is proved partly from those passages of Scripture where God is expressly called one, e.g., Deut. 6:4: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. 1 Cor. 8:4: There is no God but one; compare Eph. 4:6; 1 Tim. 2:5; partly from those sayings in which it is denied that any other God is given besides Him, e.g., Deut. 4:35: Jehovah Himself (is) God (and) there is no more (God) besides Him. Conf. Is. 44:6. § 9. Simplicity belongs to God absolutely, through which God is free from all true and real composition.

Quenstedtius: "Composition is the union of several distinct things, constituting a certain third thing. That union must be of several things. For nothing composes itself, but several things placed together effect a certain third composite thing." (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 441.) Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. II. 2 PART I. CHAP. I.

Indeed, not only from composition out of matter and form, which itself argues against the spiritual being of God, and therefore also from composition out of integral parts; but also from that by which something consists of subject and accident, likewise of nature and subsistence, which are really distinct. For a composition of reason, e.g., when we conceive of God as just and wise and good, etc., does not conflict with the highest simplicity and with God Himself.

Quenstedtius: "Nor do we suffer that composition be attributed to God, [namely] logical [composition], which is from genus and difference... If in God there is given a composition from genus and difference, God will at the very least be a monadic species, such that although by reason of existence concretely and in the act exercised there is only one thing in number that participates in the nature of the deity; yet by reason of definition, which is established by the concept of genus and difference, it will be so constituted that multiplication into many is not repugnant to it. But to wish to think of such multiplication concerning the divine essence is impious and absurd." (L. c. f. 443.)

The same: "Nevertheless, those are by no means to be censured who call Him (Christ) a υφιστάμενον σννΰετον, not from several hypostases or natures coming together into a third, but from two natures cohabiting most closely and intimately in one hypostasis." (L. c. f. 448.)

Gerhardus: "Does the Trinity of persons conflict with the simplicity of God? So it seems to the Photinians, whence they clamor that a triform, tripersonate, and composite God is introduced by us... We proceed thus: 1. Articles of faith are not to be opposed to one another. Both the simplicity of the divine essence and the trinity of persons are proposed to us in the Word; therefore, both must be accepted by the obedience of faith. 2. We do not posit that the divine essence is really distinguished from the persons..., but we assert that the divine essence and the three persons of the deity are most really and most simply one; therefore, there is no composition here. 3. Personal properties do not multiply the divine essence nor are they composed, since it is one and the same divine essence in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; in the Father άγει׳ητως, in the Son γενητώς, in the Holy Spirit ίκ,πορ'ντώς... 4. Therefore, when the Photinians urge: Where there are three truly and really distinct persons, there is not mere and highest simplicity; but in the divine essence according to our hypothesis there are three truly and really distinct persons—there we limit the major premise: where there are three truly and really distinct persons, of whom there is not one and undivided essence, there is not mere and highest simplicity. But now, of the three divine persons there is one and undivided essence." (Exeg. 1. II. § 134.)

Nempe non solum a compositione ex materia et forma, quod ipsum esse spirituale Dei arguit, adeoque etiam a compositione ex partibus integrantibus; verum etiam ea, qua quid constat subjecto et accidente, item natura et subsistentia realiter distinctis.b) Nam compositio rationis, v. g. quando concipimus Deum ut justum et sapientem et bonum etc., simplicitati etiam summae Deoque ipsi non repugnat.

Jam vero trium divinarum personarum est una atque indivisa essentia.“ (Exeg. 1. II. § 134.)


### Concerning God: It is customary to refer here to Exod

It is customary to refer here to Exod. 3:14; for there it is indicated that whatever is in God, that is God Himself. But that Holy Scripture sometimes attributes to God human members and other things which occur in creatures, especially in humans, and which argue for composition in them, this is done by metaphor, indeed that which they call άνϋρωποπάθειαν or συγκατάβασιν, and it ought to be explained ΰεοπρεπώς.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the ancient Anthropomorphites, who ascribed to God corporeal members and integral parts... Likewise of the Manichaeans, who contended that the substance of God was diffused in fragments into all creatures. But this error deserves a place among delusions rather than opinions." (L. c. f. 441.)

Thomasius: "Finally, we cannot refrain from expressing, from our concept of God, a further objection against the idea of a..."

to elevate the nature or corporeality of God. This thought, already expressed by Tertullian and frequently repeated by the mystics of all ages (Tertullian attributed corporeality, *corpus et forma*, to God, which, however, is only the anthropomorphic expression for substantiality and personality, as Baur very well remarks, p. 24), also resonates in many ways in more recent theosophy; above all in Oetinger, whom one can designate as its founder.

Starting from a justified polemic against an idealism that volatilizes all reality, this profound theosophist asserts the concept of life, *vita absoluta*, with reference to Ez. 1 and 10, as the only adequate concept of God.

Not thinking, not being, is the first thing in God, but life precedes both. This life is movement, as it were wheel-like, circling, self-generating movement, most preferably called *intensum* by Oetinger..., a living, self-developing, self-fulfilling, spiritual organism.

But Oetinger now allows this life-movement to condense outwardly into corporeality, to break out into a higher naturalness, and accordingly vindicates for God a physical essence, a spirit-corporeal nature, in which he first has his full reality; for the spiritual only attains concrete reality in the corporeal (!).

And with this, Oetinger connects backward to Jac. Böhme, whose fundamental idea of a nature in God also underlies the system of Fr. Baader and his students.

But the newest philosophy has also frequently appropriated the same. I find it in Billroth, in the younger Fichte, in Hanne, most clearly in Schwarz: *Das Wesen der Religion* [The Essence of Religion], page 185. Here it says: "The world-positing principle is not pure spirit, but the unity of spirit and nature." This nature, however, is defined as "the real side of the divine essence, which is the eternal substrate from which the temporal world emerges in the infinite multiplicity of its individual things," as "the eternal, pre-and archetypal world in God, i.e., as the world as it is still held together into unity by the penetrating spirit of God."

Here, then, the thought is quite clear. And one sees at the same time the actual reason for it. It is the total aversion to the scriptural doctrine of a creation out of nothing. Because this cannot be grasped (which is quite true), the world must proceed from the essence of God; it arises as God releases nature from himself, as it separates into space and time through his will, but as such is also continually penetrated and united by his spirit.

P. 187, 193. And precisely herein lies for us the reason why we must decidedly reject this theory; it turns creation into an emanation from God, it posits the substance of the world as essentially one with the substance of God, placing the difference between the two merely in the form of existence." (*Christi Person und Werk* [Christ's Person and Work]. I. p. 36 sq.) §

10. The immutability of God consists in this, that God is subject to no change, neither according to being, nor according to accidents, nor according to place, nor according to will or purpose. Quenstedtius: "The immutability of God is the perpetual identity of the divine essence and all its perfections, denying every motion whatsoever, both physical and ethical." (L. c. s. 1. th. 20. f. 414.) PART I. CHAP. I.

In what way God is immortal or incorruptible. See Rom. 1:23, where άφθαρτος is used; 1 Tim. 1:17, where βασιλεύς άφθαρτος is used; 1 Tim. 6:16, where He is said alone to have immortality (αθανασίαν). Thus, in James 1:17, it is said that with God there is no παραλλαγήν ή τροπής άποσχίασμα, no transmutation or shadow of turning, such as exists in men, who undergo changes of accidental perfections and imperfections of various kinds. See Jer. 23:24: Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord. But He who fills all things does not change place, nor can He change. See Num. 23:19: God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should repent. Has He said, and will He not do it? (that is, who would not want what He has hitherto willed) or has He spoken, and will He not fulfill it? And Prov. 19:21: The counsel of the Lord will stand. And Mal. 3:6: I, the Lord, do not change; but I have fulfilled and will fulfill what I have decreed and promised; I will not change My will. But that repentance, and that local motion, descent, or ascent are sometimes attributed to God in the Scriptures, that is said ά'Λρωπι,παύώς (anthropopathically). Compare the blessed Musaeus, Disp. de Vol. Dei Antec. et Conseq. § 5, 6, p. 691, 692. Similarly, affections are attributed to God; those, indeed, which in their formal concept imply imperfection, only metaphorically; but the others, which do not formally imply imperfection, truly belong to God regarding their formal concept, but without the change which they materially involve.

Gerhard: "Did the work of creation make God mutable? It is denied... In creation, two things are to be considered: 1. The principle of acting, 2. The effect produced. The principle of acting is the very essence of God, to which no change accrued through creation, because God did not will something in creation by a new motion of the will which He had not previously willed from eternity, but in time He did that which He had decreed from eternity by His immutable will. In the effect produced, there is a change from non-being to being, but this did not make God Himself mutable."

The same judgment applies to the question: Did the work of the incarnation make God mutable? Socinus affirms in defens. animadv. Posn. p. 66: "Who could deny, if God was then truly incarnated and made man, when Christ Jesus was conceived of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary and born of her, that something adventitious and new, and that of the greatest moment, happened to God Himself and His substance?" But the same νπόστασις of the Word remained, although it began to be the νπόστασις of another nature (Exeges. l. II. § 154). §

11. The infinity of essence belongs to God, insofar as the essence of God is contained by no limits. For otherwise, infinity is not a peculiar attribute of God, but extends to various positive attributes, as it is said that the knowledge, goodness, and power of God are infinite, etc. Gerhard: "Two species, as it were, of infinity are established: Eternity and immensity."

This is proved from Ps. 145:3: "Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised; and of his greatness there is no end (or searching)." For it is understood not as a greatness of mass or quantity, which does not apply to God, but as a greatness of essence.

Gerhard: "(God) is infinite below, because all things are lesser and inferior to God, and thus are distant from Him by an infinite interval. He is infinite above, because He received His being from no one, nor does He acknowledge anything higher. He is infinite before, because He is not from an efficient cause; before Him there was nothing formed, Isa. 43:10. He is infinite after, because after Him nothing shall be formed. He is infinite outside, because nothing outside of Him is higher than He. He is infinite within, because He is His own being, subsisting from Himself and through Himself." (L. c. § 169.)

The same author: "It is understood 1. not as an infinity of corporeal quantity or extension, but of essence and perfection; 2. not as a privative infinity, but a negative one. That which is privatively infinite is that which has not yet attained its ultimate perfection, like a fetus in the womb. That which is negatively infinite is that which so lacks a boundary and limitation that it neither ought to be nor can be bounded or limited. Thus, that is called privatively infinite which, although it does not actually have an end now, can nevertheless have one, such as quantity; negatively, that which simply has no end. 3. Although the etymology of 'infinite' only regards an end, it is nevertheless understood that there is a term from which, so that God is and is called infinite, because He has neither beginning nor end. 4. To the philosophers, the infinite is threefold: according to substance, according to quantity (namely, continuous and discrete), and according to quality. In created things, there is no actual infinite, neither according to substance, because every created substance is composite, nor according to quantity, nor according to quality, because infinite quantity and quality cannot exist in a finite substance. God alone is infinite, not indeed according to quantity or quality, but according to substance." (L. c. § 162.) §

12. The immensity of God consists in this, that the divine essence cannot be measured or included by any limits of place. Indeed, rather, while other things are present, God is omnipresent according to His substance, in such a way that He is circumscribed by no place, yet is present to all creatures—and that without extension of Himself—as regards His substance, and nevertheless is present without distance, just as it is customary to join omnipresence, as a positive attribute, with immensity, as a negative attribute.

Now, the immensity (and omnipresence) of God is proved from Jer. 23: 24. For He who fills heaven and earth is in heaven and on earth repletively, although He is not here or there circumscriptively.

Whence Augustine, interpreting the prophetic phrase, says that God fills heaven and earth by His present power, not by an absent nature (L. VIII. de Civ. Dei, c. XXX. p. 111. 694.), and F. L. Coquaeus defends that reading in his Notes, who also cites a passage of Hilary from L. V. de Trinit.: "There is no place without God." Similarly: "He whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain," according to 1 Kings 8:27, is rightly said to be unable to be measured by any limits of place, since the (highest) heaven is described in such a way that it is indicated that nothing created exists beyond it; yet at the same time, He is rightly said to be present to heaven alike and to all things that are contained by heaven, being absent nowhere.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Anthropomorphitarum antiquorum, qui Deo membra corporea et partes integrantes adscripserunt. . . Itemque Manichaeorum, qui contenderunt, substantiam Dei frustatim in omnes creaturas diffusam esse. Sed hic error potius inter deliria, quam opiniones locum meretur.“ (L. c. f. 441.)

Thomasius: ,,Endlich können wir nicht umhin, von unserem Gottesbegriff aus noch ein Bedenken gegen die Vorstellung von emer

Natur oder Leiblichkeit Gottes zu erheben. Dieser von Tertullian bereits ausgesprochene, von den Mystikern aller Zeiten häufig wiederholte Gedanke (Tertullian legte Gott Körperlichkeit, corpus et forma, bei, was jedoch nur der anthropoinorphische Ausdruck für Substantialität und Persönlichkeit ist, wie Baur sehr gut bemerkt, S. 24.), klingt auch in der neueren Theosophie vielfach an; vor Allen bei Oetinger, den man als den Begründer derselben bezeichnen kann.

Ausgehend von der gerechten Polemik gegen einen alle Realität verflüchtigenden Idealismus, macht dieser tiefsinnige Theosoph den Begriff des Lebens, der vita absoluta, mit Berufung auf Ez. 1. u. 10., als den allein adäquaten Gottesbegriff geltend.

Nicht das Denken, nicht das Sein ist das Erste in Gott, sondern beiden voran geht das Leben. Dieses Leben ist Bewegung, gleichsam radartige, kreisende, sich aus sich selbst gebärende Bewegung, von Oetinger am liebsten intensum genannt. . ., ein lebendiger, sich aus sich selbst entwickelnder, erfüllender, geistiger Organismus.

Aber diese Lebensbewegung lässt nun Oetinger sich nach aussen zur Leiblichkeit verdichten, in eine höhere Naturhaftigkeit ausbrechen, und vindicirt demnach Gott ein physisches Wesen, eine geistleibliche Natur, worin er erst seine volle Realität habe; denn־ zur konkreten Wirklichkeit gelangt das Geistige erst im Leiblichen (! ).

Und hiermit schliesst sich Oetinger rückwärts an Jac. Böhme an, dessen Grundgedanke von einer Natur in Gott auch dem System Fr. Bänder's und seiner Schüler zu Grunde liegt.

Aber auch die neueste Philosophie hat sich denselben vielfach angeeignet. Ich finde ihn bei Billroth, bei dem jüngeren Fichte, bei Hanne, am klarsten bei Schwarz: Das Wesen der Religion, Seite 185. Hier heisst es: ,Das weltsetzende Princip ist nicht reiner Geist, sondern die Einheit von Geist und Natur.‘ Diese Natur aber wird bestimmt als,die reale Seite des göttlichen Wesens, welche das ewige Substrat ist, aus dem die zeitliche Welt in der unendlichen Vielheit ihrer einzelnen Dinge hervorgeht‘, als,die ewige, vorund urbildliche Welt in Gott, d. h. als die Welt, wie sie noch zusammengehalten wird zur Einheit von dem durchdringenden Geiste Gottes‘.

Hier ist also der Gedanke ganz klar. Und man sieht zugleich den eigentlichen Grund desselben. Es ist die totale Abneigung gegen die Schriftlehre von einer Schöpfung aus Nichts. Weil diese nicht begriffen werden könne (was ganz wahr ist), muss die Welt aus dem Wesen Gottes hervorgehen; sie entsteht, indem Gott die Natur aus sich entlässt, indem sie durch seinen Willen in Raum und Zeit auseinandergeht, aber als solche von seinem Geiste auch immerfort durchdrungen und geeint wird.

S. 187. 193. Und eben hierin liegt für uns der Grund, warum wir diese Theorie entschieden abweisen müssen; sie macht die Schöpfung zu einer Emanation aus Gott, sie setzt die Substanz der Welt als wesentlich eins mit der Substanz Gottes, den Unterschied zwischen beiden blos in die Form der Existenz.“ (Christi Person und Werk. Agendi principium est ipsa Dei essentia, cui per creationem nulla accessit mutatio, quia nou novo voluntatis motu Deus in creatione aliquid voluit, quod prius ab aeterno voluit, sed in tempore id fecit, quod ab aeterno immutabili sua voluntate decreverat. 11. Infinitas essentiae a Deo competit, quatenus essentia Dei nullis terminis continetur. b Alias enim infinitas non est peculiare Dei attributum, sed ad attributa positiva varia se extendit, prout dicitur, scientiam, bonitatem, potentiam Dei esse infinitam etc.Gerhardus: ,,Infinitatis duae quasi species statuuntur: Aeternitas et immensitas.“

Probatur ex Ps. 145, 3.: Magnus est Dominus et laudandus valde, et magnitudinis ejus non est finis (vel pervestigatio). Intelligitur enim non magnitudo molis, seu quantitatis, quae in Deum non cadit, sed magnitudo essentiae.

Gerhardus: ״{Deus) est infinitus inferius, quia omnia sunt Deo minora et inferiora, adeoque infinito intervallo ab ipso distant. Est infinitus superius, quia a nullo suum esse accepit neque quicquam superius agnoscit. Est infinitus ante, quia non est a causa efflciente; ante eum non est formatum quicquam, Es. 43, 10. Est infinitus post, quia post eum non formabitur quicquam. Est infinitus extra, quia nihil extra ipsum est ipso superius. Est infinitus intra, quia est suum esse, a se et per se subsistens.“ (L. c. § 169.)

Idem: ,,Intelligitur 1. non infinitas corporeae quantitatis nec extensionis, sed essentiae et perfectionis; 2. non infinitas privativa, sed negativa. Nonflnitum privative est, quod nondum est assecutum ultimam suam perfectionem, sicut foetus in utero. Non-finitum negative est, quod ita caret termino et limitatione, ut finiri et limitari nec debeat nec possit. It&privative infinitum dicitur id, quod etsi finem actu jam non habet, habere tamen potest, ut quantitas; negative, quod simpliciter non habet finem. 3. Quamvis etymon infiniti tantum respiciat finem, intelligitur tamen, esse terminum a quo, ut infinitus sit ac dicatur Deus, quia nec principium nec finem habet. 4. Infinitum philosophis est triplex secundum substantiam, quantitatem, continuam scilicet et discretam, et secundum qualitatem. In rebus creatis non datur actu infinitum nec secundum substantiam, quia omnis creata substantia est composita, nec secundum quantitatem, nec secundum qualitatem, quia quantitas et qualitas infinita in substantia finita esse nequit. Deus solus infinitus est, non quidem secundum quantitatem vel qualitatem, sed substantiam.“ (L. c. § 162.) §

12. Immensitas Dei in eo consistit, quod essentia divina non potest ullis locorum terminis a mensurari aut includi.b Imo potius, exhibentibus rebus aliis, Deus secundum substantiam suam omnipraesens est, ita quidem, ut nullo loco circumscribatur, omnibus tamen creaturis, idque sine extensione sui, quoad substantiam suam, at nihilominus indistanter adsit, prout vulgo cum immensitate, tanquam attributo negativo, omnipraesentia instar attributi positivi conjungi solet.

Probatur autem immensitas (et omnipraesentia) Dei ex Jer. 23, 24. Nam qui coelum et terram implet, repletive est in coelo et in terra, quamvis non sit hic aut illic circumscriptive.

Unde Augustinus, phrasin propheticam interpretaturus, dicit, Deum implere coelum et terram praesente potentia, non absente natura, L. VIII. de Civ. Dei, c. XXX. p. 111. 694., eamque lectionem vindicat F. L. Coquaeus in Notis, qui et Hilarii locum citat ex L. V. de Trinit.: Nullus sine Deo locus est. Similiter: Quem coeli coelorum non capiunt juxta 1 Reg. 8, 27., is recte dicitur non posse mensurari ullis locorum terminis, cum coelum (supremum) ita describatur, ut ultra illud nihil creatum esse indicetur; simul autem recte dicitur, coelo pariter et his, quae coelo continentur, omnibus esse praesens, nullibi absens.


### Concerning God: PART I. CHAP. I. Gerhard

PART I. CHAP. I. Gerhard: "The immensity and essential omnipresence of God is to be understood thus: 1. That God is present to all things not only by virtue and efficacy, nor only by vision and knowledge, but also by His whole and undivided essence; for He is immense and infinite not only in power and knowledge, but also in essence. God is present here and everywhere powerfully... 2. That God is present everywhere not συνεκτικώς so that He might be comprehended, but συνεκτικώς, so that He might comprehend and contain all things; not περιεμφατικώς and περιγραπτώς, but περιεκτικώς. The Scholastics say that God is everywhere..., not definitively, in the way that intelligent forms—namely, angels and souls—are in a place or rather in a certain που, because they are essences defined by unity; but repletively, which, however, is not to be understood in a gross and corporeal manner, as if God fills all places like a body, which fills its place in such a way that it prevents another body from being located in the space it occupies, but in a divine manner, such that God, confined by no place, contains all places on account of the immensity of His essence. 3. That God is present everywhere not through the multiplication of His essence, for He is ὅλως ὅλον τι, a most simple being, and therefore, wherever He is, He is whole; nor through the division of His essence, because He is not half in half of the world, but whole everywhere; nor through extension and rarefaction, because He is not some corporeal mass, but an infinite essence, an incomprehensible virtue, and an ineffable efficacy; nor through commixtion, because He is a most simple and indivisible essence, entering into the composition of no thing. 4. That God is present everywhere by His essence not subjectively, as an accident inheres in a subject, because God is neither composite nor can He enter into composition, and just as time is excluded by the notion of eternity, so place is excluded as a subject occupying the notion of immensity; but effectively, as a principle and cause He is present to the thing which He effects; for God is not contained by place, but He Himself rather gives to place and to the things that are in place their being. His presence is α. illocal, β. impartible, γ. incomprehensible to our reason, δ. efficacious and active, ε. containing all things within Himself like a most minute point." (Exeg. 1. II. § 172.)

The same: "Is it rightly said that God exists really outside the world in imaginary space? ... Briefly, God, as He was before the world was created, so today He is outside the created world in Himself; He is to Himself both world and place and all things, as Tertullian says in *Adv. Praxeam* c. 5: 'Say, where was He then, when besides Him there was nothing: Then, where He is now, in Himself, since He suffices for Himself.' Dionys. Carthus." (L. c. § 186.)

Quenstedt: "When as yet nothing existed, there was no presence to the outside, and thus no omnipresence; yet the power of being present illocally to all things existed from eternity; thus immensity differs from omnipresence; ... the former is eternal, the latter by no means so, but began with the creatures. For when God willed that creatures should exist, He also willed to present them to Himself, not through some accession to the perfection of God, but through the calling forth of a thing not previously existing." (L. c. c. 8. s. 1. th. 18. sq. f. 414.)

Calov: "It is to be observed that these degrees succeed and follow one another in such a way that the later ones always presuppose and require the earlier ones before them, but not vice versa. Thus, the presence of grace presupposes divine omnipresence; the presence of glory includes in a certain way or requires the presence of grace; and finally, the presence of the hypostatic union assumes and requires in its own way the presence of glory, as well as the presence of grace, and indeed even universal presence or that of power, i.e., omnipresence." (System. Tom. II. p. 613.)

Luther: "The proud, arrogant spirit imagines that if he merely says, 'It does not rhyme,' or 'Such and such would follow from this,' then it must be so, and he does not need to prove it. Thirdly, he thereby brings his coarse, boorish thoughts to light, since he..."

One] thinks no differently of God’s essence in all places than as if God were a great, wide essence that fills the world and protrudes throughout. Just as when a straw sack is stuffed full of straw and yet protrudes above and below, exactly according to the first bodily, comprehensible manner. Then, indeed, Christ’s body would be a mere fiction and phantom, like a larger straw sack, in which God would be inside with heaven and earth; would that not be called speaking and thinking of God crudely enough?

But we do not speak thus, but say that God is not such an outstretched, long, broad, thick, high, deep essence, but a supernatural, unsearchable essence, which is at once in every single grain entirely and completely, and yet in all and above all and outside all creatures; therefore, no fencing in is needed here, as the spirit dreams. For a body is much, much too wide for the Godhead, and many thousands of Godheads could be inside. Conversely, also much too narrow, so that not one Godhead can be inside. Nothing is so small, God is still smaller; nothing is so great, God is still greater; nothing is so short, God is still shorter; nothing so long, God is still longer; nothing is so broad, God is still broader; nothing is so narrow, God is still narrower, and so on; it is an unspeakable essence above and outside everything that one can name or think.” (Confession Concerning Christ’s Supper. 1528. XX, 1202. sq. cf. That These Words of Christ, "This is My Body," Still Stand Firm. 1527. L. c. p. 1000—1009.) The same: “

Yet you do not treat this example rightly, and you condemn as useless the disputing before the multitude that God is in a cave or a sewer; for you think too humanly about God. I confess, indeed, that there are certain light-minded preachers who, with no religion or piety, but either out of a desire for glory, or a zeal for some novelty, or an impatience with silence, chatter and trifle most lightly: but these please neither God nor men, even if they assert that God is in the heaven of heavens.

But where there are grave and pious preachers who teach in modest, pure, and sound words, they say such things before the multitude without danger, nay, with great fruit. Must we not all teach that the Son of God was in the womb of the virgin and born from the belly? But how far does a human belly differ from any other unclean place? And who could not define it foully and basely? But we rightly condemn those [who do so], since pure words abound by which we state that necessity even with decorum and grace. Likewise, Christ’s own body was human, just as ours; what is fouler than that? Shall we therefore not say that God dwelt bodily in it, which Paul said? What is fouler than death? What is more horrible than hell? But the prophet boasts that God is with him in death and is present to him in hell. Therefore, a pious mind does not shudder to hear that God is in death or in hell, both of which are more horrible and fouler than a cave or a sewer. Indeed, since Scripture testifies that God is everywhere and fills all things, it not only says that He is in those places, but one will necessarily learn and know that He is there: unless, perhaps, if I were captured by a tyrant and thrown into a prison or a sewer, which happens to many saints, it would not be permitted for me to invoke God there, or to believe that He is present with me, until I come into some adorned temple. If you teach us to trifle so about God, and are offended by the places of His essence, you will finally not even permit Him to reside for us in heaven; for neither do the heavens of heavens contain Him, nor are they worthy.” (On the Bondage of the Will against Erasmus. 1525. See D. M. Luther’s Latin works of various subjects, ed. Schmidt. Frankfurt. Vol. VII. p. 141. sq. cf. Halle. Vol. XVIII, 2095. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Gerhard: “(They err in this place:) 4. The Calvinists, a. while some of them deny that God is present to all creatures by His essence. Crocius, P. II. of the Prussian conferences, p. 497. . . b. While they posit that the right hand of God, to which Christ was exalted in His exaltation, is a certain place in the heavens. . . c. They define the omnipresence of God by mere non-distance without operation.” (L. c. § 179.) PART I. CHAP. I.

That God is sometimes said to approach men and withdraw from them is not to be understood as if He begins or ceases to be circumscribed in some place according to His essence, but rather as an expression *anthropopathōs*; just as we said regarding immutability in § 10, note e.

For even though the Scriptures teach a certain special indwelling and nearness of God in the saints, while this presupposes the non-distant presence of God as to substance (or ἀδιάστασιν), it formally signifies a certain mode of modified presence, or such a presence by which God is said to be present where He manifests Himself to be present through certain operations—namely, that He presently confers and increases more excellent spiritual gifts upon the regenerate, or otherwise displays signs of His providence; when He is said to approach the impious, He declares His wrath, etc.

There is an advent of God to believers, by which the exhibition of grace and beneficence is noted, Exod. 20:24; John 14:23. There is also an advent of God to judge and punish, Isaiah 3:13, 14: these are the words of the blessed Glassius in *Philol. S. L. V. Tr. I. Cap. VII. p. 143. (1149.)*

Behold, the advent of God to believers in the nominative case is the very exhibition of grace and beneficence! An operation, I say, gracious and beneficent, and conversely, with respect to the impious, an operation of wrath and vindicatory justice.

However, that this implies, beyond the special gracious operation of God (who is already intimately present to all by virtue of His immensity) among believers, a special approximation of His very essence to the substance of believers, has not yet been shown clearly enough.

For the literal sense of the phrases of Scripture, e.g., "we will come to him," etc., cannot be pressed, since its rigid acceptance, as a word or phrase properly pertaining to local motion, does not apply to God; and, by virtue of the opposition between the "near" and the "remote," if the approximation is referred to the very essence or substance of God, it would necessarily signify some distance of the divine essence from the essence of man that had preceded (or that God was previously absent before He arrived) as the *terminus a quo*, and for that reason it would be necessary to deny the immensity of the divine essence.

Idem: ,,An recte dicatur Deus realiter existere extra mundum in spatio imaginario? . . .
