Tom. II. p. 613.)

Lutherus: ,,Der stolze hochmüthige Geist lässt sich dünken, wenn er blos daher sagt, es reimet sich nicht, solches und solches würde daraus folgen, so müsse es also sein und dürfe es nicht beweisen. Zum dritten gibt er damit seine groben Tölpelgedanken an Tag, da er

nicht anders von Gottes Wesen an allen Orten denket, denn als sei Gott ein grosses, weites Wesen, das dje Welt füllet und durchaus raget. Gleich als wenn ein Strohsack voll Stroh stecket und oben und unten dennoch ausraget, eben nach der ersten leiblichen begreiflichen Weise. Da würde freilich Christus Leib ein lauter Gedicht und Gespenst sein, als ein grösser Strohsack, da Gott mit Himmel und Erden innen wäre; hiesse das nicht grob genug von Gott geredt und gedacht?

Aber wir reden nicht also, sondern sagen, dass Gott nicht ein solch ausgereckt, lang, breit, dicke, hoch, tief Wesen sei, sondern ein übernatürlich, unerforschlich Wesen, das zugleich in einem jeglichen Körnlein ganz und gar, und dennoch in allen und über allen und ausser alien Creaturen sei; darum darfs keines Umzäunens hie, wie der Geist träumet. Denn ein Leib ist der Gottheit viel, viel zu weit und könnten viel tausend Gottheit drinnen sein. Wiederum auch viel zu enge, dass nicht eine Gottheit drinnen sein kann. Nichts ist so klein, Gott ist noch kleiner; nichts ist so gross, Gott ist noch grösser; nichts ist so kurz, Gott ist noch kürzer; nichts so lang, Gott ist noch länger; nichts ist so breit, Gott ist noch breiter; nichts ist so schmal, Gott ist noch schmäler, und so fort an, ists ein unaussprechlich Wesen über und ausser allem, das man nennen oder denken kann.“ (Bekenntniss vom Abendmahl. 1528. XX, 1202. sq. cf. Schrift, dass diese Worte: das ist mein Leib, noch feste stehen. 1527. L. c. p. 1000—1009.) Idem: ,,

Nec tarnen recte hoc exemplum tractas et, inutiliter disputari coram multitudine, damnas illud, Deum esse in antro vel cloaca; nimis enim humana cogitas de Deo. Fateor quidem, esse quosdam leves concionatores, qui nulla religione aut pietate, sed vel cupiditate gloriae, aut studio novitatis alicujus, aut impatientia silentii levissime garriunt ac nugantur: at ii non placent neque Deo, neque hominibus, etiamsi Deum asserant esse in coelo coelorum.

Verum ubi graves et pii concionatores sint, qui modestis, puris et sanis verbis docent, illi sine periculo, imo magno fructu, tale coram multitudine dicunt. Nonne oportet, nos omnes docere, Filium Dei fuisse in utero virginis et natum ex ventre? At quantum distat venter humanus ab alio quovis immundo loco? Et quis non foede ac turpiter posset illum definire? At illos merito damnamus, cum abundent verba pura, quibus eam necessitatem etiam cum decore et gratia dicimus. Item Christi ipsius corpus fuit humanum, sicut nostrum; quo quid foedius? Num ideo non dicemus, Deum habitasse corporaliter in eo, quod Paulus dixit? Quid foedius morte? Quid horribilius inferno? At propheta, Deum esse secum in morte et in inferno sibi adesse, gloriatur. Igitur pius animus non exhorret, audire, Deum esse in morte, vel in inferno, quorum utrumque horribilius ac foedius est, antro vel cloaca. Imo cum Scriptura testetur, Deum esse ubique et replere omnia, non solum dicit, eum esse in locis illis, verum necessario discet et noscet, eum ibi esse: nisi forte, si qua per tyrannum captus in carcerem aut in cloacam projicerer, quod multis sanctis contingit, non mihi licebit, Deum ibi invocare, vel credere, mihi adesse, donec venero in templum aliquod ornatum. Si ita nugandum de Deo nos docueris, et locis essentiae ejus offenderis, nec in coelo eum nobis residere tandem permittes; neque enim coeli coelorum eum capiunt, neque digni sunt.“ (De servo arb. c. Erasm. 1525. Vid. D. M. Lutheri opp. lat. varii arg. cur. Schmidt. Francof. Vol. VII. p. 141. sq. cf. Hal. Tom. XVIII, 2095. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Gerhardus: ״(Errant hoc loco:) 4. Calviniani, a. dum quidam ex ipsis negant, Deum sua essentia creaturis omnibus praesentem esse. Crocius, P. II. conv. Prutenicae, p. 497. . . b. Dum dextram Dei, ad quam Christus in sua exaltatione evectus est, statuunt, esse certum in coelis locum. . . c. Omnipraesentiam Dei definiunt per nudam indistantiam absque operatione.“ (L. c. § 179.) PART. I. CAP. I.

Quod autem aliquando Deus dicitur accedere ad homines et ab illis recedere, non intelligendum est, quasi secundum essentiam suam aliquo loco circumscribi incipiat aut desinat, sed tanquam per «·«״tyw־ TzoKathiav dictum; sicut de immutabilitate diximus ad § 10. not. e.

Nam et, quod Scripturae specialem quandam Dei in sanctis habitationem et propinquitatem tradunt, etsi praesentiam Dei indistantem quoad substantiam (sive άδιάστασιν) supponat, formaliter tamen significat certum aliquem modum praesentiae modificatae, seu talis, qua Deus praesens esse dicitur, ubi se praesentem esse per certas operationes manifestat, nempe quod hominibus renatis dona spiritualia praestantiora praesens confert atque auget, aut alias providentiae suae signa edit; impiis cum accedere dicitur, iram suam declarat etc.

Est adventus Dei ad credentes, quo gratiae et beneficentiae exhibitio notatur, Exod. 20, 24.. Joh. 14, 23. Est et adventus Dei ad judicandum et puniendum, Esaiae 3, 13. 14.: verba sunt b. Glassii in Philol. S. L. V. Tr. I. Cap. VII. p. 143. (1149.)

Ecce adventus Dei ad credentes in casu recto est ipsa exhibitio gratiae et beneficentiae! operatio, inquam, gratiosa et benefica, et ex adverso, respectu impiorum, operatio irae et justitiae vindicativae.

Quod autem, praeter specialem Dei (qui jam vi immensitatis suae omnibus intime praesens est) operationem gratiosam penes eredentes, etiam ipsius essentiae specialem approximationem ad substantiam credentium inferat, nondum hactenus satis clare ostensum est.

Neque enim litera phrasium Scripturae, v. g. veniemus ad eum, etc. urgeri potest, quippe cujus rigida acceptatio, tanquam verbi aut phraseos ad motum localem proprie pertinentis, in Deum non cadit, et, vi oppositionis, inter το propinquum et remotum, si ad ipsam Dei essentiam aut substantiam referatur approximatio, distantiam aliquam essentiae divinae ab essentia hominis, quae praecesserit (seu Deum prius abfuisse, antequam adveniret), tanquam terminum a quo significaverit, eaque ratione immensitatem essentiae divinae negare necesse fuerit.


### Concerning God: But if it be said that by denying a certain mode of presence, one does not…

But if it be said that by denying a certain mode of presence, one does not immediately deny all presence, much less presuppose a distance of substances; yet at the same time it must be said that the divine essence, apart from that new approximation of itself (or before that new advent), according to substance, in a certain way (though not simply, yet in a certain way, distinct from operation) was not present; and thus, of the divine and human substances, in a certain way distinct from operation, some distance will be given or presupposed.

When, however, we remember that the omnipresence of God according to substance is so founded upon the immensity of the divine essence that, once this is posited, and once the existence of things distinct from God, or created things, to which God is said to be present, is also posited, there cannot but be posited an omnipresence of such a kind that the whole divine essence i…s intimately—intimately, I say—present to all things: we shall surely acknowledge not only some presence, but a presence of such a kind that it does not admit of more or less; insofar as the presence is viewed apart from operation.

Although, therefore, the presence of God, insofar as it imports an efficacious operation of God outside Himself in creatures, receives degrees, and thus more and less; yet such is the nature of the divine essence or substance that, if you view the presence apart from operation (but not the peculiar operation itself), a new approximation of itself to the substance

of man (to whom God is present, and in whom or around whom He works) does not imply, but rather excludes it; since it is itself intimate, than which no more interior, tighter, or closer [presence] is given or can be given.

And this is what not a few of our own (especially Gerhard, *Disp. Isag. LL. Disp. IV. L. V. § ult. p. 106.*) say: that the omnipresence of God, considered relatively or in respect to creatures, is an efficacious eration conjoined with presence, which (operation) subsequently admits of different degrees, not the presence of substance to substance itself, which could be one or another, more or less close.

However, in the places of Scripture where the coming of God to men is indicated, they say it is an ἀνθρωποπάθεια, a species of metaphor, taken from man or human affairs to designate God or divine things through a certain similarity, which they also call συγκατάβαση, i.e., condescension, because in the sacrosanct discourse Jehovah as it were descends to us and expresses His heavenly mysteries in human words. See Glassius, *l. c. p. 98. 99. (1116.)*

But to sell this ἀνθρωποπάθεια and συγκατάβαση as a καταχρήσις (abuse), and by this name to render the doctrine and interpretation of the places of Scripture, founded in the very analogy of faith, suspect or hateful, is partly not permitted by the usage of speaking and the definitions in the schools of rhetoricians, and partly forbidden by the laws of truth and charity.

Certainly, the ancient teachers of our church described the different degrees of the presence of God not through different approximations of the divine essence to the essences of creatures, but through different operations of God, who is most present to all equally and always through the immensity of His essence.

You would seek in vain for that other opinion among the interpreters of the saying of Christ in John 14:23: "We will come to him (I and the Father to him who loves me) and make our abode there" (which others, however, think is the proper seat of this doctrine): Caspar Cruciger the Elder, Johann Brentius, L. Osiander, Aegidius Hunnius.

On the other hand, we know indeed that Nicolaus Selneccer, to the question: "Is the Holy Spirit given to those who already have the Holy Spirit?" answered: "He is given as to the increase of holy motions and gifts," *P. I. Exam. p. 212.* Regarding the approximation of essence, he is silent.

Similarly, Johann Wigandus, when he published his methodical consideration on the ubiquity or omnipresence of God, printed at Jena in the year 1591, proposing the doctrine concerning ubiquity in the church and concerning the indwelling in the regenerate, brings forward nothing concerning the approximation of the divine substance.

Aegidius Hunnius, however, in *QQ. et Resp. de S. Trinitate, T. I. Op. p. m. 121.*, expressly teaches and warns that it must be held that the presence of essence (by which the Holy Spirit is present even to the impious) is one thing, but His gracious indwelling is another; meanwhile, the latter undoubtedly presupposes the former.

Previously he had said that the Holy Spirit is said to be sent ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, just as God Himself is said to descend through ἀνθρωποπάθεια, namely, insofar as He who previously seemed to be absent because of the invisibility of His essence, now manifests His presence through some new work and renders it in a certain way visible. Cf. his *Comm. in Cap. VI. Joh. T. IV. Op. fol. 759.*

Similarly, Balduinus, about to declare the mystical union of God and holy men, *ad Cap. VI. prioris ad Cor. p. 17. P. H. Observ. 9. p. m. 358. a.*, maintains that it consists in the mutual adhesion of God and man.

And about to explain this further, he says: "God adheres to us through the communication of His grace, we adhere to Him through the trust of the heart, which apprehends the grace of God." Nothing about a tighter conjunction of substances. On the contrary, PART I. CHAPTER I.

When dealing with the loss of the Holy Spirit, which occurs through sins against conscience, in his *Comm. in Epist. ad Ephes.* cap. IV. P. II. Q. V. p. m. 922, he teaches nothing regarding the loss of a closer presence of the Holy Spirit in terms of substance; rather, he says: "The Holy Spirit is lost, not as if His substance departs from man (whether simply or in a certain respect), for He fills the whole world, Wis. 1:7; but because He takes away His grace, and deprives [the man] of His consolation and help." Blessed Gesner also, in *Disp. V. pro libro Conc.* Cap. VIII. § 11, distinguishes the presence of grace from the presence of universal conversation (which others call presence). He says His access occurs through the Word; regarding the duration, by which God makes μόνή in the faithful, he says it comes about that the children of God are led by the Spirit of God, and are temples of God, etc., p. m. 138. Thus, therefore, our blessed Gerhard also, in Volume I of his *Loci Theologici* (which he published in the year 1610), when about to explain the diverse degrees of divine presence, not only did not hand down a diversity of the approximation of the divine essence, but rather expressly taught that those diverse degrees differ only—NB—in their effects, or that the distinction of the manifold presence consists solely in the diversity of effects, § 219. Indeed, even after Gerhard had published his *Exegesis* fifteen years later, and in the meantime that opinion concerning the approximation of the divine essence to the substance of man had begun to please some and become known, he himself was found not to subscribe to it, but, having brought forward reasons on both sides, to suspend his judgment. In his *Harmonia Evangel.* P. III. Cap. CLXXVI. p. 598, regarding the words of John 14:23, he writes that the coming of the Father and the Son (to the faithful) occurs through the demonstration of peculiar effects, and that Christ speaks through a certain συγκατάβασιν. Regarding this matter, he brings forward the words of Augustine, Fulgentius, and Bernard. This was done in the year 1627. Indeed, even in his *Comment. ad Deuter.* (on which he died), on Chapter 4:7, he says: "By the drawing near of God is understood grace and favor, gracious presence, benevolent hearing, deliverance from dangers and adversities, etc.," p. 174, cf. p. 178, num. 5 and 6. And thus also his colleagues and successors, persisting in the simplicity of doctrine, abstained from embracing the other opinion. Cf. blessed Musaeus, *Ausführl.

Erklärung*, Qu. 74. p. 610 sqq. Quenstedtius: "Gracious divine presence, even if it presupposes a general divine nearness, by which God fills heaven and earth, nevertheless includes in itself also a special nearness of God, truly distinct from that general one, which brings about not only the operation of grace, but also a peculiar approximation of the divine essence to the substance of the faithful man. It is false, therefore, that the nearness according to substance is the same with respect to the pious and the impious, and that it differs only in this, that in the saints the nearness of God according to substance is joined with a gracious operation, but in the impious only with a general operation, consisting in the preservation of things in their being and the governing of them." (*L. C. P. III. c. 10. s. 2. f. 902.*)

Luther: "Let us also omit another question: what did God do before the beginning of the world? Did He rest, or not? To which Augustine reports in his Confessions that someone answered that God prepared hell for those who pry into curious things, namely, to elude, says Augustine, the violence of the question. Therefore, the modesty of Augustine pleases me, who surely candidly says that he draws in the sails of his genius in such questions, because even if we speculate and dispute to infinity, these things nevertheless remain incomprehensible. But if we do not understand clearly enough even those things which we see and do, how much less shall we attain these?"

For what will you determine to have been outside of time, and before time? Or what will you imagine God to have done before time existed? Wherefore let us cast these things aside, and let us hold that God, before the foundation of the world, was incomprehensible in His essential rest; but now, after creation, He is within, outside of, and above all creatures—that is, He is still incomprehensible. Nothing else can be said, because our intellect does not understand what is outside of time. Therefore, God also does not manifest Himself except in His works and in His Word, because these are in some way grasped; the rest, which are proper to the Godhead, cannot be grasped or understood, such as being outside of time before the world, etc. For this nature is so deformed by sin, nay, corrupted and lost, that it cannot know or comprehend God naked, as He is. Therefore, these wrappings are necessary. And it is madness to dispute much about God outside of and before time, because that is to wish to comprehend the naked Godhead, or the naked divine essence. Because this is impossible, God wraps Himself in works and certain forms, just as today He wraps Himself in Baptism, in absolution, etc. If you depart from these, then you go outside of measure, place, and time, and into the sheerest nothing, concerning which, according to the philosopher, there can be no knowledge.” (On Gen. 1:2. See Exegetical Latin Works, edited by Elsperger. Erlangen. Vol. I, pp. 15—17.) §

Quando autem meminimus, omnipraesentiam Dei secundum substantiam ita fundari in immensitate essentiae divinae, ut hac posita positaque simul existentia rerum a Deo distinctarum, seu creatarum, quibus Deus praesens dicatur, non possit non poni omnipraesentia ejusmodi, qua tota essentia divina rebus omnibus intime, intime inquam, praesens sit: profecto non solum aliquam adessentiam necessario agnoscemus, verum adesseutiam ejusmodi, quae non recipit magis et minus; quatenus ut adessentia, praecisa operatione, spectatur.

Quamvis ergo praesentia Dei, quatenus efficacem Dei operationem extra se in creaturis importat, recipiat gradus, adeoque magis et minus; tamen essentiae aut substantiae divinae ea est ratio, ut, si adessentiam, praecisa operatione (non autem ipsam peculiarem operationem) spectes, novam quandam sui approximationem ad substan
