Quenstedtius: ,,Praesentia divina gratiosa, etsi generalem propinquitatem divinam, qua Deus coelum et terram replet, praesupponat, tamen in se includit etiam specialem Dei propinquitatem, ab illa generali vere distinctam, quae infert non solum operationem gratiae, sed etiam peculiarem approximationem essentiae divinae ad substantiam hominis fidelis. Falsum ergo, propinquitatem secundum substantiam respectu piorum et impiorum eandem esse, in hoc autem tantum differre, quod in sanctis propinquitas Dei secundum substantiam cum operatione gratiosa, in impiis vero tantum cum operatione generali, consistente in conservatione rerum in suo esse et harum gubernatione, conjuncta sit.“ (L. C. P. III. c. 10. s. 2. f. 902.)

Lutherus: ,,Omittamus etiam aliam quaestionem, quid Deus ante principium mundi fecerit, quieveritne, an non? Ad quam sic respondisse quendam refert in confessione Augustinus, Deum praeparasse infernum curiosa scrutantibus, scilicet, ut eluderet, ait Augustinus, violentiam quaestionis. Placet ergo Augustini modestia, qui profecto candide dicit, se in hujusmodi quaestionibus contrahere sui ingenii vela, quia etiamsi in infinitum speculemur et disputemus, tamen manent haec incomprehensibilia. Quodsi etiam illa, quae videmus et gerimus, non satis plane intelligimus, quanto minus haec assequemur?

Quid enim extra tempus, et ante tempus fuisse statues? aut, quid Deum, antequam tempus esset, fecisse cogitabis? Quare abjiciamus ista, et sentiamus, Deum ante conditionem mundi fuisse incomprehensibilem in sua essentiali quiete; nunc autem post creationem esse intra, extra, et supra omnes creaturas, hoc est, etiam esse incomprehensibilem. Aliud dici non potest, quia noster intellectus, quid extra tempus sit, non intelligit. Ideo Deus quoque se non manifestat, nisi in operibus et verbo, quia haec aliquo modo capiuntur; reliqua, quae propria divinitatis sunt, capi aut intelligi non possunt, ut sunt, esse extra tempus ante mundum, etc. . . Haec enim natura sic est peccato deformata, imo corrupta et perdita, ut non possit Deum nudum cognoscere, seu comprehendere, qualis sit. Ideo involucra ista necessaria sunt. Et insania est disputare multa de Deo extra et ante tempus, quia id est velle comprehendere nudam divinitatem, seu nudam essentiam divinam. Hoc quia impossibile est, ideo involvit se Deus in opera, et certas species, sicut hodie se involvit in baptismum, in absolutionem etc. Ab his si discedas, tunc abis extra mensuram, locum, tempus, et in merissimum nihil, de quo secundum philosophum non potest esse scientia.“ (Ad Gen. 1, 2. Vid. Exeget. opp. lat. Cur. Elsperger. Erlangae. Tom. I. p. 15—17.) §


### Concerning God: The eternity of God, absolutely so called, signifies the permanent existence or…

13. The eternity of God, absolutely so called, signifies the permanent existence or duration of God, without beginning and end, and without any succession or vicissitude. For it is not taken here for long-lasting time, nor for a duration which acknowledges a beginning and only lacks an end, but in the strictest sense; which Boethius defined as the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of interminable life. For thus it imports the negation of limits, or an interminable life. By which reason it is called the possession of life "all at once," i.e., devoid of parts succeeding one another; so that "before" and "after," past and future, are excluded, and consequently a beginning, not only regarding existence simply, but also regarding motion and operation, so that it is rather a uniform duration.

The eternity of God is proved from Ps. 102:28, where, in opposition to heaven and earth—which exist for a long time indeed, but not without beginning or end of existence—God is said to persist as if devoid of all reclining, fall, or ruin; He is said to be the same (always), without any alteration or vicissitude.

Cf. Ps. 90:2, where God is said to be from everlasting to everlasting; so that no limit, neither beginning nor end, can be assigned to God. V. 4, that a thousand years are with the Lord as a day that has already passed, is to indicate that there are no intervals of time with God, before whom the times of all ages behave as a certain indivisible "now" (ἀδιαίρετον νῦν), as Aeg. Hunnius interprets (Vol. I, Works, fol. 85). Gen. 21:33 and Is. 40:28, where He is called אל עולם, God of the age; likewise 1 Tim. 1:17, where He is called Βασιλεὺς τῶν αἰώνων, King of the ages; namely, in all time. PART I. CHAP. I.

superior, coexisting with all centuries, yet not measurable by centuries or time. Finally, Rev. 1:4, 8; 11:17; 16:5: "Who is, who was, and who is to come." For although the duration of God seems to be described by these words through the differences of time, if you attend to it rightly, this is what is taught: that God exists in such a way that before He is conceived by us to exist, He already existed and can be conceived to have existed infinitely, and that He can also be conceived to exist afterwards or to be about to exist infinitely. ANTITHESIS.

Gerhard: "These things must be opposed... 5. To the Photinians, who themselves also undermine the eternity of God: a. by denying with Vorstius that this is a description of eternity properly and absolutely so called, because God is said to have been before the creation of the world..., with the end that the argument which is deduced for the true deity of Christ from Prov. 8 and parallel passages might be undermined; b. by establishing succession and differences of time in eternity." (Exeges. L. II, § 144.) § 14. The life of God, viewed in the first act, signifies the very essence or nature of God, insofar as it moves itself in a certain way, or can be conceived as the principle of vital or immanent operation; in the second act, it denotes the immanent operation itself, proceeding from the divine nature.

Gerhard: "The life of God is the act by which the divine essence demonstrates itself to be active; but the divine essence shows itself to be active in three ways, as the scholastics teach: by intellect, will, and the power of acting; therefore these three pertain to the life of God: intellect, will, and the power of acting." (L. c. § 160.) J. Ad. Osiander: "The knowledge of God... is not a habit added to the divine essence, like human wisdom, but is the very essence of God." (Colleg. theol. I, 290.)

God is called living, Gen. 16:14; Joshua 3:10; Ps. 42:3; 84:3; Is. 37:4; Acts 14:15. He is said to have life ἐν ἑαυτῷ, in Himself, John 5:26, and to swear by His life, Deut. 32:40; Ezek. 33:11. And men swear by the living God, 1 Kings 17:1. For otherwise life is taken in a double sense, insofar as it signifies in the first act the nature of any thing that moves itself in a certain way, but in the second act the motion or immanent operation itself, proceeding from such a nature, which is either material, namely vegetative or sensitive, or immaterial, such as rational or intellectual. In God, however, and on the part of the thing, life in the first act and in the second act are plainly the same, since the very being of God is His living. And this, since it must be the most perfect being, must necessarily be immaterial and therefore intellectual. Whence we must immediately proceed to treat of the intellect and will of God.

15. The knowledge of God consists in this, that God knows Himself and other things distinct from Himself, which are, and which can be, all according to their own being, which each has in itself outside of God, by one singular act, immediately through Himself, without an intelligible species or discourse; indeed, He exactly understands not only those things which truly exist or are about to exist, whether by necessity of nature or contingently through the free determination of the human will, but also those things which would be future if some condition were fulfilled, which nevertheless are not actually to be future because the condition is not fulfilled.

Or His intelligence, which, whether it be taken for the power of understanding or for the act or actual cognition, is really the same and most simply one with the divine essence, since no accident can fall into God, according to § 9 and note a. Whence the knowledge of God is distinguished into natural and free; namely, that the former belongs to God by nature and necessarily, insofar as God from eternity, and antecedently to every decree of the free will, knows both Himself as necessarily existing and all other possible things as such (for which latter reason it is also called the knowledge of simple intelligence); but the latter belongs to God consequently to the free decree concerning things to be produced at some time, and by this reason God from eternity knows all things as future after His free decree, and what each and all are to do with divine concurrence (for which reason it is called the knowledge of vision, because through it God knows things according to their own existence, as if beholding them face to face).

Gerhardus: "The knowledge of God is distinguished... into theoretical and practical. Theoretical is that by which God simply and absolutely knows all things. Practical is that by which God knows certain things in such a way that He also brings them about. It is otherwise called the knowledge of good pleasure and approbation. The former extends itself to all things, the latter only to good things. The former is distinct from the will, the latter is joined with the will. The former acts in itself, the latter acts in another. The former is not the cause of things, but the latter is the cause of things. An example of the former is proposed in a physician who foreknows that a patient will die on the morrow; of the latter, in a robber who foreknows that the one upon whom he lays violent hands will be killed on the following day." (L. c. § 244.)

J. Ad. Osiander: "The knowledge of God is called... one general, by which He knows all things and the causes of things, universals and particulars, good and evil; another special, by which He knows His elect." (L. c. p. 290.) Whence it is also called omniscience, and is proved from 1 Sam. 2:3, where God is called the Lord of knowledge, that is, possessing all knowledge. Similarly 1 John 3:20, where it is expressly said: God knows all things. Specifically, those passages are also to be observed in which God is said to know the secret PART I. CHAP. I.

the thoughts of all men, which no one else knows or can know: 1 Kings 8:39. Ps. 7:9; 34:15; 139:1 ff. Prov. 15:3. For He knows not only created things insofar as they have their being eminently in Him (God), but also in such a way that the intellect of God is terminated at their being, which they have in themselves.

For just as the power and act of understanding in God, on the part of the thing, do not differ from the essence of God, so the acts of understanding are not multiplied really according to the diversity or number of objects. For intelligible species, if they have any place, take the place of objects and are really distinct from the intellect and constitute with it one complete principle of intellection. In God, however, where there are no really produced acts of intellect, the divine intellect itself represents the object by way of an expressed species.

Indeed, although the term "science" otherwise implies the knowledge of a thing through its cause, and thus a progression from the cause, as something more known, to the effect, as something less known: yet because God, to whom nothing is unknown, does not progress from the known to the unknown, therefore knowledge through demonstration or discourse cannot be properly attributed to God. And indeed, those things are known immediately in themselves, as having a determined truth in themselves (since of contradictorily opposed things, e.g., "Adam will sin; Adam will not sin," one or the other must be true, the other false), and thus are truly knowable.

But that God knows future contingencies of such a kind, which by reason of their existence depend upon a free cause, or one indifferent to acting and not acting (namely, upon the choice of a created will), which is called by the peculiar name of the foreknowledge of God: this is proven partly by so many predictions of things future among men made divinely, and partly because God distinguishes Himself from false gods by this character, as it were. See Is. 41:22-23; 42:9; 43:12.

J. Ad. Osiander: "Foreknowledge is spoken of not with respect to God, but with respect to things. For just as 'after-knowledge' has no place in God, even though He knows past things: so, speaking accurately, foreknowledge cannot be attributed to God under the cognition of future things in time. For all things are present to God, not indeed actually, through existence, but objectively, from the perspicacity and breadth of the divine intellect." (L. c. p. 290.)

Gerhardus: "That foreknowledge is attributed to God, this is done with respect to us; for to Him all things are present which are still future to us, and with respect to the things which happen in time, since they have been known to God from eternity." (L. c. § 243.)

Lutherus: "Here in the world there is indeed a measure, that time goes one after another, the son after the father, and so on. To give an analogy: If a piece of wood lies far from you, or if you look at it lengthwise, you cannot see it all at once; but if it lies close before you, or you stand above it and can look at it crosswise, then you have it entirely in view. Thus we on earth cannot grasp this life; for it goes always from foot to foot, one after another, until the Last Day, but before God everything stands in a single moment. For before Him a thousand years are one day, Ps. 90; 2 Pet. 3. Thus the first man is just as near to Him as the one who is to be born last, and He sees it all at once: just as the human eye can bring together two things, which are even far from each other, in a single moment."

Latin:

13. Aeternitas Dei, absolute sic dicta, a significat existentiam seu durationem Dei permanentem, sine principio et fine b omnique successione c aut vicissitudine. d Non enim h. 1. accipitur pro tempore diuturno, non pro duratione, quae initium agnoscit ac tantum fine caret, sed sensu strictissimo; quam Boethius definivit, quod sit interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio. Sic enim importat negationein terminorum seu vitam interminabilem. Qua ratione dicitur possessio vitae tota simul, i. e. expers partium sibi invicem succedentium; ita ut excludatur prius et posterius, praeteritum et futurum, adeoque initium, non solum quoad esse simpliciter, verum etiam quoad motum et operationem, ut sit potius duratio uniformis.

Probatur aeternitas Dei ex Ps. 102, 28., ubi in oppositione ad coelum et terram, diu quidem, sed non sine initio aut fine existentiae, Deus dicitur perstare, tanquam omnis reclinationis, casus aut ruinae expers; dicitur idem ipse (semper) esse, sine ulla alteratione vel vicissitudine.

Conf. Ps. 90, 2., ubi dicitur Deus esse a saeculo et usque in saeculum; ita ut terminus nullus, nec principium neque finis, assignari Deo possit v. 4., quod mille anni sint apud Dominum uti dies jam praeterlapsa, ad indicandum, quod nulla sint apud Deum 'intervalla temporum, coram quo omnium saeculorum tempora velut unum quoddam άδιαίps■τυν νυν se habent, uti Aeg. Hunnius interpretatur T. I. Op. fol. 85., Gen. 21, 33. et Es. 40, 28., ubi אל עולם, Deus saeculi, item 1 Tim. 1, 17., ubi Βααι).ευ·ζ των αιώνων, Rex saeculorum dicitur; nempe omni tempore PART. I. CAP. I.

superior, omnibus quidem saeculis coexistens, non tamen saeculis aut tempore mensurabilis. Denique Apoc. 1, 4. et 8. c. 11, 17. 16, 5.: Qui esi, qui erat, qui futurus est. Quamvis enim his verbis duratio Dei describi videatur per differentias temporis; si tamen recte attendas, boc est, quod docetur, Deum ita existere, ut ante, quam a nobis concipitur existere, jam extiterit et possit concipi extitisse in infinitum, quodque possit etiam concipi postea existere aut extiturus in infinitum. ANTITHESIS.

Gerhardus: ״Opponenda haec sunt ... 5. Photinianis, qui et ipsi aeternitatem Dei labefactant: a. negando cum Vorstio, esse descriptionem aeternitatis proprie ac absolute sic dictae, quod Deus dicatur fuisse ante mundum conditura. . ., fine eo, ut argumentum, quod pro vera Christi deitate ex Prov. 8. et locis parallelis deducitur, labefactetur; b. temporis successionem et differentias in aeternitate statuendo.“ (Exeges. 1. II. § 144.) § 14. Vita a Dei, in actu primo spectata, b significat ipsam Dei essentiam seu naturam, quatenus se ipsam certo modo movet, aut concipi potest, ut principium operationis vitalis seu immanentis; in actu secundo denotat ipsam operationem immanentem, c procedentem a natura divina.

Gerhardus: ,, Vita Dei est actus, quo essentia divina se actuosam esse demonstrat; tribus autem modis, ut scholastici docent, essentia divina se actuosam esse ostendit: intellectu, voluntate et potentia agendi; haec ergo tria ad vitam Dei pertinent: intellectus, voluntas et agendi potentia.“ (L. c. § 160.) J. Ad. Osxander: ״Scientia Dei. . . non est habitus, essentiae divinae superadditus, sicut humana sapientia, sed est ipsa Dei essentia.“ (Colleg. theol. I, 290.)

Dicitur Deus vivus, Gen. 16, 14.. Josuae 3, 10. Ps. 42, 3. 84, 3. Es. 37, 4. Act. 14, 15. Dicitur vitam habere b ίαυτώ, in se ipso, Joh. 5, 26., jurare per vitam suam, Deut. 32, 40. Ezech. 33, 11. Atque homines jurant per Deum vivum, 1 Reg. 17, 1. Nam et alias vita duplici sensu accipitur, quatenus in actu primo quidem significat naturam cujusque rei, quae seipsam quodammodo movet, in actu secundo autem ipsam motionem seu operationem immanentem, a tali natura procedentem, quae vel est materialis, nempe vegetativa aut sensitiva, vel immaterialis, rationalis puta seu intellectualis. In Deo autem et ex parte rei plane idem sunt vita in actu primo et in actu secundo, cum ipsum esse Dei sit vivere ipsius. Atque hanc quidem, cum perfectissimum esse oporteat, immaterialem atque adeo intellectualem esse necesse est. Unde statim de intellectu et voluntate Dei agendum venit.

15. Scientia a Dei in eo consistit, quod Deus se et res alias a se distinctas, quae sunt, quaeque esse,possunt, b omnes c secundum esse suum proprium, d quod singulae in se ipsis extra Deum habent, uno singulari actu,e per se immediate, citra speciem intelligibilem f aut discursum, g cognoscit; imo non solum ea, quae revera existunt aut extitura sunt, sive ex necessitate naturae, sive contingenter, per liberam voluntatis humanae h determinationem, verum etiam ea, quae futura essent, si conditio aliqua impleretur, quae tamen actu futura non sunt, quia conditio non impletur, i exacte intelligit.

Seu intelligentia ejus, quae, sive pro potentia intelligendi, sive pro aetu aut actuali cognitione accipiatur, cum essentia divina realiter idem et simplicissime unum est, cum in Deum non cadat accidens, juxta § 9. et notam a. Unde distinguitur scientia Dei in naturalem et liberam; scilicet, quod illa quidem Deo per naturam et necessario conveniat, quatenus Deus ab aeterno, et antecedenter ad omne decretum liberae voluntatis cognoscit cum seipsum necessario existentem, tum res alias omnes possibiles, ut tales (qua posteriore ratione etiam vocatur scientia simplicis intelligentiae); haec autem Deo conveniat, consequenter ad liberum decretum de rebus aliquando producendis, atque hac ratione Deus ab aeterno cognoscat omnes res, velut post liberum decretum suum futuras, quidque singulae atque omnes cum concursu divino sint acturae (qua ratione scientia visionis appellatur, quod per eam Deus res cognoscat secundum propriam suam existentiam, velut coram intuendo).

Gerhardus: ,,Distinguitur Dei scientia ... in theoreticam et practicam. Theoretica est, qua Deus simpliciter et absolute omnia cognoscit. Practica est, qua Deus quaedam ea ratione scit, ut etiam eadem operetur. Vocatur alias scientia beneplaciti et approbationis. Prior extendit se ad omnia, posterior tantum ad bona. Prior distincta est a voluntate, posterior cum voluntate juncta est. Prior agit in se ipsa, posterior agit in alio. Prior non est causa rerum, posterior vero est causa rerum. Prioris exemplum proponitur in medico, qui praescit, aegrum crastino die moriturum; posterior in latrone, qui praescit, altero die occisum iri eum, cui ipse violentas manus infert.“ (L. c. § 244.)

J. Ad. Osiander: ,,Scientia Dei dicitur. . . alia generalis, qua novit res omnes et rerum causas, universalia et particularia, bona et mala; alia specialis, qua novit electos suos.“ (L. c. p. 290.) Unde et omniscientia dicitur, et probatur ex 1 Sam. 2, 3., ubi Deus scientiarum Dominus dicitur, id est, omnem scientiam possidens. Similiter 1 Joh. 3, 20., ubi expresse dicitur: Deus novit omnia. Speciatim etiam observanda sunt loca, quibus Deus dicitur nosse arcanas PART. I. CAP. I.

quorumvis hominum cogitationes, quas nemo alius norit aut nosse possit: 1 Reg. 8, 39. Ps. 7, 10. 34, 15. 139, 1. sqq. Proverb. 15, 3. Non enim solum res creatas cognoscit, quatenus in ipso (Deo) suum esse eminenter habent, verum etiam ita, ut intellectus Dei ad illarum esse, quod in se ipsis habent, terminetur.

Nam quemadmodum potentia et actus intelligendi in Deo, ex parte rei, ab essentia Dei non differunt, ita non multiplicantur realiter actus intelligendi quoad diversitatem aut numerum objectorutn. Species intelligibiles enim, sicubi locum habent, objectorum vicem gerunt suntque ab intellectu realiter distinctae et unuln cum eo principium intellectionis completum constituunt. In Deo autem, ubi non sunt actus intellectus realiter producti, ipse intellectus divinus per modum speciei expressae repraesentat objectum.

Nempe quamvis alias vox scientiae importet cognitionem rei per causam, adeoque progressum a cama, tanquam notiore, ad effectum, tanquam ignotius: quia tamen Deus, cui nihil ignotum est, non progreditur a cognito ad ignotum, ideo neque cognitio per demonstrationem aut discursum Deo proprie tribui potest. Et cognoscuntur quidem ea immediate in seipsis, tanquam in se determinatam veritatem habentia (quippe quod contradictorie oppositorum v. g. Adam peccabit; Adam non peccabit; alterutrum oportet esse verum, alterum falsum), adeoque vere cognoscibilia.

Quod autem Deus futura contingentia ejusmodi, quae ratione existentiae suae a causa libera, seu indifferente ad agendum et non agendum (videlicet ab arbitrio voluntatis creatae), pendent, cognoscat, quae praescientia Dei peculiari nomine vocatur: probant partim tot praedictiones rerum inter homines futurarum divinitus factae, partim quod Deus hoc velut charactere a diis falsis se distinguit. Vid. Es. 41, 22. 23. 42, 9. 43, 12.

J. Ad. Osiander: ״Praescientia dicitur non respectu Dei, sed respectu rerum. Ut enim in Deo non habet locum postscientia, etsi noverit praeterita: ita, accurate loquendo, sub futurorum in tempore cognitione Deo tribui non potest praescientia. Omnia enim Deo sunt praesentia, non quidem actualiter, per existentiam, verum objective, ex perspicacia et latitudine intellectus divini.“ (L. c. p. 290.)

Gerhardus: ,,Quod praescientia Deo tribuitur, id flt respectu nostri; ipsi enim omnia sunt praesentia, quae nobis adhuc futura, et respectu rerum, quae in tempore fiunt, cum ab aeterno Deo sint nota.“ (L. c. § 243.)

Lutherus: ,,Hie auf der Welt hat es wohl eine Maass, dass die Zeit nach einander geht, der Sohn nach dem Vater, und also fort. Als, dass wir ein Gleichniss geben: Wenn ein Holz fern von dir liegt, oder dass du es nach der Länge ansiehst, so kannst du es nicht übersehen; wenn es aber nahe für dir liegt, oder du oben darauf stehest, und kannst es nach der Quer ansehen, so hast du es gar im Gesiebte. Also können wir auf Erden dies Leben nicht begreifen; denn es gehet immer von Fuss zu Fuss nach einander, bis an den jüngsten Tag, aber für Gott stehet alles in einem Augenblick. Denn für ihm sind tausend Jahr Ein Tag, Ps. 90. 2 Pet, 3. Also ist ihm der erste Mensch ebenso nahe, als der am letzten geboren soll werden, und siehet es alles zugleich an: wie des Menschen Auge zwei Dinge, die auch fern von einander sind, in einem Augenblick kann zusammenbringen.“


### Concerning God: Gerhard: "In order to explain in some way how the certainty and immutability of…

Gerhard: "In order to explain in some way how the certainty and immutability of divine foreknowledge does not abolish the contingency of things and the freedom of the human will, a distinction must be made between the necessity of the consequent (which others call absolute, antecedent, or simple), which arises from the necessary connection of a cause with its effect and the intrinsic connection of terms; and the necessity of the consequence (which they call hypothetical, subsequent, concomitant, conditional, or by supposition), which arises from the act of existence from the very positing of the effect, because everything that is, by the very fact that it is, is necessarily. In respect to divine foreknowledge, those things which come to pass from causes acting contingently and freely are necessary by this latter species of necessity, and this necessity does not abolish freedom, but rather presupposes it." (L. c. § 255.)

Luther: "I would certainly wish that another, better term were used in this discussion than this common one, 'Necessity,' which is not correctly applied to either the divine or the human will. For it is of too unpleasant and incongruous a meaning for this context, suggesting to the intellect a kind of coercion, as it were, and altogether that which is contrary to the will, whereas the matter at hand does not intend this. For the will, whether divine or human, does what it does by no coercion, but by mere pleasure or desire, as if truly free, whether it be good or evil: yet the will of God is immutable and infallible, which governs our mutable will, as Boethius sings: 'Remaining stable, You cause all things to move'; and our will, especially the evil one, cannot by itself make itself good. Therefore, what the word does not provide, let the intellect of the reader supply, understanding the necessity as that which you would wish to say: the immutable will of God and the impotence of our evil will; as some have said, the necessity of immutability, though this is neither grammatically nor theologically sufficient." (De servo arbitrio. See Opp. lat. var. argum. Cur. Schmidt. Frankfurt, 1873. Vol. VII. p. 134. sq.)

Hence, it is called knowledge of the future conditional, specifically such where the condition has a connection with the effect or the future thing, but only a contingent one. It is otherwise called middle knowledge, namely because its object lies between things viewed precisely under the aspect of possibility and things that are absolutely future. That knowledge of future conditionals belongs to God is proven from Matthew 11:21, where Christ, the God-man, testifies that He knows that the citizens of the cities of Tyre and Sidon would have done penance in sackcloth and ashes, given a certain condition, that is, if such miracles as occurred in their time in the cities of Chorazin and Bethsaida had been performed before them; yet, that condition not being fulfilled, they were not in fact converted. Add 1 Samuel 23:11 sqq. Compare also the special Academic Dissertation on the knowledge of God by the blessed Frid. Bechmann.

ANTITHESIS. Gerhard: "The following undermine divine omniscience... 4. The Photinians, while they deny that God foreknows the future sins of men... Socinus in prael. theol. c. 8—11: 'No reason, no testimony of Scripture can be brought forward from which it is openly gathered that God knew the evils, which depend upon the wills of men, before they happened.'" (L. c. § 250.)

Calvin: "Nor does He foresee what is to come by any other reason than because He has decreed that it should come to pass." (Institut. III, c. 23. s. 6.) PART I. CHAPTER I.

§ 16.

The wisdom of God denotes God’s most exquisite counsel, by which He knows how to dispose and order all causes and effects in a plainly admirable manner toward their end. For although it seems to be comprehended under the knowledge of God, yet because it is commonly—and by Scripture itself, which accommodates itself to the grasp of the common people—distinguished and usually treated separately, it had to be indicated separately here as well. Quenstedtius: "The wisdom of God is distinguished from the knowledge of God in Rom. 11:33, where mention is made of the depth of the riches of σοφίας καί γνώσεως θεοῦ. The former is an absolute attribute of God, the latter a relative one; the former is conceived by us by way of a habit, the latter by way of an act." (L. c. c. 8. s. 1. th. 26. 417.) It is proved from Job ch. 12:13, where it is said that with God is wisdom, and that counsel and understanding are His; and ch. 28:20 sqq., where, when the praise of full wisdom is taken away from all others, it is taught that it must be asserted of God alone. Compare 1 Tim. 1:17, where God is called μόνος σοφός, the only wise; and Rom. 11:33, where the stupendous and unsearchable wisdom of God is celebrated. § 17.

Before we proceed to the consideration of the other attributes, something must be said about the will of God, or insofar as the divine essence conducts itself by way of an appetitive power, tending toward the good known by the intellect as something to be willed, and toward the evil known as something to be averted. For the attributes of holiness, justice, and veracity pertain to the divine will. Gerhardus: "Will signifies: 1. τὸ θελητικόν, the faculty or power of the soul itself by which we will; 2. τὴν θέλησιν, the act of willing, which the scholastics call volition, and the philosophers νοερὰν ὄρεξιν; 3. τὸ θελητόν, the object or thing which we will." (L. th. de nat. D. § 163.)

Or, as the principle of the act of willing an appetible object and of not willing or averting a disagreeable or evil object: although the essence of God and His will, and His act, do not differ from one another in reality from the divine intellect, but are really one and the same. Gerhardus: "When will is attributed to God, it is not understood as a certain faculty of willing really distinct from the essence of God itself, which exerts itself through an act of willing—which they call volition—likewise distinct from the essence; but the will of God is the essence of God itself, or God willing."

18. There are no causes of the acts of the divine will that are formally causing, yet there are causes that are virtually causing: the efficient, the internal and external impulsive, and likewise the final. For otherwise it would be necessary to posit within God something really produced and really distinct from the divine essence, since a formally causing cause and the caused differ as one thing and another; on the other hand, it implies a contradiction if we posit that the divine essence is independent, and yet that something, which in reality is the same as the divine essence, is dependent, as if truly and really produced by another.

Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Tract. de Aeterno Elect. Decr.*, ch. I, § 4 ff., p. 2 ff.

J. Scharffius: "These terms, 'formally' and 'materially,' are used and abused in various ways. 'Formally' is taken: 1. For the whole quiddity of a thing, so that it is the same as 'quidditatively.' Thus it is said: man is formally a rational animal. 2. For the ultimate difference of a thing. Thus unity formally signifies indivision. Thus genus pertains to the material; the specific difference alone, so to speak, completes the formal reason. 3. For 'actually' or for that which is present in act. Thus 'formally' is contradistinguished from 'virtually.' Thus I say: The sun is not formally hot, but virtually. 4. For an internal principle of acting. Thus man is formally animated, formally understands." (*Metaphysica*, 5th ed., Witteb. 1649, p. 18.)

Reuschius: "Causes that are formally causing are properly called causes which differ from the caused not only really, but also essentially, so that the cause and the caused are diverse beings or, as the blessed author says, one thing and another. But outside of God nothing can exist that produces an effect in God, because God is independent and, as pure act, cannot receive or suffer the actions of other beings. Likewise, no act of God can produce another act in God as a diverse being, or so that those acts differ as one thing and another; because God is so most simple that He cannot consist of multiple beings. Wherefore, neither outside of God nor within God can there be a cause properly so called of any perfection found in God or of a divine act. But in a point of reason, one perfection of God must often be conceived before another perfection can be conceived in God; e.g., before I can conceive that God is eternal, it must be presupposed in a point of reason that He is a being from Himself and exists necessarily. Since, therefore, the cognition which, from the nature of the object, must be presupposed if I wish to conceive another cognition, is called the *a priori* reason of this cognition, such an *a priori* reason is called a virtually causing cause; there are *a priori* reasons or virtually causing causes for very many divine perfections or acts." (*Annot.*, p. 175 f.)

Or *a priori* reasons of being, which in our mode of conceiving behave like causes, so that if that of which they are called the cause were caused, they would exist in reality and truly in that genus of cause. See Musaeus, *loc. cit.* Thus God Himself is the efficient cause of the acts of His will. Namely, some are said to proceed from the divine goodness, others from the divine justice, which moved God. Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. II. PART I. CHAP. I.

Thus the act of the will, by which God decrees to confer salvation upon certain men, acknowledges as its external impulsive cause the merit of Christ, to be apprehended by final faith, and thus foreseen, as we shall see below in the Book on Predestination. Thus God, in willing and doing what He does, is said to will and do it for the sake of His own glory as the final cause. § 19.

The will of God is distinguished into natural and free. By the former, God is said to will that which He cannot not will. By the latter, He is said to will that which He could also not will, or the opposite of which He could will. In the former respect, He is said to will Himself; in the latter respect, He is said to will created things. According to the diverse relation to diverse objects. As that in which every reason for goodness appears without defect, so that it is the primary object of the divine will, which imports a necessary relation to the will of God. Gerhard: "God wills Himself as the end, creatures as the means." (Exeg. L. II. § 279.)

Which, just as they are contingent and possess only finite goodness, so they do not import a necessary relation to the divine will; to which refers what is said in Ps. 115:3, that God does what He wills, and therefore freely wills and does according to His free will what He does. Thomas: "God does not necessarily will whatever He wills; but, granted that He wills something, it is necessary, because the will of God is immutable." (L. I. c. gent. c. 83.) § 20. The free will of God is distinguished 1. into efficacious and inefficacious. It is called efficacious by which God wills something as to be effected, and inefficacious by which something pleases God in itself, although He does not intend to effect it. The efficacious will is further divided into absolute, by which God wills something without condition, and conditional, by which He wills something under a condition. 2. Into absolute, by which He wills something to be effected by His absolute power, or power not bound to secondary causes; and ordained, by which He wills something to be effected by His ordained power, or power bound to secondary causes and a certain order of means instituted by Himself. 3. Into antecedent, by which He wills something from Himself alone, or precisely from His native inclination, not yet having taken into account

Latin:

Gerhardus: ,,Ut quodammodo explicetur, qua ratione certitudo et immutabilitas divinae praescientiae non tollat rerum contingentiam et libertatis humanae voluntatem, distinguendum est inter necessitatem consequentis (quam alias vocant absolutam, praecedentem, simplicem), quae oritur ex necessaria causae cum effectu ac intrinseca terminorum connexione; et inter necessitatem consequentiae (quam vocant hypotheticam, sequentem, comitantem, conditionalem, ex suppositione), quae oritur ex actu existentiae ab ipsa positione effectus, quia omne, quod est, eo ipso, quod est, necesse est esse. Hac posteriori necessitatis specie respectu divinae praescientiae necessaria sunt, quae ex causis contingenter et libere agentibus fiunt, atque haec necessitas non tollit libertatem, sed potius praesupponit.“ (L. c. § 255.)

Lutherus: ,,Optarim sane aliud melius vocabulum dari in hac disputatione, quam hoc usitatum, Necessitas, quod non recte dicitur, neque de divina, neque humana voluntate. Est enim nimis ingratae et incongruae significationis pro hoc loco, quandam velut coactionem, et omnino id, quod contrarium est voluntati, ingerens intellectui, cum tamen non hoc velit causa ista quae agitur. Voluntas enim sive divina sive humana nulla coactione, sed mera lubentia vel cupiditate quasi vere libera facit quod facit, sive bonum sive malum: sed tamen immutabilis et infallibilis est voluntas Dei, quae nostram voluntatem mutabilem gubernat, ut canit Boethius: Stabilisque manens das cuncta moveri; et nostra voluntas, praesertim mala, se ipsa non potest facere bonum. Igitur quod non praestat vox, impleat intellectus legentis necessitatem, inteliigens id quod dicere velles, immutabilem voluntatem Dei et impotentiam nostrae voluntatis malae, ut aliqui dixerunt necessitatem immutabilitatis, nec hoc satis grammatice nec theologice.“ (De servo arbitrio. Vid. Opp. lat. var. argum. Cur. Schmidt. Francof. 1873. Vol. VII. p. 134. sq.)

Unde dicitur scientia de futuro conditionato, tali quidem, ubi conditio cum effectu seu re futura connexionem habet, sed non nisi contingentem. Alias appellatur scientia media, nempe quod objectum ejus inter res sub ratione possibilitatis praecise spectatas, et res absolute futuras interjacet. Probatur autem, Deo competere scientiam futurorum conditionatorum ex Matth. 11, 21., ubi testatur Christus ^άνθρωπος, scire se, quod cives urbium Tyri et Sidonis in sacco et cinere acturi fuissent poenitentiam, posita certa conditione, seu si coram ipsis miracula talia, qualia suo tehipore in urbibus Chorazin et Bethsaida contigerunt, edita fuissent, qui tamen, non impleta conditione ista, revera conversi non fuerunt. Adde 1 Sam. 23, 11. sqq. Confer etiam de scientia Dei Dissertationem Acad. pecul. b. Frid. Bechmanni.

ANTITHESIS. Gerhardus: ,,Omniscientiara divinam labefactant ... 4. Photiniani, dum negant, Deum praescire futura hominum peccata... Socinus in praei, theoi. c. 8—11.: ,Nulla ratio, nullum Scripturae testimonium proferri potest, ex quo aperte colligitur, Deum mala, ex voluntatibus hominum dependentia, scivisse, antequam fierent.‘“ (L. c. § 250.)

Calvinus: ״Nec alia ratione, quae futura sunt, praevidet, nisi quia, ut flerent, decreverit.“ (Institut. III, c. 23. s. 6.) PAßT. I. CAP. I.

§ 16.

Sapientia a Dei importat exquisitissimum Dei consilium, quo causas et effectus omnes modo plane admirabili disponere et ordinare novit ad suum finem.b Quamvis enim sub scientia Dei comprehendi videatur; quia tamen vulgo, et ab ipsa Scriptura, ad captum vulgi se accommodante, distingui et peculiariter tradi solet, ideo et hic seorsim indicanda fuit.Quenstedtius: ״Sapientia a scientia Dei distinguitur Rom. 11, 33., ubi profunditatis divitiarum aal σοφίας καί γνόσεος θεον fit mentio. Illa est attributum Dei absolutum, haec relativum; illa concipitur a nobis per modum habitus, haec per modum actus.u (L. c. c. 8. s. 1. th. 26.

417.) Probatur ex Hiobi cap. 12, 13., ubi dicitur, penes Deum, esse sapientiam·, illius esse consilium et intelligentiam; et c. 28, 20. sqq., ubi, cum plenae sapientiae laus omnibus aliis adimitur, soli Deo eam asserendam esse docetur. Confer 1 Tim. 1, 17., ubi Deus μόνος σ<><ρυς, solus sapiens dicitur; et Rom. 11, 38., ubi stupenda et impervestigabilis sapientia Dei celebratur.§ 17. Antequam ad caeterorum attributorum considerationem progrediamur, dicendum est aliquid de voluntate Dei, a seu, quatenus essentia divina habet se per modum b potentiae appetitivae, tendentis in bonum ab intellectu cognitum, ut volendum, et ad malum cognitum, ut aversandum.

Pertinent enim attributa sanctitatis, justitiae et veracitatis ad voluntatem divinam.Gerhardus: ,, Voluntas significat: 1. το ϋελητικον, ipsam facultatem seu vim animae, qua volumus; 2. την ΰελησιν, actum volendi, quem barbari vocant volitionem, philosophi νοεράν ορεξιν; 3. το ΰελητδν, objectum sive rem, quam volumus.“ (L. th. de nat. D. § 163.) Seu, ut principium actus volendi objectum appetibile et nolendi aut aversandi objectum disconveniens aut malum: quamvis essentia Dei et voluntas, ejusque actus, inter se ab intellectu divino quoad rem non differant, sed realiter unum sint atque idem.Gerhardus: ,,Quando Deo tribuitur voluntas, non intelligitur facultas quaedam volendi ab ipsa Dei essentia realiter distincta, quae per actum volendi, quem volitionem vocant, itidem distinctum ab essentia sese exserat; sed voluntas Dei est ipsa Dei essentia vel Deus volens.“

18. Actuum voluntatis divinae non dantur causae formaliter a causantes, dantur tamen virtualiter b causantes: efficiens,c impulsiva interna d et externa, e itemque finalis.f Nam alias necesse foret statuere intra Deum aliquid realiter productum et ab essentia divina realiter diversum, cum causa formaliter causans et causatum differant, ut aliud atque aliud; ex adverso autem contradictionem implicet, si statuamus, essentiam divinam esse independentem, et tamen aliquid, quod quoad rem idem est cum essentia divina, esse dependens, tanquam vere et realiter productum ab alio.

Confer b. Musaei Tract. de Aeterno Elect. Decr. cap. I. § 4. sqq. p. 2. sqq.

J. Scharffius: ״Hisce terminis: formaliter et materialiter, varie utuntur et abutuntur. Formaliter sumitur 1. pro quidditate rei tota, ut sit idem, quod quidditative. Sic dicitur: homo est formaliter animal rationale. 2. Pro ultima rei differentia. Sic unitas formaliter dicit indivisionem. Sic genus pertinet ad materiale; sola differentia specifica, ut ita loquar, complÄt formalem rationem. 3. Pro actualiter seu pro eo, quod actu inest. Sic formaliter conträdistinguitur 7־ώ virtualiter. Ita dico: Sol non est formaliter calidus, sed virtualiter. 4. Pro principio agendi interno. Sic homo formaliter est animatus, formaliter intelligit.“ (Metaphysica. Ed. 5. Witteb. 1649. p. 18.)

Reuschius: ״Causae formaliter causantes sunt proprie dictae causae, quae adeo a causato non tantum realiter, sed etiam essentialiter differunt, ut causa et causatum sint diversa entia seu, ut b. auctor loquitur, aliud atque aliud. Sed extra Deum nihil existere potest, quod effectum in Deo producat, quia Deus est independens et tanquam purus putus actus aliorum entium actiones recipere seu pati non potest. Item nullus Dei actus potest producere alium in Deo actum tanquam ens diversum, seu ut differant illi actus tanquam aliud atque aliud; quia Deus ita est simplicissimus, ut pluribus entibus constare nequeat. Quapropter neque extra Deum, neque intra Deum esse potest causa proprie dicta alicujus perfectionis in Deo obviae seu actus divini. Sed in puncto rationis saepe una Dei perfectio ante est concipienda, quam altera perfectio in Deo concipi possit; e. g. antequam concipere queam, quod Deus sit aeternus, praestruendum est in puncto rationis, quod sit ens a se atque existat necessario. Quoniam igitur cognitio, quae ex natura objecti est praestruenda, si alteram cognitionem concipere velim, hujus cognitionis vocatur ratio a priori, atque talis ratio a priori appelletur causa virtualiter causans; perfectionum seu actuum divinorum quam plurimorum dantur rationes a priori seu causae virtualiter causantes.“ (Annot. p. 175. sq.)

Seu rationes essendi a priori, quae nostro concipiendi modo instar causarum se habent, ita ut, si illud, cujus causa dicitur, causaretur, reipsa et vere in illo genere causae ejus existerent. Vid. Mus. 1. c. Sic Deus ipse est causa efficiens actuum voluntatis suae. Nempe alii a divina bonitate, alii aj justitia divina, quae Deum moverit, proficisci dicuntur.3 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. II. PART. I. CAP. I.

Sic actus voluntatis, quo Deus decernit certis hominibus conferre salutem, agnoscit causam impulsivam externam meritum Christi, fide finali apprehendendum, atque ita praevisum, ut infra L. de Praedest. videbimus. Ita Deus, quae volens facit, gloriae suae tanquam finis causa velle et facere dicitur.§ 19.

Voluntas Dei distinguitur a in naturalem et liberam. Illa dicitur Deus velle, quod non potest non velle. Hac velle dicitur, quod etiam posset non velle, aut velle oppositum. Priore ratione seipsum,b posteriore ratione res creatas c velle dicitur. Pro diversa habitudine ad diversa objecta. Tanquam in quo omnis ratio boni sine defectu apparet, ita ut sit objectum voluntatis divinae primarium, quod ad voluntatem Dei necessariam habitudinem importat.Gerhardus: ,,Deus vult seipsum ut finem, creaturas ut media.“ (Exeg. L. II. § 279.)

Quae, sicut contingentes sunt ac bonitatem non nisi finitam habent, ita non necessariam habitudinem important ad voluntatem divinam; quo refertur, quod Ps. 115, 3. dicitur, Deum facere, quae vult, adeoque libere velle et pro libera voluntate facere, quae facit.Thomas: ״Deus non necessario vult, quicquid vult; posito autem, quod aliquid velit, est necessarium, quia voluntas Dei est immutabilis.“ (L. I. c. gent. c. 83.) § 20. Voluntas Dei libera distinguitur 1. in efficacem et inefficacem. Efficax dicitur, qua Deus aliquid vult tanquam efficiendum, a inefficax, qua Deo aliquid placet secundum se, licet non intendat illud efficere.b Efficax voluntas porro dividitur in absolutam, qua Deus aliquid vult sine conditione, c et conditionatam, qua vult aliquid sub conditione.d 2. In absolutam, qua vult aliquid potentia sua absoluta, seu ad causas secundas non alligata, efficiendum; e et ordinatam, qua vult aliquid, sua ordinata, seu ad causas secundas ac certum ordinem mediorum a se institutum alligata, potentia efficiendum. f 3. In primam, seu antecedentem, qua vult aliquid ex se solo, seu ex nativa sua inclinatione praecise, necdum habita


### Concerning God: by reason of the circumstances

by reason of the circumstances; and the second, or consequent [will], by which He wills something, having considered the circumstances, or in view of some cause or condition looked at on the part of the creature to whom He wills something. Thus the will, not only human but also divine, by which Christ the θεάνθρωπος willed to give Himself (according to His human nature, indeed) unto death, or to lay down His life, and to offer Himself as a victim for sinners, John 10:18, Heb. 7:27, was certainly efficacious, because Christ intended to effect this very thing. And some indeed define an efficacious will as that which is truly fulfilled, in such a way, namely, that not only is something intended to be effected, but it is also reached or obtained by effecting it; which indeed also has a place in the example cited.

According to the thesis, however, an efficacious will is called that by which something is intended to be effected, whether the effect follows or the intended end is obtained, or not; by which reasoning God, although He intends the salvation of all men with an efficacious will, nevertheless does not obtain it in the case of all. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. de Volunt. Dei Antec. et Conseq.*, which is annexed to the treatise *de Usu Princip. Eat.*, § 14, p. 697.

Thus Christ the θεάνθρωπος willed the preservation of human life and the turning aside of imminent death, Luke 22:42, inasmuch as that pleased Him in itself, yet so that it did not change His will to die for men.

Others call an inefficacious will that which is not fulfilled, although something is intended to be effected; which opinion we leave to its authors. Augustine: "The will of God is always fulfilled, either from us or by us." (Enchir. c. 100.)

An absolute will, as is evident from the thesis, is spoken of in various ways; but its certain meaning must be sought from that in respect to which it is called absolute. Whence, in this place, it is spoken of in respect to some condition, and in opposition to a conditional will. And in this sense God is rightly said to have willed from eternity absolutely to create the world: for He willed it without condition. He is also rightly said to will absolutely that those whom He foresaw as finally believing should be saved. For He wills this also without condition, since the foreseen final faith has the nature of a fulfilled condition, not a pending one. The will by which God wills all men to be saved, namely, if they believe, pertains here; likewise the will by which God willed many good things for the Israelites, namely, under the condition of sincere and constant obedience, Deut. 28. And that this will is not fulfilled (since God foreknew that the condition could not be fulfilled, and would not be fulfilled) is not absurd. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. cit. de Volunt. Antec. et Conseq.* § 31, p. 710.

It is called absolute from law, order, or the course of nature, or of secondary causes. Thus God willed the sun to stand still, Josh. 10:13; compare *Disp. cit.* § 28, 29, p. 708.

By which reasoning God wills to save the elect, namely, through the means of grace. Whence it is simultaneously evident that a conditional will and an ordered will do not entirely coincide, although at first glance it might seem so. But otherwise PART I. CHAPTER I.

It is certain that it is not absurd that the ordained will of God can be resisted. See the blessed Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, § 30 sqq., p. 708 sqq., § 42, p. 719. Thus, Chrysostom in Chapter I of Ephesians, homily I, and Damascenus in Book II of *De Fide Orthodoxa*, Chapter XXVI, called the will of God, by which He wills the salvation of all, προηγουμένως, although that is not understood in the same way by everyone. See Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, § 2, 3, p. 689, 690, § 10 sqq., p. 695 sqq. And some explain this precisely as that which takes its origin from our vice, or by which God wills, on account of sin, for example, to punish, to condemn, etc.; others take it more broadly as that which has its cause or occasion in us, whether from sin or elsewhere. And our theologians, in this way, refer to the consequent will not only that which pertains to the damnation of unbelievers, but also that which pertains to the salvation of those who finally believe, as such, or terminated by foreseen final faith in Christ. See Musaeus, *Disp. cit.*, § 2, 3, and 10 sqq. Manifestly, however, both of these wills of God, antecedent and consequent, are taught in Matthew 23:37, where Christ, the θεάνθρωπος, testifies that His will was first, or antecedently, terminated toward the salvation of the Jewish people, and that as if from a native and paternal inclination or affection; but then, or consequently, having first taken into account the incorrigibility of their impiety, it is terminated toward the excision and destruction of the Jews.

Dannhauer: "There is altogether in the matter of our salvation a twofold will of God, one antecedent, the other consequent; twofold, I say, not in reality and essence, but in the order of our reason, which conceives one act before another. This distinction was born: 1. From the wonderful temperament of divine justice and mercy reconciling themselves. For there exist in the Scriptures statements that show mercy prone to save all; there exist others that note justice excluding from the inheritance those who resist the divine order. A work of reconciliation, therefore, lest the Holy Spirit contradict Himself. Insinuated 2. by the parables of Christ, Matthew 22:1, 23:37, Luke 14:16; cf. Matthew 5:45 with Amos 4:7. In the former, God is said to rain upon the just and the unjust; in the latter, to rain upon one city and not upon another—namely, that the city which served God was rained upon, while that which had offered itself to idols remained unwatered and withered." (*Hodos. phaen.* 7, p. 274.)

The same: "Caspar Sanctius on Ezekiel 18, p. 419, not ineptly notes these things: 'The Lord denies that it is of His will to deliver the sinner to death, and yet He delivers him to death and condemns him to capital, nay, even to hellish punishment. Therefore, I said above that God is drawn, as if unwilling and by a resisting nature, to the punishment of men, however wicked, to whom it is proper always to show mercy and to spare, who is carried by that proneness and impetus with which rivers flow down a sloping channel. Theologians here recognize two wills in God; they call one antecedent, which most indicates the goodness of the divine nature, which wills all men to be saved, and does not think of the evil of anyone unless something happens from man that calls forth and solicits another, severe will, which will is called consequent, which is evidently not so much arisen from God according to the benignity of His nature, as stimulated on account of the sins of men, which He wills to heal, albeit with a more severe medicine, or to punish with a vindictive scourge. Antecedent, therefore, is born from the mercy and goodness of God; consequent, in a certain way, from the vice of men. This is easily understood by examples. A merchant does not will, by an antecedent will, to throw away goods which he loves dearly and sought with the greatest labor, nor does a judge will to drive to the cross him whom he destines for capital punishment, or a physician to burn and cut him whom he loves.'"

brother. Yet by a consequent will, the merchant, compelled by a storm, casts his wares into the sea, because otherwise he would perish entirely, though he would wish them to be safe if he could; and the judge, because both right reason and the merits of the condemned demand it, sentences him to punishment, from which, however, he would prefer to withhold both the avenging rod and the public power, if these things were absent; nor would a physician, by his antecedent will, cut or cauterize a patient, unless either the reason of medicine or the necessity of the patient demanded it by a consequent will. Thus, therefore, the death of the wicked is not of the will of God, namely, the antecedent will, for He does not delight in the destruction of the living, Wisd. 1:13; yet He punishes and condemns by a consequent will, because right and public reason demand it, lest sins remain unpunished.” (L. c. p. 274. sq. note.)

ANTITHESIS. Gerhard: “The following undermine orthodoxy here: . . . 2. The Calvinists, who oppose the freedom of acting, or the free will of God, to the remaining divine attributes; that is, because of the freedom of acting, they attribute to God such things as conflict with His own goodness, justice, and wisdom. Thus they say that God impels to sin, that God has made an absolute decree of reprobation, etc.; and if we say that this conflicts with the justice and holiness of God, they take refuge in the claim that God is a most free agent, subject to no laws. But God acts freely in such a way that He nevertheless does not act against His natural justice and goodness.” (Exeg. 1. II. § 278.) §

21. In a peculiar sense, a decree is called absolute in God, to exclude the consideration of an impulsive cause outside of God, to which is opposed the non-absolute, for which there is given an external impulsive cause outside of God, and one that is virtually causative. Indeed, the word "will" extends more broadly than "decree." And we are said to "will" whatever is desirable in itself, even if, when all circumstances are considered, we do not will them. But we are said to "decree" properly only those things which, all circumstances considered, we effectively will. Whence also the antecedent will (of which in the preceding §) cannot, strictly speaking, be called a decree. Compare the blessed Aegidius Hunnius toward the end of the Admonition to the Reader prefixed to the Treatise on Providence and Predestination.

Dannhauer: “A divine decree is either absolute or hypothetical. Absolute is, for example, the decree to create in this order, in this series of days, with this goal; no human condition intervenes here. The proclamation of the Gospel by the apostles was of an absolute decree, for ακατάλυτος γάρ ή βουλή αντη (i.e., His counsel is indissoluble), Acts 5:39; the reprobation of Satan to Tartarus—whence that theological proverb: ‘If Satan were to repent, he would be saved,’ is a hypothesis from an impossible condition, equivalent to a simple negative; in almost the same way is to be understood that apostolic statement in Gal. 1:8: ‘If an angel from heaven, etc.’ By an absolute decree I was born, to these parents, in this region, at this time. It was the absolute will of the Lord that John should die a natural death, John 21:22. Such divine counsel reigns in divine matters and miracles, the exhibition of which (now) depends on the nod of God alone; by this absolute nod the woman with the issue of blood recovered at this time, namely, only after medicine was finally despaired of, not before.

Latin:

ratione circumstantiarum; g et secundam, seu consequentem, qua aliquid vult, consideratis circumstantiis, seu intuitu alicujus causae aut conditionis, ex parte creaturae, cui aliquid vult, spectatae.h Sic voluntas, non solum humana, verum etiam divina, qua Christus ΰεάνΰρωπος voluit dare se (secundum humanam quidem naturam) in mortem, aut ponere animam suam, et se offerre victimam pro peccatoribus, Joh. 10, 18. Ebr. 7, 27., efficax utique fuit, quia hoc ipsum efficere intendit Christus. Et alii quidem voluntatem efficacem definiunt, quod sit ea, quae revera impletur, ita scilicet, ut non solum intendatur aliquid efficiendum, verum etiam efficiendo attingatur aut obtineatur; quod quidem in allato exemplo etiam locum habet.

Juxta thesin autem efficax voluntas dicitur, qua aliquid intenditur efficiendum, sive sequatur effectus vel finis intentus obtineatur, sive non; qua ratione Deus, cum omnium hominum salutem efficace voluntate intendat, non tamen penes omnes obtinet. Confer b. Mus. Disp. de Volunt. Dei Antec. et Conseq., quae annexa est tractatui de Usu Princip. Eat., § 14. p. 697.

Sic Christus θεάνθρωπος voluit conservationem vitae humanae et declinationem mortis imminentis, Luc. 22, 42., quippe quod ea secundum se placeret, ut tamen non mutaret voluntatem moriendi pro hominibus.

Alii inefficacem voluntatem dicunt, quae non impletur, licet aliquid intendatur efficiendum.; quam sententiam suis auctoribus relinquimus.Augustinus: ,,Voluntas Dei semper impletur, aut de nobis, aut a nobis.“ (Enchir. c. 100.)

Voluntas absoluta, ut ex thesi patet, variis modis dicitur; certa autem significatio petenda est ex eo, cujus respectu absoluta dicitur. Unde h. 1. in respectu ad conditionem aliquam, et in oppositione ad conditionatam voluntatem dicitur. Atque hoc sensu Deus recte dicitur ab aeterno absolute voluisse creare mundum: voluit enim sine conditione. Recte etiam dicitur, velle absolute, ut illi, quos finaliter credentes praevidit, salventur. Vult enim et hoc sine conditione, cum fides finalis praevisa habeat rationem conditionis impletae, non pendentis. Pertinet huc voluntas, qua Deus omnes homines vult salvam, nempe si crediderint; item qua Deus plurima bona voluit Israelitis, nempe sub conditione sincerae et constantis obedientiae, Deut. 28. Atque hanc voluntatem non impleri (cum Deus praesciverit, conditionem posse non impleri, ac non iri impletum), non est absurdum. Conf. b. Mus. Disp. cit. de Volunt. Antec. et Conseq. § 31. p. 710.

Dicitur absoluta a lege, ordine aut cursu naturae, seu causarum secundarum. Sic voluit Deus stare solem, Jos. 10, 13., conf. Disp. cit. § 28. 29. p. 708.

Qua ratione Deus vult homines electos salvare, nempe per media gratiae. Unde simul patet, voluntatem conditionatam et ordinatam non omnino coincidere, licet primo intuitu ita videri possit. Alias autem PAßT. I. CAP. I.

certum est, non esse absurdum, posse voluntati Dei ordinatae resisti. Vid. b. Mus. 1. c. § 30. sqq. p. 708. sqq., § 42. p. 719. Sic Chrysostomus in Cap. I. ad Eph. homil. I. et Damascenus lib. II. de orthod. Fide Cap. XXVI. voluntatem Dei, qua vult omnium salutem, dixerunt πρώτψ η προψουμένψ, quamvis illud non ab omnibus eodem modo intelligatur. Vid. Mus. 1. c. § 2. 3. p. 689. 690., § 10. sqq. p. 695. sqq. Et hanc quidem aliqui exponunt praecise de ea, quae ex nostro vitio ortum ducit, seu qua vult Deus propter peccatum v. g. punire, damnare etc.; alii latius accipiunt de ea, quaecunque in nobis sive a, peccato, sive aliunde causam vel occasionem habet. Et nostrates hac ratione ad voluntatem consequentem referunt non solum eam, quae ad incredulorum damnationem, verum et hanc, quae ad salutem finaliter credentium, ut talium, seu praevisa fide finali in Christum terminatur. Vid. Mus. Disp. cit. § 2. 3. et 10. sqq. Manifeste autem utraque haec voluntas Dei, antecedens et consequens, traditur Matth. 23, 37., ubi Christus ΰεάνΐίρωπος testatur, voluntatem suam primum sive anteceden· ter terminatam fuisse ad salutem populi Judaici, idque velut ex nativa ac paterna inclinatione aut affectu; deinde vero, seu consequenter, habita prius ratione incorrigibilis eorum impietatis, terminari ad excisionem et interitum Judaeorum.

Dannhauerus: ,,Est omnino in salutis nostrae negotio gemina Dei voluntas, antecedanea alia, alia consequens; gemina, inquam, non re ac essentia, sed nostrae rationis ordine, unum actum prae altero concipientis. Nata est haec distinctio: 1. E mirabili justitiae et misericordiae divinae inter se conciliandae temperamento. Extant enim in Scripturis effata, quae misericordiam ostendunt in omnes salvandos pronam; extant alia, quae justitiam notant excludentem ab haereditate eos, qui ordini divino refragantur. Opus igitur conciliatura, ne Spiritus S. sibimet contradixerit. Insinuata 2. parabolis Christi Matth. 22, 1. 23, 37. Luc. 14, 16. cf. Matth. 5, 45. cum Amos.4, 7., illic Deus dicitur pluere super justos et injustos, hic pluere super unam civitatem et nou super alteram; complutam sci. esse urbem, quae Deo serviret, incomplutam squaluisse ac horruisse, quae idolis se praebuisset.“ (Hodos. phaen. 7. p. 274.)

Idem: ,,Caspar Sanctius ad Ez. 18. p. 419. non inepte haec monet: ,Voluntatis suae esse negat Dominus morti tradere peccatorem, et tamen tradit morti et capitali, imo gehennali supplicio condemnat. Ideo supra dicebam, Deum quasi invitum et renitente natura ad hominum quantumvis sceleratorum supplicium pertrahi, cui proprium est, misereri semper et parcere, qui ea fertur pronitate atque impetu, quo per declivem alveum flumina decurrunt. Duas hic theologi in Deo voluntates agnoscunt; alteram antecedentem vocant, quae maxime indicat divinae naturae bonitatem, quae vult omnes homines salvos fleri, neque de malo cujusquam cogitat, nisi aliquid accidat ab homine, quod severam aliam voluntatem advocet ac sollicitet, quae voluntas vocatur consequens, quae videlicet non tam orta a Deo est secundum suae naturae benignitatem, quam ob hominum peccata instimulata, quod sanare vult, licet severiori medicina, aut punire vindice flagello. Antecedens itaque ex Dei misericordia nascitur et bonitate, consequens quodammodo ex hominum vitio. Hoc facile inductis intelligitur exemplis. Non vult antecedente voluntate mercator projicere merces, quas amat valde et maximo labore quaesivit, neque judex in crucem agere illum, quem supplicio destinat capitali, aut medicus urere et secare, quem amat,

fratrem. Voluntate tamen consequente jactat mercator, tempestate cogente, merces in mare, quia aliter omnino pereundum esset, quas tamen, si posset, salvas esse vellet; et judex, quia id exigit et publica ratio et damnati merita, illum supplicio destinat, a quo tamen mallet, si haec absint, et ultricem virgam et publicam potestatem cohibere; neque medicus priori voluntate secaret aut ureret aegrotum, nisi id exigeret a consequente voluntate aut medicinae ratio aut aegroti necessitas. Sic ergo non est voluntatis Dei, nempe antecedentis, mors impii, non enim laetatur in perditione vivorum, Sap. 1, 13.; punit tamen et damnat consequente voluntate, quia id exigit recta ratio atque publica, ne peccata maneant impunita.“‘ (L. c. p. 274. sq. not..)

ANTITHESIS. Gerhardus: ,,Orthodoxiam labefactant h. 1. . . 2. Calviniani, qui libertatem agendi sive liberam Dei voluntatem reliquis attributis divinis opponunt, id est, propter libertatem agendi Deo talia tribuunt, quae cum ipsius bonitate, justitia et sapientia pugnant. Sic dicunt, Deum impellere ad peccatum, Deum fecisse absolutum reprobationis decretum etc.; quodsi cum Dei justitia et sanctitate hoc pugnare dicimus, eo confugiunt, quod Deus sit agens liberrimum, nullis legibus obnoxium. Atqui Deus eo modo libere agit, ut tamen non agat contra naturalem suam justitiam et bonitatem.“ (Exeg. 1. II. § 278.) §

Peculiari sensu decretum a Dei absolutum dicitur, ad excludendum respectum causae impulsivae extra Deum,b cui opponitur non absolutum, cujus datur causa impulsiva externa extra Deum, eaque virtualiter causans. c Nempe voluntatis vox latius patet, quam decreti. Aeg. Hunnium sub finem Admon. ad Lectorem praemissae Tract. de Prov. et Praedest.

Absoluti decreti fuit praeconium evangelii per apostolos, ακατάλυτος γάρ ή βουλή αντη (i. e. insolubile consilium ejus), Act. 5, 39.; reprobatio satanae ad tartarum, unde proverbium illud theologicum: ,Si satanas resipisceret, salvaretur‘, est hypothesis ex conditione impossibili, aequipollens negativae simpliciter; eodem ferme modointelligendum illud apostolicum Gal. 1, 8.: ,Si angelus e coelo etc.‘ Absoluto decreto sum natus ego, bis parentibus, in hac regione, hoc tempore. ### Concerning God: Hypothetical is that which is sanctioned by a hypothesis, explained by the…

Hypothetical is that which is sanctioned by a hypothesis, explained by the words ‘if’ or ‘unless’: Num. 14:12; 1 Sam. 13:13; 2 Sam. 2:16; 1 Sam. 2:30; Jer. 18:8; Acts 27:31; Luke 13:3. Thus, it was of a hypothesis that the Son of God was incar- PART I. CHAP. I.

if man were to fall; but after the incarnation of the Son was decreed, the execution of the incarnation was of an absolute decree. Therefore, those Judaizers had no reason to despair regarding this, thinking that the Messiah was promised to the Jews on the condition that if the Abrahamites were righteous and good, he would come, but if not, he would not; they are refuted in Ps. 89:34, where the witness in heaven (who keeps faith even now in this latest age, which had been sanctioned by the antediluvian covenant) v. 38, and the oath v. 36, exclude every suspicion of a condition, Heb. 6:17.

Likewise, in the passion of Christ, the το άδικεισ&αι belongs to the absolute, ineluctable, and immovable decree, Acts 4:28; but that this passion was inflicted by Herod, Pilate, and Judas pertains to the hypothetical decree: If Herod, Pilate, and Judas shall crucify Christ, I decree to permit it. Let the confatalia be excluded here, for the hand of Herod, Pilate, and Judas was not necessary for the passion; the heavenly Father could have crucified, slaughtered, and sacrificed the Son immediately, just as Abraham did Isaac.

Thus: if Paul remains constant in the faith, he is elect; if not, he is reprobate. The difference must be held here between the decree of God and the νεμετικόν judgment: every avenging κρίσις is decreed, but not every decree is a νεμετικόν judgment; the former can be absolute, antecedent, predetermining, and absolutely inevitable; the latter is hypothetical, consequent, and avoidable or mitigable.

And hence, if anything is absolutely decreed, it is also absolutely immutable, irresistible, and invincible. "For who will resist his will?" Rom. 9:19. If it is hypothetical, it is mutable through the apocope of the condition, taken separately. A composite decree, whole and taken together with the supplement of the hypothesis, certainly cannot be changed. It can be changed through the apocope of the hypothesis, e.g., "Nineveh will perish," this is mutable; "it will perish, unless it repents," this is immutable. (Hodos. phaen. 3. P. p. 158. sq.)

Not only formally causing (for thus every decree of God would be absolute), but also virtually causing. See § 18. note a. For this reason our theologians say that the decree of predestination and reprobation is not absolute; for they acknowledge an external impulsive cause or reason: the former, indeed, the merit of Christ apprehended by final faith; the latter, however, final unbelief: concerning which we shall see more in its proper place. §

22. There also occurs a distinction of the divine will into the will of sign and of good pleasure. The former is so called when the name of will is attributed to the effect or object of the divine will, namely, as a sign of some will in God. The latter denotes the very act of the divine will, by which He wills something. Whence it is clear that the distinction is analogical.

One must take care, however, not to imagine such a will of sign to which the will of good pleasure, which the sign ought to signify by institution, is repugnant.

Not only in Lombard I. Sent. distinct. XL a. cap. III. sqq. and dist. XLVII. c. II. and Thomas in I. Q. XIX. art. XII., but also in our theologians, the blessed Balth. Meisner in Anthrop. Disp. XII. Q. I. th. 1. and the blessed Gerhard in Exeg. L. de Deo § 269. and others. To which Matt. 6:10 refers: Thy will be done! i.e., let the things and acts, to which your will is directed by commanding, come to pass as things to be effected.

And 1 Cor. 12:50, where those are said to do the will of the Father who perform the works which God wills to be done. Furthermore, 1 Thess. 4:3, where it is said that this is the will of God—i.e., that it is a precept and therefore a sign of the divine will—which prescribes our sanctification, that we should abstain from fornication, etc. Although at the same time, the object of the divine will or precept, or the thing willed and commanded, seems to be taken for the precept itself. Authors, however, refer other things here besides the precept, for example, counsel, prohibition, operation, and permission.

Indeed, the inequality of the members of this distinction is such that one claims the name of will for itself properly, and the other improperly, according to a figure (as they say). For example, if, with the Reformed who desert the footsteps of the Scholastics, you say that God wills the salvation of all by the will of sign, but does not will this very thing by the will of good pleasure; or that He commands man to convert, yet does not seriously will that he be converted. For these things are repugnant to the divine wisdom, goodness, and equity, and they destroy the certainty of Scripture. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Tract. de Aet. El. Dec.* c. XI. § 336. sqq. p. 253. sqq. Gerhardus: "The will is one thing of sign, another of good pleasure. Both the Scholastics and the Calvinists use this distinction, but in a different sense. The Scholastics define the will of sign as an effect of God, when He Himself goes forth outwardly, dealing with us through some covering or through external things which we can apprehend, such as the Word and the Sacraments instituted by Him. They call the will of good pleasure the essential will of God or the naked divine majesty, which is God Himself... They count five such signs: precept, prohibition, permission, counsel, operation; whence the little verse: *

Praecipit ac prohibet, permittit, consulit, implet.* (He commands and forbids, permits, counsels, fulfills.) In this sense of the Scholastics, Luther, Vol. 6 Witeb. p. 98, in his commentary on Gen. 6, repeats and approves that distinction: 'We (he says) in the N.T. have baptism, the Lord's Supper, absolution, and the ministry of the Word; these are, as the Scholastics called them, the will of sign, into which we must look when we wish to know the will of God; the other is the will of good pleasure, the substantial will of God or His naked majesty, which is God; from this, eyes are to be removed.' The Calvinists abuse that distinction while they posit that the will of sign and of good pleasure behave in a contrary manner toward one and the same object, whence they assert that the will of sign is repugnant to the will of good pleasure." (L. c. l. II. § 268.)

Quenstedtius: "Although the will of God is one and most simple, it is nevertheless distinguished in various ways... 3. Into hidden and revealed; the former is secret and unsearchable; the latter is made manifest in the Word of God and is infallible; the former is concerned with the various judgments of God, which St. Paul calls κρίματα ἀνεξερεύνητα, i.e., unsearchable judgments, because no creature can attain the reason for them by searching and investigating, Rom. 11:33. The latter is occupied with the business of our salvation. However, the revealed will of God is not to be opposed to the hidden will, as the Calvinists do, since God cannot be contrary to Himself." (L. c. c. 8. s. 1. th. 27. f. 418.) § 28. Among the attributes of the will of God, justice occurs first, by which God is partly just in Himself, which we call holiness by a peculiar name, and it implies rectitude. PART I. CHAP. I.

of the divine will, by which He wills all things that are right and good in conformity with His eternal law; partly in relation to others, so that He prescribes suitable laws to creatures and directs and governs them, and also keeps and fulfills the promises made to men, and finally rewards the good and punishes the evil.

Thus Lev. 19:2: "Be holy," says God, "for I am holy." Cf. 1 Pet. 1:15, 16, 17. See Deut. 32:4: "All His ways are judgment (are just). God is truth and not iniquity, just and upright is He." And Ps. 92:16: "The Lord is upright, and there is no iniquity in Him." Now this justice of God has a certain analogy to the universal justice which philosophers speak of (by which one lives in conformity with all laws, whence it is called the complex of all virtues). Yet it is not to be understood with the rigor with which this name is accepted by them, but rather θεοπρεπῶς. God, who has no law imposed by a superior, is Himself His own law. And to this is usually referred that passage in Heb. 2:10: ἔπρεπε τῷ θεῷ, "it became God," it was fitting for His most perfect nature.

Gerhardus: "Our theologians say that sins do not occur simply while God is unwilling or against His will; for no one can compel God, nor can anything happen while God is hindering and resisting; yet they do not occur while God is simply willing, because God neither wills nor approves of sin; but they occur while God is not willing. Now there is this difference between 'unwilling' (nolens) and 'not willing' (non volens): that the former implies a privation of will and of an active principle together with resistance and contrary action, whereas the latter has only that στέρησις without violent reluctance... Therefore, lest anyone abuse this distinction to undermine orthodoxy regarding the cause of sin, we prefer to speak thus: God wills some things as good, He permits some things as evil." (L. c. § 275.)

It is indeed the same rectitude of will as the former regarding the thing itself; but with a relation to creatures being led to their end, and to a manner of living being prescribed for them that is congruent. For to fulfill or perform promises is usually ascribed to justice, even though it is otherwise referred to veracity, of which we shall speak presently. Meanwhile, it is relevant to the present point that in Isaiah 45:23 God says: "Righteousness has gone out of My mouth, a word that shall not be revoked." And in Rom. 3, the righteousness of God is mentioned in v. 4, 5, insofar as it coincides with truth in v. 7, by which God makes His words faithful in v. 2. Whence it is usually called by the specific name of remunerative justice; concerning which see Rom. 2:5, 6, 7, where this is referred to the δικαιοκρισίαν, or just judgment of God, that He confers eternal life upon those who persevere in well-doing, and 2 Thess. 1:6, 7, where it is said to be just before God to grant relief to those who are afflicted.

Yet it is not to be thought on that account that man has any right or merit properly so called before God, by virtue of which God owes man any good, since rather, whatever good is in man is from God's grace, and God crowns His own gifts in man, or rewards them out of mere grace. And so, just as that remunerative justice in love
