nari, si sel. homo laberetur; at postquam incarnatio Filii decreta fuit, absoluti decreti fuit incarnationis exeeutio. De hac igitur non habuerunt, quod desperarent, illi judaizantes, rati, Judaeis esse promissum Messiam sub conditione, si Abrahamidae essent justi et boni, sin, non esse venturum; refutati in Ps. 89, 34., ubi testis in coelo (qui fidem servat etiam nunc in novissimo saeculo, quod antediluviano foedere sancitum fuerat) v. 38., juramentum v. 36. omnem conditionis suspicionem excludit, Hebr. 6, 17.

Item in Christi passione το άδικεισ&αι est decreti absoluti, indeprecabilis ac immobilis, Act. 4, 28.; at quod ea passio ab Herode, Pilato, Juda inflicta fuerit, pertinet ad decretum hypotheticum: Si Herodes, Pilatus, Judas Christum cruciabunt, ego decerno id permittere. Exsunto hic confatalia, non enim necessaria passioni fuit Herodis, Pilati, Judae manus socia; potuisset Pater coelestis Filium immediate cruciare, mactare, sacrificare, sicut Abraham Isaacum.

Ita: si Paulus constans in fide manebit, electus est; sin, reprobus. Tenenda hic est differentia inter decretum Dei, et judicium νεμετικόν: omnis κρίσις ultrix est decreta, non contra omne decretum est judicium νεμετικόν · illud potest esse absolutum, antecedaneum, praedeterminans, absolute inevitabile; hoc hypotheticum est, consequens et evitabile vel mitigabile.

Atque hinc, si quid absolute decretum est, est et absolute immutabile, irresistibile, impervincibile. ,Quis enim ejus voluntati resistet?‘ Rom. 9, 19. Si hypothetice, mutabile per apocopen conditionis, divisim. Decretum compositum, integrum et una cum supplemento hypotheseos sumtum, mutari utique non potest. Potest per apocopen hypotheseos, e. g. ,Ninive peribit‘, mutabile hoc; ,peribit, nisi poeniteat‘, hoc immutabile.“ (Hodos. phaen. 3. P. p. 158. sq.)

Non solum formaliter causantis (sic enim omne decretum Dei esset absolutum), sed etiam virtualiter causantis. Vid. § 18. not. a. Qua ratione dicunt nostrates, decretum praedestinationis et reprobationis non esse absolutum; agnoscere enim causam seu rationem impulsivam externam: illud quidem, meritum Christi fide finali apprehensum; hoc vero, finalem incredulitatem: de quo plura suo loco videbimus.§

22. Occurrit etiam a distinctio voluntatis divinae in voluntatem signi et beneplaciti. Illa dicitur, quando effectui aut objecto voluntatis divinae tribuitur nomen voluntatis, scilicet tanquam signo alicujus voluntatis in Deo.b Haec denotat actum ipsum divinae voluntatis, quo aliquid vult. Unde patet, distinctionem esse analogicam.c

Cavendum autem, ne voluntatem signi talem fingas, cui voluntas beneplaciti, quam signum ex instituto significare debet, repugnet.d

Non solum apud Lombardum I. Sent. distinet. XL a. cap. III. sqq. et dist. XLVII. c. II. et Thomam in I. Q. XIX. art. XII., verum etiam nostrates, b. Balth. Meimerwn Anthrop. Disp. XII. Q. I. th. 1. et b. Gerhard. Exeg. L. de Deo § 269. aliosque. Quo refertur Matth. 6, 15.: Fiat voluntas tua! i. e. fiant res et actus, ad quos tua voluntas praecipiendo terminatur, tanquam efficiendos.

Et c. 12, 50., ubi dicuntur facere voluntatem Patris, qui faciunt opera, quae Deus vult fieri. Porro 1 Thess. 4, 3., ubi dicitur, hanc esse voluntatem Dei, i. e. praeceptura atque adeo signum voluntatis divinae esse, quod praescribit sanctificationem nostram, ut abstineamus a scortatione etc. Quanquam simul objectum voluntatis aut praecepti divini seu res volita ac praecepta pro ipso praecepto accipi videatur. Auctores autem praeter praeceptum etiam alia, v. g. consilium, prohibitionem, operationem et permissionem, huc referunt.

Nempe quod membrorum distinctionis ea est inaequalitas, ut alterum proprie, alterum improprie, secundum figuram (ut illi dicunt) nomen voluntatis sibi vindicet. V. g. si cum reformatis, scholasticorum vestigia deserentibus, dicas, Deum velle omnium salutem voluntate signi, non autem hoc ipsum velle voluntate beneplaciti; aut praecipere homini conversionem, nec tamen serio velle, ut is convertatur. Haec enim sapientiae, bonitati et aequitati divinae repugnant, ac certitudinem Scripturae tollunt. Conf. b. Mus. Tract. de Aet. El. Dec. c. XI. § 336. sqq. p. 253. sqq.Gerhardus: ,,Voluntas alia signi, alia beneplaciti. Hac distinctione et scholastici et Calviniani utuntur, sed sensu diverso. Scholastici voluntatem signi definiunt effectum Dei, quando ipse foras progreditur, nobiscum agens per aliquod involucrum vel per externas res, quas possumns apprehendere, ut sunt verbum et sacramenta ab ipso instituta. Voluntatem beneplaciti vocant essentialem Dei voluntatem seu nudam majestatem divinam, quae est ipse Deus. . . Hoc scholasticorum sensu Lutherus tom. 6. Witeb. p. 98. in comm. c. 6. Gen. distinctionem illam repetit atque approbat: ,Nos (inquit) in N. T. habemus baptismum, coenam Domini, absolutionem et ministerium verbi; haec sunt, ut scholastici vocarunt, voluntas signi, in quae intuendum est, cum Dei voluntatem scire volumus; alia est voluntas beneplaciti, substantialis Dei voluntas seu nuda ipsius majestas, quae est Deus; ab hac removendi sunt oculi.‘ Calviniani ea distinctione abutuntur, dum, ad unum idemque objectum contrario modo se habere signi ac beneplaciti voluntatem, statuunt, unde voluntatem signi voluntati beneplaciti repugnare asserunt.“ (L. c. 1. II. § 268.) Quenstedtius: ,,Licet voluntas Dei una sit et simplicissima, variis tamen modis distinguitur. . . 3. In absconditam et revelatam; illa est arcana et imperscrutabilis; haec est in verbo Dei patefacta et infallibilis; illa versatur circa varia Dei judicia, quae s. Paulus vocat κρίματα άικξερευνητα, h. e. judicia imperscrutabilia, quia eorum rationem nulla creatura scrutando et indagando assequi potest, Rom. 11, 33. Haec circa negotium nostrae salutis occupata est. Non est autem cum Calvinianis opponenda absconditae voluntati Dei revelata, cum Deus sibi ipsi contrarius esse nequeat.“ (L. c. c. 8. s. 1. th. 27. f. 418.) § 28.

Inter attributa voluntatis Dei primum occurrit justitia, qua Deus partim in se justus est, quam peculiari nomine sanctitatem a vocamus, et importat rectitudinem PART. I. CAP. I.

divinae voluntatis, qua omnia, quae recta atque bona sunt, aeternae suae legi conformiter b vult; partim in ordine ad alios, ita ut creaturis leges convenientes praescribat easque dirigat c et gubernet, servet etiam et impleat promissa d hominibus facta, bonos denique remuneretur e et malos puniat.f

Sic Levit. 19, 2.: Sancti estote, ait Deus, quia ego sanctus sum» Conf. 1 Pet. 1, 15. 16. 17. Vid. Deut. 32, 4: Omnes viae ejus judicium (justae sunt). Deus (est) veritas et non iniquitas, justus et rectus ipse. Et Ps. 92, 16.: Pectus (est) Dominus, et non est iniquitas in eo. Habet autem haec justitia Dei analogiam quandam ad justitiam universalem, quam philosophi vocant (qua omnibus legibus conformiter vivitur, unde omnium virtutum complexus appellatur).' Non tamen eo rigore, quo ab illis hoc nomen accipitur, sed δεοπρεπώ intelligenda est. Deus, qui legem a superiore latam non habet, ipse sibi lex est. Et huc referri solet illud Ebr. 2, 10.: 'έπρεπε tw θεώ, decebat Deum, conveniens ejus naturae perfectissimae erat.

Gerhardus: ,,Nostrates dicunt, peccata non fieri simpliciter Deo· nolente vel invito; nemo enim Deum potest cogere, nec quidquam Deo impediente et repugnante potest fleri; nec tamen fieri Deo simpliciter volente, quia Deus nec vult nec approbat peccatum; sed fieri Deo non volente. Ea vero inter nolens et non volens est differentia, quod illud habet privationem voluntatis et principii activi una cum repugnantia et actione contraria, hoc autem tantum habet στίφησ/,ν illam absque violenta reluctatione. . . Ne quis igitur hac distinctione ad labefactandam orthodoxiam de causa peccati abutatur, ideo malumus sic loqui: Deus quaedam vult, ut bona, quaedam permittit, utmala.u (L. c. § 275.)

Est quidem quoad rem eadem rectitudo voluntatis cum priore; sed cum relatione ad creaturas ducendas ad suum finem, et rationem vivendi illis congruam praescribendam. Implere enim, aut praestare promissa justitiae adscribi solet, etsi ad veracitatem alias referatur, de qua mox dicemus. Interim ad praesens facit, quod Esaiae 45, 23. dicit Deus: Prodiit ex ore meo justitia, verbum, quod non revocabitur. Et. Rom. 3. memoratur justitia Dei v. 4. 5., quatenus cum veritate coincidit v. 7., qua Deus fidem facit dictis suis v. 2. Unde peculiari nomine appellari solet justitia remuneratoria; de qua vide Rom. 2, 5. 6. 7., ubi ad διχαιοχρισίαν, seu justum judicium Dei hoc refertur, quod perseverantibus in bene faciendo vitam aeternam confert, et 2 Thess. 1, 6. 7. justum esse dicitur apud Deum, reddere his, qui affiguntur, relaxationem.

Nec tamen propterea putandum est, homini ad Deum jus aliquod aut meritum proprie dictum esse, cujus vi Deus homini aliquid boni debeat, cum potius, quicquid boni in homine est, a Dei gratia sit, ac Deus sua dona in homine coronet, aut ex mera gratia remuneretur. Itaque sicut justitia illa remuneratoria in amore


### Concerning God: is founded upon the free divine promises, it is not usually called justice in…

is founded upon the free divine promises, it is not usually called justice in an absolute sense, but is rather referred to the goodness or veracity of God. Gerhard: "The question is asked: Is there commutative justice in God? Thomas, p. I, q. 21, art. 1, rightly denies it, because whatever we can give to God, we receive it all from Him; whence He Himself is debtor to no one, Rom. 11:35." (L. c. § 234.)

This is that which is commonly called vindicative or avenging [justice]; concerning which see the cited passages: Rom. 2:5, 8, 9, where God is said to be about to render indignation, wrath, and affliction to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, out of righteous judgment; and 2 Thess. 1:6, 7, that it is a righteous thing with God to recompense affliction to those who afflict others, and thus for God to inflict vengeance upon those who do not know God, etc. Cf. Gen. 18:20; Ps. 5:5.

Dannhauer: "God is a most righteous judge, the rewarder of good and the avenger of evil, who can pass over no sin, not even the least, unless the penalty is exacted either in the sinner or in his surety; the whole nemesis of which (to which Aristotle rightly referred κολαστικην justice) corresponds in a certain way to commutative and arithmetic proportion, and is ανταποδοτική, adequate to the guilt, so that, just as sin is an infinite evil, so its wages is infinite and eternal death." (Hodos. Phaen. III, p. 112.) §

24. There follows the veracity of God, through which God is constant in speaking the truth and in keeping promises. It is otherwise called truth in speaking or testifying, and is distinguished from truth in being and truth in knowing, both of which also belong to God. Namely, that just as He cannot be deceived through the infinite perfection of His intellect, or knowledge, so He cannot deceive through the infinite perfection of His will. See Num. 23:19 (h. l. § 10, note d) and Heb. 6:18: It is impossible for God to lie. §

25. There succeeds the power of God, through which the divine essence is efficacious for working and producing something outside of itself, and indeed everything that is in any way possible and does not imply imperfection on the part of the agent. This is either the will of God itself, His direct practical knowledge, which is believed to be so efficacious by itself that He can produce whatever He wills by willing it, without a faculty or executive power as something distinct; or it is the very being of God, insofar as it is subordinated to the divine knowledge and will for working outside of Himself; just as God is conceived through His power to work those things which He has freely willed, and thus to work through the power of the will directed and applied by a free act. PART I. CHAPTER I.

From this, it is clear that active power is to be understood; just as it is otherwise certain that God is entirely devoid of any passive power. Omnipotence is commonly spoken of as the power of effecting all things, or otherwise as extensively infinite power, since it has no limit in the breadth of its effects. And this is proven from Matt. 19:26: "With God all things are possible." And Luke 1:37: "With God nothing shall be impossible" (πᾶν ῥῆμα, every word, whatever he signifies by his words, he will perform). To the same point belongs the fact that God is called παντοκράτωρ, omnipotent, having all strength, force, or power, or κράτος εἰς τὰ πάντα, having and exercising strength or dominion over all things, 2 Cor. 6:18; Rev. 4:8; and that all virtue and fortitude (δύναμις καὶ ἰσχύς) is ascribed to him, ch. 7:12. For it is not absurd that God cannot lie, hunger, or sleep; for to be able to do these things is not a mark of perfection, but of imperfection, and therefore they are repugnant to God as the most excellent being. For the power of God is also intensively perfect, or of infinite perfection in itself, just as David, in Ps. 145, after having said that there is no end to the divine greatness, adds: "One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts" (power).

Quenstedtius: "The object of divine omnipotence is... all those things which do not involve a contradiction, such as: 1. those things which can have no reason for being; thus God cannot make what has been done to be undone; 2. those things which bring about vice or defect, such as: to be able to lie, to sin, to die. For to be able to do such things is an argument not of power, but of impotence." (L. c. c. 8. s. 1. th. 36. f. 421.)

Gerhardus: "We concede that God does not do those things which imply a contradiction and which are simply impossible, but we add that a distinction must be made between impossibilities of nature and impossibilities of essence. Impossibilities of nature are those which surpass the customary course of nature, such as the sun standing still, fire not burning, etc. Impossibilities of essence are those which are repugnant to the definition and nature of a thing and imply in themselves being and not being at the same time. The former are called impossible κατὰ τι (in a certain respect), the latter ἁπλῶς καὶ ὅλως (simply and altogether); therefore, we say that God can do the former, but not the latter... We deny, however, that it is to be judged by the principles of our reason which things are truly contradictory in the mysteries of faith. Therefore, we urge these theorems: 1. Those things which God asserts in Holy Scripture that He can do, and promises that He will do, are not truly contradictory, even if they seem so to our reason... Otherwise, the truth of God would be endangered... 4. It cannot be evidently and apodictically demonstrated that something implies a contradiction unless a full and perfect knowledge of that thing, with whose nature it is said to conflict, precedes it." (Exeges. Loc. II. § 199.)

Scherzerus: "God cannot deny Himself, die, sin, give to creatures infinite perfection so that nothing is lacking, or cause the past not to have passed, or tomorrow to be today; because it implies a contradiction either on the part of God or on the part of the thing. For if God were to lie, die, or sin, He would not be God; if a creature had infinite perfection, it would not be a creature; if the past had not passed, it would not be the past; if tomorrow existed today, it would not be today." (System, th. pag. 55.)

Gerhardus: "Just as knowledge is spoken of with respect to knowable things, so power is spoken of with respect to possible things. Impossibilities, therefore, do not fall under power, and consequently they do not in any way limit or restrict the infinity of power; for if they were to fall under power, they would not be impossible."

Scherzerus: "Just as a brute animal cannot know from its own imagination what a man can or cannot do; nor can a man, from his own ingenuity, know what an angel is capable of: so much less shall a man determine what God can or cannot do, since there exists a far greater distance in the capacity of understanding between God and man than between man and a brute. What is more? Not even from revelation can this be known. For nowhere has God revealed to us all things that are absolutely possible. Therefore, that rashness must be avoided, lest we precipitously say: God cannot do this or that, because I cannot grasp it with my intellect." (Syst. th. p. 56.) §

26. The power of God is accustomed to be distinguished into ordained and absolute. It is called ordained which is determined by God’s decree or some law to operate in a certain way. It is called absolute which pertains to Him in Himself, and is not determined by any preceding decree or law. The former can be resisted, the latter cannot. There is, indeed, one and the same infinite power of God, but it exerts itself in different ways, and thus is called ordained and absolute in different respects. Compare what we have said concerning the absolute and ordained will of God in § 20.

Or, [it is ordained] as God acts in accordance with His law or decree, and thus in accordance with the order instituted by Himself, by concurring with secondary causes and operating according to their requirements, e.g., when He preserves men by means of food, when He regenerates through the means instituted by Himself, the Word and Baptism. [It is absolute] e.g., when He causes a virgin to bring forth, raises the dead, etc.

Kromayerus: "He who freely gave laws to nature did not bind Himself to the laws and order of nature. This is a golden aphorism against those sectarians who measure the fields of the Christian religion with the measuring rod of human reason, such as the Socinians, for whom reason is religion, and the Reformed, who have persuaded themselves that God proposes nothing to us for belief that is incomprehensible to reason; whence they do not fear in the least to call into doubt the very divine omnipotence if something contrary to reason is proposed for belief.

That God, however, freely gave laws to nature—e.g., that fire should burn, that a virgin should not bring forth, that the moist should not be enclosed by its own boundaries but by foreign ones, that every heavy body should be carried downward, that every natural body should be in a place, that there should be no return from total privation to habit, that celestial bodies should be in perpetual motion, and that they should constantly observe their laws—all this is proven by the most free inhibition of the course of nature regarding the things just mentioned. For it is asserted that fire did not burn, Dan. 3:28; that a virgin brought forth, Matt. 1:25, Luke 2:7; that the moist was enclosed by boundaries not its own, Ex. 14:22; that a heavy body was carried upward, 2 Kings 6:6 (even physicists are forced to concede that an external body is not circumscribed by place, which nevertheless seems hardly comprehensible to us, who are circumscribed by places); that there was a return from total privation to habit (from death to life), John 11:43 and other places of Scripture of the Old and New Testaments; that the motion of celestial bodies was inhibited, Isa. 38:8; and that their laws were even changed and an eclipse of the sun was seen at the full moon, Luke 23:45." (Theol. pos.-pol. P. II. p. 122.) PART I. CHAP. I.

Gerhard: "God can do many things by His absolute power which He nevertheless does not do. He could liberate the damned from hell; but He does not liberate them, because justice has decreed eternal damnation for them." (L. th. de nat. Dei. § 130.)

Indeed, because secondary causes can be resisted and their influence impeded. Otherwise, the finite power of a creature would prevail over the infinite power of God. §

2. Goodness belongs to God both absolutely and in Himself, which is His very perfection, or the essence of God, insofar as it contains in itself all perfections, either formally or eminently; and also relatively, or in relation to creatures, to whom God is good, insofar as He efficiently produces all created goodness; and this is according to His own perfection, as the idea or exemplar of created perfection; He also attracts or moves [them] to the love and desire of Himself, as the highest good.

Latin:

Dei et promissionibus divinis gratuitis fundatur, ita non tam absolute loquendo justitia dici solet, quam ad bonitatem aut veracitatem Dei refertur. Gerhardus: ,,Quaeritur: An in Deo sit justitia commutativa? Thomas p. I. q. 21. art. 1. recte negat, quia, quicquid nos Deo dare possumus, id totum ab eo accipimus; unde ipse nullius est debitor, Rom. 11, 35.“ (L. c. § 234.)

Haec, illa est, quam vulgo vindicativam aut ultricem vocant; de qua vid. 11. cc. Rom. 2, 5. 8. 9., ubi Deus ex justo judicio hominibus contentiosis, veritati non obtemperantibus, sed injustitiae, indignationem, iram et afflictionem redditurus dicitur, et 2 Thess. 1, 6. 7., justum esse apud Deum, reddere affligentibus alios afflictionem, atque ita infligere Deum ultionem iis, qui non noverunt Deum etc. Conf. Gen. 18, 20. Ps. 5, 5.

Dannhauerus: ,,Deus est judex justissimus, boni remunerator et mali vindex, qui nullum, ne minimum quidem peccatum transmittere potest, nisi vel in peccante, vel ejus vade sit exacta poena; cujus tota nemesls (quorsum κολαστικην justitiam recte retulit Aristoteles) commutativae ac arithmeticae proportioni quodammodo respondet, estque ανταποδοτική culpae adaequata, ut, sicut peccatum est malum infinitum, ita ejus stipendium mors est infinita ac aeterna.“ (Hodos. Phaen. III. p. 112.) §

24. Sequitur veracitasa Dei, per quam Deus constans est in dicendo verob et servandis promissis. Dicitur alias veritas in dicendo seu testificando, et distinguitur a veritate in essendo et veritate in cognoscendo, quae tamen utraque etiam Deo competit. Nempe quod sicut per infinitam intellectus perfectionem, sive scientiam falli non potest, ita per infinitam voluntatis perfectionem non potest fallere. Vid. Num. 23, 19. (h. 1. § 10. not. d.) et Ebr. 6, 18.: Impossibile est Deum mentiri.§

25. Succedit potentia a Dei, per quam essentia divina efficax b est ad operandum ac producendum aliquid extra se, et quidem omne,c quicquid ullatenus possibile est et ex parte operantis non importat imperfectionem.d Quae vel est ipsa Dei voluntas, ejus scientia practica directa, quae per se tam efficax esse creditur, ut, quaecunque vult, absque facultate seu potentia executiva, velut distincta, volendo producere possit; vel est ipsum esse Dei, quatenus scientiae ac voluntati divinae ad operandum extra se subordinatur; prout Deus per potentiam ea operari concipitur, quae libere voluit, adeoque operari per potentiam voluntatis actu libero directam et applicatam. PART. I. CAP. I.

Unde activam potentiam intelligi constat; prout alias certum est, Deum omnis passivae potentiae plane esse expertem. Omnipotentia vulgo dicitur, tanquam potentia efficiendi omnia, alias potentia extensive infinita, quippe quod non habeat terminum in latitudine suorum effectuum. Et probatur ex Matth. 19, 26.: Apud Deum omnia sunt possibilia. Et Luc. 1, 37.: Apud Deum non est impossibile quicquam (παν fi7j.ua, omne, quicquid verbis significat, se facturum). Eodem pertinet, quod Deus dicitur παντοκ.ράτωρ, omnipotens, παν κράτος, omne robur, vim aut potentiam habens, aut κρό,τος εις τά πάντα, in res omnes robur aut imperium habens et exercens, 2 Cor. 6, 18. Apoc. 4, 8., quodque omnis virtus et fortitudo (δύναμις και Ισχύς') ei adscribitur, c. 7, 12. Sic enim non absurdum est, Deum non posse mentiri, esurire, dormire, quae posse non perfectionis, sed imperfectionis est quaeque proinde Deo, tanquam enti excellentissimo, repugnant. Nam et potentia Dei intensive perfecta, aut in se infinitae perfectionis est, prout David Ps. 145., cum dixisset, magnitudinis divinae non esse finem, addit: Generatio generationi narrabit opera tua, et fortitudinem (potentiam) tuam annuneiabunt.

Quenstedtius: ,,Objectum omnipotentiae divinae sunt. . . omnia illa, quae contradictionem non involvunt, qualia sunt: 1. illa, quae nuilam entis rationem habere possunt; sic Deus factum infectum facere nequit; 2. ea, quae vitium aut defectum inferunt, ut: posse mentiri, peccare, mori. Talia enim facere posse, non potentiae, sed impotentiae argumentum est.“ (L. c. c. 8. s. 1. th. 36. f. 421.)

Gerhardus: ,,Nos concedimus, Deum non facere ea, quae contradictionem implicant et quae sunt simpliciter impossibilia, sed addimus, distinguendum esse inter impossibilia naturae, et impossibilia natura. Impossibilia naturae sunt, quae usitatum naturae cursum superant, ut, solem stare, ignem non urere etc. Impossibilia natura sunt, quae rei definitioni et naturae repugnant ac implicant in se esse et non esse simul. Priora κ.ατα τι, posteriora άπ?ιώς κηϊ ολως dicunt impossibilia; priora igitur Deum posse, dicimus, posteriora non posse. . . Negamus vero, ex nostrae rationis principiis aestimandum esse, quaenam sint vere contradictoria in fidei mysteriis. Proinde urgemus haec theoremata: 1. Quae Deus in S. s. se facere posse asserit, seque facturum promittit, ea non sunt vere contradictoria, si vel maxime rationi nostrae talia videntur. . . Alias periclitaretur Dei veritas. . . 4. Evidenter et apodictice demonstrari nequit, aliquid implicare contradictionem, nisi plena et perfecta cognitio illius rei, cum cujus natura pugnare dicitur, antecedat.“ (Exeges. Loc. II. § 199.)

Scherzerus: ,,Deus se ipsum negare, mori, peccare, creaturis infinitam, ut nil desit, perfectionem dare, facere, ut praeteritum non praeterierit, ut dies crastina hodie sit, non potest; quia vel ex parte Dei, vel ex parte rei implicat. Si enim Deus mentiretur, moreretur, peccaret, Deus non esset; si creatura infinitam perfectionem haberet, creatura non esset; si praeteritum non praeteriisset, praeteritum non esset; si dies crastina hodie existeret, hodie non esset.“ (System, th. pag. 55.)

Gerhardus: ,,Sicut scientia dicitur respectu scibilium, sic potentia dicitur respectu possibilium. Impossibilia ergo non cadunt sub potentiam, ac proinde potentiae infinitatem nequaquam limitant aut restringunt; si enim sub potentiam caderent, impossibilia non essent.“

Scherzerus: ,,Quemadmodum brutum ex sua phantasia non potest cognoscere, quid homo possit vel non possit; nec homo ex suo ingenio, quid valeat angelus: ita multo minus homo determinabit, quid possit vel non possit Deus, cum longe major ratione intelligendi distantia inter Deum et hominem, quam inter hopiinem et brutum existat. Quid? quod ne ex revelatione quidem id cognosci possit. Nullibi enim Deus nobis omnia absolute possibilia revelavit. Ergo cavenda est temeritas illa, ne praecipitanter dicamus: Hoc vel illud Deus non potest, quia non possum intellectu meo assequi.“ (Syst. th. p. 56.) §

26. Potentia Dei distingui a solet in ordinatam et absolutam. Ordinata dicitur, quae Dei decreto vel lege aliqua determinata est ad operandum certo modo.b Absoluta vocatur, quae secundum se convenit, nec aliquo praevio decreto aut lege determinata est.c Illi potest resisti,d huic non item.e Est equidem una et eadem potentia Dei infinita, sed quae aliter atque aliter se exserit, adeoque alio atque alio respectu ordinata et absoluta dicitur. Confer, quae diximus de voluntate Dei absoluta et ordinata § 20.

Seu qua Deus agit convenienter suae legi aut decreto, et sic ordini a se instituto, concurrendo cum causis secundis, et pro exigentia earum operando, v. g. cum conservat homines mediantibus alimentis, cum regenerat per media a se instituta, verbum et baptismum. V.g. cum facit virginem parere, resuscitat mortuos etc.

Kromayerus: ,,Qui libere naturae leges dedit, seipsum naturae legibus et ordini non obstrinxit. Aureus est hic aphorismus adversus eos sectarios, qui rationis humanae decempeda Christianae religionis agros metiuntur, ut sunt Sociniani, quibus ratio est religio, et refor4mati, qui, Deum nihil incomprehensibile rationi ad credendum nobis proponere, sibi persuasum habent; unde ipsam divinam omnipotentiam, si rationi aliquid contrarium ad credendum proponitur, in dubium vocare minime verentur.

Quod autem Ubere Deus naturae leges dederit, v. g. ut ignis urat, virgo non pariat, humidum non claudatur terminis propriis, sed alienis, omne corpus grave deorsum feratur, omne corpus naturale sit in loco, a privatione totali ad habitum non detur regressus, corpora coelestia sint in perpetuo motu, suas constanter observent leges: id omne cursus naturae inhibitio liberrima circa jam ·dicta probat. Ignem enim non ussisse, Dan. 3, 28., virginem peperisse, Matth. 1, 25. Luc. 2, 7., humidum clausum fuisse, terminis propriis, Ex. 14, 22., corpus grave sursum fuisse latum, 2 Reg. 6, 6. (corpus extimum loco non circumscribi, vel ipsi physici concedere coguntur, quod tamen nobis, qui locis sumus circumscripti, vix comprehensibile videtur), a privatione totali ad habitum (a morte ad vitam) datum fuisse regressum, Joh. 11, 43. et aliis Scripturae locis V. et N. Testamentorum, corporum coelestium motum inhibitum fuisse, Jes. 38, 8., leges etiam eorum fuisse mutatas et solis eclipsin in plenilunio fuisse «conspectam, Luc. 23, 45. asseritur.“ (Theol. pos.-pol. P. II. p. 122.) PART. I. CAP. I.

Gerhardus: ,,Potentia absoluta multa potest Deus, quae tarnen non facit. Ex inferno damnatos liberare posset; sed non liberat, quia justitia aeternam damnationem illis statuit.“ (L. tb. de nat. Dei. § 130.)

Nempe quia causis secundis resisti et earum influxus impediri potest. Alias enim potentia creaturae finita praevaleret potentiae infinitae Dei.§

2;. Bonitas Deo competit cum absolute et in se, quae est ipsa ejus perfectio,a seu essentia Dei, quatenus in se continet omnes perfectiones, b vel formaliter,c vel eminenter;d tum respective, seu in relatione ad creaturas, quibus Deus bonus est, quatenus efficienter e producit omnem bonitatem creatam; idque juxta perfectionem suam, velut ideam aut exemplar f perfectionis creatae; allicit quoque aut movet in sui, tanquam summi boni,g amorem ac desiderium.


### Concerning God: Gerhard: "The question is asked

Gerhard: "The question is asked: Is God alone good by essence? — It is one thing for the essence of a thing to be good, but another for a thing to be good by its own essence. The essence of every created thing is good; whence Augustine says of the devil himself, the author of all evil: 'The devil, insofar as he is, is good; every nature, insofar as it is, is good.' (De nat. boni c. 1.) But no created thing is good by its own essence, that is, through itself and from itself. For if it were good by its own essence, then it would be essentially good; if it were essentially good, it would be good by the force of its own nature and essence, nor would it have goodness participated from elsewhere, nor could it be perfected by accidents; none of which can be said of a creature, which is accidentally, mutably, imperfectly, and participatively good; whence the scholastics rightly conclude: 'God alone is good by essence.'" (Exeg. l. II. § 210.)

For the goodness and perfection of God differ only in this, that God is called perfect absolutely and in Himself; but He is called good not only in Himself and absolutely, but also relatively. Thus, in Matthew 5, the last verse, Christ says: Be perfect (τέλειοί), as your Father in heaven is perfect: that is, I want you to imitate, as far as is permitted, the perfection proposed to you in the example of God. And in Luke 18…:19, He says: No one is good, except God alone. Indeed, creatures are perfected by those things which are superadded to their essence; but God, into whom no accident falls, [is perfected] by His own essence.

As far as pertains to perfections simply as such, which in their formal concept do not include imperfection. As for perfections in a certain respect, or those which in their formal reason imply perfection with an admixture of imperfection; which therefore are not in God according to their own proper reason, but through something more excellent, or through the power eminent to produce them

in other subjects. Thus, Ps. 94:9 says: "He who planted the ear, shall He not hear? Or He who formed the eye, shall He not behold?" Namely, because it is absurd not to attribute sight and hearing to God, who gave sight and hearing to men. Therefore, He sees and hears, yet not through a sensitive faculty, but He knows in a more excellent way that which creatures attain through sight or hearing.

Whence He is said to be good in the category of effic ient cause. To this pertains what is said, that He gives to all life and breath through all things, which are natural goods, Acts 17:25, and that in Him we live, and move, and have our being, v. 28. Thus also πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθή, καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον, every good gift and every perfect gift, ἄνωθέν ἐστι, is said to be from above, descending from the Father of lights, Jas. 1:17, and 1 Cor. 4:7: "What (good) do you have (O man!), that you did not receive (from God)?" By this reasoning, He is said to be good in the category of exemplary cause, as we shall see in the treatises on Creation and the Image of God. g) In which respect He is said to be good in the category of final cause. Compare Ps. 73:25-26, where David, despising heaven and earth and whatever is in them, even though his flesh and his heart fail, says that God is the strength of his heart and his portion (as it were, of a desired inheritance, and thus the good in which he may rest) forever. And to this pertains what we showed above, that God is the ultimate end of man and of theology, both natural and revealed. Proleg. chap. I. § 4. p. 9. sq. § 17. p. 38. § 28. As regards the divine persons, it must be held most simply that the essence and all divine perfections are common to these three distinct ones, whom Scripture calls the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, without division or multiplication.

The consideration of which follows now in the order of doctrine; see above § 5, notes c, d, e. The sum of this mystery is demonstrated by the passages 1 John 5:7 and Matt. 28:19. For in the former it is said: "There are three that bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one (ἓν εἰσί)." The authority (αὐθεντίαν) of this passage, as a part of Scripture inspired by God (θεοπνεύστου), was acknowledged by Jerome, who used the most accurate codices, and by Cyprian, who cited those words before the Arian controversy (de simplic. Cler.), and later also by Fulgentius (in Resp. ad Obj. ult. Arian.). It is also confirmed by the Complutensian, Antwerp, British, Robert Stephanus, and Vatican Library codices. Cf. the blessed Gerhard in Disp. Acad. P. III. p. m. 1306 sqq. Moreover, it is manifest that those three, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, are presented 1) as really distinct among themselves; yet at the same time 2) as bearing witness in heaven (namely, of His majesty), possessing in themselves heavenly, or supreme and truly divine authority and efficacy of operation, since 3) they are (not only think or will, but are) one among themselves, and thus one God. In the other PART I. CHAP. I.

Moreover, in the place where Christ commands the apostles to baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, 1) these three are again joined together as distinct, in such a way that 2) baptism must be administered in the name—as if it were their common name and therefore their equal authority—by which men are consecrated to God and rendered capable of His grace and the remission of sins (according to John 3:5; Acts 2:38; Titus 3:5); and since 3) there is no name of such dignity in which a rite so grave and salutary can and ought to be administered, except that of God alone (according to 1 Cor. 1:18 and Luke 20:4 sqq.), it is evident that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are that one true and eternal God.

Cf. the *Apparatus criticus* and *Gnomon* of J. A. Bengel on 1 John 5:7. Kromayer: "That there are three persons in one divine essence can be solidly proven even from the Old Testament without the aid of the New. Likewise, the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity was not unknown to the fathers of the Old Testament. . . The first class of proofs contains those sayings of Scripture in which mention is made of a plurality of persons in the Godhead, which suffices against antagonists who concede only a single person of the Godhead.

Such sayings are those in which a noun of the plural number is constructed with a verb of the singular number, as in Gen. 1:1, 3. Then, when God says in the aforementioned chapter, v. 26: 'Let us make,' etc., where both the verb and the affixed pronoun indicate a plurality; 3. when the divine majesty, through an irony—not illusory, but reproving—speaks these words to the protoplasts in Gen. 3:22: 'Behold, Adam has become as one of us,' i.e., Elohim; in which place the indivisible God is, as it were, divided into several persons; 4. when the persons of the Godhead. . . address one another thus in Gen. 11:7: 'Come, let us go down,' etc. The second class of proofs contains those sayings of Scripture in which mention is made of two persons, which also suffices against antagonists. Such are Gen. 19:24: 'Jehovah rained from Jehovah.' Exod. 34:5; Jer. 23:33; Dan. 9:17; Hos. 1:7; Zech. 3:2; 2:9; Ps. 110:1; cf. Matt. 22:44. The third class contains those sayings in which mention is made of three persons, such as Gen. 1, where a commemoration is instituted of God, of the divine Word (that is, the Son, as is explained in Ps. 33:6 and John 1:1), and of the Spirit of God brooding over the waters and bestowing vital power upon them. Ps. 33:6; Isa. 48:16; 63:10, 11; Num. 6:24–26; Ps. 67:7, 8; Isa. 6:3; Josh. 22:22. The fourth class contains those sayings of Scripture in which God is said to have a Son, not an adoptive one, but a natural one begotten from His own essence, as Ps. 2:7; Prov. 30:5 (from which place Christ seems to have derived the problem in John 3:8, 13). The fifth class of proofs contains those sayings of Scripture from which the ternary number of persons is derived. For these are not read in the Old or New Testament κατά το γράμμα (according to the letter): 'In one divine essence there are distinct persons,' but it suffices that three—and only three, neither more nor fewer—can be found in the Scriptures to whom the name, attributes, works, and divine worship belong. An argument could be constructed as follows: If, besides the Father, there are two others—neither more nor fewer—to whom the name, etc., belongs, it follows that there are three distinct persons in one divine essence. But the former is true. Therefore, the latter is also true. The minor premise is proven: The adversaries concede concerning the Father that He is that true God of Israel. But the proper name of God, the attributes, works, and worship are also attributed to a certain Angel—not a created one, but an uncreated one, the Angel of the Covenant (Mal. 3:1) and the Angel of the Great Counsel (Isa. 9:6), the Son of God. . . e.g., Gen. 16:10, 13; 22:12, 14, 16; 48:15; Exod. 3:4, 6, 8, 12, 14, 18, 20; 14:24; 13:21, 22; 23:21; 33:14; Isa. 64:9. . .

Furthermore, the proper name of God is attributed to the Holy Spirit (2 Sam. 23:1, 2; Isa. 64:10; Ps. 95:9), omnipresence (Ps. 139:6), omniscience (Isa. 40:13), divine works (Gen. 1:1, 2; Ps. 33:6; Job 33:4; Isa. 61:1; 11:2), and the worship of adoration (Isa. 6:3; Acts 28; Ps. 95:6). Therefore, if the fathers of the Old Testament either read or heard these and similar things, a concept of the three persons of the Godhead was formed in their intellect."

to have been, who would deny? Supine negligence is not lacking in the New Testament either. In the sixth class we place those testimonies which are taken partly from the Chaldean paraphrase, partly from the older Jews. . . In the seventh class we place the fact that this article is fundamental and consequently of all times. Eph. 4:6.” (Theol. posit.-pol. I, 146 sqq.)

Gerhard: “The mystery of the Trinity can and ought to be confirmed not only from the New, but also from the Old Testament. 1. We do not say this, that there is the same clarity and evidence of the testimonies concerning the Trinity in the Old and New Testaments; because a clearer revelation of this mystery was reserved for the New Testament. . . 2. Nor do we mean that in a dispute against a stubborn adversary one must make a beginning from the more obscure sayings of the Old Testament. But we assert only this, that certain testimonies can and ought to be brought forward from the Old Testament for the establishing of the dogma of the Trinity, since God has always from the beginning so revealed Himself that the Church in all ages has thus acknowledged, invoked, and celebrated God, that in one undivided essence there are three distinct persons.

Latin:

Gerhardus: ,,Quaeritur: An solus Deus per essentiam bonus? — Aliud est, rei essentiam esse bonam, aliud vero, rem per suam essentiam esse bonam. Cujuslibet rei creatae essentia est bona; unde de ipso diabolo, omnis mali auctore, Augustinus dicit: ,Diabolus, in quantum est, bonus est; omnis natura, in quantum est, bona est.‘ (De nat. boni c. 1.) Sed nulla res creata per suam essentiam, hoc est, per se ipsam et a se ipsa est bona. Si enim per suam essentiam esset bona, tunc esset bona essentialiter·, si essentialiter esset bona, vi suae naturae et essentiae esset bona nec aliunde participatam haberet bonitatem, nec posset perfici per accidentia; quorum nihil de creatura, accidentaliter, mutabiliter, imperfecte et participative bona, dici potest; unde recte concludunt scholastici: ,Solum Deum per essentiam esse bonum.“‘ (Exeg. 1. II. § 210.)

Nara bonitas et perfectio Dei per hoc tantum differunt, quod perfectus dicitur Deus absolute et in se; bonus autem non solum in se et absolute, verum etiam relative. Sic Matth. 5. v. ult. dicit Christus: Estote perfecti (τέλειοί), sicut Pater vester in coelis perfectus est: h. e. volo, vos imitari, quoad licet, perfectionem in exemplo Dei vobis propositam. Et Luc. 18, 19. ait: Nemo est bonus, nisi solus Deus. Nempe creaturae quidem perficiuntur per ea, quae essentiae suae superadduntur; Deus autem, in quem non cadit accidens, per ipsam suam essentiam.

Quantum attinet ad perfectiones simpliciter tales, quae in suo formali conceptu non includunt imperfectionem. Quod attinet ad perfectiones secundum quid, seu, quae in sua formali ratione perfectionem cum admixta imperfectione important; quae proinde non sunt in Deo secundum rationem suam propriam, sed per aliquid praestantius, aut per virtutem eminentem ad eas producendas

in subjectis aliis. Sic Ps. 94, 9. dicitur: An plantator auris, annon audiatf aut formator oculi, annon intueatur? scilicet, quod absurdum sit, Deo, qui visum auditumque dedit hominibus, visum et auditum non tribuere. Videt itaque et audit, non tamen per vim sensitivam, sed modo praestantiore cognoscit, quod creaturae per visum auditumve assequuntur.

Unde dicitur bonus esse in genere causae efficientis. Quo pertinet, quod dicitur, dare omnibus vitam et halitum per omnia, quae sunt bona naturalia, Act. 17, 25., inque ipso nos vivere, moveri et esse, v. 28. Sic etiam πασα δόσις άγαίίη, χαι παν δώρημα τέλειον, omnis donatio bona, et omne donum perfectum, avtoftsv, superne esse dicitur, descendens a Patre luminum, Jac. 1, 17., et 1 Cor. 4, 7.: Quid (boni) habes (o homo!), quod non accepisti (a Deo)? Qua ratione dicitur bonus esse in genere causae exemplaris, prout videbimus in LL. de Creatione et Imagine Dei..g) Quo respectu bonus dicitur in genere causae finalis. Confer Ps. 73, 25. 26., ubi David, coelum et terram, quaeque in illis sunt, contemnens, deficiente licet carne sua et corde suo, robur cordis sui et partem suam (veluti haereditatis optatae, adeoque bonum, in quo acquiescat) dicit esse Deum in saeculum. Eoque pertinet, quod supra ostendimus, Deum esse ultimum finem hominis et theologiae, cum naturalis, tum revelatae. Proleg. cap. I. § 4. p. 9. sq. § 17. p. 38. § 28. Quod ad personas divinas a attinet, simplicissime tenendum est, quod essentia omnesque perfectiones divinae sine divisione aut multiplicatione communes sint his tribus distinctis, quos Scriptura vocat Patrem, Filium et Spiritum Sanctum.b

Quarum consideratio ordine doctrinae nunc sequitur, vide supra § 5. notis c. d. e. Summam mysterii hujus demonstrant loca 1 Joh. 5, 7. et Matth. 28, 19. Illic enim dicitur: tres sunt, qui testificantur in coelo, Pater, Verbum et Spiritus S., et hi tres unum sunt (fiv eim). Loci αυβεντίαν, tanquam partis Scripturae ftsonνεΰστου, agnoverunt Hieronymus, accuratissimis codicibus usus, et qui ante certamen Arianum verba illa citavit, Cyprianus de simplic. Cler., postea etiam Fulgentius in Resp. ad Obj. ult. Arian. Confirmant etiam Codd. Complutensis, Antverpiensis, Britannicus, Rob. Stephani et bibliothecae Vaticanae. Conf. b. Gerh. in Disp. Acad. P. III. p. m. 1306. sqq. Manifestum autem est, tres illos, Patrem, Filium et Spiritum S., exhiberi 1) tanquam inter se realiter distinctos; simul vero 2) tanquam testantes in coelo (scilicet majestatis suae), coelesti, seu suprema ac vere divina auctoritate et operationis efficacia, ex se pollentes, quippe 3) inter se sint (non tantum sentiant aut velint, sed sint) unum, adeoque Deus unus. In altero PART. I. CAP. I.

loco autem, ubi Christus jubet apostolos baptizare in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti, rursus 1) hi tres tanquam distincti copulantur, ita quidem, ut 2) in nomine, velut communi atque adeo auctoritate aequali eorum, administrari debeat baptismus, quo homines consecrentur Deo et gratiae ejus ac remissionis peccatorum (juxta Joh. 3, 5. et Act. 2, 38. Tit. 3, 5.) reddantur capaces; cumque 3) nullum sit nomen tantae dignitatis, in quo ritus tam gravis ac salutaris administrari possit ac debeat, praeterquam solius Dei (juxta 1 Cor. 1, 18. et Luc. 20, 4. sqq.), patet, Patrem et Filium et Spiritum S. esse verum illum unum et aeternum Deum.

Cf. Apparatus criticus et Gnomon A. Bengelii ad 1 Joh. 5, 7. Kromayerus: ,,In una divina essentia tres esse personas, etiam ex V. T. absque Novi adminiculo solide probari potest. Item, mysterium SS. Trinitatis patribus V. T. non fuit incognitum. . . Prima classis probationum continet ea Scripturae dicta, in quibus pluralitatis personarum deitatis fit mentio, quod sufficit adversus antagonistas, unicam duntaxat personam deitatis concedentes. Ejusmodi dicta sunt,, in quibus nomen pluralis numeri cum verbo singularis numeri construitur, ut Gen. 1, 1.

3. Deinde cum Deus inquit cap. dicti v. 2G.: ,Faciamus‘ etc., ubi pluralitatem et verbum et pronomen affixum innuit; 3. cum divina majestas per ironiam, non illusoriam, sed objurgatoriam his verbis protoplastos Gen. 3, 22.: ,Ecce, Adam factus est, ut unus ex nobis, sci. Elohim; quo in loco Deus indivisibilis in plures personas quasi dividitur; 4. cum personae deitatis ... se ita invicem· alloquuntur Gen. 11, 7.: ,Agite, descendamus‘ etc. Secunda classis probationum continet ea Scripturae dicta, in quibus duarum personarum fit mentio, quod etiam adversus antagonistas sufficit. Talia sunt Gen. 19, 24.: ,Jehovah pluit a Jehovah.‘ Exod. 34, 5. Jer. 23, 33. Dan. 9, 17. Hos. 1, 7. Zach. 3, 2. 2, 9. Ps. 110, 1. cf. Matth. 22, 44. Tertia classis continet ea dicta, in quibus trium personarum fit mentio, utpote Gen. 1., ubi Dei, Verbi divini (id est, Filii, ut Ps. 33, 6. et Joh. 1, 1. exponitur) et Sp. Dei aquis incubantis et vim vitalem iisdem tribuentis commemoratio instituitur. Ps. 33, 6. Es. 48, 16. 63, 10. 11. Num. 6, 24—26. Ps. 67, 7. 8. Es. 6, 3. Jos. 22, 22. Quarta classis continet ea Scripturae dicta, in quibus Deus dicitur habere Filium, non adoptivum aliquem, sed naturalem ex essentia ipsius progenitum, ut Ps. 2, 7. Prov. 30, 5. (ex quo loco Christus depromsisse videtur problema Joh. 3, 8. 13.). Quinta classis probationum continet ea Scripturae dicta, ex quibus numerus personarum ternarius numerabilis eruitur. Nec enim· in V. nec N. T. haec κατά το γράμμα leguntur: In una divina essentia sunt distinctae personae, sed sufficit, tres tantum, nec plures, nec pauciores in Scripturis inveniri posse, quibus nomen, attributa, opera et cultus divinus competat. Argumentum confieri possettale: Si praeter Patrem adhuc duo sunt, nec plures, nec pauciores, quibus nomen etc. competit, sequitur, in una essentia divina tres esse distinctas personas. Sed verum est prius. E. et posterius. Minor probatur: De Patre concedunt adversarii, quod sit verus ille Deus Israelis. Sed nomen Dei proprium, attributa, opera et cultus etiam Angelo cuipiam, non creato, sed increato, angelo foederis Mal. 3, 1. et magni consilii angelo Es. 9, 6., Dei Filio. . . attribuuntur; e. g. Gen. 16, 10. 13. 22, 12. 14. 16. 48, 15. Ex. 3, 4. 6. 8. 12. 14. 18. 20. 14, 24. 13, 21. 22. 23, 21. 33, 14. Es. 64, 9. . .

Praeterea Spiritui S. nomen Dei proprium tribuitur 2 Sam. 23, 1. 2. Es. 64, 10. (Ps. 95, 9.), omnipraesentia Ps. 139, 6., omnisapientia Es. 40, 13., opera divina Gen. 1, 1.2. Ps. 33, 6. Job. 33, 4. Es. 61, 1. 11, 2., cultus adorationis Es. 6, 3. (Act. 28.) Ps. 95, 6. Ergo quodsi haec et similia patres V. T. vel legerint, vel audierint,, conceptum de tribus personis deitatis in intellectu ipsorum formatum

fuisse, quis iverit inficias? Supina negligentia neque in N. T. deest. In sexta classe collocamus ea testimonia, quae partim ex chaldaica paraphrasi, partim Judaeis vetustioribus sunt desümta. . . In septima classe ponimus, quod hic articulus sit fundamentalis et per consequens omnium temporum. Ephes. 4. 6.“ (Theol. posit.-pol. I, 146. sqq.)

Gerhardus: ,,Mysterium Trinitatis non solum ex N., sed etiam ex V. T. confirmari potest ac debet. 1. Non hoc dicimus, quod testimoniorum de Trinitate in V. et N. T. sit eadem claritas et evidentia; quia clarior hujus mysterii revelatio N. T. fuit reservata. . . 2. Nec hoc volumus, quod in disceptatione contra pertinacem adversarium ab obscurioribus V. T. dictis faciendum sit initium. Sed hoc duntaxat asserimus, quod ex V. T. pro adstruendo Trinitatis dogmate quaedam testimonia afferri possint et debeant, cum Deus semper ab initio sese sic patefecerit, ut ecclesia omnibus temporibus Deum ita agnoverit, invocarit ac celebrarit, quod in una indivisa essentia sint tres distinctae personae.


### Concerning God: We prove this thesis

We prove this thesis: 1. From the first thesis. For if the dogma of the Trinity is necessary to be known and believed by all who are to be saved, certainly its traces must exist in the sacred writings of the Old Testament; otherwise the perfection of Scripture will be undermined. 2. From the evidence of the thing itself. . .

3. From the divine prohibition Ps. 81:10: ‘There shall be no strange god in thee’ (זר, the Vulgate rendered: a new god), ‘neither shalt thou worship any strange god.’ But if the mystery of the Trinity had been entirely unknown in the Old Testament, certainly in the New Testament, through the worship of the Son and the Holy Spirit, a new god would be introduced. Is. 43:10: ‘Before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.’ But if in the New Testament the Son of God was made God, as the Photinians wish, and began to be treated with divine worship in the New Testament, certainly after God the Father another god was formed.” (Exeges. l. III. § 20 sq.)

Quenstedtius: "The question is not whether there are some indications and traces, or sayings that obscurely insinuate this mystery, in the Old Testament, but whether there are open, clear, and soul-convincing testimonies of the Holy Trinity: we affirm the latter, our adversaries the former. . .

The question is not whether all who lived in the Israelite church, whether they were pious or impious, could draw the knowledge of the Holy Trinity from the oracles of the Old Testament, or notice and understand that it is proposed and revealed there; since even today, in such clear light, many Epicureans and profane men live in the very bosom of the church who are little concerned with the knowledge of the Holy Trinity—but whether the pious and faithful could have had knowledge of that dogma from it. The illumination and illustration of the Holy Spirit is not to be excluded here, since no one can perceive the divine sense of the sayings of Scripture unless his intellect has been illuminated by a special light of grace. . .

The thesis is proven in general: 1. From the distinction between natural and revealed theology, or θεογνωσία; for the former, when compared with this knowledge of God, is very imperfect, indeed almost nothing. . . 2. From the unity of faith in the Old and New Testaments, Eph. 4:5. The salvation common to us with the church of the Old Testament presupposes a faith common to us with them. Therefore, it is not to be believed that the fathers of the Old Testament had a different and other justifying faith than we do, or that there is something in the New Testament necessary to be believed which was not necessary to be believed in the Old Testament; for it would follow that, with the passage of time, the fundamental articles of faith had been either changed or increased regarding the substance of faith, both of which are absurd. . .

3. From the express assertion of the apostles. Acts 4:12: 'There is salvation in no other,' etc. Where all other ways of salvation, both in the Old and in the New Testament, are excluded, and one alone, namely through Christ, the Son of God, is established as common to all. Cf. Acts 10:43. Peter expressly says in Acts 15:11: 'The fathers were saved by the same grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, by the same faith by which we are justified and saved.' . .

4. From the identity of the doctrine of the Old and New Testaments. Thus Paul says in Acts 26:22: 'I testify to small and great, οὐδὲν ἐκτός, saying nothing outside those things which the prophets and Moses predicted would come to pass.' Regarding these words, the blessed Dr. Huelsemannus says in *dialys. th.* 17: 'In this place, because the universal negative particle ἐκτός precedes, οὐδὲν λέγων ἐκτός, "I have spoken nothing outside or above those things which the prophets and Moses have spoken," PART I. CHAP. I. every exception of any dogma proposed by Paul is excluded, which Moses and the prophets did not likewise propose. Therefore, whatever is contained in the writings of the apostle Paul, it must likewise be contained in the writings of Moses and the prophets.'" (*Theol. did. pol.* P. I. c. 9. s. 2. q. 3. f. 509. sqq.)

The same: "With the testimonies of the Old Testament alone (Christ and the apostles) convicted the Jews and demonstrated these mysteries solely from the Scriptures of the Old Testament. Matt. 22:46; Acts 18:24, 28. Either, therefore, the ἔλεγχος of Christ and the apostles was sufficient and the Jews could be convinced from the testimonies of the Old Testament alone, or Christ and the apostles disputed with them ineptly from an invalid and unsuitable principle; which is impious to say." (*L. c.* q. 4. f. 516.)

Kromayerus: "It is surprising that this thesis (that the Trinity can be proven from the Old Testament) was impugned not many years ago by those who wish to be associates of the Augsburg Confession. For it could not have escaped them that in the conflict with the Jews, who do not receive the New Testament, this thesis was asserted so firmly by our own people from the Old Testament alone, that it has stood until now as ἀνίκητος καὶ ἀκίνητος." (*Th. posit.-pol.* I, 146.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: ... 5. Of the innovators, who dogmatize: 'The mystery of the Trinity was known to the patriarchs and prophets in their own way from a peculiar revelation of God; yet it is not contained in the books of the Old Testament in such a way that it could have been detected there by anyone in the past, or can be now, setting aside the New Testament. Traces and indications are detected there for the Trinity, rather than open and soul-convincing sayings.'" (*L. c.* q. 3. f. 510.)

Luthardt: "The scriptural proof from the O. T. . . rests almost throughout on incorrect or forced exegesis and, in general, on an unhistorical view which fails to recognize the gradual course of revelation. . . That identification, however, is explained by the fact that in the Angel of Jehovah, Jehovah Himself appears. . . Only the N. T. actually revealed the divinity of the Messiah. . . The O. T. therefore contains only the prerequisites of the Trinitarian knowledge of God, because [it contains the prerequisites] of the Trinitarian revelation of God; only the N. T. brought the latter along with the former." (Compend. 3rd ed., p. 78 sq.)

Kahnis: "In the O. T., the unity and uniqueness of Jehovah stand out so decisively that what is stated concerning the Messiah and the Holy Spirit carries within itself only the germ of divine personalities." (Die luth. Dogm. Second ed. I, 353.)

Vilmar: "The old dogmatics asserted too much when it claimed that God had not only already revealed Himself in the Father, Son, and Spirit in the Law and before the Law, but also that the 'Church of the O. T.,' i.e., those who stood firm in God's promise at that time, had known this revelation of God as Father, Son, and Spirit. Neither the one nor the other can be admitted in this way; God does not reveal Himself before He reveals Himself; and He did that as Son and Spirit only when the Logos had become flesh and the Spirit had been poured out. But where a revelation does not take place, knowledge of it cannot be posited either.

This view destroys revelation as a historical process, mixes promise and fulfillment together—which are nevertheless kept so extremely sharply apart by God Himself—and even endangers the distinction between Law and Gospel (!). Precisely the fact that the Jews did not want to acknowledge in Christ the new thing which had, however, been prophesied to them, is the reproach which Christ makes to them; not (!) that they fell away from what they had already possessed and known." (Dogmatik. 1874. I, 275.)

Hofmann: "The Old Testament teaches just as little that God is a multiple being in Himself as it teaches the unity of God with reference to a multiplicity within Him."

29. For a fuller declaration of this mystery, it is to be observed: I. That the Father differs really from the Son, the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both, so that in truth the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Here, however, this is not yet to be proposed in ecclesiastical terms, but only in a popular manner.

Apart from the operation of our mind, or with no one thinking or conceiving different nomenclatures in their mind. Thus Christ expressly says that the Father is άλλον, another than Himself, John 5:32, 37, and that the Holy Spirit, the παράκλητον, the comforter or advocate of the faithful, is άλλον, another than Himself and the Father, John 14:16.

The same is evident even from the names of Father and Son, and from the fact that the former is described as begetting, the latter as begotten, Ps. 2:7; John 1:14, 18; ch. 3:16, and that the Son is said to be sent by the Father, ch. 10:36; Gal. 4:4, and the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father, John 15:26, to be sent by the Father, John 14:26, and to be sent by the Son, John 15:26.

Indeed, no one is his own father, or his own son. No one begets himself, or is begotten by himself. No one proceeds from himself, or is sent by himself.

Compare the blessed Musaeus, Disputations held in the year 1649, Disp. III, § 11, 12, 13, pp. 57, 58, 59.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Praxeans, Noetians, Sabellians, and Samosatenes, who, as they posited one ουσίαν, so also one ΰπόστασιν or person, which, in one respect or another, assumes now the name of the Father, now of the Son, now of the Holy Spirit... Hence they were called Patripassians by the ancients. 2. Of Arius and the Arians, who... most fiercely attacked the όμοονσίαν of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whence the Arians were also called Triusians by Fulgentius... 3. Of the Tritheists, who, to avoid the heresy of Sabellius, feigned three gods or three divine essences, one essentializing, two essentialized... 4. Of the Photinians, both ancient and recent, who deny the mystery of the Trinity, whence they are rightly called Antitrinitarians; that is, they deny that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are so distinguished by persons that they are nevertheless that one true God." (L. c. c. 9. s. 2. q. 1. f. 493.)

The Swedenborgians must be added. §

30. Next, II. it is to be observed: That not only the Father, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit are the true and eternal God.

For the fact that He whom Scripture calls the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is the true and supreme God is conceded today by all who receive Scripture, and therefore it is not further proven here.

Various arguments prove that the Son is true and by nature God: I. Because Scripture expressly calls Him God (the name of God, however, properly accepted, is the name of the divine nature, see above § 3 and note b).

Latin:

Hanc thesin probamus: 1. Ex thesi prima. Si enim dogma de Trinitate omnibus salvandis scitu ac creditu necessarium est, utique ejus vestigia in sacris literis Y. T. extare oportet; alias Seripturae perfectio labefactabitur. 2. Ex ipsa rei evidentia. . .

3. Ex prohibitione divina Ps. 81, 10.: ,Non erit in te Deus alienus‘ (זר Vulg. reddidit: Deus recens), ,nec incurvabis te Deo extraneo.‘ Atqui sl Trinitatis mysterium in V. T. penitus fuisset ignotum, utique in N. T. per cultum Filii et Spiritus S. Deus recens introduceretur. Es. 43,10.: ,Ante me non est formatus Deus et post me non erit.‘ Atqui si in. N. T. Filius Dei est factus Deus, ut Photiniani volunt, ac divino cultu in N. T. affici coepit, utique post Deum Patrem alius formatus est Deus.“ (Exeges. 1. III. § 20. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Non est quaestio, an indicia aliqua et vestigiar sive dicta obscurius insinuantia hoc mysterium, sint in V. T., sed an aperta, clara, animumque convincentia S. Trinitatis testimonia: hoc nos, illud adversarii affirmant. . .

Non est quaestio, an omnes in ecclesia Israelitica degentes, sive pii fuerint, sive impii, ex oraculis V. T. notitiam SS. Trinitatis haurire, vel, id ibi proponi et revelari, animadvertere et intelligere potuerint; cum etiam hodie in tam clara luce, in ipso ecclesiae gremio multi vivant Epicuraei et profani homines, qui de SS. Trinitatis cognitione parum sunt soliciti, — sed an pii et fideles illius dogmatis notitiam inde habere potuerint. Non est hic excludenda Spiritus S. illuminatio et illustratio, cum nemo sensum divinum dictorum Scripturae percipere possit, nisi cujus intellectus speciali gratiae lumine sit collustratus. . .

Probatur thesis in genere: 1. a naturalis et revelatae theologiae sive ·δεογυωσίας distinctione; illa enim, cum hac Dei notitia collata, est valde imperfecta, imo fere nulla. . . 2. Ex fidei in V. et N. T. unitate, Eph. 4, 5. Ecclesiae V. T. communis nobiscum salus praesupponit communem nobiscum fidem. Non itaque credendum est, patres V. T. diversam et aliam fidem justificantem habuisse, quam nos, aut aliquid in N. T. creditu esse necessarium, quod in V. T. creditu necessarium non fuerit; sequeretur enim, successu temporis articulos fidei fundamentales quoad substantiam fidei vel mutatos vel auctos fuisse, quod utrumque absurdum. . .

3. Ex apostolorum diserta assertione. Act. 4, 12.: ,Non est in ullo alio salus‘ etc. Ubi omnes aliae viae salutis quam in V. tam in N. T. excluduntur, et una sola, sci. per Christum, Dei Filium, omnibus communis constituitur. Cf. Act. 10, 43. Petrus diserte ait Act. 15, 11.: ,Patres eadem gratia Domini Jesu Christi, eadem fide esse salvatos, qua et nos justificamur et salvamur.‘ . .

4. Ex doctrinae V. et N. T. identitate. Sic Paulus Act. 26, 22. ait: ,Testificor parvis et magnis, υνδεν inτό׳·, nihil extra illa dicens, quae prophetae praedixerunt futura esse et Moses.‘ Ad quae verba b. Dr. Huelsemannus in dialys. th. 17.: ,Hoc loco, inquit, quia praecedit particula εκτός universalis negativa, ονδεν Aeyuv εκτός, nihil locutus sum extra vel supra ea, quae prophetae et Moses locuti sunt, PART. I. CAP. I. excluditur omnis exceptio ullius dogmatis a Paulo propositi, quod non identidem proposuerint Moses et prophetae. Ergo quaecunque insunt Pauli apostoli scriptis, ea oportet identidem inesse scriptis Mosis et prophetarum.‘“ (Theol. did.pol. P. I. c. 9. s. 2. q. 3. f. 509. sqq.)

Idem: ,,Solis V. T. testimoniis (Christus et apostoli) Judaeos convicerunt et mysteria haec unice ex Scripturis V. T. demonstrarunt. Matth. 22, 46. Act. 18, 24. 28. Aut itaque έλεγχος Christi et apostolorum fuit sufficiens et Judaei ex solis V. T. testimoniis convinci potuerunt, aut inepte Christus et apostoli ex invalido et inidoneo principio cum illis disputarunt; quod dictu impium.“ (L. c. q. 4. f. 516.)

Kromayerus: ,,Mirari subit, quod haec thesis (Trinitatem ex V. T. probari posse) ante annos non ita multos ab iis, qui Aug. Confessionis esse volunt socii, fuerit impugnata. Nec enim ipsos praeterire potuit, quod in conflictu cum Judaeis, N. T. non recipientibus, ex solo V. T. haec thesis a nostratibus tam firmiter fuerit asserta, ut ανίκητος καϊ ακίνητος hucusque substiterit.“ (Th. posit.-pol. I, 146.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: ... 5. Novatorum, qui dogmatizant: ,Mysterium Trinitatis patriarchis et prophetis suo quodam modo ex peculiari Dei revelatione cognitum fuisse; non tamen ita in libris V. T. contineri, ut a quovis ibi deprehendi aut olim potuerit, aut nunc seposito N. T. possit. Vestigia ibi et indicia potius, quam aperta animumque convincentia dicta, pro Trinitate deprehendi.“ (L. c. q. 3. f. 510.)

Luthardtiüs: ,,Der Schriftbeweis aus dem A. T. . . ruht fast durchweg auf unrichtiger oder gewaltsamer Exegese und überhaupt auf einer ungeschichtlichen Anschauung, welche den allmäligen Gang der Offenbarung verkennt. . . Jene Identificirung aber erklärt sich daraus, dass im Engel Jeh/s Jehovah selbst erscheint. . . Erst das N. T. offenbarte thatsächlich die Gottheit des Messias. . . Das A. T. enthält also nur die Voraussetzungen der trinitarisehen Gotteserkenntniss, weil der trin. Gottesoffenbarung; erst das N. T. brachte mit dieser auch jene.“ (Compend. 3. Aufl. p. 78. sq.)

Kahnisius: ,,Im A. T. tritt die Einheit und Einzigkeit Jhvh,s so entschieden hervor, dass was vom Messias und dem Heiligen Geiste ausgesagt wird, nur den Keim göttlicher Persönlichkeiten in sich trägt.“ (Die luth. Dogm. Zweite Ausg. I, 353.)

Vilmarius: ,,Die alte Dogmatik behauptete zu viel, wenn sie behauptete, es habe nicht allein schon im Gesetz und vor dem Gesetz sich Gott im Vater, Sohn und Geist geoffenbarf, sondern auch die,Kirche des A. T.‘ d. h. die in Gottes Verheissung Feststehenden jener Zeit diese Offenbarung Gottes als Vater, Sohn und Geist gekannt. Weder das Eine noch das Andere kann in dieser Weise zugegeben werden; Gott offenbart sich nicht, ehe er sich offenbart; und das hat Er als Sohn und Geist erst gethan, als der Logos Fleisch geworden war und der Geist war ausgegossen worden. Wo aber eine Offenbarung nicht Statt findet, kann auch Erkenntniss derselben nicht statuiert werden.

Diese Ansicht zerstört die Offenbarung als historischen Prozess, mischt Verheissung und Erfüllung durch einander, die doch von Gott selbst so äusserst scharf auseinander gehalten werden, und gefährdet sogar den Unterschied zwischen Gesetz und Evangelium (!). Gerade das, dass die Juden in Christo das Neue, welches ihnen aber geweissagt worden war, nicht anerkennen wollten, ist der Vorwurf, welchen Christus ihnen macht; nicht (!), dass sie von dem, was sie schon gehabt und erkannt hätten, abfielen.“ (Dogmatik. 1874. 1,275.)

Hofmannus: ,,Das alte Testament lehrt eben so wenig, dass Gott ein in sich mehrfacher sei, als es die Einheit Gottes mit Bezug auf eine Mehrfachheit in ihm lehrt.“

DE DEQ. § 29. Ad pleniorem hujus mysterii declarationem a observandum est: I. Patrem a Filio, Filium a Patre, et Spiritum S. ab utroque realiter b differre, ut revera alius sit Pater, alius Filius, et alius Spiritus S.c Hic tamen nondum terminis ecclesiasticis, sed tantum populari modo proponendam.

Citra mentis nostrae operationem, seu nemine cogitante, aut diversas nomenclaturas animo concipiente. Sic Christus expresse dicit, Patrem esse άλλον, alium a se, Joh. 5, 32. 37., et Spiritum S. παράκλητον, consolatorem sive advocatum fidelium, esse άλλον, alium a se et Patre, Joh. 14, 16.

Idem vero vel ex nominibus Patris et Filii patet, quodque ille ut gignens, hic ut genitus describitur, Ps. 2, 7. Joh. 1, 14. 18. cap. 3, 16., quodque Filius dicitur missus a Patre, cap. 10, 36. Gal. 4, 4., Spiritus Sanctus procedere a Patre, Joh. 15, 26., mitti a Patre, Joh. 14, 26., mitti a Filio, Joh. 15, 26.

Nempe nemo sui ipsius pater est, aut sui ipsius filius. Nemo seipsum generat·, aut a se ipso generatur. Nemo a se ipso procedit, aut mittitur.

Confer b. Mus. Dispp. a. 1649. habb. Disp. III. § 11. 12. 13. p. 57. 58. 59.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Dicti inde veteribus Patripassiani. 2. Arii et Arianorum, qui. . . Patris, Filii et Spiritus S. όμοονσίαν acerrime impugnarunt, unde Ariani etiam Triusiani a Fulgentio dicti sunt. . . 3. Tritheitarum, qui, ut Sabellii haeresin vitarent, tres deos vel tres essentias divinas lingebant, unam essentiantem, duas essentiatas. . . 4.
