Addendi sunt Svoedenborgiani. §

30. Deinde II. observandum est: Non solum Patrem,a sed etiam Filium b et Spiritum Sanctum c esse verum et aeternum Deum.

Nam quod is, quem Scriptura dicit Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, sit verus ac summus Deus, ab omnibus, qui Scripturam recipiunt, hodie conceditur neque adeo hic ulterius probatur.

Probant, Filium esse verum et natura Deum, argumenta varia: I. Quod Scriptura eum expresse Deum vocat (Dei nomen autem,proprie acceptum, est nomen naturae divinae, vid. supra § 3. et not. b. Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. II. 4 PART. I. CAP. I.


### Concerning God: p. 7. 8.), see Acts 20:28, where God is said to have redeemed the church with…

p. 7. 8.), see Acts 20:28, where God is said to have redeemed the church with His own blood. However, Christ, the Son of God, is understood; for the Father and the Holy Spirit do not have blood in their own person; the Son alone, ενσαρχος, has it.

Otherwise, epithets are added, confirming the proper signification, e.g., that Christ, the Son of God, is called the true God (1 John 5:20); that the same, about to appear visibly at some time, is called the great God (Titus 2:13); that He is called God over all, blessed forever (Rom. 9:5) (by which formula the supreme God is described in Rom. 1:25).

From the collation of the sayings of the Scripture of the Old and New Testaments, or that which is said explicitly in the Old Testament concerning the supreme God is explained in the New concerning Christ the Son of God; as, for example, the argument may be: He whom the Israelites tempted in the desert besides Moses is the true and eternal God, which is proved from Num. 21:5, 6. But Christ is He whom the Israelites tempted in the desert besides Moses, according to 1 Cor. 10:9. Therefore, Christ is the true God.

Similarly: He whose glory Isaiah saw (ch. 6:1 sqq.) is the true God. But Christ is He whose glory Isaiah saw (at that time), which is proved from John 12:40, 41. Therefore, He is the true God.

By this reasoning, the following passages can also be compared: Ps. 68:19 with Eph. 4:8. For in the former, He who ascended on high and gave gifts to men, etc., is called God, יה (v. 5), Lord κατ’ ἐξοχήν, אדני (vv. 12, 18, 20), God of Israel (v. 9), from whom those stupendous works performed for the people proceeded (v. 8 sqq.). In the latter, however, that same Christ is declared to have been He.

Likewise, Ps. 97:7, Ps. 45:7, Ps. 102:26, Ps. 110:1 with Heb. 1:6, 8, 9, 10, 13. Indeed, He who in the Psalms 1) is proposed to be worshipped by the angels of God and is expressly called יהוה (v. 1); whose throne 2) is eternal, and He Himself is called God; who 3) is described as having laid the foundations of the earth, created the heavens, and being immutable in His being; and who already before in v. 1 was called by the name יהוה; who 4) is said to sit at the right hand of God: the same is taught in the cited passages to the Hebrews to be the Son of God.

Finally, Isa. 40:3 and Mal. 3:1 with Matt. 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4, John 1:23. Namely, the prophets testify that He for whom the way was to be prepared is יהוה Himself. The evangelists teach that this same one is Christ.

To invent in this matter a subordination, dependence, or similarity, or I know not what else, to be admitted under the name of accommodation, so that it might not be necessary to concede identity and equality, is foreign to the Christian religion. Conf. the blessed Hackspan’s *Disp. de Accommod.* in *Sylloge Dispp.* p. 417.

III. From the generation of the Son by God the Father, an argument arises in this way: Whoever is begotten of the substance of God the Father, He is the true and eternal God. But Christ, the Son of God, is begotten of the substance of God the Father. Therefore.

The major premise is evident from the light of nature, which teaches us that the begetter and the begotten, if they are spoken of properly, are of the same essence; so that it is a contradiction to be begotten of something, speaking properly, and yet not to have the same essence. The minor is proved from John 1:14, 18, ch. 3:16, where Christ is called the Son μονογενής, only-begotten, begotten, I say, without a trope, not precisely beloved, or begotten improperly, adopted, etc. Conf. Rom. 8:32 and John 5:18, where He is called the Son of God ἴδιος, His own.

OF GOD. IV. From the divine attributes (which we see do not differ really from the divine essence, § 5, note b), assigned to Christ, such as: 1) Eternity, described in John 1:1, in that it is an existence ἐν ἀρχῇ, in the beginning (not relatively, by reason of creation or the restoration of men, but absolutely), so that before the λόγος, or Son of God, nothing at all existed, but He Himself existed from the beginning πρὸς τὸν θεόν, with God (the Father), so that neither did the latter exist before the λόγος, but the λόγος coexisted with Him from eternity. Cf. Rev. 1:8, where for the same reason that the eternal God was described previously in v. 4 (see here § 13, note d), it is said of Christ: ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, who is, who was, and who is to come, and it is added under the person of Christ: ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος, and v. 11, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος, lacking a beginning because He is the beginning of all things that are, and having no end because He Himself is the end of all things. Cf. Heb. 1:11, where the eternity of God, described in Ps. 102, is attributed to Christ.

2) Omniscience, John 21:17: Lord, You know all things; cf. ch. 16:30. Likewise, that in Christ are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Col. 2:3, and that Christ is the searcher of hearts (which belongs to none but divine omniscience, see § 15, note e, p. 29 sq.), Matt. 9:4; John 2:24-25; 1 Cor. 4:5.

3) Omnipotence, John 10:28, where He Himself says that no one can snatch His sheep (His faithful ones) out of His hand, namely, because His power surpasses every finite power, and Rev. 1:8, where He is expressly called παντοκράτωρ, omnipotent.

Gerhardus: "Observe that one must prudently distinguish the statements that speak of the communication of the divine essence made to Christ through eternal generation according to the divine nature, from those that speak of the truly divine and infinite gifts communicated to Him personally according to the human nature; meanwhile, however, from the latter class of statements, no less than from the former, the true divinity of Christ can be proven *consequently* and by deduction. For unless the human nature were personally united to the λόγος, i.e., unless Christ in the unity of His person were true God and true man, the human nature could not have been made a participant of that dignity through the communication of idioms." (Exeg. l. IV, § 48.)

V. From the truly divine works (which argue for the divine nature and perfections in the agent), ascribed to Christ as the principal cause; such as: 1) The creation of this universe, ποίησις τῶν πάντων, John 1:3; Col. 1:16, so that not only are all things said to have been produced through Him (just as Paul says he was called through the Father, Gal. 1:1, certainly not as a less principal cause, but as the principal one), but also in the nominative case, He Himself is said to have created all things, Heb. 1:10, from Psalm 102:26: "You, Lord, in the beginning (Son of God, v. 8) founded the earth," etc.

2) The preservation of this universe, as in Col. 1:17, where all created things are said to consist (συνιστάναι) through Him and, lest they fall apart or collapse, to be held together by His power. And Heb. 1:3, He is said to be φέρων τὰ πάντα, upholding or sustaining all things, lest they perish and fall.

3) The resurrection of the dead and those long buried, and that by His own free will, and thus by way of a principal cause, John 5:21, 28-29.

And to this also 4) pertains the crushing of the serpent's head, or the destruction of the kingdom and power of the devil, which is ascribed to the seed of the woman, or the promised Messiah, Gen. 3:15. For this is in truth a divine work, and it had to be the omnipotent God who was to accomplish it; just as the blessed Musaeus also taught and showed that the mystery of the Trinity can be demonstrated from many arguments drawn from the O.T., in his manuscript collection of the Illustrious Questions of Theology, Book on God, Q. I. PART I. CHAP. I.

VI. From the fact that truly divine worship (which God denies He will give to another who is not the true God, Is. 42:8; 48:11) is ascribed to Him, as being equal with God the Father, e.g., John 5:23, where all are commanded to honor the Son, just as, καθὼς, they honor the Father, not by another kind of worship, which could not but be dissimilar. Compare Heb. 1:6 and 8.

Quenstedtius: "Blessed Chemnitius, in *Loci Theologici*, the locus on the Son of God, p. 52 sq., divides the heretics who have impugned the truth of the deity of Christ into three classes. In the first order are the ἀνυπόστατοι, who maintained that the Son of God did not have subsistence before His birth from Mary, but was in the Father, just as a feeling and thinking power is in the soul; such were Ebion and Cerinthus, Paul of Samosata, and Photinus, whom the Muhammadans and Socinians follow today. In the second order are the ἑτεροούσιοι, who acknowledged a nature in Christ more sublime than the human, yet denied that He is ὁμοούσιον and consubstantial with God the Father. The leader of these was Arius in the fourth century. In the third order are the ἀνόμοιοι, who said that Christ was of the same substance as the Father, but not of the same power. Such were Aetius and his disciple Eunomius." (L. c. c. 9. q. 6. f. 524.)

That the Holy Spirit is the true and eternal God is proved likewise: From the sayings of Scripture in which He is expressly called God; just as Peter, in Acts 5:3, says that the one to whom Ananias lied—or rather, the one to whom he had dared to foist his lie as truth—besides the apostles and especially, is the Holy Spirit, but immediately in v. 4 calls Him God Himself. Paul, in 1 Cor. 3:16, 17, says that the faithful are the temple of God by the fact that the Spirit of God dwells in them as in a temple. He indicates, therefore, that the Holy Spirit is God. Compare 2 Sam. 23:2, where David says: "The Spirit of the Lord spoke in me, and His word was upon my tongue." But he adds in v. 3: "The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me," etc. Therefore, He teaches that the same one whom he calls the Spirit of the Lord is the Lord Himself.

From a comparison of the sayings of the Old and New Testaments in this way: He who spoke to Isaiah and commanded him to go to the people, etc., Is. 6:9, is the true and supreme God. But the Holy Spirit is He who spoke to Isaiah, according to Acts 28:25. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is the true God. Similarly: He who spoke through David, Ps. 95:8, 9, 10, 11, is the true and supreme God, according to v. 1 and following up to 7. But the Holy Spirit is He who spoke (those words) through David, which is expressly stated in Heb. 3:7, 8, 9, 10. Therefore, He is the true and supreme God. However, what we warned above in note b. η. II. regarding accommodation must be repeated.

From truly divine attributes, e.g., 1) immensity, which is ascribed to the Holy Spirit in Ps. 139:7: "Whither shall I go from Thy Spirit?" etc., that is, I shall go nowhere where Thy immense Spirit is not. 2) Omniscience, which is attributed to Him in 1 Cor. 2:10, namely, that He searches, ἐρευνᾷ—not that He strives to know successively and with some labor or difficulty, but that He plainly penetrates and, with no one else revealing it, knows by Himself accurately the depths of God, all the secret senses and counsels of the divine mind, so that nothing lies hidden or remains obscure.

p. 7. 8.), vid. Act. 20, 28., ubi Dem dicitur suo sanguine redemisse ecclesiam. Intelligitur autem Christus, Filius Dei; Pater enim et Spiritus S. in sua persona sanguinem non habent, Filius solus ενσαρχος habet.

Item Ps. 97, 7. Ps. 45, 7. Ps. 102, 26. Ps. 110, 1. cum Ebr. 1, 6. 8. 9. 10. 13. Denique Es. 40, 3. et Malach. 3, 1. cum Matih. 3, 3. Marc. 1, 3. Luc. 3, 4. Joh. 1, 23. Scilicet eum, cui via paranda erat, Π'ΐΐτ ipsum esse, testantur prophetae. Hunc autem eundem esse Christum, docent evangelistae.

Fingere autem in hoc negotio subordinationem, dependentium aut similitudinem, aut nescio quid aliud, 8ub nomine accommodationis admittendum, ne necesse sit concedere identitatem et aequalitatem, alienum est a religione christiana. Conf. b. Hackspanii Disp. de Accommod. in Sylloge Dispp. p. 417.

III. Ex generatione Filii a Deo Patre argumentum nascitur hoc modo: Quicunque est genitus de substantia Dei Patris, ille est verus ac aeternus Deus. Atqui Christus, Filius Dei, est genitus de substantia Dei Patris. E.

Major ex lumine naturae evidens est, quod docemur, gignentem et genitum, si proprie dicantur, esse ejusdem essentiae; ita ut contradictio sit, esse genitum ex aliquo, proprie loquendo, nec tamen habere eandem essentiam. Minor probatur ex Joh. 1, 14. 18. c. 3, 16., ubi Christus dicitur Filius μονογενής, unigenitus, genitus, inquam, citra tropum, non praecise dilectus, aut genitus improprie, adoptatus etc. Conf. Rom. 8, 32. et Joh. 5, 18., ubi dicitur Filius Dei ίδιος, proprius.

DE DEO. IV. Ex attributis divinis (quae ab essentia divina realiter non differre, videmus § 5. not. b.), Christo assignatis, qualia sunt: 1) aeternitas, Joh. 1, 1. descripta, quod sit existentia έν άρχ%, in principio (non secundum quid, ratione creationis, aut restaurationis hominum, sed absolute), ita, ut ante λόγον, seu Filium Dei, nihil plane extiterit, ipse vero ab initio extiterit πρύς τυν θεόν, apud Deum (Patrem), ita ut neque hic extiterit ante λόγον, sed λόγος ei ab aeterno coextiterit. Conf. Ebr. 1, 11., ubi aeternitas Dei, Ps. 102. descripta, Christo tribuitur.

2) Omniscientia, Joh. 21, 17.: Domine, tu scis omnia, cf. c. 16, 80. Item quod in Christo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae ac scientiae, Col. 2, 8., quodque Christus est scrutator cordium (quod non nisi divinae omniscientiae est, vid. § 15. not. e. p. 29. sq.), Matth. 9, 4. Joh. 2, 24. 25. 1 Cor. 4, 5.

3) Omnipotentia, Joh. 10, 28., ubi ipse dicit, neminem posse oves suas (fideles suos) e manu sua rapere, nimirum quod potentia sua superet omnem potentiam finitam, et Apoc. 1, 8., ubi expresse dicitur παντοχράτωρ, omnipotens.

Gerhardus: ,,Observa, prudenter quidem distinguenda esse dicta, quae de communicatione divinae essentiae per aeternam generationem juxta divinam naturam Christo facta loquuntur, ab iis, quae de donis vere divinis et infinitis, juxta humanam naturam personaliter ipsi communicatis, loquuntur; interim tamen ex posteriori dictorum genere non minus, quam ex priori, veram Christi divinitatem επομένως et consequenter probari posse. Nisi enim humana natura τώ λόγω esset personaliter unita, h. e., nisi Christus in personae unitate esset verus Deus et verus homo, non potuisset humana natura illius dignitatis per idiomatum communicationem particeps reddi.“ (Exeg. 1. IV. § 48.)

V. Ex operibus vere divinis (quae naturam et perfectiones divinas in operante arguunt), Christo, tanquam causae principali, adscriptis; qualia sunt 1) creatio hujus universi, ποίησις τών πάντων, Joh. 1, 3. Col. 1, 16., ita ut non solum per ipsum omnia producta dicantur (prout per Patrem, non certe ut causam minus principalem, sed principalem, Paulus se vocatum esse dicit Gal. 1, 1.), verum etiam in casu recto, ipse creasse omnia dicatur, Ebr. 1, 10. ex Psalmo 102, 26.: Tu in initio, Domine! (Fili Dei v. 8.) terram fundasti etc.

2) Conservatio hujus universi, prout Col. 1, 17., ubi omnia creata per ipsum consistere (συνιστάναι) ac, ne dilabantur aut concidant, ejus virtute contineri dicuntur. Et Ebr. 1, 3. dicitur ipse ψέρων τά πάντα, portare aut sustinere omnia, ne ruant ac pereant.

3) Resuscitatio mortuorum ac pridem sepultorum, idque pro libera voluntate, adeoque per modum causae principalis, Joh. 5, 21. 28. 29.

Atque huc etiam 4) pertinet contritio capitis serpentis, seu destructio regni et potentiae diaboli, quae semini mulieris, seu Messiae promisso adseribitur, Gen. 3, 15. Est enim hoc revera opus divinum, ac Deum omnipotentem esse oportuit, qui peracturus erat; quemadmodum etiam docuit et, mysterium Trinitatis pluribus ex V. T. petitis argumentis demonstrari posse, ostendit b. Musaeus in Coli. MSto Quaest. illustrium L. de Deo Q. I. PART. I. CAP. I.

VI. Ex eo, quod cultus vere divinus (quem Deus alteri, qui Deus verus non est, se daturum negat, Es. 42, 7. c. 48, 11.) ipsi, tanquam aequali cum Deo Patre, adscribitur, v. g. Joh. 5, 23., ubi jubentur omnes honorare Filium, sicut, ν.αΠώς, honorant Patrem, non alio genere cultus, qui non posset non esse dissimilis. Confer Ebr. 1, 6. et 8.

Quenstedtius: ,,B. Chemnitius in LL. Theol. loc. de Filio Dei p. '52. sq. haereticos, qui veritatem deitatis Christi impugnarunt, in tres classes dispescit. In primo ordine sunt ανυπόστατοι, qui statuerunt, Filium Dei ante suam ex Maria nativitatem non habuisse subsistentiam, sed fuisse in Patre, velut potentia sentiens et intelligens est in anima; tales fuerunt Ebion et Cerinthus, Paulus Samosatenus et Photinus, quos hodie sequuntur Muhammedani et Sociniani. In secundo ordine sunt έτεροονσιοι, qui agnoscebant in Christo naturam sublimiorem, quam humanam, negabant tamen, ipsum Deo Patri esse όμοονσιον et consubstantialem. Horum coryphaeus fuit Arius saeculo quarto. In tertio ordine sunt ανόμοιοι, qui Christum dicebant ejusdem cum Patre substantiae, non autem cum eo potentiae. Tales erant Aetius, ejusque discipulus Eunomius.t( (L. c. c. 9. q. 6. f. 524.)

Spiritum S. esse verum atque aeternum Deum, probatur itidem: Ex dictis Scripturae, quibus diserte vocatur Deus; prout Petrus Act. 5, 3. eum, cui Ananias, praeter apostolos atque inprimis, mentitus, seu cui mendacium suum obtrudere pro vero ausus fuerat, Spiritum Sanctum esse dicit, mox autem v. 4. Deum ipsum appellat. Paulus 1 Cor. 3, 16. 17. fideles dicit esse templum Dei per hoc, quod Spiritus Dei in ipsis tanquam in templo habitet. Indicat ergo Spiritum S. Deum. Conf. 2 Sam. 23, 2., ubi David dicit: Spiritus Domini locutus est in me, et sermo ejus super linguam meam. Addit autem v. 3.: Dixit Deus Israel, mihi locutus est petra Israel etc. Eundem ergo, quem Spiritum Domini dicit, Dominum ipsum esse docet.

Ex collatione dictorum Scripturae V. et N. T. hoc modo: qui locutus est ad Esaiam, et jussit eum ire ad populum etc., Es. 6, 9., is est verus ac summus Deus. Sed Spiritus Sanctus est is, qui locutus est ad Esaiam, ׳juxta Act. 28, 25. Ergo Spiritus S. est verus Deus. Similiter: Qui locutus est per Davidem, Ps. 95, 8. 9. 10. 11., ille est Deus verus ac summus, juxta v. 1. et sqq. ad 7. Atqui Spiritus S. est is, qui locutus est (verba illa) per Davidem, quod expresse dicitur Ebr. 3, 7. 8. 9. 10. Ergo est verus ac summus Deus. Repetenda autem sunt, quae supra in nota b. η. II. de accommodatione monuimus.

Ex attributis vere divinis, v. g. 1) immensitate, quae Spiritui Sancto adscribitur Ps. 139, 7.: Quo ibo a Spiritu tuo? etc., id est, nusquam ivero, ubi non sit Spiritus tuus immensus. 2) Omniscientia, quae illi tribuitur 1 Cor. 2, 10., nempe quod scrutetur, έρευνα, non quod successive et cum labore aut molestia quadam nitatur cognoscere, sed quod plane penetret et, nemine alio revelante, per se ipse accurate cognoscat profunditates Dei, omnia arcana sensa et consilia mentis divinae, ita ut nihil lateat, aut maneat obscurum.


### Concerning God: From truly divine works, e.g., 1) creation, which Job mentions in chapter 33:4,…

From truly divine works, e.g., 1) creation, which Job mentions in chapter 33:4, saying, "The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty..."

[He] has quickened me by [His] power. And David, Ps. 33:6, declares that by the Spirit of the mouth of God all the host of the heavens was made. 2) By the voluntary bestowing and distribution of the spiritual gifts of those who minister—not only common ones, but also extraordinary and highly miraculous ones—which is attributed to the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. 12:11. 3) By the government of the church and the constitution of bishops, or ministers of the church, Acts 20:28. ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of Praxeas, the Sabellians, the Noetians, and the Samosatenes in the second and third centuries, who admitted only one person in the Godhead, and of the Macedonians, who held the Holy Spirit to be merely a certain motion or some created quality. ... 3. Of the Socinians, who most vehemently attack the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit, asserting that 'the Holy Spirit is not a divine person or the supreme God, but is a certain virtue of God, common to the Father and the Son and existing in both—naturally in the Father, but in the Son by the benefit and grace of God.'" (L. c. q. 10, f. 560.) The same: "Antithesis: 1. Of Arius and the Arians, who said that the Holy Spirit is a creature of the Word, i.e., of the Son of God, and thus a κτίσμα κτίσματος, a creature of a creature, as witnessed by Epiphanius and Theodoret. 2. Of the Macedonians, who were specifically called πνευματομάχοι, because they were occupied primarily in attacking the divinity of the Holy Spirit, saying: 'He is a mere creature.'" (L. c. q. 11, f. 564.)

ANTITHESES OF THE MODERNISTS. Kahnisius: "What reason and Scripture demand, an absolute personality, finds its truth in the fundamental doctrine that the Father is the divine primordial personality. ... If the Father is the divine primordial personality, and the Son has proceeded from the divine primordial personality in a mysterious way, then it is already undoubtedly expressed here that the Son is God only in the second sense of the word. ... The symbols and rules of faith express most definitely that the Father is God in the only and proper sense of the word, since they call only Him God." (Die lutherische Dogmatik. First Volume. Second Edition. Leipzig 1874, pp. 351, 361, 399.) "In the New Testament, Jesus Christ, in the consciousness of His pre-worldly existence (John 17:5)—thus not as man, but as the incarnate Logos—calls His Father the only true God (τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεόν), while He expressly distinguishes Himself, the Sent of God, from Him. Where God stands as the subject, the Father is always meant. ... No one (!) will appeal to the passage 1 Tim. 3:16, since the reading θεός has critically fallen (!)." (p. 353.) ... "In the doctrine that the Son and the Spirit have their ground of origin in the Father, it lies with logical necessity that the Father, who has His ground in nothing else (ἀγεννησία), is God in the only sense of the word." (p. 400.) "In and of itself, however, the divine personality of Jesus Christ is not expressed in this name (Son of God). This lies in the attributes which Jesus ascribed to Himself and the apostles ascribed to Him." (p. 360.) "Finally, it lies in the concept of a divine personality which becomes man, in order to carry humanity forever as a nature within itself, that it cannot be equal to the primordial personality, which, unchangeable as it is, cannot take finitude into itself, just as Jesus Christ subordinates Himself to the divine primordial personality not only in individual words (John 5:19 ff., 10:29, 17:3 ff.), but in His entire conduct toward the Father." (p. 362.) "In any case, this mysterious arising of a divine..." PART I. CHAP. I. personal personality, distinct from creation in God, and in the passage Col. 1:15 is only placed alongside creation (!) insofar as the generation of the Son formed the transition to creation.” (p. 361.) “What is certain, however, is that Scripture says nothing about the origin of the Holy Spirit from God. The judgment of the Church concerning the origination of the Spirit, namely that He proceeds (ἐκπορεύεται) from the Father, has its scriptural basis (?) in the words of John 15:26, which, however, as noted, signify the economic procession of the Holy Spirit.” (p. 367.) “People often appeal to the word ὁμοούσιος, which was attributed to the Son at Nicaea and Constantinople. But this word had a very different meaning... This word is only intended to express that the personality of Jesus was of a divine nature in the same way as that of the Father... We see here clearly that the *homousia* was not coordination.” (p. 379, 380.) “It only lies in the concept of every person that he, who is his own 'I' with the powers of thinking, willing, and feeling, possesses the divine attributes in a peculiar way. To have failed to recognize this is a major deficiency of the older theologians. People thought of the attributes as a possession common to the three persons. But how, then, would one want to ascribe to Christ a divine nature that was most intimately united with the human, if this nature was at the same time that of the Father and the Spirit? One was then compelled to proceed to the doctrine of an incarnation of the Godhead, which is, however, contrary to Scripture (!) and Church doctrine (!). If attributes are the moments of the divine personality, but Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct personalities, then each of the three persons must also possess the divine attributes in a particular way.” (p. 404.) “Before the foundation of the world, the Son and the Spirit were with the Father. Whether there was a heavenly time before world-time, when the Son and the Spirit were not yet? Whether the process of begetting and breathing forth ceased with the generation of the Son and the procession of the Spirit? How begetting and breathing forth differ? These are questions that cannot be answered.” (p. 403.) “Since Petavius, the father of the history of dogma, it has been generally conceded that the pre-Nicene fathers subordinated the Son and the Spirit to the Father. To this, however, more recent researchers (Baur, Dorner, Ullmann) have added the certain (!) result that the Nicene (!) fathers also teach a subordination of the Son.” (p. 398.)

The same: “The Father is therefore greater than the Son. The Son, who is God in a way conditioned by the Father, and thus in a secondary way, can never be the Father. Not to be equal to God (ἴσον εἶναι θεῷ), but divine-like being (ἴσα εἶναι θεῷ), i.e., the primordial blessedness of life following from the divine primordial personality (1 Tim. 6:15 [sic]), the pre-human Christ could possibly desire.” (L. c. I, 461.) Hofmann: “According to this most immediate conception, ὁ λόγος is a designation of the proclaimed Jesus Christ and not of a pre-worldly and supra-worldly being.” (Schriftbeweis I, 102.) “The passage (Luke 1:35) states that the child, who gains the beginning of his life in Mary through the power of God, is called the Son of God for that reason. We set this valid explanation regarding the sense in which Jesus is called the Son of God against the dogmaticians who deny that he is so called because of his conception by the Holy Spirit (see Quenstedt, Syst. II, p. 570 sqq.), and who rather distinguish a double *generatio*: a *generatio aeterna*, through which he has that he is the Son of God, and a *generatio temporalis*, through which he has that he is man or the son of man... It is the very man Jesus who, on the basis of the relationship of God to him established with the beginning of his life, calls himself the Son of God and God his Father in an exclusive sense, and [is called so] by...”

His being called the Son of God." (p. 114.) "

Where it (Scripture) speaks of the generation of the Son, we have seen above that it does not mean an eternal, but a historical process. And it is the same with the procession of the 'Holy Spirit.'" (p. 176 sq.) "

If, however, it appears that Scripture teaches the Trinitarian relationship in God as eternal only by teaching it as historical, and that it does not name it according to how it is an eternal relationship, but according to how it is a historical relationship; then the further proof is hereby also provided that, according to Scripture, the inner-divine relationship is not intended to be thought of without the relationship of God to man, and that it is therefore scriptural to teach that the inner-divine relationship exists for the sake of the relationship of God to man, or that God is triune in order to be the God of man. For as a historical relationship we have found it taught in Scripture only in connection with the history taking place between God and man, but as an eternal one only from the perspective of its historicity. Consequently, as an eternal relationship, it stands in the same relation to the eternal will of God, which is fulfilled in the history taking place between God and man, as it does as a historical relationship to this history itself." (p. 177 sq.) "

Thomas had already recognized and greeted the Risen One with the jubilant exclamation: ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου. That this exclamation is intended for Jesus, and cannot be understood as referring to God the Father, no longer needs to be proven... The Lord, whom he had often called by that name, had now become God to him: not in such a way that he recognized the subject ὁ θεός in him, but he gave him the predicate θεός. And he gave it to him in the sense in which it shone forth from the fact of his victory over death." (p. 126.) "

The man Jesus Christ, who, when the world and time had their beginning, was with God, was, of course, God before he became man, and, when the world came into being, mediated its becoming and God's creation through himself. But as Mediator he is designated by δι’ αὐτοῦ, just as it is also said of him that he was with and in such a way God. Because he can and will be distinguished from him who is God, the Father, as the one who has become man in the world and has God as his God, therefore and thus he also wishes to be designated as the mediating one for the relationship of God to the world, and thus to be distinguished from God the Creator. One will, of course, object with the passages where Jehovah and Christ allegedly appear as one and the same person. The most extensive passage of this kind would be the Old Testament citation in Heb. 1:8-9, if the Son were really addressed here as ὁ θεός, since then not only would the Son be named as Jehovah, but he would also be distinguished from Jehovah." (p. 147.) §

Latin:

Ex operibus vere divinis, v. g. 1) creatione, quam Jobus memorat cap. 33, 4., Spiritus Dei, inquiens, fecit me, et spiraculum omni

potentis vivificavit me. Et David Ps. 33, 6. Spiritu oris Dei omnem escercitum coelorum factum esse praedicat. 2) Largitione ac distributione voluntaria, tanquam a causa efficiente principali, donorum spiritualium ministrantium, nec tantum communium, sed etiam extraordinariorum ac valde miraculosorum, quae Spiritui S. tribuitur 1 Cor. 12, 11. 3) Gubernatione ecclesiae et constitutione episcoporum, seu ministrorum ecclesiae, Act. 20, 28. ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Praxeae, Sabellianorum, Noetianorum et Samosatenianorum saeculo secundo et tertio, unam tantum personam in Deitate admittentium, et Macedonianonm, Spiritum S. tantum pro motu quodam vel qualitate aliqua creata habentium. ... 3. Socinianorum, qui vehementissime hypostasin Spiritus S. impugnant, statuentes, ,Spiritum S. non esse personam divinam seu sumfflum Deum, sed esse virtutem quandam Dei, Patri et Filio communem et in utroque existentem, in Patre naturaliter, in Filio vero Dei beneficio et gratia.“ (L. c. q. 10. f. 560.) Idem: ״Antithesis: 1. Arii et Arianorum, qui Spiritum S. creaturam Verbi, i. e., Filii Dei, adeoque κτίσμα κτίσματος, creaturam creaturae dixerunt, teste Epiphanio et Theodoreto. 2. Macedonianorum, qui peculiariter πνενματομάχοι dicti sunt, quod praecipue in oppugnanda Spiritus S. divinitate occupati fuerint, dicentes: ,Eum nudam creaturam esse.‘“ (L. c. q. 11. f. 564.)

ANTITHESES NEOTERICORUM. Kahnisius: ,,Was Vernunft und Schrift fordern, eine absolute Persönlichkeit, findet seine Wahrheit in der Grundlehre, dass der Vater die göttliche Urpersönlichkeit ist. . . Ist der Vater die göttliche UrPersönlichkeit, der Sohn aus der göttlichen Urpersönlichkeit in geheimnissvoller Weise hervorgegangen, so liegt schon hier unzweifelhaft ausgesprochen, dass der Sohn nur in des Wortes zweitem Sinne Gott ist. . . . Die Symbole und Glaubensregeln drücken auf das Bestimmteste aus, dass der Vater Gott in des Wortes einzigem und eigentlichem Sinne ist, indem sie nur ihn Gott nennen.“ (Die lutherische Dogmatik. Erster Band. Zweite Ausgabe. Leipzig 1874. p. 351. 361. 399.),,Im Neuen Testamente nennt Jesus Christus im Bewusstsein seines vorweltlichen Seins (Joh. 17, 5.), also nicht als Mensch, sondern als fleischgewordener Logos, seinen Vater den allein wahren Gott (τον μόνον αληΰινον θεόν), indem er ausdrücklich sich, den Gesandten Gottes, von ihm tintersckeidet. Wo Gott im Subject steht, ist allezeit der Vater gemeint. . . Auf die Stelle 1 Tim. 3, 16. wird sich Niemand (!) berufen, da die Lesart θεός kritisch gefallen (!) ist.“ (p. 353.). . . ,,In der Lehre, dass Sohn und Geist ihren Entstehungsgrund in dem Vater haben, liegt mit logischer Nothwendigkeit, dass der Vater, der in nichts Anderem Grund hat (άγεννησία), Gott in des Wortes einzigem Sinne ist.“ (p. 400.),,An und für sich aber ist in diesem Namen (Sohn Gottes) nicht die göttliche Persönlichkeit Jesu Christi ausgesprochen. Diese liegt in den Attributen, welche Jesus sich, die Apostel ihm zuschrieben.“ (p. 360.),,Endlich liegt in dem Begriffe einer göttlichen Persönlichkeit, welche Mensch wird, um die Menschheit für immer als Natur in sich zu tragen, dass sie nicht gleichstehen kann der Urpersönlichkeit, welche, unveränderlich wie sie ist, die Endlichkeit nicht in sich aufnehmen kann, wie denn. Jesus Christus nicht blos in einzelnen Worten (Joh. 5, 19. ff. 10, 29. 17, 3. ff.), sondern in seinem ganzen Verhalten zum Vater sich der göttlichen Urpersönlichkeit unterordnet.“ (p. 362.),,Jedenfalls ist dieses geheimnissvolle Entstehen einer gött PART. I. CAP. I. lichen Persönlichkeit aus Gott von dem Schaffen verschieden und in der Stelle Kol. 1, 15. mit der Schöpfung nur insofern zusammengestellt (!), als die Zeugung des Sohnes den Uebergang zur Schöpfung bildete.“ (p. 361.),,Was allerdings feststeht, ist, dass die Schrift über die Entstehung des Heiligen Geistes aus Gott nichts sagt. Das Urtheil der Kirche über die Origination des Geistes, dass er nämlich aus dem Vater hervorgeht (εκπορεύεται), hat seinen Schriftgrund (?) in den Worten Joh. 15, 26., welche aber, wie bemerkt, das Ökonomische Ausgehn des Heiligen Geistes bedeuten.“ (p. 367.),,Man beruft sich oft auf das Wort όμοοΰσιος, welches zu Nicäa und Constantinopel dem Sohne beigelegt ward. Allein dieses Wort war von sehr verschiedener Bedeutung. . . Dies Wort soll nur ausdrücken, dass die Persönlichkeit Jesu in gleicher Weise wie die des Vaters göttlicher Art war... Wir sehen hier deutlich, dass die Homousie nicht Coordination war.“ (p. 379. 380.),,Nur liegt es im Begriffe jeder Person, dass sie, die ein eigenes Ich ist mit den Kräften des Denkens, Wollens, Fühlens, die göttlichen Eigenschaften in eigentümlicher Weise hat. Dies verkannt zu haben, ist ein grösser Mangel der älteren Theologen. Man dachte sich die Eigenschaften als einen den drei Personen gemeinsamen Besitz. Wie aber wollte man dann wieder Christo eine göttliche Natur zuschreiben, die auf das Innigste mit der menschlichen verbunden war, wenn diese Natur zugleich die des Vaters und Geistes war? Man war dann genöthigt, zur Lehre einer Menschwerdung der Gottheit fortzugehen, die doch gegen Schrift- (!) und Kirchenlehre (!) ist. Sind Eigenschaften die Momente der göttlichen Persönlichkeit, Vater, Sohn und Geist aber besondere Persönlichkeiten, so muss auch jede der drei Personen die göttlichen Eigenschaften in besonderer Weise haben.“ (p. 404.),,Vor Grundlegung der Welt waren Sohn und Geist beim Vater. Ob vor der Weltzeit eine himmlische Zeit war, da Sohn und Geist noch nicht waren? Ob der Process des Zeugens und Hauchens erloschen ist mit der Erzeugung des Sohnes und dem Hervorgehen des Geistes? Wie sich Zeugen und Hauchen unterscheiden? Das sind Fragen, die sich nicht beantworten lassen.“ (p. 403.),,Seit Petavius, dem Vater der Dogmengeschichte, ist allgemein zugestanden, dass die vornicänischen Väter Sohn und Geist dem Vater untergeordnet haben. Dazu haben aber neuere Forscher (Baur, Dorner, Ullmann) das sichere (!) Resultat gefügt, dass auch die nicänischen (!) Väter eine Subordination des Sohnes lehren.“ (p. 398.)

Idem: ,,Der Vater ist also grösser als der Sohn. Nie kann der Sohn, welcher in durch den Vater bedingter, somit secundärer Weise Gott ist, der Vater sein. Nicht gleich Gott sein (Ισον ηνηι θεώ), sondern gottgleiches Sein (Ισα είναι θε<ρ) d. h. die aus der göttlichen Urpersönlichkeit folgende Urseligkeit des Lebens (1 Tim. 5, 15.) konnte möglicher Weise der vormenschliche Christus begehren.“ (L. c. I, 461.) Hofmannus: ,,Zufolge dieser allernächst liegenden Auffassung ist ό λόγος Bezeichnung des verkündigten Jesus Christus und nicht eines vorweltlichen und überweltlichen Wesens.“ (Schriftbeweis I, 102.),,Die Stelle (Luk. 1, 35.) besagt, dass das Kind, welches durch Machtwirkung Gottes in Maria seines Lebens Anfang gewinnt, um dess willen Gottes Sohn heisst. Wir stellen diese gültige Erklärung über den Sinn, in welchem Jesus Gottes Sohn genannt wird, den Dogmatikern entgegen, welche leugnen, dass er um seiner Empfängniss aus Heiligem Geiste willen so heisse (s. Quenstedt, Syst. II, p. 570. sqq.), und welche vielmehr eine doppelte generatio unterscheiden, eine generatio aeterna, per quam habet, quod est Filius D., und eine generatio temporalis, per quam habet, quod est homo aut filius hominis. . . Eben der Mensch Jesus ist es, welcher auf Grund des mit seinem Lebensanfange gesetzten Verhältnisses Gottes zu ihm sich selbst Gottes Sohn und Gott seinen Vater in ausschliesslichem Sinn nennt, und von den

Seinen der Sohn Gottes genannt wird.“ (p. 114.) ״

Wo sie (die Schrift) von der Zeugung des Sohnes spricht, haben wir oben gesehen, dass sie nicht einen ewigen, sondern einen geschichtlichen Vorgang meint. Und eben so verhält es sich mit dem Ausgehen des,Heiligen Geistes.“ (p. 176. sq.),,

Wenn sich nun aber darstellt, dass die Schrift das trinitarische Verhältniss in Gott als ewiges nur lehrt, indem als geschichtliches, und dass sie es nicht nach dem benennt, wie es ewiges, sondern nachdem, wie es geschichtliches Verhältniss ist; so ist hiemit auch schon der weitere Erweis geliefert, dass nach der Schrift das innergöttliche Verhältniss nicht ohne das Verhältniss Gottes zum Menschen gedacht sein will, und dass es also schriftmässig ist, zu lehren, das innergöttliche Verhältniss sei für das Verhältniss Gottes zum Menschen, oder, Gott sei dreieinig, um der Gott des Menschen zu sein. Denn als geschichtliches haben wir es in der Schrift nur im Zusammenhange mit der zwischen Gott und dem Menschen sich begebenden Geschichte, als ewiges aber nur von seiner Geschichtlichkeit aus gelehrt gefunden. Folglich steht es als ewiges in gleicher Beziehung zu dem ewigen Willen Gottes, welcher sich in der zwischen Gott und dem Menschen sich begebenden Geschichte vollbringt, wie als geschiehtliches zu dieser Geschichte selbst.“ (p. 177. sq.),,

Schon den Auferstandenen hatte Thomas mit dem jubelnden Zuruf erkannt und begrüsst: b κύριός μου και ό θεός μου. Dass dieser Zuruf Jesu gelten will, und nicht von Gott dem Vater verstanden werden kann, braucht man nicht mehr zu beweisen. . . Der Herr, den er oft so genannt hatte, war ihm jetzt Gott geworden: nicht so, dass er in ihm das Subject ό θεός erkannte, sondern das Prädicat θεός gab er ihm. Und zwar gab er es ihm in dem Sinne, in welchem es aus der Thatsache seines Sieges über den Tod hervorleuchtete.“ (p. 126.),,

Der Mensch Jesus Christus, welcher, als Welt und Zeit ihren Anfang nahmen, bei Gott war, ist selbstverständlich, ehe er Mensch geworden, Gott gewesen, und hat, als die Welt geworden, ihr Werden und Gottes Schaffen vermittelt durch sich selbst. Als Mittler aber wird er bezeichnet durch δι’ αΰτηϋ, gleichwie es auch von ihm heisst, dass er bei und solchergestalt Gott gewesen. Weil er von dem, welcher Gott ist, dem Vater, unterschieden werden kann und will, als der in der Welt Mensch geworden ist und Gott zu seinem Gotte hat, darum und somit will er auch für das Verhältniss Gottes zu der Welt als der vermittelnde bezeichnet, und so von Gott dem Schöpfer unterschieden sein. Man wird nun freilich die Stellen entgegen halten, wo angeblich Jehova und Christus als eine und dieselbe Person erscheinen. Die ausgiebigste Stelle der Art wäre die alttestamentliche Anführung Hebr. 1, 8. 9., wenn hier wirklich der Sohn mit b θεός angeredet würde, indem dann nicht blos der Sohn als Jehova benannt, sondern auch von Jehova unterschieden wäre.“ (pag. 147.) §


### Concerning God: Finally, III. it is to be observed that the Father, the Son, and the Holy…

31. Finally, III. it is to be observed that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three Gods, but one God. Indeed, we have already taught above in § 8 that God is one, and that there is no other besides Him. Therefore, having shown in the meantime that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the true God, it is immediately evident that they are one God, not several gods.

Quenstedtius: "God is not divided into three persons, but the three persons, distinct among themselves, participate indivisibly in that one essence, which is numerically undivided and infinite; so that each person [possesses] the same essence..." PART I. CHAP. I.

have it without its multiplication or division; for in this mystery is given ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος, another and another, ὑποστατικῶς (hypostatically), not ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο, one thing and another, οὐσιωδῶς (essentially).” (L. c. s. 1. th. 20. f. 469.)

Calovius: “The catholic faith concerning the Trinity is not precisely situated in this formula of speaking, that there are three persons in that one divine essence, but in this, that we sincerely believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, yet in such a way that the Father is not the Son, but another than the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son, but another than the Father and the Son; according to the Athanasian Creed, the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, and yet there are not three Gods, but one is God, so that we may venerate both the Unity in the Trinity and the Trinity in the Unity in all things.” (System, loc. th. Tom. III, p. 4.)

J. Gerhardus: “The persons of the Trinity are indeed really, nay, most really distinct from one another, but in such a way that each of the persons is that whole divine essence and none of them is any part of it. For God subsists in three persons, he is not composed of them.” (Enchir. th. 1662. p. 76. sq.)

Hollazius: “The Socinians urge: In whatever the whole essence of God is, in that the whole Trinity is. But in each divine person, etc. Therefore. I answer: In that in which the whole essence of God is under all three modes of subsistence, in that the whole Trinity is, I grant. But one divine person has the essence of God not under three, but under one mode of subsistence. For God the Father subsists ἀγεννήτως (unbegottenly), the Son of God γεννητῶς (begottenly), the Holy Spirit ἐκπορευτῶς (proceedingly).” (Exam. th. P. I. c. 2. q. 55. p. 347.) §

32. In order to express this mystery more distinctly and to exclude the sophistries of heretics, the ancient Christians said—the Western or Latin ones, that there are three persons in one divine essence; the Eastern or Greek ones, that there are τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις καὶ μίαν οὐσίαν (three hypostases and one essence); just as the Nicene fathers specifically decreed concerning the Son, that He is or ought to be acknowledged as ὁμοούσιον (homoousion) to the Father, that is, coessential or consubstantial. This was done so that, while the unity of God remains, the real distinction between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as being of the same nature and equal in dignity, might be signified in manifest terms.

Gerhardus: “The rashness of those who use new terms not yet received by the Church in explaining this mystery is not to be approved. We seek the reason: 1. From the precept of the Apostle in 1 Tim. 6:20: ‘Keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding τὰς βεβήλους κενοφωνίας, profane novelties of words.’ (Some read κενοφωνίας [empty sounds], as there is the greatest kinship between these words and the things signified, new things very often being also vain, Acts 17:21.) 2. From the manifold inconvenience that follows that rashness. For an occasion for slandering is given to adversaries, seeds of dissension are scattered in the Church, a suspicion of singularity arises, etc. On the contrary, it is the mark of a moderate mind not only to think reverently with the Church but also to speak so, and it is the mark of obedient children not to disdain the voice of their mother. Augustine, lib. X. de Civitate Dei c. 23: ‘Philosophers speak with free words, nor do they fear offending religious ears in matters that are difficult to understand; but for us, it is right to speak according to a fixed rule, lest the license of words should beget an impious opinion even concerning the things which are signified by them.’”

Luther: "It is perhaps not exquisite German, nor does it sound fine, to call God by the word 'Trinity' (just as the Latin *Trinitas* does not sound exquisite), but because we have nothing better, we must speak as we can. For (as I have said) this article is so high above human understanding and language that God, as a Father, must graciously overlook it when his children stammer and babble as best they can, provided only that the faith is pure and right. For one still intends to say this much with this word: that it is to be believed that the divine Majesty is three distinct persons of one, true essence." (Kirchenpostille. Ep. D. Trin. XII, 830.)

Some of whom have said that only the Father is the true God, that the Son is a creature, and that the Holy Spirit is a creature made through the Son, or a gift of God in men; others have maintained that only diverse names are attributed to that one and eternal God on account of different respects, but that in reality the Father is the Son and the Holy Spirit himself, both using various sought-out evasions by which they might withdraw themselves from the light of the sayings of Scripture and defend and commend their errors. For although the Greeks and Latins contended among themselves for some time, and the former thought that by the name of *persona* among the Latins an office or external habit was designated, and therefore that three persons did not import or express a real distinction of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, while the Latins thought that υπόστασις denoted in the nominative case the essence itself, so that, by admitting three ύποστάσεις, three essences must be posited: yet afterwards, when they had understood one another more correctly, it came about that the Greeks said τρία πρόσωπα and the Latins three hypostases.

Luther: "We have had to use the little word 'person,' just as the Fathers also used it; for we have no other." (Ad Joh. 1, 2. VII, 1407.) Or, one who is of one and the same essence with another, not in species, but in number. For the divine essence is not multipliable after the manner of a species in several individuals, but is unique and most singular. And therefore the Son, being ὁμοούσιος with the Father, must be of the same essence in number with the Father, not in species; although otherwise, things that are the same in number are also one in species, namely, where a nature capable of multiplication in several has a place. See what I have discussed in *Disp. de concilio Nicaeno* § 72 sqq. to 78 and *Disp. de Paulo Samosateno* cap. IV. § ult. p. 55, 56.

Scharffius: "A numerical one is called one in number, which is counted as one, and is therefore determined by numerical unity. Thus every individual is called one in number; such as Peter, this man, this whiteness, Bucephalus. It is called an individual, singular, 'this something' one. By others it is defined thus: One in number is that which is so one that, according to its being, it cannot as a whole be divided into several entities of the same kind as itself. —

Things are said to be one in genus which are under one genus, whether proximate or remote; or which agree in the same genus and have opposite differences, such as species. Thus man and beast are one in genus, namely, in animal; thus temperance and fortitude are one in genus, namely, in virtue; thus heaven and the elements are one by reason of body. Things are one in species whose essence and definition is one, or which have the same specific nature. Thus all men are one in species. Similarly, this or that horse are said to be one in specific essence, although in number they are several individuals." (Metaphys. p. 44, 48.) PART I. CHAPTER I.

Luther: "Homoousios means one and the same essence or nature, or one and not two essences, as the Fathers had established in the Council and as is sung in Latin, Consubstantialis, which some later called Coexistentialis or Coessentialis.

The Arians had accepted this at the Council of Nicaea and still accept it when they have to speak before the Emperor and the Fathers.

But among their own, they fought against it exceedingly hard; they pretended that such a word was not in the Scripture, held many councils, even during the times of Constantine, so that they might weaken the Council of Nicaea, caused much misfortune, and later made our people so anxious that even Saint Jerome, confounded by it, wrote a lamentable letter to the Bishop of Rome, Damasus, and began to request that such a word, Homoousios, should be scratched out.

For I do not know (he says) what kind of poison is in the letter that the Arians make themselves so uselessly agitated over it. And there is still extant a dialogue in which Athanasius and Arius argue before an official, Probus, over this word Homoousios.

And when Arius pressed hard upon it, that such a word was not in the Scripture, Athanasius in turn caught Arius with the same art and said: 'These words are also not in the Scripture: innascibilis, ingenitus Deus, that is, God is unbegotten,' which the Arians had used to prove that Christ could not be God because He was begotten, but God was unbegotten, etc. And the official Probus judges against Arius.

For it is indeed true, one should teach nothing outside of Scripture in divine matters, as St. Hilary writes in Book 1 of De Trinitate. That means nothing other than that one should teach nothing else.

But that one should not use more or other words than those that stand in the Scripture, that cannot be maintained, especially in dispute and when heretics want to falsify matters with blind grasps and pervert the words of Scripture; there it was necessary that one should grasp the meaning of Scripture, which is set forth in many passages, into a short and summary word, and ask whether they held Christ to be homoousios, as is the meaning of Scripture in all the words which they perverted with false glosses among their own, but had freely confessed before the Emperor and in the Council.

Just as if the Pelagians wanted to trap us with the word 'original sin' or 'Adam's plague,' because such words do not stand in the Scripture; yet the Scripture powerfully teaches the meaning of those same words, as: that we are conceived in sin, Ps. 51:7, all by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2:3, and all must be sinners because of one man's sin, Rom. 5:12." (On Councils and the Church. 1539. XVI, 2702. sqq.)

Latin:

31. Denique III. observandum est, Patrem, Filium et Spiritum S. non esse tres Deos, sed Deum unum. Nempe jam supra § 8. docuimus, Deum esse unum, et praeter illum non esse alium. Itaque ostenso interim, quod Pater, Filius et Spiritus S. sint verus Deus, jam statim constat, quod sint unus Deus, non dii plures.

Quenstedtius: ,,Deus non dividitur in tres personas, sed tres personae inter se distinctae unicam illam numero essentiam indivisam et infinitam indivisim participant; ita ut quaelibet persona eandem essen PART. I. CAP. I.

tiam habeat sine ejus multiplicatione aut divisione; in hoc enims mysterio datur άλλος καϊ άλλος, alius atque alius, νποστατικως, non άλλο■ καί άλλο, aliud atque aliud, ονσιωάώς.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 20. f. 469.)

Calovius: ,,Fides catholica de Trinitate non in hac loquendi formula praecise sita est, quod tres sint personae in una illa divina essentia, sed in eo, ut sincere credamus, Patrem, Filium et Spiritum S. unumesse Deum, ita tamen, ut Pater non sit Filius, sed alius a Filio, nec Sp. S. sit Pater vel Filius, sed alius a Patre et Filio; juxta Symbolum Athanasii, Deus est Pater, Deus Filius, Deus Sp. S., et tamen non tres Dii, sed unus est Deus, ut per omnia et Unitatem in Trinitate et Trinitatem in Unitate veneremur.“ (System, loc. th. Tom. III, p. 4.)

J. Ebartus: ,,Personae Trinitatis sunt quidem realiter, imo realissime a se invicem distinctae, sed ita, ut quaelibet personarum tota illa essentia divina et nulla earum aliqua ejus pars sit. Deus enim ׳in tribus· personis subsistit, non ex illis componitur.“ (Enchir. th. 1662. p. 76. sq.)

Hollazius: ,,Sociniani instant: In quocunque est tota essentia Dei, in illo tota est Trinitas. Atqui in qualibet persona divina etc. E. Respondeo: In quo est tota essentia Dei sub omnibus tribus subsistendi modis, in illo est tota Trinitas, concedo. At una persona divina habet essentiam Dei non sub tribus, sed uno subsistendi modo. Subsistit enim D. Pater άγεννήτως, F. D. γεννήτυς, Sp. S. εκπηρεντως (Exam. th. P. I. c. 2. q. 55. p. 347.) §

32. Ad mysterium hoc distinctius exprimendum a et exeludendas haereticorum sophisticationes b dixerunt christiani veteres, occidentales quidem seu Latini, tres esse personas in una essentia divina, orientales autem sive Graeci, esse τρεις υποστάσεις xai μίαν ονσίαν;c queinadmodum peculiariter patres Nicaeni de Filio statuerunt, eum esse seu agnosci debere Patri ομοονσιον, id est coessentialem aut consubstantialem.d Scilicet ut, stante unitate Dei, distinctio realis inter Patrem, Filium et Spiritum Sanctum, tanquam ejusdem naturae ac aequalia dignitatis, manifestis terminis significaretur.

Gerhardus: ,,Non est probanda eorum temeritas, qui novis vocabulis ab ecclesia nondum receptis in hoc mysterio explicando utuntur. Rationem petimus: 1. a praecepto apostoli 1 Tim. 6, 20.: ,Depositum custodi, devitans τάς βεβήλονς κηη·οή>ωνίας, profanas vocum novitates.‘ (Quidam legunt κενοψωνίας, ut inter has voces, ita inter res significatas est maxima cognatio, nova persaepe etiam vana, Act. 17, 21.) 2. Ab incommodo multiplici, quod illam temeritatem sequitur. Datur enim adversariis calumniandi occasio, sparguntur semina dissensionum in ecclesia, singularitatis oritur suspicio etc. Contra vero moderati animi est, cum ecclesia non solum reverenter sentire, sed etiam loqui, ac obsequentium liberorum est, matris vocem non dedignari. Augustinus lib. X. de Civitate Dei c. 23.: ,Liberis verbis loquuntur philosophi, nec in rebus ad intelligendum difficillimis offensionem religiosarum aurium pertimescunt; nobis autem ad certam regulam loqui fas est, ne verborum licentia etiam de rebus, quae his significantur, impiam gignat opinionem.‘“

Lutherus: ״Es ist wohl nicht ein köstlich Deutsch, lautet auch nicht fein, Gott also zu nennen mit dem Wort: Dreifaltigkeit (wie auch das lateinische Trinitas nicht köstlich lautet), aber weil man,s nicht besser hat, müssen wir reden, wie wir können. Denn (wie ich gesagt habe) dieser Artikel ist so hoch über menschlichen Verstand und Sprache, dass Gott als ein Vater seinen Kindern muss zu gute halten, dass wir stammeln und lallen, so gut wir können, so nur der Glaube rein und recht ist. Denn man will dennoch soviel mit diesem Worte sagen, dass da soll gegläubet werden, dass die göttliche Majestät sei drei unterschiedene Personen einigen, wahrhaftigen Wesens.“ (Kirchenpostille. Ep. D. Trin. XII, 830.)

Quorum alii dixerunt, solum Patrem esse verum Deum, Filium esse creaturam, Spiritum Sanctum esse creaturam per Filium factam, aut donum Dei in hominibus; alii, tantum diversa nomina uni illi atque aeterno Deo propter diversos respectus tribui, revera autem Patrem esse ipsum Filium ac Spiritum Sanctum, statuerunt, utrique variis quaesitis effugiis, quibus luci dictorum Scripturae se subducerent atque errores suos tuerentur et commendarent. Quamvis enim Graeci et Latini aliquamdiu inter se contenderint, atque illi quidem putaverint, nomine personae apud Latinos designari officium aut habitum externum, ac propterea tres personas non importare aut exprimere realem distinctionem Patris, Filii et Spiritus Sancti, Latini vero putarent, υπόστασή denotare in casu recto ipsam essentiam, ut, admissis tribus ύποστάσεσι, statuendae sint tres essentiae: postea tamen, cum se invicem rectius intellexissent, factum est, ut Graeci dicerent τρία πρόσωπα et Latini tres hypostases.

Lutherus: ״Wir haben das Wörtlein,Person‘ müssen gebrauchen, wie es denn die Väter auch gebrauchet haben; denn wir haben kein anderes.“ (Ad Joh. 1, 2. VII, 1407.) Seu, qui est unius et ejusdem, non specie, sed numero, essentiae cum alio. Neque enim essentia divina multiplicabilis est ad modum speciei in pluribus individuis, sed unica et singularissima. Ideoque Filium, Patri ύμυυήσων, ejusdem numero cum Patre essentiae esse oportet, non specie; licet alias, quae idem sunt numero, etiam specie unum sint, nempe ubi natura multiplicabilis in pluribus locum habet. Vid., quae disserui in Disp. de concilio Nicaeno $ 72. sqq. ad 78. et Disp. de Paulo Samosateno cap. IV. § ult. p. 55. 56.

Scharffius: ״Unum numerale dicitur unum numero, quod numeratur ut unum, adeoque unitate numerica determinatum est. Sic omne individuum dicitur unum numero; ut Petrus, hic homo, haec albedo, Bucephalus. Vocatur unum individuale, singulare, hoc aliquid. Ab aliis ita definitur: Unum numero est, quod ita unum est, ut secundum suum esse totum non possit dividi in plures entitates, quale ipsum est. —

Unum genere dicuntur, quae sunt sub uno genere, sive proximo, sive remoto; vel quae conveniunt in eodem genere et habent oppositas differentias, ut species. Sic homo et bestia unum sunt genere, nempe in animali; sic temperantia et fortitudo sunt unum genere, nempe virtute; sic coelum et elementa unum sunt ratione corporis. Unum specie sunt, quorum essentia et definitio est una seu quae habent eandem naturam specificam. Sic omnes homines sunt unum specie. Similiter hic vel iste equus dicuntur unum in essentia specifica, licet numero sunt plura individua.“ (Metaphys. p. 44. 48.) PART. I. CAP. I.

Lutherus: ,,Homoousius heisst einerlei Wesen oder Natur oder einerlei und nicht zweierlei Wesen, wie die Väter im Concilio hatten gesetzt und im Latein gesungen wird, Consubstantialis, etliche Coexistentialis, Coessentialis hernach nenneten.

Solches hatten sie (die Arianer) zu Nicäa im Concilio angenommen und nehmens noch an, wo sie vor dem Kaiser und Vätern reden mussten.

Aber bei den Ihren fochten sie es überaus hart an; gaben vor, solch Wort stünde in der Schrift nicht, hielten viel Concilia, auch noch bei Constantini Zeiten, damit sie das Concilium zu Nicäa schwächen möchten, richteten viel Unglücks an, machten hernach den Unsern so bange, dass auch Sanct Hieronymus, drüber verstürzt, einen kläglichen Brief schrieb an den Bischof zu Rom, Damason, und fing an zu begehren, dass man solch Wort, Homoousius, sollte auskratzen.

Denn ich weiss nicht (spricht er), was doch für ein Gift in dem Buchstaben sei, dass sich die Arianer so unnütz darüber machen. Und ist noch vorhanden ein Dialogus, darin Athanasius und Arius zanken vor einem Amtmann, Probus, über diesem Wort Homoousius.

Und als Arius hart darauf drang, es stünde solch Wort in der Schrift nicht, Athanasius wiederum mit derselben Kunst Arium fing und sprach: ,Es stehen diese Worte auch nicht in der Schrift: innascibilis, ingenitus Deus, das ist, Gott ist ungeboren‘, welches die Arianer hatten gebraucht, zu beweisen, dass Christus nicht könnte Gott sein, weil er geboren wäre, Gott aber wäre ungeboren, etc. Und der Amtmann Probus urtheilt wider Arium.

Denn es ist ja wahr, man soll ausser der Schrift nichts lehren in göttlichen Sachen, wie St. Hilarius schreibet 1. de Trinit. Das meinet sich nicht anders, denn man soll nichts anders lehren.

Aber dass man nicht sollte brauchen mehr oder andere Worte, weder in der Schrift stehen, das kann man nicht halten, sonderlich im Zank und wenn die Ketzer die Sachen mit blinden Griffen wollen falsch machen und der Schrift Worte verkehren; da war vonnöthen, dass man die Meinung der Schrift, so mit vielen Sprüchen gesetzt, in ein kurz und Summarienwort fassete, und fragte, ob sie Christum homoousion hielten, wie der Schrift Meinung in allen Worten ist, welche sie mit falschen Glossen bei den Ihren verkehreten, aber vor dem Kaiser und im Concilio frei bekennet hatten.

Gleich als wenn uns die Pelagianer wollten gefahren mit diesem Wort,Erbsünde‘, oder,Adamsseuche‘, weil solche Worte in der Schrift nicht stehen; so doch die Schrift derselben Worte Meinung gewaltiglich lehret, als: dass wir in Sünden empfangen, Ps. 51, 7., alle von Natur des Zornes Kinder, Eph. 2, 3., und alle um eines Sünde willen Sünder sein müssen, Röm. 5, 12.“ (Von Conciliis und Kirchen. 1539. XVI, 2702. sqq.)


### Concerning God: Gerhard: "It cannot be approved simply and without an added convenient…

Gerhard: "It cannot be approved simply and without an added convenient interpretation, what Calvin writes in Book 1 of the Institutes, ch. 13, s. 15: 'Would that these names (Trinity, ὁμοουσίας, etc.) were buried, provided only that this faith were agreed upon among all, that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God.' Doubtless, that is to be understood regarding the occasion and origin of these appellations, which was heretical perversity, but not regarding the use of the appellations themselves." (L. c. § 43.) §

33. By the name of essence or οὐσίας is understood the divine nature itself, such as it is in itself absolutely, and which, together with the attributes, is most simply one and singular, and thus also is not but one of the three persons. According to those things which we said in § 5. sqq.

b) Indeed, in such a way that there is also one intellect of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, by which they understand; one will of the three, by which they will; and one power, by which they work outside the divine essence. Cf. John 5:19.

Chemnitius: "The essence of men is something communicable, but it is a universal name, which does not truly exist by itself, but is gathered only by cognition and comprehended by the intellect. The essence in divine things, however, is not something imaginary, like a genus or species, but it truly exists, even though it is communicable. Augustine expressed this elegantly. 'Essence,' he says, 'is predicated of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, not as a genus of species, nor as a species of individuals, nor as a whole of parts, but in another ineffable and incomprehensible way.' For in this whole article, that rule of Augustine must be diligently observed: 'If you cannot find what God is, yet beware of thinking about Him what He is not.' The Church therefore understands by the name of essence not a universal name, as philosophers name human essence, but the divine nature truly existing, which is communicable and common to the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and is whole in each. And this is only a definition of the name, says Nazianzen. But what it is, regarding the definition of the thing, I say this is unknown, except that we say the attributes placed in the definition of God are the very essence of God." (L. th. de Deo in specie, c. 2. s. 4. f. 36 sq.)

Quenstedtius: "Ουσία and φύσις are taken here for the same thing; 'πᾶσα γὰρ οὐσία φύσις λέγεται,' says Aristotle, IV Metaphys. The synonyms of the divine οὐσία in the Scriptures are: θεία φύσις, 'divine nature,' 2 Pet. 1:4; θεότης, 'deity,' Col. 2:9; θειότης, 'divinity,' Rom. 1:20. But the most common appellation of the οὐσία τοῦ θεοῦ and the divine essence among the doctors of the Church is [essence]. The word οὐσία does not exist in the Holy Scriptures; nevertheless, because it was according to the mind of Holy Scripture, it was used by the orthodox fathers in the Nicene synod, and thus later explained in the Chalcedonian, so that φύσις might denote more than οὐσία. For essence is the simple constitution of any thing, lacking all its properties and accidents; nature or φύσις is the essence already clothed with and joined to those properties of its own. Therefore the fathers said that in the one person of Christ there are not only the simple οὐσίαι themselves, namely the divine and the human, but also that there are φύσεις, i.e., the essences themselves joined together with their true properties." (L. c. s. 1. th. 6. f. 459.)

Dannhauerus: "He taught the distinction between essence and person... both here and in the article concerning the person of Christ; as in the former there are three persons in one essence, so here one person in two natures has been revealed from heaven." (Hodos. Phaen. 3. B. p. 93.)

Gerhardus: "They preferred to use the name of essence rather than substance: a. To indicate that God is an οὐσίαν ὑπερούσιον, not included in the categories, among which the first is substance. Damascenus lib. I. c. 12: 'God is a certain infinite ocean of substance.' See 1. de nat. Dei § 32. b. Because God does not underlie accidents, as do the essences of created things, but the attributes are His very essence. c. Because the name of substance is ambiguous, for sometimes it is put for οὐσία, but sometimes for ὑπόστασις. Thus Hilary in his book de synod. says, 'there are three substances in God,' i.e., persons, in which sense some also take what is said in the Latin version of Heb. 1:3, that the Son is the character of the substance of the Father." (Exeges. 1. III. § 60.) §

34. By the name of person or ὑπόστασις, just as elsewhere an intelligent suppositum is signified, so in this place it is indicated that three PART I. CHAP. I.

are subsistences or personalities in one divine essence, and thus three supposita, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Huelsemannus: "It is to be noted, as far as ecclesiastical writers are concerned, that hardly two or three of them have used those terms ουσίας, ΰποστάσεως, and persona with a perpetual and single meaning." (Praelectt. in F. C. p. 258.)

By this name we embrace the nature, as the material, and its subsistence, as the formal.

But if you should further ask what the Latin word persona or suppositum imports in the nominative case, whether the nature itself or the subsistence, a difficulty will occur on both sides. For if the former is said, it does not appear how, once three persons are admitted in the one essence of God, it can subsequently be denied that there are three natures or three divine essences. If the latter is admitted, this seems to be the same as if you were to say that "the black" in the nominative case denotes blackness itself.

Therefore, perhaps it must be said that persona in the nominative case imports something compounded of nature and subsistence, just as elsewhere in the concept of a material composite of matter and substantial form, neither part of the composite is placed in the nominative case. See the blessed D. Petrus Musaeus, Introd. in Loc. de persona Christi § 43 et sqq.

As far as the Greeks are concerned, the word ΰποστάσεως denotes for them sometimes subsistence itself, and sometimes a suppositum or person; just as certain Latins have sometimes used the word substantia when they defined a person by substance; although we are otherwise accustomed to call the nature itself by the name of substance.

Scharffius: "Suppositum and persona are almost one and the same. At least they differ by reason of the nature or subject. So that suppositum is common, and obtains in all complete substances that subsist ultimately by themselves, i.e., independently, whether they are rational or irrational. But persona is only in rational and intelligent natures that subsist completely, such as in men, angels, and in God. ... Therefore, persona is stricter than suppositum." (Metaphys. p. 252.)

Conf. Aug.: "They use the name persona in that signification in which ecclesiastical writers have used it in this cause, so that it signifies not a part or a quality in another, but that which properly subsists [that which exists by itself]." (Art. 1.)

Quenstedtius: "The word ΰποστάσεως is taken either concretely and materially, insofar as it implies the thing itself and the mode of the thing at the same time and denotes the essence marked with a hypostatic character, i.e., a person, in which sense Christ is called χαρηκτήρ τής ΰποστάσεως θεον, i.e., of the Father, Heb. 1:3—or abstractly and formally, insofar as it designates personality or subsistence itself, which is the act, mode, or ultimate degree by which an intelligent nature subsists completely and incommunicably, which the Greeks call τρόπον ΰπάρζεως, the ultimate mode of subsisting or, as others express it, the entitative mode, ultimately terminating and completing the substantial nature and giving to it incommunicability. In this signification, the word ΰποστάσεως is not found in Scripture; meanwhile, it can be correctly deduced from the material signification. ... Persona (taken concretely) is an individual substance (so that it may be distinguished from the universal) that is intelligent (by this it differs from suppositum, as the narrower from the broader; for every person is a suppositum, but not every suppositum is a person), subsisting ultimately and immediately by itself (so that it may be distinguished from secondary substances, which subsist by themselves, but mediately and in primary substances, i.e., individuals; likewise from the human nature of Christ, which is indeed an individual substance and

intelligent, but not a person, because it does not subsist ultimately and immediately by itself, but in the λόγος), incommunicable (namely, to another person), not sustained by or in another. Some add "living," but this is redundant and unnecessary, since it is included in the term "intelligent," for whatever is intelligent is also living, but not the reverse." (L. c. s. 1. th. 8. f. 460. sq.)

Chemnitius: "The term ὑπόστασις or person is used differently in the Church than in common parlance. We know what a person is among humans; we understand what it is among angels. Peter, Paul, and John are three persons who share one common human nature, but they differ very greatly: 1. in substance, because the whole is distinct from the whole; 2. in time, as John is younger than Peter; 3. in will, as Paul contradicts Peter (Gal. 2:11); 4. in power; thus Paul labored more than the others (1 Cor. 15:10); 5. in operation, as Peter was for the circumcision, Paul for the Gentiles (Gal. 2:8).

In the Trinity, however, the persons are not distinguished as one angel from another, or one human from another, says Cyril, where the whole of Peter is locally distinct from the whole of Paul; but in John 14:10, Christ says: 'I am in the Father and the Father is in me.' Likewise, in creatures it does not follow that where one person is, there the others also are because of a common nature; for one angel is in Persia, another in Greece (Dan. 10:13); but the Son says: 'The Father does not leave me alone, but is with me' (John 8:29). Likewise, in humans and angels, as has been said, the persons differ in time, will, power, and operation; but in the persons of the Trinity there is co-eternity, one will, one power, one operation.

These are the words of Nazianzen and Cyril. And this distinction must necessarily be observed. For it is not merely a mystery at which even the angels stand amazed, if it were simply one essence and three persons, just as Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael are three persons to whom the unique angelic nature is common and belongs equally.

Latin:

Gerhardus: ,,Non potest simpliciter et sine commoda interpretatione addita probari, quod Calvinus lib. 1. Instit. c. 13. s. 15. scribit: ,Utinam sepulta essent nomina (Trinitatis, 6μοονσίας etc.), constaret modo haec inter omnes fides, Patrem et Filium et Spiritum S. esse unum Deum.‘ Nimirum de occasione et origine harum appellationum, quae fuit haeretica perversitas, non autem de ipso appellationum usu illud accipiendum erit.“ (L. c. § 43.) §

33. Intelligitur nomine essentiae sive ουσίας ipsa natura divina, qualis in se absolute, quaeque una cum attributis simplicissime una ac singularis, a atque ita etiam trium personarum non nisi una b est. Juxta ea, quae diximus § 5. sqq.

b) Sic quidem, ut Patris, Filii et Spiritus S. unus quoque sit· intellectus, quo intelligunt, una voluntas trium, qua volunt, una potentia, qua extra essentiam divinam operantur. Conf. Joh. 5, 19.

Chemnitius: ״Essentia hominum est aliquid communicabile, sed est nomen universale, quod per se revera non existit, sed cognitione tantum colligitur et intellectu comprehenditur. Essentia vero in divinis non imaginarium quiddam est, ut genus vel species, sed revera existit, quamvis est communicabilis. Augustinus eleganter hoc expressit. ,Essentia‘, inquit, ,praedicatur de Patre, Filio et Spiritu S. non ut genus de speciebus, nec ut species de individuis, nec ut totum de partibus, sed alio quodam ineffabili et incomprehensibili modo.‘ In toto enim hoc articulo illa regula Augustini diligenter est observanda: ,Si non potes invenire, quid sit Deus, tamen caveas de eo sentire, quod non est.‘ Intelligit ergo ecclesia nomine essentiae non nomen universale, ut philosophi nominant essentiam humanam, sed naturam divinam revera existentem, quae communicabilis est et communis tribus personis, Patri, Filio et Spiritui S., et est tota in singulis. Et haec tantum nominis definitio est, inquit Nazianzenus. Quid antem sit, quoad definitionem rei, hoc nesciri dico, nisi quod attributa in definitione Dei posita dicimus esse ipsam Dei essentiam.“ (L. th. de Deo in specie, c. 2. s. 4. f. 3G. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Οΰσία et φνσις hic pro eodem sumuntur; ,πάσα yap ονσία φνσις 'λκγιται‘, inquit Aristoteles, IV Metaphys. Synonyma ουσίας divinae in Scripturis sunt: ΰεϊα φνσις, ,divina natura‘, 2 Pet. 1, 4., ·θεότης, ,deitas‘, Col. 2, 9., Οειότης, ,divinitas‘, Rom. 1, 20. Communissima vero est appellatio ουσίας του θεον et essentiae divinae apud doctores ecclesiae. — Ουσίας vox in s. Scripturis non extat, attamen, quia fuit ex mente s. Scripturae, ab orthodoxis patribus in Nicaena synodo usurpata est, sicque in Chalcedonensi postea explicata, ut φνσις plus notaret, quam ουσία. Est enim essentia simplex rei cujusque et omnibus suis proprietatibus atque accidentibus carens constitutio; natura seu φνσις est essentia jam suis illis proprietatibus vestita atque conjuncta. Itaque dixerunt patres, in una Christi persona esse non modo ipsas simplices ουσίας, divinam nempe et humanam, sed etiam esse φύσεις, i. e. ipsas essentias una cum suis veris proprietatibus conjunctas.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 6. f. 459.)

Dannhauerus: ״Essentiae et personae. . . discrimen docuit cum hic, tum articulus de persona Christi; ut illic in una essentia tres personae, ita hic in duabus naturis una persona coelitus patefacta est.“ (Hodos. Phaen. 3. B. p. 93.)

Gerhardus: ,,Maluerunt uti nomine essentiae quam substantiae, a. ut indicarent, Deum esse ουσίαν υπερούσιον non inclusam categoriis, inter quas prima est substantia. Damascenus lib. I. c. 12.: ,Deus est quoddam pelagus substantiae infinitum.‘ Vid. 1. de nat. Dei § 32. b. Quia Deus non substat accidentibus, sicut essentiae rerum creatarum, sed attributa sunt ipsius essentia, c. Quia nomen substantiae est ambiguum, quandoque enim pro ουσία, quandoque vero pro ύποστάσει ponitur. Sic Hilarius in lib. de synod. dicit, ,in Deo esse tres substantias‘, h. e., personas, quo sensu etiam quidam accipiunt, quod in latina versione Heb. 1, 3. Filius dicitur character substantiae Patris.“ (Exeges. 1. III. § 60.) §

34. Nomine personae seu υποστάσεως sicut alias significatur suppositum a intelligens, ita hoc loco indicatur, tres PART. I. CAP. I.

esse subsistentias seu personalitates b in una divina essentia,c adeoque tria supposita, Patrem, Pilium et Spiritum Sanctum.

Huelsemannus: ,,Notandum, quod scriptores ecclesiasticos attinet, vix binos aut trinos vocabula ista ουσίας, ΰποστάσεως et personae perpetuo unoque significatu usurpasse.“ (Praelectt. in F. C. p. 258.)

Quo nomine naturam, tanquam materiale, et subsistentiam ejus, tanquam formale, complectimur.

Sed si porro quaeras, quid vox latina personae aut suppositi in casu recto importet, naturam ipsam, an subsistentiam, utrinque difficultas occurret. Nam si prius dicatur, non apparet, quomodo, admissis in una Dei essentia tribus personis, negari deinceps possit, tres esse naturas, aut tres essentias divinas. Si posterius admittatur, idem' hoc fore videtur, ac si dicas, το nigrum in casu recto denotare ipsam nigredinem.

Itaque fortassis dicendum est, personam in casu recto importare aliquid conflatum ex natura et subsistentia, sicut alias in conceptu compositi materialis ex materia et forma substantiali neutra pars compositi in casu recto ponitur. Vid. b. D. Petri Musaei Introd. in Loc. de persona Christi § 43. et sqq.

Quod ad Graecos attinet, vocabulum ΰποστάσεως ipsis nunc subsistentiam ipsamp raecise, nunc suppositum aut personam denotat; quemadmodum et Latini quidam vocabulo substantiae nonnunquam usi sunt, cum perso-nam per substantiam definirent; licet alias naturam ipsam substantiaenomine appellare consueverimus.

Scharffius: ,,Suppositum et persona sunt unum et idem fere. Saltem enim differunt ratione naturae sive subjecti. Ita ut suppositum sit communis, et in omnibus completis substantiis per se ultimato, h. e., independenter subsistentibus, sive sint rationales, sive, irrationales, obtineat. Sed persona tantum est in rationalibus et intelligen־ tibus naturis, complete subsistentibus, utpote in hominibus, angelis et in Deo. . . Igitur persona strictior est supposito.“ (Metaphys. p. 252.)

Conf. Aug.: ,,Nomine personae utuntur ea significatione, qua usi sunt in hac causa scriptores ecclesiastici, ut significet non partem aut qualitatem in alio, sed quod proprie subsistit [das selbst bestehet].“ (Art. 1.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Vox ΰποστάσεως accipitur vel concrete et materialiter, prout implicat simul rem ipsam et rei modum notatque essentiam charactere hypostatico insignitam, i. e. personam, quo sensu Christus dicitur χαρηκτήρ τής ΰποστάσεως θεον, sci. Patris, Hebr. 1, 3., — vel abstracte et formaliter, prout ipsam personalitatem seu subsistentiam designat, quae est actus, modus seu gradus ultimus, quo natura intelligens subsistit complete et incommunicabiliter, quem Graeci vocant τρόπον ΰπάρζεως, modum subsistendi ultimum seu, ut alii exprimunt, modum entitativum, ultimo terminantem et complentem naturam substantialem et eidem dantem incommunicabilitatem. In hac significatione vox ΰποστάσεως in Scriptura non habetur, interim ex significatione materiali recte deduci potest. . .
