Persona (concrete sumta) est substantia individua (ut distinguatur ab universali) intelligens (per hoc a supposito, ut angustius a latiori, differt; ׳omnis enim persona est suppositum, sed non omne suppositum est persona), per se ultimato et immediate subsistens (ut distinguatur a substantiis secundis, quae per se subsistunt, sed mediate et in substantiis primis, i. e. individuis; item a natura humana Christi, quae substantia quidem est individua ct

intelligens, sed non persona, quia non per seipsam ultimo et immediate, sed in λόγω subsistit), incommunicabilis (alteri nimirum personae), non sustentata ab sive in alio. A quibusdam additur viva, sed est abundans et non necessarium, quippe cum includatur in voce intelligentis, quod enim intelligens, hoc etiam vivum, non vero contra.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 8. f. 460. sq.)

Chemnitius: ,,Vocabulum ΰποστάσεος vel personae aliter usurpatur in ecclesia, quam in vulgari consuetudine loquendi. In hominibus quid sit persona, scimus; quid sit in angelis, intelligimus. Petrus, Paulus, Johannes sunt tres personae, quibus communis est una natura humana, sed differunt valde multum: 1. substantia, quia totus a toto distinctus est; 2. tempore, ut Johannes est junior Petro; 3. voluntate, ut Paulus contradicit Petro Gal. 2, 11.; 4. potentia; sic Paulus prae caeteris laboravit 1 Cor. 15, 10.; 5. operatione, ut Petrus in circumcisione, Paulus in gentibus Gal. 2, 8.

In Trinitate vero non ita distinguuntur personae, sicut angelus ab angelo, homo ab homine, inquit Cyrillus, ubi totus Petrus a toto Paulo localiter distinctus est; sed Joh. 14, 10. Christus inquit: ,Ego in Patre et Pater in me est.‘ Item in creaturis non sequitur: ubi una persona est, ibi etiam esse reliquas propter naturam communem; quia unus angelus est in Persia, alter in Graecia Dan. 10, 13.; Filius vero dicit: ,Pater non relinquit me solum, sed mecum est‘, Joh. 8, 29. Item in hominibus et angelis, ut dictum est, differunt personae tempore, voluntate, potentia, operatione; sed in personis Trinitatis est coaeternitas, una voluntas, una potentia, una operatio.

Haec sunt Nazianzeni et Cyrilli. Et hoc discrimen necessario observandum est. Neque enim tantum est mysterium, ad quod etiam angeli obstupescunt, si ita esset una essentia, tres personae, sicut Michael, Gabriel, Raphael sunt tres personae, quibus unica angelica natura communis est et ex aequo convenit.


### Concerning God: From these foundations the common rule is taken

From these foundations the common rule is taken: The persons of the Divinity do not differ essentially, as in creatures, where each one has its own proper being; nor is there merely a distinction of reason there, as Sabellius held, but they are really distinguished, yet in a manner incomprehensible and unknown to us.

But if anyone wishes to cavil that the terms 'essence' and 'person' are not sufficiently proper to designate that arcane mystery of Unity and Trinity, let him have this answer, which Augustine says in Book 5 of *De Trinitate*: 'Human speech labors under a great lack. Yet it is said "three persons," not that this might be said, but that it might not be left entirely unsaid.'" (Loc. th. f. 36. sq.)

The same: "A person is also not carried or sustained by another being united with it; for example, you are a person, but your body alone is not a person, for it is sustained by a noble creature, namely the soul, and if the soul departs, the body falls apart and decays." (L. c. f. 37.)

Reuschius: "If it be said that 'suppositum' and 'person' denote nature in the nominative case, that which the blessed author (Baier) thinks does not follow from this, namely, the multiplication of nature according to the number of subsistences and personalities. For if you say that a 'suppositum' is a nature insofar as it is determined by the complement of existence or subsistence, it does not necessarily follow that the nature must be multiplied—for example, tripled—according to the ternary number of subsistences; since it is not repugnant for one and the same nature in number to exist or subsist in several ways with the complement." (Annotatt. p. 90.)

And these subsistences are relative, not absolute. For they are founded upon the divine relations, of which more will be said shortly. The one and simple divine essence does not admit of multiple absolute subsistences. However, we acknowledge relative subsistences in God according to revelation; although reason, left to itself, knows nothing of such things. PART I. CHAPTER I.

So that no person and no subsistence differs from the divine essence really, but only by reason (which is evident from the simplicity of God); however, the persons are distinguished among themselves really and without the operation of the mind on account of relative opposition. § 35.

Although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not expressly called three ὑποστάσεις, persons, or three supposita in the Scriptures, the thing itself, signified by these terms, is nevertheless certainly contained in the Scriptures. Indeed, those who do not wish to twist the names, but acknowledge that they are founded in a true and real generation, cannot deny that the Father and the Son are a person. Furthermore, the aforementioned attributes, especially those that have respect to operation, e.g., omniscience and omnipotence, and in particular those actions—creation, preservation, resurrection (which we saw above)—are of the supposita or persons, as of the principles which, according to the common canon [acta sunt suppositorum]. But works proper to the persons are predicated of the Holy Spirit no less properly than of the Son and the Father, e.g., that He distributes gifts to each one as He wills, 1 Cor. 12:11, that He comforts, convicts, and teaches, John 14:16 and 26, ch. 15:26, ch. 16:8 and 13. Where it is not permitted to invent a trope, as if to evade the mystery.

Scharffius: "Philosophers constantly teach that actions belong to supposita." (Metaphys. p. 337.) B. Meisnerus: "All actions and passions are most properly said of the suppositum itself, as the acting and suffering subject. For every operation requires the existence of that which acts." (Philos. sobr. 1611. P. I. p. 310. sq.)

Gerhardus: "It does not befit a bare virtue to assume a bodily form, to appear in it, and to descend; for who has ever read, heard, or seen the mercy, wisdom, etc., of God appearing in some assumed external form?" (Exeges. loc. III. § 82.) § 36. Although in this life we cannot sufficiently understand or explain how there can be …three persons of one most simple essence, distinct from the essence itself only by reason, but really distinct among themselves: nevertheless, because both are revealed, we rightly believe both.

Indeed, if our reason dares to define anything here (which, however, it ought not to do in a matter that exceeds its boundaries), it is so far from being able to bring forward a firm demonstration of this dogma from its own principles that it has rather brought forward things that are foreign to the question, or it is about to fall into manifest absurdity (as Barthol. Keckermann taught by his example

Musaeus in a special disputation, *φευδαποδείζει* [falsely demonstrates] its opposites, which is annexed to the treatise on the Use of the Principles of Reason, p. 661 sqq.), or it would deny or impugn the mystery itself. (Which is evident from the example of the Socinians and the like.) Dannhauer: "Chemnitz warns that the entire knowledge concerning God must be treated cautiously, chastely, and modestly; especially in the mystery of the Most Ho…ly Trinity, an ineffable mystery, which is the property of the Church, and is not to be sought outside of it. For although something concerning the λόγος and the υἱὸς θεοῦ may have emanated into paganism, those are nevertheless plagiarisms, snatched from Moses and the prophets. There is no force of reason in this greatest mystery of the Trinity. Hilary, in Book 8 *De Trinitate*, says excellently: 'The Church understands this; the synagogue does not believe this; philosophy does not know this: one from one, and God whole from whole, and that the Son did not, by his birth, take away from the Father that which He is in His entirety, nor did He, by this very fact of being born, fail to possess the whole with Him.' Whence those who have attempted anything here from the light of reason—for example, the scholastic summist Becanus, and after Lull and Keckermann, recently Bisterfeld—provide mockery and derision for their adversaries. For example, the argument drawn from the communicability of the highest good is solved by the pagan philosopher as easily as a fox eats a pear. The good is diffusive, not as a mother is fruitful of offspring, by generating a likeness of herself, but as the sun communicates itself to the world, not by bringing forth a new sun, but by bestowing its rays; or like a coin in the hand of a generous person, which is passed into the hand of the needy without any new fruit of usury." (Hodos. Phaenom. III. p. 92.)

Fecht: "The arguments which are brought forward from reason to prove the mystery of the Trinity prove the exact opposite." R. H. Rollius adds: "When Barthol. Keckermann, formerly a professor at Danzig, wrote in *Syst. theol.*, Book 1, ch. 3, that the Trinity of persons proceeds from the very essence of God, and that God cannot be unless He has three distinct modes of existing, or persons, he supposed, in order to prove this very thing, that intellect and will belong to God, the acts of which are not accidents in God, but substances subsisting in the divine essence itself, and therefore that one person is produced by the intellect and another by the will. But J. Musaeus opposed these things to this reasoning: It is unheard of to human reason that the intellect, by understanding itself, and the will, by loving itself, should produce persons distinct from themselves; indeed, reason will rather conclude the opposite from its own principles. For it seems to be in perpetual conflict that the essence of God is most simple, and yet that in it one person is produced by the intellect and another by the will. Moreover, if this were posited, though not granted, infinite persons would have to be established in God." (Controversiarum Sylloge ed. by Rollius. 1768. p. 56, 59 sq.) And we are certain that these things do not imply a contradiction, although to the reason of certain men, who argue poorly from the nature and condition of finite things, it may seem so. Indeed, every thought must be brought into captivity to the obedience of Christ, according to 2 Cor. 10:5. Kromayer: "There is no contradiction here, as is feigned by some, that God is one and three, but at most an ἐναντιοφανές, i.e., an apparent contradiction, because the laws of legitimate opposition are neglected, namely the law πρὸς αὐτό, i.e., in respect to the same thing. If God were one in essence and three in essence, or one and three simultaneously in persons, then perhaps the οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας [those from the opposite side] might obtain something; but unity is referred πρὸς οὐσίαν, i.e., to the essence, and trinity πρὸς ὑποστάσεις, i.e., to the persons." (Theol. pos. pol. II. p. 65.)

Luther: "Holy Scripture teaches that God is most simply one and three (as they call them) most truly distinct persons. Each of these persons is the whole God, outside of whom there is no other God. And yet it cannot be said that any person alone is God. For this would be the same as saying that there is no God, since any person... if the whole were excluded, God would be excluded, and any person would be excluded. Hence, reason, corrupted by original sin, must be taken captive, indeed extinguished, with its light and wisdom, in obedience to faith. It is one thing to say, "one person is the whole God," and "one person alone is the one God." However, how a person is distinguished from the Divinity itself is not for reason to inquire, nor is it comprehensible to the angels. Indeed, it is dangerous and to be avoided to think that there is any distinction there, since each person is the very same and the whole God. The thought of Scotus and his like, who invented a formal or other distinction here, is vain and of no account. They do not know what they are saying or affirming while they wish to aid reason with such medicines of wisdom. For however subtly these things may seem to be stated, reason nevertheless does not grasp that a formal distinction is something other than a real or essential one. Because reason does not grasp that one indistinct thing is three distinct things: therefore, mathematics and every thought of the whole creature must be excluded in believing in the Divinity. Although it seems no less impossible that, among these three things of one simple essence, one should be made man without the other: yet it is truly more impossible that one indistinct thing should be three most distinct things. Therefore, to believe that the Son of God was made man is less than to believe that He is consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit. As for what dialectic argues—that these things do not square with its rules—it must be said: "Let the woman keep silent in the church." It is no wonder if Arius, the Jew, Mahomet, and the whole world deny that Christ is God." (Disputation in 38 Theses. 1545. Thesis 1—18. Opp. Hal. X, 218—221. cf. Opp. lat. Jen. I, 534. sq.) § 37.

Latin:

Ex his fundamentis sumta est vulgaris regula: Personae Divinitatis non essentialiter differunt, ut in creaturis, ubi una quaevis suum proprium esse habet; nec tantum est ibi distinctio rationis, ut voluit Sabellius, sed realiter distinguuntur, modo tamen nobis incomprehensibili et incognito. . .

Quodsi quis cavillari voluerit, vocabula essentiae et personae non esse satis propria ad designandum arcanum illud mysterium Unitatis et Trinitatis, is sibi hoc responsum habeat, quod Augustinus dicit 1. 5. de Trin.: ,Magna prorsus inopia humanum laborat eloquium. Dictum est tamen tres personae, non ut illud diceretur, sed ne taceretur omnino.“ (Loc. th. f. 36. sq.)

Idem: ,,Persona wird auch nicht getragen oder erhalten mit einem anderen mitvereinigten Wesen, als, du bist eine Person, aber dein Leib allein ist nicht eine Person, denn er wird getragen von einer edlen Creatur, nämlich von der Seele, und so die Seele abscheidet, so zerfällt der Leib und verfaulet.“ (L. c. f. 37.)

Reuschius: ״Si dicätur, suppositum et personam denotare naturam in casu recto, illud, quod b. auctor (Baierus) putat, hinc non sequitur, sel. multiplicatio naturae pro numero subsistentiarum et personalitatum. Nam si dicas, suppositum esse naturam, quatenus complemento existentiae seu subsistentiae est determinata, non sequitur necessario, ut multiplicetur, v. g. triplicetur, natura pro numero ternario subsistentiarum; quum non repugnet, unam eandemque numero naturam aliquot modis cum complemento existere seu subsistere.“ (Annotatt. p. 90.)

Atque hae subsistentiae relativae sunt, non absolutae. Fundanfur enim in relationibus divinis, de quibus mox plura dicentur. Absolutas subsistentias plures essentia divina una et simplex non admittit. Relativas autem subsistentias in Deo agnoscimus juxta revelationem; licet ratio sibi relicta de talibus nihil noverit. PART. I. CAP. I.

Ita ut nulla quidem persona nullaque subsistentia ab essentia divina realiter, sed sola ratione differat (quod ex simplicitate Dei constat); personae autem inter se propter oppositionem relativam realiter ac citra mentis operationem distinguantur.§ 35.

Quamvis autem Pater et Filius et Spiritus S. in Scripturis expresse non dicantur tres υποστάσεις, personae, aut tria supposita, res ipsa tamen, vocibus his significata, in Scripturis utique continetur. Sane Patrem et Filium personam esse, negare non possunt, qui nomina torquere nolunt, sed in generatione vera ac reali fundari agnoscunt. Praeterea vero etiam attributa memorata, praesertim ea, quae respectum habent ad operationem, v. g. omniscientia et omnipotentia, inprimis vero actiones illae, creatio, conservatio, resuscitatio (de quibus supra vidimus), suppositorum aut personarum sunt, tanquam principiorum quae, juxta vulgatum canonem. De Spiritu S. autem non minus proprie, quam de Filio ac Patre, praedicantur opera personis propria, v. g. quod singulis distribuat dona, prout vult, 1 Cor. 12, 11., quod consoletur, arguat, doceat, Joh. 14, 16. et 26. cap. 15, 26. cap. 16, 8. et 13. Ubi tropum fingere, velut ad eludendum mysterium, non licet.

Scharffius: ״Philosophi constanter docent, actiones esse suppositorum.“ (Metaphys. p. 337.) B. Meisnerus: ״Omnes actiones et passiones de ipso supposito, veluti subjecto agente et patiente, propriissime dicuntur. Ad operationem enim omnem requiritur existentia ejus, quod agit.“ (Philos. sobr. 1611. P. I. p. 310. sq.)

Gerhardus: ״Nudae virtuti non competit corporalem speciem assumere, in ea apparere et descendere; quis enim unquam legit, audivit, vidit Dei misericordiam, sapientiam etc. in externa quadam forma assumta comparentem?“ (Exeges. loc. III. § 82.) § 36. Quamvis vero in hac vita satis intelligere aut explicare non possimus, a quomodo unius simplicissimae essentiae tres personae, ah ipsa quidem essentia tantum ratione, inter se autem realiter distinctae, esse possunt: tamen, quia utrumque revelatum est, utrumque etiam merito credimus.b

Sane, si quid ratio nostra hic ausit definire (quod tamen in re suos cancellos egrediente non debet), tantum abest, ut ex suis principiis demonstrationem firmam hujus dogmatis afferre possit, ut potius, vel quae sunt aliena a quaestione, attulerit, vel in absurditatem manifestam illapsura (quemadmodum Barthol. Keckermanni exemplo docuit

Musaeus Disp. peculiari, φευδαποδείζει ejus opposita, quae tractatui de Usu Princip. Rat. annexa est, p. 661. sqq.), vel mysterium ipsum negatura aut impugnatura sit. (Quod exemplo Socinianorum et similium constat.)Dannhauerus: ,,Caute, castigate, modeste totam de Deo notitiam tractandam, monet Chemnitius; praesertim in mysterio SS. Trinitatis, ineffabili mysterio, quod est ecclesiae proprium, nec extra eam quaerendum. Ut enim in gentilismum aliquid emanarit de λόγφ, de υΐφ θεού, tamen plagia illa sunt, e Mose et prophetis rapta. Nulla in hoc maximo Trinitatis mysterio vis est rationis. Egregie Hilarius 1. 8. de Trin. inquit: ,Hoc ecclesia intelligit; hoc synagoga non credit; hoc philosophia non sapit: unum ex uno, et totum a toto Deum, et Filium neque per nativitatem Patri ademisse, quod totus est, neque hoc ipso totum non secum nascendo‘tenuisse.1 Unde qui hic aliquid conati sunt e lumine rationis e. g. scholasticorum summista Becanus et post Lullium ac Keckermannum nuper Bisterfeld, adversariis sannas ac ludibria praebent. Quod e. g. argumentum petitur a summi boni communicabilitate, tam facile solvit philosophus ethnicus, quam pirum vulpes comest. Bonum est diffusivum, non ut mater foecunda est prolis, de se simile generando, sed ut sol se mundo communicat, non novum pariendo solem, sed radios suos indulgendo; vel ut nummus in manu liberalis, qui idem sine novo usurae alicujus fructu traditur, in manum egentis.“ (Hodos. Phaenom. III. p. 92.)

Fechtius: ,,Argumenta, quae ex ratione pro probando Trinitatis mysterio adducuntur, plane contrarium evincunt.“ Addit R. H. Rollius: ,,Quando Barthol. Keckermannus, Professor olim Gedanensis, 1. 1. Syst. theol. c. 3. scripsit, Trinitatem personarum promanare ex ipsa Dei essentia, et Deum esse non posse, nisi tres habeat distinctos existendi modos s. personas, id ipsum ut probaret, supposuit, Deo competere intellectum et voluntatem, quorum actus non sint accidentia in Deo, sed substantiae, in ipsa essentia divina subsistentes, ideoque per intellectum aliam, aliamque per voluntatem productam esse personam. Sed huic rationi J. Musaeus haec opposuit: Inauditum est rationi humanae, quod intellectus, se ipsum intelligendo, et voluntas, se ipsam amando, personas a se distinctas producant; quin ratio contrarium potius ex suis principiis concludet. Perpetuo enim pugnare inter se videntur, essentiam Dei simplicissimam esse, et tamen in ea aliam per intellectum et aliam per voluntatem produci personam. Imo posito hoc, sed non concesso, infinitae in Deo statuendae essent personae.“ (Controversiarum Sylloge ed. a Rollio. 1768. p. 56. 59. sq.) Et certi sumus, ea non implicare contradictionem, licet rationi quorundam hominum, a rerum finitarum natura et conditione male argumentantium, ita videri possit. Nempe omnis cogitatio captiva ducenda est ad obediendum Christo, juxta 2. ad Cor. 10, 15.Kromayerus: ,,Nulla hic est contradictio, quae fingitur nonnullis, Deum esse unum et trinum, sed saltem εναντωφανές i. e. contradictio apparens, quia leges oppositionis legitimae negliguntur, nominatim lex προς avTb i. e. respectu ejusdem. Si Deus unus esset essentia et trinus essentia, vel unus et trinus simul in personis, tunc forsan οί εξ εναντίας aliquid obtinerent; sed unitas προς ουσίαν, i. e. essentiam, trinitas προς υποστάσεις, i. e. ad personas, refertur.“ (Theol. pos.pol. II. p. 65.)

Lutherus: ,,Scriptura sancta docet, esse Deum simplicissime unum et tres (ut vocant) personas verissime distinctas. Harum personarum quaelibet totus est Deus, extra quam nullus est alius Deus. Nec tamen dici potest, quamlibet personam solam esse Deum. Hoc enim idem esset, dicere, Deum nullum esse, cum qualibet persona 64 PART. I. CAP. I. exclusa totus Deus esset exclusus et quaelibet persona esset exclusa. Hinc enim ratio corrupta originali peccato captivanda, imo extinguenda, est cum sua luce et sapientia in obsequium fidei. Aliud est, dicere, una persona est totus Deus, et una persona sola est unus Deus. Quomodo autem distinguatur persona a Divinitate ipsa, non est rationis inquirere nec angelis comprehensibile. Imo periculosum et cavendum est ibi, ullam esse putari distinctionem, cum sit quaelibet persona ipsissimus et totus Deus. Frustranea est cogitatio et nihili Scoti et similium, qui formulam vel aliam distinctionem hic finxerunt. Nesciunt, quid loquantur vel affirment, dum talibus sapientiae pharmacis rationem juvare volunt. Nam utcunque subtiliter ista dici videantur, ratio tamen non capit, distinctionem formalem esse aliam atque realem seu essentialem. Quia ratio non capit, unam rem indistinctam esse tres res distinctas: Excludenda igitur est mathematica et omnis totius ׳creaturae cogitatio in credenda Divinitate. Quamvis non minus impossibile videatur, inter has tres res unius simplicis essentiae unam sine alia factam hominem: Vere tamen impossibilius est, unam indistinctam rem esse tres res distinctissimas. Credere igitur, Filium Dei esse hominem factum, minus est, quam credere, ipsum esse Patri et Spiritui S. consubstantialem. Quod dialectica arguit, haec suis regulis non quadrare, dicendum est: Mulier taceat in ecclesia. Nihil mirum, si Arius, Judaeus, Mahomet et totus mundus negent, Christum esse Deum.“ (Disputation in 38 Sätzen. 1545. Thesis 1—18. Opp. Hal. X, 218—221. cf. Opp. lat. Jen. I, 534. sq.) § 37.


### Concerning God: Furthermore, the divine persons are distinguished by personal acts, properties,…

Furthermore, the divine persons are distinguished by personal acts, properties, and personal notions. Loeberus: "We see the difference of the divine persons in the personal operations (actus personales), also in the personal notions (notiones personales) and personal properties (proprietates personales) of the most holy persons of the Godhead. The personal operations are those operations within the divine essence (opera ad intra), by means of which one person of the most holy Godhead has the divine essence from another person from eternity. There are two such operations: the one, where God the Father has eternally begotten and born His Son (generatio), and the other, where God the Father and Son eternally let the Holy Spirit proceed from them (spiratio active talis). ... Upon these two personal operations are founded the personal properties, namely, that the first person is Father (paternitas), the second is the Son (filiatio), and the third is the Holy Spirit or the Proceeding One (processio s. spiratio passive talis, with the term 'passive' understood only grammatically). ... Finally, there also belong to the difference of these most holy persons their personal notions, from which we can discern their personal properties; as, namely, for the first person, that He is neither born nor has proceeded from another (innascibilitas et improcessibilitas, insofar as He is not from another, either begotten or proceeding); for the second person, that He is born of the first person (generatio passive talis); for the third, however, that He is not born, but proceeds from the Father and Son (spiratio passive in sensu grammatico talis)." (Ev.luth. Dogm. St. Louis and Leipz. 1872. p. 201. 204. 205.)

They are called otherwise *opera ad intra*, because they are terminated within the divine essence toward a certain person, who [receives] the other person (or the remaining...

TO GOD. ... which it regards as producing (producing). And those works are divided, i. e., not common to all persons of the Divinity, but proper to this or that one, in which respect they are opposed to works ad extra, which, proceeding from an active power common to the three persons, are terminated at an effect really produced outside of God. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Disp. de Deo (which is the third of those held in the year 1649) § 42, p. 70. Meanwhile, it is not to be denied that some work ad extra, or external work, is accustomed to be peculiarly ascribed to individual divine persons, by which that person has peculiarly manifested himself; just as creation is accustomed to be ascribed to the Father, reconciliation to the Son, and sanctification to the Holy Spirit, even though these individual things proceed from the three persons: which the authors call appropriation. See the blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 54, p. 75.

Gerhardus: "Some distinguish thus: The works of the Trinity are threefold: a. ad intra, b. ad extra, c. mixed, which are προς έσω by reason of the terminus, and προς έξω by reason of the principle. The former are personal, the latter essential, the mixed are both personal and essential. A mixed work is the incarnation, which is of the three persons efficiently and inchoatively, but of the Son alone formally and terminatively. From the sayings of Scripture, which speak of the work of the incarnation, that distinction is manifestly gathered. The Father sent the Son into the world. The Holy Spirit, coming upon her, sanctified those drops of blood and cleansed them from sin, from which the body of Christ was formed, so that what was born of Mary might be holy, and by divine power He worked this in the blessed virgin, that beyond the order of nature she might conceive a fetus without male seed. The Son descended from heaven, overshadowed the virgin, came into the flesh, was made flesh, participating in it, manifesting Himself in it, assuming it into the unity of His person." (Exeg. 1. IV. § 103.)

Fechtius: "Those who assert any inequality of operation in works ad extra, beyond the difference of order, with respect to the divine persons, injure the unity of the divine essence. John 5:17, 19. While creation, redemption, and sanctification are said to be appropriated to the divine persons, the reason for the appropriation cannot be sought except in the similarity of the order of the works with the order of the persons."

Rollius adds: "Therefore it cannot be said that the Father manifested Himself most especially in the work of creation, because there is no foundation for this manifestation... Because the Father is the first person of the Most Holy Trinity, it is fitting that the first divine work, which is creation, be appropriated to Him. And thus also in the rest." (L. c. p. 56, 61, sq.)

Those properties are called by some notions συστατιχαί, constitutive of each person in the being of such a person; namely, they are relations founded in personal acts. They are certain reasons of knowing, by which the divine persons are conceived by us and are distinguished among themselves ad intra, or within the divine essence. And these notions, taken more broadly, comprehend even the personal properties themselves; but taken more strictly, they are distinguished from them and are called with the addition of notions σημαντικαί and γνωριστικαί, that is, significative or indicative. §

38. The personal acts are two: generation and spiration. 5 Baier Comp. ed. Walther. II. PART I. CHAP. I.

39. Generation is an action ad intra, by which God the Father, from His own substance, from eternity produced the Son. Not figurative, but truly and properly so called, just as the Father and the Son in the divine are not improperly, but properly called Father and Son. Cf. § 28, 29.

You may call it a real action, insofar as it has a term that is really produced and distinct from the producer; although this is not an effect that acknowledges an efficient cause from which it differs as one thing from another.

But if you should inquire more distinctly about this action, it must be confessed that both the action itself and the active power of generating are inscrutable to us.

For thus also Greg. Nazianz. Orat. I. de Filio: θεου γέννησις σιωπῇ τιμάσθω, p. m. 209. med. Compare Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. XI. p. m. 118. E.

For this pertains to the formal concept of generation.

Furthermore, this divine generation does not occur, nor has it occurred, by means of seed which is separated from the substance of the generator; for the divine essence is not a material principle from which the Son was produced, but it consists only in this, that that very essence, which is of the generating Father, is perfectly communicated to the begotten Son. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Disp. cit. p. 70.

Thus in Psalm 2:7, God the Father says to the Messiah or Christ (see Acts 13:33): "You are my Son, today I have begotten you," where the word היום denotes the most present and unique moment of eternity, where there is neither anything past nor future. Compare Micah 5:2, where the prophet says the goings forth (nativity) of the Messiah are from of old, from the days of eternity: מִקֶּדֶם מִימֵי עוֹלָם.

Huelsemannus: "Nor indeed, when in Acts 13:32-33 it is said that the sonship of Christ was fulfilled in His resurrection, is it denied thereby that He existed as the Son before the resurrection; but God is said to have brought it to the highest pinnacle regarding notoriety and manifestation, concerning which it is said in Ps. 2: 'You are my Son.' It does not follow, however, that at the time when the sonship of Christ became fully known, it only then began." (Vindiciae S. Scripturae, p. 17.)

Scherzerus: "It has been shown that Acts 13:33 is objected in vain. It does not follow: the resurrection demonstrates that Christ is the Son of God; therefore Christ was begotten by God only through the resurrection. Just as it does not follow: nourishment demonstrates that Peter is Paul's son; therefore Peter was begotten through nourishment." (Syst. th. p. 68.)

ANTITHESIS. Hofmannus: "By the passage in the Psalm (Ps. 2:7) is meant his first introduction into the same (into the world), therefore also not the resurrection from the dead, nor in general any single event from the course of Jesus' history, but the beginning of the same, his incarnation." (Schriftbeweis, I, 113.)

However, that the Father produced the Son through an act of intellect reflected into Himself (God understanding Himself), or through the τό λέγειν, cannot be demonstrated or defended. See the blessed Musaeus, Disp. cit. against Keckermann, § 9 sqq. pag. 662 sqq.

Quenstedtius: "The eternal generation of the Son is a personal work ad intra, by which the eternal Father, through the communication of one and the same essence in number, begets the Son consubstantial with Himself from eternity, truly and properly, yet in a hyperphysical and inscrutable manner. This generation of the Son of God is not figurative and metaphorical, as our mind begets concepts, but true and most proper.

We argue thus: Wherever there is a communication of essence, implying the relation of father and son, there is a generation properly so called and substantial; but such is the case in the divine: therefore.

This generation of the Son of God does not take place by derivation or transfusion, nor by an action that begins and ends, but it takes place by an unceasing emanation, to which there is nothing similar in the nature of things. For God the Father has begotten His Son from eternity and is always begetting Him and will never cease to beget Him. For if the generation of the Son had an end, it would also have a beginning, and thus it would not be eternal.

Nor, however, can this generation be called imperfect and successive on that account; for the act of generation is considered perfect in the work in the Father and the Son, and perpetual in the operation.

Although this generation is most proper and most true, the mode of generation itself is nevertheless unknown and ineffable to us.

This divine generation can be shadowed forth in some way by the likeness of the rays of the sun, flowing from the solar body in constant dependence. For as the sun is not older than its rays, nor is the begetter prior in time to the begotten: so the eternal Father has begotten the Son from eternity.

And just as the sun generated its rays from the beginning and is even now generating them and will continue to generate them, and yet it cannot be inferred from this that the generation of the rays of the sun is not yet perfect: so also God has begotten His eternal wisdom from eternity and is always begetting it and will never cease to beget it, nor can it be said for that reason that the generation of the Son is not yet perfect.

Latin:

Caeterum distinguuntur personae divinae actibus personalibus,a proprietatibus b et notionibus c personalibus. Loeberus: ,,Den Unterschied der göttlichen Personen sehen wir in den persönlichen Wirkungen (actus personales), auch in den persönliehen Kenntnissen (notiones personales) und persönlichen Eigenschäften (proprietates personales) der hochheiligen Personen der Gottheit. Die persönlichen Wirkungen sind diejenigen Wirkungen innerhalb des göttlichen Wesens (opera ad intra), vermittelst welcher eine Person der hochheiligen Gottheit von einer andern Person von Ewigkeit her das göttliche Wesen hat. Solcher Wirkungen sind zwei: die eine, da Gott der Vater von Ewigkeit seinen Sohn gezeugt und geboren hat (generatio), und die andere, da Gott Vater und Sohn von Ewigkeit den Heiligen Geist von sich ausgehen lassen (spiratio active talis). .. Auf diese beiden persönlichen Wirkungen gründen die persönlichen Eigenschäften, nämlich, dass die erste Person Vater ist (paternitas), die.andere der Sohn (filiatio) und die dritte der Heilige Geist oder der Ausgehende (processio s. spiratio passive talis, termino,passive‘ tantum grammatice intellecto). . . Es gehören endlich auch noch zu dem Unterschied dieser hochheiligen Personen ihre persönlichen Kenntnisse, woraus wir ihre persönlichen Eigenschaften ersehen können; als nämlich bei der ersten Person, dass sie weder geboren, noch von einer andern ausgegangen ist (innascibilitas et improcessibilitas, quatenus non est ab alio vel genitus, vel procedens); bei der andern Person, dass sie von der ersten Person geboren (generatio passive talis); bei der dritten aber, dass sie nicht geboren ist, sondern vom Vater und Sohn ausgeht (spiratio passive in sensu grammatico talis).“ (Ev.luth. Dogm. St. Louis u. Leipz. 1872. p. 201. 204. 205.)

Dicuntur alias opera ad intra, quia intra essentiam divinam terminantur ad certam personam, quae personam alteram (aut reli

DK DEO. quas) tanquam producentem (producentes) respicit. Et sunt opera illa divisa, i. e. non omnibus personis Divinitatis communia, sed huic aut illi propria, qua ratione operibus ad extra opponuntur, quae, a potentia activa tribus personis communi proficiscentia, ad affectum extra Deum realiter productum terminantur. Conf. b. Mus. Disp. de Deo (quae III. est ex illis a. 1649. habitis) § 42. p. 70. Interim nec negandum est, quod singulis personis divinis peculiariter adscribi soleat opus aliquod ad extra, seu opus externum, quo 8e persona illa peculiariter manifestaverit; sicut creatio Patri, reconciliatio Filio, sanctificatio Spiritui S. adscribi consuevit, etsi singula haec a tribus personis proficiscantur: quam appropriationem vocant auctores. Vid. b. Mus. 1. c. § 54. p. 75.

Gerhardus: ״Quidam sic distinguunt: Opera Trinitatis sunt triplicia: a. ad intra, b. ad extra, c. mixta, quae προς έσω ratione termini, προς έξω ratione principii. Illa personalia, ista essentialia, haec et personalia et essentialia. Mixtum opus est incarnatio, quae trium personarum est efficienter et inchoative, solius autem Filii formaliter et terminative. Ex Scripturae dictis, quae de incarnationis opere loquuntur, discrimen illud manifeste colligitur. Pater misit Filium in mundum. Spiritus S. superveniens guttas illas sanguinis sanctificavit et a peccato mundavit, ex quibus corpus Christi formatum, ut, quod ex Maria natum fuerit, sit sanctum, ac divina virtute in beata virgine hoc operatus est, ut praeter naturae ordinem sine virili semine foetum conciperet. Filius descendit de coelo, obumbravit virginem, venit in carnem, factus caro, eidem participando, in ea se manifestando, eam in personae unitatem assumendo.“ (Exeg. 1.IV. § 103.)

Fechtius: ״Qui in operibus ad extra praeter differentiam ordinis quamcunque operationis inaequalitatem respectu divinarum personarum asserunt, divinae essentiae unitatem laedunt. Joh. 5, 17. 19. Creatio, redemptio, sanctificatio dum appropriari divinis personis dicuntur, ratio appropriationis non potest quaeri, nisi in similitudine ordinis operum cum ordine personarum.“

Rollius addit: ״Non ergo dici potest, Patrem in opere creationis se potissimum manifestasse, quia hujus manifestationis nullum suppetit fundamentum. . . Quia Pater prima est persona SS. Trinitatis, conveniens est, primum illi opus divinum, quod est creatio, appropriari. Atque ita et in reliquis.“ (L. c. p. 56. 61. sq.)

Vocantur proprietates illae a quibusdam notiones συστατιχολ, constitutivae cujuslibet personae in esse talis personae; nempe sunt relationes in actibus personalibus fundatae. Sunt rationes quaedam cognoscendi, quibus concipiuntur a nobis personae divinae atque inter se ad intra, seu intra essentiam divinam distinguuntur. Et hae notiones latius acceptae comprehendunt etiam ipsas proprietates personales; strictius vero sumtae distinguuntur ab illis et dicuntur cum apposito notiones σημαντικοί xa\ γνωριστιχαΐ, id est, significativae aut indimtivae.§

38. Actus personales duo sunt, generatio et spiratio. 5 BalcriComp. ed. Walther. Π. PAKT. I. CAP. I.

39. Generatio a est actio b ad intra, qua Deus Pater de substantia sua c ab aeterno d produxit e Filium. Non tropica, sed vere et proprie dicta, prout Pater et Filius in divinis non improprie, sed proprie dicuntur Pater et Filius. Conf. § 28. 29.

Realem actionem esse dixeris, quatenus habet terminum realiter productum et a producente distinctum; licet is non sit effectus, qui agnoscat causam efficientem, a qua differat tanquam aliud et aliud.

Quodsi etiam distinctius de hac actione quaeras, fatendum est, et ipsam actionem et potentiam generandi activam nobis esse inscrutabilem.

Sic enim et Greg. Nazianz. Orat. I. de Filio, θεου γέννησις σιωπjj τιμάσΰω, p. m. 209. med. Confer Oyrilli Hieros. Catech. XI. p. m. 118. E.

Hoc enim ad formalem generationis conceptum pertinet.

Caeterum divina haec generatio non fit aut facta est mediante semine, quod sit decisum de substantia generantis; nec enim essentia divina est materiale principium, ex quo productus sit Filius, sed in eo tantum consistit, quod illa ipsa essentia, quae est Patris generantis, sit filio genito perfecte communicata. Conf. b. Mus. Disp. cit. p. 70.

Sic Psalmo 2, 7. dicit Deus Pater ad Messiam seu Christum (vide Act. 13, 33.): Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te, ubi vox היום denotat praesentissimum atque unicum aeternitatis momentum, ubi nec praeteritum quicquam est, nec futurum. Confer. Mich. 5, 2., ubi propheta egressiones (nativitatem) Messiae dicit esse ab olim, a diebus saeculi: מקרם מימי עולם.

Huelsemannus: ,,Neque vero, quando Act. 13, 32. 33. dicitur impleta filiatio Christi in resurrectione ejus, negatur eo ipso, non extitisse illum Filium ante resurrectionem, sed Deus dicitur έκπεττ?.ήρωκϊ\ ad supremum fastigium deduxisse quoad notorietatem et innotescentiam, in quod Ps. 2. dicitur: ,Filius meus es tu.‘ Non sequitur autem, quo tempore filiatio Christi plene innotuit, eo demum coepit.“ (Vindiciae S. Scripturae, p. 17.)

Scherzerus: ,,Ostensum, frustra Act. 13, 33. objici. Non sequitur: resuscitatio demonstrat, Christum esse Filium Dei; ergo Christus per resuscitationem tantum fuit genitus a Deo. Sicut non sequitur: alimentatio demonstrat, Petrum esse Pauli filium; ergo Petrus per alimentationem fuit genitus.“ (Syst. th. p. 68.)

ANTITHESIS. Hofmannus: ״Mit der Psalmstelle (Ps. 2, 7.) ist seine erste Einführung in dieselbe (in die Welt), also auch nicht die Auferweckung von den Todten, überhaupt nicht irgend ein einzelnes Begebniss aus dem Verlaufe der Geschichte Jesu, sondern der Anfang derselben, seine Menschwerdung, gemeint.“ (Schriftbeweis, I, 113.)

Quod autem produxerit Filium Pater per actum intellectus, in se ipsum (Deum intelligentem) reflexum, aut per τό dicere, demonstrari aut defendi non potest. Vid. b. Mus. Disp. cit. contra Keckerm. § 9. sqq. pag. 662. sqq.

Quenstedtius: ,,Est generatio aeterna Filii opus ad intra personale, quo Pater aeternus unius ejusdemque numero essentiae communicatione Filium sibi consubstantialem ab aeterno, vere proprieque, modo tamen byperpliysico ac imperscrutabili, gignit. Est haec generatio Filii Dei non figurata et metaphorica, quomodo mens nostra gignit conceptus, sed vera et maxime propria.

Argumentamur ita: Ubicunque est communicatio essentiae, inferens relationem patris et filii, ibi est generatio proprie dicta et substantialis; atqui in divinis est talis: ergo.

Haec generatio Filii Dei non fit derivatione aut transfusione, nec actione, quae incipiat et desinat, sed fit indesinente emanatione, cui simile nihil habetur in rerum natura. Deus Pater enim Filium suum ab aeterno genuit et semper gignit nec umquam desinet gignere. Si enim generatio Filii finem haberet, haberet etiam initium, et sic aeterna non esset.

Nec tamen propterea generatio haec dici potest imperfecta et successiva; actus namque generationis in Patre et Filio consideratur in opere perfectus, in operatione perpetuus.

Licet generatio haec sit propriissima et verissima, ipse tamen generationis modus nobis est incognitus et ineffabilis.

Adumbrari utcunque potest haec divina generatio similitudine radiorum solis, fluentium a corpore solari jugi dependentia. Nam ut sol non est antiquior suis radiis, nec gignens generato prior est tempore: sic Pater aeternus ab aeterno generavit Filium.

Et sicut sol suos radios ab initio generavit et etiam nunc gignit et porro generabit, nec tamen inde potest inferri, generationem radiorum solis nondum esse perfectam: ita et Deus sapientiam suam aeternam ab aeterno genuit et semper gignit nec unquam desinet gignere, nec tamen idcirco dici potest, generationem Filii nondum esse perfectam.


### Concerning God: The Holy Spirit seems to intimate this in Ps

The Holy Spirit seems to intimate this in Ps. 2:7, where the Father addresses the Son thus: 'You are My Son; today I have begotten You.' In which words the generation of the Son is expressed in the past tense in such a way that it is nevertheless said to be happening today, because the generation of the Son is present and will never cease.

There is, however, a great difference between these two; for the sun is a substance, but the rays are an accident; but the substance of the Son is the same as the substance of the Father." (L. c. c. 9. s. 1. th. 28. f. 473. sq.)

Lutherus: "Some warn whether one should say: The Father always begat or begets the Son, or whether the Son has always been born or is always being born.

Those who hold the latter mode of speaking argue that the Son of God ought to be called 'always born,' because the perfect past tense denotes an imperfect present.

Hilary and others dare to say that the Son is always being born from the Father and lives as the living from the living and is born from the unbegotten.

But I think this is a controversy more grammatical or philosophical than theological, by which the flesh or reason is moved.

Since it is certain that in the Divinity, because it is eternity itself, there is no place for grammar or philosophy, where the past, present, and future are the same.

Whence the past tense 'born' concerning the Son does the same as the present 'is being born' and the future 'will be born'." (L. c. Thesis 20—25.)

Gerhardus: "(Adversaries) write: 'Know that generation from the essence of God is impossible in every way. For if Christ were begotten from the substance of the Father, He would be begotten either from a part of Him or from the whole; not the former, because the essence of God is most simple and indivisible, nor the latter, because the Father would no longer be the Father, since the essence of God is one in number and therefore cannot be common to many.'

Resp.: We hear again an argument not from the school of Christ, but from the principles of human reason.

We say therefore: 1. When an article of faith is proposed in Scripture in proper and clear words, philosophical principles, however plausible, are not to be urged against it.

2. That principle, upon which the whole structure of the argument rests, has a place only when the essence is finite; but it is clearly false where an infinite and immense essence is given. The Father, by begetting, communicates to the Son His whole and the same essence in number, nor is it lost by that communication, nor does anything depart from it, namely because it is infinite and immense.

3. What? PART I. CHAP. I.

which cannot even hold true in all respects in natural things. Man generates man, a light is kindled from a light, yet nothing of its essence is lost to the man through generation or to the light through the act of kindling.” (L. th. de Deo Patre et Filio, § 164.) The same: “

In this place, certain questions are raised: I. Concerning the divine nature of the Son. 1. Whether the Son is αὐτόθεος? The term is ambiguous; for either it is opposed to the communication of the divine essence, and thus we deny that Christ is αὐτόθεος, because He received the eternal essence of the Father through generation; or it is opposed to the inequality of the divine essence, and thus we concede that Christ is αὐτόθεος. Gregorius de Valentia, 1.1. de Trinit. c. 22: ‘The Son, as He is a person, is from another; as He is the most simple being, He is not from another.’ Christ is truly God by Himself, but He is not God from Himself...

It is asked: 4. Whether the Father can be called the cause of the Son? The Greek fathers use the terms ἀρχῆς and αἰτίαν indiscriminately in this mystery, as appears from Damascenus, 1.1. Orth. fid. c. 9 and 11: ‘ὁ υἱὸς οὐκ ἄναρχος, τουτέστιν, οὐκ ἀναίτιος, ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς γάρ.’ But the Latin doctors of the church repudiate the name of cause, yet they use the name of principle alone, saying that the Father is a principle without a principle, and the Son is a principle from a principle; whence the scholastics pronounce by common suffrage that the Father is not the cause of the Son, but the principle; that the Son is not the cause of the Holy Spirit, but the principle; for the word ‘principle’ extends more widely than ‘cause,’ to which it relates as genus to species; for every cause is a principle, but not every principle is a cause.” (Exeg. 1. IV. § 67. 70.) Quenstedtius: “

Not merely an act of intellect through generation to the Son, nor merely an act of will through spiration to the Holy Spirit, but the most simple, most pure, and indivisible act of the divine essence is communicated wholly in the Father to the Son, and the most simple and most pure act of the divine essence is communicated wholly in the Father and the Son to the Holy Spirit.” (L. c. q. 9. f. 562.) The same: “

If the Son of God proceeds properly through the intellect and the Holy Spirit through the will, the persons of the Most Holy Trinity are not equal. For 1. it can be said that that person who proceeds through the intellect is thus far unequal in respect of will, and that which proceeds through the will is unequal by reason of intellect... 2. No convenient reason can be shown why any person should proceed more through the intellect than through the will, and vice versa. Nor should that distinction be sought in the distinct operation of intellect and will, since that operation of both intellect and will is common to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but it arises rather immediately from the essence itself, subsisting in the Father proper to the mode of ὑπάρξεως and determined to His person, insofar as He is related to the Son and with the Son to the Holy Spirit through generation and active spiration, but not insofar as intellect and will are conceived in God. And why should it not also be said that some person proceeds through power, because the second person of the Most Holy Trinity is also called the power of God? 1 Cor. 1:24.” (L. c. f. 555.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “

Antithesis: 1. Of certain fathers... 3. Of the scholastics... 4. Of Philipp Melanchthon, who asserts in the Misnian body of doctrine: ‘That the Son of God was generated from the Father by thought, because the Father, intuiting and considering Himself, generates a certain substantial and permanent image of Himself; just as our mind generates an accidental and evanescent one.’ This dream of Philipp, his followers (Philippists) championed as a certain dogma and article of faith.” (L. c. f. 554.) §

40. Spiration is an action ad intra, by which God the Father and the Son together from their substance from eternity produced the Holy Spirit.

For 1) just as the Son is said to send the Holy Spirit, John 15:26; Luke 24:49, so it must be acknowledged that the Son also breathes the Holy Spirit, since the mission of a divine person is founded upon the substantial procession of the same from the sending person, and no other mode of proceeding, other than spiration, can be attributed to the Holy Spirit. It is added 2) that the Holy Spirit is called not only the Spirit of the Father, Matt. 10:20, but also the Spirit of the Son, Gal. 4:6; Rom. 8:9; 1 Pet. 1:11. For He is called the Spirit of that person from whom He is breathed. (Cf. John 20:22; Isa. 11:4, coll. with 2 Thess. 2:8.) And 3) otherwise the relative opposition, and therefore also the real distinction, between the Son and the Holy Spirit would be removed, unless the Son is the breather and the Holy Spirit is breathed by the Son.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: In the third age, namely, that of the more recent doctors of the Eastern Church, Theophylact, Archbishop of the Bulgarians, Michael Cerularius, abusively called Patriarch of Constantinople, and others, contended sharply that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and in no way from the Son, which error the Greek Church still stubbornly defends today against the Latin, especially the Roman, Church. In the antithesis, therefore, the following are to be noted: 1. The Nestorians, who in the creed produced at the Council of Ephesus asserted that 'the Holy Spirit does not have His subsistence through the Son, but from the Father alone.' 2. The more recent Greeks, to whom must be added the Muscovites, Russians, Armenians, as well as the Copts or Egyptians, Abyssinians, Syrians or Melkites, Jerusalemites, and Chaldeans, who in this chapter concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit all conspire by denying His έκπόρενσιν from the Son."

(L. c. s. 2. q. 12. f. 573. sq.) So that, although the Father and the Son are in reality two supposita, nevertheless through one and the same spirative power they produce the Holy Spirit, in which sense the doctors have said that the Father and the Son conduct themselves as one principle breathing the Holy Spirit. Gerhardus: "The Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father εμμέσως, that is, by the intervention of the Son; for by this reasoning He would be closer to one person than to the other; but He proceeds αμέσως from both, as if from one essential fountain; for as the Father and ὁ λόγος are one in essence, so in producing one and the same consubstantial Spirit they are 'one essential principle and, under the unity of essence, altogether one in breathing σννδναζόμενον,' yet so that the Father has that spirative faculty from Himself, while the Son receives it from the Father through ineffable generation."

(L. th. de Sp. S. § 87.) For spiration agrees with divine generation in that it denotes the emanation of the breathed person from the breathing person within the divine essence; just as generation denotes the emanation of the begotten person from the begetting person. As generation is eternal. However, we do not dare to say that the Holy Spirit is breathed through an act of will or love. Cf. Mus. Disp. cit. § 10. sqq. p. 664. sqq. §

41. It is certain that the generation of the Son and the spiration of the Holy Spirit differ; however, we cannot more fully define the mode by which they differ. PART I. CHAPTER I.

Not only by reason of the principle, since the principle of generation is the Father alone, inasmuch as He alone is said to have begotten the Son, whereas the principle of spiration is the Father and the Son, according to the preceding §, note a. b., but also by reason of the term produced. For we do not say that the Holy Spirit is begotten or has been begotten, nor that the Son is spirated. And although in the Scriptures the Son is said to be έξέρχεσθαι, yet He is not said to be έκπορεύεσθαι, but this is believed to be proper to the Holy Spirit. Cf. blessed Gerhard in *Loc. de Spiritu S.* § 71, Aug. *lib. 3. contra Maxim.*, c. 14, Nazianz. in *Orat. de Spiritu S.*, and elsewhere.

2. Principium illud, cui tota argumenti structura incumbit, tum demum locum habet, quando essentia est finita; sed falsum plane est, ubi datur essentia infinita et immensa. S. § 87.)
