Gerhardus in Loc. de Spiritu S. § 71., Aug. lib. 3. contra Maxim, c. 14., Nazianz. in Orat, de Spiritu S., et alibi.Kromayerus: ,,Quid sit nasci, quid processus, me nescire sum professus.“ (Th. pos.pol. II, 81.)


### Concerning God: Kromayerus: "What it is to be born, what procession is, I have professed that I…

Kromayerus: "What it is to be born, what procession is, I have professed that I do not know." (*Th. pos. pol.* II, 81.) The same: "The Holy Spirit emanates immanently from the Father and the Son, and remains emanently." (*L. c.* p. 78.)

Dannhauerus: "Does it not detract from the divine majesty of the Holy Spirit that He Himself produces no other person from Himself? Resp.: This diminishes nothing of His glory; rather, His eternal majesty is ineffably illustrated thereby... He can by no means be considered imperfect who, in His own substance, finishes and completes that production of persons, and thus reduces the whole Trinity, as it were, into a sphere and circle of consummate perfection, so that in this His Spirit the Father and the Son uniquely acquiesce." (*Hodos. phaen.* 3. p. 94.) § 42. The personal properties are three: a Paternity, b Filiation, c and Procession strictly so called, or passive spiration. d a Namely, according to the number of persons, each of whom is constituted in the being of a certain person by a relative subsistence. b Founded upon generation viewed actively. c Founded upon generation viewed passively or terminatively. d Not that any real passion falls upon God, but speaking grammatically, or because the Holy Spirit is said to be spirated, not to spirate; although on the part of God, spiration is a pure act, devoid of all passion. Cf. Mus. *Disp. cit. de Deo* § 6. p. 73, 74. § 43. The notions specifically so called are two: a Unbegottenness, b and active spiration.

a Or distinct from the properties. For otherwise, if the word "notion" is taken more broadly and the properties are counted among them, there are five notions. Hollazius: "’Αγεννησία indeed signifies God the Father, and indicates that He derives His origin from no other person; but it does not constitute Him in the being of the Father, and therefore it is not His hypostatic character (or personal property), but a personal notion." (*Exam. th. P. I. c. 2. q. 10. p. 286.*)

for the Father is made known through innascibility (ἀγεννησία), insofar as He is neither begotten by nor proceeding from another (for the term ἀγεννησία is accustomed to be understood in this way; although γέννησις is proper to the Son); and through active spiration, the Father and the Son, while not distinguished from each other, are nevertheless distinguished from the Holy Spirit. Nor are the persons multiplied on this account, because, according to the rules of the theologians, in divine matters all things are one, unless where relative opposition stands in the way. On the part of the Father, however, paternity, innascibility, and active spiration are not relatively opposed to one another; just as neither are filiation and active spiration on the part of the Son.

Quenstedtius: "Active spiration is not a character or property of the Son, strictly speaking, because it also belongs to the Father. For properties are characters of persons which belong to one person alone and not to another. And there are only three such: active generation, passive generation, and procession or passive spiration. Therefore, the argument of the Socinians fails: 'As many relations as there are in the divine, so many are the persons; but there are four relations, namely paternity, filiation, active spiration, and passive spiration. Therefore.' For we deny the major premise, because only opposite relations multiply persons in the Trinity; therefore, as many as are the opposite relations or hypostatic characters, so many are the persons." (L. c. s. 1. th. 46. f. 482.) §

44. The Father is the first person of the Divinity, not begotten, nor proceeding, but from eternity begetting the Son from His own substance, and with the Son from eternity spirating the Holy Spirit.

a) Yet not by time, nor by nature (which is the priority of a cause in relation to an effect), nor by dignity; for all divine persons are coeternal, and with the independent divine essence are really the same and mutually coequal to one another: but only by order, which some call that of "natural enumeration," since it is founded upon the origin or emanation of one person from another. Whence the Father, who is not from another, but from Himself, and is He from whom another proceeds, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit, holds the first place.

Quenstedtius: "From the real distinction of the persons arises their order both in subsisting and in operating... The order in subsisting among the divine persons is proved from the procession or emanation of one person from another... The order in operating is insinuated in Scripture through the distinguishing particles: *ex* (from), *per* (through), and *in* (in). Rom. 11:36: 'From Him and through Him and in Him are all things.' According to the holy fathers, the particle *ἐξ* is attributed to the Father, *διά* to the Son, *εἰς* to the Holy Spirit. Yet these particles do not induce any inequality of the persons of the Godhead in the work of creation, but only indicate the order of the same in acting. However, the particle *ἐξ* is expressly attributed to God the Father in 1 Cor. 8:6: 'One God the Father, from whom are all things'; *διά* however to the Son ibid.: 'And one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things'; likewise John 1:3: 'All things were made through Him (the Word of God, v. 1)', cf. Heb. 1:2. The particle *ἐν* is used of the Holy Spirit in 2 Thess. 2:13. But just as the natural order of the divine persons is not always used in Scripture, but is sometimes employed arbitrarily, as is evident from 2 Cor. 13:13, where the Son is placed before the Father, and Rev. 1:4-5, where the Son of God is placed after the Holy Spirit (designated metonymically by the name of the seven spirits), so also those particles are interchanged, just as *διά* is attributed to the Father in 1 Cor. 1:9, Rom. 6:4, Heb. 2:10; *ἐξ* to the Son in John 16:15; *ἐν* in Col. 1:14, 16; *εἰς* ibid. v. 16; *ἐν* to the Father and the Son in the Epistle of Jude PART I. CHAP. I. v. 1, because by that very permutation the *ὁμοουσία* and *ἰσότης* of the divine persons is evidently asserted and inequality of dignity is excluded." (L. c. s. 1. th. 17—19. f. 469.)

The same: "According to Athanasius against Greg. Sabell., the Father is ῥίζα καὶ πηγὴ τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος." (L. c. th. 22. f. 471.)

The same: "The fountain has no υπεροχήν (preeminence) or superiority in respect to the rivers, but at least a priority of order. Just as the sun is in respect to its rays, so the Father, who is the fountain of the Deity, is not more excellent than the Son; for from the order of procession to a prerogative of essence [does not follow]...

Distinguish between the first being, which is opposed to that which is created and dependent upon another, and that which is opposed to the remaining coeternal persons by reason of origin; thus the Father in the divine may be called the first being with respect to the remaining persons, so that these nevertheless are and remain coeternal, i.e., a being simply infinite and first with the Father according to essence from eternity. —

Distinguish between the denomination of cause, which cannot be attributed to the Father in the divine with respect to the Son; for thus the Son would be a dependent being, posterior to the Father by nature, and would differ from Him in the number of essences; and between the denomination not of nature or causality, but of comparison, relation, and ΰπάρξεως (subsistence) with respect to which the Greek fathers, calling the Father the αίτιον (cause) of the Son, used the term 'cause' for 'principle' καταχρηστικώς (improperly); the Latins, however, were by no means willing to admit the name of cause...

Distinguish between Christ as man constituted in the state of humiliation, and Christ considered as God. Christ says in John 14:28: 'The Father is greater than I,' but He affirms this of Himself as man, who had said of Himself as God that He is one with the Father (John 10:30) and equal to the Father (John 5:18). According to that nature He says the Father is greater than He, according to which He goes to the Father by dying and rising again. Rightly and truly the blessed Luther, Tom. VII. Jen. German, fol. 119: 'Christ’s words: "The Father is greater than I," are not to be understood concerning the origin of the Son from the Father by reason of deity, as Origen, Nazianzen, and Hilary explain, nor concerning the human nature taken by itself and precisely, but rather they are to be accepted concerning the state and condition in which Christ was then living, i.e., concerning the state of humiliation.'...

The Father is called the God of Christ (John 20:17), the head of Christ (1 Cor. 11:3), insofar as He is man or with respect to the human nature, who with the Father is one God and the head and Lord of all, insofar as He is God and the Son of God. For there is one Lord, through whom are all things (1 Cor. 8:6).

Obj.: 'Christ acknowledges the Father God as the first author of His doctrine and works, therefore He has a υπεροχήν (preeminence) over the Son.' Resp.: 1. The whole of Scripture teaches that Christ is the first cause, not merely a secondary one, of His doctrine and works and of things pertaining to salvation. 2. Although the Son is from the Father, He is nevertheless the same God with the Father, the author of the divine word and the first and supreme cause of all works. But He ascribes all things to the Father both with respect to origin and eternal generation, and with respect to His temporal mission. 'All things that the Father does, the Son also does likewise' (John 5:19).

Obj.: The Father has His essence from Himself: therefore He is more excellent than the Son, who does not have His essence from Himself. Resp.: 1. Not even among humans is a father more excellent than a son for that reason, by reason of essence. 2. Although having essence from another by dependence and causality implies inferiority, it does not, however, imply it when having it by origin and procession. 3. Those who are one in essence do not receive a prerogative and excellence of essence, one over the other. But the Father and the Son are one in essence (1 John 5:7; John 10:30). Therefore...

Hilary and not a few other ancients call the Father greater by reason of origin; but not greater than the Son as He is God, but as He is Son; not by reason of nature, but of person. Referring that superiority solely to the origin of the person, while preserving the numerical unity of essence, from which they differ as much as heaven from earth from the profane έτεροδοξίμ (heterodoxy) of M. Nicolai, who contends that the Son, as God, acknowledges the Father as God and head...

Nevertheless, the more accurate doctors of the church acknowledge that origin does not imply any excellence or superiority, and they dismiss that άκυρολογίαν (improper speech), that the Father is greater than the Son by reason of origin. Calov... No one among the Greek fathers uses this way of speaking:

The Father is more worthy or more excellent than the Son, or has greater authority than the Son, although some say that one person is prior to another in dignity. Therefore, Clichtoveus (who, by order of the theological faculty at the Sorbonne in Paris at the beginning of the last century, wrote the *Anti-Luther* against the blessed Luther, an armed hare among other things) ought not to have conceded that there is a more principal or more perfect mode of subsisting for one person than for another, because these words signify not only a priority of order, but also a greater dignity and excellence of nature.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 519—521.)

Gerhard: “It is to be noted in this place that the name ‘Father’ (just like the name ‘God’) is taken in the Scriptures either οὐσιωδῶς or ὑποστατικῶς. If it is taken οὐσιωδῶς, it belongs to the whole Trinity, indeed to the one God, who by reason of creation and preservation is the Father of all, but especially by reason of adoption and fatherly affection is the Father of believers. But if it is taken ὑποστατικῶς (where this occurs can be gathered from the fact when mention is made specifically of the second person, namely the Son begotten of the Father from eternity), then it belongs only to the first person. In short: when the Godhead is described within itself, the name of Father is taken ὑποστατικῶς; but when a comparison of the Godhead to creatures is made, the name of Father is taken οὐσιωδῶς and embraces each of the three persons.” (L. th. de Deo Patre et Filio § 8.)

Kromayer: “The Achilles of them (the Socinians) is the passage John 17:3: ‘This is eternal life, that they may know you (the Father) the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.’ From this they conclude that only the Father, and not Christ, is the true God. But we respond: The exclusive particle in this place is not opposed to the remaining persons of the Holy Trinity, but to all those things which are outside the divine essence, such as the false gods of the Gentiles, who are not the true God and yet were zealously worshipped in the world; according to the rule of the logicians: ‘An exclusive does not exclude concomitants.’ What is more? The Son (whom John in his first epistle, ch. 5, v. 20, names the true God and eternal life) is joined in this place with the Father, so that the sense is: This is eternal life, that they may know you, the Father, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent, to be the only true God. ‘Only’ because of the multitude of Gentile gods; ‘true’ because the gods of the Gentiles are not τῇ φύσει God, Gal. 4:8. If, however, anyone wished to argue that Christ, the Son of God, joined with the Father, is opposed by the exclusive particle to the false gods of the Gentiles, as the mediator is indeed distinguished from God in this place, the sense would be: The hinge of salvation turns upon the knowledge of God and the knowledge of Christ. This exclusive proposition belongs rather to the subject than to the predicate.” (Th. posit.-pol. Art. 2. p. 173.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Arians, Eunomians, and others of their accomplices, who assigned a prerogative to the Father over the Son... 2. Of the Socinians, who deny that the Father of our Lord J. C. is his true and natural father and contend that he is a father only improperly and metaphorically..., as if he is not the true Father, but only a vicar of the Father... 3. Of the Papists, such as Bellarmine, who in book I of *On Christ*, ch. 10, assigns a preeminence and a certain superiority to God the Father in respect to the Son according to the thing itself; for he writes: ‘The Father is the fountain and principle of the remaining persons and by that reason has a certain superiority.’ ... To this pertains the assertion of some scholastics, saying: ‘The Holy Spirit proceeds more principally from the Father than from the Son; in the Father there is authority, in the Son sub-authority.’ 4. Of certain Calvinists, who attribute a certain ἐξοχήν and ὑπεροχήν to the Father over the Son even by reason of deity; as Calvin in book I of the *Institutes*, ch. 13, § 29, where he says: ‘The name of God, although it is also common to the Son, is nevertheless sometimes ascribed κατ’ ἐξοχήν to the Father, because he is the fountain and principle of the Godhead’; Zanchius attempts to defend this ἐξοχήν with a great apparatus of words and arguments... 5. Of the Arminians, who make the Father superior to the Son and the Holy Spirit in dignity as well as in power, as from Episcopius, book IV of the *Institutes*.” PART I. CHAPTER I.

32. ...is to be seen. He here feigns a certain subordination... 6. M. Menricus Nicolai, a logician of Danzig, who places the Son and the Holy Spirit under the supreme God and attributes a prerogative to the Father over the Son and the Holy Spirit; likewise he maintains that "the Word and the Holy Spirit are something in that infinite essence, not the infinite essence itself," something of "that supreme God," not that one God; that God the Father is "the unoriginated and independent God; the Son is second from God the Father, originated, dependent, subordinated; the Holy Spirit is third from the Father, arisen from both, an originated God," he professes. (L. c. f. 517 sq.) § 45. The Son is the second person of the Divinity, eternally begotten of the Father, from whom also the person of the Father proceeds eternally, the Holy Spirit. a) Namely, because the Son is indeed not from Himself, yet another is from Him, namely the Holy Spirit. Quenstedtius: The consequences of ὁμοουσία are: 1. περιχώρησις or ἐνύπαρξις, circumincession, immanence, and mutual and most singular inexistence, by which one person, on account of the unity of essence, is in another, John 14:11; 17:21. 2. The equality of the persons, so that no person is greater, none lesser, nor can the Father be conveniently called God κατ’ ἐξοχήν or, by reason of the mode of subsistence, greater than the Son. 3. The most perfect communion of all essential perfections. 4. Ταὐτότης, or identity, both of the divine works ad extra and of the mode of acting, so that they act ταὐτὰ καὶ ὁμοίως, John 5:19, although not in the same order... Known is the rule of Augustine: "The works of God ad extra are undivided," i.e., common to all three persons. The reason for this rule is the ἑνότης or unity of the divine essence, the κοινότης or community of the power of acting, the ὁμοιότης or parity of operations, and the ταὐτότης or identity of the works of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and from this finally follows the ἰσότης or equality of denomination. However, this clause must be added to the Augustinian rule: "The order and distinction of the persons being preserved"; for because the Father has essence from Himself, He therefore also acts from Himself; the Son acts and works from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both, John 5:19, 20. Obs. on this statement:

1. "Οὐ δύναται οὐδὲν ποιεῖν" does not denote ἀδυναμίαν, impotence or weakness, as in John 15:5: "Without me you can do nothing," cf. 2 Cor. 3:5; but rather, when it is predicated of God simply, it designates the supreme perfection of a nature acting in the same way, so that it cannot be otherwise; just as elsewhere it is called ἀδύνατον for God to lie, since He is ἀψευδής, Heb. 6:18, Tit. 1:

2. But when it is used concerning Christ, it expresses the identity, unity, and inseparability of His and the Father’s essence, power, will, and operation, and at the same time the τρόπον ὑπάρξεως, that is, that the Son, just as He does not have His essence from Himself but from the Father through eternal generation, so also He does not have the power of acting from Himself or act from Himself, but from the Father. In the very same sense in which the Holy Spirit, on account of His procession from the Son, is said not to speak from Himself, but to receive and announce those things which are Christ’s, John 16:

13. Therefore, the Son does not act from Himself, as the Father does, since He is not from Himself, but from the Father, from whom He has His omnipotence just as He …has His essence. In short: it is ἀδύνατον, impossible, that the Son should do anything that He has not seen the Father doing, on account of the ὁμοουσία of the Son with the Father and the origin of the Son from the Father. Observe: 2. "Βλέπειν" the Father acting is said ἀνθρωποπαθῶς or in a human manner, but it is to be understood θεοπρεπῶς or in a manner befitting God, and it denotes the most exact knowledge, which the Son received from the Father not through instruction, as a disciple, but through eternal generation, as the only-begotten Son. The Son "sees" what the Father does, not after

Latin:

Idem: ,,Spiritus S. a Patre et Filio immanenter emanat et emananter immanet.“ (L. c. p. 78.) Dannhauerus: ,,Annon derogat divinae majestati Spiritus Sancti, quod nullam ipse de se personam producit aliam? Resp.: Hoc adeo de ipsius gloria nihil diminuit, ut potius aeterna majestas ejus isthinc inenarrabiliter illustretur. . . Nequaquam imperfectus haberi potest is, qui in sua substantia personarum productionem illam finit et absolvit, totamque Trinitatem in consummatae perfectionis velut orbem atque circulum sic reducit, ut in hoc suo Spiritu Pater et Filius unice acquiescant.“ (Hodos. phaen. 3. p. 94.) § 42.

Proprietates personales sunt tres:a Paternitas,b filiatio c et processio stricte sic dicta, sive spiratio passiva.d Nempe pro numero personarum, quarum quaelibet per subsistentiam relativam in esse certae personae constituitur. Fundata in generatione active spectata. Fundata in generatione passive seu terminative spectata. Non quod in Deum cadat aliqua passio realis, sed grammatice loquendo, seu quia Spiritus S. spirari, non spirare dicitur; quamvis ex parte Dei spiratio purus actus sit, omnis passionis expers. Conf.Mus. Disp. cit. de Deo § 6. p. 73. 74.§ 43.

Notiones speciatim sic dictae a duae sunt: Innascibilitas,b et spiratio activa. Seu a proprietatibus distinctae. Alias enim, latius sumta voce notionis et connumeratis proprietatibus, quinque sunt notiones.Hollazius: ,,’Aγεννησία notiflcat quidem Deum Patrem, et indicat, ipsum a nulla alia persona ducere originem; at non constituit illum in esse Patris, adeoque non ipsius character hypostaticus (s. proprietas personalis), sed notio personalis est.“

Nempe per innascibilitat&tn (άγεννηαίαν) Pater innotescit, quatenus non est ab alio vel genitus, vel procedens (sic enim vocabulum άγεννησίας accipi consuevit; licet γέννηαις sit Filio propria); per spirationem activam Pater et Filius, licet non inter se, a Spiritu Sancto tamen distinguuntur. Nec propterea multiplicantur personae, quia, juxta regulas theologorum, in divinis omnia sunt unum, nisi ubi obviat relativa oppositio. Ex parte Patris autem paternitas, innascibilitas et spiratio activa inter se non opponuntur relative; quemadmodum nec ex parte Filii filiatio et spiratio activa.

Quenstedtius: ,,Spiratio activa non est character vel proprietas Filii accurate loquendo, quia etiam Patri competit. Proprietates enim sunt characteres personarum, qui uni soli personae competunt et non alii. Et tales tantum tres sunt: Generatio activa, generatio passiva et processio seu spiratio passiva. Fallit ergo argumentum Socinianorum: ,Quot sunt in divinis relationes, tot sunt personae; sed quatuor sunt relationes, nempe paternitas, filiatio, spiratio activa et spiratio passiva. Ergo.‘ Negamus enim majorem, quia solae relationes oppositae multiplicant personas in Trinitate; quot itaque sunt relationes oppositae sive characteres hypostatici, tot sunt personae.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 46. f. 482.) §

44. Pater est prima a persona Divinitatis, non genita, nec procedens, sed ab aeterno de sua substantia gignens Filium, et cum Filio ab aeterno spirans Spiritum Sanctum.

a) Non tamen vel tempore, vel natura (qualis prioritas est causae, in ordine ad effectum), vel dignitate; omnes enim personae divinae sunt coaeternae, et cum essentia divina independente realiter idem et sibi invicem coaequales: sed tantum ordine, quem,naturalis enumerationis quidam vocant, quippe fundatum in origine seu emanatione personae unius ab alia. Unde Pater, qui non est ab alio, sed a seipso, et est is, a quo procedit alius, nempe Filius et Spiritus Sanctus, primum locum obtinet.

Quenstedtius: ,,Ex discrimine personarum reali oritur earum ordo cum in subsistendo tum in operando. . . Ordo in subsistendo inter divinas personas probatur ex unius personae ab altera processione seu emanatione... Ordo in operando insinuatur in Scriptura per particulas διακριτικάς: ex, per et in. Rom. 11, 36.: ,Ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso omnia.‘ Juxta s. patres particula εξ tribuitur Patri, διά Filio, εις Spiritui S. Nullam tamen hae particulae personarum Deitatis inaequalitatem in opere creationis inducunt, sed tantum ordinem earundem in agendo indicant. Tribuitur autem particula εξ diserte Deo Patri 1 Cor. 8, 6.: ,Unus Deus Pater, ex quo omnia‘; διά autem Filio ibid.: ,Et unus Dominus Jesus Christus, per quem omnia‘; itemque Joh. 1, 3.: ,Omnia per ipsum (Dei Verbum, v. 1.) facta sunt‘, cf. Ebr. 1, 2. Particula kv de Spiritu S. usurpatur 2 Thess. 2, 13. Uti vero ordo naturalis personarum divinarum non semper in Scriptura usurpatur, sed quandoque arbitrarius adhibetur, ut patet ex 2 Cor. 13, 13., ubi Filius Patri praeponitur, et Apoc. 1, 4. 5., ubi Filius Dei Spiritui S. (septem spirituum nomine metonymice designato) postponitur, ita et particulae illae permutantur, sicut διά Patri 1 Cor. 1, 9., Rom. 6, 4., Ebr. 2, 10., Filio εκ Joh. 16, 15., kv Col. 1, 14. 16., εις ib. v. 16., kv Patri et Filio ep. Judae PABT. I. CAP. I. v. 1. tribuatur, quia ipsa permutatione όμοονσία et ίσ6της personarum divinarum evidenter asseritur et dignitatis inaequalitas excluditur.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 17—19. f. 469.)

Idem: ״Juxta Athanasium contra Greg. Sabell., Pater est ρίζα καί πψ/η του viov και τον πνεύματος. (L. c. th. 22. f. 471.)

Idem: ״Fons nullam habet υπεροχήν et majoritatem in respectu ad fluvios, sed prioritatem saltem ordinis. Uti et sol in respectu ad radios, ita nec Pater, qui est fons Deitatis, est excellentior Filio; a processionis enim ordine ad praerogativam essentiae N. Y. C...

Dist. inter ens primum, quod opponitur creato et ab alio dependenti, et quod opponitur reliquis personis coaeternis ratione originis; sic Pater in divinis potest dici ens primum respectu reliquarum personarum, ut tamen hae sint et maneant coaeternae, h. e., ens simpliciter infinitum et primum cum Patre secundum essentiam ab aeterno. —

Dist. inter dfenominationem causae, quae Patri in divinis respectu Filii tribui non potest; sic enim Filius esset ens dependens natura Patre posterior et numero essentiarum ab eodem differret; et inter denominationempnnctjm non naturae seu causalitatis, sed comparationis, relationis et ΰπάρξεως respectu, unde Graeci patres, Patrem αίτιον (causam) Filii dicentes, causam pro principio καταχρηστικώς usurparunt; Latini vero nomen causae nullatenus admittere voluerunt. . .

Dist. inter Christum ut hominem in statu exinanitionis constitutum, et Christum ut Deum consideratum. Christus Joh. 14, 28. dicit: ,Pater major me est‘, sed hoc de se ut homine affirmat, qui se ut Deum cum Patre unum Joh. 10, 30. et Patri aequalem dixerat Joh. 5, 18. Secundum eam naturam Patrem se majorem dicit, secundum quam ad Patrem moriendo et resurgendo vadit. Recte et vere b. Lutherus Tom. VII. Jen. German, fol. 119.: ,Verba Christi: ,Pater major me est‘, non de origine Filii a Patre ratione deitatis, ut Origenes, Nazianzenus et Hilarius explicant, nec de humana natura per se sumta et praecise, sed potius de statu et conditione, in qua tum vivebat Christus, h. e. de statu exinanitionis accipienda esse docet.‘. .

Pater dicitur Christi Deus Joh. 20, 17., caput Christi 1 Cor. 11, 3., in quantum homo est seu respectu humanae naturae, qui cum Patre unus est Deus ac caput et Dominus omnium, in quantum Deus et Dei Filius est. Unus enim est Dominus, per quem omnia 1 Cor. 8. 6.

Objic.: ,Christum doctrinae suae et operum primum auctorem agnoscere Deum Patrem, hunc ergo prae Filio habere υπεροχήν. Resp.: 1. Christum doctrinae et operum suorum rerumque ad salutem spectantium primam esse causam, non secundam tantum, universa docet Scriptura. 2. Licet Filius a Patre sit, idem tamen cum Patre Deus est, verbi divini auctor et operum omnium causa prima supremaque. Patri autem transscribit omnia cum respectu originis et generationis aeternae, tum respectu missionis suae temporalis. ,Omnia, quae Pater facit, eadem similiter facit et Filius‘, Joh. 5, 19.

Objic.: Pater essentiam suam a seipso habet: ergo excellentior est Filio, qui essentiam suam a seipso non habet. Resp.: 1. Ne in humanis quidem propterea, essentiae ratione, pater excellentior est filio. 2. Licet habere ab alio essentiam per dependentiam et causalitatem inferat inferioritatem, non tamen infert, habere per originem ac processionem. 3. Qui essentia unum sunt, eorum alter prae altero essentiae praerogativam et excellentiam non recipit. Sed Pater et Filius essentia unum sunt, 1 Joh. 5, 7. Joh. 10, 30. Ergo. . .

Hilarius aliique non pauci veteres Patrem majorem dicunt ratione originis; at non majorem Filio, ut Deus est, sed ut Filius est; non ratione naturae, sed personae. Majoritatem illam unice ad personae originem referentes, salva essentiae unitate numerica, unde toto coelo distant a M. Nicolai profana έτεροδοξίμ, qui Filium, ut Deum, Deum et caput agnoscere Patrem contendit. . .

Accuratiores tamen ecclesiae doctores originem non inferre aliquam excellentiam vel majoritatem agnoscunt, eamque άκνρο'λογίαν, quod Pater ratione originis major sit Filio, dimittunt. Calov. . . Nullus Graecorum patrum utitur hoc modo loquendi:

Pater dignior seu excellentior est Pilio, vel majorem, quam Filius, habet auctoritatem, quamvis aliqui dicant, unam personam esse dignitate priorem alia. Non ergo debuit Clichtovaeus (qui jussu facultatis theol. in Sorbona Parisiensi sub initio superioris saeculi in b. Lutherum, armatus lepus, scripsit AntiLutherum inter alia) concedere, esse principaliorem seu perfectiorem modum subsistendi unius personae, quam alterius, quia haec verba non solum prioritatem ordinis, sed etiam majorem dignitatem et excellentiam naturae significant.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 519—521.)

Gerhardus: ,,Observandum hoc loco, nomen,Patris‘ (perinde ut nomen,Dei‘) sumi in Scripturis vel ονσιωδΰς vel ΰποστατιιιώς. Si ούσιωδώς accipitur, competit toti Trinitati, uni vero Deo, qui ratione creationis et conservationis Pater est omnium, specialiter autem ratione adoptionis et paterni affectus est Pater credentium. Si vero υποστατικώς accipitur (id ubi flat, ex eo colligi potest, quando nominatim fit mentio secundae personae, videlicet Filii a Patre ab aeterno geniti), tum soli primae personae convenit. Breviter: quando Divinitas intra se describitur, nomen Patris sumitur υποστατικώς; quando vero fit coilatio Divinitatis ad creaturas, nomen Patris sumitur ονσιυόώς et complectitur singulas tres personas.“ (L. th. de Deo Patre et Filio § 8.)

Kromayerus: ,,Achilles ipsorum (Socinianorum) est locus Joh. 17, 3.: ,Haec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te (Patrem) solum Deum verum et quem misisti, Jesum Christum.‘ Unde colliguut, solum Patrem, non autem Christum esse verum Deum. Sed respondemus: Exclusivam h. 1. non opponi reliquis SS. Trinitatis personis, sed omnibus iis, quae sunt extra divinam essentiam, ut deastris gentilium, qui non sunt verus Deus et tamen certatim colebantur in mundo; secundum regulam logicorum: ,Exclusiva non excludit concomitantia.‘ Quid? quod Filius (quem Johannes in epistola I. c. 5, v. 2. verum Deum et vitam aeternam nominat) h. 1. conjungatur cum Patre, ut sensus sit: Haec est vita aeterna, ut te Patrem et Jesum Christum, quem misisti, cognoscant esse solum verum Deum. ,Solum‘ propter multitudinem deorum gentilium, ,verum‘ propterea, quod dii gentilium non sunt rrj φύσει Deus, Gal. 4, 8. Si quis tamen Christum, Dei Filium, cum Patre junctim per exclusivam deastris gentilium opponi, ut mediatorem vero h. 1. a Deo distingui vellet, sensus esset: In θεογνωσία:et χριστογνωσία cardinem salutis verti. Exclusiva haec propositio potius est subjecti, quam praedicati.“ (Th. posit.-pol. Art. 2. p. 173.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Arianorum, Eunominianorum, aliorumque eorum complicum, qui Patri prae Filio praerogativam assignabant. . . 2. Socinianorum, qui Patrem Domini nostri J. C. verum et naturalem ejus patrem esse negant et saltem improprie et metaphorice patrem esse contendunt. . ., ac si non verus Pater est, sed tantum vicarius Patris. . . 3. Pontificiorum, ut Bellarmini, qui lib. I. de Christo c. 10. secundum rem praeeminentiam et majoritatem quandam Deo Patri respectu Filii assignat; scribit enim: ,Pater est fons et principium reliquarum personarum et ea ratione quandam majoritatem habet.’ . . . Huc pertinet assertio scholasticorum nonnullorum, dicentium: ,Spiritum S. principalius procedere a Patre, quam a Filio; in Patre esse auctoritatem, in Filio subauctoritatem.‘ 4. Quorundam Calvinianorum, qui Patri εξοχήν et υπεροχήν quandam prae Filio etiam ratione deitatis tribuunt; ut Calvinus lib. I. Institut, c. 13. § 29., ubi inquit: ,Dei nomen, quamvis commune quoque sit Filio, tamen ιιατ’ εξοχήν Patri interdum adscribitur, quia fons est et principium Divinitatis‘; Zanchius magno verborum et argumentorum apparatu hanc εξοχήν defendere conatur. .. 5. Arminianorum, qui Patrem dignitate pariter ac potestate superiorem faciunt Filio ac Spiritu S., uti ex Episcopio lib. IV. Instit. PART. I. CAP. I.

32. videre est. . . Subordinationem quandam hic fingit... 6. M. Menrici Nicolai, logici Dantiscani, qui Filium et Spiritum S. sub summo Deo collocat et praerogativam Patri prae Filio et Sp. ## 4 On Creation

operation, but because He is the wisdom of the Father, through whom He acts. Christ, however, willed to show Himself so joined to the Father in nature, that He nevertheless signified that He was distinct. He shows Himself joined when He says that He cannot do anything except what the Father does; He shows Himself distinct when He says, "except what He sees the Father doing"; for he who sees is one, and he who is seen is another. He makes Himself equal to the Father, yet in such a way that He speaks in a manner befitting the Son…equal to the Father, yet in such a way that He speaks in a manner befitting the Son. The "vision" (v. 19) attributed to the Son and the "demonstration" (v. 20) are related. Therefore, just as the Father demonstrates all things to the Son by working through the Son—really, not exemplarily—so also the Son sees in the unity of wisdom and power, working όμοίως (likewise) with the Father. For "He shows Him" (δείκνυσιν αὐτῷ) means "He will work in Him and through Him"; it is a vocal word for a real one (John 10:32; Acts 9:16; 2 Tim. 4:14). Because the Son is the image of the Father and the radiance of His glory (Heb. 1:3), the Father is said to demonstrate to the Son and to demonstrate Himself in the Son. Cyril of Alexandria (Book II on John, ch. 137) says beautifully: "The Father demonstrates to the Son what He Himself does, not as if depicted on tablets, nor as if helping one who is ignorant with instruction. For the Son, as God, knows all things; but [the Father] paints His whole self in the nature of the Son in such a way that whatever He has in Himself, He demonstrates in the Son," etc. 3. The particle "whatsoever" (quaecunque) is not to be extended to internal works or works *ad intra*, such as begetting, being begotten, spirating, and proceeding, which pertain only to one or two persons in the Godhead, but is to be understood only of works *ad extra*, and yet not only of miracles, as the Socinians wish, but of all external works (creation, preservation, universal governance, etc.). "For whatsoever the Father does (ad extra, that is), ταῦτα (these same things) the Son also does," not by imitating similar things, but by working the same works simultaneously... He does exactly the same things, so that nothing is excepted; "likewise" (ὁμοίως), in the same manner, not by some disparity or inequality, but from the same essence, wisdom, goodness, and power does the Son act. Nazianzen rightly says (Oration IV on Theology): "He does not say ὁμοίως because there is a similarity of works, but because the power of both is equal, and the majesty is equal." (L. c. s. 1. th. 21. f. 470. sq.) § 46. The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Godhead, not begotten, but proceeding from eternity from the Father and the Son. a) Because He is not from Himself, nor does another, or another person of the Godhead, proceed from Him.

Quenstedtius: "Regarding the name, He is called Spirit: 1. By reason of spirituality or spiritual essence and on account of spiritual effects; and thus all three persons of the Godhead are called and are Spirit (John 4:24).

2. From the mode of existence (τρόπῳ ὑπάρξεως) or hypostatic character, namely, eternal spiration; by which reason neither the Father nor the Son is Spirit, but only the third person; for that name pertains most properly to Him by reason of the Father and Son 'breathing' (πνέοντος), because He proceeds from both by spiration from eternity... He is and is called 'Holy' not only by essence, by which reason essential holiness pertains to Him with the Father and the Son (Isa. 6:3), but also from a singular character, namely, from the work of sanctification, which the Holy Spirit performs proximately and immediately, and for the performance of which He is sent by the Father and the Son into the hearts of believers." (L. c. s. 1. th. 56. 57, f. 486. sq.) Luther: "Scripture calls this Spirit of God the Holy Spirit for this reason: that just as the office of the Son is indicated in that He is called a Teacher of righteousness, so the Spirit of God is called 'holy' from His office. For He makes us holy, we who are born and are entirely unholy and godless through sin."

(On Joel 2:28, 29. Opp. Hal. VI, 2315.) PART I. CHAP. II.

§ 47.

God, viewed simultaneously in respect to His essence and His persons, may be described as a spiritual being, subsisting of Himself in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Usually, more prolix descriptions are brought forward, by which the persons are also described by their works ad extra: the Father by creation, the Son by redemption, and the Holy Spirit by sanctification. However, because these works are not coeternal with God and the divine persons, we have preferred to retain that description which pertains to God and the divine persons as they are in themselves from all eternity. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, cited Disp. III. § last, p. 76. Luther: "Therefore you see here upon what the Symbol of the holy Athanasius is founded, which is composed in such a way that I do not know whether, since the time of the Apostles, anything more important and glorious has been written in the Church of the New Testament." (On Joel 3:28. VI, 2314.) Chapter II. ON CREATION. § 1.

Among the works by which God has exercised His supreme goodness, creation must be viewed in the first place. See Chapter I, § 27, p. 44, and § 37, note a, p. 64. And thus the reason for the order is clear, as this place is immediately joined to the former. Gerhard: "When we say that God does something, we do not understand that any motion is present in Him in acting, but we signify some new effect of His eternal will; i.e., we say that by His eternal will something newly comes into existence." (L. th. 1. on creation § 4.) § 2.

The word "creation" denotes the production of a subsistent thing, either out of nothing—that is, which occurs independently of a subject—or dependently upon a subject—that is, out of some subject, but one so unfit and indisposed that such an effect cannot be produced from its potentiality by the power of a created agent. Gerhard: "We call those things 'subsistent' which do not exist in another, but in themselves." (Exeg. 1. III. § 57.)

Reuschius: "A 'subsistent thing' is called here a substance, i.e., a being which, by its own power sustained by God, or 'by itself,' as others say, can exist."

and thus that which can exist separated from other finite beings, or can have a separate and proper existence. The blessed author therefore takes "to subsist" in a different sense than it is otherwise taken among philosophers; since subsistence and to subsist are said to be the existence of a suppositum." (Annot. p. 195.)

In the style of Scripture, indeed, and speaking properly. For otherwise, in a moral sense, magistrates, consuls, leaders, etc., are also said to be created. And Scripture itself says that a new heart is created in man, i.e., new spiritual powers are conferred upon man, which they call metaphorical creation. Philosophers, however, take the term creation more strictly for the production of a thing precisely out of nothing. Quenstedtius: "Nothing else is denoted by 'out of nothing' than the term from which, that is, nothing, out of which all things are said to be made; it does not have the nature of matter, but only of the term from which, and it must be understood regarding the order of creation; and the particle 'out of' can rightly be translated as 'after,' as Thomas observes, so that the sense may be: After nothing, as the term from which, something was made." (L. c. s. 1. th. 13. f. 594.) That twofold acceptance of the word "to create" occurs in Genesis, chapter 1: the former, v. 1, concerning the creation made in the beginning; the latter, v. 21 and 27, concerning the creation of aquatic creatures out of water, and of man out of the dust of the earth; compared with chapter 2, 7. More will be evident from what follows. § 3.

Moreover, production out of nothing occurs in two ways, insofar as an effect is produced either independently of any subject, whether pre-existing or co-existing; in which manner immaterial substances, angels and the soul (of Adam), were produced; or an effect is produced, indeed independently of a pre-existing subject, but yet dependently upon a co-existing one; in which manner simple bodies were produced, e.g., the heaven and the elements. Namely, substances which in their being do not depend upon matter are, in accordance with their nature, produced also independently of all matter. Certainly, material things, and those simple ones, just as they consist of matter and form regarding their being—yet their matter did not exist separately before all form, nor did (material) form exist outside of matter—so in their coming-to-be they depend (as composites) upon matter, yet not upon pre-existing matter. Reuschius: "The blessed author added heaven as a peculiar species, distinct from the Aristotelian elements (in Baier, de creatione § 22). But heaven, as heaven, and distinct from the total bodies of the world, such as planets, comets, and fixed stars or suns, consists of ether, which fills those most vast spaces, and by that it is not distinguished from the Aristotelian elements." (Annot. p. 199.)

The same: "The blessed author asserts that simple bodies or physical elements were produced independently of pre-existing matter, and thus suppo PART I. CHAP. II.

as indubitable that the metaphysical elements, from which as from matter simple bodies are composed, did not exist individually and separately in the first creation, but on the contrary, were produced immediately from the beginning in that union by which they constitute physical elements. But the mode of creation depends upon the free will of God, determined by the principle of the best. However, whether the simultaneous production of the individual metaphysical elements without the union, in which they constitute simple bodies or physical elements—which union would have been made later in the separation of the physical elements—or whether the simultaneous production of the individual metaphysical elements immediately in that union by which they constitute physical elements or simple bodies, is the better and best mode of creating, and thus was decreed by God according to the principle of the best, cannot be determined with certainty; since no certain principles are available, either from reason or from revelation, from which one or the other mode of creating necessarily follows. Wherefore, those things which the blessed author asserts as indubitable are not such, but only probable. Yet it is not denied that they possess some probability.” (Annot. p. 199 sqq.) §

4. The remaining works of creation, or mixed bodies, were produced dependently upon pre-existing matter, namely, from the very simple bodies first produced. For although God, through His absolute power, could also produce mixed bodies independently of a pre-existing subject, it nevertheless pleased God to effect the work of creation in accordance with the order of nature, and to produce mixed bodies from pre-existing simple ones. Thus, plants were produced from the earth, and fish from the water; as we shall soon see. §

VI, 2314.) Caput II. DE CREATIONE. § 1.

Inter opera, quibus Deus summam bonitatem suam a exercuit, primo loco spectanda venit creatio. Vid. cap. I. § 27. p. 44. et § 37. not. a. p. 64. Atque ita patet ratio ordinis, quoad hunc locum, priori statim subjunctum.Gerhardus: ״Cum dicimus, Deum aliquid facere, non aliquem in operando motum illi inesse intelligimus, sed ejus sempiternae voluntatis novum aliquem significamus effectum, i. e., aeterna ejus voluntate noviter aliquid exiatere dicimus.“ (L. th. 1. de creatione § 4.) § 2.

Creationis vox denotat a productionem rei subsistentis, vel ex nihilo, seu quae fit independenter a subjecto, vel dependenter a subjecto, seu ex aliquo subjecto, verum ita inhabili et indisposito, ut ex potentia ejus non possit produci talis effectus per virtutem agentis creati.b Gerhardus: ״Illa subsistere dicimus, quae non in alio, sed in se existunt.“ (Exeg. 1. III. § 57.)

Reuschius: ״Res subsistens hic dicitur substantia i. e. ens, quod sua vi a Deo sustentata seu per se, ut alii loquuntur, existere potest,

adeoque quod separatum ab aliis entibus finitis existere seu separatam et propriam habere potest existentiam. To subsistere eapropter b. auctor alio sensu accipit, ac alias apud philosophos sumitur; cum subsistentia et subsistere dicatur existentia suppositi.“ (Annot. p. 195.)

Stylo Scripturae quidem et proprie loquendo. Nam alias etiam morali significatione dicuntur creari magistratus, consules, duces, etc. Et Scriptura ipsa dicit, creari in homine cor novum, i. e. conferri homini novas vires spirituales, quam creationem metaphoricam vocant. Philosophi autem creationis vocem strictius accipiunt pro productione rei ex nihilo praecise.Quenstedtius: ,,Non aliud notatur per rb ex nihilo, quam terminus a quo, hoc est, nihilum, ex quo omnia facta dicuntur, non materiae, sed termini a quo duntaxat rationem habet et de creationis ordine intelligi debet, et recte particula ex per post verti potest, ut Thomas observat, ut sensus sit: Post nihilum, velut terminum a quo, aliquid factum est.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 13. f. 594.) Occurrit duplex illa acceptio vocis creandi, Genes, cap. 1., et prior quidem v. 1. de creatione in principio facta, posterior v. 21. et 27. de creatione aquatilium ex aqua, hominis e pulvere terrae; collato cap. 2, 7. Plura ex seqq. patebunt.§ 3.

Fit autem etiam productio ex nihilo dupliciter, quatenus producitur effectus vel independenter ab omni subjecto seu praeexistente seu coexistente; qua ratione substantiae immateriales, angeli et anima (Adami), fuerunt productae;a vel producitur effectus, independenter quidem a subjecto praeexistente, sed tamen dependenter a coexistente; qua ratione producta sunt corpora simplicia, v. g. coelum et elementa.b Nempe substantiae, quae in esse suo a materia non dependent, naturae suae convenienter productae sunt etiam independenter ab omni materia. Sane res materiales, eaeque simplices, sicut constant materia et forma quoad esse suum, materia vero illarum non extitit seorsim ante omnem formam, nec forma (materialis) extra materiam, ita in fieri dependent (tanquam composita) a materia, non tamen a materia praeexistente.Reuschius: ״Addidit b. auctor coelum, tamquam speciem peculiarem et diversam ab elementis Aristotelicis (apud Baier. de creatione § 22.). Sed coelum, qua coelum, atque a corporibus mundi totalibus, ut planetis, cometis et stellis fixis seu solibus, distinctum, constat aethere, qui amplissima illa spatia replet, eoque ab elementis Aristotelicis non distinguitur.“ (Annot. p. 199.)

Idem: ״Corpora simplicia seu elementa physica independenter a praeexistente materia esse producta, asserit b. auctor, adeoque suppo PART. I. CAP. II.

nit ceu indubitatum, quod elementa metaphysica, ex quibus tamquam ex materia corpora simplicia composita sunt, in creatione prima singulatim et separatim non extiterint, contra, statim ab initio in ea unione, qua elementa physica efficiunt, producta sint. Sed modus creationis a libera Dei voluntate ex ratione optimi determinata dependet. Utrum vero singulorum elementorum metaphysicorum simultanea productio sine unione tamen, in qua constituunt corpora simplicia seu elementa physica, quae unio postea in separatione elementorum physicorum facta sit; an productio simultanea singulorum elementorum metaphysicorum statim in illa unione, qua elementa physica seu corpora simplicia constituunt, sit melior atque optimus creandi modus, adeoque ex ratione optimi decreta a Deo fuerit, determinari non potest cum certitudine; quum nulla certa principia vel ex ratione vel ex revelatione suppetant, ex quibus necessario sequatur alteruter modus creandi. Quapropter ea, quae b. auctor tamquam indubitata asserit, talia non sunt, sed tantum probabilia. Non tamen negatur, quod aliquam habeant probabilitatem.“ (Annot. p. 199. sqq.) §

4. Reliqua creationis opera, seu corpora mixta producta sunt dependenter a materia praeexistente,a nempe ex ipsis corporibus simplicibus primum productis.b Nam quamvis Deus per absolutam suam potentiam etiam corpora mixta posset producere independenter a subjecto praeexistente, placuit tamen Deo, efficere opus creationis convenienter ordini naturae, et producere corpora mixta ex praeexistentibus simplicibus. Sic plantae ex terra, pisces ex aqua producti sunt; ut mox videbimus.§


### On Creation: According to the history of creation, God completed the production of this…

5. According to the history of creation, God completed the production of this universe in the space of six days.

Luther: “Hilary and Augustine, as if they were the two greatest lights of the church, hold the opinion that the world was created suddenly and simultaneously, not successively over six days. And Augustine plays wonderfully in his treatment of the six days, which he makes into mystical days of knowledge in the angels, not natural ones. . . Nor is it useful to make Moses so mystical and allegorical at the beginning. For because he wishes to teach us, not about allegorical creatures and an allegorical world, but about essential creatures and a world visible and exposed to the senses, he calls, as the proverb says, a spade a spade—that is, he calls it day and evening, just as we are accustomed to do, without allegory, just as the evangelist Matthew also retains this phrase in the last chapter, when he writes that Christ rose on the evening of the Sabbath, which was dawning toward the first day of the week. But if we do not sufficiently grasp the reason for the days, nor understand why God wished to use these intervals of time, let us rather confess our ignorance than twist the words away from the matter into a foreign sense. Therefore, as far as this opinion of Augustine is concerned, we maintain that Moses spoke properly, not allegorically or figuratively; that is, that the world with all its creatures was created within six days, as the words sound.

But if we do not grasp the cause, let us remain disciples, and leave the mastery to the Holy Spirit.”

Quenstedtius: "That all things were not created by God simultaneously in one moment or instant, but over the space of six days, is proven: 1. From the history of creation described in Gen. 1, in which all words are to be understood historically and properly, nor should one depart from the clear letter unless the analogy of faith, the antecedents and consequents, and other circumstances suggest it; but in that passage, Moses teaches in the plainest words what was done by God on each day. 2. From the sanctification of the Sabbath and the reason for this matter, which is rendered in Gen. 2:3, Ex. 13:6, and 20:11, which would be of no moment if God had created all things in a single moment, and not successively over several days. 3. From reason; if all things had been made simultaneously, some reason would have to be given for the order of that Mosaic narrative. But Moses does not observe the order of nature, nor of dignity, nor of cognition; therefore, the order of time remains." (Theol. did. pol. P. I. c. 10. s. 2. q. 6. p. 613.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of some fathers, such as Origen in book 6 against Celsus, Athanasius in oration 3 against the Arians, Augustine in book 4 of *De Genesi ad litteram* c. 22 sqq. and book 2 of *De civitate Dei* c. 29 sqq., and Procopius of Gaza on Genesis, who maintain that the world was created by God in one moment and that the six days are to be interpreted allegorically... 2. Of Philo the Jew in his book *On the Creation of the World* and book 1 of the *Allegories of the Mosaic Law* p. 29... In short: that opinion, that all things were founded in one instant, devised by the Rabbis, encrusted by Cajetan and Melchior Cano (as reported by Dominicus Banne), and recently defended and enriched with new paradoxes by the Jesuit Nicolaus Abramus of Pont-à-Mousson; for the latter maintains: 'that the substance of all things, except the soul of man, was produced simultaneously in the first moment of time, and that during the six days all things emerged according to their qualities through natural emanation and strove toward their natural place by natural inclination,' which opinion Dr. Calovius refuted in Vol. III of his System." (L. c.)

Vilmar: "The investigation and answering of the question whether the days were 24-hour days dependent on the axial rotation of the earth, or creation (restitution) periods of indefinite duration, can be left freely to dogmatics without hesitation. In the application which is made of these (5 days already in Gen. 2:2–3 and later in the Law), 24-hour days are indeed meant, and the wording (evening and morning, 1st day, 2nd day, etc.) seems to speak for this. On the other hand, the determination in Ps. 90:4 and 2 Peter 3:8, according to which 1000 years are like a day and a day like 1000 years before God, is not unfavorable to the assumption of creation periods. These periods could have closed with a twilight and begun again with a twilight, thus having been separated by a night in which God did not create, but they did not depend on the axial rotation of the earth, but on other struggles between light and darkness." (Dogmatik. I, p. 247.)

Which is accurately described in Gen. ch. 1 and 2. See ch. 1, last verse, and ch. 2:2

Gen. § 6. On the first day, and since until then no thing had been created, but only God existed, God produced the heaven and the earth, and likewise the light, which would constitute the vicissitudes of day and night. PART I. CHAP. II.

See Gen. 1:1, where the word בראשית is to be explained adverbially and negatively, so that it must be said that nothing, not even any matter of this universe, existed beforehand.

Scherzerus: "In the beginning, בראשית (from which the Cabbalists make the first September by *temurah*; and Dr. Calovius, although the Fathers and other theologians choose the spring season—which opinion also pleased us at one time, *Syst.* III, f. 924—argues for the autumn, because otherwise fruits would have had to be produced twice in the first year of creation, and thus God would have immediately changed His ordinance, which is improbable), or in the first instant of time (and thus not in time, for creation and time began together), God created the heaven and the earth, Gen. 1:1. No other beginning than that of time can be understood; not of eternity, because it lacks a beginning; not of an age (*aevum*), because this duration belongs only to created spirits: therefore, it is of time. It is said ineptly: 'In the beginning of the world the world was created'; or: 'In the beginning of creation God created the heaven and the earth'; for the question remains, what beginning is understood; but Moses did not leave the reader in suspense." (*System. theol.* 1.1. § 8. p. 87 sq.)

Quenstedtius: "It is an *ἀκυρολογία* (improper speech) to say that the world at one time did not exist. For 'at one time' is the same as 'at some time'; but it cannot be said that it did not yet exist at some time, since before the world was founded, time did not exist. He speaks more cautiously who says that the world did not always exist." (*L. c. q. 2. f. 602.*)

The same: "It is proven that the world could not have existed or been created from eternity: 1. Because to exist from eternity is proper to God alone, so that whatever is eternal, it must be that it is God. 2. Because it involves a contradiction, both on the part of God creating, who cannot produce another God distinct from Himself, and on the part of creation, because this presupposes some beginning in which it takes place, and finally on the part of the creature, which is not capable of existence from eternity. That which cannot exist except after non-existence cannot exist from eternity; but no creature can exist except after non-existence, for to be created is to be produced from nothing. Therefore. That which exists from eternity exists without a beginning of itself; but a creature, whenever it is created, comes into being, because every effect, while it is produced by its cause, comes into being, and receives its existence from the same; but when a creature comes into being, it begins to exist, and if it begins to exist, it could not have existed from eternity. For it is contradictory to exist with a beginning of oneself and not to exist with a beginning of oneself." (*L. c. f. 601.*)

The same: "That dispute (whether the world could have been created from eternity) does not concern an article of faith; and therefore neither opinion is to be accused of heresy, much less of any atheism. For neither do those who deny that it could be created from eternity derogate from infinite power, since they do not deny it due to a defect of virtue in God, but because of an impossible object, which they judge to involve a contradiction; nor do those who affirm it admit an actual eternal creation, but only make it possible and do not think it involves a contradiction." (*L. c. q. 2. f. 599.*)

The same: "The creation of the world from nothing, having taken place in time, cannot be known from the light of nature or demonstrated apodictically and evidently by philosophical arguments, but becomes known from divine revelation alone, and thus is an article of pure faith and mere revelation." (*L. c. q. 1. f. 596.*)

Underst and the heaven itself under the substantial form of heaven, and the earth under the substantial form of earth; which is proven partly by the letter, or the proper meaning of the names of heaven and earth (which is not to be abandoned without significant necessity, according to the rule of interpreting Scripture, above Vol. I, p. 179, *Proleg.* c. II, § 45), and partly by the fact that Moses adds the emphatic or demonstrative ה on both, as if pointing with an extended finger, signifying *this* heaven and *this* earth. But what is added, that the earth was תהו ובהו, without form and void, equ

ally denies the cultivation and ornaments of the earth (which in this sense, and because it was enveloped by waters, could be called an unformed, rude, and indigested mass), but he does not deny the substantial form of the earth, of which there is question here. Compare Isaiah 34:11, Jeremiah 4:23, where the devastation of the earth or the region of the Jews, not the abolition of the substantial form of the earth, is designated by those wo…rds. See more in the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. Theol. V. de Creat.* § 26 sqq. p. 140 sqq., and the German treatise *Ausführliche Erklärung* Q. 23, 24, 25, p. 183 sqq.

In exactly the same way, the blessed Hutterus, *LL. Theol. de Creat.* Q. III. p. 201, taught that by the appellation of heaven and earth, one should not indeed understand those parts of the universe as they later turned out, or are now seen by the eyes, elaborated with admirable and stupendous workmanship, but an unformed, rude, and in some way confused mass, which God subsequently distinguished and elaborated according to a certain plan, in such a way that under the name of heaven comes the entire celestial body, encompassing all the spheres, perfect indeed in respect to substance and magnitude, but yet without light, without motion, and without the distinction of the stars, etc., which were only added later; and under the name of earth in the first verse of Genesis, the very element of earth is to be understood, which was subsequently distinguished and separated from the waters on the third day.

Latin:

5. Juxta historiam creationis a absolvit Deus productionem hujus universi spatio sex b dierum.

Lutherus: ,,Hilarius et Augustinus, quasi duo maxima ecclesiae lumina, sentiunt, mundum creatum subito et simul, non successive per sex dies. Ac Augustinus mirabiliter ludit in tractatione sex dierum, quos facit mysticos dies cognitionis in angelis, non naturales. . . Nec etiam utile est, Mosen in principio tam facere mysticum et allegoricum. Quia enim nos vult docere, non de creaturis allegoricis, et mundo aliegorico, sed de creaturis essentialibus et mundo visibili ac exposito sensibus, appellat, ut proverbio dicitur, scapham scapham, hoc est, diem et vesperam vocat, sicut nos solemus, sine allegoria, sicut evangelista Matthaeus capite ultimo hanc phrasin quoque retinet, cum scribit, Christum resurrexisse vespera Sabbatorum, quae in unam Sabbatorum illucescebat. Quodsi non satis assequimur rationem dierum, nec intelligimus, cur intervallis his temporis Deus voluerit uti, fateamur potius ignorantiam nostram, quam ut verba praeter rem ad alienum sensum torqueamus. Quod igitur ad hanc Augustini sententiam attinet, statuimus, Mosen proprie locutum, non allegorice aut figurate, hoc est, mundum cum omnibus creaturis intra sex dies, ut verba sonant, creatum esse.

Quodsi causam non adsequimur, maneamus discipuli, et relinquamus magisterium Spiritui Sancto.“ (Ad Gen. 1, 1. Exeget. opp. lat. Cur. Elsperger. P. I. p. 8. sq.;

Quenstedtius: ,,Non esse omnia simul in uno momento aut instanti, sed sex dierum spatio a Deo creata, probatur: 1. ex historia crea־ tionis Gen. 1. descripta, in qua verba omnia historice et proprie intelligenda sunt, nec discedendum a clara litera, nisi analogia flclei, antecedentia ct consequentia, aliaeque circumstantiae id suadeant; in illa autem planissimis verbis docet Moses, quid unoquoque die a I)eo factum sit. 2. Ex sabbathi sanctificatione et ratione hujus rei, quae redditur Gen. 2, 3. Ex. 13, 6. 20,11., quae nullius esset momenti, si Deus omnia unico momento creasset, non autem successive per dies plures. 3. Ex ratione; si omnia simul essent facta, danda esset ratio aliqua ordinis narrationis illius Mosaicae. Moses autem non observat ordinem naturae, non dignitatis, non cognitionis; relinquitur ergo ordo temporis.“ (Theol. did.pol. P. I. c. 10. s. 2. q. 6. f. 613.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Nonnullorum patrum, ut Origenis lib. 6. c. Celsum, Athanasii orat. 3. c. Arianos, Augustini lib. 4. de Gen. ad literam c. 22. sq. et lib. 2. de civit. Dei c. 29. sqq., Procopii Qazaei in Genesin, qui mundum uno momento a Deo creatum et sex dies aliegorice interpretandos esse statuunt. . . 2. Philonis Judaei lib. de opiflcio mundi et lib. 1. allegoriarum legis Mosaicae pag. 29. . . Paucis: opinio illa, quod omnia uno instanti condita, a Rabbinis excogitata, a Cajetano et Melch. Cano (referente Domin. Banne) incrustata, a Nicolao Abramo, Jesuita, Mussipontano noviter propugnata, novisque paradoxis locupletata est; statuit enim hic: ,quod omnium rerum substantia, excepta hominis anima, primo momento temporis simul producta sit, quodque sex diebus per naturalem emanationem omnia secundum qualitates suas prodierint et inclinatione naturali, ad locum naturalem contenderint‘, quam opinionem refutavit Dr. Calov. Tom. III. System.“ (L. c.)

Vilmarius: ״Die Untersuchung und Beantwortung der Frage, ob die Tage 24stündige, von der Axendrehung der Erde abhängige Tage oder Schöpfungs- (Restitutions-) Perioden von unbestimmter Dauer seien, kann die Dogmatik unbedenklich frei lassen. In der Anwendung, welche von diesen (5 Tagen schon Gen. 2, 2—3. und nachher im Gesetz gemacht wird, sind allerdings 24stündige Tage gemeint, und der Wortlaut (Abend und Morgen, 1. Tag, der 2. Tag etc.) scheint dafür zu sprechen. Dagegen ist die Bestimmung Ps. 90, 4. und 2 Petri 3, 8., wonach 1000 Jahre wie ein Tag und ein Tag wie 1000 Jahre vor Gott sind, der Annahme von Schöpfungsperioden nicht ungünstig. Diese Perioden könnten mit einer Dämmerung geschlossen und mit einer Dämmerung wieder angehoben haben, also durch eine Nacht, in weleher Gott nicht schuf, getrennt gewesen sein, haben aber nicht von der Axendrehung der Erde, sondern von andern Kämpfen um Licht und Finstemiss abgehangen.“ (Dogmatik. I, p. 247.)

Quae accurate describitur Gen. c. 1. ei 2. Vid. cap. 1. vers. ult. et cap. 2, 2.

Gen.§ 6. Prima die, et cum hactenus nulla res creata, sed solus Deus existeret,a produxit Deus coelum b et terram,c itemque lucem,d quae diei et noctis vicissitudines constitueret. PART. I. CAP. II.

Vid. Gen. 1, 1., ubi vocabulum בראשית adverbmliter et negative exponendum est, ita ut nihil, ne materiam quidem aliquam hujus universi, prius extitisse, dicendum sit.

Scherzerus: ,,Principio, בראשית (ex quo Cabbalistae per temura primum Septembrem faciunt; et Dr. Calovius, etsi patres aliique theologi vernum tempus eligant, quae sententia nobis etiam aliquando placuit, Syst. III, f. 924., pro auctumno militat, quod alias in primo creationis anno bis debuissent fructus proferri, adeoque Deus statim ordinationem suam immutasset, quod improbabile), seu primo instanti temporis (adeoque non in tempore, creatio enim et tempus simul coeperunt) creavit Deus coelum et terram, Gen. 1, 1. Nullum aliud, quam temporis principium intelligi potest; non aeternitatis, quia principio caret; non aevi, quia haec duratio tantum creatorum spirituum est: ergo temporis. Inepte dicitur: In principio mundi creatus est mundus; aut: In principio creationis creavit Deus coelum et terram; remanet enim quaestio, quodnam principium intelligatur; at Moses lectorem non in suspenso reliquit.“ (System, theol. 1.1. § 8. p. 87. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,’Ακυρολογία est dicere, mundum aliquando non fuisse. Tö aliquando enim idem est ac aliquo tempore; sed dici non potest, aliquo tempore nondum fuisse, cum ante mundum couditum non fuerit tempus. Cautius loquitur, qui dicit, mundum non semper fuisse.“ (L. c. q. 2. f. 602.)

Idem: ,,Probatur, mundum non potuisse ab aeterno esse aut creari: 1. Quia ab aeterno esse, uni et soli Deo proprium est, ita ut quicquid aeternum est, illud Deum esse necesse sit. 2. Quia involvit repugnantiam tum ex parte Dei creantis, qui Deum alium ab ipso diversum producere nequit, tum ex parte creationis, quia haec praesupponit aliquod initium, in quo fiat, tum denique ex parte creaturae, quae non est capax existentiae ab aeterno. Id quod esse non potest, nisi post non esse, non potest esse ab aeterno; at nulla creatura esse potest, nisi post non esse, creari enim est ex nihilo produci. Ergo. Quod ab aeterno existit, id sine sui initio existit; creatura autem, quandocunque creatur, fit ipsa, quia omnis effectus, dum a sua causa producitur, fit, et ab eadem suum esse accipit; quando autem fit creatura, esse incipit, si vero esse incipit, ab aeterno existere non potuit. Sunt enim contradictoria, existere cum sui initio, et non existere cum sui initio.“ (L. c. f. 601.)

Idem: ,,Disputatio illa (an mundus ab aeterno creari potuerit) non concernit fidei articulum; ideoque neutra sententia haerescos, nedum atheismi alicujus accusanda. Nam nec illi, qui negant, creari potuisse ab aeterno, infinitae potentiae derogant, cum non ob defectum virtutis in Deo id negent, sed ob objectum impossibile, quod id contradictionem involvere judicent; nec qui affirmant, creationem aeternam actualem admittunt, sed solum possibilem illam faciunt nec contradictionem involvere arbitrantur.“ (L. c. q. 2. f. 599.)

Idem: ,,Creatio mundi ex nihilo in tempore facta ex lumine naturae cognosci aut rationibus philosophicis apodictice et evidenter demonstrari nequit, sed ex sola revelatione divina innotescit, adeoque est articulus purae fidei ac merae revelationis.“ (L. c. q. 1. f. 596.)

Puta ipsum coelum sub forma substantiali coeli, et terram sub forma substantiali terrae; quod partim litera, seu propria significatio nominum coeli et terrae (quae sine insigni necessitate deserenda non est, juxta reg. de interpr. scr. supra Vol. I. p. 179. Proleg. c. II. § 45.), partim et illud probat, quod Moses ה emphaticum seu demonstrativum utrinque addit, quasi digito intenso, hoc coelum et hanc terram significans. Quod autem additur, terram fuisse תהו וברזו, vacuam et inanem, equi

dem negat cultum et ornamenta terrae (quae hoc quidem sensu, et quod aquis involuta esset, informis, rudis et indigesta moles dici potuit), non autem negat formam terrae substantialem, de qua hic sermo est. Confer Esaiae 34, 11. Jer. 4, 23., ubi devastatio terrae aut regionis Judaeorum, non abolitio formae substantialis terrae, istis vocibus designatur. Plura vide apud b. Mus. Disp. Theol. V. de Creat. § 26. sqq. p. 140. sqq. et Tract. Germ. Ausfuhrl. Erklärung Q. 23. 24. 25. p. 183. 8qq.

Eodem autem plane modo b. Hutterus LL. Theol. de Creat. Q. III. p. 201. docuit, coeli et terrae appellatione non intelligendas quidem esse partes istas universi, quales postea evaserunt, aut nunc visuntur oculis, admirando et stupendo opificio elaboratae, sed informem, rudem et confusam quodammodo massam, quam Deus postmodum certa ratione distinxit et elaboravit, ita quidem, ut coeli nomine veniat universum corpus coeleste, cunctos orbes complectens, perfectum quidem et integrum ratione substantiae et magnitudinis, sed tamen sine luce, sine motu et distinctione siderum etc., quae postea demum accesserunt; terrae quoque nomine in versu 1. Geneseos intelligendum veniat ipsum terrae elementum, quod postmodum tertio die ab aquis distinctum et separatum fuerit.


### On Creation: He adds, however, these noteworthy words

He adds, however, these noteworthy words: "Certainly, unless it is established that the earth was created in the beginning, insofar as it is considered in respect to its substance, it does not appear from Moses when it was finally created. For what some object regarding the third day is too weak; since Moses does not say that the earth was created on that third day, but that God said that the dry land or earth should appear from the waters."

Similarly, the blessed Gesnerus also taught, *Comment. in Gen.* p. 11 and 12, that the heaven which is now visible is understood in the aforementioned place; that the earth is called *Tohu*, which word denotes both the accidental στέρησις [privation] of form and figure, and that it was mixed with waters. It is called *Bohu*, which epithet denotes that the earth was 1) uncultivated, 2) sterile, as it was not yet adorned with trees, herbs, and grass, 3) destitute of inhabitants, men, and animals.

Others, however, who seem to deny that heaven and earth were produced at that time under their own form, clearly reveal that they are not speaking of the substantial form of simple bodies, but in opposition to the subsequent elaboration; certainly, they acknowledge that earth and water, although not yet separated from each other, nevertheless existed on the first day in reality and essence. See the blessed Schneccerus, *Enarr. in Gen.* p. 43; the blessed Meisnerus, *Phil. Sob. P. I. Sect. III. cap. III. Q. III.* p. m. 510, and Q. IV. p. 544; the blessed Friedlieb, *Theol. Exeg. in Genes. Q. VII.* p. 27.

But especially to our purpose, and that that common Chaos was a globe compacted of the three primary bodies—heaven, water, and earth—in places not yet distinguished, and that it is called the seed-plot of heaven, earth, and water, because none of these bodies was then distinct, and finally that in this sense (not regarding the negation of the substantial form) mention of heaven, earth, and water can be said to be made by πρóληψις [anticipation], is taught at greater length by the blessed Scherzerus in *System. L. III. § 10. p. 90*, where he also praises the blessed Musaeus’s *Disp. de Creat.* cited here by us.

Quenstedtius: "The empyrean or fiery heaven, which most scholastics and other papists, as well as Calvinists, contend was produced in the first day and the first instant of creation and placed above the firmament as the dwelling of the angels and the blessed, or even the palace of God himself, is a sweet dream without sleep... Although the heaven of the blessed is not a physical place, it is nevertheless not nowhere, but somewhere; or it is not everywhere, lest..." that it is nowhere, but somewhere. But to define precisely where it is, is rash. ... Distinguish between a certain, corporeal, and determined place created by God and destined for the blessed and the angels—such as heaven neither is, nor will be—and between the που or "where" of the blessed, as distinct from the πον of the damned, in which the souls of the pious are gathered after their release from the body and are made partakers of heavenly goods, which we also concede. ...

The falsity of the opposing view and the truth of our own is proven: 1. From reason. ... 2. From the silence of Scripture. Scripture says the heaven of the blessed is "above" in respect to us (describing the sublimity of their state and condition with words signifying place); but that it is some space created on the first day, corporeal in substance, most vast in quantity, a true place, most luminous in quality, indefectible in duration by its own nature, and in position supreme and elevated above all visible or starry heavens, circularly and on all sides surrounding them: Scripture nowhere hints at this, and therefore it is rash to wish to define it as such. ... 4. From Matthew 18:10, where angels are said to be on earth and guarding little ones, and at the same time to be in the heavens and to behold the face of God the Father δια παντός, whence we conclude invincibly that the heaven of the blessed or of the angels is not a created place most remote from the earth and situated above the starry heaven, since by that reasoning, while angels are occupied on earth, they could not be in heaven. And thus, angels, who are not absent from the earth by reason of place, are at the same time in the heavens by reason of their state and condition. That continuity of appearance before the Father does not take away their presence and διάκοviav among the saints and little ones on earth. That "where" of the angels, therefore, can be in the heavens, and these heavens of the angels can be on earth among the little ones, and thus the angels are never outside the heavens and outside the contemplation of God (which is the very heaven or blessedness of the angels), not even when they minister to the saints on earth. 5. From the conflagration of the visible heavens on the last day, 2 Peter 3:7, 10; Psalm 102:27; either, therefore, the heaven of the blessed will perish at the same time, as it is, according to the opinion of our adversaries, immediately adjacent to the starry heaven, or it must be excepted from that πανολιά/ήα, and this exception must be demonstrated from Scripture. (L. c. q. 9. f. 623. 625. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Scholastics and most Papists, who laboriously dispute and sweetly fabricate stories about the heaven of the blessed, which they call the empyrean, and its situation, location, and qualities, as well as the exercises of the blessed in that fictitious heaven, indulging at times in merely carnal and worldly speculations...

Becanus dares to write that this empyrean heaven has a most solid foundation in the Scriptures. 'For Scripture teaches,' he says, 'that the firmament and all things were produced on the second and fourth days.' He adds: 'that the firmament is in the midst of the waters, so that some waters are above, some below the firmament. If this is so, it follows that that heaven, which was created in the beginning, is above the firmament and above all the waters, which surely can be nothing other than the empyrean.' ...

2. Of the Calvinists, who posit that the heaven of the blessed is a corporeal, created place, above this corruptible world and above all the heavens, and that it has distinct local spaces and seats in which one may locally go, sit, stand, walk, etc. ... Joh. Cloppenburg, in his *Exercitationes de creatione*, disputation 3, where he says: 'The first work of the first day is the outermost and highest heaven, the third heaven, the heaven of heavens, which is corporeal and consequently local, in which the seat of God and the throne of God is,' he asserts. ... They differ, however, among themselves in some things, for some wish the heaven of the blessed to be of corporeal substance, but others say it is indeed a place and created with a local situation above, but they leave it in the middle whether it is a body. ...

3. Of the Socinians, who confine God to a certain place, and posit that He is present by His substance only in heaven, which for them is the place of immortality, the domicile of God, con[taining]..."

established above the starry expanse...

4. Of the Arminians, whose leader Episcopius (lib. 4. inst. theol. sect. 3. c. 1.) wishes the heaven to have been created first, so that it might be a suitable dwelling in which the angels could be placed, and which God willed to be His palace.” (L. c. f. 624. sq.)

Luther: “Therefore, the opinion of Moses is most simple: that all things which exist were created by God, and that at the beginning of the first day a rude mass of mud or earth, and of mist or water, was created, into which God later, throughout the remainder of the first day, infused light and caused the day to appear, which showed that rude mass of heaven and earth, not ‘unlike a rude seed, yet suitable for producing something.’” (Opp. exeg. Cur. C. S. T. Elsperger. T. I. Enarratt. in Genesin. Cap. 1, 1. pag. 11.)

ANTITHESIS. J. H. Kurtz: “We take the codex of the holy documents of revelation into our hands, and in the very first line we encounter the mysterious תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ, that waste, emptiness, and darkness in which the first glance of the holy seer beheld the earth, which through the six-day work was to become the site of light and the fullness of life... We already have, in pre-human time, an earth, and no less a history that unfolded upon it and within it. The prophet of primeval history beheld this earth as waste and emptiness. Preceding the chaotic state of devastation and desolation was a state of order, of light, of life, as befits every work of God; and likewise followed a creative restitution in the six-day work, through which light was brought forth from darkness, and order and the fullness of life from devastation and desolation, through which our present earth was founded, formed, ordered, and enlivened. The devastation was a consequence of the fall of the angels, from which we further conclude that that primeval earth was the dwelling and training ground of that portion of the angels who rebelled against God and thereby lost their principality and were compelled to leave their habitation.
