The restitution, on the other hand, was a result of the divine counsel, by virtue of which He does not allow His world-plan to be disturbed, by virtue of which He lifts up again a whole world of life that had fallen into ruin from the floods of destruction, exiles the destroyer from it, and places a new inhabitant and ruler, man, upon it—from which we further conclude that man, placed in the stead of Satan and his angels, was also called to carry out their neglected task, to restore the disturbed harmony of the universe, the broken connection of the whole, and to defeat and judge him, the destroyer and rebel, himself.” (Bibel und Astronomie. Second ed. Berlin, 1849. p. 94. 96.) “

The view defended here is already very old... Also in later, more recent, and newest times it is very widespread, and not only theosophists and theosophically tinged interpreters, such as J. Böhme, St. Martin, J. M. Hahn, Fr. v. Meyer, Hamberger, etc., are devoted to it, but also such sensible and sober men as Reichel, Stier, G. H. v. Schubert, Kniewel, Drechsler, Budelbach, Guericke, J. P. Lange, Schmieder, Ebrard, M. Baumgarten, A. Wagner, Michelis, Wichart, Lebeau, F. W. Krug, etc., have spoken out in favor of it.” (p. 95.)

The same is maintained by D. Delitzsch (See System der bibl. Psychologie. Leipz. 1855. p. 42—45.), D. Vilmar (Dogmatik. Gütersloh 1874. I, 242. sq.). But that water also was produced together with the earth, not from pre-existing matter, can be gathered from Genesis 1, 1. Compare the blessed Hutter. PART I. CHAP. II.

Latin:

Addit autem notanter haec verba: Sane nisi in principio statuatur creata esse terra, quatenus ratione substantiae consideratur, non apparet ex Mose, quando illa tandem creata sit. Nam quod de tertio die nonnulli obstrepunt, nimis dilutum est; siquidem Moses non dicit, die illo tertio creatam esse terram, sed Deum dixisse, ut appareat ex aquis arida sive terra.

Similiter autem docuit etiam b. Gesnerus Comment. in Gen. p. 11. et 12., coelum,, quod nunc aspectabile est, 1. c. intelligi; terram appellari Tohu, quae vox tum formae et figurae accidentariae στέρηαiv denotet, tum quod fuerit aquis permixta. Eandem dici Bohu, quod epitheton denotet terram fuisse 1) irwultam, 2) sterilem, utpote arboribus, herbis, gramine nondum exornatam, 3) cultoribus, hominibus et animalibus, destitutam.

Alii autem, qui negare videntur, coelum et terram sub sua forma tunc fuisse producta, non obscure produnt, se non loqui de forma substantiali corporum simplicium, sed jn oppositione ad elaborationem secutam; certe terram atque aquam, licet nondum ab invicem separata, tamen die primo revera xod nbaiav extitisse, agnoscunt. Vid. b. Sdneccerus Enarr. in Gen. p. 43., b. Meisnerus Phil. Sob. P. I. Sect. III. cap. III. Q. III. p. m. 510. et Q,. IV. p. 544., b. Friedlieb Theol. Exeg. in Genes. Q. VII. p. 27.

Inprimis vero in rem nostram, et quod vulgatum illud Chaos fuerit globus ex tribus corporibus primis, coelo, aqua et terra, locis nondum distinctis, compactus quodque seminarium coeli, terrae et aquae dicatur, quia nullum horum corporum tum distinctum fuerit, denique hoc sensu (non quoad negationem formae substantialis) coeli, terrae et aquae mentionem per πρύληψιν fieri, dici possit, pluribus docet b. Scherzerus in System. L. III. $ 10. p. 90., ubi etiam laudat b. Musaei Disp. de Creat, hic a nobis citatam.

Quenstedtius: ״Coelum empyreum sive igneum, quod primo die primoque instanti creationis productum et supra firmamentum locatum in angelorum beatorumque domicilium vel etiam ipsius Dei palatium plerique scholastici aliique pontificii, itemque Calviniani contendunt, est dulce sine somno somnium. . . Coelum beatorum etsi non sit locus physicus, nec tamen est nuspiam, sed uspiam; seu non est ubique, ne 6 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. II. PART. I. CAP. II. que nullibi, sed alicubi. Ubi vero sit praecise, definire temerarium est. ... Dist. inter certum, corporeum et determinatum locum a Deo creatum et beatis angelisque destinatum, quale ‘coelum nec est, nec erit, et inter που sive ubi beatorum a πον damnatorum distinctum, in quo animae piorum post solutionem a corpore congregantur et coelestium bonorum participes redduntur, quod et nos concedimus. . .

Probatur adversae sententiae falsitas et nostrae veritas: 1.Ex ratione. .. 2. Ex Scripturae silentio. Scriptura coelum beatorum respectu nostri sursum esse dicit (verbis locum significantibus status et conditionis sublimitatem describens); sed quod sit spatium aliquod primo die creatum, quoad substantiam corporeum, quoad quantitatem amplissimum et verus locus, quoad qualitatem lucidissimum, quoad durationem indefectibile ab intrinseco, quoad situm supremum et supra omnes coelos aspectabiles evectum sive coelos stelliferos circulariter et undiquaque ambiens: illud nuspiam Scriptura innuit, adeoque temerarium est, id ita definire velle. . . 4. Ex Matth. 18, 10., ubi dicuntur angeli in terra esse et parvulos custodire, ac simul esse in coelis et videre faciem Dei Patris δια παντός, unde invicte concludimus, coelum beatorum seu angelorum non esse locum creatum a terris remotissimum et supra coelum sidereum positum, cum ea ratione angeli, dum in terris versantur, in coelo esse nequeant. Adeoque angeli, qui ratione loci a terris non absunt, pro ratione status et conditionis eodem tempore simul in coelis sunt. Illa apparitionis coram Patre continuitas in coelis praesentiam et διάκοviav apud sanctos atque parvulos in terris non tollit. Illud ergo ubi angelorum potest esse in coelis, et hi coeli angelorum possunt esse in terris apud parvulos, atque adeo nunquam sunt extra coelos angeli et extra contemplationem Dei (quae est ipsum coelum seu beatitudo angelorum), ne quidem quando in terris ministrant sanctis. 5. Exvisibilium coelorum conflagratione in extremo die, 2Pet. 3, 7. 10. Ps. 102, 27.; aut igitur coelum beatorum simul peribit, utpote coelo stellifero proxiine incumbens ex adversariorum sententia, aut ab illa πανολιά/ήα erit excipiendum, atque haec exceptio ex Scriptura demonstranda.“ (L. c. q. 9. f. 623. 625. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum plerorumque, qui de coelo beatorum, quod empyreum vocant, ejusque situ, locatione et qualitatibus, item exercitiis beatorum in coelo isto flctitio operose disputant et suaviter fabulantur, mere carnalibus et mundanis quandoque speculationibus indulgentes...

Becanus scribere audet, coelum hoc empyreum habere solidissimum fundamentum in Scripturis. ,Nam Scriptura docet, inquit, firmamentum et omnia producta esse secundo et quarto die.‘ Addit: ,firmamentum esse in medio aquarum, ita ut quaedam aquae sint supra, quaedam infra firmamentum. Si ita est, sequitur, coelum illud, quod in principio creatum est, esse supra firmamentum et supra omnes aquas, quod sane non potest esse aliud, quam empyreum.‘ . .

2. Calvinianorum, qui coelum beatorum esse statuunt locum corporeum, creatum, supra mundum hunc corruptibilem et supra omnes coelos habereque spatia et sedes distinctas locales, in quibus localiter eatur, sedeatur, stetur, ambifletur etc. . . Joh. Cloppenburg, exercit. de creatione disput. 3., ubi dicit: ,Primum primi diei opus esse coelum extimum et summum, coelum tertium, coelum coelorum, quod corporeum et consequenter locale, in quo solium Dei et thronum Dei esse‘, asserit. . . Discrepant tamen in aliquibus inter se, quidam enim coelum beatorum corporeae substantiae esse volunt, alii vero locum quidem et locali situatione sursum ac creatum esse dicunt, an vero corpus sit, in medio relinquunt. . .

3. Socinianorum, qui Deum certo loco compescunt, nec nisi in coelo substantia sua praesto esse statuunt, quod ipsis est locus immortalitatis, domicilium Dei,

constitutum supra expansionem stelliferam.. .

4. Arminianorum, quorum antesignanus Episcopius lib. 4. inst. theol. sect. 3. c. 1. primum creatum vult coelum, ut aptum esset domicilium, in quo collocarentur angeli, quodque Deus voluerit esse palatium suum.“ (L. c. f. 624. sq.)

Lutherus: ״Mosis igitur simplicissima est sententia haec: omnia, quae sunt, esse creata a Deo, ac principio primi diei creatam esse rudem molem luti seu terrae, et nebulae seu aquae, quibus postea per reliquum primi diei spatium infuderit Deus lumen, et fecerit apparere diem, quae ostenderet istam rudem molem coeli et terrae, non ‘dissimilem rudi semini, sed tamen apto ad producendum aliquid.“ (Opp. exeg. Cur. C. S. T. Elsperger. T. I. Enarratt. in Genesin. Cap. 1, 1. pag. 11.)

ANTITHESIS. J. H. Kurtzius: ״Wir nehmen den Codex der heiligen Offenbarungsurkunden zur Hand, und treffen gleich in der ersten Zeile auf das räthselhafte Tohu va Bohu, auf jene Wüstniss, Leerheit und Finsterniss, in welcher der erste Blick des heiligen Sehers die Erde, die durch das Sechstagewerk zur Stätte des Lichts und der Lebensfülle werden sollte, erblickte. . . Wir haben bereits in vormenschlicher Zeit eine Erde, und nicht minder eine Geschichte, die sich auf ihr und in ihr entfaltet hat. Der Prophet der Urgeschichte erblickte diese Erde als Wüste und Leerheit. Voran ging dem chaotischen Zustande der Verwüstung und Verödung ein Zustand der Ordnung, des Lichtes, des Lebens, wie er jeglichem Gotteswerke geziemt; und ebenso folgte eine schöpferische Restitution im Sechstagewerk, durch welche aus der Finsterniss das Licht, aus der Verwüstung und Verödung Ordnung und Lebensfülle hervorgerufen wurde, durch welche unsere jetzige Erde gegründet, gebildet, geordnet und belebt wurde. Die Verwüstung war eine Folge des Falles der Engel, woraus wir weiter schliessen, dass jene urweltliche Erde die Wohn und Uebungsstätte desjenigen Theiles der Engel war, die sich gegen Gott empörten und dadurch ihr Fürstenthum verloren und ihre Behausung zu verlassen genöthigt waren. Die Bestitution dagegen war ein Ergebniss des göttlichen Rathschlusses, vermöge welches er sich seinen Weltplan nicht stören lässt, vermöge welches er eine ganze Welt des Lebens, die ins Verderben gerathen war, wieder aus den Fluthen des Verderbens emporhebt, den Verderber von ihr exilirt und einen neuen Bewohner und Herrscher, den Menschen, auf sie setzt, — woraus wir weiter schliessen, dass der Mensch, an die Stelle Satans und seiner Engel gesetzt, auch dessen unterbliebene Aufgäbe auszurichten, den gestörten Einklang des Weltalls, den durchbrochenen Zusammenhang des Ganzen, wiederherzustellen, und ihn selbst, den Zerstörer und Empörer, zu besiegen und zu richten, berufen war.“ (Bibel und Astronomie. Zweite Aufl. Berlin, 1849. p. 94. 96.) ״

Die hier vertheidigte Auffassung ist schon sehr alt. . . Auch in späterer, neuerer und neuester Zeit ist sie sehr verbreitet, und nicht nur Theosophen und theosophisch tingirte Ausleger, wie J. Böhme, St. Martin, J. M. Hahn, Fr. v. Meyer, Hamberger etc., sind ihr zugethan, sondern auch so besonnene und nüchterne Männer, wie Reichel, Stier, G. H. v. Schubert, Kniewel, Drechsler, Budelbach, Guericke, J. P. Lange, Schmieder, Ebrard, M. Baumgarten, A. Wagner, Michelis, Wichart, Lebeau, F. W. Krug etc. haben sich für sie ausgesprochen.“ (p. 95.)

Idem statuunt D. Delitzschius (Vid. System der bibl. Psychologie. Leipz. 1855. p. 42—45.), D. Vilmarius (Dogmatik. Gütersloh 1874. I, 242. sq.). Sed et aquam una cum terra productam fuisse, non ex praeexistente materia, colligi potest ex Genes. 1, 1. Confer b. Hutterum, PART. I. CAP. II.


### On Creation: b. Musaeus and b. Scherzer, loc

b. Musaeus and b. Scherzer, loc. cit. Indeed, it is the probable opinion of some that air and elemental fire, if such exists, were likewise created on the first day along with the other elements (just as b. Scherzer, loc. cit., notes that air is an appendage of water, as a symbolic element, and that it is not without reason that mention is made of darkness upon the face of the deep); although others think that air was produced on the second day from the more subtle parts of the water. See Gen. 1:3. However, it seems that a certain ethereal and luminous body is to be understood, produced dependently upon the substance of the heavens, and serving in the place of the sun. Cf. Hutter, loc. cit., Q. VIII, p. 211, and Musaeus, loc. cit., § 27, 28, p. 143, 144.

On the second day, God divided the elemental waters into lower and upper waters, with an aerial expanse interposed, in such a way that this expanse reached the more subtle waters gathered in the clouds from the upper part, and the thicker waters surrounding the surface of the earth from the lower part. Which were not distinct in place from the earth on the first day, but together with it constituted one confused globe, so that the earth lay hidden within them, as in an abyss. Musaeus, loc. cit., § 30, p. 145.

Namely, the same waters are understood in Gen. 1:2 and 6. It is called by Moses רָקִיעַ in ch. 1, v. 6, which properly signifies an expanse, as admitted by D. Chytraeus, L. Osiander, S. Gesner, J. Gerhard, and others. Thus, not only the Rabbis accept the word, but also b. D. Erasmus Marbach, Comm. in Gen., p. 10.

For although both the elemental waters and perhaps also the element of air were produced on the first day; yet because at that time the mass of water surrounded the earth on all sides, and the more subtle parts of the water, mixed with air, extended up to the heavens like a dense mist, it pleased God to divide them on the second day, so that the air might have the nature of an expanse and a medium intervening between both parts of the elemental water. Cf. b. Musaeus, Disp. cit., § 30, p. 145, 146, and Ausführliche Erklärung, p. 196.

For this is what the words מֵעַל and מִתַּחַת signify, which should not be translated so much as "above" and "below," but "from above" (von oben), in the upper part, and "from below" (von unten), and thus they confirm that opinion that by this רָקִיעַ, not the ethereal heaven (which certainly does not reach to the lower waters) but the aerial heaven ought to be understood, which, although not according to its whole self (which the words of the text do not require), yet in truth according to some part of itself lies between the upper and lower waters, and touches both. See Musaeus, Disp. cit., § 37, p. 150, 151, Ausführliche Erklärung, p. 198, 199, 204, 205.

Thus, moreover, Marbach, loc. cit., also thinks that God, in Gen. 1, assigns the middle region of the air to the clouds and rain waters, so that they may be contained there for

the irrigation and fertilization of the earth. And the blessed Alb. Grauerus, to the question: Whether there are true and natural waters above the starry heavens, answers: It is doubted. See *Quaest. Illustr. Disp. VIII. Coroll. I. p. 336.*

Meisnerus: "The better part of theologians has always understood (Gen. 1:7) the waters properly so-called, which they maintain God, in a singular and wonderful manner, truly and really placed above the firmament or starry heaven…nt or the starry heaven." (*Philos. sobr. P. I. s. 3. q. 3. p. 819.*) Cf. Luther, *Opp. T. I, 42. 49. sq.* For thus also in Ps. 104:3, by the name of waters, clouds are understood. Compare the blessed Geier in his *Comm.* And the blessed Marbachius believed that in Gen. 1:7, 8, rain waters are denoted. However, that region where the clouds are is not rarely called heaven. See Gen. 1:26, 28, 30, where birds are said to fly across the heaven, which certainly fly not in the ether, but in the air. Compare Deut. 4:17. And the windows of heaven, that is, the aerial [heaven], are said to be opened and closed in Gen. 7:11, ch. 8:2. But as to what is said in Ps. 148:4: המים אשר מ#ל השמים, Luther translates it: The waters that are above the heavens, and the glossators added: In the rain clouds; so that the expanse of the heavens may embrace both the expanse or the ethereal heaven and the aerial [heaven]; from which, now the one, now the other, now both, must be understood according to the diversity of the predicates and the context. Add the blessed Mus. *Disp. cit. § 33. sqq. p. 148. sqq., Ausführl. Erklärung p. 200. sqq.* § 8.

On the third day, the lower waters, washing the earth, were gathered into certain bays or channels, which God called seas.a But the remaining parts of the earth appeared dry; and from them immediately sprang herbs, trees, shrubs, etc.b See Gen. 1:9 and 10. L. c. v. 11 and 12. Indeed, in such a way that the earth had the nature of a principle, not active or efficient, but passive and material. See the blessed Mus. *Disp. cit. § 53. 54. p. 166.* Furthermore, it is not rashly believed that stones and metals, and the garden of Eden itself, or paradise, were produced on this same day. See Mus. *l. c. § 40. p. 153.* The same seems to be said concerning minerals, which they call intermediate (and to which they refer various earths, salts, sulphurs, and bitumens). § 9.

On the fourth day, God made the sun,a the moon, and the other stars,b and endowed them with a certain motion and the power of influencing, so that they might measure the times and by their influence be able to produce various effects on the earth.c PART I. CHAP. 11.

Indeed, to the imperfect luminous body, which was created on the first day, He added a fuller light and perfection, so that only then did it fully obtain the nature of the sun.

Hollazius: "The most wise Creator founded the earth so that, ordinarily and universally, it does not move, but rests. To the celestial luminaries, however, He gave the duty of defining the times by their motion." (Exam. P. I. c. 3. q. 21. p. 369.)

Calovius: "The earth was placed not to be moved, whether in a circle or by any other means, much less to define the times by its own motion—which is an office given to the luminaries—but to stand stable and unmoved. 'He founded the earth upon its bases; it shall not be moved forever and ever,' Ps. 104:5. Although the earth was drawn from the waters and is washed on all sides by the waves of waters that exceed the earth in height, it is nevertheless founded by divine power in such a way that at no time, even until the last day, can it be moved in its entirety from its place. Cf. Job 26:7; 38:6, 7; Eccl. 1:11. And therefore, those who make a planet out of the earth or establish a mobile earth, ascribing to it either both a diurnal and an annual motion, or one or the other, along with Copernicus, Kepler, and Lansberg, are opposed to the Holy Scriptures." (Syst. T. III. art. 5. c. 2. p. 952.)

The same: "Those will never be reconciled with the Christian religion who place men on the moon and assert that, if they were able to reach the lunar sphere by the rowing of wings, they would actually discover this—unless they also imagine that Christ died for the Selenites (just as Origen did for the stars) and that the apostles flew to the land of the moon, and entangle themselves in many other paradoxes that overturn the orthodox religion." (L. c. p. 961.)

Rollius: "Question: Does Scripture ever speak to the erroneous understanding of the common people? This arose from the Copernican opinion concerning the motion of the earth and the rest of the sun and other celestial bodies. For when the authority of Scripture was objected to the Copernicans—testifying that the earth stands forever, while the sun, on the contrary, rises and sets—they replied that Scripture speaks to the erroneous understanding of the common people. But this opinion is false and blasphemous against God, the author of Scripture. There exists an excellent dissertation on this matter by the blessed Dr. Rambach, delivered at the University of Halle in the year 1727. To this also pertains the dissertation of Dr. Heinrich Ascanius Engelken, a Rostock theologian, concerning statements injurious to Holy Scripture and less safe in its treatment, which he prefixed to the collection of the latest controversies of the blessed Schomer, published by himself at Rostock in the year 1703." (Vid. Fechtii Sylloge, p. 28. sq.)

Acta Eruditorum: "Hafenreffer, a theologian, advises his friend Kepler to cultivate the system of a moved earth as a hypothesis useful to an astronomer for saving the phenomena, but to abstain from reconciling it with Scripture." (Vol. of the year 1719, p. 5.) Cf. Luther on Gen. 1:6, I, 44.

ANTITHESIS. Deylingius: "Nor is there any reason for us to be offended by the division of created things into heaven and earth. For Scripture sometimes follows the experience of the senses or ideas that strike the senses most forcibly, and speaks of celestial bodies just as it does of terrestrial ones, no differently than how the senses represent them to us, because whatever we know about bodies becomes known to us through the senses. Those skilled in the arts are accustomed to call these modes of speaking 'optical' and distinguish them from physical truth. Far be it, therefore, for us to say that the more divine Scripture accommodates itself to the understanding of the common people—that is, to error—or speaks erroneously, as many from the school of R. Descartes, in particular, ignorantly and impiously opine. But what prevents us from affirming and granting that Scripture, in some places, has spoken not physically, but optically, or according to the observation of the senses and as things are comprehended by the senses? Do not astronomers themselves [refer] the moon to this..."

or do they refer to that part of the ecliptic in which it is not truly, but appears to our eyes? Do not all the tables of astronomers rely upon an optical location, which nevertheless are not indices of errors, but of true observations? He finally errs with the error of the common people who takes an optical location for a physical one, which the Holy Spirit, the author of Scripture, never did, nor did He regard the error of the common people, but our δψιν [sight]. Furthermore, the Holy Scriptures were not consigned to writing for the sake of delighting or instructing the minds of philosophers, but for the sake of instructing the souls of men eager for salvation, who are for the most part simple and unlearned. I truly think that a great argument for divine goodness lies in the fact that the construction of this universe was described not according to physical, but optical truth, so that, namely, the weaker ones and those unversed in philosophy might not be offended—for whose sake, however, we know the whole of Holy Scripture was composed, so that they might read it and easily understand it.” (Observ. s. P. I. p. 355. sq.)

Latin:

b. Musaeum et b. Scherzerum II. cc. Aerem vero et ignem, si quis detur, elementarem, similiter cum caeteris elementis die primo creata fuisse, probabilis quorundam sententia est (prout aquae appendicem esse aerem, tanquam elementum symbolieum, nec abs re tenebrarum super faciem abyssi mentionem fieri, 1. c. monet b. Scherzerus); quamvis alii aerem die secundo ex partibus aquae tenuioribus productum putent. Vid. Gen. 1, 3. Intelligi autem videtur corpus quoddam aethereum qt lucidum, dependenter a substantia coeli productum, et solis vice fungens. Conf. Hutterus 1. c. Q. VIII. p. 211. et Mus. 1. c. § 27. 28. p. 143. 144.·ל §

Secunda die divisit Deus aquas elementares a in aquas inferiores et superiores, interposito expanso b aëreo,c ita ut expansum illud attingeret d a superiore parte aquas subtiliores in nubibus e congregatas, a parte inferiore crassiores terrae superficiem ambientes. Quae prima die non fuerunt loco distinctae a terra, sed cum ea unum confuse constituerunt globum, ita ut terra in illis, tanquam in abysso, lateret. Mus. 1. c. § 30. p. 14.

Nempe aquae eaedem intelliguntur Gen. 1, v. 2. ei 6. Vocatur a Mose #רקי c. 1, vers. 6., quod proprie expansum significat, fatentibus D. Chytraeo, L. Osiandro, S. Gesnero, J. Gerhardo et aliis. Sic etiam accipiunt vocem non solum Rabbini, verum etiam b. D. Erasmus Marbachius Comm. in Gen. p. 10.

Licet enim prima die productae sint et aquae elementares et forte etiam aeris elementum; quia tamen tunc moles aquae terram undique cingebat et partes aquae tenuiores aeri permixtae ad coelum usque, instar nebulae densioris, sese porrigebant, placuit Deo die secunda jacere, ut aër haberet rationem expansi et medii intercedentis inter partes utrasque elementaris aquae. Conf. b. Mus. Disp. cit. § 30. p. 145. 146. Et Ausfuhrl. Erklärung p. 196.

Hoc enim significant voces Sj?!p et מתחת, quae non tam verti debent: supra et infra, sed a supra, desuper (von oben), in superiore parte, et ab infra, a parte inferiore (von unten), adeoque confirmant sententiam illam, quod per £ךכןי istud non aethereum coelum (quod profecto non pertingit ad aquas inferiores), sed aereum intelligi debeat, quod quamvis non secundum se totum (quod etiam verba textus non requirunt), revera tamen secundum aliquam sui partem interjacet inter aquas superiores et inferiores, et utrasque attingit. Vid. Mus. Disp. cit. § 37. p. 150. 151., Ausfuhrl. Erklärung pag. 198. 199. 204. 205.

Sic autem etiam Marbachius 1. c. existimat, Deum Genes. 1. c. notis et pluvialibus aquis mediam aeris regionem assignare, ut ibi contineantur ad

terrae irrigationem et foecundationem. Et b. Alb. Grauerus ad quaestionem: An supra coelos sidereos sint verae et naturales aquae f respondet: Dubitatur. Vid. Quaest. Illustr. Disp. VIII. Coroll. I. p.

336. Meisnerus: ״Melior pars theologorum semper intellexit (Gen. 1, 7.) aquas proprie dictas, quas Deum singulari et mirabili ratione supra firmamentum vel coelum stellatum vere et realiter reposuisse defendunt.“ (Philos. sobr. P. I. s. 3. q. 3. p. 819.) Cf. Lutherus, Opp. T. I, 42. 49. sq. Sic enim etiam Ps. 104, 3. aquarum nomine nubes intelliguntur. Conf. b. Geierum in Comm. Et b. Marbachius Gen. 1, 7. 8. pluviales aquas denotari credidit. Kegio autem illa, ubi nubes sunt, coelum appellari non raro solet. Vid. Gen. 1, 26. 28. 30., ubi aves coelum pervolare dicuntur, quae sane non in aethere, sed in aere volitant. Conf. Deut. 4,, 17. Et cataractae coeli, puta aerei, apertae et clausae dicuntur Gen. 7, 11. cap. 8, 2. Quod autem Ps. 148, 4. dicitur: המים אשר מ#ל השמים, id Lutherus vertit: Die Wasser, die oben am Himmel sind, et glossatores addiderunt: In den Kegenwolken; ut adeo expansum coelorum complectatur et expansum seu coelum aethereum et aereum; ex quibus nunc illud, nunc hoc, nunc utrumque pro diversitate praedicatorum et contextus intelligi debet. Adde b. Mus. Disp. cit. § 33. sqq. p. 148. sqq., Ausführl. Erklärung p. 200. sqq. § 8.

Tertia die congregatae sunt aquae inferiores, terram alluentes, in certos sinus aut alveos, quos vocavit Deus maria.a Reliquae autem partes terrae apparuerunt aridae; atque ex illis statim natae sunt herbae, arbores, frutices etc.b Vid. Genes. 1, 9. et 10. L. c. v. 11. et 12. Ita quidem, ut terra haberet rationem principii non activi seu efficientis, sed passivi et materialis. Vid. b. Mus. Disp. cit. § 53. 54. p. 166. Caeterum lapides et metalla, atque ipsum hortum Eden, seu paradisum hoc eodem die productum esse, non temere creditur. Vid. Mus. 1. c. § 40. p. 153. Idem de mineralibus, quae media vocant (eoque terras varias, salia, sulphura et bitumina referunt), dicendum videtur.§ 9.

Quarta die Deus fecit solem,a lunam et stellas caeteras,b iisque certum motum atque influendi virtutem indidit, ut tempora mensurarent atque influxu suo diversos in terris effectus possent producere.c PART. I. CAP. 11.

Nempe corpori lucido imperfecto, quod prima die erat conditum, pleniorem lucem ac perfectionem addidit, ut tunc demum solis rationem plane obtineret.

Hollazius: ,,Condidit creator sapientissimus terram, ut ordinarie et universaliter non moveatur, sed quiescat. Luminaribus autem coelestibus id muneris dedit, ut motu suo tempora definiant.“ (Exam. P. I. c. 3. q. 21. p. 369.)

Calovius: ,,Locata terra est, non quae moveretur, sive in gyrum, seu alia ratione, nedum quae motu suo tempora definiret, quod luminaribus datum est officium, sed quae stabilis et immota consisteret. ,Fundavit terram super bases suas, non movebitur in aeternum unquam‘, Ps. 104, 5. Quamvis terra ex aquis ducta sit et undique aquarum, terram altitudine superantium, fluctibus alluatur; ita tamen fundata est divina virtute, ut nullo unquam tempore usque ad diem novissimum tota loco suo moveri queat. Cf. Job. 26, 7. 38, 6. 7. Eccl. 1, 11. Ideoque Scripturae s. adversantur, qui e terra planetam faciunt, terramve mobilem constituunt, sive utrumque diurnum et annuum, sive alterutrum motum ei adscribentes cum Copernico, Keplero, Lansbergio.“ (Syst. T. III. art. 5. c. 2. p. 952.)

Idem: ,,Illi nunquam cum religione Christiana in gratiam redibunt, qui homines in luna collocant, seque, si alarum remigio lunarum orbem attingere valerent, reapse id comperturos, asseverant, nisi Christum etiam pro selenitis (uti Origenes pro astris) mortuum et apostolos in lunae terram volitasse fingant, multisque aliis, religionem orthodoxam evertentibus, paradoxis sese implicent.“ (L. c. p. 961.)

Rollius: ,,Quaestio: An Scriptura aliquando loquatur ad captum vulgi erroneum? orta est ex opinione Copernicana de motu telluris et quiete solis reliquorumque corporum coelestium. Cum enim Copernicanis objiceretur Scripturae auctoritas, terram in perpetuum consistere, solem contra oriri et occidere testantis, responderunt, Scripturam loqui ad captum vulgi erroneum. Falsa autem et blasphema in Deum, Scripturae auctorem, haec est sententia. Praeclara ea de re extat dissertatio b. Dr. Rambachii, in academia Halensi anno 1727. habita. Quo et pertinet dissertatio Dr. Henrici Ascanii Engelkenii, theologi Rostochiensis, de sententiis in Scripturam sacram injuriis et in tractanda illa minus tutis, quam b. Schomeri collegio novissimarum controversiarum Rostochii anno 1703. a se edito, praemisit.“ (Vid. Fechtii Sylloge, p. 28. sq.)

Acta Eruditorum: ,,Hafenrefferus, theologus, suadet Keplero, amico, ut systema terrae motae excolat tanquam hypothesin ad salvanda phaenomena astronomo utilem, abstineat autem a conciliatione cum Seriptura.“ (Vol. anni 1719., p. 5.) Cf. Lutherus ad Gen. 1, 6. I, 44.

ANTITHESIS. Deylingius: ,,Nec est, ut rerum conditarum divisione in coelum et terram offendamur. Nam Scriptura interdum sensuum experientiam sive ideas sensus maxime ferientes sequitur et de corporibus coelestibus perinde ac terrestribus non aliter loquitur, quam prout sensus illa nobis repraesentant, quia, quicquid de corporibus scimus, per sensus nobis innotescit. Quas loquendi formulas artis periti opticas appellare solent et a veritate physica distinguunt. Absit igitur, ut diviniorem Scripturam ad vulgi captum, i. e., ad errorem sese accommodare sive erronee loqui dicamus, quemadmodum multi ex R. Cartesii cumprimis schola imperite et impie opinantur. Quid autem obstat, quominus affirmemus et largiamur, Scripturam nonnullis in locis non physice, sed optice sive secundum observationem sensuum et sicut sensibus res comprehenduntur, locutam esse? Nonne ipsimet astronomi lunam ad hanc

vel illam eclipticae partem referunt, in qua vere non est, sed oculis nostris apparet? Nonne loco optico innituntur omnes astronomorum tabulae, quae tamen non sunt indices errorum, sed observationum verarum? Ille demum errorem vulgi errat, qui locum opticum pro physico habet, quod Spiritus S., Scripturae auctor, nusquam fecit nec errorem vulgi respexit, sed nostram δψιν. Accedit, quod s. literae non philosophorum vel oblectandis vel instruendis ingeniis, sed animis hominum salutis avidorum instituendis, qui simplices magnam partem sunt et indocti, consignatae fuerunt. Ego profecto ingens bonitatis divinae argumen tum in eo situm esse puto, quod non secundum physicam, sed opticam veritatem hujus universi constructio descripta fuit, ut videlicet ne offenderentur infirmiores et philosophiae rudes, quorum tamen in gratiam totam Scripturam s. confectam esse scimus, ut legant eam et facile intelligant.“ (Observ. s. P. I. p. 355. sq.)


### On Creation: Moreover, the moon and the remaining stars were made either immediately from…

Moreover, the moon and the remaining stars were made either immediately from the substance of the ethereal heaven, or from that luminous body of which we have spoken. Mus. Disp. cit. § 42. p. 155. See Gen. 1, 14. 15. 16. 17. § 10. On the fifth day, aquatic living creatures were produced from the water, a and flying creatures from the earth. b

See Gen. 1, 20. Namely, the waters bring forth, not as an effective principle, but as a material one, just as we said concerning the earth with respect to plants at § 8. n. b. And it was certainly appropriate to the nature of these living creatures that they should be produced from water, though not from water alone or pure water. Mus. l. c. § 44. p. 155. See Gen. 2, 19, where God is said to have formed the birds of the heavens, just as the beasts of the field, from the earth. The earth is also more appropriate to the nature of these living creatures than water. Luther: “The text is manifest, that the birds produced from the water sought the air in which they live.” (Ad Gen. 1, 20.) Calovius on the same verse: “The origin of birds from the waters is indicated.” (Bibl. illustr. I, 228. Cf. System. th. Th. III. p. 967. Hollazius contradicts.) § 11. On the sixth day, God produced terrestrial animals, both quadrupeds and reptiles, a from the earth. b

See Gen. 1, 24. And it is manifest that in these animals the earth is the predominant element. Hafenrefferus: “What is to be thought concerning those animals which are born today either from the various mixing of different species, or from putrefaction or some similar reason; were they also made in the first six days of creation? There was no putrefaction in the first creation of things; therefore, there were no animals of that kind then, such as are PART I. CHAP. II.

nits, lice, fleas, mites, worms, and other small animals, which are accustomed to be born from various kinds of putrefaction. Although they did not exist in act at that time, they nevertheless lay hidden in potentiality within other species of animals and in the aptitude of matter, from which they are now produced in various ways. The exact same thing must be thought concerning those species of animals which are born from the mixing of different species, as is reported by physiologists regarding the mule, the lynx, the leopard, and others.” (L. th. L. I. Loc. 2. p. 70. sq.)

Gerhardus: “If one asks about poisonous herbs, harmful beasts, etc., we respond with the words of Augustine in *De Genesi ad litteram*, lib. 3, cap. 15: ‘The harmful animals that were created would have harmed man in no way if he had not sinned. For they began to be harmful for the sake of punishing vices and for the sake of either testing or perfecting the virtue of earthly beings; therefore, they were created harmless, but because of sin they became harmful.’” (Loc. de creat. § 33.) §

12. Finally, God created man on the same day, producing his body indeed from the earth, but his soul from nothing, and joining it to the body. With all other creatures having been produced; Philo Judaeus gives the reason for this order in his book *De mundi opificio*: “As hosts,” he says, “are not called to the banquet before they have prepared what is necessary for the feast; and those who present gymnastic games and theatrical shows, before they gather the spectators into the theaters or stadiums, provide an abundance of contestants and of those things which pertain to the delight of the ears or eyes: so the Prince of the whole world, as the giver of the contest or the banquet, about to call man to the feast and the spectacle, prepared whatever pertained to both, so that upon entering the world he would immediately find both a banquet and a most sacred theater.”

See Gen. 1:26 et seqq. In Gen. 2:7, he is said to be made מן־האדמה, from the earth, just as brute animals are said to be made from the same in v. 19, so that the principle of the origin of man and beasts is common thus far. And by reason of his origin, he drew the name Adam from the earth. He is said, however, to be made עפר, dust from the earth, v. 7, where some, with Tertullian, conjecture that God, by adding liquid, coagulated the dust into mud and, as it were, clay, and thus fashioned the human body; concerning which, however, it is not sufficiently certain from the history of Moses.

Lutherus: “Gen. 2:7. Here Moses returns to the work of the sixth day, and shows whence the cultivator of the earth came. Namely, that God fashioned him from a clod, just as a potter fashions a pot from clay with his hand. Therefore, he did not say above, as he did of other creatures: ‘Let the earth bring forth man’; but: ‘Let us make man,’ so that he might show the excellence of the human race and reveal the singular counsel of God, which He used in creating man, even though hereafter man grows and multiplies in the same way as the rest of the beasts. . . But in the first creation, Moses shows that there is the greatest dissimilarity, since human nature was created by singular counsel and wisdom and formed by the finger of God. This dissimilarity, which exists between the origin of man and of cattle, also shows immortality. For although all the other works of God are full of admiration and very magnificent, yet this proves that man is the most excellent creature, since God employs counsel in creating him and uses a new method. He does not leave him to be fashioned by the earth, as beasts and trees. But He Himself [fashions] him

formed in the image of Himself, as a participant of God and one who was to enjoy the rest of God. Therefore, Adam, before he is formed by the Lord, is a dead and lying clod of earth; God takes hold of it and forms from it a most beautiful creature, a participant of immortality.

If Aristotle were to hear these things, he would burst into laughter and judge it to be, if not an unpleasant, yet a most absurd fable, that man, as to his primary origin, had been a clod of earth, but was formed by divine wisdom, and so created that he was capable of immortality. For even if some of the philosophers, such as Socrates and others, asserted the immortality of souls, they were nevertheless mocked by the remaining philosophers and all but exploded.

But is it not a great folly to be offended by reason in this way, when one sees that even today the generation of man is full of wonder? For will you not judge it absurd that a man, who is to live forever, is born as if from a single drop of seed in the loins of his father? There is almost greater absurdity in this than in what Moses says about the clod formed by the fingers of God. But reason in this way shows that it knows absolutely nothing of God, who by mere thought makes from a clod not the seed of man, but man himself, and, as Moses says later, makes woman from the rib of man.

This is the first origin of man. But with the male and female thus created, man is later generated from their blood by divine blessing.

Although this generation is common with the brutes, it does not, however, take away that glory of our primary origin, that we are vessels of God fashioned by God Himself, that He Himself is our potter, and we are His clay, as Isaiah speaks in the sixty-fourth chapter. And this pertains not only to our origin, but through our whole life and even unto death and into the grave we remain the clay of this potter.” (

Exeget. opp. lat. Cur. Elsperger. Vol. I. Erl. 1829. pp. 104—106.) Cf. S. Schmidtius, who writes: “Since Gen. ch. 1, 26 sqq. described the creation of man rather according to his qualities, i.e., the image of God and the dominion given over all things, here (Gen. 2, 7) he made a clearer mention of the essential parts, body and soul. Therefore Jehovah God formed את־האדם, man, that is, him who was to become and soon ought to be man; for He did not make the whole man, but only the body of man from the earth. He made the soul and united it to the earthly and dead body in such a way that He breathed it in, as a soul of lives, i.e., not only living immortally by itself, but also vivifying the body and breathing through the nostrils. He breathed into the nostrils of man through His Holy Spirit, through whom He impressed the image of God upon him. Thus man became a living soul, i.e., a perfect living animal according to his whole substance.” (Super Mosis librum primum. Argentor. 1697. p. 24.)

Chemnitius: “Just as the souls of brutes are dissolved, vanish, and perish together with their bodies, because the earth produced a living soul, so from the description of the creation of the human soul Solomon says in Eccles. 12, 7: ‘Let the dust return to the earth as it was; and the spirit return to God, who gave it.’ Therefore he calls the breath נשמת חיים, i.e., of lives, in the dual number, because it is not restricted only to the life of the duration of the body, but also to the spiritual life in the other age. Whence Christ says in Matt. 10, 28: ‘Do not fear those who can kill the body, but cannot kill the soul,’ and in Job 12, 10 the soul is properly attributed to the remaining living creatures, but the spirit to men. By breathing He created the soul of man, i.e., besides the vital spirit, which is common to man and beasts, God created a rational soul, and it is said to have breathed, because He infused into that soul light, wisdom, divine justice, etc., so that man might be the image and likeness of God. For Christ also, about to restore the image of God in man, used inspiration, when by breathing upon the apostles He gave the Holy Spirit, John 20, 22; and He undoubtedly wished to lead us to the thought of the first inspiration.” (Loc. th. loc. de creat, c. 5. f. 113.)

Scherzerus: “Divine insufflation sufficiently proves immortality. He who breathes in, bestows as it were from His own. However, by the words נשמת חיים this immortality is not proved; because by this reasoning the souls of brutes would also be immortal through Gen. 7, 22.” (System. Loc. V. § 5. p. 114.)

PART I. CHAP. II. Luther: "Gen. 2: 7. Here a new question arises. For just as Moses speaks here of man with a new phrase: 'God formed man of the dust of the ground'; whereas he did not speak thus of other living creatures above: so also he says something peculiar here about man, that God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, which he did not say of the remaining beasts, even though the spirit in the nostrils is present in all beasts, just as in man. The question is therefore, why did Moses wish to speak thus? Secondly, this is also asked (although it pertains to the same thing), since throughout all Scripture all animals are called living souls, why is it said only of man in this place that he was made into a living soul?

Latin:

Factae autem sunt luna et stellae reliquae vel immediate ex substantia coeli aetherei, vel ex illo, quod diximus, corpore lucido. Mus. Disp. cit. § 42. p. 155. Vid. Gen. 1, 14. 15. 16. 17.§ 10. Quinta die animantia aquatilia ex aqua, a et volatilia ex terra b producta fuerunt.

Vid. Gen. 1, 20. Nempe reptificant aquae, non ut principium effectivum, sed ut materiale, prout de terra, respectu plantarum, diximus ad § 8. n. b. Et conveniens sane erat naturae horum animantium, ut ex aqua, licet non sola aut pura, producerentur. Mus. 1. c. § 44. p. 155. Vid. Gen. 2, 19., ubi Deus volucres coeli, aeque ac bestias agri, e terra formasse dicitur. Convenientior quoque naturae horum animantium terra est, quam aqua.Lutherus: ,,Manifestus textus est, volucres ex aqua productas petiisse aërem, in quo vivunt.“ (Ad Gen. 1, 20.) Calovius ad eund. v.: ,,Ortus avium ex aquis indicatur.“ (Bibi, illustr. I, 228. Cf. System, th. Th. III. p. 967. Contradicit Hollazius.) § 11. Sexta die produxit Deus animalia terrestria, cum quadrupeda, tum reptilia,a ex terra.b

Vid. Gen. 1, 24. Atque in his sane animalibus terram esse elementum praedominans, manifestum est.Hafenrefferus: ,,Quid sentiendum est de istis animalibus, quae vel ex varia diversarum specierum commixtione, vel ex putredine aut consimili quadam ratione hodie enascuntur, num et illa in primo creationis sextiduo facta sunt? Putredo in prima rerum creatione nulla fuit, nulla igitur tum ejus generis quoque animalia fuerunt, qualia sunt PART. I. CAP. II.

lendes, pediculi, pulices, acarus, lumbrici et alia animalcula, quae ex varia putredine varia enasci solent. Licet autem istiusmodi actu tum non fuerint, potentia tamen in aliis animalium speciebus et materiae habilitate latuerunt, quae modo variis rationibus inde producuntur. Idem prorsus de istis animalium speciebus sentiendum est, quae diversarum specierum commixtione nascuntur, ut de mulo, lynce, leopardo et aliis apud physiologos traditur.“ (L. th. L. I. Loc. 2. p. 70. sq.)

Gerhardus: ,,Si quaeratur de herbis venenatis, de bestiis noxiis etc., respondemus verbis Augustini de Gen. ad literam 1. 3. c. 15.: ,Creata animalia noxia nihil homini nocuissent, si non peccasset. Puniendorum namque vitiorum et terrenorum vel probandae vel perficiendae virtutis causa nocere coeperunt; fuerunt ergo creata innoxia, sed propter peccatum facta sunt noxia.“ (Loc. de creat. § 33.) §

12. Denique a hominem eodem die creavit Deus,b corpus quidem ejus ex terra, c animam vero ex nihilo producens d et corpori conjungens.e Caeteris creaturis omnibus productis; cujus ordinis rationem reddit Philo Judaeus Lib. de mundi opific. Ut convivatores, ait, non,prius ad coenqm vocantur, quam ad epulum necessaria praeparaverint; et qui gymnicos ludos et theatrales exhibent, antequam spectatores in theatra vel stadia congregent certatorum, et earum rerum, quae ad aurium vel oculorum oblectamentum attinent, copiam parent: ita totius mundi princeps, tanquam certaminis aut convivii dator, hominem ad epulas et spectaculum vocaturus, quicquid ad utrumque pertinebat, apparavit, ut in mundum ingressus ille statim inveniret et convivium et theatrum sacratissimum.

Vid. Gen. 1, 26. et seqq. Genes. 2, 7. factus dicitur מן־האךמה, ex terra, quemadmodum animantia bruta ex eadem facta dicuntur v. 19., ut hactenus commune sit principium ortus hominis et bestiarum. Ac ratione originis suae de terra nomen Adami traxit. Dicitur autem factus פר;.’, pulvis e terra, v. 7., ubi quidam cum Tertulliano conjiciunt, Deum, liquore addito, pulverem in limum et quasi argillam coagulasse atque ita corpus humanum fabricasse; de quo tamen ex Mosis historia non satis constat.

Lutherus: ,,Gen. 2, 7. Hic redit Moses ad opus sexti diei, et ostendit, unde cultor terrae venerit. Nempe, quod Deus eum Anxerit ex gleba, sicut Agulus manu ex luto Angit ollam. Ideo supra non dixit, sicut de aliis creaturis: Producat terra hominem; sed: ,Faciamus hominem‘, ut ostendat excellentiam generis humani et revelet Dei consilium singulare, quo usus est in condendo homine, etsi posthac homo crescit et multiplicatur eodem modo, quo reliquae bestiae. . . Sed in prima conditione ostendit Moses, maximam esse dissimilitudinem, si quidem singulari tum consilio, tum sapientia, humana natura condita et digito Dei formata est. Haec dissimilitudo, quae inter originem hominis et pecudum est, etiam ostendit immortalitatem. Etsi enim omnia reliqua opera Dei plena admirationis et valde magnifica sunt, tamen hominem hoc arguit esse praestantissimam creaturam, si quidem Deus in eo condendo consilium adhibet et novo modo utitur. Non relinquit eum Angendum terrae, sicut bestias et arbores. Sed ipse eum

format ad imaginem sui, tanquam participem Dei et qui fruiturus sit requie Dei. Itaque Adam, antequam a Domino formatur, est mortua et jacens gleba; eam apprehendit Deus et format inde pulcherrimam creaturam, participem immortalitatis.

Haec si Aristoteles audiret, solveretur in cachinnum, et judicaret, esse, etsi non insuavem, tamen absurdissimam fabulam, quod homo quoad originem suam primam fuisset gleba, formatus autem sit divina sapientia, et sic conditus, ut esset capax immortalitatis. Nam etiamsi qui ex philosophis, ut Socrates et alii, asseruerunt immortalitatem animorum, tamen a reliquis philosophis irrisi, et tantum non explosi sunt.

Sed an non magna est fatuitas, sic offendi rationem, cum videat adhuc hodie plenam admirationis esse hominis generationem? An enim non absurdum judicabis, hominem, qui in aeternum victurus est, nasci quasi ex una guttula seminis in lumbis patris? Major in hoc fere absurditas est, quam quod Moses dicit, de gleba digitis Dei formata. Sed ratio hoc modo ostendit, se plane nihil scire de Deo, qui sola cogitatione ex gleba facit non semen hominis, sed ipsum hominem, et, quod postea Moses dicit, ex costa viri facit feminam.

Haec prima hominis origo est. Creato autem sic masculo et femina postea ex eorum sanguine divina benedictione generatur homo.

Quanquam autem haec cum brutis communis generatio est, non tollit tamen illam gloriam originis nostrae primae, quod sumus vascula Dei ab ipso Deo fleta, quod ipse est figulus noster, nos autem lutum ejus, sicut Jesaias sexagesimo quarto loquitur. Idque non solum ad originem nostram attinet, sed per omnem vitam et usque ad mortem et in sepulchrum manemus lutum hujus figuli.“ (

Exeget. opp. lat. Cur. Elsperger. Tom. I. Erl. 1829. p. 104—106.) Cf. S. Schmidtius, qui scribit: ,,Cum Gen. c. 1, 26. sqq. creationem hominis potius juxta qualitates, h. e. imaginem Dei datumque in omnia dominium, descripserit, hic (Gen. 2, 7.) partium essentialium clariorem mentionem fecit, corporis et animae. Formavit itaque Jehovah Deus את־האדם, hominem, hoc est, eum, qui fieti et mox esse debebat homo, non enim totum horninem, sed corpus tantum hominis e terra fecit. Animam ita fecit et univit terreno mortuoque corpori, ut spiraverit eam, tanquam animam vitarum, h. e., non tantum per se immortaliter viventem, sed et corpus vivificantem et per nares spirantem. Inspiravit autem in nares horninis per ·Spiritum suum Sanctum, per quem imaginem Dei illi impressit. Sic factus est homo in animam viventem, h. e. in perfectum animal vivens secundum totam substantiam.“ (Super Mosis librum primum. Argentor. 1697. p. 24.)

Chemnitius: ,,Sicut animae brutorum una cum corporibus dissolvuntur, evanescunt et intereunt, quia terra produxit animam viventem, ita ex descriptione creationis animae humanae dicit Salomon Eccles. 12, 7.: ,Revertatur pulvis in terram suam, unde erat; et spiritus redeat ad Deum, qui dedit illum.‘ Ideo vocat spiraculum דרים, i. e., vitarum, in duali numero, quod non tantum ad vitam durationis corporis restringatur, sed etiam ad vitam spiritualem in altero saeculo. Unde Christus dicit Matth. 10, 28.: ,Nolite timere eos, qui corpus possunt occidere, animam vero non possunt occidere‘, et Jobi 12, 10. anima proprie tribuitur reliquis animantibus, hominibus vero spiritus. Inspirando creavit animam hominis, i. e., praeter spiritum vitalem, qui homini communis est pecudibus, Deus creavit animam rationalem, et dicitur inspirasse, quia transfudit in illam animam lucem, sapientiam, justitiam divinam etc., ut esset homo imago et similitudo Dei. Nam et Christus, restauraturus imaginem Dei in homine, usus est inspiratione, cum insufflando apostolis dabat Spiritum S., Joh. 20, 22.; et voluit sine dubio nos deducere ad cogitationem primae inspirationis.“ (Loc. th. loc. de creat, c. 5. f. 113.)

Scherzerus: ,,Divina insufflatio immortalitatem sufficienter probat. Qui inflat, is de suo quasi largitur. Per voces autem נשמת חיים haec immortalitas non probatur; quia hac ratione etiam animae brutorum per Gen. 7, 22. immortales forent.“ (System. Loc. V. § 5. p. 114.)

PART. I. CAP. II. Lutherus:,, Gen. 2, 7. Hic nova quaestio oritur. Sicut enim Moses nova phrasi hic de homine loquitur: ,Formavit Deus hominem de limo terrae‘; de aliis autem animantibus supra non sic loquutus est: ita quoque hic peculiare quiddam de homine dicit, inspirasse Deum in faciem ejus spiraculum, quod de reliquis bestiis non dixit, cum tamen omnibus bestiis, sicut homini, insit spiritus in naribus. Quaeritur igitur, cur hoc Moses sic voluerit dicere? Secundo quaeritur id quoque (quanquam eodem pertinet), cum per totam Scripturam omnia animalia vocentur animae viventes, cur tantum de homine hoc in loco dicatur, factum eum esse in animam viventem?


### On Creation: Above, indeed, he said

Above, indeed, he said: 'Let the earth bring forth the living soul, each in its kind.' But here he changes much, and says: 'Man was made into a living soul.' These things without doubt moved the patriarchs, the holy fathers, and the prophets to examine such passages more diligently, because this singular manner of speaking signifies that Moses wished to show something remarkable.

For if you look at the animal life of which Moses speaks here, there is no difference between a man and an ass. For animal life has need of food and drink; it has need of sleep and rest; bodies are likewise fattened and grow by food and drink, and they wither and perish by starvation; the stomach receives food and transmits it, once digested, to the liver, which produces blood, by which all members are restored. When we consider these things, there is no difference between man and beast. And yet Moses adorns the life of man in this way, that he says of him alone that he was made into a living soul, not simply, as other beasts, but into an excellently living soul, because he was created in the image of God, which image without doubt shone forth singularly in the face of Adam and Eve in the state of innocence, just as even after sin the Gentiles, from the posture of the body—because man alone walks erect and lifts his eyes to heaven—concluded that man is a more excellent creature among all other creatures.

Paul looked to this when he cites this passage, 1 Cor. 15[:45]: 'It is written, the first man Adam was made into a living soul, but the last Adam into a life-giving spirit.' He calls the animal life a living soul, which is to eat, to drink, to beget, to grow, all of which are also in brutes. By antithesis, however, he says that the last Adam was made into a life-giving spirit, that is, such a life as does not stand in need of these conditions of animal life. Paul also teaches that, even if Adam had not sinned, he would nevertheless have lived a bodily life, needing food, drink, rest, growing, begetting, etc., until he had been translated by God to a spiritual life, in which he would have lived without animality, so to speak, namely from within, from God alone, and not from without, as before from herbs and fruits, and this in such a way that man nevertheless has flesh and bones, and is not merely a spirit, as the angels are.

I answer, therefore, to the question, that God, through the mouth of Moses, wished to show even in this place the hope of a future and eternal life, which Adam, had he persisted in innocence, would have had after this animal life. As if Moses were saying: Man was made into a living soul, not simply as beasts live, but one which God was thereafter to vivify, even without animal life. We also have this hope of immortality through Christ, although because of sin we are subject to death and all calamities.

Adam’s condition would have been better. He would have lived on earth sweetly and with the greatest pleasure, then without any trouble he would have been translated from animal life into spiritual. We are translated from animal life to spiritual only through death, and after infinite dangers and crosses.

In this manner, together with the holy prophets, we ought to examine Moses diligently, and observe why he says with singular counsel concerning man what he said otherwise concerning the remaining living creatures: namely, so that faith and the hope of immortality may be confirmed in us, that although man according to animal life is similar to the other brute creatures, yet he has the hope of immortality, which the other living creatures do not have; he bears the image and likeness of God, which the other living creatures do not bear." (L. c. p. 106—109.) Cf. A. Osiander, who

writes: "I answer that man is said to be formed from the dust of the ground not by reason of the work in progress, but by reason of the end; for Moses speaks of a perfect and formed man, not of one being formed and produced. But just as he indicates by these words what God produced and what He formed, as the completed end of creation, so he then descends to the exposition of the parts and explains how each was produced, namely, by breathing the soul, forming the body, and presupposing the formed body for that breathing." (Colleg. th. syst. I. p. 224 sq.)

Ibid. For that insufflation, which is said to have proceeded from God, cannot denote the emission of a bodily breath, since God is incorporeal; therefore, it denotes nothing other than the immateriality of the action and that the effect produced is a spirit, distinct from the body and all matter. So that in the same moment the body was produced from the dust and the soul was breathed into it. For although the word צר; is otherwise used of a potter forming some vessel from clay or mud, yet a successive production of the parts of the body or a successive introduction of a heterogeneous form into individual parts, and thus finally a subsequent animation of the body, ought not to be thought of when we contemplate the work of divine power. Nor is it permitted to go beyond the third point of the analogy.

A. Osiander: "Indeed, mention is made of three by Moses, but of two as essential parts, and of the third as a composite resulting from that union of parts; which composite is called a living soul, the denomination being made, of course, from the more excellent part." (L. c. p. 222.)

Quenstedtius: "Man consists of only two essential parts, a rational soul and an organic body; and thus neither is the spirit a third essential part of man, nor do the rational soul alone, but also the human body, essentially constitute man... Distinguish between spirit, insofar as it denotes the essence of the soul (for the soul itself is also a spirit and an incorporeal essence), and insofar as it denotes the qualities, motions, and affections of the soul, according to which the soul is said to be now joyful, now sad, now strong, now weak and timid." (L. c. c. 12. s. 2. q. 2. f. 738.)

The same: "Weigelius strives to construct his trichotomy from meager sayings of Holy Scripture, which make distinct mention of soul and spirit, such as Luke 1:46, 47; 1 Thess. 5:23; Heb. 4:12. But he washes the brick [i.e., labors in vain]; for 1. It does not follow: Holy Scripture anywhere makes distinct mention of soul and spirit, therefore there is an essential distinction between that soul and spirit. For not every διαίρεσις και μερισμός [division and partition] is an essential distinction. 2. By 'spirit' Holy Scripture in such sayings does not understand some spirit substantially different from the human soul, but the higher part of the soul (as Dr. Feuerbornius speaks). 'For the soul,' says the same, 'is accustomed to be distinguished into its higher and lower powers and faculties.' For that reason, Paul himself calls it the spirit of the mind in Eph. 4:23." (L. c. f. 739 sq.)

The same: "When the blessed Luther, Tom. VI. Witteb. f. 13. and Jen. I. f. 479, and some other writers anywhere say that there are three parts of man: body, soul, and spirit, they by no means understand three parts essentially different from themselves (for they teach expressly that the soul as to its ουσίαν [essence] is that spirit, and the latter as to substance and nature is the former), but adjunct parts. Nor is it unusual to call the division of a subject into its adjuncts a distribution of a whole into parts. Thus, for example, philosophers are accustomed to call the powers of the soul parts, as the λόγικον μέρος [rational part]. And Basil, in Ps. 33, calls the το λογικόν [rational part] of man the μέρος διορατικόν [the discerning part]; cf. Aristotle, Ethic. Nicom. book VI, ch. 1. And just as τό μέρος [the part] is sometimes taken broadly, so that even adjuncts are called τα μέρη [the parts], so also PART I. CHAP. II.

Merismos* is sometimes taken loosely and denotes an imperfect division, as some call it. Distinguish between the spirit constituting man in his natural and human being—and thus the spirit is the rational soul—and the spirit constituting man in his spiritual and Christian being—and this is the regenerating and sanctifying χάρισμα; and likewise that which places man in a state of corruption, and this is called a spirit of dizziness, Is. 19:14, or of whoredom, Hos. 5:4. (L. c. f. 740.)

Bengelius: "Jude 19: πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντες, not having the spirit; therefore the spirit is not an essential part of man." (Gnomon ad 1. c.)

Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between an instrument which a man uses, such as a soldier’s horse or a smith’s hammer, and an essential part which is informed by a form.*) The soul does not use the body as an instrument, but the body is informed by the soul; nor is the soul united with the body extrinsically, like a lyre-player with a lyre, a horse with a soldier, or a smith with a hammer, but intrinsically, which internal union makes a being *per se* and one essence. Therefore, the body is called an instrument of the soul abusively [improperly] on account of similarity, not on account of the truth of the thing and its internal nature." (L. c.)

The same: "They object: 'Our body does not always remain the same in number, how therefore can it be a part? For everyone has gradually worn away many bodies since early infancy. Therefore, the body is not essential to him, since it can be absent and present while the man remains safe.' Resp.: The body certainly remains the same in number, because the form is the same, which is the principle of individuation."**) (L. c. f. 741.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Manichaeans and Heracleonites, according to Jerome *ad Hedib.* q. 12. ep. 150. and Gennadius c. 20, who posit three essential parts of man: body, soul, and spirit. 2. Of the Paracelsians, who teach the same... 3. Of the Enthusiasts, Schwenkfeldians, Weigelians, and modern prophets, who dream that a third essential part, namely the spirit, is added to man in regeneration... 4. Of Joh. Amos Comenius, a Calvinist, who says: 'Man is composed of three: body, spirit, and soul. We have the body fashioned from the elements, we have the spirit from the spirit of the world, but the soul or mind is from God. The body is the organ and dwelling-place of the spirit, but the spirit is the dwelling-place and organ of the soul,' etc...

9. Of D. Joachim Luetkemann, formerly a professor at Rostock, who taught that 'besides the soul and body, something else is essentially required for the constitution of man, and indeed something substantial, which is corrupted when a man dies, on account of the absence of which being Christ was not a true man at the time of death, since that third requirement, being the same in number, he denied would return from the dead when the man is pressed by necessity'; but when admonished about these things, he declared that by that third thing he did not mean a part of man, but a mode of the soul and body, namely the union, which he claimed differed really from both (soul and body) and was something substantial." (L. c. f. 738. sq.) §

Latin:

Supra quidem dixit:, Producat terra animam viventem, unumquodque in suo genere. ‘ Sed hic multum mutat, et dicit: ,Homo factus est in animam viventem.‘ Haec absque dubio moverunt patriarchas, sanctos patres et prophetas, ut hujusmodi locos diligentius excuterent, quod ista singularis loquendi ratio significat, Mosen insigne quiddam voluisse ostendere.

Nam si animalem vitam, de qua hic Moses loquitur, respicias, nulla differentia est inter hominem et asinum. Habet enim animalis vita opus cibo et potu; habet opus somno et quiete; corpora pariter cibo et potu saginantur et crescunt, inedia marcescunt et pereunt; stomachus cibum accipit, et coctum transmittit ad hepar, quod sanguinem gignit, quo restaurantur omnia membra. Haec cum consideramus, nulla inter horninem et bestiam est differentia. Et tamen hominis vitam Moses ornat hoc modo, quod de eo solo dicit, esse eum factum in animam viventem, non simpliciter, sicut alias bestias, sed in animam excellenter viventem, propterea quod ad imaginem Dei est conditus, quae imago procul dubio in statu innocentiae singulariter reluxit in facie Adae et Hevae, sicut post peccatum tamen gentes ex positu corporis, quod solus homo erectus incedit et attollit oculos ad coelum, collegerunt, hominem praestantiorem esse creaturam inter omnes reliquas creaturas.

Huc respexit Paulus, cum hunc locum citat, 1 Cor. 15. (v. 45. ): ,Scriptum est, primus homo Adam factus est in animam viventem, ultimus autem Adam in spiritum vivificantem.‘ Animam viventem vocat vitam animalem, quae est edere, bibere, generare, augescere, quae omnia etiam in brutis sunt. Per antithesin autem dicit, ultimum Adam factum esse in spiritum vivificantem, hoc est, talem vitam, quae istis animalis vitae conditionibus non indigeat. Docet etiam Paulus, etiamsi Adam non peccasset, tamen victurum fuisse corporalem vitam, indigam cibi, potus, quietis, crescentem, generantem etc., donec per Deum ad vitam spiritualem esset translatus, in qua vixisset sine animalitate, ut sic dicam, nempe ab intra, ex solo Deo, et non ab extra, sicut antea ex herbis et fructibus, idque sic, ut tamen homo habeat carnem et ossa, et non sit mere spiritus, sicut angeli sunt.

Respondeo igitur ad quaestionem, Deum per os Mosi etiam hoc in loco voluisse ostendere spem futurae et aeternae vitae, quam Adam, si in innocentia perstitisset, post animalem hanc vitam habiturus fuerat. Quasi dicat Moses: Factus est homo in animam viventem, non simpliciter, sicut bestiae vivunt, sed quam Deus posthac vivificaturus erat, etiam sine animali vita. Hanc spem immortalitatis per Christum habemus nos quoque, quanquam propter peccatum morti et omnibus calamitatibus sumus subjecti.

Adae melior fuerat futura conditio. In terra suaviter et cum summa voluptate vixisset, deinde sine ulla molestia esset translatus de animali vita in spiritualem. Nos ex animali vita ad spiritualem non nisi per mortem, et post infinita pericula ac cruces transferimur.

Ad hunc modum cum sanctis prophetis debemus Mosen diligenter inspicere, et observare, cur singulari consilio de homine dicat, quod aliter de reliquis animantibus dixit: ut scilicet confirmetur in nobis fides et spes immortalitatis, quod, etsi homo secundum animalem vitam similis est caeteris animantibus brutis, tamen habet spem immortalitatis, quam caetera animantia non habent; gerit imaginem et similitudinem Dei, quam caetera animantia non gerunt.“ (L. c. p. 106—109. ) Cf. A. Osiander, qui

scribit: ,,Respondeo, hominem dici formatum ex limo terrae non ratione operis in via, sed ratione termini; de perfecto enim et formato homine Moses loquitur, non de formando et producendo. Sicut autem his verbis indicat, quid Deus produxerit, quid formaverit, ut terminum creationis completum, ita deinde ad expositionem partium descendit, et quomodo singulae sint productae, exponit, nempe anima spirando, corpus formando, et formatum isti spirationi praesupponendo.“ (Colleg. th. syst. I. p. 224. sq. )

Ibid. Insufflatio enim illa, quae a Deo profecta dicitur, non potest denotare halitus corporei emissionem, cum Deus sit incorporeus; itaque nihil aliud, quam immaterialitatem actionis denotat quodque effectus productus sit spiritus, a corpore atque materia omni distinctus. Ita ut eodem momento produceretur corpus ex limo et anima ei inspiraretur. Quamvis enim verbum צר; alias de figulo, ex argilla aut luto vas aliquod eiformante, usurpetur, non tamen ideo successiva productio partium corporis aut formae heterogeneae in singulas partes successiva introductio, atque ita demum secuta corporis animatio cogitari debet, quando divinae virtutis opus intuemur. Neque ultra tertium similitudinis egredi licet.

A. Osiander: ״Trium quidem mentio fit a Mose, sed duorum ut partium essentialium, tertii vero ut compositi, ex ista partium unione resultantis; quod compositum dicitur anima vivens, denominatione sci. facta a potiori.“ (L. c. p. 222.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Homo duabus tantum constat partibus essentialibus, anima rationali et corpore organico; adeoque nec spiritus tertia pars essentialis hominis est, nec anima rationalis solum, sed et corpus humanum essentialiter constituunt hominem. . . Dist. inter spiritum, prout notat animae essentiam (anima enim ipsa quoque spiritus est et essentia incorporea), et prout notat animae qualitates, motus et affectus, secundum quos modo laeta, modo tristis, modo fortis, modo imbecillis et timida dicitur anima.“ (L. c. c. 12. s. 2. q. 2. f. 738.)

Idem: ,,Weigelius suam trichotomiam adstruere annititur exiliis s. Scripturae dictis, quae distinctam animae et spiritus faciunt mentionem, ut Luc. 1, 46. 47. 1 Thess. 5, 23. Ebr. 4, 12. Sed laterem lavat; nam 1. non sequitur: S. Scriptura uspiam distincte meminit animae et spiritus, ergo est essentialis distinctio animae et spiritus illius. Non enim omnis διαίρεσις και μερισμός est distinctio essentialis. 2. Per spiritum Scriptura s. in ejusmodi dictis non intelligit aliquem spiritum ab anima humana substantialiter differentem, sed partem animae superiorem (ut loquitur Dr. Feuerbornius). ,Solet enim anima‘, inquit idem, ,distingui in superiores et inferiores suas potentias et facultates.‘ Proptereaque et ipse Paulus vocat spiritum mentis Eph. 4, 23.“ (L. c. f. 739. sq.)

Idem: ,,Quando b. Lutherus Tom. VI. Witteb. f. 13. et Jen. I. f. 479. et alii nonnulli scriptores uspiam dicunt, quod hominis tres sint partes: corpus, anima et spiritus, nequaquam intelligunt tres partes essentialiter a seipsis differentes (docent enim diserte, animam quoad ουσίαν esse spiritum illum, et hunc quoad substantiam et naturam esse illam), sed partes adjunctivas. Nec enim insuetum est, etiam divisionem subjecti in adjuncta vocare distributionem totius in partes. Sic v. g. philosophi potentias animae vocare solent partes, ut λόγικον μέρος. Et Basilius in Ps. 33. το λογικόν hominis vocat μέρος διορατικόν, partem perspicacem; cf. Aristotel. 1. VI. Ethic., Nicom. c. 1. Et sicut τό μέρος interdum sumitur late, ita ut etiam adjuncta dicantur τα μέρη, ita et PART. I. CAP. II.

quandoque accipitur laxe et notat divisionem imperfectam, quam sic nonnulli vocant. Dist. inter spiritum constituentem hominem in esse naturali et humanitatis, et sic spiritus est anima rationalis; et spiritum constituentem hominem in esse spirituali et christianitatis, et hic est χάρισμα regenerans et sanctificans; itemque ponentem hominem in esse corruptionis, et hic dicitur spiritus vertiginis, Es. 19, 14., scortationis, Hos. 5, 4.“ (L. c. f. 740.)

Bengelius: ״Jud. 19.: ιτνενμα μη εχοντες, spiritum non habentes; itaque spiritus non est pars essentialis hominis.“ (Gnomon ad 1. c.)

Quenstedtius: ״Dist. inter instrumentum, quo homo utitur, qualis est equus militis, malleus fabri, et partem essentialem, quae a forma informatur. *) Anima non utitur corpore ut instrumento, sed corpus ab anima informatur, nec unitur anima cum corpore extrinsece, ut citharoedus cum cithara, equus cum milite, faber cum malleo, sed intrinsece, quae unio interna facit ens per se et unam essentiam. Abusive ergo corpus instrumentum animae dicitur ob similitudinem, non ob rei veritatem ac naturam internam.“ (L. c.)

Idem: ,,Objiciunt: ,,Corpus nostrum non manet semper idem numero, quomodo igitur pars sit? Quilibet enim a prima infantia multa corpora sensim detrivit. Ergo corpus illi non est essentiale, cum salvo homine possit abesse et adesse. Eesp.: Manet utique idem numero corpus, quia idem forma, principio sci. individuationis.“**) (L. c. f. 741.)

ANTITHE SIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Manichaeorum et Heracleonitarum apud Hieronymum ad Hedib. q. 12. ep. 150. et Gennadium c. 20. tres partes essentiales hominis statuentium, corpus, animam et spiritum. 2. Paracelsistarum idem docentium. . . 3. Enthusiastarum, Schwenkfeldianorum, Weigelianorum, novellorum prophetarum, tertiam partem essentialem, sci. spiritum, in regeneratione homini accedere, somniantium. . . 4. Joh. Amosi Comenii, Calviniani, qui: ,Componitur‘, inquit, ,homo ex tribus, corpore, spiritu et anima. Corpus habemus ex elementis conflatum, spiritum habemus ex spiritu mundi, sed anima seu mens a Deo est. Corpus organon et habitaculum spiritus, spiritus vero habitaculum et organon est animae‘ etc...

9. D. Joachim Luetke· manni, professoris quondam Rostochiensis, qui docuit, ,praeter animam et corpus aliquid aliud essentialiter requiri ad constitutionem hominis, et quidem substantiale aliquid, quod moriente homine corrumpatur, ob cujus entis absentiam Christus tempore mortis non fuerit verus homo, siquidem id praeter corpus et animam ad esse hominis requiratur, quod requisitum tertium idem numero, res urgente homine, ex mortuis redire‘ negavit; sed de his monitus declaravit sese, per tertium illud non partem hominis, sed animae et corporis modum, nempe unionem, quam abi utroque (anima et corpore) differre realiter et substantiale quid esse ajebat, abs se intelligi.“ (L. c. f. 738. sq.) §


### On Creation: God created in the beginning only one human individual, namely the male;a the…

13. God created in the beginning only one human individual, namely the male;a the female b He later produced from the rib c of the sleeping d man.e *)

Scharffius: "Form is the internal cause through which a thing is constituted in its being, as in man it is the rational soul. The informing form is that through which a thing is what it is." (Metaphys. p. 115.) **) Scharffius: "The principle of individuation is the cause on account of which a thing is an individual and singular thing."

And this is that one Adam, of whom mention is made in both chapters 1 and 2 of Genesis. That Adam, however, was for some time alone without a female companion is evident from chapter 2, 18, 19, and 20.

Quenstedtius: "Adam, created by God on the sixth day of the first hexaemeron, is the first of all men and the parent of the entire human race throughout the whole world. . . Our position is not merely a problem, but a dogma of faith, and one of no slight moment, but of great difficulty; for the whole of theology is corrupted by this fiction concerning the Pre-Adamites. . . The sum of the objection is this: that in Genesis 1 the creation of the human race is described, not that of Adam himself, whose description follows only in chapter II." (L. c. c. 12. s. 2. q. 1. f. 733. sq. 736.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the ancient heretical Arabs; for the Nabataeans and Sabaeans, inhabitants of Arabia, as reported by Joh. Henr. Hottinger in his *Oriental History*, book I, ch. 8, in the thesis, say: 'They produced men older than Adam,' just as they dreamed that he was born from the sea and a woman in the manner of others. . . 2. Of Caesalpinus, following Avicenna and Cardano, who said: That men are born from putrefaction like mice and frogs. . . 5. Of the founder of the Pre-Adamites, Isaac Peyrerius, a Frenchman by nation, but who brought forth the monster of the Pre-Adamites in Belgium, formerly a Calvinist by profession, then after his *palinodia* a Roman Catholic, who in the year 1655. . . brought this portent. . . out of hell: That the Gentiles are different from the Jews in race and origin; that the Jews were formed by God in Adam, but the Gentiles were created earlier on the same day as the other living creatures. . . Likewise: That the epoch of the created world is not to be reckoned from that beginning which is commonly imagined in Adam, but that it must be sought much higher and from ages long past. A certain Johannes Meffresozotius agreed with Peyrerius." (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 734.)

Indeed, as regards the body, just as God had previously produced Adam from the dust of the earth, namely according to the body. See Gen. 2, 7, 21, and 22.

Luther: "The Hebrew word מריע signifies a rib and a side. Therefore I understand it thus, that the Lord took not a bare rib, but one clothed with flesh, just as Adam says below: 'This is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.' Furthermore, the Lord also did this by His word, lest we think that He used some incision in the manner of a surgeon. He said: From that bone, thus clothed with flesh, let a woman be made, and so it was done." (L. c. p. 162.)

Quenstedtius: "The rib, from which the woman was formed, was not dead or inanimate, but animated, as it was taken by the divine hand from a living body. And thus Eve was produced from it according to soul and body; yet the soul of Eve was not immediately created by God out of nothing and divinely infused into her, but the rib of Adam was the *tradux* [conveyance] of the human soul to Eve, i.e., it existed not by immediate creation, but by propagation and *traductio*. From the animated rib, an animated woman was formed, Gen. 2, 22." (L. c. s. 1. th. 4. f. 731.)

Heerbrandus: "The earth, from which Adam was created and formed, was not alive, but Adam's body was vivified by the inspired soul. But God afterwards built and produced Eve alive from the rib of the living Adam, and it is not written that He breathed into her, as He did before into Adam; but she was produced and built entirely from Adam, body and soul together. Which was a different mode of creation than that of Adam. Thus God always seems to create man from man, the whole from the whole, even soul from soul, just as light is kindled from light. For this order is divinely instituted in nature, that like should beget like, brute beget brute, and so also man beget man." PART 1. CHAP. II.

Nor is the generation of man more imperfect than the generation of a brute. And when Scripture speaks of the sins of men, their corruption, and their regeneration, in both it understands the whole man: "I was conceived in sins." "Unless one is born again, etc." (Compend. th. Loc. de pecc. p. 306.)

It pleased God, however, to produce the woman from a part of the man's body, partly for the ὁμοουσίαν of both spouses, and thus further so that the unity of the origin or principle of the entire human race might be recognized so much the more clearly; partly so that a notable foundation of conjugal friendship might be perceived. Although, if we listen to Hugh of St. Victor, it should be particularly observed that the part from which the woman was made was taken neither from the head nor from the feet, lest she be thought either a mistress, if from the head, or a handmaid, if from the feet: therefore, it had to be taken from the middle, that is, from the rib, so that she might be understood as a companion. It was truly a real sleep, not an ἔκστασις, although it was divinely induced. And God willed that Adam should not be a spectator of the formation, but an admirer of the formed work. God is said to have "built" the rib, so that we might observe the craftsmanship of the structure in the machine of the body. § 14. In what place, or in what part of the earth, God produced Adam and Eve, we do not define. It is thought, however, that they were created outside of Paradise and introduced into it afterwards.

For as for the fact that the Hebrews mention the field of Damascus here, it is a tradition of doubtful credibility, as Scripture is silent. Regarding Adam, the matter is indeed clear from Gen. 2:7, 8, where it is narrated that God took Adam and placed him in Paradise. For thus a local movement or translation of Adam, having stayed outside of Paradise for some time, into Paradise is certainly indicated. Basil the Great, however, thought that the woman was likewise produced outside of Paradise and finally, after she had been joined with Adam under divine auspices, was brought into Paradise together with him, whom not a few more recent authors follow. § 15. These works having been completed and the sixth day having elapsed, God rested. Nor did He create more species of creatures.
