Gerhard: "After man, God rested from His works, because man was to be the most tranquil dwelling place of the most holy Trinity." (L. de imag. § 10.) See Gen. 2:2. Although He could have added countless others. Otherwise, however, God does not entirely rest or keep holiday, as we shall see in the chapter on Providence.

16. As far as the causes of creation are concerned, it is easily established that the Triune God is the principal efficient cause. See Gen. 1 and 2, and compare Isaiah 45:12, Jer. 10:11, Ps. 146:6, Acts 4:24, ch. 17:24, Rev. 4:11, where it is shown that God alone is the cause of creation. For it is an external work. Compare Gen. 1:1 and 26, where the plurality of persons is indicated, namely, not only by the plural noun אלהים, but also by the verb and the two plural suffixes in the words: נעשה בצלמנו כדמותנו, "let us make in our image" (as of many), "according to our likeness" (of many). Let the passages be added which we proved above in ch. I, § 30, pp. 51–52, that creation pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit just as much as to the Father. One cause, I say, not three associate causes. For the power of creating of the three persons is one. Cf. Musaeus, Disp. cit. § 15, p. 113. Where he also decides the question: "Whether the three persons are rightly called three creators," in such a way as to warn that this phrase has never been accepted by ecclesiastical writers in their usage of speech, and that those who abstain from it entirely seem to act more safely, even if perhaps it might be thought that it could be defended by the force and meaning of the words.

Luther: "Now Scripture maintains the manner of speaking that the world was created through Christ and by the Father and in the Holy Spirit, all of which has its cause, although it is not sufficiently fathomable nor expressible. Yet, to mention a little, it uses such a manner of speaking in order to indicate how not the Father has the divine essence from the Son, but the Son from the Father, and that the Father is the first original person in the Godhead. Therefore it does not say that Christ made the world through the Father, but the Father through him, so that the Father remains the first person and all things come from him, yet through the Son." (Kirchenpostille. XII, 212.)

ANTITHESIS. Philippi: "If we now impress upon ourselves in what particular manner the individual persons have participated in these outward-going works of the one, whole, and undivided Godhead, the manner of their participation in creation will reveal itself to us through an analogical inference from the manner of their participation in redemption. For just as redemption has proceeded from the Father, who conceived the counsel of redemption from eternity and sent the Son for the realization of the same in time, was mediated through the Son as the organ of objective execution, and became powerful in us in the Holy Spirit as the power of the subjective appropriation of redemption: so we will also have to say in regard to creation that it is accomplished by the Father through the Son and in the Holy Spirit (hence the so-called *particulae diacriticae* εκ, διά, εν), and continues to be accomplished in the form of preservation. The Father is the ultimate ground and source of the Godhead as well as of the creature, the Son is he whose mediation the Father employed in creation, and the Holy Spirit is he in whose power the Father, through the Son, [executed] the counsel of creation in..." PART I. CAP. II.

has translated into actual reality. We see here the efficacy distributed quite evenly among all Three, even if creation appears to be referred to the Father in an original and predominant manner.” (Kirchl. Glaubenslehre. Stuttgart 1857. II, 125. sq.) § 17.

The exemplary cause of creation is constituted by the ideas of individual creatures expressed in the divine intellect. See Gen. 1, where to almost every work Moses prefixes this formula: God said. And it is subjoined: God saw what He had made, and they were very good. By this very thing it is indicated that the forms of the individual things to be produced had been observed by the divine intellect, and that the produced things had truly imitated those forms according to the intention of God, and thus had been approved by God. But this is also the nature of other causes that act through the intellect, that they produce effects in imitation of some form preconceived in the mind; and it is certain thus far that the world, and the things that are in it, were founded not by chance, but by the counsel of God. ANTITHESIS.

Lutherus: ,,Nun behält die Schrift die Weise, dass sie spricht: die Welt sei durch Christum und vom Vater und im Heiligen Geist geschaffen, welches alles seine Ursache hat, wiewohl nicht gnugsam erforschlich, noch aussprechlich. Doch, ein wenig anzuführen, brauchet sie solche Weise darum, also zu reden, dass angezeiget werde, wie nicht der Vater von dem Sohn, sondern der Sohn von dem Vater das göttliche Wesen habe und der Vater die erste ursprüngliche Person in der Gottheit sei. Darum spricht sie nicht, dass Christus habe die Welt durch den Vater gemacht, sondern der Vater durch ihn, dass der Vater die erste Person bleibe und von ihm, doch durch den Sohn, alle Dinge kommen.“ (Kirchenpostille. XII, 212.)

ANTITHESIS. Philippi: ,,Prägen wir nun, in welcher besonderen Art und Weise bei diesen nach aussen gehenden Werken der einen, ganzen und ungetheilten Gottheit sich die einzelnen Personen betheiligt haben, so wird sich uns die Art ihrer Betheiligung an der Schöpfung durch einen analogischen Rückschluss aus der Art ihrer Betheiligung an der Erlösung ergeben. Wie nämlich die Erlösung vom Vater, der den Erlösungsrathschluss von Ewigkeit gefasst und den Sohn zur Verwirklichung desselben in der Zeit gesendet hat, ausgegangen, durch den Sohn als das Organ der objectiven Ausführung vermittelt und im Heiligen Geiste als der Potenz der subjectiven Zueignung der Erlösung in uns kräftig geworden ist: so werden wir auch in Bezug auf die Schöpfung zu sagen haben, dass sie vom Vater durch den Sohn und im Heiligen Geiste (daher die so genannten Particulae diacriticae εκ, διά, kv) vollzogen ist, und in der Form der Erhaltung sich fort und fort vollzieht. Der Vater ist der letzte Grund und Quell wie der Gottheit, so auch der Creatur, der Sohn derjenige, dessen Vermittelung sich der Vater bei der Schöpfung bediente, und der Heilige Geist derjenige, in dessen Kraft der Vater durch den Sohn den Schöpfungsrathschluss in PART. I. CAP. II.

tatsächliche Wirklichkeit umgesetzt hat. Wir sehen hier die Wirksamkeit auf alle Drei ziemlich gleichmässig vertheilt, wenn auch die Schöpfung auf den Yater in ursprünglicher Weise vorherrschend bezogen erscheint.“ (Kirchl. Glaubenslehre. Stuttgart 1857. II, 125. sq.) § 17.

Causam exemplarem creationis a constituunt ideae singularum creaturarum in intellectu divino b expressae. Vid. Gen. 1., ubi singulis fere operibus a Mose praemittitur formula haec: dixit Dem. Et subjungitur: Vidit Deus, quae fecerat, et erant valde bona. Quo ipso indicatur, divino intellectui observatas fuisse singularum rerum producendarum formas, quodque res productae revera imitatae fuerint formas illas ex intentione Dei, atque ita a Deo fuerint approbatae. Sed et alias causarum, quae per intellectum agunt, haec natura est, ut effectus ad imitationem alicujus formae animo praeconceptae producant; mundum vero, et quae in eo sunt, non casu, sed consilio Dei condita fuisse, hactenus certum est.ANTITHESIS.


### On Creation: Kahnisius: “The ‘through’ expresses that He is the mediate cause

Kahnisius: “The ‘through’ expresses that He is the mediate cause; the ‘to,’ that He is the goal of all that is created. But ‘through’ and ‘to’ are only the unfoldings of the ‘in,’ which denotes first the transient, second the immanent cause, i.e., it expresses that Christ is the idea underlying all finite being, from which it follows that Christ is also the goal recapitulating all finite being.” (Die luth. Dogm. Lpz. 1861. P. I, 465.) Not indeed as accidents, such as our ideas are, but they are to be understood θεοπρεπώς. § 18.

We seek the impulsive cause of creation in the goodness of God alone. See Ps. 136:5 et seqq., where, having mentioned the works of creation, the formula is always added: For His mercy (חסדו) endureth forever. Nor will the same be difficult to recognize if we presuppose that the world was founded by the free will of God. Not by any right that creatures might have to their own production and be able to obligate God.

Quenstedtius: “Nor was there any antecedent (προηγούμενη) cause of creation besides the good pleasure of God alone, who communicates Himself not by necessity of nature, but by freedom of will.” (L. c. c. 10. s. 1. th. 12. f. 593.) § 19. We acknowledge no instrumental efficient cause.

Certainly, whether angels or anything else distinct from God could at least be an instrument of His creation, by which something is made out of nothing, is an uncertain and curious question. However, it can by no means be said that there was actually any such cause of this creation of the universe or its parts. The Son of God, through whom all things are said to have been made (having regard, of course, to the order which He has by reason of origin to the person of the Father), is nevertheless not, strictly speaking, an instrument of the Father; since the same power of creating, which is the Father’s, belongs to Him, and not a less noble one. It is permissible to excuse, but not to imitate, the improper mode of speech of certain ecclesiastical doctors. Cf. Mus. Disp. cit. § 2. p. 129.

ANTITHESIS. Kahnis: "The generation of the Son is the beginning of creation, because what is created is created in Him (Col. 1:16), i.e., the Son is the immanent mediate cause of creation." (Die luth. Dogm. Lpz. 1861. P. I, p. 464.) §

20. There is no matter for the creation of immaterial things; the matter of simple bodies is given, but it does not exist before the form; the matter of mixed bodies is to be sought in simple bodies. See above § 3, 4, and 5. Mus. l.c. § 24, 25, pages 139, 140.

Twesten: "The expression ('out of nothing') is taken from the Vulgate, which translates the words in 2 Macc. 7:28, εξ ούκ δντων ίποίησεν αντά ό θεός, as *ex nihilo illa fecit Deus*. — One must not, therefore, think of nothing as, so to speak, the material out of which things were formed; against this, the well-known axiom could rightly be asserted: out of nothing, nothing comes. We must indeed admit the correctness of that principle insofar as the meaning is: nothing comes to be without an efficient cause (in the genus of efficient causes), or: nothing cannot be the material of something (in the genus of material cause taken positively); but we do not admit it if it is intended to deny that God requires no material for creating (in the genus of material cause taken negatively). — *

Ex nihilo* means: not out of something, not out of prior matter; it does not designate matter, but excludes it.

Although this is actually already contained in the concept of creation, there was nevertheless good reason to express it specifically; for precisely thereby, in contrast to the immanence and the disjunction which lie at the foundation of pantheism and dualism, the pure relationship of dependence is designated and asserted...

Whoever considers the world as one with God... can assume no other relationship between God and the world than that which orthodox doctrine assumes between the Father and the Son and... calls generation.

Just as little, however, can one who posits a second... principle of existence outside of God, e.g., eternal matter, conceive of God as the Creator out of nothing; he can only conceive of Him as the World-Orderer or World-Architect. All religions except those which are contained in Holy Scripture or derived from it (in certain points) (the Jewish, Christian, Mohammedan), waver between these opposites, or fall into an even less admissible mixture of them, hylozoism, in which matter with the form...

or the animating principle originally connected, i.e., the Absolute is conceived as being afflicted with an original contradiction that cancels out its essence.” (Lectures on the Dogmatics of the Evangelical Lutheran Church. Vol. 2. Part 1. p. 75 sq.)

Philippi: “The concept of creation has grown solely on the soil of positive divine revelation, and where it is still found outside this sphere (as in Mohammedanism, Rationalism), it is demonstrably borrowed from there.

In pre-Christian paganism, in which the content of natural human reason is expressed unmixed with ideas of revelation, the idea of creation is not found, for all pagan speculation, which is on the one hand the root and on the other the blossom and expression of the religious view of the people, proceeds either from the pantheistic doctrine of a world-evolution or the dualistic one of a world-formation. Either God is regarded as it were as the germ from which the world has unfolded with inner necessity, or it is posited as to its substance as equally eternal with the world-forming principle, so that the primordial matter (νλη), into which the divine intellect (νους) has impressed its ideas, is placed alongside it. In the first case, God is the original substance, the dark primordial ground of the evolving world; in the latter case, the role of world-former or world-architect (δημιουργός) is assigned to him.” (Ecclesiastical Doctrine of Faith. II. p. 225 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Delitzsch: “Therefore, the Holy Scripture does not say that God created the world out of nothing (ex nihilo)... The world, far from having been nothing before its creation, had an ideal existence in God, and its creation was a transition from this ideal existence into a real one... All worldly being is born from the being of God and is not set forth from it in such a way that it would not remain conditioned, supported, and enclosed by him.” (Journal for the Entire Lutheran Theology and Church, 1876, p. 61, 65.) §

21. The mode of this creation of the universe, although congruent with the order of nature, yet entirely different from physical or natural generation, was an argument of infinite divine wisdom and power. Namely, that God first produced the simple principles of mixed bodies, and from these then the mixed ones; again, imperfectly mixed ones, e.g., clouds, earlier, afterwards perfectly mixed ones, and from the census of mixed things first plants, then fish, birds, terrestrial animals—all indeed from that element which most befits their nature, in which they are, live, and are preserved—finally, he produced man, the most perfect of corporeal creatures and the future lord of them, last. See Musaeus, Disp. cit. § 28 sqq. p. 143 sqq.

Quenstedtius: “The action of creation is completed in three stages: 1. the production of raw matter, which was as it were the nursery of the whole universe, done on the first day; 2. the distinction and disposition of simple creatures, accomplished through the first three days; for on the first day he distinguished light from darkness, on the second the lower waters from the upper, with the firmament interposed, and on the third the earth from the water; and 3. the adornment and consummation of the world, perfected in the second three days.”

For 1) physical generation always requires pre-existent matter; here, however, as far as the production of heaven and earth is concerned, matter did not exist before the form, as we saw in § 2. 2) There, a suitable subject and a passive potency not too remote are required, certainly to be altered and successively disposed to receive the form in act; here, however, even mixed bodies were so produced from an unsuitable and indisposed subject that the dispositions to the form and the forms themselves were produced in the matter in an instant. Musaeus, loc. cit., § 49, 50, p. 161, 162, 163.

Scharffius: "Passive potency is either natural or obediential. Natural potency is a real inclination implanted by nature toward some act, which can be perfected by a natural agent. Thus, in a seed there is a natural passive potency, so that from it, through nature, an animated body may be produced. Thus, according to natural potency, a hazel tree is made from a nut, and a tall oak is made from an acorn... Obediential potency is that which, beyond its own nature, can be subjected to the efficacy of another, so that an act may result therefrom. It is so called by analogy, because it as it were obeys an external agent—that is, it does not sufficiently resist. This potency is not so much in the passive subject as in the agent, namely, when the power of acting is so strong that it can produce something even from that which of itself is not suitable. Thus, it is said that children of Abraham can be made from stones; where, however, that potency for the children of Abraham is not in the stones." (Metaph. p. 82, sqq.)

This is evident from what has been said, and it must be repeated what we said in § 17, that God created all things by speaking, or by the command of His will, directed by the practical knowledge of His intellect, applied His effective power to working; or, as others teach, that God, by willing, or by the force of the act of will itself, which has the nature of productive power, effected in the work of creation what He willed. Compare what we said about the power of God in the preceding chapter, I, § 25, p. 41; Musaeus, loc. cit., § 51, p. 263, 264, 265. §

22. But in order that the world might be able to endure, God produced simple bodies on the condition that they should never be completely corrupted; but to mixed bodies, which have a life subject to corruption, He communicated the power of generating or multiplying themselves for the preservation of the species, whence He also produced two individuals of each sex of every living species at the same time. To the first man also, He immediately added a female companion, and implanted in them the power of generating. The heaven is indeed incorruptible, to be destroyed only by the power of God. The elements, however, although, insofar as they enter into the constitution of mixed bodies, they are subject to mutations, yet in themselves they never perish entirely; but mixed bodies, which are corrupted, are resolved into the elements of which they consist. Thus God created the herb yielding seed, and the tree yielding fruit after its kind, whose seed is in itself, etc. Gen. 1:11, 12, 29. Thus, blessing the aquatic and flying creatures, He said: "Be fruitful and multiply," verse 22. PART I. CHAP. II.

Dogm. Lpz. 1861. P. I, 465.) Non quidem ut accidentia, quales sunt nostrae ideae, sed Φεοπρεπώς intelligendae.§ 18.

Causam impulsivam creationis in bonitate a Dei sola b quaerimus. Vid. P8. 136, 5. et seqq., ubi memoratis operibus creationis semper additur formula: Quoniam in saeculum benignitas ejus (חסדו). Neque difficulter idem cognoscetur, si praesupponamus, voluntate Dei libera mundum fuisse conditum. Non jure quodam, quod creaturae ad sui productionem haberent ac Deum obligare possent.Quenstedtius: ,,Neque causa creationis προηγούμενη ulla fuit praeter solius Dei non ex necessitate naturae, sed ex libertate voluntatis se communicantis beneplacitum.“ (L. c. c. 10. s. 1. th. 12. f. 593.) § 19.

Causam instrumentalem efficientem nullam a agnoscimus.

Sane, an angeli aut quicquid aliud a Deo distinctum est saltem possit esse instrumentum creationis ejus, qua aliquid fit ex nihilo, incerta et curiosa quaestio est. Fuisse autem revera ejusmodi causam aliquam creationis hujus universi aut partium ejus neutiquam dici potest. Filius Dei, per quem omnia facta dicuntur (habito nimirum respectu ad ordinem, quem ratione originis ad personam Patris habet), non tamen proprie loquendo est instrumentum Patris; cum potentia creandi eadem, quae Patris est, non autem ignobilior ei competat. Impropriam vero locutionem doctorum quorundam ecclesiasticorum excusare quidem, sed non imitari licet. Conf. Mus. Disp. cit. § 2. p. 129.

ANTITHE SIS. Kahnisius: ,,Die Zeugung des Sohnes ist der Anfang der Schöpfung, weil, was geschaffen ist, in ihm geschaffen ist (Kol. 1, 16.) h. der Sohn die immanente Mittelursache der Schöpfung ist.“ (Die luth. Dogm. Lpz. 1861. P. I, p. 464.)§

20. Materia creationis rerum immaterialium nulla est; corporum simplicium materia datur, sed non existens ante formam; corporum mixtorum materia in corporibus simplicibus quaerenda est. Vid. supra § 3. 4. et 5. Mus. 1. c. § 24. 25. pag. 139. 140.

Twestenius: ״Der Ausdruck (,aus Nichts’) ist aus der Vulgata genommen, welche 2 Macc. 7, 28. die Worte: εξ ούκ δντων ίποίησεν αντά ό θεός, durch ex nihilo illa fecit Deus, übersetzt. — Man darf also nicht etwa das Nichts als gleichsam den Stoff denken, woraus die Dinge gebildet worden; dagegen liesse sich mit Recht das bekannte Axiom geltend machen: aus Nichts wird Nichts. Wir müssen nämlich die Riehtigkeit jenes Grundsatzes zugeben, inwiefern der Sinn ist: Nichts werde ohne wirkende Ursache (in genere causarum efficientium), oder: Das Nichts könne nicht der Stoff von etwas sein (in genere causae materialis positive sumtae); wir geben ihn aber nicht zu, wenn dadurch geleugnet werden soll, dass Gott zum Schaffen keines Stoffs bedürfe (in genere causae materialis negative sumtae). —

Ex nihilo bedeutet: non ex aliquo, non ex priori materia; non designat materiam, sed excludit.

Obgleich dies aber eigentlich in dem Begriffe der Schöpfung schon liegt, so hatte man doch guten Grund, es noch besonders auszudrücken; denn eben dadurch wird, im Gegensatz der Immanenz und der Disjunction, welche dem Pantheismus und dem Dualismus zu Grunde liegen, das reine Verhältniss der Dependenz bezeichnet und behauptet. . .

Wer die Welt als Eins mit Gott betrachtet..., kann zwischen Gott und Welt kein anderes Verhältniss annehmen, als was die orthodoxe Lehre zwischen Vater und Sohn annimmt und. . . Zeugung nennt.

Ebenso wenig kann aber auch derjenige, der ausser Gott ein zweites. . . Princip des Daseins setzt, z. B. eine ewige Materie, Gott als den Schöpfer aus Nichts, er kann ihn nur als den Weltordner oder Weltbaumeister begreifen. Alle Religionen ausser denjenigen, die in der heiligen Schrift enthalten oder aus ihr (in gewissen Puncten) abgeleitet sind (der jüdisehen, christlichen, muhamedanischen), schwanken zwischen diesen Gegensätzen, oder verfallen auf eine noch weniger statthafte Mischung derselben, den Hylozoismus, in welchem die Materie mit dem formenBaieri Comp. ed. Walther. II. 7 PART. I. CAP. II.

den oder belebenden Princip ursprünglich verbunden d. h. das Absolute mit einem ursprünglichen, sein Wesen aufhebenden Gegensätze behaftet gedacht wird.“ (Vorlesungen über die Dogmatik der ev.luth. Kirche. Band 2. Abtheil. 1. p. 75. sq.)

Philippi: ,,Der Begriff der Schöpfung ist allein auf dem Boden der positiven Gottesoffenbarung erwachsen, und wo er sich noch ausserhalb dieser Sphäre findet (wie im Muhamedanismus, Rationalismus), ist er nachweisbar von dort entlehnt.

Im vorchristlichen Heidenthume, in welchem der Inhalt der natürlichen Menschenvernunft unvermischt mit Offenbarungsideen ausgeprägt ist, findet sich die Idee der Schöpfung nicht, denn alle heidnische Speculation, welche einerseits Wurzel, andrerseits Blüthe und Ausdruck der religiösen Volksanschauung ist, geht entweder von der pantheistischen Lehre einer Weltentwickelung oder der dualistischen einer Weltbildung aus. Entweder wird Gott gleichsam als der Keim betrachtet, aus welchem heraus sich die Welt mit innerer Nothwendigkeit entfaltet hat, oder sie wird ihrem Stoffe nach gleich ewig mit dem weltbildenden Principe gesetzt, so dass dem göttlichen Verstände (vröf) die uranfängliche Materie (νλη), welcher derselbe seine Ideen eingebildet habe, beigeordnet wird. Im ersten Falle ist Gott die ursprüngliche Substanz, der dunkle Urgrund der sich evolvirenden Welt; im letzteren Falle ist ihm die Rolle des Weltbildners oder Weltbaumeisters (δημιουργός) übertragen.“ (Kirchl. Glaubenslehre. II. p. 225. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Delitzschius: ,,Darum sagt die heilige Schrift nicht, dass Gott die Welt aus dem Nichts (ex nihilo) geschaffen habe. . . Die Welt, weit entfernt, vor ihrer Erschaffung nichts gewesen zu sein, hatte ein ideales Dasein in Gott, und ihre Erschaffung war Ueberführung aus diesem idealen Dasein in reales. . . Alles weltliche Sein ist aus dem Sein Gottes geboren und nicht dermassen aus diesem herausgesetzt, dass es nicht von ihm bedingt, getragen und umschlossen bliebe.“ (Zeitschr. f. d. gesammte luth. Th. u. K. 1876. p. 61. 65.) §

21. Modus creationis hujus universi, etsi ordini naturae congruus,a tamen a physica aut naturali generatione plane diversus,b infinitae sapientiae ac potentiae divinae argumentum fuit.a Nempe quod Deus primum simplicia, mixtorum corporum principia, et ex his deinde mixta produxit; rursus imperfecte mixta, v. g. nubes, prius, postea perfecte mixta, et ex censu mixtorum primum plantas, deinde pisces, volucres, animantia terrestria, omnia quidem ex eo elemento, quod naturae illorum maxime convenit, in quo sunt, vivunt et conservantur, denique hominem, creaturarum corporearum perfectissimam, earumque dominum futurum, ultimo produxit. Vid. Mus. Disp. cit. § 28. sqq. p. 143. sqq.

Quenstedtius: ״Creationis actio tribus absolvitur gradibus: 1. rudis materiae, quae totius universi quasi seminarium fuit, productione, primo die facta; 2. creaturarum simplicium distinctione et dispositione, per tres dies priores peracta; nam primo die lucem a tenebris, altero aquas inferiores a superioribus, interposito firmamento, et tertio terram ab aqua distinxit; et 3. mundi exornatione et consummatione, altero triduo perfecta.“

Nam 1) physica generatio semper requirit materiam prasexistentem; hic autem, quod ad coeli et terrae productionem attinet, materia non extitit ante formam; ut vidimus § 2. 2) Illic requiritur subjectum habile et potentia passiva non nimis remota, alteranda certe et successive disponenda ad formam actu recipiendam; hic vero etiam corpora mixta ex subjecto inhabili et indisposito ita sunt producta, ut dispositiones ad formam et formae ipsae in materia in instanti producerentur. Mu». 1. c. § 49. 50. p. 161. 162. 163.

Scharffius: ,,Potentia passiva est vel naturalis, vel obedientialis. Potentia naturalis est realis inclinatio a natura insita ad aliquem actum, qui ab agente naturali potest perfici. Sic in semine est potentia naturalis passiva, ut ex eo per naturam producatur corpus animatum. Sic juxta potentiam naturalem e nuce fit corylus, de glande fit ardua quercus. . . Potentia obedientialis est, quae praeter suam naturam alterius efficaciae subjici potest, ut exinde flat actus. Dicitur ita per αναλογίαν, quod agenti externo quasi obediat, h. e., non resistat sufficienter. Quae potentia non tam est in subjecto passibili, quam in agente, nempe quando virtus agendi tam valida est, ut etiam ex illo, quod de se non est habile, possit aliquid producere. Sic dicitur posse fieri ex lapidibus filios Abrahae; ubi tamen illa potentia ad filios Abrahae non est in lapidibus.“ (Metaph. p. 82. sqq.)

Patet hoc ex modo dictis, ac repetendum est, quod diximus § 17., Deum omnia dioendo creasse, seu imperio voluntatis suae intellectus scientia practica directae potentiam effectivam applicasse ad operandum; seu, ut alii docent, Deum volendo, seu ex vi ipsius actus voluntatis potentiae productivae rationem habentis effecisse in opere creationis, quae voluit. Conf., quae diximus de potentia Dei cap. praeced. I. § 25. p. 41.; Mus. 1. c. § 51. p. 263. 264. 265.§

22. Ut autem perennare posset mundus, produxit Deus corpora simplicia quidem ea conditione, ut nunquam penitus corrumpantur;a mixtis vero, quae vitam corruptioni obnoxiam habent, vim generandi aut multiplicandi se communicavit b ad conservationem speciei, unde et cuj usque speciei animantis duo utriusque sexus individua simul produxit.c Homini quoque primo feminam sociam mox adjunxit, et vim generandi iisdem indidit.d Coelum sane incorruptibile est, non nisi per potentiam Dei destruendum. Elementa vero, etsi, quatenus mixtorum corporum constitutionem ingrediuntur, mutationibus sint obnoxia, tamen secundum se tota nunqaam intereunt; mixta autem, quae corrumpuntur, in elementa, ex quibus constant, resolvuntur. Sic Deus creavit herbam seminificantem semen, arborem quoque facientem fructum speciei suae, cujus semen in ea, etc. Gen. 1, 11. 12. 29. Sic aquatilibus et volatilibus benedicens dixit: Crescite et multiplicamini, vers. 22. PART. I. CAP. II.


### On Creation: In opposition to the other animals, Adam alone is said for some time not to…

In opposition to the other animals, Adam alone is said for some time not to have found a helper like himself, Gen. 2:20. See Gen. 1:27, where male and female are mentioned, and verse 28, where mention is made of the blessing by whose power they could multiply themselves and fill the earth.

But whether, just as brutes have the power of multiplying themselves through generation—by which, with the general concurrence of God, they produce the form and thus the whole animal, both through the seed and by means of the altered and disposed seed—man is likewise generated from man as to his soul as well as his body with only the general concurrence of God by the power of the divine blessing; or whether, in human generation, the effect is too noble to be produced by men (the parents) in its entirety with only the general concurrence of God (namely, because the rational soul is by its nature immaterial and demands a mode of production congruent with its mode of being, namely, that it be produced independently of matter or *ex nihilo*, for which secondary causes with the general concurrence of God do not suffice), and thus, by the power of that blessing, God, as the primary cause, concurs with a special influx where secondary causes fail and supplies the deficiency of the generators—this is an ancient and difficult question, regarding which we prefer to *ἐπέχειν* [withhold judgment], in accordance with what we said concerning the examples of the blessed Luther, J. Wigand, A. Musculus, M. Chemnitz, and others, in Proleg. cap. I. ad § 34. not. c. Vol. I. p. 67.

For it must be noted that the praised doctors did not speak of a special mode of the propagation of the soul by *tradux*, but of the doubts regarding the very opinion of the creation of the soul and the opinion of its propagation, which was already then coming to be known by the name of *tradux*, as distinct from creation.

Here, I say, or when it is asked whether the soul is derived from the souls of men or is produced extrinsically by God, they not so much thought as asserted that *τὸ ἐπέχειν* could rightly have a place.

And Luther indeed, as Musculus reports (LL. CC. p. 90), follows Augustine, who disputes much here (both for the opinion of the creation of the soul and for the other of its origin by *tradux*) and says that neither side is to be affirmed here, but that thought is to be suspended; although (he says) he inclines more to the opinion that the soul arises from *tradux*, yet he does not wish to assert it with certainty.

Luther continues in the same place: "I indeed, for my own belief, feel that the soul is from *tradux*; but let us know that in the church one must speak with reverence and the fear of God, and fear God, in whose sight we speak. It is not easy to establish that which we do not know."

From these things which follow in the cited place, it is manifest that the blessed Luther gave responses not only to the arguments which are opposed to the opinion of *tradux*, but also to those which are brought forward for that opinion.

Wigand, however, when he had brought forward arguments first for the opinion of the creation of the soul, and then for the opinion of *tradux*, closes the discourse thus, p. 38: "But whither am I carried? Since, however, this whole matter is still obscure, and perhaps God by a singular counsel has deferred that question until the other life, and there is no danger to the soul from it, therefore it is free to leave it in the middle."

Luther: "Those who think that vice and sin adhere to nature because it was made *ex nihilo* are not far from insulting the Creator, since such a thing is not in the angels, the sun, the stars, and the whole heaven, etc. Those who have thought that the soul is from *tradux* seem not to have thought things entirely alien to the Scriptures. Indeed, they will more easily defend the propagation of original sin than those who think otherwise, since (with Augustine as author) original sin also im..."

let there be piety. Augustine confesses that he is ignorant of which opinion is more certain and true, nor has there been anyone thus far who has determined that question. For it is sufficiently clear that those who follow Jerome from Ps. 33: "He who fashioned their hearts individually," have nothing to do with the matter. But the determinations of the Pope and his synagogue, we hold to be a most just cause for extermination or execration... In this matter, reason and the poet would better befit us, saying: "The offspring follows its father." It is certain that offspring, by common law, reflect not only the face but also the character and disposition of their parents. So there is nothing to the saying: The intellective soul is infused by creating and created by infusing. Who has proven this, or who will forbid the same from being said of every other soul? And they will make the question more difficult: how is God not unjust, who joins a pure soul to flesh and pollutes it from the outside? Although a Christian may, without danger, be ignorant of this matter along with St. Augustine and the universal Church, one must nevertheless abstain from that rashness which could verge on the insult of the Creator. Since it is certain that God also created the angels from nothing, who were to live an eternal life without corruption; what difficulty could hinder God from being able to bring forth an intellective soul both from nothing and from corrupt seed, just as He brings forth an ear of corn blighted by mildew from a blighted grain, so that many other defective things also proceed from defective ones?" (Disp. th. de distinctione personarum in Divinitate. 1545. Vol. I of all works. Jena, 1579. fol. 536.)

Quenstedtius: "The question is not: 1. Whether the soul is propagated by way of corporeal succession, as if, for instance, soul were generated from soul, just as body arises from body. Nor 2. whether it is propagated by way of transfusion, as if it were generated from some transfused seed. Nor 3. does it come into question whether, if the soul is generated, it is elicited from the potentiality of matter or even separated or made dependently upon matter. But 4. the question is whether the soul is immediately created by God and infused into a prepared body, or whether it is propagated from parents by way of transmission through the power of divine blessing... It can be known by us ἀποφατικῶς (negatively) rather than καταφατικῶς (positively)... Rightly does the blessed Hunnius say in his lectures on Gen. ch. 2: 'As God does not inspire a soul into Eve, but produces the whole from the whole Adam, living from living, in soul and body, so now through generation the whole is propagated from the whole human; therefore, just as body is propagated from body, so the soul is propagated from soul, like light from a kindled light.'" (L. c. c. 12. s. 2. q. 3. f. 741. sq. 745.)

Gerhardus: "We leave the mode of propagation to be inquired into by philosophers, since we have not yet seen it set forth in the Scriptures; meanwhile, we firmly hold the opinion concerning the propagation of souls, for the propagation of souls is not to be denied for the reason that the mode of propagation is not conspicuous. It is, as it were, a solemn rule in divine mysteries that Scripture sets forth the thing itself, but remains silent on the mode." (L. de imag. Dei § 117.)

Quenstedtius: "The thesis is proven: ... 6. from the absurdities. 1. If it be posited that the soul is immediately created by God, either original sin must be entirely denied, or God cannot be freed from injustice, both of which are absurd; for the souls that are created and infused into the body are either pure or impure; if impure, God is the author of sin; if pure, then God is unjust, who puts pure and holy souls into an impure body... 2. It follows that a human does not generate a whole human or the whole composite, but only a part of him; but he who does not give the form of a human does not generate a human; for a human without form, i.e., the soul, is not a human. 3. That the father is not the physical cause of the son, but only a moral one, i.e., a non-cause. For a moral cause is only equivocally a cause... 4. That children do not receive from their parents a soul, but only a body, and indeed an inanimate body. 5. That the generating father does not communicate his essence to the son. 6. That Christ assumed only flesh, not our soul, and thus redeemed only the body, not the soul." (L. c. f. 745. sq.) PART I. CHAP. II.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: ... 3. Of certain fathers, such as Origen in his book περὶ ἀρχῶν, ch. 7, and Gregory of Nyssa in his book *On the Making of Man*, ch. 28 and 29, and likewise of the rabbis, who teach that all human souls were created together with the angels on the first day and existed with God, and from there are sent daily into bodies... 4. Of Jerome, who contends for the creation of the soul against Rufinus and elsewhere. 5. Of Pelagius, Coelestius, and the Pelagians, mentioned in Augustine, Epist. 156, who champion the immediate creation of the soul and therefore maintain that it is immune to the stain of sin. 6. Of almost all the Scholastics and Papists, namely Lombard, Thomas, and Bellarmine in Book 4 *On the Loss of Grace and the State of Sin*, ch. 2 (where he says: 'We subscribe to the opinion which teaches that for individual men, individual souls are not created from propagation, but are then first created from nothing and infused when the fetuses are conceived in the wombs of their mothers and prepared for animation.') ... 7. Of most Calvinists, who embrace the opinion concerning the creation and infusion of the soul... 8. Of Brentius, who almost alone among the genuine Lutheran theologians explicitly asserts the creation of the soul... 9. Of the Innovators, such as D. G. Calixtus, who likewise maintain that the rational soul is produced by God immediately through creation from nothing and infused into the body, yet in such a way that the generating parents are a kind of occasion, demanding the creation of that soul." (L. c. f. 743 sq.) § 23. The ultimate end of creation is the glory of the divine wisdom, goodness, and power; the intermediate end is the utility of man. Or, that through the creatures of God, His goodness, wisdom, and power might become known, insofar as man can and ought to be stirred up to celebrate that goodness, wisdom, and power from the consideration of them. See Ps. 19:1; 104:1-2; 136:1 ff.; 148:1 ff. See Gen. 1: 28. B. Gerhard, in *Disput. Isag.* XI, Sect. VI, *de Creat.* § 6, says: "God would not have commanded other things to be made, had He not decreed to make man." For some creatures serve for the necessity of human life, others for its delight, some as remedies for diseases, others as safeguards of health, some as aids for conducting affairs, others for example and imitation. Cf. Lactantius, *de Ira Dei* c. XIII, and Damascene, *L. II. de Orthod. Fide* c. X; b. Mus. *Disp. cit.* § 56, 57, p. 167, 168. And thus, some not incorrectly maintain that the end (the *for whom*), for whose benefit all things were created, is man: that the macrocosm was founded for the sake of the microcosm. § 24. Creation is defined as the action of the Triune God *ad extra*, by which God, moved by His goodness, produced this world and all that is in it; first, indeed, simple bodies from no pre-existing matter, then from simple bodies, as from unsuitable and indisposed matter, mixed bodies, and indeed even independently of all matter

PART I. CAP. III. He produced immaterial substances, in such a way that He powerfully brought forth each of these, according to the idea of His own mind, by the sole command of His will, and completed the whole work in the space of six days, for the glory of His wisdom, power, and goodness, and for the benefit of men. See § 16, p. 95, concerning the efficient cause. See § 18, p. 96, concerning the impulsive cause. See § 6 ff., p. 79 ff., concerning the series of the works of creation. See § 17, p. 96, concerning the exemplary cause. See § 21, p. 98, concerning the mode of creation. See § 23, p. 102, concerning the end of creation.

Latin:

In oppositione ad animalia caetera solus Adam dicitur non invenisse aliquamdiu adjutorem similem sui, Gen. 2, 20. Vid. Gen. 1, 27., ubi masculi et feminae, et vers. 28., ubi benedictionis, cujus vi multiplicare se ac terram replere possent, mentio fit.

Utrum vero, sicut bruta habent vim sese multiplicandi per generationem, qua cum concursu Dei generali cum semen, tum mediante semine alterato ac disposito formam atque adeo animal totum producunt, ita vi benedictionis divinae homo ab homine quoad animam aeque atque corpus cum concursu Dei tantum universali generetur; an autem in generatione humana effectus nobilior sit, quam ut per homines (genitores) secundum se totum cum solo concursu Dei generali produci possit (nempe quod anima rationalis sua natura immaterialis sit ac modum productionis modo essendi congruum postulet, nempe ut producatur independenter a materia seu ex nihilo, ad quod causae secundae cum concursu Dei generali non sufficiant), adeoque vi benedictionis illius Deus, tanquam causa prima, ibi, ubi causae secundae deficiunt, influxu speciali concurrat et defectum generantium suppleat, antiqua ac difficilis quaestio est, in qua malumus Ιπέχειν juxta id, quod diximus de exemplis bb. Lutheri, J. Wigandi, A. Musculi, M. Chemnitii et aliorum, in Proleg. cap. I. ad § 34. not. c. Vol. I. p. 67.

Notandum enim est, laudatos doctores non esse locutos de modo speciali propagationis animae per traducem, sed de dubitationibus quoad ipsam sententiam de creatione animae et sententiam de propagatione ejus creationi contradistincta, quae nomine traducis jam tunc veniebat.

Hic, inquam, seu quando quaeritur, utrum anima de animabus hominum derivetur, an extrinsecus a Deo producatur, τό ίπέχειν locum recte habere posse, non tam putarunt, quam asseruerunt.

Ac Lutherus quidem, referente Musculo LL. CC. p. 90., Augustinum sequitur, qui multa hic disputat (pro sententia de creatione animae et pro altera de origine ejus per traducem) et dicit, neutram partem esse hic affirmandam, sed esse suspendendam cogitationem; quanquam (ait) magis inclinat in eam sententiam, ut ex traduce oriatur anima, et tamen non vult certo asserere.

Pergit Lutherus apud eundem: Ego quidem pro mea credulitate sentio, quod anima sit ex traduce; sed sciamus, quod in ecclesia loquendum sit cum reverentia et timore Dei et vereri Deum, in cujus conspectu loquimur. Non facile est statuendum hoc, quod ignoramus.

Ex his autem, quae 1. c. sequuntur, manifestum est, b. Lutherum non solum ad argumenta, quae sententiae de traduce opponuntur, sed ad ea quoque, quae pro sententia illa afferuntur, responsiones dedisse.

Wigandus autem, cum argumenta primum pro sententia de creatione animae, deinde pro sententia de traduce attulisset, ita discursum claudit, p. 38.: Sed quo feror? Cum autem ista res tota adhuc sit obscura, et fortasse Deus singulari consilio eam quaestionem usque in alteram vitam distulerit nihilque inde periculi sit animae, itaque in medio relinquere liberum est.

Lutherus: ,,Qui putant, vitium et peccatum in natura haerere, quod sit ex nihilo facta, parum absunt a contumelia creatoris, cum tale non sit in angelis, sole, stellis et toto coelo etc. Qui cogitaverunt, animam ex traduce esse, videntur non penitus aliena a Scripturis sensisse. Imo facilius defendent propagationem originalis peccati, quam il, qui aliter sentiunt, cum (Augustino auctore) peccatum originale etiam im

pietas sit. Augustinus fatetur, sese ignorare, utra sententia certior et verior sit, nec fuit hactenus, qui eam quaestionem determinaverit. Nam quod Hieronymum sequuntur alii ex Ps. 33.: ,Qui finxit singulatim corda eorum‘, nihil ad rem facere, satis patet. Determinationes vero papae et suae synagogae, pro exterminatione seu execratione justissima causa habemus. . . Melius in hac re deceret ratio et poeta dicens: ,Patrem sequitur sua proles.‘ Constat, prolem lege communi non modo faciem, sed et mores et ingenium parentum referre. Ut nihil sit, quod dicitur: Anima intellectiva creando infunditur et infundendo creatur. Quis hoc probavit, aut quis prohibebit, simile posse dici de omni alia anima? Et difficiliorem facient quaestionem: quomodo Deus non sit iniquus, qui animam puram copulet carni et ab extrinseco polluat. Quamvis istam rem sine periculo Christianus ignoret cum s. Augustino et universa ecclesia, abstinendum tamen est ab ea temeritate, quae vergere possit in contumeliam creatoris. Cum certum sit, Deum etiam angelos ex nihilo creasse victuros aeterna vita sine corruptione; quae difficultas Deum moretur, ne animam intellectivam tum ex nihilo, tum ex semine corrupto possit educere, sicut spicam uredine vitiatam educit ex grano vitiato, ut et multa alia vitiosa ex vitiosis proveniunt?“ (Disp. th. de distinctione personarum in Divinitate. 1545. Tom. primus omn. opp. Jenae, 1579. fol. 536.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Non est quaestio: 1. An anima propagetur per modum corporeae successionis, quasi sci. anima ab anima generetur, sicut corpus ex corpore oritur. Nec 2. an propagetur per modum transfusionis, ut veluti ex transfuso quodam semine generetur. Nec 3. in quaestionem venit, an, si generetur anima, a potentia materiae educatur vel etiam decidatur aut dependenter a materia fiat. Sed 4. quaeritur, an anima immediate a Deo creetur et corpori praeparato infundatur, an vero per traducem vi benedictionis divinae a parentibus propagetur. . . Άποφατικώς potius a nobis cognosci id potest, quam καταφατικως... Recte b. Hunnius in praelect. c. 2. Gen., ,Ut Evae, inquit, Deus non inspirat animam, sed totam ex toto Adamo, vivam ex vivo, anima et corpore producit, sic nunc per generationem ex toto homine propagatur totus; ut ergo corpus a corpore, sic anima propagatur ab anima tamquam lumen a lumine accenso.‘ “ (L. c. c. 12. s. 2. q. 3. f. 741. sq. 745.)

Gerhardus: ,,Nos modum propagationis inquirendum philosophis relinquimus, quippe quem in Scripturis expositum esse nondum vidimus; interim sententiam de propagatione animarum arcte tenemus, neque enim ob id neganda animarum propagatio, quia modus propagationis non est conspicuus. Mysteriis divinis hoc veluti solenne est, ut rem ipsam eorum Scriptura exponat, modum reticeat.“ (L. de imag. Dei § 117.)

Quenstedtius: ״Probatur thesis: . . . 6. ex absurdis. 1. Si statuatur, animam a Deo immediate creari, vel peccatum originis negandum plane fuerit, vel Deus ab injustitia liberari non poterit, quorum utrumque absurdum; animae enim, quae creantur, et corpori infunduntur, vel sunt purae vel impurae; si impurae, Deus peccati auctor est; si purae, ergo Deus injustus est, qui puras et sanctas animas corpori impuro immittit. . . 2. Sequitur, hominem non generare hominem totum sive totum compositum, sed tantum ejus partem; qui vero non dat formam hominis, non generat hominem; nam homo sine forma, h. e., anima, non est homo. 3. Patrem non esse causam physicam filii, sed tantum moralem, h. e. non-causam. Causa enim moralis tantum aequivoce causa est. . . 4. A parentibus liberos habere non animam, sed tantum corpus et quidem corpus inanimatum. 5. Patrem generantem non communicare filio suam essentiam. 6. Christum solam carnem, non animam nostram assumpsisse, et sic solum corpus, non animam redemisse.“ (L. c. f. 745. sq.) PART. I. CAP. Π.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: ... 3. Quorundam patrum, ut Origenis lib. περί αρχών c. 7. et Gregorii Nysseni lib. de opificio hominis c. 28. et 29., itemque rabbinorum, tradentium, animas humanas cum angelis omnes primo die simul conditas esse et apud Deum existere atque inde in corpora quotidie mitti. . . 4. Hieronymi, qui pro creatione animae adversus Ruffinum et alibi certat. 5. Pelagii, Coelestini et Pelagianorum apud Augustinum ep. 156., immediatam creationem animae propugnantium, ac proinde eam peccati labe immunem esse statuentium. 6. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum fere omnium, nominatim Lombardi, Thomae, Bellarmini lib. 4. de amissione gratiae et statu peccati c. 2. (ubi inquit: ,Nos subscribimus sententiae, quae docet, hominibus singulis animas singulas non ex propagine, sed ex nihilo tunc primum creari atque infundi, cum in uteris matrum foetus concepti atque ad animationem praeparati sunt.‘) ... 7. Calvinianorum plerorumque, ... sententiam de animae creatione et infusione amplectentium... 8. Brentii, qui solus fere ex γνησίως Lutheranis theologis creationem animae diserte asserit.. . 9. Novatorum, ut D. G. Calixti, itidem statuentium, animam rationalem a Deo immediate per creationem ex nihilo produci et corpori immitti, ita tamen, ut parentes generantes sint quaedam velut occasio, exigens creationem illius animae.“ (L. c. f. 743. sq.) § 23. Finis creationis ultimus est gloria sapientiae, bonitatis et potentiae divinae;a intermedius hominis utilitas.b Seu ut per creaturas Dei bonitas, sapientia et potentia innotesceret, quatenus ex consideratione earum bomo ad celebrandam bonitatem, sapientiam et potentiam excitari potest ac debet. Vid. Ps. 19, 1. 104, 1. et 2. 136, 1. et seqq. 148, 1. et seqq. Vid. Gen. 1, 28. B. Gerhardus in Disput. Isag. XI. Sect. VI. de Creat. § 6. dicit: Caetera Deus non jussisset fieri, nisi decrevisset hominem facere. Aliquae enim creaturae ad humanae vitae necessitatem, aliae ad ejus delectationem, quaedam ut remedia morborum, alia ut praesidia sanitatis, quaedam ut adminicula rerum gerendarum, aliae ad exemplum et imitationem serviunt. Conf. Lactant, de Ira Dei c. XIII. et Damasc. L. II. de Orthod. Fide c. X., b. Mus. Disp. cit. § 56. 57. p. 167. 168. Atque ita non male quidam statuunt, finem ώ sive cui omnia in bonum sunt creata, esse hominem: macrocosmum in gratiam microcosmi esse conditum. § 24. Definitur creatio, quod sit actio Dei trinunius a ad extra, qua Deus, bonitate sua b impulsus, mundum hunc, et quae in eo sunt omnia,c primum quidem corpora simplicia ex nulla praejacente materia, deinde ex corporibus simplicibus, tanquam inhabili et indisposita materia, corpora mixta, quin etiam independenter ab omni materia

PART. I. CAP. in. substantias immateriales produxit, ita ut quodlibet borum, juxta ideam d mentis suae, solo voluntatis imperio potenter e efficeret et sex dierum spatio totum opus absolveret, ad f sapientiae, potentiae et bonitatis suae gloriam atque hominum utilitatem. Vid. § 16. p. 95. de causa efficiente. Vid. § 18. p. 96. de causa impulsiva. Vid. § 6. sqq. p. 79. sqq. de serie operum creationis. Vid. § 17. p. 96. de causa exemplari. Vid. § 21. p. 98. de modo creationis. Vid. § 23. p. 102. de fine creationis.


## 5 Concerning Angels

Chapter III. CONCERNING ANGELS. § 1. Among the creatures that all participate in the divine goodness, those are the most perfect which Scripture calls angels. And thus the reason for the order of the doctrine is evident. Thus in the Epistle to the Hebrews 1:4, when it had to be proven that Christ is more excellent than every creature, it is said that He is better than the angels. It is necessary, therefore, that no creature be given that is more perfect than these. §

2. Although the name "angel" is a name of office and denotes a minister or legate; yet by this appellation is specifically signified a certain species of creatures, distinct by their very nature from men and from all other creatures.

Just as among the Hebrews the word מלאך, whose obsolete root לאך nevertheless survives among the Ethiopians and has the meaning of "to send." See Golius in Lex. Arab. fol. 143, Hottinger, Smegm. Orient, c. 5, p. 88, and c. 7, p. 164.

The Greek literature, however, from which the Latin name also comes, is more manifest. Whence Hilary also says that Scripture, when it calls heavenly spirits angels, testifies to the meaning of the office, Lib. V. de Trinit. And Augustine, Enarr. in Ps. 104: "Angel," he says, "is a name of office, not of nature." See blessed Musaeus, Disp. VI. de Angelis § 2, p. 69. PART I. CAP. III.

Whence also any men whatsoever are called by this name, acting in the place of ambassadors. See Gen. 18, 3. 6. James 2, 25. Especially the heralds or ministers of the divine word, e.g., various prophets, 2 Chron. 36, 15. 16. Specifically Haggai by himself, ch. 1, 13; the priests, Mal. 2, 7; John, the forerunner of the Messiah, Mal. 3, 1 and Matt. 11, 10. Indeed, Christ himself, κατ’ ἐξοχήν, is the angel of the covenant, Mal. 3, 1, namely, sent to consummate and announce the covenant of grace initiated by God with men, sent εἰς τὸ βεβαιῶσαι τὰς ἐπαγγελίας τῶν πατέρων, to confirm the promises of the fathers, Rom. 15, 8. (Although he himself was also given as לִבְרִית עָם, for a covenant of the people, Isaiah 42, 6, as the mediator of the New Testament, καινῆς διαθήκης μεσίτης, Heb. 9, 15, since by his blood the covenant was struck between God and the people.) The Son of God, however, was sent by the Father, not as an inferior by a superior, but on account of a special operation, through which he began to be somewhere in a new way or with a new effect, with a relation conceived toward God the Father, from whom he proceeded through eternal generation. Mus. l. c. § 5. p. 171.

Quenstedtius: "As often and wherever either the name of Jehovah or a divine attribute or work and divine worship is attributed to an angel appearing to the patriarchs and other believers in the O.T., there is to be understood not some created angel, but the uncreated one, namely the Son of God, the prince of the heavenly host, the Lord of all angels, since he did not once, in an ineffable condescension, appear to the fathers in the O.T. in some assumed visible form and thus preluded his future incarnation. — The apparition seems to be not a real one strictly so called, but only an objective action. For what else is 'to appear' than to be seen or to be viewed? i.e., to produce a sensible species of oneself in the sensory and thence, at least by extrinsic denomination, to be denominated as acting. See Suarez: 'That which appears is not the one who appears, but only the medium which the one who appears uses.' But the one appearing is denominated from the figure, because he reaches the eyes of the beholder under the figure." (Theol. did.-pol. P. I. c. 11. s. 2. q. 11. f. 704.)

The same: "The union παραστατική, by which the Son of God used a visible form for a time in which he might appear, is not to be confused with the union ὑποστατική." (L. c.)

The same: "We do not maintain that the persons of the Most Holy Trinity were separated in those apparitions of the O.T., nor that the Father or the Holy Spirit were there where the Son of God presented himself to be seen in an assumed figure. The Son of God indeed assumed that external form and appeared in it, not the Father, not the Holy Spirit; yet the remaining persons of the Most Holy Trinity were not separated from the very production, assumption, and apparition of that form. For the very ὁμοουσία and the highest and most intimate περιχώρησις of the divine persons does not permit this. Wherever one divine person is and operates ad extra, there the others also operate, cf. John 5, 19. Calixtus therefore confuses the apparition and the presence of the persons of the Most Holy Trinity. The ὁμοουσία requires this, that whenever and however one person of the Most Holy Trinity appears, the other is also present; yet it does not follow: the divine persons are present, therefore that very thing which is divinely ordained and arranged in the apparition pertains indiscriminately to all the divine persons. It cannot be that one person is present somewhere without the other, but it can be that one person appears in a certain body, adorned by the counsel of the Most Holy Trinity, and notifies his apparition by certain signs and characters." (L. c. f. 705.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Jews, who maintain that God revealed himself to the patriarchs only through the ministry of angels; as reported..."

Maimonides. 2. Of Paul of Samosata, who denied that the Son of God was present with the patriarchs or appeared in the O.T. He was contradicted in the Synod of Antioch. . . 3. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who, following the lead of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, maintain that God never appeared in the O.T. by Himself, but always an angel in the place of God. . . To this end they especially champion the appearances of created angels, in order to establish their ἀγγελολατρεία [angel-worship]. 4. Of certain Calvinists, who in most of the appearances of the O.T. understand a created angel, such as Calvin. . . 6. Of the Arminians, who also socinianize here, maintaining that angels appeared in the place of God in the O.T., not the Son of God Himself. . . 7. Of the Innovators, such as D. Georg. Calixtus, who. . . defends the negative, . . . contending with every effort that "not the Son of God, but some created angel was seen in those appearances. That the Son of God was neither called an angel, nor can be called one, nor appeared singularly, etc." (L. c. f. 706. sq.)

Luthardt: "Furthermore, there belongs here 1. the question concerning the Angel of Jehovah, who, according to the traditional view, is understood and defended as Jehovah Himself or as the Logos in angelic form by Hengstenberg, Kahnis, Philippi, Keil, etc.; on the other hand, as a created angel, who serves Jehovah as the bearer and organ of His manifestation, by Hofmann, Delitzsch, Kurtz, etc. For the first view it speaks that the Malach Jahve identifies himself with Jehovah and allows divine honor to be shown to him. . . For the second view, however: a. the designation itself and the other linguistic usage of this word; b. the New Testament usage of ἄγγελος κυρίου; c. the New Testament view of the angelic mediation of the revelation of God in the O.T. in general; d. the Old Testament use of Michael instead of the Angel of Jehovah in the later writings; e. the Old Testament passages in which the Angel of Jehovah is unmistakably a created angel. That identification, however, is explained by the fact that in the Angel of Jehovah, Jehovah Himself appears." (Compendium. 3rd ed. p. 78. sq.)

Which, however, is itself divinely destined for ministries and embassies. For thus they are called πνεύματα λειτουργικά ἀπεσταλμένα [ministering spirits sent forth], etc. Heb. 1: 14. As πνεύματα [spirits], complete spirits, as we shall presently say. §

3. That such natures, or angels, exist, Scripture indicates most explicitly. See on Heb. 1:4, 5, 6, 7, 13, and 14. Cf. Ps. 91:11, 104:4, Matt. 4:6, 11, and elsewhere. From the light of nature, however, it can hardly be demonstrated evidently, although it can be persuaded by probable reasons. §

4. The efficient cause of the angels is God, who produced them out of nothing, in time; although, on which day they were created, is not sufficiently distinctly known. PART I. CHAP. III.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of those who dreamed that the angels were coeval with God and had existed from eternity, which opinion is attributed to Aristotle in *Metaphysics* XII, c. 16, to Photinus and Porphyry, and likewise to the Simonians, Nicolaitans, Archontics, and others. 2. Of those who, with the Valentinians, raved that the inferior angels were created by the superior ones; see Irenaeus, I.1, c. 1, and Epiphanius, tom. II, l. 1, haeres. 23. 3. Of the ancient Greek fathers, such as Origen, Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil, Chrysostom, Damascene, and of the Latins, such as Ambrose, Jerome, Hilary, Isidore, and Cassian, all of whom asserted that the angels were created before this visible world. 6. Of the Socinians, who first doubted the pre-existence of angels before the world was created and disputed only problematically whether angels existed before the created world, as is evident from Socinus and Smalzius. Later, however, it was defined by the Socinians that the angels had pre-existed, and they defend this as an assertion certain in faith, because they believe it is a convenient way to evade the passages concerning the eternity of the Son of God, or to refute the argument for the deity of the Son of God derived from eternity. 8. Of the Arminians, from whom Episcopius adorns the same opinion—namely, that God created the angels a long time before the Mosaic hexaemeron—with new inventions. 9. Of the Rabbis, some of whom assert that the good angels were created on the first day, but the pernicious ones on the second or fifth day. Others wish for the angels or demons to have been created simultaneously 'toward the evening of the sixth day, at that same time or around the time when the woman was formed,' and that Satan took the occasion from that to tempt the woman." (L. c. c. 11. § 2. q. 1. f. 653. sq.)

Cf. Antithesis of J. H. Kurtz, see the preceding chapter, § 6, note b.

Thus, in Ps. 148:2 and 5, and Ps. 104:4, and Col. 1:16, the angels are numbered among the creatures. For they are simple substances, and just as they are independent of matter in their being, so also are they in their coming-to-be. See Proverbs 8:22, where it is said that substantial wisdom, or the Son of God, was with God before His works. And thus it is gathered that, just like the rest of God's works or creatures, the angels did not coexist with God and His Son from eternity; although it is otherwise established that eternity belongs to God alone. See here, Chapter I, § 13, p. 27 sq.

Latin:

Caput III. DE ANGELIS. § 1. Inter creaturas, quae de bonitate divina omnes participant, perfectissimae a sunt, quas Scriptura vocat angelos.b Et sic ratio ordinis doctrinae patet. Sic in Epist. ad Hebr. 1, 4.., cum probandum esset, Christum omni creatura excellentiorem esse, dicitur ille melior esse angelis. Oportet ergo, nullam dari creaturam his perfectiorem.§

2. Etsi vero angelus a nomen officii est et ministrum seu legatum b denotat; tamen peculiariter hac appellatione significatur certa creaturarum species c ab hominibus et aliis creaturis omnibus ipsa natura sua d distincta.

Sicut apud Hebraeos vox מלאן, cujus radix obsoleta לאן apud Aethiopes tamen superest et mittendi significationem habet. Vid. Golius in Lex. Arab. fol. 143., Hotting. Smegm. Orient, c. 5. p. 88. et c. 7. p.' 164.

Graeca autem literatura, a qua et Latinum nomen, manifestior est. Unde et Hilarius dicit, Scripturam, quando coelestes spiritus vocat angelos, significationem officii testari, Lib. V. de Trinit. Et August. Enarr. in Ps. 104..: Angelus, inquit, officii nomen est, non naturae. Vid. b. Mus. Disp. VI. de Angelis § 2. p. 69. PART. I. CAP. III.
