I. § 13. p. 27. sq.


### Concerning Angels: They were not created before heaven and earth, because these were created in…

They were not created before heaven and earth, because these were created in the beginning, and thus were the first of all created things. See Gen. 1:1. And it is otherwise known that the eternity of God is described by existence before the created world; see Ps. 90:2, Isaiah 48:13.

However, they were not created after, but within the hexaemeron, because, once this had elapsed, God rested from the ordinary work of creation.

That the angels were created before man is usually proven from Job 38:7. Indeed, some believe that from this very passage it can be understood that the angels were created on the first day, namely because, when God founded the earth, the angels are said to have immediately praised God.

But these things are not sufficiently clear; although we do not deny that the angels are denoted by the name "sons of God," according to chapter 1:6, and we say that their beginning is to be referred to among the origins of the other creatures.

Perhaps also, just as we know man was created after other creatures destined for his good, it is rightly gathered that the angels, who were to minister to man (according to Heb. 1:14), were created before man.

Yet it is not necessary that we say the angels are indicated by the names of either "heaven" or "light" in Gen. 1, taken metaphorically.

§ 5. Angels are, by their own nature, spirits, or spiritual or incorporeal substances, not consisting of matter and form. They are expressly called so in Hebrews 1:14. For the word "spirit" is not taken in this place for a more subtle corporeal substance, such as wind (John 3:8) or the breath of a living creature (Isaiah 2:22), but in adequate opposition to a body, namely, in the sense in which it is taken in James 2:26 and in which it must be taken when it is attributed to a nature that is not only living but also intelligent. Compare Luke 24:39, where Christ, although 1) according to His divine nature He was of a spiritual essence, 2) on the part of His human nature He possessed a spiritual soul, and 3) after the resurrection He had received a spiritual body, nevertheless denied that He was a spirit when He wished to demonstrate the reality of a body in human nature. Thus also in Ephesians 6:12, angels are opposed to flesh and blood, i.e., to a corruptible corporeal nature. Add Musaeus, *Disp. de Angel.* § 24, p. 182. Kromayer: "Angels were not produced from the substance of God. For they would have been produced from it either by generation or by some other participation. Not by generation, because the Son is μονογενής, i.e., only-begotten (John 1:14, John 3:16, 1 John 4:8), and is ἴδιος, i.e., His own (Romans 8:32), who has God as ἴδιον πατέρα (John 5:18). Not by some other participation, because the divine essence is ἀμέριστος, i.e., indivisible, ὅλως ὅλον τι, that is, a totally whole thing, incommunicable to others placed outside the bosom of the Deity." (*Theol. pos. pol.* I, 226.) Quenstedt: "Distinguish between angels considered simply and absolutely, and thus they are spirits; and viewed συγκριτικώς or comparatively, namely, in respect to God, and thus they have a greater affinity with corporeal substance, being subject to composition and mutability, than with God; and in this relation to the Creator, some ancient teachers of the church seem to have assigned bodies to angels, according to that of Damascenus, *lib. II. de orth. fide* C. 3: 'Μόνον γάρ ὄντως ἁπλοῦν τὸ θεῖόν ἐστι καὶ ἀσώματον' [For only the Divine is truly simple and incorporeal]; likewise: 'Angels are incorporeal towards us, but yet corporeal in respect to God, to whom, by a certain relation, they possess altogether density and matter.'" (*L. c. q. 2. f. 658.*) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: "Antithesis:

1. Of the Pythagoreans and Platonists, who seem to have been the first to invent that angels are not altogether immaterial and spiritual, but material and corporeal natures...

2. Of the ancient Jews; for Grotius attributes to them that angels are bodies, but most subtle ones...

3. Of the Muhammadans, some of whom trifle that demons consist of elemental, pestilential, and delegated fire, others of air...

4. Of the Messalians, ancient heretics, who posit that the devil is corporeal...

5. Of some fathers, such as Justin in his dialogue with Trypho and *Apol. I.*, Origen, *lib. 2. περὶ ἀρχῶν* c. 6, 8, and 23... Tertullian, *lib. de carne Christi* c. 6 (who asserts that angels unite bodies to themselves hypostatically), Basil, *l. de Sp. S.* c. 16, Cassian, *collat. 7. c. 13*. It is not sufficiently certain regarding Augustine whether he judged angels to be corporeal or devoid of corporeal mass: in his *Lib. de Spiritu et lit.* he writes in general: 'Every creature is corporeal.'... Lactantius, Damascenus, and others assign to angels some body, though not a fleshy one, but a subtle, celestial, fiery, or airy one... 6. Of certain Scholastics and Papists, who attributed most subtle bodies to angels... 7. Of some Calvinists, who seriously posit that angels, even when considered absolutely and in themselves, have bodies (though distinct from human ones), and those not assumed for a time, but proper and essential to them, concreated and always to be retained, such as Hieronymus Zanchius... 9. Of the Arminians, among whom Simon Episcopius, *lib. V. instit. theol. c. 2. p. 347*, says: 'It is difficult to assert what the spirituality of angels is, whether it is joined with some corporality or not?'... 10. Of Hugo Grotius (a man of no party), who in his *annot. in V. T. ad Ps. 104, 4* openly makes angels corporeal." (*L. c. f. 658. sqq.*) Kurtzius: "The angels are spirits, Heb. 1: 14. By this, both a positive and a negative statement is made regarding the essence of the angels. The positive is the concept of spirituality, of free, self-conscious personality in contrast to impersonal, unfree natural life. . . The negative. . . is, to use the words of J. T. Beck (Christi. Lehrwissensch. I, p. 176 f.), 'the negation of flesh-and-bone-ness and earthly-material life, the life-form of our earthly-spatial life-organism, and thus also the negation of dependence upon earthly-spatial life-conditions and laws of motion, without thereby denying them a bodily organ and an external life corresponding to it. For Scripture opens up to us, outside of and above our own as it now is, a sphere of bodily life which, just as the present one in its flesh-and-blood density and its earthly-material character corresponds to our earth-system (1 Cor. 15:45 ff.), so also as a faithful configuration corresponds to the heavenly world-system, and is likewise homogeneous to the nature of a pure spirit (πνεῦμα), just as our present body in its current reality is to the nature of a mere ψυχή (the life of the soul).' Rightly does the aforementioned scholar base this assertion. . . first of all on 1 Cor. 15:40. . .: 'There are heavenly bodies (σώματα) and earthly bodies.' . . The bodies designated here as heavenly can. . . only be the bodies of the inhabitants of heaven or the angels. This is also acknowledged by more recent. . . exegetes (de Wette and Meyer), and only abandoned again for insufficient reasons by the most recent interpreter (Osiander). . ., who wishes to understand by them the sun, moon, and stars according to v. 41. . . Human and animal bodies form the same contrast to the angelic bodies that prevails between earth and heaven. Just as the present human body bears within itself the character and essence of the present earthly materiality. . ., so we must conceive of the angels in a similar relationship of their bodies to heavenly materiality. . ., finer, more ethereal, purer, and more luminous than earthly human bodies. Cf. Matt. 22:30; Luke 20:36. . . Matt. 28:3. Here, it is not the merely momentarily assumed human-likeness of his (the angel's) appearance that is described, but rather precisely the extra-human and superhuman—that is, the specifically angelic—which belongs not to his passing appearance, but to his actual essence. . . The corporeality of the angels (is) by no means to be thought of as rigid and brittle, as closed and bound as our own, but rather as highly mobile and fluid, which nowhere opposes the will of the spirit with the sluggishness and immutability of earthly corporeality, but proves itself to be a perfectly adequate and submissive organ of the spirit, yielding to its every need and will. . . Indeed, even apart from the positive biblical testimonies, the concept of absolute bodilessness is in itself completely incompatible with the concept of creatureliness. . . 'Corporeality is the end of the ways of God.' A creature without corporeality is not even conceivable, because everything created, as created, can only live, act, and exist in space and time, and it is corporeality alone that binds the creature to space and time. Only God alone is an absolute spirit; only He alone stands outside of and above time and space. A cre

...a created spirit without corporeality... would have to scatter into nothingness. Within the creature, therefore, corporeality is the condition of all existence, the organ of all activity, the foil of the spirit; through it the creature receives its limitation, its definiteness, and its point of support; without it, it would drift and dissolve without hold. Corporeality is a limitation for the created spirit, because it prevents it from being eternal, infinite, and omnipresent.” (Bibel und Astronomie, pp. 78—84.)

Between those bodies, however, which angels are read to have assumed at times (whether they were fashioned from the surrounding air, or were of some other nature) and the spiritual substance of the angels themselves, no union other than an accidental one takes place. For they were in them by way of an assisting form, not an informing one. Hence, one cannot call this a natural or essential union. Cf. Mus. Disp. cit. § 38. sqq. p. 169. sqq. Scharffius: “Commonly, one form is called informing, another assisting. An informing form is that through which a thing is what it is. For this is properly the form of a thing, whereas the assisting one is only called so by analogy. An assisting form is said to be that which directs the motion and operation of a thing, but does not enter into its essence itself; just as a charioteer is an assisting form to horses, or a teacher to a student.” (Metaphys. p. 115.) Kromayerus: “When they (the angels) appeared in bodies, they were not a part of their essence, but were created by God the Creator (not by the angels themselves).” (Th. posit. pol. II, 132.)

Latin:

Ante coelum et terram non sunt conditi, quia haec initio, adeoque prima ex creatis omnibus, sunt condita. Vid. Gen. 1, 1. Atque alias notum est, quod per existentiam ante mundum conditum aeternitas Dei describatur, vid. Ps. 90, 2. Esaiae 48, 13.

Non autem post, sed intra hexaemeron creati sunt, quia, hoc elapso, quievit Deus ab opere creationis ordinario.

Ante hominem autem conditos esse angelos, probari solet ex Jobi 38, 7. Imo credunt aliqui, ex hoc ipso loco posse intelligi, angelos prima die fuisse conditos, nempe quia, cum Deus terram fundasset, illico angeli Deum laudasse dicuntur.

Sed haec non satis clara sunt; licet angelos nomine filiorum Dei denotari, juxta cap. 1, 6. non negemus, atque inter caeterarum creaturarum origines horum initium referri dicamus.

Fortasse etiam, sicut hominem post alias creaturas, bono ejus destinatas, conditum novimus: ita et angelos, homini ministraturos (juxta Ehr. 1, 14.) ante hominem creatos esse, recte colligitur.

Neque tamen necesse est, ut nominibus vel coeli, vel lucis, Gen. 1. metaphorice acceptis, angelos dicamus indicari.

§ 5. Sunt autem angeli sua natura spiritus,a seu substantiae spirituales aut incorporeae,b ex materia et forma non constantes.c Ita expresse vocantur Ebr. 1, 14. Accipitur enim hoc loco vox spiritus nm pro substantia corporea subtiliori, qualis est ventus, Joh. 3, 8., aut halitus animantis, Es. 2, 22., sed in oppositione adaequata ad corpus, eo scilicet sensu, quo accipitur Jacobi 2, 26. et quo accipi debet, quando tribuitur naturae non solum viventi, sed et intelligenti. Confer Lucae 24, 39., ubi Christus, licet 1) eecundum divinam naturam spiritualis essentiae esset, 2) ex parte humanae naturae animam spiritualem haberet, 3) post resurrectionem corpus spirituale accepisset, tamen negavit, se esse spiritum, cum veritatem corporis in natura humana demonstrare vellet. Sic etiam Ephes. 6, 12. carni et sanguini, i. e. naturae corporeae corruptibili, opponuntur angeli. Adde Mus. Disp. de Angel. § 24. p. 182.Kromayerus: ,,Angeli non ex Dei substantia fuerunt producti. Aut enim per generationem, aut per aliam quandam participationem inde producti fuissent. Non per generationem, quia Filius est μονογενής, ϊ. e., unigenitus, Joh. 1, 14. Joh. 3, 16. 1 Joh. 4, 8., est ϊΑιος, i. e. proprius, Rom. 8, 32., qui Deum habet hhov πατέρα, Joh. 5, 18. Non per ·aliam quandam participationem, quia essentia divina est άμέριστος, i. e. indivisibilis, όλως όλον τι, id est, totaliter totum quid, aliis, extra sinum Deitatis positis, incommunicabilis.“ (Theol. pos.pol. I, 226.) Quenstedtius: ״Dist. inter angelos consideratos απλώς et absolute, et sic spiritus sunt; et spectatos σνγκριτικώς seu comparate, in respectu sci. ad Deum, et sic majorem habent convenientiam cum substantia corporea, quippe compositioni et mutabilitati obnoxii, quam cum Deo, et in hac relatione ad Creatorem antiqui ecclesiae doctores nonnulli angelis corpora assignasse videntur, juxta illud Damasceni lib. II. de orth. flde C. 3.: ,Μόνον γάρ όντως ανλον το &εϊόν έστι και άσώματον‘; item: ,Angelos esse incorporeos προς ΰμας, sed corporeos tamen respectu Dei, ad quem relatione quadam omnino crassitiem obtineant et materiam.“ (L. c. q. 2. f. 658.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis:

1. Pythagoricorum et Platonicorum, qui commenti primum videntur, angelos non prorsus esse immateriales «t spirituales, sed materiales et corporeas naturas...

2. Judaeorum veterum; his enim Grotius tribuit, quod angeli corpora sint, sed subtilissima. . .

3. Muhammedanorum, quorum alii ex igne elementari, pestilenti ac deputato, alii ex aere daemones constare nugantur.

4. Messalianorum, veterum haereticorum, qui diabolum corporeum statuunt. . .

6. Nonnullorum patrum, ut Justini in dialogo cum Tryphone et apol. I., Origenis, lib. 2. περϊ αρχών c. 6. 8. et 23. . . Tertulliani lib. de carne Christi c. 6. (qui asserit, angelos unire sibi corpora hypostatice), Basilii 1. de Sp. S. c. 16., Cassiani collat. 7. c. 13. De Augustino non satis constat, utrum corporeos esse angelos censuerit, an corporeae molis expertes: Lib. de Spiritu et lit. in genere scribit: ,Creatura omnis corporea est.‘. . Lactantius, Damascenus, aliique angelis corpus aliquod, non tamen carneum, sed subtile, coeleste, igneum, vel aereum assignant. . . 6. Quorundam scholasticorum et pontificiorum, qui angelis corpora PART. I. GAP. ΠΙ. subtilissima tribuerunt. . . 7. Nonnullorum Calvinianorum, qui, angelos etiam absolute et in se consideratos corpora (etsi ab humanis distincta), eaque non ad tempus assumpta, sed sibi propria et essentialia, concreata et semper retinenda habere, serio statuunt, ut Hieronymus Zanchius. . . 9. Arminianorum, e quibus Simon Episcopius lib. V. instit. theol. c. 2. p. 347. inquit: ,Difficile esse, asserere, qualis sit angelorum spiritualitas, num cum corporalitate aliqua conjuncta, necne?‘ ... 10. Hugonis Grotii (nullarum partium hominis), qui annot. in V. T. ad Ps. 104, 4. aperte angelos corporeos facit.“ (L. c. f. 658. sqq.) Kurtzius: ״Die Engel sind Geister, Ebr. 1, 14. Dadurch ist ein Positives und ein Negatives über das Wesen der Engel ausgesagt. Das Positive ist der Begriff der Geistigkeit, der freien selbstbewussten Persönlichkeit im Gegensatz zum unpersönlichen, unfreien Naturleben. . . Das Negative . . . ist, um uns der Worte J. T. Bec^s (Christi. Lehrwissensch. I. S. 176. f.) zu bedienen, ,die Negation der Fleisch und Knochenhaftigkeit und erdstofflichen Lebens, der Lebensform unsres irdischräumlichen Lebens-Organismus, somit auch der Abhängigkeit von den irdisch-räumlichen Lebensbedingungen und Bewegungsgesetzen, ohne dass ihnen damit ein Leibes-Organ und ein demselben entsprechendes Aussenleben abgesprochen wäre. Denn die Schrift eröffnet uns ausser und über dem unsrigen, wie es jetzt ist, eine Sphäre des Leibeslebens, das wie das diesseitige in seiner Fleischund Blutverdichtung in seinem erdstoffigen Character unserm Erdsystem entspricht (1 Cor. 15, 45. ff.), so auch als treue Abgestaltung dem himmlischen Weltsystem, und ebenso der Natur eines reinen Geistes (πνεύμα) homogen ist, wie unser diesseitiger Leib in seiner jetzigen Wirklichkeit der Natur einer blossen ψυχή (des Seelenlebens).‘ Mit Recht gründet der bezeichnete Gelehrte diese Behauptung. . . zunächst auf 1 Cor. 15, 40. . .: ,Es gibt himmlische Leiber (σώματα) und irdische Leiber.‘ . . Die hier als himmlische bezeichneten Leiber können. . . nur die Leiber der Himmelsbewohner oder der Engel sein. Dies ist auch von neueren. . . Exegeten (de Wette und Meyer) anerkannt, und nur aus unzulängliehen Gründen von dem neuesten Ausleger (Osiander) wieder aufgegeben worden. . ., der darunter Sonne, Mond und Sterne nach Y. 41. verstehen will. . . Menschenund Thierleiber bilden denselben Gegensatz zu den Engelleibern, der zwischen Erde und Himmel obwaltet. Wie der jetzige Menschenleib Character und Wesen der jetzigen ErdenStofflichkeit an sich trägt. . ., so werden wir uns die Engel in einem ähnlichen Verhältnisse ihrer Leiber zur Himmelstofflichkeit zu denken haben. . ., feiner, ätherischer, reiner und leuchtender, als die irdischen Menschenleiber. Vgl. Matth. 22, 30. Luc. 20, 36. . . Matth. 28, 3. Hier wird nicht das etwa nur momentan angenommene Menschenähnliche seiner (des Engels) Erscheinung, sondern vielmehr gerade das Ausserund Uebermenschliche, also das speciflsch Angelische, nicht seiner vorübergehenden Erscheinung, sondern seinem eigentlichen Wesen Angehörige geschildert. . . Die Leiblichkeit der Engel (ist) keineswegs so starr und spröde, so abgeschlossen und gebunden zu denken, wie die unsrige, sondern vielmehr als eine höchst bewegliche und flüssige, die dem Willen des Geistes nirgends die Schwerfälligkeit und Unwandelbarkeit irdischer Leiblichkeit entgegensetzt, sondern sich als vollkommen adäquates und unterthäniges Organ des Geistes, seinem jedesmaligen Bedürfniss und Willen nachgiebig erweist. . . In der That ist auch, selbst abgesehen von den positiven biblischen Zeugnissen, der Begriff einer absoluten Leiblosigkeit an sich schon völlig unvereinbar mit dem Begriff der Creatürlichkeit. . . ,Leiblichkeit ist das Ende der Wege Gottes.‘ Eine Creatur ohne Leiblichkeit ist gar nicht denkbar, weil alles Geschaffene als Geschaffenes nur in Baum und Zeit leben, wirken und bestehen kann, und die Leiblichkeit allein es ist, welche die Creatur an Raum und Zeit bindet. Nur Gott allein ist ein absoluter Geist, nur er allein steht ausser und über Zeit und Raum. Ein ge

schaff ener Geist ohne eine Leiblichkeit... müsste in das Nichts zerstieben. Innerhalb der Creatur ist darum die Leiblichkeit die Bedingung aller Existenz, das Organ aller Thätigkeit, die Folie des Geistes; durch sie erhält die Creatur ihre Begrenzung, ihre Bestimmtheit und ihren Haltpunct; ohne sie würde sie haltungslos verschwimmen und zerfliessen. Die Leiblichkeit ist eine Beschränkung für den geschaffenen Geist, weil sie ihn hindert, ewig, unendlich und allgegenwärtig zu sein.“ (Bibel und Astronomie, p. 78—84.)

Inter ea vero corpora, quae angeli aliquando assumsisse leguntur {sive illa ex aere circumstante efficta sint, seu alterius cujuscunque naturae) et inter ipsam angelorum substantiam spiritualem non alia, quam occidentalis unio locum habet. Nam fuerunt in illis per modum formae assistentis, non informantis. Unde neque naturalem seu essentialem unionem hanc dicere licet. Conf. Mus. Disp. cit. § 38. sqq. p. 169. sqq.Scharffius: ״Vulgo forma alia dicitur informans, alia assistens. Forma informans est, per quam res est id, quod est. Haec enim proprie est forma rei, cum illa assistens saltem ita dicatur per analogiam. Assistens forma dicitur, quae motum et operationem alicujus rei dirigit, ipsam vero essentiam non ingreditur; ut auriga est forma assistens equorum, praeceptor discipuli.“ (Metaphys. p. 115.) Kromayerus: ,,Quando in corporibus apparuerunt (angeli), non fuerunt pars essentiae ipsorum, sed a Deo conditore (non ipsis angelis) creata.“ (Th. posit.pol. II, 132.)


### Concerning Angels: A. Osiander: “Men eat and drink because of need, but angels consume food like a…

A. Osiander: “Men eat and drink because of need, but angels consume food like a flame because of power.” (Colleg. th. P. II, 165.) § 6. Just as angels have a spiritual essence in common with God and the human soul, so they differ from God in that their essence is not infinite, but finite; and from the human soul in that their substance is complete.

For just as angels do not have their being from themselves, but from God, so they did not receive a being that was anything but finite and limited. Indeed, that nature of theirs is not ordered toward another with which it might constitute a *per se* unity as if with another component part. Cf. Mus. l. c. § 35. sqq. p. 294. § 7. Furthermore, angels are intelligent substances, such that intellect is of their essence.

For operations proceeding from the intellect are everywhere attributed to them in Scripture, e.g., praising God, Is. 6:3; worshipping, Heb. 1:6; knowing what is preached in the church, Eph. 3:10. And if any among men excel others in knowledge, they are said to know good and evil like an angel of God, 2 Sam. 14:20. PART I. CHAPTER III.

Taken as the power of understanding. However, the second act of understanding, or intellection or cognition, which proceeds from this, is certainly an act that is really produced, and an accident distinct from the angelic substance; as is evident from the following distinctions. § 8.

The cognition of angels is established as threefold: Natural, revealed, and beatific. For although there is one power of knowing in angels, nevertheless the acts of understanding vary according to the different manner of knowing, either in the same subject or in different ones. See Musaeus, loc. cit., § 52, 53, 54, p. 206 sqq. The former [natural cognition] is equally common to good and evil angels on account of the identity of nature, although this cognition itself admits of degrees. The latter [revealed cognition] was common to all before the fall of some. But afterwards, it was taken away from those who fell, as a punishment for the fall. The good angels, however, having been translated into the state of glory, do not need it as they once did, although they may still be said to be participants in it in their own way. The third [beatific cognition] belongs uniquely to the angels confirmed in good. § 9.

That is called natural cognition by which angels know both themselves and the angels coexisting with them, as well as the heavens and the earth, and the essences of all things contained therein, and finally God Himself; the former indeed with clear cognition, but the latter only abstractively. Thus, they know themselves without an intelligible species through their own essence, but other things through species concreated with them, or impressed upon them by God Himself in their first production. That is, *a posteriori* and through created things, yet more perfectly than our abstractive cognition. Compare Musaeus, loc. cit., § 56, p. 210 sqq. § 10.

Nevertheless, they begin to know singulars distinct from themselves, especially material things which exist at one time or another, and likewise accidents which belong to individuals, successively and in time. For we cannot attribute omniscience to them. And what is said in Ephesians 3:10 is referred to here: "so that now the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places through the church," etc. Compare 1 Peter 1:12. Certainly, they can and do proceed from things better known to things unknown, by means of discourse.

11. Future contingencies, which depend upon the free will, they do not know certainly and infallibly; although we cannot deny a conjectural knowledge to their sagacity.

However, those future events which proceed from determined causes and, according to the order of nature, always occur in the same way—for example, the constellations of the stars, eclipses, etc.—these they know certainly in their causes, and in this way they foresee the future; although they are ignorant of what God, having changed the order of nature through His absolute power, is about to do.

For this is the prerogative of God alone, by which He has willed to be recognized by men as if by a character. See Isaiah 43:12 and here, loc. cit., § 15, p. 29, etc. Namely, by the power of their natural cognition.

That God can reveal such future contingencies to them, and sometimes is accustomed to do so, so that they may know them certainly, is indeed not denied (just as they are read to have been employed at times to predict future events); but this knowledge is foreign to the present subject.

By this reasoning they know future wars and seditions of peoples, the sins and noble actions of individual men, etc., namely, by diligently observing the characters, temperaments, customs, and present circumstances of men, yet in such a way that it is nothing but a probable, uncertain, and often fallacious opinion.

Quenstedtius: "The devil, under the persona of Samuel (1 Sam. 28:19), could certainly predict the future destruction of Saul and his sons, because the execution of that matter had been entrusted to him by God, the just Judge. The strengths of both armies, the Israelite and the Philistine, were also known to him; he also held the secret counsels of both parties, and because he furthermore knew that Saul was destined for punishment by the just judgment of God and that David had already been elected king in his place, he could easily infer the outcome of the battle. Or that diabolical specter predicted those future contingencies not so much from the certainty of knowledge as from the sagacity of conjecture, estimating with himself, having compared the prophecies of the prophets—which were not unknown to him—the spirit, the strengths, and the cause of both battle lines. Nor does the 'tomorrow' exceed the condition of mere conjecture, since in the Scriptures it does not always signify precisely the next day, but also any future time indeterminately, whence that crooked prophet seems to have used its ambiguity deliberately in this passage, according to Rainoldus." (Loc. cit., s. 2, q. 3, f. 666.)

For thus they foresee future contingencies of another kind—which arise from natural causes, indeed, but ones subject to various changes, or from causes concurring by accident and chance, and which therefore turn out in diverse ways, now in this manner, now in another, e.g., storms, diseases, etc.—only probably. § 12.

Similarly, regarding the hidden thoughts of men, angels have only an opinion gathered from signs or effects. PART I. CHAP. III.

a) For God claims for Himself alone the accurate and infallible knowledge of the human heart. See 1 Kings 8:39 and in this place, Chapter I, § 15, pp. 29, 30. Quenstedtius: "Dan. 2:10, 11. The Magi and Chaldeans, faithful servants of demons, although they applied all their arts, yet could not penetrate the thoughts of Nebuchadnezzar. On the contrary, however, the devil could infer from the pursuits of Judas, and thus *a posteriori*, that he was prone to avarice... Although evil angels know those thoughts which they themselves suggest to either the pious or the impious." (L. c. f. 664, 666.) §

13. Joined with the intellect in the angelic nature is a free will, or the power of desiring good and averting evil. For the power of understanding is never without a will. And the angelic will is indicated by acts of joy, by which the will is sweetly carried toward a present good, which is ascribed to the angels in Luke 15:10; and of desire, by which the will tends toward an absent good, concerning which see 1 Peter 1:12, chapter 5:8.

Although this also pertains to the obedience of the angels, by which they conform their will to the will of their Superior (God) and act conformably; as well as to the disobedience, by which their will tends toward things other than what God wills. See concerning the former Psalm 103:20, concerning the latter 2 Peter 2:4.

And this freedom of the angelic will in the state of pilgrimage was such that an angel could indifferently desire good and evil. But what the freedom of the will of good and evil angels is today will be taught below. Whether true or apparently such, according to the diverse state of the angels. §

14. The faculty of speaking, or of manifesting the concepts of their mind to others, also belongs to the angels, in such a way that they can speak to God, to other angels, and to men. For what they speak to themselves through internal concepts of the mind does not differ from the very cognition of the angels.

Pertaining to this is that they are said to praise God in Isaiah 6:3. Compare Revelation 7:11. See Isaiah, l. c., where it is said that one cried to another. Compare Zechariah 2:8. See Luke 1:13, 19, where an angel spoke to Zechariah, the father of the Baptist, and v. 28, 30, 35, where he spoke to Mary, the mother of Christ; chapter 2:10, where he spoke to the shepherds; chapter 24:4, 5, 6, where two angels are read to have spoken to the women wishing to anoint Christ; Acts 1:10, 11, where they spoke to the disciples, the spectators of Christ’s ascension.

The question arises, however, regarding the mode of angelic speech. For although they can speak to God through mere thoughts directed toward God, for example, for the purpose of praising or petitioning Him, so that there is no need for other signs to manifest these to the omniscient divine intellect; yet, how they converse among themselves is difficult to explain. Meanwhile, the opinion that is more probable than the others is that one angel freely impresses intelligible species upon the intellect of another. Cf. Musaeus, loc. cit., § 67, 68, p. 216 sqq. They seem able to speak to humans similarly through species impressed upon their intellects, and furthermore also through phantasms presented to the human imagination. Most of the time, however, they are read in the Scriptures to have spoken with a sensible and distinct voice, formed in the air in imitation of the human voice, which, however, cannot be called natural to angels, just as it is to humans, since it is not produced by organs required for forming a natural voice, which would belong to the speaker by nature. §

15. There also belongs to the angels a power, or a certain force of acting outside themselves, which is indeed great, but limited and finite. Regarding this, it can be understood in a certain way from what has been said before. Namely, since a will is attributed to them, one must not deny them some faculty of executing or effecting what they will in a manner consistent with their nature and original state. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., § 70, p. 219, 220. And it pertains to this faculty or power that they can assume bodies for themselves, and that they can speak to humans with a sensible voice. See § 5, note e, and 14, 15.

Latin:

A. Osiander: ,,Homines edunt et bibunt ob egestatem, angeli autem instar flammae consumunt cibum ob potestatem.“ (Colleg. th. P. II, 165.) § 6. Sicut vero angeli essentiam spiritualem cum Deo et anima humana communem habent, ita differunt a Deo quidem, quod essentia ipsorum non infinita, sed finita est;a ab anima humana autem, quod completa b est illorum substantia.

Sicut enim angeli esse suum non a se, sed a Deo habent, ita non acceperunt esse, nisi finitum et limitatum. Quippe non ordinatur illa sua natura ad alterum, cum quo, tanquam cum altera parte componente, constituat unum per se. Conf.Mus. 1. c. § 35. sqq. p. 294.§ 7. Sunt porro angeli substantiae intelligentes,a ita ut intellectus b sit de essentia ipsorum.

Operationes enim ab intellectu proficiscentes passim in Seriptura illis tribuuntur, v. g. laudare Deum Es. 6, 3., adorare Ebr. 1, 6., cognoscere, quae in ecclesia praedicantur, Ephes. 3, 10. Et si qui inter homines cognitione prae aliis pollent, dicuntur cognoscere bonum et malum uti angelus Dei, 2 Sam. 14., 20. PAET. I. CAP. III.

Pro potentia intelligendi acceptus. Qui autem hinc procedit actus secundus intelligendi, seu intellectio aut cognitio est utique actus realiter productus, et accidens a substantia angelica distinctum; quemadmodum ex distinctionibus seqq. constat.§ 8.

Cognitio angelorum triplex a constituitur: Naturalis, revelata et beatifica.b Etsi enim una sit potentia cognoscendi in angelis, tamen actus intelligendi variant pro diversa ratione cognoscendi vel in eodem subjecto, vel in diversis. Vid. Mus. 1. c. § 52. 53. 54. p. 206. sqq. Illa angelis bonis et malis aeque communis est propter identitatem naturae, licet et ipsa haec cognitio magis et minus admittat. Ista fuit omnibus communis ante lapsum quorundam. Postea vero ab his, qui lapsi sunt, ablata est, in poenam lapsus. Boni vero in statum gloriae traducti eadem non ita indigent, ut olim, quamvis suo modo ejus participes adhuc esse dici possint. Haec angelis in bono confirmatis unice competit.§ 9.

Naturalis cognitio illa dicitur, qua angeli et se et angelorum sibi coexistentium, coeli quoque et terrae, et quae in his continentur, omnium essentias, Deum denique ipsum cognoscunt; illa quidem cognitione clara,a hunc vero non nisi abstracti ve.b Ita quidem, ut se ipsos sine specie intelligibili per suammet essentiam cognoscant, caetera vero per species sibi concreatas, seu in prima productione a Deo ipso impressas. Hoc est, a posteriori et rebus creatis, perfectius tamen, quam est nostra cognitio abstractiva. Conf. Musaeus 1. c. § 56. p. 210. sqq.§ 10.

Singularia tamen a se distincta, praesertim res materiales, quae alio atque alio tempore existunt, itemque accidentia, quae singulis competunt, successive et in tempore a cognoscere incipiunt.b Non enim omniscientiam illis tribuere possumus. Et refertur huc, quod dicitur Ephes. 3, 10., ut nota fiat nunc principatibus et potestatibus in coelestibus per ecclesiam etc. Conf. 1 Petr. 1, 12. Certe a notioribus ad ignota, mediante discursu, progredi possunt et solent.

11. Futura contingentia, quae a voluntate libera dependent,a certo et infallibiter b non cognoscunt;c ·licet conjecturalem notitiam d sagacitati ipsorum denegare non possimus.e

Quae autem futura a causis determinatis et secundum ordinem naturae semper eodem modo habentibus proficiscuntur, v. g. constellationes astrorum, eclipses etc., ea in suis causis certo cognoscunt atque hoc modo futura praevident; licet, quae Deus, immutato per potentiam suam absolutam ordine naturae, facturus sit, ignorent.

Hoc enim solius Dei est, quo se velut charactere agnosci ab hominibus voluit. Vid. Esaiae 43, 12. et h. 1. c. I. § 15. p. 29. 8qq. Nempe vi cognitionis suae' naturalis.

Quod autem Deus ipsis revelare possit, et aliquando soleat ejusmodi futura contingentia, ut certo sciant, equidem non negatur (prout ad praedicanda futura adhibiti aliquando fuisse leguntur); sed haec cognitio a praesenti aliena est.

Qua ratione futura bella et seditiones populorum, peccata et praeclaras actiones singulorum hominum etc. cognoscunt, nempe ex ingeniis hominum, temperamentis, moribus et rebus praesentibus diligenter spectatis, ita tamen, ut illa non sit, nisi probabilis et incerta ac saepe fallax opinio.

Quenstedtius: ,,Diabolus sub persona Samuelis 1 Sam. 28, 19. futurum interitum Saulis et Aliorum ejus certe praedicere potuit, quia ipsi demandata erat a Deo justo judice ejus rei ezecutio. Notae quoque Ipsi erant vires utriusque exercitus, Israelitici et Philistinaei; nota etiam tenebat arcana utriusque partis consilia, et quia insuper noverat, Saulem justo Dei judicio poenae esse destinatum et Davidem ejus loco jam in regem electum, inde facile colligere poterat proelii exitum. Vel praedixit illud diabolicum spectrum illa futura contingentia non tam ex certitudine scientiae, quam ex sagacitate conjecturae, aestimans secum, collatis prophetarum vaticiniis, sibi non ignotis, animum, vires, causam utriusque aciei. Neque το ,cras‘ omnem nudae conjectationis superat conditionem, quippe quod non praecise semper proximum diem, sed et quodvis tempus futurum indeterminate in Scripturis significat, unde λοξίας ille vates consulto ejus ambiguitate usus h. 1. videtur Rainoldo.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 666.)

Ita enim futura contingentia alterius generis, quae ex causis naturalibus quidem, sed variis mutationibus obnoxiis, aut ex causis per accidens et casu concurrentibus proveniunt atque adeo diversimode, nunc ita, nunc aliter eveniunt, v. g. tempestates, morbos, etc., non nisi probabiliter praesciunt.§ 12.

Similiter de cogitationibus hominum occultis angeli non nisi ex signis aut effectibus collectam opinionem habent.a PART. I. CAP. III.

a) Nam et cordis humani accuratam et infallibilem cognitionem Deus sibi soli vindicat. Vide 1 Regum 8, 39. et h. 1. cap. I. § 15. p. 29. 30. Quenstedtius: ,,Dan. 2, 10. 11. Magi et Chaldaei, fidi daemonum satellites, admotis licet cunctis suis artibus, tamen cogitationes Nebucadnezaris penetrare non potuerunt. E contrario vero diabolus ex studiis Judae et ita a posteriori colligere poterat, ipsum ad avaritiam esse proclivem. . . Quamquam mali angeli norint eas cogitationes, quas ipsi vel piis vel impiis suggerunt.“ (L. c. f. 664. 666.) §

13. Cum intellectu in natura angelica conjungitur a voluntas libera,b seu potentia appetendi bona c et aversandi mala. Nunquam enim potentia intelligendi est absque voluntate. Et voluntatem angelicam indicant actus gaudii, quo voluntas suaviter fertur in bonum praesens, qui angelis adscribitur Luc. 15, 10., desiderii, quo voluntas in bonum absens tendit, de quo vid. 1 Petr. 1, 12. cap. 5, 8.

Quanquam huc etiam pertineat angelorum cum obedientia, qua voluntatem suam superioris (Dei) voluntati conformant et conformiter agunt; tum inobedientia, qua voluntas eorum in alia tendit, quam quae vult Deus. Vid. de illa Ps. 103, 20., de hac 2 Petr. 2, 4·

Atque haec libertas voluntatis angelicae in statu viae talis erat, ut posset angelus indifferenter appetere bonum et malum. Qualis autem hodie sit libertas voluntatis angelorum bonorum et malorum, infra docebitur. Sive vera, sive apparenter talia, pro diverso statu angelorum.§

14. Competit etiam angelis facultas loquendi, seu manifestandi aliis a conceptus suae mentis, ita quidem, ut Deo,b angelis aliis,c et hominibus d loqui possint.e Quod enim sibi ipsis per internos mentis conceptus loquuntur, id non differt a cognitione ipsa angelorum.

Pertinet huc, quod dicuntur laudare Deum Esaiae 6, 3. Confer Apocal. 7, 11. Vid. Esaiae 1. c., ubi dicitur alter ad alterum clamasse. Confer Zach. 2, 8. Vid. Luc. 1, 13. 19., ubi angelus ad Zachariam, Baptistae patrem, et v. 28. 30. 35., ubi ad Mariam, Christi matrem; cap. 2, 10., ubi ad pastores, cap. 24, 4. 5. 6., ubi angeli duo ad mulieres Christum ungere volentes, Act. 1, 10. 11., ubi ad discipulos, ascensus Christi spectatores, locuti leguntur.

Quaeritur autem de modo locutionis angelicae. Quamvis enim Deo loqui possint per solas cogitationes ad Deum v. g. laudandum aut rogandum directas, ut non opus sit aliis signis ad manifestandas illas intellectui divino omniscio; tamen, quomodo inter se colloquantur, explicatu difficile est. Probabilior interim prae caeteris ea est sententia, quod species intelligibiles alter alterius intellectui libere imprimat. Conf. Mus. 1. c. § 67. 68. p. 216. sqq. Hominibus similiter per species intellectui illorum impressas, ac praeterea etiam per phantasmata phantasiae hominum objecta loqui posse videntur. Plerumque tamen in Scripturis locuti leguntur voce sensibili et distincta, ad vocis humanae imitationem efformata in aere, quae tamen angelis, aeque ut hominibus, naturalis dici non potest, cum non fiat organis ad formandam vocem naturalem requisitis, quae loquenti per se competant.§

15. Competit etiam angelis potentia, aut vis quaedam operandi extra se,a quae magna b quidem est, sed limitata ac finita.c De quo ex ante dictis quodammodo constare potest. Nempe cum voluntas illis tribuatur, denegari non debet facultas aliqua exsequendi seu efficiendi, quae naturae suae et primaevo statui convenienter volunt. Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 70. p. 219. 220. Et pertinet ad hanc facultatem seu potentiam, quod possunt sibi assumere corpora, quod possunt loqui ad homines voce sensibili. Vid. § 5. not. e. et 1 14. 15.


### Concerning Angels: Brochmand: "It cannot be denied that angels have appeared to men clothed in…

Brochmand: "It cannot be denied that angels have appeared to men clothed in bodies. For Moses, Gen. 18, 19, expressly records that they spoke, that their feet were washed, that they took food, and that, having grasped his hand, they led Lot out of the city of the Sodomites; which functions certainly could not have been truly performed without true bodies. From this, however, it cannot be inferred with any probability that angels are corporeal by the condition of their nature.". . .

Furthermore, it is disputed whether angels truly perform vital functions in assumed bodies. There is no doubt, however, that just as the angels clothed in bodies truly spoke, so they also truly ate and drank. For Moses, who records such things about the angels, does not tell fables, but things that truly happened. I am not unaware that there are those who here seek a knot in a bulrush, as the saying goes. For there are those who contend that angels do not truly perform vital functions in assumed bodies, but only in appearance, so that the angels appeared to Abraham and Lot to eat, when in reality they did not eat. For just as Moses calls the angels men, not because they were such, but because they appeared to be such, so they wish to say that Moses stated the angels ate, not because they truly ate, but because they appeared to eat. They attempt to give credence to this assertion from the words of the angel Raphael in the book of Tobit 12, 19: "I appeared to you all, yet I did not eat or drink, but it so appeared to you." It is added that angels could neither digest food nor convert it into nourishment, being spirits, which are nevertheless required for one to be said to truly eat. They add that the bodies assumed by the angels were not truly vital, wherefore the proper functions of true life could not be carried out through them.

These arguments indeed have the appearance of truth, yet they are not true. For although Moses calls the angels men, not because they were truly men, but because they appeared as such...

rent, yet he later explicitly teaches that they were not men, but angels. And nowhere in the Mosaic context do I find it written that אכל (to eat) is used in this sense regarding angels, namely that they only seemed to eat. Therefore, just as the angels truly came to Abraham, truly sat down under the tree, and truly took hold of Lot’s hand, so it is said without a trope that the angels ate.

Indeed, the passage brought forward from Tobit does not hinder our cause. For although the angel denies that he ate by necessity of nature or for the sake of nutrition, and therefore neither digested the food in the manner of men nor turned it into nourishment, this does not prevent the angel from having truly broken the food with his teeth and consumed it by a divine power unknown to us. Nor is it necessary for true eating that food be digested in the stomach and turned into juice and blood; a rich witness is Christ in Luke 24:41–43, who, after the resurrection, ate before his disciples to confirm the truth of his resurrection, even though the food was not converted into nourishment, for the nature of a glorified body did not permit this (Luke 20:36).

It is argued in vain that the bodies assumed by angels were not truly vital. For although they were not vivified by a soul, they were nevertheless so affected by the singular power of the angels that they were apt for the exercise of speech, touch, movement, and similar works of living beings. We add this: it is disputed by the fathers and scholastic doctors whether the bodies in which angels appeared clothed were created from nothing by God, or whether they were formed and assumed by the angels themselves from pre-existing matter. But here I willingly confess my ignorance.” (System, univ. theol. art. 8. c. 2. q. 2. f. 98.)

Whence they are called strong in power (Ps. 103:20), the host of the Lord (Gen. 31:ult.), strong (Matt. 12:29), strong armed men (Luke 11:21), angels of the power of Christ (2 Thess. 1:7); indeed, they are said to be much greater in strength and power than men (2 Peter 2:11), and wonderful effects are everywhere ascribed to them in Scripture. See especially 2 Kings 19:35, the slaughter of the Assyrian army, done by the work of an angel.

Quenstedtius: “Distinguish between the force and power of angels considered absolutely and nakedly—and thus it is sufficient to overturn this whole universe and its order and composition by local motion—and the virtue and power of the same viewed limitedly, or insofar as it is subjected and subordinated to divine providence and governed by it, and then it cannot do that... Good angels are more powerful than evil ones, because they keep the pious safe against their snares and assaults (Ps. 34:8; Tob. 8:3; Rev. 12:7).” (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 666. sq.)

For it cannot be denied that it is created and subject to divine power and potency. Cf. Job 1 and 2. Therefore, it neither extends itself to those things which exceed finite power (just as, for example, angels cannot produce something from nothing, or raise the dead), nor to all things that fall under finite power to be effected immediately by their own power, but only to those things which are proportionate to their nature and power. Whence, although they can produce a spiritual quality, or an intelligible species, outside themselves in another angel or in a man, they cannot, however, produce or change corporeal substances immediately and by themselves, but only through natural causes and by applying active things to passive ones. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, 1. c. § 71, 72, p. 220, 221.

Quenstedtius: “To the examples of children, whom they call supposititious infants, changelings, or ‘Kühlkröpfe,’ which are said to have been procreated by devils, I answer: they were either truly devils appearing in the form of human infants, or they were indeed true infants, but either supposititious, or [born] from women who bore them through intercourse with their own [husbands]...”

OF ANGELS. born of married women or other men. . . Distinguish between diseases which the devil himself, either through natural means, such as the disturbance of the humors, or through illusions, has effected and sent; and these he can in turn cure by applying natural remedies. . ., and diseases which depend upon God punishing the sins of men, Amos 3:6. In general, Satan can neither send nor dispel any diseases unless God permits it, Job 2:7, Luke 13:16. . .

Distinguish between metamorphosis or the transformation of species, which is feigned and fabulous, or old-wives' and poetic mutations, and true metamorphosis; or between magical transformations, and apparent ones, which occur either through the subtraction and substitution of things, or through the deception of the external senses (in the way the Egyptian magicians, by the power of the devil, produced frogs and serpents), or from one's own melancholy or corruption of the imagination, by which it happens that men falsely imagine themselves to be beasts and to be doing this or that — and true transmutations, which occur by the power of the omnipotent God either to declare justice or to show omnipotence, as in the case of Lot’s wife, Gen. 19:26, the rods of Moses, Exod. 7:11, the water, John 2:9. We concede the former to the devils, but not the latter; i.e., naturally, an angel, whether good or evil, cannot transform one species into another, e.g., a man into a dog, cat, wolf, etc., since such a transmutation is a certain new creation, which belongs to God alone. . .

Dr. Dannhauer, in his *Meletemata de miraculis*, p. 61, teaches: "Magical miracles, or those which are from satanic power, are either merely illusory or true regarding their substance. Merely illusory, he says, are those by which they delude the senses: 1. by removing the true object, 2. by presenting a false and fantastic one, or even by painting the true object with a foreign appearance (he paints objects with a foreign image when he renders his own organs invisible and takes care that they are not seen under the determined appearance of a man, but under the likeness of a beast or a tree); 3. by perverting the senses of men. Those true regarding their substance are those which have consistency; they are indeed wonders, but not miracles, because they are not above the nature and power of demons, but can be performed by them either by very swift local motion, or by the application of active things with passive ones, or by other modes which the human intellect cannot grasp." So he says. . .

Distinguish between the miracles of heretics, as they are heretics and put forth false doctrine, and to that extent they cannot perform miracles, and heretics insofar as they agree with the true church and perform miracles of God for the confirmation of doctrine and the sacraments; and thus I would not deny that the Jesuits in India and Japan have performed certain true miracles. Dr. Huelsemann, in *De auxiliis gratiae*, disput. II, th. 19, § 21, p. 156, admits that certain true miracles were performed by the Jesuits, the teachers of the Japanese, in confirmation not of the Papistic faith as such, but of the common Christian dogmas, with which they had intermingled Papal dogmas." (L. c. f. 668 sq., 671 sq.)

A. Pfeiffer: "Philo on the Giants, and others, understand Gen. 6:2 as good angels, burning with human lusts and therefore cast from heaven. . . But this opinion is repugnant both to the angelic nature, Matt. 23:30, and to the passage Acts 17:26, and to the analogy of faith concerning the confirmation of angels in good. . . The sons of God, who take wives and beget children, are not good angels, much less evil ones, but pious men and their descendants, who, although they may have fallen away here, are nevertheless called sons of God both from their former state and because of their external association with the true church. Cf. Is. 1:2, 63:8, Hos. 1:10." (*Dubia vexata*. Ed. 2, p. 59 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of David Georg, who transforms angels into thoughts and movements of the human mind, or confuses them with them. 2. Of those who deny that devils can effect anything through witches. . . 5. Of the Talmudists and Cabbalists, who dream that angels are corporeal, beget children, and die like men. . . 6. Of the Sethians, ancient heretics, who contended that angels had intercourse with women to procreate men. . . To this belongs the opinion of those who, PART I. CHAPTER III.

thought that angels begat giants from women, from a poorly understood passage in Gen. 6:2, such as Philo, Justin, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Lactantius, and Sulpicius Severus. Hence D. Dannhauer in *Christeid.* p. 271: "The monstrous incubation of angels and their commingling with antediluvian men was a fable which the ancients embraced as if in competition, against the authority of Scripture, Acts 17:26. The cause of the error, says Pamelius in his paradox, was that the old Greek LXX edition, which Tertullian and the earlier fathers, sticking in the same mire, followed, read: Οί άγγελοι τον θεον, and the Latin Itala: 'Angeli Dei'." ...

Latin:

Brochmandus: ״Angelos apparuisse hominibus vestitos corporibus, negari non potest. Nam Moses Gen. 18, 19. diserte memorat, locutos esse ipsos, lotos ipsis esse pedes, cibos sumpsisse, Lothum, apprehensa ejus manu, ex urbe Sodomitarum eduxisse; quae sane munia sine veris corporibus vere obiri non potuerunt. Hinc tamen nulla verisimilitudine exsculpi potest, angelos naturae suae conditione corporeos esse. . . .

Caeterum disputatur, an angeli in assumptis corporibus munia vitalia vere obeant? Dubium autem nullum est, quin veluti angeli corporibus vestiti vere locuti sunt, ita etiam vere comederint et biberint. Neque enim Moses, qui talia memorat de angelis, fleta narrat, sed quae vere contigerunt. Non ignoro, inveniri, qui hic modum, quod dicitur, in scirpo quaerant. Sunt enim, qui contendunt, angelos vere non obire in assumptis corporibus munia vitalia, sed tantum in speciem, ita ut angeli visi fuerint Abrahamo et Lotho comedere, cum tamen revera non comederint. Sicut enim Moses vocat angelos viros, non quod tales essent, sed quod tales esse viderentur, sic etiam dixisse volunt Mosem, angelos comedisse, non quod vere comederint, sed quod visi fuerint comedere. Fidem facere conantur assertioni e verbis Kaphaelis angeli in lib. Tobiae 12, 19.: ,Omnibus apparebam vobis, neque tamen comedebam aut bibebam, sed ita vobis videbatur.‘ Accedit, angelos nec cibos concoquere, nec in alimentum convertere potuisse, utpote spiritus, quae tamen requiruntur, ut quis vere dicatur comedere. Addunt, corpora ab angelis assumpta non fuisse vere vitalia, quare verae vitae propria munia per illa expediri non potuerunt.

Quae argumenta speciem quidem veri habent, vera tamen non sunt. Etenim licet Moses angelos vocat viros, non quod vere essent viri, sed quod tales appare Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. II. 8 PART. I. CAP. III.

rent, postea tamen diserte docet, non viros, sed angelos fuisse. Ac nuspiam in contextu Mosaico scriptum invenio, ro comedere hoc sensu de angelis usurpatum esse, quod comedere visi sint. Quocirca veluti angeli vere venerunt ad Abrahamum, vere sub arbore consederunt, Lothi manum vere apprehenderunt, ita citra tropum dictum est, angelos comedisse.

Locus vero e Tobia adductus non incommodat causae nostrae. Nam licet angelus neget, se naturae necessitate aut nutritionis causa comedisse, ac eapropter cibum more hominum nec concoxerit, nec in alimentum verterit, hoc tamen non impedit, quominus angelus cibum dentibus vere fregerit et divina virtute nobis incognita consumpserit. Nec necessarium esse ad veram comestionem, ut cibus in ventriculo concoquatur et in succum sanguinemque vertatur; testis locuples est Christus Luc. 24, 41—43., qui post resurrectionem ad confirmandam resurrectionis suae veritatem coram discipulis suis comedit, utut cibus in nutrimentum non sit conversus, hoc enim corporis glorificati natura non permittebat, Luc. 20, 36.

Frustra vero regeritur, corpora ab angelis assumpta non fuisse vere vitalia. Nam licet non vivificabantur ab anima, virtute tamen angelorum singulari ita afliciebantur, ut apta essent, per quae loquela, tactus, motus et similia viventium opera exercerentur. Hoc addimus, disputari a patribus et doctoribus scholasticis, an corpora, quibus induti angeli apparuerunt, ex nihilo a Deo creata sint, an vero ex praeexistente materia ab ipsis angelis formata et assumpta sint? Verum hic meam libens fateor ignorantiam.“ (System, univ. theol. art. 8. c. 2. q. 2. f. 98.)

Unde fortes robore dicuntur Ps. 103, 20., exercitus Domini Gen. 31. ult., fortes Matth. 12, 29., fortes armati Lue. 11, 21., angeli potentiae Christi 2 Thess. 1, 7., imo robore ac virtute multo majores hominibus esse dicuntur 2 Petri 2, 11. et effectus mirabiles passim illis adscribuntur in Scriptura. Vide inprimis 2 Reg. 19, 35. cladem exercitus Assyriorum, angeli opera factam.

Quenstedtius: ,,Dist. inter vim et potentiam angelorum absolute et nude consideratam, et sic sufficiens est ad evertendum per motum localem totum hoc universum et ordinem et compositionem ejus; et virtutem atque potentiam eorundem spectatam limitate seu quatenus illa subjecta et subordinata est divinae providentiae et ab ea gubernatur, et tunc illud non potest. . . Angeli boni sunt potentiores malis, quia pios contra ipsorum insidias et insultus tutos praestant, Ps. 34, 8. Tob. 8, 3. Apoc. 12, 7.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f; 666. sq.)

Creatam enim ac divinae potestati et potentiae subjectam esse, negari non potest. Conf. Jobi 1. et 2. Itaque nec extendit se ad ea, quae excedunt finitam potentiam (prout v. g. non possunt angeli producere aliquid ex nihilo, aut suscitare mortuos), nec ad omnia, quae sub finitam potentiam cadunt, immediate per suam potentiam efficienda, sed ad ea tantum, quae naturae et potentiae ipsorum proportionata sunt. Unde, quamvis qualitatem spiritualem, seu speciem intelligibilem extra se in alio angelo aut homine producere possint, corporeas tamen substantias immediate et per se producere aut immutare non possunt, sed mediantibus causis naturalibus et applicando activa passivis. Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 71. 72. p. 220. 221.

Quenstedtius: ״Ad exempla liberorum, quos vocant infantes supposititios, Wechselbälge, Kühlkröpfe, qui a diabolis procreati esse narrantur, respondeo: illos aut fuisse vere diabolos ln forma infantum humanorum apparentes, aut veros quidem infantes, sed vel supposititios, vel ex mulieribus, quae eos pepererunt congressu cum propriis

maritis, aut aliis viris genitos. . . Dist. inter morbos, quos diabolus ipse, vel per media naturalia, ut turbationem humorum, vel praestigias, effecit et immisit; et hos ipse rursus curare potest applicando medicamenta naturalia. . ., et inter morbos, qui a Deo hominum peccata puniente dependent, Amos 3, 6. In universum nullos satan vel immittere vel depellere morbos potest, nisi Deo permittente Job. 2, 7., Luc. 13, 16. . .

Dist. inter metamorphosin seu transformationem specierum fletam et fabulosam seu aniles et poeticas mutationes, et metamorphosin veram seu inter transformationes magicas, et apparentes, quae fiunt vel per subtractionem et suppositionem rerum, vel per deceptionem sensuum exteriorum (quomodo magi Aegyptiaci virtute diaboli produxerunt ranas et serpentes), vel ex melancholia propria aut corruptione phantasiae, qua fit, ut homines falso sibi imaginentur, se bestias esse, et haec aut illa agere, — et transmutationes veras, quae fiunt virtute omnipotentis Dei vel ad declarandam justitiam vel ostendendam omnipotentiam, ut in uxore Lothi Gen. 19, 26., baculos Mosis Exod. 7, 11., aqua Joh. 2, 9. Illas diabolis concedimus, non vero has; h. e. naturaliter angelus, sive bonus, sive malus, speciem in speciem, v. g. hominem in canem, felem, lupum etc., transformare nequit, cum ejusmodi transmutatio sit nova quaedam creatio, quae soli Deo competit. . .

D. Dannhauerus meletemat. de miraculis p. 61. docet: ,Miraculamagica, sive quae sunt a satanica virtute, esse vel mere praestigiatoria, vel vera, quoad hypostasin. Mere praestigiatoria, inquit, sunt illa, quibus illudunt sensibus: 1. verum objectum removendo, 2. falsum et phantasticum objiciendo, vel verum etiam objectum peregrina specie pingendo (peregrina vero imagine pingit objecta, quando sua organa reddit invisibilia, et curat, ne sub determinata specie hominis, sed sub effigie bestiae vel arboris videantur); 3. sensus hominum pervertendo. Vera quoad hypostasin sunt illa, quae consistentiam habent; mira quidem sunt, non tamen miracula, quia non supra naturam ac potentiam daemoniorum, sed ab iis fleri possunt vel celerrimo motu locali, vel applicatione activorum cum passivis, vel modis aliis, quos humanus intellectus capere nequit.‘ Haec ille...

Dist. inter miracula haereticorum, ut haeretici sunt et falsam doctrinam proferunt, et eatenus non possunt facere miracula, et inter haereticos, quatenus cum vera ecclesia consentiunt et ad confirmationem doctrinae et sacramentorum Dei miracula edunt; et sic nolim negare, Jesuitas in India et Japonia vera quaedam miracula edidisse. D. Huelsemannus De auxiliis gratiae disput. II. th. 19. § 21. p. 156. admittit, quaedam vera miracula a Jesuitis, Japoniensium doctoribus, esse patrata, in confirmationem non fidei papisticae, qua talis, sed communium dogmatum Christianorum, quibus dogmata pontificia immiscuerant.“ (L. c. f. 668. sq. 671. sq.)

A. Pfeifferus: ,,Philo de Gigant, aliique intelligunt Genes. 6, 2. angelos bonos, in humanas libidines exardescentes et inde coelo pulsos. . . . Verum haec opinio repugnat tum naturae angelicae Matth. 23, 30., tum loco Act. 17, 26., tum analogiae fidei de angelorum in bono confirmatione. . . Filii Dei, qui uxores ducunt et generant, non sunt angeli boni, nedum mali, sed homines pii eorumque posteri, qui, licet hic desciverint, dicuntur tamen filii Dei tum a statu priori, tum ob externam societatem cum vera ecclesia. Cf. Es. 1, 2. 63, 8. Hos. 1, 10.“ (Dubia vexata. Ed. 2. p. 59. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Davidis Georgii, qui angelos in cogitationes et motus animi humani transformat, aut cum illis confundit. 2. Eorum, qui negant, diabolos per sagas aliquid posse efficere. . . 5. Talmudistarum et Cabbalistarum, qui, angelos corporeos esse, generare et mori instar hominum, somniant. . . 6. Sethianorum, antiquorum haereticorum, contendentium, angelos cum mulieribus coiisse ad homines procreandos. . . Huc pertinet opinio eorum, qui, PAßT. I. CAP. III.

angelos ex mulieribus gigantes genuisse,, putarunt, ex male intellecto loco Gen. 6, 2., ut Philo, Justinus, Clemens Alexandrinus, Tertullianus, Lactantius, Sulpit. Severus. Hinc D. Dannhauerus in Christeid. p. 271.: ,Monstrosus angelorum incubitus et cum hominibus ante-diluvianis commixtio bucca fuit, quam veteres quasi certatim sunt osculati contra Scripturae auctoritatem, Act. 17, 26. Causam erroris, inquit Pamelius in paradoxo, dedit, quod LXX editio graeca vetus, quam et Tertullianus et patres anteriores, in eodem luto haerentes, sunt secuti, legeret: Οί άγγελοι τον θεον, et latina Italica: Angeli Dei‘. . .


### Concerning Angels: Of Bodin ... Paracelsus ..

7. Of Bodin ... Paracelsus ... and others, asserting that men can be transformed into wolves, donkeys, cats, etc. ... 8. Of most Papists, who maintain that Samuel was truly raised, 1 Sam. 28:18, and that other dead can be raised by the devil. ... 10. Of many Papists ... maintaining that the devil can perform true miracles. (L. c. f. 667 sq.)

Hofmann: "It is impossible to understand anything other than spirits by the בניהא^זים, of whom it is said there (Gen. 6:1 ff.) that they saw how beautiful the בניית האדם were, and that they took them as wives for themselves. ... The flood, which buried the then-existing generation of men, also banished the spirits, who had their sinful existence within it, from the upper world along with it: belonging to the judged world, they fell with it into the darkness into which that world was sunk." (*Schriftbeweis* I, 374 sq. 376.)

Kurtz: "That by the 'sons of God' in Gen. 6:2, 4, one is not to understand pious Sethites, but rather supernatural beings, or angels, is a fact that emerges so clearly and irrefutably from the context and is so firmly established by the ... linguistic usage of the O.T., that the stubbornness with which the opposing view is nevertheless held ... can only be explained by the power of insurmountable prejudices. ... The angel-interpretation is without question the oldest. ... However, since the end of the 4th century, it fell under the ban of absurdity and heresy. Theodoret, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, and Augustine denounced it as absurd; Philastrius counts it without further ado among the heresies. This ban weighed upon it until Rationalism, which threw off the straitjacket of dogmatic and traditional prejudices ... along with the belief in revelation, the Bible, and angels—perhaps also ... took pleasure in being able to demonstrate 'a piece of mythology' in the Bible again—until, therefore, Rationalism restored the lexicon, grammar, and context to their old rights. ... Gradually, the power of grammatical-historical exegesis also carried the day among many ... decidedly revelation-believing ... interpreters. ... I name only the old, stalwart Köppen ('The Bible, a Work of Divine Wisdom'), the orthodox Scheibel, the faith-defiant Stier, the Reformed Dietlein, the Lutheran Drechsler, furthermore Krabbe, v. Hofmann, Delitzsch, Baumgarten, Nägelsbach, Richers, etc." (*Die Ehen der Söhne Gottes mit den Töchtern der Menschen.* Berlin. 1857. p. 1, 11 sq.) §

16. From the essence of angels flow: I. Simplicity, or that they are not composed of essential parts, matter and form, nor of integral parts; II. Incorruptibility, or that they do not have within themselves a principle of corruption; III. Illocality, or that they are not in a place.

Unless, perhaps, this very spirituality formally implies a simplicity of essence opposed to physical composition. By this, however, it is not denied that they are composed of essence and subsistence, and likewise of subject and accidents, which are really distinct. See above § 8.

Scharffius: "Essential parts are those which intrinsically constitute the essence of a thing through essential union; just as matter and form are the essential parts of a body; the rational soul and the body are the essential parts of a man. Integrating or integral parts are called those which complete the integrity of a thing through quantitative union, that is, through continuous cohesion, as in animals there are heads, necks, bellies, feet, arms, hands." (Metaphys. p. 192.)

That they can be destroyed and annihilated by God, by whom they were created, and thus—although they do not have a form that can be cast off while the subject remains—can nevertheless be changed simply from being to non-being, is certain. See Musaeus, l. c. § 27, p. 185.

Meanwhile, an age or duration having a beginning, but lacking an end, is rightly ascribed to them. For because they lack matter, they are not quantitative, strictly speaking, nor can they be circumscribed by place. Yet we do not say that they are everywhere, but in a certain and definite πού, as they call it; so that they can also move themselves from one "where" to another and move material things elsewhere. See Matt. 8:32, where the demons, cast out by Christ from the possessed man in whom they had been for some time, and migrating into the herd of swine, drove this whole herd headlong into the sea. Cf. the blessed Musaeus § 34 sqq. p. 193 and § 72 sqq. p. 221, 224.

Quenstedtius: "Angels are in a certain space by designation or definitively; that is, their substantial, not only virtual, presence is defined by some space, so that they are there, and not in other spaces, much less everywhere; and because an angel is devoid of parts, he is not only whole in the whole place, but can also exist whole in any, even the smallest, part of the place, indeed in a point." (L. c.)

The same: "Angels are endowed with a certain faculty for exercising motion expeditiously, so that in a moment they can be wherever they wish, and hence, on account of their velocity and most rapid motion, they are compared to winds and a flame of fire, Ps. 104:4. I say that angels are moved from one 'where' to another in an instant; others, however, among whom are Spanheim and Maresius, maintain that angels do not acquire a new place instantly after leaving the former, but with some delay, because, although the mobile object itself is indivisible, yet the space in which it is moved is extended and continuous, which no creature can traverse in an instant." (L. c. s. 1. th. 11. f. 634.) §

17. The number of angels is great, but not definable by us. Thus, thousands of thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand angels are mentioned who serve God, Dan. 7:10. And Christ, Matt. 26:53, teaches that if He were to ask, more than twelve legions of angels would easily be sent to Him by the Father. But it is also read that in one man there was an entire legion of unclean spirits, Mark 5:8. A legion among the Romans was commonly a multitude of six thousand soldiers, although the number otherwise varied. PART I. CHAP. III.

For this is what is meant by the mention of the innumerable angels (μυριάδων) in Hebrews 12:22. Moreover, in this their number, however great it may be, the angels were created by God all at once, and were not, like men, multiplied successively through the generation of some from others. §

18. That angels differ among themselves by certain orders or degrees, there is no doubt. But whether they also differ in species and essence, is not clear.

This is gathered from their diverse names: such as Cherubim (Genesis 3, last verse), Seraphim (Isaiah 6:2), θρόνοι, ἀρχαί, κυριότητες, ἐξουσίαι, δυνάμεις (Colossians 1:16; Ephesians 1:21), and archangel (1 Thessalonians 4:16); and also because evil angels are elsewhere described as having an order among themselves, such as that of those who command and those who obey. For thus in Luke 11:15, Beelzebub is called the prince of the demons, and in Matthew 25:41, mention is made of the devil and his angels.

Quenstedtius: "That there are precisely nine orders or choirs of angels, and that these are divided into three classes or triads, which they call hierarchies, and that they are distinguished by dignity, degrees, and offices in such a way that, for instance, the first or supreme one knows God and divine things immediately and teaches the following one, and this one in turn the third, so that the first commands the second and the second the third, and likewise that the first only assists and does not minister, etc.—concerning which the Scholastics and Papists, especially Becanus, philosophize at length based on Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite—we reject as uncertain and false." (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 681.)

The same author: "At most, from the passages of Scripture that present the appellations of the angels, only these things can be gathered:1. That there are orders among the angels;2. That this order of angels can be established, so that there are a. θρόνοι, b. κυριότητες, dominions, c. ἐξουσίαι, powers, d. δυνάμεις, virtues, e. ἀρχαί, principalities, archangels, and angels (Colossians 1:16; Ephesians 1:21; 1 Peter 3:22), although in these places these names are also interchanged;3. That archangels are superior in order to angels;4. That the ἀρχαί are superior to archangels, and the δυνάμεις are superior to these (from Romans 8:38);5. That the ἐξουσίαι are superior to angels, and that the δυνάμεις also precede them in order (from 1 Peter 3:22);6. That the ἐξουσίαι intervene between the ἀρχαί and the δυνάμεις (from Ephesians 1:21);7. That the ἀρχαί are indeed superior to the angels, but inferior to all those others (from the same);8. That the κυριότητες precede them. Now, if the thrones are to be distinguished from them, this order would be established: thrones, dominions, powers, principalities, angels... Since in the aforementioned places these names are interchanged, and it is unknown whether archangels, Cherubim, and Seraphim are included in the first five terms, or whether they are to be distinguished from those orders, nothing certain can be defined here." (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 682 sq.)

Indeed, the blessed Augustine, in *Enchiridion ad Laurentium*, ch. XXVIII, speaking of the difference of the angels, says: "Let those who can, speak; I confess that I am ignorant of these things."

19. Angels may be defined as spiritual, intelligent, complete, and finite substances. Regarding the nature common to all. See § 5, p. 107. See § 7, ff., p. 109. See § 6, p. 109. §

20. In the very first creation, God bestowed upon the angelic nature certain habitual perfections, for the sake of eliciting acts suitable to themselves and for attaining a supernatural end through the grace of God. Authors call these perfections by the name of grace. For a state of pure nature, which some speak of, is not to be imagined; rather, it must be acknowledged that God, who made all things very good, made the angels at their very beginning such as they needed to be in order to be able to attain a supernatural end. Cf. the Epistle of Jude, v. 6, where the angels who became evil are said not to have kept their own origin (τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχήν). Therefore, it is necessary that they were good beforehand. See below, the note to § 25.

Quenstedtius: "The state of pure naturals, in which some Papists say angels and men were first created, is a pure and utter fiction; for there is deep silence in Scripture concerning it." (L. c. q. 5, f. 674.) For the states of the angels are distinguished into the state of grace and the state of glory, the former of which precedes, and the latter follows; these must be treated distinctly. §

Hofmannus: ,,Es ist unmöglich, unter den בניהא^זים, von welchen es dort (Gen. 6, 1. ff.) heisst, dass sie gesehen haben, wie schön die בניית האדם waren, und dass sie sich solche zu Weibern genommen haben, etwas anderes, als Geister, zu verstehen. . . Kurtzius: ״Dass unter den Söhnen Gottes in Gen. 6, 2. 4. nicht fromme Sethiten, sondern überirdische Wesen, resp. T. so fest begründet ist, dass die Hartnäckigkeit, mit welcher dennoch ... die entgegenstehende Auffassung festgehalten wird, nur durch die Macht unüberwindlicher Vorurtheile. . . erklärlich ist. . . Die Engeldeutung ist ohne Frage die älteste. . . Sie gerieth aber seit dem Ende des 4. Jahrh. unter den Bann der Absurdität und Ketzerei. Theodoret, Chrysostomus, Kyrill von Alex, und Augustin schalten sie als ungereimt, Philastrius rechnet sie ohne Weiteres zu den Ketzereien. S. 1. 11. sq.) §

16. Ex essentia angelorum fluunt I. simplicitas, seu quod non sunt compositi ex partibus essentialibus, materia et forma, neque ex partibus integrantibus;a II. incorruptibilitas, seu quod non habent in seipsis b principium corruptionis; III. illocalitas, seu quod non sunt in loco.c

Nisi forte ipsa spiritualitas essentiae simplicitatem compositioni physicae oppositam formaliter importat. Per hanc tamen non negatur, eos compositos esse ex essentia et subsistentia, itemque ex subjecto et accidentibus, realiter distinctis. Vid. supra § 8.

Scharffius: ״Partes essentiales sunt, quae essentiam rei intrinsece constituunt per unionem essentialem; quomodo materia et forma sunt partes essentiales corporis; anima rationalis et corpus sunt partes essentiales hominis. Partes integrantes s. integrales dicuntur, quae integritatem rei complent per uniouem quantitativam, h. e., per cohaesionem continuam, ut in animalibus sunt capita, colla, venter, pedes, brachia, manus.“ (Metaphys. p. 192.)

Quod autem a Deo, a quo creati sunt, destrui et annihilari adeoque, licet formam non habeant, quae remanente subjecto abjici possit, tamen ab esse ad non esse simpliciter mutari possint, certum est. Vid. Mus. 1. c. § 27. p. 185.

Interim aevum seu duratio initium quidem habens, sed carens fine, recte illis adscribitur. Quia enim materia carent, non sunt quanti, proprie loquendo, neque circumscribi possunt loco. Ideo tamen eos non dicimus esse ubique, sed in certo quodam ac definito π״ΰ, quod vocant; ita ut etiam ab uno ubi ad alterum sese movere possint et res materiales aliorsum movere. Vid. Matth. 8, 32., ubi daemones, ex homine obsesso, in quo aliquamdiu fuerant, a Christo ejecti, et in gregem porcorum demigrantes, totum hunc gregem praecipitem egerunt in mare. Conf. b. Mus. § 34. sqq. p. 193. et ^ 72. sqq. p. 221. 224.

Quenstedtius: ״Sunt angeli in certo spatio per designationem seu definitive; hoc est, eorum substantialis, non solum virtualis praesentia aliquo spatio definitur, ut ibi, non in aliis spatiis, nedum ubique sint; et quia angelus partium expers est, totus non tantum in toto loco est, sed et totus in qualibet, etiam minima, parte loci, imo in puncto, existere potest.“ (L. c.)

Idem: ״Instructi sunt angeli facultate quadam ad motum expedite exercendum, ita ut in momento possint esse, ubicunque velint, et hinc propter velocitatem et celerrimum motum conferuntur ventis et fiammae ignis Ps. 104, 4. Moveri, inquam, angelos de uno ubi in aliud in instanti, multi affirmant; alii tamen, quos inter Spanhemius et Maresius, volunt, angelos novum locum prhho deserto non acquirere in instanti, sed cum aliqua mora, quia, licet ipsum mobile sit indivisibile, tamen spatium, in quo movetur, extensum est et continuum, quod nulla creatura in instanti possit transire.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 11. f. 634.) §

17. Numerus angelorum a magnus, non autem a nobis definibilis b est.c Sic millia millium, et decies millies centena millia angelorum memorantur, qui Deo serviunt, Dan. 7, 10. Et Christus Matth. 26, 53. sibi roganti facile plus quam duodecim legiones angelorum a Patre missum iri, docet. Sed et in uno homine legio integra spirituum immundorum fuisse legitur Mare. 5, 8. Hoc enim est. quod inumerabilium anqelorum (μυριάδων) mentio fit Ebr. 12, 22. Hoc autem suo, quantus quantus is est, numero angeli a Deo simul creati, non autem instar hominum per generationem aliorum ex aliis successive multiplicati sunt.§

Ita colligitur ex diversis nominibus: qualia sunt Cherubim Genes. 3. v. ult., Seraphim, Es. 6, 2., θρόνοι, άρχάϊ, κυριότητες, έξουβίαι, δυνάμεις Col. 1, 16. Ephes. 1, 21., archangelus 1 Thess. 4, 16., quodque alias etiam mali angeli describuntur, tanquam ordinem inter se habentes, qualis est imperantium et parentium. Sic enim Eue. 11, 25. Beelzebub princeps daemoniorum dicitur, et Matth. 25, 41. mentio fit diaboli et angelorum ejus.

Quenstedtius: ״Esse determinate novem ordines seu choros angelorum, ׳hosque in tres classes seu terniones, quas hierarchias vocant, esse divisos, easque dignitate, gradibus et officiis sic distingui, ut sci. prima seu suprema Deum et divina immediate cognoscat et sequentem doceat, et haec rursum tertiam, ut prima secundae et secunda tertiae imperet, itemque, ut prima assistat tantum, non ministret etc.; de quibus ex PseudoDionysio Areopagita scholastici et pontificii, praesertim Becanus, multis philosophantur — ut incerta et falsa rejicimus.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 681.)

Idem: ״Ad summum e Scripturae locis, quae appellationes angelorum exhibent, haec colligi tantum possunt: 1. Quod dentur ordines inter angelos; 2. quod hic ordo angelorum stabiliri possit, ut a. sint ΰρόνοι, b. κυριότητες, dominationes, C. εξουσίαι, potestates, d. δυνάμεις, virtutes, e. άρχαι, principatus, archangeli et angeli, Col. 1, 16.
