19. Definiri possunt angeli,a quod sint substantiae spirituales b intelligentes,c completae et finitae.d Quoad naturam omnibus communem spectati. Vid. § 5. p. 107. Vid. § 7. sqq. p. 109. Vid. § 6. p. 109.§

20. Naturae angelicae Deus in prima statim creatione a contulit perfectiones quasdam habituales, ad eliciendos actus sibi convenientes, consequendi per Dei gratiam finis supernaturalis causa. Quas perfectiones nomine gratiae b appellant auctores. Non enim fingendus est status purae naturae, quem quidam vocant; sed agnoscendum, quod Deus, qui omnia valde bona fecit, angelos in primo ipsorum initio tales fecerit, quales esse oportebat, ut finem supernaturalem possent contingere. Conf. Epist. Judae v. 6., ubi angeli, qui mali facti sunt, dicuntur non servasse suam originem (τψ έαυτών άρχήν). Bonos itaque prius fuisse necesse est. Vid. inf. not. ad § 25.

Quenstedtius: ״Status purorum naturalium, in quo angelos et homines primum conditos esse nonnulli pontificii dicunt, purum putum figmentum est; de eo enim altum in Scriptura est silentium.“ (L. c. q. 5. f. 674.) Distinguuntur enim status angelorum in statum gratiae et gloriae, quorum ille praecedit, hic sequitur; de quibus distincte agendum est.§


### Concerning Angels: Just as the angels, tending toward their end, were obliged to know God rightly,…

21. Just as the angels, tending toward their end, were obliged to know God rightly, to love Him above all things, to believe in His truthfulness, to trust in His goodness, to obey His commands, and to hope for eternal life; so that grace, divinely granted to the angels for performing these acts, involved on the part of the intellect a certain habitual light, by the benefit of which the angels might know what needed to be known for attaining the supernatural end, but which could not be known by the light of nature; on the part of the will it involved PART 1. CHAP. III.

and habitual righteousness and holiness, by which they were able to institute and perform all actions in conformity with the eternal law of God. Certainly, the means by which the angels were to arrive at their end or blessedness had to consist in acts of the mind and will occupied with their God and the author of their blessedness. Yet, if they performed this, they could not, strictly speaking, merit their blessedness, but were able to attain it through the grace of God, or His gratuitous and unmerited favor. Whence those means are said to be not causal in the stricter sense, but in a broader signification, according to what we said in Proleg. Cap. I, § 3, Vol. I, p. 6, and § 7, p. 13.

It seems, however, that these consisted in divinely impressed species, by which God, as it were, spoke to the angels, and supernatural things to be known were exhibited to their intellect, so that they could be recognized—not indeed evidently and as they are in themselves, but with relation to God who speaks—and the angelic intellect in this way became a sufficient principle for acts of supernatural knowing and assenting.

Some call it faith or the light of faith; blessed Gerhard calls it the supernatural habit of faith, Isag. LL. Dispp. XIII, cap. IX, § 7, p. 557. Indeed, distinguishing faith from evident knowledge, they established that the angels believed, in that they recognized things under the aspect of truth; not, however, through the evidence of the object, but through the authority of God who speaks or reveals. For example, the ultimate end itself, or the beatific vision of God to be expected at some time, as a motive for the constant obedience to be rendered in the meantime; likewise also the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, which exceeds the limits of natural intelligence, but which had to be known by the angels so that God might be worshipped as He was with respect to His persons.

However, we do not say that the mystery of the Incarnation (since Christ did not take hold of angels, Heb. 2:16) and other free decrees of God were known to the angels in the state of pilgrimage through the light of grace.

Or a complex of supernatural virtues, such as ὅλη ἀρετή, or universal righteousness. And here belongs ἀλήθεια, or truthfulness, or faithfulness, integrity, and sincere holiness, from which the devil is said to have fallen, John 8:44.

The authors call them hope and charity. See Gerhard, l. c., p. m. 557. And indeed, the angels had hope in the state of pilgrimage, by which they embraced future blessedness as a good that was absent and difficult, yet possible and truly to be attained (unless they themselves stood in the way). And this hope presupposed trust placed in God as the cause of attaining blessedness, by which their will would acquiesce in God as a present good and the cause of another good. Charity, however, had as its object both God, to whom they desired to do a thing or duty pleasing, and their fellow angels as partners of their nature and future co-heirs of salvation, to be loved for the sake of God. Yet they were not necessitated to perform actions holily, but retained the freedom to act otherwise and to fall; which is evident from the subsequent fall of some.

22. And thus it is evident that it cannot be entirely denied that angels were created in the image of God. It must be admitted that this is not explicitly stated in the Scriptures, unless perhaps one wishes to refer to the fact that angels are called sons of God in Job 1:6, 2:1, and 38:7, and that a son is commonly called the image of his father. Certainly, it is surely certain that the angels were conformed in this respect to the Divine Being, and that they received this conformity from the intention of God, who bestowed it upon them. Compare the blessed Gerhard, in *Isag. Disp. XII. cap. VI. de Ang. § 26. p. 523.* §

23. Although gifts of grace were bestowed by God upon all angels, yet not all, but only some, rightly used that grace granted to them; and from this arose the distinction of angels into good and evil. §

24. Those are called good who persevered in the goodness, or righteousness and holiness, in which they had been created, and who, because God was to graciously reward their obedience, were confirmed in the good, so that they can no longer lose their goodness, sin, or become evil. §

25. Those are called evil who of their own accord departed from their primordial goodness, and, grace having been withdrawn by the just judgment of God, were so confirmed in evil that they are unable to return to goodness, to do good, or to refrain from sinning. For this is what it means not to keep their origin, but to undergo a change of their first state for the worse, Jude v. 6. (For that ἀρχή denotes not indeed the substance itself, received in the first creation, which always remains the same, but the concreated, losable perfections.) And for the same reason, he is said not to stand in the truth, John 8:44, who is supposed to have previously been in it. Quenstedtius: "In a few words: they are called evil not by origin, but by fall; not by entity, but by quality." (*L. c. s. 1. th. 29. f. 640.*) PART I. CHAPTER III.

§ 26.

How long the state of grace lasted, namely, before some of the angels were confirmed in good and others, falling away from good, became evil, is not sufficiently clear. This is certain: the distinction between good and evil angels took place before the first humans fell. For the opinion of some, that their fall occurred on the second day of creation, indicated by the fact that it is not added to the narrative of the works of that day, "God saw that those works were good," is clearly weak. Rather, the general clause at the end of Genesis 1 should be noted: "God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good." From this, one would rather conclude that after the entire six days of creation had elapsed, the angels had not yet fallen. For thus Christ calls the devil a murderer ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς [from the beginning] and the father of lies (John 8:44), the first among all to be a liar, and the cause both of the defection of humans from God and of the necessity of dying introduced to humans, and who gave an example of consummate malice in seducing Eve (Gen. 3:1 et seqq.). On the other hand, the angels who guarded paradise when humans had fallen and were cast out from it were undoubtedly confirmed in good (Gen. 3:24). See Gerhard on this passage in his Commentary, p. 124. § 27.

Good angels are confirmed in good through blessedness itself. § 28. Namely, after they had constantly exhibited their obedience to God in the state of the way, even while other angels were falling, it pleased God to fill them with the light of glory, so that they could know God Himself clearly and intuitively.

There are those who assign to these angels a peculiar operation, consisting in the battle against evil angels and the resistance opposed to their assaults; yet Scripture is silent on this. For this is what it means to see the face of the heavenly Father (Matt. 18:10). And rightly the blessed Gerhard: βλέπειν πρόσωπον θεοῦ [to see the face of God] does not precisely denote in the Holy Scriptures waiting for God’s command (although it may connote it), but the beatific vision. Isag. LL. Disp. XIII. cap. IX. de Angel. § 9. p. 558. § 29. Following this vision of God was a most intense love, by which the will of the angels began to adhere to God in such a way that it could not be turned away from Him.

Compare here the Prolegomena, cap. I. § 4. note d. Vol. I. p. 10.

30. And thus their confirmation in good, or the determination of their will toward the good, was brought about, so that whatever they do, they do in relation to God, as the infinitely perfect good perfectly known, without any stain or any defect. a) And this is that άναμαρτησία or impeccability, which is accustomed to be ascribed to the blessed angels. For sin imports άνομίαν or illegality. Now the sum of the law is to love God above all things. Therefore, those who always love God, clearly known, above all things, and incessantly embrace Him as the highest good, by this very fact cannot act άνόμως, since it implies a contradiction for someone, by loving God above all things, to be in conformity with the law, and at the same time, by sinning, to deviate from the law. §

31. Yet not every liberty of the angelic will is taken away. For although it is no longer indifferent to good and evil, it is nevertheless indifferent in relation to created goods, so that whatever one of them it wills, it can also not will, or for one, will another. Nor, indeed, did that liberty of willing evil just as much as good import perfection, and therefore it can be absent in the state of the perfection of the angels; indeed, it is absent. And thus it is free with the liberty of contradiction or of exercise. Authors call the liberty of contrariety or of specification. Namely, if the created good is not to be necessarily desired on account of the will of God; for otherwise, in this case, it is altogether desired by the blessed angels. §

32. To that blessedness, however, the good angels were indeed destined by the eternal decree of God, and thus were elected. For it cannot be said that God confers upon the angels in time what He had not decreed from eternity that He would one day confer. And compare 1 Tim. 5:21, where Paul makes express mention of τών έχλεχτών άγγίλων, the elect angels: designating that a few out of many, or out of the entire assembly of spirits, were chosen, upon whom the blessedness, of which all could have become partakers, would be conferred. Not, however, by an absolute decree, or one excluding every foreseen condition on the part of the subject, freely, but one certainly to be fulfilled. For just as God did not confer blessedness in time except upon those who in good [remained]... PART I. CHAPTER III.

severed: thus the eternal decree concerning the angels eventually being saved rested upon the foreknowledge of that condition to be fulfilled in time. And indeed, the election of the angels acknowledges an internal impulsive cause or reason in God who elects, namely His goodness, but not an external impulsive cause. And although, on the part of the divine intellect, it presupposes an act of knowing terminated at the very constant obedience of the angels, nevertheless this obedience, owed to God the Creator and temporal in nature, has no power of merit before God, nor the power of impelling His will to decree or to grant the good of eternal blessedness. Calovius: "If God in the first creation granted to all angels sufficient means to persist in the good, so that they might enjoy eternal glory, it is false that some of them were destined for eternal glory (with the rest rejected, or passed over, or not instructed by that grace) out of the absolute good pleasure of God. But the former is true. Therefore, the latter is also true." (System. T. IV, p. 71.) However, we do not say that the angels were elected in the sense in which Scripture describes the election of men, which has regard to the merit of Christ and the faith to be fixed in Him. Cf. the blessed Gerhard, Isag. LL, Disput. XIII. cap. IX. § 13. p. 561.

Latin:

21. Sicut autem angeli ad finem suum tendentes Deum recte cognoscere, super omnia diligere, veracitati ejus credere, bonitati confidere, jussis obtemperare et vitam aeternam sperare debuerunt;a ita gratia illa, angelis ad actus istos praestandos divinitus concessa, importabat ex parte intellectus lucem b quandam habitualem,c cujus beneficio cognoscerent angeli, quae ad finem supernaturalem consequendum cognoscenda erant, sed naturae lumine cognosci non poterant;d ex parte voluntatis importa PART. 1. CAP. III.

bat justitiam e et sanctitatem habitualem,f qua poterant g actiones omnes legi Dei aeternae conformiter instituere et perficere. Sane media, quibus angeli pervenirent ad finem sive beatitudinem suam, consistere oportebat in actibus mentis et voluntatis circa Deum suum et beatitudinis suae auctorem occupatis. Non tamen, si hoc praestarent, mereri proprie loquendo beatitudinem suam, sed per Dei gratiam seu favorem gratuitum atque indebitum consequi potuerunt. Unde media illa non causalia seu strictiore sensu, sed in latiore significatione dicta sunt, juxta ea, quae diximus Proleg. cap. I. § 3. Vol. I. p. 6. et § 7. p. 13.

Videtur autem illa constitisse in speciebus divinitus impressis, quibus Deus quasi locutus est angelis, et intellectui illorum res cognoscendae supernaturales sunt exhibitae, ita ut illae, non quidem evidenter, et quales in se sunt, verum cum relatione ad Deum loquentem possent agnosci, et intellectus angelicus hoc modo fieret principium sufficiens ad actus cognoscendi et assentiendi supernaturales.

Aliqui fidem aut lucem fidei; b. Gerhardus habitum supernatura־ lem fidei appellat, Isag. LL. Dispp. XIII. cap. IX. § 7. p. 557. Nempe fidem, scientiae evidenti contradistinguentes, credere angelos per fidem statuerunt, quod sub ratione veri cognoscerent; non tamen per evidentiam objecti, sed per auctoritatem dicentis aut revelantis Dei. V. g. ipsum finem ultimum, seu visionem Dei beatificam aliquando expectandam, tanquam motivum obedientiae constantis interim praestandae; simul etiam mysterium SS. Trinitatis, quod terminos naturalis intelligentiae excedit, angelis autem cognoscendum erat, ut, qualis Deus erat quoad personas, talis coleretur.

Incarnationis autem mysterium (cum Christus angelos non assumserit, Ebr. 2, 16.) et caetera Dei decreta libera angelis in statu viae per lumen gratiae fuisse cognita non dicimus.

Sive complexus virtutum supernaturalium, ut eset ολη άρετή, seu justitia universalis. Et pertinet huc άλήΰεια, seu veracitas, aut fidelitas, integritas et sincera sanctitas, a qua diabolus defecisse dicitur Joh. 8, 44.

Auctores spem et caritatem vocant. Vid. Gerh. l. c. p. m. 557. Et spem quidem habuerunt angeli in statu viae, qua beatitudinem futuram, tanquam bonum absens et arduum, possibile tamen et revera (nisi ipsi obstiterint) consequendum, amplecterentur. Atque haec spes supponebat fiduciam in Deo tanquam causa consequendae beatitudinis collocatam, qua voluntas illorum in Deo tanquam bono praesente et causa alterius boni acquiesceret. Caritas vero pro objecto habebat cum Deum, cui rem aut officium gratum facere cupiverunt, tum socios angelos tanquam consortes naturae suae futurosque cohaeredes salutis, propter Deum diligendos. Non tamen necessitabantur ad actiones sancte peragendas, sed retinebant libertatem aliter agendi ac deficiendi; quod ex sequente quorundam lapsu patet.

22. Atque ita patet, non omnino negari posse,a quod angeli ad imaginem Dei sint conditi.b Fatendum est κατά βητόν in Scripturis non extare, nisi forsan huc referre velis, quod angeli filii Dei dicuntur Jobi 1, 6. cap. 2, 1. c. 38, 7. quodque vulgo filius imago patris dicitur. Sane conformes fuisse hac ratione angelos divino Numini, et accepisse hanc conformitatem ex intentione Dei, eam illis conferentis, certum utique est. Confer b. Gerhard, in Isag. Disp. XII. cap. VI. de Ang. § 26. p. 523.§

23. Quamvis vero dona gratiae omnibus angelis a Deo fuerint collata, tamen gratia illa sibi concessa non omnes, sed aliqui duntaxat recte usi sunt; et orta hinc est distinctio angelorum in bonos et malos. §

24. Boni dicuntur, qui in bonitate seu justitia et sanctitate, in qua conditi fuerant, perseverarunt, atque a Deo obedientiam ipsorum gratiose remuneraturo confirmati sunt in bono, ut bonitatem perdere, peccare aut mali fieri amplius non possint. §

25. Mali vocantur, qui a bonitate primaeva sponte sua desciverunt a et gratia justo Dei judicio subtracta ita in malo sunt confirmati, ut ad bonitatem redire, bene agere aut non peccare nequeant. Hoc enim est non servare originem suam, sed subire mutationem status primi in deterius, Ep. Judae v. 6. (βΑρχη enim illa non quidem ipsam substantiam, in prima creatione acceptam, quae semper eadem manet, perfectiones tamen concreatas amissibiles denotat.) Et eadem ratione dicitur non stare in veritate, Joh. 8, Jßß., qui prius in ea fuisse supponitur.Quenstedtius: ,,Paucis: dicuntur mali non ortu, sed lapsu, non entitate, sed qualitate.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 29. f. 640.) PART. I. CAP. m.

§ 26.

Quamdiu autem duraverit status gratiae, nempe priusquam angelorum alii in bono confirmarentur, alii a bono desciscentes mali fierent, non satis distincte a constat. Hoc certum est, distinctionem angelorum bonorum et malorum locum habuisse, antequam b homines primi laberentur. Nam quod quidam putant, lapsum eorum die secundo creatio1118 factum per hoc indicari, quod non addatur narrationi operum ejus diei: Vidit Dem, quod opera illa sint bona, id plane infirmum est, et notanda potius clausula generalis, Gen. 1, ult.: Vidit Dem cuncta, quae fecerat, et ecce valde bona; unde potius colligas, angelos elapso toto hexaemero nondum fuisse lapsos. Ita enim Christus vocat diabolum homicidam άπ’ άρχης, et patrem mendacii, Joh. 8, 44, primum inter omnes mendacem, et causam uti defectionis hominum a Deo, ita necessitatis moriendi hominibus inductae, quique malitiae consummatae specimen dedit in seducenda Eva, Gen. 3, 1. et seqq. Contra autem procul dubio angeli in bono confirmati fuerunt, qui custodiverunt paradisum, cum homines lapsi essent inde ejecti, Gen. 3, 24.. Vid. Gerh. ad h. l. in Comment. p. 124. § 27.

Sunt autem angeli boni per ipsam beatitudinem in bono confirmati. § 28. Nempe postquam obedientiam suam in statu viae, etiam labentibus aliis angelis,a Deo constanter exhibuerunt, placuit Deo, eos lumine gloriae implere, ut ipsum Deum clare et intuitive possent b cognoscere.

Ac sunt, qui angelis his peculiarem operationem assignant, positam in pugna contra malos angelos et resistentia insultibus eorum opposita; de quo tamen Scriptura silet. Hoc enim est videre faciem Patris coelestis, Matth. 28, 10. Et recte b. Gerhardus: Βλέπειν πρόσωπυν θεοΰ, praecise in sacris literis non notat expectare Dei mandatum (quanquam connotet), sed visionem beatificam. Isag. LL. Disp. XIII. cap. IX. de Angel. § 9. p. 558.§ 29. Secutus autem est hanc visionem Dei a amor intensissimus, quo voluntas angelorum Deo ita inhaerere coepit, ut ab eo averti non posset.

Confer h. l. Proleg. cap. I. § 4. not. d. Vol. I. p. 10.

30. Et sic facta est confirmatio eorum in bono, sive determinatio voluntatis ad bonum, ut, quicquid agunt, id agant in ordine ad Deum, tanquam bonum infinite perfectum perfecte cognitum, sine labe ulla,a ullo defectu. a) Atque haec est άναμαρτησία seu impeccabilitas illa, angelis beatis adscribi solita. Peccatum enim ανομίαν sive illegalitatem importat. Summa autem legis est, diligere Deum super omnia. Itaque, qui Deum clare cognitum super omnia semper amant ac tanquam summum bonum incessanter amplectuntur, hoc ipso non possunt agere άνόμως, cum contradictionem implicet, aliquem, amando Deum super omnia, legi conformem esse, et simul peccando aberrare a lege. §

31. Nec tamen tollitur libertas omnis voluntatis angelicae. Etsi enim illa non amplius sit indifferens ad bonum et ad malum,a indifferens tamen est in ordine ad bona creata, ita ut quodlibet eorum, quod vult, possit etiam non velle,b aut pro uno c velle alterum.d Neque vero illa libertas volendi malum aeque atque bonum perfectionem importabat, ideoque in statu perfectionis angelorum abesse potest, imo abest. Adeoque libera est libertate contradictionis sive exercitii. Auctores libertatem contrarietatis seu specificationis appellant. Scilicet, si bonum creatum non sit propter voluntatem Dei necessario appetendum; alias enim hoc casu ab angelis beatis omnino appetitur.§

32. Ad illam vero beatitudinem a angeli boni utique aeterno b Dei decreto destinati, atque ita electi fuerunt.c Neque enim dici potest, Deum in tempore angelis conferre, quod non ab aeterno decreverit, se aliquando collaturum. Et confer 1 Tim. 5, 21., ubi Paulus τών έχλεχτών άγγίλων, electorum, angelorum, expressam mentionem facit: paucos ex pluribus, seu integro coetu spirituum lectos fuisse, quibus beatitudo, cujus omnes poterant fieri participes, conferretur, designans. Non autem absoluto, seu omnem praevisam conditionem ex parte subjecti, libere, sed certo implendam excludente. Sicut enim Deus in tempore beatitudinem non nisi illis contulit, qui in bono per PART. I. CAP. IH.

severarunt: ita decretum aeternum de angelis aliquando salvandis nitebatur praevisione illius conditionis in tempore implendae. Et agnoscit quidem electio angelorum causam aut rationem impulsivam in· ternam in Deo eligente, nempe bonitatem ejus, non autem causam impulsivam externam. Et licet ex parte intellectus divini supponat actum cognoscendi ad ipsam angelorum obedientiam constantem terminatum, tamen haec obedientia Deo creatori debita ac temporaria vim meriti apud Deum, aut vim impellendi voluntatem ejus ad decernendum, aut dandum beatitudinis aeternae bonum non habet. Calovius: ,,Si Deus in prima creatione angelis omnibus media sufficientia ad persistendum in bono, ut gloria aeterna fruerentur, concessit, falsum est, eorum nonnullos esse ad aeternam gloriam destinatos (reliquis rejectis, vel gratia illa praeteritis aut non instructis) ex absoluto Dei beneplacito. At prius verum est. E. et posterius.“ (System. T. IV, p. 71.) Eo tamen sensu, quo Scriptura electionem hominum describit, quaeque respectum habet ad meritum Christi et fidem in illo defigendam, angelos electos fuisse non dicimus. Conf. b. Gerhardi Isag. LL, Disput. XIII. cap. IX. § 13. p. 561.


### Concerning Angels: Quenstedtius: "Regarding the passage in Job 4:18

Quenstedtius: "Regarding the passage in Job 4:18: 'Even in his angels he found folly,' as the Vulgate has it... the sense is: If even the good and just angels were to contend with God, as you do, and wished to persuade Him that they were more just than He (in some certain cause), He would not believe their words, or conclude that the matter was so... Distinguish between the redemption of the angels and the restoration of friendship and concord between the inhabitants of heaven and earth brought about through the passion of Christ, and their reconciliation; Paul speaks of the latter, not the former, in Eph. 1:10 and Col. 1:19-20, when he says that through Christ all things in heaven and on earth have been reconciled and gathered under one head. Obs. Reconciliation presupposes an offense. But the good angels did not offend God. Therefore, all things in the heavens are said to be reconciled, because even those who were already triumphing in the heavens were reconciled to God by the blood of Christ, namely, the believers of the Old Testament who died before the coming of Christ." (L. c. f. 680.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of certain Calvinists, such as Bucanus, Pareus, Ravanellus, and others, who maintain: 'That the good angels were confirmed in the good by an absolute decree, without any intuition of perseverance and praiseworthy consistency in the truth.' Bucanus, loc. VI. on angels, where, having proposed the question: Why, when others fell away from the truth, some angels persisted in grace and truth, he replies: 'The supreme cause is the eternal, firm, and immutable decree and good pleasure of God.' And Piscator, in *Ausführlichem Bericht von den Hauptstücken christl. Lehre* [Detailed Report on the Main Articles of Christian Doctrine], p. 18, writes: 'It is certain that God has decreed from eternity to save some angels and some men, but to damn others.' 2. Of the Scholastics and Papists, such as Lombard, and likewise Thomas and Becanus, who maintain: 'That the angels not only merited their own blessedness or confirmation in the good by their obedience in the past, but that they also merit something even today...'

3. Of some Papists, such as Philippus Diez, Gregorius de Valentia, Blasius de Viegas, and Suarez, who ascribe the grace of confirmation and the glory of the blessedness of the angels to Christ the Mediator and His merit, or assert that the good angels were redeemed through Christ, who preserved them from a fall and merited grace and blessedness for them...

4. Of the Calvinists, such as Calvin on chapter 1 of Ephesians and chapter 1 of Colossians, Bucanus, Philippus Caesar, Rivetus,"

of the] Leiden professors, Zanchius, teaching that even the angels had need of Christ as mediator, not for redemption from sin, but for the preservation and confirmation of themselves in their concreated holiness and grace, partly because they were not outside the danger of falling, and partly because their own justice and obedience before God is lacking and imperfect, and thus they have need of pardon and a more perfect justice, or so that their justice, which is lacking before God, might be covered by the justice of Christ.

Otto Brunfels says: "The cross of Christ profited not only men, but also angels, and every creature has been purged by the cross of the Lord."

5. Of the Socinians, such as Enjedinus, asserting: "That regeneration or reformation made through the blood of the cross of Christ pertains also to the good angels," and also that the evil angels have been restored through Christ, because many evil spirits repented after the coming of Christ and were reconciled to God. (L. c. q. 7. f. 678.) §

33. In their blessed life, the good angels perform various operations, some of which pertain to their very blessedness, while others are ministerial, by which the angels serve God and Christ the God-man and promote the salvation of men.

For blessedness does not consist in idleness, but partly implies a certain activity in itself, and partly, moreover, admits of many operations to be exercised by those who are blessed.

For this reason, the angels, although already blessed, and that πάντες, all (with no one, not even of the highest order, excepted), are πνεύματα λειτουργικά, spirits destined for public service and performing it. Heb. 1:14.

As to their Creator and Lord and the author of their blessedness, to whom they cannot but be subject, they therefore perform His word and hearken to His voice (Ps. 103:21), and do His will in heaven (Matt. 6:10).

God, however, uses their ministry not out of any need, but by His free will and the sweet disposition of His providence. Προσκυνοῦντες αὐτῷ,

worshipping Him, as if bowed down or prostrate at His feet (Heb. 6:1), διακονοῦντες αὐτῷ, ministering to Him, executing or dispensing what is committed and entrusted to them (Matt. 4:11), and they perform this even to Christ according to His human nature (which is evident from the l. c.), since He is, even in this way, made a participant in divine majesty.

Because of the will of God, by whom they are sent, ἀπεσταλμένοι, for human services; and out of an affection of charity as toward friends and co-heirs of salvation (Heb. 1:14). §

34. The actions of the former kind are partly those in which the essential blessedness of the angels consists, and they are specifically acts of intuitively knowing God, acts of most intensely loving God who is clearly known; partly those which add a certain accidental blessedness to the angels, namely, acts of understanding other objects specially revealed by God or perceived through experience in the church, e.g., the mystery of the incarnation, the conversion of a sinful man; to which, likewise, on the part of the will, acts of love and joy are added.

See what we said in § 28 and 29. For the blessedness of the angels certainly does not reject an accidental increase; just as also on the part of men who are to be blessed, there are degrees of glory, as will be taught below.

Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between the essential blessedness of the angels... and accidental blessedness, which consists in the revelation of new mysteries, in love and joy outside of God, namely, that which arises from the conversion and repentance of sinners, and in this the angels can progress, as is evident from Luke 15:7; this increase of blessedness, however, will last only until the day of the final judgment." (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 675.)

See Luke 1:26 and 31; ch. 2:13; Luke 15:7 and 10.

For in Luke 2:15, the glorification of God itself is a sign of joy, and ch. 15:10, χαρά ἐνώπιον τῶν ἀγγέλων τοῦ θεοῦ, joy before the angels of God, is said to exist.

On both sides, the love of the angels is presupposed. For they glorify God as the good whom they love; they congratulate men as friends; they rejoice over the conversion of those whom they love as their own, and for whom they wish every best thing. §

35. The actions of the latter kind concern partly individual pious men, partly the hierarchical states themselves that are to be guarded and whose benefits are to be promoted. To whom they minister to God in such a way that they simultaneously serve men. As in general, and as men are viewed, without regard to a certain state or order. Or the sacred classes or orders of men within the church, where some preside, others are subject.

Luther: "God ordained three hierarchies against the devil, namely, the economy, the polity, and the church." (Opp. lat. Jen. I, 524. b.)

Brentius: "The state is not in the church, but the church is in the state." (Gelehrter Männer Briefe von Schumacher. III, 193. sq.) §

36. The angels minister to individual pious persons when they protect them in the very beginning of life and in infancy, serve those who are more adult in every honest function, and finally are present to those who are dying.

Whether a certain angel has been given to every man for his guardianship began to be discussed long ago. This is certain: the guardianship of a man is not to be assigned to one angel in such a way that he is deprived of the help of the rest. Yet it may probably be said that one angel is ordained for the guardianship of every pious person, and that, extraordinarily, many angels are sent to individual believers. See the blessed Gerhard, *Isag. LL. Disp. XIII. § 7*. Cf. Gen. 32:2; 2 Kings 6:17.

Quenstedtius: "Whether one or more angels have been given by God to each of the faithful for their guardianship is a problematic question, not an article of faith. ... When Christ says in Matt. 18:10: 'Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven,' it does not follow from this that one certain angel is perpetually attached to each of the τών μικρών, but only this is said, that angels are destined in general for their care. Moreover, the scope of Christ in this place is merely that little ones are not to be despised, whether they be such physically, ethically, or politically, since God employs even heavenly angels for their guardianship and protection. The inference would be more probable if the Holy Spirit spoke in the singular number about the angel of each one of those little ones, and not indefinitely about the angels of those little ones. — Obs.

The Greek fathers were confirmed in their opinion by a false interpretation of the version of the Seventy interpreters. Deut. 32:8: 'He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.' ... That passage in Acts 12:15: 'It is his angel' (these are the words of the faithful gathered in the house of Mary in Jerusalem, when St. Peter, having been miraculously freed from prison, was knocking at the doors at night), some take to refer to a human messenger sent by Peter from the prison. ... But because the word άγγελος is commonly taken in Scripture for a spirit, others more correctly understand the word άγγελον not as some human messenger, but as a heavenly spirit. Yet it does not necessarily follow from this that every believer has one assiduous and permanently attached angel. For the consequence is not valid: the Christians gathered in the house of Mary believed that the apostle Peter had a peculiar guardian angel, and indeed at the time when he was held in prison: therefore, such an angel is assigned and attached by God to all, and indeed perpetually. It is not valid, I say, to move from an eminent apostle to individual men. Nor is the reason for God’s guardianship over profane and impious men the same as it is over the pious, and indeed the eminent ones. Therefore, this passage, which Nazarius in his *Controversiae* calls a testimony more significant than all others, does not prove that individual angels are deputed by God for the guardianship of individual men, both faithful and unfaithful. Distinguish between the opinions of certain people, and indeed common people, and the dogma of the whole church. ... Distinguish between the assertion of Scripture and the assertion or conjecture of men who are introduced speaking in Scripture. Certainly, not everything is sound that was sometimes brought forth by the Jews, or even by the disciples of Christ themselves while He was still living on earth. It is not credible that guardian angels assume and mimic the appearance, figure, habit, voice, and gesture of those whose guardians they are considered to be. For such things are not simulated except for the sake of deceiving and deluding. The devil is accustomed to represent men. ... Although not a few of the fathers, and indeed Luther himself in the morning and evening prayer prescribed in the Catechism ('Let your holy angel be with me,' etc.), speak often of a guardian angel, yet that is by no means to be understood exclusively." (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 686. 690. sq.)

### Concerning Angels: Thus, they are called the angels of the children, that is, destined for their…

Thus, they are called the angels of the children, that is, destined for their care, Matt. 18:10. The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear God and delivers them, Ps. 34:7. It is commanded to the angels by God that they guard the man who trusts in God in all his ways, etc., Ps. 91:11-12. Thus, they are read to have admonished Joseph, the husband of Mary, concerning present matters, Matt. 1. PART I. CHAP. III.

19. 20. 2, 13. 19., to have forewarned Cornelius the centurion, Acts 10:3, 5, to have forewarned of future things, Rev. 1:1, 22:6, 16, to provide aid for avoiding evil, Ps. 91:11, 12, to defend in evils, as Daniel in the lions' den, Dan. 6:22, to rescue from evils, by the example of Peter, Acts 12:7, and of many apostles at once, Acts 5:18, 19, to have provided comfort to the fearful: to Zechariah, Luke 1:13, to Mary, v. 30, to the shepherds, c. 2:10, to the women coming to the sepulcher of Christ, Matt. 28:5, Mark 16: 6.

And just as evil [angels] labor to inflict upon men Typhonic winds, hailstorms, locusts, diseases, plague, and other evils of that kind: so, on the contrary, there is no doubt that good [angels] assist in their own way with εὐετηρίαν [a good season], tranquility, and moderate winds and fruitful rains, preserve the healthfulness of the air, and show remedies against diseases, writes Er. Schmidius on Heb. 1, and refers to that place in John 5:4 concerning the angel moving the water in the pool of Bethesda. He adds: Thus there is no doubt that in thermal springs, metal mines, and the like, the λειτουργίαν [ministry] of angels is present by God’s command. But how few recognize these things! p. 1297.

Just as they are said to have carried the soul of Lazarus into Abraham’s bosom, Luke 16: 22. Not as if the separated soul could not move itself, but to signify an escort, done for the sake of honor, or because angels are guides to souls, showing them where they must go, according to Chrysostom, Homily XXIX on Matthew, Vol. II of his Works, fol. m. 270. C. D. § 37.

To the office of the angels in relation to the ecclesiastical state belongs the fact that they promote the ministry of the Word, and specifically, that they were present as ministers at the promulgation of the Mosaic law;a that they announced Christ’s advent in the flesh;b that they hinder the introduction of idolatry into the church;c [and] they are present at sacred assemblies.d See Deut. 33:2 and Gal. 3:19, where it is said ὁ νόμος διαταγεὶς δι’ ἀγγέλων, the law ordained through angels. Which our theologians explain concerning the sound of trumpets stirred up by angels. Compare Acts 7:53. Luke 1:26, c. 2:9. Jude v. 9. For it is believed that that dispute of the angel with Satan over the body of Moses arose from this: that Satan was striving to bring to light the body of Moses, which had been hidden by God, in order to provide the Israelites an occasion for idolatry, and therefore the good angel opposed him.

See 1 Cor. 11:10, where Paul draws an argument to persuade women more easily to observe modesty of dress in sacred assemblies from the presence of the angels, who are lovers of good order and decorum. Compare 1 Tim. 5:21, where Paul, having exhorted Timothy at length regarding diligence in his holy office, adjures him by the sight of the angels. And it is certain that the angels, being present, celebrate God together with us, and remove not a few impediments.

38. The angels serve the political estate in such a way that they prevent the bonds of the commonwealth from being broken, assist and defend the magistrate and his ministers, ward off dangers, and afflict wicked enemies. Thus, in Dan. 10:13, it is said that God sent an angel into the court of the King of the Persians at a time when, through the zeal and work of either evil angels or evil officials and counselors, religion and justice seemed about to perish, so that, their efforts being suppressed, tranquility and public safety might be preserved. Thus we read in Daniel 6:22 that an angel sent by God shut the mouths of the lions, so that they could not harm Daniel, a chief minister of the kingdom, who was undergoing danger for the glory of God. Just as in 2 Kings 19:35 and Isa. 37:36 it is narrated that the angel of the Lord came to the aid of the pious King Hezekiah, who was attacked by the Assyrians in an unjust war, and delivered the hostile army to slaughter. §

39. They minister to the domestic economy by promoting the marriages of the pious, guarding family property, and protecting the pledges of the family, the children. Abraham testified that he hoped for this when procuring a marriage for his son, Gen. 24:7. See Job 1:10, where God is said to have hedged or surrounded his house with a wall, in the same sense in which Ps. 34:7 says that God sends an angel round about those who fear Him. See Matt. 18:10.

ANTITHESES to §§ 35—39.

Quenstedtius: " 1. Of the Gentiles; for heathendom, that fertile and prolific mother of monsters, once brought forth genii, the tutelary guardians of men, places, regions, cities, and houses... 2. Of the Rabbis and Cabbalists...

3. Of the Mohammedans. Regarding the Mohammedan opinion, see Phil. Lonizer, Vol. I of the Turkish Chronicles, where he says: 'It is the firm opinion of all Mohammedans that to every infant, as soon as they are born, two angels are added, one of whom guards the right side, the other the left.'...

4. Of some of the Fathers, especially the Greeks. For the opinion derived from the inventions of the poets, Platonists, and Stoics, and from Jewish pits, which reached Christians in the early church, is that individual angels are assigned to individual men, especially the faithful, for their custody... Primasius, in his epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 1, asserts that to each of the faithful, from the moment of birth, or rather from the time of baptism, an angel is given by God for their custody... And famous is that saying of Bernard, sermon 12 on Ps. 91: 'In every corner, in every place, have reverence for your angel, and do not dare to do in his presence what you would not dare to do in mine.'

5. Of certain of the Fathers, such as Origen..., Chrysostom, hom..." Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. II. 9 PART I. CHAP. III.

III. to the Colossians, and the author of the imperfect work on Matthew, homily V, who assert: That individual men have not only a good angel by whom they are defended, but also an evil one by whom they are attacked.

6. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who establish seven principal angels to whom the care and government of the Church and the whole world is determined.

Salmeron notes here that those seven angels are called by some: Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel, Saathiel, Ehudiel, Barachiel.

Indeed, the first three names, such as Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael, are found in the Holy Scriptures; but they added Uriel, Saathiel, Ehudiel, and Barachiel partly from the 4th book of Esdras, and partly from I know not where.

They make them, I say, certain universal guardians..., or guardians of individual men, who are specifically called guardian angels; concerning whom they posit these things as certain and indubitable:

1. That a good guardian angel is appointed to individual men, as much to the elect as to the reprobate, as much to the Gentiles as to the Christians, even to the Antichrist himself.

See the Scholastics on Book II of the Sentences. Although the Master of the Sentences, Lombard, doubts whether one angel might have the care of many; Thomas, however, in Part I of the Summa, q. 103, teaches that "individual angels are deputed to the custody of individual men." The same is maintained by those whom Gabriel Vasquez praises in great number; Becanus says: "It is the common opinion of the Fathers that a proper guardian angel is attributed to each of the faithful."

2. They maintain that an evil angel is also assigned to individual men, but deputed by the prince of demons. And this one they call the exercising demon...

7. Of certain Calvinists, such as Jerome Zanchius, who posits this thesis: "It is probable and more in agreement with the Holy Scriptures that to each of the elect, ordinarily, a certain and proper angel, who is his perpetual guardian and companion, is assigned by God from birth even to the end of life; but that extraordinarily, several are sometimes sent to him by God for the sake of greater consolation, according to God's good pleasure."

Likewise Alsted, Vossius, and Hugo Grotius, who admit the opinion concerning a good guardian angel assigned to individual believers partly as probable, and partly defend it openly.

8. D. Homeji, who thinks that the aforementioned opinion approaches most closely to the truth. (L. c. f. 686. sqq.) §

40. Finally, there will be a peculiar office of the angels, which they will perform on the last day, when they will accompany Christ as He approaches for judgment and will proclaim His advent with the sound of trumpets, will gather men from all parts of the world, will separate the pious from the impious, will place the former at the right hand of Christ, having led them to meet Him in the air, and will immediately cast the latter, established at the left of the Judge, into hell. See Matt. 25:31. 1 Thess. 4:15, 16. Matt. 24: 31. Mark 13:27. Matt. 13:41 and 49. Matt. 25:32. 1 Thess. 4:17. Matt. 25:32. Matt. 13:42, 50.

41. On account of those perfections with which we have seen the good angels to be endowed, and because they greatly favor and benefit us, it is certainly fitting that we should hold them in high regard, love them, and take care not to offend them by evil actions. For what the Augsburg Confession, Art. XXI, teaches is owed to the holy dead (namely, that their memory may be set forth so that we may imitate their good works), the same is rightly shown to the angels, especially since it is otherwise evident that the angels take an interest in our actions. See 1 Cor. 11:10; in this place, § 37, note d. §

42. However, it is not fitting to direct our prayers to the angels. For this is either impious and idolatrous, or at the very least useless and ill-advised. Namely, if we direct religious prayers with confidence to them as if they were the bestowers of spiritual goods. For whatever those prayers may be, it must be admitted that Scripture provides us with no command, nor any example or promise. And from where, I ask, will it be permitted to know that the angels understand our prayers, or that they delight in them? Indeed, in Revelation 19:10 and chapter 22:8-9, the angel simply and consistently rejects the worship of adoration, with the reason added that he is a fellow servant of John and a companion in the faith, and that God (in opposition to all who are not God, but are fellow servants among themselves, and thus God alone) is to be adored. It is indeed clear that the angel acts not out of affected humility, but seriously and for solid reasons, and does not distinguish between degrees of religious worship, of which one belongs to God alone and another to himself.

Deut. SS, 2. et Gal. 3, 19., ubi dicitur ό νόμος διαταγε)ς δι Αγγέλων, lex ordinata per angelos. Quod de sono tubarum ab angelis excitato nostrates exponunt. Conf. Act. 7, 53. Luc. 1, 26. cap. 2, 9. Creditur enim lis illa angeli cum satana super corpore Mosis hinc exorta fuisse, quod satanas corpus Mosis a Deo occultatum producere in lucem niteretur ad praebendam Israelitis occasionem idololatriae, ideoque obstitisse angelum bonum.

Vid. 1 Cor. 11, 10., ubi argumentum ad persuadendam feminis facilius modestiam vestitus in coetibus sacris observandam ab angelorum boni ordinis et decoris amantium praesentia petit Paulus. Confer. 1 Tim. 5, 21., ubi Paulus Timotheum sollicitudinis in munere sancto prolixe monitum per angelorum conspectum obtestatur. Et certum est, angelos praesentes una nobiscum celebrare Deum, neque pauca removere impedimenta.

XXI. (scilicet memoriam eorum proponi posse, ut imitemur bona opera illorum), id similiter angelis recte exhibetur, praesertim, quod angelos actionibus nostris interesse alias constet. Vid. 1 Cor. 11, 10.; h. l. § 37. not. d.§

42. Preces autem nostras ad angelos dirigere non decet. Hoc enim vel impium et idololatricum a est, vel saltem inutile et inconsultum.b Nempe si preces religiosas cum fiducia ad ipsos tanquam largitores bonorum spiritualium dirigamus. Qualescunque enim sint preces illae, fatendum tamen est, Scripturam mandatum nullum, nec exemplum aut promissum ullum nobis suppeditare. Et unde, quaeso, cognoscere licebit, angelos intdligere preces nostras, aut illis ddectarit Imo Apocal. 19, 10. et cap. 22, 8. 9. angelus simpliciter et constanter repudiat cultum adorationis, ratione addita, quod conservus Johannis et consors fidei, ac Deus (in oppositione ad omnes, qui non sunt Deus, sed inter se conservi, adeoque solus Deus) adorandus sit. Quod quidem planum est, angelum non ex affectata humilitate, sed serio et propter solidas rationes agere, nec distinguere inter gradus religiosi cultus, quorum aliquis Deo soli, alius sibi competat.


### Concerning Angels: Whence, having regard for this passage, Augustine says excellently in his book…

Whence, having regard for this passage, Augustine says excellently in his book *On True Religion*, ch. LV: "We honor the angels with charity, not with servitude, nor do we build temples to them. For they do not wish to be honored by us in such a way, because they know that we ourselves, when we are good, are temples of the Most High God." Smalcald Articles: "Even if the angels in heaven pray for us..., it does not follow that the angels and saints are to be invoked or adored by us," etc. (II, 2, p. 305.) Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between *adorare* [to adore], insofar as it signifies showing a sign of honor and reverence by an outward gesture of the body, or even civil worship itself, signified by external gestures of the body—and in this way adoration can be deferred to angels as well as to excellent men—and *adorare*, insofar as it denotes worshiping, invoking, and placing hope in someone on account of the eminence of their omnipotence and holiness and as the author and giver of every good, or religious worship itself; and in this way, only God is to be adored. And so, since *adorare* is used in the Scriptures indifferently for both civil and religious worship, one should not immediately understand religious adoration wherever the name of adoration is found. Therefore, Becanus is mistaken, who, when he reads that Abraham, Lot, and Balaam adored angels, immediately concludes that they adored them religiously..." PART I. CHAP. III.

That distinction of the Papists between *latria* and *dulia*, as if the former were owed to God alone, while the latter could be deferred to angels, is a matter fabricated and devised both in its substance and in its terminology outside of, beyond, and against Scripture. For the term «t δονλείας and λατρείας is used throughout the Scriptures just as much for the civil worship of creatures as for the religious worship of God alone; as for the substance of some intermediate worship between religious and non-religious or civil being denoted by the term δονλείας, there is no trace of it in Scripture. . . There is no doubt that an officious δουλεία can be deferred to angels, which may also be called civil, insofar as they belong to the same city with us (Heb. 12:22), (provided, of course, they appear to us), but certainly not a religious δονλεία.“ (L. c. c. 11. s. 2. q. 10. f. 692. sq.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis:

1. Of the ancient Platonists, who wished for demons to be considered as intermediaries in nature, dignity, and place between God and men. . . and therefore to be religiously worshipped and appeased with sacrifices. . .

2. Of the Jews, who were also angel-worshippers. . .

3. Of the ancient heretics, who already in the time of the apostles, under the pretext of humility, wished to introduce θρησκείαν άγγελων, the worship of angels, Col. 2:18. . . . Likewise of the successors of Simon Magus, such as the Cainites, whom Theodoret testifies, along with Epiphanius, to have worshipped and invoked angels. . .

4. Of the Socinians, who teach that angels could have been adored and religiously worshipped in the Old Testament, but that today this ought not to be done. . .

5. Of the Papists, who commonly contend that angels were rightly adored and religiously worshipped in the Old Testament, and that they are to be adored and religiously worshipped today; that is, that prayers may rightly be poured out to angels as mediators between God and men, and that they are to be pursued with some worship intermediate between civil and religious, which nevertheless must be referred to the latter; and this is evident from their theology and practice. . . The Council of Trent strikes with its brutal anathema those who deny that the saints (meaning angels and deceased saints) are to be supplicated, sess.

25. The words of the council are: ‘They think impiously who maintain that it is foolish to supplicate, by voice or mind, the saints reigning in heaven’ (to supplicate someone by mind is properly to adore religiously and divinely, as Gerhard teaches.). . . Bellarmine. . . makes them omnipresent: ‘for there is none of these,’ he says, ‘who does not see all things everywhere,’ l. I. de b. s. c. 20. respons. ad 6.; omniscient: ‘It is not true,’ he says, ‘what is assumed, that the saints are ignorant of what we ask of them’; omnipotent: ‘therefore, who can rightly deny that they (angels, or holy men) are not only powerful, but clearly omnipotent?’” (L. c. f. 693. sq.) § 43. The fall or first sin of the evil angels, through which they departed from their concreated goodness and became evil, is not sufficiently clear as to what kind it was; it is commonly thought to have been pride. Or an inordinate self-complacency and affectation of divine honor and dominion. Indeed, the spirit lurking in the serpent, Gen. 3:5, seduced Eve with the vain promise of a unique likeness to God; and because he wished to be adored by Christ, Matt. 4:9, just as he produced a specimen of consummate pride, so it is thought that he first polluted himself with this sin. Because pride is also called the beginning of all sin, Ecclesiasticus ch. 10:14, it is gathered from this that the origins of the diabolical sin, which was the first of all, are found there. Cf. Gerhard, Isag. Disp. V. § 11. cap. IX. § 8. 9.

Quenstedtius: "That pride was the first sin of the angels is probably gathered: 1. From 1 Tim. 3:6: 'Lest he be puffed up, τυφωθείς (Vulg.: lifted up into pride), and fall into the condemnation of the devil,' i.e., lest he incur the same condemnation which Satan himself suffered through arrogance. Thus Chrysostom, Gerhard, and others. . . 2. From the temptation. . . 3. From the perpetual effort by which he strives to transfer the glory of God to himself. . . This opinion is also approved by the blessed Luther in Genesis 1. Basil the Great, Cyprian, and Bernard join envy to pride." (L. c. s. 2. q. 12. f. 729.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: The Manichaeans and Priscillianists maintained that certain angels are evil not by a fall, but by origin, i.e., that they were always evil from the beginning of their existence or by their nature. . . Regarding the sin in particular, they maintain: 1. Josephus and Philo, as well as some of the fathers, such as Justin, Athenagoras, Origen, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Lactantius, etc., that the first sin of the devils was intemperance or luxury and lust. For they think that some angels defiled themselves with lusts and desired the cohabitation of women. . . 2. Others think that the devil aspired to the hypostatic union and envied that excellence of human nature, as Suarez." (L. c. f. 728.) §

44. The fall, however, is the gathering of evil angels under a certain leader or prince, whom Scripture calls the devil, and who, either by example or by his persuasion, induced the others into the fellowship of the same sin. In the singular, see John 8:44, and this is the ἄρχων τῶν δαιμονίων, the prince of the demons, Luke 11:15, the ancient serpent and Satan, Rev. 12:9. Quenstedtius: "By 'the devil' is understood in this place (John 8:44) not some prince of the devils, as in Matt. 12:24, but the whole troop of malignant spirits, because these predicates belong to all evil angels." (L. c. s. 1. th. 30. f. 640.)

Hence it is that Scripture makes mention of the angels of the devil, Matt. 25:41, Rev. 12:7.

Quenstedtius: "In what order the evil angels sinned, whether all at once, or one after another, or whether first one fell and induced others to ἀποστασίαν and the fall by his example and persuasion, the scholastics dispute about this, but it is without Scripture." (L. c. s. 1. th. 34. f. 643.) §

45. Having committed sin, all those angels lost the grace concreated in them, and thus fell into most bitter misery, without hope of restoration. PART I. CHAPTER III.

a) For God did not grant to the angels, as He did to men, a time and place for repentance, but utterly denied them the aid of grace; for the reasons for this divine counsel handed down by the fathers, see Gerhard, loc. cit., Disput., chap. IX, § 17. Quenstedtius: "Scripture nowhere teaches that any remedy was prepared for their fall, or that a space for repentance was left to those who fell; indeed, Peter, in 2 Ep. 2:4, denies that God spared the sinning angels at all. That the devils cannot perform saving repentance is evident from the fact that they are destitute of a mediator." (L. c. c. 14, s. 2, q. 5, f. 827.)

The same: "Why God, after the fall of the angels and of men, willed to show Himself φιλάνθρωπον [a lover of mankind], not φιλάγγελον [a lover of angels], the fathers and scholastics bring forward these probable reasons: 1. because the angelic nature did not perish entirely, but only a part, whereas the human nature perished entirely in one; which Augustine notes in Enchirid. c. 29; 2. because the angelic nature fell not tempted by another, while the human nature was tempted and seduced by another; the former fell through malice, the latter through infirmity." (L. c. f. 829.) §

46. Indeed, their intellect, being destitute not only of the light of grace but also of the light of glory, and fixed in the contemplation of divine wrath and their own misery, is as it were blunted and lacks a right judgment concerning the doing of good. This is what is said in John 8:44, that there is no truth in the devil. For just as the truth, in which Satan did not stand when first created, was full integrity and a power and perfection concreated for rightly exercising acts suitable to himself, which primarily implied a right judgment concerning things to be done; so, falling from the truth, and when truth is denied to be in him, by this very fact it is known that he lacks a true and sound judgment concerning things to be done; whence he is not truthful in speaking, but a liar, a deceiver, and a slanderer, etc. Moreover, the corruption of the diabolical intellect is also accustomed to be shown from this, that Satan promoted the death of Christ with such zeal, not perceiving that from it the greatest adversity was brought upon himself. But whatever natural knowledge remains in the evil angels, it adds nothing of happiness to them, being rejected by God.

Quenstedtius: "The devil says to Christ: 'If you are the Son of God,' etc. Either, therefore, he knows that Jesus is the Son of God, not by the certainty of knowledge, but by the conjecture of a firm opinion, so that he is to be considered as suspecting rather than knowing, as Hilary speaks; or, if he knows for certain that He is the Son of God, he was impudently insane, as one who thought that by his own cunning and stratagems he would subvert God Himself and entice Him to evil... There is in the evil angels some knowledge of supernatural things, but joined with extreme hatred of God and of the good angels and pious men, as well as with ignorance, doubt, error, and forgetfulness, Matt. 4:6, John 13:2, 1 Cor. 2:8... Their knowledge of natural things, both natural and experimental, is remarkable: 1. natural, from the subtlety of their spiritual nature and the sharpness of their judgment; 2. experimental, and that remarkable, from long-time usage; hence blessed Luther says somewhere: 'The devil is a doctor not promoted, but experienced.'" (L. c. c. 11, s. 1, th. 36 sqq., f. 644 sq.)

Latin:

Unde, hujus loci ratione habita, praeclare Augustinus Lib. de vera Relig. cap. LV. Honoramus angelos, ait, caritate, non servitute, nec eis templa construimus. Nolunt enim sic se honorari a nobis, quia nos ipsos, cum boni sumus, templa summi Dei esse norunt.Articuli Smalcaldici: ,,Etsi angeli in coelo pro nobis orent. . ., inde non sequitur, angelos et sanctos a nobis esse invocandos, adorandos“ etc. (II, 2. p. 305.) Quenstedtius: ״Dist. inter ro adorare, quatenus significat exteriori corporis gestu honoris et reverentiae signum exhibere vel etiam ipsum cultum civilem, gestibus corporis externis significatum, et sic adoratio deferri potest tam angelis, quam hominibus excellentibus, — et ro adorare, quatenus notat aliquem propter omnipotentiae et sanctitatis eminentiam et ut auctorem et datorem omnis boni interiori mentis intentione colere, invocare et spem in aliquem ponere sive ipsum cultum religiosum, et sic nonnisi Deus est adorandus. Adeoque cum adorare in Scripturis indifferenter de cultu tam civili, quam religioso, usurpetur, non statim, ubi adorationis nomen reperitur, adoratio religiosa intelligenda est. Fallit ergo Becanus, qui, ubi legit, Abrahamum, Lothum, Bileamum adorasse angelos, confestim colligit, adorasse religiose. . . PART. I. CAP. III.

Distinctiuncula illa pontificiorum inter latriam et duliam, quasi illa soli Deo debita sit, haec angelis deferri possit, est qua rem, qua voces extra, praeter et contra Scripturam conficta et excogitata. Vox enim «t δονλείας et λατρείας tam de cultu creaturarum civili, quam de cultu religioso solius Dei in Scripturis passim usurpatur; quoad rem cultus alicujus intermedii inter religiosum et non-religiosum sive civilem voce δονλείας denotari, in Scriptura nullum est vestigium. . . Officiosam δουλείαν angelis deferri posse, quae civilis etiam dici poterit, quatenus ad unam civitatem nobiscum pertinent Hebr. 12,12., nullum est dubium (si sci. nobis appareant), non vero δονλεία religiosa.“ (L. c. c. 11. s. 2. q. 10. f. 692. sq.) 46. Nempe intellectus illorum, non solum lumine gratiae, verum etiam lumine gloriae destitutus atque in contempiatione irae divinae ac suae miseriae defixus, velut obtunditur et caret recto de bonis agendis judicio.a Hoc est, quod Joh. 8, 44. dicitur, veritatem non esse in diabolo. Quemadmodum enim veritas, in qua satanas primum conditus non stetit, erat plena integritas et ad actus sibi convenientes recte exercendos concreata δόναμίς ac perfectio, quae rectum de rebus agendis judicium inprimis importabat; sic excidens a veritate satanas, et quando veritas in ipso esse negatur, hoc ipso cognoscitur carere vero et sano de rebus agendis judicio; unde et in dicendo verax non sit, sed mendax, deceptor et calumniator etc. Alias autem corruptio intellectus diabolici etiam hinc ostendi solet, quod satanas mortem Christi tanto studio promovit, non sentiens, inde sibi maximam contrahi adversitatem. ### Concerning Angels: …

§ 47.

The will, deprived of the supreme love of God and the joy to be drawn therefrom, and thus turned away from God, is hardened in evil, and is therefore miserably tormented and afflicted. Not by any peculiar influx or determination of God, nor by an absolute decree of God, but on account of that withdrawal of the perfections of the intellect and will, which was merited by the preceding sin. For, knowing that there is a God, whose idea they cannot fully erase from their mind; and knowing the same to be supremely powerful and, in Himself and in the other good angels, supremely good, but to themselves irreconcilably adverse and always imminent and severe, they not only do not love Him, but they turn away from Him and oppose Him; and since they know that they have brought this evil upon themselves by their own, as they say, yoke, they are angry with themselves and, as it were, quarrel with themselves (pursuing both God and themselves with hatred at the same time). Whence, since they know that it is better for others than for themselves, envy of the happiness of others and perpetual sorrow on account of the continuous presence of their own evils necessarily arise. § 48.

Therefore, the freedom of the will of the damned angels does not imply indifference toward good or evil, or toward several goods, but is concerned with particular evils, insofar as they can choose or not choose this one from among several, and likewise choose another. Under the appearance of good, indeed, but which is not truly good, their own corrupted judgment deceiving them. § 49.

The operations which the evil angels exercise are various; but those which tend toward the destruction both of individual men and of hierarchical states ought especially to be noted. § 50. Thus they endeavor to harm partly the bodies of men, so as to inflict diseases; partly external goods or wealth, so as to corrupt or take them away; partly the soul itself, so as to turn it away from God and draw it into damnation through sins. PART I. CHAP. III.

Thus, in Luke 13:11, the woman who was bent over, συγχήπτουσα, is said to have a spirit of infirmity as the cause of this, and in verse 16, it is said that Satan had held her bound until then. Quenstedtius: "Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*, ch. 2, says: 'The legion of devils had no power over the herd of swine, unless they had obtained it from the Lord; how much less, then, do they have power over the sheep of God. I might say: the very bristles of the swine were numbered by God at that time, to say nothing of the hairs of the saints.'" (L. c. th. 52, p. 651.)

See the history of Job, ch. 1:12 ff. For what Christ affirms in Luke 22:31 concerning His disciples—that Satan had demanded (by a certain right of his own, certainly quite audaciously, sought) to sift them like wheat—points to the fact that Satan had determined to agitate and disturb the minds of the apostles with various temptations, to weaken their faith, and indeed, if he could, to shake it out and lead them to total, and even final, αποστασίαν through the scandal conceived from the passion of Christ. Similarly, the fact that Paul in Ephesians 6:11 and 12 commends spiritual armor in the struggle against evil spirits presupposes the assaults of these spirits, by which the salvation of souls is brought into jeopardy. Peter, however, in 1 Epistle 5:8-9, says that one must resist the enemy with faith and Christian vigilance, as he seeks whom he may devour, or whom he may lead to the extreme destruction of the soul. § 51. Particularly relevant here are spiritual obsession, through which Satan effectively impels the minds of impious men toward the worst crimes; and bodily obsession, by which Satan, according to his substance, dwells within the bodies of men and works in them by divine permission.

See Luke 22:3, where it is said that Satan entered into the heart (that is, the soul) of Judas; cf. John 13:27; he had put it into his heart, having insinuated into his mind this counsel and purpose, that he should betray Jesus, verse 2. Thus, in Ephesians 2:2, the prince of the world, the evil spirit, is said to ένεργειν, to work effectively in the sons of disobedience, that is, unbelieving men. And in 2 Corinthians 4:4, the god of this age is said to blind the minds of the unbelievers, lest the light of the gospel should shine upon them. Finally, in 2 Timothy 2:26, those who resist the ministry are said to be ίζωγρημένοι, captured like live beasts by Satan, and as if entangled in a snare, led according to his will. Quenstedtius: "An enormous example of spiritual obsession was Judas Iscariot... Already before this, indeed, (Satan) had put it into the heart of Judas to betray Christ (John 13:2), and indeed two days before that final supper he had entered into him, when he went to the chief priests and promised his Lord to them for the agreed-upon money (Luke 22:3); but he had entered there not by a bodily, but by a spiritual είσελεύσει, by persuading Judas to promise the betrayal of Christ to the Jews; but after the morsel, he entered (John 13:27) in order to carry out the promised crime, impelling him more vehemently and possessing him entirely, not indeed bodily, but spiritually."

OF ANGELS. Hence Augustine, tract. 62 on John, says: "Before, as a stranger he urged; now, he possesses as his own." Likewise the Pharisees, whom John the Baptist calls a brood of vipers in Matthew 3:7, because of the poison of sin and malice. Whence in John 8:44 they are said to be of their father the devil, not by creation or generation, but by imitation (1 John 3:8), and by the conformity of their works with the works of the devil. And that such possessed persons are still given today, both within the church and outside the church, is confessed by all.

The subject in which the soul of the impious person exists is not merely passive, but at the same time active, and behaving as a συνεργός (co-worker) of the devil. Hence it is said in John 8:44 that the impious wish to ποιεῖν (do) the desires of their father (the devil). For although Satan, whom he spiritually besets and possesses, solicits them to sin and rules them, they themselves not only delight in sins, but also perform them with the greatest pleasure.

The efficient cause of spiritual obsession is the devil (1 Pet. 5:8; Luke 11:24 ff.).

Spiritual obsession is described by its circumstances in Matthew 12:43 ff. and Luke 11:24 ff.: "When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, and coming, finds it (his former house) swept with brooms, then he goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there."

Obs.: 1. Who? The demon, that unclean spirit, who with his foul uncleanness, namely sins, contaminates everything, so that man, who is the throne and temple of God, becomes a sewer of the devil. Such is the heart, as is the indwelling devil. 2. What? He went out ejected, he returned invited, he walks wandering far and wide seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5:8). 3. Whence and from whom did he go out? From the man whom Christ had liberated through His word from Satan who was spiritually besetting him.

4. Why did Satan return? α. Because, wandering in desert places, in empty men, he did not find a habitation pleasing and convenient for himself; therefore he thought of retaking his former dwelling. β. Because the man from whom he had been ejected, thinking that he had been liberated by Christ from the power of Satan, lived securely in sins and returned to his former ways. 5. When did he return? When he saw this abandoned house of his, idle and prepared for his palate with vices, and vacant, as is added in Matthew 12:44, empty of the fear of God, flowing with pleasures. 6. With whom did he come? With seven spirits more wicked. The number seven is taken for many, according to the custom of the Hebrews; therefore, seven more wicked spirits are many other infernal spirits. But how are they πνεύματα πονηρότερα ἑαυτόν (spirits more wicked than himself), worse? Because, just as there is order even among evil spirits, so also one surpasses another in malice. With these companions of his, therefore, Satan dwells in such a man, who is given over to sloth, security, and other sins, as a king in his kingdom, as a master in his domicile.

7. What is the outcome of this return and indwelling? That the last condition of that man will be worse and more deteriorated than the former, namely because of malice and ingratitude toward God the benefactor, who had liberated him from the power of Satan.

The meritorious cause, and that which moves God to permit it, is the zeal for sinning. The devil does not beset men at will, as Synesius calls the devil an ἀθεὸν πνεῦμα (godless spirit), but by God's permission. For God, seeing that a man stubbornly resists the Holy Spirit, by a just judgment permits Satan to spiritually beset him and lead him from sins into sins.

The form of spiritual obsession consists 1. in the closer presence of the substance of the devil to the soul of the impious. For it is said to enter into him (John 13:27), to dwell in him (Luke 11:26), which κατοίκησις (indwelling) does not imply a mere approach of the devil through operations, but a substantial approximation and presence. 2. In an efficacious συνεργεία (co-operation) that propels one to any kind of wickedness. For the devil extremely besets the intellect of the impious, lest they see the light of the Gospel and understand what makes for their salvation (2 Cor. 4:4). He besets their will, that they may consent to evils; their appetite, that they may desire the poisoned delights of sins with the greatest pleasure. He besets their heart, lest they believe; their ears, lest they hear the word of God; their eyes, lest they behold the work of God; their tongue, lest they pray; their voice, lest they praise God; their hands, lest they do any good; their feet, lest they walk in the way of the righteous, etc.

Let the work of B. Chemnitz, *Harmonia Evangelica*, be read regarding spiritual obsession. PART I. CHAP. III.

65. p. 709. sq. 758. 978. The outcome of spiritual obsession is for the most part eternal destruction, John 8:21, 24. For Satan obsesses men for this reason, that they might make shipwreck of eternal life; for the most part, I say, because such obstinate sinners rarely repent, John 8:21, 24: "You will die in your sins." Blessed Gerhard rightly says in *Disput. Isagog.* p. 610: "Bodily obsession is more horrible, since it strikes the senses; but spiritual obsession is graver and more dangerous." (L. c. s. 1. th. 44. sqq. f. 648. sq.)

Who are therefore said to be ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς τοῦ διαβόλου, of the father the devil, as the Jews, John 8:44; or ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ, children of that evil one, Matt. 13:38, or of that enemy who is the devil, v. 39, malicious imitators of satanic morals, as being listeners to his words. For which reason they are said to do the desires of their father, John 8:44.

Latin:

§ 47.

Voluntas amore Dei summo et gaudio inde hauriendo privata atque ita a Deo aversa obduratur a in malo, adeoque misere angitur et affligitur.b Non ex peculiari influxu aut determinatione Dei, neque ex absoluto Dei decreto, sed propter illam perfectionum intellectus et voluntatis subtractionem antegresso delicto promeritam. Nempe cognoscentes, esse Deum, cujus ideam ex animo plene expungere nequeunt; eundem etiam summe potentem et in se quidem atque angelis aliis bonis summe bonum, sibi vero irreconciliabiliter adversum semperque imminentem ac severum, non solum non amant, sed aversantur eum, et adversantur ei; cumque seipsos, suo, quod ajünt, jugo malum hoc sibi attraxisse cognoscunt, sibi ipsis succernent, et quasi rixantur secum (Deum ita simul et seipsos odio prosequentes).
