### Concerning Angels: It is to be noted, however, also what the blessed Gerhard writes in *Harm

It is to be noted, however, also what the blessed Gerhard writes in *Harm. Evangel.* cap. CLXVIII. pag. 1161: "This (spiritual) obsession is so subtle that both those whom it occupies and others sometimes judge that those things which follow from satanic spiritual obsession proceed from the impulse of the Holy Spirit, as appears in the example of obstinate heretics." Indeed, it is said to be present not only, but to be in the bodies of men κατ’ οὐσίαν καὶ αὐτοπροσώπως. Moreover, there are many examples of the δαιμονιζομένων, the demoniacs or those obsessed by an evil demon, in the Scriptures. See Matt. 8:28, 31, 32; Mark 7:25 sqq.; Luke 4:35, 36.

Quenstedtius: "The form of bodily obsession consists in the indwelling of an evil spirit, or even of evil spirits, in the human body, occurring not only κατ’ ἐνέργειαν, but also κατ’ οὐσίαν itself. That unclean spirits dwell in the obsessed not only κατ’ ἐνέργειαν, but also κατ’ οὐσίαν, is proven by the express assertion of Christ in Luke 11:26, and likewise by the ejection and departure of devils in Matt. 12:43, Luke 8:2, 11:14, 24. Hence the scholastics rightly teach that obsession denotes 'the intimate and substantial presence of the devil in the obsessed,' and that demons enter the bodies of the obsessed substantially. They occupy the body either totally, when they permeate and affect it entirely, or partially, when they claim certain members for themselves, such as the tongue, Mark 9:17, or the tongue and eyes, Matt. 12:22, etc. However, for the form of obsession, there is required not only the indwelling of the devil, but also torment; see Matt. 9:32, 15:22, Mark 9:18, Luke 8:27. 'It is not enough,' says Thyraeus, 'that a demon has entered a man for him to be called obsessed; it is required, furthermore, that he has obtained from God the power to rage or act against him.' Very often also Satan most miserably afflicts men externally through assistance, but not through information or indwelling, as Job and Paul teach by their own example, whom no sane person would consider obsessed; for it does not follow: This man is tormented by Satan, therefore he is possessed by him. For possession or obsession requires both: both indwelling and torment, or that he be present in the man and harm him αὐτοπροσώπως." (L. c. th. 54. f. 651.)

Not only of the impious, but sometimes also of the pious; which experience also shows, and our own theologians gather from the analogy of similar afflictions, e.g., Job 2:12, whose body Satan most miserably afflicted, and Paul, 2 Cor. 12:7. For if Paul, such a great apostle, was buffeted by Satan, lest the magnitude of the revelations should exalt him; what wonder is it if the power of Satan is also granted for a time over the bodies of the pious? says Gerhard. c. Disp. XIV. cap. VIII. § 13.

OF ANGELS. It torments the human body, to be sure, and through its members performs various, wondrous, and sinful actions, from which also, if not individually, certainly collectively, as if from signs, true bodily obsession—distinct from epilepsy and other diseases or fascinations—is recognized.

Quenstedtius: "The proper signs of obsession are: 1. Knowledge of exotic or foreign languages, as well as arts and disciplines, which the obsessed have never learned before, and do not know any longer once delivered. 2. Knowledge and indication of hidden things and things done elsewhere in the most remote regions, as well as future things. 3. Strength greater than human, or preternatural power. 4. The exact representation of the voices of birds, sheep, oxen, etc., without the disposition of the organs. To these add 5. impurity of speech, 6. deformity of gestures, 7. horrendous shouting (Mark 5:5), 8. blasphemy of God and caviling against one's neighbor, 9. savagery and ferocity both against the body itself and against spectators (Matt. 8:28; 17:15; Mark 5:5; Acts 19:16). From these and similar signs, which, however, do not all occur at the same time in individual obsessed persons, but sometimes more, sometimes fewer, bodily obsession can be recognized. Yet singular circumspection is required here, lest we take those afflicted with more serious diseases for the obsessed." (L. c. th. 56. p. 652.)

This occurs when God, either immediately or mediately—through the intervention of the work of men, whether good (e.g., ministers of the church through the greater excommunication of enormous sinners, concerning which see 1 Cor. 5:3; 1 Tim. 1:20) or evil (those striving to harm others, e.g., through witchcraft or curses)—permits that some men be subjected to Satan.

Although the end of this obsession on the part of the obsessing Satan is partly the harm and destruction of the obsessed themselves, and partly that of other men; yet on the part of God, who permits this and who, by a severe judgment, avenges even more serious sins—contempt of the Word, carnal security, blasphemies, conspiracy with the devil, etc.—or who corrects and proves the pious with bodily chastisement, the end is the manifestation of His power, justice, and goodness, and the repentance, faith, and salvation of men, if not of the obsessed themselves, at least of others watching or hearing. §

52. Similarly, it pertains to this that demons delude men through specters and strive to destroy or afflict either the soul or the body. These things the Greeks call δράματα, and the Latins, moreover, call "visions" (visa) literally; and in a general signification, some are merely imaginative, arising from a dream, disease, or an evil conscience; others are truly such; and these again are either divine, from the immediate operation of God, or angelic, from the operation of good angels, or natural, arising from ignorance of physical causes or superstition, or artificial, or finally diabolical, which last species of specters pertains to this place. Although it must be admitted that not only those things which are presented to the sight, but also those which are presented to the hearing (and perhaps to other senses), pertain to the present matter. PART I. CHAP. III.

Such were those mentioned in Wis. 17:8 ff. concerning the plagues of the Egyptians, when indalmata, or images (or specters), troubled them; when disturbing sounds echoed around them and sad visions (phasmata) appeared with mournful countenances (tois katēphesin prosōpois); when a fire full of fear appeared of its own accord (automatē pyra phobou plērēs) and they were terrified by the vision, which was not to be looked upon, etc. And these were the games played by malakhei ra'im, angels of evils, concerning whom see Ps. 78:49, which the LXX also rendered as angelous ponērous. But also belonging to the class of specters are the se'irim, commonly called satyrs, appearing in the form of goats, concerning whom see Isa. 13:21 and 34:14; compared with Lev. 17:7 and

2 Chron. 11:15, together with Rev. 18:2.

Partly by terrifying, according to Wis. 17:1 ff., partly by inducing superstition, avarice, etc. § 53.

Specifically, they oppose the ecclesiastical estate when they watch over the spreading of heresies,a hinder the pious and salutary efforts of the ministers of the church,b lead listeners away from the pious meditation of the Word, so as to subvert their conversion and salvation,c and even excite persecutions against the doctrine and the Christian church. Thus the enemy (echthros ho diabolos) is said to sow tares in the field of the church, Matt. 13:27.

Paul in 1 Tim. 4:1-2 calls heresies doctrines of demons, that is, to be attributed to these authors. That the antichrist brings so much evil upon the church is said in 2 Thess. 2:8 to be done through the operation of Satan. That which happened to Paul in 1 Thess. 2:18, where he writes that he was hindered by Satan from coming to the Thessalonians once and again. For this is to take away the word from the hearts of the hearers, Luke 8:12.

And this is done in various ways, e.g., when he presents to men things that result in the matter of foreign thoughts, or excites prejudices and various affections, by which either forgetfulness or the worthlessness of the read or preached word is induced. § 54.

In the political state, demons suggest unjust and destructive counsels to those in powera and otherwise disturb the harmony of the republic in many ways.b Such was that concerning the numbering of the people, which he supplied to David, see 1 Chron. 21:1, and that given to Ahab, that he should attack the Syrians in war, 1 Kings 22:21-22. E.g., by sowing the seeds of discord, according to that trite saying: Divide and you shall rule.

55. In the economy [of the household], they lie in wait for the spouses themselves, for their children, and for the goods of the family. For example, by sowing strife or by soliciting to lust; which twofold snare Paul commands us to notice and avoid in 1 Cor. 7: 5. See the history of Job, chap. 1, and of the daughter who was δαιμονιζομένη, Matt. 15: 22. See the history of Job and of Tobias. §

56. Meanwhile, God Himself also uses the ministry of evil angels to chastise the pious in this world and to punish the impious, both in life and after death. See again the history of Job. See Ps. 78: 49. For the "angels of evils"—whether they are said to be angels intent on inflicting evils or damages, or the angels of evil men, in opposition to those who are destined for the heirs of salvation—in both respects are rightly understood as evil spirits. Compare what we said in note b to § 51 and note c to § 52. See Matt. 18:34. For although the words seem to be parabolic, yet, because it is added: "So also will my heavenly Father do to you," it is rightly understood concerning the sending of tormentors upon irreconcilable men, by whom they are afflicted without end, and for that reason, none are believed to be more correctly denoted than evil angels. Nor will the misery of these be mitigated thereby, the sense of which they will experience unceasingly.

Scherzerus: "As far as the devils are concerned, the question remains here: Will they also be the tormentors and executioners of the damned in hell? Whatever may have seemed right to others, we prefer the negative. α.

God blesses in heaven without the ministry of angels. Therefore, He also torments in hell without the ministry of devils. β. The devils themselves will be tormented. Therefore, they will not be the tormentors of others. Whence they beg to avoid the abyss, Luke 8:31, because of the torments awaiting them. γ. The devil sinned first and most gravely of all, and enticed men to sin. Therefore, he will be tormented more gravely than men; and thus he is not going to be the tormentor of men. δ. It is contrary to God's justice that He should appoint the seducer of men as their tormentor. For thus the lot of the seducer would be better than the lot of the seduced, which is repugnant to justice. ε. No evidence of that matter exists in the Holy Scriptures... Concerning the tormentors in Matt. 18:34, the stripes in Luke 12:48, and the beatings in Prov. 19:29, parabolic Scripture is not argumentative. Nor does it follow: because devils are tormentors in this life, they will also be so in the other. For many things are permitted in this age which, with the ends of God's μακροθυμία as it were closed, cannot be granted in the other." (System, loc. 24, p. 649 sq.)

Rambachius: "The devils will not be tormentors, as many imagine and as Gerhardus in locc. th. 1. de infern. § 73 and Dannhauerus in hodosoph. p. m. 1505 suppose. Likewise Fechtius in Sylloge p. 562." (Erläuterung der Grundlegung der Theologie, p. 1085.) PART I. CHAP. III.

57. The devil and his angels also have torments and pains prepared for them from hellfire. Beyond those punishments which were treated above in § 46 and 47, we are taught in Matthew 25:41 that the devil and his angels will be banished by the penal sentence of the Judge into the fire prepared for them. Certainly, it is evident from 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude v. 6 that, beyond that punishment which they sustain thus far, they are being kept for a certain new torment to be undergone at that great and final judgment. However, to wish to explain distinctly how fire, if it be corporeal, acts upon spirits, is more curious than useful and necessary.

Quenstedtius: "The torments are described symbolically by 'eternal fire' (Matthew 25:41) and by the 'lake of fire and brimstone' (Revelation 20:10, 14). Thus Peter (2 Ep. 2:4) and Jude (v. 6). Observe: 1. Peter puts the negative for the contrary affirmative: God did not spare the evil angels, i.e., He punished them most severely. 2. Peter and Jude explain what that punishment is. Three things, therefore, are designated: 1. The bonds by which they are held constrained, which are called 'chains of darkness' and 'eternal bonds under darkness.' But the bonds that are now for custody, so that they cannot rage with freedom, will be for punishment on that great day of judgment; and those which are now looser will then be most tight and most severe. 2. 'Tartarus' (which is a name proper to Peter, l.c.), in which they are detained as in a prison, and 'darkness,' under which they are reserved. For wherever the demons go and wherever they dwell, they carry their hell around with them, as Bede says in chapter 8 of James. Therefore, one must distinguish between the infernal state and the place of hell. They do indeed wander through the world now, yet they are chained and held constrained by bonds and wrapped in darkness, and they always drag their prison with them." (L.c. c. 11, s. 1, th. 36, f. 644 sq.)

The same: "Material fire cannot act upon spirits; for nothing can act outside the sphere of its object. And if it were to act, the spirit would be weaker than the body, which is absurd." (L.c. c. 14, s. q. 4, f. 821.)

Fechtius: "Fire that is not material and yet properly so called is like water that is not wet and yet properly so called. What that [fire] will be, if it is not elementary, is not clear." Roulius adds: "A threefold opinion is given concerning hellfire. Some maintain it is metaphorical, consisting in the torments of conscience; others, that it is elementary and of the same species as ours; others, in turn, that it is indeed properly so called, but of a nature different from the elementary. However, the reason adduced in the thesis is opposed to this latter opinion." (Sylloge, p. 95, 100.) §

58. Moreover, the punishments by which the evil angels are afflicted will be eternal. a) It is indeed called πυρ αιώνιον, χόλασις αιώνιος, see Matthew 25:41 and 46; πυρ ασβεστον, inextinguishable fire, Mark 9:43. Osiander: "Regarding the eventual salvation of the devils, Origen once erred with a gross error in the older church (Homily 9 on Jeremiah), which, not without nausea, was revived in the previous century around the beginning of the Reformation by the Anabaptist Joh. Denckius, who felt that God would eventually [save] all..."

Latin:

Notandum autem etiam, quod scribit b. Gerhardus Harm. Evangel. cap. CLXYIII. pag. 1161.: Haec obsessio (spiritualis) tam subtilis est, ut tum illi, quos occupat, tum alii quandoque judicent ab impulsu Spiritus Sancti ea proficisci, quae spiritualem obsessionem satanieam consequuntur, ut apparet in pertinacium haereticorum exemplo. Nempe non solum adesse, sed χατ’ ουσίαν χαι αυτοπροσώπως inesse corporibus hominum dicitur. Exempla autem των δαιμονιζορΑνων, daemoniacorum seu obsessorum a malo daemone, multa sunt in Scripturis. Vid. Matth. 8, 28. 31. 32. Mare. 7, 25. sqq. Luc. 4, 35. 36.

Quenstedtius: ״Forma corporalis obsessionis consistit in inhabitatione maligni spiritus, vel etiam malignorum spirituum in corpore humano facta non tantum κατ’ ενέργειαν, sed etiam κατ’ ουσίαν ipsam. Quod vero immundi spiritus non modo κατ’ ενέργειαν, sed etiam κατ’ ουσίαν in obsessis habitent, probat diserta Christi assertio Luc. 11, 26., itemque diabolorum ejectio et egressio Matth. 12, 43. Luc. 8, 2. 11, 14. 24. Hinc recte docent scholastici, quod obsessio notet,intimam et substantialem praesentiam diaboli in obsessis‘, quodque daemones corpora obsessorum substantialiter intrent. Occupant autem corpus vel totaliter, cum id totum permeant et afficiunt, vel partialiter, cum membra quaedam ejus sibi vendicant, ut linguam Marc. 9, 17., linguam et oculos Matth. 12, 22. etc. Ad formam autem obsessionis requiritur non solum diaboli inhabitatio, sed etiam excruciatio, vide Matth. 9, 32. 15, 22. Marc. 9, 18. Luc. 8, 27. ,Non satis est‘, inquit Thyranus, ,daemonium hominem intrasse, ut obsessus dicatur, requiritur praeterea, ut in eundem saeviendi vel agendi a Deo obtinuerit facultatem.‘ Saepissime etiam satan miserrime affligit homines extrinsecus per assistentiam, non vero per informationem aut inhabitationem, ut suo exemplo docent Jobus et Paulus, quos nemo sanus pro obsessis habebit; non enim sequitur: Hic a satana excruciatur, ergo ab eodem possidetur. Ad possessionem enim seu obsessionem utrumque requiritur, et inhabitatio et excruciatio, sive ut αυτοπροσώπως homini insit et noceat.“ (L. c. th. 54. f. 651.)

Non solum impiorum, verum aliquando etiam piorum; quod et experientia monstrat, et nostrates colligunt ex analogia similium afflictionum, v. g. Joh. 2, 12., cujus corpus satanas miserrime afflixit, etPauli 2. ad Cor. 12, 7. Quodsi enim Paulus, tantus apostolus, a satana colapkizatus est, ne magnitudo revelationum ipsum extolleret; quid mirum, si etiam satanae potestas ad tempus in corpora piorum concedatur? ait Gerh. c. Disp. XIV. cap. VIII. § 13.

Excruciat videlicet corpus hominis et per membra ejus actiones varias, mirabiles et peccaminosas perficit, ex quibus etiam, si non singulis, certe conjunctim, tanquam ex signis, vera obsessio corporalis, ab epilepsia aliisque morbis aut fascinationibus distincta, cognoscitur.

Quenstedtius: ״Signa obsessionis propria sunt: 1. Linguarum exoticarum seu peregrinarum, artium item et disciplinarum, quas obsessi nunquam ante didicerunt, nec liberati amplius norunt, scientia. Iterum abditarum atque alibi in remotissimis regionibus gestarum, item futurarum notitia et indicatio. 3. Robur plus, quam humanum, seu praeternaturalis potentia. 4. Sine organorum dispositione avicularum, ovium, boum etc. vocum exacta repraesentatio. His adde 5. sermonis impuritatem, 6. gestuum deformitatem, 7. horrendam vociferationem Mare. 5, 5., 8. Dei blasphemationem et proximi cavillationem, 9. tum in corpus ipsum, tum in spectatores saevitiam et ferociam Matth. 8, 28. 17, 15. Marci 5, 5. Act. 19, 16. Ex his et similibus signis, quae tamen non simul omnia in singulis obsessis occurrunt, sed interdum plura, interdum pauciora, cognosci potest corporalis obsessio. Singularis tamen circumspectio hic requiritur, ne gravioribus morbis afflictos pro obsessis habeamus.“ (L. c. th. 56. f. 652.)

Quando videlicet Deus vel immediate, vel mediate, intercedente opera hominum sive bonorum, v. gr. ministrorum ecclesiae per excommunicationem majorem peccatorum enormium, de qua vid. 1. ad Cor. 5, 3. 1. ad Tim. 1, 20., sive malorum, aliis nocere studentium, v. gr. veneficiis aut exsecrationibus intercedentibus permittit, ut homines aliqui subjiciantur satanae.

Quanquam vero finis hujus obsessionis ex parte satanae obsidentis sit partim ipsorum obsessorum, partim hominum aliorum damnum et pernicies; tamen ex parte Dei, istam permittentis ac vel peccata graviora, contemtum verbi, securitatem carnalem, blasphemias, conspirationem cum diabolo etc. severo judicio vindicantis, vel pios corporali castigatione corripientis et pro liantis, finis est manifestatio potentiae, justitiae et bonitatis suae hominumque, si non ipsorum obsessorum, saltim aliorum spectantium vel audientium poenitentia, fides et salus.§

52. Similiter huc pertinet, quod daemones per spectra a hominibus illudunt b et seu animam seu corpus perdere aut affligere c student. Quae quidem δράματα Graeci, Latini praeterea ad literam visa appellant; et in generali significatione, alia quidem sunt mere imaginativa, ex somnio, morbo., aut mala conscientia; alia vere talia sunt; eaque rursus vel divina, ex immediata operatione Dei, vel angelica, ex operatione bonorum angelorum, vel naturalia, ex ignorantia causarum physicarum aut superstitione orta, vel artificialia, vel denique diabolica, quae postrema spectrorum species huc spectat. Quanquam fatendum sit, non tantum ea, quae visui, sed etiam quae auditui (forte et aliis sensibus) objiciuntur, ad praesens pertinere. PART. I. CAP. IH.

Talia fuerunt, quorum mentio fit Sap. 17, 8. sqq. de plagis Aegyptiorum, quando ινδάλματα, seu simulacra (aut spectra) eos turbabant; quando soni conturbantes ipsos circumstrepebant et visa (φάσματα) tristia flebilibus formis (τοίς χατηφέσιν προσώποις) apparebant; quando pyra timore plena ultro apparebat (αυτόματη πυρά φόβου πλήρης') ipsique a visione, quae non erat aspectabilis, terrebantur etc. Atque bos ludos fecerunt מלאכי רעים, angeli malorum, de quibus vid. Ps. 78, 49., quos etiam LXX αγγέλους πονηρούς reddiderunt. Sed et ad spectrorum classem pertinent שעירים, satyri vulgo dicti, hircorum specie apparentes, de quibus vid. Es. 13, 21. et 34, 14· collat. cum Levit. 17, 7. et 2

Chron. 11, 15. una cum Apocal. 18, 2.

Partim terrendo, juxta Sap. 17, 1. sqq., partim ad superstitionem, avaritiam etc. inducendo.§ 53.

Speciatim statui ecclesiastico adversantur, quando spargendis haeresibus invigilant,a impediunt pios et salutares ministrorum ecclesiae conatus,b abducunt auditores a pia meditatione verbi, ut conversionem et salutem eorum intervertant,c excitant etiam persecutiones ad versus doctrinam et ecclesiam christianam. Ita inimicus (έχάρος ό διάβολος) zizania in agro ecclesiae seniinare dicitur Matth. 13, 27.

Paulus in 1. ad Tim. 4, 1· et 2. haereses vocat doctrinas daemoniorum,, scilicet his auctoribus tribuendas. Quod antichristus tantum mali infert ecclesiae, id 2. ad Thess. 2, 8. per operationem satanae fieri dicitur. Quod Paulo accidit in 1. ad Thess. 2, 18., ubi se ad Thessalonicenses semel iterumque venturum a satana impeditum esse scribit. Hoc enim est tollere verbum e cordibus audientium, Luc. 8, 12.

Idque variis modis fit, v. g. quando hominibus objicit, quae in materiam cogitationum peregrinarum cedunt, aut praejudicia affectusque varios excitat, quibus vel oblivio, vel vilitas verbi lecti aut praedicati inducatur.§ 54.

In statu politico daemones iniqua et exitiosa consilia suggerunt imperantibus a atque alias multis modis turbant harmoniam reipublicae.b Quale erat illud de numerando populo, quod Davidi suppeditavit, vid. 1 Chron. 22, 1., et istud Achabo datum, ut bello peteret Syrios, 1 Reg. 22, 21. 22. V. g. dissidiorum semina spargendo, juxta tritum illud: Divide et regnabis.

55. In oeconomia conjugibus ipsis,a liberis eorum b et bonis familiae c insidiantur. V. gr. lites serendo, aut sollicitando ad libidinem; quem duplicem dolum animadvertere et cavere jubet Paulus 1 Cor. 7,5. Vid. historia Jobi, cap. 1., et filiae δαιμόνιζα μένηε, Matth. 15, 22. Vid. historia Jobi et Tobiae.§

56. Interim Deus ipse etiam utitur ministerio malorum angelorum ad castigandos in hoc mundo pios a et puniendos impios, tum in vita,b tum post mortem.c Vid. iterum historia Jobi. Vid. Ps. 78, 49. Angdi enim malorum, sive dicantur esse angeli, malis aut damnis inferendis intenti, sive malorum hominum angeli, in oppositione ad eos, qui destinati sunt haeredibus salutis, utrinque spiritus mali recte intelliguntur. Conf., quae diximus in nota b. ad §51. et nota c. ad § 52. Vid. Matth. 18, 34. Etsi enim verba parabolica esse videantur, tamen, quia additur: Sic et Pater coelestis vobis faciet, recte intelligitur de immittendis in homines irreconciliabiles tortoribus, quibus sine fine affligantur, eoque nomine non alii rectius, quam angeli mali, denotari creduntur. Neque ideo lenietur miseria horum, cujus sensum indesinenter experientur.

Scherzerus: ,,Diabolos quod attinet, quaestio hic remanet: Num et illi damnatorum tortores et carnifices in inferno sint futuri? Quicquid aliis visum fuerit, nobis placet negativa. «.

Deus sine ministerio angelorum beat in coelis. Ergo etiam sine ministerio diabolorum torquet in inferno, ß. Diaboli ipsi torquebuntur. Ergo non aliorum tortores erunt. Unde deprecantur abyssum, Luc. 8, 31., propter tormenta ipsos manentia, γ. Diabolus primus et gravissime omnium peccavit, hominesque ad peccandum pellexit. Ergo gravius hominibus torquebitur; adeoque hominum tortor non est futurus, rf. Contra Dei justitiam est, ut seductorem hominum eundem constituat tortorem. Sic enim seductoris sors melior esset sorte seducti, quod justitiae repugnat. ε. Nullum ejus rei documentum extat in sacris Literis. . . De tortoribus Matth. 18, 34., plagis Luc. 12, 48. et percussionibus Prov. 19, 29. Scriptura parabolica non est argumentativa. Nec sequitur: quia diaboli tortores sunt in hac vita, eos etiam fore in altera. Multa enim in hoc saeculo permittuntur, quae, finibus quasi μακροΰνμίας clausis, in altero concedi nequeunt.“ (System, loc. 24. p. 649. sq.)

Rambachius: ,,Die Teufel werden keine tortores sein, wie manche sich einbilden und Gerhardus in locc. th. 1. de infern. § 73. et Dannhauerus in hodosoph. p. m. 1505. vermeinet. Item Fechtius in Sylloge p. 562.“ (Erläuterung der Grundlegung der Theologie, p. 1085.) PART. I. CAP. III.

57. Habent autem diabolus et angeli ejus a etiam paratos sibi cruciatus et dolores ex igne b infernali. Praeter poenas illas, de quibus supra actum est § 46. et 47. Ita Matth. 25, 41. docemur, diabolum et angelos ejus per sententiam judicis poenalem ablegatum iri in ignem sibi paratum. Certe ultra poenam illam, quam hactenus sustinent, ad novum quoddam supplicium in judicio illo magno et extremo subeundum eos asservari constat ex 2 Petr. 2, 4.. et Judae v. 6. Distincte autem velle exponere, quomodo ignis, si corporalis sit, agat in spiritus, curiosum magis est, quam utile et necessarium.

Quenstedtius: ״Cruciatus. . symbolice describuntur per ignem aeternum Matth. 25, 41. et per stagnum ignis et sulphuris Apoc. 20, 10. 14. Sic Petrus 2. ep. 2, 4. et Judae 6. Observa: 1. Ponit Petrus negatum pro affirmato contrario: Deus non pepercit malis angelis i. e. gravissime eos punivit. 2. Explicat Petrus et Judas, qualis illa poena sit. . . Tria ergo designantur: 1. vincula, quibus constricti tenentur, quae,catenae caliginis‘ et,vincula aeterna sub caligine‘ dicuntur. Ast quae nunc sunt vincula ad custodiam, ne pro libertate grassari possint, in magno illo judicii die erunt ad poenam, et quae nunc laxiora sunt, tunc erunt arctissima et gravissima. 2. ,Tartarus‘ (quod nomen proprium Petri est 1. c.), in quo detinentur tanquam in carcere, et,caligo‘, sub qua reservantur. Quocunque enim abeunt et ubicunque degunt daemones, suum infernum circumferunt, ut ait Beda in 8. c. Jacobi. Distinguendum itaque inter statum infernalem et πον inferni. Oberrant quidem nunc per mundum, catenati tamen sunt et vinculis constricti tenebrisque obvoluti, et carcerem suum secum semper trahunt.“ (L. c. c. 11. s. 1. th. 36. f. 644. sq.)

Idem: ״Ignis materialis non potest agere in spiritus; nihil enim potest agere extra sphaeram sui objecti. Et si ageret, spiritus debilior foret corpore, quod absonum.“ (L. c. c. 14. s. q. 4. f. 821.)

Fechtius: ״Ignis non materialis et tamen proprie dictus est aqua non humida et tamen proprie dicta. Qualis ille futurus sit, si non est elementarie, non liquet.“ Addit Roulius: ״Triplex de igne infernali datur sententia. Quidam metaphoricum esse statuunt, in tormentis conscientiae consistentem; alii elementarem et ejusdem cum nostro speciei; alii vicissim proprie dictum quidem, sed diversae ab elementari naturae. Huic vero sententiae ratio in thesi adducta opposita est.“ (Sylloge, p. 95.100.) §

58. Erunt autem poenae, quibus affliguntur angeli mali, aeternae.a a) Dicitur sane πυρ αιώνιον, χόλασις αιώνιος, vid. Matth. 25, 41. et 46., πυρ ασβεστον, ignis inextinguibilis, Marc. 9, 43. Osiander: ״De salvandis aliquando diabolis crassum errorem erravit quondam in ecclesia vetustiore Origenes homil. 9. in Jeremiam, quem non sine nausea saeculo superiore circa reformationis initium refricavit Joh. Denckius anabaptista, qui sensit, Deum tandem omnium

## 6 On the Image of God Bestowed upon Man in the First Creation

ON THE IMAGE OF GOD BESTOWED UPON MAN IN THE FIRST CREATION. § 1. After the angels, men are most eminent in the assembly of creatures, concerning whom it is most clear from the history of creation that God created them in His own image.

Thus the reason for the order of doctrine is evident. And here we must treat of man, insofar as the divine goodness of the Creator shines forth in him, before he, as a sinner to be restored to salvation, is subjected to the operation of revealed theology. We do not deny that otherwise his consideration could be referred to the second part, concerning the subject. For the Triune God says in Gen. 1:26: “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.” And just as God decreed, so He effected, and in truth created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them, verse 27. Gerhard: “That God, in a new and hitherto unusual manner, as it were undertakes a deliberation concerning this miracle, argues not the infirmity of the Maker, but the excellence of the work.” (L. de imagine Dei, § 2.) Or, that God bestowed upon man a certain form, excellently expressed after His own likeness (for this is what is denoted by the name of image). Note, however, that in the cited passage the word “likeness” is added to the word “image,” so that it may be understood as a most similar image. And furthermore, it is certain that other creatures, although created according to a certain idea present to the divine intellect, are indeed called very good, yet they are not said to have been created in the image of God. PART I. CAP. IV.

Gerhard: "We do not distinguish between 'image' and 'likeness' in such a way that we refer the former to the essence of the soul and the latter to holiness, righteousness, the knowledge of God, etc., in man; rather, we maintain that the same thing is expressed by both terms and that the word 'likeness' is to be taken exegetically... When God, about to create man, says in Gen. 1:26, 'Let us make man in our image and after our likeness,' Moses immediately adds in v. 27, 'And God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him,' and there he omits the word 'likeness.' From this we gather: that which was previously expressed by both words, image and likeness, is now enunciated by the word 'image' alone, since it had already been said beforehand for the sake of clarification that that image would be similar to the prototype." (Loc. de imag. Dei. § 18. sq.)

Luther: "We said above what the likeness of God was. Although almost everyone takes the likeness and image of God as the same thing, yet, as far as I have been able to discover by diligent observation, there is some difference between these two words; for צלם they properly called an image or figure, as when Scripture says (Num. 33:52), 'Destroy the altars of your images.' There the word signifies nothing other than figures or statues that are erected. דמית, however, which signifies likeness, is the perfection of the image; for example, when we speak of a dead image, such as those on coins, we say: This is the image of Brutus, of Caesar, etc. But that image does not immediately convey a likeness; it does not show all the features. Therefore, what Moses says, that man was also made after the likeness of God, shows that man not only reflects God in that he has reason or intellect and will, but also that he has the likeness of God, i.e., a will and intellect such that he understands God, and wills what He wills, etc." (Opp. lat. Erlangens. II, 87. sq.) §

2. Therefore, it is established that the efficient cause of the divine image which is in man is the Triune God. Who is read to have decreed and likewise effected it in the aforementioned place. The plurality of the divine persons can indeed be established from the noun with the plural ending אלוזים and the plural verb נעשה, "let us make," which is followed by the double plural suffix in the words בצלמנו, "in our image" (of the many who are making), and כךמותנו, "after our likeness" (of the many persons conferring it upon man). However, the number three of the persons is precisely presupposed here from the doctrine concerning God, handed down in the preceding chapter. Nor should it be neglected that it is said elsewhere that works ad extra are undivided. For such is that by which the divine image is conferred upon man. §

3. The internal impulsive cause is the goodness of God. It is sufficient to have indicated this, since an external one ought not to be demanded. It is the same as that which we saw to be the impulsive cause of creation itself. For thus it happened here as well, that God made man very good, impelled by His own divine goodness, and man became good through the divine image conferred upon him.

Quenstedtius: "Just as a prince bestows his image as a token of special grace, so God, out of a singular affection of love and favor, impressed His image upon man, not by appending it externally, but by inserting it internally." (Th. did. pol. P. II. c. 1. s. 1. th. 11. f. 840.) §

4. That, however, which God willed to confer and did confer upon man at the time of his creation, in order to make him after His own likeness or image, is not to be sought in one certain person, but in the Triune God, as the exemplary cause. This returns to the fact that in the aforementioned place, Genesis 1:26, a verb and a double plural suffix occur. For the sense of the words is: "Let Us, who are several (persons), make man after Our (the one common to the several) image."

Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between the image of God and the image of the Most Holy Trinity. . . Indeed, Elohim says in Gen. 1:26: 'Let Us make man in Our image,' but in v. 27 it is added: 'And God created man בְּצַלְמוֹ, in His image.' Therefore, what He had previously said in the plural, He immediately repeats in the singular; whence we rightly conclude that the image is indeed the image of the several, i.e., of all three persons of the Godhead, but according to that which is one in those three persons, namely, the perfection of the essence, which belongs equally to all the persons. Chapter 3:22, the image of God is distributed in its entirety to the individual persons with these words: 'Behold, the man has become like one of Us.'" (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 858.)

The same: "The opinion of the Origenians and Osiander, who posit that 'Adam was created after the likeness of the form of the human nature of Christ preconceived in the divine mind,' is refuted: 1. From Gen. 1:26, where God the Father, speaking with the Son and the Holy Spirit, does not say: 'Let Us make man after thy image,' namely, of the Son to be incarnated, 'but Our image.' 2. From 1 Cor. 15:45, where Christ is called the 'second Adam'; now, if the idea or form of the human nature of Christ preconceived in the divine mind preceded the creation of Adam in order, to whose likeness Adam was created, Christ ought rather to be called the first Adam than the second; not to mention that we were not made like Christ in this sense, but Christ was made like us, sin excepted, Heb. 2:14. 3. Nowhere is it said in Scripture that man was created κατά τον υἱόν, according to the Son, but κατά τον Θεόν, according to God taken indefinitely. On the contrary, the Son of God is said to have been ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας, in the likeness of sinful flesh, Rom. 8:3, and to have received μορφὴν δούλου, the form of a servant, Phil. 2:7. 4. It contradicts the order of the divine decrees. For the decree concerning the forming of man after the image of God preceded the decree concerning the sending of the Son of God into the flesh to restore this lost effigy, and therefore the Son of God to be incarnated in the latter cannot be the exemplar of the divine image to be created in man in the former. 5. The mission of the Son itself stands in the way, which was done not for the sake of likeness, but for the sake of the salvation of man, 1 Tim. 1:15. 6. The image of God consists in the knowledge of God, righteousness, and holiness, as also in ἀφθαρσία, Col. 3:10, Eph. 4:24, Wisd. 2:23, but not in the members of the body, in the figure or stature of the body. 7. Through the fall, the image of God was lost, but bodily members were not lost." (L. c. f. 861. sq.)

Hollazius: "The opinion of Osiander does not agree with the appellation of Christ in 1 Cor. 15:45, that He is the second Adam. For if the form of the human nature of Christ preconceived in the divine mind preceded the creation of man in order, to whose likeness Adam was created, Christ would have to be called the first Adam rather than the second."

The same: "The Son of God is neither, nor is He anywhere in the Scriptures called, the image of the Most Holy Trinity; for thus He would be the image of Himself and of the Holy Spirit, which is άτοπου; but He is the image of the person of the Father, Heb. 1:3, on account of His eternal generation from the Father. Therefore, Moses does not precisely understand the Son of God by the image of God." (L. c. P. II. c. 1. q. 9. p. 467.) ANTITHESES.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: Of Tertullian, the Origenians, and Dr. Andr. Osiander, who thought that the first man was made in the image and likeness of the human nature which the Son of God was to assume in time into the unity of His person." (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 860.) Philippi: "The Son of God is the image of God; man is created after the image of God, that is, after the Son, to His likeness." (Kirchl. Glaubenslehre. II, 361.)

Thomasius: "Man was the creaturely image of the Son who beholds, wills, and loves the Father, and who is willed, beheld, and loved by the Father—and for this very reason the good pleasure of the Father in the Son rested upon him." (Christi Person und Werk. I, 202. Ed. 2.) Vilmarius: "The archetype of this image is God the Son, and thus the Holy Scripture of the New Testament completes the doctrine of creation as it is given in the Old Testament." (Dogmatik. I, 237.)

Hofmannus: "The second thing that we have said concerning the beginning of the self-realization of the eternal will of God is this: that the relationship to God, into which man was created on the one hand as a consciously free 'I,' and on the other hand as a nature serving as the means of itself, is an image of the unequal inner-divine relationship; thus man is an image of God, the archetypal goal of the world." (Schriftbeweis. I, 248.) § 5. And this image of God in man ought not, nor can it, be referred to all things that are in God. Nor is it in man in that degree of perfection in which it is in God.

Et quemadmodum decrevit Deus, ita effecit, ac revera creavit hominem ad imaginem suam, ad imaginem Dei creavit dium, masculum et feminam creavit illos, vers. 27.Gerhardus: ,,Quod Deus novo et hactenus insolito more de hoc thaumaturgemate deliberationem quasi suscipit, non opificis inflrmitatem, sed operis praestantiam arguit.“ (L. de imagine Dei, § 2.) Unde colligimus: quod prius utroque vocabulo imaginis et similitudinis efferebatur, id jam sola voce imaginis enunciari, quippe jam antea declarationis gratia dictum erat, imaginem illam fore similem prototypo.“ (Loc. de imag. Dei. § 18. sq.)

Ibi vocabulum nihil significat aliud, quam figuras seu statuas, quae eriguntur. דמית vero, quod similitudinem significat, est perfectio imaginis; exempli causa, cum loquimur de imagine mortua, quales sunt in numismatibus, dicimus: Haec est imago Bruti, Caesaris etc. Sed ea imago non statim refert similitudinem, non ostendit lineamenta omnia. Quod igitur Moses dicit, hominem etiam ad similitudinem Dei factum esse, ostendit, quod homo non solum referat Deum in eo, quod rationem seu intellectum et voluntatem habet, sed etiam, quod habet similitudinem Dei, h. e., voluntatem et intellectum talem, quo Deum intelligit, quo vult, quae vult etc.“ (Opp. lat. Erlangens. II, 87. sq.) §

2. Itaque imaginis divinae, quae in homine est, causam efficientem constat esse Deum a trinunum.b Qui decrevisse pariter et effecisse eam legitur l. c. Pluralitas quidem personarum divinarum constare potest ex nomine terminationis pluralis אלוזים et verbo plurali נעשה, faciamus, quod sequitur duplex suffixum plurale in vocibus בצלמנו et כךמותנו, in imagine nostra (plurium, qui facimus), secundum similitudinem nostram (plurium personarum, eam homini conferentium). Sic enim et hic factum est, ut Deus hominem faceret valde bonum, sua divina bonitate impulsus, homo autem bonus fieret per collatam sibi divinam imaginem.

### On the Image of God Bestowed upon Man in the First Creation: Thus, for example, that God is of Himself, that He is immutable, that He is…

Thus, for example, that God is of Himself, that He is immutable, that He is immense, eternal, and infinite, is not found similarly in man. Thus, while knowledge and wisdom are infinitely perfect in God, they nevertheless had a place in man only as finite. Since the holiness of God is joined with impeccability, yet in man the former was not joined with the latter. For it is also otherwise established that it is not required for an exemplar that whatever perfection is in it should also be expressed in the copy. See the blessed Musaeus, Introd. in Theol. cap. I. § 5. p. 7, 8. § 6. But that divine image which man obtained is taken in two ways: I. Generally and without restriction, by which

insofar as it contains all things in which a certain conformity of man with God the archetype has a place; then II. specially, or with restriction and κατ’ ἐξοχήν, insofar as it imports a certain principal likeness of man with God, by the power of which man, speaking absolutely, can be called the express image of God. § 7.

Taken generally, the divine image, besides the justice and wisdom concreated in the first man, includes within its scope also the very spiritual being of the human soul, and its powers, intellect and will, and at the same time also the immortality of the body and dominion over other creatures.

Thus the blessed Gerhard, *Confess. Cath.*, Book II, Part III, Art. XX, chap. II, p. 348, writes: The image of God and original justice stand to each other as whole and part. For the image of God in the first man was a certain excellent conformity with God the archetype. This conformity was twofold. One was πρώτη, primary, the other indeed δευτέρα or less principal. The primary conformity was situated in the soul, and indeed partly in the intellect, partly in the appetite, and that both rational and sensitive. These three excellencies are expressed by the one name of original justice. The less principal conformity of man with God was placed partly in the condition of the body, partly in external dominion, or, as others proceed, the less principal conformity consists, first, in the soul, both as to substance and as to attributes; second, in the body, by reason of impassibility and immortality; third, in the whole man, with respect to external dominion over all things.

The blessed Joh. Wigandus in *Syntagm. Corp. Doctr.*, p. 402, speaking of the passage Gen. 1:26, says: The image of God, he says, is there to be understood concerning the whole substance of man: because, he says, "He created man in His own image," he does not say that the soul alone was capable of such a great good. We believe, however, that this expression is general, concerning all the ornaments and gifts in the soul and body of man, by which he represented some likeness of God, finite indeed and suitable to the creature according to the judgment of the almighty God.

Cf. Chytr. *Comm. in Genes.*, chap. I, p. 57. For since there is a certain congruence between the spiritual being of God and the spiritual being of the human soul, between the intellect and will of God and the intellect and will of man, surely, unless we say that it happened by some chance that man is like God in these things, it must be confessed that he was so fashioned by God, who looked upon Himself as the exemplary cause, and that by this very fact man bears the image of God. And this is why man is called the image of God even after the fall and outside the state of renewal, Gen. 9:6, James 3:9.

For when in Gen. 9 homicide (not only that by which a faithful, renewed man, according to the image specially so called, but by which man indeterminately, whoever he may be, is rashly killed) is established to be punished by death, and the reason for the precept is sought from this, PART I. CHAPTER IV.

Since any homicide entails a violation of the divine image, which existed in the murdered man, and since God bears this violation of His image so grievously that He wills it to be avenged by the death of the violator, certainly, when original righteousness—as the image of God specifically so-called—was not in the murdered person, it is necessary that the concept of the divine image be broader and extend to those things which were mentioned in the thesis. For if you were to say that the image of God is considered here, not as it was in the murdered man, but as it once was in the first man and common parent of all, even though it did not reach the one who is killed, this would surely be a far-fetched argument and would weaken the connection of the divine precept and its foundation.

Moreover, the reason for the latter passage, James 3, is the same, because cursing a man—not precisely a regenerate one, but any man whatsoever—is condemned under this name, because it is an insult to the divine image, namely, that this image exists and can be recognized in the very person who is cursed.

Add the blessed Musaeus, *Detailed Explanation*, Q. XXVIII, p. 210 ff. Compare the blessed Grauer, *Lectures on the Augsburg Confession*, art. II, member 2, in the *Response to the Arguments of the Photinians*; the blessed Haffenreffer, *Commonplaces on the Image of God*; the blessed Gerhard, *Commentary on Genesis*, chap. IX, p. 243; the Leipzig Theologians in the *Appendix to the Consultations of Dedek*, p. 139, and the one they cite, Tilemann Heshusius.

Gerhard: "Man was created in supreme innocence, in supreme purity of soul and body, so that in him, as in a certain living mirror, the image of God might shine forth. Thus, the image of divine wisdom shone in the intellect of man; the image of goodness, μακροθυμίας, of gentleness, of tolerance, in the soul of man; the image of divine charity and mercy shone in the affections of the human heart; the image of divine justice, holiness, and purity shone in the will of man; the image of goodness, kindness, and truth in the gestures and words of man; the image of divine power in the dominion granted over all animals." (*Book on the Image of God*, § 37.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: ... 4. Of the Anthropomorphites or Anthroplani, and the Audians, who placed the reason for the divine image in the structure and lineaments of the body... 5. Of the Papists, and indeed especially the Jesuits, who distinguish between image and likeness, and refer the image of God to the very substance of the rational soul, endowed with the faculty of understanding and willing, but the likeness to supernatural perfection, or the gratuitous gifts granted to man by God, such as wisdom, justice, and holiness; from which they further conclude that by the fall, not the image of God, but only the likeness was lost... 6. Of the Calvinists, who seek the image of God partly in the substance of man, partly in the qualities... 7. Of Flacius and the Flacians, who contend that the image of God was the very substantial form of the first man, the very essence of the rational soul, which was utterly abolished by the fall of Adam... 10. Of the Jews. Galatinus, in *On the Secrets of Catholic Truth*, book II, chap. 8, writes: 'The ancient Jews placed the image of God in the soul.'" (*Loc. cit., s. 2, q. 4, f. 858 ff.*)

For this corresponds in a certain way to divine immortality, and we shall say more about it in § 14. In which a certain ray of divine majesty shows itself. See below § 15.

8. Taken specifically, the divine image imports certain accidental perfections, concreated with the intellect and will of the first humans, conformable to the perfections that are in God, and bestowed upon humans for the purpose of rightly instituting and perfecting their actions, for the sake of attaining their ultimate end. Thus, in Gen. 1, at the end, where all creatures are said to have been very good, it is rightly gathered that man also was very good, and therefore was furnished with the perfections necessary for attaining the end set before him.

Dannhauer: "(The image was) mutable and losable. Therefore, the rational soul itself is not the divine image or a part of the image, because the soul was not lost; but the image was lost; the image is only in the renewed, the soul appears even in the impious; the soul is rather a map and a mirror, in which the image shone. '1. We indeed have memory (says Luther on Gen. 1), 2. will, and 3. mind, but most corrupt and most gravely weakened, nay, to speak more clearly, utterly leprous and unclean. For if those powers are the image of God, it will follow that even Satan was created in the image of God, who surely has those natural faculties far stronger than we have. Just as he has the highest memory and intellect and a most obstinate will.' But neither does the body represent the divine image. Although Luther acknowledges an even greater perfection in the body in Gen. 1: 'For I clearly think that before the sin of Adam, the eyes were so sharp and clear that they surpassed the lynx and the eagle. And he handled lions and bears, whose strength is greatest, as being stronger himself, no differently than we handle puppies. The fruits, too, whose use is for food, had a far greater sweetness and virtue then than now.'" (Hodosoph. Phaen. V. p. 222.)

Thomasius: "To be rejected here are: a. the old rationalist conception, which thinks of the initial state of our race as animal-like and lets man only gradually emerge from bestiality to humanity; b. the Schleiermacherian view, which lets sensuality always be a power before the higher consciousness can develop, consequently deriving evil ultimately from creation; c. the Hegelian view, that the spirit begins from nature and only arrives at self-consciousness and freedom through division and particularization out of it; d. the view represented (and likely since abandoned) by Julius Müller of a transcendent, pre-temporal state of human souls, into which the God-opposing self-decision falls, which then is supposed to come to temporal appearance in the historical fall into sin." (Christi Person und Werk. I. p. 201 sq.) §

9. Namely, on the part of the intellect, God bestowed upon the first humans, for the imitation of Himself as the exemplary cause, a certain wisdom, that is, a light or some habitual perfection of the intellect, for an excellent knowledge of divine, human, and natural things, and sufficient for the primeval state. PART I. CHAP. IV.

So that the human intellect might know the essence and will of God in a timely manner, as much as was necessary for the intellect to prescribe worship convenient to God, or as much as was sufficient for living justly and holily. Thus, in the Epistle to the Colossians 3:10, it is said that the divine image in man is restored in the act of renewal by the fact that he is led to a saving knowledge of God. Namely, so that the act of knowing could be instituted rightly in all things, or in a manner convenient to the things themselves, and without error.

Latin:

Ita v. g., quod Deus a se est, quod immutabilis, quod immensus, aeternus, infinitus est, non repentur similiter in homine. Ita, cum scientia et sapientia in Deo infinite perfecta sit, in homine tamen non nisi finita locum habuit. Cura sanctitas Dei cum impeccabilitate sit conjuncta, in homine tamen illa cum hac conjuncta non fuit. Nam et alias constat, non requiri ad exemplar, ut quicquid in eo est perfectionis, exprimatur etiam in exemplato. Vid. b. Mus. Introd. in Theol. cap. I. § 5. p. 7. 8.§ 6. Ea vero, quam homo nactus est, imago divina dupliciter accipitur: I. generaliter et sine restrictione, qua

tenus continet omnia, in quibus conformitas quaedam hominis cum Deo archetypo locum habet; deinde II. specialiter, seu cum restrictione et mr’ έξοχην, quatenus importat praecipuam quandam hominis cum Deo similitudinem, cujus vi homo absolute loquendo imago Dei expressa dici potest. § 7.

Generaliter accepta imago divina praeter justitiam et sapientiam homini primo concreatam a includit suo ambitu etiam ipsum esse spirituale animae humanae, ejusque potentias, intellectum et voluntatem,b simul etiam immortalitatem corporis c et dominium in creaturas alias.d Sic b.

Gerhardus Confess. Cath. L. II. P. III. Art. XX. cap. II. p. 348. scribit: Imago Dei et justitia originalis habent se ut totum et pars. Nam imago Dei in primo homine fuit excellens quaedam conformitas cum Deo archetypo. Haec conformitas fuit gemina. Una πρώτη, primaria, altera vero δευτέρα seu minus principalis. Primaria conformitas sita fuit in anima, et quidem partim in intellectu, partim in appetitu, eoque rationali et sensitivo. Quae tres excellentiae uno justitiae originalis nomine efferuntur. Minus principalis hominis cum Deo conformitas partim in conditione corporis, partim in externo dominio fuit posita, aut, ut alii progrediuntur, consistit minus principalis conformitas, primo in anima, tum quoad substdntiam, tum quoad attributa; secundo in corpore, ratione impossibilitatis et immortalitatis; tertio in toto homine, respectu externi dominii super omnia. B.

Joh. Wigandus in Syntagm. Corp. Doctr. p. 402. de dicto Gen. 1,26. loquens: Imago Dei, ait, ibi de tota hominis substantia intettigenda est: quia, inquit, creavit hominem ad imaginem suam, non dicit, animam duntaxat istius tanti boni capacem fuisse. Oredimus autem, eam locutionem generetlern, de omnibus ornamentis ac donis in hominum anima et corpore, quibus aliquam Dei similitudinem, finitam tamen creaturaeque pro judicio omni· potentis Dei convenientem repraesentabat. Conf.

Chytr. Comm. in Genes, cap. I. p. 57. Cum enim inter esse spirituale Dei et esse spirituale animae humanae, inter intellectum et voluntatem Dei et intellectum ac voluntatem hominis congruentia quaedam sit, sane nisi dicamus, casu quodam factum esse, quod homo in his similis est Deo, fatendum erit, a Deo, seipsam tanquam causam exemplarem intuente, ita conditum fuisse, adeoque hoc ipso imaginem Dei gerere hominem. Atque hoc est, quod homo etiam post lapsum et extra statum renovationis imago Dei dicitur Gen. 9, 6. Jacobi 3, 9.

Nam quando Gen. 9. homicidium (non tantum illud, quo homo fidelis, renovatus ad imaginem specialiter sic dictam, sed quo homo indeterminate, qualiscunque sit, temere occiditur) morte puniendum statuitur et ratio praecepti hinc petitur, PAKT. I. CAP. IV.

quod homicidium quodlibet importet violationem imaginis divinae, quae in homine occiso fuerit et quam imaginis suae violationem Deus tam aegre ferat, ut morte violantis vindicari velit, certe, quando in occiso non fuit justitia originalis, tanquam imago Dei specialiter sic dicta, necesse est, conceptum imaginis divinae latius patere et ad ea se extendere, de quibus in thesi dictum est. Nam si dixeris, imaginem Dei h. l. spectari, non quae fuerit in homine occiso, sed quae olim iuerit in homine primo et communi omnium parente, licet ad eum, qui occiditur, non pertigerit, hoc profecto longius petitum erit et nexum praecepti divini ac fundamenti ejus labefactabit.

Posterioris autem loci, Jac. 3., par ratio est, quia maledictum in hominem non praecise renatum, sed quemlibet conjectum, hoc nomine damnatur, quod sit contumelia imaginis divinae, nempe quod imago haec in ipso, cui maledicitur, existat et cognosci queat.

Adde b. Mus. Ausführl. Erklärung Q. XXVIII. p. 210. sqq. Confer, b. Grauer. Praelect. ad Aug. Confess. art. II. membr. 2. in Respons. ad argumenta Photinian., b. Haffenrefferum LL. de Imag. Dei, b. Gerhard. Comment. in Genes, cap. IX. p. 243., Theol. Lipsienses in Append. Consil. Dedek. p. 139. et, quem citant, Tilem. Heshusium.

Gerhardus: ״Creatus est homo in summa innocentia, in summa animi et corporis puritate, ut in ipso, tanquam vivo speculo quodam, imago Dei reluceret. Sic imago divinae sapientiae fulgebat in intellectu hominis; imago bonitatis, μακροΰυμίας, mansuetudinis, tolerantiae in animo hominis; imago caritatis et misericordiae divinae fulgebat in affectibus cordis humani; imago justitiae, sanctitatis et puritatis divinae lucebat in voluntate hominis; imago bonitatis, benignitatis, veritatis in gestibus et verbis hominis; imago divinae potentiae in dominio concesso super omnia animalia.“ (L. de imag. D. § 37.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: ... 4. Anthropomorphitarum vel Anthroplanorum, et Audianorum, qui in structura et lineamentis corporis rationem divinae imaginis posuerunt. . . 5. Pontificiorum, et quidem praecipue Jesuitarum, qui imaginem et similitudinem distinguunt, et imaginem Dei ad ipsam animae rationalis substantiam, intelligendi volendique facultate instructam, similitudinem vero ad perfectionem supernaturalem, seu dona gratuita homini a Deo concessa, ut sapientlam, justitiam, sanctitatem, referunt, unde porro colligunt, perlapsum non imaginem Dei, 'sed solam similitudinem deperditam esse. . . 6. Calvinianorum, qui imaginem Dei partim in substantia hominis, partim in qualitatibus quaerunt. . . 7. Flacii et Flacianorum, contendentium, imaginem Dei fuisse ipsam primi hominis formam substantialem, ipsam animae rationalis essentiam, quae lapsu Adae penitus sit abolita. . . 10. Judaeorum. Galatinus de arcanis cath. veritatis l. II. c. 8. scribit: ,Priscos Judaeorum posuisse imaginem Dei in anima.‘“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 858. sqq.)

Haec enim respondet quodammodo immortalitati divinae, deque ea plura dicemus ad § 14. In quo radius quidam majestatis divinae sese ostendit. Vide infra § 15.

8. Specialiter accepta imago divina importat perfectiones quasdam accidentales, intellectui et voluntati primorum hominum concreatas, perfectionibus, quae in Deo sunt, conformes et collatas hominibus ad actiones suas recte instituendas ac perficiendas, finis a ultimi consequendi causa. Sic Gen. 1, ult., ubi omnes creaturae valde bonae fuisse dicuntur, recte colligitur, etiam hominem valde bonum, adeoque ad consequendum finem sibi praefixum perfectionibus necessariis instructum fuisse.

Dannhauerus: ״(Imago erat) mutabilis et amissibilis. Igitur anima ipsa rationalis non est imago divina aut imaginis pars, quia anima non est amissa; at imago est amissa; imago tantum est in renovatis, anima etiam in impiis apparet; anima potius est mappa et speculum, in quo imago relucebat. ,1. Memoriam (inquit Lutherus ad Gen. 1.), 2. voluntatem et 3. mentem habemus quidem, sed corruptissima et gravissime debilitata, imo, ut clarius dicam, prorsus leprosa et immunda. Si enim istae potentiae sunt imago Dei, sequetur, etiam satanam ad imaginem Dei conditum esse, qui profecto illa naturalia longe habet validiora, quam nos habemus. Sicut est memoria et intellectus summus et voluntas obstinatissima.‘ Sed nec corpus refert imaginem divinam. Quamvis in corpore etiam majorem perfectionem agnoscat Lutherus in Gen. 1.: ,Plane enim existimo, ante peccatum Adae oculos ita fuisse acutos et claros, ut lineem et aquilam superaret. Leones autem et ursos, quorum maximum robur est, ipse fortior non aliter tractavit, quam nos catulos tractamus. Fructuum quoque, quorum usus est in cibo, longe major fuit tum suavitas, tum virtus, quam nunc.‘“ (Hodosoph. Phaen. V. p. 222.)

Thomasius: ״Abzuweisen ist hier: a. die altrationalistische VorStellung, die den Anfangszustand unsere Geschlechts thierartig denkt und den Menschen erst allmählich aus der Bestialität zur Humanität herauskommen lässt; b. die Schleiermacher sehe, welche die Sinnlichkeit immer schon eine Macht sein lässt, bevor das höhere Bewusstsein sich entwickeln kann, mithin das Böse letziich von der Schöpfung herleitet; c. die Hegelsche, dass der Geist von der Natur anfange und erst aus derselben durch Entzweiung und Besonderung hindurch zum' Selbstbewusstsein und zur Freiheit gelange; d. die von Julius Müller vertretene (und wohl auch wieder aufgegebene) von einem jenseitigen, vorzeitlichen Zustand der menschlichen Seelen, in den die gottwidrige Selbstentscheidung falle, die denn in dem geschichtlichen Sündenfall zur zeitlichen Erscheinung kommen soll.“ (Christi Person und Werk. I. p. 201. sq.) §

9. Scilicet ex parte intellectus contulit Deus hominibus primis ad imitationem sui, tanquam causae exemplaris, sapientiam quandam, id est, lucem seu perfectionem aliquam habitualem intellectus,a ad cognitionem rerum divinarum, humanarum et naturalium eximiam b et pro statu primaevo c sufficientem.d PART. I. CAP. IV.

Ita ut intellectus hominis essentiam et voluntatem Dei in tardum cognosceret, quantum necesse erat ad id, ut intellectus cultum Deo convenientem, aut quantum satis erat ad juste et sancte vivendum, praescriberet. Sic in Epist. ad Col. 3, 10. dicitur imago divina in homine restaurari in actu renovationis per hoc, quod is deducitur ad salutarem Dei agnitionem. Nempe ut actus cognoscendi per omnia recte seu rebus ipsis convenienter et sine errore possent institui.


### On the Image of God Bestowed upon Man in the First Creation: Quenstedtius: "Man was conformed to divine wisdom

Quenstedtius: "Man was conformed to divine wisdom; which is proved 1. from the scriptural sayings in Col. 3:9, 10... 2. From the deeds of Adam, such as: a. ονοματοθεσία, or the convenient imposition of names in Gen. 2:19, which was not only grammatical regarding the nomenclature of the animals, but most especially logical regarding their truest definition; for immediately as the animals and the birds of the heavens were brought into his sight, they were known to him... b. The recognition of Eve, v. 23. Observe: Here is a great abyss of extemporaneous wisdom. While Adam was sleeping, Eve was fashioned from his rib, and yet he shows a. the matter from which she herself proceeded, and recognizes her as a part of his own body; β. he points out a sex different from his own, and γ. in this diversity of sexes, the order; δ. he manifests the law hitherto hidden in the counsel of God, namely, that he himself is to be joined to Eve... This knowledge of Adam was excellent, full, perfect, and as great as no man after the fall can acquire for himself, either from the book of nature or from the book of Scripture... That it was nevertheless finite and limited is evident from the fact that Adam did not know the secret decrees of God, the thoughts of hearts, future contingencies, the number of the stars, etc., [or] the mystery of the incarnation; and it is credible that the whole gospel, or the doctrine concerning Christ the Redeemer, was unknown to the integral Adam, because it was not expedient for him to know this very thing. This very concreated knowledge of Adam could also have been perfected more and more and would have admitted of increase, if you consider the perfection of degrees, both through revelation or further information from God in supernatural matters, and through experience and personal observation in natural matters." (L. c. s. 1. th. 15. f. 841. sq.)

Thomasius: "Man possessed a deep insight into nature, Gen. 2:19, 20, for language is the objectification of thought, the word the name, the sound-image for the thing; the naming of the animals is the designation of their essence, and thus presupposes an inner understanding of nature, a spiritual glance into its depths. But just as little as man gained this understanding only through reflection, just as little did he learn language only through abstraction; rather, both rested upon a kind of immediate intuition." (L. c. I, 179.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the ancient heretics, such as the Pelagians, a. who flatly deny original righteousness; b. who assert that Adam was created rude and devoid of wisdom; c. who make him ignorant of virtue and vice, and such as infants are born now... 3. Of the ancient fathers, some of whom place the formal reason of the divine image, properly so called, in the soul alone, excluding the body, such as Basil, Ambrose, Augustine, Nazianzen... Some explain the image of God solely as dominion and rule over the remaining creatures, such as Chrysostom... 4. Of the scholastics, such as Cajetan, who denies that Adam had an exquisite knowledge of the heavens, the elements, and the stars. And although the scholastics do not derogate from the knowledge of divine things in man in the state of integrity, they nevertheless derive it from the illumination of the Holy Spirit, who dwells in man. The same men also [attribute it] to human nature itself..."

attribute the rebellion of the faculties, which ought to have been restrained by the supernatural gift of original righteousness... 5. Of the Papists and especially the Jesuits, who make original rectitude proper formally to the superior part of the soul, but attribute it to the inferior only effectively, as if in the latter there had always been a certain resistance and proclivity toward evil, which was nevertheless to be restrained by the superior virtue, that is, original righteousness... 7. Of the Neophotinians, who attribute to the unfallen Adam a gross, stupid, and childish ignorance, denying that the image or likeness of God consisted in righteousness, holiness, and wisdom... They establish the sole and adequate definition of the divine image in man’s dominion over living creatures... 8. Of the Arminians, who maintain that the soul of Adam did not know good and evil. They assert, with the Socinians, that the image of God consisted solely in dominion... They contend that an inclination to sin existed in man before the fall; nay, they say that God implanted in man a repugnance against the law.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 868. sqq.)

Or regarding those things which were necessary to be known by man, created in such a state and tending toward the end divinely destined for him. And thus such [knowledge] as could nevertheless be increased by the progress of time, yet not so perfect and diffuse that it would extend even to knowing the free decrees of God, or bring about the most accurate knowledge of all natural things. §

10. On the part of the will, spiritual powers were bestowed upon man by God, or an habitual inclination and readiness to love God above all things, and to do all things according to the prescription of the intellect rightly enlightened, and to omit those things which it would judge to be omitted, and likewise to govern the inferior faculties, lest they should in any way break forth into inordinate and sinful acts. This is that righteousness and holiness of truth, not a painted, but a sincere and constant virtue; concerning which, as pertaining primarily to the divine image, see Ep. to Eph. 4: 24. Compare Eccl. 7: 30.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Pelagians, who made Adam devoid of both virtue and vice in the state of innocence, and such as infants are born now... 2. Of the Scholastics and Jesuits, who commonly teach that man was originally created in pure naturals, without the grace of God or original righteousness and without any sin; or: that man from his first origin existed only in naturals, to which grace was then added as if superinfused upon the already constituted nature of man... 5. Of the Socinians, who teach that man was created not just and holy, but only upright, simple, and innocent, just as infants are still born daily.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 847.)

For this is the first and chief object of human duty, and the love of God is considered the compendium of the whole law observed. PART I. CAP. IV.

Hofmann: "God created man as His image, created him in such a way that he resembles Him: this is what the words state, and the only question is in what the image of God in him is to consist. . . The context does not allow one to think of the God-likeness of a morally holy being. . . In contrast to the animal world, man is God-like. . . Accordingly, that which enables him to rule the world around him is also that in which his image of God consists: he is created to be a consciously free 'I,' a personal being. Therefore, the image of God does not signify a moral behavior, but a moral relationship." (Schriftbeweis. I, 251. sq.)

Not only regarding God, but also regarding himself and other men, if any coexisted. For otherwise the will is a blind power; yet it must nevertheless be inclined toward that to which the practical intellect would tend by its dictate.

According to those things which were said in the preceding § 9. Namely, that sincere and full obedience might be rendered to laws not only affirmative, but also negative, and that all things which could incline the will elsewhere could be declined or spurned.

Not only the locomotive power, but even especially the sensitive appetite, which in such a subject, where the sensitive is joined to the rational appetite, ought to be conformed to the same and therefore subjected to it or ruled by it. §

11. But the sensitive appetite itself was also then perfected, so that it would promptly and without struggle subject itself to the right judgment of the intellect and the holy command of the will, and would not give place to any inordinate motion as if it were inevitable.

For just as it is otherwise established that the sensitive appetite in man is not entirely incapable of reason and morality; so it also had to be instructed, so that it could constantly obey the superior faculties, and would not be carried toward objects pleasing to the senses, unless in a manner convenient to right reason; namely, so that man would be truly and perfectly just, holy, and very good. Gen. 1, last.

Quenstedtius: "If rebellion and an inclination toward vices follow from the condition of matter, which is from God, then God is entirely the cause and author of that evil, and sin existed before sin, and punishment preceded guilt, and Christ was in Himself subject to sin; all of which are absurd and impious." (L. c. q. 2. f. 854.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Pelagians, who posit that the rebellion of the lower part against the higher was connatural to man. . . 2. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who ascribe the rebellion of the powers to nature itself, which had to be restrained by the supernatural gift of original righteousness. . . 4. Of the Socinians, who contend that the flesh was not only rebellious to reason, but also overcame it."

This is what our first parents did not know in the state of integrity, that they were naked, nor were they ashamed; that is, they were not even slightly touched by any inordinate lust of the sensitive appetite (although an object was present which could have enticed them). Gen. 2:25. § 12.

And this wisdom, justice, and holiness of the first humans so holds the nature of the divine image that it is the sole and unique thing from which man, speaking absolutely, can be called the image of God. Certainly more so than the spiritual substance of the soul itself with its essential faculties, viewed precisely in themselves. For without that wisdom, the mind of man, blind, would have been more dissimilar than similar to the most wise divine mind; and without holiness, the will, depraved and infected by the rebellion of the sensitive appetite, would have been more dissimilar than similar to the most pure and most holy will of God. Cf. blessed Musaeus, *Detailed Explanation*, Q. 28, p. 215 and 221.

ANTITHESIS.Hofmann: "Therefore it (the image of God) is propagated also from the first-created one who had become sinful, and not from the holy man, but from man; because he is man, it is said afterwards that he bears the image of God. Gen. 9:6; Jas. 3:9... Scripture therefore does not understand by the image of God in man a moral conduct of the same, such that with the entry of sin the image of God would be lost." (*Schriftbeweis*, I, 252 sq.) § 13.

Latin:

Quenstedtius: ״Homo conformis fuit divinae sapientiae; quod probatur 1. ex Scripturis dictis Col. 3, 9. 10. . . 2. Ex Adami factis, qualia sunt: a. ονοματοθεσία sive nominum conveniens impositio Gen. 2, 19., quae erat non solum grammatica, quoad nomenclaturam animaliura, sed vel maxime logica quoad verissimam definitionem; statim autem, ac in ejus conspectum sunt deducta animalia et coeli volatilia, ipsi fuerunt cognita. . . b. Evae agnitio v. 23. Observa: Magna hic est sapientiae extemporaneae abyssus. Adamo dormiente Eva ex ejus costa erat fabricata, et tamen ostendit a. materiam, ex qua ipsa prodierit, et pro parte corporis sui ipsam agnoscit; β. monstrat sexum a se diversum, et y. in hac sexuum diversitate ordinem; A manifestat legem in Dei consilio hactenus absconditam, quod sci. ipse Evae sit conjungendus. . . Fuit haec Adami scientia excellens, plena, perfecta et tanta, quantam nullus hominum post lapsum sive ex libro naturae, sive ex libro Scripturae sibi acquirere potest. . . Finitam tamen fuisse et limitatam, inde patet, quia non novit Adam arcana Dei decreta, non cordium cogitationes, non futura contingentia, non numerum stellarum etc., mysterium incarnationis; totumque adeo evangelium sive doctrinam de Christo redemptore ignorasse Adamum integrum, credibile est, quia hoc ipsum scire non expediebat. Haec ipsa scientia Adami concreata perfici quoque magis magisque potuisset et augmentum admisisset, si perfectionem graduum spectes, tum per revelationem sive ulteriorem informationem Dei in supernaturalibus, tum per experientiam et observationem propriam in naturalibus.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 15. f. 841. sq.)

Thomasius: ״Der Mensch besass eine tiefe Einsicht in die Natur, Gen. 2, 19. 20., denn die Sprache ist die Verobjectivirung des Gedankens, das Wort der Name, das Lautbild für die Sache, die Benennung der Thiere Bezeichnung ihres Wesens, und setzt also ein inneres Verständniss der Natur, .einen Geistesblick in ihre Tiefen voraus. Aber so wenig der Mensch dieses Verständniss erst durch Reflexion gewonnen hat, so wenig hat er die Sprache erst durch Abstraction gelernt, sondern beides beruhte auf einer Art unmittelbarer Intuition.“ (L. c. I, 179.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Haereticorum antiquorum, ut Pelagianorum a. justitiam originalem plane negantium; b. Adamum rudem, expertem sapientiae conditum fuisse, asserentium; c. eundem quoque virtutis et vitii ignarum facientium, ac talem, quales nascuntur nunc infantes. . . 3. Antiquorum patrum, quorum alii formalem rationem divinae imaginis proprie dictae collocant in sola anima, excluso corpore, ut Basilius, Ambrosius, Augustinus, Nazianzenus. . . Nonnulli imaginem Dei de solo principatu et dominio in reliquas creaturas exponunt, ut Chrysostomus. . . 4. Scholasticorum, ut Cajetani, negantis, Adamum coeli, elementorum ac siderum exquisitam scientiam habuisse. Et licet scholastici notitiam rerum divinarum homini in statu integritatis non derogent, eam tamen ex illuminatione Spiritus S., inhabitantis in homine, deducunt. . . Iidem etiam ipsimet naturae

humanae rebellionem virium adscribunt, quae per donum supernaturale justitiae originalis compescenda fuerit. . . 5. Pontificiorum et inprimls Jesuitarum, qui rectitudinem originalem superiori animae parti propriam faciunt formaliter, inferiori vero tantum tribuunt effective, quasi in ista semper fuerit renitentia quaedam et proclivitas ad malum, coercenda tamen a virtute superiori, hoc est, justitia originali... 7. Neophotinianorum, qui crassam, stupidam et puerilem Adamo integro ignorantiam affingunt, negantes, imaginem vel similitudinem Dei sitam fuisse in justitia, sanctitat^et sapientia. . . Unicam et adaequatam imaginis divinae rationem in dominio hominis super animantia constituunt. . . 8. Arminianorum, qui statuunt, animam Adami nescivisse bonum et malum. Imaginem Dei sitam fuisse unice in dominio, cum Socinianis asserunt. . . Inclinationem ad peccandum in homine ante lapsum fuisse, contendunt, imo Deum homini repugnantiam adversus legem indidisse, ajunt.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 8G8. sqq.)

Seu quoad ea, quae homini in tali statu condito et ad finem sibi divinitus destinatum tendenti scitu necessaria erant. Adeoque talem, quae tamen temporis progressu posset augeri, non autem ita perfectam ac diffusam, ut se etiam ad libera Dei decreta cognoscenda extenderet, aut accuratissimam rerum naturalium omnium scientiam inferret.§

10. Ex parte voluntatis collatae sunt homini a Deo vires spirituales, seu habitualis inclinatio et promtitudo a ad Deum b super omnia diligendum et facienda omnia c ex praescripto intellectus d recte e illustrati, omittenda f autem, quae ille omittenda judicaret, regendas item facultates g inferiores, ne ullatenus in actus inordinatos et peccaminosos erumperent. Haec est illa justitia et sanctitas veritatis, non fucata, sed sincera et constans virtus; de qua, tanquam ad imaginem divinam inprimis pertinente, vid. Ep. ad Ephes. 4, 24. Confer. Eccl. 7, 30.

Scholasticorum et Jesuitarum communiter docentium, hominem primitus conditum esse in puris naturalibus, sine gratia Dei sive justitia originali et sine ullo peccato; vel: hominem a primo ortu tantum in naturalibus extitisse, quibus deinde accesserit gratia tanquam naturae hominis jam constitutae superinfusa. ... 5. Socinianorum, docentium, hominem creatum esse non justum et sanctum, sed tantum rectum, simplicem et innocentem, sicut quotidie adhuc nascuntur infantes.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 847.)

Hic enim primum ac praecipuum objectum est officii humani et dilectio Dei compendium totius legis observatae censetur. PART. I. CAP. IV.
