Hofmannus: ״Gott hat den Menschen geschaffen als sein Bild, ihn so geschaffen, dass er ihm gleicht: dies besagen die Worte, und es fragt sich nur, worin die Gottesbildlichkeit desselben bestehen soll. . . An die Gottähnlichkeit eines sittlich heiligen Wesens lässt der Zusammenhang nicht denken. . . Gegenüber der Thierwelt ist der Mensch gottähnlich. . . Demnach ist eben das, was ihn befähigt, die Welt um ihn her zu beherrschen, auch das, worin seine Gottesbildlichkeit besteht: ein bewusst freies Ich, ein persönliches Wesen zu sein, ist er geschaffen. Nicht ein sittliches Verhalten bedeutet demnach die Gottesbildlichkeit, sondern ein sittliches Verhältniss.“ (Schriftbeweis. I, 251. sq.)

Non tantum circa Deum, sed etiam circa seipsum et homines, si qui coextiterint, alios. Alias enim voluntas est potentia coeca; oportet autem nihilominus eo inclinari eam, quo intellectus practicus suo dictamine tenderet.

Juxta ea, quae dicta sunt § praeced. 9. Nimirum, ut legibus non tantum affirmativis, sed et negativis obedientia sincera ac plena praeberetur atque omnia, quae alio inclinare poterant voluntatem, declinari aut sperni possent.

Non solum potentiam locomotivam, sed vel praecipue appetitum 8ensitivum, qui in tali subjecto, ubi sensitivus rationali appetitui jungitur, eidem conformari adeoque ei subjici aut regi ab eo debebat.§

11. Sed et appetitus ipse sensitivus ita tunc perficiebatur,a ut intellectus recto judicio et voluntatis sancto imperio promte et sine lucta se subjiceret, neque ulli motui inordinato, tanquam inevitabili, locum daret.b

Nam sicut appetitum sensitivum in homine non esse omnino rationis et moralitatis incapacem, alias constat; ita illum quoque instrui oportebat, ut constanter posset obedire facultatibus superioribus, neque in objecta sensibus grata ferretur, nisi convenienter rectae rationi; scilicet ut homo revera et perfecte justus, sanctus et valde bonus esset. Gen. 1, ult.

Quenstedtius: ״Si ex conditione materiae, quae a Deo est, rebellio et inclinatio ad vitia consequitur, Deus omnino illius mali causa et auctor est, et peccatum fuit ante peccatum, et poena praecessit cuipam, et Christus per se fuit peccato obnoxius; quae omnia sunt absurda et impia.“ (L. c. q. 2. f. 854.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Pelagianorum, statuentium, rebellionem partis inferioris adversus superiorem homini fuisse connaturalem. . . 2. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum, ipsimet naturae rebellionem virium adscribentium, quae per donum supernaturale justitiae originalis compescenda fuerit. . . 4. Socinianorum, contendentium, carnem non tantum rebellem fuisse rationi, sed etiam eandem vicisse.“

Hoc est, quod primi parentes in statu integritatis non cognoverunt, se esse nudos, neque erubuerunt, id est, nulla inordinata libidine appetitus sensitivi (quanquam praesente objecto, quod allicere poterat) vel leviter tacti fuerunt. Gen. 2, 25.§ 12.

Atque haec sapientia, justitia et sanctitas primorum hominum ita obtinet rationem imaginis divinae, ut ea sola atque unica a sit, a qua homo, absolute loquendo, imago Dei appellari possit. Magis certe, quam ipsa animae substantia spiritualis cum facultatibus essentialibus, in se praecise spectatis. Nam sine sagientia illa mens hominis coeca, sapientissimae menti divinae, sine sanctitate voluntas depravata et rebellione appetitus sensitivi infecta purissimae sanctissimaeque voluntati Dei dissimilis magis quam similis fuisset. Conf. b. Mus. Ausführl. Erklärung Q. 28. p. 215. et 221.

Hofmannus: ״Daher wird sie (die Gottesbildlichkelt) fortgepflanzt auch von dem sündig gewordenen Erstgeschaffenen, und nicht von dem heiligen Menschen, sondern von dem Menschen; darum dass er Mensch ist, heisst es nachmals, er trage Gottes Bild. Gen. 9, 5. Jak. 8, 9. . . Die Schrift versteht also unter der Gottesbildlichkeit des Menschen nicht ein sittliches Verhalten desselben, 80 dass mit dem Eintritte der Sünde die Gottesbildlichkeit verloren ginge.“ (Schriftbeweis. I, 252. sq.) § 13.


### On the Image of God Bestowed upon Man in the First Creation: This divine image was therefore also a natural gift, or one owed to man by…

This divine image was therefore also a natural gift, or one owed to man by nature for the right exercise of his connatural acts, in the absence of which nature would not have been pure, but impure. In another sense, indeed, it can also be called natural, insofar as it began with nature, inhered in the nature or essential faculties of man, and adorned and perfected them, and was intended to be propagated with nature itself to descendants through carnal generation. However, it is not called natural as if it either constituted the essence of man or necessarily followed from the essence; it is certain that it was taken away while the essence of man remained.

Quenstedtius: "Something is called natural:1. Constitutively, which constitutes the nature itself, and is either the nature itself or an essential part of it, such as soul and body.2. Consecutively, which follows nature and flows essentially from the form, such as the faculties of the soul, visibility, teachability, etc.3. Subjectively, which inheres in nature most closely as a native property.4. Perfectively, which intrinsically adorns and perfects it.5. Transitively, which is naturally propagated together with nature into others. When [we say] original justice was natural or connatural to Adam..." PART I. CAP. IV.

We say that we accept [original righteousness] as natural, not in the first or second sense, but in the third, fourth, and fifth senses, namely, on account of natural inherence, perfection, and propagation. As is evident from the opposite, namely, original sin, which, because it is congenital to us, always remains fixed and passes to descendants, is rightly called natural. . . When some of our own say that original righteousness was also constitutive and natural to the first man, they are speaking not of nature itself in itself, which is now common to all, but of integral nature.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 888. sq.)

The same: “If the first man had persisted in the state of integrity, the image of God, or original righteousness, would have been propagated to descendants through natural generation and thus would have been a hereditary good; from which fact it is also manifest that original righteousness was natural to the first man. For supernatural things cannot be more hereditary than a bridle is to the foals of horses or a garland to the offspring of women.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 23. f. 846.)

The same: “One must distinguish between the divine image and those things which are necessarily connected to it. The divine image is called natural to man because it is concreated, deeply implanted, and could have passed to posterity; but things connected with the divine image, such as, for example, the indwelling of the Most Holy Trinity, are not [natural]; for wherever the divine image is, there is the Most Holy Trinity. But the indwelling of the Most Holy Trinity is supernatural: first, because it does not exist by way of a concreated quality, as the image does; second, because it presupposes man already created and established in his perfection (for the house is prior in order to its inhabitant); third, because that indwelling of the Trinity was not so deeply implanted or so constituted that it would have passed to descendants by virtue of generation or by means of it, as the image would have passed by means of generation in the state of integrity.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 891.)

For indeed, if a man lacks those perfections without which the intellect, will, and sensitive appetite cannot rightly perform their duty, why would that not import a certain stain and impurity in man? For although it is natural to man, insofar as he consists of body and soul, to have a sensitive appetite tending toward its objects; yet because man is by nature ordered toward leading a life εὐσεβῶς, δικαίως καὶ σωφρόνως—piously, justly, and temperately—as if toward acts connatural to him and required for the sake of attaining the ultimate end toward which he himself tends; surely it is also natural to man to have a sensitive appetite obedient and exactly responsive to the higher faculties; and, regarding any faculties whatsoever, to have perfections as great as are necessary for this: that man, laboring under a certain defect of powers, might not necessarily stumble or sin at some point, but that man might rather be able to perform his duty rightly and constantly without stain or enormity. Whence, in the absence of such things, it cannot be said that the natural gifts of man are integral or pure, which are rather corrupted and therefore impure.

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: Antithesis: 1. Of the Scholastics and Papists ..., who maintain that original righteousness was a gift not natural and intrinsic, but supernatural and external. . . Hence they say that original righteousness was either like a garland or wreath placed upon the head of a virgin, or like a garment adjacent to man but not inherent, or like the hair of Samson, upon the cutting of which his supernatural strength perished while his natural strength remained, or like a bridle by which an untamed horse is restrained, or like an antidote which is outside the nature of the body, yet suppresses the plague or poison inherent in the bowels of nature, lest, breaking forth into act, it despoil man of life.”

Kahnisius: "The question is whether this harmony (with God) is the product of the nature created within man, as the Lutheran Church teaches, or a supernatural gift of grace, as the Roman Church teaches. A mediation of this opposition lies in the doctrine encountered in the Fathers, namely Irenaeus, that Adam, who had sprung from the Spirit of God as a spirit of life, had in the Spirit of God indwelling him the bond of communion with God. Enlightened, as John says in the Gospel (1:9), by the Logos [who enlightens] every man (!), so the light of the Logos, i.e., the Holy Spirit, will also have indwelt the first man. And if it is indeed the Spirit of God who renews the sinner into the image of God (Eph. 4:24; Col. 3:10), which includes an eternal indwelling of the Holy Spirit, then the prerequisite of this renewal by the Spirit to the Spirit seems to be an original indwelling of the Spirit of God. But one will be justified in calling this grace." (Die Luth. Dogmatik. Leipzig. 1868. III, 290.) §

14. Furthermore, God conferred upon man, even on the part of the body, some image of Himself, insofar as not only 1. the perfections of the soul exerted themselves through the external acts of the body, but furthermore 2. the very members of the organic body have a certain analogy to the divine attributes; 3. the countenance, erected toward heaven, offers a semblance of the divine majesty; but especially 4. the immortal body, or that which was able to endure perpetually and remain free from all corruption, had from the intention of God a likeness of the divine immortality.

And thus the divine image, which was formally in the soul, belongs to the body participatively. For thus Scripture, through ἀνθρωποπάθειαν, ascribes to God eyes, ears, and hands. For just as by this man departs from the likeness of other living creatures, so he approaches in a certain way the likeness of God and is seen as the heir of heavenly life.

For although the potentiality of dying did indeed fall into the body of man, being material, nevertheless the necessity of dying and the proximate potentiality were absent, since the elementary qualities, although contrary in themselves, were nonetheless tempered by a most accurate harmony, so that they gave no place to a passion that would tend toward destruction; and thus man, on the part of the body, could have not died, through the very goodness of nature, without the special aid of God, as it were, averting the necessity of dying.

That the body of man in the state of integrity was immortal in this sense is evident chiefly from Gen. 2:17, Rom. 5:12, and ch. 6:23, where the origin of death is ascribed to sin; and thus in the first state, where sin had no place, death or the necessity of dying is also denied to have had a place. It is said, however, that the first man was immortal on the part of the body. PART I. CHAP. IV.

nature; not in the sense in which God is by nature immortal, to whom it is repugnant by essence to be mortal or to be able to be destroyed, nor in the sense in which angels, being immaterial by nature, are also said to be immortal by nature, even though they could be annihilated by God. But insofar as the very nature of the first man’s body was created such that it could live perpetually, and was not subject to death, to be undergone sooner or later.

Quenstedtius: "Regarding immortality, the question is not... about an all-encompassing and absolute inability to die..., but about a natural, proximate, immediate, absolute [inability], which inclines toward death that would certainly follow naturally. Nor is it about the body considered in the abstract, but about the whole concrete or integral man. The state of the controversy, therefore, is this: Whether Adam... could be delivered from death and preserved immortal only through the supernatural grace of God: ... Distinguish between passibility or internal passion flowing from the nature and constitution of the thing, and external [passion] coming from an external principle—heat, cold, beasts, fire, and a thousand other ways; both were absent from the integral man... The first man was impassible... by reason of external violence, e.g., lightning, and other such things; he was immortal and indissoluble by the power of divine providence, maintenance, and conservation, insofar as God was to preserve man from all external force through singular providence. Distinguish between the means preserving and serving immortality, and the remedies opposed to an emerging contrary and preventing it: food, the tree of life, etc., were of the number of the former, but there was nothing in the state of integrity of the order of the latter." (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 877. sq.)

The same: "Specifically, the impassibility of the body is proved: α. From the nakedness of our first parents, Gen. 2:25, which could not have been endured without pain if their bodies had been passible and subject to rain, heat, cold, and other inconveniences and sufferings of the air; β. from the absence of causes, both external and internal, which arose either from the image of God or from the peculiar providence of God; γ. from the plenary restoration of the divine image in the other life regarding the bodies of the glorified, which will be entirely impassible." (L. c. f. 881.) §

Latin:

Fuit ergo etiam imago haec divina donum naturale, seu homini ad actus suos connaturales recte exercendos per natura1n a debitum, quo absente, natura non fuerit pura, sed b impura. Alias equidem etiam naturale dici potest, quatenus cum natura coepit, naturae seu essentialibus hominis facultatibus inhaesit easque ornavit ac perfecit, et cum ipsa natura ad posteros per carnalem generationem propagari debuit. Non autem dicitur naturale, quasi vel constituerit essentiam hominis, vel ex essentia necessario secutum fuerit; certum est, ablatum fuisse, permanente hominis essentia.

Quenstedtius: ״Naturale aliquid dicitur: 1. constitutive, quod ipsam naturam constituit, estque vel ipsa natura, vel pars ejus essentialis, ut anima et corpus. 2. Consecutive, quod naturam consequitur et a forma essentialiter manat, ut facultates animae, visibilitas, docibilitas etc. 3. Subjective, quod naturae arctissime ut proprietas nativa inhaeret. 4. Perfective, quod eam intrinsece exornat et perficit. 5. Transitive, quod naturaliter cum natura simul in alios propagatur. Quando justitiam primaevam Adamo naturalem vel connaturalem fuisse PART. I. CAP. IV.

dicimus, non primo vel secundo, sed tertio, quarto et quinto modo naturale accipimus, videl. ob naturalem inhaesionem, perfectionem et propagationem. Ut ex opposito, videl. peccato origin., id elucescit, quod, quia nobis congenitum semper fixum haeret et ad posteros transit, recte naturale dicitur. . . Quando nonnulli e nostratibus dicunt, quod etiam constitutive justitia originalis primo homini naturalis fuerit, loquuntur non de natura ipsa in se, quae nunc omnibus communis est, sed de natura integra.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 888. sq.) Idem: ״

Si primus homo in statu integritatis perstitisset, imago Dei seu justitia originalis per naturalem generationem fuisset ad posteros propagata et sic fuisset bonum haereditarium; ex quo ipso etiam manifestum est, justitiam originalem fuisse primo homini naturalem. Supernaturalia enim non possunt magis esse haereditaria, quam fraenum pullis equorum vel sertum partui feminarum.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 23. f. 846.) Idem: ״

Distinguendum inter imaginem divinam, et quae eidem necessario connexa sunt. Imago divina dicitur homini naturalis, quia est concreata, penitus infixa et transire potuit ad posteritatem, non autem connexa cum imagine divina, qualis v. g. fuit inhabitatio SS. Trinitatis; nam ubi ubi est imago divina, ibi est SS. Trinitas. Sed inhabitatio SS. Trinitatis est supernaturalis: tum quia se non habet per modum qualitatis concreatae, ut imago; tum quia praesupponit hominem jam creatum et constitutum in sua perfectione (prior enim est domus ordine, quam illius incola); tum quia illa inhabitatio Trinitatis non fuit ita penitus infixa aut sic comparata, ut etiam vi generationis vel mediante illa transiisset ad posteros, uti mediante generatione in statu integritatis transiisset imago.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 891.)

Sane enim, carere hominem perfectionibus illis, sine quibus non possunt intellectus, voluntas et appetitus sensitivus officio suo recte fungi, quidni labem quandam et impuritatem in homine importet? Quamvis enim naturale sit homini, quatenus corpore et anima constat, habere appetitum sensitivum, in objecta sua tendentem; quia tamen homo per naturam ordinatur ad vitam εύσεβώς, δικαίως xa\ σωψρόνως, pie, juste ac temperanter ducendam, tanquam ad actus sibi connaturales et finis ultimi, ad quem ipse tendit, consequendi causa requisitos; sane et hoc homini naturale est, habere appetitum sensitivum superioribus facultatibus morigerum et exacte respondentem; quoad quaslibet vero facultates habere perfectiones tantas, quantae necessariae sunt ad hoc, ne hominem, defectu quodam virium laborantem, necesse sit aliquando impingere aut peccare, sed ut posset homo potius officio suo sine labe aut enormitate recte et constanter fungi. Unde, absentibus talibus, dici non potest, naturalia hominis esse integra aut pura, quae potius corrupta atque adeo impura sunt.

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: Antithesis: 1. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum ..., statuentium, justitiam originalem donum fuisse non naturale et intrinsecum, sed supernaturale et externum. . . Hinc justitiam originalem fuisse, inquiunt, vel instar serti aut corollae, capiti virginis impositae, vel instar vestis homini adjacentis, non inhaerentis, vel instar crinium Samsonis, quibus resectis supernaturale quidem ipsius robur perierit, naturale tamen remanserit, vel instar freni, quo equus indomitus coercetur, vel instar antidoti, quod extra corporis naturam est, pestem tamen vel venenum in naturae visceribus inhaerens reprimit, ne, in actum erumpens, hominem vita spoliet.“

Kahnisius: ״Die Frage ist, ob diese Harmonie (mit Gott) das Product der dem Menschen anerschaffenen Natur ist, wie die lutherische Kirche lehrt, oder übernatürliche Gnadengabe, wie die römische Kirche lehrt. Eine Vermittelung dieses Gegensatzes liegt in der bei den Vätern, namentlich Irenäus, uns entgegentretenden Lehre, dass Adam, der dem Geiste Gottes als Geist des Lebens entsprungen war, in dem ihm inwohnenden Geiste Gottes das Band der Gemeinschaft mit Gott hatte. Erleuchtet, wie Johannes im Evangelium sagt (1, 9.), der Logos jeden Menschen (!), so wird das Licht des Logos d. h. der Heilige Geist auch den ersten Menschen eingewohnt haben. Und wenn es doch der Geist Gottes ist, der den Sünder erneuert zum Bilde Gottes (Ephes. 4, 24. Kol. 3, 10.), welches ein ewiges Einwohnen des Heiligen Geistes einschliesst, so scheint die Voraussetzung dieser Erneuerung durch den Geist zum Geist ein ursprüngliches Eiuwohnen des Geistes Gottes zu sein. Dies aber wird man Gnade zu nennen berechtigt sein.“ (Die Luth. Dogmatik. Leipzig. 1868. III, 290.) §

14. Caeterum contulit Deus homini etiam ex parte corporis aliquam sui imaginem, quatenus non tantum 1. perfectiones animae per actus externos corporis se exseruerunt,a sed praeterea 2. ipsa membra corporis organici analogiam quandam habent ad attributa b divina; 3. vultus ad coelum erectus divinae majestatis speciem praebet;c inprimis vero 4. corpus immortale,d seu quod perpetuo poterat durare et ab omni corruptione liberum manere, immortalitatis divinae similitudinem ex intentione Dei habuit.

Atque ita imago divina, quae in anima formaliter erat, participative competit corpori. Ita enim Scriptura per άνΰρωποπάΰειαν adscribit Deo oculos, aures, manus. Nam sicut per hoc a similitudine caeterorum animantium homo recedit, ita ad similitudinem Dei quodammodo accedit et tanquam haeres vitae coelestis conspicitur.

Nam quamvis tunc potentia moriendi remota in corpus hominis, quippe materiale, utique caderet, necessitas tamen moriendi et potentia proxima abfuit, cum qualitates elementares, licet ex se contrariae, nihilominus accuratissima harmonia temperatae essent, ut passioni, quae ad interitum tenderet, locum non darent; atque ita homo ex parte corporis potuerit non mori, per ipsam naturae bonitatem, sine speciali Dei, velut necessitatem moriendi avertentis, auxilio.

Quod autem corpus hominis in statu integritatis hoc sensu immortale fuerit, patet praecipue ex Gen. 2, 17. Rom. 5, 12. cap. 6, 23., ubi origo mortis peccato adscribitur; adeoque in statu primo, ubi peccatum locum non habuit, mors quoque aut necessitas moriendi locum habuisse negatur. Dicitur autem, hominem primum ex parte corporis fuisse immortalem PART. I. CAP. IV.

natura; non eo sensu, quo Dem natura immortalis est, cui per essentiam repugnat esse mortalem aut posse destrui, neque eo, quo angeli, per naturam immateriales, etiam natura immortales dicuntur, etsi a Deo annihilari possint. Sed quatenus ipsa natura corporis primi hominis talis fuit condita, ut posset perpetuo vivere, neque obnoxia esset morti, serius ocius subeundae.

Quenstedtius: ,,Quoad immortalitatem non quaeritur ... de omnimoda et absoluta moriendi impotentia. . ., sed de naturali, propinqua, immediata, absoluta, quae ad mortem certo naturaliter sccuturam propendet. Nec de corpore in abstracto considerato, sed de toto concreto seu integro homine. Status itaque controversiae hic est: An Adam. . . nonnisi per supernaturalem Dei gratiam a morte vindicari et immortalis conservari potuerit: . . . Dist. inter passibilitatem seu passionem internam ex rei natura et constitutione fluentem, et externam a principio externo, aestu, frigore, bestiis, igne et mille aliis modis pervenientem; utraque ab homine integro abfuit. . . Impassibilis fuit homo primus. . . ratione externae violentiae, e. g. fulminum, et quae sunt alia; immortalis fuit et indissolubilis vi providentiae et manutenentiae et conservationis divinae, quatenus Deus praeservaturus erat hominem ab omni vi externa per singularem providentiam. Dist. inter media conservantia et immortalitati ancillantia, et inter remedia contrario emergenti opposita et praecaventia: cibus, arbor vitae etc. fuerunt ex numero priorum, nullum autem fuit in statu integritatis ex ordine posteriorum.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 877. sq.)

Idem: ,,In specie probatur corporis impassibilitas: a. Ex ־nuditate primorum parentum Gen. 2, 25., quae sine dolore tolerari non potuisset, si corpora fuissent passibilia et pluviae, aestui, frigori aliisque aeris incommodis et perpessionibus obnoxia; ß. ex absentia causarum, tam externarum, quam internarum, quae oriebatur vel ex imagine Dei, vel ex peculiari Dei providentia; y. ex plenaria restitutione imaginis divinae in altera vita circa corpora gloriflcatorum, quae prorsus erunt impassibilia.“ (L. c. f. 881.) §


### On the Image of God Bestowed upon Man in the First Creation: Finally, God added to man dominion over inferior creatures, especially brute…

15. Finally, God added to man dominion over inferior creatures, especially brute animals, by which he likewise bore some likeness to God, the Lord of this universe. See Gen. 1:26 and 28; ch. 2:16. That dominion was placed not only in the right and power of man over beasts and other creatures, but also in the force and power of bending them to obedience, without difficulty and fear of harm being inflicted by them. For we do not say that this dominion extended to the stars and the angels. And in the cited place, the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, the beasts and the whole earth, and all creeping things are mentioned, which can be enough for us.

Luther: "I believe that Adam could have commanded a lion with one word, just as we command a trained dog... Adam and Eve become rulers of the earth, the sea, and the air. Moreover, this dominion is committed to them not only by counsel, but also by express command... Therefore, the naked man, without weapons and walls, indeed even without any clothing, in his own naked flesh alone, ruled over all birds, wild beasts, and fish... Who can

to think of that as a kind of portion of the divine nature, that Adam and Eve understood all the affections, senses, and powers of all animals? For what kind of kingdom would it have been, had they not known this? ...

If, therefore, we wish to proclaim a distinguished philosopher, let us proclaim our first parents, while they were still pure from sin. ...

They also possessed the most certain knowledge of the stars and of all astronomy. But the things we accomplish in life are not done through the dominion that Adam had, but through industry and art. As we see, birds and fish are caught by guile and fraud; thus, beasts are tamed by art. For those that are most domestic, such as geese and hens, are nevertheless wild by themselves and by their own nature.

Therefore, this leprous body still has, by the benefit of God, some semblance of dominion over other creatures.

But that is very small and far inferior to that first dominion, where there was no need for art or guile, but the creature simply obeyed the divine voice when Adam and Eve were commanded to rule over them.

Therefore, we retain the name and term of dominion as a bare title; but the thing itself has been almost entirely lost.

And yet it is good to know and think upon these things, so that we may sigh for that coming day in which these things will be restored to us, which we lost in paradise through sin.

For we expect that life which Adam would also have expected.

And we rightly marvel at this, and give thanks to God for it, that we, so deformed by sin, so dull, stupid, and as it were dead, through the benefit of Christ expect the same glory of spiritual life that Adam was to expect if he had remained in his animal life, which possessed the image of God.” (

On Gen. 1:26.) And indeed, if you take the image of God generally, it cannot be denied that a part of it was placed in this dominion, according to those things which we said in note a. to § 7 from the blessed Gerhard and the blessed Wigand. If you take it in a special sense, it cannot be called a part, but a certain consequence or appendix of the divine image. See Gen. 1:27, where God, blessing the humans already created in His image, says: Have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heavens, and over every living thing that moves on the earth. §

16. The subject which is the bearer of the divine image was not only Adam, but also Eve, especially insofar as she was placed in original righteousness.

Meanwhile, regarding those things which were not equally necessary for attaining the end set before both, we do not assert an absolute equality between both parents.

Or the suppositum, which is denominated as bearing the divine image. See Gen. 1:27 and ch. 5:1-2, where it is expressly said that the human, whom God created in His own image, was not an individual of one male sex, but male and female.

Certainly, the passages at Col. 3:10 and Eph. 4:24, where mention is made of the image of God so-called κατ’ έξοχήν, to which men ought to be renewed, or which they ought to recover, speak not only of males but also of females, just as Gal. 3:28 says of those who are in Christ Jesus, through whom the divine image is restored in them, that in them there is not ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ, male or female, as if they were different in this state.

And the thing itself teaches that the woman, in order to rightly exercise the acts connatural to her, had equal need of the perfections of the soul, or original righteousness, as the man. PART I. CHAP. IV.

In the matter of the knowledge of natural things, Eve seems to have yielded to Adam. And it is commonly taught elsewhere that Satan preferred to attack Eve, as the weaker vessel, in his temptation; and to this is referred what is said in 1 Timothy 2:14: "Adam was not deceived, but Eve." But neither was equal dominion granted to both, since the man was also the head of the woman, and she was subject to him. Add 1 Corinthians 11:7-8. Nevertheless, the woman possessed an immortal body, and those things which otherwise pertain to the essence of man, no less than the man.

Luther: "These things were in Eve just as much as in Adam, as Eve’s speech shows when she answers the serpent concerning the tree in the midst of paradise. There it appears sufficiently that she knew her end, for which she was created, and she shows the author through whom she knows it. For she says: 'The Lord said.' Therefore, she did not hear these things from Adam alone, but her nature itself was so pure and full of the knowledge of God that she understood and saw the Word of God by herself." (L. c.)

Quenstedtius: "That dominion over living creatures was granted not only to the man, but also to the woman (for in Gen. 1:26, dominion is conferred also upon the woman through the plural ידו:, 'let them have dominion'). . . For although dominion over the man was not granted to the woman, yet dominion over the remaining living creatures was not denied to her. And certainly, from the passage 1 Cor. 11:7, it is rightly gathered that the woman also is the image of God, for otherwise it could not be said that she received the image of God from the man. Thus, a distinction must be made between the image of God taken exclusively and taken inclusively: the man is the image of God exclusively, i.e., only of God and in such a way that he is not at the same time the image of someone else; but the woman is the image of God inclusively, i.e., not only of God, but in such a way that she is at the same time the image of someone else, namely, of the man; and in this consists the man’s excellence over the woman." (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 856. sq.)

The same: "Distinguish between wisdom and the knowledge of physical things, which the woman had equally with Adam, and between the different degrees of that same knowledge, which were unequal." (L. c. f. 857.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Encratites and Severians, who condemned the female sex as an impure and inherently evil creature. . . 2. Of Diodorus of Tarsus, whom Petavius notes as denying that the woman was created in the image of God. . . and Theodoret himself restricts the image of God to the man alone. . . 4. Of the Socinians, who maintain that the woman was not created in the image of God, for this reason: because they think the image of God consists in dominion, which does not apply to the woman." (L. c. f. 855.) §

17. The subject in which the divine image, specifically so-called, resided were the faculties of the human soul: the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite. Or those parts of man according to which he bore the divine image. See above § 9, 10, 11.

18. The proximate end of the divine image, specifically and principally so called, was a holy life of man, pleasing to God; the more remote or consequent end was eternal blessedness. The common end of the divine image, taken generally, is the glory of the divine wisdom, power, and goodness. For just as the divine image itself, taken in this sense, implied in man powers—on the part of the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite—for living holily according to the will of God, who conferred these powers upon man, the intention was terminated at such a life of man as at an end. To this end, as the ultimate good, man was to have arrived, with that holy life intervening, and it would have followed without impediment if man had retained and propagated this image. Certainly, He created him with His image for eternal life.

Quenstedtius: “The adjuncts of the image of God are: 1. Its natural and mutable inherence (Gen. 1:27; Wis. 2:23; Gen. 5:3). 2. Its natural propagation (Gen. 5:3; Rom. 5:12). 3. Most pleasant habitation (Gen. 2:8). 4. The accession of supernatural gifts; such as the supernatural favor of God, the gracious indwelling of the Most Holy Trinity, and the sweetness and delight resulting therefrom.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 23. f. 846.)

The same: “Man in his integrity, after his translation from this world into the heavens, would indeed have had eternal life, yet, strictly speaking, he could not have been said to have eternal salvation, since salvation implies a twofold benefit: privative, or liberation from the evil of guilt and punishment; and positive, or the granting of life. Because, therefore, man in his integrity, when he had been translated into heaven, would have had no need of liberation from those evils, he could not properly be said to be saved, but to live forever.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 22. f. 845.)

Calovius: “How long life would have been prolonged in the state of integrity, no mortal will explain... Likewise, it is doubtful whether it would have been by the succession of children born, or whether all were to be translated at once.” (System. P. IV. p. 445.)

For what we said concerning creation in general in Chapter II, § 23, that holds no less, and indeed primarily, here. §

19. The divine image, taken specifically, can be defined as the complex of several perfections in the intellect and will, and even in the sensitive appetite of the first humans, conferred upon them by the Triune God, and out of His goodness, in the first creation, for the imitation of the divine perfections, for the sake of their holy life and blessedness, and finally for the promotion of the divine glory. PART 1. CHAPTER V.

Or primarily or principally so-called. For it imports this in the nominative case, according to § 8 and following. As the subject *quo* (by which), according to § 17, collated with §§ 9 and following. Which are the subject *quod* (which); see § 16. As the efficient cause; see § 1, note b, and § 2. Which behaves by way of an impulsive cause, according to § 3. As the exemplary cause of the image (which was given to man), as the exemplar; see § 4 and 5. In which the end of the bestowed divine image consists, according to § 18. § 20.

The divine image generally so-called can be defined as a complex of various perfections of the human soul and body, indeed even of the whole *suppositum* of our first parents, bestowed by the Triune God, out of His goodness, according to the likeness of His own perfections, in the first creation, for the sake of the holy and blessed life of men, and for the divine glory. See § 9. Of substantial and accidental, internal and external [perfections]. These and the rest, which treat of the subj ect *quod* and *quo*, and of the efficient, impulsive, exemplary, and final causes, almost agree with those things which were handed down in the prior definition. Chapter V.

Latin:

Gen. 1, 26. et 28. cap. 2, 16. Positum autem fuit dominium illud non solum in jure ac potestate hominis in bestias et creaturas alias, verum etiam in vi ac potentia flectendi ea ad obsequium, sine difficultate et metu inferendi ab illis damni. Lutherus: ״Ego credo, Adam ita potuisse uno verbo imperare boni, sicut nos imperamus assuefacto cani. . . Fiunt Adam et Heva rectores terrae, maris et aeris. Committitur autem eis hoc dominium non solum consilio, sed etiam expresso mandato. . . Ergo nudus homo sine armis et muris, imo etiam sine vestitu omni in sola sua nuda carne dominatus est omnibus volucribus, feris et piscibus. . . Quis potest

cogitare istam quasi portionem divinae naturae, quod Adam et Heva omnes omnium animalium affectus, sensus et vires omnes intellexerunt? Quale enim regnum fuisset, nisi hoc scivissent? ...

Si igitur volumus praedicare insignem philosophum, praedicemus primos nostros parentes, cum adhuc essent a peccato puri. . .
