## 7 On the Providence of God

ON THE PROVIDENCE OF GOD. § 1. The most manifest argument of the divine goodness after creation is divine providence.

Whence also the reason for the order is evident here. Namely, its impulsive cause is the divine goodness, as we shall say in § 5. § 2. The word *providentia* (providence), derived from *providendo* (foreseeing), otherwise by its native force seems to denote the knowledge or vision of future things, before they happen

tion; but from the usage of speech, and in this very place, τό providere [to provide] is the same as to consult for the salvation of creatures. And divine providence denotes not only an act of the intellect, by which God knows how to arrange and bestow those things which conduce to the things created by Him being preserved in their being and led to their ends, but also an act of the will, by which, according to that knowledge of His, He wills and ordains creatures wills and decrees to preserve and govern creatures.

To this corresponds the word πρόνοια in the apocryphal book of Wisdom, which is not read in the canonical books in the same way regarding God. From the Hebrew, it corresponds to the word for seeing, as in Gen. 22:8, יהיה יראה, "God will see," that is, "will provide." Compare 1 Sam. 16:1.

It is long established that the preposition pro, as it does not rarely elsewhere, so in composition with the verb of seeing, signifies the same as "before" or "ahead." Thus Cicero in *Pro Murena*: "to foresee the future"; and Caesar: "to foresee and foreknow." Compare the author of Book II *ad Herennium*, who says: "Providence is that by which something future is seen before it happens."

For he who sees future things in any way is not called "provident," but he who, having taken account of the present state and of the future events that are foreseen to occur, consults for the need or for his own affairs or those of others. However, when we look at divine providence, that word has respect to things other than God, distinct and created, of which God takes care and whose utility He promotes.

Opinions indeed vary here, insofar as some contend that not so much the immanent acts of the divine mind and will, as the external acts themselves of preserving and governing, are signified by the name of providence; others teach that an immanent act is indeed denoted by that name, but believe it pertains formally to the intellect and consequently to the will, or vice versa.

Yet it is easily recognized that this entire controversy is not so much about the thing itself as about the words. For all concede that to providence, viewed in its breadth, pertains both πρόγνωσιν [foreknowledge] or the act of the intellect, by which God foreknows what is conducive to creatures, and πρόθεσιν [purpose] or the act of the will, by which He wills to order and arrange what He has foreseen to be conducive, and finally διοίκησιν [administration] or the very preservation and government of creatures.

Meanwhile, if we look at the force of the words, providence seems to denote not so much external acts, as of an executive power, as the very care of creatures in God, and thus the acts of the intellect and will, from which those external acts proceed.

But the order of those internal acts is certainly such that the act of the intellect precedes, and the act of the will succeeds, or the purpose of bestowing, according to the dictate of the intellect, those things which benefit creatures; although it does not so much follow providence itself as it constitutes it intrinsically together with the preceding act of the intellect.

If, however, you look at the usage of speech, it must be admitted that the name of providence itself is not rarely wont to be ascribed, by a metonymy otherwise accepted, to the acts of preservation and government, which are the effects, signs, and characters of providence. PART I. CHAP. V.

I 3. That divine providence exists is most clear from Scripture,b beyond the fact that it is established by the light of nature.a Indeed, once the existence of God and the dependence of creatures upon a wise, powerful, and good God are admitted, providence cannot be denied.

Dannhauer: "Scripture, nature, and conscience assert providence to God... The human mind, imbued with histories from the founding of the world to the present, experiences this as an observer of fatal periods, heroic movements, the order of things, and the musical harmony of causes. For it is manifest that the world was not founded by chance or fortuitously without a cause, nor did the admirable, sudden concert and concord of infinite things responding to mutual uses coalesce rashly, as if from atoms. That everything corresponds to the end and use for which it was instituted is an indication that this world is the work of an intelligent artisan who uses reason. Add miracles, θεῖα, and the sense derived both from divine benefits and from those things which happen bitterly and troublesomely. Bread from the earth, wine from the vine—what are these but an open, constant, and perennial seal of providence? Manasseh in chains, Jonah in the whale, Julian in battle felt the power of the Divine; cf. Wis. 11:14. Add also the variety of human physiognomy, made to that end so that humans might be able to distinguish one another. Unless mortals were distinguished from one another by certain lineaments and a diversity of forms, a wondrous disturbance would follow in daily life and human society. Indeed, no commerce could take place between them; and that state of affairs would be the occasion for huge evils, monstrous crimes, and the slaughter of all, if spouses could not distinguish one another, nor friend be distinguished from foe, nor children from parents, nor these distinguish their children from strangers or their own wives by any sign. Finally, the wicked and criminal would do anything with impunity, since they would hide in that common similarity and confusion of all. Add the wondrous skill and industry in otherwise brute animals in protecting life, in procuring food, in seeking or fabricating lairs and nests, in avoiding dangers, in pursuing and capturing others." (Hodosoph. Phaen. III. p. 157.)

b) For not only is the whole of Scripture, communicated to men for their own salvation by the provident hand of God, an effect and index of providence, but especially the entire Ps. 104, Matt. 6:26 et seqq. declare it. Conf. Job ch. 38, 39, 40. Acts 17:25 sqq. Nor does the author of the book of Wisdom, ch. 14:3, speak poorly: "Your providence (πρόνοια), O Father, governs (διακυβερνᾷ) all things," he says to God. §

4. The efficient cause of providence is the entire Holy Trinity.b Understand this as virtually causing. Although, if you take the word "providence" for the external acts themselves, a formally efficient cause must truly be admitted.

Reusch: "Causes that are formally causing are properly called causes, which differ from the caused not only really, but also essentially, to such an extent that the cause and the caused are diverse beings. But no act of God can produce another act in God as a diverse being... Therefore, there cannot be within God a cause properly so-called of any..."

OF THE PROVIDENCE OF GOD. . . . divine acts. But in a point of reason, one perfection must often be conceived before another perfection can be conceived in God; e.g., before I can conceive that God is eternal, it must be established in a point of reason that He is a being from Himself and exists necessarily. Since, therefore, the cognition which is to be established from the nature of the object, if I wish to conceive another cognition, is called the reason *a priori*, and such a reason *a priori* is termed a virtually causing cause.” (Annotationes in B. Compend. p. 175 sq.)

Luther: “It is God who creates, works, and sustains all things through His almighty power and right hand, as our faith confesses; for He does not send out officials or angels when He creates or sustains something, but all such things are the very work of His own divine power. But if He is to create and sustain it, He must be there and make and sustain His creature in its innermost as well as in its outermost parts. Therefore, He must indeed be present Himself in every creature, in its innermost, outermost, all around, through and through, below and above, in front and behind, so that nothing can be more present or more inward in all creatures than God Himself with His power. For it is He who makes the skin; it is He who also makes the bones; it is He who makes the hair on the skin; it is He also who makes the marrow in the bones; it is He who makes every little piece of hair; it is He who makes every little piece of marrow; He must indeed make everything, both piece and whole: thus His hand must be there to make it; that cannot fail. To this point Scripture speaks powerfully, Isa. 66:1, 2...: The heaven is my throne and the earth my footstool. He does not say: A piece of heaven is my throne, a piece or place of the earth is my footstool; but whatever and wherever heaven is, there is my throne, be it heaven below, above, or beside the earth; and whatever or wherever earth is, be it on the floor of the sea, in the grave of the dead, or in the center of the earth, there is my footstool. Now guess, where is His head, arm, chest, body, if He fills the earth with His feet and the heaven with His legs? Far, far does He reach over and outside the world, over heaven and earth. What can or will Isaiah now [say] with this saying, but as St. Hilary also speaks concerning this, that God is essentially present at all ends, in and through every creature in all their parts and places, so that the world is full of God and He fills them all.” (Dass diese Worte Christi: Das ist mein Leib, noch feste stehen. Opp. Hal. XX, 1002—1004.)

Just as of other immanent acts and all external works. See, however, specifically concerning the Father, as providing for creatures, Matt. 6:26 and 32, where our heavenly Father is said to take care of the birds and of men. Concerning the Son, it is taught in Heb. 1:3 that He upholds all things. Concerning the Father and the Son, that which Christ says in John 5:17 holds true: My Father is working until now, and I am working. Concerning the Holy Spirit, it is said in 1 Cor. 12:11 that He distributes spiritual gifts for the preservation and government of the church.

ANTITHESIS. Hofmann: “It is not the case with this that God only works extraordinary things, instead of through the ordinary forces of nature, through angels: in the entire life of nature, Scripture sees the rule of spirits... As far as we are concerned, it is only this, that all good and evil phenomena of world-life are equally traced back to the rule and working of a multitude of spirits... They (the angels) are therefore created beings... Created life, into which the sole fullness of the being of God enters, in order therein to PART I. CHAP. V.

Latin:

DE PROVIDENTIA DEI. § 1. Bonitatis divinae post a creationem manifestissimum argumentum est b providentia divina.

Unde et hic ratio ordinis patet. Nimirum causa impulsiva ejus est bonitas divina, uti dicemus § 5.§ 2. Providentiae vox a a,providendo derivata, alias vi nativa b videtur denotare futurorum, antequam fiant,

cognitionem seu visionem; sed ex usu loquendi et hoc quidem loco τό providere idem est, quod consulere c saluti creaturarum. Et providentia divina denotat d non solum actum intellectus, quo Deus ea, quae rebus a se conditis in esse suo conservandis et ad fines suos deducendis conducunt, disponere et conferre novit, verum etiam actum volunta־ tis, quo juxta scientiam illam suam vult et statuit creaturas conservare et gubernare.

Cui in libro apocrypho Sapientiae respondet vox πρόνοια, quae in canonicis non aeque de Deo legitur. Ex Ebraeo respondet vox videndi, uti Gen. 22, 8. יהיה יראה,, Deus videbit, id est, providebit. Confer. 1 Sam. 16, 2.

Praepositionem pro enim, sicut alias non raro, ita in compositione cum verbo videndi idem significare, quod prae, vel arde, pridem constat. Sic Cicero pro Muraena: providere futurum; et Caesar: providere et praesentire. Conf. Auct. L. II. ad Herenn., qui, providentia, ait, est, per quam futurum aliquid videtur, antequam fit.

Non enim, qui quovis modo futura videt, providens dicitur, sed qui, habita ratione status praesentis et futurorum, qui eventuri praevidentur, casuum, consulit indigentiae aut rebus suis vel aliorum. Quando autem providentiam divinam spectamus, vox ea respectum habet ad res alias a Deo distinctas et creatas, quarum curam Deus gerat, utilitatem promoveat.

Variant equidem hic sententiae, quatenus alii non tam actus immanentes mentis et voluntatis divinae, quam ipsos actus externos conservandi et gubernandi nomine providentiae significari contendunt, alii actum quidem immanentem eo nomine denotari docent, credunt autem, ad intellectum formaliter, ad voluntatem consequenter pertinere, alii vice versa.

Quam tamen controversiam omnem non tam de re ipsa, quam de vocibus esse, facile cognoscitur. Omnes enim concedunt, ad providentiam in sua latitudine spectatam pertinere tum πρόγνωαΐν seu actum intellectus, quo Deus praecognoscit, quid creaturis sit conducibile, tum πρόΗεσιν seu actum voluntatis, quo, quae conducibilia praevidit, ordinare ac disponere vult, tum denique δωίχησιν seu ipsam creaturarum conservationem et gubernationem.

Interim, si ad vim vocum spectemus, videtur providentia non tam actus externos, velut executivae potentiae, quam ipsam curam creaturarum in Deo, adeoque actus intellectus et voluntatis denotare, unde actus illi externi proficiscantur.

Internorum illorum actuum autem utique hic ordo est, ut actus intellectus antecedat, succedat actus voluntatis, seu propositum conferendi, juxta intellectus dictamen, quae creaturis prosunt; etsi non tam consequatur providentiam ipsam, quam una cum actu intellectus praevio eum intrinsece constituat.

Si vero usum loquendi spectes, fatendum est, actibus conservationis et gubernationis, qui sunt effectus, signa et characteres providentiae, ipsum providentiae nomen haud raro per metonymiam alias receptam adscribi solere.BaieriComp. ed. Walther. II. 11 PART. I. CAP. V.

I 3. Dari providentiam divinam, praeterquam quod ex lumine naturae constat,a ex Scriptura clarissimum est.b Scilicet admissa Dei existentia et creaturarum a Deo sapiente, potente ac bono dependentia, negari providentia non potest.

Dannhauerus: ,,Providentiam Deo asserit Scriptura, natura et conscientia. . . Experitur mens humana, historiis a mundo condito huc usque imbuta, observatrix periodorum fatalium, heroicorum motuüm, ordinis rerum, harmoniae causarum musicae. Neque enim casu ac fortuito absque causa vel mnndum esse conditum, vel mutuis usibus respondentium rerum infinitarum admirabilem repente concentum ac concordiam quasi ex atomis temere coaluisse, palam est. Nihil non ad eum finem et usum, cujus gratia institutum est, congruere, indicium est, intelligentis ac ratione utentis artificis opus esse hunc mundum. Adde miracula, &εΐα, sensum cum ex beneficiis divinis, tum ex iis, quae acerbe accidunt atque moleste. Panis e terra, vinum e vite, quid nisi apertum est juge et perenne providentiae signaculum? Manasses in vinculis, Jonas in ceto, Julianus in praelio sensit Numinis vim cf. Sap. 11, 14. Adde et physiognomiae humanae varietatem, eo fine factam, ut se homines invicem dignoscere possent. Nisi mortales certis lineamentis ac diversitate formarum distincti invicem forent, mira in convictu quotidiano et humana societate perturbatio sequeretur. Imo nulla inter ipsos commercia fleri possent; eaque res ingentium malorum et immanium scelerum atque internecionis omnium esset occasio, si neque conjuges se mutuo discernerent, nec amicus ab hoste dignosceretur, neque liberi parentes, nec hi filias ab externis aut uxoribus suis ullo signo distinguerent. Scelerati denique ac facinorosi impune quidvis facerent, cum in illa communi omnium similitudine ac confusione delitescerent. Adde in animalibus alioquin brutis miram solertiam ac industriam in vita tuenda, in procurando pabulo, in quaerendis aut fabricandis latibulis ac nidis, in evitandis periculis, in persequendis ac captandls aliis.“ (Hodosoph. Phaen. III. p. 157.)

b) Non solum enim tota Scriptura, hominibus ad ipsorum salutem a provida Dei manu communicata, effectus atque index est providentiae, sed inprimis Ps. 104. integer, Matth. 6, 20. et seqq. illam declarant. Conf. Jobi cap. 38. 39. 40. Ad. 17, 25. sqq. Nec male auctor libri Sapientiae cap. 14., 3. Tua, ait ad Deum, Pater, providentia (πρόνοια) cuncta gubernat (διαχυβερνα). §

4. Causa efficiens a providentiae tota SS. Trinitas est.b Puta virtualiter causans. Quamvis, si providentiae vocem pro ipsis actibus externis accipias, causa formaliter efficiens revera admittenda sit.

Reuschius: ״Causae formaliter causantes sunt proprie dictae causae, quae adeo a causato non tantum realiter, sed etiam essentialiter differunt; ut causa et causatum sint diversa entia. Sed nullus Dei actus potest producere alium in Deo actum, tanquam ens diversum. . . Quapropter neque intra Deum esse potest causa proprie dicta alicujus

DE PROVIDENTIA DEI. . . . actus divini. Sed in puncto rationis saepe una perfectio ante est concipienda, quam altera perfectio in Deo concipi possit; e. g. ante־ quam concipere queam, quod Deus sit aeternus, praestruendum est in puncto rationis, quod sit ens a se atque existat necessario. Quoniam igitur cognitio, quae ex natura objecti est praestruenda, si alteram cognitionem concipere velim, hujus cognitionis vocatur ratio a priori, atque talis ratio a priori adpelletur causa virtualiter causans.“ (Annotationes in B. Compend. p. 175. sq.)

Lutherus: ״Gott ist’s, der alle Dinge schafft, wirkt und erhält durch seine allmächtige Gewalt und rechte Hand, wie unser Glaube bekennt; denn er schickt keine Amtleute oder Engel aus, wenn er etwas schaffet oder erhält, sondern solchs alles ist seiner göttlichen Gewalt selbst eigen Werk. Soll er’s aber schaffen und erhalten, so muss er daselbst sein und seine Creatur sowohl im Allerinwendigsten als im Allerauswendigsten machen und erhalten. Darum muss er ja in einer jeglichen Creatur in ihrem Allerinwendigsten, Auswendigsten, um und um, durch und durch, unten und oben, vorn und hinten selbst da sein, dass nichts Gegenwärtigeres noch Innerlicheres sein kann in allen Creaturen, denn Gott selbst mit seiner Gewalt. Denn er ist’s, der die Haut macht; er ist’s, der auch die Gebeine macht; er ist,s, der die Haare auf der Haut macht; er ist’s auch, der das Mark in den Gebeinen macht; er ist’s, der ein jeglich Stücklein am Haar macht; er ist’s, der ein jeglich Stücklein am Mark macht; er muss ja alles machen, beide, Stück und Ganzes: so muss ja seine Hand da sein, die es mache; das kann ja nicht feihlen. Hieher gehet nun die Schrift gewaltig Es. 66, 1. 2. . .: Der Himmel ist mein Stuhl und die Erde meine Fussbank. Er spricht nicht: Ein Stück des Himmels ist mein Stuhl, ein Stück oder Ort der Erden ist meine Fussbank; sondern was und wo Himmel ist, da ist mein Stuhl, es sei der Himmel unten, oben oder neben der Erden; und was oder wo Erden ist, es sei auf dem Boden des Meeres, im Grabe der Todten oder im Mittel der Erden, da ist meine Fussbank. Nu rath, wo ist noch sein Haupt, Arm, Brust, Leib, so er mit den Füssen die Erde, mit den Beinen den Himmel füllet? Weit, weit reicht er über und ausser der Welt, über Himmel und Erden. Was kann oder will nu Esaia mit diesem Spruch, denn wie St. Hilarius auch hierüber spricht, dass Gott sei wesentlich gegenwärtig an allen Enden, in und durch alle Creatur in alle ihren Stücken und Orten, dass also die Welt Gottes voll ist und er sie alle füllet.“ (Dass diese Worte Christi: Das ist mein Leib, noch feste stehen. Opp. Hai. XX, 1002—1004.)

Sicut aliorum actuum immanentium et operum externorum omnium. Vide autem speciatim de Patre, tanquam creaturis providente, Matth. 6, 26. et 32., ubi Pater noster coelestis volatilium atque hominum curam gerere dicitur. De Filio ad Ebr. 1, 3. docetur, quod portet omnia. De Patre et Filio valet illud, quod Christus ait Joh. 5, 17.: Pater meus operatur hucusque, et ego operor. De Spiritu S. 1. ad Cor. 12, 11. dicitur, quod distribuat dona spiritualia ad conservationem et gubernationem ecclesiae.

ANTITHESIS. Hofmannus: ״Nicht so verhält es sich hiemit, dass Gott nur. Ausserordentliches, anstatt durch die gewöhnlichen Naturkräfte, durch Engel wirkt: in dem ganzen Naturleben sieht die Schrift das Walten von Geistern. . . Was uns angeht, ist einzig dies, dass alle guten und schlimmen Erscheinungen des Weltlebens gleicher Massen auf das Walten und Wirken einer Geistervielheit zurückgeführt werden. . . Sie (die Engel) sind also geschöpfliche Wesen. . . Geschöpfliches Leben, in welches sich die einige Fülle des Wesens Gottes begibt, um darin zu PART. I. CAP. V.


### On the Providence of God: to become a multiplicity of faculties, serves the eternal God to make Himself…

to become a multiplicity of faculties, serves the eternal God to make Himself present to His world... If it is created life, by means of which the single fullness of the divine essence spreads itself into the multiplicity of those properties which God, being present to His world, exercises upon it; then He can and will be thought of even without this self-activity of His in the world.” (Schriftbeweis. I, 282. 313. 325. sq.) § 5.

The impulsive cause of it is the goodness of God. Or the reason for moving, and that an internal one. See Luke 11:13, where Christ, from the fact that among humans fathers provide for their children, impelled by that love with which they pursue their offspring, concludes that much more does the heavenly Father, out of His supreme goodness and φιλανθρωπία, provide for our affairs. And David, in Ps. 136, occupied with celebrating the works of divine providence, always interjects that: For the Lord is good, and His mercy endures forever. Fechtius: “If God were to withdraw His hand even for a moment from any things whatsoever, they would immediately relapse into nothingness.” Rollius adds: “Scripture itself testifies that when God withdraws His hand, creatures return to dust.” (Syllog. controvers. p. 80. 86.) § 6. The object of divine providence is all creatures, both collectively and individually, whether inanimate or animate, and among the latter, vegetables, brute animals, but especially human beings, and most of all the faithful.

That is, that to which God provides, for which He takes care, whose advantages He promotes, etc. Not God Himself; for He does not take care of preserving and governing Himself, but those dependent upon Him. Thus, in Heb. 1:3, the Son of God is said to uphold all things, as having been created through Him, and in Col. 1:17, all things are taught to consist through Him. And it must be confessed that nothing so minute or insignificant occurs in the whole universe to which divine providence does not extend itself. J. J. Rambachius: “The object of divine providence is all created things, none excepted, visible and invisible, living and lifeless, heaven, earth, and sea, and everything that is therein. As He has created everything, so His providence also extends to everything. He preserves 1. the invisible creatures, the angels; for the good ones cannot govern themselves without His wisdom nor sustain themselves without His power, and the evil ones cannot harm without His permission, and He sets goals and limits to their malice. 2. the visible creatures, and among them not only human beings, as the noblest creature, but also all irrational animals. In Egypt, frogs and lice must carry out His commands. However, such provision extends over all genera, over all species, indeed over

all individual beings of every genus; e.g., God does not only provide for the genus of creatures called birds, but for every species—storks, swallows, sparrows—indeed, for every single specimen of them, for every individual stork, swallow, and sparrow.

He provides not only that trees remain, grow, and are preserved, but also for every tree, branch, and leaf thereof. Each of these is under His government, as Christ teaches in Matthew 10:29.

A sparrow is one of the most despised and (seemingly) most useless birds; yet Christ says that not one of them shall perish, be shot, or injured without the Father’s will. Luke 12:6: "And not one of them is forgotten before God." Even the smallest, most despised, and most useless thing is subject to divine government and providence. Christ assures us of this in Matthew 10:30: "But the very hairs of your head are all numbered," so that not one can fall out otherwise than by the Father’s will.

What we consider valuable, we count. It therefore signifies precise knowledge and a diligence in preserving. Just as sunlight does not disdain the lowliest worm, neither does the providence of God. We must therefore well note that this extends even to the most trivial things.

It does not happen here as with an earthly king, who provides for all and each of his subjects in general through a universal decree, even though there are many thousands whom the king does not know. God knows the smallest thing and provides for it, as Christ, the Mouth of Truth, assures us.

Indeed, reason thinks it unbecoming to the majesty of God that He should stoop down even to the least of His creatures. The heathen Pliny thinks that the divine majesty is defiled if it provides for despised things.

But these are foolish thoughts, such as the great Church teacher Jerome also entertained. For thereby His honor is rather promoted, and indeed: 1. The honor of His infinite validity, when He embraces with the arms of His providence the lowest worm as well as the highest angel. If it is not unbecoming for God to create them, why should it be unbecoming for Him to preserve them?

2. The honor of His power and wisdom. The power of God is no less visible in the creation of a gnat than of an elephant; thus also in their preservation. Wisdom shows its excellence when it directs and leads creatures, which do not themselves know the purpose of their being, toward such an end.

There is also no difference among creatures in themselves; it arises only from their relation to us. For example, one believes that a worm is more contemptible than a lion. The latter is, of course, as we view it, better than a worm; but if we disregard the relation, the lowliest worm has just as much excellence in its kind as a lion. For this consists only in a certain constitution of the parts of which the body is composed.

It also causes God no burden, as one might think. His infinite understanding cannot be overloaded or fatigued. (Schriftm. Erläuterung der Grundlegung der Th. 1738. p. 157. sq.)

Quenstedtius: "As the sun is not defiled, though it shines upon filth, so neither is God, when He illuminates even the smallest and most abject things with His providence. A mirror represents things without any contagion to itself; how, therefore, would God be contaminated by the providence of things? Those things which God did not disdain to create, how could He judge it unworthy of His majesty to preserve? It is an impious voice in Euripides: 'The King of the world cares for great things, but leaves small things to fortune.' ...

Ammonius rightly observes that if divine providence were to be denied, it would be more reasonably denied to the immortal and heavenly beings, which require less care because they are subject to fewer and smaller changes than these sublunary, frail, and mortal things, which require far greater care. 'Immortal things do not need a guardian; but this lower realm the Artificer preserves,' says Seneca, Ep. 58." (Th. did.-pol. P. I. c. 13. s. 2. q. 1. f. 768.) PART I. CHAP. V.

To this pertains what Job declares in chapter 28, 25: that God makes a weight for the winds, weighs the waters by measure, sets a law for the rain, and a way for the thundering storms. For example, that He causes herbs, grain, oil, and wine to be produced from the earth, as David records in Ps. 104, 14. 15. 16. For example, that He is said to give food to the beasts and the young ravens in Ps. 147, 9, to feed the birds of the air in Matt. 6, 26, and to take care of every single sparrow in Matt. 10, 29 and Luke 12, 6. Thus, regarding the whole human race as the offspring of God, Paul says in his Athenian address, Acts 17, 28: In God we live, and move, and have our being. For the eye of Jehovah is said to be fixed especially upon these, Ps. 33, 19. And one must look not only at individual believers, but also at their assembly, which is called the church, the people, and the peculiar possession of God, Eph. 5, 29. Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between human and divine rest and activity; human rest is joined with sloth, idleness, inertia, and weariness, just as activity is joined with labor, effort, industry, and trouble; but 'God knows how to act while resting, and to rest while acting,' according to Augustine, Book XII, *De Civitate Dei*, ch. 17." (L. c. f. 770.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis:

1. Of Democritus, Epicurus, Pliny, Lucian, and others of the Epicurean 'herd of swine,' who utterly deny and mock providence, and indeed, with C. Velleius, a Roman senator, call it a 'fatidical old woman.' Epicurus, in Cicero, Book II, *De Natura Deorum*, is introduced as denying the providence of God, saying: 'He does nothing, is involved in no thoughts, undertakes no works. – – We would rightly call this God blessed, but yours [the Stoic God] most laborious.' . . . Known is the impious voice of Pliny, *Hist. Nat.*, Book II, ch. 7: 'It is to be mocked that He who is supreme should take care of human affairs'; with the reason added by him: 'Nothing is more futile, as if He could not be polluted by such a sad and manifold ministry.' The Epicurean Lucretius wishes the world to be carried by chance. . .

3. Of Averroes, who, in his *Paraphrase of Metaphysics*, tract 4, at the end, impiously asserts that those who attribute to God the knowledge and care of particular things necessarily attribute impiety and injustice to Him.

4. Of the Sadducees, who say that God is placed outside all care and foreknowledge of inferior or sublunary things, as witnessed by Josephus, Book II, *De Bello Judaico*, ch. 7.

5. Of R. Moses Maimonides, who posits that 'the providence of God is only in human individuals.' . . . D. Hutterus, in *Loc. Theol.*, loc. 4, *De Prov.*, q. 2, p. 223, numbers St. Jerome among those who judge it entirely unworthy of divine providence if it is established that it is occupied with minute and abject things. The words of Jerome are these: 'Otherwise, it is absurd to bring down the majesty of God to this, that He should know at every single moment how many gnats are born and how many die; what the multitude of bugs, fleas, and flies is on the earth, how many fish swim in the water – – – –. We are not such foolish flatterers of God that, while we drag His power even to the lowest things, we are injurious to ourselves by saying that the providence for rational and irrational beings is the same.' . . . B. Gerhardus, tom. II, *LL. De Prov.*, § 58, says: 'Unless you take this statement (of Jerome, just cited) in such a way that God indeed knows individual things exactly, yet not by a mode of knowing that happens successively through moments and intervals, but by an intuitive knowledge, by which He beholds all things simultaneously and at once, it detracts from the praise of divine providence.'" (L. c. f. 768 sq.)

Latin:

einer Mannigfaltigkeit von Vermögen zu werden, dient dem ewigen Gotte, sich seiner Welt gegenwärtig zu machen. . . Wenn es geschöpfliches Leben ist, mittelst dessen sich die einige Fülle des göttlichen Wesens in die Mannigfaltigkeit derjenigen Eigenschaften ausbreitet, welche Gott, seiner Welt gegenwärtig, an ihr bethätigt; so kann und will er auch ohne diese seine Selbstbetätigung an der Welt gedacht werden.“ (Schriftbeweis. I, 282. 313. 325. sq.) § 5.

Causa impulsiva a ejus est bonitas Dei.b Seu ratio movendi, eaque interna. Vid. Luc. 11, 13., ubi Christus ex eo, quod in humanis patres filiis suis prospiciunt, impulsi amore illo, quo prolem suam prosequuntur, concludit, multo magis Patrem coelestem pro sua bonitate summa et φιλανθρωπία rebus nostris prospicere. Et David Ps. 136., in operibus providentiae divinae celebrandis occupatus, illud semper interserit: Quoniam bonus (est Dominus) et in saeculum misericordia ejus.Fechtius: ״Si Deus manum suam vel ad momentum rebus quibuslibet subtraheret, e vestigio reciderent in nihilum.“ Addit Rollius: ״Ipsa Scriptura testatur, Deo manum suam subtrahente in pulverem redire creaturas.“ (Syllog. controvers. p. 80. 86.) § 6. Objectum providentiae divinae a sunt creaturae b omnes et singulae,c cum inanimatae,d tum animatae, et ex his vegetabiles,e animantia bruta,f praesertim vero homines,g et maxime omnium h fideles.

Sive id, cui Deus prospicit, cujus curam gerit, commoda promovet etc. Non Deus ipse; neque enim sui conservandi et gubernandi curam gerit, sed dependentium a se. Sic ad Ebr. 1, 3. dicitur Filius Dei portare omnia, tanquam per ipsum creata, et Col. 1, 17. omnia per ipsum consistere docetur. Et fatendum est, nihil tam minutum aut exile in tota rerum universitate occurrere, ad quod sese providentia divina non extendat.J. J. Rambachius: ״Gegenstand der göttlichen Vorsehung sind alle geschaffenen Dinge, keines ausgenommen, sichtbare und unsichtbare, lebendige und leblose, Himmel, Erde und Meer, und alles, was darinnen ist. Wie er alles geschaffen hat, so erstreckt sich auch seine Vorsehung auf alles. Er erhält 1. die unsichtbaren Geschöpfe, die Engel; denn die guten können sich ohne seine Weisheit nicht regieren und ohne seine Kraft nicht erhalten, die bösen ohne seine Erlaubniss nicht schaden und er setzt ihrer Bosheit Ziel und Schranken. 2. die sichtbaren Creaturen, und darunter die Menschen nicht allein, als das edelste Geschöpf, sondern auch alle unvernünftigen Thiere. In Egypten müssen Frösche und Läuse seine Befehle ausrichten. Es erstreckt sich aber solche Vorsorge über alle Gattungen, über alle Arten, ja über

alle Einzelwesen (Individuen) einer jeden Gattung; z. B. Gott sorgt nicht nur über die Gattung der Creaturen, die Vögel heissen, sondern für eine jede Art, Störche, Schwalben, Sperlinge, ja für ein jedes einzelne Exemplar (Stück) derselben, für einen jeden Storch, Schwalbe und Sperling.

Er sorgt nicht nur, dass die Bäume bleiben, erwachsen und erhalten werden, sondern auch für einen jeden Baum, Zweig und dessen Blatt. Jedes derselben ist unter seiner Regierung, wie Christus lehrt Matth. 10, 29.

Ein Sperling ist einer der verachtetsten und (scheinbar) Unnützesten Vögel, dennoch sagt Christus, dass deren keiner umkomme, geschossen oder verletzt werde, ohne des Vaters Willen. Luc. 12, 6.: Noch ist derselben vor Gott nicht eins vergessen. Auch das Kleinste, Verachtetste und Unnützeste ist göttlicher Regierung und Vorsehung unterworfen. Christus versichert uns solches Matth. 10, 30.: Nun sind auch eure Haare auf eurem Haupte gezählet, dass keines anders ausfallen kann, als nach des Vaters Willen.

Was wir für werthvoll halten, zählen wir. Es bedeutet also eine genaue Wissenschaft, und einen Fleiss zu erhalten. Wie das Sonnenlicht den geringsten Wurm nicht verschmähet, also auch die Vorsehung Gottes nicht. Das müssen wir also wohl merken, dass sich diese auch auf die geringsten Dinge erstreckt.

Es geht hier also nicht 80 zu, wie etwa ein irdischer König durch eine allgemeine Verordnung für alle und jeden seiner Unterthanen insgemein sorgt, obgleich viel tausend sind, die der König nicht kennt. Gott kennt das Kleinste und sorgt dafür, wie Christus, der Mund der Wahrheit, versichert.

Zwar meinet die Vernunft, es sei solches der Majestät Gottes unanständig, dass er sich auch zu den geringsten seiner Creaturen sollte herunter lassen. Der Heide Plinius meint, die göttliche Majestät werde befleckt, wenn sie für verachtete Dinge sorge.

Allein dies sind thörichte Gedanken, wie sie auch der grosse Kirchenlehrer Hieronymus geheget. Denn dadurch wird die Ehre desselben vielmehr befördert, und zwar 1. die Ehre seiner unendlichen Giltigkeit, wenn er mit den Armen seiner Vorsehung sowohl den niedrigsten Wurm, als den höchsten Engel umfasst. Ist’s Gott nicht unanständig, sie zu schaffen, warum sollt’s ihm unanständig sein, selbe zu erhalten?

2. die Ehre seiner Macht und Weisheit. Die Kraft Gottes ist nicht weniger sichtbar in der Erschaffung der Mücke, als eines Elephanten; also auch in der Erhaltung. Die Weisheit zeigt ihre Vortrefflichkeit, wenn sie die Creaturen, die selbst den Zweck ihres Wesens nicht wissen, zu solchem dirigirt und leitet.

Es ist auch unter den Creaturen an sich kein Unterschied, sondern er entsteht erst aus der Beziehung auf uns; z.B. man glaubt, dass ein Wurm verächtlicher sei, als ein Löwe. Dieser ist freilich, wie wir ihn betrachten, besser, als ein Wurm; allein sehen wir von der Beziehung ab, so hat der geringste Wurm in seiner Art eben so viel Vortrefflichkeit, als ein Löwe. Denn diese besteht nur in einer gewissen Beschaffenheit der Theile, daraus der Leib zusammengesetzt ist.

Es macht auch Gott keine Beschwerung, wie man meinen möchte. Sein unendlicher Verstand kann nicht überladen, noch abgemattet werden.“ (Schriftm. Erläuterung der Grundlegung der Th. 1738. p. 157. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ״Ut sol non inquinatur, licet sordes irradiet, ita nec Deus, cum providentia sua res etiam minimas et abjectas illustrat. Speculum repraesentat res sine ulla sui contagione, quomodo ergo Deus contaminaretur rerum providentia? Quae Deus non dedignatus est creare, quomodo conservare sua indignum judicaret majestate? Impia apud Euripidem vox est: ,Rex mundi magna curat, parva fortunae relinquit.‘ . .

Recte Ammonius advertit, si neganda esset divina providentia, rationabilius negaretur immortalibus et coelestibus, quae minorem curam postulant, quia minoribus et paucioribus obnoxia sunt mutationibus, quam hisce sublunaribus, caducis et mortalibus, quae curam requirunt longe majorem. ,Immortalia tutore non egent; haec vero inferiora conservat artifex‘, ait Seneca Ep. 58.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. I. c. 13. s. 2. q. 1. f. 768.) PART. I. CAP. V.

Huc pertinet, quod Jobus cap. 28, 25., Deum ventis pondus fa~ cere, in mensura appendere, pluviis legem ponere et viam procellis sonantibus, pronunciat. V. g. quod herbas, frumentum, oleum, vinum e terris produci a Deo memorat David Ps. 104, 14. 15. 16. V. g. quod jumentis et pullis corvorum escam dare dicitur Ps. Ilf7, 9., pascere volatilia coeli Matth. 6, 26., singulorum passerum curam gerere Matth. 10, 29. Luc. 12, 6. Sic de toto genere humano, tanquam progenie Dei, Paulus in concione Attica, Act. 17, 28.: In Deo vivimus, movemur et sumus. Super hos enim oculus Jehovae inprimis intentus esse dicitur Ps. 33, 19. Et spectari debent non solum fideles singuli, sed et coetus eorum, qui vocatur ecclesia, populus et peculium Dei, Ephes. 5, 29.Quenstedtius: ״Dist. inter quietem et activitatem humanam et divinam; quies humana conjuncta est cum ignavia, desidia, inertia et lassitudine, uti et activitas cum labore, conatu, industria et molestia; sed,Deus novit quiescens agere, et agens quiescere‘, juxta Augustinum 1. XII. de civ. Dei c. 17.“ (L. c. f. 770.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis:

1. Democriti, Epicuri, Plinii, Luciani et alii Epicuri de grege porcorum, providentiam prorsus negantium et irridentium, imo cum C. Vellejo, senatore Rom., πρόνοιαν, anum fatidicam‘ vocantium. Epicurus apud Ciceronem lib. II. de nat. deorum providentiam Dei negans ita introducitur: ,Nihil (inquit de Deo) agit, nullis cogitationibus implicatur, nulla opera molitur. – – Hunc Deum rite beatum dixerimus, vestrum vero laboriosissimum‘. . . Nota est Plinii hist. nat. lib. II. c. 7. impia vox: ,Irridendum esse, quod curam rerum humanarum agat id, quod summum est‘; ratione ab eo adjecta: ,Nihil est futilius, quasi tam tristi ac multiplici ministerio non posset non pollui.‘ Lucretius Epicureus casu vult ferri mundum. . .

3. Averrois, qui, in paraphrasi metaphysices tract. 4. in fine, Deo attribuentes cognitionem et curam rerum particularium de necessitate ei impietatem et injustitiam tribuere, impie asserit.

4. Sadducaeorum, Deum extra omnem inferiorum seu sublunarium curam et praevisionem positum esse, dicentium, teste Josepho lib. II. de bello Judaico c. 7.

5. P. Mosis Maimonidis, statuentis, ,providentiam Dei esse tantum in individuis humanis‘. . . D. Hutterus in ll. theol. loc. 4. de prov. q. 2. p. 223. S. Hieronymum illis adnumerat, qui divina providentia plane indignum judicant, si ea statuatur circa res minutas et abjectas esse occupata. Verba Hieronymi haec sunt: ,Caeterum absurdum est, ad hoc deducere Dei majestatem, ut sciat per momenta singula, quot nascantur culices, quotque moriantur; quae cimicum, pulicum et muscarum sit in terra multitudo, quanti pisces in aqua natent – –– –. Non sumus tam fatui adulatores Dei, ut, dum potentiam ejus etiam ad ima trahimus, in nosmet ipsos injurii simus, eandem rationabilium et irrationabilium providentiam dicentes‘. . . B. Gerhardus tom. II. LL. de prov. § 58. inquit: ,Nisi hoc dictum (Hieronymi jam adductum) ita accipias, quod Deus quidem singula exacte cognoscat, non tamen modo cognoscendi, qui fit per momenta et intervalla successive, sed notitia intuitiva, qua omnia α&ρόως simul aspicit, detrahet laudi divinae providentiae.“


### On the Providence of God: Specifically, providence is so occupied with men that it extends to the origin,…

7. Specifically, providence is so occupied with men that it extends to the origin, progress, and end of their life, and likewise to all their actions.

Thus Job, ch. 10:8 et seqq., addressing God, says: "Your hands, צביני#, with the utmost diligence, care, and as it were anxiety, have fashioned me and made me accurately all around; like clay you have made me."

And David, Ps. 71:6, says to God: "Upon you I have leaned from the womb; from my mother’s bowels you are my bringer-forth."

E.g., regarding the supplying of food, clothing, and other necessities of this life, Matt. 6:25 sqq.; regarding the warding off of dangers occurring in any business whatsoever, Ps. 91:1 sqq. Cf. Deut. 30:20; Job 10:12. Or regarding the determined time or number of the days and months of this life, Job 14:5. Concerning which more will be said below in § 16.

It extends to secret thoughts, to words, to external actions, and to conversation with others, Ps. 139:1 et seqq. §

8. The acts to which providence is limited in its exercise toward creatures are preservation, or the sustenance of individual creatures in existing, and governance, which implies partly a universal concurrence with secondary causes, and partly a certain special operation, not of one kind, and the direction of created agents. See here § 2 and the notes.

Which others call the continuation of creation. For it implies an unceasing influx, convenient and necessary for each thing according to its own nature, so that it may persist in its being and power of operating.

And to this pertain those phrases, φέρων τὰ πάντα, "bearing or carrying," lest they collapse, perish, or be reduced to nothing, Heb. 1:3, and πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε, "all things consist in him," Col. 1:17. "

Not only," says Theophylact, "did he create these very things, but he also sustains these same things, and in such a way that, if they were withdrawn from his providence, it would be necessary for them to perish immediately."

Fechtius: "It is in vain that the common description of preservation is chastised, which is said to be a continued creation."

Rollius adds: "Preservation is not called creation here, but continued creation or the continuation of the creative action. For God is said to preserve the creature in no other way than insofar as he positively continues the action by which he originally produced the creature. Hence, just as the duration of a thing in itself is nothing other than continued existence, so preservation is understood to be nothing other than continued creation. And just as creation gives a beginning to being, so preservation gives a continuation to being." (Sylloge controv. p. 79, 81 sq.) PART I. CHAP. V.

Thus Acts 17:25, 26: He gives to all life and breath through all things, and it is read that He made from one blood (concurring with all those who beget) the race of men.

Quenstedtius: "We are indeed accustomed to speak in this way, that God acts through creatures; the meaning of this locution is that God gives and preserves the power of acting to the one acting proximately. But insofar as the First Cause itself cooperates immediately with the creature and flows together with it into the action and the effect, it is false that the second cause mediates between the first and the effect, since the effect depends just as immediately upon the First Cause as it does upon the second." (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 781.)

The same: "Just as the same writing in number depends upon the hand and the pen, and not one part upon the hand and another upon the pen, but the whole upon the hand and the whole upon the pen: so the concurrence of God is not prior to the action of the creature by a proper priority of causality, since in reality it is entirely the same action, and thus God produces the whole effect, just as the second cause does, which is done through the external action of God, which is intimately included in the action of the creature, or rather, is one and the same with it." (L. c. f. 782.)

The same: "Nor is this concurrence of the First Cause to be placed in some action prior to the action of the second cause, which might move, excite, or apply it to these acts of its own. 'For when fire is near to combustible matter, there is no need for it to be excited by some prior action to heat, yet there is need for God to concur,' as Becanus observes. Otherwise, this concurrence would be terminated only toward the cause and not toward the effect or the action of that cause. Furthermore, that motion of God toward acting is distinct from the action of the second cause; here, however, the question is about the action of God, which is the same as the action of the second cause, not distinct." (L. c. f. 780.)

The same: "If anything were to happen without the cooperation of God, at least in that first instant in which it were to happen, it would be of itself and without God, which is one of the ίκ τών αδυνάτων. Therefore, just as created things demand to be preserved immediately by God as the supreme efficient cause, so they also demand to be brought to pass immediately. And just as God can deprive His creature of its being by the mere subtraction of the influx by which He preserves things, so He can deprive the same of its natural action by the mere negation of immediate concurrence." (L. c. f. 785.)

Gerhardus: "Created things do not subsist of themselves and by their own powers, but God carries all things by the word of His power, Heb. 1:3; in Him all things συνέστηκε, Col. 1:17; in God we live, and move, and have our being, Acts 17:28. The being of creatures is a flowing being; the being of God is a fixed being; as the being of rays is from the sun, and the shadow from the body, so all creatures depend upon divine conservation... Conservation, as defined by Scaliger, is nothing other than the continuation of existence. To be and to be preserved is attributed to the same author and the same principle. Therefore, just as all creatures received their essence, their properties, and their powers of acting from God in creation and generation, so they are preserved by the same in being and acting. Therefore, there is, as it were, a continuous influx of divine power preserving all things into all existing things, which, if subtracted even for a moment, they can neither act, nor indeed even exist. What is more natural to man than to move? And yet in God we move, Acts 17:28. What is more natural to the sun than to rise every day? And yet God ανατέλλει τον ήλιον, Matt. 5:45. Although, therefore, a property is naturally implanted in individual things, they neither exert it, nor can they exert it, unless they are (if I may so speak) given essence and vegetated by divine power. Ps. 104:29, 30: 'You hide Your face, they are troubled; You take away their breath, they die and return to their dust; You send forth Your Spirit, they are created, and You renew the face of the earth.' Deut. 8:3, Matt. 4:4, it is said that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God; by which we are not only taught that God can nourish and preserve man without natural means, but we are also warned that the power of nourishing is not so proper to bread that under..."

by the word of God, by which bread was first created and obtained the power of nourishing, it could nevertheless nourish man, but that a continuous influx, as it were, of the creating and preserving word is required, so that it may exert the power of nourishing inherent in it.

We can and ought to pronounce the same concerning the medical art. Man is not restored to health by herbs, but by the word of God, which originally implanted that power in the herbs and still instills it, as it were, to this day.” (L. de prov. § 61—63.)

Thus, for example, secondary causes, not yet constituted in act by nature, are divinely applied to act; see 1 Kings 18:44 concerning the accelerated rain.

Sometimes God confers upon secondary causes a power of acting that is either entirely supernatural, or restores and confirms a natural one that was lost or weakened, or increases it; see Judges 16:28, 29 concerning the strength of Samson restored and increased; Genesis 17:16, 17 and 19 concerning the power of procreation conferred upon Abraham, who was a centenarian, and Sarah, who was ninety years old and otherwise sterile.

Finally, God sometimes hinders secondary causes that are to be constituted in act by nature, so that the effect does not follow, just as in Deuteronomy 28:23 He threatens that He will withhold rain from a disobedient people.

For by such works God makes it manifest that He is not bound to physical causes and the order freely instituted by Himself, says the blessed Gerhard, Isag. LL. Disp. XVI. c. V. de Prov. § 12. p. 654. B.

Meisner: “There are common laws of nature, according to which (the Calvinists) examine and measure all the mysteries of faith, so that they think God can do nothing that is against the ordinary constitution of nature and natural bodies. ‘

Nothing is done singularly by God that overturns the nature created by Him,’ says Sadeel, de sacrament. manducat. c. 3. p. 93. edit. Genev. an. 96. ‘

If anything is taught that is against nature and overturns it, it must immediately be pronounced false, since it is certain that nature, constituted by the true God, is true.’ p. 91. . .

Thus it should rather be established that God can do many things that are against all nature and depart as far as possible from the common order. ‘

Nature often yields to its own laws, why not to its author?’ says Seneca in Hippol. v. 175. ‘

He commands nature, He does not obey possibility, He does not collect measures, He does not examine weight. His will is the measure of things, His word is the end of the work,’ by the testimony of Ambrose, l. 2. Hexaem. c. 2. ‘

Although the whole course of nature has its natural laws, above this natural course the Creator has it in His power to make of all these things something other than what their seminal reasons contain,’ in the words of Augustine, de Gen. ad lit. c. 17. ‘

His power is not arranged or constrained by order, but He Himself is the author of order, upon whose order all necessity depends,’ by the suffrage of Scaliger, Exer. 365. s. 8.

Hence Philip piously sang: God is not a deity shut up in the prison of the Fates, Such as the Stoic God was thought to be. He can inhibit the flying courses of the sun, He makes rivers stand still like rocks.” (Philosoph. sobr. I, 1171. sqq.) cf. Kromayer cited above p. 43.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the heresiarch Pelagius and his followers, who asserted that they could move a hand, bend a finger, sit, stand, or walk without the help of God, as Jerome testifies. . .

2. Of the scholastics, Durand of Saint-Pourçain, who admits only a remote and accidental concurrence, teaching: ‘God indeed concurs in the acts of secondary causes, but not by influencing them and their productions in Himself, but only remotely and accidentally; insofar as, namely, He first gave to particular agents being and the faculty of operating, and PART I. CHAP. V.

Latin:

7. Speciatim circa homines ita occupatur providentia, ut ad eorum vitae ortum,a progressum b et finem,c itemque actiones omnes d sese extendat.

Ita Jobus cap. 10, 8. et seqq., Deum alloquens: Manus tuae, inquit, צביני#, summa diligentia, cura et velut anxietate, elaboraverunt me et fecerunt me accurate totum in circuitu; sicut lutum fecisti me.

Et David Ps. 71, 6. ad Deum dicit: Tibi innixus sum ex utero; ex visceribus matris meae tu eductor meus.

V. g. quoad alimenta et amictum caeteraque necessaria hujus vitae suppeditanda, Matth. 6, 25. sqq.; quoad arcenda pericula in negotiis quibusvis occurrentia, Ps. 91, 1. sqq. Conf. Deut. 30, 20. Jobi 10, 12. Seu quoad determinatum tempus aut numerum dierum ac mensium hujus vitae, Jobi 14, 5. De quibus infra § 16. plura dicentur.

Cum cogitationes arcanas, tum sermones, tum actiones externas et conversationem cum aliis, Ps. 139, 1. et seqq.§

8. Actus, ad quos circa creaturas exercendos a terminatur providentia, sunt conservatio, seu sustentatio singularum creaturarum b in existendo, et gubernatio, qua q partim universalem cum causis secundis, concursum,c partim specialem quandam, neque unius generis, operationem et agentium creatorum directionem d importat. Vid. h. l. § 2. et notas.

Quam alias creationis continuationem vocant. Importat enim influxum indesinentem rebus creatis pro sua cujusque natura convenientem ac necessarium, ut in esse suo ac vi operandi persistere possit.

Atque huc pertinent illae phrases, ψέρων τά πάντα, portans aut gestans, ne collabantur, intereant aut in nihilum redigantur, Ebr. 1, 3., et πάντα iv αυτω αυνέστηχε, Col. 1, 17.

Non solum, ait Theophylaetus, haec ipsa creavit, sed eadem haec continet, et ita ut, si ab ejus providentia haec abducantur, pereant protinus necesse sit.

Fechtius: ,,Frustra castigatur conservationis trita descriptio, quae dicitur esse continuata creatio.“

Rollius addit: ,,Conservatio non dicitur hic creatio, sed continuata creatio sive creativae actionis continuatio. Neque enim Deus alia ratione creaturam conservare dicitur, quam quatenus actionem, qua creaturam primitus produxit, porro positive continuat. Hinc uti duratio rei in se nihil aliud est, quam continua existentia, ita conservatio nihil aliud esse intelligitur, quam continuata creatio. Et sicuti creatio essendi dat initium, ita conservatio dat essendi continuationem.“ (Sylloge controv. p. 79. 81. sq.) PART. I. CAP. V.

Sic Act. 17, 25. 26. Dem omnibus vitam et halitum per omnia dare atque ex uno sanguine (concurrendo cum generantibus quibusque) genus hominum fecisse legitur.

Quenstedtius: ״Ita quidem loqui consuevimus, Deum agere per creaturas; cujus locutionis hic sensus est, Deum proxime agenti dare et conservare virtutem agendi. Quatenus vero ipsa prima causa immediate cooperatur creaturae et influit una cum illa in actionem et effectum, sic falsum est, secundam causam mediare inter primam et effectum, cum aeque immediate effectus dependeat a causa prima, sicut a secunda.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 781.)

Idem: ,,Quemadmodum eadem numero scriptio pendet a manu et calamo, nec pars una a manu et alia a calamo, sed tota a manu et tota a calamo: ita concursus Dei non est prior actione creaturae propria prioritate causalitatis, cum in re sit omnino eadem actio, adeoque totum effectum producit Deus, sicut et causa secunda, quod flt per actionem Dei exteriorem, quae intime in actione creaturae includitur, imo una eademque est cum illa.“ (L. c. f. 782.)

Idem: ,,Nec c01106andus est iste causae primae concursus in actione aliqua praevia actioni causae secundae, quae vel moveat, excitet aut applicet illam ad istos actus suos. ,Quando enim ignis proximus est materiae combustibili, non opus est, ut excitetur aliqua actione praevia ad calefaciendum, tamen opus est, ut Deus concurrat‘, ut observat Becanus. Terminaretur etiam sic iste concursus solum ad causam et non ad effectum vel actionem illius causae. Praeterea motio illa Dei ad agendum distincta est ab actione causae secundae, hic autem quaeritur de actione Dei, quae eadem sit cum actione causae secundae, non distincta.“ (L. c. f. 780.)

Idem: ,,Si aliquid sine Dei cooperatione fleret, saltem in primo illo instanti, quo fleret, per se et sine Deo esset, quod est unum ίκ τών αδυνάτων. Uti ergo res creatae postulant a Deo ceu efflciente supremo immediate conservari, ita et immediate fleri. Et sicut Deus creaturam suam suo esse privare potest per solam influxus subtractionem, quo res conservat, ita potest eandem sua naturali actione privare per solam negationem immediati concursus.“ (L. c. f. 785.)

Gerhardus: ,,Non ex se et suis viribus res creatae subsistunt, sed portat Deus omnia verbo virtutis suae, Hebr. 1, 3., in ipso omnia συνέστηκε, Col. 1, 17., in Deo vivimus, movemur et sumus, Act. 17, 28. Esse creaturarum est esse fluxum, esse Dei est esse fixum; ut radiorum esse a sole, umbra a corpore, ita omnes creaturae a divina dependent conservatione. . . Conservatio, deflniente Scaligero, nihil aliud est, quam existentiae continuatio. Esse et conservari acceptum fertur eidem auctori, eidemque principio. Ut ergo omnes creaturae suam essentiam, suas proprietates ac agendi vires in creatione et generatione a Deo acceperunt: ita ab eodem in essendo et agendo conservantur. Ergo continuus est quasi divinae potentiae omnia conservantis in res existentes omnes influxus, quo vel ad momentum subtracto nec agere, immo nec esse possunt. Quid magis homini naturale, quam moveri? et tamen in Deo movemur, Act. 17, 28. Quid magis soli naturale, quam singulis diebus oriri? et tamen Deus ανατέλλει τον ήλιον Matth. 5, 45. Quamvis ergo naturaliter singulis rebus sua indita sit proprietas, eam tamen nec exserunt, nec exserere possunt, nisi divina virtute (ut ita loquar) essentientur et vegetentur. Ps. 104, 29. 30.: ,Abscondis faciem tuam, turbantur; aufers spiritum eorum, deficiunt et in pulverem suum revertuntur; mittis spiritum tuum, creantur et renovabis faciem terrae.‘ Deut. 8, 3. Matth. 4, 4. dicitur, hominem non vivere ex solo pane, sed in omni verbo, quod egreditur ex ore Dei; quo non solum docemur, Deum absque mediis naturalibus posse hominem alere et conservare, sed monemur etiam, vim alendi non esse panis ita propriam, ut sub

tracto Dei verbo, quo panis primum creatus est et alendi vim obtinuit, nihilominus hominem alere possit, sed requiri continuum quasi verbi creantis et conservantis influxum, ut alendi vim sibi insitam exserat.

Idem de re medica pronunciare possumus ac debemus. Non restituitur homo sanitati per herbas, sed per Dei verbum, quod herbis vim illam primitus insevit et adhuc hodie quasi instillat.“ (L. de prov. § 61—63.)

Ita v. g. causae secundae, in actu per naturam nondum constitutae, ad agendum divinitus applicantur; vid. 1 Reg. 18, 44. de accelerata pluvia.

Aliquando Deus causis secundis virtutem agendi vel plane supernaturalem coufert, vel naturalem amissam aut debilitatam restituit et confirmat, aut auget; vid. Judic. 16, 28. 29. de robore Simsonis restaurato auctoque, Gen. 17, 16. 17. et 19. de potentia generandi Abrahamo centenario et Sarae nonagenariae atque alias sterili collata.

Denique nonnunquam causas secundas per naturam 111 actu constituendas impedit Deus, quo minus effectus sequatur, prout Deut. 28, 23. minatur, se pluviam subtracturum populo inobedienti.

Talibus enim operibus Deus manifestum facit, se non esse alligatum ad causas physicas et ordinem libere a se institutum, ait b. Gerh. Isag. LL. Disp. XVI. c. V. de Prov. § 12. p. 654.B.

Meisnerus: ,,Sunt communes naturae leges, secundum quas (Calviniani) omnia fidei mysteria examinant et mensurant, ita ut nihil Deum posse existiment, quod sit contra ordinariam naturae et naturalium corporum constitutionem. ,

Nihil fit singulariter a Deo, quod naturam ab ipso creatam evertat‘, inquit Sadeel, de sacrament. manducat. c. 3. p. 93. edit. Genev. an. 96. ,

Si quid doceatur, quod sit contra naturam eamque evertat, statim pronuntiandum est, esse falsum, quandoquidem certum est, naturam a vero Deo constitutam veram esse.‘ p. 91. . .

Sic potius statuendum, multa Deum posse, quae sint contra omnem naturam et a communi ordine quam longissime recedant. ,

Natura saepe legibus suis ipsa cedit, quid suo auctori?‘ ait Seneca in Hippol. v. 175. ,

Imperat naturae, non possibilitati obtemperat, non mensuras colligit, non pondus examinat. Voluntas ejus mensura rerum est, sermo ejus finis est operis‘, testimonio Ambrosii 1. 2. Hexaem. c. 2. ,

Cum omnis naturae cursus naturales habeat leges, supra hunc naturalem cursum creator habet apud se, posse de his omnibus facere aliud, quam eorum seminales rationes habent‘, voce Augustini de Gen. ad lit. c. 17. ,

Non ordine disponitur aut distringitur ejus potentia, sed ipse ordinis auctor est, cujus ordinis necessitas omnis ab eo pendet‘, suffragio Scaligeri Exer. 365. s. 8.

Hinc pie cecinit Philippus: Non Deus est numen Parcarum carcere clausum, Quale putabatur Stoicus esse Deus. Ille potest solis cursus inhibere volantes, Ille velut scopulos flumina stare facit.“ (Philosoph, sobr. I, 1171. sqq.) cf. Kromayerus citatus supra p. 43.

2. Ex scholasticis Durandi de S. Portiano, qui concursum tantummodo remotum et per accidens admittit, docens: ,Deum quidem concurrere ad actus causarum secundarum, verum non per se influendo in eosdem et eorum productiones, sed solum remote et per accidens; quatenus sci. agentibus particularibus primum dedit esse et facultatem operandi, et PART. I. CAP. V.


### On the Providence of God: as well as that power of acting, he furthermore preserves.’ 

as well as that power of acting, he furthermore preserves.’ . .

3. Nicol. Taurellus, who follows in the footsteps of Durandus, asserting: ‘It is a great imprudence, indignity, and impotence if God concurs in the works of nature.’ ‘If God,’ he says, ‘willed always to work, why did he cast nature? Or do you think that God, if he wishes to do anything, stands in need of the concurrence of nature?’ . .

4. The Arminians, whose leader Episcopius, in *Inst.* lib. IV, c. 1, calls preservation ‘an act of divine providence, caring not at all whether it be called a positive act, by which God influences immediately the essences, powers, and faculties of man and of all other things; or a negative act, by which God does not will to destroy the essences, powers, and faculties of created things, but leaves them to their own vigor, insofar as they can flourish and endure by the power implanted in them through creation. For it is all the same to us (he adds) which is believed.’ . .

5. Those philosophers and scholastics who have declined to the other extreme, denying on the contrary that the effects of secondary causes are properly produced by those causes, and who wish them to be effected by God alone at the mere presence of secondary causes, with the causes themselves doing nothing. . . Suarez. . . confesses that Gabriel Biel, who was almost the last of those who became famous among the Germans for their writings on scholastic theology, leans strongly toward that opinion. See also Thomas. (L. c. f. 782.) §

9. Divine providence also has its degrees with respect to the acts to which it is directed, and above other creatures it regards men, and among the human race, especially the faithful. For something has already been said in § 6 concerning the difference with respect to the object, although this is founded upon that. So that God preserves and governs other things for the sake of others, to the preservation and government of which the preservation or government of the former serves. Hence, the division of divine providence into universal and particular, or general and special, belongs here, to which some add most special or singular, which, however, Gerhard (l. c.) determines can be reduced to special providence. For just as God first created other creatures, so he determined to preserve and direct them once created—some to satisfy the needs of human life, some for greater convenience or as aids for conducting affairs, and finally as examples and incentives for the duties to be rendered to God; which is manifest from Psalms 104 and 136, but also from Acts 17:25, 26, 27. Just as it is said in Romans 8:28 that for those who love God all things work together for good, πάντα συνεργεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν. And concerning the church, we know that by the power of divine providence it is so established that not even the gates of hell can prevail against it, Matthew 16:18. § 10. As far as the origin of man is concerned, God seems to concur in the production of man not only by a general influence, but also by a special one.

As the blessed Gerhard writes in *De Prov.*, chap. VIII, § 71, p. 67: the entrance of human life is governed in a peculiar way by divine providence. And for that reason it is rightly established that God has the character not only of a universal cause, but also of a particular one, and that He supplies the deficiency of secondary causes, or at least directs and governs them in their acting.

Some indeed explain this in such a way that, partly, when the variety, connection, and wonderful structure of the members of the body are considered, they require a particular efficient cause acting with knowledge, and thus they posit that some other and more sublime power—which cannot be thought to be anything other than that of God Himself—concurs by a special influx, rather than that which is in the seed (commonly called δύναμις πλαστική); and partly also, when the immateriality of the soul is considered, and that it must therefore be produced independently of a subject or out of nothing, and that such a production demands an infinite power of acting and is thus proper to God alone, they conclude from this that God provides a special and determined influx for the production of the human soul.

Others, however, even if they believe that the body as well as the human soul is produced by the parents themselves as secondary causes, with the concurrence of God as the universal cause, nevertheless, because they esteem the various accidents, the dangers to be averted, and many singular proofs of peculiar divine care and favor in the production and birth of man, they attribute to God, besides a universal concurrence, also a special or particular one, and refer to this the passage in Job, chap. 10:8, 9, 10, 11.

Among the actions of man, to which God concurs, a distinction must be made between good and evil, and in the category of good ones, between those that are civilly good and those that are spiritually good. For although He is concerned with both, the mode of His concern is different, as will soon be evident. They are sometimes called natural, insofar as they can be performed by man through the powers of nature. They are called by another name supernatural, because they exceed the natural powers of man and cannot be performed through them, but require more sublime powers, to be conferred by God.

Divine providence regards civilly good actions not only with respect to imparting a general concurrence, but also in respect to commanding, aiding, and approving them. It relates to spiritually good actions in the same way, but with the addition that God Himself also concurs to them by a peculiar influx. PART I. CHAP. V.

As the work of the law is written in the hearts of men, whence the Gentiles by nature do the things that are of the law, Rom. 2:15. For example, by encouraging the mind or by exciting heroic impulses, just as God is said to have called King Cyrus and to have grasped his right hand, Isaiah 45:1, 3. To this pertains, in particular, the fact that He also rewards such actions, as is evident from the example of the Egyptian midwives, to whom God is said to have done good and to have built houses after they assisted the Israelite women in labor and their offspring, Exod. 1:20, 21. Since otherwise, of ourselves, as of ourselves, we are not sufficient to think anything of this kind, much less to do it, 2 Cor. 3:5. §

13. Divine providence is terminated toward evil actions in such a way that, while they are being performed, a general concurrence is indeed imparted to them; otherwise, many actions that would have occurred are hindered; yet those that are permitted to happen are nevertheless directed so that they tend toward a good end. For thus in Him we move, whatever we do, Acts 17:28. But it is simultaneously established that evil actions are viewed thus far only as actions, not, however, insofar as they are such in their species and therefore evil.

Quenstedtius: "The acts of divine προνοίας (providence) regarding moral evils or sins are antecedent: 1. The foreseeing or eternal foreknowledge of sin... 2. The aversion to it... 3. The prohibition... 4. The hindering... The concomitant acts are: 1. The sustaining of the nature acting evilly. Thus, when Eve stretched out her hand to the forbidden fruit, God indeed sustained the locomotive power, but He did not assist the vicious action as such. And thus, often with the hand and tongue, which we move while God sustains us, we oppose God. In the very crimes and sins, God sustains the members, preserves our powers and motions, from which the stupendous long-suffering of God shines forth. 2. The concurrence with the action itself viewed as to its material. For there are two things in a sinful action: the material and the formal. The material is the subject of the viciousness, namely the action itself, and this God produces along with the agent. The formal, however, is the very viciousness adhering to the action, to which God in no way concurs. 3. The permission of 'Αταξίας (disorder). God permits sin and allows man to deflect from His law. Yet this very permission does not exclude every hindering, but only physical hindering, i.e., that by which God acts upon the will of man as it is by nature and places an impediment to the power itself; but moral hindering is joined with this permission, since God does not cease to prohibit and dissuade from sin. The consequent acts are: 1. The direction of sin to a good end. 2. The determination, so that He prescribes goals and limits, which human malice cannot overstep. Thus He set certain limits to the tyranny of Pharaoh. 3. The remission of sin... 4. The infliction of punishment." (L. c. s. 1. th. 30. f. 767.)

Thus, God hindered the adultery of Abimelech with Sarah from being completed, Gen. 20: 6. Similarly, the persecution intended by Laban against Jacob, Gen. 31:24, 29. And Ps. 33:10, it is said that Jehovah makes the counsel of the nations of no effect, and makes the thoughts of the people of no effect.

Thus God, by permitting the sins of those who seem to excel others, admonishes the sinners themselves of their infirmity, lest they be too pleased with themselves and despise others; to which pertains the fall of Peter, Luke 22:32. Sometimes He intends to amend others from the damages of those who sin and, having shaken off their security, to render them more solicitous, Luke 17:32. When He permits the pious to be afflicted by the impious, He exercises the humility and patience of the afflicted, by the example of Job, chap. 1. Cf. James chap. 5:10, 11. Sometimes He converts the affliction of the pious into an occasion for better fortune and desires that even those who afflict them be helped and amended by their works; which Joseph testifies by his own example, Gen. 50:20.

Quenstedtius: "Permission is an act of governing providence, by which God, regarding rational creatures who incline themselves of their own accord to sin, does not withdraw them from evil forbidden by law by means of impediments which a finite agent cannot resist or which He knows they will not resist, but for just causes allows them to rush into sins, Ps. 81:13; Acts 14:16; Rom. 1:24, 28. Divine permission is not: 1. a bland indulgence, as if God did not care at all when men commit crimes; nor 2. a relaxation of the law, as if He permitted them license to sin; nor 3. is it impotence in God, either of intellect, as if creatures rushed into sins without His knowledge, or of will, as if He approved or aided the crimes, or a defect of power, as if He could not restrain sin and prevent the sinful act; nor 4. does it make God an idle spectator, who neither forbids sins nor sets a limit to malice and punishes it; but 5. it is the negative act of the most wise God, by which He does not place before rational creatures who incline themselves of their own accord to sin physical and omnipotent impediments which they cannot resist or which He knows they will not resist, but allows them to deflect from His order and to sin, or does not withdraw them from evil prohibited in the law, but for just causes allows them to rush into sins.
