IV. inst. c. 1. conservationem appellat,actum divinae providentiae, susque deque habens, an actus dicatur positivus, quo Deus influit immediate in essentias, vires ac facultates hominis rerumque aliarum omnium; an actus negativus, quo Deus essentias, vires et facultates rerum creatarum non vult destruere, sed eos vigore suo relinquere, quoad vigere ac durare possunt ex vi per creationem ipsis insita. Perinde enim est (addit) nobis, utrum credatur.‘ . .

5. Eorum philosophorum et scholasticorum, qui ad alterum extremum declinarunt, negantes ex adverso, effectus causarum secundarum proprie a causis illis produci, eosque volunt a solo Deo ad praesentiam tantum causarum secundarum effici, ipsis nihil agentibus. . . Suarez. . . fatetur, Gabrielem Bielem, qui ultimus fere fuit eorum, qui inter Germanos scholasticae theologiae scriptis inclaruerunt, in eam sententiam valde inclinare. Vide etiam Thomam.u (L. c. f. 782.) §

9. Habet autem providentia divina etiam ex parte actuum, a ad quos terminatur, suos gradus b et prae caeteris creaturis respicit homines,c in genere humano autem praecipue fideles.d Nam de differentia ex parte objecti jam aliquid dictum est § 6., quamvis haec in illa fundetur. Ita ut res alias conservet Deus et gubernet propter alias, quibus conservandis et gubernandis illarum conservatio aut gubernatio serviat. Unde huc pertinet divisio providentiae divinae in universalem et particularem, seu generalem et specialem, quibus quidam addunt speciolissimam aut singularem, quam tamen Gerhardus 1. c. ad specialem providentiam reduci posse statuit. Quemadmodum enim Deus creaturas alias primum creavit, ita creatas conservare et dirigere constituit, aliquas ad humanae vitae indigentiam explendam, quasdam ad commoditatem majorem aut adminicula rerum gerendarum, denique ut exempla et incentiva officiorum Deo praestandorum; quod ex ipsis Psalmis 104. et 136., sed et Act. 17, 25. 26. 27. manifestum est. Prout diligentibus Deum omnia adjumento esse in bonum, πάντα συνεργεΐν είς άγαμον, dicitur Rom. 8, 28. Et de ecclesia novimus, vi providentiae divinae ita constitutum esse, ut ne quidem portae inferorum praevalere possint adversus eam, Matth. 16, 18.§10. Quod ad ortum hominis attinet, videtur Deus non generali solum influxu, sed speciali etiam a concurrere ad producendum hominem.

Prout b. Gerhardus de Prov. cap. VIII. § 71. p. 67. scribit: vitae humanae ingressum peculiariter divina providentia regi. Eaque ratione recte statuitur, quod Deus non tantum causae universalis, sed et particularis rationem habeat et causarum secundarum defectum suppleat, vel saltem eas in agendo dirigat et gubernet.

Quod quidem aliqui sic exponunt, ut partim, spectata membrorum corporis varietate et nexu ac structura mirabili, causam efficientem particularem cum cognitione agentem requiri adeoque aliam quandam, quam quae in semine est (βίαμις πλαστική vulgo vocata), ac sublimiorem virtutem, quae non nisi ipsius Dei esse cogitari possit, speciali influxu concurrere statuant; partim etiam, considerata animae immaterialitate quodque illa ideo independenter a subjecto sive ex nihilo producenda sit, talis autem productio virtutem agendi infinitam postulet adeoque solius Dei propria sit, colligant inde, Deum ad productionem animae humanae specialem ac determinatum influxum praebere.

Alii vero, etsi corpus pariter atque animam humanam ab ipsis parentibus, tanquam causis secundis, cum concursu Dei, tanquam causae universalis, produci credant, tamen, quod in productione et nativitate hominis varios casus et arcenda pericula ac singularia multa peculiaris curae ac favoris divini documenta aestimant, praeter universalem, etiam specialem aut particularem concursum Deo tribuunt, eoque referunt locum Jobi cap. 10, 8. 9. 10. 11.§ u.

Inter actiones hominis, ad quas Deus concurrit, distinguendae sunt a bonae a malis, et in genere bonarum, quae civiliter bonae b sunt, ab his, quae spiritualiter c sunt bonae. Quamvis enim circa utrasque versetur, modus tamen versandi alius atque alius est, ut mox patebit. Vocantur alias naturales, quatenus viribus naturae ab homine peragi possunt. Dicuntur alio nomine supernaturales, quia vires hominis naturales excedunt, nec per eas fieri possunt, sed sublimioribus viribus indigent, a Deo conferendis.§ 12.

Actiones civiliter bonas respicit divina providentia, non solum quoad impertiendum concursum generalem, verum etiam in respectu ad eas praecipiendas,a adjuvandas b et approbandas.c Ad spiritualiter bonas actiones eadem ratione se habet, sed ut praeterea etiam Deus ipse ad eas peculiari influxu concurrat.d PART. I. CAP. Y.

Prout opus legis scriptum, est in cordibus hominum, unde gentes natura faciunt, quae sunt legis, Rom. 2, 15. V. g. animum addendo, aut motus heroicos excitando, prout regem Cyrum vocasse dicitur Deus ejusque dexteram apprehendisse Esaiae 45, 1. 3. Quo speciatim pertinet, quod etiam remuneratur tales actiones, prout exemplo obstetricum Aegyptiacarum patet, quibus Deus benefecisse et domos aedificasse dicitur, postquam puerperis Israeliticis earumque foetibus auxilio fuerunt. Exod. 1, 20. 21. Cum alias ex nobis, tanquam ex nobis, non simus idonei, aliquid ejusmodi cogitare nedum facere, 2 Cor. 3, 5.§

13. Ad malas actiones ita terminatur divina providentia, ut illis quidem, cum fiunt, concursus generalis impertiatur,a caeterum actiones multae, quae alias futurae erant, impediantur,b illae vero, quae fieri permittuntur, ita tamen dirigantur, ut ad bonum finem c tendant. Sic enim in ipso movemur, quicquid agamus, Act. 17, 28. Sed ita simul constat, spectari hactenus actiones malas tantum, ut ctctiones; non autem, quatenus tales in sua specie atque adeo malae sunt.

Quenstedtius: ,,Actus divinae προνοίας circa mala moralia seu peccata antecedentes sunt: 1. peccati praevisio sive praescientia aeterna. . . 2. Ejusdem aversatio. . . 3. Prohibitio. . . 4. Impeditio. . . . Actus concomitantes sunt: 1. Naturae male agentis sustentatio. Sic quando Eva extendebat manum ad pomum interdictum, sustentabat quidem Deus locomotivam, sed non adjuvabat actionem vitiosam, qua talem. Atque ita saepe manu et lingua, quam Deo sustentante movemus, Deum oppugnamus. In ipsis flagitiis et peccatis sustentat Deus membra, conservat vires et motus nostros, ex quo stupenda Dei longanimitas elucescit. 2. Actionis ipsius quoad materiale spectatae c0eßcientia. Duo enim sunt in actione peccaminosa, materiale et formale. Materiale est subjectum vitiositatis, ipsa videlicet actio, et hanc Deus comproducit. Formale vero est ipsa actioni adhaerens vitiositas, ad quam Deus nullo modo concurrit. 3. 'Αταξίας permissio. Permittit Deus peccatum et sinit hominem a sua lege deflectere. Haec ipsa vero permissio non omnem excludit impeditionem, sed tantum physicam h. e. eam, qua Deus in voluntatem hominis agit, ut natura est et ipsi potentiae impedimentum ponit; moralis vero impeditio cum permissione hac conjuncta est, cum non cessat Deus prohibere et dissuadere peccatum. Actus consequentes sunt: 1. Directio peccati ad bonum finem. 2. Determinatio, ita ut praescribat metas et terminos, quos transilire malitia humana non potest. Sic Pharaonis tyrannidi certos limites posuit. 3. Peccati remissio. . . 4. Poenae irrogatio.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 30. f. 767.)

Sic adulterium Abimelechi cum Sara perficiendum impedivit Deus, Gen. 20, 6. Similiter persecutionem Labani Jacobo intentatam, Gen. 31, 24. 29. Et Ps. 33, 10. dicitur, Jehovam irritum facere consilium gentium, irritas facere cogitationes populi.

Sic Deus, permittens 1) peccata eorum, qui prae aliis excellere videntur, ipsos peccantes infirmitatis admonet, ne sibi nimis placeant aliosque contemnant; quo pertinet lapsus Petri, Luc. 22, 32. Aliquando 2) ex peccantium damnis alios emendare et excussa securitate solicitiores reddere intendit, Luc. 17, 32. Quando 3) pios ab impiis affligi permittit, afflictorum humilitatem et patientiam exercet, exemplo Jobi, cap. 1. Conf. Jacobi cap. 5, 10. 11. Nonnunquam 4) afflictionem piorum in occasionem melioris fortunae convertit et vel ipsos affligentes illorum opera juvari et emendari cupit; quod suo exemplo testatur Josephus Gen. 50, 20.

Quenstedtius: ״Permissio est actus providentiae gubernatricis, quo Deus creaturas rationales ad peccandum sua sponte sese inclinantes per impedimenta, quibus agens finitum resistere nequit vel quibus non restiturum novit, a malo lege vetito non retrahit, sed justis de causis in peccata ruere sinit, Ps. 81, 13. Act. 14, 16. Rom. 1, 24. 28. Permissio divina non est: 1. blanda indulgentia, quasi Deus plane non curet, quando homines scelera committunt, nec 2. relaxatio legis, quod peccandi licentiam illis permittat, nec 3. est impotentia in Deo vel intellectus, quasi inscio ipso creaturae ita in peccata ruant, vel voluntatis, quasi probet vel adjuvet scelera, vel defectus potentiae, quasi non possit peccatum cohibere et actum peccaminosum impedire, nec 4. otiosum spectatorem ex Deo facit, qui nec vetet peccata, nec metam malitiae ponat et corripiat; sed 5. est sapientissimi Dei actus negativus, quo creaturis rationalibus ad peccandum sua sponte sese inclinantibus non physica et omnipotenti actione sua impedimenta, quibus resistere nequeant vel quibus non restituras novit, ponit, sed sinit illas ab ordine suo deflectere et peccare, vel a malo in lege prohibito non retrahit, sed justis de causis in peccata ruere sinit.


### On the Providence of God: Permission 1. has as its object not the action of the creature itself, but the…

Permission 1. has as its object not the action of the creature itself, but the evil or defect of the action, which He does not will nor approve nor aid, but only permits. 2. God indeed permits, but He does not will the permitted thing, which happens, not indeed while God is absolutely unwilling—i.e., resisting and preventing—yet not willing, Ps. 5:5; 1 John 3:8. God’s not preventing is not willing, but permitting and at the same time also not willing, insofar as those things which He permits seriously displease Him. 3. Permission is not an action, but the negation of an action. For thus the self-murderer abuses the concurrence of the First Cause to kill himself; any action placing an impediment to that wicked deed is denied to him. 4. God forbids sin before it is committed; while it is being committed, He permits it, and directs the permission to a good end. 5. Permission consists in the suspension of undue resistance and of a violent and invincible impediment.

God permits sins, since He is not bound to prevent them, to which permission sin follows, not however causally, but consequently and eventually." (L. c. s. 1. th. 20. f. 763.)

Muellerus: "In the government of God, evil is also included. . . In the beginning, He either hinders it or allows it. Sometimes He hinders the ability, so that we cannot carry out the sin as we would like; either He makes the person come to nothing, as happened to Sennacherib, Isa. 37:36, or He weakens and diminishes the person's strength, as Jeroboam's hand had to wither there, which he had stretched out to seize the prophet, 1 Kings 13:4. Sometimes He hinders the ability with equal or greater ability; as He warded off the four kings who were taking Lot with them, through Abraham's march. He also often withdraws from the person that by which he wants to commit the sin, as He hid Christ when the Jews wanted to stone Him, John 8:39. Sometimes He hinders the person's will, so that he does not desire to carry out the sin to which evil lust otherwise inclines him, and he also..." PART I. CHAP. V. has enough power. This obstacle, however, is not compulsion, but persuasion, since man’s desire is convinced by certain reasons and kept away from evil. We are soon persuaded that we want to do this or that, either because it is easy to do and costs little effort, or because it brings delight, profit, and honor: so God also persuades the will not to commit sin, either because it could hardly, or perhaps even not at all, be done, or because it would only bring pain, shame, and harm. In this way, God moves the Pharisees and high priests so that they did not seize Christ; for they feared the people, who held him to be a prophet, Matt. 21:45. Now, if God hinders neither man’s power nor his will, He permits the sin; for this He has the highest right, for He is not obligated to hinder it. Who has given anything to Him that it should be repaid to him? This permission consists in the fact that God withholds His Word, by which He could break the will, or weaken the power, or even bring the person to nothing. Therefore, divine permission cannot be called a cause of sin, because God ceases to act and lets the sinner act alone.

In the progression, God orders and limits sin. He sometimes orders it to something other than what the sinner has in mind, so that it must be carried out for that purpose. For, "The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, like streams of water; He turns it wherever He wills," Prov. 21:1. Many a person thinks that he wants to harm the pious, but God governs it so wondrously that the harm must strike the godless. Sometimes God orders and directs sin to a different end than the sinner intends; this is testified to by the history of Joseph and his own words: "You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today," Gen. 50:20. Thus, many a person must often be exalted through God’s government by that very thing through which the enemy intended to humiliate him.

God also limits sin when He sets a certain measure to His permission and a certain goal for the sin. Often He does not let the sin happen at the very time when the sinner would like it to, but wisely arranges for it to happen at another time. Thus, the Jews indeed sought to seize Christ, "but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come," John 7:30. So many a person lives according to God’s will for many years, whom the wicked world would not let live for a single hour if the Man who dwells in heaven would only say "Yes." Often God lets the sin happen for only a short time, which the sinner intended to carry on for a long time. Therefore, for the sake of the elect, the days must be shortened, so that they are not subjected to the wickedness of the ungodly for too long, Matt. 24:22. God knows how to hedge up the way of sin with thorns and build a wall before it, so that the sinner cannot find his path, Hosea 2:6. Praise God! That the world cannot run any further than God permits, otherwise there would be no end to its raging and storming against the godly. Often God also does not let the sin rise as high as the sinner intends, for He is faithful and will not let the pious be tempted beyond their ability, but will make the way of escape, that they may be able to endure it, 1 Cor. 10:13.

At the outcome, God either punishes the evil or forgives it. He punishes it either temporally or eternally, and temporally, either outwardly or inwardly. The outward punishment strikes the body, takes away its property or well-being, and burdens it with all kinds of misery and wretchedness; for misery clings to sin like rays to the sun. The inward punishment concerns the soul, which God either abandons with His Spirit and grace, so that it wants and can do nothing else but sin; just as the natural body, when the spirit of life is taken from it...

is drawn, can do nothing else but fall into helplessness; or He delivers them into the power of the evil one; either that they fall into strong delusions and believe a lie, 2 Thess. 2:11, or that they are given over to a debased mind, to do those things which are not fitting, Rom. 1:28–29, or that they fall entirely into the power and snares of Satan and (if they do not come to the knowledge of salvation, so that the spirit is preserved) are finally cast, body and soul, into the maw of hell. The forgiveness of sins consists in this, that He remits the guilt and takes away the punishment; yet with the reservation of chastisement for the sake of testing.” (Himmlischer Liebeskuss, ch. 5, § 7–10, p. 35 ff.) §

14. Nevertheless, the providence of God does not take away the freedom of the human will, whether in good actions or in evil ones. For the general concurrence does not determine secondary causes, nor does it impose a necessity of acting. Likewise, to permit or not to hinder an action, and to direct an action that has been permitted toward a certain end, is not to determine the agent to perform this action. That spiritual actions are nevertheless so wrought in man by God that man can still resist God and prevent them from happening, we read clearly affirmed by Christ and shown by the example of the Israelites in Matt. 23:37. For it is said: "I would have gathered you," i.e., I not only wished for this to happen, but I contributed what was in Me so that you might receive faith, through which you might be joined to Me and be saved (for the context and the force of the simile, taken from a hen, indicate this), but you would not be gathered and you caused it to be that you were not gathered. Cf. Acts 7:51. We shall say more in the Book on Conversion.

Fechtius: “The mode by which God concurs and cooperates with creatures is universal, indifferent, and indeterminate. Indeed, every cause is either universal, which concurs with an effect in such a way that it does not determine its specific nature and proper character. Just as the sun concurs with its heat in the generation of all things, yet this heat does not cause that which is generated to necessarily be a dog or another species. For a dog is not from the sun, but from a dog giving birth. Or it is a particular cause, which concurs by determining the effect to be this specific thing. Thus, a pear tree produces a pear. Now, God concurs with all things only in the former way ordinarily, not in the latter. I say ordinarily. For we do not deny that, outside the ordinary course and in certain objects—such as in the effecting of spiritual things in man, as well as in miracles and any extraordinary events—God also concurs determinately. For unless God did this today, our prayers would be entirely in vain. This is proved: 1. From the clearest letter of Scripture, which testifies everywhere that God leaves His motions to all created things, and does not necessitate anything by determining it, except outside the ordinary course. 2. From the nature of the first and universal cause, inasmuch as it concurs with all things with an equal operation, and in no way moves or determines the secondary cause, as a principal cause does in relation to an instrumental one. And therefore, the concurrence of God imposes absolutely no necessity upon human actions, neither from without, which is that of violence, nor from within, which is that of immutability. That which compels necessitates from without; that which disposes the subject in such a way that, all things requisite for acting being posited, it cannot not act, necessitates from within. Divine concurrence brings about neither necessity, because it is indeterminate, i.e., as other theologians speak, because God tempers Himself PART I. CHAP. V. to secondary and particular causes, and permits individual agents to act according to their own natural motions.” (Compend. th., ch. 5, § 19, 20, p. 137 ff.)

Heerbrand: "Since all things are governed by the providence of God, do things happen necessarily or contingently? — By reason of the providence of God, which governs all things so that nothing happens inordinately or against His own purpose and will, and which cannot be deceived: all things are rightly said to happen necessarily. 'My counsel shall stand, and all My will shall be done.' Isa. 46. But not by compulsion. By a necessity of immutability, not of compulsion. For there is left to man a freedom of will in actions subject to reason; which, although they are governed by the providence of God, are nevertheless not compelled, but they do willingly whatever they do. Things happen, therefore, by necessity, not fatal or absolute, but, as they call it, of consequence. For nature could have things otherwise, and man could act otherwise, and it would not be impossible for the opposite to happen. Because by their own nature they are not necessary, but in reality contingent. But because they happen in this way, and God sees all things just as they happen, therefore, with respect to God who sees—who is not deceived in His vision, since He beholds all things as present, just as they happen—they are said to be necessary by a necessity, as has been said, of consequence. But if they were to happen otherwise, God would see this very thing as well. . . . Therefore, by reason and with respect to man, who is the proximate cause of his own actions, things happen and are done freely and contingently in human affairs. Thus, that David and Paris seize the wives of others, these things indeed happen by the providence of God; but by this vision of God they are not impelled or compelled to seize them; but they do this by their own most free will and contingently. For they could have abstained and not seized them. Thus Joseph, even when enticed by his master's wife, nevertheless abstained. Similarly, Alexander the Great and Scipio abstain from captives freely, willingly, contingently, and not compelled: the providence of God contributing nothing to these in either direction." (Compend. th. pp. 214—216.)

Latin:

Permissio 1. pro objecto habet non ipsam actionem creaturae, sed malum seu defectum actionis, quem non vult nec approbat nec juvat, sed permittit tantum. 2. Deus quidem permittit, sed non vult rö permissum, quod fit, non quidem Deo absolute nolente h. e. renitente ac impediente, attamen non volente, Ps. 5, 5. 1 Joh. 3, 8. Dei non impedire non est velle, sed permittere et simul etiam nolle, quatenus serio ei displicent, quae permittit. 3. Permissio non est actio, sed actionis negatio. Sic enim αύτόχεφ abutitur concursu causae primae ad se interficiendum, negatur ipsi actio aliqua, impedimentum nefando illi facinori objiciens. 4. Peccatum, antequam patratur, Deus vetat; dum patratur, permittit, et permissionem dirigit ad bonum finem. 5. Permissio constat in indebitae resistentiae ac impedimenti violenti ac invincibilis suspensione.

Permittit Deus peccata, cum impedire non teneatur, ad quam permissionem sequitur peccatum, non tamen causaliter, sed consequenter et eventualiter.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 20. f. 763.)

Muellerus: ״In der Regierung Gottes ist auch das Böse mit eingeschlossen. . . Im Anfang hindert ers entweder, oder lässets zu. Zuweilen verhindert er das Vermögen, dass wir die Sünde nicht können vollbringen, wie wir gern wollten; entweder macht er den Menschen gar zu nichte, wie dem Sennacherib geschehen ist, Esa. 37, 36., oder er schwächt und mindert des Menschen Kraft, wie dort Jerobeams Hand verdorren musste, die er ausgereckt hatte, den Propheten zu greifen, 1 Reg. 13, 4. Zuweilen hindert er das Vermögen mit gleichem oder grösserem Vermögen; wie er den vier Königen, die Loth mit sich führten, durch Abrahams Zug wehrte. Auch entzeucht er wohl dem Menschen dasselbige, daran er die Sünde begehen will, wie er Christum verbarg, da ihn die Juden steinigen wollten, Joh. 8, 39. Zuweilen verhindert er des Menschen Willen, dass er nicht begehrt die Sünde zu vollbringen, dazu ihn sonst die böse Lust neiget, und er auch PART. I. CAP. V. Vermögens genug hat. Dies Hinderniss aber ist kein Zwang, sondern eine Beredung, da des Menschen Begierde durch gewisse Gründe überzeugt und vom Bösen abgehalten wird. Wir lassen uns bald bereden, dass wir dieses oder jenes thun wollen, entweder weil es leicht zu thun ist und wenig Mühe kostet, oder weil es Ergötzung, Nutzen und Ehre bringet: so beredet auch Gott den Willen, dass er die Sünde nicht vollbringe, entweder weil es schwerlich, ja, auch wohl ganz nicht geschehen könnte, oder weil es nur Pein, Schande und Schaden bringen würde. Auf diese Art beweget Gott die Pharisäer und Hohenpriester, dass sie Christum nicht griffen; denn sie fürchteten sich vor dem Volk, das ihn für einen Propheten hielt, Matth. 21, 45. Wenn nun Gott weder des Menschen Vermögen noch Willen hindert, lässt er die Sünde zu; dazu hat er das höchste Recht, denn er ist nicht schuldig sie zu hindern. Wer hat ihm etwas zuvor gegeben, das ihm wieder vergolten würde? Diese Zulassung besteht darin, dass Gott sein Wort zurückhält, dadurch er könnte den Willen brechen, oder die Kraft schwächen, auch wohl gar den Menschen zu nichte machen. Darum mag die göttliehe Zulassung keine Ursache der Sünde heissen, weil Gott aufhört zu wirken, und lässt den Sünder allein wirken.

Im Fortgang ordnet und umschränkt Gott die Sünde. Er ordnet sie zuweilen auf etwas anderes, als der Sünder im Sinne hat, dass sie daran muss vollzogen werden. Denn,des Königs Herz ist in der Hand des Herrn, wie Wasserbäche; und er neigt es, wohin er will‘, Prov. 21, 1. Mancher meinet, dass er dem Frommen schaden will, aber Gott regiert es so wunderlich, dass das Leid den Gottlosen treffen muss. Zuweilen ordnet und richtet Gott die Sünde zu einem anderen Zweck, als der Sünder meinet; das bezeugt Josephs Historia und seine eigenen Worte: ,Ihr gedachtet es böse mit mir zu machen; aber Gott gedachte es gut (mit mir) zu machen, dass er thäte, wie es jetzt am Tage ist, zu erhalten viel Volks‘, Gen. 50, 20. Also muss oft mancher durch Gottes Regierung dadurch erhöhet werden, wodurch ihn der Feind gedachte zu erniedrigen.

Auch umschränkt Gott die Sünde, wenn er seiner Zulassung gewisses Mass und der Sünde ein gewisses Ziel setzet. Oft lässt er die Sünde nicht geschehen eben zu der Zeit, wenn der Sünder gerne wollte, sondern ordnet es weislich, dass es zur andern Zeit geschehe. Also suchten zwar die Juden Christum zu greifen, ,aber niemand legte die Hand an ihn, denn seine Stunde war noch nicht kommen‘, Joh. 7, 30. So lebt mancher nach Gottes Willen viele Jahre, welchen wohl die arge Welt nicht ein Stündlein leben liesse, wenn der Mann, der im Himmel wohnet, nur Ja sprechen wollte. Oft lässt Gott die Sünde nur eine kurze Zeit geschehen, die der Sünder eine lange Zeit gedachte zu treiben. Darum müssen um der Auserwählten willen die Tage verkürzt werden, dass sie nicht dem Frevel der Boshaftigen gar zu lange unterworfen seien, Matth. 24, 22. Gott weiss den Sündenweg mit Dornen zu vermachen, und eine Wand davor zu ziehen, dass der Sünder seinen Steig nicht finden kann, Hosea 2, 6. Gott Lob! dass die Welt nicht weiter laufen kann, als Gott zulässt, sonst wäre ihres Wüthens und Tobens wider die Gottseligen kein Ende. Oft lässt auch Gott die Sünde nicht so hoch steigen, als der Sünder meint, denn er ist getreu, und lässt die Frommen nicht versuchen über ihr Vermögen, sondern machet, dass die Versuchung so ein Ende gewinne, dass sie es können ertragen, 1 Kor. 10, 13.

Am Ausgang straft Gott entweder das Böse, oder vergibt es. Er straft es entweder zeitlich, oder ewig, und zeitlich, entweder äusserlich, oder innerlich. Die äusserliche Strafe trifft den Leib, nimmt demselben sein Vermögen oder Wohl wesen und belegt ihn mit allerlei Jammer und Elend; denn das Elend hanget an der Sünde wie die Strahlen an der Sonne. Die innerliche Strafe gehet die Seele an, die Gott entweder verlässt mit seinem Geist und Gnaden, dass sie nichts anderes thun will und kann, als sündigen; wie der natürliche Leib, wenn ihm der Lebensgeist ent

zogen ist, nichts anders thun kann, als in Ohnmacht fallen; oder er übergibt sie in die Gewalt des Bösen; entweder dass sie in kräftige Irrthümer fällt und der Lüge glaubt, 2 Thess. 2, 11., oder dass sie in einen verkehrten Sinn gegeben wird, zu thun, das nicht taugt, Rom. 1, 28. 29., oder dass sie gar in des Satans Gewalt und Stricke fällt und (wenn sie nicht zur Erkenntniss des Heils kommt, dass also der Geist erhalten wird) endlich mit Leib und Seele in der Höllen Schlund geworfen wird. Die Vergebung der Sünden bestehet darin, dass er die Schuld erlässt und die Strafe wegnimmt; doch mit Vorbehaltung der Züchtigung zur Prüfung.“ (Himmlischer Liebeskuss. c. 5. § 7—10. p. 35. sqq.) §

14. Neutrubi tamen, seu in bonis actionibus, seu malis, Dei providentia libertatem voluntatis humanae tollit. Generalis enim concursus non determinat causas secundas, aut necessitatem agendi imponit. Similiter etiam permittere seu non impedire actionem et permissam ad certum finem dirigere, non est agentem determina/re ad hoc agendum. Quod autem actiones spirituales ita fiant in homine a Deo, ut tamen possit homo Deo repugnare et facere, quo minus fiant, diserte legimus a Christo affirmatum et exemplo Israelitarum ostensum Matth. 23, 37. Dicitur enim: Ego volui vos congregare, i. e. ego non tantum id fieri optavi, sed, quod in me erat, contuli, ut acciperetis fidem, per quam mihi jungeremini et salvaremini (id enim contextus et vis similitudinis, a gallina petitae, indicat), sed vos noluistis congregari atque effecistis, ne congregaremini. Conf. Act. 7, 51. Plura dicemus in L. de conversione.

Fechtius: ״Modus, quo concurrit Deus et cum creaturis cooperatur, est universalis, indifferens, indeterminatus. Nempe omnis causa est vel universalis, quae ad effectum ita concurrit, ut speciem et rationem ejus propriam non determinet. Sicut sol ad omnium rerum generationem calore suo concurrit, nec tamen calor hic efficit, ut, quod generatur, necesse sit canis vel alia species. Canis enim non est a sole, sed cane pariente. Vel particularis, quae concurrit, effectum ad hoc tale esse determinando. Sic pirus producit pirum. Jam Deus ad rea omnes priori modo tantum ordinarie, non posteriori concurrit. Dico ordinarie. Nam extra ordinem et in quibusdam objectis, utpote in rebus spiritualibus in homine efficiendis itemque miraculis et extraordinariis quibusvis, Deum etiam determinate concurrere, non negamus. Id enim nisi hodie faceret Deus, preces nostrae plane essent früstraneae. Probatur: 1. A clarissima Scripturae littera, quae passim testatur, Deum quibuslibet rebus creatis motus suos relinquere, neque determinando quicquam, nisi extra ordinem, necessitare. 2. A natura causae primae et universalis, quippe quae ad omnia aequa operatione concurrit, neque secundam ullo modo vel movet, vel determinat, ut facit causa principalis in ordine ad instrumentalem. Atque ideo Dei concursus actionibus humanis nullam plane imponit necessitatem, neque ab extra, quae est violentiae, neque ab intra, quae est immutabilitatis. Ab extra necessitat, qui cogit; ab intra necessitat, qui ita subjectum disponit, ut, positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, non possit noü agere. Neutram necessitatem infert concursus divinus, quia est indeterminatus, h. e., ut alii theologi loquuntur, quia Deus sese attempe PART. I. CAP. V. rat causis secundis et particularibus, siugulaque agentia secundum naturales motus suos agere permittit.“ (Compend. th. c. 5. § 19. 20. p. 137. sq.)

Heerbrandus: ,,Cum omnia providentia Dei regantur, necessarione, an contingenter res flunt? — Ratione providentiae Dei, quae regit omnia, ut nihil vel inordinate fiat vel contra ipsius propositum et voluntatem, quaeque falli non potest: necessario omnia fieri recte dicuntur. ,Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet.‘ Isa. 46. Sed non coacte. Necessitate immutabilitatis, non coactionis. Relinquitur enim homini libertas voluntatis in actionibus rationi subjectis; quae, etsi providentia Dei reguntur, tamen non coguntur illa, sed volentes faciunt, quicquid faciunt. Fiunt igitur res necessitate, non fatali aut absoluta, sed, ut vocant, consequentiae. Posset enim natura res aliter habere et agere homo, ac fleri oppositum, non esset impossibile. Quia sua natura non sunt necessaria, sed revera contingentia. Sed quia sic eveniunt, et Deus videt omnia, sicuti fiunt, ideo respectu Dei videntis, qui in sua visione non fallitur, cum omnia praesens intueatur, ut flunt, necessaria dicuntur necessitate, ut dictum est, consequentiae. Quodsi aliter flerent, Deus hoc ipsum quoque videret. . . . Ratione itaque et respectu hominis, qui est proxima causa suarum actionum, libere et contingenter res fiunt et aguntur omnia in rebus humanis. Ut, quod David et Paris alienas rapiunt conjuges, flunt haec quidem providentia Dei; sed hac Dei visione non impelluntur aut coguntur, ut illas rapiant; sed liberrima voluntate sua id faciunt et contingenter. Potuissent enim abstinere, et non rapere. Sic Joseph ab herili conjuge, etiam pellectus, tamen abstinuit. Similiter et Alexander Magnus et Scipio a captivis abstinent libere, volentes, contingenter, et non coacti: nihil ad haec in utrumque faciente providentia Dei.“ (Compend. th. p. 214—216.)


### On the Providence of God: Quenstedt: "It does not take away the freedom of acting from rational agents

Quenstedt: "It does not take away the freedom of acting from rational agents; but rather man uses, and (what a stupendous long-suffering of God!) abuses that common concurrence and influx, as he does air, bread, and wine; yet without any disgrace to the divine majesty. For it is not these things themselves within themselves, but the external act (which is from God, not God Himself) that is open to abuse. Therefore, after God decreed not only to effect secondary causes but also to preserve them, He also decreed at the same time to cooperate with their actions. Which law, if taken absolutely, does not induce necessity, but is only a debt of connaturality, as Rutgersius speaks with Suarez, Instit. Metaph. lib. 2, cap. 9. Whence also God sometimes dispenses with that law by denying His concurrence: Let the fire in the Babylonian furnace serve as an example, which, by the sweet disposition of God, forgot its own power and did not burn that sacred trio of righteous men and their garments, Dan. 3." (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 781. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of Cicero, who, arguing against fate, denied the foreknowledge of future events, lib. 2 de divinit. Chrysippus also took away the same, see Augustine, lib. 5 de Civ. Dei cap. 9. And Averroes, who likewise impiously denied that the πρόγνωσιν of God embraces all things under itself, even singulars and thus even future contingencies and evils, which depend on the will of men. 2. Of the Socinians, who derogate from God the infallible foreknowledge of future contingencies, whether they be good or evil, and who maintain that if God's foreknowledge is granted, it imposes necessity upon the things foreknown. . . 5. Of the Stoics, who, from the forevision of God of all things, maintained that all things happen by a fatal order and an inevitable necessity of things. See Homer, who reveals the delirium of the Stoics with an elegant commentary, Iliad π, cf. Cicero, lib. 1 de divinit. 6. Of the Scotists and Dominicans, who contend that there is no certain forevision of future contingencies except from the determination of the divine will. . ."

7. The Calvinists, who also suspend divine knowledge upon divine ordination and an efficacious decree properly so called. Thus Piscator in his notes to Vorstius’s booklet, p. 261: "Whatever God knows will happen, that He has decreed, which also extends to sins." Thus Calvin himself, *Institutes* 1. 8. c. 23. f. 6. It is the voice of Zanchius, *Disputations on Providence*, th. 7, Vol. VII, col. 694: "That God, by His immutable providence, has not only ordained that the things which happen should happen, but has also ordained from eternity that all things should happen in the very manner in which they do happen." (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 772. sq.) §

15. Divine providence regards the term of human life not only insofar as, by a common law, a temperament is conferred upon each person, by the power of which he can reach a certain span of living with the general concurrence of God, but also insofar as life is prolonged for certain men beyond that term to which they would have arrived by the powers of nature; for others, the end of life looms sooner than it ought according to the course of nature.

Indeed, this is after the Fall; since otherwise man would have been immortal in his pristine state, as we saw in the preceding chapter, § 14, p. 155.

The term of life is otherwise called "natural," concerning which the blessed Aegidius Hunnius writes in *Questions and Responses on Providence*, Vol. I of his Works, fol. 714: "God leads man to the goal of human life ώς έπί τό πολύ through the mediation of nature. For when the radical moisture fails, together with the native heat, when the κράσις of the human body is disturbed and its powers are prostrated, it happens that man dies. But God concurs in establishing this term not only by reason of His foreknowledge, but because He Himself sustains and governs nature and secondary causes. And thus, through these mediations, God, as the primary cause, predetermines that term of which we speak."

And to this is usually referred what is said in Ps. 90:10: "The days of our years in them (or in which we live) are seventy years, and if in strengths (if the power of nature prevails, according to Kimchi, or according to others, if the number of years increases), eighty years."

The history of Hezekiah provides a manifest example, 2 Kings 20:1 sqq.

And in this sense, some call the term of physical fatality "dilatable." Thus, men of blood and deceit are read not to live out half their days, Ps. 55:23. And Ps. 102:24, David prays to his God not to cut him off in the midst of his days. And this is what others mean when they say the natural term is "abbreviable." §

16. Divine providence, however, changes the natural term of human life both in regard to pious men and in regard to the impious. Baier’s Compendium, ed. Walther. II. 12 PART I. CHAP. V.

Whence arises the preternatural term of life, which some call hyperphysical. See the blessed Gerhard, *Isag.*, Book on Providence, ch. VI, Disp. XVI, § 23, p. 667. It is called the term of grace. It is called the term of wrath, *l. e.* § 17.

For the pious, God prolongs life either as a reward for their obedience, or for the public good. He shortens the life of the same, partly so that they may not be corrupted by the wicked examples of others, and partly so that they may not see the calamities that are to come and be distressed. The promise of the fourth commandment pertains to this, Exod. 20:12. Compare Prov. 3:1-2, where length and long life are promised to those who keep the commandments of God. And ch. 4:10, the multiplication of the years of life for those who receive the words of God. That this happened to Paul is gathered from 2 Cor. 1:8 ff., inasmuch as he says he was snatched from the most imminent danger of death by subsidiary works; through the prayer offered for him by those who made use of his ministry. It happened also to Epaphroditus, Phil. 2:27, 30, whom the apostle says was healed for the good of the church and his own consolation, though he was truly near to death. Thus teaches the author of the Book of Wisdom, ch. 4:10-11. The example of Josiah, 2 Chron. 34:28, testifies to this. Compare Isaiah 26:20, ch. 57:2. § 18.

For the impious, God by a just judgment cuts off life sooner, when He either inflicts a lethal disease or death upon them Himself, or commands that death be inflicted, or permits them to contract diseases or violent death for themselves through intemperance or other crimes. For example, when a plague is sent, or, as Scripture speaks, when God strikes men so that they die. Compare the divine threatening in Deut. 28:21-22, and the examples of Er and Onan, Gen. 38:7 and 10, Nabal, 1 Sam. 25:38, and Hananiah the false prophet, Jer. 28:16-17. For example, murderers, Gen. 9:6, Exod. 21:12, 14 ff., and more so sodomites, idolaters, and the incestuous, Exod. 22:18 ff., Levit. 18 and 20. See the example of Ben-Hadad, 2 Kings 8:15, although daily experience abounds with these. Compare the blessed Hunn., *l. c.*, p. 715. The fates of Absalom, 2 Sam. 18:14 ff., and Ahithophel, ch. 17:23, are referred to this. And this last term of life which we have mentioned is said not so much to have been positively established by God, and the means by which it is reached ordained by Him, as that He does not hinder or does permit it.

19. And thus it is also established that it is not absolutely necessary that every human being should die at that specific time and by that specific kind of death by which he does die.

Gerhard: "When the question is asked concerning the term of human life, one must first of all distinguish between death considered simply and absolutely, and the hour and kind of death. Death itself, after the fall, is necessary for man according to the ordinary state and course of corrupted nature. Heb. 9:27: 'άπόκειται, it is appointed and determined for men to die once.' If the question is concerning the kind and hour of death, one must be careful not to be submerged either into the Scylla of Epicurean rashness or the Charybdis of Stoic necessity." (Loc. de provid. §78.)

That is, it is not decreed by God absolutely and immutably, without and before any regard for causes or circumstances to be found outside of God. Otherwise, the prayers and vows of the pious, and divine promises and threats, would be in vain.

Cf. the blessed Hunn. 1. c. p. 713. And the blessed Gerhard writes in Disp. Isag. 1. c. p. 667: The hyperphysical or divine term is always hypothetical, including the condition of piety, or impiety, or contempt of the means.

Meanwhile, it is not permitted for us to investigate too curiously the reason which divine providence regards concerning the term of the life of individual men, according to that passage in John 21:22, where Christ says to Peter, who was anxious about the term of John’s life: "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" And just as in other things, so in those which pertain to the term of human life, the divine judgments are often άνεξερεύνητα, unsearchable, Rom. 11:33.

Dannhauer: "You ask what is to be thought concerning the fatal term of life? I say it is fatal. For the testimonies of Scripture are too clear to be denied, when days are called חרוצים, defined, decided, measured out, decreed, Job 14:5. So that the mouth of the Epicurean who speaks offhand may be stopped.

If hairs are numbered, Matt. 10:29-30, how much more the days of life? If a little sparrow does not fall to the ground without the divine nod, how could a man fall by chance without providence?

By fatality, either absolute: 1. Regarding the determination to τόδε τι καί νῦν; for although longevity is promised to a son who is obedient to his parents, yet the term of longevity is not precisely designated—not the year, not the hour, not the moment; just as the hour of birth is of absolute decree, so also is that of dying.

2. Regarding the kind of death. Eccles. 3:2. For although the gallows is owed to a thief, it is not always imposed; thus, ordinarily, the blood of him who sheds blood is to be shed again, Gen. 9:6; yet the robber is often punished in a way other than by the shedding of blood, or he departs entirely with impunity.

3. Regarding the το ανεξερεύνητον and αντεξούσιον of divine judgment, by which it happens that a little child, though pious, is cut down sooner than expected.

Or 2. by hypothetical or physical fatality, estimated from the flow of natural causes, by which the life of man ώς έπί τό πολύ is defined as seventy years, Ps. 90:10...

Or moral, necessary by hypothesis, through extrinsic denomination; the choral connection of which is as follows: If David will honor his parents, i.e., all who are in the place of parents, not even excepting his father-in-law Saul, if he will religiously worship the heavenly Father, if he will live piously, justly, and temperately, he shall be long-lived; if not, he shall not grow to maturity. This term, taken separately, is movable by apocope, and is either dilatable through the aforementioned temperance, medical care, piety toward parents, and the grace of God outside... PART I. CHAP. V.

ordinary, such as happened to Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:1 ff.; Isaiah 38:1 ff.), or abbreviable through intemperance, neglect of medicine, or Absalom-like impiety (for who would doubt that Absalom, endowed with such good constitution of form, health, and strength, could have spun the thread of life longer than he did, had he not fallen into sedition against his father by his own doing?), through ἀυτοχειρία, through the just wrath of God the avenger, "this year you shall die, because you have counseled apostasy" (Jeremiah 28:16), or through His secret and inscrutable counsel. Otherwise, the promises of longevity and the prayers of the pious for it (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16, 33; Ephesians 6:3) would be in vain, as would the threats of μιαιροβιότης against the impious (Leviticus 26:25 ff.; Psalm 55:24); if repentance were removed, security would sail in with full sails; if the term of life were absolutely fatal, those who either fled dangers or sought remedies to preserve life would be ridiculous. For what happens by absolutely inevitable necessity can neither be prolonged by any means nor cut short by any dangers." (Hodos. Phaen. III. p. 170.) § 20.

The *proximate* end of divine providence is the utility of men, especially of the pious; the *ultimate* end is the glory of divine wisdom, power, and especially goodness. Thus, Psalm 33:19 says that the eye of Jehovah is intent upon those who fear Him and hope in His mercy, to deliver their souls from death and to keep them alive in famine. And Romans 8:28: "To those who love God, all things work together (συνεργεῖ) for good." Compare what we said about the degrees of providence in § 9. Here, however, it must be observed at the same time that the discourse concerns the utility of pious men, not precisely temporal, but especially spiritual, toward the promotion of which God tends primarily through various events and many crises of affairs. See Psalms 104 and 136 in their entirety. And God always obtains this end, even if men sometimes, by their own fault, cause the utility that God intends not to redound to themselves. § 21.

Divine providence can be defined as the benign purpose of the divine will, directed by the practical knowledge of God, concerning all creatures, especially men and, among the assembly of men, the faithful, to preserve and govern them for the utility of the men themselves and for the glory of divine wisdom, power, and goodness. For thus we have advised that providence, in the nominative case, is an act of the divine intellect and will alike. § 2, note d. By which name we indicate the impulsive cause; concerning which we spoke in § 5. The efficient cause, however, is involved in the very words "divine will" and "knowledge of God"; compare § 4. Concerning those who constitute the object of providence, see § 6. Concerning the acts to which divine providence is terminated, see § 8. These pertain to the end, concerning which see § 20.
