## 8 On Eternal Blessedness

PART I. CHAP. VI. Chapter VI. ON ETERNAL BLESSEDNESS. § 1. Since it is established that God is our highest good and the objective end of theology, we must now further inquire from the Scriptures concerning the operation by which we fully and perfectly possess and enjoy God as the highest good, as our formal ultimate end. See above, Proleg. Chap. I. § 4, Vol. I, p. 9, and § 17, p. 38.

Namely, our blessedness consists in a most perfect vital operation, which derives its perfection partly from the object and partly from the perfection of the mode by which it attains the object. Once this is obtained, our appetite is fully satisfied. For although man in the present state, under the guidance of the light of nature, can know that after this life there will be another, and that in it it will go well for the good, with God rewarding good deeds, and that the blessedness of souls also consists in knowledge; nevertheless, he cannot attain a more distinct knowledge of that blessedness and of the clear knowledge of God under the guidance of the light of nature, but must learn it from divine revelation. Compare the blessed Musaeus, Introd. Chap. II. § 9, no. IX, pp. 38-39.

Gerhard: "Just as through the most sorrowful fall the image of God in man was almost entirely extinguished and obliterated, and the good of eternal life was lost, so also the knowledge of that highest good, for which man was originally created, was miserably obscured, and the desire for it almost entirely languished. Augustine, Sermon 19 on the words of the Apostle: 'This especially distinguishes Christians from Gentile error, that the latter believe only in this life, while we believe also in the future one.' Meanwhile, however, just as certain remnants of the divine image and meager sparks of that most brilliant light have remained in the soul of man, so also a certain faint knowledge and a certain general appetite for that blessedness have remained, from which source has flowed whatever is found among the Gentiles concerning the rewards to be expected by the good after this life, concerning the immortality of the soul, and concerning the Elysian Fields. But this knowledge, as I have said, is not only imperfect and obscure... but also the assent arising from it is languid and weak; indeed, in temptations and adversities, it easily vanishes. Plato in the Phaedo: τὸ μὲν σαφὲς εἰδέναι περὶ τῆς μελλούσης ζωῆς ἐν τῷ νῦν βίῳ ἢ ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν, ἢ παγχάλεπον. ... When, therefore, it is said that 'every will tends toward blessedness,' it must be understood of blessedness considered in its generality, in the appetite for which all share; but insofar as blessedness is taken determinately for that which consists in the vision of God, it is neither desired by all, nor do all tend toward it." (Loc. on Eternal Life, § 33.) §

2. Man possesses God, however, as the highest good, through the fact that God is rendered intimately present to his intellect. PART I. CHAP. VI.

through the most perfect act of knowing, occupied with God; which is commonly called the beatific vision. Or the clear and intuitive knowledge of God. It is called a vision, by metaphorical expression, because we shall know God as distinctly and clearly as we distinctly and clearly know a thing that we see with our eyes; it is called beatific, however, because it is the formal reason by which we are constituted blessed. To this pertains what is said in Matthew 5:8: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Regarding these words, the blessed Gerhard says in his *Commentary*, p. 259: "Most people," he says, "take this to refer to the beatific vision in eternal life." And he adds: "They shall see God, that is, they shall dwell with God in eternal life and shall perfectly acknowledge Him." He also compares the passages 1 Corinthians 13:12, 1 John 3:2, and Hebrews 12:14. And indeed, in Matthew 5:8, an intellectual or spiritual vision of God is manifestly indicated, corresponding to the spiritual purity of the heart. And thus the passage in Hebrews 12:14 is also understood. Moreover, what is said in 1 Corinthians 13:12—that we, who now see through a glass in a riddle, shall one day (the imperfection of this life having been abolished) see face to face—the blessed Balduinus also explains in his *Analysis or Explication* as referring to a more exact knowledge, by which we shall know God intimately and perfectly; for it is a Hebraism in the phrase "face to face," otherwise God does not have a face. And these things, which Paul has taught thus far through comparisons, he now brings forward more clearly, as the sum of the whole matter, (when he says:) "Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I also have been known." Cf. the Paraphrase of this part, and Questions II and III, likewise Aphorism 8. And the thing itself speaks, that within the genus of intellectual vision, opposite members are presented for the state of this life and the other life. Finally, what is said in 1 John 3:2: "Beloved, now we are the children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but we know that, if He shall appear, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is," the blessed Hunnius long ago explained in his *Commentary* as referring to the knowledge of God (whose children we are), and that knowledge being as perfect as can fall to a creature, which is to be expected in the future age. Compare regarding these and other passages the blessed Dav. Chytraeus, *Book on Death and Eternal Life*, Part I, p. 172 ff.

Gerhard: "As often as either Holy Scripture or ecclesiastical writers establish blessedness in the vision and knowledge of God, it does not denote a bare act of the intellect, but also connotes an act of the will, and thus the full possession and attainment of that highest good, which is obtained through knowledge and love in eternal life. Just as words of knowledge most commonly among the Hebrews connote the affections and the following effects; concerning which matter Bonaventure discourses thus in *4 Sentences*, dist. 49, q. 5, art. 1: 'The three glorious or beatific acts—perfect vision of God, perfect love, and perf ect enjoyment—are joined and connected among themselves; therefore, through and because of this connection, that which belongs to all is attributed to one; but it is attributed more to vision for the reason that in vision the state of the fatherland is distinguished from the state of the way; not so in love, because there is love in both.'" (*Locus on Eternal Life*, § 119.) §

3. But in order to understand this operation of the intellect more correctly, a comparison must be instituted between the knowledge which we have of God in this life, and what kind [of knowledge we shall have] after this

ON ETERNAL BLESSEDNESS. life is to be expected. Indeed, in this life we can form only inadequate concepts of God, derived from created things through intelligible species and from the revealed Word; after this life, we shall know God, and all things that are formally in Him, by a simple and single act, without an intelligible species.

As Scripture itself leads the way for us in 1 Cor. 13:12, comparing what νῦν…, regarding the knowledge of God and divine things. And John writes in 1 Ep. 3:2, οὔπω ἐφανερώθη, ἐὰν δὲ φανερωθῇ, it has not yet appeared; but when it shall have appeared, etc. This is commonly called abstractive knowledge, and is otherwise described as being the knowledge either of an object not actually existing (which reason does not fit here, since God always and necessarily exists), or of an object that does exist, but not through its own proper species, nor joined to the intellect immediately and through its own substance.

Cf. the blessed P. Musaeus, *Libell. de aet. beat.* § 19, pp. 8, 9. As we said above in Chapter I, § 6, note b, p. 14, we do not have a quidditative, proper, and adequate understanding and perception of the divine essence in this life. Namely, the essence, the persons, and the divine attributes.

However, the free decrees of God (which, although on the part of that which they import in the nominative case, are within God as acts of the divine will, yet regarding that which they connote in the oblique case, they involve something outside of God, and contingent, namely, insofar as they are terminated toward things outside of God that will be in time) and likewise the perfections and actions of creatures are not equally attained by the blessed by virtue of that knowledge. To this pertains the fact that in Matt. 24:36 and Mark 13:32, the angels, even though they are blessed, are said to be ignorant of the day of the final judgment. And concerning Abraham and Israel, even though they are blessed and clearly see God, Isaiah says in chapter 63:16: He does not know us, he is ignorant of us.

Meanwhile, it is not denied that the blessed can know certain things through a special manifestation of God, which they do not know by virtue of the beatific vision of God; as we shall say in § 6 and the notes. Whence it is commonly called intuitive knowledge and is usually described as being the knowledge not only of an object actually existing, but one that is, moreover, joined and present to the intellect, whether through its own proper species or immediately through its own substance. And in this place, the latter reason holds true. Scripture calls it in 1 Cor. 13 a vision face to face, and in 1 John 3 a vision of God as He is.

Otherwise, the term comprehensive knowledge is known, from which the blessed are also called *comprehensores*, according to 1 Cor. 9:24 and Phil. 3:12, 13. For they are said, in opposition to those running in the stadium, to comprehend the prize, which formally takes place through this very vision of God. Yet this should not be understood as if the intellect of the blessed were to comprehend God in the same way that God Himself comprehends Himself; but only that nothing of those things which are formally in God will be hidden from the glorified intellect. Cf. Augustine, *Epist.* CXII, c. IX. Certainly that knowledge is τέλειος, perfect, and is contrasted with that which occurs ἐκ μέρους, in part. PART I. CHAPTER VI.

4. Therefore, for this knowledge of God, or beatific vision, it is necessary that there concur, besides the human intellect, also the light of glory, and the divine essence and persons themselves with their perfections.

Indeed, because that vision is a vital act, formally pertaining to the intellect.

For otherwise our intellect is not proportioned and capable of knowing God perfectly, inasmuch as all our natural knowledge depends in some way upon the senses. Therefore, it has need of another principle.

Now, the light of glory is, as to the thing itself, a certain spiritual habit, supernaturally infused into the intellect, elevating it beyond its natural powers to know God clearly in Himself, and, in place of an impressed species, determining it to elicit the act of intuitive knowledge.

Latin:

PART. I. CAP. VI. Caput YI. DE BEATITUDINE AETERNA. § t. Cum constet, Deum esse summum bonum nostrum et finem theologiae objectivum,a jam porro de operatione, qua Deo vel ut summo bono plene ac perfecte b potimur et fruimur, tanquam fine ultimo c formali, ex Scripturis d dispiciendum est. Vid. supra Proleg. cap. I. § 4. Vol. I. p. 9. et § 17. p. 38.

Scilicet beatitudo nostra consistit in operatione vitali perfectissima, quae suam perfectionem habet partim ex objecti, partim ex modi, quo objectum attingit, perfectione. Quo obtento, appetitus noster plane satiatur. Etsi enim homo in statu praesenti ductu luminis naturae cognoscere possit, post hanc vitam futuram esse aliam, in eaque bonis bene futurum, Deo benefacta remunerante, beatitudinem quoque animarum in cognitione constitutam; distinctiorem tamen beatitudinis illius et cognitionis Dei clarae notitiam ductu luminis naturae consequi non potest, sed ex revelatione divina discere debet. Confer, b. Mus. Introd. cap. II. § 9. num. IX. p. 38. 39.

Gerhardus: ״Ut perlapsum tristissimum imago Dei in homine ferme penitus fuit extincta et obliterata et bonum vitae aeternae amissum, ita quoque cognitio illius summi boni, ad quod homo primum conditus est, misere fuit obscurata et desiderium ejus fere totum elanguit. August, serm. 19. de verb. Apost.: ,Hoc praecipue Christianos a gentili errore discernit, quod hi hanc tantummodo vitam credunt, nos etiam futuram.‘ Interim tamen, ut quaedam imaginis divinae reliquiae et clarissimae illius lucis exiles scintillulae in anima hominis permanserunt, ita quoque tenuis quaedam notitia et generalis quidam appetitus illius beatitudinis permansit, ex quo fonte profluxit, quicquid apud gentiles de praemiis bonorum post hanc vitam expectandis, de animae immortalitate, de campis Elysiis occurrit. Sed haec notitia, uti dixi, est non solum imperfecta et obscura,... sed etiam assensus, ex ea ortus, est languidus et imbecillis, imo in tentationibus et adversis facile evanescit. Plato in Phaedone: το μεν σαφές ειδέναι τνεμι τής μελλονσης ζωής εν τώ νυν βίφ ή αόννατόν έστιν, ή παγχάλεπον. . . Quando ergo dicitur, ,quod omnis voluntas tendat ad beatitudinem‘, tum intelligendum id est de beatitudine in sua generalitate considerata, in cujus appetitu omnes communicant; sed prout beatitudo determinate accipitur pro illa, quae in visione Dei consistit, nec ab omnibus appetitur, nec omnes in illam tendunt.“ (Loc. de vita aeterna, § 33.) §

2. Potitur autem homo Deo, tanquam summo bono, per hoc, quod intellectui ejus Deus intime praesens redditur PART. I. CAP. VI.

per actum cognoscendi perfectissimum, circa Deum occupatum; quae vulgo visio a beatifica vocatur. Seu cognitio Dei clara et intuitiva. Quae visio dicitur, locutione metaphorica, quod ea tam distincte et clare Deum cognituri simus, quam distincte et clare cognoscimus rem, quam oculis videmus; beatifica autem, quod sit formalis ratio, qua constituimur beati. Quo pertinet, quod Matth. 5, 8. dicitur: Beati mundi corde, quoniam Deum videbuht. De quibus verbis b. Gerhardus Comment. p. 259. Plerique, ait, accipiunt de visione beatifica in vita aeterna. Et addit: Videbunt Deum, t. e. habitabunt cum Deo in vita aeterna et perfecte eum agnoscent. Confert etiam loca 1 Cor. 13, 12. 1 Joh. 3, 2. Ebr. 12, 14. Et sane Matth. 5, 8. manifeste indicatur visio Dei intellectualis seu spiritualis, respondens munditiei cordis spirituali. Atque ita etiam intelligitur locus Ebr. 12, llf. Quod autem 1 Cor. 13, 12. dicitur, nos ea, quae nunc cernimus per speculum in aenigmate, aliquando (abolita imperfectione hujus. vitae) a facie ad faeiem visuros esse, etiam b. Balduinus in Analysi seu Explicatione exponit de cognitione exactiore, qua Deum intime et perfecte cognoscemus; esse enim hebraismum in phrasi a facie ad faciem; alias Deum faciem non habere. Et haec, quae hactenus per similia docuit Paulus, jam clarius proferre, tanquam summam totius negotii, (quando ait: ) Nunc ex parte cognosco, tunc autem cognoscam, sicut et cognitus sum. Conf. Paraphrasin hujus partis, et Quaest. II. ac III., item Aphoris. 8. Et res ipsa loquitur, exhiberi intra genus visionis intellectualis membra opposita pro statu hujus vitae et vitae alterius. Quod denique 1 Joh. 3, 2. dicitur: Carissimi, nunc filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit, quid futuri sumus; scimus autem, quod, si apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quoniam videbimus eum, sicuti est, id de cognitione Dei (cujus filii sumus) eaque perfecta, quanta in creaturam cadere potest, quae in futuro saeculo sit expectanda, pridem exposuit b. Uunnius in Comment. Confer de his aliisque locis b. Dav. Chytraei Lib. de Morte et Yita Aet. P. I. p. 172. sqq.

Gerhardus: ,,Quoties vel Scriptura sacra vel ecclesiastici Seriptores in Dei visione ac cognitione beatitudinem statuunt, non notatur nudus actus intellectus, sed connotatur quoque actus voluntatis, adeoque plena illius summi boni possessio et adeptio, quae per cognitionem et amorem in vita aeterna obtingit. Sicut usitatissime verba notitiae apud Hebraeos affectus et effectus sequentes connotant; qua de re sic disserit Bonaventura 4. sent. dist. 49. q. 5. art. 1.: ,Tres actus gloriosi seu beatifici, perfecta Dei visio, perfecta dilectio et perfecta fruitio, sunt inter se conjuncti et connexi; ideo per et propter hanc connectionem tribuitur uni, quod est omnium; magis autem visioni tribuitur propterea, quod in visione distinguitur status patriae a statu viae; non sic in dilectione, quia utrobique est dilectio.‘“ (Loc. de vita aeterna. § 119·) §

3. Ad hanc vero operationem intellectus rectius intelligendam comparatio instituenda est a inter cognitionem, quam de Deo in hac vita habemus, et qualis post hanc

DB BEATITUDINE AETERNA. vitam expectanda est. Nempe in hac vita non nisi per species intelligibiles a rebus creatis desumtas et ex verbo revelato b conceptus inadaequatos c de Deo formare possumus; post hanc vitam Deum, et quae in eo formaliter sunt,d omnia, actu simplici et uno, absque specie intelligibili,e sumus cognituri.

Prout Scriptura ipsa nobis praeit 1. ad Cor. 13, 12., conferens, quae νΰν χα\ τότε, nunc et tunc, quoad cognitionem Dei ac rerum divinarum, nobis contingant. Et Johannes 1. Ep. 3, 2. scribit, ούπω έφανερώΗη, έά» δέ φανέρωση, nondum nunc apparuit; quando autem apparuerit etc. Quae abstractiva cognitio communiter dicitur, et describitur alias, quod sit cognitio vel objecti actu non existentis (quae quidem ratio huc non quadrat, cum Deus semper ac necessario existat), vel objecti existentis quidem, verum non per speciem propriam, neque immediate et per ipsam suam substantiam cum intellectu conjuncti.

Conf. b. P. Musaei Libell. de aet. beat. § 19. p. 8. 9. Prout supra cap. I. § 6. not. b. p. 14. diximus, nos in hac vita essentiae divinae quidditativam, propriam et adaequatam rationem cognitam et perspectam non habere. Nempe essentiam, personas et attributa divina.

Decreta autem Dei libera (quae licet ex parte ejus, quod in casu recto important, sint intra Deum, tanquam actus voluntatis divinae, tamen quoad id, quod in obliquo connotant, involvunt aliquid extra Deum, et contingens, scilicet quatenus terminantur ad res extra Deum, in tempore futuras) et similiter perfectiones et actiones creaturarum vi cognitionis illius non aeque attingunt beati. Quo pertinet, quod Matth. 24, 36. et Marci 13, 32. angeli, etsi beati, diem extremi judicii ignorare dicuntur. Et de Abrahamo atque Israele, etsi beatis ac Deum clare videntibus, Esaias cap. 63, 16. ait: Nescit nos, ignorat nos.

Interim non negatur, beatos posee ex peculiari Dei manifestatione quaedam cognoscere, quae ex vi visionis Dei beatificae non norunt; ut dicemus in § 6. et notis. Unde vulgo intuitiva cognitio appellatur et describi solet, quod sit non tantum objecti actu existentis, sed quod praeterea intellectui, sive per speciem propriam, sive immediate per ipsam sui substantiam, conjunctum et praesens est cognitio. Atque hoc quidem loco posterior ratio locum habet. Scriptura 1 Cor. 13. vocat visionem de facie ad fadem, et 1 Joh. 3. visionem Dei, sicuti est.

Alias notus est terminus comprehensivae cognitionis, a qua etiam beati comprehensores dicuntur, juxta 1 Cor. 9, 24. Phil. 3, 12. 13. Dicuntur enim, in oppositione ad currentes in stadio, comprehendere brabeum, quod formaliter fit per ipsam hanc Dei visionem. Non tamen id ita intelligi debet, quasi intellectus hominum beatorum eodem modo Deum sit comprehensurus, quo Deus ipse se comprehendit; sed tantum, quod nihil eorum, quae in Deo formaliter sunt, latebit intellectum glorificatum. Conf. August. Epist. CXII. c. IX. Certe cognitio illa τέλειος, perfecta, est, ei, quae fit έχ μέρους, exparte, contradistincta. PART. I. CAP. VI.

4. . Itaque ad hanc Dei cognitionem sive visionem beatificam necesse est concurrere praeter intellectum hominis a etiam lumen gloriae b atque ipsam essentiam et,personas divinas0 cum suis perfectionibus.

Nempe quia visio illa est actus vitalis, ad intellectum formaliter pertinens.

Nam alias intellectus noster non est proportionatus et habilis ad Deum perfecte cognoscendum, quippe quod cognitio nostra naturalis omnis a sensibus quodammodo dependet. Itaque alio opus habet principio.

Est autem lumen gloriae quoad rem habitus quidam spiritualis, intellectui supernaturaliter infusus eumque ultra vires suas naturales ad Deum in se clare cognoscendum elevans et, loco speciei impressae, ad actum cognitionis intuitivae eliciendum determinans.


### On Eternal Blessedness: And it is called "light" because it provides to the intellect, as the eye of…

And it is called "light" because it provides to the intellect, as the eye of the mind, the same thing that light properly so-called—for example, that of the sun—provides to the eye of the body by illuminating the air and brightening colors, making it so that the eye can see and know the species received therefrom.

It is called the light of "glory" because in the state of glory, or the future life, according to 1 Cor. 15:40, it is obtained by us for our intellect to behold God, who is our glory, and makes us glorious; just as Moses conceived rays from the sight of God, Exod. 34:29.

Namely, insofar as that knowledge is not of just any object, but is the clear knowledge of God. Cf. blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., § 32, pp. 17, 18. § 5.

This same beatific vision is not a free act, but a necessary one, both as to the exercise and as to the species of the act; and therefore the blessed will never cease, nor will they be able to cease, from it.

For while other acts of faith, depending on the light of grace, are indeed elicited freely, so that they might also not be elicited, and the intellect, negligent in its duty, might form for itself a different concept concerning spiritual objects;

yet here the reason is different. For the intellect, since it is not a free power but a necessary one, once all the requirements for acting (concerning which see § 4) are posited, cannot not act in this way; moreover, the will cannot turn the intellect away from the exercise of that act, because it can neither remove nor hinder the influx of the light of glory, nor the conjunction of the divine essence with the intellect. But neither does the will wish to turn the intellect away from the contemplation of that object which is the highest good and is perfectly represented to the intellect.

For what is said of the holy angels in Matt. 18:10, that they always διὰ παντός behold the face of the Father who is in heaven, that will also hold true for the blessed.

6. Although the beatific vision is occupied solely with the contemplation of God and that which is formally in Him; yet, in that state, the knowledge of other things will also pertain to the intellect of the blessed, so that each one will perfectly and clearly know his own condition or happiness, as well as the companions of his blessedness, by means of proper species, whether infused or acquired. For the vision of God is not the vision of other objects. See Matt. 17:1 and 3, where the apostles, having only a foretaste of eternal life, recognized Moses and Elijah. Cf. the blessed Dav. Chytraeus, *Lib. de Morte et V. Aet.* P. I. p. 65 sqq.; the blessed Aeg. Hunn., *Tom. I. Dispp. Marp.* disp. XLIII. p. 543; the blessed Hutter, *Comp. L. XXXIV. Qu. 5*; the blessed Gerhard, *T. VIII. L. ult. § 147. p. 1002.*

Gerhard: "In the transfiguration of Christ, Peter, James, and John see and recognize Moses and Elijah, whom they had never seen before... Just as Christ restored the son of the widow in Nain, whom He had raised from the dead, to his mother, Luke 7:15, and Peter presented Tabitha, who had been called back from the dead, to her friends and acquaintances, Acts 9:41, so on the day of the restoration of all things, Acts 3:21, pious children and relatives will be restored to their blessed parents, relatives, and friends—some of whom they did not see in this life—and conversely, parents will be restored to their children for the most sweet and pleasant conversation in the κοινωνία of the same happiness and joy. Gen. 15:15: 'You shall go to your fathers.' Deut. 32:50: 'You shall be gathered to your people.' 2 Sam. 12:23: 'I shall go to him.' Heb. 12:22, 23: 'You have come to the city of the living God and to the spirits of the perfect just.' ...

If the rich glutton, placed in the flames of hell, recognized Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham, Luke 16:23, how much more will the blessed recognize the companions and sharers of their blessedness? If John, still lurking in his mother’s womb, recognized the present Christ, Luke 1:41, how much more will the blessed, introduced into the full possession of celestial happiness, recognize Christ, the patriarchs, the prophets, the apostles, and all the sharers of their blessedness? If in this life children recognize their parents and parents recognize their children, surely also in the future life Abraham, the prophets, and the apostles—spiritual parents—will recognize their spiritual children, namely all the elect, and vice versa. For it would be absurd to posit greater knowledge in this life than in the future life." (*Loc. de vit. aet. § 147.*)

The same: "Will the blessed in eternal life see and recognize their relatives among the damned? — Just as Abraham saw the rich glutton placed in the flames of hell, whom he calls his son by reason of carnal lineage, Luke 16:25, so the blessed will also see their acquaintances and relatives, whom they held dear in this life, among the damned, as often as they wish; but without any affection of pity and without any disturbance of their joy, because their will will be perfectly conformed to the divine will. Therefore, they will not in the least desire any help or solace for those whom they know to be cast away from the face of God forever, out of an inordinate affection of love; as the example of the rich man in the same parable teaches, because he cannot obtain even a drop of water from Abraham. Ps. 58:11: 'The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance.' Therefore, a disturbance of joy is not to be feared from that vision, because every carnal affection, with which the blessed in this life pursued their relatives, will be abolished. God loved the human race much more ardently than anyone in this life..." PART I. CHAP. VI.

a parent can love his son, because He gave His only-begotten Son to the world and delivered Him unto death to redeem the human race, yet his happiness and joy can in no way be disturbed by the contemplation of the damned. Prov. 1:24: "I will laugh at your destruction." A greater affection will extinguish a lesser one, a spiritual and heavenly one a carnal one. (L. c. § 148.)

Indeed, likewise by virtue of the light of glory, which perfects the intellect and supplies its natural defect, so that it may penetrate more intimately into the nature not only of one object, but of many. Cf. the blessed Father Musaeus, l. c. § 42, p. 25. And thus also the intellect of the blessed will be able to know the free decrees of God, not through the beatific vision itself, but through the intervention of a special revelation, if God should wish to communicate any to them, with the light of glory simultaneously rendering the intellect fit to give assent without any hesitation. See the blessed Father Mascov, l. c. § 41 sqq.

Gerhardus: "In the future life, a perfect knowledge of God and of divine mysteries will follow. Then we shall fully and perfectly understand those things into whose intuitive and clear knowledge we could not penetrate in this life; namely, how God is one in essence and three in persons? How the Son of God was begotten of the Father from eternity? How the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son from eternity? Why the Son of God, and not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, assumed human nature? Why it was necessary for our mediator to be God and man? How the divine and human natures are personally united in Christ? How God created all things from nothing? On what day He created the angels? etc. Then we shall fully and perfectly understand the causes of divine counsels and works, namely, of creation, redemption, sanctification, resurrection, and glorification; how God created man with immense wisdom, preserved him with ineffable goodness, and redeemed him with infinite mercy; how He defended the Church against its enemies with His eternal omnipotence and raised the pious from death to eternal life. Then we shall fully and perfectly know the nature of the new heaven and the new earth, and therefore the inner chambers and innermost recesses of all creatures; then we shall no longer be compelled to complain that we, like Aesop’s stork, 'lick the glass but do not reach the porridge,' but we shall behold the inner forms and properties of things with a present intuition of the mind. For if Adam, through the light of his concreated wisdom, could know the natures of animals so exactly that he could impose suitable names upon each, Gen. 2:19, and could understand that Eve, whom he had not seen before, was built from his own flesh and bones, v. 23, how much more will the blessed, illuminated by divine light, be able to perfectly behold the mysteries of heaven and earth." ...

Augustine, *De triplic. habitac.*, cap. 4: "There, whatever is now hidden from us will be manifest; there the reason will be manifest why this one was elected and that one reprobated, why this one was taken into the kingdom and that one reduced to servitude, why one dies in the womb, another in infancy, another in youth, another in old age. Why one is poor and another rich; why the son of an adulteress is baptized, and sometimes the son of a legitimate spouse dies before baptism. Why he who begins to live well sometimes ends badly. All these things and many of this kind will be plain and open to all in the book of life, that is, of eternal truth and supreme wisdom. There all will know each other’s thoughts, etc." (L. c. § 73 sq.) §

7. Meanwhile, that vision of God is truly beatific and, just as it makes man a participant in the supreme good, so it leads him into that lot, that he becomes as similar to God as possible.

Indeed, our blessed life will formally consist in this very thing: that our mind will operate most perfectly within itself concerning the most perfect object. Namely, by uniting God, the most perfect being, to us, and that intimately within us. Thus it is expressly said in 1 John 3:2: ὅμοιοι αὐτῷ ἐσόμεθα. And to this pertains that participation (κοινωνία) of the divine nature, of which Peter speaks in 2 Epist. 1:4, which is indeed begun in a certain way in this life, but is perfected in the other. Compare the blessed Gerhard, in Comment. ad h. l. p. 39. § 8.

Furthermore, the same vision of God, although it formally pertains to the intellect, will nevertheless necessarily draw the will of the blessed man to the most intense love of God; and thus it will come to pass that man enjoys God as the highest good.

Namely, by this very fact, that the highest and infinite good is clearly known, there is no place in the intellect for either indifference of cognition (see notes a. b. to § 5), or comparative cognition, as some speak, or such that other goods could be known as equal to this good, or more excellent than it, or to be preferred to it and more desirable. For thus Scripture connects the cognition of God most closely with the love of Him, as we read in 1 John 4:7, 8: Everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. He who does not love does not know God, because God is love. Whence it is certain that the blessed, the more perfectly they know God, the more they love Him. And Paul says that charity will never fail, or that it will have a place not only in this life but also in the other, and, as to this, is more excellent than faith in 1 Cor. 13:8.

Latin:

Ac dicitur lumen, quod intellectui, velut oculo mentis, idem praestat, quod lumen proprie dictum, v. g. solis, illuminando aerem et collustrando colores, oculo corporis praestat facitque, ut oculus receptas inde species videre et cognoscere possit.

Gloriae lumen appellatur ideo, quod in statu gloriae, sive vitae futurae, juxta 1 Cor. 15, 40. intellectui nostro ad Deum, qui gloria nostra est, intuendum nobis obtingit et gloriosos nos facit; sicut Moses ex aspectu Dei radios concepit, Exod. 34, 29.

Nempe quatenus cognitio illa non qualiscunque objecti, sed Dei, et quidem clara cognitio est. Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 32. p. 17. 18.§ 5.

Eadem haec visio beatifica non est actus liber,a sed necessarius, cum quoad exercitium, tum quoad speciem actus,b adeoque ab eo homines beati nunquam cessabunt, nec cessare poterunt.c

Alias enim actus fidei equidem, a lumine gratiae pendentes, libere eliciuntur, ut possint etiam non elici, et intellectus, in officio suo negligens, alium de objectis spiritualibus conceptum sibi formare.

Verum hic alia ratio est. Intellectus enim, cum non sit potentia libera, sed necessaria, positis omnibus ad hoc agendum requisitis (de quibus vid. § 4.) non potest hoc non agere; voluntas autem intellectum ab exercitio actus illius avertere nequit, quia nec luminis gloriae influxum, nec essentiae divinae cum intellectu conjunctionem tollere aut impedire potest. Sed nec vult voluntas avertere intellectum a contemplatione ejus objecti, quod bonum summum est et ab intellectu sibi perfecte repraesentatum.

Quod enim de sanctis angelis dicitur Matth. 18, 10., quod semper 8tä παντός videant faciem Patris, qui in coelis est, id etiam de hominibus beatis valebit.

6. Quamvis vero visio beatifica unice circa Deum, et quae formaliter in eo sunt, contemplanda occupetur;a tamen intellectui beatorum in isto statu aliarum etiam rerum cognitio competet, ita ut suam quisque conditionem seu felicitatem, itemque socios beatitudinis,b per species quidem proprias, sive infusas, sive acquisitas,c perfecte et clare sit cogniturus.d Est enim visio Dei, 110η objectorum aliorum. Vid. Matth. 17, 1. et 3., ubi apostoli, gustum tantum vitae aeternae habentes, Mosen et Eliam agnoverunt. Conf. b. Dav. Chytraei Lib. de Morte et V. Aet. P. I. p. 65. sqq., b. Aeg. Hunn. Tom. I. Dispp. Marp. disp. XLIII. p. 543., b. Hutter. Comp. L. XXXIV. Qu. 5., b. Oerh. T. VIII. L. ult. § 147. p. 1002.

Gerhardus: ״In Christi transfiguratione Petrus, Jacobus et Johannes vident et agnoscnnt Mosen et Eliam, antea nunquam visos. . . Quemadmodum Christus filium viduae in Nain a se resuscitatum restituit matri suae, Luc. 7, 15., ac Petrus Tabitham ex mortuis revocatam παρέστηση׳ amicis et familiaribus, Act. 9, 41., sic in die restitutionis omnium, Act. 3, 21., pii liberi et cognati beatis parentibus, cognatis et amicis, quorum aliquos non viderunt in hac vita, ac vice versa parentes liberis restituentur ad suavissimam et jucundissimam conversationem in ejusdem felicitatis et gandii κοινωνία. Gen. 15, 15.: ,Ibis ad patres tuos.‘ Deut. 32, 50.: ,Jungeris populis tuis.‘ 2 Sam. 12, 23.: ,Ego vadam ad eum.‘ Ebr. 12, 22. 23.: ,Accessistis ad civitatem Dei viventis et spiritus justorum perfectorum.‘ ...

Si dives epulo, in fiammis infernalibus constitutus, Lazarum in sinu Abrahae agnovit, Luc. 16, 23., quanto magis beati socios et consortes suae beatitudinis agnoscent? Si Johannes, in utero materno adhuc latitans, Christum praesentem agnovit, Luc. 1, 41., quanto magis beati, in plenam coelestis felicitatis possessionem introducti, Christum, patriarchas, prophetas, apostolos et omnes beatitudinis suae consortes agnoscent? Si in hac vita liberi agnoscunt suos parentes et parentes agnoscunt suos liberos, utique etiam in vita futura Abraham, prophetae et apostoli, parentes spirituales, agnoscent filios suos spirituales, puta omnes electos, et vice versa. Absurdum enim foret, majorem cognitionem in hac, quam in futura vita, statuere.“ (Loc. de vit. aet. § 147.)

Idem: ״An beati in vita aeterna agnatos suos inter damnatos sint visuri et agnituri? — Sicut Abraham vidit divitem epulonem in flammis inferni constitutum, quem ratione carnalis propaginis filium suum vocat Luc. 16. vers. 25., sic beati etiam suos notos et cognatos, quos in hac vita caros habuere, inter damnatos videbunt, quotiescunque voluerint; sed absque ullo commiserationis affectu et absque gaudii sui perturbatione, quia voluntas ipsorum divinae voluntati perfecte erit conformis. Quare quos a Dei facie in aeternum abjectos noverunt, illis etiam aliquod auxilium vel solatium ex inordinato amoris affectu minime optabunt; ut in eadem parabola divitis exemplum docet, quia ne guttulam quidem aquae ab Abrahamo impetrare potest. Ps. 58, 11.: ,Laetabitur justus, cum viderit vindictam.‘ Perturbatio ergo gaudii non est metuenda ex illa visione, quia abolitus erit omnis carnalis affectus, quo beati in hac vita cognatos suos fuere prosecuti. Deus multo ardentius dilexit genus humanum, quam in hac vita ullus PART. I. CAP. VI.

parens diligere potest suum filium, quia unigenitum suum Filium mundo dedit et ad redimendum humanum genus in mortem tradidit, non tamen ex intuitu damnatorum ipsius felicitas et gaudium ulla ratione turbari poterit. Prov. 1, 24.: ,Ridebo in interitu vestro.‘ Major affectus extinguet minorem, spiritualis et coelestis carnalem.“ (L. c. § 148.)

Nempe itidem in virtute luminis gloriae, quod intellectum perficit et naturalem ejus defectum supplet, ut non 'unius tantum objecti, sed plurium naturam intimius penetrare possit. Conf. b. P. Mus. 1. c. § 42. p. 25. Atque ita etiam intellectus beatorum cognoscere poterit decreta Dei libera, non per ipsam visionem beatificam, sed intercedente peculiari revelatione, si quam Deus illis communicare voluerit, lumine gloriae simul intellectum idoneum reddente, ut sine ulla haesitatione assensum praebeat. Vid. b. P. Mas. 1. c. § 41. sqq.

Gerhardus: ,,In futura vita Dei et divinorum mysteriorum perfecta cognitio succedet. Tunc plene et perfecte intelligemus ea, ad quorum notitiam intuitivam et claram in hac vita penetrare non potuimus; quomodo scilicet Deus sit in essentia unus, in personis trinus? quomodo Filius Dei ab aeterno a Patre sit genitus? quomodo Spiritus Sanctus ab aeterno a Patre et Filio procedat? quare Filius Dei, non Pater, nec Spiritus Sanctus humanam naturam assumserit? quare mediatorem nostrum Deum et hominem esse oportuerit? quomodo divina et humana natura in Christo personaliter sint unitae? quomodo Deus ex nihilo omnia creaverit? quo die angelos condiderit? etc. Tunc plene et perfecte causas divinorum consiliorum et operum intelligemus, creationis scilicet, redemtionis, sanctificationis, resuscitationis et glorificationis; quomodo Deus hominem immensa sapientia creaverit, ineffabili bonitate conservaverit, infinita misericordia redemerit? quomodo aeterna sua omnipotentia ecclesiam adversus hostes defenderit ac pios ex morte ad vitam aeternam suscitaverit? Tunc plene et perfecte naturam novi coeli ac novae terrae, adeoqne omnium creaturarum penetralia et intimos recessus cognoscemus; tunc non cogemur ampiius conqueri, nos instar ciconiae Aesopicae,vitrum lambere, pultem non attingere‘, sed interiores rerum formas et proprietates praesenti mentis intuitu conspiciemus. Augustinus de triplic. habitae, cap. 4.: ,Ibi, quicquid nos nunc latet, manifestum erit, ibi ratio manifesta erit, cur hic electus est, et iste reprobatus, cur hic in regnum assumtus, et ille in servitutem redactus, cur alius in utero moritur, alius in infantia, alius in juventute, alius in senectute. Cur alius pauper et alius dives; cur filius adulterae baptizatur, et aliquando filius legitimae conjugis ante baptismum moritur. Cur, qui bene incipit vivere, aliquando male finit. Haec omnia et hujusmodi multa in libro vitae, hoc est, aeternae veritatis et summae sapientiae, plana et aperta omnibus erunt. Ibi omnes invicem suas cogitationes cognoscent etc.‘“ (L. c. § 73. sq.) §

Scilicet hoc ipso, quod bonum summum atque infinitum clare cognitum est neque in intellectu locum habet vel indifferentia cognitionis (vid. notas a. b. ad § 5.), vel cognitio comparativa, ut quidam loquuntur, seu talis, qua bona alia, tanquam huic bono aequalia, aut eo praestantiora, seu ei praeferenda et magis expetibilia, possint cognosci. Ita enim Scriptura cognitionem Dei cum ejus amore arctissime connectit, prout 1 Joh. 4, 7. 8. legimus: Omnis, qui diligit, ex Deo nutus est, et cognoscit Deum. Qui non diligit, non novit Deum, quoniam Deus caritas est. Unde certum est, quod beati quo perfectius cognoscunt Deum, hoc magis ament. Et Paulus caritatem nunquam defecturam, seu non in hac solum vita, verum et in altera locum habituram et, quantum ad hoc, fide praestantiorem dicit in 1. ad Cor. 13, 8.


### On Eternal Blessedness: Moreover, the chief object of charity is God

Moreover, the chief object of charity is God. Compare the blessed Chytraeus, 1. c. p. 173, 174, where he also refers to this the fact that, according to the most common phraseology of the Holy Scriptures, words of knowledge and the senses embrace not only a bare and solitary recognition or apprehension of an object in the mind or sense, but also unfeigned affections in the will and heart, and the effects or actions following that knowledge and vision. Add what he has on p. 197 sqq. Thus, indeed, although intellection is prior by nature to the love of God, yet at the same time and in the same moment of time (if one may speak thus of the state of eternity) the latter finds a place in the soul of the blessed man just as the former does. For to enjoy a good is nothing other than to adhere to it by love for its own sake, as Augustine says, Lib. I. de Doctr. Christ, cap. III. § 9. Therefore, also the will, perfectly determined to the love of God and holy, will not be able to fall away from God and sin. PART I. CHAP. VI.

See what has been said at § 5, note b, and § 8, a. Namely, when the will cannot turn the intellect away from the exercise of the intuitive vision of God, the will itself is certainly always affected by the intellect—which is fixed upon God and represents Him as the supremely good thing—and it yearns for and dwells upon that Good.

Gerhard: "God is life itself, light, essential blessedness; therefore, from the vision of God, the elect participate in life, light, and blessedness. The highest Good, perfectly known, cannot but be loved; therefore, from the vision of God arises the perfect love of God. The highest Good, perfectly known and loved, cannot but be praised and glorified; for what one loves, that one also praises; therefore, from the vision and love of God arises glorification and exultation." (Harm. ev. c. 176, f. 1271.)

The same: "Because the blessed will know God, the highest Good, intuitively and perfectly, therefore they will also inseparably adhere to that highest Good, once perfectly recognized, through a holy movement of the will; and consequently, just as every darkness of ignorance will be expelled from the mind, so every inclination toward evil will be expelled from the will. In God, as the infinite Good, all goods are contained in the most eminent way, and thus the entire breadth of the object of the will, toward which it is naturally drawn, is found [in Him], so that nothing better can be thought of or desired by man. From this it follows that the blessed cannot turn themselves away from God by their own will, nor desire anything else except in relation to that adequate object, since in Him is contained the highest perfection of man, the fulfillment of every desire, and the ultimate end, upon the attainment of which the will finds rest and desires nothing else. Therefore, the blessed will be confirmed in good by the very nature of their state—namely, from the beatific vision of God—and not merely by an extrinsic law of God, as some of the Scholastics opine. Just as in Christ there was no inordinate movement of the will, no stain of sin, no spot of iniquity, but the most exact conformity with the norm of the divine law: so in the blessed, the will immutably chooses the good recognized and shown by the intellect, without any proneness whatsoever to sin. Just as the angels, because they 'always see the face of my Father who is in heaven' (Matt. 18:10), are confirmed in good and freed from the danger of sinning: so the blessed, as being future ἰσάγγελοι, will be perfectly holy and confirmed in good through and because of the beatific vision of God." (Loc. de vita aet. § 75.)

Separated from the common, profane, and impure way of living in this age, consecrated to God and conformed to the most holy God, such that this holiness is greater than that which had been created in the first parents. This is not only because the blessed will no longer be exposed to the snares of Satan and the scandals, threats, and allurements of the world, and because the temptation and struggle of the flesh and the very root of original sin will be entirely absent, but because of that full adherence of the will to God. And this is that ἀναμαρτησία or impeccability which is accustomed to be ascribed to the blessed, similar to that which we observed in the blessed angels in Chapter III, § 30. Pertaining to this is that righteousness in which David asserted he would see the face of God after this life (Ps. 17:15), and the fact that the Church is called ἔνδοξος, glorious or triumphant, having no spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27), which is most rightly understood of inherent and most perfect holiness. Some call this holiness of the blessed humans "isangelic," alluding to Matt. 22:30. They also refer to this that "fine linen, clean and bright," which consists in the "righteous acts of the saints" (Rev. 19:8).

§ 10.

Although, through that determination of the will to embrace the highest good constantly, liberty or indifference toward good and evil is removed; nevertheless, a more excellent liberty will truly have a place, since regarding many finite and particular goods, the blessed will be able to act or not act, and to undertake the doing of this or that. Nor is this perfection said to be absolute, but only in comparison to the power which is determined solely toward evil and cannot do good; indeed, it is at the same time an imperfection to be able to sin. Compare Chapter III, on the angels, § 31. For that the highest and infinite good cannot be indifferently desired or loved by the blessed was stated at § 8. Namely, because among such things a comparative cognition has a place. Meanwhile, it is certain that the blessed, whatever they do regarding various particular goods, refer all of it exactly to the glory of God. And such liberty is most properly so called and is a perfection simply, and therefore it falls also to the angels (see above, Chapter III, § 31), and indeed even to God in His own way. § 11.

Finally, from the vision of God is born pleasure or ineffable joy, by which men are affected, beholding and loving God. As an ἐπιγινόμενόν τι τέλος, or a supervening end, or one that comes in addition, as Aristotle speaks elsewhere when he teaches that pleasure or delight arises from every perfect operation (X Ethic. cap. IV). Or by the power of which the soul of the blessed placidly rests in the possession and fruition of the present good. Whence it is rightly called heavenly and spiritual joy (Rom. 14:17), intimate and most full, or the joy of the heart (John 16:22; 1 John 1:4), as it were nuptial (Rev. 19:7), or convivial (Luke 22:30), amidst songs and dances, as of those triumphing, or of those liberated from prison (Rev. 5:9; 15:3; Ep. Jude v. 24), to which also that of Isaiah 35:10 looks, where, under the type of those returning from the Babylonian captivity, the joy of the blessed is graphically described: "The redeemed of the Lord shall return and come to Zion with singing; and everlasting joy (shall be) upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy; and sorrow and sighing shall flee away." Compare the blessed Chytraeus, loc. cit., p. 207 sqq. For thus seeing and rejoicing are conjoined (Is. 66:14; John 16:22). And Ps. 16:11, those things are conjoined among themselves: "You will make known (O God) to me the path of life; (and) fullness of joys before your face (i.e., in your sight, or, when I shall see you), pleasures at your right hand forevermore." Similarly, Ps. 17, last verse: "I shall behold your face and be satisfied," and thus, seeing, I shall rest. PART I. CAP. VI.

in You. Indeed, even the very words for "seeing" in the holy tongue, especially when they are constructed with the preposition ב, are accustomed to imply a certain acquiescence in the good or delight. See Ps. 50, last verse: "I will show him the salvation of God." Cf. Tamovius on Micah 4:11, Obadiah v. 12, and Geier on the Psalms passim.

Gerhardus: "Since God is the highest and infinite good, the highest sweetness, the highest pleasantness, etc., therefore from the vision of God there cannot but arise ineffable joy and inexplicable pleasure. If the power and efficacy of the created sun is so great that by its heat it not only imparts life to growing things, but also most sweetly refreshes and wonderfully delights the spirits of men—nay, all creatures—by the diffusion of its rays of light: how infinitely greater is the joy that must be believed to fill the breasts of the pious, when they will not only behold with their own eyes the Creator of the sun, the Sun of righteousness, the cause of all joy and salvation, but will also most fully enjoy Him through the intimate communication of the same, with the darkness of sins thoroughly dispelled! Secondary and less principal causes are the remaining goods of eternal life, as much internal as external, as much of body as of soul, as much privative as positive, to be conferred upon the elect in eternal life at some time. The elect will rejoice above themselves concerning the vision of God, within themselves concerning the glorification of soul and body, around themselves concerning the association of the holy angels and all the blessed, and below themselves concerning the escape from hell. They will have joy from Christ, in Christ, with Christ, after Christ, through Christ, and on account of Christ." (L. c. § 65.)

Indeed, men can otherwise languish or pine away with love, either when they love that of which they cannot become fully possessed, or when imperfection and satiety can have a place in the very good that is loved, or the appetite itself becomes exhausted: here, however, the perfection of both the loved object and the act itself excludes all weariness or sorrow and, on the contrary, is a fountain of perpetual joy. §

12. Moreover, that beatific vision, together with the love and joy born from it, will be equally perfect in all blessed men.a a) For not only does Scripture make no distinction here, which would have a place in different subjects (see the cited passages 1 John 3:2, 1 Cor. 13:12), but the thing itself also speaks, that when God is seen as He is, that knowledge cannot be intensified or remitted, so that it might nevertheless remain clear and intuitive. And if the vision is the same in all, the love and joy born from it will likewise be equal. It is evident, however, that the discourse is concerning the perfection of knowledge viewed intensively. For we do not deny that, extensively, there can be a greater or lesser knowledge of other objects—though not indeed of the beatific vision of God—among the blessed. See the preceding § 6. §

13. Besides these things, however, which pertain to the essence of beatitude and which furthermore consist formally in the soul,

Frui enim bono nihil est aliud, quam amore ei inhaerere propter ipsum, dicente August. Lib. I. de Doctr. Christ, cap. III.§ 9. Gerhardus: ,,Deus est ipsa vita, lux, essentialis beatitudo; ergo ex visione Dei electi participant vitam, lucem et beatitudinem. Summum bonum perfecte cognitum non potest non amari; ergo ex visione Dei oritur perfecta Dei dilectio. Summum bonum perfecte cognitum et amatum non potest non laudari et glorificari; quod enim quis amat, illud etiam laudat; ergo ex visione et dilectione Dei oritur glorificatio et exultatio.“ (Harm. ev. c. 176. f. 1271.)

Idem: ,,Quia beati Deum, summum bonum, intuitive ac perfecte cognoscent, ideo etiam summo illo bono perfecte agnito per sanctum voluntatis motum inseparabiliter adhaerebunt ac proinde, ut ex mente omnis caligo ignorantiae, ita ex voluntate omnis ad malum proclivitas erit expulsa. In Deo, utpote infinito bono, omnia bona eminentissime continentur adeoque tota latitudo objecti voluntatis, ad quod naturaliter fertur, reperitur, ut nihil melius ab homine cogitari vel appeti possit; ex quo sequitur, beatos per suam voluntatem a Deo non posse se avertere aut aliud quid, nisi in ordine ad objectum illud adaequatum, appetere, cum in illo contineatur summa hominis perfectio, desiderii omnis complementum ac finis ultimus, quo obtento voluntas acquiescit, neque aliud quicquam desiderat. Proinde ex ipsa natura sui status, ex beatifica scilicet Dei visione, non tantum ex lege Dei extrinseca, ut quidam scholasticorum opinantur, beati erunt in bono confirmati. Quemadmodum in Christo nullus fuit inordinatus voluntatis motus, nulla peccati labes, nulla iniquitatis macula, sed exactissima cum norma divinae legis congruentia: sic in beatis voluntas immutabiliter eligit bonum ab intellectu agnitum ac monstratum sine ulla omnino ad peccandum pronitate. Quemadmodum angeli, quia,semper vident faciem Patris, qui in coelis est‘, Matth. 18, 10., sunt in bono confirmati et a peccandi periculo liberati: sic beati, utpote futuri Ισάγγρλοι, perfecte sancti et in bono confirmati erunt per et propter beatificam Dei visionem.“ (Loc. de vita aet. § 75.)

Separata a vulgari, profana, impura ratione vivendi in hoc saeculo, Deo consecrata Deoque sanctissimo conformis, ita ut major sit sanctitas, quam quae protoplastis fuerat concreata. Non solum, quod satanae insidiis mundique scandalis, minis et lenociniis non amplius expositi erunt beati quodque carnis tentatio et lucta ipsaque radix peccati originalis omnino aberit, sed propter illam plenam voluntatis inhaesionem in Deo. Atque haec est άναμαρτησία aut impeccabilitas illa, quae beatis adscribi solet, similis illi, quam in angelis beatis observavimus cap. III. § 30. Pertinet huc justitia illa, in qua se post hanc vitam Dei vultum visurum esse asseruit David Ps. 17, 15. et quod dicitur ecclesia ένδοξος, gloriosa aut triumphans, non habere maculam aut rugam, Ephes. 5, 27., quod de sanctitate inhaerente ac perfectissima rectissime intelligitur. Aliqui sanctitatem hanc beatorum hominum vocant isangelicam, alludentes ad Matth. 22, 30. Referunt huc etiam byssum illam mundam et splendidam, quae consistat in justificationibus sanctorum, Apoc. 19, 14.

§ 10.

Quanquam vero per illam voluntatis determinationem, ad summum bonum constanter amplectendum, tollatur a libertas sive indifferentia ad bonum et b malum; aliqua tamen libertas praestantior revera locum habebit, quandoquidem circa bona plura, finita et particularia c poterunt beati agere et non agere hoc aut aliud agendum suscipere. Neque vero haec perfectio absolute dicta est, sed tantum in comparatione ad potentiam, quae ad malum unice determinata est et bonum agere nequit, imo simul imperfectionis est, posse peccare. Confer, cap. III. de angelis § 31. Summum enim et infinitum bonum non posse a beatis indifferenter appeti aut amari, dictum est ad § 8. Nempe quia inter haec talia locum habet comparativa cognitio. Interim certum est, beatos, quicquid agunt circa diversa bona particularia, id omne ad Dei gloriam exacte ab iis referri. Et talis libertas propriissime dicta et perfectio simpliciter est, ideoque in angelos etiam (vid. supra cap. III. § 31.), quin etiam in Deum suo modo cadit.§ 11.

Gerhardus: ,,Cum Deus sit summum et infinitum bonum, summa dulcedo, summa suavitas etc., ideo ex Dei visione non potest non oriri ineffabile gaudium et inexplicabilis voluptas. Si tanta vis et efficacia solis creati est, ut suo calore rebus nascentibus vitam non modo impertiat, sed etiam animos hominum, imo omnes creaturas, diffusione radiorum lucis suae suavissime recreet et mirifice delectet: quanto in infinitum majori gaudio credendum est completum in (iri?) pectora piorum, quando creatorem solis, solem justitiae, causam omnis laetitiae ac salutis, non modo oculis suis intuebuntur, sed etiam intima ejusdem communicatione, discussis penitus peccatorum tenebris, plenissime perfruentur! 12. Erit autem visio illa beatifica una cum amore et gaudio inde nascentibus in omnibus hominibus beatis a aeque perfecta.b a) Non tantum enim Scriptura nullum hic discrimen facit, quod in diversis subjectis locum sit habiturum (vid. loca cit. 1 Joh. 3, 2. ad Cor. 13, 12.), verum etiam res ipsa loquitur, quod, quando Deus videtur, sicuti est, non possit ea cognitio intendi, aut remitti, ut tamen clara maneat et intuitiva.
