Quod enim extensive possit, non quidem visio beatifica Dei, sed tamen cognitio aliorum objectorum, major aut minor, in beatis esse, non negamus. Vid. § praec. 6.§

13. Praeter haec autem, quae ad essentiam a beatitudinis pertinent et quae porro b in anima formaliter consistunt,


### On Eternal Blessedness: it pleases God to add also other gifts, by which the bodies of the blessed are…

it pleases God to add also other gifts, by which the bodies of the blessed are perfected and blessed in the highest degree. Indeed, the primary concept of blessedness, than which no other is prior (inasmuch as it imports the attainment and possession of the highest good, and is to be sought for its own sake, and primarily belongs to an intelligent nature), consists in the vision of God itself, conjoined with perfect love; between which, however, there is some order, such that love presupposes vision, although they do not differ in time. E.g., the knowledge of other objects, by which the intellect is perfected; concerning which see § 6 and the notes. Just as blessedness is otherwise called a state perfected by the aggregation of all goods; such as, when it is to be given to man, all the faculties of the soul and the body itself must be perfected, so that it may be the blessedness not of the soul only, but of the whole man.

Gerhard: "The body was the instrument of good works in this life, 2 Cor. 5:10; it is therefore equitable that it be assumed into the communication of the reward and the fellowship of glory. The body was made conformable to the image of the crucified Christ through sufferings and the cross; Gal. 6:17: 'I bear the marks of Christ in my body'; it is therefore equitable that it be made conformable to the image of the glorified Christ. Between the body and the soul there is a most tight union and intimate conjunction even in this life, so that sadness, grief, and other affections of the soul affect the body itself; certainly, therefore, also in the life to come, because of the most tight and indissoluble union of soul and body, the glory and joy of the soul will overflow into the body of the blessed." (Loc. de vita aet. § 80.) §

14. The blessedness of the bodies of the blessed will consist primarily in this, that the bodies will be spiritual, that is, subject to the soul, which is a spirit, in the most perfect manner, partly as an informing form, and partly as a moving principle. See 1 Cor. 15:44. However, the change of the body into a spirit, which is immaterial by essence, is not to be understood.

Luther: "It is not called a spiritual body because it should not live bodily, nor have flesh and blood; otherwise it could not be called a true body. But now it is called a spiritual body, in such a way that it shall have its life, and yet will no longer be an eating, sleeping, enduring body, but will be spiritually fed and sustained by God and have life entirely in Him. But afterwards, when it thus lives spiritually in God, it will also go out into heaven and earth, play with the sun and moon and all other creatures, and also have its joy and pleasure in them, and be so full and blessed from them that it will never again think of eating or drinking, and thus will be and be called a spiritual being or life of the whole man, which will spring from the Spirit and proceed from or through God without means; so that we will not only be enlightened by Him according to the soul and know Him, but it will also go through the whole body, so that it will become so clear and light PART I. CHAP. VI.

be, like the air, seeing and hearing as sharply as the world is wide, so that we shall have need of no other thing to sustain ourselves and live, and yet have a true body. Just as even now the stars in the heavens are so made that they have no need of any necessity for their being, and yet are also bodily creatures; although they do not have such an earthly, but a heavenly body.” (Exposition of the 15th Chapter of the 1st Epistle of St. Paul to the Corinthians, 1534. VIII, 1539.) What is the subtlety of bodies, by the power of which bodies will so subsist with their souls without imperfection, as if they themselves were spirits; and thus they will also be able to penetrate other solid bodies. See Epist. to Phil. 3:21, compared with John 20:19 and 26, and likewise Luke 24:37, 39. Indeed, the proof comes to this: If Christ with His glorified body penetrated through doors that were then truly closed and could be seen while substantially present, and our bodies, in the state of the other life, are to be conformed to the glorious body of Christ, it follows that our bodies will likewise be so subtle that, without any new change of themselves or injury to themselves or the body being penetrated, they can penetrate another solid body. The former is proved partly from the cited passages of John and Luke, and partly from chapter 8 to the Phil. Therefore, the latter is also true. Conf. *Ausführl. Erklärung* L. IV. Q. XXI. p. 175, 176. Gerhardus: “We say that the bodies of the blessed will be subtle and penetrable... A subtle body is that which penetrates and from which has been removed the repugnance of existing in the same place with another body... The blessed will be ἰσάγγελοι. Now, angels are most subtle essences, endowed with the faculty of penetrating. Acts 12:12, the angel, leading Peter out of the prison, could be restrained by no valves or bolts from standing by Peter in the prison. Therefore, the bodies of the blessed will also be subtle... Christ at the resurrection penetrated the closed tomb, after the resurrection entered to the disciples with the doors closed, in the ascension penetrated the heavens, as was demonstrated at length in *Harm. de resurr.* Therefore, the bodies of the blessed will also be endowed with this property.” (L. c. § 98.) Quenstedtius: “The bodies of the blessed will be illocal, i.e., not circumscribed by a physical, bodily place. They will not be everywhere, but in a certain που, definitely, not circumscriptively; for they will be immune from the circumscription and surrounding of an external place, e.g., from the air or another surrounding element; for those elements will be abolished.” (L. c. f. 800.) And this is the agility of bodies, by the power of which bodies will be able to be moved most easily and most swiftly, wherever their souls shall wish to move them. See 1 Cor. 15:43, where it is said that the bodies of the pious, which are sown in weakness, are to rise in power (ἐν δυνάμει), which is to say, since in this life the body of man is heavy, slow, sluggish, and lazy, the same in the resurrection is to receive a peculiar δύναμιν or power and agility, so that it may be moved most swiftly. Conf. *Ausführl. Erklärung* l. c. p. 176. To this same virtue of the bodies of the blessed is also referred that which is said in 1 Thess. 4:17, that the faithful will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air. But if you bid the mode of moving to be explained, I think I shall have spoken rightly with Augustine, L. XXII. *de Civ. D.* cap. XXX: “What the movement of such bodies will be, I dare not rashly define, because I am unable to conceive it.” Gerhardus: “We say that the bodies of the blessed will be agile, that is, instructed with a certain supernatural faculty or quality for exercising movement expeditiously, because glorified bodies will be able to be moved most swiftly by this endowment, with movement not only progressive, but also that which [corresponds] to flight.”

it will be similar; nay, the necessity of moving oneself slowly and locally will be entirely absent from the bodies of the blessed. . . Christ walked upon the waters, Matt. 14:25; after the resurrection, He was at one time around the sepulcher, at another in Jerusalem in the midst of the disciples, at another He joined Himself to those going to Emmaus; nor did He approach slowly, but suddenly, and thus in a moment He was in one place and another. If Christ had ascended to the empyrean heaven by local and successive motion, He could not have penetrated its height in the space of several years. But now, the glorified bodies will be conformed to the body of Christ. . . If the blessed could not be in a moment wherever they wished, much would be lacking to their desire and consequently also to their happiness. For if they had to be moved successively and locally, those established in one part of heaven would scarcely arrive in several years at the companions of their blessedness established in another part of heaven.” (Ibid., § 96.)

The same: “It is asked whether the blessed can move themselves in an instant, without passing through the medium? Thomas denies this in the *Additamenta*, q. 84, art. 3, since a glorified body is moved in time, albeit imperceptible due to its brevity. But we are supported by the modesty of Augustine, Book 22 of *The City of God*, ch. 30, writing thus: ‘What the motions of such bodies will be, I dare not rashly define, as I am unable to conceive it. Time will be no more there, Rev. 10:6; therefore, they will also be able to move themselves in an instant.’” (Ibid., § 153.)

The same: “It is certain that if any weight were to remain in the glorified body, no impediment would be offered to its motive power that would prevent it from being moved in a moment wherever it wishes; for it will be a spiritual body, that is, most perfectly obedient to the spirit.” (Ibid., § 153.)

Luther: “We know that, as weak as it (the body) is now, without any strength or capacity when it lies in the grave, so strong will it become when the time comes, so that with one finger it will be able to carry this church, with one toe move a tower, and play with a great mountain as children do with a ball, and in a twinkling jump up to the clouds or travel over a hundred miles. For then it shall be called pure strength (as it is now pure weakness and impotence), so that no thing will be impossible for it if it only sets its mind to it; that it might alone strike the whole world and become so light and agile that it will hover in an instant both here on earth and up in heaven.” (Ibid., p. 1356 sq.) §

15. Therefore, the bodies of the blessed will also be impassible, so that they are not subject to any corruptive passion, whether proceeding from internal or external causes, and thus they will be immortal. And perhaps indeed by that same supernatural quality through which they are rendered spiritual. See here § 14. For example, that they will be able to be harmed neither by heat nor by cold, and thus will have no need of clothing with which to be protected against the injuries of the air; that they will not be afflicted by hunger and thirst, and thus will not be in need of food or drink; that they will be subject to no intemperance of the body, nor to any internal and adverse commotion of the soul. Compare Rev. 7:16. To the same is usually referred that Ισαγγελότης of the blessed, of which Matt. 22:30 speaks.

Latin:

placet Deo etiam alia dona c addere, quibus corpora beatorum quam maxime perficiantur et beentur. Nempe primus conceptus beatitudinis, quo prior alius non datur (utpote, qui summi boni consecutionem et possessionem importat, quique per se expetendus est, ac naturae intelligenti primario competit), in ipsa visione Dei cum amore perfecto conjuncta consistit, inter quae tarnen et ipsa aliquis ordo est, ut amor visionem praesupponat, licet tempore non differant. V. g. cognitio aliorum objectorum, qua intellectus perficitur; de qua vide § 6. et notas. Quemadmodum alias beatitudo dicitur status omnium bonorum aggregatione perfectus; qualis quando homini dandus est, omnes animae facultates ipsumque corpus perfici debet, ut sit beatitudo non animae tantum, sed totius hominis.

Gerhardus: ״Corpus fuit organum bonorum operum in hac vita, 2 Cor. 5, 10., aequum igitur est, ut in communicationem praemii et consortium gloriae assumatur. Corpus per passiones et crucem conforme factum imagini Christi crucifixi; Gal. 6, 17.: ,Porto stigmata Christi in corpore‘; aequum igitur est,1 utconforme flat imagini Christi gloriflcati. Inter corpus et animam est arctissima unio et intima conjunctio etiam in hac vita, ut tristitia, moeror et alii affectus animae ipsum corpus afficiant; utique ergo etiam in vita altera propter arctissimam et indissolubilem animae et corporis unionem gloria ac laetitia animae in corpus beatorum redundabit.“ (Loc. de vita aet. § 80.) §

14. Consistet autem beatitudo corporum beatorum inprimis in eo, quod corpora futura sunt spiritualia,a id est, animae, quae spiritus est, et quidem partim, ut formae informanti,b partim ut principio moventi,c perfectissimo modo subjecta. Vid. 1. ad Cor. 15, 44. Non autem intelligi debet mutatio corporis in spiritum, qui per essentiam immaterialis est.

Lutherus: ״Er heisst nicht darum ein geistlicher Leib, dass er nicht leiblich leben, noch Fleisch und Blut haben sollte; sonst könnte er nicht ein wahrhaftiger Leib heissen. Nun aber heisst er ein geistlicher Leib, also, dass er sein Leben soll haben, und doch nicht mehr ein essender, schlafender, dauender Leib sein wird, sondern geistlich von Gott gespeiset und erhalten werden und das Leben gar an ihm haben. Darnach aber, wenn er also geistlich in Gott lebt, wird er auch herausgehen in Himmel und Erden, mit Sonn und Mond und allen andern Creaturen spielen, und auch seine Freude und Lust daran haben, und davon so satt und selig sein, dass er nimmermehr an ein Essen noch Trinken denken wird, und also gar ein geistlich Wesen oder Leben sein und heissen des ganzen Menschen, welches aus dem Geist entspringen und von oder durch Gott ohne Mittel gehen wird; dass wir nicht allein nach der Seele von ihm erleuchtet werden und ihn erkennen, sondern wird auch durch den ganzen Leib gehen, dass er so klar und leicht wird PART. I. CAP. VI.

sein, wie die Luft, so scharf sehen und hören, so weit die Welt ist, dass wir keines andern nothdürftig sein werden, dass wir uns erhalten und leben, und doch wahrhaftigen Leib haben. Gleichwie auch jetzt die Sterne am Himmel also gemacht sind, dass sie gar keiner Nothdurft bedürfen zu ihrem Wesen, und doch auch leibliche Creaturen sind; wiewohl sie nicht solchen irdischen, sondern himmlischen Leib haben.“ (Ausl, des 15. Cap. der 1. Ep. St. Pauli an die Cor. 1534. VIII, 1539.) Quae est corporum subtilitas, cujus vi corpora ita substabunt animahus suis sine imperfectione, ac si ipsa essent spiritus; et sic etiam poterunt penetrare alia corpora solida. Vide Epist. ad Phil. 3, 21. coilatum cum Joh. 20, 19. et 26. itemque Luc. 24, 37. 39. Nempe probatio huc redit: Si Christus corpore suo glorificato per fores, revera tunc clausas, penetravit ac substantialiter praesens videri potuit, nostra autem corpora, in statu vitae alterius, conformia futura sunt corpori Christi glorioso, sequitur, corpora nostra itidem sic fore subtilia, ut citra sui mutationem novam aut laesionem sui vel corporis penetrandi corpus aliud solidum penetrare possint. Prius probatur partim ex 11. cc. Johannis et Lucae, partim ex cap. 8. ad Phil. E. verum etiam est posterius. Conf. Ausführl. Erklärung L. IV. Q. XXI. p. 175.176. Gerhardus: ,,Dicimus, corpora beatorum fore subtilia ac penetrabilia. . . Corpus subtile est, quod penetrat et a quo ablata est repugnantia existendi eodem loco cum alio corpore. . . Beati erunt Ισάγγελοι. Jam vero angeli sunt essentiae subtilissimae, penetrandi facultate praeditae. Act. 12, 12. angelus, Petrum ex carcere educens, nullis potuit valvis aut claustris cohiberi, quo minus Petro in carcere astaret. Ergo etiam beatorum corpora erunt subtilia. . . Christus in resurrectione clausum sepulchrum penetravit, post resurrectionem clausis foribus ad discipulos ingressus 'est, in ascensione penetravit coelos, ut in Harm, de resurr. multis fuit demonstratum. Ergo etiam corpora beatorum hac proprietate erunt praedita.“ (L. c. § 98.) Quenstedtius: ״Erunt corpora beatorum illocalia i. e. loco physico corporeo non circumscripta. Non erunt ubique, sed in certo πον, definite, non circumscriptive; erunt enim a circumscriptione et ambitu externi loci, v. g. ab aSre aut alio elemento ambiente, immunia; elementa enim illa abolebuntur.“ (L. c. f. 800.) Et haec est corporum agilitas, cujus vi facillime ac celerrimep oterunt moveri corpora, quocunque animae eorum ea movere voluerint. Vid. 1. ad Cor. 15, 43., ubi dicitur, corpora piorum, quaeseminantur in infirmitate, resurrectura esse in potentia (έν δυνάμει), quodvidelicet, cum in hac vita corpus hominis grave, tardum, lentum etpigrum sit, idem in resurrectione peculiarem δϋναμιν seu potentiam etagilitatem sit accepturum, ut celerrime moveri possit. Conf. Ausführl.Erklärung 1. c. p. 176. Ad eandem quoque corporum beatorum vir-tutem refertur, quod 1. ad Thess. 4, 77. dicitur, fideles raptum iri inoccursum Domino in aëra. Sed si modum movendi explicari jubeas,recte opinor dixero cum Augustino L. XXII. de Civ. D. cap. XXX.:Qui motus talium corporum sint futuri, temere definire non audeo, quod ex-cogitare non valeo. Gerhardus: ״Dicimus, corpora beatorum fore agilia, id est, instructa facultate seu qualitate quadam supernaturali ad motum expedite exercendum, quia gloriflcata corpora per hanc dotem velocissime moveri poterunt, motu non solum progressivo, sed etiam eo, qui volatui

similis erit; quinimo necessitas tarde ac localiter sese movendi a beatorum corporibus prorsus aberit. . . Christus ambulabat super aquas, Matth. 14, 25., post resurrectionem modo erat circa sepulchrum, modo Hierosolymis in medio discipulorum, modo associabat se euntibus Emaunta; nec tarde aggrediebatur, sed subito, adeoque in momento in aliis atque aliis erat locis. Si motu locali ac successivo Christus in coelum usque empyraeum ascendisset, aliquot annorum spatio altitudinem ejus penetrare non potuisset. Jam vero corpora gloriflcata erunt corpori Christi conformia. . . Si beati non possent esse in momento, ubicunque vellent, plurimum ipsorum desiderio ac proinde etiam felicitati decederet. Si enim successive ac localiter moveri deberent, qui in una coeli parte constituti, vix per aliquot annos ad consortes suae beatitudinis in altera coeli parte constitutos pervenirent.“ (L. c. § 96.)

Idem: Quaeritur, an beati possint se movere in instanti, medio non pertransito? Negat Thomas in addit, q. 84. art. 3., cum corpus glorificatum moveatur in tempore, quamvis imperceptibili propter brevitatem. Sed probatur nobis modestia Augustini, 1. 22. de civ. Dei cap. 30. sic scribentis: ,Qui motus talium corporum sint futuri, temere definire non audeo, quod excogitare non valeo. Tempus ibi non erit amplius, Apoc. 10, 6., ergo etiam poterunt in instanti sese movere.‘“ (L. c. § 153.)

Idem: ,,Certum est, si quid ponderis in corpore glorificato mansurum, eo potentiae motrici nullum oblatum iri impedimentum, quo minus in momento illud moveri possit, quocunque velit; erit enim corpus spirituale, id est, spiritui perfectissime oboediens.“ (L. c. § 153.)

Lutherus; ,,Wir wissen, so schwach er (der Leib) jetzt ist, ohne alle Kraft und Vermögen, wenn er im Grabe liegt, so stark wird er hernach werden, wenn die Zeit kommt, dass er mit einem Finger wird diese Kirche tragen, mit einer Zehe einen Thurm versetzen können, und mit einem grossen Berg spielen, wie die Kinder mit einem Balle, und in einem Nu bis an die Wolken springen oder über hundert Meilen fahren. Denn alsdenn solls eitel Kraft heissen (wie jetzt eitel Schwachheit und Unkraft), dass ihm kein Ding unmöglich sein wird, wenn ers nur in Sinn nimmt; dass er allein möchte die ganze Welt schlagen und so leicht und behend werden, dass er des Augenblicks beide, hienieden auf Erden und droben im Himmel, schweben wird.“ (L. c. p. 1356. sq.) §

15. Itaque etiam a impassibilia erunt corpora beatorum, ut nulli passioni corruptivae, seu ab internis, seu ab externis causis prodeunti, sint obnoxia,b adeoque sint immortalia. c Ac fortasse quidem per eandem illam qualitatem supernaturalem, per quam spiritualia reddentur. Vid. h. 1. § 14. V. g. quod neque aestu neque frigore laedi poterunt, adeoque nee vestibus, quibus adversus injurias aeris muniantur, opus habebunt; quod fame et siti non affligentur, neque adeo cibo aut potu indigebunt; quod nulli intemperiei corporis, neque internae et adversae commotioni animorum erunt obnoxia. Confer Apoe. 7, 16. Eodemque referri solet illa Ισαγγελότης beatorum, de qua Matth. 21, 30.13 Baieri Corap. ed. Walther. II. PART. I. CAP. VI.


### On Eternal Blessedness: Gerhard: "The bodies of the blessed will be impassible in a twofold respect

Gerhard: "The bodies of the blessed will be impassible in a twofold respect: 1. In respect to internal passions, because the fuel of concupiscence, which produces vicious passions, will no longer dwell in those bodies; there will be no stain of sin in them; no disordered πάθη will be present in them, but they will be in all ways pure, holy, and uncontaminated; 2. In respect to external passions, because there will be nothing at all that could inflict passion and pain upon them; there will be a certain divine quality in them that defends them from every corruptive alteration; they will not be harmed by heat or cold; no danger will threaten them from a wild beast; nor will they be able to be penetrated by fire or sword." (L. c. § 89.) Thus, ἀφθαρσία and ἀθανασία, incorruptibility and immortality, are expressly attributed to the bodies of the blessed, 1 Cor. 15:42, 50, 52, 53, 54. It is evident how easily this is something far different from that which the protoplasts had in the state of integrity. For the bodies of the blessed will not only be able not to die, but they will not be able to die. For although God could dissolve them, He will nevertheless never will to do so. Outside of God, nothing will be able to corrupt or destroy them. § 16. Nevertheless, the blessed will be able to present their bodies to be touched and seen when they themselves wish. Just as Christ presented His glorious body to the disciples to be seen and touched, see John 20:20 and 27; Luke 24: 39. Cf. Phil. 3:21. For they will also be able to withdraw themselves from the senses of others when they wish, which Christ also did, showing Himself not to all the people, but to preordained witnesses, Acts 10:41; and the saints, rising with Christ and appearing to many (not indiscriminately to just anyone), Matthew 27:53. Quenstedtius: "It is to be noted that the bodies of the blessed are said to be invisible in relation to non-glorified eyes, at least regarding the possibility of not appearing to the eyes of others. For glorified bodies can also be seen by eyes not yet glorified, if a divine dispensation intervenes. Just as the saints who rose with Christ appeared alive not to all, but to those whose eyes were divinely opened. Now, those eyes are said to be opened to which an object, which by its own nature and heavenly strength is invisible, is rendered visible κατ’ οἰκονομίαν (by way of economy). And thus this power of appearing and not appearing depends upon the economy of the divine will, even if that economy is exercised through the glorified soul as the proximate cause. Hence, concerning the saints who rose with Christ, it is said that ἐνεφανίσθησαν, they appeared, Matthew 27:53, i.e., they made themselves visible (for the Greek word, according to Pasor in his Lexicon, has a Hithpaelic, i.e., reciprocal, meaning), but to whom? To many, therefore not to all to whom they were present." (L. c. P. I. c. 14. s. 1. th. 20. f. 800.) Gerhard: "We say that the bodies of the blessed will be impalpable, that is, that they are not necessarily touched by those whose sense of touch is not yet glorified; for here, too, one must distinguish between power and act, and likewise between a glorified and a non-glorified toucher... Christ, after the resurrection, offered Himself to His disciples to be touched and handled not by necessity of nature, but by free will, not by any essential disposition of the glorified body, but by divine dispensation, οὐ νόμῳ φύσεως, ἀλλ’ οἰκονομίας τρόπῳ (not by the law of nature, but by way of economy) (Damasc. lib. 4. orth."

(faith, ch. 1), namely, to prove the truth of the resurrection; just as for the same purpose He ate and drank with the disciples, Acts 10:41, not out of the necessity of nature, but out of a free οικονομία by a certain συγκατάβασις (Theoph. on Luke ch. 24, Bede on John ch. 20), and showed them the scars of His wounds in His glorified body; meanwhile, He could be present with His true body, although He was neither seen nor touched; as appears from the fact that, while sitting with the disciples at Emmaus, He suddenly becomes άφαντος.” (L. c. § 102.) § 17.

To the bodies of the blessed there will also be added clarity, or a vast splendor. That they may shine like the sun, Matt. 13:43. Compare 1 Cor. 15:41 sqq., Dan. 12:3. Which, while it will be too sublime for eyes not glorified, will nevertheless greatly delight those that are glorified. Quenstedtius: “Clarity, not transparency, such as that of glass, but a refulgence, such as that of the sun and moon, such as was that of the face of Moses when he returned from the mountain, and likewise of the face of Christ, Moses, and Elijah on Mount Tabor, Matt. 17:2. Dan. 12:3 says: ‘But they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament.’ Matt. 13:43: ‘Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of my Father.’” (L. c. p. 801.)

And thus, also, an elegant proportion and beauty of the bodies of the blessed is inferred, as regards their individual parts. Gerhardus: “The greatest deformity before God is sin, which is the stain and blemish of the soul; this deformity of the soul being removed, the body cannot but be most beautiful. Deformity of the body arises either from the mutilation of some member, as in the one-eyed, the maimed, etc., or from a disproportion of quantity, from a lack of due quantity, or from the addition of something incongruous, when some member is larger or smaller than it should be, or from a distemper of color, etc. But all these and similar causes of deformity will be absent from the blessed. Diseases and old age ravage beauty. But in eternal life, neither diseases nor old age will have a place.” (L. c. § 94.) § 18. And because the soul, insofar as it is sensitive, uses certain parts of the body as organs, for this reason also the blessedness of the pious will be increased, so that the eyes may be able to delight themselves by beholding the incarnate Son of God, their Savior, and the blessed men, their friends, and perhaps also the ears by more elegant hymns.

Thus Job hoped that he would see his Redeemer with his own eyes, ch. 19:25, 26. But that the blessed will see the divine essence itself with the clarified eyes of their bodies, we do not dare to assert. For not only does God, who is an infinite spirit, not have a place among the proper objects of sight, as a bodily power, regarding His essence, attributes, and persons. PART I. CHAP. VI.

their own; but even if it could be shown that sight, insofar as it is viewed as a creature of God, could be assumed through the potentia obedientialis as an instrument for producing the vision of God, nevertheless, God has never promised in the Scriptures that this will truly come to pass. Indeed, we saw above in the note to § 2 that the passages in Matthew 5, 1 Corinthians 13, 1

John 3, and Hebrews 12 speak of intellectual vision. Balduinus, in his Commentary on 1 Corinthians 13, P. III, Q. IV, p. 490, maintains that the essence of God is invisible to the eyes of the body, even if they are glorified. And, lest you think this escaped him, he repeats and demonstrates it at greater length in his Commentary on Chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Colossians, P. II, Q. II, pp. 1054–1055, stating that there is absolutely no proportion between the essence or face of God and the bodily eye. He also appeals to the consensus of the Fathers: Ambrose, Jerome, Nazianzen, Augustine, and others. Again, in his Commentary on 1

Timothy 6, P. II, Q. III, pp. 1383–1384, where he says that the epithet of God by which He is called invisible is perpetual, and that it will not cease even in the life to come, and having repeated the four arguments from the previous place in the Commentary on Chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Colossians, he bids the reader see more in Chrysostom, Tertullian, Nazianzen, Hilary, Basil, and Irenaeus, all of whom demonstrate at length that the nature of God cannot be reached by the eyes of the human body, neither in this life nor in the future life. Whatever may be the case regarding these matters, it is certain that the opinion which maintains that the beatific vision will be only intellectual is probable, even if the opposite is not therefore immediately rejected as false; which the blessed Gerhard also acknowledged in Vol. VIII, LL. § 144, p.

997. Cf. *Ausführliche Erklärung* [Detailed Explanation], L. IV, Q. XX and XXII, p. 172 sqq. And the blessed Cundisius, Notes on Comp. Hutt., pp. 1385–1386.

Quenstedtius: "Will the blessed see the Deity itself or the divine essence with glorified bodily eyes in eternal life? — Resp.

I. Some of the Fathers deny it: Irenaeus, l. 4, c. 37; Origen, c. Celsum, l. 7; Athanasius, Orat. c. Idola; Theophylact on 1

Cor. 13; Ambrose, l. 1 in Luc. c. 1; especially Augustine, ep. 112 to Paulina.

2. Most Scholastics, all the Papists, and the Calvinists. Thomas, p. 1, q. 12, a. 3, says: 'It implies a contradiction that God should be seen by a bodily eye. Therefore, it cannot happen even by absolute power.' Becanus, p. 1, Theol. Schol. c. 9, q. 6, says: 'It is the common opinion that it is impossible for God to be seen clearly and intuitively by the eyes of the body.' Among the Calvinists, P. Martyr, Class. 1, Loc. Com. c. 4, § 2, says: 'They err who think that the essence of God is seen by the eyes of the blessed.' To these is added D. Calixtus the elder, Concord. Evang. l. 2, c. 1. . .

II. Some of our own embrace the affirmative, such as Chytraeus, l. de vita et morte, p. 157; Schilterus, disp. de vita aeterna, th. 65;

D. Cramerus, tr. de sublimi corporis glorificati mysterio, c. 16, p. 187. . . III. Augustine, l. 22 de Civ. Dei c. 29; the blessed Gerhard, Loco de vita aeterna § 143 and 144; and the blessed Dorscheus, Considerat. Titulor. Dei ex 1

Tim. 6, § 32 in Pentadec, hold a middle path and determine nothing. They maintain, I say, that it should not be rashly denied that the divine essence will be seen by bodily eyes, since God can elevate the eyes of the blessed beyond their nature so that they may see the Deity itself, because the infinite power of God cannot be limited by physical reasons taken from the common and ordinary course of nature; yet, that it should not be precisely defined, since Scripture does not define the mode of vision (whether it will be mental or truly bodily), although it asserts that God is to be beheld by the blessed." (L. c. s. 2, q. 2, f. 812 sq.) See here § 6 and the note there. For that mutual recognition of the blessed in the state of restored bodies seems to extend also to the sight of these. Compare the authors cited in the same place.

### On Eternal Blessedness: I. Will the blessed also glorify God with an external voice

I. Will the blessed also glorify God with an external voice? ... Augustine, *De civ. Dei*, bk. 22, ch. 30, asserts that all the members and viscera of the incorruptible body will advance in the praises of God; but who, in this infirmity of the flesh, can attain to what the manner of this praise and proclamation will be, either by thinking or by speaking? Scripture asserts that God is to be glorified by the blessed not only with vocal praise (Rev. 7:12), but also with golden harps (Rev. 5:8; 14:2; 15:2). But anyone can see that this latter, spoken in the manner of this age, must be taken metaphorically; whence they are called κιθάραι τοῦ θεοῦ, the harps of God or divine harps.

II. In what language will the blessed glorify God and converse with one another? It is probably believed that there will be one language for all the blessed: 1. because we shall all be one people, one city in the heavenly fatherland; 2. the diversity of languages was introduced into the world in place of a punishment, but every punishment will be absent from the triumphant church; 3. the triumphant church will not be in a worse position than the militant church was, yet the latter once used one common language.

III. But what will that language of the blessed be? Galatinus, *De arcanis*, bk. 12, ch. 4, determines that the blessed will use the Hebrew language in the praises of God and in mutual conversations. ... Some, on the contrary, determine that all the languages which we use in this life will cease, since the Apostle speaks generally in 1 Cor. 13:8, and that some other sensible language, far nobler than this of ours and heavenly, will be infused into the blessed, which will befit the glorious mouth and body, by which they may also vocally praise God. Some think that the blessed will speak in whatever language they please, because all will be known to all, and therefore they will be able to use whichever they wish, at will. But these things are more rightly reserved for future blessed experience than scrupulously disputed." (L. c. § 146.) Indeed, it is hardly permitted in this life to define more about these and other perfections and operations of the senses that will have a place in the state of eternal life. § 19. Next to these accidental gifts of blessedness, especially the brightness of the bodies, a certain inequality of the blessed will be perceived, according as one has produced more specimens of Christian virtues than another in this life. See 1 Cor. 15:41; Dan. 12:3. Regarding the inequality of other gifts, although it is not equally easy to determine anything, one may nevertheless look at the passages in Matt. 19:28 and Luke 22:30, where a certain peculiar honor and glory is promised to the apostles on the day of judgment, under the words of this age, concerning a table furnished with all delicacies and sitting as it were on thrones, etc. Yet in such a way that those who will possess less accidental glory will not therefore be less satisfied, nor will they be envious toward others who are more glorified, but each will be content with his own lot, the least and the greatest. Blessed Gerhard also says wisely in *L. de Inferno* § 52, p. m. 616: "Whatever happens to one of the elect will affect the rest with as much joy as if it had been given to them themselves. Whence there will be no envy there of disparate brightness, where the unity of charity will reign in all." Gerhard: "It is certain that the happiness and glory of all the blessed will be one objectively, because the object of blessedness is God, who is common to all the blessed; one subjectively, because all the powers of the soul and... PART I. CHAP. VI.

all members of the body will be adorned in all the blessed with heavenly glory; one in respect of continuous and eternal duration, because the happiness of all the blessed will be continuous, never to be interrupted, and everlasting, never to be ended; one in respect of security, because all the blessed will be equally certain that no danger of losing this happiness and glory threatens them; one in respect of satiety, because all the blessed will be most fully and perfectly satisfied with that glory which will fall to each one from the fountain of divine kindness; one in respect of immunity from all adversities, because all the blessed will be liberated from all evils whatsoever; one in respect of the love and communion flourishing among all, because on account of the most sincere charity, the joy of any blessed one will be common to all the blessed.

It is also certain that there will be a certain inequality of the blessed and a diversity of glory. . . . However, it may be doubted whether that diversity is to be established only in the accidental glory of the soul or body, or indeed also in the essential, so that in some blessed ones there will be a greater light of glory, in others less, on account of which one blessed person sees the divine essence more perfectly and clearly than another, loves God more ardently, and enjoys Him more sweetly—a thing which is indeed taught by the Scholastics with great consensus (with the sole exception of Durandus, who in 4 Sentent. distinct. 49 argues: "All the blessed see the divine essence equally, and all are equal in the essential reward"); but our theologians more correctly establish that the difference is to be set only in the accidental rewards: " For all the saints one salvation, but unequal glory." (L. c. § 120.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of certain Calvinists, such as Peter Martyr in Loc. Com. class 3, c. 17, § 8; who was the first in the previous century to depart from the common consensus of the fathers and denied that there would be degrees of rewards and glory in eternal life; but timidly and hesitantly. ... 2. Of certain Neo-Photinians, who establish that there will be no degrees of rewards and punishments after this life, such as Smalcius... 3. Of the Jovinianists, who formerly said that all sinners would be equal in punishments just as they were in faults, following the Stoics, who themselves also made all sins equal." (L. c. q. 3, f. 814.)

Thus we read in Matt. 10:41 and 42; Luke 19:17 and 19. But these things must not be understood concerning the merit of works. For it is one thing for God, out of His liberality or unmerited favor, to render unequal rewards to those working unequally; it is another thing for God to render to those meriting unequally, by the force of meritorious works, a reward due to each and different or unequal to different people. §

20. And just as those things which we have said thus far concerning eternal beatitude are rightly held according to the Scriptures, so no one in this life has found a full and perfect declaration of it. For it has not yet appeared what we shall be, 1 John 3:2. And Isa. 64:4, and thence 1 Cor. 2:9, it is said that the eye has not seen, and the ear has not heard, and it has not ascended into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for those who love Him. Peter also, in 1 Ep. 1:8, promises to the faithful that they shall exult with χαρα άνεχλαλήτω, with ineffable joy.

ON ETERNAL BLESSEDNESS. ANTITHESIS.

Gerhardus: "Antithesis: 1. Recent Jews place the joys of eternal life in bodily pleasures, food, drink, venery, etc. ...

2. Mahomet, in the Alcoran and the Zuna—books of authentic and undoubted faith among his followers—promises the blessed in paradise most splendid palaces, royal banquets, dances, and the embraces of virgins, and imagines such a life for the blessed after the resurrection, in which they shall enjoy the sweetest waters, healthful drink, apples of many kinds, various fruits, most decent and clean women, golden rings, silken garments, curtained beds, etc. ...

3. The Chiliasts, Cerinthians, Nepotians, etc., taught that the kingdom of Christ would endure for a thousand years on this earth in bodily pleasures. ...

4. Origen, in Homily II on Numbers, thinks that 'in the future life some men will not see God, but only angels, and that God will subject some men to other angels.' The same author, in Book I, Chapter 9 of περὶ ἀρχῶν, fabricates 'a certain perpetual cycle of happiness and misery.' ...

5. Methodius, in his sermon on the resurrection, seems to hold that the blessed after the resurrection will not be in the heavens, but in paradise. 'For it is necessary,' he says, 'that each created thing remain in the proper figure of its own habit, so that all things may be filled for all: the heavens for the angels, the thrones for the powers, the lights for the ministers, the more divine places and pure lights for the Seraphim themselves, who assist the great senate containing all things, and the world for men.'

6. The Pepuzians placed eternal life and the heavenly Jerusalem in this life. For they said that Pepuza, a certain place in upper Phrygia, was the heavenly city and the Jerusalem of which the prophets prophesied, of which Hebrews 12:23 and Revelation 21:2 speak, and to which we all must aspire. Epiphanius, Heresies 49; Augustine, On Heresies, Chapter 27.

7. The Aeternales, as reported by Augustine in On Heresies, Chapter 67, from Philastrius, taught that this world, even after the resurrection of the dead, would remain in the same state in which it now is, and would not be changed so as to be a new heaven and a new earth, as the Holy Scripture promises. ...

10. The Armenians taught that men who are moderately evil will not go into the heavenly paradise after the judgment, but will remain on earth, and that the souls of the good are to be led to the earth and will fly like birds upon the trees. ...

11. The Papists ... invent certain 'aureoles' or 'laureoles,' some of which they decree are to be imposed upon virgins, others upon martyrs, and others upon doctors. ...

If you ask, what then is that beauty of the body? Scotus answers in 4 Sentences, dist. 49, q. 5, art. 2, that the aureoles are crowns, such that a red crown is seen on the head of a martyr, a white one on the head of a virgin, and a green one on the head of a doctor; he adds that the martyrs will perhaps also carry palms in their hands, the virgins white lilies, and the doctors incorruptible green branches. ...

They foster earthly, carnal, and childish thoughts concerning the heavenly joys, exercises, and dwellings of the blessed. Cassanaeus, Part 3, Preface to *Catalogus Gloriae Mundi*, Consideration I: there are twelve principal seats in paradise, namely, the seat of the Trinity and Deity itself, the seat of the Son with respect to his humanity, the seat of the blessed Virgin Mary, and nine high seats of the nine orders.

From Bernardinus, Volume 8 of the works of D. Brentius, page 890, the following discourse is brought forth concerning the exercises and dances of the blessed in heaven: 'What will the blessed do in the empyrean heaven? What kind of exercise will they have? Will there be dances and leaping there?' One indeed answers that in glory there will be no such gesticulations; but Bernardinus thinks otherwise. 'Let not the words of that doctor move you,' he says. 'For it is more likely that dances and leaping take place there. For all things that are sufficient and required for a dance are found there.' ...

Lest anyone think that those old wives' fables, concocted by idle monks, are repudiated by more recent Papists, we therefore command that you weigh what Barradius writes in Book 10, Commentary on the Harmony of the Gospels, Chapter 3. ...

Compare those things which they dispute concerning the limbo of infants, which is locally distinct from the kingdom of heaven and hell, and what Bellarmine has in Book 2, On Purgatory, Chapter 7, concerning 'a certain most flowery, most bright, fragrant, and pleasant meadow, in which souls dwell who suffer nothing, but yet remain there, because they do not...' PART I. CHAPTER VI.

while they are fit for the divine vision,’ etc., and it will appear that the Elysian fields of the poets are being brought back into the church by the Papists by way of postliminy.

12. Of the Calvinists. . . almost all of them think earthly things regarding the joys, exercises, and dwellings of the blessed. For they define heaven as a certain corporeal place, established above all visible heavens, distinguished by most ample mansions, in which one may locally sit and walk. . . They think too thinly and meagerly of the endowments of the glorified body: 1. They expressly deny its invisibility. . . 2. They no less oppose its illocality. . . 3. They likewise explain the endowment of agility and subtlety less correctly; for they deny that Christ rose from the closed sepulcher; they deny that He entered to the disciples with the doors closed, etc.

Zwingli, Part I, response to the Lutheran Confession, p. 405, denies that ‘the glorified body of Christ passed through the sealed stone of the monument, and asserts that the sepulchral stone was rolled away by the work of an angel, just as a stout praetor dressed in red breeches could exit in the same way that Christ exited the monument.’ (L. c. §§ 156—164.)

The same: “The Papists attribute to blessed Luther and the teachers of our churches that they too have strayed from the path of truth in this part of heavenly doctrine, by seeking the happiness of eternal life in corporeal delights. They prove this from the fact that Luther, in the Table Talk held on fol. 454 and 455, speaks thus: ‘God will create a new earth and a new heaven, and indeed He will create new little animals and little dogs, whose skin will be golden and whose hair will be of precious stones,’ etc. . . Note: Why do they not also add the letter which Luther wrote to his little son about the joys of paradise? The man of God imitates the style of Scripture and speaks of the state of the future age, which has not ascended into the heart of man, through a certain συγκατάβασιν [condescension] in the words of this age, which we heard from Otto of Freising, § 156, is customary for teachers of the church.” (L. c. § 165.) §

21. The causes of this blessedness are: The principal efficient cause, indeed, is the Triune God; the internal impulsive cause is the goodness of God; the principal external cause is the merit of Christ; the less principal (impulsive) cause is faith in Christ. According to those things which we said in the Prolegomena, Chap. I, § 21 ff., Vol. I, p. 40 ff. More things concerning each have been distinctly handed down in their own place and will be handed down. §

22. The subject [of this blessedness] is human beings who are finally believing and who have departed from this life, all and only.

For this was not the place to treat of the blessedness of the angels, but it has been sufficiently treated above in its own place. For it is necessary that that which is the impulsive cause of blessedness should pertain to them. For in this life no mortal actually attains to the beatific vision, and thus neither to those things which follow it. See 1 John 3:1; 1 Cor. 13:9, 10, 11, 12; Phil. 3:12, 13. Cf. our Disputation on the foretaste of eternal life.

### On Eternal Blessedness: Of Eternal Blessedness Antithesis

OF ETERNAL BLESSEDNESS.

ANTITHESIS.

Gerhardus: “Antithesis:

1. Origen, in Homily 10 on Leviticus, argues that those who have indeed believed, but have applied no amendment of life, are indeed saved, but not without a mark of infamy. The same man opined that the damned would eventually be liberated and rendered participants in heavenly glory.

2. Certain Papists attribute salvation to Gentiles destitute of true faith in Christ.

3

The same dogma pleased certain Calvinists. Zwingli, in *Expos. fid.* p. 159, places Numa, Aristides, Socrates, etc., among the blessed in heaven, the patronage of which was undertaken by Rudolph Gualter, his own son-in-law, in an *Apology* published in the year 1545

Bullinger adorned this offspring of Zwingli with a preface, in which he calls it a swan song. That horrendous utterance of Zwingli (as Bucer rightly calls it in a letter addressed to him) the Embdens attempt to defend and partly excuse in their *Commonitorium* on the book of Dr. Hunnius, p. 416

Sohnius in *Exeg. Aug. Conf.* vol. 2, p. 828

Tossanus in a writing against Marbach; Pareus in *Iren.* p. 245

Pelargus in his corrected *Comp. Theol.* p. 289; but with very frivolous sophistries. Hither must also be referred the other error of the Calvinists, by which they deny faith altogether to even baptized infants, from which it follows that either all infants without exception are damned, or that certain men are saved without faith in Christ; both of which are diametrically opposed to the Scriptures. Calvin, *Instit.* lib. 4, cap. 16, § 20: ‘Little ones are baptized into future faith.’ Sibrandus Lubertus, in his commentary on the 99 errors of Vorstius, p. 780, writes: ‘God has decreed to save some infants who, as long as they wander in this world, have not believed, do not believe, and are not going to believe.’ Piscator, on Matthew ch. 19, observation 11: ‘The kingdom of heaven can belong to infants, even if they do not yet believe, provided they are elect.’ Likewise: ‘Faith is nowhere required in Scripture, except from adults.’ 4

Franciscus Puccius Filidinus published a writing in the year 1592, *On the Efficacy of Christ the Savior in all and individual men, insofar as they are men*, in which, among other monstrous opinions, he promises heaven even to heathens outside the Church.

5. That the Photinians embrace this hypothesis—that anyone can be saved in his own religion, whatever he may have embraced, whether he be a Jew, or a Turk, or an Anabaptist, or an Arian, or a Christian—is shown by Georgius Zarnovecius the Pole.” (L. c. § 168.) Hofmannus: “The Apostle speaks (Rom. 2:14) thus of the case that heathens, without possessing a law, a revelation of the demanding will of God, do that which the will of God revealed in Israel demands, and says of such doing of theirs that it happens φύσει [by nature].... The Apostle considers it so very possible that one, by virtue of this law, might be in a position, albeit only in individual instances, to act according to the divine demand, that he holds out the prospect that there might perhaps be, on the day of judgment, a self-justification before God, arising from the thoughts called forth by the testimony of the conscience, which can be graciously accepted by Him who exercises His judgment through Jesus Christ, the Mediator of grace.” (*Schriftbeweis* I, 494, 495 sq.) The same: “Just as the Apostle in Rom. 7:14–25 is not intended to deny all doing of good by the Old Testament believers, so he says in the present passage even of individual cases of a doing of good by the heathens; without thereby contradicting what our ecclesiastical confession teaches concerning man, as he is in himself before God and apart from all effects of grace, that he is incapable of any good and inclined to all evil. He knows, in fact, of an effect of grace, not merely of the God who has sent Christ, but also of the God who will send Christ, and indeed he knows of it not merely within the Old Testament community of salvation, but also outside of it.... The Spirit of God, who dwells in them to make them alive,” PART 1. CAP. VI.

does not leave them without that testimony of God, through which they come to experience both His holiness and their sin, but also His goodness as well as their own nothingness. Through this, however, a conduct toward God can be worked in them, which He, on the day of that judgment which John saw after the resurrection of the believers, will recompense with the reward of eternal life. But this is God’s work and not their own. It is God’s love which lets them live, and through His Spirit, the Spirit of their life, He testifies Himself to them.” (L. c. 2nd ed. p. 570 sq.)

See John 3:16 and 36. By force of opposition, John 3:18 and 36. Compare Matthew 24:13, Revelation 2:10. § 23. The subject by which [subjectum quo] of blessedness are the soul, on the part of the intellect and the will, and the body and its organs.

Viewed in their integrity. To which formally pertains the beatific vision and whatever is of the accompanying knowledge. See § 2 sqq. to 7. To which pertain love and joy, concerning which it was treated in § 8 and 11. Regarding those endowments which we saw in § 14 and following, see § 18. § 24. The end of human blessedness is the eternal glory of the divine goodness, wisdom, truthfulness, and power.

Which we do not here distinguish into ultimate and intermediate, since blessedness itself on the part of men is the ultimate end, nor is there given an ulterior end, unless it be that which is simply ultimate. We have seen, however, that the joys of the blessed are contained within blessedness itself. Indeed, of the Triune God, the author of our felicity. For just as the end of election to eternal life is the glory of divine grace, Eph. 1:6, so also is it the end of the actual bestowal of eternal life. Partly on account of the sublimity of the goods themselves, such as exceed the grasp of our mind, partly if we view blessedness as to be given or having been given to such a subject, which is a sinful man, with justice preserved. Compare Ephesians 3:9. Or of faithfulness in keeping promises and fulfilling the calling to life, 1 Thess. 5:24. For we have seen those supernatural endowments to be expected only from infinite power and redounding to His praise. Some separately mention here the glory of divine justice; but it must be confessed that it pertains partly to the goodness of God (insofar as it is called remunerative), and partly to truthfulness (or the conformity of words and deeds).

In sua integritate spectatae. Ad quem formaliter spectat visio beatifica et quicquid est cognitionis accedentis. Vid. § 2. sqq. ad 7. Quo pertinent amor et gaudium, de quibus actum est § 8. et 11. Quoad dotes illas, quas § 14. et seqq. vidimus, vid. § 18.§ 24. Finis beatitudinis humanae a est divinae b bonitatis,c sapientiae,d veraci tatis e et f potentiae g gloria h aeterna.

Quem hic non distinguimus in ultimum et intermedium, cum ipsa beatitudo ex parte hominum sit finis ultimus, neque detur finis ulterior, nisi qui est simpliciter ultimus. Gaudia beatorum autem intra ipsam beatitudinem contineri vidimus. Dei quidem trinunius, auctoris nostrae felicitatis. Prout enim electionis ad vitam aeternam finis est gloria gratiae divinae, Eph. 1, 6., ita et actualis collationis vitae aeternae idem finis est. Partim propter ipsam bonorum sublimitatem, qualia mentis nostrae captum excedunt, partim si spectemus beatitudinem tali subjecto, quod est homo peccator, salva justitia dandam aut datam. Confer. Ephes. 3, 9. Seu fidelitatis in servandis promissis et implenda vocatione ad vitam, 1 Thess. 5, 24. Supernaturales enim dotes illas esse vidimus non nisi ab infinita putentia expectandas inque ejus laudem cedentes. Quidam seorsim hic memorant justitiae divinae gloriam; sed fatendum est, eam partim ad bonitatem Dei (prout remuneratoria dicitur), partim ad veraeitatem (seu dictorum factorumque conformitatem) spectare.


## 9 Concerning Eternal Death, or Damnation

PART I. CHAP. VII.

As we read in Rev. 7:11-12, the angels and the heavenly men, falling upon their faces before the throne and worshipping God, say: Amen, blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honor, and power, and might be unto our God for ever and ever, Amen. § 25. Eternal blessedness can be described as a complex of many supernatural perfections, obtained from the Triune God out of mere grace on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, by men who finally believe and have departed this mortal life, principally on the part of the intellect and the will, yet at the same time also of the body itself, by which the human appetite is fully satisfied to the eternal glory of the Triune God.

For eternal blessedness is indeed, when viewed in the nominative case and in its integrity, a certain aggregate resulting from the concurrence of various goods; see § 13, note c. Moreover, it agrees thus far also with the concreated image of God (the restoration of which it implies); concerning which see Chap. IV. In this respect it partly differs from the concreated image of God, and partly still agrees with the gifts of grace in this life. d) e) f) Thus are indicated the efficient and impulsive causes of blessedness, which were treated in § 21. Who are the subject *quod* (the subject which), according to § 22. Thus the subject *quo* (the subject by which) is indicated: partly primary, by reason of essential blessedness, in which our formal end consists; partly secondary, by reason of the other parts pertaining to the integrity of blessedness. Compare § 24. For thus the reason for blessedness absolutely so-called, or ultimate blessedness, is evident; see § 2 and 11. k) In which consists the end of blessedness, according to § 24. Chapter VII. CONCERNING DEATH OR ETERNAL DAMNATION. § 1.

Damnation is opposed to blessedness partly privatively, insofar as it implies the lack of all goods that enter into the happiness of the blessed, and partly contrarily, whereby

to the extent that it does not speak of a mere absence of blessedness, but contains positive adversities and torments and a most acute sense of evils. And therefore this second doctrine is rightly subjoined to the doctrine of blessedness, so that opposites placed next to one another may shine forth more clearly; just as it must be confessed that those who are not easily moved by the goodness of the end of theology (being corrupted by the love of earthly things) can meanwhile be terrified by the consideration of the misery otherwise to be expected. For there is no third option, and those who do not attain the highest good will not escape the highest evil; which is evident from the force of the propositions by which the ultimate lot of all men is reduced to two classes.

Dan. 12:2. John 5:28, 29. Matt. 25:32, 33, and 46. To this it is customary to refer the fact that the state of the damned is called the second death, Rev. 2:11, ch. 20:6. For death is the privation of life. And it is called second because it imports the privation of another life, which we could have attained once this life was completed. Ecclesiastical writers call it the punishment of loss. Thus, the same state sometimes comes under the name of reproach or ignominy, sometimes of eternal fire. See the cited passages of Daniel and Matthew. Otherwise, it is called the punishment of sense.

Gerhard: "If a more grievous punishment than reduction to nothingness were not to be feared by the impious, it would not be better for them not to have been born." (Loc. de inferno seu morte aeterna. § 78.) ANTITHESIS. Gerhard: "Antithesis: 1. Philo seems to have been of the opinion that hell is nothing other than the horror of conscience... Jerome in his epistle to Avitus, enumerating the heresies of Origen, among others also recounts this one in these very words: 'Origen, in book 2 of περὶ ἀρχῶν, does not place the fire of Gehenna and the torments which the Holy Scriptures threaten to sinners in punishments, but in the conscience of sinners.' 2. The Photinians maintain that the impious will either never be resurrected, or after the resurrection and judgment will be reduced to nothingness; they therefore define damnation by ἀνυπαρξίαν." (L. c. § 77. sq.) §

I. In particular, the damned will lack, on the part of the intellect, the beatific vision of God, nor will they be endowed with the light of glory, divinely bestowed upon the blessed. This is, not to see life, John 3:36. To the same is usually referred Ps. 49:20, regarding what is said of the impious, that they will not enjoy the light forever, and in the New Testament that the damned will be cast into outer darkness, Matt. 8:12, ch. 22:13, as if expelled from the Lord, who is the light of minds, according to Prosper, book III de vit. contempl. c. 12. (Conf. Gerh. T. VIII. L. de inferno, § 42. p. 590.) And that they are said to depart from Christ, Matt. 25:41, and to be left behind, Luke 17:34.

1) OF ETERNAL DAMNATION.

Indeed, they will also lack the light of grace, which they despised in this life, and a right judgment concerning divine things and their own selves. Luther: "In the damned, that same rational light remains; indeed, it becomes only brighter, so that they are tormented all the more by it." (Opp. T. XI, 256.) § 3. And thus it is also easily evident that the love of God, as the highest good clearly known, and the joy resulting therefrom, will be entirely absent from the damned.

For this [love] is born solely from the knowledge of God as our good. To this refers the "lack of water," Zech. 9:11, i.e., of refreshment, joy, and pleasure. § 4. Moreover, the endowments of the blessed bodies, through which they themselves are glorified, will in the same way be denied to the damned.

Brightness, certainly, as well as subtlety, agility, and impassibility will be absent. These are promised only to the pious and the elect. Although the bodies of the damned will indeed be incorruptible, yet that incorruptibility will neither proceed from impassibility or spirituality as an intrinsic perfection, nor will it redound to the glory of those bodies, but rather to the increase of misery, so that this may be eternal; concerning which more will be said below. Gerhard: "That the bodies of the damned are called spiritual is not to be understood in the Origenian sense, as if they were to have neither flesh nor bones; nor in that sense in which the bodies of the blessed are called spiritual and glorified, 1 Cor. 15:45, but in a broader sense, so that it is opposed to the animal body, which stands in need of the support of food, drink, clothing, etc." (Loc. de morte aet. § 66.) The same: "Just as the bodies of the blessed will be glorious, 1 Cor. 15:44, Phil. 3:21, so the bodies of the damned will be deformed, foul, and abominable. Just as the glory of the blessed will shine through their bodies like light shining through glass, so the ignominy of the damned will overflow from the soul into their bodies. For if in this life evildoers and criminals testify to the hidden impiety of their hearts with a gloomy countenance—'murder and theft look out from their eyes'—how much more will the indelible stains of sins appear in the bodies and faces of the damned!" (L. c. § 52.) § 5.

Among the positive punishments, there first occurs that knowledge of the intellect by which the damned [know] God, either abstractly or from the punishments, partly as the Lord of highest majesty, but... PART I. CHAP. VII.

they will recognize Him as most grievously offended, partly as a just judge, but by this very fact as the most severe avenger of their sins, and partly as a most benign father, yet not to them, but to others who have believed and have been made blessed.

Thus, in Revelation 6:17, they are described as recognizing Him who sits upon the throne, or God possessing supreme majesty, whose face, threatening and indeed inflicting extreme punishment, they cannot endure. Therefore, although to know God pertains to the perfection of man, yet to know Him in this way is not of perfection, but of the most grievous misery. § 6. Similarly, they will contemplate themselves in such a way that they will ponder in their minds the multitude and gravity of their sins, and also the merit, bitterness, and perpetuity of the punishments by which they are afflicted.

Thus, in Wisdom 5, near the beginning, the complaint of the damned is set forth, by which they accuse their own folly and confess that they have erred, that they have been filled with the way of truth, of iniquity, and of perdition, and have walked through pathless deserts, etc., meditating upon the vanity of their pride, their riches, and their boasting. § 7. They will look upon other men, who are blessed, as participants in that felicity of which they themselves are destitute, and as exempt from the calamities by which they themselves are oppressed.

Wisdom, loc. cit., describes them seeing the righteous standing with great confidence before them and be…ing amazed because of his unexpected salvation, etc. Gerhardus: "They will see the felicity of the blessed in heaven, not indeed in species nor πρακτικός, yet in the meantime in genus and θεωρητικός." (Loc. cit. § 52.) § 8.

Therefore, on the part of the will, there will arise hatred of God, inasmuch as He is hostile and implacable toward them;a hatred of themselves, as those who have been the cause of their own misery;b envy, resulting from the sight of the blessedness of others;c sorrow and sadness and anxiety d on account of the immense heap of present evils; and impatience e and perpetual despair.f

See Rev. 6:16–17, where a massive aversion to God, whose sight they cannot bear, is indicated. And the thing itself teaches that the will of the damned is not, and cannot be, directed toward God as a good for them, whom they have and know to be irreconcilably opposed to them. Nor will the will abstain from every act occupied with God, when God is set before their intellect as He behaves toward them, and they themselves are perpetually afflicted b…y the sense of divine wrath. Therefore, since they cannot love God, they pursue Him with hatred, which is opposed to love, just as the evil angels, the implacable (ἄσπονδοι) enemies of God and men.

Wis. 5:4, 6, 7. For that accusation indicates displeasure and detestation of themselves. Thus, in the same place, v. 3 ff., they are said to speak of the righteous blessed one: "This was he whom we once held in derision and as a common reproach. How is he numbered among the sons of God, and his lot is among the saints?" To this pertains that θλίψις καὶ στενοχωρία, that compression and constriction, of which Rom. 2:9 speaks. Compare Wis. 5:3, where they are said to groan because of the anguish of spirit.

And thus we read that terrors, confusions, gnashing, indignation, stings, and most bitter torments are ascribed to the damned. Finding no opportunity to escape their evils, seeking and desiring to die, or not to be at all, or to be utterly destroyed, Rev. 9:6.

PART. I. CAP. VII.

Prout Apoc. 7, 11. 12. legimus, augelos coelitesque homines, procumbentes ante thronum, in facies sum et adorantes Deum, dicere: Amen, benedictio, et gloria, et sapientia, et gratiarum actio, et honor, et potestas, et vires Deo nostro in saecula saeculorum, Amen.§ 25. Describi potest beatitudo aeterna, quod sit complexus a plurium perfectionum supernaturalium,b a Deo trinuno c ex mera gratia d propter meritum Christi e fide f apprehensum hominibus finaliter credentibus atque hac mortali vita defunctis g praecipue ex parte intellectus et voluntatis, simul tamen etiam ipsius corporis h obtingentium, quibus appetitus humanus plene satiatur i ad Dei trinunius gloriam k aeternam.
