### Concerning Eternal Death, or Damnation: OF ETERNAL DAMNATION

OF ETERNAL DAMNATION. § 15. The external impulsive cause is the sins of the damned, not expiated, especially those of the will, and most of all, final unbelief. Others call this the external and προκαταρκτική [pre-initiating] cause, intending to indicate the same thing regarding the matter. Each and all of these signify the ἀποστασίαν [apostasy] of the rational creature, who is bound to obedience to God, as the blessed Gerhard rightly teaches (l. c.), and thus they are worthy to be vindicated by rejection from the face of God.

To be sure, among faithful men, the heirs of eternal life, sins also occur, which, however, because they are expiated through faith in Christ, do not actually become the cause of their damnation, but are hindered in causing it, just as it is certain that the faithful are not actually damned. For thus, completed sins (which, taking their origin from depraved concupiscence, are fostered and, as it were, brought to light with the full consent of the will) are said to beget death, James 1:15. Compare Rom. 8:13; 1 Cor. 6:9, 10; Gal. 5:19, 20, 21.

Some have said that this [unbelief] is the immediate cause of damnation in the state of the new covenant, inasmuch as it alone actually, proximately, and immediately damns, whereas every other sin damns meritoriously, as the blessed Dannhauer speaks in *Hodosoph. Phaenom.* XI. p. 1412. (915.) Compare the blessed J. Fr. Koenig, *Theol. Pos.* P. I. § 328. p. m. 65.

They prove this, moreover, from Mark 16:16; John 3:18, 36. Indeed, the blessed Gerhard, *L. de Inferno* § 29. p. m. 563., writes: "Although unbelief alone is the formal and adequate cause of damnation, nevertheless, on account of that, other sins ought not to be excluded from the cause of damnation, both because they damn meritoriously, and because they are the fruits and effects of unbelief, etc."

He himself also appeals to *L. de Bon. Oper.* § 34, where likewise p. m. 41, 42, he used the distinction between the immediate or formal cause and the meritorious cause to explain the mind of Luther, who wrote in the *Book on Christian Liberty* that no evil work makes a man evil and damned, but only unbelief. Compare the same author in *L. de Inferno* § 82. p. m. 681, who also notes that unbelief, through which the merit of Christ is repelled, is the greatest of all sins, and is the cause on account of which other sins (which could have been remitted) are not forgiven; while it remains, other sins also remain, as he advises from Augustine’s *Commentary on John XVI* in *l. c. de Bon. Op.* § 34. p. 41.

However, it is well known that the phrase—that original sin is a sufficient, but not an adequate, cause of damnation—has become a matter of dispute, and therefore, because the Arminians were found to have abused that distinction to extenuate original sin, the blessed Musaeus rightly taught that one should abstain from it (*Ausführl. Erklärung* L. VII. Q. XXXIX. p. 308), though he confessed at the same time that it must be entirely admitted that those who are actually damned, if they had been without unbelief, would not have been damned on account of original sin alone.

For if unbelief had been absent, they would have believed in Christ, and on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, they would have been saved, notwithstanding original sin, which still remained in them.

Quenstedtius: "All sins by their nature are mortal, that is, of themselves they merit eternal death or damnation, because every sin..." PART I. CHAP. VII.

...it is ἀνομία and transgresses the law of God, and makes a man guilty of the whole law, Jas. 2:10, Deut. 27:26, Gal. 3:10. Rom. 6:23: "the wages of sin is death." ...

In particular, actual proaeretic sins, or those which are committed with a conscious and deliberate mind, are the meritorious cause of damnation. Hence St. James ch. 1:15: "Sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death," i.e., the mature fetus of sin admitted with full and joyful assent is death, not so much temporal as eternal, as is evident from Rom. 8:13, 1 Cor. 6:9-10, Gal. 5:19-21, 2 Thess. 1:6, 8-9.

Although all sins, as such, are the meritorious cause of damnation, yet the formal, proper, immediate, and adequate cause of damnation is final ἀπιστία or unbelief, which not only merits, but also actually brings about eternal death and damnation, by the force of the sayings in Mark 16:16: "He that believeth not shall be damned." And John 3:18: "He that believeth not is condemned already," v. 36: "He that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him." Observe: 1) "He that believeth not," i.e., he who pertinaciously perseveres in unbelief until the last breath of life, he is actually damned. Just as all diseases by their own power produce death or are lethal in themselves, but he actually dies who rejects the medicine, so every sin damns demeritoriously, but only ἀπιστία damns actually, proximately, and immediately, or only he is actually damned who has pertinaciously held heavenly aids in contempt. 2) It is said, "he that believeth not is condemned already," not according to the manifest promulgation and publication of the final condemnatory sentence, which will take place at the final judgment, but because of the certainty of the divine decree made from eternity and by reason of the judgment manifested in the Word and promulgated to the unbelieving, the execution of which will follow on the last day. 3) The word μένει denotes not only the presence of divine wrath, into which we have already fallen because of sins, but at the same time the continuous and perpetual act of that presence because of the contempt of the gospel of Christ, so that the sense is: The wrath of God will remain upon the damned like a most heavy weight forever. (L. c. P. I. c. 4. s. 1. th. 30. f. 806. sq.) Luther: "Through Christ, original sin is abolished, and after Christ's coming it condemns no one, except for him who will not let it go, i.e., who will not believe." (Marginal gloss, on John 15:22.) Scherzer: "Although original sin of itself merits damnation and infernal torments, and is thus a sufficient cause of damnation, it is not, however, the adequate cause of damnation actually inflicted (which is God's kindness). 'It is false,' says the blessed Menzer, 'that original sin in infants outside the church is the adequate cause of reprobation; nowhere in Scripture are men said to be reprobated only because of that,' Defens. part. II. Conversat. Prutenicae Doct. Crocii ch. 9. fol. 83. col. 80, 81, 82. Tom. I. Opp. fol. 951. 'No sins, however atrocious, actually bring about death and are directly and immediately deadly and actually deprive one of the salvation of grace, except for unbelief,' blessed Hoepfner. Disp. X. de justif. ch.

II. Aphor. III. § 21. fol. 911. For just as faith alone justifies, so 'unbelief alone damns,' according to the blessed Luther in Menzer f. 954. sq., namely, actually, proximately, and immediately. Otherwise, every sin damns demeritoriously, Dannhauer. Hodosoph. 1412. coll, fol. 368, 585. sqq. 1405: 'Sins, insofar as they are such, are not the proximate cause of damnation, but insofar as they remain under unbelief.' Luther on Christian Liberty, and on the Babylonian Captivity, even [says], 'that, if it were possible for unbelief to be separated from them, it would not be sin,' the same in the Response to the King of England near the end, Tom. II. Jenensis f.

144. Altenb. Tom. II. f.

204. So that he even breaks out into these words: 'That a Christian, even if he wishes, cannot lose his salvation by even the most grievous sins, unless he refuses to believe,' Lib. de Captiv. Babyl. Tom. II. Jen. Lat. fol. 285. and Tom. II. Witteberg. f. 78. In this sense must be understood that saying: 'Unbelief alone damns,' which he proves from the words of Christ ('The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, because they believe not in me,' John 16:9). Tom. VII. Jenens. fol. 85. Altenb. Tom. VIII. fol. 198. sq."

OF ETERNAL DAMNATION. § 16. The subject which is damned consists of impious men, who are finally unbelieving.

Or the supposita, which in the nominative case are said to be damned.

Some call this the object for whom hell is prepared; others call it the subject receiving infernal punishments.

This is with regard to the privative and positive, internal and external evils, which consequently affect the subject not in one way, but in various ways.

This is indeed the case in this place; for elsewhere we have said that the devil and his angels are also subject to damnation, in Chapter III, concerning angels, § 45 et seq.

In whom there is that which has the force and reason of the external impulsive causes of damnation, according to the preceding § 15.

But for a catalog of those to be damned, see, if you please, Rom. 1:29–32; 1 Cor. 6:9–10; Gal. 5:19–21; Eph. 5:3–4; Col. 3:5–6; 2 Tim. 3:2–5; Rev. 21:8, 22:15.

Those who do not know God and who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, 2 Thess. 1:8.

Those who do not believe in the Son, Mark 16:16; John 3:18, 36, and therefore do not have the Son, 1 John 5:12.

And the number of these is indeed much greater than that of the heirs of blessedness; see Matt. 7:13–14; Luke 12:32, 13:23–24. §

17. The subject in which is the soul as well as the body of those impious men.

Or that part of man according to which he suffers punishments.

To this belong formally the lack of the beatific vision, of love, and of joy, and the positive evils of the intellect and will, which were treated in § 2, 3, 5 et seq. to 9.

To which will be lacking the endowments of glorified bodies, and to which will adhere the torments of infernal fire, according to § 4 and 10. §

18. To seek or to wish to define the place of hell in this life is uselessly curious; but that a certain place is destined for the damned, there is no doubt.

Compare the blessed Gerhard, loc. cit., § 84, p. 686 et seq.

And it is certainly easier to show the difficulty of the individual opinions that define something here than to confirm one sufficiently.

For Scripture itself makes very frequent mention of hell, of a prison, etc. PART I. CHAPTER VII.

Quenstedtius: "The πού (where) of hell is certain, distinct from the πού of the blessed and separated from it by a great interval, Luke 16:26. However, what that πού is and where it is, is not established. Some place it in the world, and indeed specifically in the center of the earth, as the papists do; others, which is also probable, outside the world. Chrysostom rightly says: 'Do not ask where it is, but how we may flee it.'" (L. C. th. 34. f. 810.)

Dannhauerus: "This descent is into the κατώτερα, indeed the κατώτατα τῆς γῆς (Ephesians 4:9), or, according to the nature of the Greek idiom, into places which are themselves lower than the earth and are not contained by the body of the earth; which is truly the lowest of all lowest things, not geometrically, but mystically. Not κατὰ τὴν λέξιν (according to the letter), as Theophylactus speaks, but κατὰ τὴν δόξαν, ὁμοίωσιν, καὶ ἀναλογίαν (according to the opinion, likeness, and analogy). 'For just as (says Augustine) according to the body (ψυσικῶς) lower things are heavier, so according to the spirit (ὑπερφυσικῶς) lower things are sadder.'" (Hodos. Phaen. 8. p. 372.)

### Concerning Eternal Death, or Damnation: Fechtius: "Nor is it clear where hell is, which nevertheless, because it is…

Fechtius: "Nor is it clear where hell is, which nevertheless, because it is 'prepared' (Matthew 25:41), has been created." (Syllog. controvers. p. 95.)

Gerhardus: "Because that hypothesis, that hell is in the center of the earth, is still doubtful, and because it has not been revealed to us in the Scriptures whether that πού of hell, in which the damned will suffer punishments with the devils, is created or uncreated, corporeal or incorporeal, within or outside this visible world, it is therefore better to be concerned about escaping hell than about its creation." (L. c. § 32.)

Hutterus: "There have been not a few, both among the fathers and the scholastics, who have contended that hell, to which Christ descended, is a certain corporeal place, depressed most deeply in the bowels of the earth; or, as Bellarmine writes, established in the center of the earth.

But this assertion is so vain, futile, and trifling that it has no need of a lengthy refutation. For if hell is some subterranean place, and indeed established in the center of the earth, and if this earth will truly burn with fire on the last day (2 Peter 3:3), it would follow that hell itself would then also be reduced to nothing. Which is false and absurd.

The purer and truly orthodox opinion, on the contrary, is that which maintains that hell is by no means to be defined by any physical or corporeal place, or by any other part of this universe; but [is] outside this universe, through a certain spiritual, non-local, and entirely incorporeal system or πᾶν, in which the tortures of divine fury will rage and prevail with ineffable torments, both upon the bodies and the souls of men; just as, conversely, heaven or the seat of the blessed is not any corporeal or physical place, much less any part of the sky, but a certain spiritual and non-local πού or 'where,' in which the elect will be bathed in eternal happiness and ineffable joys.

Furthermore, where that system of hell will be, or indeed where it is even now, we certainly cannot define: especially since Scripture itself pronounces nothing openly regarding this matter. This is the reason why the opinion of the ancient fathers concerning hell was so varied and doubtful; yet the primary ones among them have nothing in common with the fables of the Esauvites [i.e., the Jesuits] and the papists. Augustine certainly writes thus in *De Genesi ad litteram*, book 12, chapter 33: 'There is indeed a substance of the lower regions, but I judge it to be spiritual, not corporeal.' And a little later: 'The lower regions (*inferi*) are so called in Latin because they are below. But just as according to the body, if they keep the order of their weight, all lower things are heavier: so according to the spirit, all lower things are sadder.' Brentius also writes to this effect: 'When there is talk of spiritual and heavenly things, these words, "above" and "below," are indeed used according to human custom, but they are not defined by places, but by dignity and indignity, majesty and abjection, joy and horror, gladness and sadness.'"

§ 19. That the punishments of all the damned, who survive perpetually, are eternal, is most certain. So that they shall never have any end; just as in Dan. 12:2 mention is made of eternal ignominy, of eternal punishment in Matt. 25:46, of eternal destruction in 2 Thess. 1:9. Compare Jude v. 6 and 13, and what we have said at § 10, note c. Gerhard: "The eternity of infernal punishments is proven: I. From the Holy Scriptures, in which it is described 1. καταφατικός, affirmatively...; 2. αποφατικός, negatively... They object: 'God threatened eternal punishments to sinners in order to restrain them from the commission of sins, because He ought to have threatened eternal torments to His creature, not to inflict them.' I answer with the words of Gregory, *Moral.* lib. 34, c. 16: 'If He threatened falsely in order to correct them from injustice, He also promised falsely in order to provoke them to justice. Who could tolerate this madness of theirs, who attempt to argue that what the Truth has threatened is not true, and while they are busy trying to represent God as merciful, they do not fear to proclaim Him a liar?' II. The same eternity of infernal punishments can be proven by reasons deduced from Scripture: 1. From the perpetual duration of divine wrath... 2. From the confirmation of the chasm, Luke 16:26... 3. From the closing of the door, Matt. 25:10... 4. From the opposition of blessedness, Matt. 25:46... 5. From the removal of repentance... 6. From the description of infernal fire... 7. From the turpitude and confusion of sin. Sin is committed against God, who is an infinite good; therefore it also merits infinite punishments. 8. From the frustration of the desire, Apoc. 9:6... 9. From the casting into bonds, Matt. 22:13... 10. From the association with demons, Matt. 25:41." (L. c. § 57 sq.) Whether they bore the name of Christians in this life, and perhaps were even truly faithful for some time (but πρὸς καιρὸν), or whether they were altogether infidels. Not that they are to be annihilated at length, but remaining in existence, they pay the penalty. Not only privative, but also positive [punishments], and of the infernal fire itself, which shall never be extinguished, Mark 9:44, 46, 48. Compare Apoc. 14:11, ch. 19:3, ch. 20:10. Notwithstanding the divine mercy, after the term of μακροθυμία has elapsed. ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Origenists, or, as some wish, the Cerinthians, who maintain that the torments of demons and wicked men are temporary and will have an end at some time, God being as it were satiated with vengeance; likewise that the devils will at long last recover their former happiness through the efficacy and virtue of the merit of Christ... Augustine, in his book *De Haeresibus*, heresy 43, writes that Origen thought 'even the devils, with all the damned, have hope of liberation from hell'... There are, however, those who attempt to free Origen from this error, contending that the former opinions were inserted into his writings by his wicked rivals, since in many places he seems to argue expressly for the eternity of infernal punishments... 2. Of the Pseudo-Ambrose, who fosters the same error. For he writes in his exposition of ch. 3 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, 'that the Pauline proclamation also profited the evil angels.'... 3. It cannot be denied that Jerome writes doubtfully in his commentary on Isaiah 24, near the end: 'It should be known'... PART I. CAP. VII.

he says, "because human frailty cannot know the judgment of God, nor pass sentence on the magnitude and measure of punishments, which has been left to the Lord’s own discretion."

4. Of the Anabaptists, who began to teach in the previous century that all the damned, and even the devils themselves, would eventually be saved and that an end would one day be put to their punishments or torments, which they have merited by their sins; which error the Augsburg Confession, Art. 17, condemns and rejects.

5. Of the Libertines, who promise God’s mercy to all men whatsoever, and even to demons after the judgment.

6. Of certain Socinians, who teach that evil angels and the impious will not be tormented eternally, but will be destroyed, abolished, and reduced to nothing by eternal fire. . .

7. Of the Arminians, in whose confession the Leyden theologians find it lacking that "it is not explained clearly enough by them whether they maintain that those infernal torments will endure forever and that the impious men themselves, affected by those punishments, will live forever in those pains"; since the words are conceived so ambiguously that some Socinian could also understand his own impious opinion regarding the eternal extinction of wicked men at the final judgment under those words. . .

8. Of Thomas and his followers, Part 1, Q. 64, Art. 2, and *Contra Gentiles* 1. 6, c. 9, where he argues that the devils could have repented if God had granted them the time and help of grace.

9. Of the "merciful" ancient doctors, against whom Augustine argues in *De Civitate Dei*, Book 21, c. 17, who did not indeed offer hope of liberation to the devils, but did to damned men." (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 826—828.) §

20. The end of that damnation on the part of God is the glory of the Judge’s vindicatory justice, truthfulness, and divine power. He indeed, of Himself and as if by a native inclination, would prefer not to damn; certainly, He cannot even will to damn a creature that is not yet viewed as fallen or about to fall, because of His infinite goodness: but insofar as He is the Judge of the whole earth (Gen. 18:25) and sinners and despisers of offered grace stand before Him, He hates the workers of iniquity (Ps. 5:6) and, after the space of long-suffering has elapsed, rejects them from His face and damns them. For from this proceeds that act of punishing, and thus it tends toward His glory by the intention of God. For this reason, it is said to be just before God (and therefore to redound to the glory of divine justice) to inflict vengeance (διδόναι ἐκδίκησιν) upon those who have not known God, that they may pay the penalty, eternal destruction, ὄλεθρον αἰώνιον, 2 Thess. 1:6, 8, 9. And Rom. 2:5, that in the day of wrath the just judgment of God is revealed. Compare Ps. 11:7, Ps. 58:11, 12, Rev. 19:1, 2, 3.

Regarding the threats made to the impious, the fulfillment of which is their actual damnation. For thus it appears that those words are faithful and true (λόγους ἀληθινοὺς καὶ πιστούς), that the unbelieving and the execrable, etc., shall have their part in the lake burning with fire and brimstone, which is the second death, Rev. 21:5, 8.

As prevailing over all the efforts and schemes of the impious in this life. Whence the blessed men, beholding the judgments of God against the impenitent, acclaim the Judge: Hallelujah. Salvation, and honor, and glory, and power (ἡ δύναμις) to our God, Rev. 19:1. In 2 Thess. 1:9, the impious are said to pay the penalty ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης τῆς ἰσχύος, from the glory of the strength (or power) of the Lord. PART I. CHAPTER VIII. 223 §

21. The state of damnation can be described as a complex of several evils, which the Triune God, by virtue of His vindicatory justice, inflicts upon impious men and those who are finally unbelieving, in respect to soul and body, on account of their sins and unbelief, in hell, to be endured eternally, to the glory of the divine justice, truthfulness, and power.

According to the analogy of the description of the opposite state of beatitude, previous chapter VI, last §. For this implies it in the nominative case. Whose series see § 2 ff. According to § 13 concerning the efficient cause. Which is the internal impulsive cause, according to § 14. As the subject *quod* (that which); see § 16. Which pertain to the subject *quo* (that by which), according to § 17. For this is the external impulsive cause; concerning which see § 15. Or the *ubi* (where) of the damned, according to § 18. k) Which is the affection of damnation, indicated in § 19. l) By which the end of damnation is indicated; concerning which see § 20.

## 10 On Temporal Death

Chapter VIII. ON TEMPORAL DEATH. § 1. Since the highest or ultimate beatitude occurs not in this life, but in the other, and similarly the opposite highest misery occurs only after this life, we must now consider those things which, according to divine revelation, pertain to the end of this life and the entrance into the further life or state.

See Prolegom. cap. I. § 4. note e. Vol. I. p. 10. And P. I. cap. VI. § 3 and 20. See cap. VII. § 1. note a. They are otherwise called the "last things," in Greek τὰ ἔσχατα, and are distinguished in that some are, and are called, the last with respect to individual men, others with respect to the universe and the whole world.

To the former class belong death and the state of the soul after death. To the latter belong the resurrection of the dead and the analogous transformation of the living, the final judgment, and the conflagration of the world; concerning each of which we must treat distinctly. PART I. CHAPTER VIII.

Quenstedtius: "We have hitherto considered the means of salvation properly so called... There follow now the means taken in a broader sense, namely, the four last things, . . . which are not so much means for obtaining salvation as the way through which we tend toward the goal or the terminus to which we are moving." (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 17. s. 1. th. 1. f. 1697.) Gerhardus: The four last things are commonly numbered, including this distich: Your death, the final judgment, the glory of heaven, And the pain of hell are to be meditated upon by you. . . The last things, taken in general, are twofold by reason of a twofold object: 1. the macrocosm, 2. the microcosm; the last thing of the macrocosm is the consummation of the age; the last things of the microcosm are four: 1. death, 2. resurrection, 3. judgment, 4. eternal abode, namely, of the pious in heaven and of the damned in hell." (Loc. de morte, § 7.) §

2. And first, indeed, death is to be considered, which is the privation of the natural life of men, proceeding from the dissolution of soul and body. As it imposes an end to the journey for individual men who are wayfarers. Although it itself is also called the way of all flesh, Josh. 23:14, namely, by which one passes to the terminus.

For not otherwise than privatively is death opposed to life, and it signifies the absence of life in a subject apt to have life, and which has had life for some time. Or, as others speak, the privation of animal life. For we are not looking here at spiritual death, of believers or unbelievers, nor at eternal death, but at temporal death, which is also called the death of the body.

Those things which are otherwise ordered and united by nature to constitute a man, as essential parts for the constitution of the whole, so that the soul exercises vital operations in the body and the body, being animated, lives by this very fact. Whence, conversely, that union being removed, the human suppositum ceases to live an animal life, or is deprived of life; yet that dissolution of soul and body is not itself the form or formal reason of death, but differs from it as an antecedent from a consequent.

For although it is not infrequent for death to be described by the noun ἀνάλυσις or the verb ἀναλῦσαι, e.g., 2 Tim. 4:6; Phil. 1:23, yet that is not its formal designation. But the body is said to καταλύεσθαι when it putrefies or falls apart, 2 Cor. 5:1.

Quenstedtius: "The form of death is not the reduction of the soul to nothing, but the dissolution from the body and the departure from the domicile of the body, or the local separation of the soul from the body, the tearing away and distraction of soul and body; I say local separation, because the soul truly departs from the body and no longer remains in it; it leaves it both as to presence and as to information; Luke 12:20: 'This night they shall require thy soul from thee.' The Savior uses the word ἀπαιτεῖν, to demand back, as if it were a foreign thing granted for use for a time. Thus the soul of the converted thief was with Christ in heaven, but his body was on earth. The essence of death, if we wish to speak accurately, consists in the λύσις alone, but its necessary consequent is the διάστασις."

8. An efficient cause of death, speaking strictly and per se, is not given. Meanwhile, those things must be considered which are the causes of the dissolution of soul and body, and these are partly physical, partly moral. For it is a privation, as we have seen. But efficient causes are properly of real and positive effects. Insofar as causes of privations are otherwise spoken of, they are those which are causes of some effect with which the privation is per se and necessarily conjoined. Or, those which act really upon the union of soul and body and destroy it. Or, those which do not indeed really destroy such a union, yet contribute something to its destruction, whence this is rightly imputed to them. §

4. Among the moral causes of death, the devil is first to be numbered, insofar as by his persuasion he induced Eve to sin and thus brought the guilt of death upon her and the associates of sin. Who is therefore called a murderer, John 8:44. See Gen. 3:1 et seqq. Thus, assuredly, the cause of the cause of death (or of sin) is also the cause of the caused (or of death itself). For without sin the protoplasts were immortal; only through sin did they become mortal, according to the preceding chapter, IV, § 15, note d. Compare Gen. 3:3, 4, 19, and Wisd. 2:24, where it is said that by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, and Heb. 2:14, that the devil has το χράτος του θανάτου, the power of death, insofar as a tyrant destines men conquered by him to death. For although we acknowledge that the discourse there is not of bodily death alone, but also of eternal death; yet this holds true here, that the devil, by inducing men into sin, has obtained χράτος or power over them, so as to subject them to death, even temporal.

Meisnerus: "If death had drawn its origin from physical necessity and the condition of nature, that threat in Gen. 2:17 would certainly have been vain and null. For the Lord willed to impose such a penalty as would never have had any place outside the state of sin. But not only eternal death is understood, but everything that comes under the name of death in Scripture, for which reason theologians rightly judge that the word for death was doubled and said by the Lord as 'dying you shall die.' ... Death in general and universally is called όψώνων της άμαρτίας, Rom. 6:23. If, therefore, death first flowed from sin, then it is not a consequence of nature as it was created by God, and therefore man was not created mortal from the beginning. For the penalty of άμαρτίας is one thing, and the condition of ονσίας is another. Scripture affirms the former of all death; therefore the latter must be denied, because two opposites cannot stand together." (Philos. sobr. P. I. p. 883 sq.) Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. II. 15 PART I. CHAP. VIII.

§ 5.

Furthermore, the first-formed are rightly called the cause of death, not only for themselves, but also for their descendants; Eve, indeed, insofar as she not only sinned herself, obeying the persuading demon, but also enticed Adam into the fellowship of sin, and thus brought the guilt of death upon herself and Adam; Adam, however, by listening to his wife and violating the law of God, not only underwent the necessity of dying himself, but was also the cause of death, just as he was the cause of sin, for all who would descend from him according to nature. Although they did not directly intend death, thinking that all other things would happen instead. See Gen. 3:3, 4; Gen. 3:6; 1 Tim. 2:14; Gen. 3:6, 17, and 19; Rom. 5:12. § 6.

God, however, is not the cause of death, except insofar as He, as a just judge, took away the gift of immortality from our first parents on account of their neglect of the prohibition and the severe threat, and thus subjected men to the death which they had merited. Speaking absolutely, lest it be thought that He Himself, without regard for sin, had so ordained it. For He created the first humans in ἀφθαρσία. Nor does He delight in death, but in the preservation and life of men, Wis. 1:13; ch. 2:23. Therefore, death is viewed here as an evil of punishment, to be inflicted in view of the intervening evil of guilt. Compare Ps. 90:7, where the wrath of God is said to consume us, and what we shall say at § 7, note c, d, and 14, note d. Fechtius: "God is not the cause of death, its merit preceding even the infliction, Ez. 33:11, and indeed He cannot be according to His nature, Matt. 19:17. Yet He is the cause of death, if merit has preceded, both threatening, Ps. 7:13, 14, and inflicting, 1 Sam. 2:6." Rollius adds: "In which way death i s viewed as an evil of punishment, inflicted in view of the antecedent evil of guilt." (Syllog. controvers. p. 373 sq. 376.)

Which is read as having been added to the law itself in Gen. 2:17. Namely, this is what is meant when man, with the gift of immortality withdrawn, is said to be destined to return to the earth from which he was taken, Gen. 3:19. § 7. The internal impulsive cause of death on the part of Satan is his supreme hatred toward God and men; on the part of God, however, the internal impelling cause is His vindictive justice, and the external cause is the fall of the first-formed.

He who undoubtedly intends the death of the human race directly, and is thus known to be impelled from somewhere to will death. For he bore it with difficulty to behold a creature who had been endowed with the gift of immortality for the praise of the Creator and for his own blessedness. And to this point looks that envy of which the author of the Book of Wisdom speaks in ch. 2:24, whether you call it envy born of hatred or hatred born of envy. W hence perhaps you might also say that the impulsive cause of death on the part of Satan was the benefit of immortality conferred upon men by God, which Satan could not behold with a calm mind. Although not by an antecedent will, yet by a consequent will, God wills and inflicts the death of sinners, according to what we have said in § 6 and notes a, b. Which He calls wrath in Ps. 90:7. It is said to consume us, because it moves God to subject us to death. For thus through sin death entered into the world, Rom. 5:12. Compare here § 5 and 6. On the part of the protoplasts themselves, we do not assign an impulsive cause, because they did not directly intend death, according to § 5, note a, § 8.

Furthermore, if we look at the particular examples of death, the moral cause of death varies greatly, and sometimes the dying themselves, at other times other men, and good or evil spirits constitute it; sometimes the dying men and others, and perhaps spirits as well, concur; whence also a manifold impulsive cause has place. For what we have seen thus far pertains mostly to death as it was first introduced into the human race, prescinding from the specific cases of the deaths of individual men. Some of these are at the same time the physical cause of a violent death by applying to themselves things that are lethal, and are commonly called αύτόχειρες; to which pertains the example of Saul, 1 Sam. 31:4. Others demand to be killed by others, as Abimelech by his armor-bearer, Judg. 9:54, or at least knowingly and willingly offer themselves to slayers, for which reason Paul set out for Jerusalem, prepared to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, Acts 21:13. Others, not by direct intention, yet by indirect, expose themselves to the dangers of dying and perish, as King Josiah, 2 Chron. 35:20 sqq. Others provoke God or the magistrate to their own killing by their offenses. See what we have said concerning the abrupt term of life in Part I, Chapter V, on Providence, § 18. For example, those who hire robbers or murderers for a price, who by their command, persuasions, threats, or promises induce or otherwise in any way promote human slaughter, just as David is said to have killed Uriah when he had ordered him to be placed in the battle line and deserted while fighting, 2 Sam. 11:15 sqq., 12:9; Absalom killed his brother Ammon by the work of his servants, ibid. ch. 13:28, 29. To the same point look those who [keep] a goring ox PART I. CHAP. VIII.

Vid. Prolegom. cap. I. § 4. not. e. Vol. I. p. 10. Et P. I. cap. VI. § 3. et 20. Vid. cap. VII. § 1. not. a. Vocantur alias novissima, Graece τά έσχατα, et distinguuntur, quod alia respectu hominum singulorum, alia respectu universorum et mundi totius, ultima sint et dicantur.

IV. c. 17. s. 1. th. 1. f. 1697.) Gerhardus: Communiter numerantur quatuor novissima, hoc inclusa disticho: Mors tua, judicium postremum, gloria coeli, Et dolor inferni sunt meditanda tibi.. . 2. Ac primum quidem spectanda est a mors, quae est privatio b vitae hominum naturalis,c ex dissolutione animae et corporis d proveniens. Tanquam singulis hominibus viatoribus viae finem imponens. Quamvis et ipsa dicatur via omnis carnis Jos. 23, 14., scilicet, qua transitur ad terminum. ‘

Neque enim hic mortem spiritualem, fidelium aut infidelium, neque mortem aeternam, sed temporalem, quae et mors corporis vocatur, spectamus.

Quae alias ad constituendum hominem, velut partes essentiales ad constitutionem totius, per naturam ordinantur et uniuntur, ita ut anima vitales operationes exerceat in corpore et corpus animatum hoc ipso vivat. Unde ex adverso, sublata unione illa, suppositum humanum vitam animalem vivere desinit, aut vita privatur; nec tamen ideo dissolutio illa animae et corporis ipsa mortis forma aut ratio formalis est, sed ab ea differt, ut antecedens a consequente.

Quamvis enim non sit infrequens, mortem nomine άναλόσεως aut verbo άναλΰσαι describi, v. g. 2 Tim. 4, 6· Phil. 1, 23., non tamen illa formalis appellatio est. Corpus autem dicitur χαταλυ^ψαι, cum putrefit aut dilabitur, 2 Cor. 5, 1.

Quenstedtius: ״Forma mortis non est animae in nihilum redactio, sed a corpore solutio et ex corporis domicilio egressio sive animae a corpore localis separatio, animae et corporis divulsio, distractio; dico localis separatio, quia anima revera a corpore discedit et non amplius in eo manet, illud relinquit et quoad praesentiam et quoad informationem; Luc. 12, 20.: ,Hac nocte animam tuam a te repetent.‘ Utitur Salvator verbo άπαιτεϊν, wiederfordern, tamquam rem alienam, usui ad tempus concessam. 8. Causa mortis efficiens per se et proprie loquendo a non datur. Interim spectari debent, quae sunt causae dissolutimis animae et corporis,b eaeque partim physicae,c partim morales.d Est enim privatio, ut vidimus. Sed causae efficientes proprie sunt effectuum realium et positivorum. Prout alias causae privationum dicuntur, quae sunt causae alicujus effectus, cum quo per se et necessario conjungitur privatio. Sive, quae realiter agunt in unionem animae et corporis eamque destruunt. Sive, quae non quidem realiter destruunt unionem talem, aliquid tamen ad ej׳s destructionem conferunt, unde haec illis recte imputatur.§

4. Inter causas morales mortis primo numerandus est diabolus,a quatenus suasione sua b ad peccatum Evam induxit et sic mortis reatum c illi et peccati sociis attraxit. Qui propterea homicida dicitur Joh. 8, 44. Vid. Gen. 3, 1. et seqq. Sic nimirum causa causae mortis (seu peccati) est etiam causa causati (seu mortis ipsius). Absque peccato enim protoplasti immortales, per peccatum demum mortales facti fuerunt, juxta cap. praeced. IV. § 15. not. d. Confer Gen. 3, 3. 4· 19. et Sap. 2, 24., ubi dicitur, invidia diaboli mortem intrasse in mundum, et Ebr. 2, 14., diabolum habere το χράτος του θανάτου, mortis imperium, prout tyrannus homines a se victos morti destinat. Quamvis enim non de sola morte corporali, sed et de morte aeterna, sermonem ibi esse fateamur; hic tamen illud valet, quod diabolus inducens homines in peccatum χράτυς seu potestatem consecutus sit in ipsos, ut morti subjiciendos, etiam temporali.

Meisnerus: ,,Si mors ex necessitate physica et conditione naturae ortum traxisset, comminatio certe ista Gen. 2, 17. fuisset frustranea et nulla. Talem enim poenam indicere voluit Dominus, quae extra peccati statum nullum unquam locum fuisset habitura. Non autem intelligitur sola mors aeterna, sed omne Id, quod nomine mortis in Scriptura venit, quam ob causam vocabulum mortis duplicatum et,morte morieris‘ a Domino dictum esse, recte existimant theologi. . . Mors in genere et universaliter vocatur όψώνων της άμαρτίας Rom. 6, 23. Quodsi igitur mors ex peccato primum promanavit, igitur naturae, prout illa a Deo creata, consequens non est, ideoque nec homo ab initio mortalis fuit conditus. Aliud enim est poena αμαρτίας et aliud conditio ονσίας. Illud de omni morte affirmat Scriptura; igitur hoc posterius negandum, quia duo opposita simul stare nequeunt.“ (Philos. sobr. P. I. p. 883. sq.) Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. II. 15 PART. I. CAP. VIII.

§ 5.

Deinde protoplasti non tantum suae ipsorum, sed et posterorum mortis causa recte dicuntur;a Eva quidem, quatenus non ipsa solum, daemoni suadenti obediens, peccavit, verum etiam Adamum ad societatem peccati pellexit b adeoque sibi et Adamo mortis reatum attraxit; Adam vero, uxori auscultans et legem Dei violans, cum ipse necessitatem moriendi subiit, tum omnibus secundum naturam ex se descensuris sicuti peccati, ita et mortis causa fuit.c Licet mortem directe non intenderint, alia omnia potius eventura putantes. Vid. Gen. 3, 3. 4. Gen. 3, 6. 1 Tim. 2, 14. Gen. 3, 6. 17. et 19. Rom. 5, 12.§ 6.

Deus autem mortis causa non est,a nisi quatenus ut justus judex b primis parentibus immortalitatis donum propter neglectum interdicti et severae comminationis c abstulit d et sic homines morti, quam meruerunt, subjecit. Absolute loquendo, ne putetur ipse, non habita ratione peccati, sic instituisse. Is enim homines primos lv άφϋαραία condidit. Neque morte, sed conservatione et vita hominum delectatur, Sap. 1, 13. cap. 2, 23. Spectatur itaque hic mors ut malum poenae, intuitu mali culpae intercedentis, infligendum. Confer Ps. 90, 7., ubi ira Dei dicitur nos consumere, et quae dicemus ad § 7. not. c. d. et 14. not. d.Fechtius: ,,Deus non est causa mortis, meritum ejus vel infligendo praecedens, Ez. 33, 11., et nec quidem secundum naturam suam esse potest, Matth. 19, 17. Est tamen causa mortem, si praecesserit meritum, et interminans, Ps. 7, 13. 14., et infligens, 1 Sam. 2, 6.“ Rollius addit: ,,Quo pacto mors spectatur ut malum poenae, intuitu mali culpae antecedentis inflictum. “ (Syllog. controvers. p. 373. sq. 376.)

Quae ipsi legi adjecta legitur Gen. 2, 17. Nempe hoc est, quod homo, subtracto immortalitatis dono, interram, unde sumtus est, reverti debere dicitur Gen. 3, 19. § 7. Causa impulsiva mortis interna ex parte satanae a est odium ejus summum erga Deum atque homines;b ex parte Dei autem c causa impellens interna est justitia ejus d vindicativa, externa lapsus e protoplastorum.f

Qui haud dubie mortem humani generis directe intendit, atque ita alicunde impulsus merito cognoscitur ad volendum mortem. Sic enim aegre tulit, creaturam, quae dono immortalitatis in laudem creatoris suamque beatitudinem praedita erat, intueri. Atque huc spectat invidia illa, de qua auctor libri Sapientiae c. 2, 24., sive invidiam ex odio, sive odium ex invidia natum dicas. Unde fortasse etiam causam impulsivam eaiernam mortis ex parte satanae dixeris esse beneficium immortalitatis hominibus a Deo collatum, quod aequo animo intueri non potuerit satanas. Licet non voluntate antecedente, consequente tamen, mortem peccatorum volentis et infligentis, juxta ea, quae § 6. et notis a. b. diximus. Quam iram appellat Ps. 90, 7. Dicitur autem ea nos cornumere, quia Deum movet, ut nos morti subjiciat. Sic enim per peccatum mors intravit in mundum, Rom. 5, 12. Confer h. l. § 5. et 6. Ex parte ipsorum protoplastorum causam impulsivam non damus, quia illi mortem directe non intenderunt, juxta § 5. not. a.§ 8.

Caeterum, si peculiaria mortis exempla a spectemus, causa moralis mortis valde variat, eamque aliquando morientes b ipsi, alias homines c alii, ac spiritus boni d aut mali e constituunt, nonnunquam homines morientes et alii, forte et spiritus simu f concurrunt; unde et causa impulsiva multiplex locum habet.g Quae enim hactenus vidimus, ad mortem, ut primum in genus humanum introductam, fere spectant, praescindendo a certis casibus mortis singulorum hominum. Quorum aliqui simul causa physica sunt mortis violentae applicando sibi ea, quae lethifera sunt, atque αύτόχειρες vulgo dicuntur; quo pertinet exemplum Saulis, 1 Sam. 31, 4· Alii postulant occidi ab aliis, uti Abimelech ab armigero, Judic. 9, 54., aut saltem scientes volentesque offerunt se occisoribus, qua ratione Paulus Hierosolymam profectus est, paratus mori pro nomine Domini Jesu, Act. 21, 13. Alii intentione non directa, indirecta tamen, periculis moriendi se exponunt et pereunt, ut Josias rex, 2 Chron. 35, 20. sqq. Alii delictis suis Deum aut magistratum lacessunt ad sui occisionem. Vid., quae diximus de termino vitae abrupto P. I. cap. V. de provid. § 18. V. g. qui latrones aut homicidas pretio conducunt, qui imperio suo, suasionibus, minis, pollicitationibus inducunt aut alias quoquo modo promovent caedem humanam, prout David dicitur occidisse Uriam, cum jussisset eum collocari in acie et pugnantem deseri, 2 Sam. 11, 15. sqq. 12, 9., Absalom servorum opera fratrem Ammonem occidit, ibid. cap. 13, 28. 29. Eodem spectant, qui bovem cornupetam PART. I. CAP. VIII.


### On Temporal Death: do not guard [them], Exod

do not guard [them], Exod. 21:29, much more those who incite beasts against a man, just as in the theaters the enemies of Christians were accustomed to do. Finally, those who do not ward off or remove the dangers and causes of a neighbor’s death, which they could have warded off or removed, such as watchmen who do not warn the citizens of an approaching enemy, according to Ezek. 33:6.

Executors of the divine will, even in such matters, [are seen] in the example of Herod, struck by an angel of the Lord so that he was eaten by worms while alive and thus perished, Acts 12:23. Some partly desire to harm the lives of men themselves, and partly have the power granted by God to chastise the pious and punish the impious, just as the destruction of the house of Job’s firstborn son and the violent killing of all his children is not undeservedly ascribed to Satan as the author, ch. 1:19. Cf. here, ch. III, on angels, § 51, 52, 56. Thus, indeed, in the slaughter of King Ahab in the battle with the Syrians, Satan and the false prophets governed by him, and at the same time Ahab himself, entering an unjust war and spurning the warnings of the prophet Micaiah—the former directly, the latter and this one indirectly—are known to have intended the death of Ahab himself and thus to have had all the reasons for the cause, 2 Chron. 18:19, 21, 25, 33, 34. There is certainly a greater variety here, due to the difference between the acting men and spirits, than can be distinctly proposed in a compendium of all classes of motives. § 9. Physical causes are divided into natural, preternatural, and violent. [

This concerns] the dissolution of soul and body, partly as first introduced, partly as actually occurring later among mortal men. Others constitute two species or classes, but in almost the same sense. For those which are here called preternatural, they refer either to natural or to violent [causes]. § 10. The natural cause of death is the consumption of the radical moisture and the extinction of the native heat, proceeding gradually from the primary qualities acting upon one another.

Namely, that which has arisen proximately from the necessity of nature (corrupt, not integral). Such as has a place in long-lived men who have enjoyed firm health, with no more serious disease intervening, just as Cicero described the long-lived in *De Senectute*, who depart only when burdened by years and by a natural death. And Aristotle called death natural when its principle is in the animal itself and is called γῆρας, old age, *Lib. de Respir.*, ch. XVII.

Or that the vigor of the native heat, which since the fall of the protoplasts has not had sufficiently pure nourishment, gradually languishes and converts the ingested food less successfully, and thus, with suitable fuel failing, that native heat or vital flame is more and more weakened and finally extinguished—a matter regarding which Aristotle called the natural corruption of life τῷ τοῦ θερμοῦ μάρανσιν διὰ χρόνου μῆκος γινομένῳ καὶ τελειότητα, the withering of the hot due to the length and completion of time passed, *l. c. cap. XVIII*. And thus there is only one cause of death that is truly natural and proximate. For besides the natural temperament, they are accustomed to refer hither also diet and, in its own way, medicine (which, since they cannot grant immortality, contribute to longevity and thus act not so much that man may not die, but that he may not die otherwise than by a natural death). § 11.

To preternatural causes pertain more vehement diseases, by which likewise the native heat is extinguished along with the radical moisture, but contrary to nature. Although these occur within man, they do not arise from the common necessity of nature, but from elsewhere, e.g., from a defect of diet in food, air, sleep and wakefulness, motion and rest, or even from passions of the sensitive appetite admitted. E.g., fevers, dropsy, phthisis, plague, and other diseases, which are excited by potent causes and overturn the substance, temperament, and remaining constitution of the parts of the body, and so dissipate or suffocate the spirits that nature no longer has the means to defend itself or to return to its pristine state.

Thus the philosopher says that θερμοῦ σβέσιν καὶ μάρανσιν, the extinction and withering of the hot, also has a place in non-natural death, but the principle of which is ἐπίκτητόν τι πάθος, some adventitious passion, *l. c. cap. XVII and XVIII*. § 12. To violent causes are referred external things, by which such force is inflicted upon the body, or upon a part of the body more noble or simply necessary for life, that the generation and distribution of the nutritive blood and spirits is impeded or removed.

E.g., a deadly weapon, fire, water, etc. For without these, the body itself is rendered inept for the functions of the soul, and life cannot subsist. PART I. CAP. VIII

13. The subject of death is human beings, not only the first ones after the fall, but also the rest, propagated from them through carnal generation, all of them.

Or that which is subject to death, and is denominated as dying. Others call it the matter in which.

According to the divine threat in Gen. 2:17, ch. 3:19, and the event corresponding to it, Gen. 5: 5. For Christ, conceived ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, was not subject to the necessity of death. Thus, death is said to have passed unto all men, Rom. 5: 12. And in Heb. 9:27, it is said that this awaits all men, that they die once.

But the fact that Enoch and Elijah were translated alive into heaven, and that those men whom the last day of the world will find alive will not undergo death (even though they themselves are mortal and would truly be about to die, unless the last day were to anticipate the end of life, or the death otherwise to be undergone), that is peculiar and extraordinary. And that these will undergo a change analogous to death, the apostle testifies in 1 Cor. 15: 51.

However, that change consists not in the troublesome or painful suffering of some adverse thing, which is similar to the dissolution of soul and body, but in the end of mortal or animal life, and the transition to another life or state (which otherwise and by common law does not happen except through the dissolution of soul and body), while in the meantime the soul and body remain joined by an essential bond; and such a change is indeed ἀνάλογος to death, yet it does not have the formal nature of death.

For thus it would not even be ἀνάλογος to death, but death itself.

And it is rightly said that this will not only happen to those men surviving on the last day, but also that it once happened to Enoch and Elijah. §

14. The final cause of death on the part of Satan is the fulfillment of hatred toward God and men; but on the part of God, the end of death, viewed in itself, is the vindication of sins, and thus also the declaration of divine justice. Which it is necessary to vary according to the diversity of the efficient or inflicting cause; concerning which see above § 4, 5, 6, 8.

Who undoubtedly intends it directly according to § 4 and 7, and that for the sake of some end, though not a true good, since he himself is most corrupt. For although that hatred of the evil spirit is insatiable, yet he strives to fulfill it in whatever way he can. Compare § 6 and 8.

Or insofar as death, such as it is by its own nature, and as it was first sent upon the human race by God, is considered. But it happened accidentally and by the grace of God that for certain subjects, namely believers in

For those reconciled to God and liberated from the guilt of sin, death is not a punishment, strictly speaking, but the end of temporal misery and a transition (μετάβασις) to a better life; see John 5:24. It is also called sleep (Matthew 9:24; John 11:11), a liberation from the body of this death (Romans 7:24), a longed-for dissolution (ἀπόλυσις) (Philippians 1:23; Luke 2:29), and an entry into rest from labors (Isaiah 57:2; Revelation 14:13).

Luther: "The tree of life, by reason of the Word, possessed the power of preserving life, and would have preserved Adam’s life as well. But God, in His wrath, does not wish to permit him, after the fall, to return to that tree—not only so that he might be admonished concerning the sin committed, but also because Adam already possessed a better promise, namely, that the seed of the woman would crush the head of the serpent. Thus, although he was subject to bodily death, he nevertheless retained the hope of immortality through the Son of God; just as an angry father, even if he does not take away his son’s right of inheritance, nevertheless chastises him, casts him out of the house, etc. The Lord God therefore wishes man to be content with the promise of a better life than that into which Adam was created. For even if Adam had eaten from the tree of life and had been restored to his former life, he would not have been safe from Satan, but would have fallen from it again through temptation. God therefore prepared for man such a state in which we may be certain that we shall never die the eternal death, through the blessed Seed, even though this bodily life is afflicted in various ways." (On Genesis 3:23-24. Exegetical Latin Works I, 291 sq.) §

15. Upon the dissolution of soul and body taking place, and thus death occurring, the soul nevertheless remains surviving and performs its operations separately outside the body. Thus Solomon, in Ecclesiastes 12:7, says that the dust or the body of man returns to the earth as it was, but the spirit returns to God who gave it. And Christ, in Matthew 10:28, says that those who kill the body cannot kill the soul.

Gerhard: "The arguments that are brought forward from the light of nature can induce a certain persuasion of probability regarding the immortality of the soul, but they by no means exhibit a firm, immovable, and ἀμετάπτωτον (unalterable) foundation of faith. 'For who knows,' says the wise man in Ecclesiastes 3:21, from natural principles and reasons, 'whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beasts goes downward?' ... That very thing is also evident from a passage in Cicero, Book I of the Tusculan Disputations, not far from the beginning. For there Atticus is introduced speaking thus: 'That sentiment delights me, that souls, when they have departed from bodies, can arrive in heaven as if it were their own home; and I would wish, first, that this is so, and second, even if it is not, that I might persuade myself of it.' Marcus replies: 'What need, then, is there for our work? Can we surpass Plato in eloquence? Unroll his book diligently, which is about the soul; there will be nothing more that you could desire.' Atticus adds: 'I have done so, by Hercules, and indeed quite often; but I do not know how it is, while I am reading, I assent; when I have put the book down and begin to think with myself about the immortality of souls, all that assent slips away.' The same doubt is proposed in Cato in Cicero’s Dialogue on Old Age. The opinions of the philosophers concerning the immortality of the soul are therefore subject to many doubts, and are not unlike the storms of winds and waves by which a ship, χειμαζομένη (tossed by a storm), is shaken at sea and driven hither and thither." (Book on Death § 147.) PART I. CHAPTER VIII.

PART. I. CAP. VIII.


### On Temporal Death: Suppose those things which formally pertain to the intellect and the will, as…

Suppose those things which formally pertain to the intellect and the will, as powers of the soul, insofar as it is human or rational, are essential; and it is rightly believed that these very things survive and are not idle, but rather that the intellect indeed retains the intelligible species which it had in the body, and thus can even continue to elicit acts of knowing, to which then certain acts of the will regarding objects exhibited by the intellect may respond. And it is to this that the passage in Rev. 6:10 is usually referred, where a knowledge of their former state and a certain desire are ascribed to the souls of the martyrs.

Gerhard: "Because he (Moses) appears together with Elijah at the transfiguration of Christ, speaking with Christ (Matt. 17:3), it is therefore probable that Moses was immediately resurrected by God after his death and translated into the heavenly paradise; in which sense it is accepted by some that no one found his sepulcher (Deut. 34:6)." (Loc. de resurr. § 28.)

Dannhauer: "That he (Moses) had risen before the transfiguration on the mountain is more than probable; for he appeared not as a phantom, but as a fellow tribesman and companion of Elijah in testimony of the resurrection and glory of Christ. Although D. Winckelmann follows a different opinion in Luke ch. 9." (Hodos. Phaen. VIII. p. 375.)

For thus we are said to be pilgrims (according to the soul, by which we are most truly human) away from the body, ἐκδημῆσαι ἐκ τοῦ σώματος; when previously we were as if at home in the body, ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι (2 Cor. 5:6 and 8), ὄντες ἐν τῷ σκήνει, existing in the tabernacle, previously (ibid. v. 1). However, we do not say that the souls of the departed know distinctly and determinately the actions and individual affairs of the living which have occurred after their departure from the body, especially the prayers and various acts of worship directed to them.

Dannhauer: "That damned souls can return by a right of postliminy, even the Romanists deny. I. That holy or heavenly souls can return, the Holy Scriptures deny (2 Sam. 12:23): 'Can I bring him back?' (by prayers); likewise: 'He shall not return' (Sirach 38:22), i.e., according to the genius of the language, he cannot return; 'οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἐπάνοδος' (Luke 16:26), 'ὅπως οἱ βουλόμενοι διαβῆναι' (scil. from heavenly glory) 'ἐντεῦθεν πρὸς ὑμᾶς μὴ δύνωνται.' If not to the damned, then neither to mortals. The same reason for the impossibility exists on both sides: filth is not to be mixed with that lot. I add a reason: A holy soul appears either in its own body, or in another's, or in one newly formed of air. None of these [is possible]. Not in its own, because it is neither honorable nor decent for glorious souls to undergo the straits of their own dissolving and decaying bodies before the resurrection, especially if they have long since rotted; not in another's, because that is less becoming and furthermore repugnant to the purpose of the apparition, which is to be recognized by the genuine and proper features and marks of the remains; not in an airy one, because a separated soul cannot move things other than itself by its own power according to the truer opinion; for it lacks bodily organs. Furthermore, it must be denied II. that holy heavenly beings ought to return, because those ψυχοφανεῖαι (soul-apparitions) would profit mortals nothing, but rather would be harmful. First, it is not useful to the living, who, if they do not believe the living, will not believe the dead either, as Abraham answers the rich man. Then, that matter could be the cause of many errors, while the devil, feigning that he is the soul of some dead person, would mock men. III. It must be denied that they would prudently wish to. For why should those who are exempt from all torments and are now blessed, being worshipped by mortals—as they say—serve mortals? It must be denied IV. that this has ever happened. For whatever is proclaimed concerning their apparitions, all of that could also be done by Satan, transforming himself into an angel of light or, like a hyena, simulating the voice of the shepherd in order to devour the sheep." (Hodosoph. Phaen. IV. p. 213 sq.)

Quenstedtius: "He whom we religiously invoke must be omnipresent, omnipotent, and omniscient, and in him we must believe and hope. But the saints are not omnipresent, not omnipotent, not omniscient, and in them we do not believe, nor do we hope. Therefore.

The major premise is established; namely, that he who is invoked is omnipresent is taught in Deut. 4:7, Ps. 91:15, 145:18, Isa. 55:6. Therefore, the prophet Elijah mocks the prayers of the priests of Baal, because Baal, when invoked, is not present. That he is omniscient and καρδιογνώστης is inculcated in 1 Kings 18:27, Ps. 18:7, 38:10, 79:11, Matt. 6:6. That he is and must be omnipotent (so that he may be able to succor our defects) Scripture shows throughout; see Ps. 46:1, 2, 62:10, 11, etc. That we must believe and hope in him whom we invoke, the apostle teaches in Rom. 10:14: 'How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?'

The truth of the minor premise is not doubtful, since God alone is καρδιογνώστης, he alone is everywhere present, he alone is omnipotent, so that he can both hear and answer. And since the already stated axiom of Paul is immovable, that one should not invoke any except him in whom we have believed (Rom. 10:14), I do not see by what reasoning the saints and angels are said to be invocable, without thereby being constituted as the pillar and object of our faith—which, how alien it is to Scripture, will be evident to anyone reading the passage in Jer. 17:5.

That the object of adoration in the Decalogue, the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, and Baptism is the same, is evident from the very coordination of these heads of religion. But in the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, and Baptism, there is no object of adoration other than God; cf. Luke 11:12, 13; Matt. 6:9. Hence the saying attributed to Celestine: 'The law of praying is the law of believing and acting.' ...

Those who are ignorant of our defects and private miseries, cares, groans, and sighs are invoked in vain. But the heavenly saints are ignorant of our defects, etc. Therefore.

We distinguish, however, here between general and special knowledge, and also between the remembrance (ἀνάμνησις) of past things and the knowledge (γνῶσις) of present things. Thus, that rich man carried with him the memory of his five brothers, etc. Although, therefore, the blessed in general know some things about the state of the militant church, with which they once served under the banner of the cross, and from that may pray in general for the church, nevertheless they are entirely ignorant of the particulars (τὰ καθ’ ἕκαστα), the private miseries, cares, groans, and sighs of each individual.

And consequently, that nothing can be obtained from them by us who are removed from this life is evident: 1) From open testimonies, Job 14:21: 'His sons come to honor, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not of them.' Eccles. 9:5: 'The living know that they shall die, but the dead know not anything anymore.' Isa. 63:16: 'Abraham is ignorant of us, and Israel acknowledgeth us not'; cf. 2 Kings 22:20. 2. From the perpetual joy of the blessed, 2 Kings 22:19, 20; Isa. 65:17, 18; Rev. 21:4. Therefore, they are ignorant of the miseries of their descendants, for by them their joy would be disturbed." (L. c. P. IV. c. 11. s. 2. q. 4. f. 1446. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Collyridians, who offered religious worship and adoration to the blessed Virgin, against whom Epiphanius, disputing in Haer. 79, speaks thus: 'Let Mary be in honor; but let the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit be adored; let no one adore Mary.' Likewise: 'Although Mary was most beautiful (καλλίστη) and holy (ἁγία) and honored (τετιμημένη), she is not for that reason to be adored.'

2. Of the Papists, who 1) in general defend the invocation of saints. For thus the Council of Trent, Sess. 25, p. 290: 'The holy synod commands all bishops and others sustaining the office and care of teaching, that according to the usage of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, etc., they diligently instruct the faithful concerning the invocation of saints, teaching them that the saints reigning together with Christ offer their prayers to God for men, and that it is good and useful to invoke them suppliantly.' The Tridentine Catechism, edited by the decree of the council and the command of Pius V, in the exposition of the Lord's Prayer, p. 544, says: 'That prayers are to be made to the saints who are in heaven is so certain in the Church of God that no doubt can occur to the pious concerning it.' ...

2) In particular, they make the deceased saints or blessed humans: a. Intercessors. Hence that common saying: 'Pray for us' ...; b. Mediators, who not only by prayer..." PART I. CHAP. VIII.

but that they intercede for us by the showing of their merits. . .

They are also, according to the Papists, redeemers. Bellarmine, L. 1. de indulgent, c. 4., pronounces that "it is not absurd if holy men are in some way called our redeemers.". .

d. Dispensers of bodily and spiritual goods. The Council of Trent, Sess. 9 and last, wills that "the saints are to be invoked with confidence, by fleeing with a suppliant mind to their help and aid.". .

However, these things which we have said thus far concerning the saints and their cult and adoration according to the mind and πράξιν of the Papists are to be understood of the saints especially canonized, or those brought by the Pope into the canon or number of the saints. For although the Papists concede that each one of the saints can be honored and invoked, yet they decree that public cult is to be rendered only to those who are canonized." (L. c. f. 1444. sq.) §

16. Indeed, we believe that the souls of the pious, immediately after they are separated from their bodies, attain essential blessedness, but that the souls of the impious undergo their damnation. See Ep. to Phil. 1:23, where Paul desires dissolution for this reason, that he might be more quickly with Christ, that is, in the glorious kingdom of Christ; so that to be with Christ is the same for him as to enjoy blessedness with Christ. And Christ Himself said to the penitent thief: Today you will be with me in paradise, that is, you will enjoy heavenly glory with me, Luke 23:43. Furthermore, what Christ says in John 5:24, that those who believe in Him pass from death into life, indicates that the faithful who die are immediately made partakers of eternal life. And in Rev. 7:4 and 15, the souls of the blessed martyrs are said to be before the throne of God and to serve Him day and night; which is certainly a description of blessedness. See Mus. Ausführl. Erklärung L. XIX. Q. XCII. p. 700. sqq.

Dannhauerus: ״Damnatas animas postliminio redire posse, ipsi Romanenses inficiantur. I. Animas sanctas seu coelites redire posse, negant sacrae literae (2 Sam. 12, 23.): ,Num potero eum‘ (precibus),reducere?‘ item: ,Non revertetur‘ (Syrae. 38, 22.), i. e. ex genio linguae, redire pqtest; ,ον γάρ έστιν επάνοδος (Luc. 16, 26.), 'όπως 01 βονλοντες όιαβτ/ναι (sci. e coelesti gloria) έντεϋ·&εν προς νμπς μη δννωνται.1, Si non ad damnatos, ergo nec ad mortales. Eadem ratio impossibilitatis utrobique: sordes cum illa sorte non miscendae. Addo rationem: Anima sancta aut apparet in proprio corpore, aut in alieno, aut aereo recens efformato. Nihil horum 1 Non in proprio, quia nec honestum, nec decens est, gloriosas animas corporum suorum diffluentium et tabidorum angustias ante resurrectionem subire, maxime si diu computruerint; non in alieno, quia id minus decet ac insuper fini apparitionis repugnat, qui est, germanis et propriis lineamentis atque notis exuviarum agnosci; non aereo, quia anima separata non potest vi propria alia a se movere ex veriore sententia; caret enim organis corporeis. Negandum insuper II., coelites sanctos debere redire, quia illae ■ψυχοφανεϊαι nihil mortalibus profuturae, imo obfuturae essent. Primum id vivis utile non est, qui, si vivis non credunt, nec mortuis quidem credent, ut Abraham diviti respondet. Deinde, ea res multorum errorum causa esse posset, dum daemon, fingens, se alicujus mortui esse animam, homines ludificaret. III. Negandum, prudenter velle. Cur enim, qui tormentis omnibus exemti ac modo beati, a mortalibus δονλείμ, ut ajunt, adorandi, servirent mortalibus? Negandum IV., aliquando id factum esse. Quidquid enim de illarum apparitionibus praedicatur, id omne a Satana quoque fleri potuit, se in angelum lucis transformante aut hyenae instar pastoris vocem simulante, ut oves deglutiat.“

Quenstedtius: ,,Quem religiose invocamus, is debet esse omnipraesens, omnipotens, omniscius, in eumque credere et sperare debemus. Atqui sancti non sunt omnipraesentes, non omnipotentes, non omniscii, in eosque non credimus, non speramus. Ergo.

Major constat; sci. quod, qui invocatur, sit omnipraesens, docetur Deut. 4, 7. Ps. 91, 15. 145, 18. Esa. 55, 6. Ridet igitur propheta Elias preces sacerdotum Baalitarum, eo, quod Baal invocatus non adsit. Quod sit omniscius et καρδιογνώστης, inculcatur 1 Reg. 18, 27. Ps. 18, 7. 38, 10. 79, 11. Matth. 6, 6. Quod sit et debeat esse omnipotens (ut sci. possit succurrere defectibus nostris), passim Scriptura ostendit; vide Ps. 46, 1. 2. 62, 10.11. etc. Quod in eum, quem invocamus, debeamus credere et sperare, docet apostolus Rom. 10, 14.: ,Quomodo invocabunt eum, in quem non crediderunt?‘

Minoris veritas non est dubia, cum solus Deus sit καρδιογνώστης, ipse solus ubique praesens, ipse solus omnipotens, ut et audire et exaudire possit. Et cum jam dictum axioma Pauli sit immotum, non invocandum, nisi eum, in quem crediderimus, Rom. 10, 14., non video, qua ratione dicantur sancti angelique invocandi, quin eo ipso fidei nostrae columen et objectum constituantur, quod quam sit a Scriptura alienum, patebit cuivis legenti locum Jer. 17, 5.

Idem esse objectum adorationis in decalogo et symbolo et oratione dominica et baptismo, ex ipsa coordinatione horum religionis capitum patet. Sed in symbolo, oratione dominica et baptismo non est objectum adorationis aliud praeter Deum, cf. Luc. 11, 12. 13. Matth. 6, 9. Hinc Coelestino tributum dictum: ,Legem orandi esse legem credendi et agendi.‘ . .

Qui defectus nostros privatasque miserias, curas, gemitus et suspiria ignorant, illi frustra invocantur. Sed sancti coelites defectus nostros etc. ignorant. Ergo.

Disting. autem hic inter notitiam generalem et specialem, item inter praeteritorum άνάμνησιν et praesentium γνώσιν. Sic dives ille memoriam quinque fratrum suorum secum extulit etc. Quamvis itaque beati in genere nonnulla de statu militantis ecclesiae, cum qua sub vexillo crucis aliquando meruerunt, sciant, indeque in genere pro ecclesia orent, attamen τα καά’ εκαστα, privatas unius cujusque miserias, curas, gemitus et suspiria omnino ignorant.

Et proinde, nihil ab illis ex hac vita a nobis ablatis impetrari posse, patet: 1) ex apertis testimoniis, Job. 14, 21.: ,Sive nobiles fuerint filii ejus, sive ignobiles, nihil intelligent.‘ Eccles. 9, 5.: ,Viventes sciunt, se morituros, mortui vero nihil noverunt amplius.‘ Esa. 63,16.: ,Abraham nescit nos, et Israel ignorat nos‘; cf. 2 Reg. 22, 20. 2. Ex beatorum perpetua laetitia, 2 Reg. 22, 19. 20. Esa. 65, 17. 18. Apoc. 21, 4. Ergo miserias posterorum suorum ignorant, quippe quibus laetitia ipsorum turbaretur.“ (L. c. P. IV. c. 11. s. 2. q. 4. f. 1446. sq.)

Collyridianorum, qui b. virgini religionis cultum et adorationem deferebant, contra quos Epiphanius haer. 79. disputans, ita loquitur: ,In honore esto Maria; Pater vero et Filius et Spiritus S. adoretur, Mariam nemo adoret.‘ Item: ,Quamvis Maria καλλίστη καϊ άγία, και τετψένη fuerit, non idcirco tamen est adoranda.‘

Sess. 25. p. 290.: ,Mandat sancta synodus omnibus episcopis et caeteris docendi munus curamque sustinentibus, ut juxta catholicae et apostolicae ecclesiae usum etc. de sanctorum invocatione fideles diligenter instruant, docentes eos, sanctos una cum Christo regnantes orationes suas pro hominibus Deo offerre, bonum atque utile esse, suppliciter eos invocare.‘ Catechismus Trid. decreto concilii et Pii V. jussu editus exposit. orat. dom. p. 544. ait: ,Sanctis, qui in coelo sunt, preces eSse faciendas, ita certum esse in ecclesia Dei, ut piis nulla de eo dubitatio possit accidere.‘ . .

bus, sed meritorum ostensione pro nobis intercedant. . .
