d. Bonorum corporalium et spiritualium largitores. Cone. Trid. Sess. 9. et ult. vult, ,fiducialiter invocandos esse sanctos, supplici mente confugiendo ad eorum opem et auxilium.‘ . .

Intelligenda autem ista, quae hactenus de sanctis eorumque cultu et adoratione juxta mentem et πράξιν pontificiorum diximus, de sanctis potissimtfln canonizatis sive a pontifice in canonem vel numerum sanctorum relatis. Quamvis enim concedant pontificii, unumquemque sanctorum coli et invocari posse, tamen cultum publicum non nisi canonizatis praestandum esse statuunt.“ (L. c. f. 1444. sq.) §

16. Imo piorum animas statim, postquam a corporibus sunt separatae, essentialem beatitudinem consequi,a impiorum vero animas damnationem suam subire,b credimus.c Vid. Ep. ad Phil. 1, 23., ubi Paulus ideo dissolutionem desiderat, ut citius sit cum Christo, id est, in regno Christi glorioso; ita ut esse cum Christo idem illi sit ac beatitudine frui cum Christo. Et ipse Christus latroni poenitenti dixit: Hodie mecum eris in paradiso, id est, coelesti gloria mecum frueris, Luc. 23, 43. Quod porro Christus dicit Joh. 5, 24., credentes in ipsum transire de morte in vitam, indicat, fideles morientes statim participes reddi vitae aeternae. Et Apoc. 7, 4. et 15. dicuntur animae beatorum martyrum esse ante thronum Dei et servire ei die ac nocte; quae utique est quaedam beatitudinis descriptio. Videatur Mus. Ausführl. Erklärung L. XIX. Q. XCII. p. 700. sqq.


### On Temporal Death: Quenstedtius: "Concerning the state of souls separated from the body, there are…

Quenstedtius: "Concerning the state of souls separated from the body, there are chiefly three opinions. The first of which maintains that they neither perceive nor understand anything, nor rejoice nor grieve, but are held in oblivion of all things and sleep as if seized by a deep slumber. Whence the defenders of this opinion are called Psychopannychites. The second is that the souls of the pious after death are indeed in refreshment and rest, and already have a foretaste of that heavenly blessedness, but that they will attain the complete and consummated possession of it only on the last day. The third, and the truer one, teaches that full and consummated blessedness, which consists in the clear and intuitive vision of God, is obtained by the souls of the pious, and that immediately from death and before the universal resurrection of bodies. D. Koenig, in Theol. positiva §291, calls this blessedness of separated souls 'consummated in a certain respect'; but he calls that absolutely consummated which belongs to the whole composite after the reunion of soul and body. . . Whence the soul, before the body is united to it, has not yet attained all-around perfection, but on account of its extension to the body, it awaits the absolutely consummated or full and perfect blessedness, viewed extensively, that is, only on the last day. Therefore, the blessedness of the soul will not be increased intensively and in itself, but extensively and extrinsically, that is, through the glory of the body, when the revived body shall be assumed into the communion of joy and the fellowship of heavenly glory. And this is what the blessed Gerhard means when, in LL. th. loc. ult. de vita aeterna § 109, he says: 'The elect men in this life perceive a certain πρόγενσιν of heavenly goods and joys.'"

Dannhauer: "The psychopannychia is a fable contrary to the Holy Scriptures, in which the martyrs in Rev. 6:10-11 cry out with a loud voice under the altar: 'How long, O Lord, do you not avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?' To them white robes were given, and it was said to them that they should rest for a little while longer, etc. But those who are clothed in white robes, which are signs of glory and festivity, are not sleepers, but watchers. Nor are they to be called sleepers who cry out and follow the Lamb wherever He goes; to whom the death of the pious is gain and a metabasis eis zoen [transition into life], John 5:24. What does he gain who sleeps for so many centuries? It would have been better to have remained in the body and enjoyed the first fruits of the Spirit. Does he who snores fully enjoy life? Why does Paul desire apolysin [departure] if he were to migrate to the slumber of so many centuries? 'If,' says Cicero, lib. 5 de finib. n. 55, p. 154, 'anyone would wish to live ninety years in such a way that, when he has lived sixty, he sleeps the rest? Not even pigs would want that.' Did Moses and Elijah sleep when they delighted in conversation with Christ? Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Matt. 17:4, when they reclined at the heavenly table? Matt. 8:11. Surely as Moses, Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu were delighted and feasted by the vision of God, Exod. 28:11." (L. c. Phaenom. p. 719.) Luther: "A man in this life, exhausted by daily labor, enters his chamber at night as if into peace, so that he may sleep there, and in that night he enjoys rest, and knows nothing of any evil, whether of fire or slaughter. But the soul does not sleep in this way, but watches and suffers visions, the speech of angels and of God." (Exeget. opp. lat. Tom. VI. p. 120.) The same: "Therefore the end makes a very great difference between the suffering of Christians and the ungodly. For although both are stabbed and killed at the same time, a Christian is led straight into eternal joy, but the ungodly into the abyss of hell." (Ad Joh. 1:11. Tom. Hai. VII. p. 1518.) The same: "Therefore we should also be firmly assured concerning our U. Rhegius... that he is blessed and has eternal life and joy in the communion of Christ and the triumphant Church in heaven, where he now presently learns, sees, and hears that which he taught here in the militant Church according to the prescription of the divine Word." (Preface to Rhegius' Explanation of the Prophecies of the O.T. concerning Christ. 1542. Tom. Hai. T. XIV, 166.) Dannhauer: "Something must be said in this place about the apparition of Samuel, which we conclude was not true, but impersonated, by this syllogism: He appeared to Saul who 1. was not a prophet; for God was not about to answer him through a living prophet, v. 6; who 2. could be disturbed, v. 15; who 3. could say that Saul would be with him tomorrow together with his sons, not only in status but also in location, v. 19; who 4. allowed himself to be worshipped, v. 14. But truly 1. Samuel was a prophet, Acts 3:24; 2. he could not be disturbed, for he was already secured in eternal rest; 3. he could not say without a lie that Saul and the sons of Saul would be with him tomorrow; for how could a fellow tribesman of Samuel (either in limbo, according to the adversaries, or in heaven according to us), who died in sin, have departed from the station of life without the command of the supreme Commander? 4. He would never have endured being worshipped with adoration bowed to the ground. This likewise by a dilemma: Either these spirits were called forth by a most impure Pythoness, or they came of their own accord, or they were returned by God Himself through the prevention of incantation. All are absurd! All are impious! The first, for how could demons thrust down from heaven pass judgment on citizens who are already triumphant in heaven? The second, because it is not credible that one who knows necromancy is forbidden by law would come of his own accord. The third, because it is blasphemous to think that God, against the law laid down by Himself, would have wished to disturb a most blessed soul for the curiosity of a most wicked king, in a work most worthy of eternal flames... 'But, it must be said either that Scripture lied, which calls him Samuel, or that the prophecy could have been from a power other than divine.' Resp.: Neither follows; for Scripture also calls Baal a god, yet it does not lie... If therefore neither damned nor blessed souls PART I. CAP. VIII. can return, it remains, as we have said, that the prince of darkness hides under these masks; for no persuasion has yet been able to convince anyone of a third state of souls, a conflict in that kingdom, for which the air is darkness, impudence is a wall, and purgatorial flame is the light of faith." (L. c. p. 214.) Cf. Luther, Opp. Hai. XIX, 1392. sqq. Fechtius: "As those twice dead, out of the ordinary, to declare divine power, twice paid the debt of nature, so it is not absurd that their souls were also out of the ordinary in a third place or state and remained stained by original sin." (Syll. controv. p. 375.) ANTITHESES: Quenstedt: "Antithesis:

1. Of the Psychopannychites, who dreamed of a certain sleep of souls resting in the grave or a common receptacle; which opinion Jerome attributes to Vigilantius (or rather Dormitantius, because he looked out for the salvation of his soul less vigilantly) in his book against the same. The Armenians held the same among the ancient heretics, establishing that all souls, even those of the saints, are kept until the last day of judgment in certain hidden receptacles, where they neither see God nor can be called blessed, except in hope. Because of which dogma they were condemned for heresy by Innocent III and Benedict XI. To this opinion (which Sixtus Senensis calls the error of the Armenians, Biblioth. s. 1. 6. annot. 345. p. m. 714.), condemned by the decretal epistles of Innocent III and Benedict XI, Roman Pontiffs (of whom Innocent III sat at the beginning of the 13th century), John XXII, Roman Pontiff after the beginning of the following 14th century, subscribed and sanctioned by decree that it is to be believed so...

2. Of some fathers of the Greek as well as the Latin church, asserting: 'The souls of the saints, released from their bodies, are not immediately admitted to the beatific vision of God, but are detained in certain fixed receptacles outside of heaven, where they neither suffer anything evil nor feel joy and refreshment, until the last day, and not until that finally dawns, and they are reunited with their bodies through the resurrection, do they become participants in their beatitude.' ... Thus Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, Lactantius, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others...

3. Of the Socinians, according to whom the separated soul before the resurrection feels, does, or suffers nothing, i.e., it neither enjoys heavenly beatitude nor is affected by infernal punishments...

9. Of the Papists, who (if their hypotheses are heeded) are forced to concede that the souls of the pious after death, if not all, at least those who bring with them venial sins not yet remitted and temporal punishments to be paid for mortal sins, do not immediately arrive at heavenly beatitude and are not admitted to the vision of God, but for a certain time and sometimes a sufficiently long one, lack this glory." (P. IV. c. 17. s. 2. q. 5. f. 1745. sqq.) Hofmann: "The state of the dead is of a similar kind in body and soul. Whoever departs without hope of salvation, his body is also hopelessly subject to death; whoever dies in faith, his soul is in a state which corresponds to the death-state of his decaying body, which is awaiting resurrection." (Schriftbeweis. Ed. 2. P. II, 480.) The same: "After Christ's transfigured corporeality has become the house of God, and the communion of the believer with God is communion with Christ, who lives super-worldly in a transfigured human nature, the Christian has the blessed certainty that his communion with Christ, when he departs from earthly life, continues in the heavenly house of God. Even bodiless, he will have as his dwelling the body in which the fullness of the Godhead dwells. If Christ let His own, as long as they were separated from Him by the nature of their condition, live personally in Him, the bodily living One; so now, after they have lost their own nature, He lets His be theirs instead of their own."

The same: "In bodily death, man ceases to possess himself as the means of his own self-activity. But what is called spiritual death, and what is called eternal death, is something other than this. Bodily death is in itself a death forever, and that a second one follows it comes merely from the fact that the annihilation of the material, which is proper to the individual for his self-activity, only occurs with the end of all history of the race, with the transformation of the entire physical creation." (Schriftbeweis. I, 430.)

Latin:

Quenstedtius: ,,De statu animarum a corpore separatarum tres sunt potissimum sententiae. Quarum prima statuit, eas nec sentire quicquam, aut intelligere, nec laetari aut tristari, sed rerum omnium oblivione detineri et profundo quasi somno correptas dormire. Unde et hujus opinionis defensores dicti sunt Psychopannychitae. Secunda est, animas piorum post mortem in refrigerio quidem ac quiete esse, jamque coelestis illius beatitudinis praegustum habere, ipsam vero completam et consummatam possessionem ejus in extremo die demum eas adepturas esse. Tertia eaque verior docet, plenam consummatamque beatitudinem, quae in clara et intuitiva Dei visione consistit, animabus piorum obtingere, idque statim a morte et ante universalem resurrectionem corporum. Hanc animarum separatarum beatitudinem D. Koenig. in Theol. positiva §291. appellat,consummatam secundum quid‘; absolute vero consummatam vocat eam, quae est totius compositi post animae et corporis redunitionem. . . Unde anima, antequam corpus ei uniatur, omnimodam perfectionem hactenus adepta non est, sed propter extensionem ad corpus absolute consummatam seu plenam et perfectam beatitudinem, extensive sci. spectatam, in extremo die demum expectat. Non augebitur ergo beatitudo animae intensive et in se, sed extensive et extrinsece, sci. per gloriam corporis, quando in communionem laetitiae et gloriae coelestis consortium corpus redivivum assumetur. Et hoc vult b. Gerhardus, quando in LL. th. loc. ult. de vita aeterna § 109. inquit: ,Homines electi in hac vita πρόγενσιν quandam coelestium bonorum ac gaudiorum percipiunt.‘ “

Dannhauerus: ,,*υχοπαννυχία fabula est sacris literis adversa, in quibus martyres Apoc. 6, 10. 11. voce magna sub altari clamant: ,Usque quo, Domine, non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his, qui habitant in terra?‘ Iisdem datae sunt stolae albae, et dictum est eis, ut requiescerent adhuc paululum temporis etc. At stolis albis, quae gloriae et festivitatis indices sunt, non dormientes, sed vigiles induuntur. Neque dormire dicendi, qui clamant et sequuntur agnum, quocunque iverit; quibus mors piorum lucrum et μετάβασις εις ζωί/ν Joh. 5, 24. vocatur. Quid lucratur, qui tot saeculis dormit? Praestitisset, in corpore mansisse et primitiis Spiritus frui. An vita plene fruitur, qui stertit? Cur apolysin Paulus optat, si ad tot saeculorum soporem illi migrandum fuerit? ,Si‘, inquit Cicero lib. 5. de finib. n.· 55. p. 154., ,quispiam ita nonaginta annos velit vivere, ut, cum sexaginta vixerit, reliquos dormiat? Ne sues quidem id velint.‘ Anne dormierunt Moses et Elias, cum Christi se colloquio oblectarunt? Abraham, Isaac et Jacob, Matth. 17, 4., cum mensae coelesti accubuerunt? Matth. 8, 11. Nimirum ut Moses, Aaron, Nadab et Abihu Dei visione oblectati epulati sunt, Exod. 28, 11.“ (L. c. Phaenom. p. 719.) Lutherus: ,,Homo in hac vita defatigatus diurno labore sub noctem intrat in cnbiculum suum tanquam in pace, ut ibi dormiat, et ea nocte fruitur quiete, neque quidquam scit de ullo malo sive incendii, sive caedis. Anima autem non sic dormit, sed vigilat et patitur visiones, loquelas angelorum et Dei.“ (Exeget. opp. lat. Tom. VI. p. 120.) Idem: ,,Darum machet das Ende gar einen grossen Unterschied unter dem Leiden der Christen und der Gottlosen. Denn ob sie schon beide zugleich erstochen und umgebracht werden, so führet doch ein Christ von Mund auf in die ewige Freude, der Gottlose aber in Abgrund der Höllen.“ (Ad Joh. 1, 11. Tom. Hai. VII. p. 1518.) Idem: ,,Derowegen sollen wir auch von unserm U. Rhegio. . . gewiss versichert sein, dass er selig sei und das ewige Leben und Freude habe in der Gemeinschaft Christi und der triumphirenden Kirche im Himmel, allwo er nun gegenwärtig dasjenige lernet, siehet und höret, davon er hier in der streitenden Kirche nach der Vorschrift göttlichen Wortes gelehret hat.“ (Vorr. über Rhegii Erkl. der Prophezeyungen A. T. von Christo. 1542. Tom. Hai. T. XIV, 166.) Dannhauerus: ,,De Samuelis apparitione aliquid dicendum hoc loco, quem verum non fuisse, sed personatum, hoc syllogismo conficimus: Is apparuit Sauli, qui 1. propheta non fuit; non enim erat illi Deus responsurus per prophetam vivum, v. 6.; qui 2. inquietari potuit, v. 15.; qui 3. dicere potuit, fore Saulem una cum filiis cras secum non status solum, sed et loci ratione, v. 19.; qui 4. se adorari passus, v. 14. At vero 1. Samuel propheta fuit, Act. 3, 24.; 2. inquietari non potuit, erat enim jam dum aeternae quieti assertus; 3. sine mendacio dicere non potuit, fore Saulem et filios Saulis cras secum; quomodo enim contribulis Samuelis (vel in limbo, juxta adversarios, vel in coelo juxta nos), qui in peccato mortuus, injussu summi Imperatoris de statione vitae decessit? 4. nunquam se adorari sustinuisset adoratione incurvata ad terram. Hoc itidem dilemmate: Aut ab impurissima Pythonissa evoeati hi manes fuerunt, aut ultro venerunt, aut per incantationis praeventionem ab ipso Deo redditi fuerunt. Omnia absurda! Omnia impia! Primum,.qui enim possint triumphantibus jam coeli civibus jus dicere coelo detrusi daemones? Secundum, quia non credibile, ultro venturum, qui sciat νεκρομαντείαν lege vetitam. Tertium, quia blasphemum, cogitare, Deum contra legem a se latam ad praevias necromantiae dispositiones, in opere aeternis flammis dignissimo, beatissimam animam ad nequissimi regis curiositatem inquietare voluisse. . . . ,At, vel dicendum, Scripturam esse mentitam, quae Samuelem appellat, vel prophetiam ex alia, quam divina, virtute esse potuisse.‘ Resp.: Neutrum sequitur; nam et Scriptura Baalem Deum vocat, neque tamen mentitur. . . Si ergo nec damnatae, nec beatae animae PART. I. CAP. VIII. redire possunt, manet, quod diximus, principem tenebrarum sub istis larvis latere; nam tertium animarum statum, in illo regno conflictum, cui caligo aer est, impudentia murus, flamma purgatoria lux fidei, nulla adhuc suada persuadere potuit.“ (L. c. p. 214.) Cf. Lutherus, Opp. Hai. XIX, 1392. sqq. Fechtius: ,,Ut bis demortui extra ordinem, ad declarandam divinam potentiam, bis naturae debitum solverunt, ita et extra ordinem eorum animas in loco statuve tertio fuisse et labe originali commaculatas mansisse, absurdum non est.“ (Syll. controv. p. 375.) ANTITHESES: Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis:

1. Psychopannychitarum, qui animarum dormitionem quandam in sepulchro vel communi receptaculo quiescentium somniarunt; quam opinionem Hieronymus Vigilantio (Dormitantio potius, quia minus vigilanter de animae suae salute sibi prospexit) in libro adversus eundem tribuit. Eandem tenuerunt ex antiquis haereticis Armeni, statuentes, quod animae omnes, quantumvis sanctorum, usque ad ultimum judicii diem serventur in quibusdam abditis receptaculis, ubi nec Deum videant, nec beatae dici possint, nisi in spe. Ob quod dogma ab Innocentio III. et Benedicto XI. haereseos sunt damnati. Opinioni huic (quam Armenorum errorem vocat Sixtus Senensis Biblioth. s. 1. 6. annot. 345. p. m. 714.), damnatae decretalibus epistolis Innocentii III. et Benedicti XI. Rom. pontif. (ex quibus Innocentius III. sedit sub initium saeculi 13.), Johannes XXII., pont. Rom. post initium saeculi sequentis 14., subscripsit et decreto sancivit, sic esse credendum. . .

2. Nonnullorum patrum graecae pariter ac latinae ecclesiae, asserentium: ,Sanctorum animas corporibus suis solutas non statim ad beatificum Dei aspectum admitti, sed certis statisque extra coelum receptaculis, ubi nec mali quicquam patiantur, nec laetitiam et refocillationem sentiant, usque ad novissimum diem detineri, nec nisi illo demum illucescente, ipsisque cum corporibus per resurrectionem redunitis, suae beatitudinis participes fieri.‘ . . Ita Justinus, Irenaeus, Tertullianus, Origenes, Lactantius, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus aliique. . .

3. Socinianorum, juxta quos anima separata ante resurrectionem nihil sentit, agit aut patitur, h. e. nec coelesti beatitudine fruitur, nec poenis infernalibus afficitur. . .

9. Pontificiorum, qui (si hypotheses eorum attendantur) concedere coguntur, animas piorum post mortem, si non omnes, saltem eas, quae peccata venialia nondum remissa et poenas temporales pro peccatis mortalibus luendas secum apportant, non statim ad beatitudinem coelestem pervenire et ad visionem Dei admitti, sed ad certum tempus et interdum satis diuturnum hac gloria carere.“ (P. IV. c. 17. s. 2. q. 5. f. 1745. sqq.) Hofmannus: ,,Der Zustand der Todten ist ein gleichartiger an Leib und Seele. Wer ohne Hoffnung des Heils absqheidet, dessen Leib ist auch hoffnungslos dem Tode verfallen; wer im Glauben stirbt, dessen Seele ist in einem Zustande, welcher dem Todeszustande seines verwesenden, aber der Auferweckung entgegenwartenden Leibes entspricht.“ (Schriftbeweis. Ed. 2. P. II, 480.) Idem: ,,Nachdem Christi verklärte Leiblichkeit das Haus Gottes geworden, und die Gottesgemeinschaft des Gläubigen Gemeinschaft mit dem in verklärter Menschennatur überweltlich lebenden Christus ist, hat der Christ die selige Gewissheit, dass sich seine Gemeinschaft mit Christo, wenn er aus dem irdischen Leben scheidet, in dem himmlischen Hause Gottes fortsetzt. Selbst körperlos, wird er den Leib, in welchem die Fülle der Gottheit wohnt, zu seiner Wohnung haben. Hat Christus die Seinen, so lange sie durch die Beschaffenheit ihrer Natur von ihm geschieden waren, persönlich in ihm, dem leiblich lebenden, leben lassen; so lässt er ihnen nun, nachdem sie ihrer Natur verlustig geworden, die seine statt der eignen sein.“

Idem: ״Im leiblichen Tode hört der Mensch auf, sich selbst zum Mittel seiner Selbstbethätigung zu besitzen. Etwas anderes aber, als dies, ist weder, was man den geistlichen, noch was man den ewigen Tod nennt. Der leibliche Tod ist an sich ein Tod für immer, und dass ihm noch ein zweiter folgt, kommt blos davon, dass die Vernichtung des Stofflichen, welches dem Einzelnen zu seiner Selbstbethätigung eignet, erst mit dem Ende aller Geschichte des Geschlechts, mit der Wandlung der gesammten körperlichen Schöpfung eintritt.“ (Schriftbeweis. I, 430.)


### On Temporal Death: For the reasoning regarding opposites is similar

For the reasoning regarding opposites is similar. And see 1 Peter 3:19, where Christ, descending to the dead, is said to have preached to the spirits who were then in prison, namely to those who were disobedient in the time of Noah, and were therefore enclosed in prison. And the souls that are in that prison are undoubtedly rejected from the face of God and are afflicted with connected punishments. Certainly, a purgatory or penal state of the faithful—who are indeed heirs of eternal life, but not yet fully purged of sins in this life—and therefore intermediate between life and damnation, ought not to be imagined.

S. Niemann: "Just as Scripture recognizes only two orders of men, of whom some are believers, others unbelievers, Mark 16:16, John 8:18; some blessed, others cursed, Matthew 25:34, 41; some sheep, others goats, ibid. v. 33: so also it mentions only two receptacles: namely, heaven, into which the souls of the faithful or pious are received, and hell, which is destined for the souls of the unbelieving or impious; likewise a twofold state of souls, namely eternal life or salvation, and eternal damnation or punishment, Luke 16:22, 23 sqq., Mark 16:16. But concerning any intermediate place or state, there is deep silence in Scripture." (Disp. th. de receptaculis etc. th. 30.) ANTITHESES.

Gerhard: "The Papists fabricate five receptacles for souls. 1. Hell, into which they banish the souls of extremely impious men who depart from this life in unbelief, impatience, and more grievous offenses or mortal sins against conscience. 2. Purgatory, next to hell, into which they relegate the souls of those who have not yet been fully purged of venial sins, and have not yet perfectly satisfied for the temporal punishments of sins, yet have departed from this life in the faith of Christ; they decree that those must sweat in purgatory for so long until, having been purged of the stains of sins, they fly up pure and clean into heaven. 3. The Limbo of children, to which they assign the souls of unbaptized infants who, on account of original sin in which they died without the remedy of baptism, are affected by the punishment of loss, though not of sense, in this subterranean cell, excluded from the joys of heaven, yet not subject to the punishments of hell. It is called a 'limbus' because it is as it were a border and extremity of hell, like the hem of a garment. 4. The Limbo of the fathers, into which they introduce the souls of the patriarchs and all the saints of the Old Testament who died before Christ’s descent into hell; they assert that these sustained the temporal punishment of loss in this cell until, the debt of original sin having been dissolved through the death of Christ, they were liberated from it and introduced to the fruition of heavenly blessedness when Christ had descended to the dead. Cat. Trid. p. 56. Sonnius in demonstr. relig. Christ, lib. 2. tract. 3. cap. 15. etc.

5. Heaven, into which they admit the souls of the saints fully purged of all sins. The order of these stories according to the Papists is as follows: hell is placed in the very center of the earth; next to this is purgatory, which is as it were the second story; contiguous to that is the limbo of infants, over which the limbo of the fathers lies immediately, which today, the fathers having been translated into heaven by Christ, is entirely empty." (Loc. de morte § 166.) PART I. CHAPTER VIII.

The same: "The Papists describe Purgatory as 'a certain place in which, as in a prison after this life, souls are purged which were not fully purged in this life, so that, being thus purged, they may be able to enter into heaven, into which nothing defiled shall enter.'" Bellarmine, lib. 1, *de purgat.*, cap. 1. Regarding the circumstances of Purgatory—namely, the persons to be purged in it, the place, the time, the punishments, the suffrages, and other things of this kind—they vary greatly among themselves.

Regarding the punishment of Purgatory, they believe "that the fire by which souls are purged is a true and proper fire, and thus of the same species as our elemental fire." Bellarmine, lib. 2, *de purg.*, cap. 6: "Almost all theologians teach that the damned and the souls in Purgatory are in the same place and are tormented by the same fire." Regarding the severity of the punishments, they hold that they are "most atrocious, and that no punishments of this life are to be compared with them. There is as much difference between the fire of Purgatory and that by which men are burned in this world as there is between glowing coals and the breath of a human mouth; and human flesh cannot endure as much torment by any kind of torture as the soul suffers, afflicted by the heat of that purgatorial fire." *c. Nullus in fin. de poenit. dist. 7.* (L. c. § 181.)

Luthardt: "Related to the pagan views of Hades as the place of the departed, shadow-like living souls, and partly connected with the idea of retribution, are the Old Testament expressions concerning Sheol, שאל. . . The New Testament takes over the Old Testament view of Hades in a developed form; thus in the parable in Luke 16:22 ff. Into this Hades, Christ himself went with his death, but he is at the same time in Paradise, and with him the thief, Luke 23:43, and he takes the Old Testament pious with him out of Hades, Matthew 27:52 f. Since then, believers no longer come into Hades, but as blessed and perfected spirits (Hebrews 12:23) into heaven to Christ (2 Corinthians 5:6, 8; Philippians 1:23; Revelation 7:9 ff.), to blessed rest (6:11; 14:13), while Hades only gives up its dead at the end, in order then to be no more (Revelation 20:13 f.). . . Dogmatics, unhistorically, lets the decision be already completely concluded with death. The pious come immediately into heaven, the godless into hell: . . . Since the time of Pietism, however, the doctrine of an intermediate state arose again and became popular in more recent times, whereby it concerns especially the questions of intermediate corporeality, the capacity for development and the possibility of conversion, and the possibility of perfected holiness." (Comp, p. 290, 291, 293.)

Kahnis: "Thus we have reason to assume in that world an intermediate state in which a decision is still possible for those who could not yet decide in this world. Even according to medieval views, there are transitions between hell and Purgatory. But in the idea of Purgatory there lies undoubtedly a truth, namely, that for many Christians a purification is still necessary. Great is the number of Christians of whom one cannot say that Christ is their life. But they nevertheless have an inclination toward him and confess what they have recognized of him in a purity, selflessness, and faithfulness of conduct which can only shame many Christians who are stronger in words than in works. Should there be no hope for them? Finally, not small is the number of Christians who, as far as men can judge, stand in true faith, but whose faith is still strongly mixed with the dross of the old man, so that one would like to judge that they, as they are, cannot come into Paradise if Paradise is to remain Paradise. Let it not be said that with the body much of the old man will also fall away. Why does one grant to the believer what one does not concede to the unbeliever? The peculiarity of a human being cannot be [removed] with a magic stroke."

remove. How is a Christian who lacks love to suddenly become a stream of love through death? And so we must indeed assume that in that world there is still room for purification and development. Thus, three places and, with them, states would have to be distinguished in that world: the place of punishment (φυλακή), the middle place of decision and purification, and the place of joy (παράδεισος).” (The luth. Dogm. III. p. 558. sq.) §

17 The lifeless bodies of men are to be committed to the earth with honor, but without immoderate luxury and superstitious rites, so that they may be resolved into ashes there, unless the preceding transgressions of the dead have merited that they be left unburied as a punishment, or at least be buried without honor. They are not to be cast into water or fire, much less consumed by beasts or men, since it is rather their lot to sleep in the dust of the earth, Dan. 12:2, to be sown, or committed to the earth like seed, 1 Cor. 15:37, as if by common law.

Gerhardus: “Those profane and heathen rites of treating the bodies of the deceased show that it was truly said by the Apostle concerning the Gentiles, Eph. 2:12, 1 Thess. 4:13, that they had no hope, namely, of the resurrection of bodies to eternal life. But in the Christian Church, the bodies of the deceased, especially of the pious, are deservedly treated more honorably. . . How much the duty of burial is esteemed before God is gathered from the fact that the Holy Spirit calls it ‘mercy,’ Ruth 1:8, 2 Sam. 2:5. . . Christ, in Matt. 26:9, calls the woman’s act of anointing His body for burial a ‘good work.’ . . .

We take care that the bodies of the deceased be brought to the earth and interred, that is, buried by heaping earth upon them: 1. Because of the promulgation of the divine oracle. Gen. 3:19: ‘Dust you are, and to dust you shall return’; Dan. 12:2: ‘Those who sleep in the dust of the earth’; Eccles. 12:7: ‘The dust returns to the earth as it was.’ 2. Because of the designation of the earth; it is called ‘the mother of us all,’ Sirach 40:1, because it receives the dead into its bosom and guards our bones in its embrace until the day of judgment, which will be the day of παλιγγενεσία, Matt. 19:28. . . 3. Because of the comparison made by Christ and the Apostle Paul, by which they compare the bodies of the piously deceased to grains cast into the earth to confirm the hope of the resurrection, John 12:24, 1 Cor. 15:37 and 38. Hence, in our vernacular language, cemeteries are most beautifully called ‘God’s fields’ (agri dominici), in which, indeed, the bodies of the pious are sown like certain grains in the hope of a future harvest.

4. Because of the imitation of the example set forth in the holy men of God. It has been received by the most ancient and perpetual custom of the Church to commit the bodies of the deceased to the earth, Gen. 23:19, ch. 50:13, etc.; indeed, God Himself confirmed this custom of burying the dead, Deut. 34:6. 5. Because of the consecration of our sepulchers effected through Christ. Just as Christ endured death on the cross for our sake, so He also willed to be buried for our sake, so that by the contact of His most holy flesh He might sanctify our graves and make them בית חיים, houses of the living, and κοιμητήρια or dormitories. Therefore, just as we have been spiritually buried with Christ through baptism into death, Rom. 6:4, so it is also fitting that we be conformed to Him in our bodily burial.” (Loc. de morte § 79. 80.) PART I. CHAP. VIII.

Having regard not only to the excellence of the human being, who is destined to perish, over brute animals, and at the same time to the status and merits of those who have gone before in this life, but especially, if they were Christian men, to a holier dignity, inasmuch as the bodies of the faithful were already in this life temples of the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. 3:16, their members the members of Christ, 1 Cor. 6:19, weapons of righteousness, Rom. 6:19, and are hereafter to be resurrected and made conformable to the glorious body of Christ, Phil. 3:21. He who insists either on the excessive adorning of the bodies of the deceased or on overly sumptuous funerals acts against both Christian order (τάξιν) and decorum (ευσχημυσύνψ). E.g., consecrating a cemetery or a grave with holy water, ringing consecrated bells as if to drive away demons, etc. As they say "buried" (humatum), he who is covered with earth (humo). Although it is not necessary that the earth touch the body directly or that coffins be excluded. For vaults or caverns also suffice. We say, however, that bodies ought to be interred, so that we may indicate the duties of the survivors and the honest desires of the dead, although we do not deny that the denial of burial by adversaries is to be borne with moderation by the pious and by confessors. Augustine says beautifully: "The earth did not cover many bodies of Christians, but no one has separated any of them from heaven and earth, which He who knows whence He may resurrect what He created fills entirely with His presence." (De Civitate Dei, Book I, ch. XII), where he soon adds that saying of Lucan: "He who has no urn is covered by the sky." According to that saying: "You are dust, and to dust you shall return," Gen. 3:19, which denotes not so much the burial itself as the resolution of the body into dust or ashes. Cf. Ps. 104:29; 146:4. E.g., the stubborn defense of heretical dogmas, joined with the seduction of others; notorious crimes continued until the very end of life without signs of repentance. Which God calls the burial of a donkey, Jer. 22:18. Or, without the customary ceremonies of the accompaniment of the people, sacred psalmody, the commendation of the deceased, perhaps even outside the cemetery. Concerning which more is taught in the schools of moral or casuistic theology. § 18. Temporal death can be described as the privation of animal life, resulting from the dissolution of soul and body, perpetrated through the sin of our first parents, with Satan hostiley instigating, proceeding from the just judgment of God, and to be undergone by all men by necessity of nature, to the glory of divine justice. As it is in itself and by reason of its origin or introduction into the world. Not as it is seen per accidens and through the intervention of various circumstances regarding various subjects. PART I. CHAP. IX. 241 For it imports this in the nominative case. Cf. § 2. By which the efficient moral and meritorious cause is indicated. Cf. § 5 and 7. This also pertains here to the moral cause, but hostile hatred to the impulsive cause on his part; see § 4 and 7. Which is the cause of death viewed by way of punishment. And when we say "just judgment," we simultaneously indicate the internal impulsive cause on the part of God; see § 6 and 7. Which are the subject "that which"; concerning which see § 13. As to the end, according to § 14. Chapter IX. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD. § 1. Just as the soul of man remains surviving after death, so also the body, which was destroyed by death, will rise again and return to life, which is most clear from the Scriptures, but by natural reason, however, it cannot indeed be known with certainty, although it is not repugnant to it. See the preceding chapter VIII, § 15. Dissolved, putrefied, reduced to ashes; see l. c. § 17, note f. Thus Job believed and professed in ch. 19:25, Isaiah also foretold in ch. 26:19, and Daniel in ch. 12:2, Christ confirmed in John 5:28, ch. 11:23, and Paul adds 1 Cor. 15:12 ff. and 1 Thess. 4:16. For although this attains to the immortality of the soul, nevertheless, whether it is to live without the body, or whether it is to be reunited to a body at some time, and to which one, cannot be defined with certainty. Cf. blessed Musaeus, Introd. ch. II, § 9, p. 39. Namely, when Scripture reveals the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead, then reason, which acknowledges God as the avenger of crimes and the rewarder of the good, finds it consistent with itself, rather than contrary, that bodies—the organs of deeds done well or ill—should be resurrected for the fellowship of punishments or rewards. And although reason does not find how bodies numerically the same, which have been resolved into ashes, can be resurrected, yet it is so far from being able to show the impossibility by an invincible argument that it is rather compelled to leave that to divine power. Cf. blessed Musaeus, Introd. in Th. P. II, ch. Y, § 12, p. 330, 331. Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. II. 16 PART I. CHAP. IX.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Gentiles outside the Church, to whom the resurrection of the bodies seemed a ληρώδης λόγος [idle tale], Acts 17:32... Acts 26:27. Pliny, *Natural History*, book 2, ch. 7, and book 7, ch. 55, calls the resuscitation of the dead 'childish ravings,' and adds: 'What, in the name of heaven, is this madness, to repeat life through death?' Aeschylus in *Eumenides*: 'Once dead, there is no resurrection'; Theocritus: 'There is no hope for the buried'; Catullus to Lesbia: 'Suns may set and rise again; for us, when once our brief light has set, there is one perpetual night to be slept.'...

2. Of the Epicureans in the visible bosom of the Old Testament Church, concerning whom see Isa. 22:13; Wisd. 2:1, 3. 3. Of the Sadducees in the New Testament, who said in the time of Christ that no resurrection was to be hoped for, Matt. 22:23; Mark 12:18; Luke 20:27; Acts 23:6, 8.

4. Of Hymenaeus and Philetus in the time of Paul, who said that the resurrection had already taken place. For they thought that no other resurrection was promised than a mystical or spiritual one (which occurs from sins through regeneration), 2 Tim. 2:17–18, as Haymo and Lyranus explain, or they established the resurrection in the succession that occurs through the procreation of children.

5. Of certain ones in the Corinthian church, 1 Cor. 15:12... 7. Of the heretics in the primitive Church, among whom the Simonians, Carpocratians, Saturninians, Basilidians, and Valentinians denied the resurrection... See Epiphanius, who teaches that Simon Magus, the parent and leader of heretics in the New Testament Church, rejected the resurrection, and that the sects that arose from him persisted in this error. Philastrius also attributes to Dositheus that 'he does not hope for a future resurrection of the flesh.' In sum: 'In no matter is the Christian faith so contradicted as in the resurrection of the flesh,' as Augustine says in Ps. 89. 'As far as I gather from the authors and history,' says Dr. Georg Calixtus, 'almost all the heretics of the earlier centuries stumbled against this stone.' Johannes Philoponus the philosopher, nicknamed 'the Grammarian,' also wrote a book on the resurrection, in which he 'τὴν τῶν σωμάτων ἀνάστασιν ἀνατρέπει' [overturns the resurrection of bodies], as Photius writes...

7. Of Amalric, a Parisian doctor, who, under Emperor Philip, son of Barbarossa, embraced this error among others... 8. Of the Albigensians... If the writers of those times are to be believed, they committed the same error...

9. Of John XXIII, the Roman pontiff, who denied the resurrection of the flesh just as he denied the immortality of the soul...

10. Of the Libertines, who mock the resurrection of the flesh and refer the sayings of Scripture that deal with it only to souls; as witnessed by P. Martyr. Calvin, in his book *Instruction against the Libertines*, ch. 3, says: 'Whatever Christians hold concerning eternal life and the resurrection is a fable to them'; and ch. 22: 'They mock every hope we have of the resurrection, and say that what we still expect has already happened to us'...

10. Of the Socinians, who utterly deny the article concerning the resurrection of the dead... Ostorodus, *Institutions*, ch. 41, indeed protests 'that he believes in the resurrection of the bodies,' but he understands those bodies that are to be ours one day, not those which we now carry about... He also miserably corrupts the w…ords of the Apostles' Creed, 'I believe in the resurrection of the flesh,' to which he attaches this meaning: 'I believe in the resurrection of the flesh, i.e., of that which was flesh, but not of this very flesh of ours'...

12. Of the Arminians, who remain in suspense as to what should be determined concerning the resuscitation of bodies." (*Theologia didactico-polemica*, Part IV, ch. 18, sec. 2, q. 1, f. 1770 ff.) § 2. The resurrection of the dead consists in this, that the body, destroyed by death, will be reproduced from the matter into which it was turned and will be reunited to the soul

Latin:

Oppositorum enim similis ratio est. Et vid. 1 Petr. 3, 19., ubi Christus, ad inferos descendens, dicitur spiritibus, qui tunc erant in carcere, illis quidem, qui tempore Noe inobedientes fuerunt, ideo autem inclusi carcere, praedicasse. Atque animae, quae in carcere illo sunt, haud dubie a facie Dei rejectae sunt et connexis poenis affliguntur. Certe purgatorium seu status poenalis fidelium, vitae aeternae quidem haeredum, sed a peccatis in hac vita plene non purgatorum, medius proinde inter vitam et damnationem fingi non debet.

S.Niemannus: ,,Scriptura sicut duos tantum ordines hominum agnoscit, quorum alii sunt credentes, alii increduli, Mare. 16, 16. Joh. 8, 18., alii benedicti, alii maledicti, Matth. 2δ, 34. 41., alii oves, alii hoedi, ibid. v. 33.: ita etiam duorum tantum receptaculorum meminit, coeli scilicet, in quod recipiantur animae fidelium sive piorum, et infemi, qui destinatus sit animabus infidelium sive impiorum; duplicis item status animarum, nempe aeternae vitae sive salutis, et aeternae damnationis sive supplicii, Luc. 16, 22. 23. sqq. Marc. 16, 16. De loco autem vel statu aliquo intermedio altum in Scriptura est silentium.“ (Disp. th. de receptaculis etc. th. 30.) ANTITHESES.

Gerhardus: ״Pontificii quinque animarum receptacula fabricant. 1. Infernum, in quem ablegant animas hominum extreme impiorum, qui incredulitate, impatientia et gravioribus contra conscientiam delictis sive peccatis mortalibus ex hac vita decedunt. 2. Purgatorium, inferno proximum, in quod relegant animas eorum, qui nondum plene a peccatis venialibus purgati sunt, necdum pro temporalibus poenis peccatorum perfecte satisfecerunt, in fide tamen Christi ex hac vita discesserunt; illis tamdiu in purgatorio sudandum statuunt, donec peccatorum maculis purgatis puri et mundi in coelum subvolent. 3. Limbum puerorum, cui assignant animas infantum non baptizatorum, qui propter peccatum originis, in quo absque baptismi remedio decesserunt, poena damni, non tamen sensus in hac cella subterranea afficiantur, exclusi a gaudiis coeli, non tamen subjecti poenis inferni. Dicitur limbus, quia est quasi ora et extremitas quaedam inferni, sicut limbus vestimenti. 4. Limbum patrum, in quem introducunt animas patriarcharum et omnium sanctorum V. Test., ante Christi ad inferos descensum demortuorum, quas in hac cellula poenam damni temporalem sustinuisse asserunt, donec, peccati originalis debito per Christi mortem dissoluto, ex ea liberatae ad fruitionem coelestis beatitudinis fuere introductae, cum Christus ad inferos descendisset. Cat. Trid. p. 56. Sonnius in demonstr. relig. Christ, lib. 2. tract. 3. cap. 15. etc.

5. Coelum, in quod animas sanctorum ab omnibus peccatis plene purgatas admittunt. Ordo illarum contignationum juxta pontificios talis est: infernus in ipso terrae centro positus est, huic proximum purgatorium, quod est contignatio quasi secunda, illi contiguus est limbus infantum, cui proxime superincumbit limbus patrum, qui hodie, translatis in coelum a Christo patribus, prorsus vacuus est.“ (Loc. de morte § 166.) PART. I. CAP. VIII.

Idem: ״Purgatorium sic describunt pontificii, quod sit,locus quidam, in quo tamquam in carcere post hane vitam purgantur animae, quae in hac vita non plene fuerunt purgatae, ut nimirum, sic purgatae, in coelum ingredi valeant, quo nihil intrabit coinquinatum.‘ Bellarminus lib. 1. de purgat, cap. 1. Dz circumstantiis purgatorii, videlicet de personis in eo purgandis, loco, ‘tempore, poenis, suffragiis et hujus generis aliis plurimum inter se variant.

De poena purgatorii credunt, ,quod ignis ille, quo animae purgantur, sit verus et proprius ignis, adeoque ejusdem speciei cum nostro elementari.‘ Bellarminus lib. 2. de purg. cap. 6.: ,Theologi fere omnes docent, eodem in loco esse et eodem igne torqueri damnatos et animas purgatorii.‘ De gravitate poenarum sentiunt, eas esse,atrocissimas, et cum illis nullas poenas hujus vitae comparandas. Tanta est differentia inter ignem purgatorii et eum, quo in hoc mundo homines uruntur, quanta inter prunas torrentes et oris humani halitum, nulloque tormenti genere caro humana tantum cruciatum ferre potest, quantum patitur anima, illius ignis purgatorii ardore afflicta.‘ c. Nullus in fln. de poenit. dist. 7.“ (L. c. § 181.)

Luthardtius: ,,Verwandt mit den heidnischen Anschauungen vom Hades, als dem Ort der abgeschiedenen, schattenhaft lebenden Seelen, theilweise verbunden mit der Idee der Vergeltung, lauten die alttestamentlichen Aeusserungen über das Scheol. שאל, . . Das Neue Testament nimmt zunächst die alttestamentliche Anschauung vom Hades in entwickelter Gestalt herüber; so im Gleichniss Luc. 16, 22. ff. In diesen Hades nun ging Christus selbst mit seinem Tode, aber er ist zugleich im Paradies, und mit ihm der Schächer, Luc. 23, 43., und nimmt die alttestamentlichen Frommen mit sich aus dem Hades Matth. 27, 52. f. Seitdem kommen die Gläubigen nicht mehr in den Hades, sondern als selige und vollendete Geister Hebr. 12, 23. in den Himmel zu Christo 2 Kor. 5, 6. 8. Phil. 1, 23. Apok. 7, 9. ff., zur seligen Ruhe 6, 11. 14, 13., während der Hades seine Todten erst am Ende herausgibt, um dann nicht mehr zu sein Apok. 20, 13. f. . . Die Dogmatik lässt, ungeschichtlich, die Entscheidung mit dem Tod schon völlig abgeschlossen sein. Die Frommen kommen alsbald in den Himmel, die Gottlosen in die Hölle: . . . Seit der Zeit des Pietismus kam aber die Lehre von einem Zwischenzustand wieder auf und wurde in der neueren Zeit beliebt, wobei es sich noch besonders um die Fragen der Zwischenleiblichkeit, der Entwicklungsfähigkeit und Bekehrungsmöglichkeit und der Möglichkeit vollendeter Heiligkeit handelt.“ (Comp, p. 290. 291. 293.)

Kahnisius: ,,Somit haben wir Grund, in jener Welt einen Mittelzustand anzunehmen, in welchem noch eine Entscheidung möglich ist für die, welche in dieser Welt sich noch nicht entscheiden konnten. Auch nach mittelalterlicher Anschauung gibt es zwischen der Hölle und dem Fegefeuer Uebergänge. In der Idee des Fegefeuers aber liegt unzweifelhaft eine Wahrheit, nämlich dass für viele Christen noch eine Läuterung nöthig ist. Gross ist die Zahl von Christen, von denen man nicht sagen kann, dass Christus ihr Leben ist. Aber sie haben doch einen Zug zu ihm und bekennen das, was sie von ihm erkannt haben, in einer Lauterkeit, Selbstlosigkeit, Treue des Wandels, welche viele Christen, die stärker in Worten als in Werken sind, nur beschämen kann. Soll für sie keine Hoffnung sein? Nicht klein ist endlich die Zahl von Christen, die, so weit Menschen urtheilen können, im wahren Glauben stehen, aber deren Glaube noch stark versetzt ist mit den Schlacken des alten Menschen, so dass man urtheilen möchte, dass sie so, wie sie sind, nicht ins Paradies kommen können, wenn das Paradies Paradies bleiben soll. Man sage nicht, dass mit dem Leibe auch viel vom alten Menschen abfallen werde. Warum lässt man den Gläubigen zukommen, was man den Ungläubigen nicht zugesteht? Die Eigenthümlichkeit eines Menschen lässt sich nicht mit einem Zauberschlag

beseitigen. Wie soll einem Christen, dem es an Liebe fehlt, durch den Tod auf einmal ein Strom von Liebe werden? Und so müssen wir wohl annehmen, dass in jener Welt noch für Läuterung und Entwickelung Raum ist. Sonach würden in jener Welt drei Orte und mit ihnen Zustände zu unterscheiden sein: der Strafort (φυλακή), der mittlere Ort der Entscheidung und Läuterung und der Freudenort (παράδεισος).“ (Die luth. Dogm. III. p. 558. sq.) §

17 Corpora hominum exanimata in a terram b cum honore, sed absque luxu c immoderato et superstitiosis d ritibus recondenda e sunt, ut ibidem in cineres f resolvantur, nisi mortuorum antegressa g delicta poenae loco vel inhumata ea h relinqui, vel saltem absque honore i sepeliri meruerint. Quemadmodum igitur spiritualiter cum Christo consepulti sumus per baptismum in mortem, Rom. 6, 4., ita quoque aequum est, ut in sepultura corporali ipsi conformemur.“ (Loc. de morte § 79. 80.) PART. I. CAP. VIII.

Habita ratione non tantum praestantiae humanae ruiturae prae brutis animantibus, simul status ac meritorum antegressorum in hac vita, sed praecipue, si homines christiani fuerint, dignitatis sanctioris, quatenus corpora fidelium jam in hac vita fuerunt templa Spiritus Sancti, 1 Cor. 3, 16., membra eorum, membra Christi, 1 Cor. 6, 19., arma justitim, Rom. 6, 19., posthac autem resuscitanda sunt et glorioso corpori Christi conformia futura, Phil. 3, 21. Qui vel in corporibus defunctorum nimium exornandis, vel in exequiis sumtuosioribus consistit, contra et τάξιν et ευσχημυσύνψ christianam. V. g. consecrandi coemeterium aut sepulchrum per aquam lustralem, pulsandi campanas consecratas velut ad abigendos daemones etc. Prout humatum dicunt, qui humo contectus est. Quanquam nec necesse sit, ut humus immediate tangat corpus aut loculi excludantur. Nam et fornices aut cavernae sufficiunt. Dicimus autem corpora debere recondi, ut officia superstitum et honesta desideria mortuorum indicemus, licet denegationem sepulturae ab adversariis factam moderate ferendam esse piis et confessoribus, non negemus. Pulchre Augustinus: Multa corpora Christianorum terra non texit, sed nullum eorum quisquam a coelo et terra separavit, quam totam implet praesentia sui, qui novit, unde resuscitet, quod creavit. L. I. de C. D. c. XII., ubi mox addit illud Lucani: Coelo tegitur, qui non habet urnam. V. g. pertinax propugnatio haereticorum dogmatum, cum seductione aliorum conjuncta: flagitia notoria ad finem usque vitae continuata absque poenitentiae notis. Quam sepulturam asini vocat Deus Jer. 22, 18. Seu, absque ceremoniis consuetis comitatus populi, psalmodiae sacrae, commendationis defuncti, forte etiam extra coemeterium. Describi potest mors temporalis,a quod sit privatio vitae b animalis, ex dissolutione animae et corporis, per peccatum primorum c parentum, satana d hostiliter instigante, patratum, justo Dei e judicio proveniens, omnibusque f hominibus ex naturae necessitate subeunda, ad justitiae divinae g gloriam. DE RESURRECTIONE MORTUORUM. § 1. Quemadmodum anima hominis post mortem superstes a manet, ita corpus etiam, quod per mortem destruotum b est, resurget et in vitam revertetur, quod ex Seripturis c clarissimum est, ratione naturali autem cognosci equidem certe non d potest, licet illi non repugnet.e Vid. cap. praeced. VIII. § 15. Dissolutum, putrefactum, in cineres redactum; vid. l. c. § 17. nota f. Ita Jobus credidit et professus est cap. 19, 25., Esaim quoque praedixit cap. 26, 19. et Daniel cap. 12, 2., Christus confirmavit Joh. 5, 28. cap. 11, 23., accedit Paulus 1 Cor. 15, 12. sqq. et 1 Thess. 4, 16. Haec enim quamvis animae immortalitatem assequatur, tamen, utrum ea absque corpore victura, an vero corporl aliquando, et cui, redunienda sit, certo definiri non potest. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. cap. II. § 9. p. 39. Nempe quando Scriptura revelat doctrinam de resurrectione mortuorum, tunc ratio, quae Deum scelerum vindicem et bonorum remuneratorem agnoscit, consentaneum sibi potius, quam adversum deprehendit, resuscitari corpora, bene aut male factorum organa, ad consortium poenarum vel praemiorum. Et quamvis non inveniat ratio, quomodo corpora numero eadem, quae in cineres resoluta sunt, resuscitari queant, tamen tantum abest, ut invicto argumento impossibilitatem ostendere possit, ut potius potentiae divinae illud relinquere cogatur. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. in Th. P. II. cap. Y. § 12. p. 330. 331.Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. Π. 16 PART. I. CAP. IX.

## 11 On the Resurrection of the Dead

OF THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD.

or, in a word, it shall rise again, and thus, together with the soul, shall arrive either at the blessedness or the damnation destined for it.b For the formal nature of the resurrection consists in these two acts, insofar as it is called transitive, or a resuscitation. And thus also the άνάστασις (which is called so in John 5:29, elsewhere έξανάστασις, Phil. 3:11, and is by the force of the word δευτέρα του πεπτωχότος στάσα του πεπτωχότος στάσις, a repeated standing of that which has fallen) and the ζωοποίησις, or vivification, as it is called in Rom. 8:11 and 1 Cor. 15:22, are one and the same action in reality; to which also corresponds the word παλιγγενεσία, or regeneration (of the reviving bodies), Matt. 19:28. And thus, just as death, so also the resurrection of the dead is a condition or medium, so to speak ώς έν πλάτει, without which, according to the common law, the full blessedness or misery of the whole suppositum does not occur. Cf. John 5:28; Dan. 12:2. § 3.

The principal efficient cause of the resurrection is the triune God and Christ the θεάνθρωπος. Or that which, by its own power, and thus according to the requirement of the work and the infinite effect, shall restore and animate bodies. For He is said to open the graves, Ezek. 37:12; to redeem from death, Hos. 13:14; to vivify the dead, Rom. 4:17; to raise the dead, 2 Cor. 1:9. Hanekenius: "The resurrection is not brought about by the powers of nature, whence those labor in vain who seek for sparks and seeds of life in the dried-up ashes of man; but by the immense power of the omnipotent God, which deservedly places a bridle upon the stubbornness of contradicting reason." (Verae th. Synopsis. Marburg, 1629, p. 155.)

For the resuscitation of the dead is an opus ad extra. It is performed through the omnipotence which He possesses essentially as God, and through communication as man; see John 5:21, where the Son is said to vivify the dead, just as the Father raises and vivifies them. It is also said in v. 28 that the dead who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God and shall come forth to judgment. However, this power of raising the dead who are to be judged, just like the power of judging, is said to have been given to Him δτι υίός άνθρώπου έστίν, that is (with the particle δτι unfolded, which is to be taken specificatively), insofar as He is the Son of Man, or according to that nature by which He is the Son of Man or man, verse 27. Walchius: "Reduplicative" is contrasted with "specificative," which are terms used for the nature of such propositions where the predicate belongs to the subject either necessarily or accidentally. If it is necessary, they say that the object is to be explained reduplicatively and repeated by the little word "quatenus" (insofar as); e.g., the King of Sweden has the right to command in Uppsala; there one could say: The King of Sweden as King of Sweden has [the right] in Uppsala... PART I. CHAP. IX.

to command. If it were accidental, then it would be only a description and, as it were, a specification of the subject; e.g., the student is a painter; here the subject is not to be repeated: the student, precisely because he is a student, is considered a painter, but it is only such a description that the person who is among the students has also done something in painting.” (Philosoph. Lexikon. Lpz. 1733. p. 2132 sq.) § 4.

The internal impulsive cause of the resurrection of the dead in general is divine justice, and specifically, with respect to the pious, remunerative justice; with respect to the impious, vindicatory justice. Thus the dead are said to be resurrected and manifested, so that each one may receive τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος, the things done through the body, whether good or evil, 2 Cor. 5:10. Or, because God, moved by His kindness, wills to transfer the bodies of the blessed, the organs of holy actions, into the fellowship of blessedness; see 2 Thess. 1:5. B. Scherzer calls it distributive justice, which altogether demands that that very body in and with which the pious struggled should be crowned. Compare what we have said concerning remunerative justice, Chapter I, § 12, note e. Or, because God, by that perfection of His whereby He is inclined to vindicate sins, is also impelled to punish the sins of the impious in their restored bodies. Compare the same place in the letter to the Thessalonians. § 5.

The external impulsive cause with respect to the resurrection of the pious is the merit of Christ apprehended by final faith; with respect to the impious, it is final impenitence. As Christ says in John 11:25: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή; ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμέ, κἂν ἀποθάνῃ, ζήσεται. And 1 Cor. 15:22, all are said to be made alive through Christ, not indeed men of every condition, but all who descend from Christ through spiritual birth; just as through Adam all die who descend from Adam through carnal birth; which the context indicates. But to be made alive through Christ is to be made alive by the virtue of His merit. Whence Christ is also called the meritorious cause of the resurrection of the pious. See 2 Cor. 5:10. Namely, the evils which each one has committed in the body move God to will to manifest him in the body, in order to receive punishments in the body. But we have no reason to call the merit of Christ the impulsive or meritorious cause of the resurrection even with respect to the impious. Namely, the merit of Christ, performed in our place and for our good by the Mediator, is called a meritorious cause in respect to some good to be obtained for us, but the resurrection of the impious does not have the character of a good with regard to them. Compare the blessed Gerhard, L. de Resurrect. Mort. § 55 et sqq.

OF THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD. ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who assert that the resurrection of the ungodly depends upon the merit of Christ rising again, or that the damned and the ungodly will also rise again by the virtue and efficacy of the merit of Christ. Thus Calvin. . . 2. Of certain of our own, such as D. Henricus Boethius, professor at Helmstadt, in a special treatise on the resurrection of the ungodly, in which he contends that 'even the infidels are to rise again by the virtue of the merit of Christ,' which opinion D. Brochmannus also made his own in his System. theol. art. XVI. de servatore Christo s. 16. q. 6." (L. c. q. 3. f. 1784.) §

6. The subject of the resurrection is dead men, all, not only the pious and faithful, but also the ungodly and infidels. Or that which is ultimately denominated as rising again, or in one word, the subject of the resurrection.

Gerhardus: "It must be said that, since actions and passions belong to the subject [suppositum], the whole man, considered ὅλικῶς [wholly], is rightly established as the subject of the resurrection, but not the whole of man, considered μερικῶς [partially], or all his parts. For to the soul, as an immortal spirit, that resurrection of which we treat in this place does not pertain, but another, namely, the spiritual, which John calls the first resurrection in Rev. 20:6, which takes place only in this life. . . But because we said above that the form of the resurrection consists in two things: in the reformation of bodies, to wit, from the dust of the earth, and in their animation, or the reunion of souls with the raised bodies, therefore, with respect to the latter work, resurrection can also be attributed to souls, but κατ' ἄλλο [in another sense], because they are again united to the rising body and return again to the original office of animation, which had been suspended in death and through death." (L. de resurr. mort. § 106.)

For those who are found alive on the last day, strictly speaking, will not rise again, since they will not have fallen through death; yet they will be changed and will lay aside the mortal condition of the body, according to 1 Cor. 15:51 sqq. Cf. the preceding chapter VIII. § 13. note d.

Indeed, John 5:28 expressly says that all who are in the graves will hear the voice of the Son of God and will rise again in one hour. For in the phrase "to be in the graves" there is a general description of the dead, taken from the more prominent part. Whence we do not exclude from this embryos extinguished in their mothers' wombs.

But that some men are not to be raised at last in the universal resurrection, but are read to have risen already long ago when Christ rose, Matt. 27:53, and are believed to have ascended into heaven with Christ, that was extraordinary. But those who in the O.T. were raised by the prophets, and in the N.T. by Christ before His passion and by the apostles after Christ's ascension from the dead to this natural life, it is rightly established that they died again and therefore are to be raised to immortal life only in the final resurrection. See our disputation, in which we examine this and the state of separated souls ordered again to natural life. PART I. CAP. IX.

Or of the just and the unjust, Acts 24:15, those who have done good and those who have done evil, John 5:29. Compare 2 Cor. 5:10.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Jews, who restrict the resurrection only to the pious, and indeed believe that those pious ones who lie buried in the blessed land of Canaan will rise first; and they wish to infer this from the desire of certain patriarchs; but that others outside of Canaan must be rolled through hidden subterranean passages with great torment until they reach the same; indeed, they roundly deny the resurrection of the wicked... 2. Of the Socinians, who maintain that the wicked will remain in death forever as to soul and body, and will feel no other punishment or torment after this life." (L. c. q. 2. f. 1777. sq.)

Hoffmannus: "In fact, the annihilation of the underworld and the cessation of the dominion of death are one and the same. We therefore receive the appropriate thought that the ungodly, with the morning after the night of death, when the dominion of death ceases, come under the dominion of the righteous, and through the annihilation of the underworld, to which their bodily part also falls victim, they lose its last sad dwelling, and thus also lose their bodily part itself, which now no longer has a place to remain." (Schriftbeweis. II, 469.) §

7. The subject by which [the resurrection occurs] is the body identical in number, which each person had in this life. Or that essential part of man according to which he is said to rise again, or which, having been destroyed before, will be reproduced through the resurrection and united to the other surviving part. Certainly, the very word ἀνάστασις, or resurrection, implies the repeated standing of that which had stood before and had fallen, according to § 2. note a., whence if you maintain that one body stood in this life and fell through death, but a different one will be produced in the future, it would not be a true resurrection, but a new creation, or something similar to the Pythagorean μετεμψύχωσις or μετενσωμάτωσις. Compare 2 Cor. 5:10, where the identity of the body is manifestly indicated, in which each person has done good or evil in this life and in which he is to receive rewards or punishments at the final judgment. Add Dan. 12:2; John 5:28, 29, where the same ones who have hitherto slept are said to be about to awaken. Since, therefore, they have not slept according to the soul, but according to the body, they are to be resurrected according to that very body in which each one slept.

DE RESURRECTIONE MORTUORUM.

sive, uno verbo, resurget atque ita una cum anima perveniet vel ad beatitudinem, vel ad damnationem sibi destinatam.b His enim duobus actibus formalis ratio resurrectionis constat, quatenus quidem illa transitive sive resuscitatio dicitur. Atque ita etiam άνάστασιν (quae Joh. 5, 29. appellatur, alias έξανάστασις, Phil. 3, 11., estque vi vocis δευτέρα του πεπτωχότος στάσις, iterata statio ejus, quod cecidit) et ζωοποίησα, seu vivificationem, juxta Rom. 8, 11. 1 Gor. 15, 22. sic dictam, quoad rem unam actionem esse credimus; cui etiam respondet vox παλιγγενεσίας seu regenerationis (corporum reviviscentium), Matth. 19, 28. Joh. 5, 28. Dan. 12, 2.§ 3.

Causa efficiens principalis a resurrectionis est Deus b trinunus c et Christus ^εάν^ρωπος.d Seu quae virtute sua, adeoque juxta exigentium operis et effectus infinita, restaurabit corpora atque animabit. Is enim dicitur aperire tumulos Ezech. 37, 12., redimere a morte Hoseae 13, 14., vivificare mortuos Rom. 4, 17., suscitare mortuos 2 Cor. 1, 19.Hanekenius: ״Fit resurrectio non naturae viribus, unde frustra laborant, qui in mortuis exsiccatis hominis cineribus vitae igniculos et semina quaeritant; sed immensa omnipotentis Dei potentia, quae merito contradicenti rationis pervicaciae capistrum injicit.“ (Verae th. Synopsis. Marpurgi, 1629. p. 155.)

Est enim resuscitatio mortuorum opus ad extra. Per omnipotentiam, quam, qua Deus, habet essentialiter, qua homo, per communicationem, vid. Joh. 5, 21., ubi Filius dicitur vivificare mortuos, sicut Pater eos suscitat et vivificat. Dicitur etiam v. 28., mortuos, qui in monumentis sunt, vocem Filii Dei audituros et prodituros ad judicium. Hanc autem, sicut judicandi potestatem, ita et virtutem suscitandi mortuos judicandos datam esse illi, δτι υίός άνΰρώπυυ έστ], id est (evoluta particula δτι, quae specificative accipienda est), in quantum filius hominis est, seu secundum eam naturam, qua filius hominis aut homo est, vers. 27.Walchius: Reduplicative wird dem specificative entgegengesetzt, welche Wörter man von solcher Beschaffenheit der Sätze braucht, da das Prädicat dem Subject entweder nothwendig, oder zufälliger Weise zukommt. Ist es nothwendig, so sagen sie, dass das Object reduplicative zu erklären und durch das Wörtchen quatenus zu wiederholen sei; z. E. der König in Schweden hat in Upsala zu befehlen; da könne man sagen: Der König in Schweden als König in Schweden hat in Upsala PART. I. CAP. IX.

zu befehlen. Wäre es zufällig, so sei es nur eine Beschreibung und gleichsam eine Specificatiori des Subjects; z. E. der Student ist ein Maler; hier sei das Subject nicht zu wiederholen: der Student, eben weil er ein Student ist, wird für einen Maler gehalten, sondern es sei nur eine solche Beschreibung, dass die Person, die sich unter den Studenten befindet, auch etwas in der Malerei gethan habe.“ (Philosoph. Lexikon. Lpz. 1733. p; 2132. sq.) § 4.

Causa impulsiva interna resurrectionis mortuorum in genere est justitia divina a et speciatim, respectu piorum, justitia remuneratoria,b respectu impiorum justitia vindicati va.c Sic mortui resuscitandi et manifestandi dicuntur, ut reportet unusquisque τά διά τoh σώματος, ea, quaecunque fecit per corpus, sive bona, sive mala, 2 Cor. 5, 10. Seu, quod Deus, benignitate sua motus, beatorum corpora, sanctarum actionum organa, in societatem beatitudinis vult transferre; vid. 2 Thess. 1, 5. B. Scherzems vocat justitiam distributivam, quae omnino postulet, ut illud ipsum corpus, in et cum quo pii certarunt, coronetur. Confer., quae diximus de justitia remuneratoria, cap. I. § 12. not. e. Seu, quod Deus ea sui perfectione, qua inclinatur ad vindicanda peccata, impellitur etiam ad peccata impiorum in corporibus restauratis punienda. Conf. 1. c. ad Thessal.§ 5.

Causa impulsiva externa respectu resurrectionis piorum est meritum Christi fide finali apprehensum,a respectu impiorum impoenitentia finalis.b Prout Christus Joh. 11, 25. dicit: Eqo sum resurrectio et vita; qui credit in me, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, vivet. Et 1 Cor. 15, 22. dicuntur per Christum vivificari omnes, non quidem homines cujuscunque conditionis, sed omnes, qui a Christo per spiritualem nativitatem descendunt; quemadmodum per Adamum omnes moriuntur, qui ex Adamo per carnalem nativitatem descendunt; quod contextus indicat. Per Christum autem vivificari, est virtute meriti ejus vivificari. Unde et Chri.stus causa meritoria resurrectionis piorum dicitur. Vid. 2. ad Cor. 5, 10. Nempe mala, quae quisque gessit in corpore, movent Deum, ut velit eum manifestare in corpore, ad reportandas in corpore poenas. Ut autem Christi meritum, etiam respectu impiorum, causam resurrectionis impulsivam seu meritoriam dicamus, causae nihil habemus. Nempe meritum Christi, nostro loco et bono a Mediatore praestitum, causa meritoria dicitur in respectu ad bonum aliquod nobis impetrandum, resurrectio autem impiorum boni rationem quoad illos non habet. Conf. b. Gerhard. L. de Resurrect. Mort. § 55. et sqq.

Gerhardus: ״Dicendum, quod, cum actiones et passiones sint suppositi, totus homo, όλικώς consideratus, recte statuatur subjectum resurrectionis, sed non totum hominis, μερικώς considerati sive omnes partes. Animae enim, utpote spiritui immortali, non competit resurrectio illa, de qua hoc loco agimus, sed alia, videlicet spiritualis, quam Johannes vocat resurrectionem primam Apoc. 20, 6., quae in hac vita duntaxat locum habet. . . Quia vero superius diximus, formam resurrectionis consistere in duobus, in corporum scii, ex terrae pulvere reformatione et in eorundem animatione sive animarum cum corporibus suscitatis redunitione, ideo respectu operis posterioris etiam animabus resurrectio tribui potest, sed κατ' άλλο, quia corpori resurgenti iterato uniuntur ac ad pristinum officium animationis, quod in morte ac per mortem suspensum fuerat, iterum redeunt.“ (L. de resurr. mort. § 106.)

Qui enim vivi deprehendentur in die ultimo, proprie loquendo non resurgent, cum per mortem non ceciderint; immutabuntur tamen ac deponent mortalem corporis conditionem, juxta 1. ad Cor. 15, 51. sqq. Conf. cap. praeced. VIII. § 13. not. d.

Sane Joh. 5, 28. expresse dicitur, omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audituros vocem Filii Dei et resurrecturos esse una hora. Est enim in phrasi, esse in monumentis, descriptio generalis mortuorum, sumta a parte potiore. Unde nec embryones in uteris matrum extinetos hinc excludimus.

Quod autem aliqui homines non demum in universali resurrectione resuscitandi sunt, sed jam olim Christo resurgente resurrexisse leguntur, Matth. 27, 53., et cum Christo in coelos ascendisse creduntur, id extraordinarium fuit. Qui vero in V. T. a prophetis, et in N. T. a Christo ante passionem suam et ab apostolis post ascensionem Christi e mortuis ad vvtam hanc naturalem resuseitati fuerunt, eos iterum mortuos adeoque in resurrectione ultima demum ad vitam immortalem resuscitandos recte statuitur. Vide disp. nostram, qua τούτο et statum animarum separatarum ad vitam naturalem rursus ordinatarum expendimus. PART. I. CAP. IX.

Sive justi et injusti, Act. 24, 15., qui bonum, fecerunt, et qui malum, Joh. 5, 29. Confer. 2 Cor. 5, 10.
