### On the Resurrection of the Dead: In the O. T., Job, chapter 19:25, about to issue a confession of faith worthy…

In the O. T., Job, chapter 19:25, about to issue a confession of faith worthy of eternal memory, said that he knew that after the passage of a very long time, or in the last time (אַחֲרוֹן), in his flesh, previously corrupted and consumed by worms, with these eyes which he had here, he would see his Redeemer (גֹּאֵל), who is joined to him (the man to be redeemed) by kinship or consanguinity (which can be understood as no one except the Messiah), appearing alive and in visible form, and, like a powerful victor, ruling over the dust.

Similarly, the Messiah himself in Isa. 26:19, concerning his martyrs, or the faithful killed for his sake and the confession of him, נִבְלָתִי יְקוּמוּן, my corpse, i. e., those who became a corpse for my sake, shall rise. Therefore, this very thing, which for some time was a corpse, will revive.

ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD. Gerhard: "The more important arguments of the adversaries are these: 1. From the oracles of the Savior, Matt. 22:30, Luke 20:36: 'The children of the resurrection will be ισάγγελοι and ὡς ἄγγελοι.' Therefore, they will be converted into an angelic nature. Resp.: a. Similarity is not identity; ὁμοιότης and ἰσότης is not immediately ταυτότης. ... c. The blessed will be ισάγγελοι not by the essence of their nature, but by the conformity of qualities and glory, whence they are not called ἄγγελοι, but will be ὡς ἄγγελοι. d. The same is gathered from the purpose...

2. From the apostolic passage 1 Cor. 15:50: 'Flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God.' Therefore, resurrected and glorified bodies will not have flesh and blood. Resp.: a. In the same chapter, the Apostle clearly asserts the resurrection of the same body in number and substance; b. Therefore, the Apostle is not speaking of the substance of the body itself, considered ἁπλῶς in itself, but of the corruption of the flesh adhering to it and its condition in this life; namely, that the body, insofar as and as long as it is animal, mortal, corrupted by sin, and subject to vicious inclinations, etc., cannot inherit the kingdom of God, but it is necessary that it be changed in respect to its qualities, not, however, in respect to its substance. ... For just as our corrupted nature cannot attain the kingdom of heaven unless it is regenerated and renewed by the Holy Spirit (John 3:5), so our bodies cannot become participants of the heavenly kingdom unless they have first put off φθοράν and corruptibility; and consequently, it is not by reason of substance, but by reason of guilt, that flesh and blood are barred from the kingdom of God. ...

3. From the apostolic analogy 1 Cor. 15:37–39: 'That which you sow, it is not quickened, except it die; and that which you sow, you do not sow that body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as it has pleased him, and to every seed his own body.' Therefore, different bodies will rise than those which were, like a seed committed to the earth. Resp.: a. Analogies of any kind are not to be extended beyond the third point, in respect to which the comparison is instituted. ... d. Christ compares His own body to a grain of wheat, which is cast into the earth and rots before it rises (John 12:24), yet the body of Christ was not putrefied, nor did another rise, but that very same one from the dead. Therefore, from the analogy of the seed, a diversity of substance can by no means be inferred, but only a diverse quality of the bodies.

e. From the apostolic words, therefore: 'You do not sow that body that shall be, but bare grain,' it ought not to be inferred: therefore, the same body in number that is sown will not rise; but this only follows: Therefore, not such a body as is sown rises. For ταυτόν, 'the same,' can be taken in two ways: either by reason of essence or by reason of qualities. The grain and the stalk that grows from the grain are the same in species, by which the stalk is born from the matter and form as the substantial parts of the grain that remain; nor is the body of the wheat grain destroyed, but the same nature and form are retained for the seed, and the substance is preserved in the same nature. However, the grain and the stalk are not the same by reason of accidents, which are different in the stalk than in the grain. Chrysostom, Homily 41 on 1 Corinthians: 'The ear is the same and not the same. It is the same because the substance is the same; it is not the same because it is better.' Gregory, Book 14 of Morals, ch. 29: 'In the grain of the seed, that which was is not lacking; but that which was not is present.'" (L. de resurr. mort. § 76.)

Fecht: "The resurrection of the same flesh conceived in the manner in which a river, although the water is always changed, remains the same river (as Thomas Browne represents the same in 'Religio Medici'), is not the resurrection of the same flesh in number." (Syllog. controvers. p. 375 sq.)

Gerhard: "The reason for resurrection is one thing, the reason for accretion is another. In accretion, the assumption of new matter occurs successively, nor is the entire prior matter consumed, but new matter, changed through various alterations, is added to the same, whence the numerical unity of the composite is not at all overturned by accretion. ... In physical accretion and alteration, matter is changed only as to quantity, not, however, as to essence." (L. de resurr. mort. § 81.) PART I. CHAPTER IX.

ANTITHESIS S. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of Origen, who thought that the same flesh would not be resurrected, but a celestial body, endowed with its former figure and appearance. . . 2. Of the Socinians, who maintain that not those same bodies which we now carry about will rise again on the day of judgment, but that others will be given to us, and those, as to substance, spiritual and celestial. . . 3. Of the Arminians, who remain in suspense of mind, μετεωρίζοντες, regarding the resurrection of bodies, 'whether the same bodies of the saints are to be resurrected, or whether others are to be created by God.'" (L. c. q. 4. f. 1789. sq.)

Kahnisius: "The resurrection will not be the reanimation of the buried flesh, but the clothing of the soul with a glorified body." (Der innere Gang etc. ed. 3. II, 279.)

The same: "The elements of which our body consists on earth are by no means essential to it. The matter of which our body consists today is excreted sooner or later. We lose some components, such as hair, nails, teeth, etc., on earth without the lost parts impairing the integrity of our body. Now, when the Apostle Paul says that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15:51), this can only mean that not this body consisting of flesh, subservient to sin, and subject to death, but a spiritual body made by God, untouched by sin and death, enters into eternal life (2 Cor. 5:1 ff.). The image of the seed grain used by the Apostle (1 Cor. 36) surely states that not this buried body rises again, but a new one that has emerged from it. And the transformation which the bodies of the living experience also demands a much greater difference between the new body and the old than is stated by the dogmatics, which, so to speak, teaches only an improved form of the old body. If we assume that already in this life the Holy Spirit forms from the earthly body the germ of the resurrection body, which envelops the soul in the state of its spiritual life in the realm of the dead, then we must think of the resurrection as a creative act through which Jesus Christ prepares from the earth a body in which that germ finds its completion, while our earthly body finds its archetype. But the matter that we bury will not rise again." (Die luth. Dogm. 2. Ausg. 1875. II, 523. sq.)

They will also receive their sex, and all parts or members which they had in this life, although not to be restored for their old use, yet for the integrity of the organic body. The bodies of the pious, however, will be rendered glorious in the very resurrection, according to those things which we said in Chapter VI, § 13 sqq., and if by chance they were deprived of certain members in this life, they will then receive them.

Gerhardus: "The question is asked: If not a hair of the head is to perish, how will the resurrected bodies not be deformed and monstrous due to the length of the hair? . . . Resp.: . . . We have warned that the pious ancients applied those words to the article of the resurrection in the sense that not even the smallest particle of the body is to perish; meanwhile, it cannot be inferred from this that superfluous and excrementitious humors, as well as the superfluities of hair and nails, which are rather refuse and excrement than members of the body and ornaments, and which burden and weigh down more than they adorn, are to be restored to man in the resurrection." (L. c. §90.)

In what stature, however, the bodies will rise again, we do not determine.

ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD. Gerhardus: "The question is asked: Of what stature will the resurrected bodies be? Schmaltz, in his *Controversies*, Disp. 7, later part, D. Frantz, p. 416, writes that theology students ought to be ashamed of that question. But this proceeds from the false hypothesis that the same bodies are not to be resurrected.

1. Lombard, Book 4, Sentences, dist. 44, lit. a, reports that some have thought all the faithful will rise according to the measure of the stature of Christ; to prove which, they have adapted the apostolic saying in Eph. 4:13: 'Until we all come to a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.'

2. The opinion of Augustine is that what the apostle asserts concerning the conformity of the resurrected bodies with the body of Christ is not to be understood of the measure of the body or stature, but of age, since each one is to receive the measure of the body that he either had at the age in which Christ died and rose again, or would have had if he had died earlier. . .

But the opinion of those who maintain that everyone will rise at that age and stature in which he died seems more probable. a. Because John sees the dead, great and small, standing before God, Rev. 11:18; 19:5; 20:12; and if not only the great but also the small will stand before the tribunal, then certainly the small will also rise. b. That which fell will rise; but when an infant died, it was not a man of tall stature that fell, but a small infant. c. Scripture nowhere asserts an equality of quantity in resurrected bodies; for those things which are brought forward to establish it are twisted into a foreign sense. . .

Therefore, the bodies of the resurrected will be χαρακτηριζόμενα [characterized], marked and, as it were, characterized by their own certain and determinate accidental forms. But the stature of the body also pertains to the proper and characteristic form of each, which varies greatly with the progress of age. e. The shortness or tallness of stature will bring no deformity to the resurrected and glorified bodies. . .

f. That variety of stature, detracting nothing from the perfection of wisdom and the fullness of joy in the elect, will rather bring a certain wondrous beauty to the assembly of the triumphant church. God desires the heavenly paradise to be adorned with those tender little plants, just as a skilled gardener decorates his garden with flowers and trees of every size. g. 'Star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead,' says the apostle, 1 Cor. 15:41-42. But a star differs from a star not only in quality, but also in quantity, namely, in magnitude; which difference of stars in glory and magnitude brings the highest beauty to the heavenly body. It is not improbably maintained that the matter will be the same in the resurrection and eternal life." (L. c. § 87.) §

8. The proximate end of the resurrection of the dead with respect to the faithful is the full participation of blessedness; with respect to the unfaithful, the consummation of damnation. The ultimate end is the glory of divine remunerative and vindicatory justice. For they will be resurrected so that they may carry away τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος [the things done through the body], etc., 2 Cor. 5:10. And in John 5:28 it is said that the resurrection is either of life or of condemnation, the denomination being taken from the end. For just as God is moved to resurrect men by that justice of His, partly remunerative and partly vindicatory, according to those things which we said in § 4, so He is rightly said to intend the glory of both. PART I. CHAP. X.

§ 9. The resurrection of the dead is described as a work of the Triune God and of Christ the θεάνθρωπος, proceeding from divine remunerative and vindicatory justice, by which all men, and indeed the faithful or pious on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by final faith, but the unfaithful and impious on account of their sins, will receive the same bodies in number which they had in this life, reunited to their souls; the former for the full participation of blessedness, the latter for the consummated participation of damnation, both for the glory of God and of divine justice. A work, I say, or the terminus of a divine action. But if the resuscitation of the dead is to be defined, it would have to be said that the action itself (transitive) is denoted in the nominative case. We indicate the efficient cause, according to § 3. This is the internal impulsive cause; concerning which we treated in § 4. Who are the subject *Quod* (that which) of the resurrection; see § 6. f) Thus we indicate the external impulsive cause, according to § 5. For this is the subject *Quo* (by which) of the resurrection; concerning which see § 7. In which the formal reason of the resurrection consists, according to § 2. The proximate end of the resurrection is indicated here, § 8. k) In which the ultimate end consists, according to the cited § 8. Chapter X. CONCERNING THE LAST JUDGMENT AND THE CONSUMMATION OF THE AGE. § 1. Since the universal resurrection of the dead has this end, that men may receive either rewards or punishments, we must now proceed to treat of that judgment by which rewards and punishments will come to men. § 2. That there will be a certain solemn judgment is most clear from the Scriptures.a It is also certain that the last judgment and the resurrection of the dead will take place on one and the same day.b But God has not willed that the day when that day is to come should be distinctly foreknown by us.c See Matt. 25, 31 et seqq. Acts 17, 31. 2 Thess. 1, 6 et seqq. It is especially to be noted that in Jude v. 6 it is called κρίσις μεγάλης ἡμέρας, the judgment of the great day; whence the solemnity of the future judgment can be known.

Jobus cap. 19, 25., confessionem fidei, aeterna memoria dignam, editurus, dixit, scire se, quod post longissimi temporis decursum, seu tempore postremo (אחיין) in carne sua, ante corrupta et a vermibus consumta, hisce oculis, quos hic habuit, Redemtorem suum (גאל), qui sibi (homini redimendo) cognatione aut consanguinitate junctus sit (qualis nemo, nisi Messias intelligi potest), vivum et visibili forma apparentem ac, victoris potentis instar, in pulverem dominaturum, visurus sit.

Similiter Messias ipse Jes. 26, 19. de martyribus suis, seu fidelibus, propter ipsum et confessionem ipsius occisis, נבלתי ןקומין, cadaver meum, i. e. propter me cadaver facti resurgent. Itaque ipsum hoc, quod aliquamdiu cadaver fuit, reviviscet.

DE RESURRECTIONE MORTUORUM. Gerhardus: ״Argumenta adversariorumpotlora haec sunt: 1. Ex oraculis Salvatoris Matth. 22, 30. Luc. 10, 36.: ,Filii resurrectionis erunt ισάγγελοι καί ΰς άγγελοι.‘ Ergo in angelicam naturam convertentur. Resp.: a. Similitudo non est identitas, ομοώτης και 'ισύτης non est statim τάντότης. . . c. Beati erunt ίσάγγελοι non per essentiam naturae, sed per convenientiam qualitatum et gloriae, unde non dicuntur άγγελοι, sed futuri ως άγγελοι, d. Idem colligitur ex scopo. . .

2. Ex loco apostolico 1 Cor. 15, 51.: ,Caro et sanguis non possidebunt regnum Dei.’ Ergo corpora resuscitata et gloriflcata non habebunt carnem et sanguinem. Resp.: a. Apostolus in eodem capite ejusdem numero et substantia corporis resuscitationem perspicue asserit; b. non ergo de ipsa corporis substantia, άπλώς in se considerata, sed de adhaerente carnis corruptione et ejusdem in hac vita conditione apostolus loquitur, quod sci. corpus, quatenus et quamdiu est animale, mortale, peccato corruptum, vitiosis inclinationibus obnoxium etc., non possit regnum Dei haereditare, sed necessarium sit, ut qualitatum, non autem substantiae ratione mutetur. . . Ut enim corrupta nostra natura non potest regnum coelorum consequi, nisi regeneretur ac renovetur per Sp. S. Joh. 3, 5., sic corpora nostra non possunt regni coelestis fleri participia, nisi prius ψ&οράν et corruptibilitatem exuerint, ac proinde non substantiae, sed culpae nomine caro et sanguis a regno Dei arcentur. . .

3. Ex similitudine apostolica 1 Cor. 15, 37—39.: ,Quod seminas, non vivificatur, nisi prius moriatur; et quod seminas, non corpus, quod futurum est, seminas, sed nudum granum, puta tritici aut alicujus caeterorum. Deus autem dat illi corpus, sicut voluit, et unicuique seminum proprium corpus.‘ Ergo alia corpora resurgent, quam quae fuerunt, instar seminis cujusdam terrae mandata. Resp.: a. Similitudines quaecunque non sunt extendendae ultra tertium, cujus respectu instituitur collatio. . . d. Confert Christus suum corpus cum grano tritici, quod in terram conjicitur et putrefit, antequam surgit, Joh. 12, 24., nec tamen corpus Christi putrefactum est, nec aliud, sed illud ipsum e mortuis est resuscitatum. Ex similitudine ergo seminis nequaquam substantiae diversitas, sed duntaxat diversa corporum qualitas inferri potest,

e. Ex verbis igitur apostolicis: ,Non corpus, quod futurum est, seminas, sed nudum granum‘, non debet inferri: ergo non idem numero corpus, quod seminatur, resurget; sed hoc tantum sequitur: Ergo non tale corpus, quale seminatur, resurgit. Duobus enim modis potest accipi ταντό, idem, vel ratione essentiae, vel ratione qualitatum. Granum et culmus, qui ex grano nascitur, sunt specie idem, qua ex materia et forma, ut substantialibus grani partibus, quae manent, culmus nascitur, nec grano fabae tritici corpus astruitur, sed eadem natura et forma sementi retinetur et substantia in eadem natura servatur. Non autem idem sunt granum et culmus ratione accidentium, quae alia sunt in culmo, quam in grano. Chrysost. Homil. 41. in priorem ad Corinth.: ,Spica eadem est et non eadem. Eadem jam haec, quia substantia eadem, non eadem, quia melior.‘ Gregor, lib 14. moral. cap. 29.: ,Grano seminis non deest, quod erat; sed adest, quod non erat.“‘ (L. de resurr. mort. § 76.)

Fechtius: ״Resurrectio ejusdem carnis ad eum modum concepta, quo fluvius, quamquam semper mutata aqua, idem fluvius manet (ut eandem in,Religione medici‘ Th. Brownius repraesentat), non est resurrectio ejusdem numero carnis.“ (Syllog. controvers. p. 375. sq.)

Gerhardus: ״Alia est ratio resurrectionis, alia accretionis. In accretione materiae novae assumtio fit successive, nec materia prior tota absumitur, sed eidem nova ־per varias alterationes mutata adjungitur, unde numerica compositi unitas per accretionem minime evertitur. . . In accretione et aTteratione physica materia mutatur tantum quoad quantitatem, non autem quoad essentiam.“ (L. de resurr. mort. § 81.) PART. I. CAP. IX.

ANTITHESE S. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Origenis, qui existimavit, non eandem carnem resuscitandam, sed corpus coeleste, praeditum pristina figura et specie. . . 2. Socinianorum, statuentium, non eadem illa corpora in die judicii resurrectura, quae nunc circumferimus, sed alia nobis danda, eaque quoad substantiam spiritualia et coelestia. . . 3. Arminianorum, qui de corporum resuscitatione. . . animo suspenso haerent μετεωρίζοντες, ,an eadem corpora sanctorum resuscitanda sint, an vero alia a Deo creanda.‘ “ (L. c. q. 4. f. 1789. sq.)

Kahnisius: ״Die Auferstehung wird nicht die Neubelebung des begrabenen Fleisches sein, sondern die Umkleidung der Seele mit einem verklärten Leibe.“ (Der innere Gang etc. ed. 3. II, 279.)

Idem: ״Unserm Leibe sind auf Erden die Elemente, aus denen er besteht, durchaus nicht wesentlich. Der Stoff, aus dem unser Leib heute besteht, scheidet früher oder später wieder aus. Manche Bestandtheile, wie Haare, Nägel, Zähne u. s. w., verlieren wir auf Erden, ohne dass das Verlorene die Integrität unseres Leibes beeinträchtigt. Wenn nun der Apostel Paulus sagt, dass Fleisch und Blut das Reich Gottes nicht ererben (1 Kor. 15, 51.), so kann dies nur heissen, dass nicht dieser aus Fleisch bestehende, der Sünde dienstbare, dem Tode verfallene Leib, sondern ein von Gott gemachter, von Sünde und Tod nicht berührter, geistlicher Leib ins ewige Leben eingeht (2 Kor. 5, 1. ff.). Das vom Apostel gebrauchte Bild vom Samenkorn (1 Kor. 15, 36.) sagt doch aus, dass nicht dieser begrabene Leib auferstehe, sondern ein aus demselben hervorgegangener neuer. Und auch die Verwandlung, welche die Leiber der Lebenden erfahren, fordert einen viel grösseren Unterschied des neuen Leibes vom alten, als die Dogmatik aussagt, die, so zu sagen, nur eine verbesserte Gestalt des alten Leibes lehrt. Nehmen wir an, dass schon in diesem Leben der Heilige Geist aus dem irdischen Leibe den Keim des Auferstehungsleibes bildet, welcher die Seele umhüllt im Zustande ihres Geisteslebens im Todtenreiche, so haben wir uns die Auferstehung als einen schöpferisehen Act zu denken, durch welchen Jesus Christus aus der Erde einen Leib bereitet, in dem jener Keim seine Vollendung findet, unser irdischer Leib aber sein Urbild. Aber der Stoff, den wir begraben, wird nicht auferstehen.“ (Die luth. Dogm. 2. Ausg. 1875. II, 523. sq.)

Recipient etiam sexum, et partes seu membra omnia, quae in hac vita habuerunt, licet' non ad veterem usum redintegrandum, tamen ad integritatem corporis organici. Piorum autem corpora in ipsa resurrectione reddentur gloriosa, juxta ea, quae diximus cap. VI. § 13. sqq., et si forte in hac vita membris quibusdam privati fuerint, tunc illa recipient.

Gerhardus: ״Quaeritur: Si non periturus est capillus de capite, quomodo corpora resuscitata ob capillorum prolixitatem non eruut deformia ac monstrosa? . . . Resp.: . . . Monuimus, pios veteres verba illa ad resurrectionis articulum applicare eo quidem sensu, quod ne minima quidem corporis particula sit peritura; interim ex eo inferri nequit, quod humores superflui et excrementitii, capillorum item et unguium superfluitates, quae sunt potius rejectamenta et excrementa, quam membra corporis et ornamenta, quaeque magis gravant et onerant, quam ornant, in resurrectione sint homini restituenda.“ (L. c. §90.)

In qua autem statura resurrectura sint corpora, non deter minamus.

DE RESURRECTIONE MORTUORUM. Gerhardus: ״Quaeritur: Corpora resuscitata cujus futura sint staturae. Schmaltz. cont. Disp. 7. poster. D. Frantz. p. 416., quaestionis illius theologiae studiosos pudere debere, scribit. Sed hoc procedit ex falsa hypothesi, quod non eadem corpora sint resuscitanda.

1. Lombardus lib. 4. sent. dist. 44. Iit. a. refert, quod nonnulli existimaverint, omnes fideles resurrecturos secundum mensuram staturae Christi; ad quod probandum accommodarint dictum apostolicum Eph. 4, 13.: ,Donec occurramus in virum perfectum in mensuram aetatis plenitudinis Christi.‘ . .

2. Augustini sententia haec est, quod non de mensura corporis vel staturae, sed aetatis accipiendum sit, quod de conformitate corporum resuscitandorum cum corpore Christi apostolus asserit, cum unusquisque recepturus sit mensuram corporis eam, quam vel habuit in ea aetate, in qua Christus mortuus est et resurrexit, vel fuerat habiturus, si ante est defunctus. . .

Sed probabilior videtur eorum sententia, qui statuunt, resurrecturum esse quemlibet in illa aetate ac statura, in qua fuit mortuus, a. Quia Johannes videt mortuos magnos et pusillos stantes coram Deo, Apoc. 11,18. 19, 5. 20,12.; atqui si coram tribunali stabunt non solum magni, sed et pusilli, utique etiam resurgent pusilli, b. Illud resurget, quod cecidit; atqui mortuo infante, non cecidit vir aliquis procerae longitudinis, sed pusillus infans. c. Scriptura aequalitatem quantitatis in corporibus resuscitatis nuspiam asserit; quae enim pro ea stabilienda adducuntur, in alienum sensum detorquentur. . .

Erunt ergo corpora resuscitatorum χαρακτηριζόμενα, certis ac determinatis suis formis accidentalibus signata et quasi characterisata. Atqui ad formam cujusque propriam et characteristicam etiam corporis statura pertinet, quae aetatis progressu eandem plurimum variat, e. Staturae brevitas vel proceritas nullam resuscitatis ac glorificatis corporibus deformitatem conciliabit. . .

f. Varietas illa staturae, perfectioni sapientiae et plenitudini laetitiae in electis nihil quicquam derogans, potius pulchritudinem quandam mirificam triumphantis ecclesiae coetui conciliabit. Deus tenellis istis plantulis coelestem paradisum cupit exornatum, sicut peritus hortulanus cujusvis magnitudinis floribus ac arboribus hortum suum condecorat. g. ,Stella differt a stella in claritate, sic et resurrectio mortuorum‘, inquit apostolus 1 Cor. 15, 42. et 43. Atqui stella differt a stella non solum in qualitate, sed etiam in quantitate, videlic. in magnitudine; quae differentia stellarum in claritate et magnitudine summam coelesti corpori pulchritudinem conciliat. Eodem modo in resurrectione et vita aeterna sese rem habituram, non improbabiliter statuitur.“ (L. c. § 87.) §

### On the Resurrection of the Dead: Antithesis Quenstedtius: "Antithesis

ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis:

1. Of the Epicureans and scoffers, who, hearing that Christ will return for judgment, mock with the Athenians and Stoic philosophers, Acts 17, 32. ...

2. Of the ancient heretics, such as the Dositheans, Samaritans, and Prodians. Philastrius attributes the same error to the Florians, Manichaeans, and Gnostics, whom Augustine asserts were also called Borborians.

3. Of the Libertines and David [Joris] in the year 1525, who also denied that there would be a future judgment." (Theol. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 19. s. 2. q. 1. f. 1809. sq.) See 1 Thess. 4, 16-17. See Mark 13, 32. And experience has hitherto shown how greatly those have fallen who believed that by divining they could know something. § 3. Meanwhile, there is no lack of signs by which God exhibits the approaching judgment as in some way to be known,a which are for the most part dividedb into common [signs], or such as do not happen in only one age, and often recur or continue, e.g., heresies,c wars and similar public calamities,d the security of men;e and proper [signs], which are to be seen only when the judgment is finally drawing nearer, and not equally in previous ages, e.g., the revelation of the antichrist,f singular eclipses of the stars and their falling to the earth,g and perhaps others.h Concerning the judgment itself, I say, it warns that it is to follow, it does not signify a determined time of judgment, even though it teaches that it is drawing nearer and nearer, just as from the tender branches of the fig tree and the leaves having sprouted, summer is known to be approaching, Matt. 24, 3 and 33, Mark 13, 29, Luke 21, 25, where they are also expressly called signs. Luther: "I do not wish to fight here, but to command Christians [to observe] whether the signs in the sun, moon, and stars have occurred. But this is my faith and certain hope, that such signs have for the most part already occurred and there are not many others to be awaited." (Tom. Jen. VII, 1360.) Others distinguish them into remote and proximate, with almost the same meaning. Namely, those common and more remote signs, although they do not seem to signify the time of the judgment, nevertheless, by the institution and intention of God, they signify...

go, and they ought to warn Christians that some solemn judgment is to be expected by virtue of divine justice and the truth of the predictions. Regarding the proper or proximate signs, the difference is that some precede the judgment by a longer interval, others by a shorter one; consequently, they do not themselves signify a determinate time, except that certain ones (or at least that which will be treated in the following § 4) are believed to be joined with the very beginning of the judicial solemnity. Thus, Christ in Matthew 24:24 makes mention of false prophets who will lead many into error. And Paul predicts that in the last times, impostor spirits and doctrines of demons will be discovered, 1 Timothy 4:1. Compare 2 Timothy 3:8, where men are mentioned who resist the truth, are corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith, seducers of the simple, etc. Therefore, while observing these things, the faithful ought at the same time to remember the final judgment, by which the truth will triumph over the oppressed heresies.

To be ended by the coming of the Supreme Lord; see Matthew 24:6 et seqq. Just as the life of the antediluvian men was then cut off by a particular judgment, so it must finally be cut off by a universal one, Matthew 24:37, 38, 39. And in 2 Timothy 3:1 et seqq., a huge catalog of vices is enumerated, which in the last times will publicly prevail not only among those who are entirely outside the church, but even among those who have a μόρφωσιν εὐσεβείας and are Christians by profession. Whence also the opinion concerning a golden age about to arise before the final judgment is manifestly refuted. Compare our Disputation on the glorious Kingdom of the Church, Chapter III.

Pfeiffer: "Chiliasm has its certain *gradus* [degrees], and we must therefore observe these well here, and right from the beginning make a reasonable distinction (between *chiliasmus crassissimus, crassus et subtilis*) between the coarsest, the coarse, and the subtle Chiliasm. The coarsest Chiliasts were Cerinthus and the Cerinthians..., who introduced Epicureanism into their Chiliasm, in that they supposed one would live in Christ’s kingdom in eating, drinking, and carnal lusts... But we call subtle Chiliasm the opinion of those who indeed hold that the thousand years of Revelation 20 have not yet been fulfilled, but that the glory promised therein is still to be awaited, yet in such a way that they posit no visible return of Christ to an earthly kingdom, no personal reign, no double resurrection, but only *halcyonia* [times of peace] and a peaceful state of the church, while leaving the actual nature, and even the time (how long it will actually last), to God, as Launäus, Rallius, Coccejus, Brenius, and others do. We hold such Chiliasm to be false and erroneous, but because the fundamental articles of the Christian faith are not thereby touched, we do not hold it to be a heresy, especially when one treats of it *problematice* and imposes one's opinion on no one; rather, the question now is concerning the middle Chiliasm, which we call the coarse, and those are the coarse Chiliasts who defend it according to its principal circumstances." (*Antichiliasmus*, p. 111 sq.)

Gerhard: "We judge that the mask must be torn from the chiliastic opinion, with whatever red lead it may be painted and with whatever white lead it may be coated, and therefore we attack it with the following general argument. Whatever opinion is 1. ἄγραφος [unscriptural], 2. ἀντιγραφής [contrary to Scripture], repugnant to Scripture, and 3. [contrary to] experience, that is deservedly to be repudiated. But such is the chiliastic opinion described by us thus far. Therefore, I. That it is ἄγραφος is evident..."

Pfeifferus: ״Es hat der Chiliasmus seine gewisse gradus, und müssen wir also dieselben hiebei wohl beobachten, und bald Anfangs einen vernünftigen Unterscheid machen (inter chiliasmum crassissimum, crassum et subtilem), zwischen dem allergröbsten, groben und subtilen Chiliasmo. Die allergröbsten Chiliasten sind gewesen Cerinthus und die Cerinthianer. . ., welche bei ihrem Chiliasmo den Epicuräismum eingeführt, indem sie vermeint, man würde in Christi Reich in Fressen, Saufen und fleischlichen Wollüsten leben. . . Den subtilen Chiliasmum aber nennen wir die Meinung derjenigen, welche zwar dafür halten, die tausend Jahre Apoc. 20. seien noch nicht erfüllet, sondern es stehe die daselbst versprochene Herrlichkeit noch zu gewarten, doch so, dass sie keine sichtbare Wiederkunft Christi zum irdischen Reich, keine persönliche Regierung, keine doppelte Auferstehung, sondem nur halcyonia und einen friedlichen Zustand der Kirche statuiren, dabei die eigentliche Art, ja auch die Zeit (wie lange es eigentlich damit währen werde) Gott heimstellen, wie Launäus, Rallius, Coccejus, Brenius und Andere thun. Solchen Chiliasmum halten wir nun zwar für falsch und irrig, allein weil dadurch die Grundartikel des christlichen Glaubens nicht angetastet werden, so halten wir denselben, zumal wenn man problematice davon handelt und seine Meinung niemand aufbürdet, für keine Ketzerei; sondern es wird jetzo die!Tage sein von dem mittleren Chiliasmo, den wir den groben heissen, und diejenigen die groben Chiliasten, welche denselben nach seinen PrincipalUmständen defendiren.“ (Antichiliasmus, p. 111. sq.)

Gerhardus: ״Nos chiliasticae opinioni, quocumque tandem minio pingatur et quacunque cerussa obducatur, larvam detrahendam esse censemus ac proinde sequenti argumento generali eam impugnamus. Quaecunque opinio est 1. άγραφος, 2. αντιγραφής, repugnans Scripturae et 3. experientiae, ea merito repudianda. Talis vero est chiliastica opinio a nobis hactenus descripta. Ergo I. Quod άγραφος sit, patet


## 12 Concerning the Last Judgment and the Consummation of the Age

regarding its first author in the church. Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis, traced its origin to apostolic traditions, but it is probable that the impure dogmas of Cerinthus were instilled into him under the feigned pretext of apostolic traditions; for it cannot be proven in any way that the apostles handed down some things by word of mouth, while committing others to writing.

It is evident from 2 Thess. 2:2 that among the means of proof by which seducers wished to persuade the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord was at hand, there was also τὸν λόγον, i.e., the pretext of apostolic tradition; there is no doubt that others also used the same argument in palliating errors. . .

Whatever is brought forward from the prophecies of Scripture to establish that opinion speaks either of the first advent of Christ in the flesh, or of the state of the N.T. church in general, or of the heavenly glory of the triumphant church to be expected only in eternal life, and therefore they are applied ἀπροσδιορίστως καὶ ἀτάκτως to confirm chiliastic dreams.

II. That it is ἀντίγραφος, we prove by reasons drawn from Scripture: 1. From the condition of the kingdom of Christ. The kingdom of Christ is described in the Holy Scriptures as spiritual and eternal, not as corporal and earthly. Therefore, the chiliasts hope in vain that Christ will administer some earthly kingdom for a thousand years. . .

2. From the constitution of the pious in these lands. The lot and state of the pious in these lands is described in the Holy Scriptures in such a way as to exclude entirely the opinions and imaginations of some most peaceful and happy kingdom. . .

3. From the approach of the last day. If the thousand years, during which Christ is said to be about to reign on earth with His own in all abundance of goods, have not yet begun, much less ended; it follows that our times are still more than a thousand years distant from the day of judgment and the consummation of the age. The reason for the connection is manifest, because they posit that that chiliastic kingdom must still be begun and finished before the day of judgment. The consequence is repugnant both to the sayings of Scripture, which testify that the end of the world is near (1 Cor. 10:11; 1 Pet. 4:7; Jas. 5:8-9; 1 John 2:18; Rev. 6:11), and to those signs which were predicted by Christ and the apostles as about to immediately precede the end of the world (Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 21; 1 Thess. 5; 2 Thess. 2; 1 Tim. 4; 2 Pet. 2), most of which have either already been fulfilled or are at the very acme of their completion. . .

It is therefore vain to delight oneself with sweet dreams about some blessed millennium still to be expected in these lands, and it is far more advisable to prepare oneself for the advent of Christ, which is immediately impending, and the last judgment, which will follow shortly, by true repentance, faith, prayers, the pursuit of piety, and patience. . .

4. From the substantial destruction and ruin of the world. At the second advent of Christ, "heaven and earth will pass away and flee from the face of Him who sits upon the throne, so that no place is found for them anymore," Rev. 20:11. . . Therefore, Christ will not reign on earth for a thousand years after His return from the heavens, for otherwise the earth would have to remain extant. . .

5. From the immediate connection of the advent of Christ with the universal resurrection of all men, the administration of the last judgment, the consummation of this age, the creation of a new heaven and earth, the meeting of the pious to encounter Christ, and the heavenly rewards of the pious and the eternal punishments of the impious. . .

6. From the assertion of the simultaneous resurrection of all men. Scripture testifies that at the second advent of Christ, all men, both the impious and the pious, will rise at one and the same time, nay, hour, nay, moment. Dan. 12:2; John 6:39, etc. . .

7. From the description of the pious recalled to life and the rewards to be rendered to them. (Loc. de consummat. saeculi § 80—87.)

Hollazius: "We prove the assertion: 1. We learn from the θεόπνευστον Word that the kingdom of Christ is threefold. For the kingdom of Christ is either the kingdom of power, or of grace, or of glory. The millennial kingdom is neither the kingdom of power, nor of grace, nor of glory. . .

We conclude: Whatever kingdom is neither the kingdom of power, nor the kingdom of grace, nor the kingdom of glory, that is not the true kingdom of Christ, but is a being of reason and a dream of waking men. . .

2. In the millennial kingdom there cannot be a greater illumination of the Holy Spirit than there was in the kingdom PART I. CHAP. X.

of grace in the times of the apostles: but the ϑεογνωσία [knowledge of God] in the kingdom of grace in the times of the apostles was imperfect. Therefore...

3. The citizens of the millennial kingdom cannot excel in a holiness more perfect than that with which the apostles were endowed: but these were endowed with an imperfect holiness, concerning which imperfection the apostles themselves complain... Therefore, in this land, until the day of the final judgment, perfect saints will not live.

4. Christ teaches in Matthew 13:30 that it will come to pass that "the tares grow together with the wheat until the harvest," and by the tares He understands the sons of τοῦ πονηροῦ, i.e., of the devil; by the wheat or good seed, the sons of the kingdom; by the harvest, the consummation of the age; and He asserts that the reapers or angels will finally gather the tares at the harvest and burn them with fire. Therefore, the field of the church before the conflagration of the world will not be devoid of tares, but the segregation of the evil goats from the holy sheep will take place only on the day of the final judgment, Matthew 25:32.

5. Whoever in this world is subject to many afflictions and persecutions cannot promise themselves perpetual halcyon days in these lands: but all the beloved children of God, etc...

6. The state of the church or the kingdom of Christ toward the end of the world, because of the most corrupt morals of the impious and the most bitter afflictions of the pious, will be most turbulent and most sorrowful. Therefore, the kingdom of Christ toward the end of the world will not flourish or excel in extraordinary holiness and earthly happiness...

7. That the solemn advent of Christ, distinguished from the daily advent of grace, is only twofold—and indeed the former humble, the latter sublime and majestic—has been made clear from the sacred scriptures and the more ancient symbols. Paul says explicitly in Hebrews 9:28: "Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, ἐκ δευτέρου, a second time, without sin, will appear to those who wait for Him for salvation."...

8. At the same time that all impious, unjust, and reprobate men rise again, at that same time all the pious, just, and elect, and thus also all the pious martyrs, are to rise again: but on the last day all impious men, etc...

9. It is incredible that those souls who receive in heaven the retribution of a most splendid reward for temporal affliction are sent back by God from heaven into bodies to participate in earthly happiness...

10. True Christians watch for their salvation at every moment for the reason that they expect the sudden and unknown advent of Christ for judgment: therefore, true Christians do not expect a blessed millennium that would precede the final judgment...

11. The hypothesis concerning the millennial kingdom of Christ does not kindle piety, but extinguishes it, or at least retards its course. For a) by the chiliastic hypothesis, men are averted from the desire for heavenly and spiritual goods, which desire, however, is that of true Christians (Rom. 8:23; Phil. 3:20). b) The chiliastic opinion fosters the security of men who think nothing or little of the final judgment. For, fascinated by this weak opinion, they persuade themselves that the advent of Christ is very far off and that one must therefore live for the day. c) By the chiliastic opinion, an opportunity is provided to men greedy for novelty and more apt for disturbing things than for managing them to incite rebellion against the ordinary magistrate. This perverse opinion in the previous century excited and stirred up the minds of the peasants to refuse the authority of the magistrates. (Exam. P. III. s. 2. c. 10. q. 15. p. 1256. sqq.)

Gerhardus: "Especially from the Apocalypse they urge that in chapter 20:2 Satan is said to be bound for a thousand years, and in verse 7 the saints are said to be about to reign with Christ for a thousand years, in which prophecy they establish the proper seat of the chiliastic kingdom... Although, indeed, both because of internal κριτήρια [criteria] and because of the testimonies of the most ancient Greek and Latin fathers, we willingly acknowledge this book to be both canonical and written by the apostle John, nevertheless, since in the primitive church there was sometimes doubt concerning the author of this book, we therefore refer it to the canonical books of the second order. Consequently, we also rightly and deservedly demand from the chiliasts that they bring forth such an interpretation of this book, and especially of this controversial passage, which in no way conflicts with the remaining canonical writings, but agrees with them most exactly." (L. c. § 93.)

Luther: "One must here, right at the beginning, remind the Christian reader that he should with the utmost diligence guard himself against the false dreams of the Jews and Chiliasts, who apply such spiritual promises of God to a bodily and earthly kingdom, and thus fall into two kinds of gross errors. For they lose and do not recognize the Lord Christ, who has a spiritual kingdom, and they wait in vain for Christ to establish a bodily kingdom on earth." (Exposition of the Prophet Micah. 1542. VI, 2846. sq.)

The same: "'I have other sheep, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.' Some have interpreted this saying to mean that it must be fulfilled shortly before the Last Day, when the Antichrist shall come, and Elijah and Enoch. That is not true, and the devil has actually contrived it so that people believe the whole world will become Christian. The devil has done this so that he might darken the true doctrine, so that it would no longer be rightly understood. Therefore, beware of this; this saying became true and was fulfilled shortly after Christ ascended into heaven, and it is still in effect today. When the Gospel began, it was preached to the Jews; this people was the sheepfold. So he says here: I have other sheep that are not of this sheepfold, them I must also bring. There he says that the Gospel shall also be preached to the Gentiles, that they also might believe in Christ, so that from Jews and Gentiles one Christian congregation might be formed; this he did afterward through the Apostles, who preached to the Gentiles and converted them to the faith. Thus, now everything is one Church or congregation, one faith, one hope, one love, one baptism, and the like. That continues even to this day, always, until the Last Day. Therefore, you must not understand it to mean that the whole world and all men will believe in Christ; for we must always have the holy cross, in that the greater part are those who persecute Christians; thus one must also always preach the Gospel, so that one may always bring some in, that they may become Christians; for the kingdom of Christ consists in becoming, not in having become." (Postill. eccles. de ev. Dom. Misericord. Dom.)

Latin:

ex primo ejus in ecclesia auctore. Papias, Hierapolitanus episcopus, ad traditiones apostolicas ejus originem revocabat, sed verisimile est, Cerinthi impura dogmata sub ementito apostolicarum traditionum praetextu ipsi fuisse instillata, neque enim ullo modo probabile fieri potest, apostolos alia viva voce tradidisse, alia vero literis mandasse.

Constat ex 2 Thess. 2, 2. inter media probandi, quibus seductores Thessalonicensibus persuadere voluerunt, diem Domini instare, fuisse etiam τον λόγον, i. e., praetextum traditionis apostolicae; eodem argumento in palliandis erroribus etiam alios fuisse usos, dubium nullum. . .

Quaecunque vero pro stabilienda illa opinione ex Scripturae prophetiis afferuntur, ea vel de primo Christi adventu in carnem, vel de statu ecclesiae N. T. in genere, vel de gloria coelesti triumphantis ecclesiae in vita aeterna demum expectanda loquuntur ac proinde άπμοςόωννσως και άττακϊί'υτως ad chiliastica somnia confirmanda adhibentur.

II. Quod sit άντίγραφος, probamus rationibus ex Scriptura petitis: 1. a regni Christi conditione. Regnum Christi in sacris literis describitur ut spirituale et aeternum, non autem ut corporale et terrenum. Ergo chiliastae frustra sperant, Christum per mille annos terrenum aliquod regnum esse administraturum. . .

2. Ex piorum in his terris constitutione. Sors et status piorum in his terris ita describitur in sacris literis, ut opinationes et imaginationes pacatissimi et felicissimi cujusdam regni prorsus excludat. . .

S. A diei novissimi appropinquatione. Si mille anni, quibus Christus in terris cum suis in omni bonorum Abundantia dicitur regnaturus, nondum sunt inchoati, nedum finiti; sequitur, ultra mille annos nostra tempora a die judicii et consummatione saeculi adhuc distare. Ratio connexionis est manifesta, quia, ante judicii diem chiliasticum illud regnum adhuc inchoandum et finiendum esse, statuunt. Consequens repugnat tum dictis Scripturae, quae mundi finem in propinquo esse testantur 1 Cor. 10,11. 1 Pet. 4, 7. Jac. 5, 8. 9. 1 Joh. 2, 18. Apoc. 6, 11., tum signis illis, quae mundi finem proxime antecessura a Christo et apostolis sunt praedicta Matth. 24. Marci 13. Luc. 21. 1 Thess. 5. 2 Thess. 2. 1 Tim. 4. 2 Pet. 2., quorum pleraque vel jamdum impleta, vel in ipsius complementi άκμί) versantur. . .

Vanum proinde est, suavibus somniis de beato quodam in his terris millenario adhuc expectando sese oblectare, ac longe consultius, ad Christi adventum proxime instantem et judicium extremum brevi secuturum vera poenitentia, fide, precibus, studio pietatis ac patientia sese praeparare. . .

4. Ex substantiali mundi interitu ac destructione. In secundo Christi adventu,coelum et terra transibunt et a facie sedentis super thronum ita fugient, ut locus illis non amplius inveniatur‘, Apoc. 20, 11. . . Ergo Christus post suum e coelis reditum non regnabit in terra mille annis, alias enim terra deberet superstes manere. . .

5. Ex immediata adventus Christi connexione cum universali omnium hominum resurrectione, judicii extremi administratione, hujus saeculi consummatione, novi coeli ac terrae creatione, piorum in occursum Christi obviatione, piorum coelestibus praemiis et impiorum aeternis suppliciis. . .

6. Ex simultaneae omnium hominum resurrectionis assertione. Scriptura testatur, in secundo Christi adventu omnes homines, tam impios, quam pios, esse uno eodemque tempore, imo hora, imo momento resurrecturos. Dan. 12, 2. Joh. 6, 39. etc. . .

7. Ex piorum in vitam revocatorum et praemiorum illis reddendorum descriptione.“ (Loc. de consummat, saeculi § 80—87.)

Hollazius: ״Probamus assertum: 1. Regnum Christi triplex esse, e verbo Θεοπνενστφ discimus. Etenim regnum Christi est vel regnum potentiae, vel gratiae, vel gloriae. Regnum millenarium neque regnum potentiae, neque gratiae, neque gloriae est. . .

Colligimus: Quodcunque regnum neque est regnum potentiae, neque regnum gratiae, neque regnum gloriae, illud non est verum Christi regnum, sed est ens rationis et somnium hominum vigilantium. . .

2. In regno millenario non potest esse major Spriritus S. illuminatio, quam fuit in regno PART. I. CAP. X.

gratiae temporibus apostolorum: atqui ΰεογνωσία in regno gratiae temporibus apostolorum fuit imperfecta. E. . .

3. Cives regni millenarii non possunt perfectiori eminere sanctitate, quam qua praediti fuerunt apostoli: at hi praediti fuerunt sanctitate imperfecta, de qua imperfectione ipsimet apostoli conqueruntur. . . Ergo in hac terra usque ad diem extremi judicii non vivent homines perfecti sancti.

4. Docet Christus Matth. 13, 30., futurum esse, ut,zizania una cum tritico crescant usque ad messem‘, et intelligit per zizania filios τον πονηρού, i. e., diaboli, per triticum sive bonum semen filios regni, per messem consummationem saeculi, atque asserit, messores sive angelos demum in messe collecturos esse zizania atque igne combusturos. E. Ager ecclesiae ante conflagrationem mundi non erit expers zizaniorum, sed segregatio malorum hircorum a sanctis ovibus fiet demum in die extremi judicii, Matth. 25, 32.

5. Quicunque in hoc mundo plurimis afflictionibus et persecutionibus subjacent, illi perpetua in his terris halcyonia sibi promittere nequeunt: atqui omnes dilecti filii Dei etc. ..

6. Status ecclesiae sive regni Christi sub finem mundi propter mores impiorum corruptissimos et afflictiones piorum acerbissimas erit turbulentissimus atque tristissimus. Ergo regnum Christi sub finem mundi eximia sanctitate terrenaqne felicitate non florebit aut eminebit...

7. Adventum Christi solemnem, quotidiano gratiae adventui contradistinctum, esse tantum geminum, et quidem priorem humilem, posteriorem sublimem et majestaticum, e sacris literis et antiquioribus symbolis patefecit. Paulus diserte dicit Heb. 9, 28.: ,Christus semel oblatus ad perferendum multorum peccata, εκ δεύτερον, secunda vice sine peccato videbitur ipsum expectantibus in salutem.‘ . .

8. Quo tempore omnes homines impii, injusti et reprobi resurgent, eodem tempore simul omnes pii, justi et electi, adeoque etiam omnes pii martyres resurrecturi sunt: atqui in die novissimoomnes homines impii etc. . .

9. Quae animae retributionem praemii splendidissimi pro temporali afflictione accipiunt in coelo, illas e coeload consortium terrenae felicitatis a Deo corporibus denuo immitti, incredibile est. . .

10. Veri christiani quovis momento in salutem suam vigilant propterea, quod subitaneum et sibi ignotum adventum Christi ad judicium expectant: ergo veri christiani beatum millennium, quod extremum judicium antecedat, non expectant. . .

11. Hypothesis de regno Christi millenario pietatem non accendit, sed extinguit, aut certe cursum ejus sufflaminat. Nam a) per hypothesin chiliasticam homines avertuntur a desiderio bonorum coelestium et spiritualium, quod desiderium tamen est verorum Christianorum Rom. 8, 23. Phil. 3, 20.. b) Alit opinio chiliastica securitatem hominum, de extremo judicio aut nihil aut parum cogitantium. Sublesta quippe hac opinione fascinati sibi persuadent, adventum Christi longissime abesse adeoque in diem esse vivendum, c) Per opinionem chiliasticam hominibus novitatis avidis et rebus turbandis, quam gerendis, aptioribus subministratur occasio ad rebellionem concitandam adversus ordinarium magistratum. Haec perversa opinio superiori saeculo animos rusticorum ad detrectandum magistratus imperium excitavit et erexit. (Exam. P. III. s. 2. c. 10. q. 15. p. 1256. sqq.)

Gerhardus: ״Cumprimis ex Apocalypsi urgent, quod cap. 20, 2. satanas dicitur ligandus per mille annos, ac v. 7. sancti dicuntur cum Christo regnaturi mille annis, in quo vaticinio propriam sedem chiliastici regni statuunt... Quamvis vero tum propter κριτήρια interna,, tum propter antiquissimorum patrum Graecorum et Latinorum testimonia librum hunc et canonicum et ab apostolo Johanne scriptum esse libenter agnoscamus, tamen cum in ecclesia primitiva de auctore hujus libri aliquando dubitatum fuerit, ideo ad secundi ordinis canonicos libros eum referimus. Proinde etiam a chiliastis jure ac merito postulamus, ut talem hujus libri ac cumprimis controversi istius loci interpretationem proferant, quae cum reliquis canonicis scriptis minime pugnet, sed exactissime consentiat.“ (L. c. § 93.)

Lutherus: ״Man muss hier bald im Anfänge den christlichen Leser erinnern, dass er sich mit höchstem Fleiss vorsehe vor den falsehen Träumen der Juden und Chiliasten, die solche geistliche Verheissung Gottes auf das leibliche und irdische Reich ziehen, und fallen also in zweierlei gröbliche Irrthümer. Denn sie verlieren also und erkennen nicht den Herrn Christum, der ein geistlich Reich hat, und warten umsonst, dass Christus ein leiblich Reich auf Erden werde anrichten.“ (Auslegung des Propheten Micha. 1542. Vl, 2846. sq.)

Idem: ״ ,Ich habe noch andere Schafe, die sind nicht aus diesem Stalle: und dieselbigen will ich herführen, und sie werden meine Stimme hören, und wird Eine Heerde und Ein Hirte werden.‘ Es haben auch etliche diesen Spruch dahin gedeutet, dass es müsse erfüllet werden bald vor dem jüngsten Tage, wenn der Endchrist werde kommen, und Elias und Enoch. Das ist nicht wahr, und hat’s eigentlich der Teufel zugerichtet, dass man glaubt, die ganze Welt werde Christen werden. Der Teufel haUs darum gethan, dass er die rechtschaffene Lehre verdunkelte, dass man sie nimmer recht verstünde. Darum hüte dich dafür, dieser Spruch ist wahr worden und erfüllet bald darnach, da Christus gen Himmel ist gefahren, und gehet noch immer im Schwange. Da das Evangelium anging, ward es den Juden geprediget; dies Volk war der Schafstall. So saget er nun hier: Ich habe noch andere Schafe, die nicht aus diesem Schafstalle sind, die muss ich auch herzubringen. Da saget er, dass den Heiden auch soll das Evangelium geprediget werden, dass sie auch an Christum glauben, dass also aus Juden und Heiden eine christliche Gemeinde werde; das hat er darnach durch die Apostel gethan, die den Heiden predigten und bekehrten sie zu dem Glauben. Also ist nun alles Eine Kirche oder Gemeinde, Ein Glaube, Eine Hoffnung, Eine Liebe, Eine Taufe und dergleichen. Das währet noch heut zu Tage immerdar, bis auf den jüngsten Tag. Darum müsst ihr es nicht also verstehen, dass die ganze Welt und alle Mensehen an Christum werden glauben; denn wir müssen immer das heilige Kreuz haben, dass ihr das mehrere Theil sind, die die Christen verfolgen; so muss man auch immer das Evangelium predigen, dass man immer etliche herzubringe, dass sie Christen werden; denn das Reich Christi stehet im Werden, nicht Geschehen.“ (Postill. eccles. de ev. Dom. Misericord. Dom.)


### Concerning the Last Judgment and the Consummation of the Age: J. E. Gerhard: "In the Augsburg Confession, Art

J. E. Gerhard: "In the Augsburg Confession, Art. 17, not only gross chiliasm, but every kind whatsoever, is rejected and condemned." (A. C. enucleata. Ed. 3. p. 85.)

S. J. Baumgarten: "In the second part (of the 17th Article of the A. C.) is... rejected the expectation of an earthly kingdom of Christ before the resurrection, which flowed from Jewish prejudices and was likewise taught by some Anabaptists; hence the defenders of such opinions cannot be genuine confessors of this article, and can defend themselves... neither with the subterfuges of a distinction between their opinion and the dreams of the Jews, and a resurrection preceding such a kingdom of Christ expected by them, or a worldly kingdom not asserted by them with the total cessation of all the ungodly, nor with the pretense of not spreading such opinions." (Erläuterung der im Concordienbuch etc. p. 102. sq.) ANTITHESES.

Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Jews, dreaming that the Messiah will be an earthly king... 2. Of Cerinthus, the heresiarch, who even in the time of the apostles... maintained that Christ would eventually rise again and spend a thousand years on earth with his own in pleasures in Jerusalem...

3. Of certain fathers, Greek and Latin, who also embraced the chiliastic error, teaching: that Christ, before..." PART I. CHAP. X. [ He will] descend again to earth at the final judgment, and will raise the most approved faithful from the dead, and together with them will reign for a thousand years before the supreme day of the world in every abundance of goods, both of body and of soul, with the greatest splendor. And they call this the first resurrection, while the second, the universal one, is to follow only then, after that period of time has been spent on earth. Eusebius reported that the author of this fable was Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, a man next in time to the apostles. . . Jerome does not indeed mention Justin, but he sufficiently betrays himself in his dialogue with Trypho. . . Eusebius also associates Irenaeus with the chiliasts. . . Regarding Tertullian. . . it cannot be denied that toward the end of book 3, *Against Marcion*, ch. 24, words favoring the millennial error are found. . . . Lactantius invents various and strange things concerning the end of the world in *Institutes*, bk. 7, ch. 24. . . .

4. Of some Papists; for the author of the book which was published under the title *Onus ecclesiae* in the year 1524, a Papist who is thought to be Johannes, Bishop of Chiemsee, shows himself to be strongly addicted to the millennial error; this author also cites other Papists in favor of this opinion. . . 5. Of some Calvinists, who defend chiliasm, such as Piscator, . . Alsted, etc. 6. Of the Arminians; Steph. Curcellaeus sets forth the opinion of the Arminians concerning the glorious kingdom of Christ on this earth. . . 7. Of certain Socinians. Smalcius and Socinus himself indeed reject chiliasm. . . 8. Of the Anabaptists, who in the previous century brought chiliasm back into the church. See Augsburg Confession, art. 17. . . 9. Of the Weigelians. . . 10. Of the Methists, new enthusiasts, followers of Ezechiel Meth; . . likewise the Rosicrucians; . . of Francesco Pucci, who among other errors also cherished this one. . . 11. Of new prophets and fanatics, such as a. Quakers. . b. Paul Nagel. . c. Adolph Held, a follower of Elias Praetorius or Christ. Hohburg. . d. Frid. Breckling, pastor of Zwolle. . e. Joh. de Labadie. . f. H. Ammersbach. (L. c. c. 20. s. 2. q. 3. f. 1862—65.)

Gerhard: "We cannot deny that Lactantius and Nepos make mention of bodily delights, and that Jerome, in book 11 on Ezekiel, indiscriminately constitutes those ancient teachers of the church as patrons of Jewish fables; to which Chemnitz undoubtedly refers when, in the oration on the reading of the fathers prefixed to the first volume of the *Loci Theologici*, he asserts: 'Irenaeus, being addicted to the chiliastic opinion, erred in the foundation.'" (L. c. § 69.) Cf. "Do the Church Fathers really teach a so-called biblical chiliasm?" See *Lehre und Wehre* Vol. XVIII, p. 97—112.

Delitzsch: "To whom do we owe it that the orthodox church of the present no longer brands the chiliastic view of the end times as a heterodoxy, as is done in all the old textbooks of dogmatics, but has instead so incorporated it into its innermost life that now there is hardly a believing Christian to be found who does not share it? To whom do we owe it that the church now believes in a glorious future for the people of Israel and for that very reason recognizes in its Old Testament prehistory a prognosis of its final history, and in Old Testament prophecy a distant view not merely of the glory of the Gentile church, but of Israel in the proper sense? To whom, that the church, in recognition of the sensible reality in which supersensible salvation is ultimately to be manifested, is enabled to restore the sensible reality of Old Testament history to its rightful place and to conceive of the spiritual and the bodily in their organic interweaving? We owe it to Bengel and no one else." (Die biblisch-prophet. Theologie. Lpz. 1845. p. 6. sq.) "

Admittedly, Crusius rejects the expression *regnum millenarium* as contrary to Scripture, because the Apocalypse indeed speaks of a *millennium regni martyrum in coelo* (20:4), but, like the whole of Scripture, knows only an eternal kingdom of Christ (11:15). . . . In any case, the expression *regnum millenarium* is misleading, and Revelation 20:4 never provides a sufficient scriptural basis for it."

This is what Paul says in 2 Thessalonians 2:3 ff., that the adversary of Christ (τὸν ἀντικείμενον) sits in the temple of God, or the Christian Church, as its head or monarch, after he has erected and stabilized his kingdom through the operation of Satan, with lying signs and wonders, having deceived a great number of men, so that for some time he is not recognized by very many for what he is, or that he is the Antichrist; yet, in his own time, he will be revealed and recognized as the Antichrist, although the day of the Lord will not come immediately even then, but rather the Antichrist himself, having now been exposed, will continue to persist until he is abolished by the splendor of the coming of Christ.

The exposure of the Antichrist, therefore, ought to signify to the faithful, like a sign, that the judgment is to follow, by which the Antichrist, now manifested, is finally to be abolished. See Matthew 24:29. For although we do not have a revealed mode or determined manner of those celestial signs, and specifically the falling of the stars to the earth, it is nevertheless better to retain the freedom of Scripture in these matters, and to leave the mode of the thing to divine wisdom and power, than to desert the literal sense and seek or embrace a metaphor, especially since express mention is made elsewhere of celestial signs, contrasted with earthly ones, in Luke 21:25.

Namely: 1) According to the opinion of some, the notable conversion of the Jews (I do not say universal in every respect, from which none of them is excepted, but a very ample and significant number of them), so that in their public assemblies the doctrine of the Gospel concerning Christ Jesus, the Nazarene, hitherto rejected by them, may be preached, and entire congregations may subscribe to it, and thus very many may be saved through faith in Christ, according to the Epistle to the Romans 11:25 ff.

For that Israel, to whom blindness has hitherto happened, is the one who is described in the same chapter by the name of the natural olive branches in opposition to the wild olive tree, and denotes Israel according to the flesh, in opposition to the Gentiles, whom Paul had also described above in chapter 9:3, 4, 5, as kinsmen according to the flesh, etc. Although it should not therefore be thought that the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem, or the restoration of the civil polity, the occupation of the land of Canaan, the discovery of the ark of the covenant and other lost sacred objects, etc., have been promised.

2) The desolation of the seven-hilled city (Rome) from Revelation 18 and the destruction of Gog and Magog from Revelation 20 are usually referred here.

Luther: "Let whoever wishes hope for the whole crowd; I have no hope for that, nor do I know of any Scripture for it. We cannot even convert our own Christians, the great crowd, and must be content with the little flock: how much less is it possible to convert all these children of the devil. For that some derive such a delusion from the 11th chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, as if all Jews were to be converted at the end of the world, is nothing; St. Paul means something quite different." (Vom Schem Hamphoras, 1541. XX, 2529. sq. cf. III, 2506. sq. VI, 1706.)

The same: "In this way one should also take the word Israel in these two chapters (Ezek. 38, 39). For the apostles and other disciples of Christ who came from the Jews were true Israelites, and have also inherited the name of the whole people of Israel, as St. Paul [inherited] the name Benjamin. Therefore, the name Israel has remained with the apostles henceforth and has been inherited by all their disciples, so that now holy Christendom, and we also, and all who believe the word of the apostles and are their disciples, are called Israel... I say this because..."

that one should not concern oneself with the interpretation of the Jews; this text does not concern them. Daniel 9:26, 27 has indicated to them their end, that they may no longer hope for any assembly. We are the ones who have been brought together from all kinds of peoples under one Lord, Christ.” (Preface to the translation of Ezekiel 38, 39. VI, 1410, 1411.)

Quenstedtius: “One is not to expect any universal or at least significant conversion of the Jews before the end of the world...

Antithesis: 1. Of many of the fathers..., who hold that all Jews without exception, or at least the majority, are to be converted to God before the end of the world. 2. Of almost all the Papists... 3. Of the Calvinists... In particular, Joh. Hoornbeck among the Calvinists undertook to defend this opinion... 4. Of many of our own, such as D. Aeg. Hunnius in his Commentary on 1 Tim. 3, vol. IV, p. 782; Winkelmann in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, ch. 11; D. Hafenreffer in *Templum Ezechielis*, p. 313; D. Menzer in his Analysis of Romans ch. 11, thesis 63; D. Balduin in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, ch. 11, p. 2, q. 11; D. Meisner, book IV *de leg.*, sect. 17, q. 18, and his Commentary on Hosea ch. 3, who also teach that almost all Jews will be converted to God before the end of the world.” (L. c. ch. 19, s. 2, q. 2, f.

Latin:

Zwar verwirft Crusius den Ausdruck regnum millenarium als einen schriftwidrigen, weil die Apokalypse zwar von einem millennium regni martyrum in coelo (20, 4.) redet, aber, wie die ganze Schrift, nur ein ewiges Reich Christi (11, 15.) kennt. . . . Hoc est, quod Paulus 2. ad Thess. 2, 3. sqq. dicit, adversarium Christi (τδν άντιχείμενον) in templo Dei sive ecclesia christiana, velut caput aut monarcham ejus, sedentem, postquam per operationem satanae, signa et prodigia mendacia decepto magno hominum numero regnum suum erexerit ac stabiliverit, ita ut aliquamdiu et a bene multis, qualis sit, seu quod sit antichristus, non agnoscatur, suo tamen tempore revelatum ac tanquam antichristum agnitum iri, licet nec tunc statim adventurus sit dies Domini, quin potius ipse antichristus, jam patefactus, porro sit perstiturus, donec splendore adventus Christi aboleatur.

Patefactio itaque antichristi fidelibus, instar signi, significare debet judicium secuturum, quo antichristus jam manifestatus denique sit abolendus. Vid. Matth. 24, 29. Quamvis enim modum ac determinatam rationem signorum illorum coelestium, ac speciatim casus siderum in terram, revelatam non habeamus, satius tamen est, liberam Scripturae in his retinere, ac modum rei sapientiae potentiaeque divinae relinquere, quam deserto literali sensu metaphoram quaerere aut amplecti, praesertim cum alias signorum coelestium, terrenis contradistinctorum, expressa fiat mentio Lucae 21, 25.

Nempe 1) ex quorundam sententia, Judaeorum notabilis (non dico universalis omnino, a qua nemo illorum excipiatur, sed valde ampla et insignis multorum) conversio, ita ut in coetibus eorum publicis doctrina evangelii de Christo Jesu, Nazareno, hactenus ab ipsis rejecta, praedicetur eique coetus integri subscribant, et sic per fidem in Christum bene multi salventur, juxta Epist. ad Rom. 11, 25. et seqq.

Israel enim ille, cui excoecatio hactenus contigit, is est, qui in eodem cap. nomine ramorum oleae naturalium in oppositione ad oleastrum describitur, denotatque Israelem secundum carnem, in oppositione ad gentes, quam etiam Paulus supra cap. 9, 3. 4· 5. descripserat, tanquam cognatos secundum carnem etc. Quanquam non ideo vel urbis Hierosolymorum reaedificationem, vel politiae civilis restaurationem, terrae Canaan occupationem, arcae foederis aliorumque sacrorum deperditorum inventionem etc. promissa esse, putari debeat.

2) Huc referri solet urbis (Romae) septicollis desolatio ex Apoc. 18. et Gogi et Magogi excidium ex Apoc. 20.
