### Concerning the Last Judgment and the Consummation of the Age: sq.) “Defending the thesis

1813 sq.) “Defending the thesis: B. Luther, Philipp Melanchthon, Brentius, Osiander, Pappus, Cramer, the blessed Gerhard, and Brochmann in their loci in the explanation and vindication of Paul’s oracle in Romans ch. 11, v. 25. To these add the blessed D. Huelsemann in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans (not yet published) and in *Calixtinischer GewissensWurm* ch. 8; the blessed Weller in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 644; D. Georg Grossehein in his diatribe *de catholica Judaeorum conversione*; Wigand in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans; Dr. Calovius in *Biblia illustrata* on Hosea 3:4, 5, and in *Systema Theologicum*, last vol., art. 4, ch. 1, q. 1.” (L. c. f. 1819.) Cf. “Is a solemn conversion of the Jews still to be expected, taught in Romans 11:25, 26?” See “Lehre und Wehre,” Vol. V, p. 307–310, 321–331. — “On the hope of a still impending general conversion of the Jews.” See “Lutheraner,” Vol. XIII, 84–87, 91–93, 97–99, 105–107, 130–133, 137–140, 147–148, 161–165. § 4. At the very moment of the judgment, a peculiar sign will be seen, which is called the sign of the Son of Man. But what kind of sign it will be is difficult to explain. It is so called in Matthew 24: 30. However, the opinion that is more probable than the others is that which teaches that this sign consists in the radiance of the very body of Christ, the splendor of the clouds, and the angelic retinue, according to Matthew l. c. and chapter 25:31, and likewise the great sound, of which we read in 1 Thessalonians 4:16. Luther: “The sign of the Son of Man that will be in heaven on the day of judgment is uncertain. The expression ‘sign of the Son of Man,’ according to the Hebrew manner, stands for: the sign [which is] the Son of Man. For that the cross is understood by that sign is nothing; that is my opinion.” (Letters etc. by de Wette. II, 400.) Gerhard: “We confess with Luther and Brentius that the coming of Christ to judgment will be local and visible, but we add that it will not be successive, as if He were to descend from heaven into the clouds with a certain passage of time, just as in the ascension He was subsequently carried up higher from the earth into the clouds while the apostles were watching (Mark 16:19, Luke 24:51, Acts 1:9), but sudden and momentary... Therefore, the comparison between the ascension of Christ into heaven and His return to judgment in Acts 1:11 is not to be extended beyond that third point in which it is instituted.”

The same: "It is better to take the designation of clouds in the literal sense, since in articles of faith one should not depart from the letter without urgent necessity. However, we believe that no man knows exactly what kind of cloud that will be." (L. c. § 36.) §

5. The Judge will be Christ Himself, who, appearing gloriously in His assumed humanity and sitting as if before a tribunal, conspicuous to all, will pass sentence by divine authority. See Matt. 25:31 ff., where the Son of Man, sitting upon the throne of glory, about to judge all nations gathered before Him, is described at length. Cf. Acts 17:31; John 5:22.

Which is one [judgment] of the whole Holy Trinity, and belongs to Christ as man through communication. With respect to that, the efficient cause of the judgment is said to be the whole Holy Trinity, distinct from others. Compare the cited passages of John and Acts, where, while it is denied that the Father judges anyone—namely, by appearing αυτοπροσώπως (in His own person) and passing sentence—it is nevertheless added that the Father has given all judgment and the power of judging to the Son, John 5:22 and 27. And in Acts 17, it is said that God judges the world έν άνδρί, through a man. Therefore, the persons distinct from the Son are not excluded, but they together bestow divine authority upon that act. To this pertain the passages Rom. 2:2, 3, 5, 6, 16; Heb. 12:23, where the judgment of God and God the judge of all are mentioned.

Gerhard: "Christ will administer that judgment not only as God, but also as man. Therefore, just as He will be a visible and conspicuous judge, so also will He pronounce an audible sentence... They will hear the sentence of judgment not only inwardly in their conscience, but also outwardly in a certain form of words." (L. c. § 69.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who... a) leave to the human nature of Christ nothing but the mere promulgation of a decisive sentence, which can be done by any minister of a judge; b) they deny Him καρδιογνωσίαν (knowledge of the heart), while they assert that Christ, as man, will administer that judgment, with the hearts and consciences of all men being laid open to His human mind by His own Deity. They also deny to the human nature of Christ the dictation and execution of the judicial sentence, which is openly νεστοριανίζειν (to Nestorianize)... 2. Of the Papists, who blow the same pipes as the Calvinists, while by εξουσίαν κρίσιν ποιείν (authority to execute judgment) communicated to Christ, insofar as He is the Son of Man or man, through and because of the hypostatic union, John 5:27, they understand at least the external visibility of the judicial act." (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 1820.) §

6. The internal impulsive cause is the justice of God, partly remunerative, partly vindictive. See 2 Thess. 1:6, 7. Which pertains to the goodness of God. Or the wrath of God, to be fulfilled through the punishment of sinners. PART I. CHAP. X.

§ 7.

The external impulsive causes are partly the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, and partly sins, and especially the final impenitence of those who are to be judged. For this moves God, in the final judgment, to be willing to adjudicate to believers not only eternal life, but also, according to the diversity of works proceeding from faith, degrees of glory regarding accidental rewards. See 2 Cor. 5:10, and compare what we said at Chapter IX, § 5, note b. Thus also in John 12:48, Christ says: "He who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day," which is the same as if He had said that a man who does not believe, by this very fact that he does not believe, moves the Judge to condemn him in the final judgment. § 8.

Christ will have, as it were, assessors and ministers of the judgment: holy men and good angels. Who, therefore, can rightly be called the ministerial and thus less principal cause of the final judgment. For even assessors, such as they are in this instance, are rightly said to minister; they certainly do not possess authority equal to the authority of the Judge, but rather authority that is entirely dependent upon Him and greatly limited. Just as the apostles are said to be about to judge the twelve tribes of Israel, Matt. 19:28, Luke 22:30. And in 1 Cor. 6:2, Paul says: "Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?" See Matt. 25:31. § 9.

And indeed, the office of the angels will be not only to accompany Christ as He approaches for judgment and to manifest His advent by sounding a great trumpet, but also to gather men—both those resurrected from death and those found alive—from all parts of the world, then to separate the pious from the impious, placing the former on the right and the latter on the left, and finally to thrust the damned into hell. Of which we have already made mention above in Chapter III, concerning angels, § 40. See Matt. 25:31, 1 Thess. 4:15, Matt. 24:31, Mark 13:27, Matt. 13:41, 49, Matt. 25:32, Matt. 13:42, 50.

§ 10. Holy men, however, shall be witnesses and approvers of the judgment of Christ. Although they themselves must also be judged first, as will be said presently. They seem, however, to be established in a higher place, according to 1 Thess. 4:14, so that the apostles are indeed nearest to the side of Christ, who appears in visible form, see Matt. 19:28; Luke 22:30; then the patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, teachers, and the rest of the faithful, in their own order, shall look upon the impious, placed in a lower position, and approve their condemnation. Cf. Rev. 19:1 et seqq. § 11. The object of the last judgment is twofold: material, which are the persons to be judged, and formal, or that according to which every person comes to be judged. According to others, the subject to be judged, not the one judging. Others would say, the subject *Quod* (that which). So that it may be the subject *Quo* (that by which). § 12. To the material object belong all men, both the pious and the impious; both those whom that day shall find alive, and the dead, who are to be resurrected first on that day; besides men, however, also the evil angels. For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, that each one may be repaid for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil, as the apostle declares in 2 Cor. 5:10. And Rom. 14:10: We shall all be set before the tribunal of Christ. Cf. Jude vv. 14, 15 and Isaiah 66:16; Matt. 25:32. For thus Christ is said to be about to judge the living and the dead, Acts 10:42; 1 Thess. 4:15, 16, 17; and 2 Tim. 4:1; 1 Pet. 4:5. 2 Pet. 2:4, where the angels who sinned are said to be kept for judgment. Cf. Epistle of Jude v. 6. And Matt. 25:41; chap. 8:29. ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of Petrus Thiraeus, who in his book *De gloriosa Christi apparitione*, ch. 12, asserts that good angels are also to be judged. ... 3. Of certain fathers, who posit that neither the faithful nor the unfaithful are to be judged, but those in between. Thus Lactantius, Hilary, Augustine, Gregory." (L. c. q. 5. f. 1831.) PART I. CHAP. X.

§ 13.

The formal object on the part of the pious is faith; on the part of the impious, it is unbelief, insofar as both are known from works. For Christ the Judge will exercise judgment in such a way that He will render to each one clear testimonies according to the works of faith or unbelief (2 Cor. 5:10. Cf. Rom. 2:6 ff.; Matt. 25:35, 36, 42, 43; Rev. 20:12, 13). However, one must be careful not to confuse the formal object (especially on the part of the pious, who, although they will receive that joyful sentence of the Judge according to works, yet not because of works) with the external impulsive cause. § 14.

The judgment itself is usually distinguished into the judgment of discussion and of retribution. It is distinct from the preliminary acts, the approach of the visible Judge, the gathering of the people to be judged, and the division of them into two classes. Not that the Judge, the heart-knower (καρδιογνώστης), Christ, has need of a discussion of causes or an inquiry to be instituted only then (for He could, even without such a solemn process, lead the pious, whom He knows, to eternal life, and cast the impious, no less distinctly known, into hell); nevertheless, so that the reason for the just judgment may be most manifestly evident to those who are being judged, He will freely enter into that judgment of discussion, and having done so, He will render to each what is his. § 15.

Et Act. 17. dicitur Deus judicare orbem έν άνδρ\, per virum. Non ergo excluduntur personae a Filio distinctae, eed auctoritatem divinam actui illi una largiuntur. Quo pertinent LL. Judicii sententiam audient non solum interius in conscientia, sed etiam exterius in certa verborum forma.“ (L. c. § 69.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antitliesis: 1. Calvinianorum, qui. . . a) humanae Christi naturae nonnisi nudam sententiae decisivae promulgationem, quae per quemvis judicis ministrum fieri potest, relinquunt, b) Denegant ipsi καρδωγνωσίαν, dum asserunt, Christum ut hominem judicium illud administraturum, patefactis humanae ejus menti ab ipsius Deitate omnium hominum cordibus et conscientiis. 6. Causa impulsiva interna est justitia Dei,a partim remuneratoria,b partim vindicativa.c Vid. 2. ad Thess. 1, 6. 7. Quae ad bonitatem Dei spectat. Seu ira Dei, per poenam peccantium explenda. PART. I. CAP. X.

§ 13.

Formale objectum ex parte piorum fides est, ex parte impiorum incredulitas, quatenus quidem utraque ex operibus a cognoscitur.b Exercebit enim Christus judex judicium, ita ut cuique juxta opera fidei aut incredulitatis testimonia luculenta redditurus sit 2 Cor. 5, 10. Conf. Rom. 2, 6. et seqq. Matth. 25, 35. et 36. 42. et 43. Apoc. 20, 12. 13. Cavendum autem est, ne objectum formale (praesertim ex parte piorum, qui, licet secundum opera, non tamen propter opera laetam illam judicis sententiam auferent) cum causa impulsiva externa male confundatur.§ 14.

Ipsum vero judicium a distingui solet in judicium discussionis b et retributionis. Ab actibus praeliminaribus, accessus judicis visibilis, congregationis hominum judicandorum et divisionis eorundem in duas classes, distinctum. Non quod judex χαρδωγνώστης, Christus, opus habeat discussione causarum aut inquisitione tunc demum instituenda (posset enim etiam, citra processum tam solennem, pios, quos novit, aa vitam aeternam deducere, impios, non minus distincte cognitos, praecipitare in infernura); attamen, ut justi judicii ratio ipsis, qui judicantur, manifestissime pateat, discussionis illud judicium libere ingredietur, eoque facto tribuet cuique, quod suum est.§ 15.


### Concerning the Last Judgment and the Consummation of the Age: It is called the judgment of discussion, by which the works of all, hidden as…

It is called the judgment of discussion, by which the works of all, hidden as well as manifest, will be brought to light; primarily so that everyone may sufficiently understand what pertains to himself and what concerns his salvation or damnation. Scripture calls this rendering an account to God, namely, as to a Judge calling the life and actions of all into examination (Rom. 14:12). Not only of those concerning whose faith or unbelief there could be doubt in this life, but also of the rest, whose faith or unbelief was established by public testimonies. For the assertion of the Apostle in the cited passage is universal, where he pronounces concerning all the dead and living, over whom Christ is Lord, that all are to render an account to God. The good works of the pious [are brought to light] to manifest their faith, and how great a difference there is between them and the unbelievers; the evil works of the impious [are brought to light] to manifest their shame, and so that it may be established that they are justly punished.

And thus some also think that the sins of the pious, although they are not to be recounted publicly, will return to their own memory, not indeed so that they may be put to shame or tormented in any way, but so that, recognizing their own unworthiness, they may the more admire and celebrate the greatness of divine grace toward them. Cf. Matthew 25:37 et seqq. Gerhard: "That all things are to be manifested in the judgment is to be understood not collectively, as if the sins of the pious as well as the impious are to be revealed to all, but distributively, in that the good works of the pious, but the evil works of the impious, even those done without witnesses or arbiters, are to be brought into the clear light, as is gathered from the judicial process in Matthew 25:34 sqq. ... Therefore, legal sayings must be distinguished from evangelical ones properly so called; the legal is: 'Men will render an account in that day for every idle word'; the evangelical is: 'He who believes does not come into judgment'; the legal is: 'You are storing up wrath for yourself in the day of the revelation of righteous judgment'; the evangelical is: 'Lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near.' ... (The righteousness of Christ) will cover all the offenses of the pious, so that they do not come into the sight of God, angels, and men." (L. c. § 65.) ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who maintain that not only the sins of the impious and unbelievers, but also those of the pious and faithful, are to be exposed and published in that most solemn judgment to the spectacle of all angels and men. Thus Thomas Aquinas. ... 2. Of certain of our own people, as Jonas Heuler, who teaches the same." (L. c. q. 6. f. 1833. sq.) J. Fechtius: "The sins of the elect also will be published generally in this judgment, yet without any reproach, indeed with praise because of the repentance performed for them." (Sylloge controvers. p. 383. sq.) § 16. The judgment of retribution will consist in the pronunciation of the sentence, which will befit the cause of each, and through which some will be sent away to life, others to eternal damnation; whereupon the execution of the sentence passed will immediately follow.

See Matthew 25:34 and 41. Which some call the judgment of absolution, although the adjudication of life implies more. Whence it is called the judgment of condemnation. Matthew 25:46, ch. 13:39 to 43. Scherzerus: "The norm of this judgment will be, in a word, the Law and the Gospel, but in a diverse and well-noted respect. The Gospel indeed with respect to the elect... The Law, however, with respect to the reprobate, but yet in such a way that it is illuminated by the light of the Gospel." (System. 1. 21. § 9. p. 598. sq.) § 17. The end of the last judgment is the glory of the wisdom, power, goodness, and vindicatory justice of God.

Which the Judge Himself, or the author of the judgment, intends. PART I. CHAPTER X.

Or of the most wise government in this universe, hitherto not rightly acknowledged by many. Which the impious for some time seemed to have eluded or escaped. Made manifest through the very remuneration of the pious, so solemn. Whose full work will appear to have been delayed, not abolished. Cf. 2 Thess. 1:10. §

18. The final judgment may be described as a solemn act by Christ, appearing in the assumed human nature, by which He, by divine authority and power and on account of divine justice, both remunerative and vindictive, will compel all men and evil angels, through the agency of the good angels, to the tribunal; and, having discussed the cause of each and taken into account final faith and sins, especially final unbelief, from their manifest works, He will assign and confer upon the pious and faithful full blessedness, but upon the unbelieving and impious men and demons, consummate misery, with the holy men approving, to the glory of His wisdom, power, goodness, and justice.

For it imports this in the nominative case, yet common to several, so that it rightly sustains the place of a genus. Who is the efficient cause, yet not excluding the other persons, according to § 5. The reason for causing is this, truly common to the three persons. Ibid. Which is the internal impulsive cause; concerning which see § 6. Who are the material object; see § 12. Thus the ministers of the judgment are denoted, according to § 8 and 9. These and the following pertain to the mode or formal reason of the proces s, regarding the prior act of judgment; see § 14, 15. By which the formal object is indicated; concerning which see § 13. As assessors of the judgment (who pertain to the ministerial cause); see § 8, 10. k) The posterior act is here, looking to the form and process of the judgment, according to § 14 and 16. l) As the final cause; concerning which see § 17. §

19. The judgment having been completed, the consummation of the world will immediately follow, by which heaven and earth, and likewise the other elements and bodies composed of elements, as to their substance, by means of fire, will perish

DE JUDICIO EXTBEMO. Or the consummation of the age, just as the word αιών denotes both the world and the age. Certainly, once the world is destroyed, time itself will also end. The Hebrews themselves also distinguish between הדה oSty and עוילים הבא, this age and the future one. Cf. our Dissertation on Rom. 12:2, regarding the avoidance of conformity with the world, in the proem. See Ps. 102:26, 27 and Heb. 1:10, 11, where it is said of the earth and the heavens: they will perish, they will grow old…y will perish, they will grow old like a garment; they will be changed like a cloak. Opposed here, however, is the immutability of God according to His essence and the mutability and change of heaven and earth; the former, indeed, when they passed from non-being to being through creation, and then the latter, by which they are to pass from being to non-being; which is, indeed, a substantial change. Cf. 2 Pet. 3:10 and 12.

Gerhard: “Man was not created primarily for this animal life, but for a heavenly one, so that, having completed the course of transitory life in these lands, he might live with God his Creator in eternal glory and joy. Therefore, the world also was not created to endure forever, but to provide what is necessary for man for this life for a certain and definite time; consequently, when the number of the elect is complete, it will be abolished, and the creation of a new heaven and a new earth will succeed, in which perfect righteousness dwells, 2 Pet. 3:13. The earth was therefore created to be the dwelling place of man the wayfarer; the whole universe was created to be a certain mirror of θεογνωσίας and to serve man on the journey of this life; therefore, when man sees God face to face and arrives at his homeland, and thus ceases to be a wayfarer, there will no longer be any use for this age. Our Luther was accustomed to say: ‘The present world is only a preparation and scaffolding of God for that world; when the house is finished, one tears down the scaffolding.’” (L. de consumm. saec. § 11.)

The same: “The consummation of the age seems to have had a place even in the state of integrity. For God had not created man to lead only an animal life in this age, but so that, after the course of animal life in these lands had been passed, he might be elevated to a heavenly and glorious life; consequently, the world was not created by God with the end that it should endure forever, but that, when the number of those whom God willed to be generated by men and to have as partakers of the heavenly kingdom was complete, it would be annihilated again, because with the cessation of the animal life of all men, there would be no further use for the world. Just as, therefore, the generation of men would not have been extended to infinity, but would have had a certain end and limit, upon the arrival of which all and individual men living on earth would have been translated to a spiritual and glorious life in the heavens, so also the duration of the world would not have been interminable and perpetual, but would have had its end together with the animal life of men. But the mode of consummation seems to have been different, namely, by simple annihilation, and not by the conflagration of fire.” (L. c. § 66.)

Kromayer: “An argument for establishing the opinion which maintains that the world will perish according to its accidents, not according to its substance, is brought forward from Rom. 8:19 sqq. But we respond that this liberation occurs not by a change for the better, but by annihilation and its own abolition. For the creature prefers not to be, rather than, subjected to the abuse of men, to war against its Creator. Thus wine, when it is forced to serve drunkenness, prefers not to be, rather than to be subjected to this vanity. Groaning and expectation are ascribed to irrational creatures by prosopopoeia... 3. From Ps. 102:25–28, God is said to be about to change the heaven, as one changes a garment. But we respond that the term for change, as appears from physics, is of such broad signification that it includes both φθοράν ... and αλλοίωσιν ... within its scope. In this place ... it denotes annihilation, just as when a garment is worn out and finally reduced to nothing.” PART I. CHAP. X.

This acceptance of the word is evident from the text itself, since the heavens are said to grow old like a garment; which change is certainly not for the better, but for the worse... " Regarding Luther’s statement that the world is already wearing its everyday garment (has the workday-garment on), and will one day wear its change-of-clothes (will have the holiday or Sunday-garment on). But we respond that these words at least establish a comparison between the old and the new world, but no transformation of one from the other is taught; cf. Rev. 21:1." (Th. posit. pol. I, 1191. sqq.)

Gerhardus: "We do not defend the opinion concerning the substantial φθορά or destruction of the world as an article of faith simply necessary to be known and believed for salvation, but we say that it is more in conformity with the emphatic sayings of Scripture which speak of the end of the world." (L. c. § 38.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of certain fathers who championed an accidental change of the world; indeed, that heaven and earth would be changed for the better regarding accidents alone without the destruction of substance, was asserted first, if I am not mistaken, by Origen... After Origen, Jerome... Augustine discourses thus: 'The substance itself will have those qualities which befit immortal bodies by a wonderful change, so that, namely, the world, renewed for the better, may be aptly accommodated to bodies, even flesh, renewed for the better.'... 2. Of the Scholastics, who posit that the world will perish not κατ’ ουσίαν, but κατά ποιότητα... 4. Of certain Calvinists, who also incline toward that opinion concerning accidental change, namely, that an instauration of heaven and earth is to be expected, not an annihilation... 5. Of some of our own, who think that the world will pass away only by a change of qualities... Brentius, hom. 53 on Luke, fol. 621: 'Will heaven and earth, he says, pass away in such a way that nothing of them remains at all? Least of all! They will not pass away entirely, but will be changed. They will cast off the garment of corruption, and put on the new garment of incorruption; the future change of heaven and earth is certain, but not a total abolition.' The same is taught by Althamerus... and Phil. Nicolai." (L. c. P. IV. c. 20. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1852. sqq.)

Thus expressly Peter, 2 Epist. 3:7, 10: The heavens and the earth which are now, are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment, etc. But concerning the nature of this fire, it is disputed more curiously than usefully. Meanwhile, the pious will also have new heavens and a new earth, i. e., a glorious habitation, 2 Pet. 3:13 and Rev. 21:1 et seqq., but the impious will have a prison and hell destined for them; see Rev. 20:14, 15.

Gerhardus: "The heaven of the blessed... can be taken in three ways: first, objectively and efficiently; second, formally; third, subjectively. If it is taken in the first way, the heaven of the blessed is God the Creator Himself; if in the second way, the heaven of the blessed is something distinct from God, namely, the glory and heavenly joy in the saints themselves, yet it is not a corporeal substance produced by God in the first creation; if in the third way, we say that the πού, its quiddity, quality, and location are not revealed to us in the Scriptures; therefore, it is better to be solicitous about its possession than about an accurate definition in this life." (L. de vit. aet. § 40.)

Latin:

Dicitur autem judicium discussionis,a quo omnium b opera, occulta pariter et manifesta, in lucem c protrahentur; inprimis, ut quilibet, quae ad se pertinent d et ad suam salutem seu damnationem spectant, satis intelligat. Scriptura hoc vocat rationem reddere Deo, scilicet tanquam judici, vitam et actiones omnium in examen vocanti, Rom. 14, 12. Non solum eorum, de quorum seu fide, seu incredulitate, dubitari in hac vita poterat, verum etiam reliquorum, quorum sive fides sive incredulitas publicis testimoniis constabat. Universalis enim assertio est apostoli l. c., ubi de omnibus mortuis ac viventibus, quibus Christus dominatur, pronunciat, quod omnes rationem reddituri sint Deo. Piorum bona opera ad manifestandam eorum fidem, et quantum intersit inter eos et infideles; impiorum mala opera ac pudorem ipsorum, et ut constet, eos juste puniri.

Atque ita etiam piorum peccata, licet non recensenda publice, Ipsis in memoriam reditura, quidam existimant, quo non quidem pudefiant aut quoquo modo angantur, sed tamen, indignitatem suam agnoscentes, gratiae divinae erga se magnitudinem magis admirentur ac celebrent. Conf. Matth. 25, 37. et seqq.Gerhardus: ״Omnia in judicio manifestanda esse, accipiendum est non collective, quasi tam piorum, quam impiorum pfeccata sint omnibus revelanda, sed distributive, quod piorum bona opera, impiorum vero mala opera, etiam sine testibus vel arbitris facta, in claram lucem collocanda sint, ut ex processu judiciali Matth. 25, 34. sqq. colligitur. . . Distinguenda igitur dicta legalia ab evangelicis proprie sic dictis; legale est: ,Rationem reddent homines in die illo de quovis verbo otioso‘; evangelicum est: ,Qui credit, non venit in judicium’; legale est: ,Thesaurizas tibi iram in die revelationis justi judicii‘; evangelicum est: ,Attollite capita vestra, quia appropinquat redemtio vestra.‘ . . (Christi justitia) teget universa piorum delicta, quo minus in Dei, angelorum et hominum conspectum veniant.“ (L. c. § 65.) ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum, statuentium, non solum impiorum et incredulorum, sed etiam piorum et fidelium peccata in judicio illo solennissimo omnium angelorum hominumque spectaculo esse exponenda et publicanda. Sic Thomas Aquinas. . . 2. Quorundam nostratium, ut Jonae Heuleri idem docentis.“ (L. c. q. 6. f. 1833. sq.) J. Fechtius: ,,Publicabuntur generaliter in hoc judicio, sine ulla tamen exprobratione, imo cum laude ob actam de iis poenitentiam, etiam electorum peccata.“ (Sylloge controvers. p. 383. sq.) § 16. Retributionis judicium consistet in pronunciatione sententiae,a quae cujusque causae conveniet, et per quam alii ad vitam,b alii ad damnationem c aeternam ablegabuntur; ubi statim sequetur sententiae latae executio.d

Vid. Matth. 25, 34. et 41. Quod judicium absolutionis quidam vocant, quanquam adjudicatio vitae plus importet. Unde judicium condemnationis vocatur. Matth. 25, 46. cap. 13, 39. ad 43.Scherzerus: ״Norma hujus judicii erit uno verbo lex et evangelium, sed diverso et probe notando respectu. Evangelium quidem respectu electorum.. . Lex vero respectu reproborum, sed ita tamen, ut sit evangelii luce collustrata.“ (System. 1. 21. § 9. p. 598. sq.) § 17. Finis judicii extremi a est sapientiae,b potentiae,c bonitatis d et justitiae vindicati vae e Dei gloria.

Quem judex ipse sive auctor judicii intendit. PART. I. CAP. X.

Sive sapientissimi regiminis in hoc universo, hactenus a multi» non recte agniti. Quam impii aliquamdiu elusisse aut sese subduxisse videbantur. Per ipsam remunerationem piorum tam solennem patefactae. Cujus plenum opus dilatum, non sublatum fuisse apparebit. Confer. 2 Thess. 1, 10.§

18. Describi potest judicium extremum, quod sit actus solennis a Christi b in assumta humana natura apparentis, quo is, auctoritate et potentia c divina et propter justitiam d divinam, remuneratoriam et vindicativam, hornines e omnes angelosque malos, mediante bonorum angelorum f opera, ad tribunal g coget et, causa cujusque discussa habitaque ratione h fidei finalis et peccatorum, inprimis incredulitatis finalis, ex operibus ipsorum apparentium, piis et fidelibus plenam beatitudinem, infidelibus autem et impiis hominibus ac daemonibus consummatam miseriam, approbantibus sanctis i hominibus, assignabit k et conferet ad sapientiae, potentiae, bonitatis et justitiae suae 1 gloriam.

19. Peracto judicio, statim sequetur mundi consummatio,a qua coelum et terra, itemque caetera elementa et corpora ex elementis composita, quoad substantiam suam,b mediante igne,c peribunt.d

DE JUDICIO EXTBEMO. Seu consummatio saeculi, prout vox αιών et mundum et saeculum denotat. Certe mundo destructo, tempus una finietur. Ipsi quoque Ebraei distinguunt inter הדה oSty et עוילים הבא, saeculum hoc et futurum. Conf. Disp. nostram ad 1. Rom. 12, 2. de conformitate cum mundo fugienda, in prooem. Vid. Ps. 102, 26. 27. et Ebr. 1, 10. 11., ubi de terra ac codis dicitur: peribunt, veterascent, sicut vestimentum; mutabuntur sicut pallium. Opponuntur autem h. 1. Dei immutabilitas secundum esse et coeli ac terrae mutabilitas et mutatio; primum quidem, cum per creationem a non esse ad esse transierint, deinde postrema illa, qua ab esse ad non esse sint transitura; quae sane mutatio substantialis est. Conf. 2 Petr. 3, 10. et 12.

Gerhardus: ״Homo non est praecipue ad hanc animalem, sed coelestem vitam conditus, ut exacto in his terris vitae transitoriae curriculo cum Deo creatore suo in aeterna gloria ac laetitia vivat. Ergo etiam mundus non est conditus, ut in aeternum perseveret, sed ut homini ad hanc vitam necessaria per certum ac definitum tempus suppeditet; proinde etiam completo electorum numero abolebitur et succedet novi coeli ac novae terrae creatio, in quibus perfecta justitia habitet, 2 Pet. 3, 13. Terra ideo condita est, ut esset domicilium hominis viatoris; tota rerum universitas ideo creata est, ut esset speculum quoddam θεογνωσίας et homini in via hujus vitae inserviret; ergo quando homo Deum a facie ad faciem videbit ac in patriam appulerit, adeoque viator esse desierit, nullus amplius erit hujus saeculi usus. Lutherus noster fuit dicere solitus: ,Die jetzige Welt ist nur eine Vorbereitung und Gerüste Gottes zu jener Welt; wenn das Haus fertig, so reisset man das Gerüste ein.‘“ (L. de consumm. saec. § 11.)

Idem: ,,Consummatio saeculi videtur etiam in statu integritatis locum habuisse. Neque enim Deus hominem ad animalem duntaxat vitam in hoc saeculo traducendam condiderat, sed' ut transacto animalis vitae in his terris curriculo ad vitam coelestem et gloriosam elevaretur; proinde etiam mundus non erat a Deo hoc fine conditus, ut in aeternum perduraret, sed ut completo eorum numero, quos Deus ah hominibus generari et consortes regni coelestis habere voluit, iterum annihilaretur, quia cessante animali omnium hominum vita nullus ampiius futurus erat mundi usus. Ut ergo generatio hominum non fuisset in infinitum exporrecta, sed certum habuisset finem ac terminum, quo adventante omnes ac singuli homines in terris viventes ad vitam in coelis spiritualem et gloriosam fuissent translati, ita quoque mundi duratio non fuisset interminabilis ac perpetua, sed una cum animali hominum vita suum habuisset finem. Sed modus consummationis videtur fuisse diversus, per simplicem sci. annihilationem, non autem per ignis conflagrationem.“ (L. c. § 66.)

Kromayerus: ״Argumentum pro adstruenda sententia, quaemundum secundum accidentia, non secundum substantiam, interiturum statuit, affertur ex Rom. 8, 19. sqq. Sed respondemus, liberationem istam fleri non mutatione in melius, sed annihilatione, suique abolitione. Creatura siquidem mavult non esse, quam, abusui hominum subjecta, contra creatorem suum militare. Sic vinum, cum ebrietati servire cogitur, mavult non esse, quam vanitati huic subjectum esse. Gemitus et expectatio creaturis irrationalibus per prosopopoeiam adscribitur. . . 3. Ex Ps. 102, 25—28. Deus dicitur coelum mutaturus, ut vestimentum mutatur. Sed respondemus, terminum mutationis, ut ex physicis apparet, tam latae significationis esse, ut et φθοράν ... et αλλοίωσιν. . . ambitu suo includat. Hoc loco. . . annihilationem denotat, veluti, cum vestis atteritur et in nihilum tandem redigitur״ PART. I. CAP. X.

Haec vocis acceptio ex ipso textu patet, cum coeli vestis instar veterascere dicuntur; quae certe mutatio non est in melius, sed deterius... Quod secundum Lutherum mundus jam indutus sit veste quotidiana (habe das Werkeltags-Kleid an), olim induendum esse veste mutatoria (werde das Feier oder SonntagsKleid anhaben). Sed respondemus, his verbis saltem comparationem inter mundum veterem et novum institui, nullam autem transformationem unius ex alio doceri, cf. Apoc. 21, 1.“ (Th. posit.pol. I, 1191. sqq.)

Gerhardus: ,,Sententiam de substantiali mundi φ&ορμ seu interitu non defendimus ut fidei articulum ad salutem scitu ac creditu simpliciter necessarium, sed, eam emphaticis Scripturae dictis, quae de fine mundi loquuntur, magis conformem esse, dicimus.“ (L. c. § 38.)

Post Origenem Hieronymus ..., Augustinus ita disserit: Ipsa substantia eas qualitates habebit, quae corporibus immortalibus mirabili mutatione conveniunt, ut sci. mundus in melius innovatus apte accommodetur corporibus, etiam carne, in melius innovatis. .. 2. Scholasticorum, statuentium, mundum non κατ’ ουσίαν, sed κατά ποιότητα interiturum... 4. Quorundam Calvinianorum, qui etiam in illam de immutatione accidentali inclinant sententiam, sci. instaurationem expectandam esse coeli et terrae, non annihilationem. . . 5. Nonnullorum ex nostris, qui existimant, qualitatum tantum immutatione mundum transiturum esse. . . Brentius hom. 53. in Lucam fol. 621.: ,Num coelum et terra, inquit, ita transibunt, ut nihil eorum omnino maneat? Minime omnium! Non transibunt omnino, sed mutabuntur. Abjicient vestimentum corruptionis, et induent uovam vestem incorruptionis; futura quidem coeli ac terrae mutatio, non autem in totum abolitio.‘ Idem docent Althamerus ... et Phil. NicoZai.“. (L. c. P. IV. c. 20. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1852. sqq.)

Sic expresse Petrus 2. Epist. 3, 7. 10.: Qui nunc sunt coeli et terra, servantur igni in diem judicii etc. De natura autem hujus ignis curiose magis, quam utiliter, disputatur. Interim habebunt et pii codos novos ac terram novam, i. e. habitationem gloriosam, 2 Petr. 3, 13. et Apoc. 21, 1. et seqq., impii vero carcerem et infernum sibi destinatum; via. Apoc. 20, 14. 15.

Gerhardus: ״ Coelum beatorum ... tripliciter potest accipi, primo objective et efficienter, secundo formaliter, tertio subjective. Si primo modo accipiatur, coelum beatorum est ipse Deus creator; si secundo modo, coelum beatorum est aliquid a Deo distinctum, videlicet gloria ac laetitia coelestis in ipsis sanctis, non tamen est substantia corporea in prima creatione a Deo producta; si tertio modo, dicimus, πον illius quidditatem, qualitatem ac situm in Scripturis non esse nobis revelata; ideo praestat, de ejus possessione, quam accurata definitione, in hac vita solicitum esse.“ (L. de vit. aet. § 40.)


## 13 Concerning Sin in General

PART TWO Chapter I. CONCERNING SIN IN GENERAL. §

1. Since the subject of the operation of revealed theology is man the sinner, therefore, having regard to the end of theology and what pertains to it, we must now speak of sin. See Prolegom. cap. I. § 20. Vol. I. p. 40. See l. c. § last. Namely, just as elsewhere in practical disciplines, when one must deal with the method of introducing an end into a subject, the subject must first be considered as lacking the end; and whether, and how far, it is capable of the end; so in theology, after having treated of beatitude, man must be considered, not only as lacking beatitude, but also as averted from God through sin and lacking the strength to obtain beatitude from God, namely, so that, being liberated from sin and reconciled to God, he may be led to beatitude. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. cap. III. § 1. p. 214. §

2. Sin is accepted in this place partly abstractively, for the very lack of conformity with the law, which concerns the life and actions of a rational creature, in which respect it is a mere privation, and not something positive; partly concretively, insofar as, besides the absence of conformity with the law, it also embraces some subject to which that privation adheres, whether it be a connate quality, or an acquired habit, or an act which behaves otherwise than it ought to behave according to a certain law, and therefore deviates from the law, or does not agree with the law; in which respect it is certain that sin is something positive. Elsewhere, sin is said more generally in relation to any rule prescribing a certain mode of operation, in which respect there is given PART II. CHAP. I.

sin of nature (which is called a monster), likewise sin of art. In this place, however, the term being taken specially and properly, it is understood as sin in respect to the rule of morals, and is called moral sin.

Thus, expressly, 1 John 3:4: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία. Now, ἀνομία is the formal reason itself, through which something has that which is ἄνομον. And thus it signifies by way of an abstract. For it imports nothing beyond the negation of a positive entity, namely, of the rectitude or conformity with the law, which ought to have been present. However, no substance, no positive accident is formally a privation. For this would be a contradiction. Thus, innate depraved concupiscence, vicious habits contracted by acting evilly, and all acts conflicting with the law are customarily and rightly called sins. For although that from which, as from a form, it has that which it is and is denominated sin, is not something positive, but a mere privation; yet because in sin taken concretively, besides that formal element, something material is also involved, therefore, as far as the material of sin is concerned, it can certainly involve a positive entity. Compare with these things, which we have said regarding this §, the blessed Musaeus’s *Theses Theologicae de Peccato*, printed and publicly debated in the year 1651, at the beginning. § 3. By the law, however, must be understood the eternal and immutable wisdom and judgment of God concerning those things which are fitting or unfitting for a rational creature, as such, joined with the will that they be done or not be done.

For because sin in its formal reason imports an aberration from a norm or rule, therefore a norm of such a kind must be sought which is primary and adequate for all sins. For a secondary norm is resolved into the primary; but a particular one is such that there are many things, partly right, partly depraved, which do not square with it. For which reason it is formally in God Himself, even though it terminates at creatures and those things which pertain to them. And thus sin must be viewed insofar as God j udges that it is unfitting for a rational nature, insofar as it is such, and wills that it not be done, or that the opposite be done. It is otherwise called the law of nature, because it is concerned with those things which are by nature or in themselves honest and base, or which are fitting or unfitting for a rational nature as such. It is also called the moral law, insofar as it looks to morals, or the manner of living, which becomes or misbecomes a rational creature. § 4.

That law was promulgated first in creation itself, when the knowledge of practical principles was conferred upon humans

their [power] and faculty, the same for applying [these] to individual actions and the circumstances of actions. For we must treat here of the promulgation of the law, so that the nature of sin may be revealed all the more clearly. For it is established that the law does not obligate unless it is promulgated, so that those who act otherwise than the law demands are not considered to act άνόμως when the law has not been promulgated. See what was s…aid above concerning the image of God on the part of the intellect, Part I, Chapter IV, § 9, p. 149.

For the law of nature, implanted in the minds of men, is a certain express image of the eternal law itself existing in God, or a communication or promulgation of the divine law, by which those things that God Himself would judge to be fitting for man, to be done and to be avoided, were manifested to man, to be observed as if by the authority of God the Creator.

These things universally prescribe what is to be done and what is to be omitted. The Schools call that knowledge συντήρησις. So that it might be clear what, according to those general precepts, is to be done and not to be done here and now. The Schools call this φρόνησις. Although this is not so much the law itself as the application of the law, or the power of applying it.

Reuschius: "Conscience and practical reasoning, by which we determine the morality (i.e., conformity and lawlessness) of free actions. Whence it requires: 1. habitual knowledge of practical principles or general judgments concerning the morality of the free actions of man, which is called συντήρησις and constitutes the major premise of that practical reasoning which we call conscience; 2. habitual knowledge of any individual actions whatsoever, by the power of which those individual actions can be subsumed under those general practical principles, which is called σννείδησις and constitutes the minor premise of that practical reasoning which is called conscience; 3. the faculty of eliciting from these two premises, which συντήρησις and σννείδησις provide, a practical conclusion which determines that this or that action is morally good and therefore to be performed, or evil and therefore to be omitted; which conclusion is called the dictate of conscience." (Annotatt. p. 392 sq.)

Balduinus: "In this place, συντήρησις is a faculty of the soul which always opposes vices and continually reproves evils that have been committed, and thus always desires to keep the soul immaculate from sin. And some have called this synteresis conscience itself... But the distinction between these two is manifest. Synteresis can never err; conscience sometimes errs in judging." (Tract. de cas. consc. p. 9.)

Ad. Osiander: "An erroneous conscience arising from invincible ignorance regarding honest and base things, especially those that are intrinsically such, and also regarding precepts and prohibitions of the divine law, does not obligate, but binds. ... To bind, however, is to constrain someone so that one cannot licitly proceed while such a conscience persists; so that one sins if one acts against it, and one also sins if one acts according to its prescription. Hence it is rightly said: 'An erroneous conscience suffices for vice, not for virtue, and it ensnares, it does not obligate.' ... An erroneous conscience proceeding from invincible ignorance in an indifferent object and deed, and also in certain (remote) consequences of the principles of law, whether natural or divine, obligates, excuses from sin, and finally diminishes [it]." (Colleg. th. system. P. V. Loc. 14. th. 48. 49. p. 288 sq.) PART II. CHAPTER I.

5. Afterwards, those perfections having been lost through the Fall, which were previously received by virtue of the divine image, that law was indeed greatly obliterated, yet some of its traces or indications remained; God, however, besides other revelations, especially repeated the sum of the law in the Decalogue by voice and in writing, and explained the individual precepts more clearly here and there in Holy Scripture. As will be said more distinctly below in the section on original sin.

As it is said in Rom. 2:15: The Gentiles, who do not have the law (externally proposed to them by a special revelation), are a law unto themselves, showing the work of the law written in their hearts, etc., inasmuch as they have a certain knowledge of discerning the honest and the base inscribed upon their hearts, as if by the finger of nature; by the power of which, when they descend into themselves after various actions have been performed, they now accuse themselves as violators of the law laid down by a superior, and now, discovering that they have acted rightly, excuse (at least in some way) and defend themselves.

Apology of the A.C.: "Since the natural law, which agrees with the law of Moses or the Ten Commandments, is innate and written in the hearts of all men, and thus reason can to some extent grasp and understand the Ten Commandments, it wants to imagine that it has enough in the law and that through the law one can obtain forgiveness of sins." (Art. IV, p. 87 sq.)

Which occurred to the patriarchs, and through them to others, not once. Compare the blessed Gerhard, L. de Lege § 15 sqq. to 24, where he shows that the practice of the moral law, comprised in the Decalogue, had a place even before Moses.

Kromayer: "An antemosaic Decalogue could easily be compiled. The first commandment can be found in Gen. 12:1, 16:7: 'I am the God who brought you out,' etc. By which words God separates Himself from other false gods to exclude idolatry. The second in Gen. 18:4, when Abraham invoked the name of God by building an altar. The third in Gen. 2:3, when God sanctified the seventh day and consecrated it to divine worship. The fourth in Gen. 9:5, when He curses the posterity of Ham, who was a mocker of his parent. The fifth in Gen. 9:6, when the divine majesty commands that whoever sheds the blood of man, his blood shall be shed by men. The sixth in Gen. 2:24, because God joined one woman to one man, and commanded that the two should be one flesh. The seventh in Gen. 44:8, because the brothers of Joseph are not a little dismayed by the fear of punishment on account of the suspicion of theft. The eighth in Gen. 3:14, because a sufficiently grave punishment is inflicted upon the devil and the serpent, his instrument, on account of a lie. The ninth and tenth in Gen. 39:8–10, because Joseph avoids wicked concupiscences, which prepare for divine wrath, worse than a dog or a snake." (Th. posit. pol. II, 266 sq.)

Vol. I. p. 40. Vid. l. c. § ult. Nempe prout alias in disciplinis practicis, quando de ratione introducendi finem in subjectum agendum est, prius considerari debet subjectum, tanquam carens fine; et an? et quousque finis capax sit? ita in theologia, postquam de beatitudine actum est, considerandus est homo, non solum ut carens beatitudine, verum etiam ut aversus a Deo per peccatum et carens viribus consequendi a Deo beatitudinem, scilicet, ut a peccato liberatus Deoque reconciliatus ad beatitudinem perducatur. Conf. b. Mus. Introd. cap. III. § 1. p. 214.§

2. II. CAP. I.

peccatum naturae (quod vocatur monstrum), item peccatum arti8. Hoc loco autem, specialiter et proprie accepta voce, intelligitur peccatum in respectu ad regulam morum, et vocatur peccatum morale.

Sic expresse Johannes 1. Ep. 8, J/.. · ή αμαρτία έατ'ιν ή άνομία. ,Ανομία autem est ipsa ratio formalis, per quam quid habet, quod est άνομον. Et sic per modum abstracti significat. Nihil enim importat, praeter negationem enti tatis positivae, nempe rectitudinis aut conformitatis cum lege, quae adesse debebat. Per legem autem intelligi debet aeterna a et immutabilis Dei sapientia ac judicium b de his, quae creaturae rationali, qua talis est, conveniunt aut disconveniunt, conjunctum cum voluntate, ut ea fiant vel non fiant. c

Quia enim peccatum in sua formali ratione importat aberrationem a norma seu regula, ideo quaerenda est norma ejusmodi, quae sit prima et adaequata omnibus peccatis. Secundaria enim norma resolvitur in primariam; particularis autem ita se habet, ut multa sint, partim recta, partim prava, quae ad eam non quadrant. Qua ratione formaliter est in ipso Deo, etsi ad creaturas, et quae ad ipsas pertinent, terminetur. Et sic peccatum spectari debet, quatenus Deus judicat, illud naturae rationali, quatenus talis est, disconvenire, et vult illud non fieri, aut fieri oppositum. Vocatur alias lex naturae, quia versatur circa ea, quae natura aut per se honesta et turpia sunt, sive, quae naturae rationali, ut tali, conveniunt, vel disconveniunt. Promulgata a est lex illa primum in ipsa creatione,b cum conferretur hominibus notitia principiorum practi

eorum c et facultas, eadem ad singulas actiones et actionum circumstantias applicandi.d Agendum enim hic est de promulgatione legis, ut ratio peccati tanto clariue patescat. Lex naturae enim, mentibus hominum implantata, est quaedam ipsius in Deo existentis legis aeternae expressa imago, seu communicatio aut promulgatio legis aivinae, qua, quae Deus ipse judicaret homini esse convenientia, agenda et fugienda, homini manifestabantur, velut ex auctoritate Dei creatoris observanda.

Quae universaliter praescribunt, quid agendum, quid omittendum sit. Scholae illam notitiam συντήρησή appellant. Ita ut constaret, quid, juxta praecepta illa generalia, hic et nunc agendum et non agendum sit. Scholae φρόνησιν appellant. Quanquam haec non tam sit lex ipsa, quam legis applicatio, aut vis eam applicandi.

Reuschius: ״Conscientia et ratiocinium practicum, quo moralitatem (i. e. kwopiav atque ανομίαν) actionum liberarum determinamus. Unde postulat illa: 1. notitiam habitualem principiorum practicorum seu generalium judiciorum de moralitate actionum hominis liberarum, qttae dicitur συντήρησις et constituit propositionem majorem illius ratiocinii practici, quod vocamus conscientiam; 2. notitiam habitualem actionum singularium quarumlibet, vi cujus subsumi possunt actiones Illae singulares sub illis principiis practicis generalibus, quae dicitur σννείδησις et constituit propositionem minorem illius ratiocinii practici, quod appellatur conscientia; S. facultatem exiliis duabus praemissis, quas suppeditat σνντήρησις atque σννείδησις, eliciendi conclusionem practicara, quae determinat, hanc vel illam actionem esse moraliter bonam, eoque perpetrandam, vel malam, eoque omittendam; quae conclusio vocatur dictamen conscientiae.“ (Annotatt. p. 392. sq.)

Balduinus: ״Hoc in loco σνντήρησις est facultas animae, quae semper adversatur vitiis et perpetrata mala continuo arguit et sic semper cupit animam a peccato conservare immaculatam. Synteresis nunquam.potest errare, conscientia interdum in judicando aberrat.“ (Tract. de cas. consc. p. 9.)

Ligare vero est aliquem constringere, ut quis non licite possit procedere, tali conscientia permanente; ita ut peccetur, si contra eam agatur, et peccetur etiam, si juxta ejus praescriptum agatur. Hinc recte dicitur; ,Conscientia erronea sufficit ad vitium, non ad virtutem, et illaqueat, non obligat.‘ . . P. V. Loc. 14. th. 48. 49. p. 288. sq.) PART. II. CAP. I.

5. Postea, amissis per lapsum perfectionibus istis, vi imaginis divinae ante acceptis, lex illa equidem valde ohliterata a fuit, sed tamen manserunt aliqua ejus vestigia aut indicia;b Deus autem, praeter caeteras revelationes,c inprimis in decalogo summam legis voce atque scripta repetiit d et singula praecepta in sacra Scriptura passim clarius explicavit.e Prout infra in loco de peccato originali distinctius dicetur.

Prout Rom. 2, 15. dicitur: Gentes, quae legem (extrinsecus per revelationem peculiarem sibi propositam) non habent, sibi ipsis sunt lex, ostendentes opus legis, scriptum in cordibus suis etc., quippe habentes notitiam quandam discernendi honesta et turpia cordibus suis, velut naturae digito, inscriptam; cujus vi etiam, cum post actiones varias patratas in se descendunt, se ipsos nunc ut violatores legis a superiore latae accusent, nunc recte se egisse deprehendentes excusent (saltem quodammodo) ac defendant.
