### Concerning Sin in General: Exod. 20:1 et seqq. And chapter 31:18, it is indicated that God, after He…

Exod. 20:1 et seqq. And chapter 31:18, it is indicated that God, after He finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, gave him the two tables of the testimony, containing the sum of the statutes, tables written by the finger (or by the immediate operation of the power) of God. Conf. Deut. 4:18, chap. 9:10.

See what the blessed Gerhard taught in *Loci*, On the Law, Section IX, regarding the individual precepts of the Decalogue, having adduced other explanatory passages of Scripture. It is especially to be noted how Christ purged the old law of Pharisaic corruptions, Matt. 5:20 ff., ch. 19:8 ff., so that it has the character of sin not only in what is repugnant to the precepts expressed in the Decalogue, but also in what is repugnant to the sense declared by Christ. He also showed that the sum of the law is comprised in the precepts of loving God and one’s neighbor, Matt. 22:37–40, and thus signifies that every sin conflicts either with the love of God, or with the love of the neighbor, or with both. §

6. And thus the greatest and most universal binding force of this law can be known, which no human being can escape. As a primary and adequate norm. For it is 1. concerning things good and evil in themselves, and 2. it has as its author God, who is most wise, most holy, and most powerful. For it is contradictory for one to be a human being and yet not be obligated, by the authority of the Legislator who is the Creator and Lord of all, to do those things which are fitting for a rational creature as such. §

7. Moreover, that is also truly sin which is committed against any positive law, whether divine or human, provided the human law does not contradict the divine. Concerning a matter not simply and in itself necessary, but only because of the free will of God, who could have not prescribed this, or could have prescribed the opposite, e.g., in ceremonial or forensic matters. Where, however, just as the law of nature commands one to obey God in all things, so the obligation to obey these precepts is founded upon the obligation of the law of nature, such that he who acts otherwise sins.

Fechtius: "Some add a third class of positive-moral laws, which are called positive because they depend upon the mere will of God, not upon natural necessity, since, if God willed, they could be otherwise and be changed; but they are called moral because they are similar to moral laws in the perpetual obligation of all men; examples of which they allege are the degrees prohibited in Leviticus and the law concerning celebrating the Sabbath every week. But, in truth, that this class of laws is devised in vain is proven: I. By the perpetual silence of Scripture. For a positive-moral law can in no way be proven, since even in the cited examples, whatever is moral in the prohibited degrees or in the Sabbath is also natural, and whatever is not natural is ceremonial and Jewish. II. By the consensus of the theologians of our church of old, since they were almost entirely ignorant of this positive-moral law until the time of Gerhard, and they referred whatever laws occur in Scripture either to natural or to positive laws." —

Very many theologians defend this positive-moral law. They prove it: I. By the examples of the prohibited degrees, since nature does not simply prohibit them, and yet they are [prohibited] as if by divine law. PART II. CHAPTER I.

are commonly considered to be prohibited by an indispensable law, to such an extent that when the Roman Pontiff sometimes grants a dispensation in them, he is said for that reason to violate the laws of God and to exalt himself above God. Resp.: 1) All the older theologians referred these degrees to the natural law, if only because God punished the nations for their transgression, who, since they did not know that positive moral law, could not have been obligated by it. . . 8) We have said above that a distinction must be made between natural law taken a little more loosely and more strictly. II. From the example of the sabbatic law concerning the keeping of a festival on every seventh day, which, since it obligates all men and does not descend from nature alone, must be a positive moral law. Resp.: 1) In the third commandment, only this is moral and natural: that some time, whatever it may be, must be celebrated publicly for God. But the fact that we keep either the seventh day or any other day as a festival is from the free determination of the church, and therefore pertains to rites. 2) In the third commandment, it is commanded not that any seventh day, but that the specifically seventh day, that is, the Sabbath day, be kept as a festival. This pertains to the Jews, not to Christians. But the consequence does not hold from a determined commandment to an undetermined commandment.” (Compend. Ed. 2, pp. 660–662.)

For because these principles—that those things which the magistrate, who is the ordinance of God, prescribes to those whose magistrate he is, provided the divine law is safe, are to be done; and those things which the magistrate similarly prohibits to them are to be avoided—are of eternal truth and are implicitly contained in the Decalogue, therefore no one can act against a positive law enacted by a superior without simultaneously acting against the eternal law of God. Otherwise, that apostolic saying would hold, Acts 4:19: “Judge whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God,” and chapter 5:29: “We must obey God rather than men.” Otherwise, however, it is established that the commands of inferior magistrates cannot derogate from the laws of a superior magistrate, nor does he sin who, observing the latter, does not obey the former. We add nothing more concerning the law in this place, as we shall treat more fully of the word of the law and the gospel below in Part III, Chapter VII. § 8. A physically efficient cause of sin, viewed abstractively, properly speaking, is not given. However, for the acts and habits to which sin adheres, insofar as they are acts and habits, a physical cause is rightly sought.

Or producing it by its real influx, as a true and real effect. For sin, as such, is a privation (see in this place § 2, note c), to which it is repugnant to be produced really by a physically efficient cause. Those things which are the material in sin taken concretively, distinct from the formal. See note e to § 2. Thus, the physically efficient cause of the sinful action of Cain, by which he killed his brother (or of the sin which they call fratricide or parricide, insofar as it is a positive action), was Cain himself, who struck his brother. The cause of vicious habits, e.g., intemperance, is the one who, by frequent acts, acquired for himself a fixed propensity toward similar acts, or the habit itself.

9. Meanwhile, a moral cause is rightly assigned to sin, as such. And that cause is always a nature which possesses intellect and will. Or, which, although it does not provide a real influx into that which is a mere privation, as if it were truly produced by itself, nevertheless contributes something, in view of which that (or the ἀνομία itself) is imputed to it as an effect, not otherwise than if it were really influencing it.

Others prefer to call it a deficient cause, with Augustine, *De Civ. Dei*, Book XII, ch. VII. Namely, that if the agent is considered precisely in relation to the ἀνομία, it is called its cause not by reason of any influx, but by reason of some defect in causing, or because it acts not in conformity with the law. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Thes.* cited, η. IX. See 1 John 3:4, where it is expressly said that he who commits τήν ἁμαρτίαν, commits at the same time τήν ἀνομίαν, namely, by the very fact that he does that which is ἄνομον. Indeed, brutes and other agents devoid of reason, when they do that which, if a man were to do it, would be judged as sin, are not, however, believed to sin, strictly speaking, just as they are not judged to act in conformity with the law when they do such things as the law prescribes for rational creatures, since they are entirely destitute of the faculty of knowing those things which the law commands and forbids. §

10. God, indeed, can rightly be called the cause of sin neither morally nor physically. For He who is supremely good and perfect cannot intend sin, either directly or indirectly. For although God concurs as a universal cause in all the actions of secondary causes, and thus in evil ones just as in good ones; yet because those actions, by reason of their positive entity, are not sins, but are so by reason of their ἀνομία, God does not provide a special influx even to their positive entity (for He neither wills nor decrees that they should happen; He does not determine the will of the sinner to sinful acts, but the particular agents determine themselves by their own will to that species of action), it is manifest that God can in no way be called the cause of sins.

But the fact that God does not prevent sins, which He could have prevented but was not bound to prevent, and that He sometimes, by virtue of His justice and supreme majesty, withdraws from sinners the grace necessary to avoid sins (but of which they have rendered themselves unworthy): yet the sins themselves do not thereby become the effects or objects of God and His actions. *

Formula of Concord*: "It must be considered with great care, when the Lord punishes sins with sins, i.e., when He, on account of subsequent carnal security, impenitence, [leaves those who had once been converted...]"

stubbornness in wicked deeds and punishes voluntary crimes with blinding and hardening, this is not to be understood as if God had never seriously willed that such persons should arrive at the knowledge of the truth and obtain salvation.” (Declar. art. 11, p. 722.) Gerhard: “How God punishes sins with sins, and yet is not the cause of sin, you will easily understand if you observe that it happens in five ways that one sin is the cause of another sin: 1. when, upon one sin being committed, the grace of the Holy Spirit is lost, and once that is lost, man can do nothing else but fall into wicked deeds; 2. when God delivers him who has sinned into the hand of Satan, who drives him to various sins; 3. insofar as from one sin a fall into similar ones becomes easy, for from acts are caused dispositions and habits inclining toward similar actions; 4. insofar as one sin cannot be perpetrated without others; thus avarice is called the root of evils by the Apostle; 5. insofar as often, because of one sin, another is also committed; just as Judas betrayed Christ out of avarice. According to the first and second modes, God punishes sins with sins, and yet does not exist as the cause or author of sin.” (L. de prov. § 140.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: “Antithesis:

Latin:

Exod. 20, 1. et seqq. Et cap. 31,18. indicatur, Deum, postquam complevit loqui cum Mose in monte Sinai, dedisse ei tabulas duas testimonii, summam statutorum complectentes, tabulas scriptas digito (seu per immediatam operationem potentiae) Dei. Conf. Deut. 4, 18. cap. 9, 10.

Vid., quae b. Gerh. L. de Lege Sect. IX., quoad singula praecepta decalogi, adductis aliis Scripturae locis explicantibus, docuit. Spedatim notandum est, quomodo Christus legem veterem a corruptelis Pharisaicis purgaverit, Matth. 5, 20. sqq. cap. 19, 8. sqq., ita ut peccati rationem habeat non solum, quod praeceptis in decalogo expressis, verum etiam, quod sensui, per Christum declarato, repugnat. Summam quoque legis praeceptis de diligendo Deo et proximo comprehendi ostendit Matth. 22, 37. aa 40. et sic omne peccatum vel cum dilectione Dei, vel cum proximi dilectione, vd cum utraque pugnare, significat..§

6. Atque ita cognosci potest legis hujus a vis obligandi maxima b et universalissima,c quam nemo hominum effugere potest. Tanquam normae primariae et adaequatae. Est enim 1. de rebus per se bonis et malis, ac 2. Deum sapientissimum, sanctissimum et potentissimum, auctorem habet. Hominem enim esse, nec tamen ad ea, quae creaturae rationali, ut tali, conveniunt, facienda per auctoritatem legislatoris, qui omnium creator ac dominus est, obligari, repugnat.§

7. Est autem etiam illud revera peccatum, quod contra legem aliquam positivam, sive divinam,a sive humanam,b committitur, modo lex humana non contrarietur c divinae.d De re non simpliciter et per se necessaria, sed tantum propter voluntatem Dei liberam, qui poterat hoc non praescribere, aut praescribere oppositum, v. g. in ceremonialibus, aut forensibus. Ubi tamen, sicut lex naturae jubet, Deo in omnibus obedire, sic obligatio ad obediendum istis praeceptis fundatur in obligatione legis naturae, ita ut peccet, qui aliter agit.

Fechtius: ״Nonnulli tertium gemis legum positivomoralium addunt, quae positivae vocentur, quia a mera voluntate Dei dependeant, non a naturali necessitate, quippe quae, Deo volente, aliter sese habere atque mutari possint; morales vero, quia in perpetua omnium obligatione hominum moralibus sint similes; quarum exempla allegant gradus 'prohibitos in Levitico et legem de sabbato qualibet septimana celebrando. Sed vero, istam legum classem frustra excogitari, probatur: I. A perpetuo Scripturae silentio. Lex enim positivomoralis nullo modo probari potest, cum et in allatis exemplis, quicquid vel in gradibus prohibitis, vel in sabbato morale est, id et naturale sit, et quicquid naturale non est, sit ceremoniale et judaicum. II. A consensu theologorum ecclesiae nostrae antiquorum, quippe qui hanc legem moralem positivam usque fere ad Gerhardi tempora plane ignorarunt, et quaecunque in Scriptura occurrunt leges, vel ad naturales, vel ad positivas retulere.—

Plurimi theologi legem hanc positivomoralem propugnant. Probant: I. Exemplis graduum prohibitorum, quippe quos natura non simpliciter prohibet, et qui tamen tanquam lege divina PART. II. CAP. I.

indispensabili prohibiti vulgo aestimentur, adeo, ut cum in iis aliquando dispenset pontifex Romanus, ideo jura Dei violare et supra Deum efferre sese dicatur. Resp.: 1) Omnes antiquiores theologi hos gradus ad legem naturalem retulerunt, vel ideo, quod ob earum transgressionem puniverit gentes, quae, cum moralem Illam positivam legem nesciverint, ideo illa eos etiam obligare non potuit. . . 8) Distinguendum esse, diximus, inter legem naturalem paulo laxius et strictius acceptam, supra. II. Exemplo legis sabbaticae de festo agendo quolibet die septimo, quae cum omnes homines obliget, nec e natura tantum descendat, moralis positiva sit, necesse est. Resp.: 1) In praecepto tertio id solum morale et naturale est, celebrandum Deo publice esse aliquod tempus, qualecunque illud sit. Quod vero vel septimum, vel quemcunque alium diem festum agimus, id ex libera ecclesiae determinatione est, adeoque ad ritus pertinet. 2) In tertio praecepto mandatum est, non ut septimus quilibet dies, sed ut determinate septimus, id est, dies sabbati festus agatur. Id quod ad Judaeos, non ad Christianos pertinet. A praecepto vero determinato ad praeceptum indeterminatum non valet consequentia.“ (Compend. Ed. 2. p. 660—662.)

Nam quia principia haec: Quae magistratus, qui Dei ordinatio «st his, quorum magistratus est, salva lege divina, praescribit, sunt facienda; quaeque magistratus his similiter prohibet, sunt fugienda, aeternae veritatis sunt et in decalogo implicite continentur, ideo nemo potest contra legem positivam a superiore latam agere, quin simul etiam agat contra aeternam Dei legem. Secus enim valet illud apostolicum, Ador. 4, 19.: Judicate, an justum sit in conspectu Dei vos potius audire, quam Deumt et cap. 5, 29.: Obedire oportet Deo magis, quam hominibus. Alias autem constat, inferiorum magistratuum jussa non posse derogare legibus sujperioris magistratus, nec peccare eum, qui, naec observans, oppositis illis non obtemperat. Plura de lege h. l. non addimus, infra P. III. cap. VII. de verbo legis et evangelii plenius acturi.§ 8. Causa physice efficiens a peccati, abstractive spectati, proprie loquendo non b datur. Actuum autem et habituum c quibus peccatum adhaeret, quatenus actus et habitus sunt, causa physica recte quaeritur.d

Seu reali influxu suo producens illud, tanquam effectum verum ac realem. Est enim peccatum, qua tale, privatio (vid. h. 1. § 2. not c.), cui repugnat, realiter produci per causam physice efficientem. Qui in peccato concretive accepto materiale sunt, a formali distinctum. Vid. not. e. ad § 2. Ita actionis peccaminosae Caini, qua fratrem interfecit (seu peccati, quod fratricidium aut parricidium dicunt, quatenus positiva actio est), causa physice efficiens fuit ipse Cain, qui percussit fratrem. Habitus vitiosi, v. g. intemperantiae, causa est is, qui crebris actibus propensionem fixam ad actus similes sive habitum ipsum sibi acquisivit.

9. Interim peccato, qua tali, causa moralis a recte assignatur.b Atque illud semper est naturae, quae intellectu et voluntate pollet.c Seu quae, licet realem influxum in illud, quod privatio mera est, tanquam a se revera producendum, non praebeat, aliquid tamen confert, cujus intuitu ei istud (seu ανομία ipsa), tanquam effectus, imputatur, non secus, ac si realiter influeret.

Alii deficientem appellare malunt cum Augustino lib. XII. de Civ. Dei cap. VII. Scilicet quod, si agens praecise in ordine ad ανομίαν consideretur, non ratione alicujus influxus, sed ratione alicujus in causando defectus, seu quod legi non conformiter agit, ejus causa dicatur. Conf. b. Mus. Thes. cit. η. IX. Vid. 1 Joh. 3, 4., obi expresse dicitur, eum, qui facit τψ άμαρτίαν, facere simul τψ ϋνομίαν, scilicet hoc ipso, quod facit id, quod est άνομον. Sane bruta et agentia alia, rationis expertia, quando id agunt, quod si homo ageret, peccare censeretur, non tamen ipsa proprie loquendo,peccare creduntur, quemadmodum nec legi conformiter agere censentur, quando talia agunt, quae lex creaturis rationalibus praescribit, cum facultate cognoscendi ea, quae lex praecipit ac vetat, plane destituantur.§

10. Deus quidem nec mor aliter,a neque physice b causa peccati recte dici potest.c Non enim sive directe, sive indirecte intendere potest peccatum, qui summe bonus ac perfectus est. Etsi enim per modum causae universalis concurrat Deus ad omnes causarum secundarum actiones, adeoque malas aeque atque bonas; tamen quia actiones illae ratione suae entitatis positivae peccata non sunt, verum ratione suae ανομίας, Deus etiam ad positivam illarum entitatem specialem influxum non praebet (neque enim vult nec decernit, ut fiant; non determinat voluntatem peccatoris ad actus peccaminosos, sed agentia particularia ipsa se sua voluntate ad illam actionis speciem determinant), manifestum est, Deum nullo modo dici posse causam peccatorum.

Quod autem Deus non impedit peccata, quae posset, non autem debebat impedire, quodque peccatoribus gratiam ad evitanda peccata necessariam (sed qua ipsi se indignos reddiderunt) vi justitiae suae ac majestatis supremae aliquando subtrahit: tamen peccata ipsa non propterea effectus, seu objecta Dei et actionum ejus fiunt.

Formula Concordiae: ,,Magna cura considerandum est, quando Dominus peccata peccatis punit, h. e., cum eos, qui aliquando conversi fuerant, propter subsequentem securitatem carnalem, impoenitentiam, BaieriComp. ed. Walther. II. 18 PART. II. CAP. I.

contumaciam in sceleribus et propter voluntaria llagitia punit excaecatione et induratione, id non ita accipiendum esse, quasi Deus nunquam serio voluisset, ut tales ad agnitionem veritatis pervenirent et salutem consequerentur.“ (Declar. art. 11. p. 722.) Gerhardus: ,,Quomodo peccata peccatis Deus puniat, et tamen peccati causa non sit, id facile intelliges, si observaveris, quinque modis contingere, ut peccatum sit alterius peccati causa: 1. cum uno peccato admisso amittitur gratia Spiritus S., qua amissa nihil aliud potest homo, quam in scelera prolabi; 2. cum Deus eum, qui peccavit, tradit in manum satanae, qui impellit eum ad varia peccata; 3. quatenus ex uno peccato facilis fit in similia lapsus, ex actibus enim causantur dispositiones et habitus inclinantes ad similes actiones; 4. quatenus unum peccatum sine aliis perpetrari non potest; sic avaritia radix malorum dicitur ab apostolo; 5. quatenus saepe propter unum peccatum alterum etiam admittitur; sicut Judas prodidit Christum ex avaritia. Juxta primum et secundum modum Deus peccata peccatis punit, nec tamen peccati causa vel auctor existit.“ (L. de prov. § 140.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis:


### Concerning Sin in General: Of Simon Magus, who blasphemously taught that God is the creator and author of…

1. Of Simon Magus, who blasphemously taught that God is the creator and author of all wicked deeds. . .

2. Of the Valentinians, who posit that malice is inherent in men from the primordial origin of things. . .

4. Of the Libertines, who by explicit affirmation posit God as the author of sin; for they posit that God worked the sin of Cain, of Saul, of Judas. . .

5. Of the Calvinists, who. . . make God directly and in Himself the cause and author of sin. For those who assert that God is the cause of all wicked deeds and sins: a. the primary, b. the supreme, c. the principal, d. the willing, e. the decreeing, f. the instigating, g. the creating, h. the providing of occasions, i. the compelling, k. the impelling, l. not only permitting, but also effecting, m. and that men and Satan are merely instruments of evil actions, n. and those often unknowing and unwilling: they altogether posit God as the author and efficient cause of sins. . . With what face, therefore, did the Reformed in a public decree at the Synod of Dort, art. 15 on predestination, sanction that ‘to constitute God as the author of sin is blasphemous to think’? . . .

6. Of certain Papists, who likewise assert in explicit words that God is the cause of sin, such as Gabriel Biel, Occam, Major, Costerus in Enchirid. Especially the Dominicans and Thomists (who also posit predetermination). . .

7. Of the Calvinists and Papists, who make God the cause of sin through their hypotheses, positing: a. that God influences by His efficacious predetermination not only natural actions, but also moral ones, both good and evil, and is therefore the cause of everything material that is in an evil act, even if the malice is inseparable from it, both by way of a moving principle and by way of concurrence. . . b. by contending that the contrary propensities and the rebellion of the flesh flowed from the very condition of nature as established by God. . .

8. Of the Socinians, who likewise constitute God as the cause of sin.” (L. c. P. II. c. 2. s. 2. q. 5. f. 973. sqq.) Fecht: “An improper and never to be imitated, nay, an unjust way of speaking against God, is that of some: that God punishes sins with sins.” (Syllog. controv. p. 109.) § 11. The devil, however, and other rational creatures, not determined to the good, can certainly become and do become the efficient cause of sin.

See John 8:44, where the devil is called a murderer, that he did not stand in the truth, that he speaks a lie from his own resources, that he is a liar and the father of it (the lie); to each of these predicates, as to one failing in acting, sins—for example, murder, lying—are attributed as to an acting cause. For those things which are determined toward the good, for example, by the light of glory, cannot fail in acting, but are impeccable, as we have said in the chapter on the angels and on eternal blessedness. § 12. Furthermore, that sin is not sin unless it is voluntary with respect to him who is thereby considered a sinner, is not universally true. To philosophers, indeed, nothing comes under the designation of sins except that in which some element of the voluntary appears, so that things done against the law are called sins only insofar as they participate in the voluntary. In the Scriptures, however, sin is taken in a much broader sense, as John in 1 Epistle 3:4 sufficiently shows by defining sin as ανομία, without the expressed condition of the voluntary. Compare what we shall teach in the following chapter, II, concerning original sin. ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of certain scholastics, such as Peter of Ailly, who in the beginning of his commentary on the 1st book of the Sentences, letter E, says: 'No act is sin in itself, but because it is prohibited by law. Prevarication is the transgression of the law. Because according to the Apostle, Rom. 4:15, "where there is no law, there is no transgression."' 2. Of Durandus and others, who contend: 'That even those acts which are condemned by natural right and law are not evil in themselves, but because they are forbidden by divine law, and therefore if God were to remove the law, they would not be sins.' ... 3. Of those scholastics who assert that all actions are indifferent by their nature, even loving God and hating God, honoring parents or not. And Peter of Ailly, the Cardinal of Cambrai cited above, notes that many scholastic doctors hold 'that God could command hatred of Himself.'" (L. c. q. 2. f. 965.) The same: "Antithesis: 1. Of certain Papists, such as Andradius in book 3 of his defense of the Council of Trent, who denies that ανομία is sin at all... 2. Of the Pelagians, ... who contend that original sin is not sin, because in infants it is involuntary. 3. Of the Papists, who establish that the voluntary is of the essence of sin, so that what is in no way voluntary is not a sin. Thus Bellarmine. ... 4. Of the Socinians, such as Socinus, Ostorodt, and Smalcius, who for the same reason (namely, because it is not voluntary) plainly deny original sin. ... 5. Of the Arminians, in the Acts of the Synod, defense of article 4, and in the Apology of the Confession, chapter 7, who require the voluntary for the definition of sin. ... 6. Of Zwingli and Calvin, in chapter 3 of Genesis, who for the same reason deny original sin, because it is involuntary." (L. c. q. 3. f. 967.) § 13. The subject of sin is a rational nature, not determined toward the good, or man as a wayfarer, who is denominated a sinner. PART II. CHAPTER I.

For brute animals and inanimate agents are not denominated as sinning, just as they are not considered moral causes of sin. See § 9, note c. Thus, God, the holy angels, and the blessed in heaven are excluded; although the first humans, even though they were mutable, were not yet the subject of sin before they freely determined themselves to sin.

For we are looking to this here, in this place, when we treat of the subject of the operation of theology. And thus we also leave the evil angels and the damned humans to their own place.

Whether regarding the act of sinning, or regarding the depraved habit, or the lack of the act commanded and the habit that ought to have been present.

However, the denomination is understood as that of the suppositum, which others call the ultimate [subject], and therefore they call it the total subject here.

J. Scharfius: "The subject is that which, beyond its own essence, receives something into itself. As: substance is the subject of accidents, because these are received and subjected in it. Thus, a wall is the subject of color, of whiteness, of blackness.—Now, a subject is either of inhesion, or of consideration, or of predication. A subject of inhesion in general is called everything to which something is said to inhere in any way.—Now, a subject of inhesion is either total, primary, or of denomination; or partial, secondary, and of information. The subject of denomination is that which is denominated by its adjunct. As: man is the subject of learning, a body of quantity; for man is denominated learned through learning, and a body is called a quantum through quantity. Hence that which is called the subject *as what* (subjectum ut quod). And this principally and properly sustains accidents, and is always a substance. The subject of information is that to which an adjunct inheres directly and in itself. As: the soul is the subject of erudition and learning; for in it is erudition directly, and it informs it. Thus, matter is the subject of quantity, because quantity informs matter accidentally. To this pertains that which is called the subject *as which* (subjectum ut quo), because it is the medium by which the accident inheres in the whole composite. E.g., a wall is the subject *as what* of whiteness, but the surface is the subject *as which*, because through the surface the whiteness inheres in the wall. Furthermore, the subject *as what* is either universal or particular. The former (universal subject) is called the πρώτον δεκτικόν, in which the adjunct inheres primarily, adequately, and reciprocally, so that it extends just as widely as its adjunct. Thus, man is the primary subject of discipline, of risibility, of docility; thus, body is the universal subject of quantity; thus, being is the primary subject of transcendental unity, truth, and goodness. A particular subject is secondary, which is narrower than its adjunct and inadequate. Th…us, man is a subject of quantity; thus, a wall is called white." (Metaphys. pp. 229—232.) §

14. The subject *as which* (subjectum quo) of sin is the soul and its faculties; although the body and its members also sometimes, and indeed secondarily, pertain to this. Others call it partial and distinguish it into primary or πρώτον δεκτικόν, and secondary. They acknowledge the former as properly so called, and they will not deny that the latter is called so less properly. From it, as from a principle, sinful acts arise, and in it, as immanent acts, they persist; to the same, likewise, they refer

DB PECCATO IN GENERB. omissions of commanded acts. In the same are the habits of vices and the privation of virtues. Thus, through the mediation of the soul, sins affect man. The intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite, which will be more fully established below from the special doctrine concerning sins, original and actual. Meanwhile, it is to be noted that these faculties are, as they are capable of reason, so undoubtedly capable of morality and sin. N amely, through the mediation of the soul, which is in the body and whose organs are the members of the body; which also will be taught more distinctly below. §

15. The consequence of every sin is the liability to guilt and to punishment properly so called, both temporal and eternal. Some call it the formal, others, with the addition, the consecutive formal of sin. And the former indeed consider sin not absolutely and in itself (for thus it must be confessed that the formal of sin is ἀνομία), but respectively and in order to the subject, which it affects and to which it gives a denomination. And thus indeed liability can be called the formal of sin; for through this, man is constituted before God as unjust, a child of wrath, and liable to eternal damnation. See the blessed Musaeus, *On Sin*, Thesis XIV.

The latter opinion, however, by which liability is called the consecutive formal of sin, agrees more openly with us. Namely, insofar as sin is inconsistent with a rational nature and renders it culpable, that is, liable to guilt. For although the name of liability extends more broadly and is sometimes said with the addition of liability to punishment, which it is certain is rightly distinguished from guilt or liability to guilt, just as it is also distinguished here in the thesis; yet guilt and liability simply so called, or liability to guilt, do not differ. For guilt is formally a certain relation resulting from sin considered in order to the rule of moral rectitude, or the law, and liability (distinguished from liability to punishment, which is otherwise called liability simply, but also liability to guilt) formally imports an obligation, by which someone is held bound under sin through the sin itself, so that he truly is and is called a sinner. Moreover, this obligation is also itself a relation to the law or rule, resulting from sin, through which man is constituted liable to sin. Nor does a difference appear between one liable to sin and one culpable or liable to guilt. Therefore, we have here spoken of liability to guilt briefly, as if by one name. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Treatise on Conversion*, Disp. III, chap. II, § 47, 48, p. 124, 125.

Latin:

1. Simonis Magi, qui blaspheme docuit, Deum esse creatorem et auctorem omnium scelerum. . .

2. Valentinianorum, statuentium, hominibus a primaeva rerum origine malitiam inesse. . .

4. Libertinorum, Deum peccati auctorem diserta affirmatione statuentium; statuunt enim, Deum operatum esse peccatum Caini, Saulis, Judae. . .

5. Calvinianorum, qui. . . faciunt Deum directe et per se causam et auctorem peccati. Qui enim asserunt, Deum esse omnium flagitiorum et peccatorum causam: a. primam, b. supremam, c. praecipuam, d. volentem, e. decernentem, f. instigantem, g. creantem, h. occasiones exhibentem, i. cogentem, k. impellentem, 1. non tantum permittentem, sed et efficientem, m. homines vero et satanam esse instrumenta tantum actionum malarum, n. eaque saepe inscia et invita: illi omnino Deum auctorem et causam efflcientem peccatorum esse statuunt. .. Qua fronte itaque reformati publico decreto in synodo Dordracena art. 15. de praedestinat, sanxerunt: ,Deum peccati auctorem constituere, cogitatu blasphemum esse‘? . . .

Deum influere efficaci praedeterminatione sua non solum in actiones naturales, sed etiam morales, bonas et malas, adeoque causam esse omnis materialis, quod in actu malo est, etiamsi malitia ab eo sit inseparabilis, tum per modum principii moventis, tum per modum concursus. . . b. contendendo, propensiones contrarias rebellionemque carnis ex ipsius naturae a Deo conditae conditione fluxisse. . .

8. Socinianorum, Deum itidem peccati causam constituentium.“ (L. c. P. II. c. 2. s. 2. q. 5. f. 973. sqq.) Fechtius: ,,Impropria nec unquam imitanda, imo in Deum iniqua quorundam locutio est: Deum peccata peccatis punire.“ (Syllog. controv. p. 109.) § 11. Diabolus a autem et creaturae rationales aliae, ad bonum non determinatae,b peccati causa efficiens utique fieri possunt et fiunt.

Vid. Joh. 8, 44״ ubi diabolus dicitur homicida, non stetisse in veritate, loqui mendacium ex propriis, mendax et pater ejus (mendacii), quibus singulis praedicatis illi, tanquam in agendo deficienti, peccata, v. g. homicidium, mendacium, ut causae agenti, tribuuntur. Quae enim ad bonum determinatae sunt, v. g. per lumen gloriae, non possunt agendo deficere, sed sunt impeccabiles, ut diximus in cap. de angelis et de beatitudine aeterna.§ 12. Caeterum quod peccatum non sit, nisi sit voluntarium respectu ejus, qui inde peccator censetur, universaliter verum non est. Philosophis quidem peccatorum appellatione nihil venit, nisi in quo aliqua ratio voluntarii apparet, ut, quae contra legem fiunt, in tantum dicantur peccata, in quantum de voluntario participant. In Scripturis autem peccatum 111 significatione multo latiore accipitur, prout Johannes 1. Epist. 3, 4· satis habet, per ανομίαν definire peccatum, non expressa ratione του voluntarii. Conf., quae cap. sq. II. de peccato originis docebimus. ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Quorundam scholasticorum, ut Petri de Aliaco, qui in prine, ad 1. sentent. Iit. E. inquit: ,Nullum est ex se peccatum, sed quia lege prohibitum. Praevaricatio est legis transgressio. Quia secundum apostolum Rom. 4, 15., ,ubi non est lex, ibi nec praevaricatio.‘ 2. Durandi et aliorum, contendentium: ,Actus etiam illos, qui sunt jure et lege naturali damnati, non esse per se malos, sed quia lege divina vetiti sunt, adeoque si Deus legem tollat, non esse peccata.‘ . . 3. Illorum scholasticorum, qui asserunt, omnes actiones esse natura sua indifferentes, etiam amare Deum et odisse Deum, parentes honorare vel non. Et nötat Petrus ab Aliaco, cardinalis Cameracensis supra citatus, quod multi doctores scholastici teneant, ,quod Deus possit praecipere odium sui‘.“ (L. c. q. 2. f. 965.) Idem: ״Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum quorundam, ut Andradii lib. 3. defens. conc. Trid., qui negat, quamvis ανομίαν peccatum esse. . . 2. Pelagianorum, ... contendentium, peccatum originale non esse peccatum, quia in infantibus est involuntarium. 3. Pontificiorum, statuentium, ro voluntarium esse de ratione peccati, adeo ut non sit peccatum, quod nullo modo est voluntarium. Ita Bellarminus. . . 4. Socinianorum, ut Socini, Ostorodi, Smalzii, qui peccatum origin. propter eandem rationem (sci. quia non est voluntarium) plane negant. . . 5. Arminianorum, in actis synodal, def. art. 4. et in apol. conf. cap. 7. voluntarium ad rationem peccati requirentium. . . 6. Zwinglii et Calvini, in cap. 3. Genes, peccatum origin. pari ratione negantium, quod involuntarium sit.“ (L. c. q. 3. f. 967.) § 13. Subjectum Quod peccati est natura rationalis,a ad bonum non b determinata, seu homo viator,c qui peccator d denominatur.e PART. II. CAP. I.

Bruta enim et agentia inanimata non denominantur peccare, prout neque causa moralis peccati censentur. Vid. § 9. not. c. Sic enim excluduntur Deus, angeli boni, homines beati; quanquam et primi homines, licet labiles, non tamen subjectum peccati fuerunt, antequam ad peccandum sese libere determinarent.

Huc enim h. l. spectamus, cum de subjecto operationis theologiae agimus. Atque ita etiam angelos malos et homines damnatos suo loco relinquimus.

Sive quoad actum peccandi, sive quoad habitum pravum, aut actus praecepti habitusque, qui adesse debebat, carentiam.

Intelligitur autem denominatio, tanquam suppositi, quam alii ultimatam vocant, ideoque totale subjectum hic appellant.

J, Scharfius: ,,Subjectum est, quod praeter suam essentiam aliquid in se recipit. Ut: substantia est subjectum accidentium, quia haec in illa recipiuntur et subjectantur. Sic paries est subjectum coloris, albedinis, nigredinis.—Est autem subjectum vel inhaesionis, vel considerationis, vel praedicationis. Subjectum inhaesionis in genere dicitur omne id, cui aliquid inesse dicitur quocunque modo.—Est autem subjectum inhaesionis vel totale, primarium sive denominationis; vel partiale, secundarium et informationis. Subjectum denominationis est, quod denominatur ab adjuncto suo. Ut: homo subjectum doctrinae, corpus quantitatis; nam homo per doctrinam denominatur doctus et corpus per quantitatem dicitur quantum. Hinc est illud, quod vocatur subjectum ut quod. Et hoc principaliter et proprie sustinet accidentia, estque semper substantia. Subjectum informationis est, cui per se directe inhaeret adjunctum. Ut: anima est subjectum eruditionis et doctrinae; in hac enim directe est eruditio, hancque informat. Sic materia est subjectum quantitatis, quia materiam accidentaliter informat quantitas. Huc pertinet id, quod dicitur subjectum ut quo, quia est medium, quo mediante inest accidens toti composito. E. g. paries est subjectum ut quod albedinis, sed superficies est subjectum ut quo, quia mediante superficie inest albedo parieti. Porro subjectum ut quod vel est universale, vel particulare. Illud (universale subjectum) dicitur πρώτον δί,κτικύν, in quo inest adjunctum primo, adaequate et reciproce, ita ut aeque late pateat cum suo adjuncto. Sic homo est primum subjectum disciplinae, risibilitatis, docilitatis; sic corpus est universale subjectum quantitatis; sic ens primum subjectum unitatis, veritatis, bonitatis transcendentalis. Particulare subjectum est secundarium, quod est angustius suo adjuncto et inadaequatum. Sic homo est subjectum quantitatis; sic paries dicitur albus.“ (Metaphys. p. 229—232.) §

14. Subjectum Quo a peccati est anima b ejusque facultates;c quanquam et corpus ejusque d membra huc aliquando, et secundario quidem, spectant. Alii partiale vocant et in primarium seu πρώτον δεχτιχόν, ac secundarium distinguunt. Illud proprie dictum agnoscunt, hoc minus proprie dici, non negabunt. A qua, tanquam principio, oriuntur et in ea, tanquam actus immanentes, persistunt actus peccaminosi; ad eandem similiter refe

DB PECCATO IN GENERB. runtur omissiones actuum praeceptorum. In eadem sunt habitus vitiorum et privatio virtutum. Sic mediante anima peccata hominem afficiunt. Intellectus, voluntas et appetitus sensitivus, quod infra ex doctrina speciali de peccatis, originali et actualibus, plenius constabit. Interim notandum est, has facultates esse, uti rationis, sic moralitatis et peccati haud dubie capaces. Mediante scilicet anima, quae est in corpore et cujus organa sunt membra corporis; quod et ipsum infra distinctius docebitur.§

15. Consequens omnis peccati a est reatus culpae b et poenae c proprie d dictae, cum temporalis,e tum aeternae.f Alii formale, quidam, cum addito formale consecutimm peccati appellant. Et illi quidem peccatum considerant non absolute et in se (sic enim fatendum est, formale peccati esse ανομίαν), sed respective et in ordine ad subjectum, quod afficit eique denominationem tribuit. Atque ita quidem reatus potest dici formale peccati; per hunc enim homo constituitur coram Deo injustus, filius irae et aeternae damnationis reus. Vid. b. Mus. de Pecc. Thes. XIV.

Posterior vero sententia, qua reatus formale consecutivum peccati dicitur, nobiscum apertius consentit. Nempe quatenus peccatum naturae rationali disconvenit eamque culpabilem reddit, id est, culpae ream. Quanquam enim reatus nomen latius pateat et aliquando cum addito reatus poenae dicatur, quem certum est a culpa seu reatu culpae recte distingui, prout etiam hic in thesi distinguitur; culpa tamen et reatus simpliciter sic dictus, seu reatus culpae, non differunt. Culpa enim formaliter est relatio quaedam ex peccato in ordine ad regulam rectitudinis moralis, seu legem, considerato resultans, et reatus (a reatu poenae distinctus, qui alias reatus simpliciter, sed et culpae reatus dicitur) formaliter importat obligationem, qua quis sub peccato per ipsum peccatum constrictus tenetur, ut revera sit et dicatur peccator. Obligatio autem haec etiam ipsa est relatio ad legem aut regulam, ex peccato resultans, per quam homo peccati reus constituitur. Neque differentia apparet inter reum peccati et culpabilem aut culpae reum. Itaque reatum culpae hic breviter, velut uno nomine, diximus. Conf. b. Musaei Tract. de Convers. Disp. III. cap. II. § 47. 48. p. 124. 125.


### Concerning Sin in General: Insofar as sin in the very violation of the law also imports an offense against…

Insofar as sin in the very violation of the law also imports an offense against God, the Lawgiver and supreme Lord, and thus constitutes the offending man worthy of punishment, or contracts for him the debt of undergoing punishment. That is, of damage or evil, which is against the inclination of the subject, contracted on account of guilt, and of undergoing it for the sake of avenging the guilt and compensating for the injury inflicted upon another (and here indeed upon God). Whence paternal chastisements of the pious must be diligently distinguished from punishments properly so called. PART II. CHAP. I.

For these are inflicted upon the faithful either for the crucifying of the lusts of the flesh, or for the testing of their faith, love, patience, and constancy, or for the bearing of witness to religion and true doctrine, and thus for the celebrating of the glory of God and Christ, but not for the avenging of guilt and the compensating of an injury brought upon God. To this latter, however, this is proper and therefore absolutely necessary. Whence, in the doctrine concerning the cross and calamities, the authors rightly distinguish χόλασιν or παιδείαν (i.e., chastisement made for the sake of amendment or correction), δοκιμασίαν (i.e., exploration or probation), and μαρτύριον (i.e., testimony provided to another by one’s own evil) from τιμωρία (i.e., punishment properly so-called, by which satisfaction is made to the injured honor of a superior).

Luther: "The thief turns around and accuses himself and confesses his sins, but hopes that he will enjoy the Lord Christ, so that his sins will not harm him regarding eternal life. Thus, he becomes an entirely different man, and his shameful death, which he has well deserved, now becomes a service to God, so that henceforth he no longer suffers as a murderer, but as a true saint; for he dies in a right confession and heartfelt trust in the grace of God through Christ, and is heartily sorry for his sin." (Hauspostille. Tom. Hal. XIII, 741 sq.)

Some [punishments] are on the part of the soul, e.g., the withdrawal of the favor of God, insofar as sins are said to separate between God and the sinning man, or to cause Him to hide His face from them, Isa. 59:2, whence, on the contrary, arises the wrath of God from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, Rom. 1:18, by the power of which men are either given over to a reprobate mind, so that they fall into various vices, ibid. verse 28, or certainly dread and flee from God as a consuming fire, with whom they cannot dwell, Isaiah 33:14.

Others, however, are on the part of the body, e.g., the heaviness of labors and sterility, whence come weariness and indigence; but also diseases and various pains, and finally death itself, Gen. 3:16, 17, 18, 19; Rom. 6:23.

Not only to some, but to every sin, as an offense against the eternal law and divine majesty, they are congruous. See Matt. 12:36, where it is said that men in the day of judgment (where their final justification, or salvation, and condemnation to eternal punishment will be dealt with) will render an account for every word ἀργὸν (or ἀεργὸν), idle—that is to say, every word that lacks either the reason of jus t necessity or the intention of pious utility, as Gregory the Great explains in his Moralia. Cf. Jerome, and from both, Gerhard ad h. l. p. m. 648. § 16.

Sins, by which the human race is stained, are accustomed to be distinguished I. into actual and habitual. II. Actual [sins] again into those which involve a real act, and those which involve the omission of an act. III. Habitual sins into connate or original, and acquired. IV. Both habitual [sins] are distinguished into vicious habits properly so-called, and the lack of a habit that ought to be present.

But because in man, such as theology

revealed, finds as its subject in the descendants of the first parents, before he actually sins, connate sin is detected, therefore the more specialized doctrine of sin is commonly proposed in such a way that first of original sin, or that which has its origin from the carnal origin or birth of every human being, then of actual sins, which arise in a human being already existing, through theaddition of their own proper acts. For although some distinguish the terms "sin" and "vice" in such a way that the former denotes acts, and the latter denotes habits that are depraved or morally evil; yet long-standing usage of speech has brought it about that the name of "sin" is taken not only for the act, but also for the habit of sinning, and vices themselves are called sins. Whence others speak of sins in act and sins in habit. ἀνομία certainly occurs in both, and thus it is the formal reason of ἁμαρτία or sin. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Tract. de Conv.*, Disp. IV, cap. I, § 2, p. 243. Concerning which division we shall see below in Chapter III. Or a propensity toward depraved acts, which has the force of a habit; such as we shall show in the following chapter (II) is born with us. Not by reason of the origin of the first humans (for this was holy and very good, according to what we have said concerning the divine image), but of the rest, who descend from the first through carnal generation. Or propensities toward similar depraved acts, contracted by repeated acts of sinning, and which are fixed and difficult to move. Namely, we rightly refer the lack of habitual righteousness—whether that which ought to be innate or that which is acquired—to habitual sin, in the same way that omissions of commanded acts are also referred to actual sins. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *de Convers.*, Disp. III, cap. I, § 7, 8, pp. 100, 101. Which is now assumed: to be proven in the following chapter (II). For thus the term "original sin" or "sin of origin" is commonly accepted. But that the fall of the first parents itself is otherwise called the "originating sin of origin" and is distinguished from the "originated [sin]," does not pertain to the present, because it cannot be held as habitual sin itself, but has its place among actual sins in its own way, even though it was the cause of original sin; as will be said shortly. Others distinguish between the "first sin" and that which arose from the first. They subdivide both; the former, indeed, into the sin that is absolutely such, which is the apostasy of the angels, and the first in the human race, which is the fall of the protoplasts; they divide the sin arising from the first into original and actual. Yet, I think, they will not deny that the first sin, both as that which is absolutely such and as that which is the first in the human race, is, by the force of the word and its meaning, actual. § 17. Sin, taken abstractively, can be described as the lack of conformity with the law, adhering to an action of a rational creature failing in acting, or even to the omission of an act, a habit, or the lack thereof, and therefore culpable and worthy of punishment, both temporal and eternal. Somewhat more fully than if you were to say only ἀνομία, so that you may embrace the rest at the same time, which have been handed down thus far. For it imports this in the nominative case. As its material; to which also pertain those things which are said concerning habit and the absence of both; see § 2. To which, as to its efficient cause and subject, it must be ascribed, according to § 8. Which are the consequences of sin viewed abstractively. § 18. Sin, viewed concretively, can be described as the action of a rational creature, or the omission of an action, a habit, or the lack thereof, conflicting with the law of God, and rendering the rational creature culpable and worthy of punishment. In that breadth by which it extends itself to the diverse species, which are to be indicated shortly. Although it is necessary, in the description itself, which they demand to be general, to enunciate disjunctively those things which pertain to the species of sin themselves, since one common name, which might embrace both entities and non-entities, is not available. To which it must be ascribed partly as a cause, partly as a subject; see § 8, 9. Which constitute the material of sin; see § 2. In which consists the formal of sin, 1. c. These are the consequences of sin; concerning which see § 13. Chapter II. ON ORIGINAL SIN. § 1. That original sin exists, although reason cannot recognize it certainly and distinctly from its own principles, is nevertheless most manifestly indicated in Scripture. For it [reason] will either suspend its judgment, or if it dares to define anything, it will deny it and think that humans are born indifferent by their own nature, although...

has detected a certain inclination of the sensitive appetite alien to the judgment of reason; see the blessed Musaeus, *Dissertation on the Insufficiency of Natural Light against E. Herbert*, § 27, pp. 22, 23, and the blessed Henricus a Lith, *Inaugural Dissertation* held under our presidency, in which he presented a Synopsis of Natural Theology compared with revealed theology, Sect. V, § 33 ff. Smalcald Articles: "This hereditary sin is so deep and foul a corruption of nature that it cannot be understood by the reason of any man, but must be acknowledged and believed from the revelation of Scripture." (p. 310.) Rollius: "The *material* of original sin is indeed not unknown to reason, since it is established by experience itself that men are carried by a certain natural impulse toward that which is evil and are accustomed to the pursuit of virtue with great difficulty. Whence that saying of the poet: 'I see the better things and approve them, but I follow the worse.' The *formal* nature of this same sin, however, entirely escapes reason, since it can be evident to no one without divine revelation that an inclination toward evil, derived from the fall of the protoplasts, has the nature of true sin and that man is on account of it liable to eternal damnation." (See Fecht’s *Sylloge controversiarum*, p. 112.) See especially Romans 5:12, where it is said that death descended upon all men for this reason, because in one man, Adam, all sinned or were constituted as sinners. For although the word ἥμαρτον otherwise denotes the *actus secundus* of sinning, it must nevertheless be confessed that it is taken in this passage also to refer to those who, by reason of age and the lack of the use of reason, do not sin in that manner, and indeed who, when the first man fell, did not even exist. Whence, that all sinned in Adam is not the same as saying that all imitated Adam’s sin with similar acts, since it is expressly said in verse 14 that death (which entered into the world through sin) passed even to those who "did not sin after the likeness of the transgression of Adam." Therefore, it must be said that all sinned in one, insofar as, when he sinned, it came to pass that all who were naturally to descend from him contracted the necessity of being born with sin and thus, each on account of his own sin, became liable to death at the very moment of birth. Compare Ephesians 2:3, where, when all men are said to be "by nature children of wrath," the cause of this guilt is presupposed, namely, that all are sinners by nature (not only truly, but by nature—which is certainly more—that is, through the condition of their corrupted nature). For to be a "child of wrath" is the same as to be liable to divine wrath and worthy of the punishment to be inflicted by God, the avenger of the law, on account of the violation of the law. Therefore, one cannot be a child of wrath by nature unless one is polluted by sin by nature or through the corruption of nature. But also in Genesis 6:5 and chapter 8:21 it is said, "Every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is only evil all the day, from his youth"; which, although it may formally denote *actus secundi* or actual sins, the universality of the subject and of the time indicates that the very faculty of thinking, which is in men, is so depraved through the corruption of nature itself that it cannot even exercise an act of good or holy thought, but is most prone to acts of evil thinking. Scherzer: "Although ἐφ’ ᾧ is sometimes causal and denotes 'in that,' yet in this place it must be rendered 'in whom' subjectively, relatively, and personally, as the anti-Socinian college proves from the *synapheia* (connection), *antithesis*, and the distinction of those sinning (for some 'did not sin in the likeness of the transgression of Adam' PART II. CHAPTER II. v. 14, i.e., as Smalcius himself explains, in their own person or immediately, whom the apostle nevertheless teaches to have sinned. Therefore, they sinned in the person of another, or Adam)." (*Systema theologiae, L. de peccato* § 7, p. 147.) Gerhard: "The other exception of the Pelagians was this: The phrase ἐφ’ ᾧ, in whom, all have sinned (Rom. 5:12), must be explained thus: because all have sinned, i.e., death passed unto all because they imitate Adam by sinning. We respond: Augustine, lib. 6 contra Julian, c. 12, disapproves of this version and accepts the word ᾧ as a relative; but the matter comes to the same thing. For whether you take ἐφ’ ᾧ to be spoken causally or relatively, nothing is lost to the truth. Varinus, Budaeus, and Suidas prove with examples that the particles ἐφ’ ᾧ are sometimes used in such a way that they signify the rendering of a cause. Whence also Dr. Luther in his German version rendered it causally. The sense will therefore be: Death passed unto all men, because all have sinned, i.e., because Adam, the parent of the human race, representing the person of all his descendants who descend from him through carnal generation, sinned—he who, created in the divine image, had received those gifts not only for himself, but also for his entire posterity. Nor does Augustine disapprove of this version, but rather that new and distorted sense which Pelagius strove to carve out of it. But if you explain the particles ἐφ’ ᾧ in a relative sense, it will follow likewise that in Adam, the first parent of men, as in a mass, all have sinned originally, just as the apostle declares in 1 Cor. 15:22: 'In Adam all die.'" (L. de pecc. orig. § 63.) ANTITHESES. Quenstedt: "Antithesis:

1. Of the philosophers, outside the church. Hence Seneca, ep. 69: 'You are mistaken if you think that vices are born with us; they have supervened, they have been introduced.' 2. Of the Pelagians, who maintain: a. that no sin passes from Adam to men through generation; b. that no one is condemned on account of Adam's sin; c. that no sin is remitted to infants in baptism, since they have none; d. that Adam's sin does not pass to men in any other way than by example...

4. Of certain scholastics, who teach that the guilt of original sin is in us, not a stain or blemish, and likewise who define original sin solely by the imputation of Adam's sin...

6. Of the Calvinists, some of whom directly deny original sin, such as Zwingli, lib. de baptismo opp. I. p. 89, 90, and in the confession prescribed to Charles V and published in the year '30 of the previous century, art. 4, and in comm. Rom. 5, and those who excuse him, teaching: 'Original sin is not properly sin, but only a disease and an effect of sin.' Others indirectly and indeed by hypothesis, saying that the children of believers are born holy, and that they are in the covenant of grace and children of God, even before they are baptized; which hypothesis being posited, original sin itself is removed...

7. Of the Socinians, who consider original sin a mere fable...

8. Of the Arminians in apol. c. 7 and in specimine 7 adv. Leidenses, and likewise of Adolphus Venator, asserting: 'That it is sin and that it is original involves a contradiction in terms.' Likewise: 'That infants are simple and stand in the same state in which Adam was before the fall.'...

9. Of the Anabaptists, who contend that original sin has been entirely removed from human nature through the death of Christ, so that infants under the New Testament are not born in sins, but are entirely innocent and immune from vices, nor do they need the washing of baptism in infancy." (L. c. q. 8. f. 999.) Hofmann: "Scripture also does not teach that there is sin and death, or what the concept of sin and death is, nor even that sin and death are hereditary, but only traces both back to the first moral self-determination of man... We are just as little in need of a specific statement that all men are sinful by birth as that all are mortal by birth. But Scripture also..."

Latin:

Quatenus peccatum in ipsa violatione legis etiam offensam Dei, legislatoris ac Domini supremi, importat, atque ita hominem offendentem poena dignum constituit, aut debitum subeundi poenam ei contrahit. Id est, damni aut mali, quod est contra subjecti inclinationem, contracti ob culpam, et ad vindicandam culpam compensandamque injuriam alteri (atque hic quidem Deo) illatam subeundi. Unde diligenter distinguendae sunt castigationes paternae piorum a poenis proprie PART. II. CAP. I.

dictis. Illae enim fidelibus vel ad concupiscentias carnis crucifigendas, vel ad explorandam fidem, dilectionem, patientiam et constantiam eorum, vel ad testimonium religioni ac doctrinae verae perhibendum, adeoque Dei et Christi gloriam celebrandam, non autem ad vindicandam culpam injuriamque Deo illatam compensandam inferuntur. His autem postremum boc proprium, atque adeo prorsus necessarium est. Unde in doctrina de cruce et calamitatibus χόλασιν seu παιδείαν (i. e. castigationem emendationis aut correctionis causa factam), δοκιμασίαν (i. e. explorationem aut probationem), μαρτύρων (i. e. testimonium suo quodam malo alteri praebitum) a τιμωρία (i. e. poena proprie dicta, qua satisfiat honori laeso superioris) recte distinguunt auctores.

Quaedam ex parte animae, v. g. subtractio favoris Dei, prout peccata disterminare dicuntur inter Deum et hominem peccantem, aut facere, ut. occultet faciem suam ab illis, Esa. 59, 2., unde ex adverso oritur ira Dei de coelo adversus omnem impietatem et injustitiam hominum, Rom. 1, 18., cujus vi homines vel in reprobam mentem traduntur, ut in varia ruant vitia, ibid. vers. 28., vel certe horrent et fugiunt Deum tanquam ignem consumentem, cum quo diversari non possint, Esaiae 33, 14..

Quaedam autem ex parte corporis, v. g. laborum gravitas ac sterilitas, unde lassitudo et indigentia; sed et morbi ac dolores varii, denique mors ipsa, Gen. 3, 16. 17. 18. 19. Rom. 6, 23.

Non ratione originis primorum hominum (haec enim sancta et valde bona fuit, juxta ea, quae de imag. div. diximus), sed caeterorum, qui a primis per generationem carnalem descendunt. Seu actibus peccandi iteratis contractas propensiones ad actus similes pravos, easque fixas et difficulter mobiles. Scilicet carentiam justitiae habitualis, sive connasci debitae, sive acquisitae, ad peccatum habituale recte referimus, eo modo, quo ad actualia peccata etiam omissiones actuum praeceptorum referuntur. Alii distinguunt inter peccatum primum et ex primo ortum. Utrumque subdividunt; illud quidem in peccatum primum absolute tale, quod sit apostasia angelorum, et primum in genere humano, quod sit lapsus protoplastorum; peccatum ex primo ortum dispescunt in originale et actuale. ## 14 On Original Sin

teaches neither the one nor the other, neither that all men are sinful and mortal—for it would have to teach the latter just as well as the former—nor that sinfulness and mortality are inherited with human nature. Everything that one brings forward to prove such a scriptural doctrine is merely a reminder of a fact that is self-evident.” (Schriftbeweis. 1, 426. 441.) §

2. Original sin imports, on the one hand, the privation of original righteousness, and on the other, the inclination of the whole nature toward evil.

As the opposite of original righteousness or the divine image. For the nature of this sin cannot be known more correctly than by making a comparison with its opposite, into whose place it has succeeded.

To this pertains that death, or the lack of spiritual life and of all active powers which were required for exercising vital acts in conformity with the divine law. And this death is attributed to men, insofar as they are by nature children of wrath, in Ephesians 2:1, 5 and Colossians 2:13.

For just as original righteousness, when it resided with the faculties of the soul of the first man, as it were animated and instructed them for living the life which is according to God, and for eliciting and exercising within themselves acts and motions that are spiritually good, so, with that primeval righteousness lost, man is like a dead person, who, through the separation of the soul from the body, is utterly destitute of all powers for eliciting and exercising vital acts and motions within himself, being indeed destitute of powers for spiritual acts and motions. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *de Conv. Disp. IV. cap. I. § 10. p. 427*.

It also pertains to original sin, taken as the lack of original righteousness, that which is said in Romans 8:10 ff., that Jews and Greeks are all subject to sin; just as it is written in Psalm 14:3 ff.: There is none righteous, no, not one (therefore all lack the righteousness which they ought to have). There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. (Therefore, a right understanding of God and divine things and the searching for them is denied to all.) There is none that doeth good, no, not one. (Therefore all lack moral goodness and the exercise and the powers of exercising acts that are morally good.)

For the same carnal man, who, on account of the privation of spiritual life, is like one dead, is said in another respect to be alive and very active, but toward a life alienated from the life of God, Ephesians 4:18, toward the life of this world and the fulfilling of the desires of the flesh, chapter 2:3.

Naturally, the faculties of the soul are by essence vital faculties, and when they are deprived of original righteousness, although they lack the powers necessary for instituting a life according to God, they are not, however, as to their vital being and the power of eliciting vital acts and motions, lost or abolished; they therefore follow another manner of life, entirely different from the former; see the blessed Musaeus, *l. c. § 11. p. 247, 248*.

With respect to this depraved propensity, Paul writes in Romans 8:7: Τό φρόνημα της σαρχός, i.e., that which the flesh, or the carnal man, as he is born, thinks, wills, and desires, is enmity against God. Which certainly [denotes] an habitual propensity, adhering to us from our very origin. PART II. CHAPTER II.

declare the depravity in every human being. And Rom. 7:17 and 20 mentions sin dwelling in us, truly; verse 21, evil lying close at hand (κακόν παρακείμενον); verse 23, the law which is in the members, warring against the law of the mind, etc., which in verses 7 and 8 was called ἐπιθυμία, concupiscence. However, this is understood not only as the lower power of desiring, which comes from the sensitive appetite, but also as the inclination of the will toward evil, and indeed even the rash proneness of the intellect itself to judge perversely concerning spiritual matters, and it embraces evil thoughts that arise suddenly. Whence also the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, Art. II, p. 55, among other things, understands concupiscence as that which seeks not only the pleasures of the body, but also carnal wisdom and righteousness, and trusts in these goods, despising God, etc.; see the blessed Musaeus, l. c., de Pecc. th. XLIV. That the Jena theologians do not teach that original sin, speaking properly and accurately, is a mere privation, nor do they exclude depraved concupiscence from original sin, the same author shows in the *Ausführliche Erklärung* [Detailed Explanation], Q. XXXI, pp. 229, 230.

Both, however, have the nature of sin: both that man is destitute of those powers which he ought to have had to exercise acts suitable to himself, and thus is inept for doing those things which the law commands, and that his faculties incline toward those things which the law prohibits, or which are repugnant to the law. § 3. Specifically, on the part of the intellect, original sin imports a total privation of spiritual light, so that he can neither rightly know God, nor perfectly prescribe in what manner God is to be worshipped, nor embrace with firm assent those things which have been divinely revealed; at the same time, it also imports a proneness of the intellect to pass rash and false judgments concerning spiritual matters, and indeed even, in those things which are subject to the light of nature, a certain impotence in the knowledge of God and in the ordering of life.

See Eph. 5:8, where men, such as they are by nature before regeneration or are born, are called σκότος, or darkness. And the abstract is put for the concrete to intensify the meaning, so that they are called darkness, that is, greatly or fully darkened, lacking all spiritual light. Compare chapter 4:18, where they are said to be ἐσκοτισμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ, darkened in their understanding, namely, on account of the ignorance that is in them, as is immediately explained. Such as He is, and… as He ought to be known by us in this life, not only according to essence and attributes, but also according to persons. For God, as He is, so must He be worshipped; and in the state after the first fall, there is that in divine worship which consists in placating God. But in both of these the intellect, corrupted by the fall, fails. See 1 Cor. 2:14, where it speaks of the natural man, or such as he is according to the condition of the soul left to itself (inasmuch as he is opposed to the spiritual man, or one having the Spirit of God, who [is] not except through a peculiar operation of God

is conferred, according to verses 10 and 12), it is said: He does not perceive, he cannot understand the things that are of the Spirit of God, or the mysteries which God has revealed through His Spirit, according to verses 7 and 10. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Disp.* IV, chap. I, § 30 ff., p. 260 ff. Thus it is said in the same place, that spiritual things are foolishness to man, or are judged by him as being foolish, absurd things, etc.

Formula of …Concord: "Although the human reason or natural intellect of man has a small, obscure spark of that knowledge remaining, that God exists, and holds some small particle of the Law (Rom. 1:19 ff.): yet that reason is so ignorant, blind, and perverse, that even if the most ingenious and learned men in this world read or hear the Gospel concerning the Son of God and the divine promises of eternal salvation, they are nevertheless unable by their own powers to perceive, understand, believe, and judge them to be true. Nay rather, the more diligently they labor in this matter, so that they might investigate and comprehend those spiritual things with the sharpness of their reason, the less they understand and believe, and they hold all those things for foolishness and mere trifles and fables, before they are illuminated and taught by the Holy Spirit." (p. 689 f.)

Such, I say, is that by which it comes to pass that the intellect errs in reasoning and in investigating the natures, causes, and affections of things, indeed even concerning God Himself and divine things, and no less in directing actions and governing life, and misapplies the principles of the light of nature to infer false, indeed impious, conclusions. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Disp.* IV, *de Convers.*, chap. I, § 25, p. 257. §

4. On the part of the will, original sin consists in the lack of original holiness, or of the powers to love God above all things and to execute what the intellect has rightly dictated, and likewise to rightly restrain the appetite, and that the will, on the contrary, inclines toward sinful works. Or the impotence of willing and performing spiritual things, according to Phil. 2:13. For when both of these are attributed entirely to God, and we are therefore commanded to work out our salvation with fear and trembling, it is certain that this is denied to our natural powers and that we are warned, lest, when we have been gifted with another’s grace, we render ourselves unworthy of it and be deprived of it. The same *adynamia* (impotence) of the will is indicated by death through trespasses, which is opposed to spiritual life. Eph. 2:5. Cf. § 2, note b. For the will does not fail or deviate only when the intellect has erred in knowing, but also when its knowledge is correct. Namely, the good is not only spiritually, but also naturally such, or honorable, and is usually joined with various troubles and difficulties, and therefore the will is more alienated from it and is almost sluggish or languid in pursuing it, even if doctrine and habituation have contributed some improvement or perfection in human affairs. The blessed Musaeus, *l. c.*, § 26, p. 258. PART II. CHAPTER II.

For it is by its own nature an appetitive faculty, and when it shrinks from the true good, it is borne all the more vehemently toward the apparent good, especially when stimulated by the motions of the sensitive appetite; cf. Musaeus, loc. cit. § 26, 27, pp. 258, 259. On account of this propensity toward evil, man, such as he is by nature, is called a slave of sin (Rom. 6:13), and sin is said to reign in his mortal body so that he obeys it through its desires (vv. 12, 14); for, since he cannot of himself do those things which are holy, he is borne conversely toward those things which are evil, as if he were obligated to act in such a way, or as if the will were bent by the command of a superior. This is also that πώρωσις, or a certain callous hardness of heart (Eph. 4:18), by which men are inclined toward carnal security, toward contempt and hatred of God, toward distrust of God, and toward confidence in temporal things, as interpreted by the blessed Gerhard, *Isag. LL. Disp. XXIV. c. III. de Pecc. Orig. § 7, p. m. 879.* § 5.

Latin:

lehrt weder das Eine, noch das Andere, weder, dass alle Menschen sündig und sterblich sind — denn sie müsste Letzteres eben so wohl lehren, als Ersteres —, noch dass Sündigkeit und Sterblichkeit mit der menschlichen Natur sich vererben. Alles, was man beibringt, eine solche Schriftlehre zu erweisen, ist nur Erinnerung an eine sich von selbst verstehende Thatsache.“ (Schriftbeweis. 1,426.441.) §

2. Importat autem peccatum originis a partim privationem b justitiae originalis, partim inclinationem c totius naturae ad prava.d

Tanquam oppositum originalis justitiae aut imaginis divinae. Neque enim rectius cognosci potest natura peccati hujus, quam facta collatione oppositi, in cujus locum successit.

Huc pertinet mors illa, seu carentia vitae spiritualis omniumque virium activarum, quae ad actus vitales legi divinae conformiter exercendos requirebantur. Atque haec mors hominibus, quatenus natura filii irae sunt, tribuitur Ephes. 2, 1. et 5. et Col. 2, 13.

Quemadmodum enim justitia originalis, cum facultatibus animae primi hominis inesset, animabat quasi et instruebat eas ad vivendum vitam, quae secundum Deum est, et ad actus motusque spiritualiter bonos intra se eliciendos et exercendos, sic deperdita justitia illa primaeva homo similis est mortuo, per separationem animae a corpore omnibus plane viribus ad actus et motus vitales in se eliciendos exercendosque destituto, destitutus quippe viribus ad actus et motus spirituales. Confer, b. Musaeus de Conv. Disp. IV. cap. I. § 10. p. 427.

Pertinet etiam ad pecc. originis pro carentia justitiae orig. acceptum, quod Rom. 8, 10. sqq. dicitur Judaeos et Graecos omnes peccato esse obnoxios; sicut seripturn est Ps. 14, 3. sqq.: Non est justus, ne unus quidem (omnes itaque carent justitia, quam habere debebant). Non est, qui intelligat, non est, qui exquirat Deum. (Denegatur ergo omnibus recta Dei ac rerum divinarum intelligentia et scrutinium.) Non est, qui exerceat bonitatem, non est usque ad unum. (Omnes itaque carent bonitate morali et exercitio ac viribus exercendi actus moraliter bonos.)

Idem enim homo carnalis, qui, ob privationem spiritualis vitae mortui instar est, alia ratione vivus et valde actuosus dicitur, sed ad vitam a vita Dei alienam, Ephes. 4, 18·, ad vitam hujus saeculi et faciendus cupiditates carnis, cap. 2, 3.

Nimirum facultates animae per essentiam sunt facultates vitales, et quando justitia originali privantur, licet careant viribus ad vitam secundum Deum instituendam necessariis, non tamen ipsae, quoad esse vitale et vim eliciendi actus motusque vitales, perditae sunt aut abolitae, sectantur itaque aliam vitae rationem, a priori plane diversam; vid. b. Mus. 1. c. § 11. p. 247. 248.

Respectu propensionis hujus pravae Paulus Rom. 8, 7. scribit: Τό φρόνημα της σαρχός, h. e., quod caro, sive homo carnalis, qualis nascitur, sapit, vult, desiderat, est inimicitia adversus Deum. Quae sane habitualem atque inde ab origine nostra nobis adhaerentem propensionem PART. II. CAP. II.

ad prava in quolibet homine declarant. Et Rom. 7, 17. et 20. memoratur peccatum in nobis habitans, vere. 21. malum adjacens (κακόν παρακείμενον), vers. 23. lex, quae est in membris, rebellans legi mentis etc., quae vers. 7. et 8. vocabatur έπιάυμία, concupiscentia. Intelligitur autem non solum inferior vis appetendi, quae ab appetitu sensitivo est, sed voluntatis etiam inclinatio in malum, quin et ipsius intellectus temeraria de rebus spiritualibus perverse judicandi pronitas, et subito exortas cogitationes malas complectitur. Unde et Apologeta Confess. Aug. art. II. p. 55. inter alia concupiscentiam intelligit eam, quae quaerit non solum voluptates corporis, sed etiam sapientiam et justitiam carnalem, et confidit his bonis, contemnens Deum etc., vid. b. Quod autem Jenenses non doceant, peccatum originis proprie et accurate loquendo esse meram privationem, neque pravam concupiscentiam a peccato originis excludant, idem ostendit in der Ausführlichen Erklärung Q. XXXI. p. 229.

confertur, juxta vere. 10. et 12.), dicitur: Non percipit, non potest intelligere, quae sunt Spiritus Dei, seu mysteria, quae Deus revelavit per Spiritum suum, juxta vers. 7. et 10. Conf. b. Mus. Formula Concordiae: ״Etsi humana ratio seu naturalis intellectus hominis obscuram aliquam notitiae illius scintillulam reliquam habet, quod sit Deus, et particulam aliquam legis tenet (Rom.. 1, 19. sqq.): tamen adeo ignorans, coeca et perversa est ratio illa, ut, etiamsi ingeniosissimi et doctissimi homines in hoc mundo evangelium de Filio Dei et promissiones divinas de aeterna salute legant vel audiant, tamen ea propriis viribus percipere, intelligere, credere et vera esse, statuere nequeant. Quin potius, quanto diligentius in ea re elaborant, ut spirituales res istas suae rationis acumine indagent et comprehendant, tanto minus intelligunt et credunt, et ea omnia pro stultitia et meris nugis et fabulis habent, priusquam a Sp. S. illuminentur et doceantur.“ (p. 689. sq.)

Talem, inquam, qua fit, ut intellectus in discurrendo et investigandis rerum naturis, causis, affectionibus, imo circa ipsum Deum et res divinas, nec minus in dirigendis actionibus et gubernanda vita erret ac principia luminis naturae male applicet ad inferendas conclusiones falsas, imo impias.
