Ex parte voluntatis consistit peccatum originis in carentia a sanctitatis originalis seu virium diligendi Deum super omnia et exequendi, quae intellectus recte dictitavit,b itemque recte coercendi appetitum, quodque voluntas ex adverso c ,propendet ad opera peccaminosa. Seu impotentia volendi et perficiendi spiritualia, ad Phil. 2, 13. Quando enim utrumque horum Deo in solidum tribuitur ac nos ideo salutem nostram cum timore ac tremore operari jubemur, certum est, naturalibus viribus nostris id denegari ac nos moneri, ne, quando donati sumus aliena gratia, ea nos indignos reddamus ac privemur. Eandem voluntatis αδυναμίαν indicat mors per delicta, spirituali vitae opposita. Eph. 2, 5. conf. § 2. not. b. Neque enim tunc solum voluntas deficit aut exorbitat, cum intellectus in cognoscendo erravit, verum etiam, quando recta est ejus cognitio. Scilicet bonum 110η solum spiritualiter, sed et naturaliter tale seu honestum, variis molestiis ac difficultatibus plerumque conjungitur, ideoque ab eo alienior est voluntas et ad sectandum illud fere torpet aut languet, etiamsi in humanis doctrina et assuefactio emendationem aliquam aut perfectionem contulerit. B. Musaeus 1. c. § 26. p. 258. PAKT. II. CAP. II.

Est enim per naturam suam facultas appetens, et quando a vero bono abhorret, in apparens tanto vehementius fertur, praesertim appetitus sensitivi motibus stimulata; conf. Mus. 1. c. § 26. 27. p. 258. 259. Ob hanc propensionem ad prava dicitur homo, qualis per naturam est, servus peccati Rom. 6, 13., et peccatum regnare in ejus corpore mortali ad obediendum illi per cupiditates ejus v. 12. 14, quod videlicet, cum ea, quae sancta sunt, agere ex se non possit, in ea, quae mala sunt, ex adverso feratur, ac si ita agere oporteret aut superioris imperio voluntas flecteretur. Haec etiam est illa πώρωσις, sive callosa quaedam durities cordis, Ephes. 4, 18., qua homines sunt propensi ad carnalem securitatem, ad contemtum et odium Dei, ad diffidentiam erga Deum et fiduciam rerum temporalium, interprete b. Gerhardo Isag. LL. Disp. XXIV. c. III. de Pecc. Orig. § 7. p. m. 879.§ 5.


### On Original Sin: On the part of the sensitive appetite, there occurs a deprivation of the…

On the part of the sensitive appetite, there occurs a deprivation of the obedience owed to the superior faculties, and it rushes, as it were, with a certain impetus—either without awaiting or having rejected the judgment of reason—toward those things which are pleasing to the senses, even though they are forbidden by divine law. § 6. For the inferior faculty ought indeed to have been conformed to the superior ones, not the latter to the former. See what we said above concerning the image of God, Part I, Chapter IV, § 11. Cf. Rom. 7:18, 19, where Paul says that in his flesh no good dwells; and that he does not do the good that he wills. See Rom. 7:8. For although depraved concupiscence, when the term is taken in a broader sense, diffuses itself through all the faculties of man, it is nevertheless referred specifically to the sensitive appetite; and for this reason it is rightly said in verse 23 to exert itself in the members against the law of the mind. § 7.

Therefore, although the power of acting, or of tending toward objects, of any faculty whatsoever, when considered precisely and in itself, is not sin, it is nevertheless rightly called sin because it is borne toward objects άνόμως (lawlessly). For thus it is something positive and only the material of sin. "We call that corruption of nature, which comprises the propensity and impetus of all the powers of the soul toward evil, a positive quality—not as if any power of acting in and of itself were sin, but because that power of acting in man is only prone and prompt toward sin; meanwhile, we do not forbid that a subtle distinction be made between the power of acting itself and the vice of that power, just as a distinction is made between the action itself and the vice of the action": these are the words of the blessed Gerhard, *T. II. LL. § 88, p. 402.* Cf. *Disp. Isag. XXIV. cap. III. thes. 10, pp. m. 880, 881.* To these correspond exactly the things which the blessed Musaeus [states in] *Disp. IV.*

Regarding Conversion § 7, p. 245, he wrote: the propensity toward evil is called sin, not insofar as it is a positive entity and a certain principle of action, but insofar as it is destitute of the due perfection and is a principle of acting wrongly. Speaking concretely, that is. Whence, if any refer it to the formal aspect of original sin, it must be understood as the form of the whole, or as the entire essence, so to speak, of original sin. Thus, that original sin taken concretely is something positive, on account of the connate habitual proneness toward an object, toward which it is inordinately borne, which it connotes by way of a subject; but that taken abstractly and formally it is a mere privation, is taught in the *Ausführliche Erklärung* [Detailed Explanation], Q. XXXI, p. 231 sqq.

And that was the ancient opinion of our people. In the year 1619, there were published, comprised in two quaternions, the testimonies of Philipp Melanchthon and Martin Chemnitz, and likewise of Aegidius Hunnius and Leonhard Hutter, that every sin—even if it is not merely a pure privation, but by reason of its material is often also a corrupt habit, a positive quality, etc., as the Apology of the Augsburg Confession most correctly teaches—nevertheless, as regards its formal aspect, does not state anything positive, but a privation. Where, among other things, from M. Chemnitz’s *Loci Theologici*, Chapter on the Cause of Sin, Response to the argument of the Manichaean, after the distinction between material and formal had been inculcated and applied to the present case, he says: "These things seem to be thorny and to suit the subtleties of dialecticians rather than theological simplicity; but because things created by God must necessarily be distinguished from sin, which is a disturbance of the divine order, such things are rightly and usefully handed down."

From the *Loci* of the blessed Hutter, however, this is to be noted among other things: that in defending the Philippean definition, by which sin is defined through privation, he brings forward in the third place this argument of the adversaries: "Whatever diminishes the atrocity of sin ought not to be taught. Privation diminishes the atrocity of sin. Therefore, it ought not to be taught." He responds, however, that in the minor proposition a false hypothesis is taken as certain and indubitable, whence a *petitio principii* [begging of the question] emerges. For, he says, by the word "privation" the atrocity of sin is not diminished, but rather exaggerated, and it is shown what great ruin and what immense damage the human race has received from this privation. There are, however, weighty reasons why the term "privation" is to be retained in the definition of sin, namely, so that the distinction may be seen between things created and the privation of things, which is not created, but draws its origin from the devil. These and more can be seen in the *Loci Theologici* of the blessed Hutter, published in the same year with a preface by the Theological Faculty of Wittenberg, p. m. 308, 309.

But if conforming testimonies of others are desired, one may see those which the blessed Musaeus brought forward from the blessed Grauer, the blessed Gerhard, the blessed Himmel, the blessed Hoepfner, and the blessed Kromayer in the *Ausführliche Erklärung*, p. 234 sqq. The blessed Grauer and the blessed Kromayer repeated those things proposed in the aforementioned places also elsewhere.

The former indeed in *Centuria Quaestionum Illustrium*, Corollary 1 of the last Disputation, whose words are these: "Original sin formally is not something positive, but materially, when these terms are used correctly and not vulgarly."

The latter, however, in *Theologia Aphoristica*, Book VIII, Aphorism X, writes: "The Apology of the Augsburg Confession indeed retains the definition of Anselm, that sin is a lack of original righteousness, but it adds concupiscence. But concupiscence itself is also considered, either as it is an inclination toward its object, or as a declination from the norm. But if by the lack of original righteousness [is meant] the privation of a connatural good that ought to be present (for the Papists wish original righteousness to have been some supernatural good, by which reasoning sin... PART II. CHAPTER II.

pius confessors felt that original sin is extenuated) is understood as drawing with it a great corruption, and we could be content with Anselm’s definition. Be that as it may, we acquiesce in the distinctions placed at the beginning of the development: namely, if sin is considered metaphysically and in the abstract, it is something privative; but if it is considered ethically and in the concrete, it may be called something positive.

In the preceding, he had said that those who posit original sin as something positive urge concrete expressions, such as the "stony heart" (Ezek. 36:26) and "flesh of flesh" (John 3:6); however, this opinion regarding the positive, properly so-called, is said by some to be a branch or ἀποσπασμάτων of Flacianism, because it is defended by arguments that labor under a confusion of the concrete and the abstract. These are the words of the blessed Kromayer, from whom, and from the preceding Gerhard and Hoepfner whom he cites, we finally note this: that the consideration of the positive, which is κατ’ ἀκρίβειαν, pertains to metaphysics, which by its own right claims the duty of distinguishing between being and non-being, the positive and the privative, so that if you call sin, viewed formally, positive, Hoepfner warns that this is done in a catachrestic sense.

If, therefore, one is provoked here to moral or ethical entity, it must nevertheless be confessed that metaphysical ἀκρίβεια ought not to be despised on that account; nor do privations, which have a relation partly to the subject which they affect morally, and partly to the form which they deny or exclude, cease to be privations because of this relation, nor, against the will of metaphysical doctrine, and yet as if ἐξ ἀκριβείας, must they be transcribed into the class of positive beings.

Carpzovius: "Just as Flacius himself later wished to defend in various writings what had once slipped out in the heat of disputation... so his sycophants spared no effort, becoming far harsher, more impudent, and more absurd than their teacher, nor did they sufficiently understand the mind of their teacher, who, if he had ever wished to correct himself at the beginning... would never have caused such disturbances, and the orthodox could easily have agreed with him. For he did not consider man absolutely or in his absolute substance, but concretely and with his state; and by essence and essential form he did not understand substance itself, insofar as it signifies a thing subsisting by itself and is opposed to the accidental predicament*), but that essence which belongs to man, not as he is man, but as he is such or corrupted—namely, the accidental form which, with the absolute subject, constitutes a concrete being and is essential to the corrupted man, so that as long as and to the extent that he is corrupted, the corruption or viciousness cannot even in thought be separated from him." (Isagog. in libb. eccles. luth. symb. p. 1160 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Manichaeans, who, according to Augustine, posited that certain evil substances originated from God, which by their own nature are sin itself... 2. Of Matthias Flacius Illyricus and his followers, Johannes Coelestinus, professor at Jena, and Cyriacus Spangenberg, dean of Mansfeld, as well as M. Christoph Irenaeus, court preacher at Weimar, asserting that original sin is the human substance itself, the substantial form of man itself, the heart itself, and the rational soul itself, so that now after the fall no distinction remains between the substance and nature of man and sin." (L. c. q. 10. f. 1022.) *)

Crusius: "That in which we think of nothing further than something which, when it is, must necessarily subsist in another, is called an ens praedicamentale." C. III §20. p. 32 sq.

Carpzovius: "Some theologians, when they taught that sin is not something privative, but also something positive, . . . wished to indicate that there is a twofold privation in original sin. One is the absence of good, the other is the presence of evil or a moral defect or a conflict with the law of God; so that human nature is not only not-just, but also unjust, not only not-holy, but also depraved; just as it is explained in the Apology, ch. 4, p. 99b. For in the intellect there is not only a lack of light, but also an inherent supreme blindness and corruption, so that it even considers the mysteries of the faith to be foolishness; in the will there is not only a lack of rectitude, but it cannot elicit any good action and is carried toward evil by its own nature; the sensitive appetite is carried inordinately toward objects and opposes itself to the dictate of right reason, etc. Otherwise, sin in itself is not something positive." (Isag. p. 1173.)

Latin:

Ex parte appetitus sensitivi locum habet privatio obsequii superioribus facultatibus debiti,a quodque ille contra in ea, quae sensibus grata sunt, licet lege divina prohibeantur, quodam quasi impetu, sive non expectato sive repudiato rationis judicio,b ruit. Debebat enim utique facultas inferior conformari superioribus, non hae illi. Vid., quae de imagine Dei supra diximus P. I. cap. IV. §11. Conf. Rom. 7, 18. 19., ubi Paulus ait, in carne sua non habitare bonum; id eoque se non facere bonum, quod velit. Vid. Rom. 7, 8. Etsi enim concupiscentia prava, vocabulo latius accepto, per omnes hominis facultates sese diffundat, speciatim tamen ad appetitum sensitivum refertur; et hac ratione v. 23. in membris sese exserere adversus legem mentis, utique recte dicitur.§ 6.

Quamvis ergo cujuslibet facultatis vis agendi, seu tendendi in objecta, quando praecise et in se consideratur, non sit peccatum,a propterea tamen, quod άνόμως fertur in objecta, peccatum b recte appellatur. Ita enim positivum quid est et materiale tantum peccati. Illam naturae corruptionem, quae complectitur omnium animae virium ad malum pronitalem ac impetum, vocamus positivam qualitatem, non quasi aliqua vis agendi in se et per se sit peccatum, sed quia illa vis agendi in homine est tantum ad peccatum prona et promta; interim non prohibemus, quin inter ipsam agendi vim, et inter vitium illius potentiae subtiliter distinguatur, sicut inter ipsam actionem et vitium actionis distinguitur: verba sunt b. Gerhardi T. II. LL. § 88. p. 402. Conf. Disp. Isag. XXIV. cap. III. thes. 10. p. m. 880. 881. Quibus plane respondent, quae b. Musaeus Disp. IV.

de Convers. § 7. p. 245. scripsit: propensio ad malum dicitur peccatum, non quatenus est entitas positiva et quoddam agendi principium, sed quatenus perfectione debita destituta et male agendi principium est. Concretive scilicet loquendo. Unde, si qui eam ad formale peccati originis referunt, intelligenda est forma totius, seu tota quasi essentia peccati originalis. Ita concretive sumtum peccatum originis esse aliquid positivi, ob connatam habitualem pronitatem in objectum, in quod inordinate fertur, quam per modum subjecti connotat, abstractive autem et formaliter sumtum esse meram privationem, docetur in der Ausführlichen Erklärung Q. XXXI. p. 231. sqq.

Ea autem antiqua fuit nostratium sententia. Prodierunt a. 1619. duobus quaternionibus comprehensa Philippi Melanchthonis et Martini Chemnitii, itemque Aegidii Hunnii et Leonhardi Hutteri testimonia, quod omne peccatum, etsi non est pura tantum privatio, sed ratione materialis sui saepe etiam habitus corruptus, posir tiva qualitas etc., ut rectissime docet Apolog. August. Confess., tamen quoad formale suum non positivum quidquam, sed privationem dicat. Ubi inter alia ex M. Chemnitii LL. Theol. Cap. de Causa Peccati, Resp. ad arg. Manichaei, inculcata ante distinctione inter materiale et formale, eaque ad praesens applicata, Videntur, inquit, haec esse spinosa et dialecticorum argutiis potius convenire, quam theologicae simplicitati; sed quia necessario discernendae sunt res conditae a Deo a peccato, quod est conturbatio ordinis divini, recte et utiliter talia traduntur.

Ex b. Hutteri LL. autem illud inter alia notandum est, quod definitionem Philippeam, qua peccatum per privationem definitur, defensurus, tertio loco hoc argumentum adversariorum adducit: Quicquid atrocitatem peccati extenuat, doceri non debet. Privatio extenuat atrocitatem peccati. E. doceri non debet. Respondet autem, quod in minore propositione falsa hypothesis pro certa et indubitata sumatur, unde principii petitio emergat. Neque enim, ait, privationis voce extenuatur, sed exaggeratur potius peccati atrocitas, et ostenditur, quantam cladem et quam ingens damnum genus humanum ex privatione hae acceperit. Graves autem sunt causae, propter quas privationis vocabulum in definitione peccati est retinendum, nempe ut conspiciatur discrimen inter res conditas et rerum privationem non conditam, sed a diabolo ortum trahentem. Quae et plura videri possunt in Locis Theol. b. Hutteri eodem anno cum praefatione Facult. Theol. Witteberg, editis p. m. 308. 309.

Quod si aliorum testimonia conformia desiderentur, videri possunt, quae ex b. Grauero, b. Gerhardo, b. Himmelio, b. Hoepfnero, b. Kromayero, adduxit b. Musaeus in der Ausführlichen Erklärung p. 234. sqq. Repetierunt autem illa 11. cc. proposita b. Grauerus et b. Kromayerus etiam alibi.

Ille quidem in Cent. QQ. Illustr. Coroll. 1. Disp. ult., cujus haec sunt verba: Peccatum originis formaliter non est aliquid positivum, sed materialiter, quando hi termini recte et non vulgariter usurpantur.

Hic vero in Theol. Aphorist. L. VIII. Aphor. X. scribit: Apologia confessionis Augustanae definitionem Anshelmi, quod peccatum sit carentia justitiae originalis, quidem retinet, sed concupiscentiam addit. Verum ipsa quoque concupiscentia, vel, ut est inclinatio ad suum objectum, vel, ut declinatio a norma, consideratur. Quod si per carentium justitiae originalis privatio boni connaturalis inesse debiti (pontificii vero justitiam originalem bonum aliquod supernaturale fuisse volunt, qua ratione peccatum PART. II. CAP. II.

originis extenuari senserunt pii confessores) magnam corruptionem secum trahens intelligatur, et nos Anshelmi definitione possemus esse contenti. Quicquid sit, in distinctionibus ab evolutionis initio positis, si nimirum peccatum metaphysice et in abstracto consideretur, quod sit privativum quid; si vero ethice et in concreto, quod positivum quid diei queat, acquiescimus.

In praecedentibus dixerat, eos, qui peccatum originis positivtim quid esse statuunt, concretivas locutiones, quoa cor lapideum Ezech. 36, 26., caro de came Joh. 3, 6. dicatur, urgere; hanc autem sententiam de positivo proprie dicto ramusculum vel αποσπασμάτων Flacianismi dici quibusdam, quod Usflem argumentis, confusione concreti et abstracti laborantibus, propugnetur. Haec b. Kromayerus, ex quo et praeeuntibus Gerhardo atque Hoepfnero, quos ille allegat, et istud denique notamus, quod consideratio toj positivi, quae sit χατ ακρίβειαν, ad metaphysicam pertineat, quae inter ens et nonens, positivum et privativum, distinguendi munus sibi suo jure arroget, ita ut, si peccatum formaliter spectatum positivum dicas, sensu catachrestico id fieri moneat Hoepfnerus.

Quod si ergo ad entitatem, moralem seu ethicam hic provocetur, fatendum tamen est, non ideo contemni debere άχρίβει v metaphysicam; neque etiam privationes, quae relationem habent partim ad subjectum, quod moraliter afficiunt, partim ad formam, quam negant aut excludunt, propter hanc relationem privationes esse desinunt, neque, invita doctrina metaphysica, et tamen velut έξ άχριβείας, in positivorum entium classem transcribi debebunt.

Carpzovius: ,,Ut ipse Flacius postea variis scriptis tueri voluit, quod semel in fervore disputationis elapsum fuerat ... ita non minus assentatores ejus nulli operae pepercerunt, longe duriores, impudentiores et absurdiores ipso praeceptore facti, nec satis intellexerunt mentem praeceptoris sui, qui, si Unguam corrigere voluisset initio, . . . nunquam tantas turbas dedisset et concordare cum eo facile potuissent orthodoxi. Non enim hominem absolute seu in absoluta sua substantia considerabat, sed concrete et cum statu suo, atque per essentiam et formam essentialem non intelligebat substantiam ipsam, prout significat rem per se subsistentem et opponitur accidentali praedicamento*), sed essentiam illam, quae homini, non qua homo est, sed qua talis sive corruptus est, competit, nempe formam accidentariam, quae cum subjecto absoluto constituit ens concretum et homini corrupto essentialis est, ita ut, quamdiu et quantum corruptus est, ne quidem cogitatione possit separari ab eo corruptio seu vitiositas.“ (Isagog. in libb. eccles. luth. symb. p. 1160. sq.)

Matthiae Flacii Illyrici et asseclarum, Johannis Coelestini, professoris Jenensis, et Cyriaci Spangenbergii, decani Mansfeldensis, itemque M. Christophori Irenaei, concionatoris aulici Vimariae, asserentium, peccatum originis esse ipsam substantiam humanam, ipsam substantialem hominis formam, ipsum cor, ipsamque animam rationalem, ut jam post lapsum inter substantiam et naturam hominis et inter peccatum nullum amplius sit relictum discrimen.“ (L. c. q. 10. f. 1022.) *)

Crusius: , ,Dasjenige, worinnen wir nichts weiterdenken, als etwas, welches, wenn es ist, nothwendig in einem andern subsistiren muss, nennt man ein ens praedicamentale." C. III §20. p. 32. sq

Carpzovius: ,,Nonnulli theologi, quando peccatum non esse privativum quid, sed etiam positivum quid docuerunt, . . . indicare voluerunt, duplicem esse privationem in peccato originali. Unam esse absentiam boni, alteram vero praesentiam mali seu defectum moralem seu pugnantiam cum lege Dei; ut humana natura non tantum sit nonjusta, sed etiam injusta, non tantum nonsancta, sed etiam prava; quemadmodum in Apologia c. 4. p. 99. b. id exponitur. Etenim in intellectu non tantum deest lux, sed etiam inest summa coecitas ac corruptio, ut etiam mysteria fidei pro stultitia habeat; in voluntate non tantum deest rectitudo, sed etiam non potest ullam bonam actionem elicere et ad mala natura sua fertur; appetitus sensitivus inordinate in objecta fertur et rectae rationis dictamini se opponit etc. Alias peccatum in se non est positivum quid.“ (Isag. p. 1173.)


### On Original Sin: Apology of the A. C.

Apology of the A. C.: "Not only the ancient fathers, such as Augustine and the like, but also the more recent teachers and Scholastics who have had any understanding, teach that these two parts together are original sin, namely, the lack and the evil desire. For thus St. Thomas says that 'original sin is not only a lack of original righteousness, but also an inordinate desire or lust in the soul. Therefore it is,' he says, 'not only a mere lack, but also *aliquid positivum* [something positive].'" (Art. 2, p. 82.) §

7. The remote efficient cause of original sin is the devil, the proximate cause is the first parents, Eve and especially Adam.

Indeed, there is no physical efficient cause of original sin formally considered, since in this respect it is a privation, as we have seen; but the deficient cause is sought, or that which, by failing or sinning, brought it about that men are born without original righteousness and with depraved concupiscence. See *Ausführliche Erklärung* Q. XXXV, p. 305.

This is why the devil is called a murderer and the father of lies, John 8:44.

For he could not be the cause of slaughter or human death unless he were the cause of sin introduced into the human race, since men were immortal before sin, but death entered the world through sin.

He is also the father of lies, who by lying drew men away from faith and the obedience owed to God and thus gave cause to the corruption that followed.

Naturally, that insidious speech which is ascribed to the serpent in Gen. 3:1ff. must be ascribed to Satan, of whom that serpent was the instrument; whence Satan himself took the name of the serpent. See 2 Cor. 11:3, Is. 27:1, Rev. 12:9.

She who was seduced by the devil became a transgressor, so that in memory of the first woman deceived by Satan (who, sinning, induced her husband to sin by her persuasion, whence that corruption of the whole human race arose), no woman should be admitted to preach publicly in the church. 1 Tim. 2:14.

See Rom. 5:12, where one man, Adam, as the common parent of the whole human race and the root and active principle of it, is declared to be the cause of sin, inasmuch as through him sin entered into the world. Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. II. PART II. CHAPTER II.

8. The first parents, and Adam in particular, are the cause of original sin by means of their fall. For by this act they rendered themselves unworthy of God continuing to grant them the influx necessary for preserving in themselves and propagating to their descendants original righteousness; rather, they rendered themselves worthy of His withdrawing it by a just judgment. Consequently, that righteousness, having been lost in the protoplasts themselves, could no longer be born with their descendants, who were descending from parents deprived of original righteousness by way of carnal generation; instead, the lack of that righteousness and the proneness of all faculties toward evil would be born with them.

Some call this the proximate and adequate cause of original sin, others call it causality, or the reason by which the protoplasts actually became the cause of original sin. Or they merited it, or moved and impelled God as Judge.

For God entered into a sort of covenant with the first humans, upon whom, out of His unmerited goodness, He had concreated the divine image, that they should use it as a natural, and not merely personal, gift, and that, through their constant obedience, they should both preserve it themselves and, with God concurring, propagate it to their children and other descendants.

Certainly, when the protoplasts sinned, they immediately lost for themselves in act the concreated or original righteousness which they had hitherto possessed in act; but for their descendants, who did not yet exist, they lost that same righteousness in potency, so that it would not be conferred upon those to be born thereafter (which some perhaps might say meant that the right or faculty of obtaining original righteousness was lost to them). However, all and every one of Adam’s descendants are deprived of original righteousness when they are born of parents who are destitute of original righteousness and laboring under depraved concupiscence.

Hence, there are those who say that the proximate cause of original sin, insofar as it is found propagated to individuals, is carnal generation itself, which is joined with the inordinate concupiscence of those generating, or which is from the lust of the flesh and the lust of man, according to John 1:13, whence it comes to pass that what is born of the flesh is flesh, John 3:6, and that humans, formed and conceived in sin, are born sinners, Psalm 51:7, so that no one is born clean from the unclean, Job 14:4.

But as for disputing more subtly: How could God so impute the fall of the protoplasts to their descendants, who did not yet exist, that for this reason it was necessary for them also to be born destitute of original righteousness and as sinners? There is no need, nor is it perhaps advisable. For it suffices that the *ὅτι* (that it is so) has been revealed, even if the *πῶς* (how it is so) is unknown.

Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between the natural and the moral head. Adam, insofar as he was the natural head of the human race, infected all the members, and thus the inherent evil passed from him through propagation into the whole posterity; in the latter way, insofar as he was the moral head, representing the whole posterity, in that measure it was derived to the descendants by imputation that he himself sinned."

The same: "Question 7: Is the Adamic sin truly and deservedly imputed by God to the whole human race? ... The controversy here concerns ... whether that first act, insofar as it was a sinful and transient act, is so appropriated and imputed to us, as if we ourselves had stretched out our hand to the forbidden evil and had sinned. ... The first sin is viewed 1. on the part of Adam himself, who by the single numerical breaking of the law implicated all his descendants in guilt, in liability, and in punishment, inasmuch as his will was the interpreter of the wills of all those who, as Scripture speaks, were in his loins or thigh, or who lay hidden in his seminal virtue, whose own deed the sin has now become interpretatively, so that they are born in the absence of the due perfection that ought to be present. The will, I say, of Adam, as the principle and root of the human race, was considered our own, not formally, but interpretatively. For the first man had the wills of all his descendants located, as it were, in his own will, whence he declared his own mind and that of his descendants against the given law.

2. With respect to God, as judge, who by the supreme right which He possesses, punishes the crime of lese-majesty even in the descendants, as having fallen in Adam, by the privation, as such, of original righteousness, and thus most justly imputes the Adamic sin to them for condemnation." (L. c. q. 7. f. 993. sq.)

Heerbrandus: "Is original sin proper or alien? It is both, both proper and alien. It is alien by reason of its first origin, because we are not its first authors, but it comes to us from elsewhere. It is called proper because it inheres in us and is not merely imputed, nor do we learn it by imitation; but it is born in us and implanted in our nature, to which it adheres." (Compend. th. p. 310.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Pelagians, who maintain that it is in no way conceded that God imputes the sins of others. ... 2. Of the Socinians. For thus Socinus, lib. IV. de serv. Christ, and praelect. theol. c. 4., where he denies that the transgression of Adam is imputed to those who do not sin in that manner, as Adam did. ... 3. Of the Arminians, such as Joh. Arnoldi, Corvinus, who says: 'We have not fallen in Adam, except by imputation.'" (L. c. q. 7. f. 995.)

Hoemannus: "We do not need an artificial assumption, such as that all who descend from Adam were in him, or that he sinned as the federal head of the human race, but we remain with the simple fact of that unity of the human race, by virtue of which every individual is not only a member of the race, but the beginning of the same is his beginning. The individual has not committed the sin of Adam, but because the beginner of the race has committed it, it is the sin of all who descend from him. In this sense, we have called it self-determination in our doctrine, not only of the first-created, but of man." (Schriftbeweis. I. 491. sq.)

Vilmarius: "One should not have identified the older and sharper Latin word *culpa* with this word *reatus*, as the imprecise Latinity of the 16th and even more of the 17th century—which was often downright frivolous in its word usage, especially in rhetorical synonymy—did: *culpa* denotes authorship; and this can only belong to the protoplasts, not to those born later. From this mixing of *culpa* and *reatus*, in which the Apology of the A. C. and then the F. C. participated, there followed then, with the beginning of the 17th century, also the concept of *imputatio* (imputation), which, strictly speaking, corresponds merely to the concept of *culpa*... According to this, one distinguished an *imputatio mediata* = imputation of guilt because of the transmitted sinfulness (*defectus* and *concupiscentia*), and an *imputatio immediata* = imputation of the sin of Adam in and of itself. This latter, the *imputatio immediata*..." PART II. CHAP. II.

the question now arises: how can a foreign guilt be imputed to me? And this question, so understood, can certainly not be given a sufficient answer. . . The *imputatio immediata* cannot be justified otherwise than through the unscriptural doctrine of the pre-existence of souls, which already existed before Adam and at his fall (or even before) were present directly, immediately, and were thus also complicit, just as they were present.” (Dogmatik. I, 370. sqq.) §

9. And that fall of the first-formed ones was indeed completed by the external act of eating from the fruit of the forbidden tree against the express law of God,a which, however, was preceded by several sinful internal acts: in the intellect, indeed, a doubting of the truth of the divine threat, and soon a fuller unbelief;b in the will, an inordinate inclination toward a greater likeness to God;c in the sensitive appetite, an inordinate motion, tending toward an object pleasing to the senses,d even though it was forbidden.

Latin:

Apologia A. C.: ,,Nicht allein die alten Väter, als Augustinus und dergleichen, sondern auch die neulichsten Lehrer und Scholastici, die etwas Verstand gehabt, lehren, dass diese zwei Stück sämmtlich die Erbsünde sind, nämlich der Mangel und die böse Lust. Denn also sagt St. Thomas, dass,Erbsünde ist nicht allein ein Mangel der ersten Gerechtigkeit, sondern auch eine unordentliche Begierde oder Lust in der Seele. Derhalben ist es‘, sagt er, ,nicht allein ein lauter Mangel, sondern auch aliquid positivum.“‘ (Art. 2. p. 82.) §

7. Causa efficiens peccati originalis a remota diabolus est,b propinqua protoplasti, Eva c et inprimis Adam.d

Equidem causa efficiens physica peccati originalis formaliter spectati nulla datur, cum hac ratione sit privatio, ut vidimus; quaeriter autem causa deficiens, seu quae deficiendo aut peccando effecit, ut homines nascantur absque justitia originali et cum prava concupiscentia. Vid. Ausführliche Erklärung Q. XXXV. p. 305.

Hoc est, quod diabolus homicida dicitur et pater mendacii Joh. 8, 44..

Causa enim caedis aut mortis humanae esse non potuit, nisi esset causa peccati in genus humanum introducti, cum homines ante peccatum immortales fuerint, mors autem per peccatum introierit in mundum.

Pater mendacii etiam est, qui mentiendo homines a fide et obsequio Deo debito abstraxit atque ita corruptioni secutae causam dedit.

Nimirum sermo ille insidiosus, qui Gen. 3, 1. sqq. serpenti adscribitur, satanae, cujus ille serpens instrumentum erat, adscribi debet; unde ipse satanas serpentis nomen traxit. Vid. 2 Cor. 11, 3. Es. 27, 1. Apoc. 12, 9.

Quae seducta a diabolo praevarieatris facta est, ita ut in memoriam deceptae a satana primae mulieris (quae peccans ad peccatum sua suasione induxit virum, unde illa corruptio totius humani generis orta fuit) nulla mulier ad praedicandum publice in ecclesia admitti debeat. 1 Tim. 2, 14..

Vid. Rom. 5, 12., ubi unus homo, Adam, tanquam communis parens totius humani generis et radix ac principium activum illius, peccati causa declaratur, quippe quod per eum peccatum in mundum venerit.19 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. Π. PART. II. CAP. Π.

8. Sunt autem parentes primi, et inprimis Adam, causa peccati originis, mediante lapsu suo.a Hoc enim facto indignos se reddiderunt,b quibus Deus influxum ad conservandam in ipsis et propagandam ad posteros justitiam originalem necessarium porro largiretur,c dignos potius, quibus eum justo judicio subtraheret, adeoque ut posteris ipsorum ex parentibus, justitia originali privatis, per generationem d carnalem descendentibus jam non posset connasci illa justitia, in ipsis protoplastis amissa, sed carentia illius justitiae ac pronitas omnium facultatum ad prava illis connasceretur.e

Quem alii causam peccati originalis proximam et adaequatam, alii causalitatem appellant, seu rationem, per quam protoplasti facti sunt actu causa peccati originalis. Sive demeruerunt, aut Deum judicem moverunt atque impulerunt.

Hoc enim quasi paetum Deus cum hominibus primis, quibus pro sua bonitate indebita imaginem divinam concreaverat, iniit, ut eo, tanquam dono naturali, non tantum personali, uterentur idque, intercedente constante obedientia sua, et servarent ipsi et ad liberos posterosque caeteros, Deo concurrente, propagarent.

Sane protoplasti, cum peccarent, statim sibi actu perdiderunt' justitiam concreatam seu originalem, quam hactenus actu possidebant; posteris autem nondum existentibus potentia amiserunt eandem justitiam, ne posthac nascituris conferretur (quod fortasse aliqui dixerint, amissum his esse jus aut facultatem consequendi originalem justitiam); privantur autem posteri Adami, omnes et singuli, justitia originali, cum nascuntur ex parentibus justitia originali destitutis et prava concupiscentia laborantibus.

Unde sunt, qui peccati originalis, quatenus ad singulos propagatum deprehenditur, causam proximam dicunt esse ipsam carnalem generationem, quae conjuncta est cum inordinata generantium concupiscentia, sive quae est ex libidine camis et libidine viri, juxta Joh. 1, 13., unde sit, ut, quod natum est de carne, sit caro, Joh. 3, 6., horninesque in peccato formati et calefacti peccatores nascantur, Ps. 51, 7., ut mundus ex immundo nascatur nemo, Jobi 14., 4.

Ut autem subtilius disputetur: Quomodo Deus lapsum protoplastorum posteris ipsorum, nondum existentibus, ita imputare potuerit, ut propterea etiam ipsos justitia originali destitutos et peccatores nasci oporteret? non opus est, nec fortasse consultum. Sufficit enim το 8rt esse revelatum, etsi τό πώς ignoretur.

Quenstedtius: ״Disting. inter caput naturale et morale. Adamus, in quantum caput naturale generis humani, infecit omnia membra, atque ita ab ipso per propagationem transiit malum inhaerens in totam posteritatem; posteriori modo, in quantum fuit caput morale, repraesentans totam posteritatem, in tantum imputatione derivatum est in posteros, quod ipse peccavit.“

Idem: ,,Quaestio 7.: An peccatum adamiticum vere meritoque toti humano generi a Deo imputetur? ... In controversiam hic venit, ... an primus ille actus, in quantum sc. fuit actus peccaminosus et transiens, nobis ita approprietur itaque imputetur, ac si ipsi manum extendissemus ad malum vetitum et peccassemus. . . Spectatur peccatum primum 1. ex parte ipsius Adami, qui unica numero legis ruptione omnes posteros cum culpae, tum reatui, tum poenae implicuit, quatenus nempe voluntas ejus interpres erat voluntatum omnium omnino eorum, qui, ut Scriptura loquitur, in lumbis vel femore ejus erant sive qui in virtute ejus seminali delitescebant, quorum jam interpretative proprium factum est peccatum, ita ut nascantur in absentia perfectionis debitae inesse. Voluntas, inquam, Adami utpote principii et radicis generis humani censebatur nostra, non formaliter, sed interpretative. Nam primus homo omnium posterorum voluntates in sua quasi voluntate locatas habuit, unde et contra datam legem pro se et posteris suis suum et posterorum declaravit animum.

2. Bespectu Dei, ut judicis, qui jure, quo pollet, summo crimen majestatis laesae etiam in posteris, utpote in Adamo lapsis, carentia, qua tali, justitiae originalis punit, adeoque peccatum adamiticum justissime illis ad damnationem imputat.“ (L. c. q. 7. f. 993. sq.)

Heerbrandus: ,,Estne peccatum originis proprium, an alienum? Utrumque est, et proprium et alienum. Alienum est ratione primae originis, quia nos non sumus primi ejus auctores, sed aliunde nobis advenit. Proprium est et dicitur, quia in nobis haeret et non tantum imputatur, nec imitatione discimus; sed innascitur nobis et implantatur nostrae naturae, cui inhaeret.“ (Compend. th. p. 310.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Pelagianomm, qui statuunt, nulla ratione concedi, ut Deus aliena peccata imputet. . . 2. Socinianorum. Sic enim Socinus lib. IV. de serv. Christ, et praelect. theol. c. 4., ubi negat illis, qui ea ratione non delinquunt, ut Adam, delictum Adami imputari. . . 3. Arminianorum, ut Joh. Arnoldi, Corvini, qui inquit: ,In Adamo non sumus lapsi, nisi imputatione.‘ “ (L. c. q. 7. f. 995.)

Hoemannus: ,,Wir brauchen keine künstliche Annahme, wie dass alle von Adam Stammenden in ihm gewesen, oder dass er als Bundeshaupt des menschlichen Geschlechts gesündigt habe, sondern bleiben bei der einfachen Thatsache jener Einheit des Menschengeschlechts, vermöge welcher jeder Einzelne nicht nur Glied des Geschlechts, sondern auch der Anfang desselben sein Anfang ist. Nicht hat der Einzelne die Sünde Adams mitgethan, sondern weil der Anfänger des Geschlechte sie gethan hat, so ist sie die Sünde Aller, welche von ihm stammen. In diesem Sinne haben wir sie in unserm Lehrsätze Selbstbestimmung nicht blos der Erstgeschaffenen, sondern des Menschen genannt.“ (Schriftbeweis. I. 491. sq.)

Vilmarius: ,,Man hätte mit diesem Wort reatus nicht das ältere und schärfere lateinische Wort culpa identificiren sollen, wie es die ungenaue und in dem Wortgebrauch zumal der rhetorischen Synonymik oft geradezu leichtfertige Latinität des 16. und noch mehr des 17. Jahrhunderts that: culpa bezeichnet die Urheberschaft; und diese kann nur den Protoplasten, nicht den Nachgebornen zukommen. Aus dieser Vermischung von culpa und reatus, woran schon die Apologie der A. C., sodann die P. C. sich betheiligt hat, folgte dann mit dem Anfange des 17. Jahrhunderts auch der Begriff der imputatio, Zurechnung, welcher streng genommen lediglich dem Begriff culpa correspondirt.. . Man unterschied hiernach eine imputatio mediata = Zurechnung der Schuld wegen der übergeleiteten Sündhaftigkeit (defectus und concupiscentia), und einer imputatio immediata = Zurechnung der Sünde Adams an und für sich. Dieser letzteren, der imputatio immediata, PART. II. CAP. II.

gegenüber stellt sich nun die Frage: wie kann mir eine fremde Schuld zugerechnet werden? und dieser Frage, so verstanden, kann eine genügende Beantwortung allerdings nicht zu Theil werden. . . Die imputatio immediata lässt sich nicht anders begründen, als durch die schriftwidrige Lehre von der Präexistenz der Seelen, welche vor Adam schon vorhanden waren und bei seinem Fall (oder vorher schon) sich direct, unmittelbar, wie gegenwärtig sich befanden so auch mitthätig waren.“ (Dogmatik. I, 370. sqq.) §

9. Et lapsus quidem ille protoplastorum perficiebatur actu externo comedendi de fructu arboris vetitae contra expressam Dei legem,a quem tamen praecesserunt plures actus interni peccaminosi: in intellectu quidem dubitatio de veritate divinae comminationis, et mox plenior incredulitas;b in wlwntate inclinatio inordinata ad similitudinem majorem cum Deo;c in appetitu sensitivo motus inordinatus, tendens in objectum sensibus gratum,d etsi prohibitum.


### On Original Sin: For the Lord God had indeed commanded the man, saying

For the Lord God had indeed commanded the man, saying: Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, Gen. 2:17; but in chapter 3, 6 and 11, it is written: The woman took of the fruit of that tree and ate, and she also gave to her husband with her, and he ate. See Gen. 3:3 et seqq. up to 6, where we are taught that Eve had first remembered the divine law and the added threat, but soon listened to and believed that serpent ἐνεργουμένῳ, teaching other things, e.g.: You shall not die, your eyes will be opened, etc.; but the man obeyed the voice of his wife, v. 7, or preferred the bland voice of his seduced wife to the divine interdict and despised the authority of God.

ANTITHESIS. Hofmann: “The biblical narrative of the sin of the first-created teaches us that it was an object of the physical world upon which his desire and action were sinfully directed. His will did not set itself against the will of God in such a hostile manner that he did not want what God wanted, for the reason that God wanted it, or in such a way that he knowingly wanted the exact opposite of what God wanted. . . For if one disregards what sin becomes when it sets itself against the grace of God, it is essentially a desire to possess the world in a way that God has not given man in general, or this man in particular, to possess it; a desire for the removal of the boundary of his world-possession. In a word, it is ἐπιθυμία. . . It is rightly said that the entire direction of life, which has proceeded from the first sin, is most comprehensively designated by the name selfishness; but it is less correct to call selfishness the root of sin, from which the first sin also proceeded. Neither the narrative of the Fall, nor the Pauline passage discussed above, agree with this: both let us perceive with what good right sin is also [described] as love of the creature

[...instead of the Creator, or has been named sensuality. According to Scripture, the beginning of human sin was not to will oneself in contradiction to God, and it is continually the beginning of its activity, but to will the world for oneself in contradiction to God; and the seductive promise of the serpent, that they would know good and evil like God, that is, what this opposition is about, changes nothing in this, in that it makes man desire not self-deification, but god-like world-knowledge and world-mastery. But this is not the selfishness of an 'I' setting itself against God and that which is God's, but that of an 'I' desiring, according to what is created by God, in a way contrary to God." (Schriftbeweis. I, 411. 413. 414. sq.)]

Indeed, Satan, Gen. 3:5, through the serpent had promised that the protoplasts would be כאלרזים, like God; but the woman, seeing that the tree was desirable to make one wise, thus took of the fruit, v. 6. Therefore, the will of the woman more greedily desired that apparent good, promised by Satan, yet false, and not to be attained by this way. Loc. cit. v. 6, the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was desirable to the eyes. And so, inflamed by the desire of enjoying it, she took and ate. § 10. God, however, even though as a just judge He denied to the fallen protoplasts the influx necessary for preserving and propagating original righteousness, nevertheless cannot be called the cause of the fall or of original sin.

For just as all evils of punishment, according to Amos ch. 3:6, so also the lack of original righteousness, viewed as an evil of punishment, could be said to be inflicted by God. But God could certainly, by the power of His justice, take away that gift which He had given to men by the power of His goodness in the first creation, after the sin of men intervened, once men had rendered themselves unworthy of that gift and of all divine benefits. Conf. b. Meisn. Consid. Theol. Photin. cap. Y. p. 701. 702. For He severely prohibited the fall: He gave the strength to prevent sin; but He neither impelled nor determined the protoplasts to the fall, although as a universal cause He could not but concur toward the material of that act. And thus it is established that God intended neither the fall of the protoplasts, nor the original sin that followed from it, by direct or indirect intention.

Luther: "St. Augustine says: God is so good that He would not let any evil happen, unless He wanted to bring a better thing out of it. He let Adam fall; but from that came such great salvation, that God became man and our Savior, and thereby honored human nature immeasurably higher than the devil had disgraced it through the fall; as St. Ambrose sings: 'O beata culpa, quae talem meruit habere redemtorem!' Not that He loves or likes evil (otherwise He would not create good upon it, but would let the evil remain and increase), but that He, to the vexation of evil and the devil, might show His goodness all the more abundantly to His praise and honor." (Preface to Dr. U. Rhegius' Exposition of Ps. 52. An. 1541. XIV, 186. sq.) PART II. CAP. II.

§ 11.

Subjectum. All men who descend from the first parents through carnal generation are subjects of original sin, and in their own way, the protoplasts themselves. Or that which is denominated a sinner from this sin and contracts the guilt of fault and punishment. See Rom. 5:12, where it is expressly said that all men have sinned, that through sin (by which all are polluted) death has passed to all, even to those who have not sinned after the likeness of the transgression of Adam—that is, who have not imitated the actual and voluntary sin of Adam by a similar prevarication, yet have been made subject to death for the reason that they sinned in Adam and thus drew original sin from him to themselves. And already before, in chapter 3:19, the apostle had said that the whole world has been made subject to God the judge. But no one is guilty except because of sin; whence sin falls upon infants from the very beginning of their existence. Similarly, what Christ says in John 3:6: "That which (whatever) is born of the flesh is flesh," in such a way indeed that it cannot enter into the kingdom of God unless it is regenerated, is nothing other than that all and individual men, such as they are by carnal generation, are excluded from the kingdom of God and thus infected with sin from their very origin. For nothing, except sin, separates men from God and the kingdom of God. ANTITHESES.

Hofmann: "As long as the 'I' is still a becoming one, one will not be able to say, just as one does later, that it is a subject of sin; rather, it becomes so to the extent that it itself becomes, as it begins to determine itself in a conscious manner, or rather, to allow itself to be determined by innate sin." (Schriftbeweis. Ed. 2. I, 562.) Pius IX: "We declare, pronounce, and define: the doctrine which holds that the most blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instant of her conception, was, by a singular grace and privilege of Almighty God, in view of the merits of Christ Jesus, the Savior of the human race, preserved immune from all stain of original guilt, is revealed by God and therefore must be firmly and constantly believed by all the faithful. Wherefore, if any shall presume to think otherwise in their hearts than as it has been defined by us, which God forbid, let them know and furthermore understand that they are condemned by their own judgment, have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith, and have fallen away from the unity of the church." (1854, Dec. 8.)

And thus we exclude Christ the man from the society of those who are stained by original sin, namely, because He was not carnally generated. And notably, the angel says to Mary in Luke 1:35: "The holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." Similarly, in Hebrews 7:26, Christ is called ὅσιος, ἄκακος, ἀμίαντος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν. J. Ad. Osiander: "It is objected: That 'in whom all have sinned' is not to be extended to the whole human race... Christ Himself would have to be considered a sinner and it would have to be said of Him that He transgressed in Adam, because He was in him. Therefore, they are called sinners, not because they were truly made sinners..."

by the Adamic transgression, but that as sinners they became subject to death. . . I deny the consequence. 1. Either it must be said that Christ was born not by the power of the primordial blessing, and thus was not naturally in Adam when he sinned, but by the power of the subsequent promise, which presupposes the fall, Gen. 3:15. Or 2. since Christ is openly called the son of Adam in Luke 3:38, a distinction must be made between Adam as he was the natural head, from whom the whole human race was to be propagated (Acts 17:26), and as he was the moral head of the whole human race, upon whose merit or demerit the happy or unhappy lot of all posterity depended; in the former way, because Christ as a child partook of flesh and blood, Christ was the son of Adam in him as the stock and head; but in the latter way, He was not in Adam; yet it was in the latter way that the legal covenant was established with Adam, so that if he did not observe the law, he would sin in his own name and in the name of all his posterity. But Christ is not subordinated to Adam in such a way as to be a descendant from him; rather, He is set over against him from the side as the second Adam.” (Colleg. theol. system. P. III. Loc. 7. th. 9. p. 116. sq.)

Insofar as that corruption, which is in us and is called original sin, truly had a place in them after the fall. See Gen. 3:7. For that knowledge of their nakedness implies a sense of inordinate and shameful concupiscence recently contracted. Whence the lack of original righteousness can be gathered entirely. It must be admitted, however, that that corruption, strictly speaking, could not be called the sin of origin with respect to the protoplasts themselves, because it was not present in them from the origin of their nature and from the beginning of their existence. §

12. The primary subject *quo* (by which) of original sin is the soul with its faculties, intellect, will, and sensitive appetite; secondarily, however, and consequently, the members of the body are also rightly referred to here. Or that by means of which original sin pertains to man, or in which original sin formally and immediately inheres. Otherwise, it is called the proper subject, in Greek πρώτον δεκτικόν. Namely, just like the opposite, original righteousness, in the place of which, once removed, original sin succeeded. Compare this place with § 4, 5, 6. And *Ausführliche Erklärung* [Detailed Explanation], L. VII. Q. 40. p. 312. sqq.

Latin:

Nam Dominus Deus quidem praeceperat homini, dicendo: Ex arbore boni et mali non comedes, Gen. 2, 17.; sed cap. S, 6. et 11. scribitur: Mulier cepit de fructu arboris illius et comedit, et dedit etiam viro suo secum, et comedit. Vid. Gen. 3, 3. et seqq. usque ad 6., ubi docemur, Evam primum quidem recordatam fuisse legis divinae adjectaeque comminationis, mox autem serpenti illi ένεργυυμένω, alia docenti v. g.: Non moriemini, aperientur oculi vestri etc., auscultasse et credidisse; virum verop aruisse voci uxoris, v. 7., seu blandam vocem uxoris seductae praetu-lisse interdicto divino Deique auctoritatem contemsisse.

ANTITHESIS. Hofmannus: ,,Die biblische Erzählung von der Sünde des Erstgeschaffenen lehrt uns, dass es ein Gegenstand der körperlichen Welt gewesen, auf welchen sich das Begehren und Thun desselben sündhaft gerichtet hat. Nicht hat sich sein Wille dem Willen Gottes in der Art feindlich entgegengesetzt, dass er, was Gott wollte, darum, weil es Gott wollte, nicht wollte, oder so, dass er wissentlich das gerade Gegentheil von dem wollte, was Gott wollte. . . Denn wenn man von dem absieht, was die Sünde wird, indem sie sich der Gnade Gottes entgegensetzt, so ist sie wesentlich Verlangen, die Welt so zu besitzen, wie Gott sie dem Menschen überhaupt oder diesem Menschen insbesondere nicht zu besitzen gegeben hat, Verlangen nach Beseitigung der Schranke seines Weltbesitzes. Mit Einem Worte, sie ist επιθυμία. . . Es ist recht gesagt, dass am umfassendsten die gesammte Lebensrichtung, welche aus der ersten Sünde hervorgegangen ist, mit dem Namen Selbstsucht bezeichnet wird; aber minder richtig ist es, Selbstsucht die Wurzel der Sünde zu nennen, aus welcher auch die erste Sünde hervorgegangen sei. Weder die Erzählung vom Sündenfalle, noch die oben besprochene paulinische Stelle stimmen hiezu: beide lassen inne werden, mit wie gutem Hechte die Sünde auch als Liebe des Geschöpf

DE PECCATO OKIGINIS.

lichen anstatt des Schöpfers, oder als Sinnlichkeit benannt worden ist. Nicht sich zu wollen im Widerspruche gegen Gott, war der Schrift zufolge der menschlichen Sünde Anfang, und ist fortwährend der Anfang ihrer Bethätigung, sondern die Welt für sich zu wollen im Widerspruch gegen Gott; und die verführende Zusage der Schlange, dass sie Gott gleich Gut und Schlimm, also was es um diesen Gegensatz sei, erkennen werden, ändert daran nichts, indem sie den Menschen nicht nach Selbstvergötteruag, sondern nach gottgleicher Welterkenntniss und Weltbeherrschung verlangend macht. Dies ist aber nicht die Selbstsucht eines sich wider Gott und das, was Gottes ist, setzenden,' sondern die eines nach Gottgeschaffenem widergöttlich begehrenden Ich.“ (Schriftbeweis. I, 411. 413. 414. sq.) Nempe satanas Gen. 3, 5. per serpentem promiserat, fore, ut sint protoplasti כאלרזים, sicut Deus; mulier autem videns, quod arbor sit concupiscibilis ad intelligendum, ita cepit de fructu, v. 6. Itaque voluntas mulieris bonum illud apparens, a satana promissum, falsum tamen, neque hac via consequendum avidius appetiit. Loc. cit. v. 6. vidit mulier, quod bona arbor ad cibum, et quod desiderabilis esset oculis. Itaque desiderio fruendi accensa cepit et comedit.§ 10.

Deus autem, etiamsi ut justus judex denegaverit lapsis protoplastis influxum ad conservandam et propagandam justitiam originalem necessarium,a tamen causa lapsus aut peccati originalis dici non potest.b Sicut enim omnia mala poenae, juxta Amosi cap. 3,6., ita et carentia justitiae originalis, tanquam malum poenae spectata, posset dici a Deo inflicta. Potuit autem profecto Deus donum illud, quod vi bonitatis suae in prima creatione hominibus dederat, intercedente postea delicto hominum, ex vi justitiae vindicativae, auferre, postquam homines dono illo ac beneficiis divinis omnibus indignos se reddiderunt. Conf. b. Meisn. Consid. Theol. Photin. cap. Y. p. 701.

702. Prohibuit enim severe lapsum: dedit vires ad praecavendum peccatum; non autem vel impulit vel determinavit protoplastos ad lapsum, licet ut causa universalis ad materiale actus illius non posset non concurrere. Et sic constat, Deum neque lapsum protoplastorum, nec peccatum originis hinc secutum intentione directa vel indirecta intendisse.Lutherus: ״St. Augustinus spricht: So gut ist Gott, dass er kein Böses liesse geschehen, wo er nicht ein Besseres daraus machen wollte. Adam hat er lassen fallen; aber daraus ist kommen solch gross Heil, dass Gott ist Mensch und unser Heiland worden, und hat damit die menschliche Natur unmässlich höher geehret, weder sie der Teufel durch den Fall geschändet hatte; wie St. Ambrosius singet: ,0 beata culpa, quae talem meruit habere redemtorem! ‘ Nicht, dass er das Böse lieb oder gerne habe (sonst würde er das Gute nicht darauf schaffen, sondern das Böse also lassen bleiben und zunehmen), sondern dass er, zu Verdruss dem Bösen und dem Teufel, seine Güte desto reichlicher erzeige zu seinem Lob und Ehren.“ (Vorr. auf Dr. U Rhegii Ausl, über den 52. Ps. An. 1541. XIV, 186. sq.) PART. II. CAP. II.

§ 11.

Subjectum Quod a peccati originis sunt omnes homines b ex primis parentibus per carnalem generationem c descendentes, et suo modo ipsi protoplasti.d Sive id, quod ab hoc peccato denominatur peccator et culpae ac poenae reatum contrahit. Vid. jRom. 5, 12., ubi expresse dicitur, homines omnes peccasse, per peccatum (quo omnes polluuntur) mortem pervasisse ad omnes, etiam illos, qui non peccarunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adami, seu, qui peccatum Adami actuale et voluntarium simili praevaricatione imitati non sunt, attamen morti obnoxii facti ideo, quod in Adamo peccassmt adeoque peccatum originale ex ipso ad se traherent. Ac jam antea cap. 3, 19. dixerat apostolus, totum mundum factum esse obnoxium Deo judici. Nemo autem reus est, nisi ob peccatum; unde et in infantes a primo sui initio cadit peccatum. Similiter, quod Christus dicit Joh. 3, 6.: Quod (quicquid) natum est de carne, caro est, ita quidem, ut non possit ingredi in regnum Dei, nisi regeneretur, nihil aliud est, quam quod homines omnes et singuli, quales per carnalem generationem sunt, exclusi sint a regno Dei adeoque peccato inde a sua origine infecti. Neque enim quicquam, nisi peccatum, separat homines a Deo et regno Dei.ANTITHESES.

Hofmannus: ,,So lange das Ich noch ein werdendes ist, wird man nicht eben so, wie nachher, sagen können, dass es Subject der Sünde sei, sondern das wird es in dem Masse, als es selbst wird, als es sich bewusster Weise selbst zu bestimmen, oder vielmehr durch die angeborne Sünde sich bestimmen zu lassen anfängt.“ (Schriftbeweis. Ed. 2. I, 5G2.) Pius IX.: ,,Declaramus, pronuntiamus et definimus: doctrinam, quae tenet, beatissimam virginem Mariam in primo instanti suae conceptionis fuisse singulari omnipotentis Dei gratia et privilegio, intuitu meritorum Christi Jesu, Salvatoris humani generis, ab omni originalis culpae labe praeservatam immunem, esse a Deo revelatam atque iccirco ab omnibus fidelibus firmiter constanterque credendam. Quapropter si qui secus, ac a nobis definitum est, quod Deus avertat, praesumserint corde sentire, ii noverint ac porro sciant, se proprio judicio condemnatos, naufragium circa fidem passos esse et ab unitate ecclesiae defecisse.“ (1854. d. 8. Decbr.)

Atque ita Christum hominem excludimus a societate eorum, qui peccato originali maculantur, nempe quia ille carnaliter genitus non fuit. Et notanter angelus ad Mariam dicit Luc. 1, 35.: Sanctum, quod ex te nascetur, Filius Dei vocabitur. Similiter ad Ebr. 7, 26. Christus appellatur υσίος, αχαχος, αμίαντος, χεχωρισμένος άπυ των Αμαρτωλών.J. Ad. Osiander: ,,Excipitur: Illud,in quo omnes peccarunt‘ non est extendendum ad totum genus humanum. . . Ipse Christus censendus esset peccator et de eo dicendum, deliquisse in Adamo, quia in eo fuerit. Peccatores itaque dicuntur, non quod vere peccatores effecti

sint transgressione Adamitica, sed quod tanquam peccatores morti facti fuerint obnoxii. . . Nego consequentiam. 1. Aut dicendum est, Christum genitum esse non vi primaevae benedictionis, adeoque naturaliter non fuisse in Adamo, cum peccaret, sed vi subsequentis promissionis, quae lapsum praesupponit, Gen. 3, 15. Vel 2. cum Christus aperte dicatur filius Adami Lue. 3, 38., distinguendum est inter Adamum, ut fuit caput naturale, ex quo proseminandum erat totum genus humanum Act. 17, 26., et ut fuit caput totius humani generis morale, ex cujus merito vel demerito pendebat sors omnium posterorum vel felix, vel infausta; pnori modo, quia Christus ut pueri participavit carnem et sanguinem, Christus fuit filius Adami in ipso, ut stirpe et capite; posteriori autem modo non fuit in Adamo; at posteriori modo pactum legale constitutum est cum Adamo, ut, si legem non observaret, suo et totius posteritatis nomine peccaret. Sic autem Christus non subordinatur Adamo, ut descendens ex ipso; sed e latere opponitur tanquam secundus Adam.“ (Colleg. theol.system. P. III. Loc. 7. th. 9. p. 116. sq.)

Quatenus corruptio illa, quae in nobis est et peccatum originale dicitur, revera in illis post lapsum locum habuit. Vid. Gen. 3, 7. Cognitio enim illa nuditatis suae importat sensum inordinatae et ignominiosae concupiscentiae recens contractae. Unde carentia justitiae originalis omnino colligi potest. Fatendum autem, quod corruptio illa proprie loquendo originis peccatum, respectu ipsorum protoplastorum, dici non potuerit, quia ab origine naturae ipsorum, atque ab initio existendi, illis non adfuit.§

12. Subjectum Quo peccati originalis primarium a est anima cum suis facultatibus,b intellectu, voluntate et appetitu sensitivo; secundario tamen et consequenter etiam c membra corporis huc recte referuntur. Sive id, quo mediante peccatum originis homini competit, aut cui formaliter et immediate inest peccatum originis. Alias subjectum proprium, Graece πρώτον δεκτικόν dicitur. Nempe sicut opposita justitia originalis, in cujus ablatae locum successit peccatum originale. Confer hoc loco § 4. 5. 6. Et Ausfuhrl. Erklär. L. VII. Q. 40. p. 312. sqq.


### On Original Sin: Thus also the blessed Balduinus, Comm

Thus also the blessed Balduinus, Comm. in Ep. ad Ephes. cap. 4. P. II. Aphor. 7. p. m. 923: The subject, he says, of original sin is indeed the whole man with all his powers: yet its primary seat is the sense of the mind, which the apostle also commands to be renewed first, verse 23. For the mind dominates the whole body, from whose corrupt dominion the corruption of the remaining parts in man easily follows. Similarly, the blessed H. Eckardus, Tom. II. Disp. Giess. Dis. XII. § 90. p. 435, when he had said that the whole man according to his whole self, and the whole of himself, that is, both the body and soul of individual men, is the proximate subject (he understands the subject *quo*) of original sin, to the objection of some that the body, because it is a brute thing, is not capable of sin and therefore cannot be a subject, he says that this single remark of a certain philosopher easily satisfies those who object in this way; namely, that sin cannot reside in the body by itself, but only insofar as it has communion with the soul. The body, he says, does not... PART II. CHAP. II.

viewed in itself, is guilty of sin, but constitutes the other part of human nature. Again, in § 94, p. 438, intending to show that the soul is the primary subject of original sin, he argues as follows: That which was the subject of original righteousness is also the subject of original unrighteousness. For a habit and its opposite privation refer to the same subject. But not only the body, but principally the soul was the subject of original righteousness. For the whole man was indeed created in the image and likeness of God, yet the soul held the chief parts of this, being most illustrious in the light of knowledge, wisdom, and science, and in the zeal for holiness and the love of truth. Therefore.

In the same way, the blessed Cundisius, in his Notes to Comp. Hutt. Loc. VIII. Q. VI. § 3. p. 579, and the blessed Joh. Frieder. Koenig, Comp. Theol. Posit. II. § 84, 85, p. 78, 79, have expressly taught that the πρῶτον δεκτικόν, or the primary subject of original sin, is the rational soul, and the secondary is the animated body. Clearly, just as in the state of integrity the body became a participant in original righteousness through this, that it served the soul by way of an instrument for works of holiness and righteousness, so also the sin of origin diffuses itself to the members of the body, as weapons of unrighteousness.

Thus the blessed Cundisius, l. c.: The secondary subject of O. S., he says, is the body. Whence Dr. Paul, Rom. 7:19, says: In my flesh dwells no good thing. Hence it is that the members of an impure man are members of a harlot, 1 Cor. 6:15. Thus, eyes full of adultery are attributed to sinners, 2 Pet. 2:14, and in Rom. 3:13, 14, 15, the mouth, lips, throat, feet, and eyes are named, all of which are instruments of that original wickedness.

But that, just as in the state of integrity, impassibility and immortality belonged to the bodies of the protoplasts, so now a certain morbid quality appears in our bodies, through which they themselves have become subject to various diseases, calamities, and death itself, this does not pertain so much to the essence of the sin of origin formally, as it follows it as its effect. Just as the blessed Cundisius, l. c. Q. VII. p. 180, reckons the diseases of the body and temporal death among those effects of original sin which are punishments only, not punishments and sins at the same time.

Cf. the blessed Gerhard, Disp. Isag. XXV. cap. VIII. § 3. p. 896. § 13. The effects of original sin are various evils: on the part of the soul, indeed, the defect of free will in spiritual matters and its infirmity in natural matters, actual sins, many in species and number, the privation of grace and the opposite wrath of God; on the part of the body, diseases and other miseries and temporal death itself; fin ally, also eternal death or damnation.

Or the consequent, which that sin, as an evil of fault, by the just judgment of God, by way of punishment or as a thing merited—that which man deserved—follows, can certainly follow by the force of divine justice. Or that man, infected with original sin, lacks the powers to act rightly concerning the spiritual good, just as he possesses the powers of acting in opposition to it. For thus in the present business the term free will is accepted, so that it is understood concerning the requirements both on the part of the intellect and on the part of the will

to exercise acts that are spiritually good, or which are and rightly behave themselves regarding matters that are merely spiritual, i.e., matters removed from the senses and the light of reason, and which lie hidden in God, who is spirit (although they are also exhibited by Him through revelation), or even regarding matters subject to reason in their own way, but which must be treated under a certain spiritual aspect.

Thus, we deny that to a man infected with original sin, before…an infected by original sin, before he is reborn, there exist powers on the part of the intellect or the will such that, apart from the special grace of the Holy Spirit and the bestowal of new and supernatural powers, the will can determine itself toward the good in spiritual matters.

Indeed, the intellect itself is so corrupted and, as it were, blind, that it cannot represent or commend spiritual goods to the will to be embraced as is fitting.

And although the doctrine of faith is sufficiently and clearly proposed in the Word and presented to the intellect, so that nothing is lacking for it to be apprehended, yet the intellect, by its own powers, cannot provide an unmoved assent of true faith.

Therefore, since it is otherwise said that liberty is radically in the intellect, here you would say that the vice is in the root, obstructing liberty in such matters and excluding it.

The will, however, not only—because in itself it is a blind power and cannot be moved toward those things which the intellect does not represent as they are and as one ought to tend toward them—but it is also itself more alien to spiritual goods, and more prone to carnal, temporal, vain, and perishable things.

Nor can it, by its own powers, be moved by an efficacious act toward spiritual goods that are distinctly proposed and apprehended by the intellect, but it subsists only in the omission of the act, and does not reach, nor can it reach, the exercise of a congruent act (and thus it is not free with the liberty of exercise or contradiction), or it even turns away from those things which it ought to pursue, and thus exercises a different and contrary act regarding these objects than that which ought to have been done. (

And thus it shows itself not to be free with the liberty of specification or contrariety.)

Compare the blessed Musaeus’s Disputation on Free Will, held in the year 1642 under the presidency of the blessed Dilherr, which exists in the *Disputationes Dilherrianae*, Vol. II, no. XVI, p. 442 sqq.

Luther: "Free will after sin is a thing of title only, and while it does what is in itself, it sins mortally." (Proposition 13, Heidelberg, a. 1518. See Luther’s Latin works pertaining to the history of the Reformation, ed. H. Schmidt. Frankfurt, 1865. Vol. I, 388.)

Gerhard: "There are two faculties of the rational soul: the mind and the will; the former performs its office by knowing, discerning, consulting, and judging; the latter by choosing and rejecting; from the συνδρομή and concurrence of both powers is born that which is commonly called free will, which is the faculty of the mind and the will; so that 'arbitrium' (judgment) pertains to the mind, and 'liberum' (free) to the will." (L. de lib. arbitr. § 2.)

The same: "Liberty is assigned to the will, first, with respect to the mode of acting, because it is such that the will, insofar as it is such, acts freely, that is, it is not compelled or violently snatched by an external motion, nor does it act solely from natural instinct, but by its own spontaneity or internal principle of motion it either embraces or rejects something. In this sense, 'free' and 'voluntary' are synonyms, and to call the will not free is the same as if one were to say 'hot without heat.' This is called liberty from coaction, by which it comes to pass that the will cannot be compelled to do something against its inclination. Likewise, liberty from necessity, insofar as necessity is taken for coaction and violence (but not for immutability)... This liberty, since it is a natural and essential property implanted in the will by God, was not lost through the fall. The substance of man did not perish; PART II. CHAP. II.

therefore neither the rational soul; therefore neither the will; therefore neither the essential freedom of the will. The will is an essential power of the soul, and the soul is nothing other than these very essential powers or faculties; consequently, while the soul remains, its essential powers, the intellect and the will, also remain. Conversely, the power of willing freely and without coercion is essential to the will; therefore, while the will remains, that power also remains. . .

In this sense and in this respect, we firmly believe and profess with a resonant voice that free choice remained in man even after the fall; so much so that we say with Augustine (Hypogn. 3): "He who denies free choice is not a Catholic." Away, therefore, with the tragic accusations leveled against our churches by Bellarmine in the preface to his books on free choice, as if we were abolishing the freedom of choice, violating nature itself, and professing ourselves to be not like beasts, but altogether beasts devoid of reason. (L. c. § 4—7. 8)

The same: "The whole question concerns freedom with respect to the object with which the will is occupied, that is, the freedom of rectitude: whether man after the fall is still endowed with that δυνάμει [power] of being equally disposed toward good and evil. . .

For we confess that some freedom has remained regarding works that are just by moral, political, and economic justice, which pertain to the lower hemisphere, as Dr. Luther speaks. A man not yet regenerate can certainly govern his external locomotion in some way; he can command his external members by the dictate of right reason; he can perform civil justice in some manner and avoid more serious external sins that conflict with external pedagogy; nay, he can even hear and meditate upon the Word of God externally; meanwhile, however, that freedom is frequently undermined by both external and internal impediments. . .

The whole question, therefore, is about the spiritually good object, about works that are just by spiritual justice and which pertain to the upper hemisphere, about spiritually good motions, whether man can of himself and his own powers initiate those spiritual motions, accept offered grace, or perform anything pleasing to God; which we deny διαρρήδην [expressly]. . .

Latin:

Sic autem etiam b. Balduinus Comm. in Ep. ad Ephes. cap. 4. P. II· Aphor. 7. p. m. 923.: Subjectum, ait, peccati originalis est quidem totus homo cum omnibus suis viribus: prir maria tamen ejus sedes est sensus mentis, quem etiam inprimis renovari jubet apostolus, vers. 23. Mens enim dominatur toti corpori, ex cujus corrupto dominio facile etiam sequitur corruptio reliquarum in homine partium. Similiter b. H. Eckardus, Tom. II. Disp. Giess. Dis. XII. §90. p. 435., cum dixisset, totum hominem secundum totum se, et totum sui, hoc est, singularum hominum tum corpus, tum animam esse subjectum proximum (intelligit subjectum Quo) peccati originalis, ad objectionem quorundam, quod corpus, quia sit res bruta, non sit peccati capax ideoque etiam subjectum esse non possit, illis, qui sic objiciunt, hoc unicum philosophi cujusdam facile satisfacere ait; nimirum, peccatum in corpore per se residere non potest, sed quatenus cum anima communionem habet. Corpus, inquit, non PART. H. CAP. II.

per se spectatum peccati reum est, sed alteram naturae humanae partem constituens. Rursus § 94. p. 438. ostensurus, animam esse subjectum primarium peccati originalis, sic argumentatur: Quod fuit subjectum originalis justitiae, idem etiam est subjectum originalis injustitiae. Habitus enim eique opposita privatio ad idem se referunt subjectum. At non corpus tantum, sed principaliter anima fuit originalis justitiae subjectum. Totus quippe homo erat ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei conditus, cujus tamen praecipuas partes tenebat anima, luce cognitionis, sapientiae et scientiae, studioque sanctitatis et amore veritatis maxime illustris. Ergo.

Eodem modo b. Cundisius Not. ad Comp. Hutt. Loc. VIII. Q. VI. § 3. p. 579. et b. Joh. Frieder. Koenig, Comp. Theol. Posit. II. § 84. 85. p. 78. 79. expresse docuerunt, ■πρώτον δεχτιχυν sive subjectum primarium peccati originalis esse animam rationalem, secundarium esse corpus animatum. Videlicet, quemadmodum in statu integritatis corpus per hoc fiebat particeps justitiae originalis, quod per modum instrumenti serviebat animae ad sanctitatis et justitiae opera, ita quoque peccatum originis ad membra corporis, tanquam arma injustitiae, se diffundit.

Sic b. Gundisius 1. c.: Subjectum P. 0. secundarium, ait, est corpus. Unde D. Paulus Rom. 7, 19. ait: In carne mea non habitat bonum. Inde est, quod membra impuri hominis membra scorti, 1 Cor. 6,15. Sic peccatoribus tribuuntur oculi pleni adulterii 2 Petr. 2, 14. et Rom. 3, 13. 14. 15. nominantur os, labia, guttur, pedes, oculi, quae omnia sunt instrumenta nequitiae illius originalis.

Quod autem, sicut in statu integritatis, impassibilitas atque immortalitas corporibus protoplastorum competierunt, ita nunc morbida quaedam qualitas in corporibus nostris apparet, per quam ipsa variis morbis et calamitatibus mortique ipsi facta sunt obnoxia, id non tam ad essentiam ipsius peccati originis formaliter pertinet, quam consequitur illud, tanquam ejus effectus. Prout etiam b. Gundisius 1. c. Q. VII. p. 180. morbos corporis et mortem temporalem inter eos effectus peccati originalis recenset, qui sint poenae tantum, non poenae et peccata simul.

Conf. b. Gerhard. Disp. Isag. XXV. cap. VIII. § 3. p. 896. § 13. Effectus a peccati originalis sunt mala varia: ex parte animae quidem defectus liberi arbitrii b in spiritualibus et infirmitas ejus c in naturalibus, peccata d actualia, specie et numero e multa, privatio gratiae et opposita ira f Dei; ex parte corporis morbi g et aerumnae aliae h ipsaque mors i temporalis; denique et mors seu damnatio k aeterna.

Seu consequens, quod peccatum illud, velut malum culpae, justo Dei judicio, per modum poenae aut tanquam res merita id, quo homo merebatur, sequitur, sequi certe vi justitiae divinae potest. Seu quod homo, peccato originali infectus, caret viribus ad recte agendum circa bonum spirituale, uti pollet viribus agendi oppositum ejus. Sic enim in praesenti negotio accipitur vox liberi arbitrii, ut intelligatur de requisitis cum ex parte intellectus, tum ex parte

voluntatis, ad exercendos actus spiritualiter bonos, seu qui sunt et recte se habent circa res mere spirituales, i. e., res a sensibus et lumine rationis remotas, quaeque in Deo, qui spiritus est, latent (quamvis etiam ab eo per revelationem exhibeantur), aut etiam circa res rationi suo modo subjectas, sed sub spirituali quadam ratione tractandas.

Sic negamus, homini peccato originali infecto, antequam renascatur, inesse vires ex parte intellectus aut voluntatis, ut citra specialem Spiritus S. gratiam novarumque et supernaturalium virium collationem voluntas ad bonum in rebus spiritualibus sese determinare possit.

Nimirum intellectus ipse ita est corruptus et quasi coecus, ut voluntati bona spiritualia amplectenda non ita, ut par est, repraesentare aut commendare possit.

Et quamvis doctrina fidei sufficienter ac perspicue in verbo proposita intellectui objiciatur, ut nihil desit, quo minus apprehendi queat, tamen intellectus ex suis viribus nequit immotum ac verae fidei assensum praebere.

Itaque cum alias dicatur, libertatem esse radicaliter in intellectu, hic vitium in radice esse dixeris, obstans libertati in talibus, eamque excludens.
