Voluntas autem non solum, quod in se potentia coeca est atque in ea, quae intellectus, qualia sunt, et prout in ea tendendum est, non repraesentat, ferri non potest, verum etiam ipsa alienior est a bonis spiritualibus, ad carnalia, temporalia, vana et caduca pronior.

Neque adeo suis viribus in bona spiritualia distincte proposita et ab intellectu apprehensa, actu efficaci ferri potest, sed in omissione actus tantum subsistit, ad exercitium actus congrui non pertingit, nec pertingere potest (et sic non est libera libertate exercitii seu contradictionis), vel etiam aversatur, quae prosequi debebat, adeoque alium et contrarium actum circa haec objecta exercet, quam eum, quem fieri oportebat. (

Atque ita prodit, se non esse liberam libertate spedficationis seu contrarietatis.)

Confer b. Musaei Disp. de Lib. Arbitrio A. 1642. sub praesidio b. Dilherri habitam, quae extat in Disputationibus DilherriaDis Tom. II. n. XVI. p. 442. sqq.

Lutherus: ״Liberum arbitrium post peccatum res est de solo titulo, et dum facit, quod in se est, peccat mortaliter.“ (Propositio 13. Heidelbergens, a. 1518. Vid. Luth. opp. lat. ad reform. hist. pert. Cur. H. Schmidt. Francof. 1865. Vol. I, 388.)

Gerhardus: ״Animae rationalis duae facultates sunt: Mens et voluntas; illa cognoscendo, discernendo, consultando, judicando, haec eligendo et repudiando suum expedit officium; ex utriusque potentiae συνδρομή et concursu nascitur id, quod vulgo vocatur liberum arbitrium, quod mentis et voluntatis facultas est; ita ut arbitrium pertineat ad mentem, liberum ad voluntatem.“ (L. de lib. arbitr. § 2.)

Idem: ,,Libertas assignatur arbitrio, primo, habito respectu ad modum agendi, quia talis est, ut voluntas, quatenus talis, libere agat, hoc est, non cogatur aut violenter rapiatur externo motu, nec ex naturali instinctu solum agat, sed sponte sua seu interno motus principio aliquid vel amplectatur vel rejiciat. Hoc sensu liberum et voluntarium sunt synonyma, et voluntatem non liberam dicere est perinde, ac si quis dicere velit calidum absque calore. Vocatur haec libertas a coactione, qua fit, ut non possit voluntas cogi ad faciendum aliquid contra suam inclinationem. Item libertas a necessitate, quatenus necessitas pro coactione et violentia accipitur (non autem pro immutabilitate). . . Haec libertas, cum sit naturalis atque essentialis a Deo indita voluntati proprietas, per lapsum non est amissa. Substantia hominis non periit; PART. II. CAP. II.

ergo nec anima rationalis; ergo nec voluntas; ergo nec libertas voluntatis essentialis. Voluntas est potentia animae essentialis et anima nihil aliud est, quam ipsae potentiae seu facultates essentiales, proinde manente anima potentiae etiam ejus essentiales, intellectus et voluntas, manent. Vicissim vis libere et absque coactione volendi est voluntati essentialis; manente ergo voluntate, etiam vis illa manet. . .

Hoc sensu et hoc respectu Uberum in homine arbitrium etiam post lapsum mansisse, firmiter credimus et sonora voce profitemur; adeo ut cum Augustino dicamus Hypogn. 3.: ,Eum, qui neget liberum arbitrium, non esse catholicum.‘ Apage igitur tragicas accusationes ecclesiis nostris a Bellarmino in praefat. libror, de lib. artk intentatas, quasi arbitrii libertatem tollamus, ipsam naturam tollamus, ipsam naturam violemus et nos ipsos non beluarum similes, sed omnino beluas rationis ׳expertes profiteamur.“ (L. c. § 4—7. 8)

Idem: ״Tota quaestio est de libertate ratione objecti, circa quod voluntas occupata est, hoc est, de libertate rectitudinis: an δυνάμει illa ad bonum et malum aequaliter se habente homo post lapsum adhuc sit instructus. ..

Fatemur enim, aliquid libertatis remansisse quoad opera, quae justa sunt justitia morali, politica et oeconomica, quae ad inferius hemisphaerium pertinent, ut loquitur Dr. Lutherus. Potest utique homo nondum renatus locomotivam externam utcunque regere; potest externis membris dictamine rectae rationis imperare; potest justitiam civilem aliquo modo praestare et peccata externa graviora, cum paedagogia externa pugnantia, vitare; quin imo potest etiam verbum Dei exterius audire, meditari; interim tamen libertas illa tum externis tum internis impedimentis saepius labefactatur. . .

Tota igitur quaestio est de objecto spiritualiter bono, de operibus, quae justa sunt justitia spirituali, quaeque ad superius hemisphaerium pertinent, de motibus spiritualiter bonis, an hotno ex se et suis viribus spirituales illos motus inchoare, oblatam gratiam acceptare, aliqua Deo grata praestare possit; quod διαρρήδην negamus. . .


### On Original Sin: Nor is the question about the natural actions of the soul, such as hearing,…

Nor is the question about the natural actions of the soul, such as hearing, reading, meditating, which in their own way can be called spiritual καταχρηστικῶς [improperly/catachrestically], because they proceed from the soul, which is a spiritual essence; for we acknowledge in these a certain freedom of choice: a man can read, he can not read; he can hear, he can turn away his ears; but the whole question is about motions properly called spiritual, such as: to know God rightly, to hear and read the Word of God with fruit." (L. c. § 32.)

Quenstedtius: "The upper hemisphere in its scope comprises things that are merely spiritual or internally sacred. . . To this hemisphere we also refer the going to the temple for the sake of receiving instruction from the preached Word, reading and hearing the Word of God with the intention of profiting, and being held by a desire for instruction from the Word; all of which are works of prevenient and incipient grace." (L. c. P. II. c. 3. s. 1. th. 29. 30. f. 1888. sq.)

The same: "Bellarmin’s argument is as follows: 'If man does not possess free choice for works of piety and even for conversion to God itself, all commands, exhortations, incitements, etc., to works of piety and conversion will be in vain.'

I answer: 1. These testimonies of Scripture—Zech. 1:2: 'Turn to me'; Joel 2:12: 'Turn to me with all your heart'; Deut. 10:16: 'Circumcise the foreskin of your heart'; Ezek. 18:31: 'Make yourselves a new heart'; Matt. 11:28: 'Come to me,' etc.—indeed show what our duty is, but not what our powers are; that is, they signify not what men can do in their own conversion, but what God demands of them under the category of debt. They urge our duty, not our strength and faculty. Precepts are not the measure of our powers, but the rule of duty. We do not learn in the law what we can do, but what we once could do. . . 3.

These testimonies urge God’s right, i.e., what God can rightfully demand from His debtors. For God..."

A creditor’s right to his indebted debtor does not perish, even if the latter is unable to pay. God justly demands from man through the Law what man unjustly lost through the fall of Adam. By commanding, ordering, and exhorting, God teaches what man ought to do, what he was once able to do, and from what state he has fallen.

4. God often commands those things which He wills to effect in us, and thus His mandates are not only imperative—what ought to be done—but at the same time they are operative and an effective medium of God, by which God effects what He commands. It is not in vain that one in shackles is commanded to run, if by that very command his shackles are loosened. It is not in vain that the blind man is commanded to see, if by those very words with which this is commanded, the eyes of the blind are opened. For the words of God effect in us what they command to be effected by us. God commands what He wills, but He also gives what He commands. And it is familiar to Scripture to say that those things are done by us which God does through us. For He joins the efficacy of the Holy Spirit to His Word; God often commands those things which He wills to effect in us, and He crowns and rewards His own works in us. Deut. 10:16, God says: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart," but in 30:6, it is declared who accomplishes this: "The Lord your God will circumcise your hearts." It is indeed said in Ez. 18:31: "Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit," but lest anyone think this is of our own free will, God Himself says in the same prophet, 36:26: "I will take away the heart of stone."

5. These exhortations themselves are not merely legal without grace, but evangelical, effective, persuasive, and drawing. When the Lord invites and says, "Come to me," etc., by inviting He admonishes, stirs up, and confers grace so that we may be able to come.

6. When God enjoins and commands conversion, He wills that men should not maliciously resist it. . .

7. Although conversion itself is not in our power, the external use of the means is, in a certain way, in our power. For man can frequent the temple and hear the external preaching of the Word, through which God wills to be effective." (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 2013. sq.)

The same: "From a precept to the ability of the natural will [N. V. C.], or from the command of God to human ability, from duty to obedience, the argumentation is invalid; this is a theological rule. Thus God says to Abraham in Gen. 15:5: 'Look toward heaven and count the stars, are you able to count them?' (This is not the sense of the Hebrew text), by which command the impossibility, rather than the possibility, of counting the stars is not obscurely hinted at. Thus in Is. 42:18 it is said: 'Hear, you deaf; and look, you blind, that you may see'; whether you understand this as natural or spiritual deafness and blindness, an impossible thing is nevertheless commanded.

Thus Christ commands the dead daughter of Jairus and says: 'Little girl, arise!' Mark 5:41, Luke 8:54. To Lazarus, buried and already stinking: 'Lazarus, come out!' John 11:43, and Peter said to the deceased disciple: 'Tabitha, arise!' Acts 9:40. Who would gather from this either that those corpses had the faculty of rising and vivifying themselves, or that Christ and Peter addressed them in vain or commanded impossible things?

It is not tyrannical to command impossible things and to bind one to those things which are not in our power. A creditor justly demands a debt from a debtor who has nothing, Matt. 18:28, and God, through the Law and legal precepts, most justly demands from men, His debtors, that which they are bound to do. The dead were not commanded by Christ and Peter to arise in vain, because with those commands the powers to arise were simultaneously conferred. Such addressings, exhortations, and invitations of God, therefore, are not in vain, because they are an effective organ of the Holy Spirit and, as it were, a rousing-tool, by which He breathes and confers new powers upon the man himself who is dead in sins, and wills to work conversion in him through His grace, provided he himself does not contumaciously resist or place obstacles in the way of His operation." (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 2014.)

J. Ad. Osiander: "Just as a ship is said to turn itself, not actively, but neutrally, because it is turned by the sailor; so conversion is indeed attributed to man, yet it does not truly belong to man, but is the action of God alone." (Colleg. th. V, 63.)

PART II. CHAP. II. ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: A. Of those sinning by excess: 1. Of Pelagius and the Pelagians. . .; for among the chief dogmas of Pelagius and the Pelagians were these: That man has no need of the grace of God, but that he can, by the proper powers of free will, believe the Gospel and perform all things necessary for salvation; that a man naturally born and not yet converted to God can, by free will alone, avoid all sins, conquer and overcome the most serious temptations, love God, and perfectly fulfill the law of God. . .

2. Of the Semipelagians. . ., (who) asserted. . ., that something must be left to free will; that preventing grace is not always necessary for producing spiritual acts. . . Another error was concerning the συνεργεία of man with God, not from a power superadded to nature, but from natural power. . .

3. Of the Scholastics, who follow in the footsteps of Pelagius; for they contend: that man, from his own natural powers, can know the true and highest good, dispose and prepare himself for grace, apply himself, avoid any mortal sin, keep the commandments as to the substance of the acts, and love God above all things, etc. . .

4. Of the Papists, especially the Jesuits. For thus they assert in the Council of Trent, sess. VI, c. 1: 'Free will (in unregenerate men) is by no means extinguished, though attenuated and inclined in its powers.' In chap. 5 of the same session, they strike with anathema those who think otherwise. They maintain, however, that the free will of man, though attenuated and inclined in its powers, is moved and excited by God in conversion, and that, once moved and excited, it cooperates by assenting to God who excites and calls, in that it disposes and prepares itself to obtain the grace of justification, as canon 4 of that session states. . .

5. Of the Socinians, who teach a. in general, that an unregenerate man, when divine external revelation is added, can do and perform in spiritual matters those things which pertain to the internal assent to the divine word, conversion to God, acknowledgment, and faith. . . b. Specifically, they teach concerning the intellect of the unregenerate man that it possesses such a perfection of powers that, if the divine things contained in the Gospel are proposed to it, it can, without the special aid of the Holy Spirit, perceive them and approve them with assent. . .

6. Of the Arminians, as they are not far from the Pelagian heresy. . . For they attribute to divine grace not an ολικήν, but only a μερικήν ενέργειαν in the converting of man, and they ascribe the cause of faith partly to the grace of God in Christ, and partly to man and his free will. . .

9. Of the Lutheran Synergists, who posit some συνεργεία or cooperation of human powers with grace in the work of conversion. . .

Philipp Melanchthon sowed the seeds of this synergistic error quite fruitfully in his various writings and books. For although in the prototype of Art. 18 of the Augsburg Confession, the Pelagianism concerning the powers of nature in spiritual matters and the Semipelagianism concerning the συνεργεία of the human will were openly condemned, he writes explicitly in the same article of the changed and adulterated Augsburg Confession: 'We are helped by the Holy Spirit in effecting spiritual righteousness in us.' So also in the earlier German edition of the Apology of the A.C., it is read: 'Free will and intellect can do nothing in spiritual matters,' and a little later: 'To be regenerated within in the heart, to be renewed in mind and senses, that the Holy Spirit alone works.' But in the corrupted edition of the German Apology, we read: 'We affirm, however, that free will and reason alone ('allein') can do nothing in spiritual matters.' And after a few words: 'To be regenerated within, and to be renewed in heart and senses, to believe and fear God, that the Holy Spirit works.' Where, first, the exclusive particle ('alone' [solus] the Holy Spirit), which is read in the earlier edition, is omitted; then the negative ('nothing'), which in the earlier edition denies every single δυναμιν to human powers, is restricted in the later corrupted edition by the added particle 'alone,' meaning that free will can do nothing *only* in spiritual matters. That by this very thing the synergistic error is established, no one fails to see.

Latin:

Neque quaestio est de naturalibus animae actionibus, quales sunt audire, legere, meditari, quae suo modo καταχρηστικάς spirituales dici possunt, quia ab anima, quae spiritualis est essentia, proficiscuntur; agnoscimus enim in hisce quandam arbitrii libertatem: potest homo legere, potest non legere; potest audire, potest aures avertere; sed tota quaestio est de motibus proprie dictis spiritualibus, quales sunt: Deum recte agnoscere, verbum Dei cum fructu audire et legere.“ (L. c. § 32.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Hemisphaerium superius ambitu suo comprehendit res mere spirituales seu sacras internas. .. Ad hoc hemisphaerium etiam referimus το ire in templum informationis ex verbo praedicato capiendae causa, legere et audire verbum Dei animo proficiendi, desiderio informationis ex verbo teneri; quae omnia opera sunt praevenientis atque incipientis gratiae.“ (L. c. P. II. c. 3. s. 1. th. 29. 30. f. 1888. sq.)

Idem: ,,Argumentum Bellarmini est tale: ,Si homo non pollet libero arbitrio ad opera pietatis et ipsam etiam conversionem ad Deum, frustra erunt omnia ad opera pietatis et conversionem mandata, adhortationes, incitationes etc.‘

Respondeo: 1. Haec Scripturae dicta Zach. 1, 2.: ,Convertimini ad me‘, Joel 2, 12.: ,Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro‘, Deut. 10, 16.: ,Circumcidite praeputium cordis vestri‘, Ez. 18, 31.: ,Facite vobis cor novum‘, Matth. 11, 28.: ,Venite ad me‘ etc., ostendunt quidem, quid sit officii nostri, non vero, quid sit virium nostrarum, h. e., significant, non quid homines in conversione sui possint, sed quid Deus ab illis sub ratione debiti exigat. Urgent nostrum debitum, non vim et facultatem. Praecepta non sunt mensura nostrarum virium, sed regula officii. Non in lege discimus, quid possimus, sed quid olim potuerimus.. . 3.

Urgent haec testimonia Dei jus, sc. quid Deus a debitoribus suis jure exigere possit. Deo enim

creditori jus in suum debitorem obaeratum non perit, etiamsi is solvere non possit. Juste Deus ab homine per legem exigit, quod homo per lapsum Adae injuste amisit. Deus praecipiendo, jubendo, hortando docet, quid homo debeat, quid aliquando potuerit et unde exciderit.

4. Deus saepe ea jubet, quae vult in nobis efficere, et sic non solum sunt mandata imperativa ejus, quid fleri oportet, sed simul operativa et efficax Dei medium, quo Deus efficit, quod imperat. Non frustra jubetur compeditus currere, si per illud ipsum mandatum compedes ejus solvuntur. Non frustra praecipitur coeco, ut videat, si illis ipsis verbis, quibus hoc jubetur, aperiuntur oculi coeci. Verba enim Dei id efficiunt in nobis, quod jubent a nobis effici. Deus jubet, quod vult, sed et dat, quod jubet. Et familiare est Scripturae, dicere, ea a nobis fleri, quae Deus per nos facit. Verbo enim suo adjungit Spiritus Sancti efficaciam; Deus saepe ea jubet, quae vult in nobis efficere, et sua in nobis opera coronat et remuneratur. Deut. 10, 16. Deus dicit: ,Circumcidite praeputium cordis vestri‘, sed 30, 6. declaratur, quis istud perficiat: ,Dominus Deus tuus circumcidet vobis corda vestra.‘ Dicitur quidem Ez. 18, 31.: ,Facite vobis cor novum et spiritum novum‘, sed ne quis putet, hoc esse nostri arbitrii, dicit ipse Deus apud eundem prophetam 36,26.: ,Auferam cor lapideum.‘

5. Sunt ipsae adhortationes non mere legales sine gratia, sed evangelicae, effectivae, persuasivae, trahentes. Cum Dominus invitat et dicit: ,Venite ad me‘ etc., invitando monet, concitat et gratiam confert, ut venire possimus.

6. Quando Deus injungit et imperat conversionem, vult, ut homines illi non malitiose resistant. . .

7. Licet ipsa conversio non sit in nostra potestate, ipse tamen externus mediorum usus in nostra potestate est quodammodo. Siquidem homo potest templum frequentare et externam verbi praedicationem audire, per quod Deus vult esse efficax.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 2013. sq.)

Idem: ,,A praecepto ad posse N. V. C., sive a mandato Dei ad posse humanum, ab officio ad obedientiam non valet argumentatio, est regula theologica. Sic Deus dicit ad Abrahamum Gen. 15, 5.: ,Suspice coelum et numera stellas, potesne numerare?‘ (Hic non est sensus textus hebraici) quo certe praecepto impossibilitas potius, quam possibilitas numerandi stellas haud obscure innuitur. Sic Es. 42, 18. dicitur: ,Surdi audite et coeci intuemini ad videndum‘; sive hic surditatem et coecitatem naturalem, sive spiritualem intellexeris, impossibile tamen praecipitur.

Sic Christus filiae Jairi mortuae praecipit et dicit: ,Fuella, surge!‘ Mare. 5, 41. Luc. 8, 54. Lazaro sepulto et jam foetenti: ,Lazare, veni foras! ‘ Joh. 11, 43., et Petrus defunctae discipulae dixit: ,Tabitha, surge!‘ Act. 9, 40. Quis hinc colliget, aut cadavera ista habuisse facultatem surgendi et semet ipsa vivificandi, aut Christum et Petrum ea frustra sic compellasse aut impossibilia praecepisse?

Non tyrannicum mandare impossibilia et obligare ad ea, quae non sunt in nostra potestate. Creditor juste exigit debitum a debitore, qui nihil habet, Matth. 18, 28., et Deus per legem et praecepta legalia ab hominibus debitoribus suis justissime exposcit id, quod facere tenentur. Non frustra jussi sunt a Christo et Petro surgere mortui, quia mandatis illis simul vires surgendi conferebantur. Tales ergo Dei compellationes, adhortationes et invitationes ideo non sunt frustraneae, quia sunt efficax Spiritus S. organon et quasi suscitabulum, quo ipsi homini in peccatis mortuo novas vires aspirat et confert et conversionem in illo per gratiam suam operari vult, modo ipse non contumaciter reluctetur aut operationi ejus obstacula ponat.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 2014.)

J. Ad. Osiander: ,,Sicut navis dicitur se convertere, non active, sed neutraliter, quia convertitur a nauta; ita conversio quidem homini tribuitur, nec tamen homini competit revera, sed actio solius Dei est.“ (Colleg. th. V, 63.)

PART. II. CAP. II. ANTITHE SE S. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: A. Peccantium in excessu: 1. Pelagii et Pelagianorum . . .; inter praecipua enim Pelagii et Pelagianorum dogmata haec fuere: Non opus esse homini gratia Dei, sed eum propriis liberi arbitrii viribus posse credere evangelio et omnia ad ^alutem necessaria praestare; hominem naturaliter genitum et nondum ad Deum conversum per solum liberum arbitrium posse evitare omnia peccata, gravissimas tentationes vincere et superare, Deum diligere, legem Dei perfecte implere. . .

2. Semipelagianorum. . ., (qui) asseruerunt. . ., esse nonnihil libero arbitrio relinquendum; gratiam praevenientem ad actus spirituales edendos non semper esse necessariam. . . Alter error fuit de συνεργεία hominis cum Deo, non ex potentia superaddita naturae, sed potentia naturali. . .

3. Scholasticorum, Pelagii vestigiis insistentium; contendunt enim: hominem ex suis naturalibus viribus posse verum ac summum bonum cognoscere, ad gratiam se disponere, praeparare, applicare, quodvis peccatum mortale cavere, praecepta quoad substantiam actuum servare et Deum super omnia diligere etc. . .

4. Pontificiorum, inprimis Jesuitarum. Sic enim illi in concilio Tridentino sess. VI. c. 1. asserunt: ,Liberum arbitrium (in hominibus non renatis) minime esse extinctum, viribus licet attenuatum et inclinatum.‘ Cap. 5. ejusd. sess. contrarium sentientes anathemate feriunt. Volunt autem, liberum arbitrium hominis viribus attenuatum et inclinatum in conversione a Deo moveri et excitari, motumque et excitatum cooperari, assentiendo Deo excitanti atque vocanti, quod ad obtinendam justificationis gratiam se disponat ac praeparet, ut habet can. 4. illius sessionis. . .

5. Socinianorum, qui docent a. in genere, hominem irregenitum accedente divina revelatione externa in spiritualibus ea facere et praestare posse, quae ad assensum verbi divini internum, conversionem ad Deum, agnitionem et fidem spectant. . . b. In specie docent de intellectu hominis non renati, illum ea virium perfectione pollere, ut, si illi proponantur res divinae in evangelio contentae, ipse possit citra speciale auxilium Spiritus S. easdem percipere et assensu approbare. . .

6. Arminianorum, utpote qui etiam a Pelagiana haeresi non longe absunt. . . Nam non όλικήν, sed μερικήν saltem ενέργειαν in homine convertendo gratiae divinae tribuunt, causamque fidei partim gratiae Dei in Christo, partim homini ejusque libero arbitrio adscribunt. . .

9. Synergistarum lutheranorum, συνέργειαν aliquam seu cooperationem virium humanarum cum gratia in opere conversionis statuentium. . .

Semina hujus synergistici erroris satis foecunda sparsit Philippus Melanchthon in variis scriptis et libris suis. Cum enim art. 18. Aug. Conf. in prototypo aperte damnaretur et Pelagianismus de viribus naturae in spiritualibus et Semipelagianismus de συνεργεία voluntatis humanae, ille in eodem articulo mutatae et adulteratae Aug. Conf. diserte scribit: ,Nos adjuvari a SpirituS. in efficienda spirituali justitia in nobis.‘ Sic quoque in priori editione Apologiae A. C. Germanicae legitur: ,Liberum arbitrium et intellectum in rebus spiritualibus nihil posse‘, et paulo post: ,Regenerari intus corde, animo et sensibus renovari, illud operari solum Spiritum S.‘ Sed in Apologiae Germanicae editione depravata legimus: ,Affirmamus tamen, liberum arbitrium et rationem in rebus spiritualibus solum (,allein‘) nihil posse.‘ Et post pauca: ,Intus regenerari, et corde ac sensibus renovari, credere et timere Deum, illud operatur Spiritus S/ Ubi primum particula exclusiva (,solus‘ Sp. S.), quae in priori editione legitur, est omissa; deinde negativa (,nihil‘), quae in priori editione viribus humanis omnem prorsus δυναμιν negat, in posteriori corrupta editione restringitur per adjectam particulam,solum‘, quod videl. liberum arbitrium in rebus spiritualibus solum nihil possit. Quo ipso errorem synergisticum stabiliri, nemo non videt.


### On Original Sin: In the *Loci Communes* of Philipp, published two years after the death of the…

In the *Loci Communes* of Philipp, published two years after the death of the blessed Luther and inserted into the body of doctrine, the definition of free will, which as erroneous in..."

Erasmus is rebuked by the blessed Luther, [where] the following is found: "Free will in man is the faculty of applying oneself to grace; that is, he hears the promise and endeavors to assent and casts off sins against conscience."

Likewise, these words, which quite clearly confirm synergism, are also found: "You will say, I cannot obey the voice of the Gospel, hear the Son of God, [or] acknowledge the Mediator." Philip [Melanchthon] responds: "Indeed, in some way you can, and when you sustain yourself with the voice of the Gospel, you are helped by God, who is petitioned," etc. . .

In the examination of ordinands on the article of free will, he established three causes of conversion, saying: "These causes concur in conversion: The Word of God, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father and the Son send to kindle our hearts, and our will, which assents to and does not resist the Word of God."

Dr. Johann Pfeffinger subsequently stubbornly followed in the footsteps of Philip Melanchthon and enshrined the idol of συνέργεια. . .

Dr. Georg Major also professed the cooperation of the unregenerate man with the Holy Spirit and the Word of God in the conversion of man to God. . .

Finally, the chief champion of this error emerged as Victorinus Strigelius, . . . Dr. Joh. Stoesselius. . .

10. Of the innovators, who also contend that the free will, excited by the Holy Spirit, can cooperate with Him in the act of conversion. . .

In the exercises on predestination held at Helmstedt under the presidency of Dr. Georg Calixtus, these are the paradoxes of Joh. Latermann, thesis 32: "Now, that the grace of God is offered, so that once offered it is in the power of man, through it, to perform those things which are necessary for conversion and salvation, and, if he wishes to indulge his own depravity, not to perform them, we demonstrate in this manner." Also thesis 33: "All," he says, "if they wish, could convert themselves.". . And thesis 34: "It is in the power of man to will to convert himself and to not will to convert himself." Thesis 35: "Man converts himself freely." And finally thesis 42: "But if exhortations are not in vain, as they certainly are not, everything will depend at once upon the cooperation of man, that is, man working freely by the virtue of grace, believing freely, persevering freely."

Regarding these words of Latermann, the theologians of Strasbourg, in their judgment on the disputes and proceedings of Joh. Latermann, p. 8, note: "He says nothing that Bellarmine, Greg. de Valentia, Becanus, and others have not also said and asserted, who nevertheless, by the great consensus of theologians, have been declared guilty of Pelagianism or Semipelagianism. He says nothing that the synergists have not said.". .

B. Of those sinning by defect: Of the ancient heretics, who defended a Stoic and fatal necessity, such as Simon Magus, Marcion, Hermogenes, [and] the Manichaeans; to which also pertain the Calvinists, who strive to introduce a certain absolute necessity depending upon their absolute decree. (L. c. f. 2000—2006.)

Kahnisius: "With Augustine, our Confession has also acknowledged that man, who has freedom in purely human matters, can perform humanly good works (A. C. Art. 18. Concordf. p. 640, 657). But this humanly good is supposed to have nothing to do with the spiritually good. However, this chasm is against Scripture (!), experience, and the reason of the matter. Scripture teaches most definitely that the Gospel connects to this humanly good. (Acts 10:35 [!], 1 Pet. 3:1 [!], John 3:21 [!]). . . It is an undeniable fact that the rapid spread of Christianity on the soil of the classical world can only be explained by its preparation for Christ, which again presupposes a point of contact for Christianity in the natural man." (Die Luth. Dogm. III, 310.)

The same: "The scriptural doctrine that through Adam’s fall sin has gained dominion in all men, Augustine exaggerates into my doctrine of the total deadness of the natural man toward the good and of the massive damnation, which is contrary to Scripture as well as to tradition and Christian experience. Scripture teaches and experience testifies that in the natural man there is an inclination toward the true, toward the good, toward peace, which, while not capable of breaking the powerful pull of the flesh downward, can nevertheless PART II. CAP. II. be a point of contact for grace. With the same dualistically rapid leap with which Augustine immediately exaggerated the conflict prevailing in natural humanity between the divine and the human will into the total unfreedom of the latter. . . Augustine now also taught that grace alone brings the entirely unfree will to salvation. . . The renewing power of grace gains a saving form in man only by setting all powers in motion and driving them to cooperation." (L. c. II, 137 sq.)

The same: "Melanchthon had, through the doctrine of the cooperation of the human will in the appropriation of salvation (synergism), entered upon the right, evangelical, and at the same time truly traditional path of holding fast to the substance of the Augustinian doctrine without its excrescences." (L. c. 539.)

Hofmann: "The Apostle speaks (Rom. 2:14) of the case that Gentiles, without possessing a law, a revelation of the demanding will, do that which the will of God revealed in Israel demands, and says of such doing of theirs that it happens φύσει (by nature). . . The Apostle (Rom. 2:14) considers it so possible that one might be able, by virtue of this law, albeit only in individual instances, to act in accordance with divine demand, that he holds out the prospect that there might perhaps be, on the day of judgment, a self-justification before God arising from the thoughts brought forth by the testimony of the conscience, which can be graciously accepted by Him who exercises His judgment through Jesus Christ, the Mediator of grace." (Der Schriftbeweis. I, 494, 495 sq.)

Luthardt: "As far as. . . the behavior of the will toward grace in conversion is concerned, orthodox dogmatics has, on the whole, in connection with the Formula of Concord, one-sidedly emphasized the divine factor in conversion (conversio transitiva). The F. C. mostly(!) allows the activity of one’s own will to enter only after conversion." (Kompend. der Dogm. 1868, p. 204.)

The same: "Martensen speaks of an innate grace which, identical with essential freedom, breaks through within the natural will in the surrender to grace. § 204, p. 336. The more decidedly ecclesiastical theologians indeed reject this synergism, but they nevertheless demand (thus Thomasius, Harless, Frank, etc.) that not only the active behavior in conversion be emphasized on the basis of the internally liberating influence of saving grace, but also that the possibility of a state of preparation for saving grace be recognized on the basis of the general effect of God through the conscience, etc." (L. c. p. 135.)

NOTE. Quenstedtius: I. Liberty of contrariety is that which is concerned between two or more specifically different acts (for the term "contraries" is to be taken more broadly here), when, namely, the will is not determined to a certain species, e.g., to only good or only evil, but can either choose or reject the one, can will the one and nill the other; for to will and to nill are contraries. It is otherwise called liberty of specification or regarding the species of the act, because it is not determined to a certain species of act or object. —

II. Liberty of contradiction is that which is concerned with one and the same object proposed to itself between contradictory terms; when, namely, someone, with one object proposed, can act or not act, will or not will. For to will and not to will, to act and not to act, are contradictorily opposed acts. It is otherwise called liberty of exercise, because it is concerned with the very exercise of the act, or because, after the will has already been determined to one species of act or object (namely, good or evil in general, or this or that particular good or evil), it freely

yet it behaves in exercise in such a way that it can will and not will, act and not act, in regard to that one and the same thing to which it is determined; e.g., when virtue and vice are proposed, and a conclusion is made in the election: "I will virtue, I do not will vice," then this is called liberty of contrariety and specification; but when a single object (e.g., virtue, temperance, fortitude) is proposed, they can choose it and not choose it, will it and not will it, and then it is named by the scholastics liberty of contradiction or of exercise. Both liberties are joined in Ecclesiasticus 15:14 ff." (L. c. s. 1. th. 12. f. 1080. sq.)

For although we do not deny that some liberty remains to man after the fall regarding things subject to reason, just as the Augsburg Confession also teaches in Art. 18, so that reason can recognize some difference between good and evil things, and from there the will can be carried toward the former as things to be sought, and flee the latter; and thus also, just as it can know God from created things, so it can love God as the author of nature and of natural goods, and can also love one's neighbor, whether because of the virtues in which he excels, or because of the utility which can be expected from him, or because of the communion of nature or closeness of blood, or because of some other suitability founded in nature; yet nowhere are there such active powers in man after the fall that do not necessarily suffer a fainting spell at some time. For the intellect is often deceived in judging, and the will, together with the sensitive appetite, often grows sluggish or languishes in pursuing the good known by the intellect, and on the contrary inclines toward the opposite evil in such a way that, not rarely and with reason protesting in vain, it breaks out into depraved acts. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Tract. de Conv. Disp. IV. cap. I. § 25. 26. 38. p. 257. 259. 266.*

Apology of the A. C.: "Nor do we take away liberty from the human will. The human will has liberty in choosing works and things which reason comprehends by itself. It can in some way effect civil righteousness or the righteousness of works; it can speak about God, offer God a certain worship by an external work, obey magistrates and parents; in choosing an external work, it can keep its hands from murder, from adultery, from theft. Since reason and judgment concerning things subject to the senses remain in the nature of man, there also remains a choice of those things and the liberty and faculty of effecting civil righteousness. For Scripture calls this the righteousness of the flesh, which the carnal nature, that is, reason by itself, effects without the Holy Spirit. Although the power of concupiscence is so great that men more often obey evil affections than right judgment. And the devil, who is effective in the impious, as Paul says (Ephes. 2:2), does not cease to incite this weak nature to various offenses. These are the reasons why even civil righteousness is rare among men, just as we see that not even the philosophers themselves attained it, who seem to have sought it." (Art. 18, p. 218.)

Latin:

In locis communibus Philippi biennio post obitum b. Lutheri tertium editis et corpori doctrinae insertis definitio liberi arbitrii, quam tanquam erroneam in

Erasmo reprehendit b. Lutherus, haec habetur: ,Liberum arbitrium in homine est facultas applicandi se ad gratiam; h. e., audit promissionem et assentiri conatur et abjicit peccata contra conscientiam.‘

Itidem etiam haec verba synergismum haud obscure confirmantia habentur: ,Non possum, inquies, voci evangelii obtemperare, Filium Dei audire, agnoscere mediatorem.‘ Respondet Philippus: ,Imo aliquo modo potes et, cum te voce evangelii sustentas, adjuvari te a Deo petito‘ etc. . .

In examine ordinand. in art. de lib. arbitr. tres conversionis causas constituit, inquiens: ,Concurrunt in conversione hae causae: Verbum Dei, Spiritus S., quem Pater et Filius mittunt, ut accendat ׳corda nostra, et nostra voluntas assentiens et non repugnans verbo Dei.‘

Philippi Melanchthonis vestigiis postmodum contumaciter institit et συνέργειας idolum incrustavit Dr. Johann. Pfeffinger. . .

D. Georgius Major quoque cooperationem hominis irregeniti cum Spiritu S. et verbo Dei in conversione hominis ad Deum professus est. . .

Tandem erroris hujus praecipuus propugnator extitit Victorinus Strigelius, . . . Dr. Joh. Stoesselius. . .

10. Novatorum, qui etiam contendunt, liberum ·arbitrium a Spiritu S. excitatum in actu conversionis ei cooperari posse. . .

Joh. Latermanni in exercitat, de praedest. sub praesidio D. Georg. Calixti habita Helmstadii haec sunt paradoxa th. 32.: ,Nunc quod gratia Dei offeratur, ut ea oblata in hominis potestate sit, per illam ea, quae ad conversionem et salutem necessaria sunt, praestare, et, si pravitati suae indulgere velit, non praestare, in hunc modum demonstramus.‘ It. th. 33.: ,Omnes‘, inquit, ,si velint, possent se convertere’... Et th. 34.: ,In potestate hominis est, velle se convertere et nolle se convertere.‘ Th. 35.: ,Homo libere se convertit.1· Et denique th. 42.: ,Quodsi adhortationes frustraneae non sunt, ut certe non sunt, pendebunt omnia simul a cooperatione hominis, h. e., homine in virtute gratiae libere operante, libere credente, libere perseverante.‘

Ad haec verba Latermanni theologi Argentorat. in judicio suo super disputatis et actitatis a Joh. Latermanno p. 8. annotant: ,Nihil dicit, quod non etiam Bellarminus, Greg. de Valentia, Becanus et alii dixerunt, asseruerunt, qui tamen magno theologorum consensu Pelagianismi aut Semipelagianismi rei dicti sunt. Nihil dicit, quod non synergistae dixerunt.‘ . .

B. Peccantium in defectu: Antiquorum haereticorum, stoicam et fatalem necessitatem defendentium, ut Simonis Magi, Marcionis, Hermogenis, Manichaeorum; quo pertinent etiam Calviniani, qui absolutam quandam necessitatem ex absoluto suo decreto pendentem introducere satagunt.“ (L. c. f. 2000— 2006.)

Kahnisius: ״Mit Augustin hat auch unser Bekenntniss anerkannt, dass der Mensch, der in rein menschlichen Dingen Freiheit hat, menschlich gute Werke vollbringen kann (A. C. Art. 18. Concordf. S. 640. 657.). Dies menschlich Gute aber soll mit dem geistlich Guten nichts zu thun haben. Allein diese Kluft ist gegen Schrift (!), Erfahrung und die Vernunft der Sache. Die Schrift lehrt auf das Bestimmteste, dass das Evangelium an dies menschlich Gute anknüpft. (AG. 10, 35. [!] 1 Pet. 3, 1. [!] Joh. 3, 21. [!]).. . Es ist eine unbestreitbare Thatsache, dass die schnelle Ausbreitung des Christenthums auf dem Boden der classischen Welt sich nur aus der Vorbereitung derselben auf Christum erklären lässt, die wieder einen Anknüpfungspunct des Christenthums im natürlichen Menschen voraussetzt.“ (Die Luth. Dogm. III, 310.)

Idem: ״Die Schriftlehre, dass durch Adams Fall in allen Mensehen die Sünde die Herrschaft gewonnen hat, übertreibt Augustin zu meiner Doctrin von der gänzlichen Erstorbenheit des natürlichen Menschen zum Guten und von der massenhaften Verdammniss, welche gegen Schrift wie gegen Tradition und christliche Erfahrung ist. Die Schrift lehrt und die Erfahrung bezeugt, dass im natürlichen Menschen ein Zug zum Wahren, zum Guten, zum Frieden ist, der zwar nicht im Stande ist, «den mächtigen Zug des Fleisches nach unten zu brechen, wohl aber PART. II. CAP. II. eine Anknüpfung für die Gnade sein kann. Mit demselben dualistisch raschen Sprunge, mit welchem Augustin den in der natürlichen Menschheit herrschenden Zwiespalt zwischen dem göttlichen und dem menschlichen Willen sogleich zur gänzlichen Unfreiheit des letzteren übertrieb, . . . lehrte nun auch Augustin, dass lediglich die Gnade den ganz unfreien Willen zum Heil bringe. . . Die erneuernde Kraft der Gnade gewinnt in dem Menschen seligmachende Gestalt nur dadurch, dass sie alle Kräfte in Bewegung setzt und zur Mitwirkung treibt.“ (L. c. II, 137. sq.)

Idem: ,,Melanchthon hatte durch die Lehre von der Mitwirkung des menschlichen Willens bei der Heilsaneignung (Synergismus) den rechten, evangelischen und zugleich wahrhaft traditionellen Weg betreten, die Substanz der augustinischen Lehre festzuhalten ohne ihre Auswüchse.“ (L. c. 539.)

Hofmannus: ״Der Apostel redet (Röm. 2, 14.) von dem Falle, dass Heiden, ohne ein Gesetz, eine Offenbarung des fordernden Willens,, zu besitzen, dasjenige thun, was der in Israel geoffenbarte Gotteswille fordert, und sagt von solchem Thun derselben, dass es ψνσει (von Natur) geschehe. . . So sehr achtet es der Apostel (Röm. 2, 14.) für möglich, dass einer vermöge dieses Gesetzes im Stande sei, obzwar nur im Einzelnen, göttlicher Forderung gemäss zu handeln, dass er in Aussicht stellt, es möge etwa am Tage des Gerichts aus den durch das Zeugniss des Gewissens hervorgerufenen Gedanken eine Selbstrechtfertigung vor Gott werden, die da gnädig angenommen werden kann von dem, weleher sein Gericht durch Jesum Christum, den Mittler der Gnade, übt.“ (Der Schriftbeweis. I, 494. 495. sq.)

Luthardtius: ״Was. . . das Verhalten des Willens zur Gnade in der Bekehrung anlangt, so hat die orthodoxe Dogmatik im Ganzen im Anschluss an die C. F. den göttlichen Factor in der Bekehrung (conversio transitiva) einseitig betont. Die C. F. lässt meistens(!) die Thätigkeit des eigenen Willens erst nach der Bekehrung eintreten.“ (Kompend. der Dogm. 1868. p. 204.)

Idem: ״Martensen spricht von einer anerschaffenen Gnade, welche, mit der wesentlichen Freiheit identisch, in der Hingabe an die Gnade zum Durchbruch innerhalb des natürlichen Willens kommt. § 204. S. 336. Die entschiedener kirchlichen Theologen weisen zwar diesen Synergismus zurück, fordern aber doch (so Thomasius, Harless, Frank u. s. w.), dass nicht nur das active Verhalten in der Bekehrung auf Grund der innerlich befreienden Einwirkung der Heilsgnade betont,, sondern auch die Möglichkeit eines Vorbereitungsstandes auf die Heilsgnade auf Grund der allgemeinen Wirkung Gottes durch das Gewissen u. s. w. anerkannt werde.“ (L. c. p. 135.)

NOTA. Quenstedtius: I. Libertas contrarietatis e st, quae versatur inter duos vel plures specie diversos actus (nam terminus contrariorum hic latius accipiendus est), quando sci. voluntas non est determinata ad certam speciem, v. g. ad solum bonum vel ad solum malum, sed alterum potest vel eligere vel rejicere, potest unum velle, alterum nolle; velle autem et nolle sunt contraria. Dicitur alias libertas specificationis sive quoad speciem actus, quia non determinatur ad certam speciem actus vel objecti. —

II. Libertas contradictionis est, quae circa unum idemque objectum sibi propositum versatur inter terminos contradictorios; quando sci. quis uno objecto proposito potest agere vel non agere, velle vel non velle. Velle vero et non velle, agere et non agere,, sunt actus contradictorie oppositi. Dicitur alias libertas exercitii, quia in ipso actus exercitio versatur vel quia, postquam voluntas jam ad unam speciem actus vel objecti (bonum sci. vel malum in communi vel in particulari hoc vel illud bonum aut malum) determinata est, libere

tamen se habet in exercitio, ut unum illud idemque, ad quod determinata est, possit velle et non velle, agere et non agere; v. g., quando virtus et vitium proponuntur, et in electione flt conclusio: Volo virtutem, nolo vitium, tum haec libertas contrarietatis et specificationis vocatur; quando vero objectum unicum (v. g. virtus, temperantia, fortitudo) proponitur, possunt illud eligere et non eligere, velle et non velle, et tum libertas contradictionis seu exercitii a scholasticis nominatur. Utraque libertas conjungitur Ecclesiastici 15, 14. sqq.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 12. f. 1080. sq.)

Quanquam enim circa res rationi subjectas libertatem aliquam homini post lapsum superesse non negamus, prout et Augustana Confessio docet Art. 18., ita ut in rebus creatis differentiam aliquam bonorum malorumque cognoscere possit ratio, indeque voluntas in illa ferri, ut appetenda, haec vero fugere et sic etiam, quemadmodum Deum ex creaturis cognoscere, ita Deum, tanquam auctorem naturae et naturalium bonorum, diligere, proximum quoque sive propter virtutes, quibus pollet, sive propter utilitatem, quae ab ipso expectari potest, sive ob communionem naturae aut propinquitatem sanguinis, sive ob aliam quandam in natura fundatam convenientiam diligere possit; nullibi tamen eae sunt vires activae in homine post lapsum, quae non aliquando deliquium necessario patiantur. Nam et intellectus in judicando saepe fallitur, et voluntas una cum appetitu sensitivo ad sectandum bonum ab intellectu cognitum saepe torpet aut languet et contra in oppositum malum ita propendet, ut non raro, ac frustra reclamante ratione, in actus pravos erumpat. Confer b. Mus. Tract. de Conv. Disp. IV. cap. I. § 25. 26. 38. p. 257. 259. 266.

Apologia A. C.: ,,Neque vero adimimus humanae voluntati libertatem. Habet humana voluntas libertatem in operibus et rebus deligendis, quas ratio per se comprehendit. Potest aliquo modo efficere justitiam civilem seu justitiam operum, potest loqui de Deo, exhibere Deo certum cultum externo opere, obedire magistratibus, parentibus, in opere externo eligendo potest continere manus a caede, ab adulterio, a furto. Quum reliqua sit in natura hominis ratio et judicium de rebus sensui subjectis, reliquus est etiam delectus earum rerum et libertas et facultas efficiendae justitiae civilis. Id enim vocat Scriptura justitiam carnis, quam natura carnalis, hoc est, ratio per se efficit sine Spiritu Sancto. Quamquam tanta est vis concupiscentiae, ut malis affectibus saepius obtemperent homines quam recto judicio. Et diabolus, qui est efficax in impiis, ut ait Paulus (Ephes. 2, 2.), non desinit incitare hanc imbecillem naturam ad varia delicta. Haec causae sunt, quare et civilis justitia rara sit inter homines, sicut videmus ne ipsos quidem philosophos eam consecutos esse, qui videntur eam expetivisse.“ (Art. 18. p. 218.)


### On Original Sin: Just as David placed the source of the adultery committed by him in original…

Just as David placed the source of the adultery committed by him in original sin, Ps. 51:7. And Paul ascribes the sins which he admits in act to the sin dwelling in him, Rom. 7:17.

For although man is not determined by the corruption of nature to a certain act of sinning in the individual, but, if he exercises any, he exercises it freely, so that he could have not exercised it; yet he is confusedly determined to some acts of sin, so that although he does not necessarily exercise this one in the individual, nor that one in the individual, yet he cannot but exercise some acts of sinning. Furthermore, of actual sins from PART II. CHAP. II.

The variety of those things proceeding from original stain, as to their species, may be seen from the catalog of the works of the flesh, Gal. 5:19 and Mark 7:21, 22, 23. It is all the less surprising that sins of the same kind, when frequently committed, sprout forth from the same root. For men are said to be φύσει, by nature, or by the condition of a corrupted nature, τέκνα οργής, children of wrath, i.e., liable to divine wrath, which implies a negation of divine favor, with a contrary effect, such as vindictive justice. Certainly, a morbid quality, with the gift of immortality withdrawn, and thus that precise χράσει of the humors and vigor of the body, arose as a punishment for the fall and the sinful stain that arose thence in all men. And diseases, the forerunners of death, are sometimes called by the name of death itself. See 2 Cor. 1:10. Whence it is not wrongly thought that they were also included in the threat of death that preceded the fall. Indeed, those calamities which afflicted the protoplasts themselves after the fall, according to Gen. 3:16 sqq., were in their own way derived to their descendants, along with sin and on account of hereditary sin. For thus temporal death is said to have spread to all men through sin, Rom. 5:12, 14. And in the last chapter, verse 23, it is called θάνατος ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας, namely, because, just as wages—both food and money—were once accustomed to be paid to soldiers, so sinners, having followed the camps of Satan, obtain death in place of a reward.

Hollazius: "Although the protoplasts did not suffer bodily death at the first moment of the fall, they nevertheless immediately became debtors to death, since this is the wages of sin." (Exam. P. II. c. 3. q. 9. p. 513.)

Luther: "The Lord forbade Adam to eat anything, otherwise he would surely die, not because the nature of this tree was to kill, but because it had been so pronounced by the Word of God, which Word grants its efficacy to all creatures and also preserves all creatures, so that they do not degenerate, but that certain species are preserved in infinite propagation. Thus, by the Word, it came to pass that the rock in the desert gave forth most abundant waters, that the bronze serpent healed those who looked upon it, etc. In this way, this one tree, or that certain species of many trees in the midst of paradise, killed Adam, who did not obey the Word of God—not indeed by its own nature, but because it had been so determined by the Word of God. Let us think the same also of the tree of life, which God commanded Adam to eat whenever he wished his strength to be restored; the tree provided this by the power of the Word. To reason, it seems very ridiculous how one apple could be so harmful as to destroy the whole human race through an almost infinite succession, and that by eternal death. But this was not the power of the apple; Adam indeed sinks his teeth into the apple; yet in reality he sinks his teeth into the sting, which was the prohibition of God and disobedience toward God. This is the true cause of the evil, namely, that he sins against God, neglects His command, and obeys Satan. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was a good tree, which brought forth most noble fruits. But because a prohibition is added, and man does not obey the prohibition, it becomes more harmful than any poison. Thus, because it is sanctioned by the Word of God that you shall not steal, whoever touches another’s property sins. In Egypt, when the Jews were commanded to ask silver from their neighbors and to take it with them, it was not a sin; for they are excused by the command of God, to whom obedience is owed in every event. When a suitor loves a girl and desires her as a wife and marries her, he does not commit adultery, even though the law prohibits concupiscence. For marriage was divinely instituted and commanded to those who cannot live chastely without marriage. The same is clearly..."

The reason for these trees is: the tree of life gives life by the power of the promising word, and thus ordains it; the tree of the knowledge of good and evil kills by the power of the prohibiting word. It has the name of the knowledge of good and evil, as Augustine says, because, after Adam sinned in it, he not only saw and experienced what good he had lost, but also into what misery he had been cast by his disobedience. Therefore, the tree was good in itself, just as the commandment that was added was also good, so that it might be for Adam a tree of divine worship, in which he might prove his obedience to God even by an external work. But because of the sin that followed, it became a tree of cursing.” (On Gen. 2:9.)

ANTITHESIS. Delitzsch: “Was the tree of knowledge a tree of blessing according to its purpose, but was it also one according to its nature? In other words: is the death which is threatened to man to be thought of only as a consequence of the transgression of the prohibition accidentally attached to this tree, or as a consequence of the forces active in this tree? The latter seems to me to lie in the sense of the narrative. For the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is not selected only when God issues the prohibition, but it stands from the beginning (v. 9) as a tree of decision in the garden; already in v. 9 one notices that it forms a contrast to the tree of life standing in the midst of the garden. But the latter imparts life by virtue of the nature created within it (3:22), therefore the tree of knowledge will also work death by virtue of its nature. But by virtue of the nature created in it by God? Death is, as we know from Gen. 1, nothing originally willed by God; therefore, the power of death in this tree will also not be something creatively established by God. If we now remember that the paradisiacal vocational calling of man has its aim at the overcoming of the evil that has penetrated into the creation, it cannot surprise us that in Paradise itself there is a tree which God indeed created, but which the power of evil has taken possession of, the consumption of which places man in relation to evil and therefore kills him, and which, so that man might not fall into the fellowship of evil and thereby into death, is hedged about by the divine prohibition.” (Die Genesis. Lpz. 1852. p. 107 sq.)

k) Concerning which we spoke above in Part I, Chapter VII, especially § 15, note e. Compare Rom. 5:18. And this eternal condemnation is drawn upon all by original sin, as a sufficient and adequate cause, in whom it is not expiated through faith in Christ. Compare *Ausführliche Erklärung* Q. XXXVIII. p. 307. § 14.

The affections of original sin are: 1. Tenacity or persistent inherence throughout the whole of life. 2. Natural propagability from parents to children. For thus also Paul, already converted, confesses that sin dwells in him as a guest that can never be expelled, Rom. 7: 17. He understands, however, concupiscence, of which he had spoken in v. 7, 8. And he openly attributes to it, just as the name, so also the formal reason or concept of sin properly so called. Compare Heb. 12:1, where it is called ἁμαρτία εὐπερίστατος, sin firmly adhering to us and surrounding us on every side, and therefore not easily to be put off, except with the body itself, or like a burden tied to us, which we cannot lay aside. PART II. CAP. II.

Apology of the Augsburg Confession: "Augustine says: 'Sin is remitted in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not imputed.'" (Art. 2.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: ... 3. Of the Papists, who recall the Pelagian dogma from hell; for concerning the remains of original sin after baptism, or concerning concupiscence, which still remains in the baptized in this life, the decree of the 5th Session of the Council of Trent holds as follows: 'If anyone denies that the guilt of original sin is remitted through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is conferred in baptism, or even asserts that the whole of that which has the true and proper nature of sin is not taken away, but says that it is only shaved off and not imputed, let him be anathema.'" (L. c. q. 12. f. 1037.)

This is what Christ says in John 3:6: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh," that is, he who is begotten by carnal parents, or those corrupted by sin, is himself also carnal and corrupted by sin. To this correspond the words of Job, chapter 14:4: "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" that is, no one will show a clean thing begotten from an unclean parent. And the words of David in Psalm 51:5: "Behold, I was shaped in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me," indicating that the contagion of sin was actually transfused into him through carnal generation.

Furthermore, just as that propagability of original sin from the begetters to the begotten is rightly held, so it may be sufficient to know that our first parents, by their fall, merited that all who were subsequently procreated should be such as they themselves were after the fall in body and soul. But how the soul contracts that evil can be ignored while maintaining the faith, because the Holy Spirit did not wish to reveal this by certain and clear testimonies—which are the words of the blessed Chemnitius, P. I. LL. CC. de Pecc. Orig. fol. 236.

He followed the footsteps of Augustine, who, when he had treated the question concerning the origin of the soul and the contracted stain of original sin in Ep. XXVIII to Jerome, making mention of the former in the following Epistle, XXIX, says that it was elegantly narrated, which fits this matter quite aptly: "When a certain man had fallen into a well, where the water was such that it received him more to keep him from dying than to stifle him from speaking, another approached, and seeing him, wondered and said: 'How did you fall in here?' But he replied: 'I beseech you, consider how you might free me from here, do not ask how I fell in here.'" Thus, since we confess and hold by the catholic faith concerning the guilt of sin, as if it were a well, that even the soul of a small infant must be freed by the grace of Christ, it is sufficient for us that we know the way by which it is saved, even if we never know how it arrived at that evil. These are the words of Augustine, l. c.

However, just as the origin of the soul has begun to be discussed somewhat more solidly in the schools of theologians, so it has come about that those who embraced the opinion of the propagation of the soul by traducianism explained the propagation of original sin through carnal generation in one way, while those who embraced the opinion of the creation of the soul explained it in another.

And indeed, when it is established that the sin of origin, taken in itself, abstractively and formally, is a privation or lack of original justice…, and therefore, by the very fact that it is not a positive entity but a mere privation, it does not acknowledge an efficient cause by whose real and positive influx it is produced; it now simultaneously appears that the mode of propagation is established as negative, since it consists in the non-production of the opposite form, original justice, or that, when the soul is efficiently produced, original justice is not simultaneously produced in and with it.

Thus, therefore, those who establish the propagation of the soul by traducianism seem to indicate that when parents, as secondary causes

produce, as if from their own, and bestow upon their offspring a rational soul, with God as the primary cause imparting a general concurrence, therefore the same persons, whose souls already lost original justice in our first parents, cannot in the act of generation transfer to their children along with the soul, or propagate, the original justice which they themselves lack, but bestow a soul destitute of original justice and thus pecca ness and thus corrupted by sin, just as God also provides His concurrence for the propagation of the soul into the offspring, but not for the propagation of original righteousness. Those, however, who posit the creation of souls believe that original sin is propagated in such a way that, since our first parents by their fall had contracted upon themselves the guilt of the removal of original righteousness and had truly lost it, indeed by their own fault and by the just judgment of God, in view of this fall and guilt, the influx from God for the co-production of original righteousness is now denied in the production of the souls of the offspring—an influx which otherwise, if men had remained in the state of integrity, would always have concurred in the act of generation by creating the soul with original righteousness. For after the fall, committed by the common parent of the human race, every man thereafter, for the generation of offspring, as if it were an effect connatural to him, does not demand the concurrence of the primary cause to produce original righteousness along with the soul of the offspring, since a connatural effect is not more perfect than its cause. But if original sin, viewed in itself, abstractly and formally, be said to be not a mere privation, but a positive entity, which requires to be produced and propagated through a real and positive influx of an efficient cause, then indeed a significant difficulty appears on both sides, lest you make God the cause of propagated original sin, whether you posit that the soul is propagated from parents by traducianism, with God nevertheless concurring as the primary cause, or that it is created immediately by God. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Ausführl. Erklärung* Q. XXX. and XXXV. p. 301 sqq. Regarding this matter, which is quite difficult and doubtful, the modesty of Augustine is pleasing, who preferred to έπέχειν [withhold judgment]. § 15.

Original sin may be described as the lack of original righteousness, propagated by the fall of Adam to all men through carnal generation, intimately corrupting the very nature of man and all the faculties of the soul, rendering them inept for pursuing spiritual goods but prone to every evil, and thus subjecting them to divine wrath and eternal death, unless the remission of sins intervenes on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. Which it signifies in the nominative case. And compare § 2 sqq. As the meritorious cause or the causality of the moral efficient cause; see § 7 and 8. Which are the subject of the *Quod*; see § 11. PART II. CHAP. III.

Which partly pertain to the efficient cause of original sin, as it is in individuals, according to § 8, note d, and partly designate the affection of this sin viewed in itself; see § 14. Indeed, capable of morality; which are the primary subject *Quo* [by which]; see § 2 ff. and § 12. In which the effect of original sin consists; see § 13. § 16.

It happens from original sin that it reigns in some, and in others it does not reign. In itself, indeed, it tends to exercise dominion in all; yet because it is not rarely hindered by the grace of God from reigning, we therefore say that both happen to it. Or to that depraved and connate concupiscence. Certainly, in the style of Scripture, the *regnare* [to reign] and *non regnare* [not to reign] is attributed to inherent sin, which is connate to us (not equally to secondary acts, or voluntary actual sins). See Rom. 6:12. Although habitual sins, acquired by frequent actions, can also be said to dominate or reign in a man, as long as they are not diminished, but flourish and stimulate the frequenting of actual sins. Or it has man obeying its irritations, just as a master has a servant under his command, or a king a subject. Compare Rom. 6:16, 17. When its motions are resisted and thus its command is snatched away, although it itself remains, so that man, having become freer, does not walk according to the flesh, but according to the spirit, Rom. 8:1, or if any evil is done, yet he himself does not do it so much willingly, as the sin inhabiting him does, while he is unwilling, just as a servant does something while the master is unwilling, or a subject while the king is unwilling. Chapter III.

Prout David adulterii a se commissi fontem in peccato originali collocavit, Ps. 51, 7. Et Paulus peccata, quae actu admittat, peccato in se habitanti adscribit, Rom. 7, 17.

Quamvis enim homo non sit per corruptionem naturae determinatus ad certum in individuo actum peccandi, sed, si quem exercet, libere exerceat, ita ut potuerit non exercere; ad aliquos tamen peccati actus confuse determinatus est, ut quamvis nec hunc in individuo, neque illum in individuo, necessario exerceat, aliquos tamen actus peccandi non possit non exercere. Dicuntur enim homines φύσει, natura, seu per naturae corruptae conditionem esse τέκνα οργής, filii irae, i. e., obnoxii irae divinae, quae negationem favoris divini importat, cum effectu contrario, velut justitiae vindicativae. Hollazius: ,,Quamvis primo lapsus momento protoplasti mortem corporis non oppetiverint, illico tamen debitores mortis facti sunt, cum isthaec peccati sit stipendium.“ (Exam. P. II. c. 3. q. 9. p. 513.)

Lutherus: ,,Dominus prohibuit, ne quid comederet Adam, älioqui futurum, ut morte moreretur, non quod natura hujus arboris fuerit occidere, sed quod per verbum Dei sic pronuntiatum erat, quod verbum omnibus creaturis tribuit suam efficaciam, et conservat etiam omnes creaturas, ne degenerent, sed ut certae serventur species in infinita propagatione. Sic verbo factum est, ut petra in deserto daret largissimas aquas, ut aeneus serpens adspicientes sanaret etc. Ad hunc modum haec una arbor, seu ista certa species plurium arborum in medio paradisi occidit Adamum, non parentem verbo Dei, non quidem sua natura, sed quia per verbum Dei sic erat definitum. Idem sentiamus de ligno vitae quoque, quo jussit Deus Adamum vesci, quoties vellet restaurari vires; virtute verbi id praestabat arbor. Rationi valde videtur ridiculum, quomodo unum pomum sic potuerit esse noxium, ut totum genus humanum per infinitam quasi successionem perdiderit, idque aeterna morte. Sed pomi haec non fuit virtus; Adam quidem in pomum figit dentes; revera tamen figit dentes in aculeum, qui erat prohibitio Dei et inobedientia erga Deum. Haec est vera causa mali, scilicet, quod contra Deum peccat, ejus mandatum negligit, et paret satanae. Euit arbor scientiae boni et mali bona arbor, quae nobilissimos protulit fructus. Sed quia prohibitio accedit, et homo prohibitioni non paret, fit quovis veneno magis noxia. Sic quia verbo Dei sancitum est, ne fureris, peccat, quisquis alienam rem attrectat. In Aegypto cum Judaei argentum a vicinis petere, et id secum auferre juberentur, non fuit id peccatum; excusantur enim mandato Dei, cui in omnem eventum debetur obedientia. Procus cum amat puellam, et concupiscit eam in uxorem ac ducit, non committit adulterium, cum tamen lex prohibeat concupiscentiam. Nam matrimonium divinitus institutum est, et mandatum iis, qui sine matrimonio non possunt caste vivere. Eadem plane

ratio est harum arborum: arbor vitae vivificat virtute verbi promittentis, et sic ordinantis; .arbor scientiae boni et mali occidit virtute verbi prohibentis. Habet autem nomen scientiae boni et mali, sicut Augustinus dicit, quia, postquam in ea peccavit Adam, non solum vidit et expertus est, quid boni amiserit, sed etiam, in quantam miseriam per inobedientiam suam conjectus sit. Fuit itaque per se bona arbor, sicut etiam mandatum, quod additum est, bonum fuit, ut esset Adae arbor cultus divini, in qua probaret Deo etiam externo opere obedientiam. Sed propter peccatum sequens fit arbor meledictionis.“ (Ad Gen. 2, 9.)

ANTITHESIS. Delitzschius: ,,Der Baum der Erkenntniss war ein Segensbaum seiner Bestimmung nach, aber war er es auch seiner Natur nach? Mit andern Worten: ist der Tod, welcher dem Menschen gedroht wird, nur als Folge der Uebertretung des zufällig gerade an diesen Baum geknüpften Verbotes zu denken oder als Folge der in diesem Baum wirksamen Kräfte? Mir scheint das Letztere im Sinne der Erzählung zu liegen. Denn der Baum der Erkenntniss Gutes und Böses wird nicht erst, als Gott das Verbot stellt, ausgewählt, sondern er steht von Anfang an V. 9. als Baum der Entscheidung im Garten, schon V. 9. merkt man, dass er einen Gegensatz bildet zu dem inmitten des Gartens stehenden Baume des Lebens. Dieser aber theilt Leben mit kraft der ihm anerschaffenen Natur 3, 22., also wird auch der Baum der Erkenntniss den Tod wirken kraft seiner Natur. Aber kraft der ihm von Gott anerschaffenen? Der Tod ist, wie wir aus Gen. 1. wissen, nichts Ursprunglieh von Gott Gewolltes; sonach wird auch die Kraft des Todes in diesem Baume nichts schöpferisch von Gott Gesetztes sein. Erinnern wir uns nun, dass die paradiesische Berufsbestimmung des Menschen ihr Absehen auf Ueberwindung des in die Schöpfung eingedrungenen Argen hat, so kann es uns nicht wundern, dass im Paradiese selbst ein Baum ist, den zwar Gott geschaffen, aber die Macht des Argen in Besitz genommen hat, dessen Genuss den Menschen in Beziehung zum Argen setzt und desshalb tödtet, und welcher, damit der Mensch nicht der Gemeinschaft des Argen und damit dem Tode verfalle, vom göttlichen Verbote umhegt ist.“ (Die Genesis. Lpz. 1852. p. 107. sq.)

k) De qua supra diximus P. I. cap. VII. praesertim § 15. not. e. Conf. Rom. 5, 18. Atque hanc damnationem aeternam peccatum originis, tanquam causa sufficiens et adaequata, attrahit omnibus, in quibus non expiatur per fidem in Christum. Confer. Ausfuhrl. Erklärung Q. XXXVIII. p. 307. § 14.

Pontificiorum, qui Pelagianum dogma ex orco revocant; de reliquiis enim peccati originalis post baptismum sive de concupiscentia, quae in baptizatis in hac vita adhuc reliqua est, decretum 5. Sess. Hoc est, quod Christus dicit Joh. 3, 6.: Quod natum est ex carne, caro est, id est, qui a parentibus carnalibus seu peccato corruptis gignitur, ipse quoque carnalis et peccato corruptus est. Cui respondent verba Jobi cap. 14, 4.: Quis dabit mundum ex immundo f id est, nemo monstrabit mundum, ex immundo parente genitum. Et verba Davidis Ps. 51, 7.: Ecce in iniquitate formatus sum, et in peccato calefecit me mater mea, indicans, contagium peccati per carnalem generationem in se actu transfusum.

Caeterum sicut propagabilitas illa peccati originalis a generantibus ad genitos recte tenetur, ita satis esse potest, scire, primos parentes lapsu suo meritos esse, ut, quales ipsi erant post lapsum corpore et anima, tales procrearentur omnes postea. Quomodo autem malum illud contrahat anima, salva fide potest ignorari, quia Spiritus Sanctus non voluit hoc certis et perspicuis testimoniis patefacere, quae verba sunt b. Chemnitii P. I. LL. CC. de Pecc. Orig. fol. 236.

Secutus autem is est vestigia Augustini, qui, cum in Ep. XXVIII. ad Hieron. quaestionem de origine animae et contracta labe peccati originalis tractasset, in Epistola seq. XXIX. mentionem faciens prioris, Eleganter, ait, dictum esse naricatur, quod huic rei satis apte convenit. Cum quidam ruisset in puteum, ubi aqua tanta erat, ut eum magis exciperet, ne moreretur, quam suffocaret, ne loqueretur, accessit alius, et eo viso admirans, ait: Quomodo huc cecidisti? At ille: obsecro, inquit, cogita, quomodo hinc me liberes, non, quomodo huc ceciderim, quaeras. Ita quoniam fatemur et fide catholica tenemus de reatu peccati, tanquam de puteo, etiam parvuli infantis animam Christi gratia liberandam, satis est ei, quod modum, quomodo salva fiat, novimus, etiamsi nunquam, quomodo in malum illud devenerit, noverimus. Haec Augustinus l. c.

Quemadmodum autem hactenus de origine animae paulo soliditius in scholis theologorum disquiri coepit, ita factum est, ut propagatiönem peccati originalis per carnalem generationem aliter explicarent, qui sententiam de propagatione animae per traducem, aliter, qui sententiam de creatione animae amplectebantur.

Et quidem, quando statuitur, peccatum originis, in se, abstractive et formaliter sumtum, esse privationem seu carentiam justitiae originalis, adeoque hoc ipso, quod non est entitas positiva, sed mera privatio, non agnoscere causam efficientem, cujus reali et positivo influxu producatur, jam simul apparet, modum propagationis statui negativum, quippe qui consistat in non-productione formae oppositae, justitiae originalis, seu quod, cum anima efficienter producitur, non simul justitia originalis in et cum ea producatur.

Sic ergo illi quidem, qui propagationem animae per traducem statuunt, id indicare videntur, quod cum parentes, velut causae

secundae, producunt, tanquam de suo, et largiuntur soboli animam rationalem, Deo tanquam causa prima concursum generalem impertiente, ideo iidem, quorum animae justitiam originalem jam in primis parentibus perdiderunt, non possint in actu generationis una cum anima transferre ad liberos aut propagare justitiam originalem, qua ipsi carent, sed largiantur animam originali justitia destitutam et sic peccato corruptam, prout etiam Deus concursum suum praebeat ad propagationem animae in sobolem, non autem ad propagationem justitiae originalis. Qui vero creationem animarum statuunt, existimant, peccatum originis sic propagari, quod cum primi parentes lapsu suo reatum auferendae justitiae originalis sibi contraxissent atque hanc revera, sua culpa quidem ac justo Dei judicio, perdidissent, intuitu hujus lapsus et culpae jam denegetur a Deo, in productione animarum sobolis, influxus ad comproducendam justitiam originalem, qui alias, si homines in statu integritatis mansissent, semper in actu generationis concursurus fuisset creando animam cum justitia originali. Post lapsum enim, a communi parente generis humani commissum, jam deinde hominem quemvis ad generationem sobolis, veluti effectus sibi connaturalis, non exigere concursum causae primae ad producendam cum anima sobolis justitiam originalem, cum effectus connaturalis non sit perfectior sua causa. Quod si vero peccatum originis, in se, abstracbive et formaliter spectatum, dicatur esse non mera privatio, sed ens positivum, quod per realem ac positivum causae efficientis influxum produci ac propagari postulet, sane utrinque difficultas insignis apparet, ne Deum causam peccati originalis propagati statuas, sive animam a parentibus per traducem, Deo tamen tanquam causa prima concurrente, propagari, sive eam a Deo immediate creari statuas. Confer b. Mus. Ausführl. Erklärung Q. XXX. et XXXV. p. 301. sqq. Cui in hac re admodum difficili atque dubia placet Augustini modestia malentis έπέχειν. § 15.

Describi potest peccatum originis, quod sit carentia justitiae originalis,a per lapsum Adami b ad omnes hornines c per carnalem generationem propagata,d ipsam naturam hominis omnesque animae facultates e intime corrumpens, ad bona spiritualia prosequenda ineptos, ad mala autem quaevis propensos reddens eosque adeo subjiciens f irae divinae et morti aeternae, nisi intercedat remissio peccatorum propter Christi meritum fide apprehensum. Quam in casu recto significat. Et confer § 2. sqq. Tanquam causam meritoriam aut causalitatem causae efficientis moralis; vid. § 7. et 8. Qui sunt subjectum Quod; vid. § 11. PART. II. CAP. III.

Quae partim ad causam efficientem peccati orig., uti in singulis est, pertinent, juxta § 8. not. d., partim affectionem hujus peccati in se spectati designant; vid. § 14. Moralitatis quidem capaces; quae sunt subjectum Quo primarium; vid. § 2. sqq. et § 12. In quibus effectus peccati originalis consistit; vid. § 13.§ 16.

Accidit a peccato originali,b quod in aliquibus regnat,c in aliis nοn d regnat. Per se quidem tendit ad dominium in omnibus exercendum; quia tamen per gratiam Dei non raro impeditur, ne regnet, ideo utrumque ei accidere dicimus. Seu pravae illi et connatae concupiscentiae. Certe Scripturae stylo το regnare et non regnare peccato inhaerenti, quod nobis connatum est (non aeque actibus secundis, seu peccatis actualibus voluntariis) tribuitur. Vid. Rom. 6, 12. Quanquam et peccata habitualia, crebris actionibus acquisita, dominari aut regnare in homine dici possunt, quoad usque non minuuntur, sed vigent et ad frequentanda actualia peccata stimulant. Seu irritationibus suis obsequentem habet hominem, velut dominus imperio suo servum, rex subditum. Confer Rom. 6, 16. 17. Quando ejus motibus resistitur atque ita imperium eripitur, quamvis ipsum supersit, ut homo, liberior factus, non ambulet secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum, Rom. 8, 1., aut si quid mali fiat, id tamen non tam faciat ipse volens, quam peccatum inhabitans, nolente ipso, prout servus aliquid facit, nolente domino, aut subditus, invito rege.Caput III.


## 15 Concerning Actual Sins

CONCERNING ACTUAL SINS. § 1. Actual sin, by the force of the word, is sin which is perfected by some act or by acting. But regarding the thing itself, it must be admitted that actual sins ought to be considered not only those which are committed by acting, but also those which are committed by not acting.

For just as some laws are about things to be done, and others about things to be omitted, so sins, being opposed to the laws, are committed some by doing what is prohibited by law, others by not doing, or by omitting, an act commanded by law.

2. Therefore, an actual sin is described as an action or the omission of an action, repugnant to the eternal law of God. Thus, the material [element], which is signified in the nominative case, and which is posited as twofold and disjunctive, is indicated. This is the formal [element], which pertains to actual sin, not insofar as it is something actual, but insofar as it is constituted in the being of sin and is distinguished from acts and omissions of actions that are right or indifferent.

Gerhard: "Some things are sins in themselves, while others are so κατ' άλλο, on account of something else. Thus, when unbelievers steal, commit fornication, plunder, etc., those are acts that are sins in themselves and by nature; but when they cover the nakedness of their neighbor, assist him, etc., those are not sins in themselves and as to the nature of the act, but they become sins through and on account of something else, because the person is not yet reconciled to God, because such works do not proceed from a pure heart, because they are not directed to the glory of God. The use of this division is manifold. Dr. Luther used to say: 'The righteous man sins in every good work'; Bellarmine gravely agitates against this; but observe, the good works of the regenerate are not called sins in themselves and as to the substance of the act, for they are a worship most pleasing to God and an odor of sweetness before Him; but because sin adheres to the regenerate as they do good, and because those very good works are not perfectly good, therefore in this respect it is most truly said that the righteous man sins in every good work and that the good works of the regenerate are sins, namely κατά τί, on account of the depraved concupiscence adhering to them and their manifold imperfection, on account of which God could repudiate the very good works of the regenerate if He were to demand them according to the rigid norm of the law, and hence it is that Is. 64:6 pronounces [as it does]." (L. de pecc. act. § 104.) §

3. The efficient cause of actual sin is the sinning man, insofar as, while he is the physically efficient cause of the positive act to which ἀνομία adheres, he thereby becomes the moral cause of the adhering ἀνομία, and insofar as, by not doing what he ought to have done, he thereby claims the ἀνομία of that omission entirely for himself. However, we look here at actual sin, not just any kind, but that which falls upon the subject of theology, that is, upon man as a wayfarer. See above, Chapter I, § 8 and 9.
