For although the omission of a commanded act, viewed in itself, is nothing but a negation, and thus is not considered something positive and really producible, nevertheless man is judged to be its cause, partly because he is the cause of some action which is incompossible with the action commanded by the law, which ought to have been done here and now, and partly because sometimes man elicits within himself an act of the will to omit a commanded act, especially an external one. PART II. CHAPTER III.

4. God is by no means, nor can He be called, the cause of actual sin, as such. As we noted above regarding sin in general in Chapter I, § 10: neither by obliging through His precept to perform a vicious act, nor by immediate or mediate, hidden or manifest persuasion, inducing one to such an act, nor by a special positive influx bending, determining, or necessitating one to it, nor by directing the action of man to an object from which it formally and per se has its character as sin. For all these things must be absent from Him who is not the cause of sin, as such. Whence we also judge, with the blessed Musaeus (*Ausführl. Erklärung* Q. XXXIX, p. 310), that one must abstain from that scandalous phrase by which it is said that God is the cause of sin *per accidens*.

Musaeus: "Those theologians, and partly philosophers, who have fallen into dispute over this phrase or form of speech (*Deum esse causam peccati per accidens*) have explained their opinion, namely, that they do not understand it *de causa peccati per accidens* on the part of the cause, but *de causa per accidens* on the part of the effect, and that in this formula the addition 'per accidens' is a *terminus alienus* and imports a negation of a true cause; that the assertion: *Deus est causa peccati per accidens* on the part of the effect, has no other meaning than this: that God is not the cause of the sin itself, but only of the effect with which the sin is conjoined beyond God's intention and without any influx of His... Whatever the case may be, this is certain: the phrase is scandalous." (*Ausführl. Erklärung der Jenaischen Theologen*. Jena 1677, p. 309 sq.)

Luther: "Regarding the evil that God does, why do you contend? You are idle, I see, in the midst of such great movements of Satan. It does not require a work, nor is it a work, that which you dispute about, but it is the omission of the work of God. For we do evil things because He ceases to work in us and allows nature to act in its own malice, which it does. Otherwise, where He Himself works, nothing but good follows. And this omitting of God, Scripture calls hardening. For evil cannot be done, since it is nothing; but it comes to be when the good is not done or is hindered." (*Briefe ges. von de Wette*, II, 181.)

The same: "The reader must be admonished concerning the property which the Hebrew language possesses. For thus it is read in the Hebrew: 'And the bones which Thou hast broken shall exult.' There is, however, a great scruple here as to why the prophets observe with singular zeal to pronounce that evils come from God Himself, when it is nevertheless true that God does not do evils *per se*, but uses intermediate instruments. For thus the Lord says in Job: 'Thou hast moved me against him, to destroy him without cause' (Job 2), when the history clearly shows that the devil burned the house, killed the children, and persuaded [him to] despair and murmuring against God. These, I say, are truly the works of the devil, and yet the Lord says: 'I have afflicted him.' In the same manner, David also says here: 'Thou hast broken my bones,' when yet God did nothing other than withdraw His hand and His Spirit, and left David to be exercised by the fiery darts of Satan... Such an instrument or medium is also the Law, through which sins are accused and condemned. God uses these means, however, so that He may humble us and take away the presumption of our works, so that we may simply learn that we live by the grace and kindness of God alone. But let us respond to the argument: Why are these things attributed to God, when He does not properly do them, but uses His means—Satan kills, the Law accuses—and yet they attribute both to God in the sacred..."

letters? The reason for this is that we may be kept in the article of our faith, that there is only one God, lest we make many gods with the Manichaeans. For they posited two principles, of which one was good and the other evil; in good things they ran to the good God, in evil things to the evil god.

But God wills that we have confidence in Him alone, both in favorable and in adverse circumstances; He does not want us to be among those of whom Isaiah says: "The people did not turn to Him who struck them." For this is what our nature is accustomed to do: in sudden terrors and dangers, it turns away from the true God because it believes Him to be angry, just as Job says: "You have become cruel to me." But this is to imagine another God and not to remain in the simplicity of faith, that there is one God. For God is not cruel, but is the Father of consolation. However, because He suspends His aid, our hearts immediately make an idol of an angry God out of the God who is always like Himself and constant. The prophets wish to forbid this when they say with one voice: "I am the Lord, who create good and evil," so that we do not think, when the sun is hindered by clouds, that the sun has been entirely removed from the world, or that it has turned from a luminous body into a black and dark one; for the sun retains its light, but we are hindered by the clouds so that we cannot see it. Thus God is good, just, and merciful, even when He strikes. He who does not believe this departs from the unity of faith, that there is one God, and imagines for himself another God who is unlike Himself, now good, now evil. But it is a distinguished gift of the Holy Spirit to believe that God, when He sends evils, is propitious and merciful." (On Ps. 51:8. Exegetical Latin Works. Ed. Irmischer. Erlangen, 1847. Vol. XIX, 104 ff.) §

5. Other causes of actual human sin occur both outside the human being and within him. There, the devil and the world, or things and people contained in this world; here, the ignorance of the intellect, the affections or passions, or the motions of the sensitive appetite, and the malice of the will. §

6. The devil is a cause of human sin, insofar as he partly proposes to man objects that invite him to sin, partly persuades him himself, or supplies the counsel for committing a crime, and partly excites certain imaginations in the fantasy, or even, by altered humors, excites passions in the sensitive appetite, by which men are induced to sin.

See John 8:44 and 1 John 3:8. For when evil men and slanderers, as such, are said to be from the devil as their father, and to comply with the desires of their father when they sin, the devil is certainly said to contribute something, and indeed a great deal, to those sins by way of a cause. Cf. 2 Cor. 4:4, where the god of this world is said to blind the minds of the unbelievers, lest the light of the gospel shine upon them. He is therefore the cause of their actual and malicious resistance, which they oppose to the Holy Spirit and the Word that is about to kindle faith. And in Eph. 2:2, the same Spirit is said to ἐνεργεῖν, to work effectively in the sons of disobedience, that is, in unbelieving men, with respect to various trespasses and sins, παραπτωμάτων καὶ ἁμαρτιῶν, in which PART II. CHAP. III.

they walk and conduct themselves in the concupiscences of their flesh, doing what is pleasing to the flesh and the mind. Cf. Acts 5:3, where the lie of Ananias is ascribed to Satan, who filled his heart. Thus, in Gen. 3:6, Satan, lurking in the serpent, is read to have presented to Eve the fruit of the forbidden tree, by which Eve’s appetite was objectively moved to covet, and so that the external act of eating might follow. Likewise, in the same place, verses 4 and 5, Satan commended the act of eating that fruit to Eve and persuaded her to perform it, using an argument taken from utility, or from a fuller conformity with God and a more excellent dignity that would follow. Cf. 1 Chron. 21:1, where it is recorded how Satan incited David to number the people. See John 13:2, where it is indicated how the devil not only induced Judas to want to betray Christ by means of arguments suited for persuasion, but also taught him the manner in which that act could be accomplished without hindrance and conveniently, εὐκαίρως; which is the mark of one who counsels. Cf. Luke 22:3 and 6. The example of Saul pertains here, whom Satan troubled and, in that state of frenzy, as it were, incited to cast a javelin at the innocent. See 1 Sam. 16:15 and ch. 18:10, 11. Although dreams proceeding from the devil, by which men are enticed to sins or commit them, may not undeservedly be referred here. § 7

Latin:

DE PECCATIS ACTUALIBUS. § 1. Peccatum actuale vi vocis est peccatum, quod actu quodam aut agendo perficitur. Sed quoad rem ipsam fatendum est, peccata actualia censeri a debere, non solum quae aqendo, verum etiam quae non agendo fiunt.

Quemadmodum enim leges quaedam sunt de faciendis, aliae de omittendis, ita peccata, legibus opposita, alia quidem agendo, quod lege prohibitum est, alia non agendo, seu omittendo actum lege praeceptum patrantur.

2. Itaque describitur peccatum actuale, quod sit actio aut actionis omissio,a pugnans cum lege b Dei aeterna. Ita materiale, quod in casu recto significatur, idque duplex ac disjunctive positum, indicatur. Hoc formale est, quod peccato actuali, non quatenus actuale quiddam est, sed quatenus in esse peccati constituitur et ab actibus atque omissionibus actionum rectis aut indifferentibus distinguitur, competit.

Gerhardus: ,,Quaedam sunt per se peccata, quaedam vero κατ' άλλο, propter aliud. Sic quando infideles furantur, fornicantur, rapiunt etc., ea sunt per se et natura actus peccata; quando vero cooperiunt nuditatem proximi, eidemque subveniunt etc., ea ex se et quoad naturam actus non sunt peccata, sed per ac propter aliud fiunt peccata, quia persona Deo nondum est reconciliata, quia talia opera non procedunt ex puro corde, quia non diriguntur ad Dei gloriam. Usus hujus divisionis est multiplex. Dicebat Dr. Lutherus: ,Justum in omni bono opere peccare‘; graviter hoc exagitat Bellarminus; sed observa, bona opera renatorum non dici peccata per se et quoad substantiam actus, sunt enim cultus Deo gratissimus et odor suavitatis coram ipso; sed quia renatis bona operantibus adhaeret peccatum et quia illa ipsa bona opera non sunt perfecte bona, ideo hoc respectu verissime dicitur, justum in omni opere bono peccare et bona opera renatorum esse peccata, nimirum κατά τί, propter adhaerentem pravam concupiscentiam et multiplicem imperfectionem, propter quam Deus ipsa renatorum bona opera repudiare posset, si ad rigidam legis normam ea velit exigere, atque inde est, quod Es. 64, 6. . . pronuntiat.“ (L. de pecc. act. § 104.) §

3. Causa efficiens peccati actualis a est homo peccans, quatenus, dum actus positivi, cui adhaeret ανομία, causa physice efficiens est, hoc ipso ανομίας adhaerentis causa moralis evadit,b et quatenus non agens, quod agere debebat, hoc ipso ανομίαν istius omissionis sibi omnino vendicat.c Spectamus autem hic peccatum actuale, non qualecunque, sed quod in subjectum theologiae, id est, in hominem viatorem cadit. Vid. supra cap. I. § 8. et 9. Etsi enim omissio actus praecepti in se spectata non nisi negatio sit, adeoque non aliquid positivum et realiter producibile censeatur, tamen homo ejus causa judicatur, partim, quod est causa alicujus actionis, quae est incompossibilis cum actione lege praecepta, quam hic et nunc fieri oportebat, partim, quod nonnunquam homo in se ipso elicit actum voluntatis de omittendo actu praecepto, inprimis externo. PART. II. CAP. III.

4. Deus peccati actualis, qua talis, causa a neutiquam b est aut dici potest.c Prout supra de peccato in genere monuimus cap. I. § 10. Neque obligando per praeceptum suum ad exercendum actum vitiosum, neque suasione immediata aut mediata, occulta aut manifesta, inducendo ad ejusmodi actum, neque influxu positivo speciali flectendo, determinando aut necessitando ad eum, neqm actionem hominis dirigendo ad objectum, a quo ea formaliter et per se habet, ut sit peccatum. Haec enim omnia abesse oportet ab eo, qui non est causa peccati, qua talis. Unde etiam ab ea scandalosa phrasi, qua dicitur, Deum esse camam peccati per accidem, abstinendum esse, censemus cum b.

Musaeo Ausführl. Erklärung Q XXXIX. p. 310.Musaeus: ,,Diejenigen Theologi, theils Philosophi, die an dieser Phrasi oder Redensart (Deum esse causam peccati per accidens) in Streit gerathen, haben ihre Meinung erklärt, nämlich dass sie solche nicht verstehen de causa peccati per accidens ex parte causae, sed de causa per accidens exparte effectus, und dass in dieser Formel der Zusatz,per accidens‘ ein terminus alienus sei und importire eine negationem verae causae; dass die assertio: Deus est causa peccati per accidens ex parte effectus, keine andere, als diese Meinung habe: Deum non esse causam ipsius peccati, sed tantum effectus, cum quo peccatum praeter Dei intentionem et absque ullo ejus influxu conjungitur. . . Quicquid tandem sit, certum hoc est, phrasin esse scandalosam.“ (Ausführl. Erklärung der Jenaischen Theologen. Jena 1677. p. 309. sq.)

Lutherus: ,,De malo, quod facit Deus, quid est quod contendatis? otiosi estis, video, in tantis motibus satanae. Non indiget opere, nec est opus, de quo disputatis, sed est omissio operis Dei. Ideo enim nos mala facimus, quia ille cessat in nobis operari, et sinit naturam in sua malitia agere, quod agit. Alioqui ubi ipse operatur, non nisi bonum sequitur. Et hoc omittere Dei vocat Scriptura indurare. Malum enim non potest fieri, cum sit nihil; sed hinc fit, cum bonum non fit vel impeditur.“ (Briefe ges. von de Wette. II, 181.)

Idem: ״Admonendus est lector de proprietate, quam habet Hebraeus. Sic enim in hebraeo legitur: Et exsultabunt ossa, quae tu contrivisti. Est autem hic magnus scrupulus, cur prophetae singulari studio hoc observent, ut pronuntient mala ab ipso Deo venire, cum tamen verum sit, Deum per se mala non facere, sed uti mediis instrumentis. Nam sic in Hiob dicit dominus: ,Tu me coegisti, ut eum affligerem frustra‘, Hiob 2., cum tamen historia clare ostendat, diabolum incendisse domum, occidisse liberos, suasisse desperationem et murmur contra Deum. Haec, inquam, vere diaboli opera sunt, et tamen dicit dominus: Ego afflixi eum. Ad eundem modum dicit hic David quoque: Tu contrivisti ossa mea, cum tamen Deus nihil aliud fecerit, quam quod subtraxerit manum et Spiritum suum, et reliquerit Davidem exercendum ignitis telis satanae. . . Tale instrumentum seu medium est lex quoque, per quam accushntur et damnantur peccata. Utitur autem his mediis Deus ideo, ut humiliet nos et eximat praesumtionem nostrorum operum, ut simpliciter discamus nos sola gratia et benignitate Dei vivere. Sed respondeamus ad argumentum: Cur ista tribuuntur Deo, cum ea proprie non faciat, sed utatur mediis suis, satan occidit, lex accusat, et tamen Deo utrumque tribuunt sacrae

literae? Ejus rei haec causa est, ut retineamur in articulo fidei nostrae, quod tantum sit unus Deus, ne cum Manichaeis plures faciamus deos. Hi enim ponebant duo principia, quorum unum bonum, alterum malum esset, in bonis currebant ad bonum Deum, in malis ad malum Deum.

Vult autem Deus nos tum in secundis tum in adversis rebus in se uno habere fiduciam, non vult nos inter eos esse, de quibus Esaias dicit: ,Non est populus conversus ad percutientem se.· Nam hoc solet na· tura nostra, in subitis terroribus et periculis a vero Deo avertitur, quia credit eum esse iratum, sicut Hiob: ,Es mihi factus in crudelem.‘ Hoc autem est alium fingere Deum, et non manere in simplicitate fidei, quod sit unus Deus. Neque enim Deus est crudelis, sed est pater consolationis. Quia autem suspendit auxilium, ideo mox corda nostra ex Deo semper sui simili et constanti faciunt idolum iratum. Hoc volunt prophetae prohibere, cum uno ore dicunt: ,Ego dominus, qui creo bonum et malum·, ne cogitemus, cum sol impeditur nubibus, omnino solem e mundo sublatum, aut ex lucido corpore atrum et obscurum factum esse, retinet enim sol lumen suum, sed nubibus impedimur nos, ne id possimus videre. Sic Deus est bonus, justus et misericors, etiam cum percutit. Qui hoc non credit, is discedit ab unitate fidei, quod sit unus Deus, et fingit sibi alium Deum, qui sui sit dissimilis, jam bonus, jam malus. Sed donum insigne Spiritus Sancti est, credere Deum, cum mala immittit, esse propitium et misericordem.“ (Ad Ps. 51, 8. Exeget. opp. lat. Cur. Irmischer. Erlang. 1847. Yol. XIX, 104. sqq.) §

5. Aliae autem causae peccati actualis humani cum extra hominem, tum intra eum occurrunt. Illic diabolus et mundus, sive res et homines, in hoc mundo contenti; hic ignorantia intellectus, affectus seu passiones, aut motus appetitus sensitivi, et malitia voluntatis. §

6. Diabolus causa peccati humani est,a quatenus,partim objecta, quae ad peccandum invitent, homini proponit,b partim suadet ipse,c aut consilium perficiendi criminis suppeditat,d partim certas imaginationes in phantasia, aut etiam alteratis humoribus passiones in appetitu sensitivo excitat,e quibus homines ad peccatum inducantur.

Vid. Joh. 8, 44. et 1. Ep. Joh. dap. 3, 8. Quando enim homines mali et calumniatores, qua tales, dicuntur esse ex diabolo, tanquam patre, et desideriis patris sui, cum peccant, obsequi, dicitur sane diabolus ad peccata illa aliquid, ac plurimum quidem, conferre per modum causae. Conf. 2 Cor. 4, 4., ubi dicitur Deus saeculi hujus excoecare sensus incredulorum, ne illucescat illis lumen evangelii. Est ergo causa actualis ac malitiosae repugnantiae illorum, quam objiciunt Spiritui S. et verbo fidem accensuro. Et Ephes. 2, 2. dicitur idem Spiritus Ινεργεϊν, efficaciter agere in filiis incredulitatis, hominibus infidelibus, respectu variorum delictorum et peccatorum, παραπτωμάτων xa\ άμαρτιων, in quibus PART. II. CAP. III.

illi ambulant et conversantur in concupiscentiis carnis suae, facientes, quae carni ac menti libent. Conf. Act. 5, 3., ubi Ananiae mendacium adscribitur satanae, cor illius implenti. Sic Gen. 3, 6. satanas, in serpente latens, fructum arboris vetitae, quo appetitus Evae objective moveretur ad concupiscendum, atque ut actus externus comestionis sequeretur, Evae exhibuisse legitur. Ita 1. c. vers. 4. 5. argumento ab utili, seu secutura pleniore conformitate cum Deo et excellentiore dignitate desumto actum comedendi fructum illum Evae commendavit satanas et persuasit, ut ex erceret. Conf. 1 Paral. 21, 1., ubi memoratur, quomodo satanas incitaverit Davidem ad numerandum populum. Vid. Joh. 13, 2., ubi indicatur, quomodo diabolus non solum argumentis ad persuadendum accommodatis Judam induxerit, ut vellet Christum prodere, verum etiam docuerit, qua ratione actus ille sine impedimento et commode, εύχαφως, posset perfici; quod consulentis est. Conf. Luc. 22, 3. et 6. Pertinet huc exemplum Saulis, quem satanas perturbavit et in illo quasi raptu ad jaciendum telum in insontes excitavit. Vid. 1 Sam. 16, 15. et cap. 18, 10. 11. Quanquam et somnia a diabolo profecta, quibus homines ad peccata pelliciuntur aut peccant, huc non immerito referantur..7 §


### Concerning Actual Sins: Meanwhile, the devil does not necessitate or immediately determine the human…

Meanwhile, the devil does not necessitate or immediately determine the human will to sin, but men consent to the impostor of their own accord. See James 4:7, where it is said that men can resist the devil, who incites them to sin, so that he may flee from them. But he who can be resisted in this way does not himself necessitate one to sin. Cf. Eph. 6:11, 12, 13; 1 Pet. 5:9. Certainly, men could withstand the beginnings—at least those who are whole or who are being governed—so that they might not be led by Satan into great sins or become his slaves, although those who have once consented to him or submitted their necks to his yoke are easily precipitated into worse or extreme things and, as it were, led captive alive to do his will, 2 Tim. 2:26. To this pertain the things we said concerning spiritual obsession in Part I, Chapter III, § 51, p. 136.

Huelsemannius: "What are the modes by which Satan acts? Are they merely moral persuasions based on the pleasant, the useful, the hateful, etc., as in the persuasion to robbery? Or are they also physical, whether through the intrinsic determination of the intellect, the will, and the affections, or through the extrinsic locomotive power of the body, the hands, and the feet? See Feurborn’s Treatise on the Sin against the Holy Spirit, ch. 2, and Meisner’s Anthropology, Dec. I, D. 3, q. 4, th. 4, which you should read cautiously. To us, it seems the matter can be resolved by a distinction between reigning sins and non-reigning sins, which are resisted daily. For in reigning sins, it is evident that the devil acts not only through persuasions and suggestions, but also through the determination of the locomotive power, as is clear from the words and examples of robbers, self-murderers, sorcerers, and others whom the devil leads captive to do his own will. 2 Tim. 2, last verse."

Kromayerus: "Nor does (the devil) force men to sin by suggesting wicked thoughts, but only persuades and incites them, to which they can also, by the grace of God, if they wish, offer resistance and oppose by pious prayers." (Th. pos. pol. II, 140.) §

8. Men, who are called by the name of the world, become the cause of another’s sin by providing objects, by persuading, by counseling, and by inviting through their own example. These things they have in common with Satan. Whence the world is called the bride of Satan, and impious men or those of the world are called the instruments of the devil.

See concerning their seductions Proverbs 1:10. Compare the examples of Jeroboam, 1 Kings 15:26; the concubines of Solomon, 1 Kings 11:3; the false prophets who persuaded Ahab to an unjust war, being instigated by Satan, 1 Kings 22:21 ff.; 2 Chronicles 18:19 ff.

And thus scandals are said to come, Matthew 18:6, 7, which are themselves sins and the proximate cause or occasion of sinning, by which, namely, men are offended in the course of this life, so that, regarding their actions, they are either drawn away from the good, so that they work more sluggishly or not at all, or are led into evil, which they would not otherwise perform, whether knowingly and willingly, or through imprudence. Conf. Wisdom 4:11, 12.

Crusius: "Scandal [Aergerniss] here means as much as a stumbling block, upon which one can strike, be damaged, or over which one can fall; hence one also says of that which brings one into misfortune that it has become a scandal to him, 1 Peter 2: 7. In the moral sense, therefore, scandal means something whereby one becomes worse or can easily become so. This meaning of the word is not to be confused with another, in which 'to be scandalized' [sich ärgern] means as much as to be angered, and 'to scandalize another' [einen andern ärgern] means as much as to provoke him to anger, Matthew 23: 16.

In such a broad meaning, scandal is to be divided into that which is given and that which is taken. A taken scandal is an occasion for error and sin which one takes from the words or actions of another without the other’s fault, because one errs oneself and judges poorly, e.g., Matthew 11:6; John 6: 61.

A given scandal, however, is an occasion for sins or errors which one gives to others through that which one oneself teaches, speaks, or does, in such a way that a moral guilt can be imputed to us for it, whereby we make ourselves partakers of the other’s sin, Matthew 18:6 f.

It happens either by one sinning oneself, or by one not observing prudence. Thereby one can give scandal not only through that which is evil, but also through the misuse or careless use of permitted things, Romans 14:13 f.

In order to judge correctly concerning scandal, the following rules of caution, among others, are to be observed: a) One must take care not to neglect one’s express duty under the pretext that one does not wish to give scandal to others... b) In particular, one should not act against truthfulness and speak now one way, then another, because one pretends that one does not wish to scandalize anyone... c) One must not allow a yoke of human ordinances or erroneous teachings to be laid upon Christendom under the pretext that one is yielding to the weak in order not to scandalize them. Weak are called, in this case, those who do not yet have enough knowledge..." PART II. CHAP. III.

have, but who nevertheless have a good Christian heart and let their purpose be to live for God, Rom. 14:1, 6, 7. . . The defiant and proud spirit of error, however, and the domineering master over consciences is not weak, but is a dangerous and harmful person, against whose undertakings the divine truth and Christian liberty must be defended, Gal. 5:1. Therefore, Paul himself withstood Peter, who nevertheless thought in complete agreement with him (Acts 15:10), when he had once been hasty only in practical application, and because of the arrival of certain zealots for the Jewish law, had not wanted to be found eating with the Gentiles, which others could quite naturally interpret as his thereby admitting himself guilty of a fault, and approving the pretense that it was necessary for salvation to combine the keeping of Jewish statutes with faith in Jesus Christ, and to place a part of righteousness in these as well, Gal. 2:11, 12. Paul himself, however, gladly yielded to the weak in this, that he had patience with their ignorance, and with a good heart on their part and with good hope of their growth in what is good, he let nothing be lacking in love toward them and gladly avoided the occasion where something contentious might have occurred, into which they had not yet known how to find their way, and where divisions were to be feared, or where the uninformed party, with a doubtful conscience, might have followed others out of timidity and thought that a Christian does not need to take everything exactly. . .

d) One must take care not to become an occasion for sin to others through the careless use of innocent and permitted things because of the weakness of their knowledge or their disposition. This can happen in various ways. Sometimes others, out of fear of man, out of shyness before those of higher rank, or in order not to suffer shame, join in something against their conscience which they do not consider permitted. Those whom they follow may have a different conscience and may even be right, but they should rather not make use of their right where it becomes a snare to others, 1 Cor. 8:9–13; 10:23, 33. Furthermore, when opinions are divided over something, and the example and reputation of one moves the other to do the same, the former not only gives offense if the matter is an actual sin, and he thus induces the other to sin, but even if it was not a sin, he offends the latter if he performed the action under such circumstances that it could become probable to the latter that the former indeed considers it a sin, but is of the opinion that one may also knowingly commit small sins, or at least sins of this kind, and that it is not necessary in Christianity to take everything exactly, and that he deserves applause and imitation therein because he has the presumption in his favor that he understands the matter better.” (Kurzer Begriff der Moraltheologie. 11, 1557–1562.)

Balduinus: “Must those Lutherans who live in the papacy necessarily abstain from meat on Friday, so as not to offend the weaker ones in the papacy? Resp.: By no means, because the rule of Paul deals with such weak ones who are brothers, i.e., who in the other chapters of the Christian religion are ομόψηφοι with us.” (See Dedekenn’s Thesaurus consil. Appendix, f. 202.)

Lutherus: “What God does not forbid, but leaves free, that shall remain free for everyone, and one is to obey no one who forbids what God wants to have free; rather, everyone is obligated to act against such prohibitions with words and deeds and always to drive the opposite in defiance against them, Gal. 2:5. . . Well then, since they simply will not listen and want to prevent and suppress such divine liberty by force, they shall see and hear, in defiance of their mad power, everything that vexes them to the highest degree and offends them most bitterly. . . I have also taken a nun in marriage, although I could have...”

[I have] advised and had no particular reason, except that I have done it in defiance of the devil with his scales, the great bigwigs, princes, and bishops, who want to be quite nonsensical in claiming that ‘spiritual’ persons should be exempt. And I would gladly cause even more offense if I only knew of something more that would please God and vex them... But that some weak ones are also offended by it, that is not our fault, but the fault of the tyrants who hinder the Gospel so that it cannot reach that point and instruct the weak; therefore they must answer for it. Also, when it comes to the point that Christian and divine freedom is to be suppressed or violated, it is to be maintained more than [the feelings of] the weak. For God’s Word is of more importance than the whole world.” (Letter to N., 1526. Opp. Hal. T. X, 962 sqq.)

It happens, however, sometimes that pious men, who are at the same time weak, provide scandal to others by certain sins, even if they are not so great. § 9. The things of the world, which are subject to our senses, move the sensitive appetite and the will toward sins by way of an object.

Latin:

Interim diabolus non necessitat aut immediate determinat voluntatem humanam ad peccandum,a sed homines sponte consentiunt b impostori. Vid. Jac. 4, 7., ubi dicitur, homines posse resistere diabolo, ad peccandum incitanti, ut fugiat ab ipsis. Cui autem sic resisti potest, is non ipse necessitat ad peccandum. Conf. Ephes. 6, 11. 12. 13. 1 Petr. 5, 9. Certe principiis obstare poterant homines, saltem integri aut regendi, ne a satana in peccata grandia perducerentur aut mancipia ejus fierent, licet semel ei consentientes aut jugo colla subjicientes facile in deteriora aut extrema praecipitentur ac velut vivi capti ad voluntatem ejus circumducantur, 2 Tim. 2. ult. Quo pertinent, quae de obsessime spirituali diximus P. I. cap. III. § 51. p. 136.

Huelsemannijs: ,,Modi, quibus agat satan, utrum sint mere raorales persuasiones a jucundo, utili, odioso etc., ut in suasione rapinae; an vero etiam physici, tum per intrinsecam determinationem intellectus, voluntatis et affectuum, tum per extrinsecam locomotivam corporis, manuum ac pedum? Vide Feurbornii Tr. de pecc. in Sp. S. c. 2. et Meisn. Anthropol. Dec. I. D. 3. q. 4. th. 4., quem caute legeris. Nobis videtur res distinctione expediri posse inter peccata regnantia et non regnantia, quibus quotidie resistitur. In regnantibus enim diabolum non solum persuasiones et suggestiones agere, sed etiam per determinationem locomotivae, tum dictis, tum exemplis constat latronum, αντοχείμων, veneficarum atque aliorum, quos diabolus captivos ducit ad suammet voluntatem. 2 Tim. 2, v. ult.“

Kromayerus: ,,Nec etiam pravas cogitationes suggerendo ad peccandum homines (diabolus) cogit, sed tantum suadet et incitat, cui etiam per Dei gratiam, si volunt, resistere piisque precibus ipsi obviam ire possunt.“ (Th. pos.pol. II, 140.)§

8. Homines, qui mundi nomine appellantur, peccati alieni causa fiunt objecta subministrando, suadendo, consulendo a et exemplo suo b invitando.c Quae cum satana habent communia. Unde et mundus satanae sponsa et homines impii seu de mundo organa diaboli dicuntur.

Vide de seductionibus illorum Proverb. 1, 10. Confer exempla Jeroboarni 1 Reg. 15, 26., pellicum Salomonis 1 Reg. 11, 3., falsorum prophetarum, qui Achabo bellum injustum persuaserunt, instincti a satana, 1 Reg. 22, 21. sqq. 2 Chron. 18, 9. sqq.

Et sic dicuntur venire scandala Matth. 18, 6. 7., quae et ipsa peccata sunt, et proxima causa vel occasio peccandi, quibus videlicet homines in hujus vitae curriculo offenduntur, ut quoad actiones suas vel a bono abstrahantur, ut segnius aut plane non operentur, vel ad malum, alias non peragendum, sive scientes ac volentes, sive per imprudentiam, perducantur. Conf. Sap. 4, 11. 12.

Crusius: ״Aergerniss heisst hier so viel als Anstoss, woran man sich stossen, beschädigen oder worüber man fallen kann, daher man auch von dem, was einen in Unglück bringt, sagt, dass es ihm zum Aergerniss geworden sei 1 Pet. 2, 7. Im moralischen Verstände heisst also Aergerniss so etwas, wodurch einer ärger wird oder leicht werden kann. Diese Bedeutung des Wortes ist mit einer andern nicht zu verwechseln, in welcher sich ärgern soviel als erzürnen, und einen andern ärgern soviel als ihn zum Zorn reizen bedeutet, Matth. 23,16׳.

In soleher weiten Bedeutung ist das Aergerniss in ein gegebenes und genommenes einzutheilen. Ein genommenes Aergerniss ist ein Anlass zum Irrthum und Sünde, den man an den Worten oder Handlungen eines Andern ohne dessen Schuld nimmt, weil man selber irret und schlecht urtheilet, z. E. Matth. 11, 6. Joh. 6, 61.

Ein gegebenes Aergerniss aber ist eine Veranlassung zu Sünden oder Irrthümern, welche man durch das, was man selber lehret, redet oder thut, Andern auf so eine Art gibt, dass uns eine moralische Schuld daher zugerechnet werden kann, wodurch wir uns der Sünde des Andern theilhaftig machen, Matth. 18, 6. f.

Es geschiehet entweder dadurch, dass man selber sündigt, oder dass man die Klugheit nicht beobachtet. Dadurch kann man nicht nur durch das, was böse ist, sondern auch durch den Missbrauch oder unvorsichtigen Gebrauch erlaubter Dinge Aergerniss geben, Rom. 14, 13. f.

Um vom Aergerniss richtig zu urtheilen, sind unter andern folgendeN Regeln der Vorsichtigkeit zu beobachten, a) Man hüte sich, dass man nicht seine ausdrückliche Schuldigkeit verabsäume, unter dem Vorwande, dass man Andern nicht Aergerniss geben wolle. . . b) Insonderheit soll man der Wahrhaftigkeit nicht entgegen handeln, und etwan einmal so, das andere Mal anders reden, weil man vorgibt, dass man niemand ärgern wolle. . . c) Man lasse' der Christenheit kein Joch der Menschensatzungen oder irriger Lehren unter dem Vorwande auflegen, dass man den Schwachen nachgebe, um sie nicht zu ärgern. Schwache heissen in diesem Fall, die noch nicht Erkenntniss genug PART. II. CAP. III.

haben, aber doch ein gut christlich Herz haben und ihren Zweck sein lassen, Gott zu leben, Rom. 14, 1. 6. 7. . . Der trotzige und stolze Irrgeist aber und der herrschsüchtige Gebieter über die Gewissen ist nicht schwach, sondern er ist ein gefährlicher und schädlicher Mensch, wider dessen Unternehmungen die göttliche Wahrheit und die christliehe Freiheit vertheidigt werden muss, Gal. 5, 1. Daher widerstund Paulus selber Petro, der doch ganz einstimmig mit ihm dachte (Ap. Gesch. 15, 10.), da er einst nur in der practischen Anwendung sich übereilt hatte, und wegen der Ankunft gewisser Eiferer für das jüdische Gesetz sich nicht über dem Essen mit den Heiden hatte antreffen lassen wollen, welches andere ganz natürlich so auslegen konnten, als gebe er sich hiermit selbst eines Fehlers schuldig, und billige das Vorgeben, dass es zur Seligkeit nothwendig sei, mit dem Glauben an Jesum Christum die Haltung der jüdischen Satzungen zu verbinden, und auch in diesen einen Theil der Gerechtigkeit zu setzen, Gal. 2, 11. 12. Paulus selbst aber gab darinnen den Schwachen gern nach, dass er mit ihrer Unwissenheit Geduld hatte, bei einem guten Herzen derselben und bei guter Hoffnung ihres Wachsthums im Guten an der Liebe gegen sie nichts abgehen liess und der Gelegenheit gern auswich, wo etwas Streitiges hätte Vorkommen müssen, worein sie sich noch nicht zu finden gewusst hätten, und wo Trennungen zu besorgen gewesen wären, oder wo der unberichtete Theil mit zweifelhaftem Gewissen Andern aus Blödigkeit es nachgethan, und gedacht hätte, ein Christ brauche nicht alles genau zu nehmen. . .

d) Man hüte sich, dass man nicht durch unvorsichtigen Gebrauch unschuldiger und erlaubter Dinge Andern eine Veranlassung zur Sünde werde wegen Schwäche ihrer Erkenntniss oder ihres Gemüths. Dieses kann sich auf verschiedene Art ereignen. Manchmal machen Andere aus Menschenfurcht, aus Scheu vor Vornehmeren, oder um nicht Schande zu haben, etwas wider ihr Gewissen mit, was sie nicht für erlaubt halten. Jene, welchen sie folgen, können ein anderes Gewissen und sie können auch Recht haben, sollten sich aber ihres Rechtes lieber da nicht gebrauchen, wo es Andern zum Fallstrick wird, 1 Cor. 8, 9—13. C. 10, 23. 33. Ferner, wenn über etwas die Meinungen getheilt sind, und das Exempel und Ansehen des Einen den Andern bewegt, es nachzuthun, so gibt jener nicht nur Aergerniss, wenn die Sache wirkliche Sünde ist, und er also den Andern zur Sünde veranlasst, sondern wenn sie auch nicht Sünde war, so ärgert er diesen, wenn er die Handlung unter solchen Umständen that, wobei es diesem wahrscheinlich werden konnte, jener halte sie allerdings für Sünde, sei aber der Meinung, dass man kleine Sünden, oder wenigstens Sünden dieser Art, auch wissentlieh thun dürfe, und dass es nicht nöthig sei, im Christenthum eben Alles genau zu nehmen, und verdiene darinnen Beifall und Nachfolge, weil er die Präsumtion für sich habe, dass er die Sache besser verstehe.“ (Kurzer Begriff der Moraltheologie. 11,1557—1562.)

Balduinus: ,,An iis Lutheranis, qui in papatu vivunt, die Veneris necessario abstinendum a carnibus, ne offendant infirmiores in papatu? Resp.: Minime, quia regula Pauli agit de talibus infirmis, qui fratres sunt, i. e., qui in caeteris capitibus religionis Christianae nobis sunt ομόψηφοι.“ (Vid. Dedekenni thesaurus consil. Appendix, f. 202.)

Lutherus: ״Was Gott nicht verbeut, sondern freilässet, das soll jedermann frei bleiben, und niemand zu gehorchen ist, der da verbeut, das Gott will frei haben; sondern schuldig ist jedermann, wider solche Verbote mit Worten und Werken zu thun und immer das Widerspiel zu Trotz darwider zu treiben Gal. 2, 5. . . Wohlan, dieweil sie denn schlechts nicht hören und mit Gewalt solche göttliche Freiheit gewehret und gedämpft haben wollen, so sollen sie wieder zu Trotz ihrer tollen Gewalt alles das sehen und hören, was sie nur auf das allerhöheste verdreusst und auf das allerbitterste ärgert. . . Ich habe auch eine Nonne genommen zu der Ehe, wiewohl ich es hätte mögen ge

rathen und nicht sonderliche Ursache gehabt, denn dass ich es dem Teufel mit seinen Schuppen, den grossen Hannsen, Fürsten und Bischöfen, zu Trotz gethan habe, welche schlecht unsinnig wollen werden, dass,geistliche‘ Personen sollen frei sein. Und wollte gerne noch mehr Aergemiss anrichten, wenn ich nur was mehr wüsste, das Gott gefiele und sie verdrösse. . . Dass aber etliche Schwache auch sich daran ärgern, das ist nicht unser, sondern der Tyrannen Schuld, die dem Evangelio wehren, dass es nicht dahin kommen und die Schwachen unterrichten kann; darum müssen sie dafür antworten. Auch wenn es dahin kommt, dass christliche und göttliche Freiheit will gedämpft oder geschändet werden, ist derselbigen mehr wahrzunehmen, denn der Schwachen. Denn an Gottes Wort liegt mehr, denn an der ganzen Welt.“ (Schreiben an N. 1526. Opp. Hai. T. X, 962. sqq.)

Fit tamen etiam aliquando, ut homines pii, simul autem infirmi, peccatis quibusdam, licet non adeo magnis, scandalum aliis praebeant.§ 9. Res mundi, quae sensibus nostris subjiciuntur, appetitum sensitivum et voluntatem objecti ve movent a ad peccata.


### Concerning Actual Sins: See 1 John 2:15 sqq., where we are forbidden to love the things that are in the…

See 1 John 2:15 sqq., where we are forbidden to love the things that are in the world, because from this are born the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. Cf. the example of David, who, upon seeing the naked body of Bathsheba, was inflamed with lust, 2 Sam. 11:2. § 10. Within man, the efficient cause of actual sin is the very corrupted nature of man or, speaking abstractly, the very perversity innate to man, consisting in the lack of original righteousness and the depravity of concupiscence.

Thus, from within, from the heart of men, are said to proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, etc. Mark 7:21, 22, 23. And Rom. 7:17, Paul says that it is not he who commits what is done against the law, but the original sin, or depraved concupiscence, dwelling within him. Compare Gal. 5:19, where the works of the flesh, which proceed from carnal concupiscence, are variously enumerated. Compare above, Chapter II, § 8, notes d, e. § 11. Specifically, on the part of the intellect, ignorance is a cause of sins, insofar as it excludes the knowledge which would otherwise have hindered the act of sinning.

Whether it is that by which one does not know what he could have known and was bound to know, and thus acts in ignorance, which is against the law, yet would not have acted so if he had known. PART II. CHAPTER III.

set; by which reasoning an act that arises from ignorance is undoubtedly a sin. Or even that which so precedes the will that one is ignorant of what one could have known in a certain matter, or at least was bound to know; from which differs concomitant [ignorance], when one is ignorant of what one is doing, yet in such a way that, if one knew, one would still wish to do the same; and consequent [ignorance], which is either affected, or such that one simply wished to be ignorant of what one could have known, or supine, when one through one's own negligence is ignorant of what one could and ought to have known. Meanwhile, even ignorance consequent to the will, from which sin proceeds, whether it be affected or supine, is a sin.

Hollazius: "Antecedent ignorance is the cause that a man wills something which he would not have willed if he had known. Such ignorance exists when one is ignorant of those things which one could be ignorant of in this or that matter, and was not bound to know, and it coincides with invincible ignorance; e.g., when someone in battle, intending to kill an enemy, kills a brother whom he neither knew nor could have known to be present in that battle." (Exam. P. II. c. 4. q. 16. p. 545.) Dannhauerus: "Ignorance of fact diminishes sin and excuses from a certain species of sin, not from all sin. Judah’s union with Tamar is excused from the crime of incest, not from the crime of fornication." (Liber conscient. I, 107.)

And thus as a remover of an impediment, just as Paul says in 1 Tim. 1:13, that he had become a persecutor because he lacked the knowledge of the true religion, which, had he possessed it, he would not have allowed himself to be induced to persecute the true believers. § 12. On the part of the sensitive appetite, the causes of sins are passions or affections, insofar as they partly distract or hinder the will, so that it tends either more remissly or not at all toward the objects commended to it by the intellect, partly disturb the imaginative faculty and thus draw the very judgment of the intellect, and through it the will, toward sensible goods, and finally, if they are very vehement, by their own weight, as it were, cast the will down toward a sensible good, against the dictate of reason.

See James 1:14. For concupiscence in that place denotes the sin innate to us, but when it is said to "conceive," it signifies the inordinate motions, or the passions proceeding from it, which are indeed themselves sins, yet at the same time are causes from which further sins, so-called κατ' ἐξοχήν, or sinful external acts, arise, and those even more grave, precipitating man from the state of grace into the guilt of death. And to this pertain the things which philosophers discuss concerning incontinence and its species, precipitation and infirmity, and their acts. Quenstedtius: "The word 'act' and 'actual' is taken here not strictly, for external works and sins of commission only, but broadly, so that it also embraces internal vicious motions, both first and second, as well as sins of omission."

For example, when sudden fear restrains a man from exercising an act of fortitude or the profession of faith, just as Peter, about to go to Jesus over the waves, but terrified by a stronger wind, cast away his courage in the act commanded by Christ, Matt. 14:29, 30, 34. The same man, also fearing the Jews, withdrew himself from the fellowship of the converted Gentiles, Gal. 2:12. Thus, the affections of love are said to "blind" the wise intellect. To this pertain those things which are handed down in the schools of the philosophers concerning the closest connection of the sensitive appetite with the rational appetite, i.e., the will. And experience teaches how love or more vehement anger sometimes degenerates into fury or insanity. §

13. On the part of the will, the cause of sin is habitual malice, from which one, knowing and willing, girds himself to sin. Acquired by more frequently repeated sinful acts; or, where, apart from the ignorance of the intellect and the passion of the sensitive appetite, and rather by previous consultation, that which is evil is freely chosen, and sorrow and repentance do not immediately follow the perpetrated action. For otherwise, evil men can also commit sins out of a certain passion. In this place, however, they are viewed insofar as, although they sin with affections, they do not, however, sin equally out of passion or a more vehement affection, but by a freer will. See 2 Tim. 3:1 sqq., where the apostle exhibits a lengthy catalog of the sins of malice. §

14. Insofar as Satan, men who are in this world, our own corrupted nature, and the affections themselves are said to tempt us to sins, whether regarding spiritual or secular matters, by flattering or by terrifying. Concerning which we spoke above in § 6. See § 8. According to § 10. See § 12. Or by way of cause they contribute something to the end that we sin, whether they obtain it without impediment, or whether, while we resist through grace, they are hindered and the sins to which we are impelled are not perpetrated. That is, to test whether they can do anything against us; to endeavor that they may abstract or restrain us from God and His true worship and the way of salvation, whether a direct intention is to be ascribed to those attempting it, or at least an indirect one. Otherwise, indeed, God is also said to tempt men when He explores their faith, obedience, patience, etc., or to provide certain proofs. PART II. CHAP. III.

provides the occasion or even the command (which is certain to be done for a good end), and a man is said to tempt God when he calls into doubt the word of God, His promises, commands, threats, as well as the perfections of His knowledge, wisdom, goodness, justice, and power, and rashly demands that they be proven by certain documents. And a man is said to tempt another man for the sake of his own (and perhaps lawful) advantage, or for the public good, or for the advantage of the one whom he is tempting, when he explores the powers of the mind or body, inclinations, studies, or progress. But these things are foreign to the present business. Dannhauer: "Augustine excellently says (Book 2, *De sermone Domini in monte*, ch. 14, and Epist. 121, ch. 11): 'It is one thing to be led into temptation, another to be tempted.' For no one can be proven without temptation, whether to himself or to another. Therefore, it is not prayed here (Matt. 6:13) that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be led into temptation, just as if someone who must be examined by fire were not to pray that he might not be touched by fire, but that he might not be burned. For although God does not of Himself lead us into temptation, yet, says Augustine, He suffers him to be led whom He has deserted by His most hidden order and for his merits; for by causes often manifest, He judges worthy the one whom He deserts and allows to be led into temptation. Jerome (on Matt. 26) says: 'It is impossible, he says, for the human soul not to be tempted, whence it is also said in the Lord’s Prayer: Lead us not into temptation, which we cannot bear; not refuting temptation entirely, but praying for the strength to sustain us in temptations.' And when Christ says: 'Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation,' this means: that temptation may not overcome and conquer you and hold you within its snares." (*Hodosoph.* p. 486.) Quenstedtius: "The apostle here (James 1:18) treats not of those temptations by which the faith, constancy, and patience of the pious are explored, but of those by which a man is solicited and instigated to evil or sin, and James affirms that these do not proceed from God. For πειράζεσθαι in this place is the same as to be incited and solicited to sin. A father tempts a son, a master a servant, a husband a wife, a teacher a disciple, in a different way, in order to explore, sharpen, and kindle their talent, affection, and zeal. 'In one signification,' says Augustine (Book 2, *De consensu evangelistarum*, ch. 30), 'is understood the temptation of which it is said: God tempts no one; and another, of which it is said: The Lord your God tempts you, that He may know if you love Him (Deut. 13). The former is of seduction, the latter of probation.'" (*L. c. P. IV. c. 10. s. 1. th. 2. f. 1432.*) For this is what we pray for in the Lord’s Prayer to our Father, that He may not lead us into temptation, i.e., that He may not suffer us to be tempted by the devil, the world, or our own flesh more severely than we can sustain and overcome by the powers of grace, and thus that He may not desert us when, if we were to fight alone, we would have to succumb, etc. Therefore, that threefold temptation is presupposed, from which not even the faithful and pious are immune, much less the unfaithful and impious, for whom the flesh is more vigorous, the world more familiar, and Satan closer. For example, to infidelity, atheism, heresy or heterodoxy, superstition, diffidence, despair, or on the contrary to hypocritical faith, to vain presumption concerning the state of grace or spiritual perfection, all of which revolve around spiritual objects: God, His word, supernatural goods, or the evils opposed to them. To this pertain the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, according to 1 John 2:16, by presenting things that delight, which excite inordinate love, hope, and joy. Thus, under the pretext of acquiring a great good, some are led to attempt things that are above their powers and their calling; under the pretext of justice, diligence, magnanimity, simplicity, liberality, recreation, peace or rest, or salutary tranquility, men are led to works of cruelty, avarice, pride, ignorance, profusion, intemperance, carnal security, etc. l) By presenting those things which are adverse, which beget fear, flight, and sadness. Just as by the singularity or novelty of a calamity, by the delay of help or liberation, by threats, deceitful reports, etc., even those who seemed to be of a strong spirit are drawn away from an honest purpose, or are cast into diffidence, despair, private vengeance, self-sufficiency, and the like. § 15. But also, preceding sins are wont to be the cause of subsequent sins, partly insofar as they incline toward similar sinful acts, and partly insofar as they shake off grace, upon the removal of which men rush into graver sins. For thus acts are commonly wont to leave behind them certain dispositions, inclining toward other similar acts, and when repeated more often, they beget a habit. And thus they are called a cause, insofar as they remove the impediment. § 16. The subject of actual sins *in which* (or of denomination) is the man himself who sins. § 17. The subject *by which* are the faculties of the human soul, which are the principles of human actions: the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite. Or that by means of which sins, as sins, affect man. And thus the ἀνομία (lawlessness) adhering to the act is referred to the same subject from which, as a principle, the act itself efficiently depends. By reason of the voluntary, however, all actual sins belong subjectively to the will, insofar as they are either commanded by it or approved. Secondarily, the members of the body are also said by some to be the subject of certain actual sins, which are conveniently called the organs of those sins by others. § 18. The effect of actual sin is partly a certain disposition of the will, through which it is inclined toward other acts.

Latin:

Vid. 1 Joh. 2, 15. sqq., ubi ea, quae in mundo sunt, diligere prohibemur, eo quod hinc nascuntur cupiditas carnis, libido oculorum et fastus vitae. Conf. exemplum Davidis, viso Bathsebae corpore denudato, libidine accensi, 2 Sam,. 11, 2.§ 10. Intra hominem causa efficiens peccati actualis est ipsa corrupta hominis natura vel, abstractive loquendo, ipsa connata homini perversitas, in carentia justitiae originalis et pravitate concupiscentiae consistens.

Sic ab interioribus, de corde hominum procedere dicuntur malae cogitaliones, adulteria, stupra, homicidia etc. Mare. 7, 21. 22. 23. Et Rom. 7, 17. dicit Paulus, non se patrare, quae fiunt contra legem, sed inhabitans in ipso peccatum originale, seu concupiscentiam pravam. Confer Gal. 5, 19., ubi opera carnis, quae a carnali concupiscentia proficiscuntur, varia recensentur. Confer supra cap. II. § 8. not. d. e. § 11. Speciatim ex parte intellectus ignorantia a causa est peccatorum, quatenus excludit scientiam, quae actum peccandi alias fuisset impeditura.b

Sive ea, qua quis nescit, quod poterat scire ac tenebatur, et sic ignorans agit, quod est contra legem, non tamen acturus, si scivis PART. II. CAP. III.

set; qua ratione actus, qui ex ignorantia oritur, haud dubie est peccatum. Sive etiam illa, quae sic antecedit voluntatem, ut quis ignoret, quod vel poterat scire in certa re, vel saltem tenebatur; a qua differt concomitam, cum quis ignorat, quod facit, ita tamen, ut, si sciret, idem facere vellet, et consequens, quae vel est affectata, seu talis, qua quis simpliciter voluit ignorare, quod scire poterat, vel supina, cum quis per negligentiam suam ignorat, quod scire poterat ac debebat. Interim et ipsa ignorantia voluntatem consequens, ex qua proficiscitur peccatum, sive affectata sit, sive supina, peccatum est.

Hollazius: ,,Antecedens ignorantia est causa, ut homo aliquid velit, quod non vellet, si scivisset. Talis ignorantia est, cum ea quis ignorat, quae nescire poterat in hac aut illa re, nec scire tenebatur, et coincidit cum ignorantia invincibili; v. g. cum quis in proelio hostem interfecturus interficit fratrem, quem nec scivit nec scire potuit proelio isti interesse.“ (Exam. P. II. c. 4. q. 16. p. 545.) Dannhauerus: ,,Ignorantia facti minuit peccatum et excusat a certa specie peccati, non peccato omni. Judae cum Thamare congressus excusatur ab incestus, non a scortationis crimine.“ (Liber conscient. I, 107.)

Adeoque tanquam removens impediens, prout Paulus 1 Tim. 1, 13. dicit, se persecutorem fuisse factum, cum careret scientia verae religionis, quam si habuisset, non fuisset passurus induci se ad persequendos veros fideles.§ 12. Ex parte appetitus sensitivi causa peccatorum sunt passiones seu affectus,a quatenus partim distrahunt aut impediunt voluntatem, ut vel remissius, vel plane non tendat in objecta ab intellectu sibi commendata,b partim turbant imaginatricem facultatem atque ita ipsum intellectus judicium eoque mediante voluntatem ad bona sensibilia trahunt,c partim denique, si admodum vehementes sint, suo quasi pondere voluntatem ad bonum sensibile, contra dictamen rationis, dejiciunt.d

Vid. Jac. 1, l4. Nam concupiscentia quidem l. c. denotat peccatum nobis connatum, sed quando dicitur concipere, significantur motus inordinati, sive passiones hinc proficiscentes, qui quidem et ipsi peccata sunt, simul tamen causae, unde porro oriantur peccata χατ έξοχηv sic dicta, seu actus externi peccaminosi, iique etiam graviores, hominem de statu gratiae in reatum mortis praecipitantes. Atque huc pertinent, quae de incontinentia ejusque speciebus, praecipitantia et infirmitate earumque actibus disserunt philosophi.Quenstedtius: ,,Sumitur vox actus et actuale h. 1. non stricte, pro externis tantum operibus et peccatis commissionis, sed late, ita ut etiam internos vitiosos motus, tam primos, quam secundos, nec non peccata omissionis complectatur.“

DE PECCATIS ACTUALIBUS. V. g. quando metus subitaneus hominem arcet ab actu fortitudinis aut professionis fidei exercendo, prout Petrus, per undas ad Jesum iturus, sed vento validiore territus, animum abjecit in actu a Christo mandato, Matth. 14, 29. 30. 34· Idem etiam metuens Judaeos subduxit se a consortio gentilium conversorum, Gal. 2, 12. Ita affectus amoris intellectum sapientem 'excoecare dicitur. Huc pertinent, quae de appetitus sensitivi cum appetitu rationali, i. e. voluntate, arctissima connexione in scholis philosophorum traduntur. Et experientia docet, quomodo amor aut ira vehementior in furorem aut insaniam aliquando degenerent.§

13. Ex parte voluntatis causa peccati est habitualis malitia,a qua quis sciens et volens b ad peccandum se accingite.c Actibus peceaminosis crebrius iteratis acquisita; aut, ubi citra ignorantiam intellectus et passionem appetitus sensitivi, ac potius praevia consultatione, libere eligitur, quod malum est, neque actionem perpetratam mox sequitur dolor et poenitentia. Alias enim homines mali etiam ex passione quadam peccata committere possunt. Hoc loco autem spectantur, quatenus, licet cum affectibus peccent, non tamen aeque ex passione aut affectu vehementiore, sed liberiore voluntate peccant. Vid. 2 Tim. 3, 1. sqq., ubi prolixum catalogum peccatorum malitiae exhibet apostolus.§

14. Quatenus satanas,a homines, qui in hoc mundo b sunt, et^corrupta nostra c natura 1psique d affectus ad peccata nos e inducunt, tentare f nos dicuntur g sive circa h spiritualia, sive i saecularia, blandiendo k aut terrendo.l De quo supra § 6. diximus. Vide § 8. Juxta § 10. Vide § 12. Seu per modum causae aliquid conferunt ad id, ut peccemus, sive absque impedimento id obtineant, sive resistentibus nobis per gratiam impediantur et peccata, ad quae impellimur, non perpetrantur. Id est, experiri, an aliquid adversus nos possint? conari, ut nos a Deo veroque cultu ejus ac via salutis abstrahant aut arceant, sive intentio directa conantibus sit adscribenda, sive saltem indirecta. Alias equidem et Deus dicitur tentare homines, quando eorum fidem, obedientiam, patientiam etc. explorat, aut certa documenta edendi PART. II. CAP. III.

occasionem vel etiam mandatum suppeditat (quod certum est bono fine fieri), et homo dicitur tentare Deum, quando Dei verbum, promissiones, mandata, minas, itemque perfectiones scientiae, sapientiae, bonitatis, justitiae, potentiae in dubium vocat ac documentis quibusdam probari temere postulat, et homo hominem tentare dicitur vel sui (ac forte liciti), vel publici, vel ejus, quem tentat, commodi causa, cum vires animi corporisve, inclinationes, studia, profectus explorat. Sed haec aliena sunt a praesenti negotio. Dannhauerus: ״Egregie Augustinus 1. 2. de serm. Dom. in monte c. 14. et ep. 121. c. 11.: Aliud est, induci in tentationem, aliud tentari.' Nam sine tentatione probatus esse nullus potest, sive sibi ipsi, sive alii. Non ergo hic (Matth. 6, 13.) oratur, ut non tentemur, sed ut non inferamur in tentationem, tanquam si quispiam, cui necesse sit igne examinari, non oret, ut non igne contingatur, sed ut non exuratur. Quanquam enim non per se Deus in tentationem nos inducit, induci tamen, ait Augustinus, patitur eum, quem suo auxilio deseruit ordine occultissimo ac meritis; causis enim saepe manifestis dignum judicat illum, quem deserat et in tentationem induci sinat. Hieronymus in Matth. 26.: ,Impossibile, inquit, est, humanam animam non tentari, unde et in oratione dominica dicitur: Ne nos inducas in tentationem, quam ferre non possumus, non tentationem penitus refutantes, sed vires sustinendi in tentationibus deprecantes.‘ Et cum Christus ait: Vigilate et orate, ne intretis in tentationem, hoc est, ne tentatio vos superet et vincat et vos intra casses teneat.“ (Hodosoph. p. 486.) Quenstedtius: ״Agit hic (Jacob. 1, 18.) apostolus de tentationibus non illis, quibus fides, constantia et patientia piorum exploratur, sed de illis, quibus homo ad malum sive peccatum solicitatur et instigatur, et has a Deo non proficisci, affirmat Jacobus. Το πεψάζεσΰαι enim h. 1. idem est ac incitari et solicitari ad peccandum. Aliter tentat pater filium, herus servum, vir uxorem, magister discipulum, ut ingenium, affectum, studium exploret, acuat, accendat. ,Alia significatione‘, ait Augustinus 1. 2. de consens. ev. c. 30., ,intelligitur tentatio, de qua dictum est: Deus neminem tentat, et alia, de qua dictum est: Tentat vos Dominus, Deus vester, ut sciat, si diligatis eum, Deut. 13. Illa seductionis est, haec probationis.“ (L. c. P. IV. c. 10. s. 1. th. 2. f. 1432.) Hoc enim est, quod in oratione dominica Patrem nostrum oramus, ne nos inducat in tentationem, i. e., ne patiatur nos a diabolo, mundo aut carne nostra gravius tentari, quam per vires gratiae sustinere et superare possimus, adeoque ne nos deserat, ubi, cum soli pugnamus, succumbere oporteret, etc. Supponitur ergo triplex illa tentatio, a qua non immunes sint etiam fideles et pii, quanto minus infideles atque impii? quibus caro vegetior est, mundus familiarior, satanas propinquior. V. g. ad infidelitatem, atheismum, haeresin aut heterodoxiam, superstitionem, diffidentiam, desperationem, aut ex adverso ad fidem hypocriticam, ad vanam de statu gratiae aut perfectione spirituali praesumtionem, quae omnia circa objecta spiritualia, Deum, verbum ejus, bona supernaturalia, aut mala eis opposita versantur. Quo spectant voluptas carnis, voluptas oculorum, superbia vitae, juxta 1 Joh. 2, 16.k) Objiciendo, quae delectant, quae amorem, spem, gaudium inordinatum excitant. Sic praetextu magni boni comparandi quidam inducuntur ad conandum ea, quae sunt supra vires et vocationem ipso DE PECCATIS ACTUALIBUS. 319 rum; praetextu justitiae, diligentiae, magnanimitatis, simplicitatis, liberalitatis, recreationis, pacis seu quietis, aut tranquillitatis salutaris perducuntur homines ad opera crudelitatis, avaritiae, superbiae, ignorantiae, profusionis, intemperantiae, securitatis carnalis, etc. l) Ea, quae adversa sunt, quae metum, fugam, tristitiam gignunt, objiciendo. Quemadmodum calamitatis singularitate aut novitate, auxilii aut liberationis dilatione, minis, fallacibus nunciis etc. ab honesto proposito abstrahuntur etiam illi, qui forti animo esse videbantur, vel in diffidentiam, desperationem, vindictam privatam, αυτυχεφίαν et similia, conjiciuntur. § 15. Sed et peccata praecedentia sequentium peccatorum causa esse solent, partim quatenus inclinant ad actus similes peccaminosos,a partim quatenus excutiunt gratiam, qua ablata homines in peccata graviora ruunt.b Sic enim communiter actus post se relinquere solent dispositiones quasdam, inclinantes ad actus alios similes, et saepius iterati gignunt habitum. Adeoque causa dicuntur, quatenus removent impediens.§ 16. Subjectum peccatorum actualium Quod, seu denominationis, est homo ipse, qui peccat. § 17. Subjectum Quo a sunt facultates animae humanae, quae sunt principia actionum humanarum,b intellectus, voluntas, appetitus sensitivus.c Seu illud, quo mediante peccata, ut peccata, hominem afficiunt. Atque ita Ανομία actui adhaerens ad idem subjectum refertur, a quo, tanquam principio, actus ipse efficienter dependet. Ratione το~> voluntarii vero peccata actualia omnia subjective pertinent ad voluntatem, quatenus vel imperantur ab ea, vel approbantur. Secundario etiam membra corporis subjectum quorundam peccatorum actualium a quibusdam dicuntur, quae aliis organa illorum commode dicuntur.§ 18. Effectus peccati actualis partim a dispositio quaedam est voluntatis, per quam haec inclinatur ad actus alios PART. II. CAP. III.


### Concerning Actual Sins: to be perfected in a similar way, and, if they are repeated more frequently,…

to be perfected in a similar way, and, if they are repeated more frequently, the hardening of the will in evil, partly the guilt of fault and punishment, both temporal and eternal. Dannhauer: " I. Every sin, even the smallest and internal, even in the regenerate, by its nature and in itself is mortal, legally, by the merit of the rigor of divine justice, Deut. 27:26, Matt. 5:22, Rom. 6:23, Gal. 5:21, Jas. 1:15; cf. Augustine, lib. 2. confess. c. 4. II. Every sin, even the greatest, e.g., that of the Ninevites, evangelically, by result under the condition of repentance, 1 John 1:9, on the part of God is venial. III. Every sin in the unregenerate, even the smallest, is actually deadly, because the wrath of God remains unremoved, John 3: 36. Moreover, the unregenerate is not only a Turk or a Jew, but also the circumcised Saul, David, a 'man of death,' 2 Sam. 12:5, 7. IV. No sin of infirmity in the regenerate actually brings about death." (Hodos. phaen. 4. p. 195.)

Indeed, if actual sins are viewed in respect to their material. Compare what we said in § 15 and note a. Insofar as an actual sin in respect to its formal aspect implies a disagreement with rational nature and with the law of God, and thus not only stains man and renders him culpable, but also moves God, whom it offends, to inflict punishment. And this also applies to every sin, even if it seems very light. See Matt. 12:36 and compare here chapter I, § 15. That, however, certain sins are venial, that is accidental, as will be said shortly. §

19. Actual sin is divided I. by reason of the efficient cause into voluntary and involuntary. It is called voluntary whose cause is a full and deliberate will determining itself to the act of sinning out of its own malice, and not hindered either by ignorance of the intellect or by a more vehement passion. It is called involuntary whose cause is not a full and deliberate will, but rather unaffected ignorance, or a more vehement passion, which nevertheless has not entirely taken away the use of reason and happens to a man without guilt. See above § 13. Hence they are called proaeretic sins, sins of malice, etc. Otherwise, every actual sin pertains to the will as to its subject, according to what we said in § 17, note c, and in this sense every actual sin could be called voluntary; but here it is understood as voluntary κατ’ ἐξοχήν.

Hollaz: "Voluntary sin is considered both in relation to the conscience and in relation to the purpose of the will. I. Sin against conscience is fourfold. For it is committed either against a right conscience, when a man in acting or omitting does not follow the dictate of conscience agreeing with the divine law, but despises it; or against..."

...erroneous knowledge, when a man in acting or omitting deviates from the dictate of a conscience imbued with error: or against a probable conscience, when someone sins against the dictate of the intellect, which for probable reasons persuades that something is to be done or omitted here and now; or against a doubtful conscience, when someone does or omits that about which he doubts whether it should be done or omitted. He who sins against the dictate of a right conscience sins most gravely... He who follows an erroneous conscience in a matter that is base in itself and prohibited by laws, he, whether he acts according to or against his conscience, sins. E.g., if a Persian had once been persuaded that the sun is to be worshipped as God, he sinned by worshipping the sun, because he venerated with religious worship that which is not the true God; he also sinned by not worshipping it, because he acted against the dictate of his conscience and thus, as far as in him lay, willed to act against the law of God, who gave us conscience as a guide for acting. ... But he who follows an erroneous conscience in an indifferent matter, neither commanded nor prohibited by laws, he sins who acts against it; he does not sin who acts according to it. E.g., toward the beginning of the New Testament, some Christians thought it was not lawful to eat idolothyta, or meats sacrificed to an idol, even though an idol is nothing in the world (by reason of divinity and divine power, which those heathens attributed to it). These would have sinned by eating against their conscience, even though it was erroneous; by not eating they would not have sinned, because they would have followed their conscience as a cynosure. See 1 Cor. 8:7. If today someone determines that it is illicit for a Christian to serve in the military, he sins by serving; he does not sin when he abstains from serving. He sins against a probable conscience who neglects the safer path. E.g., a physician sins by applying a desperate medicine to dispel a desperate disease. For although it may happen that the sick person recovers when the same is applied, he is not safe; for it may happen that the life of the sick person is extinguished by that violent medicine. He sins against a doubtful conscience who embraces either part of a contradiction, whichever it may be. E.g., if a man addicted to the Augsburg Confession were a guard of a Roman Catholic prince and remained in doubt whether it were lawful for him to accompany the prince to a Roman Catholic mass, or illicit. He would sin as much by accompanying as by not accompanying. Because 1. whatever is not of faith (i.e., whatever is undertaken with a fluctuating mind), is sin, Rom. 14:23. 2. Because he wills some evil; for since he perceives some malice in both objects, whichever he undertakes, he will have inclined toward evil. Therefore, the matter must always be settled either by one’s own prudence or by the counsel of wiser men, lest one remain in doubt and the mind hang in suspense any longer. — Voluntary sin, viewed in relation to the purpose of the will, is twofold. For one kind is that which is committed out of mere malice and a will that is plainly free; another is that which is committed out of a will inclined by force or fear and surrounding dangers. . . The betrayal of Judas, by which the Lord Jesus was delivered into the hands of enemies, was a sin simply voluntary, committed out of mere malice and a will that was plainly free. . . Peter sinned by denying Jesus three times. Which sin was not simply voluntary, in that Peter did not deny Jesus out of mere malice and a will that was plainly free. . . Yet the sin of Peter is not to be extenuated as some Romanists do.” (Exam. P. II. c. 4. q. 10—12. p. 542. sqq.)

Gerhard: “Some sins are our own, but others are alien, in which we participate. The foundation of this division stands in the following passages of Scripture: 1 Tim. 5:22: ‘Do not share in the sins of others’ (by rashly ordaining those to the sacred ministry whose learning and life have not been sufficiently explored). Eph. 5:7: ‘Do not become partakers with them,’ v. 11: ‘Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness.’ Rom. 1:32: ‘Who not only do such things, but also consent to those who do them.’ 2 John 11: ‘He who says greeting to seducers, participates in their evil works.’ Rev. 18:4: ‘Come out of her, my people, lest you be partakers of her sins.’ The ways by which one participates in the sins of others are contained in these verses: 21 Baier’s Comp. ed. Walther. II. PART II. CHAP. III.

I counsel, I command, I consent, I provoke, I praise, I do not uncover the fault, I do not punish, I do not rebuke, I do not oppose, but I command and defend the deeds of others.

All these modes can be reduced to two general headings. For we are made participants in the sin of another either by committing or by omitting.

I. By committing, when we are either the authors or the helpers of another’s sin, and this 1. either by consent and approval, when we approve with our vote those things which are committed by others (Acts 8:1; Rom. 1:32); 2. or by counsel, when we are the authors and advisors of the evil to be perpetrated (2 Sam. 16:23; John 11:49); 3. or by command and mandate, when we either follow the decrees of superiors in perpetrating evil, or command others to do evil (Exod. 1:16 ff.; 2 Kings 11:15; Matt. 2:16; John 19:16); 4. or by excuse and defense, when we defend the evil deeds of others (Isa. 5:20; Ezek. 13:18); 5. or by any participation in the crime and the profit from it, as when we allow ourselves to be received into a share of the gain from theft (Ps. 50:18), etc.

II. By omitting, when we neglect our duty, by which sins ought to be rebuked and punished, which is done by untimely silence, connivance, and excessive leniency (Ezek. 3:17, 18; 33:7; Isa. 58:1), etc. (Loc. de peccat. actual. § 89.) See above § 11.

And these sins are called by the peculiar name of sins of ignorance, to which belong the words of David in Ps. 19:12: "Who can discern his errors?" (that is, no one discerns them). "Cleanse me from hidden faults," that is, from those which are unknown to my intellect or memory, which I did not hold to be sins; such are especially those cases when one acts out of ignorance of the ἀκρίβεια (exactness) of the divine law or of certain circumstances of an action, which, if we knew what is unknown, we would not do.

For, on the contrary, concomitant ignorance, and indeed even consequent ignorance, which is affected, does not make a sin involuntary, but voluntary. That consequent ignorance, however, which is not affected, diminishes the voluntary nature in a certain way, even if it does not make the action entirely involuntary. See § 12.

These sins are called sins of infirmity, not in opposition to sins of precipitation, but in a somewhat broader sense, having regard to the weakness of our powers, partly for preventing the affections that arise in us, and partly for overcoming those that have arisen and with which we have struggled for some time.

Especially belonging to involuntary sins are the sudden inordinate motions which proceed from innate concupiscence, as if by the necessity of corrupt nature, without the consent of the will; which for this reason are accustomed by some to be referred to original sin itself.

Whence perhaps the question can also be decided: Whether actual sins fall upon infants?

Furthermore, it is very difficult in practice to distinguish involuntary sins from voluntary ones always and accurately. See the late Musaeus, Tract. Germ. de poenit. contra Stengerum, Part II, cap. II, p. 173, and P. III, c. IV, p. 499 ff.

Balduinus: "In the formula of prayers which precede baptism, mention is made of sins perpetrated by the one being baptized himself: 'And which he himself has added to it'; the question is asked, whether the minister of the church can omit those words in the baptism of infants, since infants do not seem to sin actually? . . . One must distinguish between an action προαιρετικήν (deliberate), which is joined with a deliberate purpose, and that which is proper to original sin, which one could name φυσικήν (natural), because it arises from corrupt nature, and flows as a vicious effect from original sin, as from a depraved cause. An actual sin, which [arises] from proairesis (deliberate choice) and..."

Latin:

similiter perficiendos, et, si illi crebrius iterentur, obfirmatio voluntatis in malo, partim b reatus culpae et poenae, cum temporalis, tum aeternae.c Dannhauerus: ,,I. Omne peccatum, etiam minimum et cordiale, etiam in regenitis, natura sua et per se est mortale, legaliter, ex rigore justitiae divinae merito, Deut. 27, 26. Matth. 5, 22. Rom. 6, 23. Gal. δ, 21. Jac. 1, 15., cfr. Augustin, lib. 2. confess. c. 4. II. Omne peccatum, etiam maximum, e. g. Ninivitarum, evangelice, ex eventu sub conditione poenitentiae, 1 Joh. 1, 9., ex parte Dei est veniale. III. Omne peccatum in irregenitis, etiam minimum, est actu mortiferum, quia ira Dei manet irrevoluta, Joh. 3, 36. Irrcgenitus autem non est solum Turea, Judaeus, sed et circumcisus Saul, David, ,vir mortis‘, 2 Sam. 12, 5. 7. IV. Nullum peccatum infirmitatis in regenitis actu mortem infert.“ (Hodos. phaen. 4. p. 195.)

Nempe, si peccata actualia ratione sui materialis spectentur. Conf., quae diximus § 15. et not. a. Quatenus peccatum actuale ratione sui formalis importat disconvenientiam cum natura rationali et cum lege Dei, adeoque non solum maculat hominem et culpabilem reddit, verum etiam Deum, quem offendit, movet ad infligendam poenam. Atque hoc etiam omni peccato competit, licet levissimum videatur. Vid. Matth. 12, 36. et conf. h. 1. cap. I. § 15. Quod autem peccata quaedam venialia sunt, id per accidens est, ut mox dicetur.§

19. Dividitur autem peccatum actuale I. ratione causae efficientis in voluntarium et involuntarium. Voluntarium dicitur, cujus causa est plena et deliberata voluntas ex sua malitia ad actum peccandi se determinans, non autem vel per ignorantiam intellectus, vel per vehementiorem passionem impedita.a Involuntarium dicitur, cujus causa non est plena et deliberata voluntas, sed potius ignorantia non affectata,b vel passio vehementior,c quae tamen rationis usum non omnino abstulit hominique citra cuipam obtingit.d Vid. supra § 13. Dicuntur hinc peccata proaeretica, peccata malitiae etc. Alias autem peccatum actuale quodvis ad voluntatem, tanquam ad subjectum, pertinet, juxta ea, quae diximus § 17. not. c., atque hoc sensu omne peccatum actuale dici posset voluntarium; sed hic intelligitur voluntarium χατ Ιξυχψ.

Hollazius: ,,Consideratur peccatum voluntarium tum in ordine ad conscientiam, tum in ordine ad vbluntatis propositum. I. Peccatum contra conscientiam est quadruplex. Committitur enim vel contra conscientiain rectam, cum homo in agendo vel omittendo dictamen conscientiae cum lege divina consentiens non sequitur, sed contemnit; vel contra con

scientiam erroneam, quando homo in agendo vel omittendo a dictamine conscientiae errore imbutae deflectit: vel contra conscientiamprobabilem, cum quis delinquit contra dictamen intellectus, probabiles ob causas aliquid hic et nunc agendum vel omittendum suadentis; vel contra conscientiam dubiam, quando quis id agit vel omittit, de quo dubitat, sitne agendum vel omittendum. Qui contra conscientiae rectae dictamen delinquit, gravissime peccat... Qui sequitur conscientiam erroneam in re per se turpi ac legibus prohibita, is, sive secundum, sive contra conscientiam agit, peccat. E. g. si Persa olim fuisset persuasus, solem esse Deum adorandum, is adorando solem peccavit, quia cultu religioso veneratus est eum, qui verus Deus non est; non adorando etiam peccavit, quia egit contra dictamen conscientiae atque adeo, quantum in ipso, agere voluit contra legem Dei, qui conscientiam nobis ut agendi ducem dedit. ... At qui sequitur conscientiam erroneam in re adiaphora, legibus nec praecepta, nec prohibita, is delinquit, qui agit contra eam; non peccat, qui secundum eam agit. V. g. sub initium N. T. nonnulli christiani arbitrabantur, non licere idolothytis seu carnibus idolo immolatis vesci, cum tamen idolum nihil sit in mundo (ratione divinitatis et virtutis divinae, quam ethnici illi affingebant). Hi peccassent comedendo contra conscientiam, licet erroneam; non edendo non peccassent, quia conscientiam suam tanquam cynosuram secuti fuissent. Vid. 1 Cor. 8, 7. Si hodie quis statuit, illicitum esse Christiano militare, is peccat militando; non peccat, cum a militando abstinet. Contra conscientiam probabilem peccat, qui viam tutiorem negligit. V. g. peccat medicus, morbo desperato depellendo adhibens medicinam desperatam. Quamvis enim fleri possit, ut eadem adhibita aegrotus convalescat, non tamen tutus est; nam fleri potest, ut violento illo medicamine vita aegroti exstinguatur.
