Contra conscientiam dubiam peccat, qui alterutram contradictionis partem, quaecunque ea sit, amplectitur. V. g. si homo Augustanae Confessioni addictus satelles foret principis pontificii et in dubio haereret, utrum sibi licitum sit comitari principem ad missam pontificiam, an illicitum. Is peccaret tam comitando, quam non comitando. Quia 1. quidquid ex fide non est (i. e. quidquid animo fluctu ante suscipitur), peccatum est, Rom. 14, 23. 2. Quia vult aliquod malum; cum enim in utroque objecto sentiat aliquam malitiam, quodcunque susceperit, in malum inclinaverit. Semper igitur vel propria prudentia vel aliorum sapientiorum consilio res transigenda est, ne diutius anceps haereat animique pendeat. — Peccatum voluntarium in ordine ad propositum voluntatis spectatum duplex est. Aliud enim est, quod ex mera malitia et voluntate plane libera, aliud, quod ex voluntate vi metuve et circumstantibus periculis inclinata committitur. . . Proditio Judae, qua Dominus Jesus in manus hostium traditus est, fuit peccatum simpliciter voluntarium, ex mera malitia et voluntate plane libera commissum. . . Peccavit Petrus ter Jesum abnegando. Quod peccatum non fuit simpliciter voluntarium, eo, quod Petrus non ex mera malitia et voluntate plane libera Jesum abnegavit. . . Neque tamen extenuandum est peccatum Petri cum quibusdam Romanensibus.“ (Exam. P. II. c. 4. q. 10—12. p. 542. sqq.)

Gerhardus: ,,Quaedam peccata sunt nostra, quaedam vero aliena, quibus participamus. Fundamentum hujus divisionis extat in sequentibus Scripturae locis: 1 Tim. 5, 22.: ,Ne communices peccatis alienis’ (temere eos ordinando ad sacrum ministerium, quorum eruditio et vita non satis explorata). Ephes. 5, 7.: ,Nolite fleri participes eorum‘, v. 11.: ,Nolite communicare operibus infructuosis tenebrarum.‘ Rom. 1, 32.: ,Qui talia non solum faciunt, sed etiam facientibus consentiunt.‘ 2 Joh. 11.: ,Qui dicit seductoribus ave, communicat operibus eorum malignis.‘ Apoc. 18, 4.: ,Exite ab ea populus meus, ne participes sitis delictorum ejus.‘ Modi, quibus alienis peccatis participetur, oomprehenduntur his versiculis: 21 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. Π. PART. II. CAP. III.

Consulo, praecipio, consentio, provoco, laudo, Non retego culpam, non punio, non reprehendo, Non obsto, sed praecipio et defendo aliena.

Omnes hi modi ad duo generalia capita revocari possunt. Reddimur enim participes alieni peccati vel committendo, vel omittendo.

I. Coramittendo, cum peccati alieni vel auctores sumus, vel adjutores, idque 1. vel consensu et approbatione, cum ea, quae ab aliis committuntur, nostro comprobamus suffragio (Act. 8, 1. Rom. 1, 32.); 2. vel consilio, cum mali perpetrandi auctores sumus et consultores (2 Sam. 16, 23. Joh. 11, 49.); 3. vel jussione et mandato, cum vel superiorum decreta in malo perpetrando sequimur, vel alios jubemus malum agere (Exod. I, 16. sqq. 2 Reg. 11, 1δ. Matth. 2, 16. Joh. 19, 16.); 4. vel excusatione ac defensione, cum mala aliorum facta defendimus (Es. 5, 20. Ez. 13, 18.); 5. vel quacunque criminis et commodi ex eo participatione, ut, cum in partem lucri ex furto recipi nos patimur (Ps. 50, 18.) etc.

II. Omittendo, cum officium nostrum, quo peccata reprehendi ac puniri debebant, negligimus, quod flt intempestivo silentio, conniventia ac nimia lenitate (Ez. 3, 17. 18. 33, 7. Es. 58, 1.) etc.“ (Loc. de peccat, actual. § 89.) Vid. supra § 11.

Et vocantur haec peccata peculiari nomine peccata ignorantiae, quo pertinent verba Davidis Ps. 19, 13.: Delicta quis intelligit? (id est, nemo intelligit.) Ab occultis meis munda me, id est, ab his, quae intellectui vel memoriae meae sunt incognita, quae pro peccatis non habui; qualia inprimis ea sunt, quando ex ignorantia vel äxfnßeiac legis divinae vel circumstantiarum quarundam actionis agitur, quod, si sciremus, quae ignorantur, non ageremus.

Nam ex adverso ignorantia concomitans, imo et consequens, quae affectata est, non facit peccatum involuntarium, sed voluntarium. Ea vero ignorantia consequens, quae non est affectata, minuit τύ voluntarium quodammodo, etsi non facit actionem prorsus involuntariam. Vid. § 12.

Appellantur autem haec peccata peccata infirmitatis, non in oppositione ad peccata praecipitantiae, sed paulo hxtiore sensu, habito respectu ad imbecillitatem virium nostrarum, partim ad praecavendos affectus, qui in nobis exoriuntur, partim ad superandos, qui exorti sunt et cum quibus aliquamdiu luctati sumus.

Praecipue ad peccata involuntaria pertinent motus inordinati subitanei, qui a connata concupiscentia, velut ex naturae corruptae necessitate, proficiscuntur citra voluntatis consensum; quae a quibusdam ad ipsum originale peccatum ideo referri solent.

Unde etiam fortasse decidi potest quaestio: Utrum in infantes cadant peccata actualiat

Caeterum peccata involuntaria a voluntariis semper et accurate in praxi distinguere difficillimum est. Vid. b. Musaei Tract. Germ, de poenit. contra Stengerum Part. II. cap. II. p. 173. et P. III. c. IV. p. 499. sqq.

Balduinus: ,,In formula precum, quae baptismo praemittuntur, mentio flt peccatorum ab ipso baptizando perpetratorum: ,Und die er selbst dazu gethan hat‘; quaeritur, an minister ecclesiae illa verba in baptismo infantum omittere possit, cum infantes actualiter peccare non videantur? . . . Distinguendum est inter actionem προαιρετικήν, quae cum deliberato proposito est conjuncta, et inter eam, quae peccato originis est propria, quam φυσικήν nominare posses, quia a natura corrupta oritur, et tanquam effectus vitiosus a peccato originis, tanquam a causa prava, profluit. Actuale peccatum, quod ex proaeresi et


### Concerning Actual Sins: is done with a set purpose, does not exist in infants, because they are still…

is done with a set purpose, does not exist in infants, because they are still destitute of the use of reason, Deut. 1:39, Jonah 4:11. However, actual sin, such as is wont to be in original sin, the root of which is never idle but always begets vicious actions, ought not to be denied to be in infants, even though they are unaware of it. For the evidence of it is anger, impatience, reluctance toward the good, loathing, and similar depraved motions, to which infants are subject even before the years of discretion. . . Furthermore, those words also refer to the prohaeretic act, which follows in adults after baptism. For not only is there a remission of original sin in baptism, but of all sins with which a man can be polluted during his entire life; therefore, baptism is called the stipulation of a good conscience with God, 1 Pet. 3:21, because there is no sin that can distress us in conscience for which remission has not been made in baptism.” (Tract. de cas. consc. lib. IV, q. 3, pp. 1065—67. cf. Hollazius, Exam. P. II, c. 4, q. 7, pp. 540—42.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis:

1. Of the Papists, such as Bellarmine and others, who deny all actual sin to infants, even that of omission. Bellarmine writes that it is most absurd for infants to have actual sin, at least of omission, since (as he had said a little before) ‘infants are not bound to have faith and the fear of God in act.’ . .

3. Of the Innovators. For D. G. Calixtus and Horneius, in Part II of the Apology against Buscher, q. 8, p. 217 sqq., deny that infants have actual sins immediately after birth and before the use of reason.

4. Of Zwingli and the Papists, who, from that false hypothesis of theirs—that nothing has the nature of sin unless it is committed by one who knows and wills—assert that actual sins do not fall upon infants.

5. Of the Socinians, who assert that infants are neither apt nor born for sin, and therefore cannot sin.” (L. c. q. 14, f. 1053.) § 20. Actual sins are divided II. on the part of the material into sins of commission and omission. The former are called those which consist in positive acts conflicting with a negative precept. The latter consist in the negation or omission of an act prescribed by an affirmative precept. See above § 1 and 2. Hollazius: “Although there is usually some illicit positive act in a sin of omission, either an interior one of the will, such as willing to omit what is commanded, or an exterior one, such as an operation by which one is hindered from doing what one is bound to do: yet such a positive act is not always or necessarily required, but the very act of not doing what is commanded is sin.” (Exam. P. II, c. 4, q. 26, p. 552.) § 21. Furthermore, III. sins are divided on the part of the object into sins against God, against one’s neighbor, and against the sinner himself. The former are those which immediately and directly touch God; the latter are those which immediately concern one’s neighbor; these are those which are directed immediately toward the person of the sinner himself. PART II. CHAP. III.

Immediate sins, or those regarding which sins are directly concerned, are divided by the Apostle in the same way as the opposing good acts that are conformable to the law, when he says that some things are done εὐσεβῶς, others δικαίως, and others finally σωφρόνως, at Titus 2:12.

For otherwise, εὐσέβεια denotes the entire divine worship of both tables, and conversely, every sin is committed against God, whose offense it entails.

Some refer here the distinction of actual sins into carnal, by which those things that are done against man himself and against the neighbor are comprehended, and spiritual, which are committed against God.

They coincide with the sins of the first table of the Decalogue, just as the latter two species taken together agree with the sins of the second table.

Therefore, acts of idolatry, blasphemy, superstition, etc., pertain to sins against God.

Such are the sins by which the neighbor—whether his person, his reputation, or his goods of fortune—is harmed, e.g., murder or the wounding of his body, insult, calumny, theft, fraud, etc.

E.g., fornication (through which a man is said to sin against his own body, 1 Cor. 6:18, in a truly peculiar way, because he abuses his own body against himself and converts it into the matter of illicit pleasure and makes it a member of a harlot; which the context of the place cited also indicates); drunkenness (adverse to health, and thus indeed sinning against one's own body, yet not in the way that fornication does; because that which the drunkard abuses is something outside the body, wine, beer, etc.); αὐτοχειρία (by which someone is injurious and violent toward his own life itself), etc. §

22. By reason of degree, sins are divided into sins of the heart, of the mouth, and of the deed.

According to others, they are divided into begun (in the heart) and consummated (by mouth and deed), into internal and external sins.

For here, sins of the heart, mouth, and deed are viewed insofar as they are subordinated to one another; thus, they differ regarding the degree of internal and external acts, and at the same time regarding the degree of guilt.

Otherwise, it must be admitted that some sin of the heart can be graver regarding guilt than some sin of the mouth or deed, just as habitual hatred toward an innocent neighbor, or an attempt to harm long agitated in the mind, is a graver sin than a rather harsh response to an injury inflicted upon an innocent person, or even some excess of defense, or a light wound inflicted unintentionally.

Concerning sins of the heart, mouth, and deed, see Matt. 5:21, 22, 28; ch. 15:19.

Kromayer: "There are degrees of sins, or not all sins are equal. This thesis... is opposed to the Stoics and Jovinians, who contended that all sins are equal—to kill a slave and a father of a family, nay, a rooster and a man, were equal... Besides the fact that, according to the mind of Augustine, it is against the entire sense of the human race, it is also destroyed by the following passages of Scripture: 1. From the passage Matt. 23:24, where some sins are compared to a camel, others to a gnat; 2. From Matt. 7:3, in which some sins are compared to a beam, others to a speck; 3. From John 19:11, where Christ says to Pilate: 'He who delivered me...'"

delivered to you, has the greater sin‘; 4. from 1 Tim. 5:8: ‘But if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever‘; 5. from 2 Pet. 2:20, that the latter end is worse for them than the beginning, and it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness; 6. from Luke 12:47, that the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it, shall be beaten with double stripes; 7. from those passages which speak of degrees of punishments to come after this life, such as Matt. 11:24. . . Cicero depicts the opinion of the Stoics in his Paradoxes, that to sin is to cross the lines. . . But we respond by granting the equality of sins only insofar as they transgress the prescribed norm of the law; . . . however, we establish that sins are unequal insofar as one departs further from the prescribed norm than another. . . We grant that every sin is deserving of the curse, of death, and of eternal damnation, but, just as there are degrees of sins, so also there will be degrees of punishments in the future life.“ (Th. posit.-pol. I, 516. sqq.) §

28. By reason of the consequent, sins are divided 1. into mortal or death-bringing, which are imputed to the one sinning in the second act unto death, and venial, or those which, although they are worthy of death, are nevertheless not imputed to the one sinning unto death; 2. into crying sins, or those which, even if men are silent, are accustomed to move God to public vengeance, and non-crying sins, or those which God often tolerates and overlooks in His longsuffering; 3. into remissible sins, or those which, just as they do not by their nature exclude repentance, so also can and are accustomed to be forgiven, and the irremissible sin, or that which is such by itself that it is never forgiven.

For otherwise every sin is by itself mortal, or worthy of death; none is venial, or by itself worthy of pardon or remission.

Kromayer: „There is no sin that is venial by its own nature. One must walk the middle path here between the Papist Scylla and the Calvinist Charybdis. The opinion of the Papists is that there are some sins that are venial by their own nature, such as some that are such by their kind, namely an idle word; some by surprise, such as sins of precipitation; some by the imperfection of the act, such as motions of sin that are second-first; some by the triviality of the matter, such as the theft of a single penny or a needle. Concerning these, they hold that repentance—unless it is taken only as a displeasure with the act—need not be performed, nor must they necessarily be expressed in a special enumeration of sins, nor should satisfactions be imposed for them. Indeed, they prescribe as remedies for them the making of the sign of the cross, the beating of the breast, the sprinkling of holy water, episcopal or even priestly and monastic blessing, the use of the Eucharist, the Lord’s Prayer, and whatever others there may be. . . .

The Calvinists, on the other hand, hold that all the sins of the elect, however enormous, even outside the state of repentance, are venial not only as to the possible event, but even as to the actual; but that all the acts and deeds of the reprobate, and even the sins of the τών πρόσκαιρων, are mortal. In this, some agree with us, that certain sins, or rather the sins of certain persons (because this distinction flows from the distinction of persons who are placed either in the state of grace or outside of it), are venial not by their own nature, but by the merit of Christ; but in this they differ from us, that in PART II. CHAP. III.

differently, all the sins of the elect, even if they are for a time placed outside the state of repentance, by the example of David, nevertheless, as to the actual outcome, they establish them as venial sins.” (L. c. p. 511 sq.) Luther: “The works of men, even though they may always appear specious and good, it is nevertheless probable that they are mortal sins. . . The works of the just would be mortal, unless they were feared by the just themselves as mortal out of a pious fear of God. . . Then they are truly venial sins before God, when they are feared by men to be mortal. . . A man thinking that he wishes to attain grace by doing what is in himself, adds sin to sin, so that he becomes doubly guilty.” (Disputatio Heidelbergensis. 1518. See Opp. lat. varii argum. ad reformationis hist. pert. Vol. I, 387 sq.) The same: “Peter denied Christ and was nearly lost. He falls indeed from grace, but he does not lose all reflection. . . Because he remains in the Word, he does not fall into eternal disgrace, but does true penance.” (Ad 1 Joh. 3, 23. Opp. Hal. IX, 1178.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis:

Latin:

destinato proposito fit, non est in infantibus, quia destituuntur adhuc usu rationis, Deut. 1, 39. Jon. 4, 11. Actuale autem peccatum, quale in peccato originis esse solet, cujus radix nunquam otiosa est, sed semper actiones vitiosas gignit, infantibus, licet insciis, inesse negari non debet. Ejus enim indicium est ira, impatientia, reluctatio in bono, fastidium et similes pravi motus, quibus infantes etiam ante annos discretionis sunt obnoxii. . . Deinde respiciunt etiam ista verba ad actum proaereticum, qui in adultis post baptismum sequitur. Non enim in baptismo tantum peccati originis fit remissio, sed omnium, quibus homo omni vitae suae tempore pollutus esse potest, ideo baptismus stipulatio bonae conscientiae cum Deo appellatur 1 Pet. 3, 21., quia nullum est peccatum, quod nos in conscientia angere possit, cujus remissio non sit facta in baptismo.“ (Tract. de cas. consc. lib. IV. 8. q. 3. p. 1065—67. cf. Hollazii Exam. P. II. c. 4. q. 7. p. 540—42.)ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis:

1. Pontificiorum, ut Bellarmini et aliorum, infantibus omne peccatum actuale, etiam omissionis, derogantium. Bellarminus scribit, quod absurdissimum sit, infantes habere peccatum actuale, saltem omissionis, siquidem’ (ut paulo ante dixerat),infantes non teneantur fidem et timorem Dei actu habere.‘ . .

3. Novatorum. Nam D. G. Calixtus et Hornejus parte II. apol. contra Buscherum q. 8. p. 217. sqq. negant, infantes statim post nativitatem et ante usum rationis habere peccata actualia.

4. Zwinglii etpapistarum, qui ex falsa illa sua hypothesi, quod nihil habeat rationem peccati, nisi committatur a sciente et volente, statuunt, in infantes peccata actualia non cadere.

5. Socinianorum, asserentium, infantes ad peccatum nec aptos nec natos esse, ac proinde peccare non posse.“ (L. c. q. 14. f. 1053.) § 20. Dividuntur peccata actualia II. ex parte materialis in commissionis et omissionis peccata. Illa vocantur, quae consistunt in actibus positivis, cum praecepto negativo pugnantibus. Haec in negatione aut omissione actus, praecepto affirmativo praescripti, consistunt. Vid. supra § 1. et 2. Hollazius: ,,Quamvis plerumque in peccato omissionis sit aliquis actus positivus illicitus, vel interior voluntatis, ut, velle omittere, quod praeceptum est, vel exterior, ut, operatio, qua impeditur quis ab eo, quod facere tenetur: non tamen semper aut necessario requiritur talis actus positivus, sed ipsum non facere, quod praeceptum est, peccatum est.“ (Exam. P. II. c. 4. q. 26. p. 552.) § 21. Porro III. peccata dividuntur ex parte objecti a in peccata in Deum, in proximum, et in ipsum peccantem. Illa dicuntur, quae immediate et directe Deum tangunt;b ista, quae immediate respiciunt proximum;c haec, quae in ipsam peccantis personam d directe feruntur. PART. II. CAP. in.

Immediati, seu circa quod directe versantur peccata, quemadmodum oppositos actus bonos legi conformes ita dividit apostolus, ut alios dicat fieri εΰσεβώς, alios δααίως, alios denique σωψρό^ως, ad Tit. 2, 12.

Alias enim rt ευσέβεια totum cultum divinum utriusque tabulae denotat et ex adverso omne peccatum in Deum committitur, cujus offensam importat.

Quidam huc referunt distinctionem peccatorum actualium in carnalia, quibus ea, quae in hominem ipsum et adversus proximum fiunt, comprehenduntur, et spiritualia, quae in Deum committuntur.

Coincidunt cum peccatis primae tabulaß decalogi, sicut posteriores species duae simul sumtae cum peccatis tabulae secundae conveniunt.

Pertinent itaque ad peccata in Deum actus idololatriae, blasphemiae, superstitionis etc.

Talia peccata sunt, quibus proximi seu persona, seu fama, seu bona fortunae laeduntur, e. g. caedes aut vulneraiio corporis ejus, convitium, calumnia, furtum, defraudatio etc.

V. g. scortatio (per quam homo in proprium corpus peccare dicitur 1 Cor. 6,18. peculiari sane modo, quia suo corpore abutrtur adversus se ipsum idque in materiam illicitae voluptatis convertit et membrum scorti facit; quod et contextus l. c. indicat); ebrietas (sanitati adversa, et sic quidem in proprium corpus peccans, non tamen eo modo, quo scortatio; quia quo abutitur ebrius, est aliquid extra corpus, vinum, cerevisia etc.); αυτοχεφία (qua quis in ipsam vitam suam injurius ac violentus est) etc.§

22. Ratione gradus IY. dividuntur peccata a in peccata cordis, oris et operis.

Juxta alios in peccata inchoata (in corde) et consummata (ore atque opere), in peccata interna et externa.

Spectantur enim h. 1. peccata cordis, oris et operis, quatenus sibi subordinantur; sic quoad gradum actuum internorum et externorum, simul et quoad gradum reatus differunt.

Alias fatendum est, posse aliquod peccatum cordis quoad reatum gravius esse aliquo peccato oris aut operis, quemadmodum odium habituale erga proximum innocentem, aut conatus nocendi, animo diu agitatus, gravius peccatum est responso asperiore ad injuriam insonti illatam, vel etiam excessu aliquo tutelae, aut vulnere levi praeter intentionem illato.

De peccatis cordis, oris et operis vid. Matth. 5, 21. 22. 28. cap. 15, 19.

Kromayerus: ,,Dantur peccatorum gradus vel non omnia peccata sunt aequalia. Haec ΰεσις. . . opposita est Stoicis et Jovinianis, qui omnia peccata paria esse, occidere servum et patrem familias, imo gallum gallinaceum et hominem, paria contendebant. . . tibi tradidit, majus peccatum habet‘; 4. ex 1 Tim. 5, 8.: ,Qui suorum et maxime domesticorum curam non habet, fidem abnegavit et infideli deterior est‘; 5. ex 2 Pet. 2, 20., posteriora prioribus pejora fleri, et melius fuisse talibus, justitiam non agnovisse; 6. ex Luc. 12, 47., quod servus sciens voluntatem domini et non faciens, duplo vapulaturus sit; 7. ex iis locis, quae gradus poenarum post hanc vitam futuros dicunt, ut Matth. 11, 24. . . I, 516. sqq.) §

28. Ratione consequentis V. peccata dividuntur 1. in mortalia seu mortifera,a quae peccanti actu secundo ad mortem imputantur,b et venialia, seu quae, licet morte digna sint, non tamen ad mortem peccanti imputantur;c 2. in clamantia, seu quae, etiam tacentibus hominibus, Deum ad vindictam publicam permovere solent,d et nonclamantia, seu quae Deus sua longanimitate saepe tolerat et dissimulat;e 3. in peccata remissibilia, seu quae, sicut poenitentiam sua natura non excludunt, ita quoque remitti possunt ac solent,f et peccatum irremissibile, seu quod per se tale est, ut nunquam remittatur.g

Alias enim omne peccatum per se est mortale, seu morte dignum; nullum veniale, venia aut remissione per se dignum.

Kromayerus: ,,Nullum datur peccatum sua natura veniale. Inter scyllam pontificiam et charybdin Calvinianam hic media via est incedendum. Pontificiorum sententia est, dari nonnulla peccata sua natura venialia, ut sunt quaedam ex suo genere talia, nimirum verbum otiosum, quaedam ex subreptione, ut peccata praecipitantiae, quaedam ex imperfectione actus, ut motus peccati secundoprimi, quaedam ex vilitate materiae, ut furtum unius oboli aut aciculae. De his poenitentiam, nisi sumatur tantum pro displicentia actus, non esse agendam, nec esse in speciali peccatorum enumeratione necessario exprimenda, nec satisfactiones iisdem imponendas volunt. Remedia vero iisdem formationem crucis, tunsionem pectoris, aspersionem aquae lustralis, benedictionem episcopalem vel etiam sacerdotalem et monialem, usum eucharistiae, orationem dominicam et si quae sunt alia, praescribunt. . . .

Calviniani rursus omnia electorum peccata, licet enormissima, etiam extra poenitentiae statum, non tantum quoad eventum possibilem, sed etiam actualem venialia, reproborum vero omnia acta et facta, τών πρόσκαιρων etiam peccata mortalia esse volunt. In quo quidam nobiscum conveniunt, quod non ex sua natura, sed Christi merito peccata quaedam, vel potius quorundam peccata (quia ex distinctione personarum, quae vel in statu gratiae, vel extra eandem positae sunt, haec distinctio fluit) venialia statuant; in hoc vero a nobis absunt, quod in PART. differenter omnia electorum peccata, licet ad tempus extra poenitentiae statum positi sint, exemplo Davidis, tamen quoad eventum actualem, peccata venialia statuant.“ (L. c. p. 511. sq.) Lutherus: ,,Opera hominum, ut semper sint speciosa bonaque videantur, probabile tamen est, ea esse peccata mortalia. . . Homo putans se ad gratiam velle pervenire faciendo, quod est in se, peccatum addit peccato, ut duplo reus flat.“ (Disputatio Heidelbergensis. 1518. Vid. Opp. lat. varii argum. ad reformationis hist. pert. Vol. I, 387. sq.) Idem: ,,Petrus verleugnete Christum und wäre beinahe verloren gegangen. Er fällt zwar aus der Gnade, aber verliert doch nicht alles Nachdenken. . . Weil er an dem Wort bleibt, so fällt er nicht in ewige Ungnade, sondern thut wahre Busse.“ (Ad 1 Joh. 3, 23. Opp. Hai. IX, 1178.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis:


### Concerning Actual Sins: Of the Scholastics and Papists, 

1. Of the Scholastics and Papists, . . . who establish that certain sins are in themselves and by their own nature venial or worthy of pardon, not fighting against the law of God (or not committed against, but beside the law of God), causing a stain not in the soul, but in the sensuality, and therefore deserving only a temporal punishment, which itself, however, is easily remitted. . .

2. Of the Socinians, who establish that in the N. T. not every act of sin, but only a vicious habit or a custom of sinning excludes men from the kingdom of God. . .

3. Of the Arminians, who teach the same; for thus in the Confess. c. 7. s. 6: ‘Certain sins, they say, are such that they deserve to be called lighter lapses rather than crimes, through which, according to the gracious covenant of God and paternal kindness, a man is not excluded from the hope of eternal life.’ . .

4. Of certain Calvinists, . . . who reject the use of those terms and the question as Papistic.

5. Of the Anabaptists, who explode the distinction of sin into mortal and venial altogether, and revile it as a scholastic fiction, even though it was retained by Luther.” (L. c. q. 13. f. 1048.) And to this pertain those sins of the regenerate which shake off faith; but all the sins of the unregenerate. Gerhardus: “Most scholastics embrace mortal sins within the scope of the number seven, and for the sake of memory include them in the word Saligia, signifying: pride, avarice, lust, anger, gluttony, envy, sloth. But Toletus the Jesuit rightly warns in his Instruction for Priests, treatise on mortal sin: ‘It is more correct to call them capital than mortal, since there are many more mortal sins altogether.’” (L. c. § 102.) Namely, because he who sins does not therefore cease to be a believer, and thus remains in the state of grace. And such sins are partly the indeliberate motions of faithful men, partly the sins of the same committed out of ignorance or passion, which have sorrow and repentance as their companion. Such as are numbered primarily as four: homicide, Gen. 4:10; sodomy, or lust most alien to human nature, Gen. 18:20; the oppression of the innocent, e.g., of subjects by tyrants, Exod. 3:7, but also of widows and orphans and the poor, Exod. 22:23, 27; the denial of due wages, James 5:4; yet not excluding other more grievous sins committed with unbridled license. As if by winking at them. For thus is ύπεριδών said in Acts 17:30.

And all sins pertain to this category, except for that which is called against the Holy Spirit. For even mortal sins, which, when they are committed, are actually imputed unto death, can nevertheless be remitted afterwards, because they can be retracted and expiated through repentance and faith, which may follow. Namely, that which in itself and insofar as it is such, is joined with final impenitence. And this is what is called against the Holy Spirit; concerning which we must now treat a little more distinctly. §

24. The most grievous of all actual sins, which is called against the Holy Spirit, consists in the malicious denial and the blasphemous and obstinate impugning of heavenly truth already acknowledged. The reason for the naming is taken from the object, which is the Holy Spirit, viewed in this place metonymically by reason of the office which He exercises through the ministry of the Word in converting the souls of men; such an acceptance of the term is also found in 2 Cor. 3:8, so that the sin against the Holy Spirit is a sin that is committed against the office and ministry of the Holy Spirit and the heavenly truth revealed through it. It is also called elsewhere a sin unto death, with the naming taken from the effect, because it most certainly brings about death or eternal damnation, 1 John 5:16. Compare our Disputation on this passage held last year, '88.

Dannhauer: "One can sin against the Holy Spirit in various ways: by grieving Him (Eph. 4:30), by tempting Him (Acts 5:4), by sacrilegious trafficking (Acts 8), by resisting Him (Deut. 29:18; Acts 7), by provoking Him (Isa. 63:10), by quenching Him (1 Thess. 5:19); but the enormous and consummate crime against the Holy Spirit is not exhausted by these acts of this kind. Those are sins partly tolerated by the Holy Spirit in His divine τροποφορίᾳ, and partly even actually remitted (Acts 13:18), but this one is irremissible, because it is a check upon the heavenly office of the Holy Spirit (John 5:...). Matthew 12:31-32 not only denies τὸ γινόμενον, that it will happen, but also denies τὸ δυνατόν; just as also in the opposite member, that the sin against the Son of Man is remitted, it must be understood of the power, not of the act, because for many who sin against the Son of Man, it is not remitted." (Hodos. Phaen. XI. p. 709 sqq.)

The seat of the doctrine concerning this sin is found in Matthew 12:30 et seqq., Mark 3:28, Luke 12:10. Whether that doctrine had been approved once by the assent of divine faith and public profession, or had only been so clearly perceived that the mind, being convinced, had nothing that it could oppose to the matter.

In the former way, those apostates sin against the Holy Spirit who deny and attack with revilings the truth once acknowledged and believed, such as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews describes in 6:4 sqq.

To the latter class belong the Pharisees and scribes, who had never approved the doctrine of Christ by their own confession, yet were so convinced in their minds of its truth from the Scriptures and the miracles of Christ that they had nothing to oppose to it except revilings. See the aforementioned passages: Matthew 12:24, Mark 3:22, Luke 12:10, and compare John 11:47 and 48, chapter 15:22, Acts 4:16-17, chapter 7:51. PART II. CHAPTER III.

Quenstedtius: "The opinion of those who ascribe the sin against the Holy Spirit only to those who are truly reborn, justified, and renewed seems more probable to us...

In Heb. 6:4-5, the sinner against the Holy Spirit is described: I. By gracious illumination, which does not occur except through μετοχήν του άγιου πνεύματος... II. By a taste of the heavenly gift and the powers of the age to come. A taste, I say, not light and thin, but perfect, joined with a change of the will toward loving God; for that taste is the taste of faith... III. They are called in v. 4 μέτοχοι πνεύματος αγίου. IV. It is added in v. 6: that it is impossible for such a sinner πάλιν άνακαινίζειν εις μετάνοιαν. Those who cannot πάλιν, or again, be renewed to repentance, were previously penitent and consequently reborn...

The authority of many theologians is added, e.g., the blessed Gerhard, Hutter, Lyser, Balduin, Huelsemann, who attribute this sin only to the reborn. Indeed, Scripture itself describes the subjects sinning against the Holy Spirit everywhere in such a way that this description expressly excludes the unregenerate...

Some add here the example of Francis Spira, of whom Sleidanus writes in book XXI, who at Venice before the Pope’s legate denied the truth in the year 1548. But this man is by no means to be considered a sinner against the Holy Spirit, because 1. he did not fall away to the papacy out of malice, but out of infirmity, not έκουσίως and spontaneously, but persuaded by friends. 2. He did not attack or blaspheme the doctrine of the Gospel, but grieved exceedingly that he had fallen away from the truth. There was, therefore, despair indeed, but not blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, as the blessed Meisner says; or, as Maresius says, he died in despair from the mere opinion of that sin—that he had abjured the known evangelical truth—with no consolation admitted; which is very true, provided he did not finally struggle out of that anguish.

Today, such a crime should not be rashly imputed to anyone, since we ought to despair of no one. But in the time of the apostles, when the discernment of spirits flourished among the charisms of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:9), those sinning in such a way could be known... Since today we do not know any sinner against the Holy Spirit with certainty and indubitably a priori before death by individual discernment, we also cannot know for whom, in particular, prayers are to be intermitted." (L. c. q. 16—18. f. 1060. sq. 1064. 1069.)

Huelsemannus: "The sin against the Holy Spirit is committed by men who are illuminated, and who are convicted in the truth of the faith and by the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit." (Breviar. c. 5. § 16.)

Quenstedtius: "The duration, continuation, and perseverance in this sin, or, which is the same thing, final impenitence, is not the formal reason or the definitive quiddity of the sin against the Holy Spirit, such that in its absence this sin is not definitively and essentially perfected; but it is its common, and indeed perpetual and inseparable, accident; that is, the ceaseless perdurance itself is to this sin επουσιώδης, not ουσιώδης." (L. c. q. 17. f. 1066.)

Or, so that the denial and impugning of the heavenly doctrine may be done έκουσίως (Heb. 10:26), such that the principle of the abnegation and impugning is pure, unadulterated malice. Those, however, who deny the faith out of ignorance or fear of danger are not for that reason sinners against the Holy Spirit, but can obtain the remission of sin. See the examples of Paul (1 Tim. 1:13) and Peter (Matt. 26:70 sqq.). For it is called in the aforementioned places a word that one has spoken against the Holy Spirit, and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and therefore it formally imports a contumelious statement by which the office of the Holy Spirit is attacked, e.g., when His doctrine or miraculous works, done for the confirmation of the doctrine, are ascribed to the power and operation of Satan, which the Pharisees were doing (Matt. 12:24; Mark 3:22). And so, by its own nature, it is such that it cannot be forgiven and is never forgiven to anyone, according to the aforementioned places in Matthew and Mark, namely, because by itself

and by its own nature precludes the way to repentance. But the reason why final impenitence is so closely conjoined with this sin is that men of this sort oppose themselves directly and with full malice to the means of conversion, and therefore God withdraws His grace from them and delivers them over to a reprobate mind. It is difficult, however, to pronounce concerning a man who is still alive, as if *a priori* and from the causes, that he is sinning against the Holy Spirit. Cf. the special disputation of the blessed Musaeus held on this sin in the year 1668. Quenstedtius: "The common cause of the irremissibility of the sin against the Holy Spirit is final impenitence and unbelief; but the singular cause, and the one proper to this sin, is the concurrence of the requirements essential to this sin *a priori*, such as the malicious denial, opposition, and blasphemy of the divine Word clearly and evidently acknowledged, and the obstinate and persevering rejection of all means. It is not, however, absolute reprobation, or the omission of the passion, death, and satisfaction of Christ to be provided for sinners against the Holy Spirit." (L. c. q. 19. f. 1070.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of Dr. Balth. Meisner and Feuerborn, who ascribe the sin against the Holy Spirit even to the unregenerate. 2. Of most Calvinists, who assign that sin only to the unregenerate, maintaining that the truly regenerate and renewed cannot commit the sin against the Holy Spirit (see the acts of the Synod of Dort against the Remonstrants); from these false hypotheses: a. that the reprobate are not truly regenerated, b. that the truly regenerate cannot apostatize or fall from the grace of God." (L. c. q. 16. f. 1061.) "Of Augustine, who in various places, especially in Sermon II on the words of the Lord, Epistle 50, and the book on true and false repentance, ch. 4, describes the sin against the Holy Spirit by final impenitence alone." (L. c. q. 17. f. 1066, sq.) "1. Of the Calvinists, who assign as the cause of the irremissibility of the sin against the Holy Spirit: a. the absolute reprobation of God or the absolute denial of saving grace, b. the absolute intermission of Christ’s death and satisfaction for sinners against the Holy Spirit, and c. the absolute omission of the serious divine call...

2. Of the Papists, who also bring forward three false causes of the irremissibility and non-remission of the sin against the Holy Spirit. The first is the lack of merit for the remission of sins; the second is the mostly interrupted conversion of men blaspheming the Spirit of God (Bellarminus says: 'Because for the most part such men are not converted, nor are such sins remitted'); the third is the lack of salutary repentance after this life...

3. Of Episcopius the Arminian, who maintains: 'That this kind of sin must be restricted either to the times of Christ dwelling in the flesh and confirming His doctrine with various miracles, or to the times of the apostles and the miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon them, so that afterwards there can be no place for it among Christians'...

4. Of the Socinians; Socinus contends: 'The sin against the Holy Spirit is not simply irremissible.'" (L. c. q. 18. f. 1071. sq.) SYNOPSIS OF THE SECOND VOLUME. PART ONE. page Chap. I. Latin:

1. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum,... statuentium, quaedam peccata esse ex se et sua natura venialia seu venia digna, non pugnare cum lege Dei (sive non committi contra, sed praeter legem Dei), causare maculam non in anima, sed in sensualitate, adeoque mereri tantum poenam temporalem, quae ipsa tamen facile remittatur. . .

2. Socinianorum, qui statuunt, in N. T. non quemlibet peccati actum, sed tantum vitiosum habitum seu peccandi consuetudinem homines a regno Dei excludere. . .

3. Arminianorum, qui idem docent; sic enim in confess. c. 7. s. 6.: ,Quaedam, inquiunt, peccata sunt talia, ut leviores lapsus potius dici mereantur, quam crimina, per quae juxta gratiosum Dei foedus et paternam benignitatem non excluditur homo a spe vitae aeternae.‘ . .

4. Calvinianorum quorundam, . . . usum istorum terminorum et quaestionis tanquam papisticae rejicientium.

5. Anabaptistarum, qui discrimen peccati in mortale et veniale prorsus explodunt, idque a Luthero retentum tanquam scholasticorum commentum sugillant.“ (L. c. q. 13. f. 1048.) Atque huc pertinent renatorum peccata illa, quae fidem excutiunt; non-renatorum autem peccata omnia.Gerhardus: ,,Peccata mortalia septenarii numeri ambitu amplectuntur scholastici plerique, eademque memoriae causa includunt voci Saligia, significantes: superbiam, avaritiam, luxuriam, iram, gulam, invidiam, acediam. Vere autem monet Toletus Jes. instruet, sacerd. tract. de pecc. mort.: ,Rectius ea dici capitalia, quam mortalia, cum plura sint omnino peccata mortalia.‘ “ (L. c. § 102.) Nempe quia, qui peccat, non ideo desinit esse fidelis, adeoque in statu gratiae permanet. Et talia peccata sunt partim motus indeliberati hominum fidelium, partim peccata eorundem ex ignorantia aut ex passione commissa, quae dolorem et poenitentiam comitem habent. Qualia inprimis quatuor numerantur: homicidium, Gen. 4, 10., sodomia, seu libido ab humana natura alienissima, Gen. 18, 20., oppressio insontum, v. g. subditorum a tyrannis, Ekod. 3, 7., sed et viduarum atque orphanorum et pauperum, Exod. 22, 23. 27., denegatio debitae mercedis, Jac. 5, 4·, non tamen exclusis peccatis aliis gravioribus atque effreni licentia patratis. Quasi connivendo. Ita enim ύπεριδών dicitur Act. 17, 30.

Atque huc pertinent peccata omnia, praeter illud, quod dicitur in Spiritum S. Nam et mortalia, quae, cum patrantur, ad mortem actu imputantur, tamen postea remitti possunt, quia per poenitentiam ac fidem, quae sequi potest, retractari atque expiari possunt. Nempe quod per se et quatenus tale est cum finali impoenitentia conjungitur. Et hoc est, quod vocatur in Spiritum Sanctum; de quo paulo distinctius nunc agendum est.§

24. Peccatum actuale omnium gravissimum, quod vocatur in Spiritum Sanctum,a consistit b in veritatis coelestis jam agnitae c abnegatione malitiosa d et impugnatione blasphema e et pertinaci.f Ratione denominandi ab objecto petita, quod est Spiritus S. hoc loco metonymice, ratione officii spectatus, quod per ministerium verbi in convertendis hominum animis exercet; qualis acceptio vocis etiam habetur 2 Cor. 3, 8., ut adeo peccatum in Spiritum S. sit peccatum, quod in Spiritus S. officium et ministerium patefactamque per illud veritatem coelestem commissum est. Dicitur etiam alias peccatum ad mortem, denominatione ab effectu petita, quod mortem seu damnationem aeternam certissime afferat, 1 Joh. 5, 16. Confer Disput, nostram ad h. 1. anno superiore LXXXVIII. habitam.

Dannhauerus ; ,,Varie in Spiritum S. peccari potest, contristando Eph. 4, 30., tentando Act. 5, 4., sacrilega nundinatione Act. 8., resistendo Deut. 29, 18. Act. 7., irritando Es. 64, 1., extinguendo 1 Thess. 5, 19.; sed his hujusmodi actibus non absolvitur enorme et consummatum in Sp. S. scelus. Sunt illa peccata partim divina τροποφορίμ tolerata a Sp. S., partim etiam actu remissa Act. 13, 18., at hoc est irremissibile, quia est officii Spiritus Sancti coelestis, Joh. 5. .., sufflamen ... Matth. 12, 31.32. non solum negatur το γινόμενον, quod futurum sit, sed etiam negatur όυνητόν · sicut etiam in membro opposito quod peccatum in Filium hominis remittitur, de potentia debet intelligi, non actu, quia multis in F. h. peccantibus non remittitur.“ (Hodos. Phaen. XI. p. 709. sqq.)

Sedes doctrinae de hoc peccato habetur Matth. 12, 30. et seqq. Mare. 3, 28. Luc. 12, 10. Sive doctrina illa assensu fidei divinae ac professione publica semel approbata, sive tantum ita clare percepta fuerit, ut animus convictus nihil habeat, quod ad rem possit opponere.

Priore modo peceant in Spiritum S. apostatae illi, qui veritatem semel agnitam et ereditam abnegant et convitiis petunt, quales describit auctor Ep. ad Ebr, 6, 4· sqq.

Ad posteriorem classem pertinent Pharisaei et scribae, qui doctrinam Christi nunquam sua confessione comprobaverant, interim de veritate ejus ex Scripturis et miraculis Christi ita convicti erant apud animum, ut praeter convitia nihil haberent, quod opponerent. Vid. 11. cc. Matth. 12, 24· Marc. 3, 22. Luc. 12, 10. et conf. Joh. 11, 47. et 48. cap. 15, 22. Act. 4, 16. 17. cap. 7, 51. PART. II. CAP. ΙΠ.

Quenstedtius: ״Nobis probabilior videtur eorum sententia, qui so־ lis vere renatis, justificatis et renovatis peccatum in Spiritum S. adscribunt...

Ebr. 6, 4. 5. peccator in Spiritum S. describitur: I. ab illuminatione gratiosa, quae non fit nisi per μετοχήν του άγιου ·πνεύματος. . . II. A gustu doni coelestis virtutumque futuri saeculi. Gustu, inquam, non levi ac tenui, sed perfecto, conjuncto cum immutatione voluntatis ad diligendum Deum; ille enim gustus est fidei gustus. . . III. Dicuntur v. 4. μέτοχοι πνεύματος αγίου. IV. Additur v. 6.: Non posse talem peccatorem πάλιν άνακαινίζειν elf μετάνοιαν. Qui non possunt πάλιν seu iterum renovari ad poenitentiam, illi antea poenitentes et consequenter renati fuerunt. . .

Accedit auctoritas multorum theologorum, v. g. b. Gerhardi, Hutteri, Lyseri, Balduini, Huelsemanni, qui solis renatis hoc peccatum tribuunt. Imo ipsa Scriptura subjecta peccantia in Spiritum S. ita ubique describit, ut descriptio illa irregenitos expresse excludat. ..

Addunt hic nonnulli exemplum Francisci Spierae, de quo Sleidanus lib. XXI., qui Venetiis coram legato pontificis veritatem abnegaverit anno 1548. Ast hic pro peccatore in Spiritum S. minime habendus est, quia 1. non ex malitia, sed infirmitate, non έκουσίως et sponte, sed persuasus ab amicis defecit ad papatum. 2. Non impugnavit aut blasphemavit doctrinam evangelii, sed summe doluit, quod a veritate defecerit. Fuit ergo desperatio quidem, sed non blasphemia in Sp. S., ut ait b. Meisnerus; vel ex sola opinione istius peccati, quod cognitam veritatem evangelicam abjurasset, nulla admissa consolatione desperabundus obiit, ut inquit Maresius, id quod verissimum, si modo ex illa angustia tandem non sit eluctatus.

Hodie nemini temere tantum scelus debet impingi, cum de nullo debeamus desperare. At tempore apostolorum, quo vige!bat inter charismata Spiritus S. discretio spirituum, 1 Cor. 12, 9., poterant taliter peccantes cognosci. . . Quoniam individuali discretione hodie nullum peccatorem in Sp. S. ante mortem a priori certe et indubitate novimus, non possumus etiam scire', pro quo in individuo intermittendae preces sint.“ (L. c. q. 16—18. f. 1060. sq. 1064. 1069.)

Huelsemannus: ״Peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum committitur ab hominibus illuminatis, in veritate fidei et interno Sp. Sancti testimonio convictis.“ (Breviar. c. 5. § 16.)

Quenstedtius: ״Diuturnitas, continuatio et perseverantia in hoc peccato sive, quod idem est, finalis impoenitentia non est formalis ratio sive definitiva quidditas peccati in Spiritum S., ita ut ea absente hoc peccatum definitive et essentialiter non sit perfectum, sed est accidens ejus commune et quidem perpetuum et inseparabile, hoc est, ipsa perduratio incessabilis est huic peccato επουσιώδης, non ουσιώδης.“ (L. c. q. 17. f. 1066.)

Seu ut negatio et impugnatio doctrinae coelestis fiat ίχουσίως, Ebr. 10, 26., ita ut principium abnegationis et impugnationis sit pura puta malitia. Qui autem ex ignorantia aut metu periculi abnegant fidem, non ideo peccatores in Spiritum S. sunt, sed remissionem peccati consequi possunt. Vid. exempla Pauli 1 Tim. 1, 13. et Petri Matth. 26, 70. sqq. Vocatur enim ll. cc. verbum, quod quis locutus sit adversus Spiritum Sanctum, et blasphemia in Spiritum Sanctum, ideoque formaliter importat dictum contumeliosum, quo Spiritus Sancti officium petitur, v. g. cum doctrina ejus aut opera miraculosa, ad confirmationem doctrinae facta, virtuti et operationi satanae adscribuntur, quod faciebant Pharisaei, Matth. 12, 24.· Marc. 3, 22, Adeoque suapte natura tale est, ut remitti non possit ac nemini unquam remittatur, juxta 11. cc. Matth. et Marci, nempe, quia per se

et sua natura viam ad poenitentiam praecludit. Cur autem cum hoc peccato finalis impoenitentia sit tam arcte conjuncta, cama est, quod homines ejusmodi directe et plena malitia se opponunt mediis conversionis ideoque Deus illis subtrahit suam gratiam eosque in reprobum sensum tradit. Difficile tamen est de homine adhuc vivo, velut a priori et ex causis pronunciare, quod peccet in Spiritum S. Conf. b. Musaei Disp. peculiarem de hoc peccato habitam An. 1668. Quenstedtius: ,,Irremissibilitatis peccati in Spiritum S. causa communis est impoenitentia et incredulitas finalis, causa vero singularia et huic peccato propria est concursus requisitorum huic peccato a priori essentialium, qualia sunt verbi divini clare et evidenter agniti malitiosa abnegatio, oppugnatio, blasphematio et omnium mediorum obstinata ac perseverans rejectio. Non vero absoluta reprobatio, vel passionis, mortis et satisfactionis Christi pro peccatoribus in Spiritum S. pracstandae omissio.“ (L. c. q. 19. f. 1070.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Dr. Balth. Meisneri et Feuerbornii, qui etiam nonrenatis peccatum in Spiritum S. adscribunt. 2. Calvinianorum plerorumque, qui solis nonrenatis peccatum illud assignant, statuentes, vere renatos et renovatos peccatum in Sp. II. de verbis Domini, ep. 50. et lib. de vera et falsa poenitent. c. 4., peccatum in Spiritum S. describit per solam finalem impoenitentiam.“ (L. c. q. 17. f. 1066, sq.),,1. Calvinianorum, irremissibilitatis peccati in Spiritum S. 0ausam assignantium: a. absolutam Dei reprobationem sive absolutam gratiae salvntricis denegationem, b. absolutam mortis satisfactioni· Christi intermissionem pro peccatoribus in Spiritum S., et c. absolutam seriae vocationis divinae omissionis. . .

2. Pontificiorum, qui etiam tres falsas adducunt causas irremissibilitatis et irremissionis peccati lp Spiritum Sanctum. Prima est meriti remissionis peccatorum carentia! secunda est hominum Spiritum Dei blasphemantium, ut plurimum intermissa conversio (Bellarminus inquit: ,Quia ut plurimum ejusmodi homines non convertuntur, nec ejusmodi peccata remittuntur‘); tertia est salutaris post hanc vitam poenitentiae carentia. . .

Episcopii\ Arminiani, statuentis s,Id genus peccati vel ad tempora Christi in carne versantis ac miraculis variis doctrinam suam confirmantis, vel ad tempora apostolorum et effusionis miraculosae Spiritus S. in illos debere restringi, adeo ut Illi postea locus nequeat esse inter Christianos/ . .

## 16 Concerning the Grace of God toward Fallen Men

OF POSITIVE THEOLOGY PART THREE Chapter 1. CONCERNING THE GRACE OF GOD TOWARD FALLEN MEN, THE FIRST PRINCIPLE OF OUR SALVATION. §

1. Among the principles and causes of the salvation of men, such as revealed theology finds those subject to its care, the first place is held by the grace of God, by which God did not wish to leave the human race in the common destruction which they had contracted for themselves in Adam and through original sin, but rather intended to rescue them from it through certain means and to lead them to eternal blessedness. For we must now treat of these things, after having seen in the first part concerning the objective and formal end, and in the second part concerning the subject of the operation.

Quenstedtius: "We have hitherto considered Sacred Theology in general, and its principle of knowing, Holy Scripture; then the end, both the objective, the Triune God, and the formal, the eternal fruition of God. Furthermore, the subject into which that end is to be introduced, namely, man the sinner according to his various states, namely, of institution and destitution. It remains now to treat of the principles upon which our salvation depends, and finally of the means through which fallen man is to be led to it." (Theol. did.-pol. P. III. c. 1. s. 1. th. 1. fol. 1.)

Sinners, indeed, guilty of the crime of divine lese-majesty and therefore utterly miserable and destined to perish by the force of divine justice if left to themselves, see Part II, Chapter II, § 13, Vol. II, p. 296. In which sense also it is said by Paul in Romans 3:19, πας ο κόσμος υπόδικος τω θεω, the whole world is subject to God, as judge, or to the judgment of God.

Luther: "We are not dealing here with the philosophical knowledge of man, which defines man as a rational animal, etc. These are physical matters, not theological. Thus the jurist speaks of man as the possessor and master of his own things; the physician speaks of man as healthy or sick; PART III. CHAP. I.

the theologian, however, disputes concerning man as a sinner. This is the substance of man in theology, and this is what is handled by the theologian, that man may perceive this nature of his, corrupted by sins.” (Enarrat. Ps. 51. See Exeget. opp. lat. Ed. Irmischer. Vol. XIX, 20.)

Whence, whatever belongs to those things by which our salvation is procured for us sinners, depends upon and redounds to us. Quenstedtius: “The principal cause of our salvation is the immense mercy and grace of God, which is not viewed in this place insofar as it is an attribute or essential property of God (for thus it pertains to theology specifically so-called, or to the objective end of theology, and has been treated above), but insofar as it is, in the business of our eternal salvation, the first and highest cause, the fountain and spring of all those things which pertain to the procuring of our salvation, and thus it pertains to the economy in which we are now engaged.” (L. c. th. 2. f. 1.)

Who is the efficient cause of our blessedness according to Proleg. chap. I. § 21. Vol. I. p. 40. He is, however, undoubtedly a free cause; whence it is deservedly asked concerning the impulsive causes of the divine will. For thus must the grace of God be viewed in this place, since it has long since been established from P. I. chap. I. § 26, chap. II. § 18, and chap. IV. § 3 (Vol. II. p. 43, 96, 144) that God is otherwise good to men, partly in producing them, and partly in preserving them in the state of integrity and leading them to their end, just as He is to His other creatures.

Concerning which, we shall treat distinctly in what follows. § 2. Therefore, by the name of divine grace in this place is understood the kind favor of God toward sinners, by which God, according to our mode of conceiving, is moved to will to contribute what is His own for the procuring of their salvation. It is otherwise called the mercy, love, kindness, etc., of God.

For thus the name of χάρις occurs frequently in the Scriptures, e.g., Eph. 1:7, and chap. 2:7; not only χάρις, but πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος, the riches of grace, is attributed to God in respect to the business of our salvation. Compare Rom. 3:24; Eph. 2:8; 1 Pet. 5:10. God is called the God of all grace, as if the full fountain or author. Indeed, the word grace is otherwise taken partly for the habitual gifts of grace infused into us, and partly for the actual aids of grace, but not so in the present business.

Luther: “Grace and gift are different in that grace properly means God’s favor or good pleasure, which He bears toward us in Himself, out of which He is inclined to pour Christ and the Spirit with His gifts into us; as becomes clear from the 5th chapter, v. 15, where he says: ‘Grace and gift in Christ,’ etc. Now, although the gift and the Spirit daily increase in us and are not yet perfect, so that evil desires and sin still remain in us, which strive against the Spirit, as he says in Rom. 7:14, Gal. 5:17, and as in Gen. 3:15 the strife is proclaimed between the seed of the woman...”

and the seed of the serpent; yet grace does so much that we are reckoned entirely and fully righteous before God. For His grace does not divide or parcel itself out, as gifts do, but takes us wholly and entirely into favor for the sake of Christ, our Advocate and Mediator, and because the gifts have been begun in us.” (Preface to Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. XIV, 113. sq.) “

The whole Papacy rests upon this doctrine: that grace is infused into man through a secret operation; whoever wishes to attain to it must repent, confess, and make satisfaction.” (XIII, 2078.) “

Where you do not seek forgiveness in the Word, you will gaze toward heaven in vain for grace or (as they say) for inner forgiveness.” (XIX, 1175.)

Huelsemannus: “The dispute concerning the words ‘grace’ and ‘freely’ began with the very reformation of religion. And although it pleased Philip Melanchthon, after the reconciliation of religious controversies between the princes and theologians of both parties was being treated at the Diet in the year 1530 from the 16th to the 22nd of August following the presentation of the A. C., to leave the word ‘grace’ in ambiguity, so that it might be permitted to him, just as to his associates, to take and explain it as the mere affection of divine benevolence, but to Eck and his associates, according to their custom, as virtuous qualities infused into men from the benevolence of God as the primary cause; which meaning did not prevent man from obtaining salvation through merit as a secondary cause, which was infused into him by God as the primary cause; in which equivocation Philip was wonderfully pleased with himself, as appears from the letters to Luther dated August 22nd from those proceedings, found in Chytraeus in *hist. A. C. German*, p. 400: yet this κυβεία (Eph. 4:14) displeased Luther from the very beginning... Our symbolical book, not only in the Epitome and Declaration, but also in the Apology, freed the word ‘grace’ and ‘freely’ from the equivocation concerning an infused habit, Apol. p. 73, 76, 78, 96, sqq. Although it does not deny that the name of grace is taken somewhere, by metonymy of the effect for the cause, or for gifts conferred upon us from the benevolence of God, Eph. 4:7, concerning grace given freely, or gifts required for the ministry, and also 1 Pet. 4:10: ‘Let us be good stewards of the manifold grace of God’; yet it is false that this word is ever taken for an infused gift when the discussion concerns the causes, whether instrumental or meritorious, of justification and salvation on our part.” (Praelectt. F. C. art. 11. s. 1. p. 542.)

Melanchthon: “As far as the doctrine is concerned, it stands thus: Eck cavils at the word ‘alone’ when we say that man is justified by faith alone. Yet he did not condemn the doctrine itself; but said that the inexperienced were offended by it. For I forced him to confess that righteousness is rightly attributed to faith. Yet he nevertheless desired that we should write that man is justified by grace and faith. I did not oppose that; but the fool does not understand the word ‘grace’.” (Letter to Luther, dated August 22, 1530. Luth. Opp. Hal. XVI, 1694. cf. Luther’s reply, dated August 26: “You write that Eck was forced by you to confess that we are justified by faith: I wish you had forced him not to lie.” (De Wette IV, 145.))

Quenstedtius: “Obj.: Justifying grace is called love poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, Rom. 5:5. But now, a gift poured out into the heart cannot be called the external favor of God, but something touching the heart itself, purging and renewing it, which is habitual grace, whence Augustine also explains it as the love by which we love God. Resp...: That love is said to be poured out into our hearts as to its effect, not as to subjective inhesion or inherence; add v. 8, in which the apostle explains himself as to what love he is speaking of. We argue thus: The love which God declared toward us by delivering up His Son, when we were still sinners and thus incapable of this love, is what is called here PART III. CHAP. I.

poured out; now God commends not our love, by which we love God, but that by which God loves us, by delivering up His Son, etc. Therefore.” (L. c. c. 8. s. 2. q. 2. f. 770.)

As if by way of an affection, although affections, which imply a certain change, cannot properly be ascribed to God. Yet here a certain determination of the will of God to help us is undoubtedly denoted, which has a certain likeness to human affection, but without imperfection. It has, I say, divine grace as an internal impulsive cause on the part of the divine will for procuring our salvation.

Indeed, the designation of grace has its place for the sake of excluding our merits or dignity. And thus it is opposed to debt, Rom. 4:4 sqq., c. 11:6. The remaining names are distinguished by peculiar connotations. On account of the respect to our misery, by which, as a προκαταρκτική (procatarctic) cause (which they sometimes call an external impulsive cause), He is provoked or moved to dispel it. Thus Paul celebrates the το έλεος (mercy) of God in the business of our salvation, Tit. 3:5, and calls God πλούσιον έν έλέει (rich in mercy), Ephes. 2:4. Zechariah, however, in his canticle, mentions σπλάγχνα έλέους θεού (the bowels of the mercy of God), Luke 1:78. Compare 1 Pet. 1:3.

In order to the good, namely, eternal salvation, which God wills for us. For it is of love or charity to will for another what you consider to be good, and to strive to effect those things according to one’s power. And indeed, to God is ascribed αγάπη (love) or charity toward us, such as we are after the fall, John 3:16. Πολλή αγάπη, ην ηγάπησεν ημάς (great love, wherewith He loved us), even when we were dead through trespasses, Ephes. 2:4, 5. God Himself is said to commend His love toward us as immense, nay, singular, Rom. 5:8. The same, with the object concluded together with the act itself into one word, is called φιλανθρωπία (philanthropy), love toward men, Tit. 3:4.

THEOLOGIAE POSITIVAE PARTIS TERTIAE Caput 1. DE GRATIA DEI ERGA HOMINES LAPSOS, SALUTIS NOSTRAE PRIMO PRINCIPIO. §

1. Inter principia et causas salutis a hominum, quales theologia revelata suae curae subjectos b invenit, primum locum obtinet c gratia Dei, qua Deus d humanum genus in communi e exitio, quod sibi in Adamo et per peccatum originale contraxerant, relinquere noluit ac potius per certa media inde eruere atque ad beatitudinem aeternam deducere intendit. f De his enim nunc agendum est, postquam de fine objectivo et formali in parte prima deque subjecto operationis in parte secunda vidimus.

Quenstedtius: ״Consideravimus hactenus SS. theologiam in genere, ejusque principium cognoscendi s. Scripturam; deinde finem, tum objectivum, Deum unitrinum, tum formalem, aeternam Dei fruitionem. Porro subjectum9 in quod finis ille introducendus est, hominem sci. peccatorem secundum diversos status, institutionis sci. et destitutionis. theologus autem disputat de homine peccatore. Haec hominis substantia est in theologia, et hoc a theologo agitur, ut hanc suam naturam peccatis corruptam homo sentiat.“ (Enarrat. Ps. 51. Vid. Exeget. opp. lat. Cur. Irmischer. Vol. XIX, 20.)

Unde, quicquid est eorum, quibus salus nostra peccatoribus nobis procuratur, pendet atque in nos redundat. Quenstedtius: ״Princeps salutis nostrae causa est immensa Dei misericordia et gratia, quae hoc loco non spectatur, quatenus attributum vel essentialis proprietas Dei est (sic enim ad ΰεολογίαν specialiter sic dictam sive ad finem theologiae objectivum pertinet, et supra pertractata est), sed quatenus in negotio aeternae nostrae salutis causa prima et summa, fons et scaturigo est omnium eorum, quae ad procurandam no§tram salutem spectant, sicque ad οικονομίαν, in qua nunc versamur, pertinet.“ (L. c. th. 2. f. 1.)

Sic enim h. 1. spectanda est gratia Dei, cum alias Deum hominibus partimf nt producendis, partim in statu integritatis ut conservandis et ad suum finem ducendis aeque atque caeteris creaturis suis bonum esse, jam pridem constet ex P. I. cap. I. § 26. c. II. § 18. et c.IV. § 3. Vol. II. p. 43. 96.

144. De quibus distincte agetur in sequentibus. § 2. Intelligitur ergo nomine gratiae divinae a hoc loco b benignus Dei favor c erga peccatores, quo Deus, nostro concipiendi modo, d movetur, ut velit ad salutem eorum procurandam conferre, quod suum est. Ita enim της χάριτος nomen in Scripturis crebro occurrit, v. g. Lutherus: ״Gnade und Gabe sind desUnterscheides, dass Gnade eigentlich heisst Gottes Huld oder Gunst, die er zu uns trägt bei sich selbst, aus welcher er geneigt wird, Christum und den Geist mit seinen Gaben in uns zu giessen; wie das aus dem 5. Wo du nicht die Vergebung im Worte suchest, wirst du umsonst gen Himmel gaffen nach der Gnade oder (wie sie sagen) nach der innerlichen Vergebung.“ (XIX, 1175.)

Huelsemannus: ״De vocabulis,gratiae‘ et,gratis‘ coepit disputatio cum ipsa reformatione religionis. Et quamquam Philippo Melanchthoni placeret, postquam ab exhibita A. C. in comitiis anno 1530. conciliatio controversiarum religionis inter principes et theologos utriusque partis a d. 16. usque ad 22. Augusti tractaretur, relinquere vocabulum gratiae sub ambiguitate, ut sibi, quemadmodum et sociis, liceret illud capere et exponere pro solo affectu benevolentiae divinae, Eckio autem et sociis pro more suo de qualitatibus virtuosis ex benevolentia Dei, tanquam causa principali, hominibus infusis; qui significatus non impediebat, quominus homo consequeretur salutem per meritum, tanquam per causam secundariam, quae ei infundebatur a Deo per benevolentiam, tanquam causam primariam; in qua aequivocatione Philippus sibi mirifice placebat, ut apparet ex literis ad Lutherum de 22. Aug. ex comitiis illis datis apud Chytraeum in hist. A. C. German, p. 400.: Luthero tamen haec κυβεία (Eph. 4, 14.) mox ab initio displicuit. . . Noster symbolicus liber non tantum in Epitome et Declaratione, sed in Apologia quoque liberavit vocem,gratiae‘ et,gratis‘ ab aequivocatione de habitu infuso, Apol. p. 73. 76. 78. 96. sqq. Quamquam vero non negat, alicubi sumi illud nomen gratiae, per meton. effectus pro causa, sive pro donis ex benevolentia Dei in nos collatis Eph. 4, 7., de gratia gratis data, sive donis ad ministerium requisitis, nec non 1 Pet. 4,10.: ,Simus boni dispensatores variae divinae gratiae‘; falsum tamen est, uspiam, quando de causis, sive instrumentalibus sive meritoriis, justificationis et salutis ex parte nostra agitur, accipi hoc vocabulum pro dono infuso.“ (Praelectt. F. C. art. 11. s. 1. p. 542.)

Das habe ich nicht widerfochten; aber der Narr verstehet das Wort,Gnade‘ nicht.“ (Schreiben $n Luther d. d. 22. August 1530. Luth. Opp. Hai. XVI, 1694. cf. Luthers Antwort d. d. 26. Aug.: ״Scribis Eccium a te esse coactum fateri, nos fide justifleari: utinam coegisses eum non mentiri.“ (De Wette IV, 145.)

Quenstedtius: ״Objic.: Gratia justificans dicitur caritas diffusa in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S., Rom. 5, 5. Jam vero donum in corde effusum non potest dici externus Dei favor, sed pliquid ipsum cor attingens, purgans et renovans, quod est gratia habitualis, unde et Augustinus exponit de caritate, qua nos Deum diligimus. Resp. . .: Dicitur illa caritas diffusa in cordibus nostris quoad effectum, non quoad subjectivam inhaesionem, vel inhaerentiam; adde v. 8., in quo se explicat apostolus, de qua loquatur caritate. Argumentamur ita: Quam caritatem Deus erga nos declaravit tradendo Filium, cum adhuc essemus peccatores adeoque caritatis hujus incapaces, ea dicitur hic PART. III. CAP. I.

effusa; jam non nostram caritatem, qua nos Deum diligimus, sed qua nos Deus diligit, commendat Deus tradendo Filium etc. Ergo.“ (L. c. c. 8. s. 2. q. 2. f. 770.)

Velut per modum affectus, quamvis affectus, qui mutationem quandam important, Deo proprie adscribi non possint. Propter respectum ad miseriam nostram, qua velut causa προκαταρκτική (quam impulsivam externam aliquando vocant) provocatur aut movetur ad eam depellendam. Zacharias autem in cantico suo σπλάγχνα έλέους θεού, viscera misericordiae Dei, memorat Lucae lf 78. Confer. 1 Petr. 1,3.

In ordine ad bonum, videlicet salutem aeternam, quam nobis vult Deus. Est enim amoris seu caritatis, velle alteri, quae bona putes, eaque pro viribus studere efficere. Ac Deo quidem αγάπη seu amor erga nos, quales post lapsum sumus, adscribitur Joh. 3, 16. Πολλή αγάπη, ην ηγάπησεν ημάς, multa caritas, qua dilexit rios, etiam mm essemus mortui per delicta, Ephes. 2, 4. 5. Deus ipse caritatem suam erga nos, tanquam ingentem, imo singularem, commendare dicitur Rwn. 5, 8.
