Eodem sensu cum voce amoris Graece χρηστότης Tit. 3, 4׳l.egitur; χρηστός autem dicitur, qui alteri utilis, aut causa boni, felicitatis, salutis ejus est. § 3.


### Concerning the Grace of God toward Fallen Men: In the same sense, with the word for love, χρηστότης (kindness) is read in…

In the same sense, with the word for love, χρηστότης (kindness) is read in Greek, Tit. 3:4; but he is called χρηστός (kind) who is useful to another, or the cause of his good, happiness, and salvation. § 3. The object of this grace is all and every human being, even if corrupted by sin.

Whence it is commonly called universal grace, an appellation taken from the object, which is the whole human race; as is indicated by the following words. Who, being hitherto equal in misery, agree together in the being of a creature, nay, in human nature itself, loved by God above other species of creatures, and all having once been endowed with the image of God in Adam, so equally all, with no one excepted, are the object of divine grace or mercy and benignity.

BY THE GRACE OF GOD. Indeed, God does not pursue them with His grace insofar as or because they are sinners; for God, not willing iniquity, hates those who work iniquity, Ps. 5: 5.

Nevertheless, notwithstanding the fall of the protoplasts and the sin contracted thence, but with that corruption common to all being present to the divine intellect, God, having had mercy, intends their liberation and salvation.

For it is expressly said in 1 Tim. 2:4: God wills (He does not say that He wills, but He truly wills) that all be saved, just as He commands Christians to truly seek the salvation of all through their prayers proceeding from love; of all, I say, with no one excepted, not even Nero, or others among the tyrants of that time; whence it is so much the less right to restrict that will of God to the number of a few elected out of mere good pleasure from various groups or any kind of men, but, as the letter demands, it must be referred to all men whatsoever, with no one excepted, not even Nero, or others, although they are obstinate sinners and perishing by their own fault.

Similarly, that universality of divine grace is evident from 2 Pet. 3:9: God does not will that any should perish; where He denies one of the opposites in such a way that He affirms the other all the more strongly. For he who does not will that anyone should perish, undoubtedly wills that all be saved from destruction; He destines no one to ruin out of mere good pleasure, having embraced all with equal love.

And it is to be noted that Paul and Peter in the cited places speak of men as they actually exist, and thus with regard had to the fall of Adam and the sins by which all and every descendant are polluted.

So also Christ in John 3:16: God, He says, loved the world, embracing believers and unbelievers, which is evident from the context, and thus the world is taken for the entire human race inhabiting this world, and corresponds to the whole multitude of the Jews, who were bitten by the fiery serpents, for the good of each and every one of whom, just as for all (not only for a few elected out of mere good pleasure), the bronze serpent was once erected.

Finally, in Rom. 11:32 it is said that God has concluded all under sin, that He might have mercy on all, where the same breadth is said to belong to those whom God has permitted to come into a state of sin, and those on whom He has mercy; so that just as all and every man have been constituted sinners, so all and every one, although sinners, are nevertheless also the object of divine mercy.

Gerhardus: "To this opinion (concerning the absolute decree) we first oppose that beneficent will of God, by which He seriously seeks the conversion and salvation of all, which beneficent will Scripture has made attested by words, Christ by tears, and God Himself by an oath." (De elect. et reprob. § 57.)

Lutherus: "Just as the dear sun is not darkened or eclipsed by the fact that it must shine for many, indeed, that the whole world enjoys its light, radiance, and splendor; it nevertheless retains its light entirely, nothing is lost from it, it is an immeasurable light, it could well illuminate ten more worlds. . . so Christ our Lord (to whom we must have recourse and from whom we must ask for everything) is an infinite fountain and headspring of all grace, truth, righteousness, wisdom, and life, which is without measure, end, and bottom; so that even if the whole world drew so much grace and truth from it that they all became pure angels, not a single drop would be lost from Him: the fountain always overflows with grace. Whoever, then, with no one excluded, wishes to measure His grace, let him come and fetch it from Him." (Ad Joh. 1: 16. VII, 1597.) "

It is from the PART III. CHAP. I. ... preached so finely and comfortingly of Christ, our Savior; we can never attain it with words, nor even with our thoughts. In that life, we shall have our joy and delight for eternity that the Son of God lowers Himself so deeply and takes my sin upon His back; yes, not only my sin, but also that of the whole world, which has been committed from Adam down to the very last human being; He wills to have committed them and also to suffer and die for them, so that I might be without sin and attain eternal life and salvation. . . Upon this now stands the foundation of all Christian doctrine; whoever believes this is a Christian; whoever does not believe it is no Christian, and he will also find his portion. It is indeed said clearly enough: This is the Lamb of God, who bears the sin of the world, and the text is God’s Word and not our word, nor devised by us, that God had this Lamb slaughtered for this reason and that the Lamb, out of obedience to the Father, loaded the sin of the whole world upon Himself. But the world does not want to go along; it does not want to grant the dear Lamb the honor that we are saved solely because He bears our sin. It also wants to be something, and the more it wants to do and atone for sin, the worse it makes it. . . The Lamb preaches to us Himself, saying: Look and see how I indeed bear your sin, but no one wants to accept it; and if we believed and accepted it, then no one would be damned. What more should the Lamb do? He says: You are all damned, but I will take your sin upon myself; I have become the whole world; I have assumed the person of all human beings from Adam onward, so that, just as one has received sin from Adam, so He wills to give us righteousness for it. There I should say: I will believe that my dear Lord, the Lamb of God, has taken all sin upon Himself. Yet the world will neither believe nor accept it, and if it believed it, then no one would be lost. . . That one does not believe, however, does not happen because of a lack in the Lord Christ, but the guilt is mine. If I do not believe it, then I lie in my damnation. I must say in short that God’s Lamb has borne the sin of the world; and it is earnestly commanded to me that I should believe and confess it, and even die upon it. Yes, you might say, who knows whether He also bears my sin? I believe indeed that He bore the sin of St. Peter, St. Paul, and other saints; they were pious people; if only I were also St. Peter or St. Paul! Do you not hear, then, what St. John says here: This is the Lamb of God, who bears the sin of the world! Now you cannot deny that you are also a piece of the world. . . If you (now) are in the world, and your sins are a piece of the world’s sin, then the text stands here: Everything that is called sin, the world and the world’s sin, from the beginning of the world down to the end, that lies solely upon the Lamb of God; and since you are also a piece of the world and remain in the world, then you will indeed also partake of that of which the text speaks in this place.” (On John 1: 29. VII, 1639. 1642. 1648. 1649. 1650.)

Quenstedtius: “Regarding the passage John 3:16, the Calvinists have replied that the word ‘world’ here does not denote all men in general, but only the elect from the whole world, or the body of the elect from the whole world. . . Regarding the passage 1 Tim. 2:4: ‘God desires all men to be saved,’ etc., the Calvinists except that by ‘all men’ the Apostle does not understand individual men, but any men whatsoever, i.e., men of every kind, in German: *Nicht alle, sondern allerlei Menschen* [Not all, but all sorts of men]. Thus Calvin in his commentary on this passage. . . Regarding the passage Rom. 11:32: ‘God has shut up all in disobedience, that He might have mercy on all,’ Wendelinus excepts: I. ‘That indeed all and individual men are shut up under sin, but that this is not intended by Paul in this place.’ . . II. He objects to the passage Gal. 3:22: ‘The Scripture has shut up all things under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe’; from which he presumes to demonstrate that Paul, by saying: ‘That all...’”

that He might have mercy on all‘, speaks only of believers. . .

III. Vain is the common evasion of Beza in his *Response to the Acts of the Colloquy of Montbéliard*, p. 223, and of other Calvinists, regarding the "kinds of individuals.". .

Regarding the passage 2 Pet. 3:9: "God does not wish any to perish, but all to tend toward repentance,". . Calvinists almost unanimously understand here the elect or believers, which they gather from those words: Ό κύριος μακροθυμεί εις ημας. . .

Ezek. 18:23, 32 and 33:11: "I do not desire the death of the wicked," etc. . .

Chamier, Vol. III, *Panstratia*, Bk. 7, ch. 6, no. 10, seeks his evasion I. in the distinction of the will into ευδοκίαν and ευαρεστίαν, then II. in the word חפץ, which he claims does not signify "to will" simply, but "to acquiesce in something, to take delight in, to desire.". .

Wendelinus, *Exercit.* 127, no. 13, asserts: "God does not will the death of the sinner insofar as it is the destruction of the wicked, but He does will the death of the sinner insofar as it is a just punishment dictated by the very justice of God.". .

IV. Other Calvinists deny that all sinners in general are intended in those passages in Ezekiel, and say that only those who convert themselves are designated; thus Maccovius. . .

V. Frider. Spanheim, *Exercit. de grat. univ.*, s. 5, th. 7, pp. 127 and 128, contends that the words of Ezekiel must be restricted to the house of Israel. . .

VI. Polanus in *Syntagma*, p. 613: "God," he says, "does not speak here (in Ezekiel) of the secret will and will of good pleasure, nor of all the wicked; for by His secret will and will of good pleasure He wills the death of all those who perish, i.e., of the reprobate; but He speaks of the will of the sign, revealed in the Gospel, by which He offers mercy and salvation to all, so that they may be freed from death and live." (L. c. P. III, c. 3, s. 2, q. 1, ff. 12—17.)

Latin:

Objectum hujus gratiae sunt homines a omnes ac singuli,b etiamsi peccato c corrupti.d Unde gratia universalis vulgo dicitur, appellatione ab objecto desumta, quod est universum genus humanum; uti verbis sequentibus indicatur.

Qui, hactenus miseria pares, simul in esse creaturae inter se conveniunt, imo in ipsa natura humana, Deo prae aliis speciebus creaturarum dilecta, atque olim imagine Dei donati omnes in Adamo, ita aeque omnes, nemine excepto, objectum sunt gratiae seu misericordiae et benignitatis divinae.

DB GRATIA DEI. Equidem, non quatenus, aut quia peccatores sunt, Deus sua gratia eos prosequitur; Deus enim, iniquitatem nolens, odit operantes iniquitatem, Ps. 5, 5.

Attamen, non obstante lapsu protoplastorum et hinc contracto peccato, sed obversante intellectui divino corruptione ista communi omnium, Deus misertus, eorum liberationem et salutem intendit.

Sic enim expresse dicitur 1 Tim. 2, 4.: Deus vult (non dicit, se velle; sed, vult revera) omnes salvos fieri, prout jubet christianos precibus suis ex amore profectis revera expetere omnium salutem;, omnium, inquam, nemine excepto, ne Nerone quidem, aut aliis inter tyrannos ejus temporis; unde tanto minus voluntatem illam Dei ad paucorum ex mero beneplacito electorum numerum ex variis coetibus aut quovis genere hominum restringere fas est, sed, uti litera postulat, referri ad omnes omnino homines oportet, nemine excepto, ne Nerone quidem, aut aliis, quanquam praefractis, peccatoribus et sua culpa perituris.

Similiter universalitas illa gratiae divinae patet ex 2 Petr. 3, 9.: Deus non vult ullos perire; ubi alterum oppositorum ita negat, ut alterum tanto fortius affirmet. Qui enim non vult quemquam perire, haud dubie vult omnes ab interitu servari; neminem ex mero beneplacito destinat exitio, omnes amore pari complexus.

Ac notandum est, Paulum Petrumque 1. c. loqui de hominibus, quales actu existunt, adeoque habita ratione lapsus Adami et peccatorum, quibus posteri omnes et singuli polluuntur.

Sic etiam Christus Joh. 3, 16.: Deus, ait, dilexit mundum, credentes et incredulos complectentem, quod ex contextu patet, adeoque mundum pro universo genere humano, mundum hunc incolente, acceptum ac toti multitudini Judaeorum, a serpentibus ignitis laesorum, respondentem, quorum singulorum aeque ac omnium (non tantum paucorum, ex mero beneplacito electorum) bono serpens aeneus olim erectus fuit.

Denique Rom. 11, 32. dicitur, Deum conclusisse omnes sub peccatum, ut omnium misereretur, ubi eadem amplitudo esse eorum dicitur, quos Deus in statum peccati venire passus sit, et quorum misereatur; ut quemadmodum homines omnes et singuli peccatores constituti sunt, sic omnes et singuli, quamvis peccatores, tamen etiam sint objectum misericordiae divinae.

Gerhardus: ,,Huic sententiae (de absoluto decreto) primo opponimus beniflcam illam Dei voluntatem, qua serio omnium conversionem et salutem expetit, quam beniflcam voluntatem Scriptura verbis, Christus lacrymis, Jbeus ipse juramento testatam fecit.“ (De elect. et reprob. § 57.)

Lutherus: ,,Gleichwie die liebe Sonne dadurch nicht verdunkelt oder verfinstert wird, dass sie vielen leuchten muss, ja die ganze Welt ihres Lichtes, Scheines und Glanzes geneusst; sie behält ihr Licht gleichwohl ganz, es gehet ihr nichts ab, sie ist ein unmässig Licht, könnte wohl noch zehen Welten erleuchten. . ., also ist Christus unser Herr (zu dem wir Zuflucht haben müssen und von ihm alles bitten) ein unendlicher Born und Hauptquelle aller Gnade, Wahrheit, Gerechtigkeit, Weisheit, Lebens, die ohne Mass, Ende und Grund ist; also, dass wenn auch die ganze Welt so viel Gnade und Wahrheit daraus schöpfete, dass eitel Engel daraus würden, noch ginge ihm nicht ein Tröpflein ab: die Quelle läuft immerdar über voller Gnade. Wer nun, keinen ausgeschlossen, seiner Gnade gemessen will, der komme und hole sie bei ihm.“ (Ad Joh. 1, 16. VII, 1597.),,

Es ist aus der PART. III. CAP. I. Massen fein und tröstlich von Christo, unserem Heiland, gepredigt; wir könnens mit Worten, ja auch mit unsern Gedanken nimmermehr erlangen. In jenem Leben werden wir in Ewigkeit unsere Freude und Lust dran haben, dass der Sohn Gottes sich so tief herunter lässt und nimmt meine Sünde auf seinen Rücken; ja, nicht allein meine Sünde, sondern auch der ganzen Welt, die von Adam an bis auf den allerletzten Menschen gethan ist, die will Er gethan haben und auch dafür leiden und sterben, damit ich ohne Sünde sei und das ewige Leben und Seligkeit erlange. . . Hierauf stehet nun der Grund aller christlichen Lehre; wer die gläubet, der ist ein Christ; wers nicht gläubet, der ist kein Christ, der wird sein Theil auch finden. Es ist ja klar genug gesagt: Dies ist das Lämmlein Gottes, das trägt die Sünde der Welt, und ist der Text Gottes Wort und nicht unser Wort, noch von uns erdacht, dass Gott dies Lamm darum habe geschlachtet und das Lämmlein aus Gehorsam gegen dem Vater der ganzen Welt Sünde auf sich geladen hat. Aber die Welt will nicht hinan, sie will dem lieben Lämmlein die Ehre nicht gönnen, dass wir allein selig werden darum, dass es unsere Sünde trägt. Sie will auch etwas sein, und je mehr sie thun will und Sünde büssen, je ärger sie es macht. . . Das Lamm prediget uns selber, spricht: Sehet zu, wie ich doch eure Sünde trage, aber niemand wills annehmen; und wenn wirs gläubten und annähmen, so würde niemand verdammt. Was soll das Lamm mehr thun? Es spricht: Ihr seid alle verdammt, aber ich will eure Sünde auf mich nehmen; ich bin die ganze Welt worden; habe die Person aller Menschen von Adam her angenommen, dass, so man von Adam Sünde bekommen hat, so will er uns Gerechtigkeit dafür geben. Da sollte ich sagen: Das will ich gläuben, daSs mein lieber Herr, das Lamm Gottes, alle Sünde auf sich genommen hat. Noch wills die Welt nicht gläuben noch annehmen, und wenn sie es gläubte, so würde niemand verloren. . . Dass man aber nicht gläubet, das geschieht nicht aus Mangel des Herrn Christi, sondern die Schuld ist mein. Glaube ichs nicht, so liege ich in meiner Verdammniss. Ich muss kurzum sagen, dass Gottes Lämmlein habe die Sünde der Welt getragen; und es ist mir ernstlich geboten, dass ichs gläuben und bekennen soll, auch darauf sterben. Ja, möchtest du sagen, wer weiss, ob er auch meine Sünde trage? Ich glaube wohl, dass er St. Petri, St. Pauli und anderer Heiligen Sünde getragen hat; die waren fromme Leute; wenn ich nun auch St. Petrus oder St. Paulus wäre! Hörest du denn nicht, was hier St. Johannes sagt: Dies ist das Lamm Gottes, das da trägt die Sünde der Welt! Nun kannst du ja nicht leugnen, du seist auch ein Stück von der Welt. . . So du (nun) in der Welt bist, und deine Sünden sind ein Stück der WeltSünde, so stehet hier der Text: Alles, was Sünde heisst, Welt und der Welt Sünde, vom Anfang der Welt her bis ans Ende, das liegt allein auf dem Lamm Gottes; und dieweil du denn auch ein Stück von der Welt bist und in der Welt bleibest, so wirst du ja auch dess mit geniessen, davon an diesem Ort der Text saget.“ (Ad Joh. 1, 29. VII, 1639. 1642. 1648. 1649. 1650.)

Quenstedtius: ״Ad locum Joh. 3, 16. regerunt Calvinianiy vocem mundi hic notare non omnes in universum homines, sed solos e toto mundo electos sive corpus electorum e toto mundo. . . Ad locum 1 Tim. 2, 4.: ,Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri‘ etc. excipiunt Calviniani, per omnes homines apostolum non intelligere singulos hornines, sed quosvis homines h. e. omnis generis homines, germanice: Nicht alle, sondern allerlei Menschen. Ita Calvinus comm. in h. 1. . . Ad locum Rom. 11, 32.: ,Conclusit Deus omnes sub incredulitatem, ut omnium misereatur‘, excipit Wendelinus: I., Omnes quidem et singulos homines esse sub peccatum conclusos, sed id a Paulo hoc loco non intendi.‘ . . II. Objicit locum Gal. 3, 22.: ,Conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccatum, ut promissio ex fide Jesu Christi daretur credentibus‘; ex quo demonstrare praesumit, quod Paulus, dicens: ,Ut

omnium misereatur‘, de solis credentihus loquatur. . .

III. Vanum est h. 1. Bezae in resp. ad acta coli. Mompelg. p. 223. et aliorum Calvinistarum commune effugium de generibus singulorum. . .

Ad locum 1 Pet. 3, 9.: ,Deus non vult ullos perire, sed omnes ad poenitentiam tendere‘, . . Calviniani unanimiter fere electos seu credentes hic intelligunt, quod colligunt ex illis verbis: Ό κύριος μακροθυμεί εις ημας. . .

Ezech. 18, 23. 32. et 33,11.: ,Nolo mortem impii‘ etc. . .

Chamier tom. III. Panstrat. 1. 7. c. 6. n. 10. effugium suum I. in distinctione voluntatis in ευδοκίαν et ευαρεστίαν, tum II. in verbo חפץ quaerit, quod non significet,velle‘ simpliciter, sed,acquiescere rei alicui, delectari, desiderare‘. . .

Wendelinus exercit. 127. n. 13. asserit: ,Deum non velle mortem peccatoris, quatenus est destructio improbi, velle autem mortem peccatoris, quatenus est justa poena ab ipsa Dei justitia dictata.‘ . .

IV. Alii Calviniani negant, intelligi in istis locis apud Ezechielem in genere omnes peccatores, et dicunt, illos tantum designari, qui se convertunt; ita Maccovius.. .

V. Frider. Spanhemius exerc. de grat. univ. s. 5. th. 7. p. 127. et 128. contendit, verba Ezechielis ad domum Israelis esse restringenda. . .

VI. Polanus in syntagm. p. 613.: ,Deus‘, inquit, ,hic (apud Ezech.) non loquitur de voluntate arcana et beneplaciti, neque de omnibus improbis; voluntate enim arcana et beneplaciti vult omnium eorum, qui pereunt, i. e. (reproborum, mortem; sed loquitur de voluntate signi, revelata in evangelio, quo omnibus offert misericordiam et salutem, ut liberentur a morte et vivant.‘ “ (L. c. P. III. c. 3. s. 2. q. 1. f. 12—17.)


### Concerning the Grace of God toward Fallen Men: ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the ancient heretics, who were called Predestinarians, who around the year of Christ 415, and Gottschalk the Belgian, who in the year of Christ 849, taught that God absolutely predestined some to death, and does not will the salvation of all. . .

2. Of the Calvinists, who posit that God indeed wills all to be saved by the will manifested in the Scriptures, or the will of the sign, but by His secret will, which they call the will of good pleasure, He wills to save only the elect. Thus Beza, part 2, *Response to the Acts of the Colloquy of Montbéliard*, p. 194, writes: 'There has been no time, nor is there, nor will there be, in which God has willed, wills, or will will to have mercy on individuals.' Calvin, Bk. 3, *Institutes*, ch. 23, § 1, 4, sq. . .

Especially Spanheim is very hostile to the universal will of God; for thus he writes in *Syntagma disputt. theol.*, disp. *de grat. univers.*, th. 5, p. 231: 'The sum of our opinion is: Neither can the will to have mercy on all and every human being for salvation be ascribed to God, nor the will to redeem all and every one through Christ, nor the will to call all and every one to salvation through Christ, and therefore universal grace ought neither to be posited nor can it be defended.' To this also pertain all hypothetical Calvinists, who indeed admit a certain universal benevolence of God toward all men, but under the hypothesis of faith, if they believe; inasmuch as they, what they give with one hand, they snatch away with the other, they enlarge the periphery of divine mercy, but restrict it by the impossible and unperformable condition of faith, and therefore they deserve to be numbered among the others, that is, the categorical [deniers of universal grace], such as Camero, Amyraldus, Bergius, Crocius, and others." (L. c. c. 1, s. 2, f. 11.) "

Some Calvinists are Supralapsarians, others Sub-or Infralapsarians. According to the former, God decreed to create the greatest part of men for His own good pleasure alone unto perdition and to cast them into destruction, so that He might declare His absolute power and justice; thus Calvin, Beza, Piscator, Gomarus, Maccovius; according to the latter, God decreed to pass over and leave the greatest part in the fall; thus most Calvinists today and the Synod of Dort, etc." (L. c. f. 10.)

Presbyterians: "The rest of mankind" (besides the elect), "God was pleased, according to the unsearchable counsel of his own will, whereby he extendeth or withholdeth mercy as he pleaseth, for the PART III. CHAP. I.

glory of his sovereign power over his creatures, to pass by, and to ordain them to dishonour and wrath for their sin, to the praise of his glorious justice.“ (The Confession of faith, c. 3. n. 7. See The constitution of the Presbyterian church, in the United States of Am. Philadelphia, 1840. p. 26.) §

4. This same grace of God is not some idle complacency of God, terminated upon the salvation of all, if this were to happen, but it carries with it an inclination of God to confer, on His part, those things which contribute to procuring the salvation of all, so that, as far as it depends on the part of God, it is rendered possible for all to obtain. As if it pleased God if all were saved, yet God did not wish, on His part, to confer what would necessarily have to be provided for them to be rescued from their misery or perdition. Such, I say, is not that will of God terminated upon the salvation of all. For although our own theologians sometimes call that will, by which God wills the salvation of all, conditional rather than absolute, it is not said in the sense as if God only willed the end and did not will the means, or willed the end under a condition which He Himself, out of mere good pleasure, does not wish to be fulfilled for many; but rather insofar as God, willing that men be saved, does not wish them to be saved without any satisfaction or condition to be fulfilled, but to be led to salvation under the condition of certain means; concerning which we shall see more distinctly presently.

Gerhard: „But (say those who contradict us), if God seriously wills that all be saved, then all would also be saved, because ‘all that He willed, God has done,’ Ps. 115:3; ‘who resists His will?’ Rom. 9:19. We answer: Some things God wills absolutely and simply, others under a certain condition and by certain means. The θελητά (things willed) of the first kind, since they are absolute, always come to pass; the statements alleged before are to be understood of these. The θελητά of the second kind, since they are circumscribed by a certain condition and certain means, therefore do not come to pass unless that condition is posited and those means are posited. God wills, and seriously wills, the life of the sinner; but yet He also wills the conversion of the sinner through the Holy Spirit and the Word; but if the sinner rejects that Word and resists the Holy Spirit and thus is not converted, He wills the just damnation of the sinner... Christ in Luke 14 declares this by the example of the master of the house, who prepares a great supper and seriously wills that all who are invited should appear and enjoy the good things; but after they despise his invitation and beneficence, he wills and decrees that none of them shall taste the prepared supper.“ (L. de elect. et reprob. § 75. 77.)

Quenstedt: „The antecedent will, even if strictly speaking it is not absolute, is nevertheless truly and absolutely universal... not indeed under the condition of faith: ‘if they believe,’ but neither is it absolute, but rather under a certain τάξει (order) of means; therefore this will of God is not absolute, but ordered, yet by no means (strictly speaking) conditional, as the hypothetical Calvinists hold... Therefore, when the antecedent will of God is called conditional by certain orthodox theologians, the word ‘condition’ is taken in a coarse sense, in this sense: that God wills the salvation of all not absolutely, but in an ordered manner.“

Whence they call that universal grace, or the antecedent will of God, *efficacious* in opposition to an affection of simple complacency. For the reason for God’s willing is not only the salvation of all, but also the means, insofar as these are to be ordained by God equally for all. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. de volunt. Dei Antec. et Conseq.*, which is subjoined to the *Tractatus contra Vedelium* § 12 sqq., and which we discussed above in Part I, Chapter I, § 20, Vol. II, p. 34.

Gerhard: "The will (of God) is in one respect antecedent, in another consequent. The Calvinists reject this distinction... But it is approved and proven by Chrysostom, *Hom. 1 in Ep. ad Ephes.*, where he calls the former primary and the latter secondary; by Damascenus, *lib. 2. orth. fid.*, where he calls the former θέλημα προηγούμενον and the latter ἑπόμενον; by Anselm, who calls the former the will of mercy and the latter of justice. The antecedent will is that by which God, as a most benevolent Father, wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; the consequent will is that by which God, as a most just Judge, wills that the finally impenitent and unbelieving be damned... This distinction, therefore, has its foundation in the wonderful tempering of divine justice and mercy... Maccovius, *disp. 1*, perverts our opinion. 'They posit,' he says, 'that God from eternity... had mercy on all..., but afterwards... changed this will.' But none of us posits a change of will in God; rather, we say that the consequent will is subordinated to the antecedent. This distinction can be illustrated by various examples: 1. Of a father who favors all his children equally and wills that all become heirs of his goods, but excludes the stubbornly contumacious and degenerate from the inheritance... 4. Of a physician who offers a precious medicine to all infected with the plague and desires their health; but if any spurn the offered means, he allows them to perish by their own fault." (*Exeges. l. 2. § 271.*)

Hollaz: "The will of God is called antecedent and consequent, not 1. by reason of time, ... 2. nor on the part of the divine will itself, as if there were two wills in God distinct in reality, ... 3. but from the order of our reason, which distinguishes diverse acts of willing in God according to the diverse consideration of objects and considers one act before another; so that it may at least be noted that the antecedent will precedes the consequent in the sign of divine reason. For it is prior in our mode of understanding that God wills salvation for men and provides the means of salvation, than that the same God wills to actually confer eternal salvation upon those who will finally believe in Christ, or to adjudge eternal damnation to the finally impenitent." (*Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 1. q. 5. p. 587.*)

Scharff: "It is called a distinction of reason, because it is posited and conceived not in the thing itself, but through reason, i.e., through the operation of the mind." (*Metaphys. p. 174.*)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: "Antithesis: ... 3. Of the Scholastics and Papists who posit that the will of God concerning the salvation of all is only one of simple complacency, but that the efficacious will of God prevails, by which He wills to leave many men with those aids with which He knew they would not live rightly and would finally be condemned. Thus Vasquez in *1. Thomae tom. I. disp. 83. c. 4. n. 28.* Bellarmine *de grat. et lib. arbitr. Lib. II. c. 3.* etc." (*L. c. f. 11.*)

Each of these will be treated distinctly in its proper place, e.g., concerning the common Mediator of all, concerning the universal call, etc. PART III. CHAPTER I.

§ 5. And since, besides goodness, vindicatory justice must also be acknowledged in God, it is certain that that goodness tends toward the salvation of men in such a way that nothing is detracted from justice; and therefore the very goodness of God moves God to procure a means by which divine justice may be satisfied for sinners. By which He is good not only in Himself, but also to men, even to sinners, as His creatures, and which has come to us thus far under the name of grace. As an essential attribute of God, according to Part I, Chapter I, § 23, Vol. II, p. 39. By the force of which, just as God cannot but hate sins, so He cannot but be inclined to demand satisfaction for the violation of His law. For those things which are simultaneously in God, in whom no disorder has a place, cannot be opposed to one another. Therefore, that goodness or grace of God does not tend toward the salvation of sinful men otherwise than insofar as it can be done while divine justice remains intact. Quenstedtius: "Socinus objects in *Praelect. theol.* c. 16, fol. 87: 'There is no one who cannot, by supreme right, forgive and remit injuries inflicted upon him and debts contracted with him, without any true satisfaction being received for them. Therefore, unless we wish to grant less to God than is granted to men themselves, it must be confessed entirely that God could by right forgive us our sins without any true satisfaction being received for them.' Resp.:

Latin:

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Antiquorum haereticorum, qui Praedestinatiani dicti, qui circa annum Christi 415., et Godoschalci Belgae, qui anno Christi 849. docuerunt, Deum absolute quosdam praedestinasse in mortem, nec omnium velle salutem. . .

2. Calvinianorum, statuentium, Deum quidem voluntate in Scripturis'manifestata sive signi velle omnes salvos fieri, voluntate vero arcana, quam beneplaciti vocant, velle solos electos salvare. Ita Beza part. 2. respons. ad acta colloq. Mompelgartens. p. 194. scribit: ,Nullum tempus fuit, vel est, vel erit, quo voluerit, velit, aut voliturus sit Deus singulorum misereri.‘ Calvinus lib. 3. institt. c. 23. § 1. 4. sq. . .

Eadem haec gratia Dei non est otiosa quaedam a complacentia Dei, ad salutem omnium terminata, si haec b contingeret, sed una secum importat inclinationem, Dei ad c conferendum, a sua parte ea, quae faciunt d ad procurandam salutem omnium, ut ea, quantum est a parte Dei, omnibus obtentu possibilis reddatur. Qua non solum in se, sed et hominibus, etiam peccatoribus, tanquam creaturis suis bonus est quaeque gratiae nomine hactenus nobis venit. Tanquam essentiale Dei attributum, juxta P. I. cap. I. § 23. Vol. II. p. 39. Cujus vi Deus ut peccata non potest non odisse, sic ad postulandam satisfactionem pro violatione legis suae non potest non inclinare. ### Concerning the Grace of God toward Fallen Men: Distinguish between the absolute power of God and His ordained power revealed…

1. Distinguish between the absolute power of God and His ordained power revealed in the Word. The question here is not what God could do absolutely (namely, whether He could remit sins without satisfaction), but what He willed and how He has revealed Himself. There is no need to dispute about the power of God where His will is established by revelation.

2. Regarding the argument: 'if it is permitted for any man to remit injuries inflicted upon him without satisfaction, it will also be permitted for God,' we deny both the antecedent and the consequent; the former, because the situation of man is one thing, and that of God, who is the supreme judge of the whole universe, is another; the latter, because a magistrate does not have a free hand to use or not use the sword, to avenge or not avenge injuries that are harmful to the public...

4. From debt taken properly to debt taken improperly and figuratively (such as sin is), the consequence does not follow...

7. Distinguish between a private and pecuniary creditor, and a public and judicial creditor, that is, the avenger of the law and the exacter of justice by virtue of his office. If this one does not show indignation toward delinquents nor exact punishment, he is by that very fact unjust, not munificent. Not to mention that God, in remitting sins, does not have the regard of a mere creditor, but rather of a most just judge." (L.c. P. III, c. 3, membr. 2, s. 2, q. 6, f. 436.) The same: "The Socinians object: We are justified by the absolute grace of God, therefore without the intervention of satisfaction. Thus Socinus *de justific.* f.

11. Resp.: We are indeed justified by grace (Rom. 3:24), but not by absolute grace, because we are justified by the redemption and through faith (v. 25). We are justified by grace (Rom. 4:2–7) in such a way that, through the intervention of the redemption of Christ, this act of justification and remission of sins is an ένδειξις or demonstration of divine justice (Rom. 3:24). They object: Either God could not justify otherwise, and thus the power of God is weakened, or He did not will to, and thus mercy falls. Ostorod. *Instit.* c. 36, f.

300. Resp.: 1. By a similar line of reasoning we could also press the adversaries: God [could save] all men..."

He] either did not want to save [man], or could not; if he did not want to, the glory of his mercy is taken away; but if he wanted to and could not, the glory of his omnipotence is taken away. Whatever they may answer here, they will have it in turn as a response for themselves.

2. Neither horn of the dilemma of Ostorodt strikes us. For both can be conceded in a sound sense. Both that he did not want to remit the guilt without satisfaction, and that he could not: he did not want to, indeed, because it was not fitting in such a way, because he had declared that he willed otherwise; he could not, because it was impossible in itself. For to remit sins unpunished is repugnant to divine justice and truth. Nor is this inability an impotence, but a power. For God can only do those things which are possible.” (L. c. c. 8. s. 2. q. 3. f. 774.)

H. Kromayer: “They (the Socinians) object that it flowed from the very love of God, with which he has always pursued the human race, even when corrupt, that he sent his Son into the world; therefore, there is no vindicatory justice in God that is opposed to his love and mercy. They prove the minor from Rom. 5:8: ‘God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.’ But we respond: One must distinguish between the general and the special love of God: the former wills that lost salvation be made reparable, the latter receives sinners into grace; the former is called [the love] of commiseration, the latter of complacency; the former is absolute, the latter is ordered, which cannot have a place except after satisfaction has been made to divine justice through Christ; this vindicatory justice is opposed not to the former, but to the latter. The cited verse [Rom. 5:8] speaks of the former, the effect of which is the mission of the Son; but preservation from wrath—namely, that we are not forced to pay the penalties merited by sins—presupposes the satisfaction of Christ. The verse 10 of chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Romans deals with both: ‘If, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son: much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved from wrath.’” (Theol. pos. pol. I, p. 140 sq.)

A. Osiander: “Divine love and wrath toward the human race consist together very well; for love is either of mercy, benevolence, and the ordering of means, or of complacency, the conferring of friendship; the former obtains in God even toward the human race that is under wrath, but the latter presupposes one who is appeased.” (Colleg. IV, 170.)

Gerhard: “Thomas (P. III. q. 46. art. 2) argues: ‘That God could remit sins to man without satisfaction, since he has no superior.’ ... The recent Photinians perpetually urge the subtlety of Thomas, that God, as an authentic judge, could have remitted sins to man without satisfaction. But we oppose to it this immovable foundation: God is so merciful that he is also at the same time just. ... Nor could that divine decree promulgated to man be revoked: ‘In the day that thou eatest of the fruit of the tree, thou shalt surely die.’ Therefore, no other remedy remained than that the Son of God himself should assume human nature and in it and through it make satisfaction; God ought not, man could not.” (L. de persona et off. Christi § 169 sq.)

The same: “Bellarmino sins ... in that he posits that God could have liberated either all or some in various ways; we, following Scripture, posit that no other remedy could be found for fallen man than the incarnation and passion of the Son of God himself.” (Loc. de elect. et reprob. § 197.)

The same: “Even if we should concede that the mission of the Son was hypothetical, yet we say that the mission of God, simply for the sake of accomplishing the work of our redemption—the will of God to redeem the human race being presupposed—was necessary, since in the Holy Scriptures no other mode of our redemption has been revealed, nor could there be another while saving the justice of God; meanwhile, we permit others to dispute freely concerning the absolute power of God, which is considered without respect to the other divine attributes.” (Disputt. theol. P. I. p. 54 sq.) PART III. CHAP. I.

The same: "Furthermore they say: But what is the need for Christ’s body to be in the Sacrament? Faith can surely be strengthened without it through the Gospel, which is otherwise preached. . . Do you want to set measure and manner for Him and choose? You should leap for joy that He does it, through whatever manner He wills, only that you obtain it." The same: "God could well, through His omnipotence, save the human race without Christ, without Baptism, without the Word of the Gospel; He could have enlightened the hearts inwardly through the Holy Spirit and forgiven sin without the preaching office and without the ministers of the church; but He did not want to do so." (On Gen. 32:24. II, 1139.)

Concerning which both the wisdom of God may look into it and the free will of God may establish or decree according to divine authority and power, and may actually supply or provide it. § 6. Thus, therefore, it is to be ascribed to divine grace that God willed to give, and did give, to men, who cannot satisfy Him for their sins, a mediator, Christ, who would fulfill the law for all sinners and pay the vicarious penalties for their violations.

a) No one, I say, of them, either for himself or for others. For there is no proportion between that which a man can provide of his own and the infinite justice of God that has been offended. Thus it is said in Ps. 49:7-8: No one can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their soul is precious, and it shall cease forever. Regarding this matter, Christ in John 3:16: For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, etc., and Paul in Rom. 5:8: God commends His love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Finally, 1 Tim. 2, after he had said in v. 4 that God wills all to be saved, he immediately adds that there is one mediator, just as

BY THE GRACE OF GOD. there is one God, namely, willing this one to be the mediator, who gives himself as a ransom for all. Here, at the same time, the universality of the subject, to which the grace of God in relation to the mediator to be given to it is directed, must be observed. Concerning these acts we shall treat in the following chapter. Here we consider them only insofar as the grace of God looks toward that end.

ANTITHESIS. Hofmann: "Between it (the church's doctrine) and mine there remains the very essential difference that it is not the Son who is the object of the Father's wrath, even if only vicariously, but humanity; and that the punishment to which unredeemed humanity would have fallen eternally has not been executed upon the Son, but rather his calling as Savior became the cause of all the sufferings which he brought upon himself as a consequence of his entry into Adamic humanity. It is not he, instead of us, whom the wrath of God has struck, so that the punishment is now executed and no longer needs to be executed; rather, he has suffered the evils in which God's wrath against sinful humanity is executed, in the manner established by his calling as Savior." (Schutzschriften, Part 2, p. 108.) §

7. Moreover, it is also of divine grace, regarding our salvation, to move God so that He may be willing to confer, and does confer, what is His own, to the end that we may all be able to enjoy the vicarious satisfaction of the mediator. As an efficacious intention to be promoted, according to § 4. I do not say that He determines us irresistibly to make right use of the mediator, but that He is willing to provide those things which are required on His part—God’s part—so that no one may be unable to enjoy the mediator.

Hollaz: "The following doubts seem to stand in the way of our assertion: ... If men do not believe because they resist the Holy Spirit who is about to kindle faith, then no unregenerate men can be gifted with faith; the consequent is false, therefore the antecedent is also false. The consequence of the major premise is proved from Rom. 8:7: 'The mind of the flesh is enmity against God; for it does not submit to God's law, indeed, it cannot.' But in all unregenerate men there is the mind of the flesh. — Resp.: Distinguish between natural and malicious resistance. The former the Holy Spirit breaks and restrains through prevenient grace; the latter is in some men lesser, in others greater and more ferocious, which often hinders true faith from being kindled in the heart of an unregenerate man. Objection I: Every resistance opposing the means of grace is malicious. Resp.: Malicious resistance is here called in a special sense that which proceeds from malice voluntarily contracted; natural resistance, however, flows from the very corruption of nature that is innate. Objection II: Although malicious resistance is in the power of man, yet non-malicious resistance is owed to divine grace. Resp.: Just as malicious resistance is either opposed to the external use of the means or to the grace of internal conversion, so also non-malicious resistance denotes either the negation of resistance opposed to the external use of the means, or the negation of the same opposed to the grace of internal conversion. The former is subject to the powers of the will; the latter is owed to divine grace, which takes away the heart of stone. ... Objection III: God by His omnipotence can remove all malicious resistance; since He does not do this, He Himself PART III. CHAP. I.

The cause is that many persevere in unbelief and do not cease to resist the Holy Spirit. *Example:* If God, by His absolute and irresistible power, wished to kindle faith, He could certainly remove all contumacy. But since it has pleased Him to deal with us as with human beings, not as with brutes or stones, He has therefore ordained means through which He wills to work faith in the hearts of men; he who neglects these is not converted, nor is he imbued with true faith. Yet, the blame is not therefore to be attributed to the most holy God that men remain devoid of faith; because He does not remove the malicious resistance which is an impediment to the generation of faith. For the reason is not that he who can remove an impediment, but does not do so, is immediately the cause of the impeded effect; rather, he is to be held as the cause only if he is also bound to prevent or remove the impediment. But by what right is God obligated to take away the malicious resistance from those who obstinately resist the means of grace, or to infuse faith into those who sullenly refuse it? (Exam. theol. P. III. s. 1. c. 1. q. 9. p. 602.)

Which God wills to become ours, not only insofar as it has been performed for us, but in another peculiar way, so that by virtue of it, without impediment, we may be constituted partly as heirs of salvation, and partly attain salvation itself fully. Specifically: 1) that we may apprehend it by faith and unite it to ourselves; 2) that, once apprehended by us, it may be actually imputed to us for the remission of sins; 3) that by virtue of it we may attain many spiritual goods in this life; 4) that likewise, on account of it, we may be gifted with eternal life. *

Apology of the Book of Concord:* "The Christian Book of Concord does not deny that there is a rejection in God, or that God should not reject some; thus it does not go against Luther’s statement, where he writes in *De Servo Arbitrio* against Erasmus, that this is the highest degree of faith: to believe that God is nevertheless the most merciful, who saves so few. Rather, it aims at this: that it does not ascribe to God the actual cause of such rejection or damnation, as the doctrine of the opposition does; and that when it comes to this disputation, all men should lay their finger upon their mouth, and first say with the Apostle Paul in Romans 11: 'Because of unbelief they were broken off'; and Romans 6: 'The wages of sin is death.' Secondly, however, when it is asked why the Lord God does not convert and make all men believing through His Holy Spirit (which He could well do), etc., we should speak further with the Apostle: 'How incomprehensible are His judgments and His ways past finding out!' But by no means should we ascribe to the Lord God Himself the willing and actual cause of the rejection or damnation of the impenitent. But if they press us and say: 'Because you confess the election of the elect, you must also confess the other, namely, that in God Himself there is a cause of rejection from eternity, even outside of sin, etc.': then we say that we are by no means minded to make God the cause of rejection (which actually stands not in God, but in sin) and to ascribe to Him Himself the actual cause of the damnation of the ungodly; but we wish to remain with the little verse of the prophet Hosea, chapter 13, where God says: 'O Israel, you bring yourself into misfortune; your salvation stands alone with Me.' We also wish, as heard above from Luther, not to investigate the dear God insofar as He is hidden and has not revealed Himself. For it is too high for us, and we cannot comprehend it; the more we involve ourselves in this, the further we get from the dear God, and the more we doubt His most gracious will toward us. In such a way, the Book of Concord is also not in denial that God does not work in all men in the same way; for there are many at all times whom He, through public preaching..."

has not called; but that we should therefore conclude with the opposite, that He is a real cause of the rejection of such people, and that He has decided for Himself out of mere counsel that He wills to reject and eternally cast them away, even apart from sin, they shall never persuade us to do. For it is enough that, when we come to this depth of the mystery of God, we speak with the Apostle in Rom. 11: "His judgments are unsearchable," and 1 Cor. 15: "We thank God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." What is beyond that, our Savior Christ will Himself reveal to us in eternal life." (Apology of the F. C. [Ed. Chemnitius, Selneccerus, Kirchnerus.] Dresden, 1584. f. 206. sq.) ANTITHESES. Canons of Dort: "That some are given faith by God in time, and others are not, proceeds from His eternal decree. For He knows all His works from eternity, Acts 15:18, Eph. 1:11, according to which decree He graciously softens the hearts of the elect, however hard, and bends them to believe, but leaves the non-elect to their own malice and hardness by a just judgment." (c. 1. art. 6.) "Furthermore, Scripture testifies that not all men are elect, but that some are not elect or passed over in the eternal election of God, whom, namely, God has decreed, out of His most free, most just, irreprehensible, and immutable good pleasure, to leave in the common misery into which they have plunged themselves by their own fault, and not to grant them saving and converting grace, but, having left them in their ways and under just judgment, finally to condemn and eternally punish them, not only on account of unbelief, but also for all their other sins, for the manifestation of His justice." (art. 15.) "The Synod rejects the errors of those who teach: 'That God has decreed to leave no one in the fall of Adam and in the common state of sin and damnation, or to pass them over in the communication of grace necessary for faith and conversion, out of His mere just will.'" (Reject. err. 8.) "The Synod rejects the errors of those who use the distinction of impetration and application, in order to instill this opinion into the incautious and unskilled: 'That God, as far as He is concerned, has willed to confer upon all men equally those benefits which are acquired through the death of Christ.'" (Rej. c. 2. art. 6.) § 8. The end, for the sake of obtaining which God is moved to procure the salvation of men, is the glory of the divine goodness itself. As Paul says, εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος, the good pleasure of the will of God concerning our salvation, tends εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ, Eph. 1:5, 6. § 9. The grace of God can be described in this place as being an act of the divine goodness, by which God, having looked upon the misery of men contracted through sin, is moved to desire that they all be delivered and attain to salvation, and therefore [to provide] a mediator, and those things which are necessary for the enjoyment of Him, for the good of all.

he himself may seriously desire to provide the means by which they may be rescued from that destruction and led to eternal salvation, for the sake of celebrating the glory of divine goodness.

For here the voice of grace in the nominative case signifies this; see § 2. Who conducts himself by way of a subject, as if moved within himself by that which is his own; see § 2.

As a προκαταρκτική cause, or external impulsive cause; see § 1, note c, and § 3, note c. Who are the object of this grace; see § 3. Which some call the formal acts of this grace; see regarding these § 4, 5, 6, 7. As the end; see § 8.

Latin:

1. Dist. inter potentiam Dei absolutam et ordinatam ac in verbo revelatam. Non quaeritur hic, quid Deus absolute potuerit (an sci. potuerit peccata sine satisfactione remittere), sed quid voluerit et quomodo sese revelaverit. Non opus est de potestate Dei disputare, ubi de voluntate ejus ex revelatione constat.

Argumenti: ,si cuilibet homini licet injurias sibi illatas citra satisfactionem remittere, licebit etiam Deo‘, antecedens et consequens negamus; illud, quia alia ratio hominis, alia Dei, qui summus totius universi judex est; hoc, quia magistratus non habet liberam manum utendi vel non utendi gladio, ulciscendi vel non ulciscendi injurias publico incommodantes. . .

4. A debito proprie ad debitum improprie et figurate acceptum (quale peccatum est) N. V. C. . .

Ut taceam, Deum in remittendis peccatis non habere respectum nudi creditoris, sed potius justissimi judicis.“ (L. c. P. III. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 2. q. 6. f. 436.) 300. Resp.: 1. Simili ratione et nos adversarios urgere possemus: Deus omnes homines

2. Neutrum cornu dilemmatis Ostorodi nos ferit. Utrumque enim sano sensu concedi potest. Et quod non voluerit sine satisfactione culpam dimittere, et quod non potuerit: noluit quippe, quia sic non decebat, quia aliter se velle declaraverat; non potuit, quia in se impossibile fuit. Peccata enim impunita dimittere, divinae justitiae et veritati repugnat. Nec, ista non posse, est impotentiae, sed potentiae. Ea enim Deus tantum potest, quae sunt possibilia.“ (L. c. c. 8. s. 2. q. 3. f. 774.)

H. Kromayerus: ,,Objiciunt (Sociniani), ex ipsa dilectione Dei, qua semper genus humanum, etiam corruptum, fuerit prosecutus, profluxisse, quod miserit Filium suum in mundum; ergo non dari justitiam in Deo vindicativam, quae dilectioni et misericordiae ipsius opponatur. Minorem probarit Rom. 5, 8.: ,Commendat Deus caritatem suam erga nos, quod, cum adhuc essemus peccatores, Christus pro nobis mortuus fuerit.‘ Sed respondemus: Distinguendum inter dilectionem Dei generalem et specialem: prior salutem amissam vult fleri reparabilem, posterior peccatores in gratiam recipit; prior vocatur commiserationis, posterior complacentiae; prior est absoluta, posterior ordinata, quae locum habere lion potest, quam postquam justitiae divinae per Christum fuerit satisfactum; non priori, sed posteriori justitia haec vindicativa opponitur. De priori loquitur versiculus adductus c. 6, 8. epistolae ad Rom., cujus effectus est missio Filii; sed conservatio ab ira, ne sci. poenas peccatis promeritas dare cogamur, satisfactionem Christi praesupponit. De utraque versiculus agit 10. c. 5. epistolae ad Rom.: ,Si, cum inimici essemus, reconciliati fdimus Deo per mortem Filii ejus: multo magis reconciliati servabimur ab ira.“‘ (Theol. pos.pol. I, p. 140. sq.)

Hofmannus: ״Zwischen ihr (der kirchlichen Lehre) nnd der meinigen bleibt der sehr wesentliche Unterschied, dass nicht der Sohn Gegenstand des Zornes des Vaters ist, wenn auch nur Stellvertretung sweise, sondern die Menschheit, und dass nicht die Strafet welcher die unerlöste Menschheit für ewig anheimgefallen wäre, an dem Sohn vollzogen worden, sondern ihm sein Heilandsberuf Ursache aller der Leiden geworden ist, welche derselbe in Folge seines Einkommens In die adamitische Menschheit mit sich brachte. Nicht ihn, anstatt uns, hat der Zorn Gottes betroffen, so dass die Strafe nun vollzogen ist und nicht mehr vollzogen zu werden braucht; sondern die Uehel, in welchen sich Gottes Zorn wider die sündige Menschheit vollzieht, hat er in der mit seinem Heilandsberufe gesetzten Weise erlitten.“ (Schutzschriften, Stück 2. p. 108.) §

7. Est autem etiam gratiae divinae, salutem nostram a spectantis, movere Deum, ut, quod suum b est, conferre velit et conferat ad id, ut satisfactione aliena c mediatoris omnes frui queamus.d Tanquam efficaci intentione promovendam, juxta § 4. Hollazius: ״Assertioni nostrae sequentia obstare videntur dubia: ... Si ideo homines non credunt, quia Spiritui S. fidem accensuro resistunt, nulli homines irregeniti fide donari possunt; consequens est falsum, ergo et antecedens. Consequentia majoris probatur ex Rom. 8, 7.: ,Sensus carnis est inimicitia adversus Deum, legi enim Dei non subjicit se, neque enim potest.‘ At in omnibus irregenitis est sensus carnis. — Resp.: Dist. inter resistentiam naturalem et malitiosam. Illam Spiritus S. per gratiam praevenientem frangit et refrenat; haec in aliis hominibus minor, in aliis major et ferocior est, quae saepe impedit, quominus vera fides in corde hominis irregeniti accendatur. Instantia I.: Omnis resistentia mediis gratiae se opponens est malitiosa. Resp.: Malitiosa resistentia speciali sensu hic dicitur, quae provenit ex malitia sponte contracta; naturalis autem resistentia fluit ex ipsa naturae corruptione connata. Instantia II.: Quamvis resistentia malitiosa sit in potestate hominis, non-resistentia tamen malitiosa debetur gratiae divinae. Resp.: Sicut resistentia malitiosa vel opponitur externo mediorum usui, vel gratiae conversionis internae, ita et non-resistentia malitiosa denotat vel negationem resistentiae externo mediorum usui,oppositae, vel negationem ejusdem gratiae conversionis internae oppositae. Illa viribus arbitrii subest, haec gratiae divinae, cor lapideum auferenti, debetur. . . Instantia III.: Deus omnipotentia sua omnem malitiosam resistentiam tollere potest, quod dum non facit, ipse PART. III. CAP. I.

in causa est, quod multi in incredulitate perseverent, nec Spiritui S. repugnare deshiant. Besp.: Si Deus per potentiam absolutam et irresistibilem fidem accendere vellet, utique omnem contumaciam tollere posset. At cum ipsi placuerit nobiscum agere, tanquam cum hominibus, non tanquam cum brutis aut lapidibus, ideo ordinavit media, per quae fidem in cordibus hominum vult operari, quae qui negligit, non convertitur neque vera fide imbuitur. Neque tamen ideo tribuenda est culpa Deo sanctissimo, quod homines fidei expertes manent; quia malitiosam repugnantiam, quae est impedimentum generandae fidei, non tollit; propterea quod non statim, qui potest impedimentum tollere, nec tollit, causa est impediti effectus, sed tunc demum pro causa is habendus est, si etiam teneatur impedire vel impedimentum tollere. Deus autem quo jure obligatus tenetur, ut iis, qui mediis gratiae obstinate resistunt, malitiosam repugnantiam adimat, vel fidem morose reluctantibus infundat?“ (Exam. theol. P. III. s. 1. c. 1. q. 9. p. 602.)

Quam Deus non tantum, quatenus pro nobis praestita est, sed alio peculiari modo, vult fieri nostram, ut ejus intuitu jam absque impedimento partim haeredes salutis constituamur, partim salutem ipsam plene consequamur. Speciatim 1) ut eam fide apprehendamus, nobisque uniamus; 2) ut ea a nobis apprehensa ad remissionem peccatorum nobis actu imputetur; 3) ut ejus intuitu plura bona spiritualia in hac vita consequamur; 4) ut similiter propter eam vita aeterna donemur.

Apologie des Concordienbuchs: ,,Das christliche Concordienbuch verleugnet auch nicht, dass in Gott eine Verwerfung sei oder dass Gott nicht sollte etliche verwerfen; gehet also auch nicht wider Lutheri Spruch, da er in,Servo arbitrio‘ wider Erasmum schreibet, dass dieses die höchste Staffel des Glaubens sei, glauben, dass der Gott gleichwohl der Gütigste sei, der so wenig selig macht. Sondern dahin siehet es, dass es Gott die wirkliche Ursache solcher Verwerfung oder Verdammniss nicht zuschreibe, dahin des Gegentheils Lehre gehet; und dass, wenn es zu dieser Disputation kommt, alle Menschen den Finger auf den Mund legen sollen, und erstlich sagen mit dem Apostel Paulo Röm. 11.: ,Propter incredulitatem defracti sunt‘; und Rom. 6.: ,Der Sünden Sold ist der Tod.‘ Zum andern, wann aber gefragt wird, warum denn Gott der Herr nicht alle Menschen (das er doch wohl könnte') durch seinen Heiligen Geist bekehre und gläubig mache u. s. w., mit dem Apostel ferner sprechen sollen: ,Quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus et impervestigabiles viae ejus!‘ mit Nichten aber Gott dem Herrn selbst die willige und wirkliche Ursache der Verwerfung oder Verdammniss der Unbussfertigen zuschreiben. Dringen sie aber auf uns und sprechen: weil ihr die Wahl der Auserwählten gestehet, so müsst ihr auch das Andere gestehen, nemlich dass in Gott selbst eine Ursache sei der Verwerfung von Ewigkeit, auch ausser der Sünde u. s. w.: so sagen wir, dass wir keinesweges bedacht sind, Gott zum Ursache!· der Verwerfung zu machen (die eigentlich nicht in Gott, sondern in der Sünde stehet) und ihm selbst wirklich die Ursache der Verdammniss der Gottlosen zuzuschreiben; sondern wollen bei dem Sprüchlein des Propheten Hosea Cap. 13. bleiben, da Gott spricht: ,Israel, du bringest dich in Unglück, dein Heil stehet allein bei mir.' Wollen auch, wie droben aus Luthero gehört, von dem lieben Gott, sofern er verborgen ist und sich nicht geoffenbart hat, nicht forschen. Denn es ist uns doch zu hoch und können's nicht begreifen; je mehr wir uns diesfalls einlassen, je weiter wir von dem lieben Gott kommen und je mehr wir an seinem gnädigsten Willen gegen uns zweifeln. Solchergestalt ist auch das Concordienbuch nicht in Abrede, dass Gott nicht in allen Menschen gleicher Weise wirke; denn viel sind zu allen Zeiten, die er durchs öffentliche Predigt

amt nicht berufen hat; dass wir aber darum mit dem Gegentheil schliessen sollten, dass er eine wirkliche Ursache sei der Verwerfung solcher Leute, und dass er’s für sich aus blossem Rath beschlossen, dass er sie verwerfen und ewiglich verstossen wolle, auch ausserhalb der Sünde, sollen sie uns nimmermehr dazu bereden. Denn genug ist es, dass, wenn wir an diese Tiefe der Geheimniss Gottes kommen, mit dem Apostel Rom. 11. sprechen: ,Seine Gerichte sind unerforschlich‘, und 1 Cor. 15.: ,Wir danken Gott, der uns den Sieg gegeben hat durch unsern Herrn Jesum Christum.‘ Was darüber ist, wird uns unser Seligmacher Christus im ewigen Leben selbst offenbaren.“ (Apologie F. C. [Ed. Chemnitius, Selneccerus, Kirchnerus.] Dresden, 1584. f. 206. sq.) ANTITHESES. Eph. 1, 11., secundum quod decretum electorum corda, quantumvis dura, gratiose emollit et ad credendum inflectit, non-electos autem justo judicio suae malitiae et duritiae relinquit.“ (c. 1. art. 6.),,Scriptura porro testatur, non omnes homines esse electos, sed quosdam non electos sive in aeterna Dei electione praeteritos, quos sci. Deus ex liberrimo, justissimo, irreprehensibili et immutabili beneplacito decrevit in communi miseria, in quam se sua culpa praecipitarunt, relinquere, nec salvifica et conversionis gratia donare, sed in viis suis et sub justo judicio relictos, tandem non tantum propter infidelitatem, sed etiam caetera omnia peccata ad declarationem justitiae suae damnare et aeternum punire.“ (art. 15.),,Synodus rejicit errores eorum .., qui docent: ,Deum neminem ex mera justa sua voluntate decrevisse in lapsu Adae et in communi peccati et damnationis statu relinquere, aut in gratiae ad fidem et conversionem necessariae communicatione praeterire.“ (Reject. err. 8.),,Synodus rejicit errores eorum, . . qui impetrationis et applicationis distinctionem usurpant, ut incautis et imperitis hanc opinionem instillent: ,Deum, quantum ad se attinet, omnibus hominibus ex aequo ea beneficia voluisse conferre, quae per mortem Christi acquiruntur.‘“ (Rej. c. 2. art. 6.) § 8. ## 17 Of Christ: His Person, States and Office

CONCERNING CHRIST, THE PRINCIPLE AND FOUNDATION OF OUR SALVATION. Since sinful men, who are to be led to eternal salvation, have need of a mediator, by whose benefit they may obtain happiness before God, of which they are unworthy in themselves, this mediator must by all means be considered, who is none other than He whom Scripture calls Jesus Christ.

Gerhard: "Just as the forces of enemies are occupied primarily in attacking the fortified citadel and metropolis of any region, so the devil has wished to test all the powers of his cunning and might in the mystery concerning Christ, which he knows to be the metropolis of heavenly doctrine, attacking it from the very beginning of the New Testament, indeed even from the very origin of the world; for at one time he has attempted to overturn the divine nature of Christ, at another the human, at another to dissolve the personal union, at another to weaken His office, and by dissimilar ways he has perpetually striven for the same goal, namely, to corrupt the sincerity and purity of this doctrine and consequently to snatch this treasure of salvation from men." (Exeges. loc. IV. § 3.) a) See the preceding chapter, I. § 5, and above, Proleg. cap. I. § 22. Vol. I. p.

41. Quenstedt: "The Scotists hold that in the first sign of the divine reason there was a decree, independent of the foreknowledge of sin, for the mystery of the incarnation as such, so that the final cause of the incarnation according to its substance was the excellence of the mystery and the exaltation of human nature, but the final cause—and indeed the sole one—of its passibility was the redemption of men or the remedy for sin." (Th. did.-pol. P. III. c. 3. s. 2. q. 1. f. 162.) Chapter II. § 1.

OF CHRIST.

The same: "Christ is called the firstborn of every creature in Col. 1:15, not by reason of His humanity, but of His deity, i.e., begotten by God the Father before all creatures, and thus from eternity." (L. c. f. 162 sq.) The same: "Those words, 'for whom are all things and by whom are all things,' Heb. 2:10, are a periphrasis of God the Father Himself, who, as He is the end of all things, so is He also the effector and maker of all things. Certainly, 'by whom are all things' cannot be conveniently referred to Christ according to His humanity; but τελειώσαι is not to be taken in a passive sense, as Rupertus wishes, but active, so that the sense may be: ... that He might perfect Christ through afflictions, i.e., lead Him to eternal glory." (L. c. f. 164.)

The same: "If the form of the human nature of Christ, preconceived in the divine mind, preceded the creation of man in order, to whose likeness Adam was created (Osiander), Christ ought to have been called the first Adam rather than the second." (L. c. f. 167.) ANTITHESES. Luthardt: "Representatives of that other opinion concerning an incarnation of the Son even without sin are (allegedly) Irenaeus; in the Middle Ages, mystics like Rupert and Johann Wessel from an anthropological standpoint: for the perfection of humanity and its organism; Duns Scotus from a theological standpoint: God's will had to be realized in any case; in the Reformation era, Osiander with Wesselian arguments, and pantheizing enthusiasts, the Socinians, and many Reformed with Scotist arguments. In more recent times, this proposition is widely spread, not only in the theosophical school of Baader and among theosophists like Steffens, Göschel, Chalybäus, Fischer, but also among very many theologians, such as Nitzsch, Martensen, Liebner, Lange, Rothe, Dorner, Ebrard, etc., mostly on the basis of the Schleiermacherian view of Christ as the second Adam and perfecter of creation: humanity would be without its unifying head. Against this, however, Augustine: 'Take away the diseases, take away the wounds, and there is no cause for medicine. If man had not perished, the Son of Man would not have come.'" (Compendium p. 138 sq.)

Just as Peter says in Acts 4:12: There is, he says, salvation in no other (as a cause or foundation to be placed), nor is there any other name given (no thing to be called by any name) under heaven, in whom (by whose benefit) it behooves us to be saved, except Jesus Christ, whom he had preached and in whose name he had healed the lame man. And 1 Tim. 2:5, Paul says: One, i.e., the only mediator of God and men, hitherto separated, but to be reconciled by His work, the man Christ Jesus. Gerhard: "Jesus signifies Savior, for it is from the root ישע in Hiphil הושיע, he saved, preserved, delivered. The angel shows this etymology and the reason for the etymology in Matt. 1:21: 'You shall call His name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins.'" (L. c. § 6.)

The same: "Christ signifies anointed from χρίω, because our Savior was anointed with the oil of gladness, the fullness of the Holy Spirit. As the name Jesus is Hebrew by reason of its primary origin, so the surname Christ is Greek. Therefore, because our Savior is distinguished by a Hebrew and a Greek appellation, it is insinuated by that fact that He is the Savior of both Jews and Gentiles, that is, of all men whatsoever. The name Christ corresponds to the appellation Messiah, derived from the root משח, he anointed; John 1:42, Andrew says: 'We have found the Messiah,' which is interpreted ὁ Χριστός. John 4:25, the Messiah is called Christ (Μεσαίας is formed from the Chaldean משיחא, with ש changed into σσ and ח into the Greek ending ας)." (L. c. § 13.) PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

The same: "Observe that a distinction must be made between a mediate savior; such is also the Father and the Holy Spirit, for these save through the Son, Hos. 1:7: 'I will save them by the Lord their God'; and an immediate savior; such is the Son; where again a distinction must be made between the efficacy of saving or the application of salvation, which is common to the three persons of the Trinity, and the mode of saving or the acquisition of salvation through the incarnation, namely, passion and death, which is proper to the Son." (L. c.) § 2.

The doctrine concerning Christ can be most conveniently set forth by treating: I. of the person of Christ, who is the mediator; II. of His states of humiliation and exaltation; III. of His mediatorial office, and what is joined with it. Let there be, therefore, Section I. OF THE PERSON OF CHRIST. § 1.

In the person of Christ, one must consider: I. that Christ is true God, consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal with the Father; II. that the same Christ is true man, consubstantial with us. Hollazius: "The person of our Redeemer is considered here not as άσαρκος, or as He was from eternity before the incarnation, but as ένσαρκος, or as He began to be in the fullness of time through the assumption of our human nature into His own divine hypostasis." (Exam. P. III. s. 1. C. 3. q. 6. p. 666.)

R. Tellerus: "As far as the person of Christ is concerned, this entire doctrine consists of three parts: 1. that Christ is true man, όμοούσιος with us; 2. that the same is true and supreme God, όμοούσιος with the Father; 3. that both natures constitute one person, and indeed in such a way that the divine nature does not subsist in the human, but the latter in the former. All these truths are comprehended in one statement, John 1:14: a) ό λόγος, β) σάρξ, γ) εγένετο; nor is it said of the human nature: λόγος εγένετο, but this is assigned to the divine: σάρξ εγένετο, so that we may understand that it is the divine person who assumed the human nature into… His own υπόστασις." (See Hollaz. Exam. theol. ed. Teller, p. 666.) See what we said above in Part I, Chapter I, § 29, which is now presupposed.

For Scripture expressly calls Him man, 1 Tim. 2:5; John 8:40. It is established that He is called the Son of Man eighty-two times in Scripture. The appellations concerning the seed of the woman, Gen. 3:15, the seed of Abraham, Gen. 17:7, Gal. 3:16, and the branch of David, Jer. 23:5, also pertain to this. The essential parts of man are also attributed to Christ: indeed, a soul, Matt. 26:38, Luke 23:46; a human body, John 2:21; flesh, blood, and bones,

Heb. 2:14; Luke 24:39. Finally, his genealogy is recounted, as to the ascending line, Luke 3:23 ff., and as to the descending line, Matt. 1:1 ff.

R. Teller: "I do not deny, if you say that by this name (ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου) is designated: α. the truth of the human nature in Christ; β. the origin of the same from the seed of the mother; γ. his most ardent love toward the human race; δ. the preeminence and excellence, which …e others is called ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, Ps. 46:3. But you will also grant me this, that all those reasons do not suffice, unless you add ε. the state of misery, namely, that Christ, as long as he lived on earth, experienced all the infirmities of human nature, and indeed in the place of all men." (See Hollaz, *Exam.*, p. 662.)

H. Kromayer: "Τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον, i.e., what the Son of God did not assume, he did not redeem. After Scripture had brought forward the end for which the Son of God became a partaker of flesh and blood—namely, that through his death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil—it subjoins: 'He did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham,' Heb. 2:16, as if rendering a reason why the angels were not redeemed, because, namely, the Son of God did not assume them, by participating in their nature, as he became a partaker of human flesh and blood. Whence this rule of extensive use was constructed: 'What the Son of God did not assume, he did not redeem.'

For not only do we conclude from this that the devils were not redeemed, but also that the Son of God assumed true human flesh, animated and endowed with the faculty of sensation. For if he had assumed only a schema or φάντασμα of a human body, or had brought his flesh from heaven, and had passed through Mary as through a canal... we would not have been redeemed. ...

It indeed seems that the heretics are supported by the following sayings: 1. That God is said to have sent his Son 'in the likeness of flesh,' Rom. 8:4. But the fallacy of division is committed, because the words of the text hold that he was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, on account of the infirmities, namely, that were assumed, which flow in us from sin, but which were assumed by Christ, who was separated from sinners, freely, κατ' οἰκονομίαν. The likeness, therefore, does not refer to the flesh itself, but to this accident, that it appeared sinful on account of the assumed infirmities.

Hollazii Exam. p. 662.)

H. Kromayerus: ,,Το άπρόςληπτον άΰεράπεντον i. e. quod Filius Dei non assumsit, non redemit.—Postquam Scriptura finem adduxisset, cur F. D. F. eosdem non assumserit, participando sc. naturam eorum, ut carnis et sanguinis humani particeps factus est. Unde regula haec prolixi usus fuit exstructa: ,Quod F. D. non assumsit, non redemit.'
