Similitudo itaque non ad ipsam carnem,, sed ad hoc accidens, quod propter assumtas infirmitates peccatrix visa fuerit.


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: The passage at Phil. 2:7, where Christ is said to have been found 'ἐν σχήματι…

2. The passage at Phil. 2:7, where Christ is said to have been found 'ἐν σχήματι ἀνθρώπων', i.e., in figure and schema. But we reply that the word ἄνθρωπος is not taken for the human species itself, but for an accident of man, or is not taken for man himself, but for one vile and abject, and is opposed to a man of status, just as among the Hebrews אֱנוֹשׁ, i.e., a miserable man, and אִישׁ, i.e., a man or hero, are opposed to each other. This the context teaches, where it is joined with the form of a servant in the same seventh verse.

3. The passage John 6:48, 60, where Christ is called the bread of life, 'which came down from heaven.' But we answer that these words are to be understood not of the human, but of the divine nature.

Thus, if he had assumed only an ἄψυχον (soulless) flesh, as the Apollinarians wished, the whole man would not have been redeemed. But all the faculties prove the soul: the vegetative, because he was nourished and grew; the sensitive, because he saw, heard, tasted, perceived by touch, and moved from place to place; the rational, because he willed, understood, and his soul remained surviving after being separated from the body.

Nor does it stand in the way that ὁ λόγος supplied the τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, i.e., the governing faculty, because subordinated things do not conflict. The rational soul, as an essential part governing the body, was required to constitute an integral man, even though this man was also governed by the Word, who dwelt within by the grace of the personal union." (*Th. posit. pol.* II, 89 ff.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Marcionites, Cerdonians, Manichaeans, and other ancient heretics, who dreamed that the Son of God did not assume a true human nature, but a φάντασμα and a mere external appearance of a body... These heretics were called δοκηταί." PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION I.

of the Valentinians, the Appellites, and the modern Anabaptists, as well as the Weigelians, who maintain that Christ at no time had flesh consubstantial with us, but another, and indeed a spiritual one, brought down from heaven and passing through the womb of Mary like water through a conduit. . . And these heretics are called ἑτερούσιοι. 3.

Of the Nestorians and their followers. . ., who especially attacked the truth of the incarnation of the λόγος. For they divided Christ and called him a mere man, not God incarnate; they called Mary not the Mother of God, but the Mother of Christ, etc. 4.

Of the Eutychians and Swenckfeldians, who teach that Christ indeed had flesh consubstantial with us from the beginning, but that afterwards, in the union or glorification, it was changed into the divine nature. 5.

Of the Arians, who assert that the λόγος assumed flesh πάντη ἄψυχον, i.e., destitute of every soul, even the sensitive and vegetative; these are called ἄψυχοι. 6.

Of the Apollinarists, who maintain that the λόγος indeed assumed a living body, i.e., endowed with a vegetative and sensitive soul, but destitute of a rational soul, in the place of which was his divinity. 7.

Of the Monothelites, who conceded that the Son of God assumed a body and soul, but without a human will. 8.

Of the ancient Photinians and their descendants, the Socinians and Antitrinitarians, who reject and blaspheme the incarnation of the Son of God. For all of them hold the incarnation to be a mere fiction.” (L. c. q. 3. f. 179.)

Luther: “Although, to speak thoroughly, it must follow from Nestorius’s opinion that Christ is a mere man and two persons, yet that was not his intention. For the crude, unlearned man did not see that he was proposing impossible things, that he at once seriously held Christ to be God and man in one person, and yet did not want to grant the properties of the natures to that same person of Christ. The first he wants to hold as true; but that which follows from the first is not to be true. Thereby he shows that he himself does not understand what he denies.” (On the Councils and the Church, XVI, 2727.)

This is what is said in Heb. 2:14: Just as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, so the Son of God himself also, παραπλησίως, in the very same manner (insofar as it pertains to substance), was made a partaker of the same.

Quenstedtius: “Distinguish between ὁμοουσία, insofar as it denotes unity of essence only according to species, and in this sense Christ according to his human nature is ὁμοούσιος to us, — and ὁμοουσία, insofar as it denotes unity of essence according to number, and in this sense according to his divine nature he is ὁμοούσιος to the Father, but to us according to his human nature he is not ὁμοούσιος.” (L. c. f. 178.)

Gerhard: “Because of Swenckfeld, who denied that Christ, as to his human nature, is a creature, this phrase concerning Christ according to his human nature was used at the Smalcald assembly in the year …1537. ‘We disapprove,’ they say, ‘of Swenckfeld’s delirium, and we say that the human nature in Christ both remains and is a creature; as John says: The Word was made flesh.’” (Exeges. loc. IV. § 98.)

Hollazius: “The Arians contended that the λόγος in himself, even without the human nature assumed, is a creature, made out of nothing. Therefore, the ancients, because of the snares of the Arians, rejected this proposition: Christ is a creature.” (Exam. th. P. III. s. 1. c. 3 q. 13. p. 660.) § 2. From the fact, however, that the same Christ is he whom Scripture describes now as God, now as man

describes, it is gathered, that the person of Christ is in two natures. And this is that great mystery, which ought to be regarded primarily in this place.

E.g., when the same one, who is made of the seed of David, is said to be the Son of God (Rom. 1:3), the same one who is born of Mary is said to be the Son of the Most High (Luke 1:35), the same one who is the Word (ύποστατικόν) of God and God, is said to have been made flesh (John 1:14); c…ompare ch. 20:28 and 31; Gal. 4:4. For the terms "Son of God" and "son of man" in the nominative case denote the person, who possesses a nature, whether divine or human.

For the person in the oblique case imports the nature. Gerhard: "The person of Christ consists of two natures, divine and human. The consideration of the divine nature is called by the ancients ϑεολογία, but the human is called οικονομία. There is in Christ a duality of natures, because he is not man only, and a unity of person, because there is one Christ, who consists of two and in two natures, and these two natures personally united are one Christ. And in him there is άλλο καί άλλο, because the divine essence or nature is one thing, and the human essence or nature is another; but not άλλος καί άλλος, because it is not one God and another man, but he is one ϑεάνϑρωπος, God and man, and therefore one person." (Exeg. 1.4. § 34.)

Thus Paul himself calls it υμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον, a mystery great by the confession of all, 1 Tim. 3:16; cf. Matt. 16:16 and 17. Hunnius: "Because the λόγος is written to have descended from heaven by assuming flesh, I desire the reason for his descent to be explained to me from the Scriptures. — First, the Son of God did not descend from heaven in such a way that he brought his human nature or flesh from heaven, as the Valentinians dreamed.

Secondly, neither is that descent understood as if the λόγος, according to his divinity, at the time of that incarnation, descended or flew down from some highest heaven by local motion and inserted himself into the womb of the virgin, so that he might assume flesh there. For the λόγος, being infinite by reason of his essence and essentially filling heaven and earth with the Father and the Holy Spirit, cannot by any reason be moved or transferred from place to place. Just as also, in order to become man, he did not need such a descent from some supreme place of heaven to the lowest; since even before the incarnation he was essentially in Mary, just as he was in all other creatures, and wherever the λόγος is, there he has his heaven and heavenly kingdom with him; but for that ενσάρκωσις he only needed this, that he who before and outside of the incarnation was most present to the virgin Mary, now in the incarnation should assume human nature from her and inseparably join it to himself in the unity of person.

Thirdly, therefore, the Son descended from heaven in the very same way that he is written in John 16 to have come forth from the Father, certainly not that the λόγος by reason of his divinity ever deserted the Father, in whose bosom he perpetually resides; as he says to Philip: 'Do you not believe that the Father is in me and I in the Father?'; nor that the λόγος by his divinity ever deserted heaven or withdrew from the administration of heaven for a time; but just as God himself in Gen. 11:19, Exod. 19, and other places of Scripture is said to descend from heaven not by deserting the place from which he never departs by his essence, but by manifesting himself on earth by some visible and conspicuous sign or revelation: so the Son of God descended from heaven to earth when he assumes human nature on earth and manifests himself in it, 1 Tim. 3." (Libelli 4. de persona Christi. 1690. p. 24. sq.)

Quenstedtius: "They object: The incarnation renders God mutable. Resp.: The divinity acts by assuming flesh, it does not suffer physically. Divine PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

the Divinity terminated the humanity with its own hypostasis, the humanity did not alter the Divinity. The change made here is not regarding God, but regarding the human nature. Obj.: The Incarnation removes the deity; for God having become man is no longer God. Resp.: Not God having become flesh, but God transmuted into flesh ceases to be God. Inst.: Nothing can be made without ceasing to be what it had been. Resp.: Nothing can be made through transmutation and alteration without ceasing to be what it is, but not through assumption, where the assumed and the assuming remain together. Inst.: It is one thing to assume flesh and another to become flesh. When the soul is united to the body, who would say that the soul has been made a body? Resp.: The soul is not made a body for this reason, because matter is not drawn to the hypostatic being of the form. Here two incomplete things are united, there complete things. The divine oracle suffices, even if nature does not supply an example, for it is therefore ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον, 1 Tim. 3:16. (L. c. f. 189.) §

3. However, the unity of the person having been admitted, we must further confess that the human nature of Christ does not have its own subsistence, but subsists by an alien subsistence, namely, that of the divine nature. For a person is formally constituted in its being by subsistence, and from the unity of subsistence one person must be reckoned. For it is necessary that one or the other nature, from among those which coalesce into one person, lack its own substance; and since the divine nature, which is most simply one with its own subsistence, does not demand to lack the same, it is evident that the lack of proper subsistence must be attributed to the human nature.

tas humanitatem sua hypostasi terminavit, humanitas Divinitatem non alteravit. Mutatio hic facta non circa Deum, sed circa humanam naturam. Ob}·: Incarnatio tollit deitatem; Deus enim homo factus non amplius est Deus. Resp.: Non Deus caro factus, sed Deus in carnem transmutatus Deus esse desinit. In8t.: Nil fieri potest, quin desinit esse, quod fuerat. 3. Admissa autem unitate personae, a neeesse est, porro fateamur, humanam Christi naturam non habere submtentiam propriam,b sed subsistere subsistentia aliena, nempe divinae naturae.c Nam persona per subsistentiam in esse suo formaliter constituitur et ex unitate subsistentiae persona una aestimari debet. Oportet enim naturam alterutram ex his, quae in unam pereonam coalescunt, carere sua propria substantia; cumque divina natura, quae cum subsistentia sua simplicissime una est, carere eadem non poscit; patet, humanae naturae tribuendam esse carentiam propriae subsistentiae.


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Chemnitius: "Because the person of the Word did not assume the person of a man,…

Chemnitius: "Because the person of the Word did not assume the person of a man, but the nature of a man; likewise, because the divine nature is the assuming one, but the human nature is not the assuming one, but the assumed, hence it is indeed rightly said: God was made man; but it is not so properly said: Man was made God, God assumed man; although the ancients sometimes speak in this way." (De duab. naturis in Chr. c. 14. f. 70.)

Luther: "The Symbol sings: 'Thou, to deliver, didst take upon Thee man': Augustine often does the same; although the rule (as it seems) dictates that it should be said: Thou, to deliver, didst take upon Thee humanity or human nature." (Disp. th., 1539. Tom. Jenens. lat. I, 530.)

Winckelmann: "It follows that the human nature subsists in the person of the Word or has its own subsistence; unless this is the case, it is necessary that it subsist by itself and be a person; which is Nestorian." (Disput. in Academ. Giessena hab. Tom. II, 48.)

Nor does the human nature of Christ become more imperfect through this than the human nature is in us, since the perfection of a thing is reckoned from its essence itself, not from its subsistence, and furthermore, the lack of proper personality in the human nature of Christ is supplied by the divine subsistence.

Quenstedtius: "It is one thing to lack a proper hypostasis, and another to lack every hypostasis; a complete nature can indeed subsist without a proper hypostasis (for this is not of the essence of the thing, but is the ultimate mode of subsisting), but not without any hypostasis. The Λόγος assumed the human nature, destitute of its own personality, into His own hypostasis; therefore Augustine rightly says: 'The Word did not take upon Himself the person of a man, but the nature of a man.' For because nothing subsists without a hypostasis, either proper or alien, and the human nature in Christ does subsist, but not by a proper subsistence, because the unity of the person prevents it: therefore it must be confessed that it subsists ἐν τῷ λόγου ὑποστάσει, which is the ὑπόστασις of both natures according to Damascene III. O. F. c. 9., yet in such a way that the divine nature subsists in its own person κυρίως καὶ πρώτως. For although after the union has been made, the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος is also the ὑπόστασις of the humanity, nevertheless it belongs to the divine nature πρώτως καὶ καθ' αὑτό, but to the human nature δευτέρως καὶ καθ' ἄλλο, and thus it is and remains perpetually the most proper [hypostasis] of the λόγος, even though it is participated in by the human nature." (L. c. f. 190. sq.) §

4. Next, because there are two natures in the one person of Christ, through which the same Christ is the Son of God and the son of man, a twofold generation must be considered, eternal and temporal. For in generation is founded the το esse [being] of the Son. However, through a twofold generation and the twofold filiation founded upon it, there do not come to be two Sons, since those two relations inhere in one subject, just as one father can be and is accustomed to be the father of many sons, or one master the master of many servants, to each of whom he has a peculiar relation. But that others, while ascribing one filiation to Christ, nevertheless acknowledge two modes of filiation, amounts to the same thing, I think, if you look at the matter; although you might not unreasonably doubt whether it is more conveniently stated.

Quenstedtius: "Distinguish between the prior and posterior nativity of Christ; the prior nativity is without beginning, the posterior without example; the prior without a mother, the posterior without a father; the prior is inconceivable, the posterior ineffable." (L. c. q. 3. f. 178.)

Through which He has that He is the Son of God; see Part I, Chapter I, § 30, n. III, Vol. II, p. 50.

Through which He has that He is man or the son of man; see Gal. 4:4 and the passages cited in the note to § 1, by which it is taught that Christ truly draws His human nature from other men existing beforehand, through a generation, though not entirely natural, yet true.

And this pertains most of all to the present matter.

Delitzsch: "Was then, as Mich. Baumgarten teaches, Christ according to His humanity really pre-existent in Israel?... That pre-existence collapses in itself, in that it reduces itself to the fact that Israel is the people from whom the material, which the Spirit of God was to form into human nature, was once to be taken; but this material propagates itself in Israel as a massa corrupta and requires in the fullness of time a supernaturally sanctifying operation of the Spirit in order to serve the purpose of the incarnation of the Logos. Rightly, therefore, have the dogmaticians of our Church contested the proposition: that Christ existed naturally in the loins of Adam, as an erroneous one. See Fecht, Sylloge dispp. XXII, th. 9.; Sam. Schroeder, dissert. de sanctificatione seminis Mariae virginis (Lips. 1709.); J. Geo. Stoltz, diss. de praeservatione massae, ex qua Deus nasci debuit; J. Wolfg. Jaeger, lib. de Christo sponsore, c. I. (against Pierre du Moulin, Poiret, and others); Gotthard Guenther, scheda de Christi conceptione s. purgatione massae spirituali."

OF THE PERSON OF CHRIST. PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

5. The eternal generation of Christ being presupposed, the temporal generation must be treated in such a way that, in part, the production of the human nature is explained, and in part, its union with the divine nature. Our intellect certainly conceives first of the production of the human nature; then, finally, it conceives of it, as if already existing, being united to the other nature; although, if you attend to it rightly, both actions occur simultaneously and at the same time, or perhaps, in reality, they are but one. Certainly, that statement is not inappropriately made: ἅμα σάρξ, ἅμα λόγου σάρξ, at once flesh, at once the flesh of the Word (or of the Son of God).

KROMAYERUS: "The meaning of this aphorism (ἅμα σάρξ, ἅμα λόγου σάρξ) is that that mass or drop of blood, from which the Word built a temple for Himself, did not for even a moment subsist by itself or have its own peculiar hypostasis, much less was it assumed by the Word only at that time when the term of generation was completed and the form of a man was introduced (lest we be forced to concede that the Word was united to an embryo), which would be Nestorianism itself, making the human nature even for a time self-subsistent (αὐθυπόστατον). But rather, in one act, when the Holy Spirit separated that mass in the womb of the Virgin Mary, purged it from the stain and corruption of sin, and supplied the defect of male seed, in one act, I say, it was assumed by the Son of God. These things are connected by the closest bond in Luke 1:35: 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High' (the Son of God, who is also called 'the power of God' elsewhere, 1 Cor. 1:24) 'will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God.' Where the particle διό renders the reason why the holy one born of Mary ought to be called the Son of God, namely, because of the personal union of the power of the Most High, the Son of God, with the human nature, which is most holy and liberated from all sin. And if it was not unworthy of God to be united with an infant, it will not be unworthy of Him to be united with an embryo... Christ passed through all the stages of our age, that He might radically heal our unclean conception and birth." (Theol. pos. pol. II, 91.)

Hugo de S. Victore: "He assumed the soul by creating it, and created it by assuming it." Which terminates at the human nature viewed in itself. Which terminates at that same human nature, but insofar as it constitutes one suppositum with the divine nature. It is called by one name, incarnation, from the words of John 1:14: ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο; likewise, the assumption of human nature, from Hebrews 2:16, where the Son of God is said to have assumed the seed of Abraham. However, that incarnation and assumption, even if grammatically they are not predicated of the Son in the same way—for He is said to be incarnated passively, but to assume actively (namely, to assume another nature, but not to be assumed by it)—are nevertheless not two actions in reality, but one. For by the very fact that the Son of God becomes flesh, or is incarnated, the human nature is assumed by Him, or He Himself assumes the human nature; and conversely, while He assumes the human nature, He is incarnated.

Dannhauerus: "The reasons why the second person, the Son of God, and not the first or third, was incarnated are usually given as follows: 1. That He who was the Son of God from eternity might become the Son of Man in time; 2. That He who was the natural Son might make us adopted sons; 3. That He through whom all things were made might restore those things which had failed, and through the image of God [restore them] to the lost..."

might be reformed, who had been deformed; so that the 4th, which is the middle person in the Trinity, might also be the mediator by office.” (Hodos. phaen. 8. p. 308. sq. cf. Gerhardi Exeg. 1. IV. § 104.)

Luther: “If you now ask reason why the Son and not the Father became man, it will certainly not be able to inform you; indeed, it will become a fool over it. Therefore, hear what the Holy Spirit tells you through St. John: the Word became man and suffered, and not the Father, etc. How that comes to pass, you should believe and not know nor understand, but save it until that blessed day of our redemption. Reason stumbles at this article when it wants to measure and grasp it with its cleverness; it thinks: In the Godhead there is one indivisible essence; how then can the middle person alone become man, and not all three? I would surely be as clever as any heretic if I wanted to master these words, ‘The Word became flesh,’ according to my own pleasure. It is a matter of believing, not of seeing, measuring, or grasping. In the Godhead there are three persons: the Son is the Word that was in the beginning; that same Word or utterance, not the speaker, became man; therefore, we do not let the other two persons be mixed into the humanity.” (Exposition on John 1:1–14, preached in the year 1542. VII, 1840. sq.) § 6. The efficient cause of the produced human nature of Christ is the Holy Spirit, yet with the other persons not excluded.

Thus, Luke 1:35, the Holy Spirit is said to be about to come upon Mary, in respect to producing in her the human nature of the Son of God, or as about to effect that she herself should conceive a human fetus. And in Matthew 1:18 and 20, the preposition ἐκ in the words ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου ἐστίν is causal, and a sign of the efficient cause. Gerhard: “The Holy Spirit cannot be called the father of Christ, because the flesh of Christ was not begotten from the essence of the Holy Spirit, but from the substance of the Virgin Mary; ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος does not denote the material, but the efficient cause and operation. When we say ‘of’ Mary, it is a material ‘of’; when we say ‘of’ the Holy Spirit, it is a potential ‘of’. Justin, in the *Expositio fidei*: not by sexual union, but by power. Athanasius, *Disputation against Arius*, p. 51: ‘She was found with child of the Holy Spirit, not that the Holy Spirit is to be called the father of our Savior, so that two fathers might be believed, but the same Holy Spirit is a co-worker with the Father and the Son and is of one power.’ ... Damascenus, *De fide orthodoxa*, 1: ‘Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit not spermatically, but creatively.’” (Exeg. 1. IV. § 107.)

Neque per hoc natura humana Christi fit imperfectior, quam est natura humana in nobis, cum perfectio rei ex essentia ipsa, non ex subsistentia aestimetur ac praeterea personalitatis propriae carentia in humana natura Christi suppleatur per subsistentiam divinam.

Quenstedtius: ״Aliud est carere propria hypostasi, et aliud carere omni hypostasi; potest quidem natura completa subsistere sine propria hypostasi (haec enim non est de rei essentia, sed est modus subsistendi ultimus), non vero sine omni hypostasi. Quia enim sine hypostasi vel propria vel aliena nihil subsistit, humana vero natura in Christo subsistit, non autem subsistentia propria, quia obstat personae unitas: ergo fatendum est, eam subsistere εν τον λόγον νποστάσει, quae άμφοτέρων των φύσεων νπόστασις Damasceno III. (Lic. f. 190. sq.) §

4. Deinde, quia duae naturae sunt in una Christi persona, per quas idem Christus est Filius Dei et filius hominis, consideranda est duplex generatio, a aeterna b et temporalis.c In generatione enim fundatur το esse Filii. Per duplicem autem generationem et in illa fundatam filiationem duplicem non fiunt duo Filii, quippe uni subjecto duae illae relationes insunt, prout unus pater multorum filiorum, dominus unus multorum servorum esse potest et solet, ad quos singulos relationem peculiarem habet. Quod autem alii, unam filiationem Christo adscribentes, duos tamen modos filiationis agnoscunt, eodem, opinor, redit, si rem spectes; quamvis, anne commodius dicatur, non abs re dubitaveris.

Quenstedtius: ,,Dist. inter nativitatem Christi priorem et posteriorem; prior nativitas est sine initio, posterior sine exemplo; prior sine matre, posterior sine patre; prior incogitabilis, posterior ineffabilis.“ (L. c. q. 3. f. 178.)

Per quam habet, quod est Filius Dei.; vid. Part. I. cap. I. § 30. n. ΠΙ. Vol. II. p. 50.

Per quam habet, quod est homo aut filius hominis; vid. Gal. 4, 4· et loca ad § 1. not. b, citata, quibus docetur, Christum naturam suam humanam trahere revera ex aliis hominibus antea existentibus, per generationem, licet non plane naturalem, veram tamen.

Atque haec ad praesens maxime spectat.

Delitzsch: ,,War denn, wie Mich. Baumgarten lehrt, Christus nach seiner Menschheit wirklich präexistenziell in Israel beschlossen?... Mit Recht haben somit die Dogmatiker unserer Kirche den Satz: Christum naturaliter extitisse in lumbis Adami, als einen irrigen bestritten. Vid. Fecht, Sylloge dispp. XXII, th. 9.; Sam. ### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: For it is a work *ad extra* (outward)

For it is a work *ad extra* (outward). And to this pertains what is said concerning the power of the Most High, that is, the omnipotence common to the three persons, which was to overshadow Mary, Luke 1:35. For although at other times the Holy Spirit himself is believed to be called the power from on high, Luke 24:49, it cannot, however, be denied that the word δύναμις itself denotes power and the term ὕψιστος, or Most High, denotes the supreme God; whence, literally, the power of the Most High is the power of God, and in relation to an effect actually produced outside of God, it certainly denotes the power common to the three persons, even if the work itself is attributed to one certain person, and indeed to the Holy Spirit by appropriation, and thus the same person of the Holy Spirit can be called by the name of divine power. PART III. CHAP. I. SECTION I.

7. The matter is the blood-mass of the Virgin Mary, from which the human nature of Christ was made, or produced. This is what it means to be born of a woman and thus to draw one’s substance from a woman, inasmuch as she contributed something of her own to this generation, Gal. 4:4. Hence also in Luke 1:42 it is notably called the fruit of Mary’s womb, as if drawing substance, sap, and blood from thence. And thus the subject or matter of our generation and of the human nature of Christ is, at least in part, the same, Heb. 2:14. §

8. The very impregnation of Mary and the production of the human nature of Christ effected in her can be described as a supernatural action, by which the Holy Spirit sanctified the blood-mass of the blessed Virgin and disposed and elevated it, having been brought to the customary place of generation, so that from it a perfect human fetus might be made. According to what has been said thus far in § 6 and 7. Whence we here immediately join the efficient cause and the matter with the form or mode of the action itself. Scripture calls it ἐπέλευσις and ἐπισκιασμός, Luke 1:35. For that ἐπέλευσις, or act of coming upon, is certainly such that the Holy Spirit, otherwise omnipresent as to His infinity and immensity, here, in Mary, manifested Himself to be present by a certain new and peculiar effect. And that ἐπισκιασμός, or overshadowing, is believed to have an analogy to that action by which the Holy Spirit, in the work of creation, brooding over the waters and as it were fostering them, was efficacious for the production of creatures; concerning which Gen. 1:2. However, we do not dispute whether in one moment the organic body of Christ was fully formed and the soul united to it. Kromayerus: "The Scholastics denied that the Son of God was united to an embryo, and indeed for this reason primarily, that an embryo is not yet animated, and consequently is not a human being. But they presuppose here a false hypothesis concerning the immediate infusion of souls after the completed term of generation. The truer opinion, however, is that of traducianism." (Th. pos. pol. II, 92.) §

9. Thus it is evident that that conception is most distinct from that which occurs according to the course of nature, or is miraculous, although Christ, the God-man, through it received a nature consubstantial with ours, subject to the infirmities common to nature, not equally to personal ones, much less to sin, indeed distinguished by certain prerogatives.

See Luke 1:34, 37, where Mary asks the angel, who was the messenger of the conception of the Messiah in her, a virgin, about to take place: πώς ϊσται τούτο; "How shall this be?" acknowledging that it is naturally impossible for her, not knowing a man, to conceive and give birth; but the angel agrees with Mary on this point and teaches that one must simply look to the omnipotence of God.

Heb. 2:14 and 17. Compare this place, § 1, last note. For example, hunger, thirst, sleep, sweat, weariness, tears, sorrow, indignation, etc., concerning which we shall see in Section II, on the state of exinanition. Dannhauer: " 'T ovto μέν πολλάκις,' says Chrysostom in homily 6 on Matthew, 'έστιν ιδεϊν αυτόν δακρϋοντα, γελώντα δε ονδαμον' (It is indeed often possible to see him weeping, but never laughing). Similarly, besides others, Augustine (or rather someone else, sermon 35 on the saints) and Salvian of Marseilles, book 6, *De gubernatione Dei*: 'Christ left us such an example, whom we read to have wept, but we do not read that he laughed.' But truly, it was of no concern to our salvation to know whether Christ laughed. 'That, however, it was important to know: how merciful a Lord we have, who for us miserable sinners descended from the heavens, having assumed the form of a servant, humbling himself, that he might exalt us, and by his passion and death might expiate our sins.' Thus not badly Vossius, I, 8, *De origine*." (*Hodos. phaen.* 8, p. 807.)

Such, for instance, as it was neither expedient for the human race to be assumed, nor would it have been consistent with the dignity of his nature, as Lombard, III *Sent.* dist. XV, and Thomas, P. III, Q. IV, Art. IV, speak. Such are various diseases, blindness, deformity, etc. Hollaz: "Christ assumed natural infirmities, common to all men constituted in the natural state, but not personal ones, which arise from particular causes, much less did he take on morally vicious defects. Natural infirmities of men are those which are present in all men after the fall... Personal infirmities are those which proceed from particular causes and arise either from a vice of the δννάμεως πλαστικής, or formative power, in the begetter, such as phthisis, arthritis, etc., or from a particular fault, namely from excessive gluttony, venery, or other excesses, such as fever, gout, dropsy, etc., or from a peculiar nemesis or divine judgment, such as the diseases of the family of Joab, 2 Sam. 3:29, etc. These are very far removed from the most holy humanity of Christ, since, as Lombard judges in book III, *Sent.* dist. X, it was neither expedient for the human race that they be assumed, nor would it have been consistent with the dignity of his nature." (*Exam.* P. III, § 1, c. 8, q. 11, p. 657.)

Namely, personal, actual, or habitual, whether connate or acquired. For thus he is called μή γνους αμαρτίαν, "not knowing sin," 2 Cor. 5:21; άχαχος, αμίαντος, χεχωρισμένος άπό των άμαρτωλών, "innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners," Heb. 7:26. Compare John 8:46; 1 Pet. 1:19; ch. 2:22. But that he was subject to the sins of others by imputation, we shall teach below. Kromayer: "Nor could the guilt of Adamic sin involve Christ, because he was not in the loins of Adam by the consequence of nature, but by promise, not as a mere man, but as the God-man, and consequently the Lord of the law, whom no law could bind." He was indeed made fairer than the sons of men, Ps. 45:3, most highly adorned with all gifts of grace and beauty beyond the lot of others, partly regarding the external beauty of the body, and partly and primarily regarding the excellent gifts of the soul, wisdom, righteousness, kindness, constancy, etc.

But the right of immortality can also be referred to here. For unless Christ the man had voluntarily emptied Himself, He would have been immortal by a double right: first, from the integrity of His nature; second, from the benefit and right of the union, because His body was personally united with Life itself, or the life-giving λόγος. Therefore, He willingly underwent the lot of mortality; for our sake He abdicated the right of immortality; yet in death itself He remained immune to corruption: these are the words of the blessed Aeg. Hunnius, T. I. Opp. Qq. et Respp. de Persona Christi, p. 171, 178. Fechtius: "The opinion of Franc. Vavassor is not improbable: that Christ was endowed neither with any exceptional and excellent form beyond others, nor with a base and foul one, but with an ordinary and common one; yet those who ascribe to Him a form more excellent even than Adam’s, if He is considered in His natural constitution, rely on greater arguments." (Sylloge controvers. Disp. 22. th. 8. p. 167.) §

10. The union of the human nature with the divine consists in this, that those natures are so joined that they became one person; and thus the terminus of the union is either Christ the θεάνθρωπος, or the union itself, or the human nature, viewed as personally united to the Son of God.

S. Gesnerus: "How are the two natures united in Christ? Dr. John teaches this with the proposition: 'The Word was made flesh.' For first, that the Word and flesh are united is evident from this, because things and substances that are in no way united cannot be so joined in a proposition that one is predicated of the other, and it is said that one thing is (or has been made) the other. For to be said requires to be in. Wherefore, since the λόγος was made flesh and thus joined with the flesh in reality, so that flesh can be truly predicated of the λόγος, and consequently since flesh is predicated of the Word, it must be that the flesh and the Word are united, ένωθήναι. Then John also shows the mode of the union in two ways: first, generally in the word εγένετο, then with the specific difference added, by which the union is defined. — What is the meaning of the word εγένετο in this place? There can be two meanings of this verb, and no more, based on the principle of contradiction. For when one singular thing becomes and is another, it either becomes κατά μεταβολήν, so that one is changed into the other, just as water becomes wine; to which mode belongs natural generation and the mixing of bodies; or it becomes in such a way that, with no change intervening, κατ’ άμεταβλησίαν, one singular thing is nevertheless joined and united with another in some way. Thus the dove is the Holy Spirit, the flames on the mouths of the apostles are the Holy Spirit, the blessed bread is the body of the Lord; but in different ways. Now the λόγος does not become flesh through change, so that He ceases to be the λόγος and is changed into flesh. For John says that even after the incarnation, the λόγος remains and dwells among us and gives His glory to be seen... Nor, on the other hand, does the λόγος become flesh in such a way that the flesh is absorbed into the λόγος and after the incarnation is not flesh, but merely the λόγος. For John expressly proves that the human nature is entire in Christ even after the incarnation, by the arguments that have been set forth. Since, therefore, neither the λόγος into..."

Quamobrem cum λόγος sit factus caro et ita cum carne reipsa junctus, ut caro de λόγφ vere possit praedicari, ac proinde cum caro de Verbo praedicetur, oportet, carnem et Verbum ένωθήναι, unita esse. Deinde Johannes modum quoque unionis dupliciter ostendit: primum generaliter in verbo εγένετο, deinde addita specifica differentia, per quam unio definitur. — Quae est significatio verbi εγένετο hoc loco? Duae possunt esse hujus verbi signiflcationes et non plures, ex principio contradictionis. Nam cum unum singulare fit et est alterum, id aut fit κατά μεταβολήν, ita ut unum in alterum mutetur, sicut aqua fit vinum; ad quem modum pertinet naturalis generatio et mixtio corporum; aut ita fit, ut, nulla intercedente mutatione κατ’ άμεταβλησίαν, nihilominus una res singularis cum altera conjungatur et uniatur quovis modo. Sic columba est Spiritus Sanctus, flammae in ore apostolorum sunt Spiritus Sanctus, panis benedictus est corpus Domini; sed diversis modis. Jam λόγος non fit caro, per mutationem, ita ut desinat esse λόγος et in carnem mutetur. Nam Johannes etiam post incarnationem dicit, λόγον manere et in nobis habitare et gloriam suam conspiciendam dare. . . Nec contra λόγος ita fit caro, ut caro in λόγφ absorbeatur et post incarnationem non sit caro, sed merus λόγος. Nam Johannes diserte probat, humanam naturam etiam post incarnationem esse in Christo integram, iis argumentis, quae sunt exposita. Cum igitur nec λόγος in


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: neither the flesh nor the flesh into the λόγος have been changed, and…

neither the flesh nor the flesh into the λόγος have been changed, and nevertheless the flesh is truly said of the λόγος: Ό λόγος σαρξ εγίνετο, it is necessary that the λόγος and the flesh be one, joined together κατ' άμεταβλησίαν in such a way that neither the λόγος has been converted into the flesh, nor the flesh into the λόγος.” (Orthod. conf. de persona etc. 1595. p. 47. sq.)

Such indeed is what the Greeks call συνΰετον, where one nature is not indeed composed out of several natures, yet is composed together with another.

N. Hunnius: “Hypostasis is that mode of existing by which any person or singular nature endowed with reason subsists as a perfect individual, not in another, whether by way of a part or an accident, etc., but through itself, by way of a whole, independently. This personal mode of subsisting (if we speak of man for the sake of example) is originally in the soul, and by communication in the body; when, therefore, the soul and body are united so that they become one person, then the soul communicates its hypostasis or perfect subsistence to the body, namely by receiving it within the perfection of its person; thus the soul of Abraham in its present state is a perfect person, because it now subsists as a whole, full, and perfect being, and therefore has its hypostasis; but the body of Abraham does not exist in this way, which in the resurrection from the dead the soul will receive into its hypostasis, so that it may become a participant in that perfect existence, and thus the soul then will no longer be alone, as before, but with its body will be a rational, singular substance, not sustained in another, that is, a true and perfect person.” (Διάσκεψις § 643.)

It is called the terminus qui, or the adequate [terminus], and the act of uniting terminates at it in the sense in which other actions and passions are said to be of the supposita. It is called the formal terminus, or the terminus quo. And thus this terminus of the union coincides with the union itself, which is subjectively in the human nature. For this nature alone is perfected by that union. The divine nature, however, cannot be perfected by the human nature nor receive anything from it in the same way.

Hollazius: “Unitio (the act of uniting) and unio (the state of union) strictly speaking differ: 1. Unitio is the act by which two diverse natures, divine and human, are joined; unio is the state of the natures joined through the unitio. 2. Unitio is the cause through which natures divided in themselves obtain a certain indivision in the unity of the person; unio, however, is the proximate effect of the unitio and the personal indivision itself of the two natures. 3. Unitio is transient and momentary, unio is permanent and perpetual. 4. Unio is reciprocal, for the Son of God is united to the assumed flesh and the flesh is united to the Son of God; but unitio is not reciprocal. We rightly say: The Son of God united the flesh to Himself; you would less rightly say: the flesh united the Son of God to itself. 5. Some propositions flow from the unitio, others from the unio. The subject of the former is the persona ασύνδετος or the λόγος άσαρκος; the subject of the latter is the persona σννΰετος or the λόγος ενσαρκος.” (L. C. q. 18. f. 664.) §

11. Finally, that union, resulting from the act of unitio, is not just any conjunction of two natures, divine and human, but such a one by which the divine nature, insofar as it is the nature of the Son of God, or insofar as it subsists in the hypostasis of the λόγος, within this very hypostasis, without commixtion or con- PART. III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

fusion and conversion, yet it has the human nature most closely and indissolubly joined to itself, and with it constitutes one υφιστάμενον [subsistence], which is both true God and true man.

What is the state or mode of the extremes, as being united. For God is also joined with faithful men when He dwells in them as in temples, 1 Cor. 3:16; whence he who is joined to the Lord is also said to be one Spirit with God, 1 Cor. 6:17.

However, this union or conjunction differs greatly from that personal union.

The ancients, on the occasion of the controversies of Nestorius and Eutyches, declared that union in such a way as to say that the two natures in Christ are united 1) άσυγχύτως, or inconfusedly, so that a union by mixture is excluded, by which the things that are united cease to be what they were and are united among themselves to constitute a third thing, which is called a mixture; 2) άτρέπτως, inconvertibly, so that it may be distinguished from that union by which one of the extremes is absorbed or converted into the other. Whence these two terms indicate that both natures, even after the union has taken place, have retained their essence and properties. 3) άδιαιρέτως και άχωρίστως, inseparably, with regard to intervals of time and places. For this reason, that union is called not only most close, but also indissoluble, since God neither ever wills to destroy it by His absolute power, nor could anything else destroy it.

Wherefore, even in the three days of death, although the natural union of body and soul ceased, we believe that the personal union nevertheless remained unimpaired, so that the body of the Son of God lying in the sepulchre and the soul of the Son of God separated from the body were truly the Son of God.

Gerhard: "The mode of this union is wonderfully singular and singularly wonderful, transcending the grasp not only of all men, but even of angels, whence it is confessedly called a great mystery." (L. c. § 115.)

Quenstedtius: "The formal aspect of this personal union cannot be fully known or explained by us in this darkness and infirmity of our mind, and therefore it can be determined more easily by what it is not than by what it is." (L. c. th. 33. f. 126.)

Hollazius: "The union of the two natures in Christ is not 1. merely verbal, arising either from a title without the reality, as when one is called a prince’s counselor who was never actually of his council, or from an improper locution, as when Herod is called a fox. For Christ is not only nominally, or improperly, but truly and properly Immanuel and θεάνθρωπος [God-man]. 2. It is not notional, or of reason, by which several concepts distinguished by reason are conceived as undivided by the aid of the mind. Such a union exists between genus and difference in a species. For the divine nature of Christ is not a genus, nor is His human nature a difference, or vice versa. 3. It is not relative, habitual, or respective, which can consist even if the extremes of this union are in reality separated and distant. For there is a various relative union, namely, moral between friends, whose mind is one even when they are absent; economic between spouses; political between citizens; ecclesiastical between members of the church. For the union of the two natures in Christ is far closer than a habitual one, which indeed implies a relationship of several things to one another, but without their real conjunction. The Son of God became a partaker of flesh and blood, just as the children, Heb. 2: 14. Therefore, the union of the two natures in Christ is real, because it exists between extremes that are truly coherent, with the exclusion of any separation or distance."

Quenstedtius: "The specific form of the union is altogether singular, ἐξαίρετος καὶ μονότροπος, excellent above other forms of union and exempt from all others. It consists, however, 1. in the coalition of the whole divine nature with the entire human nature in one ὑπόστασις of the λόγος, without confusion and without mixture." (L. c. s. 1. th. 26. sq. f. 121.)

The same: "This union is not V. commixtive, such as is a body composed of elements or mead made of water and honey. 'For such a drink (these are the words of the Formula of Concord) is no longer either mere water or mere honey, but a certain drink mixed from both; the matter is certainly far otherwise in that union of the divine and human nature,' etc. Some fathers indeed... used the term commixtion regarding this mystery. But they did not intend to signify a Eutychian confusion of natures, but the highest and most intimate penetration, by which the whole fullness of the deity dwells in the assumed flesh. Just as fire is united to iron not by contact alone, but penetrates and permeates the iron and is mixed with it on all sides, yet without confusion, so that no part of the iron is devoid of fire. Damascenus, lib. III. de F. O. c. 3, exchanged this for the more convenient term περιχωρήσεως... Nor is it VI. a bare παρουσία or παράστασις (by which the λόγος is present to the assumed human nature by assistance, which he sustains in actus secundus, lest it be reduced to nothing), from which παρουσία no communication arises, and which scarcely deserves to be numbered among the species of union." (L. c. s. 1. th. 30. f. 124.)

E. Hunnius: "As humanity is never turned into divinity nor divinity into humanity, so also the properties of humanity, such as: to be finite, to be moved from place to place, to be born, to suffer, to be crucified, to die, etc., are never properties of divinity; conversely, the properties of divinity never become idioms of humanity, since to be infinite, uncreated, an eternal spirit, as well as omnipotence, omniscience, and omnipresence, do not eternally become idioms of humanity." (Libelli 4 de persona Christi, p. 28.)

Kromayerus: "The Son of God, filling heaven and earth with the Father and the Holy Spirit, had his soul in paradise and his body in the sepulcher united to himself. Where, ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, we warn that we do not make our own the opinion of those who wish the body to have been united to the Son of God through the mediation of the soul. For if the matter were so, in death, i.e., with this bond dissolved, the body would not have been united to the Son of God, which neither the Papists nor the Calvinists... will concede. Nor does the question stand in our way, whether Christ was a true man at the time of his death, because one must distinguish between man considered materially and formally... Christ remained a true man in the midst of death materially, because the essential parts of man, body and soul, remained uncorrupted, though not formally, because the natural union between these two parts had ceased." (Th. pos. pol. II, 96. sq.)

Quenstedtius: "The ancients explain that intimate presence of the natures by the word ἀδιαστασία, which excludes every interval of the natures, so that the flesh is never and nowhere outside the λόγος, and the λόγος is never and nowhere outside the flesh. This intimate presence of the natures is proved from John 1:14: 'The Word was made flesh.' For if the λόγος is wholly made flesh and is flesh, therefore after the ἐνσάρκωσις has taken place, he is never and nowhere outside and apart from his flesh, but has this present everywhere with himself and in his own infinite and immense hypostasis; but the former is true; therefore. Then from Col. 2:9, where the apostle declares concerning the divine nature of the Son of God and all its fullness, that it dwells in Christ, namely in the assumed nature, σωματικώς. But if the whole divinity of the λόγος inhabits the assumed flesh everywhere, it follows that the λόγος or his whole divinity is nowhere outside the flesh. For he who is outside the house, insofar as he is situated outside the house, does not dwell in the house." (L. c. s. 1. th. 33. f. 126.) 3 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III. PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO I.

Latin:

carnem nec caro in λόγον sint mutata, et nihilo minus caro de λόγφ vere dicatur: Ό λόγος σαρξ εγίνετο, necesse est, ut λόγος et caro sint unum, κατ' άμεταβλησίαν ita conjuncta, ut nec λόγος in carnem, nec caro in λόγον sit conversa.“ (Orthod, conf. de persona etc. 1595. p. 47. sq.)

Talis quidem, quam Graeci vocant συνΰετον, ubi natura una non quidem ex pluribus naturis, attamen una cum altera est composita.

N. Hunnius: ,,Hypostasis est ille modus existendi, quo quaevis persona seu natura singularis ratione praedita ut individuum perfectum non in alio, sive ad modum partis, sive accidentis etc., sed per se, ad modum totius, independenter subsistit. Iste personalis subsistendi modus (si exempli gratia de homine loquamur) originaliter est in anima, per communicationem in corpore; quando igitur anima et corpus uniuntur, ut flant una persona, tunc anima suam hypostasin seu perfectam subsistentiam corpori communicat, nimirum recipiendo illud intra perfectionem suae personae; sic anima Abrahami in suo statu praesente est perfecta persona, quia nunc subsistit tanquam ens totum, plenum et perfectum, habet ergo suam hypostasin; at corpus Abrahami sic non existit, quod in resurrectione ex mortuis anima in suam hypostasin recipiet, ut particeps evadat perfectae illius existentiae, adeoque anima tunc non amplius sola, ut prius, sed cum suo corpore sit substantia rationalis, singularis, in alio non sustentata, hoc est, revera ac perfecta persona.“ (Αιάσκεψις § 643.)

Vocatur terminus qui, sive adaequatus, et terminatur ad illum actus uniendi eo sensu, quo alias actiones et passiones dicuntur esse suppositorum. Dicitur terminus formalis, sive quo. Atque ita coincidit hic terminus unitionis cum unione ipsa, quae in humana natura est subjective. Haec enim tantum natura per unionem illam perficitur. Divina autem natura non aeque ab humana natura perfici aut recipere quicquam potest.

Hollazius: ״Unitio et unio stricte dicta differunt: 1. Unitio est actus, quo duae diversae naturae, divina et humana, conjunguntur; unio est status naturarum per unitionem conjunctarum. 2. Unitio est causa, per quam naturae in se divisae quandam in unitate personae nanciscuntur indlvisionem; unio vero est effectus proximus unitionis et ipsa duarum naturarum personalis indivisio. 3. Unitio est transiens et momentanea, unio permanens et perpetua. 4. Unio est reciproca, nam ]Filius Dei est unitus carni assumtae et caro est unita Filio Dei; at unitio non est reciproca. Recte dicimus: Filius Dei sibi univit carnem; minus recte dixeris: caro sibi univit Filium Dei. 5. Aliae propositiones fluunt ex unitione, aliae ex unione. Illarum subjectum persona ασύνδετος sive λόγος άσαρκος; harum subjectum est persona σννΰετος sive λόγος ενσαρκος(L. C. q. 18. f. 664.) §

11. Unio denique illa, ex actu unitionis resultans, a non est qualiscunque duarum naturarum, divinae et humanae, conjunctio,b sed talis, qua natura divina, prout est Filii Dei natura, seu prout in hypostasi τον λόγον subsistit, intra hanc ipsam hypostasin, citra commixtionem seu con PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO I.

fusionem et conversionem, arctissime tamen simul et indissolubiliter c sibi conjunctam habet naturam humanam et cum ea constituit unum υφιστάμενον, quod et verus Deus et verus homo est.

Quae est status sive modus extremorum, tanquam unitorum. Nam et Deus cum hominibus fidelibus conjungitur, quando in illis velut in templis habitat, 1 Cor. 3, 16.; unde et unus Spiritus cum Deo dicitur, qui agglutinatur Domino, 1 Cor. 6, 17.

Haec autem unio seu conjunctio a pirsonali illa unione plurimum differt.

Veteres, occasione certaminum Nestorii et Eutyehis, ita declararunt unionem illam, ut dicerent, duas naturas in Christo esse unitas 1) άσυγχυτως, aut inconfuse, ita ut excludatur unio per mixtionem, qua, quae uniuntur, esse desinunt, quod fuerunt, et inter se uniuntur ad constituendum tertium, quod mixtum vocatur; 2) άτρέπτως, inconvertibüiter, ut distinguatur ab ea unione, qua alterutrum extremorum absorbetur seu in alterum convertitur. Unde haec duo vocabula indieant, naturam utramque, etiam facta unione, retinuisse essentiam et proprietates suas. 3) Άδιαφίτως xal άχωρίστως, inseparabiliter, quoad temporum et locorum intervalla. Qua ratione unio illa non solum arctissima dicitur, sed et indissolubilis, quippe quam nec Deus per absolutam suam potentiam destruere unquam velit, nec quicquam aliud destruere possit.

Quare etiam in triduo mortis, cessante licet unione naturali corporis et animae, personalem tamen unionem illibatam mansisse credimus, ita ut camus in sepulchro jacens Filii Dei corpus et mima a corpore separata Filii Dei anima revera fuerit.

Gerhardus: ״Modus unionis hujus est mirabiliter singularis ac singulariter mirabilis, omnium non modo hominum, sed etiam angelomm captum tanscendens, unde όμολογονμένως μέγα μνστήριον vocatur.** (L. c. § 115.)

Quenstedtius; ״Formale hujus unionis personalis in hac mentis nostrae caligine et infirmitate non potest plene a nobis vel cognosci vel explicari, adeoque facilius per hpaiv, quam per θ&ιν determinari potest.** (L. c. th. 33. f. 126.)

Hollazius ״ Unio duarum in Christo naturarum non est 1. mere verbalis, exsurgens vel ex titulo sine re, ut cum consiliarius principis dicitur, qui nunquam ipsi fuit a consiliis, vel ex locutione impropria, ut cum Herodes vöqatur vulpes. Christus enim non nominetenus tantum, aut improprie, sed vere proprieque Immanuel et θεάνθρωπος est. 2. Non est notionalis, sive rationis, qua plures conceptus per rationem distincti mentis ope ut indivisi concipiuntur. Talis unio datur inter genus et differentiam in specie. Neque enim natura divina Christi genus, neque natura humana ipsius differentia est, aut vice versa. 3. Non est σχετική, habitualis aut respectiva, quae consistere potest, licet extrema hujus unionis reapse separata sint et distent. Datur enim varia unio respectiv^׳, nempe moralis inter amicos, quorum etiam absentium tunus animus est, oeconomica inter conjuges, politica inter,cives, ecclesiastica inter membra ecclesiae. Longe quippe arctior est unio duarum in Christo naturarum, quam habitualis, quae importat quidem plurium rerum ad invicem habitudinem, sed sine reali earum conjunctione. Filius Dei particeps factus est,carnis et sanguinis, sicut pueri, Heb. 2,14. Est igitur unio duarum naturarum in Christo reatis, quia datur intfer extrema vere cohaerentia dum exclusione separationis alicujus ant distantiae.‘*

DB PERSONA CHRISTI. Quenstedtius: ״Forma specifica unitionis plane singularis est, εξαίρετης καί μονότροπος, prae ceteris unionum formis eximia et ab omnibus aliis exempta. Consistit autem 1. in totius naturae divinae cum integra natura humana in una τον λόγον νποστάσει coalitione inconfusa et impermixta.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 26. sq. f. 121.)

Idem: ,,Haec unio nec V. est commixtiva, qualis est corporis ex elementis compositi aut mulsi ex aqua et meile. ,Talis enim potus (sunt verba Formulae Concordiae) non amplius aut aqua est mera aut m$l merum, sed mixtus quidam ex utroque potus; longe certe aliter se res habet in illa divinae et humanae naturae unione‘, etc. nonnulli quidem patres ... vocabulum commixtionis de hoc mysterio usurparunt. Ast non confusionem naturarum Eutychi^nam, sed unionem summam et intimam penetrationem eo significare voluerunt, qua tota plenitudo deitatis in assumpta carne habitet. Sicut ignis unitur ferro non per attingentiam tantum, sed penetrat et permeat ferrum et undique ei, sine tamen confusione, miscetur, ut nulla pars ferri expers sit ignis. Hoc Damascenus lib. III. de Ο. F. c. 3. commutavit commodiori vocabulo περιχωρήσεως. . . Nec VI. est nuda παρονσΐα sive παράστασις (qua 6 λόγος assumptae humanae naturae adest per assistentiam, quam actu secundo sustentet, ne in nihilum redigatur), ex qua παρονσΐα nulla oritur communicatio, quaeque vix meretur inter unionis species numerari.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 30. f. 124.)

E. Hunnius: ,,Ut humanitas nunquam in divinitatem vertitur nec divinitas in humanitatem, sic et propria humanitatis, cujusmodi sunt: finitum esse, de loco in locum transferri, nasci, pati, crucifigi, mori etc., nunquam sunt divinitatis propria; vicissim divinitatis propria nunquam fiunt idiomata humanitatis, siquidem infinitum, increatum, aeternum spiritum esse, omnipotentia item, omniscientia et omnipraesentia humani tatis idiomata in aeternum non fiunt.“ (Libelli 4 de persona Christi, p. 28.)

Kromayerus: ״Filius Dei, cum Patre et Sp. S. coelum et terram implens, animam in paradiso, corpus in sepulchro sibi habuit unitum. Christus in media morte mansit verus homo materialiter, quia partes hominis essentiales, corpus et anima, manserunt incorruptae, licet non formaliter, quia unio naturalis inter duas hasce partes desierat.“ (Th. pos.pol. II, 96. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ״Praesentiam illam naturarum intimam exponunt veteres voce άδιαστασίας, quae omne intervallum naturarum excludit, ita ut caro nunquam et nullibi sit extra λόγον et λόγος nunquam et nuilibi extra carnem. Nam qui est extra οίκον, ille, quatenus versatur extra οίκον, non habitat εν οϊκφ.“ (L.c. s. 1. th. 33. f. 126.) 3 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III. PART. EH. CAP. II. SECTIO I.


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of Nestorius, Bishop of Constantinople, who, if not in explicit words, yet by manifest consequence dissolved the personal union, positing such a one from which neither the communication of natures nor of idioms followed; for he denied that the Son of Mary and the Son of God are one and the same, and urged that Mary should not be called Θεοτόκον, Mother of God, but χριστοτόκον, Mother of Christ...

2. Of the Papists, who, if not directly, at least obliquely deny the real communication of subsistence; for 1.) they deny the communication of all properties in general and pronounce it impossible. But if it is repugnant to a creature, through that divine and hypostatic union, to be infinitely powerful and wise, it will also be repugnant to it to be infinitely subsistent. For there is no greater repugnance between a creature and divine power and wisdom than between a creature and divine subsistence. 2.) They derogate from the personal act of the human nature. 3.) They place the entire subsistence of the λόγος outside the human nature. 4.) They deny that the human nature constitutes one υφιστάμενον [subsistent] with the λόγος. 5.) They define the union by mere sustentation; just as a tree (Bellarminus uses this simile), into which a branch of another species is grafted, sustains the same, which otherwise would exist by itself. Thus Bellarmine, lib. 3. de Christo c. 8. 15. and 17. § ad ult. says: 'Although the Word is somewhere where the humanity is not, yet even there the Word is man, because the Word existing there sustains the humanity as its own and proper, even though it exists elsewhere.'...

3. Of the Calvinists, who posit: 1.) that the human nature, insofar as it subsists in the λόγος, is locally in a place... 2.) That the human nature was indeed assumed into the ύπόστασις of the λόγος, but that the ύπόστασις itself was not communicated to it... And although others among the Reformed sometimes seem in words to assert a real communication of subsistence, most nevertheless deny the same in reality, if not directly, at least obliquely through their various hypotheses. 3.) Most define the union by mere παράστασιν, sustentation, adjunction, and the carrying of the flesh in the ύπόστασις of the λόγος." (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 192. sq.)

Kromayerus: "Eutyches, Archimandrite of Constantinople, struck against the other reef, who, in order to avoid Nestorianism, introduced a confusion of the two natures. For he taught that the human nature had been absorbed by the divine, as a drop of wine is absorbed by the sea. From this error flowed that of the Monophysites, Monothelites, Acephali, Theopaschites, Aphthartodocetae, and others... The Theopaschites, because of that very commixtion of natures, conceded that the deity itself had suffered." (L. c. p. 98.) §

12. And thus it is established that that union is neither natural nor essential, nor accidental, properly speaking. Indeed, it is a union of two natures, but not a natural one, because neit...her nature is ordered to the other by itself, or by the fact that it is such a nature, or to constitute a third nature with the other extreme. Whence it is not essential either, because the united extremes are not essential parts, nor do they coalesce as if to constitute one essential thing or one essence.

Gerhardus: "(A) natural (union is), when one essence is made from several, e.g., one composite from matter and form, one man from body and soul. This species of union in a certain way approaches that which is under discussion, whence in the Athanasian Creed, in place of a paradigm for its

whatever delineation is employed; meanwhile, however, it is not in every respect similar, much less the same.

For, speaking properly and accurately, the union of the two natures in Christ can be posited as neither natural nor essential. . . Of those things which are united naturally, there are many examples given in nature; but this union is μονότροπος and singular, of which no example is given in the whole universe of things. Those things which ...are united naturally are so disposed that neither of them is perfect without the other; but Christ is perfect man, perfect God, and the λόγος before the incarnation was a perfect person. . . An essential union constitutes one essence, but the two natures in Christ have coalesced into neither a simple nor a composite essence, since neither has the human nature been converted into the divine, nor the divine into the human, nor has some third species been composed from two different ones.” (Exeges. 1. IV. § 117.)

Hollazius: “It is a union of natures, but not a natural one; it is a personal one, but not a union of persons, for the reason that it is called personal not by reason of the term from which, as if it were made out of two persons, but by reason of the term to which, into one person.” (L. c. p. 680.)

Dannhauerus: “It is a union not 1. essential, of the kind which is the union (more truly, unity) between the persons of the Most Holy Trinity, because in Christ there is άλλο καί άλλο.” (Hodos. phaen. 8. p. 314.)

For the bond and the reason for uniting is not some accident, but ύπόστασις or personally, which is a substantial mode.

Hollazius: “The union of the two natures in Christ. . . is not 4. accidental, by which several things divided among themselves are joined into some kind of division. An accidental union of this kind is given: a) between two or more disparate accidents, coupled in one subject; thus whiteness and sweetness are united in milk; b) between an accident and a substance, such as is given in a learned man; c) between two substances so united among themselves that from them results not one per se, but per accidens. To this belongs physical union κατά σνγχνσιν, by confusion or mixture, as in mead; κατά παράστασιν, by assistance, such as exists both in things contiguous and present to one another, as when two embrace with their hands, and in continuous things, as when two planks are joined together. The mystical union belongs to accidental union, which they make threefold: sacramental, gracious, and glorious. The sacramental is given between the earthly and heavenly thing sacramentally united; the gracious between God and believers in the church militant; the glorious between God and the blessed in the church triumphant. The union of the two natures in Christ is not accidental, for the reason that no species of accidental union can be applied to it. For this union is neither between two accidents, nor between a substance and an accident, but between two substances, which are united not by mixture or confusion, for the reason that the divine nature, which is spiritual, most simple, and infinite, cannot be mixed with the human; nor by parastasis, assistance, or apposition, since that brings about no κοινωνίαν or internal communion. Furthermore, this union surpasses by its eminence the gracious conjunction of believers and the glorious conjunction of the blessed with God by a very great distance. For no believer in this life, no blessed one in the heavenly life, is one with the Son of God υφιστάμενον. In no one, equally as in Christ, does the whole fullness of the Godhead dwell bodily.” (L. c. p. 679.) §

13. From the personal union flows the communication of natures, through which it comes to pass that the human nature of the Son of God and the divine nature of the Son of Man is a nature. PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

To designate this, the term περιχώρησις began to be used, which in its native meaning denotes penetration or the existence of one in another, in such a way that the divine nature is said to penetrate (to enter into, to perfect) actively, and the human nature to be penetrated (to be entered into, to be perfected) passively. This, however, must be understood with all imperfections removed. For the divine nature does not penetrate the human in such a way that it occupies one part after another successively and diffuses itself through it extensively; but, because it is spiritual and indivisible, it simultaneously actuates and perfects every part of the human nature and the whole nature, and it is and remains whole in the whole human nature, and whole in every part of it. And to this pertains the passage in Colossians 2:9. For when πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος, the whole fullness of the deity, is said to dwell σωματικῶς, or bodily, in Christ, it is to be understood that the divine nature, together with all its perfections, is in the human nature in such a way that it allows it to be devoid of itself in no part, and thus penetrates it intimately; and that this indwelling of the deity in Christ differs greatly from that by which it once dwelt in the temple and by which it is in the saints.

GERHARD: "On account of the identity of the ὑπόστασις and the περιχώρησις of the natures into one another, the λόγος is so present to the flesh, and the flesh is so present to the λόγος, that neither is the λόγος outside the flesh, nor is the flesh outside the λόγος; but wherever the λόγος is, there he also has the flesh most present to himself, inasmuch as he assumed it into the unity of his person; and wherever the flesh is, there it has the λόγος most present to itself, inasmuch as it is assumed into his ὑπόστασις. Just as the λόγος is not outside his deity, of which he is the hypostasis, so also he is not outside his flesh, which is indeed finite in essence, yet subsists personally in the λόγος." (Exeg. l. IV. § 121.)

E. HUNNIUS: "The λόγος certainly ἐκοινώνησε, or, as the apostle says, μετέσχε, or became a participant through an admirable exchange, of flesh and blood (Heb. 2). Conversely, this same λόγος communicated himself entirely (just as he is entirely incarnate) to the assumed humanity... Which κοινωνία finally (and not a bare combination of natures without this κοινωνία) ensures that the man born of Mary is truly the Son of God; which could not be true if the human nature, by which Christ obtains the determination of man, had no true κοινωνία with the divinity; for nothing can be called God without a κοινωνία of the deity." (Libelli 4 de pers. Chr. p. 34 sq.)

Quenstedtius: "The soul does not merely assist the body as an assisting form, influencing only motion, as a pilot assists a ship, or an angel an assumed body, but it enters into, permeates, and informs the body, bestowing its own essence, life, and faculties upon the body; so the λόγος permeates the flesh and intimately communicates his divine nature to it...

The rational soul insinuates itself into the body in such a way that it could by no means have been separated from it by nature, unless, with the fall intervening as an accident, the violence of death had followed by divine judgment. Thus the λόγος is inseparable from the flesh εἰς τὸ διηνεκές, forever... The soul informs the body without any disturbance, mixture, or mutation of either. Thus the λόγος permeates his flesh, so that nothing is lost to either in its essentials, and neither is mixed with the other or confused with the other... The rational soul is in the body in such a way that it is nowhere outside or beyond it: thus the λόγος is in the flesh in such a way that he is nowhere as beyond, nowhere as outside... If the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος is truly and really communicated to the assumed flesh, then there is certainly a true and real communication between the divine and the assumed human nature, since the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος and the divine nature of the λόγος do not differ really. ... The mode of predication follows the mode of being, and to be said of something requires being in it. If, therefore, in the person of Christ, God is truly and really and is called man, and man is truly and really called God, then there is certainly a κοινωνία between the divine and human nature of Christ."

12. Proprie enim et accurate loquendo unio duarum naturarum in Christo nec naturalis nec essentialis statui potest. . . IV. § 117.)

Hollazius: ״Est unio naturarum, sed non naturalis; est persona· lis, sed non personarum, propterea, quod personalis dicitur non ratione termini a quo, quasi ex duabus personis esset facta, sed ratione termini ad quem, in unam personam.“ (L. c. p. 680.)

Vinculum enim et ratio uniendi non est aliquod accidens, sed ύπόστασις seu personaliter, quae est modus substantialis.

Hollazius: ״Unio duarum in Christo naturarum. . . non est 4. accidentalis י qua plura inter se divisa ad aliqualem in divisionem conjunguntur. Datur ejusmodi accidentalis unioj a) inter duo vel plura accidentia disparata, in uno subjecto copulata; sic albedo et dulcedo uniuntur in lacte; b) inter accidens et substantiam, qualis datur in homine docto; c) inter duas substantias ita inter se unitas, ut ex illis non unum per se, sed per accidens resultet. Huc pertinet unio physica κατά σνγχνσιν, per confusionem vel mixtionem, ut in mulso; κατά παράστασιν, per assistentiam, qualis est tum in contiguis sibi praesentibus, ut cum duo se complectuntur manibus, tum in continuis, ut cum duo asseres compinguntur. Pertinet ad accidentalem unionem mysticay quam triplicem faciunt: sacramentalem, gratiosam et gloriosam. Sacramentalis datur inter rem terrenam et coelestem sacramentaliter unitas; gratiosa inter Deum et credentes in ecclesia militante; gloriosa inter Deum et beatos in ecclesia triumphante. Unio duarum in Christo naturarum non est accidentalis, propterea, quod nulla species unionis accidentalis eidem applicari potest. Neque enim est haec unio inter duo accidentia, neque inter substantiam et accidens, sed inter duas substantias, qüae unitae sunt non per mixtionem aut confusionem, eo, quod natura divina, quae spiritualis, simplicissima et infinita est, cum humana commisceri nequit; neque per parastasin, assistentiam aut appositionem, quippe quae nullam κοινωνίαν aut internam communionem infert. Caeterum haec unio gratiosam credentium et gloriosam beatorum conjunctionem cum Deo eminentia sua longissime superat. In nullo peraeque, ac in Christo, tota plenitudo divinitatis habitat corporaliter.“ (L. c. p. 679.) §

13. Ex unione personali communicatio naturarum a fluit,b per quam fit, ut humana natura Filii Dei et divina natura filii hominis natura sit. PARTi ΙΠ. CAP. II. SECTIO I.
