### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: OF THE PERSON OF CHRIST

OF THE PERSON OF CHRIST. E. Hunnius: "Since it is established that the human nature of Christ is also in a place, is it in that same way in which it is in a place, thus also in the λόγος? By no means! For the assumed humanity of Christ is in a place naturally and locally, but in the person of the Word it exists in no way either naturally or locally, since the union is not local, nor was it brought about in any local or any other physical and earthly manner of this age. Add to this that the very person of the Word, into which the flesh of Christ was assumed, is entirely exempt from every place, needing neither time nor place nor any spatial dimensions for its existence, just as it was from eternity, before there was any place. Therefore, because the flesh of Christ subsists personally nowhere else but in this very hypostasis, to which no spatial dimensions reach: by infallible necessity (in this respect and regard) the flesh of the Word itself will also be outside and above every place, in the very purest divinity and hypostasis of the Word." (Libelli 4 de persona Christi etc. p. 30.)

Gerhardus: "Because the ϋπόστασις of the λόγος became the ϋπόστασις of the flesh, therefore the flesh, through the union, has obtained an illocal mode of subsisting. And because the ϋπόστασις of the λόγος became the ϋπόστασις of the flesh in such a way that it did not cease to be what it was, namely, true human nature, from this now arises the distinction between the natural act and the personal act. For some things are predicated of Christ as man according to the natural act, which, namely, arise from the constitutive principles of human nature and which it has in common with all men; some things according to the personal act, which, namely, belong to it by reason of the personal union; the former belong to it naturally according to essence, the latter personally according to existence." (L. c. § 121.)

Mentzerus: "Whoever says that after the incarnation has taken place, the λόγος is or subsists outside his flesh, no matter how they paint it, they dissolve, as far as in them lies, the hypostatic union, for they destroy its definition. For if the hypostatic union is the 'indwelling' of the whole fullness of the divinity of the λόγος in the assumed flesh, as the entire pious antiquity interprets the statement in Col. 2:9, it follows that the personal union is dissolved as soon as it is posited that the λόγος is outside his flesh." (Disp. theol. de praecipuis controv. in Academ. Giess. T. I. p. 36.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who contend that the λόγος, who assumed human nature, is no less wholly outside human nature than he is in human nature, and that the whole divine nature of the λόγος is both inside and outside his body after the union has taken place... Furthermore, [they contend that] the personal union is only inadequate, partial, and improper.

B. Meisnerus: "Are two primary acts to be granted in a really existing being? — By a primary act in general we understand everything from which flow and emanate certain operations, which philosophers call secondary acts... Two things occur in every substantial being, namely: 1. ουσίa or essence, and 2. ϋπαρξις or existence... Thus, iron does not burn or shine by reason of its ουσίa; yet in ignition it is rightly said to burn or shine because of the peculiar mode of subsisting which it then has... Since, therefore, these two things are found in every being, they ought not and cannot be denied concerning the humanity of Christ. For it also 1. has an essence, in species the same as ours; 2. it has a peculiar and singular subsistence. From this arise partly two acts: the natural, flowing from the common essence, and the personal, flowing from the singular subsistence; partly two kinds of attributes: some φυσικά and common, some ϋποστατικά and proper; which can be demonstrated to the eye by the clearest examples. For when it is said: 'The flesh of Christ subsists, and does not subsist; it is higher than the angels, and is not; it knows all things, and does not know many; it is God, and is not God; it is to be adored, and is not to be adored; it rules everywhere, and does not rule; it sits at the right hand of the Father, and does not sit, etc.': then these seemingly contradictory statements can in no way be reconciled unless the distinction between the natural and personal act is received, and the former members are explained concerning the ϋποστατικός act, and the latter concerning the φυσικός act. Thus, the flesh of Christ is truly food (John 6:55) and his blood cleanses us from all sin (Heb. 9:14; 1 John 1:7); and yet, conversely, it can be said that the flesh of Christ does not give life, does not cleanse from sin. For the former is true because of the personal act, the latter because of the natural act, according to which human nature is considered in itself and by itself and by reason of its own natural powers." (Philosoph. sobr. I, 955—58.) PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION I.

they make [it] primary, which is evident from the comparisons by which they explain the personal union and establish it "outside" that Nestorian [view]. For they compare the λόγος united to the human nature with the sun joined to its orb; thus Beza, *resp. ad Brentii argum.*, tom. I. *opp.* p. 511; likewise: with the ocean washing Antwerp, with a line touching a circle at one point, with the soul united to the feet of a man, etc., as may be seen everywhere in Beza and others; with a root joined to the branches in a tree, Massonius, *anat. univers.* c. 2. p. 182, Martyr in *dialog.* c. 10. . .

2. Of the Papists, according to whose opinion the Son of God was once only on earth, [and] now only in the heavens has His humanity present to Himself substantially and without distance. Thus Lombard says, *lib.* 3. *sent.* d. 22. § 6: "That Christ was not, nor is, man wherever He is, because He is everywhere according to His deity, [but] not everywhere man, because He is not everywhere united to man." The whole cohort of scholastics and Jesuits maintains the same with him. Busaeus in *apolog.* c. 7. p. 211 says: "The divinity is in infinite places where the humanity is not." Therefore, for them, Christ is Christ only in one place, i.e., consisting of two natures inseparably united there; in infinite other places He is not θεάνθρωπος, but the Word outside the flesh, who is θεάνθρωπος only somewhere. Cf. Bellarmin. *lib.* III. *de incarn.* c. 17." (*L. c. s.* 2. *q.* 5. *f.* 199. *sq.*)

The same: "Antithesis: ... 2. Of Nestorius. . . *Anathem.* 7, he asserts that 'the man born of Mary was made a participant of the Word by name alone' . . . 3. Of the Calvinists, some of whom teach that only the person of the λόγος is united to the human nature, but not at the same time His divine [nature], except consequently and by concomitance because of the identity with the personality, which alone is primarily united; and thus they invent a double union, mediate and immediate; [that] the natures are united not immediately, but through the mediation of the person of the λόγος. . . But all deny a true and real communication of the natures among themselves and acknowledge only a nominal and titular one, whatever they may protest so often. . . Beza in *colloq. Mompelg.* p. 294 says: 'The deity,' he says, 'has not been communicated to the humanity.' 4. Of the Papists and especially the Jesuits, who teach that the natures and their properties neither have been nor could have been communicated in the person of Christ, either in reality or in name." (*L. c. s.* 2. *q.* 6. *f.* 205. *sq.*)

Hofmann: "Because He (Christ) was with God before He became man, He, the One who became man, is υἱὸς θεοῦ in the exclusive sense and therefore also θεός, but θεός in the world as man, after He had previously been so super-worldly with God. Conversely, in His resurrection and transfiguration He became God, not only in that one recognized Him as such, but in that the One who became man became again what He had ceased to be in His incarnation." (*Schriftbeweis.* II, 1. p. 23.) The same: "He ceased to be God in order to become man." (*L. c.* I, 146.)

Moreover, the communication of the natures is said to flow from the personal union in our mode of conceiving. For that it differs really from it does not appear. §

14. In the unity of the person and the communion of the natures are founded, and declare it, the propositions which they call personal, by which the concrete of one nature is predicated of the concrete of the other nature; e.g., God is man, man is God, and the like. And those propositions are not merely verbal, but most highly real.

For thus the mode of predicating follows the mode of being. Reuschius: "Biblical and ecclesiastical propositions, which declare this mystery of the unition and union, and likewise of the communication, of the two natures in Christ, are called personal; those, however, which declare the communication of idioms, are called idiomatic." (Annotatt. etc. p. 557.)

These are otherwise called unusual predications, because in the whole of nature there is no example in which two disparates in the nominative case are properly predicated of one another, or can be predicated of one another without manifest falsehood. Whence they are not even safely called accidental, speaking absolutely. For although they seem to be able to be referred to the accidental mode of predicating, insofar as the predicate in them is outside the primary concept of the subject and does not flow from it by way of a property, one must nevertheless take care, lest, if these predications are called accidental, the union itself, which that mode of predicating follows as a mode of being, be believed to be accidental. See what we have said at § 12, note 6.

Gerhardus: "Question 3: Are disparates predicated of one another in personal propositions? Luther affirms this in his disputation on the saying, 'The Word was made flesh,' tom. 1. Jen. Latin, p. 567, thesis 3: 'This proposition,' he says, 'is more disparate: God is man, than that one: man is an ass.' ... This opinion of Luther is proved: 1. By the definition of disparates. Damascenus, in his book on dialectics, ch. 37 and 48, defines έτεροείδη as that which differs τῷ λόγῳ τῆς οὐσίας. Now, indeed, both deity and humanity differ τῷ λόγῳ οὐσίας or by definition. Therefore they are opposite or disparate species. 2. From the collation of similar examples. Iron and fire remain disparate even in ignited iron; body and soul remain disparate even in man: thus the two natures are and remain disparate in the union." (L. c. § 170.)

Dem est homo, homo est Deus, et similes.d Et sunt propositiones illae non verbales tantum, sed maxime reales.e

Sic enim modus praedicandi sequitur modum essendi. Reuschius: ״Propositiones biblicae et ecclesiasticae, quae declarant hoc mysterium unitionis et unionis, itemque communicationis, duarum in Christo naturarum, vocantur personales; quae vero declarant communicationem idiomatum, dicuntur idiomaticae.“ (Annotatt. etc. p. 557.)

Dicuntur alias praedicationes inusitatae, quia in universa natura nullum datur exemplum, in quo duo disparata in casu recto proprie de se invicem praedicentur, aut citra manifestam falsitatem de se praedicari possint. Unde nec satis tuto dicuntur occidentales, absolute loquendo. Quamvis enim ad modum praedicandi accidentalem eatenus referri posse videantur, quatenus in illis praedicatum est extra primum conceptum subjecti nec per modum proprii ex eo fluit, cavendum tamen est, ne, si praedicationes hae accidentales dicantur, unio ipsa, quam, tanquam modum essendi, modus ille praedicandi sequitur, accidentalis esse credatur. ### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Quenstedtius: "Obj.: Two disparates (God and man) cannot be one and the same…

Quenstedtius: "Obj.: Two disparates (God and man) cannot be one and the same subject at the same time, nor can one of the disparates be the other, nor can one be predicated of the other univocally in the nominative case. Resp.: ... 3. The objection holds regarding disparates that are not unible and are outside the state of unity. But the two natures in Christ are not such. ... 5. That other disparates are not predicated as God and man are, is because they are not united as God and man are." (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 188.)

By a concrete term is understood a word which signifies the suppositum in the nominative case, but the nature in an oblique case. Thus, God denotes the suppositum having the divine nature. Man denotes the suppositum having the human nature. And these, on account of the unity or identity of the suppositum, can certainly be rightly predicated of one another.

Abstract terms, however, which signify natures in themselves, not connoting the hypostasis, cannot equally be predicated of one another, since the natures, although joined within one person, are nevertheless diverse among themselves. For I cannot say: The divine nature is the human nature, or vice versa.

Gerhardus: "It is asked here: Whether, on account of the real communication of the natures, it should or can be said: the divine nature is human and the human nature is divine? The Calvinists and Jesuits have persuaded themselves of this, because, since divinity cannot be predicated of humanity and humanity of divinity in the abstract, they deny the real communication of the natures, but most ignorantly. For 1. essential mutation and conversion is one thing, but real communication is another. If divinity were essentially changed and converted into humanity, or humanity [were changed] by deity... PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION I.

absorbed, only then would it be rightly and truly said: divinity is humanity and humanity is deity; but because we posit not a conversion of natures, not a mutation of essence, not an abolition of either nature, but a real communication of natures resulting from the personal union, therefore we say that God is man, and man is God. . . 4. Just as on account of the union of iron and fire κατά σύνουσίαν I do not say: iron is fire, but iron is ignited; just as on account of the union of soul and body I do not say: soul is body, and body is soul, but body is animated, έμψυχον, and soul is ενσώματος: so on account of the personal union of the λόγος and the flesh I do not say: humanity is deity, and deity is humanity, but man is God, not οὐσιωδῶς, but ὑποστατικῶς, the human nature is deified, anointed with deity, the body is deified, full of deity, ένθεον, the flesh is θεωθεῖσα, deified, etc.” (Exeg. l. IV. § 153.)

In the Scriptures, indeed, we do not read those propositions expressed in so many words; but just as the names signify the same thing regarding the present: God (understanding the second person of the Divinity), Son of God, ὁ λόγος, Son of the Most High; likewise man (understanding Jesus of Nazareth), son of man, son of Mary, or born of Mary, etc.: so the personal propositions are rightly stated, when in Matthew 16:13 and 16 (with Christ approving in v. 17 seq.) Peter says: You, the son of man, are that Son of the living God; and in Luke 1:31 it is said: That which shall be born of Mary (the son of Mary) is that Son of the Most High.

Hollazius: “The foundation of this predication, ‘God is man,’ consists in the personal union and the communion of natures. If the divine and human nature, or God and man, are viewed outside of the personal union, they are disparate, and one cannot be affirmed of the other. For just as I cannot say, ‘A lion is a horse,’ so I cannot say, ‘God is man.’ But if a union intervenes between God and man, and indeed a real union, such as intervenes in Christ between the divine and human nature, they can rightly be predicated of each other in the concrete. The reason is that through the union the two natures constitute one person, and every concrete of a nature signifies that very person. Since, therefore, Christ is that same one who is God, or this person, who is God, is that very person who is man, it is also rightly said: Man is God, and God is man.” (Exam. III. s. 1. c. 3. q. 34. p. 685.)

Gerhardus: “Because the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος is not only the ὑπόστασις of His divine nature, but also of His human nature, therefore God is and is called man; because the assumed human nature subsists in the very ὑπόστασις of the λόγος, therefore man is and is called God.” (L. c. § 156.)

Quenstedtius: “I rightly say: God was made man, but I do not rightly and properly say: Man was made God, because the human nature is not the assuming, but the assumed. Thus you rightly say: Socrates was made white; not rightly: This white was made Socrates.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 29. f. 124.)

For although the predicate does not belong to the subject as such, or according to that nature from which the subject is expressly denominated—just as, for example, when it is said, God is man, the sense is not that the being man formally belongs to that suppositum or person according to the divine nature—it is sufficient, however, that there be a real identity between that which is denoted in the subject and that which is denoted in the predicate, I say, in both cases in the nominative; so that I may rightly say: He who is the Son of God is in reality the same one who is the son of Mary, and vice versa. Namely, on both sides in the nominative is signified the person, who is one and the same, whether denominated from the divine or from the human nature.

Quenstedtius: "These propositions, 'God is man, man is God,' are not improper and tropical, but most proper, because in no word of these propositions is a trope or impropriety found. They are not, I say, tropical or figurative, because they can be explained neither by metonymy, nor irony, nor metaphor, nor synecdoche (such as that: 'Man is dust,' Gen. 3, i.e., man's body is dust). Thus, the personal union would also be taken away... and the personal union would be figurative and improper; thus man would improperly be God, the Word would tropically and improperly be flesh, which is Arian." (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 211.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of Nestorius, who utterly repudiated personal propositions, whence he was accustomed to say by way of a proverb: 'Do not boast, Jew; you did not crucify God, but man.' 2. Of the Calvinists, who deny the truth of personal propositions, asserting that they are 1) only verbal, i.e., they occur only in name or σχεηκώς, without a real communication of natures... The Neustadians, admon. p. 70: 'The predication of human things concerning God and divine things concerning man, as far as the natures are concerned, is only verbal.' 2) That they are tropical and figurative; see Beza in the Colloquy of Mompelgart, p. 294, that they are to be explained by Zwingli’s αλλοίωσιν... 3) That they are customary and regular; see Fortunatus Crellius, Part of Common Logic, Book II, ch. 3, no. 2, where he contends that nothing more unusual occurs here than in other improper propositions. He adds the reason, that in those enunciations which are about the Son of God, whether God or man is the subject, the ὑπόστασις of the Word is always supposed, and the predicate is enunciated concerning Him, but man by reason of the assumed flesh, God in respect to the assuming Word... 3. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who resolve and undermine personal propositions less correctly... Occam, Book 3, Sentent. q. 6: personal propositions are 'accidental, because the human nature is outside the essence of the Word.'... 4. Of the Socinians, who reject personal propositions altogether." (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 211. sq.)

Gerhardus: "If Christ as man is truly God, then certainly Christ according to His humanity is also truly God, because man is not without humanity... Where, however, note: that the 'according to' does not express the cause, as if the human nature itself were the cause for which Christ is and is called the Son of God; nor the mode, as if Christ as man or according to human nature were God essentially; but the subject of the predication, that Christ as man is God, i.e., that He is not only God essentially by His deity, but that He is also God personally by His humanity, because, forsooth, the humanity is assumed into the Word and personally united with the divine nature." (L. c. § 167.)

Fechtius: "Christ according to the flesh is the natural Son of God, not an adoptive one, because He does not exist outside of God, just as an adopter otherwise exists outside the adopted." (Syll. disp. 23. p. 173. sq.)

Rollius adds: "That Christ cannot be called an adoptive son according to human nature is evident from the fact that the human nature, after it has been assumed into the person of the Word, is not foreign to it, but subsists within it. But for adoption, it is required that the adopter and the adopted differ not only as to essence, but also as to existence, and that he who adopts be one, and he who is adopted be another. In Christ, however, there is not 'one and another' [alius atque alius], although in Him there is 'one thing and another' [aliud atque aliud]." (Ib. p. 177. sq.)

Gerhardus: "When (Christ) is called the natural Son of God according to human nature, 'natural' is put for that which is present and exists from the very birth; just as if you were to say: Christ according to human nature is the Son..." PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

born of God, or from his very birth; for he was not adopted as the Son of God after his birth, as we are, who are by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2:3, and afterwards receive υἱοθεσίαν, John 1:12, but he himself was born the Son of God, not made.” (Exeges. l. IV. § 172.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of Felix of Urgell and Elipandus, Bishop of Toledo, who maintained that Christ, according to his humanity, is the adoptive Son of God... 2. Of certain scholastics, such as Durandus, who in 3. sent. dist. 4. q. 1. opines that ‘Christ, not indeed simply, but with the addition, *insofar as he is man*, can be called the adoptive Son of God.’ ... 3. Of D. Geo. Calixtus, who defends the same opinion in a program publicly proposed at Helmstedt in the year 1643 on the Feast of the Nativity, in which he writes: ‘I say that the opinion of those who taught that Christ according to the flesh is not the natural Son of God, but the adoptive one, is more probable; nay, I would dare to say, true.’ ... 4. Quenstedtius: ״Obj.: Duo disparata (Deus et homo) non possunt simul unum et idem subjectum esse, nec unum disparatorum alterum esse, nec unum de altero univoce in casu recto praedicari potest. Resp.: . . . 3. Valet objectio de disparatis non unibilibus et extra unitatis statum. At talia duae in Christo naturae non sunt. . . 5. Quod caetera disparata non ita ut Deus et homo praedicantur, inde est, quia non sicut Deus et homo uniuntur.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 188.)

Per concretum intelligitur vox, quae suppositum in casu recto, naturam autem in casu obliquo significat. Sic Deus denotat suppositum, habens divinam naturam. Homo denotat suppositum, habens humanam naturam. Atque haec propter suppositi unitatem seu identitatem utique recte de se invicem praedicari possunt.

Abstracta autem, quae significant naturas in se, non connotata hypostasi, non aeque de se invicem praedicari possunt, cum naturae, licet intra personam unam conjunctae, inter se tamen diversae sint. Non enim possum dicere: Divina natura est humana natura, aut vice versa.

Gerhardus: ״Quaeritur h. 1.: An propter realem communicationem naturarum dici debeat vel possit: natura divina est humana et humana natura est divina? Ita sibi persuaserunt Calviniani et Jesuitae, quia, propterea quod divinitas de humanitate et humanitas de divinitate in abstracto praedicari nequeat, realem communicationem naturarum negant, sed perquam άπαιδεντως. Nam 1. aliud est essentialis mutatio ac conversio, aliud vero realis communicatio. Si divinitas in humanitatem essentialiter mutata ac conversa esset, vel humanitas deitate ab PART. m. CAP. Π. SECTIO I.

sorpta, tunc demum recte et vere diceretur: divinitas est humanitas et humanitas est deitas; sed quia non naturarum conversionem, non essentiae mutationem, non alterutrius naturae abolitionem, sed realem naturarum communicationem ex personali unione resultantem statuimus, ideo Deum esse hominem, et hominem esse Deum dicimus. . . 4. Sicut ob unionem ferri et ignis κατά συνόύασιν non dico: ferrum est ignis, sed ferrum est ignitum; sicut propter unionem animae et corporis non dico: anima est corpus, et corpus est anima, sed corpus est animatum, έμψυχον, et anima est ενσώματος: sic propter unionem personalem λόγον et carnis non dico: humanitas est deitas, et deitas est humanitas, sed homo est Deus, non οϋσιωόώς sel., sed ϋποστατικώς, humana natura est deifleata, uncta deitate, corpus est deificatum, deitate plenum, ένθεον, caro est θεωθεισα, deifleata etc.“ (Exeg. 1. IV. § 153.)

In Scripturis equidem propositiones illas totidem verbis expressas non legimus; sed quemadmodum idem quoad praesens significant nomina: Deus (intelligendo secundam personam Divinitatis), Filius Dei, δ λόγος, Filius Altissimi; similiter homo (intelligendo Jesum Nazarenum), filius hominis, filius Mariae, aut natus ex Maria etc.: ita recte dicuntur propositiones personales, quando Matth. 16, 13. ei 16. (approbante Christo v. 17. seq.) dicit Petrus: Tu, jfili hominis, es Filius ille Dei viventis; et Lue. 1, 31. dicitur: Quod ex Maria nascetur (filius Mariae), est Filius ille Altissimi.

Hollazius:: ״Fundamentum hujus praedicationis: ,Deus est homo*, in unione personali et communione naturarum consistit. Si extra unionem personalem spectentur divina et humana natura vel Deus et homo, disparata sunt nec unum de altero affirmari potest. Sicut enim non possum dicere: ,Leo est equus*, ita dicere nequeo: ,Deus est homo.* Si autem unio intercedat inter Deum et hominem, et quidem realis unio, qualis intercedit in Christo inter divinam et humanam naturam, recte de se invicem praedicari possunt in concreto. Ratio est, quia per unionem duae naturae constituunt unam personam et quodlibet concretum naturae significat illam ipsam personam. Quoniam ergo Christus idem ille est, qui Deus est, vel haec, persona, quae Deus est, illa ipsa persona est, quae homo est, recte etiam dicitur: Homo est Deus, et Deus est homo." (Exam. III. s. 1. c. 3. q. 34. p. 685.)

Gerhardus: ,,Quia λόγου ϋπόστασις non tantum divinae suae naturae, sed etiam humanae est ϋπόστασις, ideo Deus est et dicitur homo; quia humana natura assumta ipsa τοϋ λόγου ϋποστάσει subsistit, ideo homo est ac dicitur Deus.“ (L. c. § 156.)

Quenstedtius: ״Recte dico: Deus est factus homo, sed non recte et proprie dico: Homo est factus Deus, quia humana natura non est assumens, sed assumpta. Sic recte dicis: Socrates factus est albus; non recte: Hoc album factum est Socrates.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 29. f. 124.)

Nam quamvis praedicatum non competat subjecto, ut tali, seu secundum eam naturam, a qua subjectum expresse denominatur, prout v. g. cum dicitur, Deus est homo, sensus non est, quod supposito seu personae illi, secundum divinam naturam, formaliter competat το esse nominem, sufficit tamen, inter illud, quod in subjecto et quod in praedicato, utrinque, inquam, in casu recto denotatur, realem identitatem esse; ut recte dicam: Is, qui est Filius Dei, est revera idem ille, qui est filius Mariae, et contra. Nempe utrinque in casu recto significatur persona, quae una et eadem est, sive a divina, sive ab humana natura denominetur.

Quenstedtius: ״Propositiones hae: ,Deus est homo, homo est Deus‘, non sunt impropriae ac tropicae, sed propriissimae, quia in nulla voce harum propositionum tropus vel improprietas invenitur. Non sunt, inquam, tropicae sive figuratae, quia neque per metonymiam, neque ironiam, neque metaphoram, neque synecdochen (qualis est illa: ,Homo est pulvis1, Gen. 3., h. e., hominis corpus est pulvis) possunt explicari. Tolleretur sic etiam unio personalis, ... essetque unio personalis figurata et impropria; sic homo improprie esset Deus, Verbum esset tropice et improprie caro, quod Arianum.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 211.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Nestorii, qui propositiones personales penitus repudiavit, unde proverbii loco dicere fuit solitus: ,Noli gloriari, Judaee, non Deum, sed hominem crucifixisti.‘ 2. Calvinianorum, qui negant veritatem propositionum personalium, asserentes, illas esse 1) tantum verbales, h. e., nomine tenus tantum fleri aut σχεηκώς, sine reali naturarum communicatione... Neostadienses admon. p. 70.: ,Praedicatio humanorum de Deo et divinorum de homine, quantum ad naturas, tantum est verbalis.‘ 2) Esse tropicas et figuratas; vide Bezam in coli. Mompelgart. p. 294., esse per Zwinglii αλλοίωσιν explicandas. . . 3) Esse usitatas et regulares; vid. Fortun. Crellium partis communis logices 1. II. c. 3. num. 2., ubi non magis hic inusitatum aliquid occurrere contendit, quam in propositionibus aliis impropriis. Rationem addit, quod in istis, quae sunt de Filio Dei, enunciationibus, sive Deus, sive homo subjiciatur, semper τον λόγου ύπόστασις supponatur et de eo praedicatum enuncietur, sed homo ratione carnis assumptae, Deus respectu Verbi assumentis. . . 3. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum, qui propositiones personales minus recte resolvunt et labefactant. .. Occamo lib. 3. sentent. q. 6. propositiones personales sunt,accidentales, quia humana natura est extra essentiam τον λόγον.‘.. 4. Socinianorum, qui propositiones personales prorsus rejiciunt.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 211. sq.)

Gerhardus: ״Si Christus homo vere est Deus, utique etiam Christus secundum humanitatem vere est Deus, quia homo non est absque humanitate. . . Ubi tamen nota: τό secundum non exprimere causam, quasi sci. ipsa hum. nat. sit causa, propter quam Christus sit et dicatur Dei Filius; nec modum, quasi Christus ut homo sive secundum h. n. sit Deus essentialiter; sed praedicationis subjectum, quod Christus ut homo sit Deus i. e. quod non solum deitate sua sit Deus essentialiter, sed quod etiam humanitate sua sit Deus personaliter, quia sci. humanitas est in λόγον assumta et cum divina natura personaliter unita.“ (L. c. § 167.)

Fechtius: ״Christus secundum carnem est Filius Dei naturalis, non adoptivus, quia non existit extra Deum, sicut adoptans alias existit extra adpptatum.“ (Syll. disp. 23. p. 173. sq.)

Addit Rollius: ״Adoptivum filium Christum non dici posse secundum humanam naturam, inde patet, quia natura humana personae τον λόγον, postquam in eam assumpta est, non est extranea, sed intra eam subsistit. Ad adoptionem vero requiritur, ut adoptans et adoptatus non solum quoad essentiam, sed et quoad existentiam differant, aliusque sit, qui adoptat, et alius, qui adoptatur. In Christo autem non est alius atque alius, licet in eo sit aliud atque aliud.“ (Ib. p. 177. sq.)

Gerhardus: ״Cum secundum humanam naturam (Christus) dicitur Filius Dei naturalis, naturale, ponitur pro eo, quod ab ipsa nativitäte inest et est; perinde ac si dicas: Christus secundum h. n. est Filius PART. ΠΙ. CAP. II. SECTIO I.

Dei natus vel ah ipsa nativitate; non enim post nativitatem fuit in Dei Filium adoptatus, sicut nos, qui natura sumus filii irae, Eph. 2, 3., et postea νίοΰεσίαν accipimus, Joh. 1, 12., sed ipse natus est Dei Filius, non factus.“ (Exeges. 1. IV. § 172.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Felicis TIrgelitani et Elipandi Toletani episcoporum, qui statuerunt, Christum secundum humanitatem suam esse adoptivum Dei Filium... 2. Quorundam scholasticorum, ut Durandi, qui in 3. sent. dist. 4. q. 1. existimat, ,Christum non quidem simpliciter, sed cum addito, in quantum homo est, dici posse Filium Dei adoptivum‘. ... 3. D. Geo. Galixti, qui eandem sententiam tuetur in programmate inFestoNativitatis, anno 1643. Helmstadii publice proposito, in quo scribit: ,Dico, probabiliorem esse sententiam eorum, qui docuerunt, Christum secundum carnem non esse Filium Dei naturalem, sed adoptivum; imo ausim dicere, veram.‘.. 4. Socinianorumt ex quibus Smalcius de vero et naturali Filio Dei p. 19. 20. . . asserit: ,Eundem adoptivum Filium Dei dici posse, quia non semper talis Filius Dei fuerit, qualis postea fuit, cum munus suum obiit, et qualis nunc est, postquam in coelis regnat.‘..


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Of D. Jacob Martini, who in *Colleg

6. Of D. Jacob Martini, who in *Colleg. II. Syntagm. theol.* disp. 8, rejects these propositions: ‘Christ according to human nature is the natural Son of God; Christ according to humanity is God personally,’ etc., as new and dangerous. § 38 sqq. Which opinion Mr. D. Calovius also embraced in the disputations on the Augsburg Confession, art. 3, held at Rostock, in *Exegem. Aug. Conf.* art. 3, c. 4, § 21, and in *System. theol.* l. c. art. 3, c. 3, q. 3 and 4. The aforementioned D. Jacob Martini, th. 41, says: ‘He does not see why Christ as man cannot be called a created Son of God, since he is equally created as other men,’ etc.” (L. c. s. 2, q. 8, f. 216 sq.) §

15. Those propositions also, in which a concrete of the person is predicated of a concrete of one or both natures, can in their own way be referred here; but yet they are rightly distinguished from those personal ones. Now, a concrete of the person is called a word or name of such a kind that formally signifies the person, consisting of both natures, e.g., Christ, Messiah, Immanuel, which names in the nominative case signify the suppositum, and in the oblique case do not signify either nature alone, but rather both. E.g., Christ is God or the Son of God. Christ is man or the son of man. E.g., Christ is θεάνθρωπος or is God and man at the same time. For they themselves also have something unusual; since an individual stands in the place of the subject, equally embracing two natures, divine and human, and thus does not claim the predicate for itself as a species does of an individual (whose entire essence it contains under itself), nor as a genus does of a species or individual, nor is it predicated as a specific difference, property, or accident; but in a peculiar manner. Namely, because both natures are contained in the formal concept of Christ and Messiah, therefore the predications by which a concrete of nature

of one, or of both, concerning such a subject, are judged to be formal.

Thus, the blessed Menzer in *Exeg. Aug. Confess.* Art. III. § 10, advises that predications of such a kind are conveniently and usefully distinguished from personal propositions, as their very definition clearly shows. Compare the same in T. V. *Dispp. Giess.* Disp. IX. p. 205 and 206. § 17, where he says: When it is said: Christ is God, or, Christ is man, that proposition is not, if you speak precisely, personal, describing the union itself, but it is a description of the whole composite person by one of the natures.

Gerhard: "To personal propositions, those also might seem to some to be referable in which the whole person is described by one or the other or by both natures... Nevertheless, they can be conveniently distinguished from personal propositions properly and precisely so called: 1. Because these propositions do not express the unity of the person so much as they precisely and formally express the duality of the natures in Christ... 2. Because these propositions are opposed rather to those denying either the divine nature in Christ, such as the Arians, Photinians, and Jews, or the human nature in Him, such as the Marcionites, Valentinians, and Manichaeans, than to those who evacuate the mystery of the personal union. 3. Because Nestorius, the enemy of the personal union, conceded all and each of these propositions: Christ is man, Christ is God, Christ is God and man." (L. c. § 155.) §

16. Furthermore, from the communication of the natures flows the communication of idioms, through which it comes to pass that those things which, when the two natures are compared with one another, pertain to one of them in itself and formally, truly belong also to the other nature.

Luther: "Since no human mind can attain or understand these things by its own ingenuity or wisdom, it ought to assent to them certainly by faith; and when it has done so, then at last it will feel (as pious men and those experienced in these matters testify) that this article (concerning the communication of idioms) produces consolation in all tribulations of sin and death. Likewise, it will also conceive how much light it brings to the understanding of Scripture. And all things in the history of the passion will seem idle and cold, unless these things are held." (Letter to Franz Gros. See de Wette VI, 294.)

In our way of understanding. For as to the thing itself, the communication of idioms does not seem to differ from the communication of the natures. Elsewhere, indeed, the word "idiom" is taken more strictly for that which is called a *proprium* in the fourth mode; but here it is taken more broadly for everything that belongs to either nature in itself and formally, but outside of its primary concept. And thus the idioms of the divine nature are: to be omnipotent, eternal, immortal, etc.; [the idioms] of the human nature are: to be born, to suffer, to thirst, to sleep, to be wounded, to die, etc.

Meisner: "Commonly, a fourfold *proprium* is established: 1. that which is in one only, but not in all; 2. that which is in all, but not in one only; 3. that which is in all and in one only, but not always; 4. that which is in all and in one only and always, as Porphyry recounts in c. 4 of the *Isagoge*." (*Phil. sobr.* I, 55.)

J. G. Walch: "The Peripatetics touch upon only four kinds of *proprium*, which one is accustomed to include commonly by example in the following verse: (Man) is a physician, two-footed, graying, and capable of laughter... The fourth kind would be if a certain property were present in all PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION I.

to be found in individuals of a certain species, and indeed partly only alone, partly at all times, e.g., that a human being can laugh.” (Philosophical Lexicon, s.v. Proprium, p. 2082.)

Quenstedtius: “In this place, properties or idioms are taken in a broader sense, so that besides the properties strictly so called, it also comprehends within its scope actions and passions, ενεργήματα and αποτελέσματα, because idioms exert themselves through ενεργείας and αποτελέσματα.” (L.c., s. 1, th. 53, f. 134.) Either with respect to concretes, or in relation to the nature itself viewed in the abstract; as will be evident from what follows.

Gerhardus: “Communication occurs either κατά μέθεξιν or κατά σύνδυσιν. Communication κατά μέθεξιν is an essential participation, by which one passes into the essence and definition of another... Communication κατά σύνδυσιν, which occurs according to the association of two diverse natures, through which one of the united [natures] is so connected with the other that, while the essence remains distinct, nevertheless the one truly receives and puts on the property, power, and efficacy of the other through and because of the communion that has been made, without any confusion. An example is in ignited iron and an animate body. The communication of idioms, which we establish in this place, ... is a true and real, hypostatic and supernatural communication, approaching most closely to that which is called κατά σύνδυσιν. Briefly, just as the union is not essential, nor merely verbal, nor by σνγχυσιν, or αλλοίωσιν, or μίξιν, or παράστασιν, nor is it personal or sacramental, so also such communication is not.” (L.c., § 175.) N. Hunnius: “Since the union of soul and body is such a close conjunction of those natures that the soul communicates its hypostasis to the body and both pass into one person, therefore the communication of properties follows from it, because the soul bestows life and faculties upon the body and in turn takes from the body quantity, extension, and other things: thus the union of natures in Christ is such a close combination of them that the two natures become one hypostasis, and the divine [nature] also communicates its idioms to the human, so that all the treasures of divine wisdom and knowledge are said to dwell in Christ σωματικώς, Col. 2:9.” (Διάσκεψις, § 440.)

The same: “The union of soul and body entails the communication of properties; the soul communicates its life to the body, which, as it is a true property of the soul, so the body truly becomes a participant in it. Similarly, natural and animal faculties (in their own way also rational ones) are communicated to the body; in sum: all ενεργητικά idioms, and those of which there is some operation, even if they remain proper to the soul, nevertheless become common to the body also; when this communion of life ceases, the personal union between soul and body ceases; similarly, when the communication of the remaining properties fails, the union also fails. So in turn: the soul united to the body receives certain of its properties, for it is extended to the extension of its body and thus, remaining in itself non-quantitative, it acquires a borrowed quantity; although it is also in its own nature impassible, exposed to no bodily injuries, it nevertheless becomes in a certain way passible through conjunction with the body, so that, when the human body is wounded, not only is the body wounded, but the whole man, consisting of soul and body. But as soon as that communication of properties ceases, the union of the coupled natures ends at the same time; from which it follows that the hypostatic union does not exist without the communication of properties.” (L.c., § 646.) § 17. Moreover, three kinds of communication of idioms are usually established, and the first is indeed called [the genus] from which God claims for Himself what are man’s, and man [claims] what are God’s.

Although it is commonly described through predications, the formal reason itself seems to be established not in the predications themselves, but in the real communication which provides the foundation for the predications.

J. A. Osiander: "There are as many kinds of communication of idioms as there are foundations for communications and idiomatic propositions provided by Scripture. But there are three, etc. Therefore. The major premise is proven: because in this mystery Scripture alone is our rule. The minor premise is evident from the cited passages. For it is said a. The Lord of glory was crucified; therefore, human idioms are attributed to the divine nature; whence the first kind of communication results. It is said b. All power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ; therefore, divine idioms are attributed to the human nature; whence the second kind results. It is said c. God has redeemed the church with His own blood; therefore, God and blood concur, and thus a Theandric operation is established; whence the third kind arises." (Coll. th. IV, 78.)

Gerhard: "The question is: Is it more correct to establish four kinds of communication rather than three? Some think so, whose opinion is that the predications in which the properties of the human nature are attributed to the Son of God should be distinguished from the predications in which the idioms of either nature are enunciated concerning the whole person of Christ, so that in this way four kinds of communication or modes of predication are established. Thus, therefore, the proposition 'Christ suffered' would belong to a different class than the other: 'God suffered.' ... We concede that the arguments brought forward for establishing a quaternary number of kinds of communication are not entirely without strength; meanwhile, lest we depart from the customary method of teaching prescribed in the symbolical book, the Formula of Concord, we shall retain three kinds of communication." (Exeg. l. IV. § 184.)

Latin:

6. D. Jacobi Martini, qui in Colleg. II. Syntagm. theol. disp. 8. has propositiones: ,Christus secundum humanam naturam est Filius Dei naturalis; Christus secundum humanitatem est Deus personaliter‘ etc., ut novas et periculosas simpliciter rejicit. § 38. sqq. Quam sententiam etiam Dn. D. Calovius amplexus est dispp. in Aug. Conf. art. 3. Rostochii habitis, in exegem.,Aug. Conf. art. 3. c. 4. § 21. et in systeih. theol. 1. c. art. 3. c. 3. q. 3. et 4. Jam dictus D. Jacob. Martini th. 41. ait: ,Se non videre, cur Christus ut homo non possit dici Filius Dei creatus, cum aeque creatus sit ut caeteri homines‘ etc.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 216. sq.) §

15. Illae etiam propositiones, in quibus de concreto per· sonae a enunciatur concretum b alterius aut utriusque c naturae, suo modo huc referri d possunt; sed tamen a personalibus illis recte distinguuntur.e Dicitur autem concretum personae vox aut nomen ejusmodi, quod personam, utraque natura constantem, formaliter significat, v. g. Christus, Messias, Immanuel, quae nomina in casu recto suppositum, in casu obliquo neutram naturam solam, sed potius utramque significant. V. g. Christus est Deus aut Filius Dei. Christus est homo aut filius hominis. V. g. Christus est #εάν$ρωπος aut est Dem simul et homo. Habent enim et ipsae aliquid inusitati; cum subjecti loco stet individuum, duas naturas, divinam et humanam, aequaliter complectens, adeoque praedicatum non ita sibi vendicans, prout species de individuo (cujus totam essentiam sub se continet), nec ut genus de specie vel individuo, nec ut differentia specifica, proprium aut accidens praedicatur; sed modo peculiari. Nempe, quia utraque natura in formali conceptu Christi et Messiae continetur, ideo praedicationes, quibus concretum naturae

unius, aut utriusque de tali subjecto enunciatur, formales esse judicantur.

Sic b. Menzerus in Exeg. Aug. Confess. Art. III. § 10. monet, praedicationes ejusmodi a propositionibus personalibus commode et utiliter discerni, prout ipsa earum definitio perspicue ostendat. Conf. eundem T. V. Dispp. Giess. Disp. IX. p. 205. et 206. § 17., ubi ait: Quando dicitur: Christus est Deus, vel, Christus est homo, non est illa propositio, si exquisite loquaris, personalis, describens ipsam unionem, sed est descriptio totius personae compositae ab altera naturarum.

Gerhardus: ״Ad personales propositiones videri alicui possent referendae etiam illae, in quibus tota persona ab alterutra vel.ab utraque natura describitur. . . Tamen a propositionibus personalibus proprie et exquisite sic dictis commode discerni possunt: 1. Quia hae propositiones non tam personae unitatem, quam naturarum in Christo dualitatem praecise et formaliter exprimunt. . . 2. Quia hae propositiones potius oppositae sunt negantibus vel divinam in Christo naturam, ut Arianis, Photinianis, Judaeis, vel humanam in ipso naturam, ut Marcionitis, Valentinianis, Manichaeis, quam unionis personalis mysterium evacuantibus. 3. Quia has propositiones omnes et singulas: Christus est homo, Christus est Deus, Christus est Deus et homo, Nestorius, personalis unionis hostis, concessit.“ (L. c. § 155.) §

16. Ex communicatione naturarum porro fluit a commmicatio idiomatum, per quam fit, ut ea, quae duabus naturis inter se comparatis ad unam earum per se et formaliter pertinent,b alteri etiam naturae revera competant.c

Lutherus: ״Cum nulla mens humana haec assequi aut intelligere suo ingenio aut sapientia possit, debet eis certo assentiri fide, quod ubi fecerit, tum demum sentiet (ut testantur pii et harum rerum periti homines), quod is articulus (de commun. id.) pariat consolationem in omnibus tribulationibus peccati et mortis. Item concipiet etiam, quantum lucis afferat Scripturae intelligendae. Et omnia in historia passionis videbuntur otiosa et frigida, nisi haec teneantur.“ (Brief an Franz Gros. Vid. de Wette VI, 294.)

Nostro modo intelligendi. Quoad rem enim communicatio idiomatum a communicatione naturarum differre non videtur. Alias equidem vox idiomatis strictius accipitur pro eo, quod dicitur proprium in quarto modo; sed hic latius pro omni eo, quod alterutri naturae per se et formaliter, sed extra primum ejus conceptum, competit. Atque ita divinae *naturae idiomata sunt, esse omnipotentem, aeternum, immortalem etc., humanae naturae, nasci, pati, sitire, dormire, vulnerari, mori etc.

Meisnerus: ״Vulgo proprium quadruplex constituitur: 1. quod inest μόνφ, sed non τφ π αντί, 2. quod inest τώ'παντϊ, sed non τφ μόνφ, 3. quod inest τάj παοτί και τφ μόνφ, sed non αεί, 4. quod inest τφ π αντί καί τφ μόνφ καί άεί, recensente Porphyrio c. 4. Isag.“ (Phil. sobr. I, 55.)

J. G. Walchius: ״Die Peripatetici berühren nur vier Arten des Proprium, welche man insgemein durch Exempel iri folgenden Vers einzuschliessen pflegt: (Homo) est medicus, bipes, canescens, risibilisque. . . Die vierte Art wäre, wenn eine gewisse Eigenschaft bei allen PART. m. CAP. Π. SECTIO I.

Individuis einer gewissen Art, und zwar theils nur allein, theils allezeit zu finden sei, z. E. dass ein Mensch lachen könne.“ (Philosoph, Lexik, s. t. Proprium, p. 2082.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Hoc loco in latiori significatu accipiuntur propria seu idiomata, ita ut praeter proprietates stricte sic dictas etiam actiones et passiones, ενεργήματα καϊ αποτελέσματα ambitu suo comprehendat, quia idiomata per ενεργείας et αποτελέσματα se exserunt.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 53. f. 134.) Vel respectu concretorum, vel in ordine ad naturam ipsam in abstracto spectatam; ut ex seqq. constabit.

Gerhardus: ,, Communicatio fit vel κατά μέΰεξιν, vel κατά συνδνασιν. Communicatio κατά μέΰεξιν est participatio essentialis, qua unum in alterius essentiam ac definitionem transit. . . Communicatio κατά συνόύασιν, quae fit secundum consociationem duarum diversarum naturarum, per quam alterum unitorum cum altero ita connectitur, ut, essentia distincta manente, nihilo minus alterum alterius proprietatem, vim et efficaciam per et propter communionem factam sine omni confusione vere accipiat et induat. Exemplum est in ferro ignito et corpore animato. Communicatio idiomatum, quam hoc loco statuimus, ... est communicatio vera et realis, hypostatica et supernaturalis, illi, quae κατά σννδνασιν vocatur, proxime accedens. Breviter, ut unio non est essentialis, nec verbalis tantum, nec per σνγχυσιν, vel αλλοίωσιν, vel μίξιν, vel παράστασιν, nec est προσωπική vel sacramentalis, ita quoque com· municatio talis non est.“ (L. c. § 175.) N. Hunnius: ״Quandoquidem unio animae et corporis est adeo arcta istarum naturarum conjunctio, ut anima suam hypostasin communicet corpori et utraque in unam personam transeat, ideo ex illa consequitur propriorum communicatio, quod anima corpori largitur vitam et facultates et vicissim a corpore sumit quantitatem, extensionem et alia: sic unio naturarum in Christo est tam arcta illarum combinatio, ut duae naturae flant una hypostasis, divina etiam communicet sua idiomata humanae, ut omnes thesauri sapientiae ac scientiae divinae in Christo habitare dicantur σωματικώς, Coi. 2, 9.“ (Αιάσκεψις, § 440.)

Idem: ״Unio animae et corporis infert communicationem propriorum; communicat anima corpori suam vitam, quae, ut est vera animae proprietas, sic corpus vere illius fit particeps. Similiter facultates naturales et animales (suo modo etiam rationales) communicantur corpori; summa: omnia idiomata ενεργητικά, et quorum est aliqua operatio, etsi propria maneant animae, attamen corpori quoque fiunt communia; cessante hac communione vitae, cessat unio personalis inter animam et corpus; similiter, defleiente communicatione reliquorum propriorum, deficit etiam unio. Ita vicissim: anima corpori unita recipit quasdam ejus proprietatas, extenditur enim ad sui corporis extensionem et sic, manens in se non-quanta, mutuaticiam quantitatem acquirit; quamvis etiam in sua natura sit impatibilis, nullis injuriis corporeis exposita, fit tamen quodammodo patibilis per conjunctionem cum corpore, ut, quando vulneratur humanum corpus, non solum corpus vulneratum sit, sed totus homo, constans anima et corpore. Quamprimum autem ea propriorum communicatio cessat, simul desinit naturarum copulatarum unio; ex quo sequitur, unionem hypostaticam non esse sine propriorum communicatione.“ (L. c. § 646.) § 17. Solent autem communicationis idiomatum tria constitui genera, et primum quidem appellatur,a quo Deus sibi vendicat, quae sunt hominis, et homo, quae sunt Dei.b

Etsi enim vulgo per praedicationes describatur, ipsa tamen formalis ratio non in ipsis praedicationibus, sed reali communicatione, quae praedicationibus fundamentum praebet, constituenda videtur.

J. A. Osiander: ,,Tot sunt genera communicationis idiomatum, quot suppeditantur fundamenta communicationum et propositionum idiofnaticarum a Scriptura. Atqui tria etc. Ergo. Major prob.: quia in hoc mysterio sola nobis Scriptura regula.‘ Minor autem constat ex locis allegatis. Dicitur enim a. Dominus gloriae crucifixus; ergo humana idiomata attribuuntur divinae naturae; unde primum genus communicationis resultat. Dicitur b. omnis potestas in coelo et in terra Christo data; ergo divina idiomata tribuuntur hum. nat.; unde secundum genus resultat. Dicitur c. Deus proprio sanguine redemisse ecclesiam; concurret ergo Deus et sanguis, adeoque statuetur operatio Deivirilis; unde tertium genus oritur.“ (Coll. th. IV, 78.)

Gerhardus: ״Quaeritur: An rectius quatuor, quam tria, communicationis genera sint statuenda? Ita quidam existimant, quorum haec est sententia, quod praedicationes, in quibus propria humanae naturae tribuuntur Eilio Dei, distinguendae sint a praedicationibus, in quibus alterutrius naturae idiomata de tota Christi persona enuntiantur, ut hac ratione quatuor communicationis genera seu modi praedicationum statuantur. Sic ergo propositio illa: Chnstus est passus, pertineret ad aliam classem, quam altera: Deus est passus. . . Argumentis pro quaternario generum communicationis numero stabiliendo adductis non omnino nullum robur inesse, concedimus; interim, ne ab usitata docendi ratione in libro symbolico, Formula sci. Concordiae, praescripta discedamus, retinebimus tria communicationis genera.“ (Exeg. 1. IV. § 184.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: For this communication is mutual

For this communication is mutual. Whence it is otherwise accustomed to be called άντίδοσις and τρόπος άντιδόσεως.

Hollaz: "The foundation of the first kind of communication of idioms is both the unity of the person of the θεάνθρωπος and the true and real difference of the divine and human natures." (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 3. q. 41. p. 694.)

The same: "This first kind is called by Damascenus (lib. III. de F. O. c. 4) άντίδοσις, alternation...; by Theodoret it is called εναλλαγή καί κοινωνία ονομάτων, permutation and communication of names, not merely verbal, but real...; by Cyril it is termed ίδιοποιΐα καί ίδιοποίησις, appropriation...; by Damascenus άλλοίωσις, by which both divine and human idioms are really predicated of one and the same composite person, yet κατ' άλλο καί άλλο, because the distinctive particles show according to which nature each idiom is predicated of the person. But one must accurately distinguish between determinative and distinctive άλλοίωσις, and segregative and exclusive άλλοίωσις." (L. c. q. 40. p. 693. sq.) §

18. The predications belonging to the first kind of communication of idioms are those by which an idiom of the human nature is enunciated denominatively of the concrete of the divine nature, and conversely, an idiom of the divine nature is enunciated of the concrete of the human nature. E.g., when from Acts 3:15 it is said: The Author of life was killed, the subject place is occupied by the suppositum, having a divine nature, which of itself [has] life. PART III. CAP. II. SECTION I.

He] has life and gives it to all others, and is thence denominated here; the predicate is to be killed, which formally does not fall upon the divine nature (which is of itself impassible and immortal), but pertains to the human nature. Thus, according to Rom. 8:32, concerning the own Son of God, as if concerning a subject denominated from the divine nature, and 1 Cor. 2:8, concerning the Lord of glory, it is predicated to be crucified.

Gerhard: "The foundation of this (first genus) of communication is the unity of the person. For since, after the incarnation has taken place, the one person of Christ subsists in two and from two natures, each of which is as it were clothed with its own properties, thence the properties of each nature, as well divine as human, are predicated of the one person of Christ in a composite manner." (L. c. § 186.)

The same: "Just as personal propositions are reciprocal: 'God is man, man is God,' so also are the propositions in this first genus of the communication of idioms reciprocal. For since man is truly predicated of God, therefore human attributes are also truly predicated of the same; since God is truly predicated of this man, therefore divine attributes are also truly predicated of the same." (L. c.)

The same: "It is asked, in what way is passion attributed to the Son of God? Resp.: Not passively and by way of alteration, as if He sustained a certain change and passion in the divine nature itself; but 1. hypostatically, insofar as the assumed flesh, which sustained pains and tortures, being raised into the very hypostasis of the Word, constitutes one person with Him. . . 2. Appropriatively. . . 3. Logically, relatively, objectively and relatively. By the blasphemies, reproaches, and insults which were cast upon the Son of God Himself, His eternal divinity was especially attacked, John 10:33, Matt. 26:63, 65, 27:40, 43. . . 4. Voluntarily. Christ did not suffer by compulsion, but voluntarily; therefore the Word consented to the passion through divine concurrence. . . 5. Permissively. The divinity could have repelled all passions from the flesh with a single nod; but for the sake of the salvation of the human race, He permits it to be treated in ways so unworthy, which permission Christ calls 'dereliction,' Ps. 22:1, Matt. 27: 46. Irenaeus, lib. 3, adv. haeres., c. 21, and from him Theodoret, dial. 3: 'As He was man, that He might be tempted, so also [He was] the Word, that He might be glorified, the Word remaining quiet while being tempted and crucified and dying.' Which words Philip Melanchthon, citing them in his Loci, subjoins: 'Here Irenaeus used a singular counsel in this notable description: the Word being quiet, i. e., then not exerting His power in repelling passion and death.' . . 6. Effectively, and indeed in two ways; first, by reason of the suffering human nature, by sustaining it; . . . then, by reason of the passion itself, by rendering the same, through His divine and infinite virtue, precious before God and satisfactory for the sins of the whole world." (L. c. § 197.)

Hollaz: "The Son of God truly, really, and properly suffered, was crucified, and died. . . Actions and passions belong to supposita. Wherefore when I say: 'God has suffered,' the subject of the passion is the 'what' which is God, the subject as the 'by which' is the human nature, subsisting in the very hypostasis of the Son of God. . . The passion of the flesh alone, however just it may be, does not satisfy for itself, much less for others, and least of all for the whole world. — You say: Whoever suffers really, he feels the passion; but God did not feel the passion; therefore God did not really suffer. Resp.: Whoever suffers really and physically, he feels the passion, I concede. But the Son of God, although He suffered really, yet He did not suffer physically, but hypostatically or personally and appropriatively." (L. c. q. 44, p. 698 sq.)

Gerhard: "The Calvinists resolve that proposition: 'God has suffered,' in such a way that the final analysis at last comes down to this: 'Only the human nature has suffered,' . . . whence Zwingli explains that proposition by way of alteration. . . Calvin proceeds so far as to write in lib. 2, Institut., c. 17."

s. 1.: "Indeed, I confess, if anyone were to wish to oppose Christ simply and by Himself to the judgment of God, there would be no place for merit, because there will not be found in man a dignity that could merit God." ...

To this Nestorian division we oppose: 1. The clarity of the sayings of Scripture. Scripture nowhere says: The flesh alone has suffered; but: God has suffered in the flesh; the Prince of life has been killed, etc. 2. The unity of the Person... Christ in the very act of His passion publicly professed Himself to be the Son of God, lest anyone should doubt that the Son of God Himself had suffered, Matt. 26:63; 27:54. All works, all passions are not attributed to the natures, but to the person. If, therefore, the works are torn apart, the person also will be separated.

3. The truth of appropriation... Passion and death... on account of the intimate and ineffable communion of the natures and the appropriation of the properties of the flesh, pertain no less to the Son of God than if He had sustained them in the divine nature itself; just as it is truly and properly said that a man is wounded, even if only his body is wounded... 4. The authority of the philosophical canon. Aristotle, *De Anima*, bk. 1, ch. 3: "All actions and passions belong to composite substances, but on account of the natures of which it is composed." ... It is not properly said that the hand strikes, but the man through the hand; nor is it properly said that heat heats, but fire through heat...

5. The price and dignity of the ἀντίλυτρον... Ps. 49:8... 6. The parity of examples. If it is truly and without a trope that "God is man," then certainly also truly and without a trope does Scripture assert that the Son of God was born of the Virgin Mary... 7. The absurdity of the trope... If the humanity alone has suffered, it follows that the person has not suffered for us, because the humanity alone is not a person. If the person has not suffered for us, then neither has the Son of God suffered for us, for the Son of God is a person. The consequence is repugnant to Scripture, Acts 20:28; Rom. 8:32; 1 John 1:7. (L. c. § 195.)

Luther: "Now if the old weather-maker here, Mistress Reason, the grandmother of *Allöosis*, were to say: 'Yes, the Godhead cannot suffer nor die,' you should answer: 'That is true; but nevertheless, because Godhead and humanity in Christ are one Person, Scripture, for the sake of such personal unity, attributes to the Godhead everything that happens to the humanity, and vice versa.' For you must indeed say: the Person (point to Christ) suffers, dies; now the Person is true God; therefore it is rightly said: God's Son suffers; for although the one part (if I may speak so), namely the Godhead, does not suffer, yet the Person, who is God, suffers in the other part, namely in the humanity. Just as one says: The King's son is wounded, even though only his leg is wounded; Solomon is wise, even though only his soul is wise. Absalom is beautiful, even though only his body is beautiful. Peter is gray, even though only his head is gray. For because body and soul are one Person, everything that happens to the body or soul, indeed to the smallest member of the body, is rightly and properly attributed to the whole Person. This is the way of speaking in all the world, not only in Scripture, and it is also the truth; for in truth God the Son was crucified for us, that is, the Person who is God; for it is He—I say, the Person—who is crucified according to the humanity. Thus one should attribute to the whole Person what happens to the other part of the Person, for the reason that both are one Person. So speak all the old teachers, also all new theologians, all language, and the whole of Scripture. But the cursed *Allöosis* turns this straight around and wants to exchange and attribute to the parts what is attributed to the whole Person in Scripture, making its own tropes to pervert Scripture and to tear asunder the Person of Christ... As if the Apostles had been mad and foolish, that they could not have spoken of the Godhead without having to call it humanity, and vice versa. If John had wanted to look at *Allöosis*, he could well have said: 'The flesh has become Word,' when he said: 'The Word has become flesh.'" PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION I.

They cry out against us that we mingle the two natures into one essence; that is not true. We do not say that Deity is humanity or that the divine nature is the human nature, which would be to mingle the natures into one essence. Rather, we mingle the two distinct natures into one single Person, and say: God is man and man is God. But we cry out against them in return that they tear asunder the Person of Christ, as if there were two persons; for where the *alloeosis* is to stand, as Zwingli introduces it, then Christ must be two persons, one divine and one human, because he draws the sayings concerning the suffering solely to the human nature and turns all things away from the Deity; for where the works are divided and separated, there the Person must also be divided, because all works or sufferings are attributed not to the natures, but to the Persons; for it is the Person who does and suffers everything, one thing according to this nature, the other according to that nature; as all the learned well know. Therefore, we hold our Lord Christ thus as God and man in one Person, *non confundendo naturas, nec dividendo personam* [not confounding the natures, nor dividing the person], so that we do not mingle the nature and also do not divide the Person.” (Confession Concerning Christ’s Supper. A. 1528. XX, 1181—1184.)
