Lutherus: ,,Ob nun hie die alte Wettermacherin, Frau Vernunft, der Allöosis Grossmutter, sagen würde: Ja, die Gottheit kann nicht leiden noch sterben, sollst du antworten: Das ist wahr; aber dennoch, weil Gottheit und Menschheit in Christo Eine Person ist, so gibt die Schrift um solcher persönlicher Einigkeit willen auch der Gottheit alles, was der Menschheit widerfährt, und wiederum. Denn das musst du je sagen, die Person (zeige Christum) leidet, stirbt; nun ist die Person wahrhaftiger Gott; darum ist5s recht geredet: Gottes Sohn leidet; denn obwohl das eine Stück (dass ich so rede), als die Gottheit, nicht leidet, so leidet dennoch die Person, welche Gott ist, am andern Stücke, als an der Menschheit. Gleich als man spricht: Des Königs Sohn ist wund, so doch allein sein Bein wund ist; Salomon ist weise, so doch allein seine Seele weise ist. Absalom ist schön, so doch allein sein Leib schön ist. Petrus ist grau, so doch allein sein Haupt grau ist. Denn weil Leib und Seel Eine Person ist, wird,s der ganzen Person recht und wohl zugeeignet, alles was dem Leibe oder Seele, ja dem geringsten Glied des Leibes widerfahret. Dies ist die Weise zu reden in aller Welt, nicht allein in der Schrift, und ist dazu auch die Wahrheit; denn in der Wahrheit ist Gott der Sohn für uns gekreuzigt, das ist, die Person, die Gott ist; denn sie ist, sie, sage ich, die Person ist gekreuzigt nach der Menschheit. Also soll man der ganzen Person zueignen, was dem andern Theil der Person widerfahret, um desswillen, dass beide Eine Person ist. So reden auch alle alte Lehrer, auch alle neue Theologen, alle Sprache und die ganze Schrift. Aber die verfluchte Allöosis kehret solches stracks um und will wechseln und den Stücken zueignen, das der ganzen Person in der Schrift zugeeignet wird, macht eigene Tropos, die Schrift zu verkehren und die Person Christi zu zertrennen. . . Als wären die Apostel toll und thöricht gewesen, dass sie nicht hätten mögen reden von der Gottheit, sie müssten sie denn Menschheit nennen, und wiederum. Hätte Johannes wollen Allöosin ansehen, er hätte auch wohl sagen können: Das Fleisch ist Wort worden, da er sprach: Das Wort ist Fleisch wor PART. III. CAP. Π. SECTIO I.

den.. . Sie schreien über uns, dass wir die zwo Naturen in Ein Wesen mengen; das ist nicht wahr. Wir sagen nicht, dass Gottheit sei Menschheit oder göttliche Natur sei menschliche Natur, welches wäre die Naturen in Ein Wesen gemenget. Sondern wir mengen die zwo unterschiedlichen Naturen in eine einige Person, und sagen: Gott ist Mensch und Mensch ist Gott. Wir schreien aber wieder über sie, dass sie die Person Christi zertrennen, als wären’s zwo Personen; denn wo die Allöosis soll bestehen, wie sie Zwingel führet, so wird Christus zwo Personen müssen sein, eine göttliche und eine menschliche, weil er die Sprüche vom Leiden allein auf die menschliche Natur zeucht und aller Dinge von der Gottheit wendet; denn wo die Werke zertheilet und gesondert werden, da muss auch die Person zertrennet werden, weil alle Werke oder Leiden nicht den Naturen, sondern den Personen zugeeignet werden; denn die Person ist’s, die alles thut und leidet, eins nach dieser Natur, das andere nach jener Natur; wie das alles die Gelehrten wohl wissen. Darum halten wir unsern Herrn Christum also für Gott und Mensch in Einer Person, non confundendo naturas, nec dividendo personam, dass wir die Natur nicht mengen und die Person auch nicht trennen.“ (Bekenntniss vom Abendmahl Christi. A. 1528. XX, 1181—1184.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: H. Muellerus: “Speaking properly, Christ is not a composite person

H. Muellerus: “Speaking properly, Christ is not a composite person. For the composition of two natures, strictly speaking, makes one nature composed of two, such as is the composition of man from soul and body, and such as the Monophysites impiously asserted to be one nature in Christ composed of deity and humanity. But in a mere union, one nature is not formed, but the natures remain distinct, as if you were to set an emerald into a gold ring; there, speaking properly, there occurs not a composition, but a union. God can unite another nature to Himself, but He does not enter into a composition strictly so-called with it. Nor is such a personal union like that which is perceived in creatures; for from those aggregated things a certain collective whole is constituted, which in some way is greater than any one of those things which constitute that whole. But in the mystery of the incarnation, even though a true and ever-enduring hypostatic union has been made and two distinct natures are found in one person, it is nevertheless not permitted to say that the Deity is a part of this composite person. For the Deity cannot be a part of any thing, because nothing is greater than Itself, neither in mass, nor in power, nor in dignity, nor in any other perfection; but the whole is greater than the part and the part is smaller than its whole, and every part can be exceeded and the whole is more perfect than the part; but it is contrary to the nature of the infinite to be able to be exceeded and to admit something more perfect than itself. ‘By the assumption of humanity, God is not increased or perfected, for there is nothing by which divine perfection may grow,’ says Augustine, *De Trinitate*, lib. 6, c. 8. If, however, in order to express in some way and to defend that ineffable mystery of godliness, by which the Word was made flesh, anyone wishes, speaking broadly and commonly with the orthodox antiquity, to say that Christ is a *σύνθετον* [composite] person and that the union of the two natures is an *ένωσιν κατά σύνθεσιν* [union by composition], because a new creature, namely the human, is united to the Word, while the other nature also remains, we do not morosely object, provided he acts as a right interpreter of himself where it is necessary.” (Theol. scholast. Rostochii 1669. p. 280. sq.)

Thus, when it is said in John 6:62: “The Son of Man shall ascend where He was,” our theologians elicit this proposition: The Son of Man was already long ago, before the ascension of the human nature into heaven, in heaven; where the subject is the concrete of the human nature, but the predicate does not belong to Him formally according to the human nature, but pertains formally to the divine nature. Not abstractly or so that the predicate may be the name of the denominating form itself and an attribute, quality, action, or passion in

in the nominative case. For we do not say, for example: The Son of Mary is omnipotence, the Lord of glory is crucifixion, the Son of God is passion, death, etc., but rather, so that the predicate is an adjective or participle (whether expressed or latent in the verb), where the subject is signified in the nominative case, and the attribute, quality, action, or passion, etc., is connoted in the oblique case; for example: the Son of Mary is omnipotent, i.e., he is a subject possessing omnipotence; the Lord of glory is crucified, i.e., he is a person to whom it happened to be crucified, etc.

Gerhard: "Qu. 3: Should abstract predications be used in this kind: deity has suffered, divinity has died? Some think they can be used, provided that it is added: deity has suffered in the flesh. The Württemberg theologians, in *Exam. c. 6, p. 510*: 'from which it appears that the divine nature of the Son truly suffers.' Jac. Andreae in *disp. resp. Puchenio th. 248, 299, 301*, Brentius *c. Bulling. f. 11*, Selnecc. in *Widerlegung der Auflagen p. 192* reject the phrase of Theodoret: 'insofar as he is God, he was not subject to passion.' Some also speak thus: Christ has suffered according to both natures, although not in the divine nature or according to it. But it is better to abstain from these abstract propositions... It is to be feared that, because of the use of these propositions, the error of the Theopaschites, who taught that the divinity in Christ felt pain and suffered when his flesh was fixed to the cross, might be attributed to our churches." (*L. c. § 198.*)

And these are real predications; although, as our own theologians admit, they are to be understood *κατ’ ἄλλο*, not formally, according to that nature which the subject denotes in the oblique case, but according to the other nature, from which the subject is not denominated. For this reason, *διακριτικαί* particles are also frequently added, or *ὡς, ἐν, κατά*, etc., indicating to which nature the predicate formally belongs; see Rom. 9:5, where concerning him who is God over all, and thus concerning the concrete, the divine nature, is enunciated *τὸ κατὰ σάρκα* from the fathers (which is an idiom of the human nature), but a *προσδιορισμός* is added, "according to the flesh," so that you may understand that the predicate belongs to the subject not according to that nature from which the subject is here denominated, but according to the other nature, which consists of flesh and blood.

Reusch: "The diacritic particles, which in logic are called reduplicative in a broad sense, are taken limitatively in this first kind of communication of idioms, so that they may determine the other nature of Christ, to which the predicate belongs formally, and thereby distinguish that nature, to which the predicate belongs formally, from that nature to which it belongs idiomatically or through the communication of idioms. In this respect, these particles in this first kind are also said to be taken specifically, determinatively, or diacritically, i.e., they ought to be explained by 'in respect to,' 'on the part of,' etc. Indeed, those particles can also be explained reduplicatively in the strict sense or by 'because'; but in that sense, they do not pertain to the first kind of communication of idioms." (*Annotatt. in Baieri compend. p. 580.*)

Gerhard: "Qu. 3: Should the distinctive particles be referred to the subject or to the predicate? Resp.: Scripture refers them to the predicate. Christ suffered *σαρκί* (1 Pet. 4:1), was put to death *σαρκί* (1 Pet. 3:18), which can be observed in all the remaining examples. The Calvinists, in order to establish their *ἀλλοίωσις*, prefer to refer them to the subject, but they do not thereby obtain what they seek; for it is one thing to say: Christ has suffered according to the flesh, but quite another to say: only the flesh of Christ has suffered." (*L. c. § 191.*) Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. III.4 PART. III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

The same: "Regarding these distinctive particles, it is to be noted. . . that by reason of their use, they are opposed both to the Nestorian rending asunder of the one person and to the Eutychian confusion of the two natures. For because divine and human things are predicated of one and the same Christ, therefore, against Nestorius, the unity of the person is asserted; because through the distinctive particles it is shown according to which nature each is predicated of Christ, therefore, against Eutyches, the duality of the natures is asserted; and [it is to be noted] that they are not always added actually and expressly, but are to be supplied from other passages of Scripture." (L. c. § 186.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the ancient heretics, Samosatenus, Sabellius, Nestorius, Eutyches, who either entirely denied the communication of idioms or introduced an essential confusion of the same. Especially to be noted here is Nestorius, who strove to introduce a distinction between the propositions: 'Christ suffered and died,' which he conceded, and: 'God suffered and died,' which he denied. . . Just as Eutyches subjected the deity to suffering, so Nestorius excluded God from suffering. . .

2. Of the Calvinists, who 1.) maintain that the communication of idioms is indeed real with respect to the person denominated by the deity or humanity, but with respect to the natures it is merely verbal, i.e., it is only a communication of words and locutions, not of properties. . . 2.) They call the denominations merely verbal when human things are predicated of God, or divine things of man. And they contend that those very propositions which pertain to the first genus of the communication of idioms are tropical and improper. Thus the *Admonitio Neostadiensis*, p. 70: 'The predication of human things concerning God and divine things concerning man, as far as the natures are concerned, is only verbal.' . . Indeed, they reject our opinion as Eutychian when we assert that the Son of God truly and properly suffered. The Bremenses against Hunnius, p. 70, say: 'It is Eutychian when it is said by the Lutherans that not only the humanity, but the Son of God Himself suffered for us.'

3. Of the Papists, especially the Jesuits, who deny every real communication of idioms. For thus Bellarmine, *de Christo*, lib. 3, c. 9, § *Ex unione*: 'The communication of idioms, which followed from the hypostatic union, is not real with respect to the natures themselves, as the Lutherans wish, nor is it purely verbal, as Beza and Peter Martyr wish; but it is real with respect to the hypostasis of either nature, but not with respect to the two natures.'" (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 222. sqq.) §

19. Those predications, however, in which either the subject is a concrete of that nature to which the predicate formally belongs,a or the subject is a concrete of the person and the predicate is an idiom of either nature,b indeed differ from those which properly pertain to this genus of the communication of idioms,c yet they can in their own way be referred here.d a E. g. The Son of God is immense, is eternal, etc. The Son of Man has suffered, has died, etc. b E. g. Christ is the brightness of the Father's glory, Christ is born of the fathers. c For predications by communication are wont to be distinguished from formal predications, in which the predicate is of the essence of the for

of an evil subject, or it belongs to the subject according to that which is signified by it, or according to some part comprised in its signification. Whence also the blessed Hutter, in his *Loci Communes* concerning Christ, ch. III, p. 157, when he had said that some describe the first genus of the communication of idioms thus: The first genus is that by which the property of one nature in Christ is predicated of the other in the concrete; while others describe it a little differently in this manner: The first genus is when that which is proper to one nature is attributed not only to that nature to which it is proper, separately, but to the whole person, who is God and man at the same time, and again is shown by a distinctive particle according to which nature it belongs to the person; shortly thereafter, about to offer his own judgment (*ἐπίκρισιν*), he says: Those who hold that former definition seem to have observed more properly the nature of the communication of idioms and to have looked to those locutions of Scripture which show that the *λόγος* or Son of God so appropriated the human nature together with its idioms to Himself, that now the idioms of one nature are predicated of the other in the concrete. And on the preceding page, 155, where he likewise treats of those propositions when the idioms of both natures are enunciated concerning the whole person of Christ, on account of which some have constituted a fourth genus of the communication of idioms, he explains his opinion in these words: Since these propositions, he says, do not enunciate the idioms of one nature concerning the other nature, either in the concrete or in the abstract, through any communication, but predicate of the whole person that which is attributed to the whole person with respect to one nature; therefore, in these propositions, strictly speaking, there does not seem to be a communication of idioms. Thus Hutter, *loc. cit.*

Latin:

H. Muellerus: ,,Proprie loquendo Christus non est persona composita. Duarum enim naturarum compositio proprie dicta facit unam ex duabus compositam naturam, qualis est compositio hominis ex anima et corpore, et qualem in Christo unam ex deitate et humanitate compositam naturam impie adserebant Monophysitae. At in mera unione non flt una natura, sed manent distinctae naturae, ut si annulo aureo smaragdum inferas, flt isthic proprie loquendo non compositio, sed unio. Deus unire sibi potest naturam aliam, at cum ea compositionem stricte dictam non ingreditur. Nec talis est unio personalis, qualis est ea, quae cernitur in creaturis; ex iis enim aggregatis constituitur totum quoddam collectivum, quod aliquo modo majus est qualibet una earum rerum, quae totum illud constituunt. At in mysterio incarnationis, etiamsi facta sit vera semperque duratura unio hypostatica et duae distinctae naturae in una persona inveniantur, non licet tamen dicere, deitatem partem esse hujus personae compositae. Deitas enim nullius rei pars esse potest, quia nihil ipsa majus est, nec mole, nec virtute, nec dignitate, nec ulla alia perfectione; totum autem majus est parte et pars minor est suo toto, et omnis pars potest excedi et totum parte est perfectius; contra rationem autem infiniti est, posse excedi et admittere aliquid perfectius se ipso. ,Assumtione humanitatis non augetur aut perficitur Deus, qui non est, quo crescat divina perfectio‘, inquit Augustinus lib. 6. de trin. c. 8. Si quis tamen ad effandum aliquo modo et tuendum ineffabile illud pietatis mysterium, quo Verbum caro factum est, cum orthodoxa antiquitate late et vulgariter loquendo dicere velit, Christum esse personam σύνθετον et unionem duarum naturarum esse ενωσιν κατά σϋνθεσιν, quia unita Verbo est nova creatura, nempe humana, manente etiam altera natura, non morose refragamur, modo dextrum sui ipsius agat, ubi opus est, interpretem.“ (Theol. scholast. Rostochii 1669. p. 280. sq.)

Ita quando Joh. 6, 62. dicitur: Filius hominis ascendet eo, ubi erat, nostrates hanc eliciunt propositionem: Filius hominis jam olim, ante ascensum humanae naturae in coelum, erat in coelo; ubi subjectum est concretum naturae humanae, praedicatum autem non competit ei secundum humanam naturam formaliter, sed pertinet formaliter ad divinam naturam. Non abstractive aut ut praedicatum sit nomen ipsius formae denominantis et attributum, qualitatem, actionem gtut passionem in

casu recto sigjiificet. Neque enim v. g. dicimus: Filius Mariae est omnipotentia, Dominus gloriae est crucifixio, Filius Dei est passio, mors etc., sed, ut praedicatum sit nomen adjectivum aut participium (sive expressum, sive in verbo latens), ubi in casu recto suppositum significatur, attributum, qualitas, actio aut passio etc. in obliquo connotatur; v. g. filius Mariae est omnipotens, i. e. est suppositum habens omnipotentiam, Dominus gloriae est crucifixus, i. e. est persona, cui accidit crucifigi etc.

Gerhardus: ,,Qu. 3.: An usurpandae sint in hoc gener q praedica· Mones abstracMvae: deitas est passa, divinitas est mortua? Quidam eas usurpari posse arbitrantur, ita tamen, ut addatur: deitas passa est carne. Wirtenberg, in exam. c. 6. p. 510.: ,ex quo apparet, divinam Filii naturam revera pati.‘ Jac. Andreae in disp. resp. Puchenio th. 248. 299. 301., Brentius c. Bulling. f. 11., Selnecc. in Widerlegung der Auflagen p. 192. repudiat phrasin Theodoreti: ,in quantum Deus, non fuit obnoxius passioni.‘ Quidam etiam sic loquuntur: Christus quoad utramque naturam est passus, licet non in divina natura vel seeundum eam. Sed praestat ab hisce propositionibus abstractivis abstinere. . . Metuendum, ne propter usum harum proprositionum Theopaschitarum error, qui docuerunt, divinitatem in Christo doluisse et passam esse, cum caro ejus figeretur in cruce, nostris ecclesiis affricetur.“ (L. c. § 198.)

Et sunt hae praedicationes reales; licet, fatentibus nostratibus, χατ αλλο, non formaliter, secundum eam naturam, quam subjectum in casu obliquo denotat, sed secundum alteram naturam, a qua subjectum non denominatur, intelligenda sit praedicatio. Quamobrem etiam crebro adduntur particulae διαχριτιχαϊ, sive &«, έν, χατά etc., indicantes, ad quam naturam praedicatum formaliter pertineat; vid. Rom. 9, 5., ubi de eo, qui est Deus super omnia, adeoque de concreto, divinae naturae, enuntiatur td nasd ex patribus (quod est idioma naturae humanae), additur autem προσδιορισμός, secundum carnem, ut intelligas, praedicatum competere subjecto non secundum eam naturam, a qua subjectum hic denominatur, sed secundum naturam alteram, qua carne et sanguine constat.

Reuschius: ,,Particulae diacrüicae, quae in logica vocantur redupMcaMvae in lato significatu, in hoc primo genere communicationis idiomatum sumuntur limitative, ut alteram Christi naturam, cui praedicatum competit formaliter, determinent, eoque illam naturam, cui praedicatum competit formaliter, ab ea natura, cui competit idiomatice seu per communicationem idiomatum, distinguant. Quo respectu etiam istae particulae in hoc primo genere accipi dicuntur speciflcative, determinative seu diacritice, i.e. explicari debent per,respectu‘, ,ex parte‘ etc. Possunt quidem illae particulae explicari quoque reduplicative in stricto significatu seu per quia; sed eo sensu non pertinent ad primum genus communicationis idiomatum.“ (Annotatt. in Baieri compend. p. 580.)

Gerhardus: ״Qu. 3.: An particulae distinctivae ad subjectum, an vero ad praedicatum referendae? Resp.: Scriptura eas refert ad praedicatum. Christus passus est σαρκϊ 1 Pet. 4, 1., mortificatus σαρκϊ 1 Pet. 3,18., quod ipsum in reliquis exemplis omnibus observari potest. Calviniani, ut suam άλλοίωσιν statuminare possint, ad subjectum eas referre malunt, sed nondum propterea obtinent, quod quaerunt; aliud enim est dicere: Christus secundum carnem est passus, aliud vero: sola Christi caro est passa.“ (L. c. § 191.) Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.4 PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO I.

Idem: ,,De hisce distinctivis particulis notandum, . . . quodratione usus et Nestorianae unius personae divulsioni et Eutychianae duarum naturarum confusioni opponantur. Quia enim de uno et eodem Christo divina et humana praedicantur, ideo contra Nestorium asseritur personae unitas; quia per particulas distinctivas ostenditur, secundum quam naturam utraque de Christo praedicentur, ideo contra Eutychen asseritur naturarum dUalitas; quodque non semper actu et expresse addantur, sed ex aliis Scripturae locis sint repetendae.“ (L. c. § 186.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Antiquorum haereticorum, Samosateni, Sabellii, Nestorii, Eutychis, qui vel idiomatum communicationem penitus negarunt, vel eorundem essentialem confusionem introduxerunt. Inprimis hic notandus Nestorius, qui discrimen inducere satagebat inter propositiones: ,Christus est passus et mortuus‘, quam concessit, et: ,Deus est passus et mortuus‘, quam negavit. . . Uti Eutyches deitatem passioni subjiciebat, sic Nestorius Deum a passione excludebat. . .

2. Calvinianorum, qui 1.) statuunt, idiomatum communicationem esse quidem realem respectu personae a deitate vel humanitate denominatae, sed respectu naturarum eam verbalem tantum esse, h. e. esse solum communicationem vocum et locutionum, non proprietatum. . . 2.) Denominationes solum verbales dicunt, cum de Deo humana, aut de homine divina efferuntur. Ipsasque propositiones illas tropicas et improprias esse contendunt, quae ad primum genus communicationis idiomatum pertinent. Sic admon. Neostad. p. 70.: ,Praedicatio humanorum de Deo et divinorum de homine, quantum ad naturas, tantum verbalis est.‘ . . Imo nostram sententiam ut Eutychianam reprobant, cum Filium Dei vere proprieque passum asserimus. Bremenses contra Hunnium p. 70.: ,Eutychianum est‘, inquiunt, ,cum dicitur a Lutheranis, non sola humanitas, sed ipse Filius Dei pro nobis passus est.‘

8. Papistarum, inprimis Jesuitarum, qui omnem realem idiomatum communicationem negant. Sic enim Bellarminus lib. 3. de Christo, c. 9. §. Ex unione: ,Communicatio idiomatum, ex unipne hypostatica secuta, ^on est realis respectu ipsarum naturarum, ut volunt Lutherani, nec est plane verbalis, ut volunt Beza et Petrus Martyr; sed est realis respectu hypostaseos utriusque naturae, non autem respectu duarum naturarum.‘“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 222. sqq.) §

19. Illae vero praedicationes, in quibus vel subjectum est concretum ejus naturae, ad quam praedicatum formaliter pertinet, a vel subjectum est concretum personae, et praedicatum est idioma alterutrius naturae,b differunt quidem ab illis, quae proprie ad hoc genus communicationis idiomatum pertinent,c possunt tamen suo modo huc referri.d V. g. Filius Dei est immensus, est aeternus etc. Filius hominis est passus, est mortuus etc. E. g. Christus est splendor gloriae Patris, Christus est natus ex patribus. Solent enim praedicationes per communicationem contradistingui praedicationibus formalibus, in quibus praedicatum est de ratione for

mali subjecti, aut convenit subjecto secundum id, quod per illud significatur, vel secundum aliquam partem in ejus significatu comprehensam. Unde etiam b. Hutterus LL. CC. de Christo cap. III. p. m. 157., cum dixisset, alios primum genus communicationis idiomatum sic deseribere: Primum genus est, quo unius naturae proprietas in Christo praedicar tur de altera in concreto, alios vero paulo aliter in hunc modum: Primum genus est, quando id, quod uni naturae proprium est, non soli ei naturae, cujus proprium est, seorsim, sed toti personae, quae Deus simul et homo est, tribuitur, et rursum per distinctivam particulam ostenditur, secundum quam naturam id personae competat, post paulo suam Ιπίχρισιν prolaturus: Qui priorem illam definitionem tenent, ait, magis proprie naturam communicor tionis idiomatum observasse et ad eas locutiones Scripturae respexisse videntur, quae ostendunt, λόγον sive Filium Dei humanam naturam una cum ejus idiomatibus ita sibi appropriasse, ut jam unius naturae idiomata praedicentur de altera in concreto. Et praeced. p. 155., ubi itidem de propositionibus illis, quando de tota persona Christi utriusque naturae idiomata enuntiantur, agit, quarum causa quidam quartum genus communicationis idiomatum constituerint, suam sententiam his verbis exponit: Cum propositiones hae, inquit, non per communicationem aliquam unius naturae idiomata de altera natura, vel in concreto, vel in abstracto enuntient, sed de tota persona praedicent id, quod respectu unius naturae toti personae tribuitur; ideoque in his propositionibus proprie loquendo non videtur esse communicatio idiomatum. Haec Hutterus, 11. cc.


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: To whom the blessed Scherzer adds in his *Systema Theologiae*, L

To whom the blessed Scherzer adds in his *Systema Theologiae*, L. VIII, p. 196. For although Dr. Olearius, § 12, 13, in his *Disputation on the Idiomatic Proposition of the First and Third Genus from 1 Peter 4:1*, thinks that the blessed Scherzer departs from us and the blessed Hutter, in that he warns that even in those propositions where the properties of either nature are predicated of the whole person (*συνθέτῳ*), a communication of idioms is involved, on account of the subject denominated by both natures and the communicated *ὑπόστασις*, adding this reason: For unless that were communicated, the subject could neither be denominated by both natures, nor could a divine predicate be attributed to the whole person denominated by the divine and human nature; yet at the same time it could be observed that the blessed Scherzer, with the blessed Hutter, acknowledges and expressly confesses that for the communication of idioms, strictly speaking, it is required that the idioms of one nature be communicated concerning the other nature, either in the concrete or in the abstract; for thus he speaks *loc. cit.* He acknowledges, therefore, the distinction between propositions in which the communication of idioms, strictly speaking and expressly, has a place, and propositions in which the communication of idioms is in some way involved, just as we noted in our thesis the difference between propositions which properly belong to the first genus of the communication of idioms, and those which can be referred here in their own way. Namely, just as logicians distinguish between those things which are directly and those which are reductively in the categories, so elsewhere and in this place, where the forms of predication are treated, it is not without reason that a distinction is made between those things which belong to a certain genus properly and directly, and those which involve something of that kind. But that those propositions, where the idiom of another nature is predicated of the whole person, are rightly and above others reduced to the first genus, will immediately appear from the following note and the three added reasons; so far is it from the case that we could be seen to have completely excluded them here.

d) Propositions of the former kind are indeed referred here, insofar as the place of the subject is occupied by the name of the person, who is truly σΰνΰετος [composite], or consists of another nature besides this one from which it is denominated; although, as such, it is not distinctly expressed. But especially the propositions of the latter class are reduced here, in which 1) the fact that the attributes of the two natures can be predicated of the concrete person of Christ arises from the fact that the subject is neither a mere man nor only God, and thus that mode of predication proceeds from the personal union. And 2) if you consider more deeply the relation of the predicate to both natures comprised in the subject and its meaning, it will appear that the predicate is formal only by reason of one nature comprised in the subject, not by reason of the other. Whence also 3) in those propositions the use of discretive particles has a place; e.g., Christ is born of the fathers according to the flesh, Rom. 9:5. Compare, blessed Musaeus, *Detailed Explanation*, Q. LIII, pp. 528, 529. §

20. The second kind of communication of idioms is that by which truly divine perfections, and the authority and power resulting therefrom, and the highest honor and glory, are communicated to the human nature of Christ in the abstract. R. Teller: "The abstract is one thing in mind and thought (logically so-called), and another in the thing itself (really); and the former is a mode of thinking by which our mind distinguishes a thing, which exists and inheres in a subject, from it; but the latter is a separation, by which, of course, the thing is absent from the subject. In the former way, theologians use this word in this place, but by no means in the latter way. For the human nature of Christ is never separated from the subject, nor is it ever outside the νπόστασιν [hypostasis] of the divine nature in Christ, although by our thought it can and ought to be considered separately in itself. Therefore, it is not permitted to speak thus: the human nature, separated from the subject, is of itself everywhere present, all-powerful, all-knowing (for that would be a real abstract). But this is what we profess: the human nature of Christ, which and insofar as it exists in Christ; and it exists always and everywhere (which is the logical abstract). ... We must not entirely abstain from the use of the name 'abstract,' of course, since we must oppose the errors of the followers of Calvin, and especially the Crypto-Calvinists, who deny the true and real communication of divine properties and perfections to the human nature in Christ, and indeed with the intention of drawing from this the consequence that the body and blood of Christ are not truly and in reality present in the most holy feast." (See Hollaz, *loc. cit.*, note to q. 60, p. 722 sq.)

a) Thus, with modern theologians, we place this kind of communication of idioms in the second position, which others call the communication of majesty; although formerly it almost always held the third place. It is, however, an explanation of the first kind; and it comes down to this, that just as on the part of the natures, although the divine is personally united to the human, and the human to the divine, this difference nevertheless intervenes, that the divine nature intimately penetrates and perfects the human, but the human does not in turn penetrate and perfect the divine, but is penetrated and perfected by it, so in the communication of idioms this difference intervenes on the part of the natures, that the divine nature,

PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

penetrating the human, it also makes the same, even when conceived abstractly, a participant in its own divine perfections in its own way; but the human nature does not conversely, as it neither permeates nor perfects the divine nature, possess the ability to make, nor does it make, this nature, when conceived abstractly, a participant in its own properties. Whence, that each nature in the concrete claims for itself the idioms of the other nature, this pertains to the first genus; but that the divine nature also bestows its divine properties upon the human nature itself, viewed in itself (yet within the personal union), that is referred to the second genus of the communication of idioms.

Gerhard: "Q. 2. Whether that μεταδίδοσις (by which the λόγος communicates its own proper glory and majesty to the assumed flesh) is more correctly placed in the second or the third position among the genera of communication? The Formula of Concord places it in the third position, because this genus, as being the most controversial, had to be treated and explained more copiously; but if we wish to regard the order of nature, it must be placed in the second position, because the human nature in the works of the office acts not only according to its essential properties, but also according to the divine glory communicated to it through the hypostatic union. . .; whence some of our theologians, following the authority of the symbolical books, place it in the third position, while others, insisting on the order of nature and the clarity of teaching, place it in the second; which diversity, since it does not concern the thing itself, ought to disturb no one." (L. c. § 185.)

Hollaz: "The Greeks call this (second) genus: 1. βελτίωσιν, improvement, on account of the finite gifts bestowed, by which the human nature of Christ is perfected for the undertaking of the threefold office; 2. προςθήκην μεγάλην, a great augmentation, for the reason that there is no greater augmentation given than the communicated omnipotence, omniscience, etc.; 3. νπερνψωσιν, exaltation, since through the communicated divine majesty the flesh of Christ has been raised to the most exalted state; 4. μετάδοσιν, communication, namely, of infinite majesty; 5. δόξασιν, glorification, inasmuch as the flesh of Christ is accumulated with that glory which the Son of God has from eternity, John 17:5; 6. μετάληψιν θείας αξίας, participation of divine dignity, because from the divine gifts with which the assumed flesh is adorned, its divine dignity shines forth; 7. μετοχήν θείας δννάμεως, participation of divine power, from which results the highest glory; 8. θεωσιν, άποθέωσιν, θεοποίησιν, deification, which Damascenus (lib. III. de O. F. c. 12) explains, noting that the ancients by the name of deification by no means understood a transmutation, confusion, conversion, abolition, or equalization of the natures, but that they wished to denote by that word the economy of the hypostatic union: a. because on account of that hypostatic union it is predicated of the man Christ that He is God; b. because the ancients indicated the περιχώρησιν of the natures by this word 'deification.' The Latins called it the communication of majesty for the reason that the divine and infinite gifts are the very majesty and glory of the eternal God. The occasion for this denomination was taken from the Greeks, who called the divine gifts given to Christ in time αξιώματα, dignities, and ανχήματα, excellencies. In the Holy Scriptures, the communication of majesty is called anointing, i. e., the donation of the Holy Spirit without measure, Ps. 45:8; John 3:34; Acts 10:38." (L. c. q. 47. p. 699. sq.)

Gerhard: "In this genus of communication, reciprocation does not have a place, as it does in the first; the reason for this is that the divine nature is simply αναλλοίωτος καϊ αμετάβλητος, therefore through the union it could neither be perfected, nor diminished, nor raised, nor depressed, Mal. 3:6; but the human nature, because it is humble and ενδεής, could therefore be exalted, raised, and perfected through the union." (L. c. § 201. n. 5.) And indeed all divine perfections are communicated to the human nature, insofar as on the part of God they are simply one; nor can it therefore happen that, one being communicated, the rest are not communicated; PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

yet they cannot all be predicated of the human nature in the same way, as we shall presently state. Meanwhile, what is said in Col. 2:9 pertains here: πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος, all the fullness of the deity, and thus the whole complex of divine attributes, dwells in Christ σωματικῶς, corporally, as in a man, and by the grace of the union. Cf. Matt. 11:27, where Christ Himself says: All things have been delivered to me by my Father. But whatever Scripture affirms that Christ received in time, it does not say that He received it according to His divinity (according to which He possesses all things from eternity), but that the person of Christ, by reason of and with respect to the human nature, received them in time, according to the most common rule approved by the greatest consensus of the entire orthodox church, which the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord repeats on p. 776. The ancients handed this down: Athanasius, Serm. II against the Arians, explaining the statement of Paul in Phil. 2:7, p. 146, 149, and Serm. IV, treating the statements of Matt. 28:18 and John 17:5; and from Athanasius, Theodoret, Dial. II, c. XXIX, p. 130, 131, and elsewhere in Ps. 109 (110), Vol. I, p. 176, and in the Ep. to the Phil. ch. II, Vol. II, p. 90; furthermore, Gregory of Nyssa, Orat. II de Resurrect., p. 157, and Leo the Great, Ep. LXXXIII to the Bishops of Palestine, c. VII, p.

Cui accedit b. Scherzerus System. Th. L. VIII. p. 196. Quanquam enim Dn. D. Olearius § 12. 13. Disp, de propositione primi et tertii generis idiomatica ex 1 Petr. Jf, 1. b. Scherzerum a nobis et b. Huttero discedere putet, eo quod is etiam in propositionibus illis, ubi de tqta persona (συνΜτω) alterur trius naturae proprietates praedicantur, communicationem idiomatum involvi moneat, propter subjectum ab utraque natura denominatum et communicatam υπόστασιν, addita hac ratione: Nisi enim illa esset communicata, subjectum nec ab utraque natura denominari, nec praedicatum divinum toti personae a natura divina et humana denominatae tribui posset; simul tamen observari poterat, b. Scherzerum cum b. Huttero agnoscere et expresse fateri, quod ad communicationem idiomatum stricte loquendo requiratur, ut unius naturae idiomata de altera natura vel in concreto, vel in abstracto communicent; sic enim ipse loquitur l. c. Agnoscit ergo discrimen inter propositiones, in quibus communicatio idiomatum stricte loquendo et expresse locum habet, et propositiones, in quibus communicatio idiomatum aliquo modo involvitur, aeque uti in nostra thesi notavimus differentiam inter propositiones, quae ad primum genus communicationis idiomatum proprie pertinent, et quae suo modo huc possunt referri. Scilicet, uti logici distinguunt inter ea, quae directe, et quae reductive sunt in praedicamentis, ita alias et h. l., ubi de formis praedicationum agitur, non abs re discernitur inter ea, quae ad certum genus proprie et directe pertinent, et quae aliquid ejusmodi involvunt. Quod autem propositiones illae, ubi de tota persona praedicatur idioma alterius naturae, ad primum genus recte et prae aliis reducantur, statim apparebit ex not. seq. et rationibus tribus additis; tantum abest, ut videri possimus, illas hic penitus exclusisse.

d) Prioris quidem generis propositiones huc referuntur, quatenus subjecti loco stat nomen personae, quae revera est σΰνΰετος, seu praeter hanc, a qua denominatur, etiam altera natura constans; licet, ut talis, non distincte exprimatur. Praecipue vero posterioris classis propositiones huc reducuntur, in quibus 1) quod duarum naturarum attributa de concreto personae Christi possunt praedicari, hoc inde est, quod subjectum nec est merus homo, nec tantum Deus, adeoque provenit modus ille praedicandi ex unione personali. Et 2) si habitudinem praedicati ad utramque in subjecto ejusque significatu comprehensam naturam penitius consideres, apparebit, praedicatum tantum ratione unius in subjecto comprehensae naturae esse formalem, non ratione alterius. Unde etiam 3) in propositionibus illis usus particularum discretivarum locum habet; v. g. Christus est natus ex patribus secundum carnem, Rom. 9, 5. Confer, b. Mus. Ausführl. Erklärung Q. LIII. p. 528. 529. §

20. Secundum genus a communicationis idiomatum est, quo perfectiones vere divinae b et hinc resultans auctoritas et potestas,c honor et gloria summa,d humanae Christi naturae® in abstracto communicantur/ R. Tellerus: ,, Abstractum est aliud mente‘et cogitatione (logice sic dictum), aliud re ipsa (realiter); et illud quidem est ejusmodi modus cogitandi, quo mens nostra rem, quae in subjecto inest atque inhaeret, ab eo discernit; hoc autem est separatio, qua nimirum res a subjecto abest. Priori modo hanc vocem theologi hoc loco usurpant, neutiquam vero posteriori ratione. Humana enim Christi natura nunquam subjecto sejuncta estt neque unquam est extra νπόστασιν divinae in Christo naturae, quamvis nostra cogitatione seorsim in se ipsa cowsiderari queat ac debeat. Itaque non licet ita loqui: humana natura, a subjecto separata, per se est ubique praesens, omnia valens, omnia sciens (id enim esset abstractum reale). Sed hoc est, quod profltemur: humana Christi natura, quae et quatenus in Christo inest; inest autem semper et ubique (id quod est abstractum logicum). . . Non prorsus nos abstinere debemus ab usu nominis,abstractum*, nimirum cum obviam eundum sit erroribus Calvini sectatorum, praesertim vero CryptoCalvinianorum, quippe qui divinarum proprietatum perfectionumque communicationem veram ac realem humanae in Christo naturae denegant, et ea quidem mente, ut hanc ex eo consecutionem efficiant, corpus sanguinemque Christi in sanctissimo epulo non vere et re ipsa adesse.“ (Vid. Hollaz. 1. c. not. ad q. 60. p. 722. sq.)

a) Ita cum theologis modernis secundo loco collocamus hoc genus communicationis idiomatum, quod alias majestatis communicationem appellant; licet olim tertium locum fere obtinuerit. Est autem declaratio primi generis; et huc redit, quod quemadmodum ex parte naturarum, etsi divina humanae, et humana divinae personaliter uniatur, hoc tamen intercedit discrimen, quod divina natura humanam intime penetrat et perficit, humana vero non vicissim penetrat ac perficit divinam, sed ab hac penetratur et perficitur, ita in communicatione idiomatum hoc ex parte naturarum intercedat discrimen, quod divina natura,

PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO I.

humanam penetrans, eandem etiam abstractive conceptam perfectionum suarum divinarum suo modo participem facit, non autem vicissim humana natura, quae nec permeat aut perficit divinam naturam, hanc abstractive conceptam suarum proprietatum participem aeque facere possit, aut faciat. Unde, quod utraque natura in concreto sibi vendicat idiomata alterius naturae, hoc ad primum genus pertinet; quod autem etiam divina natura suas divinas proprietates ipsi humanae naturae in se spectatae (intra unionem personalem tamen) largitur, id ad secundum genus communicationis idiomatum refertur.

Gerhardus: ,,Q. 2. An μεταδίδοσις illa (qua λόγος propriam suam gloriam et majestatem assumptae carni communicat), rectius secundo, vel tertio loco inter genera communicationis ponatur? Formula Concordiae ponit loco tertio, quia hoc genus ut maxime controversum copiosius erat pertractandum et explicandum; sed si naturae ordinem respicere velimus, secundo loco ponendum erit, quia natura humana in operibus officii non solum secundum essentiales suas proprietates, sed etiam juxta gloriam divinam per hypostaticam unionem sibi communicatam agit. . .; unde quidam ex nostris libri symbolici auctoritatem secuti tertio loco, quidam vero naturae ordini et docendi perspicuitati insistendo secundo loco illud ponunt; quae diversitas, cum non concernat rem ipsam, neminem turbare debet.“ (L. c. § 185.)

Hollazius: ,,Graeci vocant hoc (secundum) genus C. I. 1. βελτίωσιν, meliorationem, ob dona finita collata, quibus natura Christi humana ad triplex obeundum officium perficitur; 2. προςθήκην μεγάλην, magnum augmentum, ideo, quod communicata omnipotentia, omniscientia etc. nullum datur augmentum majus; 3. νπερνψωσιν, exaltationem, quoniam per communicatam majestatem divinam caro Christi in celsissimum statum evecta est; 4. μετάδοσιν,'collationem, sci. infinitae majestatis; 5. δόξασιν, glorificationem, siquidem caro Christi ea gloria cumulata est, quam habet Filius Dei ab aeterno, Joan. 17, 5.; 6. μετάληψιν θείας αξίας, participationem divinae dignitatis, quia ex donis divinis, quibus exornata est caro assumpta, illius dignitas divina relucet; 7. μετοχήν θείας δννάμεως, participationem divinae potentiae, e qua resultat gloria summa; 8. θεωσιν, άποθέωσιν) θεοποίησιν, deiflcationem, quam Damascenus lib. III. de O. F. c. 12. explicat, quod veteres nomine deiflcationis nequaquam intellexerint transmutationem, confusionem, conversionem, abolitionem aut exaequationem naturarum, sed, quod primo oeconomiam hypostaticae unionis eo vocabulo notare voluerint: a. quia propter hypostaticam illam unionem de homine Christo praedicatur, quod sit Deus; b. quia veteres vocabulo hoc,deiflcatio‘ περιχώρησιν naturarum indicarunt. Latini appellarunt communicationem majestatis propterea, quod divina et infinita dona sunt ipsa aeterni Dei majestas et gloria. Occasio hujus denominationis sumta est a Graecis, qui dona divina Christo in tempore data vocarunt αξιώματα, dignitates, et ανχήματα, excellentias. In sacris literis communicatio majestatis appellatur unctio, i. e., donatio Spiritus S. praeter mensuram, Ps. 45, 8. Joan. 3, 34. Act. 10, 38.“ (L. c. q. 47. p. 699. sq.)

Gerhardus: ,,In hoc communicationis genere reciprocatio non habet locum, ut in primo; ratio haec est, quia natura divina est simpliciter αναλλοίωτος καϊ αμετάβλητος, ideo per unionem nec perfici nec minui nec evehi nec deprimi potuit, Malach. 3, 6.; humana autem natura, quia humilis est et ενδεής, ideo per unionem potuit exaltari, evehi ac perfici.“ (L. c. § 201. n. 5.) Et omnes quidem perfectiones divinae communicatae sunt humanae naturae, quatenus ex parte Dei simpliciter unum sunt; neque adeo fieri potest, ut uno communicato non communicentur reliqua; PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO I.

non tamen ideo omnes eodem modo praedicari possunt de humana natura; ut mox dicemus. Interim huc pertinet, quod Col. 2, 9. dicitur: παν το πλήρωμα της ΰεότητος, omnem plenitudinem deitatis, adeoque totum complexum divinorum attributorum, habitare in Christo σωματιχώς, corporaliter, tanquam in homine, et per unionis gratiam. Conf. Matth. 11, 27., ubi Christus ipse ait: Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre. Quae autem Scriptura Christum in tempore accepisse affirmat, ea non dicit secundum divinitatem accepisse (secundum quam omnia ab aeterno possidet), sed quod persona Christi, ratione et respectu humanae naturae, ea in tempore acceperit, juxta communissimam maximo totius ecclesiae orthodoxae consensu approbatam regulam, quam repetit Solida Deci. F. C. p. 776. Tradiderunt autem eam olim Athanasius Serm. II. contra Arianos, explicans dictum Pauli Phil. 2, 7., p. m. 146. 149. et Serm. IV. tractans dicta Matth. 28, 18. et Joh. 17, 5., et ex Athanasio Theodoretus, Dial. II. c. XXIX. p. m. 130.131., alias etiam in Ps. 109. (110.) Tom. I. p. 176., et in Ep. ad Phil. cap. II. Tom. II. p. 90.; praeterea Gregorius Nyssenus Orat. II. de Resurrect. p. 157. et Leo M. Ep. LXXXIII. ad Episc. Palaest. c. VII. p.


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: N. Hunnius: "A mere man cannot satisfy the justice of God, conquer the devil,…

443. N. Hunnius: "A mere man cannot satisfy the justice of God, conquer the devil, destroy hell, open heaven, and reconcile us to God; therefore, in order that the λόγος might suffer, that the Lord of glory might be crucified (1 Cor. 2:8), that the Prince of life might be put to death (Acts 3:15), it was necessary for the divine nature to come into a communion of passibility, which is a human property; again, in order that a mere man might not suffer and that such weight might be added to the passion, it was necessary for the flesh to become a participant in divine omnipotence, so that by a most powerful act and a most efficacious passion through death, the devil might be destroyed, we might be healed by His stripes, sins might be expiated by death, and righteousness might be restored by the resurrection; all of which effects, mixed from divine and human actions and passions, most certainly testify to the communion and mutual concurrence of divine and human properties." (L. c. § 652.) Quenstedtius: "It is rightly said: All divine attributes are communicated to the human nature, and likewise, some are not. All are communicated as to indwelling and possession; some at least as to immediate predication and enunciation (such as ἐνεργητικά, or those which have a first and second act, such as omnipotence, omniscience, etc.; but not ἀνενέργητα, such as eternity, infinity, etc.). None are communicated as to a transfusion from subject to subject." (L. c. s. 2. q. 10. f. 228.)

Reuschius: "The quiescent attributes of God can be predicated of the human nature of Christ through the mediation of the operative ones, but not immediately; for I cannot say: The human nature of Christ is of itself, independent, exists necessarily, is eternal, simple, etc.; but I can say mediately: The human nature of Christ has omniscience or omni-wisdom, etc., which is of itself, etc." (Annotatt. etc. p. 588 sq.) Quenstedtius: "The Calvinists object: Either all the idioms of the deity are communicated, or none; not all, such as eternity, infinity, immensity, spirituality, etc.: therefore none. They prove the consequence of the major premise thus: Because the divine essence is ἀμέριστος (indivisible), and therefore the divine idioms, which do not differ from it, do not admit of division. Resp.: 1. By denying the disjunction; for the communication of idioms is not a certain physical transfusion, but a free dispensation of the divine εὐδοκία. 2. Divine idioms, as has been said more often, are some ἐνεργητικά, others ἀνενέργητα; the former admit of a second act or proceed outwardly through ἐνεργήματα and operations, such as goodness, wisdom, omnipotence, mercy..."

ON THE PERSON OF CHRIST. cordia; άνενέργητα are those which remain quiet within the divine essence and do not exert themselves outwardly in creatures through operations, such as eternity, immensity, simplicity, etc. The former are so communicated that they are predicated even of Christ’s flesh αμέσως, or immediately; the latter, however, are predicated of Christ’s flesh not immediately, but through the mediation of ενεργητικοϊς attributes; and thus all are communicated as regards common possession and inhabitation, but not all, only some at least, as regards immediate predication. Just as the soul communicates life and the faculty of sensing, etc., to the body, yet does not communicate immateriality or immortality; and just as iron is ignited by the most subtle and light fire, yet is not denominated by those attributes of lightness and subtlety: so the flesh of Christ is perfected by eternal and infinite wisdom and power, yet is not therefore called eternal and infinite αμέσως. Although they are in one subject, there is nevertheless an order in the κοινωνία and a different mode of predicating. 3. The Hypostasis is communicated, which, however, does not differ in reality from that impertible essence of God.” (L. c. q. 10. f. 235. sq.)

E. Hunnius: “(It is objected:) But if one idiom is not communicated to the humanity, it will be said that nothing at all is communicated, since the deity is άμέρίστος, or impertible; and indeed, infinity, eternity, and spirituality are not attributed to the flesh; therefore, neither are the remaining idioms. (

Resp.:) Here I answer at the beginning that in this mystery we neither affirm nor defend anything beyond what is prescribed by the divine Word. Because, therefore, we have manifest testimonies that omnipotence, infinite wisdom, the power of vivifying, and presence even unto the consummation of the age were communicated to Christ as man, we believe it for that reason. Again, because Scripture nowhere says that the humanity of Christ is from eternity, is made infinite, etc., we therefore do not assert this either.

Furthermore, it does not follow that if eternity cannot be predicated of the humanity of Christ, that for that reason the other properties, such as omnipotence, omniscience, etc., are not predicated of it. For the adversaries have not yet proven that what is said of one idiom must immediately be established for the rest as well.

For although all of God’s attributes and properties are most simply and plainly άόιαφέτως one within His essence, yet when they are considered with respect to the assumed nature or as they operate in creatures, they are discussed distinctly, so that one does not say or enunciate just anything about just anything indiscriminately.

If we say that God saves us by His goodness (which is an idiom of God), we do not say that He saves or justifies us by His infinity or eternity. Thus we say that God condemns the impious by His justice; shall we therefore, according to the dialectic of the Zwinglians, say that God condemns by His goodness, mercy, and charity (which are likewise idioms)? This would indeed be most absurd, since, although the reprobate experience and feel the justice of God, they are nevertheless utterly excluded and cast away from the sense of the charity and goodness of God.

Furthermore, even if the human nature of Christ is not infinite or from eternity, yet the power or majesty communicated to Him is infinite and eternal, just as we read in Daniel 7 that eternal power was given to the Son of Man, and, as Christ Himself explains, that all power in heaven and on earth was given to Him. By which reason infinity and eternity are communicated to the assumed nature, not indeed immediately, but through the mediation of other ένεργητίκοϊς ιδιώμασι.

To these, although eternity cannot be enunciated of the human nature by reason of its beginning, yet eternity by reason of its end is communicated to Christ as man from the personal union.” (Libelli IV. etc. p. 56. sqq.)

Ebartus: “All properties of the divine nature are in the assumed nature by reason of the κατοικήσεως παντός του πληρώματος της θεότητος of the Son of God, although not all by reason of της ενεργείας.” (Enchirid. p. 118.)

Chemnitius: “What is said, that the flesh of Christ was not made an eternal, infinite, immense, and spiritual essence by the union, and therefore that the whole fullness of the deity was not personally communicated to the assumed human nature, is easily solved. For neither does the humanity of Christ, by the personal communication of the remaining attributes, in itself...” PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

or according to itself, essentially or by essence, or by some property or condition of nature, has it become omnipotent, omniscient, and life-giving; but because the assumed humanity has those attributes of the divinity united to itself personally by the λόγος, in such a way that in it and through it He exerts His operations, just as is said of iron made fiery, therefore it is said to have communion with them,” (De duabus naturis in Christo, c. 23. f. 122.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who deny that this real communication of divine idioms has been made to the flesh of Christ. Thus Bellarmine, lib. 3. de Christo c. 8., opposes the communication of subsistence and the attributes of the deity to one another, and grants the former to the union, but denies the latter. . . 2. Of the Calvinists, who altogether deny this second genus of the communication of idioms; they explain those propositions: The flesh of Christ gives life, the Son of Man is omnipotent, etc., through the άλλοίωσις of Zwingli in this way: The Son of God, who assumed flesh, gives life; the Son of God, who is the same Son of Man, is omnipotent. . . They invent, however, a certain new communication according to analogy and similarity, by which the λόγος effects or pours into the human nature a wisdom and power similar to, but not equal to, the divine wisdom and power. . . 3. Of the Innovators, who acknowledge only one genus of the communication of idioms, namely, that in which properties suitable to one nature are attributed to the person in the concrete; likewise, that the human nature of Christ cannot be intrinsically denominated by any divine attribute. Thus D. Georg. Calixtus in the disputations on the principal chapters of the Christian religion held at Helmstedt in the year 1611, which his son, D. F. W. Calixtus, edited again in 1658, disp. III. th. 23, says: ‘That those who attribute to the humanity divine attributes, which in reality are the same as the divine essence, are not alien from Eutychianism,’ etc. Meanwhile, with the Calvinists, he grants to the human nature of Christ gifts that are supreme, but finite.” (L. c. f. 229. sq.)

Gerhardus: “Both the Papists and the Calvinists deny that a real communication of divine idioms has been made to the flesh of Christ, tied to one another here by their tails like the foxes of Samson, although in other parts of doctrine they disagree with one another in their heads.” (L. c. § 242.)

Luthardtius: “To this genus majestaticum there should logically and factually correspond a genus ταπεινωτικόν, i.e., a limitation of the divine nature through the earthly-human nature and mode of being. But the Doctors deny this because of the immutability of the divine nature. However, that the old dogmatics neither satisfy the consequence of the fundamental thought nor the Christian consciousness in this matter becomes evident in the doctrine of the exinanition.” (Compend. p. 154.)

Kahnisius: “If the communicatio idiomatum consists in the reciprocal relationship according to which both natures in Christ communicate their properties to one another (αντίδοσις), then, according to logic, this reciprocal relationship falls into two sides: first, the divine nature communicates its properties to the human (genus αυξηματικόν); second, the human nature communicates its properties to the divine (genus ταπεινωτικόν). However, the old dogmatics does not recognize this second genus at all. This is, as Thomasius has asserted, an obvious one-sidedness of the old dogmatics. If the personal unity compels the acknowledgment that the human nature has a part in the divine, then the same compels the acknowledgment that the divine nature has a part in the human. The divine nature in Christ, which is infinite, has imposed upon itself the limit of finitude in the human nature.” (Die luth. Dogm. 1868. III, 339.)

Latin:

443. N. Hunnius: ,,Nudus homo non potest justitiae Dei satisfacere, diabolum vincere, infernum destruere, coelum aperire et Deo nos reconciliare; itaque, ut ό λόγος pateretur, Dominus gloriae crucifigeretur 1 Cor. 2, 8., princeps vitae interficeretur Act. 3, 15., necessarium fuit, naturam divinam venire in communionem patibilitatis, quae est proprietas humana; rursus, ut non nudus homo pateretur et tantum pondus passioni adderetur, necessarium fuit, carnem participem fieri omnipotentiae divinae, ut sic potentissimo actu et efflcacissima passione per mortem diabolus destrueretur, nos livore ejus sanaremur, morte delicta expiarentur et resurrectione justitia redderetur; quae effecta omnia, ex actionibus et passionibus divinis humanisque mixta, certissime testantur communionem et concursum mutuum proprietatum divinarum humanarumque.“ (L. c. § 652.) Quenstedtius: ,,Recte dicitur: Omnia attributa divina esse naturae humanae communicata, item, quaedam, nulla. Omnia communicata sunt quoad inhabitationem et possessionem; quaedam saltem quoad immediatam praedicationem et enuntiationem (ut ενεργητικά sive quae habent actum primum et secundum, ut omnipotentia, omniscientia etc.; non vero άνενέργητα, ut aeternitas, infinitas etc.). Nulla sunt communicata quoad e subjecto in subjectum transfusionem.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 10. f: 228.)

Reuschius: ,,Quiescentia Dei attributa de h. Chr. n., mediantibus operativis, praedicari possunt, non vero immediate; dicere enim non possum: H. Chr. n. est a se, independens, necessario existit, est aeterna, simplex etc.; dicere autem possum mediate: H. Chr. n. habet omniscientiam vel omnisapientiam etc., quae est a se etc.“ (Annotatt. etc. p. 588. sq.) Quenstedtius: ,,Excipiunt Calviniani: Aut omnia idiomata deitatis sunt communicata, aut nulla; non omnia, ceu aeternitas, infinitas, immensitas, spiritualitas etc.: ergo nulla. Consequentiam majoris inde probant: Quia essentia divina est άμέριστος, ac proinde etiam idiomata divina, quae ab illa non differunt, divisionem non admittunt. Resp.: 1. negando disjunctum; nam communicatio idiomatum non est physica quaedam transfusio, sed libera ευδοκίας divinae dispensatio. 2. Idiomata divina, ut saepius dictum, alia sunt ενεργητικά, alia άνενέργητα; illa actum secundum admittunt sive per ενεργήματα et operationes ad extra progrediuntur, ut sunt bonitas, sapientia, omnipotentia, miseri

cordia; άνενέργητα sunt, quae intra essentiam divinam quieta manent et per operationes exterius in creaturis se non exserunt, ut sunt aeternitas, immensitas, simplicitas etc. Illa ita sunt communicata, ut etiam de Christi carne αμέσως seu immediate praedicentur; haec vero de carne Christi non immediate, sed mediantibus attributis ενεργητικοϊς praedicantur; adeoque omnia communicata sunt quoad communem possessionem et inhabitationem, non vero omnia, sed quaedam saltem, quoad immediatam praedicationem. Uti anima corpori vitam et facultatem sentiendi etc. communicat, nec tamen immaterialitatem aut immortalitatem; et uti ferrum igne tenuissimo ac levissimo ignitur, nec tamen ab illis attributis levitatis et tenuitatis denominatur: ita caro Christi aeterna et infinita sapientia et potentia perficitur, nec tamen inde αμέσως aeterna et infinita dicitur. Licet in subjecto uno sint, ordo tamen est in κοινωνία et modus praedicandi diversus. 3. Hypostasis communicatur, quae tamen ab impertibili illa Dei essentia reipsa non differt.“ (L. c. q. 10. f. 235. sq.)

E. Hunnius: ,,(Objicitur:) At uno idiomate τον λόγον non communicato humanitati nulla prorsus communicata dicentur, cum deitas sit άμέρίστος seu impertibilis; ac vero infinitas, aeternitas, spiritualitas non sunt carni tributa; ergo nec idiomata reliqua. (

Resp.:) Hic initio respondeo, nos in hoc mysterio nihil ultra praescriptum divini verbi vel affirmare, vel defendere. Quia igitur manifesta habemus testimonia, Christo homini communicatam omnipotentiam, infinitam sapientiam, virtutem vivificandi et praesentiam usque ad consummationem saeculi, propterea credimus. Rursum quia Scriptura nusquam dicit, humanitatem Christi esse ab aeterno, esse factam infinitam etc., ideo hoc etiam· non asserimus.

Praeterea non sequitur, si aeternitas non possit praedicari de humanitate Christi, ut propterea. nec caeterae proprietates, velut omnipotentia, omniscientia etc., de ea praedicentur. Nondum enim probarunt adversarii, quae de uno idiomate dicuntur, ea protinus de reliquis etiam statuenda.

Quanquam enim omnia Dei attributa et proprietates intra ipsius essentiam simplicissime et plane άόιαφέτως unum sunt, attamen quando considerantur respectu natura^ assumtae vel prout in creaturis operantur, ibi distincte de illis disseritur, ut non promiscue quidvis de quibusvis dicatur vel enuntietur.

Si dicimus, Deum bonitate sua (quae est idioma Dei) nos salvare; non dicimus, ipsum salvare aut justificare nos sua infinitate aut aeternitate. Sic dicimus, Deum sua justitia damnare impios; num ergo juxta Zwinglianorum dialecticam dicemus, Deum sua bonitate, misericordia et caritate (quae itidem sunt idiomata) damnare? Hoc vero longe fuerit absurdissimum, siquidem, licet reprobi justitiam Dei experiuntur ac sentiunt, tamen a sensu caritatis bonitatisque Dei penitus sunt exclusi et projecti.

Praeterea, ut maxime natura Christi humana infinita aut ab aeterno non sit, attamen potestas sive majestas ipsi communicata est infinita et aeterna, quemadmodum Danielis 7. filio hominis aeternam potestatem et, ut Christus ipse explicat, omnem potestatem in coelo et in terra esse traditam legimus. Qua ratione infinitas et aeternitas non quidem immediate, sed mediantibus caeteris ένεργητίκοϊς \δώμασι communicata sunt assumtae naturae.

Ad haec tametsi aeternitas ratione principii de humana natura enuntiari non possit, tamen aeternitas ratione finis ex unione personali communicata est Christo homini.“ (Libelli IV. etc. p. 56. sqq.)

Ebartus: ,,Omnes proprietates divinae naturae sunt in natura asSUmta ratione κατοικήσεως παντός τον πληρώματος τής ΰεότητος Filii Dei, licet non omnes ratione τής ενεργείας.ί1 (Enchirid. p. 118.)

Chemnitius: ,,Quod dicitur, carnem Christi non factam esse ex unione aeternam, infinitam, immensam et spiritualem essentiam, ideo non totam plenitudinem deitatis personaliter communicatam assumtae humanae naturae, facile solvitur. Neque enim ex reliquorum etiam attributorum personali communicatione humanitas Christi in se ipsa PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO I.

aut secundum se, essentialiter aut per essentiam, proprietate aut conditione aliqua naturae facta est omnipotens, omniscia, vivifica; sed quia assumta humanitas attributa illa divinitatis λόγον personaliter sibi unita habet ita, ut in illa et per illam operationes suas exserant, sicut de ferro ignito dictum est, ideo dicitur communionem cum illis habere,“ (De duabus naturis in Christo, c. 23. f. 122.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, qui, realem hanc divinorum idiomatum communicationem carni Christi esse factam, negant. Sic Bellarminus lib. 3. de Christo c. 8. communicationem sub· sistentiae et attributorum deitatis sibi invicem opponit et priorem unioni concedit, posteriorem negat. . . 2. Calvinianorum, qui hoc secundum genus commun. idiom. prorsus negant; propositiones illas: Caro Christi vivificat, filius hominis est omnipotens etc., per άλλοίωσιν Zwinglii ita exponunt: Filius Dei, qui carnem assumpsit, vivificat; Filius Dei, qui idem filius hominis est, omnipotens est. . . Comminiscuntur autem novam quandam communicationem secundum analogiam et similitudinem, qua λόγος in humanam naturam similem, non aequalem divinae sapientiae sapientiam et potentiam efficiat seu effundat.·. . 3. Novatorum, unum tantum communicationis idiomatum genus agnoscentium, illud sel., in quo proprietates uni naturae convenientes tribuuntur personae in concreto; item: humanam naturam Christi a nullo attributo divino posse denominari intrinsece. Ita D. Georg. Calixtus in disput. de praecipuis Christianae religionis capp. anno 1611. Helmstadii habitis, quas filius, D. F. W. Calixtus anno 1658. iterum edidit, disp. III. th. 23. ait: ,Quod ab Eutychianismo alieni non sint, quicunque divina attributa,.quae reipsa idem sunt cum essentia divina, humanitati attribuant‘ etc. Interea cum Calvinianis dona summa, sed finita, largitur humanae naturae Christi.“ (L. c. f. 229. sq.)

Gerhardus: ,,Realem divinorum idiomatum communicationem carni Christi factam negant tum pontificii tum Calviniani, vulpecularum Simsonianarum instar caudis invicem hic devincti, licet in aliis doctrinae partibus capitibus invicem dissideant.“ (L. c. § 242.)

Luthardtius: ,,Diesem genus majest. sollte nun eigentlich sowohl logisch als sachlich ein genus ταπεινωτικόν entsprechen, d. h. Beschränkung der göttlichen Natur durch die irdischmenschliche Natur und Seinsweise. Aber dies leugnen die DD. wegen der Unveranderlichkeit der göttlichen Natur. Allein dass hierin die alte Dogmatik weder der Consequenz des Grundgedankens noch dem christlichen Bewusstsein genüge, wird in der Lehre von der exin. offenbar.“ (Compend. p. 154.)

Kahnisius: ,,Wenn die communicatio idiomatum in dem WechselVerhältnisse besteht, nach welchem sich die beiden Naturen in Christo ihre Eigenschaften gegenseitig mittheilen (αντίόοσις), so zerfällt der Logik nach dies Wechselverhältniss in zwei Seiten: erstlich theilt die göttliehe Natur ihre Eigenschaften der menschlichen mit (genus ανχηματικον), zweitens theilt die menschliche Natur ihre Eigenschaften der göttlichen mit (genus ταπεινωτικόν). Allein die alte Dogmatik erkennt dies zweite genus gar nicht an. Dies ist, wie Thomasius geltend gemacht hat, eine offenbare Einseitigkeit der alten Dogmatik. Wenn die persönliche Einheit zur Anerkennung nöthigt, dass die menschliche Natur Theil hat an der göttlichen, so nöthigt dieselbe auch zur Anerkennung, dass die göttliche Natur Theil hat an der menschlichen. Die göttliche Natur in Christo, welche unendlich ist, hat sich in der menschlichen Natur die Schranke der Endlichkeit auferlegt.“ (Die luth. Dogm. 1868. III, 339.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Specifically, that omniscience was communicated to Christ according to his…

Specifically, that omniscience was communicated to Christ according to his human nature is evident from John 3:34, where it is said that Christ, whom God sent as man to men to speak the words of God, [has the Spirit without measure], with the added reason that

God gave him the spirit of wisdom not by measure, which is the same as saying that wisdom, immense or infinite, was given to him according to the human nature in which he spoke. Cf. John 3:34.

E. Hunnius: "Since he grew in wisdom (Luke 2), how is omniscience (which is devoid of increase) said to be attributed to Christ, as he is man? — It is most true, as Luke writes, that the boy Jesus grew in wisdom, not in pretense indeed, but in the reality of the thing and, as Luke writes, before God and men; whence Christ elsewhere professes that the hour of the last day was hidden and unknown to him in that state of humiliation. For although from his very conception he was anointed with the spirit of knowledge, wisdom, and understanding without measure, so that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were never not hidden in him: yet because that wisdom was not a natural property of the humanity nor did it inhere in it as its subject, it could certainly happen that, even though the human nature of Christ always remained united with the omniscient λόγος, not without a true κοινωνία of the same, yet the λόγος did not always exercise this his own wisdom, which is his idiom, in the humanity, but as it were withdrew the use or usurpation of the same with respect to the humanity, or, to use the word of the apostle, emptied it." (Libell. IV. p. 70.)

The same: "But since you assert that the communication of omniscience took place at the very point of conception: how will it be said that he was ignorant of certain things in the state of humiliation, if indeed the communication of omniscience excludes ignorance and ignorance in turn destroys omniscience? — The humanity had the omniscient λόγος united to itself by a real κοινωνία in the first act, although in the second act Christ as man did not then know or understand all things. . . Just as any philosopher is informed with the habit of knowledge even in sleep and retains his erudition and knowledge even while sleeping in the first act, however much he contemplates or reasons nothing in the second act. Thus, therefore, in Christ the man were all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, but they lay as if hidden, as the apostle says." (L. c. p. 72. sq.)

Quenstedtius: "Although omniscience in the deity is the purest act, yet in the humanity of Christ orthodox theologians recognize the first and second act. Therefore, the quibbling of the Calvinists and Jesuits is vain: If the majesty of divine omniscience was truly given to Christ according to the flesh in the hypostatic union, then he immediately and always exerted it and knew all things in the second act." (L. c. q. 12. f. 248.)

The same: "Even then, when the man Christ Jesus was growing in habitual wisdom, he was πληρούμενος, full of wisdom. Luke 2:40 and 52. Therefore, there was one wisdom in Christ according to human nature, of which he was full immediately from the first moment of conception, namely, divine and infinite, through and because of the hypostatic union, and another, in which he could grow and which admitted of increase, namely, human and finite. Indeed, this was the opinion of the Fathers concerning the progress of Christ, that, namely, from this first point of conception he gradually manifested divine wisdom to men through the increments of age, on account of the μορφὴν δούλου voluntarily assumed. . . Thus also some of the more recent orthodox maintain that Christ according to the flesh also progressed in divine and infinite knowledge, namely, by reason of usurpation." (L. c. s. 2. q. 11. f. 256.)

Kromayerus: "We answer: Christ grew in wisdom not infinite, communicated through the personal union, but habitual and experimental. For besides the infinite gifts in Christ, viewed according to his human nature, there were also finite ones." (Theol. posit. pol. I, 245.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the ancient Agnoetae, where it is to be observed that the Agnoetae were formerly both Arians and Nestorians, and some also Eutychians. . . The ancient Agnoetae, however, attributed to Christ PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION I.

to man a perpetual ignorance of some things, especially of the last day, without regard or distinction for the state of humiliation and exaltation. . . Or they taught that Christ, according to his human nature, did not know all things in his glory. See Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 18, ch. 50. They were condemned at the Sixth Synod of Constantinople, act 11. Furthermore, no writer of the 2nd and 3rd centuries, whether a historian of heresies or any other ecclesiastical writer, makes express mention of the Agnoetae. . .

2. Of the Calvinists, who 1.) deny that omniscience was communicated to the human nature of Christ by the λόγος, and that it is truly omniscient. . . 2.) Contend that only a certain supernatural knowledge and wisdom belongs to Christ according to his human nature, which they say is superior to the wisdom of all angels and men and indeed incomprehensible, but merely created. . . 3.) Assert that Christ, by reason of his human nature, is ignorant of certain things even in the state of exaltation. . .

3. Of the Papists, who 1.) generally deny the communication of divine idioms, from which it is rightly concluded that they also deny that divine omniscience was communicated to the assumed nature. . . 2.) in particular Becanus. . .

4. Of the Socinians, who deny that Christ had perfect knowledge from his birth, and that such knowledge does not befit an infant.” (L. c. f. 240. sq.)

Omnipotence also communicated to the same is proven by the passage John 5:19, where the power of doing all things which the Father did is said to have been given to the Son in time. And in the following verse, 21 and 28, the power of vivifying men, who are dead partly spiritually and partly corporally, is peculiarly attributed to him. The same is also indicated by what is said in Matthew 28:18, that πάσαν έξουσίαν in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ; which, although it formally denotes supreme right, authority, and all power of acting, than which no other greater is given, yet just as Christ cannot exercise that power according to his human nature unless omnipotence has been given to it and exerts itself in it and through it, so it is rightly understood that this also has been communicated to the human nature of Christ; although έξουσία is also accustomed to denote δυναμιν or effective force.

E. Hunnius: “The humanity of Christ, just as it does not subsist in itself, but in the person of the Word, so it does not have those idioms in itself, as in a subject, but in the person of the Word, into whose unity it has been assumed, it obtains them as really communicated to itself. Which is so true that, unless the λόγος had assumed his humanity within the complex and, as it were, the unity of his νποστάσεως, it could certainly never have become a sharer or participant of the omnipotence and other idioms which do not go beyond that hypostasis of the Word; and if the λόγος were to desert it or withdraw his hypostasis from it, then he would at once also withdraw all his majesty, to such an extent does the human nature not have that majesty by itself without regard to the united deity.” (Libelli IV. etc. p. 47.)

The same: “But how does that infinite majesty dwell όλικώς in the humanity, since the finite is not capable of the infinite? (Resp.:) I am not unaware that some peddle this, which is an axiom of Aristotelian physics, as some sort of gem in the discussion of this matter. But those miserable men do not weigh that by this same axiom, if it ought to have validity in this negation, the union itself is enervated. For if the human nature of Christ could not become a participant of the omnipotence and other properties of the Word on account of their infinity, certainly for the same reason it could not be capable of the λόγος himself; since the λόγος is no less infinite than his majesty. Therefore, although in nature there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite, yet in this sublime mystery, which transcends and goes beyond universal nature, such a great, I will not say proportion, but ineffable union has been made between the finite and the infinite, that the finite nature of humanity

might truly become a participant of the infinite hypostasis of the Word and, at the same time, of this most infinite divine majesty. To this, the apostle D. [Paul] has long since excluded from this mystery that axiom which these men hold up like a Gordian knot, when he writes that in Christ dwells all the fullness of the deity bodily, i.e., as in His own proper body, showing, namely, that the infinite fullness of the deity can dwell in the finite humanity in the highest degree of presence and κοινωνία. —

The adversaries, however, object that this passage of the apostle is to be understood in such a way that nothing else is to be concluded from it than that Christ is full and perfect God. (Resp.:) It is certain that by these words the eternal deity is indeed necessarily presupposed and demonstrated from this by an ineffable consequence. But since mention is made of an indwelling, it would be most absurd to say that the fullness of the deity dwells in the deity of Christ.” (L. c. p. 50. sq.)

The same: “But if the communication of properties is admitted, will not the flesh be made equal to the deity? . . . (Resp.:) Although the λόγος communicated His own proper majesty to His humanity, yet this same one and only majesty does not relate itself in an equal manner to both natures, but is attributed to the divinity in a far more sublime way than to the humanity. . . λόγος by being, the human nature by having; λόγος essence, the human nature by gift; λόγος by nature, the human nature indeed by grace; λόγος by Himself, the human nature, however, not in itself (just as it does not subsist in itself), but in the person of the λόγος, into whose κοινωνία it is assumed, is omnipotent.” (L. c. p. 52. 53. 54.)
