The same: “There are those who reason thus: If properties become common to another thing, they are no longer proper; if, therefore, omnipotence becomes common to the humanity, how will it remain proper to the deity? (Resp.:) If omnipotence were so communicated to the assumed nature that it became an idiom of it, so that the humanity of Christ were omnipotent no less than the divinity, from itself and by the condition of its own proper nature, there is no doubt that it would cease to be a property of the deity alone, since it would have become a property of the humanity as well. Now, we truly say that omnipotence is a property of the divinity alone, and indeed in the fourth mode, perpetually and immutably, and that it never becomes an idiom of the human nature. For otherwise the flesh of Christ would be omnipotent by the property of its own proper nature, even without respect to the deity, nor would it have received omnipotence from elsewhere (namely, from the union with the λόγος), and it would be attributed to it in itself as in a subject, and from the nature of the subject by itself. . . nevertheless, that this omnipotence, really communicated to the humanity, has become an idiom of the humanity, so that it is now omnipotent of itself and by its own proper virtue, that we openly deny.” (L. c. p. 48. sq.)

Latin:

Speciati m omniscientiam Christo secundum humanam naturam communicatam esse, constat ex Joh. 3, 34., ubi dicitur, Christum, quem Deus, ut hominem ad homines, misit verba Dei loqui, addita ratione, quod

Deus huic spiritum sapientiae non ad mensuram dederit, quod idem est, ac sapientiam immensam seu infinitam ei secundum humanam naturam, in qua locutus est, esse datam. Conf. Joh. 2, 24. 25.

E. Hunnius: ,,Cum creverit sapientia (Luc. 2.), quomodo omniscientia (quae incrementi expers est) Christo, qua homo est, tributa dicitur? — Verissimum est, quod.Lucas scribit, puerum Jesum sapientia crevisse, non simulate profecto, sed in rei veritate et, ut Lucas scribit, coram Deo et hominibus; unde Christus alibi profitetur, horam novissimi diei sibi in eo exinanitionis statu absconditam ignotamque fuisse. Quamvis enim jam inde a sua conceptione unctus sit spiritu scientiae, sapientiae et cognitionis sine mensura, adeo ut nunquam non in illo omnes thesauri sapientiae et scientiae essent reconditi: tamen q/uia sapientia illa non erat naturalis proprietas humanitatis nec ei tamquam subjecto inerat, fleri utique potuit, ut, tametsi humana natura, Christi semper maneret unita cum λόγφ omniscio, non absque ejusdem κοινωνίμ vera, tamen λόγος hanc suam propriam sapientiam, quae ipsius est idioma, non semper in humanitate exerceret, sed ejusdem usum sive usurpationem respectu humanitatis quasi retraheret sive, ut apostoli verbo utar, exinaniret.“ (Libell. IV. p. 70.)

Idem: ,,Sedquia omniscientiae communicationem in ipso conceptionis puncto factam asseris: quomodo in statu exinanitionis quaedam dicetur ignorasse, siquidem et communicatio omniscientiae ignorantiam secludit et ignorantia vicissim elidit omniscientiam? — Humanitas omniscium λόγον sibi reali κοινωνία habuit unitum actu primo, licet actu secundo Christus qua homo tum non sciret aut nosset omnia. . . Quemadmodum etiam philosophus quispiam habitu scientiae in somno quoque informatus est et eruditionem cognitionemque suam dormiens etiam retinet actu primo, utcunque nihil actu secundo contempletur aut ratiocinetur. Sic ergo in Christo homine erant omnes thesauri sapientiae et scientiae, sed latebant quasi absconditi, ut apostolus inquit.“ (L. c. p. 72. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Licet omniscientia in deitate sit actus purissimus, in humanitate tamen Christi agnoscunt orthodoxi theologi actum primum et secundum. Proinde Calvinistarum et Jesuitarum argutatio est vana: Si Christo juxta carnem in unione hypostatica vere data est majestas omnisapientiae divinae, ergo illam statirn et semper exseruit et omnia actu secundo scivit.“ (L. c. q. 12. f. 248.)

Idem: ,,Etiam tunc, cum cresceret sapientia habituali homo Christus Jesus, erat πλψοϋμενος, plenus sapientia. Luc. 2, 40. et 52. Alia itaque fuit sapientia in Christo secundum humanam naturam, qua plenus fuit statim a primo conceptionis momento, sc. divina et infinita, per et propter unionem hypostaticam, et alia, in qua crescere potuit, quaeque augmentum admisit, nempe humana et finita. Patrum quidem sententia haec fuit de profectu Christi, quod videl. a primo hic conceptionis puncto sapientiam divinam per aetatis tamen incrementa, ob όονλον μορφήν sponte susceptam, paulatim hominibus manifestaverit. . . Sic etiam quidam recentiorum orthodoxorum statuunt, Christum juxta carnem profecisse quoque scientia divina et infinita, sci. ratione usurpationis.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 11. f. 256.)

Kromayerus: ״Respondemus: Christum sapientia crevisse non infinita, per unionem personalem communicata, verum habituali et experimentali. Praeter dona enim infinita in Christo, secundum h. n. spectato, etiam finita fuerunt.“ (Theol. posit.pol. I, 245.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,, An tit hesis: 1. Agnoetarum veterum, ubi observandum, Agnoetas fuisse olim et Arianos et Nestorianos, et aliquos etiam Eutychianos. . . Tribuerunt autem Agnoetäe veteres Christo PART. III. CAP. H. SECTIO I.

homini ignorantiam perpetuam aliquarum rerum, inprimis diei novissimi, sine respectu aut discrimine status exinanitionis et exaltationis. . . Sive docebant, Christum secundum humanam naturam in gloria sua non scire omnia. Vid. Nicephorum lib. 18. Hist. Eccles. c. 50. Damnati sunt in synodo Constantinopol. VI. act. 11. Caeterum haeresiographorum vel etiam aliorum scriptorum ecclesiast. saeculi 2. et 3. nemo Agnoetarum disertam mentionem facit. . .

2. Calvinianorum, qui 1.) negant, humanae. Christi naturae communicatam esse omniscientiam τον λόγον eandemque esse vere omnisciam. . . 2.) Contendunt, solam scientiam et sapientiam quandam supernaturalem Christo secundum humanam naturam convenire, quam omnium angelorum et hominum sapientia superiorem et incomprehensibilem quidem dicunt, at creatam solum... 3.) Asserunt, Christum ratione humanae naturae etiam in statu exaltationis quaedam ignorare. . .

3. Pontificiorum, qui 1.) geheraliter nebant communicationem divinorum idiomatum, unde recte colligitur, eos etiam negare, communicatam esse naturae assumptae divinam omniscientiam. . . 2.) in specie Becanus. . .

4. Socinianorum, qui negant, Christum inde a nativitate sua perfectam scientiam habuisse, quodque ejusmodi scientia in infantem non cadat.“ (L. c. f. 240. sq.)

Omnipotentiam quoque eidem communicatam probat locus Joh. 5, 19., ubi vis faciendi omnia, quae Pater fecit, Filio m tempore data dicitur. Et seq. v. 21. et 28. peculiariter potentia vivificandi homines, partim spiritualiter, partim corporaliter mortuos, ei tribuitur. Eodem quoque spectat, quod Matth. 28, 18. dicitur, datam esse Christo πάσαν έξυυσίαν in coelo et in terra; quod quamvis formaliter denotat summum jus, auctoritatem et potestatem omnem agendi, qua alia superior non datur, quemadmodum tamen potestatem eam Christus exercere non potest secundum humanam naturam, nisi omnipotentia eidem sit data atque in ea et per eam sese exserat, ita hanc quoque humanae Christi naturae communicatam esse, recte intelligitur; quanquam et alias Ιξουσία ipsam δυναμιν aut vim effectivam denotare soleat.

E. Hunnius: ,,Humanitas Christi, sicut non in se ipsa subsistit, sed in persona Verbi, sic illa quoque idiomata non in semetipsa, velut in subjecto, habet, sed in persona Verbi, in cujus unitatem assumpta est, realiter ea sibi communicata obtinet. Quod adeo verum est,’ ut, nisi λόγος suam humanitatem intra complexum quasi unitatemque suae νποστάσεως assumpsisset, nunquam profecto omnipotentiae caeterorumque idiomatum, quae hypostasin illam Verbi non egrediuntur, consors sive particeps illa fieri potuisset; et si eam desereret λόγος aut suam hypostasin illi subtraheret, tum una quoque suam majestatem omnem subduceret, usque adeo humana natura majestatem illam non habet per sese sine unitae deitatis respectu.“ (Libelli IV. etc. p. 47.)

Idem: ,,Quomodo vero infinita illa majestas inhabitat όλικώς in humanitate, cum finitum non sit infiniti capax? (Resp.:) Non ignoro, quosdam hoc, quod Aristotelis est axioma physicum, pro gemma, nescio qua, in hujus negotii disceptatione venditare. Sed miseri illi homines non expendunt, eodem hoc axiomate, si in hoc negatio valere debeat, unionem ipsam enervari. Si enim humana natura Christi non potuit particeps fleri omnipotentiae caeterarumque proprietatum Verbi propter illarum infinitatem, certe propter eandem causam neque ipsius λόγον potuit esse capax; siquidem λόγος non minus, quam sua majestas, est infinitus. Proinde, etsi in natura inter finitum et infinitum nulla proportio sit, in hoc tamen sublimi mysterio, quod universam naturarp transscendit ac supergreditur, tanta est facta inter finitum et infinitum, non dicam proportio, sed ineffabilis unio, ut finita humanitatis natura

vere particeps evaderet infinitae hypostaseos Verbi atque simul infinitissimae hujus majestatis divinae. Ad haec illud axioma, quod isti homines ceu Gordium nodum obtendunt, D. apostolus jam pridem ex hoc mysterio seclusit, cum scribit, in Christo inhabitare omnem plenitudinem deitatis corporaliter, h. e., tanquam in proprio ipsius corpore, ostendens sc., infinitam deitatis plenitudinem in finita humanitate summo praesentiae et κοινωνίας gradu habitare posse. —

Excipiunt autem adversarii, hunc locum apostoli sic accipiendum,׳ ut nihil aliud hinc coneludendum sit, quam, Christum plenum perfectumque Deum esse. (Resp.:) His verbis aeternam quidem deitatem necessario praesupponi atque per ineffabilem consequentiam hinc demonstrari, certum est. Quia autem inhabitationis flt mentio, absurdissimum fuerit, dicere, plenitudinem deitatis in deitate Christi habitare.“ (L. c. p. 50. sq.)

Idem: ״At si admittatur proprietatum communicatio, nonne caro יexaequabitur deitati? . . . (Resp.:) Quanquam λόγος suae humanitati propriam suam majestatem communicavit, tamen haec ipsa una eademque majestas non aequali modo sese habet ad utramque naturam, sed longe sublimiore modo divinitati tribuitur, quam humanitati.. . Aόγος essendo, humana natura habendo; λόγος ουσία, 11. Ch. η. εξονσί$', λόγος per naturam, humana vero natura per gratiam; λόγος se ipso, humana autem natura non in seipsa (sicut nec subsistit in seipsa), sed in persona τον λόγον, in cuius κοινωνίαν assumitur, est omnipotens.“ (L. c. p. 52. 53. 54.)

Idem: ״Sunt, qui sic ratiocinentur: Propria, si alteri rei communia evadant, non esse amplius propria; si igitur omnipotentia communis evadit humanitati, quomodo propria manebit deitatis? (Resp.:) Si omnipotentia sic communicaretur naturae assumtae, ut hujus idioma evaderet, ita ut Christi humanitas non minus, quam divinitas, ex se suaeque propriae naturae conditione omnipotens esset, dubium nullum est, quin solius deitatis proprietas esse desineret, giquidem etiam humanitatis facta esset proprietas. Jam vere omnipotentiam proprietatem esse dicimus solius divinitatis, et quidem in quarto modo, perpetuo et immutabiliter, nec unquam fleri humanae naturae idioma. Alias enim caro Christi.ex proprietate suae propriae naturae esset omnipotens, etiam sine deitatis respectu, nec omnipotentiam accepisset aliunde (nempe ex unione cum λόγφ), eamque 111 semetipsa velut in subjecto, eique ex natura subjecti per sese attribuatur, . . . attamen י quod omnipotentia illa, humanitati communicata realiter, idioma humanitatis facta sit, ut jam ex sese suaque virtute propria *omnipotens sit, id aperte inficiamur.“ (L. c. p. 48. sq.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who one and all deny that divine omnipotence has been truly and really communicated to the human nature. . . The Palatine Confession p. 205 asserts: ‘Not the human nature of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, but the man Christ according to His divine nature is omnipotent.’ The Calvinists, however, are accustomed to attribute to the human nature of Christ only a created power or virtue, which is less than omnipotence and yet greater in strength and virtue than all angels and men. . . 2. Of the Papists, who likewise deny that divine omnipotence has been communicated to Christ as man. Thus Bellarmine, lib. III. de Christo c. 16: ‘The power,’ he says, ‘conferred upon the humanity of Christ is not absolutely omnipotence.’” (L. c. q. 11. f. 240. sq.)

The same: “This power of vivifying, as it is divine, so it also extends itself to a threefold vivification: one pertains to the kingdom of power and is the bestowal of life, which occurs through the union of soul and body, of which Acts 17:28 speaks, to which pertains bodily resurrection, both particular and universal, John 5:28, 29; the second looks to the kingdom of grace and is the giving of spiritual life or grace, of which John 5:21 treats; the third, however, PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

belongs to the kingdom of glory, by which He transfers the resurrected into eternal life, 1 Cor. 15:22. This divine power of vivifying is attributed to the flesh of Christ: 1. not in the abstract, in itself and through itself; 2. not formally and subjectively through the effusion of vivifying life into the flesh; but 3. by union, because that vivifying virtue, by virtue of the personal union, was truly and really communicated to the flesh of Christ; and 4. because the divine nature in the flesh, with it and through it, exerts the operation of vivifying, as if operating and effecting life through an ἐνχμηστον [in-fused/in-wrought] organ, just as heated iron, by reason of the union, both has the power of burning and also burns.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 13. f. 258.)

The same: “Antithesis: ... 2. Of the Calvinists, such as Theod. Beza; in coll. Mompelg. p. 238, he says that the power of vivifying is so proper to the deity that it can be communicated neither to the flesh of Christ nor to any creature, unless it be converted into the deity... 3. Of the Jesuits, who, just as they deny in general that divine idioms were really communicated to the assumed humanity through the personal union, so in particular they infect the power given to the man Christ of being θαυματουργικήν [miracle-working], ζωοποιητικήν [life-giving], καθαρκτικήν [cleansing], κριτικήν [judging], etc. Bellarmine, lib. III. de Christo c. 16, says: ‘Christ, as man, forgave sins as an instrument of the divinity, which does not require infinite virtue.’” (L. c. q. 13. f. 259.)

Zwingli: “When Christ says: My flesh is truly food, the flesh is properly of the human nature in Him; yet by commutation, in this place, it is put for the divine nature.” (Exegesis eucharistiae negotii. Opp. I, 1. f. 350. sq.)

Indeed, we also believe that omnipresence was communicated to the human nature of Christ, according to that which Christ Himself says in Matt. 28:20: Behold I (to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth, v. 18, and who now have sent ministers to teach and baptize, v. 19) am (according to the same nature according to which all power is given to me) with you (wherever you are to be in this world) all the days. We believe, indeed, that it is declared by this testimony of Scripture that Christ, according to that assumed nature of His, and with it, can be present, and indeed is present, wherever He wills; but especially we hold that He is present to His church on earth as mediator, head, king, and high priest; which are the words of the Solid Declaration of the F. C., article VIII, p. 783, cf. n. IV, and they manifestly describe that omnipresence, not as absolute, for a bare, non-distanced proximity to all creatures without efficacious operation, but as modified, or joined with efficacious operation, and according to the requirement of that universal dominion which Christ exercises according to both natures; just as the Electoral Saxon theologians also declared in their Decis. Solida and its Apology. Cf. b. Musaeus, Ausführl. Erklärung, Q. LVI. sqq. p. 542. sqq.

Quenstedtius: “The presence of the human body of Christ resulting from the property of the body, whether ψυχικόν [natural/soulish] or glorified, does not come into controversy here. We concede that the body of Christ, by the act of nature, was in a physical place through external circumscription from its very first conception until the resurrection, namely, for as long as it was a ψυχικόν body. We also concede that after the resurrection and ascension into the heavens, that same body, as it is a glorified body, is not everywhere by the act of nature, but determinately in its own heavenly που [place], not indeed circumscriptively, but definitively, just as in their own order and degree other glorious bodies are in their own που. But here the question is solely: whether the human nature of Christ, now raised to the right hand of the divine majesty, in this very glorious state of exaltation at the right hand of God the Father, is omnipresently present to all creatures in the universe. And thus the question is not whether this divine presence...”

does not] seek from Christ, as He is man, [this] from the property of the human nature; for this we also deny; but whether it is to be attributed to Him through and on account of the personal union, insofar as this has been inseparably joined with the exaltation of the humanity to the right hand of God the Father. Thus, therefore, the former modes of presence are to be posited, so that the infinite presence in the assumed flesh is not denied. ... Distinguish, therefore, between κτῆσις and χρῆσις; as regards κτῆσις, the human nature of Christ indeed obtained the majesty of omnipresence through and on account of the personal union, even in the very state of exinanition. But as for χρῆσις and its plenary use, concerning the presence of incessant operation, the human nature was finally admitted [to this] after the exaltation through the session at the right hand of God.” (L. c. q. 14. f. 267.)

E. Hunnius: “Therefore, do you think that the λόγος is nowhere outside the assumed humanity? — The Zwinglians indeed write that the λόγος is outside His flesh in the world; nay, they think that the λόγος is in only one place in the humanity, where, to be sure, it is by the property of essence; but besides that one place, He is in innumerable others outside it. But this opinion utterly evacuates that ineffable mystery of the hypostatic union, dissolves the union, and tears apart and severs the natures—which, apart from the consideration of place, are ἀδιαστάτως united—through and on account of the spaces of places. Which is most solidly demonstrated by this argument: For if the λόγος is said to be elsewhere outside His flesh, then it must necessarily be conceded that the λόγος, whole in His entire hypostasis, is outside it (for He does not have a part outside a part), so that He is in it by some part of Himself, but partly outside it. But if the whole λόγος is constituted outside the flesh by His whole hypostasis, how will the incarnation of the λόγος and the personal union not be denied, if the person of the Word is said to be as much outside the flesh as He is outside Peter or any other man? Consequently, it would be a certain παράστασις rather than a hypostatic union or incarnation. Furthermore, this also would follow, that that union is terminated in one place only. For because the personal union is defined by the indwelling of the fullness of the deity of the λόγος in the human nature, certainly, if He dwells in it in only that one place (where the human nature of Christ is naturally), but is outside it in the other innumerable places, it becomes manifest that in all other places the union is dissolved, and therefore that most divine union is terminated by the space of only this one place. This also would follow, that as the human nature progresses from one place to another, the union itself would also be changed from time to time according to those diverse places; for where the λόγος does not dwell in the flesh, there He is not united to it, since the union is not defined by the existence of the λόγος outside the humanity (as the Zwinglians say the λόγος is outside the flesh in all the remaining infinite places where the humanity is not by the property of its essence), but is defined by the hypostatic indwelling in the flesh.” (Libelli IV. de persona etc. p. 81. sq.)

Gesnerus: “Above and outside all creatures there is nothing but God alone. But this humanity is above and outside all creatures. Therefore, it is necessary that it be where God is. This is concluded by an infallible consequence. Naturally, however, it cannot be God; but because it reaches up to and adheres to the essential God Himself above and outside all creatures, therefore it is necessary that that human nature be present at the very least... in all places also where God is. By this argument, those voices of the Greek church are especially urged, that the union was made ἀχωρίστως, ἀδιαστάτως, ἀδιασπάστως.” (Orthodox. confess. de persona et officio Salvatoris. 1595. p. 176.)

Dannhauerus: “As the threefold kingdom of Christ, so a triple presence. I. Omnipresence in the kingdom of power; not physical, local, diffused, expanded, divisible, monstrous, but divine—that very filling of heaven and earth by which we delineated the omnipresence of God above. The Holy Scriptures vindicate this for Christ according to His human nature in the classic oracle Eph. 4:10: ‘Christ ascended far above all the heavens, that He might fill all things.’” *) *) Since there is no divine operation in imaginary spaces outside the world, no presence is to be posited there either, according to the style of Scripture; he involves himself in a contradiction who would have God present in imaginary spaces, which are absolutely nothing. (Dannh.) PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I. ...

but he filled [all things] according to his humanity, just as he ascended according to it. This is sufficiently indicated by the final particle ‘ut’ (in order that); for imagine that this is said of the deity, and such an abortion will emerge from it: Christ ascended into the heavens with his human nature for this end, that he might fill all things with his deity; as if he had needed the ascension in order that the nature by which he had already filled all things before the ascension might fill all things! Where it is evident that by τα πάντα all creatures are to be understood, from Paul’s absolute mode of speaking without restriction: from the partition of των πάντων in v. 11, and the explanation in Eph. 1:22, 23: πάντα εν πᾶσι. Moreover, this πανπλήρωσις is: 1. Not a seal of a pilgrimage, because this happened immediately after the resurrection; the forty days were not of a journey, but of a singular οικονομία (economy). 2. Not a consummation of prophecies, because these are not πάντα..., nor did he fulfill all prophecies through the ascension, for the complement of the return for judgment still remains. Not 3. a giver of gifts precisely, from which the gifts of the Church [proceed]; for neither are τά πάντα the gifts of the Holy Spirit, nor are τα πάντα filled by the gifts of the Spirit. Not 4. successive, a perambulator of all parts of the world; for this belongs even to the angels, nay, even to Satan (Job 1:7)... Finally, 5. not merely effective, because it is a filling opposed to the previous humiliation; but a divine filling described by the word in Jer. 23:24, which is the very omnipresence defined above. Whence the unanswerable argument: A nature that fills all things is omnipresent; the human nature of Christ is a filler of all things; therefore, it is Omnipresent. The same omnipresence is urged by the consequence from the session at the right hand... Every που (place) of the divine right hand is a παν (all) of omnipresence; the που of the human nature placed upon the divine throne is the που of the divine right hand; therefore, the που of the human nature is omnipresent. The same omnipresence, as an official property constituted in action, is required by the nature of the office administered according to both natures, as well the royal..., as the mediatorial..., and finally the judicial office... II. Gracious presence in the kingdom of grace, consequently solace-flowing, which it is evident belongs to Christ even as man, from power, will, and deed. He can present his flesh to us, because he is omnipotent; he wills to, because he promised it...; finally, he actually performed this gracious presence by cooperation (Mark 16:20) and by the apparitions noted in sacred history (Acts 7:56; 9:27; Rev. 1:13)... III. Glorious presence, described 1. on our part by ‘being with Christ,’ and that without any turning away of the divine face forever (1 Thess. 4:17), while we are pilgrims from the Lord in this life (2 Cor. 5:7)...; by being in the hand of God (Wisd. 3:1)... 2. On the part of Christ by dwelling with the saints and over them; by being with us (Rev. 7:17; 21:3)...; by finally being all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). (Hodosoph. Phaenom. VIII. p. 395—404.)

Latin:

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Calvinianorum, qui äd unum omnes negant, omnipotentiam divinam humanae naturae vere et realiter communicatam esse. . . Confessio Palatina p. 205. asserit: ,Non humanam naturam Eilii Dei D. N. J. C., sed hominem Christum juxta divinam suam naturam omnipotentem esse. ‘ Tribuere autem solent Calviniani humanae naturae Christi tantum potentiam seu virtutem creatam, quae minor sit omnipotentia et major tamen robore et virtute omnium angelorum et hominum. . . 2. Pontificiorum, Christo homini communi catam esse omnipotentiam divinam, itidem negantium. Ita Bellarminus lib. III. de Christo c. 16.: ,Potentia‘, inquit, ,collata Christi humanitati non est absolute omnipotentia.‘“ (L. c. q. 11. f. 240. sq.)

Idem: ״Vis vivificandi haec, ut divina est, ita etiam ad triplicem vivificationem se porrigit: una ad regnum potentiae pertinet et est vitae, quäe per unionem «animae et corporis fit, largitio, de qua Act. 17, 28., ad quäm corporalis resurrectio pertinet, tam particularis, quam universalis, Joh. 5, 28. 29.; altera ad regnum gratiae spectat et est datio vitae spiritualis seu gratiae, de qua Joh. 5, 21. agitur; tertia vero PART. III. CAP. H. SECTIO I.

ad gloriae regnum pertinet, qua resuscitatos transfert in vitam aeternam, 1 Cor. 15, 22. Vis haec vivificandi divina tribuitur cami Christi 1. non in abstracto in se et per se, 2. non formaliter et subjective per effusionem vitae vivificantis in carnem, sed 3. unione, quia virtus ista viviflcatrix vi unionis personalis vere et realiter carni Christi communicata est, et 4. quia divina natura in carne, cum illa et per illam operationem vivificandi exserit, tanquam per orgauon ενχμηστον operans et efflciens vitam, sicut ferrum ignitum ratione unionis et habet vim urendi et etiam urit.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 13. f. 258.)

Idem: ״Antithesis: ... 2. Calvinianomm, ut Theod. Bezae; in coli. Mompelg. p. 238. vim vivificandi ita dicit propriam esse deitatis, ut neque carni Christi, neque ulli creaturae communicari possit, nisi in deitatem convertatur. . . 3. Jesuitarum, qui, ut in genere negant, asshmptae humanitati per unionem personalem realiter communicata esse divina idiomata, ita in specie inficiantur datam Christo homini potestatem dανμητουργικήν, ζωοποιητικήν, κα&αρκτικήν, κριτικήν etc. Bellarminus lib. III. de Christo c. 16. ait: ,Christus, ut homo, remittebat peccata ut instrumentum divinitatis, quod non requirit infinitam virtutem.‘“ (L. c. q. 13. f. 259.)

Zwinglius: ,,Cum Christus ait: caro mea vere est cibus, caro proprie est humanae in illo naturae; attamen per commutationem hoc loco pro divina ponitur natura.“(Exegesis eucharistiae negotii. Opp. I, 1. f. 350. sq.)

Imo vero et omnipraesentiam humanae Christi naturae communicatam credimus, juxta illud, guod Christus ipse Matth. 28, 20. dicit: Ecce eqo (cui data est omnis potestas in coelo et in terra, v. 18., quique nunc misi ministros ad docendum et baptizandum, v. 19.) sum (secundum eandem naturam, secundum quam mihi data est omnis potestas) vobiscum (ubicunque in hoc mundo futuri estis) omnibus diebus. Credimus vero, hoe Scripturae testimonio declarari, quod Christus secundum illam suam assumtam naturam, et cum ea, praesens esse possit, et quidem praesens sit, ub\r cunque velit; praesertim vero sentimus, eum ecclesiae suae in terris, ut mediatorem, caput, regem et summum sacerdotem praesentem esse; quae sunt verba Solidae Decl. F. C. artic. VIII. p. 783., conf. η. IV., ac manifeste describunt omnipraesentiam illam, non ut absolutam, pro nuda indistante propinquitate ad omnes creaturas, absque efficaci operatione, sed tanquam modificatam, seu cum efficaci operatione conjunctam, et pro exigentia dominii illius universalis, quod Christus secundum utramque naturam exercet; prout etiam theologi electorales Saxonici in sua Decis. Solida ejusque Apologia declararunt. Conf. b. Musaei Ausfiihrl. Erklärung, Q. LVI. sqq. p. 542. sqq.

Quenstedtius: ,,Non venit hic in controversiam praesentia humana corporis Christi ex proprietate corporis, sive ψυχικόν sive glorificati, resultans. Concedimus, corpus Christi actu naturae per circumscriptionem exteriorem fuisse in loco physico a prima inde conceptione usque ad resurrectionem, nempe tam diu, quarndiu fuit corpus ψυχικόν. Concedimus quoque, quod post resurrectionem et ascensionem in coelos illud ipsum, ut est glorificatum corpus, actu naturae non sit ubique, sed determinate in που suo coelesti, non quidem circumscriptive, sed definitive, sicut in suo ordine et gradu alia corpora gloriosa definitive in ποϋ suo sunt. Sed hic unice quaeritur: an humana natura Christi jam ad dextram majestatis divinae evecta in hoc ipso glorioso exaltationis ad dextram Dei Patris statu omnibus in universum creaturis omnipraesenter praesit. Adeoque non quaeritur, an praesentia haec divina com

petat Christo, qua homo est, ex naturae humanae proprietate; hoc namque et nos negamus; sed an ei tribuenda sit per et propter unionem personalem, prout haec cum exaltatione humanitatis ad dextram Dei Patris indistracte copulata est. Ita ergo priores praesentiae modi ponendi, ut non negetur infinita in assumpta carne praesentia. . . Dist. ergo inter κτήσιν et χρήσιν; quoad κτήσιν quidem obtinuit humana Christi natura majestatem omnipraesentiae per et propter unionem personalem ·etiam in ipso exinanitionis statu. Quantum vero ad χρήσιν ac plenarium ·ejus usum, concernentem praesentiam operationis incessantis, admissa demum natura humana est post exaltationem per sessionem ad dextram Dei.“ (L. c. q. 14. f. 267.)

E. Hunnius: ,,Ergo censes, λόγον nullibi esse extra assumptam humanitatem? — Zwingliani quidem scribunt, λόγον extra suam carnem esse in terris; imo sentiunt, λόγον uno tantummodo in loco esse in humanitate, ubi nimirum ea est proprietate essentiae; praeter illum unieum locum vero in innumeris aliis esse extra illam. Sed haec opinio mysterium ineffabile illud unionis hypostaticae penitus evacuat, unionem solvit et naturas, extra loci considerationem άδιαστάτως unitas, per et propter locorum spatia ab invicem distrahit ac divellit. Quod hoc argumento quam solidissime demonstratur: Si enim λόγος alibi dicatur esse extra suam carnem, tum hoc necessario concedatur oportet, quod λόγος totus tota sua hypostasi sit extra eam (partem enim extra partem non.habet), ut aliqua sui parte sit in ea, partim vero extra eam. At si totus λόγος hypostasi sua tota extra carnem constituatur, quomodo non incarnatio τον λόγον et unio personalis negabitur, si persona Verbi tam vocatur tota esse extra carnem, quam extra Petrum, aut alium quemvis Hominem? proinde παράστασις potius quaedam fuerit, quam hypostatica unio seu incarnatio? Quin et hoc sequetur, ut uno du 11 taxat loco unio illa sit terminata. Nam quia unio personalis inhabitatione plenitudinis deitatis τον λόγον in humana natura definitur, certe, si uno duntaxat loco illo (ubi natura Christi humana est naturaliter) in illa habitat, in caeteris autem locis innumeris extra eam est, palam fit, in caeteris locis omnibus unionem esse solutam et proinde divinissimam illam unionem unius tantum istius loci spatio terminatam esse. Sequeretur hoc quoque, ut progrediente humana natura ex uno loco in alterum ipsa quoque unio secundum illa loca diversa subinde mutaretur; nam ubi non inhabitat λόγος in carne, ibi neque illi unitus est, siquidem unio non definitur existentia τον λόγον extra humanitatem (sicut Zwingliani λόγον in omnibus reliquis infinitis locis, quibus humanitas non est proprietate suae essentiae, extra carnem esse dicunt), sed definitur hypostatica inhabitatione in carne.“ (Libelli IV. de persona etc. p. 81. sq.)

Gesnerus: ,,Supra et extra omnes creaturas nihil est, quam solus Deus. Haec autem humanitas est supra et extra omnes creaturas. Ergo neeesse est, eam esse, ubi Deus est. Hoc infallibili consequentia conficitur. Naturaliter autem non potest esse Deus; quia vero supra et extra omnes creaturas ad ipsum usque essentialem Deum pertingit eique adhaeret, ideo oportet illam humanam naturam ad minimum. . . in omnibus etiam locis praesto adesse, ubi Deus est. Hoc argumento imprimis urgentur illae voces Graecae ecclesiae, quod unio facta sit άχωρίστως, άδιαστάτως, άδιασπάστως(Orthodox, confess. de persona et officio Salvatoris. 1595. p. 176.)

Dannhauerus: ״Ut tergeminum Christi regnum, ita triplex praesentia. I. Omnipraesentia in regno potentiae; non physica, localis, diffusa, expansa, sectilis, monstrosa, sed divina, illa ipsa impletio coeli et terrae, qua Dei omnipraesentiam supra delineavimus. Hanc Christo secundum humanam naturam vindicat S. S. in classico oraculo Ephes. 4, 10.: ,Christus ascendit super omnes coelos, ut omnia impleret‘; *) *) Cum in spatiis imaginariis extra mundum nulla sit divina operatio, ibi quoque nulla praesentia juxta Scripturae stylum statuenda est; contradictioni sese implicat, qui Deum in spatiis imaginariis, quae absolute nihil sunt, praesentem esse voluit. (Dannh.) PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO I.

impleret autem secundum humanitatem, ut secundum quam ascendit. Id quod vox,ut‘ τελική satis innuit; finge enim, de deitate hoc dici, talis prodibit hinc abortus: Christus humana sua natura ascendit in coelos hoc fine, ut deitate omnia impleat; tanquam ascensione ideo opus habuisset, ut ea natura, qua jam ante ascensionem omnia implesset, omnia impleret I Ubi per τα πάντα omnes creaturas intelligi patet ex absoluta Pauli locutione sine restrictione: ex των πάντων partitione v. 11., explicatione Ephes. 1, 22. 23.: πάντα εν 7τάσι. Est autem haec πανπλήρωσις 1. non obsignatrix peregrinationis, quia haec illico post resurrectionem contigit; quadraginta dies non fuerunt itinerarii, sed singularis οικονομίας. 2. Non consummatrix vaticiniorum, quia haec non sunt πάντα. . ., nec per ascensionem omnia vaticinia implevit, restat enim adhuc complementum reditus ad judicium. Non 3. donatrix praecise, e qua dona ecclesiae; nam nec τά πάντα sunt dona Sp. Sancti, nec τα πάντα donis Spiritus implentur. Non 4. successiva, omnium mundi partium perambulatrix; nam haec etiam angelis, imo satanae Job. 1, 7. competit. . . Denique 5. non effectiva solum, quia est impletio exinanitioni superiori opposita; sed verbo impletio divina Jer. 23, 24. descripta, quae est ipsissima omnipraesentia supra definita. Unde argumentum άλντον: Natura impletrix omnium est omnipraesens; natura Christi humana est impletrix omnium; ergo Omnipraesens. Eandem omnipraesentiam urget consequentia e sessione ad dextram. . . Omne π ον dextrae divinae est παν omnipraesentiae; π ον humanae naturae in thronum divinum collocatae est που dextrae divinae; ergo 7τον humanae naturae est omnipraesens. . . Eandem omnipraesentiam, ut idiopia officiale in actione constitutum, requirit ratio offcii secundum utramque naturam administrati, cum regii. . ., tum mediatorii. . ., denique officii judiciarii. . . II. Praesentia gratiosa in regno gratiae, consequenter solatiflua, quam Christo etiam homini competere patet ex potentia, voluntate, facto. Potest carnem suam nobis praesentem sistere, quia omnipotens; vult, quia id promisit. ..; denique gratiosam, praesentiam etiam actu praestitit cooperatione Mare. 16, 20. et apparitionibus in historia sacra annotatis Act. 7, 56. 9, 27. Apoc. 1, 13. . . III. Praesentia gloriosa, descripta 1. ex parte nostri per,esse cum Christo‘, idque sine aversione faciei divinae semper (1 Thess. 4, 17.), dum in hac vita a Domino peregrinamur (2 Cor. 5, 7.). . .; per esse in manu Dei (Sap. 3, 1.). . . 2. Exparte Christi per habitare cum sanctis et super illos; per esse nobiscum (Apoc. 7, 17. 21, 3.). . .; per denique esse omnia in omnibus (1 Cor. 15, 28.).“ (Hodosoph. Phaenom. VIII. p. 395—404.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Scherzerus: “Since divine presence denotes ἀδιαστασίαν (indistance) partially,…

Scherzerus: “Since divine presence denotes ἀδιαστασίαν (indistance) partially, and operation besides indistance totally, Christ indeed emptied himself of the dominion, but retained the ἀδιαστασίαν. The foundation is that otherwise the personal union would have been dissolved. — They urge: Christ abdicated the χρήση (use) and retained its κτήσιν (possession). Resp.: Be it so. But truly, the χρήση cannot be absent except from a total presence, or one modified with respect to dominion alone; but not from a partial presence, which consists in substantial nearness alone. What? That in that partial presence the distinction between χρήση and κτήσιν (which pertains only to active attributes) finds no place at all? And what is it to abdicate the use of substantial nearness, and to retain the possession of nearness, and yet not be near?! I argue: Whoever possesses and retains nearness, he is altogether near.” (System, th. Loc. VIII. p. 224, 237.)

Luther: "Because our faith holds that Christ is God and man and the two natures are one Person, in such a way that the same Person cannot be divided, he can indeed manifest himself according to the bodily, comprehensible manner in whatever place he wills; as he did after the resurrection and will do on the Last Day. But beyond this manner, he can also use the other, incomprehensible manner, as we have proven from the Gospel at the tomb and..."

closed door. But since He is such a man who is supernaturally one person with God, and there is no God apart from this man, it must follow that He also is and may be, according to the third supernatural mode, everywhere that God is, and that all things are through and through full of Christ, even according to His humanity; not according to the first bodily, circumscribed mode, but according to the supernatural divine mode.”*) (Confession Concerning the Supper. An. 1528. XX, 1190.)

Hutterus: “Regarding Dr. Martin Chemnitz, an incomparable theologian, the matter is settled. And Hospinian is very much mistaken, who affirms—based on the opinion of the Helmstedt theologians—that he denied or at least disapproved of a general omnipresence (but let the dream of that absolute, gross, physical, and local ubiquity be far from us). . . And lest we be too prolix in this place, we shall produce one passage out of many, and indeed one taken from the letter of Dr. Chemnitz written to Hesse, . . . where, among other things, he has this: ‘But if anyone should wish to inquire further about other creatures outside the Church of God, we know in general that all things have been put under the feet of Christ, even according to His assumed human nature, that all things are subject to His power, that all things are present to Him, and that He is present and rules over all things. But when one wishes to dispute about wood, stone, or other unclean places and matters, it is the safest way that such questions be set aside and such disputations be abolished, because they do not edify, but give cause for prolixity and offensive thoughts, and we do not sufficiently or perfectly understand the mystery of the personal union in Christ in this life; only that we hold in general to the foundation that no creature, place, spot, or time separates the two natures in the person of Christ from one another or leaves them behind, but everywhere He is, He has the same personally or according to the manner of the personal union in and with Himself. When one remains in and with such simplicity, I consider it to be the safest and simplest, and also edifying to the Church.’ You have, Hospinian, the mind and confession of the blessed Chemnitz, sufficiently clear; if you should further say that he denied the general ubiquity of Christ according to the assumed humanity among all creatures, you will truly seem to me to have lost all shame and conscience.” (Conc. concors, p. 1212 sqq.)

Huelsemannus: “Ubiquity, if it is that which depends on the immensity of God, was not communicated to the flesh of Christ, but omnipresence, which is voluntary even in God, upon the supposition of created things.” (Extens. Breviarii. Ed. 3, p. 94.)

Brentius: “They have invented a new and prodigious term, ‘ubiquity,’ so that they might more easily impose upon the ignorant and those unacquainted with the matter, and persuade them that we have also devised a new and prodigious dogma, that the body of Christ geometrically extends and diffuses itself into all places like a leather strap.” (De personali unione duarum natur. in Christo. Witeb. 1578. pref.)

Kromayerus: “They object absurdities to us; that it would follow from this that Christ is in all sewers, chamber pots, gallows, etc. But we respond *κατ’ ἔνστασιν*: thus, not even God Himself would be present to all creatures, because one would have to fear that He might be in all sewers, gallows, and chamber pots. Furthermore, one must distinguish between being *in* and being *present to* all creatures. Christ is present to all creatures—even those who are situated in sordid places, who are raised upon the gallows, who labor in flames and rivers—rather than being *in* them. If, however, the phrase of ‘being in’ is retained, it should be understood without any *σύμμειξις* with creatures.” (Theol. posit. pol. I, 247.) *)

Scherzerus: “It is evident that the blessed Feurbornius (in *Κένωσις* gr. Sect. I. fol. 9) says that the words of Luther, where ‘all things’ are said to be ‘full of Christ,’ speak of the state of humiliation according to Ephesians 1:4.” (Syst. th. loc. 8, p. 238.)

PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I. Huelsemannus: "Just as the essence of God is not defiled by material filth, even if it is most correctly said to be present in hell, in a sewer, or in a brothel, by virtue of the general statements in Jer. 23:23–24, Ps. 139:7–8, etc., Acts 17:27–28, so, if there existed such testimonies that extended the presence of the flesh of Christ as widely as the presence of the divine essence is extended, there would be nothing to fear from defilement or contamination by the presence of foul things, any more than there would be any torture or burning of the body of Christ to be feared if it pleased Him to station that presence in the midst of infernal flames." (Vindiciae S. S. Art. 20, p. 75.) cf. Luther, *De Servo Arbitrio*, XVIII, 2095 sqq. See above, Vol. II, p. 23.

Kromayerus: "Against omnipresence they object: 1. The ascension into heaven. But we respond that Christ, by His ascension, did not withdraw from us all presence, but only His visible conversation, just as He promises, when about to ascend into heaven, that He would be with us even unto the consummation of the age... Therefore, that departure to the Father is explained by non-vision in John 16:10. Nor is the heaven into which Christ ascended understood as that empyrean heaven, which they call most remote from us by intervals of space, placed above the starry heaven, but the πον of the blessed, where it is not for us to inquire. Certainly, concerning the angels who minister to the little ones on earth, it is said in Matthew 18:10 that they always behold the face of the heavenly Father.

2. They object the session at the right hand of the Father. But with Luther we immediately invert this argument: Indeed, because Christ according to His human nature sat down at the right hand of the Father, therefore He is present to us on earth. For by the session at the right hand of God, not a situation or placement of Christ in a certain place is understood, but the omnipotent and omnipresent government of this whole universe. As for our syllogism, which the Sacramentarians so greatly agitate: 'The right hand of God is everywhere. Christ according to His human nature sits at the right hand of God. Therefore, Christ according to His human nature is everywhere,' it is cryptic or an argumentative discourse, in which the proof of the major premise itself is placed in the position of the premise. Thus, however, it would be complete: 'He who sits at the right hand of God is everywhere, because the right hand is everywhere. Christ according to His human nature sits at the right hand of God. Therefore.'

3. They object the return to judgment. But we respond that Christ will return to judgment as regards visible presence. 'Every eye will see Him, and those who pierced Him,' Revelation 1:7. Whence this return is explained by επιφάνεια or appearance in Titus 2:13.

4. They object that the human nature of Christ is finite and circumscribed by its own dimensions. But we respond that this argument fights with phantoms, because we do not in any way posit the human nature of Christ as infinite, but finite, yet meanwhile, because of the personal union with the λόγος and the session at the right hand of God, we posit it as omnipresent. That gross, diffused, and expanded presence which the Calvinists falsely attribute to us, we execrate with our whole heart; meanwhile, following the guidance of Scripture, we believe that the human nature of Christ is present to all creatures by divine presence. That divine presence is described in Isaiah 40:16-17, that all creatures are like a point, subjected and exposed to it...

6. They object the passage in Matthew 26:11: 'Me you do not always have.' But we respond by distinguishing between the thing and the mode of the thing. Although Christ denies that He will be present to the apostles in the future in the way, namely, in which He could be affected by benefits, as was done at that time; yet He does not deny the presence itself, but rather promises it in Matthew 28, last verse.

7. They contend from philosophical principles that every body is in a place. But we respond by distinguishing between the phrases 'to be locatable' and 'to be in a place.' We indeed concede that every physical body is locatable, but not actually in a place, because the outermost body, whatever it may be, is not in a place, since it is not surrounded by another body, unless we wish to posit a progression to infinity. But place is the περιέχοντος πέρας ακίνητον πρώτον, that is, the first immovable limit of the container. If the body of Christ is always locatable and palpable in first act, it is not always in a place or palpated or seen in second act; as

After the ascension into heaven, He is subject neither to the intervals of places nor of times, as He was in the days of His flesh, when He was circumscribed by place, was locally in the womb of the Blessed Virgin, in the manger, on the cross, in the sepulcher, etc., and was measured by the articulations of time, as when Christ was eight days old, twelve years old, thirty years old...

Latin:

Scherzerus: ,,Cum praesentia divina partialiter άόιαστασίαν, totaliter praeter indistantiam simul operationem denotet, Christus dominio quidem se evacuavit, άόιαστασίαν vero retinuit. Fundamentum est, quia alias unio personalis fuisset dissoluta. — Urgent: Christus abdicavit se χρήση et retinuit ejus κτήσιν. Resp.: Sit ita. At vero χρήσις non nisi a praesentia totali sive modificata respectu solius dominii abesse potest; non autem a praesentia partiali, quae in sola propinquitate substantiali consistit. Quid? quod in praesentia illa partiali distinctio inter χρήσιν et κτήσιν (quae ad sola attributa ενεργητικά pertinet) nequaquam locum inveniat. Et quid est abdicare se usu propinquitatis substantialis, et retinere possessionem propinquitatis, nec tamen esse propinquum?! Arguo: Quicunque possidet et retinet propinquitatem, ille omnino est propinquus.“ (System, th. Loc. VIII. p. 224. 237.)

Lutherus: ,,Weil unser Glaube hält, dass Christus Gott und Mensch ist und die zwo Naturen Eine Person ist, als dass dieselbige Person nicht mag zertrennet werden, so kann er freilich nach der leibchen, begreiflichen Weise sich erzeigen, an welchem Ort er will; wie er nach der Auferstehung thät und am jüngsten Tage thun wird. Aber über diese Weise kann er auch der andern unbegreiflichen Weise brauchen, wie wir aus dem Evangelio bewiesen haben am Grabe und ver

schlossener Thür. Nun er aber ein solcher Mensch ist, der übernatürlieh mit Gott Eine Person ist und ausser diesem Menschen kein Gott ist, so muss folgen, dass er auch nach der dritten übernatürlichen Weise sei und sein möge allenthalben, wo Gott ist, und alles durch und durch voll Christus sei, auch nach der Menschheit; nicht nach der ersten leiblichen begreiflichen Weise, sondern nach der übernatürlichen göttlichen Weise.“*) (Bekenntniss vom Abendmahl. An. 1528. XX, 1190.)

Hutterus: ,,De D. Martino Chemnitio, incomparabili theologo, res expedita est. Et quamplurimum fallitur Hospinianus, qui ex sententia Helmstadiensium, generalem (absit autem somnium de absoluta illa crassa, physica et locali ubiquitate) omnipraesentiam ipsum negasse vel certe improbasse, affirmat. . . Et ne hoc loco prolixiores simus, unum ex multis producemus locum, et quidem petitum ex epistola D. Chemnitii in Hassiam scripta, . . . ubi inter reliqua sic habet: ,Wenn aber jemand weiter fragen wöllte von andern Creaturen, ausser der Kirche Gottes, da wissen wir ingemein, dass Christo auch nach seiner angenommenen menschlichen Natur alles unter die Füsse getlian, alles seiner Gewalt untergeben, dass ihm alles gegenwärtig sei lind er gegenwärtig über alles regiert. Wann man aber disputiren wollte von Holz, Stein oder von andern unsaubern Orten und Händeln, so ist’s der sicherste Weg, dass solche Fragen eingestellt und solche Disputationes abgeschafft werden, weil sie nicht bauen, sondern zu Weitläuftigkeit und ärgerlichen Gedanken Ursach geben und wir das Geheimniss der persönlichen Vereinigung in Christo in diesem Leben nicht genugsam oder vollkömmlich verstehen; allein, dass wir ingemein den Grund behalten, dass keine Creatur, Ort, Stelle oder Zeit die beiden Naturen in der Person Christi von einander absondere oder hinter sich lasse, sondern allenthalben, wo er sei, dieselbe persönlich oder nach Art der persönlichen Vereinigung in und bei sich habe. Wann man in und bei solcher Einfalt bleibet, achte ich, sei es am sichersten und einfältigsten und auch der Kirche erbaulich.‘ Habes, Hospiniane, mentem et confessionem b. Chemnitii satis luculentam, quem 8i generalem ubiquitatem Christi secundum assumtam humanitatem apud omnes creaturas negasse, porro dixeris: nae omnem mihi pudorem et conscientiam perdidisse videberis.“ (Cone, concors, p. 1212. sqq.)

Huelsemannus: ,,Ubiquitas, si quae ex immensitate Dei dependet, non est communicata carni Christi, sed omnipraesentia, quae etiam in Deo voluntaria est, ex suppositione rerum creatarum.“ (Extens. Breviarii. Ed. 3. p. 94.)

Brentius: ״Finxerunt novum et prodigiosum ubiquitatis vocabulum, ut eo facilius rudibus et rerum nesciis imponant, et persuadeant, nos etiam novum et prodigiosum dogma excogitasse, corpus Christi tanquam alutam in omnia loca geometrice se extendere et diffundere.“ (De personali unione duarum natur, in Christo. Witeb. 1578. praef.)

Kromayerus: ״Absurda nobis objiciunt; secuturum inde, Christum esse in omnibus cloacis, cantharis, patibulis etc. Sed respondemus κατ’ ένστασιν: ita nec Deus ipse creaturis omnibus erit praesens, quia verendum, ne sit in omnibus cloacis, patibulis, cantharis. Deinde inter ro inesse et adesse omnibus creaturis distinguendum. Christus potius adest omnibus creaturis, etiam illis, qui constituti sunt in locis sordidis, qui elevantur in patibulum, qui laborant in flammis et fluminibus, quam quod insit. Si tamen phrasis inessendi retineatur, absque omni σνμμίξει cum creaturis intelligatur.“ (Theol. posit.pol. I, 247.) *)

Scherze rus: ,,Etait b. Feurbornius (K ενωσιγρ. Sect. I. fol. 9.) manifeste, verba Lutheri, ubi,omnia‘ dicuntur,plena esse Christi‘, loqui de statu exinanitionis juxta Ephes. 1, 4.“ (Syst. th. loc. 8. p. 238.)

PART. III. CAP. Π. SECTIO I. Huelsemannus: ,,Quemadmodum essentia Dei non inquinatur sordibus materialibus, etiamsi in inferno, in cloaca, in lupanari rectissime dicatur esse praesens, vi dictorum generalium Jer. 23, 22.23. Ps. 139, 7. 8. etc. Act. 17, 27. 28., ita, si extarent ejusmodi testimonia, quae praesentiam carnis Christi extimam tam late extenderent, quam late extenditur praesentia essentiae divinae, nihil metuendum erat ab inquinatione seu contaminatione a praesentia rerum foedarum non magis, quam timendus erat ullus cruciatus, ullave ustulatio corporis Christi, si liberet illud praesens sistere in mediis flammis infernalibus.“ (Vindiciae S. S. Art. 20. p. 75.) cf. Lutherus de servo arbitrio. XVIII, 2095. sq. Vid.^gupra Vol. II. p. 23.

Kromayerus: ״Contra omnipraesentiam opponunt: 1. Ascensio־ nem in coelum. Sed respondemus, Christum per ascensionem suam non omnem praesentiam, sed visibilem duntaxat conversationem nobis subtraxisse, prout in coelum jam jam ascensurus promittit, se nobiscum futurum usque ad consummationem saeculi... Ideo abitus ille ad Patrem per non-visionem exponitur Joh. 16,10. Nec per coelum, in quod Christus ascendit, intelligitur coelum istud empyreum, quod vocant, locorum intervallis a nobis remotissimum, supra coelum stelliferum positum, sed πον beatorum, quod ubi est, nostrum inquirere non est. De angelis certe, parvulis in terra ministrantibus, dicitur Matth. 18, 10., quod faciem Patris coelestis semper videant.

2. Sessionem ad dextram Patris opponunt. Verum cum Luthero statim hoc argumentum invertimus: Imo quia Christus secundum hum. nat. consedit ad dextram Patris, ideo praesens est nobis in terris. Per sessionem enim ad dextram Dei non situatio vel collocatio Christi ad certum locum, sed totius huius universi omnipotens et omnipraesens gubernatio intelligitur. Syllogismum nostrum, quem sacramentarii tantopere exagitant: ,Dextra Dek est ubique. Christus secundum hum. nat. sedet ad dextram Dei. Ergo Christus secundum h. n. est ubique‘, quod concernit, est crypticus vel oratio argumentosa, in qua loco praemissae majoris ipsius probatio ponitur. Sic autem integer haberet: ,Qui sedet ad dextram Dei, ille est ubique, quia dextra est ubique. Christus secundum h. n. sedet ad dextram Dei. Ergo.‘

3. Peditum ad judicium obvertunt. Sed respondemus, Christum rediturum ad judicium, quoad praesentiam visibilem. ,Videbit eum omnis oculus et qui pupugerunt eum‘, Apoc. 1, 7. Unde reditus iste per επιφάνειαν vel apparitionem exponitur Tit. 2,13.

4. Humanam Christi naturam finitam suisque dimensionibus circumscriptam objiciunt. Sed respondemus, hoc argumentum cum larvis pugnare, quia humanam Christi naturam nullatenus infinitam, sed finitam, interim tamen propter unionem personalem cum λόγφ et sessionem ad dextram Dei omnipraesentem statuimus. Crassam istam, diffusam et expansam praesentiam, quam nobis affingunt Calviniani, toto pectore execramur; interim hum. Christi nat. praesentia divina praesentem esse creaturis omnibus, ductum Scripturae secuti, credimus. Praesentia ista divina Es. 40, 16. 17. describitur, quod omnes creaturae instar puncti eidem sunt objectae et expositae. . .

6. Locum Matth. 26, 11.: ,Me non semper habetis‘, obtendunt. Sed respondemus distinguendo inter rem et modum rei. Licet Christus neget, eo modo, quo sc. beneflciis affici possit, ut tum temporis factum ftferat, se in posterum praesentem futurum apostolis; praesentiam tamen ipsam non negat, sed potius promittit Matth. 20, v. ult.

7. Quod omne corpus sit in loco, ex philosophicis contendunt. Sed respondemus distinguendo inter phrases, esse locabile et esse in loco. Locabile quidem concedimus omne corpus physicum, sed non actu in loco, quia corpus extimum, quodcunque tandem sit, non est in loco, cum non circumfundatur alio corpore, nisi progressum statuere velimus in infinitum. Locus autem est περιέχοντος πέρας ακίνητον πρώτον, id est, terminus continentis immobilis primo. Si corpus Christi actu primo semper est locabile, palpabile, visibile, sed non semper est actu secundo in loco, palpatur, videtur; ut

DB PERSONA CHRISTI. post ascensionem in coelum nec locorum, nec temporum intervallis subjectum est, quemadmodum in diebus carnis, cum loco circumseribebatur, localiter erat in utero beatae virginis, in praesepio, in cruce, sepulchro etc., mensurabatur temporum articulis, ut cum Christus esset octo dierum, duodecim annorum, triginta annorum...


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: That it is contrary to the truth of human nature to be present in many places…

9. That it is contrary to the truth of human nature to be present in many places at once. But we respond by denying this: It is indeed contrary to the nature of a mere man, but not of the man [Christ], that is. Others distinguish between a man ψιλόν, i.e., mere, and υψηλόν, i.e., exalted; that it is indeed not of a mere man to be present in many places, but that an exalted man, personally united with God and sitting at the right hand of God, can well be in many places at once. ...

11. They object that the doctrine of ubiquity is new, a "Swabian theology," fabricated by the Württemberg theologians, especially Jacob Schmidelin (as they call Jacob Andreae, the son of a smith). But we respond by denying this and by appealing to the various writings of Luther, in which the majesty of omnipresence, communicated to the flesh of Christ, is established. See the "pupil" of the Evangelical estates, namely the Augsburg Confession, in the appendix of which very many passages from Luther are found collected. (Th. posit. pol. I, 248 sqq.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who not only detract from the majesty of omnipresence for the flesh of Christ, but also attack this dogma with various horrible accusations. Thus, in the Helvetic Confession, which is the most common of all, it is denied that Christ, according to His human nature, is still present in the world and is everywhere... In the preface to the *Consensus Orthodoxus*, it is called a 'ubiquitarian monster of the omnipresence of the body of Christ.' Beza, P. I. resp. ad act. p. 154, calls it a 'chimerical and futile omnipresence.' Danaeus, in *Resp. ad Laconicum* p. 1523, calls it a 'ubiquitarian Helen,' etc. 2. Of the Papists, who blow the same pipes as the Calvinists... 3. Of the Innovators, who reject the same omnipresence of the flesh of Christ and traduce it with the odious name of 'ubiquity.' See D. Georg Calixtus in the *Refutation of D. Weller* n. 125 sq., Dreierus in the *Discussion* q. 1. de persona Christi. G. Calixtus also asserts in his *Judgment on the controversies with the Reformed* and elsewhere with Tanner, etc., 'that this doctrine is new and devised by Jacob Faber Stapulensis, a Parisian Doctor, a man fond of novelty, for he is the first to make mention of the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ in his *Commentary on 2 Cor.* at ch. 12 and at ch. 10. That Luther, Brentius, Jacob Andreae, etc., followed Jacob Faber afterward.'" (L. c. s. 2. q. 14. fol. 267. sq.)

See what we have just said concerning the έξουσία (authority) communicated to Christ according to His human nature from Matt. 28: 18. To which may also be referred that all things are said to be put under His feet, 1 Cor. 15:27, 28; Eph. 1: 22. Specifically, the power of forgiving sins belongs here—that truly divine power, yet communicated to Christ as man according to Matt. 9:6—and the power of exercising judgment, given to Christ, οτι υίός ανθρώπου (because He is the Son of Man), insofar as He is the Son of Man, or according to that nature by which He is the Son of Man, John 5:22, 27. So that all ought to honor the Son, just as (καθώς) they honor the Father; or, that they are bound to pursue Christ, as man, with such honor as is exhibited to God the Father, on account of the supreme excellence of the divine nature and its perfections, and not with any other dissimilar or inferior degree of worship, John 5: 23.

Whence the object of divine worship which, or the adequate object, is said to be the suppositum itself, Christ; the object quo, or the inadequate object, is said to be not only the divine nature, but also the human. Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.5 PART III, CAP. II. SECTION I.

E. Hunnius: "According to his humanity, as the apostle asserts in express words, 'God gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, and of those on earth, and of those under the earth, and every tongue should confess him,' Phil. 2. Which name was given to him according to the flesh, as the fathers affirm with great consensus and the context of the apostolic text proves. This is shown in particular by the Greek word placed and used there by the apostle, ἐχαρίσατο, he bestowed or gave out of grace. For that adorable name could by no means be given or bestowed upon the deity of Christ out of grace, since it is adorable by nature." (L. c. p. 147.)

Scherzerus: "In Christ the man there is not ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος (another and another), but only ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο (one thing and another). Therefore, the glory granted to the humanity of Christ was not granted by God to some other person. Wherefore that worship, ascribed to the Trinity alone, does not exclude the humanity of Christ, but includes it. For 'in whom we believe, him we religiously adore,' Rom. 10:14. But we believe in Christ the man, John 3:16. Therefore. For the Father 'has given the Son authority to execute judgment, that all may honor the Son, καθὼς (just as) they honor the Father,' John 5:22, 27. But he gave the authority of judging to Christ according to his humanity. Therefore, also the glory of the same worship with which the Father himself is adored. Of the same, I say, as to the thing, not as to the manner of possessing it. For God is adored καθ’ αὑτό (of himself) and φύσει (by nature), the humanity is adored κατ’ ἄλλο (through another) and χάριτι (by grace) or through the grace of union, Phil. 2:9–11. Because the flesh of Christ is the flesh τοῦ λόγου (of the Word), not of a mere man." (System, th. Loc. II. p. 81.)

Quenstedtius: "The object of this religious worship, as it is directed toward and exhibited to the second person of the divinity, is 1. not the divine nature alone in Christ, but 2. the whole person according to both natures, so 3. that this worship terminates also in the assumed nature of Christ, not indeed 4. on account of habitual excellence, or only by accident, just as the king's purple is accustomed to be honored by a certain external kissing, but 6. because it subsists in the person τοῦ λόγου (of the Word) and possesses the essence τοῦ λόγου (of the Word) with all its properties, and in it, with it, and through it, as through an εὔχρηστον (useful) organ personally united to himself, the λόγος (Word) performs and exercises all divine things." (L. c. s. 2. q. 15. fol. 287.)

The same: "It is one thing to be the adequate object of adoration, and another to be as it were a part of the object and consequently to be adored, insofar as it subsists personally in the object. The flesh of Christ is not to be adored separately or as a certain separate person, but as a nature ὑπόστατον (hypostatic), subsisting in the person of the Son of God, made a partaker of divine majesty through personal union; which is in response to the passage Gal. 4:8: 'When you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods.' Where the discourse is about the object of adoration, not about that which is as it were a part of that object. When we adore Christ according to his human nature, we certainly do not adore him who is God by nature, but we deem worthy of the highest worship of adoration the nature which is personally united with God." (L. c. f. 296.)

The same: "They object: God himself says in Is. 48:8, 'My glory,' i.e., religious adoration, 'I will not give to another'; but the flesh of Christ is not God. Resp.: When the λόγος (Word) communicates the glory of adoration to the human nature through personal union, he does not give it to another, but to his own humanity, i.e., appropriated to himself through union and assumed into the unity of the person without any multiplication, equalization, or diminution of himself." (L. c. f. 297.)

The same: "The Calvinists urge the passage Jer. 17:5, where from the mouth of God, 'Cursed is he who makes flesh his arm and has trust in man.' But we respond by distinguishing between a ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον (mere man) from the common and promiscuous crowd of men, and one who has his own subsistence outside the person τοῦ λόγου (of the Word), and the man Christ Jesus, θεάνθρωπον (God-man), in whose name we are baptized and in whom we are bound to believe. The cited words of the prophet are to be understood not of the latter, but of the former; where he is called cursed, not he who [trusts in] flesh deified or personally united with the λόγῳ (Word) and [brought] to the fellowship..."

He] religiously worships the exalted [Christ] of the Most Holy Trinity, but he who trusts in a mere man acts idolatrously and does not desire the help of God.

Moreover, they commit the fallacy of composition and division; the words of the prophet in their entirety are as follows: "Cursed is he who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord."

But he who worships Christ as man does not depart from the Lord. (L. c. f. 296.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who assert: 'To say that the flesh of Christ is to be worshipped is the crime of horrible idolatry.' Thus Theod. Beza, Vol. 2, opp. apol. 3, ad Selnecc. p. 473. ... Most Calvinists distinguish between worship that is merely and absolutely divine, merely human, and finally mediatorial; the former they reserve for the divine nature alone, they dare not attribute the merely human to the flesh of Christ, and therefore they teach that Christ as θεάνθρωπος, or as mediator, is to be worshipped according to both natures by mediatorial worship. Thus Danaeus. ... Yet the Calvinists themselves do not agree among themselves as to what that mediatorial worship consists in, and they often change their language, but never their mind. In the question, however: Whether Christ as mediator is to be worshipped or is adorable? Gisbertus Voetius, in particular, defends the negative. ...

2. Of the Papists, who, distinguishing between λατρεία and ὑπερδουλεία, attribute λατρεία to God alone, δουλεία to angels and men, and the worship of ὑπερδουλεία to the humanity of Christ and the Blessed Virgin. ...

3. Of the Socinians or Neophotinians. Photinus indeed, their leader, bishop of the church of Sirmium in Hungary, who vomited forth his blasphemies around the year of Christ 370, although he maintained that Christ was entirely a created thing, nevertheless contended that religious adoration could not only be attributed to him, but even ought to be, which Socinus himself reports concerning this heresiarch, and also concerning his uncle Laelius, in his disp. de adorat. Christi p. 29. Around the year 1569, however, Franciscus Davidis denied entirely that Christ ought to be worshipped, whom Christianus Francken followed. ...

Socinus, in explicat. c. 6. Matth. tom. 1. opp. p. 61, says: 'It is most true that he (namely, Christ) can indeed be invoked always and perpetually, and he is by no means to be considered a Christian who does not acknowledge and confess this.' The Racovian Catechism, p. 177, contains almost the same. But the Socinians employ various limitations here.

Matth. tom. 1. opp. p. 61. inquit: ,Verissimum est, ipsum (Christum sci.) et quidem semper et perpetuo invocari posse, et pro christiano minime is est habendus, qui hoc non agnoscit et confitetur.‘ Eadem fere habet Catech. Racov. p. 177. Ast varias hic adhibent Sociniani limitationes.


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: And 1.) they distinguish between Christ glorified and not yet glorified,…

And 1.) they distinguish between Christ glorified and not yet glorified, asserting that this highest dignity of adoration could not have belonged to Christ before his glorification, but that in his glorification the heavenly Father bestowed the same upon his Son. ... 2.) They distinguish between adoration and invocation, contending that the adoration of Christ was indeed commanded, but not invocation. ... 3.) They distinguish between these two questions: Whether Christ can be invoked and whether he ought to be invoked, or whether we are obligated to invoke Christ. This is the invention of Socinus, namely, that Christ can indeed be invoked, but that it is not necessary that he be invoked. ... 4.) They establish the foundation of this adorable dignity in Christ not in his divinity, not in the personal union of both natures and the communication of divine majesty regarding the human nature, but in a certain power which God the Father bestowed upon his Son because of his blameless obedience. ... 5.) The Socinians maintain that Christ is to be invoked only in those matters which pertain to the Christian church. And by this very thing they make a distinction between the invocation of God and the invocation of Christ. ...

4. Of the Arminians, who follow the hypotheses of the Socinians in this matter, and 1.) indeed concede that Christ, as he is mediator, is to be worshipped and religiously honored. See confess. c. 16. and apolog. conf. c. 50. 'Yet they approve of that Papal-Calvinian-Socinian distinction between worship that is supremely divine and that which is inferior, yet also divine.'" (L. c. q. 15. f. 287—90.) PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

So that they belong not only to the concrete, or to the person denominated by the human nature, and to be viewed perhaps with respect to the divine, but to the human nature itself—not, however, insofar as it is considered precisely and outside of the hypostatic union, but by virtue of the union, and insofar as it is viewed within that union.

Dannhauer: "It can be said in the abstract: The flesh is life-giving, the human nature is omnipotent; not in the abstract of separation, but of precision. 'Note diligently,' says Dr. Mentzer in *Elench. Sadeel.* p. m. p. 325, 339, sq. *Opp. T. I.* p. 1218, 'when the human nature or flesh is named here, then in this argument it is not understood as humanity or flesh εϊδικώς [specifically], separately, and subsisting by itself and of its own nature, but insofar as it is personally united to the Son of God himself. And hence the analysis of such propositions is to be formed: The flesh of Christ is life-giving, that is, Christ, who according to his deity is life itself, is life-giving according to the flesh, namely, insofar as he has it personally united to him. The humanity of Christ is to be adored, that is, Christ is adored not only according to his deity, as before the incarnation, but also according to the flesh personally united to him.' Cf. Dr. Gerh. *Exeges.* p. 1458 et seqq., also p. 1359. § 261. And hence the particles *secundum* [according to], and the like, in this kind of communication do not determine the property of the nature in the same way as in the first [kind], but designate either the object *to whom* or the cause *from whence*." (*Hodos. Phaen. VIII.* p. 330 sq.)

Moreover, that communication was not made 1) by an essential or natural effusion of the properties of the divine nature into the human nature, as if the humanity of Christ possessed them separated by themselves and from the divine essence, or 2) as if through that communication the human nature in Christ had entirely laid aside its own natural properties, or 3) been converted into the divine nature, or 4) been made equal to the divine nature, with those properties of its own having been communicated to it in itself and by itself, or 5) that the natural and essential properties and operations of both natures are the same or certainly equal.

However, those words and phrases (real communication, to be communicated really) are used in opposition to a merely verbal communication; see *Sol. Decl. F. C.* p. 777, 778. § 21.

Therefore, those predications pertain to this genus of the communication of idioms in which truly divine perfections—those, indeed, which in their formal concept respect some operation, but do not involve anything that is entirely repugnant to the truth of the human nature—are predicated of Christ according to the human nature denominatively and immediately; but the remaining divine perfections, which of themselves and formally do not respect an operation, but do involve something repugnant to the human nature, are enunciated of Christ according to the human nature denominatively, not indeed immediately, but yet through the mediation of another attribute of the former kind.

Attributes are called *energetic*, and such are, for example, omniscience, omnipotence, and omnipresence. For the former concerns the act of knowing or understanding; the latter, the act of operating outside of oneself or in another; the third (modified, I say, by presence) concerns the dominion to be exercised over present creatures. For these result from those divine perfections; and he who is a participant of these, and is said to be such, cannot but also be a participant of, and be called, the divine authority and glory resulting therefrom.

Not abstractively, so that the predicate is the idiom itself viewed in itself, or the denominating form. For we do not say: Christ according to his human nature is omnipotence; or, is omniscience. Cf. what we said at § 18, note c. As, for example, I may say: Christ, as man, is omnipotent. But concerning those propositions whose subject is the abstract human nature itself, which they specifically call abstractive, questions are wont to be asked, e.g., the human nature of Christ is omnipotent; the human nature of Christ is omnipresent.

Certainly, the foundation of such propositions is contained in the Scriptures, and can be seen especially in John 6:51 ff., where this proposition is held almost in these terms: The flesh of Christ is living bread, or the flesh of Christ is truly food, having the power of conferring life; which is the same as if it were said: the human nature of Christ (to which the word "flesh" corresponds) is life-giving.

Regarding the sober and timely use of abstractive propositions, see the theologians gathered at Smalcald in the year 1578 in Hutter’s *Concordia Concors*, chap. XXI, p. 680, where they advise: 1) That they compel no one to use these phrases, provided it remains firm that Christ, according to his human nature, has been made a participant of the divine majesty. 2) That they do not use those phrases before the unlearned common people, nor will they use them elsewhere, unless necessity demands it.

Reuschius: "The unlearned and more simple-minded easily attribute this sense to these abstractive propositions, so that they understand only the human nature, with the hypostasis of the Word excluded, and then they represent to themselves in the human nature of Christ divine idioms that are clearly different from those divine perfections which the divine nature of Christ possesses. This sense of these propositions is heterodox and false, since it would imply a change of the human nature into the divine, from which, besides God, another infinite being—and thus multiple infinite beings—would arise. Hence, the more cautious advise that we abstain from these propositions among the common people and use them only among the learned." (Annotatt. in Baieri Comp. p. 602 ff.)

Such are: simplicity, eternity, immensity; of which the former imports the negation of composition, the second the negation of a beginning, and the latter the negation of measurability, which cannot stand with the truth of human nature, since it is by essence a composite thing, has a beginning of existence, and is measurable by place.

Nor is it necessary that such attributes, just as those which were of the former kind, be predicated immediately. For even in natural things, e.g., that fire is communicated to iron, and therefore it is rightly said: This iron is hot, burning, glowing, or shining; yet it is not therefore equally permissible to say: This iron is light; although the lightness of fire, along with the heat and light of fire, has been communicated to the iron. Indeed, although I cannot say: Christ according to his human nature is eternal, I can nevertheless rightly say: Christ according to...

while according to the human nature it is omnipotent by eternal and immense omnipotence, etc. Cf. blessed Scherzer, *System.* L. II. p. 200, where he teaches that only those idioms are immediately communicated to the human nature of Christ which are necessary for the end of the union (to be estimated from the use in the office) and do not overturn the origin and truth of the human nature; whence, for example, eternity is not (immediately) communicated (or in such a way that it can be immediately predicated of Christ according to the human nature), because it removes the origin of the humanity; etc.

Not indeed in the nominative case (for I cannot say: Christ according to the human nature is omnipotent, and thus eternal, immense), but in the oblique case, so that those attributes that are άνενέργητα [inactive] are appended to the attributes that are ένεργητικά [active], according to the note, preceding. Cf. what has been added to note b, § 20. § 22.

The third genus of the communication of idioms consists in this, that the operations pertaining to the office of Christ are not of one and only a certain nature, but common to both, insofar as each contributes to them what is its own, and thus each acts with the communication of the other. By others it is placed in the second position and is called χοινοποιία or χοινοποίησις, a communication or communion of operations. However, when it is called a communication of idioms, it is certain that the term "idioms" is taken more broadly, so that the works of the office, which comprise something proper to the divine nature and something that is proper to the human nature, are comprehended under them.

They are commonly called άποτελέσματα [results] or works composed of the actions of both, namely, of each nature, coordinated toward one end. Likewise, they are called θεανδρικαί [theandric] operations, or God-manly, because Christ operates according to both natures, as God and as man, so that the one suppositum or person of Christ is the principle *which* is the author of such a work, but the principles *by which* it is done are the two natures, divine and human, which act in that work distinctly, yet not dividedly. And so, insofar as each nature is left to its own powers and properties regarding that part of the common work. For otherwise, the human nature also acts by the majesty communicated to it the same things that the divine nature acts; but this pertains to the second genus of the communication of idioms, or to the communication of majesty.
