Et 1.) distinguunt inter Christum glorificatum et nondum glorificatum, asserentes, Christo ante glorificationem suam hancce summam adorationis dignitatem competere haud potuisse, in glorificatione vero Patrem coelestem eandem Filio suo gratificatum esse. . . 2.) Distinguunt inter adorationem et invocationem, contendentes adorationem Christi mandatam quidem esse, sed non invocationem... 3.) Distinguunt inter has duas quaestiones: An Christus invocari queat et an invocari debeat, sive an ad invocandum Christum obligati simus. Est hoc Socini commentum, sci. posse quidem Christum invocari, non autem necessarium id esse, ut invocetur. . 4.) Fundamentum hujus dignitatis adorabilis in Christo constituunt non ipsius divinitatem, non personalem utriusque naturae unionem et majestatis divinae communicationem, quoad humanam naturam, sed potestatem quandam, quam Deus Pater Filio suo gratificatus sit propter inculpatam suam obedientiam. . . 5.) Statuunt Sociniani, Christum in illis solum rebus invocandum esse, quae ad ecclesiam Christianam spectant. Et hoc ipso inter invocationem Dei et ifivocationem Christi discrimen faciunt. . .

4. Arminianorum, qui Socinianorum hac in re hypotheses sequuntur, et 1.) quidem concedunt, Christum, qua mediator est, adorandum et religiose colendum esse. Vid. confess. c. 16. et apolog. conf. c. 50. ' Attamen distinctionem istam pontificio ־ Calviniano Socinianam inter cultum summe divinum et inferiorem, at divinum quoque, approbant.“ (L. c. q. 15. f. 287—90.) PART. ΙΠ. CAP. Π. SECTIO I.

Ita ut non solum concreto, aut personae ab humana natura denominatae, et quoad divinam forte spectandae, verum ipsi humanae naturae, non tamen quatenus praecise et extra unionem hypostaticam, sed vi unionis, et quatenus intra unionem illam spectatur, competant.

Dannhauerus: ״In abstracto dici potest: Caro est vivifica, humana natura est omnipotens; non in abstracto separationis, sed praecisionis. ,Diligenter nota‘, ait D. Mentzerus in Elench. Sadeel. p. m. p. 325. 339. sq. Opp. T. I. p. 1218., ,quando hic nominatur natura humana, vel caro, tum in hoc argumento non intelligi humanitatem sive carnem εϊδικώς, seorsim, et per se subsistentem et ex natura sui, sed quatenus illa est unita personaliter ipsi Pilio Dei, et hinc analysis ejusmodi propositionum formanda: Caro Christi est vivifica, hoc est, Christus, qui secundum deitatem ipsa vita est, est vivificus secundum carnem, nempe quatenus personaliter habet illam unitam. Humanitas Christi est adoranda, hoc est, Christus non tantum secundum deitatem suam, sicut ante incarnationem, verum etiam secundum carnem personaliter unitam adoratur.‘ Cf. D. Gerh. Exeges. p. 1458. et seqq., it. p. 1359. § 261. Atque hinc particulae /cara, secundum, et similes in hoc communicationis genere non perinde, ut in primo, determinant naturae proprietatem, sed vel objectum Cui, vel causam Unde designant.“ (Hodos. Phaen. VIII. p. 330. sq.)

Communicatio autem illa non facta est 1) per essentialem aut naturalem effusionem proprietatum divinae naturae in naturam humanam, quasi humanitas Christi eas per se et a divina essentia separatas habeat, aut 2) quasi per illam communicationem humana natura in Christo naturales sum proprietates prorsus deposuerit, vel 3) in divinam naturam conversa, aut 4) divinae naturae, communicatis illis suis proprietatibus in se ipsa, et per se, exaequata sit, aut 5) quod utriusque naturae eaedem aut certe aequales, naturales et essentiales proprietates et operationes sint.

Vocabula autem et phrases illae (realis communicatio, realiter communicari) adhibentur in oppositione ad communicationem mere verbalem; vid. Sol. Deci. F. C. p. 777. 778. § 21.

Pertinent itaque ad hoc genus communicationis idiomatum praedicationes illae, in quibus perfectiones vere divinae, illae quidem, quae in formali conceptu suo operationem aliquam respiciunt, a non autem aliquid, quod veritati humanae naturae prorsus repugnat, involvunt; et sic etiam potestas et gloria divina b denominative c atque immediate de Christo secundum humanam naturam d praedicantur; reliquae vero perfectiones divinae, quae ex se et formaliter non respiciunt operationem, involvunt autem aliquid humanae naturae repugnans, e non quidem immediate, sed tamen mediante alio prioris generis attributo,f de Christo secundum humanam naturam denominaüves enuntiantur.

Dicuntur attributa ίνεργητιχά, et talia sunt v. g. omniscientia9 (mnipotentia, omnipraesentia. Illa enim actus sciendi seu intelligendi, i8ta actus operandi extra se aut in alio, haec (modificata inquam praesentiä) dominium in creaturas praesentes exercendum spectat. Haec enim resultant ex perfectionibus illis divinis; et qui harum particeps est et esse dicitur, non potest non etiam particeps esse et dici auctoritatis et gloriae divinae, inde resultantis.

Non abstractive, ut praedicatum sit ipsum idioma in se spectatum, seu forma denominans. Neque enim dicimus: Christus secundum humanam naturam est omnipotentia; aut, est omniscientia. Conf., quae ad § 18. not. c. diximus. Ut v. g. dicam: Christus, qua homo, est omnipotens. De illis autem propositionibus, quarum subjectum est ipsum abstractum humanae naturae, quas peculiariter abstractivas vocant, quaeri solent v. g. humana Christi natura est omnipotens; humana Clmsti natura est omnipraesens.

Sane fundamentum talium propositionum in Scripturis continetur ac videri inprimis potest Joh. 6, 51. sqq., ubi fere in terminis habetur haec propositio: Garo Christi est panis vivus, aut caro Christi vere est cibus, habens virtutem conferendi vitam; quod idem est, ac si dicatur: humana Christi natura (cui vox carnis respondet) est vivifica.

De sobrio autem et tempestivo usu propositionum abstractivarum vid. Theologi Smalcaldiae congregati anno 1578. apud Hutterum Cone. Cone. cap. XXI. p. m. 680., ubi monent 1) se neminem cogere, ut phrasibus hisce utatur, modo firmum maneat, Christum secundum naturam humanam divinae majestatis essfc factum participem. 2) Coram indocta plebe se phrasibus illis non uti, neque alibi usuros, nisi ubi necessitas postulaverit.

Reuschius: ,,Indocti ac rudiores hisce propositionibus abstractivis facile hunc tribuunt sensum, ut solam intelligant humanam naturam, exclusa hypostasi τον λόγον, atque tum sibi in humana Christi natura repraesentant idiomata divina ab iis perfectionibus divinis, quas habet divina Christi natura, plane diversa. Qui sensus harum propositionum est heterodoxus et falsus, quum mutationem naturae humanae in divinam inferat, ex qua praeter Deum aliud ens infinitum, eaque plura entia infinita, orirentur. Hinc cautiores suadent, ut ab hisce propositionibus inter plebem abstineamus atque iisdem modo inter eruditos utamur.“ (Annotatt. in Baieri Comp. p. 602. sq.)

Quales sunt: simplicitas, aeternitas, immensitas; quarum illa negationem compositionis, ista negationem initii, haec negationem mensurabilitatis importat, quae cum veritate naturae humanae stare non possunt, quippe quae per essentiam est compositum quid, habet initium existendi, est mensurabilis loco.

Neque vero necesse est, talia attributa, aeque ac ea, quae prioris generis erant, immediate praedicari. Nam et in naturalibus, v. g. quod ferro communicatur ignis, ideoque recte dicitur: Hoc ferrum est calidum, urens, candet aut lucet, non tamen ideo aeque dicere licet: Hoc ferrum est leve; quamvis levitas ignis una cum calore et luce ignis sit ferro communicata. Nempe quamvis dicere non possim: Christus secundum humanam naturam est aeternus, recte tamen possum dicere: Christus secun FAKT. 111. UAE. 11. SEUTiU 1.

dum humanam naturam est omnipotens omnipotentia aeterna et immensa etc. Conf. b. Scherz. System. L. II. p. 200., ubi docet, eatantum idiomata esse immediate communicata humanae naturae Christi, quae ad finem unionis (ex usu in officio aestimandumß sunt necessaria et originem ac veritatem humanae naturae non evertunt; unde v. g. aeternitas non sit (immediate) communicata (seu ita, ut immediate de Christo secundum humanam naturam praedicari possit), quia humanitatis origi־ nem tollit; etc.

Non quidem in casu recto (neque enim dicere possum: Christus secundum humanam naturam est omnipotens, et sic aeternus, immensus), sed in casu obliquo, ita ut attributa illa άνενέργψα attributis ένεργητίχοΐς apponantur, juxta notam/, praec. Cf., quae addita sunt ad not. b. § 20. § 22.

Tertium genus a communicationis idiomatum consistit in eo, quod operationes b ad officium Christi pertinentes non sunt unius et solius cujusdam naturae, sed utrique communes, quatenus utraque ad illas, quod suum est,c confert d et sic utraque agit cum communicatione alterius. e Ab aliis secundo loco ponitur et dicitur χοινοποαα aut χοινοποίησίς, communicatio aut communio operationum. Quando autem communicatio idiomatum dicitur, certum est, vocem idiomatum latius accipi, ita ut opera officii, quae aliquid divinae naturae proprium et aliquid, quod humanae naturae proprium est, complectuntur, 8ub ipsis comprehendantur.

Dicuntur communiter άποτελέσματα seu opera ex duabus, utriusque scilicet naturae, actionibus ad unum finem coordinatis conflata. Item operationes θεανδριχα\, seu Deiviriles, quod Christus secundum utramque naturam, qua θεός et qua ανήρ, operatur, ita ut unum suppositum seu persona Christi sit principium quod talis operis, principia quibus autem sint duae naturae, divina et humana, quae in opere isto distincte, non tamen divise agant. Adeoque quatenus utraque natura suismet viribus ac proprietatibus, quoad illam communis operis partem, relinquitur. Alias enim etiam humana natura per majestatem sibi communicatam eadem agit, quae agit divina natura; sed hoc ad secundum genus communicationis idiomatum, seu ad communicationem majestatis pertinet.


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Kromayer: "On account of the office, a composite person was also required,…

Kromayer: "On account of the office, a composite person was also required, since God alone could neither suffer nor die, and man alone could not sufficiently suffer and die. Therefore, a divine humanity and a human divinity were required. All propositions in which the prophetic, priestly, or kingly office of Christ is treated pertain here. Is. 40:10; Gal. 3:13; 1 Cor. 15:25. Certain biblical propositions, especially those which are primarily of this genus, can be considered under several genera of the communication of idioms... The proposition of 1 John 1:7: 'The blood'"

The blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from all sin," can be considered in three ways. If it is formed thus: Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from sins, it is in the second (third) genus, because the αποτέλεσμα (result) is predicated of the person. If thus: The Son of God sheds blood, it is in the first, because an Ιδίωμα, i.e., a property of the human nature, is predicated of the person. If, however, thus: The blood of Jesus Christ (a part of the human nature) has the power of cleansing, it is in the third (second), because a divine αΐχημα (attribute) is predicated of a part of the human nature. (Theol. pos. pol. I, 238, sq.)

N. Hunnius: "It is certain that if divine actions are performed through the human nature, so that they are θεανδρικαί, i.e., divine-human and human-divine, the natures also communicate their operations to one another; thus, there was a human voice: 'Young man, I say to you, arise' (Luke 7:14), but it was also a divine voice, because it was an omnipotent voice recalling the dead to life; who, indeed, would not here recognize the human voice as the vehicle of a divine action, and therefore feel with his own hands the conjunction and communication of operations?" (Διάσκεψίς. § 653.)

The same: "The communion of operations is a consequence per se of the communication of the ενεργητικών (active) idioms. For if acting properties are communicated, it is necessary that they operate as they are, namely, not only in the primary and natural subject, but also in that which possesses the idioms through communication. Thus, the soul of a man does not see with the optical faculty without an eye, but exercises and exerts the visual power communicated to the eye through the eye and in the eye; nor can it usurp this faculty of its own except through the eye, which, as it was made a participant of the power, so also of the operation. But when the soul ceases to communicate its operations to the body, the bond of the hypostatic union is broken." (L. c. § 647.)

Thus, for example, regarding the work of satisfaction or redemption, in which is included partly the endurance of the most bitter passion and death, and partly the addition of infinite value (so that the passion is not bare, but satisfactory), the former pertains to the human nature, the latter to the divine nature per se. Similarly, regarding that miraculous work by which Christ, to prove his office as Messiah, restored sight to a man born blind (John 9:6 sqq.), the human nature of Christ indeed contributed what was its own, as to the act of spitting on the ground, making clay from the spittle, and anointing the eyes of the blind man with the clay, and finally saying to him: go, wash in the pool of Siloam; but the divine nature contributed what was its own, namely, by influencing with infinite power to produce that supernatural effect.

Fechtius: "Two extremes must be avoided: first, the confusion of the natures, lest the operations of one nature be ascribed to the other as if they were proper to it, or arise from a commixture of both natures; second, the separation of actions, lest the actions of both natures be thought to flow separately from the natures, just as, for example, two rivulets flow separately to constitute one fountain or lake without any communion; but rather, the properties of both natures are to be believed to communicate intimately with one another, so that there is no particle of human passion that is not, as it were, imbued with the divinity as its soul, nor any action of the divinity that is not imbued with human blood, in the manner in which an ignited sword both cuts and burns, with the fire and the iron each contributing its own, and yet they act with a common action in such a way that neither would the iron without the fire cut so penetratingly, nor would the fire without the iron burn so penetratingly." (Compend. th. thet. c. 17. § 51. p. 469.)

Olearius: "Irenaeus, when he says in book 3, ch. 21, that Christ was crucified and died ησυχάζοντας τον λόγον, with the Word resting, by no means excludes the λόγος from the work of redemption, but only infers a retraction of power and an inhibition of its exercise through the flesh, without which it would have been impossible for Christ to suffer and die. Meanwhile, however, the humanity alone could not have provided the infinite λύτρον (ransom) in this passion if the λόγος were excluded." (Vid. Carpzovii Isag. in libb. symbol. p. 1515.)

Luther: "He (Zwingli) calls it *Allöosis* when something is said of the divinity of Christ that actually pertains to his humanity, or vice versa, as in Luke 24:26: 'Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?' Here he juggles, claiming that 'Christ' is taken for the human nature. Beware, beware, I say, of the *Allöosis*; it is a mask of the devil. For in the end, it fashions such a Christ that I would not want to be a Christian according to him—namely, that Christ henceforth is no more and does no more with his suffering and life than any other mere saint. For if I believe that only the human nature suffered for me, then Christ is a mere savior to me, and he himself would well need a savior. In sum: it is unspeakable what the devil seeks with the *Allöosis*... In particular, Zwingli is henceforth not worthy of being answered further, unless he recants his blasphemous *Allöosis*. For as the saying goes: A public lie is not worthy of an answer; thus, he who denies a public article of faith is to be avoided as a public heretic. Now Zwingli not only denies this highest and most necessary article (that God’s Son died for us), but he also blasphemes it, saying: It is the most horrible heresy that has ever existed. His conceit and the damned *Allöosis* lead him to this, that he tears asunder the person of Christ and leaves us no other Christ than a mere man who died for us and redeemed us. What Christian heart can hear or endure such a thing? For with this, the entire Christian faith and the salvation of the whole world are utterly taken away and condemned. For whoever is redeemed by humanity alone is, in truth, not yet redeemed, nor will he ever be redeemed." (Great Confession. XX, 1180. 1206. sq.)

Luther: "Ah, Lord God, concerning such a blessed, comforting article, one should always be joyful, singing, praising, and thanking God the Father for such unspeakable mercy—that he let his dear Son become man and brother like us—without strife, without doubt, and in the right faith. Yet the miserable Satan causes such displeasure through proud, ambitious, desperate people that our dear and blessed joy must be hindered and spoiled. May God lament this! For we Christians must know this: Where God is not in the scale with us and does not provide the weight, we sink to the bottom with our dish. I mean it thus: If it were not to be said, 'God died for us,' but only 'a man,' then we are lost. But when God’s death and God who has died lie in the scale, he sinks down and we rise up as a light, empty dish. But he can also rise up again or spring out of his dish. Yet he could not sit in the dish; he had to become man like us, so that it could be said: God’s death, God’s torment, God’s blood, God’s death. For God in his nature cannot die, but now that God and man are united in one person, it is rightly called: God’s death, when the man dies who is one thing or one person with God... I have also had the Nestorians before me, who fought very stiffly against me, that the divinity of Christ could not suffer, and as a sign, Zwingli also wrote against me regarding this passage: *Verbum caro factum est* (John 1:14), and simply did not want *Verbum* to be called *factum*, but wanted it to be: *Verbum caro facta est*; the reason: God could not become anything. But at that time, I myself did not know that such was the conceit of Nestorius."

The same: "This now serves, as has often been said, so that we may be able to stand against the devil and overcome him in the struggle of death and other distresses when he terrifies us with sin and hell. For if he were to accustom me to look upon Christ as a mere man who was crucified and died for me, I would be lost; but when I hang the treasure and the weight upon the fact that Christ, both true God and man, died for me, etc., that outweighs and strikes far above all sin, death, hell, and all misery and heart-sorrow.

For when I know that He who is true God has suffered and died for me, and, in turn, the same true man has risen from the dead, ascended into heaven, etc., then I can certainly conclude that my sin and death are blotted out and overcome by Him, and that now there is no wrath or disfavor from God upon me, because I see and hear nothing in this Person but pure signs and works of grace.

See, thus learn to grasp this article, that one may keep this Person of Christ whole and enclose the work of both natures within one another, although the natures are distinct. For according to the divine nature, He is not born of a human, nor was anything taken from the Virgin. And it is true that God is the Creator, but man is a creature; here, however, they have come together into one Person and are now called God and man, one Christ; so that Mary has borne a Son, and the Jews crucified such a Person, who is God and man. Otherwise, if He were a mere man, like other saints, He would not be able, with all His holiness, blood, and dying, to take away one sin from us or to quench a drop of hell-fire.

This is our art, doctrine, and comfort from the Scripture that we have concerning Christ, even though it is regarded as pure foolishness before the world and sharp-witted reason. But let others be wise in the name of their god, the devil, and have heart-sorrow with their untimely grammar and rhetoric, with which they want to master the Scripture and tear it apart or at least make it void. They are poor grammarians who want to speak and judge of these high matters out of their art. Other people are required for this than these vocabulists and grammatists, namely, those who have wrestled and struggled with sin and death or have bitten and fought with the devil several times." (On John 14:16. VIII, 170 sq.)

Latin:

Kromayerus: ,,Propter officium etiam requirebatur persona σύνθετός, cum nudus Deus nec pati nec mori, nudus homo sufficienter pati et mori non poterant. Requirebatur itaque divina humanitas et humana divinitas. Pertinent huc omnes propositiones, in quibus de officio Christi prophetico, sacerdotali aut regio agitur. Es. 40, 10. Gal. 3, 13. 1 Cor. 15, 25. Quaedam propositiones biblicae, praesertim quae πρώτως sunt hujus generis, in pluribus generibus communicationis idiomatum considerari possunt... Propositio Johannis I. ep. c. 1. v. 7.: ,Sanguis

PE PERSONA CHRISTI. Jesu Christi Filii Dei mundat nos ab omni peccato‘, in tribus generibus considerari potest. Si formatur ita: Jesus Christus, Dei Filius, emundat nos a peccatis, est in secundo (tertio) genere, quia praedicatur αποτέλεσμα de persona. Si sic: Filius Dei fundit sanguinem, est in primo, quia praedicatur Ιδίωμα i. e. proprietas humanae naturae de persona. Si vero sic: Sanguis Jesu Christi (pars humanae naturae) habet vim emundandi, est in tertio (secundo), quia praedicatur αΐχημα divinum de parte humanae naturae.“ (Theol. pos.pol. I, 238. sq.)

N. Hunnius: ,,Est certum, si actiones divinae per naturam humanam fiunt, ita ut sint ^εανδρικαϊ, h. e. divinohumanae et humanodivinae, etiam naturas communicare suas operationes invicem; sic erat humana vox: ,Juvenis, tibi dico, surge‘, Luc. 7, 14., sed erat quoque divina vox, quia vox omnipotens mortuos ad vitam revocans; quis vero hic non agnosceret vocem humanam vehiculum abtionis divinae, idcirco operationum conjunctionem et communicationem vel manibus palparet?“ (Διάσκεψίς. § 653.)

Idem: ,,Communio operationum est consequens per se communicationis idiomatum ενεργητικών. Etenim si communicantur proprietates agentes, neeesse est, illas operari, prout sunt, nempe non in solo subjecto primo et naturali, sed in eo per illud etiam, quod idiomata per communicationem possidet. Ita non anima hominis videt facultate optica absque oculo, sed visivam potentiam oculo communicatam exercet atque exserit per oculum et in oculo; nec potest hanc suam facultatem usurpare, quam unice per oculum, qui, ut potentiae, sic et operationis factus fuit particeps. Quando autem cessat, anima suas operationes communicare corpori, rumpitur unionis hypostaticae vinculum.“ (L. c. § 647.)

Ita e. g. ad opus satisfactionis aut redemtionis, in quo includitur partim toleratio acerbissimae passionis et mortis, partim additio infiniti valoris (ut sit passio non nuda, sed satisfactoria), prius ad naturam humanam, posterius ad divinam naturam per se pertinet. Similiter ad opus illud miraculosum, quo Christus ad probandum suum, velut Messiae, officium homini coeco nato visum restituit, Joh. 9, 6. sqq., humana quidem Christi natura, quod suum est, contulit, quoad actum exspuendi in terram, faciendi lutum ex sputo, et illinendo lutum super oculos coeci, dicendo denique ei: vade, lava in piscina Siloae; divina vero natura, quod suum est, contulit influendo videlicet virtute infinita ad effectum illum supernaturalem producendum.

Fechtius: ,,Duo extrema cavenda sunt: primo, naturarum con· fusio, ne nimirum operationes unius naturae alteri, quasi ei propriae sint, adseribantur aut oriantur ex commixtione utriusque naturae; secundo, actionum separatio, ne putentur actiones utriusque naturae separatim a naturis fluere, quemadmodum e/g. duo rivuli separatim fluunt ad unum fontem vel lacum constituendum sine ulla communione; sed potius utriusque naturae proprietates intime sibi invicem communicare credendae sunt, ut nulla sit particula passionis humanae, quin sit divinitatis quasi anima imbuta, nec ulla divinitatis actio, quin imbuta humano sanguine, ad eum modum, quo gladius ignitus et secat et urit, igne et ferro suum quodlibet conferente, et tamen ita actione communi agunt, ut nec ferrum extra ignem ita penetranter secaret, nec ignis extra ferrum ita penetranter ureret.“ (Compend. th. thet. c. 17. § 51. p. 469.)

Olearius: ״Irenaeus, dum lib. 3. c. 21. dicit, Christum crucifixum et mortuum esse ησυχάζοντας τον λόγον, conquiescente Verbo, nequaquam excludit λόγον ab opere redemtionis, sed solum infert potentiae retractionem et inhibitionem exercitii per carnem, sine qua impossibile PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO I. fuisset, Christum pati et mori. Interim tamen sola humanitas non potuisset infinitum λντρον in hac passione praestare, si λόγος excluderetur.“ (Vid. Carpzovii Isag. in libb. symbol. p. 1515.)

Lutherus: ,,Dasheisst er (Zwingli) Allöosin, wenn etwas von der Gottheit Christi gesagt wird, das doch der Menschheit zustehet, oder wiederum, als Luc. 24, 26.: ,Musste nicht Christus leiden, und also zu seiner Ehre gehen?‘ Hie gaukelt er, dass Christus für die menschliche Natur genommen werde. Hüte dich, hüte dich, sage ich, vor der Allöosi, sie ist des Teufels Larven; denn sie richtet zuletzt einen solchen Christum zu, nach dem ich nicht gerne wollte ein Christ sein, nämlich dass Christus hinfort nicht mehr sei noch thue mit seinem Leiden und Leben, denn ein ander schlechter Heilige. Denn wenn ich das glaube, dass allein die menschliche Natur für mich gelitten hat, so ist mir Christus ein schlechter Heiland, so bedarf er wohl selbst eines Heilandes. Summa: es ist unsäglich, was der Teufel mit der Allöosi sucht. . . Insonderheit ist der Zwingel hinfort nicht werth, dass man ihm mehr antworten solle, er widerrufe denn seine lästerliche Allöosin. Denn wie man spricht: Eine Öffentliche Lügen ist keiner Antwort werth; also ist auch der als ein öffentlicher Ketzer zu meiden, der einen öffentlichen Artikel des Glaubens leugnet. Nun leugnet der Zwingel nicht allein diesen höchsten nöthigsten Artikel (dass Gottes Sohn für uns gestorben sei), sondern lästert dasselbe dazu und spricht: Es sei die allergreulichste Ketzerei, so je gewesen ist. Dahin führet ihn sein Dünkel und die verdammte Allöosis, dass er die Person Christi zertrennet, und lässt uns keinen andern Christus bleiben, denn einen lautern Menschen, der für uns gestorben und uns erlöset habe. Welches christliche Herz kann doch solches hören oder leiden? Ist doch damit der ganze christliche Glaube und aller Welt Seligkeit allerdings weggenommen und verdammt. Denn wer allein durch Menschheit erlöset ist, der ist freilich noch nicht erlöset, wird auch nimmermehr erlöset.“ (Grosses Bekenntniss. XX, 1180. 1206. sq.)

Lutherus: ,,Ach, Herr Gott, von solchem seligen, tröstlichen Artikel sollte man ungezankt, ungezweifelt, im rechten Glauben immer fröhlich sein, singen, loben und danken Gott dem Vater für solche unaussprechliche Barmherzigkeit, dass er uns seinen lieben Sohn hat lassen uns gleich Mensch und Bruder werden. So richtet der leidige Satan durch stolze, ehrsüchtige, verzweifelte Leute solchen Unlust an, dass uns die liebe und selige Freude muss verhindert und verderbet werden. Das sei Gott geklagt! Denn wir Christen müssen das wissen: Wo Gott nicht mit in der Wage ist und das Gewichte gibt, 80 sinken wir mit unsrer Schüssel zu Grunde. Das meine ich also: Wo es nicht sollte heissen: Gott ist für uns gestorben, sondern allein ein Mensch, so sind wir verloren. Aber wenn Gottes Tod und Gott gestorben in der Wageschüssel liegt, so sinket er unter und wir fahren empor als eine leichte ledige Schüssel. Aber er kann wohl auch wieder emporfahren oder aus seiner Schüssel springen. Er könnte aber nicht in die Schüssel sitzen, er müsste uns gleich ein Mensch werden, dass es heissen könnte: Gott gestorben, Gottes Marter, Gottes Blut, Gottes Tod. Denn Gott in seiner Natur kann nicht sterben, aber nun Gott und Mensch vereiniget ist in eine Person, so heissets recht: Gottes Tod, wenn der Mensch stirbt, der mit Gott ein Ding oder eine Person ist. . . Ich habe wohl auch vor mir Nestorianos gehabt, die sehr steif wider mich fochten, dass die Gottheit Christi nicht könnte leiden, und zum Wahrzeichen schrieb auch Zwinglius wider mich über diesen Spruch: Verbum caro factum est Joh. 1, 14., und wollt schlecht nicht, dass Verbum sollt factum heissen, sondern wollte haben: Verbum caro facta est; Ursache: Gott könne nichts werden. Ich aber zu der Zeit selbst nicht wusste, dass solches Nestorii Dünkel wäre.“

Idem: ״Das dienet nun dazu, wie nun oft gesagt ist, dass wir können wider den Teufel bestehen und ihn im Todeskampf und andern Nöthen überwinden, wenn er uns schrecket mit der Sünde und Hölle. Denn wo er mir das angewönne, dass ich Christum als einen lautern Menschen für mich gekreuziget und gestorben ansähe, so wäre ich verloren; wenn ich aber den Schatz und das Gewicht daran hänge, dass Christus beide, wahrhaftiger Gott und Mensch, für mich gestorben ist u. s. w., das wiegt und schlägt weit über alle Sünde, Tod, Hölle und alle Jammer und Herzleid.

Denn wenn ich das weiss, dass der, so wahrhaftiger Gott ist, für mich hat gelitten und gestorben ist, und wiederum, derselbige wahrhaftige Mensch von Todten auferstanden, gen Himmel gefahren u. s. w., so kann ich gewisslich schliessen, dass meine Sünd und Tod durch ihn getilget und überwunden ist, und nun bei Gott kein Zorn und Ungnade über mich ist, weil ich in dieser Person Nichts, denn eitel Gnaden-Zeichen und Werk, sehe und höre.

Siehe, also lerne diesen Artikel fassen, dass man diese Person Christi ganz behalte und beider Naturen Werk in einander schliesse, obwohl die Naturen unterschieden sind. Denn nach der göttlichen Natur ist er nicht von einem Menschen geboren, noch etwas von der Jungfrau genommen. Und ist wahr, dass Gott ist der Schöpfer, der Mensch aber eine Creatur oder Geschöpf; hier aber sind sie zusammen kommen in Eine Person und heisst nun Gott und Mensch Ein Christus; dass Maria hat einen Sohn geboren und die Juden solche Person gekreuzigt, welcher ist Gott und Mensch. Sonst, wo er lauter Mensch wäre, als andere Heilige, vermöchte er mit aller seiner Heiligkeit, Blut und Sterben nicht Eine Sünde von uns zu nehmen oder ein Tröpflein des höllischen Feuers zu löschen.

Das ist unsere Kunst, Lehre und Trost aus der Schrift, so wir von Christo haben, wiewohl es vor der Welt und spitzigen Vernunft für lauter Thorheit angesehen wird. Aber lass andere klug sein in ihres Gottes, des Teufels, Namen und das Herzeleid haben mit ihrer unzeitigen Grammatica und Rhetorica, so sie damit wollen die Schrift meistern und sie zerreissen oder je nichtig machen. Es sind arme Grammatici, die da wollen aus ihrer Kunst von diesen hohen Sachen reden und urtheilen. Es gehören andere Leute dazu, denn diese Vocabulisten und Grammatisten, nämlich, die etlichemal sich mit der Sünd und Tod gerauft und gefressen oder mit dem Teufel gebissen und gekämpft haben.“ (Ad Joh. 14, 16. VIII, 170. sq.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Leo the Great preceded our [theologians] in Epistle X with these words

Leo the Great preceded our [theologians] in Epistle X with these words: "Each form (i.e., each nature in the person of Christ) acts with the communication of the other, that which is proper to itself, the Word, namely, performing that which is of the Word, and the flesh executing that which is of the flesh."

Gerhard: "Those who argue that the human nature of Christ in the works of the office and redemption acts only in ways that are human, just as the divine acts in ways that are divine, commit the fallacy of composition and division, while they propose an insufficient definition of this kind. It is indeed most true that in the works of the office each nature of Christ acts according to what is proper to it, but the complete definition is not exhausted by that; rather, that which the canon of the Council of Chalcedon adds must also be added: 'With the communication of the other.' ...

Unless this περικοπή (interpenetration) is added, there would be no κοινωνία (communion) of idioms in this genus.

Wherefore, in this genus, three things must be accurately noted, so that the κοινωνία may be more illustrious in it. First, that the operations of both natures concur in one apotelesma (effect/result) and toward one apotelesma. Second, that while one nature is acting in the office of mediation and redemption, the other is not idle and doing nothing, much less is it separated, but remains personally united to the other that is acting.

Thus, while the humanity is suffering, the divinity is not idle, but is personally present to the suffering nature and strengthens and sustains it, so that it may be able to bear that immense burden of the sins of the whole world and the divine wrath due to those sins." PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION I.

and effects those saving passions, which are precious before the whole world. Third, that the human nature in the works of the office acts not only what is proper to itself, through its essential properties, but also what is truly divine, through the majesty and power communicated to it.” (L. c. § 283.) ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: Of the Calvinists, who 1.) deny that the κοινοποίησις or communication of the αποτελέσματα or actions of the office can be referred to the κοινωνίαν ιδιωμάτων. . . 2.) Teach that each nature acts by itself, alone and without the communication of the other, and thus that the human nature of Christ in the works of the office acts only humanly from its natural properties, and is to be entirely excluded from divine actions. 3.) Maintain that the flesh of Christ concurred in miracles only as a bare and αεργον instrument. . . That the flesh of Christ contributed no more to the performing of miracles than the hem of a garment did to the healing of the woman with the issue of blood.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 16. f. 300.) § 23. Therefore, those propositions pertain here whose predicate is an operation pertaining to the office of Christ; but whose subject is a concrete name, denominating the person of Christ either from both natures, or from one nature; indeed, even those in which the very name of the office is predicated in the concrete concerning the person of Christ.

Casp. Loescherus: “In the first genus the predicate is always an Ιδίωμα of the other nature; ... in the second genus the predicate is always an Ιδίωμα of the divine nature; ... but in the third genus the predicate is always divine αποτελέσματα.” (Theol. thetica. 1701. p. 104.) Such is that one: Christ died for our sins, 1 Cor. 15:3, where the subject, Christ, is a name of the person denominated from both natures; the predicate, to die for our sins, is a work of the mediatorial office, which comprises partly to die, which is an idiom of the human nature, and partly the addition of infinite value, so that that death might have the character of a λύτρον for sins. Corresponding to this are those: Christ Jesus gave himself (namely, unto death) for our sins, Gal. 1:4. Christ gave himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor, Eph. 5:2.

J. Wandalinus: “In passions, the subject *which* is the divine person itself, the subject *by which* is the human nature: ‘Christ was put to death in the flesh,’ 1 Pet. 3:18; in actions, the principle *which* is the whole person, the principle *by which* is the divine nature: ‘Christ was quickened by the Spirit,’ ibid.” (Ύποτύπωσις sanor. verb. Havniae 1703. p. 102.) Pertaining here are these: The Son of God (which is a concrete name of the divine nature) destroyed the works of the devil (by rescuing men from his power through the merit of his obedience and gathering them into the kingdom of grace; where, consequently, are included the actions and passions of the human nature and at the same time that infinite power, sufficient for destroying the kingdom of Satan, which then exerted itself at once) 1 John 3:8. The seed of the woman (the Messiah, from the human nature

denominated) shall crush the head of the serpent (that ancient one, or the devil, whose kingdom and power He shall destroy) Gen. 3:15, the Son of Man came to save souls Luke 9:56. Gerhard: "The Calvinists resolve that proposition, 'God has suffered,' in such a way that the final analysis eventually returns to this: Only the human nature has suffered (Steinius, in *Vindic. conc. irenicae*, f. 45, denies that the Calvinists exclude the λόγου ὑπόστασιν from the κοινωνία of passion and death; but that will remain true as long as they defend this axiom of theirs: Properties cannot be really communicated to another subject, even if united; and their own words testify against them), whence Zwingli explains that proposition by way of ἀλλοίωσιν... Calvin goes so far as to write in *Inst.*, bk. 2, ch. 17, s. 1: 'Indeed, I confess that if anyone wished to oppose Christ simply and in Himself to the judgment of God, there would be no place for merit, because there will not be found in man a dignity that can merit God.' Tilenus, in his notes to Bellarmine’s book on Christ, p. 13, analyzes it thus: 'Christ, in whom is the deity, having the humanity conjoined, suffers.' Herborn, in *Rudim.*, bk. 2, p. 100: 'Only the human nature of Christ died, not the deity, not the whole person.'" (L.c. §105.)

It is notably said that the person of Christ stands in the place of the subject, whether He is denominated from both natures or from one. For we have said that the fact that those things which are truly divine are rightly predicated of the human nature in the abstract, beyond those things which are proper to it, pertains to the second genus of communication. E.g., Christ is our mediator, savior, king. For it is the same, as far as the present matter is concerned, whether you say that Christ operates according to both natures by virtue of His office, or that a function belongs to Him by whose power He operates in a certain way. Gesner: "The names of the office: mediator, redeemer, etc., are ἐνεργητικά, by which operations and actions, and their effects and application to individual men, are signified." (*Orthod. conf.*, p. 302.)

Section II. ON THE STATES OF HUMILIATION AND EXALTATION. § 1. Although the communication of idioms, and therefore also the communication of majesty, followed the personal union in an inseparable bond, yet that majesty did not always manifest itself in the same way, but it came to pass that Christ was first humiliated, then exalted. See above, Sect. I, § 16 and 20. Whence it is evident that just as the divine nature was inseparably united to the human nature, so through that same union, which lasts perpetually, the divine majesty, viewed in *actu primo*, remained always communicated to the human nature. PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION II.

See Phil. 2:6 ff., especially v. 7, where it is expressly said of Christ: έαυτόν έζένωσε, he made himself empty (emptied, divested), and v. 9: ο Θεός αυτόν υπερύψωσε, God highly exalted him, or raised him to the highest sublimity.

Gerhardus: "The emptying of Christ is taken in a 1. ecclesiastical, 2. biblical sense. Ecclesiastically, i.e., according to the style of the doctors of the church, it is taken for the merciful inclination by which ό λόγος inclined himself to have mercy upon us and to succor us, and descending from heaven, deigned to assume human nature. This emptying, spoken of improperly and in the ecclesiastical sense, is called the 'humiliation of the incarnation.' Likewise σχετική (relative), by which the Son of God is said to have humbled himself by an 'inclination of compassion,' John 1:14, 3:13, 1 Tim. 3:16, Heb. 3:16. This must be explained θεοπρεπώς (in a manner worthy of God) concerning the καταβάσει (descent) from incorporeal majesty to the vileness of the body... In the biblical sense, or according to the style of the apostle in Phil. 2, the emptying is properly taken for the very κενώσει (emptying) of Jesus Christ, or of the incarnate λόγος." (Exeg. IV. § 293 ff.) § 2. Therefore, the emptying of Christ pertains to his human nature, and consists in this, that Christ for a time renounced the plenary use of the divine majesty, which his human nature had received as communicated in the personal union, and as a lowly man endured things that were far beneath the divine majesty.

For in that the Son of God assumed human nature, the divine nature, properly speaking, was not emptied by this, nor did it divest itself of its majesty or become inferior, being altogether immutable and incessantly using its perfections. Formula of Concord: "We also reject and condemn that the saying of Christ (Matt. 28:18): 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me,' is perverted by some with a horrible and blasphemous interpretation to this meaning: that all authority in heaven and on earth was restored to Christ according to his divine nature in the resurrection and ascension into heaven, just as if, while he was in the state of humiliation, he had laid aside and divested himself of that authority even according to his divinity. For by this doctrine not only are the words of Christ's testament perverted by a false explanation, but also the way is paved anew for the long-condemned Arian heresy, so that at length the eternal divinity of Christ is denied and the whole Christ, as he is, together with our salvation, is lost, unless this impious doctrine is constantly contradicted from the solid foundations of the Word of God and our catholic faith." (Art. VIII. Epit. p. 650.)

The same: "As far as the divine nature in Christ is concerned, since 'in him there is no,' as James testifies (James 1:17), 'variation,' nothing (as regards its essence and properties) was either added to or taken away from the divine nature of Christ through the incarnation, and through it, in itself or by itself, it was neither diminished nor increased." (Art. VIII. Declar. p. 684.) Luther: "Everything that is said of Christ's humiliation and exaltation should be attributed to the man, for the divine nature can neither be humiliated nor exalted... Although the two natures are distinct, yet it is one Person, so that everything that Christ does or suffers, God has certainly done and suffered, although yet..."

Latin:

Praeivit nostris Leo M. in Ep. X. his verbis: Agit utraque forma (i. e. utraque natura in persona Christi) cum communicatione alterius, quod sibi proprium est, verbo scilicet operante, quod verbi est, et carne exequente, quod carnis est.

Gerhardus: ״Qui disputant, humanam Christi naturam in operibus officii et redemptionis agere tantum, quae sunt humana, sicut divina agit, quae sunt divina: committunt illi fallaciam compositionis et divisionis, dum insufficientem definitionem hujus generis proponunt. Verissimum quidem est, in operibus officii utramque Christi naturam agere, quod cuique proprium est, sed eo non absolvitur integra definitio, verum addendum etiam illud, quod canon concilii Chalcedonensis addit: ,Cum communicatione alterius‘. . .

Nisi haec περικοπή addatur, nulla in hoc genere esset idiomatum κοινωνία.

Quare in hoc genere tria accurate sunt notanda, ut κοινωνία in eo sit illustrior. Primo, quod utriusque naturae operationes in uno apotelesmate et ad unum apotelesma concurrant. Secundo, quod una natura in officio mediationis ac redemtionis aliquid agente altera non sit otiosa et nihil agat, multo minus sit separata, sed agenti alteri personaliter unita maneat.

Sic patiente humanitate non est otiosa divinitas, sed adest personaliter naturae patienti eamque corroborat et sustentat, ut possit immensum illud onus peccatorum totius mundi et irae divinae peccatis illis debitae sustinere, PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO I.

et efficit passiones illas salutares ac coram toto mundo pretiosas. Tertio, quod humana natura in operibus officii agit non tantum, quae sibi propria sunt, per essentiales suas proprietates, sed etiam quae vere divina, per communicatam sibi majestatem et virtutem.“ (L. c. § 283.) ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: Calvinianorum, qui 1.) negant, κοινοποίησιν seu communicationem αποτελεσμάτων sive actionum officii ad κοινωνίαν ιδιωμάτων referri posse. . . 2.) Docent, utramque naturam suum agere per se, solam et absque communicatione alterius, atque sic humanam Christi naturam in operibus officii humana tantum agere ex naturalibus suis proprietatibus, a divinis vero actionibus prorsus exeludendam esse. 3.) Statuunt, carnem Christi ad miracula concurrisse ut nudum tantum et αεργον instrumentum. . . Carnem Christi non plus contulisse ad miracula facienda, quam fimbria vestis ad sanandäm haemorrhoousam.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 16. f. 300.) § 23. Pertinent igitur huc propositiones illae, quarum praedicatum est operatio ad officium Christi pertinens; subjectum autem est nomen concretum, sive ab utraque, a sive ab una natura b personam Christi c denominans; imo ■et istae, in quibus de persona Christi ipsum nomen officii in concreto d praedicatur.

Casp. Loescherus: ,,In genere primo praedicatum semper est Ιδίωμα alterius naturae; ... in secundo genere praedicatum semper est Ιδίωμα divinae naturae; ... in tertio autem genere praedicatum semper αποτελέσματα divina.“ (Theol. thetica. 1701. p. 104.) Talis est illa: Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris, 1 Cor. 15, 8., ubi subjectum, Christus, est nomen personae ab utraque natura denominatae praedicatum, το mori pro peccatis nostris, est opus officii mediatorii, quod complectitur partim το mori, quod est idioma humanae naturae, partim additionem infiniti valoris, ut mors illa haberet rationem λύτρου pro peccatis. Cui respondent illae: Christus Jesus dedit se ipsum (scilicet in mortem) pro peccatis nostris, Gal. 1, 4. J. Wandalinus: ,,In passionibus subjectum quod est ipsa divina persona, subjectum quo natura humana: ,Christus morte fuit affectus carne‘, 1 Pet. 3, 18.; in actionibus principium quod tota persona, principium quo divina natura: ,Christus vivificatus Spiritu‘, ibid.“ ('T7roτνπωσις sanor, verb. Havniae 1703. p. 102.) Huc pertinent istae: Filius Dei (quod est nomen concretum divinae naturae) dissolvit opera diaboli (eruendo homines e potestate ejus per meritum obedientiae suae et colligendo eos ad regnum gratiae; ubi proinde includuntur’actiones et passiones humanae naturae et eimul vis illa infinita, destruendo regno satanae sufficiens, quae se una tunc exseruit) 1 Joh. 3, 8. Semen mulieris (Messias, ab humana natura

PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II. denominatus) conteret caput serpentis (antiqui illius, sive diaboli, cujus regnum et potentiam destruet) Gen. 8, 16., Filius hominis venit salvare animas Lucae 9, 56. Gerhardus: ,,Calviniani propositionem illam: ,Deus est passus*, ita resolvunt, ut ultima tandem analysis eo redeat: Humana tantum natura est passa (Steinius in vindic. conc. irenicae f. 45. negat, Calvinianos a passionis et mortis κοινων'φ excludere λόγου νπόστασιν; sed tamdiu illud verum manebit, quamdiu defendunt hoc suum axioma: Propria non possunt alteri subjecto, tametsi unito, realiter communicari; ac contra ipsos propria eorum verba testantur), unde Cinglius propositionem illam explicat per ά?.λοίωσιν. . . Calvinus eo progreditur, ut scribat lib. 2. instit. c. 17. s. 1.: ,Equidem fateor, si quis simpliciter et per se Christum opponere vellet judicio Dei, non fore merito locum, quia non reperietur in homine dignitas, quae possit Deum promereri.* Tilenus in notis ad lib. Bellarm. de Christo p. 13. sic άναλϋει: ,Christus, in quo est deitas, conjunctam habens humanitatem, patitur.* Herborn. in rudim. lib. 2. p. 100.: ,Humana natura Christi tantum mortua est, non deitas, non tota persona.‘" (L.c.§105.)

Notanter dicitur, personam Christi stare subjecti loco, sive ab utraque, sive ab una natura denominetur. Nam quod de humana natura in abstracto, praeter ea, quae ipsi propria sunt, illa quoque, quae vere divina sunt, recte praedicatur, id ad secundum genus communicationis pertinere diximus. V. g. Christus est noster mediator, salvator, rex. Perinde enim ־est, quantum ad praesens attinet, sive dicas, Christum secundum utramque naturam operari ex officio, sive, ei competere functionem, cujus vi certo modo operetur. Gesnerus: ,,Nomina officii: mediator, redemtor etc., sunt ενεργητικά, quibus operationes et actiones, earumque effectus et applicatio ad singulos homines significatur." (Orthod, conf. p. 302.)

Sectio II. DE STATIBUS EXINANITIONIS ET EXALTATIONIS. § 1. Quamvis unionem personalem indivulso nexu secuta sit communicatio idiomatum, adeoque et communicatio majestatis,“ tamen majestas illa non eodem semper modo se exseruit, sed factum est, ut Christus primum exinanitus, deinde exaltatus esset* Vid. supra Sect. I. § 16. et 20. PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II.

Vid. Phil. 2, 6. sqq., praecipue v. 7., ubi expresse dicitur de Christo: έαυτόν έζένωσε, se ipsum inanem reddidit (inanivit, exinanivit), et v. 9.: ο Θεός αυτόν υπερύψωσε, Deus illum valde exaltavit, aut in summam sublimitatem extulit.

Gerhardus: ,,Exinanitio Christi accipitur in sensu 1. ecclesiastico, 2. biblico. In sensu biblico sive secundum stylum apostoli Phil 2. exinanitio proprie accipitur pro ipsa Jesu Christi sive λόγον incarnati κενώσει.“ (Exeg. IV. § 293. sq.) § 2. Nam quod Filius Dei assumsit naturam humanam, per hoc divina natura proprie loquendo exinanita non fuit, neque majestate sua ipsa se exuit aut inferior facta est, quippe prorsus immutabilis et perfectionibus suis incessanter utens. Formula Concordiae: ,,Rejicimus etiam damnamusque, quod dictum Christi (Matth. 28, 18.): ,Mihi data est omnis potestas in coelo et in terra‘, horribili et blasphema interpretatione a quibusdam depravatur in hanc sententiam: quod Christo secundum divinam suam naturam in resurrectione et ascensione ad coelos iterum restituta fuerit omnis potestas in coelo et in terra, perinde quasi, dum in statu humiliationis erat, eam potestatem etiam secundum divinitatem deposuisset et exuisset. VIII. Epit. p. 650.)

VIII. Declar. p. 684.) Lutherus: ,,Alles, was von Christi Niedrigung und Erhöhung ist gesagt, soll dem Menschen zugelegt werden, denn göttliche Natur mag weder geniedriget noch erhöhet werden. . . Obwohl die zwo Naturen unterschieden sind, so istJs doch Eine Person, dass alles, was Christus thut oder leidet, hat gewisslich Gott gethan und gelitten, wiewohl doch


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: only. The same thing happens to one nature

...only. The same thing happens to one nature. As in the parable: when I speak of a wounded leg of a man, I say: The man is wounded, yet his soul or the whole man is not wounded, but a piece of his body; because body and soul are one thing. Just as I must speak of body and soul distinctly, so also of Christ.” (Church Postil. XII, 210.) Chemnitius: “Humiliation was not an absence, privation, lack, loss, despoiling, laying aside, or stripping away of the attributes of divinity in the divine nature of the λόγος, as if it then either did not possess them or did not exercise them in itself; such that they had to be rendered or restored to the divinity; for He says, when the passion was imminent in the height of humiliation: ‘All things that the Father hath are mine’ (John 16), and John 6: ‘My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.’ But He is said to have emptied Himself because He did not always manifest His divine majesty through the assumed flesh during the time of humiliation. In exaltation, therefore, after the humiliation was laid aside, it was given to Christ that in the flesh, with the flesh, and through the assumed flesh, the majesty of the divinity might shine forth and manifest itself in full exercise. Therefore, that glory and exaltation was not rendered to the divine nature in itself, but was given to the human nature in that manner.” (De duabus naturis in Christo etc. libellus. Francof. et Witteb. 1653. c. XXII. fol. 108. sq.) Quenstedtius: “The subject of humiliation is either the ‘what’ or the ‘by which.’ The subject ‘what’ is the person of the λόγος, not as άσαρκος (without flesh) and to be incarnated, but as ένσαρκος (in the flesh) and incarnated; for it is said expressly in Phil. 2:5, ‘Christ Jesus,’ which names are of a person σννθέτον (composite) or composed of both natures... Nor do the predicates which are attributed to Christ in this place admit any other subject, namely: to have been in the ‘form of God,’ to have assumed the ‘form of a servant,’ to have been ‘emptied,’ ‘suffered,’ ‘died,’ ‘exalted,’ etc. The incarnation of the Word is indeed a humiliation, but not a humiliation (exinanitio). By humiliation (exinanitio), however, we understand with our predecessors the ‘evacuation of divine glory, the assumption of the form of a servant, and obedience unto the death of the cross,’ according to the apostolic definition in Phil. 2:7 sqq.; but the incarnation took place without such an evacuation, and therefore the incarnation is not a humiliation (exinanitio). Humiliation (humiliatio), however, is when ‘He who is established in the highest glory and majesty performs illustrious works for the sake of abject men,’ such as the humiliation certainly is, that the λόγος assumed flesh to redeem the human race, which Athanasius in Orat. c. Sabellianos calls the λόγος επίδοσιν, the ‘inclination of the Word from incorporeal majesty to His own finitude.’ Thus also God the Father is humiliated when He is said to have descended to confound the languages of men (Gen. 11:7), when He descends to deliver His people (Ex. 3:8). And the Holy Spirit is humiliated when, sent by the Father and the Son, He comes into the hearts of men, causes prayers, and performs other works of heavenly grace. Meanwhile, neither the Father, nor the λόγος, nor the Holy Spirit are said to be emptied (exinaniri). Therefore, they err gravely, e.g., the Calvinists, Papists, Weigelians, and Innovators, by not distinguishing ταπείνωσιν (humiliation) from κενώσει (emptying/exinanition), of which the former pertains to all the persons of the Deity, but the latter only to Christ, and indeed only in the state of humiliation, while He was living from His birth until the time of His resurrection. See Consilia th. Witteberg. P. I. p. 536. n. 6. The subject ‘by which’ is the human nature, as it alone is capable of deterioration. For Christ was in the form of God and had τά ίσα τφ θεφ (the things equal to God) and could have, if He had willed, conducted Himself as equal to God, only according to the human nature; only according to the flesh could He suffer, die, be deteriorated, be improved, and be exalted. The divine nature is απαθής (impassible), impassible, inalterable, and immutable, nor is it capable of any deterioration or improvement, emptying, or exaltation.” (Th. did.-pol. P. III. c. 3. membr. 3. s. 1. th. 2. 3. fol. 475. sq.) Kromayer: "There are some among the Reformed, as they wish to be called, who maintain that Christ was emptied even according to His divine nature. Since this opinion contradicts the Scriptures and orthodox antiquity, we reject it, relying upon the following foundations: 1. Because according to PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION II. ...according to which nature Christ was made a servant and endured the death of the cross, according to that same nature He was emptied and subsequently exalted. But according to this human nature, He was made a servant and endured the death of the cross. The major premise is proven from Phil. 2:7. The minor premise is evident from the fact that the King of kings and Lord of lords, who is ἀπαθής καὶ ἀθάνατος (1 Tim. 6:15, 16), cannot serve, suffer, or die. Hence the ancients said: "The Most High cannot be exalted"; likewise: "Not the Most High, but the flesh of the Most High is exalted"; likewise: "It is not the advancement of the One assuming, but of the One assumed." 2. Because the divine nature cannot empty itself of the use of the government which belongs to it by nature. Whence John 5:17 says: "My Father is working until now, and I am working." Now, if Christ, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, governed this universe in the days of His flesh according to His divine nature, then emptying does not in the least apply to Him according to this very nature. 3. Because ὑπερύψωσις is called a χάρισμα in Phil. 2:9: "God ἐχαρίσατο, i.e., out of grace gave to Christ Himself the name which is above every name." Now, truly, as God, He can receive nothing by grace. Christ as God gives all things; as man, He receives all things. But if Christ was not exalted according to His divine nature, then neither was He emptied according to the same. 4. Because no change falls upon God (Ps. 102:28; Mal. 3:6), indeed not even a τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα, i.e., not even a shadow of turning, as James speaks in his epistle, ch. 1, v. 17. 5. Because this opinion was rejected by hoary and sound antiquity as savoring of Arianism. For thus Leo the Great, Ep. 23 (as it is cited near the end of the Formula of Concord): "Let the adversaries of the truth say when or according to which nature the omnipotent Father exalted His Son above all things, or to which substance He subjected all things? For they were always subject to the Deity as Creator. If power was added to Him, if sublimity was exalted, He was lesser than the One advancing Him and did not possess the riches of that nature whose bounty He needed; but Arius drags into his fellowship anyone who thinks such things." See more passages in the same place. Antithesis: Emptying and exaltation apply to Christ according to both natures. *Elenchus*: To establish this opinion, the Reformed bring forward:

1. That species of emptying by which the Son of God, while still ἄσαρκος, lowered Himself from the heights of heaven to these lands and assumed human nature. But we respond by distinguishing between emptying properly so-called, which is the question at hand, and catachrestic emptying. When the Son of God assumed human nature, it was not an emptying properly so-called (because through the incarnation the Son of God did not desert the divine glory nor empty Himself of the use of the government of this universe), but a catachrestic one, namely, an inclination of compassion toward the human race.

2. That Christ suffered while ἡσυχάζοντος τοῦ λόγου, i.e., the Word being at rest. But we respond: that rest of the Word is to be understood in a certain respect, namely, regarding the warding off of injuries from the human nature, not regarding abstinence from the government of this universe. Otherwise, while the flesh was subjected to the injuries of enemies, the divine nature triumphed with miracles, darkening the sun, shaking the earth, and splitting rocks.

3. That with respect to men, the divine glory of the Word was obscured. But we respond: the issue here is not about the manifestation or obscuration of divine glory with respect to men, but about the true emptying of divine majesty as to its use. Christ commands us to pray that the name of God ἄσαρκος be hallowed (Matt. 6:9), even though it is and remains holy in itself, namely, among us, in our hearts. Wherefore, although the glory of the Father Himself is not acknowledged by all, He is not therefore said to be emptied.

4. That the Son of God assumed the form of a servant. But we respond: by the form of a servant, not the human nature itself is understood, but the condition of the human nature. Nor did any ignominy redound to the Son of God because of this, nor was He made lesser than the other persons of the Deity because He assumed human nature, because the union was made ἀτρέπτως καὶ ἀσυγχύτως, i.e., without any conversion or confusion of the natures.

5. That Christ in John 17:5 asks to be glorified with the glory which He had before the foundations of the world were laid; therefore, He did not have it for a time. But we respond: that is done because of the identity of the person. Above all, however, the words omitted in the objection must be heeded: "Glorify Me, Father, with Yourself." Therefore, it is not understood merely as a manifestation of glory with respect to men. Three things in particular are elicited from this golden saying: 1.) That Christ lacked, namely, Himself...

OF EXINANITION AND EXALTATION. according to the human nature, that glory with which He asks to be glorified; 2.) that this glory is infinite, which the Son had before the foundations of the world were laid; 3.) that this glorification takes place before God, not merely before men, as the Calvinists wish regarding the divine [nature], and the Tübingen theologians regarding the human nature. Finally, when they bring forward for themselves that simile used by the Fathers concerning the sun covered by clouds, it must be held that this happens rather on account of the human nature, through which, as a very dense cloud, the rays of the communicated divine majesty could not penetrate in the state of κένωσις, while the sun meanwhile lost nothing of its light.” (Theol. posit. pol. I, 256—258.) E. Hunnius: “The adversaries object that this passage in Philippians must be explained concerning Christ according to His deity. — Both the analogy of faith and the text itself refute that exposition, preventing us from referring that passage directly to the λόγος according to His deity. For Paul does not write in this present passage that the Son of God or the λόγος assumed a human nature, but that Jesus Christ (who, to be sure, was already God and man) assumed the form of a servant. Nor can it be affirmed that the humanity of Christ is that very form of a servant of which Paul speaks. For He laid aside the form of a servant after the resurrection. But He retained His humanity. If, however, the form of a servant and the assumed human nature were simply one and the same, then Christ, upon laying aside the servile form, would have simultaneously divested Himself of His humanity, or, by retaining His humanity, would retain the form of a servant and would still be a servant in His glory at the right hand of God; which stands in direct opposition to the manifest words of Peter in Acts 2, saying that Jesus who was crucified was exalted to the right hand of God and made Lord and Christ. Furthermore, neither does the Greek word ἐκένωσε, by which that very state of exinanition is expressed, admit that this state be accommodated to the nature of the deity, which, being invariable by reason of itself, cannot empty itself, but the λόγος governed heaven and earth with the Father and the Holy Spirit even at that time when He had emptied Himself with respect to His humanity; just as Christ says in John 5: ‘My Father is working until now, and I am working.’” (Libelli IV. de persona Christi etc. p. 61. sq.) Balduinus: “Paul speaks not of the λόγος, but of Jesus Christ, which is the name of the incarnate Son of God; of Him who is in the form of God, whereas the λόγος is the very form of God; of Him who laid aside the form of a servant, but never lays aside the human nature which He assumed in the incarnation; of Him who emptied Himself, or, according to the emphasis of the Greek word, evacuated Himself, which cannot be said of the λόγος; of Him who became obedient to the Father even unto the death of the cross, which Christ did not do with respect to His deity; finally, of Him who was exalted, which again does not befit the λόγος; concerning all of which we have treated more fully in their proper place. Let the scope of our apostle be observed here, whose purpose is not to teach how the Son of God assumed flesh, but how Jesus Christ in His humanity assumed the form of a servant and by this very act left an example of humility to His own; which is so true that Calvin himself writes upon this passage: ‘Paul does not teach here what Christ was, but how He conducted Himself.’” (Disp. de cap. 2. ep. ad Phil. Witteb. 1617. B. b.) Dannhauerus: “Whom did He empty? Ἑαυτόν, not by reason of His deity, for thus ‘the Son works likewise’ (John 5:19), ‘the Son of Man is in heaven’ (3:13), but by reason of His humanity, which alone is capable of exinanition.” (Hodosoph. Phaenom. VIII. L. p. 351. sq.) ANTITHESES. Gerhardus: “1 The Jesuits pervert the doctrine concerning the exinanition and exaltation of Christ in many ways: 1.) They explain the exinanition and the assumption of the servile form absolutely and immediately concerning the work of the incarnation. Cornelius a Lapide in comm. Phil. 2 Salmeron ibid... 2 The Calvinists 1.) establish that Christ was emptied and exalted according to both natures. Beza P. I. resp. ad Coll. p. 96 Sohnius in exeg.. PART III. CAP. II. SECTIO II. p. 246. Anhald. in apol. Germ. contra Elector. p. 417. et a. . . 3.) they define the exinanition and the assumption of the servile form simply concerning the incarnation.” (L. c. § 313. sqq.) Thomasius: "As the assumption of human nature, the Incarnation is at the same time a self-limitation of God the Son." (Christi Person und Werk. Second Edition. II. § 40. p. 164.) "In it (the humiliation), the divine act of the beginning becomes the God-man act of his whole life. The difference between it and the self-limitation already contained in the incarnation consists, therefore, in the fact that the humiliation does not have as its subject, like the former, the λόγος άσαρκος, but the λόγος ένσαρκος, that is, the whole unified God-man; furthermore, that as the God-man continuation of that self-limitation, it enters through the path of lowliness and suffering, through the way of the cross, and thus ever deeper into the direction once taken. . . It (the earthly life of the Redeemer) is a revelation of the immanent divine attributes, of absolute power, truth, holiness, and love. For just as little as the Son surrendered these divine essential determinations, which as such are inseparable from the essence of God, with the Incarnation, just as little does he withhold their use as the One who became man. . . Nevertheless, the humiliation is at the same time an emptying, a continued emptying of the divine mode of being and acting, which he surrendered with the incarnation, and precisely thereby of the so-called relative divine attributes, in which the immanent ones manifest themselves outwardly and come to appearance: omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence. He renounces the possession of these attributes... He was not an omnipotent man. Even the miracles that he performed prove nothing to the contrary; for those are the works that the Father gives him; he does not do them out of his own ability, but in the power, at the behest of Him who sent him. . . It is no different with his knowledge. . . The knowledge of the Redeemer, however, even that concerning God’s counsel and will, develops in a successive manner; it matures with growing mental powers under natural mediations and conditions, and has its limits even in the matured man. . . The Mediator was not an omniscient man.—As far as presence is concerned, finally, the assumption that he existed outside the limitation of space during this stage would obviously destroy the truth of his entire historical life. . . According to this, then, the humiliation is for us not a mere veiling, but a real kenosis of the designated divine attributes, and indeed not merely of their use, but of their possession. . . We say, therefore, simply: the Redeemer was, during his earthly state of life, neither omnipotent, nor omniscient, nor omnipresent. But we say this of the whole undivided person of the same, of the Son of God who became man. Nothing could be further from us than the idea: according to his humanity he may have surrendered those divine attributes, whether their possession or use, but according to his divinity he possessed and used them." (L. c. § 43. p. 236—240.) "From the research of the later Lutheran dogmaticians. . . our doctrine of the humiliation differs in the following points: Firstly, by its concept; for while for us the humiliation is only the chronologically historical God-man continuation of the self-limitation of the Logos that coincides with the Incarnation, for them it rests upon a special act of the One who became man, which they still distinguish from the Incarnation. . . Secondly: while they designate as the subject of the humiliation the Son of God who became man, specifically as the subjectum quod the whole person, and as the subjectum quo his human nature, this distinction falls away entirely for us. We say simply, the subject is Christ. Thirdly: while they
