Es (das irdische Leben des Erlösers) ist Offenbarung der immanenten göttlichen Eigenschaften, cter absoluten Macht, Wahrheit, Heiligkeit und Liebe. Denn so wenig sich der Sohn dieser göttlichen Wesensbestimmtheiten, die al3 solche von dem Wesen Gottes unzertrennlich sind, mit der Incarnation begeben hat, so wenig hält er als der Menschgewordene ihren Gebrauch zurück. . . . Nichts desto weniger ist die Erniedrigung zugleich Entäusserung, fortgesetzte Entäusserung der göttlichen Seins und Wirkungsweise, deren er sich mit der Fleischwerdung begeben hat, und eben damit der sogenannten relativen göttlichen Eigenschaften, in denen die immanenten nach aussen hin sich manifestlren’ und zur Erscheinung kommen: der Allmacht, Allwissenheit, Allgegenwart. Auf den Besitz dieser Eigenschäften leistet er Verzicht... Er war kein allmächtiger Mensch. Selbst die Wunder, die er vollbrachte, beweisen dagegen nichts; denn das sind die Werke, die ihm der Vater gibt; er thut sie nicht aus eigenem Vermögen, sondern in der Kraft, auf das Geheiss dessen, der ihn gesandt hat. . . Nicht anders verhält es sich mit seinem Wissen. . . Das Wissen des Erlösers aber, auch das um Gottes Rath und Willen, entwickelt sich auf successive Weise, es reift mit den wachsenden Geisteskräften unter natürlichen Vermittlungen und Bedingungen, und hat auch in dem gereiften Manne seine Grenzen. . . Der Mittler war kein allwissender Mensch.—Was endlich die Gegenwart betrifft, so zerstörte offenbar die Annahme, er habe während dieses Stadiums ausserhalb der Beschränkung des Raumes existirt, die Wahrheit seines ganzen geschichtlichen Lebens. . . Hiernach ist uns also die Erniedrigung nicht eine blosse Verhüllung, sondern eine wirkliche Kenosis der bezeichneten göttlichen Eigenschaften, und zwar nicht blos ihres Gebrauches, sondern ihres Besitzes. . . Wir sagen also einfach: der Erlöser war während seines irdischen Lebensstandes weder allmächtig, noch allwissend, noch allgegenwärtig. Das aber sagen wir von der ganzen ungetheilten Person desselben, von dem menschgewordenen Sohne Gottes. Nichts kann uns ferner liegen, als die Vorstellung: seiner Menschheit nach habe er zwar jener göttlichen Eigenschaften, gleichviel ob ihres Besitzes oder Gebrauches, sich begeben, seiner Gottheit nach aber sie besessen und gebraucht.“ (L. c. § 43. p. 236—240.) ״Von der Forschung der späteren lutherischen Dogmatiker. unterscheidet sich unsere Lehre von der Erniedrigung in folgenden Puncten: Erstlich durch ihren Begriff; denn während uns die Erniedrigung nur die zeitgeschichtlich gottmenschliche Fortsetzung der mit der Incarnation zusarnmenfallenden Selbstbeschränkung des Logos ist, beruht sie ihnen auf einem besondern Act des Mensch gewordenen, den sie noch von der Incarnation unterscheiden. . . . Zweitens: während sie als das Subject der Erniedrigung den menschgewordenen Sohn Gottes, und zwar als das subjectum quod die ganze Person, als das subjectum quo die menschliche Natur desselben bezeichnen, so fällt uns diese Distinction ganz weg. Wir sagen einfach, das Subject ist Christus. Drittens: während sie


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: ON EXINANITION AND EXALTATION

ON EXINANITION AND EXALTATION. ...only let [Him] renounce the use of the divine attributes communicated to His humanity according to its nature, we posit a renunciation of the possession as well—a difference, however, which is to a certain extent balanced again by our distinction between immanent and relative attributes... The fourth difference is all the more significant: for while they limit the renunciation of the use of the divine attributes to the humanity of Christ, they nevertheless allow Him, according to His divine nature, to rule heaven and earth omnipotently and omnipresently; we refer the self-limitation to the whole person, including the divine side of the same.” (L. c. p. 253 sq.)

Luthardt: “While the Son of God assumed an earthly-human nature, He indeed preserved His divine nature and the inalienable essential glory of the same, but in the state of humiliation, He renounced, for His relation to the world, His divine mode of existence and its corresponding exercise of power, only to return to the same with the exaltation, but now as the One who has become man.” (Kompend. der Dogm. Third ed. p. 155.)

Philippi: “Finally, we must still consider that form of modern believing and at the same time speculative Christology which can be described as the most widespread in modern times. We mean the doctrine of the self-renunciation of the Logos. (Cf. Dorner, On the correct formulation of the dogmatic concept of the immutability of God, etc. This article provides a characterization and critique of the various forms of the kenosis of the Logos, in which it appears in Sartorius, König, Gaupp, Delitzsch, v. Hofmann, Ebrard, Liebner, Thomasius, Gess. It is also found in Lange, Schmieder, Steinmeyer, G. L. Hahn, Kahnis, and many others)... But if the self-renunciation is limited only to the relative attributes, this is to be called an untenable suspension of the kenotic dogma, if only because with the abandonment of omniscience, the divine self-consciousness, which is certainly to be regarded as an immanent attribute, is at the same time abandoned. The kenosis of the Logos finds its consistent completion only in the assumption that the Son of God, at His incarnation, divested Himself of all divine attributes, the immanent as well as the relative. In this completion, it is represented by Gess... We have here a complete transposition and transformation of the Godhead into the humanity.” (Kirchl. Glaubenslehre. Second ed. IV. First half, p. 386 sqq.)

For we understand this by μορφὴ τοῦ θεοῦ, or the form of God, in which Christ is said to have been, l. c. v. 6, and it is added: He did not count it a robbery, that is, He was firmly persuaded that this was by no means alien to Him, nor snatched, but rightly belonging to Him, that He should be equal to God; and yet He emptied Himself.

Quenstedtius: “Μορφὴ τοῦ θεοῦ does not primarily and principally, formally and precisely, denote the divine essence and majesty of the Logos immediately, but it consignifies and connotes it. It denotes, however, properly the glorious divine condition or the glory and the universal use of divine majesty, which cannot consist without true deity, but presuppose the same in the same hypostasis. In a few words: μορφὴ τοῦ θεοῦ designates the glorious divine state with the connotation of the divine essence, but not immediately, directly, and quidditatively, the divine essence and nature itself. For μορφὴ θεοῦ and μορφὴ δούλου are opposites, as the adversaries themselves admit; now, however, the form of a servant is not the human nature itself; therefore, the opposite deiformity is not the divine essence.” (L. c. th. 4. f. 476 sq.)

Scherzerus: “By ‘form of God’ the divine nature cannot be understood, nor by ‘form of a servant’ the human nature. Otherwise, in the exinanition, the nature... Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.6 PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II.

divine, but in the state of exaltation had laid aside the human nature, and thus in neither state would he be θεάνθρωπος, which is absurd. Therefore, the emptying is wrongly defined by the incarnation; by which logic, the exaltation would have to be described by the excarnation.” (Syst. L. VIII. p. 221.)

Balduinus: “Although some of the fathers explain the form of God and of a servant as referring to the divine and human nature itself, this cannot prejudice the truth. For they spoke somewhat more securely and freely, since there were not yet those who denied that the majesty of the λόγος had been communicated to the assumed flesh.” (Disp, de cap. 2. ep. ad Phil. Witteb. 1617. B. 2. b.)

And thus it was not so that the use of majesty was indeed perpetual and full, but occurred secretly or latently, nor as if Christ produced no specimens of divine majesty during the state of emptying; but rather that he used that majesty more rarely and as it were extraordinarily, and not ordinarily and incessantly. To this pertains what is said in Luke 2:52, that Christ increased, just as in age and stature, so also in wisdom.

Quenstedtius: “The object of the emptying, or that by which Christ emptied himself, is not the essence or divine majesty communicated to the flesh. For if he had withdrawn the communicated divine majesty from the assumed flesh, he would have rescinded or dissolved the personal union itself; but from the first moment of conception, the Son of God was and remained, and perpetually retained and possessed the whole fullness of the deity inhabiting him according to the flesh, αχωρίστως. But that which he renounced was, in general, the μορφή του θεού, i.e., the glorious divine state or deiformity, that is, the plenary, universal, and uninterrupted or ceaseless use of divine majesty; not that he never used it, but that he did not use it always, and only then, as often as the reason of his office required. Phil. 2:6, 7...

Specifically, the object of the emptying, or that which the man Christ Jesus renounced, is the plenary and universal use: 1) Of divine glory, for he asks for it from the Father, John 17:5. 2) Of all opulence, through poverty, Matt. 8:20, 2 Cor. 8:9. 3) Of omnipotence, through freely assumed infirmities, so that in his agony he had need of angelic strengthening, Luke 22:42, 43. He also suffered himself to be apprehended, bound, mocked, and crucified, ibid. v. 53, 54, 63; 23:33, 35, 37. 4) Of omniscience, through ignorance. Isa. 7:15, 16: ‘Until he knows to refuse the evil and choose the good’; therefore, as a man, he did not know from the first point of conception and immediately in infancy to discern evil from good. The same is clear from the gradual progress or proficiency of wisdom, Luke 2:52. But the progress of age and the progress of wisdom belong not to the divine, but to the human nature. 5) Of omniscience, which we prove from the ignorance of the barren fig tree, Matt. 21:19, Mark 11:13; of the final judgment, Matt. 24:36 and Mark 13:32; of the burial place of Lazarus, John 11:34. 6) Of omnipresence; for he did not universally usurp the majesty of omnipresence among creatures in the days of his flesh, but only then began to govern all creatures in the whole world omnipresently and omnipotently when he was exalted to the right hand of God the Father, Ps. 110:1, Eph. 1:20. 7) Finally, of the worship of religious adoration, as the state of exaltation is defined by its plenary use, Phil. 2:9, 10, 11; cf. Heb. 2:7.” (L. c. th. 4. 5. fol. 476. 480.)

Hollazius: “The emptying of Christ is not a mere κρύψις or concealment of divine majesty. For the emptying 1) does not fall upon the exalted Christ, upon whom, however, the concealment of majesty does fall; for we await the ἐπιφάνειαν καὶ ἀποκάλυψιν, the appearing and revelation, of Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 1:7. 2) Because Christ was truly emptied before God, angels, and men; but if Christ had only concealed the ἀρχήματα communicated to him, he would indeed have been obscure before men, but glorious before God. Yet he prayed to be glorified before God, John 17:5. 3) The concealment of gifts is not a true emptying, just as the sun covered by clouds is not truly darkened; which...”

we do not deny that Christ concealed the κτῆσις, or possession, of the communicated majesty and did not exercise it everywhere.” (Exam. th. P. III. s. 1. c. 3. membr. 3. q. 112. p. 765.)

Gerhard: “That κρύψις [concealment] can be referred both to the communication of majesty and to the use of the communicated majesty. With respect to the former, it can rightly be so called, because the divine majesty was hidden in the assumed flesh, but not entirely separated from it (Col. 2:3). With respect to the latter, however, it was not merely a κρύψις, but a true and real κένωσις [emptying], as the assumption of the form of a servant shows, which Christ subsequently laid aside in his exaltation.” (L. c. § 316.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: “Antithesis: of the Tübingen theologians D. L. Osiander, D. Melch. Nicolai, and D. Theod. Thummius, who maintained that ‘Christ, according to his human nature, even in the very state of humiliation, and indeed in death itself, powerfully and omnipresently governed heaven and earth, and thus always and incessantly fully, though secretly, exercised the majesty of omnipresence and omnipotence, which was truly communicated to him by virtue of the personal union.’ ... They further taught that, ‘just as the preceding humiliation was a withdrawal and concealment in the priestly office, but in the royal office only a concealment of the χρῆσις [use] of the divine majesty: so the subsequent exaltation was, regarding the priestly office, a true and real exaltation; but regarding the royal office, only a revelation of the preceding omnipresent, omnipotent, all-wise, and incessant dominion of Christ, as he is man.’ ... They asserted... ‘that Christ, as a man risen again and exalted to the right hand of God, did not finally arrive at the plenary use of divine majesty in the government of the world, but only received a new mode of government, namely, one that is majestically glorious and manifest.’ ... They then inculcated that ‘Christ ascended into heaven even when he was assumed into God.’” (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 560.) “

This question was agitated... between the Tübingen theologians... and the Marburg theologians D. Balth. Menzer and D. Just. Feurborn in the year 1619 et seq.” (L. c. f. 557.)

This is that form of a servant which Christ is said to have assumed (l. c.), and to which is attributed the ὁμοίωμα καὶ σχῆμα τῶν ἀνθρώπων, the likeness and appearance of men, namely, regarding his external state. To this pertains that humiliation even unto death, and death indeed on a cross (l. c.). § 8. Specifically, one must consider here a) Christ’s conception and b) nativity, c) education and d) visible conversation among men, e) and finally his passion, f) death, and g) burial. These are considered as being within the state of humiliation and its arguments, although they also deserve to be considered in themselves as parts of the course of Christ’s life on earth.

Latin:

Christum seiner Menschheit nach nur auf den Gebrauch der ihr mitgetheilteil göttlichen Eigenschaften verzichten lassen, statuiren wir eine Entäusserung auch des Besitzes —, eine Differenz, die sich jedoch durch unsere Unterscheidung zwischen immanenten und relativen Eigenschäften gewissermassen wieder ausgleicht. . . Um so bedeutender ist die vierte Differenz: denn jene beschränken die Entäusserung des Gebrauche der göttlichen Eigenschaften auf die Menschheit Christi, lassen ihn aber dabei seiner göttlichen Natur nach allmächtig und allgegenwärtig Himmel und Erde regieren; wir beziehen die Selbstbeschränkung weil auf die ganze Person, auch auf die göttliche Seite derselben.“ (L. c. p. 253. sq.)

Luthardtius: ,,Indem der Sohn Gottes irdischmenschliche Natur annahm, bewahrte er zwar seine göttliche Natur und die unveräusserliehe Wesensherrlichkeit derselben, begab sich aber im Stande der Erniedrigung für sein Verhältniss zur Welt seiner göttlichen Existenzweise und ihrer entsprechenden Machtbethätigung, um erst mit der Erhöhung in dieselbe, aber nun als Menschgewordener, zurückzutreten.“ (Kompend. der Dogm. Dritte Aufl. p. 155.)

Philippi: ,,Wir haben schliesslich noch diejenige Form der modern gläubigen und zugleich speculativen Christologie zu betrachten, welche als die in der Neuzeit am weitesten verbreitete bezeichnet werden kann. Wir meinen die Lehre von der Selbstentäusserung des Logos. (Vergl. Dorner, Ueber die richtige Fassung des dogmat. Begriffs der Unveranderlichkeit Gottes u. s. w. Dieser Artikel gibt eine Charakteristik und Kritik der verschiedenen Formen der Kenose des Logos, in welchen dieselbe bei Sartorius, König, Gaupp, Delitzsch, v. Hofmann, Ebrard9 Liebnery Thomasius, Gess auftritt. Sie findet sich ausserdem bei Lange, Schmieder, Steinmeyer, G. L. Hahn, Kahnis u. A. m.)... Wenn aber die Selbstentäusserung nur auf die relativen Eigenschaften beschränkt wird, so ist dies schon deshalb eine unhaltbare Sistirung des kenotischen Dogma’s zu nennen, weil mit dem Aufgeben der Allwissenheit zugleich das göttliche Selbstbewusstsein, welches doch gewiss als immanente Eigenschaft zu betrachten ist, auf gegeben ist. Die Kenose des Logos findet ihre consequente Vollendung nur in der Annahme, dass der Sohn Gottes bei seiner Menschwerdung sich sämmtlicher göttlichen Eigenschäften, eben sowohl der immanenten, als der relativen entkleidet habe. In dieser Vollendung vertritt sie Gess. . . Wir haben hier eine völlige Umsetzung und Verwandlung der Gottheit in die Menschheit.“ (Kirchl. Glaubenslehre. Zweite Aufl. IV. Erste Hälfte, p. 386. sqq.)

Hanc enim intelligimus per μορφψ του θεου, seu formam Dei9 in qua Christus fuisse dicitur 1. c. v. 6. et additur: Non duxit rapinam esse, id est, certo sibi persuasum habuit, hoc a se minime alienum, nec raptum, sed sibi recte competens, ut sit aequalis Deo; et tamen se ipsum inanivit.

divinam, in exaltatione vero naturam humanam deposuisset, adeoque in neutro statu ΰεάνΰρωπος esset, quod absurdum. Male igitur exinanitio per incarnationem definitur; quo pacto exaltatio per excarnationem esset describenda.“ (Syst. L. VIII. p. 221.)

Sed id, quo se abdicavit, in genere fuit μορφή τον θεον i. e. status divinus gloriosus seu deiformitas h. e. divinae majestatis plenarius, universalis et non interruptus sive indesinens usus; non, quod nunquam ea uteretur, sed quod non semper et tum solum, quoties ex officii ratione expediret. Phil. 2, 6. 7. . .

Ephes. 1, 20. 7) Denique cultus adorationis religiosae, utpote cujus plenario usu status exaltationis definitur Phil. 2, 9. 10. 11. cf. Hebr. 2, 7.“ (L. c. th. 4. 5. fol. 476. 480.)

### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Gerhard: “The state of humiliation begins at the first moment of the…

Gerhard: “The state of humiliation begins at the first moment of the incarnation and lasts until the time of the burial inclusive, which whole course of Christ’s life on these earths the apostle in Hebrews 5:7 calls ‘the days of his flesh,’ by which, through a Hebraism, is signified that time during which Christ lived among men as passible (2 Cor. 5:16), during which he was subject to the infirmities of the flesh, yet without any sin.” (L. c. § 304.) PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION II.

Gesnerus: "When did this emptying begin? — Immediately from the very incarnation of the Son of God. For as soon as He existed in the 'form of God,' that is, as soon as this man Jesus Christ received the use of divine majesty, He showed His humility in this very thing, that by the usurpation of such glory He voluntarily abdicated Himself, and by a most free will abstained from that glory which had truly accrued to Him from the union." (Orthod. confess. de persona et officio Salvatoris nostri. 1595. p. 254 sq.)

E. Hunnius: "Under the emptying of Christ is comprised that whole time which intervenes between the first origin of His conception and birth and His resurrection, excepting the special divine actions and miracles, through which certain rays of that divine majesty received through the union shone forth under that servile form.

Do you think that the miracles performed by Christ are to be attributed to His deity alone, or indeed to His deity and humanity together? — To the deity indeed principally and as the first principle of the miracles. For the power of performing miracles is an idiom of the deity alone, as it is written: 'You alone do wonders.' But because the λόγος dwells personally in the assumed flesh with the entire fullness of His deity, He therefore exerts this power of His to perform miracles through the humanity, inasmuch as He has assumed it into the κοινωνία of His power...

Nor is the blasphemy of those to be tolerated in the church of God who say and write that the most holy human nature of the Lord contributed nothing more to the miracles than His human voice and external ministry, which was also common to the prophets and the apostles. For how great a difference there is between the miracles of Christ and those of the disciples, the evangelical history clearly tells us; while it confirms that Christ indeed declared His own glory and majesty in the miracles, the apostle, however, records that he did not perform prodigies in his own name and virtue, but in the name of Jesus of Nazareth." (Libelli IV. de persona Christi etc. 1590. p. 64—66.)

Which we indeed examined above in Sect. I. § 5. and following; but now we consider it not precisely in itself, but insofar as it pertains to the state of emptying, or, insofar as the flesh of Christ, although not from male seed, was nevertheless formed in the womb of a woman and from her blood mass; by which reasoning it is certain that some infirmities concur, which could have had no place, so that the Son of God might nevertheless become true man.

Gerhardus: "Nor let it seem strange or doubtful to anyone that we refer to the state of emptying not only the passion, crucifixion, death, and burial of Christ, but also His conception and birth; because a distinction must be made between the incarnation and the mode of the incarnation. The Son of God could have formed a human nature by immediate creation, and by assuming the same into the unity of His person could have become man, even if He had not been conceived in the womb of a mother, which was, so to speak, an internal birth, carried in the womb of a mother for nine months and brought forth from the womb into the light, which was an external birth. For it is certain that Adam was a true man, who nevertheless was born neither in the womb nor from the womb. But 'for us and for our salvation' He willed not only to become man, but also to assume human nature from our flesh and voluntarily to subject Himself to the infirmities which are accustomed to happen to infants in conception and birth, so that He might sanctify our unclean conception and birth and obtain salvation for infants themselves while still enclosed in the womb." (L. c. § 304.)

Quenstedtius: "God by no means supplied or sustained the role of a father in the temporal generation of Christ, nor did He provide and add that which an earthly father is accustomed to provide or add in the procreation of children; nor is the Son of God called [the Son of God] on account of the conception from the Holy Spirit... Therefore, Socinus introduced this monster of an opinion and Smalcius defended it, with the others of this sect not denying it, lest they be forced to admit the [divine sonship] of Christ, the Savior

OF THE HUMILIATION AND EXALTATION. ours, the consubstantial deity and eternal generation from the essence of God the Father. . . We oppose the following arguments: Christ is called ἀπάτωρ with respect to his humanity and temporal birth, just as he is called ἀμήτωρ with respect to his deity and generation, Heb. 7:3. 2. Generation, properly so called, is derived only from the substance of the generator. . . But the humanity of Christ did not proceed from the substance of God. . . Christ is indeed called the Son of the Virgin Mary, but not of the Holy Spirit. . . They wish to maintain that Christ is the Son of God because of the divine conception, from the particle διὸ καί in Luke 1:35. . . Resp.: . . . "The 'power of the Most High' in this place is not the Holy Spirit or the power of the Holy Spirit, but the Son of God himself, who is called δύναμις θεοῦ in 1 Cor. 1:24. . . The heavenly messenger means to say: 'διὸ καί, therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee, Mary, shall be called and shall truly be the Son of God, because the substantial power of God, ὁ λόγος, will assume flesh in thee and from thee through a miraculous overshadowing.'" (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 570—572.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: Antithesis: 1. Of the Socinians; for thus Socinus writes in *Antiwieko* f. 221: "'The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee,' he says, 'is the same as if he had said: what is wont to happen in the begetting of a man by the work of a man, here happens by the work of divine power.'" He adds in the same place: "That some created substance was sent by God into the virgin's womb, so that Christ had not only a mother, but also a father." In *L. Quod regn. Pol.* f. 36, he writes: "The mode of conception. . . is the cause why the man Jesus of Nazareth himself, who is Christ, is called the Son of God." 2. Of the Arminians; for thus their latest leader, Steph. Curcellaeus, asserts in *Rel. Christ. institut.* l. 5. c. 3. th. 5: "that the Holy Spirit in this generation supplied that which was lacking on the part of the man, by creating immediately in the womb of the virgin a substance from which, joined with her blood, the body of Jesus was formed." (L. c. f. 570. sq.)

Hofmannus: "Accordingly, the passage (Luke 1:35) means that the child, who gains the beginning of his life in Mary through the effective power of God, is called the Son of God for that reason. We oppose this valid explanation regarding the sense in which Jesus is called the Son of God to those dogmaticians who deny that he is so called because of his conception from the Holy Spirit, and who rather distinguish a double generation: an eternal generation, through which he has that which he is as the Son of God, and a temporal generation, through which he has that which he is as man or Son of man." (*Schriftbeweis*. Ed. prim. I, 114.)

Cf. above, antithesis P. I. c. 1. § 39. In which it is especially considered that the fruit of Mary's womb, carried for the customary months, was finally brought into the light just as if according to the common lot of men. That, however, which some think—that Mary gave birth to her son with a closed womb—is uncertain; but the lowliness of his birth and the contempt and poverty of the newborn are more certain and manifest, Luke 2: 7.

Quenstedtius: "The birth of the Virgin Mary was natural and in no way different from the other accidents of natural births, and thus there happened to Mary in labor those things which are otherwise wont to happen in birth and to accompany birth." (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 576.)

Lutherus: "Some also dispute how this birth occurred, as if she were delivered of the child in prayer, in great joy, before she was aware of it, without any pain. Which devotion I do not reject; perhaps it was invented for the sake of the simple-minded. But we ought to remain with the Gospel, which says that she gave birth to him, and with the article of faith, where we say: who was born of Mary, the Virgin. There is no deception here, but, as the words sound, a true birth. . . Except that she [gave birth] without PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II.

she] bore [Him] without shame, without pain, and without injury, just as she had conceived without sin, Gen. 3:16. The curse of Eve did not pass over her, which says: ‘In pain you shall bring forth your children’; otherwise, everything happened to her just as it happens to a woman giving birth.” (Postill. eccles. Ed. Wal. Tom. XI, 169. sq.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of many ancient doctors of the church, such as Cyril, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Bernard, and others, who seek extraordinary miracles in the birth of Christ... 2. Of the Papists, who maintain the same.” (L. c. f. 575. sq.)

The same: “Those who contend that the virginity of Mary was destroyed by the birth are deservedly numbered among the heretics.” (L. c. f. 576.)

Scherzerus: “Whether the asserted virginity of Mary requires that the Lord came forth with the womb closed is a curious question. It suffices that He came forth with her virginity preserved... The Calvinists teach that He came forth with the womb opened, because they argue that He could not have come forth with it closed (on account of their denial of the communication of attributes). But we assert the communication of attributes, and therefore a passage possible even with the womb closed.” (System, th. p. 179. 181.) “

That (Mary) remained a virgin after the birth is denied by Helvidius, along with the Antidicomarianites.” (L. c. cf. Luther’s writing *On the Shem Ha-Mephorash*, 1543: “Thus Helvidius, the fool, also wanted to give Mary more sons after Christ, from these words of the Evangelist: ‘And Joseph did not know his bride Mary until she gave birth to her firstborn son’; he wanted to understand this as if she had more sons after the first, the crude fool. St. Jerome answered him well.” Tom. Wal. XX, 2617.)

Latin:

Gerhardus: ,,Status exinanitionis incipit in primo incarnationis momento et durat usque ad tempus sepulturae inclusive, quod totum vitae Christi in his terris curriculum apostolus Hebr. 5, 7. vocat,dies carnis‘, quibus per Hebraismum significatur illud tempus, quo Christus inter homines passibilis fuit versatus 2 Cor. 5, 16., quo fuit infirmitatibus carnis, absque tamen omni peccato, obnoxius.“ (L. c. § 304.) PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II.

Gesnerus: ,,Quando coepit haec evacuatio? — Statim ab ipsa incarnatione Filii Dei. Nam simulae in,forma Dei‘ extitit, h. e., divinae majestatis usum hic homo Jesus Christus accepit, in eo ipso suam humilitatem ostendit, quod usurpatione tantae gloriae se sponte abdicavit, eaque gloria, quae ipsi ex unione revera contigerat, liberrima voluntate abstinuit.“ (Orthod, confess. de persona et officio Salvatoris nostri. 1595. p. 254. sq.)

E. Hunnius: ,,Comprehenditur sub exinanitione Christi totum illud tempus, quod inter primum ortum conceptionis et nativitatis ipsius et inter resurrectionem intervenit, exceptis specialibus actionibus divinis et miraculis, per quae majestatis illius divinae per unionem acceptae radii quidam sub illa forma servili emicabant.

Num miracula per Christum facta deitati ipsius soli, an vero deitati et humanitati simul tribuenda putas? — Deitati quidem principaliter et tanquam primo principio miraculorum. Virtus enim edendi miracula solius deitatis est idioma, sicut scriptum est: ,Tu facis mirabilia solus.1 Quia autem λόγος personaliter in assumpta carne habitat universa plenitudine sua deitatis, ideo hanc suam edendorum miraculorum potentiam exserit per humanitatem, quippe quod eam in potentiae suae κοινωνίαν assumpserit. . .

Neque enim eorum blasphemia toleranda est in ecclesia Dei, qui dicunt et scribunt, sanctissimam Domini naturam humanam ad miracula plus non contulisse, nisi humanam suam vocem et externum ministerium, quod etiam prophetis et apostolis commune fuit. Quantum enim discrimen sit inter Christi et discipulorum miracula, luculenter nobis evangelica narrat historia; dum Christum quidem in miraculis suam propriam gloriam majestatemque declarasse conflrmat, apostolus vero non suo proprio nomine et virtute prodigia fecisse memorat, sed in nomine Jesu Nazareni.“ (Libelli IV. de persona Christi etc. 1590. p. 64—66.}

Quam supra quidem Sect. I. § 5. et seqq. expendimus; jam autem consideramus non in se praecise, sed quatenus ad statum exinanitionis pertinet, seu, quatenus caro Christi, licet non ex virili semine, tamen 111 utero feminae et ex massa sanguinea ejus formata fuit; qua ratione certum est, infirmitates aliquas concurrere, quae poterant locum non habere, ut tamen Filius Dei verus homo fieret.

Gerhardus: ,,Neque cuiquam mirum vel dubium videatur, quod ad exinanitionis statum referamus non solum passionem, crucifixionem, mortem ac sepulturam Christi, sed etiam ipsius conceptionem ac nativitatemf quia distinguendum inter incarnationem et incarnationis modum. Potuisset Dei Filius immediata creatione humanam naturam formare, eandemque in personae unitatem assumendo homo fleri, si vel maxime non fuisset in utero matris conceptus, quae fuit, ut sic loquar, nativitas interna, in utero matris per novem menses gestatus et ex utero in lucem editus, quae fuit nativitas externa. Constat enim, Adamum verum fuisse hominem, qui tamen nec in utero nec ex utero natus. Sed,propter nos et nostram salutem‘ non solum homo fleri, sed etiam ex nostra carne humanam naturam assumere et infirmitatibus, quae in conceptione ac nativitate infantulis accidere consueverunt, sponte seipsum subjicere voluit, ut immundam nostram conceptionem et nativitatem sanctificaret ac ipsis infantibus utero adhuc conclusis salutem impetraret.“ (L. c. § 304.)

Quenstedtius: ״Deus nequaquam vices patris supplevit aut sustinuit in generatione temporali Christi, nec id praestitit et adjecit, quod pater terrenus in procreatione filiorum praestare aut adjicere solet; nec Filius Dei vocatur ob conceptionem e Sp. Sancto. . . Ideo hoc opinionis monstrum invexit Socinus et propugnavit Smalcius, non abnuentibus caeteris de hac secta, ne admittere cogantur Christi, Salvatoris

nostri, deitatem consubstantialem et generationem aeternam ex essentia Dei Patris. . . Opponimus sequentia argumenta: Dicitur Christus respectu humanitatis et temporariae nativitatis απάτωρ, uti idem άμήτωρ dicitur respectu deitatis et generationis Heb. 7, 3. 2. Generatio proprie dicta nonnisi ex generantis substantia derivatur. . . At Christi humanitas ex Dei substantia non processit. . . Filius quidem Mariae virginis Christus dicitur, non autem Spiritus Sancti. . . Ob conceptionem divinam Christum esse Filium Bei, ex particula όώ καϊ Luc. 1, 35. obtinere volunt. . . Resp.: . . . ,Virtus altissimi' h. 1. non est Sp. S. vel virtus Sp. S., sed ipse F. D., qui δυναμις θεον vocatur 1 Cor. 1, 24. . . Vult dicere coelestis legatus: Δώ και, propterea etiam sanctum illud, quod ex te, Maria, nascetur, vocabitur et vere erit F. D., quia substantialis Dei virtus, ό λόγος, per mirabilem obumbrationem in te et ex te carnem assumet.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 570—572.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: Antithesis: 1. Socinianorum; sic enim Socinus in Antiwieko f. 221.: ,Sp. S. superveniet, perinde est', inquit, ,ac si dixlsset: quod viri opera in homine gignendo fleri solet, hic virtutis divinae opera flet.' Addit ibidem: ,A Dei in virginis uterum substantiam aliquam creatam immissam esse, ut Christus non matrem tantum, sed et patrem habuerit.' In 1. Quod regn. Pol. f. 36. scribit: ,Modum conceptionis. . . causam esse, ut ipse homo Jesus Nazarenus, qui Christus est, D. F. appelletur.' 2. Arminianorum; sic enim eorum antesignanus novissimus Steph. Curcellaeus in Rel. Christ, institut. 1. 5. c. 3. th. 5. asserit: ,quod Sp. S. in hac generatione id, quod ex parte viri deerat, suppleverit, creando immediate in utero virginis substantiam, ex qua, cum ejus sanguine conjuncta, corpus Jesu formatum fuerit.‘ “ (L. c. f. 570. sq.)

Hofmannus: ,,Demnach besagt die Stelle (Luk. 1, 35.), dass das Kind, welches durch Machtwirkung Gottes in Maria seines Lebens Anfang gewinnt, um dess willen Gottes Sohn heisst. Wir stellen die giltige Erklärung über den Sinn, in welchem Jesus Gottes Sohn genannt wird, den Dogmatikern entgegen, welche leugnen, dass er um seiner Empfängniss aus dem heiligen Geist willen so heisse, und welche vielmehr eine doppelte generatio unterscheiden, eine geperatio aeterna, per quam habet, quod est F. D., und eine generatio temporalis, per quam habet, quod est homo aut Filius hominis.“ (Schriftbeweis. Ed. prim. I, 114.)

Cf. supra antithesis P. I. c. 1. § 39. In qua praecipue consideratur, quod fructus ventris Mariae, per consuetos menses gestatus, ita demum in lucem editus est, velut juxta communem hominum sortem. Illud autem, quod quidam putant, Mariam clauso utero peperisse filium, incertum est, magis autem certa et manifesta natalium tenuitas et nascentis contemtus atque egestas, Luc. 2, 7.

Quenstedtius: ,,Fuit partus Mariae virginis naturalis et ab aliis partuum naturalium accidentibus minime diversus, adeoque Mariae parturienti usu venerunt ea, quae alias in partu fleri et partum comitari solent.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 576.)

Lutherus: ,,Es disputiren auch etliche, wie diese Geburt geschehen sei, als sei sie des Kindes genesen im Gebet, in grösser Freude, ehe sie es innen worden ist, ohne allen Schmerzen. Welcher Andacht ich nicht verwerfe; vielleicht um der Einfältigen willen also erfunden. Aber wir sollen bei dem Evangelio bleiben, das da saget, sie habe ihn geboren, und bei dem Artikel des Glaubens, da wir sagen: der geboren ist von Maria, der Jungfrauen. Es ist keine Trügerei hier, sondern, wie die Worte lauten, eine wahrhaftige Geburt. . . Ohne dass sie ohne PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II.

Sünde, ohne Schande, ohne Schmerzen und,ohne Versehrung geboren hat, wie sie auch ohne Sünde empfangen hat, 1 Mos. 3, 16. Der Fluch Hevä ist nicht über sie gangen, der da lautet: ,In Schmerzen sollst du deine Kinder gebären‘; sonst ist ihr geschehen allermassen, wie einem gebärenden Weibe geschiehet.“ (Postill. eccles. Ed. Hai. Tom. XI, 169. sq.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Plurimorum veterum ecclesiae doctorum, ut Cyrilli, Gregorii Nyss., Augustini, Bernhardi, aliorumque, qui extraordinaria miracula in nativitate Christi quaerunt. . . 2. Pontificiorum, statuentium idem.“ (L. c. f. 575. sq.)

Idem: ,,Qui per partum virginitatem Mariae destructam esse contendunt, merito suo inter haereticos referuntur.“ (L. c. f. 576.)

Scherzerus: ,,An virginitas Mariae asserta id postulet, ut Dominus clauso utero exierit, curiose quaeritur. Sufficit prodiisse salva virginitate. . . Calviniani aperto utero prodiisse ideo docent, quod clauso (ob negatam idiomatum communicationem) prodire non potuerit. At nos communicationem idiomatum adeoque possibilem etiam clauso utero transitum asserimus.“ (System, th. p. 179.181.),,

Postpartum (Mariam) virginem mansisse, negat cum Antidicomarianitis Helvidius.“ (L. c. cf. Lutheri Schrift vom Schern Hamphoras. 1543: ,,So wollte Helvidius, der Narr, auch Marien mehr Söhne nach Christo geben, aus diesen Worten des Evangelisten: ,Und Joseph erkannte seine Braut Maria nicht, bis sie ihren ersten Sohn gebar‘; solches wollte er verstehen, als hätte sie nach dem ersten Sohn mehr Söhne gehabt, der grobe Narr. Dem hat St. Hieronymus fein geantwortet.“ Tom. Hai. XX, 2617.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: The same: “The particle ‘until’ in Matt

The same: “The particle ‘until’ in Matt. 1:25 is infinite and exclusive, as it often is. Therefore, just as it does not follow: ‘Christ sits at the right hand, until His enemies are made His footstool,’ Ps. 110:2; therefore He will not sit there any longer afterward, — so it does not follow: ‘Joseph did not know her until she gave birth; therefore he knew her afterward.’ — Jerome gives this instance: ‘Helvidius did not do penance until death; did he therefore do penance after death?’ Cf. 2 Sam. 6:23: ‘Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no child until the day of her death.’ Deut. 34:6: ‘No one has known the grave of Moses to this day.’ Is. 46:4: ‘I am He, until you grow old.’ Did Michal therefore give birth after death, is the grave of Moses known today, and does God no longer exist after men have grown old? By no means. Moreover, Christ is called the ‘firstborn’ son in Luke 2:7 negatively with respect to what came before, or that no one was born before Him; but not positively with respect to what comes after, or that someone was born after Him.” (L. c. p. 179.)

In the house of the carpenter, Matt. 13:55, and in such a way that He was subject to the untimely rebuke of His mother, Luke 2: 48. For He was subject to the magistrate; He was considered equal or inferior to others; He ate and drank for the sake of satisfying hunger and thirst; He slept when weary; He endured the troubles of labors and journeys, dangers, temptations, sadness, poverty, insults, etc. Especially that confluence of afflictions which Christ drained two days before His death; to which must be referred, in particular, that desertion of which mention is made in Matt. 27:46. To be sure, Christ was deserted, not indeed as if the bond of the personal union had been broken, or as if He Himself had been utterly rejected from the face of God, never to be received into grace, nor that He truly and properly speaking despaired; but because in the greatest concurrence

of evils, on account of the sins of men imputed to Him, so felt the wrath of God, or God as alienated from Himself—who was sustaining the person of all sinners—that He felt no consolation within Himself from the fullness of the indwelling divinity. In this way, it is also to be understood what is said elsewhere, that Christ endured infernal torments.

Dorscheus: "Christ speaks (Matt. 27:46) of that degree of divine humiliation, by which, placed under the entire weight of the sins of the human race and in the winepress of divine wrath, acknowledging Himself to be the true and natural Son of God, full of all celestial majesty, He nevertheless did not seem to feel for Himself its power and efficacy and that joy of the indwelling divine strength which He felt at other times, but experienced God the Father as if turned away from Him and as an unceasing and rigorous avenger of sins. For He speaks of that dereliction regarding the reality into which the human race would have fallen by its own merit, had not divine mercy intervened. But that is not merely a casting out to external punishments, but also the infliction of internal, spiritual, and supernatural punishments of the soul. We said 'regarding the reality'; for as far as the adjunct of time is concerned, which for men would have been eternal, it was compensated by the very majesty and excellence of the Person." (Theol. Zachar. P. I. c. 8. § 168.)

Winckelmannus: "This is the very infernal punishment, to be forsaken by God and, while crying out, not to be heard for a time, which the antithesis in Ps. 22:2–7 shows." (Disputatt. th. in academ. Giessena habit. T. I, p. 509.)

Quenstedtius: "Our Savior truly endured infernal pains and torments, but He did not despair... If the Savior had despaired, He could not have redeemed us... Maldonatus well says on chapter 27 of Matthew: 'That Christ despaired of His own salvation is not only impious, but even horrible to hear, and is refuted by the very act of the dying Christ: into thy hands, He says, I commend my spirit.'" (L. c. s. 1. th. 51. f. 514.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who maintain: 1) That the soul of Christ remained ἀπαθῆ in its higher part, i.e., in the intellect and will, free from the sense of divine wrath and from the burden of sins which were to be borne and expiated... and that it appropriated passions to itself only through συμπάθειαν from the pains of the sensitive power. Thus Thomas Aquinas, Bellarmine, Fevardentius, etc. 2) They contend that it is a new and unheard-of impiety (these are the words of Bellarmine) to assert that Christ endured infernal torments in His passion... 2. Of the Socinians, who also deny that Christ was subject to infernal torments... 3. Of the Innovators, who say it is absurd that Christ endured the punishments of the damned... 4. Of the Arminians... Curcellaeus expressly denies that Christ felt infernal torments... 5. Of the Calvinists, such as Calvin in Inst. lib. 2, c. 16, § 12, and Marloratus on Matthew, who blasphemously assert that Christ despaired. 6. Of M. Flacius Illyricus, who maintains that the soul of Christ endured torments in hell after death, in his Commentary on Acts 2:24 and in his Clavis S. S. P. I. under the word 'infernus'." (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 588. sq.)

For Christ truly underwent this, that the soul was separated from the body, the natural bond being broken, and thus the body was deprived of life, although it did not see corruption. Acts 2:31; 13:35, 37.

Quenstedtius: "Whoever has a soul and body united in one ὑποστάσει is a true man; Christ at the time of death had a soul and body united in one ὑποστάσει; therefore, Christ was a true man at the time of death." (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 599.) PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION II.

Dannhauer: "‘There is one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus.’ Now, a mediator is God and man; Christ was a mediator even, and especially, in death; therefore, Christ was God and man in death." (Hodos. Phaenom. VIII. p. 317.)

Quenstedt: "A philosopher, if indeed he wishes to judge concerning the dead Christ from the common state of men, can scarcely determine otherwise than that within the three days of death He was not a man; for there, every man is an animal, is rational, is risible, etc.; but a dead man is called man equivocally. So they say. But here in Christ there is something singular, which does not pertain to philosophy, nor depend upon the principles of nature, namely: the subsistence of the human nature in the person of the λόγος, the personal union of the two natures, and the περιχώρησις of the state of the Lord’s death, and the mode of existence of the essential parts of the assumed flesh in death itself, etc. For all these things are singular, they transcend nature and depend upon the singular dispensation of God, and thus they cannot be known from nature, but from divine revelation. . .

Gerhard, Harmon. evangel. c. 202. . . speaks among other things as follows: ‘This mystery exceeds the grasp of all angels and men, for no finite intellect can comprehend how the body of Christ was truly dead, and yet in the midst of death remained the proper temple of the Word, who vivifies all things, personally united to Him, John 2:19; Col. 2:9. If the dissolution of the soul from the body which occurred in Christ’s death is denied, the truth of death is denied; if the conjunction of either the soul or the body with the λόγος remaining in death is denied, the truth of the personal union is denied. Thus, therefore, the dissolution of the essential union intervening between the body and soul of Christ must be asserted in such a way that at the same time the perpetual duration of the personal union of the λόγος and the soul, and likewise the λόγος and the body of Christ, remaining in an unsevered bond in death itself, is asserted.’" (L. c. f. 595. sq.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Scholastics, who are the first movers of this curious question. . . Lombard supports our opinion. . . Hugh of St. Victor also determined that Christ remained man in death. . . Durandus expressly rejects Lombard’s opinion with these words: ‘It must be said that Christ was not a man during that three-day period, and to assert the contrary is an error against the faith.’ Alexander of Hales: ‘Speaking materially, Christ is man during the three days, ... but formally He is not man.’*) Thomas Aquinas denies that Christ was a man during the three days of death, . . . ‘to assert that He was a man during the three days of death is heretical’... Gabriel Biel. . . posits this conclusion: ‘Christ was not a true man during the three days of death’; likewise: ‘During the three days of death, the person of the Word did not subsist in the human nature, and therefore He was not a true man.’

2. Of certain of our own theologians, such as D. H. Meisner, who in Quaest. Vexat. 2. n. 19. sq. defends this thesis: ‘That Christ did not remain or exist as a true and univocally called man during the time of His death and burial.’ But that great theologian, having been admonished by D. Hoe, D. Menzer, D. Gerhard, and other theologians of our party, did not continue to defend that opinion of his; . . . likewise D. Joach. Lütkemann. . . D. Grawer, Praelect. in A. C. art. 3, disputes on both sides of this question.

3. Of the Socinians, who contend that Christ had ceased to be entirely during the three days of death." (L. c. f. 596. sq.)

The same: "Antithesis of the Württemberg theologians, such as D. Thumm, who in ταπεινώσ. p. 471, denies that the soul of Christ was locally separated from the dead body during the three days of death. . . D. L. Osiander, who in the Appendix to his disputation on omnipresence, th. 43, writes that ‘the soul of Christ was personally in His body (during the three days of death)’; and in Defens. p. 460. sq. asserts that ‘the dead body of Christ was in paradise with the thief.’" (L. c. q. 8. f. 607.) *) Cf. the statement of H. Kromayer above p. 33.

Where the truth of His death was proven and the lifeless body was committed to rest. And thus, if you add the delay in the sepulcher until the resurrection, the state of humiliation is concluded. §

4. The state of exaltation is that by which Christ, according to His human nature, having laid aside the infirmities of the flesh, received and exercised the plenary use of divine majesty. For it is opposed to the state of humiliation, and it is easily understood that, strictly speaking, exaltation cannot fall upon the divine nature.

However, that the very assumption of the human nature into the hypostasis of the Son of God was called by some an exaltation, does not pertain to the present matter, where we are considering the exaltation that followed after the state of humiliation.

4. Exaltationis status est, quo Christus secundum humanam naturam, a depositis infirmitatibus b carnis, plenarium divinae majestatis usum c suscepit et exseruit. Opponitur enim statui exinanitionis, et in divinam naturam proprie loquendo cadere non posse exaltationem, facile constat.

Quod autem ipsa humanae naturae in hypostasin Filii Dei assumtio dicta fuit aliquibus exaltatio, id ad praesens non pertinet, ubi exaltationem post statum exinanitionis secutam spectamus.


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Gerhard: "Just as we said concerning humiliation, that it is taken in both an…

Gerhard: "Just as we said concerning humiliation, that it is taken in both an ecclesiastical and a biblical sense, so by force of opposition the same must be established concerning exaltation. Exaltation taken in the ecclesiastical sense is the elevation of the human nature into the very hypostasis of the Λόγος, which can be called the exaltation of the incarnation. Just as there was a certain humiliation when the Son of God, proceeding from the secret seat of His majesty, lowered Himself into our flesh, so it can be called an exaltation that the assumed human nature was elevated into the very hypostasis of the Λόγος through personal union, and that in the union and through the union it was made truly and really a participant of the divine idioms of divine majesty and glory; whence, in the midst of the state of humiliation, before He received the plenary usurpation of dominion in heaven and on earth, He is called King and Lord (Luke 2:11; Matt. 21:5; John 18:37). Exaltation taken in the biblical sense respects the properly so-called humiliation described in Philippians 2:5, which can be called the exaltation of glorification, the exaltation to the right hand of God." (L. c. § 306.)

Quenstedt: "Exaltation consists not in the laying aside of the human nature (for we have warned above that this differs from the form of a servant), nor in the permutation of hidden universal government with open and manifest government (which the Tübingen Doctors seem to have intended), but in the laying aside of the form of a servant, and thus of all the infirmities freely assumed, and in the bestowal of the plenary and manifest usurpation of divine majesty in and through the human nature. For there was not given to Christ in His exaltation a new power, virtue, or majesty which He did not have before, but there was conferred upon Him only the full faculty of administering that kingdom which He had received through the union itself." (L. c. s. 1. th. 70. f. 527.)

The same: "Dr. Joh. Fr. Koenig says in *Theol. pos.* § 354, that the term to which is glory and majesty, both finite and infinite... But to avoid ambiguity and for the sake of greater clarity, we here accept exaltation more specially, insofar as it has for its term to which only glory and infinite majesty regarding plenary usurpation, of which Christ speaks in John 17:5." (L. c. th. 69. f. 527.)

ANTITHESIS. Gerhard: "Antithesis: 1. The Jesuits... 2.) They say that the session at the right hand of God, in which Christ's exaltation chiefly consists, 'was given to the humanity not in itself, but in the suppositum; for it did not happen that the humanity in itself sits at the right hand of God, but that it is the humanity of that person who sits at the right hand of God.' Bellarmine, *de Christo*, lib. 3, cap. 15. ) They explain exaltation and the session at the right hand of God as 'a definite place...'"

by the power and dominion of one who is absent, just as the King of Spain rules in the new islands through his vicars; and, lest impiety lack anything, Bellarmine argues in the aforementioned place: "that sitting at the right hand was less honorable among the ancients than sitting at the left.". . 2. The Calvinists 1.) maintain that Christ was emptied and exalted according to both natures. . . 2.) They define exaltation merely through the communication of finite gifts. Sohnius, Tom. I. opp. Disp. 7. th. 55.: "Exaltation. . . does not differ in genus or species from the glorification of the blessed angels and men, but in quantity, i.e., in multitude and magnitude." (L. c. § 313—315.)

Thus, in Rom. 6:9, it is denied that death has dominion over Christ any longer, after the state of humiliation was finished. The reason for death is the same as for the other infirmities with which the human nature of Christ was previously struggling; so that it is denied that Christ is any longer liable to these or can be oppressed by them. And so, now not only as God, but also as man, He knows all things, can do all things, is present to all creatures, and has all things that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth under His feet and in His hand, as the Formula of Concord, Article VIII, § 11 teaches. Whence it is also clearly evident that the adequate foundation of the omnipresence of Christ according to His human nature is constituted in His very exaltation, namely, the actual and modified [omnipresence] (or that which is accepted for the majestic dominion of Christ according to both natures over all things, which He exercises most presently). Cf. Detailed Explanation, p. 541 sqq. § 5.

The descent into hell is to be referred to the beginning of the state of exaltation, along with the true and glorious resurrection from the dead. The ascension into heaven followed. Finally, the sitting at the right hand of the Father provided the completion. In this, Christ did not indeed undergo any difficult struggle or doubtful conflict with Satan, but rather appeared to him, already overcome by His passion and death, in the manner of a victor and triumpher, and, present according to both soul and body to the devil and all the powers of hell, He exhibited Himself as Lord, possessing supreme majesty. For this reason, it is said of Christ in 1 Pet. 3:18, 19, 20, that He was put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, or by divine power; and by the force of this same power, He also went or truly betook Himself to hell, and there preached to the spirits who were in prison (concerning whom add 2 Pet. 2:4 and Jude v. 6), or rather, showed them face to face and by the very deed that He is the One who has now crushed the head of the serpent and destroyed the works of the devil, etc.

Huelsmannus: "As far as the truth of being and the specific difference of this article (concerning the descent) are concerned, saving the judgment of others, we think that those testimonies from which the truth and definition of this article can be so proven as to generate divine faith are these two: 1 Pet. 3:18 sq. and Eph. 4:9. These are the reasons: because these testimonies alone are free from allegory or connection with allegorical sayings, and are free from metaphorical words and men, whereas, on the contrary, Hos. 13:14, Col. 2:15, Ps. 69:15, 16, and 86:13 contain a manifest allegory."

ON THE HUMILIATION AND EXALTATION. Quenstedtius: "The descent of Christ into hell is understood either improperly or properly. It is taken improperly either metaphorically, as it denotes those most exquisite and truly infernal pains and torments which Christ felt and sustained in his most holy soul at the time of his passion, Ps. 16:10; or metonymically concerning the virtue and efficacy of the passion and death of Christ, cf. Zech. 9:11. However, neither signification is that of this passage." (L. c. s. 1. th. 77. f. 632.)

The same: "The subject of the descent is Christ, the θεάνθρωπος. The subject by which it is, is not the divine nature, but the human, and that indeed in its entirety, not the soul only, 1 Pet. 3:18. The terminus to which is φυλακή, the infernal prison or receptacle and που of the damned spirits, 1 Pet. 3:19. The form is the true and real departure itself, made according to the mode of a glorified body to the που of the damned. The point of time is, according to the Petrine chain of acts in the cited place, that moment which intervened between the ζωοποίησις and the ἀνάστασις of Christ strictly so called. And the ancients probably posit that this descent occurred in that great earthquake which happened early in the morning before sunrise on Easter day. . . . This descent was a true and real motion, yet not local and natural, but supernatural, nor successive, because it was accomplished in a single νῦν, nor does the divine hypostasis of the flesh, which is everywhere, need progressive motion, but it teaches that it is present by a demonstration or operation of presence, and to that extent Christ was also present here in hell." (L. c. th. 80—§4. 87. f. 534. sq. 540.)

The same: "Christ did not descend into hell after his death and burial in order to suffer anything there, for he had declared on the cross that all things were consummated; nor was any λύτρον to be paid to Satan, who held the human race captive, as he was an executioner and a slave, but it was to be paid to the Lord God alone." (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 622.)

Hollazius: "The body of Christ, at that point in time when this descent occurred, did not lie in the sepulcher." (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 3. q. 141. p. 779.)

The same: "It does not help the Calvinists that שאל is taken for the sepulcher in Scripture, for this is not done everywhere: therefore they argue sophistically from a particular." (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 620.)

The same: "The end and effect of the descent is indicated at the same time by the word ἐκήρυξεν. This very κηρύττειν is explained from the passage in Col. 2:15, where it is said of Christ the victor that he 'made a show of principalities and powers, triumphing over them ἐν παρρησίᾳ.' From which it is clear that by κήρυγμα in this place is hinted a singular theatrical act, and thus Christ preached to the devils and damned souls not so much verbally as really, not so much by words as by deeds, signs, and triumphs, not in the manner of this age, but of the age to come, not by a bodily sound, but in a spiritual mode suitable to spirits, not for their liberation and salvation (as some Papists wish; for from hell there is no redemption; Scripture denies all consolation to the damned, Luke 16:25 sq.), but for their confusion and refutation. Therefore, the word ἐκήρυξεν is not to be rendered with the Vulgate as 'preached,' in such a way that it is thought to cohere and agree with the word εὐηγγελίσθη in chapter 4:6. . . He declared himself to have been exhibited by a certain illustrious manifestation and display of his glorious victory." (L. c. th. 86. f. 538.)

Scherzerus: "When Peter in 1 Ep. 4:6 says that the gospel was preached to the dead, he is not dealing with the descent of Christ, nor does he understand by the dead anyone other than those who had heard the gospel long ago, before they died." (System, p. 245.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis 1. Of the ancient heretics, such as 1) Marcion, who dreamed that Christ descended for the purpose of liberating the souls of all, even the extremely impious, from hell; but on the contrary, that he did not liberate the souls of the just. . . 2) Those who, with the Origenists and chiliasts PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION II. they did, and maintained, that not only were damned men, but even the devils themselves, to be saved at some time by the benefit of Christ’s descent into hell (namely, a thousand years after the day of the resurrection). . . 2. Of certain fathers... Clement of Alexandria, 1. 6. Strom., asserts: "that Christ descended into hell together with the apostles, in order to preach the gospel to the damned minds and to bring the hope of salvation to those who believe." Jerome maintains that Christ descended into hell according to his soul only. . . The same was taught by Epiphanius. . . And Nicephorus Callistus. . . 3. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who contend that Christ descended into hell according to his soul only, and not indeed with his body as well. Thus Lombard, Thomas, Durandus, Bellarmine; Cornelius a Lapide on 1 Pet. 3:18 sq., where he says: "The apostle proves that Christ, having been put to death in the flesh, was nevertheless made alive in the spirit, from the fact that in the spirit, i.e., as to his soul, he came into the prison of hell.". . "Christ having died," says the Roman Catechism, "his soul descended into hell, and remained there as long as his body remained in the sepulcher.". . John Duns Scotus taught that "the descent of Christ into hell cannot be proven at all from Scripture." He is followed by the Jesuit Forerus and others. 4. Of the Calvinists, who altogether deny the descent of Christ into hell properly so called, and understand it either as death, with Zwingli in his *Exposition of the Christian Faith*, f. 512, or as burial, with Bucer, Beza, Piscator, and Whittaker, or as the effect and fruit of the passion and death of Christ, namely, the destruction of the satanic kingdom, with Bullinger, or merely as a metaphorical descent, namely, the torments of Christ’s soul at the time of his passion, with Calvin, *Institutes*, bk. 2, ch. 16, § 10, and others, or finally as the whole state of humiliation, with Sohnius. Or they affirm that Christ descended into hell only according to his soul, as the Anhaltines do. . . 5. Of the Socinians, who interpret the descent as the state of death. . . 6. Of Weigel, who explains the descent of Christ into hell as the death of Christ, *Postilla*, Part 2, p. 44. 7. Of the innovators, who call into doubt the descent of Christ properly so called, along with the Calvinists, and do not acknowledge it as an article of faith. Thus Dr. Dreier." (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 616 sq.)
