I. opp. Disp. 7. th. 55.: ,Exaltatio. .. genere seu specie non differt a glorificatione beatorum angelorum et hominum, sed quantitate, h. e., multitudine et magnitudine.“‘ (L. c. § 313—315.)

Ita Rom. 6, 9. mortem Christo, post finitum statum exinanitionis, ultra dominari negatur. Quae autem mortis, eadem et caeterarum infirmitatum, cum quibus humana natura Christi antea conflictabatur, ratio est; ut etiam his Christum amplius obnoxium esse aut premi posse negetur. .Adeoque Jam non tantum ut Deus, verum etiam ut homo omnia novit, omnia potest, omnibus creaturis praesens est, et omnia, quae in codis, in terris et sub terra sunt, sub pedibus et in manu sua habet, docente Form. Cone, artic. VIII. % 11. Unde etiam non cjbscure constat, funr damentum adaequatum omnipraesentiae Christi secundum naturam humanam, actualis scilicet et modificata (seu pro majestatico Christi secundum utramque naturam in res omnes dominio, quod praesentissime exercet, acceptae) in ipsa ejus exaltatione constitui. Conf. Ausführl. Erklärung p. 541. sqq. § 5.

Ad initium status exaltationis referendus est descensus ad inferos,a una b cum resurrectione vera c et gloriosa d ex mortuis.e Secuta est adseensio in coelos. Complementum denique dedit sessio ad dextram P atris. f Quo Christus non quidem luctam aliquam difficilem aut crueritam dubiam ve cum satana subiit, verum illi jam superato per passionem ac mortem victoris ac triumphatoris instar apparuit et secundum animam et corpus praesens diabolo et inferis omnibus se tanquam Dominum summa majestate pollentem exhibuit. Qua ratione 1 Petr. 8,18.19. 20. de Christo dicitur, quod mortificatus carne, vivificatus autem spiritu, seu divina virtute, vi hujusdem virtutis etiam abierit aut revera se contuIerit ad inferos, ibique spiritibus, qui erant in carcere (de quibus adde 2. Epist. 2, 4· et Judae v. 6.), praedicaverit, sive coram et ipso opere ostenderit, se esse illum, qui jam contriverit caput serpentis ac dissolverit opera diaboli etc.

Huelsbmannus: ״Quod ad veritatem essendi et differentiam specificam articuli hujus (de descensu) attinet, salvo aliorum judicio, putamus, testimonia illa, ex quibus veritas et definitio hujus articuli ita potest evinci, ut fidem divinam generet, esse haec duo: 1 Pet. 3, 18. sq. Eph. 4, 9. Rationes hae sunt: quia haec sola testimonia vacant ab allegoria sive connexione cum dictis allegoricis, vacant verbis et hominibus metaphoricis, cum contra Os. 13, 14. Coi. 2, 15. Ps. 69, 15. 16. 86,13. manifestam contineant allegoriam.“

Quenstedtius: ,,Descensus Christi ad inferos accipitur vel improprie vel proprie. Improprie sumitur vel metaphorice, prout notat exquisitissimos illos et vere infernales dolores et cruciatus, quos tempore passionis Christus in sanctissima anima sua sensit ac sustinuit, Ps. 16, 10.; vel metonymice de virtute et efficacia passionis et mortis Christi, cf. Zachar. 9, 11. Neutra autem significatio est hujus loci.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 77. f. 632.)

Idem: ,,Descensus subjectum quod est Christus θεάνθρωπος. . · Subjectum quo est natura non divina, sed humana, atque ea quidem tota, non anima tantum, 1 Pet. 3, 18. . . Terminus ad quem est φυλακή, carcer infernalis seu receptaculum et που damnatorum spirituum, 1 Pet. 3, 19. . . Forma est ipsa vera atque realis et secundum modum corporis gloriflcati ad που damnatorum facta abitio. . . Temporis articulus est juxta catenam actuum Petrinam 1. c. momentum illud, quod intercessit inter ζωοποίησιν et άνάστασιν Christi stricte dictam. Et prohabiliter veteres statuunt, descensum hunc factum esse in magno illo terrae motu, qui summo mane ante solis exortum die paschatos evenit. . . . Fuit hic descensus motus verus et realis, non tamen localis et naturalis, sed supernaturalis, nec successivus, quia in unico νυν peractus, neque hypostasis carnis divina, quae ubique est, motu praegressivo indiget, sed praesentiae demonstratione vel operatione se adesse docet, atque eatenus etiam hic in inferno Christus praesto fuit.“ (L. c. th. 80—§4. 87. f. 534. sq. 540.)

Idem: ,,Non descendit Christus ad inferos post mortem ac sepulturam suam, ut aliquid ibi pateretur, nam in cruce omnia consummata esse pronuntiaverat; nec λντρην aliquod satanae, qui captivum tenebat genus humanum, utpote carnifici et servo, sed soli Domino Deo persolvendum erat.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 622.)

Hollazius: ,,Corpus Christi eo temporis puncto, quo hic descensus contigit, non jaöuit in sepulcro.“ (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 3. q. 141. p. 779.)

Idem: ,,Non juvat Calvinianos, quod שאל pro sepulchro in Seriptura sumatur, neque enim hoc flt ubique: ergo a particulari sophisticantur.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 620.)

Idem: ,,Finis et effectus descensus indicatur simul verbo εκήρνξεν. Hoc ipsum vero κηρίττειν explicatur ex loco Coi. 2, 15., ubi de Christo victore dicitur, quod,exspoliatos principatus et potestates traduxerit εν παρρησία‘. Ex quibus patet, per κήρυγμα h. 1. innui actum singularem theatricum, adeoque praedicavit Christus diabolis et animabus damnatis non tam verbaliter, quam realiter, non tam dictis, quam factis, signis, triumphis, non more hujus, sed futuri saeculi, non sono corporali, sed modo spirituali et spiritibus conveniente, non ad eorum liberationem et salutem (ut quidam papistae volunt; ex inferno enim nulla redemtio; omne solatium damnatis Scriptura denegat Luc. 16, 25. sq.), sed ad eorum confusionem et refutationem. Verbum ergo εκήμνξεν reddendum est non cum Vulgari per,praedicavit‘, ita ut cohaerere et convenire putetur cum voce ενηγγελίσθη c. 4, 6. . . Illustri quadam patefactione et manifestatione gloriosae victoriae sese exhibitum declaravit.“ (L. c. th. 86. f. 538.)

Scherzerus: ,,Quando Petrus 1. Ep. 4, 6. mortuis praedicatum esse evangelium dicit, non de descensu Christi agit, nec alios per mortuos, quam eos solum, qui olim, antequam morerentnr, evangelium audierant, intelligit.“ (System, p. 245.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis1. Antiquorum haereticorum, ut 1.) Marcionis, somniantis, Christum ideo descendisse, ut animas omnium, etiam extreme impiorum ab inferis liberaret; contra autem justorum animas non liberasse. . . 2.) Eorum, qui cum Origenistis et chiliastis PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II. faciebant, et statuebant, non lautam homines damnatos, sed etiam diabolos ipsos beneficio descensus Christi ad inferos aliquando salvos futuros (nim. post mille a die resurrectionis annos). . . 2. Quorundam patrum... Clemens Alexandr. 1. 6. Strom, asserit, ;Christum descendisse ad inferos una cum apostolis, ut evangeliam praedicaret mentibus damnatis et spem salutis adferret credentibus.‘ Hieronymus statuit, Christum secundum animam tantum descendisse in infernum. . . Idem docuit Epiphanius. . . Et Nicephorus Callistus. . . 3. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum, qui contendunt, Christum secundum animam tantum, non vero corpore simul, descendisse ad inferos. Ita Lombardus, Thomas, Durandus, Bellarminus; Cornelius a Lapide in 1 Pet. 3, 18. sq., ubi inquit: ,Probat apostolus, Christum mortiflcatum carne, vivificatum tamen fuisse spiritu ex eo, quod spiritu i. e. quoad animam venerit in carcerem inferni.‘ . . ,Christo mortuo‘, ait Catechesis Romana, ,ejus anima ad inferos descendit, ibique tamdiu mansit, quamdiu ejus corpus in sepulchro‘. . . Joh. Duns Scotus docuit, ,descensum Christi ad inferos ex Scriptura probari neutiquam posse‘. Eum sequitur Jesuita Forerus et al. 4. Calvinianorum, qui descensum Christi ad inferos proprie ita dictum prorsus negant et vel mortem cum Zwinglio in expositione fidei christ. f. 512., vel sepulturam cum Bucero, Beza, Piscatore, Wittakero, vel effectum et fructum passionis et mortis Christi, scii, destructionem regni satanici cum Bullingero, vel solum metaphoricum descensum, scii, cruciatus animae Christi tempore passionis, cum Calvino 1. 2. Institut, c. 16. § 10. et al., vel denique totunf humiliationis statum cum Sohnio intelligunt. Vel Christum tantum secundum animam descendisse in infernum, affirmant, ut Anhaltini. . . 5. Sociniano· rum, qui descensum de statu mortis interpretantur. . . 6. Weigelii, qui descensum Christi ad inferos de morte Christi exponit P. 2. Postillae p. 44. 7. Novatorum, qui descensum Christi proprie dictum cum Calvinianis in dubium vocant et pro articulo fidei non agnoscunt. Ita D. Dreierus.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 616. sq.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Calovius: "Among our own, some have also interpreted this article less…

Calovius: "Among our own, some have also interpreted this article less appropriately, who understood it as referring to torments after death, such as Dr. Epinus, Pastor of Hamburg, in the year 1553, and Dr. Draconites on Ps. 16, as also M. Flacius in *Clavis Scripturae*, under the word 'hell'." (*System.* T. VII. p. 686 sq.)

Luthardt: "The descent into hell. . . *Schriftlehre*. The state of Jesus' death, Matt. 12:40: ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ τῆς γῆς, Acts 2:24: ὠδῖνες τοῦ θανάτου (Ps. 18:5). Rom. 10:7: Hades. Eph. 4:9: τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς (so Meyer and Hölemann, *Bibelstud.* II, 89 ff. against Harless, Hofmann, and others). But also Luke 23:43: Paradise. Cf. the signs that accompanied his death: John 19:34 f., Matt. 27:53 f.— To be distinguished from this is 1 Pet. 3:19, which, according to Augustine and Gerhard (?), is to be understood as the preaching to the Noahic generation; according to the common explanation, which is justified by more recent interpreters, it refers to a preaching of Christ in Hades, though in various interpretations." (*Compend.* Ed. 3, p. 187 sq.)

Kahnisius: "The fact that Jesus Christ descended into Hades rests on Luke 23:43, Acts 2:27, 31, 1 Pet. 3: 19. However, all these passages only say that Christ descended a) as a spirit (1 Pet. 3:19), b) after death, before the resurrection, c) to the dead, and indeed both into the place of punishment (1 Pet. 3:19) and into Paradise (Luke 23:43), in order d) to preach the gospel." (*Die luth. Dogm.* Second Ed. II, 81.)

Hofmann: "No doctrine of Jesus' descent into hell. The state of death was for Jesus only a transition into a communion with God the Father that was unconditional even with regard to his nature. . . People thought they read there (1 Pet. 3:19) that Jesus, whether during his state of death or after the reunion of soul and body, had preached to the departed. But the passage says nothing of the sort." (*Schriftbeweis*, 2nd half, 1st part, p. 335 f.)

For the time of the descent into hell, although it is not sufficiently clear, we nevertheless do not dare to place it before the moment of the resurrection from death to life, according to those things which we have just seen from 1 Peter 3:18, 19, where Christ is said to have gone to hell not only after being put to death (θανατωθείς), but also after being made alive (ζωοποιηθείς), and thus, after He received life from death.

Calovius: "The vivification (ζωοποίησις) indeed precedes" (the descent of Christ into hell) "1 Pet. 3:18, because He did not go (πορενθεϊς) or proceed except as one made alive; but that is not properly a certain degree of exaltation, but a liberation from death; and therefore it is properly referred to the subject of exaltation, which is not a dead man, but one who has been brought back to life." (Theol. posit. p. 370.)

Moreover, He was raised not only by the Father, but also by Himself, according to that which He said in John 10:17, 18, that He has authority (ἐξουσίαν), power joined with effective potency, to take up again the soul, or life, which He had freely laid down; by the power of which He Himself was also to take up again the soul laid down by Himself.

Quenstedtius: "The subject which is Christ the God-man (θεάνθρωπος), the great shepherd of the sheep, Heb. 13:20, Jesus of Nazareth, Acts 2:24... The subject from which is the human nature, the proximate [subject] is the body, which had 'fallen' through death. Note: Just as He was not nailed to the cross and delivered unto death according to the divine nature, since that, considered in itself, is devoid of all passion, but according to the human nature: so also He was raised from the dead by God not according to the divine, but only according to the human nature. Yet the divine nature is not on that account entirely excluded from this act; for that nature communicated to the human nature the power of rising again and made His resurrection salutary for us, i.e., so that it might be the victor over death, sin, and hell, and the justifier of us, Rom. 4:25." (L. c. s. 1. th. 93. sq. f. 541.)

Hollazius: "Christ rose again by the divine power common to all three persons of the Godhead... Specifically, the resurrection of Christ is attributed to God the Father, as the fountain of the Godhead, for the consolation of consciences, so that we may know that the Father has been abundantly satisfied and that He is reconciled to us; otherwise, He would not have released our surety from the sepulcher." (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 3. q. 143. p. 780.)

Hunnius: "I ask, did Christ rise again by His own power?—Why not? For He says to the Jews: 'Destroy this temple (He speaks, as John interprets, of the temple of His body), and in three days I will raise it up.' Christ repeats this in John 10: 'I have power to lay down my life and I have power to take it up again.' Do you therefore judge that the human nature raised itself from the dead?—Because while Christ was in the sepulcher the state of humiliation still endured most profoundly, I would not wish to say that the body of Christ raised itself, but that the Word (λόγος) raised His body by that virtue and power which was indeed really communicated to the body of Christ, but which in death and the sepulcher had been (in respect to use) evacuated. Meanwhile, we do not hesitate to affirm that the soul of the Savior also, as vivifying, concurred in its own way to the vivification of His body by the power of its union with the Word, so that in the resurrection, by again entering His body, it effectively vivified it; although the primacy of that resuscitation remains with the Word. And in these respects, indeed, Christ is deservedly said to have risen by His own power, especially because the Word, raising His own body, is not a person separate from the body." (Libelli IV. de persona Christi etc. p. 93. sq.)

Scherzerus: "To the Jews asking what sign (σημεῖον) or miracle (John 2:18) He would perform, He replied that He would raise up the temple of His body in three days, John 2:19 sq. But if He did not raise Himself, He performed no miracle in the raising of the temple of His body destroyed by death, but only God, who raised Him." (Syst. p. 243.) PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION II.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Socinians, who bluntly deny that Christ rose again by His own power and death... Catech. Racov. c. 12, on the kingly office of Christ, q. 4: 'They are vehemently mistaken who say that Christ raised Himself from the dead.'... 2. Of the Calvinists, who deny that Christ as man, or according to His human nature, raised Himself... Zachar. Ursinus in Institut. catech. on the resurrection of Christ, p. 319, writes: 'Christ rose again by His own proper power and might, not indeed of His flesh, but of His deity.'" (L.c. s. 2, q. 10, f. 625 sq.)

For He received that very same body which He had before, but glorified, according to Phil. 3: 21. For σώμα τής δόξης, by Hebraism, denotes a glorious body, and indeed such a one whose affections are described more prolixly in 1 Cor. 15:40 sqq. Whence also He powerfully went forth from the closed sepulcher; see Matth. 28:2 and 6, where it is recounted that the angel of the Lord removed the sepulchral stone, not to open an exit, but to show others the place already abandoned by the resurrected Christ.

Gerhardus: "The end of Christ's resurrection is twofold. The end *for us* [objective] is the glory 1. of God the Father... 2. of Christ Himself, so that in the resurrection and through the resurrection He might demonstrate Himself *ipso facto* to be: 1.) The true Son of God, Rom. 1:4... 2.) The true man, and thus the θεάνθρωπον... 3.) The promised Messiah, since it had been announced by both prophecies and types that He Himself... would rise from the dead... 4. The victor over death, the devil, and all enemies, because to rise from the dead by His own power argues for the most complete victory won over death... 5. Our eternal king and priest... 6. Our mediator and savior... The end *for us* [subjective] concerns us men, which embraces the fruits flowing to us from Christ's resurrection. Such are: 1. The confirmation of our faith... 2. Our justification, Rom. 4:25... 3. Our renewal, Rom. 6:4; 2 Cor. 5:15; Col. 3:1. But our renewal is referred to among the fruits of the Lord's resurrection because not only the figure and example of our renewal, but also the cause, is proposed to us in it. Eph. 2:5... 4. The sealing of our hope concerning preservation unto eternal salvation, Rom. 5:10... 5. Our resurrection unto blessed life." (Disputatt. th. p. 1440—1444.)

Calovius: "The apostle does not say (Rom. 4:25) that Christ was raised by God so that the authority of His doctrine might be reconciled, which could have been sufficiently reconciled to Him by miracles and by testimony from heaven, had the Jews not been so hardened; but δια τήν δικαίωσιν ήμών, for our justification...

Christ is not said to be raised for our justification for the exact same reason as He was delivered by God into death for our sins; since here the death of Christ is the meritorious cause of the expiation of our sins, and He Himself was delivered into death in our place, so that we might be freed by the merit of His death from sin and its penalty, death; whereas regarding the resurrection of Christ, that cannot be asserted to the same extent, namely, that Christ by His resurrection merited righteousness for us, the merit of which had already been consummated in His death, as His exclamation on the cross, 'Τετέλεσται', it is finished, Joh. 19:30, confirmed.

Therefore, Scripture speaks differently about the death of Christ and about His resurrection. For it says that Christ suffered and died both because of us and for us, but that He rose again not for, but only because of us. Although, therefore, theologians sometimes call the resurrection of Christ the meritorious cause of our justification, they nevertheless understand the word 'merit' only in a general sense...

But in what respects the resurrection of Christ was required for our justification, the blessed Gerhardus explains thus: namely, 1. by reason of manifestation and confirmation, because the resurrection of Christ is an evident testimony that satisfaction has been fully made for our sins and perfect righteousness [has been obtained]..."

ON THE HUMILIATION AND EXALTATION. ... derived. 2. With respect to application. If Christ had remained in death, He would not have been the victor over death, nor could He have applied to us the righteousness procured at such a dear price, Rom. 5:10; 8:35. 3. With respect to the actual absolution from sin. Just as God punished our sins in Christ, which were imposed and imputed to Him as our sponsor, so also, by raising Him from the dead, He *ipso facto* absolved Him from our sins imputed to Him, and consequently also absolved us in Him; to which the following passages refer: 1 Cor. 15:17; 2 Cor. 5:21; Eph. 2:5; Col. 2:12, 13; Phil. 3:8–10; 1 Pet. 1:3. (Bibl. illustr. *ad* l. c. Rom. 4:25.)

Latin:

Calovius: ,,E nostris etiam minus commode interpretati sunt hunc articulum, qui de cruciatibus post mortem accepere, utpote D. Epinus, Pastor Hamburg., a. 1553. et D. Draconites in Ps. 16., ut et M. Flacius in Clav. Script, voc. ,inferni‘.“ (System. T. VII. p. 686. sq.)

Luthardtius: ,,Descensus ad inferos. . . Schriftlehre. Jesu Todeszustand Matth. 12, 40.: kv ry καρδίςι τής γής, Ap.-G. 2, 24. f. ωδίνες τον Φανάτυν (Ps. 18, 5.). Rom. 10, 7.: Hades. Eph. 4, 9. τα κατώτερα μέρη τής γής (so Meyer und HÖlemann, Bibelstud. II, 89. ff. gegen Harless, Hofmann u. A.). Aber auch Luk. 23, 43.: Paradies. Vgl. die Zeichen, die seinen Tod begleiteten: Joh. 19, 34. f. Matth. 27, 53. f.— Hievon zu unterscheiden ist 1 Pet. 3, 19. nach Augustin, Gerhard ( ?),, Hofmann zu verstehen von der noachischen Predigt; nach der gewöhnliehen und von den neueren Auslegern gerechtfertigten Erklärung von einer Predigt Christi im Hades, aber in verschiedener Fassung.“ (Compend. Ed. 3. p. 187. sq.)

Kahnisius: ,,Die Thatsache, dass Jesus Christus in den Hades hinabgefahren ist, ruht auf Luk. 23, 43. AG. 2, 27. 31. 1 Pet. 3, 19. Allein alle diese Stellen sagen nur, dass Christus a.) als Geist (1 Pet. 3, 19.), b.) nach dem Tode, vor der Auferstehung, c.) zu den Todten und zwar sowohl in den Strafaufenthalt (1 Pet. 3, 19.) als in das Paradies (Luk. 23, 43.) gestiegen sei, um d.) das Evangelium zu verkündigen.“ (Die luth. Dogm. Zweite Ausg. II, 81.)

Hofmannus: ״Keine Lehre von Jesu Höllenfahrt. Der Todeszustand ist für Jesus nur Uebergang gewesen in eine auch hinsichtlich seiner Natur unbedingte Gemeinschaft mit Gott dem Vater. . . Man meinte dort (1 Pet. 3, 19.) zu lesen, Jesus habe, sei es nun während seines Todeszustandes oder nach der Wiedervereinigung von Seele und Leib, den Verstorbenen gepredigt. Die Stelle besagt aber nichts der Art.

Tempus enim descensus ad inferos, etsi non satis clare constet, non tamen audemus momento resurrectionis e morte ad vitam anteponere, juxta ea, quae modo vidimus ex 1 Petr. 3, 18.19., ubi Christus non solum θανατωθείς, verum etiam ζωοποιηθείς, adeoque, postquam recepit vitam ex morte, abiisse ad inferos dicitur.

Calovius: ,,Antecedit quidem ζωοποίησις“ (descensum Christi ad inferos),,1 Pet. 3, 18., quia nonnisi vivificatus in spiritu πορενθεϊς seu profectus est; sed ille proprie non est quidam gradus exaltationis, sed liberatio a morte; ideoque ad subjectum exaltationis proprie refertur, ׳ quod est non homo mortuus, sed redivivus.“ (Theol. posit. p. 370.)

Rususcitatus autem est non solum a Patre, verum etiam a se ipso, juxta id, quod dixit Joh. 10, 17. 18., 8e habere έξουαίαν, potestatem cum potentia effectrice conjunctam, rursus sumendi animam, seu vitam, quam libere amiserit; cujus vi etiam animam a se positam ipse iterum sit sumturus.

Quenstedtius: ״Subjectum quod est Christus θεάνθρωπος, pastor ovium magnus, Hebr. 13, 20., Jesus Nazarenus, Act. 2, 24... Subjectum quo remotum est natura humana, proximum corpus, quod per mortem ״ ceciderat. Nota: Sicut non secundum divinam naturam, quippe quae in se considerata passionis omnis expers est, sed secundum humanam naturam cruci affixus et in mortem traditus fuit: ita quoque non secundum divinam, sed tantum humanam naturam a Deo suscitatus est. Non tamen propterea divina natura ab hoc actu prorsus excluditur; illa enim naturae humanae communicavit potentiam resurgendi et resurrectionem ipsius nobis fecit salutarem, h. e., ut esset mortis, peccati et inferni victrix et nostrum justiflcatrix, Rom. 4, 25.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 93. sq. f. 541.)

Hollazius: ,,Resurrexit Christus virtute divina omnibus tribus personis divinitatis communi. . . Speciatim Deo Patri, ut fonti divinitatis, tribuitur resuscitatio Christi ad consolationem conscientiarum, ut sciamus, Patri abunde satisfactum eundemque nobis reconciliatum esse, ceteroqui fidejussorem nostrum e sepulcro non dimisisset.“ (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 3. q. 143. p. 780.)

Hunnius: ,,Quaero, num Christus propria sua virtute resurrexerit?—Quidni? Dicit enim Judaeis: ,Destruite templum hoc (loquitur, Joanne interprete, de templo corporis sui), et in triduo reaedificabo illud:‘ Repetit id Christus Joh. 10.: ,Ego potestatem habeo ponendi vitam meam et potestatem habeo resumendi eam.‘ Ergone humanam naturam judicas semetipsam e mortuis excitasse? — Quia Christo in sepplchro existente profundissimus adhuc durabat exinanitionis status, nolim dicere, corpus Christi seipsum suscitasse, sed λόγον excitasse corpus suum ea virtute ac potentia, quae corpori Christi quidem realiter communicata, in morte autem et sepulchro (ratione usus) evacuata fuerat. Interim non dubitamus affirmare, animam quoque Salvatoris ut vivificam ad corporis sui vivificationem suo modo ex vi unionis ipsius cum λόγω concurrisse, ita ut in resurrectione denuo subeundo corpus suum efficaciter id vivificaret; tametsi principatus illius resuscitationis penes λό}0ν maneat. Atque his sane respectibus merito Christus propria virtute dicitur resurrexisse, praesertim quia λόγος, proprium suum corpus suscitans, alia persona non est a corpore separata.“ (Libelli IV. de persona Christi etc. p. 93. sq.)

Scherzerus: ״Judaeis quaerentibus, quale σημεΐον sive miraculum (Joh. 2, 18.) ederet, respondit, se erecturum templum corporis sui tribus diebus, Joh. 2, 19. sq. At si seipsum non resuscitavit, nullum in erectione templi corporis sui morte destructi miraculum edidit ipse, sed solus Deus, qui ipsum excitavit.“ (Syst. p. 243.) PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II.

### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Quenstedtius: “Rom. 1

Quenstedtius: “Rom. 1: 4. If Christ did not rise from the closed sepulcher by His own divine power, but through the work of an angel descending from heaven, then by that resurrection of His, He could not have been declared and effectively demonstrated to be the only-begotten Son of God.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 11. f. 635.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Socinians, who deny that Christ entered to the disciples through closed doors. 2. Of the Calvinists, who... with one voice teach: 1.) That Christ rose only when the stone had already been rolled away from the sepulcher; 2.) They contend that either the disciples opened the doors to the knocking Christ, or Christ procured entry for Himself by His own power, or the doors opened themselves to Him, or He entered through a window or some other way, or the walls were permeable to Him, etc. Thus Zwingli, P. 2. resp. ad Luth. confess. f. 456. b. Calvin, Institut. l. 2. c. 17. § 11. Peter Martyr: ‘Perhaps the doors yielded, perhaps Christ entered through the windows or the roof.’” (L. c. s. 2. q. 11. f. 634.)

The same: “The Calvinists philosophize too thinly and meagerly concerning the properties of the glorified body of Christ. 1. They precisely deny invisibility. Theophilus Mosanus... attempts to construct this thesis: ‘the body of Christ cannot but be seen, wherever it is present.’ They also deny illocality.” (L. c. p. 1435.)

The same: “Antithesis: 1. The Photinians (following the heretic Apelles, of whom Philostratus speaks) deny that Christ, after His glorification, has flesh and blood in heaven. 2. The Calvinists assert 1.) that the blood of Christ shed on the altar of the cross decayed and was not reassumed in the resurrection. Calvin on ch. 26 of Matthew. 2.) Some of them assert that Christ, just as He was humbled according to both natures, so also rose according to both natures. 3.) The Papists maintain that some part of the blood was not reassumed into the body of Christ, but was left on the earth.” (L. c. p. 1425 sqq.)

Gerhardus: “Antithesis: 1. The Papists maintain that the meritorious cause of the Lord’s resurrection was the preceding passion, through which they assert Christ merited for Himself the glory of His body and the exaltation of His name. 2. The same is approved by certain Calvinists, who depart here from their master (lib. 2. Institut. c. 17. § 6). Both parties urge the particles לכן and διό in Ps. 110:7 and Phil. 2:9. I answer: What is described here is not merit, but order and consequence, as is explained in Luke 24:26: ‘Ought not Christ to have suffered these things and thus to enter into His glory?’, where the particle οὕτως is not indeed found in all Greek manuscripts, yet it is elicited from v. 46 by the best reasoning. 1 Pet. 1:11: τὰς μετὰ ταῦτα δόξας. Those particles, therefore, do not so much express a meritorious cause as they contain a certain line of reasoning. The Greek τὸ διό is composed of the preposition διά and the article τό, so that the sense is: therefore, wherefore.” (Disputatt. th. p. 1422.)

Truly indeed and real, with the body lifted up from the earth; see Acts 1:9. Yet it is not to be scrutinized too much or according to a natural mode. PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION II.

must be defined in such a way that the presence of the body raised into heaven is denied on earth. For it is read in Ephesians 4:10 that He ascended not only into heaven, but also above all the heavens.

Formula of Concord: "From this union and communion of natures, the human nature has that exaltation after the resurrection from the dead above all creatures in heaven and on earth, which in truth is nothing other than that Christ completely laid aside the form of a servant, but did not lay aside the human nature, but retains it for all eternity, and has been exalted to the full possession and use of divine majesty according to the assumed human nature. He had that majesty immediately at His conception, even in His mother's womb, but, as the apostle speaks (Phil. 2:7), 'He emptied Himself,' and, as Dr. Luther teaches, He had it secretly in the state of His humiliation, and did not always use it, but as often as it seemed good to Him." (Art. VIII, p. 679 sq.)

Gesnerus: "Where was Christ during the space of forty days before the ascension, when He was not with the disciples? — In the state of heavenly life, as He Himself says in John 16 and 17, that He was leaving the world and going to the Father, that is, having left this earthly and visible conversation, He was entering the heavenly and invisible one; and Luke 22:16: 'For I say to you, that I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine, until the kingdom comes'; which He repeats after the resurrection in Luke 24: 'These are the words which I spoke to you, while I was still with you.' He was with the disciples and He was not. He was, according to the economy of His most free will; He was not, according to the condition of His glorious body... In this heavenly condition, therefore, He was, whether He manifested Himself to the disciples or withdrew His appearance from them... It is one thing to pass to the Father into a heavenly and invisible condition, and another to ascend to heaven. The ascension did not take place without a change of place... But the transition to the Father does not admit of local motion, since the Father is in the Son and the Son is in the Father, John 14:10. And to wish to inquire further about this matter is of ambitious audacity. It is unknown, says Thomas, in what places He was corporally during the intermediate time, since Scripture does not hand this down and His dominion is in every place." (Orthod. confess. de persona etc. p. 296 sq.)

Hollazius: "The subject *quod* (which) of the ascension is the whole θεάνθρωπος (God-man). 'The same who descended, also ascended,' Eph. 4:10. But the whole θεάνθρωπος descended; He who was made alive, descended, 1 Pet. 3:22. Therefore. — The subject *quo* (by which) of the ascension is the human nature, which was lifted up on high, Acts 1:9, which does not fit the divinity, which cannot be carried on high (for this belongs only to bodies). —

The terminus *ad quem* (to which) Christ arrived in His ascension is both common and proper. The common one is the seat and dwelling of the blessed, where Christ presents Himself to be seen face-to-face by the blessed. Christ was exalted into paradise, in which the thief was converted with Him, Luke 23:43, where Job also is, ch. 19:27, where mansions are prepared for the faithful, John 14:2, where the most glorious Redeemer will exhilarate the souls of the saints with His most pleasant sight. The proper terminus *ad quem* is the majestatic heaven of God, which is above all heavens, Eph. 4:10. 'We have a great high priest, who has passed through the heavens,' Heb. 4:14; He passed through the heavens not by reason of distance, but of most sublime and divine presence. The majestatic heaven of God is the very right hand of God, by which Christ was made higher than the heavens, Heb. 7:26, of which the apostle speaks in Heb. 8:1.

Obs. By heaven here is not understood the aerial or ethereal heaven of nature, which it is impious to think; nor the heaven of grace, which is the church militant on these earths, from which Christ withdrew His visible presence until the day of the final judgment. Therefore, the heaven of glory is understood, either finite or infinite. By finite glory, Christ indeed presents Himself to be seen in the place of the blessed by the angels and the blessed according to the manner of a true glorified body; yet so that infinite glory is also communicated to Him through the session at the right hand."

OF EXINANITION AND EXALTATION. God. Christ was therefore raised into the majestic heaven, that He might fill all things, Eph. 4:10. —

By reason of the mode, the ascension of Christ was not an ἀφανισμός or disappearance, but a true, real, successively progressive motion, Luke 24:51, and visible as far as the clouds, Acts 1:9. But being raised from the cloud in an invisible manner, He was exalted to the right hand of God. —

The visible motion of Christ as far as the clouds was local, not according to the motion of a natural body, which by its nature is borne downward, but of one glorified and endowed with supernatural gifts. Nor did Christ assume local and visible motion out of any necessity of nature, but by a free economy; for if He had willed, He could have withdrawn Himself from His disciples in a point of time and occupied heaven. But it pleased the Savior to be borne upward gradually, so that the disciples might testify to the true ascension all the more clearly and confidently. From which we gather that Christ indeed ascended as far as the clouds by local motion, but not locally or physically. (L. c. q. 148—168. p. 784. sqq.)

Quenstedtius: "The heaven into which Christ ascended is not... a glorious state or one of infinite glory, which pertains to the following article concerning the session at the right hand of God, or of finite glory, because He was in this state immediately from the resurrection, but a που, a seat and dwelling-place of the blessed... He did not wish to ascend as He came forth secretly from the tomb, but openly and plainly." (L. c. s. 1. th. 106. 108. f. 647. sq.)

The same: "The end and effect of the ascension on the part of Christ is a glorious triumph over the whole choir of enemies and the occupation of the heavenly kingdom; on our part, the unlocking of the closed paradise and the procurement of a permanent habitation in heaven... By His passion and death He merited heaven for us, but by His ascension He opened it to us." (L. c. th. 109. f. 548. sq.)

Scherzerus: "Errors: That Christ did not ascend in the body in which He suffered is a fable of the Manichaeans and Socinians. Christ, about to ascend, both required local motion and ascended into a local and created heaven, and by the ascension of His humanity, He has entirely withdrawn His substantial presence from us, according to the Calvinists... The Papists include the leading of the fathers from Limbo into heaven among the ends of the ascension." (System, p. 248. sq.)

Formula of Concord: "We therefore reject and condemn with heart and mouth: ... that Christ, on account of His ascension into heaven, is so comprehended and circumscribed in a certain place of heaven by His body, that He can neither be nor will be truly and substantially present with His body in the Holy Supper (which is celebrated on earth according to the institution of Christ), but rather is as far absent from the Holy Supper as the highest heaven is distant from the earth. For thus certain Sacramentarians have deliberately and maliciously (to confirm their error) corrupted those words in the Acts of the Apostles (3:21): 'Whom the heaven must receive,' and in place of a sincere translation have substituted these words: 'Whom the heaven must contain' (Beza), which words signify that Christ is received into heaven so as to be circumscribed and comprehended by heaven, so that He can in no way be present with us on earth in His human nature, nor does He wish to be." (Artic. VII. p. 671. 672.)

Graecum το δώ componitur ex praepositione δια et articulo ό, ut sit sensus: proinde, quocirca.“ (Disputatt. th. p. 1422.)

Vera quidem et realis, corpore ex terris sursum elevato; vid. Actor. 1, 9. Non tamen nimium scrutanda aut juxta modum naturalem PART. III. CAP. Π. SECTIO II.

ita definienda, ut negetur corporis in coelum elati praesentia in terris. Non solum enim in coelum, sed et supra omnes coelos ascendisse, legitur Ephes. 5, 10.

Formula Concordiae: ״Ex hac unione et naturarum communione humana natura habet illam exaltationem post resurrectionem a mortuis super omnes creaturas in coelo et in terra, quae revera nihil aliud est, quam quod Christus formam servi prorsus deposuit, humanam vero naturam non deposuit, sed in omnem aeternitatem retinet, et ad plenam possessionem et divinae majestatis usurpationem secundum assumtam humanam naturam evectus est. Eam vero majestatem statim in sua conceptione etiam in utero matris habuit, sed, ut apostolus loquitur (Phil. 2, 7.), ,se ipsum exinanivit‘, eamque, ut D. Lutherus docet, in statu suae humiliationis secreto habuit, neque eam semper, sed quoties ipsi visum fuit, usurpavit.“ (Art. VIII. p. 679. sq.)

Gesnerus: ״Ubi versabatur Christus quadraginta dierum spatio ante ascensionem, quando cum discipulis non erat? — In coelestis vitae statu, ut ipse dicit Joh. 16. et 17., se mundum deserere et ad Patrem proficisci, hoc est, se relicta terrena et visibili hac conversatione ingredi coelestem et invisibilem; et Luc. 22, 16.: ,Dico enim vobis, quod non amplius bibiturus sim de fructu vitis, donec regnum veniat‘; quod post resurrectionem Luc. 24. repetit: ,Hi sunt sermones, quos locutus sum, cum adhuc vobiscum essem.‘ Erat cum discipulis et non erat. E. — Subjectum quo ascensionis est natura humana, quae in altum est sublata, Act. 1, 9., quod in divinitatem, quae in altum ferri nequit (hoc enim solorum corporum est), non quadrat. —

Terminus, ad quem Christus in ascensione sua pervenit, est tum communis, tum proprius. Communis est sedes et domicilium beatorum, ubi Christus beatis se ad faciem conspiciendum praebet. Evectus est Christus in paradisum, in quo cum ipso est conversus latro, Luc. 23, 43., ubi etiam est Jobus, c. 19, 27., ubi paratae sunt fidelibus mansiones, J011. 14, 2., ubi redemtor gloriosissimus conspectu suo jucundissimo sanctorum animas exhilarabit. Terminus ad quem proprius est coelum Dei majestaticum, quod est super omnes coelos, Ephes. 4,10. ,Habemus sacerdotem principem magnum, qui penetravit coelos, Hebr. 14, 4.; penetravit coelos non ratione distantiae, sed sublimissimae et divinae praesentiae. Coelum Dei majestaticum est ipsa dextra Dei, qua coelis excelsior factus est Christus, Hebr. 7, 26., de qua apostolus Hebr. 8, 1.

Obs. Per coelum hic non intelligitur coelum naturae aereum vel aethereum, quod cogitare impium est; neque coelum gratiae, quod est ecclesia militans in his terris, cui Christus visibilem praesentiam suam usque ad diem extremi judicii subtraxit. Ergo intelligitur coelum gloriae, vel finitae, vel inAnitae. Qua gloriam finitam Christus in ποΰ beatorum se utique conspiciendum praebet angelis et beatis ad veri corporis gloriflcati modum; ita tamen, ut ipsi etiam communicata sit gloria infinita per sessionem ad dextram

Dei. Evectus igitur est Christus in coelum majestaticum, ut omnia impleret, Eph. 4, 10. —

Ratione modi ascensio Christi non fuit άφανισμος sive disparitio, sed motus verus, realis, successive progressivus, Luc. 24, 61., et visibilis usque ad nubes, Act. 1, 9. At elevatus a nube modo invisibili ad dextram Dei exaltatus est. —

Visibilis Christi motus usque ad nubes localis fuit, non secundum motum corporis naturalis, quod natura sua deorsum fertur, sed glorificati et supernaturalibus dotibus instructi. Neque per indigentiam naturae, sed per liberam oeconomiam Christus assumsit motum localem et visibilem, qui, si voluisset, in puncto temporis discipülis suis se potuisset subducere et coelum occupare. At placebat Salvatori sensim ferri sursum, ut discipuli de vera ascensione eo luculentius et confidentius testarentur. Ex quo colligimus, Christum ascendisse quidem usque ad nubes permotum localem, sed non localiter aut physice.“ (L. c. q. 148—168. p. 784. sqq.)

VII. p. 671. 672.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Which right hand of God is not some certain place, but the very omnipotent…

Which right hand of God is not some certain place, but the very omnipotent power of God, which fills heaven and earth, according to the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, Artic. VIII., and therefore he is said to sit at the right hand of God who powerfully and providently governs the whole world, especially the church, and rules over all His enemies. Cf. Ps. 110:1, 2; Acts 2:34, 35.

Luther: "First, let us take up the article that Christ sits at the right hand of God, which the enthusiasts hold, [arguing] that He does not suffer, that Christ’s body could also be in the Supper. If we now ask them here what they call God’s right hand, where Christ sits: I suspect they will rave to us, just as one is accustomed to picture for children a magic heaven, in which there is a golden chair." Baier’s Comp. ed. Walther. III.7 PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II. stand, and Christ sits next to the Father in a cope and a golden crown, just as painters depict it.

For if they did not have such childish, carnal thoughts about the right hand of God, they would certainly not allow themselves to be troubled regarding the body of Christ in the Lord’s Supper, or beat themselves with the saying of Augustine (whom they otherwise believe in nothing, nor any other), that Christ must be bodily in one place, but his truth is everywhere, etc.

From which childish thought it must then further follow that they also bind God Himself to one place in heaven on that same golden chair, because outside of Christ there is no God, and where Christ is, there the Godhead is entirely and completely, as Paul says in Col. 2:9: In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily...

But Scripture teaches us that God’s right hand is not a particular place where a body should or could be, as on a golden chair; rather, it is the almighty power of God, which at once can be nowhere and yet must be in all places.

It can be nowhere in any one place (I say): for if it were anywhere in some place, it would have to be circumscribed and contained there; just as everything that is in a place must be contained and measured by that same place, such that it cannot meanwhile be in any other place. But the divine power cannot and may not be so contained and measured. For it is incomprehensible and immeasurable, outside and above everything that is and can be.

Conversely, it must be essentially and present in all places, even in the smallest leaf of a tree.

The reason is this: for it is God who creates, works, and sustains all things through His almighty power and right hand, as our faith confesses; for He does not send out deputies or angels when He creates or sustains something, but all such things are the proper work of His own divine power.

But if He is to create and sustain it, He must be there, and make and sustain His creature as much in the innermost as in the outermost.

Therefore, He must indeed be present Himself in every creature, in its innermost, outermost, all around, through and through, below and above, front and back, so that there can be nothing more present or more inward in all creatures than God Himself with His power.

For it is He who makes the skin; it is He who also makes the bones; it is He who makes the hair on the head; it is He also who makes the marrow in the bones; it is He who makes every little piece of hair; it is He who makes every little piece of marrow; He must indeed make everything, both parts and whole: thus His hand must be there to make it, that cannot fail.” (That these words of Christ: "This is my body," still stand firm. Tom. Hal. XX, 1000. 1002. sq.) Cf. supra Kromayerus p. 64.

The same: “What can ‘to sit at my right hand’ (Ps. 110:1) mean other than to sit equal to God? For He does not sit at His head nor at His feet, neither higher nor lower, but at the right, equal to Him, so that heaven is just as much His throne and the earth His footstool; as He says in Matthew at the end, v. 18: ‘All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth.’” (Exposition of the Last Words of David. 1548. III, 2825.)

Gerhard: "Concerning God Himself, who is included in no place and excluded from no place, it is said that He dwells in the heights, that He is in the heavens, that He looks down from heaven upon the sons of men; yet no one gathers or can gather from this that He rules only in some certain place in heaven. The Holy Spirit defines that height of God and of the right hand of God not by the sublimity of place, but by the ineffable loftiness of heavenly glory and majesty. . . (Objection:) That Stephen sees Christ standing at the right hand of God in one place only. Acts 7:56. Response: It does not follow: Christ is seen or beheld standing at the right hand of God in one place; therefore, He sits at the right hand of God in one place only. For this concerns a certain peculiar revelation and vision, manifested to Stephen, which [reveals] the majesty of Christ, who is everywhere powerful"

does not weaken or limit, but rather confirms, the most present and most powerful reigning of Christ. For if, according to the hypothesis of the adversaries, the body of Christ is only in heaven, and heaven is immediately above the firmament, how could Christ, standing at the right hand of God, be seen by Stephen, since the body of Christ possesses a magnitude incomparably smaller than the most minute stars? Visibly, therefore, Christ standing at the right hand of God appears in one place, while meanwhile He invisibly sits at the right hand of God everywhere. But He appears standing, that is, prepared to bring aid and to punish enemies.” (L. c. § 221.)

Hunnius: “The Person, indeed, who is God and man, is exalted, and not one nature separately without the Person; but that Person is exalted not according to His deity, but according to His assumed humanity. First, this appears from the fact that the deity of the Word, existing as altogether immutable, can neither be humbled, nor exalted, nor transferred into a better or worse state... In expressing the exaltation of Christ, the apostles say and write that Christ was made Lord; Acts 2:36... But would it not suffice to confess that Christ was exalted to the right hand of God, so that the human nature would not be explicitly mentioned? (Resp.:) Although in instructing the simple, who do not oppose the truth, it is permitted to use this phrase as well, yet it would not be sufficiently clear by reason of which nature this was ascribed to Him. But now, because the intemperance and impiety of the adversaries is added, by which they—with wicked daring, as much as in them lies—snatch away that which is attributed to the flesh of Christ, and either refer this phrase, by which we say Christ is exalted to the right hand of infinite power, to the deity in the manner of the Arians and explain it as a restoration of power, or (as they are more changeable than Vertumnus and Proteus) explain it of Christ according to both natures and restrict it to His office, yet in such a way that the human nature only acts humanly, and thus they are entirely intent on dislodging our flesh from the throne of divine majesty: the inevitable necessity of the Church requires that, in order to uncover the fraud of those men, it be clearly shown that this exaltation happened to Christ according to His humanity.” (L. c. p. 108, 109 sq., 116 sq.)

Quenstedtius: “Christ sat at the right hand of God the Father neither from eternity nor from the beginning of the world. The reason is that this session does not belong to Him according to His deity, but according to His humanity; nor from the moment of conception, because this session has a preceding humiliation, passion, and death, and consists in υπερυψώσει, excluding all κένωσιν, but at the final term of the ascension.” (L. c. s. 2, q. 12, f. 638.)

Hunnius: “If that majesty to which Christ arrived on the day of the ascension depends upon the union, why does Scripture proclaim it as the reward and fruit of the passion, Ps. 110: ‘He shall drink of the brook in the way, therefore shall He lift up the head,’ and Phil. 2: ‘He was obedient to the Father even unto the death of the cross; therefore God hath highly exalted Him’? The cause is this, because on account of the passion the incarnation itself also took place. For the only-begotten of God came into the world and was incarnate for this reason, that He might present Himself by His passion and death as a victim for our sins. Since, therefore, the incarnation itself was undertaken on account of the passion, which otherwise would never have been, it is not a wonder that this exaltation is assigned to the passion as its fruit. For if the Son of God were not about to suffer and die, then He would neither have assumed humanity nor could He ever have been exalted according to it in time.” (L. c. p. 123.)

Kromayerus: “The right hand, of which there is question in the Scriptures, either has an opposite left hand or it does not. When it has an opposite left hand, it denotes a more honorable place, and by the left hand is understood either a lower place, as Matt. 20:21, or an ignominious one, Matt. 25:33. When it does not have a left hand, it denotes power, a metaphor taken from the right arm, which excels in strength... which can be seen from Ps. 118 in several verses and other places of Scripture. To sit and to sit at the right hand of God differ in biblical style. To sit is the same as to reign or to judge, just as God Himself PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III. is said to sit, Ps. 9:5. To sit at the right hand is to rule or to judge with communicated power, which kind of session belongs to Christ according to His human nature. For as God, He does not sit at the right hand of God, but is the very right hand of God. "Where the throne of God and the throne of Christ must also be distinguished. By the throne of God, infinite power is understood; by the throne of Christ, finite power. Christ alone sits at the right hand of God or the Father; but the elect will also be placed at the right hand of Christ, just as the Son of God distinguishes in Rev. 3:21. Therefore, as those who judge and govern sit, while those who fight stand: so Christ, being about to bring aid to the most valiant soldier Stephen against his persecutors and to crown him after the battle, is said to stand; but as governing this universe and one day to judge the world, He is said to sit." (Th. posit. pol. P. II. p. 115 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Scholastics and Papists, some of whom assert: 1.) That by the right hand of God is understood created heavenly and eternal blessedness; thus Bellarmine... 2.) They contend that a session at the right hand of God was indeed given to the humanity, but not in itself, rather in the suppositum. For the same Bellarmine argues thus: 'For when a king puts on purple and sits on his throne, he raises the purple to that throne, not in such a way that the purple is said to sit or reign, but so that it is said to be the garment of the one sitting and reigning, and also so that the purple-clad king is said to sit or reign,' etc. 3.) Some maintain that the session at the right hand of God implies only the honor next to God... 4.) Others, on the contrary, hold that the session at the right hand of God implies a certain superiority and eminence of the Son over the Father; thus Maldonatus: ... 'Wherefore to sit at the right hand is to be in a certain way greater regarding office and the administration of the church; because all judgment was given to Him by the Father.' 2. Of the Calvinists, who maintain: 1.) That the session at the right hand implies a certain occupation of a place in heaven or a position in a certain place, to which Christ is bound until He returns for judgment... 2.) That the session at the right hand of God implies not the same, but the honor next to God, and therefore that no other glory, virtue, and power was conferred upon Christ the man, as man, through that session at the right hand of God, than that which is finite and created... 3.) That Christ sits at the right hand of God according to both natures, and therefore also according to His deity; others invent a twin and double session at the right hand of God, one infinite, which belongs to Christ according to His deity, the other finite, which belongs to Him according to His humanity... 3. Of the Socinians, who assert: 1.) That the session at the right hand of God implies a more honorable place above God... 2.) That to sit at the right hand of the Father is to have God at one's right hand or to enjoy a propitious God... 4. Of the Arminians, whose leader Episcopius (Inst. theol. 1. 4, p. 342) ... attributes to Christ the man, exalted to the right hand of the Father ... only finite power... 5. Of the Weigelians, who, with the Arians and Valentinians, dream that the session at the right hand of God did not take place after the ascension into heaven, but at the very incarnation." (L. c. f. 638 sqq.)

Latin:

Quae dextra Dei non est certus aliquis locus, sed ipsa omnipotens Dei virtus, quae coelum et terram replet, juxta Solidam Declarationem Form. Cone. Artic. VIII., adeoque sedere ad dextram Dei dicitur, qui totum terrarum orbem, inprimis ecclesiam, potenter et provide gubernat omnibusque hostibus suis dominatur. Conf. Ps.110, 1. 2. Actor. 2, 34. 35.

Lutherus: ״Zum ersten, nehmen wir vor den Artikel, dass Christus sitze zur rechten Hand Gattes, welchen die Schwärmer halten, er leide nicht, dass Christi Leib im Abendmahl auch sein könnte. Wenn wir sie nun hier fragen, was sie Gottes rechte Hand heissen, da Chri>tus sitzt: achte ich, sie werden uns daher schwärmen, wie man den Kindern pflegt fürzubilden einen Gaukelhimmel, darin ein güldener Stuhl Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.7 PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO II. stehe und Christus neben dem Vater sitze in einer Chorkappe und güldenen Krone, gleichwie es die Maler malen.

Denn wo sie nicht solche kindische, fleischliche Gedanken hätten von der rechten Hand Gottes, würden sie freilich.sich nicht so lassen anfechten den Leib Christi im Abendmahl, oder sich so bläuen mit dem Spruch Augustini (welchem sie doch sonst nichts glauben noch keinem andern), Christus muss an einem Ort leiblich sein, aber seine Wahrheit ist allenthalben u. s. w.

Aus welchem kindischen Gedanken muss denn weiter folgen, dass sie auch Gott selber an einem Ort im Himmel auf denselbigen güldenen Stuhl binden, weil ausser Christo kein Gott ist, und wo Christus ist, da ist die Gottheit ganz und gar, wie Paulus sagt Col. 2, 9.: Es wohnet in ihm die ganze Gottheit leibhaftig. . .

Die Schrift aber lehrt uns, dass Gottes rechte Hand nicht sei ein sonderlicher Ort, da ein Leib solle oder möge sein, als auf einem güldenen Stuhl; sondern sei die allmächtige Gewalt Gottes, welche zugleich nirgend sein kann, und doch an allen Orten sein muss.

Nirgend kann sie an einigem Ort sein (spreche ich): denn wo sie irgend an etlichem Ort wäre, müsste sie daselbst begreiflich und beschlossen sein; wie alle dasjenige, so an einem Ort ist, muss an demselbigen Ort beschlössen und abgemessen sein, also dass es dieweil an keinem andern Ort sein kann. Die göttliche Gewalt aber mag und kann nicht also beschlossen und abgemessen sein. Denn sie ist unbegreiflich und unmässlich, ausser und über alles, das da ist und sein kann.

Wiederum, muss sie an allen Orten wesentlich und gegenwärtig sein, auch in dem geringsten Baumblatt.

Ursach ist die: denn Gott ists, der alle Dinge schafft, wirkt und erhält, durch seine allmächtige Gewalt und rechte Hand, wie unser Glaube bekennet; denn er schickt keine Amtleute oder Engel aus, wenn er etwas schaffet oder erhält, sondern solches alles ist seiner göttlichen Gewalt selbst eigen Werk.

Soll ers aber schaffen und erhalten, so muss er daselbst sein, und seine Creatur so wohl im Allerinwendigsten als im Allerauswendigsten machen und erhalten.

Darum muss er ja in einer jeglichen Creatur in ihrem Allerinwendigsten, Auswendigsten, um und um, durch und durch, unten und oben, vorn und hinten selbst da sein, dass nicht Gegenwärtigere noch Innerlichere sein kann in allen Creaturen, denn Gott selbst mit seiner Gewalt.

Denn er ists, der die Haut machet; er ists, der auch die Gebeine machet; er ists, der die Haare auf dem Haupt machet; er ists auch, der das Mark in den Gebeinen macht; er ists, der ein jeglich Stücklein am Haar macht; er ists, der ein jeglich Stücklein am Mark machet; er muss ja alles machen, beide, Stücke und Ganzes: so muss ja seine Hand da sein, die es mache, das kann nicht fehlen.“ (Dass diese Worte Christi: Das ist mein Leib, noch feste stehen. Tom. Hai. XX, 1000. 1002. sq.) Cf. supra Kromayerus p. 64.

Idem: ,,Was kann,zu meiner Rechten sitzen‘ (Ps. 110, 1.) anders heissen, denn Gott gleich sitzen? Denn er sitzet ihm nicht zun Häupten noch zun Füssen, weder höher noch niedriger, sondern zur Rechten, ihm gleich, dass der Himmel eben sowohl sein Stuhl und die Erde seine Fussbank ist; wie er spricht Matthäi am letzten v. 18.: ,Mir ist gegeben alle Gewalt im Himmel und Erden.“< (Ausleg. der letzten Worte Davids. 1548. III, 2825.)

Gerhardus: ,,De ipso Deo, nulli loco incluso, a nullo loco excluso, dicitur, quod in altis habitet, quod sit in coelis, quod e coelo respiciat super filios hominum; neque tamen quisquam inde colligit vel colligere potest, quod tantum in certo aliquo coeli loco dominetur. Altitudinem illam Dei et dextrae Dei Spiritus S. non loci sublimitate, sed gloriae et majestatis coelestis inenarrabili celsitudine definit. . . (Excipiunt:) Quod Stephanus uno tantum in loco videat Christum stantem a dextris Dei. Act. 7, 56. Resp.: Non sequitur: Christus uno in loco videtur sive conspicitur stans a dextris Dei; ergo uno tantum in loco sedet ad dextram Dei. Agitur enim hic de peculiari quadam revelatione et visione, Stephano manifestata, quae majestatem Christi ubique potentis

sime et praesentissime regnantis non labefactat nec limitat, sed potius confirmat. Quod si enim juxta adversariorum hypothesin corpus Christi est tantum in coelo, et coelum est proxime supra firmamentum, quomodo potuit Christus stans a dextris Dei a Stephano videri, cum corpus Christi quantitatem incomparabiliter minorem obtineat, quam minutissimae stellae? Visibiliter ergo Christus stans a dextris Dei in uno loco apparet, interim invisibiliter ubique ad dextram Dei sedet. Apparet autem stans, id est, paratus ad ferendum auxilium et hostes puniendos.“ (L. c. § 221.)

Hunnius: ״Persona quidem, quae Deus et homo est, est exaltata et non altera natura seorsim absque persona; exaltata autem est ea persona non secundum deitatem, sed juxta assumptam humanitatem. Primo id hinc apparet, quia deitas Verbi prorsus immutabilis existens nec humiliari, nec exaltari, nec in meliorem, nec deteriorem statum transferri potest... In exprimenda Christi exaltatione apostoli dicunt et scribunt, Christum factum esse Dominum; Act. 2, 36. . . Annon autem sufficeret confiteri, Christum esse exaltatum ad d. D., ut maxime natura humana non exprimeretur? (Resp.:) Etsi in erudiendis simplicibus, qui veritati non obsistunt, licet hac quoque phrasi uti, attamen non satis constaret, cujus naturae causa hoc ei transcriberetur. Jam vero quia adversariorum insuper intemperies accedit et impietas, qua id, quod carni Christi tributum est, nefario ausu, quantum in se est, rapiunt atque hanc phrasin, qua Christum exaltatum dicimus ad inflnitae potentiae dextram, vel ad deitatem Arianorum more referunt et de restitutione potentiae exponunt, vel (ut sunt Vertumno atque Proteo mutabiliores) de Christo juxta utramque naturam exponunt et ad offlcium restringunt, ita tamen, ut natura humana tantum agat humana, atque sic toti in hoc sunt, ut carnem nostram de solio divinae majestatis deturbent: requirit ecclesiae inevitabilis necessitas, ut ad detegendam illorum hominum fraudem dilucide monstretur, hanc exaltationem contigisse Christo juxta suam humanitatem.“ (L. c. p. 108. 109. sq. 116. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ״Sedit Christus ad dextram Dei Patris non a aeterno nec a mundi initio. Ratio est, quia haec sessio ipsi non competit juxta deitatem, sed humanitatem; nec a momento conceptionis, quia haec sessio praecedentem habet exinanitionem, passionem et mortem, et consistit in υπερυψώσει, omnem κένωσιν excludente, sed in ultimo ascensionis termino.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 12. f. 638.)

Hunnius: ״Si ab unione dependet ea majestas, ad quam Christus in die ascensionis pervenit, cur Scriptura eam ut praemium atque fructum passionis praedicat Ps. 110.: ,De torrente'in via bibet, propterea exaltabit caput‘, et Phil. 2.: ,Obediens fuit Patri usque ad mortem crucis; propter hoc extulit illum Deus in summam sublimitatem‘? Causa haec est, quia propter passionem ipsa quoque incarnatio facta est. Propterea enim in mundum venit unigenitus Dei et incarnatus est, ut seipsum passione et morte sua victimam pro peccatis nostris sisteret. Quia igitur ob passionem ipsa incarnatio suscepta, quae alias nunquam futura fuisset: mirum non est, passioni ceu fructum eam exaltationem assignari. Nisi enim passurus et moriturus fuisset F. D., tum nec assumpsisset humanitatem neque juxta illam in tempore unqnam potuisset exaltari.“ (L. c. p. 123.)

Kromayerus: ״Dextra, de qua in Scripturis agitur, vel habet oppositam sinistram, vel non habet. Quando sinistram habet oppositam, locum honoratiorem denotat, et per sinistram vel locus inferior, ut Matth. 20, 21., vel ignominiosus intelligitur, Matth. 25, 33. Quando non habet sinistram, potentiam denotat, a brachio dextro, qui robore praepollet, metaphora sumpta, . . . quod ex Ps. 118. versiculis pluribus et aliis Scripturae locis videri potest. Differunt stylo biblico sedere et sedere ad d. D. Sedere idem est, ac regnare vel judicare, prout ipse Deus PAET. III. CAP. II. SECTIO III. sedere dicitur Ps. 9, 5. Sedere ad dextram est regere vel judicare communicata potestate, cujusmodi sessio posterior Christo secundum hum. nat. competit. Ut Deus enim non sedet ad d. D., sed est ipsa dextra Dei. ’Ubi thronus Dei et thronus Christi etiam venit distinguendus. Per thronum Dei potestas infinita, per thronum Christi potestas finita intelligitur. Solus Christus ad d. D. vel Patris sedet; ad dextram vero Christi etiam electi collocabuntur, prout Filius Dei Apoc. 3, 21. distinguit. Ut itaque judicantes et gubernantes sedent, pugnantes stant: ita Christus fortissimo militi Stephano adversus persecutores opem laturus ipsum que post pugnam coronaturus stare, gubernans hoc universum et aliquando judicaturus orbem terrarum sedere dicitur.“ (Th. posit.pol. P. II. p. 115. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum, quorum alii asserunt, 1.) intelligi per dextram Dei beatitudinem coelestem et aeternam creatam; ita Bellarminus. . . 2.) Contendunt, datam esse quidem humanitati sessionen^ad dextram Dei, ast non in se, sed in supposito. Ita enim idem Bellarminus disputat: ,Cum enim rex induit purpuram et sedet in solio suo, evehit purpuram ad illud solium, non sic, ut purpura dicatur sedere aut regnare, sed ut dicatur vestis sedentis et regnantis et etiam ut dicatur purpuratus rex sedere aut regnare‘ etc. 3.) Statuunt nonnulli, sessionem ad dextram Dei inferre tantum proximum a Deo honorem... 4.) Alii contra volunt, sessionem ad d. D. inferre majoritatem et eminentiam quandam Filii supra Patrem; ita Maldonatus: . . . ,Quare sedere ad dextram est, esse quodammodo maiorem quoad officium et administrationem ecclesiae; quia omne judicium fuit illi datum a Patre.‘ 2. Calvinianorum, statuentium, 1.) sessionem ad dextram inferre certam loci in coelo occupationem vel in certo quodam loco positionem, ad quem sit alligatus Christus, donec redeat ad judicium... 2.) Sessionem ad dextram Dei inferre non eundem, sed proximum a Deo honorem, adeoque Christo homini, qua homini, per illam sessionem ad d. D. non aliam collatam gloriam, virtutem et potentiam, quam finitam et creatam... 3.) Christum ad d. D. sedere secundum utramque naturam, adeoque etiam secundum deitatem; alii geminam ac duplicem fingunt sessionem ad d. D., alteram infinitam, quae Christo secundum deitatem, alteram vero finitam, quae ipsi secundum humanitatem competat. . . 3. Socinianorum, asserentium, 1.) inferre sessionem ad d. D. locum honoratiorem supra Deum... 2.) Sedere ad d. D. P. esse, Deum sibi habere a dextris vel Deo gaudere propitio... 4. Armimianorum, quorum antesignanus Episcopius 1. 4. Institut, th. f. 342. . . Christo homini ad d. D. P. exaltato. . . finitam tantum potentiam tribuit. . . 5. Weigelianorum, cum Arianis et Valentinianis somniantium, sessionem ad d. D. non factam esse post ascensionem in coelum, sed in ipsa incarnatione.“ (L. c. f. 638. sqq.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Section III. ON THE OFFICE OF CHRIST

Section III. ON THE OFFICE OF CHRIST. § 1. It is certain that the Son of God did not assume human nature out of any necessity nor in vain, but for the sake of some end, and indeed, that in the assumed human nature, and through it, He might save sinful men.

See Matt. 1:21 and 25, where the name Jesus, of the incarnate Son of God, is said to be derived from the act or office of saving, which He performs. To save, however, is not only to preserve and deliver, but to give salvation, or to make happy. Whence it is evident that Jesus is more than a savior, and it is not without reason that the name of savior has been pleasing to Christians. And it is notably said of Christ, σώζειν εις το παντελές δΰναται τους προςερχομένους δι' αυτού τώ θεω, "He is able to save to the uttermost (perfectly) those who come to God through Him," Heb. 7:25. Furthermore, the very name of Christ, which denotes "anointed," simultaneously indicates some relation to an office, for the sake of assuming and exercising which Christ as man is anointed. Namely, just as in the Old Testament, and among the people of God, prophets, priests, and kings were accustomed to be anointed and by this means inaugurated into their respective offices, so we are taught that Christ was anointed for the sake of such offices. And in John 4:42 these are joined: '0 σωτηρ τού χόσμου, ό χριστός, "the Savior of the world, the Christ," namely, anointed for the purpose of saving.

Kromayer: "The principal names by which our Savior is distinguished are Jesus and Christ, which, although they are used interchangeably and quite often joined together in common parlance, nevertheless differ in this: that the former is a proper name, of peculiar imposition, which He received at circumcision and by which He was distinguished from other individuals; the latter, however, is an appellative, which corresponds to the name Messiah." (Th. posit.-pol. I, 83.) The same: "Ή θεότης χρίσις τής άνθρωπότητος... We wished to bring forward this saying of the Greek fathers in the place of an aphorism, in order to teach that Christ was anointed not according to His divine, but His human nature; for the divine nature was rather the anointing than the anointed. For to Him who has all things by nature, gifts are not to be conferred. . . . When, however, in Ps. 45:8 it is said that God is anointed, it is an idiomatic proposition of the first kind of the communication of idioms, in which the properties of the natures are communicated to the person in the concrete. This property, in this case, is the anointing or the bestowal of gifts, which is predicated of the person, here denominated from the divine nature, just as I say: 'God sheds His own blood,' Acts 20:28. . . . The polemical use of this aphorism is against the Reformed, namely, John Grabius, a theologian of Bremen, who vehemently defends the thesis that the anointing pertains to Christ according to both natures." (Th. posit.-pol. I, 85.)

Gerhard: "Some establish a twofold reason for the anointing in Christ. One, by which the λόγος Himself, by assuming human nature, anointed the same with the fullness of His own Spirit, Col. 2:9; of which they understand the prophecy of Dan. 9:24; the other, by which God the Father anointed Christ as man with the oil of gladness above His fellows; of which they understand the sayings of Ps. 45:8 and Isa. 61:1. But it is one and the same anointing, by which the Father anointed Christ according to His human nature with the Holy Spirit, and by which Christ anointed His own flesh with the oil of the deity and the fullness of His own Spirit, just as it is one and the same communication by which the Father is said to have placed the Son according to His human nature at His right hand, and by which the Son raised the assumed flesh to the right hand of God. Although not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, but the λόγος alone assumed the flesh into the unity of His person, and thus the term of the assumption is not the person of the Father or the Holy Spirit, but the λόγος, nevertheless it is one and the same action of the three persons." (Exeges. loc. IV. § 14.) That Christ would have assumed human nature even if Adam had not sinned cannot be proven.

Gerhard: "Would the Son of God have been incarnate if man had not sinned at all? . . . The negative part of the question is embraced by: 1. Almost all of the ancients, Athanasius, Nazianzen, Augustine..." PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III.

and others. 2. Some of the scholastics, Thomas, Bonaventure, and others. 3. Many of the papists, although hesitantly. . . 4. All of our own. The arguments are drawn: 1. From the sayings of Scripture, which 1.) everywhere establish the end of the incarnation and advent as the redemption of the human race and the restoration of that which was lost. . . 2.) set Adam as the source of sin and death and Christ as the source of righteousness in opposition to one another, Rom. 5:12; 1 Cor. 15:45, 47. 3.) From types, parables, and similitudes. If there had not been a flood, the ark would not have been built, Gen. 6. If the Israelites had not been bitten by fiery serpents on account of sin, the bronze serpent would not have been lifted up, Num. 21. If a storm had not arisen at sea, Jonah would not have been cast from the ship, Jon. 1. If the king’s servants had not been rejected, the son would not have been sent, Matt. 21. If the sheep and the drachma had not been lost, a lamp would not have been lit for searching, nor would the shepherd have gone to seek the wandering sheep, Luke 15.

2. From reasons. From this hypothesis, the foulness of sin, the atrocity of divine wrath, and the immense goodness of God shine forth more clearly, etc. (Exeges. 1. IV. § 142, 143, 144.)

Brochmand: "It is not permitted to be wise beyond what is written. But Scripture testifies that Christ would not have assumed human flesh if man had not sinned." (Syst. P. I. f. 286.)

Ambrose: "O blessed fault, which merited to have such a redeemer!" (Cf. Luther cited above P. I, 293.) For the Antithesis, see above P. II, p. 19.

Kromayer: "It is often asked why God does this or that; why He did not create the world sooner; why He did not send the promised redeemer immediately after the fall and the promulgation of the πρωτευαγγέλιον, but only after nearly four thousand years had been completed? . . . Although reasons may be brought forward by us a posteriori—and indeed regarding the first question, that even if the world had been created sooner, this question could nonetheless have been raised; regarding the second, that God wished to exercise His people first under the yoke of ceremonial laws, so that they might the more anxiously pant after the promised Messiah, and thus He imitated the method usually observed in the conversion of individuals, where contrition precedes faith, and here, because according to that well-worn saying: 'He does not feel the sweet, who has not tasted the bitter.' . . . Although, I say, such probable reasons are brought forward by us a posteriori, it is safer, however, to acquiesce in the divine will, which is the entire reason for the deed, Ps. 135:6." (Th. posit.-pol. II, 64.) §

2. Therefore, for the sake of men to be saved, Christ the θεάνθρωπος willed to execute three principal offices: 1. that He might show sinful men the way of escaping from the state of sin and obtaining salvation, which is called the prophetic office; 2. that He Himself might pay the price of redemption to God for the fallen human race and reconcile it, which is the priestly office, or mediatorial office strictly so called; 3. that He might govern, defend, and finally make blessed those who adhere to Him, which is accustomed to be called the kingly office.

Kromayer: "By office is understood the right and duty of acting in such a way, commonly [called] a function."

Quenstedtius: "The doctrine concerning the person of Christ is followed by the treatment of His office, which we call by the general name of mediatorial. This is nothing other than the function belonging to the whole person of the θεάνθρωπος, arising from the θεανδρικαῖς actions, by which Christ has perfectly executed—in both natures, with both, and through both—all things that are required for our salvation, both in acquiring and in applying it, and even now continues to execute them." (Th. did.-pol. P. III, c. 3. membr. 2. s. 1. th. 1. f. 304.)

Who were already subject to perdition; just as the Son of Man is said to have come σώσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός, to save that which was lost, Matt. 18:11; Luke 19:10. For which reason He is said to be anointed and sent to preach the gospel to the poor, to preach deliverance to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, etc., Luke 4:18. Indeed, when we were enemies, we were to be reconciled to God (as we have now been reconciled) through the death of His Son, Rom. 5:10.

Gerhardus: "The office of Christ consists in the work of mediation between God and men, which is the end of the incarnation, 1 Tim. 2:5; for the union of the divine and human nature in Christ was brought about for this reason, that the Son of God might be able to perform the office of mediator and redeemer in the assumed nature, 1 John 3:8; Matt. 20:28; John 6:38. That office of Christ is commonly established as threefold: prophetic, priestly, and kingly, the sufficiency of which distribution is proved: 1. From the coordination of the sayings of Scripture. As many classes as there are to which the titles attributed to Christ by reason of His office can be referred, and the sayings of Scripture which speak of Christ’s office, so many parts of Christ’s office are rightly established. Now, there are three classes to which the titles attributed to Christ by reason of His office can be referred. For they are attributed to Him either with respect to the prophetic, the priestly, or the kingly office. 2. From the condition of our state. On account of the ignorance of the mind introduced by sin, we stood in need of a teacher or prophet; on account of sins and the punishments of sins, we stood in need of a priest, reconciling us to God, satisfying for us, and interceding before the tribunal of God; on account of the infirmity of the will, we stood in need of a king, leading and defending us. 3. From the enumeration of the benefits of Christ. Christ expiates the guilt of our sins before God, covers the stains of our iniquities, and obtains for us a blessing from God; which is the work of a priest. Christ promulgates to us the counsel of God concerning our redemption and salvation; which is the work of a prophet. Christ effectively applies to us the benefit of redemption and salvation, obtained by His precious blood; He rules us with the scepter of the Word and the Holy Spirit, restrains our enemies, and after the final judgment transfers us into the heavenly kingdom; which is the work of a king." (Disputatt. isag. p. 406.)

Gerhardus: ״Officium Christi consistit in opere mediationis inter Deum et homines, quod est finis incarnationis, 1 Tim. 2, 5.; ideo enim divinae et humanae naturae unio in Christo facta est, ut mediatoris ac redemtoris officio Filius Dei in assumta natura fungi posset, 1 Joh. 3, 8. Matth. 20, 28. Joh. 6, 38. Officium illud Christi vulgo triplex statuitur, propheticum, sacerdotale et regium, cujus distributionis sufficientia probatur: 1. Ex dictorum Scripturae coordinatione. Quot sunt classes, in quas referri possunt appellationes, quae ratione officii Christo tribuuntur, et dicta Scripturae, quae de Christi officio loquuntur, tot etiam partes officii Christi recte statuuntur.
