### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Or His people, Matt. 1

Or His people, Matt. 1: 21. As the son of David, heir, antitype, Luke 1:31 ff.; Heb. 1:8, 9, 13. §

8. In order that these things may be understood more distinctly, it must be known that Christ was a prophet more excellent than all, and that He most clearly manifested to men the will of God concerning their salvation, and likewise both taught and rebuked, in such a way indeed that He Himself conferred divine authority and efficacy upon the preached Word. PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III.

Thus Peter, Acts 3:22, according to the prophecy of Moses in Deut 18:15, says that Christ is that prophet like unto Moses, namely in this, that just as Moses excelled all other prophets in his more familiar fellowship with God and in that he was not only a teacher but also the leader of the people, so Christ is the prophet κατ’ ἐξοχὴν; although it must be admitted that Christ is not thereby set as equal to Moses, but rather excels him, which will be evident from what follows; cf. Luke 7:16, where Christ is called προφήτης μέγας, and John 6:14, where he is called ὁ προφήτης ὁ ἐρχόμενος εἰς τὸν κόσμον.

Dannhauerus: "Deut. 18:18. Christ was truly the antitype of Moses by his royal leading out of Egypt, by his intercessory mediation, and by his immediate conversation with God." (Hodos. Phaenom. VIII. p. 413.)

Ad. Osiander: "For his prophetic office (Christ) was not taught in heaven, nor did he receive infinite knowledge through revelation, but through the personal union, John 3:34. He who does not receive the Spirit by measure and speaks the words of God by virtue of his mission and the Spirit, he has received infinite knowledge through the personal union. But Christ, etc. Therefore, etc. The major premise is proven: Because he who receives without measure, receives beyond measure, consequently in an infinite manner. However, in the passage cited, the mission and the giving of the Spirit signify a principle far more august than a certain revelation made at the beginning of Christ's ministry. Observe: that this mission is the mission into the world, i.e., the incarnation, as is proven from v. 17 and parallels, and this is laid as the foundation for the speaking of divine words... It is of such a one that there is speech here, who is said to be sent into the world and has spoken the words of God originally from the bosom of the Father, and although in the present tense, it is to be understood through an enallage of time or by the demonstration of a continuous act. Christ not only did not receive the Spirit without a certain and thus indefinite measure, but without measure, i.e., indefinitely. Furthermore, he received it in such a way that he had the power to bestow and dispense it to others, so that the oil flowed from him onto his 'companions' (Ps. 45:8), which is to receive infinitely as the primary cause dispensing to others." (Colleg. th. systemat. P. IV, 142 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Ad. Osiander: "Antithesis of the Socinians: Christ was caught up into the heavens during the time of his forty-day fast, and there was informed and inaugurated. Socin. instit. christ. relig. fol. 127." (L. c.)

No longer through types and obscure prophecies, but with clear words and by proposing the matter to be understood by men in such a way that what is said can be openly and distinctly perceived.

For to be a prophet, whom the Hebrews call נביא, is to be an interpreter of God among men, or to convey to men what has been divinely spoken or revealed to oneself.

This indeed happened in the Old Testam…ent in such a way that the prophets were taught themselves through dreams and visions, which had something of obscurity, and then taught others divine things under such signs, according to the measure of knowledge which God then imparted.

But that a fuller clarity was reserved for the times of the Messiah himself had already been signified long ago. For he informed men about those things which were necessary to be believed and done, he purged the law of God from Pharisaical corruptions, see Matt. 5, 6, 7 and elsewhere, he showed to the impenitent and unbelieving the gravity of their sins

and the wrath of God, Matt. 23; Luke 19:41 ff., but to the contrite He announced the gospel of the remission of sins, Luke 4:18; Mark 1:14, 15.

Kromayerus: "Christ was indeed a teacher of the law, but not a legislator. . . We are not speaking of the λόγος or the Son of God before He was incarnate (for we readily concede that He, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, inscribed the law upon our hearts at creation, and that when the s…ense of it was obscured after the fall, He repeated it on Mount Sinai), but of the Son of God incarnate, the great prophet, insofar as He taught His church in the days of His flesh.

That He taught the law here, purged it of Pharisaical corruptions, and demonstrated its true meaning, especially regarding the fifth and sixth commandments (from which a collection for the rest is easy), we grant with both hands, if there were four; but that He enacted new laws and added them to the Mosaic ones, we deny and utterly deny.

We rely, however, on the following foundations:

1. That Moses the lawgiver and Christ the Savior, John 1:17, are opposed to one another. 'The law was given through Moses,' says John, 'but grace and truth came through Christ.' Where 'truth' is not opposed to lies or falsehoods, as if there were no truth in the Old Testament, but to shadows.

2. That the doctrine of Christ, the great prophet, had to be different from that of Moses—namely, friendly and acceptable, full of consolation, just as Deut. 18:15–19 is opposed to the terrible voice of the law, which the Israelites could not bear. For which reason also, Christ says in Luke 4:18, from Isa. 61:1, that He was sent to evangelize. He had to teach primarily the gospel, and secondarily the law, and indeed for the sake of the gospel. Whence, since the voice of the gospel is substituted for the whole heavenly doctrine, as in Mark 16:15, the denomination is made from the more important part.

3. That Christ, when asked about the law, brings forth none other than that of Moses, Matt. 22:37–40: 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment; and the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.' But this epitome of the law is contained in Deut. 6:5 and Lev. 19:18.

4. That God prohibited any addition to the law and any subtraction from it, Deut. 4:2 and 12:32.

5. That the new laws, which those on the opposite side think were enacted by Christ, are contained in the law of Moses." (Th. posit.-pol. II, 275 ff.)

S. Schmidtius: "Nor did He come into the world for the purpose of explaining or perfecting His old law, but to bring the gospel and to prepare men for the reception of this through the explanation of the law." (Articul. Form. Conc. Repetit, p. 308.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Scholastics and Jesuits, who maintain that Christ was a new legislator and came into the world to add certain new laws and more perfect evangelical counsels to the Mosaic laws, and that His precepts are far more perfect, excellent, and severe than the Mosaic ones... Council of Trent, sess. 6, can. 21: 'If anyone shall say that Christ Jesus was given by God to men as a redeemer, in whom they should trust, and not also as a legislator, whom they should obey, let him be anathema.'...

Bellarmine adds: 'That there are many evangelical counsels truly and properly so called, but three are the principal ones': continence, obedience, and poverty.

2. Of the Socinians, who posit a twofold set of Christ's commands; for 1) they say that Christ rendered the Decalogue or moral law more perfect and added to the individual precepts of the Decalogue those things that were lacking in them; 2) they contend that Christ delivered certain commands to the apostles individually...

Hence that profane utterance of Crellius: 'The philosophers delivered more perfect duties of virtue than Moses himself.'

The primary falsehood and the scope of this impious assertion is to prove that, while no one could be justified by the righteousness of the Mosaic law, as it was imperfect and shadowed, yet now in the New Testament..." PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION III.

that a man can be justified by the works of a more perfect law. . . 3. Of the Arminians, who teach that Christ is altogether a legislator and that the gospel of Christ is a new law.” (L. c. P. IV. c. 1. s. 2. q. 8. f. 906. sq.)

For thus it is said in Matthew 7:29, that Christ taught ώς έξουσίαν εχων, as one having authority, or that in his own name and by his authority, as they say, he proposed things to be believed and things to be done, and bound the minds of men and moved them to offer him assent and obedience, with miracles added from time to time, by which their minds were struck; cf. Mark 1:27, where it is said to be χατ έξουσίαν, and Luke 4:32, where his speech is said to have been έν έξουσία. § 4. Next, in the prophetic office of Christ, it must be noted how the human and divine nature alike contributed what was proper to each. Namely, according to the human nature, Christ taught by living voice for the whole three years and more, indicated the sacraments to be celebrated in the church, and summoned to himself ministers of the Word and sacraments; but according to the divine nature, he joined infinite power and authority to the Word and sacraments instituted by him.

See Luke 4:21. For the act of speaking with a living and articulate voice through organs naturally destined for the forming of the voice is in substance human, which Scripture otherwise describes by the phrase "opening his mouth," Matthew 5:1. The space of three years, which Christ spent in the office of preaching, can be known from the history of the life of Christ and the number of Passovers which he celebrated after his baptism. See Matthew 26:26, chapter 28:19. For there the institution of the Holy Supper is held, here that of baptism.

L. c., Matthew 28:19 and John 20:21, where the mission of the apostles to gather disciples for the Master and to the ministry of absolution is recounted. Gerhardus: “The Papists, against the prophetic office, 1. attribute the magisterium of faith to the Roman Pontiff, . . . 3. introduce new sacraments unknown to Christ and the apostles, . . . 4. change the institution of the Eucharist made by Christ.” (L. c. § 327.)

Thus Mark, chapter 16, last verse, records how, when the apostles went out and preached everywhere, the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed. And in John 20:23, Christ says: Whose sins the apostles remit, they shall be remitted, and whose sins they retain, they shall be retained. § 5. Now, however, whether in the state of exaltation, where Christ no longer himself visibly performs the ministry in person

justificari posse hominem ex operibus legis perfectioris. . . 3. Arminianorum, docentium, Christum omnino legislatorem et evangelium Christi novam legem esse.“ (L. c. P. IV. c. 1. s. 2. q. 8. f. 906. sq.)

### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: teaching, but teaches through His ministers,a the prophetic office seems to…

teaching, but teaches through His ministers,a the prophetic office seems to coincide with the kingdom of grace.b Certainly, He causes the divine will to be announced to us and leads men to the acknowledgment of the truth through the Word and the Sacraments.

B. Mentzerus: "Indeed, the holy patriarchs and prophets in the Old Testament prophesied through the Spirit of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:11. And the thoughts of the ancients are pious, that through the Son of God that first promise concerning the blessed seed was promulgated in Gen. 3, and that the Son of God appeared to the fathers and spoke to them. From which it is gathered that this prophetic office belongs to Christ not only according to His humanity, but also His deity. For although in the time of the Old Testament the Son of God had not yet assumed humanity, nevertheless the decree had been made concerning its being assumed at a certain time; which pledge of the Son of God concerning the whole work of redemption was as efficacious as if all things that are required for His office had already been completed in act. To this pertain the words of Heb. 13:8: 'Jesus Christ the same yesterday and today and forever'; and Rev. 13:8: 'The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world,' understand: by reason of the eternal decree and the promise made, and the sacrifices, which were types of Christ and of the vigor and efficacy of the Lord’s passion, from which the pious fathers from the foundation of the world were saved through faith, Acts 15:11. And the reason is entirely the same regarding the prophetic office. In this prophetic office, Moses and the other prophets of the Old Testament were types of Christ, as is evident from Deut. 18:18; John 1:45; Acts 7:37." (Disp. th. in academia Giessena hab. Tom. I, 97. sq.)

This opinion certainly seems more convenient than if one were to deny outright that Christ is a prophet in the state of exaltation. For whatever is effected through those ministers, all of it depends upon Christ, who is with them always, even unto the end of the age, Matt. 28, last verse. Compare what will be said below concerning the kingdom of grace. % §

6. The priestly office consists in this, that Christ holds the middle position between God and men, who are at variance with one another,b in such a way, indeed, that He offers a sacrificec and prayersd for the sake of reconciling men with God.

That Christ is a priest is evident primarily from the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapters 3 and following up to 10. For thus He is called άρχιερεύς τής όμολογίας ήμών, the high priest of our confession, ch. 3:1; άρχιερεύς μέγας, a great high priest, ch. 4:14; ίερεύς είς τον αιώνα, a priest forever, ch. 5:6, ch. 6:20, ch. 7:17, 21; όσιος, άκακος, άμίαντος, κεχωρισμένος από των άμαρτωλών, holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, ch. 7:26, ὃς έκάλισεν έν δεξιά τού θρόνου τής μεγαλωσύνης έν τοίς ούρανοίς. Τών άγίων λειτουργός καί τής σκηνής τής άληθινής, ήν έπηξεν ό κύριος καί ούκ άνθρωπος, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens. A minister of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man, ch. 8:1, 2, 3; άρχιερεύς τών μελλόντων άγαθών, a high priest of good things to come, ch. 9:11; ίερεύς μέγας έπί τόν οίκον του Θεού, a great priest over the house of God, ch. 10:21.

For the mediatorial office of Christ and the priestly office coincide, according to 1 Tim. 2:5, 6, although otherwise not every mediator is also a priest, since arbitrators, sponsors, and guarantors, and others, sometimes claim the name of mediator for themselves, and the prophets themselves could also be called by this name. Compare Gal. 3:19. PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III.

Namely, as an expiatory sacrifice for the sins of men, as the antitype of the ancient piacular sacrifices; see Heb. 7:27; ch. 9:7, 12, 13, 14, 15, 25, 26, 28; ch. 10:4 and following up to 14. See Heb. 5:7; ch. 7:25. § 7.

Moreover, the sacrifice of Christ excels the sacrifices of the priests of the Old Testament, because these were types and shadows of that one, and had to be repeated frequently, whereas the sacrifice of Christ is the antitype and contained within itself an expiatory virtue, and that an infinite one, and needed to be performed only once. See especially the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapters 3, 7, 9, 10.

Just as those priests are said to have served the ύποδείγματι καὶ σχιᾷ, the copy and shadow, ch. 8:5, and the sacred things of the old tabernacle to have been a παραβολή τις, a certain similitude, for the time then present, ch. 9:9. Compare verses 23 and 24, where υποδείγματα and αντίτυπα are expressly opposed to one another, and ch. 10:1, where the law is said to have had the σχιάν, the shadow, of good things to come, not the very express form (αὐτὴν τὴν εἰκόνα) of the things. And thus they were of no benefit to men except by virtue of the perfect sacrifice to be performed by Christ in His own time.

For it was necessary for the man for whom a piacular sacrifice was offered in the O.T. to confess his guilt, and that he had deserved the wrath of God and punishment, yet who, by divine ordinance, causes a certain animal to be slaughtered in his stead, himself at the same time looking in his mind toward the future Messiah, who was to be slaughtered and to die in the place of a victim for the sins of all men, in view of whom God meanwhile allowed that typical act, by which a brute was slaughtered and offered—which He Himself had instituted or prescribed—to be so pleasing to Him that He would deem the man for whom the sacrifice was offered by the priest worthy of grace and mercy, on account of the value of the antitype.

Quenstedtius: "The end and use of the sacrifices is twofold: legal and evangelical. The legal use was an ανάμνησις αμαρτιών (remembrance of sins), Heb. 10:3, so that, namely, sinful men might be admonished of the gravity, atrocity, and guilt of sin, and thus they were a means of exciting contrition. . . The evangelical use was that they might show from afar that one propitiatory sacrifice to be offered for us one day on the altar of the cross, and reconcile penitent sinners to God. Lev. 1:2, 3, 9, 13, 17; 2:1, 2, 9, 12; 6:15, 21; 17:11; Gen. 8:21. . .

They had an expiatory and reconciliatory power typically, insofar as they were, as it were, vicarious and representative bodies of the victim to be offered for the sins of the world in the fullness of time; yet they did not behave as mere significant signs, but as divinely ordained organs, which set before sinners the Messiah, God to be incarnate, who in His assumed humanity would in His own time offer Himself to the Father as a sacrifice for the sins of the whole world, and would offer, apply, and seal the fruits of His bloody obedience to them.

Although there is not to be attributed to the Levitical sacrifices a power and efficacy of expiating sins of themselves and through themselves, or from the dignity of the person sacrificing, or from the work performed (ex opere operato), or on account of the mere external sacrificial work without the repentance and faith of the one performing it; to which the Epistle to the Hebrews 10:4 refers, when it says that it was impossible for the blood..."

the sins of bulls and goats to be taken away: yet the power and efficacy of the sacrifices to expiate sins under the aspect of type and shadow is not to be denied, insofar as they were vicarious and representative of the victim to be offered for the sins of the whole world in the fullness of time.” (L. c. P. IV. c. 1. s. 1. th. 46—48. p. 943. sq.) Kromayerus: “The apparent contradiction between Moses and the Apostle is easily removed; for when Moses says in Lev. 17:11, ‘The blood of goats expiates sins,’ and Paul says in Heb. 10:4, ‘The blood of goats does not expiate sins,’ it does not expiate in itself, but typically, insofar as it foreshadows the ίλαστικον (propitiatory) sacrifice of Christ for the sins of the world.” (Th. posit. pol. P. I, 775.) Dannhauerus: “The Levitical sacrifices were not salutary in and of themselves without faith; the sacrifice of Christ is salutary in and of itself, and it does not receive the power of saving from faith, but bestows it upon faith; although they do not become participants in the act of salvation unless they embrace the victim of Christ by faith.” (Hodos. Phaen. VIII, p. 341.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis:

1. Of the Socinians, especially Socinus, who denies that it is read anywhere that legal victims expiated sins, but that the priest, having performed the sacrifices, expiated the people or someone from the people; likewise, who contends that only sins of ignorance and infirmity were expiated.

2. Of Grotius, who is socinianizing; see his Annotations on Heb. 9:7.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. p. 1008.) See Heb. 9:12 ff., chap. 10:

14. And thus that [sacrifice], already long ago in the O.T., although not yet performed, yet foreseen by God, moved Him, as an impulsive or meritorious cause, to receive sinners into grace. § 8. Furthermore, since in other sacrifices victims were offered, distinct from the priests, Christ sacrificed Himself, when He voluntarily subjected Himself to passion and death, and thus offered Himself to God as a victim for the expiation of sins—not His own, but those of others, and of the whole human race. For to a sacrifice pertains 1) the destruction and slaughter of the victim, if it is an animate thing; 2) the offering or consecration of the same to the honor of God. Not by the blood of goats and calves; but by His own blood He entered once into the holy places, Heb. 9:12. Delivering Himself as a victim to God for a sweet-smelling savor, Eph. 5:2. Ad. Osiander: “Christ is the monadic priest of the N.T. Heb. 7:27, 10:14. He who by one offering has perfected forever those who are being sanctified, He is the priest, etc., nor is His priesthood to be repeated. The Popes’ exegetes distinguish 1. between a bloody and an unbloody sacrifice; they concede that He perfected all who are to be sanctified by one offering, namely, the bloody one, but they deny it regarding the unbloody one.

2. They distinguish between a propitiatory and an oblatory sacrifice; the former was unique, the latter is to be repeated, so that, namely, this benefit may be applied to individuals.

3. They say that nothing more is stated than that He offered Himself once and perfected [them] by one offering; yet the unique [sacrifice] can be repeated by turns. R. 1. The distinction is null, because a) a sacrifice requires the physical destruction of the thing offered, as Vasquez himself acknowledges; b) without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sacrifices, Heb. 9:22, therefore PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION III.

the shedding of blood is required; c) nowhere does Scripture have an unbloody sacrifice, unless metaphorically and improperly so called. 2. No distinction has been adduced, because a) there is no such thing as an applicatory sacrifice; b) the application of the sacrifice is effected through the Word and the sacraments, not through another sacrament; for in that way that work would also have a sacrifice, and so on to infinity; c) fiduciary application is one thing, sacrificial application another; the former is necessary, of the latter Scripture is silent; 3. The word ‘once’ a) denotes not only the unity of the act, but also its perfection, as in Heb. 6:4, where those who have been ‘once’—i.e., perfectly—illuminated are spoken of; b) because the word ‘once’ does not exclude a representative repetition of the sacrifice; even when Christ is said to have been born once, or tempted once in the wilderness, a representative repetition of the birth, etc., is not to be excluded; c) representative iteration was proper to the Old Testament, Heb. 10:2.” (Colleg. th. IV, 155.)

docendi, sed per ministros suos docet,a officium propheticum cum regno gratiae coincidere b videtur. Certe voluntatem divinam nobis annunciari facit et ad agnitionem veritatis per verbum et sacramenta homines deducit.

### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: For although He did not lay violent hands upon Himself, nevertheless He…

For although He did not lay violent hands upon Himself, nevertheless He intended His own passion and death when He delivered Himself to His enemies. He also died voluntarily, because He neither restored His powers, weakened by the passion, through a supernatural operation, nor did He apply medicine to the tortures that were accelerating His death; and although He could have lived longer, He did not prolong His life. Cf. John 10: 18.

But Christ could—even if as a man He might seem bound by natural law to preserve His own life—give Himself over to a death to be violently inflicted by others, because 1) as God, He had supreme power over all things, and therefore also power over His own life and death in His human nature, and because 2) it had already been decreed by the eternal counsel of God that He Himself, to save sinners, should sustain death in their stead at the appointed time.

Quenstedtius: “They object that it is unjust to punish one for another, much more an innocent person for a guilty one... One must distinguish between the voluntary acceptance of a penalty and its violent imposition. If anyone offers himself spontaneously and of his own accord to make satisfaction for another, no injury is done to him if a penalty is imposed; but if a punishment were imposed upon an unwilling person, who has acted rightly and refuses it in every way, then the judge would be unjust who would compel a reluctant person to suffer punishment and would punish an innocent person in place of the criminal. Therefore, the inference from the violent imposition of punishment, which is unjust, to voluntary acceptance, which commends the equity of the judge and the love of the one accepting, is fallacious.” (L. c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 2. q. 6. f. 438.444.)

See the aforementioned passages: Eph. 5:2, where it is said that He delivered Himself up as a προσφοράν, an oblation, and Heb. 9:12, 14: ἑαυτὸν προσήνεγκε, He offered Himself to God. And thus the killing of Christ, which, with respect to the Jews and Gentiles, was a horrendous crime, was nevertheless, with respect to Christ, a priestly act and most acceptable to God.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Socinians, who 1) posit that the priesthood of Christ is almost nothing other than the administration of His spiritual kingdom. For thus Crellius, Com. in Heb. 4:14, T. 2, Com. f. 112: ‘The priestly office of Christ,’ he says, ‘consists in this, that by the power given to Him by God, He removes the punishments of sins from His own and procures their salvation. Therefore, this office is in reality the same as the kingly office of Christ and is distinguished from it only by a certain manner of reasoning.’ 2) They contend that the death of Christ was only a preparation for His priesthood, and that the sacrifice of Christ was not performed on earth, but is finally being performed in heaven; or that the oblation indeed began on earth, but was perfected in heaven. For they wish to appear not to exclude the death on the cross, but in reality they do exclude it; nay, they utterly deny that Christ offered Himself on the cross as an expiatory victim for our sins.”

9. By that sacrifice, or by His passion and death, Christ is commonly said to have made satisfaction for us, although to the satisfaction of Christ, when viewed in its precise priestly notion, there also pertains the most perfect fulfillment of the entire divine law performed by Christ for us. Namely, on account of the supreme dignity, power, and value, and thus the sufficiency, of the passion and death of Christ for the expiation of our sins. Among ecclesiastical writers; but Scripture employs the terms of redemption in Rom. 3:24 and of reconciliation in 2 Cor. 5:18 ff. For that redemption denotes the payment of a price, which is sufficient, for a captive, and that reconciliation of God with men is described in the Scriptures in such a way that it is certain it was not accomplished without a λύτρον, which divine justice demanded from the mediator or reconciler. Cf. 1 Tim. 2:5, 6.

Quenstedtius: "Redemption, by the force of the word, is a new or repeated purchase, and the recovery of a thing once possessed and transferred into the dominion of another for a certain price. In Hebrew it is called גאלה, likewise פדות and פרין; in Greek λύτρωσις, ἀπολύτρωσις, ἀγοράσις, ἐξαγορασμός. . . We do not deny that the word 'redemption' is sometimes used in Scripture improperly and metaphorically for simple liberation without an intervening true price; but we do deny to the Socinians that this word is so taken in the Scriptures when mention is made of the redemption accomplished by Christ. . . In its proper signification, these words always denote liberation through an intervening price. Thus the noun גאלה is used eight times in the 25th chapter of Leviticus alone; cf. Ruth 3:13. And the verb גאל, if you look at the force of the word and biblical usage, denotes a properly so-called redemption and implies a λύτρον or price of redemption, which must intervene in such a redemption; or it signifies not a bare liberation, but one that is precious and arises from a communion of blood; nor does it only designate a precious redemption, but an obligation to redeem born of consanguinity. And thus it properly signifies to assert and claim for oneself, by right of kinship or consanguinity, a thing that has been alienated and, as it were, devolved to another. And from this arose the noun גואל, which denotes such a vindicator who is both joined by consanguinity to those to be redeemed, and therefore has the power of redeeming, and also interposes some price for the redemption. See Num. 35:12; Lev. 25:29, 33; Ruth 3:9, 12, 13; 4:1, 8, 6, 8, 14. In the meaning of redeeming through an interposed λύτρον, the verb פדה also occurs, which signifies to redeem something by a certain given price, and thus to draw back some thing from the power of another by right, not by mere force; see Ex. 13:13, 15; 34:20, and especially Ps. 49:7: 'No man can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him,' etc., and Hos. 13:14, where the Messiah says: 'I will ransom them from the power of the grave,' etc.; and likewise the verbs ἀγοράζειν and ἐξαγοράζειν. Where the rule is to be noted: Purchase, when it is used concerning liberation, whether the verb ἀγοράζω or ἐξαγοράζω is employed, always denotes an acquisition or liberation made by the intervention of a price." (L. c. c. 4. s. 1. th. 2. 3. f. 646. sqq.)

The same: "The redemption by which Christ the God-man. . . liberated the human race is a true and properly so-called redemption... We prove our thesis with arguments taken: 1. From the proper signification of the word 'redemption.' . . . In such a great mystery, which consists solely of the revelation of Holy Scripture, one must not depart or have recourse to tropes and figures without an urgent necessity. 2. From the emphasis and propriety of the Hebrew words פדה and גאל used concerning the redemption of Christ. Hos. 13:14. . . 3. From the mention of λύτρον and ἀντίλυτρον. Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45; 1 Tim. 2:6. . ." From the description of Christ’s άγορασμός and εξαγορασμός, as in 1 Cor. 6:20, 7:23, Apoc. 5:9, Gal. 3:13, 4:5. 5. From the description of Christ’s περιποίησις in Acts 20:28, where it is said that God (having Ιδιου αίμα, i.e., God ενσαρκον, Christ Jesus) acquired the church through His own blood. This περιποιητική, or acquisitive redemption, is altogether properly so-called and satisfactory: for it was accomplished through the intervention of the λύτρον of the blood of Christ. In Eph. 1:14, it is said to be from Christ the άπολύτρωσις τής περιποιήσεις, the redemption of acquisition or acquired, asserted, i.e., plenary redemption. 6. From the explicit determination of the λύτρον, by the interposition of which we have been redeemed. Holy Scripture calls it sometimes Christ Himself (1 Tim. 2:6), sometimes His soul (Matt. 20:28 and Mark 10:45), sometimes His death and blood (1 Pet. 1:18). Under the double species of money, silver and gold, everything is comprehended by which anything is accustomed to be bought or procured, and the blood of Christ, as something greater, is opposed to it by the very fact that it is the price. Just as gold and silver are truly the price of a purchase, not figuratively, so it is necessary that the blood of Christ be equally, or even much more, the true price of our άπολύτρωσις. Cf. Eph. 1:7, Col. 1:20, 22, Heb. 9:12, Apoc. 5: 9. In Heb. 9:15, it is said that Christ redeemed us by the intervention of death through the offering of His body. Heb. 10:10, 14. (L. c. c. 4. s. 2. q. 1. f. 653. sqq.)

The same: "In this redemption, we must consider: 1. the captive, 2. the one holding the captive, 3. the one redeeming the captive, 4. the means of redemption, 5. the form and mode, 6. the end, 7. the affections... The one holding the captive is... God. God, as the supreme Lord and most just judge, had concluded us under sin (Rom. 3:19, 11:32) and had consigned us to eternal punishment, and by the force of His justice demanded the penalty (Rom. 1:32). He, therefore, properly and principally held the human race captive, since He is the one who can and does inflict the ultimate punishment αύτεξουσίως and by His own authority. To Him, therefore, alone, and not to the devil, was the λύτρον to be paid... The devil in our captivity was nothing other than the guard and minister of the prison, or the minister of God, who had delivered us into the power of Satan by His just judgment. But he held us unjustly under his tyrannical empire, whence we are said to be 'captives held by the snare of the devil at his will' (2 Tim. 2:26)... But to him, who holds us unjustly, no λύτρον is owed, no satisfaction. For if God principally holds man captive and the devil is only like a lictor and jailer, it is manifest that the price of redemption was to be paid not to the devil, but to God." (L. c. c. 4. s. 1. th. 6. 7. 8. f. 648. sqq.)

The same: "We have been redeemed through the blood of Christ, as a precious λύτρον, not only from our sins but also from the punishments owed to sins, namely, from the wrath of God, from the execration and curse of the law, from the devil, hell, and eternal death. We are said to be redeemed from sins, as those things which consigned us to servitude and made us obnoxious to the wrath of God, condemnation, and death; from the punishments of sins, as the penalty to which we were subject." (L. c. th. 11. f. 652.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: Of the Socinians, who contend that the redemption accomplished by Christ is not properly called meritorious and satisfactory, but metaphorical and simple. They urge that the word 'to redeem' in Holy Scripture is for the most part and almost always taken metaphorically for any liberation whatsoever, and from this they infer that the metaphorical signification must obtain also whenever it is attributed to Christ."

Quenstedtius: ,,Redemtio est vi vocis nova sive iterata emtio et rei quondam possessae et in alterius dominium translatae pro certo pretio recuperatio. Captivum detinens est... Deus. Deus, ceu Dominus supremus et judex justissimus, nos sub peccato concluserat, Rom. 3, 19. 11, 32., et poenae aeternae mancipaverat ac vi justitiae suae poenam exigebat, Rom. 1, 32. Is ergo proprie et principaliter.captivum genus humanum detinuit, quippe qui supplicium ultimum infligere potest et infligit αύτεξουσίως et auctoritate propria. Ei itaque soli, non diabolo, λύτρου persolvendum erat. . . Diabolus in captivitate nostra nihil aliud erat, quam custos et minister carceris seu minister Dei, qui nos justo suo judicio in potestatem satanae, tradiderat. Hic autem nos injuste detinebat sub tyrannico suo imperio, unde dicimur,captivi detenti laqueo peccati et vinculis iniquitatum a diabolo ad ipsius voluntatem‘, 2 Tim. 2, 26. . . Huic autem, injuste nos detinenti, nullum debetur λύτρου, nulla satisfactio. Si enim Deus hominem principaliter captivum detinet ac diabolus tantum lictoris et carcerarii instar est, manifestum est, pretium redemtionis non diabolo, sed Deo solvendum fuisse.“ (L. c. c. 4. s. 1. th. 6. 7. 8. f. 648. sqq.)

Idem: ,,Redemti sumus per Christi sanguinem, ut λύτρου pretiosum, non solum a peccatis nostris, sed etiam a poenis, peccatis debitis, scii, ab ira Dei, ab exeeratione et maledictione legis, a diabolo, inferno et morte aeterna. A peccatis redimi dicimur, ut quae nos servituti mancipabant, et irae Dei, condemnationi et morti obnoxios faciebant; a peccatorum poenis, ut supplicio, cui subjecti eramus.“ (L. c. th. 11. f. 652.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: Socinianorum, qui contendunt, redemtionem a Christo factam non esse proprie dictam meritoriam et satisfactoriam, sed metaphoricam et simplicem. Urgent, redimendi verbum in S. plerumque et ferme semper metaphorice sumi pro quavis liberatione, atque hinc inferunt, metaphoricam significationem obtinere debere etiam, quoties Christo tribuitur.“


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Quenstedtius: "Reconciliation with God is attributed to distinct persons, but…

Quenstedtius: "Reconciliation with God is attributed to distinct persons, but in a different manner, 2 Cor. 5: 1.) To God the Father, v. 18, as the principal cause and first author; for he notes significantly: 'He reconciled us to Himself,' because the principle and origin of this reconciliation is not found in man, as one dead in sins, but only in God, who, having mercy on us out of mere φιλανθρωπία, sent His Son to us as a propitiation for our sins, 1 John 4:10. 2.) To Christ, v. 19, as the meritorious cause. 3.) To the ministry of the Word, v. 19, as the instrumental cause on the part of God offering it. 4.) Finally, to us, v. 20, as the instrumental cause apprehending it through faith." (L. c. s. 1. th. 22. f. 322.)

Calovius: "The Socinians object that it is not written that Christ reconciled God to us, but that we were reconciled to God through the death of Christ.

Resp.: 1. The matter comes to the same thing, whether it is said that Christ reconciled God to us, or us to God; because on both sides He destroyed the enmity that existed between us and God. For just as man was an enemy to God, so God was offended at man on account of sin, and that enmity had to be removed on both sides so that reconciliation might take place between them.

2. But that we are said to be reconciled to God rather than God to us, is because God is the offended party, while man is the offending party. Now, he who offends another is said to be reconciled to the one whom he offended. Thus, we are commanded to be reconciled to him whom we have offended, Matt. 5:23, and a woman is commanded to be reconciled to her husband, whom she had provoked, 1 Cor. 7:11; and in that manner, Christ is said to reconcile to God us, who offended God and against whose impiety the wrath of God is revealed from heaven.

Whatever the case may be, the matter, as I have said, comes to the same thing; especially if it is established that both parties, not just one or the other, held an inimical spirit. For then it will be readily evident that reconciliation was made not only with respect to one party, but to both. The dissenting parties here are God and man, who are to be reconciled. No one doubts that man was opposed to God before he was reconciled; but that God hated man as a sinner before reconciliation took place between them, we have proven elsewhere from divine holiness and justice, as well as from clear testimonies of Scripture. See Ps. 5:6, 45:8, Rom. 1:18, 32, Gal. 3: 13. Furthermore, that Christ removed the cause of wrath, i.e., expiated sin, and saves us from wrath, is again most evident from the Scriptures. And therefore He made reconciliation not only to reconcile man to God, but also to reconcile God to men." (Socinism. profligat, p. 496.)

Quenstedtius: "The word 'satisfaction' in the meaning in which we use it does not exist in so many syllables in the Vulgate version of the Bible; nor is that necessary; it is sufficient that such a thing, or its equivalent, is found in the Hebrew and Greek source. The terms equivalent to satisfaction are: payment for the robbery of the divine majesty, Ps. 69:5: 'I restored that which I took not away'; the bearing of our sins, Is. 53:4 sqq., λύτρον Matt. 20:28, ἀντίλυτρον 1 Tim. 2:6, ἱλασμός, propitiation for our sins 1 John 2:2, 4:10, ἱλαστήριον Rom. 3:24, 25, καταλλαγή, reconciliation Rom. 5:10, 11, 2 Cor. 5:18 sqq., ἀπολύτρωσις, redemption Eph. 1:7, Col. 1:14, λύτρωσις 1 Pet. 1:18, 19, ἀγορασία 1 Cor. 6:20, ἐξαγορασία, our purchase and redemption Gal. 3:13, likewise oblation, expiation, sacrifice for sin, etc., elsewhere." (L. c. membr. 2. s. 1. th. 25. f. 323.)

The same: "It is false that the remission of an offense is free and permissible for everyone. Eli, by remitting [the sins of his sons] against paternal right, offended God, 1 Sam. 2:24, 29. We have a similar case in Ahab, 1 Kings 20: 42. A man can remit [an offense] regarding his own right, unless the right of another is injured. He can and ought to do so only regarding vengeance and private satisfaction, but not regarding satisfaction owed to the laws and the public interest. In sum: a private man can and ought to remit offenses, but saving the right of God; God, saving His eternal and immutable right, cannot do so without satisfaction. Therefore, God is not less able than man. Man cannot always forgive injuries inflicted..." PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III. as regards satisfaction, although he can and ought to, as regards the desire for vengeance. That he cannot forgive an offense without satisfaction is a mark of supreme perfection, namely, of natural holiness and justice, not a mark of any impotence or imperfection.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 436. sq.) Cf. the words of Quenstedt placed above on p. 12. sq.

Calovius: “2 Cor. 5:14: ‘If one died for all, then all died.’ But if this, that one died for all, is in the divine judgment just as if all had died, then that one was indeed substituted in the place of all and died in the stead of all.” (Socinism. profligat, p. 386.)

The same: "Whether the guilt of our sins was transferred to Christ, our sponsor? The Socinians deny this; contending that Christ was afflicted not because of the imputation of our guilt, but only on the occasion of our sins. . . We, however. . . assert that our sins were imputed to Christ as our surety, and that He voluntarily took them upon Himself, and we demonstrate this with these proofs: I. From the passion of the innocent Christ. Whoever is immune from all guilt and is nevertheless treated as liable to guilt, to him must have been imputed the guilt of another; since, while divine justice remains intact, no one can be afflicted or affected by punishment unless it is either for his own guilt or for the guilt of another imputed to him. But the former is true of Christ, as can be seen in Isaiah 53:4 ff., 2 Corinthians 5:21, and elsewhere throughout. . .

II. From the bearing of sins. For if Christ bore the sins of the human race, it is necessary that the same were imposed or imputed to Him; because He could not have borne the sins of others unless the same had been imputed to Him. . .

III. From the imposition of sins. It must be established that to whomever the sins of all men were imposed, to him our guilt was imputed. But the sins of all men were imposed upon Christ, as the prophet Isaiah 53:6 testifies. . .

IV. From the description of God’s judgment. That God made Him, who knew no sin, to be sin for us, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and that Christ was made a curse and an execration for us, Galatians 3:13. For he who is made sin and a curse for others, to him must the sins and guilt of others be imputed. . .

V. From the designation of the meritorious cause of Christ’s passion. For if our sins were the meritorious cause of Christ’s passion, and He died by merit of our sins, it is necessary that the guilt of our sins was imputed to Christ. But the former is true, because He died for our sins and our iniquities, Isaiah 53:5, Romans 4:25, and for our sins, Romans 8:3, 1 Corinthians 15:3, Hebrews 10:12, and likewise τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, to sin, Romans 6:10, all of which imply a meritorious cause.

VI. From Christ’s substitution in our place. For if Christ, as our mediator, surety, and sponsor, took our place in His sufferings and death, it is certainly necessary that Christ did not suffer merely on the occasion of our sins, but also took the guilt of our sins upon Himself, and consequently suffered by the merit of our sins. . .

VII. From that prophetic phrase, that Christ was numbered with the transgressors, Isaiah 53:12. For how could Christ have been numbered with transgressors, unless our sins had been imputed to Him, which He is also said to have borne? For He was numbered with them either because of His own sins or because of others', that is, our sins. Not because of His own, because He did no violence, nor was any deceit found in His mouth, v. 9; therefore, because of our sins. . .

VIII. From the burden of sins. For Christ is presented as if burdened with sins, Hebrews 9:28, when the distinction is made between the first coming, in which He appeared for the putting away of sin by His sacrifice and was offered to bear the sins of many, and the second coming, in which He will appear without sin to those who wait for Him for salvation! For just as He will then appear χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας, so by force of opposition, at His first coming He did not appear without sin, or rather, He appeared burdened with sin, just as He then bore the sin of the world, John 1:29, and willed to be offered for the same in sacrifice. But how could He have been burdened with those sins, and how did He not appear without sin, unless the sin of the world, which He bore, was [imputed] to Him

ON THE OFFICE OF CHRIST. ... was it imputed? ... IX. From the attribution of offenses. For since offenses and foolishness—that is, sins which proceed from the foolishness and blindness of the mind—are assigned to Christ, it is necessary that our offenses and sins have been imputed to him. For those things do not belong to Christ όντως and really, καθ’ αυτό and in themselves, inasmuch as he is devoid of every offense and sin; wherefore it must be that sins were assigned to him λογιστικώς, imputatively, and σχετικώς, insofar as he, as our sponsor, took them upon himself. For thus in Ps. 69:6, God says: "You know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you." And the words immediately preceding in v. 5 confirm this: "What I did not steal, I restored," by which our mediator attributes to himself the payment of debts not his own, but ours, and of the robbery of divine majesty not his own, but ours—by which man, seduced by the devil (Gen. 3:5), wished to be like God through robbery. ... X. From the condemnation of Christ for sin, concerning which Rom. 8:3 says: "περὶ ἁμαρτίας κατέκρινε τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐν τῇ σαρκί." That the word ἐν τῇ σαρκί denotes the flesh of the Son of God is shown both by the Syriac, which teaches בבשרה, "in his flesh," and is manifest from the words immediately preceding: "Sent in the likeness of sinful flesh," which phrase is used not only because the flesh of Christ is similar to our flesh corrupted by sin as to substance, but also because it was substituted in its place as to the judgment of God (2 Cor. 5:21). Furthermore, the word κατέκρινε, "he condemned," implies a judicial act, and one that is punitory, as well as a sentence and the condemnatory execution. ... XI. From the prefiguration of types. For just as in the Levitical sacrifices the sins of those for whom they were offered were imputed to them (Lev. 4 and 5), so by the force of the analogy between type and antitype, it was likewise necessary that the sins of the whole human race be imputed to Christ, as the unique expiatory sacrifice of the New Testament." (Socinism. profligat, p. 392 sqq.) The same: "Socinus urges that here (Rom. 5:8) the love of God is commended in that Christ died for us; the praise of which is diminished by our view of satisfaction and reconciliation. I reply: nothing is taken away from the love of God by teaching that God was angry with the human race; but since Scripture declares both, both must be piously believed and explained according to the analogy of faith. The love of God consists in this, that He loved us as the work of His hands, once created in His own image. The wrath of God toward us consisted in this, that He held us, as transgressors of His law, bound under sin and its guilt by the force of His justice. It was the love of God that, when we had to die, He gave us Christ as mediator and willed that he should die in our place. It was the wrath of God that He avenged our sins in His Son and delivered him to a most ignominious death to expiate sins. Moreover, one must distinguish between the general love of God toward the human race and the special love. The former was the cause of ordaining the mediation and reconciliation of Christ; the latter is as it were the effect and consequence of the reconciliation accomplished through Christ, both of which the apostle clearly hints at here. Therefore, these things are perfectly consistent according to Scripture: that Christ reconciled God to us, and that God, out of love toward us, appointed Christ as the reconciler." (L. c. 503.) The same: "The love of God is either an affection of compassion and a will to do good, yet without friendship; in which way we are commanded to love our enemies, Matt. 5:44, just as God loved us when we were, in fact, enemies, Rom. 5:10. Or it is an affection of union and benevolent friendship; in which way we love friends whom the affection of love has joined to us, and God is said to love us after we are His friends and have been reconciled to Him through the death of His Son. The former love can be joined with just wrath, as God embraced man, who had fallen into sins, with an affection of compassion, yet was angry at his sins. The latter, however, brings about reconciliation and the appeasement of wrath, namely, where offense and wrath had preceded; just as God did not lay aside His wrath, nor did He pursue us with grace, unless reconciliation had been made through Christ." (L. c. 560.) PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III. Quenstedtius: "The Triune God does not here have the regard of a mere creditor, as the Socinians maintain, but of a most just judge, demanding an infinite price of satisfaction according to the rigor of His infinite justice. For the redemption itself, made εις ενδειξιν τής δικαιοσύνης, 'for the demonstration of divine justice,' Rom. 3:25, argues for the necessity of the penalty being exacted either from the guilty party himself, namely, the sinful man, or from his surety, namely, Christ. If God could have forgiven man his transgression without satisfaction while preserving His infinite justice, there would have been no need for such a great expenditure of His only Son. The infinite God was offended by sin, and because sin is an offense, an injury, and a violation of the infinite God and, so to speak, a deicide, it therefore has a certain infinite malice—not indeed formally (for thus, considered in itself, it admits of more and less), but objectively—and it merits infinite punishments, and thus it also demanded an infinite price of satisfaction, which Christ alone could provide. — One must distinguish between a private and pecuniary creditor and a public and judicial creditor, that is, the avenger of His own law and the exacter of justice by virtue of His office; if this one is not indignant at delinquents and does not exact the penalty, he is by that very fact iniquitous, not munificent." (L. c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 1. th. 31. f. 327.) The same: "The thesis is proved ... 2. against the Papists, who either join or subordinate our satisfaction to the satisfaction of Christ, namely, that the satisfaction of Christ does not admit any other satisfaction 1.) because of the infinity of the value which it possesses; for the person of Christ who satisfies is divine and thus of infinite dignity, whence also the value of His satisfaction will be infinite, and consequently also sufficient and equal to the offense, even though it be infinite, nay, even superabundant. 2.) Because of the rigor of justice intervening in the one satisfying and the one offended, which does not admit a double payment—one total and sufficiently compensatory, the other partial. 3.) Because of the glory of redemption, which belongs to Christ alone. 4.) Because of the imperfection and debt of human satisfactions." (L. c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 2. q. 6. f. 422.) The same: "The term from which of the duration of the satisfaction is the first moment of the humiliation; the term to which is the three days of death, as that in which the final portion of the satisfactory λύτρον was paid." (L. c. c. 3. s. 1. th. 43. f. 363.) ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis:

Latin:

Quenstedtius: ״Beconciliatio cum Deo distinctis personis tribuitur, sed diverso modo 2 Cor. 5.: 1.) Deo Patri v. 18., tanquam causae principali et primo auctori; notanter enim dicit: ,Nos sibi ipsi conciliavit‘, quia principium et origo reconciliationis hujus non reperitur in homine, utpote in peccatis mortuo, sed tantum in Deo, qui nostri misertus ex mera φιλανθρωπία nobis misit Filium suum propitiationem pro nostris peccatis, 1 Joh. 4, 10. 2.) Christo v. 19., tanquam causae meritoriae. 3.) Verbi ministerio v. 19., tanquam causae instrumental! ex parte Dei offerentis. 4.) Denique nobis v. 20., tanquam causae instrumental! apprehendenti per fldem.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 22. f. 322.)

Calovius: ״Excipiunt Sociniani, scriptum non esse, Christum nobis reconciliasse Deum, sed, nos per mortem Christi Deo reconciliatos esse.

Resp.: 1. Eodem res recidit, sive dicatur, Christum nobis Deum reconciliasse, sive nos Deo; quia utrinque inimicitiam, quae inter nos et Deum erat, interemit. Nam ut homo erat Deo inimicus, ita Deus erat homini propter peccatum offensus, eaque inimicitia utrinque poni debuit, ut inter eos reconciliatio fieret.

2. Quod autem Deo potius nos reconciliati dicamur, quam Deus nobis, inde est, quod Deus est pars offensa, homo vero pars offendens. Qui vero alterum offendit, dicitur ei, quem offendit, reconciliari. Ita imperatur nobis, ut ei, quem offendimus, reconciliemur Matth. 5, 23., et mulieri, ut marito, quem irritaverat, reconcilietur 1 Cor. 7, 11., eoque pacto dicitur Christus nos, qui Deum offendimus et contra quorum impietatem ira Dei revelata est e coelo, reconciliare Deo.

Quicquid vero sit, res, ut dixi, eodem redit; praesertim si id constet, quod utraque pars, non alterutra tantum, animum habuerit inimicum. Tunc enim non alterutrius tantum partis respectu, sed utriusque factam esse reconciliationem, ultro patebit. Partes dissidentes hic sunt Deus et homo, quae reconciliandae. Horninem fuisse Deo adversatum, priusquam reconciliaretur, nemo ambigit; Deum autem odisse hominem tanquam peccatorem, priusquam inter ipsos reconciliatio fleret, e divina sanctitate et justitia, ut et apertis Scripturae testimoniis alias probavimus. Vid. Ps. 5, 6. 45, 8. Rom. 1, 18. 32. Gal. 3, 13. Christum porro irae causam sustulisse h. e. peccatum expiasse, nosque ab ira servare, iterum e Scripturis evidentissimum est. Ideoque reconciliationem fecit non tantum, ut Deo hominem, sed ut Deum hominibus etiam reconciliaret.“ (Socinism. profligat, p. 496.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Vocabulum satisfactionis in ea, qua nos usurpamus, significatione totidem syllabis in Vulgata Bibliorum versione non extat; neque id necessarium est; sufficit, in hebraeo et graeco fonte tale quid inveniri aut illi aequipollens. Termini vero satisfactioni aequipollentes sunt solutio pro raptu divinae majestatis, Ps. 69, 5.: ,Solvi, quod non rapui‘; portatio peccatorum nostrorum Es. 53, 4. sq., λντρον Matth. 20, 28., άντίλντρον 1 Tim. 2, 6., ίλασμός, propitiatio pro peccatis nostris 1 Joh. 2, 2. 4, 10., ϊλαστήριον Rom. 3, 24. 25., καταλλα^η% reconciliatio Rom. 5, 10. 11. 2 Cor. 5, 18. sq., άπολϋτρωσις, redemtio Eph. 1, 7. Coi. 1, 14., λντρωσις 1 Pet. 1, 18. 19., άγόρασις 1 Cor. 6, 20., εξαγόρασις, nostri emercatio et redemtio Gal. 3, 13., item oblatio, expiatio, sacrificium pro peccato etc. alibi.“ (L. c. membr. 2. s. 1. th. 25. f. 323.)

Idem: ,,Falsum, quod remissio offensae cuilibet sit libera et licita. Eli remittens de jure paterno Deum offeudit, 1 Sam. 2, 24. 29. Simile habemus in Achabo, 1 Reg. 20, 42. Remittere homo potest de jure suo, nisi jus alterius laedatur. Potest ac debet tantum quoad vindictam et satisfactionem privatam, non tamen quoad satisfactionem legibus debitam et interesse publicum. Summa: offensas homo privatus, sed salvo jure Dei, remittere potest ac debet; Deus, salvo aeterno suo ac immutabili jure, absque satisfactione non potest. Non igitur miuus Deus, quam homo potest. Homo non potest semper injurias illatas condonare, 8 Baien Comp. ed. Walther. ΙII. PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO III. quantum ad satisfactionem, licet possit ac debeat, quantum ad vindictae cupiditatem. Non posse condonare oifensam citra satisfactionem, summae perfectionis, naturalis sci. sanctitatis ac justitiae, est, non alicujus impotentiae aut imperfectionis character est.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 436. sq.) Cf. Quenstedtii verba supra p. 12. sq. posita.

Calovius: ,,2 Cor. 5, 14.: ,Si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, utique omnes mortui sunt.‘ Quodsi hoc, quod unus mortuus est pro omnibus, perinde est in judicio divino, ac si mortui essent omnes, utique unus ille substitutus est omnium loco ac vice omnium mortuus est.“ (Socinism. profligat, p. 386.)

Idem: ״Utrum culpa peccatorum nostrorum translata fuerit in Christum sponsorem nostrum? Sociniani hoc negant; Christum non propter imputationem culpae nostrae, sed occasione tantum nostrorum peccatorum afflictum fuisse contendentes. . . Nos autem. . . peccata nostra Christo imputata esse ceu vadi nostro, eundemque. ultro illa in sese recepisse, asserimus, idque hisce ostendimus documentis: I. E Christi innocentis passione. Quicunque a culpa omni immunis est et nihilominus tractatur ut culpae obnoxias, eidem oportet alienam culpam imputatam esse; quum salva justitia divina nemo affligi aut poena affici possit, nisi vel ob propriam, vel ob alienam sibi imputatam culpam. At de Christo verum est prius, ut Esa. 53, 4. sqq. 2 Cor. 5, 21. et alibi passim videre est. . .

II. E peccatorum portatione. Si enim peccata generis humani portavit Christus, necessum est eadem ipsi imposita seu imputata esse; quia non potuisset aliena peccata portare, nisi eadem illi forent imputata. . .

III. E peccatorum impositione. Cuicunque peccata hominum omnium imposita sunt, ei culpam nostram imputatam esse, statuendum est. At Christo peccata hominum omnium imposita sunt, teste propheta Esa. 53, 6...

IV. E judicii Dei descriptione. Quod Deus eum, qui peccatum non npvit, pro nobis peccatum fecerit, 2 Cor. 5, 21., quodque Christus factus sit pro nobis maledictum et exsecratio Gal. 3, 13. Qui enim peccatum fit pro aliis et maledictum, illi oportet aliorum peccata et culpam imputari. . .

V. E causae passionis Christi meritoriae designatione. Si enim peccata nostra causa fuerunt meritoria passionis Christi, isque mortuus est merito peccatorum nostrorum, necessum est, Christo fuisse imputatam culpam peccatorum nostrorum. At verum est prius, quia mortuus est propter peccata nostra et iniquitates nostras, Esa. 53, 5. Rom. 4, 25., et pro peccatis nostris Rom. 8, 3. 1 Cor. 15, 3. Ebr. 10, 25., itemque ry αμαρτία, peccato Rom. 6, 10., quae omnia causam meritoriam inferunt.

VI. E Christi in nostrum locum surrogatione. Si enim Christus ceu mediator, vas et sponsor noster in nostri locum successit in passionibus et morte sua, necessum utique est, Christum non occasione tantum peccatorum nostrorum passum esse, sed culpam etiam peccatorum nostrorum in sese recepisse, ac proinde ita merito peccatorum nostrorum passum esse. . .

VII. E phrasi illa prophetica, quod Christus annumeratus sit peccatoribus, Esa. 53, 12. Quomodo enim Christus praevaricatoribus potuisset annumerari, nisi eidem peccata nostra imputata essent, quae etiam tulisse dicitur? Nam annumeratus iis est vel propter peccata propria vel ob aliena seu nostra peccata. Non ob propria, quia nulli injuriam fecit, nec dolus inventus est in ore ejus, v. 9.; ergo ob peccata nostra. . .

VIII. E peccatorum onere. Proponitur enim Christus quasi onustus peccatis Ebr. 9, 28., cum discrimen traditur adventus primi, quo apparuit ad destitutionem peccati per hostiam suam et oblatus est ad multorum exhaurienda peccata, et adventus secundi, quo sine peccato apparebit expectantibus se in salutem! Ut enim tum χωρίς αμαρτίας appariturps est, ita vi oppositionis in adventu primo non sine peccato vel onustus peccato apparuit, quemadmodum etiam tum peccatum mundi tulit, Joh. 1, 29., et pro eodem offerri voluit in sacriflcium. Quomodo vero illis peccatis onustus esse potuit, et quomodo non sine peccato apparuit, nisi peccatum mundi, quod tulit, eidem

imputatum fuit? ... IX. E delictorum attributione. Quum enim Christo assignentur delicta et stoliditas, h. e., peccata, quae e stoliditate ac caecitate animi proficiscuntur, necessum est, delicta ac peccata nostra eidem imputata esse. Illa namque όντως ac realiter, καθ’ αντο et per se Christo non conveniunt, utpote qui expers est omnis delicti atque peccati; quapropter oportet, eidem assignata esse peccata λογιστικώς, imputative, et σχετ/κώς, quatenus ceu sponsor noster in se eadem suscepit. Ita enim Ps. 69, 6. Deus inquit: ,Tu nosti stoliditatem meam, et delicta mea a te non sunt abscondita.‘ Idque comprobant verba immediate antecedentia v. 5.: ,Quae non rapui, exsolvi‘, quibus debitorum non suorum, sed nostrorum, et rapinae majestatis divinae non suae, sed nostrae, qua per rapinam Deo similis esse volebat homo, seductus a diabolo Genes. 3, 5., persolutionem sibi tribuit mediator noster. . . X. T., imputari pariter oportuit peccata totius generis humani.“ (Socinism. profligat, p. 392. sqq.) Idem: ,,Socinus urget, quod hic (Rom. 5, 8.) caritas Dei commendetur in eo, quod Christus pro nobis mortuus sit; cujus laus imminuatur nostra de satisfactione, de reconciliatione sententia. Resp., nihil hinc decedere caritati Dei, quod doceatur, Deum iratum fuisse generi humano; sed cum utrumque perhibeat Scriptura, utrumque sancte credendum, et juxta analogiam fidei explicandum. Caritas Dei in eo sita est, quod nos dilexerit ut opus manuum suarum ad imaginem suam olim conditum. Ira autem Dei erga nos in eo consistebat, quod nos ut transgressores legis suae sub peccato ejusque reatu, vi justitiae suae, constrictos teneret. Caritas Dei fuit, quod, cum nobis moriendum esset, Christum mediatorem nobis dederit, eundemque nostri loco mori voluerit. Ira Dei, quod peccata nostra vindicaverit in Filio suo, eumque tradiderit in mortem ignominiosissimam ad expiandum peccata. Distinguendum insuper inter caritatem Dei generalem erga humanum genus, et specialem. Hia fuit causa ordinandae mediationis et reconciliationis Christi; haec est velut effectus et consequens reconciliationis per Christum factae, quod utrumque apostolus hic clare innuit. Itaque optime haec secundum Scripturam consistunt, quod Christus Deum nobis reconciliarit et quod Deus ex amore erga nos Christum reconciliatorem constituerit.“ (L. c. 503.) Idem: ,,Dilectio Dei vel est affectus commiserationis et benefaciendi voluntas, citra tamen amicitiam; quomodo etiam inimicos diligere jubemur Matth. 5, 44., ita Deus dilexit nos, cum videlicet inimici essemus Rom. 5, 10. Vel est affectus conjunctionis et benevolentis amicitiae; qua ratione amicos, quos nobis junxit amoris affectus, diligimus, et Deus nos diligere dicitur, postquam ipsius amici sumus, eidemque per mortem Filii ipsius reconciliati. Pnor dilectio conjuncta esse potest cum justa ira, ut Deus commiserationis affectu complexus hominem in peccata prolapsumy.iratus tamen fuerit ejus peccatis. Posterior vero infert reconciliationem et placationem irae, sc. qua praecesserat offensio et ira; quomodo Deus non deposuit iram, neque nos gratia prosecutus est, nisi reconciliatione per Christum facta.“ (L. c. 560.) Christo. Si Deus absque satisfactione homini delictum condonare potuisset salva infinita sua justitia, tanto impendio Filii unici non fuisset opus. Infinitus Deus erat peccato offensus, et quia peccatum est offensa, injuria et violatio infiniti Dei atque, ut sic dicam, deicidium, hinc infinitam quandam malitiam habet, non quidem formaliter (sic enim in se consideratum suscipit magis et minus), sed objective, et infinitas poenas meretur, adeoque et infinitum satisfactionis pretium exigebat, quod solus Christus praestare potuit. — Distinguendum inter creditorem privatum et pecuniarium et creditorem publicum et judiciarium, h. e., legis suae vindicem et justitiae ex officio suo exactorem; hic si delinquentibus non indignetur et poenam exigat, hoc ipso iniquus est, non munificus.“ (L. .c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 1. th. 31. f. 327.) ### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Of the ancient heretics, such as Photinus and his followers, who maintained…

1. Of the ancient heretics, such as Photinus and his followers, who maintained that Christ was a mere man, and consequently did not make satisfaction to God the Father. . .

2. Of Peter Abelard, who contended that Christ did not appear in the flesh or undergo death for any other purpose than for our instruction through the Word and the attestation of His love through His death, and that there was no need for any satisfaction. . .

3. Of the Socinians, who deny that Christ was substituted in our place in His passion, that Christ by His death satisfied divine justice, expiated our sins, and reconciled God to us by His death; and they call the satisfaction of Christ for sins and due punishments a false, absurd, foully and supremely unjust, and horribly blasphemous dogma. . .

5. Of the Scholastics, who enervate the merit and satisfaction of Christ by teaching that God could remit sins to man without satisfaction, since He has no superior. . .; likewise, that the actions and passions of Christ were not, from their own internal perfection, equivalent and sufficient to satisfy divine wrath. . . apart from the liberal acceptance and promise of God. . .

6. Of the Papists, who contend that Christ has redeemed us from all sins in such a way that we ourselves must also make satisfaction for sins committed after baptism, as to temporal punishment and venial guilt, either here or in purgatory. See Council of Trent, sess. 14, c. 8. . .; likewise: that our own satisfaction is a means of applying the satisfaction and redemption of Christ. Most teachers of the Papist schools also teach that men could have attained salvation without Christ through some kind of satisfaction, by [God's] liberal acceptance."

by the offended person. ... 7. Of the Calvinists, who by their hypotheses undermine the merit and satisfaction of Christ, and deny that Christ made satisfaction for the sin against the Holy Spirit. ... The Calvinists also maintain that the satisfaction of Christ was not sufficient according to the rigor of God’s vindicatory justice, but was accepted by way of indulgence through ἐπιείκειαν. ...

Thus Calvin, Inst. lib. 2, cap. 17, sec. 1: "I indeed confess," he says, "that if anyone wished to oppose Christ simply and by Himself to the judgment of God, there would be no place for merit." ...

8. Of the Arminians, who 1) maintain that God could have pardoned all sins without satisfaction. ... 2) Call into doubt whether the satisfaction of Christ’s death was necessary. ... 3) Arminius seems to assert not so much a true and proper satisfaction, by which, namely, the divine justice was truly satisfied, as a certain acceptance." (L. c. cap. 3, membr. 2, sec. 2, q. 6, f. 418 sqq.)

Hofmann: "We have completely examined that part of the New Testament Scripture which represents the death of Christ preeminently as a high-priestly performance and sacrificial suffering, without finding in it that which is peculiar to the conception customary since (!) Anselm, in contrast to the result of our historical discussion of the same. Also, according to the Epistle to the Hebrews, Jesus’ suffering of death is not punishment, although it is a consequence of the sin of humanity; it is not the wrath, but the gracious will of God that was satisfied thereby, only indeed the latter in such a way as it had to happen after sin and death were in the world; Christ did not suffer in the place of humanity, but for its benefit, in that what happened to Him was the performance of the Mediator of salvation; and it is not that sin is now correspondingly punished, nor that it is atoned for by Jesus’ ethical action in suffering, that constitutes the essence of this reconciliation, but that the communion of God and Jesus Christ, which came about for the sake of our salvation, has proven itself even through the extreme consequence of sin. ...

Indeed, it is quite properly a task of the Epistle to the Hebrews to demonstrate that Jesus had to die. But the author does not ground this necessity on the fact that God’s punishing justice had to be satisfied, but it arises immediately from the communion with humanity entered into by Christ for the purpose of our redemption. As our Mediator of salvation, He could not have entered into God otherwise than after He had also suffered the extreme that He could suffer for that reason, because humanity stood in sins." (Der Schriftbeweis. The 2nd half, 1st part, 1853, p. 320 sqq.)

The same: "Between it (the church doctrine) and mine there remains the very essential difference that it is not the Son who is the object of the Father’s wrath, even if only vicariously, but humanity, and that the punishment to which unredeemed humanity would have fallen victim for eternity was not executed upon the Son, but His calling as Savior became the cause of all the sufferings which the same brought with it as a consequence of His entry into Adamic humanity. It is not He instead of us whom the wrath of God has struck, so that the punishment is now executed and no longer needs to be executed; but the evils in which God’s wrath against sinful humanity is executed, He has suffered in the manner established by His calling as Savior." (Schutzschriften für eine neue Weise, alte Wahrheit zu lehren. Part 2, p. 103.)

For Christ, our Mediator, truly made satisfaction for us, not only insofar as He took our punishments upon Himself, or, in our place, paid the λύτρον by His passion, so that we might be freed from enduring punishments on account of sins, but also insofar as He rendered perfect obedience to the will of God the Lawgiver in our place and obtained for us, as if we ourselves had fulfilled the Law, the rewards from God. The former is called passive obedience, the latter active. PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III.

B. Mentzerus: "The penalty, which is inflicted upon sins in the most just judgment of God, follows the violation of the law by merit, but yet it is not the law itself or the fulfillment of the law, but rather the vindication of the law in the violator. From this, it can be judged how that common distinction between active and passive obedience ought to be rightly received; namely, with a grain of salt and careful distinction. For active obedience is conformity with the law itself; and therefore it is properly and exquisitely called obedience, and that *per se*. Passive obedience, however, is usually called the suffering of the penalty inflicted upon the violator of the law; which, if it is to be called obedience, will be called *ἐν πλάτει* [in a broad sense] or *ex consequenti* [consequently]. Certainly, conformity without the concurrence of active obedience is not with the law itself, and most people suffer even the most just penalties against their will. Therefore, what is usually said: 'The law obligates either to obedience or to penalty,' is poorly applied here. Because 1. there, obedience is distinguished against penalty, and 2. the former member is understood *per se* and immediately, the latter mediately, namely on account of violation. Therefore, it is not an accurate opposition. And the threatening, added to the law, must be distinguished from the law itself, even though it is closely connected with it... Who says that the damned angels and men in hell render obedience to God? And this can have even less validity in this place, because the passion of Christ has the entire reason for its merit from the dignity and holiness of the person suffering." (

Disputatt. th. in acad. Giessena hab. T. III. p. 441. sqq.) See Matt. 5:17, where Christ says that He came to fulfill the law, i.e., that He might fully do all things which the whole law commands, and fully or thoroughly abstain from all things which the law forbids. And to this pertains the whole life of Christ in the days of His flesh, with His most holy and most illustrious works conformed to the divine law.

Quenstedtius: "By acting, Christ expiated the guilt which man had unjustly committed, and by suffering, He took away the penalty which man was justly about to suffer... For because man was not only to be liberated from the wrath of God, the just judge, but also, in order to be able to stand before God, he had need of righteousness, which he could not obtain unless the law were fulfilled; therefore Christ took both upon Himself and not only suffered for us, but also satisfied the law in all things, so that this fulfillment and obedience of His might be imputed to us for righteousness." (L. c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 1. th. 37. f. 350. sq.)

The same: "The same (Piscator) objects: Christ as true man was bound to obey God the Creator; therefore He rendered active obedience to the law for Himself. In the same way, Socinus, 1. 3. de Christo Servatore c. 5., says that Christ, as a true man, by right of creation owed to God full obedience of His whole life for Himself, and therefore that it merited nothing for us. Resp.: 1. The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, Matt. 12:8, and thus also of the whole law. 2. If Christ were a *ψιλός ἄνθρωπος* [mere man], He would have been bound by the law; but now, in the unity of the person, He is true God, and therefore, by reason of Himself, He was not bound by the law. The *πρῶτον ψεῦδος* [first falsehood] of this argument, and thus of this entire error, consists in this, that the actions and passions of Christ are considered as if they were only the actions and passions of a human nature; but it is the person who acts and suffers. The obedience of Christ is not an action of the human nature only, but of Christ the *θεάνθρωπος* [God-man], who, as He was born and given to us, Is. 9:6, so also for our sake was made under the law, Gal. 4:4, and is the *τέλος τοῦ νόμου* [end of the law], the fulfillment of the law, not for Himself, but for righteousness to every one who believes, Rom. 10:4." (L. c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 2. q. 3. f. 407.)

Gerhardus: "Although in many sayings of Scripture the work of redemption is attributed to the death and shedding of the blood of Christ, that is by no means to be taken exclusively, as if the holy life of Christ were thereby excluded from the work of redemption; but it is to be thought that this is done because it never shone more clearly that the Lord loved and redeemed us than in His passion, death, and wounds, as the pious ancients say; and because the death of Christ is as it were the final line and complement, *τέλος*, the end and..."

perfection of the entire obedience, as the Apostle says in Phil. 2:8. What is more? It is clearly ἀδύνατον [impossible] to separate the active obedience from the passive in this merit, because in the very death of Christ that voluntary obedience and most ardent love concur, of which the former respects the heavenly Father, the latter us men.” (Loc. de Justif. § 55.)

Hofmannus: ״Wir haben denjenigen Theil der neutestamentlichen Schrift, welcher vorzugsweise den Tod Christi als hohepriesterliche Leistung und Opferleiden darstellt, vollständig untersucht, ohne dasjenige darin zu finden, was der seit (!) Anselmus bräuchlichen Auffassung, im Unterschiede von dem Ergebnisse, unsrer geschichtlichen Erörterung desselben, eigenthümlich ist. Auch dem Briefe an die Ebräer zufolge ist Jesu Todesleiden nicht Strafe, obwohl Folge der Sünde der Menschheit; nicht dem Zorne, sondern dem Gnadenwillen Gottes ist damit Genüge geschehen, nur freilich letzterm so, wie es geschehen musste, nachdem Sünde und Tod in der Welt war; nicht an Stelle der Menschheit hat Christus gelitten, sondern ihr zu Gute, indem sein Widerfahrniss Leistung des Heilsmittlers war; und nicht dass die Sünde jetzt entsprechend gestraft, aber auch nicht dass sie durch Jesu ethisches Thun im Leiden gebüsst ist, macht das Wesen dieser Versöhnung aus, sondern dass sich die um unsers Heils willen gewordene Gemeinschaft Gottes und Jesu Christi auch durch die äusserste Folge der Sünde hindurch bewährt hat. . .

Allerdings ist es recht.eigentlich eine Aufgabe des Briefes an die Ebräer, darzuthun, dass Jesus sterben musste. Aber diese Nothwendigkeit begründet der Verfasser nicht damit, dass Gottes strafender Gerechtigkeit genuggethan werden musste, sondern sie erwächst unmittelbar aus der für den Zweck unserer Erlösung von Christo eingegangenen Gemeinschaft mit der Menschheit Er hat als unser Heilsmittler nicht anders zu Gott eingehen können, als nachdem er auch das Aeusserste erlitten hatte, was er um desswullen erleiden konnte, weil die Menschheit in Sünden stand.“ (Der Schriftbeweis. Der 2. Hälfte 1. Abth. 1853. p. 320. sqq.)

Idem: ״Zwischen ihr (der kirchlichen Lehre) und der meinigen bleibt der sehr wesentliche Unterschied, dass nicht der Sohn Gegenstand des Zornes des Vaters ist, wenn auch nur stellvertretungsweise, sondern die Menschheit, und dass nicht die Strafe, welcher die unerlöste Menschheit für ewig anheimgefallen wäre, an dem Sohne vollzogen worden, sondern ihm sein Heilandsberuf Ursache aller der Leiden geworden ist, welche derselbe in Folge seines Einkommens in die adamitische Menschheit mit sich brachte. Stück 2 p. 103.)

Mentzerus: ,,Poena, quae peccatis infligitur in Dei justissimo judicio, merito consequitur violationem legis, sed tamen non est ipsa lex sive legis impletio, sed potius vindicatio legis in violatore. Unde judicari potest, quomodo recte accipienda sit vulgata illa distinctio inter obedientiam activam et passivam; nempe cum grano salis et diligenti distinctione. Obedientia enim activa est conformitas cum ipsa lege; ac proinde proprie et exquisite vocatur obedientia et per se. Passiva autem dici solet obedientia perpessio poenae, violatori legis inflictae; quae si obedientia dicenda sit, vocabitur έν πλάτει sive ex consequenti. Certe sola et sine concursu obedientiae activae conformitas non est cum ipsa lege, et plerique inviti poenas etiam justissimas perpetiuntur. Quod igitur dici solet: ,Lex obligat vel ad obedientiam, vel ad poenam‘, huc male trahitur. Quia 1. ibi distinguitur obedientia contra poenam, 2. et membrum prius intelligitur per se et immediate, posterius mediate, nempe propter violationem. Accurata igitur oppositio non est. Et comminatio, addita legi, ab ipsa lege distinguenda, tametsi cum ea arcte cohaereat. . . Quis damnatos in inferno angelos et homines dicit praestare obedientiam Deo? Idque hoc loco eo minus valere potest, quia passio Christi omnem meriti sui rationem habet a personae patientis dignitate et sanctitate.“ (

I)isputatt. th. in acad. Giessena hab. T. III. p. 441. sqq.) Vid. Matth. δ, 17., ubi Christus dicit, venisse se, implere legem, i. e., ut plene faceret omnia, quae lex tota praecipit, et plene aut penitus abstineret ab omnibus, quae lex prohibet. Atque huc pertinet tota Christi vita in diebus carnis, cum sanctissimis maximeque illustribus illius operibus ad legem divinam conformatis.
