### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: The same: “The sophisms of Piscator are mainly these

The same: “The sophisms of Piscator are mainly these: ... 5. If Christ fulfilled the law for us or in our stead, we are not bound to obey the law; the consequent is false, therefore the antecedent is also.

Resp.: This argument is taken from the school of the Samosatenians, who likewise fear that through the doctrine of the satisfaction of Christ the zeal for good works might grow cold, which we have shown above is rather kindled by it.

Therefore, a distinction must be made between the obedience of the law which Moses requires and that which Christ prescribes to us.

Moses, by imposing upon us the heavy and intolerable burden of a rigid, perfect obedience, joined with the threat of eternal destruction and to be performed for the attainment of eternal life; from this burden and yoke Christ has liberated us by His most perfect obedience, which He bestows upon us through faith; meanwhile, however, He does not grant a license to sin, but with faith the Holy Spirit is given, who impels us to render spontaneous obedience to God the Creator, Redeemer, and Sanctifier, which, although it is not perfect in all respects in this life and therefore not meritorious of eternal life, yet pleases God as having proceeded from filial love and faith in Christ.” (Loc. de Justif. § 63.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who 1.) make Christ subject to the law by Himself, and thus [claim] that Christ, according to His humanity, was bound to render that active obedience for Himself a.) by right of creation, as a son of Adam, b.) by right of the divine covenant initiated with the Israelite people, as a son of Israel, Luke 2:21, and therefore could not have rendered that active obedience for others. ... 3.) Some of them exclude the active or life-obedience of Christ from the order of the meritorious cause, and contend that Christ satisfied God for us only by His passive or death-obedience, like Piscator, ... in which part he also departed from the followers of his own faith, since Calvin and others expressly state the contrary...

2. Of the Socinians, who 1.) deny that one could fulfill the law of God for all and satisfy it; ... 2.) deny that Christ fulfilled the law for us and in our stead. ... 3. Of the Arminians, who in their considerations, which they wished to observe regarding the Heidelberg Catechism, at Q. 36, have this in the *Scripta Remonstrantium Synodica*, p. 110: ‘What place of Scripture or what reason derived therefrom proves that Jesus Christ, by His innocence and perfect holiness, in which He was conceived and born, covers our sins, in which we are conceived and born, in the sight of God?’ To this belongs that horrible and impious opinion of Episcopius, ‘that Christ Jesus could have sinned, could have not obeyed.’

4. Of the Weigelians, who 1.) deny that Christ fulfilled the law for us. ... 2.) Maintain that it was not Christ who fulfilled the law by observing it.” (L. c. q. 3. f. 402. sq.)

Kahnisius: “The main argument of all who have fought against the active obedience — of Parsimonius, of Piscator, of the Socinians, of Töllner — is that the obedience of Christ was not meritorious. In fact, the reasoning of the old dogmatics, that Jesus as the Son of God was exempt from the fulfillment of the law, proves too much. ... A merit can be acquired by Christ only as a man (!). But everything to which Christ as a man was morally obligated (!) involves no merit. One cannot reckon as merit to Christ that, the omission of which would have been sin (!) for Him. It is inadmissible to elevate the obedience which Christ rendered to His parents to a merit with the help (!) of the divine nature of Christ, by saying: As the Son of God, Christ was not obligated to this obedience. Thus, one can also [not] [regard] the obedience of Christ in the fulfillment [of the law]... PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION III.

do not elevate the divine law to a merit by saying: The Son of God stood above the law. Jesus Christ, as man, was obligated to the fulfillment of the divine will. (!) That to which He was not obligated was the fulfillment of the theocratic law. If Christ submitted Himself to this, He did not do it for His own sake, but instead of humanity, in order to impute His righteousness to it.” (The Luth. Dogm. Vol. III. 1868. p. 399. sq.) § 10.

Moreover, Christ made satisfaction to the entire Most Holy Trinity,a and indeed for all men,b both the electc and the reprobate.d As the offended party, or the supreme legislator and Lord of men, whose majesty had been violated; and thus Christ in a certain way made satisfaction to Himself. For insofar as Christ made satisfaction, He is viewed precisely as Mediator; but insofar as He Himself also demanded satisfaction, He must be viewed precisely as God, the author and avenger of the law, essentially supremely just (equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit). However, it cannot be said that Christ made satisfaction for Himself or for the angels. For He Himself was not a sinner, and therefore not an offender. Moreover, as for the angels—whether you look at those who did not sin or the rest who fell—just as He did not assume their nature, so neither did He make their cause His own as Mediator. Cf. Heb. 2:16.

Kromayerus: “Christ, by His obedience, merited nothing at all for Himself. . . 1. Because Christ, just as He was not born and given for Himself but for us, so also He merited nothing for Himself, but everything for us, by both His active and passive obedience. This is proven by the sayings of Scripture: Is. 9:6; Luke 2:11; Gal. 4:4. 2. Because Christ obtained His future glory by grace, Phil. 2:9: εχαρίσατο, that is, out of grace He gave Him a name above every name. Now, truly, what one obtains by grace, one does not merit. 3. If the human nature did not merit the personal union with the Son of God, neither did it merit its consequence, future glory. But the former is true. Therefore, the antecedent is proven, because there is nothing more common in this article than the distinction between those things which Christ has by nature and those which He has by the grace of the personal union.” (Theol. posit. pol. I, 258. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who maintain that Christ, by His obedience, merited for Himself the glorious brightness and exaltation of His name. . . 2. Of certain Calvinists; thus Zanchius. . . repeats often in his writings: ‘Christ, by His obedience, merited eternal life for Himself.’ Piscator asserts. . . ‘that He was obligated to perform that obedience according to His human nature for Himself, and by it merited eternal life for Himself.’ . . Calvin, however, denies that Christ merited for Himself, Inst. 2, c. 17, n. 6. . . 3. Of the Socinians, who contend that Christ suffered for the sake of His own exaltation and offered Himself as a sacrifice for Himself. . . 4. Of the Arminians, who assert that Christ, through His death and resurrection, acquired for Himself the supreme power of saving us.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 463. sq.)

Not only insofar as the value of the satisfaction, but also insofar as the intention of the satisfying Christ extends to all men; see 1 Tim. 2: 6. For He who gave Himself as άντίλυτρον υπέρ πάντων, a ransom

He] who redeems for all, not only the elect, but truly for [all] men, for whom one must pray (according to v. 1), must certainly be acknowledged both to have been able and to have willed to pay for all, that is, in the stead and place of each and every human being, of sinners, as those to be redeemed.

Quenstedtius: "Christ satisfied for sinful men, not for some only, but for all and each, with no one at all excepted. . . This is evident I. from the sayings of Holy Scripture, which extend the merit and satisfactory death of Christ to all men whatsoever, such as Is. 53:6, Matt. 20:28, Rom. 8:32, 2 Cor. 5:14, 15, Heb. 2:6, 1 Tim. 2:6. II. From the sayings of Holy Scripture, which extend the merit and passion of Christ to the whole world, such as John 1:29, 1 John 2:1, 2. III. From the sayings which extend the merit and passion of Christ even to the reprobate themselves and those who perish by their own fault, Rom. 14:15, 1 Cor. 8:11, Heb. 6:4, 2 Pet. 2:1." (L. c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 2. th. 36. f. 342. sqq.)

The same: "Wendelinus objects I.: 'Scripture restricts the death of Christ to "many"' Matt. 26:28, 20:28, Heb. 9:16. Resp.: 1. The consequence is faulty: Many, therefore only the elect; nay, rather: Many, therefore the reprobate; for these are many, the elect are few. 2. The word 'many' abstracts from the universal and the particular, and denotes neither formally all, nor not all. Rivetus admits on Is. 57 that 'many' is understood for 'all' in some sense, because universality is a certain multitude. 'I confess,' he says, 'Rom. 6:19, "many" is taken for "all": many were constituted sinners.' Certainly, those who are called πολλοί here are called πάντες elsewhere. . . Nor does Scripture correct itself, but explains itself, when it now says 'many' whom it called 'all' elsewhere; it does not oppose 'many' to 'all,' but to 'one' or 'few.' However, a huge multitude is understood, as in Dan. 12:2. . . Moreover, in the oracle of Daniel, it is clear from the infallible interpretation of Christ in John 5:28 that 'many' stands for 'all.' . . He objects II.: 'Christ did not want to pray for the world, i.e., for the reprobate, the finally impenitent, John 17:9. Therefore, neither did He want to die for it.' . . Resp. by distinguishing between general and special prayer; Christ is not speaking of the former, but of the latter. Otherwise, Christ also prayed for the impious and transgressors, Luke 23:34, Is. 53:12." (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 459. sq.)

The same: "Was a single drop of the blood of Christ the God-man a sufficient λύτρον, or could it have been, to redeem the human race? — Certain fathers, scholastics, and papists, and some orthodox doctors have affirmed it. . . But the papists sin in this, when from the fact that one drop of the blood of Christ is a sufficient λύτρον for redeeming the world, they most wickedly conclude that the rest of the blood is superfluous, which is owed to the treasury of the church and the trafficking of indulgences. Hence they call the satisfactions of Christ superfluous, as Baradius, and Cajetanus [calls them] supervacaneous." (L. c. q. 9. f. 467.)

Luther: "What then is the treasure with which we are redeemed? Not corruptible gold or silver, but the precious blood of Christ, the Son of God. The treasure is so costly and noble that no human reason or mind can grasp that even a single drop of this innocent blood would have been enough for the sin of the whole world; yet the Father wanted to pour out His grace so richly upon us and let so much of it stand that He had His Son, Christ, shed all His blood and gifted the whole treasure to us." (Ausl. der 1. Ep. St. Petri. 1523. Tom. Hal. IX, 675.)

Latin:

Idem: ,,Sophismata Piscatoris potiora haec sunt:... 5. Si Christus pro nobis sive nostri loco legem implevit, nos non tenemur legi obedire; consequens est falsum, ergo et antecedens.

Resp.: Argumentum hoc petitum ex schola Samosatenianorum, qui itidem verentur, ne per doctrinam de satisfactione Christi frigescat studium bonorum operum, quod ea potius accendi superius ostendimus.

Distinguendum igitur inter obedientiam legis, quam requirit Moses, et quam Christus nobis praescribit.

Moses imponendo nobis grave et intolerabile onus rigidae, perfectae, cum comminatione aeterni exitii conjunctae et ad aeternam vitam assequendam praestandae obedientiae; ab hoc onere et jugo Christus perfectissima sua obedientia nos liberavit, quam per fidem nobis donat; interim tamen non tribuit licentiam peccandi, sed cum fide datur Spiritus Sanctus, qui ad spontaneam obedientiam Deo Creatori, Redemptori et Sanctificatori praestandam nos impellit, quae, quamvis in hac vita non sit numeris omnibus perfecta ac proinde nec vitae aeternae meritoria, Deo tamen utpote ex filiali dilectione et fide in Christum profecta placet.“ (Loc. de Justif. § 63.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Calvinianorumy qui 1.) Christum per se legi obnoxium faciunt, adeoque obedientiam illam activam Christum juxta suam humanitatem praestare debuisse pro se a^ jure creationis, ut filium Adami, b.) jure foederis divini cum populo israelitico initi, ut filium Israel, Luc. 2, 21., proindeque non potuisse illam activam obedientiam praestare pro aliis. . . 3.) Quidam ipsorum activam seu vitae Christi obedientiam ex ordine causae meritoriae excludunt, solaque passiva seu mortis obedientia Christum Deo pro nobis satisfecisse, contendunt, ut Piscator, . . . qua in parte etiam a suae fidei asseclis discessit, cum contrarium diserte statuant Calvinus alii que...

2. Socinianorum, qui 1.) negant, unum pro omnibus legem Dei implere, eique satisfacere potuisse; ... 2.) negant, Christum pro nobis et nostri loco legem implevisse. . . 3. Arminianorum, qui in considerationibus suis, quas circa Catechesin Heidelberg, observare voluere, ad q. 36. hanc habent in script. Remonstrant. Synodic. p. 110.: ,Quis Scripturae locus vel quae ratio inde desumta probet, Jesum Christum innocentia sua et perfecta sanctitate, in qua nim. conceptus et natus sit, peccata nostra, in quibus concipimur et nascimur, in conspectu Dei tegere?‘ Huc pertinet illa horrenda et impia Episcopii sententia, ,Christum J. potuisse peccare, potuisse non obedire.‘

4. Weigelianorum, qui 1.) negant, Christum pro nobis legem implevisse. . . 2.) Statuunt, non Christum, observando legem, eandem implevisse.“ (L. c. q. 3. f. 402. sq.)

Kahnisius: ,,Das Hauptargument Aller, welche den thätigenGehörsam bekämpft haben, — des Parsimonius, des Piscator, der Socinianer, Töllner’s — ist, dass der Gehorsam Christi nicht verdienstlich gewesen sei. In der That beweist der Grund der alten Dogmatik, dass Jesus als Sohn Gottes der Erfüllung des Gesetzes enthoben war, zu viel. . . Ein Verdienst kann Christus nur als Mensch (!) erwerben. Alles aber, wozu Christus als Mensch moralisch verpflichtet (!) war, involvirt kein Verdienst. Man kann Christo nichts zum Verdienst rechnen, dessen Unterlassung ihm Sünde (!) gewesen wäre. Es ist unzulässig, den Gehorsam, welchen Christus seinen Eltern leistete, mit Hilfe (!) der göttlichen Natur Christi zu einem Verdienste zu erheben, indem man sagt: Als Sohn Gottes war Christus zu diesem Gehorsam nicht verpflichtet. So kann man denn auch den Gehorsam Christi in Erfüllung PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO III.

des göttlichen Gesetzes nicht dadurch zum Verdienst erheben, dass man sagt: Der Sohn Gottes stand über dem Gesetze. Jesus Christus war als Mensch zur Erfüllung des göttlichen Willens verpflichtet. (!) Wozu er nicht verpflichtet war, das war die Erfüllung des theokratisehen Gesetzes. Unterzog sich Christus diesem, so that er es nicht um seinetwillen, sondern anstatt der Menschheit, um ihr seine Gerechtigkeit zuzueignen.“ (Die luth. Dogm. Bd. III. 1868. p. 399. sq.). § 10.

Satisfecit autem Christus toti SS. Trinitati,a et pro hominibus b quidem omnibus,c electis d pariter et reprobis.e Tanquam parti laesae, seu legislatori et domino hominum supremo, cujus majestas violata erat; adeoque et sibi quodammodo satisfecit Christus. Quatenus enim Christus satisfecit, spectatur praecise ut mediator; quatenus autem ipse etiam satisfactionem postulavit, sic praecise ut Deus, auctor et vindex legis, per essentiam summe justus (aeque ac Pater et Spiritus Sanctus) intuendus est. Pro se ipso autem, aut pro angelis, Christum satisfecisse, dici non potest. Ipse enim peccator non fuit, adeoque nec offendens. Angelorum autem, sive illos, qui non peccarunt, sive reliquos lapsos spectes, sicut naturam non assumsit, ita neque causam illorum, tanquam mediator, suam fecit. Conf. Ebr. 2, 16.

Kromayerus: ,,Christus obedientia sua sibi nihil quicquam meruit. . . 1. Quia Christus, ut non sibi, sed nobis natus et datus est, ita et sibi nihil, nobis omne tam activa, quam passiva obedientia meruit. Id quod probant dicta Scripturae Es. 9, 6. Luc. 2, 11. Gal. 4, 4. 2. Quia futuram gloriam Christus ex gratia consecutus est, Phil. 2, 9.: εχαρίσατο, id est, ex gratia ipsi dedit nomen super omne nomen. Jam vero quod quis ex gratia consequitur, illud non meretur. 3. Si personalem unionem cum Eilio Dei humana natura non meruit, nec istius consequens, futuram gloriam. Sed verum est prius. E. Antecedens probatur, quia nihil tritius in hoc articulo est, distinctione inter ea, quae Christus habet per naturam et quae habet per unionis personalis gratiam.“ (Theol. posit.pol. I, 258. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, statuentium, Christum obedientia sua promeruisse sibi gloriosam nominis sui claritatem et exaltationem. . . 2. Calvinianorum quorundam; sic Zanchius. . . saepius in suis scriptis repetit: ,Christum sua obedientia sibi promeruisse vitam aeternam.‘ Piscator asserit, . . . ,obedientiam illam juxta naturam suam humanam praestare debuisse pro se, eaque sibi ipsi vitam aeternam promeruisse.‘ . . Calvinus vero negat, Christum sibi meruisse, 1. 2. Institut, c. 17. n. 6. . . 3. Socinianorum, qui suae exaltationis causa Christum passum esse ac se ipsum pro seipso sacrificium obtulisse, contendunt. . . 4. Arminianorum, asserentium, Christum sibi per mortem et resurrectionem acquisivisse potestatem nos salvandi supremam.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 463. sq.)

Non solum quatenus satisfactionis valor, verum etiam quatenus intentio Christi satisfacientis ad omnes homines se extendit; vid. 1. ad Tim. 2, 6. Qui enim se ipsum dedit άντ'ίλυτρον υπέρ πάντων, pretium

redemtionis pro omnibus, non solum electis, verum hominibus, pro quibus orandum est (juxta v. 1.), sane agnoscendus est, et potuisse et voluisse solvere pro omnibus, sive vice et loco singulorum atque omnium hominum, peccatorum, tanquam redimendorum.

Quenstedtius: ״Satisfecit Christus pro hominibus peccatoribus, non aliquibus tantum, sed pro omnibus ac singulis, nemine prorsus excepto. . . Patet hoc I. ex dictis S. S., quae extendunt meritum et mortem satisfactoriam Christi ad omnes omnino homines, ut Es. 53, 6. Matth. 20, 28. Rom. 8, 32. 2 Cor. 5, 14. 15. Ebr. 2, 6. 1 Tim. 2, 6. II. Ex dictis S. S., quae meritum et passionem Qhristi extendunt ad totum mundum, ut Joh. 1,29. 1 Joh. 2, 1. 2. III. Ex dictis, quae extendunt Christi meritum et passionem ad ipsos etiam reprobos et sua culpa pereuntes, Rom. 14,15. 1 Cor. 8,11. Ebr. 6, 4. 2 Pet. 2,1.“ (L. c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 2. th. 36. f. 342. sqq.)

Idem: ״Objicit Wendelinus I.: ,Scriptura restringit mortem Christi ad multos‘ Matth. 26, 28. 20, 28. Ebr. 9, 16. Resp.: 1. Laborat consequentia: Multi, ergo soli electi; imo potius: Multi, ergo reprobi; nam hi sunt multi, pauci electi. 2. Τό multum abstrahit ab universali et particulari, nec formaliter omnes, nec non omnes notat. Fatetur Rivetus ad Es. 57., multos pro omnibus in aliquo genere intelligi, quia universalitas est quaedam multitudo. ,Fateor‘, ait, ,Rom. 6, 19. multi pro omnibus accipiuntur: peccatores constituti sunt multi.‘ Sane, qui hic πολλοί dicuntur, alibi πάντες audiunt. . . Nec se corrigit Scriptura, sed explicat, quando multos nunc dicit, quos alibi omnes dixit; non opponit multos omnibus, sed uni, vel paucis. Intelligitur autem ingens multitudo, ut Dan. 12, 2. . . In oraculo autem Danielis multos ״stare pro omnibus, liquet όχ infallibili interpretatione Christi Joh. 5, 28. . . Objicit II.: ,Christus noluit rogare pro mundo, i. e., pro reprobis, flnaliter impoenitentibus Joh. 17, 9. Ergo nec mori pro eo voluit. . . Resp. distinguendo inter precationem generalem et specialem; non de illa, sed de hac loquitur Christus. Alias quoque Christus oravit pro impiis et transgressoribus, Luc. 23, 34. Es. 53, 12.“(L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 459. sq.)

Idem: ״Num unica guttula sanguinis Christi ΰεανΰρώπον sufficiens λϋτρον aut fuerit, aut esse potuerit ad redimendum genus humanum? — Affirmafit quidam patres, scholastici ac pontificii et nunnulli doctores orthodoxi. .. Ast in eo peccant pontificii, quando ex eo, quod una gutta sanguinis Christi sit sufficiens λϋτρον pro mundo redimendo, pessime concludunt, reliquum sanguinem esse superfluum, qui thesauro debeatur ecclesiae et nundinationi indulgentiarum. Hinc satisfactiones Christi vocant superfluas, ut Baradius, et Cajetanus supervacaneas.“ (L. c. q. 9. f. 467.)

Lutherus: ״Welches ist nun der Schatz, damit wir erlöst sind? Nicht vergänglich Gold oder Silber, sondern das theure Blut Christi, des Sohnes Gottes. Der Schatz ist so köstlich und edel, dass es keines Menschen Vernunft und Sinn begreifen kann, dass nur ein Tröpflein von diesem unschuldigen Blut übrig genug wäre gewesen für aller Welt Sünde; noch hat’der Vater seine Gnade so reichlich über uns wollen ausschütten und sicffis so viel stehen lassen, dass er seinen Sohn, Christum, hat sein Blut alles vergiessen lassen und uns den Schatz ganz geschenkt.“ (Ausl, der 1. Ep. St. Petri. 1523. Tom. Hai. IX, 675.)


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: B. Meisnerus: "What theologians say about one sufficient drop is not to be…

B. Meisnerus: "What theologians say about one sufficient drop is not to be understood absolutely concerning the consummation of merit and the counsel of God, but respectively regarding the dignity of the person. For His blood was the blood of God Himself, Matt. 26:28, 1 John 1:7, Acts 20:28, and therefore in itself worthy and sufficiently suitable, of which even a single drop would be an ἀντίλυτρον for the sins of the world. Meanwhile, it pleased God, and could please Him without cruelty, PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION III. the Son was most grievously struck and wounded, Is. 53, and therefore one drop was not sufficient by reason of the whole merit and divine counsel, since God willed the New Testament to be ratified by the shedding of much blood, in order to demonstrate more openly the glory of His justice and truthfulness.” (Anthropol. Decad. 3. Disputat. 26. argum. 10. n. 70.)

Schomerus: “Q.: Did Christ also die for the people of the Old Testament, and acquire salvation for them? The Socinians deny this, such as Smalzius, who teaches: ‘Christ indeed has the salvation of those who died before Him placed in His hand, so that by divine power He will one day save them, but He by no means died for them.’ We affirm: Because 1.) The book of life from the foundation of the world is the book of the Lamb slain, Rev. 13:8, whence no one could hope for life unless the fruit of His slaughter reached him. 2.) All the sacrifices of the Old Testament were slain as a type of Christ, which could not of themselves take away sin, but only promised Him who would take it away, Heb. 10:1 sqq. cf. v. 14 and ch. 9:23, who, if He could not have absolved the matter by one death, would have had to be slain more often from the foundation of the world, v. 26. 3.) The death of Christ was made for the redemption of those transgressions which were under the Old Testament, 9:15, and to demonstrate the justice of God because of the passing over of past sins, Rom. 3:25 sq. 4.) Christ, already promised to the first parents in paradise, Gen. 3:15, and to other patriarchs and believers of the Old Testament, Acts 3:24, 25; 13:32 etc., was expected by them with great desire, Luke 10:24; Heb. 11:39 cf. Gen. 49:18; Is. 64:1, and they consoled themselves with Him, Is. 9:6; 53:4, of which they would have had no account unless they had known that His merit pertained also to them. 5.) Believers of the New Testament hope for salvation through the grace of Jesus Christ, just as the believers of the Old Testament did, Acts 15:11 cf. 4:12.” (Colleg. Antisocinian. II, 142.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of certain Calvinists, such as Calvin on Eph. 1:10 and Col. 1:20, and Bucanus, who posit that ‘the holy angels are said to be reconciled through the blood of Christ in this sense, because their justice and integrity, being as it were lacking before God, had to be covered before Him by the perfect and infinite justice of Christ.’ ... 2. Of Origen, who did not hesitate to affirm that ‘the Lord suffered and died for the saving and full restoration of the fallen angels or demons.’ ... 3. Of Theodoret, of whom Suarez reports ... that he writes on Heb. 2 that ‘Christ suffered and died for all creatures whatsoever.’ ... 5. Of the presbyter Godeschalcus, who around the middle of the 9th century A.D. taught, among other things, that ‘Christ was not crucified nor did He die for the redemption of the whole world, i.e., for the redemption and salvation of all men, but only for those who are saved.’ ... 6. Of the Calvinists, and indeed 1.) the more rigid ones, who pronounce in open words that Christ did not satisfy by His merit for all men and thus even for the reprobate, but for the elect alone. Thus Calvin, Beza, Perkins, Piscator; especially Spanheim strives with all his might to defend the particularity of the merit of Christ, and others. ... 2.) Of those Calvinists who wish to appear milder, but only play with terms. For they distinguish between the sufficiency and the efficacy or efficiency of Christ’s death, and teach that Christ indeed suffered and died sufficiently for all men, but efficiently only for the elect. Thus Andr. Rivetus. ... Nevertheless, they disagree greatly among themselves in this matter. For some admit only potential sufficiency, such as Pareus and the Hessians, ... but deny actual efficacy. ... And thus all these abstract the intention of satisfying for the non-elect from the sufficiency of the λύτρον [ransom]. ... 3.) Of those who are commonly called hypothetical (the author of which nomenclature is Rivetus), such as the French of Saumur, Moïse Amyraut and John Cameron, the Bremensians, and as many as today of their sect strive to enter into syncretism with the Lutherans, who seem to concede even a universal efficacy of the death of Christ, but...”

depending on this condition: ‘if individuals believe and repent,’ . . . but that they might perform this, God neither wills in His internal counsel and good pleasure, nor does He will to give them such grace by which they might be so moved that they actually truly believe. . . 7. Of certain Papists, who in asserting the particularity of the death of Christ do not depart from the Calvinists, such as Corn. Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres in Flanders, who taught that ‘it is Semipelagian to say that Christ died for all men,’ as is evident from volume 3 of his ‘Augustinus’. . . Thus also Guil. Estius. . . Becanus teaches the same.” (L. c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 2. q. 7. f. 447. sqq.)

For we shall teach below that election itself rests upon the foreseen satisfaction of Christ, and that the acceptance of another’s satisfaction is no obstacle, so that nevertheless both salvation and election remain gratuitous. Who, however, are nonetheless justly rejected and condemned by God, both on account of other sins and especially because they themselves reject the satisfaction of Christ; God, however, neither wills, nor is He bound, to impute the vicarious satisfaction of Christ actually for the remission of sins to any man who does not believe in Christ. § 11.

Christ, our priest, indeed performed prayers, or intercession, for all men, but in such a way that, praying for the impious, He might procure their conversion, and interceding for the pious, He might promote their constancy and growth in faith and holiness. He prayed, however, not only for those who were subsequently converted, but also for those who were not truly converted; see Luke 23:34, where Christ prayed for His crucifiers indefinitely, with no one excepted. And without doubt some among them, perhaps not a few, persisted in their impiety, yet Christ, by praying for them, showed that, as far as it depends on Him, He does not will them to be deprived of the fruit of His death, but rather to be converted and saved.

In John 17:11 He is read to have prayed: Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are. And v. 15: I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil. Furthermore v. 17: Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth. Add v. 21, 23, 24. And in this sense Christ had denied before in the same chapter, v. 9, that He was praying for the world, which is opposed to the assembly of the faithful, or for the wicked, so that that negation is to be understood not absolutely, but in a certain respect. § 12. Moreover, both natures of Christ concur in the priesthood of Christ, as regards both the sacrifice and the intercession; and the human nature indeed contributed what was its own to the sacrifice, when Christ went to meet His enemies and endured passion and death, but the divine [nature],

PART III. CHAP. II. SECTION III.

with regard to the infinite value and virtue added to His passion and death, so that it might suffice to expiate the sins of men and appease God. With regard to the intercession of Christ, the acts of praying themselves, viewed in themselves, formally pertain to the human nature, but the dignity and value of the same result from the divine nature. Gerhard: "The reasons must be repeated here, for which it was necessary that our mediator be God and man. I. He had to be God because of the magnitude of the evil to be abolished and the magnitude of the good to be brought about; for example: 1. Because of the sufficiency and perfection of the λύτρον. Unless He had been God, His own obedience and passion could not have been a sufficient λύτρον for the sins of the whole world. 2. Because of the bearing of divine wrath. A mere creature could not have borne the immense weight of the sins and the divine wrath due to the sins of the entire human race. 3. Because of the removal of evils. For a mere man, the abolition of sin, the crushing of the head of the infernal serpent, the destruction of the kingdom of the devil, and the swallowing up of death would not have been possible. 4. Because of the restoration of goods. A mere man and a finite creature could not have brought about perfect righteousness, distributed the Holy Spirit, or conferred eternal life upon believers. 5. Because of the revelation of the divine decree. A mere creature could not have known the decree of God concerning our salvation, which nevertheless had to be manifested through a mediator. John 1:18: 'No one has seen God at any time,' etc. 6. Because of the defense of the church. A mere creature could not defend the church against the devil and all the gates of hell, but for this, divine and infinite power is required. 7. Because of the preservation of the gifts obtained. Our mediator had to preserve the gifts obtained for us better than the first parent of the human race, Adam, who lost the gifts divinely entrusted to him not only for himself but also for all his descendants; but Christ faithfully preserves them for all believers. 8. Because of the hearing of prayers. It is required for the office of mediator that He be present everywhere to His church, hear those who call upon Him, and carry their prayers to God as an intercessor and mediator; therefore, it was certainly necessary that He Himself be true God. II. Conversely, He also had to be true man: 1. Because of the constitution of divine justice. Man had sinned; therefore, satisfaction had to be rendered through man, so that nothing might be lacking to the altogether unmoved and invariable divine justice. 2. Because of the restoration of human nature... Through sin, the whole human race, and thus the whole human nature, was miserably corrupted, so that all men were slaves of sin and liable to eternal death; therefore, the Son of God willed to overcome death in the assumed human nature and to raise the miserable human nature again to heavenly glory. 3. Because of our reconciliation with God. Through the sin of Adam, we were all divided from God, Isaiah 59:2. Christ, therefore, united human nature to Himself personally, so that in it and through it He might lead us back to communion with God. 4. Because of the confirmation of our faith. The Son of God willed to complete the work of redemption in and with human nature and through human nature, so that we might be made certain that those benefits obtained by the death and passion of Christ truly pertain to us, and that we shall be partakers of those goods. 5. Because of the kinship of our nature. Christ willed to deposit, as it were, all His goods and the fullness of the treasures obtained into the assumed human nature, according to which He is our brother and kinsman, so that through it they might be derived to us and come to us from the divine nature through the human. 6. Because of the sustaining of temptation. The Son of God assumed human nature for this reason, that He might be able to be tempted as another true man and might Himself experience the affections of those who are tempted, Hebrews 2:17; 4:15. 7. To confirm the promise of being heard. The Son of God willed to become our brother through the assumption of flesh, so that in all dangers and adversities, fleeing to Him by faith as our brother and kinsman, we might be certain that we are regarded and heard by Him, etc. 8. Because of what is required in the law

Infra enim docebimus, electionem ipsam niti praevisa satisfactione Christi neque obstare acceptationem alienae satisfactionis, ut tamen nihilominus et salvatio et electio maneat gratuita. Qui tamen nihilominus a Deo juste rejiciuntur et damnantur, cum propter alia peccata, tum praecipue, quod satisfactionem Christi ipsi respuunt; Deus autem nec vult, nec tenetur, alienam satisfactionem Christi ulli homini imputare actu ad remissionem peccatorum, qui in Christum 11011 credit. § 11.

Preces vero, sive intercessionem, Christus, sacerdos noster, pro hominibus omnibus quidem praestitit, sed ita, ut pro impiis a orans conversionem eorum procuraret, pro piis b intercedens constantiam eorum et incrementum in fide ac sanctitate promoveret. Oravit autem non solum pro illis, qui deinde conversi, verum etiam pro his, qui revera conversi non fuerint; vid. Luc. 23, 34., ubi Christus pro crucifixoribus suis indefinite, nullo excepto, oravit. Ac sine dubio inter eos aliqui, forte non pauci, in impietate sua perstiterunt, Christus autem, pro illis orans, ostendit, qubd, quantum in se est, non velit illos fructu mortis suae privari, sed potius converti et salvari.

Proiit Joh. 17, 11. orasse legitur: Pater sancte, serva eos per nomen tuum, quos dedisti mihi, ut sint unum, sicut et nos. Et v. 15.: Non rogo, ut tollas eos e mundo, sed ut serves eos e malo. Porro v. 17.: Sanctifica eos in veritate tua; sermo tuus veritas est. Adde v. 21. 23. 24. Atque hoc sensu Christus negaverat ante cap. ejusd. v. 9., se orare pro mundo, coetui fidelium opposito, sive pro improbis, ita ut negatio illa intelligenda sit non simpliciter, sed secundum quid. § 12. Concurrunt autem ad sacerdotium Christi, cum quod ad sacrificium, tum quod ad intercessionem attinet, duae Christi naturae; et ad sacrificium quidem humana natura, quod suum erat, contulit, quando Christus hostibus suis obviam ivit, passionem et mortem toleravit, divina vero,

PART. III. CAP. II. SECTIO ΙΠ.

quoad valorem et virtutem infinitam, passioni et morti additam, ut sufficeret ad expianda hominum peccata Deumque placandum. Quoad intercessionem Christi, actus ipsi orandi, in se spectati, ad humanam naturam formaliter pertinent, dignitas vero et valor eorundem ex divina natura resultat. Gerhardus: ,,Repetendae hoc loco causae, propter quas mediatorem nostrum Deum et hominem esse oportuit. I. Deus esse debuit ob magnitudinem mali abolendi et magnitudinem boni adducendi; puta: 1. Ob λντpov sufficientiam ac perfectionem. Nisi Deus fuisset, ipsius obedientia ac passio non potuisset esse sufficiens λντρον pro totius mundi peccatis. 2. Ob irae divinae portationem. Nuda creatura non potuisset immensum pondus peccatorum et irae divinae totius humani generis peccatis debitae portare. 3. Ob malorum remotionem. Nudo homini non fuisset possibilis peccati abolitio, capitis serpentis infernalis contritio, regni diaboli destructio, mortis absorptio. 4. Ob bonorum reparationem. Nudus homo et finita creatura non potuisset perfectam justitiam adducere, Spiritum Sanctum distribuere, vitam aeternam credentibus conferre. 5. Ob decreti divini patefactionem. Nuda creatura non potuisset scire decretum Dei de salute nostra, quod tamen per mediatorem debuit manifestari. Joh. 1, 18.: ,Deum nemo vidit unquam‘ etc. 6. Oh ecclesiae defensionem. Nuda creatura non posset ecclesiam adversus diabolum et omnes inferorum portas defendere, sed ad hoc requiritur divina et infinita potentia. 7. Ob partorum donorum conservationem. Mediator noster dona nobis parta melius conservare debuit, quam primus humani generis parens Adamus, qui non solum pro se, sed et pro omnibus posteris dona divinitus sibi concredita amisit; sed Christus ea fideliter conservat omnibus credentibus. 8. Ob precum exauditionem. Ad mediatoris officium requiritur, ut ecclesiae suae praesens ubique adsit, invocantes se audiat ac preces eorum velut intercessor ac mediator ad Deum deferat; utique ergo verum Deum ipsum esse oportuit. II. Vicissim etiam verus homo esse debuit: 1. Ob divinae justitiae constitutionem. Homo peccaverat, per hominem igitur satisfactio praestanda erat, ne quid justitiae divinae immotae prorsus ac invariabili decederet. 2. Ob naturae humanae restitutionem. . . Per peccatum totum genus humanum, adeoque tota natura humana misere erat corrupta, ita ut omnes homines essent servi peccati et mortis aeternae rei; voluit igitur Filius Dei in humana natura assumta mortem superare et miseram naturam humanam ad coelestem gloriam iterum evehere. 3. Ob nostram cum Deo reconciliationem. Per peccatum Adae omnes eramus a Deo divisi, Esa. 59, 2. Christus igitur humanam naturam sibi personaliter univit, ut in ea ac per eam reduceret nos ad communionem cum Deo. 4. Ob fidei nostrae confirmationem. Voluit Dei Filius in et cum humana natura ac per humanam naturam opus redemtionis perficere, ut certi redderemur, beneficia illa Christi morte ac passione parta ad nos vefe pertinere, nosque illorum bonorum participes fore. 5. Ob naturae nostrae cognationem. Voluit Christus omnia sua bona et partorum thesaurorum plenitudinem in hu. manam naturam assumtam quasi deponere, juxta quam est frater et cognatus noster, ut per eam ad nos deriventur et a divina natura per humanam ad nos deveniant. 6. Ob sustinendam tentationem. Filius Dei ideo assumsit naturam humanam, ut possit tentari tanquam alius homo verus et tentatorum affectus ipsemet experiri, Hebr. 2, 17. 4, 15. 7. Ad confirmandam exauditionis promissionem. Voluit Dei Filius per carnis assumtionem fleri noster frater, ut in omnibus periculis et adversis ad ipsum tanquam fratrem et cognatum nostrum fide confugientes certi simus, nos ab eo respici et exaudiri etc. 8. Ob requisitam in lege


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: the condition of the Redeemer

the condition of the Redeemer. It was provided by divine law that the *Goel*, or redeemer, should be closely related by the right of consanguinity and should provide redemption by the interposition of a certain price, Leviticus 25. Christ, therefore, by the assumption of human nature, willed to become our kinsman, so that by right He might liberate us and purchase us for Himself as a peculiar possession with His own blood. 9. On account of our adoption. Through sin we had become the slaves of the devil; therefore the Son of God willed to become the Son of man, so that through Him we men might be rendered the sons of God. 10. On account of the certification of our resurrection. The Son of God willed not only to sustain death in the assumed human nature, but also to conquer it, so that we might be rendered certain that our mortal bodies also are to be raised from the earth.” (L. c. § 41.) Calovius: “That Christ is our mediator according to both natures is established thus: I. Concerning the deity.

1. According to the same nature that our righteousness is, according to that same nature He is also our mediator. But according to the divine nature He is our righteousness, Jer. 23:6.

2. According to the same nature that He reconciled us to God, according to that He is our mediator. But He reconciled us to the Father as God, Rom. 5:11; 2 Cor. 5:19.

3. According to the same nature that He laid down His soul for us, according to that He is our mediator. But according to that same nature, according to which He is the Son of God, the image of the invisible God, He reconciled us by His death, Col. 1:15, in whom all fullness dwelt, v. 19, 20.

4. Because the Son of God came into the world for this end, that He might save us, Isa. 34:4; Matt. 18:11; Luke 19:10; 1 Tim. 1:15.

5. Therefore salvation is attributed to Jehovah, Hos. 1:7, and redemption, Hos. 13:14; the acquisition of the church is claimed for the Lord, Acts 20:28; the offering of Himself through the eternal Spirit, Heb. 9:14.

6. It was a *προςκείμενον* or requirement of the mediator that He should be no less God than man, so that, being a kinsman to both parties, He might sanction peace between both. For it is the work of friends to reconcile those who are at variance.

7. Because human nature was by no means sufficient to appease the infinite wrath of God, to satisfy the essential justice of God, to reconcile the world to God, to destroy the works of the devil, sin, death, and hell. ‘For this,’ says Anselm, *Cur Deus homo?* lib. II, c. 18, ‘the diversity of natures and the unity of person availed in Christ, so that what was necessary to be done for the restoration of men, if human nature could not do it, the divine might do,’ etc. 8. If there had been no need for the concurrence of the divine nature for the work of mediation, the union of the divine and human nature or the communication of infinite gifts through the anointing of the Holy Spirit would certainly not have been necessary; indeed, the remission of sins could have been obtained by a mere man, if not for others, at least by any mortal for himself: all of which are *ἀθεόλογα*. 9. If the human nature alone were the mediator, trust could have been placed in a mere man, indeed it would have been required, which Jer. 17:5 pronounces a curse. . . Now, that Christ is our mediator not only as God, but also as man, these things teach: 1. That the apostle expressly, 1 Tim. 2:5, states this concerning man: ‘There is one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus.’ 2. That the Son of God willed to become man and to be incarnate for this reason, that He might be able to perform the office of mediator. 3. That for the work of mediation it was required that He should shed His blood, and by its price liberate us, and lay down His soul for us, Acts 20:28; Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45; 1 Tim. 2:5. 4. That without the shedding of blood no reconciliation could take place, Rom. 5:9, no remission of sins, Heb. 9:22. 5. That for this reason it behooved Christ to suffer, Luke 24:26, and to fulfill the law, since that was impossible for us, Rom. 8:3, so that the righteousness required by the law might be fulfilled in us, v. 4. 6. That the incarnation would have been in vain if Christ could have performed the mediation by His deity alone. 7. That for mediation, ‘domesticity’ (as the ancients speak) is required toward both parties of the dissenters. Therefore Augustine, *Homil. de ovibus* c. 12: ‘Divinity without humanity is not a mediatrix; humanity without divinity is not a mediatrix; but between divinity alone and humanity alone, the human divinity and the divine humanity is the mediatrix.’ 8. That for the works of mediation the communion of both natures was necessary. No PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III.

for the theandric action, such as was the mediation, the satisfaction, the passion for the life of the world, the vicarious fulfillment for the whole human race, could not have proceeded from man alone, but had its origin from the θεάνθρωπος. Therefore, it was necessary that God should become man, so that each nature, as the Council of Chalcedon holds, might act in such a way that is its own, with the communication of the other.” (System. Th. VII. 453. 456. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of Andreas Osiander, asserting that Christ is our righteousness and our mediator only according to his divine nature. . . But by this reasoning, the necessity of the incarnation of the Son of God for the work of reconciliation and mediation is removed. . . 2. Of Francesco Stancaro, professor of the Hebrew language at the Academy of Königsberg, a Mantuan by nationality. . . In the year 1551, he contended that Christ is our mediator only according to his human nature; likewise, that the divine nature is to be entirely excluded from the office of mediation and priesthood. A rather heated dispute with Osiander at the same Academy of Königsberg provided the occasion for Stancaro’s error. Stancaro veered to the other extreme. . . 3. Of the Papists, especially the Jesuits, who embrace Stancaro’s heresy and attribute the office of mediator to Christ only according to his human nature. For thus Peter Lombard, Book 3, Sentences, dist. 19, letter G: ‘Christ is mediator, insofar as he is man; for insofar as he is God, he is not a mediator, but is equal to the Father, the same as the Father.’ Bellarmine, Book 5, On Christ, ch. 1, says: ‘The principle by which those works were performed by the mediator was the human nature, not the divine.’ . . 4. Of certain Calvinists, such as Piscator, denying that this axiom is true: ‘The names of the office belong to Christ according to both natures.’” (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 392. sq.) §

18. In the state of exaltation, it must be confessed that Christ no longer offers a sacrifice for us, but nevertheless presents to God the sacrifice once performed, and today intercedes for us; although that intercession does not take place in the form of a servant or in a humble state, as it did on earth. For he is no longer slaughtered or dying; see Rom. 6:9, 10. And in Heb. 9:12, 25, it is said that Christ the priest differs from the priests of the Old Testament in this very thing, that they offered sacrifice for sins often, but he did so once, indeed through his own blood; once, I say, he was offered to take away the sins of many, v. 28, and that having offered one sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, etc., ch. 10:10, 12, 14. Not as if the offering itself were delayed until the ascension into heaven, since it was done immediately on the altar of the cross, but because Christ always presents that victim, once consecrated and offered to God, to be looked upon and to be valid before God. Heb. 7:24, 25 says that Christ has a perpetual priesthood, living εις το έντυγχάνειν, to intercede for us. And Christ is called the παράκλητος of sinners, an advocate, pleading their cause before the Father, 1 John 2:1. For it is done by him who sits at the right hand of God, Rom. 8:34. But whether that intercession is verbal and consists in words and prayers, or is by the mind alone or

whether it consists also in words and deeds, or whether it is merely real and consists in this, that Christ, by the power of His merit and satisfaction once rendered and the prayers once made, moves God to remit our sins, it is not necessary to define; see what the blessed Musaeus collected from the German Biblical Gloss, Nuremberg edition, and the writings of Aegidius Hunnius, Balduinus, Brochmand, and Gerhard in *Der ausführlichen Erklärung*, L. X. Q. IV. p. 535 sqq.

Quenstedtius: "There is a distinction between the intercession of Christ in the state of His preceding humiliation and the intercession in the state of His subsequent exaltation. . . There, that prayer of His (joined with His entire obedience) was satisfactory for our sins and punishments and meritorious for the acquiring of our salvation and eternal life, Heb. 5:7, 9. Here, it is no longer satisfactory and meritorious (because, hanging on the cross, He said: 'It is finished,' John 19:30; Heb. 10:14), but applicatory; namely, on the part of God, it has joined to itself the divine theanthropic offering of Christ’s benefits and, unless men stubbornly resist, the collation and the graciously intended reception of men by God. For Christ intercedes for us so that, having been converted from our sins to God, we may be justified and saved through a fiducial apprehension of His merit. Heb. 7:24, 25. Feurborn. Syntagm. I. P. 3. diss. 3. thes. 49. . .

The intercession of Christ is not a bare εμφανισμός τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ or representation; for it is described as an act following it, Rom. 8:34. It is not a bare love, as Chrysostom explains; for this also belongs to the Father; indeed, intercession proceeds from the love of Christ, but it is not love itself. It is not merely an interpretative intercession through merits, but a real and express one; for the ἐντυγχάνειν is not mute, but express. Acts 25:24; Rom. 11:2. It is not a supplication consisting of genuflection, outstretched hands, and wailing; 'for it is not pious to think that this is the asking of the Father, or the suffering of the Son, nor to think this of God' (Gregory Naz. Orat. 36); but it is an ἔντευξις, εμφανισμός, παράκλησις θεανδρική καί ίλαστική (in distinction to that divine παράκλησις, by which the Father and the Holy Spirit are said to παρακαλεῖν, 2 Cor. 5:20; John 14:16), a propitiatory intercession, appearance, and advocacy of the God-man." (L. c. c. 3. membr. 2. s. 2. q. 10. f. 470 sq.)

The same: "Christ is not a metaphorical priest, therefore He does not intercede merely metaphorically. . . Smalcius objects, *de satisfact.* f. 253: 'Since Christ now has absolute power in the business of salvation, intercession must either be taken improperly, or one must deny Christ.' Resp.: 1) If intercession is taken improperly, Christ is denied; for He is not properly a priest if He does not properly intercede for us, according to Heb. 7:24, coll. 9:24. 2) A properly spoken intercession of humility removes Christ, not an authoritative intercession." (L. c. f. 472, 474.)

redemtoris conditionem. Cautum erat divina lege, ut Goel sive redemtor esset jure consanguinitatis redimendo proxime conjunctus et interposito certo precio redemtionem praestaret, Levit. 25. Christus igitur humanae naturae assumtione voluit fleri cognatus noster, ut jure nos liberare ac sanguine suo in peculium nos sibi emere posset. 9. Ob nostram adoptionem. Per peccatum eramus facti mancipia diaboli; ideo Filius Dei fleri voluit hominis filius, ut per ipsum nos homines redderemur Dei filii. 10. Ob nostrae resurrectionis certiUcationem. Calovius: ,,Quod Christus secundum utramque naturam mediator noster sit, ita constat: I. De deitate.

2. Secundum quam naturam nos reconciliavit Deo, secundum eam mediator noster est. At reconciliavit nos Patri ut Deus, Rom. 5, 11. 2 Cor. 5, 19.

3. Secundum quam naturam posuit animam suam pro nobis, secundum illam mediator noster est. At secundum eam quoque, secundum quam est Filius Dei, imago Dei inconspicui, morte sua reconciliavit nos, Col. 1, 15., qua inhabitavit omnis plenitudo in eo, v. 19. 20.

4. Quia eo fine advenit Filius Dei in mundum, ut salvaret nos, Esa. 34, 4. Matth. 18,11. Luc. 19, 10. 1 Tim. 1, 15.

### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Feurbornius: "Although Christ, after the final universal judgment, will not…

Feurbornius: "Although Christ, after the final universal judgment, will not repeat His prayers which He now pours forth, yet the fruit and effect, both of His satisfaction and of His preceding prayer, will remain forever." (Fascic. disp. IV. disp. ult. p. 561.)

Calovius affirms that Christ will still pray for the elect after the consummation of the age. See Syst. Tom. VII, 539 sqq.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Socinians, who posit that Christ does not properly intercede for us in the heavens; for thus the Racovian Catechism, c. 13, on the priestly office of Christ, q. 11: 'When Scripture testifies that Christ intercedes for us, it does not happen as if He properly pours forth prayers for us to God. . . but it happens so that it may be fixed in our minds that all the power which Christ has, He does not have from Himself, but by the gift of God the Father.' . .

2. Of certain Calvinists, who likewise deny that Christ, sitting at the right hand of God, properly intercedes for us. Thus Calvin, in c. 8 of Romans, says: 'This intercession is car[nal]...'" PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III.

in a literal sense, lest we measure it by human standards; for he is not to be thought of as a suppliant, with bended knees and outstretched hands, beseeching the Father‘ (thus far correctly), ‘but because he himself appears unceasingly with his death and resurrection, which in his stead (NB.) are an eternal intercession and have the efficacy of a living prayer, so that they may reconcile the Father to us and render him exorable, he is deservedly said to intercede.‘ . . 3. Of some Papists, who admit only a metaphorical intercession of Christ, but deny one properly so called, so that they may the more strongly establish the intercession of the saints, as D. Feurbornius says. For they distinguish between explicit and interpretative prayer, and place the latter in the presentation of the merits of Christ.“ (L. c. f. 471.) § 14.

The kingly office of Christ is threefold: the kingdom of power, of grace, and of glory. That Christ is king is evident from Ps. 2:6; Luke 1:33; Heb. 1:8.

Calovius: „Although he obtained royal power, as regards its fuller exercise, more fully through his resurrection or ascension into heaven, he nevertheless possessed the same, as regards the right and faculty of acting, already on earth and in the days of his flesh without any defect; and thus Christ was king even then, and that from his very conception, over all things.“ (Syst. VII, 595.) According to the diverse manner of those whom Christ the King regards as subject to himself and governs in diverse ways. For although, if you look at the words themselves, the kingdom of grace as well as that of glory seems to be comprehended under the kingdom of power, insofar as both truly depend upon the divine power communicated to the human nature of Christ, yet the usage of speech demands that the kingdom of grace be spoken of in relation to spiritual goods which are in this age, and the kingdom of glory in respect to the glory of the age to come, while the ‘kingdom of power‘ signifies universal dominion.

Calovius: „Is the kingdom of Christ and of God (Ephes. 5:5) distinct? — The kingdom of Christ and of God are not different kingdoms, whether by the boundaries of the empire or by the time of reigning. Nor in judgment, whether you understand the government of the church or of the whole world, or the final judgment, does Christ alone reign or will he reign without the Father, nor after the judgment does the Father alone reign without the Son. But it is called the kingdom of Christ and of God, because it was given to Christ as mediator by God, or rather because Christ as man was raised to the same government and kingdom which is God’s, that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, inasmuch as he has been exalted to the throne of divine majesty. ‘Where God is, both the Father and the Son can be understood,‘ says Jerome on this passage. Furthermore, what we say of the Father and the Son, let us think the same also of the Holy Spirit.“ (Bibl. illustr. ad Ephes. 5:5. Tom. II, f. 718.) § 15. The kingdom of power is that by which Christ powerfully dominates this universe, and preserves it and governs it most providently. And therefore the subjects in this kingdom are all creatures.

Concerning this, see Daniel 7:14, where it is read that dominion, glory, and a kingdom were given to the Son of Man, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him.

To the same point looks that πᾶσα ἐξουσία, all power in heaven and in earth, conferred upon Christ as King, who is to govern all things in this universe, Matt. 28:18. And in Eph. 1:20, concerning Christ sitting at the right hand of the Father in the heavenly places, far above all principality and power, might and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come, all things are said to be put under His feet.

To this pertain those things which we said in Section I, § 20, concerning the power to be attributed to Christ, not only as God, but also as man. Or all the works of the hands of God, even the brute animals themselves of various species, Ps. 8:7. Compare 1 Cor. 15:27; Eph. 1:20, where all things in general, with the exception of no one except God who subjected them, are said to be subject to Him.

Specifically, the enemies of Christ are referred to here, whom Christ holds under His feet, reigning in the midst of them, Ps. 110:2; Heb. 1:13. §

16. The Kingdom of Grace is that by which Christ gathers, preserves, and abundantly endows the militant church with spiritual goods through the Word and Sacraments. And thus, the subjects in this kingdom are the faithful people who constitute the militant church.

Concerning this, Jer. 23:5 and ch. 33:15, 16 foretold that He would raise up to David a righteous Branch, who shall reign as King and shall be prosperous, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth; and this shall be His name, by which (His people) shall call Him: יְהוָה צִדְקֵנוּ, The LORD our righteousness.

And Zechariah, ch. 9:9, foreseeing that kingdom of grace, stirs up the people to receive the King: Rejoice, he says, greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: He is just, and having salvation.

Christ Himself, however, having regard for this kingdom, which differs much from the worldly form of government, said, "My kingdom is not of this world," John 18:36, 37; just as Paul says: "The weapons of our warfare are not carnal," 2 Cor. 10:4.

Hollazius: "Jesus answered: 'My kingdom is not of this world.' John 18:36. The kingdom of Christ is indeed in the world and over the world, but it is not *of* the world; that is: it is not governed after the manner of the princes of this age, not with iron or carnal weapons. Christ refused the political government offered to Him, John 6:15, nor did He wish to perform the office of a civil judge, Luke 12:14." (Exam. III, S. 1. c. 3. q. 104. p. 762.)

Ad. Osiander: "The passage in John 18:36 clearly refutes the opinion of the Spaniards (the Jesuits); for if Christ had assented to the right, and had denied only the ambition, His answer would not have been simply a liberation from the fear which Pilate had conceived from the accusation. For however much the ambition might have been removed, the right of Christ would still have remained unimpaired, which consequently would have eventually flourished and oppressed the kingdom of the Romans. The phrase 'of the world' denotes that which is of a worldly nature, whether vicious, or laudable, or even indifferent. Christ, therefore, by removing His kingdom from the world, removes a kingdom of a worldly nature; consequently, He removes not so much the ambition as the right of a kingdom or of temporal dominion; this meaning is evident from John 8:23; 15:19. It is established by the added explanation." Baier Comp. ed. Walther, p. 9 PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III.

For Christ describes His kingdom under the quality of truth, communicated on the part of the King and received on the part of the subjects, v. 37. But the kingdom of truth is not coercive, but persuasive, and it does not claim right over temporal things, but over the morals of men; hence Pilate, seeing that Christ did not attribute more to Himself than the Stoics attributed to their wise man, fears nothing regarding danger, but mocks that kingdom of truth. And Eusebius notes that the kinsmen of Christ, when questioned by Domitian about the kingdom of Christ, replied: βασιλείαν ἐκείνην οὐκ εἶναι κοσμικήν, ἢ ἐπίγειον, ἀλλ' ἀγγελικὴν καὶ ἐπουράνιον. (Colleg. th. IV, 188 sq.)

By baptizing and teaching, Matt. 28:19. Even unto the end of the world. Ibid. v. last; ch. 16:18.

Walchius: "Natalis Alexander observes that the words in the Nicene Creed, 'Of whose kingdom there shall be no end' (in the Council of Constantinople), were opposed for the sake of refuting the error concerning the millennial kingdom of Christ on this earth." (Introd. in libros symb. p. 129. cf. Die symbol. BB. Edited by J. T. Müller, p. 30.)

Luther: "And then (says Paul) he, the Lord Christ, shall deliver up the kingdom to God, even the Father, etc. What is this? Does not Scripture say everywhere that he shall remain King in eternity, and of his kingdom there shall be no end: how then does it rhyme that he says here he shall deliver up the kingdom, and make himself subject to the Father, and lay his crown, scepter, and everything into his lap? Answer: He is speaking of the kingdom of Christ now on earth, which is a kingdom of faith, in which he rules through the Word, not in a visible, public state, but it is just as one sees the sun through a cloud; there one sees the light well enough, but the sun itself one does not see; but when the clouds are gone, then one sees both light and sun at the same time, in one and the same state: thus Christ now rules undivided with the Father, and it is one and the same kingdom; only there is the difference that it is now dark and hidden, or veiled and covered, entirely grasped in faith and in the Word, so that one sees nothing more of it than Baptism, the Sacrament, nor hears anything of it than the external Word: that is all his power and might, through which he rules and accomplishes everything. . . until the little hour comes when Christ will put an end to this, and present himself publicly in his majesty and dominion, where you will see and feel what you now believe, sin blotted out and drowned, death abolished and taken from your eyes, the devil and the world lying at your feet, and it will be a manifest state with God, and everything clear before your eyes, like an uncovered treasure, as we now desire and wait for it. That is what St. Paul means when he says that Christ will deliver up the kingdom to God the Father, that is, he will put aside faith and the hidden state, and present his own before God the Father, and thus place us manifestly into the kingdom which he has established and now daily carries on, so that we shall see him without veil and dark words, most clearly, and it will then be called not a kingdom of faith, but of glory and public state; and although it is one and the same kingdom, both of Christ (who became man for the sake of this, that he might establish faith in him) and of God, for whoever hears Christ, hears God the Father himself; yet it is now properly called the Lord Christ's kingdom, because God is now hidden in his majesty, and has given everything to Christ, that he might bring us to him through his Word and Baptism; to this end he also hid himself in Christ, that we should seek and recognize God nowhere but in him. . . Thus he himself interprets and clarifies it with the words that follow: when he shall have put down all rule and all authority and all power, etc."

Regium a Christi officium triplex b est: regnum potentiae, gratiae et gloriae. Christum esse regem, constat ex Ps. 2, 6. Luc. 1, 33. Ebr. 1, 8.

Calovius: ,,Quanquam potestatem regiam, quoad plenius exercitium, pleniorem nactus sit per resurrectionem vel ascensionem in coelum, eandem tamen, quoad jus et facultatem agendi, jam in terris et in diebus carnis sine ullo defectu habuit; adeoque rex tum fuit Christus, idque ab ipsa conceptione, super omnia.“ (Syst. VII, 595.) Pro diversa ratione eorum, quos rex Christus tanquam sibi subjectos respicit et diversimode gubernat. Quamvis enim, si voces ipsas spectes, regnum gratiae pariter et gloriae sub regno potentiae comprehendi videatur, quatenus revera utrumque a divina potentia humanae Christi naturae communicata, dependet, tamen usus loquendi postulat, ut regnum gratiae in ordine ad spiritualia bona, quae in hoc saeculo, et regnum gloriae in respectu ad gloriam saeculi futuri dicatur, ,potentiae regnum autem dominium universale significet.

Calovius: ״An regnum Christi et Dei (Ephes. 5, 5.) distinctum? — Non diversa regna, sive finibus imperii, sive regnandi tempore, sunt regnum Christi et Dei. Nec in judicio, sive gubernationem ecclesiae intelligas aut mundi universi, sive novissimum judicium, solus regnat aut regnabit Christus sine Patre, nec post judicium solus Pater sine Filio. Christi autem et Dei regnum dicitur, quia Christo ut mediatori datum a Deo, vel potius quia Christus ut homo ad idem evectus est regimen et regnum, quod Dei est, hoc est, Patris, Filii et Spiritus Sancti, utpote qui in thronum majestatis divinae exaltatus est. ,Ubi Deus est, tam Pater, quam Filius intelligi potest‘, inquit Hieronymus in hunc locum. Regnum gratiae est,a quo Christus ecclesiam militantem per verbum et sacramenta b colligit, conservat c et bonis spiritualibus d abunde e donat. Adeoque subditi in hoc regno sunt homines fideles, qui ecclesiam militantem constituunt.

De quo Jer. 23, 5. cap. 33, 15. 16. praedixit, excitaturum se Davidi germen justum, qui regnaturus sit rex, et felix futurus, exerciturus jus et justitiam in terra; atque hoc nomen ejus futurum, quo vocabit eum (populus suus): o Jehova justitia nostra.

Et Zacharias cap. 9, 9., regnum illud gratiae praevidens, populum ad excipiendum regem excitat: Exulta, inquiens, valde, filia Zijonis, clange filia Jerusalem, ecce, rex tuus veniet tibi, justus et salvator est.

Ipse vero Christus, habita hujus regni ratione, quae a terrena regiminis forma multum differt, Regnum meum, dixit, non est ex hoc mundo, Joh. 18, 36. 37., aeque uti Paulus: Arma militiae nostrae non sunt carnalia, 2 Cor. 10, 4.

Hollazius: ,,Respondit Jesus: ,Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo.‘ Joh. 18, 36. Est quidem regnum Christi in mundo et super mundum, sed non de mundo; hoc est: non more principum hujus saeculi, non armis ferreis aut carnalibus gubernatur. Oblatam gubernationem politicam Christus recusavit, Joh. 6, 15., nec munere judicis civilis fungi voluit, Luc. 12,,14.“ (Exam. III, S. 1. c. 3. q. 104. p. 762.)

Osiander: ״Locus Joh. 18, 36. plane profligat sententiam Hispanorum (Jesuitarum); si enim Christus annuisset de jure, et negasset solam affectationem, responsio illius non fuisset simpliciter liberativa metus, quem ex accusatione ceperat Pilatus. Utut enim affectatio fuisset remota, jus tamen Christi mansisset illibatum, quod consequenter tandem effloruisset, regnum que Romanorum oppressisset. Phrasis,ex mundo‘ notat id, quod est mundanae indolis, vel vitiosae, vel laudabilis, vel etiam indifferentis. Christus itaque, regnum a se removendo ex mundo, removet regnum mundanae indolis, consequenter non tam affectationem, quam jus regni seu dominii temporalis; patet hic sensus ex Joh. 8, 23. 15, 19.
