Regnum enim suum Christus describit sub qualitate veritatis ex parte regis communicatae, et ex parte subditorum receptae, v. 37. At veritatis regnum non coactivum, sed persuasivum est, nec jus dicit in temporalia, sed in mores hominum; hinc videns Pilatus, Christum sibi non plus tribuere, quam Stoici suo sapienti tribuebant, de periculo nil timet, sed veritatis illud regnum ridet. Et notat Eusebius, agnatos Christi, interrogatos a Domitiano de regno Christi, respondisse: βασιλείαν εκείνην ονκ είναι κοσμικήν, ή επίγειον, αλλ' αγγελικήν και επονράνιον.“ (Colleg. th. ΙΥ, 188. sq.)

Baptizando et docendo, Matth. 28, 19. Usque ad consummationem mundi. Ibid. v. ult. cap. 16, 18.

Walchius: ״Natalis Alexander observat, (Nicaeno symbolo) verba: ,Cujus regni non erit finis1 (in Concilio Constantinopolitano), erroris de millenario Christi in his terris regno refellendi causa esse opposita.“ (Introd. in libros symb. p. 129. cf. Die symbol. BB. Besorgt von J. T. Müller, p. 30.)

Lutherus: ״Und alsdenn (spricht Paulus) wird er, der Herr Christus, das Reich überantworten Gott, dem Vater u. s.w. Was ist das? spricht doch die Schrift allenthalben, dass er soll König bleiben in Ewigkeit, und seines Reichs soll kein Ende sein: wie reimet sichs denn, dass er hie sagt, er soll das Reich übergeben, und sich dem Vater unterthan machen, und ihm seine Krone, Scepter und alles in den Schooss legen? Antwort: Er redet von dem Reich Christi jetzt auf Erden, welches ist ein Reich des Glaubens, darin er regieret durch das Wort, nicht in sichtlichem, öffentlichem Wesen, sondern ist gleich wie man die Sonne siehet durch eine Wolke, da siehet man wohl das Licht, aber die Sonne selbst siehet man nicht; wenn aber die Wolken hinweg sind, so siehet man beide, Licht und Sonne zugleich, in einerlei Wesen: also regieret jetzt Christus mit dem Vater ungetheilet, und ist einerlei Reich; allein ist der Unterschied, dass es jetzt dunkel und verborgen ist, oder verhüllet und zugedeckt, gar im Glauben und ins Wort gefasset, dass man nicht mehr davon siehet, denn die Taufe, Sacrament, noch davon höret, denn das äusserliche Wort: das ist alle seine Kraft und Macht, dadurch er regieret und Alles ausrichtet. . . bis so lange das Stündlein kommt, da Christus wird dess ein Ende machen, und sich öffentlich darstellen in seiner Majestät und Herrschaft, da du wirst sehen und fühlen, was du jetzt glaubest, die Sünde ausgetilget und ersäuft, den Tod aufgehaben und aus den Augen genommen, den Teufel und Welt dir zu Füssen liegen, und wird ein offenbarlich Wesen sein bei Gott, und alles klar vor Augen, als ein aufgedeckter Schatz, wie wirs jetzt begehren und warten. Das meinet St. Paulus, als er spricht, dass Christus das Reich Gott dem Vater überantworten wird, das ist, er wird den Glauben und das verborgene Wesen beiseite thun, und die Seinen darstellen vor Gott dem Vater, und uns also offenbarlich setzen in das Reich, das er angerichtet hat und jetzt täglich treibet, dass wir ihn sehen werden ohn Deckel und dunkel Worte, aufs allerklarste, und wird denn heissen nicht ein Reich des Glaubens, sondern der Klarheit und öffentlichen Wesens; und wiewohl es einerlei Reich ist, beide, Christi (welcher um desselben willen ist Mensch worden, dass er den Glauben an ihn auf richtete) und Gottes, denn wer Christum höret, der höret Gott den Vater selbst; doch heisst es jetzt eigentlich des Herrn Christi Reich, weil Gott jetzt in seiner Majestät verborgen ist, und Christo alles gegeben hat, dass er durch sein Wort und Taufe uns zu ihm bringe; dazu auch sich selbst in Christum verborgen, dass wir Gott nirgend, denn in ihm, suchen und erkennen sollen. . . Also deutet und verkläret ers selbst mit den Worten, die da folgen: wenn er aufheben wird alle Herrschaft und alle Obrigkeit und alle Gewalt u. s. w.,


### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: that is, He will put an end to everything, both of the spiritual government…

that is, He will put an end to everything, both of the spiritual government which He now conducts in the world, which is Baptism, the pulpit, the Sacrament, the keys or absolution, etc., and also of the temporal [government], with its estates and offices, such as father, mother, child, servant, maid, lord, prince, peasant, citizen, etc., so that one will have need of none of these...

Yet He speaks with a distinction between the two, the spiritual and the temporal kingdom. For of the spiritual He does not say: He will abolish it, but deliver it to God, as that which shall nevertheless remain; but the temporal (He says) He will entirely do away with and bring to nothing. For the same is ordained, not for the sake of the pious, but for the sake of the wicked...

These seem to be empty, dark words; but everything is spoken, as I have said, to the end that He might set a distinction between the kingdom of God and of Christ; although in itself it is one and the same kingdom. But it is called Christ’s now for this reason, that we live therein here by faith, and do not see and hear Him bodily, as one sees a worldly king sitting before one’s eyes in his kingdom, with the royal crown and great, glorious splendor. For it is not yet manifest what we have in Him, and what we shall attain through the Gospel, Sacrament, and faith. Afterward, however, it shall be called God’s kingdom, when it is no longer hidden, but shall be manifest before all creatures, and faith shall cease; which He calls delivering the kingdom to the Father, that is, to present us and His whole Christendom manifestly before the Father, into eternal clarity and glory, that He Himself may reign without any veil.

Yet nonetheless Christ will remain in His dominion and majesty, for He is the same God and Lord, eternal and almighty with the Father. But because He now reigns through His Word, Sacrament, etc., in such a way that the world does not see [Him], it is called Christ’s kingdom, and everything must be subject to Him (yet excepting Him who subjects everything to Him) until the Last Day, when He will abolish everything, and then submit Himself with His whole kingdom to the Father, and say to Him: I have hitherto reigned with Thee in faith; this I deliver over to Thee, that they may now see how I am in Thee and Thou in Me, together with the Holy Spirit, in one divine majesty, and have and enjoy everything in Thee manifestly, which they have hitherto believed and awaited. Then (He says) God will be all in all, that is, everyone will have in God Himself everything that he now has in all things, so that, when He reveals Himself, we shall all have enough in soul and body, and no longer have need of such manifold things as we must now have on earth. (

Interpretation of the 15th Chapter of the First Epistle of St. Paul to the Corinthians, 1534. VIII, 1254 sqq., 1256, 1257, 1258, 1279 sqq.)

Quenstedtius: "Paul indeed says in 1 Cor. 15:24: 'Then comes the end, when He shall have delivered the kingdom to God and the Father.' But what is said here concerning the παραδόσει or delivery of the kingdom is not to be understood of the government itself, but only of the mode of reigning or the form and quality of the government, because, to wit, Christ will no longer reign through means, namely, through Word and Sacraments, through the cross and among enemies, as before; but with all enemies prostrated, the last enemy, namely death, destroyed, and the impious thrust down to hell, He will deliver the kingdom to God the Father, i.e., He will deliver the captive enemies and present the elect, in whom He obtains His spiritual kingdom. There will therefore be a triumphal delivery of the subdued enemies and a representation of the liberated faithful. By this act of delivery, He will not lay down the administration of His spiritual and heavenly kingdom, but Christ will then merely inaugurate another mode of government, the condition of the subjects being changed, but not that of the King, who will reign with His saints forever, although not economically, but with most glorious triumph, empire, and dominion." (L. c. s. 1. th. 85. f. 387.)

Dorscheus: "That delivery (1 Cor. 15:24) is not an act of deposition, but of proposition; He will not depose the kingdom, which until the consumma- PART III. CHAPTER II. SECTION III.

Christ has graciously and gloriously governed the age, but at that consummation, He will present it to God the Father for, as it were, purification and glory. Just as a military commander, having destroyed all enemies, presents and exhibits to the king—for whom he had hitherto waged war—a victorious and triumphant army, saved citizens, and free peoples, so that he may judge and by his judgment approve that these things were done excellently and to the king’s glory, yet without laying down the power he held over the army: so much more will Christ, as the Son, when the age is consummated and all enemies removed, set His ecclesiastical army before God the Father, immaculate (Eph. 5:27), which is truly His kingdom brought forth by grace, caught up to meet Him for glory (1 Thess. 4:17); He will set it before His τῷ βήματι, His tribunal (Rom. 14:10), and will say: “These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins; these are they who follow the Lamb wherever I have gone; these were redeemed from among men, being firstfruits to Thee, God the Father, and to Me, the Lamb” (Rev. 14:4). (Theol. Zach. P. II. disp. 7. p. 256.)

Both with those who sanctify and those who minister, 1 Cor. 12:4 ff. to 12; Rom. 12:3, 4 ff., where διαιρέσεις χαρισμάτων, divisions of gifts, and χαρίσματα διάφορα, various gifts, are indicated in v. 6. Compare Eph. 4:7, where it is said that grace was given to each of us κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς τοῦ Χριστοῦ, according to the measure of the gift of Christ. Therefore, the institution of the ministry, its preservation, and the concurrence of the ministers with their labor pertain to this; see Eph. 4:11; 1 Cor. 3:7, 9. More will be said in the Book on the Church, where the head of the church must be treated.

Rromayerus: “Although good ministers today are vicars of Christ in the church militant, the constitution of the same nevertheless pertains to His kingly office, according to Ephesians 4, where the giving of pastors and teachers in v. 11 is placed immediately under His royal ascension above all the heavens in v. 10, and Matthew 28, where the mission to teach and baptize in v. 19, 20 is connected with all authority which was given to Him in heaven and on earth in v. 18. Thus, the question agitated with great contention in England between the hierarchs and the Puritans—whether it pertains to the priestly, kingly, or prophetic office—is in vain.” (Th. posit. pol. P. II, 530.)

For thus it is said that Christ, the Shepherd, came so that His sheep might have life and also have it κατὰ τὸ περισσόν, and that which abounds; see John 17:6, 14, 16, where Christ says these subjects of His are not of this world, but were given to Him out of the world. And chapter 10:14, that He is known by His sheep (which recognition is of faith), and that they hear His voice and follow Him, v. 27. The same are called in 1 Pet. 2:9 a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for His own possession. §

17. The kingdom of glory is that by which Christ gloriously rules the church triumphant and fills it with eternal felicity, and thus the subjects in this kingdom are blessed men. Thus the throne of glory is attributed to Christ, as King, in Matt. 25:31. So that they themselves may see the glory of Christ, which the Father gave Him, John 17:24. And to this is referred the resurrection of the dead faithful to life; and the solemn introduction of these, and of those surviving at the end of the world, into eternal glory, Matt. 25:34; Luke 22:29, 30.

Since, however, Christ will rule in the life to come not only over the blessed, but also over the damned, some distinguish between the kingdom of glory and the kingdom of justice, and refer to the latter the resurrection of the ungodly from the dead and their condemnation, according to Matt. 25:41 sqq. Others, referring both to the same kingdom of glory, say that the glorification of the elect pertains to it in itself, but they refer the condemnation of the reprobate (which in itself pertains to the kingdom of power) to it in the same manner in which opposites are otherwise wont to be referred to the same faculty. § 18.

And Christ indeed, although from the womb he was made King by virtue of the personal union, yet he began to use his royal majesty fully only in the state of exaltation. a He received the divine majesty communicated to him then immediately according to his human nature; see above, Sect. I, § 20.

b Compare what we said in Sect. II, § 1. ANTITHESES. Gerhardus: "The Papists, against the royal office, 1) exclude the human nature of Christ from omnipresent dominion in heaven and on earth; 2) establish a vicar of Christ, the Pope; 3) transfer the honor, dignity, works, and names proper to Christ the King to the Roman Pontiff; 4) transfer temporal kingdom to the Pope under the pretext of the vicariate of Christ... The Calvinists fight against the royal office, because they exclude his human nature from omnipresent and omnipotent dominion in heaven and on earth... The Photinians, against the royal office of Christ, 1) deny that Christ, after his ascension into the heavens, rules present on earth, and they limit and restrict the power given to Christ; 2) establish that there will be an end to the kingdom of Christ." (L. c. § 326, 328, 329.)

Scherzerus: "The Jews, Papists, and Chiliasts (a noble trio!) dream that Christ is a worldly king. Concerning the fables of the Jews, see Gerson... Concerning the Papists, see Antoninus, Summa, Part III, tit. 3, c. 2, and others. For it is in their interest that the Romanist clergy themselves be temporal lords. To what end that fear of Cardinal Julian, writing to Pope Eugenius IV, who wished to dissolve the Council of Basel: 'I fear lest it happen to us as it happened' (Priscian would say: *contigit*) 'to the Jews, who said: If we let this man go, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation: so we also say: If we let the council be held, the laymen will come and take away our temporality.' In Aeneas Sylvius, not yet Pius, Opp. f. 71." (System, p. 220.) Kahnisius: "Finally, the statement 1 Cor. 15:24—28... cannot be interpreted otherwise than that the relative independence which the Son assumes as Head of the Church, in that He leads, awakens, and judges it, will cease after it has reached its goal in the overcoming of the opposition, so that the Father may become the sole reigning Principle. Thus, it is the undoubted teaching of Scripture that the Father is the divine primordial personality." (Die Luth. Dogm. III. 1868. p. 208.)

Hofmannus: "The ruling of Christ has its time just as well, in so far as His serving had its time before, in that 'it ceases when it has fulfilled its purpose.'" (Schriftbeweis. Second Half. Second Part. p. 604.) PART III. CHAP. III.

Latin:

das ist, er wird alles ein Ende machen, beide, des geistlichen Regiments, das er jetzt in der Welt führet, welches ist die Taufe, PredigtStuhl, Sacrament, Schlüssel oder Absolution u. s. w., und auch des weitliehen, mit seinen Ständen und Aemtern, als Vater, Mutter, Kind, Knecht, Magd, Herrn, Pursten, Bauer, Bürger u. s. w., dass man der keines wird bedürfen...

Er redet aber dennoch mit Unterschied von den zweien, dem geistlichen und weltlichen Reich. Denn vom geistlichen sagt er nicht: er wirds auf heben, sondern Gott übergeben, als das dennoch bleiben soll; aber das weltliche (spricht er) wird er gar abthun und zunicht machen. Denn dasselbe ist geordnet, nicht um der Frommen, sondern um der Bösen willen. . .

Das scheinen eitel dunkele Worte; ist aber alles, wie ich gesagt habe, dahin geredet, dass er einen Unterschied setze des Reichs Gottes und Christi; wiewohl es doch an ihm selbst einerlei Reich ist. Aber darum heisset es jetzt Christi, dass wir hier darin leben im Glauben, und nicht ihn leiblich sehen und hören, wie man einen weltlichen König siehet vor Augen sitzen in seinem Reich, mit der königlichen Krone und grossen, herrliehen Pracht. Denn es ist noch nicht offenbar, was wir an ihm haben, und durch das Evangelium, Sacrament und Glauben erlangen sollen. Darnach aber wirds heissen Gottes Reich, wenn es nicht mehr verborgen, sondern vor allen Creaturen offenbar werden, und der Glaube aufhören soll; welches er heisset, das Reich dem Vater überantworten, das ist, uns und seine ganze Christenheit offenbarlich darstellen vor dem Vater, in die ewige Klarheit und Herrlichkeit, dass er selbst regiere ohn alle Deckel.

Doch nichts desto weniger wird Christus in seiner Herrschaft und Majestät bleiben, denn er ist derselbige Gott und Herr, ewig und allmächtig mit dem Vater. Aber weil er jetzt so regieret durch sein Wort, Sacrament u. s. w., dass die Welt nicht siehet, so heisset es Christi Reich, und muss alles ihm unterthan sein (doch ausgenommen den, der ihm alles unterthan machet) bis an den jüngsten Tag, da ers alles wird aufheben, und sich alsdann mit seinem ganzen Reich dem Vater untergeben, und zu ihm sagen: Ich habe bisher mit dir regiert im Glauben, das gebe ich dir über, dass sie nun sehen, wie ich in dir und du in mir seiest, sammt dem Heiligen Geist, in Einer göttlichen Majestät, und alles in dir offenbarlich haben und geniessen, was sie bisher geglaubt und gewartet haben. Alsdann (spricht er) wird Gott sein alles in allem, das ist, ein jeglicher wird an Gott selbst alles haben, was er jetzt an allen Dingen hat, dass, wenn er sich offenbaret, werden wir alle genug haben an Seele und Leib, und nicht mehr so mancherlei bedürfen, wie wir jetzt auf Erden müssen haben.“ (

Auslegung des 15. Cap. der ersten Ep. St. Pauli an die Cor. 1534. VIII, 1254. sq. 1256. 1257. 1258. 1279. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ״Dicit quidem Paulus 1 Cor. 15, 24.: ,Deinde finis, cum tradiderit regnum Deo et Patri.‘ Ast quae hic dicuntur de παραδόσεt seu traditione regni, non de ipso regimine, sed de modo regnandi seu regiminis forma et qualitate tantum intelligenda sunt, quia scii. Christus non amplius regnabit per media, nempe per verbum et sacramenta, per crucem et inter hostes, ut antea; sed hostibus omnibus prostratis, ultimo hoste, morte vid., destructo, impiisque ad tartara detrusis, tradet regnum Deo Patri, i. e., tradet hostes captivos et sistet electos, in quibus obtinet regnum suum spirituale. Erit ergo traditio triumphatoria hostium subactorum et repraesentatio fidelium liberatorum. Non deponet per hunc παραδόσεως actum regni sui spiritualis et coelestis administrationem, sed saltem alium modum gubernationis tunc Christus in suo regimine auspicaturus est, mutata conditione subditorum, non autem regis, qui regnabit cum sanctis suis in aeternum, quanquam non οικονομικώς, sed gloriosissimo triumpho, imperio et dominio.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 85. f. 387.)

Dorscheus: ,,Illa traditio (1 Cor. 15, 24.) non est actus depositionis, sed propositionis; non deponet regnum, quod usque ad consumma PART. ΠΙ. CAP. Π. SECTIO III.

tionem saeculi gratiose et gloriose gubernavit Christus, in ista consummatione, sed proponet Deo Patri ad lustrationem quasi et gloriam. Zach. P. II. disp. 7. p. 256.)

Cum sanctificantibus, tum ministrantibus, 1. ad Cor. 12, 4. sqq. ad 12. Rom. 12, 3. 4. sqq., ubi διαιρέσεις χαρισμάτων, divisiones donorum, et χαρίσματα διάφορα, dona varia, v. 6. indicantur. 17. Regnum gloriae a est, quo Christus ecclesiam triumphantem gloriose regit b atque aeterna felicitate replet, adeoque subditi in hoc regno sunt homines beati. c Sic Christo thronus gloriae, velut regi, tribuitur Matth. 25, 31. Quia vero Christus in altera vita non solum beatis, verum etiam damnatis dominabitur, ideo quidam inter regnum gloriae et regnum justitiae distinguunt atque ad posterius referunt impiorum resuscitationem a mortuis et eorundem cowemnation&m, juxta Matth. 25, 41. sqq. Alii, utrumque ad idem regnum gloriae referentes, glorificationem electorum per se eo pertinere dicunt, damnationem vero reproborum (quae per se ad regnum potentiae pertineat) eum in modum istuc referunt, quo alias opposita ad eandem facultatem referri solent. § 18.

statuunt, regni Christi fore flnem.“ (L. c. § 326. 328. 329.) Scherzerus: ״Judaei, papistae, chiliastae (nobilis triga!), Christum esse regem mundanum, somniant. De Judaeorum fabulis vide Gersonem. . . De papistis vide Antoninum Summae P. III. tit. 3. c. 2. aliosque. Ipsorum enim interest, ut et ipsi clerici romanenses sint domini temporales. Quorsum ille metus cardinalis Juliani, scribentis ad papam Eugenium IV., qui volebat dissolvere concilium Basileense: ,Vereor, ne contingat nobis, sicut contingit‘ (Priscianus diceret: contigit),Judaeis, qui dixerunt: Si dimittimus hunc, venient Romani et tollent locum nostrum ac gentem: ita et nos dicimus: Si dimittimus, fleri concilium, venient laici et tollent temporalitatem nostram.‘ Apud Aeneam Sylvium, nondum Pium, Opp. f. 71.“ (System, p. 220.) Kahnisius: ,,Endlich kann der Aüsspruch 1 Cor. 15, 24—28. . . nicht anders ausgelegt werden, denn dass die relative Selbständigkeit, welche der Sohn als Haupt der Kirche einnimmt, indem er sie leitet, auf erweckt, richtet, nachdem sie in der Ueberwindung des Gegensatzes ihren Zweck erreicht haben wird, aufhören wird, damit der Väter das allein waltende Princip werde. Sonach ist unzweifelhafte Schriftlehre, dass der Vater die göttliche Urpersönlichkeit ist.“ (Die Luth. Dogm. III. 1868. p. 208.)

### Of Christ: His Person, States and Office: Chapter III

Chapter III.

Latin:

Caput III.


## 18 On Faith in Christ

ON FAITH IN CHRIST. § 1. In order that sinful men may attain eternal salvation through Christ the Mediator, faith in Christ is required, or, in other words, that they believe in Christ as the Mediator.

For although by the passion and death of Christ there was truly performed whatever satisfaction could be demanded from all men in the world to abolish the debt contracted by their offenses, and thus to appease God and reconcile them to Himself; yet God willed that sinners should acknowledge that satisfaction, performed for them by the Son of God, and, having apprehended it by faith, make it their own. And thus He willed that whoever embraces the Mediator by faith should enjoy His merit and have God actually reconciled to him and fully favorable for the bestowing of salvation; conversely, however, if anyone does not apprehend the Mediator by faith, he is, by his own fault, deprived of both His satisfaction and the grace of God, and remains in the offense of God, according to that which is written in John 3:16, 18, 36. Cf. b. Mus. de Convers. Disp. III. cap. II. § 91. p. 144. Luther: "It is not our doing and cannot be earned by our work; it is already there, given and offered; only that you open your mouth, or rather your heart, and keep still, and let yourself be filled. Ps. 81:11. That can happen through nothing else than that you believe these words; as you hear that He here demands faith and appropriates such a treasure entirely to it." (XI, 1489.)

The same: "So this is now the benefit of the suffering and resurrection of Christ, that He did such things not for Himself, but for the whole world, that He has trampled underfoot the devil and my sin, which hung upon Him on Good Friday, so that the devil also flees before the name of Christ. If you now wish to make use of such great goods: very well, He has already given them to you; do Him only so much honor, and receive it with thanks." (XII, 2048.) The same: "The two pieces must indeed come together, as Christ hangs them upon one another and says: He who believes shall be saved. In the one, being saved, there is certainly no lack nor fault; for that is entirely given and gifted in the Word or Gospel, which is God’s unchangeable truth; but there is still much lacking in our faith, that we cannot also grasp and hold such things firmly enough." (XI, 1311.)

The same: "In these words there is certainly no doubt nor lack: He who believes shall be saved, etc., so that hell is already locked, heaven is open, eternal life and joy are there; but there it is still lacking in the first piece, that you are not the man who is called, *qui credit*, a believer, or are still weak." (XI, 1327.) Calovius: "It is added that the satisfaction and redemption of Christ is not salutary to all, but only to those who by true faith appropriate and apply the same to themselves. Christ indeed died for all 1 Cor."

5, 19. Heb. 2, 9. But only those enjoy the benefits obtained by the death of Christ who apply them to themselves by faith. Just as, when a λύτρον has been paid for all captives or those held in servitude, so that they may go forth from prison or servitude, those who wish to enjoy the liberty and make the offered benefit their own—of whom it can be said that they place their trust in their liberator when they accept his liberation—so likewise it is necessary that we embrace by true faith the λύτρον paid for us, and make that liberation our own, so that we may rejoice in the fruit of Christ’s satisfaction.” (Socinism. proflig. p. 732.)

The same: “We are not redeemed, reconciled, or our sins expiated under a condition, but simply, most perfectly, most fully, as far as merit and acquisition are concerned; although, as far as the actual fruit and application are concerned, there is need of faith, which indeed is nothing other than the appropriation of that expiation and satisfaction and reconciliation of Christ. For if one died for all, this is the same (in the judgment of God) as if all had died. 2 Cor. 5, 14.” (Bibl. illustr. ad Rom. 5, 10.)

The same: “All men have been liberated, as far as the intention of God and Christ is concerned, by the liberty acquired for all through Christ; that some, however, do not actually enjoy it, that is not because, when Christ died, it was not the same as if all had died, but because they subsequently make themselves subject to death in another way.” (Socinism. profligat, p. 386.)

Hollazius: “Distinguish a. between satisfaction and its effect; b. between the satisfaction performed by Christ and that applied by man to himself. The satisfaction of Christ was performed long ago; but we do not have its effect, which is the remission of sins, before we apply to ourselves the universal satisfaction of Christ and make it our own through faith. ‘For in order that a gracious imputation may rightly take place, there must indeed be present in the agent the intention of procuring some good for another by his action; and in the recipient, the will, expressed or presumed, to receive that from him. For the imputation of a service that is thrust upon an unwilling person is rightly repelled,’ says Sam. Pufendorf in L. de I. N. et G. p. 128.” (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 8. q. 14. p. 917.)

Calovius: “Therefore, that it may be more fully explained how we have been made alive with Christ, raised up with Christ, and seated in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus (Eph. 2, 5. 6.): it must be said that this was done, first, by reason of merit, because by his being made alive, raised up, and placed in the heavenly places—as our mediator and redeemer—we have been made alive with him and raised up with him and placed in the heavenly places with him. Because he, as our mediator and redeemer, merited this for us when he himself, as our surety and sponsor, was delivered into death for us, which is the same as if we had undergone death. And therefore, he himself being raised from death, we have been raised, just as, when satisfaction has been performed by a sponsor, not only is he free, but also the one for whom he had given himself as sponsor. Then, by reason of application, because we apprehend by faith and apply to ourselves the merit and satisfaction of Christ; and by that reason we are actually spiritually made alive and awakened from the death of sin, so that we may have our πολίτευμα in the heavens, being also destined to be made alive and raised up one day to the other heavenly life.” (Bibl. illustr. ad Eph. 2, 4—6. f. 675. a.)

Faith is called by Paul faith in the blood of Christ, Rom. 3, 25, or fixed upon his merit and satisfaction, which he performed for us by his shed blood, by which reason it is also set forth to us as an ἱλαστήριον or propitiation. Compare Mus. 1. c. It is also called the faith of Christ, or that whose object is Christ, Gal. 2, 16. At other times, indeed, the doctrine of faith itself is also called faith; e.g., Gal. 1, 23. εὐαγγελίζεσθαι τὴν πίστιν, chap. 3, 2. 5., where ἀκοὴ πίστεως is the same as the preaching and hearing of the doctrine of faith. But here, faith is to be considered not that which is believed, but that by which one believes. PART III. CHAPTER III.

Gerhard: "We shall refer to three classes all the significations of faith that occur in the Scriptures. 1. By this word is denoted faith, so to speak, active, i.e., truth and constancy in words and deeds. Ps. 33:4. Rom. 3:3. Is. 11:5. Jer. 7:28. ... 2. By this word is denoted faith, so to speak, passive, by which we believe and assent to the Word. ... 3. By this term (faith) is denoted the object and principle of faith, namely, the heavenly doctrine divinely revealed.

Augustine, *De Trinitate*, 1.13, c. 2: 'Those things which are believed are one thing, and faith by which they are believed is another; and yet both are reckoned under the name of faith, both that, namely, which is believed, and that by which it is believed.'

To this class belongs: 1.) When in general the word 'faith' is taken for the whole heavenly doctrine, Gal. 6:10: 'As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith,' i.e., those who profess the same religion with us. Jude 3, mention is made of 'the faith which was once delivered unto the saints,' i.e., the heavenly doctrine preached.

2.) When it is used specifically for the doctrine of the Gospel. Rom. 3:27: 'By the law of faith,' i.e., by the doctrine of the Gospel. Gal. 3:2: 'Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?' i.e., by the preaching of the Gospel.

3.) Akin to this is the signification when it is taken for the advent of Christ in the Old Testament, in the preaching and full manifestation of those things which lay hidden under the obscurity of ceremonies. Gal. 3:23: 'Before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed.'

4.) When it is taken for the chief and fundamental heads of heavenly doctrine clearly proposed in the Word of God. Rom. 12:6: 'Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the analogy of faith.'" (*L. de justific.* § 66.) See especially John 8:14, 15, 16, 36. §

2. Moreover, knowledge pertains to faith in Christ, and that explicit, of the things to be believed, especially concerning Christ and His merit, and the grace of God or the remission of sins and salvation, to be obtained from God through Him. For we cannot believe except what we grasp with the mind or have known by simple apprehension. Whence knowledge is commonly called the first degree of faith, or the first part, or the beginning of faith. Cf. *Ausführl. Erklärung*, p. 575, 576.

Gerhard: "That knowledge belongs to the same, we demonstrate: 1. From etymology. Πίστις is derived from πείθω, which signifies to teach and to persuade. Acts 19:8. 2. From synonymy. Scripture itself defines faith by knowledge. Is. 53:11. John 17:3. Luke 1:77. Job 19:25. Heb. 11:3. 3. From conjugates. A faithful man or mind is called enlightened, understanding, wise, illuminated. Eph. 5: 8. Hos. 4: 10. Matt. 13: 23. Eph. 1:17, 18. Col. 1:9. 4. From opposites. Unbelief is called ignorance, Acts 17:23, 30; darkness, Is. 9:1, Matt. 4:15, Luke 1:79, John 1:5; blindness, Rom. 11:25, Eph. 4:18; insipience, foolishness, Rom. 10:19, Luke 24:25. Therefore, by the contrary sense, faith will be knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence.

5. From the nature and properties of faith. Faith is assent; therefore also knowledge, because we cannot assent to an unknown thing. Faith is trust; therefore also knowledge, because trust cannot be carried toward an unknown thing. Faith renders us certain, peaceful, and quiet in our heart; therefore, it certainly requires that it have the foundation upon which it rests perceived and known. 2 Tim. 1:12. By faith we recline upon the divine promises; it is required, therefore, that we thoroughly know their force and meaning.

Quamvis enim per passionem et mortem Christi revera praestitum fuerit, quicquid satisfactionis ab universis in mundo hominibus ad abolendum debitum per offensas illorum contractum, adeoque ad placandum Deum, eosque ipsi reconciliandos, exigi poterat; voluit tamen Deus, ut peccatores satisfactionem illam, pro se ipsi a Filio Dei praestitam, agnoscant et, fide apprehensam, suam faciant; et sic voluit, ut, quisquis mediatorem fide amplectitur, merito ejus fruatur Deumque aetu sibi reconciliatum et plane faventem ad salutem conferendam habeat; ex adverso autem, si quis mediatorem fide non apprehendat, satisfactione pariter ejus et gratia Dei, sua culpa, privetur maneatque in offensa Dei, juxta illud Joh. 3, 16. 18. 36. Conf. b. Mus. de Convers. Disp. III. cap. II. § 91. p. 144. Lutherus: ״Es ist nicht unsere Thuns und kann nicht durch unser Werk verdienet werden, es ist schon da, geschenkt und dargegeben; allein, dass du das Maul, oder vielmehr das Herz aufthust, und stille haltest, und lassest dich füllen. Idem: ״Non sub conditione nos rSdemti, reconciliati aut peccata nostra expiata sunt, sed simpliciter, perfectissime, plenissime, quantum ad meritum et acquisitionem; etsi quantum ad actualem fructum et applicationem fide opus sit, quae vero nihil aliud est, quam appropriatio illius expiationis et satisfactionis ac reconciliationis Christi. Hollazius: ,,Distingue a. inter satisfactionem, et ejus effectum; b. inter satisfactionem a Christo praestitam, et ab homine sibi applicatam. Nam operae, quae invito obtruditur, imputatio recte repellitur‘, ait Sam. Pufendorf. in L. de I. N. et G. p. 128.“ (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 8. q. 14. p. 917.)

Calovius: ,,Ut ergo plenius explicetur, quomodo cum Christo vivificati, cum Christo resuscitati, cum Christo in coelestibus constituti simus in Christo Jesu (Eph. 2, 5. 6.): dicendum, quod id factum sit tum ratione meriti, quod ipso, ceu mediatore et redemptore nostro, vivificato, resuscitato et in coelestibus collocato, nos vivificati cum ipso simus et resuscitati cum ipso et in coelestibus cum ipso collocati. ### On Faith in Christ: From reduction to…

6. From reduction to absurdity."

If faith is ignorance, what will be the use of the ministry? What is the fruit of preaching? What is the necessity of instruction? If faith is ignorance, why are we commanded to test the spirits, to beware of false prophets, to test all things and hold fast to what is good, to follow the voice of Christ alone, but to neglect the voice of a stranger? 1 John 4: 1. Matt. 7:16. 1 Thess. 5: 21. John 10:4, 6. But none of these things can be performed by one who does not have the truth known in the individual articles of faith.” (Loc. de justific. § 67.)

The same: “Bellarmine, l. 1. de justif. c. 7, attempts to prove that ‘justifying faith is not knowledge,’ and concludes: ‘We believe the mysteries of faith, which surpass reason, we do not understand them, and by this faith is distinguished from science.’ ... Resp.: Although faith is not knowledge deduced from the principles of human reason or built upon them (which the apostle calls ‘the wisdom of this world’ 1 Cor. 3:19, ‘human’ 1 Cor. 2:13, ‘carnal’ 1 Cor. 1:12); yet it does not follow from this that it is in no way knowledge, but ignorance; ... on the contrary, it is a certain knowledge kindled in the mind of man by the illumination of the Holy Spirit and the revelation of the Gospel. Furthermore, although faith is not intuitive knowledge, reaching all the causes and properties of an object by the light of reason, it is nevertheless spiritual knowledge, knowing as much about the object proposed to it as is required for salvation in the way of this life. Finally, although the knowledge of faith has its degrees, so that in some men it is more illustrious and clearer, while in others it is more obscure and thinner, yet ‘more and less’ do not change the species; therefore, even a weak and languid faith is not ignorance, but a certain knowledge.” (Loc. de justific. § 68.)

Or such that the thing to be believed, although it may not be evidently known or all the knowable things that are in it may not be reached by an act of cognition, is nevertheless known distinctly, or is known in such a way that it can be discerned from other objects. Opposed to this, however, is implicit knowledge, by which one is thought, for example, to believe that Christ is the mediator when he believes that the things which the church believes are true, even though he has no knowledge at all of what those things are which the church believes. Conf. b. Mus. de Convers. Disp. III. c. II. § 96. sq. p. 146. 147.

Kromayer: “A distinction must be made between distinct knowledge in respect of objects, and distinct knowledge in respect of cause or mode. We concede that the former is faith; concerning the latter it is said: Σαφής τής απιστίας έλεγχός εστι, το πώς περί θεον ζητεϊν, that is, it is a manifest argument of unbelief to inquire how a thing is concerning God. For which reason some distinguish between explicit and distinct knowledge; referring the former to the object or even the principle from which the knowledge is drawn, but the latter to the mode or cause.”

From these, a judgment can be formed concerning the implicit faith of the Papists. For implicit faith is spoken of either in a sound sense or in a heterodox sense.

In a sound sense, implicit faith is called that which occurs when spiritual things are known not distinctly, but by their common principle, which is Holy Scripture. For he who believes that Holy Scripture is true, he implicitly believes all things that are contained in it. Ps. 119:66: “All thy commandments are truth itself.”

And thus far implicit faith is spoken of either concerning things and questions not directly pertaining to salvation, in which way simpler people have implicit faith concerning certain historical circumstances, or even the minutiae of controversies, which they can be ignorant of without the loss of salvation, provided they do not deny them; or concerning fundamental doctrine, when not all articles of faith are immediately known explicitly, with the knowledge of their common principle, which is Scripture; and in this latter way is spoken of that implicit faith which is indeed good and necessary for the learner, but in such a way that it is later rendered distinct knowledge, which is necessary for apprehending the good, so that individual articles necessary for salvation are known explicitly, Heb. 6:1.

In a heterodox sense, however, implicit faith is spoken of: 1. by reason of a false common principle, which the Ponti- PART. III. CAP. III.

they make the tradition of the church the basis, and say that this or that must be believed because the church believes it. For Holy Scripture alone is the object of faith. Acts 24:14: "I worship the God of our fathers," says the apostle, "believing all things which are written in the Law and in the Prophets."

Furthermore, since implicit faith, by reason of the common true principle, that is, Scripture, is indeed "considered to be sufficient, even if those things which are believed in the common principle as articles necessary for salvation are ignored in particular; which again is the opinion of the Papists, and this is testified to by the common practice in the Papistic church, while they praise implicit faith in the laity, when they believe without explicit knowledge of the matter what the church and the prelates believe, such faith destroys religion itself, which cannot exist without knowledge." (Theol. posit. pol. I, 655 sq.)

Luther: "Thus the Papists also say now that they believe what the church believes; and as one says of the Poles, that they are supposed to say: I believe what my king believes. Why not? How could there be a better faith, which would have less trouble and care than this? Thus one says, as a doctor once asked a charcoal-burner in Prague on the bridge out of pity, as for a poor layman: Dear man, what do you believe? The charcoal-burner answers: That which the church believes. The Doctor: What then does the church believe? The charcoal-burner: That which I believe. Afterwards, when the doctor was about to die, he was so severely tempted in his faith by the devil that he could find no place to stay, nor have any rest, until he said: I believe what the charcoal-burner believes. As one also says of the great Thomas Aquinas, that at his end he could not stand before the devil until he said: 'I believe what is in this book,' and he had the Bible in his arms. But may God not grant us much of such faith. For where these have nothing else but have believed in this way, then both doctor and charcoal-burner have believed themselves into the abyss of hell. Into that also believe such spirits who say: Believe the body that Christ means; that is enough. Oh yes, it is finely and well believed; such faith does the devil no harm." (Warning to those at Frankfurt am Main, 1533. XVII, 2442 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: Of the Papists, who assert that faith is to be defined not so much by knowledge as by ignorance; thus Bellarmine on Justification, Book 1, Chapter 7, § 2, where he says: 'It is proved, therefore, that faith is not knowledge, but assent.' Toward the end of the chapter he writes: 'We believe the mysteries of faith, which surpass reason, we do not understand them, and by this faith is distinguished from science, and is better defined by ignorance than by knowledge.' ... They deny, however, that justifying faith is properly knowledge, so that a foundation may be laid for 'implicit' or 'charcoal-burner' faith, commended in the papacy, concerning which see Biel, 3 Sentences, dist. 25, q. un., and Bellarmine, l. c. Biel says: 'Implicit faith, by which a believer believes whatever the church believes, is most useful to the believer.'" (L. c. P. IV, 8, s. 2, q. 1, f. 1345.)

Concerning these, see Prolegomena, c. I, § 27 sqq. Vol. I, p. 45 sqq. See Prolegomena, § 31, 32. Vol. I, p. 52, 53.

Whence it is evident that, when faith in Christ is denominated from its object, the grace of God and the gratuitous divine promises concerning the remission of sins and salvation on account of Christ are not excluded, but included. Conf. blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 101, p. 148; § 142 sqq., p. 177 sqq.

It is proved that such knowledge is required for faith in Christ from John 6:69: "We have believed and have known that You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," and John 17:3: "This is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true [God]..."

true God and Jesus Christ, whom Thou hast sent. Thus also in Luke 1:77, saving faith is described through the knowledge of salvation, etc. And the opposite, unbelief, is called ignorance in Acts 17:23, 30; Ephesians 4:18. But the faithful themselves are γνόντες θεόν, Galatians 4:9. Cf. John 10:14. §

8. Next, assent, or the judgment of the intellect, pertains to faith in Christ, by which those things that are delivered in the Scriptures, especially concerning Christ the Mediator and the grace of God and salvation to be obtained through Him, are judged to be truly enunciated, and that on account of the divine revelation or the veracity of the God who reveals, and the grace inwardly and supernaturally exerting itself in the heart, or concurring with the word of Scripture. It is otherwise called the second degree or the other part of faith.

And it is certain that faith, in its formal concept, imports assent, leaning upon the authority of the one speaking or testifying.

Thus Paul says that the things which are of the Spirit of God are spiritually judged, άνακρινόμενα, 1 Corinthians 2:14f, 15.

Selneccerus: "He who does not believe Christ, much less believes in Christ."

Quenstedtius: "This assent ought not to be perfunctory, not doubtful, not wavering, but certain and firm; whence it is called έλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων, a certain persuasion concerning things even not appearing, Hebrews 11:1. This act of faith rests not on the evidence of things or the knowledge of causes and properties, but on the infallible authority of God speaking. Hence Damascenus (De Fide Orthodoxa, bk. 4, ch. 12) says that faith is ἀπολυπραγμόνητον συγκατάθεσιν, an inscrutable assent. By ἀπολυπραγμόνητον he removes sense and reason from faith; by συγκατάθεσιν he expresses the approval and assent itself. The object of faith is truth, but this, when known, elicits assent." (L. c. s. 1. th. 7. f. 1337.)

Hoepfnerus: "We do not mean this as if human faith is never tempted by certain temptations, since experience resists it. Wherefore we distinguish here between doubt, which overcomes faith, and that which at least attacks faith. The former is nothing other than the foolish disputation of reason, which expels all assent, let alone admits trust; and such doubt has no place in faith, since it is rather opposed to faith. For 'what is more against faith than to be unwilling to believe whatever one cannot grasp by reason?' as Bernard says (Epistle 190). Then there is the doubt of infirmity, which does not cast away all assent and trust entirely, but at least struggles in temptations and makes trust languid. And this infirmity is either in knowledge, just as the apostles did not rightly understand many articles at the beginning, or in trust, Matthew 6:30; 13:31, 32. The struggle, whether in assent or in trust, is not a sign of unbelief, but a true mark of a living and efficacious faith, which takes captive the intellect and the will into the obedience of God." (Loc. th. loc. 33. p. 449, 450.)

Ex his judicium ferri potest de fide im· plicita pontificiorum. Dicitur enim fides implicita vel in sensu sano, vel in sensu cacodoxo.

Et hactenus fides implicita dicitur vel de rebus et quaestionibus ad salutem non directe pertinentibus, qualiter fidem implicitam habent simpliciores de circumstantiis quibusdam historicis, aut etiam apicibus controversiarum, quas citra jacturam salutis ignorare possunt, modo eas non negent; vel de fundamentali doctrina, cum non statim omnes articuli fidei explicite cogniti habentur cognito eorum principio communi, quod est Scriptura; et hoc posteriori modo dicitur fldes implicita, quae bona quidem est et necessaria discenti, sed ita, ut reddatur postea distincta notitia, quae necessaria est ad apprehendendum bonum, ita, ut singuli articuli ad salutem necessarii explicite cognoscantur, Hebr. 6, 1.

I, 655. sq.)

Lutherus: ״Also sagen auch jetzt die Papisten, sie gläuben, was die Kirche gläubt; und wie man von den Polen sagt, dass sie sagen sollen: Ich gläube, was mein König gläubt. Warum nicht? ### On Faith in Christ: For although it is necessary for a man to be saved to believe that all things…

For although it is necessary for a man to be saved to believe that all things which are contained in the Holy Scriptures are true; yet in this place, when we are dealing with faith as a cause of salvation, it must be considered in order 140 PART III. CHAP. III. to the special or peculiar object, which has the power of recovering salvation lost through sin, and by whose intuition faith itself can be reckoned among the causes of salvation.

d) Just as the eunuch in Acts 8:37, after the sermon in which Philip had preached Jesus to him, answered the one asking whether he believed with his whole heart: I believe that Jesus Christ is that Son of God.

Namely, so that the doctrine of Scripture itself may be ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως, in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, according to 1 Corinthians 2:4, 13. Cf. Proleg. ch. II. § 32, 34. Vol. I. p. 53, 64. §

4. However, it is also required for faith in Christ, viewed on the side of assent, that a man descend from universal propositions concerning Christ the Mediator and the grace to be obtained through Him to himself in the individual, and believe that Christ suffered and died for him.

Whence it is also accustomed to be called special faith.

E.g., Christ gave Himself ἀντίλυτρον for all, 1 Timothy 2:6; He died for all, 2 Corinthians 5:15; He is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world, 1 John 2:2.

Gerhard: "But they say: 'If Christ truly died for all, it follows that the effect and fruit of His death must pertain to all.' Resp.: 1. Just as for an alms to be received, not only is an offering hand required, but also a receiving one; so too, 'each person possesses only as much of these goods as he gathers with the vessel of faith,' as Bernard beautifully speaks in Sermon 32 on the Song of Songs, col. 597, and Sermon 3 on the Annunciation, col. 113. It is not enough that the benefits obtained by the death of Christ be offered; they must also be received by faith. ... 5. How the universality of Christ’s merit nonetheless stands, even though some are not made partakers of its fruit, can be declared by a simile. Let, for example, one hundred Christians be held captive by the Turkish Emperor; let some Christian prince pay a certain sum of money for the redemption of them all; if any afterwards prefer to remain longer in that captivity than to enjoy the liberty offered and obtained by the price, they must blame themselves for it, nor does this in any way derogate from the universality of the λύτρον paid for all the captives. The matter stands similarly with men who were held captive in the kingdom of Satan and sin, for all of whom Christ gave His precious blood as an ἀντίλυτρον; that not all are actually liberated from that spiritual captivity does not derogate from the universality of the λύτρον." (L. th. de electione § 119.)

For this is the force of universal signs, that when added to some common term (e.g., man), they signify that what is said of the common term applies to all individuals contained under it; which, in the present matter, are read as being so often added and inculcated in the Scriptures to this end, that sinners, anxious and troubled about their sins, may raise themselves up by the universality of the satisfaction rendered by Christ for the sins of all, and hence of the grace and remission of sins restored, and may safely and firmly believe that these things pertain even to them individually. If this universality were absent, the sinner would have nothing from which, in the terrors of conscience and the sense of divine wrath on account of sins,

might raise itself up. For it is not possible for a sinner to argue from a particular, or from the fact that Christ died for some and merited the grace of God and the remission of sins for some, to subsume determinately and individually concerning himself, and to conclude that Christ also made satisfaction for him, etc. These are the words of the blessed Musaeus, *Tract. de Convers.*, Disp. III, cap. II, § 107, 108, p. 153, 154. Cf. what we have said in *Proleg.*, cap. I, § 32, Vol. I, p. 53. Thus Job, issuing a profession of his faith, said: "I know that my Redeemer liveth," ch. 19:25 [26], and Paul, Gal. 2:20: "The life," he says, "which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me."

And thus it is established that faith is not called "special" because of promises or revelations that have been made to each believer specifically and in particular, but rather from the special object upon which it is borne, namely, Christ the Mediator, and the promises concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins and salvation on account of Christ, as well as from its special application to the believer. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *l. c.*, *de Convers.*, § 110 sqq., p. 155 sqq., and *Tract. de Eccl.*, Part I, Disp. I, § 61, p. 38, 39.

Hollazius: "General faith is that by which a person to be saved believes that all things are true which have been revealed by the divine Word... special faith is that by which a converted and regenerate sinner applies to himself individually the universal promises concerning Christ the Mediator and the grace of God to be obtained through Him." (*Exam. th.*, P. III, s. 2, c. 7, q. 2, p. 1164.)

Luther: "Although these words, to which faith must hold: 'Born for us, suffered, etc.,' do not stand there explicitly, one must nevertheless take them from others afterward and draw them through all these articles; for in the third article, where we say: 'I believe the forgiveness of sins,' he glosses himself, where he sets forth the cause and benefit of this article, why he was born, suffered, and did everything. And it is indeed touched upon here in the text, where we say: 'Our Lord'; by which we confess that everything that the man is and does has happened for us, as he who was therefore born, suffered, and rose again, for the comfort that he is our Lord... Therefore, accustom yourself to look at the words in such a way that you always draw the word 'our' through all the articles of faith, so that everything applies to me (who believe in him) and becomes mine against my sin and evil conscience." (*Ausleg. des andern Artikels*, 1533, X, 1153, 1338.)

Dannhauerus: "'It is fitting,' says Chrysostom in his epistle to the Galatians, 'that each of us should give thanks to Christ no less than if He had come for him alone. For He would not have refused to undergo such a dispensation even for one; therefore He loves each individual man with the same movement of love with which He loves the whole world.'" (*Hodosoph. Phaen.*, X, p. 670 sq.)

Chemnitius: "There is a certain general faith which embraces in a general way the historical knowledge of those things which have been proposed by God in Scripture, and a general assent by which we determine that those things which have been revealed to us in the Word of God are true, not because of arguments of reason, but because we are certain that they have been handed down and proposed by God, who is truthful and omnipotent. And this general faith, indeed, because it can exist even in the ungodly, does not justify by itself; yet justifying faith presupposes and includes that general faith. For when that general foundation, which establishes that whatever has been divinely revealed in the Word of God is true and certain, is not present or wavers, then the confidence of the divine promise of mercy remitting sins on account of Christ can neither be conceived nor retained in the struggle. The article of redemption, justification, or reconciliation also cannot be rightly understood unless there is a preceding knowledge..." of the remaining parts of the Word of God. When, therefore, we say that the proper and principal object of justifying faith is the promise of the gratuitous mercy of God for the sake of Christ the Mediator, we do not subtract faith from the remaining articles or parts of the Word of God; but just as the sum, end, and scope of the whole Scripture is Christ the Mediator, Luke 24, John 5, Rom. 10, Heb. 10: so faith, when it assents to the universal Word of God, looks to the scope and end of Scripture, namely, Christ in the office of Mediator.” (Exam. Concil. Trid. Geneva 1641, p. 159.) §

5. Besides knowledge and assent on the part of the intellect, faith in Christ also includes, on the part of the will, trust, or an act of such a kind by which the will acquiesces in Christ the Mediator, as a present good and as our own, and as the cause of another good, namely, the obtaining of the remission of sins and eternal life. For just as Christ the Mediator is proposed in the Scriptures not for the sake of bare or speculative knowledge, so that He might be understood as truly existing as He is, but rather that He might have the character of our good and be presented to us in such a way, or as the cause of obtaining salvation; so it must be confessed that the will of men can and ought to be affected or moved by Him toward the pursuit of Him, or that it may rest in Him by an act of trust and raise itself up and find comfort against the wrath of God and the stings and terrors of conscience.

S. Schmidtius: “Trust or fiducial apprehension is proper to justifying faith in this business of justification, and ultimately, if I may so speak, constitutes it; whence also D. Hoepfnerus, in his disputation on justification, disp. 12, th. 32, p. 1121, did not hesitate to call it the form of saving faith, and indeed its intrinsic and essential form. For certainly, without it, knowledge and assent cannot yet justify; but if it is added to them, justification is perfected.” (Art. E. C. Repetit, p. 229.)

For thus trust, speaking generally, is defined and distinguished from hope, in that the former has as its object a present good, upon which the will relies as the cause of another good, whereas the latter has as its object an absent good, which the will desires and expects as something possible to be obtained and to be acquired. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Tract. de Convers. Disp. III, cap. III, § 121 sqq., p. 164 sqq.

However, goods are called present with respect to trust not only those which are present really and physically, but also those which are present morally, by reason of some merit and value, or are apprehended as present. And so the pious in the Old Testament could rightly place their trust in the coming Messiah and in the satisfaction for sins to be performed by Him at some time, and we (living in the New Testament, so many centuries after Christ suffered) trust in the same satisfaction, performed long ago through His passion and death. For Christ and His passion and death extend themselves morally and by reason of their merit to all past ages, as well as present and future, and were at all times the cause of the remission of sins and of obtaining salvation for believers, so that with this view also we may say with the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever, ch. 13, 8: these are the words of the blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 127, p. 166.

Gerhardus: ״At inquiunt: ,Si Christus vere pro omnibus mortuus, sequetur ipsum effectum et fructum mortis ad omnes pertinere.‘ Resp.: 1. Haec enim signorum universalium vis est, ut termino alicui communi (v. g. homo) addita, quae de termino communi dicuntur, omnibus sub eo contentis singularibus convenire significent; quae etiam in praesenti matena eo fine in scripturis toties adjecta et inculcata leguntur, ut peccatores, de peccatis suis anxii et solidti, universalitate satisfactionis pro omnium peccatis a Christo praestitae et hinc reparatae gratiae ac remissionis peccatorum sese erigere eaque ad se etiam in individuo pertinere tuto ac firmiter credere possint et credant. Absque hac universalitate si esset, peccator haud esset habiturus, unde in conscientiae terroribus et sensu irae divinae ob peccata

sese erigeret. Neque enim a particulari argumentari, aut ex eo, quod pro quibusaam Christus mortuus sit et gratiam Dei ac remissionem peccatorum aliquibus promeruerit, de se determinate et in individuo subsumere peccator quispiam, et quod pro se etiam Christus satisfecerit etc., concludere potest. Verba sunt b. Musaei Tract. de Convers. Disp. III. cap. II. § 107.108. p. 153. 154. Conf., quae diximus in Proleg. cap. I. § 32. Vol. I. p. 53. Atque ita constat, non dici fidem specialem a promissionibus aut revelationibus, quae cuique credenti specialiter et in particulari factae sint, sed cum ab objecto speciali, in quod fertur, scilicet Christo mediatore, et promissionibus de gratia Dei et remissione peccatorum ac salute propter Christum, tum ab ejus speciali applicatione ad credentem. Conf. b. Musaei 1. c. de Convers. § 110. sqq. p. 155. sqq. et Tract. de Eccl. Part. I. Disp. I. § 61. p. 38. 39.

P. III. s. 2. c. 7. q. 2. p. 1164.)

Neque enim recusaturus erat, vel ob unum tantam adhibere dispensationem; ideo singulum quemque hominem pari caritatis motu diligit, quo diligit orbem universum.“‘ (Hodosoph. Phaen. X. p. 670. sq.)

Chemnitius: ״Est fides quaedam generalis, quae complectitur in genere historicam notitiam eorum, quae in Scriptura a Deo proposita sunt, et generalem assensionem, qua statuimus, ea, quae in verbo Dei nobis revelata sunt, vera esse, non propter argumenta rationis, sed quia certi sumus, a Deo, qui verax et omnipotens est, illa tradita et proposita esse. Et haec quidem generalis fides, quia etiam in impiis esse potest, per se non justificat; fides tamen justificans generalem illam fidem praeßupponit et includit. Quando enim generale illud fundamentum, statuens, vera et certa esse, quaecunque divinitus in verbo Dei patefacta sunt, non adfuerit vel vacillaverit: nec concipi potest, nec in lucta retineri fiducia promissionis divinae misericordiae remittentis peccata propter Christum. Joh. 5. Rom. 10. Ebr. 10.: ita fldes, quando universo verbo Dei assentitur, respicit ad scopum et finem Scripturae, Christum sci. in officio mediatoris.“ (Exam. Concil. Trid. Genevae 1641. f. 159.) §

Praeter notitiam et assensum ex parte intellectus includit etiam fides in Christum ex parte voluntatis a fidiiciam, seu actum ejusmodi, quo voluntas acquiescit b in Christo ·mediatore, tanquam bono praesente c atque nostro d et causa e alterius boni, nempe remissionis peccatorum et vitae aeternae f consequendae. g Quemadmodum enim Christus mediator in Scripturis proponitur non nudae aut speculativae cognitionis causa, ut tanquam vere ita se habens intelligatur, verum, ut rationem boni nostri habeat ac taliter, sive ut causa impetrandae salutis, nobis exhibeatur; ita fatendum est, affici ea aut moveri posse ac debere voluntatem hominum ad prosecutionem ejus, seu, ut actu fiduciae in eo recumbat atque adversus iram Dei et conscientiae morsus ac pavores sese erigat ac soletur.

S. Schmidtius: ״Fiducia vel fiducialis apprehensio est fidei justiflcantis in hoc justificationis negotio propria, et ultimate, ut sic loquar, eam constituit; unde etiam D. Hoepfnerus de justif. disp. 12. th. 32. p. 1121. eam fidei salvificae formam, et quidem intrinsecam atque essentialem, dicere non dubitavit. Certe namque sine ea notitia et assensus nondum justificare possunt; quibus vero si accesserit, justificatio perflcitur.“ (Art. E. C. Repetit, p. 229.)

Sic enim fiducia generaliter loquendo definitur et a spe distinguitur, quod iUa pro objecto habeat bonum praesens, quo, tanquam causa alterius boni, voluntas nitatur, haec vero pro objecto habeat bonum absens, quod expetat voluntas et. tanquam obtentu possibile atque obtinendum expectet. Conf. b. Mus, Tract. de Convers. Disp. ΠΙ. cap. III. § 121. sqq. p. 164. sqq.

Dicuntur autem bona praesentia respectu fiduciae non tantum, quae realiter et physice, sed etiam quae moraliter, ratione alicujus meriti et valoris praesentia sunt aut tanquam praesentia apprehenduntur. Itaque pii in Vet. Test. recte potuerunt fiduciam collocare in venturo Messia et in satisfactione pro peccatis ab ipso aliquando praestanda, et nos (in Nov. Test, post tot saecula a Christo passo viventes) confidimus in eadem satisfactione, olim per ejus passionem et mortem praestita. Christus enim ejusque passio et mors extendit se moraliter et ratione sui meriti ad omnia retro saecula, praesentia item et futura, fuitque omni tempore credentibus remissionis peccatorum et salutis obtinendae causa, ut hoc etiam intuitu cum auctare epistolae ad Ebraeos dicere possimus, Jesus Christus heri et hodie idem et in saecula, cap. 18, 8.: verlia sunt b. Mus. 1. c. § 127. p. 166.


### On Faith in Christ: For goods, however excellent, are not going to be of help to us, so that we…

For goods, however excellent, are not going to be of help to us, so that we might be able to trust in them, unless they are ours, or at least, by reason of friendship and a covenant which intervenes between us and Him whose they are, they pertain to us in some way and in this regard are valued as our own. And thus, although Christ’s merit and satisfaction were not performed by us, but by Christ; yet because they were performed from the bottom for us and for our good, and God holds them in the same place as if they had been performed by us ourselves, we rightly reckon them among our own or as pertaining to us. B. Mus. de Convers. Disp. III. cap. III. § 128. p. 167.

Indeed, trust in Christ differs from the love of Christ in this: that the latter has Christ as its object absolutely, while the former has the same Christ as its object, known with a relation to obtaining another good, as the cause thereof. B. Mus. l. c. § 129. p. 167. § 139. and 140. p. 174. 175.

Indeed, just as the goods procured through Christ are many and various, according to Eph. 1:3, 2 Cor. 1:20, John 16:23, so, speaking generally, trust in Christ has as its object Christ related as a cause for obtaining various goods, both bodily and spiritual: yet here we are not dealing with just any trust, but with the trust by which a sinful man tends toward obtaining the grace of God and eternal salvation; just as it must be confessed that all trust which is in Christ, as the cause of obtaining other goods, is resolved at last into Him as the cause of reconciliation with God and the remission of sins. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 141. p. 175. 176.

Now it is proved that faith in Christ includes, besides the act of believing in the intellect, also trust in Christ on the part of the will, from Rom. 3:24 sqq., where the object of faith is established as Christ, as ίλαστήριον, or the propitiation of divine wrath, set forth in His blood, or insofar as He is the meritorious cause of appeasing divine wrath and obtaining the remission of sins before God through His shed blood, or through His passion and death.

Whence it is immediately evident that that faith is not a bare assent without any act of the will concerning Christ (for thus it would be a dead faith), and because it has joined to it some act of the will concerning Christ, this very act is the act of trust, being occupied with Christ as the cause of obtaining some good, namely, the grace of God. Conf. Mus. l. c. § 161. sqq. p. 194., where he also shows the same at length by the example of Abraham, believing in Him who justifies the ungodly, or believing in God who, although just and an avenger, yet for the sake of the Messiah the mediator grants grace to sinners, etc.

But it is also evident otherwise that τό πιστεύειν είς τόν υίόν, which is said in opposition to τό άπειθεῖν τῷ υἱῷ, John 3:36, is the same as to trust in the Son, or to place trust in Him. Add Mus. l. c. § 171. 172. p. 214. et seqq.

Hollazius: "It is proved that faith in Christ formally and intrinsically includes trust leaning upon the merit of Christ: 1) Because faith in Christ is not only an act of the intellect or knowledge and assent, but also an act of the will. This is confirmed: a) From the phrase itself: To believe in Christ, which by the force of the preposition 'in', constructed with the accusative case, insinuates a certain act of the believer tending toward Christ, by which the believing man is carried, as it were, outside of himself into Christ or adheres to Him. b) From the custom of speaking, which Augustine rightly urges in Tract. 29 on John. For demons are said to believe Christ, and also to believe Christ [as a person]; yet they are not said to believe *in* Christ. And we are said to believe Paul, to believe... PART III. CAP. III. to Peter; we also believe that Paul and Peter exist; yet we are not said to believe *in* Paul and Peter. Therefore, to believe *in* someone, beyond the act of believing or assenting, implies some act regarding the object believed, which neither falls upon demons, nor has Peter, Paul, or any creature as its object; namely, an act by which the believer tends toward the object known and believed under a certain and peculiar aspect, which does not fall upon any creature. Which certainly must be an act of the will. For it is the nature of the will to be carried out of itself toward an object; just as, conversely, it is the nature of the intellect to know an object within itself through species impressed upon it. c) The condition of the object proves the same. For Christ is not proposed in the Scriptures to the human race, having fallen into sins, to be known for the sake of speculation, but as mediator and the cause of the remission of sins and of eternal life. See 1 Tim. 2:5; John 1:29; 3:16. These goods of ours, redundant from Christ into us, are proposed in the Scriptures to be known and believed, not so that the intellect may stop at the knowledge and assent of them, but so that, being known and believed, they may be represented and exhibited to the will, so that the will may be carried toward them, rest in them, and by trust in them, the sinner may raise and console himself against the wrath of God and the terrors of conscience. We conclude: Every act of the will regarding a present good, related as a cause for obtaining another arduous and difficult good, is formally trust; but that act, which faith in Christ includes on the part of the will, is an act of the will regarding a present good for the sake of obtaining other arduous and difficult goods, related as a cause. Therefore.” (Exam. P. III. § 2. c. 7. q. 16. p. 1180. sq.)

S. Schmidtius: “That this trust is found in justifying faith, given the nature of the business of justification, is the less surprising, because in any faith whatsoever, whatever it may be, especially divine faith, some trust is found. This is taught even by the Hebrew origin. For the Hebrew word אמונה, to which the noun πίστις corresponds in the Greek New Testament text, as is manifest from the comparison of Gen. 15:6 and Rom. 4:3, is derived from firmness, strength, approval, and firm acceptance... The object of faith is always a thing not clear, or obscure. This is so true that it is found to be most true even in human faith; for if a thing is clear and evident, it is known, not believed. But if something is known to be possible, yet is at least obscure as to whether it actually exists, so that it relies solely on the authority of the speaker, then indeed it is believed. But if anyone believes something relying on the words of the speaker or revealer, does he not place all the trust of his certainty in his authority as firm and not fallacious? For he is a fool who believes a liar and a deceiver, in whose words there is no firmness. So it remains true that every true faith includes trust.” (L. c. p. 229. sq.)

Gerhard: (Bellarmino objects:) "The act of faith is to believe, not to trust." Resp.: With respect to knowledge, the act of faith is to believe, and its object is the entire Word of God revealed to us. With respect to trust, the act of faith is to trust or to apprehend trustingly, and its object is the evangelical promise concerning Christ the Mediator, or, which is the same thing, the obedience and satisfaction of Christ offered to us in the Word of the Gospel. Therefore, there is no reason for Bellarmino to say that if "to believe" is used in the Scriptures for "to trust," we are forced to explain very many passages most absurdly and ineptly; for example, John 14:10: "Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me?" Acts 8: "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God." Rom. 10: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness." And later: "If you believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved." These and similar passages (says Bellarmino) cannot be taken for trust except most ineptly. Resp.: On the contrary, Bellarmino’s argument, drawn from a particular instance, is most inept. For it does not follow: In certain sayings of Scripture, "to believe" cannot be explained as "to trust"; therefore, this explanation has no place in any [passage]; and consequently, faith is not trust. But we have shown above that Scripture itself interprets "to believe" as "to trust" in many places; nor can Bellarmino deny this, who in *De Justificatione*, Book 1, Chapter 11, concedes that "distrust" in Rom. 4 is used for "unbelief"; by the force of

Therefore, in the opposition, confidence is posited for faith. Nor will it be absurd if someone says that in the cited passages confidence is also connoted. Christ does not only want it to be believed by simple assent that the Father is in Him and He in the Father, but He also commands us to approach the Father through Him as Mediator with the confidence of the heart; whence at the beginning of the chapter He says: "You believe in God, believe also in me," which Stapleton paraphrases thus: "Have confidence in God and in me." The eunuch not only believes that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, but he also placed all the confidence of his heart in Him as the promised and exhibited Mediator.

Nor is that historical faith, by which we believe that Christ was raised from the dead, efficacious for righteousness and salvation, since even the demons believe this; but it is required that we believe that Christ "was delivered for our offenses, and was raised again for our justification," Rom. 4:25. (Loc. de justif. § 80.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, especially Bellarmine, who in his work *de justif.*, ch. 5 ff., attempts to prove with many arguments that justifying faith is not confidence. The same author notes from Thomas in ch. 4 that confidence is nothing other than strengthened hope, and therefore that faith is confused with hope if it is defined by confidence. The Council of Trent, Sess. 6, Can. 12, states: 'If anyone shall say that justifying faith is nothing other than confidence in the divine mercy, which remits sins for Christ's sake, or that it is by this confidence alone that we are justified, let him be anathema.' ... 2. Of the Socinians, who deny that the form of justifying faith is the fiducial apprehension of Christ and His satisfaction. ... They concede that faith is confidence in the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ, (but) not that Christ by His death and resurrection expiated sins and obtained the remission of them for us; rather, they say that He merely confirmed for us the certainty of the divine promises by His death and resurrection and excites us by His example to render obedience to God. ... 3. Of the Arminians, who deny that justifying faith is a certain confidence of sin remitted for Christ's sake. ... 4. Of the Schwenkfeldians and Weigelians, who posit that faith is not a created motion or confidence, but Christ Himself, indeed the very essence of God; and they define justifying faith through the life, obedience, and imitation of Christ." (L. c. P. IV. c. 8. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1348 ff.) §

Bona enim, utut pramentia, adjumento nobis futura haud sunt, ut confidere in illis queamus, nisi nostra sint, vel saltem ob amicitiam et pactum, quod cum eo, cujus sunt, nobis intercedit, ad nos quodammodo pertineant d hoc intuitu tanquam nostra aestimentur. Et sic, licet Christi meritum d satisfactio a noms non sint praestita, sed a Christo; quia tamen ah imo pro nobis et nostri beo praestita sunt, et Deus illa eodem, ac si a nobis ipsis praestita essent, loco hahd, rede ea in nostris aut ad nos pertinentibus repur tamus.
