Nimirum in hoc differt fiducia in Christum a dilectime Christi, quod haec Christum absolute, illa eundem cum relatione ad aliud bonum obtinendum, tanquam ejus causam, cognitum pro objedo habet. B. Mus. 1. c. § 129. p. 167. § 139. et 140. p. 174. 175.

Equidem prout bona per Christum parta multa ac varia sunt, juxta Ephes. 1, 3. 2 Cor. 1, 20. Joh. 16, 23., ita generaliter bquendo fiducia in Christum pro objecto habet Christum ad varia bona, cum corporalia, tum spiritualia, obtinenda per modum causae relatum: hic tamen agimus non de quavis fiducia, sed de fiducia, qua homo peccator tendit ad gratiam Dei et salutem aeternam consequendam; quemadmodum et fatendum est, fidudam omnem, quae est in Christum, ut aliorum bonorum impetrandorum causam, resolvi tandem in ipsum, ut causam reconciliationis cum Deo et remissionis peccatorum. Conf. Mus. 1. c. § 141. p. 175. 176.

Probatur autem, fidem in Christum includere praeter actum credendi in intellectu etiam ex parte voluntatis fiduciam in Christum, ex Rom. 8, 24. sqq., ubi objectum fidei constituitur Christus, ut ίλαστήptov, seu placamentum irae divinae, propositum in sanguine suo, seu quatenus per effusum sanguinem suum, sive per passionem et mortem suam, placandae irae divinae et impetrandae remissionis peccatorum apud Deum causa meritoria est.

Unde statim constat, fidem illam non esse nudum assensum, sine ullo voluntatis actu circa Christum (sic enim esset fides mortua), et quia conjunctum habet aliquem voluntatis actum circa Christum, hunc ipsum esse actum fiduciae, quippe occupatum circa Christum, ut causam impetrandi alicujus boni, nempe gratiae Dei. Conf. Mus. 1. c. § 161. sqq. p. 194., ubi etiam exemplo Abrahami, credentis in eum, qui justificat impium, seu credentis in Deum, qui, licet justus ac vindex, tamen propter Messiam mediatorem peccatoribus gratiam concedat etc., idem prolixe ostendit.

Sed et alias constat, τό πιστευειν είς τόν υίον, quod dicitur in oppositione ad τό άπει#efv τω υίψ, Joh. 8, 86., idem esse atque confidere Filb, seu fiduciam in illo collocare. Adde Mus. 1. c. § 171. 172. p. 214. et seqq.

Hollazius: ״Probatur, fidem in Christum formaliter et intrinsece includere fiduciam merito Christi innixam: 1) Quia fides in Christum non est tantum actus intellectus sive notitia et assensus, sed etiam actus voluntatis. Id quod confirmatur: a) Ex ipsa phrasi: Credere in Christum, quae vi praepositionis,in‘, cum casu quarto constructae, in« sinuat actum quendam credentis in Christum tendentem, quo homo credens quasi extra se in Christum feratur aut ipsi adhaereat, b) Ex consuetudine loquendi, quam recte urget Augustinus tract. 29. in Joannem. Nam daemones dicuntur credere Christo, ut et Christum; nec tamen credere dicuntur in Christum. Et nos credere dicimur Paulo, credere PART. III. CAP. III. Petro; credimus etiam, Paulum et Petrum esse; nec tarnen in Paulum et Petrum credere dicimur. Ergo credere in aliquem praeter actum credendi sive assentiendi importat actum aliquem circa objectum creditum, qui nec in daemones cadit, nec Petrum, Paulum aut ullam creaturam habeat pro objecto; nempe actum, quo credens in objectum sub certa quadam et peculiari ratione, quae in nullam cadat creaturam, cognitum et creditum tendit. Quem certe voluntatis actum esse oportet. Voluntatis enim est, extra se ferri in objectum; sicut contra intellectus est, objectum per species sibi impressas in se cognoscere, c) Idem evincit objecti conditio. Christus enim non proponitur in Scripturis prblapso in peccata mortalium generi cognoscendus speculationis causa, sed tanquam mediator et causa remissionis peccatorum et vitae aeternae. Vid. 1 Tim. 2, 5. Joh. 1, 29. 3, 16. Quae bona nostra, ex Christo in nos redundantia, proponuntur in Scripturis cognoscenda et credenda, non ut in illorum cognitione et assensu intellectus sistat, sed ut cognita et credita voluntati repraesententur et exhibeantur, ut voluntas in illa feratur, in iis recumbat et illorum fiducia peccator adversus iram Dei et conscientiae pavores sese erigat ac consoletur. Colligimus: Omnis actus voluntatis, circa bonum praesens ad obtinendum aliud bonum arduum e.t difficile per modum causae relatum, est formaliter fiducia; atqui actus ille, quem ex parte voluntatis fides in Christum ineludit, est actus voluntatis circa bonum praesens ad obtinenda alia bona ardua et difficilia, per modum causae relatum. Ergo.“ (Exam. P. III. § 2. c. 7. q. 16. p. 1180. sq.)

S. Schmidtius: ״Fiduciam istam in fide justiflcante deprehendi, pro natura negotii justificationis hoc minus mirum est, quod in quavis fide, quaecunque illa sit, inprimis fide divina, aliqua fiducia inveniatur. Id quod vel origo hebraea docet. Vox namque hebraea אמונה, cui in graeco N. T. textu nomen πίστις respondet, sicut ex collatipne Gen. 15, 6. et Rom. 4, 3. manifestum est, a firmitate, robore, approbatione et acceptatione firma dicta est. . . Fidei objectum semper est res non clara seu obscura. Adeo hoc verum est, ut etiam in fide humana verissimum deprehendatur; si namque res clara est et evidens, scitur, non creditur. Quod si quid possibile etiam cognoscitur, obscurum autem saltem est, num actu sit, ut sola dicentis auctoritate nitatur, tum vero creditur. Atqui si quis quid credit nixus dicentis seu revelantis verbis, nonne fiduciam omnem suae certitudinis in auctoritate ejus tanquam firma et non fallaci ponit? Stultus namque est, qui mendaci et fallaci, cujus in verbis nihil firmitatis est, credit. Ut maneat verum, quod omnis vera fides fiduciam includat.“ (L. c. p. 229. sq.)

Gerhardus: (Excipit Bellarminus:) ״,Actus fidei est credere, non confidere. Resp.: Fidei respectu notitiae actus est credere, 06jectum est omne Dei verbum nobis revelatum. Fidei respectu fiduciae actus est confidere sive fiducialiter apprehendere, objectum est promissio evangelica de Christo mediatore, sive, quod idem est, Christi obedientia et satisfactio in verbo evangelii nobis oblata. Ergo non est, quod Bellarminus dicat, si credere usurpatur in Scripturis pro confidere, nos cogi, ut absurdissime atque ineptissime loca plurima explicemus; exempli gratia Joh. 14,10.: ,Non creditis, quia ego in Patre, et Pater in me est? ‘ Act. 8.: ,Credo, Filium Dei esse Jesum Christum/ Rom. 10.: ,Corde creditur ad justitiam/ Et postea: ,Si in corde tuo credideris, quia Deus eum suscitavit a mortuis, salvus eris/ Haec et similia (ait Bellarminus) non possunt nisi ineptissime accipi pro fiducia. Resp.: Imo vero ineptissimum est Bellarmini argumentum ex particulari ductum. Non enim sequitur: In quibusdam Scripturae dictis non potest, credere per confidere explicari; ergo in nullis locum habet ista explicatio; et per consequens fides non est fiducia. Atqui ostendimus superius, Scripturam ipsam pluribus in locis credere pro confidere interpretari; neque hoc negare potest Bellarminus, qui lib. 1. de justif. cap. 11. concedit, diffidentiam Rom. 4. positam pro incredulitate; ex vi

igitur oppositionis fiducia ponitur pro fide. Neque vero absurdum erit, si quis in allegatis locis fiduciam quoque connotari dixerit. Christus non solum simplici assensu vult hoc credi, quod Pater sit in ipso et ipse in Patre, sed et fiducia cordis per ipsum tanquam mediatorem ad Patrem accedere nos jubet; unde initio capitis dicit: ,Creditis in Deum, etiam in me creditis‘, quod Stapletonus sic παραφράζει: ,In Deum fiduciam habete et in me.‘ Eunuchus non solum credit, Jesum Christum esse Dei Filium, sed et in ipsum tanquam mediatorem promissum et exhibitum omnem cordis fiduciam collocavit.

Nec historica illa fldes, qua credimus, Christum esse a mortuis suscitatum, ad justitiam et salutem efficax est, cum et daemones hoc credant; sed requiritur, ut credamus, Christum,propter peccata nostra mortuum et propter justificationem nostram resurrexisse‘, Rom. 4, 25.“ (Loc. de justif. § 80.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, inprimis Bellarmini, qui 1.1. de justif. c. 5. sq. multis argumentis probare conatur, fidem justificantem non esse fiduciam. Idem ex Thoma monet c. 4., fiduciam nihil aliud esse, quam spem roboratam, ideo fidem cum spe confundi, si per fiduciam definiatur. Concilium Trident. Sess. 6. Can. 12. sic habet: ,Si quis dixerit, fidem justificantem nihil aliud esse, quam flduciam divinae misericordiae, peccata remittentis propter Christum, vel eam fiduciam solam esse, qua justificamur, anathema sit.‘ . . 2. Socinianorum, negantium, fidei justificantis formam esse fiducialem Christi satisfactionisque ejus apprehensionem. . . Concedunt, quod fides sit fiducia in passionem, mortem et resurrectionem Christi, (at) non quod Christus morte et resurrectione sua expiarit peccata et eorum remissionem nobis impetraverit, sed ajunt, confirmasse saltem nobis morte et resurrectione sua promissionum divinarum certitudinem et exemplo suo ad obedientiam Deo praestandam excitare. . . 3. Arminianorum, negantium, fidem justificantem esse certam fiduciam remissi propter Christum peccati. . . 4. Suenkfeldianorum et Weigelianorum, qui statuunt, fidem non esse creatum motum aut fiduciam, sed ipsummet Christum, imo ipsam Dei essentiam; ac definiunt fidem justificantem per vitam, obedientiam et imitationem Christi.“ (L. c. P. IV. c. 8. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1348. sq.) §


### On Faith in Christ: This, therefore, is that faith which is said to apprehend Christ or the merit…

6. This, therefore, is that faith which is said to apprehend Christ or the merit of Christ, namely, as it is assent with confidence, or confidence joined with assent; from which acts, as if united, it consists and is called now by the name of the one, now by the name of the other, with the other always being connoted.

To this is usually referred that λαβεῖν τόν Χριστόν, John 1:11, 12; Col. 2: 6. It is understood, however, without doubt, as an apprehension not corporal, but spiritual, which takes place in the mind or soul, and is therefore metaphorical, drawn from the likeness of a hand grasping a garment or another thing, e.g., an alms. See Mus. de Conv. Disp. III. cap. IV. § 189. p. 222.

b) Elsewhere, indeed, apprehension pertains to the first operation of the mind, and is almost called simple apprehension or apprehension of simple things. But in this place, to apprehend is the same as, on the part of the intellect, to transfer the thing to oneself by knowing it, and on the part of the will, to be carried toward it by desiring it.

into the known object, as into one’s own good, and the cause of other goods to be obtained for oneself, and to hold it as if grasped by the hand, so that it may not be snatched away. See Musaeus, loc. cit., § 200, p. 220, and § 206, pp. 233–234. And to this pertains the πληροφορία (full assurance) of faith, concerning which Rom. 4:18 ff., or the fact that the mind is fully carried by belief into the object, that is, according to every reason by which the object is presented to it; by the intellect, indeed, insofar as it is presented under the aspect of truth, but by the will, insofar as it is presented under the aspect of good and desirable. Musaeus, § 183, p. 207.

Quenstedtius: "One kind of apprehension is intellectual and theoretical, which is nothing other than the cognition of a thing (for by knowing we apprehend a thing), and it is distinguished from the judgment that discerns and adjudicates what is apprehended by the intellect, whether they be true or false; and this does not suffice for faith. For in this way even unbelievers can apprehend the mysteries of faith, who nevertheless do not grant them assent. Sometimes, however, this apprehension is joined with assent, or is simultaneously assentive, when someone not only apprehends and knows something, but also holds it in his intellect as indubitable. For example, even the ungodly themselves can infer and subsume from that universal proposition that Christ died not only for all, but also for them individually, who nevertheless do not desire or conduct themselves in such a way that salvation might be obtained by them on account of Christ’s merit. But another kind of apprehension is of the will and is practical, which involves the resting of the whole heart and will in the merit of Christ, and denotes desire and access to Christ, and the fiducial application and appropriation of His merit; and this is properly trust." (Loc. cit., sect. 1, thesis 10, p. 1338 ff.)

Calovius: "The grace of God and the righteousness of Christ cannot become ours in any other way than through such an application; for just as the same is offered to us in the Gospel, so it must be apprehended by us through faith, since faith and the Word are related and mutually regard one another. Just as a beggar, in order to receive an offered gift, not only grants assent that it is seriously offered to him, but also extends his hand so that he may apprehend the gift with it: so, when we wish to be made partakers of the offered grace of God and the righteousness of Christ, not only must assent be granted, but it is required that we extend the hand of faith, and by it apprehend that [grace and righteousness] and apply it to ourselves." (Socinism. proflig., p. 731.)

Whence it is evident how faith is in different faculties, the intellect and the will, namely as an aggregate or something complex made up of different acts terminated toward the same object and having a certain order among themselves and toward that one and the same object. Musaeus, loc. cit., chap. III, § 179, p. 210.

For it is thus described, by πιστεύειν (to believe) that Jesus is the Christ, John 6:69; 1 John 5:1, 5, by which reason assent is formally signified, yet trust is to be understood; but otherwise by πιστεύειν εἰς Χριστόν (to believe in Christ), i.e., to rest in Him by an act of trust, yet with the assent of the intellect connoted or presupposed, John 8:30. Cf. here § 5, notes a and g. Similarly, πεποίθησις (confidence), which is ascribed to faith, sometimes signifies a firm persuasion of the mind, e.g., Rom. 8:38–39; 2 Tim. 1:12, and sometimes trust fixed in someone, when it is said: πέποιθα ἐν κυρίῳ (I trust in the Lord), Phil. 2:24; thus it signifies a persuasion of the mind with trust, or trust with a firm persuasion of the soul.

Quenstedtius: "Faith, considered materially, is divided into certain parts—the term 'parts' being taken broadly—by which we understand nothing other than different acts, following one another and [existing] in justifying faith..."

ON FAITH IN CHRIST. concurring. There are three parts or acts of faith: knowledge, assent, and trust. The first is that by which we believe certain things about God; the second, that by which we believe God, as God; the third, that by which we believe in God, as God, without doubt. Heretics can possess the first; only the orthodox, the second; only the regenerate, the third; and thus the latter always includes the former, but not conversely. The first two pertain to the intellect, the third to the will; the first two respect the whole Word of God, the third the promise of grace and the merit of Christ. These three parts of faith are expressed in John 14:10, 11, and 12, where verse 10 speaks of the knowledge by which something was to be known about Christ; verse 11, of the assent which ought to be given to Christ’s words; and verse 12, of the trust by which one believes in Christ as the Redeemer of the world. Thus also the ancients, namely Augustine (Tractate 29 on John) and Gregory Nazianzen (Oration 37), warn that it is a matter of knowledge to believe God [credere Deum], which even the devil believes; a matter of assent to believe God [credere Deo], which also belongs to hypocrites; and a matter of trust to believe in God [credere in Deum]. Although this distinction in the divine object is not perpetual, see Dannhauer, *Hodosophia*, p. 1323. (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 8. s. 1. th. 5. f. 1335. sq.)

Gerhard: "In this place we are dealing with justifying faith, which comprises knowledge, assent, and trust. With respect to knowledge and assent, it is referred to the intellect and has as its object the whole and only Divine Word revealed to us in the prophetic and apostolic scriptures; with respect to trust, it is referred to the heart or will and has as its object the evangelical promises concerning Christ the Mediator. Hence flows the theological rule: 'Scripture, when it speaks of faith, sometimes looks more to knowledge, sometimes more to trust.' Likewise: 'Some things are said about faith more with respect to knowledge, others more by reason of trust.'" (L. de justif. § 66.) §

7. It is evident, moreover, at the same time, how the very merit of Christ, the remission of sins, and eternal life, acquired for all men by Christ, are applied to believers through faith, so that they are truly made partakers of them. See above, Chapter II, Section III, § 10, note c. Indeed, just as the merit of Christ, so the promises concerning the gratuitous remission of sins for Christ’s sake are in themselves indeterminate and extend to all men; but when they are to benefit this or that man in the very act, it is necessary that some medium of union be given between him and them, by which the merit of Christ, indeterminate in itself, and the general gratuitous promises may be referred to this or that person, or become his. Cf. here § 1 and the blessed Musaeus, *De Conversione*, Disputation III, Chapter IV, § 215, p. 240. Whence even the promises of grace and the remission of sins themselves include faith; see John 8:16; Acts 10:43. Although it does not follow from this that one who believes in Christ must believe that he believes in Christ, as the blessed Musaeus shows in *De Conversione*, Disp. III, Chapter II, § 115 sqq., p. 159 sqq.

A. Knoesius: "The acts of faith exist in the soul either with the perception and reflection that they are present, or without this perception and reflection; in the former case, faith is called by theologians 'reflex,' in the latter, 'direct.'" (Instit. th. pract. Stockholm 1768, p. 376.) PART III. CHAPTER III.

To Osiander: "For special application, a direct act of faith suffices, nor is there need for a reflexive act. Yet a reflexive act also obtains in believers. 'For everyone sees his faith in his heart, and holds it with most certain knowledge,' as Augustine testifies." (Coll. th. P. V. p. 133.)

Zeibichius: "The act of faith is one thing, the sense of faith is another; the former does not always entail the latter simultaneously, because not every act is immediately reflexive." (De praedest. et reprob. infantium. Witeberg. 1709. p. 73.)

Kromayerus: "When we perceive no sense of faith, let us not immediately cast away our soul, since even the desire for faith is already faith itself, albeit weak. Phil. 2:13." (Th. posit. pol. II, 336.)

For otherwise that saying of Christ holds true: No one comes to the Father, to obtain grace from Him, except through Me, acknowledged and believed as the mediator of God and men, John 14:6. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Disp. de salute Gentilium, contra Curcell. § 22.

Meanwhile, God applies the merit of Christ to man in one way, and the believing man applies it to himself in another. For this application, which is performed by man through faith, does not differ in substance from faith itself in Christ, or the acts of assent and trust by which he is carried toward Christ; but that application, by which God applies the merit of Christ to man, consists in this: that God accepts that merit of Christ—even though it is not man’s own merit, but another’s—as if it were his own, namely, because it was performed in his stead and apprehended by him through faith; concerning which we shall say more in the Book on Justification. §

8. Faith in Christ, therefore, has a place among the principles and causes of salvation, not in itself and as it is an act or habit of believing, but by reason of the object toward which it is carried and which it apprehends and applies to the believer.

For the dignity, power, and value of faith itself, viewed absolutely in itself, is not, nor can it be, so great before God that we could imagine God is moved by it to confer salvation upon us. Cf. what we said in Proleg. cap. I. § 23. note b. Vol. I. p. 41., and the blessed Musaeus, Introd. cap. III. § 18. p. 138, 139. More will be said in the Books on Justification and on Predestination.

Latin:

6. Haec itaque illa fides est, quae dicitur apprehendere a Christum aut meritum Christi, scilicet, ut est assensus cum fiducia, seu fiducia cum assensu conjuncta;b ex quibus actibus, velut unitis,c constat et nunc illius, nunc hujus nomine appellatur, altero semper connotato.d

Huc referri solet illud λαβεΐν τόν Χριστόν, Joh. 1,11. 12. Col. 2, 6. Intelligitur autem haud dubie apprehensio non corporalis, sed spiritualis, quae iit mente aut animo, adeoque metaphorica, similitudine a manu, amictum aut rem aliam, v. g. eleemosynam, prehendente, petita. Vid. Mus. de Conv. Disp. III. cap. IV. § 189. p. 222.

b) Alias quidem apprehensio ad primam mentis operationem pertinet, ac fere cum apposito apprehensio simplex aut simplicium dicitur. Sed hoc loco apprehendere idem est atque ex parte intellectus cognoscendo rem ad se transferre, ex parte voluntatis autem ferri appetendo Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.10 PART. III. CAP. III.

in rem cognitam, tanquam in suum bonum, et aliorum sibi obtinendorum bonorum causam, idque velut manu conclusum tenere, ne eripiatur. Vid. Mus. 1. c. § 200. p. 220. et § 206. p. 233. 234. Et huc pertinet πληροφορία fidei, de qua Rom. 4. 18. sqq., seu quod animus credentia plene fertur in objectum, id est, secundum omnem rationem, secundum quam ei objectum objicitur; intellectu quidem, in quantum sub ratione veri, voluntate autem, in quantum sub ratione boni et appetibilis objicitur. Mus. § 183. p. 207.

Quenstedtius: ,,Apprehensio alia intellectualis est et theoretica, quae nihil aliud est, quam rei cognitio (cognoscendo enim rem apprehendimus), et distinguitur a judicio apprehensa per intellectum discernente et dijudicante, verane sint an falsa; et haec ad fidem non sufficit. Ita enim etiam infideles possunt mysteria fidei apprehendere, qui nihilominus illis assensum non praebent. Quandoque vero haec apprehensio cum assensu conjuncta sive simul assensitiva est, quum quis aliquid non tantum apprehendit et cognoscit, sed etiam id in intellectu suo pro indubitato habet. V. g., Christum non solum pro omnibus, sed etiam pro se in individuo esse mortuum, etiam ipsi impii ex universali illa propositione inferre et subsumere possunt, qui tamen non desiderant vel ita se non gerunt, ut propter Christi meritum sibi obtingat salus. Alia vero apprehensio est voluntatis et practica, quae totius cordis et voluntatis in merito Christi recumbentiam involvit, uotatque desiderium et accessum ad Christum, ejusque meriti applicationem et appropriationem flducialem; et haec proprie est fiducia.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 10. f. 1338. sq.)

Calovius: ,,Gratia Dei et justitia Christi aliter nostra fieri nequit, quam per ejusmodi applicationem; ut enim in evangelio eadem nobis offertur, ita per fidem a nobis apprehendenda est, cum fides et verbum, relata sint ac se mutuo respiciant. Quemadmodum mendicus, ut munus accipiat oblatum, non tantum assensum praebet, serio id sibi offerri, sed manum quoque extendit, ut eadem munus apprehendat: ita, cum oblatae Dei gratiae et justitiae Christi participes reddi volumus, non tantum assensus praebendus est, sed requiritur, ut manum fidei extendamus, eademque illam apprehendamus ac nobis applicemus.“ (Socinism. proflig. p. 731.)

Unde patet, quomodo fides sit in diversis potentiis, intellectu et voluntate, nempe tanquam aggregatum aut complexum quid ex diversis actibus ad idem objectum terminatis et ordinem quendam inter se atque ad unum illud idemque objectum habentibus. Mus. 1. c. cap. III, § 179. p. 210.

Sic enim describitur, per r<) credere, Jesum esse Christum, Joh. 6, 69. 1 Joh. 5, 1. ei 5., qua ratione formaliter assensus significatur, fiducia tamen subintelligenda est; alias autem per τυ credere in Christum, i. e., actu fiduciae in eum recumbere, connotato tamen aut supposito assensu intellectus, Joh. 8. 86. I, 12., nunc fiduciam in aliquo defixam, quando dicitur: πέποιΰα h χυρίω, Phil. 2, 24., itaquepersuadonem mentis cum fiducia, aut fiduciam cum firma animi persuasione significat.

Quenstedtius: ״Fides materialiter considerata dispescitur in certas partes, late sumto termino partium, per quas nihil aliud intelligimus, quam diversos actus, se invicem consequentes et in fide justifi

cante concurrentes. Harum autem partium seu actuum fidei tres sunt: Notitia, assensus, fiducia. Prima est, qua de Deo quaedam, secunda9 qua Deo, ut Deo, tertia, qua in Deum, ut Deum, indubitato credimus. Primam habere possunt haeretici, secundam tantum orthodoxi, tertiam soli renati; adeoque posterius semper includit prius, sed non contra. Priores duae ad intellectum, tertia ad voluntatem pertinet; priores respiciunt omne Dei verbum, tertia promissionem gratiae et meritum Christi. Tres hae fidei partes exprimuntur Joh. 14, 10. 11. et 12., ubi v. 10. loquitur de notitia, qua aliquid de Christo sciendum fuit, v. 11. de assensu, qui Christi verbis praeberi debuit, v. 12. de fiducia, qua in Christum, tanquam mundi redemtorem, creditur. Or. 37., monent, quod notitiae sit, credere Deum, quod etiam credit diabolus; assensus, credere Deo, quod hypocritis quoque competit; fiduciae, credere in Deum. Quamquam haec differentia in objecto divino non sit perpetua, vid. Dannhauer. Hodos. p. 1323.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 8. s. 1. th. 5. f. 1335. sq.)

Gkrhardus: ,,Hoc loco agimus de fide justificante, quae complectitur notitiam, assensum et fiduciam. Respectu notitiae et assensus refertur ad intellectum atque objecti loco habet omne et solum D. II. Sect. III. § 10. not. c. A. Knoesius: ,,Actus fidei existunt in anima vel cum perceptione et reflexione, quod adsint, vel sine hac perceptione et reflexione; in illo casu fides a theologis reflexa dicitur, in hoc directa.“ (Instit. th. pract. Holmiae 1768. p. 376.) PART. III. CAP. III.

Ad. Osiander: ״Ad specialem applicationem sufficit actus fidei directus, nec opus est actu reflexo. Etiam actus reflexus in fidelibus obtinet. ,Videt enim quisque fidem suam in corde suo, et certissima tenet scientia‘, teste Augustino.“ (Coll. th. P. V. p. 133.)

Alias enim valet illud Christi: Nemo venit ad Patrem, gratiam apud illum consecuturus, nisi per me, velut mediatorem Dei et hominum, agnitum atque creditum, Joh. 14, 6. Conf. b. Mus. Disp, de salute Gentilium, contra Curcell. § 22.

Interim aliter Deus homini applicat meritum Christi, aliter hamo credens ipse sibi. 8. Fides in Christum itaque inter principia et causas salutis locum habet, non per se a et ut actus aut habitus credendi est, sed ratione objecti, in quod fertur b et quod apprehendit et credenti applicat. c

### On Faith in Christ: Quenstedtius: "Faith does not influence justification and salvation…

Quenstedtius: "Faith does not influence justification and salvation meritoriously, as it is a work. (For 1. The efficient cause of our justification is the grace of God, Eph. 2:8. If, however, it is by grace, then faith does not justify meritoriously. 2. The meritorious cause of our justification is the obedience of Christ alone, and therefore it cannot be attributed to faith at the same time. 3. Nowhere does Scripture say that faith justifies by way of a work, but rather it denies this very thing in every way. 4. Faith is perpetually opposed to works, not indeed in itself and simply, since works are the effects and fruits of faith, but with respect to the effect, which is justification. For works do not justify in any way, neither by way of a physical, nor moral, nor meritorious, nor instrumental efficient cause. And with respect to the object, which is the merit of Christ, it is simply incompatible with our works in this article, or cannot stand with them.) But it does so by way of an organ, uniquely and solely required on the part of the man to be justified. Therefore, the causality of faith..."

in the act of justification is nothing other than organic. For faith justifies οργανικώς [organically], or by way of an instrument—that is, not by reason of itself, but by reason of the object which it apprehends and appropriates to itself, namely, Christ with all His merit. The faith that justifies is knowledge, assent, and trust; but as it justifies, it is the bare, passive apprehension of the benefits of Christ (John 1:12; Rom. 9:30; Phil. 3:12), the admission of the motions of the Holy Spirit, and a resting and reposing in the merits of Christ. Hence the great theological maxim of the ancients: Faith justifies not in the category of quality, as if it were a work or a virtue, but of relation, in its correlate or through its correlate—that is, the thing believed, the merit of Christ accepted by faith, justifies. Thus, the hand of the beggar does not enrich, but the treasure given and the alms apprehended by the hand. The mouth does not satisfy the stomach, but the food apprehended.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 15. f. 1341. sq.) See above, Proleg. I. § 23. b.

That object, indeed, is the merit of the θεανθρώπου [God-man], and through this, it is a merit of infinite price, weight, and value, and it suffices for this: that in view of it, the divine will determines itself to receive us into grace and to bestow salvation upon us.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who maintain that the proper and adequate object of justifying faith is not the special mercy of God proposed in Christ, but the whole Word of God; thus Bellarmine, l. 1. de justif. c. 4: ‘Catholics,’ he says, ‘wish the object of justifying faith to be as broad as the Word of God is broad.’ Nay, rather, they contend that a certain promise of special mercy pertains not so much to faith as to presumption. The same Bellarmine, in the same book, c. 8. § 1, says: ‘The object of justifying faith is not the special mercy of God, but all things which God has deigned to reveal.’ ... 2. Of the Socinians, who make God the primary object of justifying faith, but Christ the secondary, and deny that the merit of Christ is the object of faith. Socinus’s Rubric, P. 4. de Serv. c. 9, is: ‘To believe that our sins have been blotted out through those things which Christ suffered can in no way be that faith in Christ by which we are justified.’” (L. c. S. 2. q. 4. f. 1362. sq.)

The reason, therefore, why salvation is attributed to faith just as it is to the merit of Christ as a cause, is this very fact: that faith is intimately conjoined with the merit of Christ, not only as an act with its object, but in such a way that it unites the thing itself, about which it is concerned, to us, so that it becomes ours. Whence it is simultaneously evident how faith, or assenting trust, can do this, whereas love cannot do so equally. Conf. b. Mus. de Conv. Disput. III. c. IV. § 115. p. 240.

S. Schmidtius: “For it does not suffice, in order for justifying faith to be the instrumental cause of justification, that it be knowledge; nor does it yet suffice that it assent to those things which it knows; nor, indeed, does it suffice that there be added, moreover, a trust in itself, simply and absolutely as such; but in order for it to be what it ought to be, it is necessary that it be a trust related to the grace of God offering the remission of sins with the merit of Christ, and responding to it in a just relation—that is, apprehending that which the liberal grace of the merciful God offers. For faith can indeed exist if it has knowledge, assent, and trust; but it cannot be justifying unless it apprehends and receives from the liberal hand of God that which is offered. For those things complete the nature and essence of justifying faith in itself and absolutely, but this [apprehension] constitutes it in the office of the instrumental cause of justification and adds a relation to its nature. Which could be more fully declared by the analogy of the hand receiving alms.” (Artic. F. C. Repetit, p. 234.) PART III. CHAP. III.

Carpzovius: "The remission of sins is considered in a twofold way. First, as it has been acquired by Christ, and is offered in the Word and Sacraments as a good divinely promised and intended to be sought and possessed by sinners. Then, truly, as it has already been received and applied through faith and is possessed." (Isag. in libr. symb. p. 208.)

Gerhardus: "We urge the opposition of the Apostle in Rom. 5:19. Those many who were constituted sinners through the fall of Adam, those same many were also constituted righteous through the righteousness of Christ, that is, the benefit of righteousness was obtained for them (for the Apostle is not dealing with application): Now, however, all men were constituted sinners through the fall of Adam, verses 12 and 18. Therefore, the benefit of righteousness was also obtained for all through Christ." (Loc. de elect. § 118.)

Kromayerus: "Let it be noted in passing that faith is viewed either as it is in the heart, or as it breaks forth into the mouth. When it is viewed as it is in the heart, it is a fiducial apprehension of the grace of God or the merit of Christ; when in the latter way, it either petitions that sins be remitted to it and that it be received into grace for the sake of Christ, or it exercises itself upon other objects. If in the former way, it obtains righteousness; if in the latter, it indicates righteousness. For prayer, indeed, petitioning the remission of sins from God or invoking divine mercy is nothing other than faith proceeding outwardly and exercising itself upon its principal object. Therefore, when the Apostle says in Rom. 10:10, 'With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation,' that oral confession is occupied either with the primary object, the grace of God and the merit of Christ, or with secondary objects, e.g., goods necessary for maintaining this life, or the averting of calamities, or other benefits. If with the former, it attains salvation, i.e., the right to eternal salvation through the same; if with the latter, it indicates the right to eternal salvation conferred upon it." (Th. posit. pol. II, 334.) §

9. The principal efficient cause of faith in Christ is the Triune God. Who, by His own proper and sufficient power, produces in us the act and habit of believing. Thus Paul, in Rom. 1:8 and Col. 1:3, 4, 12, gives thanks to God as the author, when he had been made certain of the faith of his own. Similarly, in Phil. 1:3 and 5, he gives thanks to God for their κοινωνία in the εὐαγγέλιον, or that they had come into the communion of the Gospel, which happened through faith. Cf. 1 Thess. 2:13. Namely, the Father ἑλκύει, draws men, that they may come to Christ through faith, John 6:44; the Son also is called ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς τῆς πίστεως, the beginner and finisher of faith, Heb. 12:2; finally, the Holy Spirit causes us to cry out, Ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ, Rom. 8:15, and helps, συναντιλαμβάνεται, our infirmities, v. 26.

Ad. Osiander: "They object: 1. It does not follow: Faith is a gift, therefore it is the work of God alone; for even in Scripture, children are called a gift of God, where, however, man concurs causally. Therefore, concurrence is not excluded here, but at least a preceding medium; for a gift of God and merit are opposites, but not a gift of God and concurrence. R. It certainly follows: Faith is a gift of God, therefore it proceeds from God alone, 1.) because it is said: 'By grace you have been saved.' Therefore, just as salvation is attributed to grace alone, so also the divine origin is attributed to faith alone as the apprehending instrument; for if anything from us were to concur, we would not be saved by grace alone, [by] faith..."

having itself instrumentally. 2.) We are said to be saved by grace in such a way that we are not said to be saved from ourselves, and faith is submitted as a gift. Therefore, faith is removed from us by reason of its origin and transferred to God alone...

They object 3.: Faith is considered either by reason of its powers or by reason of its act. "Although it is and must be conceded that by reason of its powers it is from God alone, for He gives the powers of believing, nor do they arise from free will; yet the exercise of these powers is of the man himself and from the man himself."

R. 1.) Not only are the powers of believing from God, but faith itself in act, because before the final effect of prevenient grace, man is not yet converted; but the final effect of prevenient grace is the donation of faith. 2.) Although faith is attributed to us, it is not attributed to us under the aspect of a vital and free act, but insofar as it is considered as the final effect of God working around us and in us...

That man does not concur causally to the production of faith is evident from the fact that faith is spiritual life; but we are by nature dead in sins, Eph. 2:5. And just as a dead person does not concur to the production of life, but receives it; so also is it with those who are spiritually dead. We do not deny that man concurs to the existence of faith, but man does not concur by producing and effectively, but by admitting and subjectively, because the subject that believes is man." (Coll. th. P. V. p. 115 sq.)

Quenstedtius: "Faith is a work in no way our own, except subjectively on account of the mere reception and exercise, by which it comes to pass that the Holy Spirit is not said to believe, but man, because the act of faith is actively from the Holy Spirit, terminated in man." (L. c. s. 1. th. 17. f. 1343.)

Latin:

Quenstedtius: ״In justificationem et salvationem fides non influit meritorie, ut est opus. (Nam 1. causa efficiens justificationis nostrae est Dei gratia, Eph. 2, 8. Si vero ex gratia, ergo non meritorie fides justificat. 2. Causa meritoria nostrae justificationis est sola Christi obedientia, adeoque simul fidei ea tribui nequit. 3. Nullibi Scriptura dicit, quod fides per modum operis justificet, sed potius id ipsum omnibus modis negat. 4. Fides ׳perpetuo operibus opponitur, non quidem per se et simpliciter, cum opera sint fidei effectus et fructus, sed respectu effectus, qui est justificatio. Opera enim nullo modo justificant, neque per modum causae efficientis physicae, neque moralis, neque meritoriae, neque instrumentalis. Et respectu objecti, quod Christi meritum est, cum operibus nostris in hoc articulo simpliciter incompatibile sive stare non potest.) Sed per modum organi, ex parte hominis justificandi unice et solitarie requisiti. Causalitas ergo fidei

in actu justificationis non alia est, quam organica. Justificat enim fides οργανικώς sive per modum organi, id est, non ratione sui, sed ratione objecti, quod apprehendit sibique appropriat, scii. Christum cum omni suo merito. Fides, quae justificat, est notitia, assensus, fiducia, sed qua justificat, est nuda apprehensio beneficiorum Christi passiva, Joh. 1, 12. Rom. 9, 30. Phil. 3, 12., admissiva motuum Spiritus Sancti, recubitoria et requietoria in meritis Christi. Hinc veterum maxima theologica: Fides justificat non in praedicamento qualitatis, ut est opus aut virtus, sed relationis, in suo correlato seu per suum correlatum, id est, res credita, meritum Christi fide acceptum justificat. Sic manus mendici non ditat, sed thesaurus donatus ac eleemosyna manu apprehensa. Os non satiat stomachum, sed cibus apprehensus.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 15. f. 1341. sq.) Vid. supra Proleg. I. § 23. b.

Objectum nempe illud est meritum #εαν#ρώπου9 et per hoc pretii, ponderis ac valoris infiniti meritum est sufficitque ad hoc, ut ejus intuitu voluntas divina se determinet ad nos in gratiam recipiendos ac salute donandos.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, statuentium, objectum fidei justificantis proprium et adaequatum non esse specialem Dei misericordiam in Christo propositam, sed omne Dei verbum; ita Bellarminus 1. 1. de justif. c. 4.: ,Catholici‘, inquit, ,tam late patere volunt objectum fidei justificantis, quam late patet verbum Dei.‘ Quin potius certam promissionem specialis misericordiae non tam ad fidem, quam ad praesumptionem pertinere contendunt. Idem Bellarminus libr. ejusd. c. 8. § 1. ait: ,Fidei justificantis objectum non est specialis Dei misericordia, sed omnia, quae Deus revelare dignatus est. . . 2. Socinianorum, qui Deum fidei justificantis objectum faciunt primarium, Christum vero secundarium, negantque, Christi meritum esse fidei objectum. Socini Rubrica P. 4. de Serv. c. 9. est: ,Credere per ea, quae passus est Christus, nostra peccata deleta fuisse, nullo modo eam fidem in Christum esse posse, qua justificamur.‘“ (L. c. S. 2. q. 4. f. 1362. sq.)

Ratio igitur, quamobrem fidei itidem, ut merito Christi salus nostra tanquam causae tribuitur, haec ipsa est, quod fides cum Christi merito intime conjuncta est, non solum tanquam actus cum objecto suo, verum ita, ut rem ipsam, circa quam versatur, uniat ad nos, ut nostra fiat. Unde simul patet, quomodo fides sive fiducia assensualis hoc possit, dilectio autem aeque non possit. Conf. b. Mus. de Conv. Disput. III. c. IV. § 115. p. 240.

S. Schmidtius: ,,Non enim, ut fides justificans sit justificationis causa Instrumentalis, sufficit, ut sit notitia; nondum etiam sufficit, ut iis, quae novit, assentiatur; neque vero etiam sufficit, ut insuper accedat fiducia in se, simpliciter et absolute talis; sed ut sit, quod esse debet, oportet eandem esse fiduciam ad gratiam Dei cum Christi merito remissionem peccatorum offerentem relatam et justa relatione illi respondentem, hoc est, id, quod liberalis Dei miserentis gratia offert, apprehendentem. Fides quidem enim esse potest, si notitifcm, assensum flduciamque habeat; justificans autem esse nequit, nisi e manu Dei liberali id, quod offertur, apprehendat et recipiat. Iila namque naturam et essentiam fidei justificantis in se et absolute absolvunt, sed hoc in officio causae Instrumentalis justificationis eam constituit et relationem naturae superaddit. Quod simili manus eleemosynam recipientis uberius declarari posset.“ (Artic. F. C. Repetit, p. 234.) PART. III. CAP. III.

Carpzovius: ,,Remissio peccatorum duplici modo consideratur. Semel, ut a Christo acquisita est, et in verbo ac sacramentis tanquam bonum divinitus promissum et intentum peccatoribus quaerendum et habendum offertur. Deinde vero prout jam accepta est et per fidem applicata est atque habetur.‘‘ (Isag. in libr. symb. p. 208.)

Gerhardus: ,,Urgemus oppositionem apostoli Rom. 5, 19. Qui multi peccatores constituti sunt per Adami lapsum, illi etiam multi per Christi justitiam constituti sunt justi, id est, partum illis justitiae beneficium (non enim de applicatione agit apostolus): Jam vero omnes homines per lapsum Adami constituti sunt peccatores, vers. 12. et 18. Ergo etiam omnibus per Christum partum est justitiae beneficium.“ (Loc. de elect. § 118.)

Kromayerus: ,,Notetur obiter, fidem vel spectari, prout est in corde, vel, prout in os erumpit. Cum spectatur, ut est in corde, fiducialis apprehensio est gratiae Dei vel meriti Christi; cum posteriori modo, vel petit, peccata sibi remitti inque gratiam se recipi propter Christum, vel in objectis aliis semet exercet. Si priori modo, justitiam impetrat; si posteriori, justitiam indicat. Oratio siquidem remissionem peccatorum a Deo petens aut misericordiam divinam invocans nihil aliud est, quam fides forinsecus prodiens et in objecto suo principali sese exercens. Cum itaque Rom. 10, 10. inquit apostolus: ,Corde creditur ad justitiam, ore fit confessio ad salutem‘, vel oralis illa confessio in objecto primario, gratia Dei et Christi merito, vel secundariis objectis, v. g. bonis ad vitam hanc tuendam necessariis aut avertendis calamitatibus aut beneficiis aliis occupatur. Si priore, salutem i. e. jus ad aeternam salutem per eandem consequitur; si posterioribus, jus ad salutem aeternam sibi collatum indicat.“ (Th. posit.pol. II, 334.) §

9. Causa efficiens principalis a fidei in Christum est Deus b trinunus. c Quae virtute propria et sufficiente in nobis producit actum et habitum credendi. Sic Paulus ad Rom. i, 8. et ad Col. 1, 3. 4· 12. gratias agit Deo, velut auctori, cum de fide suorum certus factus esset. Similiter ad Philipp. 1, 3. et 5. Deo gratias agit im τη κοινωνία eorum εις τυ ευαγγέλιον, seu quod venerint in communionem evangelii, quod per fidem contigit. Conf. 1 Thess. 2, 13. Scilicet Pater έλχύζει, trahit homines, ut veniant ad Christum, per fidem Joh. 6, 44.: ·Filius quoque appellatur αρχηγός χαϊ τελειωτης της πίστεως, inchoator et consummator fidei, Ebr. 12, 2.; Spiritus S. denique facit, ut clamemus, ,Aßßä 6 πατήρ, Rom. 8, 15., et auxiliatur, συν αντιλαμβάνεται, infirmitatibus nostris, v. 26.

Ad. Osiander: ,,Excipiunt: 1. Non sequitur: Eides est donum, ergo solius Dei opus; nam etiam in Scriptura liberi dicuntur donum DeiJ ubi tamen homo causaliter concurrit. E. hic non excluditur concursus, sed saltem medium praevium; donum enim Dei et meritum sunt opposita, non vero donum Dei et concursus. R. Utique sequitur: Fides est donum Dei, ergo a solo Deo proficiscitur, 1.) quia dicitur: gratia salvati estis. Ut ergo soli gratiae tribuitur salus, ita etiam soli fidei tanquam instrumento apprehendenti tribuitur origo divina; si enim concurreret aliquid ex nobis, non tantum gratia salvaremur, fide

se instrumentaliter habente. 2.) Ita dicimur salvari gratia, ut non ex nobis dicamur salvari et fides subjiciatur tanquam donum. Ergo fides removetur a nobis ratione originis et transfertur in solum Deum...

Excipiunt 3.: Eides consideratur vel ratione virium, vel ratione actus. ׳Quamquam sit et concedatur, ratione virium esse a solo Deo, ille enim dat vires credendi, neque illae a libero arbitrio oriuntur; exercitium tamen istarum virium est ipsius hominis et ab ipso homine.

R. 1.) Non tantum vires credendi sunt a Deo, sed et ipsa fides actu, quia ante ultimum gratiae praevenientis effectum homo nondum est conversus; ultimus auteip gratiae praevenientis effectus est fidei donatio. 2.) Quamvis fides tribuatur nobis, non tamen tribuitur nobis sub ratione actus vitalis et liberi, sed quatenus consideratur tamquam ultimus effectus Dei circa nos et in nobis operantis. . .

Non concurrere hominem ad productionem fidei causaliter, inde patet, quia fides est vita spiritualis; nos autem per naturam in peccatis mortui, Ephes. 2, 5. Sicut autem mortuus non concurrit ad productionem vitae, sed recipit illam; ita quoque comparatum est cum spiritualiter mortuis. Non negamus, hominem concurrere ad fidei existentiam, sed non concurrit homo producendo et effective, sed admittendo et subjective, quia subjectum, quod credit, est homo.“ (Coll. th. P. V. p. 115. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Est fides opus nulla ratione nostrum, nisi subjective propter solam receptionem et exercitium, quo fit, ut Spiritus S. non dicatur credere, sed homo, quia actus fidei active est a Sp. S. terminatus in homine.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 17. f. 1343.)


### On Faith in Christ: Calovius: "How is that to be understood which (Latermannus) says

Calovius: "How is that to be understood which (Latermannus) says: 'That God on His part provides this, that all, if they wish, could fulfill the condition of faith, convert themselves, and thus be saved'? And how great and how burdensome are these sayings! Does God not provide on His part that we might wish? That we might believe? Does He only provide that we might be able to wish, that we might be able to convert ourselves, that we might be able to believe?" (Facultatis th. Argentorat. Resp. 1646. See Calovius, Syst. T. X. p. 50.)

Luther: "Faith is not the human delusion or dream that some hold for faith; and when they see that no improvement of life nor good works follow, and yet can hear and speak much of faith, they fall into the error and say: faith is not enough, one must do works if one is to become pious and blessed. This happens because, when they hear the Gospel, they fall away and make for themselves by their own powers a thought in their heart which says: I believe. That they then hold for a true faith. But as it is a human fabrication and thought, which the ground of the heart never experiences, so it also does nothing, and no improvement follows thereafter.

But faith is a divine work in us, which changes us and begets us anew from God, John 1:13, and kills the old Adam, makes us entirely different people in heart, spirit, mind, and all powers, and brings the Holy Spirit with it. O, it is a living, busy, active, mighty thing, this faith, so that it is impossible that it should not incessantly work good. It does not even ask whether good works are to be done, but before one asks, it has done them, and is always in the doing. But he who does not do such works is a faithless man, groping and looking about for faith and good works, and knows neither what faith nor good works are, yet washes and chatters many words about faith and good works. Faith is a living, daring confidence in God's grace, so certain that it would die a thousand times over it. And such confidence and knowledge of divine grace makes one happy, bold, and joyful toward God and all creatures; which the Holy Spirit does in faith. Hence the man without compulsion becomes willing and joyful to do good to everyone, to serve everyone, to suffer all manner of things, for the love and praise of God, who has shown him such grace." PART III. CHAP. III.

has shown. So that it is impossible to separate works from faith, indeed, as impossible as burning and shining may be separated from fire. Therefore, beware of your own false thoughts and useless chatterers, who want to be clever in judging faith and good works, and are the greatest fools. Pray to God that He may work faith in you, otherwise you will surely remain eternally without faith, no matter what you invent and do, whatever you want or can.” (Preface to the Ep. St. Paul to the Romans. XIV, 114. sq.)

The same: “It (faith) is a work of God, and not of man, as Paul teaches. All other works God works with us and through us; this one alone He works in us and without us.” (On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church. 1520. XIX, 71.) ANTITHESES. Luthardt: “On the other hand,” (in Scripture!) “repentance and faith are demanded of man as his performance: μετανοείτε και πιστεύετε — at all stages of the history of salvation... Faith is free obedience, which man performs.” (Compend. Third Edition, p. 202.)

The same: “He” (the Holy Spirit) “does not work the willing itself, but acts so liberatingly upon the bound will that it thereby receives a new ability to will.” (Doctrine of the Free Will. 1863. p. 441.) Kahnis: “Faith is an act of our ‘I.’ The person of the believer grasps Christ. The Holy Spirit cannot perform this act for man. However, man has the will and the ability to grasp Christ only through the Holy Spirit. Thus, in regeneration, the Holy Spirit works more closely the power to believe, not the act of faith.” (The Doctrine of the Lord’s Supper. 1851. p. 431.)

The same: “What is from the Holy Spirit is the power to believe. But what is from man is the act of faith... Yet, while the strict Lutherans always kept only the goal in view of cutting off all human merit, they destroyed the psychological and moral foundation in the work of the appropriation of salvation.” (The Luth. Dogm. Vol. II. 1864. p. 545.) § 10. The internal impulsive cause is the goodness or gratuitous favor of God; the external is the merit of Christ.

Moving God to excite (although also to preserve and confirm) faith in us. In respect of which Paul says in Phil. 1:29: έχαρίσθη υμϊν, it has been freely given or granted to you, το εις Χρίστον πιστεύειν, to believe in Christ. And that thanksgiving of the apostle for the faith of his own certainly refers the origin of faith to the unmerited grace of God.

Just as Paul, after having said generally that every spiritual blessing with which the Father has blessed us depends on Christ, Eph. 1:3, also says that all things were restored through Christ, v. 10, 11, and that through Him we also were κληρωθέντας, chosen by lot, i.e., made believers, v. 11.

OF FAITH IN CHRIST. M. Chemnitius: "How is it then that Judas is not received, that he does not receive forgiveness of sins, since he nevertheless repented of what he had done? And what is lacking in his repentance and penance, that he cannot obtain grace? He had no faith in Christ; he did not believe that God is gracious and forgives sins. That is what does him the harm; for where faith is not, there is also no grace of God, nor forgiveness of sins.

Now, however, our Catechism says in the third article of our Christian faith that man cannot by his own reason or strength believe in Jesus Christ or come to Him, but that the Holy Spirit must bring him to such faith, for faith is a gift of God. How is it then that God does not give such faith into the heart of Judas, so that he also could have believed that he could be helped through Christ?

There we must return with our questions and say with Romans 11: 'O, the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!' We cannot and should not investigate this and bury ourselves too deeply in such thoughts, but rather use this in such a way that we do not willfully commit ourselves to sin and tempt God, lest God withdraw His hand from us and let us sink; for where that happens, we fall ever from one sin into another, and gradually slide so deeply into sin that afterwards there is no returning, and we cannot again lay hold of the state of grace.

As it happened with Judas: he begins slowly, deals unfaithfully with the alms that were presented to Christ by good people and entrusted to him, and because he is not immediately punished by God for this, that makes him bold and daring, so that he continues in sin and ventures ever further.

When he now makes it too coarse and Christ takes him aside, admonishes, warns, and punishes him, and even wants to lead him away from his evil intent in a friendly and fatherly manner—finally even using a proper earnestness and saying, 'It would be better for that man if he had never been born'—he [Christ] stands before him again so friendly, washes his feet, feeds him with His body and blood, and admonishes him with friendly words to repentance. Yes, what is more: when he comes to Him with the band and servants of the high priests who wanted to seize Him, and he approaches Him under the guise of friendship with a treacherous heart, He permits him to come to Him and lets Himself be kissed by him.

And when Judas, after he had committed so many grievous sins, still goes on in security and regards none of this, then the Lord finally withdraws His hand from him and lets him fall into despair.

From this we should learn that we do not willfully sin against our conscience and abuse the grace of God, for God's judgments are incomprehensible and unsearchable, Rom. 11.

Therefore, no one should think: 'What harm does it do if I sin readily and delay repentance for a long time? God is gracious and merciful; He will not take it so strictly with me. When I have finished my raging, I will then convert myself, and He will soon receive me into grace.' Many a person thinks this way and goes on, and when God calls him to repentance, he thinks it is unnecessary, he will still be able to manage it in time; just as if we had it in our hands to be able to convert ourselves to God whenever we wanted.

But the Epistle to the Hebrews in chapter 3, from the 95th Psalm, warns us against this and says: 'Today, if you will hear His voice, harden not your hearts,' do not think, 'We still have enough time to improve ourselves,' as your fathers did in the wilderness, to whom I gave time for 40 years for improvement, but they provoked me, so that I swore in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest.

Therefore the Epistle to the Hebrews says: 'Take heed, dear children, that you do not have such an evil, unbelieving, and impenitent heart, but exhort one another daily.'" PART III. CAP. III.

as long as it is called today, so that you do not miss the time of grace, so that you are not also cast away, like the fathers in the wilderness.

We should not, indeed, presume to set a certain measure and limit for the grace and mercy of God, as to how far and wide it extends and where it turns; rather, it is our duty to pay diligent attention: as long as the Spirit of God performs His work in us by punishing, warning, and admonishing, and thus works in us against the flesh, it is a certain indication that God is calling us to repentance and is favorably disposed toward us in grace and would gladly convert us. But when you do not heed this, but go on without repentance and improvement, in total security, and trample underfoot all admonition from the Law and comfort from the Gospel, then you should know that God has His secret, terrible judgments and lets such willful sinners fall into a reprobate mind.” (Passion Sermons. IV, 17—19.)

Latin:

Calovius: ,,Quomodo capiendum illud, quod dicit (Latermannus): ,Deum sua parte hoc praestare, ut omnes, si velint, conditionem fidei implere, se convertere et ita salvari possent‘ ? et quanta et quam φορτικά sunt haec ακούσματα! Deusne non praestat a sua parte, ut velimus? ut credamus? Praestatne tantum, ut possimus velle, ut possimus nos convertere, ut possimus credere?“ (Facultatis th. Argentorat. Resp. 1646. Vid. Calovii Syst. T. X. p. 50.)

Lutherus: ,,Glaube ist nicht der menschliche Wahn oder Traum, den etliche für Glauben halten; und wenn sie sehen, dass keine Besserung des Lebens noch gute Werke folgen, und doch vom Glauben viel hören und reden können, fallen sie in den Irrthum, und sprechen: der Glaube sei nicht gnug, man müsse Werke thun, soll man fromm und selig werden. Das machet, wenn sie das Evangelium hören, so fallen sie daher, und machen ihnen aus eigenen Kräften einen Gedanken im Herzen, der spricht: Ich glaube. Das halten sie denn für einen rechten Glauben. Aber wie es ein menschlich Gedichte und Gedanken ist, den des Herzens Grund nimmer, erfahret; also thut er auch nichts, und folget keine Besserung hernach.

Aber Glaube ist ein göttlich Werk in uns, das uns wandelt und neu gebieret aus Gott, Joh. 1,13., und tödtet den alten Adam, machet uns ganz andere Menschen von Herzen, Muth, Sinn und allen Kräften, und bringet den Heiligen Geist mit sich. O es ist ein lebendig, schäftig, thätig, mächtig Ding um den Glauben, dass unmöglich ist, dass er nicht ohne Unterlass sollte Gutes wirken. Er fraget auch nicht, ob gute Werke zu thun sind, sondern ehe man fraget, hat er sie gethan, und ist immer im Thun. Wer aber nicht solche Werke thut, der ist ein glaubloser Mensch, tappet und siehet um sich nach dem Glauben und guten Werken, und weiss weder, was Glaube noch gute Werke sind, waschet und schwatzet doch viel Worte vom Glauben und guten Werken. Glaube ist eine lebendige, erwegene Zuversieht auf Gottes Gnade, so gewiss, dass er tausendmal darüber stürbe. Und solche Zuversicht und Erkenntniss göttlicher Gnade machet fröhlich, trotzig und lustig gegen Gott und alle Creaturen; welches der Heilige Geist thut im Glauben. Daher der Mensch ohne Zwang willig und lustig wird, jedermann Gutes zu thun, jedermann zu dienen, allerlei zu leiden, Gott zu Liebe und zu Lob, der ihm solche Gnade er PART. III. CAP. III.

zeiget hat. Also, dass unmöglich ist, Werke vom Glauben scheiden, ja so unmöglich, als Brennen und Leuchten vom Feuer mag geschieden werden. Darum siehe dich vor vor deinen eigenen falschen Gedanken und unnützen Schwätzern, die vom Glauben und guten Werken klug sein wollen zu urtheilen, und sind die grössesten Narren. Bitte Gott, dass er den Glauben in dir wirke, sonst bleibest du wohl ewiglich ohne Glauben, du dichtest und thust, was du willst oder kannst.“ (׳Vorrede auf die Ep. St. Pauli an die Römer. XIV, 114. sq.)

Idem: ,,Es (der Glaube) ist ein Werk Gottes, und nicht des Mensehen, wie Paulus lehrt. Alle andern Werke wirket Gott mit uns und durch uns; allein dieses wirket er in uns und ohne uns.“ (Von der babylon. Gefängniss der Kirchen. 1520. XIX, 71.) ANTITHESES. Luthardtius: ,,Auf der andern Seite wird“ (in der Schrift!),,Busse und Glaube vom Menschen gefordert als seine Leistung: μετανοείτε και πιστεύετε — auf allen Stufen der Heilsgeschichte. . . Der Glaube ist freier Gehorsam, den der Mensch leistet.“ (Compend. Dritte Auflage, p. 202.)

Idem: ״Nicht das Wollen selbst wirkt er“ (der Heilige Geist), ,,sondern so befreiend auf den gebundenen Willen, dass dieser dadurch ein neues Wollenkönnen empfängt.“ (Lehre vom fr. Willen. 1863. p. 441.) Kahnisius: ,,Der Glaube ist ein Thun unseres Ich. Des Glaubenden Person ergreift Christum. Diesen Act kann der Heilige Geist nicht für den Menschen verrichten. Der Mensch hat aber den Willen und die Fähigkeit, Christum zu ergreifen, nur durch den Heiligen Geist. Der Heilige Geist wirkt in der Wiedergeburt also näher die Kraft zu glauben, nicht den Act des Glaubens.“ (Die Lehre vom Abendmahle. 1851. p. 431.)

Idem: ,,Was vom Heiligen Geist ist, ist die Kraft zu glauben. Was aber vom Menschen ist, ist der Act des Glaubens. . . Indem aber die strengen Lutheraner immer nur das Ziel in’s Auge fassten, alles menschliche Verdienst abzuschneiden, zerstörten sie die psychologische und sittliche Grundlage im Werke der Heilsaneignung.“ (Die luth. Dogm. II. Bd. 1864. p. 545.) § 10. Causa impulsiva a interna est Dei bonitas seu gratuitus b favor; externa est meritum c Christi.

Movens Deum ad excitandam (quanquam et conservandam atque confirmandam) in nobis fidem. Cujus respectu dicit Paulus ad Phil. 1,29.: έχαρίσ#7) υμϊν, gratis datum aut donatum vobis est, το εις Χρίστον πιστεύει, credere in Christum. Et gratiarum actio illa apostoli pro fide suorum utique ad gratiam Dei indebitam fidei originem refert.

Prout Paulus, postquam generaliter dixisset, omnem benedictionem spiritualem, qua Pater nobis benedixit, a Christo pendere, Eph. 1, 3., omnia quoque per Christum instaurata, v. 10. 11., per eum etiam nos χληρω&έντας, in sortem adseitos, i. e. fideles factos esse dicit, v. 11.

DE FIDE IN CHRISTUM. M. Chemnitius: ,,Wie kömmts dann aber, dass Judas nicht wird auf genommen, dass der nicht Vergebung der Sünde empfähet, da es ihm doch gereuet, was er gethan hatte? Und was mangelt an seiner Reue und Buss, dass er keine Gnade erlangen kann? Er hatte keinen Glauben an Christum, gläubet nicht, dass Gott gnädig sei und Sünde vergebe, das thut ihm den Schaden, dann wo der Glaube nicht ist, da ist auch keine Gnade Gottes, noch Vergebung der Sünde.

Nun sagt aber unser Katechismus im dritten Artikel unsers christlichen Glaubens, der Mensch kann nichts aus eigener Vernunft noch־ Kraft an Jesum Christum gläuben oder zu ihm kommen, sondern der Heilige Geist müsse ihn zu solchem Glauben bringen, denn der Glaube ist eine Gabe Gottes; wie kömmt es denn, dass Gott dem Juda solchen Glauben nicht ins Herz gibt, dass er auch hätte glauben können, dass ihm könnte durch Christum geholfen werden?

Da müssen wir mit unsern Fragen wiederkehren, und sagen Röm. 11.: ,O, welch eine Tiefe des Reichthums, beide der Weisheit und Erkenntniss Gottes, wie gar unbegreiflich sind seine Gerichte und unerforschlich seine Wege! ' Wir können und sollen dies nicht ausforschen und uns in solche Gedanken zu weit vertiefen, sondern dies also gebrauchen, dass wir uns nicht vorsätzlich in die Sünde begeben und Gott versuchen, auf dass Gott nicht die Hand von uns abziehe und uns sinken lasse; denn, wo das geschieht, so fallen wir immer aus einer Sünde in die andere, und gleiten allmählich so tief in die Sünde hinein, dass hernach kein Wiederkehren ist, und wir nicht wiederum zum Stande greifen können.

Wie es mit dem Juda ist ergangen, der hebt erst gemach an, gehet mit den Almosen, die Christo von guten Leuten verehret und ihm zuvertrauet wurden, untreulich um, und als er darüber nicht alsbald von Gott gestraft wird, machet das ihn dreistig und kühne, dass er in Sünden fortfähret, und waget es immer ferner;

da er’s nu zu grob machet und Christus ihn fürnimmt, ihn ermahnet, warnet und straft, auch freundlich und väterlich ihn von seinem bösen Fürnehmen will abführen, gebraucht auch endlich einen gebührlichen Ernst und sagt: ,Es wäre dem Menschen besser, dass er nie geboren wäre‘, stellet sich hinwiederum gegen ihn so freundlich, wäschet ihm die Füsse, speiset ihn mit seinem Leib und Blut, vermahnet ihn mit freundlichen Worten zur Besserung; ja, das noch mehr ist: da er zu ihm kömmt mit der Schaar und Dienern der Hohenpriester, die ihn greifen wollten, und er unterm Schein der Freundschaft mit einem verrätherischen Herzen zu ihm tritt, gestattet er ihn zu sich und lässt sich von ihm küssen.

Und als Judas, nachdem er so viel schwere Sünde begangen hatte, noch weiter in Sicherheit dahin gehet und achtet dies alles nicht, da ziehet der Herr endlich die Hand von ihm abef und lässt ihn in Verzweiflung fallen.

Daraus sollen wir dies lernen, dass wir nicht wider unser Gewissen muthwillig sündigen und der Gnade Gottes missbrauchen, denn Gottes Gerichte sind unbegreiflich und unausforschlich, Röm. 11.

Derhalben soll niemand gedenken: Was schadet’s, ob ich bereit sündige und die Busse lange spare? Gott ist gnädig und barmherzig, der wird’s so genau nicht mit mir nehmen; wann ich ausgeraset habe, will ich mich dann einmal bekehren, so nimmt er mich bald zu Gnaden an. So gedenkt mancher und gehet darüber hin, und wann ihn Gott zur Busse ruft, meint er, es sei unverbeidet, er will noch wohl damit zu Masse kommen; gerade als wenn wir's in unsern Händen hätten, dass wir uns könnten zu Gott bekehren, wann wir nur wollten.

Aber dafür warnet uns die Epistel an die Ebräer am 3. aus dem 95. Psalm und sagt: ,Heute, so ihr hören werdet die Stimme Gottes, so verstocket eure Herzen nicht‘, gedenket nicht, wir haben noch Zeit genug uns zu bessern, wie eure Väter thaten in der Wüsten, denen ich Zeit gab 40 Jahr lang zur Besserung, aber sie entrüsteten mich, dass ich auch schwur in meinem Zorn, sie sollten zu meiner Ruhe nicht kommen.

Darum sagt die Epistel zun Hebräern: ,Sehet zu, lieben Kinder, dass ihr nicht ein solches arges, ungläubiges und unbussfertiges Herz habt, sondern ermahnet euch unter einander, PART. III. CAP. III.

so lange es heute heisst, dass ihr itzt die gnadenreiche Zeit nicht versäumt‘, dass ihr nicht auch verworfen werdet, wie die Väter in der Wüsten.

Wir sollen zwar uns nicht unterstehen, dass wir der Gnad und Barmherzigkeit Gottes wollten ein gewisse Mass und Ziel setzen, wie weit und ferne sich dieselbe erstrecke und wo sie wende; sondern das gebühret uns, dass wir fleissig Acht auf geben, so lang der Geist Gottes in uns sein Werk verrichtet mit Strafen, Warnen und Vermahnen, und in uns also arbeitet wider das Fleisch, so ist’s eine gewisse Anzeigung, dass uns Gott zur Busse ruft und uns in Gnaden gewogen ist und wollte uns gerne bekehren; wann du aber dies nicht achtest, sondern gehest dahin ohne Busse und Besserung, in aller Sicherheit, trittst alle Vermahnung aus dem Gesetz und Trost aus dem Evangelio mit Füssen, so sollst du wissen, Gott hat seine heimlichen, schrecklichen Gerichte und lässt solche muthwillige Sünder in einen verkehrten Sinn gerathen.“ (Passionspredigten. IV, 17—19.)


### On Faith in Christ: Heerbrandus: “Since faith is a special gift of God

Heerbrandus: “Since faith is a special gift of God: why is it given to one, but not to another? — God has reserved many things for Himself in this dispute which He has not revealed to us. Therefore, let us not indulge our own thoughts, but set a limit, so that we do not inquire further than what has been revealed to us in the Word.

God does whatever He can for the sake of our salvation. For He sent and gave His Son as the Savior of the world. He instituted the ministry of His Word, through which He wills that the Son be heard. And through the hearing of the Word, He works faith, through the mediation of the Holy Spirit. Since men do not wish to hear this, it is not at all surprising that they are also neglected by the Holy Spirit, and thus do not believe, nor are they saved.

For it is not for us to judge who hears with a mind to learn. And yet the Apostle rightly says that it is not of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. For the blindness and stupor of the human mind is too great for it to be able to grasp those mysteries of the kingdom of God of itself. Therefore, even if a man runs, wills, and hears for a long time, yet neither can the teacher give faith, nor can the hearer excite it in himself; but it is necessary that the motion of the Holy Spirit be added, without whom he who waters or plants is nothing, and likewise he who hears is nothing, but it is God who gives the increase; who nevertheless requires that external obedience of running, willing, and hearing, through which He Himself works faith.

But if the reason for the diversity is sought, why He gives faith to one and does not give it to another: it certainly cannot be found in God, who is equally disposed toward all. For He receives into grace all who believe in the Son, and condemns all unbelievers; according to His own words: ‘That whoever believes in the Son should not perish but have eternal life.’ And the Baptist in the same place: ‘He who believes in the Son has eternal life. But he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.’

Therefore, we have nothing else to answer here, except that it ought not to be otherwise; because He owes nothing to anyone, but has mercy on whom He wills; and that there is no injustice with Him. And let us say with the Apostle: ‘O man, who are you to reply against God? Will the thing formed say to him who formed it, Why have you made me like this?’” (Compend. th. 1582. p. 499—501.) §

11. The instrumental causes of our faith are the word of the Gospel and baptism. Which God uses freely in the production of faith, although He could also produce it without the mediation of an organ. Which is therefore called άχοή πίστεως, the preaching and hearing of faith, not only as of the object, but also as of the effect, Gal. 3:2 and 5. Namely, that ή πίστις έξ άχοής, ή δέ άχοη δίά ρήματος του θεου, faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of God, Rom. 10:17.

Augsburg Confession: "To obtain such faith, the ministry of teaching the Gospel and administering the Sacraments was instituted. For through the Word and Sacraments, as through instruments, the Holy Spirit is given, who works faith, where and when it pleases God, in those Augsburg Confession: "Concerning the use of the sacraments, they teach that the sacraments were instituted not only to be signs of profession among men, but rather that they be signs and testimonies of the will of God toward us, set forth to awaken and confirm faith in those who use them. Therefore, the sacraments are to be used in such a way that faith is added, which believes the promises that are exhibited and shown through the sacraments. They condemn, therefore, those who teach that the sacraments justify *ex opere operato*, and who do not teach that faith is required in the use of the sacraments, which believes that sins are remitted." (Art. 13, p. 42.)

Large Catechism: "In this same manner we also act with the baptism of children. We bring the child to be baptized by the minister of the church, with this hope and intention, that he certainly believes, and we pray that God may grant him faith." (Part IV, p. 494.)

Luther: "This which Cochlaeus boasts of most—that infants, since they are without faith, are justified through baptism—we strongly deny. But we say with Augustine: 'Not the sacrament, but the faith of the sacrament justifies.' And again: 'It justifies, not because it is done, but because it is believed.' But if Augustine says the contrary elsewhere, we follow him where he agrees with Scripture, and we leave him where he speaks apart from or against Scripture. In vain, therefore, has he scraped together the sayings of so many fathers, as if he would force us into the words of men, when we have so often testified that in the matter of consciences we embrace the word of no man, but of God alone, which alone pertains to God, and to no man, to rule and teach consciences. Yet we do not deny that infants are to be baptized, nor do we assert that they receive baptism without faith; but we say that they believe unto baptism through the power of the word by which they are exorcised, and through the faith of the church offering them and obtaining faith for them by its prayers. Otherwise, it would be mere and intolerable lying when the baptizer asks the infant whether he believes, not intending to baptize unless it is answered in his stead: 'I believe.' Why does he ask whether he believes, if it is certain that they do not believe, as Cochlaeus contends? Be it so, that Augustine sometimes says this, but let it be enough for Cochlaeus that it is said by a man; we want this saying proven by divine testimonies. Indeed, we assert that infants are not to be baptized at all if it is true that they do not believe in baptism, lest the sacrament and word of majesty be mocked. We owe this error of denied faith in infants to the sophists, who, like unclean animals, cite the sayings of men without judgment and at the same time teach contradictory things, while they deny that the infant has faith and yet, in order that he may be baptized, demand faith from him." (Adversus armatum virum Cocleum. 1523. Opp. lat. varii argum. Francof. ad M. 1873. VII, 54 sq. Opp. germ. XIX, 701 sq.)

The same: "Now the question is, what becomes of young children, since they have no reason yet and cannot believe for themselves, because it is written, Rom. 10:17: 'Faith comes by hearing, and hearing comes by the preaching of God's Word'? Now, young children do not hear or understand God's Word; therefore, they cannot have a faith of their own. To this question, the sophists in the high schools and the Pope's rabble have devised such an answer: that young children are baptized without their own faith, namely, upon the faith of the church, which the godparents confess at the baptism; thereafter, in the baptism, sin is forgiven the little child by the power and might of baptism, and a personal faith is infused with grace, so that a newborn child is born of water and the Holy Spirit. But when one asks them for the basis of such an answer and where that stands in Scripture, one finds it in a dark smoke-hole, or they point us to their birettas and say: 'We are the highly learned Doctors, and we say this, therefore it is right, you must not ask further.' ... Beware of this poison and error, even if it were the express opinion of all the fathers and councils; for it does not stand, it has no basis of Scripture for itself, but is vain human conceit and dreams; furthermore, it is directly and publicly..."

against the previous chief passages, where Christ says: "He who believes and is baptized," etc., so that it is briefly concluded that baptism helps no one, nor is it to be given to anyone, unless he believes for himself, and that no one is to be baptized without his own faith; just as St. Augustine himself says: *Non sacramentum justificat, sed fides sacramenti*, the sacrament does not justify, but the faith of the sacrament. . . .

Therefore we say here thus, and conclude: That children in baptism believe themselves and have their own faith, which God himself works in them through the intercession and bringing forward of the godparents in the faith of the Christian Church; and that we call the power of another’s faith; not that anyone may be saved through that same [faith], but that he may thereby, as through their intercession and help, obtain from God himself his own faith, through which he may be saved. . .

For this we have strong and firm passages: Matt. 19:13–15, Mark 10:13–16, Luke 18:15, 16; where some brought little children to the Lord Jesus that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them, he rebuked the disciples and embraced the children and laid his hands upon them and blessed them, and said: "Of such is the kingdom of God," etc. No one shall take these passages from us, nor refute them with good reason. For here it stands that Christ wants little children to be brought to him without hindrance; indeed, he commands them to be brought to him and blesses them and gives them the kingdom of heaven; let us well note that. . .

Latin:

Heerbrandus: ,,Cum fldes peculiare Dei donum sit: cur hoc uni datur, alii vero non? — Deus multa sibi in hac disputatione reservavit, quae nobis non patefecit. Ideo nostris cogitationibus non indulgeamus, sed metam ponamus, ne ultra inquiramus, quam nobis est revelatum in verbo.

Facit Deus, quicquid potest, salutis nostrae causa. Misit enim et donavit Fjlium suum mundi salvatorem. Instituit verbi sui ministerium, per quod Filium vult audiri. Et per verbi auditum fidem, mediante Spiritu Sancto, operatur. Hoc cum homines audire nolint, mirum est minime, quod etiam a Spiritu Sancto negligantur, et sic non credant, nec salventur.

Qui enim animo discendi audiat, nostrum non est judicare. Et tamen recte apostolus dicit, non esse currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Major enim est humana mentis coecitas et stupor, quam ut possit ex sese mysteria illa regni Dei capere. Igitur etsi diu homo currat, velit, audiat, tamen nec doctor fidem dare potest, nec auditor eam in se excitare; sed motus Spiritus Sancti accedat necesse est, absque quo nihil est, qui rigat aut plantat, ita nec qui audit, sed qui dat incrementum, Deus; qui tamen externam illam requirit obedientiam currendi, volendi, audiendi, per quae ipse fidem operatur.

Quodsi diversitatis ratio quaeratur, cur uni det fidem, alteri non det: certe in Deo reperiri non potest, qui aequaliter erga omnes est affectus. Kecipit enim in gratiam omnes credentes in Filium, et damnat omnes incredulos; juxta illud ipsiusmet: ,Ut omnis, qui credit in Filium, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam.‘ Et baptista ibidem: ,Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam. Qui autem incredulus est Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum.‘

Ideo hic, quid respondeamus, aliud non habemus, nisi quod aliter fieri non debeat; quia nemini quicquam debet, sed quorum vult, miseretur; et non esse injustitiam apud eum. Et cum apostolo dicamus: ,0 homo, tu quis es, qui ex adverso respondes Deo?‘ Num dicit figmentum fictori suo: Cur me ad hunc finxisti modum?“ (Compend. th. 1582. p. 499—501.) §

11. Causa instrumentalis a fidei nostrae sunt verbum b evangelii et c baptismus. Qua Deus libere utitur in productione fidei, cum hanc etiam non mediante organo producere posset. Quod propterea dicitur άχοή πίστεως, praedicatio et auditus fidei, non solum tanquam objecti, verum etiam ut effectus, Gal. 3, 2. et 5. Nimirum quod ή πίστις έξ άχοής, ή δέ άχοη δίά ρήματος του θεου, fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per verbum Dei, Rom. 10, 17.

Conf. Augustana: ,,Ut hanc fidem consequamur, institutum est ministerium docendi evangelii et porrigendi sacramenta. Nam per verbum et sacramenta tamquam per instrumenta donatur Spiritus S., qui fidem efficit, ubi et quando est visum Deo, in iis, qui audinnt evangelium, sci. quod Deus non propter nostra merita, sed propter Christum justificet hos, qui credunt, se propter Christum in gratiam recipi. Damnant (ecclesiae apud nos) Anabaptistas et alios, qui sentiunt, Spiritum S. contingere sine verbo externo hominibus per ipsorum praeparationes et opera.“ (Artic. 5. p. 39. sq.)
