Articuli Smalcaldici: ,,In his, quae vocale et externum verbum concernunt, constanter tenendum est, Deum nemini Spiritum vel gratiam suam largiri, nisi per verbum et cum verbo externo et praecedente, ut ita praemuniamus nos adversus enthusiastas, id est, spiritus, qui jactitant, se ante verbum et sine verbo Spiritum habere, et ideo Scripturam sive vocale verbum judicant, flectunt et reflectunt pro libito, ut faciebat Monetarius et multi adhuc hodie, qui acute discernere volunt inter spiritum et literam, et neutrum norunt nec, quid statuant, sciunt. Quid? quod etiam papatus simpliciter est merus entjiusiasmus, quo papa gloriatur, omnia jura esse in scrinio sui pectoris, et quidquid ipse in ecclesia sua sentit et jubet, id Spiritum et justum esse, etiamsi supra et contra Scripturam et vocale verbum aliquid statuat et praecipiat. Hoc in universum antiquus est satanas et serpens, qui ·etiam Adamum et Evam in enthusiasmum conjiciebat et ab externo verbo Dei ad spiritualitates et proprias opiniones abducebat, id quod tamen et ipse per alia externa verba perficiebat. Perinde ac hodie nostri enthusiastae externum verbum damnant, et tamen ipi non silent, sed mundum garrulitatibus et scriptionibus implent, quasi vero Spiritus per scripta et vocale verbum apostolorum venire nequeat, sed per ipsorum verba et scripta primum veniat. Cur ergo non ipsi etiam omittunt suas conciones et scriptiones, donec Spiritus ipse ad homines sine ipsorum scriptis et ante ea veniat, quemadmodum gloriantur, Spiritum se accepisse sine praedicatione Scripturarum. . . Nam etiam ii, qui ante baptismum credunt vel in baptismo credere incipiunt, per externum praecedens verbum credunt, ut adulti; audiunt enim (Mare. 16,16.): ,Quicunque crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit‘, etiamsi primum increduli post decennium accipiant Spiritum et baptismum. Cornelius Act. 10, 1. sqq. longe ante audierat apud Judaeos de venturo messia, per quem justus coram Deo preces et eleemosynas Deo gratas praestabat ex fide (sicut Lucas eum nominat justum, pium et timentem Dei) et sine praecedente illo verbo atque auditu credere et justus esse non poterat. Petrus autem patefacere ei jubebatur, messiam (in quem venturum hactenus ille crediderat) jam advenisse, ut fides ejus de venturo messia eum apud induratos et incredulos Judaeos non captivum teneret, sed ut sciret, se salvandum esse per praesentem messiam, et hunc cum Judaeorum turba non negaret nec persequeretur etc. Quid multis? Enthusiasmus insitus est Adamo et filiis ejus a primo lapsu usque ad finem mundi, ab antiquo dracone ipsis veneno quodam implantatus et infusus, estque omnium haeresium et papatus et Mahometismi origo, vis, vita et potentia. Quare in hoc nobis est constanter perseverandum, quod Deus non velit nobiscum aliter agere, nisi per vocale verbum et sacramenta et quod, quidquid sine verbo et sacramentis jactatur, ut Spiritus, sit ipse diabolus.“(P.III. art. 8. p. 321. sq.) Saltem respectu infantum, qui per baptismum concipiunt fidem (etsi non aeque nobis explicabilem, ut est fides adultorum, de qua hic maxime agimus); quod infra suo loco disertius docebitur. Quanquam et obsignandae atque confirmandae fidei adultorum, qui jam ex verbo conceperunt fidem, per modum organi efficacis destinatus est et prodest; de quo similiter infra videbimus. PART. III. CAP. ΙΠ. Confessio Augustana: ״De usu sacramentorum docent, quod sacramenta instituta sint, non modo ut sint notae professionis inter homines, sed magis ut sint signa et testimonia voluntatis Dei erga nos ad excitandam et confirmandam fidem in his, qui utuntur, proposita. Itaque utendum est sacramentis ita, ut fides accedat, quae credat promissionibus, quae per sacramenta exhibentur et ostenduntur. Damnant igitur illos, qui docent, quod sacramenta ex opere operato justificent, nec docent, fidem requiri in usu sacramentorum, quae credat remitti peccata.“ (Artic. 13. p. 42.)

Catechismus major: ״Ad hunc modum cum puerorum baptismo׳ quoque facimus. Puerum ecclesiae ministro baptizandum apportamus, hac spe atque animo, quod certo credat, et precamur, ut Deus eum fide donet.“ (IV. P. p. 494.)

Lutherus: ״Hoc, quod maxime jactat Cocleus, parvulos, cum sint sine fide, per baptismum justificari, fortiter negamus. Sed dicimus cum Augustino: ,Non sacramentum, sed fides sacramenti justificat.‘ Et iterum: ,Justificat, non quia fit, sed quia creditur.‘ Quodsi Augustinus alibi contrarium dicit, sequimur eum, ubi cum scriptura sentit, et relinquimus, ubi citra vel contra scripturam loquitur. Frustra igitur corrasit tot patrum dicta, quasi nos in hominum verba coacturus, cum toties testati simus, nos in re conscientiarum nullius hominis, sed solius Dei verbum amplecti, quod soli Deo, nulli homini conveniat, conscientias regere et docere. Non tamen negamus, parvulos esse baptizandos, nec asserimus, eos baptismum accipere sine fide, sed dicimus, ad baptismum eos credere per vim verbi, quo exorcisantur, et per fidem ecclesiae, eos offerentis et eis fidem orationibus suis impetrantis. Alioqui mera et intolerabilia essent mendacia, quando baptisans a parvulo quaerit, an credat, non baptisaturus, nisi vice ejus respondeatur: ,Credo.‘ Ut quid interrogat, an credat, si certum est, eos non credere? ut Cocleus contendit. Esto, Augustinus sic aliquanda dicat, sed Cocleo satis sit esse sic ab homine dictum, nos volumus hoc dictum divinis testimoniis probatum. Quin asserimus, parvulos prorsus non esse baptisandos, si verum est, eos in baptismo non credere, ne illudatur majestatis sacramentum et verbum. Debemus autem et hunc negatae iii parvulis fidei errorem sophistis, qui hominum dicta,, sicut animalia immunda, vocant sine judicio et simul contraria docent, dum negant parvulo esse fidem et tamen, ut baptisari possit, exigunt ab eo fidem.“ (Adversus armatum virum Cocleum. 1523. Opp. lat.. varii argum. Francof. ad M. 1873. VII, 54. sq. Opp. germ. XIX, 701. sq.)

Idem: ״Nun ist die Frage, wo die jungen Kinder bleiben, so sie doch noch keine Vernunft haben und für sich selbst nicht mögen gläuben, weil so geschrieben stehet, Röm. 10, 17.: ,Der Glaube kommt durchs Hören, das Hören aber kommt durchs Predigen Gottes Wort‘?· Nun hören noch verstehen ja die jungen Kinder Gottes Wort nicht; so mögen sie auch keinen eigenen Glauben haben. Auf diese Frage haben die Sophisten in hohen Schulen und des Pabsts Rotte eine solche Antwort erdichtet, dass die jungen Kinder werden ohn eigenen Glauben getauft, nämlich auf den Glauben der Kirche, welchen die Pathen bekennen bei der Taufe; darnach in der Taufe werde dem Kindlein aus Kraft und Macht der Taufe die Sünde vergeben und eigener Glaube eingegossen mit Gnaden, dass ein neugeboren Kind wird aus dem Wasser und Heiligen Geist. Wenn man sie aber fraget um den Grund solcher Antwort und wo das in der Schrift stehe, so findet mans im finstern Rauchloch, oder weisen uns auf ihre Birret und sagen: Wir sind die hochgelehrten Doctores, und sagen solches, darum ists recht, darfst nicht weiter fragen. . . Vor diesem Gift und Irrthum hüte dich, wenn es gleich aller Väter und Concilien ausgedrückte Meinung wäre; denn sie bestehet nicht, hat keinen Giund der Schrift für sich, sondern eitel Menschendünkel und Träume; darzu ist sie stracks und öffentlich

wider die vorigen Hauptsprüche, da Christus spricht: ,Wer gläubt und getauft wird‘ u. s. w., dass kurzum beschlossen ist, Taufe hilft niemand, ist auch niemand zu geben, er glaube denn für sich selbst, und ohn eigenen Glauben niemand zu taufen ist; wie auch St. Augustin selbst spricht: Non sacramentum justificat, sed fldes sacramenti, das Sacrament machet nicht gerecht, sondern der Glaube des Sacraments. . . .

Darum sagen wir hier also zu, und schliessen: Dass die Kinder in der Taufe selbst gläuben und eigenen Glauben haben, den selbsten Gott in ihnen wirket durch das Fürbitten und Herzubringen der Pathen im Glauben der christlichen Kirche; und das heissen wir die Kraft des fremden Glaubens; nicht, dass jemand durch denselben möge selig werden, sondern dass er dadurch, als durch seine Fürbitte und Hülfe, möge von Gott selbst einen eigenen Glauben erlangen, dadurch er selig werde. . .

Dess haben wir starke und feste Sprüche Matth. 19,13—15. Marc. 10, 13—16. Luc. 18, 15. 16.; da etliche dem Herrn Jesu Kindlein zubrachten, dass er sie anrührete, und die Jünger ihnen wehreten, strafet er die Jünger und herzet die Kinder und legt die Hände auf sie, und segnet sie, und sprach: ,Solcher ist das Reich Gottes, u. s. w. Diese Sprüche wird uns niemand nehmen, noch sie mit gutem Grund widerlegen. Denn hier stehet es, dass Christus will unverboten haben, die Kindlein zu ihm zu bringen, ja, heisset sie zu ihm bringen und segnet sie und gibt ihnen das Himmelreich; das lasset uns wohl merken. . .


### On Faith in Christ: Now he is as present in baptism as he was at that time, that we Christians know…

Now he is as present in baptism as he was at that time, that we Christians know for certain: therefore we must not forbid children baptism. Thus we must also not doubt that he blesses them all who come there, as he did those. So there remains now nothing here but the devotion and the faith of those who brought the little children to him; the same ones make and help through their bringing that the little children are blessed and attain the kingdom of heaven; which cannot be, unless they have their own faith for themselves, as has been said. Thus we also say here that the little children are brought to baptism indeed through another’s faith and work, but when they have come there and the priest or baptizer deals with them in Christ’s stead, then he blesses them and gives them faith and the kingdom of heaven; for the priest’s word and deed are Christ’s own word and work." (Kirchenpostille. XI, 667. sq. 669. 672. 673. 674. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Carpzovius: "As far as regeneration strictly so-called is concerned, which precedes justification, and indeed as it occurs in infants, there certainly baptism operates even without faith, and it behaves as an operating instrument, and operates by way of *opus operatum*, as the scholastics speak, and that Bellarmine (l. 2. de Sacr. c. 1. from Sess. VII. Can. VIII. of the Council of Trent) defines, that it does not presuppose, nor even require, a good motion in the subject, but introduces it. For in infants, baptism does not 'excite' faith, as in adults who already have it from the Word, but operates it primarily. But in order for baptism to operate faith, faith is not required; otherwise there would be a progression to infinity." (Isagog. in libb. symb. p. 1091.) §

12. The subject of faith in Christ is man, a sinner, regenerated or converted; and not only an adult, but in his own way also an infant. Or the suppositum, which is denominated believing or faithful: PART III. CHAP. III.

Both actual [faith], which is elicited and received within man; and habitual [faith], which exists in him by way of a quality perfecting its subject. For there is no longer any place to speak of the faith that was in the angels who were wayfarers. See above, Part I, Chapter III, § 21, note c, Vol. II, p. 120.

For just as Christ was given to men not as whole, but as fallen, so faith in Christ is to be sought not in the whole man, but in the sinner. For the unregenerate lack faith, which does not exist in us by nature, but proceeds by grace from the Father of lights, by whom we are begotten, James 1:17, 18. Compare 1 Pet. 1:3, 5, 21, 23, and what will be said in the following chapter IV, § 1 and 5.

Quenstedtius: "The matter of saving faith is twofold, in which and concerning which, or subjective and objective. The subject matter or the subject of faith is again twofold, total or partial. The total subject is not only the elect (as the Calvinists maintain; hence Bucanus, Book 29, question 19: 'Faith is not of all, but of the elect only'), but all regenerate men, or those instructed with the powers of believing through the grace of regeneration, whether they be infants or adults; for even infants are capable of actual (not merely potential) direct (not reflex) faith... The partial or inadequate subject is partly the intellect, partly the will, according to the different respect of faith." (L. c. P. IV. c. 8. s. 1. th. 12. p. 1340.)

For before conversion, men are in darkness, lacking the light of faith, Acts 26:18, Ephesians 5:8. Compare the following chapter, § 1 and 17.

What we have said thus far about faith undoubtedly applies to adults. Indeed, baptized infants, just as those circumcised in the Old Testament, truly believe in Christ, Matthew 18:6, Mark 9:42. Whence also the kingdom of heaven is theirs, Mark 10:14. Nor can it be said that that faith exists formally outside the infants in their parents or sponsors, or that it consists in an idle habit; but actual faith, no less than habitual faith, must be ascribed to infants.

Nevertheless, the nature of that faith is less explicable to us, since we more easily grasp the faith drawn by adults from the preached and read Word, which is commonly described.

Regarding the faith of infants, however, we judge rightly with the blessed M. Chemnitius in *Exam. Conc. Trid.*, Part II, on Baptism, to Canon XIII, p. 91: When it is said that infants believe, it is not to be imagined that infants understand or feel the motions of faith; but the error of those is rejected who imagine that baptized infants please God and are saved without any action of the Holy Spirit in them, since Christ clearly says, unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, etc. Therefore, it is necessary that the Holy Spirit be effective and work in infants who are baptized, so that they may be… able to receive the kingdom of God, which is offered and given in baptism, in a way of their own, which is neither sufficiently known to us nor explicable. See more in the same place.

Gerhardus: "We demonstrate the faith of infants inserted into the divine covenant through circumcision in the Old Testament and through baptism in the New Testament from the following foundations: 1. Scripture attributes faith to them in clear and express words. Matthew 18:6, Mark 9:42... 2. When the properties and the immediate effect of a thing are posited, the thing itself is posited. Infants circum

cised in the Old Testament and baptized in the New Testament. Scripture attributes the properties and effects of faith to them. Therefore. Ps. 8:3; 22:10; 71:6; 115:13, 14; 1 John 2:14; 5:4; Rev. 11:18. ...

3. Baptized infants are righteous and pleasing to God. But we are righteous and pleasing to God by faith in Christ alone. ...

4. Either faith must be attributed to infants, or salvation must be denied to them. To deny them salvation is cruel and impious. Therefore, neither is faith to them…and impious. Therefore, faith must not be denied to them. ...

They object that the sayings of Scripture which testify that we are made saved by faith in Christ are to be understood only of adults. Resp.: There is one Christ, one faith, one salvation, one mode of justification and salvation, as the whole of Scripture testifies. The pronouncements of the Holy Spirit are general: "Without faith it is impossible to please God." "He who does not believe will be condemned." "He who is unbelieving toward the Son, the wrath of God will remain upon him." Where, therefore, Scripture does not distinguish, neither ought we to distinguish. Besides faith, no medium can be given by which Christ, outside of whom no one can be saved, is apprehended. (Loc. de bapt. § 218—222.)

The same: "A good tree in the middle of winter is not deprived of the property of producing good fruits, although it does not appear outwardly; and shall we deny faith to infants because they do not produce the external fruits of the same? As the matter stands with seeds and shoots of trees: although they do not bear fruit, yet the power and nature are in them to produce fruit in their own time: so the faith of infants exerts its external ενέργειαν in its own time and bears fruits pleasing to God." (L. c. § 220.)

Chemnitius: "Mark 10. Christ affirms that adults receive the kingdom of God just as little children receive it. And Matt. 18 he says: 'Whoever shall offend one of these little ones who believe in me.' And among these little ones he also counts παιδίον, a little child. Furthermore, circumcision in general is called 'a seal of the righteousness of faith' (Rom. 4). But if the righteousness of faith is attributed to circumcised infants, then faith itself is also attributed to them. ... And that the Holy Spirit can effect this in infants not yet using reason, although the mode and manner can neither be comprehended nor explained by us, there is no doubt, as He shows by a manifest example in John the Baptist. For concerning his leaping, the angel says: 'He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb.' That singular example certainly does not make a common rule, yet it shows that the Holy Spirit can work even in infants." (Exam. Concil. Trid. Ed. Genev. f. 246. sq.)

Luther: "To this also agrees St. John in his first epistle, chapter 2:14, where he says: 'I write to you, fathers; I write to you, young men; I write to you, children'; he is not content that he writes to the young men, he writes also to the children; and writes that they have known the Father. From this it follows indeed that the apostles also baptized children, and held that they believe and know the Father, just as if they had come to reason and could read. Although someone might wish to interpret the word 'children' here as referring to the elders, as Christ sometimes calls his disciples, it is nevertheless certain that he speaks here of those who are younger than the young men, so that it sounds as if he is speaking of the young crowd that is under fifteen or eighteen years of age, and he excludes no one from those years down to the first year; for all these are called children. But we want to see their reason why they do not hold the children to be believers. They say: Because they have not yet come to reason, they cannot hear God's Word; but where God's Word is not heard, there can be no faith, Rom. 10:17: 'Faith comes by hearing, but hearing comes by the Word of God,' etc. Tell me, is that also Christianly spoken, thus to judge of God's works according to our own opinion: The children have not come to reason, therefore they cannot believe? What if you, through such reason, had already fallen away from faith, and the children, through their lack of reason, had come to faith? Dear friend, what good does reason do for faith and God's Word? Is it..." PART III. CHAPTER III. not it, which resists faith and the Word of God in the highest degree, so that no one can come to faith before it, nor will it suffer God’s Word, unless it be blinded and shamed; that man must die to it, and become like a fool, and indeed as unreasonable and lacking in understanding as a young child, if he is to become a believer and receive God’s grace; as Christ says in Matthew 18:3: ‘Unless you turn and become like young children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.’ How often does Christ hold before us that we must become children and fools, and condemns reason! Item, tell me, what kind of reason did the little children have, whom Christ embraced and blessed and assigned to heaven? Were they not also still without reason? Why then does He call for them to be brought to Him, and bless them? Where do they get such faith that makes them children of the kingdom of heaven? Yes, precisely because they are without reason and foolish, they are better suited for faith than the old and the reasonable, for whom reason always lies in the way and will not push its big head through the narrow door. One must not look here at reason or its works when one speaks of faith and God’s works. Here God works alone, and reason is dead, blind, and toward this work like an unreasoning block; so that the Scripture may stand, which says: ‘God is wondrous in His saints.’ Item, Isaiah 55:9: ‘As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways, and My thoughts than your thoughts.’ ... Furthermore, tell me, where does the reason of the Christian believer remain when he sleeps, while yet his faith and God’s grace never leave him? Can faith remain here without the cooperation of reason, so that it is not aware of it; why then should it not begin in children before reason knows anything about it? Item, I would also say the same of all stations in which a Christian lives, and works or has something to do, that he is not aware of faith and reason, and yet faith does not cease on that account. God’s works are secret and wondrous, where and when He wills; again, also manifest enough, where and when He wills, so that it is too high and too deep for us to judge.” (Kirchenpostille. XI. p. 675—677. 678.)

Latin:

Nun ist er in der Taufe so gegenwärtig, als er dazumal war, das wissen wir Christen gewiss: darum wir nicht dürfen wehren den Kindern die Taufe. So dürfen wir auch nicht zweifeln, er segne sie alle, die dahin kommen, wie er jenen that. So bleibt nun hier nichts mehr, denn die Andacht und der Glaube derjenigen, die die Kindlein zu ihm brachten; dieselbigen machen und helfen durch ihr Zubringen, dass die Kindlein gesegnet werden und das Himmelreich erlangen; welches nicht sein kann, sie haben denn eigenen Glauben für sich selbst, wie gesaget ist. Also sagen wir auch hier, dass die Kindlein zur Taufe gebracht werden wohl durch fremden Glauben und Werk, aber wenn sie dahin kommen sind und der Priester oder Täufer mit ihnen handelt an Christi Statt, so segnet er sie und gibt ihnen den Glauben und das Himmelreich; denn des Priesters Wort und That sind Christi selbst Wort und Werk.“ (Kirchenpostille. XI, 667. sq. 669. 672. 673. 674. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Carpzovius: ,,Quod regenerationem stricte dictam attinet, quae justificationi antecedit, et quidem prout in infantibus fit, ibi certe etiam absque fide operatur baptismus, atque se habet ut organum operans, operaturque per modum operis operati, ut scholastici loquuntur, istudque Bellarm. 1. 2. de Sacr. c. 1. ex Sess. VII. Can. IIX. Cone. Trid. definit, quod non praesupponat, neque etiam requirat bonum motum in subjecto, sed introducat eum. In infantibus enim baptismus non,excitat‘ fidem, sicut in adultis jam ex verbo eam habentibus, sed primitus operatur. Ut autem baptismus fidem operetur, non requiritur fides, alias daretur progressus in infinitum.“ (Isagog. in libb. symb. p. 1091.) §

12. ·Subjectum quod a fidei b in Christum est homo c peccator d regenitus e aut conversus;f nec solum adultus,g sed suo modo etiam infans.h Sive suppositum, quod denominatur credens aut fidele: PART. III. CAP. III.

Cum actualis, quae intra hominem elicitur et recipitur; tum habitualis, quae eidem inexistit per modum qualitatis perficientis suum subjectum. Nam de fide, quae in angelis viatoribus fuit, jam non est locus dicere. Vid. supra P. I. cap. III. § 21. not. c. Vol. II. p. 120.

Sicut enim Christus hominibus, non integris, sed lapsis, datus est mediator; ita fides in Christum non in homine integro, sed peccatore, quaerenda est. Irregeniti enim carent fide, quae per naturam nobis non inest, sed per gratiam a Patre luminum proficiscentem, a quo progignimur, Jacobi 1, 17. 18. Confer. 1 Pet. 1, 3. 5. 21. 23. et quae cap. seq. IV dicentur § 1. et 5.

Quenstedtius: ,,Materia fidei salvificae duplex est, in qua et circa quam sive subjectiva et objectiva. Materia subjecta vel subjectum fidei iterum duplex est, totale vel partiale. Totale subjectum sunt non soli electi (ut volunt Calviniani; hinc Bucanus L. 29. qu. 19.: ,Fides non est omnium, sed electorum tantum‘), sed omnes homines renati sive viribus credendi per gratiam regenerationis instructi, sive infantes illi sint, sive adulti; nam et infantes capaces sunt fidei directae (non reflexae) actualis (non nude potentialis). . . Subjectum partiale seu inadaequatum est partim intellectus, partim voluntas, pro diverso fidei respectu.“ (L. c. P. IV. c. 8. s. 1. th. 12. f. 1340.)

Ante conversionem enim homines sunt in tenebris, luce fidei carentes, Act. 26, 18. Ephes. 5, 8. Confer cap. seq. § 1. et 17.

Adultis haud dubie competunt, quae hactenus de fide diximus. Nimirum infantes quidem baptizati, uti quondam in V. T. circumcisi, revera quidem credunt in Christum, Matth. 18, 6. Marci 9, 42. Unde etiam illorum est regnum coelorum, Marci 10, lJp. Neque fidem illam vel extra infantes in parentibus aut sponsoribus formaliter esse, vel in otioso habitu consistere, dici potest; sed actualis non minus quam habitualis fides infantibus adscribenda est.

Attamen natura fidei illius nobis minus est explicabilis, cum fidem ex verbo praedicato et lecto ab adultis haustam, ac vulgo describi solitam, facilius assequamur.

De fide infantum autem cum b. M. Chemnitio in Exam. Cone. Trid. Part. II. de Bapt. ad Can. XIII. p. m. 91. juxta Formulam Concor d. inter Theologos Saxoniae et superioris Germaniae 1536. constitutam recte judicamus: Quando dicitur, infantes credere, non esse imaginan־ dum, infantes intelligere, aut sentire motus fidei; sed rejici errorem illorum, qui imaginantur, infantes baptizatoδ placere Deo et salvos fieri sine actione aliqua Spiritus Sancti in eis, cum Christus clare dicat, nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu etc. Ergo oportet Spiritum Sanctum in infantibus, qui baptizantur, efficacem esse et operari, ut regnum Dei, quod in baptismo offertur et donatur, accipere possint, suo quodam modo, nobis nec satis cognito, nec explicabili. Vid. plura 1. c.

Gerhardus: ,,Infantum per circumcisionem in V. et per baptismum in N. T. foedere divino insertorum fidem demonstramus ex sequentibus fundamentis: 1. Scriptura disertis et expressis verbis fidem illis tribuit. Matth. 18, 6. Mare. 9, 42. . . 2. Positis proprietatibus et immediato alicujus rei effectu res ipsa ponitur. Infantibus circum

cisis in V. et baptizatis in N. T. Scriptura tribuit proprietates et effecta fidei. Ergo. Ps. 8, 3. 22, 10. 71, 6. 115, 13. 14. 1 Joh. 2, 14. 5, 4. Apoc. 11, 18. . .

3. Infantes baptizati justi sunt ac Deo placent. Jam vero sola fide in Christum sumus justi ac Deo placemus. . .

4. Infantibus aut fides tribuenda, aut salus deneganda. Salutem illis denegare, crudele est et impium. Ergo nec fides eis deneganda. ..

Excipiunt, de adultis solum intelligenda Scripturae dicta, quae testantur, nos fide in Christum fleri salvos. Resp.: Unus Christus, una fides, una salus, unus justificationis et salvationis modus teste tota Scriptura. Generalia sunt Sp. Sancti pronuntiata: ,Sine fide impossibile est Deo placere. Qui non credit, condemnabitur. Qui incredulus est Filio, ira Dei manebit super eum/ Ubi ergo Scr. non distinguit, nec nos distinguere debemus. Praeter fidem nullum dari potest medium, quo Christus, extra quem nemo salvari potest, apprehendatur/‘ (Loc. de bapt. § 218—222.)

Idem: ,,Arbor bona in media hyeme non destituitur proprietate bonos fructus proferendi, quamvis exterius id non appareat, et nos fidem infantibus ex eo negabimus, quod externos ejusdem fructus non proferant? Ut in seminibus et surculis arborum res se habet: quanquam non ferunt fructus, tamen inest eis vis et natura, ut fructus suo tempore producant: sic infantum fides ενέργειαν exteriorem suo tempore exserit et fert fructus Deo placentes.“ (L. c. § 220.)

Chemnitius: ,,Mare. 10. Christus affirmat, adultos ita accipere regnum Dei, sicut parvuli illud accipiunt. Et Matth. 18. inquit: ,Qui scandalizaverit unum ex pusillis istis, qui in me credunt/ Et inter pusillos istos etiam παιόίον, puerulum, numerat. Praeterea circumcisio in genere vocatur,signaculum justitiae fidei‘ Rom. 4. Quod si infantibus circumcisis tribuitur justitia fidei, ergo etiam ipsa fides illis tribuitur. . . Et Spiritum Sanctum in infantibus, nondum ratione utentibus, hoc efficere posse, licet modus et ratio a nobis nec comprehendi, nec explicari possit, non est dubium, sicut manifesto exemplo in Joanne baptista ostendit. De ejus enim exultatione angelus inquit: ,Replebitur Spiritu Sancto adhunc in utero matris/ Singulare sane illud exempium non facit regulam communem, ostendit tamen, Spiritum Sanctum etiam in infantibus operari posse.“ (Exam. Concil. Trid. Ed. Genev. f. 246. sq.)

Lutherus: ,,Hierzu stimmet auch St. Johannes in seiner ersten Epistel Cap. 2, 14., da er spricht: ,Ich schreibe euch Vätern, ich schreibe euch Jünglingen, ich schreibe euch Kindern‘; lässt ihm nicht begnügen, dass er den Jünglingen schreibet, schreibet apch den Kindern; und schreibet, sie haben den Vater erkannt. Daraus folget je, dass die Apostel haben auch die Kinder getauft, und dafür gehalten, sie gläuben und kennen den Vater, gerade als wären sie zur Vernunft kommen und könnten lesen. Wiewohl das Wort,Kinder‘ allhier jemand möchte deuten auf die Alten, wie Christus seine Jünger etwa nennet, so ist es doch gewiss, dass er hier redet von denen, die jünger sind, denn die Jünglinge, dass es lautet, er rede von dem jungen Haufen, der unter fünf zehen oder achtzehen Jahren ist, und nimmt niemand aus von den Jahren bis auf das erste Jahr; denn das heissen alle Kinder. Aber wir wollen doch sehen ihre Ursache, warum sie die Kinder nicht gläubig halten. Sie sprechen: Weil sie noch nicht zur Vernunft sind kommen, mögen sie Gottes Wort nicht hören; wo aber Gottes Wort nicht gehöret wird, da kann kein Glaube sein, Röm. 10,17.: ,Der Glaube kommt durch das Hören, das Hören aber kommt durch Gottes Wort‘ u. s. w. Sage mir, ist das auch christlich geredet, also von Gottes Werken urtheilen nach unserm Dünken: Die Kinder sind nicht zur Vernunft kommen, darum können sie nicht gläuben? Wie, wenn du durch solche Vernunft wärest schon vom Glauben kommen, und die Kinder durch ihre Unvernunft zum Glauben kommen? Lieber, was Gutes thut die Vernunft zum Glauben und Gottes Wort? ΙΠ. nicht sie, die dem Glauben und Wort Gottes auf das höheste widerstehet, dass niemand vor ihr zum Glauben kann kommen, noch Gottes Wort leiden will, sie werde denn geblendet und geschändet; dass der Mensch muss ihr absterben, und gleich werden ein Narr, und ja so unvernünftig und unverständig, als kein jung Kind, soll er anders gläubig werden und Gottes Gnade empfahen; wie Christus spricht Matth. 18, 3.: ,Wenn ihr nicht umkehren werdet, und werdet wie die jungen Kinder, so werdet ihr nicht in das Himmelreich kommen.‘ Wie oft hält uns Christus für, dass wir zu Kindern und Narren werden müssen, und verdammt die Vernunft I Item, sage mir, was hatten die Kindlein für eine Vernunft, die Christus herzte und segnete und dem Himmel zutheilete? Waren sie nicht auch noch ohne Vernunft? Warum heisst er sie denn zu ihm bringen, und segnet sie? Wo haben sie solchen Glauben her, der sie zu Kindern des Himmelreichs machet? Ja, eben weil sie ohne Vernunft und närrisch, sind sie besser zum Glauben geschickt, denn die Alten und Vernünftigen, welchen die Vernunft immer im Wege liegt und will ihren grossen Kopf nicht durch die enge Thüre stossen. Man muss hier nicht Vernunft noch ihre Werke ansehen, wenn man vom Glauben und Gottes Werken redet. Hier wirket Gott allein, und die Vernunft ist todt, blind und gegen diesem Werke wie ein unvernünftig Block; auf dass bestehe die Schrift, die da saget: ,Gott ist wunderlich in seinen Heiligen.‘ Item Es. 55, 9.: ,So viel der Himmel höher ist, denn die Erde, so sind auch meine Wege höher, denn eure Wege, und meine Gedanken, denn eure Gedanken.‘ . . Dazu sage mir, w״o bleibet die Vernunft des Christgläubigen, wenn er schläft, so doch sein Glaube und Gottes Gnade ihn nimmer lässt? Kann hier der Glaube ohne Zuthun der Vernunft bleiben, dass sie es nicht gewahr wird; warum sollte er auch nicht anfahen in den Kindern, ehe die Vernunft darum etwas weiss? Item, so möchte ich auch sagen von allen Ständen, darin ein Christ lebet, und etwas arbeitet oder zu schaffen hat, dass er des Glaubens und Vernunft nicht gewahr wird, und doch darum der Glaube nicht ablässet. Gottes Werke sind heimlieh und wunderlich, wo und wenn er will; wiederum, auch offenbarlieh gnug, wo und wenn er will, dass uns darüber zu urtheilen zu hoch und zu tief ist.“ (Kirchenpostille. XI. p. 675—677. 678.)


### On Faith in Christ: ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who attribute a bare and idle habit of faith or a first act of faith to infants, but deny actual faith to them. This opinion was proposed at the Council of Vienne in the year 1311, the decree of which is handed down in Constit. Clement. 1. de Summa Trinit. The same is defended by Thomas, Scotus, Durandus, Gabr. Biel, etc., in 3. dist. 23., as witnessed by Bellarmine 1.1. de baptismo c. 11. The Council of Trent, sess. 7. can. 13, defined it as certain... 2. Of the Calvinists, who take away actual and saving faith from infants. Yet these themselves are carried away into various divisions of opinion. For some 1.) deny all faith to infants, and consider this doctrine, along with the Papists, to be a fabrication; thus Cunaeus 1. 3. de Rep. Hebr. c. 9.: ‘I am not unaware,’ he says, ‘that there exist writings of very serious men who maintain that there is in infants, according to their capacity, a certain power of holy faith. But this is so foolish that it is worthy of being punished with lashes. For the voice of the Apostle is Rom. 10:17: ὅτι ἡ πίστις ἐξ ἀκοῆς, that faith is from hearing; let us add, also from assent.’ ... Piscator notes on Matthew 21:14: ‘The kingdom of heaven can belong to infants, even if they do not believe, provided they are elect. For faith is nowhere required in Scripture except from adults, as those who are capable of hearing, through which faith is given.’ ... 2.) Others seize upon the ἐπέχειν [suspension of judgment] here, whence Whitaker, praelect. de Sacram, qu. 4. c. 5., praises the prudence and modesty of Calvin, ‘who dared to define nothing rashly here.’ But although Calvin, 1. 4. Instit. c. 16. § 19, says that he prefers to leave in suspense what is to be thought concerning the faith of infants in this life,”

although he rashly affirms something, yet soon § 20 and in *Antidoto Conc. Trid.* f. 280 sq., he handles the matter in such a way that he not obscurely denies true faith to them...

8.) Others attribute faith to infants neither ἐνεργείᾳ nor δυνάμει, yet they say they are saved by the faith of another, namely, the faith of pious parents or of the church, inasmuch as it is imputed to them for justification out of the covenant of God. Thus Beza teaches in *Coll. Mompelg.* resp. 2. f. 49...

4.) Some contend that infants believe by potentiality and inclination, not in the first act, but in the second; in the seed, not in the harvest... "They have an inclinative faith, or an inclination to faith," says Ursinus in *Cateches.* qu. 57. Calvin also acknowledges the seed of faith in infants, *Inst.* lib. 4, cap. 16, § 20, etc... See Altsted in *Methodo Theol.* p. 330, where he says, "believing infants have faith in existence, not in essence," which is a paradox, both in philosophy and in theology. (Essence can indeed be abstracted from existence, but not the reverse; yet it cannot be separated, see Combach in *Metaphys.* c. 9, p. 138.)

3. Of the Anabaptists, who simply deny faith to infants, since they are not capable of doctrine...

4. Of the Socinians, who utterly deny faith to infants, as those who are not apt for faith...

5. Of the Arminians, who... not obscurely deny the faith of infants, in *Apol.* f. 37. a...

7. Of the Innovators, who grant to infants some analogue of faith, but not faith itself properly so called, and ascribe to them the faith of their parents, along with certain Calvinists. Thus Brand. Daetrius, in a disputation on baptism held under the presidency of D. G. Calixtus in 1643, § 171, writes that parents and sponsors "lend, as it were, their hearts to infants for believing"... D. Hornejus, *disp. theol.* 2, sect. 1, *de praedest.* th. 21, p. 211: "The faith of the parents," he says, "and of those who offer them for baptism, is reckoned as their own proper faith." And Latermannus, th. 54, *de praedest.*, asserts that "infants believe by the confession of another." (L. c. c. 5, s. 2, q. 8, f. 1141—1143.) §

13. The subject in which [it resides] is the human soul, on the part of the intellect and the will. Or that part of man in which faith formally resides and according to which it pertains to man. Scripture sometimes calls it χαρδίαν, the heart, metaphorically, Rom. 10:10, where it is said that with the heart one believes unto righteousness. Of both powers, I say, according to those things which were said concerning the assent and trust of faith in Chapter III, § 6, notes c, d. Quenstedtius: "By reason of knowledge and assent, faith is in the intellect; by reason of trust in Christ, it is in the will; because cognition and assent pertain to the intellect, whose object is the true, but trust pertains to the will, whose object is the good." (L. c. c. 8, s. 1, th. 12, f. 1340.)

Apology of the A. C.: "If any sophist cavils: that righteousness is in the will, why can it not be attributed to faith, which is in the intellect? The answer is easy, because they themselves in the schools also admit that the will commands the intellect to assent to the Word of God. And we say more clearly: Just as the terrors of sin and death are not only thoughts of the intellect, but also horrible motions of the will, fleeing the judgment of God; so faith is not only knowledge in the intellect, but also trust in the will, i.e., it is to will and to receive that which is offered in the promise, namely, reconciliation and the remission of sins."

§ 14.

The proximate end and effect of faith is justification; then renewal; finally, the eternal salvation of believers. This is what God intends when He confers faith upon men, and this is what men themselves strive toward, as toward a good to be obtained through faith.

It is so in part as a less principal impulsive cause, if we speak of justification and salvation; and in part as a species of efficient cause, if we speak of renewal; which will be shown below, each in its proper place. For thus we are said to be justified by faith, through faith, from faith, Rom. 3:28, 30; Gal. 3:24. More will be said in the Book on Justification.

For this reason, faith is called ένεργουμένη, efficacious, through love. Gal. 5:6. Quenstedtius: "The effect of faith is twofold: immediate and mediate. The immediate effect is the remission of sins (Acts 10:43), justification (Rom. 4:5; 10:4), union with Christ, access to God, and the tranquility of the conscience (Rom. 5:1-2). Among these effects of faith, justification holds the palm, to which all other effects can be referred. The mediate effects are good works, patience in adversities (Rom. 5:3), victory over the world and Satan (1 John 5:4; Eph. 6:16), and love of God and neighbor. For faith is always efficacious through love, up and down (Gal. 5:6)." (L. c. P. IV, c. 8, s. 1, th. 15, f. 1341.)

According to that which is said in John 20:31: These are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Son of God, and that believing you may have life through His name. Quenstedtius: "The τέλος or end of faith is salvation and eternal life... Believing, 'you rejoice' (with joy inexpressible and glorified), 'obtaining το τέλος, that is, the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls' (1 Pet. 1:6, 9). Where the word τέλος can be explained both as the end, namely, regarding the intention of salvation, and as the reward, regarding the attainment of salvation; for through faith we are guarded for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time." (L. c. th. 16, f. 1342.) § 15.

The primary property of faith in Christ is certainty, both on the part of the object which is believed, to which it is repugnant that anything false should underlie it; and on the part of the subject, or the one who believes and most tenaciously adheres to and leans upon the divine promises, as those in which no deception can underlie. For this derives into the assent of faith from the formal object, which is revelation, founded upon the supreme truthfulness of God; concerning which see Prolegomena, Chapter I, § 35, Vol. I, p.

68. This is what they call the certainty (others call it firmness) of adherence, which consists in this: that the intellect, notwithstanding the non-evidence of the object, nevertheless by divine power, without fear of error and without hesitation, assents to those promises; while the will, with confidence, adheres to them, and thus, having overcome doubts, the motions of the flesh, and various temptations, with the help of God's grace, the soul of man enjoys most efficacious consolation.

This certainty of faith is proven by those passages of Scripture to which is attributed πεποίθησις, that is, the firmest adherence of the mind to divine promises, Eph. 3:12; πληροφορία, or the fact that we are carried toward those promises with the full motion of the mind, Rom. 4:18 sqq. (whence also Abraham is said to have believed in hope against hope, not to have wavered through unbelief, but to have been made strong by faith, l.c. v. 18, 20). Faith itself is also called ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων, insofar as things that are hoped for, as if they were future, are presented through faith as if they were present, and ἔλεγχος πραγμάτων οὐ βλεπομένων, insofar as things that are not seen by the eyes are nevertheless presented to the intellect through faith, as if they were known with certainty through demonstration, Heb. 11:1.

Luther: "I hold that the Epistle to the Hebrews looks here (2 Sam. 23:1) to the word הקם, where he says: 'Fides est substantia, Greek ὑπόστασις, which we have translated into German: 'Faith is a certain confidence.' One cannot say it otherwise to a German if he is to understand it. For faith is and ought to be a steadfastness of the heart, which does not waver, wobble, tremble, fidget, or doubt, but stands firm and is certain of its matters. The same word is also found in the saying of Isaiah 40: 'The word of God abides forever.' Abides, that is, it holds fast, is certain, does not yield, does not let fail. Now, where this word comes into the heart with true faith, it makes the heart like itself, also firm, certain, and secure, so that it becomes so stiff, upright, and hard against all temptation, devil, death, and whatever it may be called, that it defiantly and haughtily despises and mocks everything that wants to be doubt, timidity, evil, and wrath. For it knows that God’s word cannot lie to it. Such is a הקם, stabilitus, substantiatus, substantificatus, hypostaticus, certus passive, sicut verbum Domini certum active; as Paul says in 2 Tim. 1: 'I know and am certain,' etc.; 2 Pet. 1: 'Make your calling certain.'" (On the Last Words of David. 1543. Erl. Vol. 37, p. 7 sq.) The same: "The Holy Spirit is not a skeptic, nor has He written doubts or opinions in our hearts, but assertions more certain and firm than life itself and all experience." (De servo arbitrio. 1525. Opp. lat. var. arg. Francof. ad M. 1873. Vol. VII, 123 sq.) Cf. his preface to Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. See above § 9. c. § 16.

Proprietas fidei in Christum prima est certitudo, tum ex parte objecti, quod creditur, cui falsum subesse repugnat;a tum ex parte subjecti, sive ejus, qui credit et promissionibus divinis, tanquam quibus deceptio subesse non possit, tenacissime b adhaeret atque innititur. c Haec enim in assensum fidei derivatur ex objecto formali, quod est revelatio, in summa veracitate Dei fundata; de qua vid. !rroleg. cap. Quam vocant certitudinem (alii firmitatem) adhaesionis quaeque in eo consistit, quod intellectus quidem, non obstante inevidentia objecti, tamen virtute divina, citra metum erroris ac sine haesitatione, pro־ missionibus illis assentitur; voluntas autem cum fiducia iisdem inhaeret, atque ita, superatis dubitationibus, motibus carnis et tentationibus variis, adjuvante Dei gratia, hominis animus solatio efficacissimo fruitur.

Probant hanc fidei certitudinem loca illa Scripturae, quibus fidei tribuitur πεποίάησις, id est, firmissima animi ad divinas promissiones adhaesio, Eph. 3, 12.; πληροφορία, seu quod pleno animi motu in promissiones illas feramur, Rom. 4, 18. sqq. (unde et Abraham contra spem sub spe credidisse, non haesitasse per incredulitatem, sed fide robustus factus esse dicitur 1. c. v. 18. 20.). Lutherus: ,,Ich halte, die Epistel Ebr. sehe hieher (2 Sam. 23,1.) auf das Wort הקם, da er spricht: ,Fides est substantia, graece νπόστασις, welches wir verdeutscht haben: ,Der Glaube ist eine gewisse Zuversieht.‘ Anderst kann mans einem Deutschen nicht sagen, so ers verstehen soll. Denn der Glaube ist und soll auch sein ein Standfest des Herzens, der nicht wanket, wackelt, bebet, zappelt noch zweifelt, sondern fest stehet und seiner Sachen gewiss ist. Desselben Worts gleichen hat man auch in dem Spruch Isaiä 40.: ,Gottes Wort bleibt ewiglich.‘ Bleibt, d. i., es hält fest, ist gewiss, weicht nicht, lässt nicht feihlen. Wo nun dieses Wort ins Herz kommt mit rechtem Glauben, da machts das Herz ihm gleich, auch fest, gewiss und sicher, dass es so steif, aufrecht und hart wird wider alle Anfechtung, Teufel, Tod, und wie es heissen mag, dass es trötzlich und hochmüthiglich alles verachtet und spottet, was zweifei, zagen, böse und zornig sein will. Denn es weiss, dass ihm Gottes Wort nicht lügen kann. Solchs ist ein הקם, stabilitus, substantiatus, substantificatus, hypostaticus, certus passive, sicut verbum Domini certum active; wie Paulus 2 Tim. 1.: ,Ich weiss und bins gewiss‘ u. s. w.; 2 Pet. 1.: ,Machet euren Beruf gewiss.“‘ (Von den letzten Worten Davids. 1543. Erl. Bd. 37, p. 7. sq.) Idem: ,,Spiritus Sanctus non est scepticus, nec dubia aut opiniones in cordibus nostris scripsit, sed assertiones ipsa vita et omni experientia certiores et firmiores.“ (De servo arbitrio. 1525. Opp. lat. var. arg. Francof. ad M. 1873. Vol. VII, 123. sq.) Cf. ejusd. praefat. ad ep. Pauli ad Rom. Vide supra § 9. c. § 16.


### On Faith in Christ: Believing men can also, and are accustomed to, know with an infallible…

Believing men can also, and are accustomed to, know with an infallible certainty that they truly believe; although this is not manifested to them by a new divine revelation. If not always and in every state (for in the case of temptation it can happen, and does happen, that those who are truly faithful do not perceive their faith within themselves), yet sometimes, and with a clearer mind, they descend into themselves.

Formula of Concord: "The Apostle says (Phil. 2:13): 'It is God who works in you both to will and to do for His good pleasure.' This most sweet sentence of Scripture brings extraordinary consolation to all pious minds that feel some spark and desire for divine grace and eternal salvation in their hearts. For they are certain that God Himself has kindled that beginning of true piety like a little flame in their hearts, and that He also wills to further confirm and help them in their great infirmity, so that they may persevere in true faith even to the end." (Sol. declar. art. 2, p. 591.) PART III. CHAP. III.

L. Hartmann: "When a man has a serious desire for faith and the grace of God, that very desire must certainly be held to be true faith, even if it seems weak; for, as Augustine teaches, it is the property and operation of that same serious desire and appetite for the grace of God in Christ that it be given to man through faith; for who flees to grace, unless the steps of man are directed by the Lord and He wills his way? And through this, even to desire the help of grace is the beginning of grace. Therefore, the argument should rather be inverted and one should say: I have faith, because I feel that struggle and that desire for grace. Or the antecedent must be denied: You do not feel faith; that very desire itself is the sense and movement of faith. — Even if a person who is greatly tempted says that he does not even perceive that desire in himself, yet let it be answered to him that these very external complaints and anxious thoughts about it are the desire for faith, nay, the very faith itself, through which Christ dwells and lives in him, and in this very thing one finally arrives at those inexpressible groanings of the Holy Spirit, Rom. 8:26. Furthermore, flesh and blood itself does not work, nor can it work, such solicitude about faith, but it is the work of the Holy Spirit itself, which He works in believers, even though under the act of temptation they may think most strongly that they do not have faith." (Pastorale ev. 1697, p. 1144.)

Luther: "You will say: I cannot believe, as many are vexed by this temptation; and I remember a certain little woman coming to me at Torgau and complaining with tears that she could not believe. When I recited the articles of the Creed in order and asked about each one whether she held these to be true and to have happened in this way or not, she replied: I feel entirely that they are true; but I cannot believe. That was a satanic illusion. I said therefore: If you hold that all those things are true, there is nothing for which you should complain about your unbelief. For if you do not doubt that the Son of God died for you, you certainly believe; because to believe is nothing other than to hold these things as certain and indubitable truth." (Ad Gen. 26, 9. Exegetica opp. lat. Tom. VI. Erlang, p. 295.)

Hoepfner: "Even a weak and temporary faith can be certain and firm regarding the foundation of certainty, because it rests on the merit of Christ, although it may not insist upon it so strongly or even perpetually. Thus the father of the lunatic acknowledged his faith to be true with an infallible certainty, and indeed with divine faith, and yet with respect to the weakness adhering to it, he calls that faith, of which he was certain, ἀπιστίαν, unbelief, Mark 9:24. Thus πρόςκαιροι, temporary believers or those who believe for a certain time, have true faith, because 'they receive the word with joy,' Matt. 13:20, which is a description of fiducial apprehension; but 'they have no root,' i.e., durability and stability of faith, or, as the apostle’s phrase has it in Col. 2:7, 'they are not rooted in Christ,' and yet concerning that faith of theirs, viewed in terms of its essence, they can be infallible that it is true. Similarly, therefore, another regenerate person can have either a weak or a temporary faith... and yet concerning faith, whether weak or non-persevering, and concerning justification, he can be certain with divine certainty both of the object and of the subject. For continuity is not of the essence of faith, but concerns its duration; nor does the weakness of faith, as long as the believer struggles against it, take away the very nature of faith." (De justific. disputatt. p. 799.)

Adults indeed; for concerning the faith of infants the matter is more obscure. Without any doubt or fear of the opposite. Divine, I say, not merely human faith. Which some of the Papists call privileged, otherwise special.

For thus a progress to infinity would have to be admitted. Doubtless, just as other acts of knowing, so also the act of believing in Christ, although they are supernatural, nevertheless, when reflected upon themselves, manifest themselves to the intellect 1) through their own being, which is supernatural,

and thus according to its supernatural being. 2) through the supernatural testimony of the Holy Spirit, by which He testifies in the mind of the believer concerning those acts reflected upon themselves, according to Rom. 8:16. 3) with the addition of the acts of the faith of charity, and similar ones, as fruits of supernatural faith; which testify certainly and infallibly to the truth of that very supernatural faith.

Compare our Disputation against the Dialogues of Ebermann between Arius and Luther, § 102, pp. 95, 96.

Dannhauer: "Concerning the reflection of faith (which, as reflection in the intellect is the highest perfection of the mind—ὁ νοῦς ἂν εἴη ὁ κύκλος, says the philosopher, 1. 1. *de anima* c. 3. f. 48, while beasts indeed perceive, but do not know that they perceive: so it is the perfection and consummation of faith), the blind man testifies when he says: 'I believe,' John 9:38, i.e., I know that I believe. ...

But truly, you will say, that is infallible by divine infallibility which is revealed. That I believe is nowhere revealed. Therefore, it is not infallible by that infallibility which is the highest. Resp.: It is of the nature of any argument to have a conclusion of the same kind as its major premise, which contains the principle of believing; as in this one of ours: Whoever seals heavenly truth with his heart, he believes. I seal the heavenly truth concerning the remission of sins, made to me individually, with my heart. Therefore, I believe. The major is revealed in John 3:33: 'He that hath received his testimony hath set to his seal that God is true,' i.e., he believes! For to seal that God is true is the definition of faith. The minor is of most certain knowledge; as Augustine speaks: 'Everyone sees his own faith within himself'; likewise: 'He holds it by most certain knowledge.' L. 13 *de trin.* c. 1. Therefore, the conclusion is also revealed." (*Hodosoph. Phaen.* XI. p. 682, 684.)

Luther: "That we are God's children and may certainly hold ourselves to be such, we have not from ourselves, nor from the Law; but it is the testimony of the Holy Spirit, who testifies this in our weakness against the Law and the feeling of our unworthiness, and makes us certain of it. Such testimony proceeds in this way: that we also feel and perceive the power of the Holy Spirit, which He works in us through the Word, and our experience agrees with the Word or preaching. For you can indeed feel within yourself, when in need and anguish you receive comfort from the Gospel and thereby overcome such doubt and terror, that your heart can firmly conclude that you have a gracious God, and now no longer flee from Him, but in such faith can joyfully call upon Him and expect help from Him; and where such faith exists, there also follows the experience that you are being helped; as St. Paul says in Rom. 5:4, 5. That is the true inward testimony, by which you recognize that the Holy Spirit is working in you; besides this, you also have outward testimony and signs, that He gives you special gifts, fine spiritual understanding, grace, and success in your calling, etc., that you have desire and love for His Word, and confess the same before all the world at the risk of body and life; likewise, that you become an enemy to the godless nature and sins and resist them, etc. All of which non-Christians, who do not have the Holy Spirit, neither do nor are able to do. Although it is true that even this still happens in greater weakness among the saints, yet the Holy Spirit governs the Christians in such weakness and strengthens such testimony; as St. Paul says again in Rom. 8:26: 'The Spirit helpeth our infirmities.'" (*Kirchenpostille*. XII, 1045 sq.)

The same: "In serious terrors and struggles of conscience we do indeed apprehend Christ, and we believe Him to be our Savior. But the Law then terrifies us most, and sin disturbs us; finally, the devil attacks us with all his engines and fiery darts, and tries with all his might to snatch Christ from us and to shake off all consolations. There we are near to succumbing and despairing. For we are then PART III. CHAP. III.

that bruised reed and smoking flax (Matt. 12:20). Meanwhile, however, the Holy Spirit helps our infirmities and intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered, and gives testimony to our spirit that we are the children of God. In this way, the mind is raised up in terrors, sighs toward its Savior and High Priest Jesus Christ, overcomes the infirmity of the flesh, and again conceives consolation and says: Abba, Father! Therefore, this groaning, which we scarcely feel, Paul calls a cry and an inexpressible groaning, which fills heaven and earth. Furthermore, he also calls it the cry and groaning of the Spirit, because the Spirit excites this cry in our heart when we are infirm and tempted. . .

Exod. 14 (v. 15), the Lord speaks to Moses at the Red Sea, saying: "Why do you cry to me?" Certainly, Moses was not crying out, but trembling and almost despairing, for he was in the greatest straits. Unbelief seemed to reign in him, not faith. For he saw the people of Israel so hemmed in by the mountains, the army of the Egyptians, and the sea, that they could nowhere escape. Here Moses did not even dare to mutter; how then did he cry out? Therefore, we must not judge according to the feeling of our heart, but according to the Word of God, which teaches that the Holy Spirit is given to the afflicted, the terrified, the despairing, etc., so that He may raise them up and console them, lest they succumb in temptations and all evils, but rather overcome them—though not without the greatest dreads and labors.

Latin:

Possunt etiam et solent a homines credentes b certitudine infallibili c cognoscere, quod vere d credant; licet nova revelatione divina e id illis non f manifestetur. g Si non semper et in omni statu (nam in casu tentationis fieri potest et fit, ut, qui vere fideles sunt, fidem suam in se non sentiant), aliquando tameii et cum animo liquidiore in se ipsi descendunt.

Formula Concordiae: ,,Apostolus ait (Phil. 2, 13.): ,Deus est, qui operatur in vobis et velle et perficere pro bona voluntate.‘ Quae Scripturae dulcissima sententia omnibus piis mentibus, quae scintillulam aliquam et desiderium gratiae divinae et aeternae salutis in cordibus suis sentiunt, eximiam consolationem affert. Certi enim sunt, quod ipse Deus initium illud verae pietatis tanquam flammulam in cordibus ipsorum accenderit, quodque velit eos etiam in magna infirmitate porro confirmare et juvare, ut in vera fide ad finem usque perseverent.“ (Sol. declar. art. 2. p. 591.) PART. ΠΙ. CAP. m.

L. Hartmannus: ,,Quando homo serium desiderium fidei et gratiae Dei habet, certe illud ipsum desiderium pro vera fide, quam infirma etiam esse videatur, habendum erit; siquidem, docente Augustino, ejusdem proprietas et operatio est serium illud desiderium et appetitus gratiae Dei in Christo, ut ea homini per fidem donetur; quis enim confugit ad gratiam, nisi cum a Domino gressus hominis diriguntur et viam ejus volet? ac per hoc et desiderare auxilium gratiae initium gratiae est. Potius ergo invertendum est argumentum et dicendum: Ego fidem habeo, quia sentio illam pugnam et illud desiderium gratiae. Aut negandum est antecedens: Tu fidem non sentis; ipsum illud desiderium est sensus et motus fidei. — Si vel maxime tentatus dicat, se ne quidem desiderium illud in se deprehendere, tamen ipsi respondeatur, has ipsas externas querelas et anxias cogitationes de illo esse desiderium fidei, imo ipsam fidem, per quam Christus in eo habitet et vivat, et in hoc ipso deveniri tandem ad gemitus istos inenarrabiles Sp. S. Rom. 8, 26. Praeterea non ipsa, caro et sanguis operatur aut operari potest ejusmodi solicitudinem de fide, sed ipsa est opus Sp. S., quod ipse operatur in credentibus, quanquam sub actu tentationis vel maxime putent, se non habere fidem.“ (Pastorale ev. 1697. p. 1144.)

Lutherus: ״Dices: Non possum credere, sicut multi hac tentatione vexantur; et memini, Torgae ad me venire mulierculam quandam et cum lacrymis queri, quod non posset credere. Ibi cum articulos symboli ordine recitarem et de singulis quaererem, statueretne, haec vera et ita gesta esse, an non, respondebat: Omnino sentio, vera esse; sed non possum credere. Illa erat satanica illusio. Dicebam igitur: Si statuis, ista omnia vera esse, nihil est, cur de tua incredulitate queraris. Si enim non dubitas, Filium Dei pro te mortuum esse, certe credis; quia credere nihil, aliud est, quam habere ista pro certa et indubitata veritate.“ (Ad Gen. 26, 9. Exegetica opp. lat. Tom. VI. Erlang, p. 295.)

Hoepfnerus: ״Etiam debilis ac temporaria fides potest certa esse ac firma quoad certitudinis fundamentum, quia merito Christi nititur, licet non ita fortiter vel etiam non perpetuo ei insistat. Ita pater lunatici, fidem suam veram esse, agnoscebat certitudine infallibili et quidem fidei divinae, et tamen respectu adhaerentis debilitatis fldem illam, de qua certus erat, vocat απιστίαν, incredulitatem, Mare. 9, 24. Sic πρόςκαιροί, temporarii seu ad certum tempus credentes, habent veram fldem, quia,accipiunt verbum cum gaudio‘, Matth. 13, 20., quae est descriptio fiducialis apprehensionis; sed,non habent radicem‘, i. e., durabilitatem ac stabilitatem fidei seu, ut apostoli phrasis habet Coi. 2, 7., ,non sunt in Christo radicati‘, et tamen de ista fide sua, ratione suae essentiae spectata, possunt esse infallibiles, quod sit vera. Similiter ergo et alius renatus potest vel imbecillam vel temporariam habere fldem, . . . et tamen de fide vel infirma vel non perseverante, deque justificatione potest esse certus divina certitudine tum objecti tum subjecti. Neque enim continuitas est de essentia fidei, sed ejus durationem spectat; neque fidei debilitas, quamdiu contra eam luctatur fidelis, tollit ipsam naturam fidei.“ (De justitic. disputatt. p. 799.)

Adulti quidem; nam de infantum fide res obscurior est. Citra omnem dubitationem aut formidinem oppositi. Divina, inquam, non humana tantum, fide. Quam pontificiorum aliqui privilegiatam vocant, alias specialem.

Sic enim admittendus foret progressus in infinitum. Nimirum uti alii actus cognoscendi, ita et actus credendi in Christum, quamvis supernaturales sint, attamen in se ipsos reflexi se ipsos manifestant intellectui 1) per suum esse, quod supernaturale est,

adeoque secundum esse suum supernaturale. 2) per supernaturalem testificationem Spiritus S., qua de actibus illis in se ipsos reflexis testatur in animo credentis, juxta Rom. 8, 16. 3) accedentibus actibus fidei caritatis, et similibus, tanquam fructibus fidei supernaturalis; qui de veritate ipsius fidei supernaturalis certo et infallibili ter testantur.

Confer Disput, nostram Dialogis Ebermanni inter Arium et Lutherum oppositam § 102. p. 95. 96.

Dannhauerus: ,,De reflexione fidei (quae, ut in intellectu reflexio summa mentis perfectio est, 6 νους αν εϊη ό κϋκλος, ait philos. 1. 1. de anima c. 3. f. 48., dum bestiae quidem sentiunt, sed, se sentire, nesciunt: ita fidei perfectio est et consummatio) testatur coecus, cum dicit: ,Ego credo‘, Joh. 9, 38., h. e., ego scio, me credere. ..

At vero, inquies, id infallibilitate divina est infallibile, quod est revelatum. Me credere, nuspiam est revelatum. E. ea infallibilitate non est infallibile, quae summa est. Resp.: Ejus naturae in quolibet argumento esse conclusionem, cujus est propositio major, quae continet principium credendi; ut in hoc nostro: Qui veritatem coelestem obsignat corde suo, is credit. Ego veritatem coelestem de remissione peccatorum, mihi in individuo facta, corde meo obsigno. E. credo. Major revelata est Joh. 3, 33.: ,Qui accipit Dei testimonium, is obsignat, quod Deus verus est‘, i. e., credit! Obsignare enim, quod Deus verax sit, est de, finitio fidei. Minor est certissimae scientiae; ut loquitur Augustinus: ,Quisque suam fidem in seipso videt‘; item: ,Eam tenet certissima scientia.‘ L. 13. de trin. c. 1. Ergo et conclusio revelata est.“ (Hodosoph. Phaen. XI. p. 682. 684.)

Lutherus: ,,Dass wir Gottes Kinder sind und uns gewisslich dafür halten mögen, das haben wir nicht von uns selbst, noch aus dem Gesetz; sondern es ist des Heiligen Geistes Zeugniss, der wider das Gesetz und das Fühlen unserer Unwürdigkeit solches zeuget in unserer Schwachheit und uns dess gewiss macht. Solch Zeugniss gehet also zu, dass wir die Kraft des Heiligen Geistes, so er durchs Wort in uns wirket, auch fühlen und empfinden und unserz Erfahrung mit dem Wort oder Predigt übereinstimmt. Denn das kannst du ja bei dir fühlen, wo du in Noth und Angst Trost empfähest aus dem Evangelio und damit solchen Zweifel und Schrecken überwindest, dass dein Herz festiglich schliessen kann, du habest einen gnädigen Gott, und nun nicht mehr vor ihm fliehest, sondern in solchem Glauben ihn fröhlich anrufen kannst und Hilfe von ihm gewarten; und wo solcher Glaube bestehet, so folgt auch die Erfahrung, dass dir geholfen wird; wie St. Paulus Röm. 5, 4. 5. sagt. Das ist das rechte innerliche Zeugniss, dabei du erkennest, dass der Heilige Geist in dir wirket; daneben hast du auch äusserliche Zeugniss und Wahrzeichen, dass er dir gibt sonderliche Gaben, feinen geistlichen Verstand, Gnade und Glück zu deinem Beruf u. s. w., dass du Lust und Liebe hast zu seinem Wort, dasselbe vor aller Welt bekennest mit Gefahr Leibes und Lebens; item, dass du dem gottlosen Wesen und Sünden feind werdest und widerstehest u. s. w. Welches alles nicht thun noch vermögen die Unchristen, so den Heiligen Geist nicht haben. Wiewohl es wahr ist, dass auch noch dieses bei den Heiligen in grösser Schwachheit zugehet, aber doch der Heilige Geist in solcher Schwachheit die Christen regiert und solch Zeugniss stärkt; wie abermal St. Paulus Röm. 8, 26. sagt: ,Der Geist hilft unserer Schwachheit auf.‘“ (Kirchenpostille. XII, 1045. sq.;

Idem: ,,In seriis pavoribus et certaminibus conscientiae apprehendimus quidem Christum, et credimus eum salvatorem nostrum. Sed lex tum maxime terret, et peccatum conturbat nos, impugnat denique diabolus nos omnibus machinis ac ignitis telis suis, et conatur totis viribus eripere nobis Christum, et omnes consolationes excutere. Ibi parum abest, ne succumbamus et desperemus. Sumus enim tum PART. III. CAP. III.

arundo illa contrita et linum fumigans (Matth. 12, 20.). Interim tamen Spiritus Sanctus adjuvat infirmitates nostras, et interpellat pro nobis gemitu inenarrabili, datque testimonium spiritui nostro, quod simus filii Dei. Hoc modo in terroribus erigitur mens, suspirat ad salvatorem ac pontificem suum Jesum Christum, vincit infirmitatem carnis, atque iterum consolationem concipit et dicit: Abba pater! Istum ergo gemitum, quem nos vix sentimus, vocat Paulus clamorem et gemitum inenarrabilem, qui replet coelum et terram. Deinde etiam clamorem et gemitum Spiritus vocat, quia nobis infirmis et tentatis excitat Spiritus hunc clamorem in corde nostro. . .

Exod. 14. (v. 15.) loquitur dominus Mosi ad mare rubrum, dicens: ,Quid clamas ad me?‘ Certe Moses non clamabat, sed tremebat ac paene desperabat, erat enim in summis angustiis. Incredulitas videbatur regnare in eo, non fides. Videbat enim populum Israel ita montibus, exercitu Aegyptiorum ac mari conclusum, ut nusquam posset aufugere. Hic Moses ne mutire quidem audebat, quomodo igitur clamavit? Quare non debemus judicare secundum sensum cordis nostri, sed secundum verbum Dei, quod docet Spiritum Sanctum ideo donari afflictis, conterritis, desperabundis etc., ut eos erigat ac consoletur, ne in tentationibus et omnibus malis succumbant, sed ea vincant, non tamen sine maximis pavoribus et laboribus.


### On Faith in Christ: The Papists have dreamed that the saints possessed the Holy Spirit in such a…

The Papists have dreamed that the saints possessed the Holy Spirit in such a way that they never felt or had temptation. These speak of the Holy Spirit only speculatively, as do fanatical men today. But Paul says that the power of Christ is made perfect in our infirmity, and likewise that the Holy Spirit helps our infirmity and intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings, etc. Therefore, we have the greatest need of the Holy Spirit’s help and consolation, and He is most present to us, when we are most powerless and near to despair. If anyone endures evils with a strong and joyful spirit, the Holy Spirit has already performed His office in him. But He properly exercises His work in those who are vehemently terrified and have approached, as the Psalm says, even to the gates of death." (Commentary on St. Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, Erlangen 1844, II, 169, 172 sq.)

Quenstedtius: "Bellarmino objects (l. 3, c. 9): That this testimony is not by some expressed word, i.e., by revelation, but by the experience of a certain sweetness and internal peace, which does not beget certainty, except a conjectural one. Response: It is impious to hold the testimony of the Holy Spirit as a mere conjecture. For He neither deceives nor is deceived. A special revelation is not necessary, because the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit itself is divine and is equivalent to revelation. Although it is not an external revelation, it is nevertheless an internal revelation, and one proper to believers alone; namely, the internal operation of the Holy Spirit in our hearts, which does not exclude, but presupposes, the external revelation made in the Word. The blessed Hoepfner explains this internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, and its agreement with the testimony of the Word, most excellently in Disputation 8 on Justification, c. 3, Aph. 7, Points 21, 22, 23, where he says: 'There is no other word, viewed in terms of its form, by which the Holy Spirit testifies in our hearts than that by which He makes us certain of divine benefits through external enunciation and writing, although the acts of testifying are different; but the act of testifying, which belongs to the Holy Spirit, is twofold: one outside, the other inside. But the testimony itself always remains the same, namely, the sense contained in the divine Word, etc.'" (L. c. c. 8, s. 2, q. 9, f. 823.) §

17. Another property of faith in Christ is that it has hope and charity conjoined with it, and that necessarily; although these do not have the nature of a cause of salvation.

Which you might perhaps call the fecundity or fertility of faith. As proceeding from itself, or as its consequences and fruits. For although confidence and hope differ, in that the former is concerned with a present good, and one that is ours, which serves as a cause of another good; while the latter is occupied with a future or absent good, so that it may become ours, and is born from the will’s acquiescence in a present good, which can serve as a cause or aid for obtaining the other (see Musaeus, *De Convers.*, Disp. III, cap. III, § 130, p. 168); nevertheless, insofar as faith in Christ looks to the salvation to be obtained through Christ, it is a certain security of the will regarding the salvation to be obtained through Christ, which cannot but be conjoined with the hope of attaining it.

B. Musaeus, *De Eccles.*, P. I, Disp. I, § 80, p. 55. Gerhard: "Confidence is twofold: one of hope, the other of faith. The former looks to and expects the promised good as future; the latter, however, looks to and apprehends the same as present. The confidence of hope consists in the certain expectation of the promised good, but the confidence of faith consists in the fiducial apprehension of the offered good... Hence also πληροφορία is attributed to both faith and hope, Heb. 10:22; 6:11. To those who truly repent and believe in Christ, God’s grace, reconciliation, and the remission of sins are promised; we receive this promise by faith and embrace the promised goods offered to us as present; we do not hope that we shall finally be received into God’s favor and receive the remission of sins at some future time; but by faith we determine that we are pleasing to God on account of Christ the Mediator, and that our sins are remitted to us on account of the same; this, therefore, is the confidence of faith. Besides these goods, deliverance from the cross, the revelation of glory, the translation into the triumphant church, etc., are promised to those who truly repent and believe in Christ; we likewise embrace this promise, but since those promised goods are not yet present, we cannot apprehend them by fiducial apprehension, but we expect them by hope—which hope, since it leans upon the Word of God, is likewise certain and immovable; whence it is said 'does not put to shame,' Rom. 5:5." (*Loc. de justific.*, § 77.)

Indeed, the faith by which we desire for ourselves Christ and other goods to be obtained through Him imports an act other than that by which we love Christ, or by which we wish good to Christ Himself or desire well for Him (see Musaeus, *De Convers.*, Disp. III, cap. III, § 140, p. 175, and § 158, p. 193; cap. IV, § 207, p. 235).

Yet that confidence is not without love. For when our will looks to Christ as a present good, and to God as appeased on account of Christ and rendered propitious to us, it pursues Him not only with a love of complacency, but also with a love of benevolence, insofar as it is moved to wish Him well, or to desire to perform what will be good or pleasing to Him.

Cf. Musaeus, *ll. cc.*, and *De Eccl.*, P. I, Disp. I, § 76, p. 51; § 80, p. 55. More will be said in the *Locus de renovatione*. So that true faith is not, unless it is effective through love, Gal. 5:6, namely, otherwise it would be dead, Jas. 2:20 and 26.

Faith and the other Christian virtues are joined together, just as a good and fertile tree is joined with its fruits. For faith is a certain divine work in us, which changes us, regenerates us from God, John 1:13, mortifies the old Adam, and makes us entirely different men, and confers the Holy Spirit upon us. And that faith is something living, effective, and powerful, so that it is impossible that it should not always work good. Nor does faith finally ask whether good works are to be done. PART III. CHAPTER III.

end; but before this matter is inquired into, it has already performed many works and is always occupied in acting, just as the words of the blessed Luther in his Preface to the Epistle to the Romans are read, translated into Latin, in the *Solida Declaratio* of the *Formula of Concord*, Art. IV, p. 701. Cf. the *Disputation on the Connection of Faith and Works*, held under our presidency in the year 1686, § 8 et seqq.

Gerhard: "Question XII: Can true and justifying faith be separated from love and the remaining good works? The opinion of our theologians on this question is that faith indeed justifies alone, yet in the meantime it is not alone, that is, it is not separated from love and other good works. On the contrary, what the mind of the Romanist adversaries is, one can clearly gather from the words of Stapleton and the Council of Trent. To these, Bellarmine adds his own fitting part in *De Justificatione*, Bk. I, ch. 3, writing: 'We dissent from them (the Lutherans) in this, that while they teach that faith, which they say justifies alone, can never be alone; we contradict them, saying that it does not justify alone, but yet it can be alone.' These things, however, are diametrically opposed: 1. To the sayings of Scripture, which 1) join faith and good works, 1 Timothy 5:8: 'If anyone does not provide for his own, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.' James 2:17: 'Faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself.' Galatians 5:6. 2) They assert that those born of God do not sin, as John 5:1, 1 John 1:12-13, 1 John 3:9-10, 4:7-8. 3) They teach that Christ dwells in believers through the Holy Spirit, Ephesians 3:17, 1:13, Galatians 2:20, 3:2, 26, 4:4. Where, therefore, Christ and the Holy Spirit dwell, there men are impelled to good works of every kind. 2. To other reasons sought from Scripture. For those who still take pleasure in sins do not possess: 1) true repentance, 2) the grace of God, 3) regeneration, to which renewal is perpetually joined, 4) access to Christ, 5) love of God, 6) the perception of the sweetness that is in God, 7) the enjoyment of eternal life. But where these are not present, it is as impossible for faith to be present as it is for the sun not to shine at midday; for just as the sun is not without light, nor a generous tree without good fruits, so faith is not without works, even though it justifies alone, i.e., it does not communicate the power of justifying to the works which it brings forth." (*Explicat. ἐλεγκτική ev. Dominic.*, p. 350 et seq.)

Brentius: "Faith, if I may say so for the sake of explanation, has two hands. One, which it extends upward and apprehends Christ together with all His benefits, and in this respect we say that we are justified by faith; the other, which it extends downward to exercise the works of charity and the remaining virtues; and in this respect we indeed testify to the truth of faith, but we are not justified." (*Apolog. Confess. Wurtemberg.*, p. 319.)

For neither do hope and charity themselves have a meritorious power, so as to move God to give salvation to man by some dignity of their own, nor do they so unite the merit of Christ to us or to our benefit that it becomes ours and helps us; but faith alone, insofar as it implies the apprehension of the merit of Christ through assent and trust, accomplishes this. Cf. Musaeus, *De Conversione*, Disp. III, ch. IV, § 215, p. 240. We shall say more in the Book on Justification.

Luther: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.' The sophists drag this passage to their own opinion, by which they teach that we are justified by charity or works. For they say that faith, even if it be infused divinely (I pass over the acquired kind), does not justify unless it is informed by charity, because they call charity 'grace that makes one pleasing,' that is, justifying (to speak in our word, or rather, Paul's); charity is then acquired by our merit of congruity, etc. Indeed, they affirm that even infused faith can coexist with mortal sin. Thus they transfer justification entirely from faith and attribute it (by this reasoning) to charity alone, and they wish this..."

in this passage, as demonstrated by St. Paul: "Faith, which worketh through love," as if Paul meant to say: Behold, faith does not justify; nay, it is nothing, unless there be added a working love, which informs faith. But all these are monsters, fabricated by slothful men. For who could endure to be taught that faith, a gift of God infused into hearts by the Holy Spirit, can coexist with mortal sin? If they were speaking of acquired or historical faith, and of a natural opinion conceived from history, they could be tolerated; indeed, they would be speaking correctly regarding historical faith. But to think this of infused faith is plainly to confess that one understands absolutely nothing correctly about faith.

Papistae somniarunt sanctos ita habuisse Spiritum Sanctum, ut nunquam senserint aut habuerint tentationem. Hi speculative tantum, ut hodie fanatici homines, de Spiritu Sancto loquuntur. Sed Paulus dicit virtutem Christi in nostra infirmitate perfici, item Spiritum Sanctum adjuvare infirmitatem nostram, et interpellare pro nobis gemitu inenarrabili etc. Ergo tum maxime habemus opus Spiritus Sancti auxilio et consolatione, tumque maxime adest nobis, cum maxime sumus impotentes ac desperationi proximi. II, 169. 172. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ״Excipit Bellarminus 1. 3. c. 9.: Hoc testimonium non esse per verbum aliquod expressum, i. e., per revelationem, sed per experimentum cujusdam suavitatis et pacis internae, quae non gignat certitudinem, nisi conjecturalem.
