17. Altera proprietas a fidei in Christum est, quod habet sibi conj unctas b spem c et caritatem, d idque e necessario; licet hae non habeant rationem causae salutis. f

Quam fortasse foecunditatem aut fertilitatem fidei dixeris. Tanquam ex se proficiscentes, aut velut consequentia et fructus suos. Quamvis enim differant fiducia et spes, quod illa versatur circa bonum praesens, ac nostrum, quod sit causa boni alterius; haec vero circa bonum futurum aut absens, ut nostrum fiat, occupatur et nascitur ex voluntatis acquiescentia in bono praesente, quod ad obtinendum alterum causa aut adjumento esse potest (vid. Mus. de Convers. Disp. III. cap. III. § 130. p. 168.); tamen quatenus fides in Christum respicit salutem per Christum obtinendam, est quaedam securitas voluntatis de salute per Christum obtinenda, quae non potest non cum spe ejus impetrandae esse conjuncta.

B. Mus. de Eccles. P. I. Disp. I. § 80. p. 55. Gerhardus: ,,Duplex est fiducia, alia spei, alia fidei. Illa bonum promissum ut futurum respicit et expectat; haec vero idem ut praesens respicit et apprehendit. Spei fiducia consistit in certa expectatione boni promissi, fidei autem fiducia consistit in flduciali apprehensione boni oblati. . . Inde etiam πληροφορία et fidei et spei tribuitur Ebr. 10, 22. 6, 11. Vere agentibus poenitentiam et in Christum credentibus promissa est Dei gratia, reconciliatio et peccatorum remissio, hanc promissionem fide recipimus et promissa bona nobis oblata ut praesentia amplectimur; non speramus, nos olim demum in gratiam Dei recipiendos ac peccatorum remissionem futuro tempore accepturos; sed fide statuimus, nos propter Christum mediatorem Deo placere et peccata propter eundem nobis remitti; haec igitur est fiducia fidei. Praeter haec bona vere poenitentibus et in Christum credentibus promissa est liberatio ex cruce, revelatio gloriae, translatio in ecclesiam triumphantem etc.; hanc promissionem itidem amplectimur, sed promissa illa bona, cum nondum sint praesentia, ideo flduciali apprehensione ea non possumus apprehendere, sed spe eadem expectamus, quae spes, cum nitatur Dei verbo, itidem certa et immota est; unde dicitur,non confundere‘ Rom. 8, 5.“ (Loc. de justiflc. § 77.)

Equidem fides, qua Christum et alia per ipsum impetranda bona nobis concupiscimus, actum alium importat ab eo, quo Christum diligimus, seu, quo ipsi Christo bonum volumus aut bene cupimus (v. Mus. de Convers. Disp. III. cap. III. § 140. p. 175. et § 158. p. 193. cap. IV. § 207. p. 235.).

Fiducia tamen illa non est sine dilectione. Nam quando voluntas nostra Christum, tanquam bonum praesens, ac Deum propter Christum placatum nobisque propitium redditum respicit, non solum amore complacentiae eundem prosequitur, verum etiam amore benevolentiae, quatenus movetur, ut bene velit illi, seu cupiat praestare, quae ipsi bona aut grata sint futura.

Conf. Mus. 11. cc. et de Eccl. P. I. Disp. I. § 76. p. 51. § 80. p. 55. Plura dicentur in L. de renovatione. Ita ut fides vera non sit, nisi quae per caritatem est efficax, Gal. 5, 6., scilicet alias mortua futura, Jac. 2, 20. et 26.

Conjunguntur autem fides et virtutes christianae caeterae, quemadmodum arbor bona et fertilis cum suis fructibus. Fides enim est divinum quoddam opus in nobis, quod nos immutat, ex Deo regenerat, Joh. 1, 13., veterem Adamum mortificat et ex nobis plane alios homines facit, et Spiritum S. nobis confert. Et est fides illa quicquam vivum, efficax, potens, ita ut fieri non possit, quin semper bene operetur. Neque fides quaerit demum, an bona opera sint faci PAKT. III. CAP. ΙΠ.

enda; sed priusquam de ea re inquiratur, jam multa opera effecit et semper in agendo est occupata, prout verba b. Lutheri Praefat. in Epist. ad Rom. latine reddita leguntur in Solid. Declar. Form. Cone. art. IV. p. 701. Conf. Disp, de Connexione Fidei et Operum sub praesidio nostro liabitam anno 1686. § 8. sqq.

Dominic. p. 350. sq.)

Brentius: ,,Fides, ut ita explicandi gratia dicam, duplices habet manus. Unam, quam extendit sursum et apprehendit Christum una cum omnibus beneficiis suis, et hac parte dicimus, nos justificari per fidem; alteram, quam protendit deorsum ad exercenda opera caritatis ac reliquarum virtutum; et hac parte testificamur quidem veritatem fidei, non autem justificamur.“ (Apolog. Confess. Wurtemberg. p. 319.)

Neque enim vel ipsa spes et caritas vim meritoriam habent, ut sua quadam dignitate moveant Deum ad salutem homini dandam, vel ita uniunt nobis aut ad nos meritum Christi, ut fiat nostrum nosque juvet; sed hoc sola fides, prout apprehensionem meriti Christi perassensum et fiduciam importat, praestat. Conf. Mus. de Conv. Disp. III. cap. IV. § 215. p. 240. Plura dicemus in L. de justificatione.

Lutherus: ״ ,Nam in Christo Jesu neque circumcisio aliquid valet, neque praeputium, sed fides per caritatem efficax.‘ Hunc locum sophistae trahunt ad suam sententiam, qua docent nos caritate seu operibus justificari. Dicunt enim fidem, etiamsi sit infusa divinitus (de acquisita taceo), non justificare, nisi sit informata per caritatem, quia caritatem vocant gratiam gratum facientem, hoc est, justificantem (ut nostro verbo, seu Pauli potius, loquar); caritatem deinde acquiri nostro merito congrui etc. Quin hoc affirmant, fidem etiam infusam stare posse cum peccato mortali. Adeo in totum transferunt justificationem a fide, et soli tribuunt (hac ratione) caritati, atque hoc volunt

hoc loco per s. Paulum demonstratum habere: ,Fides, quae per caritatem operatur‘, quasi Paulus velit dicere: Ecce, fldes non justificat, imo nihil est, nisi accedat operatrix caritas, quae fidem informet. Verum haec omnia monstra sunt, per homines ignavos conficta. Quis enim ferat doceri, quod fides, donum Dei per Spiritum Sanctum infusum cordibus, possit stare cum peccato mortali? Si de fide acquisita seu historica et naturali opinione ex historia concepta loquerentur, tolerari possent, imo de historica fide recte loquerentur. At de fide infusa sip sentire, hoc est plane confiteri sese prorsus nihil de fide recte intelligere.


### On Faith in Christ: Furthermore, they read this passage of Paul through a colored (as it is called)…

Furthermore, they read this passage of Paul through a colored (as it is called) glass, and they deform the text to suit their own dreams. For Paul does not say: "Faith, which justifies through love," nor does he say: "Faith, which makes one acceptable through love." They themselves invent such a text, and force it into this passage by violence. Much less does he say: "Love makes one acceptable." Paul does not say it thus, but he says it thus: "Faith, which worketh through love." He says that works are done out of faith through love, not that a man is justified through love. But who is so crude a grammarian that he does not understand, from the force of the words, that to be justified is one thing, and to work is another? For the words of Paul are clear and open: "Faith worketh through love." Therefore, it is a manifest theft that they, having removed the true and genuine sense of Paul, understand "to justify" instead of "to work," and "justice" instead of "works," even though they are forced to admit, even in moral philosophy, that works are not justice, but that works are done by justice.

Furthermore, Paul does not here make faith an unformed and crude chaos, which has neither being nor action, but he attributes the operation itself to faith, and not to love, not imagining some crude and unformed quality, but asserting an efficacious and industrious essence, and as it were a substance or (as they call it) a substantial form. For he does not say: "Love is efficacious," but: "Faith is efficacious"; not: "Love worketh," but: "Faith worketh." He makes love, as it were, an instrument of faith, through which it may work. Now, who does not know that an instrument has force, motion, and action not from itself, but from the craftsman, the operator, or the agent? For who would say: "The axe gives the force and motion of cutting to the craftsman? The ship gives the force and motion of sailing to the sailor?" Or, to bring forward the example of Isaiah, who will say: "The saw draws the craftsman, and the staff lifts the hand"? It is not unlike what these men say, that love is the form of faith, or that it attributes force and motion to faith, or that it justifies. Since Paul does not even grant works to love, how would he grant justification? It is certain, therefore, that it is a great injury, not only to Paul, but also to faith and love itself, that this passage has been depraved for the sake of love and against faith. (Commentary on St. Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, Erl. II, 321—323.) The same: "The sophists, as they are prepared to evade the Scriptures, cavil at this passage thus: 'The just shall live by faith,' namely, faith that is efficacious, working, or formed by charity. But if it is unformed faith, it does not justify. They themselves invented this gloss, and by it they do violence to the words of the prophet. If they called 'formed faith' true and theological, or, as Paul says, ἀνυπόκριτον, which God calls faith, this gloss of theirs would not offend me at all. For then faith would not be distinguished against charity, but against a vain opinion of faith, in which way we also distinguish between feigned and true faith. Feigned faith is that which hears about God, Christ, and all the mysteries of the incarnation and redemption, and apprehends those things heard, and knows how to speak most beautifully about them, and yet it remains a mere opinion and empty hearing, which leaves only a buzzing in the heart about the Gospel, about which it chatters much, yet in truth it is not faith, because it does not renew or change the heart, it does not generate a new man, but leaves him in his former opinion and conversation; and this faith is very pernicious, which it would be better not to have; and a moral philosopher is better than such a hypocrite who has this faith. Therefore, if they distinguished 'formed faith' against false or feigned faith, that distinction of theirs would not offend me. But they speak of faith formed by charity, and they make a twofold faith, unformed and formed. This most pestilential and satanic gloss I cannot but vehemently detest. Although, they say, there is present an infused faith, which is a gift of the Holy Spirit, and an acquired one, which we ourselves produce for ourselves by many acts of believing, yet both are unformed, and are formed by charity. Thus faith without charity, as they dream, is like a painting and a specious thing in the dark, which is only then discerned when light, that is, charity, has arrived. And in this way charity is the form of faith, and faith is the pure matter of charity. To prefer this is to prefer charity to faith, and to attribute righteousness not to faith, but to charity, because that for the sake of which a thing is such, is itself more so. Therefore, since they do not attribute righteousness to faith except on account of charity, they attribute nothing at all to faith.

Furthermore, these subverters of the Gospel of Christ say that even infused faith, which is not received by hearing or acquired by any other operation, but which the Holy Spirit creates in man, can stand in mortal sin, and that the worst men can have it. Therefore, if it is alone, it is idle and useless, even if it does wonders. Thus they take away its office from faith entirely, and attribute it to charity, so that faith is of no value at all unless the form, that is, charity, has arrived. Therefore, according to this pestilent figment of the sophists, that faith, a miserable virtue, will be a certain unformed chaos, of no work, efficacy, or life, but only passive matter. All these things are blasphemous against God and satanic, which utterly obscure and overturn the doctrine of faith, and draw one away from Christ the mediator and from the faith that apprehends Him. For if charity is the form of faith, as they trifle, I am immediately compelled to think that charity itself is the principal and greatest part of the Christian religion, and thus I lose Christ, His blood, His wounds, and all His benefits, and I cling to charity, and I love and enter into moral doing, like the Pope, a Gentile philosopher, or a Turk. But the Holy Spirit, who gives mouth and tongue to all, also knows how to speak. He could well have said, as the sophists impiously trifle: 'The just shall live by formed faith.' But He deliberately omitted this, and simply said, 'The just shall live by faith.' Let the sophists therefore go to the devil with their impious and pestilent gloss." (L. c. p. 1—4.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis:

1. Of the Socinians, who assert that faith is obedience to the commandments of God, and indeed in such a way that this is the substance and form of faith, and thus they locate justifying faith formally in obedience, so that to believe is nothing other than 'to obey God under the hope of eternal life.' Thus Socinus teaches throughout chapters 11 and 12 of Part IV, *De Servatore*: 'Justifying faith is to obey the precepts of God, and to believe that those things which Christ said are true.' Cf. Smalcius against Frantz, disp. 12, f. 450, where he says: 'Just as the soul is not a secondary part of man, but essential and formal, so works or Christian piety are themselves the form and essence of Christian faith.' 2. Of the Arminians, who teach that obedience is, if not the form of faith, at least its genus or cause. See the *Confession of the Remonstrants*, ch. 10, s. 2, 3, and in the *Apology of the Confession*, pp. 110, 111. The Arminians certainly constitute obedience as the genus of the faith of justification, as such, f. 111, Apol. Therefore, it pertains entirely to its form. ...

4. Of the Papists, who contend that faith is formed by charity; whence for them one faith is 'formed,' another 'unformed' or 'informis,' which distinction they repeat from the scholastics and defend. ... With the Socinians, the Papists make works the form of faith, though the Socinians are better than them in this, that they assert works are indeed a cause of justification, but not a meritorious one.

5. Of the Weigelians, who define faith through imitating Christ and through the life of Christ, as also a heart obedient to God, or even through Christ himself; see Weigel, Part I, *Postill*, p. 178." (L. c. P. IV, c. 8, s. 2, q. 3, f. 1354, sq.)

18. It happens, even to faith in Christ, that it can be lost by men through sins against conscience, and is sometimes lost, not only for a time, but also finally, or in such a way that it is never recovered. Of true faith, I say, which, when it is present, truly reconciles a man with God and justifies him, and, as long as it is present, preserves him in a state of grace.

Hoepfnerus: "Scripture and pious antiquity are also accustomed at times to call final faith 'true' and 'unfeigned' faith, in the sense in which we estimate the truth of things by their duration, free from loss or final destruction; just as the jurists say in the penultimate law of the Senatusconsultum Syllanum: 'Nothing is considered done, if anything remains to be done.' Therefore, Gratian (De poenit. dist. 2) explains 'true' as 'persevering.' Thus, in Psalm 105, the Israelites are said to have believed in God and Moses (v. 12), yet soon after, in v. 24, not to have believed. Likewise, John 8:31: 'If you abide in my word, you will truly be my disciples.' And thus Augustine (De corrupt. et gratia, c. 9) explains that passage in 1 John 2:19: 'They were not of us (namely, as regards perseverance in faith), for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us.' In the same sense, Tertullian (Adversus Haereticos, c. 3): 'No one is a Christian, except he who has persevered to the end.' And Ambrose (in 2 Cor. cap. 6): 'It is not true faith if it is not perpetual, but can fail.' And Augustine (tract. 106 in Joh.): 'To believe truly is to believe unshakably, firmly, stably, strongly, so that you do not return to your own ways and abandon Christ.'" (De justif. Disputatt. p. 565.)

Indeed, because of the demerit of those sins, the Holy Spirit, by the power of divine justice, can withdraw that unmerited influx upon which supernatural habits depend for their existence. And so, just as grace and charity, so also supernatural faith (to which it is connatural that it cannot exist without grace and charity) can be morally and meritoriously expelled. Cf. Musaeus, De Eccl. Part. I. Disput. I. § 82 sqq. p. 58 sqq.

To this pertain those πρόσκαιροι who believe for a time, with that very faith which is born from the seed of the Word, and thus from a supernatural and divine power divinely joined to the Word, and which is therefore not human but divine faith, Luke 8:11, 13; Matt. 13:21, 22; Mark 4:16, 17. Cf. 1 Tim. 1:19 concerning those who περὶ τὴν πίστιν ἐναυάγησαν, who make shipwreck regarding the faith (or of the faith itself) and lose it.

Latin:

Deinde hunc locum Pauli per coloratum (ut dicitur) vitrum legunt, et textum deformant ad sua somnia. Non enim dicit Paulus: Fides, quae per caritatem justificat, nec dicit: Fides, quae per caritatem gratum facit. Talem textum ipsi fingunt, et huic loco per vim intrudunt. Multo minus dicit: Caritas gratum facit. Non sic dicit Paulus, sed sic dicit: ,Fides, quae per caritatem operatur.‘ Opera fieri dicit ex fide per caritatem, non justificari hominem per caritatem. At quis est tam rudis grammaticus, qui non ex vocabulorum virtute intelligat aliud esse justificari, aliud operari? Clara enim et aperta sunt verba Pauli: ,Fides per caritatem operatur.‘ Quare manifestum furtum est, quod illi vero et germano sensu Pauli sublato pro operari intelligunt justificari, et per opera justitiam, cum etiam in morali philosophia fateri cogantur, opera non esse justitiam, sed a justitia fleri opera.

Porro, Paulus hic non facit fidem informem et rude velut chaos, cujus nihil sit neque esse neque agere, sed operationem ipsam tribuit fidei, et non caritati, non fingens rudem quandam et informem qualitatem, sed asserens efficacem et operosam quidditatem ac velut substantiam seu formam (ut vocant) substantialem. Non enim dicit: Caritas est efficax, sed: ,Fides est efficax‘; non: Caritas operatur, sed: ,Fides operatur.‘ Caritatem vero facit fidei velut instrumentum, per quod operetur. Jam quis nescit, quod instrumentum habet vim, motum et actionem non a se ipso, sed a fabro, operatore seu agente? Quis enim diceret: Securis dat vim et motum secandi fabro? Navis dat vim et motum navigandi nautae? Vel, ut Esaiae exemplum adducam, quis dicet: ,Serra trahit fabrum, et baculus levat manum‘? Non dissimile est, quod isti dicunt caritatem esse forinam fidei, seu tribuere vim et motum fidei, seu justificare. Cum Paulus nec opera baritati concedat, quomodo concederet justificationem? Certum igitur est, injuria magna non solum Pauli, sed ipsius quoque fidei et caritatis hunc locum pro caritate contra fidem esse depravatum.“ (Commentar, in ep. S. Pauli ad Gal. Erl. II, 321—323.) Idem: ,,Sophistae, ut parati sunt ad eludendum Scripturas, hunc locum sic cavillantur: Justus vivit ex fide, scilicet, efficaci, operante vel formata caritate. Si vero est fldes informis, non justificat. Hanc glossam ipsi finxerunt, eaque vim faciunt prophetae verbis. Si fidem formatam vocarent veram et theologicam, vel, ut Paulus, άννπάκριτον, quam Deus fidem vocat, nihil me offenderet haec ipsorum glossa. Tunc enim fides non distingueretur contra caritatem, sed contra vanam opinionem fidei, quo modo et nos distinguimus inter fidem fictam et veram. Ficta est, quae audit de Deo, Christo et omnibus mysteriis incarnationis et redemtionis, et apprehendit illas res auditas, et pulcherrime de eis novit loqui, et tamen mera opinio et inanis auditus manet, qui tantum relinquit bombum in corde de evangelio, de quo multa garrit, re vera tamen fides non est, quia non renovat nec immutat cor, non generat novum hominem, sed relinquit eum in priori sua opinione et conversatione, estque haec fides valde perniciosa, quam satius esset non habere; et philosophus moralis melior est tali hypocrita, qui hanc fidem habet. Itaque si formatam fidem distinguerent contra falsam seu fictam fidem, nihil me offenderet ista illorum distinctio. Sed ipsi loquuntur de fide formata caritate, faciuntque duplicem fidem, informem et formatam. Hanc pestilentissimam et satanicam glossam non PART. III. CAP. III. possum non vehementer detestari. Quamvis, inquiunt, adsit fides infusa, quae donum Spiritus Sancti est, et acquisita, quam nos ipsi parimus nobis multis actionibus credendi, tamen utraque est informis, et formatur caritate. Sic fides sine caritate, ut ipsi somniant, est quasi pictura et res speciosa in tenebris, quae tum primum cernitur, cum iux, id est, caritas accesserit. Atque hoc modo caritas est forma fidei, et fides pura materia caritatis. Hoc praeferre est caritatem fidei, et tribuere justitiam non fidei, sed caritati, quia propter quod unum quodque est tale, et ipsum magis. Itaque cum non tribuunt justitiam fidei nisi propter caritatem, fidei nihil omnino tribuunt.

Deinde dicunt eversores evangelii Christi fidem etiam infusam, quae non accipitur audiendo, aut ulla alia operatione acquiritur, sed quam Spiritus Sanctus creat in homine, stare in peccato mortali, eamque pessimos homines posse habere. Ideo si sola sit, otiosam et inutilem esse, etiamsi mirabilia faciat. Ita fidei suum officium prorsus auferunt, et tribuunt caritati, ut fides prorsus nihil valeat, nisi accesserit forma, id est, caritas. Ergo juxta hoc pestilens figmentum sophistarum fides illa, misera virtus, erit quoddam informe chaos, nullius operis, efficaciae et vitae, sed tantum passiva materia. Ista omnia blasphema in Deum et satanica sunt, quae prorsus obscurant et evertunt fidei doctrinam, a Christo mediatore et a fide apprehendente ipsum retrahunt. Nam si caritas est forma fidei, ut ipsi nugantur, statim cogor sentire ipsam caritatem esse principalem et maximam partem Christianae religionis, et sic amitto Christum, sanguinem, vulnera et omnia beneficia ejus, et inhaereo caritati, et diligo ac venio in facere morale, ut papa, gentilis philosophus aut Turea. At Sanctus Spiritus, qui dat omnibus os et linguam, novit etiam loqui. Bene potuisset dicere, ut sophistae impie nugantur: Justus ex fide formata vivit. Sed consulto omisit hoc, et simpliciter dixit, ,Justus ex fide vivit.‘ Abeant igitur sophistae in malam crucem cum sua impia et pestilente glossa.“ (L. c. p. 1—4.) ANTITHESIS. ### On Faith in Christ: Such are the examples of David, who by adultery and murder became a man of…

Such are the examples of David, who by adultery and murder became a man of death, namely, subject to the wrath of God even unto his destruction, yet afterwards, having performed repentance, was received back into grace; and of Peter, who denied Christ three times in such a way that he even used imprecations, yet, being penitent, obtained the remission of his sin.

Gerhardus: "Knowledge and historical faith can remain in those who sin against conscience, and it remained even in Peter when he denied Christ; but saving faith does not remain in them, nor did it remain in Peter at the time of his denial. This very thing can be proven by these immovable arguments: He who denies Christ will again be denied by Christ, Matt. 10:33. Peter denied Christ. Therefore, he would have been denied by Christ, had he not truly been converted again. 'He who does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not His,' Rom. 8:9. Peter, in denying Christ, did not have the Spirit..." PART III. CHAPTER III.

of Christ, 2 Cor. 4:13. Therefore, he was not of Christ, and consequently, he did not have saving faith at that time. True faith and confession are αδαμαντίνες (adamantine) joined together, Ps. 116:10; 2 Cor. 4:13. Peter not only did not confess Christ, but furthermore even denied Him. Therefore, he did not have true faith at that time. True faith receives Christ, John 1:12; by denial, one repudiates Christ. Therefore, true faith could not coexist with the denial of Christ in the heart of Peter. Where there is a need for conversion, there an aversion has preceded. Peter had need of conversion, as Christ testifies: "When you have turned, strengthen your brethren." Therefore, what Christ says, that He prayed for Peter that his faith might not fail, is to be understood of the εκλείψει (failing) and εκπτώσει (falling away) finally, from which Peter was preserved by the prayers of Christ, so that he would not perish eternally, but, having been converted to God through repentance, would be saved. "

I have prayed and obtained that, after your denial, you might not fall into despair, but that you might repent, obtain the forgiveness of sin, and become a partaker of eternal salvation." (Harm. ev. on Luke 22:31, 32.)

Luther: "Peter denied Christ and was nearly lost. He falls, indeed, from grace, but he does not lose all reflection... Peter’s fall is therefore a gross fall, and he is a greater evildoer. But because he remains in the Word, he does not fall into eternal disgrace, but does true penance." (Other Exposition of the 1st Epistle of St. John. IX, 1178.)

For it is said in this way, that it is impossible for those who were once enlightened and have tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good Word of God and the powers of the age to come (by which, indeed, divine faith is described, which brings a sense of spiritual goods, so that it could not be described more correctly), if they fall away, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and putting Him to an open shame, to be renewed again to repentance, Heb. 6:4-6. Cf. 2 Pet. 2:20.

Smalcald Articles: "Whether some fanatical spirits might come, as perhaps some are already present and at the time of the uprising came before my own eyes, who hold that all those who had once received the Spirit of the forgiveness of sins, or had become believers, if they sinned thereafter, they nevertheless remained in the faith and such sin did not harm them, and thus cried out: 'Do what you will; if you believe, then it is all nothing; faith blots out all sin,' etc. They say in addition: 'Where someone sins after faith and the Spirit, he has never truly had the Spirit and faith.' I have had many such senseless people before me, and I fear that such a devil still sticks in some. Therefore, it is necessary to know and to teach that where holy people, beyond the fact that they still have and feel original sin, and also daily repent and struggle against it, sometimes fall into public sin, as David did in adultery, murder, and blasphemy, that then faith and the Spirit have departed. For the Holy Spirit does not let sin rule and gain the upper hand so that it is carried out, but steers and resists so that it must not do what it wants. But if it does what it wants, then the Holy Spirit and faith are not present; for it is written, as St. John says: 'Whoever is born of God does not sin, and cannot sin.' And yet it is also the truth (as the same St. John writes): 'If we say that we have no sin, we lie, and the truth of God is not in us.'" (P. III. Art. 3, p. 319.)

Gerhard: "Q. IX: Can faith be shaken off and lost through any mortal sin? — Stapleton, in his *Promptuarium Catholicum*, p. 60, does not fear to assert: 'From this Gospel (4th Sunday after Epiphany) that great and impious axiom of the Lutherans is overturned, that faith is shaken off and lost through any mortal sin. Which, therefore, fraudulently..."

they say, in order to appear [orthodox], when they assert that faith alone justifies and saves, that they understand faith as necessarily conjoined with virtue and good works.’ . . . The Council of Trent, Sess. 6, c. 15, Costerus in his *Enchiridion*, chapter on faith, p. 178, and Bellarmine, Book 1, *On Justification*, chapter 15, subscribe to this error, establishing that faith cannot be lost by any sins, even the most grievous.

The πρῶτον ψεῦδος [first falsehood] of this Papist error is: 1. That they define justifying faith by mere knowledge and assent, and not by trust, and that they establish that historical faith, the faith of miracles, and saving faith are one and the same; 2. That they also say that faith can exist alone without good works, nay, that faith can remain together with horrible and abominable sins. Whence they establish ‘believing fornicators, believing adulterers, believing thieves, believing misers, drunkards, revilers,’ etc., Council of Trent, Sess. 16, c. 15.

For the decision of this question, we say here that there is a maximum difference between historical faith and saving faith. For although saving faith embraces knowledge and therefore is also historical faith, yet not every historical faith is also saving faith, since saving faith, besides knowledge and assent, also embraces the fiducial apprehension of Christ. The question here, therefore, is concerning saving faith, whether it can be lost through mortal sins and against conscience.” (Explic. ελεγκτική ev. Dominical. p. 346 sq.)

ANTITHESES. The Canons of Dort: “Because of these remnants of indwelling sin, and the temptations of the world and Satan, those who are converted could not persevere in this grace if they were left to their own strength. But God is faithful, who mercifully confirms them in the grace once conferred, and powerfully preserves them in the same until the end. And although that power of God, confirming and preserving true believers in grace, is greater than that which could be overcome by the flesh; yet the converted are not always so led and moved by God that they cannot, by their own fault, depart from the leading of grace in certain particular actions, and be seduced by the lusts of the flesh, and yield to them.

Therefore, they must perpetually watch and pray, lest they be led into temptations. When they do not do this, they can not only be carried away by the flesh, the world, and the devil into even grievous and atrocious sins, but they are sometimes carried away by the just permission of God. This is demonstrated by the sad falls of David, Peter, and other saints, described in holy Scripture. By such enormous sins, however, they greatly offend God, incur the guilt of death, grieve the Holy Spirit, interrupt the exercise of faith, wound their conscience most grievously, and sometimes lose the sense of grace for a time: until, by serious repentance, the fatherly face of God shines upon them again as they return to the way.

For God, who is rich in mercy, according to the immutable purpose of election, does not altogether take His Holy Spirit from His own, even in sad falls; nor does He allow them to fall so far that they fall from the state of adoption and justification, or commit the sin unto death, or against the Holy Spirit, and, being utterly deserted by Him, precipitate themselves into eternal destruction. For, first, in these falls He preserves in them that seed of His which is immortal, from which they are regenerated, so that it does not perish or be cast out. Then, by His Word and Spirit, He certainly and effectively renews them to repentance, so that they may grieve from the heart and according to God for the sins committed, seek and obtain remission in the blood of the Mediator, through faith, with a contrite heart, feel the grace of a reconciled God again, adore His mercies through faith, and henceforth work out their salvation with fear and trembling more studiously. Thus, not by their own merits or strength, but out of the gratuitous mercy of God, they obtain that they neither fall away totally from faith and grace, nor finally remain in their falls or perish.” (Chap. V, articles 3—8.) “

The Synod rejected the errors of those who teach: ‘That the faith of temporary believers does not differ from justifying and saving faith, except in duration alone. For Christ Himself, in Matthew 13:20 and Luke 8:13 and following, manifests a threefold difference between temporary and true believers PART III. CHAP. III.

establishes, when he says that the former receive the seed in stony ground, the latter in good ground, or a good heart: that the former lack a root, the latter have a firm root: that the former are void of fruits, the latter bring forth their fruit in varying measure, constantly or perseveringly.“ (L. c. Rejection 7. See Corpus libror. symbol., which in the Reformed churches, etc. Ed. Augusti. 1827. p. 230. sq. 237.)

Confession of faith of the Presbyterians: „They whom God hath accepted in his Beloved, effectually called and sanctified by his Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end.“ (See The Constitution of the Presbyterian Church. Philadelphia 1840. p. 91.) §

Therefore, just as man immediately obtains the grace of God and the inheritance of salvation through the act of believing in Christ,a so, in order that he may actually attain to eternal salvation after this life, it is necessary that faith be final.b According to those things which we said above in § 1 and 6 and about which it will be more distinctly established from what is to be said in the Book on Justification. Meanwhile see Rom. 8, 1. 16. 17.

ANTITHESES. Canones Dordraceni: ,,Propter istas peccati inhabitantis reliquias, et mundi insuper ac satanae tentationes, non possent conversi in ista gratia perstare, si suis viribus permitterentur. Sed fidelis est Deus, qui ipsos in gratia semel collata misericorditer confirmat, et in eadem usque ad finem potenter conservat. Etsi autem illa potentia Dei, vere fideles in gratia confirmantis et conservantis, major est, quam quae a carne superari possit; non semper tamen conversi ita a Deo aguntur et moventur, ut non possint in quibusdam actionibus particularibus a ductu gratiae, suo vitio, recedere, et a carnis concupiscentiis seduci, iisque obsequi.

Quapropter ipsis perpetuo est vigilandum et orandum, ne in tentationes inducantur. Quod cum non faciunt, non solum a carne, mundo, et satana in peccata etiam gravia et atrocia abripi possunt, verum etiam interdum justa Dei permissione abripiuntur. Quod tristes Davidis, Petri, aliorumque sanctorum lapsus, in s. Scriptura descripti demonstrant. Talibus autem enormibus peccatis Deum valde offendunt, reatum mortis incurrunt, Spiritum Sanctum contristant, fidei exercitium interrumpunt, conscientiam gravissime vulnerant, sensum gratiae nonnunquam ad tempus amittunt: donec per seriam resipiscentiam in viam revertentibus paternus Dei vultus rursum affulgeat.

Deus enim, qui dives est misericordia, ex immutabili electionis proposito, Spiritum Sanctum, etiam in tristibus lapsibus, a suis non prorsus aufert; nec eousque eos prolabi sinit, ut gratia adoptionis ac justificationis statu excidant, aut peccatum ad mortem, sive in Spiritum Sanctum committant et, ab eo penitus deserti, in exitium aeternum sese praecipitent. Deinde, per verbum et Spiritum suum eos certo et efficaciter renovat ad poenitentiam, ut de admissis peccatis ex animo et secundum Deum doleant, remissionem in sanguine Mediatoris, per fidem, contrito corde, expetant et obtineant, gratiam Dei reconciliati iterum sentiant, miserationes per fldem ejus adorent, ac deinceps salutem suam cum timore et tremore studiosius operentur. Ita non suis meritis, aut viribus, sed ex gratuita Dei misericordia id obtinent, ut nec totaliter fide et gratia excidant, nec finali ter in lapsibus maneant aut pereant.“ (Cap. V. artic. 3—8.) ״

### On Faith in Christ: That is, that he either never loses throughout his whole life the habitual…

That is, that he either never loses throughout his whole life the habitual faith born from the acts of believing (which will be explained more clearly in the Book on Conversion), or perhaps, having lost it through sins, he nevertheless recovers and preserves it before death; certainly he must take care that death does not overwhelm him while he is lacking the act and habit of faith.

Whence Apoc. 2, 10 it is said: Be faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. And chap. 3, 11: Hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown. Matt. 24, 13: He that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.

Gerhard: „On the various divisions of faith. — We say that one faith is historical, another of miracles, another justifying. Historical faith is that by which we believe that those things which are revealed in the Word of God are true. The faith of miracles is established by some as twofold: active and passive. Active is a peculiar gift of God, through which those who are instructed in it work miracles by confidence in divine power, 1 Cor. 13, 2: ‚If I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains‘ etc. Passive is that confidence by which someone determines that he will be a participant in the benefits which occur through miracles; Acts 14, 9, a certain man of Lystra has faith that he will be healed by Paul. Justifying faith is the fiducial apprehension of divine mercy promised on account of Christ.

Bellarmine, Book I on Justification, chap. 4, disapproves of this division and teaches that historical faith, the faith of miracles, and the faith of promises are one and the same; to whom we oppose this argument: those things of which one can be absent from the other are not essentially one. But justifying faith can be absent from historical faith and from the faith of miracles. Therefore they are not essentially one. The truth of the minor premise is manifest regarding both parts; for although justifying faith presupposes knowledge and assent or historical faith, and therefore historical faith cannot be absent from justifying faith, nevertheless justifying faith can be absent from historical faith, as is evident from the example of hypocrites, who know and profess the truth of the Gospel, yet do not fiducially apprehend Christ. Thus the faith of miracles can be absent from justifying faith; for many who truly believe in Christ are not instructed with the gift of miracles; and conversely, justifying faith can be absent from the faith of miracles, as is evident

ON FAITH IN CHRIST. from the saying of Christ in Matthew 7:22: "Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?" v. 23: "And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity." And likewise from the apostolic pronouncement in 1 Corinthians 13:2: "Though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing." ...

The divine apostle in 1 Timothy 1:5 makes mention of true faith, πίστεως ανυποκρίτου: he implies, therefore, that there is another faith that is feigned or hypocritical. True faith is a fiducial apprehension of Christ, which is effective through love, Galatians 5:6, from which good works can no more be separated than light from the sun, or humidity from water; therefore, a hypocritical and feigned faith will be that which, removed from all piety, is defined only by profession and boasting. Akin to this distinction between true and hypocritical faith is the distinction of the apostle James between living and dead faith. Living faith, since it embraces Christ the author of life, manifests itself outwardly through the works of spiritual life; but faith, which does not have works, is dead in itself, James 2:17. ...

By reason of degrees, one faith is called small and little, which is still joined with no small amount of doubt; such as is attributed to the disciples of Christ in Matthew 8:26 and 16:8, who fluctuated in their minds during the sea storm, and did not trust themselves and their salvation to Christ with full confidence of heart, and who, having forgotten to take bread, were anxious and worried about their own feeding. Such ὀλιγοπιστία is also attributed to those who, out of anxiety, say: "What shall we eat? or what shall we drink? or wherewithal shall we be clothed?" Matthew 6:31. Likewise to Peter, who, walking on the sea and beginning to sink when a strong wind arose, cried out: "Lord, save me." Matthew 14:31.

They are called ὀλιγόπιστοι, however, either whose faith is meager, weak, and languid, or who cannot trust and rely upon God much, nor for many things, nor for great things, but can scarcely trust Him for a little, for few things, and for meager things. There is, therefore, a twofold weakness of faith: one with respect to degrees (of which we treat in this place), when we know what must be believed, yet we do not adhere to them with a faith that is so firm and robust; the other with respect to objects, when we firmly adhere to those things which we know and believe, while in the meantime there remain other things to be believed which we have not yet perceived; in this way, those who still observed the choice of foods and other legal ceremonies along with the Gospel are called by the apostle weak in faith, Romans 14:1.

Opposed to this weak and languid faith is great faith, which is joined with remarkable confidence, whence it subsists in temptations and carries off a glorious victory; such was that of the Canaanite woman in Matthew 15:28, who was victorious in the most grievous struggle of various temptations. Likewise that of the Capernaum centurion, who said to Christ: "I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: but speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed," Matthew 8:8, of whom Christ utters this eulogy: "I have not found τοσαύτην πίστιν, so great faith, in Israel," v. 10. To this pertains the fact that Peter commands us to be strong in the faith, 1 Peter 5:9. Paul mentions faith that grows exceedingly, 2 Thessalonians 1:3, and the apostles pray: "Lord, increase our faith," Luke 17:5.

From the parable of Christ concerning the seed cast into four kinds of soil in Matthew 13, Mark 4, and Luke 8, it can be gathered that some faith is πρόσκαιρος, temporary, while some is stable and persevering; hence the apostle prescribes this rule in 1 Timothy 1:19: "War a good warfare; holding (or retaining) faith, and a good conscience." And the Son of God warns gravely in Revelation 3:11: "Κράτει, ὃ ἔχεις," hold fast that which thou hast.

Faith is also called by some perfect, and by others imperfect. Perfection is attributed to faith either by reason of its kind, namely, perfect knowledge, the fullest assent, and a firm confidence excluding all doubt, or by reason of its object, namely, those things which are proposed to be believed. The former they call intensive perfection, to which we cannot aspire in this life, but the latter they call extensive.

In the writings of Dr. Luther, that distinction occurs that faith is sometimes concrete, sometimes abstract. Tom. 4. Lat. fol. 86: "We are accustomed to distinguish faith in this way, that faith is sometimes taken apart from the work, and sometimes with the work. For just as an artisan speaks in various ways about his material, and a gardener about a tree, whether it is bare or bearing fruit, so also the Holy Spirit in Scripture speaks in various ways about faith, now about faith, so to speak," 176Part.m.cap.m. abstract or absolute; now concerning concrete, composite, or incarnate faith. Faith is absolute or abstract when Scripture speaks absolutely of justification or of the justified, as can be seen in the epistles to the Romans and Galatians. But when Scripture speaks of rewards and works, then it speaks of composite, concrete, or incarnate faith, such as: "Do this, and you will live. If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. Turn away from evil and do good." Vol. I, fol. 151: "Sayings that speak of the whole Christian life or of incarnate faith must not be drawn against the part, that is, against faith alone justifying." Neander in *Theolog.*, ch. on faith, p. 546: "All sayings of Scripture that seem to attribute something to works are to be understood concerning composite, concrete, or incarnate faith; everywhere it is of faith alone, yet it is attributed to works on account of faith in the concrete, etc. And all the sayings of Scripture that seem to attribute something to works presuppose faith, so that its virginity and divinity may remain unviolated and intact, and all glory be given to God alone, and he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord alone."

These are the words of the divine Luther, which are drawn from the theological rule: Faith alone justifies, although it is never alone, that is, separated from good works; the use of which distinction and rule will appear in its proper place in the disputation concerning the righteousness of faith and the merits of works. (Locus on justification § 109—112.) §

20. Actual faith in Christ can be described as an act of the human intellect and will, by which a man so recognizes the doctrine concerning Christ the Mediator and concerning the grace of God, or the remission of sins to be obtained from God through His merit, that by the divine virtue conjoined to that doctrine, he not only judges with full persuasion that it is true and that Christ has merited grace for him before God, but also rests in Christ, as the cause of obtaining grace before God, for the sake of attaining the remission of sins and eternal salvation. In the way in which things that imply a certain aggregate or complex (of different acts) can be described. See § 6, note c. To which faith pertains, as a vital and immanent act in man. Compare § 12, 13. Thus knowledge is indicated as the first act of faith. See § 2. Or with God effecting it, through a supernatural influx; by which reason the principal efficient cause of faith is signified. See § 9. So that the doctrine itself is the organ, or the instrumental efficient cause of kindling faith. See § 11. Thus assent, or the second act of faith, is denoted. See § 3. By which the special assent of faith is denoted, according to § 4. And these things said thus far pertain to the intellect. Which is the act of trust, pertaining to the will; by which faith is completed. See § 5. Thus the end of faith is denoted. Compare § 1 and 14.

PART III. CHAP. IV. § 21. Habitual faith can be described as a habit of the intellect and will of knowing those things which are divinely revealed and to be believed, especially concerning Christ the Mediator and the grace of God and salvation to be obtained through Christ, and of assenting to the same by and because of divine revelation, and of trustfully resting in Christ, divinely conferred for the sake of obtaining the remission of sins itself and eternal salvation.

Which itself signifies a certain complex of habits pertaining to the distinct faculties of the soul.

The subject by which is indicated in this twofold manner. Namely, faith, taken in a broader signification, extends itself to all these things. Which is otherwise called the primary object of faith. Which is the formal object (according to Proleg. Chap. I. § 35, 37, Vol. I, p. 68, 74), and likewise the instrumental efficient cause.

Namely, the habit of faith is the principle of those acts of knowing, assenting, and confessing. Thus the principal efficient cause is indicated; which is the same for actual and habitual faith. The end of habitual faith, just as of actual, is this.

Latin:

Id est, ut fidem habitualem ex actibus credendi natam (quod in L. de conversione manifestius explicabitur) vel nunquam per omnem vitam amittat, vel forte per peccata amissam, tamen ante mortem recuperet ac servet; certe caveat, ne mors ipsum, fidei actu habituque carentem, obruat.

Unde Apoc. 2, 10. dicitur: Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam vitae. Et cap. 3, 11.: Tene, quod habes, ut nemo auferat coronam tuam. Matth. 2J±, 13.: Qui perseveraverit usque ad finem, salvus erit.

Gerhardus: ״De variis fidei divisionibus. — Fidem dicimus aliam historicam, aliam miraculorum, aliam justificantem. Fides historica est, qua credimus, vera esse, quae in verbo Dei revelata sunt. Fides miraculorum a quibusdam statuitur duplex: activa et passiva. Activa est peculiare donum Dei, per quam fiducia potentiae divinae miracula operantur, qui ea sunt instructi, 1 Cor. 13, 2.: ,Si habuero omnem fidem, ita ut montes transferam‘ etc. Passiva est confidentia illa, qua statuit quis, se participem fore beneficiorum, quae per miracula contingunt; Actor. 14, 9. quidam Lystrensis fidem habet, se a Paulo sanatum iri. Fides justificans est fiducialis apprehensio divinae misericordiae propter Christum promissae.

Bellarminus libr. I. de justificat, cap. 4. hanc divisionem improbat ac, fidem historicam, miraculorum et promissionum unam et eandem esse, docet; cui opponimus hoc argumentum: quorum unum ab altero abesse potest, ea non sunt essentialiter unum. Atqui a fide historica et a fide miraculorum abesse potest fides justificans. Ergo ea non sunt essentialiter unum. Minoris veritas est manifesta quoad utramque partem; quamvis enim fides justificans praerequirat notitiam et assensum sive fidem historicam ac proinde a fide justificante non possit abesse fides historica, tamen a fide historica abesse potest fides justificans, ut patet exemplo hypocritarum, qui norunt et profitentur evangelii veritatem, nec tamen fiducialiter apprehendunt Christum. Sic a fide justificante potest abesse fides miraculorum; multi enim vere in Christum credentes dono miraculorum non sunt instructi; et vicissim a fide miraculorum potest abesse fides justificans, ut constat

ex dicto Christi Matth. 7, 22.: ,Multi dicent mihi in illa die, Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo virtutes multas fecimus?‘ v. 23.: ,Et tunc confitebor illis: Non novi vos; discedite a me omnes, qui operamini iniquitatem.‘ Itemque ex pronunciato apostolico 1 Cor. 13, 2.: ,Si habuero omnem fidem, ita ut montes transferam, caritatem autem non habeam, nihil sum.‘ . .

Divus apostolus 1 Tim. 1, 5. mentionem facit verae fidei, πίστεως αννποκρίτον: innuit igitur, aliam esse fidem fletam sive hypocriticam. Fides vera est fiducialis apprehensio Christi, quae per caritatem efficax est, Gal. 5, 6., a qua tam non possunt separari bona opera, quam a sole lux, ab aqua humiclitas; hypocritica igitur et ficta fides erit, quae, ab.omni pietate remota, sola professione et jactantia definitur. Affinis est huic distinctioni inter fidem veram et hypocriticam Jacobi apostoli distinctio inter fidem vivam et mortuam. Fides viva, cum Christum vitae auctorem amplectatur, per opera spiritualis vitae exterius sese exserit; sed fides, quae non habet opera, mortua est in semetipsa, Jac. 2, 17. . .

Ratione graduum fides alia dicitur parva et modica, quae cum dubitatione non mediocri adhuc conjuncta; qualis tribuitur discipulis Christi Matth. 8, 26. 16, 8., qui in marina tempestate animis fluctuabant, nec plena cordis fiducia sese ac salutem suam Christo credebant, quique, panum ex incuria obliti, de sui cibatione angebantur ac soliciti erant. Talis ολιγοπ ιστία tribuitur etiam illis, qui ex solicitudine dicunt: ,Quid manducabimus, aut quid bibemus, aut quo operiemur?‘ Matth. 6, 31. Item Petro, qui, in mari ambulans et exorto vento valido mergi incipiens, clamabat: ,Domine, salvum me fac.‘ Matth. 14, 31.

Dicuntur autem ολιγόπιστοι, vel quorum fides est exigua, infirma et languida, vel qui Deo non multum, nec multa, nec magna, sed parum, pauca et exigua vix concredere et fidere possunt. Est igitur duplex fidei infirmitas: una respectu graduum (de qua hoc loco agimus), quando scimus, quae credenda sint, fide tamen non ita firma ac robusta illis adhaeremus; altera respectu objectorum, quando firmiter adhaeremus his, quae scimus et credimus, interim adhuc alia supersunt credenda, quae nondum percepimus; hoc pacto, qui adhuc servabant ciborum delectum et alias ceremonias legales una cum evangelio, dicuntur ab apostolo infirmi in fide, Rom. 14, 1.

Huic infirmae et languidae fidei opponitur fldes magna, quae cum insigni fiducia est conjuncta, unde in tentationibus subsistit et victoriam gloriosam reportat; talis erat mulieris Cananeae Matth. 15, 28., quae in gravissima lucta variarum tentationum victrix erat. Item centurionis Capernaitici, qui ad Christum dicebat: ,Non sum dignus, ut intres sub tectum meum, sed dic verbum unum, et sanabitur puer meus‘, Matth. 8, 8., de quo Christus hoc elogium profert: ,Non inveni τοσαντην πίστιν, tantam fidem, in Israel, v. 10. Huc pertinet, quod Petrus nos fortes esse in fide jubet 1. Epist. 5, 9. Paulus meminit fidei supercrescentis 2 Thess. 1, 3. et apostoli precantur: ,Domine, adauge nobis fidem‘, Luc. 17, 5.

Ex parabola Christi de semine in quadruplicem terram projecto Matth. 13. Mare. 4. Luc. 8. colligi potest, quod quaedam fides sit πρόςκαφος, temporaria, quaedam vero stabilis et perseverans, inde apostolus hanc praescribit regulam 1 Tim. 1, 19.: ,Milita bonam militiam, habens (sive retinens) fidem et bonam conscientiam.‘ Et Filius Dei graviter monet Apocal. 3, 11.: ,Kράτει, ο έχεις‘, fortiter tene, quod habes.

Dicitur etiam fides alia perfecta, alia vero imperfecta. Perfectio tribuitur fidei vel ratione generis, videlicet perfectae notitiae, plenissimi assensus, firmae et omnem dubitationem excludentis fiduciae, vel ratione objecti, videlicet eorum, quae credenda proponuntur. Illam vocant intensivam perfectionem, ad quam in hac vita aspirare non possumus, hanc vero extensivam.

In scriptis D. Lutheri occurrit illa distinctio, quod fides alia sit concreta, alia abstracta. Tom. 4. Lat. fol. 86.: ,Distinguere solemus fidem hoc modo, quod fides aliquando accipiatur extra opus, aliquando cum opere. Ut enim artifex varie de sua materia et hortulanus de arbore vel nuda, vel gestante fructus loquitur, ita et Spiritus Sanctus in Scriptura varie de fide loquitur, jam de fide, ut sic dicam, 176Part.m.cap.m. abstracta seu absoluta; jam de fide concreta, composita seu incarnata. Fides absoluta seu abstracta est, quando Scriptura absolute loquitur de justificatione seu de justificatis, ut cernere est in epistolis ad Romanos et Galatas. Quando vero Scriptura loquitur de praemiis et operibus, tunc de fide composita, concreta seu incarnata loquitur, ut: ,Hocfac, et vives. Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Declina a malo et fac bonum.‘ Tom. I. fol. 151.: ,Dicta, quae de tota vita Christiana seu de fide incarnata loquuntur, non debent trahi contra partem, id est, contra fidem solam justificantem.‘ Neander in Theolog. cap. de fide p. 546.: ,Omnia dicta Scripturae, quae operibus aliquid tribuere videntur, de fide composita, concreta seu incarnata intelligenda sunt; ubique solius fidei est, operibus tamen tribuitur propter fidem in concreto etc. Et cuncta dicta Scripturae, quae videntur aliquid tribuere operibus, praesupponunt fidem, ita ut ejus virginitas et divinitas illibata maneat et integra et Deo soli universa detur gloria, et qui gloriatur, in solo Domino glorietur.‘

Haec divus Lutherus, quae petita sunt ex regula theologica: Fides sola justificat, quamvis nunquam sit sola, hoc est, a bonis operibus separata; cujus distinctionis et regulae usus in disputatione de justitia fidei et meritis operum suo loco apparebit.“ (Locus de justificatione § 109—112.) §

20. Describi a potest fides in Christum actualis, quod sit actus intellectus et voluntatis b humanae, quo homo doctrinam de Christo mediatore deque gratia Dei seu remisÎÎ sione peccatorum, per illius meritum a Deo impetranda, ita c cognoscit, ut virtute d divina doctrinae illi e conjuncta non solum plane persuasus judicet,f eam esse veram et Christum sibi g promeruisse gratiam apud Deum, verum etiam in Christo, tanquam causa impetrandae gratiae apud Deum,h acquiescat consequendae ipsius remissionis peccatorum1 et salutis aeternae causa. Eo modo, quo, quae aggregatum quiddam aut complexum (ex diversis actibus) important, describi possunt. Vid. § 6. not. c. Quo pertinet fides, tanquam actus vitalis et immanens in homine. Confer § 12. 13. Sic indicatur notitia, tanquam primus actus fidei. Vid. § 2. Seu Deo efficiente, per supernaturalem influxum; qua ratione causa efficiens principalis fidei significatur. Vid. § 9. Ita ut doctrina ipsa sit organon, seu causa efficiens instrumentalis accendendae fidei. Vid. § 11. Sic assensus, seu actus alter fidei, denotatur. Vid. § 3. PART. III. CAP. IV. § 21. Fides habitualis a describi potest, quod sit habitus intellectus et voluntatis b cognoscendi ea, quae divinitus revelata c et credenda sunt praesertim d de Christo mediatore et gratia Dei ac salute per Christum impetranda eidemque per et propter revelationem e divinam assentiendi et fiducialiter in Christo acquiescendi f divinitus g collatus, consequendae ipsius remissionis peccatorum et salutis aeternae h causa.

Quae et ipsa complexum quiddam ex habitibus, ad distinctas facultates animae pertinentibus, significat.

Subjectum quo duplex hac ratione indicatur. Nempe fides, in latiore significatione accepta, ad haec omnia se extendit. Quod alias dicitur objectum fidei primarium. Quod est objectum formale (juxta Proleg. cap. I. § 35. 37., Vol. I. p. 68. 74.), itemque causa efficiens Instrumentalis.

Nempe habitus fidei est principium actuum illorum cognoscendi, assentiendi, confitendi. Ita causa efficiens principalis indicatur; quae eadem est fidei actualis et habitualis. Finis fidei habitualis aeque atque actualis hic est.


## 19 On Regeneration and Conversion

Chapter IV. ON REGENERATION AND CONVERSION. § 1. Since it is established that Christ profits no one for salvation unless he believes in Christ, it must be seen by what action faith in Christ is conferred upon men; which the Scriptures call regeneration or conversion.

From the preceding Chap. III. § 1 and the Prolegomena cited there. Thus in Titus 3:5 mention is made of παλιγγενεσίας in order to the obtaining of justification through the grace of Christ, and that we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

And Christ in John 3:3 ff. says that birth from above (or from the Spirit), which ought to follow birth from the flesh, is so necessary that, unless one is born in that manner, he cannot see the kingdom of God or

to enter into it. Therefore, since that inheritance and the entrance into eternal life are not obtained except through faith in Christ (to which the words of John 3:15, 16, 17, 18 also point), it is easily evident that regeneration consists in this: that faith is generated in men, and thus men become believers from being non-believers. Furthermore, 1 John 5:1: "Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God." Now, to be born of God is to be reborn; and thus it is manifestly evident that a man is reborn by the very fact that faith is kindled in him. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Disputations on Conversion*, edited at Halle, Disp. I, § 15, and Disp. II, § 9, 10, Disp. V, § 61.

Quenstedtius: "The form of regeneration consists in the donation of spiritual life, that is, in the bestowal of the powers of believing and of saving faith." (*Theol. didact.-pol.* P. III, c. 6, s. 1, th. 17, p. 691.) Thus, in Acts 15:3, the ἐπιστροφή τῶν ἐθνῶν, the conversion of the Gentiles, is mentioned; which Peter then explains by saying that the Gentiles believed the word of the Gospel, v. 5, 7, and that God purified their hearts by faith, v. 9. Compare v. 19 and Acts 26:18.

Quenstedtius: "The form of conversion consists in the translation of an unregenerate man from the state of wrath and sin into the state of grace and faith, from the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom of light." (*L. c.* c. 7, s. 1, th. 22, p. 706.) § 2. The term regeneration, when taken more broadly, includes justification and renewal in addition to conversion; in a stricter sense, it now denotes only justification, at other times renewal or sanctification; but it also precisely denotes the donation of faith. The latter is the meaning of this locus: to which correspond new creation, vivification, and spiritual resuscitation.

Regarding its polysemy, see *Declaration of the Formula of Concord*, Art. III, p. 686, and *Epitome of the Articles of Controversy*, Art. II, at the beginning, p. 578. Conf. the blessed Kromayer, *Theol. Posit.-Pol.* Art. XVI, Thes. 15, p. 855, 856; the blessed Joh. Olearius in *Continuation of Carpzov’s Isagoge to the Symbolic Books*, to the *Formula of Concord*, Sect. II, Art. II, M. II, Observ. VI, p. 1250, as also the blessed Carpzov, *Special Disputation on Conversion*, § 5. Add the blessed Olearius’s Index to Balduin, *Theol. Posit.* Art. 92, § 6, p. 154. Huelsemannus: "That there was already a controversy among the orthodox long ago concerning the difference between the terms justification, regeneration, renewal, vivification, adoption, salvation, and safety, is evident from J. Wigand’s treatise 'On the Necessity of Good Works,' opposed to the Majorists, printed at Magdeburg in 1555, right from the beginning, and another treatise of the same author 'On Justification,' published here at Leipzig in 1580, p. 105 sq. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession gave occasion for the dispute—not indeed the first one held at Augsburg, but the one printed in 1531—in which Philip uses in various ways, not indeed the term 'justifying,' but the terms 'vivifying,' 'regenerating,' and 'renewing.' However, I have shown above that the terms 'regeneration' and 'vivification' are sometimes taken more broadly in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession and in the Book of Concord itself."

insofar as they include the renewal of the will and the appetites in relation to new obedience; indeed, the term "renewal" is sometimes even taken for regeneration, as in the Apology, p. 90 (115): "Justification is not only the beginning of renewal, but reconciliation, by which we are also afterwards accepted before God." In the same Apology, however, on pp. 134, 138, 139, 73, 82, 109, and more frequently, the term for both regeneration and vivification is taken so broadly that it comprehends both the renewal of the affections and absolution or justification from sins. Regarding Article 10, section 1, § 8, I showed that the term "conversion" has always been used in a broader sense than any of these terms, so that it embraces not only the first illumination of man by reason of the term from which, but also the progress of those already converted by reason of the term to which, both as regards illumination and daily renewal. The term "regeneration," however, differs from the term "justification" not by reason of the term to which, but in view of the term from which. For although the adequate subject of justification is an unjust man, according to that passage in Rom. 4:5, 17: "To him who believes in Him who justifies the ungodly," yet that ungodly person must necessarily acknowledge his ungodliness. But the adequate subject of regeneration and vivification by reason of the term from which is a man who is plainly dead in sins; which is evident from a comparison of Eph. 2:1, 5; 1 Pet. 1:3, 22, 23; 2:2; John 3:5, 6. The adequate subject of regeneration is called "flesh born of flesh." Renewal and sanctification take place from day to day, 2 Cor. 4:16; Eph. 4:23; 2 Cor. 7: 1. Vivification and regeneration, however, are nowhere said to take place from day to day and successively, or to receive more and less, so that one might be said to be more regenerated or more alive than another, but the translation from death into life—namely, spiritual life—takes place in a moment, John 5:24; 1:12; 1 John 5:11, 12. See Gerh. *de justif.* n. 121 and 225. Properly and strictly speaking, therefore, justification presupposes in the one being justified an acknowledgment of sins, for it absolves the unjust person who is convicted by the ministry of the law, Rom. 3:20, 23; 10:4, 5, etc. Regeneration, however, begins in a subject endowed with no acknowledgment, no sense of sin, as in the cited place, Eph. 2. As for the term of regeneration to which, it must be confessed that it is not always used for the powers alone or the sole faculty of believing and doing good, abstracting from the exercise and good motions, both internal and external, but sometimes includes the *actus secundus* [second act], as in 1 Pet. 2:2: "Ὡς ἀρτιγέννητα βρέφη, be eager for the spiritual milk," and Matt. 19:28, when the glorious restoration of man is called παλιγγενεσία, it is manifest that this word is not restricted to the mere active or passive faculty of rising from the dead. Nevertheless, we will contend with no one about the word, provided it remains that the term "justification," by the usage of Scripture, when it is used concerning God demanding sin, never includes the renewal of the affections." (Public Lectures on the Book of Concord. See *Vindiciae S. S.*, etc. Ed. Scherzer, p. 550, etc.) By which reason it denotes the translation of the children of wrath into the state of the children of grace, both as regards their internal and real change, and as regards the external lot of the remission of sins and adoption, but also the further perfection and confirmation of those translated. By which is conferred ἐξουσία, that right or dignity to become children of God, to those who believe in His name, John 1: 12. Which follows the justification of faith; in which signification Dr. Luther used this word much, both in the book *On the Church and Councils* and elsewhere; which the Declaration of the Formula of Concord also acknowledges, l.c., p. 686. The blessed Kromayer embraced this, l.c., p. 856: "We," he says, "with most of the more recent ones, will take regeneration for the gift of faith (which justification follows)." And the blessed Hoepfner, *Disp. X. de Justif.* Aphor. VI. § 12, p. 936: "God generates us," he says, "that is, [gives] supernatural powers to be..." PART III. CHAPTER IV.

contributes to the understanding, etc., where he also treats the similarity of carnal generation and regeneration at greater length.

Finally, the blessed J. Olearius, *Isag. Libb. Symb.*, l. c., p. 1250, writes: "Regeneration, taken strictly, signifies nothing other than conversion or the very gift of faith." Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. I. de Convers.* (Halle Edition) § 15, and *Disp. II.* § 9, 10; *Disp. V.* § 61.

For thus the regenerated are called a new creature, 2 Cor. 5:17, Gal. 6:15, and in James 1:18 the reborn are called the firstfruits of God's creatures. Cf. the blessed Balduin, *Comm. in 2. ad Cor. 5*, P. II, Aphor. 16, p. m. 651, and the blessed Olearius, *Indic. Bald.*, l. c., p. 154. See Eph. 2:5. Add Rom. 6:11, where the reborn (of whom v. 3, 4 speak) are called ζώντες, living. Eph. 2:6, whence also the reborn are said to be resurrected or to have risen with Christ, Col. 3:1. §

3. Therefore, since regeneration implies some spiritual change—not indeed substantial, but accidental—its terms must be noted: from which and to which. For no other substance of the intellect and will is introduced through regeneration, with the pre-existing natural substance being deleted and extinguished, etc. See the blessed Huelsemann, *Praelect. in Form. Conc. Art. VI. Sect. IV. § 3*, p. 395.

By which new qualities are introduced into the intellect and will of man, not merely are the pre-existing ones illuminated and excited. See the blessed Huelsemann, l. c.

Namely, from which the change begins. That is, to which it tends, and in which the change is terminated.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the new fanatics, who, recalling from the abyss the gathered and conglomerated errors of the Valentinians, chiliasts, Manichaeans, enthusiasts, Donatists, Schwenkfeldians, Flacians, Osiandrians, Weigelians, and Anabaptists, assert: 'Through regeneration the substance of the former body is abolished, and, while the soul remains the same, a new body is given that differs essentially from the former.'

Let Weigel be one for all here for us, who asserts in *P. 1. Postill.*, p. 62: 'God accomplishes this creation of the new creature in such a way that He leaves Adam's flesh and blood to death, and creates new heavenly flesh and blood in its place through Christ, in which new flesh and blood we humans must enter into the kingdom of God, and not with the old body from Adam.'
