ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Novorum fanaticorum, qui, conglobatos (verba sunt D. Gerhardi Disp. th. p. 984.) et conglomeratos errores Valentinianorum, chiliastarum, Manichaeorum, enthusiastarum, Donatistarum, Suenkfeldianorum, Flacianorum, Osiandristarum, Weigelianorum, et anabaptistarum ex orco revocantes, statuunt: ,Per regenerationem aboleri corporis prioris substantiam ac, manente anima eadem, dari corpus novum essentialiter a priore differens.‘

Unus instar omnium hic nobis sit Weigelius, qui asserit P. 1. Postill. p. 62.: ,Gott vollbringet diese Schöpfung der neuen Creatur also, dass er Adams Fleisch und Blut dem Tode überlasse, und neue himmlisch Fleisch und Blut an die Stätte schaffe durch Christum, in welchem neuen Fleisch und Blut wir Menschen in das Reich Gottes müssen kommen, und nicht mit dem alten Leibe aus Adam‘. ..


### On Regeneration and Conversion: Hence he further asserts, 'the reborn have heavenly flesh, an immortal body…

Hence he further asserts, 'the reborn have heavenly flesh, an immortal body from Christ, are children of Mary, not of Eve, are from Christ, just as Eve was from Adam'; see *P. 1. Postill.*, p. 10, 35, 39; *P. 2.*, p. 11; *P. 3.*, p. 81; *Dialog. de Christianis*, p. 12.

Likewise: 'In regeneration not the soul, but only the body is changed,' he asserts, *P. 2. Post.*, p. 111, 114, and in *Dialog. de Christianis*, p. 36, he says: 'The body must be born new and differently; the soul does not need to become different; it is indeed renewed and enlightened.' Weigel is followed by..."

...are, as has been said, the new fanatics, called the Rosicrucians, who likewise say that "regeneration is the substantial abolition of the heart which we received by carnal generation from our parents." ... 2. Of Flacius and the Flacians, who maintain: "That God, in regeneration and conversion, creates a new heart, and thus a new man, in such a way that the substance and essence of the old Adam (especially the rational soul) is utterly abolished, and a new essence of the soul is created out of nothing." (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. fol. 692. sq.) § 4.

The *terminus a quo* [the point from which] is the lack of spiritual powers for faith and other spiritual acts, and thus, on the part of the intellect, an inability to know spiritual objects; on the part of the will, an inability to pursue spiritual goods; and on the part of the sensitive appetite, an ineptitude for obeying the Spirit and repressing the desires of the flesh. Just as otherwise, through generation, one tends from non-being (e.g., of a man) to being (of a man). Here, however, that from which regeneration begins and which is removed in it is called the death of sin; see Ephesians 2:1. Cf. b. Mus. Disp. II. de Convers. (Halle edition) § 5. 6. 12. Nor is the term "death" incongruous here, even though we are said to be dead spiritually before we are said to live. For it suffices, partly, that we were all created for spiritual life in Adam and in the state of integrity (according to the doctrine of the image of God), and partly, that spiritual life ought to have been actually present in us all when we were born; and therefore its absence does not imply a mere negation, but a privation.

Whence it is evident that what was said above concerning original sin pertains here. And it is to be noted what Christ says in John 6:65: "No one can come to me" (that is, no one has the powers to believe in me), "unless it has been given to him by my Father." Thus the Ephesians, such as they were before they were reborn, are called darkness by Paul in Ephesians 5:8, that is, darkened, lacking spiritual light or the powers of knowing spiritual things.

Or, that the will, such as it is by carnal condition, is not subject to the law of God, nor can it be, Romans 8:7. Namely, in that state sin has not yet ceased to reign in the body; whence men rather obey it through its lusts, Romans 6:12. § 5.

The *terminus ad quem* [the point to which] of regeneration are spiritual powers or spiritual life, which indeed, on the part of the intellect, implies spiritual light or the powers of rightly judging concerning spiritual objects or assenting to them; on the part of the will, the powers of pursuing spiritual goods, especially of trusting in Christ; on the part of the sensitive appetite, some faculty through which it begins to be brought under the obedience of the Spirit. PART III. CHAP. IV.

Viewed in actu primo; which relates to actual spiritual life by way of a principle. Whence we have also said that regeneration itself is otherwise called vivification § 2. and note h. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Disp. V. de Conv. (Hall edition) § 2. sqq. Thus the Ephesians are said to be reborn as light in the Lord, that is, endowed with spiritual light, Eph. 5:8. Elsewhere the reborn are said to be in the light, 1 John 2:9, and enlightened, Heb. 6:4. Just as the spiritual man is said to judge (and thus to possess the powers of judging) spiritual things, otherwise than the natural man, who considers them foolishness and cannot understand them, 1 Cor. 2:14. It is called habitual faith, or faith in actu primo. At least to this extent, that the generation of saving faith in the intellect and will is not hindered by the desires of the flesh. A fuller transformation and perfection of the sensitive appetite, however, pertains to renewal; concerning which in its proper place. See meanwhile the blessed Musaeus, l. c. Disp. II. § 19. § 6.

The principal efficient cause of regeneration is the triune God. Who performs the supernatural work of conferring spiritual life by His own power, and that an infinite one. Thus James, chapter 1, verse 18, says that the Father of lights, from whom every good gift descends, has begotten us. For it is a work ad extra and terminates in an effect really produced within man by a power common to the three persons; whence it is attributed to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Pet. 1:3, and to the Son, who by reason of this spiritual generation of many sons is called Father, Isa. 8:18, Heb. 2:13, and is compared with Adam, the first parent of carnal generation, regarding the origin of spiritual life no less than of justification and glorification itself, Rom. 5:14 sqq., 1 Cor. 15:45 sqq., and to the Holy Spirit, Tit. 3:5, when the washing of regeneration of the Holy Spirit, or that through which the Holy Spirit regenerates men, is mentioned.

ANTITHESIS. Kahnisius: "What seems to justify the strict Lutheran polemic against synergism is the fear that what is added to human freedom is taken away from the work of the Holy Spirit and the merit of Christ. But it happens to these theologians here as elsewhere, that in pursuing one correct and important viewpoint, they let another equally correct and important one fall. If it is God who regenerates us unto saving faith, then this cannot be a product of freedom (I, p. 605). However, it does not follow from this that man behaves in a completely unfree manner during regeneration. As soon as this is assumed, regeneration ceases to be a moral process. This is also an abstraction of theory, since the influence of grace upon man is not even conceivable without a liberating influence upon him. If it is solely the merit of Christ which makes us righteous, then the..."

Faith, which grasps it, includes no merit, because then the merit of man would be added to the merit of Christ. However, it does not follow from this that in faith man is an automaton, whom only the Holy Spirit governs.

There is an acting which includes no merit. The king’s son who assumes his father’s crown, the beggar who receives a gift, the debtor who judicially accepts the surety of another, the one in danger who grasps the saving hand, act without merit. Such a meritless acting is faith. What is from the Holy Spirit is the power to believe. But what is from man is the act of faith.

Just as the will, which is reborn, is the same subject that in the natural state can choose between good and evil, so also faith, which grasps Christ, is the same subject that in the natural state believes in God. These subjects, by the power of the Holy Spirit, grasp a content that is not from man, but is divine grace.

But while the strict Lutherans always kept only the goal in view—to cut off all human merit—they destroyed the psychological and moral foundation in the work of the appropriation of salvation. Erasmus already had enough insight to notice in Luther the same abrupt mode of reasoning to which we pointed in Augustine (p. 141 ff.). "

Luther," he says in his *Hyperaspistes*, "constantly reasons thus: free will cannot do everything, therefore it can do nothing; it does not act except with the help of grace, therefore it does not act at all," and in another place: "Luther knows no other way of exaggerating the glory of the Redeemer than by making man a Satan or something even more impious than Satan, nor does he remember that this very thing, which resides of good in man, is a gift of Christ, whose kindness is so great that He does not begrudge His gifts even to the ungrateful and the impious."

The evangelical truth, into which Augustinianism must be dissolved, indeed requires, in addition to the merit of Christ, the inability of man to come to salvation without Christ, and in addition to the regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit, the inability of the natural man to grasp the offered salvation, but not the doctrine—which slides toward Manichaeism—that the natural man has freedom only for evil and therefore can only resist grace: a doctrine which is against Scripture (Vol. I, p. 551), Tradition (Vol. II, p. 112 ff.), and all experience.

Rather, the truth, the justice, and the peace of the Gospel are for man’s salvation only when there is in him a striving for truth, justice, and peace, which finds in the Gospel what it strives for in vain outside of it. (The Luth. Dogm. 1864. II, 544 sq.) §

7. The internal impulsive cause is the mercy of God. By which God, moved, did not wish us, miserable men dead in sins, to perish, but wished to recall us from the death of sin into spiritual life.

It is proved from 1 Peter 1:3, where it is said that God, χατά τό πολυ αυτοϋ ελεος, according to His abundant mercy, has begotten us again; and Ephesians 2:4-5, where we read that God, being rich in mercy, because of His great love with which He loved us, even when we were dead in trespasses, made us alive together with Christ. Add Titus 3:5. PART III. CHAPTER IV.

§ 8.

The external impulsive and meritorious cause is Christ the Mediator. For in order that God, while preserving His justice, might deal with us according to His mercy and bring us, who were dead in sins, to spiritual life, this is owed not to our merit, but to the merit and satisfaction of another.

By virtue of His merit, passion, and death for us. For this reason, the grace through which men become children of God, believing in His name, as if born of God, is said to have come through Jesus Christ (John 1:12, 13, 17), given to us through Christ, or by virtue of His merit (2 Tim. 1:9), and we are χτισθέντες ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, created in Christ Jesus, as the work of God (Eph. 2:10). § 9. The less principal efficient causes are the Word, Baptism, and in their own way, the ministers of the Church themselves.

Latin:

Hinc porro statuit, ,renatos habere carnem coelestem, corpus immortale ex Christo, esse filios Mariae, non Evae, esse ex Christo, sicut Eva ex Adamo‘; vid. P. 1. Postill. p. 10. 35. 39. P. 2. p. 11. P. 3. p. 81. Dialog, de Christianis, p. 12.

Item: ,In regeneratione nonanimam, sed corpus tantum mutari‘, statuit,P.2. Post. p. 111. 114.et Dialog, de Christianis, p. 36. inquit:,DerLeib muss neue und anders geboren werden, die Seele darf nicht anders werden, sie wird wohl verneuert und erleuchtet.‘ Weigelium sequun

tur, ut dictum, novi fanatici, fratres roseae crucis dicti, qui itidem ajunt, ,regenerationem esse substantialem abolitionem cordis, quod carnali generatione e parentibus accepimus‘. . . 2. Flacii et Flacianorum, statuentium: Deum in regeneratione et conversione novum cor, atque adeo novum hominem ita creare, ut veteris Adami substantia et essentia (imprimis vero anima rationalis) penitus aboleatur, et nova animae essentia ex nihilo creetur.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. fol. 692. sq.) § 4.

Terminus a quo est carentia a virium spiritualium ad fidem aliosque actus spirituales,b adeoque ex parte intellectus impotentia ad cognoscenda c objecta spiritualia, ex parte voluntatis impotentia prosequendi d bona spiritualia, ex parte appetitus sensitivi ineptitudo obsequendi Spiritui et reprimendi desideria carnis. e Prout alias per generationem a non esse (v. g. hominis) ad esse (hominis) tenditur. Hic autem illud, a quo incipit regeneratio et quod in ea tollitur, dicitur mors peccati; vid. Ephes. 2, 1. Conf. b. Mus. Disp. II. de Convers. (edit. Hallens.) § 5. 6.12. Nec incongruum h. 1. est mortis vocabulum, licet prius mortui spiritualiter, quam vivere dicamur. Sufficit enim, partim, quod in Adamo inque statu integritatis ad vitam spiritualem omnes conditi sumus (juxta doctrinam de imagine Dei), partim, quod nobis, cum nascimur, omnibus vita spiritualis actu inesse debebat; ideoque ejus absentia non importat negationem meram, sed privationem.

Unde patet, huc pertinere, quae supra de peccato orig. dicta sunt. Et notandum est, quod Christus ait Joh. 6, 65.: Nemo potest venire ad me (id est, nemo habet vires credendi in me), nisi ei fuerit datum a Patre meo. Sic Ephesii, quales fuerunt, antequam renascerentur, tenebrae appellantur a Paulo Ephes. 5, 8., id est, obtenebrati, carentes luce spirituali seu viribus cognoscendi spiritualia.

Seu, quod voluntas, qualis est per carnalem conditionem, legi Dei non subjicitur, nec subjici potest, Eom. 8, 7. Nempe in eo statu nondum desiit peccatum regnare in corpore; unde nomines potius obediunt illi per concupiscentias ejus, Eom. 6, 12. § 5.

Terminus ad quem regenerationis sunt vires spirituales seu vita spiritualis,a quae quidem ex parte intellectus importat lucem spiritualem b seu vires recte judicandi de objectis spiritualibus aut assentiendi illis, c ex parte voluntatis vires prosequendi bona spiritualia, inprimis confidendi in Christo,d ex parte appetitus sensitivi facultatem aliquam, per quam incipit redigi sub obsequium Spiritus. e PART. III. CAP. IV.

In actu primo spectata; quae ad vitam spiritualem actualem per modum principii sese habet. Unde et ipsam regenerationem alias vivificationem appellari diximus § 2. et not. h. Conf. b. Mus. Disp. V. de Conv. (edit. Hall.) § 2. sqq. Sic Ephesii renati dicuntur lux in Domino, id est, luce spirituali praediti, Ephes. 5, 8. Alias renati dicuntur esse in luce, 1 Joh. 2, 9., illuminati, Ebr. 6, 4. Prout homo spiritualis dicitur dijudicare (et sic pollere viribus dijudicandi) spiritualia, aliter quam homo animalis, qui ea pro stultitia habet, nec potest intelligere, 1 Cor. 2, 14· Vocatur fiducia habitualis, sive in actu primo. Saltem eo usque, ne generatio fidei salvificae in intellectu et voluntate, per desideria carnis continuata, impediatur. Plenior autem immutatio et perfectio appetitus sensitivi ad renovationem pertinet; de qua suo loco. Vide interim b. Mus. 1. c. Disp. II. § 19. § 6.

Causa efficiens principalis a regenerationis Deus b trinunus c est. Quae opus supernaturale conferendae vitae spiritualis virtute propria eaque infinita perficit. Ita Patrem luminum, a quo omnis donatio bona descendit, 7108 genuisse dicit Jacobus cap. 1. v. 18. Est enim opus ad extra ac terminatur ad effectum intra horninem realiter productum per potentiam tribus personis communem; unde et Patri Domini nostri Jesu Christi tribuitur 1 Petr. 1, 3. et Filio, qui ratione spiritualis hujus generationis multorum filiorum Pater appellatur Es. 8, 18. Ebr. 2, 13. et cum Adamo, carnalis generationis primo parente, confertur, quoad originem vitae spiritualis non minus, quam ipsius justificationis et glorificationis Rom. 5, 14· sqq. 1 Cor. 15. 45. sqq., Spiritui Sancto Tit. 3, 5., quando lavacrum regenerationis Spiritus Sancti seu, per quod Spiritus Sanctus homines regeneret, memoratur.

ANTITHESIS. Kahnisius: ,,Was die strenglutherische Polemik gegen den Synergismus zu berechtigen scheint, ist die Furcht, dass, was der menschliehen Freiheit zugelegt, dem Werke des Heiligen Geistes und dem Verdienste Christi abgebrochen werde. Aber diesen Theologen begegnet es hier wie sonst, dass sie, einen richtigen Gesichtspunkt verfolgend, einen andern eben so richtigen und wichtigen fallen lassen. Wenn es Gott ist, der uns wiedergebiert zum seligmachenden Glauben, so kann dieser nicht ein Product der Freiheit sein (I, S. 605.). Daraus folgt aber nicht, dass der Mensch sich bei der Wiedergeburt ganz unfrei verhält. Sobald diess angenommen wird, hört ja die Wiedergeburt auf ein sittlicher Vorgang zu sein. Auch ist diess eine Abstraktion der Theorie, da ja die Einwirkung der Gnade auf den Menschen gar nicht denkbar ist ohne einen befreienden Einfluss auf denselben. Wenn es allein das Verdienst Christi ist, welches uns gerecht macht, so darf der

Glaube, welcher es ergreift, kein Verdienst einschliessen, weil dann zum Verdienst Christi das des Menschen kommen würde. Daraus folgt aber nicht, dass im Glauben der Mensch ein Automat ist, welchen nur der Heilige Geist regiert.

Es giebt ein Thun, welches kein Verdienst einschliesst. Der Königssohn, welcher die Krone seines Vaters übernimmt, der Bettler, welcher eine Gabe empfängt, der Schuldner, welcher die Bürgschaft eines andern gerichtlich annimmt, der in Gefahr schwebende, welcher die rettende Hand ergreift, handeln ohne Verdienst. Solch ein verdienstloses Handeln ist der Glaube. Was vom Heiligen Geist ist, ist die Kraft zu glauben. Was aber vom Mensehen ist, ist der Act des Glaubens.

Wie der Wille, welcher wiedergeboren wird, dasselbe Subjekt ist, welches im natürlichen Zustande zwischen Gutem und Bösem wählen kann, so ist auch der Glaube, weleher Christum ergreift, dasselbe Subjekt, welches im natürlichen Zustande an Gott glaubt. Diese Subjekte ergreifen in Kraft des Heiligen Geistes einen Inhalt, der nicht vom Menschen ist, sondern göttliche Gnade.

Indem aber die strengen Lutheraner immer nur das Ziel ins Auge fassten, alles menschliche Verdienst abzuschneiden, zerstörten sie die psychologische und sittliche Grundlage im Werke der Heilsaneignung. Schon Erasmus hatte Blick genug gehabt, um in Luther dieselbe sprunghafte Schlussweise zu bemerken, auf die wir bei Augustin hinwiesen (S. 141. ff.),

Lutherus‘, sagt er in seinem Hyperaspistes, ,perpetuo sic rationatur: liberum arbitrium non potest totum, ergo nihil potest; non agit nisi cum auxilio gratiae, ergo nihil agit‘, und an einer andern Stelle: ,Lutherus non novit aliam rationem exaggerandi redemtoris gloriam, nisi ex homine faciat satanam aut si quid est satana magis impium, nec meminit, hoc ipsum, quod in homine residet boni, esse donum Christi, cujus tanta est benignitas, ut ingratis etiam et impiis non invideat munera sua.‘

Die evangelische Wahrheit, in welche der Augustinismus aufgelöst werden muss, fordert wohl zum Verdienste Christi die Unfähigkeit des Menschen, ohne Christum zum Heil zu kommen, und zur wiedergebärenden Gnade des Heiligen Geistes das Unvermögen des natürlichen Menschen das dargebotene Heil zu ergreifen, aber nicht die zum Manichäismus abschüssige Lehre, dass der natürliche Mensch nur zum Bösen Freiheit habe und darum der Gnade nur widerstreben könne: eine Lehre, welche gegen Schrift (I. S. 551.), Tradition (II. S. 112. ff.) und alle Erfahrung ist.

Vielmehr sind die Wahrheit, die Gerechtigkeit und der Friede des Evangeliums dem Menschen nur dann zum Heile, wenn in ihm ein Streben nach Wahrheit, Gerechtigkeit und Frieden ist, das im Evangelium findet, was es ausser ihm vergebens erstrebt.“ (Die luth. Dogm. 1864. II, 544. sq.) §

7. Causa impulsiva a interna est misericordia Dei.b Qua Deus commotus 110s miseros et in peccatis mortuos hornines noluit perire, sed ex morte peccati in vitam spiritualem revocare voluit.

Probatur ex 1 Petr. 1, 3., ubi dicitur Deus χατά τό πολυ αυτοϋ ελεος, secundum multam misericordiam suam, nos regenuisse; et Ephes. 2, 4. 5., ubi legimus, Deum divitem in misericordia, propter multam caritotem suam, qua dilexit nos, cum essemus mortui per delicta, convivificasse nos Christo. Add. Tit. 3, 5. PART. HI. CAP. IV.

§ 8.

Causa impulsiva externa et meritoria a est Christus mediator.b Nam ut, salva sua justitia, Deus nobiscum juxta misericordiam suam agere nosque in peccatis mortuos ad vitam spiritualem perducere posset, hoc non nostro, sed alieno merito et satisfactioni debetur.

Vi meriti, passionis et mortis suae pro nobis. Qua ratione gratia, per quam homines filii Dei fiunt, credentes in nomen ejus, tanquam ex Deo nati, per Jesum Christum orta dicitur Joh. 1, 12. 13. 17., data nobis per Christum, aut ex vi meriti ejus, 2 Tim. 1, 9., et nos χτισ&έντες h Χριστώ Ίησου, conditi in Christo Jesu, tanquam opus Dei, Ephes. 2, 20. § 9. Causa efficiens minus principalis a sunt verbum, b haptismus c et suo modo etiam ipsi ministri d ecclesiae.


### On Regeneration and Conversion: Through which God effects conversion in man and with which He concurs to…

Through which God effects conversion in man and with which He concurs to produce the spiritual effect. Thus, we are said to be regenerated by the word of truth (James 1:18). And in 1 Peter 1:23, the word is said to behave like a seed, from which we are reborn.

Brentius: "That the Gentiles (Acts 10) were already regenerated by faith and renewed by the Holy Spirit before baptism is clearly proven by the gift of the Holy Spirit, which fell upon them miraculously... Although they did not now have a need to be baptized in order to be regenerated and renewed by the Holy Spirit, it was nevertheless necessary to obey the ordinance. To this is added that baptism is not only an instrument by which believers are initially regenerated and renewed, but also a symbol by which believers are openly declared to be the people of God and by which those tempted by various afflictions are confirmed in the faith of their regeneration. It is not, therefore, idle and superfluous that these Gentiles were baptized after their regeneration." (Homil. in Acta apostol. Homil. 51. in cap. 10.) Gerhard: "When those are baptized who have already been regenerated by the Word as by a spiritual seed, they do not have need of regeneration through baptism, but baptism is for them a confirmation and sealing of their regeneration. 'Just as in Abraham the righteousness of faith preceded, and circumcision followed as a seal of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:11), so in Cornelius spiritual sanctification preceded in the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the sacrament of regeneration followed in the washing of baptism,' writes Augustine (1. 4. de Bapt. c. 24)." (Loc. de sacramentis, § 106.)

The same: "Faithful catechumens are born of God through the word of truth and faith in Christ; therefore, they are less correctly compared to an embryo not yet formed and born. The antecedent is evident from the fact that not only is the sacrament of baptism called the 'washing of regeneration,' but the Word is also 'that incorruptible seed from which believers are reborn' (1 Pet. 1:23; James 1:18), and those who receive Christ by true faith 'are born of God' (John 1:12, 13)." (Loc. de ecclesia, § 55.) Dannhauer: "What, you will ask, did baptism accomplish in the eunuch, Cornelius, and Lydia, who were converted and regenerated by the Word before baptism? Dr. Aegidius Hunnius answers (p. 190, Qq. de sacramentis): 'For these, too, baptism is the washing of regeneration. For although they were first converted and regene-"

...though they had been moved by the hearing of the Word, yet that gift of regeneration was wondrously increased and enriched in them through baptism. Therefore, baptism was for them a washing of regeneration. First, because an increase of regeneration was conferred upon them, which, with respect to its internal motions, receives more or less. Then, because the benefit of regeneration, as well as other spiritual gifts and goods, were confirmed to them in the washing of water by the sealing of baptism.” (Hodosoph. Phaenom. X. p. 550.) ANTITHESIS.

Kahnisius: “From the understanding, therefore, the Word goes into the heart (Acts 2:37). There, the Word works repentance and the joy to grasp salvation according to the power of the Holy Spirit dwelling within it. That is the beginning of regeneration, the germ of faith. Man accepts the Word (Acts 2:41), receives Christ (John 1:12). Paul was in this state when Ananias came to him. In this faith, man is not yet righteous, not yet pure from sins, not yet a child of God, not yet one with Christ. He is only in the state of quiet submission to what God wills to do in him. The Holy Spirit now works regeneration negatively by putting the old man to death, and positively by laying the foundation of a new life, setting the beginning of life of a spiritual personality. The Holy Spirit works these two moments in baptism.” (Die Lehre vom Abendmahl. 1851. p. 429 sq.) This is what is meant when we are said to be born again of water (and the Spirit), John 3:5. And baptism is called the washing of regeneration, because this is brought about through it, Titus 3:5.

Insofar, of course, as they constitute the Word and baptism in use and apply them to men to be regenerated, not by their own authority, but by God’s, and according to divine institution. In which sense Paul says in 1 Cor. 4:15: “I have begotten you in Christ Jesus through the gospel.” Gerhardus: “What is attributed in the Holy Scriptures to the ministry of the Word and sacraments is also attributed to the ministers, the heralds of the Word and administrators of the sacraments, not by reason of their person, but by reason of their ministry, insofar as they preach the Word and administer the sacraments. Thus, the gospel is the power of God unto salvation, Rom. 1:16, and Timothy, preaching the gospel, saves himself and those who hear him, 1 Tim. 4:16.” (L. de minister. ecclesiast. § 253.)

Dannhauerus: “In the magistracy there is a principal authority, distinguished from the organic authority which is in the ecclesiastical ministry; for just as a principal secondary cause indeed depends upon the first, yet it has its own native character and active power, by which it flows of itself and by its own force into proportionate effects (just as fire burns by its own virtue): but an instrumental cause has no inherent virtue for the work, nor does it act unless moved and elevated by the principal cause; but the power attributed to the ministry for producing supernatural effects is only organic.” (Lib. conscient. P. II. p. 856.) Hoepfnerus: “When the church is called a mother, this is done only by reason of the ministry by which it dispenses the Word and baptism.” (De iustif. disp. X. p. 936.)

Quenstedtius: “Regeneration is either ordinary, which occurs through the Word, 1 Pet. 1:23, and the sacraments, John 3:5, Tit. 3:5, or extraordinary, which occurs without those external means; such is the regeneration of Christian infants who die before receiving baptism.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 7. f. 686.) PART III. CHAP. IV.

§ 10.

The subject *quod* [which] is man, lacking spiritual life, but not contumaciously resisting the operation of the Holy Spirit, without distinction of age, and whether he has never possessed spiritual life, or has lost again through mortal sins the life he once had. Or of denomination, which in the nominative case is called "to be born again."

a. For he would already be born again if he possessed spiritual life. Cf. B. Mus. 1. c. § 22, 23, and Disp. II. § 12. Fechtius: "The subject of justification, regeneration, and renewal is one and the same, but viewed only in different ways: of justification, whereby he is to be absolved from sins after grace has been received through faith; of regeneration, whereby he is to be endowed with new powers, in which spiritual life consists; of renewal, [as a] justified person, who is led away from sins and brought to the exercise of good works." (Compend. univers. th. complex, p. 596.)

For those who act otherwise and maliciously resist (which adults certainly can and sometimes do), they are not regenerated for as long as that; and they themselves are the cause of it. Cf. B. Mus. Disp. II. de Conv. (Halle ed.) § 2, 61, sqq. For what is said in John 3:3 and Titus 3:5 concerning regeneration is common to men of any age, since all infants can also be baptized; concerning which we shall see below in the Book on Baptism. Cf. B. Mus. 1. c. § 18. Regarding the regeneration of adults, however, who are capable of the preaching of the Gospel, one may look at the passages 1 Peter 1:21, 22, 23; James 1:18. ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: Of the Socinians, who contend that regeneration pertains only to adults, but by no means to infants. ... 'Let him acknowledge' (says Smiglecius, among other things), 'that the way of regeneration, which is proposed only to adults, does not suit the age of infants. For it is evident that they cannot compose their mind and will according to the norm of Christ's law.'" (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 695.) Just as infants, conceived and born in original sin, and adult Gentiles and Jews are born again.

Regarding these, however, it is to be noted that if they are to be regenerated anew, baptism is not to be repeated for that reason, but they must be brought back to repentance through the Word of Law and Gospel, and thus faith must be rekindled in them: by which method the fruit of baptism, having been interrupted for some time, is also restored. B. Mus. Disp. V. de Convers. (Halle ed.) § 58. § 11. The subject *quo* [by which] is the human soul, as regards the intellect and the will; and finally, in its own way, also the sensitive appetite.

Namely, with regard to those faculties in which, as in a subject, faith resides. Compare what we said in § 4 and 5. For the terms from which and to which the subject of the change itself easily indicate this. Add the blessed Musaeus, 1. c., Disp. II, § 3 and 18. According to those things which were said in § 5, last note. §

12. The form of regeneration consists in the very donation of faith; to the manner of which, by which the Holy Spirit acts upon the mind of an adult human being when He regenerates him through the Word, it pertains that He confers habitual faith successively through previous supernatural acts excited by Himself. See § 2, toward the end, and notes e, f.

Calovius: "Q. II: Whether regeneration is properly a change of our life and actions? Moscorovius gives this definition of regeneration in *De bapt.*, c. 7, p. 121: 'Regeneration is a reformation of the life previously led according to the doctrine of the Lord Jesus.' Of the same coinage also is the definition of Smalcius in *De natural. Dei Filio*, c. 2, p. 17: 'Regeneration is an entire change of mind and actions.' But that these descriptions are false is clear from the following: 1. Because nowhere in the Holy Scriptures is regeneration defined by the 'reformation' of a life previously led. 2. Because the Holy Spirit distinguishes between regeneration and renovation, and says that regeneration is that by which we are begotten by God into children of God, and teaches that it is prior to renovation, Tit. 3:5; John 3:5; 1 Pet. 2:3; Jas. 1:17. 3. Because not even renovation itself is properly a reformation of life, but a change of life is a consequence of renovation and a fruit of the same, since it is necessary that we be renewed before we walk in newness of life or bring forth the fruits of the Spirit, Rom. 8:12, 13; Gal. 5:16, 17." (*System.* Tom. X, 10.)

For we have already said in Chapter III, § 11, note c, and § 12, note b, that the regeneration of infants is less explicable.

Latin:

Per quam Deus conversionem in homine efficit et cum qua concurrit ad effectum spiritualem producendum. Sic verbo veritatis regenerari dicimur Jac. 1, 18. Et 1 Petr. 1, 23. verbum seminis instar se habere dicitur, unde renascamur.

Brentius: ,,Gentes (Act. 10.) jam ante baptismum per fidem regeneratas et per Sp. S. renovatas esse, manifeste comprobat donum Sp. S., mirabiliter in ipsas illapsum. . . Tametsi nunc non necesse habebant baptizari, ut regenerarentur et renovarentur a Sp. Sancto, necessarium tamen erat, ordinationi parere. Huc accedit, quod baptismus non solum sit organon, quo initio credentes regenerantur et renovantur, sed etiam symbolum, quo credentes palam declarantur esse populus Dei et quo variis afflictionibus tentati in fide regenerationis confirmantur. Non igitur otiosum et supervacaneum, quod hae gentes post regenerationem baptizentur.“ (Homil. in Acta apostol. Homil. 51. in cap. 10.) Gerhardus: ,,Quando illi baptizantur, qui per verbum tanquam spirituale semen jamdum regeniti sunt, illi non opus habent regeneratione per baptismum, sed baptismus ipsis est confirmatio et obsignatio regenerationis. ,Sicut in Abraham praecessit fidei justitia, et accessit circumcisio signaculum justitiae fidei Rom. 4,11.: ita in Cornelio praecessit sanctificatio spiritualis in dono Sp. S., et accessit sacramentum regenerationis in lavacro baptismi‘, scribit Augustinus 1. 4. de Bapt. c. 24.“ (Loc. de sacramentis, § 106.)

Idem: ,,Catechumeni fideles per verbum veritatis et fidem in Christum sunt ex Deo nati; ergo minus recte conferuntur embryoni nondum formato ac nato. Antecedens patet ex eo, quod non solum baptismatis sacramentum dicitur,lavacrum regenerationis‘, sed etiam verbum est,semen illud incorruptibile, ex quo renascuntur credentes‘ 1 Pet. 1, 23. Jac. 1, 18., et qui vera fide Christum recipiunt, ,ex Deo nati sunt‘, Joh. 1, 12. 13.“ (Loc. de ecclesia. § 55.) Dannhauerus: ,,Quid, inquies, baptismus operatus est in eunucho, Cornelio, Lydia, ante baptismum conversis, regeneratis verbo? Respondet D. Aegid. Hunnius p. 190. (Qq. de sacrameut.): ,Est etiam his baptismus regenerationis lavacrum. Etsi enim primo conversi regene

ratique fuerint per auditum verbi, tamen donum illud regenerationis per baptismum in eis mirifice auctum et locupletatum. Itaque fuit baptismus eis lavacrum regenerationis. Primo, quia illis conferebatur incrementum regenerationis, quae respectu suorum internorum motuum magis minusque recipit. Deinde, quia regenerationis beneficium, ut et reliqua spiritualia dona et bona, lavacro aquae eis obsignatione baptismi confirmabantur.“ (Hodosoph. Phaenom. X. p. 550.) ANTITHESIS.

Kahnisius: ,,Aus dem Verstände geht also das Wort in’s Herz (Apostg. 2, 37.). Dort wirkt das Wort nach der ihm einwohnenden Kraft des Heiligen Geistes Busse und Freudigkeit, das Heil zu ergreifen. Das ist der Anfang der Wiedergeburt, der Keim des Glaubens. Der Mensch nimmt das Wort an (Apostg. 2, 41.), nimmt Christum auf (Joh. 1,12.). In diesem Zustande war Paulus, als Ananias zu ihm kam. In diesem Glauben ist der Mensch noch nicht gerecht, noch nicht rein von Sünden, noch nicht Kind Gottes, noch nicht eins mit Christo. Er ist nur in dem Zustand des Stillehaltens zu dem, was Gott an ihm thun will. Die Wiedergeburt wirkt nun der Heilige Geist negativ dadurch, dass er den alten Menschen todtet, positiv dass er den Grund eines neuen Lebens legt, den Lebensanfang einer geistlichen Persönlichkeit setzt. Diese beiden Momente wirkt der Heilige Geist in der Taufe.“ (Die Lehre vom Abendmahl. 1851. p. 429. sq.) Hoc est, quod ex aqua (et Spiritu) renasci dicimur Joh. 3, 5. Et baptismus dicitur lavacrum reqenerationis, eo, quod haec per ipsum fiat, Tit. 3, 5.

Quatenus nimirum verbum et baptismum in usu constituunt et hominibus regenerandis auctoritate non sua, sed Dei, et juxta institutionem divinam applicant. Quo sensu Paulus 1 Cor. 4, 15. dicit: Ego in Christo Jesu per evangelium vos genui. Gerhardus: ,,Quod verbi et sacramentorum ministerio in S. tribuitur, illud etiam ministris, verbi praeconibus et sacramentorum administris tribuitur, non ratione personae, sed ratione sui ministerii, quatenus sci. verbum praedicant et sacramenta administrant. Sic evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem Rom. 1, 16. et Timotheus, praedicans evangelium, salvat se ipsum et eos, qui ipsum audiunt 1 Tim. 4, 16.“ (L.deminister, ecclesiast. § 253.)

Dannhauerus: ,,In magistratu est exusia principalis, organicae, quae est in ministerio ecclesiastico, contradistincta; sicut enim causa secunda principalis dependet quidem a prima, habet tamen propriam et nativam indolem, potentiam activam, qua per se suapte vi influit in effectus proportionatos (sic ignis urit suapte virtute): at causa instrumentalis non habet insitam virtutem ad opus, nec agit nisi mota ac elevata a causa principali; at ea, quae ministerio tribuitur, potestas ad effectus supernaturales edendos nonnisi organica est.“ (Lib. conscient. P. II. p. 856.) Hoepfnerus: ,,Cum ecclesia mater dicitur, hoc tantum fit ratione ministerii, quo verbum et baptismum dispensat.“ (De iustif. disp. X. p. 936.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Regeneratio est vel ordinaria, quae fit per verbum 1 Pet. 1, 23. et sacramenta Joh. 3, 5. Tit. 3, 5., vel extraordinaria9 quae sine externis illis mediis fit; qualis est regeneratio infantum Christianorum, qui ante baptismum perceptum moriuntur.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 7. f. 686.) PART. III. CAP. IV.

§ 10.

Subjectum quod a est homo carens b vita spirituali, operationi autem Spiritus S. contumaciter non repugnans, c citra differentiam aetatis,d et sive vitam spiritualem nunquam habuerit, e sive per peccata mortalia rursus amiserit, quam habuerat. f Seu denominationis, quod in casu recto dicitur renasci. .

Alias enim jam renatus erit, si habeat vitam spiritualem. Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 22. 23. et Disp. II. § 12. Fechtius: ״ Subjectum et justificationis et regenerationis et renovationis unum idemque, sed diversimode tantum spectatum: justificationis, qua a peccatis post fide receptam gratiam absolvendus; regenerationis, qua novis viribus, in quibus vita spiritualis consistit, donandus; renovationis, justificatus, qui a peccatis abducitur et ad bonorum operum exercitium deducitur.“ (Compend. univers. th. complex, p. 596.)

Nam qui secus agunt et malitiose repugnant (quod utique possunt et aliquando solent homines adulti), tamdiu non regenerantur; atque ipsi quidem sunt in causa. Conf. b. Mus. Disp. II. de Conv. (edit. Hallens.) § 2. 61. sqq. Quae enim Joh. 3, 3. et ad Tit. 3, 5. dicuntur de regeneratione, hominibus cujus vis aetatis sunt communia, cum et infantes omnes baptizari queant; de quo infra in L. de baptismo videbimus. Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 18. De adultorum autem, qui praedicationis evangelii capaces sunt, regeneratione videri possunt loca 1 Petr. 1, 21. 22. 23. Jacobi 1, 18. ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: Socinianorum, qui contendunt, regenerationem tantum adultis convenire, nequaquam autem infantibus. . . . ,Agnoscat‘ (inquit inter alia Smiglecius), ,viam regenerationis, quae adultis tantum proposita est, infantum aetati non convenire. Nec enim eos animum voluntatem que ad normam Christi legis componere posse, constat.“‘ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 695.) Prout infantes, in peccato originali concepti et nati, et adulti gentiles ac Judaei renascuntur.

De his vero notandum est, quod, si denuo regenerandi sint, non ideo iterandus sit baptismus, sed illi per verbum legis et evangelii ad poenitentiam reduci et sic fides in ipsis rursus accendi debeat: qua ratione etiam fructus baptismi, aliquamdiu interceptus, restituitur. B. Mus. Disp. V. de Convers. (edit. Hallens.) § 58. § 11. Subjectum quo est anima humana, quoad a intellectum et voluntatem; denique suo modo b etiam appetitum sensitivum.

Nempe quoad eas facultates, in quibus, tanquam in subjecto, est fides. Confer., quae diximus § 4. et 5. Nam termini a quo et ad quem ipsum subjectum mutationis facile indicant. Adde b. Mus. 1. c. Disp. II. § 3. et 18. Juxta ea, quae dicta sunt § 5. nota ult. §

12. Forma regenerationis in ipsa fidei donafione a consistit; ad cujus modum, quo Spiritus S. in hominis adulti b mentem agit, cum eam per verbum regenerat, pertinet, quod successive c per praevios actus supernaturales a se ipso excitatos d fidem habitualem confert. Vid. § 2. sub finem et notas e. f.

Calovius: ,,Q. II.: Utrum regeneratio proprie sit vitae et actionum nostrarum mutatio? Moscorovius hanc tradit regenerationis definitionem 1. de bapt. c. 7. p. 121.: ,Regeneratio est vitae ante actae seeundum doctrinam Domini Jesu reformatio.‘ Ejusdem monetae quoque est definitio Smalcii 1. de natural. Dei Filio c. 2. p. 17.: ,Regeneratio est integra animi et actionum mutatio.‘ At descriptiones hasce falsas esse, ex hisce liquet: 1. Quia nuspiam in S. definitur regeneratio per,reformationem‘ vitae ante actae. 2. Quia Sp. S. distinguit inter regenerationem et renovationem, ac regenerationem dicit, qua nos a Deo gignimur in filios Dei, eamque priorem esse renovatione, docet Tit. 3, 5. Joh. 3, 5. 1 Pet. 2, 3. Jac. 1, 17. 3. Quia ne renovatio quidem ipsa proprie est reformatio vitae, sed mutatio vitae consequens est renovationis et fructus ejusdem, cum prius nos oporteat renovari, quam in novitate vitae ambulemus aut fructus Spiritus proferamus, Rom. 8, 12. 13. Gal. 5, 16. 17.“ (System. Tom. X, 10.)

Nam infantum regenerationem minus explicabilem esse, jam diximus cap. III. § 11. nota c. et § 12. nota b.


### On Regeneration and Conversion: However, not in such a way that the habit of faith is infused into the…

However, not in such a way that the habit of faith is infused into the faculties of the soul immediately and in an instant. See the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. I. de Fide*, where he teaches against the scholastics that, just as natural habits are acquired through natural acts, so also supernatural habits of the soul are acquired through supernatural acts, excited by the Holy Spirit through the Word. Compare what we shall say shortly regarding Conversion, § 24.

Nor does the name of regeneration stand in the way, the force and meaning of which is to be estimated from the analogy of generation, yet this [latter] happens in an instant. For that similarity is not to be extended beyond its third point, and we have warned at § 3 and note a that by the act of regeneration not a new substance, but qualities, are produced. But those who have said that regeneration happens in an instant seem to have understood either justification or the conferring of the beginnings of faith, with regard to the first holy thought and pious desire.

The blessed J. Olearius, in *Indic. Bald.*, 1. c., § 17, p. 155, a. F., teaches that the form of regeneration (insofar as this coincides with conversion) consists in the successive communication of grace and the conferring of faith and spiritual life; that it is not a sudden action, but one to be perfected in a certain order. PART III. CHAPTER IV.

It must by no means be established that natural powers, and the acts depending upon them, contribute anything efficiently to the production or acquisition of faith.

Gerhard: "Just as there is nothing whatsoever in a man for which it could be said that he is generated or born, but rather the whole of that is situated in the one generating: so also there is no cause of spiritual regeneration in us." (L. de justif. § 225.) § 13. The end, from which and the effect of regeneration, is proximately justification and renovation; ultimately, the salvation of men and the glory of God.

Which God, the author of regeneration, seriously intends with respect to all whom He regenerates. Of which this is the cause of the cause. And which, once regeneration is posited, is itself immediately posited, either as to its total nature or as to its beginning.

Just as in Titus 3:5, after mention is made of the washing of regeneration, it is immediately added in v. 7: "That, being justified by His grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life." And 1 Peter 1:3-4 it is said that God has begotten us unto an immortal inheritance, etc. Fechtius: "Insofar as those powers of believing tend toward the fiducial embrace of the Savior, John 1:12, regeneration is prior to justification in the order of nature; insofar as they tend toward effecting holiness of life, Galatians 5:6, it is posterior." (Syll. p. 205.)

Just as we are said to be baptized, and thus reborn, that we might walk in newness of life, Romans 6:4. And faith itself, where it is true and living, is effective through love, Galatians 5:6, although renovation is not then immediately completed, but is to be continued throughout the whole of life. For when the inheritance and the hope of eternal life look to this, eternal life has the character of an end.

That the glory of His grace might be praised, by reason of which is every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3, 6), including by reason of regeneration. Compare 1 Peter 1:3. § 14. The affections of regeneration are: I. necessity in relation to salvation; II. perennial efficacy, as far as it is on the part of God; III. defectibility on the part of men; IV. iterability.

For unless anyone, whoever he may be, γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν, be born again, and that from above, as from the Father of lights, or ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος.

[born] of the Spirit, cannot in any way see the kingdom of God, John 3:5 and 6 Nor can the necessity of the gift of faith be denied, once the necessity of faith for salvation is admitted, which is obtained only by divine gift. Luther: "Therefore, this is our doctrine, that all the works of men are nothing and are done in vain if one is not first born anew; and for this reason we call it the most important piece, about which people should be instructed, how they must first be born anew; that one should therefore say first of all that they are all dead, and that whatever else there may be of life, orders, fasting, and other things, it helps nothing toward obtaining the forgiveness of sins until they are reborn and become new men." (Exposition of the first and second chapters of John. Erlangen, 1851. Vol. XLVI, 260.) Or that God gave the spiritual life, which He conferred in regeneration, as a durable thing; which He will continue to preserve by His grace even to the end of life, unless man himself has cast it off by his own fault. Compare Phil. 1:6, where Paul says he is persuaded that He who began a good work in them will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ, ὁ ἐναρξάμενος ἐπιτελέσει; and John 10:28, where Christ says of His sheep (the reborn and faithful): no one, He says, shall snatch them out of My hand. Namely, so that those who have begun to live spiritually through the Spirit of God and of Christ dwelling in them, but soon live according to the flesh, die in their sins, and thus cast off not only the grace of justification and renewal, but also of regeneration, Rom. 6:13 According to § 10 and note f. Although there are not wanting those who prefer to call this new gift of faith by the name of conversion rather than regeneration. Quenstedtius: "Regeneration indeed through the sacrament of circumcision (formerly in the O.T.) was unrepeatable, but regeneration and the creation of a new heart through the Word in those who have totally fallen is not absurd, says D. Dannhauer, *Hodom. Calvin*, p. 2035 There is also one baptism, Eph. 4:5, the act of which cannot be repeated; meanwhile, however, the iteration of regeneration can well stand with the unity of baptism... We prove that the grace of regeneration can be lost and recovered... 3 From Gal. 4:19, where Paul says to the seduced Galatians: 'My little children, of whom I travail in birth again.' From this it is manifest that the regeneration of one and the same man is not only one in number, because the Galatians had been regenerated through Paul, but having been seduced by false apostles, they had lost the grace of regeneration. Whence πάλιν, anew, they are regenerated, v. 19 Hence Theophylact says in the name of Paul: 'You have corrupted the form of Christ, which you had in yourselves from baptism, and there is need for you of another regeneration and reformation, so that the form of Christ may again be in you, so that you may be fashioned from Him.' 4 The same is proved by the parabolic example of the prodigal son, Luke 15:19, and the historical example of Nicodemus. Nicodemus had been regenerated in the circumcision of infancy, yet he stood in need of a new regeneration, John 3; add the examples of Adam, Lot, David, and Peter, who all lost the grace of regeneration by sinning, yet recovered it, not indeed through the sacrament of circumcision, but through the Word of God, which is also a means of regeneration. Thus all infants are regenerated through baptism; for it is the washing of regeneration, Tit. 3:5, 'and as many as are baptized, have put on Christ,' Gal. 3:27. Many, however, having become older, lose this gift of παλιγγενεσία through mortal sins... The consequence does not hold: Baptism cannot be repeated, therefore neither can regeneration be iterated; for not only the sacrament of baptism, but also the Word is a means and principle of regeneration. It does not follow: The seed of regeneration is ἄφθαρτον, immortal, therefore it cannot depart from its subject. For even the ray of the sun is ἄφθαρτος, yet it withdraws itself and yields to darkness. The seed of the Word can be taken away from the heart, Luke 8:12 He who is born of God, that is, through spiritual παλιγγενεσία, does not commit sin, 1 John 3:9, insofar as, that is, he is such and remains such and follows the leading of that heavenly birth or of the Holy Spirit." (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. fol. 698. 699.) Luther: "The keys demand faith in our hearts, and without faith you cannot use them profitably. Hollazius: "Is lost regeneration repeatable? R.: Lost regeneration can be recovered by the penitent sinner. Proved from Gal. 4:19... You say: Baptism, the ordinary means of regeneration, cannot be repeated; therefore, neither can lost regeneration be recovered. Resp.: Regeneration is recovered not through baptism, but through the seed of the divine Word, from which faith in Christ is conceived again, and thus the converted sinner begins to revive." (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 7. q. 18. p. 886. sq.) Eechtius: "Regeneration is as repeatable as it is losable, Gal. 4:19 Whence one can be called 'regenerate' who has been regenerated at some time, either by water or by the Word, by the force of the participle, or who, by the force of the noun, is presently in the state in which the regenerate ought to be. There is, however, no reason why we should delight in teaching with the term 'regenerate' more than with other more common terms that signify the same thing, such as 'converted,' 'pious,' 'faithful,' and others, especially since, because of the metaphor latent in it, simpler people often invent I know not what fanatical chimeras for themselves." Rollius adds: "The fanatics are noted here, who always use that institution indicated in the thesis, even though Scripture uses the term 'pious' and 'faithful' more frequently than 'regenerate.' Yet, by this very fact, the moderate use of the term 'regenerate' is not proscribed or eliminated." (Controvers. Sylloge p. 206, 212.) ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: Antithesis: 1 Of the Anabaptists, who maintain that those once justified cannot lose the Holy Spirit; see Aug. Confess. art. 12. 2 Of the Calvinists, who impugn the loss of the grace of regeneration and υἱοθεσία [adoption], and maintain that the iteration of regeneration is absurd. Thus Beza, P. 2. Colloq. Mompelgart. p. 74: "David," he says, "was not again endowed with the spirit of regeneration, which he had completely lost, but he who lay dormant within him was divinely awakened by the ministry of Nathan." Massonius, P. 4. c. 9. p. 95, says: "Regeneration is by no means an unstable, fickle grace, which God gives to one today and takes away again tomorrow." "How those," says Walaeus, p. 647, "who say that the grace of regeneration, once truly received, can be taken away and is in fact often taken away, defend the unity of baptism, I do not see. Because a new regeneration would have need of a new sacrament, as we see in Adam before and after the fall." But, is not the Word also a principle of regeneration, so that there is no need of a sacrament? Zwingerus in defens. Calvin, p. 323: "But if David," he says, "totally cast off the Holy Spirit by those sins of his, he therefore had need of a new regeneration, and thus there will be not only one, but a manifold rebirth of man—first, second, third, etc.—which can in no way be reconciled with the discourse of Christ to Nicodemus, John 3." (L. c. f. 698. sq.) Kahnisius: "Only the living believer may be called regenerate." That, we reply, is certainly the linguistic usage of Pietism. But just as a man is born only once, so he is also born again only once. ### On Regeneration and Conversion: renewing power of His Word, just as He calls the first effect of His Word…

renewing power of His Word, just as He calls the first effect of His Word 'begetting' (Philem. 10.)... If the baptized person, after a long walk in the flesh, now lays hold of salvation through God’s grace, this is not regeneration, as Pietism says, but the quickening of that germ implanted in him in Baptism, a renewal, an awakening. But however the life of the baptized person may be shaped, in any case he has been implanted through Baptism into the body of Christ, a link in that great chain through which the electric ray of the Holy Spirit strikes.” (Die Lehre vom Abendmahle. 1851. p. 432. 433.) § 15.

Regeneration can be defined as an action of God, by which God, out of mere grace, for the sake of Christ, through the Word and Baptism, bestows upon man—who lacks spiritual powers but does not contumaciously resist—spiritual powers in respect to the intellect and will, or produces them in him, for the purpose of believing in Christ and thus initiating a spiritual life, for the sake of obtaining justification, renovation, and eternal salvation. Although it is not always one simple action, if you consider the regeneration of adults, to whom first certain beginnings of faith, and then the habit of faith, are conferred. Cf. § 12.

Principal efficient cause; see § 6. Material cause or the subject *which* of regeneration; see § 10. Which is the internal impulsive cause; see § 7. As the external impulsive cause; see § 7.

Which are the less principal efficient cause; concerning which see § 5. Subject *by which*, that is; see § 11. Thus the term *to which* is indicated, according to § 12.

Which is the very form or formal reason of regeneration § 12. k) As the end of regeneration; concerning which see § 14. § 16. The word conversion is taken in two ways in the Scriptures: insofar as now God is said to convert man, and now man is said to convert himself; even though, as to the thing itself, it is one and the same action.

By a similitude taken from local motion; just as the meaning of reversion also obtains in Scripture; see Mus. Tr. de Conv. Jenae edit. Disp. I. cap. I. § 5. 6. p. 23. Conversion is called transitive, because it does not terminate in the agent himself, God, but passes from Him into another subject, namely, into the sinful man; whence God is said to convert, and man is said to be converted. Thus that which is said in Jer. 31:18; השיבני (which literally sounds: make me turn). PART III. CHAP. IV.

is rendered by the Greek interpreters: έπίστρεψόν με; by the Vulgate: converte me; by Pagninus: converti fac me. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Tractatus de Conversione*, Jena Edition, Disp. I, cap. I, § 2 and 11, p. 2, 11.

Conversion is called intransitive. For although the acts, through which a man is said to convert himself, depend efficiently upon the Holy Spirit; yet because they are acts of the intellect and will, and do not pass from the powers whose acts they are into another subject, but are terminated within those very powers, in this respect they are reckoned among immanent or intransitive acts.

For it always imports a spiritual change in man, through which a man, a sinner, is led—not indeed by his own powers, but by those of grace—to acknowledge his sins, to grieve over them, and to believe in Christ, etc.

Quenstedtius: "Conversion, viewed in relation to itself, is taken either broadly or strictly. Taken broadly, it indicates, with respect to the term from which, the entire state of sin and wrath into which a man precipitates himself; but with respect to the term to which, it entails not only the translation from the state of wrath and sin into the state of grace and faith, but also justification—both active on the part of God, by which God declares us righteous by absolving us from sins, and passive on the part of man, by which we accept that declaration through given faith and apply it to ourselves—as well as renovation and the continuation of this, to which the reborn man actively concurs. In this sense the word 'conversion' is taken in Acts 26:18, 20, where the apostle Paul says he announced three things to the Jews and Gentiles: 1. μετάνοιαν, 2. έπιστρέφειν έπί τον θεόν, and 3. άξια τής μετάνοιας έργα πράσσειν, i.e., aversion from sin, conversion to God, and the pursuit of good works. In the same way, the *Formula of Concord*, Art. de lib. arb., pp. 656, 663, and 675, includes renovation under the word 'conversion.' Likewise the blessed Chemnitius in *Examen Concilii Tridentini*, Part I, de lib. arb., § 'Longe enim aliud est,' etc., and § 'Exagitant etiam illud,' etc. Taken strictly, conversion is distinguished from justification and renovation. The former acceptance, although it belongs both to Scripture and to the ancient ecclesiastical writers, nevertheless, after the controversies raised by the synergists, the latter has prevailed and is attended to here." (Theol. did.-pol. P. III. c. 7. s. 1. th. 4. f. 700.)

Huelsemannus: "Second corollary: The term 'repentance' and 'conversion' has a wider scope in the sense of the Scriptures and the ancient writers than in that of most ecclesiastical writers. For it cannot be denied that good internal motions and the purpose of amendment are included in the phraseology of the Scriptures by the words 'repentance,' 'conversion from dead works,' 'resurrection,' 'resuscitation,' 'vivification,' and other synonyms, because of the most clear sayings which include both the term from which and the term to which, Acts 26:18; 11:18; 2 Tim. 2:25, 26; Heb. 6:1; Eph. 5:14; Col. 2:12. However, after the controversies of the synergists were raised, the word 'repentance' and 'conversion' began to be taken most strictly for the transitive and active conversion of God alone, who initiates in man the illumination of the intellect and the amendment of the will and affections; in which sense the *Epitome of the Formula of Concord*, pp. 680, 681, rejects that doctrine concerning the three efficient causes of the conversion of the unregenerate man, and teaches that the conversion of man to God is the work of the Holy Spirit alone, to which the will of the man being converted contributes nothing, but suffers that God may work in it, until he is regenerated. Whence it appears that the *Formula of Concord* has in some places included the conversion of man within the same terms in which regeneration is included, which is in no way the work of man, but of God alone; in which sense the word 'conversion' is sometimes used transitively concerning the operation of God alone, pp. 662, 663, 671, 674, and elsewhere. It cannot be denied, however, that the same *Formula* has elsewhere taken the word 'conversion' more broadly, and has distinguished between the initiation and the continuation of conversion, p. 674."

656. 663. 675. 681. In this sense also Chemnitz, in *Loci*, ch. 7, "On Human Powers," Part I, LL. pp. 214, 215, et seq., after the distinction of the four states of man: 1. before the fall in integral nature, 2. after the fall in corrupt nature before renovation, 3. after reparation and renovation by the Holy Spirit, affirms concerning this third state alone that in this state the will of man does not behave purely passively, and whatever he asserts concerning the three causes of a good action, he restricts only to the state after renovation begun in the Holy Spirit, and in this state the struggle of the flesh and the spirit first arises." (Praelect. Form. Conc. art. 10, s. 1, § 8, p. 500, et seq.)

Quenstedt: "Synonyms of conversion, described improperly, i.e., from the effect, are repentance, coming to one's senses, the first resurrection (Col. 2:12; Rev. 20:6). For repentance follows conversion, and is its immediate effect." (L. c. th. 9, f. 702.) § 17. Therefore, the terms of conversion are especially to be noted: one from which, the other to which; each of which is either formal or objective.

Indeed, in order to understand the nature of transitive conversion, which receives its specific essence from its term, which in reality consists in intransitive conversion itself, it is necessary that the consideration of this be premised. See the blessed Musaeus on Conversion, Disp. III, pp. 97, 98. For conversion, in its common notion and concept, is a certain spiritual change or motion, or of the mind; which is also taught by the appellations in the Scriptures, e.g., the return of the sinner, the return from sins to God. See the blessed Musaeus on Conversion, Disp. I and II. And because conversion, taken transitively and intransitively, is one and the same change in reality, it is necessary that the terms from which and to which are also one and the same in reality on both sides. Musaeus, Disput. III, § 21, p.

109. Or that from which the motion begins, and which is abolished by it. Or that toward which the motion tends, and which is acquired or obtained by it.

By this name is called that which conversion reaches by its own nature and intrinsically. Thus is called the object of the formal term, constituted outside the nature and intrinsic reason of conversion. Musaeus, Disp. I, § 7, 8, 9, pp. 3, 4, and Disp. III, ch. I, § 4. § 18.

The formal term from which are sins, both actual, whether of commission or of omission; insofar as, after they have been committed, they remain morally as if ratified, or not retracted, and offend God and contract an obligation to the punishment of sin; as well as habitual, original or connate, and acquired; not only insofar as they are habits of sinning, but also by reason of the annexed guilt and liability. Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. III.13 PART III. CHAP. IV.

For the terms נחם, μεταμέλεσθαι, μετανοεῖν, to repent, to return to one’s senses, etc., also imply a regard for past sins, which correspond to intransitive conversion. And thus in 1 Kings 8:47, conversion is attributed to those who, when they have sinned against God, turn away from their sin. And in Ezekiel 18:26, 27, to him who turns away from the iniquity or transgression which he has committed. Cf. Musaeus, loc. cit., § 9, pp. 101, 102.

For the reason here is equal, and it suffices that they agree in the common concept of sin. For physically or really they do not remain, nor are they to be abolished, because they have already passed; although even the sins of omission in themselves are not something positive, but a negation. Blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., § 31, pp. 120, 121; § 59, 60, 61, pp. 130, 131.

For insofar as they are actions against the law and concern the right of a third party, they are considered to remain for as long (like a contract) and to hold the agent as if bound under the state resulting from the action, until they are retracted. See the blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., § 42 ff., pp. 123, 124. For thus the guilt of fault and of punishment are joined. See the blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., § 46 ff., p. 124 ff.

### On Regeneration and Conversion: Scripture certainly describes conversion through the removal of the heart of…

Scripture certainly describes conversion through the removal of the heart of stone and the gift of a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 11:19; ch. 36:26 ff.), through the circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6; Colossians 2:11), through the softening of the heart (2 Kings 22:19 ff.). By these phrases, however, a change of heart or mind is manifestly indicated, insofar as habitual malice is to be removed. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., § 15 ff., p. 105 ff.; Disp. IV, cap. III, § 60 ff., p. 287 ff. Concerning which see above, Part II, Chapter II, Vol. II, p. 280. Here, however, one must also consider both the lack of original righteousness and the habitual propensity of all faculties toward evil, both of which are connate, and both of which must also be removed in their own way through conversion; as will soon be evident. Meanwhile, see the blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., Disp. IV, cap. I, § 4 ff., p. 244 ff.

h) By which name is comprehended not only the habitual propensity toward evil, contracted by acts of sinning, but also the lack of righteousness or grace, restored through Christ in the regenerate, but cast off through more grievous sins. See the blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., § 3 ff., p. 243 ff. Or insofar as they are viewed in themselves and as they imply the lack of the habitual perfection that ought to be present and the habitual propensity toward evil; both of which must be removed. Blessed Musaeus, loc. cit., and the preceding Disp. III, § 7, 8, pp. 100, 101.

k) Which indeed are common to them with actual sins (concerning which see notes d, e). For they belong to them insofar as they are sins; not precisely as they are habitual. And although the fault and guilt of sins are formally removed from the sinner in justification, which follows conversion in the order of nature, yet in conversion itself man must be so changed intrinsically and spiritually that sins may also be removed from him in respect to fault and guilt, because on the part of the man to be justified, conversion suffices for justification, and nothing more is required than to be converted.

19. The objective terminus a quo, generally speaking, consists of those things which are the objects of actual sins; specifically, however, those to which sinners are, above all others, addicted in mind and affection, and to which they have, as it were, enslaved themselves, having put God aside.

This is indicated by the very name itself. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *De Conversione*, Disp. III, cap. I, § 34, p. 118. For example: idols, from which men are said to be converted (Is. 31:6-7; Ezek. 36:25; Acts 14:15; 1 Thess. 1:9; Rev. 9:20); Satan, or the power of Satan (Acts 26:18). For this reason, the greedy are also commanded to turn away from riches, and the intemperate from harlots. Cf. Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, § 35, pp. 138-139.

For it must be admitted that the nature of those things which are the objects of sins is varied; nor must a man, when he is to be converted, turn away from all such things in the same manner, and certainly not always absolutely and simply or entirely. Harlots must be forsaken in one way, riches in another, and Satan himself in yet another. §

20. The terminus ad quem of conversion, and that which is formal, is faith in Christ, by which the sinful man is reconciled to God, who has been offended by sins. When this is acquired or obtained, the man is said to be converted. Or that which conversion, by its own nature and intrinsically, reaches in order to be produced.

Thus, in Acts 11:21, sinners are said to be converted to the Lord, πιστεύοντες, believing; that is, formally by this, that they believe, or become believers. And in Acts 26:18, we read that Christ sent Paul to the Gentiles to open their eyes, that they might turn themselves from darkness to light, namely, the light of faith; which also appears from the following verses, when they are said to be about to receive the forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified, through faith which is in Christ. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Disp. I, cap. III, § 44, pp. 24-25.

Nor does it differ in substance from what the same author says in *loc. cit.*, cap. I, § 8, p. 3: that the formal terminus ad quem (of conversion) is the restoration of the rectitude of the soul, which either ought to have been in man by virtue of his original creation and was lost in Adam, or was once restored by virtue of regeneration and was again cast off through sins against conscience. Regarding this matter, one may add what is found *ibid.*, § 9, p. 4, as well as Disp. III, cap. I, § 22 sqq., p. 109 sqq., and Disp. V, cap. I, §§ 7 and 9, p. 295.

According to what we have just said from Acts 26:18, it must be observed, however, that the forgiveness of sins itself, properly speaking, is not a part of conversion—even if conversion is taken totally, insofar as it embraces contrition and faith—but is its consequence and fruit, and pertains formally to justification. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, cap. IV, § 74, p. 39. PART III. CAP. IV.

§ 21.

The terminus ad quem, the objective [terminus], is God. Or the object of the formal terminus, according to § 17, note /.

For thus it is called μετάνοια είς τον Θεόν, repentance, or conversion to God, Acts 20:21, and men are commanded ϊπιστρέφειν έπ\ τον Θεόν, Acts 14:15 and ch. 26:18, προς τυν Θευν, 1 Thess. 1:9. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Disput. I, ch. III, § 43 ff., p. 24, 28. For although Christ the Mediator is commonly established as the object of faith, it is nevertheless certain that this faith is directed straight to God as its object, and reunites the soul of the sinner with God Himself. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, ch. I, § 9, p. 4. § 22. Therefore, in order for actual sins to be abolished through conversion, it is required first that they be retracted by the sinner, and that they be acknowledged in the intellect, not only by a speculative judgment that they are truly sins, but also by a practical one, that it is necessary to apply oneself to the abolition of sins and to consider the manner and means by which they might be abolished; on the part of the will, there is required a displeasure with sins, and that an efficacious one, or a detestation joined with sorrow.

Indeed, they can only be abolished morally, not physically, as they do not exist in act, but have long since ceased to be; as we said at § 18, note c. Retraction is also opposed to ratification, through which it comes about that sins, even if past, remain morally and affect the man. Cf. § 18, note d. Although they cannot be abolished by retraction alone for that reason. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, de Conv. Disp. III, ch. II, § 49, 50, p. 125, 126, § 62 ff., p.

131. For acknowledgment is a necessary condition, without which retraction cannot take place, since the will, as a blind power, can render nothing void unless it has first been known by the intellect. Scripture, moreover, also shows us this practice, by which, when men were to be led to conversion through the ministry of the Word, it was customary for the beginning to be made from the manifestation of sins. See the example of David, 2 Sam. 12:7 ff., Ps. 51:5. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, l. c., § 64, p. 131, 132. Whereby sins, whether they are those that present themselves to the mind (when they are more serious), or those that are known through a more diligent examination or scrutiny of one’s past life and a more accurate comparison with the norm of the divine law (by which method it happens that those things which otherwise, on account of carnal security, are not noticed, can be recognized as sins of infirmity), are known to be contrary to the divine law, hateful to God, and worthy of temporal and eternal punishments; just as it is said in Rom. 3:20, that through the law comes the knowledge of sin. Cf. ch. 7:7 and the blessed Musaeus, l. c., § 65, 66, p. 132, 133.

For otherwise that saying of James concerning a man contemplating his face in a mirror, but not thinking of wiping away the stain, will have its place, Ep. ch. 1, 23. 24. It is evident, however, from the examples of penitents in Scripture, how, once their sins were known, they solicitously sought how their sins might be abolished: e.g., Josiah, 2 Kings 22, 11. sqq., certain Jews in the time of John the Baptist, Matt. 3, 6. Mark 1, 5. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, 1. c. § 67. p. 133. 134.

For even if the intellect were to know all sins, and were to declare repeatedly that one must not persist in them, they would not yet be retracted unless they were displeasing to the will. Through displeasure, however, sins cease to be voluntary and take on the nature of involuntary actions. The blessed Musaeus, 1. c. § 69. 71. p. 134. 135. To be sure, simple displeasure, by which sins known according to some aspect of evil are displeasing to the will, without that intention of fleeing them, does not suffice for the retraction of sins; but it is necessary that we utterly turn away from sins, indeed, wishing to render them undone if it were possible, and abhorring the committing of similar ones. The blessed Musaeus, 1. c. § 70. p. 134.

11) Or, that a passion, perturbation, and restlessness of soul may arise from the apprehension of sin, as a present evil and the cause of many evils to be suffered in this life and the next. And indeed, this sorrow is the more severe, the more distinctly and accurately the nature of the evil in sins—e.g., their foulness, the offense against God, the certainty, abundance, and gravity of the punishments—is apprehended and known. Whence it is clear that the stings and terrors of conscience are contained under this sorrow. We have examples, however, especially of David, Ps. 6, 3. sqq. Ps. 32, 3. sqq. Ps. 38, 4. sqq. Ps. 88, 2. 17. sqq., and of Peter πικρῶς κλαίοντος [weeping bitterly], Matt. 27, last. Luke 22, 62. §

23. Next, it is required that the mind should tend toward the abolition of actual sins, even regarding the offense against God and the obligation of sinners to make satisfaction to God; which, indeed, is not accomplished otherwise than through faith in Christ the Mediator and His merit and satisfaction for our sins; which, when faith apprehends it, it simultaneously tends toward God, who, although offended by our sins, has nevertheless embraced us with His love and grace and is now fully reconciled through the satisfaction of Christ. For just as the cause why sins, after they have passed, remain morally and constitute man in a state of sin, is not merely ratification or non-retraction, but that sins also oppose the divine law and offend God: so, even if a sinner should seriously retract past sins in his mind, he would still remain guilty of the fault on account of the violated law of God and obligated to make satisfaction for the offense and injury brought upon God; just as the Savior, for the abolition of sin, by which PART III. CHAP. IV.

Mus. 1. c. § 15. sqq. p. 105. sqq. Disp. IV. cap. III. § 60. sqq. p. 287. sqq. De quo vid. supra P. II. cap. II. Vol. II. p. 280.
