h) Quo nomine comprehenditur non solum habitualis propensio in malum, actibus peccandi contracta, verum etiam carentia justitiae vel gratiae, per Christum reparatae in renatis, sed per peccata graviora excussae. V. b. Mus. 1. c. § 3. sqq. p. 243. sqq. Seu quatenus secundum se spectantur et prout important ca· rentiam habitualis perfectionis adesse debitae et propensionem habitualem ad prava; quarum liaec atque illa tolli debet. B. Mus. 1. c. et praeced. Disp. III. § 7. 8. p. 100. 101.

k) Quae quidem communia eis sunt cum peccatis actualibus (de quibus vid. notae d. e.). Competunt enim eis, quatenus peccata eunt; non praecise, ut sunt habitualia. Et quamvis culpa et reatus peccatorum ab homine peccatore formaliter tollantur in justificatione, quae conversionem naturae ordine sequitur, tamen in ipsa «conversione homo sic mutari debet intrinsece et spiritualiter, ut peccata etiam ratione culpae et reatus ab ipso tolli possint, quia a parte hominis justificandi et ad justificationem sufficit conversio, neque plus requiritur, quam esse conversum.

SE REGENERATIONE ET CONVERSIONE. § 19. Terminus a quo objectivus generaliter loquendo sunt res, quae peccatorum actualium objecta a sunt; speciatim vero illae, quibus peccatores prae caeteris animo et affectu addicti sunt seque, Deo posthabito, quasi manciparunt.b

Quod vel ipsum nomen indicat. Conf. b. Mus. de Conv. Disp. III. cap. I. § 34. p. 118. V. g. idola, a quibus homines convertendi dicuntur Es. 31, 6. 7. Ezech. 36, 25. Actor, 14, 15. 1 Thess. 1, 9. Apoc. 9, 20., satanas, aut potestas satanae, Act. 26, 18. Qua ratione etiam avari a divitiis, intemperantes a scortis avertere se jubentur. Conf. Mus. 1. c. §35. p. 138. 139.

Fatendum enim est, variam esse rationem earum rerum, quae sunt objecta peccatorum; neque ab omnibus ejusmodi rebus eodem modo, certe non semper absolute et simpliciter aut prorsus, hominem averti debere, quando convertendus est. Aliter sane scorta, aliter divitiae deserendae sunt, aliter ipse satanas. §

20. Terminus conversionis a ad quem, isque formalis,b est fides in Christum, c qua Deo, peccatis offenso, homo peccator reconciliatur.d Quo acquisito aut obtento, homo conversus dicitur. Seu ille, quem conversio suapte natura et intrinsece attingit, ut producatur.

Ita Actor. 11, 21. dicuntur peccatores converti ad Dominum, πιστεύοντες, credentes; seu formaliter per lioc, quod credunt, aut eredentes fiunt. Et Act. 26, 16. legimus, quod Christus miserit Paulum ad gentiles, ut aperiret oculos eorum, ut converterent se a tenebris ad lucem, nempe lucem fidei; quod etiam apparet ex seqq., quando dicuntur ilii accepturi remissionem peccatorum et sortem inter sanctificatos, per fidem, quae est in Christum. Conf. b. Mus. Disp. I. cap. III. § 44. p. 24. 25.

Neque ab eo, quoad rem, differt, quod idem 1. c. cap. I. § 8. p. 3. dicit: Terminum ad quem formalem (conversionis) esse reparandam animi rectitudinem, quae sive vi primaevae creationis homini inesse debebat et in Adamo deperdita est, sive vi regenerationis olim reparata et per peccata contra conscientiam iterum excussa fuit. Quam in rem addi possunt, quae habentur ib. § 9. p. 4., item Disp. III. cap. I. § 22. sqq. p. 109. sqq. Disp. V. cap. I. § 7. et 9. p. 295.

Juxta ea, quae modo diximus ex Actor. 26, 16., ubi tamen observandum est, ipsam remissionem peccatorum proprie loquendo non esse partem conversionis, licet haec totaliter sumatur, quatenus contritionem et fidem complectitur; sed esse ejus consequens et fructum, atque ad justificationem formaliter pertinere. Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. cap. IV. § 74. p. 39. PART. III. CAP. IV.

§ 21.

Terminus ad quem, objectivus a est Deus.b Sive objectum termini formalis, juxta § 17. not. /. Sic enim dicitur μετάνοια είς τον Θεόν, resipiscentia, sive conversio ad Deum Act. 20, 21., et jubentur homines ϊπιστρέφειν έπ\ τον Θεόν Act. 14, 15. et cap. 26, 18., προς τυν Θευν 1 Thess. 1, 9. Conf. b. Mus. Disput. I. cap. III. § 43. sqq. p. 24. 28. Quanquam enim fidei ob־ jectum vulgo constituatur Christus mediator, certum tamen est, fidem hanc recta ferri 111 Deum, tanquam suum objectum, et peccatoris animum cum Deo ipso redunire. Conf. b. Mus. cap. I. § 9. p. 4. § 22.

Itaque ad id, ut peccata actualia per conversionem aboleantur, requiritur primum, a ut retractentur b a peccatore et ut in intellectu quidem agnoscantur, c non solum judicio speculativo,d quod revera sint peccata, verum etiam practico, quod in abolitionem peccatorum incumbere et de modo ac mediis, quibus aboleantur, dispicere e oporteat; ex parte voluntatis requiritur displicentia f peccatorum, eaque efficax g seu detestatio cum dolore h conjuncta. Nempe moraliter tantum aboleri possunt, non physice, quae actu non existunt, sed pridem esse desierunt; ut diximus ad § 18. not. c.

Retractatio etiam opponitur ratihabitioni, per quam fit, ut peccata, etiamsi praeterita, moraliter maneant et hominem afficiant. Conf. § 18. not. d. Quamvis non ideo per solam retractationem aboleri possint. Conf. b. Mus. de Conv. Disp. III. cap. II. § 49. 50. p. 125. 126. § 62. sqq. p. 131. Agnitio enim conditio necessaria est, sine qua retractatio fieri nequit, cum voluntas, tanquam potentia coeca, nihil irritum reddere possit, nisi prius ab intellectu fuerit cognitum. Scriptura autem etiam nane nobis praxin monstrat, qua, cum homines per ministerium verbi ad conversionem perducendi essent, a manifestatione peccatorum initiura fieri consueverit. Vid. exemplum Davidis 2 Sam. 12, 7. sqq. Ps. 51, 5. Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 64. p. 131.

132. Quo peccata, sive per se animo bbversantia (quando graviora sunt), sive inito diligentiore examine aut excussione vitae ante actae et collatione accuratiore cum norma legis divinae (qua ratione fit, ut, quae alias ob securitatem carnalem non animadvertuntur ipsaque peccata infirmitatis agnosci possint) cognoscuntur esse adversa legi divinae, Deo exosa et poenis temporalibus atque aeternis digna; prout Rom. 3, 20. dicitur, per legem esse agnitionem peccati. Conf. cap. 7, 7. et b. Mus. 1. c. § 65. 66. p. 132. 133.

Alias enim locum habebit illud Jacobi de homine faciem suam in speculo contemplante, non autem de abstergenda macula cogitante, Ep. cap. 1, 23. 24. Constat autem exemplis poenitentium in Scriptura, quomodo, cognitis peccatis, solicite quaesiverint, quo pacto possent aboleri sua peccata: v. g. Josiae, 2 Reg. 22, 11. sqq., Judaeorum quorundam tempore Johannis Baptistae, Matth. 3, 6. Marc. 1, 5. Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 67. p. 133. 134.

Nam si maxime intellectus peccata vel omnia cognosceret, et in iis non esse persistendum dictitaret, non tamen ea retractarentur, nisi voluntati displicuerint. Per displicentiam autem peccata desinunt esse voluntaria, et rationem actionum invitarum induunt. B. Mus. 1. c. § 69. 71. p. 134. 135. Scilicet simplex displicentia, qua peccata secundum aliquam rationem mali cognita voluntati displicent, sine intentione illa fugiendi, non sufficit ad retractationem peccatorum, sed necesse est, ut peccata prorsus aversemur, quippe ea, si fieri posset, infecta reddere volentes et a similibus patrandis abhorrentes. B. Mus. 1. c. § 70. p. 134.

11) Seu, ut passio, perturbatio et inquietudo animi oriatur ex apprehensione peccati, tanquam mali praesentis et causae malorum plurium, in vita hac et altera luendorum. Atque hic quidem dolor tanto gravior est, quo magis ratio mali in peccatis, v. g. foeditas, offensa Dei, poenarum certitudo et copia atque gravitas, distincte et accurate apprehensa est atque cognita. Unde patet, conscientiae morsus et pavores sub isto dolore contineri. Exempla autem habemus, praecipue Davidis, Ps. 6, 3. sqq. Ps. 32, 3. sqq. Ps. 38, 4· sqq. Ps. 88, 2. 17. sqq., et Petri πι/φως χλαίοντης, Matth. 27, ult. Luc. 22, 62. §

23. Deinde requiritur, ut in peccata actualia, etiam quoad offensam a Dei et obligationem peccantium ad satisfaciendum b Deo, abolenda tendat animus; quod quidem non aliter fit, quam per fidem c in Christum mediatorem ejusque meritum et satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris; quam cum apprehendit fides, simul tendit in Deum,d qui, licet peccatis nostris offensus, tamen amore et gratia sua nos complexus e et nunc per satisfactionem Christi plene reconciliatus sit. f Sicut enim causa, cur peccata, postquam praeterierunt, moraliter maneant et hominem in statu peccati constituant, non est sola ratihabitio seu non-retractatio; sed quod peccata etiam legi divinae adversantur Deumque offendunt: ita, si maxime peccator serio apud animum retractet peccata praeterita, tamen adhuc reus culpae manebit ob violatam legem Dei et obligatus ad satisfaciendum pro offensa et injuria Deo illata; prout Servator ad abolendum peccatum, quo PART. III. CAP. IV.


### On Regeneration and Conversion: whoever has harmed a neighbor requires not only a retraction of the sin, but…

whoever has harmed a neighbor requires not only a retraction of the sin, but also that satisfaction be made to the neighbor, or that he be induced to forgive the injury, Matth. 5, 24. Cf. the blessed Mus. 1. c. § 49. 50. p. 125. sqq.

Namely, sins viewed by way of offense, or insofar as they offend God, and the obligation or debt of satisfying God for sins, stand as the foundation of the relation and the relation itself; and therefore the offense and the obligation to satisfy are removed by the same acts. B. Mus. 1. c. § 76. p. 137.

Certainly contrition is of no value here; to which, besides the fact that sins committed are retracted through it, nothing is to be ascribed. See what the blessed Mus. brings forward against the scholastics 1. c. § 77. sqq. p. 137. 138. 139.

But neither is the offense of God, apart from satisfaction, removed by the mere forgiveness of sins; rather, according to the Scriptures, the abolition of offenses and our reconciliation with God are ascribed partly indeed to the grace or mercy of God, namely as the internal impulsive cause, and partly indeed to Christ the mediator, as the meritorious cause, according to Eph. 1, 5. chap. 2, 4. sqq. to Tit. 3, 4. sqq. Rom. 5, 8. And this is what is said in Rom. 8, 3. 4: The right of the law (which has over us, or against us, demanding perfect obedience, or, failing that, punishment) is fulfilled in us through the Son of God, whom He Himself sent, or through the fulfillment of the law and the satisfaction performed by Him for us; and Gal. 4, 4., that Christ was made subject to the law, to redeem those who were under the law; and 1 John 2, 2., that He is the propitiation for our sins and those of the whole world, and 2 Cor. 5, 18., that God reconciled us to Himself through Christ.

Therefore, since Scripture hands down no other satisfaction acceptable to God or valid in itself besides the satisfaction of Christ, conversion also can tend toward the abolition of the offense of sins in no other way than through those acts by which it is first directed toward Christ the mediator, and through Him further toward God, reconciled by the merit of Christ. Cf. what we said in chap. III. § 6. 7. 8. And the blessed Mus. 1. c. § 81. sqq. p. 139. sqq.

For while faith is directed toward Christ as the cause of obtaining grace before God, the same is directed at the same time toward God, whose grace is to be obtained through Christ. Cf. § 21. and note b.

Willing all to be saved, according to 1 Tim. 2, 4. (compare our Disputation held on this passage concerning the universality of divine grace), and loving us, even when we were sinners and children of wrath, not indeed as such, but as creatures. Rom. 5, 8.

Thus 2 Cor. 5, 18. 19. it is said that God reconciled us and the world to Himself in Christ; with which the words of Col. 1, 20. agree, that God, peace having been made through the blood of the cross [of Christ], reconciles all things to Himself through Him.

However, they must be understood concerning reconciliation viewed from the side of satisfaction, or that it would truly perform whatever satisfaction could be demanded for reconciling men to God.

Otherwise, however, it is certain that God is reconciled to the sinful man actually only through faith itself, which apprehends the satisfaction of Christ. Cf. the blessed Mus. on Conversion 1. c. § 91. p. 244.

§ 24.

Conversion tends toward the abolition of habitual sins through the same acts by which it tends toward the abolition of actual sins,a yet in such a way that the former must be abolished or expelled not only morally,b but also physically and really,c if not entirely,d at least in a certain respect and in regard to dominion.e Namely, that man should acknowledge them and detest them with sorrow, but also believe in Christ the Mediator, according to those things which we have said in § 22 and 23.

Habitual sins must certainly be abolished no less than actual ones morally, as regards guilt and offense, and thus they must be retracted by means of serious and efficacious acknowledgment and displeasure. Moreover, the obligation to punishment contracted by those sins must be removed through those acts which are directed toward that satisfaction and merit by which God truly wills to be appeased and reconciled. For the difference between actual and habitual sins is such that the former, after they have been committed, are not something intrinsic to the sinner, whereas the latter partly import a lack of justice or habitual grace, which ought to have been present, and thus exist within man (just as other privations exist in subjects in which they remove the opposite perfection), and partly import a habitual propensity toward evil and thus some positive entity. Whence, although actual sins are only removed morally, habitual sins can nevertheless be expelled physically, just as other privations or habits are expelled from their subjects.

For as long as we live in this life, it must be confessed that in us, i.e., in our flesh, no good dwells, Rom. 7:18, and that the flesh, surviving even in the converted, lusts against the Spirit, Gal. 5:17, which would not happen if depraved concupiscence were entirely expelled or could be expelled. For there are no affections of a non-entity. Compare what we have said concerning the tenacity of original sin, Part II, Chapter II, § 14, Vol. II, p. 305. For divine grace can in a certain way and in regard to dominion remove sin within us, even if it is not abolished according to its whole self; see Rom. 6:12 ff., ch. 7:6, ch. 8:1 ff., 12 ff., Gal. 5:16 ff., and other places. That this occurs in conversion itself and through those acts by which sin is morally removed, in its own way, will be evident from what follows. See meanwhile what the blessed Musaeus brings forward concerning Conversion, Disp. III, ch. I, § 15 ff., from Ezek. 11:17 ff. and ch. 36:26, concerning the removal of the heart of stone. § 25.

Specifically, therefore, on the part of the intellect, the lack of light and strength to embrace and believe spiritual objects, and likewise the habitual propensity to judge rashly concerning them,a is abolished in conversion through the acts of faith, divine gra- PART III. CHAPTER IV.

produced in us; and indeed, simple ignorance of things to be believed is removed by the simple apprehension of things to be believed; errors, however, or false opinions in the doctrine of faith and morals are removed by acts of assenting to true doctrine, resting upon divine revelation; the rash propensity of the intellect to judge perversely concerning those things which are of the Spirit of God is restrained by the pious affection of the will to believe, excited by the power of the Word divinely; and thus, finally, the lack of habitual light or of the powers of believing is removed efficiently by acts of faith, and formally by the habit of believing, produced efficiently by means of the acts of believing.

Regarding this matter, see what we have said in § 18, note g. Such as occurs in unbelievers, especially Gentiles to be led to the Christian faith, who have not yet heard the dogmas of the faith.

Just as privatively opposed things formally expel one another from a subject. Cf. Musaeus, *De Conversione*, Disp. X, cap. I, § 4, p. 293. Such as are found in those who, when they have heard the dogmas of the faith—whether merely supernatural or naturally known (which are nevertheless referred to the former)—are occupied by prejudices and judge otherwise, and either hold those things which are proposed to them as fables, or in any way hold a different or contrary opinion.

Just as opposites, which imply a contrary disposition toward one another, also formally expel one another from a subject; see note b, Musaeus, loc. cit. And thus the act of the intellect, by which assent is offered to mysteries as divinely revealed, excludes the perverse judgment of the intellect by which the same are held as foolishness; and the acknowledgment of sins and the practical judgment, by which the intellect commands one to apply oneself to the abolition of them as foul things, hateful to God and destructive to us, certainly removes that corrupt judgment by which the intellect judges that one must persist in sins as things pleasing to the flesh. Which indeed is born in men through original sin, but afterwards is increased through depraved instruction, or the voluntary abuse of reason, and various prejudices.

For in acknowledging mysteries, especially those that are not evident, the intellect is subordinated to the will and can be captivated by it—when it is instructed by supernatural power—into the obedience of Christ, 2 Cor. 10:4 sqq., or in such a way that, with thoughts that oppose the faith being restrained, and judgment being suspended, and further instruction being admitted, it finally, through the grace of God, offers full assent. See Musaeus, loc. cit., § 6, p. 294. For acts of believing, proceeding from the preaching of the Word, leave behind in the soul of the one to be converted a disposition to elicit other similar acts, which, when these are repeated, is increased and finally passes into a fixed and firm habit, and indeed into a habit proportionate to the acts of believing and in substance supernatural. See note b, Musaeus, loc. cit., § 6, p. 294.

Since it elevates the intellect beyond its natural condition for the eliciting of subsequent acts of believing, it obtains on the part of the intellect the designation of habitual light and powers of believing, from which the eyes of our mind have it that they are habitually enlightened, according to Eph. 1:17, or that man is light in the Lord, a child of light, proving what is acceptable to the Lord, ch. 5:8, 10. Whence it is evident that the lack of habitual light is formally removed by this very habitual light; just as privations are otherwise removed by habits. B. Mus. 1. c. § 6, 7, p. 295. § 26.

Similarly, on the part of the will, the propensity toward evil and the lack of power to embrace spiritual goods unto salvation are removed by acts of serious and efficacious displeasure toward sins, partly and primarily by acts of trust, which, just as they presuppose a certain desire for grace and the remission of sins in the sinner, they themselves indeed import security and certainty concerning the obtaining of God’s grace and the remission of sins, and at the same time are also joined with love for Christ the Mediator and for God appeased through Him, and with the hope of obtaining grace and salvation; thus they formally remove the opposite acts of the will and efficiently tend toward expelling habitual sins, until they are formally expelled by the spiritual habits born therefrom. Namely, in a certain respect; as we said in § 24, note d. For when the will of man turns away from and endeavors to flee the habitual sins that have been recognized, meanwhile it is distressed and grieves over those things which it discovers within itself; certainly the contrary complacency and delight in sins and in private desires and motions of concupiscence is inhibited or removed.

Latin:

quis proximum laesit, non solum retractationem peccati, sed ut etiam proximo satisfiat, aut is inducatur, ut injuriam condonet, requirit, Matth. 5, 24· Conf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 49. 50. p. 125. sqq.

Scilicet peccata per modum offensae, sive quatenus Deum offendunt,, spectata, et obligatio seu debitum satisfaciendi Deo pro peccatis habent se ut fundamentum relationis et relatio ipsa; ac proinde iisdem actibus offensa pariter et obligatio ad satisfaciendum tollitur. B. Mus. 1. c. § 76. p. 137.

Sane contritio hic nihil valet; cui praeter hoc, quod peccata admissa per eam retractantur, nihil adscribendum est. Vid., quae b. Mus. contra scholasticos affert 1. c. § 77. sqq. p. 137. 138. 139.

Sed nec offensa Dei, citra satisfactionem, sola condonatione peccatorum tollitur; verum juxta Scripturas abolitio offensarum et reconciliatio nostra cum Deo partim quidem adscribitur gratiae seu misericordiae Dei, nempe ut causae impulsivae internae, partim vero Christo mediatori, tanquam causae meritoriae, juxta Eph. 1, 5. cap. 2, 4· sqq. ad Tit. 3, 4. sqq. Rom. 5, 8. Et hoc est, quod Rom. 8y 3. 4· dicitur: Jus legis (quod in nos, aut adversus nos habet, obedientiam perfectam, aut, deficiente ea, poenam postulans) compleri in nobis per Filium Dei, quem ipse miserit, seu per impletionem legis et satisfactionem ab ipso pro nobis praestitam; et Gal. 4, 4., Christum legi obnpxium esse factum, ut redimeret eos, qui sub lege erant; et 1 Joh. 2, 2., eum esse propitiationem pro peccatis nostris ac totius mundi, et 2 Cor. 5, 18., Deum reconciliasse nos sibi per Christum.

Itaque, cum praeter satisfactionem Christi aliam nullam Deo acceptabilem aut per se validam Scriptura tradat, ideo conversio etiam aliter in abolendam peccatorum offensam tendere non potest, quam per eos actus, quibus primo feratur in Christum mediatorem, et per eum porro in Deum, Christi merito reconciliatum. Conf., quae diximus cap. III. § 6. 7. 8. Et b. Mus. 1. c. § 81. sqq. p. 139. sqq.

Nam dum fides fertur in Christum, ut causam impetrandae gratiae apud Deum, fertur eadem simul in Deum, cujus gratia per Christum sit impetranda. Conf. § 21. et not. b.

Volens cunctos salvos fieri, juxta 1 Tim. 2, 4· (confer Disp, nostram super hunc locum habitam de universalitate gratiae divinae), et diligens nos, etiam cum peccatores et filii irae essemus, non quidem qua tales, sed qua creaturas. Rom. 5, 8.

Ita 2 Cor. 5, 18. 19. dicitur, Deum reconciliasse sibi nos et mundum in Christo; quibus consonant verba Col. 1, 20., Deum, pace per sanguinem crucis [Christi] facta, per eum reconciliare sibi omnia.

Intelligi autem debent de reconciliatione ex parte satisfactionis spectata, seu quod revera praestitura sit, quicquid satisfactionis ad reconciliandos Deo homines exigi poterat.

Alias autem certum est, Deum homini peccatori demum reconciliari actu per ipsam fidem, quae satisfactionem Christi apprehendit. Conf. b. Mus. de Conv. 1. c. § 91. p. 244.

§ 24.

Ad abolenda peccata habitualia tendit conversio per actus eosdem, per quos ad actualia peccata abolenda tendit,a ita tamen, ut illa non solum moraliter,b sed et physice ac realiter,c si non penitus,d saltem secundum quid et ratione dominii aboleri aut expelli debeant. e Nempe ut homo illa agnoscat et cum dolore detestetur, credat autem etiam in Christum mediatorem, juxta ea, quae diximus § 22. et 23.

Debent utique peccata habitualia non minus, quam actualia, aboleri moraliter, quoad culpam et offensam, adeoque retractari debent, mediante agnitione ac displicentia seria et efficaci. Obligatio autem ad poenam, peccatis illis contracta, tolli debet per actus illos, qui feruntur in satisfactionem ac meritum illud, per quod Deus revera vult placari ac reconciliari. Nam peccatorum actualium et habitualium ea est differentia, ut illa quidem, postquam patrata sunt, non sint aliquid peccatori intrinsecum, haec vero partim carentiam justitiae aut gratiae habitualis, quae inesse debebat, importent et sic homini insint (prout alias privationes sunt in subjectis, in quibus oppositam perfectionem tollunt), partim habitualem propensionem in malum adeoque entitatem aliquam positivam importent. Unde, licet actualia peccata tantum moraliter tollantur, habitualia tamen physice expelli possunt, prout alias privationes aut liabitus e subjectis sufs pelluntur.

Quamdiu enim in hac vita vivimus, fatendum est, in nobis, h. e. in carne nostra, non habitare bonum, Rom. 7, 18., et carnem, etiam in conversis superstitem, concupiscere adversus Spiritum, Gal. 5, 17., quod non fieret, si concupiscentia prava prorsus expulsa esset aut expelli posset. non-entis enim non sunt affectiones. Confer, quae diximus de tenacitate peccati orig. Part. II. cap. II. § 14. Vol. II. p. 305. Potest enim divina gratia in nobis quodammodo et ratione dominii tolli peccatum, etsi non secundum se totum aboleatur; vid. Rom. 6, 12. sqq. cap. 7, 6. cap. 8, 1. sqq. 12. sqq. Gal. 5, 16. sqq. et locis aliis. Quod autem illud in ipsa conversione et per actus istos, quibue peccatura moraliter tollitur, suo modo fiat, ex seqq. patebit. Vid. interea, quae b. Mus. affert de Conv. Disp. III. cap. I. § 15. sqq. ex Ezech. 11, 17. sqq. et cap. 86, 25. de ablatione cordis lapidei. % 25.

Speciatim igitur ex parte intellectus carentia lucis et virium ad objecta spiritualia amplectenda et credenda, itemque habitualis propensio ad temere judicandum de illis,a aboletur in conversione per actus fidei, divina gra PART. III. CAP. IV.

tia in nobis productos; et quidem simplex ignorantia credendorum b tollitur per simplicem credendorum apprehensionem, c errores autem aut falsae opiniones in do״ otrina d fidei ac morum tolluntur per actus assentiendi verae doctrinae, divina revelatione nixos;e temeraria in״ tellectus propensio ad perverse judicandum de his, quae sunt Spiritus Dei,f cohibetur per voluntatis piam affectionem g credendi, virtute verbi divinitus excitatam, et sic denique carentia lucis habitualis seu virium credendi tollitur efficienter h per actus fidei, formaliter per habitum1 credendi, mediantibus actibus credendi efficienter pro״ ductum.

Quam in rem vid., quae diximus § 18. not./, g. Qualis occurrit in infidelibus, gentilibus inprimis, ad fidem christianam perducendis, qui dogmata fidei nondum audiverunt. Prout privative opposita se invicem formaliter expellunt e subjecto. Conf. Mus. de Conv. Disp. X. cap. I. § 4. p.

293. Quales sunt penes illos, qui, cum audierint dogmata fidei seu mere supernaturalia seu naturaliter nota (quae tamen ad illa referuntur), praejudiciis occupati aliter judicant et vel ea, quae sibi proponuntur, pro fabulis habent, vel quovis modo diversam aut contrariam opinionem tenent. Quemadmodum opposita, quae contrariam ad se habitudinem important, se quoque invicem ex subjecto formaliter expellunt; vid. b. Mus. 1. c. Et sic actus intellectus, quo mysteriis, tanquam divinitus revelatis, assensus praebetur, excludit perversum intellectus judicium, quo eadem pro stultitia habentur; et agnitio peccatorum ac judicium practicum, quo intellectus jubet in abolitionem eorum, tanquam rerum foedarum Deoque exosarum et nobis exitiosarum, incumbere, tollit utique judicium illud corruptum, quo intellectus in peccatis, ut carni gratis, persistendum esse judicat.

Quae quidem hominibus per peccatum orig. connascitur, postea vero per informationem pravam, aut voluntarium rationis abusum variaque praejudicia augetur. In inevidentibus enim praesertim mysteriis agnoscendis intellectus subordinatur voluntati et ab hac, virtute supernaturali instructa, captivari potest in obsequium Christi, 2 Cor. 10, 4. sqq., seu ita, ut cohibitis cogitationibus, quae fidei obnituntur, suspensoque judicio et admissa ulteriori informatione, tandem per Dei gratiam plenum praebeat assensum. Vid. Mus. 1. c. § 6. p.

294. Actus credendi enim, ex praedicatione verbi profecti, relinquunt post se in hominis convertendi animo dispositionem ad alios actus similes eliciendos, quae iisdem iteratis aucta tandem in habitum fixum et firmum abit, et quidem in habitum actibus credendi proportionatum et in substantia mpernaturalem. Vid. b. Mus. 1. c. § 6. p. 294.

Qui cum intellectum ad actus credendi subsequentes eliciendos ultra suam naturalem conditionem elevet, sortitur ex parte intellectus appellationem luminis habitualis et virium credendi, a quo oculi mentis nostrae habent, ut sint habitualiter illuminati, juxta Eph. 1, 17., aut ut homo sit lux in Domino, filius lucis, probans, quid sit acceptum Domino, cap. 5, 8. 10. Unde patet, carentiam luminis habitualis per hanc ipsam lucem habitualem tolli formaliter; prout alias per habitus tolluntur privationes. B. Mus. 1. c. § 6. 7. p. 295. § 26.

Similiter ex parte voluntatis propensio in malum et carentia virium ad spiritualia bona salutariter amplectenda tollitur a per actus displicentiae peccatorum seriae atque efficacis,b partim et inprimis per actus fiduciae, qui, sicut desiderium quoddam gratiae et remissionis peccatorum c in peccatore supponunt, ipsi vero securitatem ac certitudinem de impetranda Dei gratia et remissione peccatorum important, d simul etiam cum amore e Christi mediatoris ac Dei per ipsum placati cumque spe f consequendae gratiae et salutis conjunguntur, ita oppositos actus voluntatis formaliter tollunt et. ad habitualia peccata expellenda efficienter g tendunt, donec ea per habitus spirituales inde natos formaliter h expellantur. Nempe secundum quid; ut diximus § 24. not. d. Quando enim voluntas hominis peccata habitualia agnita aversatur et fugere conatur, interim angitur et dolet de iis, quae penes se deprehendit; utique contraria complacentia et delectatio in peccatis privatisque desideriis et motibus concupiscentiae perseverandi inhibetur aut tollitur.


### On Regeneration and Conversion: But this is opposed to carnal security and the desires of the flesh

But this is opposed to carnal security and the desires of the flesh. And thus they are opposed to timidity and diffidence.

Which is contrary to the love of the world and earthly things. Which is opposed to despair. Namely, that while they indeed soon leave behind them dispositions which incline toward similar spiritual acts and motions, furthermore, with more acts occurring by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they tend toward a spiritual habit, in the way in which we said the acts of the intellect tend toward habits at § 25, note h.

Namely, the lack of power to embrace spiritual goods, as a privation, is removed by the opposite form, but the habitual propensity toward evil is removed by the contrary habit. PART III. CHAPTER IV.

27. Thus it is easily understood how conversion, while it is occupied in abolishing the term from which, at the same time tends toward acquiring the formal term to which, namely, habitual faith in Christ, through the very acts and motions of faith, which are excited by divine power in the mind of the man being converted and brought to a sense and sorrow for sins, at first indeed more languid or faint, then, as they are more frequently repeated, so they are stronger or firmer, until, with increased powers, habitual faith is produced. Indeed, the tendency of conversion toward acquiring the formal term to which differs only inadequately from its tendency toward the term from which to be abolished, and is included in it. For just as conversion tends toward the reunion with God of a man turned away from God, so through the very acts of faith he begins to be joined with God and is joined more and more, until, the offense having been abolished, he is fully reconciled with God and reunited through faith. For that true faith presupposes contrition in a sinful man will be easily established, partly from what has been said concerning the abolition of the term from which of conversion, and partly from what is soon to be said concerning the parts of repentance.

Thus the blessed Chemnitius, *Loci de Libero Arbitrio*, cap. VII, p. m. 199 b: "In the beginning of conversion (not for the renewal of the faithful, but for the bringing of the spiritually dead to spiritual life, whereby they are made faithful, accepted), the desire is more obscure, the assent more languid, the obedience more faint." Cf. the words of Quenstedt and Huelsemann concerning conversion taken broadly and strictly, ascribed above in § 16. d.

Quenstedt: "Dr. Musaeus, in the Jena Theologians' *Detailed Explanation*, Loc. 8, p. 423, when it is gathered from the words of his *Disputation* 5 on conversion § 30, that 'in a man not yet reborn, or before his first conversion, there are given good motions, pious desire, holy thoughts, σαρκοπνευματομαχία, and the beginnings of faith,' replies that 'he is not speaking of a man not yet reborn or before his first conversion, but of a man already converting under grace and constituted in the act of his conversion or rebirth,' and he defends this very thing ibid. p. 430, namely, 'that in a man already constituted as converting under grace, and in whom the Holy Spirit has begun conversion through the preached word perceived by hearing, there are given good motions, pious desire, holy thoughts, σαρκοπνευματομαχία, and the beginnings of faith.'

But Dr. Calovius rightly responds in *Systema*, T. 10, a. 1, c. 4, qu. 5, p. 145: 'That Latermann and his accomplices also used such an evasion,' which was obstructed in the preceding question 2. And he adds: 'Certainly, where conversion is still only being begun, there the subject is still to be converted and regenerated, but not yet already converted and reborn. Whence it is clear that before absolute conversion, good motions, holy thought, pious desire, etc., are attributed to man, even συνέργεια or cooperation toward spiritual actions, at the very least through powers excited by prevenient grace, so that through these same powers man may be able to cooperate toward the perfecting of his own conversion. Certainly, where such motions are, man is awakened from death and already lives a spiritual life, and consequently is converted.'"

Thus the blessed Chemnitz, in the place cited, after the words just now brought forward, adds: And those gifts must grow, namely in conversion itself, as the context teaches. And for this reason, the τὸ θέλειν (to will) and the τὸ ἐνεργεῖν (to work) are wont to be distinguished in conversion; both of which, however, God works, according to Phil. 2:13. Yet it cannot be shown at any mathematical point where the liberated will begins to act, says Chemnitz, in the place cited.

Furthermore, that conversion does not take place in an instant, but successively, and that faith is not infused in its entirety in one moment, but proceeds finally from antecedent acts of believing, the blessed Chemnitz taught at length in the place cited, where he begins thus: Conversion or renewal (not, however, the renewal of those who already possess habitual faith; for Chemnitz is not speaking of this in the place cited, but of how men tend toward and are led to attain habitual faith, which they have not yet had) is not such a change as is immediately completed and perfected in all its parts in one moment, but has its beginnings, its progressions, by which it is perfected in great infirmity, etc. Whence he then distinguishes between the first beginnings of faith and faith itself.

Similarly, the blessed Hutter, in his *Praelectiones* on the Formula of Concord, Art. II, on Free Will, pp. 175, 176, writes: The Holy Spirit excites good motions when He inspires pious thoughts, and by infusing a motion of good purpose, He prevents man with His grace, moves and impels the will, so that although it has not yet been fully made liberated from its enslaved state and still fluctuates and hangs as it were, yet it ceases to resist and begins to struggle with the flesh, until from an unwilling person he becomes willing, and from an enslaved person he becomes liberated. Whence it is soon clear that other point: The conversion of the ungodly to God does not take place in the way in which sometimes, by a general action of divine power, the hearts of men are changed and the counsels of the ungodly are subverted—who do not even think of such a thing, nay, more often they are even ignorant of what is being done with them, nay, sometimes they are compelled to do what they do not want to do; just as Balaam is compelled to bless the Israelite people, Num. 23:8. But the grace of God, in conversion, makes those who were unwilling more and more willing. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Ausführliche Erklärung*, Q. 47, pp. 422, 429 sqq., and the blessed Joh. Olearius, *Index Balduini*, Art. XCII, § 17, p. 155, where he teaches that the form of conversion consists in the successive communication of grace.

Quenstedt: "The form of conversion consists in the translation of the unregenerate man from the state of wrath and sin into the state of grace and faith, from the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom of light, which has its preparatory acts, with respect to which conversion is said to take place successively. Here, preparation must be properly distinguished from the translation itself from the state of wrath into the state of grace. Preparation has its degrees and takes place successively; but the translation itself from the state of wrath into the state of grace takes place in an instant and in a moment, since it is impossible that any subject should be, even for a moment, simultaneously in the state of wrath and in the state of grace, simultaneously under life and under death. For conversion is taken either broadly, in so far as it comprehends all the motions proceeding from the grace of God directed toward conversion; or strictly, in so far as it denotes only that final act, namely, the translation from the state of wrath into the state of grace. Taken in the former way, it has its preparatory acts, which take place successively: For first, preventing grace offers the Word and by means of it removes the salvific object and the natural incapacity and unfitness regarding spiritual things; then, preparing grace acts through that Word, by restraining resistance, by alluring the heart with the impulse of the Law, by explaining the Gospel. Where the man not yet reborn, through the assisting grace of the Holy Spirit, can hear the Word ἡδέως (gladly), Mark 6:20, feel the impulse of the Law and contrition, etc. And the Holy Spirit continues this His operation through preparing grace, until He renders the man capable..." PART III. CHAP. IV.

to receive that supreme good of translation from death and the state of wrath to life and the state of grace. This very translation from death into life, from the state of wrath into the state of grace, is most properly called conversion, which God alone works in an instant and in a moment, as we have said.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 22. f. 706. sq.)

The same: “Finally, conversion is either ordinary or extraordinary. . . . It is called extraordinary conversion with respect to the extraordinary mode which God sometimes uses in the conversion of certain people according to His free will. That extraordinary mode consists in this: not that it happens entirely without the Word of God, but that it does not happen through the Word of God preached by the ordinary ministry or the ministers of the church, but by the Word of God spoken by God Himself immediately, either without or with miracles, or by the Word announced through some minister, yet accompanied by certain miracles and signs; where, however, that power of converting is to be ascribed not to the miracles and signs, but to the Word of God.

Examples of extraordinary conversion are: 1) Abraham, who was an idolater. For in Joshua 24:2, 3, he is listed among the fathers of the Israelites who worshipped foreign gods. For the plural verb is twisted by Pererius and Bellarmine—not without violent forcing—to refer to Terah and other ancestors of Abraham, especially since the Israelites derive their lineage primarily from Abraham, and the idolatry of Nahor cannot be denied (Gen. 31:53); indeed, the very inference of Joshua, taken from the extreme unworthiness of the Israelites to the supreme benefit conferred upon them by God, would be entirely null unless Abraham is said to have been converted from idolatry. Cf. Philo, book on Abraham; Lindanus, lib. I. Panopl. c. II. But he was called and converted immediately by God through an external address, Gen. 12:1. 2) The Magi, who were led to Christ and converted to Him through an extraordinary medium, namely, a star, Matt. 2:1 sq. 3) The thief on the cross, who was converted immediately by Christ, Luke 23:42. And 4) Paul, whose conversion was extraordinary, with the Lord Jesus addressing him immediately [άμίσως] on the way toward Damascus and a light suddenly shining around him, Acts 9:3, 4.

Latin:

Hoc autem opponitur carnali securitati et desideriis carnis. Adeoque timiditati et diffidentiae adversantur.

Qui contrariatur amori mundi et rerum terrenarum. Quae desperationi opponitur. Scilicet quod post se quidem mox relinquunt dispositiones, quae inclinant in actus et motus spirituales similes, porro autem, actibus pluribus Spiritus Sancti gratia accedentibus, tendunt in habitum spiritualem, eo modo, quo actus intellectus in habitus tendere diximus ad § 25. not. h.

Nempe carentia virium ad bona spiritualia amplectenda, velut privatio, per oppositam formam, propensio autem habitualis ad malum per habitum contrarium tollitur. PART. III. CAP. IV.

27. Sic autem facile intelligitur, quomodo conversio, dum in abolendo termino a quo occupatur, simul tendat a in acquirendum terminum ad quem formalem, seu fidem habitualem in Christum, nempe per ipsos actus et motus fidei,b qui in animo hominis convertendi et ad sensum ac dolorem peccatorum perducti c divina virtute excitantur, primum quidem languidiores aut tenuiores,d deinde, sicut crebrius iterati, ita fortiores aut firmiores,e donec auctis viribus fides habitualis producatur. f Imo tendentia conversionis in terminum ad quem formalem acquirendum a tendentia ejus in terminum a quo abolendum inadaequate tantum differt et in hac includitur. Quemadmodum enim conversio tendit ad hominis a Deo aversi redunitionem cum Deo, ita per ipsos fidei actus incipit conjungi cum Deo et magis magisque conjungitur, donec, abolita offensa, plene reconcilietur cum Deo et reduniatur per fidem. Nam quod fides vera contritionem supponat in homine peccatore, partim ex dictis de abolitione termini a quo conversionis, partim ex mox dicendis de partibus poenitentiae facile constabit.

Sic b. Chemnitius Loc. de Lib. Arb. cap. VII. p. m. 199. b.: In principio conversionis (non pro renovatione fidelium, sed spiritualiter mortuorum ad vitam spiritualem perductione, qua fiant fideles, acceptae) desiderium est obscurius, assensus languidior, obedientia tenuior. Cf. verba Quenstedtii et Huelsemanni super conversione late et stricte accepta, supra § 16. d. asseripta.

Quenstedtius: ״D. Musaeus in der Jenischen Theologen Ausführl. Erklärung Loc. 8. p. 423., quando ex verbis ejus disput. 5. de conversione § 30. colligitur, quod,homine nondum renato vel ante primam sui conversionem dentur boni motus, pium desiderium, sanctae cogitationes, σαρκοπνενματομαχία et initia fidei': regerit, ,se non loqui de homine nondum renato vel ante primam sui conversionem, sed de homine jam sub gratia convertente et in actu conversionis sive renascentiae suae constituto‘, propugnatque hoc ipsum ib. p. 430., sc. ,in homine jam sub gratia convertente constituto et in quo Spiritus S. conversionem per verbum praedicatum et auditu perceptum inchoavit, dari bonos motus, pium desiderium, sanctas cogitationes, σηρκηπνενματο· μαχίαν et initia fldei'.

Sed recte resp. D. Calovius System. T. 10. a. 1. c. 4. qu. 5. p. 145.: ,Tali effugio etiam usos fuisse Latermannum et complices', praeced. qu. 2. obstructo. Additque: ,Sane, ubi adhuc inchoatur tautum conversio, ibi subjectum adhuc convertendum et regenerandum est, nondum vero jam conversum et renatum. Unde liquet, ante absolutam conversionem homini tribui bonos motus, sanctam cogitationem, pium desiderium etc., etiam σννέμγειαν vel cooperationem ad actiones spirituales, ad minimum per vires gratia praeveniente excitatas, ut per easdem cooperari homo possit ad perfieiendam sui ipsiusmet conversionem.‘ Certe ubi tales motus sunt, homo est excitatus a morte, et jam vivit vita spirituali, et per consequens est conversus.“

Ita b. Chemnitius 1. c. post verba modo hic allata addit: Et Ula dona oportet crescere, nimirum in ipsa conversione, uti contextus docet. Atque hac ratione alias distingui solent in conversione το velle et το perficere; quorum tamen utrumque Deus operatur, juxta PhiL 2, 13. Non tamen in puncto aliquo mathematico ostendi potest, ubi voluntas liberata agere incipiat, ait Chemnitius 1. c.

Caeterum quod conversio non fiat in instanti, sed successive, quodque fides non uno momento tota infundatur, sed demum ex antecedentibus actibus credendi proficiscatur, pluribus docuit b. Chemnitius 1. c., ubi ita infit: Conversio seu renovatio (non autem renovatio eorum, qui jam fide habituali pollent; de hac enim non loquitur Chemnitius 1. c., sed qua homines tendunt et perducuntur ad fidem habitualem consequendam, quam hactenus nondum habuerunt) non est talis mutatio, quae uno momento statim omnibus suis partibus absolvitur et perficitur, sed habet sua initia, suos progressus, quibus in magna infirmitate perficitur etc. Unde deinde inter prima initia fidei et fidem ipsam distinguit.

Similiter b. Hutterus Praei, ad F. C. Art. II. de Lib. Arb. p. 175. 176. scribit: Excitat Spiritus Sanctus bonos motus, cum cogitationes pias inspirat et boni propositi motum immittendo gratia sua hominem praevenit, movet et impellit voluntatem, ut quamvis ex serva nondum plene facta sit Uberata et adhuc fluctuet quasi ae pendeat, tamen repugnare desinat et cum carne luctari incipiat, tamdiu, donec ex nolente volens et ex serva liberata fiat. Unde mox liquet illud alterum: Conversionem impii ad Deum non eo fieri modo, quo interdum generali divinae potentiae actione corda hominum mutantur et consilia impiorum intervertuntur, qui tale quid ne cogitant quidem, imo saepius etiam ignorant, quid secum agatur, imo interdum coguntur ad agendum, quod nolunt; quemadmodum Bileam cogitur benedicere populo Israelitico, Num. 23, 8. Sed gratia Dei ex nolentibus in conversione magis magisque volentes facit. Conf. b. Mus. Ausführl. Erklärung Q. 47. p. 422. 429. sqq. et b. Joh. Olear. Indic. Balduin. Artic. XCII. § 17. p. 155., ubi formam conversionis in successiva gratiae communicatione consistere docet.

Quenstedtius: ״Forma conversionis consistit in hominis irregeniti ex statu irae et peccati in statum gratiae ac iidei, e regno tenebrarum in regnum luminis translatione, quae habet actus suos praeparatorios, respectu quorum successive fieri dicitur conversio. Probe hic distinguenda praeparatio ab ipsa ex statu irae in statum gratiae translatione. Praeparatio suos habet gradus et fit successive; ipsa vero ex statu irae in statum gratiae translatio fit in instanti et in momento, cum impossibile sit, ut subjectum aliquod vel per momentum sit simul in statu irae et in statu gratiae, simul sub vita et sub morte. Conversio enim vel late sumitur, in quantum scii, comprehendit omnes motus a gratia Dei provenientes ad conversionem directos; vel stricte, quatenus notat ultimum tantum illum actum, videl. translationem ex statu irae in statum gratiae. Illo modo sumta, habet actus suos praeparatorios, qui fiunt successive: Primo enim gratia praeveniens offert verbum et mediante eo objectum salvificum ac naturalem incapacitatem et inidoneitatem quoad spiritualia tollit; deinde gratia praeparans per illud verbum agit, repugnantiam cohibendo, cor legis pulsu alliciendo, evangelium explicando. Ubi homo nondum renatus per assistentem Spiritus S. gratiam audire verbum ήδέως Marc. 6, 20., sentire legis pulsum et contritionem etc. potest. Hancque suam operationem per gratiam praeparantem Spiritus S. continuat, quoad usque capacem hominem reddat PART. III. CAP. IV.

ad recipiendum summum illud bonum translationis e morte et statu irae ad vitam et statum gratiae. Haec ipsa vero translatio e morte in vitam, e statu irae in statum gratiae propriissime conversio est et dicitur, qftam solus Deus operatur in instanti et in momento, uti diximus.״ (L. c. s. 1. th. 22. f. 706. sq.)

Idem: ,,Conversio denique alia ordinaria est, alia extraordinaria. . . . Dicitur conversio extraordinaria respectu modi extraordinarii, quo Deus quandoque utitur in quorundam conversione pro libera sua voluntate. Modus autem ille extraordinarius in eo consistit, non quod prorsus absque Dei verbo fiat, sed quod non fiat verbo Dei per ministerium ordinarium vel ecclesiae ministros praedicato, sed verbo Dei ab ipso Deo immediate, vel sine vel cum miraculis prolato, vel verbo per ministrum aliquem annunciato, certis tamen miraculis et signis stipato; ubi tamen vis illa convertendi non miraculis ac signis, sed verbo Dei adscribenda est.

Exempla extraordinariae conversionis sunt 1) Abraham, qui fuit idololatra. Nam Jos. 24, 2. 3. refertur inter patres Israelitarum, qui deos alienos coluerunt. Verbum enim plurale non sine violenta trajectione ad Thare aliosque Abrahae majores torquetur a Pererio et Bellarmino, praesertim cum ab Abrahamo genus suum Israelitae potissimum deducant et de Nachore idololatria negari non possit, Gen. 31, 53., imo ipsius Josuae illatio, ab extrema Israelitarum indignitate ad summum beneficium ipsis a Deo collatum desumta, sic prorsus nulla esset, nisi Abraham ab idololatria conversus dicatur. Conf. Philonem lib. de Abraham, Lindanum 1. I. Panopl. c. II. Is autem immediate a Deo per alloquium externum vocatus et conversus est, Gen. 12, 1. 2)Magi, qui per medium extraordinarium, videl. stellam, ad Christum perducti, ad eumque conversi sunt Matth. 2,1. sq. 3) Latro in cruce, qui immediate a Christo conversus, Luc. 23, 42. Et 4) Paulus, cujus conversio jfuit extraordinaria, alloquente ipsum άμίσως Domino Jesu in via Damascum versus et luce subito ipsum circumfulgente, Act. 9, 3. 4.


### On Regeneration and Conversion: We add in the thesis with D

We add in the thesis with D. Koenig: ‘Such conversion does not happen by a power that is simply irresistible.’ For from the examples cited, it is clear that while extraordinary conversion was indeed brought about in various ways, none was done irresistibly; rather, all were converted by a ‘necessary will and a voluntary necessity,’ as the blessed Meisner speaks, Anthropol. Dec. 2. disp. 2. qu. 3. § 24.

But Pharaoh in Exodus 5, whom God intended to convert through the ministry of Moses and Aaron by employing many miracles, maliciously resisted the Holy Spirit, just as the Jews did in Matt. 11:20. Just as this extraordinary conversion ceases now that the church has been planted and the Word preached in the whole world, so also it is not directly treated here.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 6. 7. f. 701. sq.) §

28. Meanwhile, when the first beginnings of faith and conversion are given to a man, immediately there begins the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit; and it is manifest that that struggle d…oes not take place without the motion of our will. These words are from the blessed Chemnitz, l. c., where he also, after having warned that those gifts bestowed at the beginning of conversion must grow, adds: “But they grow in us, not as a log is moved forward by a violent impulse, or as lilies grow without laboring or caring, but by striving, struggling, seeking, asking, knocking; this is not from us, it is a gift of God.” But also, according to the Formula of Concord, Art. II, on Free Will, p. 675, this is most certain: that in true conversion, a change, renewal, and motion must take place

in the intellect, will, and heart of man, so that, indeed, the mind of man may acknowledge sins, fear the wrath of God, turn itself away from sin, acknowledge and apprehend the promise of grace in Christ (NB. thus the discourse is concerning conversion, by which one tends toward faith, not concerning the sanctification of the faithful), stir up pious thoughts in the soul, have a good purpose, and apply diligence in governing his own morals and fi…ght against the flesh.

And he notes significantly: For where none of these things occur, there is, without doubt, no true conversion to God.

See more on this matter in *Ausführl. Erklärung* 1. c. p. 429 sqq.

But also the blessed Schevzerus, in *Brev. Hülsern. enucl.* cap. IX. th. X. p. 515, teaches that the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit is proper to those who are either 1.) already actually reborn, or 2.) in the motion toward conversion, i.e., are being graciously moved by the Holy Spirit toward conversion.

No less does the blessed Joh. Olearius, in *Contin. Isag. Carpz. in Libb. Symb.* p. 1245, describe the struggle as conspicuous in the conversion of man and teaches that man struggles in the very act of conversion taking place.

So also the blessed Joh. Meisnerus, in *Disp. pecul. de Pugna Carnis et Spiritus*, on the passage Gal. 5:17, § 22, writes: The time when this struggle began can be set at that moment as soon as man feels the powers of the Holy Spirit in regeneration, and it lasts until the end of life.

But just as these speak of man constituted under converting grace, and according to the state in which the Holy Spirit works conversion in him, so it is not to be concluded from this as if it were posited that in a man not yet reborn and before his first conversion there exist good motions, pious desire, holy thoughts, σαρκοπνευματομαχίαν, and the beginnings of faith; just as the blessed Mus. also warned in *Ausführl. Erklärung* p. 423, 424.

Which indeed must be carefully distinguished from the struggle or fight of reason and the affections; just as the blessed Schevzerus 1. c. warns that the Natural Struggle of Natural Honesty with inordinate appetites is treated in Rom. 2:15, where mention is made of the mutual accusation of thoughts; but that the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit is treated in Rom. 7:15 sqq., cap. 8:6, Gal. 5:16.

From which, however, it does not follow that the will has natural powers through which it moves itself to will spiritual things against the inclination of the flesh.

And rather it is certain that those acts which occur in man in the very work and progress of conversion are not so much man’s as they are the Holy Spirit’s; concerning which, below in its proper place.

Ad. Osiander: "Hornejus excepts by distinguishing between the first beginning of conversion and its progress. In the first beginning, man is indeed dead, destitute of all spiritual life, but in the progress, he cannot be called simply dead; which he proves from D. Chemnit. in *Conc. Trid.* Sess. VI. c. 2, writing thus: 'When the Holy Spirit has begun to heal nature through the Word, having kindled some spark of efficacy and spiritual faculty' (this spark is exciting and assisting grace), 'although the renewal' (conversion) 'is not immediately perfect and absolute, but only begun in great infirmity, then, however, neither the mind nor the will is idle, but they have some new motions, which they also ought to exercise by meditating, praying, striving, struggling, etc., and this is to cooperate with divine grace.'

He adds from the locus on the powers of man, c. 7: 'After the motion of the will divinely effected, the human will does not behave purely passively, but, moved and assisted by the Holy Spirit, it does not resist, but assents and becomes a συνεργός.'

Therefore, our will becomes God’s, or cooperates with divine grace, not only when man, already reborn, converted, and justified, grows in faith and charity and [performs] works of piety through grace PART III. CAP. IV. [it] makes [him] justifying and indwelling, but also when, through the aids of preventing, preparing, and assisting grace, he is converted to God and is first justified.

For just as a man who is reborn and justified is said to cooperate with the grace of the Holy Spirit already indwelling, while he diligently trades with the gift or talent of justifying and sanctifying grace once received: so the same man also cooperates with the aids of the grace of the Holy Spirit, who is not yet indwelling our hearts, but is knocking so that He may enter and dwell therein, while, prevented, assisted, and prepared by those aids, he is converted to God, so that, justified and reborn, he may become a temple of God and of His Spirit.

Resp.: 1. That man is not only at the beginning of conversion, but also in its progress, still dead; because a) divine grace even in progress "at least prepares man, so that he does not cooperate, but is passively disposed to receive greater motions of grace successively; ß) Because man, even in the progress of conversion, before the final instant of faith being conferred and given, is not yet vivified; but lacking a vital principle, how can he cooperate vitally? Because y) whatever is done in the progress of conversion relates to man externally, as will be evident in the following.

2. Regarding the first testimony of the blessed Chemnitz: he used the term conversion in its full breadth, insofar as it denotes not only the translation from infidelity to faith, by which conversion strictly so-called is completed, but also insofar as it denotes the continuation of that conversion, vivification having already been presupposed; and thus the word conversion embraces both conversion transitively and intransitively so-called. Nor 3. does it conclude the other, inasmuch as it speaks of the assisted will; but the will cannot be assisted unless it is presupposed to be already living and endowed with vital powers, and thus to concur with grace, albeit languidly on account of the sin that surrounds [us]." (Colleg. th. IV, 333. sq.) Cf. Quenstedtius and Huelsemannus above p. 192. sq.

Response of the Theological Faculty of Leipzig to the questions proposed by the Königsberg Ministry regarding the Lateran [Council] (1640): "We indeed admit your distinction between the first and second conversion, but only in such a way that by the first we understand the action of God, by which He alone moves the soul, and by prevenient, preparing, and operating grace, as Augustine calls it, so bends the will that it begins to assent to Him and obey. This is evident from the example of Lydia, to whom, while she was listening to Paul, the Holy Spirit opened her heart so that she might attend to those things which were spoken by Paul, Acts 16: 14.

And in this sense God is said to work the ϑέλειν [willing], Phil. 2:13, when He takes away the heart of stone from the flesh of man and gives a heart of flesh and a new heart, and puts His Spirit within him, etc., Ezek. 36: 26.

This is the action and operation of God alone, and it is distinguished from the cooperation of man; as the same Augustine testifies, in his book *On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 17, and in book 2 *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, ch. 9: 'Therefore, that we may will,' he says, 'He works without us; but when we will, and so will that we may act, He works with us.' And Bernard, in his book *On the Grace of God and Free Choice*, not far from the end: 'He who finds no one good, saves no one whom He does not prevent. Therefore, the beginning of our salvation is undoubtedly from God, and certainly not through us, nor with us.' *

Formula of Concord*, p. 680: 'The conversion of our depraved will (which is in truth nothing other than its resuscitation from spiritual death) is entirely the work of God alone, just as the resuscitation of the body in the resurrection of the flesh is to be attributed to God alone'; f. sq. 681: 'The intellect and will of a man not yet reborn are only the subject to be converted; for they are the intellect and will of a man who is spiritually dead, in which man the Holy Spirit works conversion and renewal; to which work of converting man, the will contributes nothing, but suffers that God may work in it, until he is regenerated. But afterwards, in other subsequent good works, he cooperates with the Holy Spirit, etc.'

By the second conversion, however, we understand when man, after the illumination of the mind and the motion of the will, by which the Holy Spirit has excited in the heart of man a pious purpose, desire, and endeavor, as Chemnitz speaks, and man, from being unwilling, has been made willing, begins to cooperate with God Himself."

...are enlightened, and unless he has persevered in evil out of obstinate malice, he embraces the grace offered through faith, which is excited by the Holy Spirit; he also begins to prove what is the good and acceptable will of God, Rom. 12:2, and to obey God from the heart, Rom. 6:17. And indeed, he is further assisted by the subsequent and assisting grace of God, as Augustine calls it, concerning which Christ also says in John 15: "Without me ye can do nothing." For He is speaking there to disciples who were already regenerate concerning the remaining and persevering of the branches in the life into which they had once been grafted. And in this breadth or amplitude of meaning, the Formula of Concord (p. 675) accepts the term "conversion" when it says: "For this is most certain, that in true conversion a change, renewal, and movement must take place in man’s intellect, will, and heart, so that the mind of man may acknowledge sin, fear the wrath of God, turn itself away from sin, acknowledge and apprehend the promise of grace in Christ, stir up pious thoughts in the mind, have a good purpose, and apply diligence in governing his conduct, and fight against the flesh." (Dedek. Theol. Cons. App. Chr. Gruebelii (1671) f. 646 sq.) § 29.

Koenig.: ,Ejusmocji conversionem fieri potentia non simpliciter irresistibiliS Ex allatis enim exemplis patet, conversionem extraordinariam variis quidem modis esse factam, nulla tamen facta est irresistibiliter, sed omnes fuerunt conversi,necessaria voluntate et voluntaria necessitate‘, ut loquitur B. Meisnerus, Anthropol. Dec. 2. disp. 2. qu. 3. § 24.

Haec extraordinaria conversio sicut post ecclesiam plantatam verbumque in toto orbe praedicatum jam cessat, ita etiam directe de ea hic non agitur.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 6. 7. f. 701. sq.) §

28. Interim, quando a prima initia fidei et conversionis homini dantur, statim b incipit lucta carnis et,c Spiritus; et manifestum est, illam luctam non fieri sine motu nostrae voluntatis.d Verba haec sunt b. Mus. monuit in Ausführl. Erklärung p. 423. 424.

Quae quidem a lucta sive pugna rationis ei affectuum solicite distinguenda est; prout b. Unde tamen non sequitur, voluntatem habere vires naturales, per quas ipsa se moveat ad volendum spiritualia contra inclinationem carnis.

Ac potius certum est, actus illos, qui in homine in ipso opere ct progressu conversionis fiunt, non tam hominis esse, quam Spiritus· .Sancti; de quo infra suo loco.

VI. c. 2. ita scribente: ,Quando Spiritus Sanctus per verbum coepit naturam sanare, accensa aliqua scintilla efficaciae et facultatis spiritualis' (haec scintilla est gratia excitans et adjuvans), ,licet renovatio' (conversio),non statim sit perfecta et absoluta, sed in magna infirmitate tantum inchoata, tunc tamen nec mens nec voluntas est otiosa, sed aliquos motus habent novos, quos etiam debent exercere meditando, orando, conando, luctando etc., atque hoc est cooperari gratiae divinae.‘

Addit ex loco de viribus hom. c. 7.: ,Post motum voluntatis divinitus factum voluntas humana se non habet pure passive, sed, mota et adjuta a S. Spiritu, non repugnat, sed assentitur et fit obvepyog.'

Spiritus, adhuc corda nostra nondum inhabitantis, sed, ut ea intret atque inhabitet, pulsantis, cooperatur, dum auxiliis illis praeventus, adjutus et praeparatus ad Deum convertitur, ut justificatus atque renatus templum Dei et Spiritus illius fiat.

Quia 7) quicquid agitur in progressu conversionis, circa hominem externe sese habet, ut patebit in seqq.

Nec 3. concludit alterum, utpote loquens de voluntate adjuta; adjuvari autem voluntas non potest, nisi praesupponatur jam vivere et vitalibus virilius instructa, adeoque concurrere cum gratia, licet languide propter peccatum circumstans.“ (Colleg. th. IV, 333. sq.) Cf. Quenstedtius et Huelsemannus supra p. 192. sq.

Tlies. Cons. App. Chr. Gruebelii (1671) f. 646. sq.) § 29.


### On Regeneration and Conversion: The acts which enter into and constitute the business of conversion are called…

The acts which enter into and constitute the business of conversion are called and are spiritual, and are rightly distinguished from animal acts. Those are animal which have as their material object, properly and per se, things subject to the senses, or which imply causes or some other relation to sensible things, and have as their formal object the light of nature and the goodness known by the light of nature. Spiritual acts, on the contrary, are primarily those whose objects exceed the order and light of nature, but can and are wont to be known under divine revelation and desired under the aspect of good known through revelation; yet there also belong here acts which, although they are occupied with things subject to the light of nature, nevertheless tend toward them under some spiritual aspect, or tend toward things exceeding the grasp of the light of nature and include and connote some acts of a more sublime order. a) The denomination is indeed taken from the efficient cause, which is the Holy Spirit (namely, because they do not come to man from any other source than the supernatural operation of the Holy Spirit), yet it is founded in the nature of the object, as is taught later in the thesis. Thus in the Scriptures, acts of knowing are said to be done πνευματικῶς or spiritually, 1 Cor. 2:14. Otherwise they are called supernatural.

b) Those which can proceed and do proceed from the soul left to itself and its natural powers, without the supernatural grace of the Holy Spirit, even in the state after the fall, and thus fall into the "animal" man, ψυχικός, according to the aforementioned passage. And they are therefore natural in their substance as well as in their mode of production. Otherwise, indeed, natural and animal actions are taken more strictly, insofar as they are not only [distinguished] from supernatural ones, but... PART III. CHAPTER IV.

are also distinguished from civil, moral, and artificial [acts], all of which can nevertheless be performed by the powers of nature; see the blessed Meisner, *Anthropol.* Disp. XXI, Q. XII, § 107, pp. 811, 812; the blessed Gerhard, *Disp. Isag.* XXVII, cap. VI, *de Lib. Arb.* § 3, p. 961; but here it will be permitted for us, following others, to retain a somewhat broader signification.

Whence our natural cognition begins Naturally, sensible things, known in their phantasms—which have been elevated by the agent intellect—move the intellect through discourse even to the cognition of other objects, to which they relate by way of effects, or accidents, or in another manner. And thus, men naturally know not only material things, but also immaterial things and God Himself, by reason of existence, essence, and attributes, and indeed even some manner of divine worship, according to Rom. 1:19 ff. and Ps. 19:1. The will, however, with the goodness of things represented to it by the intellect, is moved to the desire for them, e.g., so that they may will to act and do act in a certain way according to the law (Rom. 2:18), and so that they may seek God (Acts 17:27). Cf. *Aug. Conf.* Art. XVIII and its *Apology*, and what is commonly taught concerning the righteousness of the flesh or legal righteousness. As the ultimate reason for knowing. Whether its own [reason] or that of another thing, to which they (as means) are ordered. For animal acts on the part of the will extend themselves so broadly that they are referred to all things which can be known under the aspect of the good by the light of nature.

And thus they are said to be the Spirit of God, because they lie hidden in God, who is Spirit, so that, just as no one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him, so also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, as the Apostle teaches in 1 Cor. 2:11 and 12. To this pertain the mysteries of the Trinity, the incarnation, and the satisfaction of Christ, the intuitive vision of God, etc. As the proper reason for assenting. Cf. what we said concerning the formal object of theology in *Proleg.* cap. I, § 35, Vol. I, p. 68, and concerning faith viewed on the part of assent in Part III, cap. III, § 4.

Insofar as the merit of Christ is to be applied to us, and the very remission of sins and eternal life are desired, Christ the mediator is loved, and trust is placed in Christ and in the reconciled God, when the intellect, illuminated by the light of revelation, represents these things to the will as goods for man. k) E.g., restraining inordinate concupiscences in view of eternal punishment or hell (which divine revelation shows), loving God who is favorable to us in Christ, etc., both of which are above natural powers; just as the reason under which, or the formal object, is something spiritual. For otherwise, some restraint of the movements of the sensitive appetite, or of the affections, out of a desire for honesty or fear of any punishments whatsoever, and a certain love of God known from creatures as the author of nature and of natural goods, can be natural.

l) Compare with these things which are said here, the blessed Musaeus, *de Convers.* Disp. IV, cap. I, § 12 ff. to 38, pp. 248 to 267.

80. To animal acts are also reckoned those which they call pedagogical; which must be exercised regarding the means of conversion, not only on the part of the body and external members, but also on the part of the intellect and the will. a

Taken in a broader signification (concerning which see note b to § 29); which are nevertheless distinguished from spiritual ones. b

By which, indeed, conversion is not intrinsically begun or perfected, yet the man to be converted is, as it were, led by the ordinary way so that the means may be rightly established in his use, and thus God, through His grace bound to His Word, may be able to work in his soul and to begin and perfect conversion, without the malicious resistance of man.

Such actions are called by some "ecclesiastical," see blessed Kromayer, *Theol. Pos.-Pol.* Art. IX. *de Lib. Arb.* Thes. II. p. 537; by others, with the addition, "ecclesiastical external," see blessed Hutter, *LL. GC.* p. 273; "sacred external actions," blessed Meisner, *Anthropol. Disp.* XXI. Q. XII. § 108. p. 812. c

The word of the Law, I say, and of the Gospel and the ministry of the Word. d

Such as: to approach the temple, to hear the Word of God, to read. e

E.g., to follow the preached or written Word with some investigation of the mind, and to meditate upon it according to human capacity. f

To which pertains the very desire of hearing or reading the Word and that carnal zeal which Hutter and others in the cited places teach. g

Kromayer: "We judge that a distinction must be made between ecclesiastical and spiritual actions. Ecclesiastical actions are such as: to read the Word of God, to go to the temple, to hear sacred sermons, and indeed with attention; spiritual actions are such as: to believe the divine Word, to believe that Christ died for oneself, etc. The former are still placed in our hand; the latter, however, are not. Concerning the former, one must hear: 1. The passage of Amos 8:11: 'Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east; they shall run to and fro to seek the word of the Lord, and shall not find it.' 2. Mark 6:20: 'Herod (unregenerate) ήδέως, i.e., gladly and with delight, heard John the Baptist.' 3. Acts 13:7: 'Sergius (unregenerate), having called for Barnabas and Saul, ἐπεζήτει, i.e., desired to hear the Word of God.' Therefore, the desire of hearing or reading the Word of God is one thing; the desire of believing is another. The former is ἐφ' ἡμῖν and can happen either from an itch for novelty, or to get a taste of eloquence, or for the sake of illusion, or for other reasons; the latter is the work of the Holy Spirit, who works in us both to will and to do, Phil. 2:13. That the passages alleged above are to be understood concerning the external hearing of the Word, not the internal—which is already συγκεκραμένος τῇ πίστει, Heb. 4:2—is evident from what has been said. This external hearing of the Word does not have the nature of merit, but of a means through which God kindles faith in our hearts. For the merit of congruity, which the Papists invent here—when, namely, a man does what he can do by nature, that it is then congruous for God to give grace to such a man—we, with Scripture, do not know." (*Th. posit.-pol.* P. I. p. 537.) Baier's Comp. ed. Walther, p. 14 PART III. CHAP. IV.

To wit, that God ordinarily confers His heavenly grace for salvation only through these [means], although by no means is merit, whether of congruity or of condignity, to be ascribed to them, as if through these actions some preparation for the grace of God or for conversion were made in man. B. Hutter, l. c., p. 274. a. Gerhard: "This distinction between merit of congruity and of condignity is established by the Papists: the former avails for the obtaining of initial grace, but the latter for the increase of grace and righteousness, and thus for eternal life itself. The former rests upon the liberality of the one accepting, the latter upon the obligation of the one rewarding; yet it is established that it is common to both that it is an act freely elicited, that it is accepted for the retribution of a reward, and that there is a certain equality between the labor and the reward. However, when it is asked whether one can merit eternal life by congruity or by condignity, some more moderate [theologians] answer: by congruity; but most answer that we can merit eternal life by condignity." (Loc. de bonis opp. § 108.) § 31. Furthermore, since intransitive conversion is the same as repentance or turning back, it is manifest that its parts are rightly constituted as contrition and faith.

Thus the blessed Musaeus, de Conv. Disp. I. § 3. p. 2. However, repentance is not understood as just any kind, speaking generally, but, taken specifically, for that which belongs to the sinful man and which, according to ecclesiastical writers, although it is sometimes taken more strictly for the part of conversion which is called contrition, is often taken for the whole conversion; just as in the Scriptures the word μεταμέλεια, or μεταμέλεσθαι, which formally signifies anxiety, displeasure, and sorrow after the fact, so that it properly signifies a part of conversion, namely contrition, yet synecdochically denotes the whole conversion. The word μετάνοια, however, or μετανοεῖν, even if it itself does not formally signify faith or believing in Christ, yet implicitly and materially includes it when it frequently denotes the whole conversion in its proper meaning. See the blessed Musaeus, cited Disp. I. cap. IV. p. 29. sqq. and Disp. II. cap. III. p. 65. sqq. Quenstedt: "The word repentance, attributed to man, is taken by theologians either for conversion taken transitively, or for the effect of conversion taken transitively or actively, and this meaning is the one for this place." (L. c. c. 9. s. 1. th. 3. f. 834.)

Latin:

Actus, qui negotium conversionis ingrediuntur et constituunt, dicuntur et sunt spirituales a et ab animalibus b recte distinguuntur. Sunt autem animales, qui pro objecto materiali, proprie et per se, habent res sensibus c subjectas, aut quae ad res sensibiles causae vel aliam habitudinem d important, pro formali objecto habent lumen naturae e et bonitatem f lumine naturae cognitam. Spirituales ex adverso sunt praecipue quidem, quorum objecta g excedunt naturae ordinem et lumen, sub revelatione autem divina h cognosci et sub ratione boni per re· velationem cogniti i appeti possunt et solent; pertinent tamen huc etiam actus, qui, licet circa res lumini naturae subjectas occupentur, tamen sub aliqua ratione spirituali k in eas tendunt, vel ad res luminis naturae captum excedentes tendunt et actus aliquos sublimioris ordinis ineludunt et connotant. l Denominatione quidem a causa effieiente, quae est Spiritus S., petita (scilicet, quod non aliunde homini obtingunt, quam ex supernaturali operatione Spiritus Sancti), fundata tamen in ratione objecti, ut postea in thesi docetur. Sic in Scripturis dicuntur actus cognoscendi fieri π>ευματι7.ως aut spiritualiter 1 Cor. 2, 14· Alias supematu· rales appellantur.

Qui ab anima sibi relicta ejusque viribus naturalibus, citra supernaturalem Spiritus S. gratiam, etiam in statu post lapsum proficisci possunt et proficiscuntur atque ita in hominem animalem, ψυχαυν, cadunt, juxta 1. c. Suntque ideo naturales in substantia sua pariter et productionis modo. Alias quidem actiones naturales atque animales strictius accipiuntur, quatenus non tantum supernaturalibus, verum PART. ΙΠ. CAP. IV.

etiam civilibus, moralibus et artificialibus, quae tamen omnes viribus naturae fieri possunt, contradistinguuntar, vid. b. Meisneri Anthropol. Disp. XXI. Q. XII. § 107. p. m. 811. 812., b. Gerhardt Disp. Isag. XXVII. cap. VI. de Lib. Arb. § 3. p. 961.; sed hic licebit nobis post alios significationem paulo ampliorem retinere.

Unde naturalis nostra cognitio incipit Nimirum res sensibiles in suis phantasmatibus, ab intellectu agente elevatis, cognitae naturaliter movent intellectum per discursum etiam ad cognitionem aliorum objectorum, ad quae sese per modum effectuum, aut accidentium, aut alio modo habent. Et sic non tantum res materiales, sed et immateriales Deumque ipsum, ratione existentiae, essentiae et attributorum, imo et aliquam cultus divini rationem naturaliter cognoscunt homines, juxta Rom. I, 19. sqq. Psal. 19, 1.
