### On Regeneration and Conversion: To wit, this is how the meaning of the word μετανοεῖν is usually rendered…

To wit, this is how the meaning of the word μετανοεῖν is usually rendered literally in Latin. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Disp. I. cap. I. § 3. p. 2. and cap. IV. § 56. and 59. p. 29. 30. 31. Indeed, that the essence of conversion (or repentance) consists in these two, contrition and faith, was also acknowledged by the blessed Musaeus, Disp. I. § 3. p. 2. cap. IV. § 66. sqq. p. 34. Ausführl. Erklärung L. XII. Quaest. 63. p. 561. sq.

Quenstedt: "Distinguish between the word repentance taken broadly for the whole conversion to God with its properties and effects, in which sense new obedience is added to the parts of repentance in the Apology of the A. C."

Art. 12: "If anyone wishes to add a third part, namely, worthy fruits of repentance, i.e., a change of the whole life and morals for the better, we shall not object"; and the term repentance is taken properly and strictly, and thus there are only two essential parts of true and saving repentance: contrition and faith; but good works are the fruits of repentance (Matt. 3:8; Acts 26:20; Rev. 2:5). Regarding these parts, the Augsburg Confession, Art. 12, says: "Repentance properly consists of these two parts: one is contrition, or the terrors struck into the conscience through the knowledge of sin; the other is faith, which is conceived from the Gospel or absolution, and believes that for Christ’s sake sins are forgiven, and comforts the conscience and delivers it from terrors. Then good works ought to follow, which are the fruits of repentance." The same is repeated in the Smalcald Articles, Part III, Art. 3, in the Formula of Concord, Art. 5, etc. (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 854. sq.)

Dannhauerus: "If," says Gerhard, "new obedience is established as an essential part of conversion, the promise of reconciliation with God and the remission of sins will not be firm, because our reconciliation with God and the remission of sins will be judged by the quality and quantity of our new obedience. The consequence contradicts the apostolic statement in Rom. 4:16: 'Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace, to the end the promise might be sure.' Observe, however: when new obedience is established as a necessary consequence of true repentance, that term is understood to include not only external good works, but also, and indeed primarily, the internal good intention, since sometimes certain external works cannot follow, e.g., at the point of death, in extreme poverty, etc.; where that saying of Augustine will have place: 'God crowns the will within, if He does not find the faculty for doing good'; and likewise that of Remigius: 'If you do not have the riches of Zacchaeus, if the two mites of the widow are lacking to you, if you cannot even offer a cup of cold water, offer God a good will.' Cf. Brochmand, p. 383, where the objection of Smalcius is refuted... Just as fruit is not a part of the tree, but an effect, so also σκληραγωγία (bodily discipline), satisfaction, new obedience, and good intention are fruits, not parts... The addition of new obedience to the parts of repentance is a Philistine plug in the fountain of consolation. For if, after absolution, some essential part was still lacking to the thief, namely, voluntary σκληραγωγία, then, being doubtful of his salvation, he should have feared some fasting of the rich man in purgatory." (Hodosoph. Phaen. XI. p. 637. sq.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who 1) deny that contrition, taken in the orthodox sense, is a part of repentance. For thus Bellarmine, Book 1, On Repentance, ch. 19, prop. 1: 'The terror struck into the soul by the Law, which the Lutherans call contrition or mortification, is not rightly numbered among the parts of repentance. This proposition is in conformity with the Council of Trent, sess. 6, ch. 6.' 2) They contend that faith can in no way be called a part of repentance. Bellarmine, in the book already cited, prop. 2: 'Faith,' he says, 'is not a part of repentance, although it is necessarily required to effect it. This proposition is also in conformity with the Council of Trent, sess. 6, ch. 6.' Roman Catechism, f. 242: 'Faith can in no way be rightly called a part of repentance.' On the contrary, they maintain that repentance consists of these three parts: contrition of heart, to which it pertains that one should grieve 'for the sin committed with the purpose of not sinning thereafter,' as the Roman Catechism has it; confession of the mouth, to which it is required that the sinner confess to the priest integrally all mortal sins of which he has memory; and satisfaction of work according to the judgment of the priest, which is indeed done primarily through prayer, fasting, and alms. Thus the Council of Florence on the sacrament of repentance and the Council of Trent, sess. 14, ch. 13. Bellarmine, Book 1, On Repentance, ch. 19, prop. 5: 'There are,' he says, 'three parts of repentance: contrition, confession, and satisfaction. In this proposition all Catholics agree.' ...

2. Of the Calvinists, who make the parts of repentance the mortification of the flesh and the vivification of the spirit, or the destruction of the old man and the [restoration of the] renewed [man]." PART III. CHAP. IV.

of the Spirit or the new man. Thus the Palatine Catechism, p. 88: "In how many parts does true repentance or conversion of man consist? In two parts: in the dying of the old man and the rising of the new man.". . . They deny, however, that contrition and faith are parts of repentance. . . 3. Of the Philippists, who make contrition, faith, and the purpose of amending one's life the parts of repentance; see the catechetical booklet of Chytraeus; but they look to the indissoluble connection between true repentance and good works. . .

4. Of the Socinians, who, with the Papists, deny that faith is a part of repentance and constitute new obedience and good works as its part. "Faith does not pertain to the nature of repentance," says Smalcius, disp. 2 on repentance, ch. Franz. f. 354, "but it is a consequence of it, which comes from divine kindness." That new obedience is a part of repentance, the same Smalcius teaches. "And this," he says on f. 356, "is almost the sole essence of repentance." They also contend with the Remonstrants, Apology ch. 15: "Repentance is nothing other than the correction of life."

5. Of the Weigelians, who construct the "essence of repentance" from "a contrite heart and the imitation of Christ, which is done through meekness, humility, patience, and obedience," as can be seen in almost all of Weigel's treatises. Likewise, for Weigel, repentance, confession, faith, and prayer are ταὐτά (the same). (L. c. f. 855 sqq.)

Hutterus: "Some Philippists oppose our purer doctrine concerning the parts of repentance, though not according to knowledge, constituting three parts of repentance: contrition, faith, and new obedience." (Loc. th. art. 21. c. 7. f. 760.)

Indeed, by this name, ecclesiastical writers are accustomed to denote the entire retraction of sins, the term being taken from the sorrow and dread of the conscience, which are accustomed to be joined seriously with the displeasure of acknowledged sins, and by which, as if by a hammer, the heart of the sinner, hard and hardened in evil, is broken or crushed, according to Ps. 51:19, Ps. 142:3, Is. 61:1, ch. 66:2, ch. 57:15, ch. 38: 13. Compare the blessed Musaeus on Conversion, Disp. III. ch. II. § 74. p. 136.

Huelsemannus: "The word for conversion, which in Greek is ἐπιστροφή, does not state, but presupposes the effect of sorrow; it states, however, the term of repentance from which and to which." (Praelect. Form. Conc. p. 498.)

Smalcald Articles: "Such an office (of the Law) the New Testament retains and also drives, as St. Paul does in Romans 1 and says: 'The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all men.' Likewise 3: 'All the world is guilty before God.' And: 'No man is righteous before Him.' And Christ in John 16: 'The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin.' That is now the thunder-axe of God, with which He strikes both the manifest sinners and the false saints into one heap and lets no one be in the right, driving them all together into terror and despair. That is the hammer (as Jeremiah says): 'My word is a hammer that shatters the rocks.' That is not *activa contritio*, a manufactured repentance, but *passiva contritio*, the true heart-sorrow, suffering, and feeling of death. And that is then called beginning true repentance, and man must here hear such a judgment: It is nothing with you all; you are public sinners or saints; you must all become different and do differently than you now are and do; you are, whoever and however great, wise, powerful, and holy you want to be, here no one is pious. . .

But now we must hold the false repentance of the Sophists against the true repentance, so that both may be understood all the better. . .

With repentance it was done thus: Because no one could remember all his sins (especially those committed throughout the whole year), they patched the fur coat in this way: if hidden sins came to mind afterward, one would have to repent of them and confess them, etc. Meanwhile, they were commended to God's grace."

Furthermore, because no one knew how great the repentance ought to be so that it might be sufficient before God, they offered such consolation: whoever could not have *contritionem*, that is, repentance, he should have *attritionem*, which I may call a half-repentance or the beginning of repentance; for they themselves understood neither of these, and still do not know what is meant by them, as little as I do.

Such *attritio* was then reckoned as *contritio* when one went to confession. And if it happened that someone said he could not repent or feel sorrow for his sin, as might have been the case with lust or a desire for revenge, etc., they asked whether he did not wish or would not like to have repentance? If he then said, 'Yes' (for who would say 'no' here, except the devil himself?), they accepted it as repentance and forgave him his sin on account of this good work of his.

Here they cited St. Bernard as an example, etc. Here one sees how blind reason gropes in the things of God and seeks consolation in its own works according to its own conceit, and cannot think of Christ or faith. Now, when one examines it in the light, such repentance is a manufactured and invented thought from one's own powers without faith, without the knowledge of Christ, in which the poor sinner, when he thought of his lust or revenge, would rather have laughed than wept, except for those who were either rightly struck by the Law or had been plagued in vain by the devil with a sorrowful spirit; otherwise, such repentance was certainly pure hypocrisy and did not kill the lust for sin.

Dannhauerus: ,,Si, inquit Gerhardus, nova obedientia statuitur pars essentialis conversionis, non erit firma promissio reconciliationis cum Deo et remissionis peccatorum, quia ex qualitate et quantitate novae obedientiae judicabitur de reconciliatione nostra cum Deo et remissione peccatorum. Articuli Smalcaldici: ״Solch Amt (des Gesetzes) behält das neue Testament und treibets auch, wie S. Paulus Röm. 1. thut und spricht: ,Gottes Zorn wird vom Himmel offenbart über alle Menschen.‘ Item3.: ,Alle Welt ist für Gott schuldig.‘ Und: ,kein Mensch ist für ihm gerecht.‘ Und Christus Joh. 16.: ,Der heilige Geist wird die Welt strafen um die Sünde.‘ Das ist nu die Donneraxt Gottes, damit er beide die offenbarliche Sünder und falsche Heiligen in einen Haufen schlägt und lässt keinen Recht haben, treibet sie allesammt in das Schrecken und Verzagen. Das ist der Hammer, (wie Hieremias spricht): ,Mein Wort ist ein Hammer, der die Felsen zerschmettert.‘ Das ist nicht activa contritio, ein gemachte Reu, sondern passiva contritio, das rechte Herzeleid, Leiden und Fühlen des Todes. Und das heisst denn die rechte Busse anfahen, und muss der Mensch hie hören solch Urtheil: Es ist nichts mit euch allen, ihr seid öffentliche Sünder oder Heiligen, ihr müsst alle anders werden und anders thun, weder. ihr jetzt seid und thut, ihr seid, wer und wie gross, weise, mächtig und heilig, als ihr wollt, hie ist niemand fromm. . .

Aber jetzt müssen wir die falsche Busse der Sophisten gegen die rechte Busse halten, damit sie beide desto bass verstanden werden. . .

Mit der Reue war es also gethan: Weil niemand alle seine Sünde kunnte bedenken (׳sonderlich das ganze Jahr begangen), flicketen sie den Pelz also, wenn die verborgene Sünde hernach ins Gedächtniss kämen, müsste man sie auch bereuen und beichten u. s. w. Indes waren sie Gottes Gnaden befohlen.

Zu dem, weil auch niemand wusste, wie gross die Reu sein sollt, damit sie ja gnugsam wäre für Gott, gaben sie solchen Trost, wer nicht künnte contritionem, das ist, Reue haben, der sollte attritionem haben, welches ich mag eine halbe oder Anfang der Reu nennen; denn sie haben selbs alles beides nicht verstanden, wissen auch noch nicht, was es gesagt sei, so wenig als ich.

Solche attritio ward denn contritio gerechnet, wenn man zur Beicht ging. Und wenn sichs begab, dass etwa einer sprach, er künnte nicht reuen noch Leide haben für seine Sünde, als möcht geschehen sein in der Hurenliebe oder Rachgier u. s. w., fragten sie, ob er denn nicht wünschte oder gern wollte, dass er Reue möchte haben? Sprach er denn, ja, (denn wer wollt hie nein sagen, ohn der Teufel selbst?) so nahmen sie es für die Reue an und vergaben ihm seine Sünde auf solch sein gut Werk.

Hie zogen sie S. Bernhard zum Exempel an u. s. w. Hie siehet man, wie die blinde Vernunft tappet in Gottes Sachen und Trost suchet in eigen Werken nach ihrem Dünkel und an Christum oder den Glauben nicht denken kann. Wenn mans nu beim Licht besiehet, ist solche Reue ein gemachter und gedichter Gedanke aus eigen Kräften ohne Glauben, ohn Erkenntnis Christi, darin zuweilen der arme Sünder, wenn er an die Lust oder Rache gedacht, lieber gelachet, denn geweinet hätte, ausgenommen, die entweder mit dem Gesetze recht troffen oder von dem Teufel vergeblich sind mit traurigem Geist geplagt gewest; sonst ist gewis solche Reu lauter Heuchelei gewest und hat der Sünden Lust nicht getödtet.


### On Regeneration and Conversion: For they had to repent, [yet] would rather have sinned more if it had been free…

For they had to repent, [yet] would rather have sinned more if it had been free to do so." (Lib. Conc. p. 312, 313, 314, sq.)

Apologia A. C.: "Moreover, they teach and write even more inept and confused things; they teach that one can merit grace through repentance, and when they are asked why Saul and Judas and the like did not merit grace, in whom there was a truly terrible contrition? — to this question they should answer that Judas and Saul lacked the Gospel and faith, that Judas did not comfort himself through the Gospel and did not believe; for faith distinguishes the repentance of Peter and Judas.

But the adversaries do not mention the Gospel and faith at all, but only the Law; they say Judas did not love God, but feared punishment. But is that not an uncertain and inept way to teach about repentance? For when will a terrified conscience, especially in the truly great anxieties which are described in the Psalms and Prophets, know whether it fears God out of love as its God, or whether it flees and hates His wrath and eternal damnation? Those people cannot have experienced much of these great anxieties, since they play with words in such a way and make distinctions according to their dreams. But in the heart, and when it comes to experience, it is found to be much otherwise, and with the simple syllables and words, no conscience finds rest, as the good, gentle, idle sophists dream. . .

But when we speak *de contritione*, that is, of true repentance, we cut off the countless useless questions where they propose questions: whether we have repentance out of the love of God, or whether we have it out of fear of punishment? For these are merely empty words and vain chatter of those who have not experienced how it is with a terrified conscience. We say that *contritio* or true repentance is when the conscience is terrified and begins to feel its sin and the great wrath of God over sin, and is sorry that it has sinned. And this same *contritio* comes about when our sin is rebuked by God's Word. . .

In these same anxieties, the conscience feels God's wrath and seriousness against sin, which is a completely unknown thing to such idle and carnal people as the sophists and their like. For there the conscience first notices what a great disobedience against God sin is; there the conscience is first truly pressed." PART III. CHAP. IV.

the terrible wrath of God, and it is impossible for human nature to bear the same if it were not raised up by God’s Word. Thus Paul says: ‘Through the law I have died to the law.’ For the law only accuses the conscience, commands what one ought to do, and terrifies it. And there the adversaries do not speak a word about faith; they teach not a word about the Gospel, nor about Christ, but empty law-teaching, and say that people earn grace with such pain, repentance, and sorrow, with such anxieties, provided that they have repentance out of the love of God or love God. Dear Lord God, what kind of sermon is that for consciences that are in need of comfort? How can we then love God when we are stuck in such high, great anxieties and unspeakable struggle, when we feel such great, terrible earnestness and wrath of God, which is felt there more strongly than any person on earth can describe or speak of? What do such preachers and doctors teach other than empty despair, who in such great anxieties preach to a poor conscience no Gospel, no comfort, only the law?” (Lib. Conc. p. 168. sq. 171. sq.)

Ad. Osiander: “They object: that contrition of itself is not salutary, since it exists even in the despairing, indeed in the devils, Jas. 2, therefore it does not have the nature of a means to salvation, since repentance is salutary in its entirety. R.: ‘Contrition is viewed in two ways: considered precisely, it is not a part of salutary repentance, but as a part of repentance it is salutary, because it is thus tempered by the hope of struggling through and by confidence in divine kindness.’” (Colleg. th. IV, 808.) Quenstedtius: “Something can be by its own nature μέσον or indifferent, which only becomes salutary by a certain manner of the user. Contrition is not therefore immediately salutary by its own nature because it is constituted as a part of repentance.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 9. f. 702.)

H. Kromayerus: “The work of God must be distinguished from the accidental effect which Satan and our flesh introduce. Contrition in itself is indeed a work of the Holy Spirit, and not a sin; yet, accidentally, by reason of our native corruption, it is a raging against God, a way to despair. Just as servile fear in itself is not evil, although it belongs to evil men, so contrition in itself is not evil, but belongs to evil men. Nevertheless, although flight from God and raging against Him is not essential to contrition, but supervenes accidentally, it is intrinsically present in the subject of contrition, namely, in the sinner. In a word: it is extrinsic by reason of its form, intrinsic by reason of its subject.” (Th. posit.-pol. II, 315.) The same: “Contrition precedes justification, and is not of a person who is pleasing [to God], but of one still placed in the state of wrath, before saving faith, apprehending the merit of Christ, approaches.” (L. c. p. 331. sq.)

The same: “The sorrow that is in contrition has its degrees, being greater in some, smaller in others. For it is not meritorious, as the Papists claim, but it drives us to recognize our need for the forgiveness of sins. Christ, who felt the power of the law and the most ardent wrath of God against sins, was contrite in our place. Is. 53, 5. 10. Matth. 26, 38.” (L. c. p. 314. sq.) However, faith in Christ, explained above, is understood, by which contrite hearts are as it were healed or raised up, and which is the chief part of conversion and, as it were, its soul; when this is posited, conversion is posited. Add blessed Musaeus, Disp. I. cap. IV. § 76. p. 41. Ausführl. Erklärung p.

562. Smalcald Articles: “To such an office (of the law) the New Testament immediately adds the comforting promise of grace through the Gospel, which one should believe, as Christ says in Mark 1: ‘Repent and believe the Gospel,’ that is, become and be made different.”

and believeth my promise. And before him John is called a preacher of repentance, yet for the remission of sins, that is, he was to rebuke them all and make them sinners, so that they might know what they were before God, and recognize themselves as lost men, and thus be prepared for the Lord to receive grace and to await and accept the forgiveness of sins from Him. Thus Christ Himself also says in Luke 24: ‘Repentance and remission of sins must be preached in my name among all nations.’ But where the Law performs such an office alone without the addition of the Gospel, there is death and hell, and man must despair, like Saul and Judas, as St. Paul says: ‘The Law killeth through sin.’” (Lib. Conc. p. 312 sq.)

Kromayerus: “The boundary between contrition and despair must be marked off by faith. Tauler, a Dominican monk who flourished as an excellent preacher in Cologne, calls this the sugar of repentance, because, to wit, the sorrows arising from the recognition of sin are sweetened by evangelical consolations apprehended by faith. Since, therefore, contrition has preceded (for it is not required as a cause, but by way of precedence, unless one should wish to name it a cause of faith *sine qua non*, just as the removal of pus is a cause *sine qua non* by which a wound can be healed), faith follows, the other part of repentance, nay, the nucleus and, as it were, the soul of true repentance.” (L. c. p. 315.) B. Mentzerus: “Calvin admits one legal repentance, another evangelical (Inst. 3.3.4). And Bucanus calls one contrition of the law, but calls the other evangelical contrition, and says that this latter is proper to the Gospel. He says the former is called μεταμέλεια, but the latter μετάνοια, and he inserts faith as a kind of middle term between the two. What a marvelous method of preaching the Gospel this will be. Thus the Catechism published at Kassel places faith in the first position; as if, forsooth, the preaching of the Law, from which sins—that is, those spiritual wounds—are to be recognized, does not precede the announcement of the Gospel, which shows medicine to sinners.” (Exeges. August. Conf. Art. 12. p. 575.) § 32.

The nature and parts of conversion having been known, it must now further be observed that its efficient cause, and that the principal one, is the Triune God, and He alone. And thus we enter upon the consideration of transitive conversion.

Which by its own sufficient power works in man the recognition of sins and serious displeasure and sorrow for them, as well as the beginnings of faith and faith itself, with the purpose of amending one’s life. Indeed, viewed transitively, conversion is formally an action of God, who is said to convert man, or to cause that man converts himself, or that he is converted. Cf. above § 12.

For it is an *opus ad extra* (work toward the outside). Specifically, however, the Father of Christ is said to draw men so that they come to Christ, John 6:44. The Son says of Himself that He willed to gather the Jews to Himself and thus to work conversion in them, Matt. 23:37. The Holy Spirit is said to convict the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment, John 16:8, and thus to contribute something efficiently to their conversion from sins to God. Cf. what we have said concerning the Efficient Cause of Faith, Chap. III, § 9. PART III. CHAP. IV.

In opposition to the proper and natural powers of man to be converted, although also to the power and faculty of angels and blessed men, inasmuch as it is entirely lacking here. Thus Paul, in Phil. 2:13, attributes both our τὸ θέλειν and our τὸ ἐνεργεῖν entirely to God working, so as to take them away from all who are not God.

ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis:

1. Of Pelagius and the Pelagians, and indeed 1.) of the cruder ones, who simply denied that the grace of God is necessary for obtaining salvation, and affirmed that the nations could be saved by the law of nature, or understood nothing else by grace than either the revelation of the divine will made in the Word, or the very powers of the soul given and granted gratuitously; whom the Scholastics follow, especially Biel and Andradius. 2.) Of the more subtle ones, who admitted the assistance of divine grace; ... whom the Jesuits follow, especially Bellarmine...

Latin:

Denn sie mussten reuen, hätten lieber mehr gesündiget, wenn es frei gewest wäre.“ (Lib. Conc. p. 312. 313. 314. sq.)

Apologia A. C.: ,,Darüber so lehren und schreiben sie noch ungeschickter und verwirreter Ding; sie lehren, man könne durch Reue Gnade verdienen, und wenn sie da gefragt werden, warum denn Saul und Juda§ und dergleichen nicht Gnade verdienet haben, in welchen gar ein schreckliche Contrition gewesen ist? — auf diese Frage sollten sie antworten, dass es Judas und Saul am Evangelio und Glauben gefehlet hätte, dass Judas sich nicht getröstet hat durchs Evangelium, und hat nicht gegläubet; denn der Glaube unterscheidet die Reue Petri und Judä.

Aber die Widersacher gedenken des Evangelii und Glaubens gar nicht, sondern des Gesetzes; sagen, Judas habe Gott nicht geliebet, sondern hab sich für der Straf gefürcht. Ist aber das nicht ungewis und ungeschickt von der Buss gelehret? Denn wenn will ein erschrocken Gewissen sonderlich in den rechten grossen Aengsten, welche in Psalmen und Propheten beschrieben werden, wissen, ob es Gott aus Liebe als seinen Gott fürchtet, oder ob es seinen Zorn und ewige Verdammnis fleuhet und hasset? Es mügen diejenigen von diesen grossen Aengsten nicht viel erfahren haben, dieweil sie also mit Worten spielen, und nach ihren Träumen Unterscheid machen. Aber im Herzen, und wenn es zur Erfahrung kömmt, findet sichs viel anders, und mit den schlechten Syllaben und Worten findet kein Gewissen Ruhe, wie die guten, sanften, müssigen Sophisten träumen. . .

Wenn wir aber de contritione, das ist, von rechter Reue reden, schneiden wir ab die unzähligen unnützen Fragen, da sie Fragen fürgeben, wenn wir aus der Liebe Gottes, item wenn wir aus Furcht der Strafe Reue haben? Denn es sind allein blosse Wort und vergebliche Geschwätz derjenigen, die nicht erfahren haben, wie einem erschrockenen Gewissen zu Sinne ist. Wir sagen, dass contritio oder rechte Reue das sei, wenn das Gewissen erschreckt wird und seine Sünde und den grossen Zorn Gottes über die Sünde anhebt zu fühlen, und ist ihm leid, dass es gesündiget hat. Und dieselbige contritio gehet also zu, wenn unser Sünd durch Gottes Wort gestraft wird. . .

In denselbigen Aengsten fühlet das Gewissen Gottes Zorn und Ernst wider die Sünde, welchs gar ein unbekannte Sache ist solchen müssigen und fleischlichen Leuten, wie die Sophisten und ihres gleichen. Denn da merkt erst das Gewissen, was die Sünde für ein grösser Ungehorsam gegen Gott ist, da drücket erst recht das Gewissen PART. III. CAP. IV.

der schreckliche Zorn Gottes, und es ist unmüglich der menschlichen Natur denselbigen zu tragen, wenn sie nicht durch Gottes Wort würde aufgericht. Also sagt Paulus: ,Durch das Gesetz bin ich dem Gesetz gestorben.‘ Denn das Gesetz klaget allein die Gewissen an, gebeut, was man thun solle, und erschreckt sie. Und da reden die Widersacher nicht ein Wort vom Glauben; lehren also kein Wort vom Evangelio, noch von Christo, sondern eitel Gesetzlehre, und sagen, dass die Leute mit solchem Schmerzen, Reue und Leid, mit solchen Aengsten Gnade verdienen, doch wo sie aus Liebe Gottes Reue haben oder Gott lieben. Lieber Herr Gott, was ist doch das für ein Predigt für die Gewissen, denen Trosts vonnöthen ist? Wie können wir denn doch Gott lieben, wenn wir in so hohen, grossen Aengsten und unsäglichem Kampf stecken, wenn wir so grossen schrecklichen Gottes Ernst und Zorn fühlen, welcher sich da stärker fühlet, denn kein Mensch auf Erden nachsagen oder reden kann? Was lehren doch solche Prediger und Doctores anders, denn eitel Verzweifelung, die in so grossen Aengsten einem armen Gewissen kein Evangelium, kein Trost, allein das Gesetz predigen?“ (Lib. Conc. p. 168. sq. 171. sq.)

Ad. Osiander: ,,Excipiunt: contritionem de se non esse salutarem, cum etiam sit in desperantibus, imo in diabolis, Jac. 2., non ergo habere rationem medii ad salutem, cum poenitentia sit salutaris ex toto. R.: «Contritio spectatur dupliciter: praecise considerata non est pars poenitentiae salutaris, sed ut pars poenitentiae est salutaris, quia ita temperatur spe eluctandi, divinaeque benignitatis fiducia.“ (Colleg. th. IV, 808.) Quenstedtius: ,,Potest aliquid sua natura esse μέσον sive indifferens, quod certa demum utentis ratione fit salutare. Non ideo statim salutaris est sua natura contritio, quia pars popnitentiae constituitur.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 9. f. 702.)

H. Kromayerus: ,,Opus Dei ab accidentario effectu, quem satanas et caro nostra ingerunt, est disterminandum. Contritio in se quidem est opus Spiritus Sancti, nec peccatum, per accidens tamen ratione nativae corruptionis nostrae est fremitus adversus Deum, via est ad desperationem. Sicut timor servilis in se non est malus, licet sit hominum malorum, ita contritio in se non est mala, sed hominum malorum. Verumtamen, licet fuga Dei et fremitus adversus eum non sit essentialis contritioni, sed per accidens superveniat, intrinsece tamen inest subjecto contritionis, homini sci. peccatori. Uno verbo: extrinseca est ratione formae, intrinseca ratione subjecti.“ (׳Th. posit.-pol. II, 315.) Idem: ,,Contritio justificationem antecedit, nec est personae piacentis, sed adhuc in statu irae positae, antequam salvifica fides Christi meritum apprehendens accedat.“ (L. c. p. 331. sq.)

Idem: ,,Dolor, qui est in contritione, suos habet gradus, in aliis major, in aliis minor existens. Nec enim est meritorius, ceu volunt pontificii, sed eo nos adigit, ut indigentiam remissionis peccatorum agnoscamus. Christus, qui vim legis et iram Dei ardentissimam adversus peccata sensit, nostro loco fuit contritus. Es. 53, 5. 10. Matth. 26, 38.“ (L. c. p. 314. sq.) Intelligitur autem fides in Christum eupra explicata, qua velut sanantur aut eriguntur corda contrita quaeque conversionis pars praecipua et ejus quasi anima est; qua posita, ponitur conversio. Adde b. Mus. Disp. I. cap. IV. § 76. p. 41. Ausführl. Erklärung p.

562. Articuli Smalcaldici: ,,Zu solchem Amt (des Gesetzes) thut das neue Testament flugs die tröstliche Verheissung der Gnaden durchs Evangelium, der man gläuben solle, wie Christus spricht Marci 1.: ,Thut Busse und gläubet dem Evangelio‘, das ist, werdet und machte anders

und gläubet meiner Verheissung. Und füf ihm her Johannes wird genannt ein Prediger der Busse, doch zur Vergebung der Sünden, das ist, er sollt sie alle strafen und zu Sündern machen, auf dass sie wüssten, was sie vor Gott wären, und sich erkenneten als verlorne Menschen, und also dem Herrn bereit würden, die Gnade zu empfahen und der Sünden Vergebung von ihm ge warten und annehmen. Also sagt auch Christus Luc. am 24. selbst: ,Man muss in meinem Namen in alle Welt predigen Buss und Vergebung der Sünden.‘ Wo aber das Gesetz solch sein Amt allein treibet ohn Zuthun des Evangelii, da ist der Tod und die Hölle und muss der Mensch verzweifeln, wie Saul und Judas, wie S. Paulus sagt: ,Das Gesetz tödtet durch die Sünde.‘“ (Lib. Conc. p. 312. sq.)

Kromayerus: ,,Contritionis et desperationis confinium per fidem est disterminandum. Hanc Taulerus, monachus Dominicanus, qui Coloniae concionator egregius floruit, poenitentiae saccharum vocat, quod sci. dolores ex agnitione peccati orti consolationibus evangelicis fide apprehensis edulcentur. Cum itaque contritio antecessit (nec enim causae, sed antecessus ratione praerequiritur, nisi quis causam fidei sine qua non, ut remotio puris est causa, sine qua non curari potest vulnus, nominare vellet) sequitur fides, altera poenitentiae pars, imo nucleus et anima quasi verae poenitentiae.“ (L. c. p. 315.) B. Mentzerus: ״Calvinus aliam admittit poenitentiam legalem, aliam evangelicam 1. 3. Instit. c. 3. dist. 4. Et Bucanus contritionem aliam vocat legis, aliam vero appellat contritionem evangelicam, et hanc posteriorem dicit esse propriam evangelii. Illam vocari, ait, μεταμέλειαν, hanc vero μετάνοιαν, et inter utramque quasi mediam inserit fidem. Quae mirabilis futura est methodus praedicandi evangelii. Sic catechesis Casellis edita fidem priori loco ponit; quasi vero legis praedicatio, ex qua peccata, h. e., vulnera ista spiritualia agnoscenda sunt, non anteeat annuntiationi evangelii, medicinam peccatoribus ostendenti.“ (Exeges. August. Conf. Art. 12. p. 575.) § 32.

Cognita natura et partibus conversionis, jam porro observandum est,a causam efficientem ejus, eamque principalem,b esse Deum c trinunum,d eumque solum.e Atque ita ingredimur considerationem conversionis transitivae.

Quae sua ac sufficiente virtute in homine operatur peccatorum agnitionem ac displicentiam seriam et dolorem de illis, itemque fidei initia et fidem ipsam, cum proposito vitam emendandi. Nempe transitive spectata conversio formaliter est actio Dei, qui hominem convertere dicitur, aut facere, ut homo se convertat, vel ut convertatur. Conf. supra § 12.

Est enim opus ad extra. Speciatim autem Pater Christi dicitur homines trahere, ut veniunt ad Christum, Joh. 69 44.. Filius de se ipso dicit, se voluisse Judaeos ad se congregare adeoque conversionem in illis operari, Matth. 23, 37. Spiritus S. dicitur arguere mundum de peccato, et de justitia, et de judicio, Joh. 16, 8., et sic conferre aliquid efficienter ad conversionem eorum a peccatis ad Deum. Conf., quae diximus de Causa Effic. Fidei, cap. III. § 9. PART. III. CAP. IV.

In oppositione ad, proprias et naturales hominis convertendi vires, quanquam et angelorum et beatorum hominum vim et facultatem, quippe hic prorsus deficientem. Sic Paulus ad Phil. 2, 13. et το velle nostrum et το perficere Deo operanti in solidum tribuit, ut omnibus, qui non sunt Deus, adimat.

Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis:

1. Pelagii et Pelagianorum9 et quidem 1.) crassiorum, qui simpliciter negabant, gratiam Dei ad salutem consequendam esse necessariam, gentesque per naturae legem salvari posse, affirmabant, aut per gratiam nihil aliud intelligebant, quam vel revelationem voluntatis divinae in verbo factam, vel ipsas animae potentias gratis datas et concessas; quos sequuntur scholastici, imprimis Biel et Andradius. 2.) Calidiorum, qui gratiae divinae adjutorium admitte« bant; . . . quos sequuntur Jesuitae, praecipue Bellarminus...


### On Regeneration and Conversion: Of the Semi-Pelagians or Massilians, of whom Augustine asserts in *De…

2. Of the Semi-Pelagians or Massilians, of whom Augustine asserts in *De Praedestinatione Sanctorum*, ch. 2, that they maintain 'that the beginning of faith is from us, the completion of faith from God.' ...

3. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who pelagianize here; for they constitute two partial causes of conversion: the grace of God and the will of man. ... The Council of Trent, Sess. 6, can. 4, holds as follows: 'If anyone shall say that the free will of man, moved and excited by God, does nothing by assenting to God who excites and calls, whereby it disposes and prepares itself to obtain the grace of justification: let him be anathema.' ...

4. Of the Socinians, who deny original sin and therefore acknowledge no conversion at all from darkness to light, but call a daily change for the better of a life that is good in itself 'conversion' and 'regeneration'; thus Socinus in his epistle on 1 John 4:6. ... When, however, they make mention of the Holy Spirit here, they understand primarily the objective offering of the Gospel, not an internal and singular operation. ...

5. Of the Arminians, who, with the Socinians, require beforehand in the man to be converted a certain natural probity of mind and an innate ardor for learning the Word of God, as well as a natural docility... And likewise, they attribute to divine grace not an ολικήν [total], but at least a μερικήν [partial] ενέργειαν [energy/operation] in the man to be converted, and ascribe the cause of faith partly to the grace of God in Christ, and partly to man and his free will. ...

7. Of the Lutheran Synergists, who admitted some συνέργειαν [synergy] or cooperation of human powers with grace in the work of conversion.

8. Of the innovators, such as Latermann, etc." (*L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 719. sqq.*) Cf. above Vol. II, p. 300 sqq. § 83. The internal impulsive cause is the mercy of God; the external or meritorious cause is Christ the Mediator. According to those things which we said concerning Regeneration in § 7 and 8. § 34. The instrumental cause is the Word, and that of the Law and of the Gospel. Through the former, the acknowledgment of sins and sorrow for them is excited or produced in men; through the latter, faith in Christ. But that the cross is also said to lead us to conversion or repentance, that is to be understood not directly, but indirectly.

Or the efficacious and operative causal medium, to which God joins His infinite power for the producing of such an effect, and through which He exerts it.

To which, therefore, not a bare moral persuasion is to be attributed, but, on account of the concurrence of God, a power much more noble and higher than that which can otherwise be attributed to doctrine or speech, even if they are most suitable for persuading. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *De Conversione* (Hall edition), Disp. IV, § 56, sqq. By this name, in this place, we understand the Word of God commanding or forbidding something, with the power of obligating to obedience and effectively denouncing the wrath of God to transgressors.

Which, when it is opposed to the Law, imports promises concerning the grace of God and the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ the Mediator and His merit apprehended by faith. According to that of Paul, Rom. 3:20: "Through the law comes the knowledge of sin," and Rom. 7:7: "I would not have known sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, 'You shall not covet.'" Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *De Conversione* (Jena edition), Disp. III, cap. II, § 65, 66, p. 133. But that the knowledge of the Law, in order to recognize sins, must be sought not from the mere light of nature after the Fall, but from Scripture, is evident from the very corruption of our intellect, which arose from the Fall. Here, however, one must also observe the divine power which God has added to the word of the Law, contained in the Scriptures, for producing in man a supernatural assent, and thus also the recognition of those things which occur in man that are at variance with the Law. For this reason, it is certain that not infrequently men, having heard the doctrine concerning the punishments of hell, are supernaturally affected and moved to believe. Cf. the blessed Scherzer, *Brev. Huelsem. auct.*, c. IX, Thes. XI, p.

519. For when, by means of the Law, the foulness of sins and the offense against God and the guilt of eternal damnation arising therefrom are exhibited to the human intellect, at the same time there is also represented to the will the very formal reason by which it may be moved to the detestation of sins, sorrow for them, and fear of divine wrath and damnation; and thus the Law itself, by divine power, works in the will of man, through the mediation of the intellect's cognition, even displeasure and detestation of sins, terrors of conscience, and a certain horror of judgment, so that it is like a hammer breaking the rock, Jer. 23:29. To this pertain the horrors born from the meditation of the final judgment or of divine threats concerning infernal punishments, which men, having heard the sacred doctrine, suffer even against their will. Cf. the blessed Scherzer, *l.c.* For there are general promises, under which a man can rightly subsume himself as an individual and, by divine power, conclude to the eliciting of the assent of faith (see above, cap. III, § 4), whence the Gospel, at the same time on the part of the will (especially after the Law has made men anxious about a remedy or a Mediator, or, like a terrifying schoolmaster, has led them, as if by an indirect path, to Christ, according to that of Gal. 3:24), excites a desire for grace and soon a fuller confidence; as we indicated before.

Or affliction divinely sent on account of sins. For which reason they also commonly call it a real sermon of the Law; nor is the example of the prodigal son, Luke 15:18, and the saying of Isaiah 28:19, "Vexation gives understanding," poorly referred to this. Cf. Ps. 119:71. Truly, the cross is profitable for repentance both for the fallen (or relapsed) and for those who stand. PART III. CHAPTER IV.

k) For this belongs only to the Word.

l) Namely, insofar as it is a stirring up of the Word previously heard and read, but less observed, regarding practical knowledge, or even urges or compels us to the use of the means of grace. § 85. Man, however, by his own natural powers, contributes nothing at all, nor can he contribute anything, to intrinsically begin or perfect his own conversion, or to exercise spiritual acts; although, regarding the external use of the means, he can conveniently exercise certain acts of the intellect and will.

For he is dead in sins, Eph. 2:1; Col. 2:13. Compare what we have said more fully regarding the *terminus a quo* [starting point] of regeneration and conversion in § 4 and 18, where we indicated that man, before regeneration or conversion, is entirely devoid of spiritual powers on the part of all the faculties of the soul, but on the contrary is inclined toward evil. Add § 32 and note e. Kromayer: "Mark 12:34: 'You are not far from the kingdom of God.' If one is now closer and more disposed to the kingdom of heaven than another, it follows that man can dispose himself to grace. For the comparative presupposes the positive. But we respond: by the particle οὐ μακράν [not far], not a greater disposition, but a lesser indisposition is indicated. For one unregenerate person is not more disposed to grace than another, but one is less indisposed than another... because sin, to which one gives more rein than another, does not dispose one to grace, but rather hinders it." (Th. posit. pol. I, 644.)

Quenstedtius: "There is a profound silence in the Scriptures regarding the natural integrity [probitas] required as a prerequisite by the Socinians and Arminians. True integrity of mind, which is pleasing to God, and a good purpose arise from the purification of the heart through faith (Acts 15:9) and consequently are subsequent to conversion itself; compare Phil. 2:13; Heb. 11:6; Rom. 14:23. Without such integrity were converted the thief (Luke 23:42), the centurion (Matt. 27:54), Saul (Acts 9:6), and the jailer (Acts 16:29). Even from those who mocked the apostles—that is, as Wolzogen explains, who were of a wicked mind—some were converted (Acts 2:12, 13, 14, 37, 41)." (L.c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 722.) Regarding the abolition of the *terminus a quo* [starting point] and the tendency toward the *terminus ad quem* [end point].

For even the first holy thought and pious will, or desire, is from the Holy Spirit, not from us, 2 Cor. 3:5; Phil. 2:13. But He who began a good work in us, the same must perfect it, Phil. 1:6.

Concerning which, see above § 29 and notes a, g, h, and following. And since we have observed two classes of spiritual acts, it must be confessed that the natural man is inept and dead not only regarding the former, but also regarding the latter class. See blessed Musaeus, l.c. § 38, 39, p. 265, 267.

V.g. that he may approach sacred places where the Word of God is taught, prick up his ears, turn his thoughts to hearing and meditating upon the Word, or take the book of Scripture into his hands, read, and meditate. Such acts we have said above (§ 30) may be called pedagogical or ecclesiastical. In this way it is said that men, before they are converted by the Holy Spirit, can not only hear the Gospel and in some way meditate upon it, but even discourse about it. Decis. Sol. Form. Conc. Art. II. p. 662. Whence also the blessed Musaeus, in his *Ausführl. Erklärung* [Detailed Explanation] Qu. XLIV. p. 344 sqq. up to 397, shows that a simple knowledge or simple apprehension of the bare literal sense of Scripture (yet without saving assent) is rightly referred to pedagogical acts. Cf. what we have said concerning the Perspicuity of Scripture, Proleg. cap. II. § 41. not. e. Vol. I. p. 169.

Of this matter, experience can be a witness, which teaches that even unregenerate men, such as Anabaptists and other fanatics, diligently pore over biblical writings, and indeed with a zeal for learning; although meanwhile, by their obstinacy in error, they resist the Holy Spirit and His operation: these are the words of the blessed Hutter, *Praei. in F. Conc.* Art. II. c. II. Q. III. M. 2. p. m. 167., to which he then refers the zeal or study of God of the Jews, Rom. 10:2; the hunger to hear the Word of the Lord, Amos 8:11 sqq.; the example of Herod, who gladly heard John the Baptist, Mark 6:20; of Sergius the proconsul, Acts 13:7 [18:7], who desired to hear Paul; of the Queen of the Ethiopians, 1 Kings 10:1, who traveled from the innermost ends of her kingdom to Jerusalem that she might hear the wisdom of Solomon, the chief part of which was religion, etc.

2. Semipelagianorum s. Massiliensium, de quibus asserit Augustinus de Praedestin. Sctor. c. 2., quod statuant, ,ex nobis esse fidei coeptum, ex Deo fidei supplementum.‘ ...

Sess. 6. can. 4. sic habet: ,Si quis dixerit, liberum arbitrium a Deo motum et excitatum nihil cooperari assentiendo Deo excitanti atque vocanti, quo ad obtinendam justificationis gratiam se disponat ac praeparet: anathema sit.'· ...

Cui proinde non nuda suasio moralis tribuenda est, sed ob concursum Dei virtus multo nobilior et altior, quam quae alias doctrinae vel orationi, etiamsi maxime idoneae ad persuadendum, tribui potest. Conf. b. Mus. de Conv. (edit. Hall.) Disp. IV. § 56. sq. Quod, cum legi opponitur, importat promissiones de gratia Dei et gratuita remissione peccatorum propter Christum mediatorem ejusque meritum fide apprehensum. Juxta illud Pauli Rom. 3, 20.: Per legem est agnitio peccati, et Rom. 7, 7.: Peccatum non cognovi, nisi per legem; nam ei concupiscenr tiam non novissem, nisi lex dixisset: Non concupisces. Hic autem observanda etiam est vis divina, quam Deus verbo legis, in Scripturis contento, addidit ad assensum supernaturalem, adeoque et agnitionem eorum, quae penes hominem legi disconvenientia occurrunt, in homine producendam. Qua ratione certum est, non raro homines audita de suppliciis gehennae doctrina supernaturaliter affici et ad credendum moveri. Confer, b. Scherzer. Brev. Huelsem. auct. c. IX. Thes. XI. p.

519. Quando enim intellectui hominis, mediante lege, peccatorum foeditas et hinc orta offensa Dei ac reatus damnationis aeternae exhibetur, simul etiam voluntati ipsa formalis ratio, qua ad peccatorum detestationem et dolorem de illis metumque irae divinae ac damnationis moveatur, repraesentatur et sic lex ipsa, virtute divina, operatur in voluntate hominis, mediante cognitione intellectus, etiam displicentiam ac detestationem peccatorum, pavores conscientiae et horrorem quendam judicii, ut sit instar mallei petram conterentis, Jerem. 23, 29. Quo pertinent horrores ex meditatione judicii extremi aut comminationum divinarum de poenis infernalibus nati, quos homines audita doctrina sacra vel inviti patiuntur. Confer, b. Scherz. 1. c. Sunt enim promissiones generales, sub quibus homo de se in individuo recte subsumere et virtute divina ad assensum fidei eliciendum concludere potest (vid. supra cap. III. § 4·), unde evangelium simul ex parte voluntatis (praesertim postquam lex homines de medicina aut mediatore solicitos effecit, aut instar paedagogi terrentis, velut obliqua via, ad Christum perduxit, juxta illud Gal. 3, 24·) desiderium gratiae et mox pleniorem fiduciam excitat; prout antea indicavimus.

Seu afflictio divinitus immissa propter peccata. Qua ratione etiam vulgo concionem legis realem vocant; nec male huc refertur exemplum acolasti Luc. 15, 18. et dietum Esaiae 28, 19.: Vexatio dat intellectum. Confer. Ps. 119, 72. Nimirum et lapsis (seu relapsis) et stantibus crux ad poenitentiam prodest. PAKT. III. CAP. IV.

k) Hoc enim tantum verbo competit.

1) Quatenus videlicet suscitabulum est verbi prius auditi et lecti, sed minus observati, quoad notitiam practicam, vel etiam ad usum mediorum salutis nos instigat aut compellit. ץ § 85. Homo autem per vires suas naturales nihil quicqüam active confert aut conferre potest a ad sui conversionem iritrinsece b inchoandam c aut perficiendam,d seu ad actus spirituales e exercendos; licet quoad externum mediorum f usum actus aliquos intellectus g et voluntatish convenienter exercere possit.

I, 644.)

Absque probitate tali conversi sunt latro Luc. 23,42., centurio Matth. 27,24., Saulus Act. 9, 6., carceris praefectus Act. 16, 21. Etiam ex iis, qui apostolos ridebant, h. e., exponente Wolzogenio, animo improbo erant, quidam conversi sunt Act. 2, 12. 13. 14. 37. 41.“(L.c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 722.) Quoad abolitionem termini a quo et tendentiam ad terminum ad quem.

Nam et prima sancta cogitatio et pium velle, seu desiderium, a Spiritu S. est, non ex nokis, 2 Cor. 3, 5. Phil. 2, 13. Is autem, qui coepit in nobis opus bonum, idem illud perficere debet, Phil. 1, 6.

De quibus vid. supra § 29. et notae a. g. h. et sqq. Cumque duas classes actuum spiritualium observaverimus, fatendum est, non solum ad qbribrem, verum etiam ad posteriorem classem, hominem animalem esse ineptum ac mortuum. Vid. b. Mus. 1. c. § 38. 39. p. 265. 267.

DE REGENERATIONE ET CONVERSIONE. V. g. ut accedat ad loca sacra, ubi verbum Dei docetur, arrigat aures, advertat cogitationes ad verbum audiendum ac meditandum, aut sumat ad manus codicem Scripturae, legat ac meditatur. Quales actus alias paedagogicos aut ecclesiasticos appellari supra diximus § 30. Qua ratione dicuntur homines, antequam per Spiritum Sanctum convertuntur, posse evangelium non solum audire et aliquo modo meditari, verum etiam de eo disserere. Deci. Sol. Form. Cone. Art. II. p. 662. Unde etiam notitiam simplicem seu apprehensionem simplicem nudi sensus literalis Scripturae (citra tamen assensum salutarem) ad actus paedagogicos recte referri, ostendit b. Hutt. Praei, in F. Cone. Art. II. c. II. Q. III. M. 2. p. m. 167., quo deinde refert Judaeorum zelum sive studium Dei, Rom. 10, 2.; famem audiendi^ verbum Domini, Amos 8, 11. sqq.; exemplum Herodis, qui Johannem Baptistam libenter audiebat, Mare. 6, 20.; Sergii proconsulis, Act. 18, 7., qui desi־· deravit audire Paulum; reginae Aethiopum, 1 Reg. 10, 1., quae ah intimis regni sui finibus Hierosolymam profecta est, ut audiret Salomonis sapientiam, cujus praecipua pars erat religio etc.


### On Regeneration and Conversion: To these responds the blessed Joh

To these responds the blessed Joh. Meisner, who in *Comp. Theol.* Disp. X. Th. VIII., having adduced the aforementioned passages from Mark 6:20 and Rom. 10:2, shows that a man can naturally hear, read, and meditate upon the Word of God, and that not without some will or προθυμία [eagerness].

And the blessed Andr. Kunadus in his *Colleg. Theol.* Disp. VIII. thes. 16. writes: We do not deny that an unregenerate man, by his own instinct, can read the sacred letters, hear the Word of God, and in a certain way meditate upon it, and likewise perform other pedagogical acts; but just as the instinct of nature and the instinct of grace differ as diverse principles, so also the end of the one and the other is diverse. For the end of a natural work is the knowledge of a thing as new, wonderful, or delightful; but the instinct of grace produces a desire for salvation.

The blessed Musaeus, intending to declare these things more fully for the benefit of those learning in the schools and to show how and how far those things are to be reckoned among the external or pedagogical acts of conversion—which nevertheless have the Word of God itself and those things which are of the Spirit of God as their object—having brought forward distinctions between the distinct and confused knowledge of spiritual goods, and likewise between acts of the will which are of simple complacency and those which are efficacious, teaches that regarding spiritual goods known only confusedly, the will can naturally have an efficacious act (that is, it can desire and seek them as things to be acquired); but regarding spiritual goods known distinctly (that is, according to their specific and proper nature), the will can have an act only of simple complacency (not an efficacious one); but that spiritual acts of the will must be efficacious, and must tend toward things judged by the spiritual judgment of the intellect, that they are truly given, and in what way they may be obtained. See *Disp. de Convers.* held in the year 1649 and edited at Halle in Saxony, Disp. II. § 38 sq. and *Ausführl. Erklärung* Qu. XLV. p. 401 sqq. PART III. CAP. IV.

§ 36.

And this is what is otherwise said, that man, such as he is by nature, does not have free will in his conversion. Or such as he is of himself, after the fall and left to himself or his own natural powers.

See Aug. Conf. art. XVIII. and F. C. art. II. The sense, however, is that the will of man to be converted, regarding goods that are merely spiritual and known in a particular and distinct way, is not indifferent, neither as to the species nor as to the exercise of the act. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Disp. III. de Convers. (Halle edition). Cf. P. II. c. 2. § 13, placed above. § 37.

That operation of God, however, by which He works conversion in man through the Word of Law and Gospel, is accustomed to be called by the name of grace and is distinguished into prevenient, operating, and cooperating. Not as if it were formally the gratuitous favor of God itself, but because it is His actual gift. See the blessed Musaeus, Disp. IV. de Convers. (Halle edition) § 11 sq. The ancients, especially those who contended with Pelagius, among whom was Augustine, used the name of grace in this doctrine.

Indeed, it is accustomed to be distinguished variously by various authors; just as the terms themselves are multiplied and are accepted in one way or another, yet in such a way that the things which are to be observed here regarding the matter itself can be referred to the members indicated here, as will be evident from what follows. By this name is understood the inspiration of the first holy thought and pious desire from God. And this grace is called prevenient because it is prior to our free consent, or because the will of the man to be converted is thus anticipated. Some add exciting grace, by which the sinner is awakened from the sleep, or rather the death, of sin and the security of the flesh; but this awakening of man seems to be brought about through that very holy thought and pious desire divinely inspired. Whence we also refer the name of preparing grace to the same thing, because that holy thought and desire certainly prepare the mind and will in a certain way to embrace spiritual goods, or to further holy motions, from which conversion may take its increase. Although by others, preparing grace is said to be that by which a man, already anticipated by the Holy Spirit, is further moved so that he may gradually begin to consent to the calling and to struggle out of doubts.

Quenstedtius: "Preparation must be properly distinguished here from the translation itself from the state of wrath into the state of grace. Preparation has its own degrees, and is done successively; but the translation itself from the state of wrath into the state of grace happens in an instant and in a moment, since it is impossible that a subject

some [person] or other, even for a moment, is simultaneously in a state of wrath and in a state of grace, simultaneously under life and under death. For conversion is taken either broadly, in which sense it comprehends all the motions proceeding from the grace of God directed toward conversion, or strictly, insofar as it denotes only that final act, namely, the translation from the state of wrath into the state of grace. Taken in the former way, conversion has its preparatory acts, which occur successively: For first, preventing grace offers the Word and, by means of it, the saving object, and removes the natural incapacity and unfitness regarding spiritual things; then, preparing grace acts through that Word, by restraining repugnance, by affecting the heart with the pulse of the Law, and by explaining the Gospel. Where the not-yet-regenerate man, through the assisting grace of the Holy Spirit, can hear the Word ήδέως [gladly] (Mark 6:20), feel the pulse of the Law and contrition, etc. And the Holy Spirit continues this operation of His through preparing grace until He renders the man capable of receiving that highest good of translation from death and the state of wrath to life and the state of grace. But this very translation from death into life, from the state of wrath into the state of grace, is most properly conversion and is so called, which God alone works in an instant and a moment, as we have said.” (L. c. sect. 1, thes. 22, p. 706 sq.)

The same [author]: “As God is one, so also the grace of God is one, but it is distinguished by reason of degrees and effects, which are various and diverse, whence also, regarding this diversity, the grace of God is considered in one way or another. Hence arose 1. the distinction of grace into preventing and subsequent. Preventing [grace] is that which leads man to the adequate means of conversion, and offers to him, still spiritually dead, the Word, which has in itself the power of converting (Rom. 1:16; Mark 4:27), and removes the natural incapacity and unfitness regarding spiritual things common to all.” (L. c. s. 2, q. 1, p. 719.)

The same [author]: “The grace of God is twofold: one assisting, which acts extrinsically around man; the other indwelling, which enters the very heart of man and dwells there by spiritually changing it. The foundation of the distinction of grace into assisting and indwelling is that common expression, that some things are done by the Holy Spirit, but not with the Holy Spirit, whereas some things are done by and with the Holy Spirit. Assisting grace is said to act extrinsically around man, not because it is occupied around him only by objectively proposing the object and showing in the Word what ought to be done (as Pelagius once spoke), so that the man himself might be able to know the proposed object salvifically or apply himself to this divine grace; but because this grace is occupied only in those things which are required around the man to be converted, so that he may both receive faith and thus, by means of faith, grace may dwell within him... There are various degrees of assisting grace, the first of which is beginning or preventing grace... The second degree is preparing grace (which by some is called subsequent)... The third species is exciting grace... The fourth degree is operating grace.” (L. c. s. 1, th. 24—28, p. 707 sqq.)

Thus they call that operation which immediately follows the beginning of conversion and looks to its continuation; through which it comes about that man, by a certain endeavor, however languid, now tends toward Christ the Mediator and the promises concerning the gratuitous remission of sins for Christ’s sake, and struggles against doubts.

According to others, however, operating grace itself is also referred to the beginning of conversion and coincides in reality with preventing and exciting grace, and is called operating because it works in us without us or without our free consent. Thus is called that operation which assists and comforts or corroborates the intellect, already in some way assenting to the promises of grace, and the will, already trusting in Christ, and thus with the will... PART III. CHAP. IV.

works through the powers received beforehand, however weak they may be. Yet it is called cooperating grace, by which God concurs with the man who is already converted, by preserving the bestowed powers, increasing them, and helping him so that he does not fall away from faith. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *De Conversione*, Disp. V. (Halle edition) § 32, 33.

Quenstedtius: "Cooperating (grace is that) by which God, after conversion has been accomplished, is effective and cooperates with the man who is already spiritually revived for the production of good works and spiritual motions, and causes the man to persist in the work begun. In short: it acts and works as 'operative' in conversion, and as 'cooperative' in those who are converted. Obs.: Insofar as God converts us without us, it is called operative grace; insofar as He makes us, together with ourselves (already instructed with new spiritual powers), persevere in that conversion and in the good that has been begun, it is termed cooperating grace. Distinguish between the grace that acts before conversion, in conversion, and after conversion; the former is called prevenient, preparing, and exciting; the middle is called operative and perfecting; the latter is called cooperating and assisting, and likewise perfecting in the second sense." (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 719.) § 38. However, it is rightly said that man at the beginning of conversion behaves merely passively, although in the progress of conversion, through the new powers already received beforehand, he behaves actively.

Thus the Formula of Concord, Art. II, p. 582: "What Dr. Luther wrote, that man's will in conversion behaves purely passively, is to be accepted rightly and skillfully, namely, with respect to divine grace in kindling new motions, etc." Cf. Solid Declaration, p. 680, 681 And this is what Luther, and with him the Formula of Concord, mean when they deny to the man being converted any natural active power, or effective ability, aptitude, or capacity, but attribute to him a passive capacity—namely, that man can be turned, unlike a log or a stone, toward the good through grace, and truly become free, for which he was created. L. c. p. 662 The same opinion concerning passive capacity (which is present in unregenerate men by nature, although according to the metaphysicians it may be called passive obediential potency, and that new passive powers do not have to be conferred supernaturally at the very moment of conversion to remove natural incapacity and passive unfitness) was diligently taught not only by the blessed M. Chemnitius, L. Hutterus, Joh. Gerhardus, D. Lobechius, G. Mylius, whose passages and words the blessed Musaeus cited in *Der Ausführlichen Erklärung*, p. 454 sqq., but also by the theologians in the Quedlinburg Colloquy, in Hutterus, *Concordia Concors*, c. XLV, p. 1056, 1057; the authors of the *Apologia Formulae Concordiae*, cap. XII, p. 201; the blessed Balthasar Meisner, *Considerationes Theologicae Photinianae*, cap. V, p. 708; the blessed Steuberus, *ad Aug. Conf. art. XVIII*, p. 153; the blessed J. Hannekenius, *Synopsis Theologiae*, § 12, p. 20, and § 29, p. 24; the blessed H. Kromayerus, in *Theologia Aphorismi*, Loc. IX, Aph. IX, p. 256 Thus the blessed Kromayerus, *Theologia Positivo-Polemica*, Artic. IX, Th. II, p. 537: "Man can contribute nothing to his own conversion, but at the beginning of conversion he behaves merely passively; in the progress of divine grace, however, he begins to cooperate, not collaterally, but subordinately." Add p. 539, 541 And *Theologia Aphorismi*, L. V, Aph. X, p. 257 The blessed M. Chemnitius preceded him, who in his *Judicium*

Latin:

Quibus respondet, quod b. Joh. Meisner. in Comp. Theol. Disp. X. Th. VIII. adductis 11. cc. ex Marc. 6, 20. et Rom. 10, 2. ostendit, hominem posse naturaliter verbum Dei audire, legere, meditari, idque non sine voluntate aut προθυμία aliqua.

Et b. Andr. Kunadus in suo Colleg. Theol. Disp. VIII. thes. 16. scribit: Non imus inficias, quin homo non renatus proprio instinctu possit sacras liter as legere, verbum Dei audire et quodammodo meditari, Itemque alia paedagogica praestare; verum sicut instinctus naturae et instinctus gratiae tanquam diversa principia differunt, ita etiam diversus est hujus et illius finis. Nam naturalis operas finis est cognitio rei, tanquam novae, mirabilis aut delectabilis; gratiae vero instinctus parit desiderium salutis.

B. Musaeus, haec in gratiam discentium in scholis uberius declaraturus atque ostensurus, quomodo et quousque actibus conversionis externis seu paedagogicis accenseantur, qui tamen ipsum verbum Dei et ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei, pro objecto habent, allatis distinctionibus inter cognitionem bonorum spiritualium distinctam et confusam et similiter inter actus voluntatis, qui sunt simplicis complacentiae, et qui efficaces sunt, docet, circa bona spiritualia confuse tantum cognita posse voluntatem naturaliter habere actum efficacem (hoc est, posse ea appetere et desiderare, ut acquirenda), circa bona spiritualia autem distincte cognita (id est, secundum rationem suam specificam et propriam) posse voluntatem habere actum tantum simplicis complacentiae (non efficacem); actus autem voluntatis spirituales oportere esse efficaces, ac tendere in res judicio intellectus spirituali dijudicatas, quod revera dentur, et qua ratione possint obtineri. Vid. Disp, de Convers. Anno 1649. hab. et Halae Sax. edit. Disp. II. § 38. sq. et Ausführl. Erklärung Qu. XLV. p. 401. sqq. PART. ΠΙ. CAP. IV.

§ 36.

Atque hoc est, quod alias dicitur, hominem, qualis est per naturam, a non habere in conversione sui liberum, arbitrium.b Seu qualis ex se est, post lapsum et sibi relictus aut suis viribus naturalibus.

Vid. Aug. Conf. art. XVIII. et F. C. art. II. Sensus autem est, quod voluntas hominis convertendi circa bona mere spiritualia in particulari et distincte cognita non sit indifferens, neque quoad speciem, neque quoad exercitium actus. Conf. b. Mus. Disp. III. de Convers. (edit. Hali.) Cf. supra posita P. II. c. 2. § 13. § 37.

Operatio autem illa Dei, qua conversionem in homine per verbum legis et evangelii operatur, gratiae a nomine appellari solet et distinguitur b in praevenientem, c operemtem d et cooperantem.e Non, quasi formaliter sit ipse gratuitus favor Dei, sed quod sit donum ejus actuale. Vid. b. Mus. Disp. IV. de Convers. (edit. Hali.) § 11. sq. Usi autem sunt nomine gratiae in hac doctrina veteres, illi inprimis, qui cum Pelagio certarunt, inter quos Augustinus.

Varie quidem a variis auctoribus hic distingui solet; prout etiam ipsi termini multiplicantur et aliter atque aliter accipiuntur, ita tamen, ut, quae quoad rem ipsam hic observanda sunt, ad membra heic indicata referri queant, ut ex seqq. patebit. Quo nomine intelligitur inspiratio primae cogitationis sanctae et pii desiderii a Deo. Et dicitur gratia haec praeveniens, quod prior sit nostro libero consensu, seu quod ita praeveniatur hominis convertendi arbitrium. Quidam addunt gratiam excitantem, qua homo peccator ex somno aut potius morte peccati et securitate carnis excitatur; verum haec excitatio hominis per ipsam illam cogitationem sanctam et pium desiderium divinitus inspiratum fieri videtur. Unde et gratiae praeparantis nomen huc eodem referimus, quod cogitatio illa et desiderium sanctum ipsa utique praeparant quodammodo mentem et voluntatem ad amplectenda bona spiritualia, sive ad ulteriores motus sanctos,, ex quibus incrementa capiat conversio. Quanquam aliis gratia praeparans dicatur ea, qua homo jam praeventus a Spiritu S. ulterius movetur, ut vocationi paulatim consentire atque e dubitationibus eluctari incipiat.

Quenstedtius: ״Probe hic distinguenda praeparatio ab ipsa ex statu irae in statum gratiae translatione. Praeparatio suos habet gradus, et flt successive; ipsa vero ex statu irae in statum gratiae translatio fit in instanti et in momento, cum impossibile sit, ut subjectum

aliquod vel per momentum sit simul in statu irae et in statu gratiae, simul sub vita et sub morte. Conversio enim vel late sumitur, in quantum scii, comprehendit omnes motus a gratia Dei provenientes ad conversionem directos, vel stricte, quatenus notat ultimum tantum illum actum, videl. translationem ex statu irae in statum gratiae. Illo modo sumpta conversio habet actus suos praeparatorios, qui fiunt successive: Primo enim gratia praeveniens offert verbum et mediante eo objectum salviflcum ac naturalem incapacitatem et inidoneitatem quoad spiritualia tollit; deinde gratia praeparans per illud verbum agit, repugnantiam cohibendo, cor legis pulsu afficiendo, evangelium explicando. Ubi homo nondum renatus per assistentem Spiritus S. gratiam audire verbum ήδέως Marc. 6, 20. sentire legis pulsum et contritionem etc. potest. Hancque suam operationem per gratiam praeparantem Spiritus S. continuat, quoad usque capacem hominem reddat ad recipiendum summum illud bonum translationis ex morte et statu irae ad vitam et statum gratiae. Haec ipsa vero translatio e morte in vitam, e statu irae in statum gratiae propriissime conversio est et dicitur, quam solus Deus operatur in instanti et momento, uti diximus.“ (L. c. sect. 1. thes. 22. f. 706. sq.)

Idem: ,,Uti Deus unus est, ita quoque una est Dei gratia, sed distinguitur ratione graduum et effectuum, qui varii et diversi sunt, unde etiam quoad hanc diversitatem gratia Dei aliter atque aliter consideratur. Hinc orta est 1. ,distinctio gratiae in praevenientem et subsequentem. Praeveniens est, quae hominem ad adaequata conversionis media ducit, eidemque adhuc spiritualiter mortuo verbum, quod potentiam convertendi in se habet, Rom. 1, 16. Marc. 4, 27., offert, naturalem incapacitatem et inidoneitatem quoad spiritualia omnibus communem aufert.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 719.)

Idem: ,,Gratia Dei duplex est: una assistens, quae extrinsecus circa hominem agit; altera inhabitans, quae ipsum hominis cor ingreditur, illudque spiritualiter immutando inhabitat. Distinctionis gratiae in assistentem et inhabitantem fundamentum est communis illa locutio, quod quaedam acti fiat a Sp. S., sed non cum Sp. S., quaedam autem a et cum Sp. S. Dicitur gratia assistens extrinsecus circa hominem agere, non quod tantum objective proponendo objectum et ostendendo! in verbo, quid fleri debeat (ut Pelagius olim locutus est), circa illum versetur, ita ut ipse homo objectum propositum salutariter cognoscere vel seipsum huic gratiae divinae applicare possit; sed ideo, quia haec gratia tantum in iis, quae circa hominem convertendum requiruntur, occupata est, quo et fidem suscipere et sic, mediante fide, gratia ipsi inhabitare possit. . . Gratiae assistentis varii gradus sunt, quorum primus est gratia incipiens seu praeveniens. . . Secundus gradus est gratia praeparans (quae a nonnullis subsequens dicitur). . . Tertia species est gratia excitans. . . Quartus gradus est gratia operans.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 24—28. f. 707. sqq.)

Sic vocant operationem illam, quae initium conversionis proxime sequitur et ad ejus continuationem spectat; per quam iit, ut homo conatu quodam, quamvis languido, jam ad Christum mediatorem ac promissiones de gratuita remissione peccatorum propter Christum tendat et contra dubitationes luctetur.

Juxta alios vero operans gratia ipsa quoque ad initium conversionis refertur et cum gratia praeveniente atque excitante quoad rem coincidit diciturque operans, quod sine nobis aut sine nostro libero consensu in nobis operetur. Ita appellatur operatio illa, quae intellectum promissionibus gratiae jam quodammodo assentientem et voluntatem in Christo confidentem adjuvat et confortat seu corroborat adeoque cum voluntate, jam PART. III. CAP. IV.

per acceptas ante, utut debiles, vires concurrente operatur. Aliis tamen cooperans gratia dicitur, qua Deus cum homine jam converso concurrit, vires collatas conservando, augendo et, ne deficiat a fide, adjuvando. Conf. b. Mus. de Conv. Disp. V. (edit. Hali.) § 32.

33. Quenstedtius: ״Cooperans (gratia est), qua Deus post peractam conversionem efficax est et homini jam spiritualiter redivivo cooperatur ad productionem bonorum operum et motuum spiritualium, facitque, ut homo in coepto opere persistat. Paucis: operans in conversione, cooperans in conversis agit et operatur. Obs.: Quatenus nos Deus sine nobis convertit, gratia operans dicitur; quatenus nos cum nobis (jam novis viribus spiritualibus instructis) in illa conversione et coepto bono perseverare facit, gratia cooperans nuncupatur. Dist. inter gratiam, quae agit ante conversionem, in conversione et post conversionem; ista praeveniens, praeparans et excitans, illa operans et perficiens, haec cooperans et adjuvans, itemque perficiens in secunda significatione dicitur.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 719.) § 38. Homo autem in initio conversionis mere passive a se habere recte dicitur, licet in progressu conversionis, per acceptas jam ante novas vires, active b se habeat.

Sic F. C. art. II. p. m. 582.: Quod D. Lutherus scripsit, hominis voluntatem in conversione pure passiv^ sese höhere, id recte et dextre est accipiendum, videlicet respectu divinae gratiae in accendendis novis motibus etc. Conf. Sol. Deci. p. 680. 681 Atque hoc est, quod Lutherus, et cum eo Formula Concord. homini convertendo naturalem vim activam, aut efficacem habilitatem, aptitudinem aut capacitatem denegant, tribuunt autem capacitatem passivam, quod scilicet verti potest homo, secus atque truncus aut lapis, ad bonum per gratiam et fieri revera liber, ad quod creatus est. L. c. p. 662 Eandem sententiam de capacitate passiva (quae in hominibus irregenitis per naturam adsit, licet juxta metaphysicos potentia obedientialis passiva appellari possit, quodque non demum in conversione novae vires passivae ad tollendam naturalem incapadtatem et inidoneitatem passivam supernatural iter conferri debeant) diligenter tradiderunt non solum bb. M. Chemnitius, L. Hutterus, Joh. Gerhardus, D. Lobechius, G. Mylius, quorum loca et verba adduxit b. Mus. in der Ausführlichen Erklärung p. 454. sqq., verum etiam theologi in colloq. Quedlinburg, apud Hutterum in Cone. Cone. c. XLV. p. m. 1056. 1057., auctores Apologiae Form. Cone. cap. XII. p. 201., b. Balthas. Meisnems Consid. Theol. Phot. cap. V. p. 708., b. Steuberus ad Aug. Conf. art. XVIII. p. 153., b. J. Hannekenius Synops. Theol. § 12v p. ,20. et § 29. p. 24., b. H. Kromayerus in Theol. Aph. Loc. IX. Aph. IX. p. 256 Ita b. Kromayerus Theol. Pos.Pol. Artic. IX. Th. II. p. 537.: Homo ad sui conversionem nihil potest conferre, sed in conversionis initic se mere habet passive; in progressu vero gratiae divinae incipit cooperari, non collateraliter, sed suborainate. Adde p. 539. 541 Et Theol. Aph. L. V. Aph. X. p. 257 Praeivit autem eum b. M. Chemnitius, qui in Judicio


### On Regeneration and Conversion: Regarding] the controversies of his time (which we published to the public in…

[Regarding] the controversies of his time (which we published to the public in the year 1676), he writes in ch. V, p. 35, 36: "That subject (he indicates the will as the subject of conversion) receives the gifts and operations of the Holy Spirit in such a way that the will, which has begun to be renewed, after the first impulse and motion of the Spirit is not idle, but as a new creature, to whom the Holy Spirit has given that it should begin to act by desiring, striving, struggling, and assenting." And a little later: "When the first beginnings of conversion are given to us by the Holy Spirit, there immediately arises a struggle of the flesh and the spirit, which it is manifest does not occur without the motion of our will. And this συνεργία [synergy] of the will—not of the old [will], but of that which has begun to be renewed—as those beginnings grow and increase in great infirmity, [occurs] not without the motion of our will. And thus it is rightly said: With grace preceding, and the will accompanying. However, this pious συνεργία always depends on the grace of God; if it is deserted by this, the gifts also cease and are lost." And in *Locis Communibus* on Free Will, ch. VII, p. 200: "What is handed down concerning preventing, preparing, and operating grace has this meaning: that our parts are not prior in conversion, but that God prevents us through the Word and divine inspiration, moving and impelling the will. But after this motion of the will, which is done divinely, the human will does not behave purely passively, but, moved and aided by the Holy Spirit, it does not resist, but assents and becomes a συνεργός [co-worker] of God." Calovius: "What the Formula of Concord designates by the work of renewal begun in us, others call the first conversion; nor is there any doubt that it is called 'begun' for this reason: because it must be continued throughout the whole life, since in this infirmity renewal is only begun, to be finally consummated in the other life. New powers are said to be begun in us because they must be perfected from time to time. However, it is not denied that only after conversion is man a συνεργός [co-worker], nor is it asserted that before conversion itself man is a συνεργός and cooperates toward his own conversion. The F.C. teaches such a thing nowhere, just as the new synergists contend." (*System*, th. T. X, 114.) Ad. Osiander: "Hornejus distinguishes between the first beginning of conversion and its progress... I answer: 1. That man is still dead not only at the beginning of conversion, but also in its progress." (*Colleg. th.* IV, 333.) See the same author above, p. 205 sq. Calovius: "Although it is beyond controversy that man and the human will are required for conversion, yet it does not concur as an efficient or cooperating cause, but as the matter and subject in which the Holy Spirit works. Since the human will is to be converted by the Holy Spirit, and thus behaves here purely passively and works nothing toward its own conversion—whether in the beginning, or in the middle, or in the consummation of conversion itself, which is to be attributed solely and entirely to divine grace—no συνεργεία [synergy] of the human will, by whatever name it may come, is admitted in the act of conversion." (*Socinism. profligat*, p. 673.) Quenstedtius: "Latermann indeed pretends (disput. on predest. th. 35) that man cooperates with divine grace in conversion through powers granted by the Lord, and that the will, prepared by God, submits itself. But he says nothing that the Jesuits, Bellarmine, Gregor de Valentia, Becanus, Tanner, etc., did not also say, who nevertheless, by the great consensus of theologians, were accused of Pelagianism or Semi-Pelagianism; nothing that the synergists did not assert. For they also presupposed the benefit of grace, and protested that they were presupposing a will prepared by the Lord, and that it freely turns itself to God—asserting not that it performs this by its own powers, but that by the virtue of grace divinely conferred it so converts itself that it could also not convert itself. Latermann says ibid. th. 42: 'If the conversion of man' (he speaks without...)" PART III. CHAPTER IV.
