(regarding the doubt about the first act of conversion), depends only on the part of God, all exhortations to conversion would be in vain.’ But this is the very argument of the Pelagians, Semi-Pelagians, Socinians, Papists, and Synergists, by which they confirm the concurrence of our powers with the assistance of grace. The assertions of our theologians are well known: that God, on His part, provides not only that we can will, but also that we actually do will; that the conversion of man is in no way free in such a way that it is in his power to will to convert himself; that not only the powers, but the act of the first conversion itself is from God as the author, without the cooperation of man. The cooperation of man follows the first act of conversion. It belongs to the converted man to cooperate, not to the man being converted. Latermann contradicts the Formula of Concord; see it in the Epitome, Art. 2, affirmative thesis 2, pages 579, 583, and in the Solid Declaration, page 681, in which places it expressly removes the cooperation of the human will from the act of conversion itself and assigns it only to the converted man; compare page 677. See the Judgment of Strasbourg in the case of Latermann, s. 1. c. 2. Dr. Huelsemann rightly warns in the *Consideranda* presented to the theological faculty of Leipzig, published in the *Censures of Orthodox Theologians* at Danzig, A.D. 1648, pp. 99–100: ‘It is false and Pelagian that in a man already aroused and moved by prevenient grace, a natural indifference to both opposites remains intact, i.e., to will to be converted and not to will to be converted. Such,’ he says, ‘indifference is found in no man: not in the unregenerate, because he is in no way free from an inclination toward the worse extreme; not in the regenerate and sanctified, who is not as free here to choose the good as he is free and prone to pursue evil, Rom. 7.’ Indifference signifies an equal latitude for the freedom of power, such as exists neither in the one being converted nor in the one converted. The Theological Faculty of Jena rightly states in the aforementioned Censures, p. 132: ‘If you say,’ it says, ‘that a man converts himself through the powers of grace, not even this is a sufficiently convenient expression. For because to convert in this sense denotes nothing other than to instruct with new powers, which is done by illuminating the mind and bending the will, it cannot be said that a man converts himself through powers already received. For those powers are not given first so that afterward a man may be converted by them, but the donation of spiritual powers is, in reality, the conversion itself.’ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 726. sq.) Calovius: "Drejerus: 'I do not hold that any sensible person would say that a man is entirely converted to God before he repents, wills the good, and believes; thus, the willing of the good and faith precede the *ultimum complementum* [final completion] of conversion, at least in nature, if not in time; and wherefore, if willing and believing are actions, through which it can rightly be said of man that he does something, then it follows correctly that man does something at the end of his conversion and to that extent does not behave merely passively.' And subsequently: 'Thus, man is not merely a *subjectum patiens* [passive subject] in his conversion, but does something good through the grace of God before he is fully converted.' But these are paradoxes, provided that the discussion here is concerning primary conversion and regeneration. To will the spiritual good of which he speaks, or the will for the good of faith itself—that is, the offspring [before] the mother, since faith is the mother of the good will—and furthermore to place the will for the good, as well as justifying faith, before regeneration and conversion in the order of nature, and to deny that man behaves merely passively, [and to claim] that man does something good (it must again be warned that the matter concerns spiritual good) before he is fully converted, when nevertheless these have hitherto been held as *κυρίαι δόξαι* [authoritative doctrines] in our schools and churches: that faith is the mother of the good will, as is taught in the Augsburg Confession, Art. 19, from Ambrose; that faith is conferred through regeneration, and that one does not believe unless one is reborn and converted, and not, however, while one is being reborn and still to be converted; [and] that in conversion man behaves merely passively and can do nothing good before he is converted, since without faith it is impossible to please God and whatever is not of faith is sin."

Osiander: "Drejer says that a man not yet converted, having been vivified by the new powers of prevenient grace, finally gives full consent and completes his own conversion. But how can he be vivified who is still to be converted, and not yet converted, when conversion itself, as it is completed by perfecting grace, is precisely the vivification of the spiritually dead? . . . How can this paradox stand, when between the dead and the vivified, the converted and the unconverted, the unbeliever and the believer, there is no middle ground, by virtue of John 20:27? Prevenient grace does not grant man the power of acting or cooperating in conversion, but a passive aptitude, by which, the resistance of the corrupt nature having been repressed, he becomes capable of further grace, until conversion is completed. For toward every motion of divine grace, man conducts himself passively; from which it is clear that the recipient of this motion cannot cooperate by the power of that motion to obtain another, nor does he cooperate, but after that motion he receives another, and conducts himself passively toward the third motion, and toward all individual motions preceding faith, until conversion is completed. Drejer is absurd when he attributes deliberation to a man placed under assisting divine grace; for deliberation concerning spiritual matters follows only after conversion; he does not yet have that liberty by which he could deliberate concerning spiritual matters; for he only possesses that liberty when he has obtained the spirit of liberty, when he has spiritual life. Nor does deliberation intervene in that succession, even though there was a struggle of flesh and spirit—not indeed of the indwelling spirit, but of the spirit knocking—because of that." (L. c. p. 337.)

The Theological Faculty of Strasbourg: "Latermann says things that are ambiguous and intricate. For what is that power of man, in whose hands it resides, through grace, to perform or not to perform those things which are necessary for conversion? In which it is situated to will to be converted and to not will to be converted? as M. Latermann speaks. He will not say that it is the very powers and faculty granted by the Holy Spirit. For what kind of assertion would this be: 'It resides in the new powers and granted faculty to perform or not to perform the things necessary for conversion, to will to be converted and to not will to be converted'? Are those new powers indifferent to conversion or aversion, to willing and not willing? There will therefore be some power in man existing before the powers and faculty granted by the Holy Spirit, in which, with the aid of supervening grace and granted powers, the things necessary for conversion are performed, by which the willing of conversion is perfected. And this is Pelagianism and Synergism itself." (Responsum, a. 1646, sent to the Königsberg ministry and published in an amended form in 1650. See Calovius, System. Vol. X, p. 50.)

Latin:

\ DE REGENERATIONE ET CONVERSIONE. de Controversiis sui temporis (quod Anno sup. 1676. luci publicae reddidimus) cap. V. p. m. 35. 36. scribit: Ita mbjectum illud (voluntatem conversionis subjectum indicat) recipit dona et operationes Spiritus Sancti, ut voluntas, quae coepit renovari, post primum impulsum et motum Spiritus non sit otiosa, sed tanquam nova creatura, cui Spiritus Sanctus dedit, ut incipiat operari desiderando, conando, luctando, assentiendo. Et paulo post: Cum prima initia conversionis per Spiritum Sanctum nobis donantur, statim oritur lucta camis et spiritus, quam manifestum est fieri non sine motu voluntatis nostrae. Et haec συνεργία voluntatis, non veteris, sed quae coepit renovari, ei initia illa in magna infirmitate crescunt et augenturf non sine motu nostrae voluntatis. Et ita recte dicitur: Praeeunte gratia, comitante voluntate. Pia autem συνεργία semper pendet a gratia Dei; a qua si deseratur, cessant et amittuntur etiam dona. Et in LL. CC. de Lib. Arb. cap. VII. p. m. 200.: Quae de gratia praeveniente, praeparante et operante traduntur, habent hunc sensum, quod non nostrae partes priores sint in conversione, sed quod Deus per verbum $t afflatum divinum nos praeveniat movens et impellens voluntatem. Post hunc autem motum voluntatis divinitus factum voluntas humana non habet se pure passive, ,sed mota et adjuta a Spiritu Sancto non repugnat, sed assentitur et fit σύνεργας Dei. Calovius: ,,Quod Formula Concordiae opere renovationis in nobis inchoato designat, id alii conversionem primam appellant, neque dubium est, ideo inchoatam dici, quia per totam vitam continuari debet, siquidem in hac infirmitate tantum inchoetur renovatio, in altera vita demum consummanda. Novae vires in nobis inchoari dicuntur, quia illae subinde perficiendae sunt. Non negatur autem, post conversionem demum hominem esse σννεργον, aut asseritur, ante ipsam conversionem hominem συνεργόν esse et cooperari ad sui ipsius conversionem. Tale quid nuspiam docet F. C., quemadmodum synergistae novi contendunt.“ (System, th. T. X, 114.) Ad. Osiander: ״Hornejus distinguit inter primum initium conversionis et ejus progressum. .. Respondeo: 1. Hominem non tantum in initio conversionis, sed etiam in progressu adhuc esse mortuum.“ (Colleg. th. IV, 333.) Vid. idem supra p. 205. sq. Calovius: ״Quamquam extra controversiam sit, hominem et voluntatem humanam requiri ad conversionem, non concurrit tamen ut causa efficiens vel cooperans, sed ut materia et subjectum, in quo operatur Sp. S. Quandoquidem voluntas humana a Sp. S. convertenda sit, adeoque pure passive hic se habeat nec quicquam operetur ad sui conversionem, sive in principio, sive in medio, sive consummatione ipsius conversionis, quae unice et in solidum gratiae divinae accepta ferenda est, nulla admissa voluntatis humanae, quocunque ea nomine veniat, συνεργεία in actu conversionis.“ (Socinism. profligat, p. 673.) Quenstedtius: ״Praetendit quidem Latermannus disput. de praedest. th. 35., hominem cooperari gratiae divinae in conversione per vires a Domino concessas, voluntatemque a Deo praeparatam se supponere. Ast nihil dicit, quod non etiam Jesuitae, Bellarminus, Gregor, de Valentia, Becanus, Tannerus etc. dixerunt, qui tamen magno theologorum consensu pelagianismi aut semipelagianismi rei acti sunt; nihil, quod non synergistae asseruerunt. Nam et illi beneficium gratiae supposuerunt, et protestati sunt, se supponere voluntatem a Domino praeparatam, eamque libere se ad Deum convertere, asserere, non quod propriis id praestet viribus, sed quod virtute gratiae divinitus collatae ita, se convertat, ut possit se etiam non convertere. Dicit Latermannus ibid. th. 42.: ,Si conversio hominis‘ (loquitur sine PART. III. CAP. IV. dubio de primo conversionis actu),a parte Dei tantum pendet, omnes adhortationes ad conversionem fore frustraneas.‘ Sed hoc est argumentum ipsorum Pelagianorum, semipelagianorum, Socinianorum, pontificiorum et synergistarum, quo concursum nostrarum virium cum adjutorio gratiae confirmant. Notae sunt nostrorum theologorum assertiones: Deum ex parte sua non tantum praestare, ut possimus velle, sed etiam ut actu velimus, nullo modo conversionem hominis eo modo liberam esse, ut in ejus potestate sit, velle se convertere; non vires tantum, sed actum conversionis primae etiam a Deo auctore sine hominis cooperatione esse. Cooperationem hominis sequi primum conversionis actum. Hominis conversi esse cooperari, non hominis convertendi. Contrariatur Latermannus Formulae Concordiae; vide eam in Epitome, Art. 2. thes. afflrm. 2. pag. 579. 583. et in Solida Declarat, pag. 681., in quibus locis cooperationem voluntatis humanae diserte removet ab ipso conversionis actu et converso duntaxat assignat, confer pag. 677. Vide Judicium Argentorat. in causa Latermanni s. 1. c. 2. Bene monet D. Huelsemannus in Considerandis collegio theologico Lipsiensi exhibitis, in Censuris theologor. orthodoxorum Dantisci A^ 1648. editis, p. 99. 100.: ,Falsura et Pelagianum esse, quod in homine per gratiam praevenientem jam excitato et moto naturalis indifferentia ad utrumque oppositorum integra maneat, h. e., velle converti et non velle converti: Talis‘, inquit, ,indifferentia in nullo homine reperitur, non irregenito, quia ille nulla ratione liber est ab inclinatione in extremum deterius; non in regenito et sanctificato, qui hic tam liber non est ad eligendum bonum, quam liber et expeditus ad sectandum malum, Rom. 7.‘ Indifferentia significat aequalem latitudinem ad libertatem potestatis, qualis neque in convertendo, neque in converso existit. Recte Facultas theologica Jenensis in Censuris jam cit. p. 132.: ,Si dicas‘, inquit, ,110minem convertere se per vires gratiae, nec sic satis commoda est locutio. Nam quia convertere hoc significatu nihil aliud notat, quam novis viribus instruere, quod fit illuminando mentem et flectendo voluntatem, dici non potest, hominem convertere se per vires jam acceptas. Neque enim vires illae prius donantur, ut postea per eas homo convertatur, sed virium spiritualium donatio secundum rem est ipsa conversio.“‘ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 726. sq.) Calovius: ,,Drejerus: ,Ich halte nicht dafür, dass ein Verständiger sagen werde, ein Mensch sei ganz zu Gott bekehret, ehe er Busse thut, das Gute will und gläubet; so gehet demnach das Wollen des Guten und der Glaube dem ultimo complemento der Bekehrung vorher, saltem natura, si non tempore, und wo derowegen Wollen und Gläuben actiones sein, dadurch recht kann gesaget werden vom Menschen, er thue etwas, so folget richtig, dass der Mensch am Ende seiner Bekehrung etwas thue und so weit sich nicht mere passive habe.‘ Et postmodum: ,So ist der Mensch nicht blos subjectum patiens in seiner Bekehrung, sondern thut was Guts durch die Gnade Gottes, ehe er völlig bekehret ist.‘ Sed haec paradoxa sunt, siquidem de prima conversione ac regeneratione hic sermo sit. Velle bonum spirituale, de quo loquitur, vel voluntatem boni fidei ipsi, hoc est, foetum matri, siquidem fides bonae voluntatis genetrix sit, ac porro voluntatem boni, ut et fidem justificantem regenerationi acconversionipraepomi ordine naturae, hominemque se habere mere passive negat, hominem boni aliquid agere (de spirituali bono, quod iterum monendum, res est), antequam plene convertatur, quum tamen hactenus κ,νρίαι δόξαι habitae sint in scholis et ecclesiis nostris, fldem bonae voluntatis genetricem esse, uti in Aug. Confess. Art. 19. ex Ambrosio docetur: per regenerationem conferri fldem, nec credere, nisi renatum et conversum, non autem regenerandum et adhuc convertendum, in conversione hominem se mere passive habere, nec quicquam boni facere posse, priusquam convertatur, cum sine fide impossibile sit Deo placere et peccatum sit, quicquid non est ex fide.“

Ad. Osiander: ,,Dicit Drejerus, hominem nondum conversum per novas vires gratiae praevenientis vivificatum verbo divino demum plane consentire et conversionem suam absolvere. At qui potest esse viviflcatus, qui adhuc est convertendus, non conversus, cum ipsa conversio, prout a gratia perficiente absolvitur, sit demum spiritualiter mortui vivificatio? . . . Qui hoc stet paradoxum, cum inter mortuum et viviflcatum, conversum et inconversum, incredulum et credentem non detur medium, vi Joh. 20, 27. Gratia praeveniens non tribuit homini vim agendi vel cooperandi in conversione, sed aptitudinem passivam, qua, repressa repugnantia naturae corruptae, jam ulterioris gratiae capax fiat, donec conversio absolvatur. Ad quemlibet enim motum gratiae divinae homo sese habet passive; ex quo patet, quod recipiens hunc motum non possit cooperari vi illius ad alium consequendum, neque cooperetur, sed post illum alium motum recipiat, et sese ad tertium motum habeat passive omnesque singulos antecedentes fidei, quousque conversio non est absoluta. Drejerus absurdus est, cum homini sub gratia divina assistente constituto tribuit deliberationem; nam deliberatio de rebus spiritualibus sequitur demum conversionem, nondum libertatem illam habet, qua de rebüs spiritualibus possit deliberare; tum demum enim illam libertatem habet, cum spiritum libertatis consecutus est, cum vitam spiritualem habet. Neque in ista successione, utut lucta fuit carnis et spiritus, non quidem inhabitantis, tamen pulsantis, propterea deliberatio intercedit.“ (L. c. p. 337.)

Argentoratensis Facultas Theologica: ,,Latermannus dicit, quae ambigua sunt et intricata. Quae enim est illa potestas hominis, penes quam residet, per gratiam ea, quae ad conversionem necessaria sunt, praestare vel non praestare? In qua situm est velle se convertere et nolle se convertere? ut loquitur M. Latermannus. Non dicet, esse ipsas vires et facultatem a Sp. S. donatam. Quae enim haec esset asseveratio: Penes novas vires et facultatem donatam residet, ad conversionem necessaria praestare vel non praestare, velle se convertere et nolle se convertere l Suntne illae novae vires indifferentes ad conversionem vel aversionem, ad velle et nolle? Erit igitur potestas aliqua in homine ante vires et facultatem a Sp. S. donatam existens, in qua adjumento gratiae supervenientis et donatarum virium praestantur necessaria ad conversionem, a qua perficitur velle conversionis. Atque hoc est ipse pelagianismus et Synergismus.“ (Responsum, a. 1646. Regiomontano ministerio missum et a. 1650. emendatius divulgat. Vid. Calovii System. Tom. X. p. 50.)


### On Regeneration and Conversion: The same: "The determination of our will in the first act of conversion has…

The same: "The determination of our will in the first act of conversion has always been ascribed by the orthodox not to the power and cooperation of man, but to the Holy Spirit working through the Word upon the will, which conducts itself passively. Yet that determination is not one of necessity and irresistible power, although, given the divine order, it is infallible. For God has bound Himself by most certain and most holy promises that He Himself wills to determine to conversion the man who is placed in the workshop of the Holy Spirit and who offers no malicious resistance to the means of salvation. Therefore, infallibly, although not by the force of an irresistible virtue, there follows in that τάξει [order] the very determination, if we may so speak, that is conversive." (L. c. p. 54.)

The Theological Faculty of Jena: "That willing of the good which precedes conversion and is designated by the name of pious desire is not a deliberate act, but, when the Holy Spirit inspires a pious thought, it is excited by Him in the will suddenly, and without us praying for any such thing, as the scholastic Doctors also commonly teach. Hence it is said less appropriately that it is in man's power to will to be converted, since no act of the will, unless it be deliberate, can properly be said to be in man's power." (Judicium, July 14, 1646, transmitted. See Calovius, System. Vol. X, 62.)

Calovius: "Latermannus says: 'If men, through grace, will [to be converted], they can be converted by the same,' th. 33. And 55: 'Man can emerge from the mire of vices by the aid of the grace of God, if he wills' . . . an *epikrisis* (critical remark). We say: if by 'willing' the very faculty of willing is denoted, it is certain that the Holy Spirit works in it in such a way that He does not impose necessity upon it, which is what the Calvinists do; and our will is required as a *passive* subject, not an *active* one, but rather *inactive* and *useless*. 'He cannot will his own conversion,' the great theologian Dr. Gesner writes excellently, disp. 4. th. 9. in the *Formula of Concord*, Art. 2. He speaks here of 'willing through grace,' for thus in th. 33 he attributes this 'willing' not to the powers of nature, but to the virtue of grace. If by this he denotes the spiritual act of willing concerning a spiritual object, such as conversion is, that must be understood of a man already regenerate in the state of grace, in whom God has worked this willing. Augustine, *lib. de spiritu et litera* c. 34: 'Indeed, God works in man even the very willing to believe, and in all things His mercy prevents us.' Therefore, just as I do not say, 'Lazarus, having been brought to life, if he wills through the power of Christ, can be brought to life by the same,' since he is already alive, so I do not say: 'Man, if he wills, can be converted through grace,' since he who thus wills through grace is already converted. Rom. 7:22; Phil. 2." (System. X, 68. sq.)

Ad. Osiander: "Hildebrandus concludes, asking: Whence comes the determination to this, that man wills to be converted, not by a simple complacency, but effectively? For if you say that grace is determined by the will, there is a danger that we might assign to free will powers denied by our own. He replies: It seems it should not be said that the will, whose *proper* duty it is to will, is determined by grace; since otherwise the indifference in acting would seem to be destroyed. For whatever is determined from elsewhere, in such a way that it cannot not act in what it does, cannot be called free; but man is freely converted, in such a way that he could also have not been converted. Therefore, just as in the general concurrence of God with secondary causes the determination is from the secondary cause, so in the special concurrence of grace, the man who is converted determines grace, not grace the man. But this is peculiar: that while man determines that general concurrence by powers inherent in nature, he determines this special concurrence by powers not connate—which we admit are none in conversion—but truly conferred by grace itself. The will, therefore, determines itself to the end that it may actually (not) be converted, yet not from itself, most freely; by which very thing the freedom of the will is saved; but no powers are granted to the will. . . I reply: It is not to be conceded: If the will is determined by grace, the necessity of conversion seems to be asserted; it will have to be said that man is not freely converted; indifference in acting is removed. Nor does the first follow, because the determination of the will made by grace is one thing, and that made by grace according to the power of omnipotence and an irresistible mode of acting is another; the former has no necessity as a companion, except that which is by hypothesis; for man, determined by grace, still retains the power of resisting; the latter, however, draws necessity after it, which determination we nevertheless reject in the Calvinists. The second is consequently absurd; for if man is freely converted according to the sense of Hildebrandus, free will will be established in spiritual matters before conversion, because a free willing of conversion is attributed to it. This indeed is certain: that man is willing to be converted, and in some way also freely, yet not positively, but privatively, insofar as he can by nature contumaciously resist grace and hinder it, so that he is not converted; but the aforementioned author does not intend this mode." (L. c. p. 336. sq. 339.)

The same: "Man does not concur in his own conversion, repentance, and vivification; neither through the powers of free will, which is the position of the Papists, as if preventing grace were to excite native powers, which might then partially concur; nor through the exercise of preventing grace, which is the opinion of Horneius and his accomplices. Spiritual death suppresses both; for he who is dead cannot concur in his own vivification through his own powers; he who possesses at least preventing grace does not yet have infused life, but life that is to be infused and awaited; therefore, he can exercise no vital operations, even by the power of preventing grace, which [merely prepares] the subject."

does it prepare passively? Nay, by the very fact that preventing grace is described under the aspect of "aid," it is assumed by them that there is something in nature to which preventing grace brings assistance, and thus this opinion agrees with the Papists. — It is absurdly said that some life precedes conversion, or that spiritual vivification is obtained in a man not yet converted; for Christ lives in us through faith, Gal. 2:20, but faith is the terminus of conversion; neither life nor vivification can yet have a place; indeed, since conversion itself is nothing other than spiritual vivification and resuscitation, it is most absurdly asserted that a man not yet finished with conversion is already vivified; [that] a man, as Drejer says, "concurs with spiritual deliberations, acts of the mind and will, toward repentance and conversion." (Colleg. th. P. IV. p. 322. sq.)

Quenstedtius: "A man is said to convert himself, just as a ship is said to turn itself when it is moved by the sailor or the wind, just as the statue of Memnon is said to have spoken when it was touched by the ray of the sun." (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 725.)

Formula of Concord: "But as regards the phrases and sayings of Chrysostom and Basil: 'God draws, but He draws the willing'; 'Only be willing, and God anticipates you'; likewise those of the Scholastics and Papists: 'The will of man in conversion is not idle, but does something,' etc., because those sayings were introduced to confirm natural free will in the conversion of man, against the doctrine of the grace of God: it is manifest from the proposed declaration that they are not analogous to the form of sound words, but conflict with it, and therefore, when the subject is conversion to God, they are deservedly to be avoided. . . For since the youth in the schools have been vehemently disturbed by that doctrine concerning the three efficient causes concurring in the conversion of an unregenerate man, while it was disputed how they (namely, the Word preached and heard, the Holy Spirit, and the will of man) concur: we wish to repeat again from the explanation set forth above, that conversion to God is the work of the Holy Spirit alone, who alone is that excellent craftsman effecting these things in us; meanwhile, however, He uses the preaching and hearing of His holy Word (as His ordinary and legitimate means or instrument). But the intellect and will of a man not yet regenerate are only the subject to be converted, for they are the intellect and will of a man spiritually dead, in which man the Holy Spirit works conversion and renewal, to which work the will of the man being converted contributes nothing, but suffers God to work in it, until he is regenerated. But afterwards, in other subsequent good works, he cooperates with the Holy Spirit, doing those things which are pleasing to God, in the manner which has already been sufficiently declared by us in this writing." (Artic. 2. Solid. declar. p. 608. sq. 610.)

Musaeus: "Do the Lutherans maintain that the cause of the distinction, why some are converted and others are not, lies solely with man? — Wendelin (lib. 1. Christian. th. c. 14. th. 7. expl. n. 10.) writes that the Lutherans indeed teach that a man in his first conversion behaves himself merely passively, i.e., that he contributes nothing of his own toward his first conversion by way of an active principle; meanwhile, they teach that the cause of the distinction, why some are converted and others are not, lies solely with man. Afterwards, having cited certain words of Eccard, he adds: 'Is this not to concur actively toward one's own conversion? What could be said more evidently for the synergy of an unregenerate man?' And after some intervening remarks: 'What could Pelagius have said more impiously?' But Wendelin proposes the mind of our people less candidly, and deliberately involves it in ambiguous language, so that he may have something to cavil at. For first, our people are not accustomed to say that the cause of the distinction, why some are converted and others are not, lies solely with man; but they all say with one mouth that the cause why those who are converted are converted is not with man, but solely with God; but that the cause why those who persevere in impiety are not converted is not with God, but solely with man." (Colleg. controversiar. p. 390.)

Latin:

Eadem: ,,Semper determinatio voluntatis nostrae in primo conversionis actu non potestati et cooperationi hominis, sed Spiritui S. per verbum in voluntatem passive se habentem operanti ab orthodoxis adscripta fuit. Neque tamen illa determinatio necessitatis est et irresistibilis potentiae, licet posito ordine divino infallibilis sit. Nimirum promissionibus certissimis sanctissimisque sese obstrinxit Deus, quod hominem in officina Sp. S. positum et mediis salutis nullam malitiosam resistentiam opponentem determinare ipse ad conversionem velit. Igitur infallibiliter, quanquam non ex vi irresistibilis virtutis, sequitur in illa τάξει ipsa determinatio, ut sic dicamus, conversiva.u (L. c. p. 54.)

Facultas Th. Jenensis: ,, Velle illud bonum, quod conversionem praecedit et pii desiderii nomine indigitatur, non est actus deliberatus, sed, cum Sp. Sanctus piam cogitationem inspirat, excitatur illud ab eodem in voluntate subito, nobisque nihil tale supplicantibus, ut communiter etiam Dd. scholastici docent. Hinc minus commode dicitur, in hominis potestate est velle se convertere, cum nullus actus voluntatis, nisi deliberatus sit, proprie in hominis potestate esse dicatur.“ (Judicium d. 14. Jul. 1646. transmiss. Vid. Calovii System. T. X, 62.)

Calovius: ,,Latermannus dicit: ,Homines si per gratiam volunt, per eandem possunt converti4, th. 33. et 55.: ,Hominem gratiae Dei 15 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III. PART. III. CAP. IV. auxilio, si velit, emergere posse e luto vitiorum‘ . . . επίκμισις. Dicimus, si per velle notetur ipsa facultas volendi, certum est, in ea sic operari Spiritum S., ut ei necessitatem non imponat, quod volunt Calviniani, et requiritur nostra voluntas ut subjectum πα&ητικον, non ενεργητικον, sed αεργον καϊ άχρηστον. ,Non potest velle sui conversionem‘, praeclare scribit magnus theologus Du. D. Gesnerus, disp. 4. th. 9. in Form. Concord. Art. 2. Loquitur hic de velle per gratiam, sic enim th. 33. ,non naturae viribus, sed virtuti gratiae velle‘ hoc attribuit. Quo si notet actum spiritualem volendi circa objectum spirituale, quale est conversio, id intelligendum est de homine jam regenito in statu gratiae, in quo Deus operatus est hoc velle. Augustinus lib. de spiritu et litera c. 34.: ,Profecto et ipsum velle credere Deus operatur in homine, et in omnibus misericordia ejus praevenit nos.‘ Quare, sicut non dico, Lazarus vivificatus, si per potentiam Christi velit, per eandem potest vivificari, cum jam vivus sit, sic non dico: Homo, si velit, per gratiam potest converti, cum jam ille conversus sit, qui sic vult per gratiam. Rom. 7, 22. Phil. 2.“ (System. X, 68. sq.)

Ad. Osiander: ,,Colligit Hildebrandus, quaerens: Unde flat determinatio ad id, ut homo voluntate non simplicis complacentiae, sed efficaci velit converti? Nam si dixeris, gratiam a voluntate determinari, periculum est, ne vires libero arbitrio a nostris denegatas assignemus. Respondet ille: non dicendum videtur, quod voluntas, cujus οίκειον munus est velle, a gratia determinetur; cum alias indifferentia in agendo perimi videatur. Quicquid enim aliunde determinatur, ita, ut hoc, quod agit, non possit non agere, id liberum dici non potest; at homo libere convertitur, ita ut etiam potuerit non converti. Proin, quemadmodum in generali concursu Dei cum causis secundis determinatio sit a causa secunda, sic in speciali gratiae concursu homo, qui convertitur, gratiam, non gratia hominem determinat. Sed hoc peculiare est, quod, cum generalem illum concursum homo viribus naturae insitis, specialem hunc concursum homo viribus non connatis, quas in conversione nullas admittimus, verum ab ipsa gratia collatis determinet. Voluntas igitur ad id, ut velit actu (non) converti, semet ipsam, at non ex seipsa, liberrime determinat; quo ipso libertas arbitrii salvatur; sed nihil virium voluntati conceditur. . . Respondeo: N. V. C.: Si voluntas determinatur a gratia, necessitas conversionis asserenda videtur; dicendum erit, hominem libere non converti; indifferentia in agendo tollitur. Nec enim sequitur primum, quia aliud est determinatio voluntatis a gratia facta simpliciter talis, aliud facta a gratia secundum vim omnipotentiae modumque agendi irresistibilem; prior nullam necessitatem habet comitem, nisi quae est ex hypothesi; homo enim determinatus a gratia retinet tamen adhuc potestatem resistendi; posterius autem necessitatem post se trahit, quam tamen determinationem nos in Calvinianis reprobamus. Secundum consequenter est absurdum; 8i enim libere homo convertitur juxta sensum Hildebrandi, statuetur liberum arbitrium in spiritualibus ante conversionem, quia tribuitur illi liberum velle conversionis. Hoc quidem certum est, hominem volentem converti · et aliquo etiam modo libere, non tamen positive, sed privative, quatenus potest per naturam contumaciter repugnare gratiae et impedire, quominus non convertatur; sed hunc modum praedictus auctor non intendit.“ (L. c. p. 336. sq. 339.)

Idem: ״Homo non concurrit ad sui conversionem, poenitentiam et vivificationem; neque per vires liberi arbitrii, quod pontiff. est, quasi scii, gratia praeveniens excitet vires nativas, quae partialiter concurrant; neque per exercitium gratiae praevenientis, quae Hornei et complicum est opinio. Utrumque reprimit mors spiritualis; qui enim mortuus est, per vires proprias ad vivificationem concurrere nequit; qui habet gratiam saltem praevenientem, is nondum habet vitam infusam, sed infundendam ac expectandam, proin nullas operationes vitales exercere potest, etiam vi praevenientis gratiae, quae saltem subjectum

passive praeparat? imo eopse, quo gratia praeveniens describitur sub ratione,auxilii‘, ab illis supponitur aliquid in natura, cui suppetias feret gratia praeveniens, adeoque haec sententia pontificiis adhinniet. — Absurde dicitur, vitam aliquam praecedere conversionem, in homine nondum converso obtinere vivificationem spiritualem; nam per fidem Christus vivit in nobis, Gal. 2, 20., fides autem est terminus conversionis; nondum potest vel vita vel vivificatio locum habere; imo cum ipsa conversio non nisi spiritualiter vivificatio et resuscitatio sit, absurdissime asseritur, conversione nondum consummata hominem esse jam vivificatum; hominem, ut ait Drejerus, deliberationibus spiritualibus, actibus mentis et voluntatis concurrere ad poenitentiam et conversionem.“ (Colleg. th. P. IV. p. 322. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Homo dicitur se convertere, ut navis se vertere dicitur, cum a nauta aut vento agitatur, ut Memnonis statua dicitur locuta, cum solis radio tangeretur.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 725.)

Formula Concordiae: ,,Quod vero attinet ad phrases et dicta Chrysostomi et Basilii: Trahit Deus, sed volentem trahit; tantum velis, et Deus praeoccurrit; item scholasticorum et pontificiorum: Hominis voluntas in conversione non est otiosa, sed agit aliquid etc., quia dicta illa pro confirmando naturali libero arbitrio in conversione hominis, contra doctrinam gratiae Dei introducta sunt: ex proposita declaratione manifeste apparet formae sanorum verborum ea non esse analoga, sed cum illa pugnare, et iccirco, cum de conversione ad Deum agitur, merito vitanda esse. . . Quandoquidem enim juventus in scholis doctrina illa de tribus causis efficientibus, concurrentibus in conversione hominis non renati, vehementer perturbata est, dum disputatum fuit, quomodo illae (verbum videlicet praedicatum et auditum, Spiritus Sanctus et hominis voluntas) concurrant: denuo repetitum volumus ex supra posita explicatione, quod conversio ad Deum sit solius Spiritus Sancti opus, qui solus est egregius ille artifex haec in nobis efficiens; interim tamen praedicatione et auditu sancti verbi sui (tanquam ordinario et legitimo medio seu instrumento suo) utitur. Hominis autem nondum renati intellectus et voluntas tantum sunt subjectum convertendum, sunt enim hominis spiritualiter mortui intellectus et voluntas, in quo homine Spiritus Sanctus conversionem et renovationem operatur, ad quod opus hominis convertendi voluntas nihil confert, sed patitur, ut Deus in ipsa operetur, donec regeneretur. Postea vero in aliis sequentibus bonis operibus Spiritui Sancto cooperatur, ea faciens, quae Deo grata sunt, eo modo, qui jam a nobis in hoc scripto abunde satis est declaratus.“ (Artic. 2. Solid, declar. p. 608. sq. 610.)

Musaeus: ,,An causam discretionis, cur alii convertantur, alii non convertantur, Lutherani unice penes hominem esse statuant? — Wendelinus (lib. 1. Christian, th. c. 14. th. 7. expl. n. 10.) scribit, Lutheranos docere quidem, hominem in sui conversione prima habere se mere passive, h. e., ad sui conversionem primam de suo nihil conferre per modum principii activi; interim docere eosdem, causam discretionis, cur alii convertantur, alii non convertantur, unice penes hominem esse. Postea citatis quibusdam Eccardi verbis, subjungit: ,Hoccine est ad sui conversionem active non concurrere? Quid evidentius pro hominis irregeniti synergia dici possit?‘ Et post aliqua interjecta: ,Quidampiius Pelagius dicere potuisset?‘ Sed Wendelinus mentem nostratium minus candide proponit, eamque studio ambigua locutione involvit, ut habeat, quod cavilletur. Primum enim, causam discretionis, cur alii convertantur, unice penes hominem esse, dicere nostrates non solent, sed uno ore dicunt omnes, causam, cur convertantur, quicunque convertuntur, non esse penes hominem, sed unice penes Deum; causam autem, cur non convertantur, qui in impietate perseverant, non penes Deum, sed unice penes hominem esse.“ (Colleg. controversiar. p. 390.)


### On Regeneration and Conversion: PART III. CHAP. IV. B

PART III. CHAP. IV. B. Meisnerus: "Whatever is assigned to free will in the conversion of man is detracted from divine grace; according to that saying of the ancients: 'The patrons of nature become the enemies of grace.' Looking to this, Augustine, *De peccatorum meritis et remissione*, lib. 2, c. 24, says: 'Grace is not grace in any way, if it is not given freely in every way.'" (*Anthropologia*, disp. 21, A. 2.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: Of the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians, the Scholastics and Papists, the Socinians and Arminians, and likewise the Synergists and Innovators, all of whom deny that man in his conversion behaves himself merely passively. In particular, the Papists agitate against this formula of speech and say that free will concurs in conversion not only by suffering, but also by acting—that is, by cooperating with divine grace. Thus, in the Council of Trent, sess. 6, can. 4, it is ordered that he be anathema who says that 'free will, moved and excited by God, behaves itself merely passively.' ... The Innovators also expressly deny that man behaves himself merely passively in his conversion, and they assert that free will, excited by the Holy Spirit, cooperates toward its own conversion. See Latermann and D. Hornejus. D. Dreier, in *Der Erörterung*, p. 522, expressly denies that 'man in his conversion is a merely passive subject.' D. Georg Calixtus, in *Annot. ad jam adductum Concilii Trid. decretum*, n. 3, p. 13, adds this *epikrisis*: 'Insofar as it is moved and excited, it indeed behaves itself merely passively. But after it has been moved and excited, it works in the power of the moving and exciting grace, with the hearing and perception of the Gospel given divinely.'" (L. c. s. 2, q. 2, f. 729.)

H. R. Frankius: "One must therefore say that the powers bestowed by God the Holy Spirit enter into such a connection with the existing potency of knowing and willing, whereby man, as a knowing and willing being, is enabled to let the center of gravity of his being fall into the divinely communicated, consciously realized thoughts of salvation: to know and to will that which is God’s with the new powers of his—man’s—knowing and willing, which have been bestowed by God. Thus, on the basis of the calling that has gone out to him, man is indeed able to cooperate with grace and to decide for it personally *ex se ipso* [from himself], so that he himself is the one acting therein and no other, yet not *tamquam ex semet ipso* [as if from himself], as though he had this self-acting out of and through himself. It stands, therefore, exactly as the Formula of Concord describes it: that first a spark of spiritual understanding is cast into the *intellectus* of man, and thereby at the same time a movement is communicated to the *voluntas*, whereby it is enabled to take a position in that thought of salvation and, despite the contradiction of the old being that hangs onto the objects of the creature and onto sin, to shift the center of gravity of the 'I' into it. ... When, therefore, the Formula of Concord points to the great difference that exists between baptized and unbaptized persons, in that the former, as truly reborn, have an *arbitrium liberatum* [liberated will] and thus can not only hear the Word but also, albeit in great weakness, give assent to it and accept it, it thereby names only the ordinary way in which, within the Christian community, the natural man born of the flesh is placed into the possibility of determining himself in personal freedom for the gifted salvation; and the proposition has its validity everywhere and throughout, that wherever the natural man is led over into the state of conversion, this happens on the basis of the *arbitrium liberatum* previously bestowed upon him by means of the Word or Baptism." (*Die Theol. der Concordienformel*, I, 163 sq., 164 sq.)

Luthardt: "At every stage (according to Chemnitz) the appropriating behavior of man is conditioned by the preceding efficacy of grace, which first makes that possible for man. So also the following dogmaticians. Only it is not always sufficiently acknowledged that this happens already *in conversione* (which the Helmstedt theologian Latermann, *De act. Dei praedest.* 1645, *De grat. et lib. arb.* 1647, particularly emphasized), but the cooperation of the human will is assumed only *post conversionem*. . . It is true that Quenstedt sets forth the stages through which conversion prepares itself, . . . but conversion is nevertheless a matter of a moment, so that only after this does *cooperatio* enter—*hominis conversi esse cooperari, non hominis convertendi*—and God does not merely work *ut possimus velle*, but *ut actu velimus* (like Augustine), although he adds that the first influences of *gratia praeveniens* are indeed *inevitabiles*, but not *irresistibiles*. But with those propositions Quenstedt goes beyond Chemnitz (?), who had denied *cooperatio* merely *ut inchoetur conversio*, while Quenstedt adds: *addo, et compleatur et absolvatur*—which is against the moral nature of this process. . .

In more recent times it has been asserted several times (esp. Jul. Müller, e.g., *Union.* p. 212; *Stud. u. Krit.* 1856, 3, p. 553) that one can only escape absolute predestinarianism if one attributes to the natural man the possibility of an independent and self-active behavior toward the effects of grace, through which alone all divine effect of grace in the interior of man is conditioned, and that the Lutheran doctrine is inconsistent in that it denies this and yet at the same time rejects absolute predestination. On the other hand, it has been replied from the Lutheran side (esp. Thomasius I, 445; III, 1, 466 sqq.) that there is a difference between being seized by grace and the actual decision for salvation. The former happens without any contribution from man and exerts through the Word an effect upon the personal thinking and willing of man, which he cannot withdraw from at all and which yet establishes a real receptivity and the possibility of a decision for salvation. The other, however, is his self-active behavior, which is only made possible by the former. This limitation of the old dogmatic proposition: *in conversione homo se habet mere passive* is now as good as generally acknowledged." (*Compend. der Dogm.* Third ed. 1868, p. 205 sq.)

The same: "It is true that the presentation of the Formula of Concord often sounds as if God alone works everything. (*Hominis conversionem non tantum ex parte, sed totam prorsus esse operationem, donum et opus solius Sp. Sancti*, p. 687, 89.) But these expressions receive their closer determination through that *potest apprehendere* (!) and the *quam primum inchoavit* discussed earlier. (674, 65.) One must indeed acknowledge that the presentation of the Formula of Concord does not keep itself cautiously enough within the limits of the necessary measure. That may well be an aftereffect of the manner of the polemical literature of that time, which placed decisiveness in the strongest and most exaggerated mode of speech possible, with which one presented and represented the opposites." (*Die Lehre vom fr. Willen.* 1863, p. 276.)

The same: "Grace may come as close to man as it will: man himself must open the door so that Jesus may enter into him." (*Die Lehre vom freien Willen.* 1863, p. 427.)

The same: "He (God's Spirit) does not work the willing itself, but works so liberatingly upon the bound will that it thereby receives a new ability-to-will." (*L. c.* p. 441.)

The same: "Scripture designates conversion partly as a work of grace, partly as an achievement of man. As a work of grace already in the Old Testament. . . but especially in the New Testament. . . On the other hand, repentance and faith are [demanded] of man." PART III. CHAP. IV.

demanded as his performance: μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε — at all stages of the history of salvation. The called person should and can comply with the demand for repentance immediately, Ps. 95:7 sqq., Heb. 4:7 sqq., and faith is free obedience which man performs, e.g., 1:5. Thus, conversion — also Jer. 31:18, "convert me," etc., the chief passage of our ancients — is man's own act, therefore also ἐπιστρέφειν is used only in the active and middle, never in the passive. — The mediation of both statements lies in the divine calling to μετάνοια, etc., in the face of which man has the freedom of rejection or acceptance. . . The older dogmaticians (e.g., König and Quenstedt) treat first of regeneration, then of conversion, but in such a way that both concepts essentially coincide in the matter itself and are distinguished from one another only formally. . . In this definition of conversion, the element of man's moral self-activity is missing, which must be designated as a deficiency (!) in the dogmatic formulation.” (Compend. p. 202 sq.)

Kahnisius: “Melanchthon, through the doctrine of the cooperation of the human will in the appropriation of salvation (synergism), had entered the right, evangelical, and at the same time truly traditional path of holding fast to the substance of the Augustinian doctrine without its excrescences. . . The proposition that the spurning of salvation has its ground in man neutralizes not only the concept of predestination but also the concept of grace in the Formula of Concord. For this proposition demands, according to irrefutable logic, that the man who can reject salvation is not without will when he grasps it. For whoever can resist and does not resist, does not want to resist. And whoever does not want to resist, just wants to receive. Melanchthon had clearly recognized that.” (Die luth. Dogm. II, 539, 543.)

Hofmannus: “Just as the Apostle in Rom. 7:14–25 is not intended to deny all doing of good by the Old Testament believers, so he says in the present passage even of individual cases of a doing of good by the heathen; without thereby contradicting what our church confession teaches about man, as he is before God, in himself and apart from all operations of grace, that he is incapable of any good and inclined to all evil. He knows, in fact, of an operation of grace, not only of the God who has sent Christ, but also of the God who will send Christ, and indeed he knows of it not only within the Old Testament community of salvation, but also outside of it. . . The Spirit of God, who dwells in them to make them live, does not leave them without that testimony of God through which they get to experience both his holiness and their sin, but also his goodness as well as their nothingness. Through this, however, a conduct toward God can be worked in them, which he, on the day of that judgment which John saw after the resurrection of the believers, will reward with the wages of eternal life. But this is God’s work and not their own. It is God’s love which lets them live, and through his Spirit, the Spirit of their life, he testifies himself to them.” (Schriftbeweis. Second ed. p. 570 sq.) Cf. Antitheses supra Vol. II, 300 sqq. §

Latin:

PART. III. CAP. IV. B. Meisnerus: ,,Quicquid in conversione hominis libero arbitrio adsignatur, hoc divinae gratiae detrahitur; juxta illud veterum: ,Patroni naturae fiunt inimici gratiae.' Quo respiciens Augustinus lib. 2. de peccat, cfrig. c. 24.: ,Gratia1, inquit, ,non est gratia ullo modo, sinon gratis datur omni modo.'" ('Αν&ρωπολογ. disp. 21. A. 2.).

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: Pelagianorum et semipelagianorum, scholasticorum et pontificiorum, Socinianorum et Arminianorum, itemque synergistarum et Novatorum, qui omnes inficiantur, hominem in sui conversione habere se mere passive. Inprimis pontificii hanc loquendi formulam exagitant et liberum arbitrium non tantum patiendo, sed etiam agendo in conversione dicunt concurrere, h. e., gratiae divinae cooperari. Sic in Concil. Trid. sess. 6. can. 4. anathema esse jubetur, qui dixerit, ,liberum arbitrium a Deo motum et excitatum mere passive se habere4. . . Novatores quoque diserte negant, hominem sese mere passive habere in sui conversione, et liberum arbitrium excitatum a Sp. S. cooperari ad sui conversionem, asserunt. Vide Latermannum et D. Hornejum. D. Dreierus in,der Erörterung4 p. 522. expresse negat, ,hominem in sui conversione subjectum mere patiens4 esse. D. Georg. Galixtus in Annot. ad jam adductum Concilii Trid. decretum n. 3. p. 13. hanc addit επίκρίσιν: ,Quatenus movetur et excitatur, ita sane se habet mere passive. Postquam vero motum et excitatum est, in virtute moventis et excitantis gratiae cum auditu et percepto evangelio divinitus datae operatur.'" (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 729.)

H. R. Frankius: ,,Man wird mithin sagen müssen, die von Gott dem Heiligen Geiste verliehenen Kräfte treten mit der vorhandenen Potenz des Erkennens und Wollens in eine solche Verbindung, wornach der Mensch als erkennender und wollender befähigt wird, den Gravitationspunkt seines Wesens in die ihm mitgetheilten, bewusstgewordenen Heilsgedanken Gottes fallen zu lassen: das, was Gottes ist, zu erkennen und zu wollen mit den von Gott verliehenen neuen Kräften seines, des Menschen, Erkennens und Wollens. So vermag der Mensch auf Grund der an ihn ergangenen Berufung wohl der Gnade zu cooperiren und für diese sich persönlich zu entscheiden ex se ipso, so dass er selbst der wirkende dabei ist und kein Anderer, aber doch nicht tamquam ex semet ipso, als hätte er dieses Selbstwirken aus und durch sich selbst. Es steht demnach allerdings so, wie es die Concordienformel beschreibt, dass zunächst ein Funke geistlichen Verständnisses in den intellectus des Menschen hineingeworfen und damit zugleich der voluntas eine Bewegung mitgetheilt wird, wodurch sie befähigt wird, in jenem Heilsgedanken Position zu nehmen und trotz des Widerspruches des alten an den Objecten der Creatur, an der Sünde hangenden Wesens in ihn den Schwerpuukt des Ichs zu verlegen. . . Wenn daher die Concordienformel auf den grossen Unterschied verweist, der zwischen den getauften und den ungetaulten Menschen Statt finde, indem die ersteren als wahrhaftig wiedergeboren arbitrium liberatum haben und somit das Wort nicht allein hören, sondern auch demselben, wiewohl in grösser Schwachheit, Beifall thun und es annehmen können, so benennt sie damit nur den gewöhnlichen Weg, auf welchem innerhalb der Christengemeinde der vom Fleische geborne, natürliche Mensch in die Möglichkeit versetzt wird, für das geschenkte Heil in persönlicher Freiheit sich zu bestimmen, und der Satz hat überall und durchweg seine Giltigkeit, dass, wo immer der natürliche Mensch hinübergeführt wird in den Stand der Bekehrung, dies geschehe auf Grund des ihm vermittelst des Wortes oder der Taufe zuvor verliehenen arbitrium liberatum.“

Luthardtius: ,,Auf jeder Stufe ist (nach Chemnitz) das aneignende Verhalten des Menschen bedingt durch die vorangehende Wirksamkeit der Gnade, welche jenes dem Menschen erst möglich macht. So auch die folgenden Dogmatiker. Nur wird nicht immer genugsam anerkannt, dass dies schon i n conversione geschehe (was besonsonders der Helmstädter Latermann, De act. Dei praedest. 1645. De grat. et lib. arb. 1647. betonte), sondern die Mitthätigkeit des menschliehen Willens wird erst post conversionem angenommen. . . Zwar führt Quenstedt die Stufen aus, durch welche die Bekehrung sich vorbereitete, . . . aber die Bekehrung ist doch Sache des Moments, so dass erst nach diesem die cooperatio eintrete — hominis conversi esse cooperari, non hominis convertendi —, und Gott nicht blos wirke ut possimus velle, sed ut actu velimus (wie Augustinus), obwohl er hinzufügt, die ersten Einwirkungen der gratia praeveniens seien zwar inevitabiles, aber nicht irresistibiles. Aber mit jenen Sätzen geht Quenstedt über Chemnitz hinaus (?),welcher die cooperatio geleugnet hatte blos ut inchoetur conversio, während Quenstedt hinzufügt: addo, et compleatur et absolvatur — was wider die sittliche Natur dieses Vorgangs ist. . .

In neuerer Zeit hat man mehrfach (bes. Jul. Müller, z. B. Union. S. 212. Stud. u. Krit. 1856, 3. S. 553.) behauptet, dass man dem absoluten Prädestinatianismus nur entgehen könne, wenn man dem natürlichen Menschen die Möglichkeit eines selbständigen und selbstthätigen Verhaltens zu den Wirkungen der Gnade zuschreibe, wodurch erst alle göttliche Gnadenwirkung im Innern des Menschen bedingt sei, und die lutherische Lehre sei inconsequent, indem sie dieses verneine und doch zugleich die absolute Prädestination ablehne. Dagegen hat man lutherischer Seits (bes. Thomas. I, 445. III, 1. 466. sqq.) erwidert, dass ein Unterschied sei zwischen dem Ergriffenwerden von der Gnade und der eigentlichen Entscheidung für das Heil. Jenes geschieht ohne Zuthun des Menschen und übt durch das Wort eine Wirkung auf das persönliche Denken und Wollen des Menschen, der er sich gar nicht entziehen kann und die doch eine Wirkliche Empfänglichkeit und die Möglichkeit einer Entscheidung für das Heil herstellt. Das andere aber ist sein selbstthätiges Verhalten, welches durch jenes erst möglich gemacht ist. Diese Beschränkung des altdogmatischen Satzes: in conversione homo se habet mere passive ist jetzt so gut wie allgemein anerkannt.u (Compend. der Dogm. Dritte Aufl. 1868. p. 205. sq.)

Idem: ,,Zwar lautet die Darstellung der Concordienformel öfter so, als ob Gott allein alles wirke. (Hominis conversionem non tantum ex parte, sed totam prorsus esse operationem, donum et opus solius Sp. Sancti, p. 687, 89.) Aber diese Aeusserungen erhalten ihre nähere BeStimmung durch jenes potest apprehendere (!) und das früher besprochene quam primum inchoavit. (674, 65.) Man muss allerdings anerkennen, dass sich die Darstellung der Concordienformel nicht vorsichtig genug innerhalb der Grenzen des nöthigen Masses hält. Das mag wohl eine Nachwirkung der Weise der damaligen Streitliteratur sein, welche die Entschiedenheit in die möglichst starke und übertriebene Redeweise setzte, mit der man die Gegensätze darstellte und vertrat.“ (Die Lehre vom fr. Willen. 1863. p. 276.)

Idem: ,,Es mag die Gnade dem Menschen noch so nahe kommen: die Thüre muss der Mensch selbst aufmachen, dass Jesus zu ihm eingehe.“ (Die Lehre vom freien Willen. 1863. p. 427.)

Idem: ,,Nicht das Wollen selbst wirkt er (Gottes Geist), sondern so befreiend auf den gebundenen Willen, dass dieser dadurch ein neues WoWenkönnen empfängt.“ (L. c. p. 441.)

Idem: ,,Die Schrift bezeichnet die Bekehrung theils als ein Werk der Gnade, theils als eine Leistung des Menschen. Als ein Werk der Gnade schon im alten Testament. . . besonders aber im neuen Testament. . . Auf der andern Seite wird Busse und Glaube vom Menschen PART. III. CAP. IV.

gefordert als seine Leistung: μετανοείτε κ<ύ πιστεύετε — auf allen Stufen der Heilsgeschichte. Der Forderung der Busse soll und kann der Berufene alsbald nachkommen, Ps. 95, 7. sq. Hebr. 4, 7. sqq., und der Glaube ist freier Gehorsam, den der Mensch leistet, z. B. 1, 5« So ist also die Bekehrung — auch Jer. 31, 18. bekehre du mich u. s. w., die Hauptstelle unserer Alten — des Menschen eigne That, desshalb auch επιστρέφε/ν nur im Activum und Medium, nie im Passivum gebraucht. — Die Vermittlung beider Aussagen liegt in der göttlichen Berufung zur μετάνοια u. s. w., welcher gegenüber der Mensch Freiheit der Abweisung oder der Annahme hat. . . Die älteren Dogmatiker (z. B. König und Quenstedt) handeln zuerst von der regeneratio, dann von der conversio, aber so, dass beide Begriffe der Sache nach im Wesentlichen zusammenfallen und mehr nur formell von einander unterschieden werden. . . Bei dieser Begriffsbestimmung von conversio fehlt das Moment der sittlichen Selbstthat des Menschen, was als ein Mangel (!) in der dogmatischen Fassung wird bezeichnet werden müssen.“ (Compend. p. 202. sq.)

Kahnisius: ,,Melanchthon hatte durch die Lehre von der Mitwirkung des menschlichen Willens bei der Heilsaneignung (Synergismus) den rechten, evangelischen und zugleich wahrhaft traditionellen Weg betreten, die Substanz der augustinischen Lehre festzuhalten ohne ihre Auswüchse. . . Der Satz, dass das Verschmähen des Heils seinen Grund im Menschen habe, neutralisirt nicht blos den Prädestinationsbegriff, sondern auch den Gnadenbegriff der Concorclienformel. Dieser Satz nemlich fordert nach unwidersprechlicher Logik, dass der Mensch, der das Heil zurückweisen kann, beim Ergreifen desselben nicht willenlos ist. Denn wer widerstreben kann und nicht widerstrebt, der will nicht widerstreben. Und wer nicht widerstreben will, der will eben empfangen. Das hatte Melanchthon klar erkannt.“ (Die luth. Dogm. II, 539. 543.)

Hofmannus: ,,Wie der Apostel Röm. 7, 14—25. nicht gemeint ist, alles Gutesthun der alttestamentlichen Gläubigen zu verneinen, so sagt er an der vorliegenden Stelle sogar von einzelnen Fällen eines Gutesthuns der Heiden; ohne damit Dem zu widersprechen, was unser kirchliches Bekenntniss vom Menschen lehrt, wie er Gotte gegenüber, an sich und abgesehen von allen Gnadenwirküngen beschaffen ist, dass er unvermögend sei zu einigem Guten und geneigt zu allem Bösen. Er weiss eben von einer Gnadenwirkung, nicht blos des Gottes, welcher Christum gesandt Λαί, sondern auch des Gottes, welcher Christum senden wird, und zwar weiss er von ihr nicht blos innerhalb des alttestamentlichen Heilsgemeinwesens, sondern auch ausserhalb desselben. . . Der Geist Gottes, welcher ihnen einwohnt, sie leben zu machen, lässt sie nicht ohne jene Bezeugung Gottes, durch welche sie beides, seine Heiligkeit und ihre Sünde, aber auch seine Güte wie ihre Nichtigkeit, zu erfahren bekommen. Hiedurch kann aber ein Verhalten gegen Gott in ihnen gewirkt werden, das er an dem Tage jenes Gerichts, welches Johannes nach der Auferstehung der Gläubigen geschaut hat, mit dem Lohne ewigen Lebens erwiedern wird. Aber dies ist Gottes Werk und nicht ihr eignes. Gottes Liebe ist es, welche sie leben lässt, und durch seinen Geist, den Geist ihres Lebens, bezeugt er sich ihnen.“ (Schriftbeweis. Zweite Aufl. p. 570. sq.) Cf. Antitheses supra Vol. II, 300. sqq. §


### On Regeneration and Conversion: It must also be observed that that grace by which God works conversion is not…

39. It must also be observed that that grace by which God works conversion is not irresistible, but resistible, insofar as men not only [resist] the means of conversion

and their external use, but they can and often do maliciously resist the grace of conversion itself, which is intrinsically operative, and thus they impede their own conversion, whether it is to be begun or perfected.

For although that power of God, through which He works the conversion of man, is infinite; yet because it ordinarily exerts itself only through certain means, it is not absurd that it can be resisted. See Matt. 23:37. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. de Volunt. Dei Antec. et Conseq.* toward the end, and *Disp. V. de Conv.* (Halle edition) § 39 et seq. Quenstedtius: "The question of the orthodox against the Calvinists is this," says the blessed Huelsemann, *disp. 3. de auxil. gratiae, qu. 7. th. 1. § 34. p. 301.*: "Whether, when all things required for conversion on the part of God have been posited—prevenient, exciting, and efficacious grace, and whatever else might be necessary on the part of the superior cause—it remains free for the man being converted not to be converted, or whether he is converted in an irresistible manner? This question is not equivalent to that one (Huelsemann continues), whether, when all things required for conversion on the part of God have been posited, it is free for man to be converted? For the liberty not to be converted, and the liberty to be converted, even when the divine requirements have been posited, flow from different principles. The liberty not to be converted flows from a principle connatural to man; but the liberty to be converted flows from a supernatural principle, namely, prevenient grace." (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 730. sq.)

The same: "It does not follow, nor is it true: If the first motion of prevenient grace is inevitable, then its result, or conversion itself, is also inevitable, and thus we are converted irresistibly. For although man cannot prevent the first motion from arising, he nevertheless has, in that very first motion, the liberty of resisting; he has it also in the second and the last (though not indifferently, i.e., equally toward being converted and not being converted; for the faculty of man, already moved by prevenient grace, always inclines more to the one than to the other), and he can, by a stubborn will, place an obstacle to prevenient grace, shake it off, and by resisting, impede his own conversion." (L. c. sect. 2. q. 3. f. 735.) The same: "The first motions, excited by prevenient grace, are indeed inevitable, i.e., an unregenerate man, hearing the Word of God, cannot prevent a spiritual motion from arising in his heart, namely, a thought concerning sin committed, concerning the avoidance of wickedness, etc.; yet they are not irresistible, for he can prevent those motions from taking root and enduring in the heart, he can stifle them, shake them off, etc., by the example of the Jews in Luke 4:22, 28, Felix in Acts 24:25, and Agrippa in Acts 26:28." (L. c. s. 1. th. 31. f. 716.)

J. Olearius: "Man can resist the Omnipotent, not by way of absolute omnipotence, but as He acts graciously through certain means; and thus he can by no means oppose the infinite power or omnipotence itself, but he can oppose grace and its order, namely, by rejecting the means of salvation and disturbing the divinely constituted order, when he scorns the counsel of God concerning his own salvation, Luke 7, and judges himself unworthy of eternal life, Acts 13." (See Carpzovius' *Isagog.*, p. 1230.) Calovius: "Rom. 9:18. It is true that there are causes in men why they do not believe, yet it is not to be thought, conversely, that there are also causes in them why they do believe. But we shall easily wrest this Herculean club from the Calvinists if it is observed that these words pertain to the objection of the Jews, and thus prove nothing. For the Jews were arguing thus: If God hardens whom He wills, why then does He find fault with those who are hardened, since no one can resist His will? — i.e., that God cannot justly find fault with those hardened by His irresistible will. But the apostolic response does not assume, but refutes this objection, which is partly indirect and..." PART III. CHAP. IV.

partly] purgatorial, because man ought not to answer back to God; partly direct and informative, by which the apostle teaches, both that God can by all means justly be angry with the hardened, since He does not harden them unless they have already become, by their own fault, vessels of the most just divine wrath, and that God does not harden by an irresistible will by positively infusing hardness of heart—which both the Jews and the Calvinists assume in that objection—but by bearing with much long-suffering and patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. But He who hardens whom He wills, yet in such a way that He is not the author, approver, or positive cause of the hardness, does not unjustly accuse those who harden themselves. . . . Although we admit that some will of God is irresistible, yet that which exerts itself in election to eternal life or in the ordinary gift of faith is not irresistible, as the apostle teaches here. That objection would certainly constrain him if this will of God were irresistible. For why does God complain of us when we do not believe, if He has determined by an absolute decree to give faith to these and deny it to others, and no one can resist His will, according to which He wills to give it or not to give it?" (Biblia illustrata, on the loc. cit.)

Ad. Osiander: "The absence of resistance is also a benefit of prevenient grace. . . They object: If man does not have in his own power the liberty to not-resist, the assertion of our theologians is false, that man does not act actively in his conversion, but passively and by not-resisting. Resp.: Non-resistance is considered in two ways, either by reason of external pedagogy or by reason of spiritual operation from the Word; in the former way, it is in the power of man, insofar as by not resisting pedagogical means he can attend the temple, or not, etc.; but not in the latter way, but it is the first effect of prevenient grace and subsequent dispensations of grace." (Colleg. th. IV, 348 sq.)

Huelsemannus: "The orthodox opinion is this: . . . no one distinguishes himself nor can boast against another who is not converted, because no one positively works anything toward the reception of first grace; but that he does not resist grace, which by itself and by its own nature works conversion, he has this from the collation of first grace, which is conferred upon all, so that they may be able not to resist." (De auxiliis gratiae, p. 274.)

Quenstedtius: "Bellarminus wrongly gathers from the cited sayings that it is in vain to be reproved for not wanting to be converted or to come, if it is not in their power to come or to convert themselves. — Christ does not simply reprove the Jews (saying in Matt. 23:37: 'How often would I have gathered you, and you would not?'), because they did not want to be converted, as if they did not want to cooperate with faith, righteousness, etc.; for Christ knew this was not in their power; but He accuses the Jews because they did not want to use even those external means which were still in their power, namely, to hear the Word of God, etc. The argument does not hold: The unregenerate can be unwilling to come, refuse to obey God calling, and resist the Holy Spirit inviting to salvation; therefore, they can likewise be willing to come, follow God calling, and leave room for the admonitions of the Holy Spirit. For the former is of disease and imperfection, and proper to those men in the state of fallen nature; the latter, however, is of restoration through grace. 'Although it is in man to be unwilling for the good, yet, unless it is given, he does not have the will for the good. Nature contracted the former through fault, nature receives the latter through grace,' says the author of the book *De vocatione gentium*. It is not permitted to argue from unwillingness to will, and from the power to reject grace to the power to embrace it and to embrace it in the state of servitude and corruption." (L. c. P. II. c. 3. s. 2. q. 2. f. 2015.)

Partly by omitting acts required for the means to be established in use, e.g., hearing, reading, meditation of the Word, etc., partly by committing acts diametrically opposed to the legitimate use of the means, e.g., contradicting the Word of God, caviling, or contumeliously attacking or blaspheming the Word, acts of repelling, defaming, or persecuting

hostilely [against] the heralds of the word, etc.; see the example of the Jews, Acts 6:10 ff., ch. 7:51, 54.

When, on the part of the intellect, one indulges in prejudices or false preconceived opinions, whence the heavenly doctrine is rashly held to be foolish or scandalous, which Paul records as having happened to the Jews and Gentiles, 1 Cor. 1:23; on the part of the will, various inordinate motions [arise], contrary to pious and holy motions, e.g., the desires of the flesh, the cares of riches, etc., Luke 8:14.

For we distinguish between malicious resistance (which others call morose, voluntary, habitual, or stubborn) and natural resistance (which others call congenital). The latter flows directly from the corrupted nature of man and is common to all mortals; the former, however, is brought on by the peculiar fault of man and by deliberate effort, and thus proceeds from malice contracted of one's own accord; it is greater and more stubborn in some, and lesser and less stubborn in others, according as the acquired malice itself varies.

That natural resistance is gradually diminished in conversion itself through grace conjoined with the Word of God, and is finally overcome, nor does it, precisely taken, hinder conversion. But the other, or malicious resistance, which is added to the natural, just as it is not equally common to all the unregenerate, so men can abstain from it by the powers of free will, or, if they cannot now after vicious habits have been contracted, they could nevertheless have been without it to some extent before, if a right education and habituation to virtues had been present.

See the blessed Musaeus discussing these things at greater length in *De Aet. El. Decr.*, ch. XI, § 38 ff. Compare the blessed J. Olearius, *Contin. Isag. Carpzov. in Libb. Symbol.*, p. 1230.

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who maintain that God converts the elect by an irresistible motion, so that they are converted infallibly and absolutely, and cannot resist the efficacious grace or repel it. . . Thus in the acts of the Synod of Dort, the British [delegates] p. 131: 'For this very work of regeneration, man conducts himself merely passively' (so far, so good) 'nor is it in the power of the human will to hinder God thus immediately regenerating.' Thus the Palatines p. 139: 'God works conversion by the supereminent magnitude of His power and by the efficacy of the strength of His forces, by which He can subject all things to Himself. Such an efficacious, such a powerful operation of God can most rightly be called irresistible. Both on the part of the grace of God and on the part of the will. On the part of grace, because the efficacious operation of God is placed in act, which no one can resist, Rom. 9:19, Luke 21, Acts 11:17. On the part of the will, for [the will] being subjected to efficacious grace now does not wish to resist, and because it does not wish to, it necessarily does not wish to, and thus it cannot wish to resist while preserving its liberty. For everything, while it is, is necessary,' etc. And later: 'As if dust and ashes could hinder and elude the most omnipotent action of God!' . . .

Latin:

39. Observandum etiam est, gratiam illam, qua Deus conversionem operatur, non esse irr esis ti bilem, sed resistibi· lem,a quatenus homines non solum mediis conversionis

eorumque usui externo,b verum ipsi gratiae conversionis intrinsecus operaturae c malitiose d repugnare possunt et saepe solent, atque ita impediunt conversionem suam, seu inchoandam, seu perficiendam.

Etsi enim vis illa Dei, per quam hominis conversionem operatur, infinita sit; quia tamen ordinarie non nisi per certa media se exserit, non absurdum est, ei posse resisti. Vid. Matth. 23, 37. Conf. b. Mus. Disp, de Volunt. Dei Antec. et Conseq. sub finem et Disp. V. de Conv. (edit. Hali.) § 39. sqq. Quenstedtius: ,,Quaestio orthodoxorum adversus Calvinianos haec est, inquit b. Huelsem. disp. 3. de auxil. gratiae, qu. 7. th. 1. § 34. p. 301.: ,An positis ex parte Dei omnibus ad conversionem requisitis, gratia praeveniente, excitante, efficaci et si quid porro ex parte causae superioris necessarium fuerit, homini convertendo liberum maneat non convertif an vero convertatur modo irresistibili? Haec quaestio non est aequipollens illi (inquit porro Huelsem.), an positis ex parte Dei omnibus ad conversionem requisitis homini liberum sit convertif Nam libertas non converti, et libertas converti, etiam positis divinis requisitis, manant ex diversis principiis. Libertas non converti manat ex principio homini connaturali; libertas autem converti manat ex principio supernaturali, praeveniente scii, gratia.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 730. sq.)

Idem: ,,Non sequitur, nec verum est: Si primus motus gratiae praevenientis est inevitabilis, est etiam inevitabilis ejus eventus seu ipsa conversio, et sic convertimur irresistibiliter. Nam licet homo non possit impedire, ne primus motus oriatur, habet tamen in ipso primo motu libertatem resistendi, habet etiam in secundo et ultimo (licet non indifferenter i. e. aequaliter ad convertendum et non convertendum; semper enim facultas hominis jam moti a gratia praeveniente magis propendet ad hoc, quam ad illud) et potest per morosam voluntatem gratiae praevenienti obicem ponere, eam excutere et resistendo ipsam sui conversionem impedire.u (L. c. sect. 2. q. 3. f. 735.) Idem: ,,Motus primi, a gratia praeveniente excitati, sunt quidem inevitabiles, i. e., non potest homo irregenitus, verbum Dei audiens, impedire, ne oriatur in corde suo motus spiritualis, sci. cogitatio de peccato admisso, de vitandis flagitiis etc.; non tamen irresistibiles sunt, potest enim illos motus, ne radices agant et in corde perdurent, impedire, eos suffocare, excutere etc., exemplo Judaeorum Luc. 4, 22. 28., Felicis Act. 24, 25., Agrippae Act. 26, 28." (L. c. s. 1. th. 31. f. 716.)

J. Olearius: ,,Resistere potest homo omnipotenti non per modum omnipotentiae absolutae, sed per certa media gratiose agenti adeoque nequaquam ipsi infinitae potestati vel omnipotentiae, sed gratiae, ejusque ordini se opponere potest, scii, media salutis rejiciendo et ordinem divinitus constitutum perturbando, cum consilium Dei de salute sua spernit, Luc. 7., et se ipsum vita aeterna indignum judicat. Act. 13." (Vid. Isagog. Carpzovii, p. 1230.) Calovius: ,,Rom. 9, 18. Verum est, causas esse in hominibus, ut non credant, non tamen vicissim censendum est, in iis causas etiam osse, ut credant. Calvinianis autem hanc clavam Herculeam facile extorquebimus, si observatum fuerit, verba haec pertinere ad Judaeorum objectionem, adeoque nil probare. Sic enim regerebant Judaei: Si Deus indurat, quos vult, quid ergo succenset induratis, cum nemo ejus voluntati resistere possit? — q. d., Deum non posse jure succensere irresistibili ejus voluntate induratis. Responsio autem apostolica non assumit, sed refellit hanc objectionem, quae partim indirecta est et ob PART. III. CAP. IV.

jurgatoria, quod homo non debeat respondere Deo ex adverso, partim directa et informatoria, qua docet apostolus, tum quod Deus omnino jure succensere possit induratis, quandoquidem non induret, nisi jam culpa sua justissimae irae divinae vasa factos, tum quod Deus non in־ duret voluntate irresistibili duritiem cordis positive immittendo, quod et Judaei et Calviniani in ista objectione assumunt, sed perferendo multa lenitate et patientia vasa irae ad interitum coagmentata. Qui autem indurat, quem vult, ita tamen ut duritiei non sit auctor vel approbator seu causa positiva, is non immerito accusat eos, qui indurescunt. . . . Quamquam vero admittamus, voluntatem aliquam Dei esse irresistibilem, ea tamen, quae exserit sese in electione ad vitam aeternam vel in fidei donatione ordinaria, irresistibilis non est, quemadmodum hic docet apostolus. Quem certe objectio illa stringeret, si irresistibilis haec Dei voluntas foret. Quid enim conqueritur Deus de nobis, quum non credimus, si fidem his dare, aliis negare absoluto decreto constituit ejusque voluntati, secundum quam illam dare aut non dare vult, nemo resistere possit.“ (Bibi, illustrata ad 1. d.)

Ad. Osiander: ״Absentia repugnantiae est quoque praevenientis gratiae beneficium. . . Excipiunt: Si homo non in sua potestate habeat libertatem ad non-resistendum, fallere assertum nostrorum theol., hominem se non active habere in sua conversione, sed passive et nonresistendo. Resp.: non-resistentiam dupliciter considerari, aut ratione paedagogiae externae aut ratione spiritualis operationis ex verbo; priori modo est in potestate hominis, quatenus mediis paedagogicis non resistendo potest adire templum, vel non, etc.; non autem modo posteriori, sed est primus effectus gratiae praevenientis et subsequentium gratiae dispensationum.“ (Colleg. th. IV, 348. sq.)

Huelsemannus: ,,Orthodoxa sententia haec est: . . . neminem sese discernere neque gloriari posse adversus alterum non conversum, quia nemo positive aliquid operatur ad receptionem primae gratiae; quod autem gratiae, per se et sua natura conversionem operanti, non resistit, hoc habet ex primae gratiae collatione, quae omnibus confertur, ut possint non resistere.“ (De auxiliis gratiae, p. 274.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Male Bellarminus ex allatis dictis colligit, frustra reprehendi, quod noluerint converti aut venire, si in eorum potestate non sit, venire aut se convertere. — Christus non simpliciter reprehendit Judaeos (inquiens Matth. 23, 37.: ,Quoties volui te congregare, et tu noluisti?‘), quod noluerint converti, quasi noluerint cooperari fidem, justitiam etc.; hoc namque sciebat Christus non esse in illorum potestate; sed incusat Judaeos, quod etiam externa illa media noluerint usurpare, quae erant adhuc in eorum potestate, scii, audire verbum Dei etc. Non valet argumentum: Possunt irregeniti nolle venire, renuere obsequi Deo vocanti, Spiritui S. ad salutaria invitanti resistere, ergo pariter possunt velle venire, Deum vocantem sequi, Spiritus S. admonitionibus locum relinquere. Nam illud prius est morbi et imperfectionis, illisque hominibus in statu naturae lapsae propyium; hoc vero est restaurationis per gratiam. ,Licet insit homini, nolle bonum, tamen, nisi donatum, non habet velle bonum. Illud contraxit natura per culpam, hoc recipit natura per gratiam‘, inquit auctor lib. de voc. gent. A noluntate ad voluntatem et a potestate gratiam repudiandi ad potestatem eam amplectendi et amplexandi in statu servitutis et corruptionis argumentari non licet.“ (L. c. P. II. c. 3. s. 2. q. 2. f. 2015.)

Partim omittendo actus ad id, ut media in usu constituantur, requisitos, v. g. auditus, lectionis, meditationis verbi etc., partim committendo actus usui mediorum legitimo e diametro adversantes, v. g. contradicendi verbo Dei, cavillandi aut contumeliose insectandi vel blasphemandi verbum, actus repellendi, infamandi vel persequendi
