hostiliter praecones verbi etc.; vid. exemplum Judaeorum, Act 6, 10. sqq. cap. 7, 51. 54.

Quando ex parte intellectus indulgetur praejudiciis seu praeconceptis opinionibus falsis, unde doctrina coelestis pro stulta aut scandalosa temere habetur, quod Judaeis et gentilibus accidisse memorat Paulus 1 Cor. 1, 23.; ex parte voluntatis varii motus inordinati, motibus piis et sanctis contrarii, v. g. desideria carnis, curae divitiarum etc. Luc. 8, 14.

Distinguimus enim inter repugnantiam malitiosam (quam alii morosam, voluntariam, habitualem, pertinacem vocant) et naturalem (quae aliis congenita appellatur). Quarum haec quidem ex natura hominis corrupta proxime fluit et mortalibus omnibus communis est; illa vero peculiari hominis culpa et data opera accersita, et sic ex malitia sponte contracta, profecta est et in aliis major ac pertinacior, in aliis minor ac minus pertinax est, prout ipsa malitia acquisita variat.

Naturalis illa repugnantia per gratiam verbo Dei conjunctam in ipsa conversione sensim minuitur, tandemque vincitur, neque adeo ipsa praecise sumta impedit conversionem. Altera vero seu malitiosa resistentia, quae naturali superadditur, sicut non omnibus irregenitis aeque communis est, ita ab ea abstinere possunt homines ex viribus liberi arbitrii, aut, si non nunc possunt post habitus vitiosos contractos, ante tamen, si educatio recta et assuefactio ad virtutes accessisset, carere quadantenus ea potuissent.

Vid. pluribus de his differentem b. Musaeum de Aet. El. Decr. cap. XI. § 38Ö. sqq. Conf. b. J. Olear. Contin. Isag. Carpzov. in Libb. Symbol, p. m. 1230.

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Galvinianorum, qui statuunt, Deum electos convertere per motum irresistibilem, ita, ut infallibiliter et absolute convertantur, nec resistere operosae gratiae queant aut eam repellere. . . Sic in judiciis Synodi Dordracenae Britanni p. 131.: ,Ad hoc ipsum opus regenerationis habet se homo mere passive‘ (hactenus bene) neque est in voluntate potestatis humanae, impedire Deum sic immediate regenerantem.‘ Sic Palatini p. 139.: ,Deus operatur conversionem supereminente magnitudine potentiae suae et pro efficacitate roboris virium suarum, qua omnia sibi potest subjicere. Tam efficax, tam potens Dei operatio optimo maximo jure dici potest irresistibilis. Tum ex parte gratiae Dei, tum ex parte voluntatis. Ex parte gratiae, quia efficax Dei operatio est in actu posita, cui nemo potest resistere, Rom. 9, 19. Luc. 21. Act. 11, 17. Ex parte voluntatis, nam subdita gratiae efficaci jam non vult resistere, et quia non vult, necessario non vult, sicque resistere velle non potest salva sua libertate. Nam unumquodque, dum est, necessarium‘ etc. Et post: ,Quasi omnipotentissimam Dei actionem impedire possit et eludere pulvis et cinis!‘ . . .


### On Regeneration and Conversion: Of the Scholastics and Papists, who also assert that free will in the *sensus…

2. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who also assert that free will in the *sensus compositus* cannot resist assisting grace. . . Where it is further to be observed: Although the Papists do not defend the irresistibility of man against efficacious grace as evidently and notoriously as the Calvinists, yet most of them defend the irresistibility or infallibility of the subsequent conversion when the efficacious grace of God is applied. . .

3. Of Jansenius and the Jansenists, who heterodoxly assert: 1) That the grace of conversion is never lacking the effect of consummated salvation. 2) That that grace works irresistibly. 3) They acknowledge no sufficient grace except that which by *actus secundus* infallibly consummates blessedness." PART III. CHAPTER IV.

see T. 3, Augustine’s own L. 2, c. 24, 25; L. 3, c. 1, sqq.; L. 8, de Gratia Christi, c. 3, sqq.

The Jansenists indeed do not wish to call the grace of conversion irresistible with the Calvinists, but they do call it invincible, unconquerable, insuperable, ineluctable, etc., which amounts to the same thing.

4. Of the Anabaptists or Mennonites, the Waterlanders in Belgium, who maintain that the Word of God operates without any resistance in the moment of regeneration; see Episcopius’s judgment on the ordinary means of conversion.” (L. c. s. 2, q. 3, f. 732, sqq.) §

40. The subject of conversion is an adult human being, turned away from God through sin, and who does not contumaciously resist the operation of the Holy Spirit.

Or the suppositum, which is spiritually changed, or in whom God works the acknowledgment of sins with sorrow for them, and faith in Christ, and who therefore himself, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, acknowledges sins, sorrows for them, apprehends by faith the promises concerning the grace of God for the sake of Christ, etc.

For infants, when they conceive faith through baptism, are indeed said to be regenerated, but not equally commonly said to be converted. Nor are they capable by reason of age of hearing the Word and the acknowledgment of sins, etc., arising from it.

Conf. blessed Joh. Olear. Contin. Isag. Carpzov. in Libb. Symbol, p. 1246.

Thus the terminus a quo of conversion is signified; see above § 18.

Now, those are said to be turned away from God through sin both those who have never had faith before, such as men born and educated outside the church in Gentilism, Judaism, or Mohammedanism, whom they call infidels, as well as those who have shaken off the faith which they once had through sins, whom consequently some name the fallen, others the relapsed.

They call the conversion of the former the first, since no other has preceded it in that subject.

They call the conversion of the latter the second or repeated or to-be-repeated, because another prior conversion (or regeneration) had preceded it in the same subject.

Indeed, there is also the repentance of those standing, or of reborn and faithful men, who still persist in the state of rebirth and grace; yet because they have sins, which they ought daily to acknowledge, detest, and, having been converted to God by faith, pray against, they are therefore rightly said to be capable of conversion from sins to God in this respect.

But it must be admitted that the term conversion is then taken more generally, which in a more special signification has as its subject only the wicked man, who is constituted in potency for union with himself to God, but is not actually united.

Quenstedtius: “By reason of the subjects, they commonly make a threefold conversion; of which the first is of infidels, never reborn and constituted outside the boundaries of the church; and thus it denotes conversion from infidelity to faith... The second is continued and of the reborn who are standing, which is nothing other than daily repentance and the mortification of the flesh or the continuous resuscitation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is in those standing or the faithful; this conversion is treated in Jer. 31:18, 19; Lam. 5:21: ‘Convert me, O Lord, and I shall be converted, for You are my God.’ The third

is reiterated, which others call reassumed, and it belongs to the reborn who have fallen into sins against conscience or from προαίρεσις [deliberate choice], and who return in turn to God and a sounder mind through true and serious repentance. This is called by the Greeks μετάνοια, resipiscence or a change of mind. This is treated in Deut. 30:2, where God’s mercy is promised to those who have fallen but are seriously repentant. Jer. 3:7, 12: "Return, backsliding Israel, and I will not cause mine anger to fall upon you" [lit: "I will not turn my face from you"]; by which words God recalls rebellious Israel to conversion, with this promise added: "I will not turn my face from you," i.e., I will not look upon you with an angry face. Ezek. 18:30: "Repent [convert yourselves] to me"; v. 32: "Turn yourselves, and live." Joel 2:12: "Turn ye even to me with all your heart," etc.

Others distinguish conversion into primary and secondary. The primary is when someone is led for the first time from a state of wrath into a state of grace; the secondary is when one who has turned away from God through mortal sins returns again to God through true and serious repentance. The Calvinists, indeed, at Wetterau in the *Acts of the Synod of Dort*, Part I, p. 711, also employ this distinction into primary and secondary conversion, but in a most false sense; for by the primary they understand the operation of irresistible grace, by which the habit of grace and the principle of acting well is infused—such an infusion of irresistible grace is totally denied by us; but by the secondary, they understand the exercise of the habit itself and the continuation of pious acts. See D. Huelseman, *de auxiliis grat.*, c. 1, § 6, p. 9." (L. c. s. 1. th. 3. f. 699. sq.)

For those who, by contumaciously resisting, place an obstacle to divine grace, as long as they conduct themselves in this way, not only are they not converted, but they themselves are the cause why they are not converted. See what we said at § 39, note d. § 41.

The subject *quo* [by which] of conversion is the human soul, on the part of the intellect and the will, and in its own way regarding the sensitive appetite. For conversion is not received in the whole man, but the man is said to be converted regarding the nobler part of himself, as the proximate and immediate subject. As is evident from what was said concerning the terms of conversion, from which and to which, § 17 sq. For although a fuller perfection of the sensitive appetite pertains to renovation, it is certain here that the sensitive appetite must at least be so far subjected to the Spirit that the production of saving faith is not hindered by the lusts of the flesh. Compare what we said concerning Regeneration, § 4 and 5, note e. § 42.

The proximate end of conversion is justification; the ultimate end on the part of men is eternal salvation, on the part of God, His glory. Which God Himself intends and for the sake of which He converts men. PART III. CHAPTER IV.

Whence men are commanded μετανοεῖν, or to do penance, εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν, Acts 2:38. Thus God is said to have granted to the Gentiles τὴν μετάνοιαν εἰς ζωήν, Acts 11:18; and Paul, 2 Cor. 7:9, 10, teaches that there is a certain μετάνοιαν εἰς σωτηρίαν. Cf. Ezek. 33:11. See the same place, Acts 11:18. § 43.

The consequence or fruit of conversion is new obedience, and therefore a purpose not to sin, but to live piously; which, indeed, if it be habitual, is born not so much of contrition as of faith. Thus John commands to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, Matt. 3:8.

According to that passage, 1 John 3:9: He who is born of God (insofar as he is reborn, and as long as he remains reborn) certainly does not commit sin (namely, sin against conscience and proceeding from a deliberate purpose and counsel of the mind). Indeed, he cannot sin (in the manner just explained), so that he might sin and nevertheless remain reborn. Rather, as soon as he sins knowingly and willingly by purpose, he immediately ceases to be reborn, as interpreted by the blessed Aegidius Hunnius in his Commentary on this passage. Just as we showed in Chapter III, § 17, that charity (the mother of holy works) is joined with faith in Christ by an inseparable bond.

For serious contrition and a purpose of sinning cannot coexist, since the former implies a serious displeasure with sins, while the latter implies complacency in sins. Whence, by force of opposition, as long as contrition lasts, a purpose of sinning cannot have a place in the same subject. But yet it must be confessed that a constant purpose not to sin, or a constancy of the will in fleeing sin, or an habitual hatred of sin, depends upon the powers of grace and the special motive of charity, which proceeds from faith kindled by the Gospel. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, German Treatise on Repentance, against J. M. Stenger, Part I, ch. I, pp. 12, 13; Part II, p. 205; Part III, ch. IX, n. I, p. 709 sqq., 715 sqq. §

44. Meanwhile, it can happen, and sometimes does happen, that reborn and converted men fall away from the state of regeneration and grace through sins, not only once but many times, and are restored to the same through conversion repeated as many times. Indeed, not only after the first and second regeneration, but always within the reborn there is depraved concupiscence; which, although it is weakened by conversion so that it may no longer reign as it did before, is nevertheless not so thoroughly subdued—either by the first, or the second, third, or fourth conversion—that it does not oppose the Spirit or affect dominion.

See Galatians 5:17; Romans 7:18. Thus, it is possible for concupiscence, when it has conceived, to bring forth sin and death, according to James 1:15. Moreover, outside of the regenerate, the world and Satan always remain and lie in wait, no less after the third and fourth conversion than after the first. However, the will of the regenerate in this life is not so thoroughly confirmed in good that it is entirely exempted from the danger of falling; although it must be confessed that, through the converting grace itself, some habit is conferred upon the will, by which it is rendered capable of the pursuit of holiness, and the more a man exercises himself in this pursuit, the more he becomes firm in good through the grace of renewal, so that he is less prone to falls, especially more serious ones, than before. For God offers grace and the forgiveness of sins to all sinners without restriction, without regard to whether they have fallen once or many times, and He asserts with an oath that He does not desire the death of any sinner, but rather that all, having repented, should live; just as the words in Ezekiel chapters 18 and 33, set forth indefinitely, teach that they are to be taken in a universal sense, as Paul in 1 Timothy 2:4 and Peter in 2 Peter 3:9 do. Therefore, it cannot be said that men who relapse after a repeated conversion are not converted except through an extraordinary grace, conferred or to be conferred from the secret and inscrutable counsel of God, apart from the common power of the Word. See entirely the blessed Musaeus, *German Treatise on Repentance against Stenger*, Part II, Chapter I, p. 126 ff., and Part III, Chapter VIII, p. 677 ff. Thus also Chrysostom: Χιλιάκις μετανοήσας, χιλιάκις εἴσελθε. Compare the blessed Kromayer, *Theological Aphorisms*, Book XII, Aphorism VII, p. 329. Gerhard: "In previous centuries, around the year 220, there were the Novatians, named after Novatus, an African and crafty man, who determined that pardon should be denied to those who repent... Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, Chapter 7, reports that the Emperor Constantine replied to Acesius the Novatian—who said that those who have fallen into sin unto death after baptism should be exhorted to repentance, but that the hope of remission should be expected not from priests, but from God—saying: 'Θὲς, Ἀκέσιε, κλίμακα, καὶ μόνος ἀνάβηθι εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν.' The occasion of the Novatian error was the apostasy of certain ones during the time of persecution, against whom Novatus judged that a certain severity should be used. To this also pertain the inconvenient expressions of the ancients. Clement, *Stromata*, Book 2: 'It appears, but it is not repentance, to ask often for those things which are often sinned.' Tertullian, *On Repentance*, 1, p. 557: 'The bolt of the font' (baptism) 'having been shut, God has placed in the vestibule a second repentance, which may open to those who knock, but only once, because it is already the second time; but never again, because it would be in vain; for is not even this once enough?' where the blessed Beatus Rhenanus shrewdly notes: 'Nay, not only once, or seven times, but seventy times seven.'... The Novatians, as is the custom of the race of heretics, varied the state of the controversy several times. For sometimes they simply denied that there was a place for repentance after baptism; sometimes they conceded that the fallen should be exhorted to repentance, but that the hope of remission should be expected not from priests, but from God; sometimes they made a distinction between more serious sins, among which the crime of denial during persecution stands out, and lighter or daily ones, granting the remission of the latter to the ministers of the church, but leaving the former to God alone. But these heretics were condemned in the Roman council, which Eusebius, Book 6, Chapter 33, says was most celebrated.... The strongest foundation of the Novatians was the saying in Hebrews 6:4–6. And indeed, this passage troubled the ancients, and therefore various explanations were sought.... The most convenient is the opinion of those who take this passage concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit, which Christ Himself denies will be forgiven either in this [age or the age to come]. PART III. CHAPTER IV.

Latin:

2. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum, qui etiam asserunt, liberum arbitrium in sensu composito non posse resistere gratiae adjuvanti.. . Ubi insuper observandum: Licet papistae irresistibilitatem hominis adversus efficacem gratiam non tam evidenter et notorie propugnent, sicuti Calvinistae, irresistentiam tamen sen infallibilitatem subsequentis conversionis, quando admovetur efficax Dei gratia, plerique defendunt. . .

3. Jansenii et Jansenistarum, qui heterodoxe asserunt: 1) quod gratia conversionis effectu consummatae salutis nunquam careat. 2) Quod illa gratia irresistibiliter operetur. 3) Nullam agnoscunt gratiam sufficientem, nisi quae actu secundo beatitudinem infallibiliter consummat, PART. III. CAP. IV.

vide T. 3. ,Augustini‘ ipsius L. 2. c. 24. 25.1. 3. c. 1. sq. 1. 8. de Gratia Christi c. 3. sq.

Nolunt quidem Jansenistae gratiam conversionis irresistibilem vocare cum Calvinianis, appellant vero eam invictissimam, invincibilem, insuperabilem, ineluctabilem etc., quod eodem recidit.

4. Anabaptistarum seu Mennonitarum, Waterlandorum in Belgio, qui statuunt, verbum Dei sine ulla resistentia in momento regenerationis operari; vide Episcopii judicium de ordinario conversionis medio.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 732. sqq.) §

40. Subjectum quod a conversionis est homo adultus,b per peccatum a Deo aversus,c quique operationi Spiritus Sancti contumaciter non d repugnat.

Sive suppositum, quod spiritualiter immutatur, seu in quo Deus agnitionem peccatorum cum dolore de illis serio et fidem in Christum operatur quodque adeo ipsum per gratiam Spiritus S. peccata agnoscit, de illis dolet, promissiones de gratia Dei propter Christum fide apprehendit etc.

Infantes enim, quando per baptismum fidem concipiunt, regenerari quidem, non autem aeque usitate converti dicuntur. Neque etiam verbi audiendi et hinc oriturae agnitionis peccatorum etc. per aetatem capaces sunt.

Conf. b. Joh. Olear. Contin. Isag. Carpzov. in Libb. Symbol, p. 1246.

Ita significatur conversionis terminus a quo; vid. supra § 18.

Dicuntur autem per peccatum aversi a Deo cum illi, qui fidem nunquam ante habuerunt, quales sunt homines extra ecclesiam in gentilismo, Judaismo aut Muhammedismo nati atque educati, quos infideles appellant, tum qui fidem, quam olim habuerant, per peccata excusserunt, quos proinde lapsos, alii relapsos nominant.

Illorum conversionem primam vocant, quippe quam alia nulla in subjecto illo antegressa est.

Horum conversionem secundam aut iteratam vel iterandam dicunt, quod in eodem subjecto alia prior conversio (aut regeneratio) antecesserit.

Datur equidem et poenitentia stantium, seu hominum renatorum et fidelium, qui in statu renascentiae et gratiae adhuc persistunt; quia tamen peccata habent, quae quotidie agnoscere, detestari et fide ad Deum conversi deprecari debent, ideo et conversionis a peccatis ad Deum hac ratione capaces esse recte dicuntur.

Sed fatendum est, conversionis vocem tunc accipi generalius, quae specialiore significatu pro subjecto habet solum hominem improbum, qui ad conjunctionem sui cum Deo in potentia constitutus, non actu conjunctus est.

Quenstedtius: ״Ratione subjectorum triplicem communiter faciunt conversionem; quarum prima est infidelium, nunquam renatorum et extra ecclesiae pomoeria constitutorum; et sic notat conversionem ab infidelitate ad fidem... Altera est continuata et renatorum stantium, quae nihil aliud est, quam quotidiana poenitentia et carnis mortificatio sive continua gratiae Spiritus S., quae in stantibus seu fidelibus est, resuscitatio; de hac conversione agitur Jer. 31, 18. 19. Thren. 5, 21.: ,Converte me, Domine, et convertar, quia tu Deus meus es.‘ Tertia

est reiterata, quam alii reassumtam vocant, estque renatorum, in peccata contra conscientiam sive ex προαφέσει lapsorum et per veram ac seriam poenitentiam vicissim ad Deum et saniorem mentem redeuntium. Haec Graecis dicitur μετάνοια, resipiscentia sive mentis mutatio. De hac agitur Deut. 30, 2., ubi lapsis, sed serio poenitentibus, promittitur Dei misericordia. Jer. 3, 7. 12.: ,Reverte, aversatrix Israel, et non avertam a vobis faciem meam‘; quibus verbis revocat Deus rebellem Israelem ad conversionem, addita hac promissione: ,Non avertam faciem meam‘, i. e., non intuebor vos irata facie. Ezech. 18, 30.: ,Convertimini ad me‘; v. 32.: ,Revertimini, et vivite.‘ Joel 2, 2.: ,Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro‘ etc.

Alii distinguunt conversionem in primam et secundam. Prima est, cum quis e statu irae in statum gratiae deducitur primum; secunda, cum aversus a Deo per peccata mortalia iterum ad Deum redit per veram ac seriam poenitentiam. Calviniani quidem Wetteravi in Actis Synod. Dordrac. P. I. p. 711. distinctionem hanc in conversionem primam et secundam etiam adhibent, sed in falsissima acceptione; per primam enim intelligunt irresistibilis gratiae operationem, qua habitus gratiae et principium bene agendi infunditur, qualis infusio irresistibilis gratiae a nobis in totum negatur; per secundam vero ipsius habitus exercitium et piorum actuum continuationem. Vide D. Huelseman. de auxiliis grat. c. 1. § 6. p. 9.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 3. f. 699. sq.)

Nam qui contumaciter resistendo gratiae divinae obicem ponunt, quamdiu se ita gerunt, non solum non convertuntur, sed etiam ipsi jn causa sunt, cur non convertantur. Vid., quae diximus ad § 39. not. d. § 41.

Subjectum quo a conversionis est anima humana ex parte intellectus ac voluntatis,b et suo modo quoad appetitum sensitivum.c Non enim in toto homine recipitur conversio, sed quoad nobiliorem sui partem, tanquam subjectum proximum et immediatum, homo converti dicitur. Quemadmodum constat ex dictis de terminis conversionis a quo et ad quem § 17. sq. Quamvis enim plenior perfectio appetitus sensitivi ad renovationem pertineat, hic tamen certum est, saltem eo usque appetitum sensitivum subjici debere Spiritui, ne, per concupiscentias carnis, fidei salvificae productio impediatur. Conf., quae de Kegener. diximus § 4. et 5. not. e. § 42.

Finis conversionis a proximus est justificatio;b ultimus ex parte hominum est salus aeterna,c ex parte Dei gloria d ejus. Quem Deus ipse intendit et cujus gratia homines.convertit. PART. III. CAP. IV.

Unde jubentur homines μετανοεί» seu poenitentiam agere, εις αφεσιν αμαρτιών, Act. 2, 38. Sic Deus dicitur dedisse gentibus την μετάνοιαν εις ζωήν Act. 11,18. et Paulus 2 Cor. 7, 9. 10. docet, esse quandam μετάνοιαν εις σωτηρίαν. Conf. Ezech. 33, 11. Vid. 1. c. Act. 11, 18. § 48.

Consequens seu fructus conversionis est nova obedientia a adeoque propositum non peccandi,b sed pie vivendi;c quod quidem, si habituale sit, non tam ex contritione, quam ex fide d nascitur. Ita Johannes jubet facere fructus dignos poenitentia Matth. 3, 8.

Juxta illud 1 Joh. 3, 9.: Qui natus est ex Deo (quatenus is est renatus, et quamdiu renatus permanet), peccatum certe non committit (peccatum scilicet contra conscientiam et ex deliberato animi proposito consilioque profectum). Imo non potest peccare (modo jam explicato), ut scilicet simul peccet, ac nihilominus renatus maneat. Quin potius, quam primum ex proposito sciens volensque peccat, confestim remtus esse desinit, interprete b. Aegid. Hunnio in Comm. ad h. 1. Prout caritatem (matrem sanctorum operum) cum fide in Christum indivulso nexu conjungi ostendimus cap. III. § 17.

Nam contritio quidem seria et propositum peccandi consistere una nequeunt, cum illa importet seriam displicentiam peccatorum, hoc autem importet complacentiam in peccatis. Unde, ex vi oppositionis, quamdiu contritio durat, propositum peccandi in eodem subjecto locum habere non potest. Sed tamen fatendum est, propositum non peccandi constans, seu constantiam voluntatis in fugiendo peccato aut habituale odium peccati, pendere a viribus gratiae et motivo speciali caritatis, ex fide per evangelium accensa proficiscentis. Conf. b. Mus: Tract. Germ, de Poenitentia, contra J. M. Stengerum. Part. I. cap. I. p. 12.13. P. II. p. 205. P. III. cap. IX. η. I. p. 709. sqq. 715. sqq. §

44. Interim fieri potest et fit nonnunquam, ut homines renati et conversi non solum semel, sed pluribus vicibus renascentiae et gratiae statu per peccata a excidant et per conversionem toties iteratam b in eundem restituantur. Nempe non solum post primam et secundam regenerationem, sed semper intra renatos est prava concupiscentia; quae, licet per conversionem infirmetur, ne regnet amplius, ut antea, non tamen vel per primam vel per secundam, tertiam aut quartam conversionem ita subigitur penitus, ut Spiritui se non opponat, aut dominium affectet.

Vid. Galat. 5, 17. Rom. 7, 18 Sic autem fieri potest, ut concupiscentia concipiens pariat peccatum et mortemf juxta Jacobi i, 15 Extra renatos autem semper supersunt et insidiantur mundus et satanas, non minus post tertiam et quartam, quam post primam conversionem. Voluntas autem renatorum in hac vita non penitus in bono confirmatur, ut a periculo lapsus plane eximatur; quamvis fatendum sit, per ipsam gratiam convertentem habitum aliquem voluntati conferri, per quem ipsa potens reddatur ad sanctitatis studium, quoque magis homo in hoc studio se exercet, hoc magis eum per gratiam renovationis fieri firmum in bono, ut lapsibus, praesertim gravioribus, minus obnoxius sit, quam antea. Deus enim gratiam et remissionem peccatorum sine restrictione omnibus offert peccatoribus, non habita ratione, utrum una an pluribus vicibus fuerint lapsi, ac jurejurando asseverat, se nolle mortem ullius peccatoris, velle autem, ut omnes acta poenitentia vivant; prout verba apud Ezechielem cap. 18. et 33. indefinite posita, sensu universali accipienda docent Paulus 1 Tim. 2, 4. et Petrus 2. Ep. 3, 9 Neque ergo dici potest, homines, qui post iteratam conversionem relabuntur, non converti, nisi per gratiam extraordinariam, ex arcano et inscrutabili Dei consilio, praeter communem verbi virtutem, collatam aut conferendam. Vid. omnino b. Mus. Tract. Germ, de Poenitentia contra Stengerum, P. II. cap. I. p. 126. sqq. et P. III. cap. VIII. p. 677. sqq. Sic autem et Chrysostomus:Χιλίάχιςμετανοήσας, χύιάχις εϊσελ&ε. Confer, b. Kromayeri Theol. Aph. L. XII. Aph. VII. p. 329. Gerhardus: ״Fuerunt superioribus saeculis circa annum 220. Novatiani, a Novato, homine Afro et vafro, dicti, qui poenitentibus veniam negandam statuerunt. . . Socrates 1.1. Histor. c. 7. refert, imperatorem Constantinum Acesio Novatiano, dicenti, eos, qui post baptismum in peccatum ad mortem inciderint, ad poenitentiam cohortandos, sed remissionis spem non a sacerdotibus, sed a Deo expectandam, respondisse: ,θέζ־, ,Aκέσιε, κλίμακα, και μόνος ανάβηΟι είς τον ουρανόν.‘ 'Αφορμή erroris Novatiani fuit quorundam apostasia tempore persecutionis, contra quos severitate quadam utendum censuit Novatus. Quo pertinent etiam incommodae locutiones veterum. Clemens lib. 2. Strom.: ,Apparet, sed non est poenitentia, saepe petere de iis, quae saepe peccantur.' Tertullianus 1. de poenit. p. 557.: ,Intinctionis' (baptismi),sera obstructa, collocavit Deus in vestibulo poenitentiam secundam, quae pulsantibus patefaciat, sed jam semel, quia jam seeundo; sed amplius nunquam, quia proxime frustra; non enim et hoc semel satis est?‘ ubi tecte annotat B. Bhenanus: ,Imo non solum semel, aut septies, sed septuagies septies.‘.. Variarunt Novatiani, ut solet haereticorum genus, aliquoties controversiae statum. Quandoque enim simpliciter negarunt, post baptismum esse poenitentiae locum; quandoque concesserunt, lapsos ad poenitentiam cohortandos esse, sed remissionis spem non a sacerdotibus, sed a Deo expectandam esse; quandoque distinctionem fecerunt inter peccata graviora, inter quae eminet crimen abnegationis in persecutione, et leviora sive quotidiana, horum quidem remissionem ecclesiae ministris concedentes, illorum vero soli Deo relinquentes. Sed damnati sunt haeretici isti in concilio Romano, quod Eusebius lib. 6. c. 33. dicit fuisse celeberrimum. . . . Potissimum Novatianorum fundamentum fuit dictum Ebr. 6, 4—6 Et sane torsit hic locus veteres, ideo variae quaesitae sunt explicationes. . . Commodissima est eorum sententia, qui locum hunc accipiunt de peccato in Spiritum S., quod Christus ipse negat remitti vel in hoc PART. III. CAP. IV.


### On Regeneration and Conversion: or in the world to come..

or in the world to come... The remaining arguments of the Novatians are of less importance. "Esau found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears," Heb. 12:17. Resp.: The little word "repentance" is taken passively for the repentance of Isaac. Esau did not find a place of repentance, that is, he could not move the mind of his father with tears and prayers so that he would revoke the blessing conferred upon Jacob, but he was forced to hear: "I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed," Gen. 27:33. (Loc. de poenit. § 14. sqq.) §

45. True repentance also, even if it be late and occurs only at the very end of life, can nevertheless be saving, although it is most dangerous to delay repentance for so long. For God offers grace to the penitent without restriction. And thus the ancients said that true repentance is never (too) late. See the blessed Krom. 1. c. Aph. V. p. 327. Cf. the blessed Mus. Tr. against Stenger P. II. cap. I. p. 145. sqq. cap. II. p. 185. sq. P. III. cap. IV. p. 479. sqq.

J. G. Walchius: "J. Melchior Stenger (of Erfurt, later of Wittstock, removed from the sacred office in the year 1670) maintained that a great repentance is either never performed by the faithful, or at most only once again: if anyone should fall away from God a third time through sins of malice, and be restored to his former state of grace and holiness through repentance, that this happens to him outside the ordinary course; that no one can attain eternal salvation unless he remains in the pursuit of a pious life until the end of mortality." (Bibliotheca th. selecta. Tom. II, 700. sq.)

The same: "Among the struggles of the Lutheran Church, and those of great importance, the Terministic controversies also hold a place, which received their name from the term of grace and salvation set by God for men. . . . He who is the author of this dispute, or provided its first material and occasion, maintained that God has established a peremptory term of grace for all men, such that if they repent before that term is completed, grace and eternal salvation are to be obtained by them; but otherwise, if the prescribed space of time is finished without repentance. . . Jo. Georg. Boesius maintained and wished to prove that God has set a peremptory term of grace for all men in a booklet of this title: 'The Peremptory Term of Human Salvation, that is, the Time of Grace set by God in His secret counsel, etc. Frankfurt, 1698,' with the censure of the theological faculty of Halle, as the inscription has it. . .

Adam Rechenberg did indeed defend a term of divine grace, but in such a way that he did not entirely agree with Boesius. For first, he maintained that a term of divine grace was established not for all men, as Boesius opined, but only for certain ones. Who these are, he defines neither accurately and distinctly, nor always clearly, and he shows himself to be inconsistent in this matter. Now he says that a term of divine grace is set for all relapsed, apostate, refractory, obstinate, blinded, and hardened sinners, as he himself speaks; now he writes that the term of divine grace pertains only to the plainly hardened, and when he establishes certain classes of them, he refers to this those who sin against the Holy Spirit, and besides these, other hardened ones, whose reason and state, however, he does not show clearly and distinctly enough. Then, he adds that the foundation of the term of divine grace is the will of God, not the antecedent [will], to which Boesius seems to refer this term, but the consequent [will], and he affirms that it is judicial. . . By these writings of Rechenberg, [they were] refuted

Ittig, the chief adversary and assailant of the term of divine grace, devoted his efforts to this. . . Not only was there a dispute between Adam Rechenberg and Thomas Ittig concerning the term of divine grace, but others also entered into the same contest, though with a different purpose. Among these, some took up arms to defend the opinion concerning the term of divine grace and took the side of Rechenberg. . . Many joined themselves with Ittig in this contest and placed their common effort into refuting the dogma of the term of divine grace and demonstrating that all sinners, of whatever condition they may be, can at any time, even up to the end of life, approach God and obtain from Him grace and eternal salvation, if they truly grieve over their sins and place their trust in the merits of Christ; and that for no one has a term of grace been established, inasmuch as it is universal and has been restored to all men by the Savior.” (L. c. p. 783, sqq.) To this pertain those sayings: Late repentance is rarely true. How will he who does not remember himself remember God at death? One day is hidden, so that all may be on guard. He who promised forgiveness did not promise tomorrow; concerning which see the blessed Kromayer, l. c. Aph. VI. p. 318. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Tract. against Stenger, P. II. cap. I. p. 150, 151, and P. III. cap. III. p. 408, 409 (and the places cited there from Matt. 24:38, 42, 44, 50; ch. 25:10, 13; Luke 21:34), likewise cap. IV. p. 479, sqq. § 46. Conversion, taken transitively, can be defined as the action of God, by which God, in an adult human—either not yet previously reborn, or after regeneration turned away from Him (God) by sins—works in his intellect and will, out of mere grace, on account of Christ, through the word of the Law the recognition of sins with serious sorrow over them, and through the word of the Gospel faith in Christ with the purpose of amending his life, for the sake of conferring upon him justification and eternal life. See above § 16 and note b. Who is the principal efficient cause of conversion; see § 32. The subject *quod* of conversion, and at the same time the term *a quo* are indicated; see § 40 and § 18. Which are the subject *quo* of conversion, according to § 41. The internal and external impulsive cause are joined here, according to § 33. This is the instrumental cause; see § 34. Which pertain to the abolition of the term *a quo*, and the term *ad quem* itself; see § 23, sqq. This is the immediate consequence of conversion and faith; see § 43. In which the end of conversion consists, according to § 42. PART III. CHAPTER V.

§ 47.

Conversion taken intransitively, or repentance, is described as an immanent action of man, by which he, anticipated and further assisted by divine grace, acknowledges his sins from the law, grieves over them, and detests them; he apprehends by faith the promises concerning the gratuitous remission of sins for the sake of Christ, offered in the Gospel, and raises himself up with confidence placed in the merit of Christ, with the purpose of a better life, for the sake of obtaining the remission of sins and eternal salvation. a See § 16, note e. b Loc. cit. c See § 35, 36. d These pertain to the retraction of sins and the former part of repentance, which they call contrition.

e These look to the abolition of sins, not only moral, on the part of the offense, but also physical, and thus to the acquisition of the very terminus ad quem of conversion, and so to the other part of repentance; see § 20, § 23. f According to those things which we said in § 43. g The final cause of conversion and repentance; see § 42. Chapter V.

Latin:

vel in futuro saeculo... Reliqua Novatianorum argumenta minoris sunt momenti. . . ,Esau non invenit poenitentiae locum, quamvis cum lacrymis eam quaereret‘, Ebr. 12, 17. Resp.: Poenitentiae vocula passive accipitur pro poenitentia Isaaci. Esau non invenit locum poenitentiae, hoc est, non potuit lacrymis ac precibus parentis animum promovere, ut benedictionem Jacobo collatam revocaret, sed audire coactus fuit: ,Benedixi ei, et benedictus erit.‘ Gen. 27, 33.“ (Loc. de poenit. § 14. sqq.) §

45. Vera quoque poenitentia, etsi sera sit et sub finem vitae demum contingat, tamen* salutaris esse potest, licet differre poenitentiam tamdiu periculosissimum* sit. Deus enim poenitentibus sine restrictione offert gratiam. Et sic veteres dixerunt, veram poenitentiam nunquam esse (nimis) seram. Vid. b. Krom. 1. c. Aph. V. p. 327. Conf. b. Mus. Tr. contra Stengerum P. II. cap. I. p. 145. sqq. cap. II. p. 185. sq. P. III. cap. Iv. p. 479. sqq.

J. G. Walchius: ״J. Melchior Stengerus (Erfurtensis, postea Wittstockiensis, a. 1670. munere sacro remotus) statuit, magnam poenitentiam a fidelibus vel nunquam, vel non nisi semel denuo peragi: si quis tertium per peccata malitiae a Deo deficiat, isque per poenitentiam in pristinum gratiae ac sanctimoniae statum restituatur, illi contingere quid extra ordinem; neminem salutem aeternam consequi posse, nisi qui in studio vitae piae usque ad finem mortalitatis permaneat.“ (Bibliotheca th. selecta. Tom. II, 700. sq.)

Idem: ,,Inter certamina ecclesiae Lutheranae, eaque magni momenti, locum etiam tenent controversiae terministicae, quae nomen suum acceperunt a termino gratiae ac salutis, a Deo hominibus positis. . . . Qui litis hujus auctor est aut praebuit primam illius materiam occasionemque, is statuit, Deum omnibus hominibus terminum gratiae peremtorium ita constituisse, ut, si isti resipiscant, antequam terminus ille absolvatur, ab iis gratia ac salus sempiterna sint impetrandae; minus autem, ubi praescriptum temporis spatium sine poenitentia conflciatur. . . Deum omnibus hominibus terminum gratiae peremtorium posuisse, statuit ac probare voluit Jo. Georg. Boesius in libello tituli hujus: ,Terminus peremtorius salutis humanae, das ist, die von Gott in seinem geheimen Rath gesetzte Gnadenzeit etc. Francof. 1698‘ cum censura facultatis theologicae Halensis, ut inscriptio habet. . .

Adamus Bechenbergius defendit quidem terminum gratiae divinae, eo autem modo, ut non penitus cum Boesio consentiret. Primum enim, non omnibns hominibus, ut Boesius opinatus est, sed quibusdam tantum terminum gratiae divinae constitutum esse, statuit. Quales isti sint, nec accurate distincteque, nec perspicue semper definit, variumque se hac in re praebet. Nunc, terminum gratiae divinae positum esse, dicit, omnibus relapsis, apostatis, refractariis, obstinatis, excaecatis et induratis peccatoribus, quemadmodum ipse loquitur; nunc, terminum gratiae divinae ad solos plane induratos spectare, scribit, ac quando certa illorum genera constituit, eos huc refert, qui in Spiritum Sanctum peccant, ac praeter hos, alios induratos, quorum rationem autem ac statum non dilucide ac distincte satis ostendit. Deinde, fundamentum termini gratiae divinae esse voluntatem Dei, addit, non liberam, ad quam Boesius terminum hunc referre videtur, sed consequentem, eamque judiciariam esse, adflrmat. . . Scriptis his Rechenbergii confutan

dis operam dedit Ittigius, princeps illius adversarius atque oppugnator termini gratiae divinae. . . Non solum inter Adamum Rechenbergium et Thomam Ittigium de termino gratiae divinae disceptatum est, sed etiam alii in idem certamen descenderunt, diverso tamen consilio. Inter hos nonnulli arma sumpserunt ad sententiam de termino gratiae divinae defendendam ac partes pro Rechenbergio susceperunt. . . Plures in certamine hoc cum Ittigio se conjunxerunt ac communem operam in eo collocarunt, ut dogma de termino gratiae divinae refellerent ac monstrarent, cunctos peccatores, cujuscumque illi sint conditionis, omni tempore usque ad vitae finem, Deum adire atque ab eo gratiam ac salutem aeternam consequi posse, si de noxis suis vere doleant atque in meritis Christi fiduciam ponant; nec ulli terminum gratiae, utpote quae universa atque a servatore omnibus hominibus reparata sit, constitutum esse.“ (L. c. p. 783, sqq.) Quo pertinent illa dicta: Sera poenitentia raro est vera. Quomodo in morte recordabitur Dei, qui non reminiscitur sui? Latet unus dies, ut observentur amnes. Qui veniam promisit, crastinum non promisit; de quibus vide b. Kromayer. 1. c. Aph. VI. p. 318. Conf. b. Mus. Tract. contra Stengerum P. II. cap. I. p. 150. 151. et P. III. cap. III. p. 408. 409. (et loca ibi citata ex Matth. 24, 38. 42. 44· 50. cap. 25, 10. 13. Duc. 21, 34.), item cap. Consequens conversionis et fidei proximum hoc est; vid. § 43 In quibus finis conversionis consistit, juxta § 42. PART. ΙΠ. CAP. V.

§ 47.

Conversio intransitive sumta,a seu poenitentia, describitur, quod sit actio immanens b hominis, qua is, gratia divina praeventus et porro adjutus,c peccata sua ex lege agnoscit, de illis dolet eaque4 detestatur, promissiones de gratuita remissione peccatorum propter Christum, in evangelio oblatas, fide e apprehendit et fiducia in Christi merito posita sese erigit, cum proposito vitae melioris,f remissionis peccatorum et salutis aeternae consequendae causa.g Vid. § 16. not. e. Loc. cit. Vid. § 35. 36. Quae pertinent ad retractationem peccatorum et partem priorem poenitentiae, quam contritionem vocant.

Spectant haec ad abolitionem non solum moralem peccatorum, ex parte offensae, verum etiam physicam, adeoque ad acquisitionem ipsius termini ad quem conversionis, et sic ad alteram poenitentiae partem; vid. § 20. § 23. Juxta ea, quae diximus § 43. Causa finalis conversionis et poenitentiae; vid. § 42. Caput V..


## 20 On Justification

ON JUSTIFICATION. § 1. Justification, which immediately follows conversion, has a forensic meaning and denotes that act by which God the Judge pronounces a man who is a sinner, and thus guilty of fault and punishment, but who believes in Christ, to be righteous; concerning which it is established not from reason, but from evangelical Scripture.

Smalcald Articles: "From this article nothing can be yielded or conceded, even if heaven and earth or whatever will not remain should fall. 'For there is no other name given among men by which we can be saved,' says Peter, Acts 4:12. 'And by his stripes we are healed,' Isa. 53:5. And upon this

In this article stands everything that we teach and live against the Pope, the devil, and the world. Therefore, we must be quite certain of it and not doubt, otherwise it is all lost, and the Pope and the devil and everything else retain the victory and the right against us." (P. II. artic. 1. p. 300.)

Apology of the Augsburg Confession: "In the fourth, fifth, and sixth, and subsequently in the twentieth article, the adversaries condemn our confession, that we teach that believers obtain forgiveness of sin through Christ without any merit, solely by faith, and they reject both quite insolently. First, that we say 'no' to the idea that sins should be forgiven to men through their own merit. Second, that we hold, teach, and confess that no one is reconciled to God, no one obtains forgiveness of sin, except solely through faith in Christ. But since such a dispute is over the highest and most important article of the entire Christian doctrine, so that a great deal depends upon this article, which also serves primarily for a clear and correct understanding of the entire Holy Scripture, and points the way alone to the unspeakable treasure and the true knowledge of Christ, and also alone opens the door into the entire Bible, without which article no poor conscience can have any true, constant, certain comfort or recognize the riches of the grace of Christ:—therefore we pray that His Imperial Majesty will graciously hear us regarding this great, weighty, and highly important matter as necessity requires." (Artic. 4. p. 86. sq.)

Luther: "This gift of God, above others, I love and venerate in you singularly, that you urge the righteousness of faith so faithfully and sincerely in all your writings. For this topic is the head and cornerstone, which alone begets, nourishes, builds, preserves, and defends the Church of God, and without it the Church of God cannot subsist for one hour." (Joh. Brentii in prophet. Amos expositio. 1530. Praefat. See Letters etc. collected by de Wette P. IV. p. 150.)

The same: "Therefore, everything depends on this article concerning Christ, and everything hangs upon it; whoever has this, has everything, and Christians must stand in the highest battle over it and constantly strive that they may remain with it; therefore, Christ and the Apostles do not without cause urge it everywhere.

For the other articles, although they are also founded in Scripture (such as: that Mary, a pure virgin, gave birth to Christ), yet it does not drive them so hard that St. Paul (when he contends over this article) even cares to name the mother, nor does he mention the honor of the virgin, but simply says in Gal. 4:4: 'Natum ex muliere,' i.e., born of a woman. But in this he is entirely and completely focused, that we do not obtain grace and salvation before God through works and the law, but solely through this Mediator, Christ.

For this is also the only article that must always suffer persecution from the devil and the world. Just as it was announced soon in the beginning in the first divine sermon that was given to man after the Fall, Gen. 3:15: 'I will put enmity between your seed and the serpent, and that same seed shall bruise your head, but you shall bruise his heel,' etc. That is precisely the enmity of which Christ speaks here, that his Christians, for the sake of his knowledge and because they preach of him, must both be excommunicated and killed.

Other articles have also had opposition, but none has caused so much bloodshed and martyrdom as this one. For it began so soon in the two brothers Cain and Abel, that the one had to die at the hands of the other, and it will not cease as long as the world stands.

Where this [article] arises, there the devil is mad and foolish and burns the world in sheer fire and bright flames out of wrath and rage.

And one sees in all histories that all heresy and error have arisen where this ar[ticle]..." Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.16 PART III. CHAP. V. fallen into, as people became secure, as if they could understand it very well, and thus fell from this into other things and began to dispute about the person of Christ, whether He were true God or mere man, and with such speculating and questioning introduced all misfortune, where one denied the divinity of Christ, another the humanity, likewise, some the person of the Holy Spirit, some the virginity of Mary: but all of them, as many as there were, also erred and were led astray in this chief article.

For in this hangs and stands everything, and it draws all the others with it, and everything is concerned with this, that whoever errs in the others, certainly does not have this one rightly either; and even if he holds the others, and does not have this one, it is all in vain.

Conversely, this article also has the grace, where one remains with it with diligence and earnestness, that it does not let one fall into heresy, nor run against Christ and His Christendom. For it certainly brings the Holy Spirit with it, who thereby illuminates the heart and keeps it in a right, certain understanding, so that it can give a pure and dry distinction and judge of all other articles of faith and powerfully maintain and defend them.

As one also well sees in the ancient Fathers: where they remained with such an article and founded their doctrine upon it and derived it from it, they remained fine and pure in all points; but where they departed from it and disputed outside of it, they also went astray and stumbled mightily; as also happened at times to the oldest, Tertullian and Cyprian.

And what is lacking not only in the Papists, but in all our sectarians who swarm against Baptism and other articles, but that they, having already fallen from this, did not concern themselves with it and instead brought up other things, and thereby lost their understanding, so that they can teach nothing right about this and cannot certainly maintain any article?

As one can well see in their books: thereafter they fall further from one error into another, until they finally lead themselves and other people into ruin.

For where this knowledge of Christ is gone, there the sun has lost its shine and it is vain darkness, so that one understands nothing more rightly and can defend oneself against no error nor false doctrine of the devil.

And even if one retains the words about faith and Christ (as they remained in the Papacy), yet there is no foundation of any article in the heart, and what more remains there is vain foam and uncertain persuasions or conceits or a painted, colored faith.

As they themselves call their faith *fidem acquisitam et informem*, that is, a loose, rotten, empty thought, which does nothing nor is of any use, neither holds nor fights when it comes to the encounter where it should hold and prove itself.

And indeed, that their boasting of faith and Christ is entirely false and lied, they prove themselves by the deed, that they will not suffer this article of the knowledge of Christ and right faith, but rage against it with excommunications and murders.

Conversely, where this sun shines and glows in the heart, there is a right certain understanding of all things, so that one can stand firm and hold to all articles, such as: that Christ is true man, born of the Virgin Mary, and also true almighty God, born of the Father from eternity, Lord over angels and all creatures; likewise, thus he believes and teaches rightly of the Holy Spirit, of Baptism, Sacrament, good works, resurrection of the dead; thus he walks simply in faith, does not dispute or be clever about God's Word, stirs up no strife nor doubt.

And where someone comes who attacks one or more of such articles, a Christian can defend himself and beat them back: for he has the right Master (the Holy Spirit), who alone reveals this article from heaven and is given to all those who hear and accept this Word or sermon of Christ.

Therefore, such a one will not let himself be led into heresy and error, and even if he perhaps errs or stum

yet, provided he does not fall away from this, he soon returns to the path; for this light consumes and drives away the clouds and darkness, and points him back and sets him upright. But if he loses this light, then there is no helping him. For where this knowledge is gone, it takes everything with it, and you may thereafter profess and confess all the articles (as the Papists do), but there is no earnestness nor right understanding, but rather one gropes in the dark, like a blind man hearing talk of colors he has never seen. That is what those do who are the best and most pious among them. For the other great multitude must fulfill what Christ says here, that they run headlong against it, blaspheme and persecute, excommunicate and murder the true Christians, for no other reason than for the sake of this knowledge, and thus they become possessed, blinded, and hardened—indeed, mere devils—out of those who do not have the knowledge of this article (even if they otherwise earnestly strive to be holy and pious), just as those who know and believe it become mere children of God.” (Exposition of the 14th, 15th, and 16th Chapters of St. John, 1538. VIII, 502—506.)

The same: “Where this doctrine remains in the pulpit, there is no danger; one is safe from all heretics and errors; this article suffers no error alongside it; thus the Holy Spirit is also present, and those who believe such things tolerate no error. But if they are led astray, it is a certain sign that they have not understood the article. Had they grasped it rightly, they would not have been deceived.” (Exposition of the 6th, 7th, and 8th Chapters of St. John, 1530—1532. VII, 2107.)

Latin:

DE JUSTIFICATIONE. § 1. Justificatio, quae conversionem proxime a sequitur, forensem significationem b habet et actum illum denotat,c quo Deus judex d hominem peccatorem adeoque reum e culpae et poenae, sed in Christum credentem,f justum pronunciat;g de quo non ex ratione, sed Scriptura h evangelica i constat.

Articuli Smalcaldici: ,,Von diesem Artikel kann man nichts weichen oder nachgeben, es falle Himmel und Erden oder was nicht bleiben will. ,Denn es ist kein ander Name den Menschen gegeben, dadurch wir können selig werden‘, spricht Petrus Actor. 4, 12. ,Und durch seine Wunden sind wir geheilet‘, Esa. 53, 5. Und auf diesem

Artikel stehet alles, das wir wider den Pabst, Teufel und Welt lehren und leben. Darum müssen wir des gar gewiss sein und nicht zweifeln, sonst ist es alles verloren und behält Pabst und Teufel und alles wider uns den Sieg und Recht.“ (P. II. artic. 1. p. 300.)

Apouogia Conf. August.: ,,Im vierten, fünften und sechsten, und hernach im zwanzigsten Artikel verdammen die Widersacher unser Bekenntniss, dass wir lehren, dass die Gläubigen Vergebung der Sünde durch Christum ohne alle Verdienst allein durch den Glauben erlangen, und verwerfen gar trötzlich beides. Erstlich, dass wir nein dazu sagen, dass den Menschen durch ihren Verdienst sollten die Sünden vergeben werden. Zum andern, dass wir halten, lehren und bekennen, dass niemand Gott versühnet wird, niemand Vergebung der Sünde erlanget, denn allein durch den Glauben an Christum. Dieweil aber solcher Zank ist über dem höchsten fürnehmsten Artikel der ganzen cfiristliehen Lehre, also dass an diesem Artikel ganz viel gelegen ist, welcher auch zu klarem richtigen Verstände der ganzen heiligen Schrift fürnehmlich dienet, und zu dem unaussprechlichen Schatz und dem rechten Erkenntniss Christi allein den Weg weiset, auch in die ganze Bibel allein die Thür aufthut, ohne welchen Artikel auch kein arm Gewissen einen rechten beständigen gewissen Trost haben oder die Reichthümer der Gnaden Christi erkennen mag: — so bitten wir, kaiserl. Majestät wollen von dieser grossen, tapfern, hochwichtigen Sachen nach Nothdürft und gnädiglich uns hören.“ (Artic. 4. p. 86. sq.)

Lutherus: ,,Hoc donum Dei, prae caeteris, in te singulariter amo et veneror, quod justitiam fidei tam fideliter et sincereurges in omnibus scriptis tuis. Hic locus enim caput et angularis lapis est, qui solus ecclesiam Dei gignit, nutrit, aedificat, sei'vat, defendit, ac sine eo ecclesia Dei non potest una hora subsistere.“ (Joh. Brentii in prophet. Amos expositio. 1530. Praefat. Vid. Briefe etc. gesammelt von de Wette P. IV. p. 150.)

Idem: ,,Darum liegt es gar an diesem Artikel von Christo und hanget alles daran; wer diesen hat, der hat alles, und müssen die Christen darob im höchsten Kampf stehen und stetigs streiten, dass sie dabei bleiben mögen; darum auch Christus und die Apostel nicht ohne Ursach allenthalben darauf dringen.

Denn die andern Artikel, wiewohl sie auch in der Schrift gegründet sind (als: dass Maria eine reine Jungfrau Christum geboren habe), doch treibet sie solche nicht so hart, dass St. Paulus (da er über diesem Artikel streitet) auch nicht achtet, die Mutter zu nennen, noch die Ehre der Jungfrauen anzeucht, sondern schlechts dahin sagt Gal. 4, 4.: ,Natum ex muliere‘, d. i. von einem Weibe geboren. Aber in dem ist er gar und ganz, dass wir nicht durch Werk und Gesetz, sondern allein durch diesen Mittler, Christum, Gnade und Seligkeit bei Gott erlangen.

Denn das ist auch allein der Artikel, der da allezeit muss Verfolgung leiden vom Teufel und der Welt. Wie denn davon verkündiget ist bald im Anfang in der ersten göttlichen Predigt, so zu dem Menschen nach dem Fall geschehen ist, 1 Mos. 3, 15.: Ich will Feindschaft legen zwischen deinem Samen und der Schlange, und derselbige Same wird dir den Kopf zertreten, du aber wirst ihn in die Ferse stechen u. s. w. Das ist eben die Feindschaft, davon Christus hier sagt, dass seine Christen um seines Erkenntnisses willen und dass sie von ihm predigen, müssen beide, in Bann gethan und getödtet werden.

Andere Artikel haben auch Anfechtung gehabt, aber keiner so viel Blutvergiessen und Marter gemacht, als dieser. Denn es auch so bald angefangen hat in den zweien Brüdern Cain und Abel, dass der eine darum hat müssen sterben von des andern Händen, und wird nicht aufhören, so lange die Welt stehet.

Wo dieser aufgehet, da ist der Teufel toll und thöricht und brennet die Welt in eitel Feuer und lichterlohe vor Zorn und Toben.

Und man siehet in allen Historien, dass alle Ketzerei und Irrthum entstanden sind, wo dieser Ar Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.16 PART. III. CAP. V. tikel gefallen ist, da die Leute sicher worden, als könnten sie ihn sehr wohl, und also von diesem auf andere Dinge gefallen und angefangen zu disputiren von der Person Christi, ob er wahrhaftiger Gott, oder lauter Mensch wäre, und mit solchem Speculiren und Fragen alles Unglück eingeführet, da einer die Gottheit Christi, ein anderer die Menschheit, item, etliche die Person des Heiligen Geistes, etliche die Jungfrauschaft Mariä verleugnet: aber alle zumal, so viel ihrer gewesen sind, auch in diesem Hauptstück ge irret und verführet haben.

Denn in diesem hanget und stehet es alles und zeucht die andern alle mit sich und ist alles um diesen zu thun, dass, wer in den andern irret, hat gewisslich auch diesen nicht recht, und ob er gleich die andern hält, und diesen nicht hat, ist es doch alles vergeblich.

Wiederum hat auch dieser Artikel die Gnade, wo man mit Fleiss und Ernst dabei bleibet, dass er nicht lässt in Ketzerei fallen, noch wider Christum und seine Christenheit laufen. Denn er bringet gewisslich den Heiligen Geist mit sich, welcher dadurch das Herz erleuchtet und hält in rechtem gewissem Verstände, dass er kann rein und dürre Unterscheid geben und richten von allen andern Artikeln, des Glaubens und dieselben gewaltiglich erhalten und vertheidigen.

Wie man auch wohl siehet in den alten Vätern: wo sie bei solchem Artikel blieben und ihre Lehre darauf gegründet und daraus geführet, sind sie in allen Stücken fein rein blieben; wo sie aber davon gegangen und ausser diesem disputirt, sind sie auch irre gangen und weidlich gestrauchelt; wie auch den ältesten, Tertulliano und Cypriano, unterweilen geschehen ist.

Und was mangelt noch nicht allein den Papisten, sondern unsern Rottengeistern allen, so wider die Taufe und andere Artikel schwärmen, denn dass sie, schon von diesem gefallen, sich nicht damit bekümmert und dafür andere Dinge aufgeworfen, und damit den Verstand verloren haben, dass sie hievon nichts Rechtes lehren und keinen Artikel gewiss erhalten können?

wie man in ihren Büchern wohl sehen kann: darnach weiter von einem Irrthum in den andern fallen, bis sie zuletzt sich und andere Leute ins Verderben führen.

Denn wo dies Erkenntniss Christi hinweg ist, da hat die Sonne ihren Schein verloren und ist eitel Finsterniss, dass man nichts mehr recht verstehet und kann sich keines Irrthums noch falscher Lehre des Teufels erwehren.

Und ob man wohl die Worte vom Glauben und Christo behält (wie sie im Pabstthum blieben sind), so ist doch kein Grund einiges Artikels im Herzen, und was mehr da bleibt, das ist eitel Schaum und ungewisse Persuasiones oder Dünkel oder ein gemalter, gefärbter Glaube.

Wie sie selbst ihren Glauben nennen Fidem acquisitam et informem, das ist, ein loser, fauler, lediger Gedanke, der nichts thut noch taugt, weder hält noch kämpft, wenn es zum Treffen gehet, dass er halten und sich beweisen soll.

Und zwar, dass ihr Rühmen vom Glauben und Christo ganz falsch und erlogen ist, beweisen sie selbst mit der That, dass sie diesen Artikel vom Erkenntniss Christi und rechtem Glauben nicht leiden wollen, sondern dawider toben mit Bannen und Morden.

Wiederum, wo diese Sonne scheinet und leuchtet im Herzen, da ist ein recht gewisser Verstand von allen Sachen, dass man kann fest stehen und halten ob allen Artikeln, als: dass Christus wahrhaftiger Mensch ist, geboren von der Jungfrau Maria, und auch wahrhaftiger allmächtiger Gott, vom Vater in Ewigkeit geboren, Herr über Engel und alle Creaturen; item, also gläubet und lehret er recht von dem Heiligen Geist, von der Taufe, Sacrament, guten Werken, Auferstehung der Todten; gehet also einfältiglich im Glauben, disputiret und klügelt nicht über Gottes Wort, richtet kein Gezänk noch Zweifel an.

Und wo jemand kömmt, der solcher Artikel einen oder mehr anficht, so kann sich ein Christ wehren und dieselben Zurückschlagen: denn er hat den rechten Meister (den Heiligen Geist), welcher allein diesen Artikel vom Himmel offenbaret und allen denen gegeben wird, so dies Wort oder Predigt von Christo hören und annehmen.

Darum wird sich ein solcher nicht lassen verführen in Ketzerei und Irrthum und ob er schon etwa fehlt oder strau

chelt, doch, so er nur hiervon nicht fället, kommt er bald wieder auf die Bahn; denn dies Licht die Wolken und Finsterniss verzehret und vertreibet und ihn wieder weiset und auf richtet. Verlieret er aber dies Licht, so ist ihm nicht zu helfen. Denn wo diese Erkenntniss weg ist, so nimmt sie es alles mit ihr, und magst darnach alle Artikel führen und bekennen (wie denn die Papisten thun), aber es ist kein Ernst noch rechter Verstand, sondern wie man im Finstern tappet, und ein Blinder von der Farbe höret reden, die er nie gesehen hat. Das thun die, so unter ihnen die Besten und Frömmsten sind. Denn der andere grosse Haufe müssen dies erfüllen, so hier Christus sagt, dass sie mit dem Kopf dawider laufen, lästern und verfolgen, bannen und morden die rechten Christen, aus keiner andern Ursache, ohne allein um dieser Erkenntniss willen und werden also besessen, verblendet und verstockt, ja eitel Teufel aus denen, so dieses Artikels Erkenntniss nicht haben (ob sie gleich sonst ernstlich trachten heilig und fromm zu sein), gleichwie aus denen, die ihn erkennen und gläuben, eitel Gottes Kinder werden.“ (Ausleg. des 14. 15. u. 16. Cap. St. Joh. 1538. VIII, 502—506.)

Idem: ,,Wo diese Lehre auf der Canzel bleibet, so hat es keine Noth, man ist sicher vor allen Ketzern und Irrthümern; dieser Artikel leidet keinen Irrthum bei sich; so ist der Heilige Geist auch dabei, und die solches gläuben, dulden keinen Irrthum. Werden sie aber verführt, so ist es ein gewisses Zeichen, dass sie den Artikel nicht verstanden haben. Hätten sie ihn recht gefasset, so wären sie nicht betrogen worden.“ (Ausleg. des 6. 7. u. 8. Cap. St. Joh. 1530—1532. VII, 2107.)


### On Justification: The same: “In my heart this one article reigns, namely, faith in Christ

The same: “In my heart this one article reigns, namely, faith in Christ; from whom, through whom, and into whom all my theological thoughts flow and reflow day and night.” (Preface to the Epistle to the Galatians. See Commentary on the Epistle of St. Paul to the Galatians. Ed. Irmischer. 1843. Vol. I, p. 3.) “

In my heart reigns, and should also reign, this one article alone, namely, faith in my dear Lord Christ, which is the sole beginning, middle, and end of all my spiritual and divine thoughts, which I may have evermore day and night.” (Opp. ed. Walch. VIII, 1524.)

The same: “And although the weary saints consider it an unnecessary thing to urge such things so firmly and evermore (for they imagine that they know it well enough and have long since learned it by heart); yet I know well how far such conceit of theirs misses the mark, and they know nothing at all of how much depends upon this piece. For where this one piece remains pure on the field, there Christendom also remains pure and fine and harmonious, and without any sects; since this piece alone, and nothing else, makes and maintains Christendom. All other pieces may also shine among false Christians and hypocrites: but where this does not remain, it is not possible to ward off any error or sectarian spirit. This I know for a truth, and have tested it so much, that I could refute neither the Turk nor the Jew, were I to act without this piece. And where sects arise or begin, have no doubt that they have certainly fallen away from this chief article, regardless of the fact that they chatter much about Christ with their mouths and adorn and decorate themselves greatly. For this piece allows no sects to arise, since it cannot be; the Holy Spirit must also be there, who does not allow sects to begin, but gives and maintains harmony. And especially where you hear an untimely and immature saint who boasts that he knows well enough that we must be saved without our works, by God’s grace, and acts as if it were a simple art for him, there doubt nothing at all that the same person does not know what he is saying, and perhaps shall never experience nor taste it. For it is not an art that lets itself PART III. CHAP. V. to finish learning, or to boast that one knows them: it is an art that wishes to keep us as students and remain the mistress. And all who truly know and understand it do not boast that they know it all; rather, they feel something of it, like a lovely taste and scent, which they pursue and run after, marvel at, and cannot grasp or fully comprehend as they would like; they thirst, hunger, and yearn for it more and more, and never grow weary of hearing or acting upon it; just as St. Paul himself confesses that he has not yet attained it; and Christ in Matthew 5 calls those blessed who feel such hunger and thirst for righteousness. And whoever desires to do so, let him think of me in this example, which I wish to confess herewith. The devil has caught me several times when I did not think of this chief article, and has so tormented me with passages of Scripture that heaven and earth became too narrow for me. Then all human works and laws were right, and there was no error in the entire Papacy. In short, no one had ever erred except Luther alone; all my best works, doctrine, preaching, and books had to be condemned. Indeed, the shameful Mahomet would almost have become a prophet to me, and both Turks and Jews would have become pure saints. Therefore, dear brother, be not proud, nor too secure and certain that you know Christ well. You hear now how I confess and acknowledge to you what the devil has been able to do against Luther, who nevertheless ought to be almost a doctor in this art: he has surely preached, composed, written, spoken, sung, and read so much about it, and yet must remain a student in this, and at times is perhaps neither student nor master. Therefore, let yourself be advised and do not say, "Hui! You are standing." But take heed and do not fall. "You know it all"; but take heed that the art does not fail you. Fear, be humble, and pray that you may grow in this art and be protected from the clever devil who is called "Little-Wise" or "Little-Knower," who knows everything and learns everything on the fly." (Exposition of Psalm 117. 1530. Walch. V, 1698. sqq.)

Chemnitius: "This single locus especially distinguishes the Church from all other nations and superstitions, just as Augustine says: 'The Church distinguishes the just from the unjust, not by the law of works, but by the law of faith.' Indeed, this locus is like a citadel and the chief bulwark of the entire Christian doctrine and religion, and if it is obscured, adulterated, or subverted, it is impossible to retain the purity of doctrine in other loci. But if this locus is preserved, all idolatries, superstitions, and whatever corruptions exist in almost all other loci collapse of their own accord; not unlike the example in 1 Kings 5:1-4, when the ark of the Lord was placed in the temple of the Philistines next to the idol Dagon, that idol was immediately moved from its place, and although it was replaced repeatedly, yet, while the ark of the Lord stood, it could not remain, and indeed was finally completely shattered. . .

We must, therefore, exert ourselves all the more to retain the genuine sense and apostolic purity of the doctrine of justification and to propagate it to posterity, nor should we allow it to be shaken from us or adulterated by any sophistic tricks, nor by force, nor by fraud. And we shall be able to accomplish this all the more easily, with God’s help, because we enter into the labors of others, John 4:38. For it was a task of immense and more than Herculean labor to extract the true light from the densest darkness and the foulest filth and pits of the Antichrist and to restore apostolic purity to the fountains of Israel; nor could this have been done unless the Holy Spirit Himself, having kindled the light of the Word, had gone before.

Therefore, it would be a shameful and impious sloth on our part if we were to lose these things, which have been handed down and demonstrated to us in this article from the prophetic and apostolic foundations with such great labor and by the wondrous benefit of God, either by learning them negligently and teaching them coldly, or by allowing them to be snatched from us in conflicts through some sort of softness. Nor should we think that in such great light there is no darkness to be feared. For we carry that treasure not in vessels of iron or bronze, but in earthen vessels, 2 Cor. 4:7, and on this path, by which

we walk, many stumbling blocks are placed here and there, against which we easily (such is our infirmity) strike. I often shudder, because Luther, I know not by what omen, very often repeats that saying in his Galatians and in Genesis: “This doctrine will be obscured again after our death.” (Loc. theol. ed. Leyser., P. II, f. 200 sq.)

Gerhard: “The greatest dignity of this article is joined with equal utility and necessity, since its pious and sincere treatment asserts the due honor to Christ, shows firm consolation to terrified consciences, establishes the distinction between Law and Gospel, excites the πληροφορίαν [full assurance] of faith necessary in true and God-pleasing invocation, and inflames the souls of the pious to a serious zeal for good works. Therefore, what Augustine says concerning the remission of sins in Enchirid. ad Laurent, cap. 64: ‘By this the church stands, which is on earth; by this that which had perished and was found does not perish,’ we can pronounce the same concerning justification, since it consists in the remission of sins. Rom. 4:7.” (Loc. de justificatione, § 2.)

Meisner: “This article is as it were the center of theology, toward which all things aim; it is the sacred ocean into which all things flow; it is the ark of faith, which keeps all things safe and uncorrupted. If one errs here with the Papists, soon the grace of God is changed into an infused habit, the merit of Christ is diminished, faith is held as a mere disposition, something inherent is substituted for evangelical righteousness, the distinction between Law and Gospel is confused, the πληροφορία [full assurance] of faith is taken away, the merit of works is established, satisfactions are urged, suffrages are sought, masses are celebrated, saints are invoked, purgatory is kindled, monasticism is chosen, and many other elective cults are introduced; as Luther most correctly pronounced in his enarration of the argument on the Epistle to the Galatians: ‘With the loss of the article of justification, the whole Christian doctrine is lost at the same time.’ But if the true sentiment is perceived in this chapter of doctrine, then almost the whole papacy is already conquered and the entire business is finished, since the rest fall beyond it and can no longer stand. So very true is that proverb of Luther, which he used quite often: ‘Justification is the article of the standing and falling church.’” (Ανθρωπολογίας sacr. Disp. XXIV. p. A. 2. b.)

Kromayer: “That the locus on justification is the most fundamental of all, extremely necessary to be known for salvation, and is truly the ομφαλόν τής θεολογίας [navel of theology] (a metaphor taken not from physics, but from architecture), anyone who is not entirely a stranger to theology will grant άκονιτί [without a struggle]. For just as all lines meet in the navel or dome of some arch, so the remaining articles of faith tend toward this center, namely, the article of justification. For whatever it behooves us to know concerning the image of God, sin, free or rather enslaved will, in short, concerning our misery, and conversely concerning the remedy, the person and office of Christ, concerning repentance, concerning faith, is carried to this article, by which we are justified and saved before God. Conversely, those things which are contained in this article concerning our misery and the remedy diffuse themselves widely through all the articles. Worthy of cedar are those things which the great Luther pronounced in ch. 21 of Genesis: ‘This is the highest article of faith, which, if you take it away, as the Jews do, or corrupt it, as the Papists do, neither can the church stand nor can God retain His glory, which is that He is merciful and that for the sake of His Son He wills to forgive sins and save.’ ... If we examine this article according to those things which enter into the definition of faith, which are presupposed, which follow, it is the nucleus and marrow of those things which enter into the definition of faith: that God, for the sake of the merit of His Son, wills to receive sinners into grace and save them eternally. This article is necessary to be known not only by a necessity of expediency, but by a simple one; not only for certain Christians who enjoy solid food, but also for those who are nursed on milk; not only for those who have space to think, but also for those placed on the threshold of conversion and in the jaws of death. ‘For whom He justified, these He also...’” PART III. CHAP. V.
