Idem: ,,In corde meo iste unus regnat articulus, scilicet, fides Christi; ex quo, per quem et in quem omnes meae diu noctuque fluunt et refluunt theologicae cogitationes.“ (Praefat. in ep. ad Gal. Vid. Commentar, in ep. S. Pauli ad Gal. Cur. Irmischer. 1843. T. I. p. 3.) ״

In meinem Herzen herrschet allein und soll auch herrschen dieser einige Artikel, nemlich der Glaube an meinen lieben Herrn Christum, welcher aller meiner geistlichen und göttlichen Gedanken, so ich immerdar Tag und Nacht haben mag, der einige Anfang, Mittel und Ende ist.“ (׳Opp. ed. Walch. VIII, 1524.)

Idem: ״Und obs die überdrüssigen Heiligen ein unnöthiges Ding achten, so fast und immerdar solches zu treiben (denn sie lassen sich dünken, dass sie es fast wohl wissen, und habens längst ausgelernt); so weiss ich doch wohl, wie weit solch ihr Dünkel fehlet, und wissen nichts überall davon, wie viel an diesem Stück gelegen ist. Denn wo dies einige Stück rein auf dem Plan bleibt, so bleibt die Christenheit auch rein und fein einträchtig, und ohne alle Rotten; sintemal dies Stück allein, und sonst nichts, macht und erhält die Christenheit. Alle andern Stücke mögen bei falschen Christen und Heuchlern auch gleissen: wo es aber nicht bleibt, da ists nicht möglich, dass man einigem Irrthum oder Rottengeist wehren möge. Das weiss ich fürwahr, und habs versucht also viel, dass ich weder Türken noch JudenGlauben könnte verlegen, wo ich ohne dies Stück sollte handeln. Und wo auch Rotten aufkommen oder anfahen, da habe du keinen Zweifel, dass sie gewisslich von diesem Hauptstück gefallen sind, unangesehen, dass sie mit dem Maul viel von Christo plaudern, und sich fast putzen und schmücken. Denn dies Stück lässt keine Rotten aufkommen, sintemal es nicht kann sein, der Heilige Geist muss auch da sein, der nicht Rotten lässt anfahen, sondern Eintracht gibt und erhält. Und sonderlich, wo du einen unzeitigen und unreifen Heiligen hörest, der sich rühmet, er wisse fast wohl, dass wir ohne unser Werk, durch Gottes Gnaden selig werden müssen, und stellet sich, als sei es für ihm eine schlechte Kunst, da zwTeifle du nichts überall, dass derselbige nicht weiss, was er sagt, solls vielleicht auch wohl nimmermehr erfahren noch schmecken. Denn es ist nicht eine Kunst, die sich lasst PART. III. CAP. V. auslernen, oder rühmen, dass man sie könne: es ist eine Kunst, die uns will zu Schülern behalten, und Meisterin bleiben. Und alle, die sie recht können und verstehen, die rühmen sich nicht, dass sie es alles können; sondern fühlen wohl etwas davon, als einen lieblichen Schmack und Geruch, dem sie nachtrachten und laufen, verwundern sich, und könnens nicht fassen noch zu Ende ergreifen, wie sie gern wollten, dürsten, hungern und sehnen sich immer mehr und mehr darnach, und werdens nicht satt zu hören noch zu handeln; wie S. Paulus selbst bekennet, dass crs noch nicht ergriffen habe; und Christus Matth. 5. selig spricht, die solchen Hunger und Durst fühlen nach der Gerechtigkeit. Und wen es gelüstet, der denke mein bei diesem Exempel, das ich hiemit bekennen will. Es hat mich der Teufel etlichemal erwischt, da ich an dies Hauptstück nicht gedacht, und mit Sprüchen der Schrift also zerplagt, dass mir Himmel und Erden zu enge ward. Da waren Menschenwerk und Gesetze alle recht, und im ganzen Pabstthum kein Irrthum. Kürzlich, es hatte niemand jemals geirret, ohne der Luther allein, alle meine besten Werke, Lehre, Predigt und Bücher mussten verdammt sein. Auch wäre mir beinahe der schändliche Mahomet zum Propheten, und beide, Türken und Juden, eitel Heiligen worden. Darum, lieber Bruder, sei nicht stolz, noch allzu sicher und gewiss, dass du Christum wohl kennest. Du hörest jetzt, wie ich dir beichte und bekenne, was der Teufel vermocht hat wider den Luther, welcher doch auch sollte schier ein Doctor sein in dieser Kunst: er hat wohl so viel davon gepredigt, gedichtet, geschrieben, geredet, gesungen und gelesen, und muss dennoch ein Schüler hierin bleiben, und zuweilen wohl weder Schüler noch Meister ist. Darum lass dir rathen und sprich nicht Hui. Dustehest; siehe aber zu und falle nicht. Du kaunsts alles; siehe aber zu, dass dir die Kunst nicht fehle. Fürchte dich, sei demüthig, und bete, dass du in dieser Kunst mögest wachsen, und behütet werdest für dem kündigen Teufel, der da heisst Klügel oder Kündelin, der alles kann und alles im Flug lernet.“ (Ausleg. des 117. Psalms. 1530. Walch. V, 1698. sqq.)

Chemnitius: ,,Hic unicus locus praecipue discernit ecclesiam a reliquis omnibus gentibus et superstitionibus, sicut Augustinus inquit: ,Ecclesia discernit justos ab injustis, non lege operum, sed lege fidei.‘ Imo hic locus est tanquam arx et praecipuum propugnaculum totius doctrinae et religionis Christianae, quo vel obscurato vel adulterato vel subverso impossibile est, puritatem doctrinae in aliis locis retinere. Salvo autem hoc loco corruunt per se omnes idolom&niae, superstitiones, et quicquid est corruptelarum in omnibus fere aliis locis; non dissimili exemplo, sicut 1 Reg. 5, 1. 2. 3. 4., cum arca Domini in templo Philistinorum collocaretur juxta idolum Dagon, statim idolum illud suo loco motum fuit, et licet saepius reponeretur, tamen, stante arca Domini, consistere non potuit, imo tandem plane disjectum fuit. . .

Eo vero magis nobis opera danda est, ut genuinum sensum et apostolicam puritatem doctrinae de justificatione retineamus et ad posteritatem propagemus, nec ullis sophisticis praestigiis, nec vi, nec fraude nobis illam vel excuti, vel adulterari patiamur. Idque eo facilius, Deo juvante, praestare poterimus, quia in aliorum labores ingredimur, Joh. 4, 38. Immensi enim et plus quam herculei laboris fuit, ex densissimis tenebris et foeditissimis antichristi sordibus et lacunis veram lucem eruere et apostolicam puritatem fontibus Israel restituere; nec potuisset hoc fieri, nisi ipso Spiritu Sancto, accenso lumine verbi praeeunte.

Flagitiosa igitur et impia esset nostra ignavia, si haec, quae tanto labore et mirando beneficio Dei ex fundamentis propheticis et apostolicis nobis in hoc articulo tradita et monstrata sunt, vel negligenter discendo, et frigide docendo amitteremus, vel in certaminibus mollitie quadam nobis eripi pateremur. Nec cogitandum est, in hac tanta luce non esse metuendas tenebras. Thesaurum enim illum gestamus non in ferreis aut aheneis, sed in fictilibus vasis, 2 Cor. 4, 7., et in via hac, qua

ambulamus, multa hinc inde offendicula posita sunt, in quae facile (quae est nostra infirmitas) impingimus. Saepe cohorresco, quod Lutherus, nescio quo omine, valde saepe in Galatis et in Genesi vocem illam repetit: ,Haec doctrina post mortem nostram rursus obscurabitur.1 “ (Loc. theol. ed. Leyser., ·P. II, f. 200. sq.)

Gerhardus: ,,Maxima hujus articuli dignitas est cum pari utilitate et necessitate conjuncta, siquidem pia et sincera ejus tractatio debitum honorem Christo asserit, firmam consolationem territis conscientiis ostendit, discrimen legis et evangelii communit, πληροφορίαν fidei in vera ac Deo grata invocatione necessariam excitat, et ad serium bonorum operum studium animas piorum inflammat. Quod igitur de remissione peccatorum Augustinus dicit in Enchirid. ad Laurent, cap. 64.: ,Per hanc stat ecclesia, quae in terris est; per hanc non perit, quod perierat et inventum est‘, idem de justificatione pronunciare possumus, quippe quae in peccatorum remissione consistit. Rom. 4, 7.“ (Loc. de justificatione, § 2.)

Meisnerus: ,,Articulus hic quasi centrum theologiae est, ad quod omnia collimant; sacer oceanus est, in quem omnia confluunt; arca fidei est, quae omnia servat tuta et illibata. Hic si erretur cum pontiflciis, mox Dei gratia mutatur in habitum infusum, Christi meritum extenuatur, fides pro sola dispositione habetur, justitiae evangelicae quiddam inhaerens substituitur, discrimen legis et evangelii confunditur, πληροφορία fidei tollitur, meritum operum stabilitur, satisfactiones urgentur, suffragia conquiruntur, missae celebrantur, sancti invocantur, purgatorium succenditur, monastice eligitur, multique alii cultus electitii introducuntur; ut rectissime pronunciarit Lutherus in enarratione argumenti super epistolam ad Galatas: ,Amisso articulo justiflcationis, amissa est simul tota doctrina Christiana.‘ Quod si vero in hoc doctrinae capite vera sententia fuerit percepta, jam totus ferme papatus expugnatus et omne negotium confectum est, siquidem caetera ultra ruunt et diutius consistere haud queunt. Adeo verissimum est illud Lutheri proverbium, quo saepius fuit usus: ,Justificatio est articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae.‘ “ (,Ανθρωπολογίας sacr. Disp. XXIV. p. A. 2. b.)

Kromayerus: ,,Locum de justificatione omnium fundamentalissimum, ad salutem cognitu extreme necessarium et vere δμφαλον τής θεο~ λογίας esse (non ex physicis, sed architectonicis metaphora petita), quilibet in theologia non plane hospes άκονιτϊ dabit. Ut enim in umbilico vel tholo alicujus fornicis omnes lineae coeunt, ita reliqui articuli fidei ad hoc centrum, articulum scilicet de justificatione, tendunt. .. Quicquid enim de imagine Dei, peccato, libero vel potius servo arbitrio, paucis, de miseria nostra, et vicissim de remedio, Christi persona et officio, de poenitentia, de fide, scire nos convenit, ad hunc articulum, quo coram Deo justificamur et salvamur, fertur. Rursus, quae continentur in hoc articulo de miseria nostra et remedio, per omnes articulos late se diffundunt. Cedro digna sunt, quae de justificationis articulo pronunciavit Megalander Lutherus in c. 21. Gen.: ,Hic summus fidei articulus est, quem, si tollas, ut Judaei, vel depraves, sicut Papistae, neque ecclesia consistere.potest neque Deus retinere potest suam gloriam, quae est, quod sit misericors et quod propter Filium condonare peccata et salvare velit.‘ . . Si secundum ea, quae fidei definitionem ingrediuntur, quae praesupponuntur, quae consequuntur, articulum hunc examinamus, nucleus est et medulla eorum, quae fidei definitionem ingrediuntur: quod Deus propter Filii sui meritum peccatores in gratiam recipere, et aeternum salvare velit. Non necessitate duntaxat expedientiae, sed simplici, non quibusdam duntaxat Christianis cibo solido gaudentibus, sed et lactis alumnis, non spatium cogitandi saltem habentibus, sed et in conversionis limine ac faucibus mortis constitutis articulus hic cognitu necessarius est. ,Quos enim justificavit, hos sal PART. III. CAP. V.


### On Justification: he justified‘, Rom. 8:30

he justified‘, Rom. 8:30. But how can those be justified to whom it is hidden in what justification consists? If the articles of faith are divided into fundamental, circum-fundamental, and non-fundamental, this one is the most fundamental of all, the ignorance of which is joined with the loss of salvation. If regard is had to the analytical order, this article constitutes the internal end of theology, through which we obtain the external end, eternal salvation; unless, perhaps, one might wish to call it the means leading most directly to salvation and therefore extremely necessary. For man the sinner is considered in theology as one to be justified and eternally blessed.“ (Theol. posit.-pol. P. I, 605 sq.) “

For when faith is posited, and through faith, which is kindled in conversion, man is immediately justified, so that in time the act by which faith is conferred upon man and the act by which man is justified are simultaneous; although the former is prior by nature, the latter posterior. Conf. the blessed Musaeus, Disp. de Justif. Hom. Pecc. coram Deo, held in the year 1650, § 12. Otherwise, indeed, the word justification is sometimes taken more broadly, so that it comprehends all the benefits of Christ’s restoration (regeneration, justification, adoption, renovation or sanctification, salvation, glorification) as if accumulated in one complex, as the blessed Hafenreffer speaks, praef. LL. Theol. p. 9. But here we follow the stricter signification, which is also the more customary one.” For although the Latin word *justificare* is composed of the noun *justus* and the verb *facere*, it does not, according to the usage of speech, especially in the Scriptures when a sinful man is said to be justified before God, denote the infusion of habitual righteousness, but rather according to the nature of the word הצדיק (see 2 Sam. 15:4, where Absalom, affecting the kingdom, offers himself as ready to justify anyone. In the divine law itself, Deut. 25:1, it is established that there must be judges who justify, i.e., absolve the just and disapprove or condemn the wicked. Whence, conversely, he is said to be an abomination to Jehovah who justifies, i.e., absolves, the wicked and who condemns the just, Prov. 17:15) and of the word δικαιοῦν among the LXX interpreters in the aforementioned places and Paul in Rom. 3 and 4, also δικαιοῦν, to justify, which Luther rightly translates: *rechtfertigen*, has been transferred from the external court to the spiritual court, in which men are placed as if before a divine tribunal and, the case being heard and the sentence passed, are absolved. Why the Holy Spirit wished to express the doctrine of justification by a judicial word, the blessed Chemnitz teaches gravely in Exam. Concil. Trident. Part I, p. 239. And the sum of these statements returns to this: that that genuine property of the word *justificare* preserves and defends the purity of the doctrine of justification both from Pharisaic leaven and from Epicurean opinions, and that the whole doctrine of justification cannot be understood more simply, more correctly, and more conveniently, and accommodated to serious use in the exercises of repentance and faith, than from the true observation of the judicial signification of the word *justificare*.

J. A. Osiander: “Just as in other trials, if a criminal is brought forward and justified, a habit of righteousness is not infused into him, but he is either absolved or condemned: so the matter stands in this place.” (Colleg. th. V, 64.) The same: “Man is justified before God having no righteousness of his own (Phil. 3:9), therefore he is justified according to the forensic acceptance of the word. For if he has no righteousness, then he is not justified physically, but in the forensic sense, because he is absolved, even though he is guilty.” (L. c. p. 64 sq.)

Dannhauer: “Justification is a moral change, not a physical act, such as it is when by the work of a physician a sick man becomes healthy, a blind man seeing,”

the work of a bath-attendant, where cold water is made hot through the removal of the former form and the induction or infusion of a new one; but moral and forensic [justification] is such as occurs when a defendant is made a free man, and an enemy is made a friend.” (Hodosoph. Phaenom. IX. p. 445.) The same: “Isa. 5:23; Prov. 17:15, where the מַצְדִּיק רָשָׁע [he who justifies the wicked] cannot mean to infuse righteousness into the wicked; for if a judge were to do that, it would not be abominable.” (Hodos. p. 445.) Scherzerus: “In the same way that God made Christ sin for us, in that same way are we made righteousness through Christ (2 Cor. 5:21). But Christ was made sin by imputation. Therefore, we also are rendered righteousness by imputation.” (System. th. p. 417.) Reuschius: “Just as the terms of accusation and condemnation here (Rom. 8:33, 34) are forensic and judicial terms, so the opposite term of justification will be forensic and judicial; which is also evident from the seat of this doctrine in Rom. 3 and 4. Thus, if to condemn a defendant is to pronounce a sentence in court against the defendant, that which is opposed to it will be to pronounce a sentence in court for him or in favor of the defendant, i.e., to absolve him; since opposites must be under the same genus, by the force of logical rules.” (Annotat. in Baieri Compend. p. 750 sq.) Quenstedtius: “Bellarminus objects (ad Rom. 5:19): ‘Adam condemned us not only forensically, nor by judging, but by imprinting original guilt; so also Christ justifies us by deleting sin and infusing grace.’ Resp.: ... 6. Bellarminus sins by extending the apostolic statement beyond the third point of comparison. The apostolic comparison is such: as condemnation is from Adam through sin, so justification is from Christ through obedience. Nor does the apostle proceed further here, since he had taught the mode of application in the preceding chapters, namely, that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us by faith (ch. 3 and 4), but the sin of Adam is propagated into us by carnal generation. See these things more at length in Gerhard in Loci Communes, on the topic of justification, § 11.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 763 sq.) The seat of the doctrine is found in Rom. ch. 3 and 4. For he is the one who is said to be justified (Rom. 8:33). As ὑπόδικος τῷ θεῷ [guilty before God], which Paul pronounces of the whole world (Rom. 3:19). The Law, however, acts like a prosecutor and renders man ὑπόδικον [guilty]. Cf. John 5:45. Indeed, it does not merely accuse man, but by bringing forward the points of the case and firm proofs, it overcomes the defendant. This is shown by the force of the word αἰτιᾶσθαι (and that προῃτιασάμεθα in Rom. 3:9) by the blessed Dannhauer, Hodos. Phaen. IX. p. 880 (643). Cf. Erasm. Schmid in Not. ad Rom. 3:9. For conscience also, like a witness or a written bond, confirms the accusation of the Law and convicts man (Rom. 2:15; Col. 2:14). And he who, although he has not been found innocent, nevertheless has one who has satisfied for his offense and pleads his case before God the Judge (Rom. 3:25; 1 John 2:1). For thus justification is opposed to accusation and condemnation (Rom. 8:33, 34). And thus it undoubtedly signifies a sentence passed by a judge in favor of the defendant, yet while preserving the justice of the judge himself. This absolution of man or reckoning of him as righteous takes place within the divine mind (not by an external act, as will happen in that final and solemn judgment), as will be evident from what follows. Although the word "to justify" sometimes also signifies the act by which, in this life, that which has been done before God is declared and continued before men by external signs, as... PART III. CHAPTER V.

Although some interpret the words of James in chapter 2 of his Epistle, verses 21 and 24, in a certain way, it must be admitted, and the same authors acknowledge, that this meaning is less proper. Quenstedtius: "The Hebrew הצדיק and the Greek δικαιονν, as often as they occur in the Scriptures, signify either 1. the acknowledgment of divine justice and the celebration of it once acknowledged, as Ps. 51:6, Luke 7:29... Or 2. the making known of a received justification by good works, as James 2:12: 'Abraham was justified by works.' Where the apostle does not speak of that justification by which we are reckoned righteous by God, but of the showing and demonstration of faith by works, by which a man proves and declares to man that he is truly righteous and faithful...

Or 3. a leading by the hand to the pursuit of justice, i.e., doctrinally, for information unto justice, as Dan. 12:3... Or 4. the continuation of justification, as Rev. 21:11... or the reiteration of an act... Or 5. a comparative probity in relation to others who sin more enormously, Ezek. 16:51: 'You have justified your sisters in all the abominations which you have committed,' i.e., you are contaminated with such impiety that your sisters, if compared with you, can in a certain way be reckoned righteous and pious...

Or 6. a Pharisaical seeking after the reputation of justice, or the imagination and arrogance of one's own justice, Luke 10:29... Or 7. a translation and reproof, Matt. 11:19 and Luke 7:35: 'Wisdom is justified by her children.' According to the blessed Luther, Brentius, etc., to be justified in this place is to be rebuked, to be accused, to be reproved, to master, to judge, to declare in the wrong, to muster. Or 8. liberation from sin, Rom. 6:7: 'He who has died has been justified from sin,' where the word δεδικαίωται is put for ήλενθέρωται, which word the apostle uses in verses 18 and 22, i.e., he has been liberated from sin. For he who is justified, or absolved in judgment, is liberated from the guilt of sin.

Or finally 10. the forensic action of a judge and of a judgment, consisting in the absolution of the accused, opposed to condemnation, or a judicial act by which someone is judicially declared and pronounced righteous. Deut. 25:1, Prov. 17:5, Matt. 12:37. And in this forensic meaning, the word 'to justify' is perpetually used in places where the justification of a sinful man before God is treated. This is evident from the opposite, condemnation (see Rom. 5:16, 8:33, 34)... Then from the exposition of Christ and the apostle, for whom δίκαιονσθοι in this matter is 'not to be condemned, not to be judged' (John 3:18), 'not to come into judgment' (John 5:24), 'to be reconciled to God' (Rom. 5:10), 'to be constituted righteous through the obedience of another' (v. 19), 'to become a participant of the blessing' (Eph. 1:3), 'to receive the remission of sins' (Acts 10:43).

We conclude, therefore, that the word 'to justify' never signifies in the Scriptures the infusing of a quality of justice into someone, but in this place denotes nothing other than to constitute one righteous judicially, or to make one righteous by an action purely extrinsic to man and which only extrinsically denominates its subject...

Latin:

vavit‘, Rom. 8, 30. Sed quomodo justificari possunt, quos latet, in quibus justificatio consistat? Quodsi articuli fidei dividantur in fundamentales, circumfundamentales et praeterfundamentales, hic omnium fundamentalissimus est, cujus ignorantia cum jactura salutis est conjuncta. Quodsi ad ordinem analyticum habetur respectus, hic articulus finem theologiae internum, per quem finem externum, salutem aeternam, obtinemus, constituit; nisi forsan medium ad salutem proxime ducens et proin extreme necessarium quis dicere velit. Ut enim justificandus et aeternum beandus est homo peccator, in theologia consideratur.“ (Theol. posit.-pol. P. I, 605. sq.),

Nam posita fide, et per fidem, quae in conversione accenditur, statim justificatur homo, ita ut tempore simul sint actus, quo homini confertur fides, et actus, quo homo justificatur; licet ille natura prior sit, hic posterior. Conf. b. Mus. Disp, de Justif. Hom. Pecc. coram Deo, Anno 1650. hab. § 12. Alias equidem vox justificationis latius nonnunquam accipitur, ita ut omnia restaurationis Christi beneficia (regenerationem, justificationem, adoptionem, renovationem seu sanctificationem, salvationem, glorificationem) uno complexu quasi cumulata comprehendat, uti loquitur b. Hafenrejfer. praef. LL. Theol. p. 9. Sed hic strictiorem significationem, quae etiam usitatior est, sequimur. Quamvis enim vox Latina justificare composita sit ex nomine justus et verbo facere, non tamen ex usu loquendi, praesertim in Seripturis, quando homo peccator coram Deo justificari dicitur, infusionem habitualis justitiae denotat, verum juxta indolem vocis הצדיק (vide 2 Sam. 15, j., ubi Absolom, regnum affectans, promturn se offert ad justificandum quemvis. In ipsa vero lege divina Deut. 25, 1. statuitur, judices esse debere, qui justificent i e. absolvant justum et improbent aut condemnent improbum.. Unde ex adverso abominabilis Jehovae esse dicitur, qui justificaverit, i. e. absolverit, improbum et qui condemnaverit justum, Proverb. 17, 15.) et vocis duat<r^ apud LXX interpretes 11. cc. et Paulum Rom. 3. et lf.., etiam 'Εο,ύηιιηι justificare, quod Lutherus recte vertit: rechtfertigen, a foro externo ad forum spirituale translatum est, in quo homines velut coram tribunali divino sistantur et cognita causa lataque sententia absolvantur. Quare autem Spiritus S. doctrinam justificationis verbo judiciali exprimere voluerit, graviter docet b. Chemnitius in Exam. Concil. Trident. Part. I. p. 239. Ac summa dictorum eo redit, quod genuina illa proprietas verbi justificare puritatem doctrinae justificationis et a pharisaico fermento et ab Epicuraeis opinionibus conservet et defendat, quodque tota doctrina justificationis non possit simplicius, rectius et commodius intelligi et ad serium ׳usum in exercitiis poenir tentias et fidei accommodari, quam ex vera observatione judicialis significationis verbi justificare.

### On Justification: Whence also this whole act of our justification is described by the Holy Spirit…

Whence also this whole act of our justification is described by the Holy Spirit through a forensic process and through forensic or judicial words. The 'accused' or υπόδικος is the sinful man, Rom. 3:19. The actor or 'accuser' is Moses, as legislator, John 5:45, and the devil, for he is the κατήγορος, the accuser of our brethren, accusing them before the sight of our God day and night, Rev. 12: 10. The 'witness' is the conscience, Rom. 2: 15. The 'advocate' is Christ, 1 John 2:2, and the Holy Spirit, Rom. 8: 26. The 'judge,' but sitting on the throne of grace, is God, 1 Cor. 4:4, 2 Tim. 4:8. There is also expressed the 'judgment' (Ps. 143:2), the 'tribunal of Christ' (Rom. 14:20, 2 Cor. 5:10), the 'handwriting' (Col. 2:14), the 'debt' (Matt. 6:12 and 18:20), the 'absolution' (Ps. 32:2)." (L. c. s. 1. th. 3. f. 737—739.)

ANTITHESIS S. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who maintain that 'to justify' in this matter denotes two things: 1.) To make one righteous out of an unrighteous one, namely, through an internal change of qualities, by which inherent sin is removed and justice is infused. 2.) To make one more righteous out of a righteous one, [by increasing] the habit of justice."

to the increasing of grace. And thus they make a twofold justification: the first, which consists in the expulsion of sin and the infusion of a habit of righteousness, and the second, which consists in the increase of the same. Thus Costerus in *Enchirid.* c. 8. p. 227: "To justify signifies to make righteous or to give righteousness, just as to heat signifies to make hot or to give heat." Becanus, P. II. Th. schol. t. 1. tr. 4. c. 2. on justification, writes: "It" is "a change... just as the change by which one becomes healthy from being sick." Bellarmine, l. 1. *de justif.* c. 3: "Just as it is commonly said that one is heated, not only he who becomes hot from being cold, but also he who becomes hotter from being hot: so also he is said to be justified, not only he who becomes righteous from being ungodly, but also he who becomes more righteous from being righteous." 3. Of the Anabaptists and Schwenkfeldians, who assert that the word "to justify" in this article does not signify to pronounce righteous, but to make a man righteous and upright by renewing, regenerating, and giving a new heart and a new spirit. (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 760. sq.)

For although human reason, even without the illumination of the Holy Spirit, understands that God delights only in the company of the righteous and admits them into the fellowship of heavenly glory and communicates Himself to be enjoyed by righteous and holy men as His friends; yet, what the true righteousness of man before God is, which one happens to attain in act and by the intuition of which one happens to be absolved, cannot be taken from the judgment of the human mind. See the blessed Rungius, *Disp. Acad.* VII., which is on the Justification of a Sinful Man before God, § 2. sqq. Indeed, from the Gospel alone, if the discourse is concerning the righteousness by the intuition of which we are pronounced righteous before God. For the Law, although it drags us to the tribunal of the judge and makes us guilty of condemnation, does not, however, show the way of escaping or obtaining absolution. Conf. the blessed Rungius, l. c. § 12. sqq. to 43. § 2.

Although justification does not import a real and intrinsic change of man; yet because through it a man becomes righteous judicially from being unrighteous, and thus the state of man is truly changed, therefore the terms from which and to which are not noted without reason. For this indeed happens in the business of regeneration or conversion and further in renovation, but not likewise in the act of justification.

Which cannot be denied, provided the judicial signification of the terms is retained. The Apology of the A. C. certainly led the way, pp. 73, 74, 82, 125. But it is said in that sense in which we otherwise say that one is made guilty, is rendered guilty, and is made immune or free from guilt, just as one is made a freedman from a slave, yet not through an intrinsic change of the subject. I say state, which imports a relation to some good or evil to be undergone; even if formally it does not import a quality, inherent in the subject, that is good or evil.

By analogy, of course, to the acts of regeneration and renovation, but an improper one and for a very different reason. Conf. the blessed Hutter, *LL. Theol. de Causa Form. Justif.* p. m. 474. b. at the end, where he writes: In the act of justification two terms are given: One is of evil, from which we are freed; the other, however, is of good, to which we are transferred. PART III. CHAP. V.

§ e.

The *terminus a quo* [the starting point] is the state or guilt of wrath and of punishment, not only temporal, but eternal, privative, and positive; which, through justification, is to be judicially removed from the subject. Here, the state and the guilt of wrath coincide entirely; although, in other contexts, the state of wrath in its breadth denotes also the intrinsic corruption of man himself.

Others say that the *terminus a quo* of justification is sin, both original and actual. They understand sin, however, considered relatively—namely, with respect to the punishment which it has merited. But this merit of sin we commonly call by the name of guilt. Wrath, however, in this place denotes the vindicatory justice of God, the effect of which is the punishment of the sinner. And thus, "children of wrath" are men obnoxious to divine wrath, or those upon whom the vindicatory justice of God terminates, as those to be punished. Eph. 2:3: to whom nothing else is owed than divine hatred and eternal rejection from the face of God, as the blessed Quistorp speaks (Comm. on Ep. to Eph. 2:3, p. 19). Indeed, the matter comes to the same thing, whether you say that a man is obnoxious to wrath or to the vindicatory justice of the judge for the inflicting of punishment, or that he is obnoxious to the punishment to be inflicted by the judge out of justice.

That this is a consequence of sin is evident from what was said above in Part II, Chapter 1, concerning sin. To this is usually referred that ύστέρησις τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ, the lack of the glory of God, Rom. 3:23, into which we fall through sins, and which is to be removed through justification.

Quenstedtius: "We say that the subject of justification, by reason of the *terminus a quo*, is man the sinner... The Apostle describes the subject to be justified: 1. From the common state of corruption, when he says that all have sinned without distinction, whether Jews or Gentiles, Rom. 2:9, 10; 3:9. 2. From the lack of glory, when he adds that they are ὑστερούμενοι τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ. Now, the glory of God is the original justice and holiness with which man, created in the image of God (Eph. 4:24), shone, so that thus the ὑστέρησις τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ, or the destitution of the glory of God, here denotes the loss of original justice and integrity, which is followed by natural ἀδυναμία, or the inability to perform justice worthy of God and equal to that which was lost. Thus, therefore, the Apostle describes the subject of justification negatively and privatively, and indeed with respect to the *terminus a quo*." (L. c. s. 1. th. 4. f. 739.) These things are certainly joined with privative punishments as if by one common guilt of both.

For insofar as man is to be intrinsically changed, so that from a sinner he may be made a believer and thus justifiable (if one may speak so), or such a one who, while divine justice is preserved, can be absolved from the guilt of sins, that pertains to regeneration or conversion. Here, however, we are bound to consider the judicial act. From man, I say, the sinner. For guilt is not to be taken away from sin, but from the sinner.

4. The *terminus ad quem* (the end point) of justification is righteousness, not indeed inherent in us, yet ours, by which we are held righteous before God, as if we ourselves had fulfilled the law of God and had made satisfaction for our sins. According to that which Paul says in 2 Cor. 5:21: "that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him (Christ)," that is, righteous by reason of the righteousness which is valid in the divine court and which imports full immunity from accusation and from the liability of privative and positive punishments, so that οὐδὲν κατάκριμα, no condemnation, remains. Rom. 8: 1. In which sense the apostle again says of himself, being justified, in Phil. 3:9: Μὴ ἔχων τὴν ἐμὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ νόμου, "not having my own righteousness, which is of the law." Although it is derived to us from elsewhere, namely through the imputation of an alien righteousness, by the power of which, however, we ourselves are reckoned or pronounced righteous and are absolved; just as Paul, in the place cited, continues, saying that he has the righteousness which is through the faith of Christ, which is of God, righteousness in faith.

B. Meisnerus: "We assert that there is primarily a fivefold righteousness of man, considered according to distinct states. The first is concreated righteousness, which by another name is called original righteousness and was nothing other than the very image of God. ... The Papists indeed presume that Adam in the state of innocence could have merited salvation through good works, but falsely. For 1. Adam was created for life, so that he did not have the necessity to merit it in the first place. 2. Good works were already owed beforehand, inasmuch as the Creator demanded them as a sign of gratitude. 3. And that righteousness was a part of the blessed life and the kingdom of heaven, Rom. 14:17, 18. Therefore it could not be the meritorious cause of salvation. ... The second righteousness is Pharisaical, when justification is presumed from the works of the law. ... The third species is imputed or evangelical righteousness, which is not to be sought in us on account of the depravity of nature and the impossible fulfillment of the law, but outside of us. ... There follows the fourth species, namely, inchoate righteousness. For since we have been absolved from sins on account of Christ’s merit imputed to us through faith, new obedience and the pursuit of good works ought to follow. For although these are not necessary for salvation, they are nevertheless required as fruits of faith. ... And this is righteousness before men in the forum of the world, which is the token of evangelical justification before God and is commended by James in chapter 2. But this inherent righteousness is only inchoate, not full, as the Papists imagine for themselves. ... The last fifth species remains, namely, consummated righteousness, with which we shall be adorned in the other life after the glorious resurrection of the bodies. ... Liability is taken away by justification, dominion by renovation, sense by death, the root by reduction to ashes and resurrection." (Meditationes sacrae in evangelia dominicalia. Witebergae, 1635. p. 576 sqq.)

ANTITHESE S. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, statuentium, rd justificare in hoc negotio duo notare: 1.) ex injusto justum facere, sci. per mutationem internam qualitatum, qua inhaerens peccatum tollatur et justitia infundatur. 2.) Ex justo justiorem efficere, habitum justi

tiae adaugendo. Atque ita duplicem faciunt justificationem: primam, quae in expulsione peccati et infusione habitus justitiae, et secundam, quae in ejusdem augmento consistat. Sic Costerus in Enchirid. c. 8. p. 227.: ,Justificare significat justum facere seu justitiam dare, sicut calefacere significat calidum facere seu calorem dare.‘ Becanus P. II. Bellarminus 1. 1. de justif. c. 3.: ,Quemadmodum usitate dicitur calefieri, non solum, qui fit calidus ex frigido, sed etiam qui ex calido fit calidior: sic etiam justificari dicitur non solum is, qui ex impio fit justus, sed ille quoque, qui ex justo fit justior‘. . . 3. Quamvis enim ratio humana etiam sine Spiritus Sancti illustratione intelligat, Deum non nisi justorum commercio delectari eosque in coelestis gloriae societatem admittere et se hominibus justis et sanctis tanquam amicis suis f ruendum communicare; tamen, quae sit vera hominis justitia coram Deo, quam actu consequi ejusque intuitu absolvi contingat, ex mentis humanae judicio sumi nequit. Vid. b. Rungii Disp. Acad. VII., quae est de Justif. Hom. Pecc. coram Deo § 2. sqq. Imo ex solo evangelio, si sermo sit de justitia, cujus intuitu coram Deo justi pronunciamur. Licet autem justificatio non importet realem et intrinsecam a hominis mutationem; quia tamen per eam.homo ex injusto b fit justus judicialiter atque ita status c hominis revera mutatur, ideo non abs re d notandi sunt termini a quo et ad quem. Haec enim in regenerationis seu conversionis et porro in renovationis negotio quidem fit, in justificationis actu non item.

Quod negari non potest, modo judiciaria vocum significatio retineatur. Praeivit certe Apologia A. C. p. 73. 74. 82. 125. Dictum autem est eo sensu, quo alias reum fieri, reum effici et immunem aut liberum a reatu fieri dicimus, aeque atque ex servo libertum, non tamen per intrinsecam subjecti mutationem. Statum dico, qui relationem importat ad bonum aliquod aut malum subeundum; etsi formaliter non importet qualitatem, subjecto inhaerentem, bonam aut malam.

Per analogiam scilicet ad actus regenerationis et renovationis, sed impropriam et ratione valde diversa. Conf. b. Hutteri LL. Theol. de Causa Form. Justif. p. m. 474. b. in fine, ubi scribit: In actu justijicationis duo dantur termini: Unus est mali, a quo liberamur; alter vero est boni, ad quod transferimur. PART. ΠΙ. CAP. V.

§ e.

Terminus a quo est status seu a reatus irae b ac poenae c non tantum temporalis, sed aeternae,d privativae e et positivae;f qui per justificationem judicialiter g a subjecto h tollendus est. Hic autem judicialem actum considerare tenemur. Ab homine, inquam, peccatore. Non enim reatus a peccato, sed a peccatore auferendus est.

Rom. 8, 1. Quo sensu iterum apostolus Phil. 3, 9. de se justificato dicit: Μή εχων την έμήν διχαιοσύνην την έχ νόμου, non habens meam justitiam, quae sit ex lege. Etsi aliunde in nos derivata, per imputationem scilicet alienae justitiae, cujus vi 1108 tamen ipsi justi reputamur aut pronunciamur et absolvimur; quemadmodum Paulus 1. c. pergit, dicens, se habere justitiam, quae per fidem Christi est, quae est ex Deo, justitiam in fide.

B. Meisnerus: ״Quintuplicem dari imprimis justitiam hominis, secundam distinctos status considerati, asserimus. Prima est justitia concreata, quae alio nomine justitia originalis dicitur et nihil fuit aliud, quam ipsa Dei imago. . . ׳Papicolae quidem autumant, Adamum in statu innocentiae per bona opera mereri potuisse salutem, sed falso. Nam 1. Adamus erat ad vitam conditus, ut primum illam mereri necesse non habuerit. 2. Bona opera jam ante erant debita, quippe quae creator in signum gratitudinis exigebat. 3. Et illa justitia pars fuit vitae beatae regnique coelorum, Rom. 14,17. 18. Ergo non potuit esse causa salutis meritoria. . . Secunda justitia est pharisaica, quum ex operibus legis justificatio praesumitur. . . Tertia species est justitia imputata vel evangelica, quae non est quaerenda in nobis ob naturae depravationem et impossibilem legis impletionem, sed extra nos. . . Sequitur species quarta, nempe justitia inchoata. Quum enim a peccatis absoluti sumus ob Christi meritum nobis per fldem imputatum, subsequi debet nova obedientia et studium bonorum operum. Licet enim haec ad salutem necessaria non sint, requiruntur tamen ut fructus fidei. . . Et haec est justitia coram hominibus in foro soli, quae justificationis evangelicae coram Deo tessera et a Jacobo commendatur c. 2. Est autem justitia inhaerens tantum inchoata non plena, ut papicolae sibi imaginantur. . . Restat ultima quinta species, nimirum justitia consummata, qua decorabimur in altera vita post gloriosam corporum resurrectionem. . . Reatus aufertur per justificationem, dominium per renovationem, sensus per mortem, radix per cinefactionem et resurrectionem.“ (Meditationes sacrae in evangelia dominicalia. Witebergae, 1635. p. 576. sqq.)


### On Justification: Dannhauerus: "Justifying grace ..

Dannhauerus: "Justifying grace ... is positive grace through the imputation of Christ’s righteousness, which righteousness is not I. essential, by whose indwelling a man might be justified and do righteous things, to which all sins relate as drops of water to a great sea; for 1. this is common to Christ with the Father and the Holy Spirit, 2. it is incommunicable *ad extra*, 3. it condemns rather than justifies, for if we were justified by it, we could not be righteous unless we were made gods. ... But V. righteousness (which alone is most perfect by merit, most precious by infinite value, most worthy of a station in the forum of justification), namely the righteousness of Christ, performed by Christ, i.e., the obedience of Christ, both active (Is. 9:6; Luke 2:11; Rom. 5:19; 10:4) and passive, performed in our stead, otherwise 'the righteousness of God,' because it is valid before God; the righteousness of the Gospel, because it is revealed in the Gospel alone; the righteousness of faith, because it is apprehended by faith (so D. Mentzerus); righteousness (acquired for all, but in act only for the faithful) imputed by λογισμῷ." (Hodosoph. Phaenom. IX. p. 456, 459—461.)

Aeg. Hunnius: "Just as the remission of sins (in which, as David and Paul testify, both the justification and the beatification of man consist) happens and is renewed daily, since we sin daily even when justified, whence we must also pray daily: 'Forgive us our debts': so also our justification is not indeed increased daily (as sanctification is), but is renewed daily. And justifying faith is not only imputed to man for righteousness at the first moment of our reconciliation with God (as if it were no longer imputed for righteousness afterwards), but always and daily, especially when it exerts its justifying ἐνέργειαν, namely, a faithful gaze upon the promise and Christ, in act, just as Abraham did when he heard the voice of God: 'So shall your seed be.' While he believes this word, the Lord continues to impute to him for righteousness his faith, by which he had also been justified before." (Exposit. ep. ad Rom. c. 4. p. 365.)

Kromayerus: "If we are justified before God through the imputation of the meritorious righteousness of Christ, justification will not admit of more and less, but will be equal for all believers, nor will it be acquired by degrees, but will be accomplished in an instant, yet it will be continued for those who persevere in faith." (Th. posit.-pol. II, 356.)

Lutherus: "I had (in 1519) a heartfelt desire and longing to understand St. Paul’s Epistle to the Romans properly, and nothing had hindered me in this until then, except for the single little word 'Justitia Dei' (righteousness of God) in the first chapter, verse 17, where Paul says: The righteousness of God is revealed in the Gospel. I was very hostile to this word, 'the righteousness of God,' and according to the usage and custom of all teachers, I had been taught and instructed no otherwise than that I must understand it in a philosophical sense as that righteousness by which God is righteous in Himself, does and works what is right, and punishes all sinners and the unrighteous, which righteousness one calls essential (formal) or actual (active) righteousness. Now, my situation was this: although I lived as a holy and blameless monk, I still found myself to be a great sinner before God and, moreover, one with an anxious and restless conscience, and I did not trust that I could reconcile God with my satisfaction and merits. Therefore, I did not love this righteous and angry God at all, who punishes sinners, but I hated Him, and (if this was not blasphemy or worthy of condemnation) I was secretly and with real earnestness angry at God; I often said: Is it not enough that God, through original sin, has already condemned us poor, miserable sinners to eternal death with all kinds of misery and tribulation of this life, alongside the terrors and threats of the Law, that He must still add more to this misery and heartache through the Gospel, and through its preaching and voice further threaten and proclaim His righteousness and stern wrath? Here I often raged in my confused conscience; yet I persisted with more reflection on the dear Paul, as to what he meant in that very place, and I had a heartfelt thirst and desire to know the same. With such thoughts I spent day and night, until through God’s grace I noticed how the words hung together, namely thus: the righteousness of God is revealed in the Gospel, as it is written: The righteous shall live by his faith. From this I learned to understand that same righteousness of God, in which the righteous lives by God’s grace and gift solely through faith,"

and noted that the Apostle’s meaning was this: that through the Gospel is revealed the righteousness which avails before God, in which God justifies us out of grace and pure mercy through faith, which in Latin is called *justitia passiva* [passive righteousness], as it is written: the righteous shall live by his faith. Here I felt at once that I was wholly reborn and had now found an open door into Paradise itself; the dear Holy Scripture also looked upon me now in a much different way than it had before. I therefore ran through the whole Bible, as I could recall it, and gathered together in other words according to this rule all its interpretations, such as: that the work of God is called that which God works in us ourselves; the power of God, whereby He makes us powerful and strong; the wisdom of God, whereby He makes us wise; and likewise the others: the strength of God, the salvation of God, the glory of God, and the like. Just as I had previously hated this little phrase, "the righteousness of God," with true earnestness, so I began, on the contrary, to esteem it as my most beloved and comforting word, and that same passage in St. Paul was in truth the right gate to Paradise for me." (Preface to the first part of his Latin books. Published Anno 1545. Opp. Hal. Tom. XIV, 460 sqq.)

The same: "I saw that first point well, that there was an absolute need for a gratuitous gift to obtain heavenly light and life, and that one must labor anxiously and diligently to understand that sentence, Rom. 1:17: 'The righteousness of God is revealed in the Gospel.' There I sought and knocked for a long time. For that term, 'the righteousness of God,' stood in the way, which was customarily explained thus: The righteousness of God is the virtue by which God Himself is formally righteous and condemns sinners. All the doctors had interpreted this passage in this way, except Augustine: The righteousness of God, that is, the wrath of God. But as often as I read this passage, I always wished that God had never revealed the Gospel. For who could love a God who is angry, judging, and condemning? Until at last, with the Holy Spirit illuminating me, I weighed the passage in Habakkuk 2:4 more diligently: 'The righteous lives by faith.' From there I gathered that life must exist from faith, and thus I referred the abstract to the concrete, and the whole of Holy Scripture was opened to me, and heaven itself." (In Genesin Enarration. Exeget. opp. lat. Erlangae. 1831. Tom. VII, 74.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who contend that that for which, or by whose intuition, a man is justified and constituted an heir of eternal life, is not, and cannot be called, the imputed righteousness of Christ, but an infused habit of righteousness and charity or newness, that is, a righteousness inherent in us, by which we observe the law. And thus they commonly make this inherent righteousness the formal cause of our justification, so that they acknowledge no imputed righteousness of Christ. Council of Trent, sess. 6, c. 7: 'The sole,' it says, 'formal cause is the righteousness of God, not that by which He Himself is righteous, but that by which He makes us righteous, by which, namely, being gifted by Him, we are renewed in the spirit of our mind, and are not only reputed, but are truly named and are righteous, receiving righteousness in ourselves, each one according to the measure which the Holy Spirit distributes to each as He wills, and according to the proper disposition and cooperation of each.'

Canon 10 holds thus: 'If anyone shall say that men are formally righteous through the righteousness of Christ, let him be anathema.' ...

2. Of the Socinians, who deny that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, or who maintain that not the merit of Christ, but our own obedience, is the cause of our justification. ...

3. Of the Arminians, who not only do not use that phrase concerning the righteousness of Christ, but even revile and cavil at it. ...

4. Of the Weigelians, who likewise, as much as in them lies, overturn the imputed righteousness of Christ entirely, along with the Papists and Socinians. For thus Weigelius ... P. 3. Postill. p. 15: 'If Christ’s suffering, dying, and merit are to be of use to us, PART III. CAP. V.

so it must not remain outside of us and be imputed to a fictitious *imputativa justitia* (imputed righteousness). No, indeed, *Christus extra nos non salvat* (Christ outside of us does not save), that is, Christ’s death outside of us is no life; his death must be in us, so that Christ is first in us.’

5. Of the Schwenkfeldians and Anabaptists, who assert that we teach a broad way of justification, ... and on the contrary maintain that justification ... is a formation toward righteousness and piety.

6. Of Andreas Osiander, who taught that we are formally righteous before God by the very essential righteousness of God dwelling in man. In a certain confession and disputation held in the year 1549, he contended: ‘The fulfillment of the Law and the obedience performed by Christ, and the remission of sins, are a preparation for righteousness; but the righteousness itself, by which we are reckoned righteous before God, is the divine nature of Christ, entering into us through faith and dwelling in us, or the essential and eternal righteousness of God, which, dwelling in us, makes us do righteous things.’ (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 777. sqq.)

Hofmann: ‘Thus I believe I am teaching according to Scripture when I call faith in the Word—which has as its content God’s present relationship to sinful humanity—the sinful man’s righteousness, or, what is the same thing, the obedience demanded of him.’ (*Schriftbeweis*, 2nd ed., I, 651.)

Latin:

Dannhauerus: ,,Gratia justifica. . . est gratia positiva per justitiae Christi imputationem, quae justitia non est I. essentialis, cujus inhabitatione homo et justificetur et justa agat, ad quam se omnia peccata habeant ut guttulae aquae ad magnum mare; nam 1. haec Christo cum Patre et Spiritu Sancto communis, 2. ad extra incommunicabilis, 3. damnat potius quam justificat, qua si justificaremur, non possemus justi esse, nisi dii efficeremur. . . Sed V. justitia (quae sola merito perfectissima, infinito valore preciosissima, statione in justificationis foro dignissima), justitia sci. Christi, a Christo praestita h. e. obedien PART. III. CAP. V. tia Christi tam activa, Es. 9, 6. Luc. 2, 11. Rom. 5, 19. 10, 4., quam passiva, vice nostri praestita, alias,justitia Dei‘, quia coram Deo valida; justitia evangelii, quia in solo evangelio revelata; justitia fidei, quia fide apprehensa (ita D. Mentzerus); justitia (omnibus acquisita, solis tamen fidelibus actu) imputata λογισμώ(Hodosoph. Phaenom. IX. p. 456. 459—461.)

Aeg. Hunnius: ,,Sicut remissio peccatorum (in qua, teste Davide et Paulo, cum justificatio, tum beatificatio hominis consistit) fit et renovatur indies, siquidem quotidie peccamus etiam justificati, unde etiam quotidie nobis orandum: ,Remitte nobis debita nostra‘: sic et justificatio nostra, non quidem augetur indies (sicut sanctificatio), sed innovatur indies. Et fides justificans non tantum in primo momento nostrae cum Deo reconciliationis imputatur homini ad justitiam (quasi postea non amplius ad justitiam imputetur), sed semper et quotidie, praesertim quando justificam suam hepyeiav, nempe fidelem intuitum in promissionem ac Christum, actu exserit, sicut Abraham faciebat, cum audiret Dei vocem: ,Sic erit semen tuum‘. Cui verbo dum credit, Dominus fidem ejus, qua et prius erat justificatus, jam quoque ad justitiam illi imputare pergit.“ (Exposit. ep. ad Rom. c. 4. p. 365.)

Kromayerus: ,,Si per imputationem justitiae Christi meritoriae coram Deo justificamur, justificatio non suscipiet magis et minus, sed omnibus credentibus erit aequalis, nec per gradus acquiretur, sed in instante peragetur, perseverantibus tamen in fide continuabitur. “ (Th. posit.-pol. II, 356.)

Lutherus: ,,Ich hatte (1519) in der Wahrheit eine herzliche Begierde und Lust, St. Pauli Epistel an die Römer eigentlich zu verstehen, und hatte mich bisher daran nichts anders gehindert, denn allein das einzige Wörtlein Justitia Bei (Gerechtigkeit Gottes) im ersten Capitel Vers 17., da Paulus spricht: Die Gerechtigkeit Gottes werde im Evangelio offenbaret. Diesem Wort,Gottes Gerechtigkeit‘ war ich sehr feind, und war nach Gebrauch und Gewohnheit aller Lehrer nicht anders berichtet und unterwiesen, denn dass ichs philosophischer Weise von solcher Gerechtigkeit verstehen müsste, in welcher Gott für sich gerecht ist, recht thut und wirket und alle Sünder und Ungerechten strafet, welche Gerechtigkeit man die wesentliche (formalem) oder wirkliche (activam) Gerechtigkeit nennt. Nun stund es um mich also: ob ich gleich als ein heiliger und unsträflicher Mönch lebte, befand ich mich doch einen grossen Sünder vor Gott und dazu eines angstliehen und unruhigen Gewissens, getrauete auch nicht mit meiner Genugthuung und Verdiensten Gott zu versöhnen. Derwegen liebete ich diesen gerechten und zornigen Gott gar nicht, welcher die Sünder strafet, sondern ich hassete denselbigen und (so dieses keine Lästerung gewesen oder zu ächten ist) zürnete heimlich und mit rechtem Ernst wider Gott; sagete oftmals: Genüget denn Gott an diesem nicht, dass er uns arme, elende Sünder und durch die Erbsünde zum ewigen Tod allbereit Verdammte mit allerlei Jammer und Trübsal dieses Lebens neben des Gesetzes Schrecken und Bedräuung beleget, dass er noch muss durchs Evangelium dieses Jammers und Herzeleides mehr machen und durch desselbigen Predigt und Stimme seine Gerechtigkeit und ernsten Zorn ferner dräuen und verkündigen? Hier ergrimmete ich oftmals in meinem verwirreten Gewissen; hielt aber dennoch mit mehrerem Nachdenken bei dem lieben Paulo an, was er doch an demselbigen Orte meinete, und hatte herzlichen Durst und Begierde, dasselbige zu wissen. Mit solchen Gedanken brachte ich Tag und Nacht zu, bis ich durch Gottes Gnade merkete, wie die Worte an einander hingen, nämlich also: die Gerechtigkeit Gottes wird im Evangelio offenbaret, wie geschrieben stehet: Der Gerechte lebet seines Glaubens. Hieraus habe ich dieselbige Gerechtigkeit Gottes, in welcher der Gerechte durch Gottes Gnaden und Gabe allein aus dem Glauben lebet, verstehen lernen,

und gemerkt, dass des Apostels Meinung diese wäre: es würde durchs Evangelium clie Gerechtigkeit offenbaret, die vor Gott gilt, in welcher uns Gott aus Gnaden und eiteler Barmherzigkeit durch den Glauben rechtfertiget, welche man zu Latein Justitiam passivam nennet, wie geschrieben stehet: der Gerechte lebet seines Glaubens. Hie fühlete ich alsbald, dass ich ganz und neu geboren wäre und nun gleich eine weit aufgesperrte Thür, in das Paradies selbst zu gehen, gefunden hätte; sähe mich auch die liebe heilige Schrift nunmals viel anders an, denn zuvor geschehen war; lief derhalben bald durch die ganze Bibel, wie ich mich derselben ׳erinnern konnte, und sammelte auch in andern Worten nach dieser Regel alle ihre Auslegungen zusammen, als: dass Gottes Werk dies heisse, dass Gott in uns selbst wirket; Gottes Kraft, damit er uns kräftig und stark machet; Gottes Weisheit, damit er uns weise machet; also die andern: Gottes Stärke, Gottes Heil, Gottes Herrlichkeit u. dgl. Wie ich nun zuvor dieses Wörtlein,Gottes Gerechtigkeit‘ mit rechtem Ernst hassete, so fing ich auch dagegen an, dasselbe als mein allerliebstes und tröstlichstes Wort theuer und hoch zu achten, und war mir derselbige Ort in St. Paulo in der Wahrheit die rechte Pforte des Paradieses.“ (Vorrede über den ersten Theil seiner lateinischen Bücher. Anno 1545 ausgangen. Opp. Hai. Tom. XIV, 460. sqq.)

Idem: ,,Ego id primum bene videbam, omnino opus esse gratuita donatione ad lucem et vitam coelestem consequendam atque anxie et sedulo laborandum de illa sententia intelligenda, Rom. 1, 17.: ,Justitia Dei revelatur in evangelio.‘ Ibi diu quaerebam et pulsabam. Obstabat enim vocabulum illud: ,Justitia Dei‘, quod usitate sic exponebatur: Justitia Dei est virtus, qua ipsa Deus est formaliter justus et damnat peccatores. Sic omnes doctores hunc locum interpretati fuerant, excepto Augustino: Justitia Dei, id est, ira Dei. Quoties vero legebam hunc locum, semper optabam, ut Deus nunquam revelasset evangelium. Quis enim possit diligere Deum irascentem, judicantem, damnantem? Donec tandem illustrante Spiritu Sancto locum Abacuc 2, 4. diligentius expenderem: ,Justus ex fide vivit.‘ Inde colligebam, quod vita deberet ex fide existere, atque ita abstractum referebam in concretum, et aperiebatur mihi tota sacra Scriptura et coelum ipsum.“ (In Genesin Enarration. Exeget. opp. lat. Erlangae. 1831. Tom. VII, 74.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 11. Pontificiorum, contendentium, illud, propter quod vel cujus intuitu homo justificatur et haeres aeternae vitae constituitur, non esse nec dici posse justitiam Christi imputatam, sed infusum justitiae et caritatis habitum vel novitatem, sive justitiam nobis inhaerentem, per quam legem observemus. Sicque communiter hanc inhaerentem justitiam faciunt justificationis nostrae formam, ut nullam agnoscant justitiam Christi imputatam. Concil. Trid. sess. 6. c. 7.: ,Unica‘, inquit, ,formalis causa est justitia Dei, non qua ipse justus est, sed qua nos justos facit, qua videl. ab eo donati renovamur spiritu mentis nostrae et non modo reputamur, sed vere justi nominamur et sumus, justitiam in nobis recipientes, unusquisque secundum mensuram, quam Sp. S. partitur singulis, prout vult et seeundum propriam cujusque dispositionem et cooperationem.‘

Canon 10. ita habet: ,Si quis dixerit, homines per Christi justitiam formaliter justos esse, anathema sit.‘ . .

2. Socinianorum, justitiam Christi nobis imputari negantium, sive statuentium, non Christi meritum, sed nostram obedientiam justificationis nostrae causam esse. . .

3. Arminianorum, qui phrasin illam de justitia Christi non modo non usurpant, sed etiam sugillant et cavillantur. . .

4. Weigelianorum, itidem imputatam Christi justitiam, quantum in ipsis est, cum pontificiis et Socinianis in totum evertentium. Sic enim Weigelius. . . P. 3. Postill. p. 15.: ,Soll uns nun nütze sein Christi Leiden, Sterben und Verdienst, PART. III. CAP. V.

so muss es nicht ausser uns bleiben und der erdichteten imputativae justitiae zugerechnet werden. Nein traun, Christus extra nos non salvat, d. i., Christi Tod ausser uns ist kein Leben, sein Tod muss in uns sein, so ist erst Christus in uns.‘

5. Schwenkfeldianorum et anabaptistarum, asserentium, nos latam justificationis viam docere, ... et e contrario statuentium, justificationem. .. esse formationem ad justitiam et pietatem. . .

6. Andreae Osiandri, qui docuit, ipsa Dei essentiali justitia in homine habitante formaliter nos justos esse coram Deo. In confess. et disputatione quadam, a. 1549. habita, contendit: ,Legis impletionem a Christo factam et obedientiam, remissionemque peccatorum esse praeparationem ad justitiam; ipsam vero justitiam, qua coram Deo justi censemur, esse divinam Christi naturam, ingredientem in nos per fidem et in nobis habitantem vel essentialem atque aeternam Dei justitiam, quae, in nobis habitans, faciat, nos justa agere.“‘ (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 777. sqq.)

Hofmannus: ,,So meine ich schriftgemäss zu lehren, wenn ich den Glauben an das Wort, welches Gottes nunmehriges Verhältniss zur sündigen Menschheit zum Inhalt hat, des sündigen Menschen Gerechtigkeit oder, was dasselbe ist, den von ihm geforderten Gehorsam nenne.“ (Schriftbeweis. 2. Aufl. I, 651.)


### On Justification: Hasius: ‘The Rationalists stand here on the side of Catholicism

Hasius: ‘The Rationalists stand here on the side of Catholicism. Hofmann also endangers the jewel of Protestant justification through his doctrine of reconciliation, since he cannot grasp it as the imputation of the merit of Christ, but rather as an actual reception into his fellowship.’ (*Hutterus redivivus*, 11th ed., p. 230.)

Luthardt: ‘Even the authority of a Hengstenberg has not been able to gain approval in the circles of church theology for his alleged improvement of the common church doctrine of justification, in which he sought to bring the Epistle of James into harmony with Paul by assuming degrees of justification (Ev. K.Z. 1866, No. 93, 94) and then believed he could exegetically justify this theory from the history of the sinful woman (Ev. K.Z. 1867, No. 23–26).’ (*Kompend. der Dogm.*, 3rd ed., p. 226.)

Thus some refer to this the right of the children of God and the inheritance of eternal life, which is conferred or adjudged to us in the divine court.

Some add the dignity of the rewards of righteousness, which we obtain in this act of justification.

Others, however, and indeed most, distinguish that act by which sonship or that inheritance, or the right to rewards, is conferred upon the faithful, from justification and refer it among its consequences.

Indeed, just as on the part of the term *a quo* (from which) there occurs such a guilt of man, originally created in the image of God and for eternal life, which imports the privation of grace and glory, otherwise to be conferred upon him, together with the obligation to undergo positive punishments (according to those things which we said in the notes b, c, d, e, f to § 3), so it is not without reason that, on the contrary, the very grace of God, as of one reconciled, paternal and at the same time ἐξουσία (authority), the right and dignity of the children of God, and the very right o...of the inheritance of eternal life, seem to be adjudged to the faithful by one act and judicial sentence of God, so that, just as when we were dragged as guilty to the tribunal of God, pressed by the guilt of habitual and actual sins, of omission and commission, we appeared as those to be excluded from eternal life and subjected to eternal torments, so in justification and through the absolutory sentence of God the Judge we are reckoned righteous, or as such, as if we had not sinned, but as if by reason of the acts committed and omitted and the habits with which we ought to have been endowed...

...we would be entirely conformed to the divine law, no longer to be deprived of, but to be gifted with eternal life, just as we are free from the obligation to undergo other torments. Nevertheless, Scripture not infrequently distinguishes them as two things: immunity from the guilt of sins and the υἱοθεσία (adoption) of the sons of God and the heavenly inheritance, the latter of which presupposes the former and is obtained by the justified through an interior or new benefit, namely, that when the an interior or new benefit—namely, that once the judicial process is finally concluded, that υἱοθεσία or adoption as sons follows; concerning which Rom. 8:15, 23, Gal. 4:5, and Eph. 1:5 may be consulted. § 5.

Therefore, it pertains to the very process of justification that God, as the judge of a man accused by the law and convicted of sins, yet at the same time believing in Christ, so examines his cause that He indeed discovers him to be destitute of his own righteousness and guilty of death and eternal damnation, but judges or imputes the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, to belong to him in such a way that, on account of it, He no longer regards him as a sinner, but absolves him from the accusation and the obligation to punishment. I say, the process by which a man is judicially transferred from a state of wrath to a state of grace.

For the first thing in a judicial process is the examination of the cause. For this remains fixed and firm: that a man, even if he is a believer, does not possess his own righteousness that would avail in the tribunal of God.

This is that application of the merit of Christ to the believing man, concerning which, as pertaining to the Topic of Justification, we said something above in Chapter III, On Faith in Christ, § 7, note d. It is called imputation, not as if it were an idle or imaginary relation of another’s merit to someone else, lacking foundation and fruit, but because it is an act of the intellect (as it were, practical) and of the will of Him who exercises judgment, by which He judges that the merit of another, which was performed in the stead of another and apprehended by faith by him for whom it was performed, can be accepted with justice preserved, as if it were his own merit, and He wills to accept it in this way, as if he himself had performed this, whatever it is, from his own resources. This λογισμός Paul himself sets forth in Rom. 4:3, 4, 5, 6; he declares it otherwise, if we compare how he requested that the debt by which Onesimus was bound to Philemon be imputed to himself, Ep. to Philem. v. 18. And more examples of serious and efficacious imputation may be seen in Mark 15:27, Rom. 8:36.

Dannhauerus: "Imputed righteousness (is) a λογισμός, not 1. feigned, putative, and imaginary, as Bresser slanders, who lacks foundation and terms, relegating it to the schools of mathematicians; not 2. of debt, whose foundation and term are in man, rejected by St. Paul; not 3. of justification, where either the foundation is without the term, consisting of a bare judgment of the just without actual application, or the term is without the foundation, PART III. CHAP. V.

when righteousness is attributed to man without satisfaction having been rendered: much less to the unrighteous, such as that λογισμός of Christ in the midst of the robbers, when referred to human judgments. But [it is] first a λογισμός (a phrase taken from arithmetic) that is serious and real, the foundation of which is in Christ, the termination [of which is] toward us; 2. a gracious λογισμός, κατά χάριν; 3. a satisfactory λογισμός, the foundation of which is the λύτρον to be rendered for us; 4. a true, formal λογισμός, terminated toward us through formal appropriation and application, by which the righteousness of Christ becomes our righteousness, by which Christ himself is put on by us.” (Hodosoph. Phaenom. IX, p. 461. sq.) Ού μή λογίσηται Κύριος ἁμαρτίαν, not imputing sin, Rom. 4:8. Broad, or [it is] a final sentence, directly opposed to accusation and condemnation; so that that [word] of Paul may have place: “Who shall lay anything to the charge? Who is he that condemneth? It is God that justifieth,” etc. Who shall accuse? Who shall condemn? No one, I say. It is God who justifies, Rom. 8:33, 34. § 6. The efficient cause of the act of justification is the triune God. [It is] so called according to our mode of conceiving, or [it is] a cause virtually causing, because justification as to the thing itself is not an act really produced in God, as the acts of our will are, but, according to the nature of other immanent acts of God, it is the very essence of God, conceived by way of an act on account of the connoted object. V. b. Mus. 1. c. § 16. and in the Detailed Explanation § 63. p. 584, 585. As the act of imputing righteousness to man and not imputing sin is ascribed to God, Rom. 8:33. Thus the act of justifying is attributed to the Father, whose Son is Christ, Rom. 8:33. Of the Son it is said that He remits sins, Luke 7:47, 48, 49; Matt. 9:6. Of the Holy Spirit, that in Him, as cause and author, we are justified, 1 Cor. 6:11. And it is otherwise established that divine immanent acts are similar to works ad extra in this, that they themselves are also undivided. But nevertheless, it is to be observed concerning the Son that He not only stands in relation to justification as an efficient cause and justifies us by one act with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but also by way of a meritorious cause, insofar as He, as mediator between God and men, gave Himself as the price of redemption for all. 1 Tim. 2:5, 6. Quenstedtius: “Christ concurs in our justification under three respects:

1. Meritoriously, by obtaining for us by His merit the grace of justification.

2. Efficiently, insofar as justification is a work ad extra, common to the whole Most Holy Trinity.

3. Formally, in the application itself; for by no other thing are we righteous before God than by the righteousness acquired by Chri…Paul, in Rom. 4, presents Abraham as the father of believers, even of those who are in the New Testament, and proves by didactic induction from his example that all who believe in Christ, whether they lived in the Old or in the New Testament, are justified. This he could not do unless there were one and the same mode of justification in both testaments after the state of integrity. Those who deny this, as if con

specto Gorgonis capite turbantur axiomate philosophico, effectum sua causa non posse priorem esse. Sed inter causas physicas et morales isti distinguere deberent. Licet in causis physicis res ita se haberet (saepius autem causa et effectus temporum intervallis ne quidem in naturalibus disterminantur), in moralibus tamen fallit. Quoties enim, antequam actu solveretur λύτραν, captivum temporibus pro… ...troubled by the philosophical axiom that an effect cannot precede its cause, as if by the head of a Gorgon. But they ought to distinguish between physical and moral causes. Although in physical causes the matter might be so (though often, even in natural things, cause and effect are not separated by intervals of time), in moral matters, however, it fails. For how often, before the ransom (λύτραν) was actually paid, have we seen a captive in the times immediately preceding a wa r, before the λύτραν (ransom) was actually paid, provided that sufficient security had been given!

But the divine decree and promise, by their own certainty, surpass every connection that intervenes between physical causes and their effects.

As to why God did not send the Messiah immediately after the fall, but only in the fullness of time (Gal. 4:4), we indeed consider the will of the Doer to be the entire reason for the deed; meanwhile, *a posteriori*, certain reasons can be brought forward, namely, that grace might stand long-awaited, and that men, pressed by the yoke of ceremonial laws, might yearn all the more anxiously for the future Messiah.

For as it is held in the trite verse: "He does not feel the sweet, who has not tasted the bitter." Therefore, however much the act of redemption was performed only in the fullness of time, its fruit nevertheless extended both forward and backward.

And so, as many as were saved, whether in the Old or New Testament, were saved through the merit of Christ; and as many as were damned, whether in the Old or New Testament, were damned on account of the contempt of the merit of Christ, or, which is the same thing, on account of unbelief.

Sie aliqui huc referunt jus filiorum Dei et haereditatem vitae aeternae, quae nobis in foro divino conferatur sive adjudicetur.

Quidam dignitatem praemiorum justitiae, quam in hoc justificationis actu consequamur, addunt.

Alii tamen, et fere plerique, actum illum, quo fidelibus filiatio aut haereditas illa, aut jus praemiorum confertur, a justificatione distinguunt et inter consequentia ejus referunt.

Equidem quemadmodum ex parte termini a quo occurrit hominis ad imaginem Dei vitamque aeternam primum conditi reatus talis, qui privationem gratiae gloriaeque, alias ipsi conferendae, una cum obligatione ad poenas positivas subeundas importat (juxta ea, quae ad § 3. notis b. c, d. e. f. diximus), ita non abs re est, quod ex adverso ipsa gratia Dei, tanquam reconciliati, paterna et simul ίςουσία, jus ac dignitas filiorum Dei ipsumque jus haereditatis vitae aeternae uno actu et sententia judiciaria Dei fidelibus adjudicari videatur, ut, quemadmodum, cum ad Dei tribunal rei traheremur, peccatorum habitualium et actualium, omissionis et commissionis, reatu pressi, tanquam a vita aeterna exeludendi, cruciatibus autem aeternis subjiciendi, comparebamus, sic ia justificatione et per sententiam Dei judicis absolutoriam reputemur justi, seu tales, quasi non peccassemus, sed quasi ratione actuum commissorum atque omissorum habituumque, quibus pollere debeba

mus, legi divinae prorsus conformes essemus non amplius privandi, sed donandi vita aeterna, prout liberi ab obligatione ad cruciatus alias subeundos. Attamen Scriptura etiam non raro tanquam duo distinguit, immunitatem a reatu peccatorum et ίξουσίαν filiorum Dei atque haereditatem coelestem, quarum haec illam supponat et justificatis idteriore aut novo beneficio obtingat, scilicet, quod finito demum processu judiciali sequatur υιοθεσία illa seu adoptio in filios; de qua Rom. 8, 15. 23. Gal. 4, 5. et Eph. 1, 5. videri possunt. § 5.

Itaque ad ipsum processum a justificationis pertinet, quod Deus, tanquam judex hominis a lege accusati et peccatorum convicti, simul tamen in Christum credentis causam sic b cognoscit, ut illum quidem propria justitia destitui et mortis ac damnationis aeternae reum esse c deprehendat, Christi meritum autem fide apprehensum ita ad eum pertinere d judicet seu ei imputet,e ut propterea non amplius pro peccatore f habeat, sed ab accusatione et obligatione ad poenam g absolvat. Eum, inquam, quo homo ex statu irae in statum gratiae judicialiter transfertur.

Primum enim in processu judiciario est cognitio causae. Hoc enim fixum ac firmum manet, quod homo, etiamsi credens, non habeat propriam justitiam, quae in tribunali Dei valeat.

Quae est illa applicatio meriti Christi ad hominem credentem, de qua, tanquam ad Locum de Justificatione spectante, aliquid diximus supra cap. III. de Fide in Christum § 7. nota d. Dicitur imputatio, non quasi sit otiosa vel imaginaria, aut fundamento et fructu carens relatio meriti alieni ad alium, sed quod sit actus intellectus (velut practici) et voluntatis ejus, qui judicium exercet, quo judicat, meritum alienum, quod vice alterius praestitum et ab eo, pro quo praestitum fuit, fide apprehensum est, posse salva justitia acceptari, quasi illius proprium meritum esset, et vult illud hoc modo acceptare, quasi ille hoc, quicquid est, de suo praestitisset. Quem λογισμόν Paulus ipse tradit Rom. 4, 3. 4. 5. 6., alias autem declarat, si conferamus, quomodo is sibi debitum, quo Onesimus Philemoni obstrictus erat, imputari petiit, Ep. ad Philem. v. 18. Ac plura imputationis seriae atque efficacis exempla videri possunt Mare. 15, 27. Rom. 8, 36.

Paulo; non 3. justihabitorio, ubi vel fundamentum sine termino, constans nuda justi censura sine actuali applicatione, vel terminus sine fundamento, PART. III. CAP. V.

Phaenom. IX, p. 461. sq.) Ού μή λογιζό μένος Αμαρτίαν, non imputans peccatum, Rom. 4, 8· Lata vel at finali sententia, accusationi et condemnationi directe opposita; ut locum habeat illud Pauli: Τίς έγχαλέσει; τίς ό χαταχρίνων; Θεός ό διχαιών etc. Quis accusabitt Quis condemnabitt Nemo, inquam. Deus est, qui justificat, Rom. S, 33. 34· § 6. Causa efficiens a actus justificationis Deus b triunus c est. Secundum nostrum modum concipiendi sic dicta, seu causa virtualiter causans, quia justificatio quoad rem non est actus realiter in Deo productus, prout nostrae voluntatis actus sunt, sed juxta indolem aliorum actuum Dei immanentium ipsa Dei essentia, ob connotatum objectum per modum actus concepta. V. b. Mus. 1. c. § 16. et in der Ausführlichen Erklärung § 63. p. 584. 585. Prout actus imputandi homini justitiam et non imputandi peccor tum Deo adscribitur Rom. 6, 6. 8. Sed tamen de Filio observandum est, illum non solum tanquam causam efficientem ad justificationem se habere et uno actu cum Patre et Spiritu Sancto nos justificare, verum etiam per modum causae meritoriae, quatenus ut mediator inter Deum et homines se ipsum redemtionis pretium dedit pro omnibus. 1 Tim. 2, 5. 6. Quenstedtius: ,,Christus sub tribus rationibus ad justificationem nostram concurrit:

3. Formaliter, in ipsa applicatione; nulla enim alia re coram Deo sumus justi, quam justitia a Christo acquisita et nobis per fidem imputata.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 771.) Kromayerus: ״Meritum Christi profuit, antequam fuit; contemtus ejusdem obfuit, antequam fuit. . . Paulus c. 4. Rom. T. vixerint, justificari. Quod facere non posset, nisi unus idemque justificandi modus esset in utroque testamento post statum integritatis. Qui negant hoc, quasi con

specto Gorgonis capite turbantur axiomate philosophico, effectum sua causa non posse priorem esse. Sed inter causas physicas et morales isti distinguere deberent. Licet in causis physicis res ita se haberet (saepius autem causa et effectus temporum intervallis ne quidem in naturalibus disterminantur), in moralibus tamen fallit. Quoties enim, antequam actu solveretur λύτραν, captivum temporibus proximis bellicis dimissum fuisse vidimus, modo sufficienter cautum fuisset!

Sed decretum et promissio divina sua certitudine nexum omnem, qui causas physicas et earum effectum intercedit, superat.

Ut enim habetur in trito versiculo: ,Dulcia non sentit, qui non gustavit amara.‘ Quantumvis itaque redemtionis actus in plenitudine demum temporis praestitus fuerit, fructus tamen ejusdem antrorsum et retrorsum fuit extensus.

Quotquot itaque sive in V. sive in N. T. fuerunt salvati, per meritum Christi salvati fuerunt; et quotquot sive in V. sive in N. T. damnati fuerunt, propter contemtum meriti Christi vel, quod idem est, propter incredulitatem damnati fuerunt.


### On Justification: The use of this aphorism in didactic theology is so that we may be certain…

The use of this aphorism in didactic theology is so that we may be certain concerning the fruit of the Lord’s passion, the matter imputable to us for righteousness, and the common mode of justification.

In polemics, it can be used against the Papists, who wish the fruit of the Lord’s passion to have begun only after the word τετέλεσται, i.e., "it is finished," was uttered on the cross (John 19:30); against the Socinians and certain Remonstrants, who contend that the fathers had only a shadow of future goods (when, however, it is not the benefits of Christ’s death, but Christ Himself who is exhibited in Heb. 10:1 through this word) and that they beheld the grace of God only through a lattice; and against the Calvinists, who, contrary to their own hypotheses and conscience, object that Christ is not a universal redeemer because He could not have suffered for those who were in hell at the time of His death." (Theol. posit. pol. II, 369, 370, sq.)

Scherzerus: "Cocceius abuses the apostolic passage, as if in Rom. 3:25, αφεσις and πάρεσις were distinguished in such a way that πάρεσις is a mere toleration of sins, but αφεσις is a perfect remission. This is most false and rests upon a false hypothesis.
