Quemadmodhm ex. gr. quando manus famelici oblatum ‘panem apprehendit, apprehensio ista, qua talis, hominem non saturat, posset enim apprehendere lutum vel lapidem vel alia, quibus saturari non posset; sed tota saturatio pendet ab objecto apprehenso et manducato, nempe a pane; et veluti cum ossitibundi aquam aliunde, ex fonte scii., acceptam haurit per situlam, haustio ista, quatenus talis, sitim non sedat, posset enim per situlam haurire etiam arenam aut sanguinem; verum ideo sedat sitim, quia potus, quem haurit, habet vim sedandi sitim: sic esuriens vel sitiens justitiam Matth. 5, 6. apprehendit equidem fide, ceu manu mendicante, panem, qui de coelo descendit Joh. 4, 50. 51. et situla hac animae sitibundae haurit aquam salientem in vitam aeternam Joh. 4, 14., neque tamen apprehensio et haustio ista, qua talis, sive famem spiritualem pellit, sive sitim talem restinguit, posset enim ejusmodi homo aliud quippiam heterogeneum, quod divina hac efficacia non pollet, ex. gr. merita propria imaginaria et satisfactiones, quas synagoga Romana fingit, sanctorum apprehendere, sed tota apprehensionis vis dependet a re apprehensa per fldem, απολυτρώσει scii, ac sanguine Jesu Christi, in quo fundari illam apostolus diserte innuit Rom. 3, 25.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 8—11. f. 742. sqq.)

Idem: ,,Quando fides a nobis instrumentum appellatur (quia non vi propria, sed aliena justificat), non adeo haeremus in voce instrumenti, an sc. significatu famosissimo fides instrumentum sit. Nolumus enim ea de re cum quoquam contendere, modo certum maneat, quod per fidem unice accipiamus remissionem peccatorum, quodque fides sit medium apprehendens gratiam Dei et meritum Christi. Sumimus enim causam instrumentalem vel instrumentum in latiore significatione pro medio quovis aliquid recipiente et continente. Justificare ergo fides dicitur όργαν/κώς, non quod fides remittat peccata aut absolvat a peccatis, non quod imputet nobis justitiam Christi instrumentaliter, uti Deus id facit principaliter, sed quod remissionem peccatorum et absolutionem, quam Deus per verbum et sacramenta nobis offert et conferre vult, fides apprehendat, quodque acceptet justitiam Christi, nobisque eandem applicet.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 794.)

Carpzovius: ,,Significanter dicimus, fidem esse organum apprehensivum. Non enim unius generis sunt instrumenta seu organa. Quaedam enim instrumenta sunt operativa, quae causae principali cooperantur seu quae cum agente suo operantur effectum, sicut serra instrumentum est in findendo ligno; quaedam autem dativa, per quae aliquid ab altero praestitum exhibetur, seu quae effectum ab alio productum aliis porrigunt, sicut manus divitis pauperi erogat eleemosynam; quaedam vero apprehensiva sunt, quibus res oblata accipitur et in nostram rem convertitur, sicfUt manus pauperis capit eleemosynam. Et ex ultimo hoc instrumentorum genere est fides, quia correlative ad PART. III. CAP. V. objectum suum sese habeat, ad obedientiam seil. Christi, qui est finis legis ad justitiam omni credenti, Rom. 10, 4., quam recipit ad sese, unde vocatur αποδοχή, receptio, 1 Tim. 1, 15., et per verba λαμβάνειν, καταλαυβάνειν Joh. 1, 5. 11. 12. exponitur. Ad secundum genus enim referri fides non potest, quia hac ratione cum evangelio et sacramentis confunderetur, quae sunt organa offerentia et exhibentia justitiam Christi; multo minus vero ad primum. Nihil enim confert aut cooperatur fides ad justificationem, sed tantum justitiam ad salutem imputabilem apprehendit, nec alio fine requiritur et adhibetur, quam ut obedientia per evangelium oblata etiam nostra per imputationem fiat, sicut manus, qua mendicus eleemosynam apprehendit, nihil ad ipsam eleemosynam, v. gr. nummum vel panem, confert, quae jamjam a monetario aut pistore suum esse consecuta sunt, et sicut situla non est causa restinctionis sitis, sed aqua, et non alium in finem adhibetur, quam ut aqua etiam nostra fiat. Hinc dubitari potest, an fides recte dici possit Instrumentalis causa justificationis nostrae, cum non sit operativum instrumentum justificationis nostrae.“ (Isagog. in lib. symbol. p. 206.)


### On Justification: Gerhardus: "Faith ought not to be compared to the hand apprehending a cup in…

Gerhardus: "Faith ought not to be compared to the hand apprehending a cup in which a salutary potion is contained, but it is that spiritual mouth by which we drink from the fountain of salvation; it is the spiritual food of the soul, it is the very spiritual drinking, the heavenly drink, as is evident from the 6th chapter of John." (L. de justif. § 181.)

The same: "It is one thing to be justified διὰ τὴν πίστιν, another to be justified διὰ τῆς πίστεως; the former denotes a meritorious cause, the latter, however, an instrumental one. We are not justified because of faith, as if it were some merit, but through faith, which apprehends the merit of Christ." (L. de justif. § 179.)

The same: "The particle 'if' is either αἰτιολογική or συλλογιστική, i.e., it designates a cause or a consequence. In legal discourses: 'If you do this, you shall live,' the particle 'if' is αἰτιολογική, since obedience is the cause for which eternal life is given to those who keep the law; but in evangelical promises: 'If you believe, you shall be saved,' the particle 'if' is συλλογιστική, for it denotes the mode of application divinely constituted, pertaining to faith alone." (L. de Ev. § 26.)

J. Olearius: "Faith, when related to salvation, is not our work, but pertains to the order divinely instituted, and therefore it is by no means a condition properly so called, depending on man, but a benefit divinely conferred or a requirement of the passive subject and an organ apprehending salvation, but by no means an active principle proceeding from man or influencing the effect of salvation by way of a cause properly so called." (See Carpzovius' Isag. in lib. symbol. p. 1361.)

Heerbrandus: "Faith is not a condition, nor is it required as a condition, properly speaking. Because justification is not promised or offered because of its dignity or merit, or insofar as it is a work. For faith is also imperfect; but it is a certain mode, receiving the benefit offered and given through and because of Christ... The hand is not called a condition, but a medium and instrument by which alms is received." (Compend. p. 379 sq.)

S. Schmidtius: "Indeed, justifying faith has long been called a condition by our theologians. But the condition is to be understood not as moral, but as physical, so to speak, of a necessary instrument. For when I say: If you believe, you will be saved, I do not signify a moral condition under which you are to be saved, but the necessity of the instrument through which you are to be saved. Thus we also observe the matter in natural things. If you have wings, you will fly, by which I indeed state a condition for flying, yet not a moral condition, but one of a necessary instrument or means, without which it will not be permitted for you to fly and you will attempt to fly in vain. Therefore, faith alone justifies on the part of man, which the Apostle also intends in the epistles to the Romans and Galatians, Rom. 3:20, Gal. 2:16. Faith indeed has"

OF JUSTIFICATION ... justifying others besides the fiducial apprehension, for it desires, seeks, asks, insists, promises new obedience, and whatever other act there may be. But in truth, neither are these acts the formal acts of justifying faith, but only that act which we mentioned above: that act of fiducial and appropriative apprehension, reception, or application. For if we consider the offering of divine grace and the merit of Christ, and with these the remission of sins, certainly all those other acts do not have the due relation to it, but are absolute with respect to it; only the act of fiducial, appropriative apprehension has a relation to that offering, so that it may apprehend and receive what is offered in the offering. "I was found," says the Lord, "by those who did not seek me." Behold, God offers His grace, the merit of Christ, and the remission of sins even to those who do not desire, seek, ask, or insist, and He is found by them certainly through the fiducial apprehension alone, by which what is freely offered is accepted. In these, faith soon works desire and unceasing prayers for the continuation of the grace and remission of sins once received, although even here it cannot be satisfied unless a firm trust applies the promise concerning the perpetual grace of God contained in the Scriptures." (Repetition of the Formula of Concord, p. 235.)

Osiander: "Faith does not justify as it is obedience and under a precept; for thus it behaves actively, it is a work, and therefore something legal; but insofar as it receives, and thus concurs to justification by way of a passive instrument." (Colleg. V, 140.)

Gerhard: "Just as a ring, in which a most precious gem is enclosed, is said to be worth several crowns, where the ring is not the gem and yet the ring is valued so highly on account of the gem, so faith, which apprehends the righteousness of Christ, is said to be imputed to us for righteousness, as it is the apprehending organ." (L. de justif. § 180.)

Hoepfner: "When faith is said to be imputed to the believer, the word 'faith' belongs to the class of those terms which are called μετά συμπλοκής, that is, they are complex and include a twofold concept. For faith here denotes both the thing believed and the condition of the organ, namely, the fiducial apprehension, by which the righteousness of Christ (not inherent in us, but imputable to us by the fact that it was performed by Christ in our stead for the divine law) is received, and by that fiducial reception it becomes and is reckoned by God as our righteousness. Therefore, faith is said to be imputed for righteousness when an alien righteousness, namely, that inherent in Christ, is imputed to the believer, that is, is adjudged by God, pronouncing from the tribunal of grace, to the believer as his own righteousness, no differently than if the faithful man himself had performed that righteousness valid before God. A similar meaning of the word 'faith,' including both the object and the organic act of believing, is found in Galatians 3:23 and 25: 'Before faith came,' that is, Christ to be apprehended by faith, just as a little before, namely, in verse 9 of that chapter, the apostle said: 'Until the seed should come,' that is, Christ, in whom according to the promise of grace all nations are to obtain the blessing through faith in Him. Therefore, the interpretation is false that faith, taken as an act of believing, is imputed to us, because the sole object of this imputation is righteousness. Faith, however, is the medium through which the thing imputable for righteousness or justifying is imputed to us." (Disputations on Justification, p. 1065.)

Calov: "That is, what our churches mean is that faith is indeed our act, since it is not God who believes in us, but we who believe, with God working in us; but it is not valued in the judgment of God, when faith is imputed for righteousness, as our act, and that it performs what is attributed to it either by its own dignity or even by divine exaltation beyond its own power, but [it is valued] as it apprehends the grace of God and the merit of Christ; not on account of the power of apprehension or the act itself, but on account of the object apprehended, so that all dignity, power, and virtue may be uniquely ascribed to the object, namely, the merit of Christ; faith, however, [does] this very thing only for itself... PART III. CHAP. V. appropriates it, and makes it his own, or rather applies it to the believer, so that the faithful one apprehends it through faith and claims it for himself.” (Consider. Arminianismi, Disp. 13. p. 258.)

Osiander: “Paul would argue foolishly, nay, he would contradict himself, if he were to maintain that we are justified by formed faith, yet not by works. For if we are justified by formed faith, then we are certainly justified partly by works and partly by faith, whereas faith in this matter is opposed to all works whatsoever.” (Colleg. V, 90.)

Calovius: “How could faith be an impelling cause, or how could it impel God to justify and predestine believers, and that by its own virtue, when faith here possesses no virtue or activity at all, but behaves itself merely passively and only receives the grace of God and the merit of Christ, while God, out of grace, imputes that to us as if it were our own merit? Therefore, man behaves himself here more passively, receiving and admitting Christ through faith—who insinuates Himself into our heart through the Word—than actively; so that it is properly the work of God, and not our own, while it is being produced. And whatever activity of ours there is in that reception of Christ or in the apprehension of the divine grace offered and conferred—after, namely, faith has been produced in our hearts by the Holy Spirit—that very thing certainly does not come into the account when our justification is being dealt with, so much so that faith itself, insofar as it is an instrument, is rightly said to be opposed not only to all works of obedience and piety, but even to faith itself, insofar as it is our work or act, and to its virtue. Unless this is holily asserted, the Arminian heresy concerning faith as a quality or our own work and act justifying us can easily creep in.” (System. X, 632. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who contend that faith does not justify by way of an organic or instrumental cause, or by way of a receiving instrument, but as some quality and virtue of ours and a disposition inherent in us; or that faith justifies dispositively, because as the beginning and first root of justification it disposes and prepares the mind of man to receive righteousness, as if it were opening the doors to hope and charity, which are works necessary for obtaining and acquiring righteousness, as Andradius says; see Bellarmine, T. 4, l. 1, de justificat, c. 13, where he says: “The first disposition for justification, according to the doctrine of the Council (of Trent), is faith.” The same is said in c. 17 of the same book. They likewise assert that faith justifies, not having that form or power from Christ, whom it apprehends and possesses, but from our charity. See the Censura Coloniensis, pp. 92 and 114. Note here the words of D. Calovius, which are found in T. 10, System, a. 2, c. 2, qu. 3: “Faith,” he says, “is considered by the Papists in two ways: first, before justification, and thus it is believed to justify dispositively, insofar as it precedes and disposes man to the habit of righteousness, which they say is infused into no one unless he has given assent to the Gospel; then, in the act of justification, where it is said to justify formally, insofar as it is posited as some part of the infused habit of righteousness or charity.” Concerning the former, Becanus says, P. 2, Theol. Scholast. tr. 4, qu. 3: “Among the dispositions, faith holds the first place, which is the foundation and root of salvation and justification; as the Council of Trent, sess. 6, c. 8, speaks.” Bellarmine, l. 1, de justific. c. 17, contends that the remission of sins is imputed through faith and that man is justified through this by faith, not because faith merely looks to the promise and apprehends it by believing, but because it obtains remission and in its own way merits it. 2. Of the Socinians, who also deny that faith is the instrumental cause of justification. They affirm, however: 1) That faith is an assisting cause and a cause without which justification would not be... 2) They contend that justifying faith is not to believe that Christ suffered for us, or to apply His merit to oneself trustingly, but under the hope of life

Latin:

Gerhardus: ,,Fides non debet conferri manui apprehendenti poculum, in quo continetur salutaris potio, sed est spirituale illud os, quo ex fonte salutis bibimus, est spiritualis pastus animae, est ipsa spiritualis bibitio, coelestis potus, ut patet ex cap. 6. Johannis.“ (L. de justif. § 181.)

Idem: ,,Aliud est Sta την πίστιν, aliud δια τής πίστεως justificari; illud causam meritoriam notat, hoc vero instrumentalem. Non justiflcamur propter fidem, tanquam meritum aliquod, sed per fidem, quae meritum Christi apprehendit.“ (L. de justif. § 179.)

Idem: ,,Particula,si‘ aut est αιτιολογική, aut συλλογιστική, i. e., designat causam, vel consequentiam. In concionibns legalibus: ,Si feceris hoc, vives‘, particula,si‘ est αιτιολογική, siquidem obedientia est causa, propter quam servantibus legem datur vita aeterna; sed in evangelicis promissionibus: ,Si credideris, salvus eris‘, particula,si‘ est συλλογιστική, denotatur enim modus applicationis divinitus constitutus, soli fidei competens.“ (L. de Ev. § 26.)

J. Olearius: ,,Fides ad salutem relata non est opus nostrum, sed pertinet ad ordinem divinitus institutum, adeoque nequaquam est conditio proprie dicta, pendens ex homine, sed beneficium divinitus collatum sive requisitum subjecti patientis et organum salutem apprehendens, nequaquam vero principium activum, ab homine procedens aut in effectum salutis per modum causae proprie ita dictae influens.“ (Vid. Carpzovii Isag. in lib. symbol. p. 1361.)

Heerbrandus: ,,Fides non est conditio, neque ut conditio requiritur, proprie loquendo. Quia non propter ejus dignitatem vel meritum, aut quatenus est opus, promittitur aut offertur justificatio. Est enim fldes quoque imperfecta; sed est modus quidam, oblatum benefleium et donatum per et propter Christum accipiens. . . Manus non conditio dicitur, sed medium et instrumentum, quo eleemosyna accipitur.“ (Compend. p. 379. sq.)

S. Schmidtius: ,,Equidem conditio vocata pridem etiam est fides justificans a nostratibus theologis. Sed conditio intelligenda est non moralis, sed physica, ut sic loquar, instrumenti necessarii. Quando namque dico: Si credideris, salvaberis, non conditionem moralem, sub qua salvandus sis, sed necessitatem instrumenti, per quod salvandus es, significo. Sic etiam rem in naturalibus deprehendimus. Si alas habueris, volabis, quo conditionem quidem ad volandum dico, non conditionem tamen moralem, sed necessarii instrumenti seu medii, sine quo volare tibi non licebit et volare frustra conaberis. Sola itaque fides justificat ex parte hominis, quod etiam vult apostolus in epistolis ad Romanos et Galatas, Rom. 3, 20. Gal. 2, 16. Habet quidem fldes

DE JUSTIFICATIONE justificans alios praeter appprehensionem fiducialem actus, quippe desiderat, quaerit, petit, instat, novam obedientiam promittit, et si quis actus alius est. Verum enim vero neque lii actus sunt fidei justiflcantis formales, sed solus, quem supra diximus, actus ille apprehensionis, receptionis seu applicationis fiducialis et appropriativus. Si namque oblationem gratiae divinae et meriti Christi et cum his remissionis peccatorum consideraverimus, certe omnes isti actus relationem ad eam debitam non habent, sed respectu ejus absoluti sunt; solus autem actus apprehensionis flducialis appropriativus eam ad oblationem habet relationem, ut quod in oblatione offertur, ille apprehendat et recipiat. ,Inventus sum‘, inquit Dominus, ,non quaerentibus me.‘ En, Deus gratiam suam, meritum Christi et remissionem peccatorum offert etiam non desiderantibus, quaerentibus, petentibus, instantibus, et invenitur ab his certe per solam flducialem apprehensionem, qua, quod ultro offertur, acceptatur. In his mox fides operatur desiderium, precesque indesinentes pro continuanda semel accepta gratia et remissione peccatorum, licet et hic exsatiari nequeat, nisi firma fiducia promissionem de perpetua Dei gratia in Scripturis comprehensam applicet.“ (Articulor. Form. Cone. Repetitio, p. 235.)

Osiander: ״Fides non justificat, ut est obedientia et sub praecepto; ita enim active se habet, est opus, adeoque legale quid; sed in quantum recipit, adeoque per modum instrumenti passivi concurrit ad justificationem.“ (Colleg. V, 140.)

Gerhardus: ״Quemadmodum annulus, cui inclusa est gemma pretiosissima, dicitur valere aliquot coronatis, ubi annulus non est gemma et tamen propter gemmam annulus tanti aestimatur, ita fides, quae apprehendit Chrjsti justitiam, dicitur nobis imputari ad justitiam, quippe cujus est organum apprehendens.“ (L. de justif. § 180.)

Hoepfnerus: ״Cum fides credenti dicitur imputari, vox fidei pertinet ad classem eorum vocabulorum, quae dicuntur μετά συμπλοκής, id est, complexa sunt geminumque includunt conceptum. Nam fides h. 1. denotat et rem creditam, et conditionem organi, nempe flducialis apprehensionis, qua justitia Christi (nobis non inhaerens, sed eo, quod vice nostri legi divinae a Christo praestita est, nobis imputabilis) accipitur et ista receptione flduciali fit ac a Deo censetur nostra justitia. Proinde imputari fides ad justitiam dicitur, cum justitia aliena, nempe Christo inhaerens, credenti imputatur, id est, a Deo, e tribunali gratiae pronunciante, credenti adjudicatur pro justitia propria, non secus ac si fidelis homo ipse illam justitiam coram Deo valentem praestitisset. Similis significatus vocis fidei, objectum simul et actum credendi organicum includentis, habetur ad Gal. 3, 23. et 25.: ,Priusquam venit fides‘, id est, Christus fide apprehendendus, sicut paulo ante, nempe v. 9. illius capitis, dixit apostolus: ,Donec veniret semen‘, id est, Christus, in quo secundum promissionem gratiae omnes gentes benedictionem adepturae sint per fidem in illum. Falsa itaque est interpretatio, quod fides pro actu credendi sumta nobis imputetur, quia imputationis hujus unicum objectum est justitia. Fides autem est medium, per quod res imputabilis ad justitiam seu justifica nobis imputatur.“ (De justificatione disputationes, pag. 1065.)

Calovius: ״Id est, quod ecclesiae nostrae volunt, fidem esse quidem actum nostrum, quum non Deus in nobis credat, sed nos, operante Deo in nobis, credamus; non autem aestimari in judicio Dei, cum fides imputatur ad justitiam, ceu actum nostrum atque vel dignitate sua, vel etiam exaltatione divina ultra virtutem propriam id praestare, quod tribuitur, sed qua apprehendit gratiam Dei et meritum Christi; non propter vim apprehensionis aut actum ipsummet nostrum, sed propter objectum apprehensum, ut ita omnis dignitas, vis et virtus unice transeribatur objecto, Christi nempe merito; fides vero hoc ipsum tantum sibi PART. III. CAP. V. appropriet, suumque faciat vel potius credenti applicet, ita ut fidelis id per fidem apprehendat sibique vendicet.“ (Consider. Arminianismi, Disp. 13. p. 258.)

Osiander: ,,Paulus inepte disputaret, imo sibi ipsi contradiceret, si statueret, nos justificari fide formata, nec tamen operibus. Nam si ex formata fide justificamur, utique per opera justificamur partim et partim ex fide, cum tamen fides in hoc negotio omnibus omnino operiribus opponatur.“ (Colleg. V, 90.)

Calovius: ,,Quomodo fides causa esset impellens vel impelleret Deum ad justificandum et praedestinandum credentes, idque virtute propria, quum fides hic nullam vel virtutem vel activitatem obtineat, sed nude tantum passive sese habeat et gratiam Dei ac meritum Christi solummodo recipiat, Deus autem nobis ex gratia illud imputet, ac si proprium nostrum meritum esset? Magis ergo hic sese passive habet homo, recipiens Christum et admittens per fidem, qui per verbum in cor nostrum sese insinuat, quam active; ut ita opus sit Dei proprie, non vero nostrum, dum procreatur. Et quicquid est activitatis nostrae in illa Christi receptione vel gratiae divinae oblatae et collatae apprehensione, postquam nempe fides per Sp. S. producta est in cordibus nostris: id ipsum certe in censum non venit, cum de justificatione nostra agitur, adeo ut fides etiam ipsa, quatenus instrumentum est, recte dicatur opponi non tantum operibus omnibus obedientiae et pietatis, sed ipsi fidei, qua opus vel actus noster est, ejusque virtuti. Quod nisi sancte adseratur, facile Arminiana haeresis de fide ceu qualitate vel opere et actu nostro, nos justiflcante, subrepere potest.“ (System. X, 632. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ØAntithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, contendentium, fldem non per modum causae organicae seu Instrumentalis sive per modum instrumenti recipientis, sed ut qualitatem ac virtutem aliquam nostram atque dispositionem nobis inhaerentem justificare, sive fldem justificare dispositive, quia tanquam initium et prima radix justificationis disponat ac praeparet animum hominis ad accipiendam justitiam, quod quasi fores aperiat ad spem et caritatem, quae opera sint ad consequendam et comparandam justitiam necessaria, ut inquit Andradiusj vide Bellarminum T. 4.1. 1. de justificat, c. 13., ubi ait: ,Prima justiflcationis dispositio ex doctrina Concilii (Tridentini) fides est.‘ Idem dicit c. 17. ejusd. lib. Idem asserunt, quod fides justificet, illam formam sive vim non habere ex Christo, quem apprehendit et possidet, sed a caritate nostra. Vide Censuram Coloniensem pag. 92. et 114. Notanda hic sunt verba D. Calovii, quae habentur T. 10. System, a. 2. c. 2. qu. 3.: ,Fides‘, inquit, ,bifariam a pontificiis consideratur, tum ante justificationem, atque ita dispositive justificare creditur, quatenus praecedit et hominem disponit ad habitum justitiae, quam nemini, nisi qui assensum evangelio praebuerit, infundi ajunt; tum in actu justiflcationis, ubi formaliter justificare dicitur, quatenus pars aliqua habitus infusi justitiae vel caritatis statuitur.‘ De priori ait Becanus P. 2. Theol. ׳Scholast. tr. 4. qu. 3.: ,Inter dispositiones primum locum tenet fides, quae est fundamentum et radix salutis et justificationis; ut loquitur Concil. Trident, sess. 6. c. 8.‘ Bellarminus 1. 12. de justiflc. c. 17. contendit, perfidem imputari remissionem peccatorum et per hoc justiflcari hominem ex fide, non quia fides tantum respiciat promissionem et illam credendo apprehendat, sed quia remissionem impetret et suo quodam modo mereatur. 2. Socinianorum, qui etiam inficiantur, fidem causam justificationis instrumentalem esse. Affirmant autem 1.) fldem causam adjuvantem et sine qua non justificationis esse. . . 2.) Contendunt, fldem justificantem non esse credere, Christum pro nobis passum, aut fiducialiter ejus meritum sibi applicare, sed sub spe vitae


### On Justification: to obey God eternally, so that this obedience or observance of the commandments…

to obey God eternally, so that this obedience or observance of the commandments of God constitutes the form and essence of justifying faith. . . 3. Of the Arminians, who deny that justifying faith is the medium and instrument of our justification and hold it to be some condition prescribed by an evangelical covenant.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 789. sq.)

Luther: “Thus the Gospel of God and the New Testament is a good message and cry, sounded into all the world by the apostles, concerning a true David, who has fought with sin, death, and the devil and overcome them, and thereby has redeemed, made righteous, alive, and blessed all those who were caught in sins, plagued by death, and overcome by the devil, without their merit.” (On the N. T. according to the edition of A. 1522 and 1527. XIV, 99.)

Large Catechism: “The treasure is indeed opened and laid before everyone at the door, yes, upon the table; but it is required that you also accept it and surely hold it to be as the words declare.” (Lib. Conc. p. 504.)

The same: “Therefore there is here again great need to pray and cry: Dear Father, forgive us our trespasses. Not that He would not forgive sin even without and before our praying (for He has given us the Gospel, in which there is pure forgiveness, before we asked for it or ever thought of it). But it is a matter of our recognizing and accepting such forgiveness.” (L. c. p. 478.)

Formula of Concord: “Because the obedience is of the whole person, it is a perfect satisfaction and reconciliation of the human race, whereby the eternal, unchangeable righteousness of God, which is revealed in the Law, is satisfied, and thus our righteousness, which avails before God, which is revealed in the Gospel, upon which faith relies before God, which God imputes to faith: as it is written Rom. 5:19: ‘For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so also by one Man’s obedience shall many be made righteous.’” (Artic. 3. Solid. Declar. p. 623.)

Gerhard: “It is to be noted that Christ concurs in justification chiefly under three respects: 1. Meritoriously, for He Himself by His most holy and most perfect merit obtained for us the grace of justification; 2. Efficiently, for He not only liberated us from sins, death, and the devil and procured for us the righteousness which avails before God, but He also offers these precious goods, so dearly acquired, to us in the word of the Gospel and applies them through faith; 3. Formally, in the application itself, since we are righteous before God by no other thing than the righteousness acquired by Christ and imputed to us through faith.” (Loc. de justific. § 33.)

The same: “We urge the opposition of the apostle in Rom. 5:19: Those many who were constituted sinners through the fall of Adam, those same many were constituted righteous through the righteousness of Christ, that is, the benefit of righteousness was procured for them (for the apostle is not dealing with the application). Now, however, all men were constituted sinners through the fall of Adam, v. 12 and 18. Therefore, the benefit of righteousness was also procured for all through Christ.” (Loc. de elect. § 118.)

Carpzov: “The remission of sins is considered in a twofold way. First, as it has been acquired by Christ and is offered in the word and sacraments as a good divinely promised and intended to be sought and had by sinners. Then, however, as it has already been accepted and applied through faith and is possessed.” (Isag. in lib. symbol. p. 208.)

Gerhard: “How did the δικαίωμα of Christ in Rom. 5:18 redound to all men unto justification, when not all are justified? Resp.: The apostle is not speaking of the application, but of the acquisition of the benefit. If we wish to descend to the application, that universality must be restricted to those who are engrafted into Christ through faith.” (Annotationes in ep. ad Rom. p. 177.) PART III. CAP. V.

Ad. Osiander: "However this passage (2 Cor. 5:14) may be explained in various ways, it is nevertheless proven that it must be accepted as if it were written: 'If one died in the place of all, then it is the same as if all had died, namely, with that death which they had deserved.' Nor does the opposing argument stand (that it follows from this that all men were *ipso facto* liberated, since Christ died for them). For it is understood either regarding acquisition or regarding application; if the former, then certainly all men were actually liberated when Christ died for them, paying the price for all; but since application involves faith and men are distinguished into believers and unbelievers, it does not follow regarding application." (Colleg. th. IV, 167 sq.)

Chr. Chemnitius: "'Many' in Rom. 5:19, when it is said: 'By the disobedience of one man many were made sinners,' signifies the whole multitude of men; and in the following verses likewise the whole multitude of men, if they are understood as 'many made righteous' with respect to the acquisition of salvation through the merit of Christ." (Commentariolus in ep. ad Rom. p. 86.)

Calovius: "To explain more fully how we have been made alive with Christ, raised with Christ, and established in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus (Eph. 2:4–6), it must be said: that this was done, first, by reason of merit, because he, as our mediator and redeemer, having been made alive, raised, and placed in the heavenly places, we have been made alive with him and raised with him and placed in the heavenly places with him. Because he, as our mediator and redeemer, merited this for us, when he, as our surety and sponsor, was delivered into death for us—which is the same as if we had undergone death—and therefore, he having been raised from death, we have been raised, not otherwise than when satisfaction has been rendered by a sponsor, not only is he free, but also the one for whom he had given himself as sponsor. Then, by reason of application, because we apprehend by faith and apply to ourselves the merit and satisfaction of Christ, and by that means we are actually spiritually made alive and awakened from the death of sin, so that we have our πολίτευμα in the heavens, being also destined to be made alive and raised one day to the other, heavenly life." (Bibl. illustr. ad Ephes. 2:4–6. Tom. II. N. T. f. 675.)

J. Wandalinus: "The primary end" (of the resurrection of Christ) "is that he might declare his victory over death and his plenary satisfaction (for he would not have come out unless he had paid the last farthing for us, Matt. 5:26), and thus our justification. Therefore it is said in Rom. 4:25: 'Jesus, our Lord, was raised for our justification,' and 2 Tim. 1:10: 'Our Savior Jesus Christ both abolished death and brought life and immortality to light.'" ('Ύποτύπωσις sanor. verb. Havniae, 1703. p. 116 sq.)

J. J. Rambachius: "Christ was, in his resurrection, first of all justified for his own person, Isa. 50:8, 1 Tim. 3:16, since the righteousness of God declared that it was perfectly paid and satisfied by this our surety, and issued to him, as it were, a receipt for it; and that happened in his resurrection, when he was released from his debtor's prison and set at liberty. But since the surety has been justified, all the debtors have also been justified in him." (Ausführliche Erklärung der Ep. an die Römer, p. 322.)

The same: "Since Christ has risen, he has not risen for himself alone, but also meritoriously; all those have risen with him whose place he took in death. But he took the place of all, etc., etc. Therefore all. In justification, however, man enters into this communion and becomes a partaker of all the fruits of the resurrection."

Conr. Rieger: "With and in Christ, all men have been justified at the same time. This is evident, first of all, from the connection and relationship that Christ had on our behalf before the divine tribunal, namely, as a surety... If He is released, then we are released with Him... As we have all been made guilty of eternal death and condemned in Adam, so have we all been justified in Christ and absolved from the sentence of eternal death. Just as the sentence of death and condemnation pronounced over Adam has affected us all, because Adam represented us all before God, so the absolution that occurred over Christ through His resurrection affects us all, because Christ also represented us all. What happened to Christ, our Mediator, is also regarded as if it had happened to us ourselves... Which is also confirmed by clear passages of Holy Scripture. Thus Paul says in Ephesians 2:5, 6: 'God has raised us up with Christ, when we were dead in sins'; especially he speaks in Romans 5:18: 'As by the sin of one, condemnation came upon all men, so also by the righteousness of one, the justification of life came upon all men.'... We have all died with the dying Adam; we have all been justified with the justified Christ. As in death the Just One died for the unjust, so in the resurrection the Just One, who needed no justification of life for Himself, was justified for us unjust ones, and thus we are justified with Him... What has been said so far applies to the acquisition; now it must also be grasped and utilized by each one... Faith then grasps for itself in particular what has been acquired in general." (Herzens-Postille. Sermon on the 1st Holy Easter Day, p. 653 sqq.)

Ph. D. Burk: "Indeed, it cannot be denied that Scripture speaks in many places of justification as a general benefit of God's grace over all men; e.g., Romans 5:18: 'By the righteousness of one, the justification of life came upon all men.' Likewise 2 Corinthians 5:19: 'God was reconciling the world to Himself, not imputing their trespasses to them.' And a witness of the truth must in every way proclaim the Gospel so that he makes the general offer of God's grace to all men his main work. And every soul that is to come to faith must lay the foundation in the knowledge of this general justification over all men." (Die Rechtfertigung. Stuttg. 1763. p. 62 sq.)

Cf. what was said above in Part III, Chapter 2, Section 2, § 5, p. 94; Chapter 3, § 1, p. 134 sq.

Latin:

aeternae Deo obedire, ita ut haec obedientia seu observantia praeceptorum Dei fidei justificantis formam et essentiam absolvat. . . 3. Arminianorum, qui fidem justificantem medium et instrumentum nostrae justificationis esse negant et eandem pro conditione aliqua evangelico ioedere praescripta habent.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 789. sq.)

Lutherus: ״Also ist das Evangelium Gottes und Neue Testament eine gute Märe und Geschrei, in alle Welt erschollen durch die Apostel, von einem rechten David, der mit der Sünde, Tod und Teufel gestritten und überwunden habe, und damit alle die, so in Sünden gefangen, mit dem Tode geplagt, vom Teufel überwältigt gewesen, ohne ihr Verdienst erlöset, gerecht, lebendig und selig gemacht hat.“ (Auf das N. T. nach der Edition von A. 1522 u. 1527. XIV, 99.)

Catechismus major: ״Der Schatz ist wohl aufgethan und jedermann für die Thür, ja, auf den Tisch gelegt; es gehört aber dazu, dass du dich sein auch annehmest und gewisslich dafür haltest, wie die Wort geben.“ (Lib. Conc. p. 504.)

Idem: ״Darum ist hie abermal grosse Noth zu bitten und rufen: Lieber Vater, verlasse uns unsere Schuld. Nicht dass er auch ohne und vor unserm Bitten nicht die Sünde vergebe (denn er hat uns das Evangelium, darin eitel Vergebung ist, geschenkt, ehe wir darum gebeten oder jemals darnach gesunnen haben). Es ist aber darum zu thun, dass wir solche Vergebung erkennen und annehmen.“ (L. c. p. 478.)

Formula Conc.: ״Weil der Gehorsam der ganzen Person ist, so ist er eine vollkommene Genugthuung und Versühnung des menschliehen Geschlechts, dadurch der ewigen unwandelbaren Gerechtigkeit Gottes, so im Gesetz geoffenbaret, genug geschehen, und also unsere Gerechtigkeit, die für Gott gilt, so im Evangelio geoffenbaret wird, darauf sich der Glaube für Gott verlässet, welche Gott dem Glauben zurechnet: wie geschrieben stehet Röm. 5,19.: ,Gleichwie durch Eines Menschen Ungehorsam viel Sünder worden sind, also auch durch Eines Gehorsam werden viel gerecht.‘ “ (Artic. 3. Solid. .Declar. p. 623.)

Gerhardus: ״Notandum, quod Christus sub tribus potissimum rationibus ad justificationem concurrat: 1. meritorie, ipse enim sanctissimo et perfectissimo merito suo gratiam justificationis nobis impetravit; 2. efficienter, neque enim a peccatis solum, morte ac diabolo nos liberavit et justitiam, quae coram Deo valet, nobis peperit, sed etiam pretiosa ista bona tam care acquisita in verbo evangelii nobis offert et per fidem applicat; 3. formaliter, in ipsa applicatione, siquidem nulla alia re coram Deo sumus justi, quam justitia a Christo acquisita et per fidem nobis imputata.“ (Loc. de justiflc. § 33.)

Idem: ״Urgemus oppositionem apostoli Rom. 5, 19.: Qui multi peccatores constituti sunt per Adam lapsum, illi etiam multi per Christi justitiam constituti sunt justi, id est, partum illis justitiae beneficium (non enim de applicatione agit apostolus). Jam vero omnes homines per lapsum Adami constituti sunt peccatores, v. 12. et 18. Ergo etiam omnibus per Christum partum est justitiae beneficium.“ (Loc. de elect. § 118.)

Carpzovius: ״Remissio peccatorum duplici modo consideratur. Semel, ut a Christo acquisita est et in verbo ac sacramentis tanquam bonum divinitus promissum et intentum peccatoribus quaerendum et habendum offertur. Deinde vero, prout jam accepta est et per fidem applicata est atque habetur.“ (Isag. in lib. symbol. p. 208.)

Gerhardus: ״Quomodo Rom. 5, 18. δικαίωμα Christi redundavit in omnes homines in justificationem, cum non omnes justificentur? Resp.: Apostolus non de applicatione, sed de acquisitione beneficii lo PART. III. CAP. V. quitur. Si ad applicationem descendere velimus, universalitas illa restringenda ad eos, qui Christo per fidem inseruntur.“ (Annotationes in ep. ad Rom. p. 177.)

Ad. Osiander: ,,Utut diversimode hic locus (2 Cor. 5, 14.) explicetur, evictum tamen est, debere accipi, ac si scriptum esset: Si unus omnium loco mortuus est, ergo perinde est, ac si omnes essent mortui, morte scii, ea, quam erant meriti. Nec obstat opposita ratio (inde sequi, omnes homines ipso facto fuisse liberatos, cum Christus pro ipsis fuerit mortuus). Aut enim intelligitur de acquisitione, aut de applicatione; si prius, utique omnes homines fuerunt actu liberati, cum Christus pro illis fuerit mortuus, pro omnibus solvens pretium; applicatio autem cum fidem involvat et homines distinguantur in fideles et infideles, ideo de applicatione non procedit.“ (Colleg. th. IV, 167. sq.)

Chr. Chemnitius: ,,,Multi‘ in Rom. 5, v. 19., quando dicitur: ,Per inobedientiam unius hominis peccatores constituuntur multi‘, significat totam hominum multitudinem; et in sequentibus itidem totam hominum multitudinem, si intelligantur justi constituti multi respectu acquisitionis salutis per meritum Chrisii.“ (Commentariolus in ep. ad Rom. p. 86.;

Calovius: ,,Ut plenius explicetur, quomodo cum Christo viviflcati, cum Christo resuscitati, cum Christo in coelestibus constituti simus in Christo Jesu (Eph. 2, 4—6.), dicendum: quod id factum sit tum ratione meriti, quod ipso ceu mediatore et redemtore nostro viviflcato, resuscitato et in coelestibus collocato nos vivificati cum ipso simus et resuscitati cum ipso et in coelestibus cum ipso collocati. Quia ipse nobis ceu mediator et redemtor noster id promeruit, cum ipse tanquam vas et sponsor noster pro nobis in mortem traditus est, quod perinde est, ac si nos mortem subiissemus, ideoque resuscitato ipso e morte nos resuscitati sumus, non secus, atque praestita satisfactione a sponsore non solum hic liber est, sed etiam ille, cujus sponsorem se dederat. Tum ratione applicationis, quod fide apprehendamus, nobisque applicemus meritum Christi et satisfactionem, atque ea ratione actu spiritualiter vivificamur et a morte peccati excitamur, ut πολίτευμα nostrum in coelis habeamus, vivificandi etiam ac resuscitandi olim ad alteram coelestem vitam.“ (Bibi, illustr. ad Ephes. 2, 4—6. Tom. II. N. T. f. 675.)

J. Wandalinus: ״Finis primarius“ (resurrectionis Christi) ״est, ut suam de morte victoriam et plenariam satisfactionem (nam non exivisset, nisi ultimum pro nobis solvisset quadrantem, Matth. 5, 36.), adeoque nostram justificationem declararet. Ist Er losgelassen, so sind wir mit ihm losgelassen. . . Wie wir in Adam alle sind des ewigen Todes schuldig und verdammt worden, also sind wir alle in Christo gerechtfertigt und vom Urtheil des ewigen Todes losgesprochen worden. ### On Justification: Thus we are said to be justified by faith, from faith, through faith, Romans…

Thus we are said to be justified by faith, from faith, through faith, Romans 3:28 and 30; Galatians 3:24. However, when it is said of faith in the nominative case that it justifies, the expression seems to be metonymical. For the meaning is not that faith absolves man from sins and reckons him righteous, but faith is said to justify because, in view of it, God reckons us righteous, or because faith (not indeed by its own dignity, but by the dignity of the merit of Christ) moves God to justify us. See the blessed Musaeus, Disp. cit. de Justif. § 38.

Kromayer: "We are not justified on account of faith, but through faith... If perhaps any of the orthodox theologians have used these expressions: 'on account of faith' or 'because of faith we have justification,' they used the particle 'on account of' in a broader sense in place of the preposition 'through'; however, saying that we are justified 'because of faith,' they understood faith insofar as it grows together with its object, namely, the merit of Christ, and on account of the dignity of this, they valued faith so highly. Although we are not justified and saved on account of faith considered in itself, yet on account of unbelief we are dam[ned]... Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. III.18 PART III. CHAPTER V.

for it deserves condemnation, but faith deserves nothing; it is only the medium or instrument by which the righteousness of Christ becomes ours.” (Th. posit.-pol. II, 376.)

The same: “Faith is considered in the article of justification not qualitatively, as it is a virtue, nor quantitatively, as it is great or small, but relatively, as it is referred to Christ as its object and looks to Him.” (L. c.) The same: “‘Faith raised must be brought down.’ Certain Julian professors, namely Georg Calixtus, seeing that our justification is frequently ascribed to faith in the Scriptures, determined that it is raised (or extolled) in comparison to other works and imputed to us for righteousness. But in truth, although this phrase is read in the Scriptures, as in Rom. 4:5, ‘faith is imputed for righteousness,’ it must nevertheless be explained according to the analogy of faith. By distinguishing in the same chapter between imputation according to grace and according to debt, Paul shows us the way to interpret this phrase. Faith, of course, which otherwise considered in itself is quite languid, is taken concretively, insofar as it grows together with the object it apprehends, the merit of Christ.” (L. c. p. 377.)

Concerning its nature, see the preceding chapter, III. § 10. Beyond this faith, however, nothing else can be held on our part as a cause of justification.

See Rom. 3:28; Gal. 2:16; Rom. 4:2–6, where Paul distinguishes faith from any works whatsoever—not only those which are done according to the law of nature from the powers of nature, but in general from the works of the law, which are done according to the prescription of the law by any powers whatsoever—in this, that by the former man is justified, but by the latter he is not. Whence it is rightly said that faith alone justifies, or that faith is that which, on our part, is the thing in view of which God justifies us, and whatever is not faith itself (even if it be joined with faith) ought not to be held on our part as a cause of justification. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, the cited Disp. de Justif. § 38, and Tract. de Eccles. P. II. Disp. V. § 56, p. 377 sqq., § 75 sqq., p. 395 sqq.; Vindic. Bibl. Gloss. contra Erberm. Disp. II. § 18 sqq., p. 96 sqq. Apology of the A. C.: “The remission of sins is a thing promised for Christ’s sake. Therefore, it cannot be received except by faith alone. For a promise cannot be received except by faith alone. Rom. 4:16: ‘Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace, to the end the promise might be sure’; as if he were to say: if the matter depended on our merits, the promise would be uncertain and useless, because we could never determine when we had merited enough. And experienced consciences can easily understand this.” (Art. 4, p. 102.)

Formula of Concord: “We believe, teach, and confess that for the preservation of the pure doctrine of the righteousness of faith before God, one must hold with special diligence to the *particulis exclusivis*, that is, to the following words of the holy Apostle Paul, by which the merit of Christ is entirely separated from our works and the honor is given to Christ alone, since the holy Apostle Paul writes: By grace, without merit, without law, without works, not of works; which words all together mean as much as that we are justified and saved by faith in Christ alone.”

Luther: "I have received your letter with the two questions in which you desire my report; first, why I have translated the words of St. Paul in Romans chapter 3, 'Arbitramur, hominem justificari ex fide absque operibus,' as: 'We hold that a man is justified without the works of the law, by faith alone.' And you point out at the same time how the Papists make themselves uselessly busy beyond measure because the word *sola*, 'alone,' does not stand in Paul's text, and that such an addition is not to be tolerated by me in God's words, etc. . .

I have known quite well here in Romans 3 that the word *solum* does not stand in the Latin and Greek text, and the Papists did not need to teach me that. It is true, these four letters, *sola*, do not stand therein, which letters the donkey-heads look at as a cow looks at a new gate. But they do not see that the meaning of the text nevertheless contains it, and if one wishes to translate it clearly and powerfully into German, it belongs in there. For I wanted to speak German, not Latin or Greek, since I had undertaken to speak German in my translating. But it is the nature of our German language that when a speech occurs concerning two things, of which one is affirmed and the other denied, one uses the word *solum* (alone) alongside the word 'not' or 'no.' As when one says: The farmer brings only grain, and no money. No, I truly have no money now, but only grain. I have only eaten, and not yet drunk. Have you only written, and not read over? And countless similar ways in daily usage. In all these speeches, even if the Latin or Greek language does not do it, the German does, and it is its nature to add the word 'alone' so that the word 'not' or 'no' may be the more complete and clear. For although I also say: The farmer brings grain and no money, yet the word 'no money' does not sound as complete and clear as when I say: The farmer brings only grain and no money; and here the word 'alone' helps the word 'no' so much that it becomes a complete, clear German speech. For one must not ask the letters in the Latin language how one should speak German, as these donkeys do; rather, one must ask the mother in the house, the children in the alley, the common man in the market about it, and look at their mouths to see how they speak, and translate accordingly; then they understand it and notice that one is speaking German with them. . .

But now I have not only trusted and followed the nature of the languages in adding *solum* (alone) in Romans 3 (v. 28); rather, the text and the meaning of St. Paul demand and force it with power. For he is dealing there with the main article of Christian doctrine, namely, that we are justified through faith in Christ, without all works of the law, and he cuts off all works so cleanly that he even says the works of the law (which is nevertheless God's law and word) do not help toward righteousness. And he sets Abraham as an example, that he was justified so completely without works that even the highest work, which was then newly commanded by God, before and above all other laws and works, namely circumcision, did not help him toward righteousness, but he was justified without circumcision and without all works through faith, as he says in chapter 4 (v. 2): If Abraham was justified by works, he may boast, but not before God. But where one cuts off all works so cleanly, there the meaning must indeed be that faith alone makes one righteous. And whoever wishes to speak clearly and plainly about such a cutting off of works must say: faith alone, and not works, makes us righteous. The matter itself forces this, alongside the nature of the language.

Yes, they say, it sounds offensive, and people learn from it to understand that they do not need to do any good works. Dear friend, what should one say? Is it not much more offensive that St. Paul..." PART III. CHAP. V. [ The text] does not say "faith alone" itself, but rather pours it out more crudely, and knocks the bottom out of the cask, and says, "without the works of the law"? And Galatians 1 (2:16): "Not by the works of the law," and much more so in other places. For the word "faith alone" might still find a gloss; but the word "without works of the law" is so crude, offensive, and shameful that one cannot help it with any gloss. How much more might people learn from this not to do good works, since they hear the preaching of the works themselves in such dry, strong words: no works, without works, not by works. If it is not offensive that one preaches "without works, no works, not by works," what then should be offensive about preaching this "faith alone"?

And what is even more offensive, St. Paul does not reject bad, common works, but the works of the law itself.

From this, someone might be even more offended and say that the law is condemned and cursed before God, and that one should do nothing but evil, as those did in Romans 3 (v. 8): "Let us do evil, that good may come," as a sectarian spirit also began in our time. Should one, for the sake of such offenses, deny St. Paul’s word, or not speak freshly and freely of faith? Dear friend, St. Paul himself and we want to have such offense, and we teach so strongly against works for no other reason, and urge faith alone, so that people should be offended, stumble, and fall, so that they may learn and know that they do not become righteous through their good works, but only through Christ’s death and resurrection. If they cannot become righteous through the good works of the law, how much less will they become righteous through evil works, and without the law? Therefore, it does not follow: good works do not help; therefore, evil works help. Just as it does not follow well: the sun cannot help the blind man to see; therefore, the night and darkness must help him to see.

Latin:

Non enim sensus est, fidem absolvere liominem a peccatis et reputare eum justum, sed dicitur fides justificare, quia ejus intuitu Deus nos justos reputat, seu, quia fides (non sua quidem, sed meriti Christi dignitate) Deum movet, ut nos justificet. Rom. 3, 2—6., ubi Paulus fidem operibus quibuslibet, non solum, quae juxta legem naturae ex viribus naturae fiunt, sed in genere operibus legis, quae ad praescriptum legis quibuscunque viribus fiunt, in hoc contradistinguit, quod per illam homo justificetur, per haec non item.
