Idque facile intelligere queunt peritae conscientiae.“ (Xrt. 4. p. 102.)

Form. Conc.: ״Wir gläuben, lehren und bekennen, dass zuErhaltung reiner Lehre von der Gerechtigkeit des Glaubens für Gott über den particulis exclusivis, das ist, über nachfolgende Wort des heiligen Apostels Pauli, dadurch der Verdienst Christi von unsern Werken gänzlich abgesondert und Christo die Ehre allein gegeben, mit besonderm Fleiss zu halten sei, da der heilige Apostel Paulus schreibt: Aua Gnaden, ohne Verdienst, ohne Gesetz, ohne Werk, nicht aus den Werken, welche Worte alle zugleich so viel heissen als allein durch den Glauben an Christum werden wir gerecht und selig.“

Lutherus: ״Ich habe eure Schrift empfangen mit den zwo Quästioneu oder Fragen, darin ihr meines Berichts begehrt; erstlich, warum ich zun Römern am 3. Cap. die Worte St. Pauli: ,Arbitramur, hominem justificari ex fide absque operibus‘, also verdeutscht habe: ,Wir halten, dass der Mensch gerecht werde ohne des Gesetzes Werk, allein durch den Glauben‘. Und zeigt daneben an, wie die Papisten sich über die Massen unnütze machen, weil im Text Pauli nicht stehet das Wort sola, allein, und sei solcher Zusatz von mir nicht zu leiden in Gottes Worten u. s. w. . .

Ich habe hie Röm. 8. fast wohl gewusst, dass im lateinischen und griechischen Text das Wort solum nicht stehet, und hätten mich solches die Papisten nicht dürfen lehren. Wahr ists, diese vier Buchstaben, sola, stehen nicht drinnen, welche Buchstaben die Eselsköpf ansehen, wie die Kuh ein neu Thor. Sehen aber nicht, ׳dass gleichwohl die Meinung des Textes in sich hat, und wo mans will klar und gewaltiglich verdeutschen, so gehöret es hinein. Denn ich habe Deutsch, nicht Lateinisch noch Griechisch reden wollen, da ich Deutsch zu reden im Dolmetschen vorgenommen hatte. Das ist aber die Art unsrer deutschen Sprache, wenn sich eine Rede begibt von zweien Dingen, der man eins bekennet, und das andere verneinet, so braucht man des Worts solum (allein) neben dem Wort,nicht oder kein‘. Als wenn man sagt: Der Bauer bringt allein Korn, und kein Geld. Nein, ich habe wahrlich jetzt nicht Geld, sondern allein Korn. Ich habe allein gegessen, und noch nicht getrunken. Hast du allein geschrieben, und nicht überlesen? Und dergleichen unzählige Weise im täglichen Brauch. In diesen Reden allen, obs gleich die lateinische oder griechische Sprache nicht thut, so thuts doch die deutsche, und ist ihre Art, dass sie das Wort,allein‘ hinzu setzt, auf dass das Wort,nicht oder kein‘ desto völliger und deutlicher sei. Denn wiewohl ich auch sage: Der Bauer bringt Korn und kein Geld, so lautet doch das Wort,kein Geld‘ nicht so völlig und deutlich, als wenn ich sage: Der Bauer bringt allein Korn und kein Geld; und hilft hie das Wort,allein‘ dem Wort,kein‘ soviel, dass es eine völlige deutsche klare Rede wird. Denn man muss nicht die Buchstaben in der lateinischen Sprache fragen, wie man soll deutsch reden, wie diese Esel thun; sondern man muss die Mutter im Hause, die Kinder auf der Gasse, den gemeinen Mann auf dem Markt drum fragen, und denselbigen auf das Maul sehen, wie sie reden, und darnach dolmetschen, so verstehen sie es denn, und merken, dass man deutsch mit ihnen redet. . .

Aber nun habe ich nicht allein der Sprachen Art vertrauet und gefolget, dass ich Rom. 3. (V. 28.) solum (allein) habe hinzu gesetzt; sondern der Text und die Meinung St. Pauli fordern und erzwingens mit Gewalt. Denn er handelt ja daselbst das Hauptstück christlicher Lehre, nämlich, dass wir durch den Glauben an Christum, ohne alle Werke des Gesetzes, gerecht werden, und schneidet alle Werke so rein ab, dass er auch spricht, des Gesetzes (das doch Gottes Gesetz und Wort ist) Werke nicht helfen zur Gerechtigkeit. Und setzt zum Exempel Abraham, dass derselbige sei so gar ohne Werke gerecht worden, dass auch das höchste Werk, das dazumal neu geboten ward von Gott, vor und über allen andern Gesetzen und Werken, nämlich die Beschneidung, ihm nicht geholfen habe zur Gerechtigkeit, sondern sei ohne die Beschneidung und ohne alle Werke gerecht worden durch den Glauben, wie er spricht Kap. 4. (V. 2.): Ist Abraham durch Werke gerecht worden, so mag er sich rühmen, aber nicht vor Gott. Wo man aber alle Werke so rein abschneidet, da muss ja die Meinung sein, dass allein der Glaube gerecht mache. Und wer deutlich und dürre von solchem Abschneiden der Werke reden will, der muss sagen: allein der Glaube, und nicht die Werke, machen uns gerecht. Das zwinget die Sache selbst neben der Sprachen Art.

Ja, sprechen sie, es lautet ärgerlich, und die Leute lernen daraus verstehen, dass sie keine gute Werke thun dürfen. Lieher, was soll man sagen, ists nicht viel ärgerlicher, dass St. Paulus PART. III. CAP. V. selbst nicht sagt, allein der Glaube, sondern schüttete wohl gröber heraus, und stosset dem Fass den Boden aus, und spricht, ohne des Gesetzes Werke? Und Galat. 1. (2, 16.): Nicht durch die Werke des Gesetzes, und dess viel mehr an andern Orten. Denn das Wort,allein der Glaube‘ möchte noch eine Glosse finden; aber das Wort,ohne Werke des Gesetzes‘ ist so grob, ärgerlich, schändlich, dass man mit keiner Glosse helfen kann. Wie viel mehr möchten hieraus die Leute lernen keine gute Werke thun, da sie hören mit so dürren starken Worten von den Werken selbst predigen: keine Werke, ohne Werke, nicht durch Werke. Ist nun das nicht ärgerlich, dass man,ohne Werke, keine Werke, nicht durch Werke‘ predigt, was sollts denn ärgerlich sein, so man diess,allein der Glaube‘ predigt.

Und das noch ärgerlicher ist, St. Paulus verwirft nicht schlechte gemeine Werke, sondern des Gesetzes selbst.

Daraus möchte wohl Jemand sich noch mehr ärgern, und sagen, das Gesetz sei verdammt und verflucht vor Gott, und man solle eitel Böses thun, wie die thäten Roman. 3. (v. 8.): Lasst uns Böses thun, auf dass es gut werde; wie auch ein Rottengeist zu unserer Zeit anfing. Sollte man um solcher Aergernisse willen St. Paulus Wort verleugnen, odör nicht frisch und frei vom Glauben reden? Lieber, eben St. Paulus und wir wollen solch Aergerniss haben, und lehren um keiner andern Ursache willen so stark wider die Werke, und treiben allein auf den Glauben, dass die Leute sollen sich ärgern, stossen und fallen, damit sie mögen lernen und wissen, dass sie durch ihre guten Werke nicht fromm werden, sondern allein durch Christus Tod und Auf erstehen. Können sie nun durch gute Werke des Gesetzes nicht fromm werden, wie viel weniger werden sie fromm werden durch böse Werke, und ohne Gesetz? Darum folget es nicht: gute Werke helfen nicht; darum helfen böse Werke. Gleich als nicht fein folgt: die Sonne kann dem Blinden nicht helfen, dass er sehe; darum muss ihm die Nacht und Finsterniss helfen, dass er sehe.


### On Justification: But I am amazed that one can be so resistant in this public matter

But I am amazed that one can be so resistant in this public matter. Tell me, pray, whether Christ’s death and resurrection is our work, which we do, or not? It is certainly not our work, nor any work of the law. Now, Christ’s death and resurrection alone makes us free from sins and righteous, as Paul says in Romans 4 (v. 25): "He was delivered for our offenses, and was raised again for our justification." Furthermore, tell me, what is the work by which we grasp and hold Christ’s death and resurrection? It must be no external work, but only the one faith in the heart; that same one, yes, even alone, and without any works, grasps such death and resurrection, where it is preached through the Gospel. What is it then that one rages and storms, calls heresy and burns, when the matter itself lies clearly at the foundation and proves that faith alone grasps Christ’s death and resurrection without any works, and that the same death and resurrection is our life and righteousness? Since it is then publicly so in itself, that faith alone brings, grasps, and gives us such life and righteousness; why then should one not also speak thus? It is not heresy that faith alone grasps Christ and gives life; but it must be heresy to say or speak such things. Are they not mad, foolish, and senseless? They confess the matter to be right, and yet punish the speech about the same matter as wrong. One and the same thing must be both right and wrong at the same time.

Also, I am not alone, nor the first, who says that faith alone makes one righteous; Ambrose, Augustine, and many others have said it before me. And whoever is to read and understand St. Paul must say so, and cannot do otherwise; his words are too strong and suffer no, indeed, absolutely no work. If it is no work, then it must be faith alone. Oh, how it would be such a fine, improving, inoffensive doctrine if people learned that, alongside faith, they might also become righteous through works. That would be as much as...

said] that not only does Christ’s death take away our sin, but our works also contribute something to it. That the Mass honors Christ’s death finely, that our works help Him, and could do what He does, so that we would be just as good and strong as He. It is the devil who cannot leave the blood of Christ unprofaned. Since, therefore, the matter itself fundamentally demands that one say, faith alone makes one righteous, and the nature of our German language, which also learns to express such things in this way, has the example of the holy fathers for it, and the danger to the people also compels it, so that they do not remain hanging on works and lack faith and lose Christ—especially at this time, when they have been accustomed to works for so long and are to be torn away from them with force—so it is not only right, but also highly necessary, that one state most clearly and completely: faith alone without works makes one pious.” (An Open Letter on Translating, etc., 1530. Luther’s Collected Works. Erlangen. Vol. 65, p. 104, 109 sq., 115–118.)

H. Kromayerus: “Although the exclusive [particle] is not found κατὰ τὸ γράμμα in c. 3 of the Epistle to the Romans, v. 28, where Luther placed it in his German version, it can nevertheless be proven partly from the opposition, partly from other places in Scripture. The opposition is found both in this and in many other places of Scripture. If we compare parallel passages, in Galatians 2:16, the words ἐὰν μὴ, ‘not unless by faith,’ are read to the very letter. In Mark 5:36, the particle μόνον is found, when the Savior says to the ruler of the synagogue: Μόνον πίστευε, i.e., ‘only believe.’” (Th. posit. pol. II, 374.)

The same: “It is to be noted concerning this expository proposition, which is referred by logicians to the class of exclusives: ‘Faith alone justifies,’ that it is held by some of our own as an exclusive of the subject, and by others as an exclusive of the predicate. Those who refer it to the exclusive of the predicate resolve this proposition thus: It is faith that alone justifies. However, those who refer it to the exclusive of the subject seem to approach more closely to the equilibrium of truth. For not many predicates are excluded from participation in the subject by that exclusive, because far more things can be predicated of faith than justification—e.g., that it pleases God, that it is kindled by the Holy Spirit, that it apprehends the merit of Christ, that it is effective through love—but rather, many subjects are excluded from participation in the predicate. For there is nothing on our part of which justification can be said and predicated other than faith, as the Lord D. Hoepfner correctly notes with the more elegant logicians in his first disputation on justification. If anyone objects regarding the Word and the Sacraments, of which justification can also be said, we reply with this logical canon: An exclusive does not exclude concomitants.” (Th. posit. pol. I, 660.)

Quenstedtius: “Bellarminus, 1. 1. de justif. c. 12: ‘If,’ he says, ‘faith alone justified, it would also do so if it were alone without love, and in this way even dead faith would justify, because faith without works is a dead thing.’ Resp.: 1. Faith justifies while those virtues are absent as regards the act of justification or the cause, because it is the proper office and proper act of faith to apply the merit of Christ. It does not, however, justify while they are absent as regards existence or the act of the effect. 2. It is the same as if I were to say: The eye alone sees, therefore it also sees if it is alone and torn from the head. It does not follow; for vision is indeed ascribed to the eye alone, yet not when separated from the remaining members of the body, because then it is not even properly an eye. Thus, justification is ascribed to faith alone, yet not when torn away from the other pursuits of piety. As often as Scripture attributes our justification to faith, that faith is understood which is not alone, but living and effective through love, so that love is nevertheless the mark, the adjunct, and the necessary consequence of justifying faith, but not indeed a co-cause of justification, nor does it concur socially with faith toward justification. Faith alone is naturally suited for the apprehension of the righteousness of Christ imputed to us and the remission of sins in His blood, in which our justification before God [consists].” PART III. CHAP. V.

is [it, and since the works of the law are removed from justification by faith, charity, which is the fulfillment of the law, Rom. 13:10, must also be removed from it.” (L.c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 804.)

Hollazius: “Objection: Whatever faith is never alone, that never justifies alone. Justifying faith is never alone, therefore. Resp.: I deny the major and distinguish between the existence of faith and its office or ἐνέργεια and justifying power. Faith justifies alone, even though it is never alone, but is joined with charity, hope, and other internal motions. Thus, the intellect alone understands, although it is joined with the will; the eyes alone see, although ears and nostrils coexist with them; the flavor of an apple alone affects the taste, however much the odor and color of the same apple accompany it.” (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 8. q. 9. p. 908.) Gerhardus: “Faith, insofar as it justifies, concurs alone to that act; meanwhile, justifying faith itself is not alone, much less does it consist with vices, i.e., sins against conscience; how, therefore, would it justify with vices? To act presupposes to be; true faith does not consist with vices, therefore it does not justify with vices.” (L. de justif. § 175.)

For faith is not opposed to divine grace and the merit of Christ, but is subordinated to them. See Rom. 3:24, 25. Quenstedtius: “The exclusive particle ‘alone’ in this proposition, ‘Faith alone justifies,’ does not exclude different kinds of causes, but subordinates them. For it is not opposed 1. to the grace of God or, which is the same thing, to the gratuitous favor of God, the principal efficient cause of justification; 2. not to the merit of Christ, the meritorious cause of the same; nor 3. to the Word and Sacraments, which are the instrumental causes of our justification on the part of God offering and giving; but to our works, inasmuch as they are excluded by this proposition; just as this proposition, ‘Faith alone justifies,’ is equivalent to this: ‘Faith justifies without works.’” (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 795.)

Grauerus: “There are indeed several instrumental causes of justification, namely, the preaching of the Word and the Sacraments, through which the benefits of Christ are offered to us; but yet there is only one instrumental cause that apprehends. From which it appears in what sense it is said by our churches that we are justified by faith alone, namely, by faith alone as the apprehending instrumental cause. Yet it remains true at the same time that we are justified by the obedience of Christ alone, namely, as the meritorious cause; and this also remains true, that we are justified by the mercy of God alone, namely, as the original and προκαταρκτική cause. And thus the particle ‘alone’ can be used or employed in any kind of cause of justification in a sound sense, so that no contradiction at all arises. All these three causes are comprehended in that most common saying of Christ in John 3: ‘God so loved the world,’ etc.” (Grauerus redivivus, i.e., praelection. in A. C. p. 690. sq.) Whether it be said to contribute as much to justification as faith contributes, or somewhat less.

Form. Conc.: “Therefore we reject and condemn all the following errors: ... 11. That faith does not justify without good works, so that good works are necessarily required for righteousness, and without their presence a person cannot be justified.” (Epitom. art. 3. p. 529. sq.) Loescherus: “The presence of works is one thing, and their operation or influence upon the effect is another. For true faith always (therefore also in the work of justification and glorification) has good works with it, which are most present to it; but that those works should flow into justification together with faith is not necessary; just as a striking hand has with it heat and color, which nevertheless do not flow into the effect of the striking at all or effect anything of it.”

Latin:

Mich wundert aber, dass man sich in dieser öffentlichen Sache so mag sperren. Sage mir doch, ob Christus Tod und Auf erstehen unser Werk sei, das wir thun, oder nicht? Es ist ja nicht unser Werk, noch einiges Gesetzes Werk. Nun macht uns ja allein Christus Tod und Auferstehen frei von Sünden, und fromm, wie Paulus sagt Rom. 4. (v. 25.): Er ist gestorben um unserer Sünde willen, und auferstanden um unserer Gerechtigkeit willen. Weiter sage mir, welches ist das Werk, damit wir Christus Tod und Auferstehen fassen und halten? Es muss ja kein äusserlieh Werk, sondern allein der einige Glaube im Herzen sein; derselbige allein, ja gar allein, und ohne alle Werke, fasset solchen Tod und Auferstehen, wo es gepredigt wird durchs Evangelion. Was ists denn nun, dass man so tobet und wüthet, ketzert und brennet, so die Sache im Grunde selbst klärlich da liegt und beweiset, dass allein der Glaube Christus Tod und Auferstehen fasse ohne alle Werke, und derselbige Tod und Auf erstehen sei unser Leben und Gerechtigkeit? So es denn an ihm selbst öffentlich also ist, dass allein der Glaube uns solch Leben und Gerechtigkeit bringet, fasset und gibt; warum soll man denn nicht auch also reden? Es ist nicht Ketzerei, dass der Glaube allein Christum fasset und das Leben gibt; aber Ketzerei muss es sein, wer 801ches sagt oder redet. Sind sie nicht toll, thöricht und unsinnig? Die Sache bekennen sie für recht, und strafen doch die Rede von derselbigen Sache für unrecht. Einerlei zugleich muss beide recht und unrecht sein.

Auch bin ichs nicht allein, noch der erste, der da sagt, allein der Glaube macht gerecht; es hat vor mir Ambrosius, Aug. und viele Andere gesagt. Und wer St. Paulum lesen und verstehen soll, der muss wohl so sagen, und kann nicht anders; seine Worte sind zu stark, und leiden kein, ja gar kein Werk. Ists kein Werk, so muss der Glaube allein sein. 0 wie sollte es so gar eine feine, besserliche, unärgerliche Lehre sein, wenn die Leute lernten, dass sie neben dem Glauben auch durch Werke fromm möchten werden. Das wäre so viel

gesagt, dass nicht allein Christus Tod unsere Sünde wegnähme, sondern unsere Werke thäten auch etwas dazu. Das Messe Christus Tod fein geehret, dass unsere Werke ihm hülfen, und könnten das auch thun, das er thut, auf dass wir ihm gleich gut und stark wären. Es ist der Teufel, der das Blut Christi nicht kann ungeschändet lassen. Weil nun die Sache im Grunde selbst fordert, dass man sage, allein der Glaube macht gerecht, und unserer deutschen Sprache Art, die solches auch lernt also auszusprechen, habe dazu der heiligen Väter Exempel, und zwinget auch die Gefahr der Leute, dass sie nicht an den Werken hangen bleiben, und des Glaubens fehlen, und Christum verlieren, sonderlich zu dieser Zeit, da sie so lange her der Werke gewöhnet, und mit Macht davon zu reissen sind: so ists nicht allein recht, sondern auch hoch vonnöthen, dass man aufs Allerdeutlichste und Völligste heraussage, allein der Glaube ohne Werke macht fromm.“ (Ein Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen u. s. w. 1530. Luther’s Sämmtliche Werke. Erlangen. Band 65, p. 104. 109. sq. 115—118.)

H. Kromayerus: ,,Quantumvis exclusiva in c. 3. ep. ad Rom. v. 28., ubi Lutherus eam in versione sua germanica posuit, κατά rö γράμμα non inveniatur, partim tamen ex oppositione, partim ex aliis scripturae locis probari potest. Oppositio tum in hoc, tum in aliis scripturae locis pluribus habetur. Loca parallela si conferimus, in ep. Gal. 2, 16. voces εάν αή, nonnisi fide, quoad totidem apices leguntur. Mare. 5, 36. particula μόνον habetur, cum salvator ad principem synagogae dicit: Μόνον πίστευε, i. e., tantum crede.“ (Th. posit.pol. II, 374.)

Idem: ,,Notandum circa propositionem hanc exponibilem, quae ad classem exclusivarum a logicis refertur: ,Fides tantum justificat‘, eandem a quibusdam nostratium pro exclusiva subjecti, a quibusdam pro exclusiva praedicati haberi. Qui ad exclusivam praedicati referunt, propositionem hanc ita resolvunt: Fides est, quae tantum justificat. Verumenimvero propius ad veritatis aequilibrium videntur accedere, qui ad exclusivam subjecti referunt. Non enim plura praedicata per exclusivam istam a participatione subjecti excluduntur, quia de fide longe plura praedicari possunt, quam justificatio, v. 9. quod Deo placeat, quod a Sp. S. accendatur, quod meritum Christi apprehendat, quod per caritatem sit efficax; sed plura subjecta potius a participatione praedicati excluduntur. Nihil enim est ex parte nostra, de quo justificatio dici et praedicari queat, quam fides, ut recte cum logicis elegantioribus notat dominus D. Hoepfnerus in disp. sua prima de justif. Si quis verbum et sacramenta, de quibus etiam justificatio dici potest, objiciat, canonem istum logicum reponimus: Exclusiva non excludit concomitantia.“ (Th. posit.pol. I, 660.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Bellarminus 1. 1. de justif. c. 12.: ,Si‘, inquit, ,fides sola justificaret, id etiam faceret, si esset sola absque dilectione, et hoc modo fidem etiam mortuam justificare, quia fldes sine operibus sit res mortua.‘ Resp.: 1. Fides justificat virtutibus illis absentibus quoad actum justificationis seu causae, quia proprium fidei officium est et actus proprius, applicare meritum Christi. Non autem justificat illis absentibus quoad existentiam seu actum effectus. 2. Ideik. est, ac si dicerem: Solus oculus videt, ergo etiam videt, si solus sit et revulsus a capite. Non sequitur; nam soli quidem oculo adseribitur visio, attamen non separato a reliquis corporis membris, quia tunc neque proprie oculus est. Ita fidei soli adseribitur justificatio, non tamen avulsae a caeteris pietatis studiis. Quoties Scriptura justificationem nostram tribuit fidei, sic intelligitur illa fides, quae non sola est, sed viva et per caritatem efficax, ut tamen caritas sit nota, adjunctum et consequens necessarium fidei justificantis, non vero concausa justificationis et quae socialiter cum fide concurrat ad justificationem. Sola fides apta nata est ad apprehensionem imputatae nobis justitiae Christi et remissionis peccatorum in sanguine ipsius, in qua nostra coram Deo justificatio PART. III. CAP. V.

sita [est, et cum legis opera removeantur a justificatione ex flde, ab eadem etiam debet removeri caritas, quae legis est complementum, Rom. 13, 10.“(L.c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 804.)

Hollazius: ,,Instantia: Quaecunque fides nunquam est sola, illa nuncquam sola justificat. Fides justificans nunquam est sola, ergo. Resp.: Neg. maj. et dist. inter fidei existentiam et officium seu ενέργειαν et vim justificam. Fides justificat sola, tametsi nunquam sit sola, sed cum caritate, spe et aliis internis motibus conjuncta. Sic solus intelligit intellectus, licet cum voluntate sit conjunctus; soli vident oculi, quamvis ipsis coexistant aures et nares; solus sapor pomi afficit gustum, quantumvis ipsum comitetur odor et color ejusdem pomi.“ (Exam. P. III. s. 1. c. 8. q. 9. p. 908.) Gerhardus: ,,Fides, quatenus justificat, sola ad illum actum concurrit; interim ipsa fides justificans non est sola, multo minus cum vitiis, h. e., peccatis contra conscientiam, consistit, quomodo ergo cum vitiis justificaret? Agere praesupponit esse; fides vera non consistit cum vitiis, ergo non justificat cum vitiis.“ (L. de justif. § 175.)

Nam gratiae divinae et merito Christi fides 11011 opponitur, sed subordinatur. Vid. Rom. 3, 24. 25. Quenstedtius: ,,Particula exclusiva,sola‘ in hac propositione: ,Sola fides justificat‘, non excludit diversa causarum genera, sed eadem subordinat. Non enim 1. opponitur gratiae Dei seu, quod idem est, gratuito I)ei favori, justificationis causae efficienti principali; 2. non merito Christi, causae ejusdem meritoriae; nec 3. verbo et sacramentis, quae causae instrumentales justificationis nostrae a parte Dei offerentis et dantis sunt; sed nostris operibus, utpote quae hac propositione exeluduntur; sicut propositio haec: ,Fides sola justificat‘, aequipolleat huic: Fides absque operibus justificat.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 795.)

Grauerus: ,,Plures quidem sunt causae instrumentales justificationis, nempe praedicatio verbi et sacramenta, per quas beneficia Christi nobis offeruntur; sed tamen est unica causa Instrumentalis apprehendens. Ex quibus apparet, quo sensu dicatur a nostris ecclesiis, nos sola fide justificari, nempe sola flde tanquam causa iustrumentali apprehendente. Manet tamen simul verum, quod sola Christi obedientia justificemur, nempe tanquam causa meritoria; manet et hoc verum, quod sola misericordia Dei justificemur, nempe tanquam causa originali et προκαταρκτική. Atque sic 'in quolibet genere causarum justificationis particula,sola‘ adhiberi seu usurpari potest sano sensu, ut nulla fiat prorsus contradictio. Omnes hae tres causae comprehenduntur in usitatissimo illo Christi dicto Joh. 3.: ,Sic Deus dilexit mundum‘ etc.“ (Grauerus redivivus, h. e., praelection. in A. C. p. 690. sq.) Sive tantumdem conferre dicatur ad justificationem, quantum fides confert, sive aliquanto minus.

Form. Conc.: ,,Demnach verwerfen und verdammen wir alle nachfolgende Irrthum: ... 11. Dass der Glaube nicht rechtfertige ohne die guten Werke, also, dass die guten Werke nothwendig zur Gerechtigkeit erfordert, ohne derselben Gegenwärtigkeit der Mensch nicht gerechtfertigt werden könne.“ (Epitom. art. 3. p. 529. sq.) Loescherus: ,,Alia est operum praesentia, et alia eorum operatio sive influxus in effectum. Vera enim fides semper (ergo etiam in opere justificationis et glorificationis) secum habet bona opera, quae ipsi praesentissima sunt; at vero ut opera ea simul cum flde in justificationem influant, necesse non est; quemadmodum manus verberans praesentem secum habet calorem et colorem, qui tamen in effectum verberationis neutiquam coinfluunt aut aliquid ejus efficiunt.“


### On Justification: Kromayer: "Faith alone justifies, but it does not exist in solitude." (Th

Kromayer: "Faith alone justifies, but it does not exist in solitude." (Th. posit.-pol. II, 374.)

Formula of Concord: "It remains as Luther rightly says: 'Faith and works agree well and are inseparably connected; but it is faith alone that apprehends the blessing without works, and yet it is never alone.'" (Solid Declar. Art. 3, p. 619.)

The same: "But here, if the article of justification is to remain pure, very diligent and careful attention must be paid that that which precedes faith, and that which follows it, not be mixed or inserted into the article of justification as if necessary and belonging thereto, because it is not one and the same thing to speak of conversion and of justification. For not everything that belongs to conversion also belongs at the same time to the article of justification, in and to which alone belongs and is necessary the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and faith, which accepts such things in the promise of the Gospel, whereby the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, from which we obtain and have forgiveness of sins, reconciliation with God, sonship, and the inheritance of eternal life." (Art. 3, Sol. Declar. p. 615.)

Gerhard: "That the Papists argue that the grace of God attributes to our works the power of justifying, and that the merits of our works concur with the merit of Christ, is asserted without Scripture and does not agree with the apostolic oppositions between grace and works, between believing and working." (L. c. § 152.)

The same: "Justification by works is denied to Abraham; now, in the time of Abraham, the ceremonial laws had not yet been enacted: therefore, works done according to the ceremonial laws cannot be meant... If righteousness were to be attributed to works, how could the works of the ceremonial law be excluded, since the observance of ceremonies, pertaining to the first table of the Decalogue, was not the least part of divine worship?" (L. de justif. § 151.)

Quenstedt: "Distinguish in Luke 7:47 between cause and effect. Christ says to Simon concerning Mary: 'Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much.' Hence the Papists infer the merit of charity, although it is sufficiently manifest that the remission of sins was the cause and not the effect of love. Solution: Because here 'for' (ὅτι) is not the cause why the thing is, but the cause why it is known; it is not the cause of the consequent, but of the consequence, such as a deduction from premises. Thus we say: There is fire, because there is smoke, although smoke is not the cause of fire. Thus the servant girl said to Peter: 'You are a Galilean, for your speech betrays you.' That speech was not the cause why Peter was a Galilean, but an indication. And so Christ does not argue from love to the remission of sins, as from cause to effect, but rather proceeds by reasoning from the effect to declare the preceding cause. He himself indicates the cause of the remission of sins by adding: 'Your faith has saved you,' v. 50. Therefore, the particle ὅτι is not causal, but ratiocinative, or rather, it does not denote the cause of the thing, but of the conclusion. The same must be answered regarding the passage 1 John 3:14." (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 802. sq.)

Hülsemann: "The saying of the Apostle in Rom. 10:10: 'With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation,' by no means signifies that the confession of the mouth or any other good work, distinct from the faith of the heart, is necessary for salvation, whether as a cause without which it is not, or as a causal medium, or as an analogous, congruent, or condign merit; nor does it signify that salvation has causes distinct from the causes of obtaining righteousness, or that the faith of the heart alone is sufficient to obtain righteousness, but that to obtain salvation, besides the faith of the heart, confession of the mouth is also required...

As for the meaning of the particle 'unto' (εἰς), it is manifest that it [denotes] whatever... PART III. CHAP. V. the analogy of one to another is to be noted, not the cause, as in Phil. 1:19, "Tribulation profits for salvation," 2 Cor. 7:10, 2 Thess. 2:11, Luke 1:35, Rom. 3:26, John 11:4: "The sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God," and in infinite other places. . . whence it follows that the mode of cohesion, by which salvation coheres with the confession of the mouth, and by which righteousness coheres with the faith of the heart, must be determined from elsewhere. . .

The true solution, therefore, of this saying in Rom. 10 is this: 1. That the apostle, by the confession of the mouth in this place, does not understand the confession of praise and gratitude, which is properly called a good work, but the confession of acknowledgment and knowledge, i.e., a sign of the knowledge acquired concerning Christ, which is proven from the cited passage, Deut. 30:14: "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.". . . 2. That the apostle did not intend to divide the attainment of salvation and righteousness between the confession of the mouth and the faith of the heart as distinct effects of distinct causes, but that he cited the confession of the mouth and the faith of the heart as a mere sign of knowledge and of present faith, on the occasion of the Mosaic saying which precedes it. This is also evident from the fact that in the declaration of his sentiment in verses 11 and 13, he attributes salvation and eternal glory and the aversion of eternal ignominy to faith alone, when by the ratiocinative particle γάρ in verse 11: "For the Scripture says: Whoever believes," etc., he renders the reason why he had said in the preceding verse 10 that one believes with the heart unto righteousness, and makes confession with the mouth unto salvation, namely, because all righteousness and salvation are from faith. From these testimonies, I say, by which the apostle confirms the saying in verse 10 and attributes salvation to faith alone, it appears that he did not posit the confession of the mouth as a co-cause of salvation, but as a sign of the true cause. . .

Heb. 12: 14. Children know that the force of a preposition with something and through something is not the same. How does it not follow: No one will see God without joy, the devil without terror, therefore joy is a cause without which one cannot see God, and terror is a cause without which one cannot see the devil? These are attributes of the one seeing, not causes nor means of seeing God or the devil, just as the damned are said to see the just with great confusion, Wisd. 5:2, and just as the crucifiers of Christ are said to see Him whom they pierced with great consternation, Zech. 12:10, and there are infinite examples of this kind. However, since the particle "without" is indefinite, and by the force of its indefiniteness denies only the attribute, just as the opposite particle "with" posits only the attribute, and is not a sign of a cause—which is learned from logic, for the particles "from," "through," and "by" are causal signs—therefore, it must be concluded or determined from the σχέσις or relation that exists between the subject and the predicate, which are separated or connected by the particle "without" or "with." As, for example, when it is said in Rom. 3:28: "We are justified χωρὶς ἔργων, without works"; Heb. 11:22: "Without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins"; and again in the same place, verse 28: "Christ will be seen at His second coming χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας, without sin"; Heb. 2:6: "Without faith it is impossible to please God"; it is manifest that the particle does not have the same meaning in every case, but this must be elicited from the σχέσις that the extremes have with one another, as the Holy Scripture testifies. But the Holy Spirit testifies that holiness and whatever other works of holiness have no σχέσις of a causal medium, whether principal or less principal, toward the acquisition of eternal salvation, in the same Epistle to the Romans. Whence it remains that nothing at all follows from the particle "without" alone, except the negation of the attribute alone, just as nothing at all follows from the opposite particle "with" except the presence of the attribute alone; but it does not pertain to these prepositions "without" and "with" to determine the mode and effect of the attribute, but these must be determined from elsewhere. That holiness is predicated of the one who attains or will see God in the mode of a mere attribute is evident from the connection of this attribute with others preceding it, such as the tolerance of afflictions, the zeal and diligence of amendment, the zeal for peace, verses 12, 13, and 14, and the parallels in Matt. 5:8, 9, etc.: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God; blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be the children of God; blessed are they, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." These and similar attributes of those who are to be saved cannot, except by manifest violence...

to be set forth as the scope of Christ concerning the cause without which not, or as a means of obtaining eternal salvation, since the grammatical position of the words shows that they are bare attributes of those who are to be saved, not causes.” (Vindiciae S.S. per loca classica system. theol. p. 121 sq.)

Form. Conc.: “It is also wrong when it is taught that a person must be saved in another way or through something else than how he is justified before God, so that we are indeed justified by faith alone without works, but that it is impossible to be saved without works or to obtain salvation without works. This is therefore false, for it is directly against the saying of Paul in Romans 4: ‘Blessed is the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works.’ And Paul’s reason is that we obtain salvation in the same way as we obtain righteousness; indeed, that by the very same means, when we are justified through faith, we also at the same time receive the sonship and inheritance of eternal life and salvation; and therefore Paul sets and presses the *particulae exclusivae*, that is, such words by which works and one’s own merit are entirely excluded, namely, ‘by grace,’ ‘apart from works,’ just as strongly in the article of salvation as in the article of justification.” (Art. 3. Sol. Declar. p. 621 sq.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who... not only deny that faith alone justifies, but also deny that faith justifies primarily, since the primary parts are owed to charity. The Council of Trent pronounces anathema upon those who say that we are justified by trust alone, Sess. 6, can. 12; cf. can. 14... They say that faith does not justify alone, but together with six other acts, namely, fear, hope, love, repentance, the purpose of receiving the sacraments, and the purpose of a new life... 2. Of the Anabaptists, asserting that faith alone in Christ without one’s own proper works and sufferings justifies no one before God... 3. Of the Socinians and Arminians, who, even if they concede that we are justified by faith alone, nevertheless describe that faith by obedient assent or the purpose of obeying God, or by obedience itself.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 797.)

Latin:

Kromayerus: ,,Sola fides justificat, sed solitaria non existit.“ (Th. posit.-pol. II, 374.) "

Form. Conc. ; ,,Manet, quod Lutherus recte dicit: ,Bene conveniunt et sunt connexa inseparabiliter fides et opera; sed sola fides est, quae apprehendit benedictionem sine operibus, et tamen nunquam est sola." (Solid. Declar. Art. 3. p. 619.)

Eadem: ,,Aber hier muss mit sonderm Fleiss darauf gar gute Acht gegeben werden, wenn der Artikel der Rechtfertigung rein bleiben soll, dass nicht dasjenige, was vor dem Glauben hergehet, und was demselben nachfolget, zugleich mit in den Artikel der Rechtfertigung, als darzu nöthig und gehörig, eingemenget oder eingeschoben werde, weil nicht eins oder gleich ist von der Bekehrung und von der Rechtfertigung zu reden. Denn nicht alles, was zur Bekehrung gehöret, auch zugleich in den Artikel der Rechtfertigung gehöret, in und zu welchem allein gehöret und vonnöthen ist Gottes Gnade, der Verdienst Christi, der Glaube, so solches in der Verheissung des Evangelii annimmet, dadurch uns die Gerechtigkeit Christi zugerechnet wird, daher wir erlangen und haben Vergebung der Sünden, Versühnung mit Gott, die Kindschaft und Erbschaft des ewigen Lebens.“ (Art. 3. Sol. Declar. p. 615.)

Gerhardus: ״Quod pontificii disputant, gratiam Dei tribuere nostris operibus vim justificandi, cum merito Christi concurrere operum nostrorummerita, illud άτερ γραφής asseritur nec convenit cum oppositionibus apostolicis inter gratiam et opera, inter credere et operari.“ (L. c. § 152.)

Idem: ״Derogatur Abrahae justificatio ex operibus; jam vero tempore Abrahae leges ceremoniales nondum erant latae: ergo non possunt intelligi opera juxta leges ceremoniales facta. . . Si operibus accepta ferenda esset justitia, quomodo opera legis ceremonialis exeluderentur, cum ceremoniarum observatio, ad primam decalogi tabulam pertinens, divini cultus pars fuerit non postrema?“ (L. de justif. § 151.)

Quenstedtius: ״Disting. Luc. 7, 47. inter causam et effectum. Christus ad Simonem de Maria dicit: ,Remissa ei peccata multa, nam dilexit multum.‘ Hinc pontificii caritatis meritum inferunt, cum tamen satis manifeste liqueat, remissionem peccatorum causam fuisse et non offectum dilectionis. Lysis: Quia h. 1. non est causa, cur res sit, sed causa, cur cognoscatur, non est causa consequentis, sed consequentiae, qualis est deductio ex praemissis. Sic dicimus: Ibi est ignis, quia est fumus, cum tamen fumus non est causa ignis. Sic ancilla dicebat Petro: ,Tu es Galilaeus, quia sermo tuus te prodit.‘ Sermo ille non erat causa, cur Petrus esset Galilaeus, sed indicium. Adeoque Christus non a dilectione ad peccatorum remissionem argumentatur, tamquam a causa ad effectum, sed potius ab effectu ad causam antegressam declarandam ratiocinando progreditur. Causam vero remissionis peccatorum ipse indicat subjiciens: ,Fides tua te salvam fecit‘, v. 50. Particula itaque οτι non est causalis, sed ratiocinativa, sive non notat causam rei, sed conclusionis. Idem respondendum ad locum 1 Joh. 3, 14.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 802. sq.)

Huelsemannus: ״Dictum apostoli ad Rom. 10, 10.: ,Corde creditur ad justitiam, ore fit confessio ad salutem‘, nequaquam significat, confessionem oris vel quodcunque aliud bonum opus, contradis tinctum fidei cordis, necessarium esse ad salutem, sive tanquam causam sine qua non, sive tanquam medium causale, sive tanquam meritum analogum, congruum aut condignum; neque significat, salutem distinctas causas habere a causis justitiae impetrandae, aut ad justitiam consequendam sufficere quidem solam fidem cordis, ad salutem autem consequendam requiri praeter fidem cordis etiam confessionem oris. ..

Quoad significatum particulae ad manifestum est, eo qualemcunque PART. III. CAP. V. analogiam unius ad alterum notari, non causam, ut Phil. 1, 19.ז,Tribulatio prodest ad salutem‘, 2 Cor. 7, 10. 2 Thess. 2, 11. Luc. 1, 35. Rom. 3, 26. Joh. 11, 4.: ,Morbus non est ad mortem, sed ad gloriam Dei‘, aliisque locis infinitis, . . . unde sequitur, modum cohaesionis, quo salus cohaeret cum confessione oris, quo justitia cohaeret cum fide cordis, aliunde determinandum esse. . .

Vera igitur solutio hujus dicti ad Rom. 10. haec est: 1. Quod apostolus per confessionem oris h. 1. non intelligit confessionem laudis et gratitudinis, quae proprie bonum opus dicitur, sed confessionem agnitionis, et notitiae, i. e., signum acquisitae de Christo notitiae, quod probatur ex loco allegato׳ Deut. 30, 14.: ,Prope est illud verbum in ore tuo et in corde tuo.‘ . . . 2. Quod apostolus consecutionem salutis et justitiae non voluerit partiri inter confessionem oris et fidem cordis tanquam distinctos effectus distinctarum causarum, sed quod confessionem oris et fidem cordis tanquam nudum signum notitiae et fidei praesentis allegaverit, ex occasione dicti Mosaici, quod antecedit, vel ex eo patet, quod in declaratione sententiae suae v. 11. et 13. salutem et gloriam aeternam atque aversionem ignominiae aeternae soli fidei tribuit, quando per particulam ratiocinativam yap v. 11.: ,Dicit enim Scriptura: Quicunque credit‘ etc., rationem reddit, cur v. anteced. 10. dixisset, corde credi ad justitiam, ore fieri confessionem ad salutem, quia nempe ex fide omnis justitia et salus sit. Ex his, inquam, testimoniis, quibus apostolus dictum v. 10. comprobat et salutem soli fidei tribuit, apparet, quod confessionem oris non tanquam concausam salutis posuerit, sed tanquam signum verae causae. . .

Ebr. 12, 14. Norunt pueri, praepositionis cum aliquo et per aliquid non esse eandem vim. Quomodo non sequitur: Deum nemo videbit sine gaudio, diabolum sine terrore, ergo gaudium est causa sine qua non videndi Deum, terror est causa sine qua non videndi diabolum. Attributa sunt videntis, non causae nec media videndi Deum, diabolum, quomodo damnati dicuntur visuri justos cum magna confusione, Sap. 5, 2., quomodo crucifixores Christi dicuntur visuri eum, quem confoderunt, cum magna consternatione, Zach. 12, 10., atque ejusmodi sunt infinita. Particula autem sine cum sit indefinita et vi indefinitudinis neget solum attributum, quemadmodum opposita particula cum ponit solum attributum, non autem est nota causae, quod ex logicis addiscitur, particulae enim ex, per, a sunt notae causales: ideo finiendum seu determinandum est ex σχέσει seu habitudine, quae est inter subjectum et praedicatum, quod per particulam sine vel cum separantur vel connectuntur, ut e. g., quando Rom. 3, 28. dicitur: ,Justificamur χωρϊς έργων, sine operibus‘; Ebr. 11, 22.: ,Sine effusione sanguinis non fit remissio peccatorum‘; et rursus ibidem v. 28.: ,Christus in secundo adventu videbitur χωρίς αμαρτίας, sine peccato‘; Ebr. 2, 6.: ,Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo‘, manifestum sit, non esse utrobique particulae idem significatum, sed hoc demum eruendum esse ex σχέσει, quam extrema, teste Scriptura Sacra, inter se habent. Testatur autem Spiritus S., sanctimoniam et quaecunque alia sanctimoniae opera ad salutis aeternae acquisitionem non habere ullam σχέσιν medii causalis, sive principalis sive minus principalis, eod. 1. ad Rom. Unde relinquitur, ex sola particula sine nihil omnino sequi, nisi solius attributi negationem, quemadmodum ex opposita particula cum nihil omnino, quam sola attributi praesentia, sequitur; modum autem et effectum attributi determinare non spectat ad has praepositiones sine et cum, sed aliunde ista determinanda sunt. Per modum autem nudi attributi praedicari sanctimoniam comprehensoris sive futuri visoris Dei, patet ex connexione hujus attributi cum aliis praecedentibus, ut tolerantia afflictionum, studio et diligentia emendationis, studio pacis, v. 12. 13. et 14. et parallelis Matth. 5, 8. 9. sq.: ,Beati mundo corde, quia videbunt Deum; beati pacifici, quia erunt filii Dei; beati, quia illorum est regnum coelorum.‘ Haec et similia attributa salvandorum non possunt, nisi per manifestam violentiam

in scopum Christi de causa sine qua non aut medio consequendi salutem aeternam exponi, cum positus vocum grammaticus ostendat, esse nuda attributa salvandorum, non causas.“ (Vindiciae S.S. per loca classica system. theol. p. 121. sq.)

Form. Conc.: ,,Es ist auch das unrecht, wann gelehret wird, dass der Mensch anderergestalt oder durch etwas anders selig müsse werden, denn wie er für Gott gerechtfertiget wird, also dass wir wohl allein durch den Glauben ohne Werk gerecht werden, aber ohne Werk selig zu werden oder die Seligkeit ohne Werke zu erlangen sei unmöglich. Dieses ist darum falsch, denn es ist stracks wider den Spruch Pauli Röm. 4.: ,Die Seligkeit ist des Menschen, welchem Gott die Gerechtigkeit zurechnet ohne Werk.‘ Und Pauli Grund ist, dass wir auf eine Weise, wie die Gerechtigkeit, also auch die Seligkeit erlangen, ja dass wir eben darmit, wenn wir durch den Glauben gerecht werden, auch zugleich empfangen die Kindschaft und Erbschaft des ewigen Lebens und Seligkeit; und derhalben Paulus die particulas exclusivas, das ist, solche Wort, dadurch die Werk und eigner Verdienst gänzlich ausgeschlossen wird, nämlich aus Gnaden, ohne Werk, ja so stark bei dem Artikel der Seligkeit, als bei dem Artikel der Gerechtigkeit setzet und treibet.“ (Art. 3. Sol. Declar. p. 621. sq.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, qui. . . nec solum negant, solam fidem justificare, sed etiam inficiantur, fldem praecipue justificare, cum praecipuae partes caritati debeantur. Concil. Trid. anathema dicit iis, qui sola fiducia nos justificari ajunt, Sess. 6. can. 12. cf. can. 14. . . . Dicunt, fidem non solum justificare, sed una cum sex aliis actibus, nempe timore, spe, dilectione, poenitentia, proposito suscipiendi sacramenta et proposito novae vitae. . . 2. Anabaptistarum, asserentium, solam fidem in Christum sine suis propriis operibus et passionibus coram Deo neminem justificare. . . 3. Socinianorum et Arminianorum, qui, etiamsi concedant, nos sola fide justificari, eam tamen fldem per obsequiosum assensum seu propositum obediendi Deo vel per obedientiam ipsam describunt.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 797.)


### On Justification: The same: “Antithesis

The same: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who maintain: 1.) That good works justify entirely, yet not formally, but meritoriously, i.e., that good works are not the formal cause of justification, but the efficient and meritorious cause... 2.) That justification is derogated by the Apostle only from the works of the ceremonial law, but not from the works of the moral law... 3.) Or if even the works of the moral law are excluded from the act of justification, that only those are excluded which are done by the unregenerate before faith, but not those which proceed from the regenerate after faith. 2. Of the Socinians, who also ascribe justification to our obedience or our works. ‘That justifying faith is to obey the precepts of God, and to believe that those things which Christ said are true,’ Socinus teaches throughout chapters 11 and 12 of Part 4 of *De Servatore*. The same Socinus, *De fide et opp.* f. 55, T. 1. Op. f. 623, says: ‘Works themselves justify, insofar as they are the execution and perfection and, as it were, the form of faith itself.’... They further assert that the works excluded by the Apostle are those that are absolute and perfect in every respect, but not works *τὰ πρὸς δυνατόν* [things according to ability], or those which are possible... 3. Of the Arminians, who in *Apolog.* c. 10, p. 111, say: ‘Nor is there any cause or reason that can move the Censors to judge this opinion of the Remonstrants concerning faith or the obedience of faith—namely, that it should be considered in the matter of justification as our work or act—to be Socinian.’... 4. Of the Anabaptists, who attribute to their own works the power of justifying before the tribunal of God, and suspend the gift of eternal life upon their own righteousness... 5. Of the Innovators, who teach: ‘That a man is justified not only by faith, but at the same time by works, applying to himself and apprehending salvation while he walks in the divine precepts’; likewise: ‘That good works cooperate with man toward justification; that a good purpose...’ PART III. CAP. V.

to be required along with faith for justification; likewise: "The purpose of loving God and observing His commandments is the cause without which not and the condition under which we are justified." Thus D. Hornejus asserts: "Man is also justified by works," P. 2. Disp. 4. s. 1. Ed. 1653. th. 51. And in Disp. de summa fidei non qualislibet, sed quae per caritatem operatur, necessitate ad salutem th. 4. he maintains: "The purpose of the love of God and neighbor must be present before justification." (L. c. q. 8. f. 806. sq.) §

11. The form or formal reason of justification is the remission or non-imputation of sins. For otherwise it must be confessed that justification is not a substance composed of matter and form. A distinction must also be made between the formal reason of the entire judicial process (concerning which see here § 5) and the form of that act which, in the process, is opposed to condemnation and removes it, and which Scripture calls by the name of justification. We are considering not the former, but the latter here.

Apology of the A. C.: "To obtain the remission of sins is to be justified, according to that (Ps. 32:1): 'Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven.'" (Artic. 4. p. 100.)

Smalcald Articles: "Upon such faith, renewal and forgiveness of sins follow good works. And whatever is still sinful or lacking in them shall not be reckoned as sin or lack, precisely for the sake of Christ Himself, but the person shall be called and be entirely righteous and holy, both in his person and his works, out of pure grace and mercy, poured out and spread over us in Christ." (P. III. art. 13. p. 324. sq.)

Kromayerus: "Sin is removed in justification, not so that it does not exist, but so that it does not harm." (Th. posit.-pol. II, 382.) Quenstedtius: "The form of justification in general does not consist in a certain physical change, such as heating, by which someone becomes hot from being cold, a likeness which Becanus adapts here concerning Justification, c. 2. th. 2. For our justification does not occur by the real expulsion of sin and the infusion of righteousness, or by a change from injustice to inherent righteousness; but it consists in a moral change, which constitutes a man righteous by a judicial action that is purely extrinsic to him, that is, one which is performed not in the man, but around and outside the man, and from that it denominates him, at least extrinsically, yet most truly." (L. c. s. 1. th. 12. f. 744.)

That ἄφεσις ἀνομιῶν, concerning which see Rom. 4:7 and Luke 11:4. It is called elsewhere ἄφεσις τῶν ὀφειλημάτων, remission of debts, Matt. 6:12, and shortly after ἄφεσις τῶν παραπτωμάτων, of lapses, errors, or transgressions, v. 14, 15. Therefore, it is not the total expulsion of sins from man, just as we, who forgive debts or offenses to our neighbor, do not by this very act really remove anything in him; but, using a locution taken from contracts between a creditor and a debtor, it denotes the relaxation of the obligation to pay the debt, as if it were a certain bond (certainly a moral one). From this, πάρεσις ἁμαρτημάτων, Rom. 3:25, does not differ, which certainly does not denote a mere delay of the demand of the debt, or a passing over of the debtor, whom the creditor allows to be quiet or does not compel. Rather, by both words is denoted the remission of a debt, such as otherwise, when it occurs among men, also

it implies the restitution of a promissory note, or when a creditor writes that he has received payment (ἀπέχει), and credits the debtor with the debt paid, and declares that he will never be called upon by him. Thus, indeed, God is said to forget our sins (Ezek. 18:22), to cast them into the depths of the sea (Mic. 7:19), to cast them behind His back (Isa. 38:17), to remove them far from us (Ps. 103:12), to hide His face from them (Ps. 51:9), all of which signify, in an anthropopathic manner, the removal of the guilt of sins. Meanwhile, the blessed Gerhard rightly observes that God does not remit sins rashly, as if He did not care for them; nor unjustly, as if He loved them; nor ignorantly, as if He were unaware of them or deceived in their estimation; but, so that justice and mercy may shine forth simultaneously, He remits them with a view to the plenary satisfaction rendered by Christ and apprehended by believers through faith. *Annott. in Ep. ad Rom. cap. III. v. 25. p. 216.* Or that God wills to judge that the sins of the man to be justified do not so pertain to him that he must be afflicted with punishments on their account. See Rom. 4:7-8; 8:1. See above § 4. And thus the guilt of sins, although it is not taken away from the sins themselves (which, by the very fact that they are sins, are also worthy of punishment), is nevertheless taken away from the sinful man. Cf. § 2, last note. Thus, certainly, the blessed Gerhard wrote in *L. de Justif. § 202. p. 1037*: Justification is defined by the remission of sins and the non-imputation of iniquities (Rom. 4:6-8), which definition, N.B., is full and perfect. And to this he refers the parallel passages of Scripture: Luke 1:77; 18:13; Acts 13:38; 1 John 1:7, coll. with Rom. 5:9. Furthermore, we do not deny that a certain variation, extension, or even restriction of justification is found in the writings of our own people, which the blessed Huelsemann also acknowledges and explains with examples in *Praelect. in F. C. art. XI. Sect. II.*, where he deals with the definition, form, and difference of Justification, pp. 545, 546. And thus it is certain that when we say the form of justification is the remission or non-imputation of sins, the imputation of the righteousness of Christ—that is, His obedience, both active and passive—is not excluded, nor is the imputation of faith itself for righteousness. We merely think that the imputation of the righteousness of Christ and of faith itself is, in the order of reason, prior to that forensic act of justification by which men are absolved from the guilt of sins, because to the question: "Why does God justify a man?" the answer given by *a priori* reasoning is: "Because God imputes the righteousness or merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, to the man, or judges it to pertain to the man in such a way that he is therefore absolved from the guilt of sins." As far as the matter itself is concerned, the statement of the blessed Gerhard, *l. c. de Justif. § 198. p. m. 1034*, is manifest and grave: Before the judgment of the most just God, he says, justification without righteousness has no place; therefore, the remission of sins, N.B., is founded upon the righteousness of Christ, on account of which, when apprehended by faith, God receives us into favor and remits our sins. The blessed Huelsemann gives a more detailed reason why he thinks the imputation of the merit of Christ should be placed in order before the non-imputation of sins, and he draws the cause 1) from the words of the Apostle in Rom. 3:24-25; 4:3-4, etc.; 2) from the analogy of faith, or because it is necessary that the application of some meritorious cause precede before sin can be remitted to a sinful man; unless we wish to say that remission occurs from a fullness of power without the intervention of any satisfaction or alien merit, which the Socinians maintain. The blessed Scherzer follows him in *Brev. Huelseman. aucto, cap. XI. § 16. pp. 671, 672.* But when 284 PART III. CAP. V. Since the remission of sins is founded upon the righteousness of Christ imputed to the man to whom sins are to be remitted, one may now not undeservedly distinguish between the form of the righteous man, in view of whom he is reputed righteous in the act of justification, and the form of the act of justification itself. As the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, Article on Justification (p. 273, post-mortem ed.), teaches, the term "to be justified" can be taken in two ways: In one way, as it is the same as being made or constituted righteous from unrighteous by a righteousness that avails before God, which indeed is none other than the righteousness of Christ, the active and passive obedience obtained for us; in the other way, as it is the same as being pronounced or reputed righteous.

Namely, in the former sense we are justified or made righteous when we apprehend the righteousness of Christ by faith, so that it becomes ours, and thus we are formally constituted righteous before God through the righteousness of Christ apprehended by faith (by which reasoning it can also be said that the formal cause of justification is the righteousness of Christ apprehended by faith, insofar as it happens in the very process of justification that God imputes to man the alien righteousness of Christ); in the latter sense, it must be confessed that the formal cause of justification is the non-imputation or remission of sins, while the righteousness of Christ, apprehended by faith and accepted by God as ours, or imputed to us by God, is its foundation, and therefore prior in the order of nature. See the blessed D. Musaeus, *Ausführliche Erklärung*, L. XIII, Qu. 73, p. 586 ff. To these responds what the blessed Th. Thummius, in a special treatise in which he explains the terms and distinctions occurring in the article on justification (no. CXLIII, p. 246), taught in these words: "The remission of sins is the same as justification, and differs from it in a different respect.

praerequiri cum fide ad justificationem‘; item: ,Propositum diligendi Deum et praecepta ejus observandi esse causam sine qua non et conditionem, sub qua justificemur‘. Sic D. 11. Forma seu ratio formalis a justificationis est remissio b sive non-imputatio c peccatorum.d Alias enim fatendum est, justificationem non esse substantiam ex materia et forma compositam. Distinguendum quoque est inter rationem formalem totius processus judiciarii (de quo vid. h. 1. § 5.) et formam iUius actus, qui in processu condemnationi opponitur eamque tollit, quemque Scriptura justificationis nomine appellat. Non illam, sed hanc h. 1. consideramus.

Apologia A. C.: ,,Consequi remissionem peccatorum est justiflcari, juxta illud (Ps. 32, 1.): ,Beati, quorum remissae sunt iniquitates‘.“ (Artic. 4. p. 100.)

Articuli Smalcald.: ,,Auf solchen Glauben, Verneuerung und Vergebung der Sünden folgen denn gute Werke. Und was an denselben noch sündlich oder Mangel ist, soll nicht für Sünde oder Mangel gerechnet werden eben um desselben Christi willen, sondern der Mensch soll ganz, beide nach der Person und seinen Werken, gerecht und heilig heissen und sein aus lauter Gnade und Barmherzigkeit, in Christo über uns ausgeschüttet und ausgebreitet.“ (P. III. art. 13. p. 324. sq.)

Kromayerus: ,,Peccatum in justificatione tollitur, non ut non sit, sed ut non obsit.“ (Th. posit.-pol. II, 382.) Quenstedtius: ,,Eorma justificationis in genere non consistit in mutatione quadam physica, qualis est calefactio, qua quis ex frigido fit calidus, quod simile huc accommodat Becanus de Justif. c. 2. th. 2. Neque enim fit justificatio nostra reali peccati expulsione et justitiae infusione, vel ab injustitia ad justitiam inhaerentem mutatione; sed consistit in mutatione morali, quae constituit hominem justum actione judiciali et eidem pure extrinseca, h. e., tali, quae non in homine, sed circa et extra hominem peragitur, indeque ipsum extrinsece saltem, verissime tamen denominat.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 12. f. 744.) illa ανομιών) de qua vid. Rom. 4, 7 et Luc. 11, 4. Dicitur alias άφεσιτ των όφειλημάτων^ remissio debitorum, Matth. 6, 12., et mox αψεσις των παραπτωμάτων, lapsuum, erratorum aut delictorum, v. 14. 15. Neque ergo est totalis expulsio peccatorum ex homine, quemadmodum nec nos, qui proximo debita aut offensas remittimus, hoc ipso aliquid in eo realiter tollimus; sed, locutione a contractibus inter creditorem et debitorem petita, denotat obligationis ad solvendum debitum, quasi vinculi cujusdam (moralis certe), relaxationem. A qua non differt πάρεσις Αμαρτημάτων, Rom. 3, 25., quae sane non denotat nudam dilationem exigentiae debiti, seu praetermissionem debitoris, quem quietum sinat aut non compellet creditor. Utroque potius verbo denotatur remissio debiti, qualis alias, cum inter homines fit, etiam

restitutionem chirographi importat, aut cum scribit creditor, se απέχει, ac debitori accepto fert aes solutum et declarat, ipsum a se nunquam compellatum iri. Sic profecto Deus dicitur oblivisci peccatorum nostrorum Ezech. 18, 22., projicere ea in profundum maris Midi. 7, 29., post tergum rejicere Esaiae 38, 17., elongare a nobis Ps. 103, 12., abscondere faciem suam ab eis Ps. 51, 11., quae omnia άν&ρωποπαΰώς sublationem reatus peccatorum significant. Rom. 4, 7. 8. cap. 8, 1. Eoque refert parallela Scripturae loca Luc. 1, 77. cap. 18, 13. Actor. 13, 38. 1 Joh. 1, 7. coll. cum Rom. 5, 9 Caeterum non negamus, variationem quandam, extensionem vel etiam restrictionem justificationis in nostratium scriptis deprehendi, quam etiam agnoscit et exemplis declarat b. Huelsemannus Praelect. in F. C. art. XI. Sect. II., ubi de definitione, forma et differentia Justif. agit, p. 545. 546 Atque ita certum est, quando formam justificationis dicimus esse remissionem aut non-imputationem peccatorum, non excludi imputationem justitiae Christi seu obedientiae, cum activae, tum passivae, neque imputationem ipsius fidei ad justitiam. Scilicet existimamus tantum, imputationem justitiae Christi ipsiusque fidei in signo rationis priorem esse actu illo forensi justificationis, quo homines absolvuntur a reatu peccatorum, quia ad quaestionem: Quare Deus hominem justificet? ratione a priori data respondetur: Quia Deus justitiam seu meritum Christi fide apprehensum homini imputat, seu ita judicat ad hominem pertinere, ut is propterea a reatu peccatorum absolvatur. Quod ad rem attinet, manifesta et gravis est sententia b. Gerhardi 1. c. de Justif. § 198. p. m. 1034.: Coram Dei justissimi judicio, ait, justificatio sine justitia non habet locum; proinde peccatorum remissio NB. fundatur in Christi justitia, propter quam fide apprehensam Deus nos in gratiam recipit et peccata nobis remittit. Prolixius autem b. Huehernannus rationem reddit, cur imputationem meriti Christi ordine praeponendam putet non-imputationi peccatorum, et causam 1) arcessit ex verbis apostoli Rom. 3, 24. 25. cap. 4, 3. 4. sq.; 2) ex analogia fidei, seu quod oporteat praecedere applicationem alicujus causae meritoriae, antequam homini peccatori possit remitti peccatum; nisi dicere velimus, remissionem fieri ex plenitudine potestatis sine interventu alicujus satisfactionis aut meriti alieni, quod Sociniani volunt. Sequitur eum b. Scherzerus in Brev. Huelseman. aucto, cap. XI. § 16. p. 671. 672 Quando autem 284PART.III.CAP. V. remissio peccatorum fundatur in justitia Christi imputata homini, cui peccata sint remittenda, jam non immerito distingui potest inter formam hominis justi, cujus intuitu in actu justificationis justus reputatur, et inter formam ipsius actus justificationis; prout Apologia Conf. Aug. artic. de Justif. p. m. 273, docet, vocem justificari accipi posse dupliciter: Uno modo, prout idem est, atque ex injustis justos effici sive constitui per justitiam, quae coram Deo valet, quae quidem non est alia, quam justitia Christi obedientia activa et passiva nobis parta; altero modo, prout idem est, quod justos pronunciari aut reputari. Nempe priore sensu justificamur aut justi efficimur, quando justitiam Christi fide apprehendimus, ut nostra fiat, et sic per justitiam Christi fide apprehensam coram Deo formaliter constituimur justi (qua ratione etiam dici potest, formale justificationis esse justitiam Christi fide apprehensam, quatenus in ipso processu justificationis fit, ut Deus homini imputet justitiam alienam Christi); posteriore sensu fatendum est, formale justificationis esse non-imputationem seu remissionem peccatorum, justitiam Christi autem fide apprehensam et a Deo acceptatam ut nostram, sive a Deo nobis imputatam, esse ejus fundamentum, adeoque ordine naturae priorem. Vid. b. D. Musaei Ausführliche Erklärung L. XIII. Qu. 73. p. 586. sqq.

Quibus respondet, quod b. Th. Thummius Tract. peculiari, quo terminos et distinctiones in articulo de Justif. occurrentes explicat, numer. CXLI1I. p. 246. docuit his verbis: Remissio peccatorum eadem est cum justificatione, et ab ea differt, diverso respectu. Remissio enim peccatorum considerari potest vel solitarie, quatenus distincta et peculiaris nostrae justificationis causa est, (NB.) formalis scilicet, vel junctim, quatenus caeteras justificationis causas, gratiam scilicet Dei, meritum Christi et fidem complectitur. Priori modo differt a justificatione (videlicet pro toto processu accepta) ceu pars a suo toto; posteriori vero justificatio cum remissione peccatorum est ταύτό quiddam seu idem.


### On Justification: For the remission of sins can be considered either solitarily, insofar as it is…

For the remission of sins can be considered either solitarily, insofar as it is a distinct and peculiar cause of our justification—namely, the formal cause—or conjunctively, insofar as it embraces the other causes of justification, namely, the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and faith. In the former way, it differs from justification (namely, taken as the whole process) as a part from its whole; in the latter way, however, justification is one and the same thing with the remission of sins." B. Meisnerus: "The formal cause either denotes the entire quiddity of a thing itself, or the cause of the quiddity, that by which a thing is what it is. For one is called a metaphysical form, which indicates the whole quiddity, such as humanity; another is a logical form, which precisely posits the cause of the quiddity, such as rationality. If it denotes the whole quiddity, then we say the form of justification is the remission of sin or absolution from the punishment of sin and acceptance into grace for eternal life on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. For in these consists our entire justification, according to that passage in Romans 3:25: 'To declare his righteousness δια τήν πάρεσιν των προγεγονότων αμαρτημάτων,' that he offers righteousness by forgiving sin. Here our δικαίωσις is expressly said to be placed in the remission of sins. If by 'form' you understand precisely not the whole quiddity, but only that by which a thing is what it is, I say that this is nothing other than the merit of Christ imputed through faith, or the imputation of the merit apprehended by faith. For if you ask: 'Why are we absolved from the punishment of sin and accepted into grace?' the entire Scripture answers: 'Because the passion and obedience of Christ is imputed through faith, as if we ourselves had satisfied for our sins.' And if this distinction is rightly held, our theologians, to whom a perpetual dissension from the Papists is otherwise objected, can easily be reconciled."

(*Anthropol. Disput. XXVII, p. C. 1.*) Quenstedtius: "Therefore, our justification before God consists in the remission or non-imputation of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ. These very parts (so to speak) are not diverse or...

distinct not in essence, but only in reason. For the imputation of the righteousness of Christ is, materially, the very remission of sins, and the remission of sins is the very imputation of the righteousness of Christ, so that either term, taken separately, can express the whole nature of justification. Note: The remission or non-imputation of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, on account of their supreme affinity, embrace one another, and necessarily the one includes the other, nor can one ever be torn away or separated from the other. For it is one act of imputation; the mode is merely twofold, privative and positive, consisting in the imputation of an alien righteousness and the non-imputation of one’s own iniquity; and both imply a real judgment of God, so that our justification formally is nothing other than the transfer of our sin unto Christ and of the righteousness of Christ unto us through imputation. Whence also the Apostle Paul, in Romans 4, interchanges the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness in his description of justification, which he defines now by the remission of sins, now by the imputation of righteousness, but does not constitute two integral parts. For just as it can be rightly said at one and the same time and by one action that the expulsion of darkness from the air is the very introduction of light into the air, so one and the same impious man, at one and the same time and by an act of justification that is entirely indivisible, is both absolved from guilt and pronounced righteous, as Dr. Weller well teaches in his Commentary on Romans 4:7, 8, p. 271 sq. (L. c. s. 1. th. 14; f. 753.)

J. Olearius: “Just as they differ only by reason and with respect to the terms from which and to which—covering a naked body and putting on a garment—for as regards the formal aspect itself, it is one act, namely, clothing; for by putting on, nakedness is covered, and by covering, the body is clothed: so also in justification, by covering sin, righteousness is put on, and by putting on righteousness, sin is covered; and when one is posited, the other is always posited as well.” (See Carpzov’s Isag. in lib. symbol. p. 1301.)

Carpzovius: “Regarding the remission of sins, one must attend to how and to what extent it is held and posited by the Augsburg Confession as the object of justifying faith, in order to refute the sophistical objections of Bellarmine, lib. 1. de justif. c. 10. For the remission of sins is considered in a twofold way. First, as it has been acquired by Christ and is offered in the Word and Sacraments as a good divinely promised and intended to be sought and possessed by sinners. Then, indeed, as it has already been accepted and applied and is possessed through faith. Just as also the merit of Christ can now be considered as it is offered in the Word and Sacraments, as imputable unto righteousness; now as it has already been imputed through faith and is possessed by faith. In the former way, the remission of sins is the object of justifying faith, insofar as it justifies and apprehends that remission as a benefit acquired by Christ and offered to us in the Gospel as a good destined for our salvation; in the latter way, it is also the object of justifying faith, but not insofar as it justifies, but insofar as it is occupied with a good object—namely, the accepted remission of sins—and delights in it and has joy in it. Therefore, when in Article 4 of the Augsburg Confession and in the Apology the remission of sins is sometimes posited and alleged as the object of justifying faith, insofar as it justifies, then it is considered not in the latter way, but in the former way and manner. The Apology of the A.C. expresses this significantly when it says: ‘The object of justifying faith is the promised mercy,’ p. 96.” (Isagog. in lib. symbol. p. 208 sq.) §

12. The subject of justification is a man who is a sinner, but converted or regenerate. Who not only is in need of justification, but is also justifiable, or, while preserving the vindicatory justice of God, is capable of the remission of sins. PART III. CHAP. V.

See Rom. 3:23, 24, where these two are joined: ήμαρτον and δικαιούμενοι, they sinned, and are justified, etc. But afterwards, in ch. 4:5, it is expressly said: δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ, to justify the ungodly.

Osiander: "The ungodly person here (Rom. 4:5) is not called such by the apostle in an ampliative sense regarding a past state, in the way (according to the papist explanation) wine is called water; but in the sense that the dead are called those whom God makes alive, and all things that are, are called nothing, ch. 4:17—in that sense the apostle here calls the ungodly person whom God justifies... God justifies the ungodly in that state; this is proved from the parallel in Matt. 9, where Christ says: 'I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.' If, therefore, sinners as such are called to repentance, it follows also that the ungodly as such is justified. But the ungodly as such, reduplicatively, is one thing, who is not justified; and the ungodly as such, specifically, is another, who is indeed justified." (Colleg. V, 188.) See here § 1. Cf. Epistle to Titus 3:5, 7. Whence it is simultaneously established that God justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5) not insofar as he is and remains ungodly, but the ungodly person who, led by repentance, has retracted the sins committed and has presented to God the satisfaction of Christ for sins, apprehended by faith, as a λύτρον for his sins. For otherwise God hates those who work iniquity, Ps. 5:5, and he who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him, John 3:36.

S. Schmidtius: "The receiving or accepting subject, or the object of justification, which we have already said is man, we can, and indeed must, constitute as twofold: remote or proximate. The remote subject is every sinful or ungodly man, still constituted under the wrath of God and the guilt of condemnation, indeed capable of reconciliation, yet not yet believing... The proximate subject... of total justification we say is that which is so disposed that nothing further is required in it for the full act of justification. And this is every ungodly or sinful man believing in Him who justifies the ungodly." (Artic. Form. Conc. Repetitio, p. 159, 165 sq.) Huelsemannus: "It is necessary that the adequate subject of justification be, at least in the order of nature, instructed with justifying faith before the absolution or justification itself follows, even if they are simultaneous in time." (Praelect. Form. Conc. p. 606.) ANTITHESIS.

Theologians of Wittenberg (a. 1597): "It vexes him (Dr. Huber) greatly that we could not let his phrase pass, since he wrote in thesis 59 at Tübingen: 'Christus contulit redemptionem proprie, facto et opere ipso toti generi humano,' that is, Christ has actually and in deed itself handed over (or gifted) the redemption to the whole human race. That we censure this speech of his is said to be acting against the Gospel, and therefore he accuses us of Calvinistic doctrine, but with pure groundlessness. For the reason that we do not let the aforementioned proposition pass for him is because such *conferre*, as it is taken in theological schools, does not properly refer to the acquisition, but rather to the application, delivery, or appropriation, when through the preaching of the Gospel the merit of Christ is offered and handed over to us, and also received and accepted, which cannot happen without faith; and yet Huber also writes expressly in thesis 270 concerning those who do not believe, indeed concerning all men, 'quod remissionem peccatorum acceperint,' that they have received the forgiveness of sins; by which he then gives sufficiently to understand how he intended his *contulit* to be meant. If one now asks whether"

Christ has actually, in work and in deed, acquired, obtained, and brought about redemption from eternal death for the entire human race; to this we answer without any wavering, firmly and irrevocably: Yes. But when it is asked whether Christ confers this redemption upon the entire human race, and therefore the entire human race has received the forgiveness of sins, there we answer a loud No, and leave it to the judgment of all Christians whether we are Calvinistic in this regard.

For such conferring means as much as bestowing, imputing, and appropriating the same to us humans in the word of the Gospel, which happens in no other way than through faith. Just as such redemption and the forgiveness of sins arising therefrom are accepted by no other means than through faith.

Latin:

B. Meisnerus: ״Causa formalis vel notat ipsam totam rei quidditatem, vel causam quiclditatis eam, per quam res est id, quod est. Nam alia dicitur esse forma metaphysica, quae totam innuit quidditatem, ut humanitas, alia logica, quae praecise ponit causam quidditatis, ut rationalitas. Si totam quidditatem notat, tunc dicimus justificationis formam esse remissionem peccati seu absolutionem a poena peccati et acceptationem in gratiam ad vitam aeternam propter Christi meritum fide apprehensum. In his enim consistit omnis nostra justiflcatio juxta illud Rom. 3, 25.: ,Ad ostensionem justitiae δια τήν πάρεσιν των προγεγονότων αμαρτημάτων', dass er die Gerechtigkeit darbiete, indem, dass er die Sünde vergibt. Hic expresse δικαίωσις nostra in remissione peccatorum posita esse dicitur. Si enim quaeras: Cur a poena peccati absolvimur et in gratiam acceptamur? respondet universa Scriptura: Quia passio et obedientia Christi per fidem imputatur, ac si nos ipsi pro peccatis satisfecissemus. Atque haec distinctio si rite teneatur, facile conciliari nostrates poterunt, quibus alias perpe tua objicitur dissensio a pontificiis.“ (Anthropol. Disput. XXVII. p. C. 1.)

distinctae τψ είναι, sed duntaxat τφ λόγφ.
