Ut enim uno eodemque tempore et actione recte dici potest, tenebrarum expulsionem ex aere esse ipsius luminis in aerem introductionem, ita unus idemque homo impius uno eodemque tempore et actu justificationis plane individuo et a reatu absolvitur et justus pronunciatur, ut bene docet D. Wellerus Comm. in Rom. 4, 7, 8. p. 271. sq.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 14; f. 753.)

J. Olearius: ,,Sicut non nisi ratione differunt et respectu terminorum a quo et ad quem, tegere nudum corpus et induere vestimentum; quoad ipsum enim formale unus actus est, scii, vestitura; induendo ·enim nuditas tegitur et tegendo corpus induitur: ita etiam in justificatione tegendo peccatum induitur justitia et induendo justitiam tegitur peccatum, unoque posito semper etiam alterum ponitur.“ (Vid. Carpzovii Isag. in lib. symbol. p. 1301.)

Carpzovius: ,,Circa remissionem peccatorum attendendum modo est, quatenus et in quantum pro objecto fidei justificantis illa habeatur atque ponatur ab Augustana Conf., ad diluendas sophisticas objectiones Bellarmini lib. 1. de justif. c. 10. Remissio enim peccatorum duplici modo consideratur. Semel, ut a Christo acquisita est et in verbo ac sacramentis tanquam bonum divinitus promissum et intentum peccatoribus quaerendum et habendum offertur. Deinde vero, prout jam accepta est et per fidem applicata est atque habetur. Sicut etiam meritum Christi nunc considerari potest, ut offertur in verbo et sacramentis, tanquam imputabile ad justitiam; nunc ut jam per fidem imputatum est ac fide possidetur. Priori modo remissio peccatorum objectum fidei justificantis est, quatenus justificat et apprehendit remissionem istam tanquam beneficium a Christo acquisitum et in evangelio nobis, tanquam bonum ad salutem nostram destinatum, oblatum; posteriori modo etiam objectum fidei justificantis illa est, sed non quatenus justificat, sed in quantum circa objectum bonum, remissionem sci. peccatorum acceptam, occupatur et in eo sese delectat atque gaudium habet. Quando igitur in artic. 4. Aug. Conf. et in Apologia aliquoties remissio peccatorum pro objecto fidei justificantis, quatenus justificat, ponitur et allegatur, tunc non in posteriori modo, sed priori modo ac ratione consideratur. Hoc significanter Apologia A. C. exprimit, quando dicit: ,Objectum fidei justificantis esse misericordiam promissam‘, p. 96.“ (Isagog. in lib. symbol. p. 208. sq.) §

12. Subjectum a justificationis est homo peccator,b sed conversus aut renatus. c Quod non solum justificationis indiget, sed et justificabile aut, salva Dei justitia vindicativa, remissionis peccatorum capax est. PART. III. CAP. V.

Sed aliud est impius, qua talis reduplicative, qui non justificatur; et aliud impius, qua impius specificative talis, qui justificatur utique.“ (Colleg. V, 188.) Vid. h. 1. § 1. Conf. Form. Cone. p. 606.) ANTITHESIS.

Theologi Witebergenses (a. 1597.): ״Es verdreusst ihn (Dr. Huber) sehr, dass wir ihm seine Phrasin nicht haben können lassen gut sein, da er thesi 59. Tübingens! geschrieben: ,Christus contulit redemptionem proprie, facto et opere ipso toti generi humano‘, das ist, Christus hat dem ganzen menschlichen Geschlecht übergeben (oder geschenket) die Erlösung eigentlich und in der That selbst. Dass wir diese Rede an ihm strafen, soll wider das Evangelium gehandelt sein, und daher beschuldigt er uns Calvinischer Lehre, aber mit lauterm Ungrund. Denn dass wir berührte Proposition ihm nicht passiren lassen, ist die Ursach, weil solch conferre, wie es in theologischen Schulen genommen wird, nicht eigentlich auf die Erwerbung, sondern vielmehr auf die Application, lieber gab oder Zueignung gehet, wenn durch die Predigt des Evangelii das Verdienst Christi uns angetragen und übergeben, auch empfangen und angenommen wird, welches ohne Glauben nicht geschehen kann; und doch Huber auch von denen, die nicht glauben, ja von allen Menschen thesi 270. ausdrücklich schreibet, ,quod remissionem peccatorum acceperint‘, dass sie die Vergebung der· Sünden empfangen haben; damit er dann genugsam zu verstehen gibt, wie er sein contulit gemeint haben wolle. Wenn man nun fraget, ob

Christus dem ganzen menschlichen Geschlechte eigentlich, im Werk und in der That selber die Erlösung vom ewigen Tod erworben, erlanget und zuwege gebracht, antworten wir ohne alles Wanken, fest und unwiderruflich: Ja. Wenn aber gefragt wird, ob Christus die Erlösung dem ganzen menschlichen Geschlechte conferirt, und daher das ganze menschliche Geschlecht Vergebung der Sünden empfangen habe, da antworten wir lauter Nein und stellens zu aller Christen Urtheil, ob wir hierum Calvinisch sein.

Denn solch Gonfenren heisst so viel, als dieselbige im Wort des Evangelii uns Menschen schenken, zurechnen und zueignen, welches anders nicht als durch den Glauben geschiehet. Wie auch solche Erlösung und die daher entspringende Vergebung der Sünden durch kein ander Mittel als durch den Glauben angenommen wird.


### On Justification: Whoever has never believed in Christ (as, indeed, all hardened Jews and Turks…

Whoever has never believed in Christ (as, indeed, all hardened Jews and Turks and many others never believe), they have certainly never received the forgiveness of sins; how else could it be true what John the Baptist says: "He who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him"? John 3.

Thus it is also evident how St. Paul considers the forgiveness of sins and our justification before God to be entirely one and the same, Rom. 4, and proves from the words of the 32nd Psalm, where the forgiveness of sins is spoken of, that we are made righteous through faith.

Yet, according to Huber’s opinion, Christ is supposed to have so conferred and given redemption to the entire human race that (as the context of his words in th. 270, Tubing. indicates) the entire human race is supposed to have received the forgiveness of sins.

Therefore, he also consecrated the entire human race (under which, of course, alongside the orthodox, all hardened Jews, Turks, and Mahometans are included) by perverting the passage of St. Peter, 1 Epist. 2, to be a chosen race (in the Greek is the little word ἐκλεκτόν) and a priesthood of God, in his *Discovery of the Calvinistic Doctrine*, p. 163.

So far has he extended his *contulit*, and because we cannot be at peace with such Puccianian manner of speaking, we are to be Calvinistic to him, who (according to his false testimony) deny the universal redemption of the human race." (Confession of the Eternal Election of Grace. See *Consil. Witeberg.* I, 622. sq.)

Theologians of Württemberg: "The second point, in which you seem to dissent from your master colleagues and from us (though more in phrase and manner of speaking than in the thing itself), is that you establish a certain universal justification, which corresponds to the universal fall of this race." (Writing of the Württemberg theologians to D. Samuel Huber. Acted 8 Decemb. Year 1593. Subscribed by Heerbrand, Gerlacius, Haffenreffer, L. Osiander, E. Bidembach, and others. See *Fortgesetzte Sammlung von Alten und Neuen theol. Sachen.* Leipz. 1730. p. 567.) §

13. The end of justification on the part of the men who are justified is their eternal salvation,a on the part of God who justifies, it is His glory.b Thus Rom. 4, 6. 9. justification itself is called μακαρισμός or beatification, namely, because it happens to men for the sake of eternal salvation, the inheritance of which it also confers. Eph. 1, 6.

Luther: "From this Gospel is born the true glory of God, while we are taught that we are justified not by our own works, but by the grace of the merciful God in Christ." PART. III. CHAP. V.

the law is fulfilled and is being fulfilled, not by working, but by believing; not by offering something to God, but by receiving and partaking of everything from Christ, of whose fullness we all partake and receive. (Resolutions on the Power of Indulgences. Conclusion 62. See *Various Latin Works*. Frankfurt, 1865. Vol. II, 275 ff.)

The same: "Workers lacking faith indeed do many things; they fast, they pray, they impose a cross upon themselves. But because they think that by these things they appease the wrath of God and merit grace, they do not give glory to God—that is, they do not judge Him to be merciful, truthful, and one who keeps His promises, etc., but rather an angry judge to be appeased by works. In this way, they despise God, accuse Him of lying in all His promises, deny Christ and all His benefits; in sum, they cast God down from His seat and place themselves in His stead. For, having neglected and despised the Word of God, they choose forms of worship and works not commanded by God. They dream that God is delighted by these, and they hope to receive a reward from Him for them. Thus, they do not slaughter reason, the most atrocious enemy of God, but rather keep it alive, and they take away majesty and divinity from God and attribute it to their own works. Therefore, faith alone gives glory to God, as Paul testifies in Romans 4:3 regarding Abraham: 'Abraham,' he says, 'strengthened by faith, gave glory to God, knowing most certainly that whatever God has promised, He is powerful also to perform. Therefore, it was reckoned to him as righteousness.'" (Commentary on St. Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, Erlangen 1843. Vol. I, p. 330 ff.) §

14. The effects of justification are peace of conscience with God,a adoption as sons of God,b the gift of the Holy Spirit,c sanctification and renewal,d and the hope of eternal life.e

a) That is, the soul, although conscious of its sins, is nevertheless not tormented, nor does it fear and flee from an angry God, but is content with its lot and rests secure in the grace of God. See Romans 5:1.

Luther: "This peace of God (Phil. 4:7) is not to be understood as that by which God is quiet and content within Himself, but that which He gives into our hearts so that we are content. Just as the Word of God is called that which we speak, hear, and believe from Him. It is God’s gift; therefore, it is called His peace; also because it makes peace with God, even if we have strife among men. This same peace surpasses all senses, reason, and understanding. You must not understand it in such a way that no one can feel or perceive it. For if we are to have peace with God, we must indeed feel it in our heart and conscience; how else could our heart and mind be guarded by it? Rather, you should understand it thus: When tribulation and adversity come upon those who do not know how to flee to God with prayer and are anxious, they rush about and seek peace, but only that which reason grasps or attains. Reason, however, knows of no peace other than when the evil ceases. This peace does not surpass reason, but is in accordance with it. Therefore, they rage and strive according to reason until they attain that same peace through the removal of the evil, be it by force or by cunning. Thus, whoever has a wound understands and seeks health. But those who rejoice in God are content that they have peace with God; they remain manly in tribulation, they do not desire the peace that reason dictates—namely, the cessation of evil—but stand firm and wait for the inward strength through faith, asking nothing as to whether..."

Whether the evil be short, long, temporal, or eternal; they do not think or worry about how the end will turn out, but let God rule regardless; they do not wish to know when, how, where, or through whom. Therefore, God in turn shows them grace and brings their evil to such an end, with such great benefit, that no human could have thought of or wished for it. See, that is called the peace of the cross, the peace of God, the peace of conscience, the Christian peace; it makes a person quiet even outwardly, content with everyone, and troubling no one. For no reason can grasp or perform this: that a person should have pleasure under the cross, and peace under discord. It is a gift of God, known to no one except him who has experienced it.] (Tom. Hal. XII, 131 sq.)

The same: “When the soul is fully occupied with the sense of sin, then not even the righteous can have enough peace; but there remains a sorrow mixed with the hearing of joy, which does not allow them to take as much of the hearing of joy as is sufficient. For they have the firstfruits, and as it were a tiny drop on the tip of a finger, by which their souls are refreshed; they do not have the fullness of joy, but hang as if by a thin thread, where a very thick rope was needed to sustain the weight of the body. Thus the saints only begin to perceive this hearing; they have not yet drunk to the point of intoxication.” (Exeget. opp. lat. Erlangae 1847. Vol. XIX, 106 sq.)

For there is indeed a certainty of justification, insofar as the faithful feel that they are seriously grieving over their sins and perceive in themselves a struggle against despair, and, this having been overcome, joy from the righteousness of Christ imputed through faith. For although they simultaneously acknowledge and lament the remnants of concupiscence, with which they must struggle in this life, they nevertheless conclude from this that they possess faith and are justified before God. Cf. the blessed Hoepfner, *de Justif.* Disp. VII, VIII, and IX, especially Disp. IX, Aph. V, § 3 sqq., p. 739 sqq.

Chemnitius: “The true state of this controversy between us and the papists is this: they teach that a sinner, when in serious repentance he apprehends by true faith—conceived from the Word of God through the Holy Spirit—the promise of gratuitous mercy, and in it simultaneously apprehends the Mediator Himself, the Son of God, who is our righteousness, can neither be able nor ought to determine with certain confidence that his sins are forgiven him; that he may indeed hope well and promise himself the best things from the mercy of God, but that these things must nevertheless be left suspended in the midst of fluctuating doubt without certain confidence, because falsehood can underlie faith and hope can deceive. And they count this doubt not among the infirmities and stains of the flesh, but among the virtues of faith, so that unless doubt is present to adorn and commend faith, it is the empty confidence of heretics, not justifying faith.

But because they see that these two things are manifestly contradictory—to believe and to doubt—they feign that faith in general indeed determines that the divine promises concerning the mercy of God, the merit of Christ, and the efficacy of the sacraments are true and certain, but that regarding their application to the believers, faith must remain suspended in perpetual doubt: namely, whether my faith, which relies on the promise of God, ought to determine with certainty according to the evangelical sayings: ‘Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven you’; likewise: ‘Your faith has made you well.’ According to the papists, therefore, faith will flutter, suspended in general persuasion, among universals—whether real or nominal—among Platonic ideas in the air, either unconcerned or uncertain about the application to the believing person.

But because that doctrine which is proper to the Gospel is useful and necessary—how consciences that are tormented by the dread of the wrath of God on account of sins can have certain and firm consolation, in which they can rest with certain confidence regarding the remission of sins—we shall certainly not rhetorize at length, but shall note only the principal foundations of that doctrine.” Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III. 19 PART III. CHAP. V.

Latin:

Wer an Christum nie gegläubet hat (wie denn alle verstockte Juden und Türken und viele andere nimmermehr gläuben), die haben freilich die Vergebung der Sünden niemals empfangen; wie könnte sonst wahr sein, das Johannes, der Täufer, sagt: ,Wer an den Sohn nicht glaubet, über dem bleibet der Zorn Gottes‘? Joh. 3.

So ist auch offenbar, wie St. Paulus die Vergebung der Sünden und unsere Rechtfertigung vor Gott durchaus für eins hält Röm. 4., und aus den Worten des 32. Ps., da von der Vergebung der Sünden geredet wird, erweiset, dass wir durch den Glauben gerecht werden.

Noch soll nach Hubers Meinung Christus die Erlösung dem ganzen menschlichen Geschlecht also conferirt und gegeben haben, dass (wie der Context seiner Worte th. 270. Tubing. gibt) das ganze menschliche Geschlecht Vergebung der Sünden empfangen haben soll.

Daher er auch das ganze menschliehe Geschlecht (unter welchem freilich neben den Rechtgläubigen alle verstockte Juden, Türken und Mahometisten begriffen sind) durch Verkehrung des Spruchs St. Petri 1. Epist. 2. zum auserwählten Geschlecht (im Griechischen ist das Wörtlein εκλεκτόν) und Priesterschaft Gottes geweihet hat in seiner Entdeckung der Calvinischen Lehr p. 163.

So weit hat er sein contulit erstrecket, und weil wir mit solcher Pucci anischen Art zu reden nicht friedlich sein können, so sollen wir ihm Calvinisch sein, welche die allgemeine Erlösung des menschlichen Geschlechte (seinem falschen Zeugniss nach) verleugnen.“ (Bekenntniss von der ew. Gnadenwahl. Vid. Consil. Witeberg. I, 622. sq.)

Theologi Wuertembergenses: ,,Secundum est, in quo a dominis collegis tuis et nobis dissentire videris (in phrasi tamen magis ac loquendi modo, quam reipsa), quod videl. justificationem quandam statuis universalem, quae lapsui universali generis hujus respondeat.“ (Scriptum theologorum Wurtembergensium ad D. Samuelem Huberum. Actum 8. Decemb. Anno 1593. Subscripserunt Heerbrandus, Gerlacius, Haffenrefferus, L. Osiander, E. Bidembachius et al. Vid. Fortgesetzte Sammlung von Alten und Neuen theol. Sachen. Leipz. 1730. p. 567.) §

13. Finis justificationis ex parte hominum, qui justificantur, est salus aeterna eorum,a ex parte Dei justificantis est gloria b ejus. Sic Rom. 4, 6. 9. justificatio ipsa dicitur μακαρισμός seu beatir jwatio, scilicet quod hominibus obtingat salutis aeternae causa, cujus naereditatem ipsa quoque conferat. Eph. 1, 6.

Lutherus: ״Ex hoc Evangelio nascitur vera gloria Dei, dum docemur, non nostris operibus, sed gratia miserentis Dei in Christo im PART. III. CAP. V.

pletam legem et impleri, non operando, sed credendo, non Deo aliquid offerendo, sed ex Christo omnia accipiendo et participando, de cujus plenitudine participamus omnes et accipimus.44 (Resolutiones disputat, de indulgentiarum virtute. Conclus. 62. Vid. Opp. lat. varii argumenti. Francof. 1865. Vol. II, 275. sq.)

Idem: ,,Operarii carentes fide multa quidem faciunt, jejunant, orant, sibi ipsis crucem imponunt. Quia vero his rebus existimant se placare iram Dei et gratiam mereri, non tribuunt Deo gloriam, hoc est, non judicant, eum esse misericordem, veracem, servantem promissa etc., sed iratum judicem, placandum operibus, atque hoc modo contemnunt Deum, arguunt eum mendacii in omnibus suis promissis, negant Christum et omnia beneficia ejus, in summa, deturbant Deum e sede sua et sese in locum ipsius collocant. Neglecto enim et contempto verbo Dei eligunt cultus et opera a Deo non praecepta. His Deum delectari somniant et se pro illis mercedem recepturos ab eo sperant. Itaque rationem, atrocissimum Dei hostem, non mactant, sed vivificant, auferuntque Deo majestatem et divinitatem et eam operibus suis tribuunt. Quare sola fides tribuit Deo gloriam, ut testatur Paulus Rom. 4, 3. de Abraham: ,Abraham4, inquit, ,fide confortatus dedit gloriam Deo, certissime sciens, quod, quaecunque promisit Deus, potens est et facere. Ideo reputatum est illi ad justitiam4.44 (Commentar, in ep. S. Pauli ad Gal, Erlangae 1843. Tom. I, p. 330. sq.) §

14. Effecta justificationis sunt pax conscientiae cum Deo, a adoptio in filios Dei, b donatio Spiritus Sancti,c sanctificatio et renovatio,d spes vitae aeternae.e

a) Seu quod animus, etsi peccatorum sibi conscius, non tamen angitur, aut Deum iratum formidat ac fugit, sed sorte sua contentus est et de Dei gratia securus acquiescit. Vid. Rom. 5, 1.

Lutherus: ,,Dieser Friede Gottes (Phil. 4, 7.) ist nicht zu verstehen von dem, damit Gott bei ihm selbst stille und zufrieden ist, sondern den er uns gibet ins Herz, dass wir zufrieden sind. Gleichwie das Wort Gottes heisset, das wir aus ihm reden, hören und gläuben. Es ist Gottes Gabe, darum heissets sein Friede; auch darum, dass er mit Gott Friede mache, ob wir bei den Menschen Unfrieden haben. Derselbige Friede überschwebet alle Sinne, "Vernunft und Verständniss. Das musst du nicht also verstehen, dass ihn niemand fühlen noch empflnden möge. Denn sollen wir mit Gott Friede haben, so müssen wirs je fühlen im Herzen und Gewissen; wie könnte sonst unser Herz und Sinn bewahret werden durch ihn? sondern also sollst du es verstehen: Wenn Trübsal und Widerwärtigkeit kommt über die, so nicht wissen mit Gebet zu Gott fliehen und sorgfältig sind, so fahren sie zu und suchen auch Friede, aber nur den, den die Vernunft begreifet oder erlanget. Die Vernunft aber weiss von keinem Frieden, denn von dem, wenn das Uebel aufhöret. Dieser Friede schwebet nicht über Vernunft, sondern ist ihr gemäss. Darum toben und streben sie auch der Vernunft nach, bis dass sie denselbigen Friede durch Abthun des Uebels erlangen, es sei mit Gewalt oder mit List. Also wer eine Wunde hat, der verstehet und suchet die Gesundheit. Aber die an Gott sich freuen, lassen ihnen begnügen, dass sie mit Gott Friede haben, bleiben männlich in Trübsal, begehren nicht den Friede, den die Vernunft stimmet, nämlich des Uebels Aufhören, sondern stehen fest und warten der inwendigen Stärke durch den Glauben, fragen nichts darnach, ob das

Uebel kurz, lang, zeitlich oder ewig sei und bleibe; denken und sorgen auch nicht, wie das Ende werden wolle, lassen Gott walten immerhin, wollen nicht wissen, wenn, wie, wo und durch welchen. Darum thut ihnen auch Gott wieder Gnade und schaffet ihrem Uebel ein solch Ende, mit so grossem Vortheil, dass kein Mensch hätte können gedenken fund wünschen. Siehe, das heisset der Friede des Kreuzes, der Friede Gottes, der Friede des Gewissens, der christliche Friede; der machet, dass der Mensch auch auswendig stille und mit jedermann zufrieden ist und niemand verunruhiget. Denn das begreifet noch thut keine Vernunft, dass ein Mensch sollte unter dem Kreuze Lust, unter dem Unfrieden Friede haben. Es ist ein GottesGeschenk, das niemand bekannt ist, denn dem, der es erfahren hat.“ (Tom. Hai. XII, 131. sq.)

Idem: ,,Quando animus sensu peccati plene occupatus est, tunc ne justi quidem satis pacis habere possunt, sed manet cum auditu laetitiae mixtus dolor, qui non patitur, ut tantum de auditu laetitiae sumant, quantum satis est. Primitias enim habent et tanquam guttulam extremi digiti, qua refrigerantur animi; plenitudinem gaudii non habent, sed pendent ceu ex tenui filo, ubi bene crasso fune opus erat ad sustinendam molem corporis. Sic sancti incipiunt tantum sentire hunc auditum, nondum hauserunt enim ad ebrietatem.“ (Exeget. opp. lat. Erlangae 1847. Vol. XIX, 106. sq.)

Datur enim omnino certitudo justificationis, quatenus fideles, qui se serio dolere ob peccata sua sentiunt et in se deprehendunt certamen cum desperatione, hac vero superata, gaudium ex Christi justitia per fidem imputata. Quamvis enim simul reliquias concupiscentiae, cum quibus sibi in hac vita luctandum sit, agnoscant et deplorent, inde tamen coiligunt, se habere fidem et esse justificatos coram Deo. Conf. b. Hoepfner. de Justif. Disp. VII. VIII. et IX., praesertim Disp. IX. Aph. V. § 3. sqq. p. 739. sqq.

Chemnitius: ״Verus controversiae hujus internos et pontificios status hic est, quod ipsi docent, peccatorem, quando in seria poenitentia vera fide, ex verbo Dei per Spiritum Sanctum concepta, apprehendit promissionem gratuitae misericordiae et in ea simul apprehendit ipsum mediatorem Filium Dei, qui est justitia nostra, nec posse nec debere certa fiducia statuere, peccata sibi remitti; posse quidem bene sperare et de Dei misericordia optima quaeque sibi polliceri, sed haec tamen sine certa fiducia in medio fluctuantis dubitationis suspensa esse relinquenda, quia fidei possit subesse falsum et spes possit fallere. Et hanc dubitationem numerant non inter infirmitates et maculas carnis, sed inter virtutes fidei, ut nisi dubitatio adsit, ornet et commendet fidem, sit inanis haereticorum fiducia, non fides justificans.

Quia vero vident, duo haec manifeste esse pugnantia, credere et dubitare, fingunt, fidem in genere quidem statuere, promissiones divinas de misericordia Dei, de merito Christi et sacramentorum efficacia veras et certas esse, sed de applicatione ad credentes fidem debere in perpetua dubitatione suspensam manere: an sc. mea fides, quae promissione Dei nititur, certe juxta dicta evangelica statuere debeat: ,Confide, fili, remittuntur tibi peccata tua‘; item: ,Fides tua te salvum fecit.‘ Juxta pontificios igitur fides inter universalia, sive realia, sive nominalia, inter ideas Platonicas in aere generali persuasione suspensa volitabit, de applicatione ad personam credentem vel non solicita, vel non certa.

Quia vero utilis et necessaria est illa doctrina, quae evangelii propria est, quomodo conscientiae, quae pavore irae Dei propter peccata anguntur, possint habere certam et firmam consolationem, in qua certa fiducia de remissione peccatorum acquiescere possint, non prolixe sane rhetoricabimur, sed praecipua tantum fundamenta ejus doctrinae notabimus. liaieri Comp. ed. Walther. IU.19 PART. III. CAP. V.


### On Justification: First, a firm and manifest foundation is taken from the nature and property of…

First, a firm and manifest foundation is taken from the nature and property of the gratuitous promise. For the confidence of our salvation does not rest upon the idea that the perspicacity of our own intellect could, by its own sharpness, penetrate the heavens of heavens and scrutinize what has been decreed concerning me in the secret counsel of the Trinity; rather, it rests upon this foundation: that God, proceeding from secret light, has revealed His will to us in the Word, so that Paul, in 2 Cor. 2, does not hesitate to affirm that we have the mind of Christ. And in the Law, the will of God is revealed thus: "He who does these things shall live by them." But if eternal life could be apprehended through doubt, no promise would be more suitable than that of the Law; for because of the annexed condition of perfect fulfillment, it leaves consciences in perpetual doubt, Rom. 4. But because it is not doubt, but faith, that justifies, and not he who doubts, but he who believes, that has eternal life, therefore God has proposed the gratuitous promise of the Gospel, which rests not on our works, but on the mercy of God because of the obedience of the Son, the Mediator. And Paul shows why this promise was proposed, Rom. 4: "Therefore it is of faith, that it might be according to grace, so that the promise might be firm." But is the promise firm only in a general sense and in itself? "Nay," says Paul, "that it might be firm to all the seed." But how? "It is written," he says, "for us, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe." For in a general sense and in itself, the promise of the Law is also firm. But in order for it to be firm for us, it is therefore according to grace and of faith. Thus, in Heb. 6, there exists a most beautiful sentiment: that God, in the gratuitous promise, interposed an oath, "that by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us." You hear that the promise is not only firm in a general sense or in itself, but that we, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us, might have strong consolation. From this foundation, John draws an argument in 1 John 5: "He who does not believe God makes Him a liar." Nor does John speak of a general assent; for he adds: "These things I write to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life." For if I believe in the Son of God, and yet doubt whether I have eternal life, I do not believe this promise: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life"; according to John, therefore, I make God a liar.

Second, from the property of justifying faith. For to faith are attributed πληροφορία, υπόστασις, ἔλεγχος, παρρησία, πεποίθησις, which certainly signify not doubt, but a certain and firm confidence, as I could prove by examples, were I not afraid of prolixity. John, with a particular purpose, speaks of faith thus in 1 John 3: "We know that we have passed from death to life," and ch. 5: "That you may know that you have eternal life, you who believe in the name of the Son of God." 1 Pet. 1: "Hope perfectly for the grace that is brought to you." Heb. 3: "If we hold the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end." Heb. 10: "Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, holding fast the confession of our hope without wavering." In Heb. 6, there exists the sweetest metaphor of an anchor. For when an anchor falls into fabulous ground, it cannot hold the ship firmly; but when it is cast into a firm and tenacious bottom, it holds the ship firmly against all waves. Thus, he says, the anchor of our hope is cast into heaven itself, and indeed where Christ is our High Priest, who apprehends, supports, and retains that anchor; just as He says in John 10: "No one shall snatch them out of my hand," and as Paul says in Phil. 3: "I have apprehended, nay, rather I have been apprehended." Thus Rom. 5: "Being justified by faith, we have peace with God." Likewise: "We stand in grace and rejoice in the hope of the glory of God." Rom. 4: "Therefore it is of faith, that the promise might be firm." These sweetest consolations the Papist academics wickedly attempt to corrupt and snatch away from us with their doubt. But if doubt were a virtue, it would not be rightly commanded that we must struggle against doubt, nor would we be ordered to ask: "Increase our faith, help our unbelief." This is also a very firm argument against Papist doubt, that in 2 Cor. 13 Paul says: "Examine and prove yourselves, whether you are in the faith. Do you not know yourselves, that..."

Jesus Christ is in you, unless perhaps you are reprobates.’ You hear that everyone ought to test himself, whether he is in the faith, and that those who do not acknowledge that Christ is in them are reprobates. These things could be explained in a copious discourse, but we are only showing the foundations now. I will only add with what various artifices the Papists attempt to mock the passage in Rom. 8. Pighius, following Thomas, says that Paul is speaking there only of the certainty of his own salvation, which he had from a special revelation, and not affirming that every believer in Christ has such certainty; but this is manifestly false. For Paul, in that whole sentence, speaks in the plural and lays down the foundations of that certainty: ‘Christ died, nay rather, He sits at the right hand of the Father, interceding for us.’ Andradius, therefore, seeing that these mockeries cannot stand, says that the word πέπεισμαι signifies not a certain trust, but a probable estimation or persuasion, which nevertheless could be mistaken, because it is used in that way in certain places of Scripture. But it is also used for a certain, firm, and indubitable persuasion in 2 Tim. 1: ‘I am certain that He is able to keep my deposit.’ And from this theme πεποίθησις is derived. The question now is: Which meaning fits Rom. 8? But the whole context all but cries out: ‘If God is for us, who is against us? How will He not also with Him graciously give us all things? Who shall accuse? Who shall condemn? It is God who justifies, Christ who died. Who shall separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord? Shall danger, shall the sword? etc. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us.’ And after these things follows the word πέπεισμαι. It is manifest, however, that he is (as they say) mad with reason who would attempt to explain that whole discourse in terms of doubt. And among the Papists themselves, no one has hitherto dared to say that Paul in Rom. 8 was also uncertain and doubting about his own salvation, except that the impudence of the Jesuits attempted this, which Andradius strives not only to equal, but even to surpass.” (Examen Concil. Trid. Ed. Genev. 1641. f. 168. sq.)

Quenstedtius: “The fountains and hypotheses of the Papists, from which the dogma of doubt flows, are these: 1. That they take faith only for assent, not for trust; 2. that they suspend the virtue of the sacraments from the intention of the minister, which is doubtful; 3. that they do not believe sins are remitted unless they have been enumerated one by one to a confessor, which is uncertain; 4. that they place hope in their own merits and works, which are imperfect; 5. that they consider only the doubts which sometimes befall the saints from the infirmity of the flesh; and 6. that they distinguish between faith and trust.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 818. sq.) Luther: "Even if everything else were safe in the papacy, that monster of uncertainty surpasses all monsters. And although it is manifest that the enemies of Christ teach uncertain things, because they command consciences to doubt, they are nevertheless so filled with satanic rage that they most confidently condemn and kill us, who dissent from them and teach certain things, as heretics, as if they were most certain of their own doctrine. Let us therefore give thanks to God that we have been liberated from this monster of uncertainty, and now we can certainly establish that the Holy Spirit cries out and utters an inexpressible groaning in our hearts. And this is our foundation: the Gospel commands us to look not at our own good deeds and perfection, but at God Himself promising, at Christ Himself the mediator. Conversely, the Pope commands us to look not at God promising, not at Christ the high priest, but at our own works and merits. There, doubt and despair necessarily follow; here, however, certainty and joy of spirit, because I cling to God, who cannot lie. For He says: 'Behold, I deliver my Son to death, that He may redeem you by His blood from sins and death.' There I cannot doubt, unless I wish to deny God entirely. And this is the reason why our theology is certain: because it snatches us from our own sight and places us outside of ourselves, so that we do not rely on our own powers, conscience, sense, person, or works, but rely on that which is outside of us, that is, on the promise and truth of God, which cannot deceive. The Pope does not know this; therefore, he impiously trifles with his PART III. CAP. V. furies, [saying] that no one knows, not even the righteous and wise, whether they are worthy of love, etc. Indeed, if they are righteous and wise, they certainly know that they are loved by God, or else they are not righteous and wise." (On Gal. 4:6. Commentary on St. Paul's Epistle to the Galatians. Erlangen 1844. Vol. II, 177 sq.) The same: "Where the Papists might otherwise have won in all matters, they are nevertheless lost in this chief article, since they teach that one must doubt God's grace if we are not first worthy enough through our own satisfaction or merit and the intercession of the saints. There are their books, letters, and seals, monasteries, foundations, and also their current tonsures and masses. But because they teach this point, that they stand upon their works and doubt, as they cannot do otherwise: so it is certain that they must be the devil's church; for there are and can be no more ways than these two: one, which relies upon God's grace; the other, which builds upon our merit and work. The first is the way of the ancient church and of all the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, as the Scripture testifies; the other is the way of the Pope and his church." (Against Hans Wurst. 1541. Halle Ed. XVII, 1681.) ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who deny the certainty of justification and present grace, and maintain that a man, without a special revelation, cannot be certain of his justification and the present grace of God infallibly, but only with a conjectural certainty. . . . However, the Papists differ greatly in this matter; for some grant certainty to all the righteous, others only to the perfect, and others to no Christian at all. . . This matter was discussed at length among the fathers of the Council of Trent, and in particular, Dominicus a Soto and Catharinus disputed it vehemently, the former defending doubt, the latter certainty. . . Indeed, after a long debate, a decree was finally conceived in favor of the uncertainty of grace, but in such a way that the signs of a wavering mind were sufficiently betrayed in it, and each party thought the decree was in favor of their own opinion. . . . The decree of the Council of Trent, sess. 6, c. 9, states as follows: 'Although it is necessary to believe that sins are not remitted, nor ever have been remitted, except gratuitously by divine mercy for Christ's sake: yet it must not be said that sins are remitted or have been remitted to anyone who boasts of a confidence and certainty of the remission of his sins and rests in that alone, since this vain confidence, which is far removed from all piety, can exist—and in our own time does exist and is preached with great contention against the Catholic Church—among heretics and schismatics.' (But the question is not, as the blessed Gerhard rightly advises in *Confess. cathol.* p. 727, about the faith of heretics, nor about a proud boasting of confidence far removed from all piety, which is a specter of faith, not faith.) And later: 'But neither must it be asserted that those who are truly justified are bound to determine within themselves, without any doubt whatever, that they are justified, and that no one is absolved and justified from sins except him who believes with certainty that he is absolved and justified, and that by this faith alone absolution and justification are perfected, as if he who does not believe this doubts the promises of God and the efficacy of the death and resurrection of Christ.' . . . Compare Andradius in his defense of the Council of Trent, and Bellarmine, Vol. 4, Book 3, *de justificatione*, ch. 3–7 and 18. In ch. 3 he says: 'The opinion common to almost all theologians is that which teaches that men cannot have in this life the certainty of faith regarding their own righteousness, except for those to whom God deigns to indicate this by special revelation.' . . Furthermore, the Council of Trent, sess. 6, can. 15, thunders as follows: 'If anyone shall say that a man who is reborn and justified is bound by faith to believe that he is of the number of the predestined, let him be anathema.' . . 2. Of the Latermannians, who in *disputat. de praedestinatione* th. 43, do not hesitate to write: 'Because a man is certain that he can fall from the hope of salvation, therefore he cannot but be doubtful regarding his final perseverance.'" (*L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 818. sq.*)

Latin:

Primo, fundamentum firmum et manifestum sumitur ex natura et proprietate promissionis gratuitae. Fiducia enim salutis nostrae non eo nititur, quasi ingenii nostri perspicacia acumine suo possit penetrare coelos coelorum et scrutari, quid de me in arcano consilio Trinitatis decretum sit, sed hoc fundamento nititur, quod Deus, ex arcana luce prodiens, voluntatem suam nobis in verbo patefecit, ut Paulus 2 Cor. 2. non dubitet affirmare, nos mentem Christi tenere. Et in lege voluntas Dei ita patefacta est: ,Qui fecerit haec, vivet in eis/ Quod si per dubitationem apprehendi posset vita aeterna, nulla magis idonea esset promissio, quam legis; propter annexam enim conditionem perfectae impletionis conscientias relinquit in perpetua dubitatione, Rom. 4. Quia vero non dubitatio, sed fides justificat, nec qui dubitat, sed qui credit, habet vitam aeternam, ideo Deus proposuit gratuitam promissionem evangelii, quae nititur non nostris operibus, sed misericordia Dei propter obedientiam Filii mediatoris. Et quare haec promissio sit proposita, Paulus ostendit Rom. 4.: ,Ideo ex fide, ut secundum gratiam, ut sit firma promissio/ Num vero, ut tantum in genere et per se firma sit promissio? ,Imo4, inquit Paulus, ,ut firma sit omni semini/ Quomodo vero? ,Scriptum est4, inquit, ,propter nos, quibus imputabitur credentibus/ In genere enim et per se firma est etiam legis promissio. Ut vero nobis sit firma, ideo secundum gratiam et ex fide. Ita Hebr. 6. extat pulcherrima sententia, Deum in gratuita promissione interposuisse jusjurandum, ,ut per duas res immobiles, quibus impossibile est mentiri Deum, firmam consolationem habeamus, qui confugimus ad tenendam propositam spem/ Audis, non 111 genere tantum nec per se firmam tantum esse promissionem, sed ut nos, qui confugimus ad apprehendendam propositam spem, firmam consolationem habeamus. Ex hoc fundamento Johannes ducit argumentum 1 Joh. 5.: ,Qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum/ Nec vero de generali assensione Johannes loquitur; subjungit enim: ,Haec scribo vobis, qui creditis in nomen Filii Dei, ut sciatis, quod vitam aeternam habetis/ Nam si credo in Filium Dei, et tamen dubito, an habeam vitam aeternam, non credo huic promissioni: ,Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam4; juxta Johannem igitur facio Deum mendacem.

Secundoy ex proprietate fidei justificantis. Tribuitur enim fidei πληροφορία, υπό· στασις, έλεγχος, παρρησία, πειτοίΰησις, quae certe non dubitationem, sed certam et firmam fiduciam significant, sicut exemplis probare possem, nisi vererer prolixitatem. Joannes peculiari consilio de fide ita loquitur 1 Joh. 3.: ,Scimus, quod translati sumus a morte ad vitam4, c. 5.: ,Ut sciatis, quoniam vitam habetis aeternam, qui creditis in nomen Filii Dei/ 1 Pet. 1.: ,Perfecte sperate in eam, quae ad vos defertur, gratiam/ Ebr. 3.: ,Si fiduciam et gloriationem spei ad finem usque flrmam tenuerimus/ Ebr. 10.: ,Accedamus vero corde in plerophoria fidei, tenentes confessionem spei ά κλίνη.‘ Ebr. 6. extat dulcissima metaphora ancorae. Quando enim ancora in terram fabulosam incidit, non potest navem firmiter retinere; quando vero in fundum firmum et tenacem jacta est, firmiter retinet navem contra omnes fluctus. Ita, inquit, ancoram spei nostrae jactam esse in ipsum coelum, et quidem ubi Christus pro nobis pontifex est, qui apprehendit, fulcit et retinet ancoram illam; sicut inquit Joh. 10.: ,De manu mea nemo rapiet eas4, et sicut Paulus inquit Phil. 3.: ,Apprehendi, imo magis apprehensus sum/ Ita Rom. 5.: ,Justificati fide, pacem habemus apud Deum/ Item: ,Stamus in gratia et gloriamur spe gloriae Dei/ Rom. 4.: ,Ideo ex fide, ut firma sit promissio/ Has dulcissimas consolationes scelerate nobis dubitatione sua depravare et eripere conantur pontificii academici. Quod si virtus esset dubitatio, non recte praeciperetur, esse luctandum contra dubitationem, nec juberemur petere: ,Adauge nobis fidem, adjuva incredulitatem/ Est et hoc valde firmum argumentum • contra pontificiam dubitationem, quod 2 Cor. 13. Paulus inquit: ,Tentate et probate vos ipsos, an sitis in fide. Anne cognoscitis vos ipsos, quod

Jesus Christus ia vobis sit? nisi forsan reprobi estis.‘ Audis, quemque debere se ipsum probare, an sit in fide, et illos, qui non agnoscunt, Christum in se esse, reprobos esse. Haec copiosa oratione possent explicari, sed nos tantum fundamenta nunc monstramus. Illud tantum addam, quam variis artificiis locum Rom. 8. ludificare conentur pontificii, Pighius ex Thoma dicit, Paulum ibi tantum de suae salutis certitudine, quam ex peculiari revelatione habuerit, loqui, non vero affirmare, omnem Christi fidelem ejusmodi certitudinem habere; sed hoc manifeste falsum est. Paulus enim in tota illa sententia in plurali loquitur et fundamenta illius certitudinis ponit: ,Christus mortuus est, imo sedet ad dexteram patris, interpellans pro nobis.‘ Andradius igitur, videns, has ludificationes non posse consistere, dicit, verbum πέπεισμαι significare non certam fiduciam, sed verisimilem existimationem seu persuasionem, quae tamen falli possit, quia in quibusdam Scripturae locis ita usurpetur. Atqui usurpatur etiam pro certa, firma et indubitata persuasione 2 Tim. 1.: ,Certus sum, quod potens est, depositum meum servare.‘ Et ab hoc themate πεποίϋησις deducitur. Quaestio jam est: Utra signiflcatio conveniat Rom. 8.? Illud vero totus contextus tantum non clamat: ,Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Quomodo non omnia cum Filio nobis donaret? Quis accusabit? Quis condemnabit? Deus justificat, Christus mortuus est. Quis separabit nos a caritate Dei, quae est in Christo Jesu, Domino nostro? Num periculum, num gladius? etc. Imo in his omnibus plus quam vincimus per eum, qui dilexit nos.‘ Et post haec sequitur verbum πέπεισμαι. Manifestum autem est, eum cum ratione (quod dicitur) insanire, qui totam illam orationem de dubitatione conaretur explicare. Et inter ipsos pontificios nemo hactenus ausus fuit dicere, Paulum Rom. 8. de sua etiam salute incertum dubitare, nisi quod Jesuitarum impudentia hoc tentavit, quam Andradius non aequare tantum, sed et superare contendit.“ (Examen Concil. Trid. Ed. Genev. 1641. f. 168. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Fontes et hypotheses papisticae, ex quibus fluit dubitationis dogma, hae sunt: 1. Quod fidem habent tantum pro assensu, non pro fiducia; 2. quod sacramentorum virtutem ab intenr tione ministri suspendunt, quae dubia; 3. quod remitti peccata non censent, nisi enumerata sint confessionario singula, quod incertum; 4. quod spem ponunt in meritis et operibus propriis, quae imperfecta; 6. quod dubitationes, quae sanctis nonnunquam ex infirmitate carnis obveniunt, unice considerant; et 6. quod inter fidem et fiduciam distinguunt.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 818. sq.) Lutherus: ,,Si in papatu etiam omnia salva essent, tamen istud monstrum incertitudinis superat omnia monstra, et quanquam palam est, inimicos Christi incerta docere, quia jubent dubitare conscientias, tamen adeo satanica rabie pleni sunt, ut nos, qui ab ipsis dissentimus et certa docemus, condemnent et occidant securissime tanquam haereticos, velut certissimi de sua doctrina. Agamus igitur Deo gratias, quod liberati sumus ab hoc monstro incertitudinis, ac jam certo statuere possumus, Spiritum Sanctum clamare et inenarrabilem gemitum edere in cordibus nostris, hocque fundamentum est nostrum: Evangelium jubet intueri nos, non benefacta et perfectionem nostram, sed ipsum Deum promittentem, ipsum Christum mediatorem. Contra papa jubet respicere non Deum promittentem, non Christum pontificem, sed nostra opera et merita. Ibi necessario sequitur dubitatio et desperatio, illic vero certitudo et gaudium spiritus, quia in Deo haereo, qui mentiri non potest. Dicit enim: Ecce trado filium meum in mortem, ut te sanguine suo redimat a peccatis et morte. Ibi non possum dubitare, nisi velim prorsus Deum negare. Atque haec est ratio, cur nostra theologia certa sit, quia rapit nos e conspectu nostro, et ponit nos extra nos, ut non nitamur viribus, conscientia, sensu, persona, operibus nostris, sed eo nitamur, quod est extra nos, hoc est, promissione et veritate Dei, quae fallere non potest. Hoc papa nescit, ideo impie nugatur cum suis PART. III. CAP. V. furiis neminem scire, ne justos quidem et sapientes, utrum digni sint amore etc. Imo si justi et sapientes sunt, certo sciunt se diligi a Deo, vel justi et sapientes non sunt.“ (Ad Gal. 4, 6. Commentar, in ep. St. Pauli ad Gal. Erlangae 1844. Tom. II, 177. sq.) Idem: ,,Wo sonst die Papisten in allen Sachen hätten gewonnen, sind sie doch in diesem Hauptstück verloren, da sie lehren, dass man zweifeln müsse an Gottes Gnaden, wo wir nicht zuvor würdig genug sind durch unsere eigene Genugthuung oder Verdienst und Fürbitte der Heiligen. Da sind ihre Bücher, Briefe und Siegel, Klöster, Stift und auch noch ihre jetzigen Platten und Messen. Weil sie aber dieses Stück lehren, dass sie auf ihren Werken und Zweifel stehen, wie sie nicht anders können: so ist es gewiss, dass sie des Teufels Kirche sein müssen; denn es sind und können nicht mehr Wege sein, denn diese zween: einer, der auf Gottes Gnade sich verlässt; der andere, so auf unser Verdienst und Werk bauet. Der erste ist der alten Kirchen und aller Patriarchen, Propheten und Apostel Weg, wie die Schrift zeuget; der andere ist des Pabsts und seiner Kirchen.“ (Wider Hans Wurst. 1541. Tom. Hai. XVII, 1681.) ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, qui justificationis et gratiae praesentis certitudinem negant, sfatuuntque, hominem absque peculiari patefactione non infallibili ter, sed conjecturali tantum certitudine certum esse posse de justificatione et gratia Dei praesente. . . . Valde autem hac in causa discrepant papistae; alii enim omnibus justis, alii solis perfectis, alii nulli prorsus christiano certitudinem concedunt. . . Actum hac de re prolixe est inter patres Concilii Trident., et inprimis vehementer de ea disceptarunt Dominicus a Soto et Catharinus, quorum ille dubitationem, hic certitudinem defendebat. . . Conceptum quidem tandem post longam disceptationem decretum est pro incertitudine gratiae, sed ejusmodi, ut fluctuantis animi signa satis in eo proderentur et quilibet pro sua sententia decretum esse putaret. . . . Decretum Concil. Trid. sess. 6. c. 9. ita habet: ,Quamvis necessarium sit, credere, neque remitti, neque remissa unquam fuisse peccata, nisi gratis divina misericordia propter Christum: nemini tamen fiduciam et certitudinem remissionis peccatorum suorum jactanti et in ea sola quiescenti, peccata dimitti vel dimissa esse, dicendum est, cum apud haereticos et schismaticos possit esse, imo nostra tempestate sit et magna contentione contra ecclesiam cathol. praedicetur vana haec et ab omni pietate remota fiducia.‘ (At non est quaestio, ut recte monet b. Gerhardus Confess. cathol. p. 727., de fide haereticorum, nec de superba fiduciae jactantia ab omni pietate remota, quae est spectrum fidei, non fides.) Et postea: ,Sed neque illud asserendum est, oportere eos,' qui vere justificati sUnt, absque ulla omnino dubitatione apud eemetipsos statuere, se esse justificatos, neminemque a peccatis absolvi ac justificari, nisi eum, qüi certo credat, se absolutum et justificatum esse atque hac sola fide absolutionem et justificationem perfici, quasi, qui hoc non credit, de Dei promissis, deque mortis et resurrectionis Christi efficacia dubitet.‘ . . . Confer Andradium in defensione Concil. Trid., Bellarminum T. 4. 1. 3. de justiflc. c. 3—7. et 18. C. 3. inquit: ,Sententia communis fere omnibus theologis est, quod docent, non posse homines in hac vita habere certitudinem fidei de sua justitia, iis exceptis, quibus Deus speciali revelatione hoc indicare dignatur.‘ . . Porro Concil. Trid. sess. 6. can. 15. ita fulminat: ,Si quis dixerit, hominem renatum et justificatum teneri ex fide ad credendum, se esse ex numero praedestinatorum, anathema esto.‘ . . 2. Latermanni, qui in disputat, de praedestinatione th. 43. scribere non dubitat: ,Quia homo certus est, quod spe salutis excidere possit, propterea eum non posse non esse dubium de finali perseverantia.‘ “


### On Justification: Whence pertains to this that liberation from the curse of the law and eternal…

Whence pertains to this that liberation from the curse of the law and eternal damnation, which some call the first degree of Christian liberty. Brochmandus: "Christian liberty is a liberation from spiritual servitude, acquired by the blood of Christ, by which those believing in the only-begotten Son of God are free before God in conscience from the curse of the law, from the servitude of sin, from the yoke of Mosaic ceremonies, and from the burden of human traditions, being finally to be liberated from every sense of sin and from all servitude of corruption and death itself to the praise of God and their own salvation...

1. This liberty is called Christian, both because its efficient cause is Christ, Christ himself testifying in John 8:36: 'If the Son shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed'; and because it is the property of Christians, as Paul admonishes in Galatians 5:13: 'Ye have been called unto liberty, brethren.'

2. Christian liberty is said to be a liberation from spiritual servitude for two principal reasons. One is because it is not a liberation from civil servitude; for it does not prevent one who obeys another and is his servant from being truly free in Christ, as Paul explains in 1 Corinthians 7:20–22: 'Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called. Art thou called being a servant? care not for it: but if thou mayest be made free, use it rather. For he that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord's freeman: likewise also he that is called, being free, is Christ's servant.' The other is because this liberty does not consist in a license to do whatever one pleases; for he who commits sin is the servant of sin, John 8:34 ff.; but Christian liberty is placed in the liberation of the soul from depraved desires through the Holy Spirit, according to that of Paul in 2 Corinthians 3:17: 'Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.'

3. That the entire Christian liberty, taken as a whole, is to be referred to Christ Jesus, Scripture clearly testifies, as it reports that those whom the Son has liberated are truly free, John 8:36; Galatians 5: 1. Moreover, the sacred page does not conceal by what reason the Son has obtained this spiritual liberty for us, namely, by redeeming us from sins and the punishments of sin and vain conversation in the world, not with gold and silver, but with precious blood; as may be read in Isaiah 6:33 [sic], 1 Peter 1:18–19, Colossians 1:19.

4. The matter of Christian liberty, or those who are truly free with Christian liberty, are only those who truly believe in Christ. These sayings testify to this: John 1:12: 'As many as received him (Christ), to them gave he εξουσίαν, that they should become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.' And 8:36: 'If the Son shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.' Romans 8:2: 'The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death.' Galatians 3:26: 'Ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus.'" (Univers. theol. System. Tom. II, 520 ff.)

Indeed, by the power of regeneration we are born sons of God; but being reborn and having our sins remitted, we are adopted as sons of God, or we obtain the right of sons of God by adoption. Which is τήν υιοθεσίαν άπολαβεϊν, Galatians 4: 5. Conf. Ephesians 1:5 and John 1: 12. Namely, that He Himself, being substantially present in the justified, by conferring more abundant gifts of grace, may manifest Himself as present and as it were indwelling. See Galatians 4:6, where the Holy Spirit, sent into the hearts of the justified, is said to cry out; otherwise, to dwell in them as in a temple, 1 Corinthians 3: 16.

And to the same point looks that mystical union of believers and the justified with Christ; the formal cause of which the blessed Gerhard, intending to explain, writes in Part III of the *Harmonia Evangelica*, cap. CLXXVI, p. 551: "Although this mystical union is in a certain way reciprocal, because Christ unites Himself to us and we are united to Christ, nevertheless on the part of Christ it is rather active, on our part it is rather passive. For Christ is in us in such a way that He may live in us, Galatians 2:20, that He may make us partakers of all His goods, of righteousness and eternal life, that He may impart the Holy Spirit to us, that He may rule us by His word and Spirit, that He may protect and defend us as the apple of His eye. But we are in Christ in such a way that from... PART III. CAP. V.

as from him as the head we may receive spiritual life, righteousness, and salvation, so that we may be engrafted into his mystical body as true and living members, and that we may be ruled, sustained, and defended by him. It makes no mention of an approximation of the substance of Christ, regarding either one or both natures, to the substance of the believing man.

Quenstedtius: "As soon as a sinful man is justified through faith, his mystical union with God begins, Eph. 3:17... It is called a spiritual union: 1. from the principal efficient cause, because it proceeds from the Holy Spirit, to whom it is also usually appropriated in a special way; 2. from the mode, because it is accomplished not in a carnal, but in a spiritual manner; 3. from the effect, because it makes men spiritual, Rom. 8:9. In particular, this appellation took its origin from 1 Cor. 6:16, 17, where κολλώμενος τώ κυρίω εν πνεύμα, 'joined to the Lord,' i.e., the believer adhering to God, is said to be 'one spirit with the Lord.' It is also called a mystical union, because this union is a great mystery, the mode of which cannot be exactly known by mortals, Eph. 5:32. It is also called by some of our own a substantial union, not formally and by reason of the mode, but objectively, from the terms, i.e., the extremes of the union, which are substances. It is therefore a union of substances, but not a substantial union, speaking properly and accurately... The extremes or terms of the mystical union are the very essences of those being united; and on the one hand, the divine substance of the whole Holy Trinity, 2 Pet. 1:4, and the substance of the human nature of Christ, John 15:1, 2, 4; 1 Cor. 6:15-17; Eph. 5:30; Gal. 2:19, 20; on the other hand, the substance of the believers regarding soul and body, 1 Cor. 6:15, 19; Eph. 5:30... The form of the mystical union consists in a true, real, intrinsic, and most close conjunction of the substance of the believing man with the substance of the Holy Trinity and the flesh of Christ, without extension or contraction of the divine or human essence, the united extremes remaining essentially distinct even in the state of union, John 14:23; Gal. 3:27... The end of this union is the assurance of the believer, struggling with the miseries of this life, of the perpetual assistance, influence, and favor of God, preservation in the state of grace, the hearing of prayers, the sealing of certainty regarding present grace and future or following glory, Rom. 8:10, 11, 16, 26, 35; John 6:54-57. [Also] the union of believers among themselves in faith and love... for he who is united to the head cannot but also love the remaining members of the body and succor them according to his strength, John 17:20 sq." (L. c. c. 10. § 1. th. 1. 5. 6. 14. 17. f. 886. sqq.)

The same: "That common and general presence of God, by which he is present to all creatures and thus also to believers, does not come into consideration here... The mystical union does not consist in mere harmony and tempering of affections, as the soul of Jonathan is said to be knit to David, 1 Sam. 18:1... It does not consist in the mere gracious operation of the Holy Spirit in believers... Nor does it consist in μετονσία or transubstantiation... Nor in συνουσία or consubstantiation, so that from two united essences one essence is made... Nor, finally, does it consist in a personal union... Luther indeed, in his Commentary on Galatians chapter 2, says that a believer is so glued to Christ through faith that from him and the believer one 'quasi' person is made, so that he can say with confidence: 'I am Christ'; but he immediately explains himself, adding: i.e., Christ's righteousness, life, and victory are mine; and conversely, Christ may say: 'I am that sinner,' i.e., his sins, death, etc., are mine... The mystical union also differs from sacramental union and communion. For there the extreme, participating in the substance of the sacrament, extends itself more broadly than here, since there the unworthy and hypocrites are included, whereas here only believers are united; there the communion consists in a transitory act, here in a permanent one, etc." (L. c. s. 2. f. 900. 901. 902.)

Fechtius: "Luther... understood the union not as mystical and analogous to the physical, but as moral, i.e., of faith, which in justification makes all things of Christ ours through interpretative identity."

Rollius: "It cannot be denied that the ancient theologians, from Luther down to Gerhard, explained the mystical union in such a way that what is said concerning the closer approach of God to the faithful person, they understood as a closer approach regarding grace and operation." (See Fecht’s *Syllog.* p. 242.) Cf. the statement of Quenstedt concerning the approximation of God; see above P. I, c. 1. § 12. b. p. 26. Formula of Concord: "Therefore we unanimously reject and condemn, beyond the aforementioned and also the following and all such errors...: Where it is taught... 6. that not God, but only the gifts of God dwell in the believers." (Sol. Declar. art. 3. p. 623. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of certain Scholastics, who, as reported by P. Lombard, lib. 1. Sent. dist. 14. lit. C., maintained that 'not God Himself, the Holy Spirit, is given to believers, but only His gifts, which are not the Holy Spirit Himself,' and consequently that the Holy Spirit dwells in the heart and body of believers, not as a person according to His substance, but only ενεργητικώς and effectively; just as the sun is said to be in a field when its rays and operations are there, not the body of the sun itself... 2. Of the Papists, who contend that the union of the faithful with Christ θεάνθρωπος is spiritual, consisting in the communication of Christ’s gifts and in a singular gracious operation...

For just as they deny the substantial presence of Christ according to His humanity on earth, so also they deny the union of the faithful with the substance of Christ’s flesh... 3. Of the Calvinists, who 1.) teach that in the union of God with the faithful, only an operation, and not the divine substance, is joined more closely to them...

2.) From this spiritual union they exclude the substantial presence of Christ’s flesh altogether, for they imagine that it resides far removed from us and transfuses its spiritual properties into us through the channel of His Spirit. Thus Calvin, lib. 4. Instit. c. 18. § 12... 5. Of the Schwenkfeldians, Weigelians, and Stifelians, who dream here of an essential union, ἀποθέωσιν, a substantial μεταμόρφωσιν, and χριστουσίαν. Among more recent enthusiasts, Jacob Boehme and others belong here."

Latin:

Unde huc pertinet liberatio illa a maledictione legis et damnatione aeterna, quam aliqui primum gradum libertatis christianae appellant. Brochmandus: ״Libertas Christiana est e servitute spirituali liberatio, sanguine Christi acquisita, qua in unigenitum Dei Filium eredentes a maledictione legis, a servitute peccati, a jugo ceremoniarum Mosaicarum et ab onere traditionum humanarum coram Deo in conscientia liberi sunt, liberandi tandem a sensu omni peccati et ab omni servitute corruptionis et ipsa morte ad laudem Dei et suam salutem...

1. Libertas haec dicitur Christiana, tum quia ejus causa efficiens est Christus, teste ipso Christo Joh. 8, 36.: ,Si Filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi estis4; tum quia Christianorum proprium est, monitore Paulo Gal. 5, 13.: ,Vos in libertatem vocati estis, fratres.4

2. Libertas christiana esse dicitur e spirituali servitute liberatio duabus potissimum de causis. Una est, quia non est e servitute civili liberatio; nam non impedit, quominus qui alteri paret ac ipsius servus est, in Christo vere liber sit, ita explicante Paulo 1 Cor. 7, 20—22.: ,Unus quisque maneat in ea vocatione, in qua vocatus est. Servus vocatus es, ne sit tibi curae, sed si potes etiam liber fieri, potius eo utere. Etenim qui in Domino vocatus est servus, libertus Domini est; similiter et qui liber vocatus est, servus est Christi.' Altera est, quia haec libertas non consistit in licentia faciendi pro arbitratu quaevis; nam qui operam dat peccato, servus est peccati, Joh. 8, 34. sq.; sed libertas Christiana posita est in liberatione animae a pravis desideriis per Spiritum S., juxta illud Pauli 2 Cor. 3, 17.: ,Ubi Spiritus Domini est, ibi libertas.'
