### On Justification: L. c. c. 10. s. 2. § 902

(L. c. c. 10. s. 2. § 902. sqq.)

See Rom. 6:22, where our sanctification (ἁγιασμός) is expressly called the fruit of manumission from sin. Add verses 18, 19. We shall say more about Renovation shortly. Luther: "You must have heaven and already be blessed before you do good works; the works do not earn heaven, but rather, heaven, given out of pure grace, produces the good works, without the seeking of merit, only for the benefit of the neighbor and to the honor of God, until the body also is redeemed from sin, death, and hell."

(Tom. Hal. XII, 183.) Apology of the Augsburg Confession: "Christ often attaches the promise of the remission of sins to good works, not because He wishes good works to be a propitiation (for they follow reconciliation), but for two reasons. The one is because good fruits must necessarily follow. He warns, therefore, that it is hypocrisy and feigned repentance if good fruits do not follow. The other reason is because we need to have external signs of such a great promise, because a fearful conscience needs manifold consolation. Therefore, just as Baptism and the Lord’s Supper are signs that repeatedly admonish, raise up, and confirm fearful minds so that they may believe more firmly that sins are remitted, so the same promise is written and depicted in good works, so that these works may admonish us to believe more firmly. And those who do not do good do not stir themselves up to believe, but despise those promises. But the pious embrace them and rejoice to have signs and testimonies of such a great promise. Therefore they exercise themselves in those signs and testimonies. Just as, therefore, the Lord’s Supper does not justify *ex opere operato* without faith, so alms do not justify without faith *ex opere operato*." (Artic. 4. p. 135.) Luther: "But how does he, with these words, base forgiveness precisely upon our work, saying: 'If you forgive your neighbor, you shall be forgiven,' and again, etc.? Does that not mean that forgiveness is placed upon faith?" Answer: The forgiveness of sin, as I have often said before, happens in two ways: first, through the Gospel and the Word of God, which is received inwardly in the heart before God through faith; secondly, outwardly, through works, of which 2 Peter 1 speaks when it teaches about good works: "Beloved brothers, make every effort to confirm your calling and election," etc. There he wants us to make it certain that we have faith and the forgiveness of sin—that is, that we demonstrate it through works, so that the tree may be known by its fruits, and it may become manifest that it is a good and not a rotten tree. For where there is true faith, good works certainly follow. Thus, a person is both outwardly and inwardly pious and righteous, both before God and before people. For this is the consequence and fruit by which I make myself and others certain that I truly believe; which I otherwise could neither know nor see. Thus, the outward forgiveness here, which I show by deed, is a certain sign that I have the forgiveness of sin with God. Conversely, where such is not shown toward the neighbor, I have a certain sign that I also do not have the forgiveness of sin with God, but am still stuck in unbelief. See, that is the two-fold forgiveness: one inwardly in the heart, which hangs solely upon God's Word; and one outwardly, which breaks forth and makes us certain that we have the inward one... Where the outward sign and proof is not present, I cannot be certain of the former, but deceive both myself and others. But when I see and feel that I gladly forgive my neighbor, I can conclude and say: I do not do this work by nature, but feel myself to be different through God's grace than before... But it is also true that this work, as he calls it here, is not a mere work like others that we do of ourselves; for faith is not forgotten in it. For he takes such a work and places a promise upon it, so that one might well call it a sacrament, to strengthen faith thereby. Just as Baptism is also to be viewed as a work that I do, I who baptize or let myself be baptized; but because God's Word is joined to it, it is not a simple work that counts or accomplishes something by itself: rather, it is a divine Word and sign to which faith clings. Thus also, our prayer, as our work, would count for nothing and accomplish nothing; but it does so because it proceeds according to His command and promise, so that it may well be considered a sacrament, and more a divine work than our own. I say this because the Sophists look only at the works we do as mere things, without God's Word and promise. Therefore, when they hear and read such passages that speak of works, they must say that man earns such things through his doing. But Scripture teaches us thus: that we should not look to ourselves, but to God's Word and promise, and cling to them with faith, so that when you do a work out of the Word and promise, you have a certain token that God is gracious to you; so that your own work, which God has now taken to Himself, shall be a certain sign to you of forgiveness, etc. Now God has presented to us various manners, ways, and paths by which we grasp grace and the forgiveness of sin; as, first, Baptism and the Sacrament; likewise (as I have just said), prayer; likewise, absolution; and here, our forgiveness: so that we might be abundantly provided for, and everywhere [find] grace.

and can find mercy. For where would you seek it closer than with your neighbor, with whom you live daily, and also have sufficient cause daily to practice such forgiveness? For it cannot fail that you should be offended much and often: so that we have a daily Sacrament or Baptism, not only in the church or with the priest, but in the midst of our life, one brother with another, and everyone at home in his own house. For if you grasp the promise through this work, you have the very thing that you receive in Baptism.

How could God now grace us more abundantly than by hanging such a common Baptism about our necks, and binding it to the Lord’s Prayer, which everyone finds in himself when he prays and forgives his neighbor? So that no one has cause to complain or excuse himself that he cannot attain to it, and that it is too high and too far, or too difficult and costly, since it is brought to his very door and his neighbor’s, indeed, laid in his bosom.

See, if you look at it not according to the work in itself, but according to the Word that is attached to it, you find therein an excellent, precious treasure, so that it is now no longer your work, but a divine Sacrament; and a mighty great comfort, that you come to the grace of being able to forgive your neighbor, even if you could not come to other Sacraments. That should move you to do such a work gladly from the heart, and thank God that you are worthy of such grace: you should, after all, run to the ends of the earth for it, and consume all your goods for it; as we previously did for the invented indulgence.

Whoever will not accept this, he must be a shameful, cursed person, especially where he hears and recognizes such grace, and yet remains so stubborn and stiff-necked that he will not forgive, whereby he loses both Baptism and Sacrament, and everything else at once. For they are all bound together, so that whoever has one, he shall have them all, or keep none. For whoever is baptized shall also receive the Sacrament; and whoever receives the Sacrament must also pray; and whoever prays, also forgives, etc. But if you do not forgive, then you have here a terrible judgment, that your sins shall also not be forgiven you, even if you are among the Christians and partake of the Sacraments and other goods: rather, they shall only be the more harmful and damnable to you. (Exposition of the 5th, 6th, and 7th Chapters of Matthew. A. 1532. Opp. Wal. Tom. VII, 751—55.)

Gerhardus: "From the righteousness of faith arises in the regenerate the righteousness of works, which is likewise in many ways more perfect in the regenerate than that external Pharisaic righteousness (Matt. 5:20): since it proceeds from the renewal of the Spirit and has joined to it the interior obedience of the heart, since it is spontaneous and voluntary, not mercenary, since it respects the whole law, not just a certain particle of the law, since it proceeds from a sincere heart, and not a hypocritical one, from a sincere love of God, and seeks only the glory of God, and not one's own advantage or honor.

Both the righteousness of faith and the righteousness of works in the regenerate is more perfect and abundant than Pharisaic righteousness; meanwhile, however, since the regenerate, although they serve the law with their mind, yet serve the law of sin with their flesh, Rom. 7:25, since imperfections and filth adhere to the very works of the regenerate, therefore through and because of their works, because they are imperfect and unclean, they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, and consequently in this question, so that they may enter the kingdom of heaven, they do not flee to the Pharisaic righteousness of the flesh, nor to their own spiritual imperfect obedience, but to the most perfect righteousness of Christ by faith." (L. de Evang. § 22.)

Thus in Rom. 5:2 they are said to be justified to boast in the hope of the glory of God, namely, having obtained the foundation of hope and the hope itself of eternal life and PART III. CAP. V.

to be obtained from God and in God. And ch. 8, 17. 23. 24. 25. not only an inheritance, but also the hope and expectation of future salvation born from this is attributed to them. Cf. Gal. 3, 29.

E. Hunnius: "Whatever doctrine fights against the hope of Christians is necessarily false and erroneous, since the entire Scripture tends toward this, 'that through patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.' But the dogma of the Papists concerning doubting is opposed to Christian hope; therefore, it must be false and dissonant from the mind and scope of Scripture.

The Word of God describes the hope of the faithful, which does not put those who hope to shame, according to these most weighty oracles and testimonies of the divine Spirit: Ps. 25: 'In thee I trust, let me not be ashamed'; and shortly after: 'All who wait for thee shall not be ashamed'; Ps. 31 and 71: 'In thee, O Lord, have I hoped, let me not be ashamed forever'; and Rom. 5: 'Affliction produces patience, patience indeed probation, probation indeed hope, furthermore hope does not put to shame.'

Hence the epistle to the Hebrews 6 compares it to a safe and firm anchor, upon which the ship, leaning, stands against the onslaught of winds and storms. 'We,' he says, 'who have fled for refuge, to lay hold upon the hope set before us, which we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast.' Hence the same [apostle] admonishes that we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.

Especially ἀξιόλογον [noteworthy] is what he writes in Heb. 10: 'Let us draw near with a true heart, in certainty of faith, having our hearts sprinkled and an evil conscience cast away and our bodies washed with pure water, let us hold fast the confession of our hope, not wavering, for he is faithful who promised.' To which saying there are almost as many arguments against the doubting of the Papists as there are words, and especially that which calls the confession of our hope ἀκλινή, not wavering.

Whence Peter also reports that Christians are begotten again by God unto a living hope. And a little later he subjoins: 'Girding up the loins of your mind, be sober, hope perfectly for the grace that is brought to you.'

But those who teach that a man ought still to dispute with himself by doubting whether he is in the grace of God, or whether he is an heir of eternal life, they cannot teach with the prophets and apostles a hope that does not put to shame, a hope firm, a hope safe and like a most firm anchor, a hope living, a hope ἀκλινή or not wavering, a hope by which one hopes perfectly in the grace of God; but, having most unworthily condemned and trampled upon this Christian hope, they substitute a hope that can put to shame, one that is fluctuating, wavering, and finally casting a man from doubt into the abyss of despair, which kind of doubtful and uncertain hope the prophetic and apostolic Scripture is entirely ignorant of. —

But since hope is occupied with the future goods of eternal life, who will be able to be certain that he will struggle through all temptations, since there are so many impediments in the world, such great power of Satan, and in turn such great infirmity of our flesh?

If we wish to fix our eyes either on the infirmity of our flesh, or the power of Satan, or those obstacles which are set before the pious in the world, we must not only doubt concerning salvation, but we must plainly despair.

But against all these must be opposed the firm consolations of the Holy Spirit, namely, that he who is in us is greater than he who is in the world, as one who, as Christ testifies, has been judged and cast out; and that the Savior says: 'Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world'; and again, what is read, that those who are born of God overcome the world, 1 John 5; nay, that in all the evils of this world they are far superior through him who loved them; and also that saying of Peter, saying that the faithful are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation.

Just as Christ also says: 'No one shall snatch my sheep out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of my Father's hand.' '

He is faithful,' says Paul, 'who does not allow us to be tempted above that which we are able, but will even with the temptation make a way of escape, that we may be able to bear it,' 1 Cor. 10.

And Phil. 1: 'Being persuaded that he who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ.'

2 Thess. 3: 'Not all have faith, but the Lord is faithful, who will establish you and keep you from evil.'

But if anyone by study and deliberate effort turns himself away again from God, since he who

PART III. CHAP. VI. by the power of the Spirit, with which he had been regenerated and endowed, he could have persevered in goodness and retained the beginning of his substance unto the end, this is the head and cause of his own destruction, nor can this be a deception to those who are touched by a serious concern for their own salvation. Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit makes these certain of salvation by the promises set forth, so that, if they do not willingly fall away from the good, but desire to persevere in the grace of God, no diabolical power can tear them away from God and Christ, so also, conversely, He warns that they should crucify the flesh with its desires, that they should abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul, that, when they stand, they should take heed lest they fall, that they should hold fast what they have, lest anyone take away their crown or intercept their palm, that they should work out their own salvation with fear and trembling. All these admonitions together look not to the fostering of popish doubt or the weakening of the hope of Christians, but only to the shaking off of carnal security and spiritual lethargy.” (Artic. de justific. 1590. p. 81—85.) §

15. Justification can be defined as an act of the divine Will, by which the Triune God, out of His gratuitous favor, on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, remits sins to a sinful man, who is reborn or converted, for the sake of obtaining eternal salvation.

Which holds the place of the genus. Cf. § 1. note g. and § 6. note a. The efficient cause of justification, according to § 6. Which is the internal impulsive cause; concerning which see § 7. Which is the external impulsive cause, and that the principal one, according to § 7. Which is the less principal external impulsive cause; see § 9. As the subject, or object of justification, according to § 12. In which the formal reason of justification consists; see § 11. The end of justification is this, according to § 13.

Lutherus: ,,Du musst den Himmel haben und schon selig sein, ehe du gute Werke thust; die Werke verdienen nicht den Himmel, sondern wiederum, der Himmel, aus lauter Gnaden gegeben, thut die guten Werke dahin, ohne Gesuch des Verdienstes, nur dem Nächsten zu Nutz und Gott zu Ehren, bis dass der Leichnam auch von Sünden, Tod und Hölle erlöset werde.“ (Tom. Hai. XII, 183.) Apologia Aug. Conf.: ,,Christus saepe annectit promissionem remissionis peccatorum bonis operibus, non quod velit, bona opera propitiationem esse (sequuntur enim reconciliationem), sed propter duas causas. Altera est, quia necessario sequi debent boni fructus. Monet igitur, hypocrisin et fictam poenitentiam esse, si non sequantur boni!ructus. Altera causa est, quia nobis opus est habere externa signa tantae promissionis, quia conscientia, pavida multiplici consolatione opus habet. Ut igitur baptismus, ut coena Domini sunt signa, quae subinde admonent, erigunt et confirmant pavidas mentes, ut credant firmius, remitti peccata, ita scripta et picta est eadem promissio in bonis operibus, ut haec opera admoneant nos, ut firmius credamus. Et qui non benefaciunt, non excitant se ad credendum, sed contemnunt promissiones illas. Sed pii amplectuntur eas et gaudent, habere signa et testimonia tantae promissionis. Ideo exercent se in illis signis et PART. III. CAP. V. testimoniis. Sicut igitur coena Domini non justificat ex opere operata sine fide, ita eleemosynae non justificant sine fide ex opere operato.“ (Artic. 4. p. 135.) Lutherus: ״Wie setzet er aber mit diesen Worten die Vergebung eben auf unser Werk, und spricht: Wenn ihr dem Nächsten vergebt, so soH euch vergeben sein, und wiederum u. s. w.? Das heisst ja nicht die Vergebung auf den Glauben gestellt? Antwort: Die Vergebung der Sünde, wie ich sonst oft gesagt habe, geschieht zweierlei, einmal, durchs Evangelium und Wort Gottes, welches empfangen wird inwendig im Herzen vor Gott, durch den Glauben; zum andern, äusserlich, durch die Werke, davon 2 Petri 1. sagt, da er von guten Werken lehret: Lieben Brüder, thut Fleiss, euern Beruf und Erwählung fest zu machen u. s. w. Da will er, dass wir solches sollen gewiss machen, dass wir den Glauben und Vergebung der Sünde ^aben, das ist, dass wir beweisen die Werke, dass man den Baum an den Früchten spüre, und offenbar werde, dass es ein guter und nicht ein fauler Baum sei. Denn wo ein rechter Glaube ist, da folgen gewisslich auch gute Werke. Also ist ein Mensch beide, auswendig und inwendig, fromm und gerecht, beide vor Gott und den Leuten. Denn das ist die Folge und Frucht, damit ich mich und andere gewiss mache, dass ich recht gläube; welches ich sonst nicht wissen noch sehen könnte. Also ist hier auch die äusserliche Vergebung, so ich mit der That erzeige, ein gewiss Zeichen, dass ich Vergebung der Sünde bei Gott habe. Wiederum, wo sich solches nicht erzeigt gegen den Nächsten, so habe ich ein gewiss Zeichen, dass auch ich nicht Vergebung der Sünde bei Gott habe, sondern stecke noch im Unglauben. Siehe, das ist die zweierlei Vergebung: eine inwendig im Herzen, die allein an Gottes Wort hanget; und auswendig, die heraus bricht, und uns gewiss machet, dass wir die innerliche haben. . . Wo die äusserliche Zeichen und Beweisung nicht ist, sa kann ich jener nicht gewiss sein, sondern beide, mich und andere, betrügen. Wenn ich aber sehe und fühle, dass ich gerne dem Nächsten vergebe, so kann ich schliessen und sagen: Das Werk thue ich von Natur nicht, sondern fühle mich durch Gottes Gnade anders, denn zuvor. . . Das ist aber auch wahr, dass dies Werk, wie ers hier nennet, nicht ein bloss Werk ist, wie andere, so wir von uns selbst thun; denn es ist auch des Glaubens nicht dabei vergessen. Denn er nimmt solch Werk und stellet eine Verheissung darauf, dass mans mit guten Ehren mochte ein Sacrament nennen, den Glauben dadurch zu stärken. Gleich als, die Taufe ist auch wohl ein Werk anzusehen, das ich thue, der ich taufe oder mich taufen lasse; aber weil Gottes Wort dabei ist, ist es nicht ein schlecht Werk, als das für sich selbst etwas gelte oder schaffe: sondern ein göttlich Wort und Zeichen, daran sich der Glaube hänget. Also auch, unser Gebet, als unser Werk, würde nichts gelten noch schaffen; aber das thuts, dass es gehet in seinem Gebot und Verheissung, dass es auch wohl mag ein Sacrament, und mehr ein göttlich, denn unser Werk geachtet werden. Das rede ich darum, dass die Sophisten allein die Werke, so wir thun, so bloss ansehen, ohne Gottes Wort und Verheissung. Derhalben, wenn sie solche Sprüche hören und lesen, so auf die Werke lauten, müssen sie wohl sagen, dass der Mensch durch sein Thun solches verdiene. Die Schrift aber lehret uns also: dass wir nicht auf uns, sondern auf Gottes Wort und Verheissung sollen sehen, und daran mit dem Glauben haften, dass, wenn du ein Werk aus dem Wort und Verheissung thust, so hast du ein gewiss Wahrzeichen, dass dir Gott gnädig ist; also, dass dein eigen Werk, das Gott nun zu sich genommen hat, soll dir ein gewiss Zeichen sein der Vergebung u. s. w. Nun hat uns Gott mancherlei Weise, Weg und Stege vorgestellt, dadurch wir die Gnade und Vergebung der Sünde ergreifen; als, erstlich, die Taufe und Sacrament; item (wie ich jetzt gesagt), das Gebet; item, die Absolution; und allhier, unsere Vergebung: dass wir ja reichlich versorget wären, und allenthalben Gnade

und Barmherzigkeit finden können. Denn wo wolltest du sie näher suchen, denn bei deinem Nächsten, bei dem du täglich lebest, und auch täglich Ursache genug hast, solche Vergebung zu üben? denn es kann nicht fehlen, dass du nicht solltest viel und oft beleidigt werden: also, dass wir nicht allein in der Kirche oder bei dem Priester, sondern mitten in unserm Leben ein täglich Sacrament oder Taufe haben, ein Bruder am andern, und ein jeglicher daheim in seinem Hause. Denn wenn du die Verheissung dtfrch dies Werk ergreifest, so hast du eben das, was du in der Taufe überkommst.

Wie könnte uns nun Gott reichlicher begnaden, denn dass er uns so eine gemeine Taufe an den Hals hängt, und ans Vater Unser bindet, die ein jeglicher an ihm selbst flndet, wenn er betet und seinem Nächsten vergibt? dass ja niemand Ursache hat zu klagen oder sich zu entschuldigen, er könne nicht dazu kommen, und sei ihm zu hoch und zu fern, oder zu schwer und theuer, weil es ihm und seinem Nächsten heim vor die Thür gebracht, ja in Busen gelegt wird.

Siehe, wenn du es also nicht nach dem Werk an ihm selbst, sondern nach dem Wort, so daran geheftet ist, ansiehest, so findest du darin einen trefflichen, köstlichen Schatz, dass es jetzt nicht mehr dein Werk, sondern ein göttlich Sacrament ist; und mächtigen grossen Trost, dass du zu der Gnade kommest, dass du deinem Nächsten vergeben kannst, ob du gleich zu andern Sacramenten nicht kommen könntest. Das sollte dich bewegen, dass du solch Werk von Herzen gerne thätest, und Gott dazu dankest, dass du solcher Gnaden werth bist: solltest du doch bis an der Welt Ende darnach laufen, und alle dein Gut darum verzehren; wie wir zuvor um den erdichteten Ablass gethan haben.

Wer nun das nicht will annehmen, der muss ein schändlicher, verfluchter Mensch sein, sonderlich, wo er solche Gnade höret und erkennet, und dennoch so kropfisch und halsstarrig bleibt, dass er nicht will vergeben, damit er beide, Taufe und Sacrament, und alles andere auf einmal verliert. Denn sie sind alle an einander gebunden, dass, wer eines hat, der soll sie alle haben, oder keines behalten. Denn wer getauft ist, soll auch das Sacrament empfahen; und wer das Sacrament empfähet, muss auch beten; und wer da betet, auch vergeben u. s. w. Vergibst du aber nicht, so hast du hier ein schrecklich Urtheil, dass dir deine Sünden auch nicht sollen vergeben sein, ob du gleich mit unter den Christen bist, und der Sacramente und anderer Güter mit geniessest: sondern sollen dir nur desto schädlicher und verdammlicher sein.‘4 (Auslegung des 5. 6. u. 7. Cap. Matthäi. A. 1532. Opp. Hai. Tom. VII, 751—55.)

Gerhardus: ,,Ex fidei justitia oritur in renatis operum justitia, quae itidem multis modis perfectior est in renatis, quam externa illa pharisaica justitia (Matth. 5, 20.): cum procedat ex renovatione Spiritus et conjunctam habeat obedientiam interiorem cordis, cum sit spontanea et voluntaria, non mercenaria, cum respiciat totam legem, non tantum particulam quandam legis, cum ex sincero corde, non autem hypocritico, ex sincera Dei dilectione, procedat et solam Dei gloriam, non autem proprium commodum vel honorem quaerat.

Et justitia fidei et justitia operum in renatis perfectior est et abundantior, quam pharisaica justitia; interim tamen, cum renati, licet mente serviant legi, tamen carne serviant legi peccati, Rom. 7, 25., cum ipsis renatorum operibus imperfectiones et sordes adhaereant, ideo per et propter opera sua, quia imperfecta sunt et immunda, non possunt ingredi regnum coelorum, ac proinde in hac quaestione, ut ingredi possint regnum coelorum, non ad justitiam carnis pharisaicam, nec ad spiritualem suam imperfectam obedientiam, sed ad perfectissimam Christi justitiam fide confugiunt.44 (L. de Evang. § 22.)

Ita Rom. 5, 2. dicuntur justificati gloriari sub spe gloriae Dei, videlicet nacti fundamentum spei spemque ipsam vitae aeternae et PART. III. CAP. V.

gloriosae a Deo et in Deo consequendae. Et cap. 8, 17. 23. 24. 25. non solum haereditas, sed et hinc nata spes atque expectatio salutis futurae illis tribuitur. Conf. Gal. 3, 29.

E. Hunnius: ,,Quae doctrina pugnat cum spe Christianorum, est necessario falsa et erronea, quandoquidem universa Scriptura tendit eo, ,ut per patientiam et consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus.‘ At pontificiorum dogma de dubitatione adversatur spei Christianae; ergo falsum et a Scripturae mente atque scopo dissonum sit oportet.

Spem fidelium describit verbum Dei, quod non confundat sperantes, secundum haec gravissima oracula et testimonia divini Spiritus: Ps.25.: ,In te confido, non erubescam‘; ac mox: ,Universi, qui ex־ pectant te, non confundentur‘; Ps. 31. et 71.: ,In te, Domine, speravi, non confundar in aeternum‘; et Rom. 5.: ,Afflictio parit patientiam, patientia vero probationem, probatio vero spem, porro spes non pudefacit.‘

Hinc epistola ad Ebr. 6. comparat eam ancorae tutae ac firmae, cui innixa navis adversus impetum ventorum tempe^tatumque consistit. ,Qui‘, inquit, ,huc confugimus, ut potiamur spe, quam velut ancoram tenemus animae, cum tutam, tum firmam.‘ Hinc idem monet, ut flduciam et gloriationem spei ad finem usque firmam teneamus.

Imprimis άξιόλογον est, quod Hebr. 10. scribit: ,Accedamus cum vero corde, in certitudine fidei, aspersi cordibus ac depulsa conscientia mala et abluti corpore aqua pura teneamus confessionem spei, non vacillantem, fidelis enim, qui promisit.‘ Cui dicto paene tot sunt argumenta contra Papistarum dubitationem, quot verba, et imprimis illud, quod spei nostrae confessionem vocat ακλι,νή, non vacillantem.

Unde Petrus quoque refert, Christianos regenitos a Deo in spem vivam. Et paulo post subjungit: ,Succincti lumbis mentis vestrae, sobrii, perfecte sperate in eam, quae ad vos defertur, gratiam.‘

At qui docent, debere hominem dubitando adhuc secum disceptare, anne sit in gratia Dei, an sit haeres vitae aeternae, 111 non possunt cum pfophetis et apostolis docere spem non confundentem, spem firmam, spem tutam et firmissimae ancorae similem, spem vivam, spem άκλινή seu non vacillantem, spem, qua perfecte speretur in Dei gratiam, sed, hac Christiana spe indignissime damnata et conculcata, substituunt spem, quae confundere possit, fluctuantem, vacillantem et hominem ex dubitatione in desperationis voraginem tandem conjicientem, cujusmodi spem dubiam et ancipitem prorsus ignorat Scriptura prophetica et apostolica. —

Cum autem spes circa ventura vitae aeternae bona sit occupata, quis poterit esse certus, quod per omnes tentationes sit eluctaturus, cum tot sint in mundo impedimenta, tanta sit potentia satanae, tanta vicissim carnis nostrae infirmitas?

Si vel in carnis nostrae infirmitatem, vel satanae potentiam, vel obstacula illa, quae piis in mundo objiciuntur, velimus oculos defigere, de salute non modo dubitandum nobis, sed plane desperandum erit.

Verum his omnibus opponendae sunt firmae consolationes Spiritus Sancti, puta, quod major sit is, qui in nobis, quam qui in mundo est, utpote qui, teste Christo, judicatus et foras ejectus est; et quod Salvator ait: ,Confidite, ego vici mundum‘; atque rursum, quod legitur, eos, qui ex Deo nati sunt, vincere mundum, 1 Joh. 5.; imo in universis hujus mundi malis longe esse superiores per eum, qui dilexit illos; nec non illud Petri, dicentis, fideles virtute Dei per fidem custodiri ad salutem.

Plane ut et Christus inquit: ,Non rapiet oves meas quisquam de manu mea. Pater meus, qui dedit mihi, major omnibus est, et nemo potest rapere de manu Patris mei.‘ ,

Hic fidelis est‘, inquit Paulus, ,qui non sinit nos tentari supra id, quod possumus, imo dat una cum tentatione eventum,<quo possumus sufferre‘, 1 Cor. 10.

Et Phil. 1.: ,Persuasum habeo, quod is, qui coepit in vobis opus bonum, perficiet usque ad diem Jesu Christi.‘

2 Thess. 3.: ,Non omnium est fides, sed fidelis est Dominus, qui stabiliet vos et custodiet a malo.‘

VI. dem virtute Spiritus, quo regeneratus et donatus erat, potuerit in bonitäte perseverare et initium substantiae usque ad finem retinere, hic proprii exitii caput et causa est, neque hoc fraudi potest esse his, qui salutis suae seria tanguntur cura. ## 21 On Renewal and Good Works

Chapter VI. ON RENEWAL AND GOOD WORKS. § 1. The term renewal is sometimes taken so broadly that it embraces even conversion or regeneration itself, and indeed justification along with the subsequent work of sanctification; in this place, however, it is taken more strictly, so that it may be distinguished from conversion and follow justification itself. It is otherwise called sanctification. PART III. CHAP. VI.

Indeed, renewal in general denotes any action by which old things, or those which have been worn away, weakened, or corrupted by age or otherwise, are restored. And thus, in the spiritual renewal of man, taken in a broader sense, it is understood that the old man, according to his entire condition—that is, his total lack of spiritual powers, his guilt, and the dominion of sin—is abolished, and the new man, according to his full extent—that is, the spiritual powers themselves, the absolution from guilt, and the habitual gift by which the dominion of sin is suppressed—is produced. See 2 Cor. 5:17 ff., where men who are in Christ are said to be a new creature. To this, moreover, the very reconciliation with God and justification through Christ are referred (v. 19 and 21). Compare the blessed Musaeus, *De Conversione* (Jena ed.), Disp. III, cap. I, § 29, p. 113, where he shows that the conversion of man itself is truly and not unusually called a certain renewal. Add *Ausführl. Erklärung* L. XV, Q. 78, p. 653 ff.

Fechtius: "Both terms, renewal and sanctification, are by their nature so general that they embrace every grace and its operation. For when a man is pronounced righteous, and when he is instructed with the divine power of doing good, and when he actually conforms his life to the divine law, he is renewed and sanctified—that is, he becomes new from old, and holy from impure." (*Compendium, universam th. complex.* Cap. XXII, § 1, p. 608.) *Large Catechism*: "So learn now to understand this (3rd) Article most clearly. When one asks: 'What do you mean by the words: I believe in the Holy Spirit?' that you may answer: 'I believe that the Holy Spirit makes me holy (sanctificari), as his name is.' With what does he do this, or what is his manner and means for it? Answer: Through the Christian Church, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and the life everlasting." (*Liber Conc.* p. 455 f.)

J. B. Carpzov the Elder: "There does not occur a text in the Bible where the term 'sanctification' is interchanged with the term 'justification,' but the distinction between justification and sanctification is always kept intact in Holy Scripture, even in the terminology. As Chemnitz rightly noted, T. II, *Loc. th.*, p. 621: 'Augustine, deceived by the breadth of the term "to sanctify" and "to justify," was sometimes led beyond the mind of Scripture and bent the meanings of the terms justification and sanctification.' That we are holy through justification—namely, by that imputed holiness which is one in number with the obedience and holiness of Christ, which He performed for the divine law in our place—is read in Scripture. Under the word 'to sanctify,' justification is also sometimes included therein, which, among other things, the texts Eph. 5:26, 27 and Heb. 10:29 prove; but justification itself is never called sanctification in Scripture; which can be proven by induction." (*Disputatt. isagog. in Chemnitium*. Ed. J. B. Carpzov. Lips. 1701, p. 1142.) For thus we enumerated renewal among the effects of justification in Chapter V, § 14 and note d. And the following will teach this special meaning.

See Rom. 6:22, where men, having been set free from sin and having become servants to God, are said to have their fruit εις αγιασμον, unto sanctification. And 1 Thess. 5:23, the Apostle prays for his own that the God of peace may sanctify them wholly. By this is understood the bestowal and attainment of internal holiness, whereas in the very act of justification, the imputation of an alien holiness—namely, that of Christ—takes place; to which the passages 1 Cor. 1:30 and Heb. 10:14 refer, here

but the men themselves are *πιτελοῦντες ἁγιωσύνην ἐν φόβῳ Θεοῦ*, perfecting holiness in the fear of God, 2 Cor. 7: 1. Carpzovius: "Immediately and at that very moment in which faith is kindled in us, and by it, insofar as it apprehends the offered righteousness, we are justified, we are also renewed in mind and body; but whatever may be the case regarding this simultaneity of time, in themselves and by their own nature the benefits remain distinct, as the Apostle not only signifies this by his manner of treating the doctrine of justification and renovation in the epistles to the Romans and Galatians, while he treats justification first and separately in Rom. 3, 4, 5 and Gal. 1, 2, 3, 4, but afterwards treats sanctification in Rom. 6 and 7 and Gal. 5 and 6. But the very nature of the benefits also makes this apparent. For 1. Justification is a forensic act and corresponds to a moral action; renovation, however, approaches a physical action. 2. Justification consists in the remission of sins; renovation, however, in inherent righteousness and in the habit and zeal for new obedience. 3. Justification frees from the guilt of sin; renovation, however, from its dominion. 4. Justification is equal, and neither the act nor the imputable righteousness is increased or diminished; renovation, however, is unequal and receives increments, and is not only continued, as is justification, but is also increased. 5. In justification, the righteousness of Christ is considered as a gift, by the imputation of which we are constituted righteous; in renovation, however, Christ is set forth as an example, to which and according to which our inherent righteousness ought to be conformed." (L. c. p. 1135 sq.) §

2. Renovation, strictly so-called, imports a certain real and intrinsic change in the regenerate or converted man; which is sometimes taken transitively, sometimes intransitively. Which the Apostle designates by the word *μεταμορφώσεως*, by which a man changes his form—not an external one, but an internal one, albeit accidental. *Μεταμορφοῦσθε*, he says, "be transformed by the renewing of your mind," Rom. 12:2. As an action of God producing in us holy motions and actions; just as He is said to give a new heart and a new spirit, Ezek. 36:26, and to renew a right spirit within us, Ps. 51:10. Insofar as men are said to renew themselves, making for themselves a new heart and a new spirit, Ezek. 18:31, putting off the old man, putting on the new, Eph. 4:22, 24. Compare, regarding this double acceptation, the blessed Olearius, *Index*; Balduinus, *Gener. Th. Posit.*, art. XCVII, observ. ad § 5, p. 165 a.; and the blessed Scherzer, *Brev. Hülsem. auct.*, cap. XII, Thes. III, p. 684. §

3. On both sides its terms are to be noted: that from which and that to which. For it is, as to the thing itself, one action, although there is a difference on the part of the principles or causes, of which one is subordinated to the other. Which occurs in every change; where one term is to be abolished or deserted, and the other is to be produced or acquired. PART III. CAP. VI.

§ 4. The *terminus a quo* [the starting point] consists of the remnants of sin, which remain after conversion; namely, a certain deficiency of good powers: on the part of the intellect, indeed, for knowing spiritual things; on the part of the will, for pursuing spiritual goods; on the part of the sensitive appetite, for obeying the superior faculties; and at the same time, also the proneness of these same faculties of the soul toward evil. This must be abolished, if not entirely and root and branch (which cannot happen in this life), at least *secundum quid* [in a certain respect], so that it may be diminished, weakened, or suppressed. Or, the old way of living and sinning, which includes both sin itself as innate and the vices contracted by living wickedly. It is otherwise called the "old man," Eph. 4:22, not by reason of substance, but by reason of the vicious qualities and accidents from the ancient fall, from which man has drawn, as it were, the rot of antiquity. "Flesh with its lusts," Gal. 5:24. That, indeed, which in the carnal man, or after the fall through carnal generation, has been transferred to him and by which he is inclined from spiritual things toward sensible things. It is called the "body of sin," because it is a complex of many sins, as if they were parts or members, Rom. 6:6, whence also the various species of sins are called "earthly members," Col. 3:5. See the complaint of Paul (who was certainly regenerate and instructed with spiritual powers according to the inner man, according to vv. 18 and 22), that he does not do the good that he wills; nor does he find (sufficient powers) to do the good; but he does the evil that he does not will, and that by the power of sin dwelling in him, lying close to him, etc., Rom. 7:15 ff. Quenstedtius: "That he (the apostle) speaks in that chapter (Rom. 7) of himself as regenerate, all orthodox theologians maintain, relying on firm reasons... Blessed Huelsemannus in *Vindiciae* A. 9. § 33. p. 42 says: 'Rom. 7:16, 19, 23 does not deal with the repugnance of the pure natural powers of the intellect and will of the unregenerate, nor does it deal with the quality of a man imbued with some knowledge of the Mosaic law, such as the apostle was when he was taught according to the strictness of the state of Pharisaism, Acts 22:3, yet not yet brought into the state of adoption, or not yet regenerate or renewed; but it deals entirely with a man regenerate and renewed, and indeed expressly with the imperfection of renewal in this life, as Article 20 of the Augsburg Confession explains.' And this the most consummate theologian demonstrates at length in the same place with four most firm reasons, which deserve to be read entirely. The sum of the reasons is this:

1. That the apostle in the whole of chapter 6 exhorts the faithful who are already regenerate concerning their duty, and he says that this is evident from all the verses, and especially the last verses of the chapter, and from the phraseology carried over from chapter 6 into the seventh, namely, that the discourse is about those who have been liberated, v. 18, 20, 21, 22 of ch. 6, and v. 1, 2, 3, 6 of ch. 7.

2. That the apostle describes the past state through verbs of the past tense; 'Such I was,' and 'such you were,' etc., 'you had that fruit,' ch. 6:18–22, and he repeats the same difference in ch. 7, from v. 1 up to 14, where the apostle uses verbs of the past tense, namely, 4, 5, 9, 12; but from v. 14 to the end of the chapter, Paul speaks with verbs of the present tense, to which present he opposes not in this, but in eternal life, the future, v. penultimate and ultimate.

Latin:

Caput VI. DE RENOVATIONE ET BONIS OPERIBUS. § 1. Renovationis vox aliquando ita late accipitur, ut ipsam quoque conversionem sive regenerationem, imo et justificationem cum sequente opere sanctificationis a complectatur; hoc loco autem strictius,b ut a conversione distinguatur atque ipsam etiam justificationem sequatur. Dicitur alias sanctificatio.c PART. III. CAP. VI.

Nempe renovatio in genere denotat quamlibet actionem, qua vetera, aut quae vetustate vel aliunde detrita seu infirmata aut corrupta sunt, restaurantur. Atque ita in renovatione hominis spirituali, latius sumta, vetus homo secundum omnem suam rationem, i. e. carentiam virium spiritualium omnimodam, reatum et dominium peccati, aboleri, et novus homo secundum suam latitudinem, id est, ipsas vires spirituales, absolutionem a reatu et donum habituale, quo supprimatur dominium peccati, produci intelligitur. Vid. 2 Cor. 5, 17. sqq., ubi homines, qui in Christo sunt, nova creatura esse dicuntur. Eo autem refertur ipsa reconciliatio cum Deo et justificatio per Christum v. 19. et 21. Conf. b. Mus. de Conv. (ed. Jen.) Disp. III. cap. I. § 29. p. 113., ubi ostendit, ipsam conversionem hominis esse revera nec inusitate dici renovationem quandam. Add. Ausführl. Erklärung L. XV. Q. 78. p. 653. sqq.

Fechtius: ,,Utraque vox renovationis et sanctificationis ita sua natura generalis est, ut omnem gratiam ejusque operationem in se complectatur. Nam et cum homo justus pronuntiatur, et cum divina virtute bene operandi instruitur, et cum vitam suam actu ipso ad legem divinam conformat, renovatur et sanctificatur, i. e., ex ve te re fit novus et ex impuro sanctus.44 (Compendium, universam th. complex. Cap. XXII. § 1. p. 608.) Catechism. major: ,,So lerne nun diesen (3.) Artikel aufs deutlichste verstehen. Wenn man fraget: Was meinest du mit den Worten: ,Ich gläube an den Heiligen Geist?4 dass du könnest antworten: Ich gläube, dass mich der Heilige Geist heilig machet (sanctificari), wie sein Name ist. Womit thut er aber solches oder was ist seine Weise und Mittel dazu? Antwort: Durch die christliche Kirche, Vergebung der Sünden, Auferstehung des Fleisches und das ewige Leben." (Liber Conc. p. 455. sq.)

### On Renewal and Good Works: That the apostle says in the past that he served sin, and of the present, that…

3. That the apostle says in the past that he served sin, and of the present, that he serves..." [He] served as a slave ignorant of a better condition, but now serves unwillingly with struggle and resistance, as one detained by a tyrant; there he committed sins spontaneously and by choice, here not except by surprise and through infirmity and imprudence. The former is evident from verses 4–6 of chapter 7, compared with the parallels 1 Cor. 4:10, 11; 11:2; Eph. 2:3, 11–13; 4:17–19. The latter is evident from the periphrasis both of the subject sinning after regeneration and of the sins committed after regeneration. The subject is described as one who delights in the law of God according to the inner man, v. 22, which "inner man," when opposed to the "outer," always signifies the regenerate state, Rom. 2:29; 2 Cor. 4:16; Eph. 3:

16. Moreover, the attributes—such as delighting in the law of God, hating sin, fleeing from sin—which the apostle mentions regarding his present state in vv. 17–20, 22, do not fit the unregenerate; for these do not delight in the law of God, but it is hateful to them, etc. 4. That antiquity and the symbolical books, such as Augustine (Book 1, *Retract.*, ch. 23) and the *Apology of the Augsburg Confession* (ad art. 4, pp. 82, 84, and 117), explain the subject, of whom it is predicated in v. 18, 19, and following of chapter 7, as a subject already justified.” (*Theol. did.-pol.* P. III, c. 11, s. 2, f. 922 sq.) Not indeed a total lack of them (because in conversion itself some good powers have already been obtained), yet some lack. For although some spiritual light is present after conversion, it is nevertheless joined with a lack of that fuller perfection which ought to be present. For the powers that were conferred in conversion are slender, so that the just or more perfect holiness, which ought to be present, is absent. See what we said in Chapter IV on Regeneration and Conversion, § 5, last note. From this it is evident that the lack of prompt obedience, which is owed by the higher faculties, has not yet been removed by conversion. Indeed, even in the regenerate, the flesh (concerning which see note b) lusts (and by lusting resists) against the spirit (or against those new powers which the Holy Spirit began to confer in the act of conversion or regeneration), Gal. 5:17. From this it appears that there remains in the intellect some proneness (though not as strong as before conversion) to rash judgments concerning spiritual things; in the will, a certain inclination toward fleeting goods to be preferred over spiritual ones; in the sensitive appetite, some propensity toward goods pleasing to the senses, even if forbidden. § 5. The term to which of renewal are those greater spiritual powers, which are only to be acquired after conversion; namely, on the part of the intellect, a fuller knowledge of spiritual things; of the will, a more perfect holiness; and of the sensitive appetite, a more prompt and constant obedience to be rendered to the higher faculties. Which is to be acquired and which renewal ought to reach by its acts. PART III. CHAPTER VI.

However, full perfection without any defect, which does not fall to men in the state of this life after the fall and the tenacity of original sin, is something toward which one must strive or aspire through renewal itself.

Luther: "This is how it is with the Christian life: whoever has begun it thinks to himself as if he has nothing, but he stretches himself toward it and goes ever further forward, so that he may grasp it. Therefore Paul says in Phil. 3:13-14: 'My brothers, I do not consider myself to have grasped it. But one thing I say: I forget what is behind and stretch myself to what is in front; and I press on toward the set goal, the prize, which the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus holds out.'

For in truth, nothing is more harmful to a believer than when he imagines that he has already grasped it, and that it is not necessary to keep seeking. For from this it comes that many fall back and wither and become weary from security and laziness.

Thus also Bernard says: 'If one stands still on the way of God, it is the same as if one goes backward.' Therefore, whoever has begun to be a Christian is obligated to do this: to remember that he is not yet a Christian, but that he is still seeking to bring it about that he becomes a Christian; that he may boast with Paul in Phil. 3:12, 15-16: I am not it, but I seek to be it; 'not that I have already grasped it, or am already perfect, but I press on, if I might also grasp it, after I have been grasped by Christ Jesus. And as many of us as are perfect, let us remain by this rule.'

For a Christian is in the becoming, not in the having-become. For it is said to him: 'Ask, seek, knock'; it does not say: You already have it, you have found it, you have already entered; but: 'Ask, seek, etc.'

Whoever is a Christian, therefore, is not a Christian; that is, whoever thinks to himself that he has already become a Christian, when he should only be becoming a Christian, he is nothing. For we stretch ourselves toward heaven, but we are not yet in heaven. And just as he will never come into heaven who imagines that he is already in heaven; so he is already in heaven who stretches himself toward heaven and seeks to get into it. For God considers him as one who is already in heaven.

In sum: One must always go further forward and increase, and not stand still, nor snore in security. 'Our old man must,' as Paul says, 'perish, and the inner one be renewed from day to day.' 2 Cor. 4:16.

Woe to him who is already completely renewed, that is, who imagines that he is already renewed. That person has without doubt not yet begun to be renewed, and has never yet tasted what it is to be a Christian. For whoever has begun to be a Christian does not consider himself to be a Christian, but he longs greatly to become a Christian; and the more he grows and increases, the more he seeks to become it, and the less he considers himself to be it.

So truly wonderful are the works of the kingdom of Christ. 'Whoever stands,' says Paul, 'let him take heed lest he fall.' 1 Cor. 10:12. And again: 'If anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself.' Gal. 6:3." (Notes on the Evangelist Matthew. A. 1538. Tom. Hal. VII, 324—326.)

Quenstedtius: "It is objected that the regenerate are called 'perfect' in Phil. 3:15; 1 John 4:12; and indeed as the heavenly Father is perfect in Matt. 5:48. I respond: 1. The same ones who are called 'perfect' and holy in Scripture are also called 'carnal' according to another mode of consideration, 1 Cor. 3:3. 2. They are called perfect παραστατικώς, preceptively—but from a precept to the ability to perform it, the consequence does not hold—or λογιστικώς, imputatively, or ἀνυποκρίτως, sincerely and inchoatively, or τελικώς, consummately, in respect to the other life; or they are called perfect not νομικώς, but εὐαγγελικώς, not

not according to the ἀκρίβεια [strictness] of the law, but according to the ἐπιείκεια [gentleness/equity] of the gospel; not on account of a full effect, but a pious affection; not on account of a perfect execution, but a good intention; not on account of integrity, but sincerity; not on account of consummation, but initiation.” (L. c. s. 2. f. 924.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Socinians, who contend that a perfect fulfillment of the law is possible in this life. . . Socinus, in his persuasive book, p. 60, c. 2, affirms it to be probable that a man, aided by the Spirit of God or supported by the help of God, can perfectly obey the law of God. The same author, in his disputation on the passage of the Apostle in Rom. 7, ed. Racov. an. 1612, in his response to a friend’s epistle, p. 56, establishes certain degrees of the regenerate, and adds: ‘I have no doubt that in some of Christ’s faithful, that struggle between the flesh and the spirit ceases in this life, with the spirit now clearly dominating and the flesh not daring to join battle with it.’ . . 2. Of the Arminians, who also imagine that there are perfect and ‘adult’ persons, as they call them, among the regenerate in this imperfection. Arminius, in his response to the 31 articles falsely ascribed to him, p. 164, and in a. 9, p. 307, and likewise in his Commentary on c. 7 of Romans, seems to attribute such perfection to the regenerate in this mortality that he does not hesitate to affirm that their good works are so perfect that they are not defiled by any vice of the flesh nor worthy of any punishments. Cf. Apol. Remonstrant. c. 10, 11, p. 131. 3. Of the Anabaptists, who boast of the perfection of good works in this life, and think that the regenerate can rise to such a degree of perfection that they are without any sin. . . 4. Of the Schwenkfeldians and Weigelians, who likewise contend that the regenerate rise to such perfection in this life that they fulfill the law of God both easily and perfectly. V. Schwenckfeld, tr. de abusu evangelii p. 75 sq., likewise de verbo Dei p. 135; cf. Wigand, tr. de Schwenckfeldian. p. 24; Weigel, P. 1. Postill. p. 35 and 73; P. 2. Postill. p. 240, and P. 3. p. 16. 5. Of the Papists, who contend that the perfect fulfillment of the law does not exceed the powers of a regenerate man, and that therefore a regenerate man, aided by the grace of God, can perfectly fulfill the moral law, and that their good works in this life are absolutely and simply good and perfect. Thus Conc. Trident, sess. 6, c. 18: ‘If anyone shall say that the commandments of God are impossible to observe even for a man who is justified and placed under grace: let him be anathema.’” (L. c. s. 2. f. 921 sq.)

They are called by one name the new man, Eph. 4:24, in an accidental signification, because they are, as it were, a new face, a similar quality, etc., of the divine image bestowed upon the first man but lost through the fall. So that we may grow up in Christ in all things and arrive at a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, Eph. 4:13, 15, i.e., that just as the Lord Himself made certain progressions from the years of His infancy, being strengthened by the Spirit, increasing in wisdom and stature and favor with God and men, until He proceeded from one stage of age to another into His full manly age, so also Christians, by the increase of the Spirit in faith and the knowledge of Christ, may progress into a perfect man. Paul does not understand this of an all-encompassing perfection, which is expected in the other life, but only that perfection is noted by which, with the roots of faith having been cast, a man can neither be ensnared by their craftiness nor moved by any of Satan’s frauds and deceits from the foundation of salvation, Jesus Christ; which is the paraphrase of the blessed Aegidius Hunnius in his Commentary. Thus, l. c. ad Eph. 4:13, that increase and perfection is referred to faith and the knowledge of the Son of God. And Phil. 1:9, Paul prays for the converted to have an exuberance in knowledge and all intelligence. Conf. Coloss. 1. Baier’s Comp. ed. Walther. III.20 PART III. CAP. VI.

Latin:

3. Quod dicat apostolus in praeterito, se serviisse peccato, et de praesenti, ser״ DB BONIS OPERIBUS.303 vire. Serviisse tanquam mancipium ignarum melioris conditionis, nunc autem servire invitum cum lucta et repugnantia, tanquam detentum a tyranno; illic commisisse peccata spontanea et proaeretica, hic non nisi sub et obreptitia per infirmitatem et imprudentiam. Prius patet ex v. 4—6. c. 7. collato cum parallelis 1 Cor. 4, 10. 11. 11,2. Eph. 2, 3.11—13. 4, 17—19. Posterius ex periphrasi tum subjecti post regenerationem peccantis, tum peccatorum post regenerationem commissorum. Subjectum describitur, quod delectetur lege Dei quoad interiorem hominem, v. 22., qui interior homo exteriori oppositus semper significat statum regeneratum, Rom. 2, 29. 2 Cor. 4, 16. Eph. 3, 16. Attributa autem, qualia sunt, delectari lege Dei, odisse peccatum, fugere peccatum, quae apostolus de statu suo praesente commemorat v. 17—20. 22., non quadrant irregenitis; hi enim non delectantur lege Dei, sed exosa est ipsis etc.

4. Quod antiquitas et libri symbolici, ut Augustinus 1. 1. Retract. c. 23. Apologia Aug. Conf. ad art. 4. p. 82. 84. et 117. subjectum, de quo praedicantur v. 18.19. et seq. c. 7., exponant de subjecto jam justificato.“ (Theol. did.-pol. P. III. c. 11. s. 2. f. 922־. sq.) Non quidem omnimoda illarum carentia (quia in ipsa conversione jam aliquid bonarum virium impetratum est), aliqua tamen. Quamvis enim aliqua lux spiritualis post conversionem adsit, conjuncta k tamen est cum defectu plenioris perfectionis, quam adesse oportebat. Quae enim in conversione collatae fuerunt vires, tenues sunt, ita ut absit justa seu perfectior sanctitas, quae adesse debebat. Vid., quae diximus cap. IV. de Regen, et Conv. § 5. not. ult. Unde constat, carentiam obsequii prompti, quod superioribus facultatibus debetur, per conversionem nondum esse sublatam. Nempe etiam in renatis caro (de qua vid. not. b.) concupiscit (et concupiscendo reluctatur) adversus spiritum (seu adversus novas illas vires, quas Spiritus Sanctus in actu conversionis aut regenerationis conferri coepit), Gal. 5, 17. Ex quo apparet, in intellectu superesse pronitatem aliquam (licet non aeque fortem, sicut ante conversionem) ad temeraria judicia de rebus spiritualibus, in voluntate inclinationem quandam ad bona caduca, spiritualibus praeferenda, in appetitu sensitivo propensionem aliquam ad bona sensibus grata, etsi prohibita. § 5. Terminus ad quem a renovationis sunt majores b illae vires spirituales,c quae post conversionem demum aequirendae d sunt; videlicet ex parte intellectus plenior cognitio e rerum spiritualium, voluntatis perfectior sanctitas,f et appetitus sensitivi g promptius et constantius obsequium superioribus facultatibus praestandum. Qui acquirendus est et quem renovatio suis actibus attingere debet. PART. III. CAP. VI.

Non autem plena perfectio sine ullo defectu, quae in homines pro statu hujus vitae post lapsum et tenacitate peccati orig, non cadit, licet ad eam enitendum aut aspirandum sit per ipsam renovationem.

Lutherus: ,,Also ist es mit dem christlichen Leben beschaffen, dass, wer es angefangen hat, sich dünken lässt, als ob er nichts habe, sondern er strecket sich darnach und gehet immer weiter fort, auf dass er es ergreife. Daher spricht Paulus Phil. 3, 13. 14.: ,Meine Brüder, ich schätze mich selbst noch nicht, dass ich es ergriffen habe. Eins aber sage ich: Ich vergesse, was dahinten ist, und strecke mich zu dem, das da vorne ist; und jage nach, dem vorgesteckten Ziel nach, dem Kleinod, welches vorhält die himmlische Berufung Gottes in Christo Jesu.'

Denn es ist in der That einem Gläubigen nichts schädlicher, als wenn er sich einbildet, er habe es schon ergriffen, und es sei nicht nöthig, erst zu suchen. Denn daher kommt es, dass viele zurückfallen und vor Sicherheit und Faulheit verwelken und lass werden.

Also spricht auch Bernhardus: ,Wenn man auf dem Wege Gottes still steht, ist es ebensoviel, als wenn man zurück geht.4 Dero wegen, wer angefangen hat, ein Christ zu sein, der ist schuldig, noch dieses zu thun, dass er gedenke, er sei noch kein Christ, sondern er suche es noch dahin zu bringen, dass er ein Christ werde; dass er mit Paulo Phil. 3, 12. 15. 16. rühmen könne: Ich bin es nicht, sondern ich suche es zu sein; ,nicht dass ich es schon ergriffen habe, oder schon vollkommen sei, ich jage ihm aber nach, ob ich es auch ergreifen möchte, nachdem ich von Christo Jesu ergriffen bin. Und wie viel unser vollkommen sind, die lasset uns bei dieser Regel bleiben.‘

Denn ein Christ ist im Werden, nicht im Wordensein. Denn es wird zu ihm gesagt: ,Bittet, suchet, klopfet an‘; es heisst nicht: Ihr habt es bereits, ihr habt es gefunden, ihr seid schon eingegangen; sondern: ,Bittet, suchet u. s. w.‘

Wer derohalben ein Christ ist, der ist nicht ein Christ; das ist, wer sich dünken lässt, er sei schon ein Christ worden, da er nur ein Christ werden soll, der ist nichts. Denn wir strecken uns nach dem Himmel, wir sind aber noch nicht im Himmel. Und gleichwie derjenige nimmermehr in den Himmel kommen wird, der sich einbildet, er sei schon im Himmel; also ist derjenige bereits im Himmel, der sich nach dem Himmel strecket, und da hinein zu kommen sucht. Denn Gott hält ihn dafür, als der schon im Himmel sei.

In Summa: Man muss immer weiter fortgehen und zunehmen, und nicht still stehen, noch sicher schnarchen. ,Unser alter Mensch muss‘, wie Paulus sagt, ,verwesen, und der innerliche von Tage zu Tage erneuert werden.‘ 2 Cor 4, 16.

Wehe demjenigen, der schon ganz erneuert ist, das ist, der sich einbildet, er sei schon erneuert. Selbiger hat ohne Zweifel noch nicht angefangen erneuert zu werden, und noch niemals geschmeckt, was da sei, ein Christ sein. Denn wer da angefangen hat, ein Christ zu sein, der hält sich nicht dafür, dass er ein Christ sei, sondern er verlanget sehr, ein Christ zu werden; und je mehr er wächst und zunimmt, desto mehr suchet er es zu werden, und desto weniger hält er sich dafür, dass er’s sei.

So gar wunderbar sind die Werke des Reiches Christi. ,Wer stehet‘, sagt Paulus, ,der sehe wohl zu, dass er nicht falle.‘ 1 Cor. 10, 12. Und abermal: ,So sich jemand lässt dünken, er sei etwas, so er doch nichts ist, der betrügt sich selbst.‘ Gal. 6, 3.“ (Anmerkungen über den Evangelisten Matthäum. A. 1538. Tom. Hai. VII, 324—326.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Objicitur, quod renati dicantur,.perfecti' Phil. 3, 15. 1 Joh. 4, 12.; et quidem ut Pater coelestis perfectus est Matth. 5,48. Respond.: 1. Iidem, qui,perfecti‘ et sancti dicuntur in Seriptura, etiam,carnales' vocantur secundum alium considerandi modum, 1 Cor. 3, 3. 2. Dicuntur perfecti 7ταμαστατικώς, praeceptive, a praecepto autem ad posse non valet consequentia, vel λογιστικός, imputative, vel άνυποκρίτως, sincere et inchoative, vel τελικός, consummate, respectu alterius vitae; vel dicuntur perfecti non νομικός, sed ευαγγελικός, non

juxta legis ακρίβειαν, sed juxta evangelii επιείκειαν, non propter plenum effectum, sed pium affectum, non propter perfectam executionem, sed bonam intentionem, non propter integritatem, sed sinceritatem, non propter consummationem, sed inchoationem.“ (L. c. s. 2. f. 924.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Socinianorum, qui contendunt, perfectam legis impletionem in hac vita esse possibilem. . . Socinus libro suasorio p. 60. c. 2. probabile esse affirmat, hominem Dei Spiritu adjutum vel Dei auxilio suffultum posse legi Dei perfecte obedire. Idem ad disp. de loco apostoli Rom. 7. ed. Racov. an. 1612. in resp. ad epistol. amici p. 56. certos gradus renatorum constituit, et addit: ,Ego nihil dubito, quin in aliquibus ex Christi fidelibus in hac vita pugna illa inter carnem et spiritum cesset, jam plane spiritu dominante et carne cum ipso manus conserere non au dente‘.. . 2. Arminianotum, qui etiam fingunt in hac imperfectione perfectos et,adultos‘, ut vocant, inter renatos. Arminius in resp. ad 31 articulos sibi falso adscriptos p. 164. et in a. 9. p. 307., Itemque Comm. in c. 7. Rom. tantam videtur regenitis in hac mortalitate tribuere perfectionem, ut affirmare non dubitet, bona ipsorum opera adeo perfecta esse, ut nullo carnis vitio sint inquinata neque ullis digna poenis. Cf. Apol. Remonstrant. c. 10. 11. p. 131. 3. Anabaptistarum, qui bonorum operum in hac vita perfectionem jactitant, eoque perfectionis assurgere posse putant renatos, ut sint sine omni peccato. . . 4.
