Schwenckfeldium tr. de abusu evangelii p. 75. sq., item de verbo Dei p. 135., cf. Wigandum tr. de Schwenckfeldian. p. 24., Weigelium P. 1. Postill. p. 35. et 73. P. 2. Postill. p. 240. et P. 3. p. 16. 5.Pontificiorum, qui perfectam legis impletionem vires hominis renati non excedere, ac proinde hominem renatum gratia Dei adjutum legem moralem perfecte implere posse, eorumque bona opera in hac vita absolute et simpliciter bona et perfecta esse contendunt. Ita Cone. Trident, sess. 6. c. 18.: ,Si quis dixerit, Dei praecepta homini etiam justificato et sub gratia constituto esse ad observandum impossibilia: anathema siti“‘ (L. c. s. 2. f. 921. sq.)

Dicuntur uno nomine novus homo Eph. 4, 24· significatione accidentali, eo, quod sint imaginis divinae, primo homini collatae, sed per lapsum amissae, nova velut facies, similis qualitas etc. Ita ut crescamus in Christo per omnia et perveniamus in virum perfectum, in mensuram aetatis plene adultae Christi, Eph. 4, 13. 15., i. e. ut, quemadmodum ipse Dominus ab infantiae suae annis progressus quosdam fecit, corroboratus Spiritu, proficiens sapientia et aetate et gratia apud Deum atque homines, donec ab uno aetatis gradu ad alterum in plenam aetatem virilem suam processit, sic et christiani Spiritus incremento in fide et agnitione Christi in virum perfectum proficiant. Quod non de omnimoda perfectione Paulus intelligit, quae in altero expectatur saeculo, sed haec tantum notatur perfectio, qua jactis fidei radicibus homo neque haeretir eorum astutiis, neque ullis satanae fraudibus atque dolis a fundamento salu· tis Jesu Christo demoveri potest; quae paraphrasis est b. Aea. Hunnii in Comm. Sic 1. c. ad Eph. 4, 13. incrementum et perfectio illa refertur ad fidem et agnitionem Filii Dei. Et Phil. 1, 9. precatur Paulus conversis exuberantiam in agnitione omnique intelligentia. Conf. Coloss. 1, Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.20 PART. HI. CAP. VI.


### On Renewal and Good Works: and chapter 3, 10, in which latter place we are expressly commanded to put on…

10. and chapter 3, 10, in which latter place we are expressly commanded to put on the new (man), who is renewed unto knowledge and thus unto the image of Him who created him.

Namely, that we be renewed in the spirit of our mind, putting on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and holiness of truth (that is, true or sincere), Eph. 4:24. Righteousness is understood as a universal [virtue], or a complex of all virtues which pertain to Christian morals and which are otherwise accustomed to be variously distributed according to the two tables of the Decalogue, or, according to the method of moral theology, according to the duties of man toward God, regarding internal and external worship, toward the (regenerate) man himself, and toward his neighbor and his soul, body, reputation, wealth, etc. A brief syllabus of Christian virtues may be seen in Gal. 5:22-23; 1 Tim. 6:11; 2 Tim. 2:22; 2 Pet. 1:6-7. In opposition to the obedience rendered to the desires of the flesh, Rom. 6:12. § 6.

The *terminus a quo* (the starting point) of renewal is abolished, partly when man, having entered into a diligent and accurate examination of his life, observes and retracts more solicitously the sins committed or left behind after conversion through a serious displeasure and sorrow for them, and partly when he is occupied in the exercise of any spiritual acts according to the various kinds of Christian virtues. And to this pertains the struggle of the spirit against the flesh in the regenerate. Scripture uses phrases such as "to put off," ἀποθέσθαι (like a worn-out, filthy, torn garment) according to the former old conversation, Eph. 4:22; "to put off the old man with his deeds," Col. 3:9; "to crucify" (to finish off with a slow and, as it were, painful torture) the flesh with its lusts, Gal. 5:24; "to mortify" (to exert effort so that they lose their power and ἐνέργειαν) his members which are upon the earth, Col. 3:5. But that sin is never in this life completely and radically extirpated in man, but must be diminished, weakened, and, as far as possible, expelled, we have said at § 4, note a. Cf. b. Musaeus, *Tractatus de Poenitentia contra Stengerum*, Part III, chap. VII, pp. 634, 635.

According to those things which we said in Chapter IV concerning Conversion. Whence it pertains to this, what was said concerning the repentance of those who are standing, and that contrition cannot stand with a purpose of sinning; see § 43. Therefore, the more often and accurately a regenerate man is occupied in the chastisement of himself or his sins, the more frequently the dominion of sin is inhibited and thus diminished, although it was likewise said in the same place, from the blessed Musaeus’ *Tractatus contra Stengerum*, Part III, chap. IX, p. 709 sqq., that such more frequent or constant contrition is born from the motive of charity after conversion. Of which it will be spoken shortly. Thus, however, while one tends toward those greater perfections, by which the *terminus a quo* of renewal is partly privatively,

partly it is opposed contrarily, it happens entirely that one tends toward the abolition of the opposites or of the very term from which one departs. After they are regenerated and converted. For that struggle, which occurs in the very business of conversion, has already been treated above, Chap. IV, § 28. For corrupt concupiscence does not easily suffer itself to be crucified, mortified, etc.; rather, there are always efforts or contrary strivings. Carpzovius: "The Apostle in Rom. 7:14 and 24 complains that he has been sold under sin and is a captive. These things are to be understood not of the dominion of indwelling sin and corruption, but of the sense and the first motions thereof. For one is sold and captivated under sin in a twofold manner: first, when one sells oneself and gives oneself over to obedience, 1 Kings 21:20; 2 Tim. 2:26; secondly, when one feels the suggestions of the flesh, while wicked thoughts are excited in the mind and inclinations in the will and the remaining faculties, so that evil thoughts are as it were messengers and wicked inclinations are the edicts of indwelling sin, to which, however, obedience is denied and against which one fights. The Apostle, however, is speaking here not of the former, but of the latter captivity. For as long as the regenerate person is in the struggle, the flesh does not have full dominion, but the Spirit resists it and suppresses the sprouting shoots in the blade, as the saying goes, and crucifies the flesh, so that he not only restrains and compresses the first motions of the flesh, and does not act as the flesh wills, but also weakens the flesh more and more from time to time, 2 Cor. 4:16; Gal. 5:24. And the regenerate person, insofar as he is regenerate, always not only resists but also conquers. For he is equipped with so many and such great powers and weapons that, with their help, he can always carry off the victory over the flesh, and the Apostle John also testifies for this reason in 1 John 3:9: 'Everyone who has been born of God does not commit sin, nor can he sin,' namely, insofar as he is regenerate and as long as he possesses and guards the grace of regeneration and faithfully uses his means and weapons. But if it happens that the regenerate person sins and succumbs to the temptations of the flesh, either through precipitation or even from deliberate choice, then he either does not use his weapons rightly, as he ought, or he even grieves the Holy Spirit and, if he does not return immediately, casts Him off and falls from the grace of regeneration." (Disputatt. isag. p. 1167 sq.) § 7. And thus, at the same time, toward the acquisition of the term to which renovation tends, when through more frequent spiritual acts the spiritual powers of the intellect and will, previously bestowed, are increased and receive growth, so that they may reach a fuller habitual perfection. Thus Paul writes to Timothy: Γύμναζε σεαυτόν, exercise yourself, like an athlete, unto godliness, 1 Tim. 4:7. Elsewhere he compares Christians to runners, 1 Cor. 9:24 sqq. And to the Philippians, chap. 3:13, proposing his own example to be imitated: I, he says, do not consider myself to have already attained (the due perfection, of which he speaks in v. 12), but one thing (I do), forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth (ἐπεκτεινόμενος, as if with a body leaning or rushing forward, stretched out toward the things before, like those running toward the goal; namely, that he does not stop in those things which he has already attained, but strives toward ever more abundant progress and toward perfection, as Aeg. Hunnius explains) unto those things which are before. And in chap. 4:8, 9 he writes: PART III. CHAP. VI.

Whatever things are true, whatever things are honest, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely (προσφιλῆ), whatever things are of good report, if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things. To this pertains the parable in which Christ relates that servants, having received from their master ten, or five, or two talents, acquired as many more; i.e., that men, having diligently used the gifts of grace first bestowed, have attained to greater perfection, Matt. 25:14 ff.; Luke 19:12 ff. § 8. The principal efficient cause of renewal is the Triune God. Just as it is the cause of regeneration. For just as the primary powers of grace are conferred through the supernatural and infinite power of God, so also their increase and confirmation are owed to God. Whence Paul writes in Phil. 1:6: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. Compare 1 Thess. 5:23 and this place, § 2. For it is a work *ad extra* (external). Which, however, by appropriation is attributed to the Holy Spirit, Tit. 3:5, who for this reason is also called the Spirit of sanctification, Rom. 1:4, who dwells in the regenerate as in a temple, 1 Cor. 3:16, leads them, Rom. 8:14, and helps their infirmities, ibid. v. 26. § 9. The instrumental cause on the part of God is the Word of the Law and the Gospel, and the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist. The Law indeed dictates throughout the whole of life what things are to be done, even for the regenerate. See Ps. 1:2; the entirety of Ps. 119. The same suppresses the concupiscences of the flesh remaining in the regenerate; see Gal. 5:16. We understand, however, the Law of Moses and of Christ, which in reality is one and the same, and is to be observed by the regenerate for their renewal. Compare blessed Musaeus, *De poenit. contra Steng.*, Part II, chap. I, p. 160; chap. II, p. 199; Part III, chap. VI, p. 561 ff. Indeed, the Gospel not only excites faith in the act of conversion, but also preserves, confirms, and increases it once excited. Whence in 1 Pet. 1:22, the regenerate are said to purify their souls in obeying the truth. Compare blessed Musaeus, *Disp. de Renov.*, § 38, 39. Carpzovius: "That the Word of God is this instrument of our renewal, the clearest texts of Scripture do not allow anyone to doubt, which ascribe illumination, the changing of the heart, etc., to the Word, Ps. 19:8, 11; 119:105; Acts 26:18; Jer. 20:9; 23:29; 1 Cor. 1:6; 2:4, 5; 3:8; 2 Cor. 4:4; 1 Thess. 1:5, etc. In all these texts, however, it is a matter of the Gospel alone. 'Through the Gospel,' says the *Formula of Concord*, Art. II, p. 605, 'the Holy Spirit wills to work and perfect conversion or renewal in us.' The Law is indeed said to be 'written in the hearts,' Jer. 31:33; Heb. 8:10, but not to write itself. The inscription is done through the Gospel alone. From that alone we are reborn; from that alone we are also renewed. Now, we are reborn from the Gospel alone. Therefore, we are also renewed from the Gospel alone."

we are renewed. Nor is it an objection that the law provides some use in renewal and is the norm according to and by which new obedience ought to be instituted. For this use is at least a normative one in obedience, or in the powers and capacity of obeying already effected by the Gospel, and it pertains to that third use of the law which the law has in the regenerate and justified, as this is declared in Article VI of the Formula of Concord, p. 642.

The law indeed inculcates that it is the will and command of God that we walk in new life, but it does not bestow the powers and faculty by which we might be able to begin and perform new obedience. The Holy Spirit, however, who is given and received not through the preaching of the law, but through the preaching of the Gospel, renews the heart of man. Furthermore, the same Holy Spirit uses the ministry of the law in order to teach the regenerate through it. . . It is one thing to be the organ of renewal, and another thing to be assumed by the organ of renewal for some use at least.” (Disputatt. isagog. p. 1146 sq.)

Latin:

10. et cap. 3, 10., quo postremo loco expresse jubemur induere novum (hominem), qui renovatur ad agnitionem et sic ad imaginem ejus, qui condidit illum.

Nempe ut renovemur spiritu mentis nostrae, induentes novum hominem, qui juxta Deum conditus est in justitia et sanctitate veritatis (id est, vera aut sincera), Eph. 4, 24. Intelligitur autem justitia velut universalis, s'eu complexus omnium virtutum, quae ad mores christianos pertinent et alias juxta duas decalogi tabulas, aut pro ratione methodi theologiae moralis juxta officia hominis circa Deum, quoad cultum internum et externum, circa hominem (renatum) ipsum et circa proximum ejusque animam, corpus, famam, opes etc. varie dispesci solent. Brevem virtutum Christianarum syllabum videre licet Gal. 5, 22. 23. 1 Tim. 6, 11. 2Tim. 2, 22. 2 Pet. 1, 6. 7. In oppositione ad oblequium cupiditatibus carnis praebitum, Rom. 6, 12. § 6.

Aboletur a autem terminus a quo renovationis partim, quando homo, inito diligenti et accurato examine vitae suae, peccata post conversionem admissa aut relicta solicitius observat et retractat per seriam illorum displicentiam et dolorem,b partim, quando in exercitio actuum spiritualium quorumvis occupatur c juxta varia virtutum Christianarum genera. Atque huc pertinet renatorumά lucta spiritus adversus carnem. e Scriptura utitur phrasibus deponere, άπο&έσΰαί (velut vestimentum detritum, sordidum, lacerum) juxta priorem conversationem veterem Jwmimrn Eph. 4, 22., exuere veterem hominem cum factis suis Coloss. 3, 9., crucifigere (lento velut et doloroso cruciatu conficere) carnem cum concupiscentiis suis Gal. 5, 24 mortificare (dare operam, ut vim et hipyetav suam amittant) membra sua terrestria Col. 3, 5. Quod autem peccatum in hac vita nunquam penitus et radicitus in homine extirpetur, minui autem, infirmari et, quantum fieri potest, expelli debeat, diximus ad § 4. not. a. Conf. b. Mus. Tractat, de Poenit. contra Stengerum P. III. cap. VII. p. 634.

635. Juxta ea, quae cap. IV. de Conversione diximus. Unde huc pertinet, quod de poenitentia stantium dictum est, quodque contritio stare non possit cum proposito peccandi; vid. § 43. Quo saepius itaque et accuratius homo renatus occupatur in castigatione sui aut peccatorum suorum, eo frequentius inhibetur et sic minuitur dominium peccati, quanquam contritionem ejusmodi frequentiorem aut constantiorem ex motivo caritatis post conversionem nasci, itidem dictum est 1. c. ex b. Musaei Tract. contra Steng. P. III. cap. IX. p. 709. sqq. De quo mox dicetur. Sic autem, dum ad majores illas perfectiones tenditur, quibus terminus a quo renovationis partim privative,

partim contrarie opponitur, fit omnino, ut in abolitionem oppositorum seu ipsius termini a quo una tendatur. Postquam regeniti et conversi sunt. Nam de ea lucta, quae fit in ipso negotio conversionis, jam supra actum est, cap. IV, § 28. Neque enim prava concupiscentia facile patitur se crucifigi, mortificari etc., semper potius dantur nisus aut connatus contrarii. Carpzovius: ,,Apostolus Rom. 7, 14. et 24. conqueritur, se venundatum esse sub peccatum et captivum. Quae non de imperio inhaerentis peccati ac corruptionis, sed de sensu et primis ejus motibus intelligenda sunt. Nam duplici modo quis venundatus et captivatus sub peccatum est: semel quando quis se vendit ac dedit in obsequium, 1 Reg. 21, 20. 2 Tim. 2, 26.; deinde quando quis suggestiones carnis sentit, dum in ipso excitantur pravae cogitationes in mente et inclinationes in voluntate ac reliquis viribus, ita ut cogitationes malae sint quasi tabellarii et inclinationes pravae edicta peccati inhabitantis, quibus tamen obedientia denegatur et adversus quae pugnatur. Non de priori autem, sed posteriori captivitate hic loquitur apostolus. Quamdiu enim in lucta est renatus, tamdiu plenum dominium non habet caro, sed spiritus Illi repugnat et pullulantes surculos in herba, quod dicitur, reprimit atque carnem crucifigit, ita ut non tantum motus primos carnis refrenet et comprimat, nec agat, quomodo velit caro, sed etiam carnem subinde magis magisque debilitet, 2 Cor. 4, 26. Gal. 5, 24. Et renatus, quatenus renatus, semper non tantum repugnat, sed etiam vincit. Tot et tantis enim viribus atque armis instructus est, ut illorum ope victoriam de carne reportare semper possit, ac apostolus Johannes etiam propterea testetur 1 Joh. 3, 9.: ,Omnem, qui natus fuerit ex Deo, non committere peccatum nec posse peccare‘, sci. quatenus renatus est et quamdiu gratiam regenerationis possidet atque custodit et media ac arma sua fideliter usurpat. Si vero contingat, ut peccet et succumbat renatus in tentationibus carnis, vel per praecipitantiam, vel etiam ex proaeresi, tunc vel arma non rite usurpat, ut deberet, vel etiam contristat Spiritum S. atque, si non statim redeat, excutit eum et gratia regenerationis excidit.“ (Disputatt. isag. p. 1167. sq.) § 7. Atque ita simul ad acquisitionem termini ad quem renovationis tenditur, quando per crebriores actusa spirituales intellectus et voluntatis vires spirituales antea collatae augentur et incrementa capiunt, ut ad pleniorem perfectionem habitualem pertingant.b Sic Paulus Timotheo scribit: Γυμναζέ σε, exerse te ipsum, instar athletae, ad pietatem, 1 1Ep. 4, 7. Alias cursoribus comparat christianos, 1 Cor. 9, 24· sqq. Et Philippensibus cap. 3, 13. exemplum suura imitandum propositurus: Ego, ait, me ipsum nondum arbitror assecutum esse (perfectionem debitam, de qua loquitur v. 12.), unum autem illud (ago), ea quidem, quae a tergo sunt, oblivisceris, ad ea, quae a fronte sunt, enitens (έπεχτε^ομένος, velut prono aut praecipiti corpore protensus ad anteriora, instar currentium ad metam; nempe quod, quae pridem assecutus est, in iis non subsistat, sed ad uberiores subinde profectus et ad perfectionem contendat, exponente Aeg. Hunnio). Et cap. 4, 8. 9. scribit: PART. ΙΠ. CAP. VI.

Quaecunque sunt vera, quaecunque honesta, quaecunque pura, quaecunque accommodata (προςφάη), quaecunque bonae famae, si qua virtus et si qua laus, haec cogitate. Huc pertinet parabola, qua Christus servos, talentis decem, aut quinque, aut duobus, a domino suo acceptis, alia talenta totidem acquisivisse memorat, 1. e. donis gratiae primum collatis diligenter usos homines ad majorem pertigisse perfectionem, Matth. 25, 14. sqq. I/uc. 19, 12. sqq. § 8. Causa efficiens principalis renovationis Deus* trinunusb est. Aeque* ut regenerationis. Quemadmodum enim primae vires gratiae per virtutem supernaturalem et infinitam Dei conferuntur, ita et augmentum et confirmatio earum Deo debetur. Unde Paulus Phil. 1, 6. scribit: Persuasum habeo, quod is, qui coepit in vobis opus bonum, perficiet usque ad diem Jesu Christi. Confer. 1 Thess. 5, 28. et h. 1. § 2. Est enim opus ad extra. Quod tamen per appropriationem tribuitur Spiritui Sancto Tit. 3, 5., qui etiam ideo spiritus sanctificationis appellatur Rom. 1, 4·, qui iu renatis tanquam in templo habitat, 1 Cor. 3, 16., agit eos, Rom. 3, 14., auxiliatur infirmitatibus eorum, ibid. v. 26. § 9. Causa ins frumen talis ex parte Dei sunt verbum legis a et evangelii,b et sacramenta baptismi c et eucharistiae. d Lex sane per omnem vitam dictat, quae sint facienda, etiam renatis. Vid. Psal. 1, 2. Psal. 119. integer. Eadem concupiscentias carnis in renatis reliquas supprimit, vid. Gal. 5, 15. 16. Intelligimus autem legem Mosis et Christi, quae revera una est et renatis ad renovationem sui observanda. Conf. b. Mus. de poenit. contra Steng. P. II. cap. I. p. 160. cap. II. p. 199. P. III. cap. VI. p. 561. sqq. Nempe evangelium non solum excitat fidem in actu con versionis, sed etiam excitatam conservat, confirmat atque auget. Unde 1 Pet. 1, 22. dicuntur renati animas suas purificare obediendo veritati. Conf. b. Mus. Disp, de Renov. § 38. 39. Carpzovius: ״De verbo Dei, qui istud instrumentum renovationis nostrae sit, neminem ambigere sinunt clarissimi Scripturae textus, qui verbo illuminationem, mutationem cordis etc. asscribunt, Ps. 19, 9.12. 119, 105. Act. 26, 18. Jer. 20, 9. 23, 29. 1 Cor. 1, 6. 2, 4. 5. 3, 8. 2 Cor. 4, 4. 1 Thess. 1, 5. etc. In omnibus autem hisce textibus de solo evangelio agitur. ,Per evangelium‘, inquit Form. Cone. art. 2. p. 605., ,Sp. S. conversionem vel renovationem in nobis operari et perfleere vult.‘ Lex quidem in renovatione dicitur,inscribi in corda‘. Jer. 31, 33. Ebr. 8, 10., sed non inscribere. Inscriptio fit per evangeliurri solum. Ex quo solo renascimur, ex eo solo etiam renovamur. Jam ex solo evangelio renascimur. Ergo ex solo evangelio etiam

renovamur. Neque obest, quod lex aliquem usum in renovatione praestet et sit norma, ad et secundum quam nova obedientia institui debet. Hic enim usus saltem normalis est in obedientia seu viribus et potentia obediendi jam jam effectis per evangelium, et ad tertium illum legis usum pertinet, quem in renatis et justificatis lex habet, prout in 6. art. Form. Cone. p. 642. hoc declaratur.

Lex inculcat quidem, esse voluntatem et mandatum Dei, ut in nova vita ambulemus, at vires et facultatem non donat, quibus novam obedientiam inchoare et praestare possimus. Sp. S. autem, qui non per legis, sed per evangelii praedicationem datur et accipitur, cor hominis renovat. Deinde idem Spiritus S. ministerio legis utitur, ut per eam renatos doceat. . . Aliud est, esse organum renovationis, et aliud est, ad aliquem saltem usum ab organo renovationis assumi.“ (Disputatt. isagog. p. 1146. sq.)


### On Renewal and Good Works: See on Titus 3:5, where baptism is expressly called the washing of renewal,…

See on Titus 3:5, where baptism is expressly called the washing of renewal, namely because this depends upon it as if from a cause. For not only does the Holy Spirit, when baptism is actually received, work the benefit of regeneration and renewal in the heart of a man who does not place an obstacle—which baptism (as that for the sake of which it was instituted) signifies outwardly, and thus the powers of grace are efficiently conferred upon the man who is baptized by the Holy Spirit through baptism as an effective organ, and these powers certainly provide or contribute something to the subsequent spiritual acts—but also through baptism received long ago, yet recalled to memory, the Holy Spirit similarly works and confers further spiritual powers, or increases those already conferred. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Disput. de Renov. § 42.

For in it we receive the body of Christ, which is the bread of life or life-giving, John 6:54, 55. And we are more closely united to Christ, as to the vine, so that in Him, as branches, we may bear fruit, John 15:1, 5. Thus it is also said that many have drunk of one Spirit, as it were, 1 Cor. 12:13. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 43. §

10. On the part of man, the powers of grace received in conversion efficiently concur toward renewal. For thus men are commanded to purify their own hearts, 1 Pet. 1:22; to put off the old man and put on the new, Eph. 4:22 sqq., Col. 3:10; to cleanse themselves, 2 Tim. 2:21; to sanctify themselves, 1 John 3:3; to perfect holiness, 2 Cor. 7: 1.

This, however, happens dependently upon God or the grace of God, as is evident from what has been said. Cf. Ausführl. Erklärung L. XV. Q. 79. p. 693 sqq. and here § 2, note c. And this is what the blessed Scherzer teaches in System. Theol. L. XVII. § 4. p. 458: that the justified man is a cause of renewal; for he is said to renew himself, 1 Pet. 1:22. He is, however, a secondary cause, because he is subordinated to God, and the grace of God by nature moves the man before he, moved by grace, acts. Cf. the same, Brev. Hülsemann. auct. cap. XII. Thes. III. and V. p. 684, 688 sqq. Formula of Concord: “From this then it follows: as soon as the Holy Spirit, as has been said, has begun this His work of regeneration and renewal in us through the Word and holy Sacraments, it is certain, PART III. CHAP. VI.

that we can and should cooperate through the power of the Holy Spirit, albeit still in great weakness, yet this not out of our own fleshly natural powers, but out of the new powers and gifts which the Holy Spirit has begun in us at conversion; as St. Paul expressly and earnestly admonishes that we, as fellow workers, do not receive the grace of God in vain, which indeed can be understood in no other way than that the converted man does good for as much and as long as God governs, leads, and guides him with His Holy Spirit; and as soon as God were to withdraw His gracious hand from him, he could not stand for a moment in obedience to God.

But if it were to be understood that the converted man cooperated alongside the Holy Spirit in such a way as two horses pulling a wagon together, such could by no means be admitted without prejudice to divine truth.” (Declar. art. 2. p. 604.)

Quenstedtius: “The instrumental cause on the part of God are the Word and the Sacraments. . . The mediate and subordinate cause on the part of man is justifying faith, through which God purifies the hearts of men not only from error of mind, but also from the vices of the affections and the will, Acts 15:9. The subaltern, assisting cause is the will of man, sanctified through faith in Christ. Thus the Epitome of the Formula of Concord, art. 2, p. 526: ‘The new will of man is an instrument and organ of God the Holy Spirit, so that it not only apprehends grace, but also cooperates with the Holy Spirit in the works that follow.’ And concerning the influence of faith upon renewal, the Declaration of the Formula of Concord, p. 626, says: ‘That faith is something living, efficacious, powerful; so that it cannot be otherwise than that it always works good.’ Gal. 5:6; 2 Pet. 1:5.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 5. 6. f. 915. sq.)

By no means, however, are these natural powers, which always are and remain inept for spiritual things. 1 Pet. 1:28. For this reason, faith is said to be ἐνεργουμένη, working effectively (according to the analogy of the passages Eph. 3:20; Col. 1:29; Jas. 5:16) through love, Gal. 5:6.

Whence it is especially to be noted that faith performs a twofold duty in relation to renewal. First, it determines the intellect to assent, both in general to all things that are revealed in the Holy Scriptures, and in particular to the promises concerning the gratuitous remission of sins for Christ’s sake. For thus, having deduced practical conclusions, it prescribes what is to be done and what is to be avoided, with the addition of reasons and motives by which the will is impelled to pursue the study of piety.

In the second way, faith inclines the will itself (in which it likewise subjectively resides) to resist the depraved concupiscence of the flesh and to do that which the intellect, concerning any spiritual object now believed, prescribes by way of practical judgment; from which repeated acts the will is rendered daily more prompt to act, and various Christian virtues are acquired, the principle and root of which is faith itself. Cf. blessed Musaeus, Disp. de Renov. § 21. sq.

Huelsemannus: “From the saying of the apostle in Phil. 2:13, it is solidly concluded that divine grace obtained through Christ (not that creative grace, as Pelagius equivocated against Eph. 1:3) is the …origin, the efficient and perfecting cause of every good ordered and fitted for attaining eternal salvation, with the concurrence of man excluded not only from the origin of the first motion, which is fitted for attaining supreme blessedness, but also excluded from the communion of that causality by which God perfects the good that has been begun, or by which He concurs toward the renewal of man. The first reason is because the apostle brings forward this statement before those who are reborn and and already established in the state of regeneration and renewal. . . Even in the reborn, for daily

renewal, although it is denied that their own renovation concurs with God, the same species of causality in the concurrence toward their own renovation is evident from the opposition of God and man, not only in the willing (ἐν τῷ θέλειν), but also in the working (ἐν τῷ ἐνεργεῖν). For if God and man had the same mode of concurring toward the renovation of man, the mere good pleasure (εὐδοκία) of God cannot be alleged as the reason why it is right for m an to tremble and fear in the way of his salvation, or in that very act when he seeks or works out (κατεργάζεται) his own salvation. (Vindiciae Scr. S. per loca class. p. 32. sq.) §

11. The subject which (subjectum quod) of renovation is the converted and justified man. Or the whole suppositum, which is said to be renewed. For we are dealing with renovation strictly so called. Otherwise, the subject of renovation more broadly defined coincides with the subject of regeneration, insofar as the same man who is reborn is also said to be renewed. However, the passages of Scripture cited above, especially Eph. 4:22 sqq. and Col. 3:10, speak manifestly of the reborn. §

12. The subject by which (subjectum quo) is the soul with respect to its faculties, the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite; secondarily also the members of the body. According to those things which we said concerning the terms from which and to which in § 3, 4 sqq. For from this the subject of any change is to be estimated. Cf. the blessed Scherzer, Brev. Hülsemann. auct. cap. XII. Thes. VI. p. 692, where he writes: The proximate subject and the adequate matter in which renovation takes place are the faculties of man corrupted by sin, as much of the intellect as of the will and the sensitive appetite. Insofar as the members of the renewed or sanctified soul are instruments necessary for performing holy actions. To this may be referred that passage in 1 Thess. 5:23, where Paul prays for his own that the God of peace may sanctify them wholly, so that their whole spirit, and soul, and body may be preserved blameless. Cf. Rom. 6:12 sqq. and 19, where Paul demands that the reborn present their members as instruments of righteousness unto holiness. Confer the blessed Musaeus, Disp. de Renov. § 14. and Ausführl. Erklärung LXV. Q. 80. p. 665. §

13. The form, therefore, or the formal reason of renovation consists in a complex of several spiritual acts, through which man tends more and more toward subduing depraved concupiscence and acquiring an increase of the habitual gift, by which he is rendered more apt for performing those things which are conformable to the divine will. PART III. CHAPTER VI.

According to those things which we stated in § 5 and following. This is what Paul teaches in 2 Cor. 6:16, that renewal must take place ημέρα και ημέρα, day by day. Cf. Eph. 4:22, 25 ff.; 2 Pet. 1:5, 8. For the things commanded there do not require the effort of a single hour or day, but a prolonged and continuous study, so that we must be occupied daily in putting off the old man and daily in putting on the new man, and in the exercises of many virtues. Thus also the blessed Olearius, in his Index to Balduin’s *General Theology*, Art. XCVII, § 5, teaches that renewal is the successive suffocation of the old Adam and the restoration of the powers of the intellect, will, and appetite, so that the inherent righteousness, which arises from sanctification, may follow day by day the imputative righteousness that arose from justification, along with its increases and fruits.

For sin is not entirely abolished in man in this life, nor is fully perfect holiness acquired; see Rom. 7:14 ff. to the end; Gal. 5:17. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Treatise on Repentance against Stenger*, Part III, chap. VII, p. 634. And this is why our theologians say that our holiness, which belongs to this life and inheres in us (distinct from the imputed righteousness which is derived to us from Christ), is begun, and they maintain that its consummation is deferred to the state of glorification in eternal life. Carpzovius: "If God had wished to act absolutely here and demonstrate His power, He would have extinguished in a moment the corruption brought on by the Fall and restored the divine image, just as He had concreated it in Adam in a moment. But it pleased Him to act here by degrees and, by grace, to restore in man through succession and increments the divine image that had been withdrawn by His just judgment." (*Disputatt. isagog.*, p. 1161.) § 14.

### On Renewal and Good Works: The proximate end of renewal coincides with its term to which

The proximate end of renewal coincides with its term to which. The ultimate end on the part of men is eternal life, on the part of God, His own glory. For it is for the sake of acquiring this that renewal takes place.

As we read in Rom. 2:7, that men who persevere in well-doing seek glory, honor, and immortality, and thus strive toward the proposed goal of eternal life, as the blessed Gerhard explains in his *Annotations*, p. 68. Beware, however, of inferring from this that renewal is the efficient or meritorious cause of eternal life. For it is expressly said that this is the χάρισμα του Θεοΰ, Rom. 6:23. Carpzovius: "Although the Apostle in Rom. 6:22 calls eternal life the end of sanctification, he does not understand by 'end' the final cause, but merely the terminus." (*L. c.*, p. 1169.)

Quenstedtius: "The ends on our part are good works, viewed both by reason of their purpose and by reason of their extrinsic exercise, Rom. 6:2, 4, 6 ff.; Eph. 2:10, 4:22 f., 5:8; Gal. 5:22; Col. 3:9 ff." (*L. c. s. 1. th. 11. f. 918.*) A. Osiander: "The end of renewal is not eternal salvation, to which renewal relates either by way of means or merit... Paul in Eph. 2:8, 9 does not say: 'by grace you have been converted or justified,' but 'by grace you have been saved,' to indicate that final salvation also does not depend on renewal as if it were a merit or a means, but depends entirely upon it [grace] itself."

grace. The subordinate end of renewal is: α. our daily progress in the pursuit of piety, 2 Cor. 4:16...; β. the confirmation of our justification *a posteriore* (from what follows), 2 Pet. 1:4 ff...; γ. manifestation with respect to others, Jas. 2:21... The end of renewal is also to invite and improve others by our example, 1 Pet. 2:12. (Colleg. th. P. V, 221 ff.) See Phil. 1:10, 11, where Paul prays that they may be renewed and sanctified in mind and morals to the glory and praise of God. Cf. Eph. 1:13, 14; Col. 1:9–12. §

15. The adjuncts of renewal are: I. Necessity.a II. Difficulty.b III. Imperfection.c IV. Utility.d By divine precept in the cited passages, Ezek. 18; Eph. 4; Col. 3, and by our own need, for we fail unless we progress, and we easily lose faith itself. Indeed, just as without sanctification, so also without renewal, which is the same thing, no one shall see God, Heb. 12:14.

Luther: "My Antinomians preach very finely and (as I cannot think otherwise) with true earnestness about the grace of Christ, about the forgiveness of sins, and whatever else is to be said concerning the article of redemption. But this *consequens* they flee like the devil, that they should tell the people about the third article, sanctification, i.e., about the new life in Christ. For they think one should not frighten or trouble the people, but always preach comfortingly about grace and the forgiveness of sins in Christ, and by all means avoid these or similar words: 'Do you hear? You want to be a Christian, and yet remain an adulterer, a whoremonger, a drunken sow, proud, greedy, a usurer, envious, vengeful, malicious, etc.' Instead, they say: 'Do you hear? Are you an adulterer, a whoremonger, a miser, or some other kind of sinner—if you only believe, you are saved; you need not fear the Law, Christ has fulfilled everything.' Dear friend, tell me, does that not mean the *antecedens* is conceded and the *consequens* denied? Yes, it means to take away and annihilate Christ in the very same act, even when He is being preached most highly. And it is all vain 'yes' and 'no' in the same matter. For such a Christ is nothing and nowhere, who would have died for such sinners who do not, after the forgiveness of sins, cease from sins and lead a new life. Thus they preach Christ finely according to Nestorian and Eutychian dialectics, so that Christ is, and yet is not; and they are indeed fine Easter preachers, but shameful Pentecost preachers. For they preach nothing *de sanctificatione et vivificatione Spiritus Sancti*, about the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, but only about the redemption of Christ—yet Christ (whom they preach highly, as is right) is Christ or has acquired redemption from sin and death for this reason: that the Holy Spirit should make us into new men out of the old Adam, that we should be dead to sin and live to righteousness, as St. Paul teaches in Rom. 6:2 ff., beginning and increasing here on earth and completing it there.

For Christ has merited for us not only *gratiam*, grace, but also *donum*, the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that we might have not only the forgiveness of sins, but also a ceasing from sins, John 1:16, 17. Whoever, then, does not cease from sins, but remains in his former evil nature, must have a different Christ from the Antinomians. The true Christ is not there, even if all the angels cry out in vain, 'Christ! Christ!'—and he must be damned with his new Christ." (On the Councils and the Church. A. 1539. Tom. Hal. XVI, 2741 ff.) PART III. CHAP. VI.

Huelsemannus: "From the negative (Heb. 12:14), that without holiness God will not be seen, it follows at least that holiness is necessary so as not to fall away, or so as not to be deprived of the beatific vision, or, which is the same thing, so as not to lose that benefit; but by no means is it necessary for obtaining that benefit. For not every opposite of a destructive cause is a constitutive of that which the opposite privation destroys or corrupts. Now, that God is not seen without holiness states the destructive cause of that vision, not, however, its positive contrary; thus it is rightly said: Respiration, food, clothing, etc., are necessary to man, lest he lose natural life; but it is wrongly said: Respiration, food, clothing are necessary to man for obtaining natural life." (Praelect. F. C. art. 12. s. 5. p. 614. sq.)

Ad. (Colleg. th. V, 35.) On account of that sharp reluctance of the flesh; whence come such grievous complaints of the saints. Ps. 13:1, 42:16, Rom. 7:24.

According to those things which we have said at § 4. note a., § 5. note b., and at § 13. note b. For the perfection or imperfection of an action is estimated from the nature of the end toward which it is directed. Notwithstanding the imperfection. Indeed, piety, not only if any perfect piety is given, but that which is actually found in faithful men, is profitable for all things, 1 Tim. 4:8; concerning which Balduinus notes: To worship and fear God, to walk in His commandments, and to serve one's neighbor for His sake, this has use at all times and in all things. To this pursuit of piety is joined the most ample promise of present and future benefits in this life and the next, p. m. 1310. b.; cf. Aphor. pract. XV. and XVI. p. 1331.
