Renewal can be defined as the complex of spiritual acts which a reborn man, with God graciously concurring through the Word and Sacraments by the spiritual powers bestowed upon him, exercises regarding the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite, for the sake of abolishing the remnants of sin and acquiring greater holiness on the way of salvation, to the glory of God. See § 13.

Which is the subject of renewal, according to § 11, yet in such a way that he also conducts himself actively or efficiently, according to § 10. Who is the principal and primary cause; see § 8.

What the organic or instrumental causes are; see § 9. What is the principle by which, on the part of man; see § 10. The subject by which is signified, according to § 12. The term from which is denoted, according to § 4. What is the term to which; see § 5. The ultimate end on the part of man is indicated; see § 14. k) The absolutely ultimate end, also on the part of God, l. c. § 17.

The doctrine of good works pertains to the doctrine of renovation, which in part stand in relation to renovation as an end and effect, and in part pertain to its formal nature. The nature of which will be explained shortly.

If works are considered, they are to be performed by powers acquired and more perfect through renovation, and in this manner intended and performed. For renovation formally consists in good and holy acts or works, which are performed by the powers of grace and through which one tends toward the increase of spiritual powers; whence they also have the nature of a principle or cause in relation to the term to which of renovation. See B. Mus. de Renov. § 51. sqq. § 18.

In this place, however, by good works are understood the free actions of a regenerate man, which he himself exercises by the powers of grace received and increased in conversion, according to the norm of the divine word, to the glory of God.

Yet not only positive works, which are done according to the prescription of affirmative precepts, but also the omissions of acts prohibited by negative precepts; which, however, themselves also involve or presuppose internal acts of the mind and a certain purpose to omit those acts.

Quenstedtius: "Some are internal, others external; internal are the interior thoughts of the mind, motions of the will, and good affections of the heart. . . . For it is a good work when that is done which is commanded by God, and with that affection, manner, and end with which it is commanded." (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 9. s. 1. th. 4. f. 1371.)

For otherwise there are many holy motions which are performed by the Holy Spirit in the very business of conversion in man, yet they are not, according to the usage of speech in the schools of theologians, called good works absolutely.

Luther: "Therefore these two sayings are true: Good, pious works never make a good, pious man; but a good, pious man makes good, pious works. Evil works never make an evil man, but an evil man makes evil works. Thus, the person must always be good and pious before all good works, and good works follow and proceed from the pious, good person. Just as Christ says, Matthew 7:18: 'A bad tree does not bear good fruit. A good tree does not bear bad fruit.' Now it is evident that the fruits do not bear the tree; nor do the trees grow upon the fruits: but conversely, the trees bear the fruit and the fruits grow upon the trees. Just as the trees must be before the fruits; and the fruits do not make the trees either good or bad, but the trees make the fruits: so the man must be pious or evil in his person before he does good or evil works; and his works do not make him good or evil, but he makes good or evil works. We see the same in all crafts. A good or bad house does not make a good or bad carpenter; but a good or bad carpenter makes a bad or good house. No work makes a master according to the work; but as the master is, so is his work. Thus it is also with the works of man; as it stands with him in faith or unbelief, so are his works good or evil. And not conversely, that as his works stand, so is he pious or believing. Works, just as they do not make one believing, so they do not make one pious. But faith, just as it makes one pious, so it also makes good works." (Sermon on the Freedom of a Christian. A. 1520. Tom. Hal. XIX, 1225. sq.)

Latin:

Finis renovationis proximus coincidit cum termino ejus ad quem. a Finis ultimus ex parte hominum est vita aeterna,b ex parte Dei gloria ipsius.c Hujus enim acquirendi gratia fit renovatio. Prout Rom. 2, 7. legimus, homines perseverantes in bene agendo quaerere gloriam, et honorem, et immortalitatem, atque ita contendere ad propositum vitae aeternae scopum, uti b. Gerhardus exponit in Annotat, p. 68. Cave autem, ne hinc inferas, renovationem esse causam efficientem aut promerentem vitae aeternae. Expresse enim dicitur, hanc esse χάρισμα του Θεοΰ Rom. 6, 23.

Carpzovius: ,,Quamvis apostolus Rom. 6, 22. finem sanctificationis vitam aeternam appellet, tamen per finem non intelligit causam finalem, sed terminum saltem.“ (L. c. p. 1169.) Quenstedtius: ״Finis exparte nostri bona opera sunt, tum ratione propositi sui, tum ratione exercitii extrinseci spectata, Rom. 6, 2. 4. 6. sqq. Eph. 2, 10. 4, 22. sq. 5, 8. Gal. 5, 22. Coi. 3, 9. sqq.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 11. f. 918.)

A. Osiander: ״Renovationis finis non est salus aeterna, ad quam se habeat renovatio vel per modum medii vel meriti. . . Paulus Eph. 2, 8. 9. non dicit: gratia conversi aut justificati estis, sed gratia salvi facti estis, ut indicet, ultimam quoque salutem non dependere a renovatione, tanquam merito aut medio, sed in solidum pendere ab ipsa

gratia. Finis renovationis subordinatus est a. quotidianus noster pro־ gressus in studio pietatis, 2 Cor. 4, 16. . .; ß. confirmatio justificationis nostrae a posteriore, 2 Pet. 1, 4. sq. . y. manifestatio respectu aliorum, Jac. 2, 21. . . Renovationis etiam finis est, alios exemplo nostro invitandi et emendandi, 1 Pet. 2, 12.“ (Colleg. th. P. V, 221. sqq.) Vid. Phil. 1, 10. 11., ubi Paulus optat, ut illi renoventur et quoad mentem ac mores sanctificentur ad gloriam et laudem I)ei. Conf. Eph. 1, 13. 14· Col. 1, ,9. ad 12. §

15. Adjuncta renovationis sunt I. Necessitas.a II. Difficultas.b III. Imperfectio. c IV. Utilitas.d Ex praecepto divino 11. cc. Ezech. 18. Eph. 4· Coi. 3., nostraque indigentia, qui deficimus, nisi proficiamus, fidemque ipsam facile am itiimus. Imo quemadmodum sine sanctificatione, ita et sine renovatione, quae idem est, nemo videbit Deum, Ebr. 12, 14·

Lutherus: ,,Meine Antinomer predigen sehr fein und (wie ich nicht anders denken kann) mit rechtem Ernst von der Gnade Christi, von Vergebung der Sünden und was mehr vom Artikel der Erlösung zu reden ist. Aber dies Consequens fliehen sie wie der Teufel, dass sie den Leuten sagen sollten vom dritten Artikel, der Heiligung, d. i. vom neuen Leben in Christo. Denn sie meinen, man solle die Leute nicht erschrecken noch betrüben; sondern immer tröstlich predigen von der Gnade und Vergebung der Sünden in Christo, und beileibe ja meiden diese oder dergleichen Worte: Hörest du es, du willst ein Christ sein, und gleichwohl ein Ehebrecher, Hurenjäger, volle Sau, hoffärtig, geizig, Wucherer, neidisch, rachgierig, boshaftig bleiben u. s. w.; sondern so sagen sie: Hörst du es, bist du ein Ehebrecher, ein Hurer, ein Geizhals, oder sonst ein Sünder — gläubest du nur, so bist du selig, darfst dich vor dem Gesetz nicht fürchten, Christus hats alles erfüllt. Lieber, Sage mir, heisst das nicht Antecedens concedirt, und Consequens negirt? Ja, es heisst, eben in demselben Christum wegnehmen und zu nichte machen, wenn er am höchsten gepredigt wird. Und ist alles eitel Ja und Nein in einerlei Sachen. Denn solcher Christus ist nichts und nirgend, der für solche Sünder gestorben sei, die nicht nach Vergebung der Sünden von den Sünden lassen und ein neues Leben führen. Also predigen sie fein auf Nestorianische und Eutychische Dialectica Christum also, dass Christus sei, und sei es doch nicht, und sind wohl feine Osterprediger, aber schändliche Pfingatprediger. Denn sie predigen nichts de sanctificatione et vivificatione Spiritus Sancti, von der Heiligung des Heiligen Geistes, sondern allein von der Erlösung Christi, so doch Christus (den sie hoch predigen, wie billig) darum Christus ist oder Erlösung von Sünden und Tod erworben hat, dass uns der Heilige Geist soll zu neuen Menschen machen aus dem alten Adam, dass wir der Sünden todt und der Gerechtigkeit leben, wie St. Paulus lehret Röm. 6, 2. ff., hie auf Erden anfahen und zunehmen und dort vollbringen.

Denn Christus hat uns nicht allein Gratiam, die Gnade, sondern auch Donum, die Gabe des Heiligen Geistes, verdienet, dass wir nicht allein Vergebung der Sünden, sondern auch Aufhören von den Sünden hätten, Joh. 1, 16. 17. Wer nun nicht auf höret von Sünden, sondern bleibt im vorigen bösen Wesen, der muss einen andern Christum von den Antinomern haben. Der rechte Christus ist nicht da, und wenn alle Engel schreien eitel Christus! Christus! — und muss mit seinem neuen Christo verdammt werden.“ (Von den Conciliis und Kirchen. A. 1539. Tom. Hai. XVI, 2741. sq.) PART. III. CAP. VI.

Huelsemannus: ,,Ex negativa (Ebr. 12, 14.), sine sanctimonia non visum iri Deum, hoc saltem sequitur, sanctimoniam esse necessariam aci non excidendum sive ad non privandum beatifica visione seu, quod perinde est, ad beneficium illud non amittendum, nequaquam vero ad beneficium illud consequendum. Non enim omne oppositum causae destructivae est constitutivum ejus, quod opposita privatio destruit seu corrumpit. Sine sanctimonia autem non videri Deum, dicit causam destructivam ejus visionis, non vero contrariam positivam; sic recte dicitur: Respiratio, victus, amictus etc. necessaria sunt homini, ne perdat vitam naturalem; sed perperam dicitur: Respiratio, victus, amictus necessaria sunt homini ad consequendam vitam naturalem.“ (Praelect. F. C. art. 12. s. 5. p. 614. sq.)

Ad. Osiander: ,,Uti non nisi verbum et sacramenta generant salvificam fidem, ita quoque conservant, Luc. 8, 15. Rom. 10, 17.; quam licet excutiant regnantia peccata, sine tamen ullo nexu dicetur, vitae novitatem seu renovationem esse causam fidei vel procreatricem, vel conservatricem; cum causa destruens unius rei, e. g. sanitatis, possit esse multiplex; proin ab uno negato ad affirmationem causae procreantis vel conservantis minus firmiter concluditur; e. g. homicida non haereditabit regnum Dei, nec tamen omnes, qui homicidae non sunt, regnum Dei et Christi haereditabunt.“ (Colleg. th. V, 35.) Ob acrem illam carnis reluctantiam; unde tam graves querelas sanctorum. Psal. 13, 1. 42, 16. Rom. 7, 24.

Juxta ea, quae diximus ad § 4. not. a. § 5. not. b. et ad § 13. not. b. Aestimatur enim perfectio aut imperfectio actionis ex ratione termini ad quem. Non obstante imperfectione. Nimirum pietas, non solum, si quae perfecta detur, sed quae actu in hominibus fidelibus invenitur, ad omnia utilis est, 1 Tim. 4, 8.; ad quae Balduinus notat: Deum colere ac timere, in mandatis ejus ambulare, et propter ipsum proximo inservire, hoc omni tempore et in omnibus usum habet. Huic studio pietatis adjuncta est promissio amplissima praesentium et futurorum beneficiorum in hac et altera vita, p. m. 1310. b.; conf. Aphor. pract. XV. et XVI. p. 1331.

b., ubi etiam citantur dicta 1 Tim. 6, 6. Prov. 3, 4. 16. 14, 32. Deut. 28. § 16. Definiri potest renovatio, quod sit complexus a actuum spiritualium, quos homo renatus,b Deo c per verbum et sacramenta d gratiose cöncurrente viribus spiritualibus e sibi collatis, quoad f intellectum, voluntatem et appetitum sensitivum, ad abolendas reliquias peccati g et majorem sanctitatem h acquirendam in via salutis i exercet ad Dei gloriam.k Vid. § 13.

Qui subjectum quod renovationis est, juxta § 11., ita tamen, ut etiam active seu efficienter se habeat, juxta § 10. Qui causa principalis et prima est; vid. § 8.

Quae causae organicae aut instrujnentales sunt; vid. § 9. Quae sunt principium quo, ex parte hominis; vid. § 10. Significatur subjectum quo, juxta § 12. Terminus a quo denotatur, juxta § 4. Quae est terminus ad quem; vid. § 5. Indicatur finis ultimus ex parte hominis; vid. § 14. k) Finis absolute ultimus et ex parte Dei, 1. c. § 17.

Ad doctrinam de renovatione pertinet doctrina de bonis operibus,a quae partim ut finis et effectus b ad renovationem sese habent, partim ad rationem formalem c ejus spectant. Quorum natura mox explicabitur.

Si spectentur opera, viribus perfectioribus per renovationem acquisitis perficienda, atque hac ratione intenta ac praestita. Renovatio enirn formaliter consistit in actibus aut operibus bonis et sanctis, quae viribus gratiae perficiuntur et per quae ad incrementum virium spiritualium tenditur; unde etiam rationem principii vel causae habent in ordine ad terminum ad quem renovationis. Vid. b. Mus. de Renov. § 51. sqq. § 18.

Intelliguntur autem hoc loco per bona opera actiones a hominis renati b liberae,c quas ipse viribus gratiae d in conversione acceptis atque auctis juxta normam verbi divini e exercet ad gloriam Dei.f

Non tamen solum opera positiva, quae ad praescriptum praeceptorum affirmativorum fiunt, verum etiam omissiones actuum, praeceptis negativis prohibitorum; quae tamen et ipsae involvunt aut supponunt internos actus mentis et propositum quoddam de omittendis istis actibus.

Quenstedtius: ,,Alia sunt interna, alia externa; interna sunt interiores mentis cogitationes, voluntatis motus, cordisque affectus boni. . . . Est enim bonum opus, cum id fit, qifod a Deo jubetur et eo affectu et modo ac fine, quo jubetur.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 9. s. 1. th. 4. f. 1371.)

Nam alias dantur plures motus sancti, qui a Spiritu Sancto in ipso negotio conversionis in homine perficiuntur, neque tamen ex usu loquendi in scholis theologorum bona opera absolute dicuntur.

Lutherus: ,,Darum sind die zwei Sprüche wahr: Gute, fromme Werke machen nimmermehr einen guten, frommen Mann; sondern ein PART. III. CAP. VI. guter, frommer Mann machet gute, fromme Werke. Böse Werke machen nimmermehr einen bösen Mann, sondern ein böser Mann machet böse Werke. Also dass allewege die Person zuvor muss gut und fromm sein vor allen guten Werken und gute Werke folgen und ausgehen von der frommen, guten Person. Gleichwie Christus sagt, Matthäus 7, 18.: ,Ein böser Baum trägt keine gute Früchte. Ein guter Baum trägt keine böse Früchte.‘ Nun ist’s offenbar, dass die Früchte tragen nicht den Baum; so wachsen auch die Bäume nicht auf den Früchten: sondern wiederum, die Bäume tragen die Frucht und die Früchte wachsen auf den Bäumen. Wie nun die Bäume müssen eher sein, denn die Früchte; und die Früchte machen nicht die Bäume weder gut noch böse, sondern die Bäume machen die Früchte: also muss der Mensch in der Person znvor fromm oder böse sein, ehe er gute oder böse Werke thut; und seine Werke machen ihn nicht gut oder böse, sondern er machet gute oder böse Werke. Desgleichen sehen wir in allen Handwerken. Ein gutes oder böses Haus macht keinen guten oder bösen Zimmermann; sondern ein guter oder böser Zimmermann macht ein böses oder gutes Haus. Kein Werk macht einen Meister, darnach das Werk ist; sondern wie der Meister ist, darnach ist auch sein Werk. Also sind die Werke des Menschen auch; wie es mit ihm stehet im Glauben oder Unglauben, darnach sind seine Werke gut oder böse. Und nicht wiederum, wie seine Werke stehen, darnach sei er fromm oder gläubig. Die Werke, gleichwie sie nicht gläubig machen, so machen sie auch nicht fromm. Aber der Glaube, gleichwie er fromm macht, so macht er auch gute Werke.“ (Sermon von der Freiheit eines Christenmenschen. A. 1520. Tom. Hai. XIX, 1225. sq.)


### On Renewal and Good Works: The same: "Christian doctrine therefore instructs us that we must first become…

The same: "Christian doctrine therefore instructs us that we must first become other people, that is, be born anew. But how does that happen? Through the Holy Spirit and through water. When I am then born anew, having become pious and God-fearing, then I go forth, and what I do in the new birth, that is good. Just as Adam, if he had remained in innocence and in the state in which he was created, would have gone forth and done whatever he had wanted, such as fishing for minnows, catching robins, or planting trees: these would have been purely good, holy works and no sin; and Eve would have suckled the children, washed them: these would have been purely precious, good works. For the person was created good, upright, pure, and holy: therefore all his works were also good; whether he ate or drank, it was all right. But after man has fallen into sin, he does nothing good after the Fall, but sins in all his works, even when he prays. For he does it as a sinner; everything he does is not right, even if he fasts, prays, leads a strict life like a Carthusian, wears a monk’s habit, or goes barefoot. For such things are all sinful because the person is evil and not yet born anew, and everything he does helps him nothing at all. Therefore Christ says to Nicodemus: I have come to preach another doctrine, namely, how you must be born anew, so that you may become good. Such preaching is also contained and described beforehand in the Holy Scripture, but you do not read it, and even if you do read it, you do not understand it, namely, that before one does good works, one must be born anew, for from sinners only other sinners are begotten; the person is corrupted there. The Lord Christ says in the 7th chapter of Matthew: Where the tree is evil, it bears no good fruit; thistles do not bear figs, nor thorns grapes. . . . Thus the Holy Spirit’s preaching stands in the Word: new birth, which He teaches and writes. Whoever believes in Christ, that He was born, died, and was buried for us, and also rose again from the dead, that same person is reborn or born anew."

There a person is a new man, for you have such thoughts that no Papist or Turk otherwise has, namely, that Christ died for you and rose from the dead, and now sits at the right hand of God. If you now remain in this faith, then the Holy Spirit is there and baptizes you, strengthens and increases your faith, and gives you a new understanding in your heart; He also awakens in you holy and new thoughts and affections, so that you begin to love God and desist from all godless dealings, and do from the heart what God wants, love your neighbor, and avoid wrath, hatred, and envy. Such works are done by those who are previously born anew, namely through Baptism, in which the Holy Spirit then is and makes the person new.

When the person is then born anew, the new man begins to use all kinds of clothing, food, and drink, and a Christian says: If you do not want to wear a cowl, then put on a coat; if you do not have a gray coat, then take a red one. It does not matter how you dress, just as it does not matter whether you are a woman or a man. For that does not make you born anew, but rather that I believe in Christ, who died for me. This I know from the divine Word through the Holy Spirit, and also from Baptism.

What need have I of cowls for this? A Christian has no need of these ceremonies for anything, but only that he let himself be baptized by the Holy Spirit and through Him obtain faith; that is what makes one born anew; and thereafter I serve God in the three commandments of the first table of the Law of Moses; thereafter, in the other tables, I attend to my office and calling according to my ability, love my neighbor, and have a fine, quiet life with my wife. If the cross then comes, I suffer it also with joy, go then to the sermon and hear Christ, my Bishop, and do not need to run to Rome or to St. James.

That will be the new preaching, how we become new men, and thereafter as the newborn also do good works; and that is the chief part of our Christian doctrine, that men should be instructed how one must be born anew through water and the Holy Spirit, not that they should put on a cowl and wear a tonsure. For the cowl only covers the old rogues and does not make new men. (Sermon on the 3rd and 4th chapters of John, A.D. 1537–1540. Luther’s Complete Works. Erlangen, 1851. Vol. XLVI, p. 261 sq., 270 sq.) Cf. supra P. III, c. 3, § 9, note c, p. 151 sq.; c. 4, § 14, note a, p. 189.

For the will after conversion, in relation to spiritual acts and the external works corresponding to them, is not only active, but also indifferent, so that it can act and not act, act in this way and in another.

Quenstedtius: "Good works must be spontaneous and voluntary, not coerced, insofar as, you know, something of an external work is extorted from the unwilling against the sentiment of their mind, see 2 Cor. 9: 7. All coercion must be absent from a good work; for he is not only unworthy of praise, but not even worthy of pardon, who does his duty unwillingly. For he himself condemns his own action, intending to do otherwise if the option were given." (L. c. s. 1, th. 10, f. 1374.)

The same: "Huelsemann says well: 'Such indifference,' he says, 'is found in no man; not in the unregenerate, because he is in no way free from an inclination toward the extreme worse; not in the regenerate and sanctified, who is not as free here to choose the good as he is free and ready to pursue evil. Rom. 7.' Indifference signifies an equal breadth of freedom of power; such as exists neither in the one being converted, nor in the one who is converted." (L. c. P. III, c. 7, s. 2, q. 1, f. 726.) Cf. supra P. III, c. 4, § 27 and 38, p. 202, 223 sq.

Namely, with the Spirit leading or acting, Rom. 8: 14. Whence also they are called the fruits of the Spirit, Gal. 5: 22. PART III. CHAPTER VI.

Or according to divine laws, whether moral or natural, common to all men, or positive, enacted for certain men and for a certain time. Although works also pertain to this which are done according to the prescription of human, ecclesiastical, or civil law, which does not conflict with divine laws and rather tends toward edification and public utility. For those things are also said to be commanded by God not only which are commanded formally and immediately, but also those which are commanded mediately and by consequence. Otherwise, however, if neither has a place, elective works are not good, according to that of Matt. 15:9.

Quenstedtius: "The directing norm, according to which good works are to be performed and judged, is not the dictate of right reason or the law of nature, but solely the Word of God; yet not the Word of the Gospel properly so called, for this is not a doctrine of works, but the Word of the divine law, which contains the most perfect rule of divine justice and holiness and prescribes both what is to be done and what is to be omitted. —

Because the law of nature shows both vices and virtues only confusedly and obscurely, and indeed does not show or even extenuates certain enormous vices, while it is ignorant of or sells as virtues and plainly opposes certain virtues, hence the law promulgated peculiarly by God is the genuine norm of moral works. —

Distinguish between the Gospel taken γενικώς [generally] or in a general sense and improperly for the entire doctrine handed down by Christ and the apostles and comprised in the writings of the prophets and apostles, in which sense we concede that there is contained in it not only the doctrine concerning faith and the gratuitous remission of sins, but also the precepts of morals; and the Gospel taken εΐόικώς [specifically] or specially and in its most proper signification, insofar as it is opposed to the law of God, and in this way it does not prescribe works or precepts of morals, but solely faith. —

The norm of good works is not, as the Papists feign, 'evangelical counsels,' from which works of supererogation and greater perfection than we are bound to might be performed, since there is no one who perfectly performs even that to which we are bound, and no one can truly say that he has no sin, 1 John 1:8. They foolishly burden themselves with additions and offer to God what is not owed, who fail in what is owed.

Nor are they the traditions of the church and the commandments of men, concerning which there is the constant rule: 'In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' Isa. 29:13; Matt. 15:9.

But the law of God, since that alone is, on the contrary, sin by itself, directly and by the nature of the thing, which is committed against it, 1 John 3:4. —

Distinguish between voluntary and elective acts of worship. We teach that voluntary acts of worship performed according to the prescription of divine law are pleasing to God, as the Scriptures say in Ps. 54:8, Ps. 110:3, 2 Cor. 9:7, but God by no means approves of ἐθελοθρησκείας [will-worship] or elective acts of worship, devised by one's own judgment.

We do not require that works of love be shown in the law as specifically prescribed, but we say it is sufficient if they are contained in the divine law by reason of their genus. —

Distinguish between the ordinary rule and extraordinary or singular examples of the saints, who did this or that by a peculiar instinct of the Holy Spirit and His otherwise familiar guidance; the question here is not about these, but about the former. —

The question between us and the Papists is not absolutely this, whether any work is good unless its species is defined in detail by God, but whether any work of worship or merit, as the Papists call it, can be justly offered by us to God which has not been specifically commanded by God. —

Distinguish between the species of the good and divinely commanded work itself and its various circumstances regarding time, place, manner, order, and other things that do not change the species itself. The former is prescribed in the Word of God, but the latter are not, but are left to the judgment of the church or even of any regenerate man." (L. c. c. 9. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1387. sq.)

The same: "Those works are truly good, not which anyone devises himself with a good intention, or which are done according to human traditions, but which God Himself has prescribed and commanded in His Word, for

Latin:

Idem: ,,Die christliche Lehre unterrichtet uns also, dass wir erstlieh müssen andere Leute werden, das ist, neu geboren werden. Wie geschieht aber das? Durch den Heiligen Geist und durchs Wasser. Wenn ich denn neu geboren bin, fromm und gottesfürchtig worden, so gehe ich hin, und was ich in der neuen Geburt thye, das ist gut. Als, Adam, wenn er in der Unschuld und in dem Stande, darinnen er geschaffen war, geblieben wäre, so wäre er hingangen und hätte gethan, was er nur gewollt hätte, als irgends Schmirlen gefischt, Rothkehlchen gefangen oder Bäume gepflanzet: das wären eitel gute, heilige Werke gewesen und keine Sünde; und Eva hätte die Kinder gesäuget, sie gewaschen: das wären eitel köstliche, gute Werke gewesen. Denn die Person war gut, rechtschaffen, rein und heilig geschaffen: drum waren auch alle ihre Werke gut, sie esse oder trinke, so wars alles recht. Aber nachdem nun der Mensch in die Sünde gerathen, thut er nach dem Fall nichts Gutes, sondern sündiget in allen seinen Werken, auch wenn er betet. Denn er thuts wie ein Sünder, alles, was er thut, ist nicht recht, auch wenn er fastet, betet, ein gestrenges Leben führet als ein Karthäuser, ein Mönchskleid an trägt, gehet barfuss. Denn Solches ist alles sündlich darum, dass die Person böse ist und nicht wieder neu geboren, und hilft sie alles nichts, was sie nur thut. Derhalben spricht Christus zu Nicodemo: Ich bin kommen, dass ich eine andere Lehre predige, nämlich, wie ihr neu geboren werden müsset, dass ihr gut werdet. Solche predigt ist zuvor in der heiligen Schrift auch begriffen und beschrieben, aber ihr lesets nicht, und ob ihrs schon leset, so verstehet ihrs doch nicht, nämlich, dass eher man gute Werke thue, so müsse man neu geboren sein, denn aus Sündern werden eitel andere Sünder gezeuget, die Person ist da verderbt. Der Herr Christus saget Matthäi am 7. Capitel: Wo der Baum böse ist, da trägt er keine gute Früchte, Disteln tragen nicht Feigen, noch Dornen Trauben. . . . So stehet nun des Heiligen Geistes Predigt in dem Wort: neue Geburt, das er lehret und schreibet. Wer da gläubet an Christum, dass er für uns geboren, gestorben und begraben, auch von den Todten wieder auferstanden sei, derselbige ist wiedergeboren oder neu geboren.

Da ist einer ein neuer Mensch, denn du hast solche Gedanken, die sonst kein Papist oder Türke hat, nämlich, dass Christus für dich gestorben und von den Todten auf erstanden sei, und jetzt zur rechten Hand Gottes sitze. Bleibest du nun in diesem Glauben, so ist der Heilige Geist da und taufet dich, stärkt und mehret dir den Glauben und gibt dir neuen Verstand ins Herz, er erweckt auch in dir heilige und neue Gedanken und Affekt, auf dass du anfähest, Gott zu lieben und ablässt von allen gottlosen Händeln, und thust von Herzen, was Gott.haben will, liebest den Nächsten, meidest den Zorn, Hass und Neid. Solche Werke thun diejenigen, so zuvor neu geboren sind, nämlich durch die Taufe, darinnen dann der Heilige Geist ist und machet die Person neu.

Wenn denn die Person neu geboren ist,^so fähet der neue Mensch an zu gebrauchen allerlei Kleider, Speise und Trank, und ein Christ saget: Willst du nicht eine Kappe tragen, so ziehe einen Rock an; hast du nicht einen grauen Rock, so nimm einen rothen. Es liegt nichts dran, wie du dich kleidest, wie denn auch nichts dran liegt, ob du ein Weib oder ein Mann seiest. Denn das macht dich nicht neu geboren, sondern dass ich gläube an Christum, der für‘mich gestorben ist. Solches weiss ich aus dem göttlichen Wort durch den Heiligen Geist, auch aus der Taufe.

Was bedarf ich hierzu der Kappen? Ein Christ bedarf dieser Ceremonien nirgends zu, sondern dass er sich nur taufen lasse durch den Heiligen Geist und durch ihn den Glauben erlange, das macht neu geboren werden; und darnach diene ich Gott in den dreien Geboten der ersten Tafel des Gesetzes Mosi; darnach in den andern Tafeln warte ich meines Amts und Berufs nach meinem Vermögen, liebe den Nächsten, und habe ein fein still Leben mit meinem Weibe. Kommt dann das Kreuz, so leide ichs auch mit Freuden, gehe dann zur Predigt und höre Christum, meinen Bischof, darf dann nicht gen Rom oder zu St. Jakob laufen.

Das wird die neue Predigt sein, wie wir neue Menschen werden, und darnach als die Neugebornen auch gute Werke thun; und das ist das Hauptstück unsrer christlichen Lehre, dass die Menschen unterrichtet würden, wie man müsse durch das Wässer und den Heiligen Geist neu geboren werden, nicht dass sie eine Kappen anziehen und Platten tragen. Denn die Kappe decket nur die alten Schälke, und machet nicht neue Menschen.“ (Pred. über das 3. u. 4. Cap. Joh. A. 1537—1540. Luthers sämmtliche Werke. Erlangen, 1851. .P. XLVI. p. 261. sq. 270. sq.) Cf. supra P. III. c. 3. § 9. not. c. p. 151. sq. c. 4. § 14. not. a. p. 189.

Voluntas enim post conversionem, in ordine ad actus spirituales et his respondentia opera externa, non solum active, verum etiam indifferenter se habet, ut possit agere et non agere, agere sic et aliter.

Quenstedtius: ,,Debent bona opera esse spontanea et voluntaria, non coacta, quatenus scii, vel ab invitis praeter animi sententiam aliquid externi operis extorquetur, vid. 2 Cor. 9, 7. A bono opere abesse debet omnis coactio; non modo enim indignus est laude, sed ne quidem dignus est venia, qui invitus officium facit. Damnat enim ipse actionem suam, aliter facturus, si daretur optio.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 10. f. 1374.)

Idem: ,,Bene Huelsemannus: ,Talis‘, inquit,,indifferentia in nullo homine reperitur; non irregenito, quia ille nulla ratione liber est ab inclinatione in extremum deterius; non in regenito sanctificato, qui hic tam liber non est ad eligendum bonum, quam liber est et expeditus ad sectandum malum. Rom. 7.‘ Indifferentia significat aequalem latitudinem ad libertatem potestatis; qualis neque in convertendo, neque in converso existit.“ (L. c. P. III. c. 7. s. 2. q. 1. f. 726.) Cf. supra P. III. c. 4. § 27. et 38. p. 202. 223. sq.

Ducente videlicet aut agente Spiritu, Rom. 8, 14. Unde etiam fructus Spiritus dicuntur Gal. 5, 22. PART. III. CAP. VI.

Seu juxta leges divinas, cum moralem seu naturalem, omnibus bominibus communem, tum positivas, certis hominibus atque ad certum tempus latas. Quanquam huc etiam spectent opera, quae ad praescriptum legis humanae, ecclesiasticae aut civilis, divinis legibus non repugnantis ac potius ad aedificationem et utilitatem publicam tendentis, fiunt. Nam et mandata a Deo dicuntur non solum, qua e formaliter et immediate!, verum etiam quae mediate et per consequentiam fieri jubentur. Alias autem, si neutrum habeat locum, opera electilia non sunt bona, juxta illud Matth. 15, 9.

Quenstedtius: ״Norma directrix, secundum quam opera bona praestanda et dijudicanda sunt, non est dictamen rectae rationis aut lex naturae, sed unice verbum Dei; non autem verbum evangelii proprie sic dicti, hoc enim non est doctrina operum, sed verbum legis divinae, quod perfectissimam regulam justitiae et sanctitatis divinae continet et tum facienda tum omittenda praescribit. —

Quia lex naturae confuse tantum et obscure ostendit tum vitia tura virtutes, quaedam vero vitia enormia vel non ostendit aut extenuat, contra quasdam virtutes ignorat aut pro vitiis venditat planeque aversatur, hinc lex peculiariter a Deo promulgata genuina est operum moralium norma. —

Dist. inter evangelium acceptum γενικώς seu generaliter et improprie pro universa doctrina a Christo et apostolis tradita et scriptis prophetarum et apostolorum comprehensa, quo sensu concedimus, contineri in eo non tantum doctrinam de fide et gratuita peccatorum remissione, sed et praecepta morum; et evangelium sumptum εΐόικώς seu specialiter et in propriissima sua significatione, quatenus legi Dei opponitur, et hoc modo non praescribit opera aut praecepta morum, sed unice fidem. —

Norma bonorum operum non sunt, ut fingunt pontificii, vel,consilia evangelica‘, ex quibus praestentur opera supererogationis et majoris perfectionis, quam teneamur, cum id ipsum, ad quod tenemur, nemo sit, qui perfecte praestet, et nemo vere possit dicere, se peccatum non habere, 1 Joh. 1,8. Inepte se onerant auctariis et Deo offerunt non debita, qui in debitis deficiunt.

Vel ecclesiae traditiones et hominum mandata, de quibus est constans regula: ,Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas, quae sunt mandata hominum.‘ Esa. 29, 13. Matth. 15, 9.

Sed Dei lexf quandoquidem id demum e contrario per se, directe et ex natura rei peccatum est, quod in illam committitur, 1 Joh. 3, 4. —

Dist. inter cultus voluntarios et electitios. Cultus voluntarios juxta praescriptum legis divinae factos Deo gratos esse, docent Scripturae dicta Ps. 54, 8. Ps. 110, 3. 2 Cor. 9, 7., sed έ&εΤϋο&ρησκείας sive cultus electitios, proprio arbitrio excogitatos, Deus minime probat.

Non requirimus, ut opera dilectionis in specie praescripta in lege monstrentur, sed sufficere dicimus, si ratione generis in lege divina contineantur. —

Dist. inter regulam ordinariam et extraordinaria sive singularia exempla sanctorum, qui ex peculiari Spiritus S. instinctu et familiari ejusdem alioquio hoc vel illud fecerunt; non de his, sed de illa hic est quaestio. —

Quaestio inter nos et pontificios non est absolute haec, an nullum opus sit bonum, nisi cujus species a Deo sigillatim definita sit, sed an opus aliquod cultus seu meritif ut pontificii vocant, a nobis juste Deo exhiberi possit, quod speciatim a Deo praeceptum non sit. —

Dist. inter ipsam operis boni et divinitus praecepti speciem et inter varias ejus circumstantias quoad tempus, locum, modum, ordinem, aliaque speciem ipsam non mutantia. Illa in verbo Dei praescripta est, hae vero non, sed arbitrio ecclesiae seu etiam cujusvis hominis regeniti relictae.“ (L. c. c. 9. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1387. sq.)

Idem: ,,Ea demum opera vere bona esse, non quae quisque bona intentione ipsemet excogitat, aut quae secundum humanas traditiones fiunt, sed quae Deus ipse in verbo suo praescripsit atque praecepit,


### On Renewal and Good Works: was argued: α. From those sayings of Scripture in which human reason and…

was argued: α. From those sayings of Scripture in which human reason and commandments are rejected, such as Deut. 12:8: "You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes." Ezek. 20:18: "Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers." Isa. 1:12: "Who has required this from your hand?" In these sayings it is to be observed that there is rejected 1) the judgment of the senses and the eyes, 2) the example of the fathers, by which no one ought to be led astray, 3) everything that is affixed and stitched onto the commandments of God, 4) that concerning all these things it is said that they are vain and do not please God. β.

From the sayings by which it is evidently taught that the one and only norm of truly good works that please God is the Word of God or the Law. ... The Jesuits do not escape by limiting these sayings to that addition which is directly contrary to the Word of God. For to oppose is not to add. In divine worship, also, that which is disparate is contradictory. The phrase "neither to the right hand nor to the left" stops the mouth of every exception; just as the strange fire in Lev. 10:1, cf. Num. 3:4, Jer. 19:4, which God did not command, is strange, so worship not commanded by God is strange. γ.

From reasons taken 1) from the perfection of the divine law...; 2) from the clarity of the prohibition opposed to elective worship...; 3) from the gravity of the sin committed through elective worship...; 4) from the blindness of human reason, which knows nothing of worship that pleases God, 1 Cor. 2:14, 2 Cor. 3:5.

The Papists paint this fictitious worship with the diluted color of "good intention"; for if anything is done by them against or beyond the commandment of God, they judge it to be a good work because it is done from a good intention. But an intention is wrongly called good which is opposed to the intention of God. Certainly, that "good intention," such as it was, destroyed Uzzah when he put forth his hand to steady the ark as it was shaking on the cart. Saul pleaded a good intention when, having been commanded to destroy the Amalekites utterly and to destroy their flocks, he spared the king and reserved the choice animals for sacrifices, which good intention, however, turned out very badly for him." (L. c. P. IV. c. 9. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1389. sq.)

Luther: "Before the Gospel came, people preached thus: Good works are those which we ourselves devise and choose out of our own devotion; as, for instance, that one should go to St. James, another on a different pilgrimage; this one gave to the monks in the monastery and had many masses said; that one lit little wax candles, fasted on bread and water, and prayed so many rosaries, etc. But now that the Gospel has come, we preach thus: Good works are not those which we ourselves choose out of our own intention, but those which God has commanded; as, when everyone does what God has commanded and laid upon him in his station here on earth. A servant does good works when he fears God, believes in Christ, and walks in the obedience of his master. First, he is righteous before God through faith in Christ; thereafter, he walks in faith, leads a godly life, keeps himself temperate and chaste, serves his neighbor, cleans out the stable, gives fodder to the horses, etc. When he walks in such works, he does better works than any Carthusian. For because he is baptized, believes in Christ, and waits in certain hope for eternal life, he goes about his business, is obedient to his master, and knows that what he does in his calling is well-pleasing to God. Therefore, they are all good, precious works, whatever he does in his station. It may not appear that they are great, excellent works when he rides to the field, drives to the mill, etc.; but because God’s commandment and order are there, such works, however lowly they may seem, cannot be anything other than entirely good works and services to God. Likewise, a maidservant does good works when she carries out her calling in faith and does what her mistress bids her, when she sweeps the house, washes and cooks in the kitchen, etc. Although such works do not appear like the works of a Carthusian, which have a mask about them and make people gape; yet they are much better and more precious works before God than those of a Carthusian, who wears a hair shirt, his early..." PART III. CHAP. VI. keeps hours, rises at night and sings for five hours, eats no meat, etc. For although these are glittering and shining works before the world, they nevertheless have no commandment or order from God; how then can they be good works that please God? Likewise, when a citizen or a farmer is helpful to his neighbor, serves him with what he can, warns him when he sees that he might suffer harm to his body, wife, children, servants, cattle, and goods, helps him where he needs his help, etc.: such works also do not shine; but nonetheless, they are vainly good, precious works. When worldly authority punishes the wicked and protects the pious, when subjects are submissive and obedient to their authority, and do such things in faith in Christ and in hope of eternal life, then they are good works, even if they do not glitter or shine before reason. For what God does on earth through His Christians and saints, that shall not glitter or shine before the world; but be black, despised, and condemned by the devil and the world. Conversely, what the devil does through his hypocrites and false saints, that shall glitter and shine, so that the whole world opens its mouth and nose in wonder, as if it were an excellent, precious thing, when it is yet vain devilish deception and lies. If one takes reason into counsel, then the works of a manservant, a maid, a master, a wife, a mayor, and a judge are common, lowly works compared to a Carthusian who keeps vigil, fasts, prays, and eats no meat: but if one takes God’s Word into counsel, then the works of all Carthusians and monks, even if one were to melt them all together into one heap, are not as good as the work of one single poor servant girl who has been placed into God’s kingdom through Baptism, believes in Christ, and in faith waits for the blessed hope. St. Paul wanted to preserve these two pieces in Christendom: the knowledge of our Savior Jesus Christ, and the knowledge of our commanded office; so that we might learn to rightly recognize our Christian station; namely, first, that we are called through Baptism and the Gospel to be heirs of eternal life, for which reason we should also wait for the blessed hope and appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. Secondly, because we have now become Christians and heirs of the kingdom of heaven, that everything we do out of faith in our calling and station are vainly good, precious works; for which reason we should also be diligent in good works. And we should learn these two pieces well. The first piece, concerning the blessed hope, we must have for that life, so that we know where we shall remain when this life comes to an end. The other piece, concerning good works, we must have for this life, so that we know how we should conduct ourselves in our station and office. Therefore, because we have heard what our blessed hope is, for which we should wait, we should now also learn what good works are, namely, those that happen out of faith, in our commanded office, according to God’s commandment and Word. Although such works do not glitter before reason, they are nevertheless precious before God, and no Carthusian or monk is worthy to see and recognize them. Thus, I am a preacher, that is my office; if I now believe in Christ, and wait for the blessed hope, and go forth thereafter, attend to my preaching, and do my office, even though my work has a lowly appearance; yet I would not trade it for all monks and nuns, and all their works that they do in the monastery. And thus, through Baptism and through faith in Christ, I have my assurance for that life, and through God’s Word a report for this present life, as to how I should conduct myself therein. Likewise also, a wife is a living saint if she believes in Christ, waits for the blessed hope and appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, and thereafter

goes forth, and does from that same [state of life] what is incumbent upon a wife. For our works, which we do in our commanded office, even if they are regarded by the world as common and lowly works, become precious before God when they are done out of faith in Christ and in the hope of eternal life. But, as has been said, the world is not worthy that it should see and recognize a single good work. For just as reason knows nothing of the blessed hope of eternal life, so it also does not understand what good works are. It thinks, therefore: This maid milks the cows, this farmer plows the field: these are all common, lowly works, which even the heathen do; how then can they be good works? But this one becomes a monk, that one becomes a nun, looks sour, puts on a cowl, wears a hair shirt: these are special works, which other people do not do; therefore they must be good works. Thus thinks reason. Thereby one comes away from the knowledge of both the blessed hope and the good works." (Sermon on our blessed hope. A.D. 1531. Tom. Wal. IX, 615—619.)]

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who 1.) hold this hypothesis, that true moral good can be known by the powers of nature alone. Hence they afterwards infer that nature is so constituted that the appetite is carried toward the good that is known or shown by the intellect. See Bellarmine in his books on grace and free choice. 2.) They teach that the proper doctrine of the Gospel is: 'If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.' ...

3.) In ἐθελοθρησκείαις, or self-chosen and humanly devised forms of worship, they spend almost more time and effort than on those which have been divinely prescribed. Hence the Council of Trent, when it decrees concerning the good works to be performed by the justified, declares that 'we are bound to the observance of the commandments of God and the Church,' but also asserts that the justified, through the observance of the commandments—as of God, so also of the Church—grow in justice itself and are more justified. ... Indeed, the entire religion of the Pope, as such, is an ἐθελοθρησκεία, confirmed neither by the word of the promise nor by divine command, which is the very essence of superstition. ...

Latin:

probatur: a. ex illis Scripturae dictis, in quibus ratio et mandata hominum rejiciuntur, ut Deut. 12, 8.: ,Non faciat quisque, quod in oculis ipsius rectum videtur.‘ Ezech. 20, 18.: ,In praeceptis patrum vestrorum nolite incedere.‘ Esa. 1,12.: ,Quis quaesivit haec de manibus vestris?‘ In quibus dictis observandum est rejici 1.) judicium sensuum et oculorum, 2.) exemplum patrum, quibus nemo seduci debeat, 3.) omne illud, quicquid mandatis Dei affingitur et assuitur, 4.) de his omnibus dici, quod frustanea sint nec Deo placeant. . .

ß. E dictis, quibus evidenter docetur, vere bonorum et Deo placentium operum norm,am unicam et solam esse verbum Dei seu legem. . . Non effugiunt Jesuitae limitatione dictorum ad eam additionem, quae verbo Dei directe contraria. Nam oppo· nere non est apponere. In cultu divino etiam, qui disparatus est, est contradictorius. Phrasis neque dextrorsum neque sinistrorsum omni exceptioni os obstruit; ut ignis peregrinus Lev. 10,1. conf. Num. 3, 4. Jer. 19, 4., quem Deus non mandavit, ita cultus non mandatus a Deo peregrinus est.

y. Ex rationibus, desumtis 1.) a legis divinae perfectione. . .; 2.) a prohibitionis electitiis cultibus oppositae perspicuitate. . .; 3.) a peccati per cultus electitios commissi gravitate. . .; 4.) a rationis humanae coecitate, quae de cultu Deo placente nihil novit, 1 Cor. 2, 14. 2 Cor. 3, 5.

Commentitio isti cultui pontificii dilutum bonae intentionis colorem allinunt; nam si qui ab eis fit contra aut praeter Dei mandatum, censent esse bonum opus, quia fit ex bona intentione. Ast perperam intentio bona appellatur, quod Dei intentioni adversatur. Sane ista qualiscunque bona intentio Uzam perdidit, quando nutantem in plaustro arcam injecta manu sustentavit. Bonam intentionem obtendebat Saul, quando jussus internecione delere Amalecitas et greges perdere, regi pepercit et opimas pecudes reservavit ad sacrificia, quae tamen bona intentio pessime ei cessit.“ (L. c. P. IV. c. 9. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1389. sq.)

Lutherus: ,,Ehe das Evangelium kam, predigte man also: Gute Werke wären, die wir selber aus eigner Andacht erdichteten und erwähleten; als, dass einer ginge nach St. Jacob, der andere zu einer andern Wallfahrt; dieser gab den Mönchen ins Kloster, und liess viel Messen halten; jener steckete Wachslichtlein auf, fastete zu Wasser und Brod, und betete so viel Rosenkränze u. s. w. Aber nun das Evangelium kommen, predigen wir also: Gute Werke sind nicht, die wir seiber erwählen aus eignem Vornehmen, sondern die Gott geboten hat; als, wenn ein jeder thut, was ihm Gott befohlen und aufgelegt ist in seinem Stande hier auf Erden. Ein Knecht thut gute Werke, wenn er Gott fürchtet, an Christum gläubet, und in dem Gehorsam seines Herrn herein gehet. Zuerst ist er gerecht vor Gott durch den Glauben an Christum; darnach gehet er im Glauben dahin, führet ein gottselig Leben, hält sich mässig und züchtig, dienet seinem Nächsten, mistet den Stall aus, gibt den Pferden Futter u. s. w. Wenn er in solchen Werken herein gehet, so thut er bessere Werke, denn kein Carthäuser. Denn weil er getauft ist, an Christum gläubet und in gewisser Hoffnung auf das ewige Leben wartet, so gehet er unterdess hin, ist seinem Herrn gehorsam, und weiss, was er in seinem Beruf thut, dass es Gott wohlgefalle. Darum sind es eitel gute köstliche Werke, was er in seinem Stande thut. Es scheinet wohl nicht, dass es grosse, treffliche Werke sind, wenn er auf den Acker reitet, in die Mühle fähret u. s. w.; aber weil Gottes Gebot und Befehl da ist, so können solche Werke, wie geringe sie auch scheinen, anders nicht, denn eitel gute Werke und Gottesdienste sein und heissen. Also auch, eine Magd thut gute Werke, wenn sie im Glauben ihren Beruf ausrichtet, und thut, was sie die Frau heisset, wenn sie das Haus kehret, in der Küchen spület und kochet u. s. w. Obschon solche Werke nicht scheinen, wie eines Carthäusers Werke, welche eine Larve um sich haben, und den Leuten das Maul aufsperren; so sind es doch viel bessere und köstlichere Werke vor Gott, denn eines Carthäusers, der ein hären Hemde an hat, seine Früh PART. III. CAP. VI. stunden hält, des Nachts aufstehet und fünf Stunden singet, kein Fleisch isset u. s. w. Denn obschon das gleissende und scheinende Werke sind vor der Welt, so haben sie doch kein Gebot und Befehl Gottes; wie können es denn gute Werke sein, die Gott gefallen? Des־ gleichen, wenn ein Bürger, Bauer seinem Nächsten behülflich ist, ihm dienet, womit er kann, ihn warnet, wenn er siehet, dass er Schaden leiden möchte an seinem Leibe, an Weib, Kind, Gesinde, Viehe und Gütern, ihm hilfet, wo er seiner Hülfe bedarf u. s. w.: solche Werke scheinen auch nicht; aber nichts desto weniger sind es eitel gute, köstliche Werke. Wenn weltliche Obrigkeit die Bösen strafet und die Frommen schützet, wenn die Unterthanen ihrer Obrigkeit unterthan und gehorsam sind, und thun solches im Glauben an Christum, und in Hoffnung des ewigen Lebens, so sind es gute Werke, ob sie schon nicht gleissen, noch scheinen vor der Vernunft. Denn was Gott auf Erden thut durch seine Christen und Heiligen, das soll nicht gleissen noch scheinen vor der Welt; sondern schwarz sein, verachtet und verdammet werden vom Teufel und der Welt. Wiederum, was der Teufel durch seine Heuchler und falsche Heiligen thut, das soll gleissen und scheinen, also, dass alle Welt Maul und Nasen aufsperret, und sich darüber verwundert, als wäre es trefflich, köstlich Ding, so es doch eitel Teufelstrug und Lügen ist. Wenn man die Vernunft zu Rathe nimmet, so sind eines Knechtes, einer Mdgd, Oines Herrn, einer Frauen, eines Bürgermeisters und Richters Werke gemeine, geringe Werke gegen dem, dass ein Carthäuser wachet, fastet, betet, nicht Fleisch isset: wenn man aber Gottes Wort zu Rathe nimmet, so sind aller Carthäuser und Mönche Werke, wenn man sie gleich allesammt auf einen Haufen schmelzet, nicht so gut, als einer einigen armen Dienstmagd Werk, die durch die Taufe in Gottes Reich gesetzt ist, an Christum gläubet, und im Glauben auf die selige Hoffnung wartet. Diese zwei Stücke wollte St. Paulus in der Christenheit gerne erhalten: das Erkenntniss unsers Heilandes Jesu Christi, und das Erkenntniss unsers befohlenen Amts; auf dass wir unsern christlichen Stand recht erkennen lerneten; nämlieh, zum ersten, dass wir durch die Taufe und durchs Evangelium berufen sind zu Erben des ewigen Lebens, darum wir auch auf die selige Hoffhung und Erscheinung unsers Herrn Jesu Christi warten sollen. Zum andern, weil wir nun Christen und Erben des Himmelreichs worden sind, dass alles, was wir aus dem Glauben thun in unserm Beruf und Stande, eitel gute köstliche Werke sind; darum wir auch fleissig sein sollen zu guten Werken. Und solche zwei Stücke sollen wir wohl lernen. Das erste Stück, von der seligen Hoffnung, müssen wir haben zu jenem Leben, auf dass wir wissen, wo wir bleiben sollen, wenn dies Leben ein Ende nimmt. Das andere Stück, von guten Werken, müssen wir haben zu diesem Leben, auf dass wir wissen, wie wir uns in unserm Stande und Amte halten sollen. Darum weil wir gehöret haben, was unsere selige Hoffnung sei, darauf wir warten sollen, sollen wir nun auch lernen, was gute Werke sind, nämlich, die aus dem Glauben geschehen, in unserm befohlenen Amte, nach Gottes Gebot und Wort. Obschon solche Werke nicht gleissen vor der Vernunft, so sind sie doch köstlich vor Gott, und ist kein Carthäuser, noch Mönch werth, dass er die sehen und erkennen soll. Als, ich bin ein Prediger, das ist mein Amt; wenn ich nun an Christum gläube, und auf die selige Hoffnung warte, und darnach hingehe, meines Predigens warte, und mein Amt thue, obschon meine Arbeit ein geringes Ansehen hat; so wollte ich doch nicht mit allen Mönchen und Nonnen, und mit allen ihren Werken, die sie im Kloster thun, beuten. Und habe also durch die Taufe und durch den Glauben an Christum meinen Bescheid in jenes Leben, und durch Gottes Wort einen Bericht für dies gegenwärtige Leben, wie ich mich darinnen halten solle. Also auch, eine Ehefrau ist eine lebendige Heilige, wenn sie an Christum glaubet, auf die selige Hoffnung und Erscheinung unsers Herrn Jesu Christi wartet, und darnach

hingehet, und aus demselbigen thut, was einer Ehefrau zuständig ist. Denn unsere Werke, die wir in unserm befohlenen Amte thun, ob sie schon für gemeine und geringe Werke angesehen werden von der Welt, werden köstlich vor Gott, wenn sie geschehen aus dem Glauben an Christum und in der Hoffnung des ewigen Lebens. Aber, wie gesagt, die Welt ist es nicht werth, dass sie ein einiges gutes Werk sehen und erkennen soll. Denn gleichwie die Vernunft nichts weiss von der seligen Hoffnung des ewigen Lebens: also verstehet sie auch nicht, was gute Werke sind. Sie denkt also: Diese Magd milket die Kühe, dieser Bauer pflüget den Acker: solches sind alles gemeine, geringe Werke, welche auch die Heiden thun; wie können es denn gute Werke sein? Aber dieser wird ein Mönch, jene wird eine Nonne, siehet sauer, zeucht eine Kappe an, trägt ein hären Hemde: solches sind sonderlich Werke, die andere Leute nicht thun; darum müssen es gute Werke sein. So denkt die Vernunft. Damit kommet man denn von dem Erkenntniss, beide, der seligen Hoffnung und der guten Werke.“ (Predigt von unserer seligen Hoffnung. A. 1531. Tom. Hai. IX, 615—619.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, qui 1.) hanc tenent hypothesin, posse verum bonum morale cognosci solis naturae viribus. Hinc postea inferunt, natura ita comparatum esse, ut appetitus feratur in bonum cognitum vel ab intellectu ostensum. V. Bellarminum in libris de grat. et lib. arb. 2.) Docent, evangelii propriam doctrinam esse". ,Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata‘. . .

3.) In έΰt?ιο&ρησκείαις sive cultibus electitiis et humanitus excogitatis plus fere temporis atque operae ponunt, quam in illis, quae divinitus praescripta sunt.
