### On Renewal and Good Works: Of the Antinomians, such as John Agricola, who taught that repentance is to be…

2. Of the Antinomians, such as John Agricola, who taught that repentance is to be taught not from the Law or the Decalogue, but from the Gospel. Likewise, that the Gospel immediately shows the magnitude of the offense and the deformity of sin; that the Law is not only not the norm of things to be done, but is not even to be taught or tolerated among Christians, as the blessed Luther reports, T. 1. Jen. p. 533.

3. Of the Socinians and Arminians, who assert that Christ promulgated three singular precepts not contained in the Law, but pertaining to the Gospel, such as: to deny oneself, to take up one's cross daily, to follow Christ, Matt. 16: 24. See Smalcius, book on the divinity of Christ, c. 6, p. 22; the Arminians, Apol. c. 12 and 13.

4. Of the Canonists and Scholastics (as can be seen from Thomas and his commentators and D. Georg Calixtus in his *Epitome Theol. Moral.*, published at Helmstadt in 1634, p. 40 sq.), who place the goodness of human actions in the natural agreement of the mode of acting regarding this or that object with the instinct of an intelligent and free nature. And it is to be noted that when D. Calixtus, l.c., the Scholastics, and likewise the moralists dispute here as to what constitutes the formal [nature] of a good or evil action, they are disputing not only about civil or ethical moral good, but also about the formal nature of supernatural goodness or supernatural actions, the rule of which is conformity or difformity with the judgment of natural reason—which is clearly false, as D. Huelsemann teaches in *Prae. F. C.* to a. 12, sect. 3, § 5." (L.c. c. 9, s. 2, q. 2, f. 1388.)

f) See 1 Cor. 10:31. Col. 3:17. ad 28. Brochmandus: "There are those who attribute too much, and there are also those who attribute less than is right, to intention in constituting an action as good or evil."

They follow the royal and straight path who are undoubtedly persuaded that a good intention does not suffice for a good work. For, first, it is the will of God that we should not constitute our own will, but the will of God, as the rule of good works, Deut. 12:8; Num. 15:39; Matt. 15:9; Mark 7:7. Next, nothing is more certain than that a work, even the most wicked, can be performed with a good intention or with a view to an optimal end; cf. Gen. 19:31-32. Christ also testifies that the most cruel persecutors of Christians intend the glory of God by the slaughter of Christians, John 16:2; the Jews also conspire for the death of Paul with zeal, but a misguided one; they are driven by the glory of God, Acts 26:9. Shall we pronounce these works good because of a good intention? Third, since for a truly good work there is required both the command of God and the efficacy of the operating Holy Spirit and a living faith and the glory of God as the ultimate end of the work: everyone easily understands that a good intention alone does not suffice for any work to be good. But the matter stands differently regarding an evil intention. For there is no work, however excellent in terms of its act and substance, that an evil intention does not infect and turn from the best into the worst. On this opinion, read the Savior Christ discoursing at length and professedly in Matt. 6:1 sqq. (System. univers. th. Artic. 25. c. 3. cas. 9. f. 258.)

ANTITHESIS. Busenbaum (theologian of the Society of Jesus, d. 1668): "A criminal, even if he is truly guilty, is permitted to flee before and after sentencing (regarding death, or a punishment equivalent to death, e.g., perpetual imprisonment)... Regularly, a criminal is permitted to flee, even if the prison guard is to suffer grave harm from it... It is also permitted, at least in the forum of conscience, to deceive the guards (excluding force and injury) by handing over, for example, food and drink so that they may be lulled to sleep, or by arranging for them to be absent; likewise, to break chains and prisons: because, when the end is licit, the means are also licit. And if other captives escape at the same time through the broken wall, he will not be held responsible for the damage, because he is only the cause of it by accident, since he is using his own right... Those who are not ministers of justice are permitted not only to help the criminal with advice to flee, but also by supplying instruments, e.g., ropes, a file, etc., because it is permitted to persuade another of a licit end and to propose the means to the same." (Medulla th. moral. Antwerp, 1723. p. 447 sq.)

Institute of the Society of Jesus: "It has seemed good to us in the Lord that no constitutions, declarations, or any order of living can induce an obligation to mortal or venial sin, unless the superior should command it in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ or in virtue of obedience; which, in those matters or persons in which it shall be judged that it will be very conducive to the particular good of each or to the universal good, it may come to pass that in place of the fear of offense, love and the desire for all perfection may succeed, and that greater glory and praise of Christ, our Creator and Lord, may follow." (Institut. soc. Jesu, augmented and reprinted by the authority of the 18th general congregation. Prague, 1757. Vol. I. f. 414 sq.)

Cf. Index: "Superiors can obligate to sin in virtue of obedience, when it is very conducive to it, part 6. c. 5. p. 414." (Vol. II. Index under the title: Obedience.) §

19. The works of the unregenerate, which are done in a certain way according to the prescription of the moral law, cannot be called good in the same way as the works of the regenerate; and although not in themselves and simply, yet insofar as they are destitute of the requirements of good works, they are rightly called sins.

For this is known even to the light of nature. Thus the Gentiles are said to do τά τού νόμου, those things which are of the law, Rom. 2:15. And the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, Art. XVIII, p. 218 (in the edition of the time), teaches that the human will can in some way effect civil righteousness or that of works, can speak about God, exhibit to God a certain worship by an external work, obey magistrates and parents in choosing an external work, and can restrain the hands from murder, from adultery, from theft. However, the unregenerate cannot perform moral works that are exactly conformable to the law, without any defect.

Whence some have said that those works of the unregenerate, even if as to the substance of the act they imply conformity with the law and right reason, nevertheless fail in many ways in their circumstances from the rule of rectitude. See *Ausführl. Erklärung* [Detailed Explanation], Book VIII, Q. 62, p. 333.

Kromayer: "Good works do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the one who has been justified." (*Th. posit. pol.* II, 390.)

Not only because they are not simply and in all ways conformable to the law without any defect (which does not fall even to regenerate men), but because they are not performed—as are the works of the regenerate—from faith and with delight to the glory of God; for they are performed rather by the compulsion of the law, without faith and interior complacency, more for the sake of men than to be referred to God; whence they do not please God equally.

Meanwhile, insofar as they agree with the law, to that extent they can be called good, just as the blessed M. Chemnitz said in *Exam.* P. I, p. 200 (in the edition of the time), that they are honest and good in their own kind. He also adds this reason: "What," he says, "nature still has remaining from the first creation, information, life, senses, mind, etc., are good in themselves, but through sin they are wounded, vitiated, and contaminated."

The blessed Josua Stegmann writes in *Photinian. Disput.* XL, Q. 2, p. 647: "We concede that the good works of the heathen were morally good in some way, because they were done according to the dictate of reason, such as it was; but that they are spiritually good, that does not follow from it." And because some have said that those works are good as to the substance of the act, which displeased others (who, under the name of substance, comprehend also those things which pertain to the circumstances), therefore Stegmann, *loc. cit.*, p. 648, distinguished between the substance of the act as to the genus and as to the είδος or species, and refers to the latter signification the special causes from which the act proceeds.

This flows from what has been said. And it is indeed useful to distinguish between the actions of the unregenerate, which are vicious in their kind and prohibited by the law of God, and those which are not vicious in their kind, or whose very matter or substance is not evil, or by whatever other words this may be expressed, according to the blessed Chemnitz, *l. c.*, in whose footsteps the blessed Gerhard insists in *L. II. Conf. Cath. P. III. art. XXII. cap. 3*, saying: "The external works of the unregenerate, such as covering the naked, helping one in danger, etc., are not sins in themselves and by the kind of act." And again: "Certain actions of unregenerate men are not vicious in themselves and as to the substance of the act. They are called sins not as to the substance of the act." Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Ausführl. Erklärung*, Book VIII, Q. 42, p. 336, 337.

Just as it is otherwise said that evil is born from any defect whatsoever. And indeed, this defect of actions is not supplied by the imputation of alien righteousness, which is not apprehended by faith. However, those actions are sins with respect to the efficient, formal, and final cause, as Chemnitz and Gerhard teach in the places cited. PART III. CHAPTER VI.

Kromayer: "Good works are to be judged not by nouns, but by adverbs, i. e., they must not only be good, but also be done well... Whoever, therefore, does works congruent with the law, but directs them not to the glory of God, but to his own, he does not do good works well. Wherefore Augustine called the good works of the Gentiles, by which they sought the fame of immortality, 'splendid sins,' i. e., sins that strike the eyes, accidentally, on account of the omitted, i. e., due end." (*Th. posit. pol.* II, 395.)

Luther: "Moses describes the patriarch Jacob, how he came into Haran, found there his uncle’s daughter, loved the girl, took her as his wife, begat sons, and tended the flocks—all of which are such foolish and carnal things that one could not find more carnal things even among the heathens themselves. For no one sees the essential difference, which is the greatest, between a gentile and this patriarch Jacob. For Esau and Ishmael also till the fields, graze sheep, milk cows, have a family, and provide fodder for the cattle, which are works similar to the works of the saints: and yet they are not holy. Why? Because there is a great and incomprehensible difference between the works of both parties. Here, with Jacob, there is faith and the Word: there, there is no Word, but mere unbelief. Therefore, the works of Jacob are as distant from the works of Ishmael or Esau as heaven is from earth, however much they may be the same works in appearance.

Latin:

2. Antinomorum, ut Joh. Agricolae, qui docuit, poenitentiam docendam esse non ex lege seu decalogo, sed ex evangelio. Item evangelium immediate magnitudinem offensae et deformitatem peccati ostendere; legem non tantum non esse normam faciendorum, sed ne quidem apud Christianos docendam et tolerandam, uti refert b. Lutherus T. 1. Jen. p. 533.

3. Socinianomm et Arminianorum, qui asserunt, Christum tria singularia praecepta lege non comprehensa, sed ad evangelium pertinentia, promulgasse, qualia sunt, se ipsum abnegare, crucem quotidie tollere, Christum sequi, Matth. 16, 24. Vide Smalcium lib. de divin. Christi c. 6. p. 22., Arminianos Apol. c. 12. et 13.

4. Canonistarum et scholasticorum (ut videre est ex Thoma ejusque commentatoribus et D. Georg. Calixto in Epitome Theol. Moral, a. 1634. Helmstadtii edita p. 40. sq.), ponentium bonitatem actionum humanarum in naturali convenientia modi agendi circa hoc vel illud objectum cum instinctu naturae intelligentis et libeiae. Et notandum, quando D. Calixtus 1. c., scholastici, item et moralistae hic disputant, in quo consistat formale bonae vel malae actionis, eos disputare non de bono civili aut morali ethico solum, sed etiam de formali bonitatis supernaturalis sive actionum supernaturalium, quarum regulam esse conformitatem vel difformitatem cum judicio rationis naturalis, plane falsum est, ut docet D. Huelsemannus in Praei. F. C. ad a. 12. sect. 3. § 5.“ (L. c. c. 9. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1388.)

f) Vid. 1 Cor. 10, 31. Col. 3, 17. ad 28. Broch&andus: ,,Sunt qui nimium, sunt etiam qui minus, quam fas sit, tribuant intentioni in actione bona vel mala constituenda. 21 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. IH. PART. III. CAP. VI.

Regiam et rectam sequuntur viam, qui indubie persuasi sunt, non sufficere ad opus bonum intentionem bonam. Nam primo, Dei voluntas est, ne nostram, sed Dei voluntatem regulam constituamus bonorum operum, Deut. 12, 8. Num. 15, 39. Matth. 15, 9. Mare. 7, 7. Deinde, nihil est certius, quam opus, etiam sceleratissimum, intentione bona seu finis optimi intuitu patrari posse, cf. Gen. 19, 31. 32. Perhibet etiam Christus, crudelissimos Christianorum persecutores intendere Christianorum caede honorem Dei, Joh. 16, 2.; qui etiam in necem Pauli conjurant Judaei, zelo, sed praepostero; gloriae Dei aguntur, Act. 26, 9. An haec opera ob intentionem bonam pronuntiabimus bona? Tertio, cum ad opus vere bonum requiratur et mandatum Dei et efficacia operantis Sp. Sancti et viva fides et gloria Dei, tanquam ultimus operis finis: nemo non facile intelligit, non sufficere solam intentionem bonam, ut opus aliquod sit bonum. At secius se res habet de intentione mala. Non enim est ullum opus, ratione actus et substantiae adeo praestans, quod intentio mala non inficiat et ex optimo non faciat pessimum. In quam sententiam lege fuse et ex professo disserentem salvatorem Christum Matth. 6, 1. sqq.“ (System, univers. th. Artic. 25. c. 3. cas. 9. f. 258.)

ANTITHESIS. Busenbaumius (Societatis Jesu theologus f 1668.): ״Reo, etiamsi vere reus sit, licet ante et post sententiam (quoad mortem, vel poenam morti aequivalentem, v. g. perpetuum carcerem) fugere. . . Regulariter reo licet fugere, etiamsi custos carceris grave damnum inde passurus sit. . . Licet etiam saltem in foro conscientiae, custodes (praecisa vi et injuria) decipere, tradendo v. g. cibum et potum, ut sopiantur, vel procurando, ut absint; item, vincula et carceres effringere: quia, cum finis est licitus, etiam media sunt licita. Et licet alii captivi per effractum parietem simul elabantur, non tenebitur de damno, quia tantum est ejus causa per accidens, cum jure suo utatur. . . Illis, qui non sunt ministri justitiae, licet non solum consilio juvare reum, ut fugiat, sed etiam suppeditatis instrumentis, v. g. funibus, lima etc., quia finem alteri licitum illi suadere et ad eundem media proponere licet.“ (Medulla th. moral. Antwerpiae, 1723. p. 447. sq.)

Institutum Societatis Jesu: ״Visum est nobis in Domino, nuilas constitutiones, declarationes vel ordinem ullum vivendi posse 05ligationem ad peccatum mortale vel veniale inducere, nisi superior ea in nomine Domini nostri Jesu Christi vel in virtute obedientiae juberet; quod in rebus vel personis illis, in quibus judicabitur, quod ad particulajre uniuscujusque vel ad universale bonum multum conveniet; fieri poterit, ut loco timoris offensae succedat amor et desiderium omnis perfectionis, et ut major gloria et laus Christi, creatoris ac Domini nostri, consequatur.“ (Institut, soc. Jesu, auctoritate congregationis generalis 18. auctum et recusum. Pragae, 1757. Vol. I. f. 414. sq.)

Cf. Index: ״Superiores possunt obligare ad peccatum in virtute obedientiae, quando id multum conveniat, par. 6. c. 5. p. 414.“ (Vol. IL Index sub titulo: Obedientia.) §

19. Opera non-renatorum, quae ad praescriptum legis moralis a quodammodo b fiunt, non aeque dici possunt bona,c uti opera renatorum; et licet non per se et simpliciter,d tamen quatenus requisitis bonorum operum destituuntur, peccata e recte appellantur.

Haec enim etiam lumini naturae nota est. $ ic dicuntur gentes facere τά τού νόμου, ea, quae, sunt legis, Rom. 2, 15. Et Apolog. Aug. Conf. Art. XVIII. p. m. 218. docet, humar nam voluntatem posse aliquo modo efficere justitiam civilem seu operum, posse loqui de Deo, exhibere Deo certum cultum externo opere, obedire magistratibus, parentibus in opere externo eligendo, posse continere manus a caede, ah adulterio, a furto. Non autem possunt non־renati efficere opera moralia, legi exacte conformia, sine ullo defectu.

Unde quidam dixerunt, opera illa non-renatorum, etsi quoad substantiam actus importent conformi־ tatem cum lege et ratione recta, ini circumstantiis tamen a rectitudinis regula multis modis deficere. Vid. Ausführl. Erklärung L. VIII. Q. 62. p. 333.

Kromayerus: ״Bona opera non praecedunt justificandum, sed sequuntur justificatum.“ (Th. positiv.pol. II, 390.)

Non solum quod legi non sunt simpliciter et modis omnibus conformia, absque omni defectu (quod nec in homines renatos cadit), sed quod non aeque ut renatorum opera ex fide et cum delectatione ad Dei gloriam fiunt, quippe quae potius, lege cogente, absque fide et interiore complacentia fiunt, hominum causa magis, quam ut referantur in Deum; unde nec Deo aeque placent.

Interim quatenus legi conveniunt, eatenus dici possunt bona, prout b.. M. Chemnitius P. I. Exam. p. m. 200. dixit, eas suo genere honestas et bonas esse. Addit etiam hanc rationem: Quae, inquiens, natura adhuc reliqua habet ex prima creatione, informatione, vita, sensibus, mente etc., per se sunt bona, sed per peccatum sunt sauciata, vitiata et contaminata.

B. Josua Stegmannus in Photinian. Disput. XL. Q. 2. p. 647. scribit: Quod bona opera ethnicorum fuerint moraliter aliquo modo bona, concedimus, quia secundum rationis dictamen, qualiter etiam illud se habebat, facta sunt; quod autem spiritualiter sint bona, id inde non sequitur. Et quia aliqui dixerunt, opera illa esse bona quoad substantiam actus, quod aliis displicuit (substantiae nomine comprehendentibus ea quoque, quae ad circumstantias pertinent), ideo Stegmannus loc. cit. p. 648. distinxit inter substantiam actus quoad genus et quoad είδος seu speciem, et ad posteriorem significationem refert speciales causas, unde actus proficiscatur.

Fluit hoc ex dictis. Atque utile sane est, distinguere inter actiones non-renatorum, quae sunt genere suo vitiosae et lege Dei prohibitae, atque illas, quae suo genere non sunt vitiosae, seu quarum ipsa materia sive substantia non est mala, aut quibuscunque aliis verbis hoc exprimatur, juxta b. Ghemnit. 1. c., cujus vestigiis insistens b. Gerhardus L. II. Conf. Cath. P. III. art. XXII. cap. 3. dicit: Opera externa nonrenatorum, utpote cooperire nudum, subvenire periclitanti etc., ex se et genere actus non sunt peccata. Et rursus: Quaedam hominum non-renatorum actiones per se et quoad substantiam actus non sunt vitiosae. Dicuntur peccata non quoad substantiam actus. Conf. b. Musaei Ausführl. Erklärung L. VIII. Q. 42. p. 336. 337.

Prout alias dicitur malum nasci ex quavis defectu. Atque hic quidem defectus actionum non suppletur per imputationem justitiae alienae, quae fide apprehensa non est. Sunt autem actiones illae peccata, respectu causae efficientis, formalis, finalis, ut docent Chemnitius et Gerhardus 11. cc. PART. HI. CAP. VI.

Kromayerus: ,,Bona opera non nominibus, sed adverbiis sunt dijudicanda, i. e., non tantum bona esse, sed et bene fleri debent. . . Quisquis itaque facit opera cum lege congruentia, sed illa non ad Dei, verum suam gloriam dirigit, is bona opera bene non facit. Quare Augustinus bona gentilium opera, quibus immortalitatis famam captabant, per accidens, propter intermissum sci. debitum flnem, splendida i. e. in oculos incurrentia peccata vocavit.“ (Th. posit.pol. II, 395.)

Lutherus: ,,Describit Moses patriarcham Jacob, quomodo venerit in Haran, invenerit ibi filiam avunculi, amaverit puellam, duxerit uxorem, genuerit filios, paverit pecudes, quae omnia stulta et carnalia sunt, ut non magis apud ethnicos ipsos carnalia inveniri queant. Quia nemo videt differentiam essentialem, quae maxima est inter gentilem et hunc patriarcham Jacob. Esau enim et Ismael etiam colunt agros, pascunt oves, mulgent vaccas, habent familiam, praebent pabulum pecudibus, quae sunt similia opera sanctorum operibus: et tamen non sunt sancta. Quare? Quia magna et incomprehensibilis differentia est inter opera utriusque partis. Hic apud Jacob est fides et verbum: illic nullum verbum est, sed incredulitas mera. Tantum igitur distant opera Jacob ab operibus Ismael aut Esau, quantum coelum a terra, quantumvis sint eadem opera in speciem.


### On Renewal and Good Works: Thus, Erasmus magnificently praises the virtues of the heathens, of Socrates,…

Thus, Erasmus magnificently praises the virtues of the heathens, of Socrates, Cicero, Atticus, etc., and makes a comparison: You would scarcely find, he says, among Christians those who have excelled in what Pomponius Atticus or others did; indeed, among Christians many are found who are openly evil and flagitious, to whom these heathens were far superior. But one must answer: Philosophically and in their matter they agree, that is, in the kind of life; but not in species and difference. For if even Cicero or Socrates had sweated blood, he would not for that reason please God. Nor is the question what and how great works Alexander the Great, Hannibal, Julius Caesar, or Scipio performed, for it is certain that they accomplished greater things than any Christian ever has. For you will not easily find that military strength, nor likewise the patience and tolerance of evils and labors, in any Christian king, indeed not even in the kings of the people of Israel, David or others. Why then do you not extol them, or prefer them to all Christian kings, David and others? I answer: If the choice were given to me, I would choose the most sordid and most rustic work of a single Christian peasant or maidservant over all the victories and triumphs of Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, etc. Why? Because here is God, there is the devil, which is the essential difference.

The matter of the works is the same, but the species and difference are infinitely diverse, because God says: 'The works and domestic duties of this little woman, that she sweeps the house, obeys the mistress of the house, please me; because He has regarded the lowliness of His handmaid,' where there is nothing of great and glorious works, except that she humbly performs the duties of a maidservant at home, whether in culinary or pastoral matters. Such were those two, Leah and Rachel, who grazed their father’s flocks, went to fetch water, milked cows and goats: these works pleased God. Hannibal, however, Alexander, Scipio, Cicero do not please Him. Why? Because they indeed agree in kind, or rather surpass, but in species and difference they are surpassed. Not everyone can discern this; not even Erasmus saw it.

Only believers discern the value and weight of Christian works. But the greatest weight and value of works is faith and the Word. For there God Himself and the Spirit are in the one who works.

Men, however, who are like horses and mules, are vehemently moved by external appearance. I, too, was once in the monastery far holier than I am now, as far as the external mask is concerned; I prayed more, kept vigil, abstained, macerated my flesh: in short, my whole life was most specious in the eyes of others, although not so in my own; for I was greatly contrite and afflicted. Now, however, I eat and dress in a general and customary way; nothing special or singular stands out in my life compared to others. Then, when I was a monk, I did nothing other than waste my time, afflict my health, and indeed even wound my conscience with those..."

of the] righteousness of works, so that it can even now be healed only with difficulty. Because, besides nature, in which boasting about works is ingrained, I have also acquired the habit and custom of looking to my own works and my own dignity. Furthermore, I know for certain that now one reading, one Lord’s Prayer, is worth more and is more pleasing to God than all those prayers which I mumbled for fifteen whole years; because I know that I am heard. Nor is there any need for any vigils or special fasts and abstinence, because God has given a messenger of Satan with other difficulties and crosses of this world, which exercise me more than all those things.” (On Gen. 29. Exegetical Latin Works, Erlangen, 1831. Vol. VII. pp. 212—214.)

Gerhardus: “Through errors directly fighting against the foundation and stubbornly defended, no less than through sins against conscience, the grace of the Holy Spirit is excluded. Therefore, the works of heretics, truly and properly so called, cannot be spiritually good. Heretics ‘have departed from the faith,’ 1 Tim. 4:1; ‘they have made shipwreck of the faith,’ 1 Tim. 1:19: how then can their works be done from faith? ‘If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples,’ says Christ, John 8:31. Therefore, by contrary sense: ‘If anyone teaches otherwise and does not consent to the wholesome words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine which is according to godliness, he is proud, knowing nothing,’ 1 Tim. 6:3, 4, nor can he be a true disciple of Christ; how then can his works be pleasing to God? Heretics are no longer true and living members of the church, which is the mystical body of Christ; therefore they are not partakers of the spiritual life, which is ‘from God,’ Eph. 4:18; they are not ‘branches’ drawing fruit from the vine of salvation, Christ, John 15:4; their works, therefore, are dead before God. Heretics, truly and properly so called, are idolaters, because the Old Testament was accustomed to call new dogmas ‘strange gods’ in allegorical speech, namely, in that ‘their opinions are observed by heretics just as their gods are by the Gentiles,’ as Vincent of Lérins writes in his work against heresies; how then are their works directed to the true glory of the true God?” (Book on Good Works, § 9.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Pelagians, who, according to Augustine (Book 4 against Julian), asserted that even those alienated from the faith of Christ can possess true righteousness, in that they naturally do the things that are of the law. 2. Of the Papists, such as the Council of Trent, sess. 6, can. 7, which anathematizes: ‘If anyone shall say that all works which are done before justification, in whatever way they may be done, are truly sins.’ ... Costerus in Enchiridion, ch. 6, p. 276, says: ‘The works of infidels do not arise from infidelity, but from elsewhere, such as from natural instinct and the judgment of right reason, and no one would call these sins.’ 3. Of the Socinians, who establish that even the unregenerate can perform good works. ‘It is certain,’ says Smalcius (Disp. 6 on Good Works, ch. Franz, f. 167), ‘that a man, even if unregenerate, can perform good works under the guidance of nature and reason, although not as perfectly as he who is regenerate, nor as perfect, nor as acceptable to God as those which one does out of the love of Christ’; compare the same, f. 174. 4. Of the Arminians, who, with Socinus, require integrity of mind in a man before conversion; see the Remonstrants in their Apology to the Censure, f. 118.” (Loc. cit., s. 2, q. 1, f. 1380.) §

20. The efficient cause of good works is the same as that of renewal. According to those things which we said in § 17. PART III. CHAPTER VI.

Huelsemannus: "Whether the free will of man, even when renewed, ought to be called the proximate cause of continued sanctification and its exercises, or good works, is not without reason doubted. . . A notable passage exists in the Epitome of the Book of Concord, Art. 2, p. 603, that even the regenerate, after they have already been renewed, do good 'only as much and as long' as the Spirit effects in them. Therefore, the opinion of the Papists and Arminians is false, that the renewed will of man determines the concomitant grace of God toward the specification and exercise of any good work; and that to use or not to use the present grace of God is indifferent and equally possible for the renewed man. . . The contrary is true, namely, that divine grace determines the will of the renewed man toward the specification and exercise of any good work; not vice versa, not indifferently, not with equal ease, so that just as a man, even when renewed, can abuse divine grace, so he can also use it; for the faculty, or rather the weakness, of abusing is natural, but the faculty of using is determined by grace itself, without which, just as we can do nothing, so we cannot determine anything. Wherefore this error was rightly condemned in the Synod of Dort, Art. 3 and 4, in the Rejection of Errors, Art. 9." (Praelect. F. C. p. 577 sq.) § 21.

The form or formal reason of good works, when they are viewed in themselves, is conformity with the law of God; but when they are viewed insofar as, although they do not exactly conform to the law, they nevertheless please God, then their form is faith in Christ. For thus the goodness of every work, which is to be done according to the prescription of a certain norm, consists in its agreement with its norm.

Indeed, by the very fact that they do not exactly conform to the law, they cannot, as if by reason of agreement with the norm, simply and absolutely please God; and therefore the form, by virtue of which they please God, is not that imperfect law-abidingness. For through this faith, while the merit of Christ is apprehended, it comes to pass that the infirmities adhering to the works of the faithful are covered. § 22.

The affections of good works are: 1. that they are done spontaneously; 2. that they are imperfect; 3. that they are necessary for those who are to be saved. Indeed, the law does not compel the regenerate with its threats and curses, but only directs or teaches them with its precepts. In this sense, 1 Tim. 1:9 says that the law is not laid down for the just, nor does it lie upon them like a burden against their will, pressing them with its threats. And Rom. 7:6 says that the regenerate serve (God) in newness of spirit (that is, through new powers received from the Holy Spirit, promptly and with a certain delight) and not in the oldness of the letter (i.e., not by the force of the ancient law, which urges with its threats and urges and drives those who are either hesitating or unwilling). Clearly, the regenerate would serve God, even if there were no coercive force or

the threat annexed to the laws, since they willingly do all things out of love for God, who is propitious to them. In this way, the authors here observe the second degree of Christian liberty (since the first pertains to the locus on Justification; concerning which see here, Chapter V, § 14, note a, toward the end), namely, that men, having been gifted by God with new and spiritual powers and liberated from the servitude of dominating sin, now perform works pleasing to God, or new obedience, with a free and spontaneous spirit.

Gerhardus: "Bellarminus argues that it is lawful to perform good works with a view to an eternal reward. . . The question is not whether the promises concerning the rewards of good works ought to stir up in the regenerate a zeal for doing good. For since 'the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,' Matt. 26:41; and since 'the flesh lusts against the spirit,' Gal. 5:17, we ought therefore to stir up and inflame that sluggishness of the flesh in ourselves and in other regenerate persons by the consideration of rewards and punishments—the former being proposed for good works, the latter for evil ones. Likewise, when we are cast down in spirit in adversities and persecutions because of the weakness of the flesh, let us lift ourselves up with pious meditations on the glory of eternal life that will follow the afflictions. . . But if the question is asked. . . concerning rewards in this life and the future life, whether we ought to do good with a view to them (so that we hope to obtain them by our merits), we command that the following foundations be considered:

Latin:

Sic Erasmus magnifice ethnicorum virtutes praedicat, Socratis, Ciceronis, Attici etc., et facit comparationem: Vix, inquit, invenias apud Christianos, qui praestiterint hoc, quod Pomponius Atticus aut alii; imo apud Christianos multi inveniuntur aperte mali et flagitiosi, quibus ethnici hi longe fuerunt meliores. Respondendum est autem: Philosophice et in materia conveniunt, hoc est, in genere vitae; sed non in specie et differentia. Si enim vel Cicero vel Socrates sanguinem sudasset, tamen propterea non placeret Deo. Neque est quaestio, quae et quanta opera fecerint Alexander magnus, Hannibal, Julius Caesar, Scipio, quos quidem majores res gessisse constat, quam ullum unquam Christianum. Illud enim robur militare, patientiam item et tolerantiam malorum et laborum non facile reperies in ullo rege christiano, imo ne quidem in populi Israelitici regibus, Davide aut aliis. Quare igitur non extollis eos, aut praefers omnibus Christianis regibus, Davddi et aliis? Respondeo: Si daretur mihi optio, eligerem unius Christiani rustici aut ancillae sordidissimum et maxime agreste opus prae omnibus victoriis et triumphis Alexandri magni, Julii Caesaris etc. Quare? Quia hic est Deus, illic est diabolus, quae est differentia essentialis.

Materia operum est eadem, sed species et differentia in infinitum diversa est, quia Deus dicit: Hujus mulierculae opera et officia domestica, quod verrit domum, obtemperat matrifamilias, mihi placent; quia respexit ad humilitatem ancillae suae, ubi etiam nihil magnorum et gloriosorum operum est, nisi quod domi humiliter fungitur officiis ancillae, sive in re culinaria, sive pecuaria. Tales erant istae duae, Lea et Rachel, quae pascebant greges patris, agebant aquatum, mulgebant vaccas et capras: haec opera placebant Deo. Hannibal autem, Alexander, Scipio, Cicero non placent. Quare? Quia genere quidem conveniunt, vel superant potius, sed specie et differentia superantur. Hoc non omnes possunt cernere, ne Erasmus quidem vidit.

Soli credentes cernunt pretium et pondus operum Christianorum. Pondus autem et pretium maximum operum est fides et verbum. Ibi enim Deus ipse est et Spiritus in operante.

Homines vero, qui sunt sicut equi et muli, vehementer moventur externa specie. Ego quoque olim ih monachatu longe eram sanctior, quam nunc sum, quoad externam larvam, plus orabam, vigilabam, abstinebam, macerabam carnem meam: breviter tota vita mea erat speciosissima in aliorum oculis, tametsi in meis non item; quia valde contritus et afflictus eram. Jam vero comedo et vestio generali et usitato modo, nihil praecipuum aut singulare prae aliis in vita mea eminet. Tum cum essem monachus, nihil aliud feci, quam quod perdidi tempus, afflixi meam valetudinem, quin etiam conscientiam meam sauciavi illis

justitiis operum, ut etiamnum aegre sanari queat. Quia praeter naturam, cui insita est gloriatio de operibus, etiam comparavi habitum et consuetudinem respiciendi ad mea opera et dignitatem meam. Caeterum certo scio, jam unam lectionem, unum Pater noster plus valere et Deo magis probari, quam omnes illas precationes, quas murmuravi totis quindecim annis; quia scio, me exaudiri. Nec opus est ullis vigiliis aut singularibus jejuniis et abstinentia, quia Deus dedit angelum satanae cum aliis difficultatibus et crucibus hujus mundi, quae magis me, quam illa omnia, exercent.“ (Ad Gen. 29. Exeget. opp. lat. Erlangae, 1831. Tom. VII. p. 212—214.)

Gerhardus: ,,Per errores contra fundamentum directe pugnantes et pertinaciter defensos non minus, quam per peccata contra conscientiam, excluditur Spiritus S. gratia. Ergo haeretitorum vere et proprie sic dictorum opera non possunt esse spiritualiter bona. Haeretici,discesserunt a fide‘, 1 Tim. 4, 1.; ,fecerunt naufragium fidei‘, 1 Tim. 1, 19.: quomodo ergo opera eorum ex fide poterunt fieri? ,Si in sermone meo manseritis, vere discipuli mei eritis‘, dicit Christus Joh. 8, 31. Ergo a contrario sensu: ,Si quis aliter docet et non acquiescit sanis sermonibus Domini nostri Jesu Christi et ei, quae secundum pietatem est, doctrinae, inflatus est, nihil sciens‘, 1 Tim. 6, 3. 4., nec potest esse verus Christi discipulus, quomodo ergo opera illius Deo placere poterunt? Haeretici non amplius sunt vera et viva membra ecclesiae, quae est corpus Christi mysticum; ergo non sunt participes spiritualis vitae, quae est,ex Deo‘, Eph. 4, 18.; non sunt,palmites‘, haurientes fructum ex vite salutis, Christo, Joh. 15, 4.; opera ergo eorum coram Deo sunt mortua. Haeretici vere et proprie sic dicti sunt idololatrae, quia nova dogmata V. T. allegorico sermone,deos alienos‘ appellare consuevit, eo sc., quod,ab haereticis ipsorum opiniones, sicut a gentilibus dii sui observentur‘, ut scribit Vincent. Lyrinensis adv. haereses; quomodo ergo opera eorum ad veram veri Dei gloriam sunt directa?“ (L. de bonis opp. § 9.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Pelagianorum, apud Augustinum 1. 4. c. Julianum asserentium, etiam alienos a fide Christi posse habere veram justitiam, eo quod naturaliter, quae legis sunt, faciant. 2. Powtificiorum, ut Concilii Trid. sess. 6. can. 7. anathematizantis: ,Si quis dixerit, omnia opera, quae ante justificationem fiunt, quacunque ratione facta sint, vere esse peccata‘. . . Costerus in Enchir. c. 6. p. 276. inquit: ,Infidelium opera non ex infidelitate oriuntur, sed aliunde, velut ex naturali instinctu et rectae rationis judicio, et haec nemo dixerit esse peccata.‘ 3. Socinianorum, opera bona etiam non-renatos facere posse, statuentium. ,Certum est‘, inquit Smalcius Disp. 6. de B. O. c. Franz. f. 167., ,hominem etiam non-renatum natura et ratione duce bona opera praestare, licet non ita perfecte, quemadmodum is, qui renatus est, nec ita perfecta nec Deo etiam ita accepta, quemadmodum ea sunt, quae quis facit amore Christi‘; confer eundem f. 174. 4. Arminianorurn, qui animi probitatem ante conversionem in homine cum Socino requirunt; vide Remonstrantes in Apolog. ad Censur. f. 118.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 1380.) §

20. Causa efficiens bonorum operum eadem est, quae renovationis. Juxta ea, quae diximus § 17. PART. III. CAP. VI.

Huelsemannus: ,,An liberum hominis arbitrium etiam renovatum dici debeat causa proxima continuatae sanctificationis et exercitiorum ejus sive bonorum operum, non immerito dubitatur. . . Insignis locus extat in Epitome lib. Cone, ad art. 2. p. 603., etiam renatos, postquam jam renovati sunt, ,tantum et tam diu‘ bene agere, ,quantum et quam diu‘ Spiritus in illis efficit. Proinde falsa est pontificiorum et Arminianorum opinio, voluntatem hominis renovatam determinare concomitantem Dei gratiam ad specificationem et exercitium cujuscunque boni operis; uti et non uti praesenti Dei gratia, esse indifferens et perinde homini renovato. . . Contrarium est verum, nempe gratiam divinam determinare voluntatem hominis renovati ad specificationem et exercitium cujuscunque boni operis; non vice versa, non perinde, hon aeque facile, ut homo etiam renovatus potest abuti divina gratia, ita potest eadem uti; abutendi enim facultas sive imbecillitas potius naturalis est, utendi autem facultas determinatur ab ipsa gratia, sine qua ut nihil facere, ita nec determinare possumus. Quamobrem hic error recte damnatus est in Concilio Dordraceno ad artic. 3. et 4. in Rejectione errorum in artic. 9.“ (Praelect. F. C. p. 577. sq.; § 21.

Forma seu ratio formalis operum bonorum, quando in se spectantur, est conformitas a cum lege Dei; quando autem spectantur, quatenus, licet legi exacte non convenientia, tamen Deo placent, sic forma eorum b est fides in Christum.c Sic enim omnis operis, ad praescriptum certae normae faciendi, bonitas in convenientia ipsius cum sua norma consistit.

Nempe hoc ipso, quod exacte non conveniunt cum lege, non possunt Deo, velut ob convenientiam cum norma, simpliciter et absolute placere; adeoque forma, cujus intuitu Deo placent, non est Ιννομία illa imperfecta. Per hanc enim, dum Christi meritum apprehenditur, iit, ut infirmitates operibus fidelium adhaerentes tegantur. § 22.

Affectiones bonorum operum sunt: 1. quod sponte a fiunt; 2. quod sunt imperfecta;b 3. quod sunt necessaria c salvandis. d Nempe lex comminationibus et maledictionibus suis renatos non cogit, sed praeceptis suis dirigit tantum seu docet. Quo sensu 1 Tim. 1, 9. dicitur, legem justo non esse positam aut instar oneris incumbere invito, quem suis comminationibus premat. Et Rom. 7, 6. dicuntur renati servire (Deo) per novitatem spiritus (seu per vires novas, a Spiritu Sancto acceptas, promte et cum quadam delectatione) et non per vetustatem literae (i. e. non ex vi legis antiquae, suis comminationibus urgentis, et vel cunctantes aut invitos urgentis ac propellentis). Scilicet renati servituri essent Deo, si maxime nulla vis coactiva aut

comminatio legibus annexa esset, cum ex dilectione Dei sibi propitii omnia libenter agant. Qua ratione secundum gradum libertatis christianae hic observant auctores (cum primus ad Locum de Justif. pertifieat; de quo vid. h. 1. cap. V. § 14. not. a. sub finem), scilicet, quod homines viribus novis ac spiritualibus a Deo donati et a servitute peccati dominantis liberati jam libero et spontaneo spiritu opera Deo grata praestant seu novam obedientiam.

Gerhardus: ,,Disputat Bellarminus, licitum esse operari bona intuitu mercedis aeternae. . . Non est quaestio, an promissiones de praemiis bonorum operum in renatis excitare debeant studium bene operandi. Cum enim,spiritus quidem promtus, caro autem infirma' sit, Matth. 26,1.; cum,caro adversus spiritum concupiscat‘, Gal. 5,17., ideo torporem illum carnis in nobis atque aliis renatis consideratione praemiorufti et poenarum, quorum illa bonis, hae vero malis operibus propositae, excitare atque inflammare debemus; Itemque cum in adversitatibus et persecutionibus propter carnis infirmitatem animo dejicimur, erigamus nos ipsos piis de gloria vitae aeternae afflictiones secutura meditationibus. . . Si vero quaeratur ... de praemiis in hac et futura vita, an intuitu eorum bene operari debeamus (ita ut meritis nostris ea nos obtinere speremus), jubemus considerari sequentia fundamenta:


### On Renewal and Good Works: A son does not obey his parents with a view to a reward, but out of a sincere…

1. A son does not obey his parents with a view to a reward, but out of a sincere and filial heart. The regenerate are children of God. Therefore, they obey their heavenly Father not with a view to a reward, but out of a sincere and filial heart. The major premise is sufficiently manifest. For if filial obedience were performed or ought to be performed with a view to a reward, there would be no difference between a son and a servant; likewise, greater obedience would be owed to those parents from whom a greater reward is hoped. The minor premise rests upon the clearest pronouncements of Scripture. John 1:12, Rom. 8:16, etc. . .

2. Whoever obeys God with a spontaneous spirit does not look to punishments or rewards in this manner and in this respect; for what is extorted by the threat of punishments or elicited by the promise of rewards does not, to that extent, proceed from a spontaneous spirit. But the regenerate obey God with a spontaneous spirit. Ps. 110:3, 119:108. Therefore, they do not look to rewards or punishments in this manner and in this respect. . .

3. The sounder philosophers recognized from the light of nature that virtue is to be loved for its own sake, with no hope of reward; and that vice is to be detested and fled for its own sake, not out of fear of punishment. . . 4. Matt. 6:3, this rule is proposed to us to be observed in good works: 'When you do alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does.' If we ought to forget our good works, they are certainly not to be done with a view to a reward. . .

5. The laborers of the first hour in the parable of Matt. 20, who bargain with the householder for a wage and will not work until the wage is fixed, etc., become the last of all and are forced to hear: 'Take what is yours and go!' . . . 6. The elect, when they hear in Matt. 25:34: 'Come, possess, etc.,' marvel at the immense generosity and munificence of the One rewarding, and by that very fact declare that they did good with a simple heart, and not with a view to a reward. . .

7. 'Charity does not seek its own,' 1 Cor. 13:5; it does not seek a reward in its works, but obeys freely; therefore, love even loves enemies, from whom, however, no remuneration is to be hoped. Now, the good works of the pious proceed from charity." (L. de bonis opp. § 126.)

For after sin entered into the world and tenaciously clings even to regenerate men, so that the flesh always struggles against the spirit, it happens that we do not do whatever we will, as Paul testifies in Gal. 5: 17. And thus, we sometimes err and stumble in the very circumstances of good actions, or we do not perform them with the promptness and alacrity that is due. PART III. CHAPTER VI.

tate, but we work more sluggishly, or with φιλαυτία (self-love) intervening or accompanying, we sprinkle a stain upon our works, however good they may be. Luther: "Augustine does not say: Woe to some good life; but: Woe to the most praiseworthy life, if it is judged without grace. . . A good work, done in the best way, is a daily sin, according to mercy; and a mortal sin, according to the strict judgment of God." (Grund und Ursach aller Artikel, so durch die römische Bulle unrechtlich verdammt worden. Tom. Hal. XV, 1852. sq.)

The same: "Just as a fig tree or another tree sometimes bears a worm-eaten fruit, yet it is a good fruit according to its kind, without sting or thorn; indeed, before it should be without fruit, it must rather have worm-eaten fruits, yet without its own fault: so also all the works of a Christian are good by nature, because the tree is good and lives in such a way that it would gladly bring forth purely good fruits, although sometimes, out of the weakness of the flesh or other obstacles, something evil creeps in." (Ad Matth. 7, 20. T. Hal. VII, 934.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, whose fervent assertion is (the words are Brochmann’s, l. c.), 'the good works of the justified in this life are absolutely and simply good and perfect,' or 'the works of the just in this life can be perfectly good, so that they have no vice at all.' Thus Bellarmine, T. 4. l. 4. de justif. c. 15. . . 2. Of the Socinians, as Smalcius c. Franz. p. 176. sq. disp. 6. ref. th. 9.: 'A twofold consideration of perfection in piety is given,' he says: 'the one is most absolute, when someone has never, not even once, sinned; the other is comparative, when someone has contracted no habit of sin or has never stuck or does not stick in any sin. The former perfection, as it is not absolutely necessary for salvation, so it is also not necessarily and absolutely required of men now under the N. T. . . The latter, however, as it is altogether necessary for salvation, so it is required of all absolutely.' 3. Of the Arminians, contending that works can be performed by the regenerate which are so perfect that they are not defiled by any vice of the flesh nor can be judged worthy of punishment, in Apolog. c. 11. p. 131. 4. Of the Schwenckfeldians and Weigelians, who champion the perfection of good works; see Weigel, P. 1. Post. p. 35. 5. Of Jean de Labadie and his followers, contending that 'the faithful are not only immune from mortal sins, but also from inordinate motions' or depraved concupiscence, 'altogether,' in Declaratione fidei p. 180. Cf. Schurmannia, ευκλημ. p. 116. 141. 192." (L. c. c. 9. s. 2. q. 3. f. 1395.)

For there are various causes, which concern either God, or our neighbor, or ourselves. God, by the right of creation, redemption, regeneration, and adoption, holds us obligated to Himself, that we should do His will. Thus in Malachi 1:6, God says: A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If then I am your Father, where is My honor? And if I am a Master, where is My reverence? 1 Cor. 6, end: You were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s. Furthermore, to Eph. 2:10: We are His (God’s, who saves us out of His grace through faith) workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them. Finally, Tit. 2:11-12: That saving grace of God has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in the present age. But we are also commanded to provide an occasion for others to glorify God, "seeing our good works and as it were our light shining forth," Matt. 5:16. 1 Pet.

2, 12. We are bound, however, to take heed that God be not offended, or His name evil spoken of, Rom. 2:24; Tit. 2:5, but rather to imitate Him and His Son Jesus Christ, Eph. 5:1, 2; Matt. 11:29. We are obligated to our neighbor, that we may assist him with our services, just as the members of the body are a help to one another, Rom. 12:4–8; 1 Cor. 12:14–26, to bear one another’s burdens, relieving the troubles of his life, Gal. 6:2 ff., to go before him with a good example, Phil. 2:15, and to flee scandals, becoming ἀπρόσκοποι, 1 Cor. 10:23 ff. to 32, μηδεμίαν ἐν μηδενὶ διδόντες προσκοπήν, 2 Cor. 6:3, and to silence the calumnies of the wicked by doing good, Tit. 2:8; 1 Pet. 2:12; ch. 3:16. With respect to ourselves, diligence must be used that we make our calling and election sure, namely, that from our works we may be rendered more certain of our faith, and from this, of our calling and election, 2 Pet. 1:10. We must take heed, however, lest by acting wickedly or living carelessly we cast away faith, or grieve the Holy Spirit and fall from eternal life, 1 Tim. 1:19; Eph. 4:30; Rom. 8:13, but rather strive to attain the rewards promised to piety, 1 Tim. 4:8. Luther: “Outside the matter of justification, no one can sufficiently praise the good works commanded by God. For who can sufficiently proclaim the utility and fruit of even one work which a Christian does from faith and in faith? For it is more precious than heaven and earth. Therefore, neither can the whole world in this life render a worthy reward even for one such work, nor does the world have this grace, that it should magnify the good works of the pious, much less compensate them, because it does not discern them, or, if it does discern them, it judges them not to be good works but most wicked misdeeds, and drives those who do such things out of the world as the most harmful pests to the human race.” (Ad Gal. 3:22. Commentar. in ep. S. Pauli ad Gal. Erlangen, 1844. II, 100.) The same: “See how finely they teach about good works; they say they give their good works for a groschen. With this they want to be our apes and imitate our teaching, because they have heard that we teach that good works do not make one pious, nor do they blot out sin, nor do they reconcile God. Over this, the devil here adds his own supplement and despises good works so much that he wants to sell them all for a groschen. There I praise God, my Lord, that the devil must so shamefully besmirch and befool himself in his cleverness. We teach, therefore, that to reconcile God, to make one pious, to blot out sin, is such a high, great, and glorious work that only Christ, the Son of God, must do it, and it is properly a pure, bare, special work of the one true God and His grace, to which our works are nothing and can do nothing. But that for this reason good works should be nothing, or worth a groschen, who has ever taught or heard that, except now from the lying mouth of the devil? I would not give one of my sermons, one of my lectures, one of my writings, one of my Lord’s Prayers—yes, however small the works I have ever done or still do—for all the goods of the world; yes, I esteem it dearer than the life of my body, which is and should be dearer to everyone than the whole world. For if it is a good work, then God has done it through me and in me. If God has done it, and it is God’s work, what is the whole world compared to God and His work? Although I do not become pious through such a work (for that must happen beforehand through Christ’s blood and grace, without works), nevertheless it is done to the praise and honor of God, and to the use and salvation of the neighbor, which no one can pay for or compare with the world’s goods. And this fine rabble takes a groschen for it. Ah, how finely the devil has hidden himself here! Who could fail to grasp him here?” (Preface to Justus Menius’s writing: *Der Wiedertäufer Lehre u. s. w.* A. 1530. Tom. Hal. XIV, 281 ff.) PART III. CHAP. VI. The same: "That we may provide some parables for this, the works of a Christian, who has been justified and saved by his faith and out of the pure grace of God for nothing, should be regarded no differently than the works of Adam and Eve were in Paradise. Concerning this, it is written in Genesis 2:15: that 'God placed the created man into Paradise, that he should work and keep it.' Now Adam was pious and well-created before God without sin, so that he did not need to become pious and justified through his working and keeping; yet, so that he would not be idle, God gave him work to do, to plant, build, and preserve Paradise. These would have been purely free works, done for the sake of nothing other than to please God, and not to attain piety, which he already possessed; which would also have been naturally innate to us all. Thus, also, the work of a believing man, who through his faith is again placed into Paradise and created anew, needs no works to become pious; but so that he may not be idle and that his body may work and be preserved, such free works are commanded him to be done solely to please God." (Sermon on the Freedom of a Christian. Tom. Jen. XIX. 1224. sq.) Formula of Concord: "As concerns the necessity or voluntariness of good works, it is evident that in the Augsburg Confession and its Apology these expressions are used and often repeated, that good works are necessary; likewise, that it is necessary to do good works, which also must necessarily follow faith and reconciliation; likewise, that we necessarily ought to and must do good works, which God has commanded. Thus, also, in the Holy Scripture itself, the words 'need,' 'necessary,' and 'necessity,' likewise 'ought' and 'must,' are used in such a way as to signify what we are obligated to do by reason of God’s order, command, and will, as in Romans 13:5, 1 Corinthians 9:16, Acts 5:29, John 15:12, 1 John 4:21. Therefore, the aforementioned expressions or propositions are unjustly censured and rejected by some in this Christian and proper sense, whereas they ought justly to be cited and used to censure and reject the secure Epicurean delusion, where many imagine for themselves a dead faith or a delusion that is without repentance and without good works, as if true faith and an evil intention to persist and continue in sins could well be in one heart at the same time, which is impossible; or as if one could well have and keep true faith, righteousness, and salvation, even if he is and remains a lazy and unfruitful tree, from which no good fruits follow at all; indeed, even if he persists in sins against his conscience, or intentionally commits himself again to such sins; which is wrong and false. However, the reminder of this distinction must also be noted here, namely, that it should be understood as *necessitas ordinis, mandati et voluntatis Christi ac debiti nostri, non autem necessitas coactionis*; that is: when this word 'necessary' is used, it should not be understood as referring to compulsion, but solely to the order of the unchangeable will of God, whose debtors we are, to which also His command points, that the creature should be obedient to its Creator; for otherwise, as in 2 Corinthians 9:7 and in the Epistle of St. Paul to Philemon 14, likewise 1 Peter 5:2, that is called 'of necessity' which is extorted from one against his will, through compulsion or otherwise, so that he does it outwardly for appearance's sake, but yet without and against his will. For God does not want such sham works, but the people of the New Testament shall be a willing people, Psalm 110:3, and offer willingly, Psalm 54:6, not with reluctance or out of compulsion, but be obedient from the heart, 2 Corinthians 9:7, Romans 6:17; for God loves a cheerful giver, 2 Corinthians 9:7. In this sense and with such meaning, it is rightly said and taught that true good works are willing or out of

Damit wollen sie uns§re Affen sein, und uns nachlehren, weil sie gehört haben, dass wir lehren, gute Werke machen nicht fromm, tilgen auch die Sünde nicht, versöhnen auch Gott nicht. Ueber solches thut hier der Teufel seinen Zusatz, und verachtet die guten Werke so gar, dass er sie alle um einen Groschen verkaufen will. Da lobe ich Gott, meinen Herrn, dass der Teufel sich selbst in seiner Klugheit so schändlich muss beschmeissen und bethören. Wir lehren also, dass Gott versöhnen, fromm machen, Sünde tilgen, sei so hoch, gross, herrlich Werk, dass allein Christus, Gottes Sohn, thun müsse, und sei eigentlich ein lauter, bloss, sonderlieh Werk des einigen rechten Gottes und seiner Gnade, .dazu unsere Werke nichts sind noch vermögen. Aber dass darum gute Werke sollten nichts sein, oder eines Groschen werth sein, wer hat das je gelehret oder gehöret, ohne jetzt aus dem Lügenmaul des Teufels? Ich wollte meiner Predigt eine, meiner Lection eine, meiner Schrift eine, meiner Vater Unser eins, ja wie kleine Werke ich immer gethan oder noch thue, nicht für der ganzen Welt Güter geben; ja, ich achte es theurer, denn meines Leibes Leben, das doch einem Jeglichen lieber ist und sein soll, denn die ganze Welt. Denn ists ein gut Werk, so hats Gott durch mich und in mir gethan. Hats Gott gethan, und ist Gottes Werk, was ist die ganze Welt gegen Gott und sein Werk? Ob ich nun wohl durch solch Werk nicht fromm werde (denn das muss zuvor geschehen durch Christus Blut und Gnade, ohne Werk), dennoch ists Gott zu Lob und Ehren geschehen, dem Nächsten zu Nutz und Heil, welcher keines man mit der Welt Gut bezahlen oder vergleichen kann. Und diese feine Rotte nimmt einen Groschen dafür. Ah, wie fein hat sich der Teufel hier verborgen! Wer könnte ihn doch hier nicht greifen?“ (Vorrede zu Justi Menii Schrift: Der Wiedertäufer Lehre u. s. w. A. 1530. Tom. Hal. XIV, 281. sq.) PART. III. CAP. VI. Idem: ,,Dass wir dess etliche Gleichnisse geben, soll man die Werke eines Christenmenschen, der durch seinen Glauben und aus lauterer Gnade Gottes umsonst ist gerechtfertigt und selig worden, nicht anders achten, denn wie die Werke Adams und Evä im Paradies gewesen waren. Davon 1 Mos. 2, 15. stehet geschrieben: Dass,Gott den geschaffenen Menschen setzte in’s Paradies, dass er daselbst arbeiten und hüten sollte‘. Nun war Adam vor Gott fromm und wohlgeschaffen ohne Sünde, dass er durch sein Arbeiten und Hüten nicht durfte fromm und gerechtfertigt werden; doch dass er nicht müssig ginge, gab ihm Gott zu schaffen, das Paradies zu pflanzen, bauen und bewahren. Welches wären eitel freie Werke gewesen, um keines Dinges willen gethan, denn allein Gott zu gefallen, und nicht um Erömmigkeit zu erlangen, die er zuvor hatte; welche uns auch allen natürlich wäre angeboren gewesen. Also auch eines gläubigen Menschen Werk, welcher durch seinen Glauben ist wiederum in’s Paradies gesetzet und von neuem geschaffen, bedarf keiner Werke, fromm zu werden; sondern dass er nicht müssig gehe und sein Leib arbeite und bewahre, sind ihm solche freie Werke zu thun allein Gott zu gefallen befohlen.“ (Sermon von der Freiheit eines Christenmenschen. Tom. Hai. XIX. 1224. sq.) Formula Conc.: ,,Was belangt Nothwendigkeit oder Freiwilligkeit der guten Werke, ist offenbar, dass in der Augsburgischen Confession und derselben Apologia gebraucht und oft wiederholt werden diese Reden, dass gute Werke nöthig seien; item, dass es nöthig sei, gute Werke zu thun, welche auch nothwendig dem Glauben und der Versöhnung folgen sollen; item, dass wir noth wendig gute Werke, so Gott geboten, thun sollen und thun müssen. So wird auch in der heiligen Schrift selber das Wort noth, nöthig und noth wendig, item, sollen und müssen also gebraucht, was wir von wegen Gottes Ordnung, Befehl und Willen zu thun schuldig sind, als Röm. 13, 5. 1 Cor. 9, 16. Act. 5, 29. Joh. 15, 12. 1 Joh. 4, 21. Werden derhalben gemeldte Reden oder Propositiones in diesem christlichen und eigentlichen Verstand unbillig von etlichen gestraft und verworfen, welche billig, den sichern epikurischen Wahn zu strafen und zu verwerfen, sollen geführt und gebrauchet werden, da viele ihnen einen todten Glauben oder Wahn, der da ohne Busse und ohne gute Werke ist, dichten, als könnte wohl zugleich in einem Herzen sein rechter Glaube und böser Vorsatz, in Sünden zu verharren und fortzufahren, welches unmöglich ist; oder, als könnte wohl einer wahren Glauben, Gerechtigkeit und Seligkeit haben und behalten, wenn er gleich ein fauler und unfruchtbarer Baum ist und bleibet, da gar keine guten Früchte folgen; ja, wenn er gleich in Sünden wider das Gewissen verharret, oder wiederum sich auf solche Sünden vorsätzlich begibt; welches unrecht und falsch ist. Es muss aber auch die Erinnerung von diesem Unterschied hierbei gemerket werden, dass nämlich verstanden werden solle necessitas ordinis, mandati et voluntatis Christi ac debiti nostri, non autem necessitas coactionis; das ist: wenn dies Wort nöthig gebraucht, soll es nicht vop einem Zwang, sondern allein von der Ordnung des unwandelbaren Willens Gottes, dess Schuldner wir sind, verstanden werden, dahin auch sein Gebot weiset, dass die Kreatur ihrem Schöpfer gehorsam sei; denn sonst, wie 2 Cor. 9, 7. und in der Epistel St. Pauli an Philemonem 14., item 1 Petr. 5, 2., aus Noth genennet wird, was einem wider seinen Willen, durch Zwang oder sonst abgenöthigt wird, dass er äusserlich zum Schein, aber doch ohne und wider seinen Willen thue. Denn solche Schein werke will Gott nicht haben, sondern das Volk des neuen Testaments soll sein ein williges Volk, Ps. 110, 3., und willig opfern, Ps. 54, 8., nicht mit Unwillen oder aus Zwang, sondern von Herzen gehorsam sein, 2 Cor. 9, 7. Röm. 6, 17.; denn einen willigen Geber hat Gott lieb, 2 Cor. 9, 7. In diesem Verstand und solcher Meinung ists recht geredet und gelehret, dass rechte gute Werke willig oder aus


### On Renewal and Good Works: should be done with a willing spirit by those whom the Son of God has set free

should be done with a willing spirit by those whom the Son of God has set free; for it is with this meaning that the disputation concerning the voluntariness of good works has been conducted by some.” (Declar. art. 4. p. 627. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the ancient heretics, such as Simon Magus, the Gnostics, the Valentinians, Aetius, etc., who formerly permitted a free license for all crimes, as may be read in Irenaeus, book 1, ch. 9 and 24. 2. Of the Libertines among the Anabaptists, who permit the same license.

3. Of the Antinomians, who, partly while Luther was living and partly after his death, impugned the necessity of good works; for they taught that good works are not only not necessary, but even pernicious, see Formula of Concord, f. 591. sq. But since the Formula of Concord distinguishes between the necessity of coercion and the necessity of command and order, the Antinomians seem to speak only of a coercive necessity, and indeed to deny it in such a way that they say the regenerate perform from a spontaneous spirit what is commanded to the carnal by the Law. For thus they themselves speak in their latest confession: ‘

The question is, whether the Law is laid upon the righteous or the new man, etc.; whether the Law teaches the new man good works, demands them from him, requires them, asks for them; whether the Law is imposed upon him, proposed to him, to teach him what is to be done; or whether he who is created in Christ Jesus for good works does all things of the Law without the Law teaching, urging, or commanding,’ Catal. haeretic. 1. 4. p. 46, 49.

From which it appears that, although they denied the Law a coercive (βιαστικον) authority over the new man, they nevertheless did not make good works so free and arbitrary for him that it is all the same whether he works well or ill, but they derived them from his new nature and made them necessary by the force of natural consequence, so that, since he is a new creature in Christ Jesus, he cannot but do good works of his own accord.

But it is no wonder if fanatical men establish what is inconsistent (ἀσύστατα) and fight no less with themselves than with the truth.

Thus the blessed Luther, having rejected their false hypothesis concerning the elenchtic office of the Gospel, or that they might preach the spontaneous obedience of the regenerate, nevertheless accurately showed that from the removal of the Law, the most certain barbarism and most pestilential security and the subversion of all honest discipline follow, disp. 2 against the Antinomians.

Where the man of God rightly concludes from the removal of the Law to the removal of sin and to the license of life, in this manner: Where there is no Law, there is neither sin condemning, nor obligation to render obedience to God, nor necessary good works, but mere security and license; now, however, according to the Antinomians, there is no Law in the Church; therefore.

That it follows from their opinion that good works are not necessary is evident from the fact that, as has been said, the necessity of command is understood. But a command consists in the Law. Therefore, the Law being removed, the command is removed, and the necessity of working well by force of command is removed, etc.

4. Of Andreas Musculus, who contended that the proposition, ‘Good works are necessary,’ is not to be tolerated. For he claimed that the new obedience of the regenerate and their good works are free; which error, however, he acknowledged and revoked when he subscribed to the Formula of Concord.” (L. c. c. 9. s. 2. q. 4. f. 1400. sq.)

Yet good works are not necessary by way of cause, in relation to salvation.

And it is rightly to be avoided, just as that phrase by which it is said that good works are pernicious to salvation, so also this one, which says that good works are necessary to salvation.

For whatever may be the case regarding the interpretations or explanations by which either or both might be thought capable of being drawn into a convenient sense, it is nevertheless certain that they were rejected as ambiguous and long-suspected, and as “seeds of dissensions and scandals.”

Conf. regarding the latter phrase, the Preface of the blessed Musaeus to the Tract against Stenger, quire fol. 4. b. sqq.

Similarly, neither is that, strictly speaking, PART III. CHAPTER VI.

That it can be said that faith is preserved through the pursuit of holiness, or that life—or the acquired right to attain eternal life—is guarded by that very thing, is shown by the blessed Musaeus, *Ausführl. Erklärung* Loc. XIII. Q. 70. p. 578.

Formula of Concord: "Here one must take very good heed that works are not drawn into and mingled with the article of justification and salvation. Therefore, the propositions are rightly rejected that good works are necessary for the believers for salvation, in such a way that it is impossible to be saved without good works.

For they are directly contrary to the doctrine *de particulis exclusivis* [concerning the exclusive particles] in the article of justification and salvation; that is, they contend against the words with which St. Paul has entirely excluded our works and merit from the article of justification and salvation, and has ascribed everything solely to the grace of God and the merit of Christ, as explained in the preceding article.

Likewise, they take from tempted, troubled consciences the comfort of the Gospel, give cause for doubt, are dangerous in many ways, strengthen the presumption of one's own righteousness and trust in one's own works, are furthermore accepted by the Papists and used to their advantage against the pure doctrine of the alone-saving faith; thus they are also against the pattern of sound words, where it is written: 'Blessed is the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works,' Rom. 4:6. . . .

Therefore, and for the reasons just recounted, it should rightly remain the case in our churches that the aforementioned ways of speaking are not taught, defended, or excused, but are exposed and rejected from our churches as false and wrong, as those which, at the time of persecution—when the most clear, correct confession against all manner of *corruptelae* [corruptions] and falsification of the article of justification was necessary—were renewed, flowed forth, and were brought into dispute from the Interim.

Thirdly, because it is also disputed whether good works preserve salvation, or whether they are necessary to preserve faith, righteousness, and salvation, and yet much and a great deal depends upon this; for 'he who endures to the end will be saved,' Matt. 24:13; likewise, Heb. 3:6, 14: 'We have become partakers of Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of our confidence steadfast to the end': it must also be very well and properly explained how righteousness and salvation are preserved in us, so that they are not lost again. . . .

On the other hand, however, it is not the meaning that faith alone grasps righteousness and salvation in the beginning and thereafter hands over its office to works, so that the same must henceforth preserve faith, the received righteousness, and salvation; but, in order that the promise of righteousness and salvation—not only to be received, but also to be kept—may be firm and certain for us, Paul, in Rom. 5:2, gives to faith not only the access to grace, but also that we stand in grace and rejoice in the hope of the glory to come; that is: beginning, middle, and end, he gives everything to faith alone. Likewise Rom. 11:20: 'They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand through faith.' Col. 1:22: 'He will present you holy and blameless before himself, if indeed you continue in the faith.' 1 Pet. 1:5, 9: 'We are kept by the power of God through faith for salvation'; likewise: 'You will receive the end of your faith, namely, the salvation of souls.'

Since it is therefore manifest from God's Word that faith is the proper and only means by which righteousness and salvation are not only received, but also preserved by God, that which was concluded in the Council of Trent and whatever else is directed toward the same opinion—that our good works preserve salvation, or that the received righteousness of faith or even faith itself..."

[...are] either entirely or at least in part obtained and preserved by our works. For although before this controversy some very pure teachers used such and similar expressions in the interpretation of Holy Scripture, yet they by no means intended thereby to confirm the aforementioned errors of the Papists; however, because subsequently a dispute arose over such a way of speaking, from which all sorts of scandalous complications followed, it is safest, according to the admonition of St. Paul, to hold to the pattern of sound words as well as to the pure doctrine itself, whereby much unnecessary wrangling may be cut off and the Church may be guarded against much offense.” (Declar: art. 4. p. 628. sq. 629. sq.) Huelsemannus: “'Necessary for obtaining something' in common usage denotes the necessity of a means for obtaining something, which we deny regarding good works for obtaining salvation.” (Praelect. F. C. p. 572.) Quenstedtius: “Good works are not, nor can or ought they to be called, necessary for salvation, whether for meriting it by way of merit, or acquiring it by way of a means, or obtaining it by way of a condition or a cause without which it is not, or attaining it by way of perfection toward the final goal.” (L. c. q. 5. f. 1403.) The same: “Distinguish between necessity for a true and living faith, and necessity for salvation.

We concede that good works can be called necessary for faith in a certain way; partly as regards the truth of knowing, or so that faith may be known from them. . . , partly as regards the attainment or by reason of consequence.” (L. c. f. 1404.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis:

1. Of the Papists, who teach that good works are necessary not only by reason of presence, but also by reason of efficiency for acquiring, meriting, and preserving salvation; thus Bellarmine, bk. 4, *de justificat.*, ch. 7, th. 2, 3, whom the rest of the Papists follow.

2. Of the Calvinists, such as Piscator on Luke 2:28, asserting that our good works are the procreative causes of blessedness; Jacobus ad Portum in *orthod. fidei defens.*, 33, p. 432, 433, that they are its efficient causes; Pareus in bk. 4 of Bellarmine *de justific.*, ch. 7, that good works are necessary for salvation by the necessity of a means and of a condition, without which there is no righteousness and salvation; Zanchius, bk. 5, *de natura Dei*, ch. 2, qu. 3, *de praed. sanctor.*, p. 630, that good works are the instrumental cause of salvation and the possession of eternal life; Molinaeus in *anatomia Arminianismi*, ch. 17, § 10, p. 110, that the pursuit of good works is no less a prerequisite condition for salvation than faith.
