freiwilligem Geist von denen, die der Sohn Gottes gefreiet (hat), geschehen sollen; wie denn auf diese Meinung vornehmlich die Disputation von Freiwilligkeit der guten Werke von etlichen geführet ist.“. (Declar. art. 4. p. 627. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Antiquorum haereticorum, ut S1monis magi, Gnosticorum, Valentinianorum, Aetii etc., qui liberam omnium scelerum licentiam olim permiserunt, ut legere est apud Irenaeum 1.1. c. 9. et 24. 2. Libertinorum inter anabaptistas, eandem licentiam permittentium.

3. Antinomorum, qui, partim vivente Luthero, partim post ejus obitum, necessitatem bonorum operum impugnarunt; docuerunt enim, bona opera non modo non necessaria esse, sed etiam perniciosa, v. Formul. Concord. f. 591. sq. Cum autem Formula Concordiae inter coactionis et inter mandati atque ordinis necessitatem distinguat, videntur antinomi de necessitate solum coactiya loqui, et eam quidem ita negare, ut renatos ex spiritu spontaneo praestare dicant, quod carnalibus a lege imperatur. Sic enim illi ipsi in sua novissima confessione loquuntur. ,

Quaeritur, an justo seu novo homini lex sit posita etc.; an lex novum hominem doceat bona opera, exigat ab illo, requirat, postulet bona opera; an illi lex imponatur, proponatur, ut doceat facienda; an vero sine lege docente, urgente, mandante faciat legis omnia conditus in Christo Jesu ad bona opera‘, Catal. haeretic. 1. 4. p. 46. 49.

Ex quibus apparet, eos, licet legi imperium βιαστικον in hominem novum denegarint, ei tamen bona opera ita libera et arbitraria non fecisse, ut perinde sit, sive bene, sive male operetur, sed illa ex nova illius indole deduxisse et vi consequentiae naturalis necessaria fecisse, ut, cum nova creatura sit in Christo Jesu, non possit non ultro bona opera facere.

Sed mirum non est, si homines fanatici ασύστατη statuant et secum ipsis non minus ac cum veritate pugnent.

Ita b. Lutherus, rejecta falsa ipsorum hypothesi de officio evangelii elenchtico, aut ut illi spontaneam renatorum obedientiam praedicarent, accurate tamen ostendit, ex legis exauctoratione certissimam barbariem et pestilentissimam securitatem omnisque honestae disciplinae convulsionem sequi, disp. 2. contra antinomos.

Ubi vir Dei recte coneludit a remotione legis ad remotionem peccati et ad licentiam vitae, in hunc fere modum: Ubi non est lex, ibi nec peccatum damnans nec obligatio ad obedientiam Deo praestandam nec necessaria bona opera, sed mera securitas et licentia; jam vero secundum antinomos in ecclesia non est lex; ergo.

Quod vero ex illorum sententia sequatur, quod bona opera non sint necessaria, inde patet, quia intelligitur, uti dictum, necessitas mandati. Mandatum autem consistit in lege. Quare sublata lege sublatum est mandatum, sublata necessitas vi mandati bene operandi etc.

4. Andreae Musculi, contendentis, non ferendam illam propositionem: ,Bona opera sunt necessaria‘. Novam quippe obedientiam renatorum, bonaque eorum opera esse libera; quem tamen errorem agnovit et revocavit, quando Formulae Concordiae subscripsit.“ (L. c. c. 9. s. 2. q. 4. f. 1400. sq.)

Non tamen necessaria sunt bona opera per modum causae, in ordine ad salutem.

Ac merito abstinendum est, sicut ab ea phrasi, qua dicitur, bona opera esse perniciosa ad salutem, ita etiam ab hac, quae dicit, bona opera esse necessaria ad salutem.

Quicquid enim sit de interpretationibus aut explicationibus, quibus alterutra aut utraque in commodum sensum, trahi posse putetur, certum tamen est, ambiguas,ac pridem suspectas et, tanquam dissidiorum et scandalorum semina/ rejectas fuisse.

Conf. de posteriore phrasi b. Musaei Praef. Tract. contra Stenger. quatern. fol. 4. b. sqq.

Similiter nec illud proprie loquendo PART. III. CAP. VI.

dici posse, quod fides per sanctimoniae studium conservetur aut vita sive acquisitum jus adeundae vitae aeternae per id ipsum custodiatur, ostendit b. Musaeus Ausführl. Erklärung Loc. XIII. Q. 70. p. 578.

Formula Conc.: ,,Hie muss man sich gar wohl vorsehen, dass die Werke nicht in den Artikel der Rechtfertigung und Seligmachung gezogen und eingemengt werden. Derhalben werden billig die Propositiones verworfen, dass den Gläubigen gute Werke zur Seligkeit vonnöthen seien, also, dass es unmöglich sei, ohne gute Werke selig‘ werden.

Denn sie sind stracks wider die Lehre de particulis exclusivis in articulo justificationis et salvationis, das ist, sie streiten wider die Worte, mit welchen St. Paulus unsere Werke und Verdienst aus dem Artikel der Rechtfertigung und Seligmachung gänzlich ausgeschlossen und alles allein der Gnade Gottes und dem Verdienst Christi zugeschrieben hat, wie in dem vorhergehenden Artikel erkläret.

Item, sie nehmen den angefochtenen betrübten Gewissen den Trost des Evangelii, geben Ursache zum Zweifel, sind in viel Wege gefährlich, stärken die Vermessenheit eigener Gerechtigkeit und das Vertrauen auf eigene Werke, werden dazu von den Papisten angenommen und zu ihrem Vortheil wider die reine Lehre von dem allein seligmachenden Glauben geführt; so sind sie auch wider das Vorbild der gesunden Worte, da geschrieben stehet: ,Die Seligkeit sei allein des Menschen, welchem Gott zurechnet die Gerechtigkeit, ohne Zuthun der Werke‘, Röm. 4, 6. . . .

Demnach und aus jetzt erzählten Ursachen soll es billig in unsern Kirchen dabei bleiben, dass nämlich gemeldte Weisen zu reden nicht gelehret, vertheidigt oder beschönet, sondern aus unsern Kirchen als falsch und unrecht ausgesetzt und verworfen werden, als die zur Zeit der Verfolgung, da am meisten klare, richtige Bekenntniss wider allerlei corruptelas und Verfälschung des Artikels der Rechtfertigung vonnöthen war, aus dem Interim wiederum verneuert, hergeflossen und in Disputation gezogen sind.

Zum dritten, weil auch disputirt wird, ob gute Werke die Seligkeit erhalten, oder ob sie nöthig seien, dQU Glauben, Gerechtigkeit und Seligkeit zu erhalten, und aber hieran hoch und viel gelegen; denn,werverharret bis ans Ende, wird selig werden“, Matth. 24, 13.; item, Ebr. 3, 6. 14: ,Wir sind Christus theilhaftig worden, so wir anders das angefangene Wesen bis ans Ende fest behalten‘: muss auch gar wohl und eigentlich erklärt werden, wie die Gerechtigkeit und Seligkeit in uns erhalten, dass sie nicht wiederum verloren werden. . .

Dagegen aber hat es die Meinung nicht, dass der Glaube allein im Anfang die Gerechtigkeit und Seligkeit ergreife und darnach sein Amt den Werken übergebe, dass dieselbigen hinfürder den Glauben, die empfangene Gerechtigkeit und Seligkeit erhalten müssten, sondern, auf dass die Verheissung der Gerechtigkeit und Seligkeit, nicht allein zu empfangen, sondern auch zu behalten, uns fest und gewiss sein möge, gibt Paulus Röm. 5, 2. dem Glauben nicht allein den Eingang zur Gnade, sondern auch, dass wir in der Gnade stehen, und uns rühmen der zukünftigen Herrlichkeit, das ist: Anfang, Mittel und Ende gibt er alles dem Glauben allein. Item Röm. 11, 20.: ,Sie sind abgebrochen um ihres Unglaubens willen, du aber stellest durch den Glauben.‘ Col. 1, 22.: ,Er wird euch darstellen heilig und unsträflich vor ihm selbst, so ihr anders bleibet im Glauben.‘ 1 Petr. 1, 5. 9.: ,Wir werden aus Gottes Macht durch den Glauben bewahret zur Seligkeit‘; item: ,Ihr werdet das Ende eures Glaubens davon bringen, nämlich der Seelen Seligkeit.‘

Weil denn aus Gottes Wort offenbar, dass der Glaube das eigentliche einige Mittel ist, dadurch Gerechtigkeit und Seligkeit nicht allein empfangen, sondern auch von Gott erhalten wird, soll billig verworfen werden, das im Trientischen Concilio geschlossen und was sonst mehr auf dieselbige Meinung ist gerichtet worden, dass unsere guten Werke die Seligkeit erhalten, oder dass die empfangene Gerechtigkeit des Glaubens oder auch der Glaube selbst

durch unsere Werke entweder gänzlich oder ja zum Theil erhalten und bewahret werden. Denn obwohl vor diesem Streit etliche viel reine Lehrer solche und dergleichen Reden in Auslegung der heiligen Schrift gebraucht, hiemit aber keineswegs gesinnet, obvermeldte Irrthümer der Papisten zu bestätigen: jedoch, weil nachmals über solcher Weise zu reden Streit entstanden, daraus allerlei ärgerliche Weiterung erfolgete, ist es am allersichersten, nach der Vermahnung St. Pauli, über dem Vorbilde der gesunden Worte sowohl, als über <jer reinen Lehre selbst zu halten, dadurch viel unnöthiges Gezänks abgeschnitten und die Kirche vor vielem Aergerniss behütet werden mag.“ (Declar: art. 4. p. 628. sq. 629. sq.) Huelsemannus: ,,Necessarium ad consequendum aliquid communi significatu notat necessitatem medii ad consequendum aliquid, quam de bonis operibus ad salutem consequendam negamus.“ (Praelect. F. C. p. 572.) Quenstedtius: ,,Bona opera non sunt nec dici possunt aut debent necessaria ad salutem, vel promerendam per modum meriti, vel acquirendam per modum medii, vel consequendam per modum conditionis vel causae sine qua non, vel obtinendam per modum pervectio· nis ad ultimam metam.u (L. c. q. 5. f. 1403.) Idem: ״Dist. inter necessitatem ad fidem veram ac vivam, et necessitatem ad salutem. Concedimus, bona opera dici quodammodo posse necessaria ad fidem; partim quoad veritatem cognoscendi seu ut fides inde cognoscatur. . . , partim quoad consecutionem sive ratione consequentiae.“ (L. c. f. 1404.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis:

1. Pontificiorum, docentium, bona opera esse necessaria non solum ratione praesentiae, sed etiam ratione efficientiae ad acquirendam, promerendam et conservandam salutem; ita Bellarminus 1. 4. de justificat, c. 7. th. 2. 3., quem sequuntur reliqui pontificii.

2. Calvinianorum, ut Piscatoris in Luc. 2, 28. asserentis, bona nostra opera esse beatitudinis causas procreantes; Jacobi ad Portum in orthod, fidei defens. 33. p. 432.433., esse causas ejusdem efficien· tes; Parei in 1.

4. Bellarmini de justiflc. c. 7., bona opera esse necessaria ad salutem necessitate medii et conditionis, sine qua non est justitia et salus; Zanchii 1. 5. de natura Dei c. 2. qu. 3. de praed. sanctor, p. 630., bona opera esse causam instrumentalem salutis et possessionis vitae aeternae; Molinaei in anatomia Arminianismi c. 17. § 10. p. 110., studium bonorum operum non minus esse conditionem praerequisitam ad salutem, quam fidem. Sam. Maresius quoque, hanc propositionem, bona opera esse necessaria ad salutem, non esse rejiciendam, arbitratur in system. loc. 12. th.


### On Renewal and Good Works: Sam. Maresius also thinks that this proposition, that good works are necessary…

Sam. Maresius also thinks that this proposition, that good works are necessary for salvation, is not to be rejected, in *system. loc.* 12, th. 11 Ludovicus Crocius in *syntagm.*, p. 1213, says: ‘If (good works) in all adults have the character of a way, a means, a condition, a cause without which it is not, or a necessary antecedent for blessedness, how will they not be necessary for salvation?’ 3 Of the Socinians, who also require good works from those to be saved as necessary for salvation. Smalcius, *disp.* 2, *de poenit.*, ch. Franzium, f. 356, says: ‘It is therefore an absurdity to Franz that the very evangelical truth and its chief part should be considered to be that good works are necessary for salvation.’ 4 Of the Arminians, who indeed contend that faith is necessary for salvation, but because by faith they understand, with the Socinians, obedience to the commandments of God, whence it follows that obedience rendered to the divine command is necessary in the same way that faith is necessary; see the preceding chapter on faith, s. 2, qu. 3. 5 Of D. Georgius Major, Professor at Wittenberg, a contemporary and colleague of the blessed Luther and Philip Melanchthon, and also a disciple of the latter, who after Luther’s death, due to the Interimistic and Adiaphoristic controversies, was led to establish the necessity of good works for salvation and to defend not only that one proposition, that good works are necessary for salvation, but also the other two [propositions] prior to it... PART III. CHAP. VI. added worse things, namely, that it is impossible for anyone to be saved without good works, and that no man has ever been saved without good works. Dr. Major also added that he would judge and pronounce anathema upon anyone who teaches and thinks otherwise, even if he were an angel from heaven. . . Nicolaus Amsdorf, a Lutheran theologian, opposed Dr. Georg Major and disputed against him in public writings; but while he attempted to overturn Dr. Major’s false propositions, he struck the other extreme and defended this absurd opinion: that good works are pernicious to salvation; which opinion, no less than that of Dr. Major, was disapproved and rejected by sincere theologians, as Dr. Osiander teaches more fully in his epitome of ecclesiastical history. The Misnian or Electoral Saxon theologians followed Dr. Major against the Thuringian or Ducal theologians at the Colloquy of Altenburg in the year 1568. . . 6 Of the innovators, especially Dr. Com. Hornejus, who cooked up this Majoristic cabbage anew and championed that phrase and doctrine, as is evident from their writings. See Dr. Hornejus, P. 2, disp. theol., disp. 4, s. 3, th. 173. . . Dr. Georg Calixtus in his history of Joseph, p. 14 sq., where he says: "Acts of abstinence from adulteries, homicides, and the remaining works of the flesh are necessary for having or obtaining the heavenly kingdom"; p. 16: he says that "good works in order to acquire salvation are a cause without which it is not"; in his moral theology, p. 3, 4, he says: "the pursuit of piety and holiness is a medium upon which the preservation of faith and the state of grace and the attainment of the end, namely eternal life, depend." Cf. the preface of the same to his dissertation on the knowledge of the Trinity in the O.T., and Dreier in his *Erörterung* [Discussion], p. 566. (L. c. qu. 5, f. 1406.) Apology of the A.C.: "We teach that rewards are proposed and promised to the works of the faithful. We teach that good works are meritorious, not of the remission of sins, of grace, or of justification—for these we obtain only by faith—but of other bodily and spiritual rewards, in this life and after this life." (Art. 4, p. 120.) Luther: "Christ speaks in this sermon (Matt. 5–7) nothing about how we become Christians, but only about the works and fruits which no one can do unless he is already a Christian and in grace; as the words show, that they must suffer poverty, misery, and persecution because they are Christians and have the kingdom of heaven, etc. Now, when one speaks of such fruits, which follow after grace and the forgiveness of sin, we are well content that one calls them merit and reward: but we contend that such works of ours are not the principal good, which must be present beforehand, and without which they neither happen nor please God. If we only keep this point pure, that it is not merit but sheer grace, we will not fight over whether one gives the following fruits that name; only that one does not falsely pervert such passages and draw them against Scripture toward our merit of grace, but interprets them rightly, where they belong, to comfort Christians especially in suffering and opposition, where it is felt and appears as if our life, suffering, and doing were in vain and accomplished nothing; as Scripture comforts everywhere where it exhorts to persevere in good works, as in Jeremiah 31: *Est merces operi tuo*, your work is not in vain; likewise St. Paul, 1 Cor. 15: *Labor vester non est inanis in Domino*, your labor is not in vain in the Lord. For if we did not have this comfort, we could not endure such misery, persecution, and wretchedness, that we should do so much good and have our teaching and preaching repaid with sheer ingratitude and disgrace; and we would finally have to desist from such works and sufferings as we encounter before our eyes... In this way, we now allow that Christians have merit and reward with God: not so that they may become God’s children and heirs of eternal life, but for the comfort of believers who already possess this, so that they know that He does not wish to leave unrewarded what they..."

here suffer for Christ’s sake: but rather, when they suffer and labor much, He desires to adorn them especially on the Last Day, more and more gloriously than others, as special great stars before others. Thus St. Paul will shine forth brightly and clearly before others in the most beautiful way. That is not called forgiveness of sin, nor earning heaven, but a recompense of suffering with greater glory. But we will not tolerate it there, where they place it; for that is to disgrace and blaspheme Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit, and everything that God has given us through Him, and we would rather be called heretics and knaves and be burned with fire than abandon or deny such a treasure: rather, we want to hold to this comfort, even if we must suffer every plague, disgrace, and persecution on account of it. For nothing else will come of it. For the devil will not concede such things to us, nor come to an agreement with us; but he wants to maintain the Pope’s doctrine and bring us to believe as he believes; and because he sees that we do not want to, he sets himself against us with all his might. For he knows well that if the article stands—that the forgiveness of sin and Christ is a pure gift—then everyone can well count on their fingers and conclude that the Papacy with its masses, monkery, purgatory, saint-worship, etc., must be nothing, and everything falls away of itself. So learn now to answer such passages where it speaks of merit and reward. I hear well that Christ says: Blessed are the poor, for they shall have the kingdom of heaven; and: Blessed are you when you suffer persecution for my sake; for your reward is great in heaven, etc. But with that, He does not teach me to build the foundation of my salvation, but gives me a promise of what comfort I should have from it in my suffering and Christian life. You must not make a mixture for me there, and brew the two together, nor make my merit out of that which God gives me in Christ, through Baptism and the Gospel. For it does not stand here that I can earn such things, and need no Christ and Baptism for it; but that those who are Christ’s disciples, to whom He has preached here, and who must suffer all kinds of things for His sake, know what they have to comfort themselves with, because people on earth do not want to tolerate them, that they shall have everything all the more abundantly in heaven for it; and whoever works and suffers the most shall also have the more glorious recompense.” (Exposition of the 5th, 6th, and 7th Chapters of Matthew. A. 1532. Tom. Hal. VII, 969. sq. 972. sq.) Gerhard: "That to which the properties of merit do not pertain cannot be meritorious. But the properties of merit do not pertain to our good works; therefore, they cannot be meritorious. The assumption is proven in this way: The nature and definition of merit require these four things:

1. That the work by which we merit be our own. For that which we do not bring forth from the shrine and grove of our own powers, but obtain from the liberality of another, cannot be used to merit his gifts; rather, we are merely rendering a due service.

2. That it be an undue work. For that which is already owed beforehand does not bind the one to whom it is rendered to new benefits. It is a contradiction to render a work owed to someone and, by that work already owed, to merit something. One must be quite impudent to demand a reward as if one had merited well for doing that which one was already obligated to pay.

3. That it be useful and advantageous to the one to whom it is rendered; for if no utility accrues to another from our work, he will never acknowledge it as a merit.

4. That it be equal in both price and dignity to that which is rendered for our work. For if there is a certain inequality between the labor and the wage, between the work and the reward, then merit *ex condigno* (from worthiness) has no place. A minister distributing alms in the name of a prince does not merit anything by that act, because he does not give from his own. He who pays a wage to a laborer does not merit anything from him, because he gives nothing that he does not already owe. He who gives a cup of water to a thirsty king, if he were gifted a city by him, could not be said to have merited such a great gift by his own liberality, since between what was given and what was received PART III. CAP. VI. there is no proportion. Now, however, good works 1. are not our own, but are the works of God effectively acting in us through His Spirit... 2. Our good works are already owed to God beforehand on many accounts by the right of creation, preservation, dominion, redemption, sanctification, etc. Indeed, whatever we do is not the whole of what we owe to God, but only a certain part of our duty toward God; therefore, 'if we were to do even all that has been commanded us, we would still have to say that we are unprofitable servants' (Luke 17:10). Therefore, since our works are already owed to God beforehand, the reward is not rendered to them as a debt. If works are owed, the reward is not owed; if the reward is owed, the works are not owed. 3. Our works bring no utility to God (Job 22:2-3; Ps. 50:12)... 4. There is no equality between our works and eternal life, which is an infinite good. 'The sufferings are not worthy (τὰ παθήματα οὐκ ἄξια) of the future glory' (Rom. 8:18). Therefore, neither are works worthy... To the first man, the possession of eternal life would have been rendered for his holy obedience toward God and for his perseverance in good works; meanwhile, however, if we wish to speak properly and accurately, that obedience of the first man would not have been meritorious of eternal life, since it was already owed beforehand, since no advantage accrued to God from it, and since no proportion exists between temporal obedience and eternal blessedness. What presumptuous audacity, then, is it to ascribe to man after the fall—who, though indeed renewed by the Spirit of God, is meanwhile still in part carnal and sold under sin—that which would not even have pertained to him in the state of integrity?" (*Loci de bonis operibus* § 102.) Formula of Concord: "The works which belong to the maintenance of outward discipline, which are also done and required of the unbelieving and unconverted, although they are praiseworthy before the world and are also rewarded by God in this world with temporal goods, yet, because they do not proceed from true faith, they are sin before God, etc." (Declar. art. 4, p. 626.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who assert that the aids of actual grace and justification itself can be merited by good works *ex congruo* [by congruity]. . . Likewise, they maintain that the good works of the justified are truly meritorious of eternal life. The Council of Trent, sess. 6, can. 16, while it confesses that good works are gifts of God, nevertheless insists that they are merits of the justified man and strikes with anathema those who think otherwise. . . Regarding this merit of eternal life, the Papists speak in various ways. For some are more moderate, others more crude. The former assert that eternal life is obtained at least by merit *de congruo* [by congruity]. . . Hence that distinction was born, by which it is said that good works have the power of meriting not of themselves, but from the merit of Christ and insofar as they are tinctured by the blood of the Redeemer. . . The cruder ones are those who say that the good works of the just are meritorious of eternal life *ex condigno* [by condignity] by reason of the work performed out of grace, by its intrinsic value so constituted that eternal life is owed to it as an equivalent price, even if God had not stipulated that He would receive those works as such a merit; thus Cajetan. . . And Vasquez judges this opinion to be more probable and more agreeable to Catholic doctrine. This Jesuit (Vasquez) has rubbed off all shame and so deals with God that he owes Him nothing and attributes solid praise to himself for his own salvation. His words in the place already cited are these: 'It is more agreeable to Catholic doctrine that the primary value and dignity of eternal life should be ascribed to the works of the just without any pact or favor.' And a little later he adds: 'No accession of dignity comes to the works of the just from the merits of Christ or from His person.' 2. Of the Arminians, who maintain that good works have no proportion to eternal life if they are considered in themselves, yet they do have it if they are accepted by God out of grace and are estimated κατ' επιείκειαν [according to equity], in *Confessio*, ch. 18, p. 3." (L. c. q. 6, f. 1421, sq.)

Socinianorum, qui etiam bona opera a salvandis tanquam ad salutem necessaria requirunt. . . Smalcius disp. 2. de poenit. c. D. Georgii Majoris, Profess. Witteberg., b. Lutheri et Philip. Melanchthonis σνγχρόνον et collegae, illius etiam discipuli, qui post Lutheri mortem ex interimisticis et adiaphoristicis contentionibus eo adductus fuit, ut bonorum operum necessitatem ad salutem statueret et non solum illam unam propositionem defenderet, quod bona opera ad salutem sint necessaria, sed et reliquas duas priori PART. III. CAP. VI. deteriores apponeret, nempe, quod impossibile sit, sine bonis operibus quenquam salvari, nec unquam ullum hominem sine bonis operibus esse salvatum. Addidit quoque D. Major, se anathema judicaturum et pronunciaturum eum, qui aliter doceät ac sentiat, etiamsi sit angelus de coelo. . . Opposuit sese D. Horneji, qui crambem hanc Majoristicam denuo recoxerunt et pro phrasi et doctrina illa propugnarunt, ut patet ex illorum scriptis. Vid. D. Horneji P. 2. disp. theol. disp. 4. s. 3. th. 173.. . D. Georg. Galixtus in historia Josephi p. 14. sq., ubi inquit: ,Actus abstinentiae ab adulteriis, homicidiis et reliquis operibus carnis ad habendum vel obtinendum regnum coeleste sunt necessarii‘; p. 16.: ,bona opera in ordine ad salutem acquirendam‘, dicit, ,causam esse sine qua non‘; in theol. morali p. 3. 4. ait: ,studium pietatis et sanctimoniae esse medium, a quo conservatio fidei et status gratiae ac consecutio finis, vitae sc. aeternae, pendeat.‘ Cf. ejusdem praefat. dissert. de Trinitatis in V. T. cognitione et Dreierum in der Erörterung p. 566.“ (L. c. qu. 5. f. 1406.) Apologia A. C.: ,,Docemus, operibus fidelium proposita et promissa esse praemia. Docemus, bona opera meritoria esse, non remissionis peccatorum, gratiae aut justificationis, haec enim tantum fide consequimur, sed aliorum praemiorum corporalium et spiritualium, in hac vita et post hanc vitam.“ (Art. 4. p. 120.) Lutherus: ,,Christus redet in dieser Predigt (Matth. 5—7.) Nichts davon, wie wir Christen werden, sondern allein von den Werken und Früchten, die niemand thun kann, denn der zuvor ein Christ, und in der Gnade ist; wie die Worte zeigen, d^iss sie müssen Armuth, Elend, Verfolgung darüber leiden, dass sie Christen sein, und das Himmelreich haben u. s. w. Wenn man nun von solchen Früchten redet, so da folgen nach,der Gnade und Vergebung der Sünde, so lassen wir wohl geschehen, dass mans einen Verdienst und Lohn heisse: aber da fechten wir, dass solche unsere Werke nicht das Hauptgut seien, welches zuvor muss da sein, und ohne welches sie nicht geschehen, noch Gott gefallen. Wenn wir nur das Stück rein erhalten, dass es nicht Verdienst, sondern eitel Gnade sei, so wollen wir nicht fechten, ob man den folgenden Früchten den Namen gebe; allein, dass man solche Sprüche nicht fälschlich verkehre, und wider die Schrift auf unser Verdienst der Gnade ziehe, sondern recht deute, dahin sie gehören, zu trösten die Christen sonderlich in Leiden und Widerstand, da sichs fühlet und scheinet, als sollte unser Leben, Leiden und Thun vergebens sein und Nichts schaffen; wie die Schrift allenthalben tröstet, wo sie vermahnet anzuhalten an guten Werken, als Jeremiä 31.: Est merces operi tuo, deine Arbeit ist nicht umsonst; item St. Paulus 1 Cor. 15.: Labor vester non est inanis in Domino, eure Arbeit ist nicht vergeblich in dem Herrn. Denn so wir den Trost nicht hätten, so könnten wir nicht ertragen solch Jammer, Verfolgung und Elend, dass wir so viel Gutes thun sollten, und unser Lehren und Predigen mit eitel Undank und Schmach bezahlen lassen; und müssten aufs Letzte von solchen Werken und Leiden, so uns unter Augen stosset, ablassen. . . Auf diese Weise lassen wir nun zu, dass die Christen Verdienst und Lohn bei Gott haben: nicht dazu, dass sie Gottes Kinder und Erben des ewigen Lebens werden, sondern den Gläubigen, die bereits solches haben, zu Trost, dass sie wissen, dass er nicht wolle unvergolten lassen, was sie

hie um Christi willen leiden: sondern, wenn sie viel leiden und arbeiten, so wolle er sie am jüngsten Tage sonderlich schmücken, mehr und herrlicher, denn Andere, als sonderliche grosse Sterne vor Andern. Also wird St. Paulus vor Andern hell und klar daher leuchten aufs allerschönste. Das heisset nicht Vergebung der Sünde, noch den Himmel verdienet, sondern Vergeltung des Leidens mit desto grösserer Herrlichkeit. Aber da wollen wirs nicht leiden, da sie es hinsetzen; denn das ist Christum, Gott und den Heiligen Geist geschändet und gelästert, und Alles, was uns Gott durch ihn gegeben hat, und wollen lieber Ketzer und Buben gescholten und mit Feuer verbrannt werden, denn solchen Schatz verlassen oder verleugnen: sondern wollen uns auch dieses Trostes halten, ob wir wohl drüber leiden müssen alle Plage, Schmach und Verfolgung. Denn es wird doch nichts Anderes draus. Denn der Teufel wird uns solches nicht einräumen, noch mit uns eins werden; sondern will des Pabstes Lehre erhalten, und uns dazu bringen, dass wir glauben, wie er glaubt; und weil er siehet, dass wir nicht wollen, legt er sich wider uns mit aller Macht. Denn er weiss wohl, wenn der Artikel stehet, dass die Vergebung der Sünde und Christus ein lauter Geschenk ist, dass ein jeglicher darnach wohl an Fingern rechnen und schliessen kann, dass das Pabstthum mit seinen Messen, Möncherei, Fegfeuer, Heiligendienst u. s. w. Nichts sein muss, und Alles dahin fällt von sich selbst. So lerne nun auf solche Sprüche antWorten, wo vom Verdienst und Lohn stehet. Ich höre wohl, dass Christus spricht: Selig sind die Armen, denn sie sollen das Himmelreich haben; und: Selig seid ihr, wenn ihr um meinetwillen Verfolgung leidet; denn euer Lohn ist gross im Himmel u. s. w. Aber damit lehret er mich nicht den Grund meiner Seligkeit bauen, sondern gibt mir eine Verheissung, was ich für Trost davon haben soll in meinem Leiden und christlichen Leben. Da musst du mir nicht ein Gemenge machen, und die zwei unter einander brauen, noch mein Verdienst machen aus dem, was mir Gott gibt in Christo, durch die Taufe und Evangelium. Denn es stehet nicht hie, dass ich Solches verdienen könne, und keines Christus und Taufe dazu bedürfe; sondern dass die, so Christus Schüler sind, welchen er hie gepredigt hat, und um seinetwillen Allerlei leiden müssen, wissen, wess sie sich zu trösten haben, weil man sie auf Erden nicht leiden will, dass sie dafür im Himmel desto reichlicher sollen Alles haben; und wer am meisten arbeitet und leidet, soll auch desto herrlichere Vergeltung haben.“ (Auslegung des 5. 6. u. 7. Cap. Matthäi. A. 1532. Tom. Hal. VII, 969. sq. 972. sq.) Gerhardus: ,,Cui non competunt proprietates meriti, illud non potest esse meritorium. Atqui bonis operibus nostris non competunt proprietates meriti, ergo non possunt esse meritoria. Assumptum probatur hoc modo: Meriti natura et ratio postulat haec quatuor:

1. Ut opus illud, quo meremur, sit nostrum. Quod enim non afferimus ex nostrarum virium phano ac luco, sed ex alterius liberalitate obtinemus, per illud non possumus dona ejus mereri, sed debitum obsequium tantummodo reddimus.

2. Ut sit opus indebitum. Quod enim jam ante debitum est, illud non obstringit ad nova beneficia eum, cui ex debito praestatur. Contradictoria haec sunt, opus debitum alicui exhibere, et opere illo jam ante debito aliquid mereri. Admodum impudens sit oportet, qui quasi bene meritus praemium ob id poscit, quod debita solvit.

3. Ut sit utile atque commodum illi, cui praestatur; si enim ex opere nostro nulla accedit alteri utilitas, nunquam id pro merito agnoscet.

4. Ut sit et pretio et dignitate aequale illi, quod pro opere nostro redditur. Si enim inaequalitas quaedam est inter laborem et mercedem, inter opus et praemium, tunc meritum ex condigno non habet locum. Minister principis nomine distribuens eleemosynam non meretur ea re qüippiam, quia non dat de suo. Qui solvit mercedem laboranti, non meretur quippiam apud eum, quia nihil dat, quod nisi debet. Qui regi sitienti dat phialam aquae, si ab eo donaretur civitate, non posset dici liberalitate sua tantum donum meruisse, cum inter datum et acceptum PART. III. CAP. VI. nulla sit proportio. Jam vero opera bona 1. non sunt nostra, sed Dei per Spiritum suum in nobis efficaciter agentis opera. . . 2. Opera nostra bona jam ante multis nominibus Deo sunt debita jure creationis, conservationis, dominii, redemptionis, sanctificationis etc. Imo quicquid agimus, non est totum id, quod Deo debemus, sed nostri erga Deum officii pars duntaxat quaedam; proinde,si vel maxime omnia, quae praecepta nobis sunt, faceremus, tamen dicendum nobis foret, quod simus servi inutiles.‘ Luc. 17, 10. Ergo cum nostra opera sunt jam ante Deo debita, merces non redditur illis ex debito. Si opera sunt debita, merces est indebita; si merces est debita, opera sunt indebita. 3. Opera nostra nullam utilitatem Deo afferunt, Job. 22, 2. 3. Ps. 50, 12. . . 4. Nulla est aequalitas inter opera nostra et vitam aeternam, quae est bonum infinitum. ,Passiones non sunt condignae (rd παΰήματα ονκ εισιν αξία) ad futuram gloriam‘, Rom. 8, 18. Ergo nec opera sunt condigna... Primo homini pro sancto erga Deum obsequio et pro perseverentia in operibus bonis vitae aeternae possessio esset reddita; interim tamen, si proprie et accurate loqui velimus, illa primi hominis obedientia non fuisset vitae aeternae meritoria, cum fuerit jam ante debita, cum nihil commodi ex ea Deo accesserit, cum nulla inter obedientiam temporalem et aeternam beatitudinem proportio intercedat. Quae ergo praesumptuosa audacia est, homini post lapsum, qui, renovatus quidem Dei Spiritu, interim tamen ex parte adhuc carnalis est et sub peccatum venundatus, hoc adscribere, quod ne quidem in statu integritatis ipsi competeret?“ (L. de bonis opp. § 102.) Formula Conc.: ,,Die Werke, so zur Erhaltung äusserlicher Zucht gehören, welche auch von den Ungläubigen und Unbekehrten geschehen und gefordert werden, obwohl vor der Welt dieselben löblich, dazu auch von Gott in dieser Welt mit zeitlichen Gütern belohnet werden, jedoch, weil sie nicht aus rechtem Glauben gehen, sind sie vor Gott Sünde u. s. w.“ (Declar. art. 4. p. 626.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Scholasticorum et pontificiorum, qui, auxilia gratiae actualis ipsamque justificationem mereri posse ex congruo bonis operibus, asserunt. . . Itemque statuunt, bona opera justificati vere esse meritoria vitae aeternae. Concil. Trident, sess. 6. can. 16., cum fateatur, bona opera esse Dei dona, pertendit tamen, esse merita hominis justificati et contra sentientes ferit anathemate. . . De hoc tamen vitae aeternae merito diversimode loquuntur papistae. Quidam enim modestiores sunt, quidam crassiores. Illi vitam aeternam saltem ex merito de congruo haberi asserunt. . . Inde distinctio illa nata, qua dicitur, bona opera non ex se, sed ex merito Christi et quatenus sanguine Redemtoris tincta sunt, virtutem merendi habere. . . Crassiores sunt, qui dicunt, opera bona justorum esse meritoria vitae aeternae ex condigno ratione operis ex gratia praestiti ex intrinseco suo valore ita comparati, ut vita aeterna illi tanquam aequivalenti pretio debeatur, etiamsi Deus non fuisset stipulatus, se recepturum illa opera pro tali merito; ita Cajetanus. . . Atque hanc sententiam Vasquez probabiliorem judicat et catholicae doctrinae magis consentaneam. Jesuita hic (Vasquez) frontem omnem perfricuit et sic agit cura Deo, ut qui nihil ei debeat et solidam laudem sibi ipsi tribuat salutis suae. Verba ejus haec sunt loco jam citato: ,Est catholicae doctrinae magis consentaneum, primum valorem et dignitatem vitae aeternae absque ullo pacto et favore operibus justorum adscribendam esse.‘ Et paulo post subjungit: ,Operibus justorum nullam accessionem dignitatis provenire ex meritis Christi aut ex ejus persona.‘ 2. Arminianorum, statuentium, bona opera nullam habere proportionem cum vita aeterna, si ex se considerentur, habere tamen, si a Deo ex gratia acceptentur et κατ' επιείκειαν aestimentur, in confession. c. 18. P. 3.“


## 22 Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel

PART III. CHAP. VII. Chapter VII. CONCERNING THE WORD OF LAW AND GOSPEL. § 1. After it has been stated that regeneration, and conversion, and indeed also renewal, are effected by God through the mediation of the Word, we must now treat more distinctly of this very Word of God in relation to these works. See Chap. IV. § 4. L. c. § 34. Chap. VI. § 8 and 9. For above, in the Prolegomena, Chap. I. § 25, 35, Vol. I, p. 43, 68, and in the entirety of Chap. II, we treated of the Word of God as it is contained in the Holy Scriptures and constitutes the primary principle of knowing for revealed theology. But just as we indicated there in Chap. I. § 24, that the Word of God can be viewed specifically as the instrument for kindling saving faith, which is in Christ, so under that aspect, and regarding those things which are related to it, it must certainly be examined more deeply.

Quenstedtius: "We have acted thus far concerning the principles of our salvation; there follow now the means through which one arrives at it, and these are both those more properly so called, and those termed ὡς πλάτει [in a broad sense]. The means properly so called on the part of God are the Word and the Sacraments, the salutary antidotes to our spiritual disease." (Th. didact. polem. P. IV. c. 1. s. 1. th. 1. 2. f. 925.)

Hollazius: "The means of salvation are the means divinely ordained, through which God, out of grace, offers to all men who have fallen into sin the salvation acquired by the Mediator Christ, and grants and preserves true faith, just as He introduces all who embrace the merit of Christ with final faith into the kingdom of glory. — The means strictly so called on the part of God, δοτικά [giving] or exhibiting salvation, are the Word and the Sacraments; on our part, the medium ληπτικον [taking] or that which apprehends the offered salvation, is faith resting upon the merit of Christ. The means of salvation in a broad sense are εισαγογικά [introductory] or executive and introducing into the kingdom of glory, viz., death, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment, and the consummation of the age. — They are called executive, insofar as through them God executes the sentence of glorification and damnation; they are called isagogic, insofar as through their immediate intervention men persevering finally in faith are introduced into the kingdom of glory." (Exam. th. P. III. s. 2. c. 1. q. 1. 2. p. 991. sq.)

The same: "The Word of God is not considered here as a principle of γνώσεως [knowledge] or knowing, but as a medium of πράξεως [action] or working, by whose intervention the sinner is led by God to eternal salvation. The Word of God, considered as a principle of knowing, ... pertains to the prolegomena of theology; in the present instance, it is weighed as a medium of calling, illuminating, converting, etc." (L. c. q. 8. p. 992.)

Ad. Osiander: "It must be observed that the hearing of the Word acts by way of a necessary requirement for introducing the ability to receive grace; but repentance and prayer act by way of an inseparable fruit, which presupposes the Holy Spirit already indwelling." (Colleg. P. IV. p. 296.)

Calovius: "The Word of God is attended to here ... as a principle of acting or effecting, or ποιητικόν [productive] or effective, insofar as it is the medium of converting, regenerating, justifying, and saving. Since these works cannot be attributed to the mere striking of the air or the sound of the wind, it is necessary that the Word of God have something more, which is 'Spirit and life,' John 6:63. Moreover, those effects, even though they belong to the spoken Word on account of the union with the hypostatic Word, who is one in essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, 1 John 5:7, are not to be claimed for the Word in such a way that they are denied to the Word with Schwenkfeld, but so that they are attributed to the Word on account of that union." (System. Tom. IX. p. 2.)

J. Olearius: "God calls, draws to Himself, converts, regenerates, and sanctifies men unto eternal salvation only through the Word and the Sacraments. This is proven: 1. because He saved those who believe through the foolishness of preaching, 1 Cor. 1; 2. because the words which Peter speaks to Cornelius save him and his entire household, Acts 10; 3. because faith comes by hearing, Rom. 10; 4. because through the word of truth they believe and those who are to be saved will believe, John 17; 5. because it is said from heaven concerning our Savior to all who desire the remission of sins, and it is commanded to all and each: 'Hear Him!' Matt. 17. Whence it is concluded: By whatever means God makes us saved, in such a way that faith arises from it, the effect of which is the remission of sins and eternal salvation, and which is promised to all who hear that instrument: that must also be acknowledged by all as the sole means of divine calling, conversion, regeneration, and sanctification. But the preaching of the Word, joined with the Sacraments, is that means by which God makes us saved, etc. Therefore." (See Carpzov’s Isagog., p. 1249.)

Luther: "God will not suffer that we should rely upon anything else or hang with our hearts upon anything that is not Christ in His Word, be it as holy and full of spirit as it may. Faith has no other foundation upon which it can stand... We must seek Christ in that which is the Father’s, that is, that we hold simply and solely to the Word of the Gospel, which shows us Christ rightly and makes Him known. And learn only in this and all spiritual temptations, if you wish to comfort others or yourself rightly, to say thus with Christ: Why is it that you run here and there, tormenting yourself with anxious and troubled thoughts, as if God would have no more grace for you and as if no Christ were to be found, and you will not be satisfied until you find Him within yourself and feel yourself holy and without sin? Nothing will come of that; it is vain, lost effort and labor. Do you not know that Christ will not be, nor let Himself be found, except in that which is the Father’s? Not in that which you or all men are and have? The fault is not in Christ and His grace; He is and remains surely unfound-lost and lets Himself be found at all times. But the fault is in you, that you do not seek Him rightly, where He is to be sought, because you judge according to your feeling and think to grasp Him with your thoughts. You must come to this, that not your business nor any man’s, but God’s business and government, namely where His Word is, there you will meet Him, hear and see that neither wrath nor disfavor is there, as you fear and tremble, but pure grace and heartfelt love toward you... But it becomes difficult before it (the heart) comes to this and grasps such: it must first run against the wall and experience that everything is lost and that it is called seeking Christ in vain, and finally there is no counsel but that you surrender yourself outside of yourself and all human comfort solely into the Word." (Kirchenpostille. Tom. Hal. XI, 623 sqq.)

Gerhard: "Since there is no real distinction between the written and the unwritten Word of God, therefore those honorable proclamations concerning the efficacy and fruit of the Word are deservedly considered to pertain also to Holy Scripture."

Just as the Word did not cease to be divine through being written, so too it did not cease to be an efficacious instrument of conversion and salvation; therefore, that it is said in Rom. 10:17, "faith comes by hearing," is not to be taken exclusively, so that the hearing of the preached Word is opposed to the reading of the written Word, but inclusively, so that God is established as efficacious unto faith and salvation through the Word not only heard, but also read, since it is and remains the same Word, whether it is preached and heard, or written and read; whence John says notably concerning the evangelical history reduced to writing, and thus concerning the entire Scripture of the Old and New Testaments: "These are written, that you may believe," John 20:31; "These things we write to you, that your joy may be full," 1 John 1:4. Therefore, faith and spiritual joy, and consequently eternal salvation, can also be drawn from the written Word of God when it is applied to use through reading and meditation. (Exeges. Loci de S. S. § 364.)

Formula of Concord: "But that it is said that no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him, is right and true; but the Father does not wish to do this without means, but has ordained His Word and Sacraments as ordinary means and instruments for this purpose, and it is the will of neither the Father nor the Son that a man should not hear or should despise the preaching of His Word and wait for the drawing of the Father without Word and Sacraments. For the Father indeed draws with the power of His Holy Spirit, yet, according to His common order, through the hearing of His holy divine Word, as with a net, by which the elect are snatched from the jaws of the devil, to which every poor sinner should betake himself, hear the same with diligence, and not doubt the drawing of the Father; for the Holy Spirit wishes to be present with His power in the Word and to work through it; and that is the drawing of the Father." (Artic. XI. Declar. p. 720.)

Cf. supra Prolegom. c. 2. § 39. Vol. I. p. 153-161. P. III. c. 3. § 11. Vol. III. P. 3. § 11. p. 154. sq.

ANTITHESIS. Carpzovius: "In the antithesis, which is subjoined to the thesis (of Article V of the Augsburg Confession), the assembly of Protestants separates itself from the assemblies: 1. Of the Anabaptists, Enthusiasts, Schwenkfeldians, and Celestial Prophets, who maintain that faith is received and given partly without the external Word, and partly through their own preparations, of which they make certain degrees. 2. Of Zwingli and other Calvinists, who partly deny that faith is drawn from the Word, partly teach that faith is given without the Word, and partly also do not correctly explain the operation of the Word regarding faith, and either entirely separate the operation of faith from the Word, or attribute to the Word nothing but the presentation of the object and a naked signification of the divine will, but entirely strip the Word of the operation of faith itself. 3. Of the Papists, who also wish for God to work faith without the Word, and wish to merit faith through their own preparations and dispositions by merit of congruity; just as Johannes a Daventria in 'Refut. Artic. 5' and Johannes Hoffmeister in 'Judic. super Artic. 5' openly confessed, and rightly perceived that they had been noted by our people in this antithesis." (Isagog. in lib. Symbol, p. 246.) §

Latin:

PART. III. CAB. VII. Caput VII. DE VERBO LEGIS ET EVANGELII. § 1. Postquam dictum est, regenerationem a et conversionem,b imo et renovationem c fieri a Deo inediante verbo, jam de ipso hoc verbo Dei in ordine ad haec opera c distinctius agendum est. Vid. cap. IV. § 4. L. c. § 34. Cap. VI. § S\ et 9. Nam supra quidem in Prolegomenis cap. I. § 25. 35., Vol. I. p. 43. 68., et cap. II. integro actum est de verbo Dei, prout in Scripturis sacris continetur et theologiae revelatae principium cognoscendi primum constituit. Sicut autem ibidem cap. I. § 24. indicavimus, verbum Dei peculiariter spectari posse ut organon accendendae fidei salvificae, quae est in Christum, ita sub ea habitudine, et quoad ea, quae cognata sunt, utique penitius spectandum venit.

Quenstedtius: ״Actum hactenus de principiis nostrae salutis, sequuntur jam media, per quae ad eam pervenitur, eaque tum magis proprie ita dicta, tum ως h πλάτει nuncupata. Media proprie ita dicta a parte Dei sunt verbum et sacramenta, salutaria spiritualis nostri morbi alexipharmaca.“ (Th. didact.polem. P. IV. c. 1. s. 1. th. 1. 2. f. 925.)

Hollazius: ,,Media salutis sunt media divinitus ordinata, per quae Deus acquisitam a mediatore Christo salutem omnibus hominibus, in peccatum prolapsis, ex gratia offert, veramque fidem donat et conservat, juxta atque omnes, meritum Christi finali fide amplectentes, in regnum gloriae introducit. — Media stricte dicta ex parte Dei, δοτικά seu salutem exhibentia, sunt verbum et sacramenta; ex parte nostri, medium ληπτικον seu oblatam salutem apprehendens, est fides merito Christi innixa. Media salutis late dicta sunt εισαγογικά sive exsecutiva et in. regnum gloriae introducentia, sci. mors, resurrectio mortuorum, extremum judicium et consummatio saeculi. — Exsecutiva dicuntur, quatenus per ea Deus sententiam glorificationis et damnationis exsequitur; isagogica vocantur, quatenus eorum proximo interventu homines in fide finaliter perseverantes in regnum gloriae introducuntur.“ (Exam. th. P. III. s. 2. c. 1. q. 1. 2. p. 991. sq.)

Idem: ״Verbum Dei hic non consideratur ut principium γνώσεως sive cognoscendi, sed ut medium πράξεως sive operandi, cujus interventu hOmo peccator a Deo ad aeternam salutem perducitur. V. D., consideratum ut principium cognoscendi, . . . pertinet ad prolegomena theologiae; in praesenti pensitatur ut medium vocandi, illuminandi, convertendi etc.“ (L. c. q. 8. p. 992.)

Ad. Osiandek: ״Observandum, auditum verbi habere se per modum x requisiti necessarii ad introducendam habilitatem suscipiendi gratiam; poenitentiam autem et ·precationem per modum fructus inseparabilis, qui S. Spiritum jam inhabitantem supponit.“ (Colleg. P. IV. p. 296.) Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. ΙΠ.22 PART. III. CAP. VII.

Calovius: ,,Verbum Dei hic attenditur. . . ut principium operan di vel efficiendi seu ποιητικόν vel effectivum, quatenus sci. est medium convertendi, regenerandi, justificandi, salvandi. Quae opera cum nudae aeris percussioni vel venti sono tribui nequeant, necessum est, ut V. D. quid amplius habeat, quod est,Spiritus et vita‘, Joh. 6, 63:.. Effectus autem illi, etsi propter unionem cum Verbo hypostatico, quod cum Patre et Spiritu S. unum est essentia, 1 Joh. 5, 7., verbo προφορική conveniant, non tamen ita λόγω vindicandi sunt, ut verbo denegentur cum Schwenkfeldio, sed ut verbo propter unionem illam tribuantur.“ (System. Tom. IX. p. 2.)

J. Olearius: ״Deus nonnisi per verbum et sacramenta homines ad aeternam salutem vocat, ad se trahit, convertit, regenerat et sanctificat. Probatur: 1. quia salvos fecit credentes per stultitiam praedicationis, 1 Cor. 1.; 2. quia verba, quae Petrus loquitur Cornelio, salvant ipsum et universam ejus familiam, Act. 10.; 3. quia fides est ex auditu, Rom. 10.; 4. quia per verbum veritatis credunt et credituri sunt salvandi, Joh. 17.; 5. quia de Salvatore nostro omnibus remissionem peccatorum desiderantibus coelitus dicitur et universis atque singulis mandatur: ,Hunc audite! ‘ Matth. 17. Unde concluditur: Per quodcunque medium Deus nos salvos facit, ita, ut ex illo fides oriatur, cujus effectus peccatorum remissio et aeterna salus, omnibus illud organum audientibus promittitur: illud etiam ab omnibus velut unicum divinae vocationis, conversionis, regenerationis et sanctificationis medium agnoscendum est. Atqui verbi praedicatio sacramentis conjuncta, est illud medium, per quod Deus nos salvos facit etc. Ergo.“ (Vid. Isagog. Carpzovii, p. 1249.)

Lutherus: ״Gott will nicht leiden, dass wir uns sollen auf etwas anders verlassen oder mit dem Herzen hangen an etwas, das nicht Christus in seinem Wort ist, es sei, wie heilig und voll Geistes es wolle. Der Glaube hat keinen andern Grund, darauf er bestehen könne. . . Wir müssen Christum suchen in dem, das des Vaters ist, das ist, dass wir uns schlecht und bloss an das Wort des Evangelii halten, welches uns Christum recht zeigt und zu erkennen gibt. Und lerne nur in dieser und allen geistlichen Anfechtungen, so du willst andere oder dich selbst recht trösten, also mit Christo sagen: Was ist es, dass du so hin und wieder laufest, dich selbst so zermarterst mit ängstigen und betrübten Gedanken, als wolle Gott dein nicht mehr Gnade haben und als sei kein Christus zu finden, und willst nicht ehe zufrieden sein, du findest ihn denn bei dir selbst und fühlest dich heilig und ohne Sünde; da wird nichts aus, es ist eitel verlorne Mühe und Arbeit. Weisst du nicht, dass Christus nicht sein will, noch sich finden lassen, denn in dem, das des Vaters ist? nicht in dem, das du oder alle Menschen sind und haben? Es ist nicht der Fehl an Christo und seiner Gnade; er ist und bleibet wohl unverloren und lässt sich allezeit finden. Aber es fehlet an“ dir, dass du ihn nicht״ recht suchest, da er zu suchen ist, weil du deinem Fühlen nach richtest und meinest, ihn zu ergreifen mit deinen Gedanken. Hieher musst du kommen, dass nicht dein noch einiges Menschen, sondern Gottes Geschäfte und Regiment, nämlich da sein Wort ist, da wirst du ihn treffen, hören und. sehen, dass weder Zorn noch Ungnade da ist, wie du fürchtest und zagest, sondern eitel Gnade und herzliche Liebe gegen dir. . . Aber schwer wird es, ehe es (das Herz) dazu kommt und solches ergreifet: es muss zuvor anlaufen und erfahren, dass alles verloren und vergeblich Christum gesucht heisset, und zuletzt doch kein Rath ist, denn dass du dich ausser dir selbst und allem menschlichen Trost allein in das Wort ergebest.“ (Kirchenpostille. Tom. Hai. XI, 623. sqq.)

Gerhardus: ״Cum inter verbum Dei scriptum et non-scriptum nullum reale discrimen intercedat, ideo honorifica illa de verbi efficacia ac fructu praeconia merito etiam ad Scripturam S. pertinere censentur.

Sicut per scriptionem verbum non desiit esse divinum, ita quoque non desiit esse efficax conversionis et salutis organum; proinde quod Rom. 10, 17. ,fides ex auditu‘ esse dicitur, id non accipiendum est exclusive, ut auditus verbi praedicati opponatur lectioni verbi scripti, sed inclusive, ut per verbum non solum auditum, sed etiam lectum l)eus ad fidem et salutem efficax statuatur, cum idem sit et maneat verbum, sive praedicetur et audiatur, sive scribatur et legatur; unde notanter dicit Johannes de historia evangelica in literas redacta, adeoque de tota Vet. et N. T. scriptura: ,Haec scripta sunt, ut credatis‘, Joh. 20, v. ult. ,Haec scribimus vobis, ut gaudium vestrum sit perfectum‘, 1 Joh. 1, 4. Ergo etiam ex scripto Dei verbo per lectionem et meditationem ad usum translato fides et spirituale gaudium, et consequenter salus aeterna hauriri potest.“ (Exeges. Loci de S. S. § 364.)

Formula Conc.: ,,Dass aber gesagt wird, niemand komme zu Christo, der Vater ziehe ihn denn, ist recht und wahr; aber der Vater will das nicht thun ohne Mittel, sondern hat dazu sein Wort und Sacramente als ordentliche Mittel und Werkzeuge verordnet, und ist weder des Vaters noch des Sohnes Wille, dass ein Mensch die Predigt seines Worts nicht hören oder verachten und auf das Ziehen des Vaters ohne Wort und Sacramente warten solle. Denn der Vater zeucht wohl mit der Kraft seines Heiligen Geistes, jedoch, seiner gemeinen Ordnung nach, durch das Gehör seines heiligen göttlichen Worts, als mit einem Netze, dadurch die Auserwählten aus dem Rachen des Teufels gerissen werden, dazu sich ein jeder armer Sünder verfügen, dasselbe mit Fleiss hören und an dem Ziehen des Vaters nicht zweifeln soll; denn der Heilige Geist will mit seiner Kraft bei dem Wort sein und dadurch wirken; und das ist das Ziehen des Vaters.“ (Artic. XI. Declar. p. 720.)

Cf. supra Prolegom. c. 2. § 39. Vol. I. p. 153-161. P. III. c. 3. § 11. Vol. III. P. 3. § 11. p. 154. sq.

ANTITHESIS. Carpzovius: ,,In antithesi, quae thesi (articuli V. Aug. Conf.) subjuncta est, separat sese Protestantium coetus a coetibus: 1. Anabaptistarum, Enthusiastarum, Schwenkfeldianorum, Coelestium prophetarum, qui partim sine verbo externo, partim per praeparationes suas, quarum certos gradus faciunt, fidem accipi et dari statuunt. 2. Zwinglii et aliorum Calvinistarum, qui partim negant, fidem ex verbo hauriri, partim, sine verbo fidem dari, jocent, partim etiam operationem verbi circa fidem non recte exponunt, et vel plane operationem fidei a verbo separant, vel nonnisi praesentationem objecti et significationem nudam voluntatis divinae verbo tribuunt, ipsam autem fidei operationem verbo plane detrahunt. 3. Papistarum, qui etiam sine verbo Deum operari fidem volunt, et per suas praeparationes ac dispositiones fidem mereri merito de congruo volunt; prout id ipsum Joh. a Daventria in,Refut. Artic. 5.‘ et Joh. Hoffmeister, in,Judic. super Artic. 5.‘ aperte confessi sunt, et probe senserunt, in antithesi hac a nostratibus se fuisse notatos.“ (Isagog. in lib. Symbol, p. 246.) §


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: The Word of God is divided into Law and Gospel

2. The Word of God is divided into Law and Gospel. And this division must be diligently known and held, since it is certain that the confusion of Law and Gospel has generated many harmful errors.

Formula of Concord: "We believe, teach, and confess that the distinction between the Law and the Gospel is to be maintained in the Church with great diligence as a particularly glorious light, by which the Word of God... PART III. CHAPTER VII. (according to the admonition of St. Paul) is rightly divided.” (Epitome, Art. V, p. 533 sq.) “

Since the distinction between the Law and the Gospel is a particularly glorious light, which serves to ensure that God’s Word is rightly divided and the writings of the holy prophets and apostles are properly explained and understood, it must be held to with special diligence, so that these two doctrines are not mixed together, or a law made out of the Gospel, whereby the merit of Christ is obscured and troubled consciences are robbed of the comfort which they otherwise have in the holy Gospel when it is preached pure and unadulterated, and by which they can sustain themselves in their highest temptations against the terror of the Law.” (Declaration, Art. V, p. 633.)

Luther: “St. Paul’s opinion is this: That in Christendom, both by preachers and hearers, a certain distinction should be taught and grasped between the Law and the Gospel, between works and faith; just as he commands this to Timothy when he admonishes him in 2 Epist. 2:15, ‘rightly to divide the word of truth,’ etc. This distinction between the Law and the Gospel is the highest art in Christendom, which all and everyone who boast of or assume the Christian name ought to be able to do and know. For where this piece is lacking, one cannot distinguish a Christian from a heathen or a Jew; so much depends upon this distinction. Therefore, St. Paul insists so strongly that the two doctrines, namely of the Law and the Gospel, be well and rightly separated from one another among Christians. Both are indeed God’s Word—the Law or the Ten Commandments, and the Gospel—the latter given by God initially in Paradise, the former on Mount Sinai. But the power lies in rightly distinguishing the two words and not mixing them together; otherwise, one will be able to know or retain the right understanding of neither the one nor the other; indeed, when one thinks one has both, one will have neither...

Therefore, it is highly necessary that these two kinds of words be rightly and well distinguished; for where that does not happen, neither the Law nor the Gospel can be understood, and consciences must perish in blindness and error. For the Law has its goal, how far it is to go and what it is to accomplish, namely, up to Christ, to terrify the impenitent with God’s wrath and disfavor. Likewise, the Gospel also has its special office and work, to preach the forgiveness of sins to troubled consciences. Therefore, these two may not, without falsification of the doctrine, be mixed together, nor one taken for the other. For the Law and the Gospel are indeed both God’s Word, but not the same doctrine.

Just as it is God’s Word in Ex. 20:12: ‘Honor your father and your mother.’ And again in Eph. 6:2, 3, 4: ‘You fathers, bring up your children in the fear of God,’ etc. But because it is not spoken of the same office and persons, what disorder would follow if it were thrown together under the pretext that it is all God’s Word? Then the son would want to be the father, the father the son; the mother the daughter, the daughter the mother... But if it is necessary in laws that one separate them from one another and rightly consider the persons to whom they are directed, how much more must a distinction be made between the Law and the Gospel? Therefore, whoever knows this art of separating the Law from the Gospel well, set him at the top and call him a Doctor of Holy Scripture. For without the Holy Spirit, it is impossible to hit upon this distinction. I experience it in myself, and I see it daily in others, how difficult it is to separate the doctrine of the Law and the Gospel from one another. The Holy Spirit must be the Master and Teacher here; or no man on earth will be able to understand or teach it. Therefore, no Pope, no

no] false Christian, no enthusiast, [ought] to separate these two from one another, especially in *causa materiali* and in *objecto*.” (Sermon on the Distinction between the Law and the Gospel, A.D. 1532. IX, 410 sqq.)

The same: “For how the devil now, through the enthusiasts, mixes Law and promise, faith and works together, and tortures poor consciences, lets them see neither Law nor Gospel rightly distinguished, drives and chases them into the Law, spreads a net before them, which says: This you must do and leave undone. If I do not distinguish well here between Moses and Christ, then I am and remain captive, cannot become free and loose, but must despair. But if I knew how to divide Law and Gospel rightly, then there would be no need; then I could say: Has God then given only one kind of word, namely the Law? Has He not also commanded the Gospel of grace and the forgiveness of sins to be preached? Yes, says the conscience, where there is no faith in the promise, there the Law soon presses upon it: This and that is commanded to you, this you have not done, therefore you must pay. In such a struggle and death-agony, it is high time and necessity that faith take courage and break forth with all power and step before the eyes of the Law, and confidently say to it: Hey, dear Law, are you alone God’s Word? Is the Gospel not also God’s Word? Has the promise then come to an end? Has God’s mercy ceased? Or are the two, Law and Gospel, or merit and grace, now mixed and boiled together, become one thing? We will not have the God who can do nothing more than give the Law, that know well; so we also want to have the Law unmixed with the Gospel. Therefore, let us let this distinction go free, unhindered and unimpeded: that you press for duty and right, [while] the Gospel points us to pure grace and gift. Therefore, when the Law accuses me: I have not done this and that; I am unrighteous and a sinner, written in God’s register of debts: I must confess that it is all true. But the conclusion: Therefore you are damned, I must not concede, but defend myself with strong faith and say: According to the Law, which reckons my guilt to me, I am indeed a poor, damned sinner, but I appeal from the Law to the Gospel; for God has given another word above the Law, which is called the Gospel, which grants us His grace, forgiveness of sins, eternal righteousness and life, and furthermore speaks [us] free and loose from your terror and damnation, and comforts me that all debt is paid through the Son of God, Jesus Christ Himself. Therefore it is highly necessary that one knows how to rightly direct and handle both words, and diligently sees to it that they are not mixed together.” (L. c. p. 419—421.)

The same: “We distinguish the Law as far from righteousness as death from life, hell from heaven, and that we may establish this, that famous passage of Paul moves us: The Law is not given to justify, to vivify, and to save, but simply to condemn, to kill, and to destroy, contrary to the opinion of all men, who naturally judge that the Law was given to obtain righteousness, life, and salvation. This proper distinction of the offices of the Law and the Gospel preserves the entire sincere theology in its true use, likewise constitutes believers as judges over all kinds of life, over all the laws and dogmas of all men, and finally provides the ability to test all spirits.” (Ad Gal. 3, 21. Commentary on the Ep. of St. Paul to the Galatians, Erlangen, 1844. Tom. II, 95 sq.)

The same: “It is difficult and dangerous to teach that we are justified by faith without works, and yet at the same time to demand works. Here, unless there are faithful and prudent ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, who rightly divide the word of truth, faith and works are immediately confounded. Both the place of faith and [the place] of works must be diligently taught and urged, yet so that PART III. CHAP. VII.

let each remain within its own limits. Otherwise, if works alone are taught, as happens in the papacy, faith is lost. If faith alone is taught, carnal men immediately dream that works are not necessary, etc.” (On Gal. 5:15, ibid., Vol. III, 5.)

b) Indeed, the terms are sometimes taken more broadly, so that the Law in its concept embraces the Gospel, or the latter in some way embraces the former; for example, when the Law is taken for the whole of Scripture, Ps. 1:2, or more specifically for the Scriptures of the Old Testament, John 15:25; 1 Cor. 14:21, or finally, particularly for the Mosaic writings, Luke 24:44. The Gospel is also sometimes taken more broadly for the whole doctrine of the New Testament delivered by Christ and the apostles, Mark 1:14; ch. 16:15; Luke 9:6. Here, however, the terms of Law and Gospel are taken insofar as they are adequately contradistinguished from one another.

Quenstedtius: “These two heads of heavenly doctrine do indeed sometimes receive common names in the Scriptures, as in Isa. 2:3; Mic. 4:2; Rom. 8:2, etc. Yet that communication of the names of Law and Gospel is not mutual or ἀντίστροφος [convertible], but only ἀναστρέφονσα [one-way], since in the Scriptures the name of Law is indeed more often assigned to the Gospel, but the appellation of Gospel is never attributed to the Law.” (Ibid., ch. 2, sec. 2, q. 4, p. 1027.)

S. Schmidtius: “In the Holy Scriptures, no passage has been found or produced to this very day in which either the Law properly so-called, consisting of precepts, or the threatening, or the reproof of sin, is called the Gospel.” (Repetition of the Articles of the Formula of Concord, p. 297.) §

3. In this place, the Law properly denotes the Word of God by which some things are commanded and others are forbidden, with the power of binding. Thus Paul takes the term when he denies that a man is justified by the Law in the Epistles to the Romans and to the Galatians. Specifically, he calls it the law of works, Rom. 3:27. Whence the precepts of the Law are called some affirmative, others negative. Immediately, indeed, [it binds] to obedience; but if obedience is lacking, to the most severe and eternal punishments.

Latin:

2. Verbum Dei dividitur a in legem et evangelium.b Atque haec divisio diligenter cognoscenda ac tenenda est, cum confusionem legis et evangelii multos noxios errores genuisse constet.

Formula Conc.: ,,Wir glauben, lehren und bekennen, dass der Unterschied des Gesetzes und Evangelii als ein besonder herrlich Licht mit grossem Fleiss in der Kirche zu erhalten, dadurch das Wort Gottes PART. III. CAP. VII. (nach der Vermahnung St. Pauli) recht getheilet wird.“ (Epitom. artic. V. p. 533. sq.),,

Nachdem der Unterschied des Gesetzes und Evangelii ein besonder herrlich Licht ist, welches dazu dienet, dass Gottes Wort recht getheilet und der heiligen Propheten und Apostel Schriften eigentlich erkläret und verstanden: ist mit besonderem Eleiss über demselben zu halten, damit diese zwo Lehren nicht mit einander vermischt oder aus dem Evangelio ein Gesetz gemacht, dadurch der Verdienst Christi verdunkelt und die betrübten Gewissen ihres Trosts beraubt, den sie sonst in dem heiligen Evangelio haben, wenn dasselbige lauter und rein gepredigt, und sich in ihren höchsten Anfechtungen wider das Schrecken des Gesetzes aufhalten können.“ (Dedar. artic. V. p. 633.)

Lutherus: ״St. Pauli Meinung ist diese: Dass in der Christenheit soll, beides von Predigern und Zuhörern, ein gewisser Unterschied gelehret und gefasset werden zwischen dem Gesetz und Evangelio, zwischen den Werken und dem Glauben; wie er denn solches auch Timotheo befiehlet, da er ihn vermahnet 2. Epist. 2, 15., ,das Wort der Wahrheit recht zu theilen‘ u. s. w. Dieser Unterschied zwischen dem Gesetz und Evangelio ist die höchste Kunst in der Christenheit, die alle und jede, so sich des christlichen Namens rühmen oder annehmen, können und wissen sollen. Denn wo es an diesem Stück mangelt, da kann man einen Christen vor einem Heiden oder Juden nicht erkennen; so gar liegt es an diesem Unterschied. Darum dringet St. Paulus so hart darauf, dass die zwo Lehren, nämlich des Gesetzes und Evangelii, bei den Christen wohl und recht von einander geschieden werden. Beides ist wohl Gottes Wort, das Gesetz oder die zehen Gebote und Evangelium, dieses anfänglich im Paradies, jenes auf dem Berge Sinai von Gott gegeben. Aber daran liegt die Macht, dass man die zwei Wörter recht unterscheide und nicht in einander menge; sonst wird man weder von diesem noch von jenem rechten Verstand wissen noch behalten können, ja, wenn ·man meinet, man habe sie beide, wird man keines haben. . .

Darum ist hoch vonnöthen, dass diese zweierlei Worte recht und wohl unterschieden werden; dass, wo das nicht geschieht, kann weder das Gesetz noch Evangelium verstanden werden, und müssen die Gewissen in Blindheit und Irrthum verderben. Denn das Gesetz hat sein Ziel, wie weit es gehen und was es ausrichten soll, nämlieh bis auf Christum, die Unbussfertigen schrecken mit Gottes Zorn und Ungnade. Desgleichen hat das Evangelium auch sein sonderlich Amt und Werk, Vergebung der Sünden betrübten Gewissen zu predigen. Mögen darum diese beide, ohne Verfälschung der Lehre, nicht in einander gemenget, noch eines für das andere genommen werden. Denn Gesetz und Evangelium sind wohl beide Gottes Wort, aber nicht einerlei Lehre.

Gleichwie das Gottes Wort ist 2 Mos. 20, 12.: ,Du sollst deinen Vater und deine Mutter ehren.‘ Und wiederum Ephes. 6, 2. 3. 4.: ,Ihr Väter, ziehet eure Kinder auf in Gottesfurcht‘ u. s. w. Aber weil es nicht von einerlei Amt und Personen geredet ist, was würde wohl für Unordnung draus folgen, wenn es mit dem Schein, dass es alles Gottes Wort wäre, in einander geworfen werden sollte? Da würde der Sohn wollen Vater, der Vater wollen Sohn sein; die Mutter Tochter, die Tochter Mutter. . . Ist es aber in Gesetzen vonnöthen, dass man sie von einander scheide und die Personen, darauf sie gerichtet sind, recht ansehe, wie viel mehr ist Unterschied zwischen dem Gesetz und Evangelio zu machen? Darum, welcher diese Kunst, das Gesetz vom Evangelio zu scheiden, wohl kann, den setze obenan, und heisse ihn einen Doctor der heiligen Schrift. Denn ohne den Heiligen Geist ist es unmöglich, diesen Unterschied zu treffen. Ich erfahre es an mir selbst, sehe es auch täglich an andern, wie schwer es ist, die Lehre des Gesetzes und Evangelii von einander zu sondern. Der Heilige Geist muss hier Meister und Lehrer sein; oder es wird kein Mensch auf Erden verstehen noch lehren können. Darum vermag kein Pabst, kein

falscher Christ, kein Schwärmer diese zwei von einander zu theilen, sonderlich in causa materiali et in objecto.“ (Sermon vom Unterschied zwischen dem Gesetz und Ev. A. 1532. IX, 410. sqq.)

Idem: ,,Wie denn jetzt der Teufel durch die Schwärmer in einander gemenget Gesetz und Verheissung, Glaube und Werk, und zermartert die armen Gewissen, lässt sie weder Gesetz noch Evangelium recht unterschiedlich ansehen, treibt und jagt sie in das Gesetz, spannet ein Netz vor, das heisst: Das soll ich thun und lassen. Unterscheide ich hier nicht wohl Mosen und Christum, so bin ich und bleibe gefangen, kann nicht frei und los werden, sondern muss verzweifeln. Wenn ich aber das Gesetz und Evangelium recht wüsste zu theilen, so hätte es nicht Noth, so könnte ich sagen: Hat denn Gott nur einerlei Wort, als nämlich das Gesetz gegeben? Hat er nicht auch das Evangelium von Gnade und Vergebung der Sünden predigen heissen? Ja, spricht das Gewissen, wo nicht Glaube ist an die Verheissung, da dringet das Gesetz bald darauf: Diess und das ist dir geboten, das hast du nicht. gethan, darum musst du herhalten. In solchem Kampf und Todesangst ist hohe Zeit und Noth, dass sich der Glaube ermanne und mit ganzer Macht hervor breche und dem Gesetz unter die Augen trete, und ihm getrost zuspreche: Ei, liebes Gesetz, bist du allein Gottes Wort? Ist das Evangelium nicht auch Gottes Wort? Hat denn die Verheissung ein Ende? Hat Gottes Barmherzigkeit aufgehöret? Oder sind die zwei, Gesetz und Evangelium, oder Verdienst und Gnade, nunmehr in einander gemenget und gekocht, Ein Ding worden? Wir wollen den Gott nicht haben, der nicht mehr kann, denn Gesetz geben, das wisse gar eben; so wollen wir auch das Gesetz mit dem Evangelio unvermenget haben. Darum lasse uns diesen Unterscheid ungewehret und ungehindert frei gehen: dass du auf Pflicht und Recht dringest, das Evangelium auf eitel Gnade und Geschenk uns weise. Darum, wenn mich das Gesetz beschuldiget: Ich habe diess und das nicht gethan; ich sei ungerecht und ein Sünder, in Gottes Schuldregister geschrieben: muss ich bekennen, es sei alles wahr. Aber die Folgerede: Darum bist du verdammt, muss ich nicht einräumen, sondern mich mit starkem Glauben wehren und sagen: Nach dem Gesetz, welches mir meine Schuld rechnet, bin ich wohl ein armer, verdammter Sünder, aber ich appellire vom Gesetz zum Evangelio; denn Gott hat über das Gesetz noch ein ander Wort gegeben, das heisst das Evangelium, welches uns seine Gnade, Vergebung der Sünden, ewige Gerechtigkeit und Leben schenket, dazu frei und los spricht von deinem Schrecken und Verdammniss, und tröstet mich, alle Schuld sei bezahlt durch den Sohn Gottes, Jesum Christum selbst. Darum hoch vonnöthen, dass man beide Worte recht wisse zu lenken und handeln, und fleissig zusehe, dass sie nicht in einander vermenget werden.“ (L. c. p. 419—421.)

Idem: ,,Discernimus legem tam longe a justitia, quam mortem a vita, infernum a coelo, et ut hoc statuamus, movet nos ille clarus Pauli locus: Lex non est data ad justificandum, vivificandum et salvandum, sed simpliciter ad damnandum, occidendum et perdendum, contra opinionem omnium hominum, qui naturaliter judicant, legem datam esse ad justitiam, vitam et salutem consequendam. Hoc proprium discrimen officiorum legis et evangelii conservat in vero usu universam sinceram theologiam, item constituit credentes super omnia vitae genera, super omnes omnium hominum leges et dogmata judices, denique facultatem suppeditat probandi omnes spiritus.“ (Ad Gal. 3, 21. Commentar, in ep. S. Pauli ad Gal. Erlangae, 1844. Tom. II, 95. sq.)

Idem: ,,Difficile et periculosum est docere nos fide justificari sine operibus, et tamen simul exigere opera. Hic nisi sint fideles et prudentes ministri Christi et dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, qui recte secant verbum veritatis, statim fides et opera confunduntur. Uterque locus et fidei et operum diligenter doceri et urgeri debet, sic tamen, ut PART. III. CAP. VII.

uterque intra suos limites maneat. Alioqui si opera sola docentur, ut in papatu accidit, fides amittitur. Si fides sola docetur, statim somniant carnales homines, opera non esse necessaria etc.“ (Ad Gal. 5,15. 1. c. Tom. III, 5.)

b) Equidem aliquando latius accipiuntur voces, ita ut lex sub suo conceptu evangelium aut hoc illam quodammodo complectatur, v. g. quando lex sumitur pro tota Scriptura, Psal. 1, 2., aut specialius pro Scripturis V. T., Joh. 15, 25. 1 Cor. 14, 21., denique peculiariter pro scriptis Mosaicis, Luc. 24., 44. Evangelium quoque interdum latius accipitur pro tota doctrina N. T. a Christo et apostolis tradita, Mare. 1, 14. cap. 16, 15. Luc. 9, 6. Hic autem accipiuntur vocabula legis et evangelii, quatenus sibi adaequate contradistinguuntur.

Quenstedtius: ,,Sortiuntur quidem haec duo coelestis doctrinae capita quandoque in Scripturis nomina communia, ut Es.· 2, 3. Mich. 4, 2. Rom. 8, 2. etc. Illa tamen nominum legis et evangelii communicatio non est mutua sive αντίστροφος, sed tantum άναστρέφονσα, siquidem in Scripturis evangelio quidem assignatur saepius nomen legis, nunquam vero legi tribuitur appellatio evangelii.“ (L. c. c. 2. s. 2. q. 4. f. 1027.)

S. Schmidtius: ,,In S. S. nullus ad hunc usque diem inventus aut productus est locus, in quo sive lex proprie dicta, praeceptis constans, sive comminatio, sive redargutio peccati dicatur evangelium.“ (Articulor. F. C. Repetitio, p. 297.) §

3. Lex hoc loco proprie a denotat verbum Dei, quo aliqua b praecipiuntur, alia prohibentur, cum vi obligandi.c Sic Paulus accipit vocem, quando negat hominem justificari per legem in Epist. ad Rom. et ad Gal. Speciatim appellat legem operum Rom. S, 27. Unde praecepta legis alia affirmativa, alia negativa appellantur. Proxime quidem ad obsequium; deficiente autem obsequio, ad poenas gravissimas atque aeternas.


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: Formula of Concord: “Therefore we unanimously believe, teach, and confess that…

Formula of Concord: “Therefore we unanimously believe, teach, and confess that the Law is properly a divine doctrine, in which the righteous, unchangeable will of God is revealed, how man should be constituted in his nature, thoughts, words, and works, so that he may be pleasing and acceptable to God, and it threatens the transgressors of the same with God’s wrath, temporal and eternal punishments. For, as Luther speaks against the Antinomians: ‘Everything that punishes sin is and belongs to the Law, whose proper office is to punish sins and lead to the knowledge of sin,’ Rom. 3:20 and 7:7; and since unbelief is a root and fountainhead of all punishable sins, the Law also punishes unbelief. It is, however, nevertheless also true that the Law with its doctrine is illustrated and explained by the Gospel, and yet the proper office of the Law remains to punish sin and to teach about good works. Thus the Law punishes unbelief, when one does not believe God’s Word. Since now the Gospel, which alone properly teaches and commands to believe in Christ, is God’s Word, so the [Law] punishes...”

Holy Spirit through the office of the Law also [convicts] unbelief, that they do not believe in Christ, which Gospel, however, alone properly teaches concerning the saving faith in Christ.” (Artic. V. p. 636, sq.)

Luther: “Everything is a preaching of the Law that preaches of our sins and God’s wrath, let it happen how or when it will. . . . Yea, what is a more earnest, more terrible indication and preaching of God’s wrath over sin than the suffering and dying of Christ, His Son! But as long as all this preaches God’s wrath and terrifies man, it is not yet the Gospel, nor Christ’s own preaching, but that of Moses and the Law over the impenitent. . .
