Und Tage und Zeit sollen nicht Herrn sein über die Christen, sondern die Christen sind freie Herren, über Tage und Zeit zu setzen, wie sie wollen, oder wie es ihnen eben ist. Denn Christus hat alles frei gemacht, da er Mosen aufgehaben hat, ohne dass wirs wollen lassen bleiben, wie es jetzt geht, weil da keine Gefahr, Irrthum, Sünde noch Ketzerei ist und ohne Noth oder aus eigener einzelner Durst nichts andern wollen um der andern willen, die gleich mit uns an solchen Ostern hangen. Denn wir ohne Ostern und Pfingsten, ohne Sonntag und Freitag wissen selig zu werden und um der Ostern, Pfingsten, Sonntag, Freitag willen nicht können verdammt werden, wie uns St. Paulus lehret.“ (Von den Conciliis und Kirchen, a. 1539. Opp. Hal. XVI, 2682. sq.) Cf. III, 1620—1623.

J. Fechtius: ,,Lex positivomoralis a theologis antiquioribus merito ignoratur. . . ,Jus morale tertii praecepti est, cultum Deo publicum praestare indefinite certo tempore. Nulla sufficiens ratio ex lege divina elucet, quae indicet voluntatem Dei de uno praecise ex hebdomade dierum. Non in libertate nostra positum est extendere diem sanctificationis ad vicesimum vel tricesimum, contra caritatem Dei et proximi. Septimus dies, e permutatione septidui recurrens, non est juris moralis positivi.‘ JDorscheus." —

Addit Bollius: ,,Legibus moralibus et positivis quidam tertium genus positivomoralium addiderunt. Et positivas quidem vocarunt, quod a mera voluntate divina dependeant, non a naturali necessitate; morales vero, quia in perpetua omnium obligatione moralibus sint similes. Exempli loco allegarunt gradus in Levitico prohibitos, itemque legem de sabbato, qualibet hebdomade celebrando. Recte autem ab aliis oppositum est, legibus hisce positivomoralibus obstare perpetuum Scripturae silentium, quodque non commemorentur ullibi aliae leges, quam quae vel ad morales sive naturales, vel ad positivas pertinent. . .

In eo conveniunt theologi omBaieri Comp. ed. Walther. ΙΠ.23 PART. III. CAP. VII. nes, quod in praecepto tertio habeatnr morale et ceremoniale quid. In definiendo autem utroque aliqua datur differentia. Plerorumque tamen nostratium sententia est, morale esse, quod unus cujuslibet septimanae dies cultui publico destinandus sit; ceremoniale autem, quod septimus a Judaeis, primus a Christianis celebretur. Nonnulli solum hoc morale esse agnoscunt, quod tempus aliqdod cultui publico destinandum sit; pro ceremonia vero habent unum ex septem diebus. Ita Dorscheus in thesi allegatus, ante eum Jo. Brentius, et post eum Sebast. Schmidius, cum aliis quibusdam putans, liberum fuisse christianis, vel sextum vel octavum vel decimum diem ad cultum publicum eligere, atque ita vel intra circulum hebdomadarium manere, vel eundem egredi.“ (Controvers. Sylloge. p. 262. 263. 268. 269.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Eorum, qui tantum non omne ceremoniale Sabbatho abjudicant, statuentes, omnia, quae in hoc tertio praecepto habentur, esse moralia, ac proinde, sabbathum non potuisse abrogari, colligunt. Ita Sabbatharii, Ebionitae apud Nicephorum 1. 3. Hist. eccles. c. 13., Eusebium 1.3. H.E. c. 2i., Epiphanium Haeres. 30. (Sic et nonnulli veteres Christiani, praesertim in oriente, sabbathum et diem Dominicum una sanctiflcarunt, teste Socrate H. E. 1. 6. c. 8. Et pseudoapostol. Constitutiones 1. 7. c.24. mandant, ,ut festa sint cujusque septimanae sabbathum et dies Dom.‘ Hinc Gregarius Nyss. Orat, adv. eos, qui castigationes aeque ferunt: ,Quibus‘, inquit, ,oculis diem Dom. intueris, qui despicatus es sabbathum? An nescis, hos duos dies, Dominicum et sabbathum, germanos esse, et si in alterum injurius sis, te in alterum quoque impingere?‘ ... Anastasius Nicaenus ita: ,Sabbathum et dies Dominica sunt dies festi et sancti, neque licet in eis jejunare‘ etc. Alii tamen Christiani particulam tantum sabbathi, praeparationis ad divinum cultum causa, segregabant, uti ex Eusebio 1. 4. de vita Constantini c. 18. colligere est, qui mos etiam hodie in nostris ecclesiis viget.) ...


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: Of those who acknowledge no morality here, but assert that this entire third…

2. Of those who acknowledge no morality here, but assert that this entire third commandment is ceremonial and was abolished by Christ in the New Testament. Thus the Socinians, as in the Racovian Catechism, q. 69: 'What do you think of this commandment? Resp.: I think it has been abolished under the New Covenant, just like other ceremonies, as they are called'; cf. ibid., q. 70 and 71. ...

3. Of the Anabaptists, who maintain the same. ... They conspire here, as in many other things, amicably with the Socinians, whence it is said that 'an unlearned Anabaptist is a Socinian, but a learned Socinian is an Anabaptist.'" (L.c., ch. 1, s. 2, q. 4, p. 978.)

Quenstedtius: "The Apostles ... sanctioned and instituted the first day of the week, by the divine authority with which they were endowed, as the ordinary Sabbath of Christians." (L.c., p. 977.) "

Hence others proceed so learnedly regarding the morality of this commandment concerning the Sabbath that they hold: 1. That a certain external worship, some time for divine worship, and rest from labors hindering sacred things belong to the law of natural morality. For it is naturally impressed upon man to have fixed and designated days for divine worship. 2. That the circumstance of the seventh day, indefinitely in any weekly cycle after the completion of six days of labor, from wherever you begin the weekly cycle, belongs to the law of positive morality. And 3. That the seventh day, i.e., the last day of the Jewish week, is of merely ceremonial law, in itself and by its own nature mutable, though by the hypothesis of the still-standing Jewish polity immutable, which has actually been varied and changed in the New Testament. Thus the blessed Dannhauer in Coll. decal., disp. 8, § 4, p. 546." (L.c.)

Ph. J. Spener: "In particular, I would not like for such a question concerning the obligation of the Sabbath to come into too much public disputation; for I am certain that it would cause a great schism in our church, and therefore I would not like it to become generally known how very different our own people are on such points. A few years ago, it was the case that such a fire might have broken out, and already..."

ON LAW AND GOSPEL. such movements were shown, at which I shuddered, and I thanked God when the matter became quiet again.” (A. 1675. See *Last Theological Considerations*, edited by C. H. v. Canstein. II, 41.)

The same: “To prove the necessity of observing the Sunday for the entire day against an adversary becomes more difficult than one might believe. For not only about 30 years ago was this controversy *de moralitate sabbathi* [on the morality of the Sabbath] strongly pursued for a while, but by God’s grace it soon subsided again; since I noticed that at that time the theologians at the most prominent universities were divided among themselves on this matter, and in one *collegio* [lecture course] one sided with one party, the other with the other. Thus, the two famous theologians, Dr. Seb. Schmidt of Strasbourg and Dr. Wagner, Chancellor of Tübingen, as commissioners requested by the city of Augsburg in the case of a deacon there, who had been challenged partly because of his zeal against those who visited Sunday fairs, spoke against him. I also still remember two old theologians, still living at universities, who contradict the *sententiae de moralitate sabbathi* [opinion on the morality of the Sabbath]; and I fear that if the fire of such a dispute were to break out anew, the opposing party would prove itself much stronger.” (A. 1703. *L. c.* I, 476.)

The same: “Since those who do not acknowledge the same view of the third commandment as we do surpass us in number, and since I have seen what opinions from our older theologians before the blessed Gerhard lend authority to their position, the minds of most have always been more easily drawn by that dispute to their side than to ours. Whence it seemed more useful to me if we obtain at least this from the civil power, that the more glaring scandals be abolished.” (A. 1689. See *Latin Theological Consultations and Judgments*. II, 26.)

Indeed, for this reason primarily is the Sabbath observed among Christians: that on the Sabbath day, when it is otherwise not permitted to be free for this matter, leisure and time may be taken to serve divine worship; so that we may assemble to hear and treat of the Word of God, and subsequently praise God with hymns, psalms, canticles, and prayers. And these things ought indeed to be done daily, but since the multitude is hindered by business and cannot attend, at the very least one day per week must be chosen to serve this purpose. Furthermore, since the Lord’s Day has been ordained for this by our ancestors, this harmless and already accepted custom of the ancients is not to be rashly changed, so that a unanimous and consenting order may remain, lest anyone disturb everything with their unnecessary innovation.

These are the words of Luther in the *Large Catechism*, explanation of the 3rd commandment, p. 424. Compare § *Quare* [Wherefore], and § *Et profecto* [And indeed] p. 425.

According to those things which we have just said; yet not excluding or neglecting private exercise, by which individuals perform their duties, being free for holy words, works, and life, as is said *l. c.* § *Quare*. For holidays are not to be observed so strictly and superstitiously that, for their sake, labors which cannot be avoided or interrupted are forbidden; as is said *l. c.* § *Hujus* [Of this] p. 425. Compare § *Quare adversus hoc* [Wherefore against this] p. 427.

Whence our people commonly teach that not only works which are formally divine worship are lawful, but also those of charity, necessity, and those which pertain to the sustenance of life; but that there are prohibited not only works which are otherwise sinful in themselves, but also works of ordinary civil function which either fatigue the body or distract the mind with cares and render it unfit for sacred things; finally, also works of untimely or inordinate recreation, by which the devotion of public or private worship is hindered. PART III. CHAPTER VII.

§ 10.

The fourth [commandment] enjoins the honor and obedience to be rendered to parents and those who are in their place;b it forbids contemptc and offensesd against them. At the same time, it obligates parents and those like them to provide for the advantagese of their children and subjects, etc., and to take care not to harmf them, or make themselvesg contemptible.h b For example, guardians and curators, masters and mistresses, magistrates, ministers of the churches, teachers, those who are older in age, etc. For when precepts or prohibitions are given in some specific form, the related forms, or the whole genus, are also commanded or forbidden, according to the ancient rule.

c While preserving, however, the honor and obedience that is owed primarily to God. d Whether it be declared through external signs or suppressed in the mind.

e Through disobedience or contumacy. f Namely, that they conduct themselves in a manner worthy of the character divinely granted to them and be as it were an instrument of divine goodness toward those inferiors committed to their care and trust, regarding their spiritual and temporal happiness. g By neglecting them, or by corrupting them through unjust commands, solicitations, promises, threats, examples, etc., and by seizing for themselves, wasting, etc., what ought to have been prepared for or left to their inferiors.

h By the aforementioned ways or other ways by which they themselves hinder a good opinion of themselves and the estimation appropriate to their status. For the scope of this commandment is to preserve the order of superiors and inferiors, instituted for the good of the human race, and to assign to each party their duties. § 11.

The fifth [commandment] prohibits homicide, whether committed by deed or intended in the mind,a along with any injuries whatsoeverb or the desirec for injury to the life or body of one’s neighbor;d but it commands that aid be brought to him in his necessities,e and that works of mercy, humanity, and gentlenessf be studiously exhibited. Whence it is recognized that those things which pertain… to the care of our owng life and body also belong here. a Whence likewise rash and unjust wars, and the duels of private individuals, and all acts in which the intention, at least indirectly, involves the use of force against a neighbor. Capital punishments, however, which the magistrate inflicts upon evildoers, and necessary wars are not prohibited here, since they are not homicides according to the usage of speech.

b Not those which charity commands and prudence directs toward the greater good of the neighbor, such as those which are performed by surgeons; but those which harm the neighbor

… whether by the work itself, or by gesture, or by words, or are only conceived in the mind.

Whether it is manifested by external signs, of gestures, imprecations, threats, betrayal, etc., or is kept suppressed in the mind and comes under the names of wrath, hatred, ἐπιχαιρεκακία, or others. Whether he be a friend or an enemy. According to those things which we said in note c to § 7.

By which human life and conve…rsation are rendered better or more pleasant. See what we said in note c to § 6, from which it is evident that self-murder [αὐτοχειρία] is prohibited here, but that care for one’s own soul, life, and health is commended. § 12.

The sixth [commandment] forbids adultery and all related impurities, of work, of speech, and of gestures, and of the heart itself, and whatever else conflicts with marital fidelity; but it requires chastity to be cultivated within and outside of marriage, along with marital duties. Compare note a to § 10. Such as fornication, concubinage, incest, sodomy, etc.

Obscene songs, or poems, or jokes. To which pertains the lasciviousness of the eyes, the uncovering of parts of the body that ought to be covered to avoid the enticements of lust, and unchaste kisses. Obscene thoughts, and delight in them. Malicious desertions, rash divorces, quarrels, brawls, and animosities between spouses.

For there is given not only virginal and widowly chastity, but also marital chastity; the former of which implies complete abstinence from carnal union and related pleasures, the latter implies abstinence with the prior use withdrawn, and this [marital chastity] implies the moderate and holy use of them. Whether entirely mutual, or proper to husband and wife; concerning which more in its proper place. § 13.

The seventh [commandment] prohibits theft and every taking away of another’s goods and injustice, by which we attribute to ourselves more than is fitting, and to our neighbor less. But it commands that we give what is proper and to whom it is proper, and that we leave and preserve for each his own. By which reasoning, those things also which pertain to the care of honestly acquiring and guarding our own goods are to be observed. PART III. CHAPTER VII.

Latin:

2. Eorum, qui nihil moralitatis hic agnoscunt, sed totum hoc praeceptum tertium ceremoniale esse et a Christo in N. T. antiquatum esse asserunt. Sic Sociniani, ut Catechism. Racov. q. 69.: ,Quid de hoc praecepto censes? Resp.: Esse sublatum sub novo foedere, quemadmodum alias ceremonias, ut vocantur, censeo‘; cf. ib. q. 70. et 71. . . .

3. Anabaptistarum, idem statuentium. ... Conspirant hic, ut in multis aliis, cum Socinianis amice, unde et,anabaptista indoctus Socinianus, Socinianus‘ autem,doctus anabaptista‘ dicitur.“ (L. c. c. 1. s. 2. q. 4. f. 978.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Apostoli ... primum septimanae diem, divina, qua pollebant, auctoritate sanciverunt et instituerunt in sabbathum Christianorum ordinarium.“ (L. c. f. 977.),,

Hinc alii in moralitate hujus praecepti de sabbatho ita erudite procedunt, ut ipsis 1. juris moralis naturalis sit cultus quidam externus ac tempus aliquod cultus divini et vacatio a laboribus sacra impedientibus. Naturaliter enim est impressum homini, habere statos et destinatos dies cultui divino. 2. Juris moralis positivi circumstantia septimi diei indefinite in quovis orbe hebdomadario post exactos sex laboris dies, undecunque orbem hebdomadarium incipias. Et 3. juris mere ceremonialis sit septimus h. e. ultimus septimanae judaicae dies in se et sua natura mutabilis, ex hypothesi vero stantis adhuc politiae judaicae immutabilis, qui actu in N. T. variatus et immutatus est. Ita b. Dannhauerus in Coll, decal. disp. 8. § 4. p. 546.“ (L. c.)

Ph. J. Spewerus: ,,Sonderlich wollte ich nicht gerne, dass solche quaestio de sabbathi obligatione zu vieler öffentlichen Disceptation käme; indem ich versichert bin, dass es eine grosse Spaltung in unserer Kirche geben würde, und daher nicht gerne wollte, dass insgemein bekannt würde, wie sehr different in 801· chen Punkten die Unsrigen selber sind. Vor etlichen Jahren war es an dem, dass ein solch Feuer aufgebrochen wäre, und haben sich schon

solche motus gezeigt, davor mir gegrauet, und Gott gedanket, als die Sache wiederum stille worden.“ (A. 1675. Vid. Letzte theol. Bedenken, herausg. von C. H. v. Canstein. II, 41.)

Idem: ,,Die Nothwendigkeit der Sonntagsfeier auf den ganzen Tag gegen einen Widersacher zu erweisen, wird schwerer, als man glauben möchte. Wie denn nicht allein vor ungefähr 30 Jahren diese Controverse de moralitäte sabbathi eine Weile stark getrieben worden, aber durch Gottes Gnade sich bald wieder geleget hat; da ich bemerkte, dass damals auf den vornehmsten Universitäten die Theologen in dieser Materia unter sich uneins waren und in einem Collegio einer der einen, der andere der anderen Partei zufiel. So haben die beiden berühmten Theologen Hr. Dr. Seb. Schmidt von Strassburg und Hr. Dr. Wagner, Canzler von Tübingen, als von der Stadt Augsburg erbetene Commissarien in der Sache eines dasigen Diakonus, der zum Theil wegen seines Eifers wider die, so die Sonntags-Jahrmärkte besuchten, in Anspruch genommen worden, wider ihn gesprochen. So entsinne mich noch zwei alter noch jetzt lebender Theologen auf Universitäten, die der sententiae de moralitate sabbathi widersprechen; und fürchte ich, wo das Feuer solches Streites wieder aufs neue ausbrechen sollte, es würde die Gegenpartei sich viel stärker weisen.“ (A. 1703. L. c. I, 476.)

Idem: ,,Cum numeros eorum, qui non eandem nobiscum praecepti tertii religionem agnoscunt, nos vincat, et quae ex vetustioribus nostris theologis ante b. Gerhardum sententiae ipsorum auctoritatem concilient, vidi semper plerorumque animos illa disputatione ad horum facilius partem, quam ad nos, pertractos. Unde illud mihi utilius visum est, si a potestate civili saltem hoc obtineamus, ut extantiora duntaxat scandala aboleantur.“ (A. 1689. Vid. Consil. et judic. th. latina. II, 26.)

Nempe ob eam rem potissimum apud christianos sabbatum servatur, ut die sabbati, qmndo alias ei rei vacare non licet, otium et tempus sumatur cultui divino serviendi; ita ut conveniamus ad audiendum et trdctandum Dei verbum, ac deinceps Deum hymnis, psalmis, canticis et precibus laudemus. Et haec quidem quotidie jieri debebant, sed quando multitudo praepedita negotiis interesse nequeat, ad minimum unus aliquis dies per hebdomadam huic rei servandae eligendus est. Porro autem cum a majoribus nostris ad hoc dies dominica ordinata sit, non est immutanda temere haec innoxia veterum consuetudo jam recepta, ut unanimis et consentiens ordo consistat, ne quis sua non necessaria innovatione conturbet omnia.

Verba sunt Lutheri in Catech. Maj. explic. praec. III. p. m. 424. conf. § Quare, et § Et profecto p. 425.

Juxta ea, quae modo diximus; non tamen excluso aut neglecto exercitio privato, quo singuli fungantur, sanctis verbis, operibus et vitae vacantes, ut dicitur 1. c. § Quare. Neque enim tam arcte et superstitiose colendae sunt feriae, ut earum gratia labores, qui vitari et intermitti non possunt, interdicantur; prout dicitur 1. c. § Hujus. p. 425. Conf. § Quare adversus hoc. p. 427.

Unde vulgo nostri non solum opera, quae formaliter sunt cultus divini, verum etiam sunt caritatis, necessitatis, et quae ad sustentationem vitae pertinent, licita esse docent, prohiberi autem opera non solum alias ex se peccaminosa, verum etiam opera functionis civilis ordinariae, quae vel corpus fatigant, vel animum curis distrahunt et ad sacra ineptum reddunt; denique etiam opera recreationis intempestivae aut inordinatae, quibus devotio cultus publici aut privati impeditur. PART. in. CAP. vn.

§ 10.

Quartum praecipit honorem et obsequia, parentibus, et qui eorum a loco sunt, praestanda;b vetat contemtum c et offensas d eorundem. Simul parentes et his similes obligat ad procuranda commoda e liberorum ac subditorum etc. et cavendum, ne noceant f illis, aut se ipsos faciant g contemtibiles.h V. gr. tutores et curatores, domini dominaeque, magistratus, ecclesiarum ministri, praeceptores, seniores aetate etc. Praecepta enim aut prohibita specie aliqua praecipua, etiam cognatae species, sive totum genus praecipitur aut prohibetur, juxta regulam veterem.

Salvo tamen honore et obsequio, quod Deo inprimis debetur. Sive per signa externa declaretur, sive animo comprimatur.

Per inobedientiam aut contumaciam. Nimirum, ut se dignos gerant charactere divinitus concesso et sint velut instrumentum bonitatis divinae erga inferiores suae curae ac fidei commissos quoad spiritualem et temporalem eorum felicitatem. Negligendo, aut injustis imperiis, solicitationibus, promissis, minis, exemplis etc. eos corrumpendo, quaeque inferioribus parari aut relinqui debebant, ad se rapiendo, perdendo etc.

Modo memoratis aut aliis modis, quibus bonam de se opinionem statusque sui congruam aestimationem ipsi impediant. Scopus enim hujus praecepti est, servare ordinem superiorum et inferiorum, generis humani bono institutum, et utrique parti sua officia assignare. § 11.

Quintum prohibet homicidium, seu facto commissum, seu animo intentum, a cum quibuslibet laesionibus b aut desiderio c laesionis, vitae aut corporis proximi;d jubet autem ei auxilium ferre in necessitatibus, e et opera misericordiae, humanitatis, mansuetudinis f studiose exhibere. Unde et quae ad nostrae g vitae atque corporis curam spectant, huc pertinere cognoscitur. Unde bella pariter temeraria atque injusta, et duella privatorum omnesque actus, in quibus intentio, saltem indirecta, vim faciendi proximo involvitur. Supplicia autem capitalia, quae magistratus maleficis infert, et bella necessaria hic non prohibentur, cum nec ex usu loquendi sint homicidia.

Non, quas caritas imperat ac prudentia dirigit ad majus bonum proximi, quales sunt, quae a chirurgis fiunt; sed quae nocent

proximo, sive opere ipso, aut gestu, aut verbis fiant, sive tantum animo concipiantur.

Sive signis externis, gestuum, imprecationis, minarum, proditionis etc. manifestetur, sive animo clausum prematur atque irae, odii, έπιχαιρεχαχίας aliisve nominibus veniat. Sive amicus sit, sive inimicus. Juxta ea, quae diximus in nota c. ad § 7.

Quibus humana vita et conversatio melior aut suavior reddatur. Vide, quae diximus in nota c. ad § 6., unde constat, prohiberi h. 1. αυτοχειρίαν, commendari autem curam animae, vitae ac valetudinis propriae. § 12.

Sextum vetat adulterium et cognatas a impuritates omnes, operis,b oris c ac gestuum,d et ipsius cordis,e quaeque praeterea cum fide conjugali f pugnant; exigit autem castitatem intra et extra g conjugium colendam, una cum officiis h conjugalibus. Confer notam a. ad § 10. Quales sunt scortatio, concubinatus, incestus, sodomia etc.

Cantica, aut carmina, aut joci obscoeni. Quo pertinet lascivia oculorum, denudatio partium corporis ob vitandas libidinis illecebras tegendarum, oscula impudica. Cogitationes obscoenae, et oblectatio in illis. Desertiones malitiosae, divortia temeraria, jurgia, rixae et simultates conjugum.

Datur enim non solum virginalis ac vidualis, sed et conjugalis castitas, quarum illu abstinentiam a copula carnali et cognatis voluptatibus plenam, ista abstinentiam subducto usu priore, haec moderatum et sanctum illarum usum importat. Seu plane mutuis, seu marito atque uxori propriis; de quibus suo loco plura. § 13.

Septimum prohibet furtum atque omnem a opum alienarum ablationem et injustitiam,b qua plus, quam decet nobis, minus proximo tribuimus. Praecipit autem, ut demus, quae et quibus oportet, sua cuique relinquamus et conservemus. Qua ratione et quae ad nostrarum opum c honeste acquirendarum ac tuendarum curam d pertinent, observanda sunt. PART. III. CAP. VII.


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: And thus also rapine, embezzlement, etc

And thus also rapine, embezzlement, etc. Cf. note c. to § 6. In contracts of buying and selling, loaning, leasing and hiring, etc. And otherwise, when either the magistrate imposes excessive burdens, or subjects deny their debts, or pay them too slowly; when laborers or servants are unfaithful or negligent; or when wages are not rightly paid to them by those who owe them (by whatever name they may be called); when found items are not returned to their owners; when a living is sought through dishonest arts or by begging rashly; when alms are either entirely denied to the needy, or are given too sparingly and grudgingly, etc. Cf. note c. to § VII.

Luther: "Where one lends money and demands or takes more or better in return, that is usury, condemned in all laws. Therefore, all those who take five, six, or more per hundred from loaned money, they are usurers; let them know how to govern themselves accordingly, and they are called idolatrous servants of greed or Mammon, and they cannot be saved unless they do penance. Thus, one must say exactly the same thing about grain, barley, and other such goods, that where one demands more or better for them, that is usury, stolen and robbed property. For lending means this: when I give someone my money, property, or tools so that he may use them as long as he needs them, or as long as I can and will, and he returns the same to me at his time, as good as I have lent it to him; just as one neighbor lends another dishes, pitchers, beds, clothes, and thus also money or money's worth, for which I should take nothing. We are not speaking this time of giving or gifting, nor of buying or selling, nor of redeemable interest; but of lending, in which usury now conducts almost all its business, especially in money-lending. Therefore, this point is to be diligently impressed upon the people, and it is no great, high wisdom, but is quite easy to understand, and a very crude text, namely: whoever lends something and takes something over and above it, or (which is the same thing) something better, that is usury. For lending should take back nothing more, but exactly the same thing that was lent, as the prophets, Christ himself, and also the secular laws teach. . . .

Fourthly, Squire Usury speaks thus: 'My dear fellow, as the times are now, I am doing my neighbor a great service by lending him a hundred at five, six, or ten, and he thanks me for such a loan as a special favor; he even begs me for it, and offers himself, willingly and unforced, to gift me five, six, or ten guilders per hundred; should I not be able to take that without usury and with a good conscience? Who would consider a gift to be usury?' Here I say: Let whoever wants to boast, adorn, and dress it up do so, but do not let yourself be moved by it; remain firm by the text: one shall take nothing more or better upon a loan. But whoever takes more or better, that is usury, and it is not called a service, but harm done to one's neighbor, just as happens with stealing and robbing. Not everything that is called a service and a good deed is a service and a good deed to one's neighbor; for an adulteress and an adulterer do each other a great service and favor; a rider does a great service to an incendiary by helping him rob on the road and feud against land and people. . . .

This case can happen, or often does happen: that I, Hans, lend you, Balthasar, a hundred guilders, with the understanding that I must have them back at Michaelmas for my necessities, or else I will (if you delay) come to harm because of it. Michaelmas comes, you do not give me the hundred guilders back, so the judge takes me by the throat, or puts me in the tower or in custody, or some other such trouble comes upon me, until I am—

pay: there I sit or remain stuck, neglecting my sustenance and improvement to my great detriment; there you bring me down with your dallying, and reward me so poorly for my kindness. What am I to do here? My "damage-watch" [accrued loss] wakes because you dally and sleep, and daily expense or damage is incurred as long as you dally and sleep. Who, then, is to bear or atone for the damage here? For the "damage-watch" will eventually be an intolerable guest in my house, until I am utterly ruined.

Well then, here we must speak of the matter in a worldly and legal sense (we must save the theology for later). Thus, you, Balthser, are obligated to give me, in addition to the hundred guilders, everything that the "damage-watch" has driven up with all the costs, for it is your fault that you have left me in this state, and it is just as much as if you had taken it from me wickedly. Therefore, it is fair, even according to reason and natural law, that you reimburse me for everything, both the principal sum and the damage; for I did not lend you the hundred guilders so that I should ruin myself, or that you should ruin me with them, but I wanted to help you without suffering damage myself. All this is so clear and bright that, even if all laws and law books were lost, reason would still have to establish it, however weak it might be.

The books of the jurists call such a "damage-watch" *interesse* in Latin, and such lending is certainly no usury, but a right, praiseworthy, honest service and a good work shown to one's neighbor. And where the person is a Christian, it is also a Christian work, which God will reward not only here on earth, as He does worldly works, but also in that world, as David says in Ps. 112:6: *In memoria aeterna erit justus etc.* For God will never forget a Christian good work; the worldly good works He pays for here on earth, and thereafter they are forgotten; thus, laws and worldly government can do no more than teach and maintain such worldly, perishable good works.

Beyond this "damage-watch," another can now occur, and it is this: if you, Balthser, do not return the hundred guilders to me at Michaelmas, and a purchase presents itself to me, such that I could buy a garden, field, house, or whatever property it may be, from which I might have great profit or sustenance for myself and my children, then I must let it pass, and you cause me the damage and hindrance with your dallying and sleeping, so that I can never again come to such a purchase. If I had not lent you my hundred guilders, but kept them at home, I could pay the judge with half and buy the garden with the other half; now that I have lent them to you, you make a twin out of the "damage-watch" for me, so that I can neither pay here nor buy there, and thus must suffer damage on both sides; this is what they call *duplex interesse, damni emergentis et lucri cessantis*, as well as they are able to speak of it.

Here one must leave to the jurists their manifold disputations as to whether a single hundred guilders, if neglected, can bring both damages or the twin at once. For if Hanns owes a hundred guilders, only one "damage-watch" is there; if he owes fifty, both "damage-watches" may be there; for no one can pay with a hundred guilders and at the same time buy the garden for a hundred guilders. Likewise, it is another matter whether the garden was for sale, or was conditionally purchasable when Hanns lent out the hundred guilders; for what is not yet for sale, even if cash is present, no one can buy. Item, that Hanns could well have lost the hundred guilders through theft, robbers, fire, and the like, whereby he could neither pay nor buy; for money is an uncertain, fickle thing, upon which one cannot trade with certainty. Such and countless similar circumstances or contingencies it behooves the jurists to calculate and weigh, so that the "damage-watch" or *interesse* does not become a rogue and a usurer. PART III. CHAP. VII. become; and wise people can well err here.

But how can one make everything so pure in the impure law, which the world must use in this miserable life? It is enough that it be coarse, simple, and plain law; it cannot be subtle and sharp, or it will get such notches that it cannot even cut butter, whereas it ought to split blocks and logs. It is another matter with Christ and His Gospel.

But you, preacher, have enough in this to be able to distinguish what usury is; namely, if Balthser has not returned the hundred guilders at Michaelmas, and Hanns has had to pay because of it, and suffered damage, then Balthser should reimburse him for the payment damage according to worldly law. If he has thereby prevented Hanns from being able to buy the garden: if Hanns wants to proceed strictly, then Balthser must also yield something; or let good friends settle and reconcile it (that is better); for it is difficult and dangerous to estimate and hit upon that same purchase damage exactly, because the purchase was never made nor concluded, as to how dearly the garden would have been bought, and perhaps another garden just as good could have turned up instead. In the other damage of payment, one can easily calculate the expenses; but the Gospel will judge much more simply in this matter; as hereafter.

But look into this and note well, my pastor, that such lending, where *Schadewacht* [compensation for damage] or interest governs within, does not happen in these dealings now, but it is all vain usury with them. For after they have heard that Hanns has suffered damage with his lent hundred guilders, and demands fair reimbursement of his damage, they proceed bluntly and slap onto every hundred guilders such two *Schadewacht*, namely: the expenses of payment, and the missed garden purchase; just as if such two *Schadewacht* had naturally grown onto the hundred guilders: where a hundred guilders are present, they lend them out, and calculate such two damages upon them, and take from them reimbursement for such damages, which they have not, however, suffered.

For, because you have a hundred guilders, you are not therefore obligated to pay at Michaelmas, and there is therefore no garden for sale that you could buy at Michaelmas; nor do you calculate such two null damages upon your certain, secure hundred guilders, and take for them five, six, ten guilders yearly, just as if you were the Hanns who is neglected and hindered by Balthser. No, listen now, you are not that same Hanns; for there is no Balthser there who makes such a Hanns; you imagine for yourself that you are such a Hanns, without any Balthser; therefore you are a usurer, who yourself atone for your imagined damage with your neighbor's money, which no one has done to you, and you can neither prove nor calculate it. Such damage the jurists call *non verum, sed fantasticum interesse*, a damage that everyone dreams up for himself.

Latin:

Adeoque et rapinam, peculatum etc. Conf. not. c. ad § 6. In contractibus emtionis et venditionis, mutui, locationis et conductionis etc. Et alias, quando vel onera nimia magistratus imponit, vel debita subditi denegant, aut segnius praestant; quando operarii, aut servi, infideles aut negligentes sunt; vel merces illis ab bis, qui debent (quocunque nomine veniant) non recte solvitur; quando inventa non restituuntur dominis; quando artibus inhonestis, aut temere mendicando, victus quaeritur; quando indigentibus eleemosynae vel prorsus denegantur, vel parcius atque aegre dantur etc. Conf. not. c. ad § VII.

Lutherus: ,,Wo man Geld leihet, und dafür mehr oder Besseres fordert oder nimmt, das ist Wucher, in allen Rechten verdammt. Darum alle diejenigen, so fünfe, sechs, oder mehr aufs Hundert nehmen vom geliehenen Gelde, die sind Wucherer; darnach sie sich wissen zu richten, und heissen des Geizes oder Mammons abgöttische Diener, und mögen nicht selig werden, sie thun denn Busse. Also eben soll man von Korn, Gersten und ander mehr Waare auch sagen, dass, wo man mehr oder Besseres dafür fordert, das ist Wucher, gestohlen und geraubt Gut. Denn Leihen heisst das, wenn ich jemand mein Geld, Gut oder Geräthe thue, dass ers brauche, wie lange ihm noth ist, oder ich kann und will, und er mir dasselbe zu seiner Zeit wiedergebe, so gut als ichs habe ihm geliehen; wie ein Nachbar dem andern leihet Schüssel, Kannen, Bette, Kleider, also auch Geld oder Geldeswerth, dafür ich nichts nehmen soll. Wir reden diesmal nichts von Geben oder Schenken, auch nicht von Kaufen oder Verkaufen, noch vom wiederkäuflichen Zinse; sondern von dem Leihen, darin der Wucher fast alle seine Geschäfte jetzt treibet, sonderlich im Geldleihen. Darum ist das Stück fleissig dem Volk einzubilden, und ist keine grosse, hohe Klugheit, sondern ist ganz leicht zu verstehen, und ein sehr grober Text, nämlich, wer etwas leihet, und nimmt dafür etwas drüber, oder (das gleich so viel ist) etwas Besseres, das ist Wucher. Denn Leihen soll nichts mehr wiedernehmen, sondern eben dasselbe, das geliehen ist, wie die Propheten, Christus selbs, auch die weltlichen Rechte lehren. . . .

Zum Vierten, spricht Junker Wucher also: Lieber, als jetzt die Läufte sind, so thue ich meinem Nächsten einen grossen Dienst dran, dass ich ihm leihe hundert auf fünfe, sechse, zehen, und er dankt mir solches Leihens, als einer sonderlichen Wohlthat; bittet mich wohl darum, erbeut sich auch selbs, willig und ungezwungen, mir fünf, sechs, zehn Gulden vom Hundert zu schenken; sollte ich das nicht ohne Wucher mit gutem Gewissen mögen nehmen? Wer will ein Geschenk für Wucher achten? Hie sage ich: Lass du rühmen, schmücken und putzen, wer da will, kehre dich gleichwohl nichts dran, bleibe fest bei dem Text: man soll auf Leihen nichts mehr oder BessCrs nehmen. Wer aber mehr oder Bessere nimmt, das ist Wucher, und heisst nicht Dienst, sondern Schaden gethan seinem Nächsten, als mit Stehlen und Rauben geschieht. Es ist nicht alles Dienst und wohlgethan dem Nächsten, was man heisst Dienst und wohlgethan; denn eine Ehebrecherin und Ehebrecher thun einander grossen Dienst und Wohlgefallen; ein Reuter thut einem Mordbrenner grossen Reuterdienst, dass er ihm hilfet auf der Strasse rauben, Land und Leute befehden. ...

Es kann geschehen, oder geschieht auch wohl oft dieser Fall: dass ich, Hanns, leihe dir, Balthser, hundert Gulden, mit solcher Masse, dass ich sie muss auf Michaelis wieder haben zur Nothdurft, oder werde (wo du säumest) drob zu Schaden kommen. Michaelis kommt, du gibst mir die hundert Gulden nicht wieder, so nimmt mich der Richter bei dem Halse, oder setzt mich in Thurm oder Gehorsam, oder kommt dergleichen ander Unrath daraus über mich, bis ich be-

zahle: da sitze oder bleibe ich stecken, versäume meine Nahrung und Besserung mit grossem Schaden; da bringest du mich zu mit deinem Säumen, und lohnest mir so übel für meine Wohlthat. Was soll ich hie thun? Mein Schade wacht, weil du säumest und schlafest, und gehet täglich Unkost oder Schaden drauf, so lange du säumest und schläfest. Wer soll nun denn hie den Schaden tragen oder büssen? Denn der Schadewacht wird zuletzt ein unleidlicher Gast in meinem Hause sein, bis ich zu Grund verderbe.

Wohlan, hie ist weltlich und juristisch von der Sache zu reden (die Theologiam müssen wir sparen bis hernach). So bist du, Balthser, mir schuldig hinnach zu geben über die hundert Gulden alles, was der Schadewacht mit aller Unkost drauf getrieben hat, denn es ist deine Schuld, dass du mich so gelassen hast, und ist eben so viel, als hättest du mirs genommen frevelich. Darum ists billig, auch der Vernunft und natürlichem Rechte nach, dass du mir alles wieder erstattest, beide die Hauptsumma mit dem Schaden; denn ich habe dir die hundert Gulden nicht geliehen, dass ich mich selbs, oder du mich damit solltest verderben, sondern ich habe dir wollen ohne meinen Schaden helfen. Dies alles ist so klar und helle, dass, wenn alle Jura und Juristenbücher verloren würden, so müsste es doch die Vernunft noch setzen, wie schwach sie wäre.

Solchen Schadewacht heissen der Juristen Bücher zu Latein Interesse, und solch Leihen ist freilich kein Wucher, sondern ein rechter löblicher, ehrlicher Dienst und gut Werk, dem Nächsten erzeigt. Und wo die Person dazu ein Christ ist, so ists auch ein christlich Werk, welches Gott nicht allein hie auf Erden, wie er den weltlichen thut, sondern auch in jener Welt belohnen will, wie David sagt Ps. 112, 6.: In memoria aeterna erit justus etc. Denn eines christlichen guten Werkes will Gott nimmermehr vergessen; die weltlichen guten Werke bezahlet er 11ie auf Erden, darnach sind sie vergessen; so können auch Jura und weltliche Herrschaft nicht mehr, denn solche weltliche, vergängliche gute Werke lehren und erhalten.

Ueber diesen Schadewacht kann nun noch einer vorfallen, und ist der: wenn du, Balthser, mir nicht wiedergibest auf Michaelis die hundert Gulden, und stehet mir vor ein Kauf, dass ich könnte kaufen einen Garten, Acker, Haus, oder was für ein Grund ist, daran ich grossen Nutzen oder Nahrung möchte haben, für mich und meine Kinder, so muss ichs lassen fahren, und du thust mir den Schaden und Hinderniss mit deinem Säumen und Schlafen, dass ich nimmermehr kann zu solchem Kauf kommen. Hätte ich nun meine hundert Gulden dir nicht geliehen, sondern daheim behalten, so könnte ich mit der Hälfte den Richter bezahlen, mit der andern Hälfte den Garten kaufen; nun ich dir sie geliehen habe, machst du ■mir einen Zwilling aus dem Schadewacht, dass ich hie nicht bezahlen, und dort nicht kaufen kann, und also zu beiden Theilen muss Schaden leiden; das heisst man duplex interesse, damni emergentis et lucri cessantis, so gut sie es haben können reden.

Hie muss man nun den Juristen lassen die mancherlei Disputation, ob einerlei hundert Gulden versäumet, zugleich beide Schaden oder den Zwilling bringen. Denn ist Hanns hundert Gulden schuldig, so ist allein der eine Schadewacht da; ist er fünfzig schuldig, so mögen beide Schadewacht da sein; denn cs kann niemand zugleich mit einem hundert Gulden bezahlen, und zugleich den Garten für hundert Gulden kaufen. So ists auch ein anderes, ob der Garten feil gewest, oder käuflich mit einbedingt ist, da Hanns die hundert Gulden von sich geliehen hat; denn was noch nicht feil ist, wenn schon baar Geld da ist, kann niemand kaufen. Item dass Hanns die hundert Gulden wohl hätte mögen verlieren durch Diebstahl, Räuber, Feuer und dergleichen, damit er weder bezahlen noch kaufen könnte; denn es ist Geld ein ungewiss, wankelbar Ding, darauf man kein Gewisses kann handeln. Solche und derselben unzählige Umstände oder Zufälle gebührt den Juristen zu rechnen und zu bewegen, damit der Schade wacht oder Interesse nicht ein Schalk und Wucherer PART. III. CAP. VII. werde; und können weise Leute hier wohl fehlen.

Aber wie kann man alles so rein machen in dem unreinen Recht, so die Welt in diesem elenden Leben muss brauchen? Ist genug, dass es grob, schlecht, einfaltig Recht sei; subtil und scharf kanns nicht sein, oder kriegt solche Scharten, dass es auch nicht Butter schneiden kann, da es wohl sollte Blöcke und Klötze scheitern. Es ist ein ander Ding mit Christo und seinem Evangelio.

Aber du, Prediger, hast hieran genug, damit du könnest unterscheiden, was Wucher ist; nämlich, hat Balthser die hundert Gulden auf Michaelis nicht wiedergegeben, und Planns hat drüber müssen bezahlen, und Schaden gelitten, so soll ihm Balthser den Bezahlschaden wieder erstatten nach weltlichem Recht. Hat er dazu damit verhindert, dass Hanns den Garten nicht hat können kaufen: will Hanns strenge fahren, so muss Balthser auch was nachgeben; oder lasses (das ist besser) gute Freunde vertragen und schlichten; denn es ist schwer und fährlich, denselben Kaufschaden eben gleich zu schätzen unditreffen, weil der Kauf zuvor nie gemacht, noch beschlossen, wie theuer der Garten erkauft wäre worden, und vielleicht ein andrer Garten dagegen ja so gut konnte noch vorfallen. In dem andern Schaden der ]Bezahlung kann man die Unkosten leichtlich rechnen; das Evangelium aber wird viel einfältiger hierin richten; wie hernach.

Darein siehe aber und merke wohl, mein Pfarrherr, dass solch Leihen, da Schadewacht oder Interesse innen regiert, in den Händeln jetzt nicht geschieht, sondern ist alles eitel Wucherei mit ihnen. Denn nachdem sie gehöret, dass Hanns mit seinen verliehenen hundert Gulden hat Schaden gelitten, und billige Erstattung seines Schadens fordert, fahren sie plumps einhin, und schlahen auf ein jeglich hundert Gulden solche zween Schadewacht, nämlich·, des Bezahlens Unkosten, und des versäumten Gartenkaufs; gerade als wären den hundert Gulden natürlich solche zween Schadewacht angewachsen: wo hundert Gulden vorhanden sind, die thun sie aus, und rechnen drauf solche zween Schaden, und nehmen davon Erstattung solcher Schaden, die sie doch nicht erlitten haben.

Denn, dass du hundert Gulden hast, darum bist du nicht schuldig, dass du auf Michaelis bezahlen müssest, und ist darum kein Garten feil, den du auf Michaelis kaufen könntest; noch rechenst du solche nichtige beide Schaden auf deine gewisse sichere hundert Gulden, und nimmst dafür fünf, sechs, zehen Gulden jährlich, gerade als wärest du der Hanns, der von Balthser versäumt und verhindert ist. Nein, hörest nun es, du bist nicht derselbe Hanns; denn es ist kein Balthser da, der einen solchen Hannsen mache; du erdichtest dir selbs, dass du ein solcher Hanns seiest, ohne alle Balthser; darum bist du ein Wucherer, der du selbs deinen erdichteten Schaden von deines Nächsten Geld büssest, den dir doch niemand gethan hat, und kannst ihn auch nicht beweisen noch berechnen. Solchen Schaden heissen die Juristen non verum, sed fantasticum Interesse, ein Schaden, den ein jeglicher ihm selber erträumet.


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: Yes, you say, it is possible, and it could nevertheless happen, that my hundred…

Yes, you say, it is possible, and it could nevertheless happen, that my hundred guilders might suffer such two damages someday. There you are right. Let us now deal with each other equally: your hundred guilders might perhaps someday suffer such two damages, so I could someday well give you five, six guilders; let it be equal, and let the guilders lie still; as long as your hundred guilders do not suffer such two damages, so long will I give you nothing; thus we are agreed on the matter, and the lending is right.

It does not hold to say: the damages could happen, that I could neither pay nor buy; but it means: the damages have happened, that I have not been able to pay nor buy. Otherwise it is called: *Ex contingente Necessarium*, out of that which is not, to make that which must be; out of that which is uncertain, to make a vain certain thing; should such usury not devour the world in a few years? In sum, it is now said enough that lending should take nothing over and above, and should be

...are done for the service or benefit of the needy. Hold fast to the text, and it is also easy to understand that to pay for damages is not the same as giving or taking more than what was lent; for it is an accidental misfortune that befalls the lender without his will, for which he must recover. But in business dealings it is the reverse, and quite the opposite; there, one seeks and fabricates damages against the needy neighbor, wishing thereby to feed oneself and become rich, to be lazy and idle, to carouse and show off from other people’s labor, worry, danger, and loss; so that I sit behind the stove and let my hundred guilders work for me in the country; and yet, because it is lent money, I keep it safely in my purse, without any danger or worry. My dear friend, who would not want that? And what is said of lent money, that should also be understood of lent grain, wine, and similar goods, that such two damages may occur therein; but that those damages should not have naturally accrued to the goods, but rather have occurred accidentally, and therefore are not to be counted as damages until they have happened and are proven, where they are demanded and taken without that, one knows that it is usury and injustice. . . . They say: the world cannot be without usury. That is certainly true. For no government in the world will ever become so rigid and stately, nor has it ever been, that it could prevent all sins. And if a government could prevent all sins, still original sin, the source of all sins, together with the devil (of which the laws know nothing), must remain, which one must always resist anew, as much as is possible. Therefore, the world cannot be without usury, without greed, without pride, without whoredom, without adultery, without murder, without stealing, without blasphemy, and all kinds of sins; otherwise it would not be the world, and would have to be a world without a world, a devil without a devil. But whether they are excused by this, they will surely find out. The Lord says in Matthew 18:7: "Woe to the world for temptations to sin! For it is necessary that temptations come, but woe to the man by whom the temptation comes." Usury must be, but woe to the usurers. . . . But how? If the case were to arise that, for instance, old people, poor widows or orphans, or otherwise needy persons who until then had learned no other trade, had a thousand or two florins in trade; and if they were to let them go, they would have nothing else, and would have to warm their hands on a beggar’s staff, or die of hunger. Here I would gladly wish that the jurists would establish a mitigation of the strict law; and it should be considered that all the aforementioned princes and lords who have curbed usury, such as Solon, Alexander, the Romans, could not or would not make everything pure, nor did Nehemiah restore everything (Nehemiah 5:15). And here the saying mentioned above might belong: the world cannot be without usury; yet so that it is not strictly usury, nor a right, but a "little necessity-usury," almost a half-work of mercy for the needy who would otherwise have nothing, and which does not particularly harm others. It could also be disputed whether an interest or damage might not be justified here, because they were misled and neglected, in that they learned nothing else in the meantime, and it would be unkind to make them beggars or let them die of hunger, because no one is helped by that, and it would happen without the ruin of the neighbor, as *ex restitutione vaga*.... I have by no means meant the purchaseable interest here; for what is a right, honest purchase, that is no usury. Thus, God be praised, one knows well what a purchaseable interest is according to secular laws, namely, that there should be a pledge, and that it should not be sold for too much per hundred, of which there is no need to speak now. Let everyone see to it for himself that it is a right, honest purchase." (Admonition to the Pastors to Preach against Usury. A.D. 1540. Opp. Hal. X, 1025. sqq.)

PART III. CHAPTER VII. The same: "That you indicate it seems strange to you that another should improve his property with your money, and you have nothing from it, is indeed a superfluous, unnecessary good work, like one who might give 100 florins to someone who did not need it. But by this, no usury is excused; why did I not keep it or use it for something more necessary? To a repurchase [Wiederkauf] belongs: Primo, a hypotheca, a pledge, such as a field, house, city, or land, upon which the interest has been purchased. For that which yields nothing can bear no interest. And where the pledge perishes or is lost in war by enemies, such as the Turks, there both lose their own, the buyer and the seller. Therefore, to take five or more, or even 1 gulden or a heller, on mere base money—that is, on a hundred (or however much it is) gulden—without an expressed and named pledge, is usury. Secundo, that the buyer (who buys the interest) remains obligated to permit the seller (who takes the sum of money upon his property) the redemption of the interest with an equal sum, if he can or will. Therefore, when the buyer reserves for himself the right to demand back the sum of his money with which he buys the interest after one, two, three, etc., years, which the jurists call repetitio sortis, that is also usury, a true whore-child, for it wants to be at once a loaned money (which one may demand back) and yet also a purchase-money (which I may not demand back after the goods have been received). Although one wants to dispute here when the seller himself requests or consents to the reclamation, as one who no longer wishes to have it sold, which is strange, and one must indeed take good care that it is not a semblance of light." (Letter to S. Weller. A.D. 1543. Luther’s Collected Works, Frankf. a. M. and Erlangen. Vol. LVI, p. LVIII sq.) Cf. Larger Sermon on Usury. A.D. 1519. Opp. Hal. X, 1010—1015. Chemnitius: "Many and various things have been disputed concerning usury. For some have contended that political society, such as human affairs are now, cannot subsist without usury; therefore, if political constitutions are observed in the exacting of usury, it can be done without injury to the conscience. Others, however, under the name of usury, rescind all legitimate contracts and condemn honest profits. . . It must be established from certain and clear testimonies of Scripture that usury is not a thing good in itself and by its own kind, nor is it a middle thing, such that it should be judged by its use or abuse, and that moderation is approved while only excess is condemned; but rather that it is an action evil, vicious, and condemned in itself and by its own kind. For many think that, just as in other legitimate contracts only excess, vices, and abuses are condemned, so also moderate usury is not a sin, but only excess is condemned. . . Now, however, we shall remove that pretext, as if Scripture approves of any usury. And first we shall speak concerning the passage Deut. 23:19, 20. . . God in the Old Testament was both theologian and legislator. For elsewhere He hands down how God is to be served in justice and holiness before Him. Elsewhere, however, for the external society of civil life in the Israelite republic, He prescribes certain political constitutions for that people. This is, as we commonly say, He treats of the law of the forum and the law of the pole, He orders the political forum and the forum of conscience. In political laws, however, which God gave to the people of Israel, justice and holiness of conscience before God are not always prescribed; but they are accommodated to the preservation of external and civil society in that polity, according to the condition of the temperaments and morals of that people, to whom God Himself attributed the epithet of stiff-necked. Because, therefore, God was prescribing forensic laws to the political magistrate, He saw that it was not possible for the vices which were to be punished by civil penalties to be entirely restrained by civil penalties through political laws due to the unbridled malice of men. In order, therefore, that worse evils might be avoided in the civil society of that people, He did not indeed approve of certain lesser evils, but permitted them to be tolerated for a forensic and political end, insofar as they were not punished by the civil magistrate. Thus Exod. 21:21: 'He who strikes his servant, so that he dies from it,' is not punished."

civilly as a murderer, but he was not thereby excused in conscience before God. Thus, the bill of divorce and usury toward foreigners were permitted in the political forum of the Republic of Israel, insofar as they were not punished by the civil magistrate. But because the Jews judged those forensic permissions as if they were precepts that inform the conscience before God, in this way: "God permits in the law of Moses; therefore, He approves; therefore, it does not conflict with the will of God; therefore, it is also valid in conscience before God." God, therefore, through Moses himself and later through the prophets, delivered by frequent repetition the explanation that those promises were to be understood politically, not theologically; in the civil forum, not in the forum of conscience; before the magistrate, not before God—as if it were not a sin before God because it is not punished by the magistrate.

Latin:

Ja, sprichst du, es ist möglich, und könnte gleichwohl geschehen, dass meine hundert Gulden solche zween Schaden litten dermaleins. Da bist du recht. Lasst uns nun gleich gegen einander handeln: deine hundert Gulden könnten vielleicht dermaleins solche zween Schaden leiden, so könnte ich dermaleins wohl dir fünf, sechs Gulden geben; lass gleich sein, und die Gulden stille liegen; so lange deine hundert Gulden solche zween Schaden nicht leiden, so lange will ich dir nichts geben; so sind wir der Sache eins, und ist das Leihen recht.

Es gilt nicht also Sagens: es könnten die Schaden geschehen, dass ich weder bezahlen noch kaufen könnte; sondern es heisst: es sind die Schaden geschehen, dass ich nicht habe können bezahlen noch kaufen. Sonst heissts: Ex contingente Necessarium, aus dem, das nicht ist, machen das, das sein müsse; aus dem, das ungewiss ist, eitel gewiss Ding machen; sollte solcher Wucher nicht die Welt auffressen in kurzen Jahren? Summa, es ist nun genug gesagt, dass Leihen soll nichts drüber nehmen, und soll ge

schehen dem Dürftigen zu Dienst oder Nutz. Den Text halte fest, und ist auch leicht zu verstehen, dass den Schaden bezahlen, nicht sei über das Leihen mehr geben oder nehmen; denn es ist zufälliges Unglück, das dem Leiher widerfahret ohne seinen Willen, dess er sich erholen muss. Aber in den Händeln ists umgekehrt, und gar das Widerspiel; da sucht und erdichtet man Schaden auf den benöthigten Nächsten, will damit sich nähren und reich werden, faul und müssig, prassen und prangen von andrer Leute Arbeit, Sorge, Fahr und Schaden; dass ich sitze hinter dem Ofen, und lasse meine hundert Gulden für mich auf dem Lande werbeii; und doch, weil es geliehen Geld ist, gewiss im Beutel behalte, ohne alle Fahr und Sorge. Lieber, wer möchte das nicht? Und was vom geliehenen Gelde gesagt ist, das soll auch vom geliehenen Getreide, Wein und dergleichen Waare verstanden sein, dass solche zween Schaden mögen darinnen vorfallen; aber dass dieselben Schaden nicht sollen der Waare natürlich angewachsen sein, sondern zufälliglich widerfahren mögen, und darum nicht eher für Schaden zu rechnen, sie seien denn geschehen und überweiset, wo sie ohne das gefordert und genommen werden, dass man wisse, es sei Wucher und Unrecht. . . . Sie sagen: die Welt könne nicht ohne Wucher sein. Das ist gewisslich wahr. Denn so steif und stattlich wird kein Regiment in der Welt werden, ist auch nicht gewest, das allen Sünden könnte wehren. Und wenn ein Regiment könnte allen Sünden wehren, so wird dennoch die Erbsünde, die Quelle aller Sünden, sammt dem Teufel (davon die Jura nichts wissen), müssen bleiben, welchen man muss immer aufs neue wehren, so viel es möglich ist. Darum kann die Welt nicht ohne Wucher, ohne Geiz, ohne Hochmuth, ohne Hurerei, ohne Ehebruch, ohne Mord, ohne Stehlen, ohne Gotteslästerung und allerlei Sünden sein; sonst wäre sie nicht Welt, und müsste Welt ohne Welt, Teufel ohne Teufel sein. Aber ob sie damit entschuldiget sind, das werden sie wohl erfahren. Der Herr spricht Matth. 18, 7.: Es müssen Aergerniss kommen, aber wehe dem Menschen, durch welchen Aergerniss kommt. Wucher muss sein, aber wehe den Wucherern. . . . Aber wie? Wenn der Fall vorkäme, dass etwa alte Leute, arme Wittwen oder Waisen, oder sonst dürftige Personen, die bis daher keine andere Nahrung gelernt, hätten im Handel ein tausend Floren oder zwei; und sollten sie davon lassen, so hätten sie sonst nichts, und müssten die Hand am Bettelstab wärmen, oder Hungers sterben. Hie wollte ich wohl gern, dass die Juristen eine Linderung des scharfen Rechtes setzten; und wäre zu bedenken, dass alle obgenannten Fürsten und Herren, die dem Wucher gesteuert, als Solon, Alexander, die Römer, nicht haben alles rein können oder wollen machen, Nehemia auch nicht alles wieder stattet (Nehem. 5, 15.). Und hieher möchte der Spruch gehören, der droben gesagt ist: die Welt könne nicht ohne Wucher sein; doch dass es nicht stracks ein Wucher, auch nicht ein Recht, sondern ein Nothwücherlein wäre, schier ein halbes Werk der Barmherzigkeit für die Dürftigen, die sonst nichts hätten, und den Ändern nicht sonderlich schadet. Würde sich auch disputiren, ob nicht hie ein Interesse oder Schade wacht sein könnte, weil sie verführet und versäumet, dass sie nichts anders dieweil gelernt haben, und unfreundlich wäre, sie zu Bettlern zu machen, oder lassen Hungers sterben, weil niemand damit beholfen, und ohne Verderben des Nächsten solches geschähe, als ex restitutione vaga.... Den käuflichen Zins habe ich hier mit nichten gemeinet; denn was ein rechter, redlicher Kauf ist, das ist kein Wucher. So weiss man, Gott Lob, wohl, was ein käuflicher Zins ist nach den weltlichen Rechten, nämlich, dass da soll sein ein Unterpfand, und nicht zu viel aufs Hundert verkauft werde, davon jetzt nicht zu reden ist. Ein Jeglicher sehe für sich, dass ein rechter, redlicher Kauf sei.“ (Vermahnung an die Pfarrherrn wider den Wucher zu predigen. A. 1540. Opp. Hai. X, 1025. sqq.) PART. HI. CAP. VII.

Idem; ,,Dass ihr anzeiget, es sei euch seltsam, dass ein anderer mit euerm Gelde sein Gut soll bessern, und ihr nichts davon haben, ist wohl ein übriges, unnöthiges gutes Werk, wie ich einem möchte geben 100 Fl., der es nicht bedürfte. Aber damit ist kein Wucher entschuldigt, warum habe ich es nicht behalten oder nöthiger gebraucht? Zum Wiederkauf gehöret: Primo hypotheka, ein Unterpfand, als Acker, Haus, Stadt, Land, auf welchem die Zins gekauft worden. Denn was nichts trägt, das kann nichts zinsen. Und wo das Unterpfand verdirbt oder im Krieg von Feinden, als Türken, verloren würde, da verlieren alle beide das Ihre, der Käufer und Verkäufer. Darum auf bloss schlecht Geld, als auf hundert (oder wie viel dess ist) Gulden, ohne Unterpfand ausgedrückt und genannt, fünf oder mehr, ja auch 1 Gulden, einen Heller nehmen, ist Wucher. Secundo, dass der Käufer (der die Zins kauft) schuldig bleibt, dem Verkäufer (der die Summa des Geldes auf sein Gut nimmt) wiederum die Ablösung der Zinsen mit gleicher Summe zu gestatten, wenn er kann oder will. Darum wann der Käufer ihm vorbehält, die Summa seines Geldes, damit er die Zins kauft, wieder zu fordern über eins, zwei, drei u. s. w. Jahre, welches die Juristen heissen repetitio sortis, das ist auch Wucher, ein recht Hurkind, denn es will zugleich ein geliehenes Geld (das man wieder fordern mag), und doch auch ein Kaufgeld sein (das ich nicht mag wieder fordern nach der empfangenen Waare). Wiewohl man hier will disputiren, wenn der Verkäufer von ihm selber die Wiederforderung begehrt oder bewilliget, als der es nicht länger will verkauft haben, welches seltsam ist, und darf wohl gut aufsehen, dass nicht ein Schein sei an Licht.“ (Brief an S. Weller. A. 1543. Luthers sämmtliche Werke, Frankf. a. M. u. Erlangen. P. LVI. p. LVIII. sq.) Cf. Grösser Sermon vom Wucher. A. 1519. Opp. Hai. X, 1010—1015. Chemnitius: ״Multa et varia de usura disputata sunt. Quidam enim contenderunt, societatem politicam, quales nunc sunt res humanae, non posse consistere sine usuris; ideo, si constitutiones politicae in exigendis usuris serventur, posse id fieri sine laesione conscientiae. Alii vero nomine usurarum omnes legitimos contractus rescindunt et honesta lucra damnant. . . Constituendum est ex certis et perspicuis Scripturae testimoniis, usuram non esse rem per se et suo genere bonam, nec ita mediam, ut ex usu vel abusu judicetur, et moderatio quidem probetur, excessus vero tantum damnetur; sed esse actionem per se et suo genere malam, vitiosam et damnatam. Multi enim cogitant, sicut in reliquis legitimis contractibus tantum excessus, vitia et abusus damnantur: ita etiam moderatam usuram non esse peccatum, sed tantum excessum damnari. . . Nunc vero tantum illum praetextum removebimus, quasi Scriptura probet aliquam usuram. Et primo dicemus de loco Deut. 23, 19. 20. . . Deus in Veteri Testamento fuit et theologus et legislator. Alibi enim tradit, quomodo serviendum sit Deo in justitia et sanctitate coram ipso. Alibi vero pro externa societate vitae civilis in republica Israelitica certas quasdam politicas constitutiones praescribit isti populo. Hoc est, sicut vulgo loquimur, tractat de jure fori et de jure poli, ordinat forum politicum et forum conscientiae. In legibus autem politicis, quas Deus populo Israel dedit, non semper justitia et sanctitas conscientiae coram Deo praescribitur; sed sunt accommodatae ad conservationem externae et civilis societatis in illa politia, pro conditione ingeniorum et morum istius populi, cui Deus ipse tribuit epitheton durae cervicis. Quia igitur leges forenses Deus praescribebat politico magistratui, quae vitia, quibus civilibus poenis punienda forent, vidit fieri non posse, ut effrenata hominum malitia ex toto compesceretur poenis civilibus per leges politicas. Ut igitur in societate civili istius populi pejora vitarentur, minora quaedam mala, non quidem approbavit, sed forensi et politico fine toleranda permisit hactenus, quod per magistratum civilem non puniebantur. Ita Exod. 21, 21.: ,Qui servum suum percusserit, ut inde moriatur', non punitur

civiliter tanquam homicida, sed non ideo in conscientia coram Deo excusatus erat. Sic libellus repudii et usurae erga extraneos in foro politico reip. Israel permissa sunt hactenus, quod a magistratu civili non puniebantur. Quia vero Judaei de forensibus illis permissionibus judicabant, sicut de praeceptis, quae informant conscientiam coram Deo, hoc modo: Deus in lege Mosis permittit. Ergo probat. Ergo non pugnat cum voluntate Dei. Ergo etiam in conscientia coram Deo valet. Deus igitur per ipsum Mosen et postea per prophetas crebra repetitione tradidit explicationem, promissiones illas intelligendas esse politice, non theologice, in foro civili, non in foro conscientiae, coram magistratu, non coram Deo, quasi ideo coram Deo non sit peccatum, quia a magistratu non punitur.


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: From this foundation, the explanation of the sentence in Deut

From this foundation, the explanation of the sentence in Deut. 23 can be rightly taken. For God, as the legislator in the polity of Israel, prescribing to the magistrate the form of external discipline to be maintained—which crimes they ought to coerce with which civil penalties (as much as can be done through political judgments), because the judgment of the magistrate and the judgment of God do not consist in equal degrees, and those things which cannot be coerced without greater detriment to political society, He permits to be tolerated; not as things that are good before God in conscience, but for a political end and manner, so that they might not be punished civilly. Thus, He civilly permitted usury toward foreigners, so that it would not be practiced toward those of the household of faith. But lest that permission be drawn into the forum of conscience before God, by often-repeated inculcation, God generally and expressly condemned usury with atrocious words. This explanation shows the causes why the reprehension of usury is so often repeated in the prophets with the most atrocious words. In this way, usury is permitted in the Old Testament, namely civilly; but it is condemned theologically, in conscience before God.

In the New Testament, however, this distinction is handed down more clearly and manifestly by the Son of God Himself. For because there are two chief permissions in the Old Testament which were being depraved by the Pharisees in the way mentioned—namely, concerning divorce and usury—Christ opposes to both permissions the perpetual rule of justice in God (Matt. 5:32, 42; likewise ch. 19:8 and Luke 6:34, 35).

The Δευτερωταί (Deuterotai) interpreted it thus: "Because Moses in the laws concerning loans and usury makes a difference between neighbors or brothers and foreigners, therefore the will of God is satisfied if only friends are relieved by the duty of a loan; but it is not a sin if others are exhausted by usury." But Christ, who was sent not to be a political legislator, but to inform the conscience before God by the manifestation of His own eternal and immovable will, says that in the forum of conscience that distinction between neighbor and foreigner, which has its place in political society, does not hold, but: "Give to everyone who asks," whether he be friend or enemy. And concerning that general giving of a loan, whether it be done to the poor or the rich, to friends or enemies, He says, "hoping for nothing therefrom." Therefore, just as the law of divorce has also been abrogated politically, so the same must be the reason for the constitution concerning usury, as is manifest from these things which we have said. . .

It is to be observed that Scripture taxes usury, not as the law of God argues many flaws even in the saints in this life; but let the atrocity of the words with which usury is condemned be considered in the individual testimonies; Deut. 23:19: "You shall not lend at interest to your brother," etc., but without interest you shall lend what he needs, "that God may bless you in your work in the land," etc. Therefore, usuries are punished by the curse of God in works and by ejection from the fatherland. Thus Prov. 28:8. . .

It is worthy of admiration, however, since in this corruption of nature avarice devises various pretexts, that usury has been atrociously condemned even by the sounder heathens and philosophers and legislators. And this is a most shining testimony that it conflicts not only against Scripture, but also against the very law of nature, which Paul says is the truth of God, inscribed on the hearts of men.

The Fathers rightly take the detestation of usury from the seventh commandment. Hieron.: "To seek usury, or to defraud, or to rob, it makes no difference, because the seventh commandment prohibits all these things." Am PART III. CHAP. VII. Ambrosius: "If anyone accepts usury, he commits theft: therefore he shall not live." Augustine to Macedonius: "Which is more cruel: he who takes something from the rich, or he who slaughters the poor with usury?" Therefore, just as theft, robbery, etc., are evil in themselves and cannot be done well, so too is usury. And when the question is asked about moderate usury, it is the same question as whether moderate adultery is good. And just as it is the office of the magistrate to punish robberies, adulteries, homicides, etc., so too ought he to restrain usury. . .

To the definition of usury belongs: I. That it occurs in a contract of loan, Exod. 22:25; Deut. 23:20. And these four things belong to the substance of a loan: 1. When a thing is transferred in such a way that it becomes the recipient's. For it is called a loan (*mutuum*) because it is made from mine into yours (*de meo fiat tuum*). 2. It must be a gratuitous service; otherwise, it would be either a sale or a lease. 3. Power is given to use the loan, not in perpetuity, but for a certain time; otherwise, it would be a gift. 4. An obligation is added that it be restored, not indeed the same thing in number, but another of the same kind, or quantity, and value. Psa. 37:21: "The wicked borrows, and does not pay back," etc. And indeed, by law, the risk of the principal belongs to the recipient, so that if it is lost by accident, theft, or fire.

II. To the definition of usury belongs the fact that something beyond the restoration of the principal is demanded, either by pact or by intention. Hence it is called מרבית and הרבית, as was said above. III. When something is demanded beyond the principal on account of the use of the money lent or on account of the service of lending. For a legitimate compensation for what is of interest (*id quod interest*), when the debtor has provided an effective cause of loss, is not usury. Likewise, when a debtor has either avoided some loss or gained something by the use of the borrowed money, and, understanding that he is obligated to return favors (*antidora*) out of gratitude, has given something to the creditor beyond the principal, if he accepts it without a pact, exaction, or usurious intention, it is not usury. . .

When Christ says: "hoping for nothing in return," He censures the pact and the intention, that he would not otherwise have given the loan unless he hoped to receive something beyond the principal. The definition must be adapted to use in the explanation of the questions that are proposed, which are many and various regarding this business. And while the foundations of judgments are rightly sought from definitions, it often happens that the explanation of questions is not so easy and obvious to everyone that it can be constructed from bare definitions by simpler people at first glance. I have therefore noticed and observed in Luther a certain method, which Aepinus and Brentius later used to explain this doctrine plainly and clearly. And I judge that the true and solid explanation of all questions of this kind can be most rightly sought and taken from there. . .

Scripture distributes the human race into certain orders, and assigns to each certain contracts or modes of communication. For first, there are beggars, who have neither money, nor goods, nor labor, by the exchange of which they might acquire something; such as Lazarus, Luke 16:20; Acts 3:2; Luke 18:35; John 9:8, etc. Now, purchase is a contract that is approved by God; if, therefore, a rich man offers Lazarus the communication of his goods through purchase, or: "If you will give or do, I will give" according to unnamed contracts; or if he offers a loan in this way: "If you will stipulate that you will return the principal, I will give"; this would certainly not be a legitimate communication, but an illusion. And those contracts are not approved by God, but it is a discrimination of persons. For God did not institute purchase so that it might be exercised with beggars, but He wills that the destitution of such be relieved by the giving of alms.

2. There are some who have neither goods nor money, but can provide labor, work, and trade; just as Lev. 25:35 says most beautifully: "If your brother has been depressed and his hand has faltered," etc. He has a hand, it says, but one depressed and faltering from poverty, so that he cannot exercise the labors or works of his vocation. Him, the text says, you ought to apprehend and sustain before he is reduced to extreme destitution or beggary. But should that be done by purchase or exchange? Certainly, Scripture says he is attenuated and faltering. By alms? Paul answers in 2 Thess. 3:12: "He who can work, ought to eat his own bread." And 1 Thess.

4, 12: "that you may lack nothing." To this order of men, therefore, God prescribes two forms and modes: that either their labor be hired; for in the same place, Lev. 25:39, He gives commands concerning hired servants and slaves who, because of poverty, sell themselves to others; or, if their vocation does not conveniently allow for the hiring out of labor, that they be relieved by the duty of exchange. And God wills that this duty be gratuitous, so that he who ought to be relieved is not oppressed and exhausted.

3. There are those who have the blessing of God, both things and resources, by which they can acquire and maintain the necessities of life. But because God has not bestowed all things upon the rich in such a way that they can do without contracts, He therefore wills that they also be associated with the rest of men through those legitimate communications and exchanges in civil society. It is manifest, however, that with this order, if they are in need of anything of ours, whether in goods or in labor, communication is not to be made through alms. And when Scripture commands that we relieve the needy and the impoverished by gratuitous exchange, it shows that this duty is not prescribed for the sake of those who abound of themselves. To this order, therefore, the remaining legitimate contracts are proposed, such as buying, hiring, exchange, etc. These things are so manifest that they are understood even from the law of nature. For God willed that there be such communication among all orders of men that there might be association, as was said in the chapter on contracts. ...

Some do not wish to appear usurious, and they do not give loans to the poor who ask, but sell certain goods more dearly than is just because of the delay in payment. These flatter themselves because they do not practice usury. But they oppress and exhaust their neighbor more than by usury. And Paul says: "The Lord is the avenger of all these things," 1 Thess. 4:6. ...

If such a person gives a loan to a rich man, who can make a profit by the use of another's money, and stipulates something beyond the principal, when indeed the other can repay without his own inconvenience and detriment, and the other has his sustenance from it, can this be done with a good conscience, or is it indeed usury, which God so atrociously condemns in Scripture? ...

Latin:

Ex hoc fundamento recte potest sumi explicati o sententiae Deut. 23. Deus enim tanquam legislator in politia Israel, praescribens magistratui formam externae disciplinae custodiendae, quae flagitia, quibus civilibus poenis (quantum quidem per politica judicia fieri potest) coercere debeant, quia judicium magistratus et judicium Dei non consistunt in aequalibus gradibus, quae sine majori societatis politicae detrimento coerceri non possunt, permittit, ut tolerentur; non tanquam quae bona sunt coram Deo in conscientia, sed fine et modo politico, ne civiliter puniantur. Ita civiliter permisit usuram erga extraneos, ne erga domesticos fidei exerceretur. Ne vero illa permissio traheretur in foium conscientiae coram Deo, saepe repetita inculcatione Deus generaliter et expresse atrocibus verbis usuram damnavit. Haec explicatio ostendit causas, quare in prophetis toties repetita sit reprehensio usurarum verbis atrocissimis. Hoc modo usura in Veteri Testamento permittitur, scilicet civiliter; damnatur autem theologice, in conscientia coram Deo.

In Novo vero Te«tamento haec distinctio clarius et manifestius tradita est ab ipso Filio Dei. Quia enim duae potissimum extant permissiones in Veteri Testamento, quae ita, sicut dictum est, depravabantur a Pharisacis, de repudio scii, et usura: Christus utrique permissioni opponit perpetuam regulam justitiae in Deo Matth. 5, 32. 42., item cap. 19, 8. et Luc. 6, 34. 35. . . Αεντερωταί

ita interpretabantur: Quia Moses in legibus de mutuo et usura facit differentiam inter proximos seu fratres et extraneos, ideo voluntati Dei satisfieri, si amici tantum officio mutui subleventur; non autem esse peccatum, si alii usuris exhauriantur. Christus vero, qui missus erat, non ut esset politicus legislator, sed ut conscientiam coram Deo patefactione aeternae et immotae ipsius voluntatis informaret, inquit, in foro conscientiae discrimen illud inter proximum et extraneum, quod in politica societate suum locum habet, non valere, sed: ,Da omni petenti‘, sive amicus sit, sive inimicus. Et de illa generali datione mutui, sive pauperibus, sive divitibus, sive amicis, sive inimicis fiat, inquit, ,nihil inde sperantes'.
