Sicut igitur lex repudii etiam politice abrogata est, ita eadem etiam debet esse ratio constitutionis de usuris, sicut ex his, quae diximus, manifestum est. . .

Observandum est, Scripturam taxare usuram, non sicut lex Dei multos naevos etiam in sanctis in hac vita arguit; sed consideretur in singulis testimoniis atrocitas verborum, quibus damnatur usura; Deut. 23, 19.: ,Non foeneraberis fratri tuo ad usuram' etc., sed absque usura, quo indiget, ,commodabis, ut benedicat tibi Deus in opere tuo in terra‘ etc. Ergo usurae puniuntur maledictione Dei in operibus et ejectione ex patria. Ita Prov. 28, 8. . .

Dignum est autem admiratione, cum in hac naturae corruptione avaritia varios praetextus excogitet, quod etiam ab ethnicis sanioribus et philosophis et legumlatoribus usura atrociter damnata est. Et hoc luculentissimum testimonium est, eam pugnare non tantum contra Scripturam, verum etiam contra ipsam legem naturae, quam Paulus dicit esse veritatem Dei, inscriptam cordibus hominum.

Patres detestationem usurarum recte sumunt ex septimo praecepto. Hieron.: ,Usuras quaerere, aut fraudare, aut rapere nihil interest, quia septimum praeceptum haec omnia prohibet.‘ Am PART. III. CAP. VII. brosius: ,Si quis usuram accipit, furtum facit: vita ergo non vivet.' Augustinus ad Macedonium: ,Uter crudelior est, an qui aliquid aufert diviti, aut qui usura trucidat pauperem?‘ Sicut ergo furtum, rapina etc. per se mala sunt nec possunt bene fieri, ita etiam usura. Et quando quaeritur de moderata usura, eadem est quaestio, an adulterium moderatum sit bonum. Et sicut magistratus officium est, rapinas, adulteria,, homicidia etc. punire, ita etiam debet usuras coercere. . .

Ad definitionem usurae pertinet: I. Quod fit in contractu mutui, Exod. 22, 25.. Deut. 23, 20. Et de substantia mutui sunt haec quatuor: 1. Quando· res ita transfertur, ut fiat accipientis. Mutuum enim inde dictum volunt, quia de meo fiat tuum. 2. Debet esse officium gratuitum; alias enim esset vel venditio vel locatio. 3. Datur potestas utendi mutuo׳ non in perpetuum, sed ad certum tempus; alias enim esset donatio. 4. Additur obligatio, ut restituatur, non quidem eadem res numero, sed alia ejusdem vel generis, vel quantitatis et aestimationis. PsaL 37, 21.: ,Peccator mutuo accipit, et non solvit‘ etc. Et quidem de jure periculum sortis pertinet ad accipientem, ut si vel casu, vei furto, vel incendio amittatur.

II. Ad definitionem usurae pertinet, quod ultra restitutionem sortis aliquid, vel pacto, vel intentione interveniere, exigitur. Inde enim vocatur מרבית et הרבית, sicut supra dictum est. III. Quando ultra sortem aliquid exigitur propter mutuo datae pecuniae usum vel propter officium mutuationis. Nam legitima compensatio ejus, quod interest, quando debitor efficacem causam damni dedit, non est usura. Item, quando debitor usu mutuae pecuniae vel damnum aliquod evasit, vel lucratus est aliquid, et intelligens, se gratitudinis ergo obligatum esse ad antidora, aliquid creditori ultra sortem donaverit, si absque pacto, exactione et intentione usuraria accipiat, non est usura.. ״

Quando Christus dicit: ,Nihil inde sperantes‘, taxat pactum et intentionem, quod alias non esset mutuo daturus, nisi speraret, aliquid ultra sortem se recepturum. Accommodanda est definitio ad usum in explica״ tione quaestionum, quae de hoc negotio multae et variae proponuntur. Et ex definitionibus quidem fundamenta dijudicationum recte petuntur; sed saepe accidit, quod explicatio quaestionum non ita expedita, et cuivis obvia est, ut ex nudis definitionibus a simplicioribus primo statim intuitu extrui possit. Animadverti igitur et observavi in Luthero methodum quandam, qua usi postea Aepinus et Brentius plane et perspicue explicarunt hanc doctrinam. Et judico, inde rectissime posse peti et sumi veram et solidam explicationem omnium quaestionum hujus generis. . .

Scriptura distribuit genus humanum in aliquot ordines, et singulis attribuit certos contractus seu modos communicatio״ num. Primo enim sunt mendici, qui nec pecuniam, nec res, nec operas habent, quarum commutatione aliquid possint acquirere; ut Lazarus Luc. 16, 20. Actor. 3, 2. Luc. 18, 35. Joli. 9, 8. etc. Jam emptio est contractus, qui Deo probatur; si igitur dives Lazaro offerat rerum sua״ rum communicationem per emptionem, vel: Si dederis aut feceris, dabo juxta contractus innominatos; vel si mutuum offerat hoc mödo: Si stipulatus fueris, te sortem redditurum, dabo; haec certe non legi״ tima communicatio, sed illusio esset. Et contractus illi Deo non probantur, sed est discrimen personarum. Non enim instituit Deus emp״ tionein, ut cum mendicis exerceatur, sed talium inopiam vult sublevari largitione eleemosynarum.

2. Sunt quidam, qui nec res, nec pecuniam habent, sed possunt operas praestare, laborare, negotiari; sicut Lev. 25, 35. textus pulcherrime inquit: ,Si depressus fuerit frater et manus ejus nutaverit‘ etc. Manum, inquit, habet, sed depressam et nutantem paupertate, ut non possit operas seu labores suae vocationis exercere. Illum, inquit textus, debes apprehendere et sustentare prius, quam ad extremam inopiam seu mendicitatem redigatur. Sed num emptione vel permutatione illud debet fieri? Certe Scriptura dicit esse attenuatum et nutantem. Num eleemosynis? Respondet Paulus 2 Thes. 3, 12.: ,Qui potest laborare, debet proprium panem manducare.‘ Et 1 Thes.

4, 12.: ,μηόενυς χρείαν εχητε.‘ Huic igitur hominnm ordini Deus praescribit duas formas et modos: ut vel opera ipsorum conducatur; nam in eodem Levit. 25, 39. praecipit de mercenariis et de servis, qui propter egestatem se vendunt aliis; vel, si vocatio ipsorum elocationem operarum non commode patitur, ut officio mutationis subleventur. Et illud officium Deus vult esse gratuitum, ne is, qui sublevari debet, opprimatur et exhauriatur.

3. Sunt, qui Dei benedictionem habent et res et facultates, quibus acquirere et tueri possunt vitae necessaria. Quia vero etiam divitibus Deus non ita omnia contulit, ut possint carere contractibus, vult igitur etiam, illos consociatos esse reliquis hominibus legitimis illis communicationibus et commutationibus in societate civili. Manifestum autem est, cum 110c ordine, si qua nostra vel re vel opera indigent, non faciendam esse communicationem per eleemosynas. Et quando Scriptura praecipit, ut egentes et attenuatos gratuita mutatione sublevemus, ostendit, non praescriptum esse hoc officium propter illos, qui per se abundant. Huic igitur ordini propositi sunt reliqui legitimi contractus, ut emptio, locatio, permutatio etc. Haec adeo sunt manifesta, ut etiam ex lege naturae intelligantur. Voluit enim Deus, inter omnes ordines hominum esse talem communicationem, ut sit consociatio, sicut in capite de contractibus dictum est. . .

Quidam nolunt usurarii videri, et pauperibus petentibus non dant mutuo, sed merces quasdam propter moram solutionis carius justo vendunt. Hi blandiuntur sibi, quia non exercent usuram. Sed magis opprimunt et exhauriunt proximum, quam usuris. Et Paulus dicit: ,Vindex est Dominus de his omnibus‘, 1 Thes. 4, 6. . .

Si talis mutuo det diviti, qui usu alieni aeris potest lucrum facere, et paciscatur aliquid ultra sortem, cum quidem alter sine suo incommodo et detrimento possit reddere, et alter inde sustentationem suam habeat, num bona conscientia id fleri possit, an vero sit usura, quam Deus tam atrociter in Scriptura damnat? ...


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: If Scripture, in the description of usury, established such a distinction—that…

If Scripture, in the description of usury, established such a distinction—that when something is exacted from a poor man beyond the principal in a loan, it is a sin, but when from a rich man, it is a legitimate and pious business transaction—then the answer would be plain. But now, it condemns usury in general and simply, and every superabundance that is exacted in a loan beyond the principal, without distinction, from whomever it is received, Ps. 15, last verse; Ezek. 18:8; Luke 6:35. Since, therefore, God judges according to the revealed word, certainly the conscience cannot be certain if it invents such a distinction for itself without the manifest word of God.

For whatever reasonings may be devised, those general sentences will always cry out against them: "He who has not given his money to usury," etc. That mention is made of the poor in certain testimonies is done for the same reason that in the fifth and seventh commandments widows, orphans, and the poor are usually named, so that no injury may be inflicted upon them. But it does not follow from that: therefore, an injury that is done to married persons, adults, the powerful, the rich, etc., is not a sin.

Likewise, the duty of a loan is commanded especially for the sake of the poor and needy, therefore they are also mentioned in the testimonies of Scripture. Furthermore, it pertains to the definition and substance of a loan that it be a gratuitous duty and that the recipient is obligated to restore only the same in kind or quantity. Therefore, when the lender stipulates something beyond the principal, this is done against the nature of the contract of a loan; therefore, it is invalid. Whatever name may be imposed upon it, when the right of reclaiming the principal remains with the creditor, it is a true loan. And whatever is exacted in a loan beyond the principal is usury.

And Scripture prohibits usury generally for this reason: because in the communication of political society it does not want all things to be venal, but wants certain duties to be gratuitous, which are certainly deformed and depraved when they are either sold as if they were venal or hired out as if they were mercenary. And if Scripture were to concede the practice of usury in a loan toward the rich, the gratuitous duty of a loan would be quickly and easily abolished. Therefore, lest liberality fail, Scripture frequently condemns usury simply and in general. Does the Gospel, therefore, command that in such a case, concerning which now... PART III. CHAP. VII.

we ask, is it the other, who is not impoverished, that he should use my money in such a way that he is enriched to my detriment? This is certainly not commanded, just as the sentiment of 2 Cor. 8:13 is manifest. Two things, therefore, have now been established: 1. That in this case, a gratuitous sharing to the detriment of another is not owed to men of the third order. 2. That it is not permitted to exact profit above the principal on account of the duty of lending, neither from the poor nor from the rich. For usury is generally condemned, so that it can in no case be practiced with a good conscience.

What, therefore, shall he do who, in order to sustain the burdens of the republic and to tolerate economic expenses, cannot do without the use of his money? The answer is manifest from the foundations shown above. For there are many other legitimate contracts which are approved in Scripture; let him, therefore, use those.

But he says: "I cannot exercise the negotiations of buying, leasing, exchanging, etc." I answer: He who flees those legitimate contracts for this reason, because he does not wish to undergo labors and dangers, but seeks another easier method which is joined with less labor and no danger, he sins against the doctrine concerning the sharing of goods in civil society. For the rule is that charity should be exercised in those political duties, but it certainly does not befit this rule that others should alone undergo labors and sustain dangers, while you, idle and unharmed, are fattened by the labors and dangers of others.

But if it be a matter of health, or age, or condition (as in widows, or those who manage the republic at private expense), or lack of skill, or another honest reason, certain other contracts are also approved by the laws, so that those who have money and cannot negotiate themselves may be able, through an honest and legitimate use of money, to acquire that by which they may sustain themselves, namely, contracts of redemption and partnership." (Loc. Theol. II. fol. 158—166.)

Not only gladly proclaiming those things which redound to his praise, but also abstaining from more iniquitous suspicions; [being] more equitable in

interpreting the part, which are doubtful; covering or excusing errors and weaknesses as far as possible, and hoping for his amendment and procuring it by fraternally rebuking him, or by causing him to be rebuked by others.

For as in other matters, so also here, everyone is commanded to love himself, and thus his neighbor; according to note c on § VI. § 15. By the ninth and tenth commandments, inordinate concupiscence for the house, wife, servants, beasts of burden, and other goods of one's neighbor is prohibited, not only the actual [concupiscence], to which delight is added, but every kind whatsoever; on the other hand, however, a full and constant rectitude and purity of our desires and inclinations regarding those things which belong to one's neighbor is required.

These commandments are rightly distinguished by our countrymen: just as in Exodus the word תחמוד stands placed twice, so that by the repetition of the word of prohibition you may understand that two commandments are formally delivered; but in Deuteronomy ch. 5, 21, the word תחמוד is used once, and once in its place the word is substituted, namely, so that not only actual concupiscence joined with delight is prohibited, but specifically that depraved concupiscence itself, viewed in its first act with its first motions; the latter indeed formally, expressly, and directly, but the former virtually, implicitly, and indirectly. Just as it is also certain that the inordinate acts or motions of concupiscence, which are formally prohibited in the latter commandments, are implicitly prohibited in the former commandments. See b. Mus. Tract. contra Steng. P. III. cap. VI. p. 593. 594. Indeed, it is certain that it is declared what is against the law, and that that depraved concupiscence should not be present or have a place, in which sense it is rightly said to be prohibited; although, if you look at that innate habitual evil, which is already present inevitably, it seems to be accused and condemned rather than prohibited. See b. Musaei Tr. contra Stenger. P. III. cap. VI. p. 594. Conf. b. Chemn. L. de Lege cap. II. near the beginning, and Sect. de Praec. Nono et Dec., where he frequently warns that original concupiscence is accused, argued, and taxed, so that we may understand that the chief end of the law (after the fall) is to reveal the knowledge of sin, and to accuse us that we do not have that conformity with the law; which are the words p.

and prescribes the celebration of Him and His office and benefits, together with the persons and things pertaining thereto, with the power of binding.

Gerhard: "Since the moral law is distinguished from the rest by such a great difference, it must be accurately observed which commandments pertain to the moral law, and which, in truth, are merely ceremonial and forensic. Two criteria, above all, are handed down by which this can be detected and investigated.

The first is the light of nature, still remaining in the notions born with us. For whatever agrees with natural notions, implanted in the minds of men at creation and still remaining in part after the fall, pertains to the moral law. Thus, the honoring of parents is approved by the sounder heathens and agrees with the law of nature itself. The verses of Euripides are well known: οστις δέ τους τεκόντας έν βίφ σέβει, όό1 έστι και ζών και ΰανών βεοϊς φίλος. Whoever in his life honors his parents, this man is dear to the gods both living and dead. Therefore, the precept concerning the honor of parents is moral.

The second criterion is the light of grace proposed in the explanation of Moses and the prophets, and especially of Christ and the apostles in the New Testament. For since natural notions have been greatly obscured by sin, the light of nature is not clear enough for the judgment of this matter; rather, the light of grace, kindled for us in the sermons of the prophets and apostles, must be added. Therefore, this rule is added: whatever Moses and the prophets show to pertain not only to the Israelites, but to all nations, those are precepts of the moral law. Thus, it is gathered that the laws concerning the reverence of blood to be observed in marriages pertain to the moral law, from the fact that Moses expressly adds in Leviticus 18:24 that the Canaanites were to be punished by God on account of the transgression of those laws. Likewise, also, when the prophets condemn vices practiced among the nations on the basis of the law, then it is certain that those prohibiting commandments pertain to the Decalogue.

In the New Testament, a clearer light of this knowledge is handed down through Christ and the apostles; for whatever is repeated and commanded in the New Testament, which pertains to all nations, those things pertain to the moral law and bind all men.

Latin:

Si Scriptura in descriptione usurae talem constitueret differentiam, quando in mutuo a paupere aliquid ultra sortem exigitur, esse peccatum, quando vero a divite, esse legitimam et piam negotiationem, tunc plana esset responsio. Jam vero in genere et simpliciter damnat usuram et omnem superabundantiam, quae in mutuo ultra sortem exigitur, sine discrimine, a quocunque accipiatur, Psal. 15, v. ult. Ezech. 18, 8. Luc. 6, 35. Quia igitur Deus juxta verbum patefactum judicat, certe conscientia non potest certa esse, si absque manifesto verbo Dei ipsa sibi talem differentiam fingat.

Qualescunque enim excogitentur ratiocinationes, semper obstrepent generales illae sententiae: ,Qui pecuniam suam non dedit ad usuram‘ etc. Quod vero in quibusdam testimoniis pauperum fit mentio, eadem ratione fit, sicut in quinto et septimo praeceptis plerumque nominantur viduae, pupilli, pauperes, ne illis inferatur injuria. Sed inde non sequitur: ergo injuria, quae fit conjugatis, adultis, potentibus, divitibus etc., non est peccatum.

Item officium mutui praecipitur praecipue propter pauperes et egentes, ideo eorum etiam fit mentio in testimoniis Scripturae. Praeterea ad definitionem et substantiam mutui pertinet, ut sit officium gratuitum et quod recipiens obligatur, ut restituat tantum idem in genere seu quantitate. Ergo quando mutuans paciscitur aliquid ultra sortem, hoc fit contra naturam contractus mutui; igitur non valet. Quodcunque autem nomen ei imponatur, quando jus repetendae sortis manet penes creditorem, est verum mutuum. Et quicquid in mutuo ultra sortem exigitur, est usura.

Et Scriptura ideo generaliter prohibet usuram, quia in communicatione societatis politicae non vult omnia esse venalia, sed vult quaedam officia esse gratuita, quae certe deformantur et depravantur, quando vel tanquam venalia venduntur, vel tanquam mercenaria locantur. Et si Scriptura concederet, in mutuo erga divites usuram exercere, cito et facile gratuitum officium mutui aboleretur. Ne igitur liberalitas deficiat, frequenter Scriptura simpliciter et in genere damnat usuram. Num igitur evangelium jubet, ut in tali casu, de quo nunc PART. III. CAP. VH.

quaerimus, alter, qui nou est attenuatus, mea pecunia ita utatur, ut cum meo damno locupletetur? Hoc certe non jubet, sicut manifesta est sententia 2 Cor. 8,13. Duo igitur jam constituta sunt: 1. Quod in hoc casu hominibus tertii ordinis non debetur gratuita communicatio cum damno alterius. 2. Quod propter officium mutuationis supra sortem lucrum exigere, nec a pauperibus, nec a divitibus licet. Usura enim generaliter damnata est, ut in nullo casu bona conscientia exerceri possit.

Quid igitur faciet is, qui ad sustinenda reipublicae onera et tolerandos sumptus oeconomicos usu suae pecuniae non potest carere? Responsio manifesta est ex fundamentis supra monstratis. Sunt enim multi alii legitimi contractus, qui in Scriptura approbantur, illis igitur utatur.

Sed inquit: Non possum exercere negotiationes emptionis, locationis, permutationis etc. Respondeo: Qui legitimos illos contractus fugit hoc nomine, quia labores et pericula non vult subire, sed quaerit aliam rationem faciliorem, quae minori cum labore et nullo cum periculo conjuncta sit, is peccat contra doctrinam de communicatione rerum in societate civili. Regula enim est, ut in politicis illis officiis exerceatur caritas, at huic certe non convenit, ut alii tantum labores subeant et pericula sustineant, tu vero ociosus et indemnis aliorum laboribus et periculis sagineris.

Sed si sit valetudinis, vel aetatis, vel conditionis (ut in viduis, vel qui privatis sumptibus rempublicam gerunt), vel imperitiae, vel alia honesta ratio, approbati sunt legibus etiam alii quidam contractus, ut qui habent pecuniam et non possunt ipsi negotiari, possint honesto et legitimo usu pecuniae acquirere, unde se sustentent, scilicet, contractus redemptionis et societatis.“ (Loc. Theol. II. fol. 158—166.)

Gerhardus: ,,Cum lex moralis tanto a reliquis secernatur discrimine, accurate observandum erit, quae mandata ad legem moralem pertineant, quae vero sint tantum ceremonialia et forensia. Traduntur autem duo potissimum κριτήρια, quibus deprehendi ac investigari istud possit.

Prius est lumen naturae in notitiis nobiscum natis adhuc reliquum. Quaecunque enim conveniunt cum notitiis naturalibus, in creatione mentibus hominum insitis et post lapsum κατά μέρος adhuc reliquis, ea pertinent ad legem moralem. Sic honor parentum a sanioribus ethnicis comprobatur et cum ipsa naturae lege congruit. Noti sunt Euripidis versiculi: οστις δέ τους τεκόντας έν βίφ σέβει, όό1 έστι και ζών και ΰανών βεοϊς φίλος. Quisquis in vita sua parentes colit, hic et vivus et defunctus diis carus est. Ergo praeceptum de honore parentum est morale.

Posterius κριτήpiov est lumen gratiae in explicatione Mosis ac prophetarum, praesertim vero Christi et apostolorum in N. T. propositum. Cum enim notitiae naturales per peccatum valde obscuratae sint, ideo lumen naturae ad dijudicationem hujus rei non satis clarum, sed accedat oportet lumen gratiae in concionibus prophetarum et apostolorum nobis accensum; ideo additur haec regula: quae Moses et prophetae ostendunt pertinere non tantum ad Israelitas, sed ad omnes gentes, ea sunt legis moralis praecepta. Sic leges de reverentia sanguinis in conjugiis observandas ad legem moralem pertinere, colligitur ex eo, quod Moses diserte addit Levit. 18, 24., propter transgressionem istarum legum Cananaeos a Deo puniendos. Ita quoque quando prophetae ex lege contra vitia inter gentes usitata condonantur, tum certum est, mandata illa prohibentia pertinere ad decalogum.

In N. T. clarior lux hujus notitiae per Christum et apostolos tradita est; quaecunque enim in N. T., quod ad omnes gentes pertinet, repetuntur et praecipiuntur, illa ad legem moralem pertinent et omnes homines obligant.


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: Where, however, this exception must be observed

Where, however, this exception must be observed: that the apostles observed and ordered to be observed abstinence from blood and from what is strangled, as well as the rite of circumcision in the first sprout of the New Testament church (Acts 15:29; 16:3; 21:26), not because they thought that these pertained to the moral law and to all Christians of all times and places whatsoever, but so that 'the Jewish synagogue might be buried with honor,' and that scandal might not be offered to the weak by an untimely use of Christian liberty—that is, so that the minds of the Jews converted to Christ might not be alienated, and the bond of concord between those converted from the Jews and the Gentiles might not be disrupted.

Lyranus on Acts 15: 'What is strangled and blood was indeed a lawful food, but for the sake of friendly society it was written to the Gentiles that they should abstain from such things, just as it frequently happens that someone abstains from food which he knows is abominable to his companion.' But as time went on, the cause ceasing, the effect ceased, the truth of evangelical doctrine having been manifested." (Loc. de legibus ceremon. et forens. § 6.)

Or the offerings of certain gifts consecrated to God from things either inanimate, whether solid, e.g., bread, salt, incense, etc., or liquid, e.g., oil, wine, or animate, to be slaughtered or sacrificed in honor of God; whence the various species of sacrifices: burnt offerings, peace offerings, and those either votive or voluntary; finally, piacular offerings, either for the sin of ignorance, or for a fault or more serious offense.

Gerhard: "Some doubt whether a certain divine command was given to Abel, Noah, and the remaining patriarchs before Moses regarding the offering of sacrifices, since no such κατά ρητόν appears to be expressed in the book of Genesis.

But indeed, although Moses, having encompassed the histories of so many centuries with admirable brevity, does not make express mention of that revelation and command promulgated by God concerning the offering of sacrifices, far be it from us to conclude that those most holy patriarchs devised the rite of sacrificing merely by their own judgment and private intention. For, first, the history of the church of all times testifies that έΰελοθρησκείας have always been hateful and adverse to God; who, therefore, would believe that in that first flower of the early church they were pleasing to Him?

Deut. 4:2, ch. 12:32: 'What I command you, that only shall you do; you shall not add anything, nor take away.' V. 8: 'You shall not do everyone what seems right to you.' Num. 15:39: 'They shall not follow their own thoughts and eyes, after which you are accustomed to commit fornication, but rather, mindful of the commandments of God, they shall do them.' Is. 1:12: 'Who has required this from your hands?' Is. 29:13; Matt. 15:9: 'In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men,' etc. The examples of the Aaronical μηχολατρείας, the Teraphim of Micah, and the calves of Jeroboam prove the same.

Next, all sacred histories make it attested that the merciful God, through His superabundant grace, has always established some external and visible sign of His grace alongside the Word, so that men, admonished by an external work and sign, might more certainly conclude that God favors them and is propitious to them. Therefore, the patriarchs also had such a sign divinely established, which is the argument of the blessed Luther in ch. 4 of Genesis.

Third, whatever worship God approves and regards, it must necessarily have God as its author. God approved and regarded the sacrifices of the patriarchs. Therefore, the sacrifices of the patriarchs have God as their author and institutor. The major premise is proven by those apostolic aphorisms: Rom. 14:23, 'Whatever is not done from faith is sin.' Heb. 11:6, 'Without faith it is impossible to please God.' Now, faith and the Word, both of command and of promise, stand in correlation; therefore, whatever is done without the Word cannot be done from faith, and consequently cannot please God. The truth of the minor premise is undoubted. Gen. 4:4: 'God had regard for Abel and his sacrifice.' Let the same judgment be held regarding the sacrifices of the other patriarchs.

Fourth, from the fact that in Gen. 7:2 Noah is commanded to receive into the ark seven of the clean animals, but only two of the unclean, Ambrose (lib. de Noah et arca c. 22), Chrysostom (hom. 24 in Gen.), and Theodoret most correctly conclude that the will of God concerning the rite of sacrificing became known to him from this command. 'He commanded the three pairs to be preserved for the increase of the species, and the one remaining for sacrifice.'

Fifth, whatever sacrifices are offered from faith, they must necessarily have a divine institution. But the sacrifices of the patriarchs were offered from faith. Therefore, they had a divine institution. The truth of the major premise is evident, 'because faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God' (Rom. 10:17). True faith cannot arise except from the Word, in which God has revealed His will; έΰελοΰρησκεϊαι cannot leave consciences certain and tranquil that they are approved by God, for the mind of man always thinks: 'Who knows whether this pleases God?' Therefore, for anything to be done from faith, it is necessary that the Word of God be present and shine before us; furthermore, it is required that one believe in Christ, that through and because of Him one pleases God.

The truth of the minor premise is έγγραφος. Heb. 11:4: 'By faith Abel offered to God a sacrifice of greater value than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts.' The same is evident from the fact that the sacrifices of the patriarchs were approved and accepted by God, the cause of which Chrysostom (in ch. 8 of Genesis) rightly refers to faith in the promised Messiah, whose ίλαστικόν sacrifice, to be offered on the altar of the cross, the sacrifices of the Old Testament prefigured.

Finally, human reason could find or devise no αναλογίαν between God, who is spirit, and the external rite of sacrifices." ‘ Not by the slaughter of an ox do the heavenly powers rejoice, But by the faith that must be rendered, and without a witness,’ Baier’s Comp. ed. Walther. III.24 PART III. CHAP. VII. says the poet. As far as the sacrifices of the Gentiles are concerned, they did not devise them so much for the sake of appeasing the incorporeal God Himself, as they borrowed them from the Israelite people out of a certain perverse κακοζηλία (emulation). (L. c. § 14.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of certain Jews, who, in order to crush all the more strongly the typical prefiguration of the Messiah made in the sacrifices, assert that men were first induced to offer sacrifices to God by natural reason and their own free will; such as R. Levi Ben Gerson, Maimonides, Abarbanel.

2. Of the Papists, who derive the rite of sacrificing either from the very law of nature, or from a mere instinct of nature, or at least from the proper devotion of the offerers, which reason dictated, so that from this they may carve out the moral and perpetual use of sacrifice properly so called, required in all religion at all times, and specifically the use of their own mass-sacrifice, or show that the Deity is not averse to ε’θελοθρησκείαις (will-worship). Thus Thomas, P. 3. Summae q. 60. a. 5. ad tert., says: ‘Just as in the state of the law of nature men were moved to worship God by no externally given law, but by an interior instinct alone, so also it was determined for them by an interior instinct which sensible things they should use for the worship of God.’ Gregorius de Valentia contends that this kind of divine worship proceeds from a right inclination of nature, and that the patriarchs, as well as the Gentiles, were compelled by it to sacrifice, 1. 1. de missae sacrificio c. 4., with whom Bellarmine is ομόψηφος (of the same opinion) 1. 1. de missa c. 20. § 2. Becanus and others teach the same.

3. Of Simon Episcopius, the leader of the Arminians, who in Instit. th. 1. 1. c. 8. p. 18.b. T. 1. Opp. says: ‘Abel by faith alone, induced by no divine precept’ (faith without the Word is a baseless thing), ‘i. e., by the instinct of right reason alone, judged that God should be worshipped with the things which he had in his own possession, the best, i. e., sacrifices from the firstlings of his flocks and from their fat. Gen. 4, 4. Heb. 11, 4.’

4. Of H. Grotius, who judges in his notes on Gen. 4, 3 that Cain and Abel sacrificed not by any command of God, but by the dictation of reason; cf. the same on Ex. 15, 27 and 1. 5. de V. R. Chr. c. 8.” (L. c. c. 1. s. 2. q. 8. f. 1004. sq.)

Hofmannus: “Not to comply with a divine command, but out of their own impulse, did Cain and Abel offer a portion of the yield of their labor. They returned the gift of God with this embodied prayer.” (Der Schriftbeweis. The first division of the 2nd half, p. 140.)

Quenstedtius: “The end and use of the ceremonial law is partly principal, partly less principal. The principal is both the signification and foreshadowing of the benefits of Christ, Col. 2, 16; Heb. 8, 4. 5; 10, 1, and the application of the same through the mediation of sacrifices and sacraments. . . The less principal is: 1. a reminder of sin, Heb. 10, 3; 2. εὐταξία (good order) in ecclesiastical assemblies and actions; 3. the distinction of the Jewish church from all idolatrous assemblies of the Gentiles, Deut. 4, 8; Eph. 2, 14; 4. an exercise of obedience toward God; 5. the preservation of the sacred ministry.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 58—60. f. 953. sq.)

The same: “The sacrifices of the O.T. truly expiated not only sins of ignorance and infirmity, or those committed ignorantly and involuntarily, but also all others, yet not by their own power and virtue, nor ex opere operato (by the work performed), or on account of the mere external sacrificial work without the repentance and faith of the offerers; but 1. typically, insofar as they were types and figures of Christ, the Lamb of God, to be immolated for the sins of the world and immolated in the fullness of time, 1 Cor. 5, 7; John 1, 29; 2. instrumentally and organically, insofar as they proposed Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God, to sinful men by the ordinance of God, offered to them the fruits of that future bloody obedience, and applied them to those who confessed their sins and believed in the future Messiah.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 1007.) Cf. above P. III. c. 2. s. 3. § 7. p. 108. sq.

Dorscheus: "It is said (Heb. 9:9) that the gifts and sacrifices of the O.T. could not purify and perfect the consciences of those who offered them, not because the Holy Spirit did not use those gifts and sacrifices of the O.T. as certain instruments by which justifying and sanctifying grace was applied. For they were nothing other than a certain visible sermon and proposition of those mysteries which were to be represented in the N.T. And so, to that extent, they possessed that power which the audible word also has, and were the power unto salvation, Rom. 1:16. For even though by reason of the act they pertained to the law, yet by reason of the image—whether the image in act, or, as Paul speaks above in ch. 8:5, by reason of the ὑπόδειγμα—they looked toward the Gospel, and received from it certain justifying rays, but for the reason that in this very apparatus and body, so to speak, of sacrifices and gifts, there was not that virtue by which wounded consciences could be succored." (Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews. 1717. 4. On Heb. 9:9.)
