### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: ANTITHESES. Antithesis 1

ANTITHESES. Antithesis 1. Of the Socinians, especially Socinus, and 2. Of Grotius, who is socinianizing, see above p. 109.

Luthardtius: "Through the Law, a priestly mediation and a constant order of reconciliation were established, which permeate the entire cultus, since man should never be permitted to approach God without a preceding atonement. This atonement and reconciliation is not merely depicted in the sacrifice, but rather accomplished by means of it—but only for the theocratic, not for the inwardly personal relationship to God (Heb. 9:9, 13, 14; 10:3, 4; Thomasius III, 1, 45)." (Compendium of Dogmatics. Third Ed. 1868. p. 171.)

To this pertain the sacraments of the O.T. themselves, insofar as they had to be frequented as external rites sanctioned by divine law. Cf. the blessed Gerhard, L. XVI, on Ceremonial and Forensic Laws, Sect. II, § 11. (Concerning the requirements and manner of administering these, we shall speak specifically below.)

Furthermore, the festivals, inaugurations, washings, and various purifications. Of which it was also required that they be marks of distinction from other nations.

For thus they are called a shadow of things to come (certainly not by accident, but by the very intention of the Author), but the body (the truth and complement of the things prefigured through the shadows of the law) is called Christ, or is to be sought in Christ Himself, Col. 2:16. For which reason it is also said in Heb. 10:1 that the law has a shadow of good things to come, not the very image of the things, or the things shadowed forth or represented.

And beautifully Augustine, L. VII, De Civ. Dei, ch. XXXII: "Sacred rites, priesthoods, the tabernacle or temple, altars, sacrifices, ceremonies, feast days, and whatever else pertains to that service which is owed to God and is properly called λατρεία in Greek, these signified and foretold those things which, for the sake of the eternal life of the faithful in Christ, we believe have been fulfilled, we perceive are being fulfilled, and we trust will be fulfilled." Cf. here, Part III, ch. II, § 7.

For divine constitutions also exist concerning the high priest and the remaining priests and ministers of sacred things from the tribe of Levi.

Not only those things which were to be handled in a certain way in the sacrifices, but also the sacred vessels and utensils, garments, places, and times divinely defined.

And under the threat of wrath and punishment; which is common to all divine law. PART III. CHAPTER VII.

§ 17.

The forensic law is that which contains the civil constitutions prescribing the form of public judgments and of external discipline to be maintained among the Jewish people. For they are distinguished from the ceremonial laws in that the latter pertained properly to the church, while the former pertained to the Jewish polity.

For example: concerning magistrates, the process of judgments, contracts, the division of inheritances, and punishments. To this category, besides those mentioned, belong the laws that regulate economic society, such as the laws concerning marriages, servants, parents and children, and indeed also those that deal with foreigners, military service, etc.

These were adapted entirely to the state of that people, not equally to the forms of every commonwealth. Gerhard: "The error of Carlstadt is to be rejected, which the Anabaptists of Münster later followed, who strenuously argued that Roman law should be exterminated from Christian commonwealths and that judgments in civil cases should be rendered according to Mosaic laws; against whom Dr. Luther sharply opposed himself." (Loc. de legib. ceremon. et forens. § 40.) § 18.

The ceremonial laws were abrogated upon the manifestation of the Messiah, and the forensic laws upon the removal of the Jewish polity; but the moral law was not. For God did not will that they should endure and bind perpetually, but only for a time; whence, the appointed time having elapsed, the power of binding ceased. And this is the third degree of Christian liberty among those which are commonly established, namely, that the faithful in the New Testament are no longer bound to the observance of the Mosaic ceremonial and forensic laws.

Hebrews 9:10 states that they were imposed μέχρι καιροῦ διορθώσεως, until the time of reformation, when more perfect things were to be substituted for the shadowy ones. Cf. Heb. 7:22; 8:6. See Acts 10; 11 regarding the removal of the distinction of foods. And Gal. 2:8; ch. 4:10; ch. 5:2; Col. 2:16 regarding the removal of the laws of circumcision, festivals, and the like. Moreover, with the destruction of the Jerusalem temple and the tabernacle, to which most of those sacred rites were bound, it is recognized all the more clearly that this very worship has expired.

These also did not bind those converted from the Gentiles in former times, since they were left to their ancestral and hereditary laws. For neither Christ nor the apostles imposed upon the newly converted the necessity of observing those laws, but rather left them subject to the laws of their own magistrates under whom they were; see the examples of the centurion in Matt. 8:13, Cornelius in Acts 10:1 sqq., and Sergius the proconsul in Acts 13:7.

IS, 12. And Paul wishes the Romans to be subject to imperial laws, Rom. 13:1 sqq. He himself demands to be judged according to Roman laws, Acts 25:10, 25. Cf. 1 Peter 2:13, 14.

But when the republic is overturned, it is manifest that the laws are likewise abolished.

Although not a few of the Jewish forensic laws, insofar as and to the extent that they are suitable for other republics, may be freely introduced by a Christian magistrate and proposed to be observed. For it does not look precisely to the church or the synagogue, or the Jewish polity, but to men as rational creatures.

Therefore, although the moral law is invalid and useless for justification, due to corrupt human nature, Rom. 8:3, and although its curses do not touch men who rely by faith upon an alien satisfaction, Rom. 8:1, yet the law itself is not therefore abrogated, since it does not cease to bind all to exact and constant obedience; even if those who do not perform this are not therefore condemned, but their imperfect obedience also pleases God.

See the blessed Gerhard, *L. de Legg. Cerem. et For.* ch. IV, § 43; the blessed Musaeus, *Tract. contra Stenger.* P. II, ch. II, p. 204, and P. III, ch. VI, p. 618.

Quenstedtius: "Some include the abrogation of the law among the adjuncts, insofar as it concerns the vigor of its exaction. For the moral law is not abrogated and abolished *ὅλως* (wholly), from the whole, but *μερικῶς* (partially), in part; namely: 1. Regarding justification, for which it is ineffective and invalid. For it is not a law that can *ζωοποιῆσαι* (make alive), Gal. 3:2, 21; which, however, happens by impotence, not of the law itself, but brought about by the vice of the flesh. 2. Regarding the curse; for Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, Gal. 3:13. 3. Regarding the rigor of exaction; for because Christ perfectly fulfilled the law for us, God remits to believers something of the rigor of the law, and does not impute to the regenerate the defects that adhere to them, for the sake of the Son. 4. Regarding servile coercion, which appears in the unregenerate, who do not perform the things of the law except with weariness, for fear of punishment. Hence Paul says in Gal. 5:18: 'Those who are led by the Spirit are not under the law,' namely, the condemning and cursing law (for the regenerate remain under the norm of the law). For 'not to be under the law' does not signify an absolute immunity from the law and a license to do anything, but signifies being liberated from the curse and coercion of the law; but because the regenerate are led by the Spirit, they now delight in the law according to the inner man and do the things of the law spontaneously." (*L. c. s. 1. th. 35. f. 939 sq.*)

Cf. the Sentences of Luther and Fecht, which follow.

Luther: "A Christian, properly defined, is free from all laws, and subject to absolutely no one, neither within nor without. But I say significantly: insofar as he is a Christian (not insofar as he is a male or a female), that is, insofar as he has a conscience imbued, adorned, and enriched with that faith, with that great and incomprehensible treasure, or, as Paul says, with the ineffable gift, which cannot be sufficiently magnified and praised, because it makes them children and heirs of God." (On Gal. 2: 16. See *Commentar.*, ed. Irmischer, Erlangen 1843, Vol. I, 197.)

The same: "Nor does Paul speak here (Gal. 2:19) of the ceremonial law, because he sacrificed in the temple, circumcised Timothy, and shaved his head in Cenchreae; he would not have done those things if he had been dead to the ceremonial law; but he speaks of the whole law. Therefore, simply put, the whole law, whether it be ceremonial or of the Decalogue, is abrogated to the Christian, because he is dead to it; not that the law perishes; indeed, it remains, lives, and reigns in the impious; but the pious man is dead to the law, just as he is dead to sin, the devil, death, and hell, which nevertheless remain, and the world and the impious will have them. Therefore, when the sophist understands the law to be abrogated, and that it is the ceremonial law, you understand Paul, and every Christian, to be abrogated and dead to the universal law, and yet the law remains." (On Gal. 2: 19. *L. c. p. 229.*) PART III. CHAPTER VII.

The same: "The Law is not so abolished by grace that the truth should also remain behind (John 1:17), that one should not love God, etc.; but through it, it is granted to us that we do not satisfy the Law, and yet should do so, in the kingdom of forgiveness or grace. But for this purpose, the Holy Spirit is also given to us, who kindles in us a new flame and fire, namely, love and desire for God’s commandments. This shall begin in the kingdom of grace and continue forever until the Last Day, when it will no longer be called grace or forgiveness, but pure truth and entirely perfect obedience." (Postill. eccl. Tom. Hal. XI, 2274.)

The same: "Where now the Law of Moses and the Law of Nature are one thing, there the Law remains, and is not abolished outwardly, except spiritually through faith; which is nothing other than fulfilling the Law." (Against the Heavenly Prophets. 1524. Tom. Hal. XX, 210.)

The same: "The saying in John 10:35 remains nonetheless true, that 'the Scripture cannot be broken,' and Matthew 5:18, that 'one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the Law, till all be fulfilled.' Therefore, when I say thus: I may break the commandment, the Law, that is as much as to say: I may break its wrong understanding (as David did) and keep the right one." (Judgment on Monastic Vows. A. 1522. Tom. Hal. XX, 2025.)

Latin:

ANTITHESES. Antithesis 1. Socinianorum, imprimis Socini, et 2. Grotii, socinizantis, vid. supra p. 109.

Luthardtius: ״Durch das Gesetz wurde eine priesterliche Mittlerschaft und stetige Versöhnungsordnung gestiftet, welche den ganzen Cultus durchdringt, da der Mensch nie ohne vorangegangene Sühne Gott soll nahen dürfen. Diese Sühne und Versöhnung wird im Opfer nicht bloss abgebildet, sondern vielmehr mittelst desselben vollzogen — aber nur eben für das theokratische, nicht für das innerlich persönliche Verhältniss zu Gott (Hebr. 9, 9.13.14. 10, 3. 4. Thomasius III. 1, 45.).“ (Compend. der Dogm. Dritte Aufl. 1868. p. 171.)

Quo pertinent ipsa sacramenta V. T., quatenus ut ritus externi, lege divina sanciti, frequentari debebant. Conf. b. Gerhard. L. XVI. de Legg. Cer. et For. Sect. II. § 11. (De quorum requisitis et administrandi ratione infra peculiariter dicemus.)

Praeterea festivitates, inaugurationes, lotiones et purgationes variae. Cujus etiam notae discreti vae ab aliis gentibus esse ista debebant.

Sic enim dicuntur umbra futurorum (non certe ex accidenti, sed ex ipsa intentione auctoris), corpus autem (veritas et complementum rerum per umbras legis praefiguratarum) dicitur Christus, aut in ipso Christo quaerendum, Col. 2, 16. Qua ratione etiam Ebr. 10, i. dicitur, legem umbram habere futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum, aut res adumbratas seu repraesentatas.

Et pulchre Augustinus L. VII. de Civ. Dei cap. XXXII.: Sacra, sacerdotia, tabernaculum sive templum, altaria, sacrificia, ceremoniae, dies festi, et quicquid aliud ad eam servitutem pertinet, quae Deo debetur et Graece proprie latria dicitur, ea significata et praenunciata sunt, quae propter aeternam vitam fidelium in Christo et impleta credimus, et impleri cernimus, et implenda confidimus. Conf. h. 1. P. III. cap. II. § 7.

Nam et de summo sacerdote et sacerdotibus reliquis et ministris sacrorum de tribu Levi constitutiones divinae extant.

Non solum, quae in sacrificiis certo modo tractandae essent, verum etiam vasa ac utensilia sacra, vestes, loca, tempora divinitus definita.

Et sub comminatione irae ac poenae; quod commune est omni legi divinae. PART. III. CAP. VII.

§ 17·

Lex forensis ea dicitur, qua constitutiones a civiles, formam publicorum b judiciorum et externae disciplinae c in populo Judaico d conservandae praescribentes, continentur. Per hoc enim distinguuntur a ceremonialibus, quod hae ad ecclesiam, istae ad politiam Judaicam proprie spectarent.

V. g. de magistratibus, de processu judiciorum, de contractibus, de divisione haereditatum, de poenis. Quo praeter istas pertinent, quae societatem oeconomicam ordinant, quales sunt leges de conjugiis, de servis, de parentibus et liberis, imo et illae, quae de advenis, de militia agunt etc.

Ad cujus statum plane accommodatae fuerunt, non aeque ad formas cujusvis reipublicae. Gerhardus: ,,Improbandus Carolostadii error, quem anabaptistae Monasterienses postea sunt secuti, qui strenue pugnarunt, jus romanum ex Christianis rebuspublicis exterminandum ac secundum leges Mosaicas in causis civilibus pronuntiandum esse; quibus acriter se opposuit D. Lutherus.“ (Loc. de legib. ceremon. et forens. § 40. § 18.

Abrogatae a sunt leges ceremoniales,b exhibito c Messia, et forenses, d sublata politia e Judaica; moralis vero non f item. Neque enim voluit Deus, eas perpetuo, sed ad tempus, durare et obligare; unde, elapso tempore statuto, cessabat vis obligandi. Atque hic est tertius gradus libertatis christianae ex his, quos vulgo constituunt, nimirum quod fideles in N. T. ad legum ceremonialium et forensium Mosaicarum observationem non amplius sunt obligati.

Ebr. 9, 10. dicitur, impositas illas fuisse μέχρι χαφοΰ δωρΰώσεως, usque ad tempus correctionis, quo perfectiora umbraticis substituerentur. Conf. Ebr. 7, 22. 8, 6. Vid. Actor. 10, 11. de sublato discrimine ciborum. Et Gal. 2, 8. cap. If, 10. cap. 5, 2. Col. 2, 16. de sublatis legibus circumcisionis, festorum, et similibus. Destructo autem templo Hierosolymitano ac tabernaculo, ad quod alligata erant pleraque illa sacra, ipsum hunc cultum expirasse, tanto clarius agnoscitur.

Quae etiam olim conversos ex gentibus non obligarunt, quippe relictos patriis avitisque legibus. Nam et Christus et apostoli recens conversis necessitatem observandi leges istas non imposuerunt, verum legibus eorum magistratuum, sub quibus erant, obnoxios reliquerunt; vid. exempla centurionis Matth. 8, 13., Cornelii Act. 10, 1. sqq., Sergii proconsulis Actor.

IS, 12. Et Paulus Romanos legibus imperatoriis subjectos esse vult Rom. 18, 1. sqq. Ipse juxta leges Romanas judicari se postulat Actor. 25, 10. 25. Conf. Petri 1. Epist. 2, 13. 14.

Eversa autem republica, leges simul tolli manifestum est.

Quanquam possint leges forenses Judaicae non paucae, quae et quousque rebuspublicis aliis conveniunt, a magistratu christiano libere introduci atque, ut observentur, proponi. Neque enim vel ecclesiam aut synagogam, vel politiam Judaicam praecise spectat, sed homines, ut creaturas rationales.

Quamvis itaque lex moralis ad justificationem invalida et inutilis sit, corrupta natura humana, Rom. S, S., quamvis etiam maledictiones ejus non tangant homines, satisfactione aliena per fidem nixos, Rom. 8, 1., non tamen ideo lex ipsa abrogata est, quippe quae non desinit obligare omnes ad exactam et constantem obedientiam; etiamsi qui hanc non ita praestant, propterea non damnentur, sed etiam imperfecta illorum obedientia placeat Deo.

Vid. b. Gerhard. L. de Legg. Cerem, et For. cap. IV. § 43., b. Mus. Tract. contra Stenger. P. II. cap. II. p. 204. et P. ΓΙΙ. cap. VI. p. 618.

Quenstedtius: ,,Inter adjuncta referunt nonnulli legis abrogationem, quantum ad vigorem exactionis. Lex enim moralis non όλικώς, ex toto, sed μερικώς, ex parte, est abrogata et abolita; sc. 1. quoad justificationem, ad quam inefficax est et invalida. Non enim est lex, quae possit ζωοττυιήσαι, vivificare, Gal. 3, 2. 21.; quod tamen accidit impotentia, non legis propria, sed vitio carnis accersita. 2. Quoad maledictionem; Christus enim nos a maledictione legis redemit, factus pro nobis maledictum, Gal. 3, 13. 3. Quoad rigorem exactionis; quia enim Christus pro nobis legem perfecte implevit, Deus remittit credentibus aliquid de rigore legis, et defectus renatis adhaerentes propter Filium non imputat. 4. Quoad servilem coactionem, quae apparet in nonrenatis, qui non nisi cum taedio faciunt, quae legis sunt, metu poenae. Hinc Paulus dicit Gal. 5,18.: ;Illos, qui spiritu ducuntur, non esse sub lege‘, sc. damnante et execrante (sub legis enim norma manent renati). Nam,non esse sub lege‘ non significat omnimodam a lege immunitatem et licentiam quidvis faciendi, sed significat, liberatum esse a maledictione et coactione legis; quia vero spiritu ducuntur renati, jam delectantur lege secundum interiorem hominem et sponte faciunt, quae legis sunt.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 35. f. 939. sq.)

Cf. Sententiae Lutheri et Fechtii, quae sequuntur.

Lutherus: ״Christianus proprie definitus est liber ab omnibus legibus, et nulli prorsus nec intus nec foris subjectus. Sed signiflcanter dico: in quantum Christianus (non in quantum masculus aut foemina), hoc est, in quantum habet conscientiam imbutam, ornatam et ditatam illa fide, illo magno et incomprehensibili thesauro, vel, ut Paulus ait, inenarrabili dono, quod non potest satis magnifleri et laudari, quia facit filios et heredes Dei.“ (Ad Gal. 2,16. Vid. Commentar, cur. Irmischer. Erlanggte 1843. T. I. 197.)

Idem: ״Nec Paulus hic (Gal. 2, 19.) loquitur de lege ceremoniali, quia sacrificavit in templo, circumcidit Timotheum, rasit caput in Cenehraeis; ista non fecisset, si fuisset mortuus legi ceremoniali; sed loquitur de tota lege. Itaque simpliciter tota lex, sive sit ceremonialis, sive decalogi, abrogata est christiano, quia ei mortuus est; non quod lex pereat; imo manet, vivit et regnat in impiis; sed pius est legi mortuus, sicut et peccato, diabolo, morti, inferno mortuus est, quae tamen manent, et mundus ac impii ea habebunt. Ideo cum sophista intelligit legem abrogari, eamque ceremonialem, tu intellige Paulum, et quemlibet Christianum universae legi abrogari et mori, et tamen legem manere.“ (Ad Gal. 2, 19. L. c. p. 229.) PART. III. CAP. VII.

Idem: ,,Das Gesetz wird nicht also aufgehoben durch die Gnade, dass auch die Wahrheit sollte nachbleiben (Joh. 1,17.), dass man nicht sollte Gott lieben n. s. w.; sondern durch ihn wird es uns geschenkt, dass wir dem Gesetz nicht genugthun, und doch thun sollten, im Reich der Vergebung oder der Gnade. Aber dazu wird uns auch gegeben der Heilige Geist, welcher in 11ns eine neue Flamme und Feuer anzündet, nämlich Liebe und Lust zu Gottes Geboten. Das soll in dem Gnadenreich aniahen, und immer fortgehen bis an den jüngsten Tag, da es nicht mehr wird Gnade noch Vergebung heissen, sondern eitel Wahrheit und ganz vollkommener Gehorsam.“ (Postill. eccl. Tom. Hal. XI, 2274.)

Idem: ,,Wo nun Mosis Gesetz und Naturgesetz ein Ding ist, da bleibet das Gesetz, und wird nicht aufgehoben äusserlich, ohne durch den Glauben geistlich; welches ist nichts anderes, denn das Gesetz erfüllen.“ (Wider die himmlischen Propheten. 1524. Tom. Hal. XX, 210.)

Idem: ,,Der Spruch Joh. 10, 35. bleibet gleichwohl wahr, dass,die Schrift nicht kann aufgelöset werden‘, und Matth. 5, 18., dass,ein Buchstab oder ein Tüttel vom Gesetz nicht wird umkommen, bis dass alles erfüllet werde.‘ Darum, wenn ich also sage: das Gebot, das Gesetze mag ich brechen, das ist so viel gesagt, seinen Unrechten Verstand mag ich brechen (wie David gethan) und den rechten halten.“ (Urtheil von den geistlichen und Klostergelübden. A. 1522. Tom. Hal. XX, 2025.)


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: The same: "The Law is thus fulfilled in a twofold way, namely, through faith…

The same: "The Law is thus fulfilled in a twofold way, namely, through faith and through love. Through faith it is fulfilled in this life, in that God imputes to us by grace the righteousness or fulfillment of the Law acquired through Christ. Through love it will be fulfilled in that life, when we as a new creature of God shall be perfect. Although one cannot properly say that the Law will be fulfilled there, because then there will be no Law, but rather that very thing itself which the Law requires in this life." (Five Disputations on Rom. 3:28. A. 1535. Opp. Hal. XIX, 1770.)

Fechtius: "The moral law has not been abrogated regarding justification, nor regarding the curse, nor regarding the rigor of exaction, nor regarding coercion, but it always remains the same in the Old and New Testaments."

Bollius adds: "Certain ones among the Calvinists in the previous century, namely David Pareus and Andr. Rivetus, taught that the moral law, as it was delivered through Moses, has been abrogated for Christians. Afterward, some among our own also said the law was abrogated, not entirely, but in those ways indicated in the thesis. But the truer opinion, without doubt, is that of most of our own, that it has been abrogated in none of these ways: not regarding justification, since the law did not justify even in the Old Testament; nor regarding the curse, since it did not curse the faithful in the Old Testament; nor, finally, regarding coercion, since it obtains even today with respect to those who are placed outside the state of grace." (Syll. controv. p. 263, 269 sq.) §

19. The Mosaic moral law, or that of the Decalogue, is the same as the law of Christ; for Christ indeed purged that law from Pharisaical corruptions and declared it more correctly, but He did not give entirely new moral precepts to the faithful. For on both sides, perfect obedience and the rectitude of all human faculties and actions are required; and not only sins

more serious and ethical matters, but also those which are called matters of human infirmity, and original sin itself, are prohibited on both sides. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Tract. contra Stetiger.* Part II, chap. I, p. 160, etc.; chap. II, p. 199; Part III, chap. VI, p. 561 sqq., p. 598 sqq. See Matthew 5:20 sqq., where the phrases: "You have heard that it was said to those of old: But I say to you, etc.," are easily understood to be directed with respect to the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, who adhered to the shell of the law while neglecting its sense, and therefore stood in need of correction, especially if we attend to that which Christ premised in verse 17: "I have not come to abolish the law (to relax or remove its power of obligation), but (by my perfect obedience) to fulfill it." For the precepts which Christ inculcated, if not expressly, are nevertheless implicitly contained in the Decalogue.

Luther: "But if you ask from what cause they make such counsels out of it, or with what they prove it, they say: 'Alas, if one were to teach thus, that would be called *nimis onerativum legis Christianae* [too burdensome for the Christian law], that is, it would be too great a burden upon Christendom,' as those of Paris have publicly and shamelessly written against me. Yes, truly a fine cause and a great burden, that a Christian should be friendly to his neighbor and not forsake him in need, just as everyone would wish that it be done to him. And because it seems too difficult to them, it must not be called a commandment, but stand in free choice, for whoever wants to do it gladly; but whoever does not want to or cannot do it, shall not be burdened with it. Thus one should seize Christ by the mouth, master His Word, and make of it what we please. But He will not let Himself be deceived, nor revoke His judgment, which He has set forth here and said: Whoever does not have a better righteousness, to him heaven shall be closed, and he shall be damned; and, as follows thereafter, he shall also be guilty of hell fire who says to his brother, 'You fool.' From which it is well to calculate whether it be a counsel or a commandment." (*Exposition of the 5th, 6th, and 7th Chapters of Matthew*, A.D. 1532. *Opp. Hal.* VII, 641.)

Gerhard: "Neither Christ nor the apostles prescribed new counsels of perfection in the Gospel." *Έκΰεσις* [Exposition]: 1. If counsels defined indifferent works, which are good or bad according to the ratio of circumstances, and permitted them to the judgment of each, we would not deny that certain counsels are given. 2. If the doctrine concerning external exercises were handed down in this way—that they are not in themselves worship or merits, much less above the commandments or a certain perfection, but are undertaken according to the diversity of gifts, so that one may be more free and ready to attend to those things which pertain to true piety—it could be tolerated in some way. But the Papists do not stop within those bounds, but fight for perfection and the supererogation of merits in such works. They maintain that those who observe the evangelical counsels acquire more merits than are necessary for themselves, and therefore they can be applied to others for the remission of sins and the merit of eternal life. 3. By 'counsel' the apostle in 1 Corinthians 7:25 does not understand such a counsel of perfection that is above God's commandments and by whose observation a work of supererogation is performed and a certain merit is collected to be dispensed to others, but he prescribes in a doubtful case what should be followed and chosen. For in the Greek there is the word γνώμη, which properly signifies an opinion." (*Conf. cath.* L. II, P. II, art. 7, c. 3, f. 894.)

Chemnitz: "They call them evangelical counsels because they pretend that the Old Testament only had exercise in the commandments of God, but that Christ in the New Testament added certain other more perfect, better, more sublime, and more excellent things above those commandments. But lest those be too burdensome, because it is written in Matthew 11, last verse: 'My yoke is easy, and my burden is light.'"

PART III. CHAPTER VII. they say, are counsels, which do not simply bind under the penalty of mortal sin. Therefore, they derive the number of counsels chiefly from Christ’s sermon on the mount, because Christ speaks there as follows: "It was said to them of old; but I say unto you," etc. Luther, in a certain disputation, recounts that 12 evangelical counsels are enumerated by the sophists: 1. Matt. 19:21, 29, voluntary poverty; 2. Luke 9:23, self-denial or monastic obedience; 3. Matt. 19:12, chastity; 4. not to seek revenge, Matt. 5:39; 5. patience under injury: "If anyone strikes you," Luke 6:29, etc.; 6. almsgiving, Luke 6:30: "Give to everyone who asks of you"; 7. not to swear, Matt. 5:34; 8. to avoid the occasion of sinning, Matt. 18:9: "If your eye causes you to stumble," etc.; 9. Matt. 6:1: "Do not do your righteousness before men," etc., that is, to form the intention rightly in good works; 10. to do what you teach, Matt. 23:3: "They say and do not," Matt. 7:5: "First cast out the beam," etc.; 11. not to be anxious about food and clothing, Matt. 6:31; 12. "If your brother sins, go, rebuke him," Matt. 18: 15. Others enumerate them differently, such as: to dismiss signs of rancor before reconciliation; not to look at a woman to lust after her; to show offices of love to an enemy outside the case of necessity; to pray in one's room; to fast; not to judge. . . For from these passages, especially Matt. 5, 6, 7, Luke 6, Matt. 18, 19, 1 Cor. 7, they take their catalog of counsels. They call three, however, the substantial counsels of perfection: concerning poverty, chastity, and obedience. But after the opinion was once received that counsels are above precepts and that life according to the counsels is a state of perfection, the ternary and duodenary number seemed to make the limits of monastic religion too narrow. Therefore, in order to extend the boundaries, they fabricated counsels from all the testimonies of Scripture wherever they read the word "perfection." Likewise, wherever they found those particles: "If you wish, he who wishes, if you wish," etc., because those particles seem not to command, but to leave to our discretion what pertains to the counsels. But in order that the burden of religion and merit might be increased even more, they added to the number of counsels the eight beatitudes, Matt. 5:3 ff." (Loc. theol. II. f. 104.)

ANTITHESIS. Hollazius: "The antithesis is that of the Anabaptists, Socinians, and Arminians, who assert that Christ is a new legislator, who rendered the moral law more perfect and completed it with new precepts. Their stronger arguments are: 1. Christ and Moses, as two legislators, are opposed to each other, Heb. 3:5, 6. Resp.: They are opposed to each other as master and servant, as a son in the house of God and a domestic. . .

3. Christ gave a new law, John 13:34. Therefore, he was a new legislator. Resp.: Distinguish between a law that is simply new and one that is new in a certain respect or comparatively. The law of Christ is called new not absolutely and simply, because it is the same law as the Sinaitic law, but it is called new in a certain respect and comparatively, because it has been renewed by Christ, vindicated from the false interpretations of the Pharisees, and confirmed by the new example of Christ.

4. He who opposes his own precepts to Mosaic precepts is a new legislator: but Christ does so, etc., Matt. 5:21, 22. Resp.: Christ opposed his precepts not to the Mosaic laws, but to the corruptions of the Pharisees, who thought that homicide was committed only by an external act, not by the heart, not by gesture, not by the mouth. . .

6. Christ gave three moral precepts which do not exist in the Mosaic law: 1. to deny oneself, 2. to take up or tolerate one's cross, and 3. to imitate Christ, Matt. 16:24. Resp.: Self-denial pertains to the first commandment, which deals with loving God with all one's heart and with all one's soul. For he denies himself who subordinates self-love to the love of God. The tolerance of the cross is patience, commended to us in the first commandment, because it flows from filial fear of God. The imitation of Christ (as the Racovian Catechism, ch. 2, on the precepts of Christ, quest. 8, explains) consists in trust toward God, perfect charity, humility, and perseverance in prayers, and thus pertains both to the first and to the second commandment of the Decalogue.

Latin:

Idem: ,,Es wird also das Gesetz auf eine zweifache Art erfüllt, nämlich durch den Glauben und durch die Liebe. Durch den Glauben wirds erfüllt in diesem Leben, indem uns Gott die durch Christum erworbene Gerechtigkeit oder Erfüllung «des Gesetzes aus Gnaden zurechnet. Durch die Liebe wirds in jenem Leben erfüllt werden, da wir als eine neue Creatur Gottes vollkommen sein werden. Obwohl man eigentlich nicht sagen kann, dass dorten das Gesetz erfüllt werde, weil alsdann kein Gesetz, sondern vielmehr dasjenige selbst, was das Gesetz in diesem Leben erfordert, sein wird.“ (Fünf Disputat, über Rom. 3, 28. A. 1535. Opp. Hal. XIX, 1770.)

Fechtius: ,,Lex moralis neque quoad justificationem, neque quo ad maledictionem, neque quoad rigorem exactionis, neque quoad coac tionem abrogata est, sed in Vet. Novoque T. eadem semper manet.“

Addit Bollius: ,,Quidam inter Calvinianos superiori saeculo, nominatim David Pareus et Andr. Bivetus, docuerunt, legem moralem, prout per Mosen tradita est, abrogatam esse penes Christianos. Postmodum et quidam inter nostrates abrogatam dixerunt legem non omnino, sed modis illis in thesi indicatis. Verior autem haud dübie sententia est plerorumque nostratium, nullo horum modorum abrogatam eam esse, non quoad justificationem, cum nec in V. T. lex justificaverit, nec quoad maledictionem, cum nec maledixerit fidelibus in V. T., nec denique quoad coactionem, cum ea et hodie obtineat respectu illorum, qui extra statum gratiae positi sunt.“ (Syll. controv. p. 263. 269. sq.) §

19. Lex moralis Mosaica, seu decalogi, eadem est cum a lege Christi; illam enim quidem a pharisaicis corruptelis purgavit b et rectius declaravit Christus, non autem praecepta moralia plane nova c dedit fidelibus. Utrinque enim perfecta obedientia et omnium facultatum atque actionum humanarum rectitudo exigitur; et non solum peccata

graviora ac proaeretica, verum etiam ea, quae vocantur humanae infirmitatis, ipsumque peccatum originis utrinque prohibetur. Confer, b. Mus. Tract. contra Stetiger. Part. II. cap. I. p. 160. etc. cap. II. p. 199. P. III. c. VI. p. 561. sqq. p. 598. sqq. Vid. Matth. 5, 20. sqq., ubi phrases: audivistis, quod dictum sit veteribus: Ego'autem dico etc., habito respectu ad justitiam scribarum et Pharisaeorum, cortici legis, sensu vero neglecto, adhaerentium ideoque correctione opus habentium, intelligendas esse facile cognoscitur, praesertim si attendamus ad illud, quod v. 17. praemisit Christus: Non veni solvere legem (vim obligandi ejus relaxare aut tollere), sed (mea perfecta obedientia) implere. Quae enim Christus inculcavit praecepta, si non expresse, implicite tamen in decalogo continentur.

Lutherus: ,,Fragst du aber, aus was Ursach sie solche Räthe draus machen, oder womit sie es beweisen, so sprechen sie: Ei, wenn man also sollte lehren, das heisse nimis onerativum legis Christianae, das ist, es wäre die Christenheit zu hoch beschwert, wie die von Paris öffentlich und unverschämt wider mich geschrieben haben. Ja, wahrlieh eine schöne Ursache und grosse Beschwerung, dass ein Christ sollte seinem Nächsten freundlich sein und nicht lassen in Nöthen, wie ein jeglicher wollte, dass ihm geschehe. Und weil sie es zu schwer dünkt, muss es nicht geboten heissen, sondern in freier Willkür stehen, wer es gerne thun will; wer es aber nicht thun will oder kann, soll nicht damit beschwert sein. So soll man Christo ins Maul greifen, sein Wort meistern und daraus machen, was uns gefällt. Er wird aber sich nicht so täuschen lassen, noch sein Urtheil widerrufen, das er hier gestellt und gesagt hat: Wer nicht eine bessere Frömmigkeit habe, dem 8011 der Himmel zugeschlossen, und verdammt sein; und, wie hernach folgt, auch der des höllisehen Feuers schuldig sein, wer zu seinem Bruder sagt, du Narr. Aus welchem wohl zu rechnen ist, ob es gerathen oder geboten sei.“ (Ausl, des 5. 6. u. 7. Cap. Matthäi. A. 1532. Opp. Hai. VII, 641.)

Gerhardus: ,,Nec Christus nec apostoli praescripserunt in evangelio nova consilia perfectionis. 'Έκΰεσις: 1. Si consilia definirent opera indifferentia, quae pro ratione circumstantiarum bona vel mala, ac permitterent ea cujusque arbitrio, non negaremus, dari quaedam consilia. 2. Si doctrina de externis exercitiis hoc modo traderetur, quod per se non sint cultus vel merita, multo minus supra praecepta seu perfectio quaedam, sed pro diversitate donorum suscipiantur, ut liberius et expeditius iis, quae ad veram pietatem pertinent, vacari possit, utcunque tolerari posset. Sed pontificii intra terminos illos non consistunt, sed pugnant pro perfectione et supererogatione meritorum in talibus operibus. Statuunt, illos, qui observant consilia evangelica, plura aequirere merita, quam quae sibi ipsis sint necessaria, ideo aliis ad peccatorum remissionem et vitae aeternae meritum ea applicari posse. 3. Per consilium apostolus 1 Cor. 7, 25. non intelligit tale consilium perfectionis, quod sit supra Dei praecepta et cujus observatione supererogationis opus praestetur ac meritum quoddam aliis erogandum colligatur, sed in casu dubio, quid sequendum et eligendum sit, praescribit. In Graeco enim habetur vox γνώμη, quae sententiam proprie significat.“ (Conf. cath. L. II. P. II. art. 7. c. 3. f. 894.)

Chemnitius: ,,Consilia vocant evangelica, quia fingunt, V. T. tantum habuisse exercitium in mandatis Dei, Christum vero in N. T. supra illa praecepta addidisse quaedam alia perfectiora, meliora, sublimiora, praestantiora. Ne autem illa essent nimis onerativa, quia scriptum est Matth. 11. vers. ult.: ,Jugum meum suave, et onus meum leve est‘>

PART. III. CAP. VII. dicunt, esse consilia, quae non simpliciter sub poena peccati mortalis obligant. Numerum igitur consiliorum sumunt praecipue ex concione Christi in monte, propterea, quia Christus ibi sic loquitur: ,Dictum est antiquis; Ego vero dico vobis‘ etc. Lutherus in disputatione quadam recitat, numerari a sophistis 12 consilia evangelica: 1. Matth. 19, 21. 29. paupertatem voluntariam; 2. Luc. 9, 23. abnegationem sui seu obedientiam monasticam; 3. Matth. 19, 12. castitatem; 4. non vindicare Matth. 5, 39.; 5. patientiam injuriae: ,Si quis te percusserit‘ Luc. 6, 29. etc.; 6. eleemosynas Luc. 6, 30.: ,Omni petenti a te tribue‘; 7. non jurare Matth. 5, 34.; 8. vitare occasionem peccandi Matth. 18, 9.: ,Si oculus te scandalizat‘ etc.; 9. Matth. 6, 1.: ,Ne justitiam vestram faciatis coram hominibus‘ etc., id est, in bonis operibus intentionem recte formare; 10. facere, quod doces Matth. 23, 3.: ,Dicunt et non faciunt‘; Matth. 7, 5.: ,Ejice primum trabem‘ etc.; 11. non esse solicitum de victu Matth. 6, 31.; 12. ,Si peccaverit frater tuus, vade, corripe eum‘ Matth. 18, 15. Alii aliter numerant, ut: signa rancoris ante reconciliationem dimittere; non aspicere mulierem ad concupiscendum; inimico extra casum necessitatis officia dilectionis exhibere; orare in cubiculo; jejunare; non judicare. . . Ex his enim locis, praecipue Matth. 5. G. 7. Luc. 6. Matth. 18. 19. 1 Cor. 7. sumunt catalogum consiliorum. Tria vero vocant consilia substantialia perfectionis: de paupertate, castitate et obedientia. Postquam vero semel recepta fuit opinio, consilia esse supra praecepta et vitam secundum consilia esse statum perfectionis, visus est numerus ternarius et duodenarius nimis angustos facere limites religionis monasticae. Ut igitur terminos proferrent, ex omnibus Scripturae testimoniis fabricarunt consilia, ubicunque legerunt vocabulum,perfectionis‘. Item, ubicunque illas particulas invenerunt: ,Si vis, qui vult, si vultis‘ etc., quia illae particulae videntur non praecipere, sed in arbitrio nostro relinquere, quod ad consilia pertinet. Ut autem gravamen religionis et meritum adhuc magis augeretur, numero' consiliorum addiderunt octo beatitudines Matth. 5, 3. sqq.“ (Loc. theol. II. f. 104.)

ANTITHESIS. Hollazius: ,,Antithesis est Anabaptistarum, Socinianorum et Arminianorum, asserentium, Christum esse novum legislatorem, qui legem moralem perfectiorem reddiderit, et novis praeceptis compleverit. Quorum potiora argumenta sunt: 1. Christus et Moses, tanquam duo legislatores, sibi opponuntur Hebr. 3, 5.6. Resp.: Opponuntur sibi ut dominus et servus, ut filius in domo Dei et famulus. . .

3. Christus dedit novam legem, Jo. 13, 34. Ergo fuit novus legislator. Resp.: Dist. inter legem simpliciter novam et secundum quid seu comparate novam. Lex Christi nova dicitur non absolute et simpliciter, quia est eadem lex cum lege Sinaitica, sed dicitur nova secundum quid et comparate, quia est a Christo renovata, a falsis interpretationibus pharisaeorum vindicata, et novo Christi exemplo confirmata.

4. Qui praecepta sua Mosaicis praeceptis opponit, ille est novus legislator: atqui Christus etc. Matth. 5, 21. 22. Resp.: Christus praecepta sua opposuit non legibus Mosaicis, sed corruptelis pharisaeorum, qui putabant, homicidium tantum fieri opere externo, non corde, non gestu, non ore. ..

6. Christus tria dedit praecepta moralia, quae non exstant in lege Mosaica: 1. seipsum abnegare, 2. crucem suam tollere sive tolerare, et 3. Christum imitari, Matth. 16, 24. Resp.: Abnegatio sui pertinet ad praeceptum primum, quod agit de Deo diligendo ex toto corde et ex tota anima. Nam seipsum abnegat, qui amorem sui postponit amori Dei. Crucis tolerantia est patientia, commendata nobis in praecepto primo, quia fluit ex timore Dei filiali. Imitatio Christi (exponente catech. Racov. c. 2. de praecept. Christi, quaest. 8.) consistit in fiducia erga Deum, caritate perfecta, humilitate ac perseverantia in precibus, adeoque tum ad primum, tum ad secundum decalogi praeceptum per-


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: pertains. Furthermore, that the imitation of God and Christ was not unknown to…

...pertains. Furthermore, that the imitation of God and Christ was not unknown to the fathers and prophets, we learn from Lev. 11:44: "I am the Lord your God; you shall be holy, for I am holy." This is repeated in Matt. 5:48 and 1 Pet. 1:15. And lest anyone suppose that the imitation prescribed to the fathers was one thing, and the imitation prescribed to us of Christ is another, let him hear Paul in Eph. 5:1–2: "Therefore be imitators of God as dear children, and walk in love, as Christ also has loved us." (Exam. P. III. s. 2. c. 1. q. 38. p. 1019 sq.) See the antithesis of the Papists above, p. 105 sq.

Luther: "Many books and doctrines have been provided to instruct the life of men, so that there is neither number nor end to them, and there is still no ceasing to make books and laws, as we see in spiritual and secular laws and in spiritual orders and estates. And all that would still be tolerable and a special grace if such laws and doctrines were all drawn and handled according to the chief law, rule, and measure of love, as the Holy Scripture does, which also gives many and various laws, but draws and gathers them all into love, and subjects them all to love. So that they all must yield and no longer be law, nor count for anything, where love is concerned. We read very many examples of this in Scripture, and in particular Christ Himself cites in Matt. 12:3–5 how David and his companions ate the holy showbread. For although there was a law there that no one should eat such holy bread except the priests alone, yet love was here a free empress over that law and forced it under itself, so that at that time it had to yield and cease when David suffered hunger, and had to suffer such a judgment: David suffers hunger, one must help him, as love says: Do good to your neighbor where he needs it. Therefore, desist, you law, and do not hinder him from doing such good, but rather do the good to him yourself and serve him in his need, and do not catch me with your prohibitions. Likewise, he also says there that one should do good to the neighbor on the Sabbath who needs it, however much the law forbids doing anything on the Sabbath; but because there is a need to help the neighbor, love should take precedence and the Sabbath should count for nothing. Now, if the laws were thus drawn into love and were all mastered according to love, it would not matter how many of them there were. For whoever could not hear or learn them all could still hear and learn some, one or two, in which he would nevertheless learn the same love that is taught in all of them. And if he hears and learns them all: if he could not recognize love in all of them, he might yet recognize it in one law. St. Paul also gives this rule and way of mastering and understanding the laws here, when he says: 'Owe no one anything, except to love one another.' Item: 'He who loves another has fulfilled the law.' Item: 'All commandments are summed up in the commandment: Love your neighbor as yourself.' Item: 'Love does no evil to the neighbor.' Item: 'Love is the fulfillment of the law.' All the words of this epistle conclude and say that love is mistress over all laws. Conversely, where one teaches and drives the laws without love and outside of love, there is no greater misfortune, no greater injustice, no more miserable wretchedness on earth. For there the law is nothing else than a plague and ruin. There the proverb is true: 'Summum jus, summa injustitia,' the strictest right is the strictest injustice. And Solomon, Eccl. 7:16: 'Noli nimium esse justus,' be not overly righteous. Yes, there one lets the beam stick in one's own eye and does not recognize it, and goes about plucking the splinter out of one's neighbor's eye; there one makes dull, frightened, and despairing consciences without any need and [original]— PART III. CHAP. VII.

thing, and with great harm to body and soul. And great effort and labor occur there, and yet everything is lost. Let us prove this with examples. Where, in the aforementioned case, when David was hungry (1 Sam. 21:6), the priest had not wanted to give him the holy bread and had been so blind that he had insisted upon the law and had not recognized love, and had refused him the food, what would have come of it? As much as it depended on him, David would have had to die of hunger, and the priest would have committed murder for the sake of the law; there would then certainly be nothing other than *summum jus, summa injuria*—the strictest law, the greatest injustice.

Furthermore, if you look into the heart of such a mad priest, you find the horrible abomination that he creates sin and conscience where there is no sin and conscience; for he holds that it would be a sin to eat the bread, when it is actually love and a good work. Conversely, he considers murder to be no sin—that he would let David die of hunger—but rather a good work and service to God. But who can sufficiently recount such horrible, blind, perverted folly? For with such conduct he does so much evil that the devil could not do worse, namely, in that he creates sin and conscience where there is none, he takes away from man grace, salvation, virtue, and God with all His goods, and all that without cause and also falsely and deceitfully, whereby he denies and damns God through and through. Conversely, because he makes a good work and service to God out of murder and injustice, he sets the devil and lies in God’s place and establishes the highest idolatry that can be, and thus ruins body and soul, murders the body through hunger and the soul through conscience, makes a devil out of God and a God out of the devil, a hell out of heaven and a heaven out of hell, right out of sin, and sin out of right. That is what I call perverted, and the strictest law becoming the strictest injustice. . .

Thus, all kinds of laws should be given, ordained, and kept so that they are not kept for their own sake, nor for the sake of the works, but solely for the sake of the exercise of love; which is also the true meaning of the law, as St. Paul says here: "He who loves another has fulfilled the law"; so that, where one sees that it does not redound to the benefit of the neighbor, but to his harm, it should be omitted. For one and the same law can well be useful to the neighbor at one time, and harmful at another. . .

Thus it goes when one wants to govern people according to the law and work, and not the laws according to the people, just as the wagoner directs the path according to the wagon. Now, it is true that the path often fits nicely to the wagon, goes straight ahead, but then again it sometimes goes crooked and uneven; there it truly wants to have the wagon crooked and uneven to match itself. Thus it must indeed be that people fit themselves to the law and work where they can and it is good for them. But again, where it is harmful to them, the law should truly bend and give way, and the ruler be wise so that he leaves room for love and suspends the works and laws. (Epistolische Kirchenpostille. Opp. Hal. XII, 488–497.) §

20. The moral law was given for eternal life, but under the condition of perfect fulfillment. However, after the fall, no one can perform this, and therefore no one can be saved by the law.

Hence it is called ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ εἰς ζωήν (the commandment which was unto life), Rom. 7:10; ἡ ἐντολὴ ἁγία (the holy commandment), v. 12, 13. According to that saying: "Do this, and you shall live," Luke 10:28. And what is read in Gal. 3:12: "The man who does them shall live by them."

The Wittenberg Theologians: "Thus, there are also found elsewhere all sorts of questionable (dubious) phrases and assertions therein (in the writing of D. Gottfried Huber), as can easily be shown. For 1. he pretends in thesis 10 and 11, as if God had given the Law to man in the state of innocence so that he should attain eternal life by the fulfillment of the same, *ut praestando legi debitam obedientiam viverent* (that by rendering due obedience to the law they might live), as he speaks; and to this he draws the passages Lev. 18:5, Deut. 27:26, Col. 3:10; which, however, does not have the *τύπον ὑγιαινόντων λόγων* (pattern of sound words); for man was created for eternal life without this, and already had it *alio principio creationis* (by another principle of creation), so that it was not necessary to earn the same only by the fulfillment of the Law." (Censura, concerning Huber’s fanaticism, A. 1612. See Consil. Witeberg. I. f. 652. b.)

S. Schmidtius: "In the state of man’s integrity, there was no need for any rigorous merit for the acquisition of salvation, but the goodness or benignity of God could, by merit from a covenant alone, promise and give eternal life to man fulfilling His law and precepts. The reason for this matter is that the justice of God did not have to be satisfied there, since it had not yet been injured. Whereas, on the contrary, there was room for benignity where no rigorous merit was given, for the reason that man already owed everything to God, his Creator and Lord; whereas rigorous merit arises only from works that are not owed. Therefore, the benignity of God, with His justice in no way hindering, made a covenant with integral man, that if he fulfilled His law and precepts, he would be transferred into eternal life, even if he did not merit it by rigor. But in truth, in the state of the fall, the same room was not left for divine benignity, and that is because the offended justice of God intervenes, which must be satisfied. However, the offended justice of God cannot be satisfied except through rigorous merit... There is also a great difference between the persons meriting... For if we compare Christ with men, even integral ones, it must be said that every work of Christ, rendered to the divine law, is rigorously meritorious; but of man, even an integral one, no work rendered to the divine law is called rigorously meritorious. The reason for the former is: because every work of Christ rendered to the divine law is not owed and was undertaken voluntarily, and at the same time, because of the dignity of His person, it is of infinite value and price; moreover, man can perform nothing that is not already owed to God for another reason." (Articul. F. C. Repetit. 1696. p. 183. sq.)

et Christi non fuisse ignotam patribus et prophetis, discimus ex Lev. 11, 44.: ,Ego sum Dominus, Deus vester; sancti estote, quia ego sanctus sum.‘ Quod repetitur Matth. 5, 48. 1 Pet. 1, 15. Et ne quis opinetur, aliam esse Dei, patribus praescriptam, et aliam esse Christi, nobis praescriptam, imitationem, audiat Paulum Eph. 5, 1. 2.: ,Estote imitatores Dei, sicut liberi dilecti, et ambulate in dilectione, sicut etiam Christus dilexit nos.‘“ (Exam. P. III. s. 2. c. 1. q. 38. p. 1019. sq.) Vid. antithesis Pontificiorum supra p. 105. sq.

Lutherus: ,,Man hat viel Bücher und Lehre gegeben, der Mensehen Leben zu unterrichten, dass derselben weder Zahl noch Ende ist, und ist noch kein Aufhören, Bücher und Gesetze zu machen, wie wir sehen in geistlichen und weltlichen Rechten und geistlichen Orden und Ständen. Und wäre das alles noch zu leiden und eine sondere Gnade, wo solche Gesetze und Lehre alle würden gezogen und gehandelt nach dem Hauptgesetz, Regel und Mass der Liebe, wie die heilige Schrift thut, welche auch viel und mancherlei Gesetze gibt, aber allesammt in die Liebe zeucht und fasset, der Liebe auch dieselben alle unterwirft. Also, dass sie alle müssen weichen und nimmer Gesetz sein, noch etwas gelten, wo es die Liebe trifft. Dess lesen wir gar viel Exempel in der Schrift und sonderlich zeucht Christus selbst Matth. 12, 3. 4. 5. an, wie David mit seinen Gesellen die heiligen Schaubrote ass. Denn wiewohl daselbst ein Gesetz war, dass solche heilige Brote niemand sollte essen, ohne allein die Priester, so war doch die Liebe hier eine freie Kaiserin über dasselbe Gesetz und zwang es unter sich, dass es zu der Zeit musste weichen und aufhören, da David Hunger leidet, und musste ein solch Urtheil leiden: David leidet Hunger, dem soll man helfen, wie die Liebe spricht: Thue deinem Nächsten Gutes, wo ers bedarf. Darum lass ab, du Gesetz, und wehre ihm nicht, solch Gut zu thun, sondern selbst thue ihm das Gute und diene ihm in der Noth und fange mir ihn nicht mit deinem Verbieten. Item, also saget er auch daselbst, dass man am Sabbath solle Gutes thun dem Nächsten, der es bedarf, wie hoch auch das Gesetz verbeut, etwas zu thun am Sabbath; sondern weil da Noth ist dem Nächsten zu helfen, soll die Liebe vorgehen und der Sabbath nichts gelten. Wo nun die Gesetze also wären in die Liebe gezogen und würden alle nach der Liebe gemeistert, so läge nichts daran, wie viel ihrer wären. Denn wer sie nicht möchte alle hören oder lernen, der könnte doch etliche, eins oder zwei, hören und lernen, in welchen er doch dieselbe Liebe lernete, die in allen gelehret wird. Und wenn er sie alle höret und lernet: könnte er die Liebe nicht in allen erkennen, so möchte er doch dermaleins in einem Gesetz sie erkennen. Diese Regel und Weise, die Gesetze zu meistern und zu verstehen, gibt auch hier St. Paulus, da er spricht: ,Seid niemand nichts schuldig, ohne dass ihr euch unter einander liebet.‘ Item: ,Wer den andern liebet, hat das Gesetz erfüllet.‘ Item: ,Alle Gebote werden in dem Gebot verfasset: Liebe deinen Nächsten, als dich selber.‘ Item: ,Die Liebe thut dem Nächsten kein Böses.‘ Item: ,Die Liebe ist des Gesetzes Erfüllung.‘ Alle Worte dieser Epistel schliessen und sagen, dass die Liebe Meisterin sei über alle Gesetze. Wiederum, wo man die Gesetze lehret und treibt ohne Liebe und ausser der Liebe, da ist kein grösser Unglück, kein grösser Unrecht, kein elenderer Jammer auf Erden. Denn daselbst ist das Gesetz nichts anders, denn eine Plage und Verderben. Da ist das Sprüchwort wahr: ,Summum jus, summa injustitia‘, das strengste Recht ist das allerstrengste Unrecht. Und Salomon Pred. 7, 17.: ,Noli nimlum esse justus‘, sei nicht allzu streng gerecht. Ja, da lässt man den Balken in ünserm Auge stecken und kennen ihn nicht und gehen damit um, dass wir das Spänlein aus unsers Nächsten Auge reissen; da macht man blöde, erschrockene und verzagte Gewissen ohne alle Noth und UrPART. ΙΠ. CAP. VII.

sache, dazu mit grossem Schaden an Leib und Seele. Und geschieht allda' grosse Mühe und Arbeit, und ist doch alles verloren. Dass wir das mit Exempeln beweisen. Wo in dem obgesagten Fall, da David hungrig war (1 Sam. 21, 6.), der Priester ihm nicht hätte wollen die heiligen Brote geben und wäre so blind gewesen, dass er auf dem Gesetz gestanden wäre und die Liebe nicht erkennet und ihm die Speise versagt hätte, was wäre daraus worden? So viel, als an ihm gelegen wäre, hätte David musst Hungers sterben und hätte der Priester da einen Mord begangen um des Gesetzes willen; da wäre denn gewisslich nichts anders, denn summum jus, summa injustitia, das schärfeste Recht, das schärfeste Unrecht. '

Ueber das, wenn du in solches tollen Priesters Herz siehest, so findest du den greulichen Greuel, dass er Sünde und Gewissen machet, da keine Sünde und Gewissen ist; denn er hält, dass da Sünde wäre, das Brot zu essen, so es doch Liebe und ein gut Werk wäre. Wiederum hält er den Mord für keine Sünde, dass er David Hungers sterben liesse, sondern für ein gut Werk und Gottesdienst. Wer kann aber solche greuliche, blinde, verkehrte Thorheit genugsam erzählen? Denn mit solchem Handel thut er so übel, dass der Teufel nicht ärger thun könnte, nämlich damit, dass er Sünde machet und Gewissen, da keine ist, nimmt er dem Menschen weg Gnade, Heil, Tugend und Gott mit allen seinen Gütern, und das alles ohne Ursache und auch fälschlich und betrüglich, damit er Gott verleugnet und verdammt durch und durch. Wiederum, weil er ein gut Werk und Gottesdienst aus dem Mord und Unrecht machet, setzet er den Teufel und die Lügen an Gottes Statt und richtet die höchste Abgötterei an, die sein kann, und verderbet also Leib und Seele, mordet durch Hunger den Leib und durchs Gewissen ctie Seele, machet aus Gott einen Teufel und aus dem Teufel einen Gott, aus dem Himmel eine Hölle und aas der Hölle einen Himmel, aus Sünden Recht, aus Recht Sünden. Das heisset, meine ich, verkehret, und das schärfeste Recht das schärfeste Unrecht werden. . .

So sollten nun allerlei Gesetz dazu gegeben, verordnet und gehalten werden, dass sie nicht für sich selbst, noch um der Werke willen gehalten würden, sondern allein um Uebung willen der Liebe; welche auch ist die rechte Meinung des Gesetzes, wie hier St. Paulus sagt: ,Wer den andern liebet, hat das Gesetz erfüllet‘; also, dass, wo man sähe, dass es nicht zum Nutz des Nächsten gereichet, sondern zu Schaden, sollte es nachbleiben. Denn es kann wohl einerlei Gesetz auf eine Zeit dem Nächsten nütze, auf eine andere Zeit schädlich sein. . .

Also gehet es zu, wenn man die Leute nach dem Gesetz und Werk will regieren, und nicht die Gesetze nach den Leuten, eben wie der Fuhrmann den Weg nach dem Wagen richtet. Nun ist,s wahr, dass der Weg sich oft schicket fein nach dem Wagen, gehet stracks vor sich, aber wiederum gehet er zuweilen krumm und ungleich, da will er wahrlich den Wagen nach sich gekrümmet und ungleich haben. Also muss es ja sein, dass die Leute sich nach dem Gesetz und Werk schicken, wo sie können und ihnen gut ist. Aber wiederum, wo es ihnen schädlich ist, soll wahrlich das Gesetz sich beugen und weichen, und der Regierer klug sein, dass er der Liebe Raum lasse und die Werke und Gesetze auf hebe.“ (Epistolische Kirchenpostille. Opp. Hai. XII, 488—497.) §

S. Schmidtius: ,,In statu integritatis hominis ad acquisitionem salutis nullo rigoroso merito opus erat, sed bonitas seu benignitas Dei per meritum ex pacto tantum homini legem et praecepta ipsius implenti vitam aeternam promittere et dare poterat. Cujus rei ratio haec est, quod justitiae Dei ibi non satisfaciendum, quippe quae nondum laesa erat. Cum contra benignitati locus esset ibi, ubi meritum rigorosum nullum dabatur, ideo, quod homo Deo, creatori et domino suo, jamjam omnia debebat; cum vero meritum rigorosum non nisi ex operibus indebitis oriatur. Pactum itaque benignitas Dei, non impediente ullo modo justitia ejus, cum hoiniiie integro fecit, ut, si legem et praecepta ipsius impleret, iu vitam aeternam transferretur, etiamsi ex rigore eam non mereretur. Verum enimvero in statu lapsus non idem benignitati divinae locus relictus, idque propterea, quod offensa Dei justitia intercedit, cui satisfaciendum est. Offensae autem Dei justitiae satisfieri non potest, nisi per meritum rigorosum... Inter personas quoque merentes magnum discrimen est. . . Christum namque si cum hominibus etiam integris comparemus, dicendum est, quod omne Christi opus, legi divinae praestitum, sit rigorose meritorium; at hominis, etiam integri, nullum opus, legi divinae praestitum, dicitur rigorose meritorium. Ratio prioris est: quia omne opus Christi legi divinae praestitum est indebitum et sponte susceptum, simulque ob personae dignitatem infiniti valoris atque pretii est; nihil insuper homo operari potest, quod non prius ex alia ratione Deo sit debitum.“ (Articul. F. C. Repetit. 1696. p. 183. sq.)


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: For that rigor, by which exact obedience is demanded, and the natural impotence…

For that rigor, by which exact obedience is demanded, and the natural impotence contracted through the fall, with a habitual propensity toward evil, are mutually opposed to each other. Whence it is said that *τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός* (the mind of the flesh) is not subject to the law, nor can it be, Rom. 8:7. Cf. v. 3; ch. 7:15 sqq. But that the precepts of Christ are said not to be grievous, 1 John 5:3, that is not to be understood simply, or in respect to any men whatsoever, but in respect to the faithful, who, by the powers granted by Christ, do not work grudgingly, and whose imperfect obedience, because of the perfect obedience of Christ, apprehended by faith and imputed by God, is accepted as if it were perfect, so that they are not oppressed by the burden of the precepts. Cf. Mus. Tract. contra Stenger. Part. III. cap. VI. p. 588.

Kromayerus: "The Law in this life after the fall is impossible for us to fulfill... (Which) thesis we build upon the following foundations, and 1. because— PART III. CAP. VII. ...to the saying of Peter in the apostolic council, Acts 15:10: "Why do you tempt God, by putting a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?" Where the controversy was not only about the ceremonial law, but the entire Mosaic law. Nor is the ceremonial law a burden impossible to bear, but only difficult. 2. The passage Acts 13:38: "Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man (Christ) is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: and by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses." If we cannot be justified by the law, then it certainly cannot be fulfilled by us in this life. 3. The passage Rom. 8:3-4: "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh" (i.e., on account of the infirmities assumed) "and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh: that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us," namely, by believing in Christ, who is the τέλος, that is, the τελείωσις, the perfection of the law. Rom. 10:4. Whence a new argument arises for us: If the perfection of the law is to be sought in Christ through faith, it follows that the law is impossible for us to fulfill. Truly, the exception is quite insipid, that Christ merited for us the fulfillment of the law, so that we might fulfill it by our own works. For as often as the fulfillment of the law is denied to us, even though we are regenerate, so often is this figment struck down as if by a lightning bolt. 4. The passage Rom. 3:20 and Gal. 2:16: "That by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified." This the apostle, a good analyst, undoubtedly took from Ps. 143:2, where David, regenerate, declining the tribunal of God, says that "no man living shall be justified in his sight." 5. The passage Gal. 2:21: "If righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain." 6. The passage Gal. 3:21: "If there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law. But the Scripture hath concluded all" (all our powers and actions) "under sin." Now, if we cannot have life from the law, it also cannot be fulfilled by us. "For whosoever shall do these things shall live in them," Gal. 3: 12. We do not deny that the law, as the word of God, is life-giving; but that it does not give us life in the state of transgression happens accidentally, on account of the intimate and most profound corruption of our nature. Wherefore spiritual life is to be sought by us from faith, according to that of Habakkuk 2:4: "The just shall live by his faith," which is repeated several times in the N.T., Rom. 1:17, Gal. 3:11, Heb. 10:38. 7. The passage Rom. 7:14: "That the law is spiritual," but regenerate men, such as the apostle Paul was, are "carnal, sold under sin." For in those in whom there is σαρκοπνευματομαχία, they are still in part carnal, namely, as regards the sense of sin and the first motions of concupiscence. Now, those who have concupiscence cannot fulfill the law. 8. The passage Luke 10:27, that we cannot love God with all our heart, on account of the remnants of the flesh, by which that love is contaminated. Where we can by no means admit the explanation of the Papists, that to love God above all things is to love God principally. For the "whole" is that which has all its parts and to which nothing is lacking. Nor is that particle repeated so often in vain: "With all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind," but that the πηναρμονία (perfect harmony) of all our faculties and powers might be indicated. 9. The passage Rom. 7:19, that the regenerate "cannot fulfill the good that they will," and therefore acknowledge themselves to be miserable. 10. The passage Gal. 3:10 and James 2:10, 3:2, that perseverance in all the precepts of the law is required, so that the continuous tenor of observance is not disturbed by even one little thought against the law, and "whosoever shall offend in one point, he is guilty of all." (Th. posit. pol. I, 766 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Scholastics, who teach that the fulfillment of the law is possible through the powers of free will alone; thus Gabriel Biel in 2 Sent. dist. 28, qu. un. a. 3, and 1 Sent. dist. 3, qu. 2, a. 3, and 3 Sent. dist. 27, qu. un. a. 3. 2. Of the Papists, that the perfect fulfillment of the law does not exceed the powers of a regenerate man, and therefore that a regenerate man, aided by the grace of God, can perfectly fulfill the moral law, sta-"

defenders. Thus the Council of Trent, sess. 6, c. 18: "If anyone shall say that the commandments of God are impossible to observe for a man who is even justified and placed under grace, let him be anathema." Bellarmine, bk. 3, *de R. Pontif.*, c. 23, antithesis 6, says: "We do not fear to assert that a man justified by the grace of God can, by the aid of that same grace, both fulfill the law and by that fulfillment merit eternal life." The same is maintained in bk. 2, *de monachis*, c. 13, and bk. 4, *de justif.*, c. 10, and the three following chapters. Costerus in *Enchir.*, p. 244; Alphonsus de Castro, *adv. Haeres.*, bk. 2, under the word "Praeceptum," heresy 4; Lindanus, *Panopliae*, bk. 3, c. 19; Dominicus a Soto, *de nat. et grat.*, bk. 3. 3. 4

The Socinians, who likewise assert that the perfect fulfillment of the law is possible in this life. Thus Socinus in his *Libro Suasorio*, p. 60, c. 11, where he affirms it to be probable that a man, aided by the Spirit of God or supported by the help of God, can perfectly obey the law of God. Thus also the *Catechism. Racov.*, p. 289. 4

The Arminians, who also imagine that there are perfect and "adult," as they call them, persons among the regenerate; see Arminius in *resp. ad 31. a.*, p. 164, and *ad a. 9.*, p. 176; the *Apology of the Remonstrants*, c. 10 and 11 Vorstius in *Apol. Exeg.*, pp. 111, 112. 6

The Weigelians, who contend that the law can be fulfilled; see Weigel, Part 2, post., p. 240. 6 The Anabaptists, who boast of the perfection of good works in this life and call the sins of the saints "slight little faults and blemishes, not in themselves staining, but lightly bedewing the Christian life like a very thin rain"; in the *Confession* opposed to Faukel, pp. 210 sq., and *Protoc. Embd.*, Act. 68. 7 The Labadists, who contend that the law can be perfectly fulfilled by the regenerate; thus with Labadie in *Protestatione*, pp. 58, 62; Schurmannia, *ενκληρ.*, pp. 64, 121, 129, 201; in *Declar. Fidei*, p. 93 sq. (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 984.) Thus it is said in Gal. 3:21: "There is no law given which could give life." And in Rom. 7:10 sqq., Paul says that the commandment which was given for life resulted in death for him, etc. § 21. The Gospel, properly speaking, is the doctrine of the grace of God and the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ the Mediator and His merit apprehended by faith, which was revealed in its own way not only in the New Testament but also in the Old Testament. a In opposition to the law and favored by the etymology itself. For by the force of the name it denotes "good news." Thus it is said in Matt. 11:5 that the gospel is preached to the poor. b Or a complex of promises which are pleasing, joyful, and salutary to sinful men; the sum of which is held in John 3:16. c That is, of the gratuitous favor, love, and mercy with which God pursues men, though they be sinners, and is intent upon procuring their salvation. See 1 Tim. 2:4. d In which we taught in Part III, chap. V, § 11 and 14, that the justification of a sinful man consists, and from which peace with God, adoption as sons of God, etc., flow. Cf. Rom. 3:21 sqq., where it is declared that without the law (and thus through the gospel) the righteousness of God (or that by which we are constituted righteous before God) has been manifested. PART III. CHAPTER VII.

Let the voice of the angel to Joseph in Matt. 1:21 be noted: "He shall save his people from their sins"; to Mary in Luke 1:31 ff.: "You shall call his name Jesus," etc.; to the shepherds in ch. 2:10, 11: "There is born to you this day a Savior." Cf. Acts 4:12: "There is no salvation in any other," etc. John 1:12, 14, 16, 18, 29, 36 concerning the ἐξουσία of believers as children of God, and concerning grace to be received from his fullness, etc. Whence the gospel itself is called the law of faith in Rom. 3:27, and the phrase πιστεύειν εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον arises, Mark 1:15.

Which is evident from the passages cited thus far.

For here pertain the promises concerning the seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the serpent, whose heel the serpent would meanwhile crush; that is, concerning the one to come from the posterity of Eve, a true man, who by his own greater power—which is truly divine—would destroy the kingdom and power of Satan (who, through the serpent, persuaded man to sin and thereby plunged men into death and held them reduced to his power), yet not without passion or blood, and would liberate the human race, Gen. 3:15; concerning the seed of Abraham, in whom all the nations of the earth are to be blessed (with every spiritual blessing to be bestowed through faith in him), Gen. 12:3, ch. 15:6, ch. 22:18; concerning the Messiah, Shiloh, to be born from the tribe of Judah, to whom the nations would adhere, Gen. 49:10; concerning the prophet like Moses, Deut. 18:15, 18. Cf. what is contained in the Psalms, 2, 8, 22, 16, 18, 68, 110, and in Isaiah ch. 7:14, ch. 53:4 ff., ch. 61:1 ff., in Jeremiah ch. 23:5, ch. 33:15, Daniel ch. 9:24, Hosea ch. 13:14, Micah ch. 5:2, Haggai 2:8, Zechariah 9:9, ch. 13:1, Malachi 1:11, ch. 3:1, ch. 4:2. And it is certain that those things which were contained in the ceremonial laws, even if they had the force of law insofar as they commanded certain actions and rites, were nevertheless rightly reckoned as gospel insofar as they represented Christ the mediator and his merit, which was to be embraced by faith, through certain rites, as if by types or shadows.
