### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Disputatio contra Curcellaeum de salute gentilium*, §…

Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Disputatio contra Curcellaeum de salute gentilium*, § 46, 47. For although there is one and the same gospel in the Old and New Testaments, yet the evangelical promises were from time to time more clearly exposed and illustrated, until at length the full light arose in the New Testament.

Isaiah certainly had as much light of knowledge as we can observe in any of his predecessors. Indeed, with respect to the light of the New Testament, the doctrine concerning the Messiah in the Old Testament is compared to night and darkness, namely κατὰ σύγκρισιν; for it was covered by figures and shadows, from whose wrappings, once removed, the most clear radiance of knowledge shone forth in the New Testament, which is therefore compared to the day: these are the words of the blessed Gerhardt, *Loci de Evangelio*, § 37.

Quenstedtius: "A divine testament, as it is distinguished from the Old and New, is nothing other than the most free disposition of the will of God concerning divine worship, the means of salvation, and the form of the government of the church, confirmed and sealed by blood and death—either by a typical animal or by the testator himself—by which God promises his goods to men and confers them through certain symbols, while men in turn bind themselves to render to God the faith and worship prescribed by him, to the praise of divine grace and justice and for the salvation of men... The term 'Old Testament' is taken: 1. in the common usage of speaking, systematically or dogmatically, for the sacred canonical books consigned before the coming of Christ in the flesh, or for the writings of Moses and the prophets, or for the doctrine contained in them, to which is usually referred..."

that of Paul, 2 Cor. 3:14: "Until this very day the same veil remains unlifted in the reading of the παλαιάς διαθήκης, the Old Testament (which is abolished in Christ)." By the O.T. are understood the books of Moses, says Grotius in his notes to this passage, the most important part of which is the Sinaitic covenant. And the blessed Aeg. Hunnius on this passage: "In the reading of the O.T., namely, of the writings of Moses and the prophets, just as they read them not only publicly every Sabbath, but also privately at home, Acts 15:21."

2. The O.T. is accepted in a sense and meaning not indeed of Scripture, but common among ecclesiastical writers, chronologically, for the state of the church from the beginning of the world until the advent of the Messiah in the flesh. In which sense the patriarchs, Moses, and the prophets are said to have lived under the O.T. But that chronology does not properly effect a distinction between the O.T. and N.T. And that statement, that the fathers lived under the O.T., is spoken ambiguously; for it either denotes that those who lived before Christ was born had only the legal covenant, and were destitute of the evangelical or the goods of the N.T.; or that they lived while only the promises and types concerning the Messiah were still in force, with the fulfillment and the body still to come. The former sense is false, as will appear from what follows; the latter can be admitted.

3. Federally, for that solemn economy or dispensation of the Jewish religion and polity made on Mount Sinai. Briefly, the term O.T. is taken 1. for the code and federal tables or canonical books written at that time. 2. Broadly, for the time preceding the fulfillment of the N.T. 3. Properly, for that legal covenant entered into with the Israelites. And this third meaning is that of this passage.

In this sense it is also taken in Jer. 31:31, 32: "I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, not according to the covenant that I made with your fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt." In this passage 1. the prophet opposes the N.T. or the fact to the former or old one, as is evident from Heb. 8:7 sq. and 9:15, 18, where the difference between both testaments is confirmed from this prophecy. 2. He testifies that the old covenant was entered into and promulgated after the exodus from Egypt, namely, on Mount Sinai. 3. It is added that the Jews made this old covenant void, namely, through frequent idolatry and rebellion.

Likewise Gal. 4:24, where Paul says: "There are two testaments: one testament is from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery," etc.

This Sinaitic O.T. differs from the most ancient legal covenant sanctioned with Adam before the fall, because the latter was not struck under a testamentary form (which includes the death of the testator, whether in type or in truth), nor with a vicarious end looking toward grace. For in the divine covenant before the fall, there was no place for Christ the Mediator, nor for the remission of sins to be obtained through Him, because no sin yet existed there. Cf. the blessed Chemnitz, Part 3, Loci Communes, Locus on the O. and N.T. and their distinction, pp. 86 and 90.

Moreover, the O.T. is called in the Scriptures διαθήκη πρώτη, Heb. 8:7, παλαιά, 2 Cor. 3:14. (L. c. c. 7. s. 1. th. 9.11. f. 1301. sq.)

WINCKELMANN: "The O.T. is properly the covenant of the law entered into on Mount Sinai between God and the Israelites with Moses as mediator, by which He promised the people blessing, bodily goods, and eternal life on the condition that they perfectly keep the law given, but on the contrary threatened punishments and temporal and eternal curses to all who transgressed the law, dedicated and confirmed by the blood of bulls and calves." (Disput. Giess. P. IV. disp. 18. th. 16. p. 407.)

Quenstedt: "The term New Testament is accepted: 1. Systematically or dogmatically for the books of the evangelists and apostles or for the doctrine contained in their writings. 2. Chronologically for the whole state of the church from the birth of Christ until the end of the world. 3. Federally, and thus it is taken either for that covenant of grace or evangelical covenant, which was sanctioned by God immediately after the fall in paradise with our first parents and then with the fathers, and finally confirmed, established, and consummated through the advent of the Messiah in the flesh and His actual and sacrificial satisfaction and death; or for that new and solemn disposition and dispensation of heavenly doctrine first revealed through Christ and afterwards promulgated through the ministry of the apostles throughout the whole world." PART. III. CAP. VII.

which Christ sealed with His own blood on the altar of the cross, and which is the peculiar ταμεῖον [treasury] of our salvation. And in this latter signification, the term New Testament is accepted by us here, and is called in Scripture ברית חדשה, a new covenant (Jer. 31:31), διαθήκη κρείττων, a better testament (Heb. 7:22; 8:6) (in comparison to the Old Testament), of which Christ Himself has been made ἔγγυος, a sponsor (Heb. 7:22), and μεσίτης, a mediator (Heb. 5:6; 9:15; 12:24), and the apostles, ministers (2 Cor. 3:6). It is called καινή [new] (ibid. and Heb. 9:15), δεύτερα [second] (Heb. 8:7), ἁγία [holy] (Luke 1:72), νέα [new] (Heb. 12:24), αἰώνιος [eternal] (Heb. 13:20), because it had its confirmation in Him who offered Himself through the eternal Spirit and found αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν, eternal redemption (Heb. 9:12, 14).

It is called the New Testament peculiarly: 1. Because it made the former inveterate and, as it were, antiquated (Heb. 8:13). 2. Because it pertains to the new man, just as the old pertains to the old man, according to Augustine (lib. contra Adimantum Manich. c. 16). 3. Because it is always to endure and will not have another succeeding it, as the old did; or it is called new as if it were the last. Especially 4. in opposition to: a. the most ancient and first of all legal covenants, which preceded in time the προτευαγγέλων [protoevangelium] (Gen. 3:15); β. the Mosaic legal covenant, which is called the New Testament to the extent that it long preceded in time the public promulgation of the Gospel concerning Christ sent in the flesh (Jer. 31:32, 33); then also γ. with respect to the evangelical covenant of the old economy, which flourished in the Abrahamic and Israelitic Old Testament church. (L. c. c. 7. s. 1. th. 21. f. 1309. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis:

1. Of the Pelagians, who maintain that men before Moses were justified and saved by the law of nature alone, after Moses by the law of Moses alone, and in the New Testament by the evangelical law; see Augustine (l. 1. contra duas epist. Pelagii c. 1). The Scholastics, who for this reason are called naturalists, Pelagianize in this part, as in many others.

2. Of the Socinians, who affirm that the Gospel, or the preaching concerning the gratuitous remission of sins through faith in Christ, began first with Christ manifested in the flesh; and that it is proper to the New Testament alone; and that justification and salvation through faith in Christ had no place in the Old Testament. Thus Catechism. Racov. p. 231; Socinus (l. Suasorio c. 5. p. 60).

3. Of the Arminians, who in Conf. c. 10. p. 21. and in Conf. Apol. c. 7. f. 157 say: 'It is certain,' they assert, 'that the precept of faith in Christ nowhere clearly appears handed down in the Old Testament, just as the promise of eternal life does not appear in those terms.'

4. Of the Anabaptists, who assert that the patriarchs in the Old Testament knew nothing of the Gospel and the promises of eternal life, and that we are saved in one way in the Old Testament and in another way today; see their Confession opposed to Faukelio, p. 43—48." (L. c. c. 2. s. 2. q. 1. f. 1014. sq.) §

22. The Law and the Gospel therefore agree I. regarding the author, who is God on both sides; II. regarding the subject to whom they are given, which is all human beings; III. regarding the end intended by itself, which is eternal salvation on both sides; IV. regarding the term of duration, which is the end of the world. For both are the Word of God, as is evident from what has been said. We speak, however, of the moral law, given to all, by which they are obligated to obedience; but the Gospel itself, destined for the good of all, [was revealed] at different times, especially regarding those more significant periods: 1.) in Adam, 2.) in Noah, 3.) through the Israelitic church in the whole

illustrious throughout the world, 4.) through the apostles filling the whole world with their preaching, Matt. 28:19, Mark 16:15, Rom. 10:18, it has come to the whole human race. V. b. Mus. Disp. against Curcell. § 37 sqq. Concerning the law, it was spoken of in § 20, note a. Concerning the gospel, the matter is even more manifest, and the passage Rom. 1:16 is to be noted, where the gospel is called the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. But it is by accident that the law results in death according to Rom. 7:10 sqq., and that the gospel becomes to some a savor of death unto death, 2 Cor. 2:16. Conf. 1 Cor. 1:18 sqq. Thus, we have said in § 18 and note f that the moral law is perpetual, and not abrogated or to be abrogated.

### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: But that the gospel is to be preached until the end of the world is expressly…

But that the gospel is to be preached until the end of the world is expressly stated in Matt. last, last verse. § 28. The law and the gospel differ 1. in the mode of manifestation and cognition. For the law is known by nature a even after the fall b in a certain way; but the gospel is a mystery, to be known only by supernatural revelation c. 2. By reason of the object. For the law is concerned with things to be done and omitted d; the gospel delivers gratuitous promises e to be embraced by faith. 3. By the diversity of the promises. For the promises of the law f are compensatory, those of the gospel are altogether gratuitous g. 4. By the diversity of office. For the law prescribes h perfect obedience, and accuses, terrifies, i and condemns all delinquents, but does not confer new powers k for a spiritual and holy life; but the gospel neither commands l works, nor reproves m sinners, but shows n the mediator, consoles, and promises grace and salvation.

Whence 5. the law is to be proposed to secure sinners, o so that they may be led to contrition, the gospel to the contrite, p so that they may conceive faith. Luther: "Here I pray and exhort all lovers of godliness, and especially those who in time are to teach other people, that they learn with all diligence from St. Paul’s writings this article, which teaches what the right and proper work of the law is, and how one ought to use it rightly; which, as I greatly fear, will after our times again be darkened and altogether suppressed. For even now, while we are still alive and most diligently point out what both the law and the gospel, each in particular, serve for, there are very, very few, even among those who profess the gospel and know how to boast of it most gloriously, who rightly and properly understand and know such office of the law. What do you think will happen when we have now laid down our heads? I will not now speak of the Anabaptists, the new Arians, and the enthusiast spirits, who blaspheme and profane the holy sacrament of the body and blood of our dear Lord Jesus Christ, all of whom [are] upon one..." Baier’s Comp. ed. Walther.

III. 25 PART III. CHAP. VII. the masses understand or know as little what the proper work of the Law is and what it serves, as the Papists themselves, even if they let themselves be heard otherwise with many words; for they have long since fallen away from the pure doctrine of the Gospel back to the doctrine of the Law; therefore, they also do not teach Christ. They do indeed do this, that they boast with a great outcry and may even swear dearly to it, that they teach nothing else and seek or intend nothing else with their doctrine than God’s honor, the salvation of the brethren, and that God’s Word might be spread and preserved pure and unadulterated; but when one wants to examine it in the light and at the foundation, one finds that they falsify God’s Word and pervert it into an erroneous misunderstanding, so that it must sound and signify to them whatever they dream and want according to their own pleasure. Therefore, under the name of Christ they teach their own dreams, and under the name of the Gospel, vain laws and ceremonies, thus remaining always one way or the other, as they have been from the beginning, namely, monks, work-righteous, teachers of the Law and of ceremonies, except that they invent new names and also other or new works for their essence. . .

Therefore, the Law is also a light that shines there and makes visible and manifest, not God’s grace, nor the righteousness by which one attains life, but sin, death, God’s wrath, and judgment. For just as it was in the minds of the children of Israel when they stood at the foot of Mount Sinai and heard the cruel thundering, saw the lightning, the black, dark clouds, the mountain burning and smoking, and whatever other terrible things happened there, which was certainly no pleasant or joyful spectacle for them, but rather terrified them, indeed, caused them to nearly die from great fear, and taught them how they could not stand before God with all their holiness and uprightness, nor hear His voice, which was nevertheless of the most friendly and comforting sort, namely: "I, the Lord, thy God," etc.: so it is also in the minds of all hypocrites when the Law begins to carry out its own work or office, that is, to reveal sin, to stir up wrath, to accuse the consciences, to terrify them, and to drive them into despair.

That is the Law’s own and proper work, with which it should rest and proceed no further. The Gospel, however, is a very different light, namely, one that illuminates, enlivens, comforts, and helps up the terrified hearts. For it indicates how God is gracious to the unworthy and condemned sinners for Christ’s sake, when they believe that they are redeemed from the curse through His death, that is, from sin and eternal death, and that through His victory and overcoming, the blessing is gifted to them, that is, grace, forgiveness of sins, righteousness, and eternal life.

When we distinguish the Law and the Gospel in such a way, we give to each its right, proper, and due work and office that belongs to it. But of such a distinction between the Law and the Gospel, you will not find a single letter in all the books of all the monks, canonists, and sophists, indeed, not even in those of the ancient Fathers. St. Augustine understood and indicated this distinction in part, but Jerome and others knew little of it. In sum, for several hundred years now, nothing upright has been taught or preached in all schools and churches regarding such a distinction between the Law and the Gospel, whereby the poor, miserable consciences have come into great danger and harm." (Detailed Explanation of the Ep. to the Gal. A. 1535. Opp. Hal. VIII, 2257—60.)

The same: "Some imagine that they understand these things very well; but you must guard yourselves against presumption and remember that you remain students of the Word. For Satan is such a master that he can very easily abolish the distinction and foist upon us the Law instead of the Gospel, and again the Gospel instead of the Law. How often does it happen to people in

in the final throes of death, that poor consciences seize upon certain evangelical sayings which, however, actually belong to the Law, and thus lose the comfort of the Gospel? Such as this saying in Matthew 19:17: "If you want to enter into life, keep the commandments of God"; likewise also this one in Matthew 7:21: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven." Through these and similar sayings, hearts are often made so confused that they see nothing but only what they have done and what they ought to have done, likewise what God demands and forbids. When hearts look upon such things, they forget everything that Christ has done and that God has promised to do through Christ. Therefore, let no one presume as if he had attained perfection. In words, one can easily make the distinction, but in death and in danger, one finds what poor dialecticians we are when a disputation arises concerning what we have done and what we ought to do, when the Law accuses us: "This God commanded you to do, but you have not done it, but rather the opposite; therefore you must be damned, according to the saying of your Lawgiver in Deuteronomy 27:26." Whoever is a skillful dialectician here makes a distinction between the Law and the Gospel and admits that he has not kept the Law, but answers that it does not follow from the foregoing that I should therefore despair and must be damned; for the Gospel means to believe in the Lord Christ and to build upon the works and righteousness of the Lord Christ." (Exposition on the 15 Psalms in the Higher Choir, A.D. 1532. Ps. 181, 1. Tom. IV, 2881 sq.)

Chemnitius: "What other light dispelled the densest darkness of the pontifical kingdom, if not this one especially, that the true distinction between the Law and the Gospel was demonstrated?" (Loc. th. II. De justif. f. 206. b.) Cf. what is noted above at § 2.

Gerhardus: "The reasons why that distinction must be accurately established and strictly maintained are many. 1. The integrity of the article of justification will not stand, nay, it cannot stand, if the distinction of these doctrines is neglected, which the ecclesiastical history of former times proves more than enough. 2. The benefits of Christ are not insignificantly obscured unless the doctrine of the Gospel is separated from the Law by accurate boundaries. 3. The confusion of the Law and the Gospel necessarily brings with it perturbations of consciences, since in great and serious terrors of conscience no true and solid consolation remains, if the gratuitous promises of the Gospel are adulterated. Wherefore, since these two are established as the chief heads of the whole Christian doctrine, to which all other things can be referred in a certain manner and order, not undeservedly does the Apostle, among the virtues which he requires in a faithful minister of the church, assign the first place to the art of ὀρθοτομεῖν, rightly dividing the word of truth, 2 Tim. 2: 15. They posit the metaphor as drawn from the office of the Levitical priests in the O.T., whose duty it was to rightly cut and divide the flesh of the sacrifices. Some think the metaphor is drawn from the arrangers of banquets, because the ministers of the church in the N.T. are, as it were, arrangers of a spiritual banquet. Isa. 25:6." (Loc. de ev. § 52.)

The same: "Although the distinction between the Law and the Gospel is to be retained everywhere, yet it must be observed especially: 1. In the article of justification, since our justification is not from the Law, to which, on account of the corruption and infirmity of our flesh, a certain ἀδυναμία is attributed, though accidentally, in this part, Rom. 8:3, but from the Gospel, in which the righteousness of God is revealed without the Law, Rom. 3:21, which is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, Rom. 1:16. Men are therefore to be admonished, nay, urged, to perform works according to the norm of the Law, but they are not to be brought into the theater of our justification before God; for there is a perpetual opposition between working and believing, between grace and works, between the Law and the Gospel. 2. In the use of the ecclesiastical keys. To the impenitent and... PART III. CHAP. VII.

Lex enim natura nota a est etiam post lapsum b quodammodo; evangelium autem mysterium est, sola revelatione c supernaturali cognoscendum. 2. Ratione objecti. Lex enim circa agenda et omittenda d versatur; evangelium promissiones e gratuitas fide amplectendas tradit. 3. Promissionum diversitate. Legis enim promissiones f compensatoriae, evangelii prorsus gratuitae g sunt. 4. Diversitate officii. Lex enim praescribit h perfectam obedientiam, et delinquentes quosvis accusat, terret,1 damnat, non autem confert novas vires k ad vitam spiritualem et sanctam; evangelium autem nec mandat1 opera, nec arguitm peccatores, sed n mediatorem ostendit, solatur, promittit gratiam et salutem. Unde 5. lex proponenda est peccatoribus securis,o ut ad contritionem perducantur, evangelium contritis,p ut fidem concipiant.

Luthertjs: ,,Hier bitte ich und ermahne ich alle Liebhaber der Gottseligkeit und sonderlich die, so mit der Zeit andere Leute lehren sollen, dass sie diesen Artikel, der da lehrt, was des Gesetzes rechtes und eigenes Werk sei, und wie man sein recht brauchen soll, aus St. Pauli Schriften mit allem Fleiss wohl lernen, welcher, wie ich grosse Sorge habe, nach unsern Zeiten wiederum wird verdunkelt und ganz und gar unterdrückt werden. Denn auch jetzund bereitan, da wir noch im Leben sind und aufs allerfleissigste anzeigen, wozu beide, das Gesetz und Evangelium, ein jedes insonderheit diene, ihrer sehr, sehr wenig sind auch unter denen, so sich zum Evangelio bekennen und gar herrlich davon zu rühmen wissen, die solches Amt des Gesetzes recht und eigentlich verstehen und wissen. Was meint ihr, dass werden wird, wenn wir nun das Haupt gelegt haben? Ich will jetzt der Wiedertäufer, der neuen Arianer und der Schwärmergeister, so das heilige Sacrament des Leibes und Blutes unsers lieben Herrn Jesu Christi lästern und schänden, geschweigen, welche allesammt auf einen Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. ΠΙ.25 PART. III. CAP. VII.

Haufen ja so wenig verstehen oder wissen, was des Gesetzes eigen Werk sei und wozu es diene, als die Papisten selbst, ob sie sich mit viel Worten wohl anders vernehmen lassen; denn sie sind vorlängst von der reinen Lehre des Evangelii zurückgefallen auf des Gesetzes Lehre; darum lehren sie auch nicht Christum. Das thun sie wohl, dass sie mit grossem Geschrei rühmen und dürfen auch wohl theuer dazu schwören, dass sie nichts anders lehren und mit ihrer Lehre nichts anders suchen, noch meinen, denn Gottes Ehre, der Brüder Heil und dass Gottes Wort möge rein und lauter ausgebreitet und erhalten werden; aber wenn mans beim Licht und im Grunde besehen will, so befindet man, dass sie Gottes Wort fälschen und verkehren in einen irrigen Missverstand, dass es ihnen lauten und deuten muss, was sie träumen und wollen ihres Gefallens. Darum lehren sie unter Christi Namen ihre eigenen Träume, unter dem Namen des Evangelii eitel Gesetze und Ceremonien, bleiben also immerhin einen Weg wie den andern, wie sie von Anfang je und je gewesen sind, nämlich, Mönche, Werkheilige, des Gesetzes und der Ceremonien Lehrer, ohne dass sie ihrem Wesen neue Namen und auch andere oder neue Werke erdichten. . .

Derhalben ist das Gesetz auch ein Licht, das da leuchtet und sichtbar und offenbar macht, nicht Gottes Gnade, auch nicht die Gerechtigkeit, dadurch man das Leben erlangt, sondern die Sünde, den Tod, Gottes Zorn und Gericht. Denn gleichwie den Kindern Israel zu Sinne war, da sie unten am Berge Sinai stunden und hörten das grausame Donnern, sahen das Blitzen, die schwarzen finstern Wolken, den Berg brennen und rauchen, und was schreckliche Dinge sonst mehr da geschahen, das ihnen freilich kein lustig noch fröhlich Schauspiel war, sondern erschreckte sie vielmehr, ja, machte, dass sie vor grösser Angst schier gestorben wären, und lehrte sie, wie sie mit aller ihrer Heiligkeit und Beinigkeit vor Gott nicht bestehen könnten, noch seine Stimme hören, die doch aufs allerfreundlichste und tröstlichste war, nämlich: ,Ich, der Herr, dein Gott‘ u. s. w.: also ist auch allen Heuchlern zu Sinne, wenn das Gesetz sein eigen Werk oder Amt beginnt auszurichten, das ist, die Sünde offenbaren, Zorn anrichten, die Gewissen verklagen, sie schrecken und in Verzweiflung treiben.

Das ist des Gesetzes eigen und recht Werk, dabei es bewenden und weiter nicht schreiten soll. Das Evangelium aber ist viel ein ander Licht, nämlich, das die erschreckten Herzen erleuchtet, lebendig macht, tröstet und ihnen aufhilft. Denn es zeigt an, wie Gott den unwürdigen und verdammten Sündern gnädig sei um Christi willen, wenn sie gläuben, dass sie durch seinen Tod vom Fluch, das ist, von der Sünde und ewigem Tod erlöst sein, und dass ihnen durch seinen Sieg und Ueberwindung geschenkt sei der Segen, das ist, Gnade, Vergebung der Sünden, Gerechtigkeit und ewiges Leben.

Wenn wir das Gesetz und Evangelium auf solche Weise unterscheiden, so geben wir einem jeden sein recht eigen und gebührlich Werk und Amt, das ihm zusteht. Aber von solchem Unterschied des Gesetzes und des Evangelii findest du nicht einen einigen Buchstaben in allen Büchern aller Mönche, Canonisten und Sophisten, ja, auch der alten Väter dazu. St. Augustinus hat diesen Unterschied zum Theil verstanden und angezeigt, Hieronymus aber und andere mehr haben wenig davon gewusst. Summa, es ist in allen Schulen und Kirchen etliche hundert Jahre daher nichts Rechtschaffenes von solchem Unterschied des Gesetzes und des Evangelii gelehrt oder gepredigt worden, dadurch denn die armen, elenden Gewissen in grosse Gefahr und Schaden kommen sind.“ (Ausführliehe Erkl. der Ep. an die Gal. A. 1535. Opp. Hal. VIII, 2257—60.)

Idem: ,,Etliche lassen sich bedünken, sie verstehen diese Dinge sehr wohl; ihr aber sollt euch vor der Vermessenheit hüten und gedenken, dass ihr Schüler des Wortes bleibt. Denn der Satan ist ein solcher Meister, dass er den Unterschied sehr leichtlich aufheben und anstatt des Evangelii das Gesetz, wiederum anstatt des Gesetzes das Evangelium uns eindringen kann. Wie oft begegnet es den Leuten in

den letzten Todeszügen, dass die armen Gewissen etliche evangelische Sprüche ergreifen, welche doch eigentlich zum Gesetz gehören, und also den Trost des Evangelii verlieren? Wie dieser Spruch Matth. 19, 17.: ,Willst du ins Leben gehen, so halte die Gebote Gottes‘; desgleichen auch dieser Matth. 7, 21.: ,Nicht ein jeder, der zu mir spricht: Herr, Herr, wird in das Himmelreich gehen.‘ Durch die und dergleichen Sprüche werden die Herzen oftmals so irre gemacht, dass sie nicht sehen, denn nur allein was sie gethan haben und hätten thun sollen, item was Gott fordert und verbeut. Wenn die Herzen solches anschauen, vergessen sie alles dess, was Christus gethan und Gott verheissen hat durch Christum zu thun. Derohalben soll sich niemand vermessen, als hätte er Wiehes vollkömmlich erlangt. Mit Worten kann man den Unterschied leichtlich machen, aber im Tode und in der Gefahr befindet man, wie böse Dialectici wir sind, wenn eine Disputation einfällt von dem, was wir gethan haben und thun sollen, wenn uns das Gesetz vorwirft, das hat dir Gott befohlen zu thun, du aber hast es nicht gethan, sondern das Gegenspiel, darum musst du verdammt sein, nach dem Spruch deines Gesetzgebers 5 Mos. 27, 26. Wer allhier ein geschickter Dialecticus ist, der macht einen Unterschied zwischen dem Gesetz und Evangelio und gibt nach, dass er das Gesetz nicht gehalten habe, antwortet aber, dass auf das Vorgehende das nicht die Folge sei, dass ich darum verzweifeln soll und muss verdammt sein; denn das Evangelium heisst an den Herrn Christum glauben und auf des Herrn Christi Werke und Gerechtigkeit bauen.“ (Ausl, über die 15 Lieder im höhern Chor. A. 1532. Ps. 181, 1. Tom. IV, 2881. sq.)

Chemnitius: ,,Quae alia lux discussit densissimas tenebras regni pontificii, nisi haec praecipue, quod demonstratum est verum discrimen legis et evangelii?“ (Loc. th. II. De justif. f. 206. b.) Cf. quae supra annotata sunt ad § 2.

Gerhardus: ,,Causae, propter quas discrimen illud accurate constituendum et arcte tenendum, sunt complures. 1. Articulo justificationis sua non constabit, imo nec constare poterit integritas neglecto harum doctrinarnm discrimine, id quod ecclesiastica superiorum temporum historia plus satis comprobat. 2. Beneficia Christi non mediocriter obscurantur, nisi doctrina evangelii a lege accuratis limitibus secernatur. 3. Confusio legis et evangelii necessario secum affert perturbationes conscientiarum, siquidem in magnis et seriis conscientiae pavoribus nulla superstes manet vera ac solida consolatio, si gratuitae promissiones evangelii adulterentur. Quare cum totius doctrinae christianae haec duo praecipua constituantur capita, ad quae reliqua omnia certo modo ac ordine referri possunt, haud immerito inter virtutes, quas in fideli ecclesiae ministro requirit apostolus, primum locum tribuit artificio ορ&οτομεlvy recte secandi sermonem veritatis 2 Tim. 2,15. Metaphoram statuunt ductam ab ofticio sacerdotum Leviticorum in V. T., quorum erat carnes sacrificiorum recte secare ac dividere. Quidam existimant metaphoram ductam a structoribus conviviorum, quia ministri ecclesiae in N. T. sunt vel structores quidam spiritualis convivii. Esa. 25, 6.“ (Loc. de ev. § 52.)

Idem: ,,Quamvis legis et evangelii discrimen ubique sit retinendum, cumprimis tamen illud observandum erit: 1. In articulo justificationis, siquidem justificatio nostra non est ex lege, cui propter carnis nostrae corruptionem et infirmitatem αδυναμία quaedam, accidentia tamen, hac in parte tribuitur Rom. 8, 3., sed ex evangelio, in quo justitia Dei sine lege revelatur Rom. 3, 21., quod est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. 1, 16. Monendi igitur, imo urgendi sunt homines ad opera juxta legis normam praestanda, sed in theatrum justificationis nostrae coram Deo non sunt inferenda, ibi enim perpetua est oppositio inter operari et credere, inter gratiam et opera, inter legem et evangelium. 2. In usu clavium ecclesiasticarum. Impoenitentibus et sePART. III. CAP. VII.


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: to the secure, the remission of sins is not to be announced, but rather the…

to the secure, the remission of sins is not to be announced, but rather the wrath of God from the Law. Rom. 2:9: "Tribulation and anguish upon every soul of man that worketh evil." 1 Tim. 1:9: "The law is laid down for the unjust, the ungodly, the wicked, etc.," whom it presses down with the weight of their own accusation and condemnation. To contrite hearts, the threats of the Law are not to be exacerbated, but rather the oil of evangelical consolation is to be instilled. Isa. 66:1: "Where is the place of my rest?" v. 2: "I will look to the poor and contrite in spirit and him who trembles at my words." Matt. 11:5: "To the poor the gospel is preached." (Loc. de ev. § 55.)

By God, as the author of nature, implanted through creation and inscribed upon the hearts of men. Cf. Rom. 2:14 ff. See Part II, chap. I, § 4, 5, 6. Vol. II, p. 268 ff. A fuller knowledge of it, however, because of the corruption of the human intellect through the fall, must be sought from the revelation contained in the Scriptures. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, Tr. contra Steng. P. II, chap. I, p. 161. See Rom. 16:25; 1 Cor. 2:6, 7 ff. See here § 3.

According to § 21. Luther: "Law is when God commands to do or to leave undone and demands something from us. Gospel is when He proclaims something good that He Himself wants to do and give to us. Thus the two are quite contrary to one another: the one drives, the other gives; the one demands, the other bestows. Thus one should call all sayings that promise God’s grace and favor nothing other than Gospel, which means as much as a good message." (Sermon on the 1st Book of Moses. A. 1527. Opp. Hal. III, 391.)

The same: "By the Law, nothing else should be understood than God’s Word and commandment, in which He commands us what we should do and leave undone, and demands our obedience or works from us." Such is easy to understand in the formal cause, but very difficult in the final cause. The laws or commandments, however, that speak of works which God demands of everyone in particular, according to nature, station, office, time, and other circumstances, are manifold. Therefore, they also tell every person what God has laid upon him according to his nature and office and demands of him, such as: the wife should care for the children, let the master of the house rule, etc.; that is her commandment; a servant should be obedient to his master, and whatever else belongs to a servant’s office; likewise, a maid also has her command. The common law, however, that concerns us all as humans, is this, Matt. 22:39: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," to advise and help him in his need, as it occurs; if he is hungry, feed him; if he is naked, clothe him; and whatever else is of the like. That is what it means to mark out the Law correctly and measure it off from the Gospel; namely, that the Law is called and is that which presses upon our works. On the other hand, the Gospel or faith is such a doctrine or Word of God that does not demand our works nor command us to do anything, but tells us simply to accept the offered grace of the forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation and to let it be given to us. There we do nothing at all, but only receive and let ourselves be given what is bestowed and offered to us through the Word, that God promises and lets you be told: This and that I bestow upon you, etc. As in Baptism, which I did not make, nor is it my work, but God’s Word and work, He says to me: Hold still, I baptize you and wash you from all your sins, accept it, it shall be yours. When you now let yourself be baptized in this way, what more do you do than that you [accept] such grace

do you receive and accept gifts? Thus, the difference between the Law and the Gospel is this: Through the Law, what we ought to do is demanded; it presses for our work toward God and our neighbor. In the Gospel, however, we are called to a donation or a rich alms, where we are to take and receive God’s grace and eternal salvation. This difference is easily noted from this: The Gospel offers us God’s gift and presents, help or salvation; it tells us only to hold out the sack and let ourselves be given to. The Law, however, gives nothing, but takes and demands from us. Now, these two—giving and taking—are indeed very far separated from one another. For when something is gifted to me, I do nothing toward it, but take and receive it and let it be given to me. Conversely, when I carry out in my calling what I am commanded, or advise and help my neighbor, I receive nothing, but give to another whom I serve. Thus, the Law and the Gospel are distinguished by their *formalis causa*: the latter promises, the former commands; the Gospel gives and tells us to take, the Law demands and says: "This you shall do." (

Sermon on the Difference between Law and Gospel, A. 1532. IX, 416. sqq.)

The same: "Those err mightily who interpret the 'yoke of Christ' here as the evangelical law—that is, through the commandments, insofar as they were given by Christ. And the Sophists have made it very difficult for themselves here to show how the yoke of Christ is lighter than the yoke of Moses, when Moses only forbade the work, but Christ also forbade every useless word and the whole heart in addition. Finally, these blind people concluded that the Law and the Gospel relate to one another as *excedentia* and *excessa*, namely, that the Law is easier in that regard than the Gospel because it forbids not the heart, but the hand (or external, gross deeds); conversely, the Gospel is easier therein than the Law because it has abolished circumcision and the ceremonies. O blindness! Which is well-suited for such people who, out of contempt, do not want to read the Gospel." (Notes on the Gospel of Matthew, A. 1538. VII, 214.)

Namely, under the condition of perfect obedience and merits. See § 20. With all respect to our works excluded, according to Rom. 11:6.

Whence also our theologians deny that evangelical promises are conditional, excluding not any condition whatsoever, but specifically the condition of our merits, so that in this way "conditional" is opposed to "gratuitous." Therefore, the condition of faith is different from the condition of works: these are the words of the blessed Gerhard, *L. de Evang.* § 26. Conf. ibid. § 42.

J. Olearius: "Evangelical promises are not conditional. For 1. A condition, properly so-called, is the suspension of a future event, by which, being posited or not posited, that event either follows or does not follow, for the reason that he in whose power it was not only to reject that condition but also to fulfill it by his own powers, did not fulfill it. Thus, all who were sailing with Paul were given to him (Acts 27:24), yet with an express condition, which he himself repeats to the sailors who were contemplating flight (v. 31): 'Unless these remain in the ship, you' (the centurion and the soldiers) 'cannot be saved.' 2. Faith, when related to salvation, is not our work, but pertains to the order divinely instituted, and therefore is by no means a condition properly so-called, depending on man, but a benefit divinely conferred, or the requirement of a passive subject and an instrument apprehending salvation, but by no means an active principle proceeding from man or influencing the effect of salvation by way of a cause properly so-called." (See Carpzov’s *Isag. in lib. symb.* p. 1361.)

PART III. CAP. VII. Gerhard: "Bellarmine draws a fifth argument from our own concession. 'The adversaries,' he says, 'do not deny that faith is required in the evangelical promises; from which it follows, first, that it is false that the promises of the Gospel are denied to be conditional, since some condition, namely faith, is required in them; second, that it is false that the condition of fulfilling the law is not required, for in the same words, or even clearer ones, in which Scripture teaches that the condition of faith is required for salvation, it teaches that the condition of fulfilling the law is required; as is evident from the cited passages.' Resp. 1. When we deny that evangelical promises are conditional, we do not exclude any condition whatsoever, but specifically the condition of our own merits, so that in this way 'conditional' is opposed to 'gratuitous.' ... The particle 'if' is either αιτιολογική or συλλογιστική, that is, it designates a cause or a consequence. In legal pronouncements: 'If you do this, you shall live,' the particle 'if' is αιτιολογική, inasmuch as obedience is the cause on account of which eternal life is given to those who keep the law; but in evangelical promises: 'If you believe, you shall be saved,' the particle 'if' is συλλογιστική, for it denotes the mode of application divinely constituted, which pertains to faith alone." (Loc. de ev. § 26.)

The same: "Although the good things offered in the Gospel are received by faith and cannot be received except by faith, they nevertheless do not cease to be gratuitous for a twofold reason: first, because that very faith is a gift of God, not our work, inasmuch as the Holy Spirit kindles faith in our hearts through the word of the Gospel; then, because faith does not concur as a certain merit, the dignity of which God might regard, but only as an organ, as a begging hand, which, even if it receives the alms of a rich man, the alms does not for that reason cease to be gratuitous." (L. c. § 42.)

Quenstedt: "When we deny that evangelical promises are conditional, we exclude not the condition of the means or instrument, but the condition of merit or works on our part. We say that faith is required, yet more as an organ of apprehension and a medium of the divine τάξις than as a condition." (L. c. c. 2. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1019.)

The same: "Distinguish between the condition of the subject, to whom the possession of eternal life actually happens, and the condition under which eternal life is promised in the Gospel: the pursuit of good works and holiness is the condition of the subject to whom the possession of eternal life actually happens, not that under which it is promised." (L. c. f. 1022.)

Luther: "Therefore he wants to say: I lay no heavy burdens and loads upon you, many sacrifices or divine services or other things that require great cost or effort. I have laid the Gospel, Baptism, and the Sacrament upon you; that is no commandment, but your treasure, which I have given you for nothing; and I force no one to it, as Moses did, with coercion and punishment, but I leave the choice to everyone, whoever wishes to accept it gladly. It is not commanded to you that you must do it as a service to God, but for your own good, that you may fetch your salvation there, if you otherwise wish to be saved." (Exposition of the 14th, 15th, and 16th Chapters of John, A. 1538. Hall. T. VIII, 403.)

Latin:

curis non est annuncianda peccatorum remissio, sed potius Dei ira ex lege. Eom. 2, 9.: ,Tribulatio et angustia in omnem animam hominis operantis malum.‘ 1 Tim. 1, 9.: ,Lex posita est injustis, impiis, sceleratis etc., quos accusationis et damnationis suae pondere premit. Contritis cordibus non sunt legis comminationes exasperandae, sed potius evangelicae consolationis oleum instillandum.‘ Esa. 66, 1.: ,Quis est locus quietis meae?‘ v. 2.: ,Respiciam ad pauperem et contritum spiritu et trementem sermones meos.‘ Matth. 11, 3.: ,Pauperibus evangelium praedicatur.“‘ (Loc. de ev. § 55.)

A Deo, ut auctore naturae, per creationem implantata et cordibus hominum inscripta. Conf. Rom. 2, llf. sqq. Vid. Part. II. cap. I. § 4. 5. 6. Vol. II. p. 268. sqq. Plenior autem ejus notitia, ob corruptionem intellectus humani per lapsum, ex revelatione in Scripturis comprehensa peti debet. Conf. b. Mus. Tr. contra Steng. P. II. cap. I. p. 161. Vid. Rom. 16, 25. 1 Cor. 2, 6. 7. sqq. Vid. h. 1. § 3.

Juxta § 21. Lutherus: ״Gesetz ist, wenn Gott heisst thun oder lassen und etwas von uns fordert. Evangelium ist, wenn er etwas Gutes verkündigt, das er selbst thun und uns geben will. So gehen die zwei gar wider einander: eines treibt, das andere gibt; das fordert, jenes schenkt. So soll man alle Sprüche, die Gottes Gnade und Huld verheissen, nicht anders heissen, denn Evangelium, welches soviel heisst, als eine gute Botschaft.“ (Pr. über das 1. Buch Mose. A. 1527. Opp. Hai. III, 391.)

Idem: ,,Durchs Gesetz soll anders nichts verstanden werden, denn Gottes Wort und Gebot, darinnen er uns gebeut, was wir thun und lassen sollen, und unsern Gehorsam oder Werk von uns fordert. ״ Solches ist leicht zu verstehen in causa formali, aber in causa finali sehr schwer. Die Gesetze aber oder Gebote, so von Werken reden, die Gott von einem jeden insonderheit, nach Natur, Stand, Amt, Zeit und andern Umständen mehr, fordert, sind mancherlei. Daher sie auch einem jeden Menschen sagen, was ihm Gott seiner Natur und Amte nach aufgelegt hat und von ihm fordert, als: das Weib soll die Kinder warten, den Hauswirth regieren lassen u. s. w.; das ist ihr Gebot; ein Knecht soll seinem Herrn gehorsam sein, und was mehr zu eines Knechts Amt gehört; gleicherweise hat eine Magd auch ihren Befehl. Das gemeine Gesetz aber, das uns Menschen alle betrifft, ist dies Matth. 22,39.: ,Du sollst deinen Nächsten lieben, als dich selbst‘, ihm in seiner Noth, wie die vorfällt, rathen und helfen; hungert ihn, so speise ihn; ist er nacket, so kleide ihn; und was desgleichen mehr ist. Das heisst das Gesetz recht abzirkeln und vom Evangelio abmessen; nämlich, dass das Gesetz heisse und sei, welches auf unsere Werke dringt. Dagegen das Evangelium oder der Glaube ist solche Lehre oder Wort Gottes, das nicht unsere Werke fordert noch gebeut uns etwas zu thun, sondern heisst uns die angebotene Gnade von Vergebung der Sünden und ewiger Seligkeit schlecht annehmen und uns schenken llssen. Da thun wir ja nichts, sondern empfahen nur und lassen uns geben, was uns durchs Wort geschenkt und dargeboten wird, dass Gott verlieisst und dir sagen lässt: Dies und das sehenke ich dir u. s. w. Als in der Taufe, die ich nicht gemacht noch mein Werk, sondern Gottes Wort und Werk ist, spricht er zu mir: Halt her, ich täufe dich und wasche dich von allen deinen Sünden, nimm sie an, sie soll deine sein. Wenn du dich nun so täufen lässt, was thust du mehr, denn dass du solch Gnaden

geschenke empfähst und annimmst? So ist nun der Unterschied des Gesetzes und Evangelii dieser: Durch das Gesetze wird gefordert, was wir thun sollen, dringt auf unser Werk gegen Gott und den Nächsten; im Evangelio aber werden wir zur Spende oder zum reichen Almosen gefordert, da wir nehmen und empfahen sollen Gottes Huld und ewige Seligkeit. Dieser Unterschied ist leichtlich hieraus zu merken: Das Evangelium beut uns an Gottes Gabe und Geschenke, Hülfe oder Heil, heisst uns nur den Sack herhalten und uns lassen geben; das Gesetz aber gibt nichts, sondern nimmt und fordert von uns. Nun sind je die zwei, geben und nehmen, sehr weit von einander geschieden. Denn wenn mir etwas geschenkt wird, so thue ich nichts dazu, sondern nehme und empfahe es und lasse mir es geben. Wiederum, wenn ich in meinem Beruf ausrichte, was mir befohlen ist, item, rathe und helfe meinem Nächsten, so empfahe ich nichts, sondern gebe einem andern, dem ich diene. Also wird das Gesetz und Evangelium formali causa unterschieden: dieses verheisst, das andere gebeut; Evangelium gibt und heisst nehmen, Gesetz fordert und sagt: Das sollst du thun.u (

Sermon vom Unterschied des Ges. und Ev. A. 1532. IX, 416. sqq.)

Idem: ,,Diejenigen irren gewaltig, die allhier das,Joch Christi' auslegen durch das evangelische Gesetz, das ist, durch die Gebote, insofern sie von Christo gegeben worden. Und haben sichs die Sophisten allhier sehr sauer werden lassen, zu zeigen, wie das Joch Christi leichter sei, als das Joch Mosis, da doch Moses nur allein das Werk verbot, Christus aber auch noch darzu nur ein jegliches unnützes Wort und das ganze Herz untersagte. Endlich haben diese blinden Leute den Schluss gemacht, das Gesetz und Evangelium verhielten sich gegen einander, wie excedentia und excessa, nämlich, das Gesetz sei in dem Stück leichter, als das Evangelium, weil es nicht das Herz, sondern die Hand (oderäusserliche grobe That) verbiete, hingegen das Evangelium sei darinne leichter, als das Gesetz, weil es die Beschneidung und die Ceremonien aufgehoben hätte. O Blindheit! welche sich wohl für solche Leute schickt, die das Evangelium aus Verachtung nicht lesen wollen.“ (Anmerk, über den Ev. Matthäus. A. 1538. VII, 214.)

Scilicet sub conditione perfectae obedientiae ac meritorum. Vid. § 20. Excluso omni respectu ad opera nostra, juxta Rom. 1/, J/. et 5. cap. 11, 6.

Unde etiam nostri negant, promissiones evangelicas esse conditionatas, non quamvis conditionem, sed in specie conditionem nostrorum meritorum excludentes, ut hac ratione conditionatum opponatur gratuito. Alia igitur est conditio fidei a conditione operum: verba sunt b. Gerh. L. de Evang. § 26. Conf. ib. § 42.

J. Olearius: ״Promissiones evangelicae non sunt conditionatae. Nam 1. conditio proprie dicta est suspensio futuri eventus, qua posita vel non posita ille vel sequitur vel non sequitur, ideo, quia is, in cujus potestate erat conditionem illam non solum repudiare, sed etiam ex propriis viribus illam adimplere, eandem non implevit. Sic donati erant Paulo omnes cum ipso navigantes Act. 27, 24., cum expressa tamen conditione, quam ipse fugam meditantibus nautis repetit v. 31.: ,Nisi hi in navi manserint, vos‘ (centurio et milites),salvi fieri non potestis.‘ 2. Fides, ad salutem relata, non est opus nostrum, sed pertinet ad ordinem divinitus institutum, adeoque nequaquam est conditio proprie dicta, pendens ex homine, sed beneficium divinitus collatum sive requisitum subjecti patientis et organum salutem apprehendens, nequaquam vero principium activum ab homine procedens aut in eflectum salutis per modum causae proprie ita dictae influens.“ (Vid. Carpzovii Isag. in lib. symb. p. 1361.)

PART. III. CAP. VII. Gerhardus: ,,Quintum argumentum Bellarminus petit ex ipsamet nostrum concessione. ,Fidem (inquit) in promissionibus evangelicis requiri non negant adversarii; ex quo sequitur primo, falsum esse, quod promissiones evangelii negantur esse conditionales, cum aliqua in illis conditio, scilicet fidei, requiratur; secundo, falsum esse, quod non requiratur conditio legis implendae, nam quibus verbis Scriptura docet requiri conditionem fidei ad salutem, iisdem, vel etiam clarioribus, docet, requiri conditionem legis implendae; ut patet ex adductis locis.‘ Resp. 1. Quando, evangelicas promissiones conditionales esse, negamus, non quamvis conditionem, sed in specie conditionem nostrorum meritorum excludimus, ut hac ratione conditionale opponatur gratuito. . . Particula,si‘ aut est αιτιολογική aut συλλογιστική, id est, designat causam, vel consequentiam. In concionibus legalibus: ,Si feceris hoc, vives‘, particula,si‘ est αιτιολογική, siquidem obedientia est causa, propter quam servantibus legem datur vita aeterna; sed in evangelicis promissionibus: ,Si credideris, salvus eris‘, particula,si‘ est συλλογιστική, denotatur enim modus applicationis divinitus constitutus, soli fidei competens.“ (Loc. de ev. § 26.)

Idem: ,,Quamvis bona in evangelio oblata fide recipiantur ac nonnisi fide recipi possint, ex eo tamen non desinunt esse gratuitae; duplici ratione: primo, quia illa ipsa fides est donum Dei, non opus nostrum, siquidem Spiritus Sanctus per verbum evangelii accendit in cordibus nostris fidem; deinde, quia fides non concurrit ut meritum quoddam, cujus dignitatem Deus respiciat, sed tantum ut organum, ut mendica manus, quae si vel maxime divitis eleemosynam recipiat, non tamen ex eo eleemosyna desinit esse gratuita.“ (L. c. § 42.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Quando promissiones evangelicas conditionatas esse negamus, non conditionem medii seu instrumenti, sed conditionem meriti seu operum ex parte nostra excludimus. Fidem requiri dicimus, magis tamen ut organon apprehensionis et medium τάξεως divinae, quam ut conditionem.“(L. c. c. 2. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1019.)

Idem: , ,Dist. inter conditionem subjecti, cui ipso actu vitae aeternae possessio contingit, et conditionem, sub qua vita aeterna in evangelio promittitur: studium bonorum operum et sanctimonia est conditio subjecti, cui possessio vitae aeternae actu contingit, non sub qua illa promittitur.“ (L. c. f. 1022.)

Lutherus: ״Darum will er sagen: Ich lege euch keine schwere Bürden und Last auf, viel Opfer oder Gottesdienst oder andere Dinge, dazu grosse Kost oder Mühe gehört. Das Evangelium, Taufe und Sacrament habe ich euch aufgelegt; das ist kein Gebot, sondern euer Schatz, den ich euch umsonst geschenkt habe; und zwinge niemand dazu, wie Moses, mit Zwang und Strafe, sondern lasse jedermann die Wahl, wer es gern will annehmen. Es ist dir nicht geboten, dass du es müssest Gott zu Dienst thun, sondern dir selbst zu gut, dass du deine Seligkeit da holest, so du anders willst selig werden.“ (Ausl, des 14., 15. u. 16. Cap. Joh. A. 1538. Hai. T. VIII, 403.)


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who contend that evangelical promises require the condition of inherent righteousness, or of works, or of the perfect observation of the commandments of God. Thus the Council of Trent, sess. 6, can. 20: 'If anyone shall say that a man who is justified and however perfect is not bound to the observance of the commandments of God and the Church, but only to believe (as if the Gospel were a bare and absolute promise of eternal life without the condition of observing the commandments): let him be anathema.' Bellarmine, 1. 4. de justific. c. 2. §: 'Nor do we contend,' he says, 'concerning this, that the Gospel contains all those things which the adversaries attribute solely to the law, which are principally..."

ON LAW AND GOSPEL. three: laws properly so-called, threats, and promises with the condition of obedience.’ The same is maintained by Gregor. de Valentia, T. 2, Controv. disp. 7, q. 6, p. 992.

2. Of the Socinians and Arminians, who require perfect obedience not indeed absolutely, but comparatively; as Socinus, Comm. in Joh. f. 51; Arminius, respons. ad q. 9, f. 176; Apolog. Arminian. c. 15, f. 152.

3. Of the Innovators, who assert that salvation is promised under the condition of good works. See Hornejus, disp. de fidei non qualislibet necessitate, th. 37, and elsewhere passim. The same author, in his repeated assertion, th. 53, says: ‘The distinction of the legal covenant does not consist in the fact that the law has the condition of works and the gospel has none; for both have it, but in a different way; but the law demands exact obedience, perfect in every respect, whereas the gospel provides grace and remission, but to those who are penitent and propose to themselves to begin a new life, as far as can be done in this fragility.’ Dr. Georgius Calixtus, however, inverts the doctrine concerning the distinction between law and gospel, both elsewhere and in his Disp. de pactis.

He calls the covenant entered into with Moses and the Israelites an evangelical covenant (these are the words of Dr. Hulsemann in Praelect. ad Breviar. c. 8, p. 1176), and distinguishes it into old and new. He calls the old the demands and promises brought through Moses under the rigorous fulfillment of the law; he calls the new the doctrine of Christ and the apostles under the possible fulfillment of the law, n. 39, 40, 41, 45, 46, 55, 56. This again is a πρῶτον ψεῦδος [first falsehood], through those things which the apostle handed down concerning the difference between law and gospel in Rom. 10:5, 6 sqq. and Gal. 3:18, 21 sqq., where the difference between law and gospel is established in this, that the law required the performance of works, to be done both by nature and by grace; but the gospel requires not works, but faith alone.

He establishes that common distinction of the Scholastics, that the law and the gospel equally require works, but the gospel alone also confers the strength to perform them, etc.” (L. c. c. 2, s. 2, q. 2, f. 1019 sqq.) h) See § 3, 5, 6 sqq. and § 20. i) See Rom. 4:15, where it is said: ὁ νόμος ὀργὴν κατεργάζεται, it works wrath, i.e., it constitutes men guilty of divine wrath and strikes terror into consciences from that guilt, as the blessed G. Mylius explains, p. 205. For the curse of the law itself, see Gal. 3:10, from Deut. 27: 26. Luther: “Whatever indicates sin, wrath, or death, that the office of the law exercises and drives, whether it happens in the Old or New Testament.” (Disput. against the Law-stormers. Opp. Hal. XX, 2041.) The same: “The law cannot refresh the soul, for it is a word that demands of us and commands that we should love God with all our heart, etc., and our neighbor as ourselves. Whoever does not do this, it condemns him and speaks such a judgment over him: ‘Cursed be everyone who does not do everything that is written in the book of the law,’ Deut. 27:26. Now, however, it is certain that no one on earth does this; therefore, the law comes with its judgment in its own time, it only saddens and terrifies the soul, and where no counsel is provided, it presses forward so that they must despair and be eternally damned. Therefore St. Paul says in Rom. 3:20: ‘Through the law comes only the knowledge of sin.’ Likewise Rom. 4:15: ‘The law only works wrath,’ etc. The Gospel, however, is a blessed word; it demands nothing from us, but proclaims all good things, namely, that God has given his only Son to us poor sinners, that he should be our Shepherd, who sought us languishing, lost, and scattered sheep again, and laid down his life for us, so that he might thus redeem us from sin, from eternal death, and from the power of the devil.” (Exposition of the 23rd Psalm. A. 1536. Ib. V, 400.) PART III. CHAP. VII.

k) For it neither removes the agonies or stings of conscience, nor the blindness of the intellect in spiritual matters and the resulting resistance through doubts concerning the truth of revelation, nor does it kindle faith or charity.

See the blessed Musaeus, *Tractatus contra Steng.*, Part III, ch. IX, pp. 712, 736. l) For it is not a law of works, but of faith, Gal. 3:2. m) For although the Gospel, taken in a broader sense, can be called a preaching of repentance, this is not to be stated of the Gospel strictly so called. For it does not of itself and directly treat of things to be done and omitted, nor does it of itself and directly reveal or reprove sins. However, the Passion of Christ, which, insofar as it is λύτρον for sins and thus the cause of recovered divine grace, pertains to the Gospel, nevertheless, insofar as it arises from our sins and sets the wrath of God before our eyes, pertains to the Law, as a real preaching of repentance. See *Formula of Concord*, Art. on Law and Gospel, p. 593. *Formula of Concord*: "Therefore, and in order that both the doctrine of the Law and of the Gospel may not be mingled and mixed with each other, and that what belongs to the one may not be ascribed to the other, whereby the merit and benefits of Christ are easily obscured and the Gospel is again turned into a doctrine of the Law, as has happened in the Papacy, and thus Christians are robbed of the true comfort which they have in the Gospel against the terrors of the Law, and the door is again opened to the Papacy in the Church of God: therefore, the true and proper distinction between the Law and the Gospel must be diligently urged and maintained, and everything that might give cause for confusion between the Law and the Gospel—that is, whereby both doctrines, Law and Gospel, are confused and mixed into one doctrine—must be diligently avoided. It is therefore dangerous and wrong to want to make a sermon of repentance or punishment out of the Gospel, when it is properly so called, as it is distinguished from the Law. For otherwise, when it is understood in a general sense as the whole doctrine, the Apology also says several times that the Gospel is a preaching of repentance and the forgiveness of sins. But the Apology also indicates at the same time that the Gospel, properly speaking, is the promise of the forgiveness of sins and of justification through Christ, but the Law is a word that punishes and condemns sin." (Art. V, p. 639.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis:

1. Of the Papists, who affirm that the Gospel, properly accepted, is not only a preaching of grace, but also of repentance and terror; see Bellarmine, Vol. 4, Book 4, *de justific.*, ch. 2, where he says: 'Since, therefore, Christ and all the apostles terrify by evangelizing, and in the Apostolic Creed, which contains the sum of the Gospel, there is also one article concerning the future judgment, the Lutherans falsely teach that it is the proper office of the Law to terrify and that it does not pertain to the Gospel.' ... 2. Of the Antinomians, such as John Islebius, the apostate, and his associates, who assert that repentance is learned more conveniently and correctly from the Gospel than from the Law. Likewise, that the Gospel in its most proper and most specific use and office is a preaching of repentance and the remission of sins at the same time. See Schlusselburg’s *Catalogus Haereticorum*, Vol. 4, p. 39, and the *Confessio Antinom.*, ibid., p. 46; compare the blessed Luther, Vol. 1, Latin, Jena, f. 553. 3. Of Philip Melanchthon, who, after the death of the blessed Luther, made this error of the Antinomians his own, not obscurely, in the final edition of the *Loci*, where he quite manifestly restored the errors of the Antinomians in this very article; see articles 4, 5, and 20 of that spurious and changed and varied Confession."

...following Augustinus Philippus [Melanchthon] were Paulus Crellius and Caspar Cruciger the Younger; the former in a disputation against Joh. Wigandus held at Wittenberg in the year 1571; the latter in a disputation on the justification of man instituted at Wittenberg in the year 1570, thesis 10 See D. Hutter in *F. C.* ad a. 5, p. 559 sq. 4 Of the Wittenberg Crypto-Calvinists, who defended antinomian *ἀκυρολογίας* [improper expressions], as appears from the Catechism and theses published at Wittenberg in the years 70 and 71 of the previous century, and also from the writing of Pezelius, which contains an apology for the definition of the Gospel as being the preaching of repentance, published in the year 71 Compare Hemmingius in *Syntagm. vol. theol.* p. 713 sq. These are followed by the Calvinists Ursinus, P. 2, *Cateches.* p. 139; Bucanus, L. 20, p. 193 Pareus in *epist. ad Rom.* p. 88 Tossanus in *Not. margin.* 1 Tim. 1, 11. 5 Of the New Prophets, who make the Gospel a preaching of repentance, see Vorhof, preface, p. 17 and 18.” (*L. c. c. 2. s. 2. q. 3. f. 1023 sq.*) n) See John 1:17, where, in opposition to the law given through Moses, it is said that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ and are therefore to be known from the Gospel. Compare Rom. 8:21f. sqq., add Isa. 61:1, Luke 4:18, 19, 20, Matt. 11:5, ch. 12:5 Although not exclusively, as will be taught shortly; yet these [are the primary ones], and because of the end added. See 1 Tim. 1:9. p) See Matt. 11:5 and 28. Luther: “The art is common; it is soon said that the Law is one word and doctrine, and the Gospel another, but to distinguish them *practice* [in practice], and to put the art into effect, is toil and labor.” (Sermon on the Distinction of Law and Gospel, 1532. *Opp. Hal.* IX, 422.) The same: “Therefore, this is the highest art and wisdom of Christians, that (when the Law accuses and terrifies them on account of sin, they hold simply to Christ, who has paid for sin, and) they know nothing at all of the Law, nor of works, nor of any righteousness of their own doing. Just as otherwise, outside of Christendom, this is the highest wisdom, that one knows the Law, works, and the righteousness of our own doing in the best way and always has them before one’s eyes. Therefore, it is indeed a wonder, a strange and entirely unheard-of thing in the world, that one proposes to Christians and teaches them that they should learn to forget the Law and know nothing more of it, but live before God as if there were absolutely no Law at all. For where you do not thus entirely forget the Law, put it away from you, and think as if, in short, there were no Law anymore, but only pure grace, you cannot be saved. For through the Law comes only the knowledge of sin, etc. Rom. 3:20. Conversely, one must urge the Law and the doctrine of works in the world as if there were absolutely no promise or grace. And this for the sake of the stiff-necked, arrogant, and wild people, to whom one should otherwise set forth and present nothing else but the Law, so that they may also be terrified and humbled. For it is precisely for this reason that the Law is given, that it should terrify and kill the secure and hardened, and should only properly attack the old Adam, quickly plague and torment him; and thus both, the Word and preaching of grace and of wrath, should be rightly divided according to the counsel of the Apostle. 2 Tim. 2:2. Therefore, one certainly needs a faithful and wise teacher for this, who knows how to urge and use the Law in such a way that it does not go further than is fitting and good. For if I wanted to preach the Law to people in such a way that they should thereby become righteous and pious before God, I would have already done far too much and overstepped the mark, and would be mixing these two kinds of righteousness.” PART III. CHAP. VII. namely, the righteousness which comes from the Law and is of my own doing, with the other righteousness, which comes without the Law from grace and is given and gifted to me by God (for Christ’s sake) without any of my works and contribution. And therefore, he would be a very crude, inept teacher who, without any distinction, threw the hundreds into the thousands and mingled one with the other. But when I hold forth and preach the doctrine of the Law and works to the old Adam, but the promise and grace to the new man, then I divide them rightly. For the flesh or old Adam, Law and works belong together, just as the Spirit or new man, promise and grace also belong together. Therefore, when I notice that a person has broken himself sufficiently with the Law, suffers need under it, torments himself with his sins, and desires grace, it is truly high time and necessary that I tear the Law together with the righteousness of his own doing away from his eyes and show him through the Gospel the other righteousness, which God offers and gifts to him without the merit and contribution of his own works, solely out of grace (for the sake of His Son), which righteousness bids Moses with his righteousness to yield and holds the promise of Christ before the terrified person through the Law, as He who has come for the sake of such miserable consciences and poor sinners. Then the poor person is truly helped, so that he draws a right, comforting hope and good confidence, and is henceforth no longer under the Law, but under grace. But how is he no longer under the Law? Answer: According to the new man, whom the Law does not concern at all, but is directed solely toward Christ, as St. Paul also says later in 3:24: “The Law lasted until Christ.” (Detailed Explanation of the Ep. to the Gal. A. 1535. Ib. VIII, 1545—47.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis:

tria: leges proprie dictae, comminationes et promissiones cum conditione obedientiae.‘ Idem statuit Gregor. de Valentia T. 2. Controv. disp. 7. q. 6. p. 992.

3. Novatorum, salutem sub conditione bonorum operum promissam esse, asserentium. Videatur Hornejus disp. de fidei non qualislibet necessitate, th. 37. et alibi passim. Idem in iterata assertione th. 53. inquit: ,Discrimen pacti legalis non in eo consistit, quod lex conditionem operum habeat, evangelium nullam habeat; utrumque enim, sed diversimode, habet; sed lex exactam obedientiam et omnibus numeris perfectam postulet, evangelium gratiam et remissionem praestet, sed poenitentibus et novam vitam, prout in hac fragilitate fieri potest, inchoare sibi proponentibus.‘ D. Georgius Calixtus vero doctrinam de discrimine legis et evangelii invertit, tum alibi, tum in Disp, de pactis. Pactum cum Mose et Israelitis initum vocat pactum evangelicum (verba sunt D. Hulsemanni in Praelect. ad Breviar. c. 8. p. 1176.), idque distinguit in vetus et novum. 56. Quod iterum πρώτον ψενόος est, per ea, quae apostolus tradidit de differentia legis et evangelii Rom. 10, 5. 6. sq. et Gal. 3,18. 21. sq., ubi differentia inter legem et evangelium statuitur in hoc, quod lex operum praestationem requisiverit, tum per naturam, tum per gratiam faciendorum; evangelium vero non opera, sed solam fidem requirat. Vulgatum illud Scholasticorum discrimen constituit, quod lex et evangelium pariter requirant opera, solum autem evangelium conferat etiam vires praestandi etc.“ (L. c. c. 2. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1019. sq.) h) Vid. § 3. 5. 6. sqq. et § 20. i) Vid. Rom. J, 15., ubi dicitur: 6 νόμος ό,ογψ χατεργάζεταί, iram operatur, i. e. reos irae divinae constituit et ex reatu isto conscientiis terrorem incutit, ut exponit b. G. Mylius p. ra.

205. Ipsam vero maledictionem legis vide Gal. S, 10. ex Deut 27, 26. Lutherus: ,,Was die Sünde, den Zorn oder Tod anzeigt, das übet und treibet des Gesetzes Amt, es geschehe im Alten oder Neuen Testamente.“ (Disput, wider die Gesetzstürmer. Opp. Hai. XX, 2041.) Idem: ,,Das Gesetz kann die Seelen nicht erquicken, denn es ist ein Wort, das von uns fordert, und gebeut, dass wir Gott lieben sollen von ganzem Herzen u. s. w., unsern Nächsten als uns selbst. Wer solches nicht thut, den verdammt es und spricht ein solch Urtheil über ihn: ,Verflucht sei jedermann, der nicht alles thut, was im Buch des Gesetzes geschrieben steht‘, 5 Mos. 27, 26. Nun aber ist es gewiss, dass niemand auf Erden solches thut, darum kömmt das Gesetz mit seinem Urtheil zu seiner Zeit, betrübt und erschreckt nur die Seelen, und wo nicht Rath geschafft wird, dringt es fort, dass sie verzweifeln und ewig verdammt sein müssen. Daher spricht St. Paulus Röm. 3, 20.: ,Durch das Gesetz kömmt nur Erkenntniss der Sünde.‘ Item Röm. 4, 15.: ,Das Gesetz richtet nur Zorn an‘, u. s. w. Das Evangelium aber ist ein selig Wort, fordert nichts von uns, sondern verkündigt alles Gutes, nämlich, dass Gott seinen einigen Sohn uns armen Sündern geschenkt habe, dass er soll unser Hirte sein, der uns verschmachtete, verlorne und zerstreute Schafe wieder suchte, sein Leben für uns Hesse, auf dass er uns also von Sünden, vom ewigen Tod und des Teufels Gewalt erlösete.“ (Auslegung des 23. Psalms. A. 1536. Ib. V, 400.) PART. III. CAP. VII.

k) Nam neque angores aut morsus conscientiae, neque coecitatem intellectus in spiritualibus et hinc nascentem repugnantiam, per dubitationes de veritate revelationis, tollit, neque fidem aut caritatem accendit. Vid. b. Mus. Tract. contra Steng. P. III. c. IX. p. 712. 736.

1) Non enim est lex operum, sed fidei, Gal. 3, 2. m) Nam, quamvis evangelium, in latiore significatione acceptum, dici possit concio poenitentiae, non tamen de evangelio stricte sic dicto id enunciandum est. Non enim per se directe tractat agenda et omittenda, neque adeo per se et directe revelat aut arguit peccata. Passio Christi autem, quae, quatenus $st λύτρο» pro peccatis et sic causa recuperatae gratiae divinae, ad evangelium pertinet, tamen quatenus ex peccatis nostris orta iram Dei ob oculos ponit, ad legem pertinet, velut realis concio poenitentiae. Vid. Form. C. Art. de Lege et Evang. p. 593. Form. Conc.: ,,Demnach, und auf dass beide Lehre des Gesetzes und Evangelii nicht in einander gemengt und vermischt und der einen zugeschrieben werde, was der andern zugehört, dadurch dann leichtlich der Verdienst und die Gutthaten Christi verdunkelt und das Evangelium wiederum zu einer Gesetzlehre gemacht, wie im Pabstthum geschehen, und also die Christen des rechten Trosts beraubt, den sie im Evangelio wider das Schrecken des Gesetzes haben, und dem Pabstthum wiederum die Thür in der Kirchen Gottes aufgethan werde: so muss mit allem Fleiss der wahre eigentliche Unterscheid zwischen dem Gesetz und Evangelio getrieben und erhalten, und was zur Confusion inter legem et evangelium, das ist, dadurch die beide Lehren, Gesetz und Evangelium, verwirrt und in eine Lehre gemengt, Ursach geben möchte, tieissig verhütet werden. Ist derhalben gefährlich und unrecht, dass man aus dem Evangelio, wenn es eigentlich also genennt, wie es vom Gesetz unterschieden wird, eine Buss oder Strafpredigt machen wolle. Dann sonst, wann es ingemein verstanden wird von der ganzen Lehre, so sagt auch die Apologia etzlichmal, das Evangelium sei ein Predigt von der Buss und Vergebung der Sünden. Es zeigt aber darneben die Apologia auch das an, dass Evangelium eigentlieh sei die Verheissung der Vergebung der Sünden und der Rechtfertigung durch Christum, das Gesetz aber sei ein Wort, das die Sünde straft und verdammt.“ (Art. V. p. 639.) ANTITHESIS.

Antinomorum, ut Johannis Islebii, apostatae, et sociorum, asserentium, poenitentiam commodius et rectius addisci ex evangelio, quam ex lege.
