Lutheri errorem istum Antinomorum haud obscure suum fecit in editione postrema Locorum, ubi errores Antinomorum in hoc quidem articulo satis manifeste reposuit; vide a. 4. 5. et 20. spuriae illius et mutatae ac variatae Confessio-

nis August. Philippum secuti sunt Paulus Crellius et Caspar Cruciger jun.; ille in disp., adv. Joh. Wigandum A. 1571. Witteb. habita; hic in disp. de justific. hominis A. 1570. Witt, instituta th. 10. Vide D. Hutterum in F. C. ad a. 5. p. 559. sq.


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: Of the Scholastics, who posit that the Law and the Gospel differ

1. Of the Scholastics, who posit that the Law and the Gospel differ: 1. in time, 2. in precepts, 3. in promises, 4. in sacraments; see Lombard, 3 Sent. dist. 40. lit. A. and B., Thomas on c. 5 of Matthew and in Summa P. I. 2. q. 91. a. 5, Scotus 3 Sent. dist. 40, Gabriel Biel, ibid. qu. unica. 2. Of the Papists, especially Bellarmine, who asserts that the first difference between the Law and the Gospel is that which exists between an incipient and a perfect doctrine, l. 4 de justif. c. 3, 4. The second, that the Law comes alone, but the Gospel together with grace, or that the Law was given through Moses, who was only a legislator, but the Gospel through Christ, whom he says was not only a legislator but also a redeemer. The third, that the Law of Moses was given to one nation only, the Law of Christ to all nations. The fourth, that the Law of Moses for the most part embraces the shadow and figures of future things, while the Gospel has the body itself and the truth. The fifth, that the Law of Moses had to be changed upon the arrival of the Law of Christ, but no other law ought to succeed the Law of Christ; to all of which the blessed Gerhard responds in L. de evangel. § 58, 59, 60, 61, and D. Dannhauer in Hodom. Papaea, phant. 6, p. 1031 sq.; compare the blessed Hemnitius from the beginning of the locus on justification.

3. Of the Socinians and Arminians, as also of Vorstius, who constitute the difference between the Law and the Gospel by reason of the promises, namely, that in the former the promises are only corporal, in the latter spiritual. See Socinus in his persuasive book p. 63, Ostorod in Instit. Germ. c. 5, Smalcius c. Franzium p. 220, Arminius disp. de lege et evangelio th. 6, Vorstius de auctorit. Script. p. 58.

4. Of the Schwenkfeldians, who imagine that the Law demanded only a figurative, shadowy, and external righteousness; see Schwenkfeld de V. D. p. 130.

5. Of the Anabaptists and Socinians, and likewise the Remonstrants or Arminians, who, with the Dominicans and Jesuits, pervert the true difference between the Law and the Gospel with this hypothesis: that the Gospel is a new law of a new legislator, Christ, which has succeeded the old law of Moses, the legislator.

of the old. Thus Petrus a Soto says, "to believe that a new law was given to the catholic church by Christ." Bellarmine, *de justif.*, bk. 4, ch. 3, *et seq.*, calls the New Testament or the gospel "the law of Christ" throughout. Greg. de Valentia, Vol. 2, disp. 7, q. 8, calls it "the new law" everywhere. See the Apology of the Arminians, ch. 13. 6. Of the Synergists, who extended the term "gospel," taken strictly, even to the precepts of legal works, against whom it was decreed in Part 3 of the Smalcald Articles, p. 329; the Formula of Concord in the Epitome, p. 591; and in the Declaration, p. 709. 7. Of the Innovators, who confuse law and gospel, while they make one law old and another new (by which they understand the gospel), and, recalling not only things to be believed but also things to be done to the gospel, they say that the law requires perfect obedience; but the gospel, at least, that we do not permit sins to reign, nor obey the desires of the flesh. See D. Georg. Calixtus, *Epitom. theol. mor.*, p. 7, 10, 70; Horneius in *iterata assert.*, th. 53. (L. c. s. 2, q. 4, f. 1027, *et seq.*) §

24. Although the law and the gospel differ in this way, in practice, however, they must be most closely joined, and indeed, as far as the conversion of men pertains, the law, which delivers what is to be done and what is to be omitted and obligates them to the most accurate observance thereof, denouncing the most grave guilt to any transgressors whatsoever, by this very thing leads men to the acknowledgment of sins and sorrow for them, and thus renders them solicitous for a mediator; the gospel, however, shows the mediator himself, and through him the grace of God and the remission of sins to be obtained. Whence the law indeed prepares the minds of men to receive faith, but the gospel kindles faith itself, by which sinners are reconciled with God.

See blessed Musaeus, Preface to the Treatise against Steng., quire B. I. a. Luther: "Here we see again that the law and the gospel, which are separated from each other most widely and are more than contradictory, are most closely joined in affection. . . For although those two are most remote in their very nature, yet they are also most closely joined in the same heart. Nothing is more joined than fear and trust, law and gospel, sin and grace. For they are so joined that one is absorbed by the other. Therefore, no mathematical conjunction can be given that would be similar to this." (Commentary on the Epistle of St. Paul to the Galatians, ed. Irmischer. Erlangen II, 105, 113.) See l. c. and here, ch. IV, § 34.

To be sure, this is the first and perpetual and common thing that the law provides. Whence, although a threefold use of the law is commonly established, and that which they call the political holds the first place, which looks to the preservation of external discipline and public tranquility in civil society against savage and untamed men, for whom their punishments are established, it is nevertheless certain that even here some didactic use is presupposed. PART III. CHAPTER VII.

by the force of which the law acts as a norm or rule for maintaining that discipline. However, in this place, the law must be viewed in relation to men who are to be spiritually converted and renewed. Here is the second use of the law, which they commonly establish and call pedagogical, taking the occasion from Galatians 3:24, namely, that the law, like a strict schoolmaster, by reproaching men for their lapses and rendering them terrified and anxious, causes them to desire a liberator and to look toward all ways, if by any means they might be liberated.

Luther: "Thus the law is not given so that we should become righteous through it, because it is able to give neither righteousness nor life. In sum, as high as the heaven is above the earth, so far should the law be separated from justification. And one should teach, say, or think nothing in the article concerning justification except only the word of grace shown to us in Christ. From this, however, it does not follow that the law should be abolished and removed from the pulpit in the church. Indeed, for that very reason it is all the more necessary that it be diligently taught and urged, that it is not only unnecessary but also impossible for righteousness. So that man, who is proud and relies upon his own powers and abilities, may be instructed from it that he cannot become righteous through the law. For sin and death should be shown to man primarily for this reason, not that they are necessary for life and innocence, but that man may recognize his unrighteousness and damnation and thus be humbled. When sin remains unrecognized, man is presumptuous regarding his false, fabricated innocence, as can be seen in the case of the heathens and later also in the Pelagians... Also, it is false and a lie that the law punishes sin without the Holy Spirit, since the law is written with the finger of God (Exodus 32:16). And all truth, wherever it is, is from the Holy Spirit, and to forbid the law is to forbid the truth of God... Therefore, the law will never be abolished in eternity, but remains either to be fulfilled in the damned or fulfilled in the blessed. But these, the devil's disciples, have these thoughts, as it seems, that the law was given only for a time and was abolished after Christ's coming, like circumcision... And even if the law could be done away with according to grammar and the dead letter (for that must be the opinion of these fanatics), as one erases something written on a tablet: My dear friend, who will tear out of our conscience the living law, which is written in the hearts and is a handwriting against us that cannot be blotted out (which is of the very same kind as the law of Moses)?" (Second and Third Disputation against the Antinomians, 1539. XX, 2040 sq. 2043. 2044. 2048.)

Gleichwie sonst ausserhalb der Christenheit dies die allerhöchste Weisheit ist, dass man das Gesetz, Werk und die Gerechtigkeit unsers eigenen Thuns aufs allerbeste wisse und allewege vor Augen habe. Darum ists wohl ein Wunder, seltsam und ganz unerhörte Sache in der Welt, dass man denChristen vorgibt und sie lehrt, dass sie des Gesetzes vergessen lernen und davon gar nichts mehr wissen sollen, sondern vor Gott also leben, als ob allerdings gar kein Gesetz wäre. Denn wo du des Gesetzes nicht also allerdings vergisst, dich sein abthust, und denkst, als wäre kurzum gar kein Gesetz mehr, sondern eitel lauter Gnade, so vermagst du nicht selig zu werden. Denn durchs Gesetz kommt nur Erkenntniss der Sünden u. s. w. Röm. 3, 20 Wiederum muss man das Gesetz und Werklehre in der Welt also treiben, als wäre allerdings keine Verheissung noch Gnade nicht. Und dies um der halsstarrigen, hochfahrenden und wilden Leute willen, denen man sonst nichts anders vor die Augen stellen und fürbilden soll, denn das Gesetz, auf dass sie auch erschreckt und gedemütliigt werden. Denn eben darum ist das Gesetz gegeben, dass es die Sichern und Verstockten erschrecken und tödten und den alten Adam nur wohl angreifen, flugs plagen und martern soll, und soll also beiderlei, Wort und Predigt der Gnaden und des Zorns, nach Rath des Apostels recht ausgetheilt werden. 2 Tim. 2, 2 Darum bedarf man hierzu wohl eines treuen und klugen Lehrers, der das Gesetz dermassen zu treiben und zu gebrauchen wisse, dass es nicht weiter gehe, denn sichs gebührt und gut ist. Denn wenn ich den Leuten das Gesetz also predigen wollte, als, dass sie dadurch vor Gott sollten gerecht und fromm werden, so hätte ich ihm schon bereits allzuviel gethan und über die Schnur gehauen und vermengte diese zweierlei Gerechtigkeit, PART. III. CAP. VII. als nämlich die Gerechtigkeit, so ans dem Gesetz kommt und meines eigenen Thuns ist, mit der andern Gerechtigkeit, so ohne Gesetz aus Gnaden kommt und ohne alle meine Werke und Zuthun mir von Gott (um Christi willen) gegeben und geschenkt wird. Und wäre derhalben allzugar ein grober, ungeschickter Lehrer, der ohne allen Unterschied das Hunderte ins Tausende würfe und eins ins andere vermengte. Wenn ich aber die Lehre vom Gesetz und Werken dem alten Adam, die Verheissung aber und Gnade dem neuen Menschen Vorhalte und predige, so theile ichs recht. Denn das Fleisch oder alte Adam, Gesetz und Werk gehören zusammen, gleichwie der Geist oder neue Mensch, Verheissung und Gnade auch zusammen gehören. Darum, wenn ich merke, dass der Mensch mit dem Gesetz sieh genugsam gebrochen hat, darunter Nothleidet, sich mit seinen Sünden martert und der Gnaden begehrt, ists wahrlich hohe Zeit und vonnöthen, dass ich ihm das Gesetz sammt der Gerechtigkeit seines Thuns aus den Augen hinwegreisse und zeige ihm durchs Evangelium die andere Gerechtigkeit, die ihm Gott ohne seiner eigenen Werke Verdienst und Zuthun allein aus Gnaden (um seines Sohnes willen) anbeut und schenkt, welche Gerechtigkeit denn den Mosen mit seiner Gerechtigkeit weichen heisst und hält dem erschrockenen Menschen durchs Gesetz die Verheissung von Christo für, als der um solcher elender Gewissen und der armen Sünder willen kommen ist. Da wTird denn dem armen Menschen recht aufgeholfen, dass er eine rechte tröstliche Hoffnung und gute Zuversicht schöpft, ist hinfort nicht mehr unterm Gesetz, sondern unter der Gnade. Antwort: Nach dem neuen Menschen, welchen das Gesetz allerdings nichts angeht, sondern ist allein auf Christum gerichtet, wie St.Paulus hernacher 3, 24. auch sagt: ,Das Gesetz währet bis auf Christum‘.“ (Ausführliche Erkl. der Ep. an die Gal. Lutherus: ,,Also ist das Gesetz niclit gegeben, dass wir dadurch gerecht sollten werden, weil es weder Gerechtigkeit noch Leben zu geben vermag. Summa, so hoch der Himmel über der Erden ist, so׳ fern soll das Gesetz von der Justification geschieden werden. Und man soll nichts lehren, sagen, gedenken in dem Artikel die Justification belangend, denn allein das Wort der Gnaden, uns in Christo erzeiget. Daraus folget aber nicht, dass das Gesetz soll abgethan und in der Kirche von der Kanzel weggenommen werden. Ja, eben darum ists desto mehr vonnöthen, dass mans fleissig lehre und treibe, dass es nicht allein unnöthig, sondern auch unmöglich ist zur Gerechtigkeit. Auf dass der Mensch, so stolz ist und sich auf seine Kräfte und Vermögen verlässt, daraus unterrichtet, werde, dass er durch das Gesetz nicht könne gerecht werden. Denn die Sünde und der Tod sollen darum vornehmlich dem Menschen angezeigt werden, nicht dass sie vonnöthen sein zum Leben und Unschuld, sondern dass der Mensch erkenne seine Ungerechtigkeit und Verdammniss und also gedemüthiget werde. Wenn die Sünde unerkannt bleibet, ist der Mensch vermessen auf seine falsche, erdichtete Unschuld, wie solches an den Heiden und hernach auch an den Pelagianern zu sehen ist. . . Auch ist das falsch und erlogen, dass das Gesetz ohne den Heiligen Geist die Sünde strafe, so doch das Gesetz mit dem Einger Gottes geschrieben ist. 2 Mos. 32, 16. Und alle Wahrheit, wo sie nur ist, ist von dem Heiligen Geist, und das Gesetz verbieten, ist die Wahrheit Gottes verbieten. .. Darum wird das Gesetz nimmermehr in Ewigkeit aufgehaben, sondern bleibet entweder in den Verdammten zu erfüllen, oder in den Seligen erfüllet. Diese aber, des Satans Schüler, haben diese Gedanken, wie es scheinet, dass das Gesetz nur eine Zeitlang gegeben und nach Christi Zukunft aufgehaben sei,, wie die Beschneidung. . . Und obgleich das Gesetze nach der Grammatik und dem todten Buchstaben könnte weggethan werden (denn das muss dieser Schwärmer Meinung sein), wie man etwas an einer Tafel geschrieben auslöschet: Lieber, wer will aber das lebendige Gesetz, so in die Herzen geschrieben, und eine Handschrift uns entgegen ist,, die sich nicht austilgen lässt (welche eben der Art ist, wie Moses Gesetz), aus unserm Geioissen reissen?“ (Zweite und dritte Disput, wider die Gesetzstürmer. 1539. XX, 2040 sq. 2043. 2044. 2048.)


### Concerning the Word of Law and Gospel: Which is expressly stated in Romans 3:20

Which is expressly stated in Romans 3:20. Conf. ch. VII. and in this place, ch. IV. § 34. note e. See 1. c. note f.

For although the law itself does not know a mediator, nor can it show or promise one, it nevertheless brings it about by its terrors that the mind of man, despairing of itself according to the law, seeks help elsewhere, from wherever it may shine forth. Luther: "They have invented for themselves a new method, that one should first preach grace, and afterwards the revelation of wrath, so that one might by no means hear or speak the word (the law). That is a fine cat's-chair; it pleases them exceedingly well."

and think they want to pull the whole Scripture in and out, and thereby become the light of the world. Such things St. Paul should and must grant, Rom. 1; but they do not see how St. Paul teaches the very opposite, beginning and showing first the wrath of God from heaven and making all the world sinners and guilty before God; thereafter, once they have become sinners, he teaches them how one obtains grace and becomes righteous, as the first three chapters powerfully and clearly show.” (Against the Antinomians. 1539. XX, 2024.) Cf. the notes above on Part III, ch. 6, § 15, p. 313.

The same: “The Church and Christ Himself, and furthermore righteousness, mean nothing to us where the harmful presumption has not first been overcome and killed. Therefore, the Antinomians are rightly worthy of everyone’s enmity, who want to hold to and defend themselves with our example, when the cause is nevertheless manifest as to why we taught of God’s grace in the beginning in such a way. The cursed Pope had completely oppressed poor consciences with his human ordinances; he had taken away all right means, help, and comfort by which poor, despairing hearts might have been saved from despair. What else were we to do at that time than to raise up again the oppressed and burdened hearts and set before them the right comfort? But we also know well that one must speak differently to those who are full, tender, and fat. We were all cast out and greatly plagued at that time. The water in the bottle was gone; that is, there was no comfort present. We lay like the dying, just as Ishmael under the shrub. Therefore, such teachers were necessary for us who would set God’s grace before us and teach us how we might be refreshed. The Antinomians, however, want it to be that one should simply begin the doctrine of repentance with grace, but I did not follow that process. For I knew well that Ishmael had first been driven out and had despaired before he heard the comfort from the angel. Therefore, I followed the example and comforted no one except only those who had previously had repentance and sorrow over their sin and had despaired of themselves, whom the Law had terrified, the Leviathan had attacked, and had made completely dismayed.” (Exposition of the First Book of Moses. A. 1536—1545. I, 2143—45.)

Kromayerus: “We note that the pedagogue to Christ, as the Law is called in Gal. 3:24, is either one who leads us to Christ directly or one who leads us to Him indirectly. It leads us directly to Christ (as far as signification is concerned), as the ceremonial law did formerly even in the O.T. (as far as observation is concerned), which contained σκίαν τῶν μελλόντων, i.e., a shadow of things to come; indirectly, the moral [law leads us], because it only indicates the disease and commands us to seek a physician, whoever that may be. But the Gospel shows us this one.” (Th. posit. polem. I, 771.)

According to those things which we said in § 21. However, it does not concur efficiently to generate faith, but only by removing the impediment of security and contempt, born from unretracted sins, and thus by this reason disposing the subject, although the Law does not even adequately remove all impediments, as is evident from note k to § 23. Conf. b. Mus. Tract. contra Steng. p. 736.

k) See above, ch. IV, § 34, note g. §

25. In the matter of renewal, the Law, by teaching what things are to be done and what things are to be omitted, directs the regenerate to works that are truly PART III. CHAP. VII.

good things to be performed and sins to be avoided. By its threats, it also causes the desires of the flesh to be more strongly repressed. Indeed, by showing the imperfection of new obedience, it leads to daily repentance. The Gospel, however, just as it preserves and increases the faith bestowed in conversion, so it confers ever greater spiritual strength for the acts of charity and other virtues, and lifts up the spirit that is wavering under the sense of imperfect obedience and sin. See 11. 1. chap. VI. § 9. Conf. blessed Musaeus, Preface to the Treatise against Stengelius, quire B. I. b. That which they commonly establish as the third use of the law and call didactic, namely in a special sense, since otherwise the law can also be said to teach in the first and second use. Luther: "As the law is given without doubt so that it should not be rejected, but taught, in order that through it people may recognize both sin and death or the wrath of God, so it is also given to the godly, insofar as they have not died and still live in the flesh. In Christ, raised from the dead, there is certainly no sin, no death, no law, to which He was nevertheless subject in life. But this same Lord Christ is not yet perfectly raised in His saints; indeed, He begins in them as the firstfruits to rise from the dead. In the ungodly, however, who are mingled in the church—and their number is greater than that of the pious—He is still dead in all things; indeed, He is nothing at all in them. These same people are simply under the law and must be terrified by the law, indeed, if it were possible, with physical thunderclaps. Insofar as Christ is raised in us, we are without law, sin, and death. But insofar as He is not yet raised in us, we are and remain under the law, sin, and death. Therefore, the law (as also the Gospel) must be preached without distinction to both the righteous or believers and the ungodly. To the ungodly, so that they may thereby be terrified and recognize their sin, death, and the unavoidable wrath of God, by which they are humbled. To the godly, so that they may thereby be reminded to crucify and put to death their flesh together with its desires and vices, so that they do not become secure. Gal. 5:24. For security takes away both faith and the fear of God and causes the last state to become worse than the first." (Fifth Disputation against the Antinomians. 1539. XX, 2055. sq.) Cf. Article VI of the Formula of Concord concerning the third use of the divine law. ANTITHESIS. Hutterus: Antithesis: "That Islebius and his accomplices spread such doctrines, the blessed Luther is a witness worthy of faith, who in Vol. I of the Jena edition (Latin) assigns these emblems to them on pp. 554 and 555: '1. The law is not worthy to be called the Word of God. 2. If you are a harlot, if you are a fornicator, if you are an adulterer, only believe, and you are on the way of salvation. 3. The Decalogue belongs to the courthouse, not to the pulpit. 4. Those who have business with Moses are heading for the devil; therefore, Moses should be relegated to the gallows. 5. Men are not to be prepared for the Gospel through the law, but God does it' (namely, without the law). '6. As soon as such a thought enters your mind, that the state of the church ought to be such and such, or that Christians ought to be holy, righteous, pious, and chaste, then you have immediately strayed from the Gospel. 7. Re

one must side with those who teach that the Gospel is not to be preached unless souls have first been shattered and contrited by the Law. 8. The Law does not teach good works, nor is it to be preached so that we may do good works. 9. The Holy Spirit does not work conversion through the Law, but effects this by Himself without the ministry of the Law; nor is it the work of the Holy Spirit to convict the world of sin. 10. These phrases are not to be used in the Church of Christ: "Christian life," "Christian obedience," "works of Christians," because Christians cannot be recognized by their works or fruits." —

But what need is there to add more, when from these things the prodigious impiety of Antinomian fury shines forth more than enough? Some Anabaptists, who called themselves Libertines, attempted to defend this fury in the age of our fathers, and indeed in our own age as well, contending that there is no need for the regenerate person to regulate his life according to the norm of the divine Law, since he has been liberated from it and everything he proposes, thinks, and does is from the Spirit; indeed, they raved that it lay within the simple liberty of the regenerate man either to perform the precepts of the Law or to neglect them, because the regenerate man is entirely indifferent and free in regard to either.

Akin to this fury are the Schwenckfeldians, who, just as they simply reject every written Word of God and attribute everything to secret raptures or enthusiasms, so also do they turn away from the entire Law of God. (Explanation of the Books of Concord. 1611. pp. 503—505.)

Into which the regenerate are then carried by a spontaneous spirit, having a rule and norm for rightly ordering their life. See the example of David, Psalm 119 in its entirety.

Namely, once it is known through the Law what things are sins, and therefore must be distinguished from things to be done. For although the regenerate, insofar as they are such and regarding their spiritual powers, greatly desire to do good themselves and do not wait for threats by which they might be compelled; yet because, besides the spirit, the flesh also remains in them, it is necessary for this to be terrified, lest by resisting the spirit it should prevail.

For the Law always demands more and better things than we are able to provide. See here § 11. Which they commonly call the "standing" [Law], and which it is established that the regenerate have need of, from Chapter IV, § 20, note c.

For by the same causes through which faith is generated, it is also preserved. See Detailed Explanation, L. XIII, Q. 70, p. 578.

For just as, when faith apprehending the merit of Christ is kindled in the heart of a man contrited by the Gospel, at the same time love toward a propitious God also arises—which inclines the will of the regenerate man to love God above all things, to perform all things that are pleasing to God, to pursue with hatred and flee from those things that are adverse, to trust in God, to hope for every good thing from Him, to love and help one's neighbor for God's sake, etc.—so, when faith is increased and strengthened through the use of the Gospel, it is certain that these things also take on increments through the Gospel at the same time.

k) For it shows that our defects are supplied and our sins are covered by the perfect obedience of Christ, imputed to the faithful. PART III. CHAPTER VIII.

Latin:

Quod expresse dicitur Rom. 3, 20. Conf. c. VII. et h. 1. cap. IV. § 34. not. e. Vid. 1. c. nota f.

Quamvis enim mediatorem ipsa lex nesciat neque ostendere aut polliceri possit, facit tamen terroribus suis, ut' mens hominis de se juxta legem desperans alibi auxilium quaerat, undecunque illud affulserit. Lutherus: ,,Sie haben ihnen erdichtet einen neuen methodum, dass man solle zuerst die Gnade predigen, darnach Offenbarung des Zorns, auf dass man das Wort (Gesetze) ja nicht hören noch reden dürfe. Das ist ein fein Katzenstühlchen, gefallet ihnen trefflich wohl

und meinen, sie wollen die ganze Schrift hinein und heraus ziehen, und damit lux mundi werden. Solches soll und muss St. Paulus geben Röm. 1.; sehen aber nicht, wie St. Paulas gerade widersinnisch lehret, fähet an und zeigt erstlich den Zorn Gottes vom Himmel und macht alle Welt zu Sündern und schuldig vor Gott, darnach, so sie zu Sundern worden sind, lehret er sie, wie man Gnade erlanget und gerecht werde, wie die drei ersten Capitel gewaltiglicli und klärlich weisen.“ (Wider die Antinomer. 1539. XX, 2024.) Cf. supra annotata ad P. III. c. 6. § 15. p. 313.

Idem: ,,Es gehet uns die Kirche und Christus selbst, darzu auch ’die Gerechtigkeit nichts an, wo nicht erst die schädliche Vermessenheit überwunden und getödtet ist. Darum sind die Antinomer billig werth, dass ihnen jedermann feind sei, welche sich mit unserm Exempel auf halten ifnd vertheidigen wollen, so doch die Ursach am Tag ist, warum wir im Anfang also von Gottes Gnade gelehrt haben. Der verfluchte Pabst hatte die armen Gewissen mit seinen Menschensatzungen gar unterdrücket, hatte alle rechte Mittel, Hülfe und Trost, damit die armen verzagten Herzen wider die Verzweiflung hätten mögen gerettet werden, hinweg genommen; was sollten wir denn dazumal anders thun, denn die unterdrückten und beschwerten Herzen wiederum aufrichten und ihnen den rechten Trost Vorhalten? Wir wissen aber auch wohl, dass man anders reden muss mit denen, die da satt, zart und fett sein. Wir waren dazumal alle verstossen und sehr geplaget. Das Wasser in der Flaschen war aus, das ist, es war kein Trost vorhanden. Wir lagen wie die Sterbenden, gleichwie Ismael unter dem Strauch. Darum waren uns solche Lehrer vonnötlien, die uns Gottes Gnade vorhielten und lehreten, wie wir uns erquicken möchten. Die Antinomer aber wollen haben, dass man die Lehre von der Busse schlecht mit der Gnade anfangen soll, ich aber habe den Process so nicht gehalten. Denn ich wusste wohl, dass Ismael erst ausgetrieben und verzaget worden war, ehe denn er vom Engel den Trost gehört hat. Derohalben habe ich dem Exempel nachgefolget und niemand getröstet, denn nur allein die, so zuvor Reu und Leid über ihre Sünde gehabt und an ihnen selbst verzaget hatten, welche das Gesetz erschrecket, der Leviathan überfallen und gar bestürzt gemacht hatte.“ (Ausl, des 1. B. Mose. A. 1536—1545. I, 2143—45.)

Kromayerus: ,,Notamus, paedagogum ad Christum, ut lex vocatur Gal. 3,34., vel esse, qui directe vel qui per indirectum ad Christum nos adducit. Directe ad Christum nos ducit (quantum ad significationem), ut olim etiam in V. T., quantum ad observationem, lex ceremonialis, quae continebat ακιαντών μελλόντων, i.e., umbram futurarum; indirecte moralis, quia tantum indicat morbum et quaerere jubet medicum, quicunque tandem sit ille. Hunc vero nobis evangelium ostendit.“ (Th. posit.polem. I, 771.)

Conf. b. Mus. Tract. contra Steng. p. 736.

Lutherus: ,,Wie das Gesetz gegeben ist ohne Zweifel darum, dass es nieht verworfen, sondern gelehret solle werden, auf dass durch dasselbige die Leute beide Sünd und Tod oder den Zorn Gottes erkennen, also ists auch den Gottseligen gegeben, so ferne sie nicht gestorben und noch im Fleisch leben. In Christo, vom Tod auferweckt, ist gewisslich keine Sünde, kein Tod, kein Gesetz, welchen er doch im Leben unterworfen war. Aber derselbe unser Herr Christus ist noch nicht vollkömmlich auferweckt in seinen Heiligen, ja, fdhet in ihnen als Erstlingen an vom Tode aufzustehen. In den Gottlosen aber, so in der Kirche mit eingemenget sind und ihre Zahl grösser, denn der Frommen ist, ist er noch aller Dinge todt, ja, er ist gar nichts in ihnen. Dieselbigen sind schlechte unter dem Gesetz und müssen durch das Gesetz, ja, wo es möglich wäre, mit leiblichen Donnerschlägen erschreckt werden. Sofern nun Christus in uns auferweckt ist, sofern sind wir ohne Gesetz, Sünde und Tod. Sofern er aber in uns noch nicht auferweckt ist, sofern sind und bleiben wir unter dem Gesetz, Sünde und Tod. Darum muss das Gesetz (wie auch das Evangelium) ohne Unterscheid, beide den Gerechten oder Gläubigen und Gottlosen, gepredigt werden. Den Gottlosen, dass sie dadurch erschreckt, ihre Sünde, den Tod und unvermeidlichen Zorn Gottes, durch welchen sie gedemüthigt werden, erkennen. Den Gottseligen, dass sie dadurch erinnert werden, dass sie ihr Fleisch kreuzigen und tödten sammt den Lüsten und Lastern, dass sie nicht sicher werden. Gal. 5, 24. Denn Sicherheit nimmt hinweg beide Glauben und Gottesfurcht und macht, dass das letzte ärger wird, denn das erste war.“ (Fünfte Disp. wider die Antinomer. 1539. XX, 2055. sq.) Cf. Artic. VI.
