Sed quid opus est plura addere, cum ex istis furoris antinomici prodigiosa impietas plus satis elucescat? Hunc furorem patrum nostrorum, imo nostra quoque, aetate defendere conati fuerunt nonnulli Anabaptistae, qui se Libertinos appellabant, contendentes, haud opus esse, ut renatus vitam suam exigat ad normam legis divinae, siquidem ab illa sit liberatus et omne, quod proponit, cogitat, facit, illud sit ex spiritu; imo delirabant, in simplici libertate hominis renati positum esse, vel facere praecepta legis, vel eadem negligere, propterea quod renatus prorsus indifferens sit et liber in quodlibet.

Affines huic furori sunt Schwenckfeldiani, qui uti simpliciter omne verbum Dei scriptum repudiant et arcanis raptibus sive enthusiasmis omnia tribuunt, ita legem etiam Dei universam aversantur.“ (Libri Concordiae explicatio. 1611. p. 503—505.)

In quae deinde renati spiritu spontaneo feruntur, habentes regulam et normam vitae recte instituendae. Vid. exemplum Davidis, P8. 119. integro.

Nempe cognito per legem, quod sint peccata, ideoque ab agendis discernenda. Quamvis enim renati, quatenus tales et quoad vires spirituales, valde ipsi cupiant bene agere neque minas, quibus cogantur, expectent; quia tamen in illis, praeter spiritum, etiam caro superest, terreri hanc oportet, ne spiritui reluctando praevaleat.

Semper enim lex plura et meliora poscit, quam praestare queamus. Vid. h. 1. § 11. Quam vulgo stantium vocant et qua renatos opus habere constat ex cap. IV. § 20. nota c.

Per easdem enim causas, per quas generatur fides, etiam conservatur. Vid. Ausführl. Erklärung L. XlII. Q. 70. p. 578.

Nam sicut, quando fides meritum Christi apprehendens in corde hominis contriti per evangelium accenditur, simul etiam caritas erga Deum propitium oritur, quae voluntatem hominis renati ad Deum super omnia amandum et omnia, quae Deo grata sunt, praestanda, quae autem adversa sunt, odio prosequenda ac fugienda, in Deo etiam confidendum, bona quaevis ab eo speranda, proximum propter Deum diligendum et juvandum etc. inclinat: ita, quando per usum evangelii fides augetur et roboratur, haec quoque simul per evangelium incrementa capere certum est.

k) Ostendit enim, defectus nostros suppleri et peccata tegi per obedientiam Christi perfectam, fidelibus imputatam. PAET. III. CAP. VIII.


## 23 On the Sacraments in General

ON THE SACRAMENTS IN GENERAL. § I. Since, besides the Word of God, the sacraments are also instruments of regeneration, conversion, and renewal, and thus of the conferring, sealing, and increasing of faith, these must also be treated more distinctly. See Chapter IV, § 9. Loc. cit., § 34. Chapter VI, § 9.

Gerhard: "The most merciful God, consulting both the salvation of men and the weakness of our faith, not content to manifest His more than paternal will through the Word of evangelical promise, has furthermore given it confirmed by external signs, so that that which is proposed concerning our salvation in the Word, being confirmed by an external sign, might be apprehended by us with a firm and immovable faith, and every doubt might be excluded from our souls. 'If you were incorporeal,' writes Chrysostom (Hom. 60 to the people of Antioch and Hom. 83 on Matthew), 'God would have handed over to you the incorporeal gifts themselves in a naked manner; but since your soul is joined to a body, intelligible things are handed over to you in sensible ones.' Therefore, just as He had bound man to render Him due obedience—when he still stood in the state of concreated integrity—by both Word and external sign; so after the fall, He restored him by the Word of promise and confirmed his faith by an external sign, inasmuch as to the promise concerning the seed of the woman—that is, concerning the Messiah who would crush the head of the serpent, that is, who would destroy the works of the devil and restore the righteousness and life that had been lost by His own obedience and death—He added an external sign, namely, the rite of sacrificing, which we have proven with immovable evidence in the treatise *De Legibus Ceremonialibus et Forensibus*, § 14, to have been not devised by human judgment, but divinely sanctioned. ... After the flood, God proposes to Noah the Word of promise and adds the rainbow as a sign of the covenant (Gen. 9:13). There followed then the institution of circumcision (Gen. 17) and the paschal lamb (Ex. 12), to which in the New Testament succeeded Baptism and the Lord’s Supper, which are called 'sacraments or mysteries, visible words and visible signs of invisible grace' (Aug., *Contra Faustum*, Bk. 19, ch. 16, and *Quaest. in Levit.*, 84). For by them, that which is announced to the ears through the Word is, in a certain way, placed before the eyes." (*Loc. de sacramentis*, § 1, 2.)

Luther: "God has never wanted to have His worship in the world without external means. In the Old Testament, He gave the Jews a way by which one should find Him; there was a certain place of the tabernacle or the tent of meeting, the altar, the lampstand, the Levites, and God did not let Himself be found without external means and ways. He always proposed to them an external means, so that they might certainly find Him; He did not let them wander about in error without a way and external means. But, just as our enthusiasts now run about and depart from this way which God has given us in the New Testament, so the Jews also abandoned the same way and sought other paths. God cannot be our God unless He gives us something external in which we may find Him, such as the oral..."

the Word and the two Sacraments. If I do not grasp God through external things, how then can I encounter Him? Therefore, all heretics have been against the first commandment and have laid hands upon it with all manner of human works, and they cut out the promise and grace of God that is placed therein; indeed, they deny God Himself, rejecting the benefit and use, so that one might not come to grace." (Exposition on several chapters of the 5th book of Moses. A.D. 1529. Opp. Hal. III, 2503 sq.)

The same: "God has generally given, in all His promises, alongside the Word, also a sign for the greater assurance or strengthening of our faith. Thus, He gave Noah the rainbow as a sign, Gen. 9:10, 13. To Abraham He gave circumcision as a sign, Gen. 17:16. To Gideon He gave the rain upon the land and the fleece, Judg. 6:37 ff., and so on; one finds many such signs given in Scripture alongside the promises. For this is also done in worldly testaments, that not only are the words written down, but seals and notary marks are also attached to them, so that it may be constant and credible. Thus, Christ also has done in this Testament and has attached a powerful, most noble seal and sign to and in the words; that is His own true flesh and blood under the bread and wine. For we poor humans, because we live in the five senses, must at the very least have an external sign alongside the words, by which we may hold fast and come together, yet so that the same sign be a Sacrament—that is, that it be external and yet have and signify spiritual things, so that we may be drawn through the external into the spiritual; to grasp the external with the eyes of the body, and the spiritual inwardly with the eyes of the heart." (Sermon on the New Testament. A.D. 1520. Ib. XIX, 1274.) Cf. Luther’s Collected Works. Erlangen. Vol. XLVII, 82 sq.

Gerhardus: "It can be said without any absurdity that the tree of life was for our first parents like a sacrament and a symbol of immortality. For although that sacrament was not a remedy for sin (such as are the sacraments properly so-called after the fall), nevertheless it was a sign of divine grace. Therefore, omitting the figurative, temporary, and analogically so-called ancient sacraments—such as the tree of life before the fall, the passage through the Red Sea, the eating of manna, the eruption of water from the rock, and even the preservation in the ark at the time of the flood, the dew on Gideon’s fleece, the shadow of the sun in the sundial of Ahaz going backward, etc.—we shall treat of the ordinary, perpetual, and properly so-called sacraments of the O.T., namely, circumcision and the paschal lamb." (Loc. de circumcis. § 7.) §

2. The term *sacramentum* is ecclesiastical, when it is understood of sacred rites, which are signs and means or instruments of conferring and sealing grace. It is not read expressly in the Scriptures; but just as it is of Latin origin, so in the Hebrew and Greek language, and specifically in the books of the O. and N. T., there has not yet been found a certain word that corresponds exactly to it. And although the word *sacramentum* occurs in the Latin version of the Bibles, yet it is not properly used specifically for those external and visible signs of grace of which we treat in this place, but was transferred to them only by ecclesiastical writers, says the blessed Gerhard, L. d. Sacram. § 5. Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.26 PART. III. CHAP. VIII.

Gerhard: "Far be it from us to approve the error of Carlstadt, who wished to reject the term 'sacrament' simply because it is άγραφος [unwritten]; Dr. Luther refutes him diligently in his book against the celestial prophets. Bellarmine, in Book 1, Chapter 7, *De Sacramento*, attempts to prove that Luther initially abhorred this name, since in his book *De Captivitate Babylonica*, in the chapter on matrimony, he states: 'The name of sacrament is not found in Scripture in the signification in which it is used here.'

Yet both are true, and both are accepted by Luther; for although the name 'sacrament' is not found in the Scriptures, the thing itself denoted by this name is found in them. The case of the term 'sacrifice' is different, for neither the name nor the thing, or the proper requirements of the Holy Supper, are attributed to it in the Scriptures. Bellarmine would have acted more correctly had he ascribed the Carlstadtian rejection of this word to Zwingli; for the latter writes as follows in his book *De Vera Religione*, p. 2, *Opera* p. 197: 'I would greatly wish that this word "sacrament" had never been accepted by the Germans, unless it were understood in the German sense.' He adds the reason: 'For when they hear this word "sacrament," they immediately understand something great and holy, which by its own power frees the conscience from sin.'" (L. c. § 5.)

Among profane writers, it is read to have signified not only money deposited by litigants with a judge, to the end that he who had won might recover his own, and he who had lost his case would have his money ceded to the treasury, but also a wager of money to be paid by him who was defeated in judgment, and indeed even an oath, especially a military one. Tertullian seems to have had this latter meaning in mind; he was the first of the Latin fathers to use the word to denote the act by which those to be baptized bind themselves to God and religiously promise that they will faithfully and strenuously fight under the banners of Christ against Satan, in his book *De Corona Militis*. Hence it came about that not only the entire rite of baptism, but also the Holy Supper was called a sacrament, although this name has also been used more generally for any sacred and secret things, and likewise for signs of sacred things, even if instituted by men. Cf. the blessed Gerhard, l. c. § 3 and 7.

Gerhard: "In ecclesiastical usage, the term 'sacrament' is used primarily in three ways: 1. Most generally for an arcane and secret thing, as appears from the Latin translation of the Bible in 1 Tim. 3:16, Rev. 17:7, and elsewhere passim. In this sense, Tertullian, in Book 4 *Against Marcion*, calls Christianity the 'sacrament of the Christian religion.' Jerome, vol. 9, p. 59: 'The sacraments of God are to preach, to bless and confirm, to administer communion, to visit the sick, to pray.' Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm 33 and elsewhere passim, calls the mystical or allegorical exposition of Scripture a 'sacrament.'

2. More specially, it is taken for any sign of a sacred thing, even if it is not divinely instituted in the New Testament, but either taken from the Old, like chrism, or devised by pious men, like the sign of the cross. Augustine, in Book 2 *Against the Letters of Petilian*, chapter 104, calls 'anointing' a 'sacrament,' and says it must be distinguished from the invisible anointing of charity in Book 19 *Against Faustus*, c. 14; he counts the 'sign of the cross' among the sacraments in his exposition of Psalm 141, and adds the reason: 'because it is a cause of shame on the forehead, it establishes the very ignominy which the pagans mock in the place of our modesty, so that we may not be ashamed of the cross'; in Book 4 *De Symbolo ad Catechumenos*, c. 1, and in Ps. 65, he calls all the 'rites' that were used at that time in the action of 'baptism' sacraments. Hence Lombard defines it in general in Book 4, dist. 1, B: A sacrament is 'a sign of a sacred thing.'

Latin:

Caput VIII. DE SACRAMENTIS IN GENERE. § I. Cum, praeter verbum Dei, etiam sacramenta sint regenerationis, a conversionis b et renovationis,c atque adeo fidei conferendae, obsignandae et augendae organa, de his etiam distinctius agendum est. Vid. cap. IV. § 9. L. c. § 34. Cap. VI. § 9.

Gerhardus: ,,Misericordissimus Deus, et hominum saluti et fidei nostrae imbecillitati consulens, non contentus voluntatem suam plusquam paternam verbo evangelicae promissionis manifestare, externis insuper signis eandem confirmatam dedit, ut id, quod de salute nostra in verbo proponitur, externo signo confirmatum, firma et immota fide a nobis apprehenderetur, omnisque ex animis nostris dubitatio excluderetur. ,Si incorporeus esses‘, scribit Chrysost. hom. 60. ad pop. Antioch. et hom. 83. in Matth., ,nude tibi ipsa dona incorporea (Deus) tradidisset, quoniam vero conjuncta corpori est anima tua, in sensibilibus intelligenda tibi traduntur.‘ Ut ergo hominem, cum in statu concreatae integritatis adhuc consisteret, et verbo et signo externo ad debitum obsequium sibi praestandum astrinxerat; ita post lapsum et verbo promissionis eundem restituit et signo externo fidem ejus confirmavit, siquidem promissioni de semine mulieris, hoc est, de messia, caput serpentis contrituro, hoc est, opera diaboli destructuro ac sua obedientia et morte amissam justitiam et vitam restituturo, addidit signum externum, ritum scilicet sacrificandi, quem non'liumano arbitrio excogitatum, sed divinitus sancitum fuisse, immotis documentis in tract. de Legg. cerem, et forens. § 14. comprobavimus. . . Post diluvium proponit Deus Noae verbum promissionis et arcum coelestem addit in signum foederis Gen. 9,13. Secuta deinde fuit institutio circumcisionis Gen. 17. et agni paschalis Exo. 12., quibus in N. T. successit baptismus et coena dominica, quae dicuntur,sacramenta sive mysteria, verba visibilia et invisibilis gratiae visibilia signa‘, Aug. 19. contra Faustum cap. 16. et in Levit, quaest. 84. Siquidem per ea oculis quodammodo subjicitur, quod auribus per verbum annunciatur.“ (Loc. de sacramentis, §1.2.)

Lutherus: ,,Gott hat nie ohne äusserliche Mittel seinen Gottesdienst in der Welt haben wollen. Im Alten Testament hat er den Juden eine Weise gegeben, darbei man ihn sollte finden; da war ein gewisser Ort des Tabernakels oder Hütten des Stifts, der Altar, Leuchter, die Leviten, und liess Gott sich nicht finden ohne äusserliche Mittel und Weise. Er hat ihnen allewege ein äuss,erliches Mittel vorgeschlagen, damit sie ihn ja finden sollten; er liess sie nicht ohne Weise und äusserlich Mittel in der Irre herumgehen. Aber, wie unsere Schwärmer jetzt laufen und lassen von dieser Weise, welche uns Gott gegeben hat im Neuen Testament, also verliessen die Juden auch dieselbige Weise und suchten andere Wege. Gott kann nicht unser Gott sein, er gebe uns denn etwas Aeusserliches, daran wir ihn finden, als, das münd

liehe Wort und die zwei Sacramente. Wenn ich Gott nicht ergreife durch äusserliche Ding, wie kann ich ihn denn antreffen? Darum sind alle Ketzer wider das erste Gebot gewesen und haben sich daran vergriffen in allerlei Menschenwerken und schneiden aus die Verheissung und Gnade Gottes, so darein gesteckt ist, ja, verleugnen Gott selbst, verwerfen den Nutzen und Brauch, dass man zu der Gnade nicht kommen möge.“ (Auslegung über etliche Capp. des δ. B. Mose. A. 1529. Opp. Hal. III, 2503. sq.)

Idem: ,,Gott hat in allen seinen Zusagen gemeiniglich neben dem Wort auch ein Zeichen geben zu mehrer Sicherung oder Stärke unsers Glaubens. Also gab er Noä zum Zeichen den Regenbogen, 1 Mos. 9, 10. 13. Abrahä gab er die Beschneidung zum Zeichen, 1 Mos. 17, 16. Gideon gab er den Regen auf das Land und Lammfell, Rieht. 6, 37. ff., und so fortan findet man viel derselben Zeichen in der Schrift neben den Zusagen geben. Denn also thut man auch in weltlichen Testamenten, dass nicht allein die Worte schriftlich verfasst, sondern auch Siegel und Notarienzeichen daran gehängt werden, dass es je beständig und glaubwürdig sei. Also hat auch Christus in diesem Testament gethan und ein kräftiges alleredelstes Siegel und Zeichen an und in die Worte gehängt; das ist sein eigen wahrhaftig Fleisch und Blut unter dem Brot und Wein. Denn wir arme Menschen, weil wir in den fünf Sinnen leben, müssen je zum wenigsten ein äusserlich Zeichen haben neben den Worten, daran wir uns halten und zusammen kommen mögen, doch also, dass dasselbe Zeichen ein Sacrament sei, das ist, dass es äusserlich sei und doch geistliche Dinge habe und bedeute, damit wir durch das Aeusserliche in das Geistliche gezogen werden; das Aeusserliche mit den Augen des Leibes, das Geistliche innerlich mit den Augen des Herzens begreifen.“ (Sermon von dem Neuen Testament. A. 1520. Ib. XIX, 1274.) Cf. Luthers sämmtliche Werke. Erlangen. P. XLVII, 82. sq.

Gerhardus: ,,Sine ulla absurditate dici potest, arborem vitae primis parentibus fuisse instar sacramenti et symboli immortalitatis. Quamvis enim sacramentum illud non fuit peccati remedium (qualia sunt proprie dicta sacramenta post lapsum), tamen fuit gratiae divinae signum. Omissis ergo κηφικοϊς, temporariis atque analogice sic dictis veteribus sacramentis, qualia sunt arbor vitae ante lapsum, transitus per mare rubrum, esus mannae, aquae de petra eruptio, quin et conservatio in arca tempore diluvii, ros in vellere Gideonis, umbra solis in horologia Achas retrograda etc., de ordinariis, perpetuis et proprie sic dictis V. T. sacramentis, videlicet circumcisione et agno paschali, agemus.“ (Loc. de circumcis. § 7.) §

2. Vox sacramenti a ecclesiastica est, cum de ritibus sacris,b qui sunt signa c et media sive organa conferendae et obsignandae gratiae, accipitur.d In Scripturis expresse non legitur; sed sicut origine latina est, ita in ebraeo atque graeco sermone, ac speciatim in libris V. ac N. T. non reperta est hactenus vox certa, quae illi exacte respondeat. Et quamvis vox sacramenti in latina bibliorum versione occurrat, proprie iamen ei specifice non usurpatur de externis illis ac visibilibus gratiae signis, de quibus hoc loco agimus, sed a scriptoribus ecclesiasticis ad ea demum translata est, ait b. Gerh. L. d. Sacram. § 5. Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.26 PART. III. CAP. VIII.

Gerhardus: ,,Absit, ut öarolstadii errorem probemus, qui sacramenti appellationem, cum sit άγραφος, simpliciter rejectam voluit; quem diligenter refellit D. Lutherus in lib. contra coel. proph. Bellarm. 1. 1. de sacram, c. 7. probare conatur, Lutherum initio ab hoc nomine abhorruisse, cum in lib. de capt. Babyl. cap. de matrim. statuat, ,in Scriptura non haberi nomen sacramenti in ea significatione, qua hic usurpatur.‘

Atqui utrumque verum, utrumque a Luthero acceptatur; quamvis enim nomen sacramenti non habeatur in Scripturis, tamen res ipsa hoc nomine denotata in eis habetur. Alia ratio est appellationis,sacrificii‘, cujus nec nomen, nec res sive propria requisita sacrae coenae in Scripturis tribuuntur. Rectius fecisset Bellarminus, si Cinglio Carolstadianam hujus vocabuli rejectionem asscripsisset; is enim in lib. de vera religione p. 2., Operum p. 197. sic scribit: ,Vocem istam sacramenti magnopere cupiam Germanis nunquam fecisse receptam, nisi germane esset accepta.‘ Rationem subjungit: ,Cum enim hanc vocem sacramentum audiunt, jam aliquid magnum sanctumque intelligunt, quod vi sua conscientiam a peccato liberet.‘ “ (L. c. § 5.)

Apud profanos scriptores legitur significasse non solum pecuntam, a litigantibus apud judicem depositam, eo fine, ut, qui vicisset, suam reciperet, qui causa cecidisset, ejus pecunia fisco cederet, sed et sponsionem solvendae ab eo, qui judicio victus fuerit, pecuniae, imo et juramentum, praecipue militare. Postremam significationem respexisse videtur Tertullianus, qui primus Latinorum patrum ad denotandum actum, quo baptizandi Deo se obligant et fideliter ac strenue sub vexillis Christi contra satanam pugnaturos religiose promittunt, vocem adhibuit, L. de Corona militis. Unde factum est, ut non solum ritus totus baptismi, sed et 8. coenae sacramentum diceretur, quamquam et alias hoc nomen generalius ad res sacras et secretas quasvis, itemque signa rerum sacrarum, etsi ab hominibus instituta, adhibitum sit. Conf. b. Gerhard. 1. c. § 3. et 7.

Gerhardus: ״In usu ecclesiastico sacramenti vocabulum tripliciter potissimum usurpatur: 1. Generalissime pro re arcana et secreta, ut apparet ex latina bibliorum translatione 1 Tim. 3, 16. Apoc. 17, 7. et alibi passim. Hoc sensu Tertullianus lib. 4. contra Marcion. christianismum vocat,religionis Christianae sacramentum‘. Hieron. tom. 9. p. 59. ,Sacramenta Dei sunt praedicare, benedicere ac confirmare, communionem reddere, visitare infirmos, orare.‘ Augustin. in enarr. Psal. 33. et alibi passim mysticam sive allegoricam Scripturae expositionem vocat,sacramentum‘.

2. Specialius accipitur pro quavis rei sacrae signo, si vel maxime non sit divinitus in N. T. institutum, sed vel ex veteri desumptum, ut chrisma, vel a piis viris excogitatum, ut signum crucis. Aug. lib. 2. contra lit. Petii, cap. 104. ,unctionem‘ appellat,sacramentum‘, idque discernendum dicit ab invisibili unctione caritatis lib. 19. contra Faustum c. 14.; ,signum crucis‘ inter sacramenta numerat in enarr. Psal. 141., et addit rationem: ,quia in fronte erubescitur, ipsam ignominiam quodammodo et quam pagani derident, in loco pudoris nostri constituit, ne de cruce erubescamus‘; lib. 4. de Symb. ad Catechum. c. 1. et in Ps. 65. omnes,ritus‘, qui in actione,baptismi‘ tunc temporis adhibebantur, vocat sacramenta. Inde Lomb. in genere definit lib. dist. 1. B.: Sacramentum est,sacrae rei signum‘.


### On the Sacraments in General: Most specially and most properly, it is taken for a solemn action divinely…

3. Most specially and most properly, it is taken for a solemn action divinely instituted, in which the proper promise of the Gospel is applied and sealed through an external and visible sign; in this sense, only two sacraments of the New Testament are counted: baptism and the Lord's Supper. Augustine, Book 3 *De Doctrina Christiana*, c. 9: 'The Lord himself and apostolic discipline have handed down a few things instead of many, and those most easy to perform, most august to understand, and most chaste to observe, such as the sacrament of baptism and the celebration of the body and blood of the Lord.'" (*Loc. de sacr.* § 6.)

OF THE SACRAMENTS IN GENERAL They are expressly called so in the Augsburg Confession, Art. XIII, partly because they are marks of profession among men, and partly and especially by virtue of divine institution, so that they may be signs and testimonies of the will of God toward us, proposed to excite and confirm faith in those who use them.

And the blessed G. Mylius, on Chapter IV, 12 of the Epistle to the Romans, p. 200, writes: "If we wish to call the sacraments by the proper term of the Scriptures, we shall simply call them signs. However, sacraments are signs, not by reason of an earthly thing present being referred to an absent heavenly thing (for in the Holy Supper this is also substantially present), but because the action occupied with the external thing and the subject, or man, signifies a spiritual action which God is about to perform through the external rite, when man does not resist. Although the external thing itself, or the earthly matter, can also be a sign of the heavenly matter, which is indeed substantially but invisibly present." This is to be observed entirely. "

For the sacraments are not merely naked signs, mere σημαντιχά [signifying things], but at the same time instruments through which the Spirit is given, who effects or confirms faith, according to Art. V of the Augsburg Confession." And the blessed Mylius, loc. cit., p. 199, dealing with the Sacrament of Circumcision, wrote that God did not wish to deal with the patriarch (Abraham) by word alone, but also by a visible sign, so that grace might flow into the mind of the patriarch, NB, not only through hearing, but also through a visible mark, so that by the intuition of that sign his mind might be rendered even more certain and confirmed concerning the righteousness freely received through faith. These things indeed pertain not only to Abraham alone, nor to circumcision alone, but likewise to all sacraments and to men who rightly use the sacraments.

Gerhardus: "It appears that the genus in the definition of a sacrament is established by Bellarmine as a 'sign.' Although we do not unwillingly admit that sacraments, by reason of their office and end, are and can be called signs, because they signify, effect, apply, and seal the benefits of the Gospel to those using them by faith, nevertheless we deny that the proximate and adequate genus of a sacrament is a 'sign.' 1. Because the thing itself is one thing, its office and end another; its appellation from its office is one thing, its definition from its essence another. A definition is a λόγος ουσίας [account of the essence]; therefore, the genus in a definition ought to be sought from the essence of the thing defined; but now, to be a sign does not pertain to the quiddity of a sacrament, but to its end and use. Therefore, it is not a true and proper genus. 2. A definition ought to consist of things prior and better known. That sacraments are signs and seals is not from things prior and better known, because the knowledge of them depends upon the actions and ceremonies; for these, when joined with the end, which is to signify, are called signs and seals. 3. A proper genus ought to be proximate. But 'sign' is a remote genus of a sacrament, both because this denomination is sought from the end, and because they signify through the mediation of actions consisting of a certain word and an external element. 4. A part of a thing is not the genus of the thing as a whole. Signs that strike the eyes are a part of the sacraments, namely the earthly one, to which the invisible heavenly thing joined constitutes the sacrament properly so called. 5. A genus ought not to be ambiguous. But the word 'sign' is ambiguous, for it is used by some in the definition of a sacrament so that it may be denoted that the whole essence of the sacraments consists in signifying; but by others, so that the end of the sacraments, placed in signifying and sealing, may be expressed by this appellation.

Those who follow Calvin likewise define sacraments by signs. They establish a twofold signification in the sacraments: one, by which the earthly thing signifies an absent heavenly thing; the other, by which the entire sacrament signifies spiritual grace."

Cingi, lib. de peccato originis: "Signs are nothing but external things, by which nothing is effected in the conscience." In Con- PART III. CHAP. VIII.

Confession to the Emperor: "I believe, nay, I certainly know, that all sacraments are so far from conferring grace that they do not even bring or dispense it." Calvin in his Catechism: "A sacrament is nothing other than an external testimony of divine benevolence toward us, which figures spiritual graces by a visible sign." ...

The water of baptism is nowhere called a sign of spiritual washing, but regeneration is said to occur "of water and the Spirit" (John 3:5). We are said to be saved "by the washing of regeneration and renewing" (Titus 3:5). The church is said to be cleansed "with the washing of water by the word" (Eph. 5:27). Baptism is said to "save us" (1 Pet. 3:21). The eucharistic bread is not called a sign, but the "communion of the body," and the eucharistic wine is not called a sign, but the "communion of the blood of Christ" (1 Cor. 10:16); therefore, sacramental signs consist not merely in signifying, but in conferring and applying. ...

We place the sacraments in the category of action and seek the genus of the definition from the same, since the defined and the genus of the definition must be in the same category. Furthermore, we prove that a sacrament is an action: 1. From the divine institution of the individual sacraments, in which God expressly requires and prescribes an action. ...

But since there are various kinds of actions, it must be added that sacraments are divine, sacred, and solemn actions, namely because they are divinely instituted and because God acts with us in them, and conversely, we have business with God in them. ...

Furthermore, by this qualification (προσδιορισμῷ), that sacraments are sacred and solemn actions, this genus is in a way restricted and distinguished from any political, natural, or playful action, since this entire action depends upon God’s institution, and therefore it is sacred and solemn and requires due reverence." (Loc. de sacram. § 22—25.) §

3. For a true sacrament, properly and strictly so called, there is required: 1. that it be an action commanded by God; 2. that it have a visible element divinely prescribed; 3. that it have a promise of evangelical grace.

Indeed, the requirements of a sacrament in general, just as the name itself, are not expressly read in the Scriptures, but the general doctrine concerning the sacraments must be deduced from those things which are held in Scripture specifically concerning each one, as the blessed Gerhard warns (L. de Sacram. § 11.), where he also treats of the requirements of true and properly so-called sacraments first of all by this reasoning, and alleges the words of the blessed Chemnitz (P. II. Exam. Conc. Trid. p. 14.): "Baptism and the Eucharist are by the confession of all truly and properly sacraments: from them, therefore, we shall gather what is required as substantial, so that something may be truly and properly a sacrament (of the New Testament). For this will be the simplest and most certain demonstration." Thus, therefore, from the common concepts of those things which are without doubt sacraments, in which these agree, it is recognized that those things which are perhaps called sacraments, but do not have those common requirements, are not sacraments of the same nature and essence as those which are properly so called, but are called so equivocally.

Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Detailed Explanation*, L. XVI. Qu. 81. p. 667, 668, and the blessed D. Carpzov, *Inaugural Dissertation on the Sacraments in General*, Aphorism I, *Refutation of the Papists* § 6, whom the blessed Scherzer follows in *Brev. Hülsem. auct.*, chap. X, Thes. III, p. 549. And indeed, it is necessary that a mandate of this kind exist expressly in the Scriptures.

Or a certain thing or substance, corporeal and sensible, about which the external act or rite of the sacrament is occupied in a sacred manner.

Which is concerning the remission of sins and the spiritual benefits connected therewith. Quenstedtius: "The human nature of Christ, which has been assumed, is not to be excluded from the institution and dispensation of the sacraments of the New Testament. For according to that nature, 'all authority in heaven and on earth' belongs to Christ; according to it, the power to institute sacraments also belongs to Him; but according to the human nature, by virtue of the personal union, all authority belongs to Him, Matt. 28:18. Therefore. The minor premise is proved from the word 'given'; for that which was given to Christ in time was given to Him according to His human nature; but all authority, etc., was given to Him. Therefore, also the power to institute sacraments. However, this power does not belong to Christ according to His humanity organically and by delegated authority, as Bellarmine (1.1. de Sac. c. 23, where he says: 'Christ's humanity is an instrument conjoined hypostatically to the divinity, and therefore a certain ministerial power is attributed to Christ as man') and Becanus (c. 5. de Sacram, q. 1. n. 2.) maintain; but in a higher and communicative way, on account of the infinite virtue received from the hypostatic union." (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 3. s. 1. th. 5. f. 1032.) § 4.

The principal efficient cause of the sacraments is the Triune God, and Christ in the assumed flesh. Or He who not only by His own authority institutes and determines which actions or which rites, as means of grace, and how or in what manner they ought to be celebrated, and commands that they be celebrated (so that He is the cause, both as to the species and as to the exercise of the act), but also elevates the sacraments themselves, as organs, to confer spiritual grace.

And He indeed alone; who alone is the author of grace, and therefore alone can define the means through which He wills to confer that grace which He freely bestows, and alone can communicate to them the infinite power by which the sacraments are rendered apt for conferring grace. Luther: "When the devil saw that God was building such a holy Church, he did not rest, but built his chapel right next to it, larger than God's Church, and did this: he saw that God took external things, such as Baptism, the Word, the Sacrament, the Keys, etc., by which He sanctified His Church (for he is always God's ape and wants to imitate all of God's things and make them better), so he also took external things for himself, which were also supposed to sanctify, just as he does with weather-makers, sorcerers, exorcists, etc.; there he also allows the Lord's Prayer to be prayed and the Gospel to be read over them, so that it might be a great sanctuary. Thus, through the Popes and Papists, he has had water, salt, candles, herbs, bells, images, Agnus Dei, palls, altars, chasubles, patens, fingers, hands consecrated or sanctified; who can recount it all? Finally, even monks' cowls are so sanctified that many people have died and been buried in them, as if they wanted to be saved thereby. Now, it would be fine if one were to speak God's Word, blessing, or prayer over a creature, as children do at the table, and

Latin:

3. Specialissime et maxime proprie.accipitur pro solenni actione divinitus instituta, in qua per externum et visibile signum applicatur et obsignatur promissio evangelii propria, quo sensu duo tantum N. T. numerantur sacramenta, baptismus et coena domini. Aug. lib. 3. de doctr. christ. c. 9.: ,Pauca pro multis, eaque factu facillima et intellectu augustissima et observatione castissima ipse Dominus et apostolica tradidit disciplina, sicut est baptismi sacramentum et celebratio corporis et sanguinis Domini.‘“

DE SACRAMENTIS IN GENERAL Sic expresse appellantur in August. Conf. art. XIII., partim videlicet, quod sint notae professionis inter homines, partim et praecipue ex vi divinae institutionis, ut sint signa et testimonia voluntatis Dei erga nos ad excitandam et confirmandam fidem in his, qui utuntur, proposita>

Et b. G. Mylius ad cap. IV, 12. Epist ad Rom. p. 200. scribit: Sacramenta si proprio Scripturarum vocabulo appellare velimus, signa simpliciter appellabimus. Sunt autem sacramenta signa, non ratione rei terrenae praesentis, ad rem coelestem absentem referendae (haec enim in s. coena etiam substantialiter praesens est), sed quod actio circa rem externam et subjectum seu hominem occupata significet actionem spiritualem, quam Deus raediante ritu externo praestiturus est, quando homo non repugnat. Quamquam et ipsa res externa seu materia terrena signum materiae coelestis, substantialiter quidem sed invisibiliter praesentis, esse potest. Quod omnino observandum est. '

Neque enim sacramenta nihil aliud sunt, quam signa nuda, mere σημαντιχά, sed simul instrumenta, per quae donatur Spiritus, qui fidem efficit aut confirmat, juxta Art. V. Aug. Confess. Et b. Mylius 1. c. p. 199. de Sacramento Circumcisionis agens scripsit, noluisse Deum verbo duntaxat agere cum patriarcha (Abrahamo), sed visibili etiam signo, ut non per auditum tantum, 8ed per visibilem etiam notam gratia coelestis animo patriarchae NB. influeret, adeo ut signi istius intuitu certior etiam et confirmatior redderetur ipsius animus de justitia per fidem gratuito accepta. Quae quidem nec ad solum Abrahamum, neque circumcisionem solam, sed ad omnia sacramenta et sacramentis recte utentes homines similiter spectant.

Gerhardus: ,,Apparet, genus in definitione sacramenti a Bellarmino constitui signum. Quamvis vero non inviti fateamur, sacramenta ratione officii et finis esse ac dici posse signa, quia significant, efficiunt, applicant et obsignant fide utentibus beneficia evangelii propria, tamen proximum et adaequatum sacramenti genus negamus esse signum. 1. Quia aliud est res ipsa, aliud ejus officium ac finis, aliud appellatio ejus ex officio, aliud definitio ex essentia. Definitio est λόγος ουσίας, ergo genus in definitione peti debet ex rei definitae essentia; jam vero esse signum non pertinet ad quidditatem sacramenti, sed ad ejus finem et usum. Ergo non est genus verum et proprium. 2. Definitio debet constare ex prioribus et notioribus. Sacramenta esse signa et sigilla, non est ex prioribus et notioribus, quia ipsorum cognitio pendet ex actionibus et ceremoniis; hae enim cum fine, qui est signare, conjunctae dicuntur signa et sigilla. 3. Proprium genus debet esse propinquum. Signum autem est genus sacramenti remotum, tum quia a fine petita est haec denominatio, tum quia mediantibus actionibus certo verbo et externo elemento constantibus signant. 4. Pars rei non est genus rei ut totius. Signa in oculos incurrentia sunt pars sacramentorum, una terrena scilicet, cui adjuncta res coelestis invisibilis sacramentum proprie dictum constituit, δ. Genus non debet esse ambiguum. Atqui vox signi est ambigua, usurpatur enim a quibusdam in definitione sacramenti, ut denotetur sacramentorum totam essentiam in significando consistere; ab aliis vero, ut finis sacramentorum in significando et obsignando positus hac appellatione exprimatur.

Qui Calvinum sequuntur, itidem sacramenta definiunt per signa. Duplicem autem significationem in sacramentis constituunt; unam, qua res terrena significet rem coelestem absentem; alteram, qua integrum sacramentum significet gratiam spiritualem.

Cingi, lib. de peccato originis: ,Signa nihil quam externae res sunt, quibus in conscientia nihil efficitur.‘ In ConPART. III. CAP. VIII.

fess. ad Imp.: ,Credo, imo certo scio, omnia sacramenta tam abesse ut gratiam conferant, ut ne afferant quidem et dispensent.‘ Calvinus in Catech.: ,Sacramentum nihil aliud est, quam externa divinae erga nos benevolentiae testificatio, quae visibili signo spirituales gratias figurat.‘ .' . .

Aqua baptismatis nullibi dicitur signum spiritualis ablutionis, sed,ex aqua et spiritu‘ dicitur fieri regeneratio Joh. 3, 5. ,Per lavacrum regenerationis et renovationis salvari‘ dicimur Tit. 3, 5. ,Lavacro aquae in verbo mundari‘ dicitur ecclesia Eph. 5, 27. ,Baptisma nos salvare‘ dicitur 1 Pet. 3, 21. Panis eucharisticus non dicitur signum, sed,communicatio corporis‘ et vinum eucharisticum non dicitur signum, sed,communicatio sanguinis Christi‘, 1 Cor. 10, 16.; utique ergo non in significando tantum, sed in conferendo et applicando signa sacramentalia consistunt. . .

Sacramenta nos ponimus in praedicamento actionis et ex eodem genus definitionis petimus, cum definitum et genus definitionis in eodem oporteat esse praedicamento. Ceterum sacramentum esse actionem, probamus: 1. Ex institutione divina singulorum sacramentorum, in qua Deus expresse requirit et praescribit actionem. . .

Cum autem varia sunt actionum genera, ideo addendum, quod sacramenta sint actiones divinae, sacrae et solennes, nimirum quia divinitus sunt institutae et quia Deus nobiscum in illis agit et vicissim cum Deo nobis in illis res est. . .

Praeterea hoc 7rροςδωρισμψ, quod sacramenta sint actiones sacrae et solennes, restringitur quodammodo hoc genus et distinguitur a quavis actione politica naturali ac ludicra, cum tota haec actio ex Dei institutione dependeat, ideoque sacra sit et solennis ac reverentiam debitam requirat.“ (Loc. de sacram. § 22—25.) §

3. Requiritur a vero ad sacramentum proprie et stricte sic dictum, 1. ut sit actio a Deo mandata; b 2. ut habeat elementum c visibile divinitus praescriptum; 3. ut habeat promissionem gratiae d evangelicae.

Equidem requisita sacramenti in genere, aeque ac nomen ipsum, in Scripturis expresse non leguntur, sed generalis doctrina de sacramerdis ex iis, quae in specie de singulis in Scriptura habentur, deducenda est, monente b. Gerhardo L. de Sacram. § 11., ubi etiam hac ratione primo omnium de requisitis verarum et proprie sie dictorum sacramentorum tractat, et allegat verba b. Chemnitii P. II. Exam. Cone. Trid. p. 14.: Baptismus et eucharistia omnium confessione vere et proprie sunt sacramenta: inde igitur colligemus, quae tanquam substantialia requirantur, ut aliquid vere et proprie sit sacramentum (N. Test.). Haec enim erit simplidssima et certissima demonstratio. Sic ergo ex eorum, quae sine dubio sacramenta sunt, conceptibus communibus, in quibus ista conveniunt, cognoscitur, ea, quae forte dicuntur sacramenta, requisita autem illa communia non habent, non esse ejusdem rationis et quidditatis sacramenta cum his, quae proprie sic dicuntur, verum aequivoce sic dicta.

Conf. b. Mus. Ausführliche Erklärung L. XVI. Qu. 81. p. 667. 668. et b. D. Garpzov. Disp. Inaug. de Sacram, in Genere, Aphorisrai I. Pontificii Confutatione § 6., quem sequitur b. Scherzerus Brev. Hülsem. auct. cap. X. Thes. III. p. 549. Et quidem expresse in Scripturis mandatum ejusmodi extare, necesse est.

Sive rem aut substantiam quandam, corpoream et sensibilem, circa quam sacro modo tractandam occupetur actus externus aut ritus sacramenti.

Quae est de remissione peccatorum et beneficiis spiritualibus connexis. Quenstedtius: ,,Ab institutione et dispensatione sacramentorum N. T. assumta humana natura Christi non est excludenda. Secundum quam naturam enim Christo competit,omnis potestas in coelo et in terra‘, secundum eam etiam ipsi competit potestas instituendi sacramenta; sed secundum humanam naturam vi unionis personalis ipsi competit omnis potestas, Matth. 28, 8. Ergo. Minor probatur ex voce dationis; quod enim Christo in tempore datum est, id ei secundum humanam naturam datum est; sed omnis potestas etc. Ergo etiam potestas sacramenta instituendi. Non competit autem Christo haec potestas secundum humanitatem organice et potestate delegata, ut volunt Bellarminus 1.1. de Sac. c. 23. (ubi ait: ,Christi humanitas est instrumentum conjunctum divinitati hypostatice, et ideo Christo, ut homini, tribuitur quaedam potestas ministerialis‘) et Becanus c. 5. de Sacram, q. 1. n. 2.; sed altiori modo et communicative, ob virtutem infinitam ex unione hypostatica acceptam.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 3. s. 1. th. 5. f. 1032.) § 4.

Causa efficiens principalis a sacramentorum Deus b trinunus c est, et Christus in assumta d carne. Seu quae non solum sua auctoritate instituit ac determinat, quaenam actiones aut qui ritus, tanquam media gratiae, et quomodo aut qua ratione celebrari debeant, ac mandat, ut celebrentur (ita ut sit causa, cum quoad speciem, tum quoad exercitium actus), verum etiam sacramenta ipsa, tanquam organa, elevat ad gratiam spiritualem conferendam.

Et is quidem solus; qui solus auctor gratiae est, ideoque solus media, per quae gratiam illam, quam libere confert, conferre velit, definire potest, solus etiam vim infinitam, per quam sacramenta apta reddantur ad conferandam gratiam, communicare illis potest. Lutherus: ,,Da der Teufel sähe, dass Gott eine solche heilige Kirche bauete, feierte er nicht und baute seine Capelle dabei, grösser denn Gottes Kirche ist, und thät ihm also: er sähe, dass Gott äusserliehe Dinge nahm, als Taufe, Wort, Sacrament, Schlüssel u. s. w., dadurch er seine Kirche heiligte (wie er denn allezeit Gottes Affe ist und will alle Dinge Gotte nachthun und ein bessers machen), nahm er auch äusserlich Ding vor sich, die sollten auch heiligen, gleichwie er thut bei den Wettermachern, Zauberern, Teufelsbannern u. s. w.; da lässt er auch wohl das VaterUnser beten und Evangelium über lesen, auf dass es gross Heiligthum sei. Also hat er durch die Päbste und Papisten lassen weihen oder heiligen Wasser, Salz, Kerzen, Kräuter, Glocken, Bilder, Agnus Dei, Pallia, Altar, Casein, Platten, Finger, Hände; wer wills alles erzählen? zuletzt die Mönchskappen so heiligen, dass viel Leute drin gestorben und begraben sind, als wollten sie dadurch selig werden. Nun wäre das wohl fein, wenn man Gottes Wort, Segen oder Gebet über die Creatur spräche, wie die Kinder über Tische thun, und


### On the Sacraments in General: over themselves when they go to sleep and rise, of which St

over themselves when they go to sleep and rise, of which St. Paul says in 1 Tim. 4:5: ‘Every creature is good and is sanctified by the word and prayer.’ For from this the creature does not receive a new power, but is confirmed in its former power. But the devil seeks something else; he wants the creature to receive a new power and might through his monkey-tricks. Just as water becomes a Baptism through God’s Word, a bath for eternal life, which washes away sin and saves—which is not the nature or power of the water—and bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, and sins are forgiven through the laying on of hands according to God’s institution, so the devil also wants his juggling and monkey-tricks to be powerful and to do something beyond nature. Holy water is supposed to blot out sin, it is supposed to drive out devils, it is supposed to ward off poltergeists, it is supposed to protect the woman in childbirth, as the Pope teaches us, etc. *Aquam sale*; so holy salt is also supposed to do this; the *Agnus Dei*, consecrated by the Pope, is supposed to do more than God Himself is able to do...

Therefore, the *ecclesia*, the holy Christian people, does not have mere external words, sacraments, or offices, as God’s ape, Satan, also and even more has, but has them commanded, instituted, and ordained by God, so that He Himself (no angel) intends to work through them with the Holy Spirit... Such a piece is missing in the devil’s sacraments and churches; there no one can say: God has commanded, ordered, instituted, and established it; He Himself wants to be there and Himself do everything; rather, one must say: God has not commanded it, but forbidden it; men have invented it, or rather, God’s ape has invented it and thereby seduced the people. For he also works nothing but what is temporal, or where it is supposed to be spiritual, it is vain deception. For he cannot thereby eternally forgive sin and save, as he lies, through holy water, masses, and monkery, even if he can let a cow get back its milk, which he himself previously stole through his prophetess and priestess.” (On the Councils and the Church. 1539. Opp. Wal. XVI, 2807 sqq. 2811. 2812.)

Indeed, those things which we have said concerning the institution, mandate, and concurrence of God, behave by way of an *opus ad extra* [work toward the outside], Namely, with respect to the sacraments of the N. Testament, concerning which we shall see distinctly in their proper place. §

5. The internal impulsive cause is the goodness of God; the external or meritorious cause is the merit of Christ. This is easily evident if we consider that the sacraments are means of grace. And furthermore, our theologians remind us that God looked upon our infirmity (which some therefore call the *prokatarktike* [pre-initiating] cause), from which it happens that we easily doubt the evangelical promises; therefore, out of His love for us, He was not content with the revelation of the Gospel, but wished to confirm with external signs what is taught in the Word concerning our salvation. Cf. the blessed Gerhard, *l. c.* § 1. 2. For thus, *en Christo*, in Christ, as Mediator, and thus on account of Him, we are blessed with every spiritual blessing according to Eph. 1:3, whence it is rightly inferred that we are also gifted with the sacramental means of grace on account of Him.

6. The less principal cause is ordinarily the minister of the church, but in a case of necessity, a layman or a woman. Or, that which constitutes the sacrament in use and applies it to the causing [of the effect], dependently indeed upon the authority, and exactly according to the institution, of the principal cause, God. Whence it is evident that that act is to be celebrated not through play and jest, but as a serious and holy thing, so that it may be sacramental, although the dignity or intention of the administrator is not therefore required for the truth and efficacy of the sacrament.

Smalcald Articles: “And the person does nothing at all toward such a Word and Office, commanded by Christ; let whoever will preach and teach it; where there are hearts that believe it and hold to it, to them it happens as they hear and believe.” (Tract. de potest. et prim. papae, p. 333.) Cf. Aug. Conf. art. VIII. p. 40. Apol. A. C. art. 4. p. 162. § 47.

Quenstedtius: “Concerning the intention of the minister, the dispute is more intricate. It is of decency that he who exhibits the sacraments should offer at the altar the intention of doing well what the Lord instituted, with a mind not wandering, but present. It is of necessity that the intention of Christ be observed in the external act. I say in the external act, for the internal intention of the minister to do what the church does is by no means necessary. For (1.) if no quality of the minister in general adds or takes away anything from the integrity of the sacrament, then the defect of intention will take nothing away from it, and presence will add nothing; (2.) thus human infidelity could render the faithfulness of God void, contrary to Paul, 1. c.; (3.) the greater the intention, the greater also would be the effect of the sacrament; (4.) just as the affection of the minister adds or takes away nothing from the audible Word, Phil. 1:17, so neither from the visible Word. A sermon, whether it proceeds from one intending not to preach, or preaching for an evil end, is equally efficacious; (5.) because no one could thus be certain of the baptism received.” (L. c. s. 1. th. 7. f. 1033. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Donatists, who ascribed the efficacy of the sacraments to the holiness and dignity of the ministers. See Augustine, 1. 7, against the Donatists. 2. Of the Anabaptists, who also require the holiness of the minister for the integrity of the sacrament, to whom is opposed the aphorism in the A. C. art. 8: ‘The sacraments and the Word are efficacious on account of the ordination and command of Christ, even if they are exhibited by evil men.’ 3. Of the Papists, who teach that for the integrity, truth, and virtue of the sacrament, the intention of the minister is required, which should regard not only the external act of conferring the sacrament according to the form of the institution, but also the very end and effect of the sacrament. For thus the Council of Trent, sess. 7, can. 11: ‘If anyone shall say that, while they perform and confer the sacraments, the intention at least of doing what the church does is not required, let him be anathema.’ . . . Note, however, that not all scholastics and Papists think and speak in the same way here. And there is a wonderful contradiction here in Papal doctrine; for they wish the sacraments to confer grace *ex opere operato* and to work grace infallibly, and yet they suspend not only their efficacy, but their entire existence, upon the intention of the ministers. Certainly, they fight among themselves wonderfully concerning the nature of that intention; for some require an actual one, others only a habitual one, others, establishing that the first is unnecessary and the second insufficient, urge a third entirely, which they call virtual. Thomas rests in the habitual, P. 3. q. 64. art. 8. But Scotus found a middle way between the actual and the habitual, which may be called vir- PART III. CHAP. VIII.

tual, which the Jesuits seize upon. 4. Of the innovators, who require the intention of the baptizer for the form of baptism, see D. Georg. Calixtus, Annotations on the aforementioned canon of the Council of Trent, p. 24, and in his disputation on Baptism, thesis 131, where the intention of the baptizer is required for the form of baptism. But observe: the words of the Tridentines, "The intention of doing what the Church does is required" (which D. Calixtus also sometimes uses), can be understood not only of the act itself but also of the end of the sacrament, which Bellarmine himself will not deny; see him in c. 28, § 17. And Chemnitz himself, in the place cited, shows that neither intention of the minister is necessarily required for the integrity of the sacrament. (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 1039.)

See 1 Cor. 4:1. Namely, the stewards of the mysteries of God are stewards not only of the Word but also of the sacraments, in which the benefits of God are hidden. Furthermore, Christ himself also, in the state of humiliation, administered one sacrament (that of the Supper) when He instituted it, just as He otherwise performed the office of teaching. For if a man cannot without danger of losing salvation be without the sacrament, and the ordinary minister is absent, it is better that what cannot be omitted without danger be done by another person than that a man who ought to be gifted with the sacrament should suffer loss. And God is efficacious through the sacraments, whoever it may be who administers them, provided he administers them rightly. See what will be said below concerning Circumcision and Baptism.

Luther: "The holy place or Church teaches, therefore, that neither priest nor Christian makes a single sacrament, not even the holy Christian Church herself... Thus, the baptizer does not make a baptism, but Christ has made it beforehand; the baptizer only reaches and gives it. For there stands Christ’s ordinance, which is, as St. Augustine says: 'The word comes to the element and it becomes a sacrament,' when one takes water and adds His word to it, then it is a baptism, as He commands in Matthew at the end, v. 19: 'Go therefore, teach all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.' This command and institution does it; they make it so that water and word are a baptism; our work or doing, *ex opere operato*, does not do it. For it is not called a baptism because I baptize or do the work, even if I were holier than St. John or an angel; but my baptizing is called a baptism because Christ’s word, command, and institution have so ordained that water and His word shall be a baptism...

Thus also, that bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood is not the fault of our doing, speaking, or work, much less of the chrism or consecration, but it is the fault of Christ’s ordinance, command, and institution; He Himself has commanded (as St. Paul says, 1 Cor. 11:23): When we come together and speak His words over bread and wine, it shall be His body and blood; so that we here also do nothing more than reach and give bread and wine with His words according to His command and institution. And such command and institution of His enables and effects that we do not reach and receive mere bread and wine, but His body and blood, as His words sound: 'This is my body, this is my blood'; so that it is not our work or speaking, but the command and order of Christ that makes the bread into the body and the wine into the blood, from the beginning of the first Supper until the end of the world, and it is daily reached through our service or office...

Latin:

über sich selbst, wenn sie schlafen gehen und aufstehen, davon St. Paulus sagt 1 Tim. 4, 5.: ,Alle Creatur ist gut und wird geheiligt durchs Wort und Gebet.‘ Denn daraus kriegt die Creatur keine neue Kraft, sondern wird bestätigt in ihrer vorigen Kraft. Aber der Teufel sucht ein anders, sondern will, dass durch sein Affenspiel die Creatur eine neue Kraft und Macht kriege. Gleichwie das Wasser durch Gottes Wort eine Taufe wird, ein Bad zum ewigen Leben, die Sünde ab wäscht und selig macht, welches ist nicht des Wassers Natur noch Macht, und Brot und Wein Leib und Blut Christi wird, durch Auflegen der Hände Sünden vergeben werden nach Gottes Einsetzung, also will der Teufel auch, dass sein Gaukelwerk und Affenspiel kräftig sei und über die Natur etwas thue. Weihwasser soll Sünde tilgen, es soll Teufel austreiben, soll den Poltergeistern wehren, soll die Kindbetterin schirmen, wie uns der Pabst lehret u. s. w. Aquam sale; so soll Weihsalz auch thun; Agnus Dei, vom Pabst geweiht, soll mehr thun, weder Gott seiher zu thun vermag. . .

Darum hat nun ecclesia, das heilige christliche Volk, nicht schlecht äusserliche Worte, Sacramente oder Aemter, wie der Gottes Affe, Satan, auch und viel mehr hat, sondern hat sie von Gott geboten, gestift und geordnet, also dass er selbst (kein Engel) dadurch mit dem Heiligen Geist will wirken. . . Solch Stück fehlet in des Teufels Sacramenten und Kirchen; da kann niemand sagen: Gott hats geboten, befohlen, eingesetzt, gestift, er will selber da sein und selber alles thun; sondern so muss man sagen: Gott hats nicht geboten, sondern verboten, Menschen habens erdichtet, oder vielmehr der Gottes Affe hats erdichtet, und die Leute damit verführt. Denn er wirket auch nichts, denn was zeitlich ist, oder wo es geistlich soll sein, ists eitel Trügerei. Denn er kann damit nicht ewiglich Sünde vergeben und selig machen, wie er leuget, durchs Weihwasser, Messen und Möncherei, ob er gleich eine Kuh kann wieder lassen ihre Milch kriegen, die er selbst zuvor durch seine Prophetin und Pfäffin gestohlen hat.“ (Von den Conciliis u. Kirchen. 1539. Opp. Hai. XVI, 2807. sqq. 2811.2812.)

Nempe ea, quae de institutione, mandato et concursu Dei diximus, habent se per modum operis ad extra, Scilicet respectu sacramentorum N. Test., de quibus suo loco distincte videbimus. §

5. Causa impulsiva interna est bonitas a Dei, externa seu meritoria est meritumb Christi. Quod facile patet, si cogitemus, sacramenta esse media gratiae. Ac praeterea monent nostri, Deum infirmitatem nostram spectasse (quam ideo quidam causam προζαταρχτιχψ vocant), ex qua fiat, ut de promissionibus evangelicis facile dubitemus; ideo pro suo in nos amore non fuisse contentum revelatione evangelii, sed signis externis confirmare voluisse, quod de salute nostra in verbo docetur.
