Sic enim h Χρκττω, in Christo, ut mediatore, et sic propter illum, benedicimur omni benedictione spirituali juxta Eph. 1, S., unde recte infertur, quod etiam propter eum mediis gratiae sacramentalibus donemur.

DB SACRAMENTIS IN GENERE. § 6. Causa minus,principalis a ordinarie est minister b ecclesiae, in casu necessitatis autem laicus aut femina.c Sive, quae sacramentum in usu constituit atque ad causandum applicat, dependenter quidem ab auctoritate, et exacte juxta institutionem causae principalis, Dei. Unde constat, actum illum non per ludum et jocum, sed tanquam serium et sanctum celebrandum esse, ut sit sacramentalis, licet non ideo ad sacramenti veritatem atque efficaciam requiratur administrantis dignitas aut intentio.

Articuli Smalcaldici: ,,Und thut die Person gar nichts zu solchem Wort und Amt, von Christo befohlen; es predige und lehre es, wer da wolle; wo Herzen sind, die es gläuben und sich daran halten, denen widerfährt, wie sie es hören und gläuben.“ (Tract. de potest, et prim, papae, p. 333.) Cf. Conf. Aug. artic. VIII. p. 40. Apolog. A. C. art. 4. p. 162. § 47.

Quenstedtius: ,,De intentione ministri intricatior est disputatio. Ει׳ίτ χημοσυνης est, eum, qui sacramenta exhibet, ad aram offerre In tentionem bonam faciendi, quod Dominus instituit, animum non peregrinantem, sed praesentem. Necessitatis est, observari actu externo intentionem Christi. Dico actu externo, nequaquam enim necessaria est intentio ministri interna faciendi, quod facit ecclesia. Nam (1.) si nulla qualitas ministri in genere addit demitque aliquid sacramenti integritati, nihil igitur eidem adimet in specie intentionis defectus, nihil addet praesentia; (2.) sic infidelitas humana Dei fidem posset in irritum revocare, contra Paulum 1. c.; (3.) quo major intentio, hoc quoque major esset effectus sacramenti; (4.) uti verbo audibili nihil addit adimitve affectus ministri, Phil. 1,17., ita nec verbo visibili. Concio sive prodeat ab intendente non concionari, sive ob malum finem concionari, aeque est efficax; (5.) quia nemo sic de accepto baptismo certus esse posset.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 7. f. 1033. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Donatistarum, qui efficaciam sacramentorum ministrorum sanctitati et dignitati adscribebant. Vid. 1.7. Augustini c. Donatistas. 2. Anabaptistarum, qui etiam ministri sanctitatem ad sacramenti integritatem requirunt, quibus oppositus est aphorismus in A. C. a. 8.: ,Sacramenta et verbum propter ordinationem et mandatum Christi sunt efficacia, etiamsi per malos exhibeantur.4 3. Pontificiorum, docentium, ad sacramenti integritatem, veritatem et virtutem requiri ministri intentionem, quae non tantum respiciat externum actum conferendi sacramentum juxta formam institutionis, sed et ipsum finem et effectum sacramenti. Sic enim Concil. Trident. sess.7. can. 11.: ,Si quis dixerit, dum sacramenta conficiunt et conferunt, non requiri intentionem, saltem faciendi, quod facit ecclesia, anathema sit.4. . . Obs. tamen, non omnes scholasticos et Pontificios eodem modo hic sentire et loqui. Miraque hic est contradictio in doctrina pontificia; volunt enim sacramenta conferre gratiam ex opere operato et infallibiliter gratiam operari, et tamen eorum non efficaciam modo, sed existentiam omnem a ministrorum intentione suspendunt. Certe circa naturam istius intentionis mire inter se digladiantur; alii enim actualem requirunt, alii habitualem tantum, alii, primam non necessariam et seeundam insufficientem statuentes, tertiam omnino urgent, quam virtualem vocant. Thomas in habituali acquiescit P. 3. q. 64. art. 8. Sed Scotus mediam reperiit inter actualem et habitualem, quae dicatur virPART. IH. CAP. VIII.

tualis, quam Jesuitae arripiunt. 4. Novatorum, intentionem baptizantis ad formam baptismi requirentium, vid. D. Georg. Calixti Annot. ad Concil. Trid. canonem praedictum p. 24. et in disp. de Bapt. th. 131., ubi intentio baptizantis ad formam baptismi requiritur. Obs. vero, verba Tridentinorum: ,Requiri intentionem faciendi, quod facit ecclesia‘ (quibus etiam quandoque D. Calixtus utitur), non solum de ipso actu, sed etiam de fine sacramenti intelligi posse, quod ipse Bellarm. non negabit, vid. ipsum c. 28. § 17. Ipseque Chemnitius 1. citando neutram intentionem ministri ad integritatem sacramenti necessario requiri ostendit.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 1039.)

Vid. 1 Cor. 4, 1. Nempe dispensatores mysUriorum Dei sunt dispensatores non solum verbi, sed et sacramentorum, in quibus abscondita sunt beneficia Dei. Caeterum ipse quoque Christus in statu exinanitionis sacramentum unum (s. coenae) administravit, cum institueret, prout officio docendi alias functus fuit. Si enim sine periculo amittendae salutis homo carere non possit sacramento et absit ordinarius minister, satius est, ab alia persona fieri, quod omitti sine periculo nequit, quam ut homo sacramento donandus damnum ferat. Et Deus per sacramenta efficax est, quisquis sit, qui administrat, modo recte administret. Vid., quae de Circumcisione et Baptismo infra dicentur.

Lutherus: ״Die heilige Stätte oder Kirche lehret also, dass weder Priester noch Christen ein einiges Sacrament machen, auch die heilige christliche Kirche selbst nicht. . . Also der Täufer macht keine Taufe, sondern Christus hat sie zuvor gemacht; der Täufer reicht und gibt sie allein. Denn da stehet Christus Ordnung, die ist, wie St. Augustinus spricht: ,Accedit verbum ad elementum et fit sacramentum‘, wenn man Wasser nimmt und thut sein Wort dazu, so ists eine Taufe, wie er befiehlt Matth, am letzten V. 19.: ,Gehet hin, lehret alle Heiden und täufet sie im Namen des Vaters und des Sohnes und des Heiligen Geistes.‘ Dieser Befehl und Einsetzung die thuts, die machen, dass Wasser und Wort eine Taufe ist, unser Werk oder Thun, ex opere operato, thuts nicht. Denn es heisst nicht darum eine Taufe, dass ich täufe oder das Werk thue, wenn ich auch heiliger denn St. Johannes oder ein Engel wäre; sondern darum heisst mein Taufen eine Taufe, dass es Christi Wort, Befehl und Einsetzung also geordnet hat, dass Wasser und sein Wort sollen eine Taufe sein. . .

Also auch, dass Brot und Wein Christi Leib und Blut werde, ist nicht unsers Thuns, Sprechens, noch Werks, viel weniger des Chresems oder Weihe Schuld, sondern es ist Christi Ordnung, Befehl und Einsetzung Schuld; derselbe hat befohlen (wie St. Paulus sagt 1 Cor. 11, 23.): Wenn wir zusammen kommen und seine Worte über Brot und Wein sprechen, so soll es sein Leib und Blut sein; dass wir hier auch nicht mehr thun, denn reichen und geben Brot und Wein mit seinen Worten nach seinem Befehl und Einsetzung. Und solch sein Befehl und Einsetzung vermag und schafft, dass wir nicht schlecht Brot und Wein, sondern seinen Leib und Blut darreichen und empfahen, wie seine Worte lauten: ,Das ist mein Leib, das ist mein Blut‘; dass nicht unser Werk oder Sprechen, sondern der Befehl und Ordnung Christi das Brot zum Leibe und den Wein zum Blut macht, von Anfang des ersten Abendmahls bis an der Welt Ende und durch unsern Dienst oder Amt täglich gereicht wird...


### On the Sacraments in General: For we must believe and be certain of this, that Baptism is not ours, but…

For we must believe and be certain of this, that Baptism is not ours, but Christ’s; the Gospel is not ours, but Christ’s; the preaching office is not ours, but Christ’s; the Sacrament is not ours, but Christ’s; the keys or the forgiveness and retention of sins are not ours, but Christ’s."

In sum, the offices and sacraments are not ours, but Christ’s; for He has ordained all such things and left them behind in the Church, to be practiced and used until the end of the world, and He neither lies nor deceives us; therefore, we can make nothing else out of them, but must act according to His command and observe them as such.

But where we change or improve them, it is nothing, and Christ is no longer there, nor is His order; and I will not say, like the Papists, that no angel or Mary could change them, etc., but I say this: even if the devil himself were to come (if he were so pious that he wanted or could do it), but I assume that I later discovered that the devil had sneaked into the office or had let himself be called to the pastoral office, perhaps in the form of a man, and had publicly preached the Gospel in the church, baptized, held Mass, absolved, and exercised and administered such office and sacrament as a pastor according to the command and order of Christ; then we would still have to confess that the sacraments were right, that we had received right Baptism, heard the right Gospel, received the right Absolution, and taken the right Sacrament of the Body and Blood of Christ.

For our faith and sacrament must not stand upon the person, whether he be pious or wicked, consecrated or unconsecrated, called or having sneaked in, the devil or his mother, but upon Christ, upon His Word, upon His office, upon His command and order. Where these proceed, there it must go and stand rightly, let the person be who and how he will or can.

And if one were to look at the person, what kind of preaching, baptism, and sacrament is it that Judas and all his descendants have done and administered according to Christ’s command and still do, other than the devil’s preaching, baptism, and sacrament, that is, reached and given to us through the devil’s members? But because the office, Word, sacrament, and order are Christ’s and not Judas’s nor the devil’s, we let Judas and the devil be Judas and the devil, yet we receive through them the goods of Christ.

For when Judas went to the devil, he did not take his apostolic office with him, but left it behind, and Matthias received it in his place. The offices and sacraments remain forever in the Church; the persons change daily.

One need only call and place into them those who can carry them out, and they proceed and happen certainly. The horse is bridled and saddled; place even a naked boy upon it who can ride, and the horse goes just as well as if the Emperor or Pope were riding it. (On the Private Mass and the Consecration of Priests. 1533. Opp. Wal. XIX, 1547—1552.)

Gerhardus: "Bellarmine lashes out (lib. 1. de Sacram, c. 24. et lib. 4. de Euchar. c. 16.) at Dr. Luther, because he taught that 'every baptized person has the power and right to administer the sacraments.' But Bellarmine knows that we by no means approve of confusion in the Church, nor do we grant to anyone, unless lawfully called to the ministry, the power to administer the Holy Supper, not even in a case of necessity, since there is a different reason between baptism and the Holy Supper.

As far as Luther is concerned, he does not grant to all baptized persons absolutely and simply the power to administer the sacraments, but he speaks of a certain general aptitude which Christians have toward the sacraments with respect to unbelievers, that because they have been received into the covenant of God through baptism, they are fit and apt for this office, provided, of course, they are lawfully called; this general aptitude Luther opposes to the priestly character, about which the Scholastics and Pontificians dispute, namely, that through the sacrament of order a certain spiritual power is caused in the soul of the recipient, through which the priest becomes capable of consecrating the Eucharist, so that without it it could in no way be consecrated, and they say that a character is imprinted on the soul as a sign of this power." (L. de sacramentis § 29.)

Tilem. Heshusius: "In a case of necessity, where one cannot have regularly called ministers of the church, there is no doubt that every Christian has the power, from God’s Word and according to Christian love..." PART III. CHAP. VIII. authorized to perform the church ministry by proclaiming God’s Word and distributing the Sacraments. . .

But we are speaking here of the case of necessity, when one cannot have upright and true ministers of the church, and what is then permitted to a Christian.

As when several Christians are in a place where there is no appointed pastor at all; when several Christians are imprisoned for the sake of the truth or are in danger on the sea; or when several Christians are living among the Turks or in the Papacy, where there are no true pastors; when several Christians are living among the Calvinists or Schwenkfeldians or Adiaphorists or Majorists, from whom, as from false teachers, they must separate themselves according to God’s command; or when several Christians are living under such pastors or church ministers who exercise public tyranny and cruelly persecute the true confessors of the truth, thereby sufficiently demonstrating that they are not members of the true Church, and therefore godly Christians are obligated to refrain from their fellowship, so that they do not strengthen their tyranny and help condemn the innocent Christians:

in such and similar cases of necessity, which occur quite often, that one cannot have true church ministers whose doctrine and confession would be upright and in agreement with God’s Word, it is permitted even to a single private person and believing Christian to absolve the penitent sinner of sins, to comfort the weak with God’s Word, to baptize little children, and to distribute the Supper of Christ; and such a Christian in such a case need not fear or have a troubled conscience as if he were encroaching upon a foreign office, but should know that he is walking in a right and orderly calling of God, and that his service is just as powerful as if he had been confirmed for the preaching office before the whole Church and before all the angels of God by the laying on of hands;

which, to prove this foundation, is sufficiently set forth and confirmed with Holy Scripture in the booklet *On the Power to Call Preachers* [von Gewalt Prediger zu berufen]: that the entire church ministry, which consists in preaching, admonishing, comforting, forgiving sins, retaining sins, and administering the Sacraments, was not committed by the Lord Christ to a special estate, neither the spiritual nor the secular, but to the whole congregation of God, as the passage testifies: "Whatever you bind on earth," etc.

Whoever, then, is an orthodox Christian and a living member of Christ has his share and right to the holy preaching office and to everything that belongs to the church ministry. Christ gives the whole Church the power, according to God’s Word and promise, to forgive the sins of the penitent, and that the called preachers exercise such power, they do not do so by their own authority, but by the power and command of the Church, which has commanded the preachers to administer such glory, bestowed upon it by Christ.

Now, when church ministers are not present, then every Christian is indeed authorized to exercise such power. For if the preachers do not perform their office as they are obligated to do, or if none are present, the office indeed reverts to the Church, to whom it belongs to bestow it; just as when a fief-holder dies or forfeits the fief, the fief-property falls back to the fief-lord.

But what now belongs to the whole Church and is the right of every Christian, that may also every Christian, in case of necessity, according to God’s Word, in the common spirit of all believers, distribute and perform. . .

I do not say that two or three should separate themselves from the true Church, flee the appointed, orderly preachers, and start separate sects, but in the case of necessity, when either no preachers are present, or they pour out false doctrine and are therefore to be fled, and in addition the necessity arises that one cannot seek the use of the Sacraments in other places, that then every Christian, upon the consent of one or two, [may] administer the Sacraments to

is authorized and entitled to reach out and to strengthen the weak in the throes of death. The papal asses have been possessed by the delusion that no one may baptize, nor confirm, nor pronounce absolution, nor distribute the Lord’s Supper, unless he be an ordained priest; but such an error, which contains many kinds of lies, has long since been refuted and overturned by God’s Word.” (See Bidembach, *Consil. decad.* 3, pp. 138–140.) §

7. The matter of a sacrament implies two things: first, a certain external and visible element; second, a certain action occupied with that element.

Indeed, a sacrament is not a substance composed of matter and form, but a rite and an action. Therefore, the matter here is the same as the material, or that which is, or can be, common to a sacrament and to other actions that are not sacraments, such that it must finally be determined by something else that is added to it to become the existence of a sacramental action. Regarding this, see § 3, note c.

Others call this the "thing of the sacrament," distinguishing between the "thing" as the matter *about which*, as they say, and the "thing" as the fruit of the sacrament received; it is not the latter, but the former, that pertains to the present discussion. But this will be clear from what follows.

However, the claim by some that in every sacrament there is a twofold matter, earthly and heavenly, is not without difficulty, nor can it be defined except where the nature and essence of individual sacraments have been established from their proper seat—that is, from the words of their institution. This is acknowledged by the blessed Gerhard (*L. de Sacram.* § 45) and the blessed Himmel (*Synt. Disp.* XIX, § 38).

Latin:

Denn das müssen wir gläuben und gewiss sein, dass die Taufe nicht unser, sondern Christi sei; das Evangelium nicht unser, sondern Christi sei; das Predigtamt nicht unser, sondern Christi sei; das Sacrament nicht unser, sondern Christi sei; die Schlüssel oder Vergebung und Behaltung der Sünden nicht unser, sondern Christi sei.

Summa, die Aemter und Sacramente sind nicht unser, sondern Christi; denn er hat solches alles geordnet und hinter sich gelassen in der Kirche, zu üben und gebrauchen bis an der Welt Ende und leuget noch treuget uns nicht; darum können wir auch nichts anders daraus machen, sondern müssen seinem Befehl nach thun und solches halten.

Wo wirs aber andern oder bessern, so ists nichts, und Christus nicht mehr da, noch seine Ordnung; und ich will nicht sagen, wie die Papisten, dass kein Engel noch Maria könne wandeln u. s. w., sondern so sage ich: wenn gleich der Teufel selbst käme (wenn er so fromm wäre, dass ers thun wollte oder könnte), aber ich setze, dass ichs hernach erführe, dass der Teufel so herein in das Amt geschlichen wäre oder hätte sich gleich lassen, als in Mannsgestalt, berufen zum Pfarramt und öffentlich in der Kirche das Evangelium gepredigt, getauft, Messe gehalten, absolvirt und solch Amt und Sacrament als ein Pfarrherr geübt und gereicht nach dem Befehl und Ordnung Christi; so müssten wir dennoch bekennen, dass die Sacramente recht wären, wir rechte Taufe empfangen, recht Evangelium gehöret, rechte Absolution krieget, recht Sacrament des Leibes und Blutes Christi genommen hätten.

Denn es muss unser Glaube und Sacrament nicht auf der Person stehen, sie sei fromm oder böse, geweihet oder ungeweihet, berufen oder eingeschlichen, der Teufel oder seine Mutter, sondern auf Christo, auf seinem Wort, auf seinem Amt, auf seinem Befehl und Ordnung. Wo dieselben gehen, da muss es recht gehen und stehen, ·die Person sei wer und wie sie wolle oder könne.

Und so man die Person sollte ansehen, was ists für eine Predigt, Taufe und Sacrament, so Judas und alle seine Nachkommen nach Christi Befehl gethan und gereicht haben und noch thun, anders, denn des Teufels Predigt, Taufe, Sacrament, das ist, durchs Teufels Glieder uns gereicht und gegeben? Aber weil das Amt, Wort, Sacrament, Ordnung Christi und nicht Judas noch des Teufels ist, lassen wir Judam und den Teufel Judas und Teufel sein, nehmen gleichwohl durch sie die Güter Christi.

Denn da Judas zum Teufel fuhr, nahm er sein Apostelamt nicht mit sich, sondern liess es hinter sich, und kriegts Matthias an seine Statt. Die Aemter und Sacramente bleiben immerdar in der Kirche, die Personen andern sich täglich.

Man berufe und setze nur drein, die sie können ausrichten, so gehen und geschehen sie gewiss. Der Gaul ist gezäumt und gesattelt, setze darauf auch einen nackten Knaben, der reiten kann, so gehet der Gaul eben so wohl, als wenn ihn der Kaiser oder Pabst ritte.“ (Von der Winkelmesse und Pfaffenweihe. 1533. Opp. Hai. XIX, 1547—1552.)

Gerhardus: ,,Flagellat Beilarm. lib. 1. de Sacram, c. 24. et lib. 4. de Euchar. c. 16. D. Lutherum, quod docuerit, ,quemvis hominem baptizatum potestatem et jus habere administrandi sacramenta'. Sed novit Bellarminus, nos haudquaquam confusionem in ecclesia probare, neque cuiquam, nisi legitime ad ministerium vocato, potestatem administrandi sacram coenam concedere, ne quidem in casu necessitatis, cum dispar ratio sit inter baptismum et sacram coenam.

Lutherum quod attinet, is non concedit omnibus baptizatis absolute et simpliciter potestatem administrandi sacramenta, sed loquitur de generali quadam aptitudine, quam christiani ad sacramenta respectu infidelium habent, quod per baptismum in foedus Dei recepti idonei et apti sint ad hoc officium, si scilicet legitime vocentur; hanc generalem aptitudinem opponit Lutherus characteri sacerdotali, de quo scholastici et pontificii disputant, quod per ordinis sacramentum in anima suscipientis causetur potestas quaedam spiritualis, per quam sacerdos fiat habilis ad conflciendam eucharistiam, ita ut sine illa nullo modo confici possit, et in hujus potestatis signum animae characterem imprimi dicunt.“ (L. de sacramentis § 29.)

Tilem. Heshusius: ,,Im Fall der Noth, da man ordentlich berufene Kirchendiener nicht haben kann, ist kein Zweifel, dass ein jeglieher Christ Macht habe aus Gottes Wort und nach christlicher Liebe PART. III. CAP. VIII. befugt sei, den Kirchendienst mit Verkündigung Gottes Worts und Austheilung der Sacramente zu verrichten. . .

Von dem Nothfall aber reden wir hie, wenn man rechtschaffene und wahre Diener der Kirche nicht haben kann, was alsdann einem Christen zustehe.

Als wenn etliche Christen an dem Orte sind, da überall kein bestellter Seelsorger ist; wenn etliche Christen um der Wahrheit willen gefangen liegen oder in Gefährlichkeit wären auf dem Meer; oder wenn etliche Christen unter den Türken sässen oder fm Pabstthum, da keine rechten Pfarrer sind; wenn etliche Christen unter den Calvinisten oder Schwenkfeldianern oder Adiaphoristen oder Majoristen sässen, von denen, als von falschen Lehrern, sie sich nach Gottes Befehl müssten absondern; oder wenn etliche Christen unter solchen Pfarrern oder Kirchendienern sässen, die öffentliche Tyrannei übeten und die rechten Bekenner der Wahrheit grausamlich verfolgten, damit sie dann auch genugsamlich an den Tag geben, dass sie nicht Gliedmassen der wahren Kirche wären, und derhalbe» gottselige Christen schuldig, sich ihrer Gemeinschaft zu enthalten, auf dass sie ihre Tyrannei nicht stärken und die unschuldigen Christen nicht helfen verdammen:

in solchen und dergleichen Nothfällen, die denn gar oft sich zu tragen, dass man wahre Kirchendiener, deren Lehre und Bekenntniss rechtschaffen wäre und mit Gottes Wort stimmte, nicht kann, haben, ist auch einer einzelnen Privatperson und gläubigen Christen erlaubt, den bussfertigen Sünder von Sünden loszusprechen, die Schwachen mit Gottes Wort zu trösten, Kindlein zu taufen und das Nachtmahl Christi auszuspenden, und darf sich ein solcher Christ in solchem Fall nicht befahren oder Gewissen darüber machen, als griffe er in ein fremd Amt, sondern soll wissen, dass er in rechtem, ordentlichem Berufe Gottes einhergehe, und dass sein Dienst ebenso kräftig ist, als wäre er mit Auflegung der Hände zum Predigtamt für der ganzen Kirche und für allen Engeln Gottes bestätigt;

welches denn, auch diesen Grund zu beweisen, im Büchlein,von Gewalt Prediger zu berufen‘ ist zur Nothdürft genugsam ausgeführt und mit heiliger Schrift bestätiget: dass der ganze Kirchendienst, welcher stehet in Predigen, Vermahnen, Trösten, Sünden vergeben, Sünde behalten, Sacramente administriren, sei vom Herrn Christo nicht einem besondern Stande, weder dem geistlichen noch dem weltlichen, übergeben, sondern der ganzen Gemeinde Gottes, wie der Spruch bezeuget: Was ihr auf Erden binden werdet u. s. w.

Wer denn nun ein rechtgläubiger Christ und ein lebendiges Gliedmass Christi ist, der hat sein Theil und Gerechtigkeit zum heiligen Predigtamt und zu allem, was zum Kirchendienst gehört. Christus gibt der ganzen Kirche Macht, nach Gottes Wort und Verheissung den Bussfertigen die Sünde zu vergeben, und dass solche Gewalt die berufenen Prediger üben, thun sie nicht aus eigener Autorität, sondern in Kraft und aus Befehl der Kirche, die solche Herrlichkeit, ihr von Christo verehret, den Predigern zu verwalten befohlen hat.

Wenn nun die Kirchendiener nicht vorhanden sind, so ist ja ein jeder Christ berechtigt, solche Gewalt zu üben. Denn wenn die Prediger ihr Amt nicht verrichten, wie sie schuldig sind, oder keine vorhanden sind, kommt je das Amt wieder auf die Kirche, der es gebührt zu verleihen; als wenn ein Lehenträger verstirbt oder das Lehen verwirkt, fällt das LehenGut wieder zum LehenHerrn.

Was aber nun der ganzen Kirche zustehet und eines jeden Christen ist, das mag auch ein jeder Christ im Fall der Noth nach Gottes Wort in gemeinem Geist aller Gläubigen austheilen und verrichten. . .

Nicht sage ich, dass zween oder drei sich von der wahren Kirche absondern sollen, die bestellten ordentlichen Prediger fliehen und besondere Rotten anrichten, sondern auf den Nothfall, wenn entweder keine Prediger fürhanden sind, falsche Lehre ausgiessen und derhalben zu fliehen sind, dazu die Noth fürfället, dass man den Brauch der Sacramente an andern Orten nicht kann suchen, dass alsdann ein jeder Christ auf Eines oder Zweier Verwilligung die Sacramente zu

reichen und den Schwachen in Todesnöthen zu stärken befugt und berechtigt sei. Die Pabstesel sind in dem Wahn gesteckt, es möchte niemand tanfen, noch confirmiren, noch die Absolution sprechen, noch das Nachtmahl Christi ausspenden, er müsste ein geweihter Priester sein; aber solcher Irrthum, der mancherlei Lügen in sich hat, ist längst aus Gottes Wort widerlegt und umgestossen.“ (Vid. Bidembachii consil. decad. 3. p. 13δ—140.) §

7. Materia a sacramenti duo importat: primo elementum quoddam b externum et visibile;c deinde d actionem quandam e circa elementum occupatam.

Equidem sacramentum non est substantia ex materia״ et forma composita, sed ritus et actio. Itaque materia h. 1. idem est, quod matenaky sive illud, quod sacramento et actionibus aliis, quae non sunt sacramenta, commune est aut esse potest, ita ut per aliud quiddam, quod accedat, determinari demum debeat ad esse actionis sacramentalis. De quo vid. § 3. not. c.

Alias rem sacramenti appellant, distinguentes inter rem, pro materia circa quam, ut ajunt, et inter rem, pro fructu sacramenti acceptam; non hanc, sed illam pertinere ad praesens. Sed de hoc ex sequentibus constabit.

Quod autem quidam dicunt, in quolibet sacramento esse materiam geminam, terrenam et coelestem, non caret difficultate, neque potest definiri, nisi ubi de singulorum sacramentorum natura et essentia ex propria sede, hoc est, ex verbis institutionis ejus constiterit; quod agnoscunt b. Gerhardus L. de Sacram. § 45. et b. Himmelius Synt. Disp. XIX. § 38.


### On the Sacraments in General: Certainly, if for every sacrament there is given a matter, besides the earthly,…

Certainly, if for every sacrament there is given a matter, besides the earthly, also a heavenly one, there must also be a certain union between the former and the latter; and thus, when we speak of the sacrament in general, something must also be defined concerning the union of this twofold matter in the sacrament in general.

Yet the blessed Menzer (*Tom. II. Dispp. Giess. Disp.* V, § 49, p. 164), arguing against the Calvinists concerning the heavenly and earthly matter of the sacraments and the union of both, writes: "To wish to define a general mode and manner of that union, common indiscriminately to all and individual sacraments of the Old and New Testaments, is truly to fight against the very institution of the individual sacraments."

These things being admitted, it will be better to remain silent about the heavenly matter of the sacrament in general, just as about the general union of the twofold matter, than to say doubtful things.

For even the older teachers of our church, when they delivered the doctrine concerning the sacraments in general, did not teach that in every sacrament there must be a heavenly matter, sacramentally united to an earthly element.

Certainly, the blessed Chemnitz (*in Exam. Conc. Trident. P.* II, *de Num. Sacram.*, p. 14), in reviewing the substantials of a sacrament, does not mention a heavenly matter. Compare the *Ausführliche Erklärung* by the blessed Musaeus (*L.* XVI, *Qu.* 84 sqq., p. 683).

Similarly, the blessed Aegidius Hunnius, in his book *de Sacram.*, to the question: "How many things are required for the substance or substantial integrity of each sacrament?" answers: "Two, namely, the element, or the thing that meets the eyes, and the word joined to it, according to that saying of Augustine: 'Let the word be added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.'" PART III. CAP. VIII.

is silent regarding the heavenly matter. Thus, however, also the blessed Eras. Sarcerius in *Exam. Ordin.* f. CCLVI. a. b., the blessed Jac. Heerbrandus in *Comp. Theol.* L. de Sacram, p. 511. 512., the blessed Ambr. Reudenius in *P. V. Catech. Theol.* Cap. II. p. 178. 179., the blessed Alb. Grauerus in *Supplem. Praei, in Aug. Conf.* ad art. IX. p. m. 78., the blessed Matth. Hafenrefferus in *LL. Theol.* L. III. Stat. III. L. VII. p. 465., the blessed Joh. Gerhardus in *Aph. Theol.* L. XVI. Aph. 37. 38.

But as for the fact that others call the other part of the sacrament, namely the word of institution—from which and the element, treated by a certain action, the sacrament consists—the heavenly and invisible matter of the sacrament, it must be confessed that this is rather the form, or the formal of the sacrament, as we shall soon see.

And although others, by the name of heavenly matter, understand some thing signified, relatively opposed to the element as a sign, yet not the fruit of the sacrament itself, but the thing upon which the operation and fruit of the sacrament depends, they nevertheless confess that this very thing, which they call heavenly matter, is sometimes not even really present; as we shall see regarding the sacraments of the Old Testament.

However, it is difficult to hold as matter, and thus as an essential part of the sacrament, something which, while the sacrament exists, does not itself also exist at that time.

Otherwise, even if that which is held as heavenly matter were indeed present, some again warn that the consequence from presence to matter is not valid, but that it is required that it be present by way of matter, in order to be called matter.

But what it is to "be present by way of matter" in a sacrament, they themselves do not sufficiently declare regarding the sacrament in general, but leave it to be learned regarding individual sacraments from the institution of each.

Whence you may gather that the heavenly matter of a sacrament in general cannot be acknowledged unless it has been detected in the individual sacraments.

And since in the Holy Supper the body and blood of Christ are called the heavenly matter for the reason that the act of dispensing, eating, and drinking is occupied not only with the bread and wine, but also with the body and blood of Christ themselves truly and really, so that when bread is dispensed and eaten, the body of Christ is also truly and really dispensed and eaten at the same time, and when wine is dispensed and drunk, the blood of Christ is also truly and really dispensed and drunk at the same time, it must be confessed that heavenly matter of such a kind does not have a place equally in all sacraments (especially those where that which is called by the name of heavenly matter is acknowledged not to be really present).

Therefore, even if we should posit some heavenly matter when dealing with the sacrament in general, the term "matter" would have to be so broadened that it would not be the case that in the same way in which something is in one sacrament by way of matter, another thing would also be in another sacrament by way of matter.

Whence it will further follow that in one sacrament something is present by way of matter speaking properly, and in another speaking improperly. By which reasoning it will not be difficult to judge whether the clarity and solidity of the doctrine is consulted.

There are indeed those for whom the thing or heavenly matter of the sacrament is the same as the intelligible signified, which sacraments require as sensible signs. Thus we shall have such a union as exists between the signified and the sign. But whether being the signified is sufficient for the definition of matter, especially since the signified can also be really absent from the sign, will be a matter for further investigation.

Meanwhile, that in all sacraments there is given in its own way a heavenly thing, not only as the fruit of the sacrament, but also as the thing upon which, as a cause, depends

the fruit of the sacrament and must be distinguished from the earthly thing, we do not deny, but gladly concede, although we do not for that reason attribute to it the name and nature of matter; as we shall explain in its proper place concerning the individual sacraments.

Some here use the distinction between remote and proximate matter; by the former name they designate the element, by the latter the action occupied about it. They call it remote matter, however, not because it is locally absent from the sacrament, but because it does not have the nature of matter in the sacrament except insofar as it is subject to a certain action and is treated through it. The action is understood as commonly considered, which is indifferent to a vulgar and a sacramental action, but is determined to the being of a sacramental action only from elsewhere (by the accession of the word of institution, of which we shall see presently), e.g., the act of washing with water, the act of dispensing, eating, and drinking bread and wine; of which in their proper place. Otherwise, however, the action, determined by the accession of the word of institution, constitutes the very formal nature of the sacrament; as we shall say immediately. Meanwhile, see blessed Gerhard, l. c. § 46. § 8.

The form of the sacrament is the word of institution, to be added to the action occupied about the sensible element. Or the formal principle, from which, when it approaches or is united to the action occupied about that element, the action formally has that which makes it a sacrament or a sacramental action.

Some say the form of the sacrament is the action about the proper subject of the sacrament, determined by the word of institution. And this indeed is the form of the whole, or the entire formal nature of the sacrament; which they also sometimes call the essence of the sacrament. But in this place we are dealing with the formal principle, which is distinguished from the material. The word, I say, not of promise, which looks to the fruit or effect of the sacrament, but of institution, which enters entirely into the constitution of the sacrament.

Therefore, although the word of institution pertains in its own way to the efficient cause, as its causality, or that which God has efficiently determined through the word of institution, which pertains to the nature of each sacrament; yet insofar as the word of institution is to be added to the external sacramental action itself in such a way that by this very thing that action is distinguished from other vulgar actions and is constituted in the being of a sacramental action, thus the word of institution pertains entirely to the form of the sacrament. § 9. The end of the sacraments is men born carnally and living.

PART III. CHAP. VIII.

Or the subject, for whose benefit any given sacrament is instituted by God and to whom, consequently, it ought to be applied. Some call this the object, understanding it as the personal object, which they distinguish from the real object, or the thing itself, which the sacramental action treats.

Nothing else. This is evident partly from an induction of the individual sacraments and their express institution, and partly from their common end, which will be treated in the following paragraph. Meanwhile, not all sacraments are equally intended for all, such that they may be admitted indiscriminately; which will be clearly shown below. However, not fetuses hidden in their mothers' wombs; to whom, although salvation is not denied, these means, lacking a mandate, ought not therefore to be applied; as we shall say below regarding baptism. But that Christ Himself used certain sacraments, that was done through that dispensation by which He freely took upon Himself other things that pertain to infirm men for their benefit.

For those who are dead are no longer in the way of salvation, so that they might be helped by the means of grace, but are either blessed or damned. § 10. The end of the sacraments, which also has the nature of an effect, is indeed proximately the bestowing or sealing of evangelical grace; the ultimate end, on the part of men, is their eternal salvation.

Or that for the sake of effecting or obtaining which the sacrament was instituted by God the author, and therefore ought to be applied to men and received by them. Namely, insofar as it is conferred upon men through the sacraments as effective organs and means. Cf. what we said at § 2, last note. But as for that question: Whether the efficacy of the sacraments is physical or moral, the blessed Musaeus replied: If this remains fixed and firm, that the sacraments are effective organs of conferring grace, and that God works through them and confers grace in an undivided action, which the Holy Scriptures teach quite clearly, let us not be too scrupulous about the mode of working and conferring grace, but rather leave it to divine wisdom. See *Ausführliche Erklärung* L. XVII. Q. 83. p. 675. (It is manifest, however, that this opinion is not thereby approved, by which the sacraments are said to be a moral, but not a physical, cause of conferring grace, in such a way that it is simultaneously denied that God and the sacraments work in one and an undivided action to confer evangelical grace.) Thus also the blessed Gerhard, L. de Sacram. § 86, when he had fallen into that question, left it undecided. Cf. the same in *Conf. Cathol.* L. II. Part. II. Art. XI. cap. II. p. 813. and in *Bellarmino ’Opftod. teste*, Disp. XVIII. § 39. Add the blessed Cundisius in *Notis ad Compend. Hutteri* L. XX. Qu. IV. p. 1065.

Latin:

Certe si cujusque sacramenti detur materia, praeter terrenam, etiam coelestis, oportebit etiam unionem quandam esse inter hanc et illam, atque adeo, cum de sacramento in genere loquimur, etiam de unione duplicis materiae sacramenti in genere aliquid definiendum erit.

Atqui b. Menzerus, Tom. II. Dispp. Giess. Disp. V. § 49. p. 164. de materia coelesti ac terrena sacramentorum et unione utriusque contra Calvinianos disputans, scribit: Generalem unionis illius modum ac rationem omnibus et singulis sacramentis F. et N. Test, promiscue communem definire velle, vere est pugnare cum ipsa institutione singulorum sacramentorum.

Quibus admissis, satius erit, uti de unione generali duplicis materiae, sic de ipsa materia coelesti sacramenti in genere silere, quam dubia dicere.

Nam et antiquiores ecclesiae nostrae doctores, cum doctrinam de sacramentis in genere traderent, non docuerunt, quod in omni sacramento oporteat esse materiam coelestem, elemento terreno sacramentaliter unitam.

Certe b. Chemnitius in Exam. Cone. Trident. P., II. de Num. Sacram, p. 14., substantialia sacramenti recensens, materiae coelestis non meminit. Confer. Ausführliche Erklärung b. Musaei L. XVI. Qu. 84. sqq. p. 683.

Similiter b. Aegid. Hunnius Lib. de Sacram, ad Quaest.: Quot requiruntur ad substantiam vel integritatem substantialem cujusque sacramenti? respondet: Duo, videlicet elementum, seu res in oculos incurrens, et verbum adjunctum, juxta illud, Augustini: Accedat verbum ad elementum, et fiat sacramentum. De PART. III. CAP. VIII.

materia coelesti tacet. Sic autem etiam b. Eras. Sarcerius in Exam. Ordin. f. CCLVI. a. b., b. Jac. Heerbrandus Comp. Theol. L. de Sacram, p. 511. 512., b. Ambr. Reudenius P. V. Catech. Theol. Cap. II. p. 178. 179., b. Alb. Grauerus in Supplem. Praei, in Aug. Conf. ad art. IX. p. m. 78., b. Matth. Hafenrefferus in LL. Theol. L. III. Stat. III. L. VII. p. 465., b. Joh. Gerhardus in Aph. Theol. L. XVI. Aph. 37. 38.

Quod autem alii alteram sacramenti partem, nempe verbum institutionis, ex quo et elemento, certa actione tractato, constat sacramentum, materiam sacramenti coelestem atque invisibilem dicunt, fatendum est, hanc potius esse formam, seu formale sacramenti, quam materiam; ut mox videbimus.

Quodque alii nomine materiae coelestis rem aliquam signatam, elemento velut signo relative oppositam, non autem ipsum fructum sacramenti, sed rem, a qua pendet operatio et fructus sacramenti, intelligunt, fatentur tamen, hanc ipsam rem, quam materiam coelestem dicunt, aliquando ne quidem realiter praesentem esse; prout de sacramentis Vet. Test, videbimus.

Difficile autem est, pro materia et sic pro parte essentiali sacramenti habere aliquid, quod, sacramento existente, non tamen et ipsum tunc existit.

Alias etiam, si maxime id, quod pro materia coelesti habetur, praesens sit, tamen iterum aliqui monent, a praesentia ad materiam non valere consequentiam, requiri autem, ut adsit per modum materiae, quod materia appellari queat.

Quid autem sit‘, adesse per modum materiae in sacramento, ne ipsi quidem quoad sacramentum in genere satis declarant, sed quoad singula sacramenta ex institutione cujusque discendum relinquunt.

Unde coiligas, materiam coelestem sacramenti in genere agnosci non posse, nisi in singulis sacramentis ea deprehensa fuerit.

Cumque in s. coena corpus et sanguis Christi dicantur materia coelestis ideo, quod actus dispensandi, manducandi et bibendi non solum circa panem et vinum, verum etiam circa ipsum corpus et sanguinem Christi vere et realiter occupetur, ita ut, quando panis dispensatur et manducatur, simul etiam corpus Christi vere et realiter dispensetur ac manducetur, et quando vinum dispensatur et bibitur, simul etiam vere ac realiter sanguis Christi dispensetur et bibatur, fatendum erit, materiam coelestem ejusmodi non aeque in omnibus sacramentis (praesertim his, ubi illud, quod nomine materiae coelestis appellatur, realiter praesens non esse agnoscitur) locum habere.

Itaque si maxime, cum de sacramento in genere agitur, materiam aliquam coelestem statuamus, terminus materiae ita ampliandus erit, ut non ea ratione, qua aliquid per modum materiae est in uno sacramento, etiam aliud quiddam in alio sacramento per modum materiae fuerit.

Unde porro sequetur, in uno sacramento aliquid esse per modum materiae proprie loquendo, in alio improprie loquendo. Qua ratione utrum perspicuitati et soliditati doctrinae consulatur, non difficile erit judicare.

Sunt profecto, quibus res aut materia coelestis sacramenti idem est ac signatum intelligibile, quod sacramenta tanquam signa sensibilia requirant. Itaque unionem talem habebimus, qualis est inter signatum et signum. An vero ad rationem materiae sufficiat τό esse signatum, praesertim quod signatum etiam realiter potest abesse a signo, ulterioris disquisitionis res erit.

Interim dari in sacramentis omnibus suo modo rem coelestem, non solum pro fructu sacramenti, verum etiam pro re, a qua tanquam causa pendet

fructus sacramenti quaeque a re terrena distinguenda sit, non negamus, sed libenter concedimus, licet nomen et rationem materiae ei propterea non tribuamus; prout de sacramentis singulis suo loco explicabimus.

Quidam hic utuntur distinctione inter materiam remotam et proximam; illo nomine elementum, hoc actionem circa illud occupatam appellant. Vocant autem materiam remotam, non quod localiter absit a sacramento, sed quod non habeat rationem materiae in sacramento, nisi quatenus actioni certae subest et per eam tractatur. Intelligitur autem actio communiter considerata, quae per semdifferens est ad vulgarem et sacramentalem actionem, ad esse sacramen· talis actionis autem aliunde demum (accedente verbo institutionis, de quo mox videbimus) determinatur, v. g. actus abluendi aqua, actus dispensandi, comedendi ac bibendi panem et vinum; de quibus suo loco. Alias autem actio, accedente verbo institutionis determinata, ipsam rationem formalem sacramenti constituit; ut statim dicemus. Interim vide b. Gerhardum 1. c. § 46. § 8.

Forma a sacramenti est b verbum institutionis, c actioni circa elementum sensibile occupatae addendum.d Sive formale, a quo ad actionem, circa elementum illud occupatam, accedente aut ei unito actio formaliter habet, quod est sacramentum aut sacramentalis actio.

Quidam formam sacramenti dicunt esse actionem circa subjectum sacramenti proprium, verbo institutionis determinatum. Et haec quidem est forma totius, seu tota ratio formalis sacramenti; quam etiam aliquando essentiam sacramenti appellant. Verum h. l. agimus de formali, quod materiali contradistinguitur. Verbum, inquam, non promissionis, quod ad fructum aut effectum sacramenti spectat, sed institutionis, quod constitutionem sacramenti omnino ingreditur.

Itaque quamvis verbum institutionis suo modo ad causam efficientem pertineat, velut causalitas ejus, seu, quod Deus per verbum institutionis efficienter determinavit, quae ad naturam cujusque sacramenti pertinent; quatenus tamen verbum institutionis ipsi actioni sacramentali externae addendum est ita, ut hoc ipso actio illa ab aliis vulgaribus actionibus distinguatur et in esse sacramentalis actionis constituatur, sic ad formam sacramenti verbum institutionis omnino pertinet. § 9. Finis cui a sacramentorum sunt homines b carnaliter nati c ac viventes.d

PART. III. CAP. VIII.

Sive subjectum, in cujus bonum institutum est a Deo sacramentum quodvis et cui proinde applicari debet. Quidam objectum appellant, intelligentes objectum personale, quod a reali, seu ipsa re, quam actio sacramentalis tractat, distinguunt.

Non aliud quidquam. Quod patet partim ex inductione singulorum sacramentorum eorumque institutione expressa, partim ex fine cujus communi, de quo § seq. agetur. Interim non omnia sacramenta aeque omnibus sunt destinata, ita ut indiscriminatim admitti queant; quod infra distincte patebit. Non autem foetus in uteris matrum latentes; quibus etsi salus non denegetur, haec autem media, deficiente mandato, propterea applicari non debent; ut infra de baptismo dicemus. Quod autem Christus ipse sacramentis quibusdam usus fuit, id per eam dispensationem factum est, qua alias ea, quae ad homines infirmos pertinent, eorum bono libere suscepit.

Qui enim mortui sunt, non amplius sunt in via salutis, ut mediis gratiae juvari queant, sed vel beati, vel damnati sunt. § 10. Finis cujus a sacramentorum, qui et effectus b rationem habet, proximus quidem est gratiae evangelicae c collatio aut d obsignatio; ultimus ex parte hominum est salus aeterna e eorundem.

Seu illud, cujus efficiendi aut obtinendi causa institutum est ab auctore Deo sacramentum ideoque applicari debet hominibus et ab iis suscipi. Scilicet in quantum per sacramenta, tanquam organa ac media efficacia, hominibus confertur. Conf., quae diximus ad § 2. not. ult. Quod autem attinet ad quaestionem illam: Num efficacia sacramentorum sit physica an moralis, respondit b. Musaeus: Si hoc maneat fixum et firmum, sacramenta; esse organa efficacia conferendae gratiae, et Deum um indivisa actione operari per illa et conferre gratiam, quod Scripturae s. satis diserte docent, de modo operandi et conferendi gratiam ne simus nimis scrur pulosi, sed eum potius divinae sapientiae relinquamus. Vid. Ausführliche Erklärung L. XVII. Q. 83. p. 675. (Manifestum vero est, non ideo probari eam sententiam, qua sacramenta ita dicuntur esse causa moralis, non autem physica, conferendae gratiae, ut simul negetur, Deum et sacramenta um et indivisa actione operari ad conferendam gratiam evangelicam.) Sic autem etiam b. Gerhardus L. de Sacram. § 86., cum in quaestionem istam incidisset, indecisam reliquit. Conf. Eundem in Conf. Cathol. L. II. Part. II. Art. XI. cap. II. p. 813. et in Bellarmino ’Opftod. teste, Disp. XVIII. § 39. Adde 6. Cundisium in Notis ad Compend. Hutteri L. XX. Qu. IV. p. 1065.


### On the Sacraments in General: Apology of the A. C.

Apology of the A. C.: "God moves hearts simultaneously through the Word and the rite, that they may believe and conceive faith, as Paul says (Rom. 10:17): 'Faith comes from hearing.' And just as the Word strikes the ears in order to strike the hearts:"

Thus the rite itself strikes the eyes, so that it moves the hearts. The effect of the word and the rite is the same, as has been excellently stated by Augustine, that a sacrament is a "visible word," because the rite is received by the eyes and is as it were a picture of the word, signifying the same thing that the word signifies. Wherefore the effect of both is the same." (Art. 13. p. 202. § 5.)

Luther: "We know indeed that external things do not save, if you take 'external' to mean 'ours'; but God also works salvation through external things, and has so ordained that He does not wish to give His Spirit without signs and some external thing. Therefore He instituted in the church the ministry of the word, baptism, and the supper of the body and blood of His Son. Thus, on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended and was given to the apostles not invisibly, but with a mighty wind and tongues of fire. Therefore the Sacramentarians err, and they posit here a false principle when they say: 'No external thing profits for salvation.' Nay, you invert it and say: 'Without an external thing, no salvation occurs.' ... For just as the Holy Spirit moves through the word, so He also moves through signs, which are nothing other than, if I may say so, a 'real' word, where that which the word sounds is expressed by the thing." (Scholia on Isaiah. See Exeget. opp. lat. Erlangen, 1860. Vol. XXII, p. 185 sq.)

M. Chemnitius: "How does baptism save us, 1 Pet. 3? How is it the washing of regeneration, Tit. 3? Paul declares this simply when he says in Eph. ch. 5: 'Cleansing the church with the washing of water by the word.' And Augustine gathers the same from that statement of Christ: 'You are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.' Rightly, therefore, the Apology of the Augsburg Confession says that the effect, the same virtue or efficacy, is the same for both the word and the sacraments, which are seals of the promises; which is why Augustine also calls them visible words. Just as, therefore, the gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes—not because some magical power inheres in the characters, syllables, or the sound of the words, but because it is a medium, an organ, or an instrument through which the Holy Spirit is efficacious, proposing, offering, exhibiting, distributing, and applying the merit of Christ and the grace of God unto salvation to everyone who believes—so also is virtue or efficacy attributed to the sacraments, not because grace is to be sought in the sacraments outside of or apart from the merit of Christ, the mercy of the Father, and the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, but because the sacraments are instrumental causes, such that through these media or organs the Father wills to exhibit, donate, and apply His grace, the Son wills to communicate His merit to believers, and the Holy Spirit wills to exercise His efficacy unto salvation to everyone who believes. In this way, His grace remains God's, so that grace is not to be sought elsewhere than with God the Father; the price or cause of the remission of sins and eternal life is not to be sought elsewhere than in the death and resurrection of Christ; the efficacy of regeneration unto salvation is not to be sought elsewhere than in the operation of the Holy Spirit. The sacraments, however, propose, bring, exhibit, and seal those benefits to us in the word, and thus lead us to Christ, to the grace of God, and to the efficacy of the Spirit. For because God wills to deal with us in those things which pertain to our salvation through certain media, and He Himself has ordained and instituted this use of the word of the promise of the gospel, which is sometimes proposed simply by itself or naked, but sometimes clothed or made visible by certain rites or sacraments instituted by God. The word and the sacraments, therefore, show us where faith ought to seek and where it can find Christ the Mediator, the Father, and the Holy Spirit, so that they may deal with us, exhibit, apply, and seal the benefits which Christ merited and of which the gospel preaches. And in the use of the sacraments, faith does not seek or look to some essential virtue or efficacy inherent in the external elements of the sacraments themselves, but in the promise which is annexed to the sacrament, it seeks, apprehends, and receives the grace of the Father, the merit of the Son, and the efficacy of the Spirit." (Exam. concilii Trid. De efficacia et usu sacram. Ed. Genev. f. 215.)

Carpzovius: "Sacraments, viewed not μερικώς (partially) but όλικώς (wholly), are signs—not naked signs, which are only σημεῖα (signs) and [signify] some thing or..." PART III. CHAP. VIII.

at least represent or indicate by way of notification, or at least make one certain of it, and move the object and excite assent; but they are προςφερόμενα [things offered], which truly work as organs and instruments, and indeed once by way of physical action, insofar as they either originally confer and work faith and inherent divine charisms, or increase and strengthen those already given. Then, indeed, by way of moral action, regarding the justifying good, which they do not merely offer to the believer, but also confer and seal when received by faith. Hence, by the Augsburg Confession, they are called instruments through which the Holy Spirit is given (Art. IV, p. 10), and testimonies of the will of God proposed and offered through them. They are likewise said to excite and confirm faith and to exhibit and show forth the promises, ibid.” (Isagog. p. 406.) Cf. the annotations above to Part III, ch. 5, § 8, pp. 260—265.

Christ. Chemnitius: “Question A: What is the use of the sacraments, since all things are in the Word? Answer: They are necessary 1. by divine institution as organs of grace and the visible Word. 2. On account of the infirmity of faith, so that they may specially offer, apply, and seal to us the grace of God contained in the general promises. The sacraments are therefore necessary for salvation as an instrumental cause, but not as precisely as the Word and faith; for the thief on the cross was saved without baptism, and the children who died in the wilderness, or before the eighth day, were saved without circumcision, by virtue of that promise: ‘I will be God to you and to your seed after you.’ Whence also Bellarmine (p. 100) makes faith and the sacraments associate causes, but he errs in that he says the sacraments are more necessary than faith. Question B: What, therefore, did Abraham receive in circumcision and Cornelius through baptism? Answer: The same grace of God which they had before and which the sacraments confer, but through other means. Whence they also had the same grace fully before, as far as it was on God’s part, but as far as it was on their own part, they were rendered the more certain of grace because they had received it through a double means.” (Annot. in Catechesin C. Dieterici, p. 141.)

The sacraments confer or seal evangelical grace when they confer faith, or seal and confirm it. For thus are men regenerated, justified, and renewed; which we shall show below regarding the individual sacraments. Meanwhile, it is simultaneously evident how the sacraments do not profit unless faith intervenes.

Apology of the A. C.: “We condemn the whole crowd of scholastic doctors, who teach that the sacraments confer grace *ex opere operato* [by the work performed] to one not placing an obstacle, without a good motion of the user. This is a simply Jewish opinion, to think that we are justified by a ceremony without a good motion of the heart, that is, without faith.” (Art. 14, p. 204, § 18.)

Augsburg Confession: “Concerning the use of the sacraments, they teach that the sacraments were instituted not only to be marks of profession among men, but rather that they should be signs and testimonies of the will of God toward us, proposed for the purpose of exciting and confirming faith in those who use them. Therefore, the sacraments are to be used in such a way that faith may be added, which believes the promises that are exhibited and shown forth through the sacraments. They therefore condemn those who teach that the sacraments justify *ex opere operato*, and who do not teach that faith is required in the use of the sacraments, which believes that sins are remitted.” (Art. 13, p. 41 sq.)

Luther: “They say that they (the sacraments) profit all, even the impious and unbelieving, provided they do not place an obstacle; as if unbelief itself were not the most obstinate and hostile obstacle of all to grace, so much so that they have labored to make a precept out of the sacrament, and a work out of faith. For if the sacrament gives me grace because I receive it, then I truly obtain grace by my own work, not by faith.”

ON THE SACRAMENTS IN GENERAL. Indeed, the matter stands differently regarding infants than it does regarding adults. For in the latter, faith must already be present in order for them to use the sacraments unto salvation; in the former, however, faith is produced precisely through the sacrament itself. Cf. the annotations above to Part III, ch. 3, § 11, c., p. 156 sq. For God, in conferring evangelical grace, always intends the salvation of men in this manner. Gerhard: "Since the best and wisest God does nothing and institutes nothing in vain, therefore the sacraments also have certain and divinely established ends; and these are either principal or less principal. There are two principal ends of the sacraments: the first is that they are organs, media, and οχήματα, through which God offers, exhibits, and applies to believers the proper promise of the Gospel concerning the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life. . . The latter principal end follows, that they are σφραγίδες, seals and signets, sealing the promise of divine grace exhibited to believers. For in the sacraments, God offers His grace, applies the offered grace to believers, and seals the applied grace to them. . . Secondary and less principal ends of the sacraments can be enumerated in many ways. Such as:

Latin:

Apologia A. C.: ״Corda simul per verbum qjb ritum movet Deusr ut credant et concipiant fidem, sicut ait Paulus (Rom. 10, 17.): ,Fides ex auditu est.4 Sicut autem verbum incurrit in aures, ut feriat corda:

ita ritus ipse incurrit in oculos, ut moveat corda. Idem effectus est verbi et ritus, sicut praeclare dictum est ab Augustino, sacramentum esse,verbum visibile‘, quia ritus oculis accipitur et est quasi pictura verbi, idem significans, quod verbum. Quare idem est utriusque effectuß.“ (Art. 13. p. 202. § 5.)

Lutherus: ״Scimus quidem, externa non salvare, si accipias externa, id est, nostra, verum Deus etiam per externa salutem operatur, et sic ordinavit, quod nolit dare spiritum suum sine signis et externa re aliqua. Ideo instituit in ecclesia ministerium verbi, baptismum et coenam corporis ac sauguinis Filii sui. Sic in die pentecostes descendit et datus est apostolis Spiritus Sanctus non invisibiliter, sed vento valido et linguis igneis. Quare sacramentarii errant, et ponunt hic falsum principium, quod dicunt: Nulla externa res prodest ad salutem. Imo tu inverte, et dic: Sine externa re nulla salus contingit. . . Quemadmodum enim per verbum movet Spiritus Sanctus, ita etiam per signa movet, quae nihil sunt, quam verbum, ut sic dicam, reale, ubi re exprimitur, quod verbum sonat.‘4 (In Esajam scholia. Vid. Exeget. opp. lat. Erlangae, 1860. Vol. XXII, p. 185. sq.)

M. Chemnitius: ״Quomodo baptisma nos salvos facit, 1 Pet. 3., quomodo est lavacrum regenerationis, Tit. 3.? Hoc Paulus simpliciter declarat, cum Ephes. c. 5. inquit: ,Mundans ecclesiam lavacro aquae in verbo.1 Et Augustinus idem colligit ex illa Christi sententia: ,Mundi estis propter verbum meum, quod locutus sum vobis.‘ Recte ergo Apologia Augustanae Confessionis dicit, eundem esse effectum, eandem virtutem seu efficaciam et verbi et sacramentorum, quae sunt sigilla promissionum; quae ideo etiam Augustinus vocat verba visibilia. Sicut igitur evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, non, quod magica quaedam vis characteribus, syllabis aut sono verborum inhaereat, sed quia est medium, organon seu instrumentum, per quod Spiritus Sanctus efficax est, proponens, offerens, exhibens, distribuens et applicans meritum Christi et gratiam Dei, ad salutem omni credenti; ita etiam sacramentis tribuitur virtus seu efficacia, non, quod in sacramentis extra seu praeter meritum Christi, misericordiam Patris et efficaciam Spiritus Sancti quaerenda sit gratia ad salutem, sed sacramenta sunt causae instrumentales, ita quod per illa media seu organa Pater vult gratiam suam exhibere, donare, applicare, Filius meritum suum communicare credentibus, Spiritus Sanctus efficaciam suam exercere ad salutem omni credenti. Hoc modo manet Deo gratia sua, ut gratia non alibi quaeratur, quam apud Deum Patrem; pretium seu cauia remissionis peccatorum et vita aeterna non alibi quaeratur, quam in morte et resurrectione Christi; efficacia regenerationis ad salutem non alibi quaeratur, quam in operatione Spiritus Sancti. Sacramenta vero illa beneficia in verbo nobis proponunt, afferunt et exhibent et obsignant, atque ita ducunt nos ad Christum, ad gratiam Dei, ad efficaciam Spiritus. Quia enim Deus in iis, quae ad salutem nostram pertinent, per certa media vult nobiscum agere, et hunc usum ipse ordinavit et instituit verbum promissionis evangelii, quod aliquando simpliciter per se sive nudum proponitur, aliquando vero vestitum seu visibile factum, certis a Deo institutis ritibus seu sacramentis. Verbum igitur et sacramenta monstrant nobis, ubi fides debeat quaerere et ubi possit invenire Christum mediatorem, Patrem et Spiritum Sanctum, ita ut nobiscum agant, exhibeant, applicent et obsignent beneficia, quae Christus promeruit et de quibus evangelium concionatur. Et in usu sacramentorum fides non quaerit aut respicit essentialem aliquam virtutem seu efficaciam inhaerentem ipsis externis sacramentorum elementis, sed in promissione, quae annexa est sacramento, quaerit, apprehendit et accipit gratiam Patris, meritum Filii et efficaciam Spiritus.“ (Exam. coneil. Trid. De efficacia et usu sacram. Ed. Genev. f. 215.)

Carpzovius: ״Sacramenta non μερικώς, sed όλικώς spectata sunt signa, non signa nuda, quae σηαεκύτικα tantum sunt et rem aliquam vel PART. III. CAP. VIII.

repraesentant saltem aut per modum notificationis indicant vel de ea certum aliquem saltem faciunt, et objecti ve movent atque assensum excitant; sed προςφερόμενα, quae revera operantur ceu organa et instrumenta, et quidem semel per modum physicae actionis, quatenus fidem et divina charismata inhaerentia sive primitus conferant ac operentur, sive jam ante data augeant ac roborent. Deinde vero per modum actionis moralis, quoad justificum bonum, quod credenti non offerunt saltem, sed fide receptum etiam conferunt et obsignant. Hinc ab A. C. dicuntur instrumenta, per quae donatur Sp. S., art. IV. p. 10., et testimonia voluntatis Dei per illa propositae et oblatae. Dicuntur item excitare et confirmare fidem et promissiones exhibere atque ostendere, ibid.“ (Isagog. p. 406.) Cf. supra ad P. III. c. 5. § 8. annotata p. 260—265.

Christ. Chemnitius: ״Inquis a.: Quid prosunt sacramenta, cum omnia sint in verbo? Resp.: Sunt necessaria 1. ex institutione divina ut organa gratiae et verbum visibile. 2. Propter fidei infirmitatem, ut nobis specialiter gratiam Dei, in generalibus promissionibus contentam, offerant, applicent et obsignent. Sunt igitur sacramenta necessaria ad salutem tanquam causa Instrumentalis, sed non tam praecise, ac verbum et fides; latro n. in cruce salvatus est sine baptismo et liberi, qui mortui sunt in deserto, aut ante octavam diem, salvati fuerunt sine circumcisione, vi illius promissionis: ,Ero Deus tuus et seminis tui post te.‘ Unde et Bellarm. p. 100. fidem et sacramenta facit causas socias, sed errat in eo, quod sacramenta dicit magis esse necessaria, quam fidem. Inquis ß.: Quid igitur acceperunt Abraham in circumcisione et Comelius per baptismum? Resp.: Eandem gratiam Dei, quam antea habebant et quam sacramenta conferunt, sed per alia media. Unde eandem gratiam etiam antea habebant plenam, quantum erat ex parte Dei, sed quantum est ex parte sua, eo certiores reddebantur de gratia, quod duplici medio eam accepissent.“ (Annot. in Catechesin C. Dieterici. p. 141.)

Conferunt autem sacramenta aut obsignant gratiam evangelicam, quando fidem conferunt, aut obsignant et confirmant. Sic enim homines regenerantur, justificantur et renovantur; quod de sacramentis singulis infra ostendemus. Interim simul constat, quomodo sacramenta non prosint, nisi intercedat fides.

Apologia A. C.: ״Damnamus totum populum scholasticorum doctorum, qui docent, quod sacramenta non ponenti obicem conferant gratiam ex opere operato, sine bono motu utentis. Haec simpliciter judaica opinio est, sentire, quod per ceremoniam justificemur, sine bono motu cordis, hoc est, sine fide.“ (Artic. 14. p. 204. § 18.)

Aug. Confessio: ״De usu sacramentorum docent, quod sacramenta instituta sint, non modo ut sint notae professionis inter hornines, sed magis ut sint signa et testimonia voluntatis Dei erga nos ad excitandam et confirmandam fidem in his, qui utuntur, proposita. Itaque utendum est sacramentis ita, ut fides accedat, quae credat promissionibus, quae per sacramenta exhibentur et ostenduntur. Damnant igitur illos, qui docent, quod sacramenta ex opere operato justificent, nec docent, fidem requiri in usu sacramentorum, quae credat remitti peccata.“ (Artic. 13. p. 41. sq.)

Lutherus: ״Ea (sacramenta) prodesse dicunt omnibus etiam impiis et incredulis, modo non ponant obicem; quasi ipsa incredulitas non sit omnium obstinatissimus et hostilissimus obex gratiae, adeo ex sacramento praeceptum, ex fide opus facere moliti sunt. Nam si dat gratiam mihi sacramentum, quia suscipio, jam vere ex opere meo, non ex fide gratiam obtineo.“

Nempe aliter sese res habet circa infantes, aliter circa adultos. In his enim fidem jam adesse oportet, ut sacramentis salutariter utantur; in illis vero fides per ipsum sacramentum demum producitur. Cf. supra annotata ad P. III. c. 3. § 11. c. p. 156. sq. Semper enim Deus, gratiam evangelicam conferens, hac ratione intendit hominum salutem. Gerhardus: ״Cum Deus optimus et sapientissimus nihil faciat aut instituat frustra, ideo etiam sacramentorum sunt certi ac divinitus constitutiones; iidemque vel principales vel minus principales. Fines sacramentorum principales duo sunt, prior, quod sint organa, media et οχήματα, per quae Deus offert, exhibet et credentibus applicat promissionem evangelii propriam de remissione peccatorum, justitia et vita aeterna. . . Succedit finis principalis posterior, quod sint σφραγίδες, sigilla et signacula, promissionem divinae gratiae credentibus exhibitam obsignantia. Sicut milites tesseris et oves ex notis impressis dignoscuntur, ita Deus ecclesiam certis notis voluit esse insignitam. 2 Quod sint nervi publicorum congressuum; ut enim praedicatio verbi, ita quoque administratio sacramentorum est pars publici ministerii, ideoque non nisi in casu necessitatis privatim peragi debet. Sic baptismus significat mortificationem veteris adami et resurrectionem novi hominis, Rom. 6 Sacra Domini coena est symbolum concordiae, ,unum enim corpus sumus, qui de uno pane participamus.4 1 Cor. 11. etc.44 (L. de sacram. §§ 55. 87. 94.)
