Trid. sess. 7. can. 2. . . Negant quoque pontificii, sacramenta esse sigilla gratiam Dei obsignantia, ut Bellarminus 1. 1. de Sacram, c. 14.


### On the Sacraments in General: That they are symbols of confession, marks, and tokens of the Church, by which…

1. That they are symbols of confession, marks, and tokens of the Church, by which the people of God are distinguished from other assemblies. Just as God distinguishes Himself from the idols of the Gentiles, so He also wills His Church to be distinguished from idolatrous assemblies. Just as soldiers are recognized by tokens and sheep by impressed marks, so God willed the Church to be distinguished by certain marks.

2. That they are the nerves of public gatherings; for just as the preaching of the Word, so also the administration of the sacraments is a part of the public ministry, and therefore it ought not to be performed privately except in a case of necessity. To this must be referred what Augustine writes in *Lib. 19 contra Faustum*, c. 14: 'Men have never been able to be gathered into any name of religion without sacraments.' 3. That they are as it were pledges, by which we are bound to God for faith and obedience.

4. That they are types and images of virtues, especially of love. Thus, Baptism signifies the mortification of the old Adam and the resurrection of the new man, Rom.

6 The Lord's Supper is a symbol of concord, 'for we are one body, who partake of one bread,' 1 Cor. 11, etc." (L. de sacram. §§ 55, 87, 94.) ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1 Of the Calvinists, who maintain that the sacraments are bare signs signifying divine grace, either already conferred or to be conferred afterward; thus Zwingli in *Conf. a. 7.*, Calvin in *Inst. 4.14*, Bucanus in *Loc. 46. Instit. Theol.* p. 59, Beza in *resp. ad acta colloq. Mompelg. P. 2.* p. 115, where he says: 'That it is a palpable error by which a causative power—as the Scholastics say—of conferring grace is attributed indeed to God, but an instrumental power to the sacraments'; cf. p. 116, 118. Aretius, *P. 2. probi*, p. 441, criticizes those 'who call the sacraments exhibitive signs,' adding this reason: 'because the things themselves, of which they are exhibitive signs, are not present in the sacraments'; Wolfg. Musculus, *Loc.* p. 615, says: 'It is proven by no Scriptures that a sacrament is a medium through which the remission of sins is conferred.' 2 Of the Papists, who deny that the sacraments of the Old Testament were effective media of divine grace, whether for offering, conferring, or sealing it. Thus Bellarmine, *l. 2. de Sacram., c. 13*, based on the Council of Florence and Trent, maintains: 'This is the difference between the sacraments of the Old and New Law, that ours confer grace, while those only signified it.' See *Concil. Trid. sess. 7. can. 2.* . . The Papists also deny that the sacraments are seals sealing the grace of God, as Bellarmine, *l. 1. de Sacram., c. 14*. 3 Of the Socinians, who deny that the grace of God is conferred or. . . sealed through the sacraments. . . 4 Of the Anabaptists, who deny that the sacraments of the New Testament are seals of grace, and [consider] them to be nothing but bare tokens of discretion and signs." Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. III.27 PART III. CAP. VIII. they wish them to be memorials and reminders of our duty. Thus Menno Simons against Gellius Faber, p. 135. . . 5 Of the Schwenkfeldians, who maintain that "the sacraments are not means of conferring grace, but are only foreshadowings of an external profession and of the mortification of the flesh and similar things." See Schwenkfeld, Ep. 23, Vol. I, p. 177, and Ep. 89, Vol. I, p. 749 sq. 6 Of the Weigelians, who assert that "the sacraments, being sensible and visible elements, do not contribute even the slightest bit to salvation." See Weigel, Part 2, Phil. Myst., p. 184." (L. c. q. 2, f. 1043.) Luthardt: "After rationalistic theology denied the objectivity and the supernatural content of the sacraments and left them with only a subjective significance, unionistic theology retreated to the concept of the 'pledge,' while modern Lutheran theology seeks to obtain a specific gift and effect of the sacrament in distinction from that of the Word. Cf. Höfling, *Sacram. der Taufe*, I, § 13: 'a completely concentric, immediate divine effect not merely upon the spirit and the spiritual personality, but upon the entire spiritual and bodily nature of man which underlies it'; this is a necessary 'further development of ecclesiastical dogmatics'; for no one will be able to resist the impression that between the teaching of our dogmaticians regarding what a sacrament is, and what and how it effects, there prevails no proper and satisfying agreement." (*Compend. der Dogm.*, Third Ed., p. 281.) Thomasius: "While the Word with its testimony turns to the self-conscious personality of man in order to work upon it and, by means of it, upon the whole man, the sacrament turns to human nature—by which, however, we here deliberately repeat, we by no means understand merely corporeality, but the entire spiritual-bodily essence of man, which the 'I,' reflecting, distinguishes from itself just as it knows itself to be joined with it in unity. To this side of human existence, to this realm which never fully opens itself to consciousness and yet stands in an intimate rapport with it, the effect of the sacraments relates immediately. . . For this very reason, the mode of operation of the sacraments is of a different kind than that of the Word. The Word works because it works upon the self-conscious human personality, psychologically—that is, attaching itself to the law innate to the human spirit, through the organs of the same, through intelligence and will, upon the heart; and for this very reason it also works successively, by way of gradual unfolding; only in this way can it open up and mediate its rich content to the human personality and determine it to a new behavior (in repentance and faith). The sacrament, on the other hand, works because it works upon nature, concentrically, drastically, all at once; by means of one act, Baptism plants man completely into Christ and into His communion; in one moment, Christ imparts to us in the Lord's Supper His glorified corporeality for our enjoyment. While there, with the Word, the effect spreads out in breadth, here it gathers itself into the act of a sacramental performance; and while there the result is a new behavior of the personality, here it is a new relationship to Christ, into which the whole man is placed, and which he is given to experience." (*Christi Person und Werk*, III, 2 [ed. 2], p. 116—118.) Luther: "Because the Word of God is the greatest, most necessary, and highest part in Christendom (for the sacraments cannot exist without the Word, but the Word can indeed exist without the sacraments, and in case of necessity one could be saved without a sacrament, but not without the Word, as is the case with those who die before they obtain the desired Baptism),"

419 "...

in this, Christ has also performed all the more and greater wonders, namely, that they (the Papists) have had to preach the text of the Gospel freely and publicly, not only in Latin, but also in the language of every land, so that it might indeed remain known before all the world and in all languages among the elect, even though they handled the Sacrament and Baptism in no other than the Latin language, with secret words that no one was to hear." (Writing on the Private Mass and the Consecration of Priests. 1533. Opp. Hal. XIX, 1537.) § 11. A sacrament in general may be defined as an action divinely instituted out of the grace of God on account of the merit of Christ, occupied with an external and sensible element, through which, with the word of institution added, the grace of the Gospel concerning the remission of sins unto eternal life is conferred or sealed to men.

A general definition of a sacrament nowhere exists in Scripture. However, it must be formed from an induction of all the sacraments (strictly so called), which are divinely instituted, both in the Old and in the New Testament. Thus the blessed Himmelius, Synt. Disput. XIX. § 18. p. 192. Yet it is not one simple action, but a certain aggregate of several actions ordered toward one another. Conf. Cundisius, Not. ad Comp. Hutt. L. XX. Q. III. § 2. p. 1028.

Quenstedtius: "In this, sacraments differ from the Word; sacraments are nothing outside of their use; but the Word, even before and outside of its use, has intrinsic power and efficacy to produce spiritual effects." (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1042.) Thus, it is indicated not only that it is a serious and sacred action, but also what is its principal efficient cause. See § 4.

Which is the internal impulsive cause, according to § 5. As the external impulsive cause; concerning which see § 5.

The matter, or the material, is denoted. See § 7. Which bestows form upon the sacramental action. See § 8. The end for which it is signified. See § 9. The end of which, which is also the effect of the sacraments, is this. See § 10. § 12.

Some sacraments are of the Old, others of the New Testament. The former are called those which, instituted before the coming of Christ, pointed to Him from afar and shadowed Him forth by certain figures, and were abrogated when He was finally exhibited; the latter are those which, instituted by Christ Himself, testify to Him as exhibited and offer Him as present, to endure in the Church until the end. PART III. CHAP. VIII.

They agree, indeed, in that both are instituted by God, both consist of the Word and an element, and both are means of conferring or sealing grace.

Luther: "It is an error that the sacraments of the new law differ from the sacraments of the old law in the efficacy of their signification. Both signified equally; for the same God, who now saves us through baptism and bread, saved Abel through sacrifice, Noah through the ark, Abraham through circumcision, and all others through their signs.

Therefore, the sacrament of the old and new law does not differ regarding signification, provided you call 'old law' whatever God worked in the patriarchs and other fathers during the time of the law.

For those signs which were made among the patriarchs and fathers are to be distinguished far from the legal figures which Moses instituted in his law, such as the priestly rites in vestments, vessels, foods, houses, and the like. For the sacraments of the new law differ not only most widely from these, but also from the very signs which God gave for a time to the fathers living under the law, such as that of Gideon in the fleece (Judg. 6), of Manoah in the sacrifice, and such as Isaiah offered to Ahaz (Isa. 7). For in these, something was promised at the same time, by which faith in God was required.

In this, therefore, legal figures differ from new and old signs: that legal figures do not have an annexed word of promise that requires faith, whence they are not signs of justification, because they are not sacraments of faith, which alone justifies, but are sacraments of work only; for their entire force and nature was work, not faith, for he who performed them fulfilled them, even working without faith.

But our signs or sacraments, and those of the fathers, have an annexed word of promise which requires faith, and can be fulfilled by no other work; therefore, they are signs or sacraments of justification, because they are sacraments of justifying faith and not of work, whence also their entire efficacy is faith itself, not the operation. For he who believes in them fulfills them, even if he performs no work.

Hence that proverb: 'Not the sacrament, but the faith of the sacrament justifies.' Thus, circumcision did not justify Abraham and his seed, and yet the Apostle (Rom. 4) calls it a seal of the righteousness of faith, because faith in the promise, to which circumcision was joined, justified and fulfilled that which circumcision signified. For faith was the circumcision of the foreskin of the heart in the spirit, which the circumcision of the flesh in the letter figured. Thus, the sacrifice of Abel clearly did not justify him, but the faith by which he offered himself wholly to God, which the external sacrifice figured." (De captivit. babyl. eccl. 1520. See Opp. lat. ad reform. hist. pert. Francof. 1868. Vol. V. p. 62 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Luthardt: "The equating of the Old Testament sacraments (circumcision and Passover) with the New Testament ones (the same oblation, collation, sealing of evangelical grace, and the application through faith as a medium receptivum) rests upon a misunderstanding of the difference in the progress of the history of salvation." (Compend. der Dogm. Third Ed. 1868. p. 281.) See above at this place § 10. e. antithesis 2 of the Papists. The words are those of the blessed Himmelius, Syntagm. 1. c. §§ 66. 68.

Latin:

3. Socinianorum, negantium, per sacramenta gratiam Dei conferri aut. . . obsignari. . .

4. Anabaptistarum, qui N. T. sacramenta negant esse sigilla gratiae, eademque non nisi nudas discretionis tesseras et signa Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III.27 PART. III. CAP. vm. memorialia, nostrique officii commonitoria esse volunt. Ita Menno Simonis adv. Gellium Fabrum p. 135. . .

5. Swenkfeldianorum, statuentium, ,sacramenta non esse gratiae conferendae media, sed tantum adumbrationes esse externae professionis et mortificationis carnis et similium rerum.‘ Vide Swenkfeldium Ep. 23. T. I. p. 177. et Ep. 89. T. I. p. 749. sq.

6. Weigelianorum, asserentium, ,sacramenta, quippe elementa sensibilia et visibilia, nec tantillum facere ad salutem.‘ Vide Weigeliuui P. 2. Phil. Myst. p. 184.“ (L. c. q. 2. f. 1043.) Luthardtius: ,,Nachdem die rationalistische Theologie die Objectivitat und den übernatürlichen Inhalt der Sacramente verneint und ihnen nur eine subjective Bedeutung übrig gelassen, zog sich die Unionstheologie auf den Begriff des Unterpfändlichen zurück, während die moderne lutherische Theologie eine specißsche Gabe und Wirkung des Sacraments im Unterschied von der des Wortes zu gewinnen sucht. Vgl. Höfling, Sacram, der Taufe. I. § 13.: ,eine ganz concentrische unmittelbare göttliche Wirkung nicht blos auf den Geist und die geistliche Persönlichkeit, sondern auf die ganze dieser zum Grunde liegende geistliehe und leibliche Natur des Menschen‘; dies eine nothwendige,Fortbildung der kirchlichen Dogmatik‘; denn Niemand wird sich des Eindrucks erwehren können, dass zwischen der Lehre unsrer Dogmatiker von dem, was Sacrament ist, und der, was und wie es wirkt, keine rechte und befriedigende Zusammenstimmung herrscht.“ (Compend. der Dogm. Dritte Aufl. p. 281.) Thomasius: ,,Während das Wort mit seinem Zeugniss sich an die selbstbewusste Persönlichkeit des Menschen wendet, um auf sie und mittelst ihrer auf den ganzen Menschen zu wirken, wendet sich das Sacrament an die menschliche Natur, unter der wir aber — was wir hier geflissentlich wiederholen — keineswegs blos die Leiblichkeit verstehen, sondern den ganzen geistleiblichen Wesensbestand des Menschen, welchen das Ich reflectirend eben so von sich unterscheidet, als es sich mit ihm zur Einheit zusammengeschlossen weiss. Auf diese Seite des menschlichen Seins, auf dieses Gebiet, das sich dem Bewusstsein nie völlig erschliesst und doch in einem innigen Rapport mit ihm steht, bezieht sich unmittelbar die Wirkung der Sacramente. . . Eben deshalb ist die Wirkungsweise der Sacramente eine andersartige, als die des Wortes. Das Wort wirkt, weil auf die selbstbewusste menschliche Persönlichkeit, psychologisch, d. h., sich anschliessend an das dem menschlichen Geiste eingeborne Gesetz, durch die Organe desselben, durch Intelligenz und Wille hindurch, auf das Herz; und es wirkt eben deshalb auch successiv, auf dem Wege allmählicher Entfaltung; nur so kann es seinen reichen Inhalt der menschlichen Persönlichkeit erschliessen, vermitteln und sie zu einem neuen Verhalten (in Busse und Glaube) bestimmen. Das Sacrament hingegen wirkt, weil auf die Natur, concentrisch, drastisch, mit einem Male; mittelst Eines Aktes pflanzt die Taufe den Menschen vollständig in Christum und in seine Gemeinschaft, in einem Momente theilt uns Christus im Abendmahle seine verklärte Leiblichkeit zum Genüsse mit. Während sich dort, bei dem Wort, die Wirkung in die Breite auseinanderlegt, fasst sie sich hier in den Akt eines sacramentlichen Vollzugs zusammen, und während dort das Resultat ein neues Verhalten der Persönlichkeit ist, ist es hier ein neues Verhältniss zu Christus, in das der ganze Mensch versetzt, und welches ihm zu erfahren gegeben wird.“ (Christi Person und Werk. III, 2. [ed. 2.] p. 116—118.) Lutherus: ,,Weil das Wort Gottes das grösste, nöthigste und höchste Stück ist in der Christenheit (denn die Sacramente ohne das Wort nicht sein können, aber wohl das Wort ohne die Sacramente, und zur Noth einer ohne Sacrament, aber nicht ohne das Wort könnte selig werden, als die so da sterben, ehe sie die begehrte Taufe erlangen),

DE SACRAMENTIS IN GENERE.419

hat hierin Christus auch desto mehr und grössere Wunder gethan, nämlich dass sie (Pontificii) den Text des Evangelii haben müssen frei öffentlich predigen, nicht allein in lateinischer, sondern auch in eines jeglichen Landes Sprache, dass es ja vor aller Welt und in allen Sprachen kund bliebe bei den Auserwählten, so sie doch das Sacrament und die Taufe in keiner andern, denn in lateinischer Sprache, mit heimliehen Worten, die niemand hören musste, handelten.“ (Schrift von der Winkelmesse und Pfaffenweihe. 1533. Opp. Hai. XIX, 1537.) § 11. Definiri a potest sacramentum in genere, quod sit b actio divinitus c ex gratia Dei d propter meritum Christi e instituta, circa elementum f externum et sensibile occupata, per quam, accedente verbo g institutionis, hominibus h confertur aut obsignatur gratia i evangelii de. remissione peccatorum ad vitam aeternam.

Definitio sacramenti generalis in Scriptura nuspiam extat. Formanda autem est ex inductione omnium sacramentorum (exquisite dictorum), quae sunt divinitus instituta, tum in Vet. tum in Nov. Testam. Ita b. Himmelius Synt. Disput. XIX. § 18. p. 192. Non tamen una simplex actio, verum aggregatum quid ex pluribus ad se invicem ordinatis actionibus. Conf. 6. Cundisium Not. ad Comp. Hutt. L. XX. Q. III. § 2. p. 1028.

Quenstedtius: ״In hoc differunt sacramenta a verbo; sacramenta extra usum nulla sunt; verbum autem etiam ante et extra usum intrinsecam habet vim et efficaciam ad spirituales effectus producendos.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1042.) Ita non solum esse actionem seriam et sacram, verum etiam quae sit ejus causa efficiens principalis, indicatur. Vid. § 4.

Quae est causa impulsiva interna, juxta § 5. Tanquam ob causam impulsivam externam; de qua vid. § 5. Materia, seu materiale, denotatur. Vid. §7. Quod formam actioni sacramentali largitur. Vid. § 8.

Finis cui significatur. Vid. § 9. Finis cujus, qui et effectus sacramentorum, hic est. Vid. § 10. § 12. Sacramenta alia a sunt veteris, alia novi testamenti. Illa b dicuntur, quae, ante Christi adventum instituta, eminus ipsum monstrarunt et quibusdam figuris adumbrarunt, quo demum exhibito abrogata fuerunt; haec sunt, quae ab ipso Christo instituta ipsum exhibitum testantur et praesentem offerunt, duratura in ecclesia usque ad finem.

PART. III. CAP. VIII.

Conveniunt quidem, quod utraque a Deo sunt instituta, utraque constant verbo et elemento suntque media conferendae aut obsignandae gratiae.

Lutherus: ,,]Error est, sacramenta novae legis differre a sacramentis veteris legis penes efficaciam significationis. Utraque aequaliter significabant; idem enim Deus, qui nos nunc per baptismum et panem salvat, salvavit Abel per sacrificium, Noe per arcam, Abraham per circumcisionem et alios omnes per sua signa.

Nihil itaque differt sacramentum veteris et novae legis quoad significationem, modo veterem legem appelles, quidquid in patriarchis et aliis patribus tempore legis operatus est Deus.

Nam ea signa, quae in patriarchis et patribus facta sunt, longe sunt discernenda a figuris legalibus, quas Moses in lege sua instituit, quales sunt ritus sacerdotales in vestibus, vasis, cibis, domibus et similibus. Ab his enim non modo longissime differunt novae legis sacramenta, sed et ipsa signa, quae pro tempore Deus patribus dedit, in lege viventibus, quale fuit Gedeonis in vellere (Judic. 13.), Manue in sacrificio, quale et Isaias obtulit Achas Isa. 7. In iis enim simul promittebatur aliquid, quo fides in Deum exigebatur.

In hoc ergo differunt legales figurae a signis novis et vetustis, quod legales figurae non habent annexum verbum promissionis, quod fidem exigat, unde non sunt signa justificationis, quia non sunt sacramenta fidei, quae sola justificant, sed sunt sacramenta operis tantum; tota enim eorum vis et natura erat opus, non fides, qui enim ea faciebat, implebat ea, etiam sine fide operans.

At nostra et patrum signa seu sacramenta habent annexum verbum promissionis, quod fidem exigit, et nullo opere alio impleri potest, ideo sunt signa seu sacramenta justificationis, quia sunt sacramenta justificantis fidei et non operis, unde et tota eorum efficacia est ipsa fides, non operatio. Qui enim eis credit, is implet ea, etiamsi nihil operetur.

Inde proverbium illud: ,Non sacramentum, sed fides sacramenti justificat.4 Sic circumcisio non justificavit Abraham et semen ejus, et tamen apostolus (Rom. 4.) eam appellat signaculum justitiae fidei, quia fides in promissionem, cui juncta fuit circumcisio, justificabat et implebat id, quod circumcisio significabat. Fides enim fuit circumcisio praeputii cordis in spiritu, quam figurabat circumcisio carnis in litera. Sic sacrificium Abel plane non eum justificabat, sed fides, qua se Deo totum obtulit, quam sacrificium externum figurabat.44 (De captivit. babyl. eccl. 1520. Vid. Opp. lat. ad reform. hist. pert. Francof. 1868. Vol. V. p. 62. sq.)

Luthardtius; ,,Die Gleichstellung der alttestamentlichen Sacramente (Beschneidung und Passah) mit dem neutestamentlichen (dieselbe oblatio, collatio, obsignatio gratiae evangelicae und die Application durch den Glauben als medium receptivum) beruht auf einer Verkennung des Unterschiedes des heilsgeschichtlichen Fortschritts.44 (Compend. der Dogm. Dritte Aufl. 1868. p. 281.) Vide supra h. 1. § 10. e. antithesin 2. Pontificiorum. Verba sunt b. Himmeln Syntagm. 1. c. §§ 66. 68.


## 24 On the Sacraments of the Old Testament

PART III. CAP. IX. Chapter IX. ON THE SACRAMENTS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT. § I.

After the human race had fallen into sin, and God, before the advent of the Messiah, willed to enter into a peculiar covenant, especially with Abraham and his posterity, and to endow them with His grace, it pleased Him to exhibit His grace to men not only through the revealed Word, but also through the singular rite of circumcision instituted by Him.

Luther: "You have heard that Abraham is the first patriarch who was commanded to circumcise the little boys. That was a shameful, disgraceful, mad, and nonsensical commandment in the eyes of reason, that they should circumcise themselves, and in that place which one does not like to name or hear mentioned. But Abraham is obedient to God and lets himself be circumcised, even though it is a disgraceful and shameful thing. But it happened for this reason, that God wanted to break our pride and make human wisdom into foolishness. Therefore, the Jews had to hear much scorn and mockery among the Gentiles. People spoke of them mockingly and scornfully and considered circumcision a foolish thing. Therefore, many did not want to endure or suffer the evil gossip and did not let themselves be circumcised. Just as one also finds many among us Christians who cannot endure the world’s slander, when we are called factions, sects, and heretics, and would rather let Christianity go on that account. Thus Moses’ wife also acted; when he was a guest with her in a foreign land, he would have gladly had his son circumcised for his own part, but he could not; his wife did not want to enter into this disgrace, that her son should be circumcised, but he should live as one lived among the Gentiles; she did not want to have this mark and stain of shame. For circumcision was a shame among the Gentiles." (Exposition on several chapters of the 2nd Book of Moses. 1524. III, 1137. sq.)

For in the state of integrity, sacraments properly so-called had no place, since sins were absent from the human race, and thus there was no need for the remission of sins or for the means of obtaining it.

By which men were initiated or inserted into the divine covenant; just as circumcision itself is called ברית, i.e., covenant, pact, Gen. 17:10, διαθήκη περιτομῆς Acts 7:8.

The seat of the doctrine is found in Gen. 17. § 2.

The principal efficient cause of circumcision is the Triune God. Who, by the act of institution, indeed determined by His own sufficient authority what pertained to the nature or essence of circumcision, or to...

pertain to the species of the act, as they say, but at the same time He commanded the exercise of the act and not only annexed a promise of grace, but also conferred grace itself through this medium. See Gen. 17:1 and 9.

For circumcision is an external work. § 3. The internal impulsive cause is the goodness and φιλανθρωπία of God; the external and meritorious cause is the merit of Christ.

For God, moved within Himself by nothing but His own goodness, instituted this sacrament, by which men might be so joined with God that, being reborn and having their sins remitted and being adopted, they might enjoy God as their own. Compare what we shall say regarding the end for which [it was instituted] in the first book. And specifically, indeed, it was limited to the house and descendants of Abraham; to this pertain the things that will be delivered regarding the end to whom or the subject.

For to this pertains not only what we said about the sacrament in general from Eph. 1:8, but also that circumcision itself prefigured Christ who was to be born from this nation; whence you may gather that that type was instituted on account of this antitype, and that God, having regard for the Messiah and His merit, therefore also willed to be efficacious through circumcision. § 4. The ministerial cause of circumcision was first Abraham, then the succeeding patriarchs; afterwards the Levitical priests. Extraordinarily, however, circumcision was also performed by laymen and women.

Regarding which, indeed, no express command exists either in the history of the institution of circumcision, Gen. 17, or in the repeated institution, Lev. 12, but the example of the first act of circumcision is deservedly held as the norm for the ministry of circumcision to be performed thereafter. See Gen. 17:25 ff., chap. 21:4. However, Abraham is to be viewed not precisely as a head of a household, but as a minister of sacred things in the church of his house. Yet Abraham himself seems not so much to have circumcised himself as to have been circumcised by Eliezer, the steward of the house and vicar of sacred things.

They also, not so much as heads of families, but rather as ministers of sacred things and teachers of the church. Just as they claimed for themselves the other parts of the ecclesiastical ministry by divine institution; therefore they were distributed throughout all the Israelite tribes, so that they could perform such offices everywhere. Compare 1 Macc. 2:18.

Thus Zipporah circumcised her son (God indeed approving, and removing the plague which He was about to inflict on account of the omitted act of circumcision), Exod. 4:25, and many women during the time of persecution, 1 Macc. 1:63 and 2 Macc. 6:10, did the same. §

5. The material of circumcision constituted the foreskin, as the external element, and the amputation of it, as the action occupied about it. Or that which was common, or could be common, to that sacred or sacramental circumcision and to others which are not a sacramental action. Which some think is called so from *praeputando* [pruning/cutting off], others from the Greek προπόσιον. And it is the anterior skin on the male member, to be amputated through circumcision.

But by this material destined for circumcision, God seems to have wished to admonish the Israelites partly of the coming of the Messiah, who was to be born from the posterity of Abraham (though not in a carnal manner), partly of original sin, propagated through carnal generation, and partly of spiritual regeneration, which was effected through circumcision itself.

For it is not precisely required for the matter or element of a sacrament that it be exhibited and dispensed to the user from the outside, but it suffices if it be treated by an external sacramental action, or if this action be directly occupied about it, and with a relation to man as a personal object. Which is expressly handed down, together with the thing to be amputated, in Gen. 17:11.

However, the instrument by which the amputation was to be performed is not read to be defined. Meanwhile, the amputation of the foreskin itself, viewed in itself, is certainly indifferent to a sacramental and non-sacramental action, so that it may rightly be held as the material of this sacrament.

We do not dare to assert a heavenly matter, which some seek here in addition to that earthly one or external element, and think it to be the body and blood of Christ.

For (1.) it is confessed that the body and blood of Christ were not really present in the administration of circumcision in the Old Testament (since the Son of God had not yet been made man). But it is difficult to assert a matter, and thus an essential part of a sacrament, which does not yet really exist. (2.) Since the heavenly matter of the sacraments cannot and ought not to be judged more correctly from elsewhere than from the divine institution, or, which is the same thing, from the proper seat in which the divine institution is described, according to the received rule, nothing is had in the institution of circumcision from which that heavenly matter could be gathered. (3.) The union between the earthly matter of this sacrament and that heavenly matter which is handed down can be declared with difficulty, unless you take refuge in that relation which imports the relation of the sign to the thing signified, and the fact that the merit of the future passion of Christ was applied to men through this sacrament; yet whether these suffice to assert a heavenly matter of the sacrament comes into question.

Therefore, with the blessed Gerhard in his *Loci* and the blessed Himmel in his *Syntagma*, we have preferred to omit mention of a heavenly matter in this sacrament. PART III. CHAP. IX.

Quenstedtius: "Finally, the ὀνοματοθεσία or imposition of a name was joined with circumcision, which indeed does not have a divine command, nor was it a perpetual adjunct; for those adults who accepted circumcision with Abraham retained their own names; yet it was a most ancient custom. It is probable from Gen. 21:3 that Abraham imposed upon his son Isaac the name which God had previously destined for him in Gen. 17:19, though it is not certain. But the examples of John the Baptist and Jesus Christ, our Savior, in Luke 1:59 and 2:21, are clear." (L. c. s. 1. th. 17. f. 1062.) § 6.

The formal element of circumcision was the very word of institution applied to the act of circumcision. Or that by which the amputation of the human foreskin was formally constituted in the being of a sacramental action.

Which is found in Gen. 17:10: "This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: (which commands) every male among you shall be circumcised." However, the word of promise had been set forth in verse 7. For just as God, through those words, made circumcision in its species, so to speak, and in the *actus signatus* a sacrament, so in the exercise, through words founded upon that institution, every individual act must be performed, writes Dr. Sebast. Schmidt, *Tract. de Circumc.* p. 395, who also in the following pages, 398-399, among several ancient formulas of Jewish blessings, recounts this sacramental one, which especially regards the words of institution: "Blessed are You, O Lord our God, King of the world, who has sanctified us with Your commandments, and commanded us to initiate him into the covenant of Abraham, our father."

Quenstedtius: "Circumcision was not without some ἄκουστον or audible word, which is shown both by the generic condition of all sacraments, for which the word of institution and promise is required, and by the explicit description of circumcision as instituted and commanded, where the promise of grace is annexed, Gen. 17:7: 'I will be your God and the God of your offspring after you.' Without a doubt, there was also added in the very dispensation a word of application and invocation, which is found either formally or at least in its traces among the rabbis; see Dr. Schmidt, l. c. p. 390 sq., where he recounts various blessings, and indeed: 1. of the circumciser, 2. of the father, 3. of those standing by." (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 4. s. 1. th. 10. f. 1058.) N. Hunnius: "Philosophers call the *actus signatus* an act abstracted from particulars, multiplied in the exercise of particulars; as a thing is apprehended in the *actus signatus* when it is conceived just as it is signified by a common definition and is not apprehended under its own sign (which is a name); but in the *actus exercitus*, when something is conceived not in a common and indefinite notion, but under a particular name, just as man in the *actus signatus* is a species, in the *actus exercitus* he is an individual, Socrates, Peter, etc." (Διάσκεψις, § 97. p. 63.) § 7.

Latin:

PART. ΠΙ. CAP. IX. Caput IX. DE SACRAMENTIS VETERIS TESTAMENTI. § I.

Postquam genus humanum in peccata prolapsum fuit, a ac Deus ante Messiae adventum, inprimis cum Abrahamo et posteritate ejus, peculiare foedus inire eosque gratia sua donare voluit, placuit ei, non solum verbo revelato, sed etiam ritu singulari circumcisionis b instituto hominibus gratiam suam exhibere. c

Lutherus: ,,Ihr habt gehört, dass Abraham der erste Patriarche ist, dem befohlen worden, die Knäblein zu beschneiden. Das war ein schändlich, schmählich, toll und unsinnig Gebot vor der Vernunft, dass sie sich selbst beschneiden sollten und an dem Orte, den man nicht gerne nennen und hören mag. Aber Abraham ist Gott gehorsam und lässt sich beschneiden, ob es wohl ein schmählich und schändlich Ding ist. Aber es ist darum geschehen, dass Gott unsern Sinn brechen und die menschliehe Weisheit zur Thorheit machen wollte. Deshalben haben die Juden viel Hohn und Spott unter den Heiden hören müssen. Man hat spöttlich und höhnisch ihnen nachgeredet und die Beschneidung für ein närrisch Ding geachtet. Darum wollten viele die böse Nachrede nicht dulden noch leiden und Hessen sich nicht beschneiden. Wie man denn auch unter uns Christen viel findet, die der Welt Lästerung, da man uns heisst Rotten, Secten und Ketzer, nicht ertragen können, und lassen eher das Christenthum darüber fahren. Also hat Mosis Weib auch gethan; da er mit ihr ein Gast im fremden Lande gewesen, hätte er für seine Person den Sohn wohl gerne beschneiden lassen, aber er hat nicht gekonnt, sein Weib hat nicht gewollt in diese Schinachtreten, dass ihr Sohn beschnitten würde, sondern er sollte leben, wie man unter den Heiden lebte; sie wollte diesen Klick und Schandfleck nicht haben. Denn die Beschneidung war eine Schande unter den Heiden.“ (Ausl, über etliche Capp. des 2. B. Mose. 1524. III, 1137. sq.)

Nam in statu integritatis sacramenta proprie sic dicta locum non habuerunt, cum abessent a genere humano peccata, adeoque nec remissione peccatorum aut mediis ejus consequendae opus esset.

Quo homines initiarentur aut insererentur foederi divino; prout circumcisio ipsa dicitur 11,ברית. e. foedus, pactum Gen. 17, 10., dtaüήχη περιτομής Act. 7, 8.

Sedes doctrinae habetur Gen. 17. & 2·

Causa efficiens principalis a circumcisionis est Deus b trinunus. c Quae actu institutionis quidem sua ac sufficiente auctoritate determinavit, quae ad naturam aut essentiam circumcisionis, sive ad PART. III. CAP. IX.

speciem actus, ut ajunt, pertinent, simul autem exercitium actus mandavit ac non solum promissimem gratiae annexuit, verum etiam gratiam ipsam per hoc medium contulit. Vid. Gen. 17, 1. et 9.

Est enim circumcisio opus ad extra. § 3. Causa impulsiva interna est a bonitas et φιλαα&ρω7ιία Dei;b externa et meritoria est meritum c Christi.

Deus enim intra se non nisi sua bonitate impulsus sacramentum boc instituit, quo homines ita cum Deo jungerentur, ut renati et remissis peccatis adoptati Deo, velut suo, fruerentur. Confer., quae de fine cujus b. 1. dicemus. Ac speciatim quidem ad domum et posteros Abrabami terminata; quo pertinent, quae de fine cui aut subjecto tradentur.

Huc enim non solum pertinet, quod de sacram, in genere diximus ex Ephes. 1, S., verum etiam, quod ipsa circumcisio Christum ex hac gente nasciturum praefiguravit; unde colligas, typum illum propter hunc antitypum esse institutum ac Deum, habito respectu ad Messiam ejusque meritum, ideo etiam per circumcisionem esse voluisse efficacem. § 4. Causa ministerialis a circumcisionis primum Abraham b fuit, deinde patriarchae c succedentes; postea sacerdotes d Levitici. Extraordinarie vero etiam a laicis et feminis e circumcisio peracta fuit.

De qua quidem expressum mandatum nec in historia institutae circumcisionis, Gen. 17., nec in repetita institutione, Levit. 12., ullum extat, exemplum autem primi actus circumcisionis merito habetur pro norma ministerii circumcisionis deinceps obeundi. Vid. Gen. 17, 25. sqq., cap. 21, 4. Spectandus autem est Abraham non praecise, ut paterfamilias, sed ut minister sacrorum in ecclesia domus suae. Ipse tamen Abraham non tam se ipsum circumcidisse, quam ab Eliesare, praefecto domus et sacrorum vicario, circumcisus esse videtur.

Ipsi quoque, non tam ut capita familiarum, sed magis ut ministri sacrorum ac doctores ecclesiae. Prout caeteras ministerii ecclesiastici partes sibi vendicarunt ex institutione divina; ideo per omnes tribus Israeliticas distributi, ut ubique talibus officiis fungi possent. Conf. 1 Macc. 2, Iß.

Ita Zippora filium circumcidit (approbante quidem Deo et pia· gam, quam propter omissum actum circumcisionis illaturus erat, aufefente), Exod. 25., et feminae plures tempore persecutionis, 1 Macc. 1, 63. et 2 Macc. 610 ר., idem fecerunt. §

5. Materiale a circumcisionis constituebat praeputium,b tanquam elementum externum,c et amputatio d ejus, tanquam actio circa illud occupata.e Seu quod circumcisioni illi sacrae aut sacramentali et aliis, quae non sunt sacramentalis actio, commune erat, aut esse poterat. Quod alii a praeputando, alii a Graeco προπόΰζον dictum putant. Estque pellicula anterior in membro virili, per circumcisionem amputanda.

Dem autem hoc materiali ad circumcisionem destinato videtur admonere voluisse Israelitas partim adventus Messiae ex Abrahae posteritate (licet non carnali modo) nascituri, partim peccati originalis, per carnalem generationem propagati, partim regenerationis spiritualis, quae per ipsam circumcisionem fiebat.

Neque enim ad materiam sive elementum sacramenti praecise requiritur, ut utenti sacramento extrinsecus exhibeatur et dispensetur, sed sufficit, si actione externa sacramentali tractetur, aut haec circa illud, et cura relatione ad hominem, tanquam objectum personale, directe occupetur. Quae expresse, una cum re amputanda, traditur Gen. 17, 11.

Instrumentum vero, quo fieri debebat amputatio, definitum non legitur. Ipsa interim amputatio praeputii in se spectata utique indifferens est ad sacrmentalem et non-sacramentalem actionem, ut pro materiali hujus sacramenti recte habeatur.

Materiam coelestem, quam aliqui praeter terrenam illam seu elementum externum h. 1. quaerunt eamque corpus ac sanguinem Christi esse putant, non audemus asserere.

Nam (1.) in confesso est, corpus et sanguinem Christi in V. Test, (cum Filius Dei nondum factus esset homo) non fuisse in administratione circumcisionis realiter praesentia. Atqui difficile est materiam adeoque partem essentialem sacramenti asserere, quae realiter nondum existat. (2.) Cum de materia coelesti sacramentorum non aliunde rectius judicari possit ac debeat, quam ex divina institutione, sive, quod idem est, ex propria sede, in qua divina institutio describitur, juxta regulam receptam, in institutione circumcisionis nihil habetur, unde materia illa coelestis colligi queat. (3.) Unio inter materiam terrenam hujus sacramenti et materiam illam coelestem, quae traditur, difficulter declarari potest, nisi ad σχετιχψ illam, quae relationem signi ad rem signatam importat et quod meritum passionis Christi futurae per sacramentum hoc hominibus applicatum fuit, confugias; quae tamen an sufficiant ad materiam coelestem sacramenti asserendam, in quaestionem venit.

Ideo.cum b. Gerhardo in LL. et b. Himmelio in Syntagmate materiae coelestis in hoc sacramento mentionem omittere maluimus. PART. III. CAP. IX.

Quenstedtius: ,,Conjuncta denique fuit cum circumcisione ovouaßεσίη seu nominis impositio, quae quidem mandatum divinum non habet, nec fuit perpetuum adjunctum; qui enim adulti cum Abrahamo circumcisionem admiserunt, sua nomina retinuerunt; fuit tamen antiquissima consuetudo. Abrahamum filio suo Isaaco nomen, quod prius Deus ipsi destinaverat, Gen. 17, 19., in ipsa circumcisione imposuisse, probabile est ex Gen. 21, 3., non tamen certum. Sed exempla Johannis Baptistae et Jesu Christi, Salvatoris nostri, Luc. 1, 59. et 11, 21., clara sunt/‘ (L. c. s. 1. th. 17. f. 1062.) § 6.

Formale circumcisionis a erat ipsum verbum institutionis b ad actum circumcisionis adhibendum.c Sive illud, a quo amputatio praeputii humani in esse actionis sacramentalis formaliter constituebatur.

Quod habetur Gen. 17, 10.: Hoc est foedus meum, quod serva· bitis inter me et vos, et inter semen tuum post te: (quod praecipit) circum· eidi vobis omnem masculum. Praemissum autem erat v. 7. verbum promissionis. Nam sicut Deus per verba ista circumcisionem in sua specie, ut sic loquar, et in actu signato fecit sacramentum, ita in exercitio, per verba in institutione ista fundata, individualis quilibet actus faciendus est, scribit Dn. D. Sebast. Schmidt, Tract. de Circumc. p. 395., qui etiam in seqq. p. 398. 399. inter plures vetustas benedictionum Judaicarum formulas hanc sacramentalem, quae inprimis ad verba institutionis respiciat, recenset: Benedictus tu, Domine Deus noster, Rex mundi, qui sanctificasti nos praeceptis tuis, et praecepisti, ut initiemus eum foederi Abrahami, patris nostri.

Quenstedtius: ,,Non fuit circumcisio sine verbo aliquo άκονστφ sive audibili, quod ostendit cum conditio generica omnium sacramentorum, ad quae requiritur verbum institutionis et promissionis, tum diserta circumcisionis institutae et praeceptae descriptio, ubi annexa est promissio gratiae, Gen. 17, 7.: ,Ero Deus tuus et seminis tui post te.' Accessit quoque sine dubio in ipsa dispensatione verbum applicationis et invocationis, quod vel formaliter, vel quoad vestigia saltem apud rabbinos reperitur; vide D. Schmidt 1. c. p. 390. sq., ubi varias recenset benedictiones, et quidem: 1. circumcidentis, 2. patris, 3. adstantium.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 4. s. 1. th. 10. f. 1058.) N. Hunnius: ,,Actum signatum dicunt philosophi actum a singularibus abstractum, exercitum in singularibus multiplicatum; ut res apprehenditur in actu signato, quando ita concipitur, prout communi definitione signatur nec sub proprio signo (quod nomen est) apprehenditur; in actu autem exercito, quando aliquid non in communi et indefinita notione, sed sub particulari nomine concipitur, qualiter homo in actu signato est species, in actu exercito est individuum, Socrates, Petrus etc.“ (Δίάσκεψίς, § 97. p. 63.) § 7.


### On the Sacraments of the Old Testament: The end-to-whom of circumcision were the Israelite males and their household…

The end-to-whom of circumcision were the Israelite males and their household members and proselytes, and indeed infants, when they were in their eighth day of life.

Concerning the benefit for whom circumcision was divinely instituted and who were the subjects to whom this rite, as a means of grace, was to be applied, or in one word, the subject to be circumcised. And indeed males only, which is evident from the very seat of this doctrine; although females were not on that account deprived of federal grace. For that covenant, initiated with Abraham, was derived from him to Isaac, from him to Jacob, and thus to the Israelites, with collateral branches not being equally received into the covenant.

Quenstedtius: " 1. The subject which was 1. every male in the house of Abraham. Circumcision was commanded for the sealing of the covenant not to Abraham and Isaac alone, but also to all Abraham’s descendants, whether they drew their origin from Sarah, or from Hagar, or from Keturah. I say, they were obligated to the sacrament of circumcision, both by the necessity of the means and by the necessity of the precept, not only the descendants of the patriarch Jacob, but also the Ishmaelites, the Edomites, and the Keturahites; which must be maintained against the Jews, who contend that the sacrament of circumcision pertained only to the descendants of Jacob; to whom Corn. a Lapide (Comm. in Gen. 17, 10) and Suarez (P. 3. q. 70. in Gen. 17, 20. 21) assent. The lineage of the Messiah is restricted to Isaac, not the covenant of circumcision; compare Gerhard (Comm. in Gen. ad h. l. p. 368) and D. Calov (in Comm. in Gen. p. 882).

And not only Abraham’s seed, but also his servants born in the house and bought with money were to be circumcised by the command of God, Gen. 17, 12. 13: 'He who is born in your house' (i.e., a home-born servant or slave) 'and he who is bought with your money' (or, he who became a servant not by right of birth, but of purchase), 'from any foreigner who is not of your seed himself'—that is, a servant who has passed into your power—'shall be circumcised,' even if he was bought not from the Israelite people, but from some foreigner. It was optional for hired servants and day laborers to receive circumcision, Ex. 12, 45. However, servants were not to be forced to circumcision, but rather dismissed and not retained in the house, or sold again. 2. Proselytes, who, namely, desired to be admitted to the Israelite sacred rites.

For express mention is made of these, not indeed in Gen. 17, but in Ex. 12, 48, from which passage it is evident that proselytes were not absolutely obligated to circumcision unless they wished to eat the paschal lamb, to which the ἀπερίτμητος, the uncircumcised, could not be admitted, Ex. 12, 44. 48. There were, however, two kinds of proselytes in Israel: proselytes of righteousness and proselytes of the dwelling; proselytes of righteousness acknowledged all Jewish sacred rites and received the ceremonies; not so the proselytes of the gate or of the dwelling. Therefore, those who desired to be initiated into the religion of the Jews and betook themselves to the Jewish worship of God, they were obligated by the law of circumcision." (L. c. s. 1. th. 7. f. 1056. sq.)

According to Gen. 17, 12, where express mention is made of foreigners to be circumcised, if any were born in the house or bought with money; although they were not on that account to be forced to circumcision. Provided that they wished to approach the other Israelite sacred rites, especially the sacrament of the paschal lamb. See Levit. 12, 3. Meanwhile, infants dying before the eighth day could nevertheless be saved.

By that delay of circumcision, God seems to have provided for the tender bodies of the newborn; just as it is believed to have been given as a consolation to parents that He did not wish the sacrament of initiation, by which their children were immediately received into the covenant of grace, to be deferred longer.

Otherwise, however, on account of dangerous illness and journeys, it was permitted to defer circumcision longer; just as God allowed it to be omitted for forty years, while the people of the Israelites were making their journey into the land of Canaan. PART III. CHAP. IX.

See Joshua 5:5, 6, 7, and 8. No fixed time was assigned for the circumcision of proselytes. However, circumcision had to precede admission to the remaining sacred rites of the Jews.

Quenstedtius: "The third adjunct was the necessity of circumcision in the Old Testament. For it was required under the most severe threat of εξολοθρεύσεως [extermination] from all Abraham's descendants; Gen. 17:14: 'The male, whose flesh of his foreskin shall not be circumcised' (εξολοθρευθήσεται, LXX), 'that soul shall be cut off' (exscindetur) 'from his people' (by excision not only civil and temporal, but also eternal from the fellowship of the saints in heaven), 'because he has broken' (made void) 'my covenant.' Circumcision was therefore necessary by the necessity both of the means and of the precept, if one asks about the ordinary way and means of being saved; and thus this precept is to be interpreted not absolutely, but with limitations: 1. under the condition of possibility, 2. outside the case of inevitable necessity, 3. regarding the ordinary way of salvation. That necessity was to be opposed to supine negligence, contempt, and unbelief, not to any and every case." (L. c. s. 1. th. 17. f. 1062.) § 8. The proximate and principal end of the sacrament of circumcision was the bestowal of federal grace regarding the remission of sins; the less principal end was the segregation of the Israelites from other peoples and an admonition concerning original sin and the coming Messiah; the ultimate end was the eternal salvation of the circumcised.

Intended by God the author and to be conferred or effected by the thing itself through circumcision, as an organon. See Gen. 17:7, where God promises that He will be the God of Abraham who is to be circumcised and of his seed who are to be circumcised; which must be explained primarily regarding spiritual benefits divinely conferred and adoption into the covenant of grace. Whence it is also said to have been a seal of righteousness, Rom. 4:11. Thus, therefore, just as God in the first institution of circumcision simultaneously promised that He would receive those who were to be circumcised into the covenant of grace, so He also concurred with circumcision when established in act, in such a way that He might excite or seal the faith to be placed in that promise in those who were being circumcised, and render them certain of the grace of the covenant and of righteousness obtained before God. For although through circumcision the descendants of Abraham were to testify to their faith before others and invite them to believe, yet he himself also was to be reminded through circumcision and his faith excited, so that circumcision had the nature of a means for the increase of that faith; which double end of circumcision the Apology of the Augsburg Confession also noted on pp. 97 and 276. Compare C. Hoepfner, Disput. VIII. de Justif. c. IV. Aph. II. § 2. sqq. p. 637. sqq., and what we noted from the blessed Mylius above at chapter VIII. § 1. last note.

For thus the very names of circumcision and uncircumcision denote and distinguish the peoples, the Jewish and the others, Rom. 3:30. See what we said above at § 3. note c. Namely, because of the connection between the remission of sins and eternal salvation.

9. Circumcision may be defined as a sacred action instituted by God, by which God in the Old Testament, through the amputation of the foreskin, with the word of institution accompanying it, conferred faith upon male Israelites and their households and proselytes—upon infants, indeed—and sealed and confirmed it to believing adults, for the sake of obtaining the remission of sins and eternal salvation.

The common genus of all sacraments. Thus the principal efficient cause is indicated. See § 2. This is the material of circumcision. See § 5. This is the formal element. See § 6. Thus the subject, or the end for whom, is indicated. See § 7. These and the following points pertain to the end of which circumcision is; concerning which see § 8. §

10. The other sacrament of the Old Testament is called by the name of the Passover or the Paschal lamb. In Hebrew: פֶּסַח, which is derived from the passing over, the act of passing or leaping over, such as that by which the smiting angel, while killing the firstborn of the Egyptians throughout all the houses, leaped over the houses of the Israelites; whence that sacrament has its name, both so that the Israelites might be saved as the angel passed over, and furthermore to be celebrated in memory of this passing over. See Exod. 12:11, 12, 13, 27.

Namely, that sacramental action was occupied with the lamb to be treated with a certain rite; and hence it came about that the name פֶּסַח and the Greek πάσχα sometimes denoted the sacramental lamb itself by metonymy.

The seat of this doctrine is found in Exod. 12. Hollazius: "The Paschal lamb was not a sacrifice properly so called; yet analogically it can be so called.

Obs. 1. A sacrament is one thing, a sacrifice is another. In a sacrament, God offers and confers grace to men; in sacrifices, men offer a gift to God to obtain His grace. . .

Proof: 1. No sacrifice, properly so called, could be made in Egypt because of the abominations of the Egyptians, Exod. 8:26.

2. Every sacrifice, properly so called, was performed by a priest at an altar, with a sacrificial rite which the delineation of the Levitical priesthood prescribes. The Paschal lamb was ordinarily slaughtered not by a priest, but by the head of the household, Exod. 12:4, and not on a solemn altar, but in private dwellings.

3. If the Paschal lamb was a sacrifice properly so called, it was either a מִנְחָה or a זֶבַח. It was not a mincha, because that was a meal offering, consisting of fine flour and cakes and fruits with salt, wine, and oil, partly burned and partly destined for the priest, Lev. 2, Num. 15. But the lamb, a living animal, was not such a thing. Nor was it a sebach strictly so called, because neither PART III. CHAP. IX.

it was neither a burnt offering, nor a sacrifice for sin and guilt, nor a peace offering; it was not a burnt offering, because the whole lamb was not burned; nor a sacrifice for sin, because the sins of the people were not laid upon it; nor a peace offering, because it was not eaten by the priests in the holy court itself. Therefore, it is not a זבח under the special notion of a sacrifice, although it may be called a זבח under the notion of a slaughter.” (Exam. P. III. s. 2. c. 3. q. 40. p. 1075. sq.)

Gerhard: “Although, once the Levitical priesthood was established, the paschal lambs were brought to the Levites, as we have shown above with probability, yet that was not perpetual, as is evident from the first celebration of the paschal lamb, nor was it done for the purpose that the paschal lamb should be sacrificed, but that it might be inquired whether the qualities divinely required were present in it. Sacrifices properly so called were slaughtered at the altar of the Lord. The paschal lamb was slaughtered by families and households. It is proper and essential to a sacrifice that either the whole or at least a certain part of it is offered to God and consumed by fire; but nothing of the paschal lamb was offered to God or consumed by fire, but rather the whole was roasted and eaten.” (Loc. de circumcis. § 50.) Quenstedt: “Nor is it necessary that the type and the antitype should agree with each other even in particulars. . . What is said elsewhere about the sacrifice of the Passover being administered by the priests does not pertain to the lamb slaughtered for the use of the paschal feast, but to other victims which were offered in the temple at the time of the Passover, which were also understood by the name of the Passover; see Deut. 16:2.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1078.) Cf. Luther’s Interpretation of the III. Ps. V, 1569. § 11.

Latin:

Finis cui a circumcisionis erant masculi b Israelitici c eorumque domestici d ac proselyti,e et infantes quidem, cum octavum vitae diem agerent. f

Quorum bono circumcisio divinitus instituta fuit quique subjectum erant, cui ritus hic, tanquam medium gratiae, applicari debebat, seu uno verbo, subjectum circumcidendum. Et quidem soli, quod patet ex ipsa hujus doctrinae sede; quamvis feminae non propterea gratia foederali privatae fuerint. Nempe foedus illud, cum Abrahamo initum, inde ab eo ad I8aacum, ab hoc ad Jacobum, et sic ad Israditas derivatum est, collateralibus non aeque in foedus receptis.

Quenstedtius: "1. Subjectum quod 1. fuit omnis masculus in domo Abrahae. Imperata erat ad foederis obsignationem circumcisio non uni Abrahamo et Isaaco, sed etiam Abrahamidis omnibus, sive ex Sara, sive ex Agar, sive ex Kethura originem traherent. Obligati inquam, erant ad circumcisionis sacramentum tum necessitate medii, tum necessitate praecepti non solum Jacobi patriarchae posteri, sed et Ismaelitae, Idumaei, Kethuraei; quod contra Judaeos tenendum, qui contendunt, ad solos Jacobi posteros circumcisionis sacramentum pertinuisse; quibus adstipulantur Corn. a Lapide Com. in Gen. 17, 10. et Suarez. P. 3. q. 70. in Gen. 17, 20. 21. Prosapia messiae ad Isaacum restringitur, non foedus circumcisionis; confer Gerhardum Com. in Gen. ad h. 1. p. 368. et D. Calov. in Com. in Gen. p. 882.

Nec solum Abrahae semen, sed etiam ejus servi vernaculi et emptitii erant circumcidendi ex mandato Dei, Gen. 17, 12. 13.: ,Circumcidendo circumcidetur natus domus tuae‘ (i. e. verna seu servus in domo natus),et emp« tus argento tuo‘ (sive, qui non nativitatis, sed emptionis jure servus factus), ab omni alienigena, qui non de semine tuo ipse‘, h. e. servus, qui in potestatem tuam transierit, circumcidetur, etiamsi non a populo Israelitico, sed ab alienigena quodam emtus fuerit. Mercenariis et conductitiis liberum fuit, circumcisionem suscipere, Ex. 12, 45. Non erant autem servi ad circumcisionem cogendi, sed potius dimittendi et in domo non retinendi aut iterum vendendi.

2. Proselyti, qui sc. ad sacra Israelitica admitti cupiebant. Horum enim expressa mentio fit, non quidem Gen. 17., sed Ex. 12, 48., ex quo loco patet, non fuisse proselytos absolute obligatos ad circumcisionem, nisi vellent agno paschali vesci, ad quem non poterat admitti απερίτμητος, incircumcisus, Ex. 12, 44. 48. Erant autem duo 7τμοσ?/λντων genera in Israel: proselyti justitiae et proselyti domicilii; proselyti justitiae omnia sacra Judaica agnoscebant et ritus suscipiebant; non proselyti portae seu domicilii. ### On the Sacraments of the Old Testament: The principal efficient cause of this sacrament is the Triune God

The principal efficient cause of this sacrament is the Triune God. By His own authority He institutes and commands it, and effectively concurs with it according to the promise for a spiritual effect. See Exod. 12:1. § 12.

The internal impulsive cause is the goodness and gratuitous favor of God; the external or meritorious cause is Christ the Mediator. For moved by this, just as God willed to spare the Israelites, although they were not entirely free from sin, so He Himself instituted and offered a means of grace which they might use unto salvation.

In which the antitype of the paschal lamb is contained, we shall say presently; meanwhile, it is easily understood that the prefigurative sacrament was divinely instituted with a view to Him. § 13. The less principal causes were partly Moses and Aaron, partly the heads of families of the Israelite nation, and partly the Levites.

Which provided ministry to God the author, so that this sacrament might either be first introduced into the church, or subsequently established in use.

As ministers of the divine institution to be promulgated. See Exod. 12:1, 28. Undoubtedly administering the sacrament when it was first to be celebrated in Egypt. See the same chapter, vv. 3, 6, 21, 28. But afterwards, when the Levitical priesthood was instituted, if they were not slaughtering, they were at least roasting the paschal lamb.

However, it is taught elsewhere that circumcised proselytes had the same right to the sacred rites as the Jewish heads of families. For it is established elsewhere that these were the ministers of the sacred rites. And it is certain that in the case where heads of families labored under legal uncleanness, the Levites prepared the Passover for them. See Ezra 6:20; 2 Chron. 30:17, 18. Whether, however, outside of this case, they performed the work of slaughtering as ordinary ministers is disputed. Yet the passage in 2 Chron. 35:10 and 11 is usually referred to in this regard. And it is probable that after God bound the celebration of this sacrament to the place where the temple was (concerning which see Deut. 16:5, 6, 7), the ministerial labor of the Levites and priests was also required more than before.

Gerhard: "As regards the place, the first Passover was celebrated in Egypt, the second in the desert. But afterwards, by an explicit law, the celebration of the Passover, like the other festivals, was bound to a certain place. Deut. 16:2: 'You shall sacrifice the pesach to Jehovah your God in the place which Jehovah shall choose, to make His name dwell there'; v. 5: 'You shall not be able to sacrifice the pesach in any of your cities which the Lord your God is giving you'; v. 6: 'But in the place which Jehovah your God shall choose, to make His name dwell there.' Therefore, all males from the entire Israelite kingdom had to assemble at that place where the tabernacle of the covenant, and afterwards the temple of the Lord, was. Exod. 34:23: 'Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Sovereign Jehovah, the God of Israel.' By that express determination of place, 1. self-chosen worship was prevented, 2. concord among the confessors of one true religion was nourished, and 3. the sacrifice of the Messiah to be offered in the city of Jerusalem was prefigured." (L. de circumcis. etc. § 43.) § 14. The matter of this sacrament was a lamb, whole and free from blemish, a male, and of one year, for the acts were occupied about it, namely, the separation from the flock, the slaughtering and roasting, then the eating, and finally the sprinkling of the blood upon the lintel and the doorposts of the houses.

If not always, yet most frequently, or even a kid in its place, as is gathered from Exod. 12:5, where the common noun שֶׂה occurs; then indeed it is added that it could be taken from the different species of small cattle, כְּשָׂבִים and עִזִּים, lambs and kids; and it is certain that not only the lamb, but also the kid was a type of Christ, although it is not as customary for Christ to be called a kid as a lamb (concerning which see John 1:29). PART III. CHAP. IX.

To this corresponds the antitype in 1 Pet. 1:19, where Christ is called αμνός αμωμος και άσπιλος, cf. ch. 2:22; Heb. 7:26.

With respect to the excellence which this sex has, not one over the other. And the antitype, the Son of Man, agrees, in whom is masculine strength and perfection. That is, born in the previous year, so that he would either soon complete the first year of his age, or had completed it; yet not so as to have exceeded it, such that he could be considered a two-year-old. Regard was had, however, to the flower of Christ’s age, at which he was to die.

This act and the following two were preparatory, yet necessary. And the segregation indeed seems to have prefigured the captivity of Christ. Moreover, the slaughtering had to take place between the two evenings, l.c. v. 6, i.e., around the third hour after midday, or a little later, before the setting of the sun. At which time Christ also willed to die. But that Christ, as our Passover, was slaughtered, Paul teaches in 1 Cor. 5:7.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, who, in order to maintain that the sacrament of the Supper, or the Mass, is also a sacrifice properly so called, contend: 'The paschal lamb, as a type of the holy Eucharist, was offered to God by way of a certain sacrifice properly so called.' Thus Bellarmine, T. 3, Op. 1.1, de missa c. 7, throughout, where he argues immediately from the beginning thus: 'The celebration of the paschal lamb was an express figure of the celebration of the Eucharist, but that was a certain immolation of a victim offered to God; therefore, the celebration of the Eucharist must be an immolation of a victim offered to God, so that the figure may correspond to the thing figured.' Becanus, T. 2, opusc. 11, c. 7, where he says: 'This sacrifice of the paschal lamb was instituted by God a little before the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt,' etc. Gregorius de Valentia, book 1, de Messiae Sacrificio, and Suarez, T. 2, Disp. 40, sect. 24, 50, also wish the paschal lamb to be a sacrifice. 2. Of certain of our own theologians, who assert that the Passover was a sacrifice properly so called, such as Theod. Hackspan in Not. philologicotheol. Lat. col. 996, and D. Brochmann, System, c. 4, de A. P. p. 270 sq." (L.c. s. 2, q. 2, f. 1074.)

For it was not to be eaten boiled in water, but roasted, according to Exodus loc. cit. verses 8 and 9. It also had to be roasted whole, …with no part broken. In which manner Christ also was, as it were, roasted and intimately penetrated, partly by the fire of divine wrath toward the sins which he himself had taken upon himself, and partly by the fire of his own love toward us who were to be redeemed. He remained, however, whole as to the members of his body; see John 19: 36.

According to the practice of the Jews, which Maimonides mentions, the paschal lamb was roasted tied to a wooden spit. And Justin Martyr in his Dialogue with Trypho, p. m. 74 and 75, edit. Paris. An. 1575, writes: That lamb (paschal) in the form of a cross is

spread out and roasted. For one straight spit is thrust through from the bottom to the head, and another transverse one through the back of the neck, to which the shoulders of the lamb are bound; and he rightly notes that Christ to be crucified was signified in this way.

See the loc. cit. v. 8. And this was the principal act of the sacrament.

It is to be noted, however, that the whole lamb was to be eaten, and nothing of it was to be left.

It is also certain that the mandu…It is also certain that the eating of Christ was signified, both the sacramental eating in the Eucharist and the spiritual eating, or that of faith; it is agreed that in both cases the whole Christ is received.

Furthermore, unleavened bread and bitter herbs were to be added; to which corresponds, partly, what Paul in 1 Cor. 5:8 notes concerning the purging out of the leaven of malice and the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth to be used in the Passover of Christians, and partly, that daily repentance is necessary for those who are to enjoy Christ unto salvation.

L. c. v. 7. And this act was first to be employed so that, seeing the blood, the Lord would pass over the houses of the Israelites and not kill any of them, v. 13 and 22, 23.

But whether that act was to be practiced at a stated time, along with the others, in memory of those things which happened at the time of the first Passover, there are those who infer from the l. c. v. 24 sqq.

If we look at the practice of the Jews, it is certain that the smearing of the houses was discontinued and all the blood of the paschal animals was poured out at the foundation of the altar.

Meanwhile, both methods of religiously treating the blood of the paschal lamb undoubtedly prefigured the shedding of the blood of Christ, upon which our redemption and the remission of sins depend. See 1 Pet. 1:19, Rev. 13:8, Heb. 9:22.

k) Here, too, the question is usually asked concerning the heavenly matter of this sacrament; those who acknowledge it maintain that it is the body and blood of Christ.

And it is certain that these are the thing signified by the earthly matter of the sacrament, as a sign; as is evident from what has been said.

It is also certain that they are a thing of a higher order than that which constitutes the earthly matter, so that they deserve to be called the heavenly thing entirely; just as they are so called in the sacrament of the Supper.

Finally, it is certain that the efficacy of the paschal sacrament depended upon Christ’s body being delivered unto death and His blood being shed, as its antitype.

But whether those things which are not really present in the sacramental act, nay, not yet existing, much less having been truly and really handled by the sacramental act, can be called the matter of the sacrament, strictly speaking, is not without reason doubted by others.

And we, indeed, with the blessed Gerhard, are content with the earthly thing or external element of this sacrament and the sacramental action occupied with it. L. de Circumcis. et Agno Pasch. Cap. IV. § II. § 31. § 15.

The form a of this sacrament was the word of institution b.

Or that by which it had that which was sacramental, when applied to the eating of the slaughtered and roasted lamb.

For thus the words of Exod. 12:11 have it: ליהויה פסח הוא, this is the Lord’s Passover. And God commanded that these words also be used in the progress of time, so that this rite might be distinguished from other similar non-sacramental acts, l. c. v. 27. PART III. CHAP. IX.

§ 16.

The end for whom, by whom, and the subject to be admitted to the eating of the paschal lamb, were all Israelites, without distinction of sex or age, as well as servants and circumcised male proselytes. For whose benefit God instituted the sacrament. See Exod. 12:8, 4, 21. Meanwhile, it is not denied that sickness or other defects, on account of which men could not eat the flesh, and indeed even legal uncleanness and legitimate absence from the house, excused those who did not use the sacrament at the appointed time. See Num. 9:10. But the unclean, once cleansed, and those traveling, once returned home, were nevertheless commanded to use the sacrament, even if after others and after the time otherwise appointed had elapsed.

For boys and girls, in whom the use of reason had developed, were accustomed to be admitted. See Exod. 12:43, 44, 48. § 17.

The end of which paschal sacrament was, first, that men using the sacrament might be rendered more certain of the grace of God, who does not impute sins, and who, by passing over their houses while others were being slain, would avert every harm; then, that the memory of this benefit might be preserved and celebrated in succeeding times; on both sides, however, the confirmation of faith in the promised Messiah, and finally, eternal salvation. Which God, the author of the sacrament, seriously intended, so that you may also call it the fruit or effect of the sacrament.

Namely, regarding that first celebration performed in Egypt. See Exod. 12:13, 14. And it is evident from verses 11 and 24 that the very name פסח was divinely imposed upon this sacrament for this reason: that in view of it, God was about to pass over the houses of the Israelites and grant His grace and the remission of sins. Regarding the exercise of the sacramental act to be celebrated annually after that benefit of the passing over and the miraculous liberation, according to verse 24 ff.

For the sacrament itself was a type of the Messiah and of the benefits to be expected through Him and to be embraced by faith, according to those things which we said at § 12, note b, and § 14, note a, ad i. And it is certain that God Himself, by His power, concurred with that sacramental rite established in use, for the purpose of exciting and confirming faith in the men using the sacrament through it, so that this end also had the nature of an effect with respect to the sacrament, as an efficacious means or organ.

Luther: "Passah [Passover] means a passing, because the Lord went through the land of Egypt by night and struck all the firstborn dead. But it signifies Christ’s dying and rising again, by which He departed from this world and in the same struck down sin, death, and the devil, and led us out of the true Egypt to the Father; that is our Passover, or Easter." (Glossa ad Exod. 11, 43. XXI, 427.*)

According to the connection of faith and the remission of sins and eternal life. § 18. The Passover may be defined as an action divinely instituted, by which a lamb or a kid, whole and a year old, separated from the flock, was slaughtered, roasted, and eaten by the Israelites and circumcised proselytes, while its blood was sprinkled upon the doorposts and lintels of the houses to excite faith in the Messiah and to obtain and celebrate the grace of God and the remission of the plague, and to attain eternal salvation.

The genus is that which is predicated of the Passover speaking properly and in the nominative case, according to Exod. 12:11 and 27, where not so much the passing of the Lord itself, as that which was to be celebrated by the Israelites in view of that passing, or the sacred action which was to be performed, is called ןסח. Luther: "When Moses says: 'Eat in haste, it is the Lord’s Passover,' Zwingli cannot prove that it signifies the Easter lamb. For one has soon answered thus: Eat in haste, it is the Lord’s Passover, just as we say in German: Eat meat, for it is Sunday; drink water, it is Friday. Here no one will force out of me that meat signifies Sunday, or water signifies Friday. So also here: 'Eat in haste, for it is the Lord’s Passover,' that is, it is the day when the Lord went into Egypt, etc." (That these words of Christ: This is my body, still stand firm. 1527. XX, 979. sq.)
