CAP. X.


## 25 On Baptism

Chapter X. ON BAPTISM. § 1. Among the two sacraments of the New Testament, baptism holds the prior place. Furthermore, that there are no other sacraments of the same order, nature, and essence besides these two (baptism and the Holy Supper); but if there are any others to which the word "sacrament" can be attributed, they nevertheless do not possess the same common concept and definition of a sacrament, and therefore the others are not called sacraments univocally; and that this can be taught from the Scriptures, insofar as those two special sacraments exist in the Scriptures, and the reason, essence, and definition of each can be taught from the Scriptures, namely baptism and the sacrament of the Lord’s Supper; that from these a certain concept can be abstracted, common to both univocally; and thus, having shown that the others which go by the name of sacraments do not, however, agree with those two regarding a univocal and common concept, it is easily evident that they are not equally properly called

sacraments, Musaeus also asserted. See *Ausführl. Erklär.* L. XVI. Q. 81. p. 667. Quenstedtius: "One must distinguish between the broader and improper signification of the word 'sacrament,' and thus we concede that more can be numbered as sacraments of the N.T., and between the strict and proper signification, and thus we assert that only two sacraments of the N.T. are given." (*Th. did.-pol.* P. IV. c. 3. s. 2. q. 3. f. 1049.)

The same: "The word 'sacrament' is taken: 1. most generally for any thing άκαταλήπτῳ [incomprehensible] or arcane and secret. Thus the incarnation of Christ 1 Tim. 3:16, the union of Christ and the church Eph. 5:32, the calling of the Gentiles Eph. 3:3, our redemption Col. 1:26 are called μυστήριον [mystery], which the old Latin interpreter rendered as 'sacrament.' Thus also the holy fathers called any mystery whatsoever and any sacred and not obvious doctrine a sacrament, such as the sacrament of the Trinity, the sacrament of the incarnation and of the faith; 2. more specially for an external sign of a sacred and heavenly thing; thus seed, a grain, a pearl, etc., are sacraments or signs of the kingdom of heaven Matt. 13:23, 31, 46, in which way Augustine also numbers the sign of the cross among the sacraments, *l. c. c. 143*. The same says in *Epist. 5 to Marcellinus*, 'signs, when they pertain to divine things, are called sacraments'; 3. most specially for a sacred, arcane, symbolic thing, not only signifying, but also at the same time conferring the thing which it signifies, or for a solemn action divinely instituted, commanded, and prescribed, in which, through an external and visible sign, invisible goods are graciously offered, conferred, and sealed." (*L. c. s. 1. th. 3. f. 1031.*)

Gerhardus: "Bellarminus accuses us of perjury, because we have made a secession from the Augsburg Confession, which reckons repentance among the sacraments (in the *Apology* under the title on the number and use of the sacraments). Resp.: The name of sacrament is attributed to repentance with respect to the end, which it has in common with the other properly called sacraments, which is the confirmation of our faith concerning the remission of sins; for thus the words hold: 'If we call sacraments the rites which have the command of God and to which the promise of grace has been added, it is easy to judge which are properly sacraments,'"

namely, baptism, the Lord’s Supper, and absolution.”

But a little later it follows: “If all things that have a command of God and to which promises have been added ought to be numbered among the sacraments, why do we not add prayer, which can most truly be called a sacrament, for it has a command of God and very many promises,” etc. From this passage we conclude as follows: It is not sufficient for a sacrament, strictly so called, to have a command of God and a promise of grace. Yet it was on this foundation that it was asserted that absolution is referred to the sacraments. Therefore, the Apology did not intend for it to be a sacrament strictly so called.

The Apology of the Confession therefore looks to this: that among all the other things which are joined to the true and properly called sacraments—namely, baptism and the Lord’s Supper—absolution approaches most closely to their nature; for through it, the benefits of Christ are dispensed to the penitent and those who truly believe according to the command of God, the evangelical promises are applied to them specifically, and the gratuitous remission of sins is announced. What, however, is still lacking, so that the formal and specific definition of a sacrament does not apply to it, will be explained immediately.

Observe, therefore, that the Apology numbers absolution among the sacraments in a sense far different from that of the Papists; for they maintain that the word of absolution confers a sacramental power upon the actions of the penitent person, so that they concur effectively to cause and merit the remission of sins and, together with the absolution, constitute an entire sacrament—a notion that did not even enter the minds of the authors and confessors of the Augsburg Confession.” (L. on Repentance, § 22.) Cf. Apology of the Augsburg Confession, pp. 202–204, §§ 2–17, and the Large Catechism, p. 496 sq., §§ 74–76.

The same: “Bellarmine, in *De Sacramento ordinis*, ch. 1, writes that Luther, Illyricus, and Chemnitz deny that ordination is a sacrament properly so called, but that Philip [Melanchthon] in the *Loci* published in the years ’36, ’52, and ’58, as well as in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, Art. 13, teaches quite openly that ordination is a sacrament properly so called, whence he accuses Chemnitz of opposing the principal Lutherans in this controversy and joining himself to the fewer and more obscure ones.

Resp.: The term ‘sacrament’ is used by Philip in the *Loci* and in the Apology in a broader sense. The words of the Apology are as follows: ‘If order is understood as the ministry of the Word, we would not hesitate to call order a sacrament. For the ministry of the Word has a command of God and has magnificent promises, Rom. 1, Isa. 55. If order is understood in this way, we would not hesitate to call the laying on of hands a sacrament. For the church has a command to appoint ministers; which ought to be most pleasing to us, because we know that God approves of that ministry and is present with the ministry,’ etc. (From these, anyone understands that the Apology is dealing not so much with the rite of ordination as with the ministry of the Word and sacraments itself, and not in the most proper and most specific signification, but in a certain more general signification of a sacrament. Whence it is immediately added:) ‘If all things that have a command of God and to which promises have been added ought to be numbered among the sacraments, why do we not add the Lord’s Prayer, which can most truly be called a sacrament? For it has both a command of God and very many promises. Alms can also be numbered here. Likewise afflictions, which are themselves signs to which God has added promises.’ From this we conclude as follows: The Apology accepts the name of sacrament in such a way that it includes prayer, alms, and the afflictions of the pious. But the name of sacrament, accepted in that way, does not yet obtain the most proper and most specific signification. Therefore, the Apology does not accept the name of sacrament in the most proper and most specific signification.” (Confess. cath. L. II. P. III. art. 18. f. 1328.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists, the first of whom, Peter Lombard, determined the number of the sacraments of the N.T. to be seven, which the Council of Trent later [enjoined] under anathema to be believed— PART III. CHAPTER X.

as he proposed in session 7, canon 1, and as all Papists hold today; whence Becanus, *Manual.*, bk. 1, ch. 2, no. 39: "We constantly teach, with the Council of Trent, that there are seven sacraments of the New Law: baptism, confirmation, the eucharist, penance, orders, extreme unction, and matrimony." ...

Eugenius IV, Roman Pontiff, preceded the Tridentines in his *Commonitorium* to the Armenians, but without an anathema. Bellarmine says, bk. 2, *de Sacram.*, ch. 24: "The opinion of the Catholics is one and has always been that there are seven sacraments properly so called." Where it is to be observed that Gregor de Valentia, Vol. 4, disp. 3, q. 6, and others acknowledge that the seven sacraments cannot be proven from the Scriptures. But ατερ γραφής we acknowledge no sacrament. "That there are seven sacraments," says Vasquez, "to confirm by the testimonies of the fathers is superfluous, because none of them defined anything specifically regarding their number." 2. G. Calixtus, who in his *Response opposed to the slanderous vindications of the Mainz theologians*, § 103, says: "It is certain that what a sacrament is, or what properly constitutes a sacrament, and consequently how many sacraments there truly and properly are, cannot be gathered from Scripture." And in *Considerations of Papal Doctrine according to the Council of Trent*, on session 7, § 1: "The defined number of the sacraments can be proven neither by Scripture nor by the consensus of the ancients." (Loc. cit., vol. 2, q. 3, p. 1049 sq.)

As the sacrament of Initiation. Denoting an ablution by the force of the word, whether it occurs by immersion or by sprinkling. Concerning the former, see Matthew 8:16; concerning the latter, Mark 7:4, Luke 11:38, where the βαπτισμυς of hands used by those coming to dine is mentioned; which it is certain was accustomed to be performed among the Jews no less by the pouring or sprinkling of water than by the immersion of hands into water, such that they would use a minister pouring water and a sprinkling vessel, and sometimes there was not even room for immersion. The seat of the doctrine concerning the sacrament of baptism is held in Matthew 28:19 and John 3:5. Quenstedtius: "This word (baptism) is taken either improperly or properly. Taken improperly, it is understood either metaphorically or synecdochically. And indeed it is used metaphorically: 1. for the cross, calamity, martyrdom, or the baptism of blood, Matthew 20:22, Mark 10:38, Luke 12:50; 2. for the outpouring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit or the baptism of the Spirit, Matthew 3:12, Mark 1:8, Luke 3:16, Acts 1:5, 11:16; 3. for the miraculous transition of the Israelites through the Red Sea, 1 Corinthians 10:1. Synecdochically it signifies instruction in the doctrine of faith, Matthew 21:25, Mark 9:30, Acts 18:25, 1 Corinthians 10:2. It is called by some the baptism of light or of doctrine. It is taken properly either generally for any washing, Hebrews 9:10,… Mark 7:4, Luke 11:38, or specifically for the first sacrament of the N.T. or the baptism of water. Which is the meaning of this place." (L. c. ch. 5, s. 1, th. 2, p. 1080.) §

Latin:

Caput X. DE BAPTISMO. § 1. Inter duo a Novi Testamenti sacramenta priorem locum b obtinet baptismus.c Praeter duo haee autem (baptismum et s. coenam) non dari alia ejusdem ordinis, naturae et quidditatis sacramenta; sed si quae alia sint, quibus sacramenti vox tribui possit, iis tamen conceptum et rationem sacramenti non esse eandem communem atque adeo reliqua non esse univoce dicta sacramenta; et hoc doceri posse ex Scripturis, quatenus duo illa specialia sacramenta extant in Scripturis, et quae cujusque ratio, quidditas et definitio sit, ex Scripturis doceri potest, nempe baptismus et sacramentum coenae Dominime; ab his abstrahi posse conceptum aliquem, utrique univoce communem; et sic, ostenso, quod reliqua, quae sacramentorum nomine veniunt, non tamen cum duobus istis quoad conceptum univocum et communem conveniant, facile constare, quod non sint aeque proprie dicta sacramenta,

b. Musaeus etiam asseruit. Vid. Ausführl. Erklär. L. XVI. Q. 81. p. 667. T., et inter significationem strictam et propriam, et sic duo tantum dari sacramenta N. T. asserimus.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. IV. c. 3. s. 2. q. 3. f. 1049.)

Idem: ,,Accipitur vox sacramenti: 1. generalissime pro quavis re άκαταλήπτφ seu arcana et secreta. Sic Christi incarnatio 1 Tim. 3, 16., Christi et ecclesiae conjunctio Eph. 5, 32., gentium vocatio Eph. 3, 3., nostra redemtio Col. 1, 26. dicuntur μυστήριον, quod vetus Latinus interpres,sacramentum‘ reddidit. Sic quoque s. patres quodlibet mysterium et quamlibet doctrinam sacram et non obviam sacramentum appellarunt, ut sacramentum trinitatis, sacramentum incarnationis et fidei; 2. specialius pro signo externo rei sacrae et coelestis; sic semen, granum, margarita etc. sunt sacramenta seu signa regni coelorum Matth. 13, 23. 31. 46., quomodo etiam Augustinus signum crucis inter sacramenta numerat, 1. c. c. 143. Idem ait Epist. 5. ad Marcellinum, ,signa, cum ad res divinas pertinent, sacramenta appellantur‘; 3. specialissime pro re sacra, arcana, symbolica, non significante tantum, sed et conferente simul rem, quam significat, sive pro actione solemni divinitus instituta, mandata et praescripta, in qua per externum et visibile signum bona invisibilia gratiose offeruntur, conferuntur et obsignantur.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 3. f. 1031.)

Gerhardus: ,,Perjurii Bellarminus nos accusat, quod ab Augustana Confessione, quae poenitentiam sacramentis accenset (in Apolog. sub titulo de numero et usu sacram.), secessionem fecerimus. Resp.: Sacramenti nomen poenitentiae tribuitur respectu finis, quem cum reliquis proprie dictis sacramentis communem habet, qui est fidei nostrae de remissione peccatorum confirmatio; sic enim habent verba: ,Si sacramenta vocamus ritus, qui habent mandatum Dei et quibus addita est promissio gratiae, facile est judicare, quae sint proprie sacramenta,

scilicet baptismus, coena Domini et absolutio.'

Sed paulo post sequitur: ,Si omnes res annumerari sacramentis debent, quae habent mandatum Dei, et quibus additae sunt promissiones: cur non addimus orationem, quae verissime potest dici sacramentum, habet enim mandatum Dei et promissiones plurimas‘ etc. Ex quo loco sic colligimus: Non sufficit ad sacramentum propriissime dictum, habere mandatum Dei et promissionem gratiae. Atqui ex hoc fundamento assertum erat, absolutionem referri ad sacramenta. Ergo noluit Apologia eam esse sacramentum propriissime sic dictum.

Eo igitur respicit Apologia Confessionis, quod inter reliqua omnia, quae veris et proprie dictis sacramentis, baptismo scii, et coenae Dominicae, conjunguntur, absolutio proxime ad eorum naturam accedat; per illam enim poenitentibus ac vere credentibus juxta Dei mandatum dispensantur beneficia Christi, evangelicae promissiones in specie ipsis applicantur et remissio peccatorum gratuita annunciatur; quid vero adhuc desit, quo minus formalis et specifica ratio sacramenti ei conveniat, statim expeditum dabitur.

Observa igitur, longe alio sensu ab August. Confess. Apologia numerari absolutionem inter sacramenta, quam fit a pontificiis; illi quippe statuunt, verbum absolutionis vim sacramentalem conferre actionibus hominis poenitentis, ut ad remissionem peccatorum causandam et promerendam effective concurrant atque una cum absolutione integrum sacramentum constituant, quod auctoribus et confessoribus August. Confess. ne in mentem quidem venit.“ (L. de poenitentia, § 22.) Cf. Apolog. Aug. Conf. p. 202—204. §§ 2—17. et Catechism. Major, p. 496. sq. §§ 74—76.

Idem: ,,Bellarminus de Sacramento ordinis c. 1. scribit, Lutherum, Illyricum et Chemnitium negare, quod ordinatio sit sacramentum proprie dictum, sed Philippum in Locis editis Ann. 36. 52. 58., item in Apol. A. C. art. 13. satis aperte docere, ordinationem esse sacramentum proprie dictum, unde Chemnitium accusat, quod in hac controversia repugnet praecipuis Lutheranis, seque adjungat paucioribus et obscurioribus.

Resp.: Vox sacramenti a Philippo in Locis et in Apol. sumitur in significatione laxiore. Verba Apologiae sic habent: ,Si ordo de ministerio verbi intelligatur, non gravatim vocaverimus ordinem sacramentum. Nam ministerium verbi habet mandatum Dei et habet magnificas promissiones Rom. 1. Esa. 55. Si ordo hoc modo intelligatur, neque impositionem manuum sacramentum vocare gravabimur. Habet enim ecclesia mandatum de constituendis ministris; quod gratissimum esse nobis debet, quod scimus, Deum approbare ministerium illud et adesse ministerio‘ etc. (Ex his quilibet intelligit, non tam de ritu ordinationis, quam de ipso verbi et sacramentorum ministerio, nec de propriisima et specialissima significatione, sed de generaliore quadam sacramenti significatione Apologiam agere. Unde statim additur:),Si omnes res annumerari sacramentis debent, quae habent mandatum Dei et quibus sunt additae promissiones, cur non addimus orationem Dominicam, quae verissime potest dici sacramentum? Habet enim et mandatum Dei et promissiones plurimas. Possunt hic numerari etiam eleemosynae. Item afflictiones, quae et ipsae sunt signa, quibus addidit Deus promissiones.‘ Inde sic colligimus: sacramenti nomen Apologia eo modo accipit, ut complectatur orationem, eleemosynas et piorum afflictiones. Atqui sacramenti nomen, eo modo acceptum, nondum obtinet propriissimam et specialissimam signiflcationem. Ergo Apol. non accipit sacramenti nomen in propriissima et specialissima significatione.“ (Confess. cath. L. II. P. III. art. 18. f. 1328.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Pontificiorum, quorum primus Petrus Lombardus septenarium numerum sacramentorum N. T. determinavit, quem postea Concilium Tridentinum sub anathemate ad credenPART. HI. CAP. X.

dum proposuit sess. 7. can. 1. ac hodie omnes tenent Pontificii; unde Becanus Manual. 1. 1. c. 2. n. 39.: ,Nos constanter docemus cum Concilio Tridentino, septem esse sacramenta Novae Legis: baptismum, confirmationem, eucharistiam, poenitentiam, ordinem, extremam unetionem, matrimonium.‘ . .

Praeivit Tridentinis Eugenius IV., P. R., in Commonitorio ad Armenios, sed sine anathemate. Bellarminus inquit 1. 2. de Sacram, c. 24.: ,Sententia catholicorum una est ac semper fuit, septem esse sacramenta proprie dicta.‘ Ubi observandum, Gregor, de Valentia T. 4. disp. 3. q. 6. aliosque agnoscere, septem sacramenta e Scripturis probari non posse. Sed ατερ γραφής nullum agnoscimus sacramentum. ,Quod septem sint sacramenta‘, ait Vasquez, ,patrum testimoniis confirmare, supervacaneum est, quia nullus cie eorum numero quicquam speciatim definivit.‘ 2. D. G. Galixti, qui in Responso maledicis theologorum Moguntinorum vindiciis opposito § 103. inquit: ,Certum est, quid sacramentum sit vel quid proprie sacramentum constituat, et proinde, quot vere et proprie sacramenta sint, ex Scriptura non posse colligi.‘ Et in Considerat, doctrinae pontificiae juxta Concil. Trid. ad sess. 7. § 1. :,,Definitus sacramentorum numerus nec Scfiptura probari potest, nec consensu veterum.“‘ (Loc. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 1049. sq.)

Tanquam sacramentum Initiationis. Ablutionem vi vocis denotans, sive illa immergendo, sive asper״ gendo fiat. De illa vid. Matth. 8, 16., de hae Marci 7, 4·, Luc. 11, 38., ubi βαπτισμυς manuum accessuris ad prandium usitatus memoratur; quem constat non minus affusione aut aspersione aquae, quam immersione manuum in aquam etiam apud Judaeos peragi consuevisse, ita ut ministro affundente et vase aspersorio uterentur et aliquando ne quidem locus esset immersioni. Sedes autem doctrinae de sacramento baptismi habetur Matth. 28, 19. et Joh. 3, 5. Quenstedtius: ,,Accipitur vox haec (baptismus) vel improprie vel proprie. Improprie accepta sumitur vel metaphorice vel synecdochice. Et quidem metaphorice usurpatur 1. pro cruce, calamitate, martyrio seu baptismo sanguinis Matth. 20, 22. Mare. 10, 38. Luc. 12, 50.; 2. pro donorum Spiritus S. effusione seu baptismo flaminis Matth. 3, 12. Marc. 1, 8. Luc. 3, 16. Act. 1, 5. 11, 16.; 3. pro miraculosa transitione Israelitarum per mare rubrum 1 Cor. 10, 1. Synecdochice significat informationem in doctrina fidei Matth. 21, 25. Mare. 9, 30. Act. 18, 25. 1 Cor. 10, 2. Vocatur a nonnullis baptismus luminis seu doctrinae. Proprie accipitur vel generaliter pro quavis lotione Hebr. 9, 10. Mare. 7, 4. Luc. 11, 38., vel specialiter, pro sacramento primo N. T. seu baptismo fluminis. Quae significatio est hujus loci." (L. c. c. 5. s. 1. th. 2. f. 1080.) §


### On Baptism: The principal efficient cause of baptism is Christ, together with the Father…

2. The principal efficient cause of baptism is Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, who not only determined what pertains to the constitution of baptism, but also commanded that this rite be frequented and rendered it efficacious for conferring saving fruit. As God and as man. See Matthew 28:18, 19, 20, where Christ, instituting baptism, appeals to the πασαν έξουσιαν [all authority] given to Him in time

and thus as given to man, which, however, as the Son of God, He had from eternity. For it is otherwise established that the authority and power which Christ used there are common to the three persons, and that their wisdom and will are one; whence also Christ commanded to baptize in the name, as if by the authority, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, l. c. v. 19. Compare John 1:33, where John the Baptist mentions his divine missionion to baptize, and Luke 7:30, where those who refused to be baptized are said to have rejected the counsel of God.

Kromayer: "The baptism of John was a sacrament of the New Testament and the same as the baptism of Christ."

Exegesis: The Papists maintain a negative position based on false principles concerning the effect of the death of Christ and the distinction between the two testaments, to whom we oppose:

1. That in the baptism of John all those things which occur in the baptism of Christ are contained. Let us look at the principal efficient cause; that was God, as it is said in Luke 3:2: "The word of God came unto John in the wilderness." John 1:33: "God sent me to baptize with water." In Matthew 21:25, the baptism of John is said to have been "from heaven." Let us look at the material cause; that was water. For John baptized with water in the Jordan, as is said in Matthew 3, Mark 1, Luke 3, John 1, Acts 1, and near Salem, where there was an abundance of water, John 3:23. Let us look at the formal cause, the application of water for baptizing in the name of the Most Holy Trinity, nor shall that be denied to the baptism of John. Indeed, for whom the manifestation of the Most Holy Trinity took place when He baptized Christ in the Jordan. To which Christ also seems to have looked in His formula in Matthew 28:19.

Let us look at the final cause, the remission of sins, the turning away of divine wrath, regeneration; nor is this end to be denied to the baptism of John. For John was baptizing in the wilderness, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, Mark 1:4. John addresses the Pharisees and Sadducees who were about to receive baptism with these words: "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" Matthew 3:7. Concerning the baptism of John, about which Nicodemus was holding a conversation with Christ (this conversation was held before the passion and resurrection of Christ), the Savior says in John 3:5: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God."

2. If the baptism of John was not the same as the baptism instituted by Christ in Matthew 28:19, it follows that Christ received a different baptism than the one He Himself later instituted, and that Christ did not sanctify our baptism by His own.

3. It would follow that the disciples of Christ, previously baptized by John, were rebaptized; of which, however, not even a tittle is found in the Scriptures; or that they administered a different baptism after the ascension of Christ than before, and a different one than that by which they themselves were baptized." (Th. posit. pol. I, 826 sq.)

The same: "A pretext can be drawn against this opinion: ... 2. That it is nowhere read that John baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But we answer by distinguishing between that which exists in the Scriptures κατά το γράμμα (according to the letter), and that which exists κατά το πράγμα (according to the reality). Even if it is not read in the Scriptures as far as the same letters and points are concerned, it is nevertheless not difficult to elicit it by good consequence. For he baptized in the name of Him by whom he had been sent to baptize, namely, the true God, who is one in essence, three in persons, as He had revealed Himself at the baptism of Christ at the Jordan, the Father by voice, the Son in the body, the Spirit as a dove. Nor are we easily led to believe that this ceremony was mute.

3. That those baptized by John were rebaptized by the apostles. Acts 19... But we answer this argument by distinguishing between the words of Paul and those of Luke the historian. The words, "When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus," are not those of Luke the historian, but of Paul, which the suspensive particles μέν and δέ, corresponding to each other, prove. Nor was the question primarily Paul's... PART III. CHAP. X. of baptism, but of the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit, which those disciples also received afterward through the laying on of hands. But when Paul asks a second time, "Into what baptism were you baptized?", he is looking to the words of Christ in Acts 1:5: "John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now." In these words, therefore, there is no opposition between the baptism of water, as it was administered by John and as it was administered by the apostles after the resurrection of Christ, but rather between the baptism of water and of the Spirit, insofar as the latter is understood as the miraculous gifts poured out upon believers in the primitive church.

I add that the baptism of water was frequently accompanied by the baptism of the Spirit in the primitive church after Christ’s ascension into heaven. The term "Holy Spirit" in verse 2 is understood not of the person, but of these extraordinary gifts, as it is taken in John 7:39: "But this He spoke concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in Him would receive; for the Holy Spirit was not yet given" (although the Scripture of the Old Testament was full of testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit), "because Jesus was not yet glorified." 4. That John baptized with water, Christ with the Spirit and fire. Matthew 3:11." (L. c. p. 827 sq.)

Gerhard: "Bellarmine attempts to prove the dissensions of our people, because Luther, in his disputation concerning the baptism of the Law, of John, and of Christ, maintained that the baptism of John was not a sacrament, nor did it remit sins, and that those baptized by John had to be baptized again. Resp.: That disputation was held in the year 1520; therefore, it must be understood concerning it what Luther writes in the preface to Volume I of his works: ... Remember that I was one of those who, as Augustine writes of himself, have progressed by writing and teaching... What Luther maintained concerning the baptism of John is evident from the sermons on infant baptism held at Dessau in the year 1541." (Loc. de bapt. § 54.)

M. Chemnitz: "In all controversies, those things which have a necessary use in the exercises of repentance, faith, and piety must be distinguished from other disputations in which a diversity of opinions, or even some slight hallucination, does not bring about the loss of faith and salvation. Thus, concerning the baptism of Christ, by which the New Testament church now baptizes, many things—the necessary use of which is clear—can be usefully said: what it is, what its efficacy is, how it is rightly dispensed and received, what its use is throughout the entire life of the baptized person, etc. But the disputation concerning the baptism of John is not equally necessary; for no one is now baptized, nor has anyone been baptized, with the baptism of John; but it is only a question concerning a ceremony of a time long since past, and indeed a brief one. For when John was cast into chains, his baptism ceased. The series of the evangelical history indicates not obscurely that he was detained in prison for more than a full year. Therefore, the baptism of John did not last for a full year and a half. Therefore, those who dispute a little differently than certain ancients concerning this question, having compared the sentences of Scripture, should not immediately be slaughtered with anathema, if this is done while preserving the truth of the doctrine concerning repentance, faith, and piety." (Exam. Concil. Trid. De baptismo. Ed. Genev. f. 230.)

Calov: "Although we by no means think that a mark of heresy should be branded or an anathema hurled because of a disagreement on this question (concerning the baptism of John), since that question does not pertain to salvation today, yet the opinion and the disputation on either side should by no means be left free where the decision of the Holy Spirit Himself is held." (System. Tom. I, 953.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of certain fathers, such as Augustine and others, who thought that the baptism of John was different from the baptism of Christ, and that John thus baptized in the water of repentance for the remission of sins, so that sins would be remitted in hope to those baptized by him, but in reality it would be done in the sacrament of God; thus Augustine, Book 5 against the Donatists, ch. 10. 2. Of the Papists, who maintain that 'the baptism of John was not the same sacrament as the baptism of Christ'; thus Bellarmine, Book 1, de bap-"

baptism c. 19; that it was only a preparation for the baptism of Christ, and therefore those who were baptized by John had necessarily to be baptized by the apostles.

Likewise, that the baptism of John did not have the same power and efficacy as the baptism of Christ; that the baptism of John was offered for repentance, but that of Christ for the remission of sins.

Thus the Council of Trent, sess. 7, on baptism, can. 1: "If anyone shall say that the baptism of John had the same power as the baptism of Christ, let him be anathema." ...

3. Of the Socinians, who contend that the baptism of John was different from the baptism of Christ or the apostles: 1.) by reason of the principle, because John baptized by a special mandate, but the apostles did not; 2.) by reason of the object, because the baptism of John pertained to the Jews, but that of Christ also to the Gentiles; Volkelius, bk. 3, *de V. R.*, c. 8, p. 49; 3.) by reason of the adjunct, namely, the necessity of baptism, because not all from the Israelite people who heard John had need to be baptized, but only those who were in need of repentance and the remission of sins; Socinus, *de baptism.*, p. 239; 4.) by reason of the end, because John baptized so that men might be kept in the pursuit of piety through baptism; Volkelius, *l. c.*, c. 9, p. 53; 5.) by reason of the form, because the baptism of John was only a profession of repentance, but that of the apostles a profession of faith, and thus those baptized by John were only those who did not yet believe in Christ; Socinus, *l. c.*, c. 64; 6.) by reason of the authority and the formula used in baptism, because the baptism of John was not administered in the name of Christ; but the apostles administered baptism in this way; Socinus, *l. c.*, p. 72; 7.) by reason of the efficacy, because the baptism of John did not suffice, and thus those baptized by John had need of ἀναβαπτισμός; 8.) finally, by reason of the duration, because the baptism of John was abrogated after Christ was taken up into heaven. ...

Latin:

2. Causa efficiens,principalis baptismi est Christus a una cum b Patre et Spiritu S., qui non solum, quae ad constitutionem c baptismi pertinent, determinavit, verum etiam ritum illum frequentari d praecepit atque efficacem e reddidit ad conferendum salutarem fructum. Qua Dem et qua homo. Vid. Matth. 28, 18. 19. 20., ubi Christus, baptismum instituens, provocat ad παβαν έξουσία» sibi in tempore

adeoque ut homini datam, quam tamen, ut Filius Dei, ab aeterno habuit. Auctoritatem enim et potentiam, qua Christus illic usus est, tribus personis communem atque unam earum sapientiam et voluntatem esse, alias constat, unde et Christus jussit baptizare in nomine, velut ex auctoritate, Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti, 1. c. v. 19. Confer. Joh. 1, 33., ubi Johannes Baptista divinam missionem sui ad baptizandum memorat, et Luc. 7, 30., ubi, qui baptizari noluerunt, dicuntur consilium Dei sprevisse.

Kromayerus: ,,Baptismus Johannis fuit sacramentum N.T. et idem cum baptismate Christi. νΕκϋεσ(ς:

Negativam ex falsis principiis de effectu mortis Christi et discrimine utriusque testamenti tuentur pontificii, quibus opponimus:

1. quod in baptismo Johannis omnia ea, quae in baptismo Christi occurrunt, contineantur. Videamus causam efficientem principalem; illa Deus erat, ut dicitur Luc. 3, 2.: ,Factum est verbum Domini ad Joliannem in deserto.‘ Joh. 1, 3.: ,Deus misit me ad baptizandum aqua.‘ Matth. 21, 25. baptismus Johannis,e coelo‘ fuisse dicitur. Videamus materialem; illa erat aqua. Johannes enim baptizavit aqua in Jordane, ut Matth. 3. Marc. 1. Luc. 3. Joh.l. Act.l. dicitur, et prope Salem, ubi aquarum suppetebat copia, Joh. 3, 22. Videamus causam formalem, applicationem aquae ad baptizandum in nomine S. S. Trinitatis, nec illa Johannis baptismo erit deneganda. Quippe cui S. S. Trinitatis manifestatio, cum Christum in Jordane baptizaret, facta est. Quorsum et formula sua Matth. 28, 19. Christus respexisse videtur.

Videamus causam finalem, remissionem peccatorum, irae divinae declinationem, regenerationem; nec Johannis baptismo finis hic est denegandus. Baptizabat enim Johannes in deserto, praedicans baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem peccatorum, Mare. 1,4. Baptismum suscepturos Pharisaeos et Sadducaeos his verbis Johannes alloquitur: ,Progenies viperarum, quis vobis monstravit, ut fugeretis a ventura ira?‘ Matth. 3, 7. De baptismo Johannis, super quo colloquium Nicodemus cum Christo instituebat (ante passionem et resurrectionem Christi colloquium hoc fuit habitum), Salvator inquit Joh. 3, 5.: ,Nisi quis regeneratus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu, non poterit ingredi regnum coelorum.‘

2. Si baptismus Johannis non fuit idem cum baptismate Matth. 28, 19. a Christo instituto, sequitur, Christum alium suscepisse baptismum, quam ipse postmodum instituit, nec Christum suo baptismo nostrum sanctiflcasse.

3. Sequeretur, quod Christi discipuli, prius a Johanne baptizati, fuerint rebaptizati; de quo tamen ne apiculus quidem in Scripturis habetur; aut quod alium baptismum administraverint post ascensionem Christi, quam prius, et alium, quam quo fuerunt ipsi baptizati.“ (Th. posit.pol. I, 826. sq.)

Idem: ,,Color obduci potest huic sententiae: ... 2. Quod Johannes in nomine Patris, Filii et Sp. S. baptizasse nullibi legatur. Sed respondemus distinguendo inter id, quod in Scripturis extat κατά το γράμμα, et quod extat κατά το πράγμα. Etiamsi quoad totidem literas et apices non legatur in Scripturis, per bonam tamen consequentiam haut difficulter elicitur. Baptizavit enim in nomine istius, a quo missus fuerat ad baptizandum, nimirum veri Dei, qui est unus in essentia, trinus in personis, ut se revelaverat in baptismo Christi ad Jordanem, voce Pater, Natus corpore, Flamen ave. Nec enim ceremoniam hanc mutam fuisse, ut credamus, faicile adducimur.

3. Quod a Johanne, baptizati ab apostolis rebaptizati fuerint. Act. 19. . . Respondemus autem ad hoc argumentum distinguendo inter verba Pauli et Lucae historici. Verba: ,His vero auditis baptizati sunt in nomine Domini Jesu‘, non sunt Lucae historici, sed Pauli, quod particulae suspensivae ξΐεν et sibi respondentes, probant. Nec quaestio primum erat Paulo PART. III. CAP. X. de baptismo, sed de donis miraculosis Sp. S., quae per manuum impositionem etiam acceperunt postmodum isti discipuli. Cum autem Paulus secundo quaerit: ,Quo baptismate baptizati estis‘, ad verba Christi Act. 1, 5. respicit: ,Johannes quidem baptizavit aqua, vos autem baptizabimini Spiritu S. post dies hos non multos.‘ In verbis itaque hisce non est oppositio baptismi fluminis, ut a Johanne fuit administratus et prout ab apostolis post resurrectionem Christi administrabatur, sed inter baptismum fluminis et flaminis, quatenus hic de donis miraculosis, in ecclesia primitiva super credentes effusis, accipitur.

Addo, quod baptismum fluminis baptismus flaminis in ecclesia primitiva post ascensionem Christi in coelum saepius comitatus fuerit. Vox Spiritus S. non de persona, sed donis his extraordinariis v. 2. accipitur, ut sumitur Joh. 7, 39.: ,Hoc autem dicit de Spiritu, quem accepturi erant credentes in ipsum; nondum enim erat Spiritus S.‘ (cum Scriptura V.T. plena fuerit testimoniis de Sp. S.), ,quia Jesus nondum erat glorificatus.‘ 4. Quod Johannes baptizaverit aqua, Christus Spiritu et igni. Matth. 3, II.“ (L. c. p. 827. sq.)

Gerhardus: ,,Bellarminus dissensiones nostrorum evincere conatur, quia Lutherus in disputatione de baptismo legis, Johannis et Christi statuit, baptisma Johannis non esse sacramentum, nec remittere peccata ac baptizatos a Johanne iterum fuisse baptizandos. Resp.: Habita est illa disputatio a. 1520., de ea igitur accipiendum, quod in praefatione Tom. I. opp. Lutherus scribit: . . . Memor sis, me unum fuisse ex illis, qui, ut Augustinus de se scribit, scribendo et docendo profecerint. . Quid Lutherus statuerit de baptismo Johannis, patet ex concionibus de paedobaptismo habitis Dessaviae a. 1541.“ (Loc. de bapt. § 54.)

M. Chemnitius: ,,In omnibus controversiis ea, quae necessarium usum habet in exercitiis poenitentiae, fidei et pietatis, discernenda sunt ab aliis disputationibus, in quibus opinionum diversitas, vel etiam levis quaedam hallucinatio non infert jacturam fidei et saluti. Ita de baptismo Christi, quo nunc ecclesia N.T. baptizat, multa, quorum necessarius usus est, utiliter possunt dici, quid sit, quae sit ejus efficacia, quomodo rite dispensetur et suscipiatur, quis sit ejus per totam baptizati hominis vitam usus etc. Disputatio vero de Johannis baptismo non aeque est necessaria; nemo enim nunc vel baptizatur, vel baptizatus est Johannis baptismo; sed tantum quaestio est de ceremonia temporis jam dudum praeteriti et quidem exigui. Johanne enim in vincula conjecto, baptismus ejus desiit. Detentum autem fuisse in carcere ultra integrum annum, series historiae evangelicae non obscure indicat. Ergo non per totum sesquiannum duravit baptismus Johannis. Non igitur anathemate statim jugulandi erant, qui de hac quaestione, coilatis Scripturae sententiis, paulo aliter, quam veteres quidam, disputant, si id fiat salva veritate doctrinae de poenitentia, fide et pietate.“ (Exam. Concil. Trid. De baptismo. Ed. Genev. f. 230.)

Calovius: ,,Quamquam ob dissensum in hac quaestione (de baptismo Johannis) haereseos notam inurendam vel anathema vibrandum esse minime censeamus, quum ea quaestio salutem hodie non attineat, minime tamen libera relinquenda opinio et in utramque partem disceptatio, ubi habetur ipsius Sp. S. decisio.“ (System. Tom. I, 953.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Quorundam patrum, ut Augustini et aliorum, existimantium, Johannis baptismum alium fuisse a Christi baptismo, atque ita baptizasse Johannem in aqua poenitentiae in remissionem peccatorum, ut ab eo baptizatis in spe remitterentur peccata, reipsa vero in Dei sacramento id fieret; ita August. 1. 5. c. Donatistas c. 10. 2. Pontificiorum, statuentium, ,baptismum Johannis non fuisse idem sacramentum cum baptismo Christi‘; ita Bellarminus 1.1. de

baptismo c. 19.; fuisse tantum praeparationem ad baptismum Christi ac proinde illos fuisse necessario ab apostolis baptizandos, qui a Johanne baptizati.

Item, baptismum Johannis non habuisse eandem vim et efficaciam cum baptismo Christi; baptismum Johannis in poenitentiam, Christi autem in remissionem peccatorum exhibitum esse.

Ita Concil. Trident. sess. 7. de baptismo can. 1.: ,Si quis dixerit, baptismum Johannis habuisse eandem vim cum baptismo Christi, anathema sit.‘ . .

3. Socinianorum, contendentium, diversum fuisse baptismum Johannis a baptismo Christi seu apostolorum: 1.) ratione principii, quia Johannes baptizarit e peculiari mandato, apostoli non item; 2.) ratione objecti, quia Johannis baptismus pertinuerit ad Judaeos, Christi vero etiam ad gentes; Volkelius 1. 3. de V. R. c. 8. p. 49.; 3.) ratione adjuncti, sc. necessitatis baptismi, quod non omnes e populo Israelitico, qui Johannem audierunt, baptizari opus habuerint, sed solum, qui poenitentia et remissione peccatorum indiguerunt; Socinus de baptism. p. 239.; 4.) ratione finis, quod Johannes baptizarit, ut in studio pietatis homines contineantur per baptismum; Volkelius 1. c. c. 9. p. 53.; 5.) ratione formae, quod Johannis baptismus tantum fuerit professio poenitentiae, apostolorum vero professio fidei, adeoque a Johanne baptizati tantum, qui nondum crediderunt in Christum; Socinus 1. c. c. 64.; 6.) ratione auctoritatis et formulae in baptismo adhibitae, quod Johannis baptismus non fuerit administratus in nomine Christi; sic autem administrarunt baptismum apostoli; Socinus 1. c. p. 72.; 7.) ratione efficaciae, quod non suffecerit baptismus Johannis, adeoque άναβαπτ/,σμψ opus habuerint baptizati a Johanne; 8.) denique ratione durationis, quod Johannis baptismus abrogatus sit, postquam Christus in coelum assumtus est. . .


### On Baptism: Of certain Calvinists, such as Zwingli, who in his book *de vera et falsa R.*,…

4. Of certain Calvinists, such as Zwingli, who in his book *de vera et falsa R.*, chapter on Baptism, calls the baptism of John one consisting only of elemental water, by which they marked themselves so that they might be reckoned among the penitent who were about to amend their life and morals." (*L. c.*, s. 2, q. 3, f. 1108, sq.)

And thus it is the cause of baptism, viewed as to the species of the act. See what will be said shortly concerning the matter and form of baptism. Thus they are considered as causes of baptism regarding the exercise of the act.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Arminians, who affirm that 'the doctrine concerning baptism is not necessary, nor are we bound to baptize by virtue of any command of God,' in their *Apologia*, p. 247, 248.

2. Of the Socinians, who contend 1.) that baptism was freely used by the apostles without the institution and command of Christ; 2.) that the baptism of water is not equally commanded for all in perpetuity who wish to be Christians." Thus Socinus, preface to the book *de baptismo*, f. 4: "Whence it seems to be established," he says, "that the ministry of that baptism was not enjoined upon the apostles themselves by Christ"; *ibid.*, c. 2, p. 14, T. 1, Op., f. 712. And he attempts to show throughout the whole book that baptism is an indifferent matter, such that it should be left free to everyone whether he wishes to receive the baptism of water or whether he wishes to abstain from it; f. 752, T. 1, Op., he says: "It is not at all established that the apostles were impelled to baptize by the force of a divine command. It is more probable that they were incited by a desire to imitate John, with Christ consenting in His wisdom, especially in an indifferent matter." The same Socinus, Ep. 3 to Radecc., f. 128, T. 1, Op., f. 384: "We maintain that the baptism of water is an indifferent matter." The same is taught by Volkelius, bk. 3, *de Ver. Relig.*, c. 9, f. 53; and bk. 4, f. 670, he says: "It is not established that the baptism of water was instituted by Christ... It is an error that Christ instituted that the baptism of water should be spread and used among the Gentiles by the apostles." PART III. CHAP. X.

The opinion of the Socinians, therefore, is: "that the baptism of water was not instituted by Christ nor commanded for all in perpetuity." (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1111.)

Concerning this, we shall see more when we come to treat of the end and effect of baptism. See, meanwhile, Mark 16:16. § 3. The internal impulsive cause is the goodness of God; the external is the merit of the Mediator Christ.

Thus Paul, in Titus 3:5, ascribes it to the goodness, love toward man, and mercy of God our Savior that we are saved through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit. Just as Christ is said to have given Himself for the church, that He might sanctify it, cleansing it with the washing of water by the word, and thus by giving Himself unto death, He merited that men should be cleansed by the washing of baptism, Eph. 5:26. Compare what we have said concerning the Sacraments in general, Chapter VII, § 5. § 4.

The less principal efficient cause is ordinarily the minister of the church; extraordinarily, in a case of necessity, even a layman or a woman. That is, one who establishes baptism in use and applies it to men by the authority of another, as of a superior, and according to His institution.

See Matt. 28:19, where Christ addresses the apostles as ministers of the church. And it is evident that John the Baptist made mention of his mission as a minister, John 1:33. Add 1 Cor. 4:1. Christ Himself, however, abstained from the office of baptizing. See John 4:2. When, namely, it appears that a person, especially a weaker infant, is about to die without baptism, the ordinary minister of the church being absent, it is better that another should baptize him than that a means of regeneration and salvation so necessary (according to John 3:5) should be omitted, not without danger; especially since he who administers baptism does not bestow efficacy upon it, but only establishes in use the medium which, with God concurring, is efficacious, whereas it is committed peculiarly to the ministers of the church for the sake of εὐταξίας (good order).

Namely, thus far a layman and a woman are equivalent. And since in the Old Testament circumcision was to be administered by women rather than be omitted entirely (see Chapter IX, § 4), it is certain that the same is permitted no less in the New Testament regarding baptism. Gerhardus: "As far as the question concerning the baptism of heretics is concerned, its decision rests upon certain distinctions. 1. Certain heretics impugn the substantials of baptism, such as those who use something else in place of water, or who stubbornly and directly deny the mystery of the Trinity, and do not administer baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit."

they] administer. Some, however, although they otherwise corrupt parts of the heavenly doctrine with their leaven, nevertheless think rightly concerning the substance of this sacrament and follow the divine institution in substantial matters. As far as the heretics of the first class are concerned, their baptism is not to be considered true and efficacious; and therefore, those baptized by them, if they flee to the bosom of the true church, must be baptized entirely, since they have not yet received true baptism. . . What we have said concerning baptism conferred by a heretic who directly denies the mystery of the Holy Trinity must again be accepted with a certain distinction. For either the minister alone is infected with that heresy, or the church to which the minister belongs is infected along with him. But if a heresy attacking some substantial part of baptism has occupied an entire church, we deny that the baptism is true, because it is administered by such a heretic in such a church, since the definition of baptism does not apply to it. If, however, a minister of a church privately and secretly fosters a heresy contrary to the institution and truth of baptism, while the church openly holds a different view, we maintain that true baptism is conferred there. For the sacraments are goods of the church; therefore, the secret error of the minister detracts nothing from the integrity of the baptism, provided he observes its substantial elements and changes nothing in the external element or word. Such a thing happened in the memory of our fathers in Heidelberg in the Palatinate; for there Adam Neuser, the primary pastor of the church of the Holy Spirit, fostered the Arian heresy privately for several years, who, finally fleeing to Constantinople, having abjured the Christian religion and undergone circumcision, gave his name to Mohammedanism. Osiand. cent. 16. Hist. Eccles. l. 2. c. 22. Yet the baptism was not pronounced, nor even ought it to have been pronounced, invalid, which he administered in the name of a church that thought rightly on this article.” (L. c. § 25. 26.)

P. Tarnovius: “The question is asked, whether heretics administer true baptism? I answer by a double distinction: one of heresy, the other of the subject in whom the heretic [is found]. For one heresy strikes at the substantials of baptism, such as that of the Antitrinitarians, Arians, Photinians, Macedonians, Manichaeans, Valentinians, and the like, who deny and blaspheme the Trinity, in whose name baptism is to be given. Another [strikes at] the end and effect of baptism, such as that of the Calvinists; another, besides this error concerning the end and effect of baptism, adds human traditions to its ceremonies, such as that of the Papists. Of these, the latter, because they do not change true baptism in its substantials, can baptize legitimately; but the former [can do so] only if the error and heresy is fostered privately and secretly by the minister alone or by a few; but if it rages openly and publicly and occupies the whole church, its minister can by no means administer a true and legitimate baptism. The argument upon which this opinion of ours rests is as follows: such as is the faith of the church concerning the substantials of this article, such also is the baptism, as is evident from the institution in Matt. 28:19 and from Basil’s epistle 78: ‘We must,’ he says, ‘be baptized as we have received, and believe as we are baptized, and glorify as we have believed: the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.’ But the faith of those heretical churches of which we have spoken is not true in its substantials. Therefore, neither is their baptism. The same argumentation holds in reverse concerning an orthodox church and a heretical minister. For baptism is a good of the church, not of the minister. This man, therefore, however unfaithful and heretical he may be, gives what is the public and common [property] of the orthodox mother church, not what is his own private and singular [property].” (De ministrorum verbi officio disput. 2. th. 11. See Dedekenn’s thesaur. etc. II, f. 29.)

Balduinus: "Even if they retain the most customary words of the institution, the sound of the words is not what should be attended to, since we attribute no magical power to them, but rather that true sense which Christ intended in the institution of baptism. Therefore, in the assemblies of the Arians, who tear down the article concerning the Trinity, there is no true baptism; for this reason, those who have received baptism among them are to be held as unbaptized. Whence Damascenus writes in *De fide orthodoxa*, bk. 4, ch. 5: 'Whoever has not been baptized into the most holy Trinity, them it behooves to be rebaptized,' and for this reason the Paulianists were formerly rebaptized, because they had been baptized in the assemblies of the Samosatenians, who deny the article concerning the Trinity, regarding which matter a canon exists in the Council of Nicaea, the nineteenth in order, and in the Council of Arles, the eighth in order." (*Tract. de cas. consc.*, p. 200 sq.)

Deylingius: "A man who is at least by external and public profession a Lutheran and sustains the person of a Lutheran minister does not give his own baptism, but the baptism of God and the Church. And his baptizing is not held to be a private action of the minister, but a public act of the Church. The matter stands otherwise with one who has received baptism in the assembly of Arians or Photinians or Sabellians and the like, who tear down the mystery of the Trinity. For although they use the formula prescribed by the Savior and baptize an infant in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, using water; nevertheless, by their own mind and in the name of their own church and public profession of doctrine, they corrupt and overturn a substantial part of the sacrament. For the follower of Arius acknowledges three persons of the Trinity, different and unequal in essence among themselves. The Sabellian man understands by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit not three persons, but merely three names of one person. Thus, if a Socinian comes to our church, he must be washed by the sacred font entirely, even if he has already received baptism among his own using the customary formula. Indeed, Hornbeckius affirms in *Apparatus ad controversias Socinianas*, f. 78, that these sectarians in Transylvania, by the order of the prince, administered their baptism in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But the recitation of the words of the institution is not sufficient; rather, it is required that it be done in the orthodox Church, to which Christ has bound His benefits, Matt. 16:18, 19. The sect of the Socinians, however, is not a true Church. And just as they do not have one Lord and one faith with us, so neither do they have one baptism, Eph. 4:4. Nor are Socinians true Christians, because they deny and impugn the mystery of the Trinity, as well as the divinity and satisfaction of Christ." (*Institut. prud. past.*, Ed. 3, p. 347 sq.)

Latin:

4. Quorundam Calvinianorum, ut Zwinglii, qui lib. de vera et falsa R. cap. de Baptism. baptismum Johannis vocat elementari solum aqua constantem, quo se signarint, ut inter poenitentes censerentur, qui vitam et mores erant emendaturi.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 1108. sq.)

Et sic baptismi, quoad speciem actus spectati, causa est. Vid., quae de materia et forma baptismi mox dicentur. Ita considerantur, tanquam causae baptismi quoad exereitium actus.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Arminianorum, qui affirmant, ,doctrinam de baptismo non esse necessariam, nec teneri nos, ex vi alicujus mandati Dei baptizare‘, in Apologia sua p. 247. 248.

2. Socinianorum, contendentium 1.) baptismum ab apostolis citra Christi institutionem et mandatum libere usurpatum esse; 2.) baptismum aquae non esse omnibus in perpetuum, qui Christiani esse velint, peraeque praeceptum.‘ Ita Socinus praef. lib. de baptismo f. 4.: ,Unde constare videtur‘, inquit, ,baptismi illius ministerium ipsis apostolis a Christo non fuisse injunctum‘; ibid. c. 2. p. 14. tentia ergo Socinianorum est: ,baptismum aquae non esse a Christo institutum ac omnibus in perpetuum mandatum.‘ “ (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1111.)

De quo plura, cum de fine et effectu baptismi agendum erit, videbimus. Vid. interim Marc. 16, 16. § 3. Causa impulsiva interna est bonitas a divina; externa est meritum b mediatoris Christi.

Ita Paulus ad Tit. 8, 5. bonitati et amori erga homines ac misericordiae Servatoris nostri Dei ad scribit, quod per lavacrum regenerationis et renovationis Spiritus Sancti salvamur. Prout Christus dicitur tradidisse se pro ecclesia, ut illam sanctifir caret, mundans lavacro aquae per verbum, adeoque tradendo se in mortem meruisse, ut homines mundarentur lavacro baptismi, Eph. 5, 26. Confer, quae diximus de Sacramentis in genere, cap. VII. § 5. § 4.

Causa efficiens minus principalis a ordinarie est minister b ecclesiae; extraordinarie in casu necessitatis c etiam laicus autd femina. Sive quae baptismum auctoritate aliena, tanquam superioris, et juxta institutionem ejus in usu constituit et hominibus applicat.

Vid. Matth. 28, 19., ubi Christus apostolos ut ministros ecclesiae alloquitur. Et constat, Johannem Baptistam missionis suae ut ministri mentionem fecisse Joh. 1, 33. Adde 1 Cor. 4, 1. Christus autem ipse abstinuit a munere baptizandi. Vid. Joh. 4, Quando videlicet homini, praesertim infanti imbecilliori, deficiente ordinario ministro ecclesiae, absque baptismo moriendum esse apparet, satius est, ut alius eum baptizet, quam ut medium regenerationis et salutis tam necessarium (juxta Joh. 3, 5.) non sine periculo omittatur, praesertim quod, qui administrat baptismum, non largitur ei efficaciam, sed tantum in usu constituit medium, quod Deo concurrente est efficax, ministris ecclesiae autem peculiariter demandatum est, ευταξίας causa.

Nempe hactenus aequipollent vir laicus et femina. Et cum Vet. Testam, circumcisio per feminas administranda fuerit potius, quam ut prorsus omitteretur (vid. cap. IX. § 4.), certum est, non minus in N. T. quoad baptismum idem licere. Gerhardus: ,,Quod ad quaestionem de haereticorum, baptismo attinet, certis quibusdam distinctionibus ejus decisio innititur. 1. Quidam haeretici substantialia baptismi impugnant, utpote qui loco aquae aliud quippiam usurpant, vel mysterium trinitatis praefracte et directe negant, nec in Patris, Filii ac Spiritus Sancti nomine baptismum admi-

nistrant. Quidam vero, quamvis alias doctrinae coelestis partes fermento suo corrumpant, tamen de substantia hujus sacramenti recte sentiunt et in substantialibus divinam institutionem sequuntur. Quod ad haereticos prioris classis attinet, illorum baptismus non est verus et efficax censendus, ideoque baptizati ab illis, si ad verae ecclesiae gremium confugiant, omnino baptizandi sunt, cum verum baptismum nondum acceperint. . . Quod de baptismo ab haeretico, qui mysterium S. 8. Trinitatis directe negat, collato diximus, iterum cum quadam distinctione accipiendum. Vel enim solus minister haeresi illa infectus est, vel una cum eo etiam ecclesia illa, cujus est minister. Quod si haeresis substantialem aliquam baptismi partem impugnans totam aliquam ecclesiam occupavit, negamus, verum esse baptismum, quia ab ejusmodi haeretico in tali ecclesia administratur, cum definitio baptismi illi non conveniat. Si vero minister ecclesiae privatim et occulte haeresin institutioni et veritati baptismi contrariam foveat, ecclesia aperte diversum sentiente, statuimus, verum ibi conferri baptismum. Sacramenta enim sunt bona ecclesiae, ideo occultus ministri error baptismi integritati nihil detrahit, modo substantialia ejusdem observet nec in externo elemento vel verbo quicquam mutet. Tale quid patrum nostrorum memoria Heidelbergae in Palatinatu contigit; ibi enim Adamus Neuserus, pastor ecclesiae ad S.S. primarius, aliquot annis privatim haeresin Arianam fovit, qui Constantinopolin tandem profugiens abjurata religione Christiana circumcisione suscepta Mahomethismo nomen dedit. Osiand. cent. 16. Hist. Eccles. 1. 2. c. 22. Nec tamen baptismus pronunciatus est vel etiam pronunciari debuit irritus, quem ecclesiae in hoc articulo recte sentientis nomine administravit.“ (L. c. § 25. 26.)

P. Tarnovius: ,,Quaeritur, an haeretici verum baptismum administrent? Respondeo per distinctionem duplicem: unam haereseos, alteram subjecti, in quo haeret. Haeresis enim alia impingit in substantialia baptismi, ut Antitrinitariorum, Arianorum, Photinianorum, Macedonianorum, Manichaeorum, Valentinianorum et similium abnegantium et blasphemantium trinitatem, in cujus nomine dandus est baptismus. Alia finem et effectum baptismi, ut Calvinianorum, alia praeter hunc de fine et effectu baptismi errorem ejusdem ceremoniis humanas traditiones adjungit, ut Pontificiorum. Ex his posteriores, quia verum baptismum in substantialibus non mutant, legitime baptizare possunt; priores vero tum demum, si error et haeresis privatim, occulte a ministro tantum aut paucis foveatur; quod si palam et publice grassetur et totam ecclesiam occupet, nequaquam verum et legitimum baptismum ejus minister administrare potest. Argumentum, quo haec sententia nostra nititur, est tale: qualis est fides ecclesiae de hujus articuli substantialibus, talis quoque est baptismus, ut patet ex institutione Matth. 28, 19. et ex Basilii epistola 78. ,AeZ, inquit, ?)μας βαπτίζεσϋαι μεν, ως לταρελάβομεν ‘ πιστενειν όε, ως βαπτιζόμεΦα · όοξάζειν όέ, ως πεπιστενκαμεν, πατέρα, και νΐον, και άγων πνεύμα. At fides ecclesiarum haereticarum illarum, de quibus dictum, non est in substantialibus vera. Ergo nec baptismus. Eadem argumentatio valet in contrarium de ecclesia orthodoxa et ministro haeretico. Baptismus enim bonum est ecclesiae, non ministri. Hic igitur, quantumvis infidelis et haereticus, dat, quod est orthodoxae matris ecclesiae publicum et commune, non quod suum est privatum et singulare.“ (De ministrorum verbi officio disput. 2. th. 11. Vid. Dedekenni thesaur. etc. II, f. 29.)

Balduinus: ,,Quod si maxime usitata verba institutionis retinent, non tamen sonus verborum attendendus esset, cum nullam illis tribuamus vim magicam, sed verus ille sensus, quem Christus in institutione baptismi intendit. In coetibus ergo Arianorum, convellentibus articulum de trinitate, non est verus baptismus; ideo pro non baptizatis habendi sunt, qui apud illos baptismum acceperunt. Nie., in ordine decimus nonus, et in Concil. Arelanensi in ordine octavus.“ (Tract. de cas. consc. p. 200. sq.)

Deylingius: ,,Homo, qui minimum professione externa et publica Lutheranus est et ministri Lutherani personam sustinet, non dat suum, sed Dei et ecclesiae baptismum. Et ejus baptizatio non pro actione ministri privata, sed pro actu ecclesiae publico habetur. Aliter se res habet cum eo, qui baptismum suscepit in coetu Arianorum aut Photinianorum aut Sabellianorum similiumque, qui mysterium trinitatis convellunt. Quamvis enim formulam a servatore praescriptam usurpent et infantem in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus S. adhibita aqua baptizent; tamen ex propria sua mente et suae ecclesiae nomine ac publica doctrinae professione substantialem sacramenti partem corrumpunt et evertunt. Nam Arii sectator tres agnoscit trinitatis personas, essentia inter se diversas ac inaequales. Homo Sabellianus per Patrem, Filium et Spiritum S. non tot personas, sed tria dumtaxat unius personae nomina intelligit. Sic, si Socinianus ad nostram ecclesiam veniat, omnino sacro fonte abluendus est, etsi apud suos adhibita consueta formula jam baptismum accepit. Affirmat quippe Hornbeckius in Apparatu ad controversias Socinianas f. 78., hos sectarios in Transylvania principis jussu in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus S. suum baptismum administrasse. Verum non sufficit verborum institutionis recitatio, sed requiritur, ut id fiat in ecclesia orthodoxa, ad quam Christus sua beneficia alligavit, Matth. 16, 18. 19. Socinianorum autem secta non est ecclesia vera. Et quemadmodum nobiscum non unum Dominum et unam fidem habent, ita nec unum baptismum, Eph. 4, 4. Nec Sociniani veri sunt Christiani, quia mysterium trinitatis, nec non Christi divinitatem et satisfactionem negant atque impugnant.“ (Institut, prud. past. Ed. 3. p. 347. sq.)


### On Baptism: Gerhardus: "Q.: Whether anyone ought to baptize himself

Gerhardus: "Q.: Whether anyone ought to baptize himself? . . . We leave it in the middle whether a catechumen in a case of extreme necessity can baptize himself. Q. 2: Whether baptism administered by one who is himself not baptized is to be held valid? Gregory II, Roman Pontiff, pronounces it invalid in the chapter 'Quos a paganis,' dist. 4, *de consecrat*. Nicholas I holds it valid in a rescript which is read among the decrees, vol. 3 of the councils. Thomas establishes the same, part 3, q. 67, art. 5. Augustine, *de bapt.*, bk. 7, ch. 53, and *contra ep. Parmen.*, bk. 2, ch. 13, leaves it in doubt. In favor of the affirmative part of the question, we bring forward these arguments: ... 4. Just as the Word preached by one who is not yet regenerated and truly converted is effective in others through the grace and operation of the Holy Spirit: so baptism conferred by one not baptized is to be judged effective and valid." (*L. c.* §§ 66, 67.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of Marcion, who permitted women to baptize even outside a case of necessity and, indeed, in public assemblies; thus Epiphanius writes in *Haereses* 42 concerning Marcion: 'He permits women to baptize'; cf. the same, *Haereses* 79, *Collyridiani*. 2. Of the Socinians, as Volkelius against Smiglecius, p. 19, who maintain that baptism can be administered by anyone, even outside a case of necessity. 3. Of the Anabaptists, who contend that all Christians indiscriminately, without any regard for whether they are ministers of the church or not, can ordinarily administer baptism. 4. Of the Calvinists, who contend that a legitimate calling is necessarily required in the baptizer, and who simply disapprove of baptism administered by a private person in a case of necessity. Thus Calvin says in *Institutes*, Book 4, ch. 15, § 20: 'The dispensation of this (baptism), as well as of the Supper, is a part of the ecclesiastical ministry; for neither to women nor to"

Christ did not command all men whatsoever to baptize, but gave this mandate to those whom He had constituted as apostles.

Ibid. § 22. And in 1. 2. def. c. Westph. he says: "It is better that baptism be omitted entirely than that it be administered by a woman"; Ep. 278, 326, he calls the baptism of women "a putrid profanation of the ministry." Theod. Beza, Ep. 12, calls it "a pseudo-baptism," and P. 2. qq. Qu. 139, "a fable." Qu. 144, he prefers the baptism of Satan to the baptism of a woman administered in a case of necessity.

Altingius in Syllab. Controv. p. 261: "The administration of baptism," he says, "cannot be permitted to women by any right, whatever necessity may arise." And ibid. p. 263: "Women administering a baptism of necessity and haste, *Jachtaufe* [hurried baptism], intrude into the ecclesiastical ministry, because they baptize without being called, and they attach eternal salvation to an external act, because they think it is all over for the infant if death forestalls the baptism of water, being ignorant that the salvation of infants depends upon the grace of election and the covenant."

Chamier, 1. 5. de bapt. c. 14. n. 8. p. 137, says: "We say that the right of conferring baptism resides only with those who hold a public office in the church. Therefore, [a baptism] conferred by anyone who has no person other than a private one has no force, that is, it is no sacrament, but a rash mockery, in no way to be tolerated in the church." (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 1115. sq.) §

5. The material of baptism is true and natural water, and the act of washing, which can be done either by immersion or by aspersion, once or three times. Which is common to this sacrament and other non-sacramental actions.

As an element or a corporeal and sensible earthly thing, about which some action is directly occupied and treats it.

Moreover, water was determined for baptism by Christ Himself, John 3:5, where it is certain that Nicodemus, being anxious about the baptism of water already introduced at that time by John, was more correctly informed by Christ.

But the apostles also, baptizing with water, testified not obscurely that they were following the institution of Christ. See Acts 10:47 and compare Matthew 28:19; Acts 8:36 sqq.

Hollazius: "The reason why God destined water for the sacrament of baptism has not been revealed in the written Word of God. It is certain, however: a. That water is a common medium, available to all nations. Everywhere among the nations there is as much water given as suffices for baptism. b. That there is no clearer symbol of the Holy Spirit and the efficacy of baptism than water. God the Father is the fountain, the Son of God is the mouth of the fountain, the crystalline river flowing from both is the Holy Spirit. Water cleanses the body; baptism, the vehicle of the Holy Spirit, purges the soul. Water refreshes the thirsty, vivifies drooping plants, and makes trees fruitful; baptism, when called to memory, slakes the thirst of the soul, vivifies the sad, and brings forth the fruits of repentance. Water cools; baptism provides refreshment against the heat of concupiscence." (L. c. p. 1084. sq.)

Not another liquid, or any other thing, lest the substance of baptism be changed. But what kind of water it is, e.g., river or spring, cold or tepid, makes no difference, because Christ determined nothing concerning that.

Deylingius: "Nor does it matter whether the baptismal water is drawn from a spring, river, sea, or pond, or whether it is rainwater, dew, hot, cold, or... PART III. CHAP. X.

is lukewarm, because nothing definite is read about that matter in Holy Scripture. It suffices if true, natural, and pure water is used, which represents the purifying power of baptism. Those who wish to substitute another liquid in its place, and—for example—use medicated, scented, or rose water (a foolishness that sometimes enters the minds of the nobility and the wealthier classes), or who wish to use wine, milk, or beer under the pretext of necessity, must be warned that the sacrament is corrupted in this way, because true water is required for the substance of baptism, which is the "washing of water by the word," Eph. 5:26; John 3:5; Acts 8:36 and 10:49.

Hence, when a certain young Hebrew was once baptized by having sand poured over his head three times, because water was lacking in the wilderness, Dionysius, Bishop of Ascalon, most correctly judged that he must be baptized again. He therefore immediately sent him to the Jordan and ordered him to be baptized there. . . We see, therefore, that the ancients disapproved of such a baptism as illegitimate, because it did not have water.

Indeed, in the collections of canon law, there exists a decree under the name of Pope Siricius to this effect: "To a presbyter who baptizes in wine out of necessity, so that a sick person might not be in danger, no blame can be ascribed for such a thing." However, Antonius Augustinus in *De Emendat. Gratiani*, p. 200, and Steph. Baluzius in his notes, p. 431, observed that this is not a decree of Siricius, but of Stephen II, who lived only in the middle of the eighth century. See Jo. Harduin’s *Diss. de baptismo in vino*, which exists among his *Opera Selecta*, f. 223.

The primitive church consistently denied that one could be validly baptized without water. Our Evangelical Church also denies that baptism can be rightly conferred without true water.

At the beginning of the reformed religion, it once happened at Kahla on the Saale in Thuringia that a midwife baptized certain weaker infants there and in the vicinity under the pretext of necessity without water, with only the words pronounced: "I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." B. Luther and Bugenhagen, consulted on this case, replied on March 26, 1542: "The woman is suspected of heresy, which has been rampant in those places in recent years. Baptism is openly scorned and corrupted, which cannot be done without water, nor does it suffice that that old woman says she is baptizing with the Word of God. For the Word of God does not suffice, but water must also be present in that sacrament." See the illustrious Seckendorff’s *History of Lutheranism* for that year, bk. 3, sect. 25, no. 101, f. m. 416, who narrates from Bugenhagen that some in Holstein also taught that baptism could be done without water. Neither wished to tolerate the abuse, and both, as much Luther as Bugenhagen, contended that such infants must be baptized again and legitimately.

I am therefore surprised that the scholastics in Jo. Gerhard, in the *Locus de baptismo* § 72, substituted lye or another liquid, and that Theod. Beza could write in *Epist. 2, vol. 3, Tractat. theolog.*, p. 196: "I would baptize with any other liquid no less rightly than with water."

For it is no more permitted to invent a baptism without water than the Holy Supper without bread and wine. For once the essential part is removed, the essence of the whole cannot remain intact.

As for the rest, if some foreign liquid, e.g., oil or chrism, happens to have been poured into the natural water, nothing is lost from the integrity of the baptism. (Institut. prud. pastoral. p. 338 sqq.)

Hollazius: "The earthly matter is natural, pure water. . . By pure water, mixed, muddy, and dreggy water—such as lye, broth mixed with pieces of bread and meat, salt water, and the like—is excluded. However, purity is not understood as exact and absolute, to which nothing of a foreign element adheres, but common or natural purity is understood." (Exam. th. P. III. s. 2. c. 4. q. 7. p. 1084.)

Gerhardus: "Bellarmine, in book 1 *de baptismo* c. 2, gravely accuses Luther because in his table talks, when asked whether it is permitted to baptize in milk or beer if water is lacking, he first replied that 'that must be left to divine judgment,' but then added: 'Whatever can be called by the name of a bath, that is water for baptizing, whether it be wine, or milk, or beer.' Resp.: 1. The book

that of the table-talks is such that it was neither seen, nor read, nor approved by Luther. 2.

Luther holds the contrary in the sermons on baptism delivered at Dessau, sermon 2, Jena Edition, Vol. 7, German, p. 469: "Suppose (he says) the person is impious and unbelieving, provided he keeps the institution of Christ inviolate, and does not use wine, beer, lye, or any other thing, but water with the added Word of God, then it is and is called holy baptism." (L. c. § 71.) Cf. Opp. Luth. Hal. T. VII, 1015. Erlang. P. XIX, 81.

Which some call the proximate material, just as they call water the remote material, according to those things which we said about the sacraments in general in Chapter VIII, § 7. See Rom. 6:4, Col. 2:12, where men are said to be buried together with Christ through baptism, namely, that baptism, conferred by immersion into water, would represent the burial of Christ. This not only the force of the word baptism admits, as we showed at § 1, note c, but also the institution of the sacrament, which determined neither mode.

Q. 2.: An baptismus administratus ab eo, qui ipse non est baptizatus, ratus sit habendus? Gregorius II., pont. rom., irritum eum pronuntiat cap. ,Quos a paganis‘ dist. 4. de consecrat. Parmen. c. 13. in dubio relinquit. Pro affirmante quaestionis parte proferimus haec argumenta: ... 4. Sicut verbum ab eo, qui nondum regeneratus et vere conversus est, praedicatum in aliis per Sp. S. gratiam et operationem est efficax: ita baptismus a non baptizato collatus judicandus est efficax et ratus.“ (L. c. §§ 66. 67.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Marcionis, qui mulieribus etiam extra casum necessitatis et quidem in publicis coetibus baptizare permisit; ita Epiphanius haeres. 42. de Marcione scribit: ,Permittere eum mulieribus, ut baptizent‘; cf. eundem haeres. 79. Collyrid. 2. Socinia· norum, ut Volkelii c. Smiglecium p. 19., statuentium, baptismum a quovis administrari posse etiam extra casum necessitatis. 3.
