Controv. p. 261.: ,baptismi administratio4, inquit, ,mulieribus nullo jure, quaecunque etiam ingruat necessitas, permitti potest.4 Et ib. p. 263.: ,mulieres baptismum necessitatis et festinationis, Jachtaufe, administrantes et involant in ministerium ecclesiasticum, quia non vocatae baptizant, et rei externae salutem aeternam affingunt, quia actum de infante putant, si aquae baptismum mors praeveniat, ignorantes, salutem infantum ab electionis foederisque gratia pendere.4

Cliamier. 1. 5. de bapt. c. 14. n. 8. p. 137. ait: ,Nos dicimus, baptismi conferendi penes eos duntaxat jus esse, qui publicum munus gerunt in ecclesia. Itaque collati a quocunque, cujus praeter privatam nulla persona sit, nullam vim esse, id est, sacramentum nuilum esse, sed temerariam ludificationem, nullo modo tolerandam in ecclesia. 4 4 4 (L. c. s. 2. q. 4. f. 1115. sq.) §

5· Materiale a baptismi est b aqua vera c et naturalis, et actus d abluendi, qui vel e immergendo vel f aspergendo, semel aut tribus vicibus g fieri potest.h Quod commune est huic sacramento et actionibus aliis non sacramentalibus.

Velut elementum aut res terrena corporea et sensibilis, circa quam actio aliqua directe occupatur eamque tractat.

Est autem aqua ad baptismum a Christo ipso determinata Joh. 3, 5., ubi certum est, Nicodemum de baptismo aquae, per Johannem jam tunc introducto, solicitum, a Christo rectius informatum fuisse.

Sed et apostoli, aqua baptizantes, institutionem Christi se sequi, non obscure testati fuerunt. Vid. Ad. 10, 47. et conf. Matth. 28, 19. Ad. 8, 36. sqq.

Hollazius: ״Causa, cur Deus sacramento baptismi aquam destinaverit, verbo Dei scripto revelata non est. Certum tamen est: a. Quod aqua sit medium παλνκοινον, omnibus nationibus obvium. Ubivis gentium tantum datur aquae, quantum baptismo sufficit, b. Quod nullum sit clarius symbolum Spiritus S. et efficaciae baptismi, quam aqua. Deus Pater est fons, fontis os Filius Dei, fluvius crystallinus ex utroque profluens est Spiritus S. Aqua emundat corpus; baptismus, vehiculum Spiritus S., purgat animam. Aqua recreat sitientem, vivifleat plantas flaccidas arboresque foeeundat; baptismus in memoriam revocatus sedat sitim animae, quam tristem vivificat, et fructus poenitentiae parit. Aqua refrigerat; baptismus praestat refrigerium contra concupiscentiae ardorem.44 (L. c. p. 1084. sq.)

Non liquor alius, aut res alia ulla, ne mutetur substantia baptismi. Qualis autem sit aqua, v. gr. fluvialis aut fontana, frigida aut tepida, nihil refert, quia Christus de eo nihil determinavit.

Deylingius: ,,Nec refert, utrum aqua baptismalis ex fonte, fluvio, mari aut stagno hausta, an pluviatilis, rorulenta, calida, frigida aut PART. III. CAP. X.

tepida sit, quia ea de re in Scriptura s. nihil legitur definitum. Sufficit, si aqua adhibeatur vera et naturalis et pura, quae vim baptismi purificantem repraesentet. Qui alium liquorem in ejus locum substituere, et e. g. aquam medicatam et muscatam aut rosaceam, quae stoliditas proceribus et ditioribus ex statu nonnunquam in mentem venit, adhibere, vel vino, lacte aut cerevisia, sub necessitatis praetextu, uti volunt, commonendi sunt, sacramentum hac ratione corrumpi, quia vera aqua requiritur ad substantiam baptismi, qui est,lavacrum aquae in verbo‘, Eph. 5, 26. Joh. 3, 5. Act. 8, 36. et 10, 49.

Hinc quum certus quidem adolescens Hebraeus ter effusa super caput ejus arena, quoniam aqua in solitudine deerat, olim baptizatus esset, ׳Dionysius, episcopus Ascalonensis, rectissime judicavit, eum denuo baptizandum esse. Continuo igitur eum ad Jordanem misit et baptizari illic jussit. . . Videmus igitur, veteres ejusmodi baptismum tanquam illegitimum improbasse, quia aquam non habebat.

Equidem in juris canonici collectionibus exstat decretum sub Siricii papae nomine, in hanc sententiam: ,Presbytero, qui in vino baptizet ex necessitate, ut aeger non periclitetur, pro tali re nullam culpam adscribi‘ posse. Verum Antonius Augustinus de Emendat. Gratiani p. 200. et Steph. Baluzius in notis p. 431. observarunt, non esse hoc decretum Siricii, sed Stephani II., qui octavo demum saeculo medio vixit. Vid. Jo. Harduini Diss. de baptismo in vino, quae inter Opera ejus Selecta extat f. 223.

Primitiva ecclesia, sine aqua valide baptizari posse, constanter negavit. Negat et ecclesia nostra evangelica, sine aqua vera baptismum recte conferri posse.

Sub emendatae religionis initium Kahlae ad Salam in Thuringia olim evenit·, ut obstetrix aliqua infantes quosdam infirmiores ibi et in vicinia sub necessitatis praetextu absque aqua baptizaret, verbis solum pronunciatis: ,Ego te baptizo in nomine Patris, Filii et Spiritus S.‘ B. Lutherus et Bugenhagius, hoc de casu consulti, responderunt d. 26. Mart. 1542.: ,feminam haereseos suspectam esse, quae superioribus annis iis in locis grassata fuerit. Sperni et corrumpi aperte baptismum, qui sine aqua fieri non possit, neque sufficere, quod anus illa dicat: se verbo Dei baptizare. Verbum enim Dei non sufficere, sed simul aquam in sacramento illo adesse debere.‘ Videatur illustris Seckendorffii Historia Lutheranismi ad illum annum, 1. 3. sect. 25. num. 101. f. m. 416., qui ex Bugenhagio narrat, quosdam in Holsatia etiam docuisse, baptismum sine aqua fieri posse. Neuter tolerare voluit abusum et uterque, tam Lutherus quam Bugenhagius, contendit, infantes istiusmodi denuo et legitime baptizandos esse.

Miror igitur, scholasticos apud Jo. Gerhardum in loco de baptismo § 72. lixivium vel alium liquorem substituisse et Theod. Bezam Epist. 2. vol. 3. Tractat, theolog. p. 196. scribere potuisse: ,Ego quovis alio liquore non minus rite, quam aqua, baptizarim.‘

Non magis enim baptismum licet fingere sine aqua, quam sacram coenam sine pane et vino. Sublata quippe parte essentiali, non potest salva manere essentia totius.

De reliquo, si aquae naturali nonnihil alieni liquoris, e. g. oleum vel chrisma, forte affusum fuerit, integritati tamen baptismi nihil decedit.“ (Institut, prud. pastoral. p. 338. sqq.)

Per aquam puram mixta, lutosa et faeculenta, qualis est lixivium, jusculum cum partibus panis et carnis mixtum, aqua salsa, similisque excluditur. Puritas autem non intelligitur exacta et omnimoda, cui nihil alieni elementi adhaereat, sed intelligitur puritas communis sive naturalis.“ (Exam. th. P. III. s. 2. c. 4. q. 7. p. 1084.)

Gerhardus: ,,Bellarminus lib. 1. de baptismo c. 2. Lutherum graviter accusat, quod in colloquiis convivalibus, interrogatus, num deflciente aqua liceat baptizare in lacte vel cerevisia, primum quidem responderit, ,id divino judicio committendum‘, deinde vero subjunxerit: ,Quicquid balnei nomine appellari potest, illud י esse» aquam ad baptizandum, sive sit vinum, sive lac, sive cerevisia.‘ Kesp.: 1. Liber

ille convivalium colloquiorum talis est, qui Luthero nec visus, nec lectus, nec approbatus. 2.

Contrarium habet Lutherus in concionibus de baptismo Dessaviae habitis, concione 2. T. 7. Jenensi Germ. p. 469.: ,Esto (inquit), persona sit impia et incredula, dummodo institutionem Christi inviolatam servet, et non vino, cerevisia, lixivio vel alia quapiam re, sed aqua cum adjuncto verbo Dei utatur, tunc est et vocatur sacrum baptisma.‘“ (L. c.‘§ 71.) Cf. Opp. Luth. Hal. T. VII, 1015. Erlang. P. XIX, 81.

Quem quidam materiale proximum vocant, prout aquam, remotum, juxta ea, quae de sacramentis in genere diximus cap. VIII. § 7. Vid. Rom. 6, 4. Coloss. 2, 12., ubi dicuntur homines sepulti una cum Christo per baptismum, scilicet quod baptismus, immergendo in aquam collatus, repraesentaret sepulturam Christi. Quod non solum vis vocis baptismi admittit, ut ostendimus ad § 1. not. c., sed et institutio sacramenti, quae neutrum modum determinavit.


### On Baptism: Indeed, examples of aspersion used in baptism are wont to be brought from those…

Indeed, examples of aspersion used in baptism are wont to be brought from those places where certain persons are read to have been baptized within private houses, e.g., Saul or Paul in the house of Judas, Acts 9:11, 18; Cornelius the centurion with his relatives and necessary friends in his own home, ch. 10:24, 27, 44, 48; that they were lowered into water can hardly be affirmed with sufficient reason, and certainly cannot be shown.

In northern regions, however, and in colder weather, especially regarding the tender bodies of infants, aspersion is deservedly used in place of immersion.

Gerhardus: "It is asked: 3. Whether immersion or aspersion ought to be total, i.e., whether the whole body must be washed? Resp.: This also is an αδιάφορον (indifferent matter), since in the words of institution there exists no precept concerning it, since in the sacramental action one must distinguish between the giving and the mode of giving, between the receiving and the mode of receiving; the giving and receiving are necessary, the mode of giving and receiving is arbitrary; finally, since the end of baptism is not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, so that for that reason the whole body must be washed and scrubbed, but regeneration and spiritual purification from all filthiness of sin. Although that regeneration looks to the whole man, it is not, however, necessary that the whole body be washed by the water of baptism, since the power of regenerating is not from the water, but from the Holy Spirit effectively acting through the water sanctified by the Word; therefore, by one member of the body being washed with the water of baptism, the regeneration of the whole man is perfected by the Holy Spirit; this was declared above by the example of circumcision.

The people were sprinkled with the blood of the covenant, so that it was said to be sprinkled upon all, even if the whole body of each one was not covered, Exod. 24.

The Scholastics ask 4.: Which member of the body is to be sprinkled with water? Resp. Richard in 4 Sent. dist. 4, q. ult.: 'Principally the head or face, because the senses are active in it, afterwards the chest, which is the seat of the heart.' Comp. theol. verit. 1. 6. c. 9. p. 434: 'The washing ought to be done on the more dignified part of the body, namely, on the head.' Rightly, however, the Summa Angelica adds, in the word *baptismus* c. 4. q. 2: 'It is held more commonly that, however one is tinged, he is baptized, and that an aspersion, however slight, suffices in a case of necessity.'" (L. c. § 98, 99.)

Quenstedtius: "They object: 'The Apostle institutes a comparison between the death and resurrection of Christ and baptism, Rom. 6:3, 4, or that by immersion we are buried together with Christ, but by emersion we rise again, which shadowing forth can in no way be done by aspersion with a little water; see Col. 2:12.' Wolzogenius on the same place, Matt. T. 1. Op. f. 152; Slichting. on the same, 1. T. 1. Op. f. 210. — Resp.: 1. This proves that immersion is lawful and was used in the ancient church, but not that it is therefore necessary or even always used by the apostles (see PART III. CHAPTER X.

Acts 2:38) is proven. 2. The Church herself, even in the time of Cyprian—which Slichtingius admits in the aforementioned place—administered baptism by aspersion to the bedridden and to infants; therefore, baptism performed by aspersion was held to be legitimate at that time.

3. We concede that immersion relates to the death of Christ (Rom. 6:3), but aspersion can also signify that we are sprinkled with the blood of Christ in baptism (1 Pet. 1:2) and cleansed (1 John 1:8). Some similarity is sufficient here, which is also found in aspersion or affusion. For he whose head is sprinkled or poured upon is, as it were, buried by those waters; as Vossius rightly says in *De baptismo*, thesis 9, p. 40.

4. Col. 2:12 compares baptism with the burial and resurrection of Christ in such a way that the preceding verse calls circumcision its type. Now, this end—that we may be spiritually circumcised and buried with Christ—is obtained just as much by affusion as by immersion, as is known; which is sufficient for us here. We are saved by the washing of water in the word (Tit. 3:5); and it is a washing, whether we are immersed or sprinkled with water. (Loc. cit., sec. 2, q. 5, p. 1124.)

Cyprian: "You have also asked, dearest brother, what my opinion is regarding those who obtain the grace of God in infirmity and sickness, whether they are to be considered legitimate Christians, because they have not been washed with the saving water, but poured upon. In this matter, our diffidence and modesty do not prejudice anyone, so as to prevent each person from thinking what he wishes and doing what he thinks. We, as far as our mediocrity conceives, believe that the divine benefits can in no way be mutilated or weakened, nor can anything less happen there, where what is drawn from the divine gifts is received with the full and entire faith of both the giver and the receiver. For the contagion of sins is not washed away in the saving sacrament as the filth of the skin and body is washed away in a carnal and secular bath, such that soap, nitre, and other aids, as well as a tub and a pool, are needed for the little body to be washed and cleansed. The breast of the believer is washed in one way, the mind of man is cleansed through the merits of faith in another. In the saving sacraments, when necessity compels and God grants His indulgence, divine compendia confer the whole upon believers.

Nor should it disturb anyone that the sick appear to be sprinkled or poured upon when they obtain the Lord’s grace, since the Holy Scripture speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and says: 'And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your filthiness and from all your idols, and I will cleanse you, and I will give you a new heart and a new spirit I will put within you.' Likewise in Numbers: 'And the man who is unclean shall be purified until evening on the third day and on the seventh day, and he shall be clean. But if he is not purified on the third day and on the seventh day, he shall not be clean and that soul shall be cut off from Israel, because the water of sprinkling has not been sprinkled upon him.' And again: 'And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take the Levites from among the children of Israel and you shall purify them. And thus you shall perform their purification for them: you shall sprinkle them with the water of purification.' And again: 'The water of sprinkling is purification.' Whence it appears that the sprinkling of water also obtains the likeness of a saving bath, and when these things are done in the Church, where the faith of both the giver and the receiver is whole, all things stand and are consummated and perfected, and they have obtained the grace of Christ by the saving water and legitimate faith, and cannot be [invalidated] by the majesty of the Lord and the truth of the faith.

Furthermore, as to the fact that some call them not Christians but 'clinics' [bedridden], I do not find whence they assume this name, unless perhaps those who have read more and more secret things in Hippocrates or Soranus have discovered these 'clinics.' For I, who know the 'clinic' from the Gospel, know that for that paralytic and weak man, lying in bed for long periods of his life, his infirmity was no hindrance to his attaining most fully to heavenly strength. And not only was he roused from his pallet by the Lord’s indulgence, but he himself carried his own pallet with restored and invigorated strength. And therefore, as far as it is given to us to conceive and feel by faith, my opinion is this: that anyone who has obtained divine grace in the Church by the law and right of faith should be judged a legitimate Christian. Or if anyone thinks that they have obtained nothing because they have only been poured upon with the saving water, if they are empty and..."

are empty, let them not be deceived, so that if they escape the inconvenience of their illness and recover, they are not to be baptized. But if they cannot be baptized, who have already been sanctified by the ecclesiastical baptism, why are they scandalized in their faith and the indulgence of the Lord? Have they indeed obtained the grace of the Lord, but in a shorter and lesser measure of the divine gift and the Holy Spirit, so that they are indeed held to be Christians, yet are not to be equaled to others? Nay, rather, the Holy Spirit is not given by measure, but is poured out in full upon the believer.” (D. Caecilii Cypriani Opp. repurg. per Des. Erasmum. Basii. 1530. p. 132.)

Quenstedtius: “They object: Luther, T. 1. Jen. f. 186, judges that the German word *taufen* is derived from the word *Tiefe*, i.e., depth, because those who were baptized were deeply immersed in water; so Wolzogenius, Com. ad Matth. 3, 6. T. 1. Op. f. 151. Resp.: Luther, l. c., indeed says, ‘it ought to be so,’ yet he does not deny that baptism performed by sprinkling is legitimate. See T. 2. Isleb. f. 365, where the baptism of infants by the sprinkling of the head alone is approved.” (L. c. q. 5. f. 1123. sq.)

Cf. the following sayings of Luther: “I would that those who are to be baptized were dipped entirely into the water, as the word sounds and the mystery signifies. Not that I consider it necessary, but that it would be beautiful if a thing so entirely perfect were also given a perfect sign. As it is, without doubt, instituted by Christ.” (Von d. babyl. Gef. d. Kirche. 1520. Opp. Hal. XIX, 80.) “The little word ‘baptize’ (*taufen*) brings water with it, for it means to bathe, or to immerse, or to make wet with water.” (Brief an Churf. Joh. Friedrich, a. 1542. Opp. Hal. X, 2615. sq.)

For Scripture determines nothing. In the church, however, both customs flourished in former times; the former indeed to indicate the unity or singularity of the divine essence, which the ancient Christians asserted against the heretics, but the latter to denote the trinity of the divine persons and to confess it against other heretics.

We omit the mention of the heavenly matter in this sacrament, which some add at this point. It is certain, however, that even the older teachers of our church did not make mention of it when they were setting forth the substance or the essential, or (as they say) principal, parts of baptism.

Blessed Luther, in the Smalcald Articles, P. III, art. V, p. 329 of the Book of Concord, writes: Baptism is nothing else than the Word of God with immersion in water, according to His own institution and command, or, as Paul says, the washing in the Word, just as Augustine also says: Let the Word be added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament. Where it is manifest that Luther taught that the whole essence of baptism is completed by (1) water, (2) the act of immersion or washing, (3) the word of institution, in such a way indeed that the water and the action occupied about it obtain the nature of a sacrament through the word of institution being added; which is the same as if he had said that the matter of the sacrament is the element of water together with the act of washing, but the form, which gives being to the thing (the sacrament), is the word of institution.

Latin:

Exempla vero aspersionis, in baptismo adhibitae, ex iis locis adduci solent, ubi quidam intra aedes privatas baptizati leguntur, v. gr. Saulus sive Paulus in domo Judae, Actor. 9, 11. 18., Cornelius centurio cum cognatis et necessariis amicis suis domi suae, cap. X, 24. 27. 44. 48., quos in aquam fuisse demissos, vix satis rationabiliter affirmari, certe non ostendi potest.

Gerhardus: ,,Quaeritur: 3. An immersio vel aspersio debeat esse totalis, 11. e., an totum corpus abluendum? Resp.: Et hoc αδιάΦορον est, cum in verbis institutionis nullum de eo extet praeceptum, cum in actione sacramentali distinguendum sit inter δόσιν καί δόσεως τρόπον, inter λί/ψιν καϊ λήψεως τρόπον, δόσ/.ς και λήψις necessaria SUnt, τρόπος δόσεως καϊ λήψεως arbitrarius; denique cum finis baptismi non sit depositio sordium carnis, ut propterea totum corpus abluendum ac fricandum sit, sed regeneratio et ab omni immunditie peccati purificatio spiritualis. Cyprianus: ,,Quaesisti etiam, frater carissime, quid mihi de illis videatur, qui in infirmitate et languore gratiam Dei consequuntur, an habendi sint legitimi christiani, eo quod aqua salutari non loti sint, sed perfusi. Qua in parte nemini verecundia et modestia nostra praejudicat, quo minus unusquisque, quod voluerit, sentiat et, quod senserit, faciat. Nos, quantum concipit mediocritas nostra, existimamus, in nullo mutilari et debilitari posse beneficia divina, nec minus aliquid illic posse contingere, ubi plena et tota fide et dantis et sumentis accipitur, quod divinis muneribus hauritur. Neque enim sic in sacramento salutari delictorum contagia, ut in lavacro carnali et saeculari sordes cutis et corporis abluuntur, ut et sapone et nitris et ceteris quoque adjumentis et dolio et piscina opus sit, quibus ablui et mundari corpusculum possit. Aliter pectus credentis abluitur, aliter mens hominis per fidei merita mundatur. In sacramentis salutaribus, necessitate cogente et Deo indulgentiam suam largiente, totum credentibus conferunt divina compendia.

Nec quenquam movere debet, quod aspergi vel perfundi videntur aegri, cum gratiam dominicam consequuntur, quando Scriptura sancta per Ezechielen prophetam loquatur et dicat: ,Et aspergam super vos aquam mundam et mundabimini ab omnibus immunditiis vestris et omnibus simulacris vestris, et mundabo vos et dabo vobis cor novum et spiritum novum dabo in vobis.4 Item in Numeris: ,Et homo, qui fuerit immundus, usque ad vesperam hic puriflcabitur die tertio et die septimo, et mundus erit. Si autem non fuerit purificatus die tertio et die septimo, non erit mnndus et exterminabitur anima illa de Israel, quoniam aqua asperginis non est super eum aspersa.4 Et iterum: ,Et locutus est Dominus ad Mosen dicens: Accipe Levitas de medio filiorum Israel et purificabis eos. Et ita facies eis purificationem eorum, circumsperges eos aqua purificationis.4 Et iterum: ,Aqua aspersionis purificatio est.4 Unde apparet, aspersionem quoque aquae instar lavacri salutaris obtinere, et quando haec in ecclesia fiunt, ubi sit et dantis et accipientis fides integra, stare omnia et consummari ac perfici eos, salutari aqua et fide legitima Christi gratiam consecutos, non posse majestate Domini et fidei veritate.

Porro autem quod quidam non Christianos, sed clinicos vocant, non invenio, unde hoc nomen assumant, nisi forte, qui plura et secretiora legerunt apud Hippocratem vel Soranum, clinicos istos deprehenderunt. Ego enim, qui clinicum de evangelio novi, scio, paralytico illi et debili, per longa aetatis curricula in lecto jacenti, nihil infirmitatem suam obfuisse, quo minus ad firmitatem coelestem plenissime perveniret. Nec tantum indulgentia Dominica excitatum de grabato esse, sed ipsum grabatum suum reparatis et vegetatis viribus sustulisse. Et idcirco, quantum fide concipere et sentire nobis datur, mea septentia haec est, ut christianus judicetur legitimus, quisquis fuerit in ecclesia lege et jure fidei divinam gratiam consecutus. Aut si aliquis existimat, eos nihil consecutos, eo quod ab aqua salutari tantum perfusi sint, si inanes et

vacui sunt, non decipiantur, ut, si incommodum languoris evaserint et convaluerint, non baptizentur. Si autem baptizari non possunt, qui jam baptismo ecclesiastico sanctiflcati sunt, cur in fide sua et Domini indulgentia scandalizantur? An consecuti sunt quidem gratiam Domi« nicam, sed breviore et minore mensura muneris divini ac Spiritus Sancti, ut habeantur quidem Christiani, non sint tamen ceteris adaequandi? Quin imo Spiritus Sanctus non de mensura datur, sed super credentem totus infunditur.“ (D. Caecilii Cypriani Opp. repurg. pej Des. Erasmum. Basii. 1530. p. 132.)

Wie es denn ohn Zweifel von Christo gestiftet ist.“ (Von d. babyl. Gef. d. Kirche. 1520. Opp. Hai. XIX, 80.),,Das Wörtlein,taufen‘ bringt mit sich Wasser, denn es heisst baden, oder eintauchen, oder nass machen mit Wasser.“ (Brief an Churf. Joh. Friedrich, a. 1542. Opp. Hai. X, 2615. sq.)

Scriptura enim nihil determinat. In ecclesia autem mos uter· que olim viguit; prior quidem ad unitatem seu singularitatem essentiae divinae, quam adversus haereticos christiani veteres asserebant, indicandam, ,posterior vero ad personarum divinarum trinitatem denotandam et contra haereticos alias confitendam.

Omittimus mentionem materiae coelestis in hoc sacramento, quam aliqui h. 1. addunt. Certum autem est, etiam antiquiores ecclesiae nostrae doctores mentionem ejus non fecisse, cum baptismi substantiam aut partes essentiales, sive principales (ut loquuntur), traderent.

B. Lutherus m Artic. Smalc. P. III. art. V. p. 329. Libri Cone, scribit: Baptismus nihil est aliud, quam verbum Dei cum mersione in aquam, secundum ipsius institutionem et mandatum, sive, ut Paulus inquit, lavacrum in verbo, sicut et Augustinus ait: Accedat verbum ad elementum, et fit sacramentum. Ubi manifestum est, Luther um totam essentiam baptismi docuisse absolvi (1.) aqua, (2.) actu mersionis sive ablutionis, (3.) verbo institutionis, ita quidem, ut aqua et actio, circa illam occupata, rationem sacramenti nanciscantur per verbum institutionis accedens; quod idem est, ac si dixisset, materiam sacramenti esse elementum aquae una cum actu abluendi, formam autem, quae dat esse rei (sacramento), esse verbum institutionis.


### On Baptism: To these respond the things which are held in the Large Catechism, p

To these respond the things which are held in the Large Catechism, p. 587: Being asked what baptism is, answer thus: It is not altogether simple water, but such as is comprehended in and included with the Word and command of God, and is thereby sanctified, so that it is nothing else than God’s or divine water; not that this water is in itself more excellent than any other, but that the Word and command of God have been added to it. Conf. Small Catechism, to the Question: What is baptism? p. 876. In this simplicity also persisted the blessed Erasmus Sarcerius in Exam. ordinand. fol. PART. III. CAP. X.

CCLXI. b., b. Joh. Wigandus in *Syntagm. Corp. Doctr. ex Nov. Test.* P. I. p. 240. and P. II. p. 854., b. Mart. Chemnitius in *LL. P. III. L. de Baptism.* § IV. p. m. 161. a., b. Nicol. Selneccerus in *Exam. Ordin.* § IV. p. 122. 124., b. Tilem. Heshusius in *Examine*, which he composed while engaged in the ecclesiastical visitation under the auspices of John William, Duke of Saxony, etc., and dedicated first to the aforementioned prince, and then to his son John, Duke of Saxony, etc., b. Jacob Andreae in the volume of *Dispp.* (which Jacob Heerbrand edited collectively) *Disp.* XXXI. § 5. p. 452., b. Jac. Heerbrand himself in *Compend. Theol. L. de Baptism.* p. 534., all of whom taught that the substance of baptism is completed by water, treated by the act of washing, and by the word of institution; but that the rationale or essence of the sacrament is conferred upon that action, by which the element of water is treated, through the word of institution itself, and that therefore the former is the material, and the latter the formal part of this sacrament, making no mention of a heavenly matter.

The occasion for the question concerning the heavenly matter of baptism was provided by the Calvinists, especially Beza, who in the Colloquy of Montbéliard asserted that the blood of Christ is required for the substance of baptism as a second, and indeed principal, part; and he accused Jacob Andreae and Lucas Osiander—who in their *Theses on Baptism* (which they had brought forward as being beyond controversy) had placed this in the first position, that baptism consists of water and the word—and repeated even to the point of nausea that those who defined baptism in this way did not do so correctly, since they excluded the blood of Christ, which is a substantial part of baptism. See *Actor. Colloq. Mompelg.* p. 428, 432, 437, 438, 442, 446, 448.

But because Beza simultaneously brought forward a distinction between external and internal baptism, and asserted that the former consists of the element and the word, but that to the latter pertains the thing signified by the element as a sign, and that this is the blood of Christ, just as in the sacrament of the Supper (p. 437, 438), Jacob Andreae therefore impugned that distinction of a twofold baptism above all else, showing from Ephesians 4:5 that there is one baptism. And since he also remembered that he had to prove, especially against Beza, that baptism is not merely a sign, but a washing (an efficacious medium) of regeneration and renewal (as is evident from Thesis IV and V, p. 429), and that regeneration and renewal cannot be attributed to baptism efficiently except dependently upon the Holy Spirit, he therefore immediately adds from John 3 that this one baptism consists of water and the Spirit, and that Christ in that place joins water with the Spirit and attributes regeneration to both—namely, that the Spirit regenerates unto eternal life through water (as he speaks on p. 444), or that the Spirit is the principal efficient cause of regeneration, which He works through water (of baptism) as through an instrument (as his words are on p. 451).

However, on this occasion, when he was removing Beza’s opinion—which asserted that the blood of Christ, following the example of the sacrament of the Supper, should also be referred to the substance of baptism (for which see p. 439, 442, 445, and 450)—and was showing how individual sacraments have their own certain and mutually distinct rationales, and at the same time wished to disti...nguish the effect of baptism, which is regeneration, from the substance of baptism, it happened that he said the substance of baptism consists of water and the Spirit and that these are the substantial parts of baptism (p. 439); yet in such a way that soon after (p. 441), repeating the same thing, that the Holy Spirit is a principal and substantial part of baptism, he notably added the words: "If it is permitted to speak thus," from which (1.) it is manifest that the blessed Doctor did not so much wish to give laws of precision (*ἀκριβείας*) to others here, as he was occupied only with this...

that he had been, in order to teach that the Holy Spirit and the entire most holy Trinity are substantially and ἀδιαστάτως present in baptism, and that they intimately conjoin their own infinite power, as the principal cause, with the water of baptism, as the instrument, to produce one and the same effect of regeneration and renewal by one undivided action; so that this effect ought not to be attributed to the water alone, without the concur rence of the Holy Spirit or the Triune God, nor to God or the Holy Spirit as acting separately outside the sacrament, but to both conjointly. This is indeed the true and orthodox opinion, and it was diametrically opposed to the Calvinian or Bezian opinion concerning a double baptism. Compare pp. 442, 443.

Next (2.), it is to be noted that the blessed Doctor not only did not use the term "celestial matter," but asserted only the "thing of the sacrament"—and indeed the internal thing—as distinct from the external and visible thing, although joined with it in its own way.

It must also be observed (3.) that, since he did not wish to call the blood of Christ a substantial part of baptism, or to say that baptism consists of water and the blood of Christ, he rendered this reason: that in the words of the institution of baptism there is no mention at all of the blood of Christ expressed, but only the mention of the Trinity is made, in whose name one is to be baptized (see p. 450). Meanwhile, he taught that the blood of Christ pertains to baptism insofar as men are regenerated in baptism by its power (p. 444), or insofar as through the water of baptism, by the power of the blood of Christ, the Holy Spirit works that which Christ merited for us by His blood (p. 445), or that the merit of the shed blood of Christ is applied to the baptized man through the aspersion of the baptismal water; without which application, the shedding of the blood of Christ would profit an unbaptized and unregenerate infant nothing for the purging of sins (p. 446).

Finally (4.), since he referred now to the Holy Spirit and now to the entire Most Holy Trinity as the substantials of baptism, he explained himself thus on p. 443: "Concerning individual sacraments," he says, "one must both think and speak just as the Word of God sounds. Nor do we speak an empty word, but it truly contains what it sounds. Now the word of Christ in baptism is: 'Baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.' This word embraces the presence of the three persons of the Holy Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And therefore the work of regeneration in baptism is also the work of the entire Trinity. But because the Father and the Son work regeneration and renewal through the Holy Spirit, Christ therefore attributes this work of regeneration peculiarly to the Holy Spirit when He says: 'Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit.' Wherefore, in baptism, we say the thing of the sacrament is the Holy Spirit, who by the power of the blood of Christ regenerates men unto eternal life."

Whence it is again evident that the "thing of the sacrament" is said by the blessed Jacob Andreae to be that upon which the effect of the sacrament—which is regeneration and renewal—depends as upon a cause; and that, besides the water, the Spirit or the entire Most Holy Trinity is also said to be the thing of the sacrament of baptism, because in baptism, and in order to the effect which is to be produced through baptism, the Most Holy Trinity and the water are conjoined, or (because the work of regeneration is attributed by appropriation to the Holy Spirit) the Holy Spirit and the water are conjoined, as the principal efficient cause with its organ or instrument; just as he adds on p. 444: "But it is one thing for the Holy Spirit and the water, or the Most Holy Trinity and the water, to be conjoined in baptism as subordinate efficient causes—principal and instrumental—working by one, undivided action and pro[ducing]..." Baier's Comp. ed. Walther. III, 29 PART III. CHAP. X.

leading to the same effect; it is another thing to be joined as a double matter from which one complete matter of baptism arises. Certainly, he did not affirm the latter, but the former; and furthermore, regarding that phrase by which he said these things are joined as substantial parts of baptism, the blessed Dr. Andreas guarded himself equally and warned his readers by the added formula: "If one may speak so."

Meanwhile, given this occasion, it happened that others of our own, when they wished to distinguish their doctrine from the opinion of the Calvinists concerning a double baptism, made mention of a heavenly thing, and some even of a heavenly matter, though they entered upon various paths in delivering or explaining it.

When the blessed Aegidius Hunnius, in *L. de Sacram.* Tom. I. Op. fol. 1020, had answered the question: "What, therefore, are the substantial parts of baptism?" by saying: "Two; the former is the word of institution and the annexed promise, the latter is the visible element added to the word," he indeed soon warned that the Holy Spirit also pertains to the substance of baptism, and that not only insofar as baptism is dispensed in the name of the Most Holy Trinity, but also under that specific consideration, insofar as He is the σφραγίς, the pledge and earnest of the covenant between God and the men who are baptized, *l. c.* fol. 1023.

However, it is evident that the blessed Hunnius did not teach on that account that the Holy Spirit is, properly speaking, a substantial—and indeed material—part of baptism.

For not only does nothing appear in the aforementioned places to this effect, but it also militates against it that, on fol. 1023 and 1024, when he is about to explain the sense in which it should be understood that he asserted the Holy Spirit pertains to the substance of baptism, he teaches that one must first look to the formula of Matthew 28, and then that baptism imports a covenant of God with the man who is baptized; and that the covenant of God always has an earnest annexed to it; and that this in baptism is the Holy Spirit, namely, substantially present in baptism, inasmuch as He establishes a pact of eternal favor toward the baptized man, of which he who believes immediately becomes a participant; but the hypocrite, who does not perceive the fruit at present, may nevertheless perceive it whenever he returns through faith and repentance.

Latin:

Quibus respondent, quae in Catechismo majore p. 587. habentur: Interrogatus, quid baptismus sit t ita responde: Non esse prorsus aquam simplicem, sed ejusmodi, quae verbo et praecepto Dei comprehensa et illi inclusa sit, et per hoc sanctificata, ita ut nihil aliud sit, quam Dei seu divina aqua; non quod aqua haec per sese quavis alia sit praestantior, sed quod ei verbum ac praeceptum Dei accesserit. Conf. Catech. min. ad Quaest. Quid est baptismus t p. 876. In hac quoque simplicitate perstiterunt b. Erasmus Sarcerius in Exam. ordinand. fol. PART. III. CAP. X.

CCLXI. b., b. Joh. Wigandus in Syntagm. Corp. Doctr. ex Nov. Test. P. I. p. 240. et P. II. p. 854., b. Mart. Chemnitius in LL. P. III. L. de Baptism. § IV. p. m. 161. a., b. Nicol. Selneccerus in Exam. Ordin. §. IV. p. 122. 124., b. Tilem. Heshusius in Examine, quod, cum visitationi ecclesiasticae, auspiciis Johannis Wilhelmi, Ducis Saxoniae etc., intentus esset, concinnavit et laudato principi primum, deinde filio Johanni, Duc. Sax. etc., dedicavit, b. Jacob. Andreae in volum. Dispp. (quas Jacob. Heerbrandus junctim edidit) Disp. XXXI. § 5. p. 452., b. Jac. Heerbrandus ipse in Compend. Theoi. L. de Baptism. p. 534., qui omnes substantiam baptismi aqua, actu ablutionis tractata, et verbo institutionis absolvi, actioni autem illi, qua elementum aquae tractatur, rationem aut esse sacramenti per ipsum verbum institutionis conferri adeoque illud materiale, hoc formale hujus sacramenti esse docuerunt, mentionem materiae coelestis nullam facientes.

Occasionem autem quaestioni de materia coelesti baptismi praebuerunt Calviniani, praesertim Beza, qui in Colloquio Mompelg. sanguinem Christi ad baptismi substantiam, tanquam partem alteram, eamque principalem, requiri statuit et Jacobum Andreae ac Lucam Osiandrum, qui in Thesibus de Baptismo (quas tanquam extra controversiam positas attulerant) primo loco hanc collocaverunt, baptismum aqua et verbo constare, accusavit et ad nauseam usque repetiit, quod baptismum haud recte definiverint, quippe excludentes sanguinem Christi, qui substantialis pars baptismi sit. Vid. Actor. Colloq. Mompelg. p. 428. 432. 437. 438. 442. 446. 448.

Quia vero Beza simul attulit distinctionem inter baptismum externum et internum, et illum quidem constare elemento et verbo, ad hunc autem pertinere rdm elemento tanquam signo significatam, et hanc quidem esse sanguinem Christi aeque atque in sacramento coemie asseruit p. 437. 438., ideo Jacobus Andreae ante omnia distinctionem illam duplicis baptismi impugnavit, unum baptismum esse ostendens ex Ephes. 4, 5. Et cum simul meminisset, sibi praecipue contra Bezam evincendum esse, quod baptismus non sit signum duntaxat, sed lavacrum (medium efficax) regenerationis et renovationis (ut constat ex thesi IV. et V. p. 429.), regenerationem autem ac renovationem baptismo efficienter tribui non posse, nisi dependenter a Spiritu Sancto, propterea ex Joh. 8. mox addit, unum hunc baptismum aqua et Spiritu constare et Christum 1. c. conjungere cum Spiritu aquam, et utrique regenerationem tribuere, quod videlicet Spiritus per aquam ad vitam aeternam regenerat (ut loquitur p. 444.), aut quod Spiritus sit causa efficiens regenerationis principalis, quam per aquam (baptismi) tanquam per instrumentum operetur (prout ee habent verba ejus p. 451.).

Hac autem occasione, cum removeret sententiam Bezae, statuentis, sanguinem, Christi, juxta exemplum sacramenti coenae, etiam ad baptismi substantiam referendum esse (quam in rem vid. p. 439. 442. 445. et 450.), et monstraret, quomodo singula sacramenta suas certas et a se invicem distinctas rationes habeant, simul autem effectum baptismi, qui est regeneratio, a substantia baptismi distinguere vellet, accidit, ut substantiam baptismi aqua et Spiritu constare et haec esse substantialia baptismi diceret (p. 439.), ita tamen, ut mox (p. 441.), idem repetens, quod Spiritus S. sit principalis et substantialis pars baptismi, notanter adderet verba: Si ita loqui licet, unde (1.) manifestum est, b. Doctorem non tam leges άχριβυλυγίας hic dare aliis voluisse, quam in eo solum occu-

patum fuisse, ut doceret, Spiritum Sanctum totamque sacrosanctam Trinitatem in baptismo esse substantialiter et άδίαστάτως praesentem ac suam, velut causae principalis, virtutem infinitam, cum aqua baptismatis, velut organo, intime conjungere ad unum eundemque effectum regenerationis ac renovationis, una indivisa actione producendum, ita ut effectus hic nec soli aquae, sine concursu Spiritus Sancti, aut Dei trinunius, neque Deo aut Spiritui Sancto, velut extra sacramentum separatim agenti, sed utrique conjunctim, tribui debeat; quae sane vera et orthodoxa sententia Calvinianae autem aut Bezianae sententiae de duplici baptismo e diametro opposita fuit. Confer, p. 442. 443.

Deinde (2.) notandum est, b. Docto rem non solum termino materiae coelestis non fuisse usum, sed tantum rem sacramenti, et quidem internam, ab externa et visibili distinctam, licet cum ea suo modo conjunctam, asseruisse.

Observandum quoque (3.) quod, cum sanguinem Christi nollet dicere partem substantialem baptismi, aut, baptismum constare aqua et sanguine Christi, rationem reddiderit hanc, quod in verbis institutionis baptismi nulla prorsus mentio sanguinis Christi expressa, sed solius Trinitatis mentio jacta sit, in cujus nomine sit baptizandum, vid. p. 450., interim sanguinem Christi ad baptismuqi spectare docuerit, quatenus virtute ejus homines in baptismo regenerantur, p. 444., seu quatenus per aquam baptismi, virtute sanguinis Christi, Spiritus Sanctus id operatur, quod nobis Christus suo sanguine meruit, p. 445., aut quod meritum effusi sanguinis Christi homini baptizato per aspersionem aquae baptismi applicetur, sine qua applicatione facta effusio sanguinis Christi infanti non baptizato et non regenerato ad purgationem a peccatis nihil prodesset, p. 446.

Denique (4.) quod, cum nunc Spiritum Sanctum, nunc totam SS. Trinitatem ad substantialia baptismi referret, ita se explicaverit p. 443.: De singulis sacramentis, inquiens, et sentiendum et loquendum est, sicuti verbum Dei sonat. Neque inane verbum dicimus, sed continet hoc vere, quod sonat. Est autem verbum Christi in baptismo: Baptizate eos in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti. Hoc verbum praesentiam trium personarum Sanctae Trinitatis complectitur, Patris, Filii et Spiritus Sancti. Ideoque etiam opus regenerationis in baptismo opus totius Trinitatis est. Quia vero Pater et Filius per Spiritum Sanctum regenerationem et renovationem operantur, ideoque Christus regenerationis hoc opus peculiariter Spiritui Sancto tribuit, cum inquit: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu. Quapropter in baptismo rem sacramenti dicimus Spiritum Sanctum esse, qui virtute sanguinis Christi homines ad vitam aeternam regener at.

Unde rursus constat, rem sacramenti a b. Jac. Andreae dici, a qua effectus sacramenti, qui est regeneratio ac renovatio, pendet, tanquam a causa, et dici, praeter aquam, etiam Spiritum aut totam SS. Trinitatem esse rem sacramenti baptismi, quia in baptismo et in ordine ad effectum, qui per baptismum producendus sit, conjunguntur SS. Trinitas et aqua, aut (quia opus regenerationis per appropriationem tribuitur Spiritui Sancto) Spiritus Sanctus et aqua, tanquam causa efficiens principalis cum suo organo aut instrumento; quemodmodum addit p. 444. Aliud autem est, Spiritum S. et aquam, aut S. Trinitatem et aquam conjungi in baptismo, ut causas efficientes subordinatas, principalem et instrumentalem, una, indivisa actione operantes et proBaieri Comp. ed. Walther. III,29 PART. III. CAP. X.

ducentes eundem effectum; aliud est, conjungi, ut duplicem materiam, ex qua oriatur una completa materia baptismi. Certe non hoc, sed illud affirmavit ac de caetero, quoad istam phrasin, qua dixit conjungi ista ut partes substantiales baptismi, per adjectam formulam: Si ita loqui licet, sibi pariter cavit et lectores monuit b. D. Andreae.

Interim data isthac occasione factum est, ut alii nostratium, cum doctrinam suam a Calvinianorum sententia de duplici baptismo distinguere vellent, rei coelestis, aliqui etiam materiae coelestis mentionem facerent, in ea vero tradenda seu explicanda vias varias inirent.

B. Aegid. Hunnius cum in L. de Sacram. Tom. I. Op. fol. 1020. ad quaestionem: Quae sunt ergo baptismi partes substantiales f respondisset: Duae; prior est verbum institutionis annexaeque promissionis, posterior est visibile elementum verbo additum, mox equidem monuit, Spiritum S. pertinere etiam ad substantiam baptismi, et quidem non tantum, quatenus in nomine SS. Trinitatis baptismus dispensatur, verum etiam sub illa pecidiari ratione, quatenus est σφραγϊς, pignus et arrha foederis inter Deum et hornines, qui baptizantur, 1. c. fol. 1023.

Patet autem, b. Hunnium non ideo docuisse, quod Spiritus S. sit proprie loquendo pars substantialis, et quidem materialis^ baptismi.

Non solum enim 11. cc. nihil in hanc rem apparet, verum etiam contra militat, quod fol. 1023. et 1024. explicaturus sensum, quo intelligendum sit, quod asseruit, Spiritum S. pertinere ad substantiam baptismi, docet, spectandam primum esse formulam, Matth. 28., deinde, quod baptismus importet foedus Dei cum homine, qui baptizatur; foedus Dei autem semper habere arrham adjunctam; et hanc in baptismo esse Spiritum Sanctum, nempe in baptismo substantialiter praesentem, quippe pactum aeterni favoris ad hominem baptizatum statuat, cujus statim particeps fiat, qui credit; hypocrita autem, qui in praesenti non percipit fructum, possit tamen percipere, quandocunque per fidem et poenitentiam redierit.


### On Baptism: Therefore, it is said to pertain to the substance of baptism because, even if…

Therefore, it is said to pertain to the substance of baptism because, even if the fruit does not actually accrue, yet when baptism is administered, it truly has a place at the same time, as that upon which the fruit of baptism depends.

Furthermore, others, while indeed employing the term of an invisible matter distinct from the visible, said that by that name the Word is to be understood, containing the command, Matt. last, verse 19, and the promise, Mark 16:16: thus the blessed Ambrosius Reudenius, *P. V. Catech.* cap. VI. p. 283, and the blessed P. Piscator in the XX Disputations, in which he embraces the Theological Commonplaces, Disp. XIV. § 31, 32.

But these did not on that account judge that either the blood of Christ, or the Holy Spirit, or the Most Holy Trinity should be called the heavenly matter of baptism, as is evident from the cited places and will soon be more fully evident when we have indicated what the opinion of the blessed Johannes Himmelius was, who at the same time appeals to the blessed P. Piscator.

Meanwhile, in the Academy of Wittenberg, on April 30, 1596, the blessed David Rungius, having held a special Disputation on Baptism, thes. 4, 6, 32, 37, etc., when about to deliver the constituent parts of this sacrament, the matter and form of baptism, says that the former is the visible and external element, namely water, but the latter, or form, is the word of institution.

And he subsists in this ancient simplicity, making no mention of a heavenly matter.

But this disputation also appeared a second time, inserted into the eight disputations of the blessed Rungius, published together in the year 1606, p. 170, etc.

It is also worth joining the blessed Matthias Hafenreffer from the Academy of Tübingen, who in *LL. Theol.* Lib. III. Stat. III. L. VII. p. 492, [discusses] the substantials

He] who delivers the baptism, mentions only the element and the word, and refers the word of institution to the form of baptism (p. 493), but is entirely silent regarding the heavenly matter.

Furthermore, others indeed, having progressed a little further, not only conceded but argued that the very blood of Christ is the heavenly matter of baptism. Regarding this matter, one may especially look at the blessed Leonhard Hutter, who, in his *Locis*, when he had arrived at the question concerning the other essential part of baptism—which is the heavenly and invisible thing—reviewed four opinions. He openly attacked the first, by which the word is substituted in the place of the heavenly thing (reasoning that the word is not a constitutive principle or a substantial part, but only an efficient principle of baptism). However, he proposed the remaining ones, in which the substantial heavenly part is said to be the Holy Spirit or the blood of Christ, or both together, in such a way that he left it free for each to follow whichever of those three he might wish, though he himself not obscurely established that the blood of Christ, either alone or together with the Holy Spirit, is the heavenly matter of baptism; see *l. c.*, pp. 580, 636, 637.

Notwithstanding these things, the blessed Johann Foerster, in the same academy, when he had descended to the doctrine concerning the substantial parts of baptism in his *Thesaurus Catecheticus*, Chapter on Baptism, Decade II, Problem VIII, § 9, writes in § 31: "The constitutive or essential parts of baptism are expressly designated in Scripture: the element and the word."

And that this is indeed the case, and is to be desired; but whether, just as the sacrament of the Eucharist consists of a thing not simple but double: 1. terrestrial and visible, 2. heavenly and invisible, so also in baptism that same thing occurs, and besides the terrestrial and visible thing, some heavenly thing—for example, the blood of Christ or the Holy Spirit—united sacramentally to the water (just as the body of Christ to the bread and his blood to the wine) enters into and completes the constitution of the material causes—he says that this question so intrudes itself that it converts ease into difficulty, that is, it renders a matter otherwise easy to explain intricate and perplexed; see § 34 *et sqq.*

Specifically, in Problem VIII, intending to propose the Lutheran opinion concerning the blood of Christ in baptism, he says in § 41 that it is nowhere openly and explicitly taught in the Holy Scriptures that the blood of Christ constitutes a substantial and heavenly part *materially* in the sacrament of initiation, and he continues in § 42: "Indeed, no mention at all is made of it in the words of the institution of baptism, from which alone one must judge concerning its substance, as is the case in the words of the institution of the Supper."

And § 43: "And yet we are bound to hold the pattern of sound words, and to turn away with our whole mind from those things which differ from this. 2 Tim. 1:13." (§ 44.)

To which these truly golden words of Chrysostom in Homily 49 on Matthew agree: "Christians wishing to receive the firmness of faith ought to flee to no other thing than Scripture." Likewise in the Homily on the Progress of the Gospel: "Whatever is decreed against Scripture is error." (§ 45.) Nor do such opinions occur anywhere in the writings of the blessed Luther or the ancient fathers, by which the blood of Christ is touted as a *material* part of baptism.

Similarly, in Problem IX, "Is the Holy Spirit a substantial part of baptism?" Foerster answers in Thesis LXIII: "The Holy Spirit pertains to the substance of baptism, not indeed properly as a *material* heavenly part, united to the water by a sacramental union..." (

And § 49:) "For what that part or heavenly thing of baptism is, is not explicitly defined in Holy Scripture. And therefore we prefer to confess a cautious ignorance than to profess a false knowledge, as Augustine admonishes in Epistle 78." (§ 65.) "

But in another way, and that a double one: one common, the other singular." (§ 66.) "And indeed in a common way, insofar as baptism is in the sacred name..." PART III. CHAPTER X.

is dispensed among the persons of the Holy Trinity, the third of whom is the Holy Spirit, and those who are baptized, a covenant is ratified, which on the part of the most holy Trinity always remains ἀμεταμέλητον and ἀμετακίνητον, Rom. 11:29; 2 Tim. 2:13. Luther, Vol. IV, Jena, German, fol. 284. (§ 67.)

But in a special way, as a σφραγίς, pledge, and earnest of the υιοθεσίας, which the covenant in every baptism always has conjoined and retains as to presence, even if it is not presently perceived as to fruit and efficacy by those who are baptized as hypocrites.

Thus the blessed Foerster: whence it is evident that he believed that the Holy Spirit and the entire most holy Trinity could be present in baptism in these respects and pertain to the substance of baptism, even if it is not properly a substantial, ὕλικη, or material heavenly part.

Indeed, he rather teaches at the same time that those things which we have seen from the blessed Hunnius (to which these statements of Foerster entirely correspond) are to be understood in such a way that the opinion by which the Holy Spirit or the most holy Trinity is posited as the heavenly matter of baptism is not proven thereby.

He himself, however, as we have seen, acquiesces in the two συστατιχοῖς or essential parts of baptism expressly designated in Scripture: the element and the word.

In a similar manner, the blessed Zacharias Schilterus treated the matter at the University of Leipzig. For he argues with several points against that opinion which posits that the blood of Christ pertains to the substance of baptism as the matter from which it is made.

As far as the Holy Spirit is concerned, he indeed refers Him to the substance of baptism, but in that sense which we have seen also handed down by Foerster. He does not say that He is heavenly matter, although he calls the word by this name.

It is to be noted, however, that he asserts that the matter from which it is made fully agrees with the substantial parts. But since it is otherwise certain that the substantial parts are matter and form (not matter only, even if perhaps a double one) and that the whole, which is called essential, or composed of matter and form, consists of matter and form as its parts, of which he grants that the former is common and the latter is proper and determined, it is now easily evident that the word in Schilterus is called matter, that is, the other essential part, which others have called form or the formal; whence an argument cannot be sought from Schilterus for heavenly matter, taken in the sense in which Foerster and others deny it.

See the blessed Schilterus, *Exet. Catech. Thes. de Baptism.*, pp. 440, 446, 485 ff., and the *Dispp.* of the same and the blessed Burch. Harbarti, edited together, p. 464 ff.

And with these things observed, one can understand what the blessed A. Reudenius and the blessed P. Piscator (in the cited places) handed down concerning invisible matter, especially if we listen to the blessed Joh. Himmel, who, when he himself in *Disp. XXII. Syntagm. Theol.*, p. 220 and § 47, had distinguished the matter of baptism into visible and invisible, and had taught that the former is the element of water and the latter the word of God, in § 48 and 51, soon added in § 52: "Therefore, it is certain that water and the word, as the συστατιχάς xai ουσιώδεις parts of this sacrament, are so joined by sacramental union that without water the word, and vice versa, does not at all obtain the nature of baptism, nor deserve that name; b ut water and the word, joined together by an ένώσει and sacramental union, complete and constitute the το είναι or the ύλιχάς αίτιας of baptism."

Certainly, baptism has its το είναι or its being through its form or formal, joined to the matter or material, and matter, although it is an ουσιώδης or essential part, does not, even if it is perhaps double, complete the ύλιχάς αίτιας without the form, but only with the form.

Therefore, here too, there is no reason why you should seek heavenly matter in Himmel, speaking properly and in the sense in which others of our party heavenly matter äs

they wish to sow. But it is especially to be observed that Himmelius, § 32, proceeds thus: There are those who posit as a συστατικόν [constitutive] and essential or material part of baptism either the whole Most Holy Trinity from that passage in Matthew 28:19, or the Holy Spirit from that in John 3:5, or the blood of Christ from that in 1 John 1:7; but we doubt whether the opinion of either of these can be solidly proven from the institution (from which every sacrament is to be judged) of baptism aptism (whence one must judge concerning any sacrament). See the Disputation on Baptism publicly held here in the year 1616 by D. Pet. Piscator, of blessed memory, theses 131, 132. Gerhard, § 82, 88.

Itaque ad substantiam baptismi pertinere dicitur, quod, si maxime fructus actu non accedat, tamen cum baptismus administratur, revera simul locum habet, tanquam illud, a quo pendet fructus baptismi.

Alii porro, terminum quidem materiae invisibilis a visibili distinctae adhibentes, eo nomine verbum intelligendum dixerunt, continens mandatum, Matth. ult. vers. 19., et promissionem, Mare. 16, 16.: ita b. Ambr. Reudenius P. V. Catech. cap. VI. p. 283. et b. P. Piscator in XX. Dispp., quibus LL. CC. Theologicos complectitur, Disp. XIV. § 31. 32.

Sed hi non ideo vel sanguinem Christi, vel Spiritum S. vel SS. Trinitatem materiam coelestem baptismi dicendam judicarunt, uti constat ex locis cit. et mox plenius constabit, ubi, quae b. Joh. Himmelii sententia fuerit, provocantis simul ad b. P. Piscatorem, indicaverimus.

Interim in Academia Witteb. A. 1596. d. 30. April, b. David Rungius, habita peculiari Disp. deBapt. thes. 4. 6. 32. 37. sqq., partes hujus sacramenti constituentes, materiam et formam baptismi, traditurus, illam quidem dicit esse elementum visibile et externum, nempe aquam, hanc vero, seu. formam, esse verbum institutionis.

Atque in hac antiqua simplicitate subsistit, nullam materiae coelestis faciens mentionem.

Sed haec disputatio etiam altera vice prodiit, inserta disputationibus octo b. Bungii, junctim editis Anno 1606. p. 170. sqq.

Jungi quoque meretur ex acad. Tubingensi b. Matthias Hafenrefferus, qui in LL. Theol. Lib. III. Stat. III. L. VII. p. 492., substantialia

baptismi tradens, elementum et verbum tantum memorat et verbum institutionis ad formam baptismi refert p. 493., de materia coelesti prorsus silet.

Caeterum alii quidem, paulo longius progressi, ipsum quoque sanguinem Christi materiam coelestem baptismi esse non concesserunt solum, sed propugnaverunt, quam in rem praecipue videri potest b. Leonh. Hutterus, qui in LL. suis, cum ad quaestionem de parte altera essentiali baptismi, quae sit res coelestis ac invisibilis, delatus esset, quatuor sententias recensuit ac primam quidem, qua loco rei coelestis substituitur verbum, aperte impugnavit (ratus, verbum non esse principium συσταπχόν, aut partem substantialem, sed tantum principium, ποιητικόν baptismi), reliquas vero, quibus pars substantialis coelestis dicitur esse Spiritus S. vel sanguis Christi, vel ambo simul, ita proposuit, ut liberum relinqueret, quam quisque ex tribus illis sequi velit, ipse tamen sangitinem Christi, vel solum, vel una cum Spiritu S. materiam coelestem baptismi esse, non obscure statuens; vid. 1. c. p. 580. 636. 637.

His autem non obstantibus, b. Joh. Foersterus, in eadem academia, cum in Thesauro Catechetico, Cap. de Bapt. Decade II. Problem. VIII. § 9. ad doctrinam de partibus substantialibus baptismi descendisset, § 31. scribit: Partes συστατικά) vel essentiales baptismi duae in Scriptura expresse designantur: elementum et verbum.

Atque hoc quidem in vado et ex voto se habere; an autem, quemadmodum eucharistiae sacramentum re non simplici, sed duplici constat: 1. terrestri et visibili, 2. coelesti et invisibili, ita etiam in baptismo illud occurrat ac praeter rem terrestrem et visibilem res aliqua coelestis, v. g. sanguis Christi, aut Spiritus Sanctus, aquae sacramentaliter unita (sicut corpus Christi pani et sanguis ejus vino) σΰστασιν υλικών αιτιών ingrediatur et absolvat, hanc quaestionem ita se ingerere, ait, ut ευπορίαν in απορίαν convertat, id est, rem alioqui facilem expeditu intricatam et perplexam reddat; vid. § 34. et sqq.

Speciatim problemate VIII. Lutheranorum sententiam de sanguine Christi in baptismo propositurus, § 41. dicit, nullibi sacris in literis aperte et diserte tradi, quod sanguis Christi partem substantialem eamque coelestem ΰλικώς in sacramento initiationis constituat, et pergit § 42.: Imo nulla plane ejus, in verbis institutionis baptismi, e quibus solis de substantia ejus judicandum, fit mentio, sicut in verbis institutionis coenae,

et §43.': Atqui nos tenemur omnes εχειν ύποτύπωσιν ύγιαινόντων λόγων, ea vero, quae ab hac discrepant, tota mente aversari. 2 Tim. 1, 13. (§ 44.)

Lutheri aut antiquorum patrum uspiam tales occurrunt sententiae, quibus sanguis Christi pro parte baptismi υλική (materiali) venditetur.

Et § 49.) Quae enim pars illa vel res coelestis baptismi, in sacra Scrip. tura non diserte definitum est. Ideoque malumus cautam ignorantiam, confiteri, quam falsam scientiam profiteri, monitore Augustino, Ep. 78.. (§ 65.)

Verum alia ratione eaque duplici, una communi, singulari altera. (§ 66.). Et communi quidem ratione, quatenus baptismus in nomine sacroPART. III. CAP. X.

sanctae Trinitatis dispensatur inter que hujus personas, quarum tertia Epiritus Sanctus, et eos, qui baptizantur, foeaus sancitur, quod ex sacrosanctae Trinitatis parte semper manet άμεταμέλητον et άμεταχίνητον, Rom. 11, 29. 2 Tim. 2, 13. Lutherus Tom. IV. Jen. Germ. fol. 284. (§ 67.)

Speciali autem ratione, ut σψραγ\ς, pignus et arrha, υιοθεσίας, quam foedus in omni baptismo semper adjunctam habet et retinet quoad praesentiam, licet ab illis, qui hypocritae baptizantur, in praesenti non percipiatur quoad fructum et efficaciam.

Haec b. Foersterus: unde patet, credidisse eum, posse Spiritum S. totamque SS. Trinitatem in baptismo quoad istas rationes praesentem esse et pertinere ad substantiam baptismi, etsi non sit proprie pars substantialis ύλιχη, aut materialis coelestis.

Imo potius ille simul docet, ea, quae ex b. Hunnio vidimus (quibus ista Foersteri omnino respondent), sic intelligenda esse, ut non inde probetur sententia ista, qua Spiritus S. aut SS. Trinitas materia coelestis baptismi ·statuatur.

Acquiescit autem ipse, ut vidimus, in partibus συστατιχοϊς aut essentialibus baptismi duabus in Scriptura expresse designatis, elemento et verbo.

Simili ratione in academia Lipsiensi rem tractavit b. Zacharias Schilterus. Nam adversus eam sententiam, quae statuit, sanguinem Christi ad substantiam baptismi, tanquam materiam ex qua, pertinere, aliquot argumentis disputat.

Ad Spiritum Sanctum quod attinet, eum equidem ad substantiam baptismi refert, verum ea ratione, quam a Foerstero quoque tradi vidimus. Materiam coelestem esse, non dicit, licet verbum hoc nomine appellet.

Notandum autem est, quod materiam ex qua cum partibus substantialibus plane congruere perhibet. Sed cum alias certum sit, partes substantiales esse materiam et formam (non materiam tantum, utut forte duplicem) et ex materia et. forma, velut partibus, constare totum, quod vocatur essentiale, seu compositum ex materia et forma, quarum illa esse commune, haec esse proprium ac determinatum largitur, jam facile constat, verbum apud Schilterum dici materiam, id est, partem essentialem alteram, quam alii formam, seu formale appella verint; unde pro materia coelesti, eo sensu accepta, quo Foersterus et alii eam negant, argumentum ex Echiltero peti non poterit.

Atque his observatis, intelligi possunt, quae b. A. Reudenius et b. P. Piscator 11. cc. de materia invisibili tradiderunt, praesertim si audiamus b. Joh. Himmelium, qui cum et ipse Disp. XXII. Syntagm. Sane baptismus habet το είναι sive esse suum per suam formam aut formale, materiae,seu materiali conjunctum, et materia, licet sit pars ουσιώδης seu essentialis, non tamen ea, licet fortasse duplex, sed sine forma, absolvit τάς ύλιχάς αίτιας, sed cum forma demum.

Itaque et hic non est, cur materiam coelestem apud Himmelium quaeras proprie loquendo et eo sensu, quo alii nostratium materiam coelestem äs

serere volunt. Inprimis vero observandum, quod Himmelius § 32. ita pergit: Sunt, qui partem συστατιχψ ac essentialem seu materialem baptismi statuunt vel totam SS. Trinitatem ex illo Matth. 28, 19. vel Spiritum S. ex illo Joh. 3, 5. vel sanguinem Christi ex illo 1 Joh. 1, 7., sed utrum horum sententia ex institutione (unde de quolibet sacramento judicandum) baptismi solide pro· bari possit, subdubitamus. Vide Disp, de Baptism. publice hic anno 1616. D. Pet. Piscatore p. m. habitam thes. 131. 132. Gerhard. § 82. 88.


### On Baptism: Therefore, the blessed Himmelius believed that the word of institution pertains…

Therefore, the blessed Himmelius believed that the word of institution pertains to the τά ουσιώδη [essentials] and συστατικά [constitutive elements] or essentials of baptism in such a way, however, that neither the Most Holy Trinity, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the blood of Christ is for that reason an essential or material part of baptism, even though mention is made of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the word of institution; namely, because the word of institution is not, in the nominative case, the Most Holy Trinity itself, or the Holy Spirit, or the blood of Christ; and he affirmed that P. Piscator and Joh. Gerhard also agreed with him in this.

And certainly, concerning the blessed Joh. Gerhard, to speak more distinctly, it is certain that in his *Aphor. Theol. de baptismo*, although he taught that the efficacious presence of the whole Most Holy Trinity in baptism is to be gathered from the words of institution, and that Christ, the θεάνθρωπος [God-man], is present with His blood and cleanses man, he nevertheless did not employ the designation of "heavenly matter." Similarly, when in his *Harmonia Hist. Evang. de Resurr. Christi*, chap. XII, p. 461 sqq., he dealt at greater length concerning the institution of baptism, he did not teach that the word of institution or the most holy Trinity is the other material part of baptism.

However, in his *Locis*, Vol. IV, *L. de S. Bapt.*, § 70, he considers the matter and the external element in baptism to be the same, as is evident from the marginal lemma.

Although in that chapter, which he entitled "On the matter of baptism," he deals in section I with the earthly thing and in section II with the heavenly thing of baptism, yet, when he treats of the heavenly thing, he abstains from the designation of "matter" and only teaches the conjunction of the heavenly thing with the earthly thing, or matter; but he says in § 80 that this heavenly thing is the Word of God, and indeed the word of divine ordination concerning the administering of baptism in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Whence he further infers in § 83 that the whole Most Holy Trinity is present in baptism by His grace, and in § 84 that the Holy Spirit acts effectively in, with, and through the water, indeed in such a way, according to § 85, that in every baptism administered according to the institution of Christ, the Holy Spirit is present: 1. by reason of essence, as are also the remaining persons of the Trinity; 2. as regards the offering of saving efficacy and the benefits of Christ; 3. as regards the sealing of the covenant initiated between God and the baptized, ratified at any time on the part of God; specifically, and besides these, in the baptism of believers, He concurs by reason of saving efficacy in actual regeneration and renewal, and likewise by reason of the actual and reciprocal obligation of the covenant initiated between God and the baptized; but in the baptism of hypocrites, He concurs not only as regards the obligation (offering) of benefits and the sealing of the covenant on the part of God, but also as regards the judgment which the Holy Spirit exercises through baptism upon the unbelieving.

And in this sense he finally concludes in § 81: Although the most holy Trinity is the efficient and ordaining cause of this sacrament, nothing prevents us from saying that the name of the most holy Trinity is the other substantial part, since the word of institution and promise testifies that God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, with all the benefits of grace, are present in baptism.

But that Gerhard established that the Holy Spirit or the whole Most Holy Trinity is present in baptism through a peculiar approximation of His essence to PART III. CHAP. X.

that the substance of water, or what is properly speaking the heavenly matter of baptism, is such that by virtue of the sacramental union between water and the Holy Spirit it can be said that those who are baptized are, properly speaking, sprinkled not only with water but also with the Holy Spirit (just as in the Holy Supper, by virtue of the sacramental union between the earthly and heavenly matter, it comes to pass that all communicants, together with the blessed bread and wine, eat and drink the body and blood of Christ, not metaphorically but properly speaking and orally, albeit not in a natural way), we certainly cannot gather from the words of the blessed Doctor.

Indeed, as far as the blood of Christ is concerned, although Gerhard (l.c. § 86) maintains that it is not to be excluded from baptism, since it is present 1. by reason of substance, insofar as Christ as θεάνθρωπος is present in His entirety; 2. by reason of merit, because the fruit of baptism proceeds from it; 3. by reason of efficacy, or the efficacious application of merit (partaken of by the blood of Christ) conferred through faith in baptism; 4. because we are baptized into the death of Christ; nevertheless, in § 87 he openly approves the opinion of those most serious theologians who maintain that the blood of Christ cannot be quite conveniently called the other material part of baptism, and he acquiesces in the reasons they adduce.

For this reason also, when it is acknowledged (1.) that the word of institution pertains to the substance of baptism in addition to the water, and (2.) it is further recognized by the power of this word that the Holy Spirit and the entire Holy Trinity is the author of this sacrament as a means of grace; when (3.) it is acknowledged that the Holy Spirit and the Triune God, wherever and as often as baptism is rightly administered, are present by their immense essence and likewise (4.) by their grace in such a way that they not only seriously offer spiritual benefits present through this sacrament and (5.) enter into a covenant of grace with the baptized person, never to be retracted on their part, and seal it through baptism, but also (6.) in the person who is baptized and does not resist divine grace, perform the work of regeneration or renewal through this sacrament in the very act, so that (7.) not separately and by a peculiar action, but conjointly with the water of baptism and through it in one and an undivided action, they kindle or confirm faith, and that (8.) on account of the merit of Christ the θεάνθρωπος, who is really present according to both natures, and His blood shed for our sins: for just as (9.) when faith is conferred through baptism, the blood of Christ is sprinkled in this very sense, insofar as His merit is applied through faith: when these things, I say, are acknowledged and taught, it will be permissible for the rest, regarding the name of heavenly matter and its scarcely explicable nature, to be silent with the older doctors or, with the blessed Foerster, to distinguish between εὐπορία and ἀπορία and to confess a cautious ignorance rather than to profess a false knowledge.

L.c. § 34 and 64. It also happens conveniently that the blessed Scherzer, in *Brev. Hülsemann. auct.* cap. X. thes. XII. p. 588, left it noted: The term heavenly matter is here taken not in the ἀκρίβεια of philosophers, but in a certain latitude for a heavenly th ing.

For strictly speaking, he says, neither the Holy Spirit, nor the word, nor the most holy Trinity can be or be called a material cause. Therefore, by matter we understand the thing itself. For since these things are so, there is no reason why those who have taught the heavenly thing entirely and long ago should be accused of error, but had no cause to call it matter.

We add nothing more here. For it is not our intention to dispute, but to propose what pertains to positive theology.

And just as elsewhere in these matters that are asserted, so here, where that which is asserted is omitted

while it seemed that it could be, we wished to show the consensus of our own people in a few words, which, however, contrary to expectation, have grown into many pages.

Scherzerus: The question is asked concerning the heavenly matter of baptism, whether it exists and what it is? That it is given together with the earthly is evident from the words of Christ, which express both through the little word ἐξ: "Unless one is born of water and (of)… the Spirit," John 1. c. Just as, therefore, the word "of" (ἐξ) in relation to water denotes the matter or the earthly thing, so also the same particle ἐξ (unless you violently invent a double literal sense in the same proposition) will denote the heavenly thing in relation to the Spirit. And that a heavenly thing is indeed given, united to the earthly, is a constant opinion among the orthodox. But as to what that heavenly thing is, they disagree. Blessed Hülsemann names the Word (that is, the thing promised by the Word) Eph. 5:26, the Spirit, John 3:5, 1 Cor. 6:11, the blood 1 John 5:6, and the whole Most Holy Trinity, Matt. 28:19. "These," he says, "internal denominations of matter, not separately or individually, but simultaneously and conjunctively, constitute the heavenly matter of baptism, is rightly demonstrated from the cited sayings." Breviar. c. 10. th. 8. Others, with Dannhauer, f. 351. Mysteriosoph., do not acknowledge all these as heavenly matter. Dannhauer himself argues for the Spirit alone. α. From "of water and Spirit" John 3:5, "of" (ἐξ) denotes matter, as in Gal. 4:4, etc. For just as I rightly conclude: Of water; therefore water is the matter: so I rightly infer: Of the Spirit; therefore the Spirit (which, however, does not exclude the Trinity) is the matter or thing of baptism. β. Just as the eucharistic bread is not bare bread, but united to a heavenly thing, so the water of baptism is not bare water. γ. Water in the nominative case saves us, 1 Pet. 3:21. But bare water, not united to a saving thing, does not accomplish this. Therefore, the sacramental effect requires the union of both. δ. God "regenerates us through water" John 3:5, cleanses us Eph. 5:26, and saves us Tit. 3:5. Therefore, water is God’s instrument and consequently, not as separated, but joined and sacramentally united to the saving thing. ε. We are regenerated "of water and Spirit" in such a way John 3:5, that out of these two one baptism is made Eph. 4:5. But water and Spirit are not one and the same. Therefore, they are united into one, otherwise baptism would become twofold, which is an absurdity. ζ. Whatever is poured out upon us in baptism, that is its matter. But both water Eph. 5:26 and the Holy Spirit himself Tit. 3:5, 6 are poured out upon us in baptism itself. Therefore, both water and the Holy Spirit (the former indeed earthly, the latter truly heavenly) are the matter or thing of baptism. And we think we can rest in this simplicity. η. "We do not assert that the Word is a material part in baptism and a heavenly thing, because thus the Word in the Eucharist would also be a heavenly matter," says B. Affelmann, Disp. de baptismo, th. 3. I add θ. The Word of institution pertains to the efficient cause, the promise (or the thing promised) pertains to the effect of the sacrament, and this also has a place in the Eucharist, which by this reasoning would have a double heavenly matter. In sum: The Word is not so much the heavenly matter itself, as it promises and offers the heavenly matter. ι. Regarding the blood, the others judge that it pertains to the meritorious cause, but has the character of heavenly matter only in the Eucharist. For they think that mention of the blood is made in no place that deals with baptism *ex professo*. κ. The Most Holy Trinity (in whose name, institution, and authority we are baptized, Matt. 28:19), insofar as it is referred to the efficient cause, cannot be the matter of baptism. λ. We acknowledge the opinion of B. Wilhelm Lyser in *Summar. Theolog.* num. 274, who substitutes the water flowing from the side of Christ, as indeed pious, but less certain. For Christ did not say: "Unless one is born of water and water" (that is, earthly and lateral), John 3:5. (System, th. Loc. XIV. § 16. p. 361. sqq.) Quenstedtius: "We, with Menzer, Meisner, Affelmann, Gerhard, Brochmand, Calov, and others, establish that the heavenly thing is the Most Holy Trinity, in which neither Christ the God-man nor his blood is excluded, but terminatively the Holy Spirit." (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1085.) PART III. CHAP. X.
