### On Baptism: Hutterus: "Just as in the Supper the unworthy eat the very body and blood of…

Hutterus: "Just as in the Supper the unworthy eat the very body and blood of Christ, yet do not become partakers of the vivifying virtue of Christ’s flesh, their unbelief standing in the way: so also hypocrites are sprinkled in baptism not only with water, but with the Holy Spirit Himself, yet they are not rendered partakers of the saving fruit or operation of the Holy Spirit; for the Holy Spirit, thus bestowed upon them, indeed intends that saving operation, but in the very act does not perfect or exert it because of their infidelity. For it is not a necessary consequence that where the Holy Spirit is substantially, there He must also be according to the saving effect of regeneration." (LL. th. f. 636.)

Hollazius: "We take the name of 'heavenly matter' here not in the strict sense (ἀκριβείᾳ) of the philosophers, but in a certain breadth for a heavenly thing. Strictly speaking, neither the Holy Spirit nor the venerable Trinity is or can be called a material cause." (L. c. q. 8. p. 1056.)

Lutherus: "Therefore it is a godless speech concerning holy baptism, that water is and remains water, since with this water stands God’s Word and the command and the promise, and it is like a fiery iron; which, just as it is truly iron, so it is also truly fire, and does everything that fire is accustomed to do. But the Word in baptism is seen only by the believers; the godless, however, like a cow or a dog, see nothing but the bare water. With such bovine and canine eyes these enthusiasts look upon the external ceremonies of baptism, judge and pass sentence solely according to their bovine sight, but bring with them no ears that would hear God’s Word, command, and promise, which is in and with this ceremony." (Exposition of the 15 Psalms in the higher choir. Opp. Hal. IV, 2488.)

The same: "Thus St. John (1 John 5:6) portrays for us dear baptism, that we should not regard nor look upon the white water alone. For Christ (he says) 'comes not with water only' (as the Anabaptists blaspheme, that it is nothing more than water), 'but with water and blood.' He wishes through such words to admonish us to look with spiritual eyes in baptism upon the beautiful, rose-colored blood of Christ, which flowed and was shed from His holy side. And thus to be baptized means nothing else than to be bathed and cleansed in that same rose-colored blood of Christ... Therefore, such preaching and baptizing upon it is as much as if the blood of Christ itself were sprinkled over us. Only that it happens here spiritually (for bodily sprinkling would not do it), that we believe and say: I am washed from sins and death through the blood of my Lord Christ." (Two sermons on the third chapter of the Evangelist Matthew, a. 1540. Ib. VII, 1019. sq.) §

6. The formal [cause] of baptism is the word of institution, or that the washing is in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Or that by which the act itself, when joined with the act of washing, formally possesses that which is sacramental or a sacrament.

Musaeus: "Baptism is not a substance composed of matter and form, but an action occupied about a certain matter in a certain way, of which there is not properly given an internal form that, with the matter, constitutes a being in itself. However, the form of baptism is called that from which the action of baptism has [the quality] that it is baptism and is distinguished from any other action."

As we indicated in the last note to the preceding § at the beginning, we have shown what the blessed Luther and the orthodox theologians who followed him most closely have held. The blessed Aegidius Hunnius also expressly states (Tom. 1. op. fol. 1016, 1020) that the word of institution is the form of baptism, as a substantial part, and having cited the passage in Ephesians 5:26 concerning the washing of water by the word, he says: "You see that the divine apostle makes mention of both water and the word as substantial parts of baptism." For water, without the word, would not have the power of sanctifying. But through the word of God who institutes it, it acquires this supernatural faculty of sanctifying. And the blessed David Rung (Disp. de Bapt. A. 1596, held § 37), where he treats of the form of baptism and establishes that it is the word of institution itself: "This word," he adds, "is that by which the water of baptism is truly sanctified and by which Christ cleanses His church with the washing of water, and which imparts, as it were, life and soul to it, so that it not undeservedly deserves to be called the form of baptism."

And for this purpose, he himself cites the words of Luther from the Small Catechism in § 38.

But as for the fact that others refer the word of institution to the matter of baptism (as we saw in the note to the preceding §), it is to be observed that they believed the twofold matter and the substantial parts of baptism to be equally extensive (see Reudenius, Piscator, Schilterus, Himmelius in the cited places). Indeed, even those who reckon that word among the ποιητιχοίς (productive) principles still refer it also to the form of baptism. See Hutterus in the cited place. Gerhardus: "The form of baptism consists in the action, namely, in the immersion of the person to be baptized into water, or, which is the same thing, in the affusion of water, and then in the recitation of the words of institution: 'I baptize thee in the name,' etc., so that in general three substantial parts of baptism are to be established, which cannot be torn away or changed, namely, water, the word, and the action." (L. c. § 87.) Cf. above, what was said concerning the form of the sacraments, Part III, Chapter 8, § 8.b.

Some call it the word of mandate or precept, understanding not so much that by which the exercise of the act is commanded, but that by which the act of washing is formally determined to a certain species of act. Whence others prefer to say the word of ordination.

d.) "One name, one deity," says Theophylactus in this place, "because to baptize into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit is to baptize by the authority and power of these three persons; wherefore, since there is one authority and power and therefore one essence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, for this reason (the apostles) are commanded to baptize not in the names, but in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit," as interpreted by Gerhard in Harm. Evang. de Besurr. Christ, chapter XII, p. 463, and Tom. IV, L. de Bapt. § 81, 82. Gerhardus: "I say that this is the meaning of the words of baptism: I, a minister of the word, not by my own name or private daring or whim, but by the mandate, authority, institution, and ordination, and therefore in the name and place of Christ, the supreme high priest of the church, our only Mediator and Savior, baptize thee, that is, I wash thee with water sanctified by the word of God in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, that is, by the mandate and invocation of the true God, one in essence and three in persons, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; I pray Him that He may receive thee into grace, remit thy sins, and confer eternal life, and I truly testify that thou art received into grace by God the Father, washed from sins by the blood of the Mediator the Son, and sealed by the Holy Spirit, who regenerates and renews thee unto eternal life, and know that thou art baptized into the name of that one true God, that is, bound to the acknowledgment, invocation, and worship of Him, etc. That this is the power..." PART III. CHAPTER X.

of this phrase, "to be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit," is evident from the following passages of Scripture. Exod. 5:23: "Moses spoke in the name of God to Pharaoh." Deut. 18:7: "The Levites serve in the name of God," v. 20: "When a prophet presumes to speak in my name what I have not commanded him." 1 Sam. 17:45: "I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts." 2 Sam. 6:18: "David blessed the people in the name of the Lord." 1 Kings 18:32: "Elijah built an altar in the name of the Lord." Matt. 18:20: "Where two or three are gathered in my name." Mark 9:39: "To do mighty works in Christ’s name." John 16:23: "Whatever you ask the Father in my name," etc. From these and similar passages, it appears that to speak or act in the name of God is the same as to speak or act by the command of God, in the place of God, in true invocation of God, by the power of God, in true trust toward God, for the glory of God, etc. (L. c. § 81.)

And we acknowledge that this full formula, just as it was constantly observed by the apostles and their disciples, must be studiously and necessarily retained. Yet, this is left to Christian liberty: whether one who baptizes according to the custom of the Latin church says actively, "I baptize you in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit," or with the Greek church, in the third person passive: "Let this servant of the Lord be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit," or finally, whether one joins the invocation of the most holy Trinity—that is, the words "In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit"—with the act of washing, which already strikes the senses by itself, provided the church is not disturbed by an untimely change.

Brentius: "There are those who think that Christ instituted baptism in this place in such a way that it must be administered with these very words: 'I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,' and they believe that if we do not use these words, it is not a true baptism. For the phrase 'in the name,' they think one must understand 'with these words.' It must be observed, therefore, that in baptism these customary words, 'I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,' are by all means to be retained, nor is anyone permitted to change these words according to his own whim and rashness, or to use other words in baptism at his own discretion. For there are most weighty reasons, which it is superfluous to recount here, why the use of these words should be diligently retained.

And yet, this use must be rightly understood. For Christ did not place the foundation of his baptism upon certain letters, syllables, or expressions. Nor did he bind us to certain words. For he did not institute magic, which is bound to a certain form of words and rites, but he instituted heavenly sacraments, which consist in his own meaning and will, signified to us by these or those words.

Sancti redduntur compotes; siquidem Sp. S., sic ipsis collatus, intendit quidem operationem illam salutiferam, sed ipso actu non perficit aut exserit propter infidelitatem ipsorum. Lutherus: ״Derowegen ist das eine gottlose Rede von der heiligen Taufe, dass Wasser Wasser sei und bleibe, dieweil bei diesem Wasser Gottes Wort und der Befehl und die Verheissung stehet, und einem feurigen Eisen gleich ist'; welches wie es wahrhaftig Eisen ist, also ist es auch wahrhaftig Feuer, und thut alles, was Feuer zu thun pfleget. Ib. VII, 1019. sq.) §

6. Formale a baptismi est verbum b institutionis,c seu quod ablutio sit in nomine d Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti.e Sive illud, per quod cum actu abluendi conjunctum actus ipse formaliter habet, quod est sacramentalis aut sacramentum.

Dicitur autem forma baptismi id, a quo actio baptismi habet, quod baptismus est et ab alia quavis actione distinguitur.“

Prout b. Lutherum, et qui eum proxime secuti sunt, theologos orthodoxos sensisse indicavimus, not. ult. ad § praeced. sub initium. Expresse etiam b. Aegid. Hunnius Tom. 1. op. fol. 1016. 1020. verbum institutionis dicit esse formam baptismi, tanquam partem substantialem, et adducto loco Ephes. 5, 26. de lavacro aquae per verbum: Vides, ait, et aquae et verbi, tanquam substantialium baptismi partium, meminisse divum apostolum. Aqua enim, sine verbo, virtutem sanctificandi non haberet. Per verbum autem instituentis Dei acquirit hanc supernaturalem sanctificandi facultatem. Et b. David Rung. Disp, de Bapt. A. 1596. hab. §37., ubi de forma baptismi agit eamque ipsum verbum institutionis esse statuit: Hoc verbum (addit) illud est, per quod baptismi aqua vere sanctificatur et per quod Christus lavacro aquae ecclesiam suam mundat quodque vitam quasi et animam impertit, ut non immerito baptismi forma dici mereatur.

Atque eam in rem verba Lutheri ex Catech. min. ipse citat § 38.

Quod autem alii verbum institutionis ad materiam baptismi referunt (uti ad § praeced. not. h. vidimus), observandum est, quod materiam duplicem et partes substantiales baptismi aeque late patere crediderunt (vidd. Reudenius, Piscator, Schilterus, Himmelius 11. cc.). Imo etiam illi, qui verbum illud principiis ποιητιχοίς accensent, tamen etiam ad formam baptismi referunt. Vid. Hutterus 1. c. Gerhardus: ,,Forma baptismi in actione consistit, videl. in mersione hominis baptizandi in aquam sive, quod perinde est, in affusione aquae, ac deinde in recitatione verborum institutionis: ,Ego baptizo te in nomine‘ etc., ut in universum tres substantiales baptismi partes sint statuendae, quae non possunt divelli aut mutari, sc. aqua, verbum et actio.“ (L. c. § 87.) Cf. supra, quae dicta sunt de forma sacramentorum P. III. c. 8. § 8.b.

Quidam verbum mandati aut praecepti appellant, intelligentes non tam istud, quo exercitium actus praecipitur, sed quo actus abluendi formaliter determinatur ad certam speciem actus. Unde alii malunt dicere verbum ordinationis.

d.) Unum nomen, una deitas, ait Theophylactus h. 1., quia in nomen Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti baptizare, est auctoritate et virtute harum trium personarum baptizare, quare, cum sit una auctoritas et virtus adeoque una essentia Patris, Filii, et Spiritus S., ideo non in nominibus, sed in nomine Patris, Filii, et Spiritus S. baptizare jubentur (apostoli), interprete Gerhardo Harm. Evang. de Besurr. Christ, cap. XII. p. m. 463. et Tom. IV. L. de Bapt. § 81. 82. Gerhardus: ,,Dicipaus, hunc esse verborum baptismi sensum: Ego minister verbi non meo nomine aut privato auso vel arbitrio, sed mandato, auctoritate, institutione atque ordinatione, adeoque nomine et loco Christi, summi ecclesiae pontificis, Mediatoris et Salvatoris nostri unici, baptizo te, hoc est, aqua verbo Dei sanctificata te perfundo in nomine Patris, Filii et Spiritus Sancti, hoc est, mandato et invocatione veri Dei, unius in essentia ac trini in personis, videlicet Patris, Filii et Spiritus Sancti; illum oro, ut in gratiam te recipiat, peccata tibi remittat et salutem aeternam conferat, ac vere testificor, te in gratiam a Deo Patre recipi, sanguine Filii Mediatoris a peccatis ablui et Spiritu Sancto, ad vitam aeternam te regenerante ac renovante, obsignari, ac scias, te ^ ,όνομα in nomen unius illius veri Dei baptizari, id est, obiigari ad illius agnitionem, invocationem ac cultum etc. Hanc esse vim PART. III. CAP. X.

hujus phraseos,in nomine Patris, Pilii et Spiritus Sancti‘ baptizari, patet ex sequentibus Scripturae locis. Exod. 5, 23.: ,Moses loquebatur in nomine Dei ad Pharaonem.‘ Deuter. 18, 7.: ,Levitae serviunt in nomine Dei‘, v. 20.: ,Quando propheta praesumserit loqui in meo nomine, quod non praecepi ei.‘ 1 Sam. 17, 45.: ,Venio ad te in nomine Dei Zebaoth.‘ 2 Sam. 6, 18.: ,David benedicebat populo in nomine Dei.‘ 1 Reg. 18, 32.: ,Elias extruit altare in nomine Dei.‘ Matth. 18, 20.: ,Ubi duo vel tres congregati in nomine meo.‘ Mare. 9, 39.: ,In Christi nomine virtutes facere.‘ Joh. 16, 32.: ,Quicquid rogaveritis Patrem in nomine meo‘ etc. Ex his et similibus locis apparet, in nomine Dei aliquid loqui vel agere idem esse, quod mandato Dei, loco Dei, in vera invocatione Dei, virtute Dei, in vera erga Deum fiducia, ad gloriam Dei etc. aliquid loqui vel agere.“ (L. c. § 81.)

Atque hanc plenam formulam, sicut 0U7n ab apostolis eorumque discipulis constanter observatam, ita studiose ac necessario retinendam usse agnoscimus. Christianae tamen libertati hoc relictum est, utrum, qui baptizat juxta morem ecclesiae Latinae, active dicat: Ego baptizo te in nomine Patris, Filii et Spiritus S., an cum ecclesia Graeca, in persona tertia passiva: Baptizetur hic servus Domini in nomine Patris, Filii, et Spiritus S., an denique cum actu abluendi, qui jam per se in sensus incurrit, conjungat invocationem sanctissimae Trinitatis, seu verba: In nomine Patris, Filii, et Spiritus Sancti, modo intempestiva mutatione ecclesia non turbetur.

Brentius: ,,Sunt, qui sentiunt, quod Christus hoc loco sic instituerit baptismum, ut etiam his verbis: ,Ego baptizo te in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti‘, distribuendus sit et, nisi his verbis utamur, existimant non esse verum baptismum. Hi pro eo, quod dicitur ·,in nomine‘, putant intelligendum esse, ,his verbis‘. Observandum igitur, quod 111 baptismo haec usitata verba,ego baptizo te in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti‘ omnino retinenda sunt, nec cuiquam permittendum est, ut haec verba pro sua libidine et temeritate mutet ac aliis verbis pro suo arbitrio in baptismo utatur. Sunt enim gravissimae causae, quas supervacaneum est hoc loco commemorare, cur horum verborum usus diligenter retinendus sit.

Et tamen hic usus recte est intelligendus. Nam Christus non collocavit fundamentum baptismi sui super certis literis, syllabis, aut dictionibus. Nec aliigavit nos ad certa verba. Non enim instituit magiam, quae ad certam verborum formam et ritus alligata est, sed instituit coelestia sacramenta, quae constant sua ipsius sententia et voluntate, his vel illis verbis nobis significata.


### On Baptism: For when Christ commended that baptism be spread among the nations, he spoke…

For when Christ commended that baptism be spread among the nations, he spoke with his disciples in Hebrew or Aramaic. What then? If baptism were bound to certain letters and syllables, it would certainly not be permitted to baptize in any language other than Hebrew or Aramaic. But it is well. Just as Christ spread his gospel on the day of Pentecost into all the languages of the nations, so he also wills that his sacraments be distributed in those languages which can be understood by the hearers and those who receive the sacraments, and by which the meaning of his gospel is rightly known.

Therefore, if someone, after the recitation of the Apostles' Creed in baptism, were to say to the one being baptized these words: 'I have now heard from you the confession of your faith, that you believe in God the Father Almighty, Creator of heaven and earth, and in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit. Into this confession and faith, therefore, I dip you into the water or pour water upon you, that by this sign you may be made certain that you have been inserted into Jesus Christ and the communion of all his goods. Go therefore in peace.' This would certainly be a true baptism, because it contains those things which are necessary for baptism, and the meaning of Christ's words has been recited, even if the sound..."

the words themselves seem slightly changed. This was added for this reason, not that a change of the customary words, "I baptize thee in the name of the Father," etc., should be permitted; but that the words of Christ might be rightly understood and that we might learn to distinguish magic far from the true consecration of the heavenly sacraments. (Catechismus illustrat. 1551. p. 55—57.)

Luther: "Beware, do not so distinguish baptism as to attribute the external to man and the internal to God; attribute both to God alone, and do not accept the person of the one conferring it as anything other than a vicarious instrument of God, through whom the Lord, sitting in heaven, immerses you into the water with His own hands and promises the remission of sins on earth, speaking to you with the voice of a man through the mouth of His minister.

The very words themselves tell you this, when He says: 'I baptize thee in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, Amen.' He does not say: 'I baptize thee in my name,' as if He were saying: 'That which I do, I do not by my own authority, but in the stead and name of God, so that you may regard it no differently than if the Lord Himself had done it visibly.' The author and the minister are different, but the work is the same for both, or rather, it is the work of the author alone through my ministry. For I think that 'in the name' refers to the person of the author, so that it is not merely a matter of pretending and invoking the name of the Lord in the work, but of fulfilling the work itself as if it were another's, in his name and stead. By which trope Christ says in Matthew 24: 'Many shall come in my name'; and Romans 1: 'Through whom we have received grace and apostleship, for obedience to the faith among all nations for his name.' I most gladly follow this opinion, because it is a most full source of comfort and an effective aid to faith to know that one has been baptized not by a man, but by the Trinity Itself through a man who acts in His name among us.

By this, that idle contention ceases, by which they wrangle over the form of baptism (which they call the words themselves), with the Greeks saying: 'Let the servant of Christ be baptized,' and the Latin: 'I baptize.' Likewise, others, trifling most rigidly, condemn the saying: 'I baptize thee in the name of Jesus Christ,' by which rite it is certain the apostles baptized, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, and they want no other to be valid henceforth than this: 'I baptize thee in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, Amen.' But they contend in vain, for they prove nothing; they merely assert their own dreams. In whatever way baptism is administered, provided it is not administered in the name of man, but in the name of the Lord, it truly saves." (De Captivitate Babylonica ecclesiae. 1520. See Opp. lat. ad reformat. histor. pertin. Francof. ad M. 1868. Vol. 5, 60. sq.)

Scherzer: "We note II., that it is an idle question whether one should say 'into the name' or 'in the name' of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Whence both 'into the name' (Matt. 28:19; 1 Cor. 1:13) and 'in the name' (Acts 2:38; 10:48) are explicitly read. But the custom of the Church must be regarded, and it is not to be changed by the minister. We note III., that baptism performed 'in the name of Christ' (Acts 2:38; 10:ult.; 19:5) does not exclude the Most Holy Trinity. For 'the profession of Christ is a confession of the whole Trinity. For it manifests the anointing God, the anointed Son, and the oil of anointing, the Holy Spirit,' as Basil the Great says in *On the Holy Spirit*... Since, however, Christ expressly says that one must be baptized into the name, εις το όνομα, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19), no one can justly disapprove of this formula. Although we reject the opinion of those who, with Richard (IV. Dist. III. art. 2. q. 2.), assert that one baptized 'in the name of Christ' must be rebaptized conditionally." (System. th. p. 356.)

Calov: "They err who, with the Marcionites, Paulianists, and Cataphrygians, denied that one must be baptized in the name of the Trinity; see Canon VII. of the Council of Laodicea... Nor is conditional baptism to be admitted: 'If you are baptized, I do not baptize you; but if you are not yet baptized, I baptize you,' etc., which is approved in Lib. III. decretal. Greg. M. t. 42. c. 2. from Innocent; if, that is, there is doubt whether one has been baptized; which the blessed Luther rightly reproves (T. VIII. Jen. Germ. f. 50)... Nor is the formula 'in the name of Jesus Christ' to be reproved, provided it is not understood exclusively; which baptism Hugo and Lombard acknowledge as valid. Not PART. III. CAP. X.

the opinion of the Calvinists is to be rejected, that it is permissible to baptize "in the names," because the name conveys the authority, majesty, and virtue of God, which is μονοτάτως μόνος; nor is that formula, approved by Bernard (Ep. 740 to Henry), "in the name of God and of holy truth," to be approved. Perhaps that rite of the Eunomians mentioned in Socrates (Bk. 5, ch. 27), who baptized "into the death of the Lord," could be more easily excused, which was also done in the primitive church, if the Apostolic Canons deserve credit, in whose 50th canon this is read. (System. loc. th. Vol. X, 227 sq.)

Gerhard: "The question is: Must a baptism be considered valid if another letter or syllable is changed in the words? Resp.: If the sense remains whole and uncorrupted, and nothing is corrupted intentionally, such a baptism is to be held as legitimate; for the institution of Christ is to be accepted not so much for the sound as for the sense of the words.

Aventinus (Bk. 3, Annal. p. 207): 'Around the year of Christ 745, a certain Bavarian presbyter, ignorant of the Latin language, had baptized a boy "in the name of Patria, Filia, and Spiritua Sancta"; Boniface of Mainz had ordered the boy to be rebaptized. Virgil, Bishop of Salzburg, and Sidonius, Bishop of Laureacum, wished the baptism to be valid among the Bavarians; great disturbances were stirred up. Zachary, Roman Pontiff, resolved the dispute and confirmed Virgil's opinion.'

The decree exists in c. Retulerunt, dist. 4, de consec. to Boniface: 'The messengers reported that there was a priest in the same province who was completely ignorant of the Latin language, and while he was baptizing, not knowing how to speak Latin, he broke the language and said: "I baptize you in the name of Patria and Filia and Spiritua Sancta," and on account of this your reverend holiness considered rebaptizing them; but, most holy brother, if he who baptized, not introducing error or heresy, but only out of ignorance of the Roman speech, said this while breaking the language, we cannot consent that he be rebaptized.' The Gloss adds the reason, 'because an error of a syllable does not harm, especially at the end of a word.'" (L. c. § 93.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Gnostics, who baptized 'in the name of the unknown father of all, and in the truth of the mother of all, and in the name of him who descended into Jesus for the union and redemption and communion of powers,' as Irenaeus testifies (Bk. 1, ch. 18), Epiphanius (haer. 34), and Eusebius (Bk. 4, Hist. ch. 10). 2. Of the Marcionites, Paulianists, and Cataphrygians, who denied that one must be baptized in the name of the Trinity; see Council of Laodicea, can. 7.

3. Of the Arians, Aetians, and Eunomians, who baptized 'in the Father alone, Jesus the Savior and creature, and the Holy Spirit, his fellow-servant'; likewise: 'In the name of the uncreated God, the created Son, and the sanctifying Spirit created by the Son'; in Epiphanius (haer. 76); or also: 'In the name of the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit,' as Nicephorus reports (Bk. 4, ch. 36), Sozomen (Bk. 6, ch. 26). 4. Of Bernard (Ep. 348) and Hugh of St. Victor (Bk. 2, de Sacram. P. 6, ch. 2), because they approved a baptism administered with this formula: 'I baptize you in the name of God and of the holy cross.'

5. Of certain Papists, who baptized in the name of the Father, Son, Holy Spirit, and Mary. For not only did William of Baptis (ch. 2) add Mary, as did Fabius Incarnatus in Scrutin. Sacerd. (tr. 2, p. 1), but also (Bk. 1, Nov. Sacerd. p. 25) approved the same formula. 6. Of Bellarmine (Bk. 1, de Sacram, ch. 19, §: 'quod igitur' and Bk. 1, de Bapt. ch. 3), denying that the formula of baptism used in our churches—'I baptize you in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit'—can be demonstrated from the Gospel alone, but that one must necessarily have recourse to traditions and the declaration of the church, §: 'Porro hanc.' But we oppose to him the command of Christ himself in Matthew 28.

7. Of the Socinians, denying that this formula of baptism was commanded by Christ and used by the apostles; see Ostorodt in Instit. Germ. p. 252, ch. 39. Wolzogenius on Matthew 28:19 (Vol. 1, Op. f. 449) writes: 'That a certain formula "in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit" is to be used by the baptizer, is neither from Scripture nor any...'"

OF BAPTISM. ... can be demonstrated by an ecclesiastical writer.’ ...

8. Of the Calvinists, who invent a double form of words that is to be used in baptism: one, ‘I baptize you in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,’ the other, ‘I baptize you in the name of Christ.’ See Sohnius in *Methodo theol.* p. 262; indeed, Zwingli asserts that ‘no certain form of words is necessary,’ in his book *de vera et falsa relig.*, chapter on baptism.” (*L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 1121.*)

Latin:

Cum enim Christus baptismum inter gentes vulgandum commendaret, locutus est cum discipulis suis hebraice aut syriace. Quid ergo? Si baptismus ad certas literas ac syllabas aliigatus esset, certe non liceret, nisi hebraica aut syriaca lingua baptizare. Sed bene habet. Sicut Christus vulgavit evangelion suum in die pentecostes in omnes linguas gentium, ita etiam vult, ut sacramenta sua distribuantur his linguis, quae ab auditoribus et his, qui accipiunt sacramenta, intelligi possunt et quibus sententia evangelii ejus recte cognoscitur.

Itaque si quis post recitationem symboli apostolici in baptismo diceret ad baptizandum haec verba: ,Audivi jam ex te confessionem fidei tuae, quod credas in Deqm Patrem omnipotentem, creatorem coeli et terrae, et in unigenitum Filium ejus, Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, et in Spiritum Sanctum. In hanc igitur confessionem et fidem intingo te in aquam seu perfundo te aqua, ut hoc signaculo certus fias, te insertum esse in Jesum Christum et communionem omnium bonorum ejus. Vade ergo in pace.‘ Hic certe baptismus esset verus baptismus, quia continet ea, quae ad baptismum necessaria sunt et recitata est sententia verborum Christi, etsi sonus

ipse verborum paululum immutatus videtur. Hoc idcirco visum est addere, non quod permittenda sit mutatio usitatorum verborum: ,Ego baptizo te in nomine Patris4 etc.; sed ut verba Christi recte intelligantur et ut magiam a vera coelestium sacramentorum consecratione longe discernere discamus.44 (Catechismus illustrat. 1551. p. 55—57.)

Lutherus: ,,Cave, sic discernas baptismum, ut externum homini, internum Deo tribuas, utrumque soli Deo tribue, nec conferentis personam aliam, quam instrumentum vicarium Dei accipe, per quod Dominus in coelo sedens te in aquam suis manibus propriis mergit, et remissionem peccatorum promittit in terris, voce hominis tibi loquens per os ministri sui.

Hoc et ipsa verba tibi dicunt, cum dicit: Ego baptizo te in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti, Arnen. Non dicit: Ego baptizo te in nomine meo, quasi dicat: Id, quod facio, non mea auctoritate, sed vice et nomine Dei facio, ut non aliter habeas, quam si ipse Dominus visibiliter fecisset. Auctor et minister diversi sunt, sed opus idem utriusque, imo solius auctoris per ministerium meum. Sic enim ego arbitror, ,in nomine4 referre personam auctoris, ut non tantum sit, nomen Domini praetendere et invocare in opere, sed ipsum opus tanquam alienum alterius nomine et vice implere. Quo tropo Matth. 24. Christus dicit: ,Multi venient in nomine meo4; et Rom. 1.: ,Per quem accepimus gratiam et apostolatum, ad obediendum fidei in omnibus gentibus pro nomine ejus.4 Hanc sententiam ego libentissime sequor, quod sit plenissimum solatii et efficax fidei adjutorium, nosse, se esse baptizatum non ab homine, sed ab ipsa Trinitate per hominem, qui nomine ejus rem gerat apud nos.

Quo cessat illa otiosa contentio, qua de forma baptismi (quam appellant ipsa verba) litigant, Graecis dicentibus: ,Baptizetur servus Christi4, Latinus: ,Ego baptizo.4 Item alii rigidissime nugantes damnant, sic dici: ,Ego baptizo te in nomine Jesu Christi4, quo ritu certum est apostolos baptizasse, ut in Actis apostolicis legimus, voluntque nullam aliam deinceps valere quam istam: ,Ego baptizo te in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti, Arnen.4 Sed frustra contendunt, nihil enim probant, sua somnia duntaxat asserunt. Quocunque modo tradatur baptismus, modo non in nomine hominis, sed 111 nomine Domini tradatur, vere salvum facit.44 (De Captivitate Babylon, ecclesiae. 1520. Vid. Opp. lat. ad reformat, histor. pertin. Francof. ad M. 1868. Vol. 5, 60. sq.)

Scherzerus: ,,Notamus II., otiose quaeri, an dicendum sit,in nomen1, an,in nomine4 Patris, Filii et Spiritus Sancti. Unde et in nomen Matth. 28, 19. 1 Cor. 1, 13. et 111 nomine Actor. 2, 38. 10, 48. diserte legitur. Sed usus ecclesiae respiciendus, nec a ministro mutandus est. Notamus III., quod baptismus, ,in nomine Christi4 Actor. 2, 38. 10, ult. 19, 5. peractus, non excludat Sacrosanctam Trinitatem. Nam,Christi professio est totius Trinitatis confessio. Manifestat enim ungentem Deum, unctum Filium et oleum unctionis, Spiritum Sanetum4, dicente Basilio M. de Spiritu Sancto. . . Quia tamen Christus expresse dicit, baptizandum esse in nomen, εις το,όνομα, Patris, Filii et Spiritus Sancti, Matth. 28, 19., nemo hanc formulam jure potest improbare. Quanquam rejiciamus sententiam eorum, qui cum Richardo IV. Dist. III. art. 2. q. 2. ,in nomine Christi4 baptizatum cum conditione rebaptizandum asserunt.44 (System, th. p. 356.)

Calovius: ,,Errant, qui, cum Marcionistis, Paulianistis, Cataphrygibus, in nomine Trinitatis baptizandum esse negarunt; vid. Canon VII. Concil. Laodic... Neque admittendus conditionalis baptismus: ,Si baptizatus es, non te baptizo; sed si nondum baptizatus es, ego te baptizo4 etc., quem probat 1. III. decretal. Greg. M. t. 42. c. 2. ex Innocentio; si sci. dubium sit, an quis baptizatus sit; quod reprobat merito b. Lutherus T. VIII. Jen. Germ. f. 50. . . Neque etiam reprobanda formula,in nomine Jesu Christi4, modo non exclusive intelligatur; quem baptismum ratum agnoscunt Hugo et Lombardus. Non PART. III. CAP. X.

probanda tamen Calvinianorum sententia, quod baptizare liceat in nominibus, quia nomen auctoritatem, majestatem et virtutem Dei infert, quae μονοτάτως μόνος est; neque illa, Bernhardo Ex. 740. ad Henric. probata, ,in nomine Dei et sanctae veritatis‘ p. 3. Excusari forsan magis posset ritus ille Eunomianor. apud Socratem 1. 5. c. 27., qui baptizarunt,in mortem Domini‘, quod etiam factum in primitiva ecclesia, si Can. apostol. fidem merentur, in quorum L. id legitur.“ (System. loc. th. T. X, 227. sq.)

Gerhardus: ,,Quaeritur: Num baptismus ratus sit habendus, si alia litera aut syllaba in verbis mutetur. Resp.: Si sensus maneat integer et. incorruptus, neque ex industria aliquid corrumpatur, baptismus ejusmodi pro legitimo habendus; neque enim tam de sono, quam sensu verborum institutio Christi accipienda.

Aventinus lib. 3. annal. p. 21)7.: ,Circa annum Christi 745. presbyter quidam Bavarus, latinae linguae ignarus, baptizarat puerum,in nomine Patria, Filia et Spiritua Sancta‘; Bonifacius Moguntinus puerum jusserat rebaptizari. Salisburgensis episc. Virgilius et Sidonius, pontifex Laureacensis, apud Bojos baptismum ratum esse volebant; turbae excitatae maximae. Zacharias, Pontif. Rom., dissidium solvit et Virgilii opinionem confirmavit.

Decretum extat c. Retulerunt, dist. 4. de consec. ad Bonifacium.: Retulerunt nuncii, quod fuit in eadem provincia sacerdos, qui latinam linguam penitus ignorabat et dum baptizaret, nesciens loqui latine, infringens linguam diceret: Baptizo te in nomine Patria et Filia et Spiritua Sancta, et per hoc tua reverenda sanctitas consideravit eos rebaptizare; sed, sanctissime frater, si ille, qui baptizavit, non errorem introducens aut haeresin, sed pro sola ignorantia romanae locutionis infringendo linguam hoc baptizans dixisset, non possumus consentire, ut denuo baptizetur.‘ Glossa addit rationem, ,quia error syllabae non nocet, maxime in fine dictionis.“‘ (L. c. § 93.)

Qnosticorum, qui baptizarunt in nomine ignoti patris omnium et in veritate matris omnium et in nomine descendentis Jesu ad unitionem et redemptionem et communionem virtutum; ut testatur Irenaeus 1. 1. c. 18., Epiphanius haer. 34. et Eusebius 1. 4. Hist. c. 10. 2. Marcionitarum, Paulianistarum et Cataphrygum, qui negarunt, in nomine trinitatis esse baptizandum; vide Concil. Laodic. can. 7.

3. Arianorum, Aetianorum et Eunomianorum, qui baptizarunt, in solo Patre, Jesu Servatore et creatura, et Spiritu S., ejusdem conservo‘; item: ,In nomine Dei increati, Filii creati et Spiritus sanctiflcativi et a Filio creati‘; apud Epiphanium haer. 76.; vel etiam: ,In nomine Patris per Filium in Spiritu S.‘; ut refert Nicephorus 1. 4. c. 36., Sozomenus 1. 6. c. 26. 4. Bernhardt Ep. 348. et Hugonis de S. Victore 1. 2. de Sacram. P. 6. c. 2., quia approbarunt baptismum administratum hac formula: ,Baptizo te in nomine Dei et sanctae crucis.‘

5. Quorundam Papistarum, qui baptizarunt in nomine Patris, Filii, Spiritus S. et Mariae. Nam non tantum Guilhelmus de Baptis, c. 2. b. Mariam adjecit, ut et Fabius Incarnatus in scrutin. Sacerd. tr. 2. p. 1., sed etiam 1. 1. Nov. Sacerd. p. 25. eandem formulam approbavit. 6. Bellarmini 1. 1. de Sacram, c. 19. §: ,quod igitur‘ et 1. 1. de Bapt. c. 3. negantis, formulam baptismi in ecclesiis nostris usitatam: ,Ego te baptizo in nomine Patris, Filii et Spiritus S.‘ ex solo evangelio demonstrari posse, sed necessario ad traditiones recurrendum esse et ecclesiae declarationem, §: ,Porro hanc.‘ Sed opponimus ipsi Christi mandatum Matth. 28.

7. Socinianorum, negantium, hanc formulam baptismi a Christo esse mandatam et ab apostolis usurpatam‘; vide Ostorodum in Instit. Germ. p. 252. c. 39. Wolzogenius ad Matth. 28, 19. T. 1. Op. f. 449. scribit: ,Formulam certam in nomine Patris, Filii et Spiritus.S. a baptizante usurpandam esse, nec ex Scriptura nec ullo

scriptore ecclesiastico demonstrari posse.‘ ...

8. Calvinianorum, fingentium duplicem formam verborum, qua in baptismo sit utendum, unam: baptizo te in nomine Patris, Filii ac Spiritus S., alteram: baptizo te in nomine Christi. Vide Sohnium in Methodo theol. p. 262., imo Zwinglius, ,non esse necessariam ullam certam verborum formam‘, asserit libro de vera et falsa relig. c. de baptismo.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 1121.)


### On Baptism: Gerhard: “The Papists consecrate the water to be used in baptism on the vigils…

Gerhard: “The Papists consecrate the water to be used in baptism on the vigils of Easter and Pentecost with certain rites and exorcisms, which they afterwards call ‘blessed.’ *Catech. Rom.* p. 308: ‘The water which we use for baptism must first be prepared and consecrated by the addition of the oil of mystical blessing, and this must not be done except on the vigils of Easter and Pentecost.’ Response: 1. That consecration of water is destitute of the Word of God. 2. It lacks the example of John and the apostles, who used whatever water they encountered for baptism. Justin, *Apol. 2. pro Christ.*, p. 73, says: ‘Believing catechumens are led to where there is water, by which they are washed and regenerated,’ from which it is evident that simple and common water was used for baptizing in former times. 3. It disparages the element of water, which is in itself a good creature of God, needing no exorcisms; indeed, it is consecrated to baptism by the institution of Christ, sanctified in the very baptism of Christ, and in the very act of baptizing, through the Word of God, through prayers, and the Holy Spirit, it becomes water that is salutary and fit for washing away sins. Augustine, *serm. 37. de temp.*: ‘All waters were consecrated by Christ in the Jordan.’ 4. The Papists do not consider that consecration of water an adiaphorous rite, but a necessary part of divine worship.” (*L. c. § 74.*)

Höfling: “In the *Sacramentarium Gelasianum* it is said: ‘The consecration of the water’ (which is expressly compared to the transformation of water into wine that happened at Cana) ‘fecundates the whole substance of this water with the power of regeneration,’ and makes it effective for cleansing souls.” (*Das Sacr. der hl. Taufe. I, 453.*)

ANTITHESIS. Fecht: “Hearers must be diligently admonished not to administer baptism unless these (words of institution) have preceded; but if, in the meantime, before these are pronounced, the infant should die, they should rather commit the same to the mercy of God than hasten to baptism with, as they say, unwashed hands. For unless those are premised, the consecration has not preceded, and therefore it is not a sacrament. For the words which are spoken while the infant is being baptized, ‘I baptize you,’ etc., are not consecratory, but applicatory. Just as in the distribution of the Holy Supper the words, ‘Take and eat,’ etc., are not consecratory, but another consecration must necessarily precede. Nor does the consecration consist in the Lord’s Prayer alone, but also in the repetition of the words of institution, and that by the example of Christ. Therefore, neither is to be omitted, and unless both can precede, the infant is not to be baptized.” (*Instruct. pastoralis. Ed. 2. p. 109.*) §

7. The end for which and the subject of baptism are humans carnally begotten and brought into the light; and all of these, males as well as females; and not only those who are older, but also infants. PART III. CHAP. X.

Or those for whose benefit baptism was instituted by God and is thus to be administered. To whom baptism, as a means of grace, ought to be applied. Others call this the object, which some, with the addition, call the personal object. However, no other thing, of whatever nature it may be, nor even all human fetuses, unless it is certain that they are alive and truly human.

Gerhard: "The baptism of the dead is to be condemned. The Cerinthians, as Epiphanius reports (Haer. 28 against Cerinthus), baptized the dead, relying on a perverse understanding of the Apostle’s words in 1 Corinthians 15:29: 'What shall they do which are baptized for the dead, ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, if the dead rise not at all? why are they then baptized for the dead?' Yet this custom of baptizing the dead was used among some in the primitive church, as appears from the 3rd Council of Carthage, chapter 6. The Papists sprinkle the dead and their graves with holy water. Chrysostom, in Homily 1 on Acts, reports that in his time some even poured baptismal water on the dead, which he there rebukes and teaches that 'this is nothing else than casting holy things into the dirt.' The Marcionites, as Tertullian reports (Book 5 against Marcion), had a certain vicarious baptism, which was conferred upon the living in place of the unbaptized dead, as a testimony to the article concerning the resurrection of the dead. But neither the νεκροβαπτισμός of the Cerinthians nor that of the Marcionites can be proven from the words of the Apostle; the former conflicts with the institution and end of baptism, the latter with manifest sayings of Scripture: 'The just shall live by his faith; it is impossible to please God without faith; where the tree falls, there it shall remain,' etc. Nor does the Apostle say: 'If the dead do not rise, why are the dead baptized?'—which could be urged with some appearance for νεκροβαπτισμός—but: 'What shall they do who are baptized ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, over the dead?' ... We embrace that simplest exposition concerning the rite of baptizing Christians at the graves of the dead, which was a symbol of faith and a confession concerning the resurrection of the dead and the spiritual gathering and association of the baptized living with the members of one and the same mystical body, and indeed a public profession concerning the death to be undergone for the glory of Christ and the article of the resurrection. That this custom was received in the primitive church is testified to by the letter of the church of Smyrna in Eusebius (Eccl. Hist. Book 4, ch. 15), Augustine (De Civitate Dei, Book 20, ch. 9), and Luther in his explanation of this passage." (L. c. § 165.)

Quenstedt: "The object of baptism, to whom it is to be administered, are I. human beings alone; for these alone are capable of baptism, not bells, ships, or other inanimate things, which in the Papacy are accustomed to be dipped in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, with human names imposed upon them, and godparents or baptismal witnesses employed; which rite is prohibited in the Constitutions of Charlemagne edited by Busaeus, p. 266, where this chapter is found: 'Let them not baptize bells.' Cf. John Bale in the Acts of the Roman Pontiffs, under John XIV, who ordered a great bell at St. John Lateran to be baptized and his own name to be imposed upon it." (L. c. s. 2, th. 11, f. 1092.)

Gerhard: "A certain singular virtue and efficacy is attributed (by the Papists) to baptized bells for the expulsion of every diabolical influence, for putting to flight thunder and lightning, for the salvation of departed souls, etc. ... From the description (of the rites of baptizing bells) it is easily understood what is to be determined concerning the exception of Stanislaus Hosius, who says that bells are not baptized by his people, but consecrated." (L. c. § 166.)

Thus, that they may be flesh of flesh, according to John 3:6. Christ, however, not having need of baptism, was baptized by the same οἰκονομία (economy) by which He was circumcised. Cf. Matthew 3:14, 15. 463 ON BAPTISM.

Those, however, who have not yet been perfectly born are not commanded to be reborn through baptism. For the saying of Christ is universal: Unless one (whoever he may be) is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God (John 3:5). And in Matthew 28:19, Christ commands to baptize πάντα τά ἔθνη, not only the Gentiles, as distinguished from the Jews, but all the peoples of the world, whom Mark calls "every creature" (ch. 16:15). Nor did these things pertain only to the planting of the church, but to its preservation; just as the doctrine or preaching of the Gospel must continue until the end of the age, so too must baptism (Matt. 28, last verse). Thus, we know from Acts 16:15 that Lydia was baptized.

That infants are to be baptized is rightly gathered from the combined passages of John 3:5 and Mark 10:14, in this manner: Whosoever Christ wills to attain salvation, yet who cannot attain eternal life by the ordinary way except through the mediation of baptism, to them baptism, as the ordinary means, ought to be conferred and not denied. But Christ wills that infants be saved (according to Mark 10:14), and they cannot attain eternal life by the ordinary way except through the mediation of baptism (by virtue of the universal saying in John 3:5). Therefore. Furthermore (2), in this manner: Whosoever Christ wills to be brought to Him, that they may enjoy spiritual blessing, they are to be brought to Christ through baptism as the ordinary means. But Christ wills that infants be brought to Him, that they may enjoy spiritual blessing (according to Mark 10:14, which Luke, by explaining it as τά βρέφη—children of the tenderest age, such as still hang from the breasts of their mothers or nurses—teaches to be designated). Therefore. Furthermore (3), the command in Matthew 28:19 to baptize all nations is rightly extended also to infants, who are contained within the scope of the nations. And (4), the examples which teach that entire households were baptized, e.g., Acts 16:15 and 33, ch. 18:8, 1 Cor. 1:16, are rightly believed to include infants, who undoubtedly constituted a part of those households. Added to this (5) is the analogy of circumcision, which was conferred upon infants, and (6) that, just as the promise of the covenantal grace (Acts 2:39) pertains to infants, so too does the seal of the covenant, baptism. Finally (7), since the whole church has been cleansed by the washing of water through the word (according to Eph. 5:26), this is also rightly referred to infants, since they, though naturally unclean, must nevertheless be grafted into the church.

Quenstedtius: "If those who wished to be saved at the time of the flood necessarily had to enter the ark, then infants, outside the case of necessity, must also be baptized in order to be saved, because that salvation was a type of baptism (1 Pet. 3:21). But the former is true. Therefore." (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1126.)

Luther: "That infant baptism is pleasing to Christ is sufficiently proven by His own work, namely, that God makes many of those who are thus baptized holy and has given them the Holy Spirit; and even today there are many in whom one perceives that they have the Holy Spirit, both in regard to doctrine and life; just as it has been given to us by God’s grace that we are indeed able to interpret the Scripture and recognize Christ, which cannot happen without the Holy Spirit. But if God did not accept infant baptism, He would not give the Holy Spirit, nor any part of Him, to any of them; in sum, there would have been no person on earth who was a Christian from that long time ago until this day. Since God now confirms baptism by the infusion of His Holy Spirit, as one [sees] in certain Fathers, such as St. Bern— PART III. CAP. X.

Latin:

Gerhardus: ,,Pontificii aquam in baptismo adhibendam in vigilia paschatos et pentecostes certis ritibus et exorcismis prius consecrant, quam postea vocant benedictam. Catech. Rom. p. 308.: ,Aqua, qua ad baptismum utimur, prius paranda et addito mystici benedictionis oleo consecranda est, idque non nisi in vigiliis paschae et pentecostes fieri debet.‘ Resp: 1. Consecratio illa aquae destituitur verbo Dei. 2. Caret exemplo Johannis et apostolorum, qui obviam quamvis aquam baptismati adhibuerunt. Justin. Apol. 2. pro Christ, p. 73.: ,Credentes catechumenos eo adduci‘, ait, ,ubi est aqua, qua loti regenerantur‘, ex quo constat, simplicem et communem aquam ad baptizandum olim fuisse adhibitam. 3. Derogat elemento aquae, quae per se est bona Dei creatura, nullis indigens exorcismis, quin etiam per institutionem Christi baptismo consecrata, in ipso Christi baptismo sanctiflcata, imo in actu ipso baptizandi per verbum Dei, per preces et Spiritum S. fit aqua salutaris abluendis criminibus apta. August, serm. 37. de temp.: ,Omnes aquae a Christo in Jordane consecratae sunt.‘ 4. Consecrationem illam aquae Pontificii non habent pro ritu adiaphoro, sed necessaria divini cultus parte.“ (L. c. § 74.)

Hoeflingius: ,,Im Sacrament. Gelasii heisst es: ,Die Weihung des Wassers‘ (welche ausdrücklich mit der zu Cana geschehenen VerWandlung des Wassers in Wein verglichen wird),befruchtet die ganze Substanz dieses Wassers mit der Kraft der Wiedergeburt‘, macht es wirksam, die Seelen zu reinigen.“ (Das Sacr. der hl. Taufe. I, 453.)

ANTITHESIS. Fechtius: ,,Admonendi sunt diligenter auditores, ne, nisi his (verbis institutionis) praeviis, baptismum administrent; sed si interea, donec haec pronuncientur, infans moriatur, eundem Dei misericordiae committant potius, quam ut illotis, quod ajunt, manibus ad baptismum properent. Nisi enim illa praemittantur, consecratio non antecessit, adeoque sacramentum non est. Verba enim, quae, dum baptizatur infans, dicuntur: ,Ego baptizo te‘ etc., non suntconsecratoria, sed applicatoria. Quemadmodum in sacrae coenae distributione verba: ,Nehmet hin und esset‘ etc., non sunt consecratoria, sed necessario alia consecratio antecessit. Nec etiam consecratio in sola oratione Dominica oonsistit, sed in repetitione etiam verborum institutionis, idque exemplo Christi. Quare neutrum omittendum, et nisi utrumque prae· cedere possit, infans baptizandus non est.“ (Instruet, pastoralis. Ed. 2. p. 109.) §

7. Finis cui a qui et subjectum,b baptismi, sunt homines c earnaliter geniti d editique in lucem;e atque hi omnes,f masculi pariter et femellae; g nec solum adultiores, verum etiam infantes.h PART. III. CAP. X.

Seu illi, quorum bono baptismus a Deo institutus atque ita administrandus est. Cui baptismus, tanquam medium gratiae, applicari debet. Alii objectum dicunt, quod quidam, cum addito, personale objectum vocant. Non autem alia res ulla, cujuscunque rationis sit, ac ne foetus· quidem humani omnes, nisi, eos vivos ac vere homines esse, constet.

Gerhardus: ,,Improbandus baptismus mortuorum. Cerinthianiy referente Epiph. haeres. 28. contra Cerinth., mortuos baptizarunt, freti pravo intellectu verborum apostoli 1 Cor. 15, 29.: ,Quid faciunt, qui baptizantur pro mortuis, νπερ των νεκρών, si omnino mortui non resurgent? cur igitur baptizantur pro mortuis?‘ Atqui haec consuetudo baptizandi mortuos apud quosdam in primitiva ecclesia usitata fuit, ut apparet ex Cone. Carthag. 3. cap. 6. Pontificii mortuos et sepulcra aspergunt aqua lustrali. Chrysost. homil. 1. in Act. refert, a quibusdam suo tempore etiam mortuis infusam baptismi aquam, quod ibi reprehendit ac docet, ,hoc nihil esse aliud, quam sancta in terram projicere.‘ 3Iarcionitae, referente Tertull. lib. 5. contra Mare., habebant vicarium quendam baptismum, qui vivis conferebatur loco mortuorum non baptizatorum, in testimonium articuli de resurrectione mortuorum. Sed nec Cerinthianorum nec Marcionitarum νεκροβαπτισμός ex verbis apostoli probari potest, quorum ille pugnat cum institutione et fine baptismi, hic vero cum manifestis Scripturae dictis: ,Justus sua fide vivet; impossibile est Deo placere sine fide; lignum ubi ceciderit, permanebit‘ etc. Neque vero dicit apostolus: ,Si mortui non resurgunt,, quare baptizantur mortui?‘ id quod specie quadam pro νεκρόβαππσμώ urgeri posset; sed: ,Quid faciunt illi, qui baptizantur υπέρ των νεκρών, super mortuos?‘ . . . Amplectimur simplicissimam illam expositionem de ritu baptizandi Christianos ad sepulcra mortuorum, qui symbolum fidei fuit et confessionis de resurrectione mortuorum ac de collectione et consociatione baptizatorum vivorum spirituali cum membris unius· ejusdemque corporis mystici, quin et publica professio de morte pro Christi gloria et articulo resurrectionis obeunda. Hunc autem morem in primitiva ecclesia receptum fuisse, testatur epistola ecclesiae Smyrnensis apud Eusebium lib. 4. Hist. Eccles. cap. 15., August, lib. 20. de C. D. cap. 9. et Lutherus in explic. hujusdoci.“ (L. c. § 165.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Objectum baptismi, cui is est administrandus, sunt I. soli homines; hi enim soli baptismi sunt capaces, non campanae» naves aut aliae res inanimatae, quae in papatu in nomine Patris, Filii et Spiritus S. tingi solent, impositis hominum nominibus, adhibitisque susceptoribus seu baptismi testibus; qui ritus in Caroli M. Constitutionibus a Busaeo editis p. 266. est prohibitus, ubi hoc habetur capitulum: ,Ne elocas baptizent.‘ Cf. Joh. Balaeum in Actis Rom. Pontificum, in Johanne XIV., qui campanam magnam ad Johannem Lateranensem baptizari et de suo nomine nomen ipi imponi jussit.“ (L. c. s. 2. th. 11. f. 1092.)

Gerhardus: ,,Tribuitur (a pontificiis) baptizatis campanis singularis quaedam virtus et efficacia ad expulsionem omnis diabolici insuitus, ad fuganda tonitrua et fulmina, ad salutem defunctarum animarum etc. . . Ex descriptione (rituum baptizandi campanas) facile intelligitur, quid statuendum sit de exceptione Stanislai Hosii, qui campanas a suis non baptizari, sed consecrari dicit.“ (L. c. § 166.)

Ita, ut sint caro de carne, juxta Joh. 3, 6. Christus autem, baptismo opus non habens, per eandem οΐχονομίαν baptizatus, qua circumsisus est. Conf. Matth. 4, 14. 15. 463, DE BAPTISMO.

Qui autem nondum perfecte nati sunt, renasci per baptismum, non jubentur. Universale enim est dictum Christi: Nisi quis (quisquis sit) natus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei Joh. 3, 5. et Matth. 28, 19. Christus baptizare jubet πάντα τά &%η, non solum gentiles, Judaeis contradistinctos, sed omnes populos orbis terrarum,, quos Marcus appellat omnem creaturam, cap. 16, 15. Nec solum ad ecclesiam plantandam haec spectabant, sed servari, prout doctrina aut. praedicatio evangelii, sic baptismus debet usque ad consummationem saeculi, Matth. 28, ult. Sic Lydiam baptizatam novimus ex Act. 16, 15.

Infantes baptizandos esse, recte colligitur ex locis Joh. 3, 5. et Marci 10, 14. conjunctis, hoc modo: Quoscunque Christus vult ad 8alutem pervenire, ipsi vero via ordinaria ad vitam aeternam pervenire non possunt, nisi raediante baptismo, illis baptismus, tanquam medium ordinarium, conferri, non autem denegari debet. Atqui infantes Christus vult salvos fieri (juxta Mare. 10, 14.), ipsi vero via ordinaria ad vitam aeternam pervenire non possunt, nisi mediante baptismo (vi dicti universalis Joh. 3, 5.). Ergo. Deinde etiam (2.) hoc modo: Quoscunque Christus vult sibi offerri, ut benedictione spirituali fruantur, illi per baptismum, vel ut medium ordinarium, sunt adducendi ad Christum. Atqui infantes Christus vult sibi offerri, ut benedictione spirituali fruantur (juxta Marci 10, 14., quod Lucas explicans τά βρέφη, tenerrimae aetatis liberos, quales adhuc ab uberibus matrum aut nutricum pendent, designari docet). Ergo. Porro (3.) praeceptum Matth. 28, 19. de baptizandis omnibus gentibus ad infantes etiam, qui gentium complexu continentur, recte extenditur. Et (4.) exempla,, quae docent integras familias fuisse baptizatas, v. gr. Act. 16, 25. et 33. cap. 18, 8. 1 Cor. 1, 16., recte creduntur complecti infantes, qui partem familiarum haud dubie constituerunt. Accedunt (5.) analogia circumcisionis, infantibus collatae, et (6.) quod, sicut promissio gratiae foederalis, Actor. 2, 39., ita et sigillum foederis, baptismus, ad infantes pertinet. Denique (7.) cum ecclesia tota mundata sit lavacro aquae per verbum (juxta Eph. 5, 26.), recte etiam hoc ad infantes refertur, quando et illi, natura immundi, tamen inseri debent in ecclesiam.

Quenstedtius: ,,Si istis, qui sub diluvii tempus servari voluerunt, arca necessario fuit ingredienda: etiam infantes extra casum necessitatis erunt baptizandi, ut salventur, quia ista servatio typus fuit, baptismi, 1 Pet. 3, 21. Ast prius est. Ergo.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1126.)

Lutherus: ,,Dass die Kindertaufe Christo gefalle, beweiset sich genugsam aus seinem eigenen Werk, nämlich, dass Gott deren viel heilig macht und den Heiligen Geist gegeben hat, die also getauft sind,, und heutiges Tags noch viel sind, an denen man spüret, dass sie denHeiligen Geist haben, beide der Lehre und Lebens halben; als uns von Gottes Gnaden auch gegeben ist, dass wir ja können die Schrift auslegen und Christum erkennen, welches ohne den Heiligen Geist nicht geschehen kann. Wo aber Gott die Kindertaufe nicht annähme, würde er derer keinem den Heiligen Geist noch ein Stück davon geben; Summa, es müsste so lange Zeit her bis auf diesen Tag kein Mensch auf Erden Christ sein. Weil nun Gott die Taufe bestätigt durch Eingeben seines Heiligen Geistes, als man in etlichen Vätern, als St. BernPART. III. CAP. X.


### On Baptism: Hard, Gerson, John Huss, and others who were baptized in infancy, one clearly…

Hard, Gerson, John Huss, and others who were baptized in infancy, one clearly perceives, and the holy Christian Church does not perish until the end of the world, so they must confess that such infant baptism is pleasing to God; for He certainly cannot be against Himself, or aid falsehood and knavery, nor give His grace and Spirit to it. This is almost the best and strongest proof for the simple and unlearned. For one will neither take from us nor overturn this article: ‘I believe in one holy Christian Church, the communion of saints,’ etc.” (Large Catechism. See Book of Concord, p. 492 sq.)

Melanchthon: “Since there is no reason why the baptism of infants should be disapproved, there is no need for them to be baptized again; but those who demand that we be baptized again think that baptism is a work for a certain time; namely, when you have begun to repent and believe, only then do they order baptism to be used, so that the sign may agree with the mind. What will these people do? Will they baptize as many times as those who have relapsed repent?” (On the Anabaptists. A.D. 1528. See Corpus Reformatorum, Vol. I, p. 968.)

Gerhard: “The Anabaptists object: It is a command that we first teach, then baptize; therefore, infants must be taught before they are baptized. Resp.: Christ sends His disciples to the nations, to whom nothing at all was known about baptism; therefore, instruction and information certainly had to precede; but when parents who have been rightly instructed concerning baptism have received it, the example of the apostles manifestly proves that their children also are to be baptized; and therefore a distinction must be made between a church being established and one already established, just as between adults and infants. In a church being established, adults are to be taught before they are baptized, but in a church long since established, the infants of Christians are to be baptized before they are taught. This can be declared from the sacrament of circumcision, which was a figure of baptism. Since in Genesis 17:10 Abraham circumcised all the males of his household by the power of a divine command, he undoubtedly instructed the adults first concerning this ceremony; but when Isaac was born to him, he did not wait for years of discretion in him, but circumcised him immediately on the eighth day, Gen. 21:4. Add that in the Greek text the word μαθητεύσατε, ‘make disciples,’ is used, which is done not only by the preaching of the Word in adults, but also by the administration of baptism, which is the sacrament of initiation and the first entry into the church in infants; whence these two means are expressed later in the words of Christ: ‘Make disciples,’ or gather a church for me, first ‘baptizing,’ second ‘teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you.’ Thus the word μαθητεύσατε is explained in John 4:1: ‘The Pharisees heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John.’” (L.c. § 185.)

The same: “The argument of the Anabaptists is: Christ was baptized only in the thirtieth year of His age, Matt. 3:16, Luke 3:22; now, however, every action of Christ is our instruction, Matt. 11:29, 16:24; therefore our baptism also must be deferred until the years of discretion. Resp.: 1. If Christ had wished to prescribe a certain time for baptism by the use of His own baptism, it would follow that baptism should be received only in the thirtieth year of age; but not even the Anabaptists themselves observe this, but baptize people in the very first years of discretion. Some teachers of the Anabaptists, however, contend that baptism should not be received until the 30th year of age because of this example of Christ, a matter upon which they should first settle among themselves. See Calvin, Book IV, Institutes, chap. 6, § 29. 2. Christ did not wish to be baptized in infancy because baptism had not yet been instituted, since John the Baptist first administered baptism in the 29th year of Christ. 3. Furthermore, Christ was circumcised in infancy itself, and now baptism has succeeded to the place of circumcision, Col. 2: 11. Therefore, just as Christ was circumcised in infancy, so also baptism is to be administered to infants. 4. There is a great dissimilarity between the baptism received by Christ and that received by others, which Nazianzen explains in his oration on

s. bapt., which is 40.: “Christ had no need of baptism for His own person, since He was innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners; but by His own baptism He willed to consecrate and sanctify ours; yet we stand in need of baptism in our very infancy, since we were born and conceived in sins.”

Christ could defer baptism without any danger, having the most full power over His own death and life, John 10:18…fer it without the most present danger to our salvation, since we do not know what will happen on the morrow, James 4:14. Christ willed to be baptized only then, when He was beginning His ministry, for reasons to be explained shortly; but at this time the ministry of the New Testament has long since begun, and the nations have been called to its communion." (L. c. § 193.)

The same: "The Anabaptists object: That baptism is of no benefit, nor does anyone become a participant in the benefits of Christ without repentance. Now, infants do not know how to repent. Resp.: In the same way that the Holy Spirit works faith in infants, in that same way He also excites repentance in them; now, the Holy Spirit excites faith in infants in a way incomprehensible to us, as will be demonstrated later. Therefore, repentance as well." (L. c. § 188.)

Luther: "What is strange about the Holy Spirit being effective in infants in a way that we do not understand? Although they have life, flesh, and bones, they are not nourished in the womb in the way that we, who live in this light, are nourished. Truly, therefore, the dogma of the Anabaptists is hateful and impious, who deny baptism to children for the reason that they lack sense and mind, and do not understand what is being done with them; to us they do not understand, to us they are judged to lack mind and sense, but not so to God, whose work they are. For God, just as He nourishes them in a different way than He does us, so also He moves their hearts in a different way." (In ch. 12 of Hosea. See Tom. IV. lat. f. 665.)

Cf. the things said above concerning the faith of infants, P. III. c. 3. § 12. note h. p. 158. sqq.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Socinians, who indeed admit infant baptism, but consider it a folly. 'We consider infant baptism itself as a childish and altogether indifferent matter,' says Smalcius, Exam. CLVII Err. f. 37. Err. 140...

2. Of the Anabaptists, who attack infant baptism with great tumults, contending that it has no basis in divine law, and who have derived their name from the fact that they initiated into their church with a new baptism anyone baptized in infancy who would give their name to them. For they posit that only adults, who are sufficiently imbued with Christian doctrine and are able to profess their faith with their own mouth and demand baptism themselves, are worthy of baptism; that baptism given to infant age is not the holy baptism of Christ, but the profane baptism of the Antichrist; and that all who were dipped in infancy must be rebaptized once they are older and have attained the use of reason. That infant baptism rests neither on the precept nor the example of Scripture, etc. See Colloqu. Embdan. Act. p. 82, 83, and the Frankenthal Colloquy, likewise the Confession opposed to Faukel, p. 263, 278; let Menno, the leader and torch of the Anabaptists, be compared in his book *Fundament* or *On the Foundation of the Christian Religion*, ch. on baptism...

3. Of the Calvinists, who deny that the children of unbelievers, even if they are in the power of Christians, are to be baptized; see Bucanus in *Instit. theol.* p. 624... 4. Of the Papists, who posit that infant baptism can neither be expressly taught in the Scriptures nor deduced from them by evident reason; see Bellarmine, l. 4, *de Verbo Dei*, c. 4." (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1125. sq.) §

8. Meanwhile, the infants of faithful parents, if by chance they are deprived of baptism, are regenerated and saved by the extraordinary grace of God.

we believe; however, we commit the unbaptized infants of unbelievers to the divine judgment; indeed, we do not even dare to snatch them away by force against the will of their parents and thus baptize them.

For the necessity of baptism is not absolute. On our part, we are obligated to the reception of baptism; meanwhile, however, one must not deny the extraordinary act of God in infants who are offered to Christ by pious parents and the Church through prayers and who die before the opportunity for baptism can be provided to them, since God has not so bound His grace and saving efficacy to baptism that, in a case of deprivation, He both cannot and will not act extraordinarily; these are indeed the words of the blessed Gerhard, *L. de Baptismo* § 237.

Augustine: "Contempt of the sacrament damns, not deprivation." (*Contra Donat.* IV, 22.)

Kromayer: "Between the Scylla of the Calvinists, who deny the necessity of the means, and the Charybdis of the Papists, who invent an absolute necessity of baptism, we walk a middle path, asserting the highest necessity of both the precept and the means from John 3:5, 6, yet not an absolute one." (*Theol. posit. pol.* II, 437.)

Carpzov, on the words of the Augsburg Confession, Art. 9, "Of Baptism": "That it is necessary for salvation," adds: "1. Not absolutely, but 2. by necessity of precept, and because Christ has thus ordained to save man ordinarily; and 3. by necessity of means, because it pleased Him to use this means in the application of the salvation merited by Him. It is significantly said: 'Necessity of means.' For the Calvinists, especially Alting (*Exeg. Aug. Confess.* p. 62), restrict it only to the 'necessity of rite and ceremony,' because there is no power of saving inherent in baptism, p. 63, where he even commends the altered confession for that reason. *Tom. III. Opp.*, containing the *Explic. Catech. Palatinae*, calls it 'necessity of precept' in contradistinction and opposition to the means, p. 316." (*Isag. in lib. symb.* p. 332.)

For although the determined mode of acting with the unbaptized infants of believers through extraordinary grace, and of working regeneration and faith in them, and thus applying the merit of Christ to them, is not expressly revealed in the Scriptures, nevertheless, relying on theological reasons drawn from Scripture, we can conceive a pious and undoubting hope concerning that extraordinary regeneration of those infants. See the blessed Musaeus, *Ausführliche Erklärung* Q. 61, p. 358 sqq.

Latin:

hard, Gerson, Johann Huss und andern, so in der Kindheit getauft sind, wohl spüret, und die heilige christliche Kirche nicht mitergehet bis ans Ende der Welt, so müssen sie bekennen, dass solche Kindertaufe Gott gefällig sei; denn er kann je nicht wider sich selbst sein, oder der Lüge und Büberei helfen, noch seine Gnade und Geist dazu geben. Dies ist fast die beste und stärkste Beweisung für die Einfältigen und Ungelehrten. Denn man wird uns diesen Artikel: ,Ich glaube Eine heilige christliche Kirche, die Gemeine der Heiligen‘ u.s. w. nicht nehmen noch umstossen.“ (Catechism. major. Vid. Lib. Conc. p. 492. sq.)

Melanchthon: ,,Cum nulla sit causa, cur improbetur baptismus infantium, nihil necesse est denuo baptizari; sed qui postulant, ut denuo baptizemur, hi cogitant, baptismum certi alicujus temporis opus esse; videlicet, cum coeperis agere poenitentiam et credere, tum demum jubent baptismo uti, ut signum cum animo consentiat. Quid facient isti? Totiesne baptizabunt, quoties relapsi agunt poenitentiam?“ (De Anabaptistis. A. 1528. Vid. Corp. Reform. Vol. I, p. 968.)

Gerhardus: ,,Excipiunt Anabaptistae: Mandatum esse, ut prius doceamus, postea baptizemus; prius ergo infantes docendos esse, quam baptizandos. Resp.: Ablegat Christus discipulos suos ad gentes, quibus nihil quicquam de baptismo constabat; utique ergo institutio et informatio praemitti debebat; sed quando parentes de baptismo recte instituti eundem susceperunt, etiam liberos eorum baptizandos esse, exemplum apostolorum manifeste probat; ac proinde distinguendum est inter ecclesiam constitutam et constituendam, uti et inter adultos ac infantes. In ecclesia constituenda adulti prius docendi, quam baptizandi, sed in ecclesia jam dudum constituta infantes Christianorum prius baptizandi, quam docendi. Declarari hoc potest ex sacramento circumcisionis, quae fuit figura baptismi. Cum Gen. 17, 10. omnes familiae suae masculos Abrahamus vi mandati divini circumcideret, adultos dubio procul de hac ceremonia prius instituit; sed cum Isaac ipsi nasceretur, non expectat annos discretionis in ipso, sed octavo statim die eundem circumcidit, Gen. 21, 4. Adde, quod in graeco textu habeatur vocabulum μαθητεύσατε, discipulos facite, id quod fit non solum praedicatione verbi in adultis, sed etiam administratione baptismi, qui est sacramentum initiationis et primus in ecclesiam introitus in infantibus; unde haec duo media in verbis Christi postea exprimuntur: ,Discipulos facite‘, vel ecclesiam mihi colligite, primo,baptizantes‘, secundo,docentes servare, quae ego praecepi vobis‘. Sic declaratur verbum μαθητεύσατε Joh. 4, 1.: ,Pharisaei audiverunt, Christum plures discipulos facere et baptizare, quam Johannem.‘“ (L. c. § 185.)

Idem: ,,Argumentum Anabaptistarum est: Christus trigesimo demum aetatis anno baptizatus est, Matth. 3, 16. Luc. 3, 22.; jam vero omnis Christi actio est nostra institutio, Matth. 11, 29. 16, 24.; ergo et noster baptismus ad annos discretionis differendus. Resp.: 1. Si Christus usu baptismi sui certum tempus baptizandi praescribere voluisset, consequens fuerit, non nisi trigesimo aetatis anno baptismum suscipiendum esse; id vero ne ipsi quidem Anabaptistae observant, sed in primis statim discretionis annis homines baptizant. Quidam tamen Anabaptistarum magistri contendunt, nonnisi 30. aetatis anno propter hoc exemplum Christi baptismum suscipi debere, de quo prius inter se transigant. Vide Calv. lib. IV. instit. cap. 6. § 29. 2. Ideo Christus in infantili aetate baptizari noluit, quia baptismus tunc nondum erat institutus, siquidem Johannes Baptista annb Christi 29. primum baptismum administravit. 3. Quinimo in ipsa infantia Christus est circumcisus, jam vero baptismus successit in locum circumcisionis, Col. 2,11. Ergo ut Christus in infantili aetate circumcisus, ita quoque baptismus infantibus administrandus. 4. Magna est dissimilitudo baptismi a Christo et aliis suscepti, quam exponit Nazianzenus orat, in

s. bapt., quae est 40.: ,Christus non opus habuit baptismo pro sua persona, cum fuerit innocens, impollutus et a peccatoribus segregatus; suo autem baptismo nostrum consecrare et sanctificare voluit; sed nos in ipsa infantia baptismo indigemus, cum in peccatis nati et concepti simus.‘

Christus baptismum sine ullo periculo differre potuit, mortis et vitae suae potestatem habens plenissimam, Joh. 10, 18.; nos autem sine periculo salutis praesentissimo differre eundem non possumus, cum ignoremus, quid die crastino futurum sit, Jac. 4, 14. Christus tum demum baptizari voluit, curn inchoaret ministerium propter causas paulo post exponendas; sed hoc tempore ministerium N. T. jamdudum inchoatum et gentes ad ejus communionem vocatae.“ (L. c. § 193.)

Idem: Excipiunt Anabaptistae: Baptismum non prodesse, nec quemquam beneficiorum Christi participem fieri absque poenitentia. Jam vero infantes poenitere nesciunt. Resp.: Quomodo Spiritus Sanctus fidem operatur in infantibus, eo etiam modo poenitentiam in illis excitat; jam vero Spiritus Sanctus modo nobis incomprehensibili fidem in infantibus excitat, ut postea demonstrabitur. Ergo et poenitentiam.“ (L. c. § 188.)

Lutherus: ,,Quid mirum est, Spiritum Sanctum in infantibus esse efficacem eo modo, quem nos non intelligimus? Cum habeant vitam, carnem et ossa, non tamen aluntur in utero eo modo, quo nos, qui in hac luce vivimus, alimur. Vere igitur odiosum et impium Anabaptistarum dogma est, qui ideo pueris baptismum negant, quod sensu et mente careant, nec intelligant, quae cum eis agantur; nobis non intelligunt, nobis mente et sensu judicantur carere, sed Deo non sic, cujus opus sunt. Deus enim, sicut alio modo eos alit, quam nos, ita quoque alio modo movet eorum corda.“ (In cap. 12. Hoseae. Vid. Tom. IV. lat. f. 665.)

Cf. supra dicta de fide infantum P. III. c. 3. § 12. not. h. p. 158. sqq.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: 1. Socinianorum, paedobaptismum quidem admittentium, sed pro insania habentium. ,Ipsum baptismum infantum pro re puerili et adiaphora prorsus habemus‘, inquit Smalcius Exam. CLVII Err. f. 37. Err. 140...

2. Paedobaptismum nec praecepto, nec exemplo Scripturae niti etc. Vide Colloqu. Embdan. Christ, c. de bapt. . .

3. Calvinianorum, negantium, infidelium liberos, etiamsi sint in potestate Christianorum, esse baptizandos; vide Bucanum in Instit. theol. p. 624. . . 4. Pontificiorum, qui, paedobaptismum in Scripturis nec expresse tradi, nec evidenti ratione inde deduci posse, statuunt; vide Bellarminum 1. 4. de Verbo Dei c. 4.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1125. sq.) §

8. Interim infantes parentum fidelium, baptismo forte privatos, extraordinaria Dei gratia“ regenerari et salvari1‘ 30 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III. PART. ΙΠ. CAP. X.

credimus; infidelium autem infantes non baptizatos divino judicio c committimus, imo neque eos invitis parentibus 1per vim abripere et sic baftizare audemus.d

Necessitas enim baptismi non absoluta. Ex parte nostra ad baptismi susceptionem obligati sumus; interim tamen non neganda est actw Dei extraordinaria in infantibus, Christo a piis parentibus et ecclesia per preces oblatis atque extinctis, priusquam baptismi copia illis fieri possit, cum Deus suam gratiam et salutarem efficaciam non ita alligarit baptismo, quin in casu privationis extraordinarie agere et velit et possit; quae quidem verba b. Gerhardi sunt L. de Baptismo § 237.

Augustinus: ,,Contemtus sacramenti damnat, non privatio.“ (Contra Donat. IV, 22.)

Kromayerus: ,,Inter Scyllam Calvinianam, necessitatem medii negantem, et Charybdim Pontificiam, necessitatem baptismi absolutam fingentem, via media incedimus, summam quidem tum praecepti, tum medii necessitatem ex Joh. 3, 5. 6., non tamen absolutam, asserentes.“ (Theol. posit.pol. II, 437.)

Carpzovius ad verba Augustanae Conf. art. 9. ,,De baptismo“: ,,Quod sit necessarius ad salutem“, addit: "1. Non absolute, sed 2. necessitate praecepti, et quia Christus ita instituit ordinarie hominem salvare; et 3. necessitate medii, quia placuit ei hoc medio in applicatione salutis a se promeritae uti. Significanter dicitur: ,Necessitate medii.‘ Nam Calviniani, imprimis Alting. Exeg. Aug. Confess. p. 62., non nisi ad,necessitatem ritus ac ceremoniae‘ adstringunt, quia non insit ulla vis salvandi baptismo, p. 63., ubi mutatam confessionem propterea etiam commendat. Tom. III. Opp., continente Explic. Catech. Palatinae, ,necessitatem praecepti‘ vocat in contradistinctione ac oppositione medii, p. 316.“ (Isag. in lib. symb. p. 332.)

Quanquam enim determinatus modus agendi cum infantibus fidelium non baptizatis per gratiam extraordinariam et operandi in illis regenerationem et fidem, atque ita meritum Christi iis applicandi, non sit expresse in Scripturis revelatus, tamen rationibus theologicis, ex Scriptura petitis, nixi, spem piam neque dubiam concipere possumus de regeneratione illa extraordinaria infantum illorum. Vid. b. Musaeus Ausführliche Erklärung Q. 61. p. 358. sqq.


### On Baptism: Thus also the blessed Gerhard, *l

Thus also the blessed Gerhard, *l. c.*: Concerning infants born in the Church, he says, we hope for the better. And a little later: We neither can nor ought to rashly condemn those infants who are extinguished either in the maternal womb or by some sudden accident before the reception of baptism; rather, we maintain that the prayers of pious parents, or, if the parents have been negligent in this regard, the prayers of the Church poured out to God for these infants are mercifully heard, and that they are received by God into grace and life. And he brings forward several arguments to this effect in § 238, 239. However, he does not equally touch upon the determined mode of acting by which God might use extraordinary grace.

Luther: "Christ lets it suffice that He says in the first part of this passage: 'He who believes and is baptized'; and in the second: 'But he who does not believe,' etc., [He] does not repeat baptism; surely because it is sufficiently indicated by the first and commanded further elsewhere, as in Matthew 28:19: 'Teach all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father,' etc. And it does not follow from that—"
