Docentque Calvinisequae, ,baptismum (quem vocant, externum) esse tantum nudum signum, symbolum et sigillum regenerationis, non autem ejusdem medium.‘ Adeoque virtutem regenerandi, peccata remittendi et salvandi baptismo simpliciter adimunt, totum ejus finem et effectum ponentes in significando, repraesentando, testificando etc. Zwinglius in Confess. ad Carolum V. a. 7. scribit: ,Credo, imo scio, omnia sacramenta tantum abesse, ut gratiam conferant, ut ne afferant quidem aut dispensent.‘ Idem ait t. 2. p. 96. ,Externum quiddam est (baptismus) et ceremoniale, quo, ut aliis rebus externis, ecclesia digne et honeste uti potest, vel idem hoc omittere et rite tollere, quatenus ipsi ad aedificationem et salutem omnium facere videtur.‘ Confess. Belgica p. 96. ita habet: ,Significat aqua, sanguinem Christi per Spiritum S. idem praestare et efficere interne in anima, quod aqua externe operatur in corporibus.‘ . . Beza in Actis Colloq. Mompelgart. P. 2. p. 115. vocat,errorem palpabilem, ex foetidis Scholasticorum lacunis haustum, si vis conferendae gratiae principalis quidem Deo, Instrumentalis autem sacramentis tribuatur.‘ Johannes Gryneus P. 1. Theol. Theorem, in praefat. ait: ,Evangelio, baptismo et eucharistiae tribuitur remissio peccatorum cohonestandi causa.‘ Admonitio Neostadiens. c. 2. p. 510.: ,Baptismus signum tantum est et testimonium regenerationis.‘

ß. Socinianorum, statuentium, ,baptismum Spiritum S. non conferre, nec regenerationis et salutis medium, sed nudam externam humanam ecclesiasticam ceremoniam, omnis divinae operationis expertem esse.‘ . .

y. Arminianorum, qui de efficacia et usu baptismi non sentiunt honorificentius, quam praedicti Sociniani; vide eorum Confessionem cap. 23. sect. 3., Episcopium disp. 29. th. 8. Contendunt enim, quod,baptismus ex parte Dei tantum sit gratiae quaedam significatio, ex parte nostri solum publica nominis Christi professio.‘ Sic enim Episcopius loc. jam alleg.: ,Effectus sive finis baptismi non est realis aliqua gratiae collatio, sed tantum sola divinae gratiae et professionis nostrae significatio.‘ δ.

Ad peccantes in defectu referendi quoque Pontificii, qui baptismum appellant primam tabulam post naufragium, sicut lapsis post baptismum regenerationis illud lavacrum non prosit, sed eo tantum momento, quo baptizantur. Volunt ergo, quod gratiae foedere fracto alio indigeamus remedio et tabula alia, nostra nempe contritione et satisfactione, cujus ope ad salutis portum enatemus. Vide Concil. Trident, can. 20. de bapti3., Bellarm. de baptis. 1. 1. c.,18.“

10. Hic autem, quod ad finem proximum attinet, diversitas occurrit, respectu subjectorum diversorum. Nam infantibus quidem aeque omnibus a per baptismum primum b confertur et obsignatur c fides,d per quam meritum Christi illis applicetur. Adultis vero illis tantum, qui fidem ex verbo e conceperunt ante baptismi f susceptionem, baptismus eam obsignat et confirmat. Nec solum nunc, quando suscipitur, sed et postea, ac per omnem g vitam, fidelibus efficaciter prodest ad confirmationem h fidei et renovationem 1 ulteriorem.k Neque enim per aetatem possunt obicem ponere aut malitiose repugnare gratiae divinae adeoque mediis gratiae in usu constitutis, neque impeditis, gratiam utique statim obtinent. Hactenus enim natura immundi et filii irae sunt, non autem sancti coram Deo, velut jure nativitatis ex parentibus fidelibus. Huc enim se non porrigit gratia foederalis.


### On Baptism: Luther: "Furthermore, St

Luther: "Furthermore, St. Paul speaks in 1 Cor. 7:14: 'For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the [believing] wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the [believing] husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are holy.' That is spoken in the Hebrew manner and after St. Paul’s style, that to him who is holy, all things are holy, as he says in Tit. 1:15: 'To the pure all things are pure'; and Rom. 8:28: 'All things work together for the good of the saints.' And he means to say: A Christian spouse must not divorce, but can well remain with his non-Christian spouse, and also beget and raise children with non-Christians. The reason is this: If the non-Christian spouse does not hinder his Christian spouse from living as a Christian, then faith is such a powerful thing that it does not harm him to be with non-Christians, and it is all the same to him whether that with which he associates is holy or not holy. . . . Thus the children are also holy, even if they are not yet baptized nor are they Christians. They are not holy in their own person—of which holiness St. Paul does not speak here—but to you they are holy, so that your holiness can associate with them and raise them, so that you are not defiled by them, as if they were an unholy thing. For St. Paul means to say: If a Christian spouse had grown children with a non-Christian spouse (as often happened at that time) and the children did not yet want to be baptized or become Christians—since no one should be forced to faith, but should be drawn willingly by God through the Gospel—then the mother or father should not for that reason abandon the children, nor withdraw or deny maternal or paternal duty, as if they were committing sin thereby and defiling themselves with the unbelieving children; but they should provide for them bodily and care for them, just as if they were the most holy Christians. For they are not unclean nor unholy (he says), that is, your faith can exercise itself upon them, so that it remains pure and holy." (Exposition of the 7th Chapter of the 1st Epistle of St. Paul to the Corinthians. Anno 1523. VIII, 1111. sqq.) PART III. CAP. X.

Kromayerus: "The Calvinists also undermine original sin indirectly, when they teach that the children of Christians are holy from their mother’s womb, before they are even baptized, and are established in grace and in covenant with God. However, although they do not deny the corruption of nature through the sin of our first parents, they nevertheless deny the guilt of it, by denying that they are born children of wrath and liable to eternal damnation. Spiritual, federal, and ecclesiastical holiness differ. Spiritual holiness is the excitation of good motions produced by the Holy Spirit, from which the fruits of the Spirit described in Galatians 5 spring forth. Both we and the Reformed deny this to the children of Christians before they are baptized. Federal holiness is the reception into grace with God, or the establishment in a covenant with God. The Reformed attribute this to the children of Christians even before baptism; we deny it. ... It must be noted, however, that the Calvinists do not understand what we have said about federal holiness as applying to all children of Christians, but only to those absolutely elected to eternal life." (Th. posit.polem. I, 501 sq.)

Gerhardus: (The Calvinists retort:) "The infants of believers are in God’s covenant before baptism, by virtue of the divine promise in Genesis 17:7: 'I will be your God and the God of your seed.' Therefore, they are not received into the covenant of grace through baptism, but the seal of a benefit already received is given to them. Resp. 1. The infants of believers are no less than others 'by nature children of wrath' (Eph. 2:3), 'conceived and born in sins' (Ps. 51:5), 'born of unclean seed' (Job 14:4), and are 'flesh born of flesh' (John 3:6); how, then, are they actually in the covenant of grace before the use of baptism? 2. The statement in Genesis 17:7 contains a notable promise of grace, that God wills to receive the seed of Abraham—and thus the seed of all those who are of the faith of Abraham—into His covenant, not without a certain medium, nor because of a carnal birth from believing parents, but in the Old Testament through the sacrament of circumcision, and in the New Testament through the sacrament of baptism. Hence, in verse 10, it is expressly added: 'This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised.' In verse 14, the threat is added: 'The uncircumcised male, who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant.' 3. In Acts 2:39, an illustrious explanation of this saying is proposed: 'Repent,' says Peter in verse 38, 'and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Christ'; in verse 39, he adds causally: 'For the promise is to you and to your children.' If the infants of Israelites had been in God’s covenant by virtue of that promise before circumcision in the Old Testament and before baptism in the New Testament, how could Peter have exhorted them to receive baptism by bringing forward this very promise as the reason? 4. Therefore, by virtue of that promise, the infants of believers have access to circumcision in the Old Testament and to baptism in the New Testament; and if by some chance they should depart from this life before receiving the sacrament of initiation, divine grace, by virtue of the same promise, extraordinarily works regeneration and salvation in them; yet from this it cannot be inferred that baptism is not the ordinary medium of regeneration and salvation." (Loc. de bapt. § 122.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: Of the Calvinists, who teach that the children of believing parents are born holy, immune from all guilt, pleasing to God, and accepted by hereditary right from their mother’s womb—indeed, that even before they are born, they are contained in the covenant and are in the people of God. They teach that the very propagation from pious parents opens to them an access to salvation, and that the right to eternal life is acquired for them by being born of pious parents. Thus Calvin, Inst. 4.5.20: 'But, you say, there is a danger that he who is ill may be deprived of the grace of regeneration if he departs without baptism. By no means; God declares that He adopts our infants as His own (NB) before they are born, when He promises that He will be God to us and to our seed after us. In this word their salvation is contained,' etc. ... The same Calvin"

1. 4. Inst. c. 16. sect. 24. teaches: "An infant, born of a faithful parent, is contained in the covenant by hereditary right according to the formula of the promise, even from the mother’s womb." Likewise: "Because infants derive their origin from Christians, they are received by God into the inheritance of the covenant as soon as they are born." Likewise 1. 4. c. 15. s. 22.: "The children of faithful parents are not baptized so that they may then first become children of God, having previously been strangers to the church, but rather they are received into the church by a solemn sign because, by the benefit of the promise, they already belonged to the body of Christ.". . . The public Confessions of the Reformed churches propose similar things. (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 1156. sq.)

For it is the seal of the covenant of grace, just as circumcision was of old, in whose place it succeeded. And indeed, faith is proper to infants, consisting not in an idle habit, but in spiritual acts and motions, though not sufficiently explicable, yet certain. Cf. what we said in Chapter III, § 11, note c, and 12, note b. Nor indeed should it be thought that the actual benefit of regeneration or the conferring of faith in infants is deferred until the years of discretion, and that they are nevertheless received into grace in the meantime; but it must be believed that when baptism is conferred upon them, they are simultaneously regenerated and faith is produced in them.

Frankius: "Admittedly, it cannot be denied that differences prevailed among the authors of the Confession regarding the appropriation of baptismal grace to the children to be baptized, insofar as Andreä, on the basis of the presupposition that baptism is of no use without faith, allowed the latter to be given to children in and at baptism, but not through it; Chemnitz, on the other hand (?), leans toward the view represented by Melanchthon—but also once expressed by Luther in his later period (?)—which later became common in Lutheran theology, that by means of baptism itself faith, without which baptism is indeed of no use, is bestowed upon children. . . . I intentionally say no more than that Chemnitz leans toward this view. For even in the *Examen Concilii Tridentini* II, 90 ff., he contents himself with asserting the children's own faith at baptism (*in baptismo, parvuli, qui baptizantur, dum baptizantur*)." (Die Th. der Concordienf. IV, 211. sq. 304.)

Luther: "Secondly, as I hear from your reports, baptism is also correct among you, without that giving me great concern, that you baptize young children upon a future faith, which they are to learn when they come to reason; not upon a present one: for you hold that young children do not believe (as I am informed), and yet you baptize them. There I have said: It would be better to baptize no child at all anywhere than to baptize without faith, since the Sacrament and God’s holy name are thereby used in vain, which is a great thing to me. For the Sacraments should and cannot be received without faith, or they are received to greater harm. On the contrary, we hold according to the words of Christ, 'He who believes and is baptized,' etc., that faith must be present before or at least at the same time when one baptizes, or else it becomes a mere mockery of divine Majesty, as if He were present and offering grace, and no one were receiving it. Therefore we believe that young children are cleansed from unbelief and the devil through the faith and prayer of the Church and are endowed with faith and thus baptized; because such a gift was also given to children through the circumcision of the Jews; otherwise Christ would not have said in Matthew 19:14: 'Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.' Without faith, however, no one has the kingdom of heaven. And where one could overturn this opinion of ours, as I think it cannot be overturned— PART III. CHAPTER X. should happen, I would rather not teach a child to be baptized, for (as has been said) that one should baptize him without faith; for one should not take God’s name in vain, even if the salvation of the whole world depended upon it.” (On the Worship of the Sacrament. A. 1523. XIX, 1625.) Cf. what was noted above on Part III, c. 3, § 11, p. 156 sq.)

Latin:

Lutherus: ״Weiter spricht St. Paulus 1 Kor. 7, 14.: ,Denn der ungläubige Mann ist geheiligt durch das [gläubige] Weib, und das nngläubige Weib ist geheiligt durch den [gläubigen] Mann. Sonst wären eure Kinder unrein; aber nun sind sie heilig.‘ Das ist auf ebräische Weise, und nach St. Pauli Art geredt, dass dem, der da heilig ist, sind alle Dinge heilig, wie er spricht Tit. 1, 15.: ,Dem Reinen ist alles rein‘; und Röm. 8, 28.: ,Alle Dinge dienen den Heiligen zum Besten.‘ Und will also sagen: Ein Christengemahl darf sich nicht scheiden, sondern kann wohl bleiben bei seinem Unchristengemahl, und auch Unchristen״ kinder zeugen und aufziehen. Ursach ist die: Wenn der unchristliche Gemahl seinem christlichen Gemahl nicht wehret, christlich zu leben, so ist der Glaube so ein mächtig Ding, dass ihm nicht schadet, bei Un״ Christen zu sein, und gilt ihm gleich so viel, es sei heilig oder nicht heilig, damit er umgehet. . . . Also sind die Kinder auch heilig, ob sie gleich nicht getauft, noch Christen sind. Nicht sind sie heilig an ihrer eignen Person; von welcher Heiligkeit St. Paulus hier nicht redet; sondern dir sind sie heilig, dass deine Heiligkeit mit ihnen kann um״ gehen und sie aufziehen, dass du an ihnen nicht entheiliget wirst, gleich als wären sie ein unheilig Ding. Denn St. Paulus will also sagen: Wenn ein christlich Gemahl grosse Kinder hätte mit einem nnchristliehen Gemahl (wie es dazumal oft geschah) und die Kinder sich noch nicht wollten taufen lassen, noch Christen werden; sintemal niemand soll zum Glauben gezwungen, sondern von Gott williglich gezogen werden durchs Evangelium; so soll darum die Mutter oder der Vater die Kinder nicht lassen, noch mütterliche oder väterliche Pflicht entziehen oder versagen, als thäten sie Sünde daran und sich verunreinigten an den ungläubigen Kindern; sondern sollen ihnen leiblich vorstehen und sie versorgen, ebensowohl, als wären sie die allerheiligsten Christen. Denn sie sind nicht unrein noch unheilig (spricht er), das ist, dein Glaube kann sich an ihnen üben, dass er rein nnd heilig bleibe.“ (Ausl, des 7. Kap. der 1. Ep. St. Pauli an die Kor. Anno 1523. VIII, 1111. sqq.) PART. IH. CAP. X.

Kromayerus: ,,Per indirectum peccatum originale labefactant quoque Calviniani, cum Christianorum liberos ab utero matris, priusquam adhuc baptizentur, sanctos, in gratia et foedere cum Deo constitutos docent. Quantumvis autem corruptionem naturae per peccatum primorum parentum non negent, reatu tamen per hoc ipsum, quod filios irae, damnationis aeternae reos nasci negent. Differunt sanctitas spiritualis, foederalis et ecclesiastica. Sanctitas spiritualis est motuum bonorum a Sp. S. facta excitatio, ex qua progeminant fructus Spiritus ad Gal. 5. descripti. Hanc et nos et Reformati Christianorum liberis, antequam baptizentur, denegamus. Sanctitas foederalis est in gratiam cum Deo receptio, vel in foedere cum Deo constitutio. Hanc Reformati Christianorum liberis adhuc ante baptismum tribuunt, nos negamus. ... Notandum vero, non de omnibus Christianorum liberis, sed tantum de absolute ad vitam aeternam electis, quod de sanctitate foederali diximus, Calvinianos intelligere.“ (Th. posit.polem. I, 501. sq.)

Gerhardus: (Calviniani regerunt:),,Infantes fidelium ante baptismum sunt in Dei foedere, vi divinae promissionis Gen. 17, 17.: ,Ero Deus tuus et Deus seminis tui.‘ Ergo non per baptismum in foedus gratiae recipiuntur, sed beneficii jam ante accepti sigillum ipsis datur. Resp. 1. Infantes fidelium non minus ac reliqui sunt,natura filii irae‘ Ephes. 2, 3., ,concepti et nati in peccatis‘ Psal. 51, 7., ,ex immundo semine geniti‘ Job. 14, 4., ,sunt caro de carne‘ Joh. 3, 6.; quomodo ergo actu sunt in foedere gratiae ante baptismi usum? 2. Dictum Gen. 17, 17. continet insignem promissionem gratiae, quod Deus semen Abrahae, adeoque semen eorum omnium, qui sunt ex fide Abrahae, in foedus suum recipere velit, non sine certo quodam medio, vel ob carnalem ex fidelibus parentibus nativitatem, sed in V. Testamento per sacramentum circumcisionis, in N. Testamento per sacramentum baptismi, unde v. 10. diserte additur: ,Hoc autem foedus meum, quod servabitis inter me et vos et semen vestrum, circumcidetur in vobis omne masculinum‘, v. 14. additur comminatio: ,Masculus, cujus praeputii caro non circumciditur, ejus anima eradicabitur ex populo suo, eo quod foedus meum fecerit irritum.‘ 3. Actor. 2, 39. proponitur illustris hujus dicti explicatio: ,Poenitentiam agite‘, inquit Petrus v. 38., ,et baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Christi‘; v. 39. αιτιολογ/,κώς addit: ,Vobis enim facta est promissio et liberis vestris.‘ Si infantes Israelitarum vi illius promissionis ante circumcisionem in V. et ante baptismum in N. T. fuissent in Dei foedere, quomodo Petrus ad baptismum suscipiendnm eos fuisset cohortatus adducta rationis loco hac ipsa promissione? 4. Ergo vi illius promissionis infantes fidelium habent aditum ad circumcisionem in V. et baptismum in N. T., ac si casu quodam contingat, ipsos ante susceptum initiationis sacramentum e vita decedere, divina gratia vi ejusdem promissionis extraordinarie in illis regenerationem et salutem operatur; ex eo tamen non potest inferri, quod baptismus non sit ordinarium regenerationis ac salutis medium.“ (Loc. de bapt. § 122.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: Calvinianorum, qui docent, liberos fidelium parentum nasci sanctos, ab omni reatu immunes, Deo gratos, acceptos haereditario jure a matris utero, imo antequam nascantur, contineri in foedere et esse in populo Dei. Ipsam ex piis parentibus propagationem aperire ipsis aditum ad salutem, jus vitae aeternae ipsis acquiri ex piis parentibus nascendo. Sic Calvinus 1. 4. Instit. c. 5. s. 20.: ,At, inquis, periculum est, ne is, qui aegrotat, si absque baptismo discesserit, regenerationis gratia privetur. Minime vero; inf antes nostros, antequam nascantur, se (NB.) adoptare in suos, pronunciat Deus, cum se nobis in Deum fore promittit, seminique nostro post nos. Hoc verbo continetur eorum salus‘ etc. . . . Idem Calvinus

1. 4. Inst. c. 16. sect. 24. docet: ,Infantem, ex fideli parente progenitum, haereditario jure secundum promissionis formulam jam a matris utero in foedere contineri.‘ Item: ,Quia a Christianis originem ducunt infantes, in foederis haereditatem statim, ac nati sunt, a Deo excipiuntur.‘ Item 1. 4. c. 15. s. 22.: ,Non ideo baptizantur fidelium parentum liberi, ut filii Dei tum primum fiant, qui antea alieni fuerint ab ecclesia, sed solenni potius signo in ecclesiam ideo recipiuntur, quia promissionis beneficio jam ante ad Christi corpus pertinebant.‘ . . . Similia proponunt publicae reformatarum ecclesiarum Confessiones.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 9. f. 1156. sq.)

Est enim sigillum foederis gratiae, prout olim circumcisio, in cujus locum successit. Ac fides quidem infantibus propria, neque in habitu otioso, sed actibus et motibus spiritualibus, licet non satis explicabilibus, certis tamen, consistens. Conf., quae diximus cap. III. § 11. not. c. et 12. not. b. Nec sane putandum est, actuale regenerationis beneficium aut collationis fidei in infantibus usque ad annos discretionis differri, interim illos nihilominus in gratiam recipi, sed, cum baptismus eis confertur, simul eos regenerari et fidem in eis produci, credendum est.

Frankius: ״Zwar lässt sich nicht leugnen, dass über die Aneignung der Taufgnade an die zu taufenden Kinder auch unter den Verfassern des Bekenntnisses insofern Differenzen obwalteten, als Andreä auf Grund der Voraussetzung, dass die Taufe nichts nütze sei ohne den Glauben, letzeren in und bei der Taufe, aber nicht durch dieselbe den Kindern geschenkt werden liess, Chemnitx dagegen (?) der von Melanchthon vertretenen, aber auch von Luther in seiner spätem Zeit einmal ausgesprochenen (?), nachher in der lutherischen Theologie gewöhnlichen, Anschauung sich zuneigt, dass mittelst der Taufe selbst der Glaube, ohne welchen die Taufe allerdings nichts nütze, den Kindern verliehen werde. . . . Absichtlich sage ich nicht mehr, als dass Chemnitz sich dieser Anschauung zuneige. Denn noch in dem Examen Trident. Cone: II, 90. ff. begnügt er sich, den eignen Glauben der Kinder bei der Taufe (in baptismo, parvuli, qui baptizantur, dum baptizantur) zu behaupten.“ (Die Th. der Concordienf. IV, 211. sq. 304.)

Lutherus: ״Aufs andere, wie ich von euren Geschickten höre, so ist die Taufe auch recht bei euch, ohne dass mir das eine grosse Bewegung gibt, dass ihr die jungen Kinder täufet auf zukünftigen Glauben, den sie lernen sollen, wenn sie zur Vernunft kommen; nicht auf gegenwärtigen: denn ihr haltet, die jungen Kinder gläuben nicht (wie sie mich bericht), und taufet sie dennoch. Da habe ich gesagt: Es wäre besser, gar überall kein Kind taufen, denn ohne Glauben taufen, sintemal daselbst das Sacrament und Gottes heiliger Name vergebens wird gebraucht, welches mir ein Grosses ist. Denn die Sacrament sollen und können ohne Glauben nicht empfangen werden, oder werden zu grösserm Schaden empfangen. Dagegen halten wir nach den Worten Christi: ,Wer da glaubet und getauft wird‘ u. s. w., dass zuvor oder je zugleich Glaube da sein muss, wenn man täuft, oder ein lauter Spott göttlicher Majestät daraus werde, als die da gegenwärtig sei und Gnade anbiete, und niemand nehme sie an. Darum achten wir, die jungen Kinder werden durch der Kirchen Glauben und Gebet vom Unglauben und Teufel gereinigt und mit dem Glauben begabt und also getauft; weil solche Gabe auch durch Beschneidung der Juden den Kindern gegeben ward; sonst hätte Christus Matth. 19, 14. nicht gesagt: ,Lasset die Kindlein zu mir kommen, solcher ist das Himmelreich.‘ Ohne Glauben aber hat niemand das Himmelreich. Und wo man solche unsere Meinung könne umstossen, als ich achte nicht umPART. m. CAP. X. zustossen sei, wollte ich lieber kein Kind taufen lehren, denn (wie gesagt) dass man es ohne Glauben taufen sollte; denn Gottes Namen soll man nicht umsonst brauchen, obgleich aller Welt Seligkeit daran läge.“ (Vom Anbeten des Sacraments. A. 1523. XIX, 1625.) Cf. quae supra adnotata sunt ad Part. III., c. 3. § 11. p. 156. sq.)


### On Baptism: Apologia A. C.: “Confirmation and extreme unction are rites received from the…

Apologia A. C.: “Confirmation and extreme unction are rites received from the fathers, which not even the church requires as necessary for salvation, because it does not have a command of God.” (Art. XIII, § 6, p. 203.)

Chemnitius: “Our people have often shown that the rite of confirmation, once useless, superstitious, and unscriptural traditions are removed, can be used piously and for the edification of the church, in accordance with the consensus of Scripture, in this way: namely, that those who were baptized in infancy (for such is the current state of the church), when they have reached the years of discretion, should be diligently instructed in a certain and simple catechism of the church’s doctrine. And when they seem to have moderately grasped the basics, they should afterwards be presented to the bishop and the church, and there the child, baptized in infancy, should first be admonished by a brief and simple reminder concerning his baptism—namely, by whom he was baptized, how, why, and into what he was baptized, what the whole Trinity conferred upon and sealed to him in that baptism, namely, the covenant of peace and the pact of grace, and how there the renunciation of Satan, the profession of faith, and the promise of obedience were made. Second, the child himself should give his own public profession of this doctrine and faith before the church. Third, he should be questioned on the principal heads of the Christian religion, answer to each, or, if he understood anything less well, be more correctly instructed. Fourth, he should be admonished and show by this profession that he dissents from all heathen, heretical, fanatical, and profane opinions. Fifth, a grave and serious exhortation from the Word of God should be added, that he might persevere in the covenant of baptism and in that doctrine and faith, and be confirmed by progressing continually. Sixth, a public prayer should be made for those children, that God might deign to govern, preserve, and confirm them in this profession by His Holy Spirit. To this prayer, the laying on of hands could be applied without superstition. Nor would that prayer be empty, for it rests upon the promises concerning the gift of perseverance and the grace of confirmation. Such a rite of confirmation would confer very much utility for the edification of the youth and the whole church; it would also be consistent with both Scripture and the purer antiquity.” (Exam. Concil. Trid. ed. Genev. f. 258 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Vilmarius: “Confirmation, absolution, and ordination can be called sacramental acts, i.e., such as are preparations and conditions for the power of eternal life to be communicated by God, which proceed from God and therefore must not be omitted by men. Confirmation (Firmung) is represented in its foundation in Acts 8:14–17 and 19:6. It is a laying on of hands for the communication of the Holy Spirit under prayer; it follows baptism as a strengthening of the germ of life received in baptism (as it were, to use an apostolic image, as the watering belonging to the planting), thus not merely as an external confirmation of baptism, but indeed especially as an implantation of charisms, and can therefore only be given to and received by one who is prepared to effect the appropriation of baptismal grace. Thus it was also regarded in the church as an entry into the army of Christ (Ps. 110), the *militia Christi*... In confirmation, as has been said, the direction of the will to allow the Holy Spirit to be communicated belongs to the reception of the Holy Spirit, so that if the direction of the will of the one to be confirmed toward this reception is lacking, the act must (subjectively) become void; but it also requires that the one being confirmed be filled with the Holy Spirit, if not the con firmed person makes themselves guilty of a sin against the Holy Spirit, or at least wishes to prepare such a one within themselves. That, however, the communication of the Holy Spirit can also occur through the action of an unbeliever, must not be denied unconditionally, and least of all here, because the communication of the Holy Spirit is also mediated through prayer, and indeed the prayer of the congregation.” (Dogmatik. Gütersloh 1874. II, 227. sq.) See Acts 2:41; ch. 8:12, 36, 37, 38; 16:14, 15, 31, 33; 18:8.

Gerhardus: “We demonstrate that adults who are to be instructed in the Christian religion must embrace and profess the same before they are admitted to baptism: 1. From the sequence of the words of institution in Matthew 28:19: ‘Go, teach all nations, and baptize them,’ where Christ first commands to teach, and only afterwards to baptize; Mark 16:15, 16: ‘Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized will be saved.’ 2. From the example of John the Baptist and the apostles; for they first taught their hearers, and afterwards baptized them. Matthew 3:1; Luke 3:3: ‘In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea; then Jerusalem and all Judea went out to him, etc. And they were baptized by him in the Jordan.’ Acts 2:38: Peter first preaches repentance, and only afterwards baptizes those who receive his word. ‘As many as received his word were baptized,’ v. 41. Therefore, by the contrary sense, those who did not receive his word, but contradicted it, were not baptized. Join Acts 8:12, 13, 38; 9:17; 10:44; 16:14, 15, 32; 18:8, where the perpetual practice of the apostles shows that instruction must precede the baptism of adults. 3. From the type of circumcision. For since not only Isaac, but also the rest of the household of Abraham were circumcised, there is no doubt that the holy patriarch first informed them about this rite; otherwise they would never have undertaken circumcision, joined as it was with such bitterness of pain. Genesis 18:19: ‘For I know that Abraham will command his children and his household after him, that they keep the way of the Lord, and do justice and judgment.’ Thus, children are commanded to be instructed by their parents regarding the rite of the paschal lamb, Exodus 12:26, 27: ‘When your children say to you, What is this service? you shall say to them, It is the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passover,’ etc. 4. From necessity itself. For since baptism is a new ceremony of the New Testament, it was certainly necessary that John the Baptist and the apostles first inform their hearers about its divine institution, use, and efficacy. 5. From the nature of the sacraments, which are seals of divine promises. For just as the tables of the covenant and the letters of contracts are written first, and only afterwards are the seals appended: so hearers must first be informed about the divine promises before the same are sealed in them by the use of the sacraments. 6. From the analogy of the Word. Just as the Word of God is not to be preached to those who furiously and violently reject it; Matthew 7:6: ‘Do not give what is holy to the dogs.’ Matthew 10:14: ‘If anyone does not receive you, nor hear your words, depart from that city.’ Acts 13:46: ‘Because you repel the word, etc., behold, we turn to the Gentiles’: so, much less are the sacraments to be forced upon the unwilling.” (L. c. § 175.)

Apology of the Augsburg Confession: “Thirdly, James said a little before concerning regeneration, that it happens through the gospel. For thus he says (1:18): ‘Of his own will he begat us with the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.’ When he says that we are reborn by the gospel, he teaches that we are reborn and justified by faith.” (Concord. ed. Mueller. p. 130.)

Cf. what has been noted on the preceding § concerning regeneration effected by the Word. Otherwise, however, if they lack faith and thus resist divine grace, they will not receive spiritual goods, nor will they be regenerated or renewed. 31

Baier’s Compendium, ed. Walther. III. PART III. CHAPTER X.

Dietericus: "If baptism is the washing of regeneration, are all the baptized regenerated in the same way? No; for a distinction must be made here between infants and adults. Indeed, all and every infant who is baptized according to the institution of Christ is regenerated; but not all adults, only those who believe and do not resist the operation of the Holy Spirit. Regarding the former, there are testimonies: 'All of us who have been baptized into Christ,' etc. (Rom. 6:3); 'As many of you as have been baptized have put on Christ' (Gal. 3:27). Regarding the latter: 'He who believes and is baptized,' etc. (Mark 16:16). But what is to be determined concerning adult hypocrites who are baptized, who do not believe? A distinction must be made here between the substance and the fruit of baptism. An adult hypocrite, if he is baptized, truly receives baptism as to its substance, but he by no means perceives the salutary fruit and effect, which happens only to the faithful, as long as he persists in hypocrisy." (Institut. catechet. p. 763.)

Theologians of Wittenberg: "We reject as erroneous and false that D. Huber pretends that regeneration belongs to the substance and essence of holy baptism, whereas the Holy Spirit in Scripture, as well as the Children’s Catechism, refers the same to the effect, fruit, and salutary benefit of baptism. Secondly, that even unbelieving hypocrites, when they are baptized in their adulthood in the midst of such unbelief, not only receive the true baptism (which we also hold), but that they are furthermore born anew of God and truly cleansed from sins. Item, that the same hypocrites, even if they are not truly converted when they receive baptism, nevertheless (by virtue of the institution) have certainly and truly received regeneration and grace (that God has adopted them as children) in holy baptism. Item, that they receive regeneration without the renewal of the Holy Spirit, which is an absurd, manifest contradiction that refutes itself. Item, that such godless hypocrites have also been accepted in baptism as children of God by virtue of the institution, even in the midst of impenitence, and have been counted among the children of God. Item, that the same, according to D. Huber’s teaching, are at once and at the same time children of God, and yet, while they are thus children of God, such grace of sonship results in their judgment. Which mixing of the substance and the benefit of baptism, separation of regeneration and renewal in the Holy Spirit, reception of regeneration without conversion, reception without faith in Christ, and grace of sonship resulting in judgment, we clearly and roundly reject and condemn as unheard-of paradoxes and palpable contradictions, of which no apostle ever dreamed." (Bekenntniss v. d. ew. Gnadenwahl. A. 1597. Vid. Consil. Witeberg. I, 642.)

Latin:

Apologia A. C.: ,, Confirmatio et extrema unctio sunt ritus accepti a patribus, quos ne ecclesia quidem unquam necessarios ad salutem: requirit, quia non habet mandatum Dei.“ (Art. XIII. § 6. p. 203.)

Chemnitius: ,,Nostri saepe ostenderunt, ritum confirmationis, remotis inutilibus, superstitiosis et cum Scriptura pugnantibus traditionibus, pie et ad ecclesiae aedificationem, juxta Scripturae consensum, hoc modo posse usurpari, ut scilicet illi, qui in infantia baptizati sunt (talis enim nunc est ecclesiae status), cum ad annos discretionis pervenissent, diligenter in certa et simplici catechesi doctrinae ecclesiae instituerentur. Et cum initia mediocriter percepisse viderentur, postea episcopo et ecclesiae offerrentur, atque ibi puer, in infantia baptizatus, primo brevi et simplici commonefactione admoneretur de suo baptismo, quo scilicet sit baptizatus, quomodo, quare et in quid sit baptizatus, quid in illo baptismo tota Trinitas ipsi contulerit et obsignarit, foedus scilicet pacis et pactum gratiae, quomodo ibi facta sit abrenunciatio satanae, professio fidei et promissio obedientiae. Secundo, puer ipse coram ecclesia ederet propriam et publicam professionem hujus doctrinae et fidei. Tertio, interrogaretur de praecipuis Christianae religionis capitibus, ad singula responderet, aut, si quid minus intelligeret, rectius erudiretur. Quarto, admoneretur et hac professione ostenderet, se dissentire ab omnibus ethnicis, haereticis, fanaticis et profanis opinionibus. Quinto, adderetur gravis et seria exhortatio ex verbo Dei, ut in pacto baptismi et in illa doctrina et fide perseveraret et proficiendo subinde confirmaretur. Sexto, fleret publica precatio pro illis pueris, ut Deus Spiritu suo sancto illos in hac professione gubernare, conservare et confirmare dignaretur. Ad quam precationem sine superstitione adhiberi posset impositio manuum. Nec inanis esset ea precatio, nititur enim promissionibus de dono perseverantiae et gratia confirmationis. Talis ritus confirmationis valde multum utilitatis ad aedificationem juventutis et totius ecclesiae conferret, esset etiam consentaneus et Scripturae et puriori antiquitati.“ (Exam. Concil. Trid. ed. Genev. f. 258. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Vilmarius: ,,Confirmatio, absolutio und ordo kann man sacramentale Handlungen nennen, d. h. solche, welche Vorbereitungen und Bedingungen der von Gott mitzutheilenden Kraft des ewigen Lebens sind, von Gott ausgehen und mithin von den Menschen nicht unterlassen werden dürfen. Die Confirmation (Firmung) ist in ihrer Grundlage Act. 8, 14—17. und 19, 6. dargestellt. Sie ist eine Handauflegung zur Mittheilung des Heiligen Geistes unter Gebet, folgt der Taufe als Kräftigung des in der Taufe empfangenen Lebenskeims (gleichsam, um ein apostolisches Bild zu brauchen, als das zum Pflanzen gehörige Begiessen), also nicht blos als äussere Bestätigung der Taufe, wohl aber besonders als Einpflanzung von Charismen, und kann mithin nur dem ertheilt und von dem empfangen werden, welcher die Aneignung der Taufgnade zu bewirken bereit ist. So wurde sie denn auch in der Kirche als Eintritt in das Streiterheer Christi (Ps. 110), die militia Christi, betrachtet... Es gehört bei der Confirmation, wie gesagt, zur Empfangnahme des Heiligen Geistes die Richtung des Willens, sich den Heiligen Geist mittheilen zu lassen, so dass bei mangelnder Richtung des Willens des zu Conflrmirenden auf diese Empfangnahme hin der Act (subjectiv) nichtig werden muss; aber es gehört auch das Erfülltsein des Conflrmirenden vom Heiligen Geist dazu, wenn nicht der Confirmirende sich einer Sünde wider den Heiligen Geist schuldig machen, wenigstens eine solche in sich anbahnen will. Dass jedoch die Mittheilung des Heiligen Geistes auch durch die Handlung eines Ungläubigen erfolgen könne, darf nicht unbedingt, und hier am wenigsten geleugnet werden, weil die Mittheilung des Heiligen Geistes auch durch Gebet, und zwar das Gebet der Gemeinde vermittelt wird.“ (Dogmatik. Gütersloh 1874. II, 227. sq.) Vid. Act. 2, 41. cap. 8, 12. 36. 37. 38. 16, 14. 15. 31. 33. 18, 8.

Gerhardus: ״Adultos in christiana religione instituendos, eandemque amplecti et profiteri debere, antequam ad baptismum admittantur, demonstramus: 1. Ex serie verborum institutionis Matth. 28, 19.: ,Euntes docete omnes gentes, et baptizate eos‘, ubi Christus primo jubet docere, postea demum baptizare; Mare. 16,15.16.: ,Ite in orbem universum et praedicate evangelium omni creaturae. Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit.‘ 2. Ex Johannis baptistae et apostolorum exemplo; illi enim auditores suos primo docuerunt, postea eosdem baptizarunt. Matth. 3, 1. Luc. 3, 3.: ,In diebus illis venit Johannes baptista, praedicans in deserto Judaeae; tunc exibat ad ipsum Hierosolyma et omnis Judaea etc. Et baptizabantur ab eo in Jordane.‘ Act. 2, 38. Petrus prius poenitentiam praedicat, postea demum eos, qui recipiunt sermonem ejus, baptizat. ,Quotquot receperunt sermonem ejus, baptizati sunt‘, v. 41. Ergo a contrario sensu, qui sermonem ejus non receperunt, sed illi contradixerunt, non sunt baptizati. Conjunge Act. 8,12.13. 38. 9,17. 10, 44. 16, 14.15. 32. 18, 8., ubi perpetua praxis apostolorum ostendit, institutionem baptismo adultorum praemittendam esse. 3. Ex typo circumcisionis. Cum enim non solum Isaac, sed et reliqui domestici Abrahae circumcisi fuerint, dubium nuilum, quin de hoc ritu sanctus patriarcha eosdem prius informarit; alias circumcisionem, cum tanta dolorum acerbitate conjunctam, nunquam suscepissent. Gen. 18, 19.: ,Scio, quod praecepturus sit Abraham filiis suis et domi suae post se, ut custodiant viam Domini, et faciant judicium et justitiam.‘ Sic de ritu agni paschalis liberi a parentibus erudiri jubentur Exod. 12, 26. 27.: ,Cum dixerint vobis filii vestri, quae est ista religio? dicetis eis, victima transitus Domini est‘ etc. 4. Ex ipsa necessitate. Cum enim baptismus sit nova N. T. ceremonia, utique necessarium fuit, ut Johannes baptista et apostoli auditores suos de divina ejusdem institutione, usu et efficacia prius informarent. 5. Ex natura sacramentorum, quae sunt sigilla divinarum promissionum. Ut enim tabulae foederis et literae contractuum prius conscribuntur, postea demum sigilla appenduntur: sic de divinis promissis informandi prius auditores, antequam usu sacramentorum eadem in illis obsignentur. 6. Ex analogia verbi. Quemadmodum verbum Dei non est praedicandum illis, qui furenter et violenter illud repudiant; Matth. 7, 6.: ,Nolite sanctum dare canibus.‘ Matth. 10, 14.: ,Si quis non receperit vos, nec audierit sermonem vestrum, exite ab illa civitate.‘ Act. 13,46.: ,Quia repellitis verbum etc., ecce convertimur ad gentes‘: ita multo minus invitis obtrudenda sacramenta.“ (L. c. § 175.)

Apologia A. C.: ״Tertio Jacobus paulo ante dixit de regeneratione, quod flat per evangelium. Sic enim ait (1, 18.): ,Volens genuit nos verbo veritatis, ut nos essemus primitiae creaturarum ejus.‘ Quum dicit nos evangelio renatos esse, docet, quod fide renati ac justificati sumus.“ (Concord. ed. Mueller. p. 130.)

Cf. quae adnotata sunt ad § anteced. de regeneratione verbo facta. Alias autem, si fide careant atque adeo repugnent gratiae divinae, non recipient spiritualia bona neque regenerabuntur aut renovabuntur. 31

Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. ΙΠ. PART. ΠΙ. CAP. X.

Dietericus: ״Quodsi baptismus est lavacrum regenerationis, anne omnes baptizati eodem modo regenerantur? Non; distinguendum enim bic est inter infantes et adultos. Omnes quidem et singuli infantes regenerantur, qui juxta institutionem Christi baptizantur; adulti vero non omnes, sed ii tantum, qui credunt et operationi Spiritus S. non resistunt. De istis extant testimonia: ,Quicunque baptizati sumus in Christum‘ etc. (Rom. 6, 3.),Quicunque baptizati estis, Christum induistis.‘ (Gal. 3, 27.) De his: ,Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit' etc. (Mare. 16,16.) Quid vero de adultis hypocritis baptizatis, qui non credunt, statuendum? Distinguendum hic est inter substantiam et fructum baptismi. Homo adultus hypocrita, si baptizetur, verum quidem baptismum suscipit quoad substantiam, salutarem autem fructum et effectum, qui non nisi fidelibus contingit, quamdiu in hypocrisi perseverat, nequaquam percipit.“ (Institut, catechet. p. 763.)

Theologi Witebergenses: ,,Wir verwerfen als irrig und falsch, dass D. Huber vorgibt, die Wiedergeburt gehöre zur Substanz und Wesen der heiligen Tauf, so doch der Heilige Geist in der Schrift, wie auch der Kinder Catechismus, dieselbe zum effectu, Frucht und heilsamen Nutzen der Tanfe referiren thut. Fürs andere, dass auch die glaublosen Heuchler, wenn sie mitten in solchem Unglauben getauft werden in ihrem Alter, nicht allein die rechte Tauf empfahen (welches auch wir halten), sondern dass sie noch über das aus Gott neu geboren und wahrhaftig von Sünden gereiniget werden. Item, dass dieselbigen Heuchler, ob sie gleich, wenn sie die Tauf empfangen, nicht wahrhaftig bekehret sind, nichts desto weniger (vermög der Einsatzung) die Wiedergeburt und die Gnad (dass sie Gott zu Kindern angenommen) in der heiligen Tauf gewiss und wahrhaftig empfangen haben. Item, dass sie die Wiedergeburt empfangen ohne die Verneuerung des Heiligen Geistes, welches ein ungereimte, offenbare Contradiction ist, die sich selber widerlegt. Item, dass auch solche gottlose Heuchler in der Tauf für Kinder Gottes vermög der Einsetzung auch mitten in der Unbnssfertigkeit angenommen und unter die Kinder Gottes gerechnet worden sein. Item, dass dieselbigen zugleich und zu einer Zeit, nach D. Hubers Lehr, Kinder Gottes sein, und doch, indem sie also Kinder Gottes sind, solche Gnad der Kindschaft ihnen zum Gericht gereiche. Welche Vermischung der Substanz und des Nutzens der Tauf, Trennung der Wiedergeburt und der Verneurung im Heiligen Geist, Empfahung der Wiedergeburt ohne Bekehrung, Aufnehmung ohne Glauben an Christum, zum Gericht gereichende Gnade der Kindschaft, wir als unerhorte Paradoxa und handgreifliche Contradictiones, darvon kein Apostel ihm jemals hat träumen lassen, deutlich und rund verwerfen und verdämmen.“ (Bekenntniss v. d. ew. Gnadenwahl. A. 1597. Vid. Consil. Witeberg. I, 642.)


### On Baptism: ANTITHESIS. Delitzschius

ANTITHESIS. Delitzschius: "The body of a baptized person is a member of Christ through the act of God; if a man, upon whom such an act of God has been performed, commits fornication, then his body is a member of Christ made into a member of a harlot... Whoever is once baptized is a member of Christ; that cannot be changed." (Vier Bücher von der Kirche. Dresden 1847. p. 43 sq.) (

Calovius: "That statement of Ambrose is most true: 'Members adhering to a harlot cannot be members of Christ.' Whence it is most false what Cornelius a Lapide holds here according to the mind of the Council of Trent: 'A fornicator remains a member of Christ and the Church when he retains true faith (!) or can retain knowledge of the things of faith.' He cannot retain true faith." Bibl. illustr. Adnotat. ad 1 Cor. 6:15, 16.)

For the covenant of grace itself, of which baptism is the seal, remains always valid and firm on the part of God. Cf. what we said in Chapter VI, § 9, notes c and b; Hunnius, loc. cit., fol. 1024. Wandalinus: "The question is asked: Does the efficacy of baptism extend only to the remission of past sins, and not likewise to future ones? We deny this, against the Papists. For in baptism, as the covenant of God (1 Pet. 3:21), which on the part of God is ἀμεταμέλητον (Rom. 11:29), this promise was made, that God 'will forgive their iniquity, and remember their sin no more' (Jer. 31:34). Hence the Apostle says in Rom. 8:1: 'There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit.' Cf. Jer. 3:14; Acts 3:19; Tit. 3:7." (Ύποτύπωσις san. verb. p. 262.)

Calovius: "Unless the efficacy of baptism extends into the future, how can hypocrites, who approach baptism feignedly and have subsequently fallen, raise themselves up by the baptism once received by them—to which, in the case of true repentance (if indeed baptism is joined with faith, without which there is never true repentance), Alensis and Rada grant [efficacy], just as the Apostle also raises up the Galatians (ch. 3:27), the Corinthians (1 Ep. 6:11; 12:13), and the Hebrews (ch. 10:23 sq.)?" (System. IX, 283.)

For while it renders them certain of the covenant of God’s grace through Christ, it certainly comforts and raises up their souls, so that they may continue to rest more securely in Christ. Indeed, when it increases faith, it simultaneously excites them to greater love, hope, and the exercise of other virtues.

Hollazius: "By baptism the guilt and dominion of sin are removed, not the root or the fuel of sin." (Exam. th. ed. Tellerus, p. 1096.)

k) Indeed, even baptism, once conferred, although faith and the grace of God may have been expelled by intervening sins against conscience, nevertheless effectively profits those who return to repentance for the confirmation of faith. Cf. the blessed Hunnius, loc. cit.

Luther: "Where Satan could not extinguish the power of baptism in infants, he nevertheless prevailed so as to extinguish it in all adults, so that now there is almost no one who remembers that he is baptized, much less glories in it, so many other ways of having sins remitted and of coming to heaven having been found. That dangerous word of St. Jerome—whether poorly stated or poorly understood—by which he calls repentance the 'second plank after shipwreck,' as if baptism were not repentance, gave occasion for these opinions. For hence, when they have fallen into sin, despairing of the first plank or ship as if it were lost, they begin to rely and trust only in the second plank, that is, repentance. Hence were born those infinite burdens of vows, religious orders, works, satisfactions, pilgrimages, indulgences, and sects, and from these, those seas of books, questions, opinions, and human traditions, which the whole world can no longer contain, so that that tyranny has afflicted the Church of God incomparably worse than it ever did the synagogue or any nation under heaven. . . .

Therefore, first of all, the divine promise is to be observed in baptism, which says: 'He who believes and is baptized will be saved.' This promise is to be preferred incomparably above all the pomp of works, vows, religious orders, and whatever has been introduced by human invention. For our entire salvation hangs upon this, and it is to be observed in such a way that we exercise faith in it, not doubting at all that we are saved after we have been baptized. For unless this faith is present or is prepared, baptism profits nothing; indeed, it is a hindrance, not only when it is received, but for the whole time of life thereafter." PART III. CHAPTER X.

For unbelief of this kind argues that the divine promise is a lie, which is the greatest of all sins.

If we grasp this exercise of faith, we shall immediately understand how arduous it is to believe this divine promise. For human weakness, conscious of its own sins, finds it most difficult of all to believe that it is saved or to be saved, and yet, unless it believes this, it cannot be saved, because it does not believe the divine truth that promises salvation.

This was the preaching that needed to be diligently inculcated to the people, that promise that needed to be assiduously recited, baptism that needed to be constantly repeated, and faith that needed to be continually awakened and fostered.

For just as the divine promise once made over us persists in its truth until death, so faith in the same must never be interrupted, but must be nourished and strengthened until death, with a perpetual remembrance of that same promise made to us in baptism.

Therefore, while we rise again from sins or repent, we do nothing other than return to the virtue and faith of baptism, from which we had fallen, and return to the promise made at that time, which we had deserted through sin. For the truth of the promise once made always remains, ready to receive us with outstretched hand when we return.

And this, if I am not mistaken, is what they mean who obscurely say that baptism is the first and the foundation of all sacraments, without which none of the others can be obtained.

Hence, it will be of no small profit if the penitent, first of all, lays hold of the memory of his baptism, and, remembering with confidence the divine promise which he deserted, confesses the same to the Lord, rejoicing that he still has such a safeguard of salvation in that he is baptized, and detesting his own impious ingratitude in that he has fallen away from the faith and truth of the same.

For his heart will be wondrously comforted and animated to the hope of mercy if he considers the divine promise made to him—which it is impossible to lie—to be still intact and unchanged, nor changeable by any sins, just as Paul says in 2 Timothy 2: "If we are faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself." This, I say, the truth of God will save him, so that if everything else collapses, this, once believed, will not abandon him.

For through this he has something to oppose to the insulting adversary; he has something to object to the sins that disturb his conscience; he has something to answer to the horror of death and judgment; he has, finally, something that is a comfort against all temptations, namely this one truth, saying: God is truthful in His promises, the sign of which I received in baptism. If God is for me, who is against me? (Rom. 8).

For if the children of Israel, when they were to return to repentance, remembered first of all the exodus from Egypt, and by this memory returned to God who had led them out—which memory and this very safeguard is so often inculcated to them by Moses and repeated by David—how much more ought we to remember our exodus from our Egypt, and by the memory of it return to Him who led us out through the washing of new regeneration, the memory of which was commended to us for this very purpose?

This can be done most conveniently of all in the sacrament of bread and wine.

For thus, in former times, those three sacraments—penance, baptism, and bread—were frequented together in the same office, and one helped the other.

Thus it is read of a certain holy virgin who, as often as she was tempted, resisted with nothing but her baptism, saying most briefly: "I am a Christian"; for the enemy immediately understood the power of baptism and faith, which hung upon the truth of the promising God, and fled from her.

Thus you see how rich the Christian or baptized man is, who, even if he wishes, cannot lose his salvation by any sins whatsoever, unless he refuses to believe. For no sins can condemn him except unbelief alone.

All other things, if he returns or stand s faithful to the divine promise made to the baptized, are in a moment absorbed by that same faith, or rather by the truth of God, because He cannot deny Himself if you have confessed Him and and have faithfully clung to the One who promises.

Contrition, however, and the confession of sins, and then satisfaction, and all those pursuits devised by men will suddenly desert you and render you more unhappy if, having forgotten this divine truth, you have stretched yourself out in them. For it is vanity of vanities and a striving of the Spirit, whatever is labored outside the faith of the truth of God.

is labored. At the same time, you see how dangerous, nay, how false it is to opine that repentance is a second plank after shipwreck, and how pernicious an error it is to think that the power of baptism has been lost through sin, and that this ship has been dashed to pieces.

That one, solid, and invincible ship remains, nor is it ever dissolved into any planks; in it are carried all who are carried to the harbor of salvation, which is the truth of God in the sacraments promisin…ruth of God promising in the sacraments. It certainly happens that many rashly leap from the ship into the sea and perish; these are they who, having deserted faith in the promise, cast themselves into sin. But the ship itself remains and passes intact on its course; and if any grace can return to the ship, it will be carried to life not by any plank, but by the solid ship itself; this is he who returns through faith to the stable and abiding promise of God.

Whence Peter, in 2 Pet. 1, argues against those who sin, that they receive forgetfulness of the cleansing of their old sins, undoubtedly taxing the ingratitude of the baptism received and the impiety of their unbelief.

What profit is there, then, in writing so much about baptism and not teaching this faith in the promise? All sacraments are instituted for the nourishing of faith, and they so far from touching this very thing that impious men even assert that a man ought not to be certain of the remission of sins, or of the grace of the sacraments—by which impiety they drive the whole world mad, and utterly extinguish, not to say captivate, the sacrament of baptism, in which the first glory of our conscience stands, meanwhile raging against miserable souls with their contritions, anxious confessions, circumstances, satisfactions, works, and infinite trifles of that kind.

Latin:

ANTITHESIS. Delitzschius: ״Der Leib eines Getauften ist ein Glied Christi durch die That Gottes; treibt nun ein Mensch, an dem solche That Gottes geschehen ist, Unzucht, so ist sein Leib ein zum Hurengliede gemachtes Glied Christi. . . Wer einmal getauft ist, der ist ein Glied Christi, das lässt sich nicht andern.“ (Vier Bücher von der Kirche. Dresden 1847. p. 43. sq.) (

Calovius: ״Illud Ambrosii est verissimum: ,Membra adhaerentia meretrici non possunt esse membra Christi.' Unde falsissimum est, quod hic ex mente concilii Trident, habet Cornelius a Lapide: ,Christi et ecclesiae membrum manet fornicator, quando veram fidem retinet (!) seu cognitionem de rebus fidei retinere potest.' Fidem veram retinere non potest." Bibi, illustr. Adnotat. ad 1 Cor. 6, 15. 16.)

Ipsum enim foedus gratiae, cujus sigillum baptismus est, a parte Dei semper ratum et firmum manet. Confer., quae diximus cap. VI. § 9. not. c. et b. Hunnium 1. c. fol. 1024. Wandalinus: ״Quaeritur: An baptismi efficacia ad remissionem peccatorum tantum praeteritorum, non item futurorum se extendat? Neg. cont. pontificios. Etenim in baptismo, ut foedere Dei 1 Pet. 3,21., quod ex parte Dei est άμεταμέλητον Rom. 11, 21., promissio haec facta est, Deum,condonare iniquitatem et peccati non recordari amplius.‘ Jer. 31, 34. Hinc apostolus Rom. 8, 1.: ,Nulla nunc est condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Christo Jesu, qui non secundum carnem ambulant, sed secundum spiritum.‘ Conf. Jer. 3, 14. Act. 3, 19. Tit. 3, 7.“ (Ύττοτϋπωσις san. verb. p. 262.) Calovius: ״

Nisi efficacia baptismi sese in futurum extendat, quomodo hypocritae, ficte accedentes ad baptismum et postea prolapsi, erigere se possunt baptismo, abs se quondam suscepto, cui in casu verae poenitentiae, si nempe baptismus cum fide conjunctus sit, sine qna poenitentia vera nunquam est, Alensis et Rada largitur, quemadmodum et Galatas c. 3, 27. et Corinthios 1. ep. 6,11. 12, 13. et Ebraeos c. 10, 23. sq. evergit apostolus?“ (System. IX, 283.)

Dum enim certos reddit de foedere gratiae Dei per Christum, utique solatur et erigit animos, ut in Christo porro et securius acquiescant. Nempe, quando fidem auget, simul etiam excitat ad majorem dilectionem, spem et virtutum caeterarum exercitia. Hollazius: ״

Tollitur per baptismum reatus et dominium peccati, non radix aut fomes peccati.“ (Exam. th. ed. Tellerus, p. 1096.) k)

Imo etiam baptismus, olim collatus, licet intercedentibus peccatis contra conscientiam fides et gratia Dei expulsa fuerit, tamen redeuntibus ad poenitentiam efficaciter prodest ad confirmationem fidei. Conf. b. Hunnium 1. c. Lutherus: ״

Ubi virtutem baptismi in parvulis non potuit satan exstinguere, praevaluit tamen, ut in omnibus adultis exstingueret, ut jam fere nemo sit, qui sese baptizatum recordetur, nedum glorietur, tot repertis aliis viis remittendorum peccatorum et in coelum veniendi. Praebuit his opinionibus occasionem verbum illud periculosum divi Hieronymi, sive male positum, sive male intellectum, quo poenitentiam appellat secundam post naufragium tabulam, quasi baptismus non sit poenitentia. Hinc enim, nbi in peccatum lapsi fuerint, de prima tabula seu nave desperantes velut amissa, secundae tantum incipiunt niti et fidere tabulae, id est, poenitentiae. Hinc nata sunt votorum, religionum, operum, satisfactionum, peregrinationum, indulgentiarum, sectarum infinita illa onera, et de iis maria illa librorum, quaestionum, opinionum, traditionum humanarum, quas totus mundus jam non capit, ut incomparabiliter pejus habet ecclesiam Dei ea tyrannis, quam unquam habuit synagogam aut ullam nationem sub coelo. . . .

Primum itaque in baptismo observanda est divina promissio, quae dicit: Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit. Quae promissio praeferenda est incomparabiliter uuiversis pompis operum, votorum, religionum, et quicquid humanitus est introductum. Nam in hac pendet universa salus nostra, sic autem est observanda, ut fidem exerceamus in ea, prorsus non dubitantes nos esse salvos, postquam sumus baptizati. Nam nisi haec adsit aut paretur fides, nihil prodest baptismus, imo obest, non solum tum, cum suscipitur, sed toto post tempore vitae. PART, III. CAP. X.

Incredulitas enim ejusmodi mendacem arguit promissionem divinam, quod est summum omnium peccatorum.

Hoc exercitium fidei si apprelienderimus, statim intelligemus, quam arduum sit credere promissioni huic divinae. Humana enim imbecillitas, peccatorum suorum sibi conscia, difficillime omnium credit se esse salvam aut salvandam, et tamen, nisi id credat, salvari non poterit, quia non credit veritati divinae promittenti salutem.

Haec erat praedicatio sedulo inculcanda populo, assidue recantanda ista promissio, semper repetendus baptismus, jugiter excitanda fovendaque fides.

Sicut enim semel super nos lata divina hac promissione usque ad mortem veritas ejus perseverat, ita fides in eandem nunquam debet intermitti, sed usque ad mortem ali et Roborari, perpetua memoria promissionis ejusdem in baptismo nobis factae.

Quare, dum a peccatis resurgimus sive poeniternus, non facimus aliud, quam quod ad baptismi virtutem et fidem, unde cecideramus, revertimur, et ad promissionem tunc factam redimus, quam per peccatum deserueramus. Semper enim manet veritas promissionis semel factae, nos extenta manu susceptura reversos.

Atque id, ni fallor, volunt, qui obscure dicunt, baptismum esse primum et fundamentum omnium sacramentorum, sine quo nullum queat aliorum obtineri.

Proinde non parum profuerit, si poenitens primo omnium baptismi sui memoriam apprehendat, et promissionis divinae, quam deseruit, cum fiducia recordatus, eandem confiteatur Domino, gaudens se tantum adhuc in praesidio habere salutis, quod baptizatus sit detestansque suam impiam ingratitudinem, quod a fide et veritate ejusdem defecerit.

Mire enim cor ejus confortabitur, et ad spem misericordiae animabitur, si consideret divinam promissionem sibi factam, quam impossibile est mentiri, adhuc integram et non mutatam nec mutabilem ullis peccatis esse, sicut Paulus dicit 2 Timoth. 2.: Si non credimus, ille fidelis permanet; se ipsum negare non potest. Haec, inquam, veritas Dei eum servabit, ita ut, si cetera omnia ruant, haec tamen eum credita non derelinquet.

Habet enim per hanc, quod insultanti adversario opponat, habet, quod turbantibus peccatis conscientiam objiciat, habet, quod horrori mortis et judicii respondeat, habet denique, quod universis tentationibus solatium sit, nempe hanc unam veritatem, dicens: Deus est verax in promissionibus suis, cujus signum in baptismo suscepi. Si Deus pro me, quis contra me? (Rom. 8.)

Si enim filii Israel ad poenitentiam reversuri primo omnium exitum de Aegypto memorabant, et hac memoria ad Deum, qui eduxerat eos, revertebantur, quae memoria et hoc ipsum praesidium eis toties a Mose inculcatur, et a David repetitur, quanto magis nos nostrum de Aegypto nostra exitum debemus memorare, et ejus memoria redire ad eum, qui nos eduxit per lavacrum regenerationis novae, cujus memoria in hoc ipsum nobis commendata est?

Id quod omnium commodissime fleri in sacramento panis et vini potest.

Sic enim olim tria ista sacramenta, poenitentia, baptismus, panis, simul eodem officio frequentabantur, et alterum alterum juvabat.

Ita legitur de quadam sancta virgine, quae, quoties tentabatur, non nisi baptismo suo repugnabat, dicens brevissime: Christiana sum; intellexit enim hostis statim virtutem baptismi et fidei, quae in veritate Dei promittentis pendebat, et fugit ab ea.

Ita vides, quam dives sit homo Christianus sive baptizatus, qui etiam volens non potest perdere salutem suam quantiscunque peccatis, nisi nolit credere. Nulla enim peccata eum possunt damnare, nisi sola incredulitas.

Cetera omnia, si redeat vel stet flcles in promissionem divinam baptizato factam, in momento absorbentur per eandem fidem, imo veritatem Dei, quia se ipsum negare non potest, si tu eum confessus ftieris, et promittenti fideliter adhaeseris.

Contritio autem et peccatorum confessio, deinde et satisfactio, et omnia illa hominum excogitata studia subito te deserent, et infeliciorem reddent, si oblitus veritatis hujus divinae in ipsis tete distenderis. Vanitas enim vanitatum et afflictio Spiritus est, quicquid extra fidem veritatis Dei labo-

ratur. Simul vides, quam periculosum, imo falsum sit opinari, poenitentiam esse secundam tabulam post naufragium, et quam perniciosus sit error putare, per peccatum excidisse vim baptismi, et navem hanc esse illisam.

Manet illa una, solida, et invicta navis, nec unquam dissolvitur in ullas tabulas, in qua omnes vehuntur, qui ad portum salutis vehuntur, quae est veritas Dei in sacramentis promittens. Hoc sane fit, ut multi e nave temere in mare prosiliant et pereant, hi sunt, qui deserta promissionis fide in peccatum sese praecipitant. Verum navis ipsa permanet, et transit integra cursu suo; quod si qua gratia ad navem reverti potest, nulla tabula, sed solida ipsa nave feretur ad vitam, hic est, qui ad promissionem Dei stabilem et manentem per fidem revertitur.

Unde Petrus 2 Pet. 1. arguit eos, qui peccant, quod oblivionem accipiant purgationis veterum delictorum suorum, sine dubio ingratitudinem accepti baptismi et impietatem infidelitatis eorum taxans.

Quid ergo prodest de baptismo tam multa scribere et hanc fidem promissionis non docere? Omnia sacramenta ad fidem alendam sunt instituta, et hanc ipsam adeo non tangunt, ut etiam asserant impii homines, non debere hominem esse certum de remissione peccatorum, seu gratia sacramentorum, qua impietate orbem totum dementant, et sacramentum baptismi, in quo stat prima gloria conscientiae nostrae, funditus exstinguunt, nedum captivant, interim insanientes in miseras animas suis contritionibus, anxiis confessionibus, circumstantiis, satisfactionibus, operibus, et id genus infinitis nugis.


### On Baptism: Be therefore a prudent reader, nay, a contemner of the Master of the Sentences,…

Be therefore a prudent reader, nay, a contemner of the Master of the Sentences, Book 4, with all his scribes, who write only of the matter and form of the sacraments, while they write best—that is, they treat the dead and killing letter of the sacraments, but otherwise leave the spirit, life, and use, that is, the truth of the divine promise and our faith, entirely untouched.

See to it, therefore, that the pomp of works and the fallacies of human traditions do not deceive you, so that you do not do injury to divine truth and your own faith.

You must begin with faith in the sacraments, without any works, if you wish to be saved; but works themselves will follow faith—only do not hold faith cheap, which is the most excellent and arduous work of all works, by which alone, even if you were compelled to lack all others, you will be saved.

For it is the work of God, not of man, as Paul teaches; other things He works with us and through us, this one thing He works in us, and without us.” (

De captivitate Babylonica ecclesiae. A. 1520. See Opp. lat. varii argum. cur. Dr. H. Schmidt. Francof. ad M. 1868. Vol. V. p. 56. 57—60.)

Luther: “It is clear: let no one rely too much on such a bath and rebirth; there is still more there.” (Epistol. Kirchenpostille. Tom. Hal. XII, 193.) §

11. To signify the efficacy of baptism, by which infants are transferred from the power of Satan into spiritual liberty, the ancient rite of exorcism, with the sign of the cross and the votive renunciation of Satan, although indifferent, is rightly observed, just as sponsors or godparents are also employed by a pious rite to designate the covenant of grace which the baptized enter into with God.

On which see § 9.

I do not say obsession, especially bodily, but from the power of Satan, which he has over men carnally through sin, according to Eph. 2:2. PART III. CHAP. X.

Formerly, indeed, it had a place when the miraculous gift of casting out demons from the possessed was in effect. Afterward, however, it was preserved not only in the baptism of adults, but also in the baptism of any infants whatsoever, as witnessed by Greg. Nazianz. Orat. XL., August. de Fide et Oper. cap. VI., and Lib. II. contra Pelag. cap. XL. By words conceived in the mode of commanding, but to be understood in the sense of prayer to God, with confidence and the courage born therefrom against the enemy to be repelled. With regard had to the power of the merit of the crucified Christ, upon which the very efficacy of baptism depends. By which those to be baptized solemnly and in express words renounce Satan and all his pomp. Gerhardus: "We distinguish the ceremonies and rites used in the administration of baptism into three classes:

1. Some are divinely commanded;

2. Some were freely used by the apostles;

3. Some were added by ecclesiastical men. Regarding each, these rules are to be held: 1. The rites of baptism divinely instituted are to be accurately distinguished from the rites used by the apostles and those added by ecclesiastical men for the sake of honest decorum, order, and pious admonition; for the former are substantial and necessary, but the latter are accidental and in a certain way free. ... 2. The rites freely used by the apostles in the administration of baptism, although they are not necessary to the same degree as the rites of the former kind that were divinely instituted, are nevertheless to be distinguished from merely ecclesiastical rites and are to be diligently preserved. It is gathered from the history of the apostles that in the administration of baptism they employed explanations of the doctrine of the sacraments, exhortations, prayers, thanksgivings, etc., Acts 2:38, etc. We also retain these rites in our churches, because the sacraments are not bare and idle spectacles, but were instituted so that they might both confirm faith and explain the promise more clearly; therefore, the doctrine concerning their substance, use, and efficacy is to be proposed and explained to those present from the Word of God in a language known to them, so that they may be diligently admonished concerning the legitimate and salutary reception of the sacraments. It is to be noted, however, that while the foundations are indeed shown in the Scriptures from which explanations, exhortations, prayers, and thanksgivings ought to be taken—namely, from the institution and the doctrine concerning baptism as it is handed down in the Word of God—a certain form in conceived words is not prescribed, but this is permitted to be free for the sake of edification according to the circumstances, provided the foundation is preserved. 3. The rites added by ecclesiastical men are adiaphora and indifferent; therefore, they are not to be simply rejected, nor are they, however, necessary to the same degree as the rites divinely commanded." (L. de bapt. § 255.) Rudelbachius: "What is required for ecclesiastical validity, the Church has always understood under two points, namely: The renunciation of the devil (abrenuntiatio) and the confession of the Christian faith. ... It is true, the first express mention of a renunciation formula appears only in Tertullian in the well-known passage of his writing de corona militis c. 3. However, if unbelieving theologians conclude further from this: Therefore, the renunciation at baptism is not an apostolic institution, they would thereby only betray a complete lack of judgment, if one did not know that a quite different interest drove them to fight against this formula—a testimony of living Christianity. Let us visualize the state of the matter! Tertullian wrote his work de cor. mil. after his transition to Montanism in the year 201. He mentions the renunciation at baptism not as a matter that required further explanation, but as one that was manifest, and from which one was therefore justified in drawing conclusions. Now, one will surely not want to claim that he invented the matter, but rather that which..."

had attained general ecclesiastical validity toward the end of the second century, it must indisputably have been known as an apostolic institution already in the first. Thus we stand at the boundary of the apostolic age, and how would it be conceivable that any church teacher from the first or second apostolic διαδοχή (succession) could have invented such a thing, in a time when immediate disciples of the apostles (like Polycarp, the disciple of John) were still living—and these, indeed the whole church, would not have loudly and solemnly contradicted such a fabrication or unchurchly private opinion? No, on the contrary, the testimony of Tertullian, when well considered, must strike dumb all those who, from the history of the church, wish to undermine the foundation of the church itself and tear down the bulwarks of Christianity. But even among still older church teachers, the attentive observer will find at least traces of renunciation at baptism as a fundamental Christian institution. How, we ask, will one explain ‘the vow of a Christian life,’ which, according to Justin Martyr, all those being baptized had to make in connection with the confession of faith (Apol. I, c. 61)? Yet we truly do not need these testimonies, since the matter as such is already brought to light by the testimony of the apostles themselves, so that evidently there can only be further talk of the formula as such.” (Die Sakramentworte, p. 25 sqq.)

Not certainly commanded by Christ, but freely received and therefore abrogable, if circumstances so require, or at some time to be omitted without fault.

Gerhardus: “One must take care, 1. that this ceremony (of exorcism) is not established as an essential and necessary part of baptism; 2. that one does not think of some bodily obsession of the infant, since it demonstrates only its spiritual captivity in the kingdom of Satan. . .; 3. nor that the use of exorcism be established as effective, as if by the power of those words the infant were liberated from the kingdom of Satan, since this is to be attributed entirely to the sacrament of baptism, but [that it be] at least significative. . . . Therefore, as regards the thing itself shadowed forth by the exorcism, and likewise the explanation of the words used in this ceremony—namely, that it is a reminder and testimony concerning the spiritual captivity of the infant in the kingdom of Satan, concerning the miserable state into which we have been reduced by the fall of our first parents, concerning the salutary efficacy of baptism, etc.—since it is analogous to the faith, it cannot be simply disapproved; meanwhile, however, since the words are harsher and, if that explanation is set aside, suggest a certain obsession of the infant, from which liberation is effected by that very ceremony, therefore, as D. Chemnitius speaks in Part 3 of the Loci theologici, p. 178, ‘the church has the liberty to propose and explain that doctrine concerning original sin, concerning the power and kingdom of Satan, and concerning the efficacy of baptism in other words, more agreeable to Scripture.’ . . . This liberty of abrogating an adiaphorous ceremony, so that the church might demonstrate this fact in the exorcism, would perhaps not be useless for reasons not to be despised.” (Loc. de bapt. § 264 sqq.)

Huelsemannus: “Nor do we deny that it would be more useful if, by the consent of the whole church, that imperative apostrophe were converted into an epiphonema or doctrine concerning the manner and means of exiting from the power of Satan.” (Praelect. Form. Conc. p. 495.)

For the sake of pious admonition concerning the remarkable operation of the sacrament itself. Whence, for the sake of heterodox persons who lie in wait for our liberty, or who ascribe to Christian infants a holiness as if it were hereditary, by which they are already in a state of grace, it ought not to be abrogated or omitted. See § 10, notes c, g, h.

k) Not only witnesses of the baptism conferred, but also those bearing the cause of those being baptized, especially infants, as if their person were assumed into themselves. PART III. CHAP. X.

B. Meisnerus: "The question is asked, whether the interrogation of godparents is rightly retained in our churches? — This ceremony is retained in our churches usefully on account of its ends and uses: 1. Because we interrogate not so much the infants as the sponsors themselves in their own name and in the name of the infants, so that the godparents may thus profess their own faith before the church. 2. So that they may know what kind of testimony they ought to bear to the baptized person when he has reached the years of discretion. 3. So that he may recognize in what faith the baptized person is to be instructed. Among others, some reject that formula, 'Do you believe?' 'I believe!' 'Do you renounce?' 'I renounce,' thinking that this ceremony was wrongly transferred from the baptism of adults to infant baptism...

Menzerus, however, considering this matter more deeply, uses these words: Because the Savior has testified in express words that little children believe (Matt. 18:6) and that the kingdom of God belongs to them (Mark 10:14), and that adults must become like them in order to obtain eternal life (Matt. 18:3), therefore the sponsors or godparents repeat this very thing in their response at the baptism of the infant, which Christ clearly testified for them as the mouth of the infants. And to this he refers the saying of Augustine, which is alleged in *De consecrat.*, dist. 4, c. 139: 'Mother Church lends her maternal mouth to the little ones, so that they may be imbued with the sacred mysteries,' namely, by repeating and applying that which Christ himself expressly testified and confirmed for the infants." (*Colleg. adiaphorist. disp. VI. § 79—81. 83. 84.*) §

12. Baptism, according to the institution of Christ, once conferred, ought not to be repeated upon the same subject. a

Namely, provided that nothing has been changed in the essentials, but that those things were in conformity with the institution. Otherwise, it would not have been a true baptism. b

Even if it was administered by a heretic or a wicked person, provided it is certain that it was administered correctly. c

Although he may have fallen away from God through open denial or other crimes and violated the covenant of grace. d "

For not only does no command or example exist for repeating baptism, but neither does any necessity or solid reason appear otherwise. Indeed, the very nature of the sacrament of initiation excludes repetition more than it demands it." §

13. Baptism can be defined as a sacred action instituted by Christ, in which humans, without distinction of sex or age, are washed with water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that they may thus be regenerated and renewed, for the sake of obtaining eternal salvation. a This is the common genus of the sacraments. b The principal efficient cause is indicated thus, see § 2. c The subject or the end to whom it is denoted, according to § 7. d This is the matter of baptism, see § 5. e Thus the form of baptism is signified, see § 6. f These pertain to the end for which, according to § 9.

Latin:
