### Of the Holy Supper: can do abundantly beyond all that we ask or think, Eph

can do abundantly beyond all that we ask or think, Eph. 3, 20., nor is anything difficult for him, Gen. 18, 14. Zech. 8, 36., much less impossible, Luke 1, 37. Since he is a faithful and true witness, it is right that we should have faith in his words, taking captive our intellect into his obedience. 2 Cor. 10, 5. Since he is omniscient and all-wise, it is right that we should determine that he himself knows the reason and the manner by which he can fulfill his promises, nor is it fitting that wisdom should be justified by her children, Luke 7, 35. But above all, those two pronouncements should be kept before our eyes and minds, one of which is of Christ himself, the other of the apostle Paul, whenever we think or speak about this mystery: John 12, 48: "The word that I have spoken, that will judge you in the last day"; 1 Tim. 6, 3. 4: "If anyone teaches otherwise, έτεροόίόασκαλει [teaches differently], and does not consent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness, he is proud, knowing nothing." (Loc. de S. C. § 14.)

But he who has the authority and power, and likewise the omnipotence, which Christ used in effecting this sacrament, in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, therefore it can also be rightly said that the triune God is the principal efficient cause of this sacrament. § 3. The internal impulsive cause of the institution of this sacrament is the goodness and love of Christ toward his own; the external is the very merit of his passion and death. Specifically regarding the real presence of the body and blood of Christ in every administration of the supper, the institution of Christ itself holds the status of the principal impulsive cause; the less principal impulsive cause is the consecration of the symbols, performed by the minister according to the institution of Christ.

By which Christ is good to others, or his gratuitous favor; as is evident from the following. To this pertains what we read in John 13, 1 concerning the love with which Christ loved his own who were in the world, even to the end; to which also those things which were done at the last supper and after it are ascribed.

For although in the holy supper the very body of Christ, delivered into death for us, and the blood of Christ, shed for us, are exhibited to us; yet just as Christ merited for us spiritual benefits through that delivery of his body into death and the shedding of his blood, so also he merited that those benefits should be applied, sealed, and confirmed through this seal of the new covenant. Namely, that act by which the body and blood of Christ are presented as present in the holy supper and united with the earthly symbols depends at once on the divine power and the free will of Christ. But after Christ determined to present his body and blood as present with the bread and wine in the holy supper, as often as it is celebrated in conformity with his institution, and to unite them sacramentally, and that with these words: This is my body; this

OF THE SACRED SUPPER is my blood (concerning which we shall see more distinctly presently), he openly declared, it is certain that the will of Christ is moved by the power of his very institution to effect that very thing which the words: This is my body; this is my blood, signify. Concerning which we shall speak immediately in the following paragraph. In the meantime, it is to be noted that the words of consecration move the will of Christ not by their own power, and as they are uttered by the minister, but by the power of the institution itself which proceeded from Christ.

Formula of Concord: "Since also concerning the consecration and the common rule that nothing is a sacrament apart from the instituted use, misunderstanding and division have arisen among some teachers of the Augsburg Confession, we have also declared ourselves fraternally and unanimously with one another concerning this matter in the following opinion, namely: that the true presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Supper is not brought about by any word or work of man, be it the merit or the speaking of the minister, or the eating and drinking or the faith of the communicants, but all such things should be ascribed solely to the power of Almighty God and the word, institution, and ordinance of our Lord Jesus Christ. For the true and almighty words of Jesus Christ, which he spoke in the first institution, were not only powerful in the first Supper, but endure, are valid, operate, and are still powerful, so that in all places where the Supper is held according to Christ’s institution and his words are used, by the power and virtue of those same words which Christ spoke in the first Supper, the body and blood of Christ are truly present, distributed, and received;

for Christ himself, wherever one observes his institution and speaks his words over the bread and cup, and distributes the blessed bread and cup, is powerful through the spoken words, by the power of the first institution, still through his word, which he wills to have repeated there; as Chrysostom says (in serm. de pass.) in the sermon on the Passion: 'Christ himself prepares this table and blesses it; for no man makes the set-forth bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ, but Christ himself, who was crucified for us. The words are spoken through the priest’s mouth, but by God’s power and grace, by the word where he says: This is my body, the presented elements in the Supper are blessed; and as this speech: Increase and multiply and fill the earth, was spoken only once, but is always powerful in nature, so that it grows and multiplies, so also this speech was spoken once, but until this day and until his coming it is powerful and operates so that in the Supper of the Church his true body and blood is present.'

And Luther, tom. 6. Jen. fol. 99.: 'Such his command and institution is able to and brings it about that we do not offer and receive mere bread and wine, but his body and blood, as his words sound: This is my body, etc. This is my blood, etc.; that not our work or speaking, but the command and order of Christ makes the bread into the body and the wine into the blood from the beginning of the first Supper until the end of the world, and is daily offered through our service and office.'

Item, tom. 3. Jen. fol. 446: 'So also here, if I were to speak over all bread: this is Christ’s body, surely nothing would come of it; but when we, according to his institution and command, say in the Supper: This is my body, then it is his body, not because of our speaking or word of action, but because of his command, that he has bidden us so to speak and to do, and has bound his command and action to our speaking.'" (Solid. Declar. artic. VII. §§ 73—78. p. 663. sq.) PART III. CAP. XI.

4. The ministerial cause is the minister of the church, the ordinary one, who consecrates the external elements and distributes them to the communicants. Or, that which, by the authority of another, as of a superior, establishes the sacrament in use. Indeed, Christ himself, on the night in which he was betrayed, first administered the Eucharist, still clothed in the form of a servant, although, as #εάν&ρωπος, he used his own authority. But after that first celebration of the Eucharist, he handed down and left this duty to the ministers of the church. See 1 Cor. 4:1; ch. 11:23.

Not equally, as in baptism, [may] a layman sometimes, or a woman [administer it]. For there is not the same necessity for both sacraments. However, when, in the absence of an ordinary minister, a faithful person anxiously desires this sacrament, it is nevertheless better to persuade him in every way of the sufficiency of spiritual eating and to point out the danger of other temptations that could arise if the sacrament were administered by another, without a legitimate calling, and thus with a doubtful mind and outcome. Z. Grapius: "Priests are laymen, but they are fit for any duties of the church, and thus also for the administration of the Eucharist, only by internal Ικανότψι; lest we think that it would be a less true sacrament which a layman might have given, perhaps led by necessity or error. See Schomer in his treatise on collegialism, Dissert. I. § 34." (System. novissim. controvers. Tom. IV. p. 89.) Cf. the notes above on P. III. c. 8. § 6. p. 408. sqq.)

Namely, bread and wine; of which more will be said shortly.

That is, by prayers poured out to God, he separates the external symbols from common use and designates them for sacred use (which others call a blessing or thanksgiving, and which among us is accustomed to be performed by the Lord's Prayer); then, by the words of Christ, which he himself used in the first institution of the Supper, pronounced in the person of Christ, he causes the body and blood of Christ, united with the symbols of bread and wine, to be simultaneously dispensed, eaten, and drunk (which is consecration strictly so called).

He causes this, however, not by his own physical or intrinsic power of acting, whether principal or instrumental, but by moving the free will of Christ, so that He himself, through his omnipotence as the physical efficient cause, or the one really influencing, may really present his body and blood in the Holy Supper for true eating and drinking along with the earthly symbols.

Indeed, those words of consecration, just as they are the words of the omnipotent Son of God, so, as soon as they are uttered, have a divine operation joined to them, by which what they themselves signify is actually performed. Compare the blessed Musaeus, Dissert. de Coena, against J. Vorstius § 75, and what we have said in the notes d. e. to § 3.

Quenstedtius: "Because it is not expressed in the institution of the Holy Supper with what words the Lord consecrated the bread and wine, nor is any peculiar formula prescribed, hence in the primitive church consecration was indeed performed through prayers and thanksgivings, but the manner of them was αδιάφορος and left to Christian liberty. But at first..."

That the Lord’s institution of the Eucharist was recited in the act of consecration by the priest is evident not only from the pseudo-apostolic Constitutions of Clement (Book 8, ch. 12) and the ancient liturgies which circulate under the names of the evangelist Mark, the apostles Peter and James, Basil, Chrysostom, etc., but it is also manifest from other certain and indubitable monuments of the Fathers, such as Justin Martyr’s *Apology* 2, near the end; Ambrose, *On the Mysteries of Those Who Are Initiated*, ch. 9 (Vol. 4, Works, f. 381) and Book 4 *On the Sacraments*, ch. 4 (ibid., p. 392); and others.

Latin:

cumulate potest facere ultra omnia, quae petimus aut cogitamus, Eph. 3, 20., neque quicquam est ei difficile, Gen. 18, 14. Zach. 8, 36., nedum impossibile, Luc. 1, 37. Cum sit fidelis et verax testis, aequum est, ut verbis ejus fidem habeamus, captivantes intellectum nostrum in obsequium illius. 2 Cor. 10, 5. Cum sit omniscius et omni sapiens, aequum est, ut statuamus, ipsum scire rationem ac modum, quo possit suas promissiones implere, nec convenit, ut sapientia a filiis suis justificetur, Luc. 7, 35. Cumprimis vero obversentur oculis et animis nostris illa duo pronunciata, quorum alterum est ipsius Christi, alterum vero apostoli Pauli, quotiescunque de hoc mysterio cogitamus aut loquimur: Joh. 12, 48.: ,Sermo, quem locutus sum, ille judicabit vos in novissimo die'; 1 Tim. 6, 3. 4.: ,Si quis aliter docet, έτεροόίόασκαλει, et non quiescit sanis sermonibus Domini nostri Jesu Christi, ei, quae secundum pietatem est, doctrinae, inflatus est, nihil sciens.4 “ (Loc. de S. C. § 14.)

Qui vero auctoritatem et potestatem, Itemque omnipotentiam, qua usus est Christus in efficiendo hoc sacramento, cum Patre dt Spiritu S. communem habet, ideo etiam Deum trinunum hujus sacramenti camam efficientem principalem esse, recte dici potest. § 3. Causa impulsiva interna instituti hujus sacramenti est bonitas a atque amor Christi erga suos;b externa est ipsum meritum c passionis et mortis ejus. Speciatini quoad realem praesentiam corporis et sanguinis Christi in qualibet administratione coenae, causae impulsivae principalis rationem habet ipsa d institutio Christi; causa impulsiva minus principalis est consecratio e symbolorum, a ministro juxta institutionem Christi facta.

Qua Christus aliis bonus est, seu gratuitus favor ejus; ut ex seqq. patet. Huc spectat, quod Joh. 13, 1. legimus de dilectione, qua Christus aüexerit mos, qui in mundo erant, mque ad finem; cui etiam ea, quae in coena ultima et post eam acta sunt, adscribuntur.

Quamvis enim in sacra coena ipsum corpus Christi, in mortem pro nobis traditum, et sanguis Christi, pro nobis effusus, nobis exhibeantur; sicuti tamen Christus per illam corporis sui traditionem in paortem et sanguinis effusionem beneficia spiritualia nobis meruit, ita quoque meruit, ut beneficia illa per hoc signaculum novi foederis applicarentur, obsignarentur et confirmarentur. Scilicet actus ille, quo corpus et sanguis Christi in s. coena praesentia sistuntur et cum symbolis terrenis uniuntur, a potentia divina simul et libera voluntate Christi pendet. Postquam autem Christus constituit, corpus et sanguinem suum cum pane et vino in s. coena, quoties illa institutioni suae conformiter celebratur, praesentia sistere et sacramentaliter unire, idque verbis istis: Hoc est corpus meum; hoc

DE SACRA COENA* est sanguis meus (de quibus mox distinctius videbimus), aperte declaravit, certum est, voluntatem Christi vi ipsius institutionis suae moveri ad illud ipsum efficiendum, quod verba: Hoc est corpus meum; hoc est sanguis meus, significant. De qua statim ad §. seq. dicemus. Interim notandum est, verba consecrationis movere voluntatem Christi non vi propria, et ut a ministro proferuntur, sed vi ipsius institutionis a Christo profectae.

Formula Concordiae: ,,Dieweil auch von der Consecration und von der gemeinen Regel, dass nichts Sacrament sei ausser dem eingesetzten Gebrauch, Missverstand und Spaltung zwischen etlichen der Augsburgischen Confession Lehrern eingefallen sind, haben wir auch von dieser Sache uns brüderlich und einträchtig mit einander auf nachfolgende Meinung erkläret, nämlich: dass die wahre Gegenwärtigkeit des Leibes und Blutes Christi im Abendmahl nicht schaffe einiges Menschen Wort oder Werk, es sei das Verdienst oder Sprechen des Dieners, oder das Essen und Trinken oder Glaube der Communicanten, sondern solches alles solle allein des allmächtigen Gottes Kraft und unsers Herrn Jesu Christi Wort, Einsetzung und Ordnung zugeschrieben werden. Denn die wahrhaftigen und allmächtigen Worte Jesu Christi, welche er in der ersten Einsetzung gesprochen, sind nicht allein im ersten Abendmahl kräftig gewesen, sondern währen, gelten, wirken und sind noch kräftig, dass in allen Orten, da das Abendmahl nach Christi Einsetzung gehalten und seine Worte gebraucht werden, aus Kraft und Vermögen derselbigen Worte, die Christus im ersten Abendmahl gesprochen, der Leib und Blut Christi wahrhaftig gegenwärtig ausgetheilet und empfangen wird;

denn Christus selbst, wo man seine Einsetzung hält und seine Worte über dem Brot und Kelch spricht, und das gesegnete Brot und Kelch austheilt, durch die gesprochenen Worte, aus Kraft der ersten Einsetzung, noch durch sein Wort, welches er da will wiederholt haben, kräftig ist; wie Chrysostomus spricht (in serm. de pass.) in der Predigt von der Passion: ,Christus richtet diesen Tisch selbst zu und segnet ihn; denn kein Mensch das Vorgesetzte Brot und Wein zum Leib und Blut Christi macht, sondern Christus selbst, der für uns gekreuzigt ist. Die Worte werden durch des Priesters Mund gesprochen, aber durch Gottes Kraft und Gnade, durch das Wort, da er spricht: Das ist mein Leib, werden die vorgestellten Elemente im Abendmahl gesegnet; und wie diese Rede: Wachset und vermehret euch und erfüllet die Erde, nur einmal geredet, aber allezeit kräftig ist in der Natur, dass sie wächst und sich vermehret, also ist auch diese Rede einmal gesprochen, aber bis auf diesen Tag und bis an seine Zukunft ist sie kräftig und wirket, dass im Abendmahl der Kirche sein wahrer Leib und Blut gegenwärtig ist.‘

Und Lutherus tom. 6. Jen. fol. 99.: ,Solch sein Befehl und Einsetzung vermag und schaffet, dass wir nicht schlecht Brot und Wein, sondern seinen Leib und Blut^darreichen und empfangen, wie seine Worte lauten: Das ist mein Leib u. s. w. Das ist mein Blut u. s. w.; dass nicht unser Werk oder Sprechen, sondern der Befehl und Ordnung Christi das Brot zum Leib und den Wein zum Blut macht vom Anfang des ersten Abendmahls bis an der Welt Ende, und durch unsern Dienst und Amt täglich gereicht wird.‘

Item, tom. 3. Jen. fol. 446: ,Also hie auch, wenn ich gleich über alle Brote spräche: das ist Christi Leib, würde freilich nichts daraus folgen; aber wenn wir seiner Einsetzung und Heissung nach im Abendmahl sagen: Das ist mein Leib, so ists sein Leib, nicht unsers Sprechens oder Thätelworts halben, sondern seines Heissens halben, dass er uns also zu sprechen und zu thun geheissen hat, und sein Heissen und Thun an unser Sprechen gebunden hat.“‘ (Solid. Declar. artic. VII. §§ 73—78. p. 663. sq.) PART. m.

CAP. XI.

4. Causa ministerialis a est minister b ecclesiae c ordinarius, qui elementa externa d consecrat e et communicantibus f distribuit. Seu quae auctoritate alterius, velut superioris, sacramentum in usu constituit. Equidem Christus ipse, ea nocte, qua traditus est, eucharistiam primus administravit, servi forma tunc adhuc indutus, quamvis, ut #εάν&ρωπος, sua auctoritate uteretur. Sed post primam illam eucharistiae celebrationem ecclesiae ministris hoc munus tradidit et reliquit. Vid. 1 Cor. 4, 1. cap. 11, 23.

Non aeque, ut in baptismo, etiam laicus aliquando, aut femina. Non enim eadem necessitas est utriusque sacramenti. Quando autem, deficiente ministro ordinario, homo fidelis anxie desiderat hoc sacramentum, satius tarmn est, illi quoquo modo persuaderi sufficientiam manducationis spiritualis et ostendere periculum aliarum tentationum, quae nasci possent, si sacramentum ab alio, citra vocationem legitimam, adeoque dubia mente et eventu, administretur. Z. Grapius: ״Sacerdotes sunt laici, sed nonnisi interna Ικανότψι apti ad quaevis ecclesiae munia et sic quoque ad eucharistiae administrationem; ne putemus, minus verum sacramentum fore, quod laicus dederit necessitate forsitan vel errore adductus. Vid. Schomer. in tr. de collegiatismo. Dissert. I. § 34.“ (System, novissim. controvers. Tom. IV. p. 89.) Cf. supra adnotata ad P. III. c. 8. § 6. p. 408. sqq.)

Panem videlicet et vinum; de quibus mox dicetur.

Id est, precibus ad Deum fusis, symbola externa ab usu vulgari segregat et ad usum sacrum destinat (quam alias benedictiomm sive gratiarum actionem vocant, quaeque apud nos oratione dominica peragi solet), deinde verbis Christi, quibus ipse usus est in prima coenae institutione, in persona Christi pronunciatis, efficit, ut corpus et sanguis Christi, cum symbolis panis et vini unita, simul dispensentur, edantur ac bibantur (quae est consecratio stricte sic dicta').

Efficit autem, non sua vi agendi physica aut intrinseca, principali vel instrumental!, sed movendo liberam Christi voluntatem, ut ipse per omnipotentiam suam tanquam causam efficientem physicam, seu realiter influentem, corpus suum et sanguinem in sacra coena realiter praesentia sistat ad veram cum symbolis terrenis manducationem et bibitionem.

Imo verba illa consecrationis, sicut sunt verba omnipotentis Filii Dei, ita, simul ac proferuntur, divinam operationem habent conjunctam, qua, quod ipsa sonant, reapse praestetur. Confer, b. Mus. Dissert. de 15. Coena, contra J. Vorstium § 75. et quae diximus in notis d. e. ad § 3.

Quenstedtius: ״Quia in institutione s. coenae non exprimitur, quibus verbis Dominus panem et vinum consecraverit, neque praescribitur peculiaris quaedam formula, hinc in primitiva ecclesia consecratio quidem fiebat per preces et gratiarum actiones, modus vero earum erat αδιάφορος et Christianae libertati relictus. Primo autem

Dominicam eucharistiae institutionem recitatam esse in actu consecrationis a sacerdote, patet non solum ex Constitutionibus pseudoapostolicis Clementis 1. 8. c. 12. et antiquis liturgiis, quae sub nomine Marci evangelistae, Petri et Jacobi apostolorum, Basilii, Chrysostomi etc. circumferuntur, sed etiam ex aliis certis ac indubitatis patrum monumentis, ut Justini Martyris Apolog. 2. prope finem, Ambrosii de his, qui initiantur, mysteriis c. 9. T. 4. Op. f. 381. et 1. 4. de sacram, c. 4. ibid. p. 392., aliorumque, manifestum est.


### Of the Holy Supper: However, prayers and acts of thanksgiving were joined by the ancients to the…

However, prayers and acts of thanksgiving were joined by the ancients to the words of institution in the act of consecration, and indeed in the earliest times, the Lord’s Prayer alone. (L. c. s. 1. th. 11. not. 2. f. 1187.) Luther: "I know for a truth that all Christians are obligated by the institution and command of Christ to speak such words in the Lord’s Supper, and I do not hold the enthusiasts themselves to be so bold as to leave them out with a good conscience." (Confession concerning the Lord's Supper, A. 1528. XX, 1145.)

Whether by giving the blessed bread and cup into the hands of the communicants, or by bringing both to the mouths of the communicants. For nothing is determined here; yet the distribution can be performed in either way. Quenstedtius: "Most Calvinists contend that Christ our Savior placed the consecrated bread into the hands of the apostles, but did not put it into the mouths of each one as they reclined. They gather this from the word λαμβάνειν, which they translate as 'to take with the hand,' 'to receive with the hand.' ... But the word λαμβάνειν in general denotes any taking, performed by any part of the body, and that it is used in the Scriptures even for an acceptance that occurs by the mouth is evident from Mark 15:23 and John 19:30. For Christ, already nailed to the cross, received the sour wine mixed with myrrh, offered to his mouth by a sponge, not with his hands, which were fixed to the cross by nails, but by his mouth alone. Rightly does the blessed Gerhard in *L. de coena* § 169 say: 'The evangelists testify,' he says, 'that Christ gave the blessed bread and the cup to the disciples, but they nowhere express whether he moved it to their hand or to their mouth; they would have done so entirely if either one were absolutely and simply necessary.'

In the primitive church, for several centuries, the use of εγχείρισις was in effect; for the faithful received those sacred portions of bread, the άγίας μερίδας, from the hand of the priest with their own hand, as we have shown in the place cited from Dionysius of Alexandria, Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, and other fathers; but because that custom introduced superstition—namely, the making of certain δοχεία, receptacles, and linens out of gold or other precious material, which the communicants used instead of their hand (which superstition was condemned and abolished by canon 7 of the Council of Constantinople, which is called the Trullan, in the seventh century), and the carrying away with them and taking to their homes the particles of the sacred bread handed into their hands—therefore the pious antiquity judged that in place of εγχείρισις, μετάδοσις should be used. ... Which custom is still rightly preserved in many places for the sake of Christian liberty." (L. c. s. 1. th. 11. not. 4. f. 1188. sq.)

Whence there is no need for the breaking of bread in the very act of administration, but it suffices if it is brought forward already adapted, broken, or divided for distribution. For we know that Christ, in the first administration, broke the bread for no other purpose than for the sake of distribution. Luther: "Note secondly, that Paul indeed speaks of the bread in the Sacrament, which Christ broke and which the apostles afterwards also broke; which breaking is nothing else than making pieces or distributing, in the Hebrew manner, Isaiah 58:7: 'Break thy bread to the hungry'; Lamentations 4:4: 'The young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them.' So that we are not here again scolded by the sectarians as traitors to Christ, because we do not break or crumble it with our fingers, but take many particles and hosts. For that is what they call breaking, and they are not satisfied that it is otherwise made into pieces, whether it be done by hand, knife, or however it may be, as it is called 'broken' in the Hebrew manner." (Against the Heavenly Prophets, A. 1524. XX, 314.) PART III. CHAPTER XI.

Aeg. Hunnius: "Certainly, just as from the fact that it is written that Christ and the apostles reclined, that they are recorded to have celebrated these mysteries in the upper room of an inn, and that it was in the evening, it is not permitted to conclude that we also must perform these sacred rites only in inns, only in the evening, and while reclining—however much Christ may expressly say, 'Do this'—so too, by the force of this command ('Do this'), we are not compelled to the breaking of bread properly so called; but only to those things which, in this divine action, are necessary for the sacramental κοινωνία or salutary by reason of their fruit. Furthermore, it is established that the word 'breaking' is taken in the Hebrew idiom for distribution. In this sense, the sons of Jacob are read to have heard that bread was being broken in Egypt. And in Isaiah 58, the Lord admonishes us to break bread for the hungry; yet there is no one so ignorant as to think that for the fulfillment of this command, it is necessary to dissect a single mass of bread into several pieces. Indeed, even he who gives an entire mass of bread to a poor person complies with this command. Nay, he approaches this command of God (break bread for the hungry) even more closely, because he bestows more than the other, who communicates only a part or a fragment of bread." (Artic. s. locus de sacramentis, p. 332 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who urge the breaking of bread in the very act of the Supper as necessary... Ursinus, p. 117, says: 'The breaking of bread is of the essence and form of the Lord's Supper, and therefore is not to be omitted; and Christ used it, not for the sake of dividing and distributing, but for the sake of representing His death.' ... 2. Of the Socinians; thus Ostorodus, Instit. germ. c. 38, f. 344: 'One must break the bread.' ... Therefore, the Calvinists also defend the breaking, 'so that thereby the idolatrous, false delusion of the body of Christ in or under the bread may be most powerfully broken and cleared out of the hearts of the common, misguided people'; these are the words of Pareus in his book *Vom Brot und Brotbrechen* [On Bread and Bread-Breaking], f. 198. No egg can be more like an egg, no milk more like milk." (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 1241 sq.)

Theological Faculty of Wittenberg: "The question sent to us by you: 'Whether, during the administration of the Holy Supper, these or other such words: "The body and blood of Jesus Christ preserve your body and soul unto eternal life," must necessarily be spoken and referred to the place where Christ says, "Do this in remembrance of me,"' certainly rests upon the institution of the holy sacrament performed by Christ, and especially upon the words also cited: 'Do this,' etc., as thereby the final cause of this administration is regarded. In consideration of this, it is first of all quite certain that for the salutary and proper administration of the Holy Supper, the Lord Christ should and must be thankfully remembered and His death proclaimed. Besides this, however, it stands beyond doubt that such a commemoration and proclamation of the Lord's death can also take place without this or a similar formula being repeated to every communicant, namely, through a preceding admonition. Likewise, the recitation of the words of institution, Christian hymns which are performed during the distribution, and also the right and proper devotion of every Christian; for which reason one should not consider the words set forth in the question as an essential, which belongs to the essence, nor as an integral part, which belongs to the right perfection of the Supper—

[...cannot hold them to be properly, or likewise necessary for the benefit and salutary use of the Lord’s Supper. In particular consideration that they: 1. are not incorporated into the original institution nor expressly commanded therein; 2. are not cited by St. Paul as necessary for the holy Sacrament; 3. are nowhere read to have been used by Christ, the Apostles, or the first apostolic Church, in which, however, everything necessary for the holy Sacrament regarding its substance and benefit was performed. Meanwhile, it cannot be denied that it is very conducive to the prosperity and edification of the Church if one does not let the performance of the Communion be an *actionem mutam* [mute action], but rather reminds each communicant individually of the benefits of the Lord Christ, as well as the benefit and effect of this Sacrament, informs and instructs the simple, and also awakens many a person who, through the recitation of such a *formula*, is led to a deeper contemplation of his action; finally, there is also more compliance with the words of Christ: "Do this in remembrance of me," and Paul: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death"; so that no congregation, for the reasons mentioned and others, should neglect to use a certain *formula* in the performance of the holy Supper." (Anno 1619. See Dedekenn’s *Thesaurus* II, 267.) Guerickius: "Thus, the words of distribution were certainly not entirely the same in the various ancient liturgies; but all testify to the true presence of the body and blood of Christ, and the words of institution themselves, historically reported (the new Union formula), were nowhere and never used in the ancient Church during the distribution. The reported word of the Lord, it was clearly recognized (here, as analogously in Baptism), belongs to the consecration; the confession, the open, free, unambiguous confession of the Church, belongs to the distribution; and one was most distant from the thought—which one would have considered satanic and abhorred—of wanting to transform the confession to the honor of the Lord in the distribution into a relation that intentionally bypasses this confession, and thus into a non-confession to dishonor, i.e., into a denial, out of distrust in the unconditional truth of the clear testament-word of the Lord, and in order to place its validity or non-validity into freedom out of human love of peace." (*Lehrbuch der christl. Archäologie*. 2nd ed. 1859, p. 310.) § 5. The matter of the holy Supper is twofold, earthly and heavenly. That thing, I say, which is to be handled in this sacrament and applied to men. Thus our theologians commonly [speak], led by Irenaeus, who writes in *Lib. IV. adv. haeres.*, cap. XXXIV, p. m. 363, edit. Feuard.: "The bread which is from the earth, receiving the invocation of God, is no longer common bread, but the eucharist, consisting of two things, earthly and heavenly." Regarding the genuine sense of these words, see the blessed Musaeus, *Disert. de S. Coena* § 81 sq., pp. 73, 74, 75.

Latin:

Cum verbis autem institutionis jungebantur in actu consecrationis preces et gratiarum actiones a veteribus, et quidem primis temporibus sola oratio Dominica.44 (L. c. s. 1. th. 11. not. 2. f. 1187.) Lutherus: ״Ich weiss fürwahr, dass alle Christen schuldig sind aus der Einsetzung und Gebot Christi, solche Worte im Abendmahl zu sprechen, und halte die Schwärmer selbst so kühne nicht, dass sie dieselbigen mit gutem Gewissen aussen lassen.44 (Bek. vom Abendm. A. 1528. XX, 1145.)

Sive in manus communicantium dando panem et poculum benedictum, sive utrumque ori communicantium admovendo. Nihil enim hic determinatum est; utroque autem modo fieri potest distributio. Quenstedtius: ״Christum salvatorem nostrum panem consecratum in apostolorum manus reposuisse, non vero in ora discumbentibus singulis ingessisse, contendunt plerique Calviniani. Colligunt id ex verbo λαμβάνειν, quod vertunt manu prehendere, manu accipere. . . . Ast verbum λαμβάνειν in genere sumtionem notat omnem, quacunque corporis parte factam, atque etiam de acceptione, quae ore fit, in Scripturis accipi, patet ex Mare. 15, 23. et Joh. 19, 30. Christus enim, jam in crucem actus, acetum myrrhatum, ori per spongiam oblatum, non manibus, quae clavis affixae erant cruci, sed ore tantum accepit. Recte b. Gerhardus in L. de coena § 169.: ,Testantur evangelistae4, inquit, ,Christum benedictum panem et calicem discipulis dedisse, sed an manui, an ori eorum admoverit, nuspiam exprimunt; facturi illud omnino, si alterutrum absolute et simpliciter foret necessarium.4

In primitiva ecclesia per aliquot saecula in usu fuit εγχείριας; άγίας enim μερίδας seu particulas illas sacras panis fideles de manu sacerdotis manu sua accipiebant, ut 1. c. ex Dionys. Alexand., Tertulliano, Cypriano, Ambrosio, aliisque patribus ostendimus; ast quia.consuetudo illa superstitionem invexit, conficiendi sc. ex auro vel alia materia pretiosa quaedam δοχεία, receptacula et linteamina, quibus pro manu utebantur communicantes (quae superstitio damnata et sublata est canone 7. Concilii Constantinopol., quod Trullanum vocatur, saeculo septimo), asportandique secum ac deferendi in domos suas particulas sacri panis in manus traditi, ideo judicavit pia antiquitas, εγχεφίσεως loco μετάδοσιν esse usurpandam. . . . Qui mos Christianae libertati jure etiamnum passim servatur.44 (L. c. s. 1. th. 11. not. 4. f. 1188. sq.)

Unde neque fractione panis opus est in ipso actu administrationis, sed sufficit, si ad distributionem aptatus, fractus aut divisus afferatur. Nam et Christum in prima administratione non in alio consilio, nisi distributionis causa, panem fregisse novimus. Lutherus: ״Merke zum andern, dass Paulus ja redet vom Brot im Sacrament, welches Christus brach und hernachmals die Apostel auch brachen; welches Brechen nichts anders ist, denn Stück machen oder austheilen, auf ebräische Weise Jes. 58, 7.: ,Brich dem Hungrigen dein Brot4; Klagl. 4, 4.: ,Die Jungen hieschen Brot, und niemand brachs ihnen.4 Auf dass wir hier nicht abermal von den Rottengeistem gescholten werden als Christus Verräther, dass wirs nicht mit Eingern PART. m. CAP. XI. brocken oder brechen, sondern viel Partikel und Hostien nehmen. Denn das heissen sie brechen, und haben nicht Genüge daran, dass es sonst zu Stücken gemacht wird, es gesche mit Hand, Messer oder wie es wolle, wie es in ebräischer Weise gebrochen heisst.“ (Wider die himmlischen Propheten. A. 1524. XX, 314.)

Aeg. Hunnius: ״Certe quemadmodum ex eo, quod Christus et apostoli scribuntur discubuisse, quod memorantur in palatio diversorii celebrasse haec mysteria, quod vesperi, non licet colligere, nobis etiam in diversoriis et vesperi tantum et discumbendo haec sacra esse peragenda; quantumvis Christus expresse dicat: ,Hoc facite‘, sic quoque vi hujus mandati (hoc facite) non adigimur ad illius panis fractionem proprie sic dictam; sed ad sola illa, quae in actione hac divina sunt ad κοινωνίαν sacramentalem vel ratione substantiae necessaria vel ratione fructus salutaria. Praeterea constat, frangendi vocem phrasi hebraea sumi pro distributione. Quo sensu filii Jacob leguntur audivisse, quod frangeretur in Aegypto panis. Et Esaias 58. monet Dominus, ut esurienti frangamus panem; nec tamen est quisquam tam rudis, qui ad huius mandati complementum putet esse necessariam dissectionem unius massae panis in frusta plura. Quin obsecundat huic mandato is etiam, qui integram massam panis dat pauperi. Imo hic propius etiam accedit ad mandatum hoc Dei (frange esurienti panem), quia plus largitur, quam alter, qui duntaxat partem aut frustum panis communicat.“ (Artic. s. locus de sacramentis, p. 332. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Calvinianorum, qui fractionem panis in ipso coenae actu ut necessariam urgent. . . . Ursinus p. 117. inquit: ,Fractio panis est de essentia et forma coenae Dom., ideoque non omittenda, eaque Christus est usus, non gratia dividendi et distribuendi, sed mortis suae repraesentandi gratia. ... 2. Socinianorum; sic Ostorodus Instit. germ. c. 38. f. 344.: ,Man soll das Brot brechen.‘ . . . Ideo etiam Calviniani fractionem propugnant, ,dass dadurch der abgöttische falsche Wahn vom Leibe Christi in oder unter dem Brot am allerkräftigsten zerbrochen und dem gemeinen verirrten Volk aus dem Herzen geräumet werde‘; sunt verba Parei lib. Vom Brot und Brotbrechen, f. 198. Non ovum ova, non lac lacti similius esse potest.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 1241 sq.)

Facultas theol. Wittebergensis: ״Eure an uns geschickte Frage: ,Ob unter der Administration des heil. Nachtmahls diese oder andere dergleichen Worte: Der Leib und Blut Jesu Christi bewahre deinen Leib und Seele zum ewigen Leben, nothwendig müssen gesprochen und dahin, da Christus sagt: Solches thut zu meinem Gedächtniss, gezogen werden‘, beruht allerdings auf der Einsetzung des heil. Sacraments, von Christo beschehen, insonderheit aber auf den mitangezogenen Worten: ,Solches thut‘ u. s. w., als damit auf die EndUrsache dieser Administration gesehen wird. In Erwägung dessen ist zuvörderst ganz gewiss, zu heilsamer und gebührlicher Administration des heil. Abendmahls solle und müsse des Herrn Christi dankbarlich gedacht und sein Tod verkündigt werden. Daneben aber stehet ausser Zweifel, dass eine solche Commemoration und des Herrn Todes Verkündigung auch ohne dieses oder gleiches Formular, so zu jedem Communicanten repetirt werde, geschehen könne, als durch vorgehende Admonition. Item, der Wort der Einsetzung Recitation, christliche Gesänge, die unter Ausspendung verrichtet werden, auch wohl eines jeden Christen rechte und gebührliche Andacht; deswegen man die in der Frage gesetzte Worte nicht für ein Essential, das zum Wesen, auch nicht für ein Integralstück, das zu rechter Vollkommenheit des Nacht-

mahls gehörig, wie imgleichen zum Nutz und heilsamen Gebrauch des Abendmahls nothwendig nicht halten kann. In sonderer Betrachtung, dass sie: 1. der ersten Einsetzung nicht einverleibet oder ausdrücklich darinnen befohlen; 2. von St. Paulo als nothwendig zum heil. Sacrament nicht angezogen; 3. nirgends gelesen wird, dass Christus, die Apostel oder erste apostolische Kirche eine gleiche oder auch diese Formulam gebrauchet, bei welchem jedoch alles dasjenige, so zum heil. Sacrament seiner Substanz und Nutzens halben nothwendig ist, verrichtet worden. Indessen mag nicht geleugnet werden, dass zu der Kirchen Wohlstand und Erbauung sehr dienlich, wenn man die Verrichtung der Communion nicht ein actionem mutam sein lässet, besondern einem jeden Communicanten des Herrn Christi Wohlthaten, auch dieses Sacraments Nutz und Wirkung absonderlich erinnert, die Einfältigen informiret und unterrichtet, auch sonsten manchen Menschen, der durch einer solchen formulae Recitation zu desto tieferer Betrachtung seiner Verrichtung angeführt wird, erwecket; geschieht auch endlich desto mehr Folge den Worten Christi: ,Solches thut zu meinem Gedächtniss‘ und Pauli: ,So oft ihr von diesem Brot esset und von diesem Kelch trinket, sollt ihr des Herrn Tod verkündigen‘; dass also keine Gemeine angeregter und auch anderer Ursachen wegen unterlassen sollte, in des heil. Nachtmahls Verrichtung sich eines gewissen Formulars zu gebrauchen.“ (Anno 1619. Vid. Dedekenni thesaur. II, 267.) Guerickius: ,,So waren allerdings in den verschiedenen alten Liturgieen die Spendeworte nicht ganz gleich; die wahre Gegenwart aber des Leibes und Blutes Christi bezeugen alle, und die Einsetzungsworte selbst, historisch referirt (das neue Unionsformular), wurden in der alten Kirche bei der Austheilung nirgends und nie gebraucht. Das referirte Wort des Herrn, erkannte man ja klar (hier, wie analog bei der Taufe), gehört in die Consecration, das Bekenntniss, das offene, freie, unzweideutige der Kirche in die Distribution; und am allerentferntesten war man von dem Gedanken, den man als satanisch betrachtet und verabscheut haben würde, aus Misstrauen in die unbedingte Wahrheit des klaren Testamentsworts des Herrn, und um dessen Geltung oder Nichtgeltung aus menschlicher Friedensliebe in Freiheit zu stellen, das Bekenntniss zur Ehre des Herrn in der Distribution in eine dies Bekenntniss absichtlich umgehende Relation, also in ein Nichtbekenntniss zu Unehren, d. h. in eine Verleugnung, verwandeln zu wollen.“ (Lehrbuch der christl. Archäologie. 2. Aufl. 1859. p. 310.) § 5. Materia"a s. coenae duplex est, terrena et b coelestis. Res illa, inquam, quae in hoc sacramento tractanda et hominibus applicanda est. Ita nostrates communiter, praeeunte Irenaeo, qui Lib. IV. adv. haeres, cap. XXXIV. p. m. 363. edit. Feuard. scribit: Qui est a terra panis, percipiens invocationem Dei, jam non communis panis est, sed eucharistia, ex duabus rebus constans, terrena et coelesti. De quorum verborum genuino sensu vid. b. Musaeus Disert. de S. Coena § 81. sq. p. 73. 74. 75. 32 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. IU. PART. ΠΙ. CAP. XI.


### Of the Holy Supper: The earthly matter consists of true bread and true wine, as to substance

6. The earthly matter consists of true bread and true wine, as to substance; yet unleavened bread just as much as leavened, and finer or thinner just as much as coarser or common and usual; not only wheat, but also other grain. Wine also, red just as much as white, and whether it be pure or slightly diluted with water. This [matter] is also not abolished by consecration, but retains its substance. For thus in 1 Cor. 11:26, 27, communicants are said to eat bread, certainly already blessed or consecrated; not, I say, something that was bread and ceased to be, but the bread itself, still existing.

Quenstedtius: "In 1 Cor. 10:16, the Eucharistic bread is called by Paul the κοινωνία of the body, and the Eucharistic cup the κοινωνία of the blood of Christ. Now, sacramental κοινωνία involves the presence of the earthly substance, which communicates with the heavenly thing to be communicated, and overturns transubstantiation. For the bread is the κοινωνία of the body, the wine of the blood of Christ. Therefore, it is not the body itself, the blood itself, by substantial change. Κοινωνία exists between two things that exist. If existence is removed, the relation of communion is taken away." (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1249.)

Hafenrefferus: "It is by no means valid to say: Christ truly said, 'This is my body'; therefore, the substance of the bread is converted into the substance of the body of Christ. For just as it is not valid to say: Peter truly said of Christ, 'You are the Son of the living God'; therefore, the substance of the Son of Man is converted into the substance of the Son of God: so neither is the former valid: Christ truly said, 'This is my body'; therefore, the substance of the bread is converted into the substance of the body of Christ. The reason is: because in both cases, namely both in this (of which Christ pronounces that it is His body) and in Christ (of whom Peter says that He is the Son of God), not one, but two things or substances or natures are comprehended. For the person of Christ consists of two natures, human and divine, which are united through the personal union. Therefore, it can truly be said: Christ is the Son of God. And by a clearly similar reasoning, this 'this' (of which Christ says: 'This is my body') consists not of one thing only, but of two: the one earthly, which is bread; the other heavenly, which is the body of Christ, sacramentally united to that bread by means of which it is exhibited. Therefore, for the truth of this statement, 'This is my body,' popish transubstantiation is by no means required. For bread is bread and remains bread; the body of Christ is the body and remains the body of Christ, without any conversion or transubstantiation. But because of that sacramental union, by which the bread and the body of Christ are now a certain sacramental 'one'—which is demonstrated by this—it is most plainly and most truly said: '

This is the body of Christ.' — Could this matter not be declared more clearly at some point? Indeed, it can be illustrated not only by certain examples, but also by an elegant rule. For it is familiar and customary, not only in the Holy Scriptures but also in all languages, that when two things are offered or pointed out joined together, the whole, consisting of two parts, is indeed offered or pointed out, and the one of them, which is not so exposed to the senses, is truly predicated of it; as if, offering a purse, I should say: 'These are a hundred florins'; or pointing to a cask, I should say: 'This is Rhine wine, this is Italian, this is claret'; or touching a glass,"

I shall say: 'This is water, this is beer, this is ointment,' etc. By all these examples it appears that the demonstrative particle "this" certainly embraces both the vessel and the drink, and that, on account of that union, the other thing, which is not so obvious to the senses, can most truly be predicated of that whole which is pointed out, and that it can most truly be pointed out or exhibited through the intervention of the other thing with which it is united or conjoined.” (Loc. th. Tübingen, 1601, p. 347 sqq.)

Hollazius: “Distinguish between essential and accidental change. When the holy fathers wrote that bread and wine in the Eucharist are changed or trans-elemented through consecration, they did not understand an essential change, but an accidental one, namely, by reason of office and mystical use, i.e., the elevation of the elements into a nobler state, so that the bread is and remains, by reason of its essence, the same that it was before consecration, but according to the institution and promise of Christ, by His own omnipotent power, it becomes a symbol communicative of the body of Christ, whereas before consecration it was common bread. . . . (The Papists object:) If the Eucharistic bread is not changed essentially into the body of Christ, it follows that the proposition: 'Bread is the body of Christ,' is false. But that proposition is true and used by the holy fathers and Luther. Therefore. Resp.: Distinguish between a biblical and an ecclesiastical proposition. That proposition, 'Bread is the body of Christ,' is not biblical, but ecclesiastical, to be understood by reason of the sacramental union.” (Exam. P. III. s. 2. c. 5. q. 14. p. 1129.)

Quenstedtius: “That the Papal transubstantiation is not a substantial conversion, but an annihilation, is proved from this, because in a substantial conversion the matter ought to remain as the subject of the conversion of both the term from which and the term to which; but according to the Papists, the matter of the bread does not remain. In creation, that which was not comes to be; in annihilation, that which was ceases to be; in conversion, something passes from non-being to another.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1247.)

Gerhardus: “If transubstantiation is posited. . . it follows that Christ has two bodies: one which He assumed from Mary, and another which is formed from the bread.” (L. de s. c. § 130.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: Of the Papists, who imagine that the substance of bread and wine in the Holy Supper, after the words of consecration, passes into the substance of the body and blood of Christ, so that nothing remains except the species and accidents of bread and wine, or that by the power of the divine words the nature of bread and wine is transmuted so that it is converted into the body and blood of the Lord, as Costerus explains the opinion of the Roman Church (Enchir. controv. p. 313). . . . The Council of Trent, sess. 13, c. 4, decreed concerning transubstantiation as follows: 'Since Christ our Redeemer said that that which He offered under the species of bread was truly His body, it has therefore always been believed in the Church of God, and this holy synod now declares it anew, that by the consecration of the bread and wine a conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the body of Christ our Lord, and of the whole substance of the wine into the substance of His blood, takes place; which conversion has been aptly and properly called transubstantiation by the holy Catholic Church.'” (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1247 sq.)

But it is not permitted to use other elements, foods, or drinks, substantially different from those, in their place. Such as Christ is believed to have used, when He had just celebrated the sacrament of the paschal lamb. PART III. CAP. XI.

Which the Greek Church has used since the most ancient times, and indeed the Latin Church as well, up to the times of Alexander I, Bishop of Rome. Just as round loaves or small cakes, which they called hosts and oblations, are rightly used in our churches. For they are, as to matter and form, and thus as to substance, true bread, because they consist of purer wheat flour, mixed with water, and baked by the heat of an oven; they can also serve for the nutrition of the body if taken in greater quantity, although such a quantity is not required in the Eucharist, where the nutrition of the body is not to be sought.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Greeks, who are persuaded that Christ used leavened bread, ένζυμα, not unleavened, άζυμα, at His Passover, whence they themselves use leavened bread in this mystery and convert a matter that is by its nature αδιάφορου and indifferent into a dogma of faith; but they rely on a false hypothesis, namely, that the legitimate day for celebrating the Passover was anticipated by the Lord. . . . To deny, however, that the Passover which Christ solemnly celebrated with His disciples in the upper room shortly before the institution of the Supper was legitimate, is not without its impiety. The Abyssinians also use leavened bread in their sacred rites, prepared on the same day. ... 2. Of certain Calvinists, who 1. having abrogated the unleavened bread which Christ Himself used, champion the necessity of leavened, common, or usual bread in the Holy Eucharist; 2. urge a larger bread that can be broken in the act of the Supper; and 3. accuse the nature, quantity, external form, and efficacy of the sacramental bread customarily used by our churches. The nature, when they deny that our hosts are true bread, and call them 'foam of bread,' 'foam of bread unworthy of the name,' 'an invention of the Antichrist,' 'unleavened mists,' 'coin-like mists,' 'paper-like wafers,' 'farinaceous leaves,' etc. . . . Antonius Praetorius says that we do not institute the memory of the dead Christ with these coin-like breads so much as the memory of the betraying Judas... 3. Of some Calvinists, such as Beza, asserting that 'a substance similar to bread can be used in those regions where there is no use of bread'.... To which pertains the decree of Innocent VIII in Volaterranus 1.2. Georg.: 'In those places where there is no use of either grain or wine, another food is to be used in place of bread, and water in place of wine.' ... 5. Of the Socinians, who maintain that the host cannot be accepted as bread. Smalzius against Franz, p. 349, says: 'It can in no way be defended that a host is used for bread.' 6. Of the Papists, who maintain that 'the use of unleavened bread in the administration of the Eucharist is simply necessary.' . . . Although the Council of Trent calls the use of unleavened bread an ecclesiastical precept, yet, on the contrary, the Jesuits refer it to the institution of Christ and the apostles; see Bellarmine, l. c." (L. c. q. 4. f. 1234. sq.)

For although they differ as to the species of grain, they nevertheless agree in the being of bread. For Christ determined only wine, or γέννημα της αμπέλου, in Matthew 26:29; the rest He left to Christian liberty. Indeed, in those regions where stronger wines are scarcely used for common consumption otherwise than tempered with water, it is certain that the same has long since come into use in the Eucharist. In our regions, however, where wines are not so strong, there is no cause why they should be tempered with water. Certainly, Christ made mention of wine, and not likewise of water to be mixed in, at the institution of the Holy Supper.

Latin:

6. Materia terrena a sunt panis verus et vinum verum, quoad b substantiam; azymus c tamen panis aeque ac fermentatus,d et subtilior aut tenuior e aeque atque crassiorr sive vulgaris et usualis; triticeus non solum, verum etiam frumentarius f alius. Vinum quoque rubrum perinde atque album,g et sive merum sit, sive aqua paulis״ perh dilutum. Quae etiam per consecrationem non aboletur, sed retinet substantiam suam. Sic enim 1 Cor. 11, 26. 27. communicantes dicuntur edere panem, utique jam benedictum aut consecratum; non, inquam, aliquid, quod fuit panis, et esse desiit, sed panem ipsum, adhuc exsistentem.

Quenstedtius: ,,1 Cor. 10, 16. vocatur panis euchar. a Paulo κοινωνία corporis et poculum euchar. κοινωνία sanguinis Christi. Κοινωνία autem sacramentalis involvit substantiae terrenae, communicantis cum communicanda re coelesti, praesentiam et evertit transsubstantiationem. Panis enim est κοινωνία corporis, vinum sanguinis Christi. Ergo non est ipsum corpus, ipse sanguis substantiali commutatione. Κοινωνία est inter duo nhita existentia. Sublata existentia, tollitur relatio communionis.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1249.)

Hafenrefferus: ,,Nequaquam val^t: Christus vere dixit: Hoc est corpus meum; ergo substantia panis conversa est in substantiam corporis Christi. Quemadmodum enim non valet: Petrus vere dixit de Christo: Tu es Filius Dei vivi; ergo substantia Filii hominis conversa est in substantiam Filii Dei: ita nec prius illud valet: Christus vere dixit: Hoc est corpus meum; ergo substantia panis conversa est in substantiam corporis Christi. Ratio est: quia utrobique, videlicet et in hoc (de quo Christus pronunciat, quod sit corpus suum) et in Christo (de quo Petrus ait, quod sit Filius Dei) non una, sed duae res vel substantiae aut naturae comprehenduntur. Nam Christi persona duabus naturis constat, humana et divina, quae per unionem personalem unitae sunt. Vere igitur dici potest: Christus est Filius Dei. Et simili plane ratione illud hoc (^de quo Christus ait: Hoc est corpus meum) non una tantum re, sed duabus constat, altera terrena, quae panis est, altera coelesti, quae corpus Christi est, illi pani, cujus medio exhibetur, sacramentaliter unitum. Ad veritatem igitur hujus enunciati: Hoc est corpus meum, papistica transsubstantiatio nequaquam requiritur. Panis enim est panis et manet panis, corpus Christi est corpus et manet corpus Christi, sine omni conversione aut transsubstantiatione. Sed propter sacramentalem illam unionem, qua panis et corpus Christi jam quoddam sacramentale unum sunt; quod per hoc demonstratur, planissime et verissime dicitur: Hoc est corpus Christi. —

Annon haec res aliquando dilucidius declarari possit? Imo vero non tantum exemplis quibusdam, sed eleganti quoque regula illustrari potest. Nam familiare et usitatum est, non tantum in Scripturis s., sed etiam in omnibus linguis, ut cum duae quaedam res conjunctae porriguntur aut demonstrantur, id totum quidem, duobus constans, porrigitur aut demonstratur, atque alterum eorum, quod non ita sensibus expositum est, de illo vere enunciatur; ut, si marsupium porrigens, dicam: Hi sunt centum floreni; aut dolium monstrans, dicam: Hoc est vinum Rhenanum, hoc Italicum, hoc rubellum; aut vitrum tangens,

dicam: Haec est aqua, haec cerevisia, hoc unguentum etc. Quibus omnibus exemplis apparet, particulam demonstrativam hoc utrunque sane et vas et potum complecti et propter istam unionem de illo toto, quod monstratur, verissime enunciari posse alterum, quod sensibus non ita obvium est, alterius autem, quocum unitum aut conjunctum est, interventu verissime monstrari aut exhiberi posse.“ (Loc. th. Tubingae, 1601. p. 347. sqq.)

Hollazius: ״Dist. inter mutationem essentialem et accidentalem. Quando sancti patres scripserunt, quod panis et vinum in eucharistia per consecrationem mutentur aut transelemententur, non intellexerunt mutationem essentialem, sed accidentalem, nempe ratione officii et usus mystici, i. e., evectionem elementorum in nobiliorem statum, ita, ut panis sit et maneat ratione essentiae idem, qui ante consecrationem fuit, sed juxta institutionem atque promissionem Christi omnipotente ipsius virtute flat symbolum corporis Christi communicativum, cum ante consecrationem esset panis vulgaris. . . . (Pontificii objiciunt:) Si panis euchar. non mutatur essentialiter in corpus Christi, sequitur, quod illa propositio: Panis est corpus Christi, sit falsa. At illa propositio est vera et usurpata a sanctis patribus et Luthero. Ergo. Resp.: Dist. inter propositionem biblicam et ecclesiasticam. Propositio illa: panis est corpus Christi, non est biblica, sed ecclesiastica, ratione unionis sacramentalis intelligenda.“ (Exam. P. III. s. 2. c. 5. q. 14. p. 1129.)

Quenstedtius: ״Transsubstantiationem pontificiam non esse substantialem conversionem, sed annihilationem, inde probatur, quia in substantiali conversione materia manere debet, tanquam subjectum conversionis utriusque termini a quo et ad quem, sed juxta pontificios materia panis non manet. In creatione fit, quod non erat; in annihilatione desinit esse, quod erat; in conversione transit aliquid de non esse ad aliud.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1247.)

Gerhardus: ״Posita transsubstantiatione. . . sequitur, Christum habere duo corpora, alterum, quod ex Maria assumsit, alterum, quod ex pane formatur.“ (L. de s. c. § 130.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: Pontificiorum, qui fingunt, substantiam panis et vini in s. coena post verba consecrationis transire in substantiam corporis et sanguinis Christi, ita ut nihil remaneat, nisi species et accidentia panis et vini, sive vi divinorum verborum transmutari naturam panis et vini, ut convertatur in corpus et sanguinem Domini, ut sententiam Romanae ecclesiae exponit Costerus Enchir. controv. p. 313. . . . Concilium Trid. sess. 13. c. 4. de transsubstantiatione ita decrevit: ,Quoniam Christus redemtor noster corpus suum id, quod sub specie panis efferebat, vere esse dixit, ideo persuasum semper in ecclesia Dei fuit, idque tiunc denuo sancta haec synodus declarat, per consecrationem panis et vini conversionem fieri totius substantiae panis in substantiam corporis Christi, D. n., et totius substantiae vini in substantiam sanguinis ejus, quae conversio convenienter et proprie a s. catholica ecclesia transsubstantiatio est appellata.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 1247. sq.)

Alia autem elementa, cibos aut potus, substantialiter ab illis diversos, eorum loco adhibere non licet. Qualem Christus adhibuisse creditur, cum agni paschalis sacramentum modo celebrasset. PART. III. CAP. XI.

Qualem ecclesia Graeca inde ab antiquissimis temporibus adhibuit, imo et Latina usque ad tempora Alexandri I. episcopi Rom. Prout panes orbiculares seu placentulae, quas hostias et oblatas appellarunt, in nostris ecclesiis recte adhibentur. Sunt enim, quoad materiam et formam, adeoque quoad substantiam, verus panis, quia constant ex farina triticea puriore, aqua permixta et calore fornacis cocta; possunt etiam servire nutritioni corporis, si in majore quafititate sumantur, licet in eucharistia tanta quantitas non requiratur, ubi nec nutritio corporis quaerenda est.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Graecorum, quibus persuasum est, Christum ad pascha suum fermentata ένζυμα, non άζυμα adhibuisse, unde et ipsi pane fermentato in hoc mysterio utuntur atque rem sua natura αδιάφορου et indifferentem in dogma fidei convertunt; sed falsa nituntur hypothesi, sc. legitimum diem paschatis celebrandi a Domino esse anticipatum. . . . Negare vero, pascha fuisse legitimum, quod Christus solemniter in coenaculo paulo ante institutionem coenae celebravit cum discipulis, impietate sua non caret. Etiam Abissini fermentato pane in sacris utuntur, eodem die confecto. ... 2. Calvinianorum quorundam, qui 1. abrogato pane azymo, quem ipse Christus usurpavit, necessitatem panis fermentati, cibarii seu usualis in s. euchar. propugnant; 2. panem grandiorem, qui possit in actu coenae frangi, urgent; et 3. panis sacramentalis a nostris ecclesiis adhiberi soliti incusant naturam, quantitatem, formam externam et efficaciam. Naturam, cum hostias nostras verum panem esse negant, easque spumam panis, spumam panis nomine indignam, antichristi inventum, nebulas azymas, nebulas nummuläres, chartaceas crustulas, farinacea folia etc. . . . Antonius Praetorius ait, nos nummulariis his panibus non tam mortui Christi, quam prodentis Judae memoriam instituere... 3. Nonnullorum Calvinianorum, ut Bezae, asserentis, ,substantiam pani similem adhiberi posse in illis regionibus, ubi panis nullus sit usus‘.... Quo pertinet Innocentii VIII. decretum apud Volateranum 1.2. Georg.: ,Iis in locis, quibus nullus est vel frumenti vel vini usus, loco panis alium cibum et loco vini aquam esse usurpandam. ... 5. Socinianorum, hostiam pro pane accipi non posse, statuentium. Smalzius c. Franzium p.349. inquit: ,Defendi nullo modo potest, quod pro pane hostia usurpatur.‘ 6.
