Trid. azymi usurpationem praeceptum appellet ecclesiasticum, ast contra Jesuitae rejiciunt illud ad Christi et apostolorum institutionem; vide Bellarminuml. c.“ (L. c. q. 4. f. 1234. sq.)

Quamvis enim quoad species frumenti differant, tamen in esse panis conveniunt. Vinum enim tantum, seu γέννημα της αμπέλου, determinavit Christus Matth. 26, 29., caetera libertati christianae reliquit. Nempe in illis regionibus, ubi vina fortiora vix aliter, quam aqua temperata, ad communem usum adhibentur, etiam in eucharistia idem jam olim usu venisse constat. In nostris autem regionibus, ubi vina adeo fortia non sunt, cur aqua temperari debeant, causa non est. Certe Christus vini, non item aquae admiscendae, in institutione s. coenae mentionem fecit.


### Of the Holy Supper: ON THE HOLY SUPPER. § 7

501. ON THE HOLY SUPPER. § 7. Bread and wine have the character of matter in the Holy Supper, insofar as they are dispensed and received, eaten, and drunk. Whence some here also apply a distinction of matter into remote and proximate; the former they say are the symbols themselves, the latter the aforementioned acts occupied about those symbols. So that bread is taken separately, and wine also separately, just as Christ administered it. Yet these actions, as such, do not have the character of form in this sacrament. For they are actions indifferent in themselves and are only determined from elsewhere to be sacramental actions, namely, by the accession of the word of institution, as will be said shortly. §

8. The heavenly matter of the Holy Supper is the true and substantial body, and the same blood of Christ, true as to substance, of which the former is united sacramentally with the bread, and the latter with the blessed wine, so that the body of Christ is truly and really dispensed with the bread, and the blood of Christ with the wine, and are received by all communicants equally by the mouth of the body, the former being eaten, the latter being drunk. It is called heavenly matter, not as if it only adheres in heaven or is of a heavenly or sidereal substance, but because it is present in a heavenly or supernatural manner, yet truly and really, and is joined with the earthly matter. This very body, which was given for us. See Luke 22:19; 1 Cor. 11:24. That very same, which was poured out for us and for many for the remission of sins. Matt. 26:28; Mark 14:24; Luke 22:20.

Kromayer: "From the epistle Phil. 3, last verse, they object that He will conform our humble body to His glorified body, although we deny omnipresence to glorified bodies. But we answer by distinguishing between a glorified body and a majestic body. Christ will conform our humble body to His glorified body, not to His majestic body. What a glorified and spiritual body is, we learn from the body of Christ after the resurrection and certain particular acts before His resurrection; e.g., when He became αφαντον, when He penetrated closed doors, when He shone like the sun on Mount Tabor; Christ obtains a majestic body from the personal union with the λόγος and His session at the right hand of God. That it is omnipresent pertains to His majestic body." (Th. posit. pol. I, 913. sq.) PART III. CHAP. XI.

Fechtius: "The Papists contend that the whole Christ is the celestial matter of this sacrament, because they do not wish to appear to be subtracting anything of Christ from the communicants through communion under one kind. Therefore, they say that under one species the whole Christ is received just as much as under both." (Compend. p. 706.)

Luther: "See, the rays of the sun are so near to you that they prick your eyes or your skin, so that you feel them; yet you are not able to grasp them and lay them in a little box, even if you were to grope for them eternally. You can indeed hinder them so that they do not shine into the window; but you cannot grope for them or grasp them. So also Christ, even though He is everywhere, does not let Himself be grasped and groped for; He can indeed peel Himself out, so that you get the shell of it and do not grasp the kernel. Why is that? Because it is one thing when God is present, and another when He is present for you. But He is present for you when He adds His Word to it and binds Himself to it, and says: 'Here you shall find Me.'" (That these words of Christ: "This is My body," still stand firm. A. 1527. XX, 1015. sq.)

Dannhauerus: "In the Holy Supper, the whole of Christ is present, yet not the whole of Christ is present sacramentally, but only the flesh and blood. Therefore, the fallacy of Bellarmine (l. 3. de incarn. c. 13) vanishes into smoke: 'Ubiquity,' he says, 'conflicts with the sacrament of the Eucharist itself, for the establishing of which it was devised. For if the flesh of Christ is everywhere, we certainly do not need the Eucharist.'" (Hodos. phaen. 8. p. 400. not.)

Luther: "The finest thing, however, in the bishop’s note is that the pastors should teach the people how, under one form, the whole Jesus Christ, God’s Son, God and man, along with His body and blood, is present and is eaten and drunk by the laity. ... To this now belongs the 'concomitances,' that is, the consequence. Because Christ’s body is not without blood, it follows from this that His blood is not without the soul; from this it follows that His soul is not without the Godhead; from this it follows that His Godhead is not without the Father and the Holy Spirit; from this it follows that in the sacrament, even under one form, the soul of Christ is present, and the Holy Trinity is eaten and drunk, together with His body and blood; from this it follows that a mass-priest in every single mass sacrifices and sells the Holy Trinity twice; from this it follows that, because the Godhead is not without the creature, heaven and earth must also be in the sacrament; from this it follows that the devils and hell are also in the sacrament; from this it follows that whoever eats the sacrament (even in one form) devours the Bishop of Meissen with his mandate and note; from this it follows that a Meissen priest devours and drinks his bishop twice in every single mass; from this it follows that the Bishop of Meissen must have a body larger than heaven and earth—and who could ever recount all the consequences? But finally, it also follows from this that all such followers are donkeys, fools, blind, mad, senseless, raving, foolish, and raging: this consequence is certain." (Report on both kinds, etc. A. 1528. XIX, 1688. 1689. sq.)

This sacramental union is neither substantial, nor personal, nor merely παραστατική [representative] or local, much less merely significative, but it is such that of those things which are said to be united, each remains in its own being, yet both are also received simultaneously, truly, and really, by one act by those who use the sacrament. Whence it is manifest that impanation and consubstantiation, which adversaries have falsely attributed to the Lutherans, are rather excluded. See our peculiar Disputation on Impanation and Consubstantiation held in the year 1677.

Kromayerus: (The Calvinists object:) "That we must posit a συνουσία, that is, consubstantiation. But we respond that, walking a middle path between μετουσίαν, that is, the Papal transubstantiation, and ἀπουσίαν, that is, the Calvinian absence, as between two opposing cliffs, we assert the παρουσίαν, that is, the presence of the body and blood of Christ with the symbols. As regards συνουσίαν, if by it were signified the sacramental union of two disparate things, by which they are posited as present together in the Supper, we could admit the term; but because the Calvinists wish to signify by it the local inclusion of the body of Christ in the bread, the hiding of a small corpuscle under the bread, impanation, or *artocreas*—that is, a meat pie—we not unjustly abstain from it." —

Instance: "But we posit the body and blood of Christ as present in the Supper *in*, *with*, and *under* the symbols." Resp.: * In, cum, sub*—these monosyllables trouble the whole world. It is not the mode of presence, which is ἀκατάληπτος, that is, incomprehensible (οὐ κατ' ἄρσιν, that is, not by removal, but κατά θέσιν, that is, by the position of a certain mode), but rather, on one hand, the substantial presence of the body of Christ is built up by these little words, and on the other, the figment of Papal transubstantiation is destroyed. Moreover, in imitation of the personal propositions, the doctors of the church explained the sacramental propositions with these little words. It is said of Christ in 2 Cor. 5:19, "God was *in* Christ," and Acts 10:38, "God was *with* Christ," by which an intimate presence is hinted; thus also the doctors of the church posit that the body of Christ is present in the Supper *in* and *with* the bread. The particle *sub* (under), however, which Luther uses in the Small Catechism, does not hint at the hiding of a small corpuscle under the bread, but at the highest mystery. —

Instance: "Thus the sacramental and personal union will be the same." Resp.: By distinguishing between genus and species. They agree in genus, they differ in species. In the hypostatic union (since unions derive their denomination not from the terms *from which*, but *to which*), two natures tend toward the constitution of one person; in the sacramental, two things—the earthly and the heavenly, the visible and the invisible—tend toward the constitution of one sacrament. The hypostatic is indissoluble; the sacramental, after the oral manducation has been completed, is dissoluble. For example, when it happens that the eucharistic bread and blood are vomited by the sick, it is not the body and blood of Christ that are vomited, but the bare symbols. The hypostatic union is followed by a κοινωνία φύσεων [καὶ] ἰδιωμάτων; in the sacramental, nothing of the sort is found. —

Instance: "But we confess impanation or local inclusion in the hymn which Luther translated from Huss’s song into the German language: *'verborgen im Brot so klein'* (hidden in the bread so small)." But we respond: If the interpreter is good, bad words will never do harm; If the interpreter is bad, good words will never do help. The sense is: in the small bread He gave us His body to be eaten mystically. "In the small bread He gave us His body to eat in a hidden way." (Th. posit. pol. I, 917 sq.)

Gerhardus: "When we profess that we believe in the true, real, and substantial presence of the body (and blood) of Christ, we by no means posit either impanation, or incorporation, or consubstantiation, or physical inclusion, or local presence, or the hiding of a corpuscle under the bread, or the essential conversion of bread into body, or the durable affixing of the body to the bread outside the use of the Supper, or a personal union of bread and body; but we believe, teach, and confess, according to the institution of Christ Himself, in a mode known to God alone but incomprehensible to us, that the body of Christ is truly, really, and substantially present and united to the eucharistic bread as a divinely ordained medium, so that through that bread we receive and eat the true body of Christ in a sublime mystery; which presence is called sacramental, not because it is merely a σχετική (relative) and significative presence, but because the heavenly thing is conferred upon us in this mystery through the mediation of external symbols and— PART III. CHAP. XI.

Latin:

501. DB SACRA COENA. § 7· Habent autem panis et vinum rationem materiae in s. coena, quatenus a dispensantur et accipiuntur, mandu· cantur et b bibuntur.c Unde quidam hic quoque adhibent distinctionem materiae in remotam et propinquam; illam dicunt esse symbola ipsa, hane actus memoratos, circa symbola illa occupatos. Ita ut seorsim panis, vinum quoque seorsim sumatur, prout Christus administravit. Neque vero actiones hae, ut tales sunt, formae rationem in hoc sacramento habent. Sunt enim actiones ex se indifferentes atque aliunde demum determinantur ad esse actionum sacramen talium, nempe accedente verbo institutionis, ut paulo post dicetur. §

8. Materia coelestis a s. coenae est verum et substantiale b corpus, verus idem quoad substantiam c sanguis Christi, quorum illud cum pane, hic cum vino benedicto sacramentaliterd unitur, ita ut corpus Christi cum pane et sanguis Christi cum vino vere et realiter e dispensentur et a communicantibus aeque f omnibus ore g corporis accipiantur, illud manducetur, hoc bibatur.h Coelestis materia dicitur, non quasi tantum in coelo haereat aut quod coelestis sive sidereae sit substantiae, sed quod coelesti sive supernaturali modo, vere tamen et realiter sit praesens et cum materia terrena conjuncta. Hoc ipsum corpus, quod pro nobis traditum est Vid. Luc. 22, 19. 1 Cor. 11, 24. Is ipse, qui pro nobis, ac pro multis effusus est in remissionem peo catorum. Matth. 26, 28. Mare. 14, 24. Luc. 22, 20.

Kromayekus: ״Ex epistola Phil. 3. v. ult., quod corpus nostrum humile conformaturus sit corpori suo glorificato, cum tamen corporibus glorificatis omnipraesentiam derogemus, objiciunt. Sed respondemus distinguendo inter corpus glorificatum et majestaticum. Christus humile corpus nostrum conformabit corpori suo glorificato, non majestatico. Corpus glorificatum et spirituale quid sit, ex corpore Christi post resurrectionem et quibusdam actibus particularibus ante resurrectionem ipsius, discimus; v. g. quando factum fuit αφαντον, quando fores clausas penetravit, quando fulsit instar solis in monte Tabor; corpus majestaticum Christus ex unione personali cum λόγω et sessione ad dextram Dei obtinet. Quod omnipraesens sit, ad majestaticum ipsius corpus pertinet.“ (Th. posit.pol. I, 913. sq.) PART. ΠΙ. CAP. XI.

Fechtius: ,,Pontificii, totum Christum esse materiam coelestem hujus sacramenti, contendunt, quia nolunt videri per communicationem sub una quicquam Christi communicantibus subtrahere. Dicunt itaque, sub una specie totum Christum perinde ac sub utraque sumi.“ (Compend. p. 706.)

Lutherus: ״Siehe, die Glänze der Sonne sind dir so nahe, dass sie dich gleich in die Augen oder auf die Haut stechen, dass du es fühlest; aber doch vermagst du es nicht, dass du sie ergreifest und in ein Kästlein legest, wenn du gleich ewiglich darnach tappest. Hindern kannst du sie wohl, dass sie nicht scheine zum Fenster ein; aber tappen und greifen kannst du sie nicht. Also auch Christus, ob er gleich allenthalben da ist, lässt er sich nicht so greifen und tappen; er kann sich wohl ausschälen, dass du die Schale davon kriegest und den Kern nicht ergreifest. Warum das? Darum, dass ein anderes ist, wenn Gott da ist, und wenn er dir da ist. Dann aber ist er dir da, wenn er sein Wort dazu thut und bindet sich damit an, und spricht: Hie sollst du mich finden.44 (Dass diese Worte Christi: Das ist mein Leib, noch fest stehen. A. 1527. XX, 1015. sq.)

Dannhauerus: ״In sacra coena praesens est totum Christi, non tarnen totum Christi praesens est sacramentaliter, sed sola caro et sanguis. In fumos igitur abit fallacia Bellarmini 1. 3. de incarn. c. 13.: ,Pugnat4, inquit, ,ubiquitas cum ipso sacramento eucharistiae, pro quo stabiliendo est excogitata. Nam si caro Christi est ubique, certe non egemus eucharistia. 4 4 4 (Hodos. phaen. 8. p. 400. not.)

Lutherus: ״Das Allerfeinste aber in des Bischofs Zettel ist, dass die Pfarrherrn sollen das Volk lehren, wie unter der einen Gestalt der ganze Jesus Christus, Gottes Sohn, Gott und Mensch, dazu sein Leibund Blut sei, und von den Laien gegessen und getrunken werde. ... Hiezu schlägt nun die Concomitantien, das ist, die Folge. Weil Christi Leib nicht ohne Blut ist, so folget daraus, dass sein Blut nicht ohne Seele ist; daraus folget, dass seine Seele nicht ohne die Gottheit ist; daraus folget, dass seine Gottheit nicht ohne den Vater und Heiligen Geist ist; daraus folget, dass im Sacrament auch unter einer Gestalt die Seele Christi ist, die heilige Dreifaltigkeit gegessen und getrunken wird, sammt seinem Leib und Blut; daraus folget, dass ein Messpfaffe in einer jeglichen Messe die heilige Dreifaltigkeit zweimal opfert und verkauft; daraus folget, weil die Gottheit nicht ohne die Creatur ist, so muss Himmel und Erden auch im Sacrament sein; daraus folget, dass die Teufel und die Hölle auch im Sacrament sind; daraus folget, dass wer das Sacrament (auch einerlei Gestalt) isset, der frisset den Bischof zu Meissen mit seinem Mandat und Zettel; daraus folget, dass ein Meissnischer Priester seinen Bischof in einer jeglichen Messe zweimal frisset uud säufet; daraus folget, dass der Bischof zu Meissen muss einen grössern Leib haben denn Himmel und Erden, und wer will alle Folge immermehr erzählen? Aber zuletzt folget auch draus, dass alle solche Folger Esel, Narren, blind, toll, unsinnig, rasend, thöricht und tobend sind: diese Folge ist gewiss.44 (Bericht von beiderlei Gestalt u. s. w. A. 1528. XIX, 1688. 1689. sq.)

Quae quidem unio sacramentalis neque substantialis, neque per80nali8, neque mere παραστατική aut localis, nedum mere significativa, sed talis est, qua eorum, quae uniri dicuntur, utrumque in esse suo permanet, utrumque tamen etiam simul, vere et realiter, uno actu accipitur ab his, qui sacramento utuntur. Unde impanationem et consubstantiatimem, quam Lutheranis affinxerunt adversarii, excludi potius manifestum est. Vid. Disp, nostra peculiaris de Impan. et Consubst anno 1677. habita.

Kromayerus; (Calviniani objiciunt:),,Quod συνουσία, id est, consubstantiatio9nobis sit statuenda. Sed respondemus, nos, inter μετονσίαν, id est, transsubstantiationem pontificiam et απουσίαν, id est, absentiam Calvinianam, tamquam inter duos scopulos oppositos, media via incedentes, παρουσίαν, id est, praesentiam corporis et sanguinis Christi cum symbolis asserere. Συνουσίαν quod attinet, si per eandem duarum rerum disparatarum sacramentalis unio, qua simul praesentes in coena statuuntur, significaretur, vocem admittere possemus; verum quia Calviniani corporis Christi localem inclusionem in pane, delitescentiam parvi corpusculi sub pane, impanationem, artocreas, id est, eine Fleischpastete, per illam significari volunt, ab eadem non immerito abstinemus. —

Instantia: Sed in, cum et sub symbolis corpus et sanguinem Christi praesentia in coena statuimus. Resp.: In, cum, sub totum turbant monosyllaba mundum. Non modus praesentiae, qui est ακατάληπτος, id est, incomprehensibilis (ου κατ' άρσιν, id est, non per remotionem, sed κατά ΰέσιν, id est, per certi modi positionem), verum ex una parte substantialis corporis Christi praesentia per hasce voculas adstruitur, ex altera figmentum transsubstantiationis pontificiae destruitur. Ad imitationem autem propositionum personalium ecclesiae doctores propositiones sacramentales hisce voculis explicarunt. De Christo dicitur 2 Cor. 5, 19.: ,Deus erat in Christo‘, Act. 10, 38.: ,Deus erat cum Christo‘, quibus intima praesentia innuitur; sic etiam in et cum pane corpus Christi praesens esse in coena doctores ecclesiae statuunt. Particula vero sub, qua Lutherus in catechesi minore utitur, non delitescentia parvuli corpusculi sub pane, sed summum mysterium innuitur. —

Instantia: Sic eadem erit unio sacramentalis et personalis. Resp.: Distinguendo inter genus et speciem. Conveniunt genere, differunt specie. In hypostatica (denominationem siquidem uniones non a terminis a quibus, sed ad quem sortiuntur) duae naturae ad constitutionem unius personae, in sacramentali duae res, terrena, et coelestis, visibilis et invisibilis, ad constitutionem unius sacramenti tendunt. Hypostatica est insolubilis; sacramentalis, postquam oralis manducatio peracta est, solubilis. V. g. cum ׳contingit, ut ab aegrotis panis et sanguis eucharisticus evomantur, non corpus et sanguis Christi, sed nuda symbola evomuntur. Unionem hypostaticam sequitur κοινωνία φύσεων Ιδιωμάτων, in sacramentali nihil ejusmodi reperitur. —

Instantia: Sed impanationem aut localem inclusionem fatemur in cantico, quod Lutherus ex Hussi cantilena transtulit in linguam germanicam: ,verborgen im Brot so klein.‘ Sed respondemus: Sit bonus interpres, nunquam mala verba nocebunt, Sit malus interpres, nunquam bona verba juvabunt. Sensus est: in parvo pane corpus suum mystice nobis comedendum dedit. ,Im kleinen Brot gab er uns seinen Leib verborgener Weise zu essen.“‘ (Th. posit.pol. I, 917. sq.)

Gerhardus: ,,Quando veram, realem et substantialem corporis (et sanguinis) Christi praesentiam nos credere profitemur, nequaquam vel impanationem, vel incorporationem, vel consubstantiationem, vel physicam inclusionem, Vel localem praesentiam, vel delitescentiam corpusculi sub pane, vel essentialem panis in corpus conversionem, vel durabilem corporis ad panem extra usum coenae affixionem, vel personalem panis et corporis unionem statuimus; sed credimus, docemus et confitemur, juxta ipsius Christi institutionem modo soli Deo cognito, nobis vero incomprehensibili, pani eucharistico tanquam medio divinitus ordinato corpus Christi vere, realiter et substantialiter praesens uniri, ut medi ante illo pane verum Christi corpus in sublimi mysterio sumamus et manducemus; quae praesentia dicitur sacramentalis, non quod sit tantum σχετική ac significativa praesentia, sed quia res coelestis mediantibus externis symbolis in hoc mysterici nobis confertur et exPART. III. 0AP. XI.


### Of the Holy Supper: is held. It is called a true and real presence to exclude a figurative,…

is held. It is called a true and real presence to exclude a figurative, imaginary, and representative presence; it is called a substantial presence to exclude the opinion concerning the mere efficacy of the body of Christ being present in this mystery; it is called a mystical, supernatural, and incomprehensible presence, because the body (and blood) of Christ are present, distributed, and received in this mystery not in any manner of this age, but in a mystical, supernatural, and incomprehensible manner.” (Harm. ev. contin. cap. 171. f. 784.)

The same: “Some of our own, following Cyril (1. 10. on John c. 13), have called it a corporeal presence with regard to the object, but by no means with regard to the mode; they meant to say this: that not only the virtue and efficacy, but the very substance of the body and blood of Christ is present in the Holy Supper; for they opposed this term to a spiritual presence, as it is defined by the adversaries; but they by no means meant that the body of Christ is present in a corporeal and quantitative mode. Thus Hilary (1. 8. de trin. p. 101) asserts: ‘that the flesh of Christ remains in us naturally,’ which he explains there as follows: ‘that Christ is in us by the truth of nature, not merely by a harmony of will.’” (L. de s. c. § 98.) Luther: “We say that the disciples murmured both against the understanding of the Spirit and against the bodily eating of the flesh of Christ; for they understood neither rightly, because they thought they would have to tear His flesh with their teeth, like other perishable flesh. But it does not follow from this that the flesh of Christ, as an imperishable spiritual flesh, may not be eaten bodily in the Lord’s Supper with faith. The Spirit was to overturn such things; thus He teaches us how the disciples understood the bodily eating of Christ’s flesh, just as if we did not know such things without His mastery.” (Bek. vom A. Christi, 1528. XX, p. 1225.)

The same: “Therefore it is certainly rightly said that, when one points to the bread and says: ‘This is Christ’s body,’ and whoever sees the bread sees the body of Christ, just as John says that he saw the Holy Spirit when he saw the dove, as is heard. Thus, furthermore, it is rightly said: whoever touches this bread touches Christ’s body, and whoever eats this bread eats Christ’s body, whoever crushes this bread with teeth or tongue crushes the body of Christ with teeth or tongue, and yet it remains true at all times that no one sees, touches, eats, or bites the body of Christ as one visibly sees and bites other flesh. For what is done to the bread is rightly and properly attributed to the body of Christ because of the sacramental union.” (Bek. vom Abendmahl Christi 1528. XX, 1294.) Indeed, although it is not necessary to define the moment of time in which the body and blood of Christ begin to be sacramentally united with the bread and wine; it is nevertheless certain that the sacramental union pertains to the use in such a way that, according to the ancient rule, nothing has the nature of a sacrament outside the use which has been instituted by God. Whence we also believe that the symbols, when reserved after consecration and placed outside of use, do not obtain the nature of a sacrament, nor are the body and blood of Christ sacramentally united with them outside of use.

Luther: “‘Let the word be added to the element and it becomes a sacrament.’ To understand this saying is the more useful, the more the Papists have abused it and derived the greatest errors from it. For they conclude thus: Augustine assures us that a sacrament consists of two parts, namely, of the word and the external sign (elementum). Consequently, as soon as the mass-priest, in the presence of the bread and wine, [utters] the words of the Supper...” has spoken, the body and blood of Christ must immediately be present. Furthermore, in order that the due honor be shown to Christ, this bread must be enclosed in a sturdy little house, so that it does not become food for worms and mice, and afterwards it must be worshipped by men. Thus, under the Papacy, a similar opinion was impressed upon the minds of the people, so that they thought their prayers were never more pleasing to God and would never be more easily heard than when they prayed in the place where said bread is enclosed. But in order to avoid these errors, one must know that Augustine is not speaking only of the pronunciation of the words of Christ, but rather includes the command to take and eat the bread. And afterwards he adds: *Hic est corpus meum*, which is as much as to say: outside of this use, my body and my blood are not joined with these external signs. For one must not think that this Supper is like magical jugglery, in which Christ could be bound without words through mere human superstition. Therefore, just as Baptism, when there is no child present to be baptized, is nothing other than mere water, so we also assert most certainly that where there are no eating and drinking people present according to the institution of Christ, there is nothing other than bread and wine, even if one were to repeat the words a thousand times.” (Luther’s opinion on the words of Augustine: *Accedat etc.* XXI, 1588 sq.)

Quenstedtius: “In that theological rule: *Nihil habet rationem sacramenti extra usum a Christo institutum* (Nothing has the nature of a sacrament outside the use instituted by Christ), by the name of ‘use’ is understood the whole or entire sacramental action prescribed by Christ, namely, consecration, distribution, eating, and drinking; for these acts, all and each taken together, complete that sacramental use of which the rule treats, i.e., not one particular action, but all taken and joined together constitute the nature of the Eucharistic sacrament, and thus it consists simultaneously in the word and in the reception. The sacramental union of the body of Christ with the bread and of His blood with the wine, by the immutable institution of Christ, respects the use and the action: ‘Do this,’ ‘as often as you do it’; therefore, when the use and action cease, the sacramental union also ceases. . .

Obj. Bellarmine, Book 4, *de euchar.*, ch. 2: ‘The words of the Lord: *Hoc est corpus meum* etc., were spoken before the action of eating and drinking took place; therefore, before that action, the body of the Lord was present in the Supper, and consequently the sacrament of the Eucharist was also completed. The consequence is proven: 1. because if the word is added to the element, a sacrament is made; 2. the words of the Lord, as soon as they were uttered, were true.’

Resp.: 1. Christ did not say: *Hoc est corpus meum, hic est sanguis meus*, before the action of eating and drinking took place, but He uttered those words in the midst of the sacramental action: i.e., *h. e. c. m.* etc., so that the distribution and reception of the bread and wine of the Eucharist took place simultaneously with the utterance of the words. Luther well says that by saying He gave, and by giving He said: *h. e. c. m.* 2. The words of Christ are most true in that sense and order which He Himself intended and intimated when He pronounced those words; but in the order of Christ’s words, those things precede which command the reception, eating, and drinking; but those which promise the presence of the body and blood follow. Therefore, the fulfillment of the latter requires the fulfillment of the former by reason of order. 3. Nor does Christ pronounce absolutely concerning the consecrated bread that it is the body of Christ, but concerning the bread broken and given to be eaten. For He first said: ‘Take and eat’; then He said: ‘This is my body.’ 4. The saying of Augustine: ‘Let the word be added to the element and a sacrament is made,’ is to be understood of the word and element existing in the very act and use; otherwise, what the Papists intend to prove from this concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist would also apply to the other sacraments.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 1265. 1268.)

Kromayerus: “A theological aphorism (is): The sacramental union occurs when the eating and drinking occur. Instance: Thus the words of the Savior— PART III. CHAP. XI.

their dispositive [words] will lack their efficacy if the elements become the body and blood of Christ only when the eating and drinking take place. But we respond by distinguishing between efficacy viewed in the first act and in the second act. Through the words of institution, the elements indeed receive this vocation, so that they are media for exhibiting the body and blood of the Lord, but they exert their efficacy in the second act when the eating and drinking take place. (Th. posit. pol. I, 968 sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: Of the Papists, who contend that the Eucharist does not consist in the action alone, i.e., in the use or reception, but in a permanent thing, for instance, in the consecrated host itself; that is, they assert that the sacramental union continues perpetually even outside of use, so that the blessed bread is a sacrament outside of use. . . II. They contend that the consecrated Eucharistic bread is to be reserved in a shrine (in a ciborium, as Johannes Fabri calls it; in a canopy, as Harding calls it), to be carried about, and to be adored. . . Council of Trent, sess. 13, c. 5: 'No room is left for doubt that all the faithful of Christ, according to the custom always received in the Catholic Church, should offer in veneration the worship of latria, which is due to the true God, to this most holy sacrament; nor is it to be adored any the less because it was instituted by Christ the Lord in order to be received.' Bellarmine, l. 4, de euchar. c. 29, §. Sed haec etc.: 'Christ is to be adored by the worship of latria in and of Himself and properly, and that adoration pertains also to the symbols of bread and wine, insofar as they are apprehended as one thing with Christ, whom they contain.' . . . Some of the Papists do not deny that, since they cannot be certain that Christ is present there and that this particular host is to be adored, because it can be certain to no one whether all things required for consecration have concurred there, . . . therefore the danger of at least material idolatry, as they call it, underlies the daily adoration of the host. Hence many, in order to prevent this inconvenience (among whom are named Bonaventure, Marsilius, Alexander of Hales), since it is no more a matter of faith that this particular host is to be adored than that these particular relics are to be adored, grant no adoration of any host in particular, except conditionally: 'I adore you, if you are Christ.' But the modern Jesuits reject this, maintaining that that material idolatry would be immune from all guilt on account of an insuperable ignorance of the fact; as can be seen in Bresserus, l. 5, de consecr. c. 12." (L. c. s. 2, q. 8, f. 1266 sq.)

Latin:

hibetur. Dicitur vera et realis praesentia ad excludendum figurativam, imaginariam ac repraesentativam praesentiam; dicitur substantialis praesentia ad excludendam opinionem de sola corporis Christi efficacia in hoc mysterio praesente; dicitur mystica, supernaturalis et incomprehensibilis praesentia, quia non modo aliquo hujus saeculi, sed mystico, supernaturali et incomprehensibili corpus (et sanguis) Christi in hoc mysterio adsunt, distribuuntur et accipiuntur.“ (Harm. ev. contin. cap. 171. f. 784.)

Idem: ,,Quidam ex nostratibus, secuti Cyrillum 1.10. in Joh. c. 13., corporalem praesentiam vocarunt respectu habito ad objectum, nequaquam vero ad modum; voluerunt hoc dicere, non solam virtutem et efficaciam, sed ipsam substantiam corporis et sanguinis Christi in sacra coena praesentem esse; opposuerunt enim hanc vocem praesentiae spirituali, prout ab adversariis ea definitur; nequaquam vero hoc voluerunt, quod modo corporali et quantitativo corpus Christus praesens sit. Sic Hilarius 1. 8. de trin. p. 101. asserit: ,Christi carnem naturaliter in nobis manere‘, quod ibid. sic exponit: ,Per naturae veritatem Christum in nobis esse, non tantum per concordiam voluntatis.‘“ (L. de s. c. § 98.) Lutherus: ,,Wir sagen, dass die Jünger murreten beide wider den Verstand des Geistes und wider das leibliche Essen des Fleisches Christi; denn sie verstunden keines recht, weil sie dachten, sie müssten sein Fleisch mit Zähnen zerreissen, wie ander vergänglich Fleisch. Aber daraus folget noch nicht, dass Christi Fleisch, als ein unvergänglich geistlich Fleisch, nicht möge mit dem Glauben im Abendmahl leiblich zu essen sein. Solches sollte der Geist umstossen; so lehret er uns, wie die Jünger haben Christi Fleisch leiblich zu essen verstanden, gerade als wüssten wTir solches nicht ohn seine Meisterschaft.“ (Bek. vom A. Christi, 1528. XX, p. 1225.)

Idem: ,,Darum ists allerdings recht geredt, dass, so man aufs Brot zeiget und spricht: Das ist Christus Leib, und wer das Brot siehet, der siehet den Leib Christi, gleichwie Johannes spricht, dass er den Heiligen Geist sähe, da er die Taube sähe, wie gehöret ist. Also fortan ists recht geredt: wer dies Brot angreift, der greifet Christi Leib an, und wer dies Brot isset, der isset Christi Leib, wer dies Brot mit Zähnen oder Zungen zerdrückt, der zerdrückt mit Zähnen oder Zungen den Leib Christi, und bleibt doch allewege wahr, dass niemand Ghi'isti Leib siehet, greifet, isset, oder zerbeisset, wie man sichtlich ander Fleisch siehet und zerbeisset. Denn was man dem Brot thut, wird recht und wohl dem Leibe Christi zugeeignet um der sacramentlichen Einigkeit willen.“ (Bek. vom Abendmahl Christi 1528. XX, 1294.) Nempe licet momentum temporis, quo corpus et sanguis Christi cum pane et vino sacramentaliter uniri incipiunt, non necesse sit definire; certum tamen est, unionem sacramentalem ita spectare ad usum, ut juxta regulam veterem nihil habeat rationem sacramenti extra usum, qui institutus est a Deo. Unde et symbola post consecrationem reservata et extra usum constituta rationem sacramenti non obtinere, neque corpus et sanguinem Christi extra usum cum illis sacramentaliter unita esse, credimus.

Lutherus: ,, ,Accedat verbum ad elementum et fit sacramentum/ Diesen Spruch zu verstehen, ist desto nützlicher, jemehr die Papisten denselben gemissbraucht und daraus die grössten Irrthümer hergeleitet haben. Denn also schliessen sie: Augustinus versichert, dass ein Sacrament aus zwei Stücken bestehe, nämlich aus dem Wort und dem äusserlichen Zeichen (elemento). Folglich, sobald der Messpfaffe in Gegenwart des Brotes und Weines die Worte des Abendmahls hergesagt hat, muss sogleich der Leib und das Blut Christi da sein. Ferner, damit Christo die gebührende Ehre erzeiget werde, muss dieses Brot in ein festes Häuslein eingeschlossen werden, dass es nicht eine Speise der Würmer und Mäuse werde, und hernach muss es von Menschen angebetet werden. Also ist unter dem Pabstthum eine ähnliehe Meinung den Gemüthern des Volkes eingepräget worden, dass sie gemeinet, ihre Gebete wären Gott nie angenehmer und würden nie leichter erhöret, als wenn sie an dem Orte beteten, wo benanntes Brot eingeschlossen ist. Damit man aber diese Irrthümer vermeide, muss man wissen, dass Augustinus nicht allein von der Aussprache der Worte Christi rede, sondern vielmehr den Befehl vom Nehmen und Essen des Brotes mit darunter begreife. Und hernach thut er hinzu: Hic est corpus meum, welches soviel ist, als: ausser diesem Gebrauche wird mein Leib und mein Blut nicht mit diesen äussern Zeichen verbunden. Denn man muss nicht denken, dass dieses Abendmahl magisehen Gaukeleien gleich sei, darin Christus ohne Worte durch blossen menschlichen Aberglauben könne angebunden werden. Darum, gleichwie die Taufe, wenn kein Kind da ist, das getaufet werde, nichts anders ist, als blosses Wasser, also behaupten wir auch ganz gewiss, wo nicht essende und trinkende Menschen da sind nach der Einsetzung Christi, dass nichts anders als Brot und Wein da sei, wenn man auch die Worte tausendmal hersagen sollte.“ (Lutheri Meinung von den Worten Augustini: Accedat etc. XXI, 1588. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ,,In regula illa theologica: Nihil habet rationem sacramenti extra usum a Christo institutum, nomine usus intelligitur tota seu integra actio sacramentalis a Christo praescripta, videlicet consecratio, distributio, manducatio et bibitio; hi enim actus omnes et singuli conjunctim sumti absolvunt usum illum sacramentalem, de quo regula agit, h. e., non una aliqua actio particularis, sed omnes simul sumtae et conjunctae rationem sacramenti eucharistici constituunt, adeoque h όόσει καϊ εν λήψει simul consistit. Unio sacramentalis corporis Christi cum pane et sanguinis ejus cum vino ex institutione Christi immutabili respicit usum et actionem: ,Hoc facite‘, ,quotiescunque feceritis‘; cessante ergo usu et actione, cessat quoque unio sacramentalis. . .

Objic. Bellarminus 1. 4. de euchar. c. 2.: ,Verba Domini: hoc est corpus meum etc., prius dicta sunt, quam fleret actio manducandi et bibendi; ergo ante illam actionem fuit corpus Domini praesens in coena, et proinde etiam sacramentum eucharistiae confectum. Consequentia probatur: 1. quia si accedit verbum ad elementum, fit sacramentum; 2. verba Domini, mox atque prolata sunt, vera fuerunt.‘

Resp.: 1. Christus non prius dixit: Hoc est corpus meum, hic est sanguis meus, quam fieret actio manducandi et bibendi, sed in media actione sacramentali verba illa protulit: h. e. c. m. etc., ita ut distributio atque acceptio panis et vini eucharistiae simul facta sit cum verborum prolatione. Bene Lutherus ait, quod dicendo dederit et dando dixerit: h. e. c. m. 2. Verba Christi verissima sunt eo demum sensu et ordine, quem ipse intendit et innuit, cum verba illa pronunciavit; in ordine autem verborum Christi illa praecedunt, quae acceptionem, manducationem et bibitionem praecipiunt; quae vero praesentiam corporis et sanguinis promittunt ea sequuntur. Horum ergo impletio illorum impletionem ratione ordinis praerequirit. 3. Nec Christus absolute pronunciat de pane consecrato, quod sit corpus Christi, sed de pane fracto et dato ad manducandum. Prius enim dixit: Accipite et manducate; deinde dixit: ,Hoc est corpus meum.‘ 4. Dictum Augustini: ,Accedat verbum ad elementum et fit sacramentum‘, intelligendum est de verbo et elemento in ipso actu et usu existente, alioqui, quod pontificii de sacramento eucharistiae hinc probare intendunt, de caeteris etiam sacramentis procederet.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 1265. 1268.)

Kromayerus: ,,Aphorismus theologicus (est); Unio sacramentalis fit, quando fit manducatio et bibitio. Instantia: Sic verba salvaPART. III. CAP. XI.

toris dispositiva sua carebunt efficacia, si tunc demum elementa fiunt corpus et sanguis Christi, quando fit manducatio et bibitio. Sed respondemus distinguendo inter efficaciam in actu primo et secundo spectatam. Per verba institutionis elementa quidem vocationem hanc accipiunt, ut sint media exhibitiva corporis et sanginis Dominici, sed efficaciam suam actu secundo exserunt, quando fit manducatio et bibitio. (Th. posit.pol. I, 968. sq.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״ Anlithesis: Pontificiorum, qui I. eucharistiam non in sola actione h. e. usu vel sumtione, sed in re permanente, puta, in ipsa hostia consecrata, consistere contendunt, h. e., asserunt, unionem sacramentalem extra usum etiam perpetuo durare, ita ut panis benedictus extra usum sit sacramentum. . . II. Contendunt, panem eucharisticum consecratum in sacrario (in ciborio, ut vocat Johannes Fabri, in conopeo, ut Hardingus) esse reponendum, circumgestandum, adorandum. . . Concilium Trid. sess. 13. c. 5.: ,Nullus dubitandi locus relinquitur, quin omnes Christi fideles pro more in ecclesia Christi semper recepto latriae cultum, qui vero Deo debetur, huic sacramento sanctissimo in veneratione exhibeant, neque enim ideo minus adorandum, quod fuerit a Christo Domino, ut sumatur, institutum. Bellarminus 1. 4. de euchar. c. 29. §. Sed haec etc.: ,Cultu latriae per se et proprie Christus est adorandus, et ea adoratio ad symbola etiam panis et vini pertinet, quatenus apprehenduntur, ut quid unum cum Christo, quem continent.4 .. Quidam pontificiorum non diffitentur, cum non possint esse certi, Christum ibi praesentem esse, et hanc numero hostiam esse adorandam, eo quod nemini constare queat, an requisita omnia ad consecrationem ibi concurrerint, . . . ideo periculum subesse idololatriae saltem materialis, ut loquuntur, in hostiae quotidiana adoratione. Hinc plures, ut huic incommodo praeverterent (quos inter nominantur Bonaventura, Massilius, Alexander Halensis), cum non sit magis de fide, hanc numero hostiam esse adorandam, quam has numero reliquias esse adorandas, nullam hostiae cujuslibet in particulari concedunt adorationem, nisi conditionatam: Adoro te, si tu es Christus. Sed hanc rejiciunt hodierni Jesuitae, pertendentes, illam materialem idololatriam ab omni culpa fore immunem propter insuperabilem facti ignorantiam; ut videre est apud Bresserum 1. 5. de consecr. c. 12." (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 1266. sq.)


### Of the Holy Supper: Not only by the worthy or believers, but also by the unworthy or unbelievers…

Not only by the worthy or believers, but also by the unworthy or unbelievers and the impious, whom Paul (1 Cor. 11:27) says are guilty not only of the sacred symbols which they abuse, but of the body and blood of the Lord Himself, and that for the reason that they do not discern the body (and blood) of the Lord, or because they eat the body of the Lord itself unworthily, while, namely, they approach this feast, in which they receive the true body of the Lord, without faith and religious reverence, just as they would to a common meal. Compare the blessed Musaeus, Dissert. de S. Coena, contra Johan. Vorstium § 10, p. 6, 8.

Luther: "I lump them all into one cake, as they are, who do not want to believe that the Lord's bread in the Supper is His true, natural body, which the godless or Judas receives orally just as much as St. Peter and all the saints. Whoever (I say) does not want to believe that, let him leave me alone with letters, writings, or words, and let him expect no fellowship from me; nothing else will come of it." (Kurzes Bek. vom h. Sacr. A. 1544. XX, 2212. Vid. Concord. ed. Müller p. 653.)

Quenstedtius: "Nor does Christ say: 'Eat, this is then my body, when you believe, etc.'; but He says simply, that which is offered with the bread,"

to be His body; for the body of Christ is not distributed with the bread, and the blood with the wine, because it is believed, but in order that it may be believed, and that faith in the remission of sins may be more and more established; faith adheres to the sacrament accidentally.” (L. c. q. 11. f. 1290.)

The same: “The apostle speaks in 1 Cor. 10:21, not of the fact, but of the right; not of drinking considered simply and ἁπλῶς, but worthily and decently. You cannot, i.e., worthily and decently, ὡς προσήκει and as is of right, not salutarily and with a good conscience, become partakers of the table of the Lord and of demons.” (L. c. f. 1294.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who maintain that the unworthy and hypocrites receive only half of the sacrament, i.e., only the external signs, and not the entire sacrament; that is, that they do not become partakers of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper, but receive only naked and empty signs. Thus Danaeus in resp. p. 122: ‘The unworthy and impenitent receive only half the sacrament, namely, the signs only, but the penitent receive the entire sacrament.’ Calvin writes in an epistle to Jacob Andreae: ‘I am so far from being moved by your arguments that I wonder it did not occur to you that the impious, by rejecting Christ, bring destruction upon themselves more than by receiving Him.’ Some of the Calvinists make a distinction between unworthy eating in the Holy Supper and the eating of the unworthy. A worthy person, i.e., a man believing in Christ, sometimes eats the bread and wine worthily, sometimes unworthily, but always perceives the body and blood through faith. Thus in Supplem. Panstrat. Chamier. c. 3: ‘Unworthily, he who does not rightly prepare himself for this great banquet, which often happens even to believers, as the apostle teaches in 1 Cor. 11; on the contrary, an unworthy person is one who is not endowed with true faith.’ ...

2. Of the Socinians, Arminians, Anabaptists, and Schwenckfeldians, who, just as they deny all real presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper, so they deny, reject, and traduce with dire blasphemies all oral perception of the same.

3. Of the Labadists, who assert that in the Holy Supper only believers partake of the body and blood of Christ, and that the worthiness of the communicants is not to be sought in faith. See Declarat, p. 144.” (L. c. s. 2. q. 11. f. 1290.)

Indeed, that sacramental eating comprises in one act both the natural and sensible eating of the blessed bread, and the eating—not indeed sensible and natural, yet true—of the body of Christ sacramentally united with the bread. And the sacramental drinking, which is performed by the mouth of the body, comprises at the same time the sensible and natural drinking of the blessed wine, and the drinking—not indeed sensible, yet true—of the blood of Christ. And hence that sacramental eating and drinking is also accustomed to be called oral on account of the unity and identity of the act, or so that the organ of the mouth may be connoted, by which the eating of the bread and body, and likewise the drinking of the wine and blood of Christ, is performed; although the food and drink are different on both sides, and the mode of eating the bread differs greatly from the mode of eating the body, and the mode of drinking the wine from the mode of drinking the blood of Christ; just as it is not of the formal nature of eating (but only of the nature of natural eating) that food be received in a sensible mode, be crushed by the teeth, and be sent down into the stomach; nor is it of the formal nature of drinking (but only of the nature of natural drinking) that we experience the moisture and flavor of the drink with the tongue and palate; here, however, the presence, and likewise the eating of the body and the drinking of the blood of Christ, is insensible, supernatural, and unknown to the human mind and PART III. CHAP. XI.

incomprehensible, yet in such a way that it exists in reality without anyone conceiving it. We may, however, profess our ignorance regarding the determination of the mode by which the body and blood of the Lord are present and received in the Supper, even though we firmly hold to the τό ὅτι.

Cf. b. Mus. Dissert. de S. Coena contra Johan. Vorst. § 91. 92. p. 83. sqq.

Luther: "We stand upon, believe, and teach that in the Lord’s Supper one truly and bodily eats and partakes of Christ’s body. But how that happens or how He is in the bread, we do not know; nor should we know. We ought to believe God’s Word and not set for Him any manner or measure. We see bread with our eyes, but we hear with our ears that the body is there." (Dass diese Worte u. s. w. XX, 968.)

ANTITHESIS S. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the ancient heretics, who deny the truth of Christ’s human nature. . . 2. Of the Calvinists, from whose words and hypotheses it is evident that they themselves 1.) deny that the body and blood of Christ are a substantial part of the Holy Supper. 2.) Deny that the body and blood of Christ are truly and substantially present in the Holy Supper; where, however, observe: some of the Calvinists openly profess the ἀπουσία or absence of the body and blood of Christ in the Supper, such as Calvin, Inst. bk. 4, ch. 17, th. 21; Zwingli in expos. fid. christ.; Zanchius in Confess. p. 177; Beza, vol. 1, f. 228; Polanus, p. 269; others do so covertly and deceptively, namely those who claim that the question is not about the presence itself, but about the mode of presence; see Bezelium 1. de coena p. 44, cf. Musculum Loc. Com. p. 822. . . The Palatine Catechism proclaims our doctrine concerning the corporal presence of Christ to be the 'foundation of the Mass and of papistic idolatry,' qu. 80. . . Therefore, the Calvinists do not believe the body of Christ is present in the Holy Supper any more than the body of the sun is present on earth, that is, as Theodore Beza frankly professed, 'they believe the body of Christ is now as far removed from the place where we celebrate the Lord’s Supper as heaven is removed from the earth.' . . 3. Of the Socinians, who establish that the food and drink in the Holy Supper are merely naked bread and wine, and deny the real presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper. . . The Racovian Catechism, ch. 3, de coen. Dom., holds the same. For it says: 'The native and genuine sense of these words of Christ is: this action of breaking and eating this bread is a commemoration and a certain foreshadowing of that which is to happen to my body, and this action of pouring and drinking this wine is a commemoration and a certain representation of what will happen to my blood.' 4. Of the Arminians, who deny the sacramental union of the eucharistic bread and the body of Christ, and of the blessed wine with His blood, and impiously argue that it is papistic idolomania in their Apology, f. 250. 5. Of the Schwenckfeldians and Anabaptists, who deny that the body of Christ is exhibited in the Holy Supper, partly because 'Christ, now exalted, is no longer bodily on earth,' and partly because 'the bodily presence of Christ in the Supper and in the assembly of the church is a humiliation, which has long since ceased.'" (L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 1208. sqq.)

The same: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who not only deny the oral manducation of the body of Christ but even blaspheme it. Zwingli, T. 2, in Exeges. p. 372, does not fear to call it a 'plague.' Beza calls it such a 'figment and invention, of which even Satan himself would be ashamed,' and proclaims us to be 'sarcophagi' and 'Capernaites.' The same Beza in Creophagia, f. 262, calls oral manducation a 'brutish and cyclopean eating'; vol. 1, f. 216, he says: 'We say that symbols are given on earth by the ministers, but by faith we are carried up as if by ladders to heaven, where we finally seek the flesh of Christ.' Polanus, bk. 6, ch. 56, distinguishes between ὅμον and ἅμα. 'With bread and wine,' he says, 'it is exhibited by Christ and partak—

the body and blood of Christ are received by true believers, which ought not to be understood as ὁμοῦ, i.e., in the same place, as if the body were in or under the bread, and likewise the blood of Christ in or under the wine in the same place here on earth, but ἅμα, i.e., at the same time, so that the sense is: When a faithful man eats the bread of the Lord and the wine of the Lord with the mouth of the body, then at the same time he eats the body and drinks the blood of Christ with the mouth of the soul."

The Helvetic Confession, ch. 21, p. 71, says: "The flesh (of Christ) cannot be eaten corporally without wickedness or savagery." "To eat the crucified body of Christ and to drink his shed blood means to believe in Christ and to be united with him in faith," says the Heidelberg Catechism, q. 76. 2.

The Photinians or Socinians, who admit no manducation and drinking of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper, neither oral nor spiritual, but grant a spiritual one outside the Supper." (L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 1224. sq.)

Delitzsch: "Whoever is baptized and partakes of the Lord's Table is a member of the body of Christ. The body of Christ is the totality of all those who are baptized into one body and made to drink into one Spirit. Be it Hengstenberg or Wislizenus—by the power of God's act, which faith does not produce and unbelief does not thwart, they are both members of one and the same body." (Four Books on the Church. Dresden 1847. p. 33. sq.)

Latin:

Non solum a dignis sive credentibus, verum etiam ab indignis sive incredulis et impiis, quos Paulus 1 Cor. 11, 27. dicit reos esse non tantum symbolorum sacrorum, quibus abutantur, sed ipsius corporis et sanguinis Domini, idque ideo, quod non dijudicent corpus (et sanguinem) Domini, seu, quod ipsum corpus Domini indigne edant, dum videlicet ad hoc epulum, quo verum corpus Domini accipiunt, ita accedunt sine fide ac religiosa reverentia, sicut ad epulum vulgare. ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Calvinianorum, statuentium, indignos et hypocritas dimidium tantum sacramentum, sc. signa duntaxat externa, accipere, non vero integrum sacramentum, h. e., non fieri participes corporis et sanguinis Christi in s. coena, sed tantum nuda et inania signa percipere. Ita Danaeus in resp. p. 122.: ,Indigni et impoenitentes dimidium tantum sacramentum, videl. signa duntaxat, sumunt, poenitentes vero integrum sacramentum/ . . Calvinus epist. ad Jacob. Andreae scribit: ,Tantum abest, ut tuis argumentis dimovear, ut mirer, tibi non venisse in mentem, impios Christum respuendo magis, quam recipiendo, sibi accessere interitum/ Quidam Calvinianorum discrimen faciunt inter manducationem in s. coena indignam et indignorum. Persona digna i. e. homo credens in Christum interdum digne, indigne interdum sumit panem et vinum, semper vero percipit corpus et sanguinem per fidem. Ita in Supplem. Panstrat. Chamier. c. 3.: Indigne, qui non recte se praeparat ad hoc tantum convivium, id quod saepenumero accidit et credentibus, ut docet apostolus 1 Cor. 11.; contra indignus est, qui non est praeditus vera fide. ..

2. Socinianorum, Arminianorum, Anabaptistarum, Svenckcfeldianorum, qui, uti omnem corporis et sanguinis Christi in s. coena realem praesentiam, ita omnem oralem perceptionem eorundem negant, reprobant, dirisque traducunt blasphemiis.

3. Labadistarum, asserentium, in s. coena non nisi credentes de corpore et sanguine Christi participare, neque dignitatem communicantium in fide quaerendam esse. Vide Declarat, p. 144.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 11. f. 1290.)

Nempe sacramentalis illa manducatio uno actu complectitur et manducationem naturalem ac sensibilem panis benedicti, et manducationem, non quidem sensibilem et naturalem, veram tamen, corporis Christi cum pane sacramentaliter uniti. Et bibitio sacramentalis, quae ore corporis peragitur, complectitur simul bibitionem sensibilem ac naturalem vini benedicti, et bibitionem, non quidem sensibilem, veram tamen, sanguinis Christi. Atque hinc manducatio et bibitio illa sacramentalis etiam oralis dici solet propter unitatem et identitatem actus, seu ut connotetur organon oris, quo manducatio panis et corporis, itemque bibitio vini ac sanguinis Christi peragitur; licet cibus et potus utrinque sit diversus et modus manducandi panem a modo manducandi corpus, ac modus bibendi vinum a modo bibendi sanguinem Christi plurimum differat; quemadmodum nec de ratione formali manducationis (sed tantum de ratione manducationis naturalis) est, ut cibus modo sensibili accipiatur, dentibus comminuatur et in ventriculum demittatur, nec de ratione formali bibitionis (sed tantum de ratione bibitionis naturalis) est, ut lingua et palato humorem saporemque potus experiamur; hic autem praesentia pariter et manducatio corporis ac bibitio sanguinis Christi est insensibilis, supernaturalis humanaeque menti incognita et PART. III. CAP. XI.

incomprehensibilis, ita tamen, ut nemine cogitante reapse existat. Possumus autem quoad determinationem modi, quo corpus et sanguis Domini adsit et accipiatur in coena, ignorantiam nostram profiteri, etsi τό δτι firmiter teneamus.

Conf. b. Mus. Dissert. de S. Coena contra Johan. Vorst. § 91. 92. p. 83. sqq.
