### Of the Holy Supper: However, the true and real presence, manducation, and drinking of the body and…

However, the true and real presence, manducation, and drinking of the body and blood of Christ are proved chiefly from the very words of institution, where Christ, having offered the bread, said to the disciples: Take, eat, this is my body; and having offered the cup, in which was wine: Drink, this is my blood. As these words speak indubitably of oral manducation and drinking, so, if they are viewed in their native force and character, they most clearly signify that this, which Christ commands to be taken and eaten with the mouth of the body, and which he testifies is actually present, is his own body, and this, which he likewise commands to be drunk with the mouth from the blessed cup, is his own blood.

Indeed, the sense of the statement by which Christ, having offered the bread and pronounced the words: Take, eat, continues: This is my body, with the words taken properly and without a trope, is this: This, which I give to you, and which I command you to take and eat, is my body.

Similarly, the sense of the words by which Christ, having offered the cup in which was wine, and having added the words: Take, drink, further said: This is my blood, is this: This, which I offer to you, and command you to take and drink, is my blood.

And although nothing but bread and wine were shown to the senses, yet another thing, and indeed the very body and blood of Christ, not equally obvious to the senses, is nevertheless declared by the added words to be conjoined and united with that which is shown to the senses, as being really present and actually exhibited. Compare, blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 109. sqq. p. 103. § 111. p. 134. § 144. p. 137. § 158. p. 153.

That those words of Christ are to be taken in their native force and character, and that one should not deflect from their proper signification to a trope, is evident (1.) from the common rule of interpretation, founded in natural reason itself, concerning the retention of the proper signification, unless an urgent necessity compels one to descend to an improper signification; which rule, indeed, is to be observed with particular care in those matters which contain supernatural things and pertain to faith. (2.) Because, although three evangelists and Paul, at different times and places, commemorated the institution of the Holy Supper, yet no one indicated by a word that a tropical signification of the words was to be embraced to the extent that not the body, but a sign of the body is eaten, not the blood, but a sign of the blood. PART III. CHAP. XI.

it must be believed. (3.) From the consensus of the Holy Scriptures, 1 Cor. 11:27, 28 and ch. 10:16. For there, the unworthy guest of the Eucharist is said to be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord himself, as if he had received them unworthily or with contumely, because the bread and wine are κοινωνία, a communion, of the body and blood of Christ, which is taught in the latter passage. This communion, however, is not a bare signification, but a real conjunction. (4.) From the nature of testaments, in which the propriety and perspicuity of words are most required, and it is least of all to be thought that Christ, most wise and most truthful, either deliberately or imprudently gave occasion for disputes and quarrels in his testament through the impropriety of words. Confer, blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 4. sqq. ad 13. p. 2. sqq. "

Luther: To instruct you further, as our own, you should know that it is a pure fabrication for anyone to say that this little word 'is' means as much as 'signifies.' No human being can ever prove this in any place of Scripture; indeed, I will go further: if the enthusiasts can bring a single passage in all the languages that are on earth where 'is' counts for as much as 'signifies,' then they shall have won. But they will surely have to leave it be; these high spirits lack the ability to properly look at rhetoric, grammar, or what they call a trope, which one is taught in the children's schools. That same art teaches how a boy should make two or three words out of one, or how he might give one and the same word a new usage and further meanings. For example, to prove it with a few instances: the word 'flower,' according to its first and old meaning, signifies a rose, lily, violet, and the like, which grows and blooms from the earth. Now, if I wanted to praise Christ with a fine eulogy and saw how he comes from the Virgin Mary, such a beautiful child, I may take the word 'flower' and make a trope, or give it a new meaning and usage, and say: 'Christ is a flower.' Here all grammarians or rhetoricians say that 'flower' has become a new word and has a new meaning, and no longer signifies the flower in the field, but the child Jesus; and the word 'is' must not here become a 'signification,' for Christ does not signify a flower, but he is a flower—yet a different flower than the natural one. For thus speaks the poet Horace: *Dixeris egregie, notum si callida verbum reddiderit junctura novum* (De arte poetica, v. 47. 48.), that is, it is spoken very finely when you can well renew a common word. From this one has it that one and the same word becomes two or many words when it receives other new meanings beyond its common meaning. As, 'flower' is one word when it signifies Christ, and another when it signifies natural roses and the like. Likewise, another when it signifies a golden, silver, or wooden rose. Thus, when one speaks of a stingy man: 'He is a dog'; here 'dog' signifies the stingy miser, and from the old word a new word has been made; according to the teaching of Horace, 'is' must not here be a 'signification,' for the stingy man does not signify a dog. Thus one speaks now in all languages and renews the words, as when we say: 'Mary is a dawn'; 'Christ is a fruit of the womb'; 'the devil is a god of the world'; 'the Pope is Judas'; 'St. Augustine is Paul'; 'St. Bernard is a dove'; 'David is a wood-worm,' and so forth; the Scripture is full of such speech. And it is called a trope or metaphor in grammar when one gives two different things the same name, because there is a likeness in both, and then that same name is indeed one word according to the letter, but *potestate et significatione plura*, according to power, usage, and meaning, it is two words, an old one and a new one, as Horace says and the children well know. We Germans are accustomed with such renewed words to [say] 'rightly' or 'otherwise'..."

or to set it anew and say: You are a true dog, the monks are true Pharisees, the nuns are true daughters of Moab, Christ is a true Solomon. Likewise, Luther is another Huss, Zwingli is another Korah, Oecolampadius is a new Abiram.

In such expressions, all Germans will give me testimony and confess that these are new words, and it is the same as if I say: Luther is Huss, Luther is another Huss, Luther is a true Huss, Luther is a new Huss. Thus, one feels how in such expressions, according to the teaching of Horace, a new word is made from the previous one; for it clatters and does not ring true if I say: Luther signifies Huss, but rather, he is a Huss.

One speaks of the essence in such sayings, what one is, and not what one signifies, and makes a new word for his new essence. So you will find it in all languages, that I know for a truth, and thus all grammarians teach and the boys in school know, and you will never find that "is" can mean "signifies."

Now when Christ says: John is Elijah, no one can prove that John signifies Elijah, for it would also be ridiculous that John should signify Elijah, when it would be much more reasonable that Elijah signifies John. And according to Zwingli’s art, Christ would have to reverse it and say: Elijah is John, that is, he signifies John. But Christ wants to say what John is, not what he signifies, but what kind of essence or office he has, and says: he is Elijah. Here Elijah has become a new word and does not mean the old Elijah, but the new Elijah, as we Germans say: John is the true Elijah, John is another Elijah, John is a new Elijah.

Just so it is also spoken: Christ is a rock, that is, he has an essence and is truly a rock, but yet a new rock, another rock, a true rock; likewise: Christ is a true vine.

Dear friend, how does it clatter if you want to interpret such things according to Zwingli’s conceit: Christ signifies the true vine? Who then is the true vine that Christ signifies? So I hear indeed, Christ should be a sign or signification of the wood in the vineyard? Oh, that would be a fine thing! Why then would Christ not have more reasonably said: The true vine is Christ, that is, the wooden vine signifies Christ? It is indeed more reasonable that Christ should be signified than that he should first have to signify, since that which signifies is always lesser than that which is signified, and all signs are lesser than the thing which they signify; as even fools and children well understand.

But Zwingli does not look at the word *vera* [true] in this passage: Christ is the true vine. If he looked at that, he could not have made a "signification" out of the "is." For no language, according to reason, allows one to say that Christ signifies the true vine. For no one can say that in this place the true vine is the wood in the vineyard. And thus the text forces with violence that "vine" is here a new word, which denotes another, new, true vine and not the vine in the vineyard. Therefore, "is" here cannot be a "signification," but Christ is truly and has the essence of a true, new vine.

Although, even if the text stood thus: Christ is a vine, it still does not sound as if I wanted to say: Christ signifies the vine, but rather the vine should signify Christ;

thus also this passage: Christ is the Lamb of God, John 1:29, cannot be understood thus, Christ signifies the Lamb of God, for then Christ would have to be lesser than a sign, namely the Lamb of God. But what then is the Lamb of God that Christ signifies? Is it to be the Passover lamb? Why then does he not reverse it and say more reasonably: The Lamb of God is Christ, that is, the Passover lamb signifies Christ, as Zwingli interprets? Now, however, because the little word "of God" stands by the word "Lamb," it forces with violence that "Lamb" here is another, new word, also called a PART III. CAP. XI.

Latin:

Probatur autem vera et realis praesentia, manducatio et bibitio corporis et sanguinis Christi praecipue ex ipsis verbis institutionis, ubi Christus, porrecto pane, ad discipulos dixit: Accipite, comedite, hoc est corpus meum, et porrecto poculo, in quo vinum erat: Bibite, hoc est sanguis meus. Quae ut indubie de manducatione et bibitione ovali loquuntur, ita, si in sua nativa vi et indole spectentur, clarissime significant, hoc, quod accipere et ore corporis comedere Christus jubet atque adeo reapse praesens esse testatur, esse suum ipsius corpus, et 110c, quod de poculo benedicto itidem ore bibere jubet, esse suum ipsius sanguinem.

Nempe enuntiationis, qua Christus porrecto pane et pronuntiatis verbis: Accipite, comedite, pergit: Hoc est corpus meum, verbis proprie ac sine tropo acceptis hic est sensus: Hoc, quod vobis do, et quod vos accipere et comedere jubeo, est corpus meum.

Similiter verborum, quibus Christus porrecto poculo, in quo vinum erat, additisque verbis: Accipite, bibite, porro dixit: Hoc est sanguis meus, sensus hic est: Hoc, quod vobis porrigo, et accipere ac bibere jubeo, est sanguis meus.

Ac licet.non nisi panis et vinum ad sensum monstrata fuerint, aliud tamen, et quidem ipsum corpus et sanguis Christi, sensibus non aeque obvium, nihilominus cum eo, quod ad sensum monstratur, conjunctum et unitum, tanquam realiter praesens ac reapse exhibitum verbis adjectis declaratur. Confer, b. Mus. 1. c. § 109. sqq. p. 103. § 111. p. 134. § 144. p. 137. § 158. p. 153.

Quod autem verba illa Christi in sua nativa vi atque indole accipienda, neque a propria illorum significatione ad tropum deflectendum sit, constat (1.) ex communi et in ipsa ratione naturali fundata regula interpretationis de retinenda propria significatione, nisi urgens necessitas ad significationem impropriam descendere cogat; quae quidem regula in iis, quae res supernaturales continent atque ad fidem pertinent, inprimis solicite observanda est. (2.) Quod, cum tres evangelistae atque Paulus, temporibus ac locis diversis, institutionem s. coenae commemorarent, nemo tamen verbo significavit, tropicam significationem verborum eatenus amplectendam esse, ut, non corpus, sed signum corporis edi, non sanguinem, sed signum sanguinis PART. III. CAP. XI.

bibi, credendum sit. (3.) Ex consensu LL. 1 Cor. 11, 27. 28. et cap. 10, 16. Illic enim indignus conviva eucharistiae dicitur reus ipsius corporis et sanguinis Domini, tanquam indigne aut cum contumelia acceptorum, quia panis et vinum sunt κοινωνία, communicatio, corporis et sanguinis Christi, quod altero loco docetur. Communicatio autem haec non est nuda significatio, sed realis conjunctio. (4.) Ex indole testamentorum, in quibus verborum proprietas et perspicuitas maxime requiritur ac minime omnium putandum est, Christum sapientissimum ac veracissimum in testamento suo verborum improprietate litium ac rixarum materiam vel data opera vel imprudenter dedisse. Confer, b. Mus. 1. c. § 4. sqq. ad 13. p. 2. sqq. ״

Lutherus: ״Euch, als die Unsern, weiter zu unterrichten, sollt ihr wissen, dass ein lauter Gedicht ist, wer da sagt: Dass dies Wortlein,ist6 so viel heisse, als,deutet6. Es kann kein Mensch nimmermehr beweisen an einigem Ort der Schrift; ja, ich will weiter sagen: wenn die Schwärmer in allen Sprachen, so auf Erden sind, einen Spruch bringen, darinnen,ist6 so viel gelte als,deutet6, so sollen sie gewonnen haben. Aber sie sollens wohl lassen, es mangelt den hohen Geistern, dass sie die Redekunst, Grammatik, oder wie sie es nennen, Tropus, so man in der Kinderschulen lehret, nicht recht ansehen. Dieselbige Kunst lehret, wie ein Knabe solle aus einem Wort zwei oder drei machen, oder wie er einerlei Wort neuen Brauch und mehr Deutungen geben möge. Als, dass ich mit etlichen Exempeln beweise: das Wort Blume, nach seiner ersten und alten Deutung, heisst es eine Rose, Lilie, Violen und dergleichen, die aus der Erden wächst und blüht. Wenn ich nun Christum wollt mit einem feinen Lobe preisen und sähe, wie er von der Jungfrau Maria kommt, so ein schon Kind, mag ich das Wort Blume nehmen und einen Tropum machen, oder eine neue Deutung und Brauch geben und sagen: Christus ist eine Blume. Hie sprechen alle Grammatici oder Redenmeister, dass Blume sei ein neu Wort worden und habe eine neue Deutung und heisse nun nicht mehr die Blume auf dem Feld, sondern das Kind Jesus, und müsse nicht hie das Wort,ist‘ zur Deutelei werden, denn Christus bedeutet nicht eine Blume, sondern er ist eine Blume, doch eine andere Blume, denn die natürliche. Denn so spricht der Poet Horatius: Dixeris egregie, notum si callida verbum reddiderit junctura novum (De arte poetica, v. 47. 48.), das ist, gar fein ists geredt, wenn du ein gemein Wort kannst wohl verneuen. Daraus man hat, dass einerlei Wort zwei oder vielerlei Wort wird, wenn es über seine gemeine Deutung andere neue Deutung kriegt. Als, Blume ist ein ander Wort, wenn es Christum heisst, und ein anders, wenn es die natürliche Rosen und dergleichen heisst. Item, ein anders, wenns eine güldene, silberne oder hölzerne Rosen heisst. Also, wenn man von einem kargen Mann spricht: Er ist ein Hund; hie heisst ein Hund den kargen Filz und ist aus dem alten Wort ein neu Wort worden; nach der Lehre Horatii muss nicht hie,ist‘ eine Deutelei sein; denn der Karge bedeutet nicht einen Hund. Also redet man nun in allen Sprachen und verneuet die Wörter, als, wenn wir sagen: Maria ist eine Morgenröthe; Christus ist eine Frucht des Leibes; der Teufel ist ein Gott der Welt; der Pabst ist Judas; St. Augustin ist Paulus; St. Bernhard ist eine Taube; David ist ein Holzwürmlein, und so fortan, ist die Schrift solcher Rede voll. Und heisst Tropus oder Metaphora in der Grammatik, wenn man zweierlei Dingen einerlei Namen gibt, um deswillen, dass ein Gleichniss in beiden ist, und ist denn derselbige Name nach dem Buchstaben wohl einerlei Wort, aber potestate et significatione plura, nach der Macht, Brauch, Deutung zwei Wort, ein altes und neues, wie Horatius sagt und die Kinder wohl wissen. Wir Deutschen pflegen bei solchen verneueten Worten recht, oder ander,

oder neu zu setzen und sagen: Du bist ein rechter Hund, die Mönche sind rechte Pharisäer, die Nonnen sind rechte Moabiter Töchter, Christus ist ein rechter Salomon. Item, Luther ist ein ander Huss, Zwingel ist ein ander Korah, Oecolampad ist ein neuer Abiram.

In solchen Reden werden mir alle Deutsche Zeugniss geben und bekennen, dass neue Wörter sind und gleich so viel ist, wenn ich sage: Luther ist Huss, Luther ist ein ander Huss, Luther ist ein rechter Huss, Luther ist ein neuer Huss. Also, dass man es fühlet, wie in solchen Reden nach der Lehre Horatii ein neu Wort aus dem vorigen gemacht wird, denn es klappet noch klinget nicht, wenn ich sagt: Luther bedeut Huss, sondern, er ist ein Huss.

Vom Wesen redet man in solchen Sprüchen, was einer sei, und nicht, was er bedeute, und macht über seinem neu Wesen auch ein neu Wort, So wirst du es finden in allen Sprachen, das weiss ich fürwahr, und also lehren alle Grammatici und wissen die Knaben in der Schule, und wirst nimmer finden, dass,ist‘ möge,deuten‘ heissen.

Wenn nun Christus spricht: Johannes ist Elias, kann niemand beweisen, dass Johannes bedeute Elias, denn es auch lächerlieh wäre, dass Johannes sollte Elias bedeuten, so viel billiger Elias Johannem bedeutet. Und nach Zwingeis Kunst müsste es Christus umkehren und sagen: Elias ist Johannes, das ist, er bedeutet Johannem. Sondern Christus will sagen, was Johannes sei, nicht was er bedeute, sondern was er vor ein Wesen oder Amt habe, und spricht: er sei Elias. Hie ist Elias ein neu Wort worden und heisst nicht den alten Elias, sondern den neuen Elias, wie wir Deutschen sagen: Johannes ist der rechte Elias, Johannes ist ein ander Elias, Johannes ist ein neuer ^Elias.

Eben so ists auch geredt: Christus ist ein Fels, das ist, er hat ein Wesen und ist wahrhaftig ein Fels, aber doch ein neuer Fels, ein ander Fels, ein rechter Fels; item: Christus ist ein rechter Weinstock.

Lieber, wie klappets, wenn du solches also willt deuten nach Zwingeis Dünkel: Christus bedeutet den rechten Weinstock? Wer ist denn der rechte Weinstock, den Christus bedeutet? So hör ich wohl, Christus sollte ein Zeichen oder Deutung sein des Holzes im Weinberge? Ach, das wäre fein Ding! Warum hätte denn Christus nicht billiger also gesagt: Der rechte Weinstock ist Christus, das ist, der hölzerne Weinstock bedeutet Christum? Es ist ja billiger, dass Christus bedeutet werde, denn dass er allererst bedeuten sollte, sintemal das da deutet, allemal geringer ist, denn das bedeutet wird, und alle Zeichen geringer sind, denn das Ding, so sie bezeichnen; wie das alles auch Narren und Kinder wohl verstehen.

Aber der Zwingel siehet nicht auf das Wort vera in diesem Spruch: Christus ist der rechte Weinstock. Wenn er dasselbige ansähe, hätte er nicht können Deutelei aus dem,ist‘ machen. Denn es leidet keine Sprache nach Vernunft, dass man sage, Christus bedeute den rechten Weinstock. Denn es kann ja niemand sagen, dass an diesem Ort der rechte Weinstock sei das Holz im Weinberge. Und zwinget also der Text mit Gewalt, dass Weinstock sei hie ein neu Wort, das einen andern, neuen, rechten Weinstock heisse und nicht den Weinstock im Weinberge. Drum kann auch,ist‘ hie nicht Deutelei sein, sondern Christus ist wahrhaftig und hat das Wesen eines rechten, neuen Weinstocks.

Wiewohl, wenn gleich der Text also stünde: Christus ist ein Weinstock, so lautets doch nicht, dass ich sagen wollte: Christus bedeutet den Weinstock, sondern vielmehr sollte der Weinstock Christum bedeuten;

Also auch dieser Spruch: Christus ist das Lamm Gottes, Joh. 1, 29., kann nicht also verstanden werden, Christus bedeutet das Lamm Gottes, denn so müsste Christus geringer sein, als ein Zeichen, denn das Lamm Gottes. Welches will aber denn das Lamm Gottes sein, das Christus bedeutet? Solls sein das Osterlamm? Warum kehret ers denn nicht um und spräche billiger: Das Lamm Gottes ist Christus, das ist, Osterlamm bedeutet Christus, wie Zwingel deutet? Nun aber, weil das Wortlein Gottes bei dem Wort Lamm stehet, zwingt es mit Gewalt, dass Lamm hie ein ander, neu Wort ist, heisset auch ein PART. III. CAP. XI.


### Of the Holy Supper: other, new, and the true Lamb, which Christ truly is, and not the old Passover…

other, new, and the true Lamb, which Christ truly is, and not the old Passover lamb. And so forth, regarding the other examples they bring forward, such as: The seed is the Word of God, Luke 8:11 ff., the field is the world, etc., Matt. 13:38, they cannot make any mere interpretation out of the "is" with good reason; rather, the children in school say that "seed" and "field" are *tropi* or renewed words according to metaphor. For *vocabulum simplex et metaphoricum* are not one, but two words. Thus, "seed" here does not mean grain or wheat, but the Word of God, and "field" means the world, for Christ (the text itself says) speaks in parables and not of natural grain or wheat.

But whoever speaks in parables makes mere *tropos* out of common words—new and different words—otherwise they would not be parables if he used the common words in their previous meaning. That is a truly foolish, senseless spirit that wants to take words in parables according to their common meaning, against the nature and manner of parables; such a person must surely have to busy himself with interpretation and jugglery. (Confession Concerning the Lord’s Supper, A.D. 1528. Vol. XX, 1131—1136.)

The same: "Here perhaps the other faction will boast and say: 'By this you will confirm Oecolampadius’s sign-theory, because he, according to such teaching of Horace, also makes a new word and *tropum* out of the common one and says, "my body" here means "the sign of my body."' To this, the answer is soon given: that the *grammatici*, and also all Christian teachers, forbid that one should ever depart from the common, old meaning of a word and adopt a new meaning, unless the text and the sense compel it, or it is proven by force from other places of Scripture; otherwise, one would never retain any certain text, sense, speech, or language. As when Christ says: John is Elijah; here the text and faith compel that 'Elijah' must be a new word, because it is certain that John is not, nor can be, the old Elijah. Likewise: Christ is a rock; again, the text itself and faith compel that 'rock' here is a new word, because Christ is not, nor can be, a natural rock.

That Oecolampadius now makes 'sign of the body' out of the word 'body' here, one does not concede to him, for he does it willfully and cannot prove that the text or faith so compels it. Just as if someone willfully wanted to *tropisize* or renew a word thus: 'The Gospel is the power of God,' Rom. 1:16, should mean as much as, 'The Gospel is Roland’s sword.' Thus, one might call or interpret Christ as Belial, or Paul as Judas; who would stop him? But one does not accept it unless he proves it and compels it from the text. Thus, Oecolampadius also argues no further than that he makes mere bread and wine in the Lord’s Supper. But even if he were to prove that (which he cannot), he still cannot argue or prove that 'body' means 'sign of the body.' ...

Furthermore, it is also a perverse, improper *tropus* against all *tropos* of Scripture, such that one must grasp that it is a willful fabrication; I must make that clear.

Where a *tropus* or renewed word is used in Holy Scripture, there are also two meanings, a new one over the first old or previous one, as was said above; as, the word 'vine' in Scripture has two meanings, an old and a new one. According to the old or first, it simply means the shrub or plant in the vineyard; according to the new, it means Christ, John 15:5: 'I am a vine'; or it means a mother of children, Ps. 128:3: 'Your wife shall be like a vine,' or whatever is similar, because it has a parable with the vine on account of the fruit, as the rhetoricians teach, *quae transferuntur, secundum similitudinem transferuntur*, that is, all renewal or *tropi* occur on account of a likeness. Now, those same *tropi* in Scripture are done in such a way that the words, according to the old or first meaning, show the thing,

is the new parable, and according to the new interpretation, they point to the new, real thing or essence itself, and not back again. As in this saying: "I am the true vine." Here the word "vine" has become a trope or a new word, which cannot point back to the old vine, which is the parable of the new one, but points for itself to the true new vine itself, which is not a parable. For Christ is not a parable of the vine, but rather the vine is a parable of Christ, etc. Likewise, "the seed is the word of God," Luke 8:11; here "seed" does not point to the grain, which is a parable of the Gospel, but (as a renewed word or trope should) it points to the Gospel, the true new seed itself, which is not the parable.

And so on, all tropes in Scripture point to the true new essence and not to the parable of that same new essence.

But Oecolampadius reverses this and makes such a trope or renewed word that points back to the parable of the new essence, and says that "body" should be called a sign or parable of the body, in the saying: "This is my body," when he, if he wanted to follow Scripture, should much rather renew the word "body" in such a way that it means the true new body, to which the natural body of Christ would be a parable.

For Scripture does not trope backward in such a way, and it does not sound right if I wanted to trope thus: "Christ is a vine," John 15:5, that is, a sign of a vine. "The Gospel is a seed," that is, a sign of a seed. "Christ is a lamb," John 1:29, that is, a sign of a lamb. "Christ is a rock," Matt. 16:18, that is, a sign of a rock. "Christ is our Passover," that is, a sign of our Passover. "John is Elijah," Matt. 11:14, that is, a sign of Elijah. Summa summarum, such a trope is not in Scripture, and none is valid.

Therefore, Oecolampadius’s trope cannot hold when he says: "Bread is my body," that is, a sign of my body, for it is a regressive, perverted trope; it makes a parable or sign out of the true essence, which is not the manner of Holy Scripture; therefore, it is a pure fabrication.

But if the text stood thus: "Take, eat, this is my true bread," then one could make a proper trope and say quite finely: "Bread" is here a renewed word, which according to the first interpretation means simple bread, which is a parable of the body of Christ, and according to the new interpretation, it means the true new bread itself, which is the body of Christ.

But now that the text stands thus: "This is my body," and he wants to make a trope there, he must, according to Scripture, say: The word "body" according to the old interpretation means the natural body of Christ, but according to the new interpretation, it must mean another new body of Christ, to which his natural body is a parable. That would be, according to the manner of Scripture, the word rightly and well renewed, so that the new text would stand thus: "This is my true new body, which is not a parable," just as I say of Christ: "This is our vine," that is, a new true vine, of which the old vine in the vineyard is a parable.

Now if someone here wanted to claim that one finds such an Oecolampadian trope in common speech, as when one says of pictures: "This is St. Peter, this is St. Paul, this is Pope Julius, this is Emperor Nero," and so on, in which speeches the words Peter, Paul, Julius, Nero are taken for pictures.

I answer firstly: I do not care about that; Oecolampadius did not undertake to trope in common speech, but in Scripture, and there he must remain and follow its manner and way.

But if he could show me an example of his troping in Scripture, then he would have won, and I would agree with him in all points.

But if he brings up no example, then he has lost, and his trope is nothing and a pure fabrication.

For Holy Scripture conducts itself with speaking as God conducts himself with acting.

Now God always creates in such a way that the mean- 33 Baier’s Compendium, ed. Walther. III. PART III. CHAPTER XI. ...or parable must happen first, and thereafter follows the true essence and fulfillment of the parables. For thus the Old Testament goes before as a parable, and the New Testament follows thereafter as the true essence.

Just so does she [the language] also act when she makes a trope or a new word, in that she takes the old word, which is the parable, and gives it a new meaning, which is the true essence.

For how would it sound if I were to say: The Gospel is a new testament, that is, a parable of the New Testament? That would be saying as much as: The Gospel is the Old Testament. Likewise, Christ is God’s Lamb, that is, an image or parable of God’s Lamb; that would be saying as much as: Christ is the old Easter lamb of Moses.

Just so does Oecolampadius also act with his perverse trope, where he makes an old word out of the new word "body" and says: It should mean, "this is a sign of my body," which is saying as much as, "this is bread." Now, here bread should rightly be the old word and body the new, and the word "bread" should signify the body, not the word "body" signify the bread.

Thus his trope turns to water and cannot stand in the Scripture.

Secondly, it is also not true that such a trope of Oecolampadius exists in any common speech or language in the whole world, and whoever brings me a consistent example of this, to him I will give my neck.

They indeed say that such a trope exists in this speech: "Here is St. Peter, that is, an image of St. Peter"; but I say no to that, and they cannot prove it; it is their own false invention.

For this is a certain rule in all languages: where the little word "is" is used in a speech, there one speaks certainly of the essence of that same thing and not of its meaning.

Note this in this regard: I take a wooden or silver rose before me and ask, "What is that?" Then one answers me, "It is a rose." Here I do not ask what it signifies, but after the essence, what it is; so one answers me also what it is, and not what it signifies. For it is a very different question when I say, "What does that signify?" and when I say, "What is that?" "Is" always goes to the essence itself; that never fails.

Latin:

ander, neu und das rechte Lamm, welches Christus wahrhaftig ist, und nicht das alte Osterlamm. Und so fortan, was sie mehr vor Exempel führen, als: Der Same ist Gottes Wort, Luc. 8,11. ff., der Acker ist die Welt u. s. w., Matth. 13, 38., können sie keine Deutelei aus dem,ist4 machen mit gutem Grunde, sondern die Kinder in der Schule sagen, dass Same und Acker seien tropi oder verneuete Wörter nach der Metaphora. Denn vocabulum simplex et metaphoricum sind nicht ein, sondern zwei Worte. Also heisst Same hie nicht Korn noch Weizen, sondern Gottes Wort, und Acker heisset die Welt, denn Christus (spricht der Text selbst) redet in Gleichnissen und nicht von natürlichem Korn oder Weizen.

Wer aber in Gleichnissen redet, der machet aus gemeinen Worten eitel tropos, neue und andere Wörter, sonst wärens nicht Gleichnisse, wo er die gemeinen Wort brauchet in der vorigen Deutung. Dass gar ein toller, unverständiger Geist ist, der in Gleichnissen will die Worte nehmen nach gemeiner Deutung, wider die Natur und Art der Gleichnissen; der muss denn wohl mit Deutelei und Gaukelei zu schaffen gewinnen.44 (Bekenntniss vom Abendmahl. A. 1528. Tom. XX, 1131—1136.)

Idem: ״Hie wird vielleicht die andere Rotte sich brüsten und sagen: Hiermit wirst du bestätigen des Oecolampadii Zeichelei, weil derselbige, nach solcher Lehre Horatii, auch ein neu Wort und tropum machet aus dem gemeinen und spricht, ,mein Leib4 heisse hie,meines Leibes Zeichen1. Hierauf ist bald geantwortet: dass die Grammatici, dazu auch alle christliche Lehrer verbieten, man solle nimmermehr von gemeiner alten Deutung eines Wortes treten und neue Deutung annehmen, es zwinge denn der Text und der Verstand, oder werde aus andern Orten der Schrift mit Gewalt bewiesen; sonst würde man nimmermehr keinen gewissen Text, Verstand, Rede noch Sprache behalten. Als, wenn Christus spricht: Johannes ist Elias; hie zwinget der Text und Glaube, dass Elias ein neues Wort sein muss, weil das gewiss ist, dass Johannes nicht ist noch sein kann der alte Elias. Item: Christus ist ein Fels, zwinget abermal der Text selbst und der Glaube, dass Fels hie ein neues Wort ist, weil Christus nicht ist, noch sein kann ein natürlicher Fels.

Dass nun Oecolampad hie aus dem Wort Leib macht Leibes-Zeichen, gestehet man ihm nicht, denn er thuts muthwilliglich und kanns nicht beweisen, dass der Text oder Glaube so erzwinge. Gleich als wenn einer muthwilliglich wollte also tropisiren oder Wort verneuen: Das Evangelium ist Gottes Kraft, Röm. 1, 16., sollte so viel gelten, das Evangelium ist des Rolands Schwert. Also möchte einer Christum Belial, Paulum Judas heissen oder deuten, wer wills ihm wehren? Aber man nimmts nicht an, erbeweise es denn, und zwinge es aus dem Text. Also streitet Oecolampad auch nicht weiter, denn, dass er eitel Brot und Wein im Abendmahl mache. Aber wenn er dasselbige schon erstritte (als er nicht vermag), so kann er doch nicht erstreiten noch beweisen, dass Leib Leibes Zeichen heisse. . . .

Ueber das, so ists auch ein verkehrter unartiger Tropus wider alle Tropos der Schrift, dass man greifen muss, es sei ein muthwillig Gedichte; das muss ich klar machen.

Wo ein Tropus oder verneuert Wort wird in der heiligen Schrift, da werden auch zwo Deutungen, eine neue über die erste alte oder vorige, wie droben gesagt ist; als, das Wort,Weinstock4 in der Schrift hat zwo Deutungen, eine alte und neue. Nach der alten oder ersten heisst es schlecht den Strauch oder Gewächse im Weinberge, nach der neuen heisst es Christum, Joh. 15, 5.: ,Ich bin ein Weinstock4; oder heisst eine Kindermutter, Ps. 128, 3.: ,Dein Weib wird sein wie ein Weinstock4, oder was desgleichen ist, darum, dass es mit dem Weinstock ein Gleichniss hat der Frucht halben, wie die Redenmeister lehren, quae transferuntur, secundum similitudinem transferuntur, das ist, alle Verneurung oder Tropi geschehen einer Gleichniss halben. Nun sind dieselbigen Tropi in der Schrift also gethan, dass die Worte nach der alten oder ersten Deutung zeigen das Ding,

so des neuen Gleichniss ist, und nach der neuen Deutung zeigen sie das neue rechte Ding oder Wesen selbst und nicht wiederum zurücke. Als in diesem Spruch: Ich bin der rechte Weinstock. Hie ist das Wort Weinstock ein Tropus oder neu Wort worden, welches nicht kann zurück deuten den alten Weinstock, der des neuen Gleichniss ist, sondern deutet für sich den rechten neuen Weinstock selbst, der nicht ein Gleichniss ist. Denn Christus ist nicht ein Gleichniss des WeinStocks, sondern wiederum der Weinstock ist ein Gleichniss Christi u. s. w. Item, ,der Same ist Gottes Wort‘, Luc. 8,11., hie zeiget Same nicht das Korn, welches ein Gleichniss ist des Evangelii, sondern (wie ein verneuet Wort oder Tropus soll) deutet es das Evangelium, den rechten neuen Samen selbst, der nicht die Gleichniss ist.

Und so fortan alle Tropi in der Schrift deuten das rechte neue Wesen und nicht das Gleichniss desselbigen neuen Wesens.

Solches aber kehret Oecolampad um und macht einen solchen Tropum oder verneuet Wort, das zurücke deutet die Gleichniss des neuen Wesens, und spricht, Leib solle Leibes Zeichen oder Gleichniss heissen, in dem Spruch: das ist mein Leib, so er doch, wo er der Schrift nachfolgen wollt, vielmehr soll das Wort Leib also verneuen, dass es den rechten neuen Leib heisst, welchem der natürliche Leib Christi ein Gleichniss wäre.

Denn die Schrift troppet nicht also zurücke und lautet auch nicht, wenn ich also wollte troppen: Christus ist ein Weinstock, Joh. 15, 5., das ist, ein Zeichen des Weinstocks. Evangelium ist ein Same, das ist, ein Zeichen des Samens. Christus ist ein Lamm, Joh. 1, 29., das ist, ein Zeichen des Lamms. Christus ist ein Fels, Matth. 16, 18., das ist, ein Zeichen des Felsen. Christus ist unser Passah, das ist, ein Zeichen unsers Passah. Johannes ist Elias, Matth. 11, 14., das ist, ein Zeichen Elias. Summa Summarum, solcher Tropus ist keiner in der Schrift und taugt auch keiner.

Darum kann auch Oecolampads Tropus nicht gelten, da er spricht: Brot ist mein Leib, das ist, meines Leibes Zeichen, denn es ist ein rücklinger, verkehrter Tropus, macht aus dem rechten Wesen ein Gleichniss oder Zeichen, welches der heiligen Schrift Art nicht ist, darum ists ein lauter Gedicht.

Wenn aber der Text also stünde: Nehmet, esset, das ist mein rechtes Brot, da könnt man einen artigen Tropum machen und gar fein sagen: Brot ist hie ein verneuet Wort, welches nach der ersten Deutung heisst schlecht Brot, das ein Gleichniss ist des Leibes Christi, und nach der neuen Deutung heisst es das rechte neue Brot selbst, welches ist der Leib Christi.

Aber nun der Text also stehet: Das ist mein Leib, und er will einen Tropum da machen, muss er der Schrift nach also sagen: Das Wort Leib nach der alten Deutung heisst den natürlichen Leib Christi, aber nach der neuen Deutung muss es einen andern neuen Leib Christi heissen, welchem sein natürlicher Leib ein Gleichniss ist. Das wäre nach der Schrift Weise das Wort recht und wohl verneuet, dass der neue Text also stünde: Das ist mein rechter neuer Leib, der nicht ein Gleichniss ist, gleichwie ich sage von Christo: das ist unser Weinstock, das ist, ein neuer rechter Weinstock, welches Gleichniss ist der alte Weinstock im Weinberge.

Ob nun jemand hie wollt vorgeben, man finde gleichwohl solchen Oecolampadstropum in gemeiner Rede, als, wenn man von den Bildern saget: das ist St. Peter, das ist St. Paulus, das ist Pabst Julius, das ist Kaiser Nero und so fortan. In welchen Reden die Worte Petrus, Paulus, Julius, Nero für Bilder genommen werden.

Antworte ich erstlich: da frage ich nichts nach; Oecolampad hat nicht für sich genommen zu troppen in gemeiner Rede, sondern in der Schrift, da muss er auch in bleiben und derselbigen Art und Weise folgen.

Wo er aber mir ein Exempel seines Troppens in der Schrift könnte zeigen, sa sollt er gewonnen haben und ich wollt ihm in allen Stücken zufallen.

Wo er aber kein Exempel aufbringet, so hat er verloren und ist sein Tropus nichts und ein lauter Gedicht.

Denn die heilige Schrift hält sich mit reden, wie Gott sich hält mit wirken.

Nun schafft Gott allwege, dass die Deu33 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III. PART. III. CAP. XI. tung oder Gleichniss zuvor geschehen, und darnach folge das rechte Wesen und Erfüllung der Gleichnissen. Denn also gehet das alte Testament als ein Gleichniss vorher, und folget das neue Testament hernach als das rechte Wesen.

Eben also thut sie auch, wenn sie Tropos oder neue Wort macht, dass sie nimmt das alte Wort, welches die Gleichniss ist, und gibt ihm eine neue Deutung, welche das rechte Wesen ist.

Denn wie sollts lauten, wenn ich spräche: Evangelium ist ein neu Testament, das ist, ein Gleichniss des neuen Testaments. Das wäre so viel gesagt: Das Evangelium ist das alte Testament. Item, Christus ist Gottes Lamm, das ist, ein Bild oder Gleichniss Gottes Lamms; das wäre so viel gesagt: Christus ist das alte Osterlamm Mosis.

Eben so thut auch Oecolampad mit seinem rücklingen Tropo, da er aus dem neuen Wort Leib ein alt Wort macht und spricht: Es soll heissen, das ist meines Leibes Zeichen, das ist so viel gesagt, das ist Brot. Nun soll hie billig Brot das alte Wort sein und der Leib das neue, und das Wort Brot den Leib, nicht das Wort Leib das Brot bedeuten.

Also wird sein Tropus zu Wasser und kann nicht bestehen in der Schrift.

Zum andern ists auch nicht wahr, dass solcher Tropus Oecolampads in einiger gemeinen Bede oder Sprache sei in der ganzen Welt, und wer mir des ein beständig Exempel bringet, dem will ich meinen Hals geben.

Sie sagen wohl, dass ein solcher Tropus sei in dieser Rede: Hie ist St. Petrus, das ist, ein Bilde St. Petrus; ich sage aber nein dazu, und sie könnens nicht beweisen, es ist ihr eigen falsch Gedicht.

Denn das ist eine gewisse Begel in allen Sprachen: wo das Wörtlein,ist4 in einer Bede geführt wird, da redet man gewisslich vom Wesen desselbigen Dinges und nicht von seinem Deuten.

Das merke dabei: ich nehme eine hölzerne oder silberne Rose vor mich und frage, was ist das? so antwort man mir, es ist eine Rose. Hie frage ich nicht, was es bedeute, sondern nach dem Wesen, was es sei; so antwortet man mir auch, was es sei, und nicht, was es bedeute. Denn es ist viel eine andere Frage, wenn ich sage, was bedeut das? und wenn ich sage, was ist das? ,Ist4 gehet immer aufs Wesen selbst, das fehlet nimmermehr.


### Of the Holy Supper: Yes, you say; it is indeed not a rose, but wood

Yes, you say; it is indeed not a rose, but wood? Answer: That is good; nevertheless, it is a rose; even if it is not a grown, natural rose in the garden, nevertheless it is also essentially a rose in its own way, for there are many kinds of roses, such as silver, golden, cloth, paper, stone, wooden; nevertheless, each one for itself is essentially a rose in its essence, and there cannot be a mere meaning there.

Yes, how could a meaning be there that did not first have an essence? What is nothing, that signifies nothing; but what signifies, that must first have an essence and a parable of the other essence.

Therefore, in a wooden rose, both are to be separated from one another, the essence and the meaning, *sicut actum primum et secundum, sicut verbum substantivum et activum*; according to the essence it is truly a rose, namely a wooden rose; thereafter, when the essence thus stands, one may then say: this rose signifies or is made after another rose. For these are two different speeches or *propositiones*: "that is a rose," and "that signifies a rose"; and whoever makes one speech out of them, he does as much as one who would hold a *propositionem hypotheticam* and *categoricam* to be one proposition, *quod est impossibile*. How clumsy a thing that is, the learned know well.

Now, just as the essence of the rose is manifold—wooden, silver, golden, etc.—and yet each one is and is called truly a rose for itself, so also the word "rose" becomes a different new word (even if it remains the same letters) according to the meaning, as often as the essence of the rose becomes different and different.

Thus, one may nowhere use Oecolampadius’s trope, or say: "that is an image of a rose."

For it is also not true that whoever says, "that is a rose," intends to have said or understood, "that is a parable of a rose," but he wants to say what it is in essence. And when he wants to say further what...

it means, he makes two different statements and says: this is a rose, and this signifies a rose. And everyone must confess that such two statements are not of equal value, nor do they speak of the same kind of rose, but each one says something different for itself than the other.

This I know for a truth, that it is so with all this, and no one will be able to deny it. Therefore, Oecolampad cannot stand with his trope, in that he wants to let these two statements be of equal value: this is my body, and this is the likeness of my body; for no tongue or language suffers that.

Just as it cannot be of equal value when I say of the image of St. Paul: this is St. Paul, and: this signifies St. Paul. For the first statement wants to say what the image is, that it is St. Paul, namely a wooden St. Paul, a silver St. Paul, a golden St. Paul, a painted St. Paul. In short, the little word "is" speaks of the essence, whatever essence it may be, and "St. Paul" has here become a new word that does not mean the living St. Paul.

Thereafter, when I ask further: what does it signify then? there is immediately another statement, which now speaks not of the essence, but of the signifying. Thus, just as essence and signifying are not the same, so they cannot be expressed with the same words or statements; each must have its own particular statement.

If Oecolampad is to stand with his trope, he must also make two statements in the Lord's Supper, the one concerning the essence, thus: this is my body; for there stands an "is," which wants to and must speak of the essence. Since now there stands in the Lord's Supper no more than the one statement which speaks of the essence, namely: this is my body, so it must be spoken of an essential body of Christ, God grant that the same body be wooden, silver, or whatever he wills; for there stands an "is," which wants to have a body of Christ that is and is called Christ's body, as is the manner of common speech, that a Paul must be there when one says of the image: this is Paul. Thus Oecolampad must let a body of Christ be in the Lord's Supper; he may ponder whether he wants to make the same out of bread, wood, clay, or stone; the trope must have a body of Christ, because the other statement does not stand there, "this signifies," or "this is the sign of my body," but rather thus: "this is my body."

Summa Summarum, as I have said of the rose, where in a statement the word "rose" is to become a new word or trope, there must come together two roses, which both truly bear the name "rose," one that signifies, the other that is signified, and each of the two roses must truly be and be called a rose, although each in its own way, one wooden, the other natural. So also, if the word "my body" in the statement of the Lord's Supper is to become a new word or trope, there must also come together two bodies of Christ, which both truly bear the name "my body," one that signifies, the other that is signified.

So that each of the two bodies of Christ is truly and rightly called a body of Christ and is essential, be it wooden, silver, or bread-like.

If Oecolampad can now prove that bread is truly a body of Christ and can say it is a bread-like body of Christ, which is a likeness of the natural body of Christ, just as the wooden rose is truly a rose and a likeness of the natural rose, then he has achieved so much that an example of his trope may be found, and his trope is equal to that which goes in common speech of images, "this is St. Peter," "this is St. Paul," etc. Even though it is not yet a trope according to the manner of Scripture.

But where not, there his trope is also nothing outside of Scripture. How will he now bring forth such a thing, that bread is and is called Christ's body, or that Christ has a bread-like body, as St. Paul has a wooden St. Paul?

Now he must do it, or it is nonsense; and even if he found it, what does it help, since such a trope would nevertheless not be valid in Scripture?

Because then his PART III. CHAP. XI. "If a trope has no example either in Scripture or outside of Scripture, nay, is contrary to Scripture and the nature of all languages, then one can surely grasp that it is a mere useless fiction." (Ibid. p. 1137. sq. 1234—1242.)

Calovius: "We refute the opinion of the Calvinists. . . 15.) by the induction of the individual words and their native meaning. For in no place is a figure found, or if one is posited, it will not be found where a foothold can be established, and it will be a mere μετεωρισμός [suspension/vacillation]. On the contrary, however, all the words cry out that the proper sense must be retained. For if you wish, with Carlstadt, to accommodate the το δεικτικόν [the demonstrative] to the body of Christ sitting at the table, Mark protests, accommodating the same pronoun also to the blood of Christ: τούτο έστι το αιμά μου [this is my blood], where no visible pointing to the blood of Christ sitting there can take place. Not to mention that a λεπτολογία [subtlety/hair-splitting] is feigned to be in the words of Christ by that inept distortion of the words: 'eat, here you see my body; drink, for here sits my blood.' Likewise, if you wish, with Zwingli, to place the trope in the copula 'is,' not only does the consensus of the evangelists protest, who have nothing about 'is' being significant, but the phrasing of Luke also stands in the way, who omits the substantive verb entirely; and that which does not exist cannot be modified, much less should the remaining words be drawn into a foreign meaning on account of it. Furthermore: if one presumes to defend the opinion by means of the signs of Oecolampadius, who speaks in direct opposition to Zwingli, and to substitute a figure of the body in the predicate in place of the body, or with John Calvin the benefits of the body of Christ, Luke and Paul protest, asserting that that very body is exhibited which was delivered into death for us, so that you are necessarily compelled to understand it concerning the very substance of the body, as Beza himself urges. Thus, therefore, the unanimous consensus of the amanuenses of Christ most solidly refutes all tropes, which are reduced to these general heads, although otherwise they are innumerable. Hence I argue: Those individual words which are so determined that they block the cracks against all tropes, these are not to be understood tropically, but literally; but that the essential words of the Supper are such, has already been proven. Therefore. ὅπερ έδει δεῖξαι [which was to be demonstrated]." (System. IX, 296.)

Gerhard: "This is also very often objected to us by our adversaries, that we ourselves depart from the ρητόν of the words, namely in this mystery with these propositions: in, with, and under the blessed bread the body of Christ is given; in, with, and under the blessed wine the blood of Christ is given; whence they have devised a shameful verse: 'In, cum, sub, these monosyllables deceive the whole world.'"

Walther's Note 1: Let the true, real, and substantial presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper be granted to us; let it be granted that the words of Christ are to be taken κατά το ρητόν in their genuine, native, and proper sense, and we will easily come to an agreement with them regarding the use of these particles. 2. Sacramental predications—"this is my body," "this is my blood"—are comprehensive and exhibitive, that is, they denote the union and joint exhibition of two distinct things, as we have shown above; therefore, they cannot be resolved more conveniently than by the particles: in, with, under, by which the conjunction of the united things and their joint exhibition is expressed. Just as this exhibitive proposition, "Take, this is wine," cannot be resolved more skillfully and conveniently than in this way: "In or with this vessel, wine is exhibited"—for whatever other analysis you might bring forward will be trifling and absurd—so also that sacramental predication, "This is my body," is most conveniently resolved: "In, with, and under this bread I exhibit my body," because by the institution of Christ the Eucharistic bread is the instrument, όχημα, and symbol with which and under which the body of Christ is given. ...

Grammatical synonymy, oratorical paraphrase, logical equipollence, and theological interpretation, which expresses the same thing in other words, detract nothing from the ρητόν, as D. Major rightly writes in his treatise περί τω ρητω, title 3, chapter 1, thesis 17. ...

Latin:

Ja, sprichst du; es ist ja nicht eine Rose, sondern ein Holz? Antwort: das ist gut; dennoch ists eine Rose, obs nicht eine gewachsen natürliche Rose ist im Garten, dennoch ists auch wesentlich eine Rose auf seine Weise, denn es sind mancherlei Rosen, als silbern, gülden, tüehern, papierern, steinern, hölzern; dennoch ist eine jegliche für sich wesentlich eine Rose in ihrem Wesen, und kann nicht ein blos Deuten da sein.

Ja, wie wollte ein Deuten da sein, das nicht zuvor ein Wesen hätte? Was nichts ist, das deutet nichts; was aber deutet, das muss zuvor ein Wesen und ein Gleichniss des andern Wesens haben.

Darum ist an einer hölzern Rosen beides von einander zu scheiden, das Wesen und das Deuten, sicut actum primum et secundum, sicut verbum substantivum et activum; nach dem Wesen ists wahrhaftig eine Rose, nämlich eine hölzerne Rose; darnach, wenn das Wesen also stehet, mag man denn sagen: diese Rose bedeut oder ist nach einer andern Rosen gemacht. Denn dies sind zwo unterschiedliche Reden oder propositiones: das ist eine Rose, und, das bedeut eine Rose; und wer eine Rede draus macht, der tliät so viel, als der propositionem hypotheticam und categoricam für eine Proposition hielte, quod est impossibile. Wie ungeschickt Ding das sei, wissen die Gelehrten wohl.

Wie nun der Rosen Wesen mancherlei ist, hölzern, silbern, gülden u. s. w., und doch eine jegliche wahrhaftig für sich selbst eine Rose ist und heisst, also wird auch das Wort Rose so oft ein ander neu Wort (obs wohl einerlei Buchstaben bleibt) nach der Deutung, so oft d׳es Wesen der Rosen anders und anders wird.

Also, dass man nirgend darf des Oecolampads Tropos brauchen, oder sagen: das ist einer Rosen Bilde.

Denn es ist auch nicht wahr, dass, wer da spricht: das ist eine Rose, dass er wolle gesagt oder verstanden haben, das ist einer Rosen Gleichniss, sondern er will sagen, was es sei am Wesen. Und wenn er weiter sagen will, was

es bedeute, so macht er zwo unterschiedliche Reden und spricht: das ist eine Rose und bedeut eine Rose. Und jedermann muss bekennen, dass solche zwo Reden nicht gleich viel gelten, noch von einerlei Rosen reden, sondern eine jegliche für sich ein anders sagt, denn die andere.

Das weiss ich fürwahr, dass diesem allem so sei, und niemand wirds leugnen können. Darum kann Oecolampad mit seinem Tropo nicht bestehen, dass er diese zwo Reden gleich viel will gelten lassen: das ist mein Leib, und das ist meines Leibes Gleichniss; denn das leidet keine Zunge noch Sprache.

Gleich als nicht kann gleich viel gelten, Wenn ich sage vom Bilde St. Pauli: das ist St. Paulus, und: das bedeut St. Paulus. Denn die erste Rede will sagen, was das Bild sei, dass es sei St. Paulus, nämlich ein hölzerner St. Paulus, ein silberner St. Paulus, ein güldener St. Paulus, ein gemalter St. !Paulus. Kurzum, vom Wesen redet das Wörtlein,ist‘, es sei, was es auch für ein Wesen sei, und ist St. Paulus hie ein neu Wort worden, das nicht den lebendigen St. Paulus heisst.

Darnach, wenn ich weiter frage: was bedeut es denn? da ist so balde eine andere Rede, die nun nicht vom Wesen, sondern vom Deuten redet. Dass also, gleich wie Wesen und Deuten nicht einerlei sind, also auch nicht mit einerlei Worten oder Reden mögen ausgesprochen werden; ein jegliches muss seine besondere Rede haben.

Soll nun Oecolampad mit seinem Tropo bestehen, so muss er im Abendmahl auch zwo Reden machen, die eine vom Wesen, also: das ist mein Leib; denn es stehet ein,ist‘ da, das will und muss vom Wesen reden. Dieweil nun im Abendmahl nicht mehr denn die eine Rede stehet, so vom Wesen redet, nämlich: das ist mein Leib, so muss es von einem wesentlichen Leibe Christi geredet sein, Gott gebe, derselbige Leib sei hölzern, silbern, oder wie er will; denn es stehet ein,ist‘ da, das will einen Leib Christi haben, der da sei unci heisse Christus Leib, wie gemeiner Sprache Art ist, dass ein Paulus da sein muss, wenn man vom Bilde sagt: das ist Paulus. Also muss Oecolampad einen Leib Christi im Abendmahl sein lassen, da mag er nachdenken, ob er denselbigen aus Brot, Holz, Thon oder Stein machen wolle; der Tropus muss einen Leib Christi haben, weil nicht die andere Rede dabei stehet, das bedeut, oder das ist meines Leibes Zeichen, sondern also: das ist mein Leib.

Summa Summarum, wie ich von der Rose gesagt habe, wo etwa in einer Rede das Wort Rose soll ein neu Wort oder Tropus werden, da müssen zwo Rosen zukoramen, die alle beide den Namen Rose mit Wahrheit führen, eine, die bedeute, die andere, die bedeutet werde, und eine jegliche der beiden Rosen muss wahrhaftig eine Rose sein und heissen, wiewohl eine jegliche auf ihre Weise, eine hölzern, die andere natürlich. Also auch, so das Wort,mein Leib‘ in der Rede des Abendmahls ein neu Wort oder Tropus werden soll, so müssen auch zween Leibe Christi darzu kommen, die alle beide den Namen: mein Leib, mit Wahrheit führen, einer, der da bedeute, der andere, der bedeutet werde.

Also, dass ein jeglicher der beiden Leibe Christi wahrhaftig und recht ein Leib Christi heisse und sei wesentlich, er sei gleich hölzern, silbern oder brötern.

Kann nun Oecolampad beweisen, dass Brot sei wahrhaftig ein Leib Christi und mag sagen, es sei ein brötern Leib Christi, der da sei ein Gleichniss des natürlichen Leibes Christi, wie die hölzern Rose wahrhaftig eine Rose ist und ein Gleichniss der natürlichen Rose, so hat er damit so Viel ausgericht, dass seines Tropi Exempel mag funden werden, und sein Tropus sei dem gleich, so in gemeiner Rede gehet von Bildern, das ist St. Petrus, das ist St. Paulus u. s. w. Obs wohl noch nicht ein Tropus ist nach der Schrift Art.

Wo aber nicht, so ist sein Tropus auch ausser der Schrift nichts. Wie will er nun solches beibringen, dass Brot Christi Leib sei und heisse, oder dass Christus einen brötern Leib habe, wie St. Paulus einen hölzern St. Paulus hat.

Nun muss ers thun, oder ist Lurzsch; und wenn ers gleich fünde, was hilfts, so dennoch in der Schrift solcher Tropus nichts gülte?

Weil denn sein PART. III. CAP. XI. Tropus weder in der Schrift noch ausser der Schrift Exempel hat, ja wider der Schrift und aller Sprachen Art ist, so kann man ja wohl greifen, dass ein lauter unnütz Gedicht sei.“ (Ibid. p. 1137. sq. 1234—י 1242.)

Calovius: ,,Calvinianorum sententiam refellimus. . . 15.) singulorum verborum inductione ac sententia nativa. In nullo enim reperitur figura, aut si statuatur, non invenietur, ubi pes figatur, merusque erit μετεωρισμός. Ex adverso autem omnia verba clamant, proprium sensum retinendum esse. Nam si cum Carlstadio τον το δεικτικόν ad corpus Christi mensae assidens accommodare velis, reclamat Marcus, idem pronomen etiam ad sanguinem Christi accommodans: τούτο έστι το αιμά μου, ubi nulla ostensio visibilis sanguinis Christi assidentis locum habere potest. Ne dicam, quod λεπτολογία fingatur verbis Christi inesse, inepta ista verborum detorsione: edite, hic cernitis corpus meum, bibite, hic enim sedet sanguis meus. Ita, si cum Zwinglio tropum velis locare in copula est, non modo reclamat consensus evangelistarum, qui nil de esse significativo habent, sed et obstat Lucae locutio, qui verbum substantivum plane omittit, id vero quod non est, modificari nequit, multo minus propter id reliqua verba in alienam trahi debent sententiam. Ulterius: signis Oecolampadii, Zwinglio adversa fronte obloquentis, praesumat tueri sententiam et loco corporis in praedicato substituere figuram corporis, vel cum Johanne Calvino beneficia corporis Christi, reclamant Lucas et Paulus, asserentes illud ipsum corpus exhiberi, quod pro nobis in mortem est traditum, ut de ipsamet corporis substantia, urgente ipso Beza, intelligere necessario cogaris. Ita ergo consensus unanimis amanuensium Christi solidissime omnes tropos refutat, qui ad ista generalia capita reducuntur, quamvis caeteroquin innumeri sint. Hinc argumentor: Quae verba singula ita determinantur, ut omnibus tropis rimas obstruant, ea non tropice, sed literaliter intelligenda sunt, atqui essentialia coenae verba talia esse, jam evictum est. Ergo. 0״περ έόει δεϊξαι.“ (System. IX, 296.)

Gerhardus: ,,Saepius etiam hoc ab adversariis nobis objicitur, quod ipsimet a ρητω verborum discedamus, μ8ί sc. in hoc mysterio hisce propositionibus: in, cum et sub pane benedicto.datur corpus Christi, in, cum et sub vino benedicto datur sanguis Christi, unde propudiosum excogitarunt versum: ,In, cum, sub totum fallunt monosyllaba mundum/ . .

Besp. 1.: Concedatur nobis vera realis et substantialis corporis et sanguinis Christi in s. coena praesentia; concedatur, verba Christi /cara το ρητόν in genuino, nativo et proprio sensu accipienda esse, ac de usu harum particularum facile cum illis transigemus. 2. Praedicationes sacramentales: ,hoc est corpus meum‘, ,hoc est sanguis meus‘, sunt comprehensivae et exhibitivae, id est, duarum rerum distinctarum unionem et conjunctam exhibitionem notant, ut superius ostendimus, ideo non possunt commodius resolvi, quam per particulas: in, cum, sub, quibus unitorum conjunctio et conjuncta exhibitio exprimitur. Sicut haec exhibitiva propositio: accipe, hoc est vinum, non potest dexterius et commodius resolvi, quam eo modo: in vel cum hoc vase exhibetur vinum; quamcunque enim aliam proferas analysin, nugatoria erit et absurda; ita quoque praedicatio illa sacramentalis: hoc est corpus meum, commodissime resolvitur: .in, cum, sub hoc pane exhibeo corpus meum, quia ex instituto Christi panis eucharisticus est organum, όχημα et symbolum, cum quo et sub quo datur Christi corpus, . . Τώ ρητω

nihil derogat synonymia grammatica, paraphrasis oratoria, aequipollentia logica, interpretatio theologica, quae aliis eandem rem verbis effert, ut recte scribit D. Major in tractatu περί τψ 'ρητω tit. 3. c. I. th. 17. . .


### Of the Holy Supper: That the use of these particles denotes local inclusion is proven false by the…

That the use of these particles denotes local inclusion is proven false by the fact that in the mystery of the personal union of the two natures in Christ, the Holy Spirit uses the same ones, yet no one would say that the divine nature is locally included in the assumed flesh τω λόγω. What the Word is said to have become—flesh (John 1:14)—the Apostle expresses thus in 1 Timothy,

1 Tim. 3:16: "God was manifested in the flesh." That Christ is called true God in Rom. 9:5 is expressed in Col. 2:9 thus: "In Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily"; 2 Cor. 5:19: "God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself"; John 3:2; Acts 10:38: "God was with Him." Just as, on account of the personal union of the divine and human nature, it is rightly said: God is man and man is God, i.e., personally; so, on account of the sacramental union of the bread and the body of Christ, it is rightly said: the eucharistic bread is the body of Christ, i.e., sacramentally. Just as the personal union is explained by the particles *in* and *with*: "God is in Christ, God is with Christ," so the sacramental union can also be declared by the same. . . Whenever something invisible manifests itself or is even given in some external, visible, bodily symbol, these particles can be most conveniently employed. Thus, it is most correctly said that the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ in the bodily form of a dove (Matt. 3:16; Luke 3:21), was given to the apostles with a breath (John 20:22), and descended upon the apostles under the form of tongues of fire (Acts 2:1), where, however, no one dreams of a local inclusion of the Holy Spirit in the dove or the breath or the tongues of fire, but only a peculiar presence and the manifestation and bestowal of the invisible Holy Spirit through these external visible symbols is expressed; so also in the article concerning the Supper, the use of the particles *in*, *with*, *under* denotes nothing other than the sacramental union and participation." (L. c. § 96.)

Chemnitius: "Does this dogma not conflict with the articles of our faith: 'He ascended into heaven, from thence He shall come,' etc.? By no means. For while Christ indeed ascended into heaven visibly and locally with His body according to the true and natural mode or property of a body, just as in the same way He is to return from thence for judgment (Acts 1:9, 11; Matt. 24:30), the aforementioned articles do not assert that He does not know or have at hand another, heavenly and supernatural mode by which He can be present with His body and blood according to the words of institution in the Supper; rather, they teach and confirm the contrary. For the articles of our faith testify that Christ ascended into heaven with His body not in the way that little birds, having left the surface of the earth, sit upon the top of a tree, nor as Elijah was taken up into heaven, but in such a way that He sat down at the right hand of God the Father Almighty. Now, the right hand of God is not a circumscribed place or a peculiar seat or region in heaven by which Christ is held circumscribed and enclosed, but Scripture calls it the right hand of the majesty and power of God, which fills all things (Ps. 139:7 ff.), to which Christ has been exalted according to His human nature, 'far above all principality and power and might and dominion and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in that which is to come' (Eph. 1:20; 1 Pet. 3:22: 'who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, angels and authorities and powers having been made subject to Him'). So that even according to His human nature all things are subject to Him (Ps. 8:6; Eph. 1:22; Heb. 2:8; 1 Cor. 15:27; Matt. 28:18; John 13:3). Could He not, therefore, perform with His body and blood that which He spoke and ordained in His testament in express and clear words? Indeed, the aforementioned articles most strongly prove the true and essential presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Supper according to the words of His own testament. For although this itself is not possible according to the natural and essential properties of a true human body, yet because He affirms it—He who ascended into heaven with His body in such a way that He sat down at the right hand of the majesty and power of God the Father Almighty—it would be a horrible blasphemy either to say or to think that this is impossible and can in no way come to pass. And from this consideration it can be perceived of what flour the faction of the Sacramentarians is made." (Enchiridion 1600, p. 326 ff. Cf. the notes above from Kromayer’s *Theologia Positivo-Polemica*, P. III, c. 2, s. 1, p. 64 ff.)

Luther: "Thus, their second best piece is the saying in John 6:63: 'The flesh profiteth nothing,' which Oecolampadius boasts is his iron wall... Christ, as often as He speaks in the Scripture of His flesh or body, adds the little word 'my' and says: 'My flesh,' 'my body'; just as He says in the same chapter, John 6: 'My flesh is meat indeed.' Item: 'Whoso eateth of my flesh,' etc. Item: 'Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man,' etc... Thus, the iron wall is blown over with one little word, that is: 'mea,' my. For because it does not stand there: 'My flesh profiteth nothing,' but simply: 'Flesh profiteth nothing,' we have first of all gained this, that it cannot be understood of Christ's body. For because He does not add it Himself and say: 'My flesh,' it is forbidden to improve His words and add something; we are also certain and sure when we do not understand it of His flesh. Secondly, that they cannot prove with any letter that 'flesh' here means Christ's flesh." (That these words, etc., XX, 1027, 1028, 1030, sq.)

The same: "Secondly, besides these four powerful sayings, we have yet another, 1 Cor. 10:16, which reads thus: 'The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?' That is indeed, I think, a saying, indeed a thunder-axe upon Doctor Carlstadt's head and all his factions. The saying has also been the living medicine of my heart in my temptation concerning this Sacrament. And if we had no more sayings than this one, we could still sufficiently strengthen all consciences with it and mightily strike down all opponents. O, how D. Carlstadt feared this saying! And he began to build a great, strong vault over himself against this thunder-axe." (Against the Heavenly Prophets, A. 1525, XX, 313.)

The same: "We poor sinners are surely not so mad as to believe that Christ's body is in the bread in the coarse, visible manner as bread is in a basket or wine in a cup, as the enthusiasts would gladly like to impute to us, to tickle themselves with our folly; but we believe straightway that His body is there, as His words sound and point: 'This is my body,' etc. But that the Fathers and we sometimes speak thus: 'Christ's body is in the bread,' happens with the simple intention that our faith wishes to confess that Christ's body is there; otherwise, we can well tolerate it if one says: He is in the bread, He is the bread, He is where the bread is, or however one wishes. We do not want to quarrel over words, only that the meaning remains, that it is not mere bread that we eat in the Supper of Christ, but the body of Christ." (That these words, etc., XX, 1011, sq.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who abandon the literal sense (τό 'ρητόν) in the words of the Supper and wish the sacramental propositions—"This is my body," etc.—to be figurative and tropical. Beza and his associates in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, regarding Dogma I on the Lord’s Supper, state: "We judge that the words of the Lord’s institution cannot be accepted according to the literal sense (κατά τό 'ρητόν) while preserving the analogy of faith." P. Ramus writes in *De Religione Christiana*, book 4, chapter 14, that the whole mystery of the Supper is filled with tropes. They seek these tropes, however, by various paths: Calvin, along with Oecolampadius, places the trope in the predicate and takes "body" metonymically for a figure and symbol of the body. Walaeus also preferred to seek the seat of the trope in the predicate in *Loci Communes de Coena Domini*, p. 989, but Chamier himself shows the absurdity of this trope in *Panstratia Catholica*, book 10, *De Eucharistia*, chapter 4, no. 5, which see. Although Calvin, in his *Second Defense against Westphal*, took "body" to mean the virtue and efficacy of the body—for which he was rebuked (though without being named) by Beza in *Epistle 5 to Aleman*, vol. 3, p. 203—Carlstadt fosters the trope in the subject, and affirms that Christ, while handing the bread to the disciples, pointed with his finger to his own body and said: "This (which you see sitting at the table) is my body." To which class

Those belong here who, by the δεικτικόν, "this," understand only the bread, like the Marburg and Cassel Calvinists; as if Christ had said: "This, [which is] bread, is my body." Ulrich Zwingli seeks a trope and figure in the copula "is," and explains it by "signifies"; see Zwingli to Matthaeus Alber, fol. 155 sq., where he says: "We think the hinge of this matter turns on a very short syllable, namely, on this word 'is,' the significance of which is not always taken for 'to be,' but also for 'to signify.'" Zwingli is followed by Polanus, t. 2, Syntagm., p. 252, where he says: "The trope is not in the subject, nor in the predicate, but in the copula 'is'." Musculus in *Ll.*, p. 822 Beza in *Summa doctrinae de re sacram.*, q. 2 Danaeus in *Resp. ad Selnec.*, p. 199 Carolstadius in his book *De sacramentis*. Zanchius *De coena Dom.*, c. 4. Chamier, *Panstr.*, l. 10, *de euchar.*, c. 2. 11. 3 Thus also Bucanus, l. 48, q. 44, asks: "Must the word 'is' be taken ονσιωδώς, essentially, or νπαμκτικώς, substantially, and in its native signification? Resp.: By no means; but αημαντικως, significatively, representatively, figuratively," etc. Wendelinus, l. 1, *Christ. Theol.*, c. 23, to the objection: "Rhetoricians do not place a trope except in the subject or predicate, nor has anyone ever written that a trope can be fixed in the copula or the word 'is'?" responds: "And yet theologians, both ancient and recent, have very often said and written that the copula 'is' is sometimes taken improperly; these have greater authority among us than rhetoricians, whether pagan or Christian, who serve their own error." Likewise, to eat in those words of institution is to believe. Thus Zwingli to Matth. Alber, *l. c.*: "Thus, therefore, you will teach what Christ understands here by 'to eat,' namely, to believe." And Musculus, *l. c.*: "The word 'eating' in this case must be taken in a metaphorical sense, not a proper one; which no one, I suppose, will deny"; the same is taught by Beza, *l. c.* Keckerman, *Syst. Th.*, l. 3, c. 8, p. 444 sq., asserts clearly and confirms with appropriate arguments: "No word is transferred here from its own signification into a foreign one." *Ib.*, p. 443, he calls these propositions: "Bread is the body of Christ; wine is the blood of Christ," "relative" propositions; likewise "extrinsic and analogical" predications. Which he explains thus: Bread is the body of Christ, i.e., there is a supreme and sacred union between the bread and the body, namely, a union of signification and confirmation. See D. Menzer, *Exeges. A. C.*, p. 482 sq. "Finally, that trope of Keckerman (which Combachius repeats in *De eucharist.*, c. 2)," says D. Dannhawerus (*Hodomor. Spiritus Calvin.*, p. 3147), "is also absurd, in the whole proposition, yet in such a way that the individual words remain proper, i.e., the whole statement is tropical, the whole statement is proper—a monster of a kind never heard of in any rhetoric." 2 Of the Socinians, who with the Calvinists maintain: "The words of the Supper are not to be taken properly, as they sound, but are to be explained tropically." (*L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 1196 sq.*)

Quod particularum istarum usus localem inclusionem denotet, ex eo falsitatis convincitur, quod in mysterio unionis personalis duarum naturarum in Christo Spiritus S. eisdem utatur, nemo tamen dixerit, divinam naturam τφ λόγω in assumta carne localiter inclusam. 3, 16.: ,Deus manifestatus est in carne.‘ Quod Christus dicitur verus Deus Rom. 9, 5., id Col. 2, 9. sic effertur: ,In ipso habitat tota plenitudo deitatis corporaliter‘, 2 Cor. 5, 19.: ,Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi ipsi‘; Joh. 3, 2. Actor. 10, 38.: ,Deus erat cum illo.‘ Quemadmodum propter unionem personalem divinae et humanae naturae recte dicitur: Deus est homo et homo est Deus, sc. personaliter, ita propter unionem sacramentalem panis et corporis Christi recte dicitur: panis euchar. est corpus Christi, sc. sacramentaliter. Quemadmodumuniopemmabs exponitur per particulas in et cum: ,Deus est mChristo, Deus est cum Christo‘, ita per easdem etiam unio sacramentalis declarari potest. . . Quandocunque invisibile quid in externo quodam symbolo corporeo visibili sese manifestat vel etiam datur, commodissime hae particulae adhiberi possunt. Sic Spiritus S. in corporali specie columbae super Christum descendisse Matth. 3, 16. Luc. 3, 21., cum flatu apostolis datus Joh. 20, 33., sub specie linguarum ignearum in apostolos descendisse Actor. 2, 1. rectissime dicitur, ubi tamen nemo somniat localem inclusionem Spiritus S. in columbam vel flatum vel linguas igneas, sed peculiaris tantummodo praesentia et per haec externa visibilia symbola invisibilis Spiritus S. manifestatio et collatio tantummodo exprimitur, ita quoque in articulo de coena usus particularum in, cum, sub nihil aliud, quam sacramentalem unionem et participationem denotat.“ (L. c. § 96.)

Chemnitius: ,,Nonne hoc dogma pugnat cum articulis fidei nostrae: ascendit ad coelos, inde venturus est etc.? Minime. Nam Christus quidem corpore suo secundum verum et naturalem corporis modum seu proprietatem visibiliter et localiter ascendit ad coelos, sicut eodem etiam modo inde rediturus est ad judicium, Act. 1, 9.11. Matth. 24, 30. Quod vero alium, coelestem et supernaturalem modum non norit aut in promptu habeat, quo juxta verba institutionis in coena corpore et sanguine suo adesse possit, hoc ipsum praedicti articuli non asserunt, sed contrarium potius docent et confirmant. Testantur enim articuli fidei nostrae, Christum corpore suo ad coelos ascendisse non eo modo, sicut aviculae, relicta superficie terrae, summa super arbore sidunt, neque sicut Elias 111 coelum assumptus est, sed ita ut consederit ad dexteram Dei Patris omnipotentis. Dextera autem Dei non est locus circumscriptus vel peculiaris sedes seu regio in coelo, qua Christus circumscriptus et conclusus teneatur, sed Scriptura vocat eam dexteram majestatis et virtutis Dei, quae implet omnia (Ps. 139, 7. et sqq.), ad quam Christus secundum humanam naturam exaltatus est, ,super omnem principatum, potestatem, dominationem et omne nomen, quod nominatur, non solum in hoc saeculo, sed etiam 111 futuro‘, Ephes. 1, 20. lPet.3,ult.: ,qui est ad dexteram Dei profectus in coelum, subjectis sibi angelis et potestatibus ac virtutibus.‘ Ita ut ipsi etiam secundum humanam naturam omnia sint subjecta, Ps. 8, 7. Ephes. 1, 22. Ebr. 2, 8. 1 Cor. 15, 27. Matth. 28, 18. Joh. 13, 3. Num igitur non posset corpore et sanguine suo hoc praestare, quod in testamento suo verbis expressis et perspicuis elocutus est et ordinavit? Imo praedicti articuli maxime comprobant veram et essentialem praesentiam corporis et sanguinis Christi in coena juxta verba testamenti ipsius. Licet enim hoc ipsum juxta naturales et essentiales veri corporis humani proprietates possibile non sit; quia tamen ille affirmat, qui corpore suo in coelum ascendit, ita ut consederit ad dexteram majestatis et virtutis Dei Patris omnipotentis, horrenda esset blasphemia, vel dicere, vel cogitare, impossibile idipsum esse et fieri nullo modo posse. Atque ex hac consideratione animadverti potest, cujus farinae sit factio sacramentariorum.“ (Enchiridion 1600. p. 326. sqq. Cf. supra annotata ex Kromayeri th. posit.-pol. P. III. c. 2. s. 1. p. 64. sq.)

Lutherus: ,,So ist nun ihr ander bestes Stück der Spruch Joh. 6, 63.: ,Fleisch ist kein nütze‘, welchen Oecolampad rühmet, er sei seine eiserne Mauer. . . Christus, so oft er in der Schrift von seinem PART. III. CAP. XI. Fleisch oder Leib redet, thut er das Wörtlein,mein4 hinzu und spricht': ,Mein Fleisch, ,mein Leib4; wie er in demselbigen Capitel, Joh. 6.,, spricht: ,Mein Fleisch ist die rechte Speise.4 Item: ,Wer meines Fleisches isset4 u. s. w. Item: ,Wo ihr nicht esset vom Fleisch des Menschensohnes4 u. s. w. . . Also liegt die eiserne Mauer mit einem Wortlein umgeblasen, das heisst: ,mea4, mein. Denn weil da nicht stehet: Mein Fleisch nützet nicht, sondern schlechthin: Fleisch nützet nicht,, haben wir erstlich also gewonnen, dass nicht mag von Christi Leib verstanden werden. Denn weil ers nicht selbst hinzusetzt und spricht: Mein Fleisch, so ists verboten, seine Worte zu bessern und etwas hinzuthun, sind auch gewiss und sicher, wenn wirs nicht von seinem Fleisch verstehen. Zum andern also, dass sie nicht mögen beweisen mit einigem Buchstaben, dass Fleisch hier Christi Fleisch heisse.44 (Dass diese Worte u. s. w. XX, 1027. 1028. 1030. sq.)

Idem: ,,Aufs andere haben wir über diese vier gewaltige Sprüche· noch einen andern, 1 Cor. 10, 16., der lautet also: ,Der Kelch der Benedeiung, welchen wir benedeien, ist der nicht die Gemeinschaft des. Blutes Christi? Das Brot, das wir brechen, ist das nicht die Gemeinschaft des Leibes Christi?' Das ist ja, meine ich, ein Spruch, ja eine Donneraxt auf Doctor Carlstadts Kopf und aller seiner Rotten. DerSpruch ist auch die lebendige Arznei gewesen meines Herzens in meiner Anfechtung über diesem Sacrament. Und wenn wir keine Sprüche mehr hätten denn diesen, könnten wir doch damit alle Gewissen genugsam stärken und alle Widerfechter mächtiglich genugsam schlagen. O, wie hat D. Carlstadt den Spruch gefurcht! und fing an, ein gross. stark Gewölb über sich zu bauen wider diese Donneraxt. (Wider die himmlischen Proph. A. 1525. XX, 313.)

Idem: ,,Wir armen Sünder sind ja nicht so toll, dass wir gläuben,.
