Christi Leib sei im Brot, auf die grobe sichtbarliche Weise, wie Brot im Korbe oder Wein im Becher, ,wie uns die Schwärmer gerne wollten auf legen, sich mit unsrer Thorheit zu kützeln; sondern wir gläuben stracks, dass sein Leib da sei, wie seine Worte drauf lauten und deuten: ,Das ist mein Leib4 u. s. w. Dass aber die Väter und wir zuweilen sa reden: Christi Leib ist im Brot, geschieht einfältiger Meinung darum, dass unser Glaube will bekennen, dass Christus Leib da sei; sonst mogen wir wohl leiden, man sage: er sei im Brot, er sei das Brot, er sei, da das Brot ist, oder wie man will. Ueber Worten wollen wir nicht zanken, allein dass der Sinn da bleibe, dass nicht schlecht Brot sei, das. wir im Abendmahl Christi essen, sondern der Leib Christi.44 (Dass diese Worte u. s. w. XX, 1011. sq.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Calvinianorum, qui τό 'ρητόν in verbis coenae relinquunt et propositiones sacramentales: hoc est corpus meum etc., figuratas et tropicas esse volunt. Beza et socii in Colloq. Mompelg. ad dogma I. de coena Domini inquiunt: ,Existimamus, verba institutionis Domini κατά τό 'ρητόν accipi salva fidei analogia non posse.' Totum coenae mysterium tropis esse refertum, scribit P. Ramus 1. 4. de relig. christ. c. 14. Tropos vero diversis viis quaerunt: Calvinus cum Oecolampadio tropum in praedicato constituit et corpus metonymice pro figura et symbolo corporis accipit. In praedicato etiam sedem tropi quaerere maluit Walaeus in L. Comm. de coena Dom. p. 989., sed absurditatem hujus tropi ostendit ipse Chamier. Panstr. cathol. 1.10. de euchar. c. 4. n. 5., quem vide. Quanquam Calvinus defens. 2. c. Westphal. corpus acceperit pro virtute et efficacia corporis, eo nomine reprehensus (at sine nomine) a Beza Ep. 5. ad Aleman. V. 3. p. 203, Carolstadius in subjecto tropum fovet, Christumque panem discipulis porrigendo corpus suum digito designasse et dixisse: Hoc (quod in mensa assidere cernitis) est corpus meum, affirmat. Ad quam classem

pertinent illi, qui per δεικτικόν, hoc, intelligunt solum panem, ut Calviniani Marpurgenses et Cassellani; quasi dixerit Christus: Hoc, panis, est corpus meum. Ulricus Zwinglius tropum et figuram quaerit in copula,est‘, eamqueper significat exponit; vide Zwinglium ad Matthaeum Alberum f. 155. sq., ubi ait: ,Nos cardinem hujus rei in brevissima syllaba versari arbitramur, vid. in hoc verbo est, cujus significantia non perpetuo pro esse accipitur, sed etiam significare.‘ Zwinglium sequuntur Polanus t. 2. Syntagm. p. 252., ubi inquit: ,Tropus non est in subjecto, neque in praedicato, sed in copula est.‘ Musculus in Ll. p. 822 Beza in summa doctrinae de re sacram, q. 2 Danaeus in resp. ad Selnec. p. 199 Carolstadius in lib. de sacramentis. Zanchius de coena Dom. c. 4. Chamier. Panstr. 1.10. de euchar. c. 2.11. 3 Sic et Bucanus L. 48. q. 44. quaerit: ,anne verbum est ονσιωδώς, essentialiter, seu νπαμκτικώς, substantialiter, et nativa sua significatione accipiendum est? Resp.: Nequam; sed αημαντικως, significative, repraesentative, flgurative‘, etc. Wendelinus 1.1. Christ. Theol. c. 23. ad objectionem: ,Rhetores non collocant tropum, nisi in subjecto vel praedicato, neque quispiam unquam scripsit, tropum posse figi in copula seu verbo est?‘ resp.: ,Atqui theologi, cum veteres, tum recentes, improprie quandoque copulam est accipi, saepissime dixerunt et scripserunt; horum major apud nos auctoritas est, quam rhetorum sive gentilium, sive Christianorum, errori suo servientium.‘ Item rb edere 111 verbis institutionis illis est credere. Sic Zwinglius ad Matth. Alberum 1. c.: ,Sic ergo docebis, quid hic Christus per edere intelligat, nempe credere.‘ Et Musculus 1. c., ,verbum manducandi in hac causa accipiendum est sensu metaphorico, non proprio; quod nemo, opinor, negabit‘; idem docet Beza 1. c. Keckerman. Syst. Th. 1. 3. c. 8. p. 444. sq. diserte asserit et appositis argumentis confirmat: ,Non transferri liic ullam vocem de sua significatione in alienam.‘ Ib. p. 443. propositiones has: ,Panis est corpus Christi; vinum est sanguis Christi‘, vocat propositioues,relativas‘; item,extrinsecas et analogicas‘ praedicationes. Quas sic explicat: Panis est corpus Christi, i. e., summa est et sacra unio inter panem et corpus, nempe unio significationis et confirmationis. Vide D. Menzeri Exeges. A. C. p. 482. sq. ,Absurdus denique etiam ille Keckermanni (quem repetit Combachius de eucharist. c. 2.) tropus‘ (inquit D. Dannhawerus Hodomor. Spiritus Calvin, p. 3147.),in tota propositione, ita tamen, ut singula verba maneant propria, totum sc. enunciatum est tropicum, totum enunciati proprium, cujusmodi monstrum in nulla unquam rhetorica auditum est.‘ 2. Socinianorum, cum Calviniaiiis statuentium: ,Verba coenae non esse proprie, ut sonant, accipienda, sed tropice exponenda.‘ “ (L. c. s. 2. q. 1. f. 1196. sq.)


### Of the Holy Supper: Kahnisius: "The Lutheran Church has on its side the irrefutable principle of…

Kahnisius: "The Lutheran Church has on its side the irrefutable principle of hermeneutics that literal interpretation has the first right, which comes into consideration especially in the case of words of such great importance (which were revealed to the Apostle Paul especially by the Lord, 1 Cor. 11:25; see my *Lehre v. Abendm.*, p. 14 ff.), if it maintains the literal understanding wherever at all possible. But this is only possible if, in the sentence: 'This is my body (my blood),' the subject is not = bread (wine). Where it is a matter of determining a subject, the context decides on the one hand, and the predicate on the other. The context demands bread (wine) as the subject, the predicate demands body (blood). And so the interpretation found itself directed to an interpenetration of bread (wine) and body (blood), from which the predicate extracts the main substance. Thus the physician says, while giving an essence in water: 'This is life-essence.' The 'this' is here essence and water, the predicate the main substance. When Christ says: 'My words are spirit and life,' he extracts from the subject 'word,' which is partly spirit and partly letter, the essential substance. This mode of speech, designated by Luther as synecdoche, is in itself permissible. The question can only be whether it is permissible here. One according to the principle *dies diem docet* [one day teaches another]." PART III. CHAP. XI.

upon renewed consideration, the difficulties of this assumption have emerged to an increasing degree. According to the context, the "this" is that which Jesus took, broke, and gave to eat, i.e., the bread. In the case of the cup, however, the subject is explicitly designated as τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον. Now, the cup (beaker) stands, according to the well-known metonymy *continens pro contento* (the container for the thing contained), for that which it contains. But that which the cup contains is the wine. Christ does not say: That which you are now eating is my body, that which you are now drinking is my blood, but rather: that which I give you to eat, to drink: thus, even before the consumption.

The ποτήριον is the drink as it was in the cup, even before the disciples drank. Yet, according to Lutheran doctrine, bread and wine are not the body and blood of Christ before consumption.

That the ποτήριον is to be taken as the as-yet-undrunk wine that was in the cup is stated by the interpretation of Paul in 1 Cor. 10:16: Τὸ ποτήριον τῆς εὐλογίας, ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν, οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐστίν; τὸν ἄρτον ὃν κλῶμεν, οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐστίν; — in which, without doubt, the bread as that which is broken for eating, and the cup as that which is blessed for drinking, is called the communion, i.e., that which puts us into communion with the body and blood of Christ (Abendm. p. 127 ff.): thus, even before the consumption.

But if bread (wine) is the subject, then the literal interpretation must be abandoned. The sentence "This cup is the new covenant in my blood" already compels this; since a cup of wine cannot possibly be the covenant relationship between Godhead and humanity itself, which was established by Christ in his death, it can only be interpreted as: this cup is a sign of the new covenant in my blood.

The assumption that body (blood) stands metonymically for a sign of the body (blood) (Oecolampadius, Calvin) is inadmissible, since such a metonymy cannot be proven (Abendm. p. 48 ff.). The sentence is, like countless others, a trope in which the predicate stands figuratively. Thus, one says of a statue: This is Blücher, and of a snake biting its own tail: This is eternity.

However, the obviously symbolic nature of the entire action justifies the assumption of a symbol. The bread which is broken is the body which is broken (κλώμενον) for us; the wine which is poured out from a larger vessel into the cup is the blood which is poured out (ἐκχυνόμενον) for us. That the breaking of the bread has a special significance is proven by the designation of the bread as the bread which we break (1 Cor. 10:16), parallel to the cup which we bless.

Thus, in baptism, the immersion under water is also a symbolic act (p. 615). If it were the glorified body which Jesus offered in the bread at the institution, then a communication of the same could somehow be conceived, even if always in a mysterious and obscure way. But the one who was to be put to death, who stood before the disciples, could not be the object of consumption. Up to this point reaches the validity of Zwingli’s interpretation." (Die luth. Dogm. 1861. I, 617. sqq.) §

9. The form of the Supper consists in the words of institution. Or the formal reason, through which the action, by which the symbols of bread and wine are dispensed to and received by the communicants, formally possesses that which is the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ. Namely, that the dispensation of the symbols is a sacramental dispensation of the body and blood of Christ, it has this from the fact that it is performed according to the institution of Christ and is joined with the word of institution. And

that the eating of the bread and the drinking of the wine is formally the sacramental eating of the body and drinking of the blood of Christ, it has from the fact that it is the eating and drinking of symbols, performed according to the institution of Christ and joined with the word of institution. Nor does it stand in the way that the word of institution behaves itself on the part of the efficient cause. For just as elsewhere in accidental things and beings by aggregation, so also here it can happen and does happen that the thing (the action of the sacred supper) is constituted in its specific being and receives its formal reason from that (the word of institution), which in its own way also pertains to the efficient cause.

Luther: "Likewise I also speak and confess concerning the Sacrament of the Altar, that therein the body and blood are truly eaten and drunk orally in the bread and wine, even though the priests who distribute it, or those who receive it, do not believe or otherwise misuse it. For it does not stand upon human faith or unbelief, but upon God’s Word and ordinance. Unless it be that they first change God’s Word and ordinance and interpret them differently, as the present-day enemies of the Sacrament do, who indeed have mere bread and wine; for they do not have the words and the instituted ordinance of God, but have perverted and changed the same according to their own conceit." (Confession concerning the Lord's Supper. A. 1528. XX, 1381.) §

10. The end to which,a or the subjectb to be admitted to the participation of the sacred supper, are Christian men,c who are able to examine themselves.d a For whose benefit this sacrament was instituted by its author. b Or, to whom this sacrament, as a means of grace, ought to be applied. Some call it the object, understanding the personal object, which is the correlate of the person administering the sacred supper. c Those professing the faith or the Christian religion and endowed with the sacrament of initiation, or baptized. d See 1 Cor. 11:28.

Moreover, to examine oneself here means to examine oneself according to those things which ought to be absent or present in a man who is to use the sacred supper rightly and profitably, so that sins, which are opposed to the salutary use of the sacrament, may be retracted through repentance, and on the contrary, faith may exert itself in a contrite heart and be carried toward the body and blood of Christ, as present, and as the cause of the remission of sins. §

11. To alla those who are admitted to the communion of the sacred supper, bothb of the blessed symbols must altogetherc be given. a No difference is to be admitted between clergy and laity; just as it must be confessed that this sacrament, as a means of grace, is destined for the faithful, as such, without difference of ecclesiastical and secular status and in PART III. CHAP. XI.

in the first administration the apostles themselves were regarded not as apostles or ministers of the church, but as Christians and believers. See the blessed Musaeus, *On Communion under Both Kinds*, second dissertation, § 15 et seqq.

Not only bread, but also wine, is consecrated, and that not for the ablution of the bread or host, but as the other part of the sacrament.

They are commonly called "both kinds," not as if only external species or bare accidents of the symbols were present without the substance itself, or in a foreign substance, but because the symbols of bread and wine themselves differ from one another in species. See the blessed Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, first dissertation, § 2.

Namely, because of the institution of Christ, which by its own nature implies a precept concerning the specification of the act; nor does it leave to the church such liberty that it is permitted to administer this sacrament in this way or another. See the blessed Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, first dissertation, § 3 et seqq.

Gerhard: "Communion under one kind was decreed first in the Council of Constance, sess. 13, A.D. 1415, and confirmed in the Council of Trent, sess. 21, 22, A.D. 1562. The decree of the Council of Constance states: 'The general council declares, decrees, and defines, against this error (concerning the communion of the laity under both kinds), that although Christ after supper instituted and administered to His disciples this venerable sacrament under both kinds of bread and wine; yet, notwithstanding this, the authority of the sacred canons and the approved custom of the church has preserved and preserves that... in the primitive church such a sacrament was received by the faithful under both kinds, and [that it] be received by the laity only under the species of bread, since it must be most firmly believed and in no way doubted that the entire body and blood of Christ are truly contained as much under the species of bread as under the species of wine.'" (*Loc. cit.*, § 48.)

Luther adds: "The praiseworthy city has a fine name: 'Constantia,' which means constancy or a firm, manly spirit, hence they call it the Council of Constance (*Constantiense concilium*). But I, Dr. Martin, baptize it by its true name, which they have given themselves herein: the Council of Obstancy (*obstantiense concilium*); for *obstantia* means resistance. For here they have not only acted in deed against Christ and His Church, but they boast of it and confirm that Christ may well ordain what He wills; but the lords of the Council of Obstancy wish to ordain against it and pay no heed to Him, nor to His Church either. *Non obstante Christo et ecclesia* (notwithstanding Christ and the Church), they say openly; Christ together with His Church shall not stand in our way; we are indeed a higher and different Christ and Church than those are." (*Several Sayings against the Council of Constance*, A.D. 1535, XIX, 1699.)

Latin:

Kahnisius: ,,Die lutherische Kirche hat den unumstösslichen Grundsatz der Hermeneutik, dass die wörtliche Auslegung das erste Recht hat, welche bei Worten von so grösser Bedeutung (die dem Apostel Paulus besonders vom Herrn offenbart wurden 1 Cor. 11, 25. m. Lehre v. Abendm. S. 14 ff.) besonders in Betracht kommt, für sich, wenn sie, wo irgend möglich, das wörtliche Verständniss aufrecht hält. Dies ist aber nur möglich, wenn in dem Satze: Dies ist mein Leib (mein Blut), das Subject nicht = Brot (Wein) ist. Wo es sich um die Bestimmung eines Subjectes handelt, entscheidet einerseits der Zusammenhang, anderseits das Prädicat. Der Zusammenhang fordert als Subject Brot (Wein), das Prädicat Leib (Blut). Und so fand sich denn die Auslegung an ein Ineinander von Brot (Wein) und Leib (Blut) gewiesen, aus welchem das Prädicat die Hauptsubstanz herauszieht. So sagt der Arzt, indem er in Wasser eine Essenz gibt: Dies ist Lebensessenz. Das,dies‘ ist hier Essenz und Wasser, das Prädicat die HauptSubstanz. Wenn Christus sagt: Meine Worte sind Geist und Leben, zieht er aus dem Subjecte Wort, welches theils Geist, theils Buchstabe ist, die wesenhafte Substanz heraus. Diese von Luther als Synecdoche bezeichnete Redeweise ist an sich zulässig. Die Erage kann nur sein, ob sie hier zulässig ist. Einer nach dem Grundsatz dies diem docet PART. HI. CAP. XI.

erneuten Betrachtung haben sich die Schwierigkeiten dieser Annahme in steigendem Grade herausgestellt. Nach dem Zusammenhänge ist das,dies‘ das, was Jesus nahm, brach, zum Essen gab, d. h. das Brot. Beim Kelche aber wird als das Subject ausdrücklich τοντο το ποτήριον bezeichnet. Nun steht der Kelch (Becher) nach der bekannten Metonymie continens pro contento für das, was er enthält. Das aber, was der Becher enthält, ist der Wein. Christus sagt nicht: Das, was ihr jetzt esset, ist mein Leib, das, was ihr jetzt trinket, mein Blut, sondern das, was ich euch zu essen, zu trinken gebe: also noch vor dem Genüsse.

Das ποτήριον ist der Trank, wie er in dem Becher war, noch ehe die Jünger tranken. Vor dem Genüsse aber ist doch auch nach lutherischer Lehre Brot und Wein nicht Leib und Blut Christi.

Dass ποτήριον aber als der noch ungetrunkene Wein, der im Becher war, zu nehmen ist, besagt die Auslegung des Paulus 1 Cor. 10, 16.: Το ποτήριον τής ευλογίας, δ εί>λ0}0νμεν1 ονχι κοινωνία τον αίματος τον Χρίστον εστίν; τον άρτον ον κλώμεν ονχι κοινωνία του σώματος τον Χρίστον εστίν; — in welcher ohne Zweifel das Brot als das zum Essen gebrochene, der Kelch als der zum Trinken gesegnete die Gemeinschaft, d. h., was uns in Gemeinschaft setzt mit Leib und Blut Christi (Aben,dm. S. 127 ff.), heisst: also noch vor dem Genüsse.

Ist aber Brot (Wein) das Subject, so ist die eigentliehe Fassung aufzugeben. Dazu nöthigt schon der Satz: Dieser Kelch ist der neue Bund in meinem Blute, der, da ein Becher Weines unmöglieh das von Christo in seinem Tode gestiftete Bundesverhältniss zwischen Gottheit und Menschheit selbst sein kann, doch nur ausgelegt werden kann: dieser Kelch ist ein Zeichen des neuen Bundes in meinem Blute.

Die Annahme, dass Leib (Blut) für Zeichen des Leibes (Blutes) metonymisch stehe (Oecolampadius, Calvin), ist, da eine solche Metonymie sich nicht nachweisen lässt (Abendm. S. 48 ff.), unstatthaft. Der Satz ist, wie unzählige, ein Tropus, in welchem das Prädicaf; uneigentlich steht. So sagt man von einer Statue: Dies ist Blücher, und von einer in den Schwanz sich beissenden Schlange: Dies ist die Ewigkeit.

Zur Annahme eines Symbols aber berechtigt das offenbar Symbolische der ganzen Handlung. Das Brot, welches gebrochen wird, ist der Leib, welcher für uns gebrochen (κλώμενον) wird; der Wein, welcher aus einem grössern Gefässe in den Becher ausgegossen ist, ist das Blut, welches für uns vergossen wird (εκχννόμενον). Dass das Brechen des Brotes eine besondere Bedeutung hat, beweist die Bezeichnung des Brotes als des Brotes, welches wir brechen (1 Cor. 10, 16.), parallel dem Kelche, welchen wir segnen.

So ist ja auch in der Taufe das Untertauchen unter das Wasser ein symbolischer Act (S. 615). Wäre es der verklärte Leib, welchen Jesus bei der Einsetzung im Brote böte, so Hesse sich irgendwie, wenn auch immer in geheimnissvoller und dunkler Weise, eine Mittheilung desselben denken. Der zu Tödtende aber, welcher vor den Jüngern stand, konnte nicht Gegenstand des Genusses sein. Bis hieher reicht das Recht der Auslegung Zwinglis.“ (Die luth. Dogm. 1861. I, 617. sqq.) §

9. Forma a coenae consistit in verbis b institutionis. Sive ratio formalis, per quam actio, qua symbola panis et vini communicantibus dispensantur et accipiuntur, formaliter habet, quod est sacramentum corporis et sanguinis Christi. Nempe, quod dispensatio symbolorum est sacramentalis dispensatio corporis et sanguinis Christi, hoc inde habet, quod juxta institutionem Christi peragitur et cum verbo institutionis est conjuncta. Et

quod manducatio panis et bibitio vini formaliter est sacramentalis manducatio corporis et bibitio sanguinis Christi, hoc inde habet, quod est symbolorum manducatio et bibitio, juxta institutionem Christi peracta et cum verbo institutionis conjuncta. Neque obstat, quod verbum institutionis ex parte causae efficientis sese habet. Sicut enim alias in accidentalibus et entibus per aggregationem, ita et hic fieri potest et fit, us res (actio s. coenae) in esse suo specifico constituatur et rationem formalem accipiat ab eo (a verbo institutionis), quod suo modo etiam ad causam efficientem pertinet.

Lutherus: ,,Ebenso rede ich auch und bekenne das Sacrament des Altars, dass daselbst wahrhaftig der Leib und Blut im Brot und Wein werde mündlich gegessen und getrunken, obgleich die Priester, so es reichen, oder die, so es empfahen, nicht gläubeten oder sonst missbrauchten. Denn es stehet nicht auf Menschen Glauben oder Unglauben, sondern auf Gottes Wort und Ordnung. Es wäre denn, dass sie zuvor Gottes Wort und Ordnung andern und anders deuten, wie die jetzigen SacramentsFeinde thun, welche freilich eitel Brot und Wein haben; denn sie haben auch die Wort und eingesetzte Ordnung Gottes nicht, sondern dieselbigen nach ihrem eigenen Dünkel verkehret und verandert.“ (Bek. vom Abendmahl. A. 1528. XX, 1381.) §

10. Finis cui,a sive subjectum, b ad participationem sacrae coenae admittendum, sunt homines christiani,c qui se probare possunt.d Quorum bono institutum est ab auctore suo hoc sacramentum. Seu, cui sacramentum hoc, tanquam medium gratiae, applicari debet. Quidam objectum vocant, intelligentes personale, quod est correlatum personae administrantis s. coenam. Fidem seu religionem christianam profitentes et sacramento initiationis donati, seu baptizati. Vid. 1 Cor. 11, 28.

Est autem probare se h. 1. examinare se ipsum, juxta ea, quae in homine sacra coena recte et utilitel· usuro abesse aut adesse debent, ita ut peccata, quae salutari sacramenti usui adversantur, per poenitentiam retractentur, contra autem fides in corde contrito sese exserat et in corpus Christi ac sanguinem, ut praesentia, et causam remissionis peccatorum feratur. §

11. Omnibus a illis, qui ad communionem s. coenae admittuntur, symbolum benedictum utrumque b dari omnino c debet. Nulla differentia inter clericos et laicos admittenda; prout fatendum est, sacramentum hoc, tanquam medium gratiae, fidelibus, ut talibus, citra differentiam status ecclesiastici ac saecularis destinatum et in PART. III. CAP. XI.

prima administratione apostolos ipsos, non ut apostolos aut ministros eccle~ siae, sed ut christianos ac fideles spectatos fuisse. Vid. b. Musaei de Comm. sub utraque Disp, poster. § 15. sqq.

Non solum panis, sed etiam praeterea vinum consecratum, idque non ad ablutionem panis sive hostiae, sed tanquam ut altera pars sacramenti.

Vulgo utramque speciem appellant, non quasi externa tantum species, aut nuda accidentia symbolorum, sine substantia ipsa, aut in aliena substantia, adsint, sed quod symbola ipsa panis et vini inter se specie differant. Vid. b. Mus. 1. c. Disp, prior. § 2.

Scilicet propter institutionem Christi, quae sua natura importat praeceptum de specificatione actus; neque relinquit ecclesiae eam libertatem, ut sic vel aliter administrare hoc sacramentum liceat. Vid. b. Mus. Disp. cit. prior. § 3. et seqq.

Gerhardus: ,,Communio sub una specie decreta est primum in concil. Constant, sess. 13. A. 1415. et confirmata in concil. Trid. sess. 21. 22. A. 1562. Decretum concilii Constantiensis sic habet: ,Generale concilium declarat, decernit et definit, contra hunc errorem (de communione laicorum sub utraque specie), quod licet Christus post coenam instituerit et suis discipulis administrarit sub utraque specie panis et vini hoc venerabile sacramentum; tamen hoc non obstante, sacrorum canonum auctoritas et approbata consuetudo ecclesiae servavit et servat, quod ... in primitiva ecclesia hujusmodi sacramentum reciperetur a fidelibus sub utraque specie et a laicis tantummodo sub specie panis suscipiatur, cum firmissime credendum sit et nullatenus dubitandum, integfum Christi corpus et sanguinem, tam sub specie panis, quam sub specie vini veraciter contineri.‘“ (L. c. §48.)

Lutherus addit: ,,Die löbliche Stadt hat einen feinen Namen: ,Constantia‘, das heisst Bestand oder fest männlich Gemüthe, daher sie es nennen Constantiense concilium. Aber ich, Dr. Martinus, täufe sie nach ihrem rechten Namen, den sie ihnen selber hierinnen gegeben, obstantiense concilium; obstantia aber heisst Widerstand. Denn hie haben sie nicht allein mit der That wider Christum und seine Kirche gehandelt, sondern rühmen sich dazu und bestätigen, dass Christus wohl möge setzen, was er will; aber die Herren obstantiensis concilii wollen dawider setzen und ihn nicht ansehen, noch seine Kirche dazu. Non obstante Christo et ecclesia, sagen sie frei heraus; Christus sammt seiner Kirchen soll uns nicht widerstehen, wir sind wohl ein höher und ander Christus und Kirche, denn jene sind.“ (Etliche Sprüche wider das Concilium zu Constanz. A. 1535. XIX, 1699.)


### Of the Holy Supper: ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: The Council of Constance, sess. 13, decreed the communion under one kind with the denunciation of anathema and under the necessity of law... Finally, the Council of Trent, sess. 21, held on the 16th day of July in the year 1562, in chapter 1, declared and taught: 'By no divine precept are the laity and non-consecrating clerics obligated to receive the sacrament of the Eucharist under both kinds, nor can it be doubted in any way, while faith is preserved, that communion under one kind is sufficient for them for salvation. If anyone shall say that by the precept of God or by necessity of salvation all and every one of the faithful of Christ ought to receive both kinds of the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist, let him be anathema.' ... But in order that the Romanists may deceive the unlearned common people with some image of the Lord's cup, the sacrificing priests offer them wine for rinsing the mouth; that is, after the sacred bread has been taken, they present a cup to the communicating laity and non-consecrating clerics, but one which contains simple and unconsecrated wine, as Alphonsus Tostatus testifies." (*Loc. cit.*, s. 2, q. 7, f. 1254 et seq.)

§ 12.

The end of this sacrament, which is also its fruit or effect, and which is intermediate, is (1.) the remembrance and commemoration of the death of Christ, which is performed by faith; (2.) the sealing of the promise concerning the remission of sins, and the confirmation of our faith; (3.) our ingrafting into Christ and spiritual nourishment unto life; (4.) the mutual love of the communicants, and many similar things. The ultimate end is the eternal salvation of the communicants. For the sake of attaining which this sacrament is instituted and to be celebrated.

Indeed, the sacraments are efficacious means in relation to their end; which we shall also show here specifically regarding the Sacred Supper. Thus Christ Himself says in Luke, chapter 22, 19: "Do this εις την εμην ανάμνησιν." Paul, repeating this in 1 Cor. 11, 24. 25, adds in v. 26: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death till He comes." Now this sacrament, in which Christ Himself really exhibits His body and blood to us, certainly has a huge power to move souls to the remembrance of Him who has performed and continues to perform such great things for us.

Luther: "I hope it is not necessary to teach at length here what is meant by 'Christ's remembrance,' of which we have often and much taught elsewhere, namely, that it is not the contemplation of the suffering, with which some, as if with a good work, want to have served God and obtained grace, going about with mourning for the bitter suffering of Christ, etc. But this is Christ's remembrance: when one teaches and believes the power and fruit of His suffering. Thus, that our works and merits are nothing, the free will is dead and lost, but that we become free from sins and pious solely through the suffering and death of Christ, that it is a teaching or remembrance of the grace of God in Christ and not a work done by us toward God." (How one should prepare oneself for the Lord's Supper, A. 1530. X, 2689.) Gerhard: "Christ does not say: 'Do this in remembrance of my pains and torments endured for you,' but εις την εμην, i. e., την εμην ανάμνησιν, in remembrance of Me, i. e., in grateful and faithful memory of My immense love, out of which I have suffered and died for you, by which I was also prepared to suffer more for you, if this My passion and death had not been a sufficient price for your sins." (Harmon. ev. cap. 171. f. 788.)

Indeed, that we may weigh and believe that Jesus Christ, θεάνθρωπος, our King and Priest, Himself offered His body to God the Father as a victim for us on the altar of the cross and shed His blood for us, that He might obtain for us the grace of God and the remission of sins. And thus faith, insofar as it is directed toward the body of Christ delivered to death for us, is called the spiritual eating of the body of Christ, and insofar as it is directed toward the blood of Christ shed for us, it is called the spiritual drinking of the blood of Christ; concerning both of which see John 6, 35. 53. sqq. PART III. CAP. XI.

For we eat that very body of Christ which was delivered unto death for us, by means of the blessed bread, and we drink that very blood of Christ which was shed for our sins, by means of the wine; and thereby we are made certain (and Christ wills that we be made certain in this way) that whatever Christ merited upon the altar of the cross by the delivery of His body and the shedding of His blood—which are the remission of sins, the grace of God, and eternal life—are bestowed upon us by grace through faith. Thus the blessed Johann Gerhard, joining the end and the fruit of the Holy Supper, *Loci Theologici*, Vol. V, *De S. Coena* § 212.

Quenstedtius: "Truly penitent and believing Christians receive through the Holy Supper, as a divine and efficacious *δοτικόν* [giving] medium, the remission of their sins and eternal salvation. . . Our thesis is proved: 1. From the explicit mention of the remission of sins in the institution of the Holy Supper, Matt. 26:26 ff.: 'Take, eat; this is my body, which is given for you for the remission of sins. Take, drink; this is the blood of the New Testament, which is shed for you for the remission of sins; do this, as often as you do it, in remembrance of me.' And consequently, through the eating of this body delivered for us and through the drinking of this blood shed for us, the remission of sins is applied in the individual to everyone to whom it is said: Eat, i.e., this is my body, which was delivered for you, and drink, i.e., this is my blood, which was shed for you for the remission of sins; and we are made certain of the same by means of this sacramental fruition of the blessed bread and wine; hence Ambrose, *De Sacramentis*, bk. 4, ch. 6: 'As often as you drink, you receive the remission of sins and are inebriated with the Holy Spirit.'

2. From the designation of the New Testament; whoever receives the flesh of Christ given for him and the blood of Christ shed for him for the remission of sins, in such a way that the eating of this flesh and the drinking of this blood is the New Testament and applies the benefits of the covenant, he also receives the remission of sins and spiritual life, unless he himself has hindered the application of these benefits; but those who approach the Holy Communion receive the flesh of Christ given for them, etc. Therefore, those who approach the Holy Communion also receive the remission of sins, spiritual and eternal life, unless they themselves have hindered the application of these benefits. Christ Himself calls the Eucharistic cup the New Testament, Luke 22:20, and Jeremiah affirms that this covenant is contained in the New Testament: 'I will be merciful to their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more,' Jer. 31. Therefore, since the cup is the New Testament in the blood of Christ, by it the new covenant of grace is confirmed and sealed (for in no other sense can it be called the New Testament); but the Eucharistic cup is the New Testament in the blood of Christ, *l.c.* Therefore.

3. From the condition of the Eucharistic food and drink; those who actually receive in the Holy Supper that very body of Christ which was delivered unto death for our sins, and that very blood of Christ which was shed for our sins upon the altar of the cross, are made certain that whatever Christ merited upon the altar of the cross by the delivery of His body and the shedding of His blood—which are the remission of sins, the grace of God, and eternal life—are bestowed upon them by grace through faith. He who communicates the sun (Mal. 4:2) also communicates its rays.

4. From our insertion into Christ; by that medium through which we are inserted into Christ and are made to drink into one Spirit, by that same medium we are made partakers of the remission of sins and spiritual benefits. But through the Eucharist we are 'inserted into Christ,' 1 Cor. 10:17, *coll.* [compare] analogously John 6:56, 'and are made to drink into one Spirit,' 1 Cor. 12: 13. Therefore.

Hence Hilary, *De Trinitate*, bk. 8, from the passage already alleged, John 6:56: 'These things taken and drunk cause that we remain in Christ and Christ in us.' (*L.c.*, Part 2, q. 10, f. 1282, 1284 ff.)

Luther: "Therefore Luther taught rightly, that whoever has an evil conscience because of sins, he should go to the Sacrament and seek comfort, not in the bread and wine, not in the body and blood of Christ, but in the Word, which in the Sacrament offers, bestows, and gives to me the body and blood of Christ as given and shed for me." (*Against the Heavenly Prophets*, A.D. 1524, XX, 364.)

The same: "We answer, therefore, that these words in Luke 22:20, 'This is the cup, the new testament in my blood,' should not and cannot be understood as if the words 'in my blood' were to belong to the words 'this is the cup,' as this spirit, out of sheer, loud, wanton malice, pretends, but rather to the words 'a new testament,' just as they naturally stand and follow one after another; so that this much is said: This cup is a new testament, not through itself—for it is perhaps of glass or silver—but because my blood is there; through that same blood it is a new testament. For whoever receives the cup in such a way that he receives there Christ’s blood, which is shed for us, he receives the new testament, that is, the forgiveness of sins and eternal life." (Against the Heavenly Prophets, 1525. XX, 368.)

The same: "What, then, is this testament, or what is promised to us therein by Christ? Truly a greater, eternal, unspeakable treasure, namely, the forgiveness of all sins, as the words clearly sound: This is the cup of a new eternal testament in my blood, which is shed for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. As if He were to say: Behold, man, I promise you and grant you with these words the forgiveness of all your sins and eternal life. And so that you may be certain and know that such a vow remains irrevocably yours, I will die for it and give my body and blood for it, and leave both behind for you as a sign and seal, by which you should remember me, as He says in Luke 22:19: 'As often as you do this, remember me.'" (Sermon on the New Testament, 1520. XIX, 1273.)

The promise of the Gospel, that everyone who believes in Christ shall not perish but have eternal life, is indeed universal; meanwhile, however, because consciences that are anxiously terrified by the sense of sin, divine wrath, and their own unworthiness often doubt whether this promise pertains to them individually—so that they might be able to rely upon it with true faith before the judgment of God and raise themselves up against the accusation of the law, sin, and Satan—therefore Christ distributes His body and blood to them individually, so that, as ὁ μάρτυρ ὁ πιστός (Rev. 1:5), He may confirm them against all the assaults of various temptations (thus the end and the effect are joined again), that the promise of the Gospel and the goods offered in it truly pertain to them also, when they are fed and given to drink in the Sacred Supper with the body of Christ delivered unto death and His blood poured out for sins (which are the source and foundation of the evangelical promise):

Latin:

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: Pontificiorum, communionem sub una specie cum anathematis denunciatione et sub legis necessitate decrevit concil. Constantiense sess. 13. . . Denique concilium Trid. sess. 21., habita die 16. Julii anno 1562., capitulo 1. declaravit et docuit, ,nullo divino praecepto laicos et clericos non conficientes obligari ad eucharistiae sacramentum sub utraque specie sumendum, neque ullo pacto salva fide dubitari posse, quin illis alterius speciei communio suificiat ad salutem. Si quis dixerit ex Dei praecepto, vel necessitate salutis omnes et singulos Christi fideles utramque speciem sanctissimi sacramenti eucharistiae sumere debere, anathema sit.‘ . . Ut vero calicis Dominici imagine aliqua imperitam plebem fallant Romanenses, vinum ori abluendo illi porrigunt sacrificuli h. e. sumto pane sacro, calicem exhibent communicantibus laicis et non conficientibus, sed qui vinum simplex et non consecratum contineat, ut testatur Alphonsus Tostatus.“

DB SACRA COENA. § 12.

Finis cujus a qui etiam fructus aut effectus b hujus sacramenti, isque intermedius, est (1.) recordatio et commemoratio c mortis Christi, quae fide d peragitur; (2.) obsignatio e promissionis de remissione peccatorum, et fidei nostrae f confirmatio; (3.) insitio nostra g in Christum et spiritualis nutritio h ad vitam; (4.) dilectio mutua 1 communicantium, et similia k plura. Ultimus finis est salus1 aeterna communicantium. m Cajus consequendi gratia institutum ac celebrandum est hoc sacramentum.

Nempe sacramenta sunt media efficacia in ordine ad finem suum; quod etiam h. 1. de S. Coena sigillatim ostendemus. Ita Christus ipse apud Lucam cap, 22, 19.: Hoc facite εις τψ■ ίμψ ανάμνησή. Quae repetens Paulus 1 Cor. 11, 24. 25, addit v. 26,: Quotiescunque enim comederitis panem hunc et de poculo hoc biberitis, mortem Domini annunciate, donec venerit. Habet autem utique hoc sacramentum, quo Christus ipse suum corpus et sanguinem nobis realiter exhibet, vim ingentem movendi animos ad sui, qui tanta nobis praestitit et praestat, recordationem.

Lutherus: ,,Ich hoffe, es sei nicht noth, hier lange zu lehren, was. da heisse,Christi Gedächtnisse davon wir anderswo oft und viel gelehret haben, nämlich, dass es nicht sei das Betrachten des Leidens, damit etliche, als mit einem guten Werk, wollen Gott gedienet und Gnade erlanget haben, gehen um mit Trauren für das bittere Leiden Christi u. s. w. Sondern das ist Christi Gedächtniss: so man die Kraft und Frucht seines Leidens lehret und glaubt. Also, dass unsere Werk und Verdienste nichts sind, der freie Wille todt und verloren sei, sondern allein durch Christi Leiden und Tod von Sünden los und fromm werden, dass es sei ein Lehren oder Gedächtniss von der Gnade Gottes in Christo und nicht ein Werk von uns gegen Gott gethan.“ (Wie man sich zum Abendmahl zubereiten soll A. 1530. X, 2689.) Gerhardus: ,,Christus non dicit: hoc facite in meorum dolorum ac cruciatuum pro vobis toleratorum recordationem, sed εις την εμήν h. e. την εμον άνάμνησιν, in mei recordationem, h. e., in gratam et fidelem memoriam immensae meae caritatis, ex qua pro vobis passus et mortuus sum, qua etiam paratus eram, plura pro vobis pati, si haec mea passio et mors non fuisset sufficiens pro peccatis vestris precium.“ (Harmon. ev. cap. 171. f. 788.)

Nempe ut expendamus et credamus, quod Jesus Christus,, ΰεώΛρωπος, rex et sacerdos noster, ipse corpus suum Deo Patri victimam pro nobis obtulerit in ara crucis et sanguinem suum pro nobis, effuderit, ut impetraret nobis Dei gratiam et remissionem peccatorum. Atque ita fides, quatenus fertur in corpus Christi pro nobis in mortem traditum, dicitur corporis Christi manducatio spiritualis, et quatenus fertur in sanguinem Christi pro nobis effusum, dicitur spiritualis bibitio sanguinis Christi; de qua utraque vid. Joh, 6, 35. 53. sqq. PART. III. CAP. XI.

Quia enim illud ipsum Christi corpus pro nobis in mortem tradi' tum, mediante benedicto pane, manducamus et illum ipsum Christi sanguinem, qui pro peccatis nostris effusus est, mediante vino bibimus, inde certi reddimur (et Christus vult, ut hac ratione certi reddamur), quod ex gratia per fidem nobis donentur, quaecunque traditione sui corporis et effusione sui sanguinis Christus in ara crucis promeruit, quae sunt remissio peccatorum, gratia Dei et vita aeterna. Ita b. Joh. Gerhardus, finem et fructum s. coenae conjungens, T. V. L. de S. Coena § 212.

Quenstedtius: ,,Tere poenitentes ac credentes Christiani per s. coenam, ceu divinum et efficax medium δοτικόν, accipiunt suorum peccatorum remissionem et aeternam salutem. . . Probatur thesis nostra: 1. ex remissionis peccatorum in institutione s. coenae diserta mentione, Matth. 26,26. sq.: ,Accipite, manducate, hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur in remissionem peccatorum. Accipite, bibite, hoc est sanguis N. T., qui pro vobis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum; hoc facite, quotiescunque feceritis, in mei commemorationem.‘ Ac proinde per esum hujus pro nobis traditi corporis et per potum hujus pro nobis effusi sanguinis remissio peccatorum in individuo applicatur unicuique, cui dicitur: Ede, h. e. c. m., quod pro te traditum, et bibe, h. e. s. m., qui pro te effusus est in remissionem peccatorum, et certi de eadem reddimur, mediante hac benedicti panis et vini sacramentali fruitione; hinc Ambrosius 1. 4. de sacram, c. 6.: ,Quotiescunque bibis, remissionem peccatorum accipis et inebriaris Spiritu S.‘

2. Ex novi testamenti denominatione; quicumque accipit carnem Christi pro se datam et sanguinem Christi pro se effusum in remissionem peccatorum, ita ut comestio hujus carnis et bibitio hujus sanguinis sit n. t. et applicet bona foederalia, ille accipit etiam remissionem peccatorum, vitam spiritualem, nisi ipse impediverit horum beneficiorum applicationem; at qui accedunt ad s. synaxin, accipiunt carnem Christi pro se datam etc. Ergo, qui accedunt ad s. synaxin, etiam accipiunt remissionem peccatorum, vitam spiritualem ac aeternam, nisi ipsimet impediverint horum beneficiorum applicationem. Ipse Christus poculum euchar. nominat n. t. Luc. 22, 20. et Jeremias affirmat, in n. t. comprehendi hoc pactum; ,Propitius ero iniquitati eorum et peccati eorum non recordabor ampiius‘, Jer. 31. Quod poculum itaque est n. t. in sanguine Christi, eo novum gratiae foedus confirmatur atque obsignatur (alio enim sensu n. t. dici nequit); atqui poculum euchar. est n. t. in sanguine Christi 1. c. Ergo.

3. Ex cibi ac potus euchar. conditione; qui actu accipiunt in s. coena illud ipsum corpus Christi, quod pro peccatis nostris inmortem traditum, et illum ipsum sanguinem Christi, qui pro peccatis nostris in ara crucis effusus est, illi certi redduntur, quod ex gratia per fidem ipsis donentur, quaecunque Christus traditione corporis sui et effusione sanguinis sui in ara crucis promeruit, quae sunt remissio peccatorum, gratia Dei et vita aeterna. Quod communicat solem (Mal. 4, 2.), communicat etiam radios.

4. Ex nostra in Christum insertione, per quod medium Christo inserimur et ad unum spiritum potamur, eo medio remissionis peccatorum et spiritualium beneficiorum participes reddimur. Atqui per eucharistiam,Christo inserimur‘ 1 Cor. 10, 17., coli, άναλόγως Joh. 4, 56., ,et ad unum spiritum potamur‘, 1 Cor. 12, 13. Ergo.

Hinc Hilarius 1. 8. de trin. ex loco jam alleg. Joh. 6, 56.: ,Haec sumta et hausta faciunt, ut nos in Christo et Christus in nobis maneat.‘ (L. c. S. 2. q. 10. f. 1282. 1284. sq.)

Lutherus: ,,Darum hat der Luther recht gelehret, dass wer ein böse Gewissen hat von Sünden, der solle zum Sacrament gehen und Trost holen nicht am Brot und Wein, nicht am Leibe und Blut Christi, sondern am Wort, das im Sacrament mir den Leib und Blut Christi, als für mich gegeben und vergossen, darbeut, schenkt und gibt.“

Idem: ,,Wir antworten also, dass diese Worte Luc. 22, 20.: ,Das ist der Kelch, das Neue Testament in meinem Blut‘, nicht sollen noch mögen also zu verstehen sein, dass dies Wort,in meinem Blut‘ solle gehören zu dem Wort,das ist der Kelch‘, wie dieser Geist für grösser lauter muthwilliger Bosheit vorgibt, sondern zu dem Wort,ein neu Testament‘, wie sie auch nacheinander natürlich stehen und folgen; dass also so viel sei gesagt: Dieser Kelch ist ein neu Testament, nicht durch sich selbst; denn er vielleicht in Glas oder Silber ist; sondern darum, dass mein Blut da ist; durch dasselbige Blut ist er ein neu Testament. Denn wer den Keleh also empfähet, dass er da Christus Blut, das für uns vergossen ist, empfähet, der empfähet das neue Testament, das ist, Vergebung der Sünden und ewiges Leben.“ (Wider die himml. Pr. 1525. XX, 368.)

Idem: ,,Was ist denn nun dies Testament oder was wird uns darinnen bescheiden von Christo? Fürwahr ein grösser, ewiger, unaussprechlicher Schatz, nämlich, Vergebung aller Sünden, wie die Worte klar lauten: Dies ist der Kelch eines neuen ewigen Testaments in meinem Blut, das für euch und für viele vergossen wird, zu Vergebung der Sünde. Als sollte er sagen: Siehe da, Mensch, ich sage dir zu und bescheide dir mit diesen Worten Vergebung aller deiner Sünde und das ewige Leben. Und dass du gewiss seiest und wissest, dass solch Gelübde dir unwiderruflich bleibe, so will ich darauf sterben und mein Leib und Blut dafür geben und beides dir zum Zeichen und Siegel hinter mir lassen, dabei du meiner gedenken sollt, wie er saget Luc. 22, 9.: ,So oft ihr das thut, so gedenkt an mich.“‘ (Sermon von dem neuen Test. 1520. XIX, 1273.)

Promissio evangelii, quod omnis, qui in Christum credit, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam, est quidem universalis; interim tamen, quia anxie, et peccati, irae divinae et propriae indignitatis sensu territae conscientiae saepius dubitant, an ad se quoque in individuo haec promissio pertineat, ut vera fide coram Dei judicio eadem niti seque contra accusationem legis, peccati et satanae ea erigere queant, ideo Christus ipsis in individuo corpus et sanguinem suum distribuit, ut tanquam ό μάρτυρ ό πιστός, Apoc. 1, 5., contra omnes variarum tentationum insultus ipsos confirmet (sic rursus finis et effectus conjunguntur), quod vere ad ipsos quoque evangelii promissio et bona in eadem oblata pertineant, cum corpore Christi in mortem tradito et sanguine ejus pro peccatis effuso (equae sunt evangelicae promissionis fons et fundamentum) in sacra coena cibentur ac potentur:


### Of the Holy Supper: these are the words of the blessed Gerhard, l

these are the words of the blessed Gerhard, l. c. Nothing is joined more closely and tightly to the Son of God than the assumed human nature, which He united to Himself by a personal covenant. Conversely, nothing is joined more closely to us than that which we eat and drink, since it is converted into the substance of our flesh. Christ, therefore, desiring that He be most closely united with us and we with Him, instituted this sacrament, in which, by means of the blessed bread, we eat His body, and by means of the blessed wine, we drink His blood, writes Gerhard again, from the observation of Tauler, § 213.

He warns, however, that he does not posit that that spiritual food is altered and transmuted in us, but that it transmutes and alters us, so that we may become partakers of the divine nature (2 Pet. 1:4) and members of the mystical body, whose head is Christ (Eph. 5:30). And thus it is evident that not only does the intention of Christ the author look toward this as an end, but also that that grafting of us into Christ is efficiently conferred through the sacrament itself. PART III. CHAPTER XI.

Gg. Koenigius: "Can it be established with a clear conscience that, through the intervention of communion, an essential union of Christ with us is effected?" We do not wish to dispute here with others, except with Weigel alone, who thinks that from communion—that is, the use of the Lord’s Supper, by which the body of Christ is distributed through the bread and His blood through the cup—there follows an essential conjunction of our body and blood with the body and blood of Christ. It may be pleasing to hear his own words. . . He explains his mind most clearly in Part I of his postil, p. 214: "Christ," he says, "gives us the bread of heaven not only spiritually in faith without bread and wine, but also in the Supper with bread and wine; not that the visible bread and wine are evidently Christ’s body and blood, but therein He is given to us. For the bread of heaven is His Word, and He is the Word, and the Word is in the bread, and this invisible bread from heaven, or the Word, becomes flesh and blood in us and lays itself upon our flesh and blood. Therefore, when we receive such food of remembrance, we are united with Christ’s crucified body and are bodily united with Him.". .

This assertion of Weigel is so constituted that we can offer it no assent with a good conscience for the following reasons: 1. Because it has no foundation in Scripture. . . For where did Christ say: "Take and drink, so that My body and blood may be transmuted into a common substance with you"? Where did He say: "Take, eat, and drink; these things taken and drunk will effect in you a common essence with Me"? Where did He say: "Eat, this is the invisible bread from heaven, from which flesh and blood will be made in you and will be glued to your flesh and blood"? Where did He say: "Eat, so that you may be substantially united to My crucified body"? ... 2. That is conferred upon us in the sacrament which is promised in the Word. For the sacraments are seals of the Word, but seals do not confirm more than the letters to which they are appended contain. But nowhere in the words of Scripture is it promised to us that Christ must be essentially united with us, either within communion or outside of it. . .

3. If communicants are essentially united to Christ by the mere use of the Lord’s Supper, then even the impious would be made participants of this union. The reason is that they also use the Lord’s Supper, and that in its entirety. For when one treats of the integrity and holiness of the sacrament, it makes no difference what he believes or with what kind of faith he who receives the sacrament is imbued. It matters a great deal for the way of salvation, but for the question of the sacrament, it matters nothing. For it is possible that a man may have the entire sacrament and a perverse faith, says Augustine (Book 3 against the Donatists, ch. 14; see the same, Book 4, ch. 24). But the consequence is absurd. For by this reasoning: 1) the most pure and the most impure essence, the Son of God and the son of the devil, Christ and Belial, would be joined together, against the manifest Scripture, 2 Cor. 6:15. . .

You will say: "Is there, therefore, not to be established, besides the spiritual, a certain sacramental union between Christ and the faithful, flowing from the participation of the body and blood of Christ?" There are some, even among our own, who maintain that such a sacramental union exists, which proceeds by the power and efficacy of communion and is common equally to the worthy and the unworthy. . .

For me, to tell the truth, it seems otherwise, and I think this can neither be asserted nor defended while preserving the truth: I. Because in this way the term "union" is dragged into manifest abuse. For "sacramental union" has simply been used hitherto to describe that which intervenes between the earthly thing and the heavenly, from which sacramental propositions were also deduced, just as personal ones are from personal union. Now a new sacramental union would be added, of which Scripture is entirely ignorant and provides no foundation. Paul, indeed, in 1 Cor. 10:16-17, makes mention of at least a twofold communion which takes place by the power of the Eucharist: 1) sacramental, looking to the eucharistic symbols joined with the heavenly thing; 2) mystical, which looks to the mystical body of Christ and its members. But just as hypocrites are not members of that mystical body, except equivocally, so it is not to be thought that any properly so-called union, arising from the Eucharist, looks to them or intervenes between them and Christ.

whether it be called sacramental or otherwise.

II. That sacramental union, if it can derive its origin from anywhere, will do so only from the eating of the body and the drinking of the blood. But it is one thing for the impious to eat the body of Christ and drink the blood of Christ, and another for the same to be united with Christ mystically by the power of the sacrament. The former we necessarily admit because of the truly sacramental union which intervenes between the earthly and heavenly thing, and which depends upon the authority of the Institutor, not upon the condition of the communicant. The latter, however, we necessarily reject because of the deficient condition required of the one eating and drinking, which is faith. Therefore, upon whom faith does not fall, to him the salutary effect of the sacrament—within the circle of which union with Christ must also be included—can in no way pertain; and unless we concede this, it would follow that some salutary effect must be attributed to the Eucharist *ex opere operato* without a good movement of the user; which opinion of certain ancient scholastics is for the most part deserted even by the modern Jesuits themselves.

III. The comparison instituted with the baptism of adults stands in the way. What spiritual effect, I ask, does that have which is common to the faithful and to hypocrites? None at all, insofar as it regards salvation; but only an external communion of the church, in that both have been received within the boundaries of the church through baptism. The reason here is the same and no other. We cannot, indeed, deny that the fathers sometimes spoke rather harshly concerning the effect of the Eucharist... for many things are so constituted that they can easily be distorted to apply to hypocrites themselves, but such things ought to be read with a grain of salt.” (Casus consc. p. 484. sqq. 494. sq.)

For when spiritual eating and drinking are joined with sacramental eating and drinking, the contrite heart, burdened with sins, is truly refreshed by the body and blood of Christ, received in both ways; the fearful mind is lifted up, sustained, and nourished unto eternal life, so that it does not hunger nor thirst, but has life in itself, has eternal life, according to the passages of Scripture, John 6:33, 34, sqq. Cf. the blessed Gerhard, l. c., where he teaches that from this union with Christ it results that we obtain new strength, like branches from the vine, to fight against Satan, to resist the desires of the flesh, to progress in grace, etc.

Luther: “The heart knows well what the mouth eats. For it grasps the words and eats spiritually that which the mouth eats bodily. But because the mouth is a member of the heart, it must finally also live in eternity, for the sake of the heart, which lives eternally through the Word, because it also eats here bodily the same eternal food which its heart eats with it spiritually.” (That these words, etc., XX, 1037.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of the Papists; the Council of Trent, sess. 13, can. 5, pronounces anathema against those who posit that the remission of sins is either the principal fruit of the most holy Eucharist, or that no other effects proceed from it. Bellarmine, T. 3, l. 4, de euchar. c. 18, writes: ‘It is nowhere taught that the Eucharist was instituted for the remission of sins, but only for the leading and preserving of the spiritual life.’ ... 2. Of the Socinians; for thus the Racovian Catechism, c. 3, de coena Dom. q. 5: ‘Is there any other cause (besides the commemoration of the Lord’s death) for which the Lord instituted the Supper? Resp.: None at all.’ ... 3. Of the Arminians, who insist upon the perverse footsteps of the Socinians, positing that ‘the sacrament of the Eucharist makes merely a commemoration of the death of Christ,’ in Confess. c. 23, s. 4. They do not acknowledge other spiritual uses or ends of the Eucharist. ... 4. Of the Calvinists, who posit that ‘the sacrament in general is a naked sign signifying divine grace either already conferred before, or to be conferred afterwards.’” PART III. CHAP. XI. “To bestow, increase, and confirm faith is the work of the Holy Spirit alone, not of that external body eaten corporally,” writes Zwingli, Tom. II, Resp. ad lib. Lutheri de sacram., p. 397. (L.c.s. 2, q. 10, f. 1283, sq.)

Luthardt: "Modern Lutheran theology attempted a further development of dogma through a stronger emphasis on the bodily, natural life of Christ. Sartorius, *Meditations on the Revelation of the Glory of God*, pp. 222 f., also for the body: 'the sensual nature, the bodily life, is thereby to be sanctified, spiritualized, and prepared for the future glory.' Martensen, § 265, p. 412: 'The Lord's Supper is the union with Christ as the principle of the holy marriage of the Spirit with nature, which is the final goal of creation,' therefore 'a nourishment for the whole new man, and thus also for the future man of the resurrection, who is already germinating and developing in secret' (thus a mystery of nature). Hofmann, *Schriftbeweis* I, 51: 'in the Lord's Supper the Church celebrates its (still transcendent) possession of the glorified corporeality of human nature in Jesus.' II, 2, 244: the effect is a 'demonstration of the state of affairs of the forgiveness of sins, procured in Christ's death and present in his glorification, which imparts to the Christian living in the flesh a spiritual natural power for his life of faith.' On the same path also Thomasius, III, 2, § 76. Against which Kahnis abandons the Lutheran interpretation of the words of institution (I, 618 f.) and conceives of bread and wine as the sacramental word, i.e., as sign and medium at the same time, which he places in connection with the sacrificed corporeality of Christ, i.e., with his sacrificial death and its reconciling grace (I, 622 f.). 'If that which the body of Christ suffered in death now inheres in the glorified body, then whoever receives the atoning power immanent in the glorified body likewise receives the glorified body itself, and in and with it the whole Christ into himself. — This receiving is, of course, not eating and drinking, but a spiritual receiving through the medium of faith.'" (*Compend. d. Dogm.* 3rd ed. 1868, p. 278.)

Latin:

verba sunt b. Gerh. 1. c. Filio Dei nihil propius atque arctius est conjunctum, quam assumta natura humana, quippe quam personali foedere sibi univit. Vicisdm nobis nihil propius conjungitur, quam quod manducamus ac bibimus, quippe quod in carnis nostrae substantiam convertitur. Christus igitur, arctissime sese nobiscum et nos sibi uniri desiderans, instituit hoc sacramentum, in quo mediante benedicto pane corpus ipsius manducemus et mediante benedicto vino sanguinem ejus bibamus, scribit iterum, ex Tauleri observatione, Gerhardus § 213.

Monet autem, se non statuere, quod cibus ille spiritualis alteretur et transmutetur in nobis, sed quod nos transmutet et alteret, ut divinae naturae consortes, 2 Petr. 1, 4., et membra corporis mystici, cujus caput est Christus, efficiamur, Ephes. 5, 30. Et sic patet, non solum intentionem Christi auctoris huc, tanquam ad finem, spectare, verum etiam insitionem illam nostri in Christum per sacramentum ipsum efficienter conferri. PART. III. CAP. XI.

Gg. Koenigius: ,,An per rectam conscientiam statui queat, interventu communionis effici unionem Christi nobiscum essentialemf — Nolumus hic controvertere cum aliis, nisi cum solo Weigelio, qui putat, ex communione, h. e., usu coenae Dom., qua mediante pane corpus Christi, mediante calice ejusdem sanguis distribuatur, sequi essentialem corporis et sanguinis nostri cum corpore et sanguine Christi conjunctionem. Placeat propria illius audire verba. . . Clarissime mentem explicat part. I. postillae suae, p. 214.: ,Christus4, spricht er, ,gibt uns das Himmelbrot nicht allein im Glauben geistlich ohne Brot und Wein, sondern auch im Nachtmahl mit Brot und Wein, nicht dass das sichtbare Brot und Wein sei Christi Leib und Blut augenscheinlich, sondern darinnen ist er uns gegeben. Denn das Himmelbrot ist sein Wort, und er ist das Wort, und das yVort ist im Brot und dies unsichtig Brot vom Himmel, oder das Wort wird in uns Fleisch und Blut und leget sich an unser Fleisch und Blut. Derhalben, wenn wir solche Speis der Gedächtniss empfangen, so werden wir vereiniget mit Christi gekreuzigtem Leib und sind mit ihm leiblich vereiniget.‘ . .

Haec Weigelii assertio ita comparata est, ut bona cum conscientia nullum ei possimus praebere assensum propter sequentes rationes: 1. Quod nullum habet fundamentum in Scriptura. . . Ubi enim Christus dixit: accipite et bibite, ut corpus et sanguis meus in communem vobiscum transmutetur substantiam? Ubi dixit: accipite, edite et bibite; haec sumta et hausta efficient in vobis communem mecum essentiam? Ubi dixit: edite, hic est panis invisibilis de coelo, ex quo in vobis iiet caro et sanguis et agglutinabitur vestrae carni ac sanguini? Ubi dixit: edite, ut crucifixo meo corpori snbstantialiter uniamini? ... 2. Id in sacramento nobis confertur, quod in verbo promissum est. Nam sacramenta sunt verbi sigilla, sigilla autem non plus confirmant, quam literae, quibus appensa sunt, continent. At verbis Scripturae nuspiam nobis promissum est, quod, vel intra communionem, vel extra eam, Christum nobiscum essentialiter uniri debeat. . .

3. Si communicantes nudo coenae Dom. usu uniuntur Christo essentialiter, etiam impii hujus unionis reddentur participes. Ratio est, quia et illi utuntur coena Dom., eaque integra. Nam nihil interest, cum de sacramenti integritate et sanctitate tractatur, quid credat aut quali fide imbutus sit ille, qui accipit sacramentum. Interest quidem plurimum ad salutis viam, sed ad sacramenti quaestionem nihil interest. Fieri enim potest, ut homo integrum habeat sacramentum, et perversam fidem, inquit Aug. 1.3. contra Donat, c. 14., vide eundem 1. 4. c. 24. At consequens est absurdum. Etenim hac ratione 1.) coadunarentur essentia purissima et impurissima, Filius Dei et filius diaboli, Christus et Belial, contra manifestam Scripturam, 2 Cor. 6, 15. . . .

Dices, an igitur praeter spiritualem non erit statuenda sacramentalis quaedam unio inter Christum et fideles, fluens ex participatione corporis et sanguinis Christi? Sunt, qui ita statuant etiam ex nostratibus, dari talem sacramentalem unionem, quae promanet vi et efficacia communionis et tam dignis, quam indignis aeque communis sit? . .

Mihi, ut dicam quod res est, aliter videtur et hoc salva veritate nec asseri nec defendi posse existimo: I. quia hoc modo terminus unionis in manifestum abusum trahitur. Nam unio sacramentalis simpliciter hactenus dicta fuit illa, quae intercedit rei terrenae cum coelesti, ex qua etiam deductae fuere propositiones sacramentales, uti personales ex unione personali. Jam nova accederet sacramentalis unio, quam tamen Scriptura prorsus ignorat, nec ullum ejus fundamentum suppeditat. Paulus sane 1 Cor. 10, 16. 17. duplicis saltem communionis facit mentionem, quae.locum habet vi eucharistiae: 1.) sacramentalis, spectantis symbola euchar. collata cum re coelesti; 2.) mysticae, quae spectat corpus Christi mysticum, ejusque membra; uti vero hypocritae corporis illius mystici membra non sunt, nisi aequivoce, ita putandum non est, proprie dictam aliquam unionem, ex eucharistia oriundam, eosdem spectare aut ipsis cum Christo intercedere,

sive illa jam sacramentalis vocitetur, sive aliter.

II. Unio illa sacramentalis, sicunde potest ortum trahere, faciet id, non nisi ex manducatione corporis et bibitione sanguinis. At aliud est, impios manducare corpus Christi et bibere sanguinem Christi, aliud, eosdem uniri cum Christo mystice vi sacramenti. Illud necessario admittimus ob unionem vere sacramentalem, quae intercedit inter rem terrestrem et coelestem, et ab auctoritate instituentis, non a conditione manducantis dependet. Hoc contra necessario rejicimus ob deficientem conditionem, a manducante et bibente requisitam, quae est fides. In quem itaque non cadit fides, ad illum etiam effectus sacramenti salutaris, cujus circulo etiam includi debet unio cum Christo, nullatenus spectare potest, idque nisi concesserimus, sequetur, eucharistiae tribuendum effectum aliquem salutarem ex opere operato sine bono motu utentis; quae sententia scholasticorum quorundam veterum ab ipis etiam novellis Jesuitis ut plurimum deseritur.

III. Obstat instituta collatio cum baptismo adultorum. Quem, quaeso, spiritualem effectum habet ille fidelibus et hypocritis communem? Nullum plane, qui quidem salutem respiciat; sed externam solum communionem ecclesiae, quod utrique per baptismum intra ecclesiae pomoeria sint recepti. Eadem et hic ratio est et non alia. Negare quidem non possumus, patres de effectu eucharistiae interdum duriuscule fuisse locutos, . . nam multa sic sunt comparata, ut facile ad ipsos hypocritas possint detorqueri, sed talia cum grano salis legi debent.“ (Casus consc. p. 484. sqq. 494. sq.)

Quando enim cum sacramentali manducatione et bibitione spiritualis manducatio et bibitio conjungitur, utique corpore et sanguine Christi, utraque ratione acceptis, cor contritum et peccatis oneratum reficitur, pavida mens erigitur, sustentatur et ad vitam aeternam nutritur, ita ut non esuriat, neque sitiat, sed habeat vitam in se, habeat vitam aeternam, juxta LL. Joh. 6, 33. 34. sqq. Conf. b. Gerhard. 1. c., ubi docet, quod ex ista uyvione eum Christo proveniat, ut novas vires, tanquam palmites ex vite, consequamur pugnandi contra satanam, resistendi desideriis carnis, proficiendi in gratia etc.

Lutherus: ,,Das Herz weiss wohl, was der Mund isset. Denn es fasset die Worte und isset das geistlich, welches der Mund leiblich isset. Weil aber der Mund des Herzens Gliedmass ist, muss er endlich auch in Ewigkeit leben, um des Herzens willen, welches durchs Wort ewiglich lebt, weil er hier auch leiblich isset dieselbige ewige Speise, die sein Herz mit ihm geistlich isset.“ (Dass diese Worte u. s. w. XX, 1037.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ,,Antithesis: Pontificiorum; concilium Trid.sess. 13. can. 5. anathema pronunciat adversus illos, qui statuunt, vel praecipuum fructum sanctissimae eucharistiae esse remissionem peccatorum, vel ex ea non alios effectus provenire. Bellarminus T. 3.1. 4. de euchar. c. 18. scribit: ,Nusquam docetur, eucharistiam institutam esse ad peccata remittenda, sed tantum ad vitam spiritualem agendam et conservandam.‘ . . 2. Socinianorum; sic enim Catech. Racov. c. 3. de coena Dom. q. 5.: ,Nonne alia causa‘ (praeter commemorationem mortis Domini), ,ob quam coenam instituit Dominus, superest? Resp.: Nulla prorsus.‘ . . 3. Arminianorum, qui Socinianorum perversis insistunt vestigiis, statuentes, ,sacramentum eucharistiae meram tantum facere mortis Christi commemorationem‘, in Confess. c. 23. s. 4. Alios usus aut fines spirituales eucharistiae non agnoscunt. . . 4. Calvinianorum, qui statuunt, ,sacramentum in genere esse nuda signa significantia gratiae divinae vel jam ante collatae, vel postmodum conferendae.‘.. PART. III. CAP. XI. ,Fidem largiri, augere, confirmare, solius Sp. S. est, non corporis illius externi corporaliter manducati‘, scribit Zwinglius Tom. II. Resp. ad lib. Lutberi de sacram, p. 397.“(L.c.s. 2. q. 10. f. 1283. sq.)

Luthardtius: ,,Die moderne lutherische Theologie versuchte eine Fortbildung des Dogmas durch stärkere Betonung des leiblichen Naturlebens Christi. Sartorius, Meditationen über die Offenbarung der Herrlichkeit Gottes, S. 222 f. auch für den Leib: ,die sinnliche Natur, das leibliche Leben soll dadurch geheiligt, vergeistigt, für die dereinstige Herrlichkeit zubereitet werden.‘ Martensen, § 265. S. 412.: ,Das Abendmahl ist die Vereinigung mit Christo als dem Prinzip der heil. Vermählung des Geistes mit der Natur, welche das Endziel der Schöpfung ist‘, daher,eine Nahrung für den ganzen neuen Menschen, also auch für den künftigen Menschen der Auferstehung, der im Verborgenen schon keimt und sich entwickelt‘ (also ein Naturmysterium). Hof mann, Schriftb. I, 51.: ,im Abendmahl feiert die Kirche ihren (noch jenseitigen) Besitz der in Jesu verklärten Leiblichkeit menschlicher Natur.‘ II, 2, 244.: die Wirkung ist eine,Erweisung des in Christi Tod beschafften, in seiner Verklärung vorhandenen Thatbestands der Sündenvergebung, welche dem im Fleisch lebenden Christen eine geistliehe Naturkraft für sein Glaubensleben dargibt.‘ Auf derselben Bahn auch Thomasius, III, 2, § 76. Wogegen Kahnis die lutherische Auslegung der Einsetzungsworte;aufgibt (I, 618. f.), und Brot und Wein als das sacramentliche Wort, d. h. als Zeichen und Medium zugleich, fasst, welches in Verbindung mit der geopferten Leiblichkeit Christi, d.h. mit seinem Opfertod und dessen Versöhnungsgnade setzt (1,622. f.). ,Inhärirt nun das, was der Leib Christi im Tode erlitten, dem verklärten Leibe, so nimmt ebensomit, wer die dem verklärten Leibe immanente Sühnkraft empfängt, den verklärten Leib selbst, in und mit ihm den ganzen Christus in sich auf. — Dieses Aufnehmen ist freilich kein Essen und Trinken, sondern ein geistliches Empfangen durch das Medium des Glaubens.“‘ (Compend. d. Dogm. 3. Aufl. 1868. p. 278.)


### Of the Holy Supper: Kahnis: "One must say openly that the Lutheran purpose of the Lord's Supper is…

Kahnis: "One must say openly that the Lutheran purpose of the Lord's Supper is unfounded. If the truth is entirely on Luther's side in the defense of the reception of the true body and blood of Christ, he withdraws the power from this fundamental fact if he does not see in it the purpose of the Lord's Supper, but only a guarantee of the appropriation of the word of the forgiveness of sins... This whole concept, that the forgiveness of sins is received in the Lord's Supper, rests upon the reversal of the relationship of the word to the specific content of the sacrament in general, and upon a false interpretation of the words: 'given for you,' 'poured out for you,' in particular. In general, the concept of the sacrament of the Lutheran Church has not reached its full development. The fundamental concepts of word and faith have been applied to it too directly. To the Apology, the sacrament is only a qualified word, *verbum visibile* (p. 200), *quasi pictura verbi seu sigillum* (p. 267), which, like the word, has the power of the forgiveness of sins only through faith (p. 267). Before the word, the specific saving good of each sacrament falls into the shadows, just as the specific saving effect does before faith... The purpose of the Lord's Supper can only be derived from its essence. We partake in the Lord's Supper of the glorified body of Christ, and in and with it Christ's Spirit and life. What other purpose can the Lord's Supper have than union with Christ's body and life? This purpose is pointed to already by the character of the Lord's Supper as a sacrificial meal; secondly, John 6:56: 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him'; thirdly, the parallel with the marital communion, which is drawn in Eph. 5:31, 32." (*Die Lehre vom Abendm.* 1851, pp. 327, 328, 470 sq.)

Indeed, the administration of the Holy Supper in the public assemblies of the church looks to this, among other things, as the sinew and bond of ecclesiastical gatherings, 1 Cor. 11:20. And when Paul exhorts to the cultivation of Christian charity and concord, with schisms and dissensions excluded, among other arguments he says: πάντες, he says, εις ἓν πνεῦμα ἐβαπτίσθημεν. 1 Cor. 12:13. k) Which may be seen in the blessed Gerhard, l. c. Gerhard: "Several less principal ends (of the Holy Supper) can be enumerated.

1. That we may be stirred up to give thanks to Christ for the work of redemption, 1 Cor. 11:26. ...

2. That we may testify our obedience toward Christ’s institution and ordination. For He did not leave the use of this sacrament free and arbitrary to us, but enjoined it upon us by an express command, saying: 'Do this.' 3. That we may testify that we wish, by Christ’s example, to bear the cross patiently and are prepared to shed our blood for Christ’s glory, since in the Holy Supper we drink the blood of Him who died for us on the altar of the cross, Luke 14:27. ...

4. That we may preserve the public assemblies of Christians, the sinew and bond of which is the celebration of the Holy Supper, 1 Cor. 11:20. ...

5. That we may prove by the very act that we are performing serious repentance for sins acknowledged, etc.

6. That we may testify that we approve the doctrine which sounds forth in that church in which, together with others, we eat the same Eucharistic bread and drink from one cup, 1 Cor. 10:17, 21.

7. That we may publicly profess that we wish to forgive our neighbor his faults, to serve him to the best of our ability, and to acknowledge him as a brother and a member of one mystical body, Matt. 5:24." (L. de s. c. § 214.) l) For all sacraments, as means and organs of evangelical grace, ultimately tend toward this. m) However, we deny that the celebration of this sacrament, which is performed by others *ex opere operato* [by the work performed], or by the force of the work itself, or by way of a sacrifice properly so called, profits the absent and the dead. For the celebration of the Holy Supper cannot even be called a commemorative sacrifice if it is distinguished from the Eucharistic genus of sacrifices. See *Ausführl. Erklärung* [Detailed Explanation] L.

XVIII. Q. 90. p. 695 sqq. Cf. the blessed Chemnitz, *Exam. Conc. Trid.* P. II. p. m. 250 sq., where he teaches in what sense the liturgical action can rightly be called a sacrifice according to Scripture, and p. 275 sqq., where he explains in what sense the ancients called the liturgy a sacrifice. Hollaz: "The Mass is not a sacrifice properly so called, propitiatory for the sins of the living and the dead. ... Our assertion is proved: 1. Whatever animate thing is properly sacrificed is killed and destroyed by death; the animate body of Christ is not killed in the Mass, nor is it destroyed by death. Therefore, the body of Christ is not properly sacrificed in the Mass. The major premise is clear from the nature of a sacrifice properly so called. The minor is clear from the testimony of Paul, Rom. 6:9. 2. That which must be repeated is imperfect and argues an imperfect priesthood; Christ’s sacrifice is neither imperfect, nor does it argue an imperfect priesthood. Therefore, it ought not to be repeated. The major and minor are evident from Heb. 7:27; 9:25, 26. 3. If the Mass were a sacrifice properly so called, it would have been instituted by Christ at the Last Supper. But it was not instituted there. Therefore, it is not a sacrifice properly so called. The reason for the consequence is that, according to the Papists, the Mass does not differ from the Eucharist regarding the thing itself, but the Eucharist [was instituted] at the Last Supper." was finally instituted. The consequence is proven, because the institution of a sacrifice properly so-called, by which a living thing is offered, carries with it a command to slaughter that which is to be offered. But in the institution of the Supper, there is no command, neither explicitly nor implicitly, to slaughter Christ. 4. According to the mind of the adversaries, the Mass is an unbloody sacrifice. From this we gather: no propitiatory sacrifice properly so-called is made without blood, Heb. 9:22. But the sacrificial Mass is made without blood. Therefore, it is not a propitiatory sacrifice properly so-called. 5. No sacrament can be a sacrifice; the Eucharist is a sacrament. Therefore. The major premise is proven: because in the sacraments God offers and confers His grace to men; but in sacrifices, men offer certain gifts to God.*) *) There is also in the sacrificial Mass a great heap of false principles, the worst of which are these: that Christ underwent only temporal vicarious punishments; that for temporal punishments man himself must make satisfaction; that sins must be expiated and temporal punishments endured in some purgatorial fire or other, unless satisfaction for them has been made before departure from this life, or liberation has been effected by the benefit of indulgences; and that by the works of those who are still among the living, especially by the office of the priests, by which Christ is immolated daily, the torments of the dead in that fictitious fire can be made both more tolerable and shorter. The Antithesis is that of the Papists, who maintain that Christ is sacrificed in the Mass properly, but in an unbloody manner. Their stronger arguments are: 1. If the sacrifice of the New Testament must be daily and universal, it follows that the sacrificial Mass is not to be called into doubt (for this is daily and universal); the antecedent is true, as Malachi 1:11 testifies. Therefore, the consequent is also true. Resp. The passage cited does not refer to an expiatory sacrifice properly so-called, but to a spiritual sacrifice, namely, the preaching of the Gospel throughout the whole world, Rom. 15:16, the sacrifice of charity or beneficence, the sacrifice of prayers, and the host of praise. 2. Whoever is a priest after the order of Melchizedek, his office must be performed by offering bread and wine; but Christ, etc., Heb. 5:6. Therefore. The major premise is proven, because Melchizedek is said to have sacrificed and offered bread and wine to Abraham, Gen. 14:18. Resp. 1. Melchizedek did not sacrifice, but brought bread and wine to refresh Abraham and his soldiers. 2. Christ sacrificed and immolated Himself once on the altar of the cross, Heb. 9:12. Objection: But the sacrifice of Christ must be eternal, because He is a priest after the order of Melchizedek forever. Resp. The sacrifice of Christ performed on the altar of the cross is eternal not because of a perennial reiteration, but because of its perpetual value, Heb. 9:10. 3. No true religion can exist without a constant and perennial sacrifice. But the Christian religion is a true religion. Therefore. The major premise is proven, because the Israelite religion was not without daily sacrifices; indeed, even the Gentiles sacrificed. Resp. 1. The Christian religion rests upon the sacrifice of Christ, which is eternal in its value, Heb. 10:14. 2. The Christian religion is exercised by daily eucharistic sacrifices, which are the hosts of praise and prayer. (Exam. p. 1139, 1140, etc.) ANTITHESIS.
