Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: Of the Papists; the Council of Trent, sess. 6, c. 1, calls the Mass 'a singular sacrifice, by which Christ at the Last Supper offered His body and blood to God the Father under the species of bread and wine, and by which that bloody sacrifice performed on the cross is represented, and its saving virtue is applied for the remission of those sins which are committed by us daily.' Canon II calls it 'a divine sacrifice, by which that same Christ is contained and immolated in an unbloody manner, who once offered Himself bloodily on the altar of the cross'; and also 'a propitiatory sacrifice, by the oblation of which the Lord, being appeased, forgives even great crimes and sins.'"

Kahnisius: ,,Man muss sich offen sagen, dass die lutherische Zweckbestimmung des Abendmahles unbegründet ist. Wenn die Wahrheit ganz auf Luthers Seite ist in der Vertheidigung des Empfangs des wahren Leibes und Blutes Christi, so entzieht er dieser Grundthatsache ihre Kraft, wenn er in ihr nicht den Zweck des Abendmahles sieht, sondern nur eine Bürgschaft der Aneignung des Wortes von der Vergebung der Sünden. . . Es beruht dieser ganze Begriff, dass im Abendmahle die Vergebung der Sünden empfangen werde, auf der Umkehr des Verhältnisses des Wortes zum speciflschen Inhalt des Sacraments im Allgemeinen, auf falscher Interpretation des Wortes: für euch gegeben, für euch vergossen, ins Besondere. Ueberhaupt ist der Sacramentsbegriff der lutherischen Kirche nicht zur vollen Entwickelung gekommen. Die Grundbegriffe Wort und Glauben sind zu unmitelbar ihm angelegt worden. Das Sacrament ist der Apologie nur ein qualifleirtes Wort, verbum visibile (p.200.), quasi pictura verbi seu sigillum (ρ.267Λ, welches wie das Wort nur durch den Glauben die Kraft der Vergebung der Sünden hat (p. 267.). Vor dem Wort tritt das specifische Heilsgut jedes Sacraments ebenso in Schatten, wie vor dem Glauben die specifische Heilswirkung. . . Der Zweck des Abendmahles kann nur aus dem Wesen desselben entnommen werden. Wir gemessen im Abendmahle den verklärten Leib Christi, in und mit ihm Christi Geist und Leben. Welchen andern Zweck kann das Abendmahl haben, als Vereinigung mit Christi Leib und Leben? Auf diesen Zweck!weist schon der Charakter des Abendmahles als Opfermahl; zweitens Joh. 6,56.: ,Wer mein Fleisch isst und trinkt mein Blut, der bleibt in mir und ich in ihm‘; drittens die Parallele mit der ehelichen Gemeinschaft, welche Eph. 5, 31. 32. gezogen ist.“

Scilicet huc inter alia spectat administratio s. coenae in publicis ecclesiae conventibus, tanquam nervus et vinculum congressuum יecclesiasticorum, 1 Gor. 11, 20. Et cum ad caritatem atque concordiam christianam, exclusis schismatibus et dissidiis, colendam hortatur Paulus, inter caetera argumenta: πάντες, inquit, εις £v πνεύμα έπυτίσΰημεν. 1 Cor. 12, 18. k) Quae apud b. Gerhard. 1. c. videri possunt. Gerhardus: ״Fines minus principales (sacrae coenae) enumerari possunt complures.

1. Ut excitemur ad gratias Christo agendas pro opere redemtionis, 1 Cor. 11, 26. . .

2. Ut nostram erga Christi institutionem et ordinationem testemur oboedientiam. Neque enim liberum et arbitrarium nobis reliquit hujus sacramenti usum, sed expresso mandato eum nobis injunxit, dicens: ,Hoc facite.‘ 3. Ut testemur, nos Christi exemplo velle patienter ferre crucem et paratos esse ad fundendum nostrum pro Christi gloria sanguinem, cum in s. c. bibamus sanguinem illius, qui pro nobis in ara crucis mortuus est, Luc. 14, 27. . .

4. Ut conservemus publicos coetus Christianorum, quorum nervus et vinculum est sacrae coenae celebratio, 1 Cor. 11, 20. . .

5. Ut ipso facto comprobemus, nos peccatis agnitis seriam agere poenitentiam etc.

6. Ut testemur, nos approbare doctrinam, quae sonat in ecclesia illa, in qua una cum aliis eundam panem eucharisticum manducamus et ex uno calice hibimus, 1 Cor. 10,17. 21.

7. Ut publice profiteamur, nos velle proximo condonare suos naevos, pro virili eidem inservire ac pro fratre et membro unius corporis mystici agnoscere, Matth. 5, 24.“ (L. de s. c. § 214.) 1) Huc enim omnia sacramenta, tanquam media et organa gratiae evangelicae, tandem tendunt. m) Absentibus autem et mortuis sacramenti hujus celebrationem, quae ab aliis fit ex opere operato, seu ex vi operis ipsius, aut per modum sacrificii proprie dicti, prodesse negamus. Nam neque sacrificium commemorativum dici potest celebratio s. coenae, si ab eucharistico sacrificiorum genere distinguatur. Vid. Ausführl. Erklärung L.

XVIII. Q. 90. p. 695. sqq. Conf. b. Chemn. Exam. Cone. Trid. P. II. p. m. 250. sq., ubi docet, quo sensu actio liturgiao juxta Scripturam recte possit sacrificium appellari, et p. 275. sqq., ubi explicat, quo sensu veteres liturgiam appellarint sacrificium. Hollazius: ״Missa non est sacrificium proprie dictum, propitiatori um pro peccatis viventium et mortuorum. . . Probatur assertio nostra: 1. Quae res animata proprie sacrificatur, ea occiditur et per mortem destruitur; corpus Christi animatum in missa non occiditur, neque per mortem destruitur. E. corpus Christi in missa proprie non sacrificatur. Major liquet ex natura sacrificii proprie dicti. Minor claret testimonio Pauli Rom. 6, 9. 2. Quod sacrificium repeti debet, illud est imperfectum et arguit sacerdotium imperfectum; Christi sacrificium nec est imperfectum, nec sacerdotium arguit imperfectum. E. repeti non debet. Major et minor patet ex Hebr. 7, 27. 9, 25. 26. 3. Si missa esset sacrificium proprie dictum, esset institutum a Christo in ultima coena. Sed in ea institutum non est. E. non est sacrificium proprie dictum. Ratio consequentiae est, quia juxta pontificios missa ab eucharistia non differt quoad rem, eucharistia autem in ultima coena 34 BaieriComp. ed. Walther. IU. PART. III. CAP. XI. demum fuit instituta. Consequens probatnr, quia institutio sacrificii proprie dicti, quo res animata offertur, importat mandatum de mactando eo, quod offerendum est. De Christo autem mactando nullum in institutione coenae mandatum, neque explicite neque implicite, continetur. 4. Ex mente adversariorum missa est sacrificium incruentum. Ex quo colligimus: nullum sacrificium propitiatorium proprie dictum fit sine sanguine, Hebr. 9, 22. At sacrificium missaticum fit sine sanguine. E. non est sacrificium propitiatorium proprie dictum. 5. Nuilum sacramentum potest esse sacrificium; eucharistia est sacramentum. E. Major probatur: quia in sacramentis Deus gratiam suam hominibus offert et confert; in sacrificiis autem homines quaedam munera Deo offerunt.*) *) Est etiam in sacrificio missatico magnus cumulus errorum falsorumäue principiorum, quorum pessima haec sunt: quod Christus vicarias poenas duntaxat aeternas subierit; quod pro temporalibus homo ipse satisfacere debeat; quod igne purgatorio, nescio quo, expianda sint peccata ac poenae temporales perferendae, nisi aut ante discessum ex hac vita satisfactio pro iis praestita sit, aut indulgentiarum beneficio liberatio facta, quod eorum, qui adhuc in vivis sunt, opera, inprimis^ue sacerdotum officio, quo Christus quotidie immoletur, cruciatus mortuorum in illo igne commentitio et tolerabilior et brevior eifici queat. Antithesis est pontificiorum, statuentium, Christum in missa proprie, sed modo incruento sacrificari. Quorum argumenta potiora sunt: 1. Si sacrificium novi testamenti debet esse quotidianum et universale, sequitur, quod sacrificium missaticum in dubium non sit vocandum (nam hoc est quotidianum et universale); antecedens est verum, teste Malachia 1, 11. Ergo et consequens. Resp. L. c. non intelligitur sacrificium expiatorium proprie dictum, sed sacrificium spirituale, nempe praedicatio evangelii in toto terrarum orbe, Rom. 15, 16., sacrificium caritatis sive beneficentiae, sacrificium precum et hostia laudis. 2. Quicunque est sacerdos in morem Melchisedechi, illius officium offerendo panem et sanguinem est peragendum; atqui Christus etc. Hebr. 5, 6. E. Major probatur, quia Melchisedechus dicitur sacrificasse et obtulisse Abrahamo panem et vinum Gen. 14, 18. Resp. I. Melchisedechus non sacrificavit, sed attulit panem et vinum ad reficiendum Abrahamum et ipsius milites. 2. Christus semel sacrificavit et immolavit seipsum in ara crucis, Hebr. 9, 12. Instantia: Sed sacrificium Christi debet esse aeternum, quia est sacerdos in morem Melchisedechi aeternum. Resp. Sacrificium Christi in ara crucis peractum est aeternum non ob perennem reiterationem, sed ob perpetuum valorem, Hebr. 9, 10. 3. Nulla vera religio potest esse sine sacrificio constanti et perenni. Atqui Christiana religio est vera religio. E. Major prob., quia religio Israelitica non erat sine sacrificiis quotidianis, quin immo gentiles sacrificarunt. Resp. 1. Religio christiana nititur sacrificio Christi, quod qua valorem aeternum est, Hebr. 10, 14. 2. Religio christiana exercetur quotidianis sacrificiis eucharisticis sine hostiis laudis et precum.“ (Exam. p. 1139. 1140. sq.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: Pontificiorum; Concil.Trid. sess. 6. c. 1. missam vocat,sacrificium singulare, quo Christus in novissima coena corpus et sanguinem suum sub speciebus panis et vini Deo Patri obtulerit, quoque cruentum illud in cruce peractum repraesentetur, atque illius salutaris virtus in remissionem eorum, quae a fiobis quotidie committuntur, peccatorum applicetur.‘ Can. II. nominat,sacriflcium divinum, quo idem ille Christus contineatur et incruente immoletur, qui in ara crucis semel seipsum cruente obtulit‘; nec non,sacrificium propitiatorium, cujus oblatione placatus Dominus crimina et peccata etiam ingentia dimittat.‘ “


## 27 On Predestination and Reprobation

PART. III. CHAP. XII. § 12. The Holy Supper can be defined as a sacred action instituted by Christ, in which, with blessed bread, His body is given to be eaten, and with blessed wine, His blood is given to be drunk to the communicating Christians, and by them both are received, the body is eaten with the bread, the blood is drunk with the wine, in commemoration of the death of Christ, the sealing of the remission of sins, and the confirmation of faith unto eternal life. The common genus of the sacraments is denoted. The principal efficient cause is indicated. See § 2. This is the earthly matter. See § 6. Or consecration, using the words of institution; which is the form of the H. Supper. See § 9. This is the heavenly matter. See § 8. Thus the final cause or the subject of the H. Supper is denoted. See § 10. The end for which it is, is here, according to § 12. Chapter XII. CONCERNING PREDESTINATION AND REPROBATION. § 1. Those men whom God brings to salvation in time, and the manner in which He does so, He has decreed from eternity that He would bring those same ones to salvation in time and in the same manner. And to this point look the names of predestination and election. Formula of Concord: "The doctrine of this article, when it is conducted from and according to the pattern of the divine Word, one cannot and should not consider useless or unnecessary, much less offensive or harmful, because the Holy Scripture does not mention the article in one place only by chance, but treats and urges the same thoroughly in many places; thus, one must also not omit or reject the doctrine of the divine Word for the sake of abuse or misunderstanding, but for that very reason, to avert all abuse and misunderstanding, the right understanding must be explained from the foundation of Scripture." (Art. XI. de aet. praedest. Declar. p. 704.) Cf. p. 713. sqq. § 43—51. Luther: "The apostle Paul in the epistle to the Romans does not discuss these things in a corner, but in public and before the whole world, with a most free mouth, and even in harsher words, saying (Rom. 9.): 'Whom He wills, He hardens', and again: 'God willing to make known His wrath' etc. What is harsher (but to the flesh) than that word of Christ (Matt. 20.): 'Many are called, few are chosen'? and again (John 12.): 'I know whom I have chosen.' Of course, all these things are such, by your account, that nothing more useless could be said, because, namely, from this, impious men slide into despair and hatred and blasphemy. . . Two things demand that such things be preached; the first is the humiliation of our pride and the knowledge of the grace of God, the other is faith itself, the Christian faith. First, God has certainly promised His grace to the humbled, i.e., to the deplored and desperate. But a man cannot be thoroughly humbled until he knows that his salvation depends entirely outside his own powers, counsels, efforts, will, and works, and entirely upon the will, counsel, will, and work of another, namely, of God alone. For as long as he is persuaded that he can do even the slightest thing for his salvation, he remains in confidence of himself, nor does he despair of himself thoroughly; therefore he is not humbled before God, but presumes for himself a place, a time, some work, or hopes, or at least wishes, by which he might finally arrive at salvation. But he who doubts nothing, but trusts entirely in the will of God, he despairs of himself entirely, chooses nothing, but waits for God to work, he is closest to grace, so that he may be saved. Therefore, for the sake of the elect, these things are published, so that in this way, humbled and reduced to nothing, they may be saved; the others resist this humiliation, nay, they condemn that this despair of self should be taught, they want something, even a little bit, to be left to them, which they can do; these remain secretly proud and adversaries of the grace of God. This is, I say, one reason, so that the pious, humbled, may know, invoke, and receive the promise of grace. The other is that faith (Heb. 11.) is of things not appearing; so that there may be room for faith, it is necessary that all things which are believed be hidden, and they are not hidden more remotely than under a contrary object, sense, and experience. Thus God, while He gives life, does it by killing, while He justifies, He does it by making guilty, while He carries to heaven, He does it by leading to hell, as Scripture says: 'The Lord kills and makes alive, He brings down to the underworld and brings back up', 1 Sam. 2." (De servo arb. See opp. lat. var. arg. Francof. ad M. 1873. Vol. VII, 151. 153. sq.) U. Rhegius: "That there is predestination, is certain, Eph. 1, 4.: 'The Father chose us in Christ, before the foundations of the world were laid'; and Rom. 9, 11. 12.: 'When the children were not yet born, Esau and Jacob, when they had done neither any good nor evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might remain, not from works, but from Him who calls, it was said to Rebecca, the greater shall serve the lesser', just as it is written in Mal. 1, 2. 3.: 'Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.' But this mystery of predestination is solid food for adults, not milk for infants. Wherefore it is very necessary to treat this topic cautiously and not to speak of it indiscriminately among just anyone. For Paul commands that all things be done for edification. For we see with what fear of God and with what reverence the apostle treated this topic, Rom. 9. 10. 11." (Formulae caute loquendi. Ed. Feustking. p. 36. sq.) Chemnitius: "Should a preacher also teach something about this article? Or may a Christian also know something about this? — Because the holy divine Scripture does not mention the article—that God provided, chose, and ordained the elect for salvation in Christ before the time of the world—in one place only by chance, but treats and urges the same thoroughly in many places, so one cannot and should not consider the same doctrine useless, unnecessary, or offensive and harmful, when it is conducted from and according to the pattern of the divine Word, as much as is revealed therein. And the most important passages of this article should be known to the pastors, as Matt. 20. and 22. Luke 10. John 13. and 15. Acts 13. Rom. 8. 9. 10. and 11. 1 Cor.

1. Eph. 1. 2 Tim. 1. and 2. Gal. 1. 2 Thess.

2. Apoc. 20. But this article is often spoken of very indiscreetly; so does many a one also grasp dangerous thoughts from this, whereby either impenitence is strengthened, or faith is driven into despair? — For the sake of abuse and misunderstanding

the doctrine of the divine Word must not be omitted or rejected on account of the will, but every misunderstanding should be diligently separated and rejected, and one should also faithfully warn against every abuse. Whoever then wishes to abuse the pure doctrine because of this, his condemnation is just. Rom. 3.” (Handbüchlein. 1574. See Frank, Th. d. Concordienf. IV, 329. sq.) Hutterus: “Before the Pelagians, certain heretics taught that neither were evil works to be avoided by men elected and predestined by God, nor could they be harmed by them, nor should the reprobate strive for good works, because they could in no way be confirmed or helped by them; but that those who were once predestined could not fall away, and those who were not predestined could not return to grace with God. The foulness of this error imposed a name upon these heretics, so that they were called Predestinarians or Predestinati. Pelagius, therefore, believed that this error could not be refuted unless he attributed to man free will, by which he would be equally inclined to choose and perform both good and evil. Indeed, he progressed to such a degree of impiety that he slandered the entire doctrine of predestination as useless, nay, even harmful to the church, as Augustine testifies in book 6 of the Hypognosticon.” (Lib. Concord. explic. p. 1160. sq.) Gerhardus: “There exist letters of Prosper and Hilary to Augustine, which are prefixed to the books on the predestination of the saints and on the gift of perseverance, Tom. 7, which testify that certain men, conspicuous at that time for their authority in Gaul, judged that the definition of predestination was adverse to the utility of preaching. But. . . what the Holy Spirit has revealed in Scripture ϑεοπνεύστω, concerning which Christ and the apostles dealt in their sermons, which suppresses every tumor of spiritual pride in us, which excites us to the love of God and to giving thanks to Him, which inflames us to the study of piety, that certainly must by no means be wrapped in silence. But such is the mystery of predestination that it is easy to show it κατά μέρη. Therefore, this mystery must be discussed in the schools of Christians, but in a due manner.” (Loc. de elect. §§ 19. 20. 21.) The same: “A sober treatment of this mystery, consonant with Scripture, shows us the abyss of divine mercy, to which alone our election to eternal life is to be attributed in its entirety; it suppresses all boasting about our own merits and all confidence in ourselves; it confirms the certainty of our salvation, placed in the omnipotent and most beneficent hand of God; it stimulates us to a sincere love of God, who loved us before the foundations of the world were laid; it nourishes mutual love and φιλαδελφίαν toward those whom we hope to have as companions in eternal life, having likewise been elected out of mere grace; it excites us to an ardent study of the divine Word and the frequent use of the sacraments, through which means the Holy Spirit wishes to kindle, preserve, and increase faith in us; it inflames us to prayers and a serious study of piety, for we were chosen that we might be holy and blameless, Eph. 1, 4. Finally, it fortifies us to bear all adversities with an even mind, ‘for those whom God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son of God; we know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are the called according to His purpose.’ Rom. 8, 28. 29.” (Loc. de elect. § 216.) B. Meisnerus: “Beza, in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. 308, ed. Witteb. A. 1605, proposed these words: ‘Nor is it advisable to confer about this article before everyone, lest perhaps more be offended than instructed, who cannot grasp these things.’ And p. 310: ‘This dispute cannot be held in a public assembly without grave offense to those who are not capable of such a mystery, whether they assent to our opinion or the contrary. Whence a new seedbed of dissension could arise, so that this dispute should be debated in the schools, among trained theologians, rather than in a public assembly of any and all.’ We, however, maintain that this meticulous concealment of the truth is pernicious and highly suspect, and therefore [it should be taught] not only in the schools from the learned to the learned, but in PART. III. CAP. XII. ... that this doctrine ought also to be treated and explained by pastors to the unlearned in the churches. . . . They object 1: If it is preached that the elect are not damned and the reprobate are not saved, then the effort to rise again will be taken away from those who have fallen, and torpor and sloth in not progressing will be added to those who are standing. Resp.:

ΡΑΕΤ. ΠΙ. CAP. ΧΠ. § IB. Definiri potest sacra coena, quod sit actio sacra a a Christo b instituta, in qua cum pane c benedicto d corpus e ipsius manducandum, et cum vino benedicto sanguis ejus bibendus datur communicantibus f christianis, et ab his utrumque accipitur, corpus cum pane manducatur, sanguis cum vino bibitur, in g commemorationem mortis Christi, obsignationem remissionis peccatorum et confirmationem fidei ad vitam aeternam. Denotatur genus commune sacramentorum. Causa efficiens principalis indicatur. Vid. § 2. Materia terrena haec est. Vid. § 6. Seu consecratio, adhibitis verbis institutionis; quae est forma s. coenae. Vid. § 9. Materia coelestis haec est. Vid. § 8. Sic finis cui seu subjectum s. coenae denotatur. Vid. § 10. Finis cujus hic est, juxta § 12. Caput XII. DE PRAEDESTINATIONE ET REPROBATIONE. § 1. Quos homines et qua ratione Deus in tempore ad salutem a perducit, eosdem et eadem ratione ad salutem in tempore se perducturum, ab aeterno b decrevit. Atque huc spectant nomina praedestinationis c et d electionis. Formula Concordiae: ,,Die Lehre von diesem Artikel, wenn sie aus und nach dem Vorbilde des göttlichen Worts geführt, man nicht kann noch soll für unnütz oder unnöthig, viel weniger für ärgerlich oder schädlich halten, weil die heilige Schrift des Artikels nicht an einem Ort allein etwa ungefähr gedenket, sondern an vielen Oertern denselben gründlich handelt und treibet; so muss man auch um Missbrauchs oder Missverstandes willen die Lehre des göttlichen Worts nicht unterlassen oder verwerfen, sondern eben derhalben, allen Missbrauch und Missverstand abzuwenden, soll und muss der rechte Verstand aus Grund der Schrift erklärt werden.“ (Art. XI. de aet. praedest. Declar. p. 704.) Cf. p. 713. sqq. § 43—51. Lutherus: ,,Paulus apostolus in epistola ad Romanos non in angulum, sed in publicum ac coram toto mundo, liberrimo ore, eadem etiam durioribus verbis palam disserit, dicens (Rom. 9.): ,Quos vult, PART. III. CAP. XII. indurat‘, et iterum: ,Deus volens notam facere iram suam‘ etc. Quid durius (sed carni) illo Christi verbo (Matth. 20.): ,Multi vocati, pauci electi‘? et iterum (Joh. 12.): ,Ego scio, quos elegerim.‘ Scilicet haec omnia talia sunt, te auctore, ut nihil possit inutilius dici, quod videl. hinc ad desperationem et odium et blasphemiam prolabantur homines impii. . . Duae res exigunt, talia praedicari; prima est humiliatio nostrae superbiae et cognitio gratiae Dei, altera ipsa fides christiana. Primum Deus certo promisit humiliatis, i. e., deploratis et desperatis, gratiam suam. Humiliari vero penitus non potest homo, donec sciat, prorsus extra suas vires, consilia, studia, voluntatem, opera, omnino ex alterius arbitrio, consilio, voluntate, opere suam pendere salutem, nempe Dei solius. Siquidem, quamdiu persuasus fuerit, sese vel tantulum posse pro salute sua, manet in fiducia sui, nec de se penitus desperat; ideo non humiliatur coram Deo, sed locum, tempus, opus aliquod sibi praesumit, vel sperat, vel optat saltem, quo tandem perveniat ad salutem. Qui vero nihil dubitat, totum in voluntate Dei pefidere, is prorsus de se desperat, nihil eligit, sed exspectat operantem Deum, is proximus est gratiae, ut salvus fiat. Itaque propter electos ista vulgantur, ut isto modo humiliati et in nihilum redacti salvi fiant; caeteri resistunt humiliationi huic, imo damnant, doceri hanc desperationem sui, aliquid vel modiculum sibi relinqui volunt, quod possint; hi occulte manent superbi et gratiae Dei adversarii. Haec est, inquam, una ratio, ut pii promissionem gratiae humiliati cognoscant, invocent et accipiant. Altera est, quod fides (Ebr. 11.) est rerum non apfcarentium; ut ergo fidei locus sit, opus est, ut omnia, quae creduntur, abscondantur, non autem remotius absconduntur, quam sub contrario objectu, sensu, experientia. Sic Deus, dum vivificat, facit illud occidendo, dum justificat, facit illud reos faciendo, dum in coelum vehit, facit id ad infernum ducendo, ut dicit Scriptura: ,Dominus mortificat et vivificat, deducit ad inferos et reducit‘, 1 Sam. 2.“ (De servo arb. Vid. opp. lat. var. arg. Erancof. ad M. 1873. Vol. VII, 151. 153. sq.) U. Rhegius: ,,Esse praedestinationem, certum est, Eph. 1, 4.: ,Pater elegit nos in Christo, antequam jacerentur fundamenta mundi‘; et Rom. 9, 11. 12.: ,Nondum natis pueris Esau et Jacob, cum neque boni quippiam fecissent, neque mali, ut secundum electionem propositum Dei maneret, non ex operibus, sed ex vocante dictum est Rebeccae, major serviet minori‘, sicut Mal. 1, 2. 3. scriptum est: ,Jacob dilexi, Esau vero odio habui.‘ Sed hoc mysterium praedestinationis est solidus cibus adultorum, non lac infantium. Quare valde necessarium est, caute tractare hunc locum et non apud quoslibet indiscriminatim de eo loqui. Paulus enim jubet omnia fleri ad aedificationem. Videmus enim, cum quanto Dei timore, quantaque reverentia hunc locum apostolus tractarit, Rom. 9. 10. 11.“ (Formulae caute loquendi. Ed. Feustking. p. 36. sq.) Chemnitius: ,,Soll auch ein Prediger von diesem Artikel etwas lehren? Oder darf ein Christ auch etwas hievon wissen? — Weil die heilige göttliche Schrift dieses Artikels, dass Gott die Auserwählten vor der Zeit der Welt in Christo zur Seligkeit versehen, erwählet und verordnet habe, nicht an einem Orte alleine ohngefähr gedenkt, sondern an vielen Orten denselbigen gründlich handelt und treibet, so kann und soll man auch dieselbige Lehre nicht für unnütz, unnöthig oder ärgerlich und schädlich halten, wenn sie aus und nach dem Fürbild des göttlichen Worts, so viel darin geoffenbaret ist, geführt wird. Und sollen die fürnehmsten Sprüche von diesem Artikel den pastoribus bekannt sein, als Matth. 20. und 22. Luk. 10. Joh. 13. und 15. Act. 13. Röm. 8. 9. 10. und 11. 1 Kor.

1. Eph. 1. 2 Tim. 1. und 2. Gal. 1. 2 Thess.

2. Apoc. 20. Es wird aber oft von diesem Artikel gar unbescheiden geredet; so fasset auch mancher hieraus gefährliche Gedanken, dadurch entweder Unbussfertigkeit gestärket, oder der Glaube in Verzweiflung getrieben wird? — Um Missbrauchs und Missverstands

willen muss die Lehre des göttlichen Worts nicht unterlassen oder verworfen werden, sondern allen Missverstand soll man mit Fleiss absondern und verwerfen, auch für allem Missbrauch treulich warnen. Wer dann darüber der reinen Lehre missbrauchen will, des Verdammniss ist billig. Röm. 3.“ (Handbüchlein. 1574. Vid. Frank, Th. d. Concordienf. IV, 329. sq.) Hutterus: ,,Ante Pelagianos docuerunt haeretici quidam, quod neque mala opera hominibus a Deo electis et praedestinatis fugienda vel obesse possint, neque reprobis studendum sit bonis operibus, quia nullo modo iis confirmari juvarique possint; sed qui semel sint praedestinati, ii excidere, qui non praedestinati, illi in gratiam cum Deo redire haud possint. Cujus erroris foeditas nomen haereticis istis imposuit, ut praedestinatorii sive praedestinati dicerentur. Hunc igitur errorem Pelagius refutari haud posse censebat, nisi homini liberum arbitrium, per quod aeque ad bona atque mala eligenda perpetrandaque ferretur, tribueret. Quin eo tandem impietatis progressus est, ut totam doctrinam de praedestinatione calumniaretur, tanquam inutilem, imo noxiam ecclesiae, teste Augustino lib. 6. Hypognosticän.“ (Lib. Concord. explic. p. 1160. sq.) Gerhardus: ,,Extant epistolae Prosperi et Hilarii ad Augustinum, quae praefixae sunt libris de praedestinatione sanctorum et de bono perseverantiae Tom. 7., quae testantur, quosdam in Gallia tum temporis auctoritate conspicuos viros judicasse, praedestinationis definitionem utilitati praedicationis adversam esse. Sed. . . quod Sp. S. in Scriptura ΰεοπνενστω revelavit, de quo Christus et apostoli in suis concionibus egerunt, quod omnem spiritualis superbiae tumorem in nobis deprimit, quod ad Dei amorem et gratias ipsi agendas excitat, quod ad studium pietatis inflammat, illud utique silentio minime est involvendum. Sed, tale est praedestinationis mysterium, ut κατά μέρη ostendere in proclivi est. Disserendum igitur in Christianorum scholis de hoc mysterio, sed modo debito.“ (Loc. de elect. §§ 19. 20. 21.) Idem: ,,Sobria et Scripturae consona mysterii hujus tractatio monstrat nobis abyssum divinae misericordiae, cui soli electio nostrum ad vitam aeternam in solidum tribuenda; deprimit omnem de nostris meritis gloriationem atque in nobis ipsis confidentiam; confirmat salutis nostrae certitudinem in omnipotente ac beneficentissima Dei manu repositam; exstimulat nos ad sincerum Dei amorem, qui prior ante jacta mundi, fundamenta nos dilexit; alit mutuam dilectionem ac φιλαδελφίαν erga eos, quos itidem ex mera gratia electos in aeterna vita speramus habere socios; excitat nos ad verbi divini ardens studium et frequentem sacramentorum usum, per quae media Sp. s. fidem in nobis vult accendere, conservare et augere; inflammat nos ad preces et serium pietatis studium, electi enim sumus, ut sancti et inculpati simus, Eph. 1, 4. Denique ad omnia adversa aequo animo perferenda nosmet munit, ,quos enim praescivit Deus, hos etiam praedestinavit conformes fieri imagini Filii Dei; scimus, quod diligentibus Deum omnia cooperentur in bonum iis, qui secundum propositum vocati sunt sancti.‘ Rom. 8, 28. 29.“ (Loc. de elect. § 216.) B. Meisnerus: ,,Beza in Colloquio Mompelg. m. p. 308. ed. Witteb. A. 1605. haec verba proposuit: ,Neque consultum est, coram omnibus de hoc articulo conferre, ne forte plures offendantur, quam erudiantur, qui illa capere non possunt.‘ Et p. 310.: ,In publico coetu haberi haec disputatio non potest sine gravi eorum offendiculo, qui tanti mysterii capaces non sunt, sive nostrae sive contrariae sententiae assenti antur. Unde novum exoriri dissensionis seminarium possit, ut haec disputatio potius in scholis, inter exercitatos theologos, quam in publico quorumvis coetu disceptanda sit.‘ Nos autem statuimus, perniciosam et maxime suspectam esse illam meticulosam veritatis occultationem, ideoque non solum in scholis a literatis ad literatos, sed in PART. ### On Predestination and Reprobation: Those who are offended in such a way are either weak or contumacious

1. Those who are offended in such a way are either weak or contumacious. If they are weak, let them be instructed; if they are contumacious, let them be abandoned.

2. Because of the abuse and mockery of the wicked, the elect are not to be defrauded of this doctrine...

3. This objection is opposed to the Holy Spirit Himself. For if these stumbling blocks accompany the doctrine of election by their very nature, why was it recorded in the Scriptures and commended to us?

4. Things that are subordinate are held to be opposites. For election does not remove the pursuit of good works and perseverance in faith, but promotes it, since they stand in relation to one another as end and means, which are subordinate, not contradictory. For those who are elected from eternity perform repentance in time, believe in Christ, and persevere in piety; if the opposite occurs, election is falsely presumed. Therefore, this reasoning is impious: "If I am elected, I shall obtain life even without piety." For the argument must be inverted: "If I am elected, I ought to renounce worldly pursuits." For God chose us that we should be holy and blameless, Eph. 1:4. . . . They object 2: The mystery of election is too deep to be grasped by the common people. "For who has known the mind of the Lord?" Rom. 11: 33. Therefore, it is better to be silent about it than to speak of it. Resp.: 1. Although it cannot be known in its entirety, it can be known to a certain extent, and therefore Christ inculcated it even before the common people. Augustine aptly says in *De bono perseverantiae*, ch. 15: "Must that which is manifest be denied because that which is hidden cannot be comprehended?" 2. Election is considered with respect to either its causes or its specific cases. The former can be known, even if an account cannot be rendered for all of the latter. 3. This doctrine is obscure to the slow and to those who are perishing, 2 Cor. 4:3, but not to pious and devout investigators, for whom light shines out of darkness, v. 6. 4. Heralds of the Word ought to apply themselves to treat this article both soberly and prudently. Soberly, so that they explain it solely from the Word of God, not from the judgment of reason. Prudently, so that they use sound words for sound doctrine, and direct the matter so that every occasion is snatched away from both Pharisaical presumption and Judaic despair, so that the pious may be preserved in humility and the impious may be thrust down from their security. If this is done, this doctrine will be proposed appropriately, heard usefully, and clearly understood." (Anthropology, Disp. XII, A 2. sq. A 3. sqq.) Brochmand: "When the question is asked whether it is safe to publicly propose and teach the doctrine of predestination to the people in the Church of God, we do not hesitate to concede to the affirmative opinion. For although we acknowledge that it must be diligently ensured, with all moderation and spiritual prudence, that when predestination is discussed, neither vain questions that do not serve for edification are proposed to the people, nor anything beyond what is written is rashly urged; nevertheless, we judge it advisable, indeed absolutely necessary, that the people be piously instructed in the doctrine of predestination. For since the entire Holy Scripture has been left to us for the purpose that we might meditate upon it both publicly and privately (Rom. 15:4; 2 Tim. 3:16–17), and since the doctrine of predestination or eternal election is a principal part of Holy Scripture (Mark 13:20, 27; Rom. 8:30; Eph. 1:3–4, etc.), everyone easily understands how gravely one would err who attempted to hide this doctrine of eternal election from the unlearned people. And to press even further those who, with preposterous care and uncommendable circumspection, deny that it is safe to propose the doctrine of eternal election to the unlearned people, see how many benefits they deprive men of by this rash solicitude. 1. The doctrine of eternal predestination or election to eternal life is supremely useful for confirming the certainty of our salvation. For since election to eternal life is firmly founded not in human wisdom, not in the will or works of men, but in the mere mercy and εὐδοκία of God, who, hearing this, could fail to conceive from it a sure confidence regarding the indubitable and entirely immovable certainty of his own salvation?"

And to this point pertain these sayings of the Holy Scriptures: Luke 10:20; 12:23; John 6:37; 10:28; 17:14, 15. 2. There is nothing that can more vehemently kindle in us the love of God and neighbor than a serious and devout meditation on predestination. For you cannot help but love God, who, when you were dead in sins and adjudged to eternal death because of sins, freely chose you for eternal life. Eph. 1:3, 4, etc. And it would be shameful to hate your brother, a partaker of the same grace as you. Hear 1 John 3:16. 3. The doctrine of predestination, when rightly taught, is a most effective means and remedy for curbing pride, so that, namely, we do not arrogate anything to ourselves or attribute even the slightest bit to our own powers or righteousness. John 15:16; Rom. 5:8; 2:5, 6, 31, 32, etc.; 1 Cor. 1:28, 29, etc.; 1 Cor. 4:2–4. Lastly, the doctrine of predestination is a spur by which we are stirred up to the pursuit of good works. Eph. 1:4; 2:8, 9, 10. Since the doctrine of predestination brings these and similar fruits, it is immense how much he sins against the benefit of his hearers who hides the true doctrine of predestination from his hearers!” (System. I. f. 248, etc.)

Indeed, what we have hitherto treated concerning the causes and means of obtaining salvation returns to this. For God does nothing in time that He has not decreed from eternity that He would do in time. And thus the acts which God exercises in time stand, as an execution, in relation to the eternal decree of God; and therefore the exact agreement of both must be acknowledged. And concerning the eternal decrees, which perhaps might otherwise lie hidden, we can be most rightly informed if we have known, according to revelation, what and in what manner God does in time; whence, in this place, the reason and way being known by which God leads men to salvation in time, we shall be taught all the more easily concerning the eternal decree of saving men.

In Greek, προορισμός, according to Eph. 1:5; Rom. 8:29, 30. In this place, however, it denotes the destination of some subject, and indeed by the force of the particle πρό, or "pre-," the destination of a subject, before it itself exists, to a certain end.

And we, insisting on the footsteps of Scripture, which nowhere uses the word προορίζειν, "to predestinate," regarding men in a bad sense, take predestination for predestination to life only. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Dissert. Inaug. de Aetern. Praedest. Decret.*, ch. I, § 8.

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: “Antithesis: 1. Of some of the fathers, who interpreted the term predestination generically, and took it for the decree concerning both the saving of the elect and the damning of the unbelieving and reprobate. In which sense Isidore said (l. 2, *de summo bono*, c. 5, 6): ‘Predestination is twofold, either of the elect to rest, or of the reprobate to death.’ Augustine (l. 15, *de civ. Dei*, c. 1, and in *Enchir.* c. 100), Prosper (in *resp. 14, 15 ad Capitula Gallorum*), and Fulgentius (l. 1, *ad Monimum*, c. 14) are in the same boat. Much more rightly Leo (in his epistle to Peter of Antioch) says: ‘I believe,’ he says, ‘that God only predestinated good things, but foreknew both good and evil things.’

2. Of the Calvinists, in whose logic predestination has obtained the nomenclature of a genus, which they divide into two species, election and reprobation; that is, they extend the word predestination, taken in its proper signification, even to the reprobate and constitute two species of predestination: election, which is predestination to life, and reprobation, which is predestination to death. Thus Calvin (l. 3, *Inst.* c. 21). . . D. Affelmann (l. c. to the question: Whether a certain predestination of the infidels can be called to death, or whether predestination contains two species under itself, election and reprobation— PART III. CAP. XII.

nem? Resp.: We deny that we are in unanimous agreement. The Genevan, Basle, Lausanne, and English Calvinists affirm it, above all Matthew, Archbishop of York. The Tigurines, Sedanensians, Gedanensians, and the Cantabrigian Whittaker contradict them; the Marburgers, Lugdunensians, Herbornensians, and Neustadians fluctuate; the Heidelbergers dispute among themselves concerning it. So he says.” (Th. did.-pol. P. III. c. 2. s. 2. q. 1. f. 37. sq.) ' Εκλογή

in Greek, according to Eph. 1:4, Rom. 8:33. However, regard is had to the number of those who are saved and therefore have been destined for salvation by an eternal decree; who are indeed few, chosen from a great number of men, and separated from the rest. Some call this election, with the addition of the term, election to glory, distinguishing it from that which they call election to grace, or to the means of salvation. But, according to the custom received in our churches, the word election, when spoken of absolutely, denotes that which looks to eternal life itself. And thus election, as to the thing itself, is the same as predestination; although, on account of diverse connotations—namely, here the priority of ordination, there the respect to the promiscuous assembly of sinful men—some distinction of reason may be admitted. Cf. b. Mus. 1. c. § 11.

The Wittenberg Theological Faculty: “The synonyms which periphrastically denote those whom the Lord has chosen are these: they are called predestined, called κατά πρόθεσιν, Rom. 8, ordained to eternal life, Acts 13, given to Christ by the Father, John 6, 10, 17, bought from among men, the firstfruits to God and the Lamb, Rev. 14, bought from the earth, in the same place.” (Bek. von d. ewigen Gnadenwahl. A. 1597. Vid. Consil. Witteberg. I, 632. b.)

Chr. Cornerus: “Lest anyone think that the faithful attain this by their own love, that they might be saved, and that they perceive the fruit only from hard things, it is rightly added in Rom. 8:28, by way of correction or explanation, who those are of whom he speaks here, namely: who are κλητοί κατά πρόθεσιν, called according to the purpose of God, that is, chosen to salvation by his counsel and benign will.” (In ep. ad. Rom. commentar. 1583. p. 110.)

Meisnerus: “There is some difference between the will of God, the purpose of God, and the decree of God. The term will is general and comprehends even those things which do not come to pass. Thus God wills that all men listen attentively to his word, which nevertheless never happens. The purpose of God, however, embraces only those things which certainly come to pass. For what God purposes, that happens without any exception. The decree of God is a still stricter degree; namely, when God decrees that he will effect by certain means that which he has purposed within himself. Thus, therefore, these things follow: God wills something, he purposes what is willed, he decrees what is purposed, and so these three differ as the broader and the stricter, the antecedent and the consequent...

Latin:

1. Qui taliter offenduntur, aut sunt infirmi, aut contumaces. Si infirmi, erudiantur, sin contumaces, deserantur.

2. Propter improborum abusum et irrisionem non sunt hac doctrina defraudandi electi...

3. Haec objectio ipsi Spiritui S. opponitur. Si enim offendicula ista per se doctrinam electionis comitantur, cur in Scripturas relata et nobis commendata est?

4. Pro oppositis habentur, quae subordinata sunt. Electio enim studium bonorum operum et perseverantiam in fide non tollit, sed promovet, siquidem habent se, ut finis et media, quae subordinantur, non contrariantur. Nam qui ab aeterno electi sunt, illi in tempore poenitentiam agunt, in Christum credunt et in pietate perseverant; secus si fiat, electio falso praesumitur. Quare impia est haec ratiocinatio: si electus sum, etiam sine pietate vitam consequar. Invertendum enim est argumentum: Si electus sum, secularibus studiis renunciare debeo. Elegit enim nos Deus, ut essemus sancti et irreprehensibiles, Eph. 1,4.... Objiciunt 2.: Electionis mysterium altius est, quam ut a vulgo capi possit. ,Quis enim cognovit mentem Domini?‘ Rom. 12, 33. Ergo potius silendum de illo, quam loquendum. Resp.: 1. Etsi non in totum, tamen in tantum cognosci potest, ideoque Christus coram vulgo etiam illud inculcavit. Scite Augustinus 1. de bono persev. c. 15.: ,Numquid ideo negandum est, quod apertum est, quia comprehendi non potest, quod occultum est?‘ 2. Electio consideratur respectu vel causarum, vel specialium casuum. Illae cognosci possunt, quamvis de his omnibus ratio reddi nequeat. 3. Doctrina haec obscura est tardis et pereuntibus 2 Cor. 4, 3., non autem piis et devotis indagatoribus, quibus lux e tenebris exsplendescit, v. 6. 4. Operam adhibere debent praecones verbi, ut hunc articulum tractent tum sobrie, tum prudenter. Sobrie, ut ex solo Dei verbo, non rationis judicio, illum explicent. Prudenter, ut ad sanam doctrinam sana verba adhibeant, eoque rem dirigant, ut omnis occasio praeripiatur tum pharisaicae praesumptioni, tum Judaicae desperationi, ut in humilitate conserventur pii, a securitate detrudantur impii. Quod si fiat, doctrina haec convenienter proponetur, utiliter audietur, luculenter intelligetur.“ (״Avϋρωπολ. Disp. XII, A 2. sq. A 3. sqq.) Brochmandus: ,,Quando quaeritur, an tutum sit, doctrinam de praedestinatione populo in ecclesia Dei publice proponere ac tradere, nulli dubitamus in ajentem sententiam concedere. Licet enim agnoscamus, cum omni moderatione et spirituali prudentia sedulo curandum, ne, ubi de praedestinatione agitur, aut vanae quaestiones nec aedificationi servientes populo proponantur aut quidquam ultra id, quod scriptum est, temere urgeatur; attamen consultum, imo plane necessarium judicamus, ut populus de praedestinationis doctrina pie instituatur. Cum enim universa sacra scriptura eo fine nobis, relicta sit, ut eam qua publice, qua privatim meditemur Rom. 15, 4. 2 Tim. 3, 16. 17., pars autem praecipua sacrae scripturae sit doctrina de praedestinatione seu aeterna electione, Mare. 13, 20. 27. Rom. 8, 30. Eph. 1, 3. 4. sq., nemo non de facili intelligit, quam graviter erraret, qui rudem populum hanc de aeterna electione doctrinam celare tentaret. % Et ut adhuc magis eos premam, qui praepostera cura nec probanda circumspectione negant, tutum esse, doctrinam de aeterna electione populo rudi proponere, vide mihi, quantis commodis privent homines hac solicitudine temeraria. 1. Summe utilis est doctrina de aeterna praedestinatione seu ad vitam aeternam electione ad confirmandam salutis nostrae certitudinem. Cum enim electio ad vitam aeternam non in sapientia humana, non in voluntate aut operibus hominum, sed in mera Dei misericordia et ευδοκία solide fundata sit, quis, haec audiens, non poterit non hinc concipere certam fiduciam de salutis suae indubitata et plane immota certitudine?

Et huc pertinent haec Literarum s. dicta Luc. 10, 20. 12, 23. Joh. 6, 37. 10, 28. 17, 14. 15. 2. Non est quidquam, quod potest vehementius accendere in nobis amorem Dei et proximi, quam seria et devota praedestinationis meditatio. Non enim potes non amare Deum, qui te, in peccatis mortuum et ob peccata aeternae morti adjudicatum, gratis ad vitam aeternam elegit. Eph. 1, 3. 4. sq. Et türpe fuerit odisse te fratrem, ejusdem tecum gratiae consortem. Audi Joh. 1. ep. 3, 16. 3. Praedestinationis doctrina recte tradita efficacissimum medium et remedium est ad retundendam superbiam, ne videl. quidquam arrogemus nobis aut viribus justitiaeve nostrae vel tantillum tribuamus. Joh. 15, 16. Rom. 5, 8. 2, 5. 6. 31. 32. sq..l Cor. 1, 28.29. sq. 1 Cor. 4, 2—4. Ultimo, calcar est doctrina praedestinationis, quo ad studium bonorum operum excitamur Eph. 1, 4. 2, 8. 9. 10. Hos et consimiles fructus cum afferat doctrina praedestinationis, immane quam peccet in commoda auditorum, qui veram praedestinationis doctrinam auditores suos celat!“ (System. I. f. 248. sq.)

Nempe huc redeunt, .quae hactenus tractavimus de causis et mediis consequendae salutis. Nihil enim Deus facit in tempore, quod non ab aeterno decreverit, se in tempore facturum. Et sic actus, quos Deus in tempore exercet, habent se, tanquam executio, ad aeternum Dei decretum; ideoque agnoscenda est exacta convenientia utriusque. Ac de decretis quidem aeternis, quae forte alias latere possunt, rectissime informari possumus, si, quid et qua ratione Deus in tempore faciat, juxta revelationem cognoverimus; unde h. 1. cognita ratione et via, qua Deus homines in tempore ad salutem perducit, de decreto aeterno salvandi homines tanto facilius docebimur.

Et sic electio quoad rem idem est, quod praedestinatio; licet ob diversa connotata, nempe hic prioritatem ordinationis, illic respectum ad coetum hominum peccatorum promiscuum, distinctio rationis aliqua admitti possit.
