Rom. commentar. 1583. p. 110.)

Meisnerus: ,,Datur aliquod discrimen inter voluntatem Dei, propositum Dei, ut et decretum Dei. Voluntas terminus generaliter est et comprehendit eas etiam res, quae non fiunt. Sic Deus vult, omnes homines attente audire verbum suum, quod tamen nunquam fit. Propositum autem Dei tantum complectitur ea, quae certo fiunt. Quod enim Deus proponit, illud absque omni exceptione fit. Decretum Dei adhuc strictior gradus est; quando videl. Deus decernit, se certis mediis effecturum id, quod apud se proposuit. Ita ergo haec sequuntur: Deus aliquid vult, volitum proponit, propositum decernit, adeoque tria ista differunt, ut latiora et strictiora, antecedentia et consequentia. . .


### On Predestination and Reprobation: The name of election and the word to choose have many meanings in the…

The name of election and the word to choose have many meanings in the Scriptures, of which five are primary... In the most special signification, it is taken for the election of the faithful to eternal life made before the foundations of the world were laid, which they therefore designate as saving. And in this last signification we take the word election, from which are properly and κατ' εξοχήν called εκλεκτοί or εξελεγμένοι, i.e., chosen nominally and principally. For that there is no difference between these two words is evident from that in Mark 13:20: διά τους εκλεκτούς, οΰς εξελέξατο ο θεός. From all these significations, however, it appears that the word to choose 1. includes a certain separation, by which a thing or person is set apart from others and selected for a certain thing. Hence these terms are interchanged, so that what Moses calls to choose in Deut. 7:6, Solomon renders by to separate in 1 Kings 8:53. Thus the election of the disciples in Luke 6:13 is named a separation in Acts 13:2. To have observed this will be of no small benefit for refuting the universal and indiscriminate Huberine election; 2. to presuppose

gratuitous love, from which it always proceeds. This is intimated in Deut. 4:37: "Because He loved thy fathers, He chose their seed after them," which is found in Deut. 7:6, 7, 8. And the reason is at hand, since those things which are chosen must be pleasing and dear to us before others, which ought to be noted against the champions of works and merits. . . What the Latins call *praedestinare*, whence *praedestinatio*, the Greeks call προορίζειν, whence προορισμός. Now, προορίζειν signifies to decree and predetermine something before you do it; for όρος denotes a boundary, hence όρίζειν means to terminate, and προορίζειν means to determine before or beforehand, as in 1 Cor. 2:7: "We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which ό θεός προώρισεν before the ages," i.e., which He had decreed and preordained to reveal to us. Thus the elect are called προορισμένοι, predestined, i.e., destined to life before they existed." (Άνθρωπολ. Disp. XIV. p. A 3. b. A 4. b.) §

2. Moreover, by the names of predestination and election is denoted now the decree concerning the whole work of bringing men to salvation, and now, in particular, the decree concerning certain men, known to the divine intellect under a certain aspect, to be certainly saved. And this is indeed the broader acceptance of the terms, by which the whole, if I may so speak, process of God in the business of salvation, which is to take place in time, is conceived to have been decreed from eternity; by which reasoning predestination, or the eternal election of God, is said to procure the salvation of the children of God and to dispose those things which pertain to it. See F. C. Art. XI, n. IV, p. 618. And certain degrees, in which election or predestination consists, are enumerated; see Sol. Decl. Form. Conc. Art. XI, p. 802. Add the blessed Musaeus, *Dissert. de Aet. El. Decr.*, published in the year 1668, § 266 sq., p. 205, 206.

Formula of Concord: "First, the distinction between the eternal providence of God and the eternal election of His children to eternal salvation is to be diligently noted. For *praescientia vel praevisio*, that is, that God sees and knows everything beforehand, before it happens, which is called the providence of God, extends over all creatures, good and evil, namely, that He sees and knows beforehand everything that is or will be, what happens or will happen, be it good or evil, because before God all things, whether past or future, are unhidden and present. As it is written in Matt. 10:29: 'Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father'; and Psalm 139:16: 'Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them'; likewise, Isa. 37:28: 'I know thy abode, and thy going out, and thy coming in, and thy rage against me.'

But the eternal election of God, *vel praedestinatio*, that is, God's ordinance unto salvation, does not extend at all over the godly and the wicked, but only over the children of God, who are chosen and ordained to eternal life 'before the foundation of the world was laid,' as Paul says in Eph. 1:5: 'He hath chosen us in Christ Jesus and ordained us unto the adoption of children.' The providence of God (*praescientia*) also sees and knows the evil beforehand, but not in such a way that it would be God's gracious will that it should happen; but what the perverse, evil will of the devil and of men will purpose and do, that God all sees and knows beforehand, and holds PART III. CAP. XII. his *praescientia*, that is, foreknowledge, also has its order in evil dealings or works, in that God sets a goal and measure for the evil which God does not will, how far it should go and how long it should last, when and how He will hinder and punish it; yet all of this the Lord God governs in such a way that it must redound to the glory of His divine name and the salvation of His elect, and the ungodly must be put to shame thereby.

But the beginning and cause of evil is not God’s providence (for God does not create or work evil, nor does He help or promote it), but the evil, perverted will of the devil and of men, as it is written: “Israel, you bring yourself into misfortune; but your salvation rests in Me alone.” (Hos. 13:9.) Item: “You are not a God who takes pleasure in wickedness,” Ps. 5:4 [5].

But the eternal election of God not only foresees and knows the salvation of the elect, but is also, out of the gracious will and good pleasure of God in Christ Jesus, a cause which creates, works, helps, and promotes our salvation and whatever pertains to it; upon which our salvation is also so founded that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; as it is written: No one shall tear My sheep out of My hand; and again: And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. (Matt. 16:18; John 10:28; Acts 13:48.)” (Concordia. Ed. Muellerus. p. 704 sqq.)

Faculty of Theology at Wittenberg: “Regarding this so clear and undeniable declaration of the Book of Concord, S. Huber seeks such a vain subterfuge that he writes: ‘I concede such a description of the election of the children of God,’ he says, ‘in the sense in which the Book of Concord uses it there; for there the election of grace is used *particulariter* [particularly] in the application and in the event or outcome of salvation. When the word *praedestinatio* (ordination to life) is used in that sense, we allow it,’ he says, ‘that predestination belongs solely to the children of God.’ But the Christian reader should know in opposition to this that this pretext of Huber’s will only be valid when he has first proven from the Book of Concord that the Book of Concord mentions any other election than just this one alone, which is written there, that it does not extend to both the evil and the good, but solely to the godly, believing children of God. Furthermore, it is a pure fabrication, intended to deceive the simple-minded, that he pretends he allows the particular election, which extends only to the children of God, and does not contend against it, when he nevertheless most vehemently attacks the very same doctrine that we hold according to the guidance of God’s Word and the Book of Concord, and slanders it as a Calvinistic error.” (Consil. Witeb. I, 606.)

Aeg. Hunnius: "Now, if one descends to the question of to whom this gratuitous election of God, initiated in the very counsel of God before the foundations of the world were laid, should be referred, the Book of Concord answers thus: 'Predestination or the eternal election of God pertains only to the good and beloved children of God.' In the formula itself, eternal election, or the predestination of God to salvation, is not referred simultaneously to the good and to the evil, but only to the children of God. Huberus, on the other hand, reviewing these words of the Book of Concord, contradicts it with his own dogma: 'Predestination or the eternal election of God is by no means to be referred only to the good and beloved children of God (for this is extremely Calvinistic), but equally to the evil and the unbelieving, because it is simply to all, whether they were to believe in the only-begotten Son of God or not to believe. Indeed, God chose only the unbelieving, such as we all are by nature,' *Rettung*, p. 5. If, however, by election one understands the application of election (which is nothing other than justification), in this sense alone does Huberus concede that election, i.e., justification, pertains only to the children of God. But the election itself, of which the Book of Concord speaks from Scripture, [he claims pertains] no less to the children of the devil (such as are the impenitent...

all those who tempt), which He extends to the children of God, and that against the clear, express, and irrefragable letter of the Formula of Concord.” (Volum. Disputatt. 1598. p. 304. sq.)

Philippi: “According to the Formula of Concord, God has from eternity decreed the salvation of all men and, for the execution of this counsel, in the fullness of time gave His Son unto death for the reconciliation of the sins of the whole world. This universal counsel of grace, accomplished in Christ, He earnestly offers to all men through the Word, which, as the bearer of the Spirit, is in itself a means of salvation powerful for conversion. All those, therefore, who are led by the Word of God to faith and thereby to righteousness and life, owe this solely to the divine mercy, which chose them from eternity in Christ and saved them in time in Him; those, on the other hand, who do not attain to this goal of salvation must attribute it to their own resistance against God’s gracious will and against His Word and His Spirit. The Formula of Concord, therefore, by the way in which it grasps the conversion of man purely as an effect of divine grace, excludes every Pelagian, semi-Pelagian, and synergistic way of viewing it, without thereby falling into the opposite extreme of predestinarianism, in that it represents God’s grace, Christ’s sacrifice, and God’s Word as extending to all men.” (Kirchl. Glaubensl. IV. First Half. 1868. p. 62. sq.)

Latin:

Nomen electionis et verbum eligendi multa habet in Scripturis significata, quorum quinque sunt primaria... In specialissima significatione pro electione fidelium ad vitam aeternam facta, priusquam jacerentur fundamenta mundi, quam propterea salutarem indigitant. Atque in hac significatione ultima sumimus vocabulum electionis, a qua denominantuf proprie et κατ'' εξοχήν εκλεκτοί vel εκλε?ιεγμειοι, h. e., electi nominaliter et principaliter. Nam inter haec duo vocabula nihil esse discriminis, patet ex illo Mare. 13, 20.: διά τους εκλεκτούς, οΰς εξελεξατο ο ΰεός. Ex omnibus vero his significationibus apparet, vocem eligendi 1. includere quandam separationem, qua res vel persona ab aliis secernitur et ad certum quid seligitur. Hinc isti termini permutantur invicem, ut, quod Moses vocat eligere Deut. 7, 6., Salomon reddit per separare 1 Reg. 8, 53. Sic electio discipulorum Luc. 6, 13. nominatur separatio, Act. 13, 2. Id quod observasse non parum proderit ad refutandam universalem et indiscretam electionem Huberianam; 2. praesupponere

gratuitam dilectionem, a qua semper procedit. Innuitur hoc Deut. 4,37.: ,Quoniam dilexit Jehovah patres tuos, elegit semen eorum post eos‘, quod reperitur Deut. 7, 6. 7. 8. Et ratio est in promptu, quoniam, quae eliguntur, prae aliis grata nobis et dilecta esse oportet, quod contra operum et meritorum propugnatores notari debet. . . Quod Latini dicunt praedestinare, unde praedestinatio, Graeci προορίζειν nominant, unde προορισμός. Significat autem προορίζειν aliquid decernere et praefinire, antequam illud agas; όρος enim terminum notat, hinc όρίζειν terminare, et προορίζειν pro vel prius determinare, ut 1 Cor. 2, 7.: ,Loquimur Dei sapientiam in mysterio, quam προώρισεν ό ΰεος ante saecula‘, i. e., quam decreverat et praeordinaverat nobis revelare. Sic electi dicuntur προορισμένοι, praedestinati, h. e., antequam existerent, ad vitam destinati.“ (Άνΰρωπολ. Disp. XIV. p. A 3. b. A 4. b.) §

2. Denotatur autem nominibus praedestinationis et electionis nunc decretum de toto opere a perducendi homines ad salutem, nunc peculiariterb decretum de certis hominibus sub certa ratione intellectui divino cognitis certo salvandis. Atque haec quidem latior est vocabulorum acceptio, qua totus, ut sic loquar, processus Dei in negotio salutis, in tempore locum habiturus, ab aeterno decretus esse concipitur; qua ratione praedestinatio, seu aeterna Dei electio, salutem filiorum Dei procurare et ea, quae ad ipsam pertinent, disponere dicitur. Vid. F. C. artic. XI. n. IV. p. 618. Et certi quidam gradus, in quibus consistat electio aut praedestinatio, numerantur; vid. Sol. Deci. Form. Cone. art. XI. p. 802. Adde b. Mus. Dissert. de Aet. El. Decr. an. 1668. edita. § 266. sq. p. 205. 206.

Formula Concordiae: ,,Erstlich ist der Unterschied zwischen der ewigen Vorsehung Gottes und ewigen Wahl seiner Kinder zu der ewigen Seligkeit mit Fleiss zu merken. Denn praescientia vel praevisio, das ist, dass Gott alles vorher siehet und weiss, ehe es geschieht, welches man die Vorsehung Gottes nennet, gehet über alle Kreaturen, gute und böse, dass er nämlich alles zuvor siehet und weiss, was da ist oder sein wird, was da geschieht oder geschehen wird, es sei gut oder bös, weil vor Gott alle Dinge, sie seien vergangen oder zukünftig, unverborgen und gegenwärtig sind. Wie geschrieben stehet Matth. 10,29.: ,Kauft man nicht zween Sperlinge um einen Pfennig? noch fällt derselben keiner auf die Erde ohne euren Vater‘; und Psalm 139,16.: ,Deine Augen sahen mich, da ich noch unbereitet war, und waren alle Tage auf dein Buch geschrieben, die noch werden sollten, und derselben keiner da war; item, Jes. 37, 28.: ,Ich kenne deinen Auszug und Einzug und dein Toben wider mich.‘

Die ewige Wahl Gottes aber vel praedestinatio, das ist, Gottes Verordnung zur Seligkeit, gehet nicht zumal über die Frommen und Bösen, sondern allein über die Kinder Gottes, die zum ewigen Leben erwählt und verordnet sind, ehe der Welt Grund gelegt ward', wie Paulus spricht Eph. 1, 5.: ,Er hat uns erwählet in Christo Jesu und verordnet zur Kindschaft.‘ Die Vorsehung Gottes (praescientia) siehet und weiss zuvor auch das Böse, aber nicht also, dass es Gottes gnädiger Wille wäre, .dass es geschehen sollte; sondern was der verkehrte, böse Wille des Teufels und der Menschen vornehmen und thun werde und wolle, das siehet und weiss Gott alles zuvor, und hält PART. III. CAP. XII. seine praescientia, das ist, Vorsehung, auch in den bösen Händeln oder Werken ihre Ordnung, dass von Gott dem Bösen, welches Gott nicht will, sein Ziel und Mass gesetzt wird, wie fern es gehen und wie lang es währen solle, wann und wie ers hindern und strafen wolle; welches doch alles Gott der Herr also regieret, dass es zu seines göttlichen Namens Ehre und seiner Auserwählten Heil gereichen und die Gottlosen darob zu Schanden werden müssen.

Der Anfang aber und Ursache des Bösen ist nicht Gottes Vorsehung (denn Gott schafft und wirkt das Böse nicht, hilft und beförderts auch nicht), sondern des Teufels und der Menschen böser, verkehrter Wille, wie geschrieben stehet: ,Israel, du bringest dich in Unglück; aber dein Heil stehet allein bei mir.‘ (Hos. 13, 9.) Item: ,Du bist nicht ein Gott, dem gottlos Wesen gefalle‘, Ps. 5, 5.

Die ewige Wahl Gottes aber siehet und weiss nicht allein zuvor der Auserwählten Seligkeit, sondern ist auch aus gnädigem Willen und Wohlgefallen Gottes in Christo Jesu eine Ursache, so da unsere Seligkeit, und was zu derselben gehöret, schaffet, wirket, hilft und befördert; darauf auch unsere Seligkeit also gegründet ist, dass die Pforten der Höllen nichts dawider vermögen sollen; wie geschrieben stehet: Meine Schafe wird mir niemand aus meiner Hand reissen; und abermals: Und es wurden gläubig, so viel ihrer zum ewigen Leben verordnet waren. (Matth. 16, 18. Joh. 10, 28. Act. 13, 48.)“ (Concordia. Ed. Muellerus. p. 704. sqq.)

Facultas Th. Witebergensis: ״Bei diesem so hellen undunverneinlichen Ausspruch des Concordienbuchs sucht Et, Huberus eine solche nichtige Ausflucht, dass er schreibt: ,Ich gebe solche Beschreibung der Erwählung der Kinder Gottes nach‘, spricht er, ,in dem Verstand, wie es daselbst das Concordienbuch gebraucht; denn daselbst wird die Gnadenwahl particulariter gebraucht in der Application und in dem Event oder Ausgang der Seligmachung. Wenn das Wort praedestinatio (Verordnung zum Leben) in dem Verstand gebraucht wird, so lassen wir es‘, spricht er, ,zu, dass die Praedestination allein die Kinder Gottes angehöret.‘ Es soll aber der christliche Leser dargegen wissen, dass dieser Schein Huberi alsdenn wird gelten, wenn er zuvor aus dem Concordienbuch wird erwiesen haben, dass das Concordienbuch irgend einer andern Wahl gedenke, als eben nur allein dieser einigen, welche allda geschrieben ist, dass sie nicht zugleich über Böse und Gute, sondern allein über die gottseligen gläubigen Kinder Gottes gehe. Darnach so ist es ein lauter Gedichte, damit die Einfältigen zu bethören, dass er vorgibt, er lasse die ParticularElection, welche allein über die Kinder Gottes gehet, zu und streite nicht wider dieselbe, da er doch eben dieselbe Lehre, die wir nach Anleitung Gottes Worts und des Concordienbuchs führen, zum heftigsten anflehtet und als einen calvinischen Irrthum verlästert.“ (Consil. Witeb. I, 606.)

Aeg. Hunnius: ״Jam si descendatur ad quaestionem, ad quos haec gratuita Dei electio ante mundi jacta fundamenta in ipso consilio Dei inita referenda sit, ibi sic respondet Concordiae liber: ,Praedestinatio seu aeterna Dei electio tantum ad bonos et dilectos filios Dei pertinet.‘ In formula ipsa aeterna electio, seu praedestinatio Dei ad salutem, non simul ad bonos et ad malos refertur, sed tantum ad filios Dei. Huberus econtra, haec libri Concordiae verba recensens, eidem sic obloquitur suo dogmate: ,Praedestinatio seu aeterna Dei electio nequaquam tantum ad bonos et dilectos Dei filios est referenda (hoc enim extreme Calvinianum est), sed aeque ad malos et infideles, quia simpliciter ad omnes, sive in unigenitum Dei Filium fuerint credituri, sive non credituri. Imo Deus elegit tantum infideles, quales omnes natura sumus‘, Rettung, p. 5. Si autem per electionem intelligatur electionis applicatio (quae nihil aliud est, quam justificatio), in hac demum significatione concedit Huberus, ad solos Dei filios pertinere electionem, i. e., justifleationem. Ipsammet vero electionem, de qua Concordiae liber ex Scriptura loquitur, non minus ad filios diaboli (quales sunt impoeni-

tentes omnes), quam ad Dei filios extendit, idque contra claram, expressam et irrefragibilem literam Formulae Concordiae.“ (Volum. Disputatt. 1598. p. 304. sq.)

Philippi: ,,Nach der Concordienformel hat Gott von Ewigkeit das Heil aller Menschen beschlossen und zur Ausführung dieses RathSchlusses in der Fülle der Zeit seinen Sohn zur Versöhnung der Sünden der ganzen Welt in den Tod gegeben. Diesen allgemeinen, in Christo vollzogenen Gnadenrathschluss erbietet er ernstlich allen Mensehen durch das Wort, welches als Träger des Geistes in sich selbst bekehrungskräftiges Heilsmittel ist. Alle diejenigen demnach, welche durch das Wort Gottes zum Glauben und damit zur Gerechtigkeit und zum Leben geführt werden, verdanken dies lediglich dem göttlichen Erbarmen, das sie von Ewigkeit in Christo erwählet und in derZeit in ihm errettet hat; diejenigen hingegen, welche nicht zu diesem Heilsziele gelangen, haben es ihrem eigenen Widerstreben gegen Gottes Gnadenwillen und gegen sein Wort und seinen Geist zuzuschreiben. Die Concordienformel schliesst also durch die Art, wie sie die Bekehrung des Menschen rein als Wirkung der göttlichen Gnade fasst, jede pelagianische, semipelagianische und synergistische Anschauungsweise aus, ohne dadurch dem entgegengesetzten Extreme des Prädestinatianismus zu verfallen, indem sie Gottes Gnade, Christi Opfer und Gottes Wort als auf alle Menschen sich erstreckend darstellt.“ (Kirchl. Glaubensl. IV. Erste Hälfte. 1868. p. 62. sq.)


### On Predestination and Reprobation: ANTITHESIS. Loescherus

ANTITHESIS. Loescherus: “Although those who impugn this doctrine are accustomed to object not a few things; yet it does not stand in the way... 3. that predestination does not constitute a peculiar article of faith and religion, but rather wanders through all the articles, e.g., concerning redemption, vocation, conversion, etc. And the Formula of Concord teaches this very thing in Art. XI.; it is therefore erroneously separated from those articles and taught as something disjointed. For we reply: the word ‘predestination’ certainly has a certain broad signification, not in the sacred code, but in the symbolic books. Whence we again distinguish between the symbolic and the biblical signification of that word: the former is broad, the latter is strict and contracted. The former has no place here, except negatively; the latter, however, obtains here. For we propose this doctrine from Scripture; therefore, it must also be presented in the words of Scripture and in that sense which they obtain in Scripture.” (Th. thet. 1694. p. 247. sq.)

The blessed G. Cundisius, Notes on Comp. Hutt. L. XIII. Q. V. § 1. p. 797: The term ‘predestination’ is taken either broadly or strictly. Broadly, where it is accepted, it comprehends the entire apparatus of the means of salvation; in this sense, the Formula of Concord uses the same word in the Solid Declaration, Art. XI. Used strictly, this word signifies the very ordination of the faithful unto salvation, instituted according to God’s purpose. For which reason πρόθεσις, or purpose, and προορισμός, or predestination, as distinct, ought to be considered here. The blessed Balth. Meisnerus also acknowledged this stricter acceptation in Anthrop. Dec. II. Disput. IV. Q. III. n. IV. § 31., when he writes: First, (God) ordained the means for all; but because not all were going to accept them, therefore He did not choose all. Thus, therefore, the decree of the means is prior in order to the decree of election, and therefore the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith and considered from eternity, is not a means of the decree, but a cause. But more will be said about these things in what follows. Add the blessed Musaeus, l. c.

Heilbrunnerus: “Although it is true in itself, as the Word of God teaches, that with respect to the multitude of the reprobate few are elect, yet the doctrine of the Calvinists is false, that by an absolute, secret, and inscrutable [decree] of God PART III. CHAP. XII. decree, without any regard for unworthiness, the greater part of the human race was created and destined for eternal destruction; the same thing which is rightly censured in the Apology of the Articles of Visitation. In this opinion, some famous and orthodox theologians taught that the election of God is universal, using the word "election" in a broader sense. Whence the Book of Concord confesses in the introduction to that article that theologians do not always use similar expressions regarding this article, and in the aforementioned Saxon Apology it is written that certain orthodox doctors of the church refer the word "election" to all men in a broader sense, because (as far as the will of God is concerned) no human being has been excluded from the grace of life by a decree or purpose of God; just as the Calvinists falsely teach. But because not long ago a certain dispute arose from this phrase or proposition, while one party wished it to be proper, but the other less proper, and the former came under suspicion among some as if it taught that all men, whether they believe or do not believe, are actually elected: it would be better and more advisable, indeed necessary for the sake of the tranquility of the church, while retaining the mind or sentiment declared above, to oppose the Calvinistic particularity with the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures concerning the universal love of God, the universal merit of Christ, and also the universal promises of the Gospel, and to abstain in the future from the aforementioned phrase, which was accepted under the name of ambiguity and is nowhere expressed in the sacred oracles, out of a desire for peace and concord.” (Theses on Predestination, A.D. 1597. See Consil. th. Wittebergens. I, 649, et seq.)

Winckelmannus: “They say, moreover, that many theologians of great name have affirmed the universal election of all men. R.: I do not deny it; but they spoke more freely before the controversy was stirred up (a thing which happened to Augustine and other fathers before the conflicts were stirred up in other chapters of doctrine), using the word 'election' improperly for the general will of God toward all men. Now, therefore, the mind is to be retained and the language corrected.” (Disp. th. in academ. Giessena hab. P. V, p. 179.)

Gerhardus: “To those who posit that all believers without exception, even the προςκαίρους [temporary ones], are elected, . . . we oppose this immovable argument: All the elect are saved. Those who believe for a time and afterwards fall away again are not saved; therefore, those who believe for a time and afterwards fall away again are not the elect. . . To the fourth class belong the sayings in which election is said always to attain its end, Rom. 11:7: 'What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it; the rest, however, were blinded.' Certainly, therefore, election is never frustrated of its end, and consequently the elect also always obtain the end of election, 2 Tim. 2:19: 'The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, the Lord knows those who are His.'” (Disp. isagog. p. 754, et seq.)

S. Schmidtius: “Christ is the meritorious cause of predestination, who by His satisfaction obtained it for us. Whence we are said to be elected in Christ, Eph. 1:4, predestined through Jesus Christ, v. 5, predestined according to the purpose of God’s own and the grace given to us in Christ Jesus, 2 Tim. 1:9, Eph. 1: 11. So that the reason for predestination is not the same as that of God’s purpose concerning the redemption of men. For here the philanthropy of God was moved to destine a redeemer for the human race, but the predestination of God is solicitous about applying the benefits of redemption to this or that man according to that purpose, which actual application and solicitude Christ has already merited.” (Aphorism. th. p. 292.)

Hannekenius: “And not only are those who believe finally in general elected, so that this is the whole decree of eternal election—that all who believe finally will be saved—without an application being made to certain individuals, but also certain persons, e.g., Peter, Paul, David, etc., are elected. Rom. 8:35, Eph. 1:4, 2 Tim. 1:9. Truly F. C. Art. 11: 'And indeed God, in that counsel, purpose, and ordination of His, not only procured the salvation of His own in general, but also mercifully foreknew all and singular the persons of the elect (who are to be saved through Christ) unto salvation'

He] chose and decreed that, in that manner (which we have already recited), He wills to make them participants of eternal salvation, to help them, to promote their salvation, and to confirm and preserve them through His grace, gifts, and efficacy.” (Verae th. Synops. p. 58 sq.)

Calovius: “The Remonstrants falsely assert that the decree of election is not a decree concerning certain persons to be destined by name to eternal life, but only a decree concerning the condition by which God wills that persons, that is, all men, be destined for salvation. . . And the Arminians themselves confess (f. 102. b.) that this decree of the Remonstrants ‘in fact predestines, segregates, or inscribes no certain persons in the book of life (for this cannot be done unless divine foreknowledge intervenes).’ But what kind of decree of predestination will that be, which predestines no certain persons? What kind of decree of election, which segregates none, and inscribes none in the book of life?” (Consideratio Arminianismi. 1657. p. 239 sq.)

ANTITHESES. Antithesis of the Arminians: “It is evident that it is false that election was made from eternity; there is only one passage in Scripture which seems to affirm this, from which this common error was born, namely, the passage at Eph. 1:4.” (Apologia Remonstrantium, c. 18. f. 190.)

J. Fechtius: “The modern Tübingen theologians dissent from all other Lutheran theologians on this subject, regarding whose opinion it must be observed: 1. That the same does not appear in the writings of the older Tübingen theologians, who with one voice with us made the man who finally believes the object of election. We have produced the testimonies of this matter in ‘Apparatus ad epp. Marbachianas’ c. 7. p. 276. 2. That this opinion of the Tübingen theologians is clearly one and the same with the opinion of the Arminians. . . 3. That the opinion of the Tübingen theologians is that election is either taken broadly, and then has as its object all believers as such, that is, insofar as and as long as they believe; or strictly, and then has as its object only those who finally believe.” (Compend. univers. th. complex, p. 426 sq.)

Melch. Nicolai: “Predestination is the eternal decree of God concerning the human race, which had fallen into sin and death, to restore it through Christ—without any merit of its own or the dignity of foreseen works, which do not precede to constitute, but follow to declare—and to lead it through the Word and Sacraments by the efficacious and yet resistible operation of the Holy Spirit through faith unto eternal life and glory. . . Those who restrict the term ‘election’ only to those persevering in faith, and define the decree of election by perseverance as the ultimate and specific difference, we do not refute, because they defend the same dogma of truth with us, albeit with differing terms, for we do not have the custom of litigating over terms with our brethren. Yet we cannot grasp, saving the peace of those very great men, how perseverance constitutes election, which posits nothing, but only continues what has been posited. ‘Hold fast what you have,’ says the Son of God (Rev. 2:25). Therefore, those who persevere do not acquire some new gift of God which they did not have, but preserve what they had. Just as he who was cut off from Christ through unbelief was not therefore not in Christ, so he who ceased to be elect through the vice of unbelief was not therefore not elect.” (Compend. did. et elencht. 1654. p. 157, 168 sq.)

Hofmannus: “According to Scripture, the object of this eternal will of God is not men as individuals, but it is man, or, which amounts to the same thing, humanity. . . It will now be decidedly false to say of ‘being chosen’ (ἐκλέγεσθαι) that it denotes the eternal destination of certain individuals to salvation. . ., since it is rather primarily the congregation, and indeed the whole congregation of Christ or an individual as a member of the same, of which it is said,” PART III. CAP. XII.

Latin:

ANTITHESIS. Loesciierus: ,,Quamquam, qui hanc doctrinam impugnant, non pauca objicere soleant; non tamen obstat, ... 3. praedestinationem non peculiarem fidei et religionis articulum constituere, sed potius vagari per omnes articulos, e. g. de redemtione, vocatione, conversione etc. Atque id ipsum docere Formulam Concordiae art. XI.; erronee igitur ab iis articulis separari et disjunctum doceri; Nam regerimus: habet certe praedestinationis vox significationem aliquam amplam, non in sacro codice, sed in libris symbolicis. Unde denuo distinguimus inter significationem ejus vocis symbolicam et biblicam: illa est ampla, haec stricta et contracta. Illa hic nullum habet locum, nisi remotive; haec vero hic obtinet. Proponimus enim doctrinam hanc ex scriptura, ergo id praestandum quoque est verbis scripturae et in eo sensu, quem in scriptura obtinent.“ (Th. thet. 1694. p. 247. sq.) $

ic b. G. Cundisius Not. ad Comp. Hutt. L. XIII. Q. V. § 1. p. 797.: Praedestinationis vocabulum sumitur vel late vel stricte. Late ubi accipitur, comprehendit universum mediorum salutis apparatum,; in hoc sensu vocem eandem usurpat Formula Concordiae in solida Dedar. Art. XI. Stricte usurpata haec vox significat ipsam ordinationem fidelium ad salutem, secundum Dei propositum institutam. Qua ratione πρόΰεσις, seu propositum, et προορισμός, seu praedestinatio, ut distincta, hic considerari debent. Eandem acceptionem strictiorem agnovit etiam b. Balth. Meisnerus in Anthrop. Dec. II. Disput. IV. Q. III. η. IV. § 31., cum scribit: Primum media ordinavit (Deus) pro omnibus; quia vero non omnes accepturi erant, ideo non omnes elegit. Sic ergo decretum mediorum ordine prius est decreto electionis, ideoque meritum Christi fide apprehensum et ab aeterno consideratum non est medium decreti, sed causa. Sed de his in seqq. plura dicentur. Add. b. Mus. 1. c.

Heilbrunnerus: ,,Etsi per se verum est, quod verbum Dei docet, respectu multitudinis reproborum paucos esse electos, tamen falsa est Calvinistarnm doctrina, quod absoluto, arcano et imperscrutabili Dei PART. III. CAP. XII. decreto, nullo indignitatis respectu, major pars generis humani ad aeternum exitium creata et destinata sit; idem quod in Apologia articulorum visitationis jure reprehenditur. In hac sententia aliquot celebres et orthodoxi theologi electionem Dei universalem esse docuerunt, vocabulo electionis in latiore significatione usi. Unde fatetur liber Concordiae in exordio istius articuli, quod theologi non similes semper de hoc articulo locutiones usurpent, et in praedicta Apologia Saxonica scriptum extat, quod doctores quidam ecclesiae orthodoxi in latiore significatione vocem electionis ad omnes homines referant, quia (quoad voluntatem Dei) nemo hominum a gratia vitae decreto vel proposita Dei exclusus sit; sicut Calvinistae falso docent. Quia vero haud ita pridem ex hac phrasi vel propositione lis quaedam orta est, dum una pars propriam, altera vero eam minus propriam esse voluit, ac prior illa in eam apud nonnullos venit suspicionem, quasi doceret, omnes homines, sive credant, sive non credant, actu electos esse: satius et consultius, imo propter ecclesiae tranquillitatem necessarium fuerit, retenta mente vel sententia superius declarata, Calvinianae particularitati Scripturae S.S. doctrinam de universali Dei dilectione, universali Christi merito, promissionibus quoque evangelii universalibus, quam propositionem ambiguitatis nomine susceptam et in sacris oraculis nuspiam expressam opponere et a praedicta phrasi pacis et concordiae studio in posterum abstinere.“ (Theses de praedest. A. 1597. Vid. Consil. th. Wittebergens. I, 649. sq.)

Winckelmannus: ,,Ajunt praeterea, multos magni nominis theologos affirmasse universalem omnium hominum electionem. R.: Non inficior; verum ante motam controversiam liberius locuti sunt (id quod Augustino et aliis patribus ante mota certamina in aliis doctrinae capitibus accidit), usi vocabulo electionis improprie pro generali Dei voluntate erga omnes homines. Jam igitur retinenda mens et corrigenda lingua.“ (Disp. th. in academ. Giessena hab. P. V, p. 179.)

Gerhardus: ,,Illis, qui omnes omnino credentes, etiam προςκαίρους, electos esse statuunt, . . opponimus irtimotum hoc argumentum: Omnes electi salvantur. Qui ad tempus credunt et postea iterum deflciunt, non salvantur; ergo qui ad tempus credunt et postea iterum deficiunt, non sunt electi. . . Ad quartam classem pertinent dicta, in quibus electio finem suum semper dicitur assequi, Rom. 11, 7.: ,Quod quaerebat Israel, non est consecutus; electio autem est consecuta; caeteri vero excaecati sunt.‘ Utique ergo electio fine suo nunquam frustratur, ac proinde etiam electi finem electionis semper sortiuntur, 2 Tim. 2, 19.: ,Firmum stat fundamentum Dei, habens signaculum hoc, novit Dominus, qui sint sui.‘“(Disp, isagog. p. 754. sq.)

S. Schmidtius: ,,Christus praedestinationis causa meritoria est, qui satisfactione sua eam pro nobis impetravit. Unde electi dicimur in Christo Ephes. 1,4., praedeflniti per Jesum Christum v. 5., praedefiniti secundum propositum Dei proprium et gratiam, datam nobis in Christo Jesu 2 Tim. 1, 9. Ephes. 1, 11. Ut neque eadem praedestinationis ratio sit, quae propositi Dei de redemtione hominum. Nam hic philanthropia Dei mota est ad destinandum humano generi redemtorem, sed praedestinatio Dei solicita est de redemtionis beneficiis huic illive homini juxta propositum istud applicandis finaliter, quam actualem applicationem et solicitudinem Christus jam promeruit.“ (Aphorism. th. p. 292.)

Hannekenius: ,,Nec tantum finaliter credentes in genere sunt electi, ut hoc sit totum electionis aeternae decretum, omnes finaliter credentes salvabuntur, non facta applicatione ad certa individua, sed et certae personae, v. g. Petrus, Paulus, David etc., sunt electi. Rom. 8,35. Eph. 1, 4. 2 Tim. 1, 9. Vere F. C. art. 11.: ,Et quidem Deus illo suo consilio, proposito et ordinatione non tantum in genere salutem suorum procuravit, verum etiam omnes et singulas personas electorum (qui per Christum salvandi sunt) clementer praescivit, ad salutem

elegit et decrevit, quod eo modo (quem jam recitavimus) ipsos per suam gratiam, dona atque efficaciam, salutis aeternae participes facere, juvare, eorum salutem promovere, ipsos confirmare et conservare velit.‘ “ (Verae th. Synops. p. 58. sq.)

Calovius: ,,Decretum electionis non esse decretum de personis certis nominatim vitae aeternae destinandis, sed tantum decretum de conditione, qua Deus personas, id est, homines omnes saluti vult destinari, falso asserunt Bemonstrantes. . . Et fatentur ipsi Arminiani f. 102. b., decretum istud Remonstrantium,de facto nullas certas personas praedestinare, segregare vel libro vitae inscribere (hoc enim fieri non posse, nisi intercedat divina scientia)‘. Quale vero illud decretum praedestinationis erit, quod nullas personas certas praedestinet? quale electionis decretum, quod nullas segreget, nullas libro vitae inscribat?“ (Consideratio Arminianismi. 1657. p. 239. sq.)

ANTITHESES. Antithesis Arminianorum: ,,Patet, falsum esse, quod electio facta sit ab aeterno; unus tantum in Scriptura locus est, qui id affirmare videtur, unde communis error iste natus est, locus videl. ad Eph. 1, 4.<‘ (Apologia Remonstrantium, c. 18. f. 190.)

J. Fechtius: ,,Dissentiunt in hoc argumento a caeteris Lutheranis theologis omnibus theologi Tubingenses hodierni, circa quorum sententiam observandum est: 1. Eandem in veterum Tubingensium theologorum scriptis non comparere, quippe qui uno nobiscum ore objectum electionis hominem flnaliter credentem fecerunt. Testimonia ejus rei produximus in,apparatu ad epp. Marbachianas‘ c. 7. p. 276. 2. Esse lianc Tubingensium sententiam plane unam eandemque cum opinione Arminianorum ... 3. Sententiam Tubingensium esse, electionem vel late sumi, et tum pro objecto habere omnes credentes, qua tales, id est, quatenus et quamdiu credunt; vel stricte, atque tum habere pro objecto tantum eos, qui flnaliter credunt.“ (Compend. univers. th. complex, p. 426 sq.)

Melch. Nicolai: ,,Praedestinatio est aeternum Dei decretum de humano genere, in peccatum et mortem prolapso, per Christum, nullo suo merito aut praevisorum operum dignitate, quae non antecedunt, ut constituant, sed consequuntur, ut declarent, reparando et per verbum et sacramenta efficaci et tamen resistibili Spiritus S. operatione per fidem ad vitam et gloriam aeternam perducendo. . . Qui vocabulum electionis tantum ad perseverantes in fide restringunt et decretum electionis perseverantia, tanquam ultima et specifica differentia, definiunt, eos, quia discrepantibus vocabulis idem nobiscum veritatis dogma tuentur, non redarguimus, quia de vocabulis cum fratribus nostris litigandi consuetudinem non habemus. Capere tamen non possumus, salva maximorum virorum pace, quomodo perseverantia constituat electionem, quae nihil ponit, sed tantum, quod positum est, continuat. ,Tenete, quod habetis‘, inquit Filius Dei Apoc. 2, 25. Perseverantes ergo non novum aliquod Dei donum, quod non habuerunt, acquirunt, sed quod habuerunt, conservant. Sicut non ideo non fuit in Christo, qui per incredulitatem excisus fuit e Christo, ita non ideo non fuit electus, qui incredulitatis vitio desiit esse electus.“ (Compend. did. et «elencht. 1654. p. 157. 168. sq.)

Hofmannus: ,,Gegenstand dieses ewigen Willens Gottes sind nach der Schrift nicht die Menschen als einzelne, sondern der Mensch ist es, oder, was gleichviel sagen will, die Menschheit. . . Entschieden falsch wird es nun sein, von,Erwähltwerden‘ (εκλέγεσ&αι) zu sagen, es bezeichne die ewige Bestimmung gewisser Individuen zur Seligkeit. . ., da es vielmehr zunächst die Gemeinde ist, und zwar die ganze Gemeinde Christi oder eine einzelne als Glied derselben, von welcher es heisst, PART. III. CAP. XH.


### On Predestination and Reprobation: God has chosen them. It is said of individual Christians because they are, and…

God has chosen them. It is said of individual Christians because they are, and in so far as they are, members of the congregation.” (Schriftbeweiss. I, 193. 199. 201.)

Thomasius: “Considered in itself, the divine purpose has no relation to individual persons; it is not a decree regarding the election of individuals, but rather ordered love. In other words: God’s love rests upon Christ, the Beloved, and in Him upon all who unite themselves with Him in faith, becoming one person with Him through faith. Who these are is not the content, not a determination that that decree has in itself—it is therefore not closed on this side, and indeed not, because it is directed toward the conduct of men. . . . And so it fulfills itself, if I may say so, only gradually with the individual persons; who these are, God indeed knows beforehand by virtue of His prescience, but that is not the content, not the determination of that general decree concerning the men who are to be saved.” (Christi Person und Werk. 1853. I, 400. sq.) “

The eternal purpose. . . is not individual election, but. . . a universal will of grace, encompassing the whole lost human race, yet not a simply universal one, but decided and contained in Christ, Eph. 1:4, for it consists precisely in this, that God wills to save humanity in Christ, the object of His love and the acquirer of our salvation, and only in Christ, i.e., insofar as it surrenders itself to Him in faith, not without and outside of Him.” (Das Bekenntnis der ev.lutherischen Kirche u. s. w. 1848. p. 219.)

Vilmar: “More fruitfully. . . the Lutheran dogmaticians could have developed the doctrine of the Formula of Concord without any question, if they had posed to themselves the question whether there was not occasion in the Apology to conceive of election as the representation of the founding of the Christian Church, as an institution of salvation as a whole, and consequently to eliminate entirely election as relating to individual persons, i.e., to assert election for individuals only insofar as these individuals, in the separation of the Christian congregation from the world, are included among the saints.” (Dogmatik. 1874. p. 16. sq.)

Luthardt: “The fundamental error from the beginning is the too immediate relation to individuals, instead of to humanity as God wills it in Christ, into whose fellowship then only the individuals enter through faith. These individual believers are then, however, not the object of a special and particular predestination, but in them the one and general decree of the love of God is merely realized historically.” (Compend. ed. 3. p. 95.) §

3. In order to recognize the decree of predestination, insofar as it concerns the whole business of human salvation, the order of the divine acts must be diligently observed, as they follow one another in the sign of reason according to divine revelation. To this pertain those degrees of which predestination consists, according to the F. C. l. c., and of which we shall see shortly.

Formula of Concord: “Therefore, if one wishes to think or speak rightly and fruitfully of the eternal election or of the predestination and ordination of the children of God to eternal life, one should

“...one must accustom oneself not to speculate about the bare, secret, hidden, unsearchable providence of God, but rather how the counsel, purpose, and ordinance of God in Christ Jesus, who is the right and true Book of Life, is revealed to us through the Word; namely, that the entire doctrine concerning the purpose, counsel, will, and ordinance of God, concerning our redemption, calling, justification, and salvation, be summarized; just as Paul treats and explains this article in Rom. 8:29 ff., Eph. 1:4 ff., as also Christ in the parable in Matt. 22:1 ff.” (Concordia, p. 707.)

Quenstedtius: “Divine decrees are eternal, and therefore one is not prior to another in terms of time; but if you look at the order, the decree of redemption ... is prior to election, that is, in the sign of the divine reason, with respect to external objects, and thence according to the moments of our conception.” (Th. did.-pol. P. III. c. 2. s. 2. q. 3. f. 51.) For as regards the thing itself, it must be confessed that there are not, within God, acts of intellect or will that are really distinct and succeeding one another, on account of the supreme simplicity and immutability of God.

For it is not permitted to invent either the acts themselves or their series and order according to our own ingenuity, but we must look to what God Himself teaches us concerning the acts of His intellect and will, and how, according to the Scriptures, this act presupposes that one, and not that one this one, especially so that we may take care not to attribute some act to God in such a way that we exclude or pervert another, which ought to have been acknowledged no less, or indeed as prior. § 4. Therefore, because God, out of His supreme goodness, not only loved men from Himself, when He created them in the first man according to His own divine image, but also pursues them, even when viewed in the fallen Adam as sinners, with such love that for the sake of procuring their salvation He gave His Son as Redeemer to all; it must also be acknowledged that, although God from all eternity had foreseen that men would be corrupted by sin, He nevertheless decreed, for the sake of procuring their salvation, to give His Son, who would pay the price of redemption for all.

As He is good not only in Himself, but also to others, His creatures, and intends to lead them to their ends, for which they were created. As His work, which is very good, hitherto undefiled or corrupted by any stain.

For thus Paul testifies in 1 Tim. 2:4, that God wills (not merely to signify by an external word, as if He wills, but truly and seriously to will) all (men, for whom the faithful ought to pray, all, I say, and each one who exists, not in the state of integrity, but after the fall, and therefore sinners, with no one excluded, not even the tyrants under whom they lived, and Nero himself, who was never converted) to be saved (to attain true and eternal salvation). Cf. our Disputation on the Universal PART III. CAP. XII.

of Divine Grace, held at this place in the year 1675. Furthermore, we shall not, strictly speaking, call that will which terminates in the salvation of all a decree; however, the term "will" has a broader scope. And to this also pertains the distinction between the antecedent and consequent will; concerning which see the special Disputation of the blessed Musaeus, and what we have adduced from it in Part I, Chapter I, § 19, 20, Vol. II, p. 34.

ANTITHESES. Confession of faith: "By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life, and others foreordained to everlasting death. — Neither are any other redeemed by Christ, effectually called, justified, adopted, sanctified, and saved, but the elect only." (The constitution of the Presbyterian church in the U. S. of A. Philadelphia. Presbyterian Board of publication. 1840. p. 23. 25.)

To this pertains what Christ said in John 3:16: "So" (with such and so great, serious and efficacious love) "God loved the world" (the whole multitude of the inhabitants of the world, or the entire human race, which embraces believers and non-believers, just as it is divided into those and these in verse 18; here, however, it is viewed as the antitype of the promiscuous multitude of Israelites who, having once been attacked by the bites of fiery serpents on account of their rebellion against God, were near to death, according to verses 14 and 15), "that He gave His only begotten Son" (namely, to the world itself, or to the human race otherwise destined to perish, He gave the antitype of the bronze serpent, to be lifted up on the cross, according to verse 15), "that it might not be necessary for sinful men to perish, but that" (rather) "the world might be saved through Him," or, that all men contained in the world might have one through whom, by the serious intention of God, who is most loving toward them, they could be saved and would be saved, provided they did not reject Him, just as the bronze serpent had been erected for the good of all the wounded, so that all might have that from which they could be healed, according to verses 14, 15, and 17.

Cf. Romans 8:2-3, where it is said that God saw that men could not be saved by the law, since by carnal generation and the contracted original stain they had become inept for fulfilling the law, and therefore God, wishing to succor human infirmity, and so that that defect might be supplied, sent His own Son, who in the place of miserable men would fulfill the law and in the assumed flesh would satisfy the law, etc.

Add what we have said in Chapter II, Section III, § 10, and the blessed Musaeus’s Dissertation on the Insufficiency of Natural Light for Salvation against Edward Herbert, § 87 ff., p. 54 ff. For God knew from eternity all things that would happen in time, even though contingently, and He knew them immediately in themselves. See Part I, Chapter I, § 15, note h, Vol. II, p. 30.

And it is certain that the will of God concerning sending a redeemer for the sins of men presupposes the knowledge of those human sins themselves. For the act of the will, which terminates in the mission of the redeemer, did not finally begin in God in time, but it must be confessed that God, who sent the mediator in time, sent Him according to an eternal decree. And thus, when it is established that He was sent for the good of all sinful men, it must be confessed that it was so decreed of old, that He was sent not for the good of a few chosen out of a mere good pleasure, but for the good of all. Cf. what was said above, Part III, Chapter 1, § 3, p. 6 ff.; Chapter 2, Section 3, § 10, p. 120 ff.

§ 5. Furthermore, just as God declares in time that those who believe in Christ shall actually obtain salvation through the merit of Christ; and that all might be able to believe in Christ, God Himself promulgated the doctrine of faith in such a way that it could reach the ears and minds of all, so it must be acknowledged that God willed from eternity that all men should believe, and decreed to offer the Mediator, whom He had determined to send, to all to be embraced, once the doctrine concerning Him had been promulgated. To this point pertain the things we said in Part III, Chapter III, concerning Faith in Christ, § 1, and the fact that in the cited passage, John 3:16, the love of God is referred to all men in such a way that, nevertheless, the actual deliverance from destruction and the attainment of eternal life is restricted to believers, just as in the following verse, 18, after a division of men into believers and non-believers has been made, it is said of the former that they are not condemned, but of the latter that, by virtue of their very unbelief, they are subject to condemnation. According to that saying: "How shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard?" Rom. 10:14. "Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." Ibid., v. 17. See above, Chapter VII, § 22, note b, and Musaeus, Dissertation against Edward Herbert, § 90 ff., p. 55 ff., and what we discussed in the German treatise, *Gründliche Erweisung wider die Quäker* [Thorough Proof against the Quakers], § 25 and 49, p. 27 and 105. From this it is simultaneously evident that for a universal vocation it is not necessary that the doctrine of the Gospel be announced to each and every person face-to-face and immediately by heralds sent specifically by God; but it suffices that the doctrine be promulgated, or has been promulgated, in such a way that all (who are obligated to search for the true and saving religion and are able, through the use of reason, to know that a certain and saving religion, revealed by God Himself, exists somewhere) can arrive at the knowledge of it, and that none are barred by God out of an absolute good pleasure (by His being unwilling to provide them with the supply of that doctrine and denying every way by which they might arrive at that knowledge). Quenstedtius: "Taken in a broad sense, it also includes the indirect vocation, which occurs both in view of this universe, its governance, and the divine beneficence toward creatures, Rom. 1:20, 2:14-15, Acts 17:27, and through a general and confused report concerning a certain assembly in which it is said that the only true God is acknowledged and worshipped, 1 Kings 10:1 ff., 2 Kings 5:2-3, 1 Thess. 1:8... These species of vocation are more in the nature of invitations and incitements to inquire about the true worship of God and the assembly in which it flourishes, rather than a vocation properly so called; the reason is that they do not have as their proximate and immediate end the eternal salvation of man itself or the knowledge of Christ the Redeemer and the mysteries necessary for obtaining eternal salvation, but at least the bringing of them to the door of the true church... Just as the law promulgated on Mount Sinai did not bind only the Israelites then living and present, but also all their descendants, and indeed the nations themselves as well, Deut. 1:6, 4:11, so also that threefold vocation..." time of the fallen protoplasts, of Noah, and of the apostles) pertained not only to those present, or those to whom it was immediately made, but also to their posterity. . . The divine calling remains, according to the mind, will, purpose, and intention of God, truly general and universal, even if for someone among the remaining nations, who have merited by their sins the withdrawal of the grace of God and the interruption of the gracious calling, the solemn act itself does not flourish, and God does not restore the deposit of His Word once justly taken away. And that calling, which in itself and by the intention of God would always have been universal, becomes particular by accident on account of the negligence and contempt of men, not indeed simply, but only at this or that time. . . That God bestows the light of the Gospel upon one nation, while another is neglected; that some of the Turks, Americans, and other barbarians are converted to the faith, while the rest, who are their equals, are left in their infidelity, is to be ascribed to the secret and unsearchable judgment of God, and we must exclaim with Paul in Romans 11:33: „ώς ανεξερεύνητα, how unsearchable are His judgments and His ways past finding out.“ It must also be acknowledged that God does certain things regarding the order, manner, time, and degrees of the calling out of His absolute will.“ (L. c. P. III. c. 15. s. 1. th. 3. 13. 14. p. 662. sqq.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: „Antithesis:

3. Ad agnoscendum decretum praedestinationis, quatenus totum salutis humanae negotium spectat, diligenter observandus est ordo a actuum divinorum, prout in signo rationis b juxta revelationem divinam c alii alios sequuntur. Formula Concordiae: ,,Derwegen, wenn man von der ewigen Wahl oder von der Prädestination und Verordnung der Kinder Gottes zum ewigen Leben recht und mit Frucht gedenken oder reden will, soll

man sich gewöhnen, dass man nicht von der blossen, heimlichen, verborgenen, unausforschlichen Vorsehung Gottes speculire, sondern wie der Rath, Vorsatz und Verordnung Gottes in Christo Jesu, der das rechte wahre Buch des Lebens ist, durch das Wort uns geoffenbaret wird, nämlich, dass die ganze Lehre von dem Vorsatz, Rath, Willen und Verordnung Gottes, belangend unsere Erlösung, Beruf, Gerechtund Seligmachung, zusammengefasst werde; wie Paulus also diesen Artikel handelt und erkläret Röm. 8, 29. f. Eph. 1, 4. f., wie auch Christus in der Parabel Matth. 22, 1. f.“ (Concordia, p. 707.)

Quenstedtius: ,,Decreta divina sunt aeterna, adeoque unum altero non est prius ratione temporis; ordinem vero si spectes, decretum redemtionis ... prius est electione, puta in signo rationis divinae, respectu objectorum externorum, indeque juxta momenta conceptus nostri.“ (Th. did.-pol. P. III. c. 2. s. 2. q. 3. f. 51.) Nam quoad rem ipsam fatendum est, non dari intra Deum realiter distinctos et sibi invicem succedentes actus intellectus aut voluntatis, propter summam simplicitatem et immutabilitatem Dei.

Non enim fingere licet vel actus ipsos, vel eorum seriem atque ordinem pro nostro ingenio, sed spectandum est, quid Deus ipse de actibus intellectus ac voluntatis suae nos doceat, et quomodo juxta Scripturas actus hic illum, non autem ille hunc praesupponat, praesertim, ut attendamus, ne actum aliquem Deo sic tribuamus, ut alium, qui non minus, imo ut prior, agnoscendus erat, excludamus aut pervertamus. § 4. Itaque, quia Deus pro summa bonitate a sua homines non solum, cum in primo homine ad imaginem suam divinam crearet,b dilexit, verum etiam in Adamo lapso spectatos, tanquam peccatores, eo amore c prosequitur, ut procurandae salutis eorum causa Filium redemtorem d omnibus dederit; agnoscendum etiam est, quod, cum Deus ab omni aeternitate e praevidisset, homines peccato corruptum iri, tamen procurandae salutis illorum causa decreverit dare Filium, qui pro omnibus f solveret pretium redemtionis.

Qua bonus est non solum in se, verum etiam aliis, creaturis suis, easque ad suos fines, ad quos conditae sunt, perducere intendit. Tanquam opus suum valde bonum, hactenus nulla labe foedatum aut corruptum.

Sic enim Paulus 1 Tim. 2, 4. testatur, Deum omnes (homines, pro quibus orare debent fideles, omnes, inquam, et singulos, qui exsistunt, non in statu integritatis, sed post lapsum, adeoque peccatores, nemine excluso, ne quidem tyrannis, sub quibus vivebant, ipsoque Nerone, qui nunquam conversus fuit) velle (non tantum significare verbo externo, quasi velit, sed revera ac serio velle) salvos fieri (veram atque aeternam salutem consequi).
