salit. Gratiae Divinae, ad h. 1. habitam anno 1675. Caeterum voluntatem quidem illam, quae terminatur ad omnium salutem, non dicemus decretum, proprie loquendo; voluntatis autem vox latius patet. Atque huc etiam pertinet distinctio inter voluntatem antecedentem et carnequentem; de qua vid. Disp, peculiaris b. Musaei, et quae inde attulimus Part. I. cap. I. §. 19. 20. Vol. II. p. 34.

ANTITHESES. Confession of faith: ,,By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life, and others foreordained to everlasting death. — Neither are any other redeemed by Christ, effectually called, justified, adopted, sanetified, and saved, but the elect only.“ (The constitution of the Presbyterian church in the U. S. of A. Philadelphia. Presbyterian Board of publication. 1840. p. 23. 25.)

Quo pertinet, quod Christus Joh. 3, 16. dixit: Sic (tali ac tanto, serio atque efficaci amore) Deus dilexit mundum (totam incolarum orbis multitudinem, seu universum genus humanum, quod complectitur credentes et non credentes, prout deinde vers. 18. in illos et hos dividitur; hic autem spectatur ut antitypus promiscuae multitudinis Israelitarum, qui olim serpentum ignitorum morsibus ob rebellionem adversus Deum petiti, morti vicini erant, juxta vers. 14. 15.), ut filium suum unigenitum daret (nempe ipsi mundo, sdu generi humano alias perituro, daret antitypum serpentis aenei, in cruce erigendum, juxta vers. 15.), ne necesse esset homines peccatores perire, sed ut (potius) mundus servaretur per eum, seu, ut omnes in mundo contenti homines haberent, per quem, ex intentione seria Dei, ipsorum amantissimi, servari possent et servarentur, qui non respuerent, prout serpens aeneus omnium vulneratorum bono erectus fuerat, ut omnes haberent, unde sanarentur, juxta v. 14. 15. et 17.

Conf. Rom. 8, 2. 3., ubi dicitur, Deum vidisse, quod homines per legem non possent salvari, quippe per carnalem generationem contractamque labem originalem inepti facti ad legem implendam, ideoque Deum, humanae infirmitati succurrere volentem, atque ut defectus ille suppleretur, misisse proprium filium, qui loco hominum miserorum impleret legem et in assumpta carne legi satisfaceret etc.

Add., quae diximus Cap. II. Sect. III. § 10., et b. Mus. Dissert. de Insuffic. Lum. Nat. ad sal. contra Ed. Herbert. § 87. sqq. p. 54. sqq. Cognovit enim Deus ab aeterno omnia, in tempore, licet contingenter, futura, et cognovit quidem ea immediate in se ipsis. Vid. Part. I. Cap. I. § 15. not. h. Vol. II. p. 30.

Ac certum est, voluntatem Dei de mittendo redemtore pro peccatis hominum supponere cognitionem ipsorum peccatorum humanorum. Neque enim actus voluntatis, qui terminatur ad missionem redemtoris, demum in tempore coepit in Deo, sed fatendum est, Deum, qui mediatorem misit in tempore, misisse eum juxta decretum aeternum. Et sic, quando constat, missum esse illum omnium hominum peccatorum bono, fatendum est, ita olim decretum fuisse, ut non paucorum ex mero quodam beneplacito praelectorum, sed omnium bono mitteretur. Cf. supra dicta P. III. c. 1. §3. p. 6. sqq. c. 2. s. 3. § 10. p. 120. sqq.

PE PRAEDESTINATIONE ET REPROBATIONE. § 5. Deinde, sicut Deus in tempore declarat, quod per meritum Christi salutem actu consecuturi sint, qui a in Christum credunt; ut autem omnes in Christum credere possent, Deus ipse doctrinam b fidei ita promulgavit, ut ad omnium c aures mentesque posset pertingere, ita agnoscendum est, Deum ab aeterno voluisse, ut d homines omnes crederent, ac e decrevisse, mediatorem, quem mittere constituerat, promulgata doctrina de eo, omnibus offerre amplectendum. Huc spectant, quae diximus P. III. cap. III. de Fide in Christum § 1. et quod 1. c. Joh. 8, 16. dilectio Dei ita refertur ad omnes homines, ut tamen actualis liberatio ab interitu et consecutio vitae aeternae restringatur ad credentes prout in 8eq. v. 18. facta divisione hominum in credentes Jet non credentes de illis dicitur, quod non condemnentur, de his vero, quod vi ipsius incredulitatis obnoxii sint dam· nationi. Juxta illud: Quomodo credent, de quo non audiverunt f Rom. 10, 14. Fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per verbum Dei. Ibid. v. 17. Vid. supra cap. VII. § 22. not. b. et b. Mus. Dissert. contra jEd. Herbert. § 90. sqq. p. 55. sqq. et quae disseruimus in Tr. Germ. Gründliche Erweisung wider die Quäker § 25. et 49. p. 27. et 105. Unde simul constat, quod ad vocationem universalem non sit necessarium, ut doctrina evangelii omnibus et singulis coram et immediate per praecones peculiariter a Deo missos annuncietur; sed sufficiat, sic promulgari aut promulgatam esse doctrinam, ut omnes (qui ad veram et salutarem religionem scrutandam obligati sunt ac median te usu rationis cognoscere possunt, extare alicubi religionem certam et salutarem, a Deo ipso revelatam) in illius notitiam pervenire possint, non autem aliqui a Deo, ex absoluto beneplacito (copiam doctrinae illius ipsis facere nolente et viam omnem, qua in notitiam illam pertingant, denegante) arceantur. Quenstedtius: ״Late sumta includit etiam vocationem indirectam, quae iit tum intuitu hujus universi, ejusdemque gubernationis et divinae in creaturas beneficentiae, Rom. 1, 20. 2, 14. 15. Act. 17, 27., tum per famam generalem et confusam de coetu quodam, in quo dicitur agnosci et coli solus verus Deus. 1 Reg. 10, 1. sqq. 2 Reg. 5, 2. 3. 1 Thess. 1, 8 ... Hae vocationis species sunt magis invitamenta et incitamenta quaedam ad inquirendum de vero Dei cultu et coetu, in quo ille viget, quam vocatio proprie dicta; ratio est, quia pro fine proximo et immediato non habent ipsam hominis aeternam salutem vel cognitionem Christi redemtoris et mysteriorum ad salutem aeternam adipiscendam necessariorum, sed saltem adductionem ad januam verae ecclesiae. . . Sicut lex in monte Sinai promulgata non solos Israelitas tunc viventes et praesentes obligabat, sed omnes etiam eorum posteros, imo ipsas quoque gentes, Deut. 1, 6. 4, 11., sic quoque trina illa vocatio (tem35 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III. PART. III. CAP. XII. pore protoplastorum lapsorum, Noachi et apostolorum) non tantum pertinebat ad praesentes seu eos, quibus immediate facta est, sed etiam ad eorum posteritatem. . . Manet divina vocatio ex mente, voluntate, proposito et intentione Dei vere generalis et universalis, licet alicui apud reliquas gentes, qui gratiae Dei subtractionem et vocationis gratiosae intermissionem suis peccatis promeriti sunt, ipse solennis actus non vigeat et Deus verbi sui depositum semel juste ablatum non restituat. Et quae vocatio per se et ex intentione Dei semper fuisset universalis, illa per accidens ob incuriam et contemtum hominum fit particularis, non quidem simpliciter, sed tantum hoc vel illo tempore. . . Quod Deus uni nationi largitur evangelii lucem, altera neglecta; quod Turearum, Americanorum et aliorum barbarorum aliqui ad fidem convertuntur, reliqui, qui illis aequales sunt, in sua infidelitate relinquuntur, arcano et impervestigabili Dei judicio est adseribendum et exclamandum cum Paulo Rom. 11, 33.: ,ώς ανεξερεύνητα, quam inscrutabilia sunt judicia ejus et inpervestigabiles viae ejus.‘ Agnoscendum quoque est, Deum quaedam circa ordinem, modum, tempus et gradus vocationis ex absoluta voluntate agere.“ (L. c. P, III. c. 15. s. 1. th. 3. 13.14. f. 662. sqq.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis:


### On Predestination and Reprobation: Of the Papists, but especially of the Dominicans, who, embracing with the…

1. Of the Papists, but especially of the Dominicans, who, embracing with the Calvinists the absolute decree of predestination, assert that the grace of God was destined by God for only a few men, whom He chose by an absolute and efficacious will unto glory and a certain degree of glory. . .

2. Of certain fathers, who thought that the Gospel had not been preached by the apostles and their disciples throughout the whole world, and consequently that the fullness of the Gentiles had not yet entered in, and that therefore the universal calling commanded by Christ was still to be completed before the last day by the successors of the apostles in the ministry of the Word; thus Origen, Tr. 28 in Matt., and Augustine, Ep. 89 to Hesychius. . .

3. Of those Papists who, following Origen, assert that the Gospel of Christ has not yet reached all provinces, such as Bellarmine, l. 3 de Pontif. Rom. c. 4. . .

4. Of the Calvinists, who deny the catholicity of the calling and of the preaching of the Gospel because it directly opposes the fiction of absolute reprobation. For they commonly teach that God never willed to have mercy on all and each, never willed to send the Son to all and each, and never willed to offer His benevolence to all and each, as is evident from the Hague Conference, the Synod of Dort, and other of their writings, both public and private. . . Frequent in their mouths is the distinction between external and internal, efficacious and inefficacious calling. See Molinaeus in his letter sent to the Synod, pp. 410, 411: ‚I assert,‘ he says, ‚that an external calling can exist without the internal efficacy of the Spirit.‘ At Emden, p. 595, they say: ‚Many are called externally and hear the Word, who nevertheless are not drawn internally by the power of the Spirit, neither sufficiently nor efficaciously.‘ . . Furthermore, the Calvinists teach that the apostles preached the Gospel to all nations not collectively, but synecdochically or distributively, i.e., to a great part of the world, to these or those nations; whence they prefer to call that calling not universal, but common, viz., of the Jews (who alone, according to them, were called in the O.T. and at the beginning of the N.T.) and of the Gentiles (to some of whom the grace of calling happened, while the rest were plainly passed over by the mere good pleasure of God). . . Moses Amyraldus, professor at Saumur, c. 7 of his treatise on predestination, published in the French language in 1634, asserts a twofold preaching or calling: one through the ministry of divine providence only, which produces faith in the mercy of God, though destitute of the true and clear knowledge of the Redeemer, of whom the Gospel preaches to us, yet nevertheless sufficient for salvation, etc. . . . But that opinion was long ago exploded among the Pelagians and Scholastics, and was abjured by Amyraldus himself at the Synod of Alençon in 1637.“

For although it is rightly said that God willed all to be saved, if they believe, it must nevertheless also be confessed that God willed that all should believe, or that all should arrive at the knowledge of the truth (or of the true, divinely revealed doctrine), which He testifies that He wills in 1 Tim. 2:4. Cf. blessed Musaeus, *Diss. de Aet. El. Decr.* § 279, p. 207. Indeed, we do not call that will, by which God wills that all should believe (just as we do not call that by which God wills that all should be saved; concerning which see note c to § 4), a decree; yet this act of the divine will, by which God determined to promulgate the doctrine concerning the Mediator of God and men in such a way that it could reach the knowledge of all and obtain faith, is rightly called a decree. Cf. what was said above, Part III, Chap. 1, § 7, p. 15, et seq. §

6. And just as God in time joins divine power to His Word, through which the assent of supernatural faith, which is to be offered to the Word itself, and thus faith in Christ, can be and is excited, as often as man admits the Word itself without malicious resistance: so it is certain that God has decreed from eternity, when the Word is to be promulgated in time, to concur powerfully and graciously toward producing the effect of faith in such a way that no one shall lack faith, unless he has despised the means of conferring faith or the grace itself. See Prolegomena, Chap. II, § 39, and Part III, Chap. IV, § 29. Prolegomena, Chap. II, § 39, note Z, and Part III, Chap. IV, §§ 34, 35.

And to this pertains what is said in 1 Tim. 2:4, that God wills all to arrive at the knowledge of the truth, through which they may be saved, and thus at saving faith. Whence it follows entirely that God, as far as it depends on Him, is prepared and ready to confer the powers of arriving at that saving knowledge, or the powers of believing, so that no one is excluded by God, as if by His mere or absolute good pleasure; but if any do not arrive at it, it is necessary that the cause and the blame lie with them. And thus also Christ, in Matt. 23:37, expressly teaches that it is not absurd, but happens quite often (although it happens wickedly), that those whom He Himself seriously wills to gather to Himself, or, as far as it depends on Him, to contribute to their conversion and faith, by which they might be joined with their Mediator and obtain grace and salvation, the men themselves nevertheless do not wish to be converted and hinder and exclude the faith that would otherwise be obtained.

Formula of Concord: "But when a man will not hear the preaching, nor read God's Word, but despises the Word and the congregation of God, and thus dies and perishes in his sins: he can neither comfort himself with God's eternal election, nor obtain His mercy; for Christ, in whom we are elected, offers to all men..." PART III. CHAP. XII. offers His grace in the Word and holy Sacraments, and earnestly wills that one should hear it, and has promised that where two or three are gathered in His name and deal with His holy Word, He will be in the midst of them. But when such a person despises the instrument of the Holy Spirit and will not hear, then no injustice is done to him if the Holy Spirit does not enlighten him, but lets him remain stuck in the darkness of his unbelief and perish, of which it is written: "How often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you would not!" Matt. 23:37. And in this case, one may well say that man is not a stone or a block. For a stone or a block does not resist the one who moves it, nor does it understand or feel what is being done with it, as a man resists God the Lord with his will until he is converted. And it is nevertheless true that a man before conversion is still a rational creature, who has an intellect and a will, yet not an intellect in divine matters, or a will to desire anything good and salutary; however, he can do absolutely nothing toward his own conversion (as was also mentioned above), and in such a case is much worse than a stone and a block; for he resists the Word and will of God until God awakens, enlightens, and renews him from the death of sin. And although God does not force man so that he must become pious (for those who always resist the Holy Spirit and continually oppose the recognized truth, as Stephen speaks of the hardened Jews in Acts 7:51, they are not converted); yet God the Lord draws the man whom He wills to convert, and draws him in such a way that from a darkened intellect an enlightened intellect is made, and from a refractory will an obedient will is made. And that is what Scripture calls creating a new heart." (Concordia, p. 602 sq.)

Quenstedtius: "Although no one can escape the first impulse of grace, one can nevertheless, after having felt the first motions excited by prevenient grace, maliciously shake off that grace, Matt. 23:37 sq., Luke 7:30. But this shaking off does not occur from any resistance whatsoever... but from an actual, pertinacious resistance, and especially one that perseveringly opposes the means of salvation. For 'whenever men oppose the extreme perversity of malice and openly struggle and pertinaciously resist the drawing of the Holy Spirit, not out of a lack of strength, but out of a just judgment, He neglects the rebels and does not extend the most efficacious drawing beyond the order established from heaven.' See the blessed Huelsemann on the aids of grace, p. 238, D. Dorscheus, Pentadec. Disp. 9, p. 317, and diss. 3, ep. on grace... Preparing grace, applied through the Word to the individual to be converted, acts efficaciously by restraining natural and actual resistance, so that it does not resist morosely, or so that he ceases here and now from the exercise of this natural resistance (which cessation, or delay and space of not resisting pertinaciously, is certainly not from the will of man, but from the Spirit of God)." (L. c. c. 7, s. 1, th. 25, 26, f. 709.)

Hollazius: "Non-resistance is twofold: pedagogical and spiritual. Pedagogical non-resistance is in the power of the sinful man in external matters that invite him to the church. E.g., some unregenerate men refuse to go on foot to the temple, some do not refuse. This pedagogical non-resistance, corresponding to external hearing, is of the free will. But spiritual non-resistance, corresponding to internal hearing or assent, is from the assisting and preparing grace of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as it breaks and inhibits natural and actual simple resistance, so that it does not become malicious, affected, and morose; although through the extreme malice of men it does not always attain this intended end." (Exam. th. p. 873.)

Cf. the things said above in Part III, ch. 4, § 39, p. 230 sqq.

Huelsemannus: "Holy Scripture asserts both: that the Word of God has in itself a certain life-giving power, through the statements in 1 Thess. 2:13 and Rom. 1:16; and that God either intends and increases that intrinsic power, or does not intend and does not increase it; yet it is never said that He entirely takes away the life-giving power from the Word. Cf. the statements in Deut. 29:3-4, Ezek. 24:12, as well as the comparison of the sufficiency of the same means of salvation for converting the Tyrians and Sidonians, with the insufficiency for converting the Bethsaidans, Capernaites, etc., Matt. 11:21, Luke 11:31-32. Where it is to be noted that the issue is not only the greater indisposition of the passive subject—that is, of the Chorazinites—than was the indisposition of the Tyrians, but the issue is also the greater or lesser intrinsic efficacy of the means of conversion. Therefore, although a medicinal power resides in every Word of God, and it is never entirely taken away, we nevertheless confess that it is increased by God more or less, or is not increased, but left in a state of ordinary efficacy. See Ps. 86:10, Isa. 5:5-7, and following." (Praelect. in lib. Con. p. 440.)

Latin:

1. Pontificiorum, praecipue vero Dominicanorum, qui, cum Calvinianis absolutum praedestinationis decretum amplectentes, gratiam Dei paucis tantum hominibus a Deo destinatam asserunt, quos absolute et efficaci voluntate elegerit ad gloriam certumque gloriae gradum. . .

2. Quorundam patrum, qui existimarunt, non fuisse evangelium per apostolos eorumque discipulos in toto mundo praedicatum et consequenter plenitudinem gentium nondum intrasse, adeoque vocationem universalem a Christo mandatam adhuc perficiendam esse ante extremum diem ab apostolorum in ministerio verbi successoribus; ita Origenes Tr. 28. in Matth. et Augustinus ep. 89. ad Hesych. ...

3. Pontificiorum illorum, qui, Origenem secuti, evangelium Christi nondum omnes provincias pervasisse asserunt, ut Bellarminus 1. 3. de Pontif. Rom. c. 4...

4. Calvinianorum, qui catholicismum vocationis et praedicationis evangelicae, quia directe flgmento absolutae reprobationis adversatur, negant. Docent enim communiter, Deum nunquam voluisse omnium et singulorum misereri, nunquam voluisse omnibus ac singulis mittere Filium, nunquam voluisse omnibus et singulis suam benevolentiam offerre, ut ex collatione Hagiensi, Synodo Dordrac. aliisque tum publicis tum privatis eorum scriptis constat. . . Frequens in ore ipsorum distinctio vocationis externae et internae, efficacis et inefficacis. Vide Molinaeum in sua ad Synodum missa epistola p. 410. 411.: ,Assero‘, inquit, ,vocationem externam posse esse sine interna Spiritus efficacia.‘ Embdani p. 595. dicunt: ,Multos externe vocari et audire verbum, qui tamen vi Spiritus non trahuntur interne, neque sufficienter, neque efficaciter.‘ . . Porro docent Calviniani, apostolos praedicasse evangelium omnibus gentibus non collective, sed synecdochice vel distributive, h. e., magnae orbis parti, his vel illis gentibus; unde vocationem istam non universalem, sed communem, sc. Judaeorum (qui soli juxta eos in V. T. et initio N. T. vocabantur) et gentium (quibus aliquibus gratia vocationis contigit, caeteris ex mero Dei beneplacito plane praeteritis) appellare malunt. .. MosesAmyraldus, professor Salmuriens., c. 7. tr. de praedest. A. 1634., gallica lingua editi, duplicem asserit praedicationem seu vocationem, unam per ministerium providentiae divinae tantum, quae pariat fidem de misericordia Dei, destitutam quidem vera et dilucida cognitione redemtoris, de quo evangelium nobis praedicat, nihilominus tamen sufficientem ad salutem etc. . . . Ast illa opinio jam olim in Pelagianis et Scholasticis explosa est, et ab ipso Amyraldo in Synodo Alenconensi A. 1637. ejurata.“

Quamvis enim recte dicatur, Deum voluisse omnes salvos fieri, si credant, fatendum tamen etiam est, Deum voluisse, ut credant omnes, seu ut omnes ad agnitixmem veritatis (seu doctrinae verae, divinitus revelatae) perveniant, quod sese velle, testatur 1 Tim. 2, 4. Conf. b. Mus. Diss. de Aet. EI. Decr. § 279. p. 207. Equidem voluntatem illam, qua Deus vult, ut omnes credant (aeque ut illam, qua Deus vult, ut omnes salvi fiant; de qua vid. not. c. ad § 4.), non appellamus decretum; hic tamen actus voluntatis divinae, quo Deus constituit, doctrinam de mediatore Dei atque hominum ita promulgare, ut ad omnium notitiam pervenire et fidem obtinere posset, decretum recte appellatur. Cf. supra dicta P. III. c. 1. §7. p. 15. sqq. §

6. Et quemadmodum Deus in tempore verbo suo virtutem divinam a conjungit, per quam assensus fidei supernaturalis, verbo ipsi praebendus, atque ita fides in Christum excitari potest et excitatur, quoties homo absque malitiosa repugnantia b verbum ipsum admittit: ita certum est, quod Deus ab aeterno decreverit, cum verlo in tempore promulgando potenter et gratiose ad effectum fidei producendum c ita concurrere, ut nemo fide cariturus sit, nisi qui media conferendae fidei gratiamve ipsam contemserit. Vid. Proleg. cap. II. § 39. et P. III. c. IV. § 29. Proleg. cap. II. § 39. not. Z. et P. III. cap. IV. § 34. 35.

Atque huc pertinet, quod 1 Tim. 2, 4. dicitur, Deum velle omnes ad agnitionem veritatis, per quam salvi fiant, adeoque ad fidem salvificam pervenire. Unde omnino sequitur, Deum, quantum in se est, vires perveniendi ad salutarem agnitionem illam, seu vires credendi, /conferre paratum ac promtum esse, ita ut nemo a Deo, velut ex mero aut absoluto ejus beneplacito, excludatur; si qui vero ad eam non perveniant, causam atque culpam penes ipsos esse necesse sit. Et sic etiam Christus Matth. 28, 86. expresse docet, non esse absurdum, sed saepe admodum fieri (licet male fiat), ut, quos ipse serio vult ad se colligere, seu, quantum in ipso est, conferre ad ipsorum conversionem et fidem, qua cum mediatore suo jungantur et gratiam ac salutem obtineant, ipsi tamen homines nolint converti fidemque alias obtinendam impediant et excludant.

Formula Concordiae: ,,Da aber ein Mensch die Predigt nicht hören, noch Gottes Wort lesen will, sondern das Wort und die Gemeine Gottes verachtet und stirbet also und verdirbt in seinen Sünden: der kann weder Gottes ewiger Wahl sich trösten, noch seine Barmherzigkeit erlangen; denn Christus, in dem wir erwählet sind, allen Menschen PART. III. CAP. XII. seine Gnade im Wort und heiligen Sacramenten anbeut, und ernstlich will, dass man es hören soll, und hat verheissen, wo zween oder drei in seinem Namen versammelt sind und mit seinem heiligen Wort umgehen, will er mitten unter ihnen sein. Da aber ein solcher Mensch verachtet des Heiligen Geistes Werkzeug und will nicht hören: so geschieht ihm nicht unrecht, wenn der Heilige Geist ihn nicht erleuchtet, sondern in der Finsterniss seines Unglaubens stecken und verderben lässt, davon geschrieben stehet: ,Wie oft habe ich deine Kinder versammeln wollen, wie eine Henne versammelt ihre Jungen unter ihre Flügel, und ihr habt nicht gewollt.‘ Matth. 23, 37. Und in diesem Fall mag man wohl sagen, dass der Mensch nicht · sei ein Stein oder Block. Denn ein Stein oder Block widerstrebt dem nicht, der ihn bewegt, verstehet auch nicht und empfindet nicht, was mit ihm gehandelt wird, wie ein Mensch Gott dem Herrn widerstrebet mit seinem Willen, so lang bis er bekehret wird. Und ist gleichwohl wahr, dass ein Mensch vor der Bekehrung dennoch eine vernünftige Kreatur ist, welche einen Verstand und Willen hat, doch nicht einen Verstand in göttlichen Sachen, oder einen Willen, etwas Gutes und Heilsames zu wollen; jedoch kann er zu seiner Bekehrung (wie droben auch gemeldet) ganz und gar nichts thun, und ist in solchem Fall viel ärger, denn ein Stein und Block; denn er widerstrebt dem Wort und Willen Gottes, bis Gott ihn vom Tode der Sünde erweckt, erleuchtet und verneuert. Und wiewohl Gott den Menschen nicht zwinget, dass er müsse fromm werden (denn welche allezeit dem Heiligen Geist widerstreben und sich für und für auch der erkannten Wahrheit widersetzen, wie Stephanus von den verstockten Juden redet Act. 7, 51., die werden nicht bekehret); jedoch zeucht Gott der Herr den Menschen, welchen er bekehren will, und zeucht ihn also, dass aus einem verfinsterten Verstand ein erleuchteter Verstand, und aus einem widerspenstigen Willen ein gehorsamer Wille wird. Und das nennet die Schrift ein neues Herz erschaffen.“ (Concordia, p. 602. sq.)

Quenstedtius: ״Licet primum gratiae pulsum nemo possit effugere, potest tamen aliquis, postquam primos motus a gratia prae veniente excitatos sensit, illam gratiam malitiose excutere, Matth. 23, 27. sq. Luc. 7, 30. Quae vero excussio non fit a quavis repugnantia,.. sed ab actuali repugnantia pertinaci et imprimis mediis salutis perseveranter opposita. ,Quandocunque‘, enim, ,opponunt homines extremam malitiae proterviam et aperte reluctantur pertinaciterque tractui Spiritus S. resistunt, non ex defectu roboris, sed ex justo judicio negligit rebelles et tractum efflcacissimum ultra ordinem coelitus positum non extendit.‘ Vide b. Huelsemannum de auxil. gratiae, p. 238., D. Dorscheum Pentadec. Disp. 9. p. 317. et diss. 3. ep. de gratia. . . Gratia praeparans, per verbum ad individuum convertendum applicata, efficaciter agit, repugnantiam naturalem et actualem cohibendo, ne resistat morose, sive ut cesset hic et nunc ab exercitio hujus naturalis repugnantiae (quae sane cessatio seu mora ac spatium non resistendi pertinaciter non est ab hominis voluntate, sed a Spiritu #.)“ (L. c. c. 7. s. 1. th. 25.26. f. 709.)

Hollazius: ,,Non-resistentia est duplex, paedagogica et spiritualis. Paedagogica non-resistentia est penes hominem peccatorem ·in rebus externis, ad ecclesiam invitantibus. V. g. Quidam homines irregeniti renuunt ire pedibus in templum, quidam non recusant. Haec paedagogica non-resistentia, auditui externo respondens, est liberi arhitrii. Spiritualis autem non-resistentia, auditui interno sive assensui respondens, est a gratia Sp. S. assistente et praeparante, quippe quae repugnantiam naturalem et actualem simplicem frangit et inhibet, ne flat malitiosa, affectata et morosa; quamvis per extremam hominum malitiam intentum hunc finem non semper assequatur.“ (Exam. th. p. 873.)

Cf. supra dicta P. III. c. 4. § 39. p. 230. sqq.

Huelsemannus: ,,Utrumque asserit s. scriptura, tum quod verbum Dei in se habeat vivificamquandam vim, per dicta 1 Thess. 2, 13. Rom. 1, 16., tum, quod Deus intrinsecam illam vim sive intendat et augeat, sive non intendat et non augeat; nunquam autem dicitur, quod vim vivificam plane auferat a verbo. Cf. dicta Deut. 29, 3. 4. Ezech. 24,12., nec non comparationem sufficientiae eorundem mediorum salutis ad convertendos Tyrios et Sidonios, cum insufficientia ad convertendos Bethsaidanos, Capernaitas etc. Matth. 11, 21. Luc. 11, 31. 32. Ubi notandum est, agi non tantum de majori indispositione subjecti passi, h. e. Chorazinorum, quam fuit indispositio Tyriorum, sed agi etiam de majori vel minori intrinseca efficacia mediorum conversionis. Itaque quanquam omni verbo Dei insit vis medicinalis, eaque nunquam plane auferatur, fatemur tamen eam a Deo augeri magis vel minus, vel non augeri, sed relinqui in statu ordinariae efficaciae. Vid. Ps. 86, 10. Jes. 5, 5. 6. 7. et sq.“ (Praelect. in lib. Con. p. 440.)


### On Predestination and Reprobation: For if God in time, willing it, gives faith through the Word to all who do not…

For if God in time, willing it, gives faith through the Word to all who do not resist, and gives it according to the eternal decree of His will, it must be confessed that this very eternal decree of God is terminated toward the faith to be conferred in time upon all who do not resist through the Word. §

7. Furthermore, just as God in time justifies all who believe in Christ, and, unless they themselves cast off faith and the Holy Spirit by sins against conscience, renews or sanctifies them more and more, and preserves and confirms faith itself until the end of life: so it must be acknowledged that God from eternity decreed to confer upon all who would believe in Christ the grace of justification and renewal in time, and to further sanctify those who would rightly use the means, and to preserve and confirm their faith until the end of their lives. See Part III, Chapter V, § 1 and 9.

Which they indeed can do; as is evident from Part III, Chapter III, § 17. See Part III, Chapter VI, note a. Compare Chapter VII, § 25.

For when God in time justifies all believers, sanctifies them, and preserves and confirms faith in all who continue to use the means of grace, and does so willingly and according to His eternal decree, it must be confessed that the eternal decree of God itself is terminated, just as it is toward the justification of all believers, so also toward the renewal of all the justified who will continue to use the means of grace rightly and are foreseen as such, and toward the final preservation and confirmation of the faith of all those.

Huelsemannus: "Although it is not impious to say that a certain peculiar grace has been prepared by God for the elect, by which they are infallibly converted and preserved in faith: yet that grace which converts the temporary believers is, by its own nature and by God’s institution, sufficiently efficacious with intrinsic efficacy, so that through it, had it not been cast off, they could have persevered and been saved." (De auxiliis gratiae, p. 317.) PART III. CHAPTER XII.

8. Finally, just as God in time actually saves all who finally believe in Christ, it must also be acknowledged that there is an eternal decree of God concerning all who will finally believe being saved at a certain time. See Part III, Chapter III, § 19. Or, as others express it, glorifies, from Romans 8:30. For God, willing to confer blessedness upon those who finally believe in time, does so by virtue of an eternal decree, according to Matthew 25:34; and therefore His very eternal decree concerning the saving of certain men was terminated toward them as those who would finally believe. §

9. And because God from eternity foresaw which men would finally believe, and determined to save these as such, thus the eternal decree concerning the imparting of eternal salvation to those who will finally believe, in view of the merit of Christ and foreseen faith in Christ, when made and precisely considered, is specifically called by the name of predestination or election. By virtue of His omniscience, by which He knows all things, even those that will happen contingently, immediately in themselves. According to the preceding §. And what we said in § 2, note b, pertains here. Cf. the annotations below to §§ 15 and 17. §

10. On the other hand, however, just as God in time punishes with eternal damnation men who either never believed or have cast off faith again and end their life without faith, so it must be confessed that God decreed from eternity to damn eternally those who lack final faith. See Part I, Chapter VII, § 1; Part III, Chapter III, note a. And by reason of opposites, just as we have said the matter stands in the business of procuring salvation, regarding the decree of God.

11. And just as God foresaw from eternity which men would depart in time without faith in Christ, so He decreed to condemn those same ones, as such and distinctly known. And this decree is called reprobation. The reason here is the same as that of the opposite, predestination. That is, the rejection and repudiation of men. In Greek, you might call it ἀποδοκιμασία, although this word does not appear in the Holy Scriptures in opposition to predestination. However, it suffices that the sense exists. And it is certainly more correctly called reprobation than predestination to death. §

12. To the causes of election, taken in the stricter sense, that are virtually causative, belongs I. the efficient cause, which is the Triune God. For this must now be viewed more distinctly. And although some causes can also be assigned to election taken in the broader sense, it is nevertheless certain that in the schools, when the causes of election are discussed, the stricter meaning of the term is rather attended to; as will be evident from what follows.

For the acts of the divine will, such as election, do not really differ from the divine essence, and therefore, just like the divine essence itself, they are not really produced, nor do they acknowledge causes of themselves strictly so called, or formally causative, which would influence being into another. See the blessed Musaeus, *De Aet. Praed. Dec.*, ch. I, § 22, and *Diss. de Aet. El. Decr.*, ch. I, § 4, sqq.

Thus, our theologians long ago taught against Conr. Vorstius, e.g., the blessed J. Gerhard, *Exeg. L. II. de Not. Dei* § 277: God does not produce in Himself new actions of intellect and will, as men and angels do, which are accidents distinct from His own essence, but the act of intellect and will is the very essence of God. Cf. the blessed Christ. Scheibler, *Metaph. L. III. cap. III. § 264, sqq.* Moreover, the blessed Scherzer also used the distinction between a cause formally and virtually causative in this matter (*System. L. XVIII. p. 511, 512*).

Therefore, those are not to be thought subtle beyond necessity who, while retaining here the term "cause" according to the manner of speaking hitherto received in the church, at the same time rightly warn—out of the necessity of distinguishing sound doctrine from Vorstian and Socinian error, and likewise to avoid the cavils of the Reformed, who pretend that our opinion regarding the causes of election corresponds to those errors—that one must not understand here a cause of such a kind that it looks to a caused object really distinct from the infinite and unproducible essence of God, which is required for a cause formally and strictly so called.

But those who acknowledge that it is self-evident that the most simple essence of God does not admit the differences of causes and effects must also acknowledge that between those acts, which are really the same as the essence of God, and God Himself, there is no... PART III. CAP. XII.

such a distinction of causes and effects, nor can it exist on account of that same simplicity. And when the term "cause" is taken in a purified sense, insofar as it can have a place in God, one must certainly return to that very thing which was said concerning a cause that is virtually causing. Furthermore, the distinction between the immanent acts of God, such as predestination, and the transient acts, such as the calling and glorification of men, must not be neglected. For if the latter, just as they import something outside of God really produced in creatures, do indeed acknowledge a cause formally causing them, the former do not.

To whom, as agent, election or predestination is attributed, so that you may consequently call Him the predestinating or electing one. Just as God is otherwise accustomed to be called the cause of the acts of His own will.

Indeed, in Ephesians 1:5, it is ascribed to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ that He predestined or elected us; but the remaining persons are not excluded, whose acts of will, just as their essence is one, belong equally to all. However, in the aforementioned passage, there is a peculiar respect of the electing one toward Him in whom He elected, as we shall say presently. § 13. The internal impulsive cause is the goodness or mercy and the gratuitous favor of God.

Not formally, but virtually causing, or the reason *a priori*; which, according to our mode of knowing, in the genus of impulsive cause, behaves like a cause toward that act of the divine will, as if that act were caused or really produced, this would truly and in reality exist, in the genus of impulsive cause, as the cause of that act. Compare the blessed Musaeus and Scherzer in the aforementioned places. Just as Paul in 2 Timothy 1:9 joins the πρόθεσιν and χάριν of God, in opposition to our works, and says that it was given to us before eternal times. And when he writes in Ephesians 1:5 and 6 that God predestined us so that the glory of His grace might be praised, he manifestly indicates that predestination proceeded from or took its origin from that grace of God, as an impulsive cause or reason. And when the act by which believers are saved in time acknowledges the grace of God as an impulsive cause, it must be confessed that the decree concerning the saving of believers also rests upon the same reason or impulsive cause. Compare what we said in the note to § 1, and what we shall say more fully in the following §.

Formula of Concord: "Through this doctrine and explanation of the eternal and saving election of the chosen children of God, God is given His honor entirely and completely, that He, out of pure mercy in Christ, without any merit or good works of ours, saves us according to the purpose of His will, as it is written in Eph. 1:5: 'He has ordained us to sonship unto Himself through Jesus Christ according to the good pleasure of His will, to the praise of the glory of His grace, by which He has made us acceptable in the Beloved.' Therefore it is false and wrong when it is taught that not only the mercy of God and

the most holy merit of Christ, but also that there is a cause of God’s election within us, for the sake of which God has chosen us to eternal life. For not only before we had done anything good, but even before we were born, He chose us in Christ; indeed, before the foundation of the world was laid, and ‘that the purpose of God according to election might stand, it was said to her, not of the merit of works, but of the grace of Him who calls, thus: the elder shall serve the younger; as it is written: Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.’ Rom. 9:11. Gen. 25:23. Mal. 1:2 sq.” (Concordia, p. 723. §§ 87. 88.) Luther: “‘According to the foreknowledge of God the Father.’ These are chosen, he says. How? Not by themselves, but according to God’s ordinance (ordinatio = ordinance. Hunnius). For we shall not be able to bring ourselves to heaven, or create faith within ourselves. God will not let all men into heaven; He will count His own very precisely. Here, human teaching concerning free will and our own powers is of no account; it does not depend on our will, but on God’s will and election. ‘And through sanctification of the Spirit.’ God has foreknown us that we should be holy, and thus, that we should become spiritually holy... This is what Peter means to say: God has foreknown you to this end, that you should be truly holy, as St. Paul also says in Eph. 4:24: ‘In righteousness and holiness of truth,’ that is, in a genuine and fundamentally good holiness.” (Exposition of the 1st Epistle of St. Peter. A. 1523. IX, 631. sq.) Gerhard: "Augustine strongly opposes this Pelagian opinion concerning the foresight of merits, on account of which election is said to have been made, in many places, especially in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints* and his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, in which: 1. He shows that the very beginning of faith is from the grace of God, that perseverance is a gift of God, and indeed that eternal life itself is a gratuitous gift. 2. He brings forward the example of infants, who, having been regenerated by grace through baptism, become partakers of salvation without any merits. 3. He teaches that in Christ, as the head and mediator of the elect, the pattern of gratuitous election is set forth. 4. He urges many passages of Scripture against that Pelagian opinion: 1 Kings 19:18: 'I have left for myself seven thousand'—he does not say, 'they have left themselves for me,' but 'I have left.' John 15:16: 'You did not choose me, but I chose you.' Romans 9:11: 'Though they (Jacob and Esau) were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad, in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls, it was said to her, "The older will serve the younger."' Ephesians 1:5: 'God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless' (not because we were going to be holy). Prosper and Fulgentes follow Augustine. Many arguments can be added from the aforementioned place in Ephesians, which is the proper seat of this article. 1. The very word 'to choose' denotes a gratuitous love, as we showed in Thesis 26. § 2. 'By nature we are all children of wrath,' Eph. 2:3. 2. God chose us in Christ, Eph. 1:4. Therefore, He found nothing in us ourselves for the sake of which He would choose us. If we could have been chosen on account of our own dignity, what need would there have been for Christ? 3. The end does not enter into the act of the thing; good works are, on the part of the end, the result of election, Eph. 1:5: 'He chose us, that we should be holy.' 4. God chose us before the foundation of the world. Therefore, our works did not move Him to predestine us. 5. God predestined us 'in Himself,' Eph. 1:5; therefore, He found nothing in us ourselves for the sake of which He predestined us. 6. He predestined us according to the purpose of His will, Eph. 1:5. Therefore, that is the cause of predestination, not the purpose of our will. 7. God chose us to the praise of His glorious and praiseworthy grace, Eph. 1:6. Therefore, not on account of our works; for if it is by grace, it is no longer by works, Rom. 11:6. 8. That grace of God is the cause of our election, by which God held us dear to Himself in His beloved Son, Eph. 1:6. But that favor of God is entirely gratuitous. 9. God chose us from eternity κατώς, just as in time He blesses us in Christ, Eph. 1:4. But we are blessed in time out of the mere and gratuitous grace of God. Justification does not depend on the merit of works; therefore, neither does election. Neither works before justification nor works after justification can be the cause of election; not the former, because works do not please God before the person pleases God; nor the latter, because those works are gifts of grace, not merits of grace." (L. c. § 193.) The same: "Christ confirms and emphasizes His love by the gratuitous election of the apostles. 'You did not choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain...' Some think that Christ is speaking here of temporal election, i.e., of that election by which the apostles were called by Christ both to the fellowship of the church and to the highest degree of ecclesiastical ministry... Others, on the contrary, maintain that Christ is speaking here of eternal election, i.e., of that election by which the apostles were chosen for eternal salvation... But these two interpretations are not opposed, but subordinate. For in both ways He demonstrated His love toward the apostles: both by calling them in time to the fellowship of the church and the apostolate, and by choosing them from eternity for eternal salvation. Both elections are gratuitous, both were made through Christ, Eph. 1:4; 4:11, and both were made with the end that the elect should bear fruit and that their fruit should remain." (Harmon. ev. c. 177.) f. 1022. sq.) Quenstedtius: "The moving cause is partly internal, partly external; the internal is the merely gratuitous grace of God, excluding altogether every merit of human works, or everything that comes under the name of work or action, whether done through the grace of God or out of the powers of nature. For God chose us not according to works, but out of His mere grace. Even faith itself does not belong here, if it is viewed as a condition more or less worthy, whether in itself or from an estimation added to faith by the will of God; for none of these things enters into the decree of election as a moving or impelling cause for God to make such a decree, but it is to be ascribed to the pure and unmixed grace of God; as the blessed Huelsemannus teaches, Breviar, c. 15. θ. 6. This position is proved from Rom. 9:15, 16: 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy. It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.'" (Th. did.-pol. L. c. s. 1. th. 10. f. 25.) Calovius: "We profess and teach that it is false and conflicts with the Word of God when it is taught that not only the mercy of God and the sole most holy merit of Christ, but also something in us, is a cause of divine election, on account of which God has predestined these to eternal life... We reject those who teach that it is not without regard to works of mercy or lack of mercy, but according to them, that the place of both eternal life and hell was prepared from the foundation of the world and destined for men, and that charity is some condition under which God decreed to save us. Thus teaches D. Conradus Hornejus in part II of his theological disputations, disp. 2, which treats of predestination, § 32, p. 225, in these words: 'By no means, therefore, is it without regard to works of mercy or lack of mercy, but according to them, that both places were prepared from the foundation of the world and destined for men. The parable of the laborers in Matt. 20 also looks to this, because it shows that eternal life is not decreed to anyone absolutely, but with the condition that he has labored diligently in the vineyard of the Lord.' And in the same place, § 42, or the last, p. 237: 'But it was not made out of the dignity of faith or the works of faith, yet only according to the foreknowledge of faith, which is effective through charity, as some condition under which God decreed to save us gratuitously.' To this also Joh. Latermannus seems to have aimed in his Exercise on the eternal predestination of God and the ordered will to save all, § 18, using these words: 'As these things cohere most excellently, so they beautifully agree with those things which Scripture hands down; for in it few are said to be chosen before many, not for the performing of a duty, but in view of a duty already performed.'" (Consens. repetit. See Consil. Witteberg. I, 962.) Olearius: "Question XVII: Is the Lutheran doctrine concerning election akin to Pelagianism? No, because it attributes everything to God, to man..."

Latin:

Si enim Deus in tempore, volens, fidem per verbum dat omnibus non repugnantibus et dat juxta decretum voluntatis aeternum, fatendum est, hoc ipsum decretum Dei aeternum terminari ad fidem in tempore omnibus non repugnantibus per verbum conferendam. §

7. Porro sicut Deus in tempore omnes, qui in Christum credunt,a justificat et, nisi ipsi pecpatis contra conscientiam fidem et Spiritum Sanctum b excutiant, magis magisque c renovat, aut sanctificat, fidemque ipsam conservat et confirmat usque ad finem vitae: ita agnoscendum est, quod Deus ab aeterno d decreverit, omnibus, qui in Christum credituri essent, in tempore gratiam justificationis et renovationis conferre, et mediis recte usuros sanctificare ulterius, fidemque eorum conservare et confirmare usque ad finem vitae illorum. Vid. Part. III. cap. V. § 1. et 9.

Quod quidem possunt; uti constat ex Part. III. cap. III. § 17. Vid. Part. III. cap. VI. not. a. Conf. cap. VII. § 25.

Nam quando Deus in tempore credentes omnes justificat, sanctificat, et in omnibus, qui mediis gratiae porro utuntur, fidem conservat et confirmat, idque volens et juxta decretum suum aeternum, fatendum est, ipsum Dei decretum aeternum, sicut ad omnium credentium justificationem, ita ad justificatorum omnium, qui mediis gratiae porro recte usuri sunt atque ut tales praevidentur, renovationem fideique illorum omnium conservationem et confirmationem finalem terminari.

Huelsemannus: ,,Quamquam non sit impium, dicere, electis esse peculiarem quandam gratiam a Deo praeparatum, qua infallibiliter convertantur et in fide conserventur: illam tamen gratiam, quae προςκαίρους convertit, ex natura sua et ex Dei instituto satis efficacem esse efficacia intrinseca, ut per eam, non excussam recidive, potuerint perseverare et salvari.“ (De auxiliis gratiae, p. 317.) PART. ΠΙ. CAP. XU.

8. Denique, sicut Deus in tempore omnes finaliter a in Christum credentes actu salvat,b agnoscendum etiam est aeternum Dei decretum c de orrmibm finaliter credituris in tempore certo salvandis. Vid. Part. III. cap. III. § 19. Seu, ut alii loquuntur, glorificat, ex Rom. 8, 30. Nam Deus in tempore finaliter credentibus volens confert beatitudinem, idque vi decreti aeterni, juxta Matth. 25, 84·, ideoque ipsum ejus decretum aeternum de salvandis certis hominibus terminabatur ad eos, ut finaliter credituros. §

9. Et quia Deus ab aeterno praevidit,a quinam homines finaliter credituri sint, atque hos, ut tales,b salvare con· stituit, sic decretum aeternum de impertienda finaliter creditwris salute aeterna, intuitu meriti Christi et praevisae fidei in Christum, factum ac praecise spectatum praedestinationis aut electionis nomine speciatim c appellatur. Vi omniscientiae suae, qua omnia, etiam contingenter futura, immediate in se ipsis cognoscit. Juxta § praeced. Et huc pertinent, quae diximus § 2. not. b. Cf. infra ad §§ 15. et 17. adnotata. §

10. Ex adverso autem, sicuti Deus in tempore homines, qui vel nunquam crediderunt, vel fidem rursus excusserunt ac sine fide vitam finiunt, aeterna damnatione a punit, ita fatendum est, decrevisse b Deum ab aeterno, eos, qui fide finali caruerint, aeternum damnare. Vid. Part. I. cap. VII. § 1. Part. III. cap. HI. not. a. Et ratione oppositorum, prout in negotio procurandae salutis, quoad decretum Dei, rem sese habere diximus.

u. Et sicut Deus praevidit a ab aeterno, quinam homines absque fide in Christum in tempore decessuri sint, ita eosdem, ut tales ac distincte cognitos, aeternum damnare decrevit. Atque hoc decretum dicitur b reprobatio. Eadem hic ratio est, quae oppositae praedestinationis. Id est, abjectio et repudiatio hominum. Graece αποδοκιμασίαν dixeris, quamvis vox haec in oppositione ad praedestinationem in Scripturis sacris non extet. Sufficit autem, extare sensum. Et rectius sane dicitur reprobatio, quam praedestinatio ad mortem. §

12. Ad electionis strictiore sensu dictae a causas virtualiter b causantes pertinet I. efficiens c quae est Deus d trinunus.e Haec enim jam distinctius spectanda est. Et licet etiam electioni, latiore sensu acceptae, possint aliquae causae assignari, certum tamen est, in scholis, cum de causis electionis agitur, strictiorem potius significationem vocis attendi; quemadmodum ex sequentibus constabit.

Nam actus voluntatis divinae, qualis est electio, ab essentia divina realiter non differunt adeoque, sicut ipsa essentia divina, ita et illi non producuntur realiter, neque causas sui in rigore sic dictas, seu formaliter causantes, quae influant esse in aliud, agnoscunt. Vid. b. Mus. de Aet. Praed. Dec. cap. I. § 22. et Diss. de Aet. EI. Decr. cap. I. § 4. sqq.

Sic autem et nostrates contra Conr. Vorstium pridem docuerunt, e. g. b. J. Gerhardus Exeg. L. II. de Not. Dei § 277.: Deus non producit in se novas actiones intellectus et voluntatis, ut homines et angeli, quae sint accidentia ab ipsius essentia distincta, sed actus intellectus et voluntatis est ipsa Dei essentia. Conf. b. Christ Scheibleri Metaph. L. III. cap. III. § 264. sqq. Distinctione autem inter causam forrnaliter et virtualiter causantem in hoc negotio usus etiam est b. Scherzerus System. L. XVIII. p. 511. 512.

Neque ergo praeter necessitatem subtiles esse putandi sunt, qui, terminum causae, juxta modum loquendi in ecclesia hactenus receptum, hic retinentes, simul tamen et ex necessitate distinguendi sanam doctrinam ab errore Vorstiano ac Sociniano itemque ad declinandos cavillos Reformatorum, sententiam nostram de causis electionis erroribus illis respondere fingentium, merito monent, non esse hic intelligendam causam ejusmodi, quae spectet causatum ab infinita et improducibili Dei essentia realiter distinctum, quod ad causam formaliter et in rigore sic dictam requiritur.

Qui autem agnoscunt, quod per se pateat, differentias causarum et effectuum simplicissimam Dei essentiam non admittere, agnoscant etiam necesse est, inter actus illos, qui cum essentia Dei realiter idem sunt, et inter ipsum Deum non esse PART. III. CAP. XII.

talem differentiam causarum et effectuum, nec esse posse propter eandem simplicitatem. Et quando vox causae in sensu purificato accipitur, quatenus in Deo locum habere potest, redeundum sane est ad id ipsum, quod de causa virtualiter causante dictum est. Caeterum nec negligenda est distinctio inter actus Dei immanentes, qualis est praedestinatio, et transeuntes, quales sunt vocatio et glorificatio hominum. Si enim, sicut aliquid extra Deum in creaturis realiter productum important, ita causam sui formaliter causantem utique agnoscunt; illi vero non item.

Cui tanquam agenti electio seu praedestinatio tribuitur, ut proinde praedestinantem, seu eligentem, appellare possis. Prout Deus actuum voluntatis suae causa alias dici solet.

Equidem Ephes. 1, 5. Patri Domini nostri Jesu Christi adscribitur, quod nos praedestinaverit seu elegerit; sed non excluduntur reliquae personae, quarum sicut una essentia est, ita et actus voluntatis omnibus aeque competunt. Habetur autem 1. c. peculiaris respectus elir gentis ad eum, in quo elegit; ut mox dicemus. § 13. Causa impulsiva a interna est bonitas seu misericordia et gratuitus b favor Dei.c

Non formaliter, sed virtualiter causans, seu ratio a priori; quae juxta nostrum modum cognoscendi, in genere causae impulsi vae, ad actum illum voluntatis divinae instar causae se habet, ׳ut si actus ille causaretur seu realiter produceretur, ista vere et re ipsa, in genere causae impulsivae, causa actus illius existeret. Conf. b. Musaeum et Scherzerum 11. cc. Prout Paulus 2 Tim. 1, 9. conjungit πρό&εσιν et χάριν Dei, in oppositione ad opera nostra, atque illam nobis datam dicit ante tempora aeterna. Et quando ad Ephes. 1, 5. et 6. scribit, Deum praedestinasse nos, ut laudetur gloria gratiae suae, manifeste indicat, ex gratia illa Dei, velut causa aut ratione impulsiva, profectam esse aut originem ducere praedestinationem. Et quando actus, quo salvantur credentes in tempore, gratiam Dei tanquam causam impulsivam agnoscit, fatendum est, etiam decretum de salvandis credentibus eadem ratione aut causa impulsi va niti. Confer, quae ad § 1. not. b. diximus, et ad § seq. dicemus pluribus.

Formula Concordiae: ,,Durch diese Lehre und Erklärung von der ewigen und seligmachenden Wahl der auserwählten Kinder Gottes wird Gott seine Ehre ganz und völlig gegeben, dass er aus lauter Barmherzigkeit in Christo, ohne allen unsern Verdienst oder gute Werke, uns selig mache, nach dem Vorsatz seines Willens, wie geschrieben stehet Eph. 1, 5.: ,Er hat uns verordnet zur Kindschaft gegen ihm selbst durch Jesum Christum nach dem Wohlgefallen seines Willens, zu Lobe seiner Herrlichkeit und Gnade, durch welche er uns hat angenehm gemacht in dem Geliebten.‘ Darum es falsch und unrecht, wenn gelehrt wird, dass nicht allein die Barmherzigkeit Gottes und

allerheiligste Verdienst Christi, sondern auch in uns eine Ursache der Wahl Gottes sei, um welcher willen Gott uns zum ewigen Leben erwählt habe. Denn nicht allein, ehe wir etwas Gutes gethan, sondern auch, ehe wir geboren werden, hat er uns in Christo erwählet, ja, ehe der Welt Grund gelegt war, und,auf dass der Vorsatz Gottes bestünde nach der Wahl, ward zu ihm gesagt, nicht aus Verdienst der Werke, sondern aus Gnaden des Berufers, also: der Grösste soll dienstbar werden dem Kleinern; wie davon geschrieben stehet’: Ich habe Jacob geliebet, aber Esau habe ich gehasset.‘ Rom. 9,11. Gen. 25, 23. Mal. 1, 2. sq.“ (Concordia, p. 723. §§ 87. 88.) Lutherus: ,, ,Nach der Versehung Gottes des Vaters.‘ Die sind erwählet, spricht er. Wie? Nicht von ihnen selber, sondern nach Gottes Ordnung (ordinatio = Verordnung. Hunnius). Denn wir werden uns selber nicht können zum Himmel bringen, oder den Glauben in uns machen. Gott wird nicht alle Menschen in Himmel lassen; die Seinen wird er gar genau zählen. Da gilt nun nichts mehr Menschenlehre vom freien Wülen und unsern Kräften;. es liegt nicht an unserm Willen, sondern an Gottes Willen und Erwählung. ,Und der Heiligung des Geistes.‘ Gott hat uns versehen, dass wir heilig sein sollten, und also, dass wir geistlich heilig werden. . . Das will nun Petrus sagen: Gott hat euch dazu versehen, dass ihr wahrhaftig sollet heilig sein, wie St. Paulus auch spricht Eph. 4, 24.: ,In Gerechtigkeit und Heiligkeit der Wahrheit‘, d.i., in einer rechtschaffenen und grundguten Heiligkeit.“ (Ausl, der 1. Ep. St. Petri. A. 1523. IX, 631. sq.) Gerhardus: ,,Huic sententiae pelagianae de prae visione meritorum, propter quam facta sit electio, graviter in plurimis locis adversatur Augustinus, praesertim in libro de praedestinatione sanctorum et lib. de bono perseverantiae, in quibus: 1. Ostendit, ipsum initium fidei esse ex Dei gratia, perseverantiam esse donum Dei, imo ipsam vitam aeternam esse donum gratuitum. 2. Profert exemplum infantum, qui ex gratia per baptismum regeniti absque meritis salutis fiunt participes. 3. In Christo tanquam electorum capite et mediatore exemplar gratuitae electionis propositum esse docet. 4. Urget multa Scripturae loca contra pelagianam illam sententiam: 1 Reg. 19, 18.: ,Reliqui mihi septem millia‘, non ait, reliquerunt se mihi, sed ego reliqui. Joh. 15, 16.: ,Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos.‘ Rom. 9, 11.: ,Cum nondum nati fuissent (Jacobus et Esau), aut aliquid boni vel mali fecissent, ut secundum electionem propositum Dei maneret; non ex operibus, sed ex vocante dictum est: major serviet minori.‘ Eph. 1, 5.: .,Elegit nos Deus in Christo ante jacta mundi fundamenta, ut essemus sancti et immaculati‘ (non quia futuri eramus sancti). Augustinum sequuntur Prosper et Fulgentius. Possunt addi multa argumenta ex 1. c. Eph., quod est propria sedes hujus articuli. 1. Ipsa vox eligendi notat gratuitam dilectionem, ut ostendimus thesi 26. § 2. ,Natura sumus omnes filii irae‘, Eph. 2, 3. 2. Elegit nos Deus in Christo, Eph. 1, 4. Ergo in nobis ipsis nihil invenit, propter quod nos eligeret. Si propter nostram dignitatem eligi potuissemus, quid opus fuisset Christo? 3. Finis non ingreditur rei actum; bona opera sunt ex parte finis electionis Eph. 1, 5.: ,Elegit nos, ut essemus sancti.‘ 4. Elegit nos Deus ante jacta mundi fundamenta. Ergo opera nostra non moverunt eum, ut nos praedestinaret. 5. Deus praedestinavit nos,in se ipso‘ Eph. 1, 5., ergo in nobis ipsis nihil invenit, propter quod nos praedestinavit. 6. Praedestinavit nos secundum propositum voluntatis suäe, Eph. 1, 5. Ergo illud est causa praedestinationis, non propositum voluntatis nostrae. 7. Elegit nos Deus in laudem gloriosae et praedicandae gratiae suae, Eph. 1, 6. Ergo non propter opera nostra; si enim ex gratia, jam non ex operibus Rom. 11,6. 8. Illa Dei gratia est electionis nostrae causa, qua nos Deus sibi gratos habuit in dilecto Filio suo, Eph. 1, 6. Atqui ille Dei favor est plane gratuitus. 9. Elegit nos Deus ab aeterno καΰώς, sicut in tempore nobis benedicit in Christo, Eph. 1, 4. Atqui benedicimur in PART. III. CAP. ΧΠ. tempore ex mera et gratuita Dei gratia. Justificatio non pendet ex operum merito; ergo nec electio. Nec opera ante justificationem, nec opera post justificationem possunt esse causa electionis; non illud, quia opera non placent Deo, antequam persona Deo placeat; nec hoc, quia illa opera sunt dona gratiae, non merita gratiae.“ (L. c. § 193.) Idem: ,,Confirmat et exaggerat Christus dilectionem suam a gratuita apostolorum electione. ,Non yos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos, et constitui vos, ut eatis et fructum afferatis, et fructus vester maneat... Quidam existimant, Christum hic loqui de electione temporaria, h. e., de ea electione, qua apostoli erant a Christo vocati tum ad ecclesiae consortium, tum ad summum ecclesiastici ministerii gradum. . . Quidam contra statuunt, Christum hic loqui de electione aeterna, h. e., de ea electione, qua apostoli erant ad salutem aeternam electi. . . Sed hae duae interpretationes non sunt oppositae, sed subordinatae. Utroque enim modo suam erga apostolos dilectionem demonstravit, tum ad ecclesiae consortium et apostolatum eos in tempore vocando, tum ad aeternam salutem $b aeterno eos eligendo. Utraque electio est gratuita, utraque facta est per Christum, Eph. 1,4. 4,11., utraque facta est fine eo, ut electi fructum afferant et fructus eorum maneat.“ (Harmon. ev. c. 177. f. 1022. sq.) Quenstedtius: ,,Causa movens alia interna est, alia externa; interna est gratia Dei mere gratuita, excludens omne omnino operum humanorum meritum sive omne id, quod nomine operis vel actionis, sive per gratiam Dei, sive ex viribus naturae factae, venit. Elegit enim nos Deus non secundum opera, sed ex mera sua gratia.Etiam fides ipsa huc non pertinet, si spectatur tanquam conditio magis vel minus digna, sive per se sive ex aestimio per voluntatem Dei fidei superaddito; quod nihil horum decretum electionis ingreditur tanquam causa movens aut impellens Deum ad tale decretum faciendum, sed id purae putae gratiae Dei est adscribendum; ut docet b. Huelsemannus, Breviar, c. 15. θ. 6. Probatur haec positio ex Rom. 9, 15. 16.: ,Miserebor, cujus misereor. Non volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei est.‘ “ (Th. did.-pol. L. c. s. 1. th. 10. f. 25.) Calovius: ,,Profitemur et docemus, falsum esse et cum verbo Dei pugnare, cum docetur, quod non sola Dei misericordia et unicum sanetissimum Christi meritum, verum etiam aliquid in nobis causa sit electionis divinae, propter quod Deus Hos ad vitam aeternam praedestinaverit. . . Rejicimus eos, qui docent, non citra intuitum operum misericordiae aut immisericordiae, sed secundum ea et vitae aeternae et inferni locum a jacto mundi fundamento paratum et hominibus destinatum esse, ac caritatem esse conditionem aliquam, sub qua nos Deus salvare decrevit. Ita docet D. Conradus Hornejus parte II. disp. theol. disp. 2., quae agit de praedestinatione § 32. p. 225., hisce verbis: ,Nullatenus ergo citra intuitum operum misericordiae aut immisericordiae, sed secundum ea uterque locus a jacto mundi fundamento paratus et hominibus destinatus est. Spectat huc etiam parabola operariorum Matth. 20., quia vitam aeternam non absolute cuiquam decerni monstrat, sed cum conditione, si in vinea Domini sedulo laborarit.' Et ibidem § 42. seu ult. p. 237.: ,Sed nec ex fidei seu operum fidei dignitate facta est, veruntamen tantum secundum praevisionem fidei, quae per caritatem efficax est, ut conditionem aliquam, sub qua nos Deus gratis salvare decrevit.4 Quo etiam videtur collineasse Joh. Latermannus in Exercitatione de aeterna Dei praedestinatione et ordinata omnes salvandi voluntate § 18., usus hisce verbis; ,Quae ut optime cohaerent, ita cum iis, quae scriptura tradit, pulchre consentiunt; in ea enim pauci prae multis electi dicuntur, non ad officium faciendum, sed intuitu officii jam ante praestiti.‘ “ (Consens. repetit. Vid. Consil. Witteberg. I, 962.) Olearius: ,,Quaest. XVII.: An doctrina Lutheranorum de electione affinis sit pelagianismo? Neg., quia Deo tribuit omnia, homini


### On Predestination and Reprobation: nothing. Since He alone grants both the willing and the performing, Phil

nothing. Since He alone grants both the willing and the performing, Phil. 2, as is evident from the foundations explained above, where the book of life, the certainty of election, and final perseverance were treated. Cf. the Wittenberg theologians in *dem gründl. Beweis* [the thorough proof], p. 617 sq., where the Bergian objections have been satisfied.

Nor is there any obstacle from 1. the external hearing of the Word, because pedagogical actions are most distinct from conversion itself and salutary hearing; nor 2. faith, which is by no means our work, but God’s gift, nor a condition to be fulfilled by us, but a requirement divinely conferred, out of grace, through the ordinary means of salvation; nor 3. the desire for salvation, because even that is not natural, but supernatural, gifted by the Holy Spirit and arising from the Word; nor 4. non-resistance assigned to man above. Because even this itself is a gift of the Holy Spirit, who removes and inhibits resistance—which alone is from us—through the ordinary means of salvation. For not-resisting is by no means to influence causally, but only not to impede the operation of the agent, just as the leper in Matt. 8 and Lazarus in John 11, by not resisting Christ, were by no means the cause of the miraculous healing or resuscitation.

Nor 5. prayers, and their continuation in the agony. For the Holy Spirit excites those also in us. Rom. 8. (See Carpzov’s *Isag. in lib. symb.*, p. 1684 sq.)

S. Schmidtius: "In the predestined man there is just as little cause for predestination as there is in the reprobate; rather, it proceeds from a mere divine ordination, resting upon universal grace and the merit of Christ, by its nature excluding every cause on the part of man." (*Aphorism. th.*, p. 295.)

Ad. Osiander: "Predestination is an act on the part of God not provoked by us, as if from us; nor does the predestined person have anything from himself by which he is distinguished from the reprobate. This is the antithesis of the Pelagians and those who pelagianize." (*Colleg. th.* VI, 134.)

Gerhardus: "The third argument by which they (the Calvinists) wish to establish absolute reprobation: 'If the cause of reprobation is in man, then certainly the cause of election will also be in him. The latter is false. Therefore, the former is also.' Resp.: Although according to the ordinary mode of acting, God does not convert those who do not hear the Word, who despise and persecute the ministers of the Word, who blaspheme the Word and resist the Holy Spirit, yet it does not follow from this that it lies within man to be converted, since the fact that man is converted through the hearing of the Word is the work of the Holy Spirit, and not of human powers." (*L. c.* § 188.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Pelagians, who maintain that men are elected by God on account of foreseen works; see Augustine *de praedest. sanctorum* c. 18 and ep. 105. 2. Of Johannes Erigena Scotus, who, when he drew his pen in the 9th century against the predestinarians, especially Godeschalcus, veered to the opposite—namely, that election was made from the foresight of merits—and for that reason perished, pierced by the writing styli of his own disciples. See the blessed Huelsemann, *Praei. in F. C.* a. 14. s. 1. § 3.

3. Of the Scholastics, who approach very closely to the camp of Pelagius and contend that God preordained that He would grant glory based on merits; thus Thomas P. 1. q. 23. a. 5., Biell. *sent.* distinct. 41. q. unic. 4. Of the Papists, who closely follow the footsteps of the Scholastics... Although others among the Papists deny that God chose us on account of foreseen merits, they cannot, however, free themselves from that error or maintain otherwise, while their hypotheses remain, namely, when they maintain that the righteous merit eternal life by their works... Cornelius a Lapide, *com. in Matth.* c. 20. p. 379, and others establish a twofold order of the predestined; one common, of those who are elected to glory from the foresight of merits; the other of those who are elected to glory before foreseen merits, whom they therefore call 'eximiously' [specially] predestined, and they think these are the ones noted when it is said: 'But few are chosen.' For such few are, namely, the blessed Virgin, the apostles, and a few others; the former, however, are by far more numerous, and therefore it is said of them: 'Many...'" PART III. CHAP. XII. are called. To the latter class they also refer baptized infants who are taken from life before the years of discretion, where no foreseen merits can be feigned, and no good use of free will or grace. Thus Bellarmine, *de grat. et lib. arbit.*, bk. 2, ch. 12, § *Tertia ratio*, etc., col. 554.

5. Of the Socinians, who assert that predestination was made according to the foreknowledge of obedience and works. Thus Socinus, *Prael.*, ch. 13, p. 62 sq., asserts that "the firmness of election depends mostly on our zeal and our diligence"; likewise, he says, p. 63, "that election can in no way exist or consist without some free action of our will." Where it is to be observed that the Socinians distinguish between predestination and election; they say the former was made from eternity, but they wrongly confuse the latter with vocation, which was made only in time, and they subordinate the former to the latter.

6. Of the Arminians, who, following the Socinians, 1) deny that the election of certain persons to eternal life was made from eternity. For thus the *Apol.*, ch. 18, p. 190: "It is evident that it is false that election was made from eternity. There is only one passage in Scripture that seems to affirm this, from which this common error was born, namely, the passage Eph. 1:4." Cf. p. sq. and Episcopius, P. 3, disp. 27, last thesis. 2) They place the cause of election in the obedience of man or establish that election was made from the foreknowledge of works; thus Sim. Episcopius, P. 3, disp. 7, th. 8: "The Scriptures," he says, "everywhere assert that God decreed salvation for men under the condition of obedience and faith rendered either to the law or to the gospel," and *Apol.* Cf. p. 74: "Scripture never asserts that anyone pleased God unto eternal life, except through faith and the works that are joined to faith." Cf. p. 76. (L. c. s. 2, q. 2, p. 40 sqq.)

Ambrose: "He did not predestine before He foreknew, but He predestined the rewards of those whose merits He foreknew." (On Rom. 8:29.)

Hutter: Melanchthon "places election not in the sole will and mercy of God, but partly in the will of man. For he expressly says: 'There is and must be some cause in man why some are elected to salvation, others are rejected and damned.' And again: 'Since the promise is universal, and these are not contradictory wills in God, it is necessary that there be some cause of the distinction in us, why Saul is rejected and David is received, i.e., it is necessary that there be some dissimilar action in these two.' In *loc. de lib. arb.*" (*Conc. concors*, p. 345.)

Pfeffinger: "Because the promise of grace is universal and it is necessary that we obey the promise: it follows that some distinction between the elect and the rejected must be taken from our will, namely, that those who resist the promise are rejected, but on the contrary, those who embrace the promise are received." (*De libertate vol. humanae qq. quinque*. Lips. 1555, thes. 30.)

The same: "If the will were idle or behaved purely passively, there would be no distinction between the pious and the impious, or the elect and the damned, as between Saul and David, between Judas and Peter. And God would become a respecter of persons and the author of contumacy in the impious and damned. And contradictory wills would be established in God, which conflicts with the entire Scripture. It follows, therefore, that there is some cause in us why some assent and others do not assent. But Scripture expressly says that there is no respect of persons with God, as in Deut. 10, Acts 10, Rom. 2, etc. And let not the respect of persons be understood of those things which are conspicuous in man, as some interpret, but that it is not to treat equals unequally. Moreover, this is the highest praise of the justice of God, that He is equal to equals, according to the rule which He has handed down." (L. c. Thes. 17—19.)

Kahnis: "It depends essentially on man whether he remains in the state of grace until the end... If, therefore, only he is saved who perseveres to the end, but perseverance depends on the will of man, then it follows irrefutably that salvation has its foundation not in grace alone, but also in the will of man." (*Die luth. Dogmatik*. Leipzig 1875, II, 254.)

ON PREDESTINATION AND REPROBATION. Or the antecedent will itself, as they call it, the fountain and origin of our salvation. See the blessed Musaeus, *Dissertatio Inauguralis de aeterna Praedestinationis Decreto*, chap. III, § 31 ff. Philippi: "Already John of Damascus, in *De fide orthodoxa* II, 26, 29, 30, distinguishes between θέλημα προηγούμενον, antecedent will, and θέλημα ἑπόμενον, consequent will; only with him this distinction rests upon semi-Pelagian presuppositions." (*Kirchliche Glaubenslehre*, Vol. IV, First Half, 1868, p. 64.) §

14. The external impulsive cause, and that the principal one, is the merit of Christ. Virtually causing, as we indicated in the notes to § 12 and 13. Which, by the power of its own dignity, perfection, and value, relates to the decree of predestination as an impulsive reason, in view of which God decreed eternal life for us from eternity. See the blessed Musaeus, *Dissertatio de Aeterno Electionis Decreto*, held in the year 1668, chap. II, § 37, pp. 23–24.

It is otherwise called meritorious, because under the aspect of merit it moves the will of God to decree salvation for us; by which very fact, however, it must be acknowledged as an impulsive cause or reason, namely, importing a twofold relation: one indeed to the thing merited, the other to the will of the efficient or decreeing cause. See the blessed Musaeus, *loc. cit.*, chap. V, §§ 109–110, p. 76 ff.

For this is taught to be the impulsive cause of every spiritual blessing that comes to us from God, and thus also of our predestination or election to eternal life, Ephesians 1:3–4, where it is also expressly said that God chose us ἐν Χριστῷ, and ἐν is used for διά, as it is frequently elsewhere; so that it is said that God chooses us on account of Christ, or in view of Christ as the impulsive cause.

That this explanation alone is consistent with the context, while the others that are circulated are either twisted or, when rightly understood, coincide with this one, the blessed Musaeus shows at length in his *Dissertatio Inauguralis*, chap. V, § 74 ff.

nihil. Cum ille solus det velle et perficere, Philip. 2., uti patet ex supra explicatis fundamentis, ubi de libro vitae, certitudine electionis et finali perseverantia actum fuit. Cf. theologos Witteb. in dem Griindl. Beweis p. 617. sq., ubi Bergianis exceptionibus satisfactum est.

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Pelagianorum, propter opera praevisa homines a Deo electos esse statuentium; vid. Augustinum dd praedest. sanctorum c. 18. et ep. 105. 2. 3. Scholasticorum, qui ad Pelagii castra proxime accedunt et, Deum praeordinasse, se daturum gloriam ex meritis, contendunt; ita Thomas P. 1. q.23. a. 5., Biell. sent. distinet. 41. q.unic. 4. Pontificiorum, Scholasticorum vestigia presse sequentium. . . Cf. f. 74.: ,Nunquam Scriptura asserit, quenquam Deo placuisse ad vitam aeternam, nisi per fidem et, quae fidei conjuncta sunt, opera.‘ Cf. f. 76.“L. c. s. 2. q. 2. f. 40. sqq.)

Ambrosius: ,,Nonante praedestinavit, quam praesciret, sed quorum merita praescivit, eorum praemia praedestinavit.“ (Ad Rom. 8, 29.)

Expresse enim dicit: ,In homine esse et esse oportere causam aliquam, cur alii ad salutem eligantur, alii abjiciantur et damnentur.‘ Et rursus: ,Cum promissio sit universalis, liec sint in Deo contradictoriae voluntates, necesse est in nobis esse aliquam discriminis causam, cur Saul abjiciatur, David recipiatur, h. e., necesse est esse aliquam actionem dissimilem in his duobus.‘ In loc. de lib. arb.“ (Cone, concors, p. 345.)

Pfeffingerus: ,,Quia promissio gratiae universalis est et necesse est, nos obedire promissioni: sequitur, aliquod discrimen inter electos et rejectos a voluntate nostra sumendum esse, videl. repugnantes pro· missioni rejici, contra vero amplectentes promissionem recipi.“ (De libertate vol. humanae qq. quinque. Lips. 1555. thes. 30.)

Seu ipsa voluntas antecedens, quam vocant, fons et origo nostrae salutis. Vid. b. Musaei Diss. Inaug. de aetern. Praed. Decr. cap. III. § 31. sq. Philippi: ,,Schon Johannes Damascenus de fide orth. II, 26.29.30. unterscheidet zwischen ΰέλημα προηγονμενον, voluntas antecedens, und ΰελημα επόμενον, voluntas consequens; nur ruht hei ihm diese UnterScheidung auf semipelagianischen Voraussetzungen.“ (Kirchliche Glaubenslehre. IV. Erste Hälfte. 1868. p. 64.) §

14. Causa a impulsiva externa, eaque principalis,b est meritum c Christi.d Virtualiter causans, ut indicavimus in notis ad § 12. 13. Quae vi propriae dignitatis, perfectionis et valoris ad decretum praedestinationis sese habet, ut ratio impulsiva, cujus intuitu Deus vitam aeternam nobis ab aeterno decrevit. Vid. b. Mus.
