Quod autem sola haec explicatio contextui conformis, reliquae vero, quae circumferuntur, omnes vel contortae sint, vel recte intellectae cum ista tandem coincidant, prolixe ostendit b. Musaeus Dissert. Inaug. cap. V. § 74. sqq.


### On Predestination and Reprobation: And to this point also pertains especially the argument drawn from the…

And to this point also pertains especially the argument drawn from the execution, to wit: That which is the (impulsive) cause why God confers salvation upon us in time, that also is the cause why He chose us to salvation. But the merit of Christ is the (impulsive) cause why God confers salvation upon us in time. Therefore, the merit of Christ is also the cause why God chose us.

The major proposition of which can be proved *a posteriori*—or that we are accustomed to judge commonly in this way concerning those things which are done from a preceding decree of the will, nor do we doubt the impulsive cause of the decree when we are certain of the impulsive cause of the execution, since we acknowledge that the impulsive causes are the same on both sides—as well as *a priori*, or from the nature and formal reason of an impulsive cause, through which it itself imports a relation to the will of the efficient cause by alluring or moving it (formally or virtually) to the act of willing or decreeing, to do that which is said to be done by its impulse, so that it is necessary to incur a contradiction if anyone, while admitting the impulsive cause of the execution, denies that the same is the cause of the decree, when, namely, the decree [relates] to the execution, and PART III. CHAP. XII.

He answers this accurately, and no change intervenes either on the part of the object or on the part of the will of Him who decrees and executes. See the blessed Musaeus, *Disp. Inaug. de Aet. Praed. Decr.*, ch. IV, § 51 ff., and *Dissert. de Aet. Elect. Decr.*, published in the year 1668, ch. III, § 82 ff., p. 59 ff., and ch. VII, § 166 ff., p. 123 ff.

The minor proposition of the argument is confirmed by those places of Scripture which teach that we are saved on account of Christ; and thus, just as they teach that the merit of Christ is the meritorious cause of salvation to be actually conferred, so they teach that the same holds the status of an impulsive cause with respect to the divine will. Compare what we have said before, and the blessed Musaeus, *Dissert. de Elect.*, held in the year 1668, ch. V, § 102 ff.

Nor does the acceptance of another’s merit conflict with the fact that election is ascribed to the gratuitous favor of God. See 2 Timothy 1:9, especially if we remember how God Himself gave us a mediator who might perform for us what we owed. Romans 8:3; John 3:16.

And the merit of Christ, although performed in time, could nevertheless have the status of an impulsive cause in relation to the eternal decree of God. For it suffices that it was objectively present, or foreseen by God, as something to be performed in its own time. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Dissert. de Aet. Elect. Decr.*, ch. VII, §§ 177, 178, pp. 132, 133.

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Calvinists, who exclude the merit of Christ from the causes of election and refer it to the means of execution supplied in time, and thus deny that Christ is the meritorious cause of our election. Nothing sounds in the Calvinistic school except the absolute decree, authorized at the Synod of Dort, confirmed by the religious obligation of an oath at the French Synod of Alais, as witnessed by Episcopius, Part 2 of the first part of his *Opera*, p. 388: 'The heart and palladium of the (Reformed) church is the doctrine of the most absolute grace of God,' according to the Genevans. *Actor. Synod. Dord.*, p. 212, Hannov. ed., according to the peremptory decree of Dort in the judgment on the first article, ibid., p. 30: 'The impulsive cause of this election is solely the most free and gratuitous good pleasure of God; and therefore not the merit of Christ, nor anything outside of God. Especially since the gift of Christ is a means subordinated to the election of men unto salvation. And therefore it is not the cause of election, but a consequent effect of election.' According to Ravanellus, p. 523: 'Christ, considered as θεάνθρωπος and mediator, is not the foundation and cause of election, but the means of executing election, or He through whom we are led to the end of our election.' In the *Acts of the Synod of Dordrecht*, f. 531, the Hessians of the same year say, 'The Reformed churches teach that Christ is the means of election (not of the decreeing, but of the executing), ... indeed in such a way that the decree concerning sending Christ and delivering Him to the ignominious death of the cross is in order posterior to the decree of election or to election.' 2. Of the Papists, who also defend an absolute decree of predestination; for thus Thomas Aquinas, P. 1, q. 23, a. 5: 'Why God chose these for glory and reprobated those has no reason except the divine will.' ... Bellarmine, *de amiss. grat. et lib. arb.*, bk. 2, ch. 8, § 2: 'We believe that God by an absolute will wills to save many, both infants and adults, and by an absolute will does not will to save others, both infants and adults.' 3. Of the Socinians, who deny the merit of Christ entirely, and exterminate it from the article of election just as they do from the article of justification. 4. Of the Labadists, who defend the absolute decree with the Calvinists." (*L. c. s. 2. q. 3. f. 46. sq.*) *

Formula consensus Helvetica*: "In that gracious decree of divine election, Christ Himself is also included, not as the cause

meritorious or the foundation, preceding the election itself, but as He Himself is also the εκλεκτός, the elect (1 Pet. 2:4, 6), foreknown before the foundations of the world were laid, and thus chosen as the primary mediator for the execution of it, and our firstborn brother, by whose precious merit He willed to use in order to confer salvation upon us, while preserving His justice. For Holy Scripture not only testifies that election was made according to the mere good pleasure of the divine counsel and will (Matt. 11:26; Eph. 1:5, 9), but also derives the destination and giving of Christ, the mediator, from the intense love of God the Father toward the world of the elect.” (§§ 14, 15. A. 1675. See *Collectio conf. in eccles. Reform. publ. ed. Niemeyer*, 1840, p. 731 sq.) § 15.

The less principal external impulsive cause of the decree of election is faith in Christ, and that is the final one. Virtually causing, or the reason *a priori*, just as we said the term is to be understood in the preceding sections as well.

Or that which, in our mode of conceiving, is prior to the decree of election and stands in relation to it as that by whose intuition we are elected, so that to one asking why those who are saved (precisely, and no others) were elected to life from eternity, one might respond appropriately by adducing or expressing that (namely, in this instance, faith, as we shall see): yet it does not itself possess its own merit, goodness, dignity, and perfection by which the will of the agent, or the one electing, is moved to act or to elect, but is elevated by the merit, goodness, or perfection of another, as the principal impulsive cause, or by the power of another’s merit, goodness, or dignity, it stands as the reason by whose intuition the will of God determines itself to decree salvation for us and had determined itself from eternity. Cf. the blessed Musaeus, *Diss. de Elect.*, An. 1668, cap. II, § 18 sq., p. 24, 25; § 63, p. 45. To the decree itself, I say, or the act of election, reference is made here, which is evident from the formal reason of an impulsive cause. See note c to § 14. However, the impulsive cause or reason is understood here not in relation to the decree concerning the whole process or business of procuring salvation, or concerning predestination taken more broadly, but more strictly, as we have already warned in § 12.

Namely, the merit of Christ, viewed absolutely in itself, without regard to the men who apply it to themselves through faith, is universal and extends even to the reprobate; however, it moves [God] to decree salvation for certain men insofar as it is apprehended by them through faith. And yet, faith also is to be considered here in this way: not in itself, as it is a supernatural habit or act (in which respect, even if it has some proper dignity, it does not, N.B., in any way move God to decree salvation for us through it), but on the part of the merit of Christ, which it apprehends and includes by way of an object. See the blessed Musaeus, *l.c.*, cap. II, § 40 to 44. Furthermore, some of our own have called faith in Christ the instrumental cause of the decree of election, others its condition, some a condition on the part of the object to be elected, and others a part of the order of predestination, but in the same sense, among themselves and with those who call it the less principal impulsive cause. For all acknowledge that faith is neither a bare condi- PART III. CHAP. XII.

that it is a condition which exercises no causality, but just as it relates to the act of saving, so it relates to the act of decreeing salvation by way of a cause (at least as a virtual cause), as that in view of which we were elected, yet without being able by its own dignity to move God to elect us, so as to be the principal cause.

Hence, when faith is otherwise said to behave like a hand or an organ by which the grace of God electing and the merit of Christ as the cause of salvation are apprehended, and for this reason is also accustomed to be called an instrument here, it must nevertheless be indicated here how faith relates to the decree of election itself; where our theologians do not say that it behaves by way of an instrument which the principal efficient cause, the electing God, uses to produce the act of election by a real influx. Those, however, who have spoken of a moral instrumental cause cannot understand anything other than a less principal impulsive cause.

Furthermore, when faith is said to be a part of the predestinarian order, it must be added what kind of respect it has (within those things which the whole order of the acts of predestination, broadly speaking, contains) to the very act of decreeing salvation for certain men, namely, those who will finally believe. And so, there finally remains that formula of speaking by which faith is called an impulsive cause or reason, yet not κατ’ ἐξοχήν or principal, but rather, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, with the addition of "less principal," in relation to the act of election itself. And those who formerly did not want to say that faith is an impulsive cause of election were looking at the principal impulsive cause, not thinking of the less principal impulsive cause.

See by all means the blessed Musaeus, l. c. § 50 sqq. p. 32 sqq., whom the blessed D. J. A. Scherzer also says must be consulted entirely in this whole matter, and he fully agrees with him in System. LXVIII. p. 488 sqq., especially p. 510, where he proposes and urges the argument taken from the execution of the decree of election in exactly the same way, and teaches in terms that the merit of Christ is the principal external impulsive and meritorious cause of the decree of election, but that faith is the less principal external impulsive cause and organ. Compare p. 512, 513, 514.

Latin:

Atque huc etiam praecipue pertinet argumentum ab executione petitum, h. m.: Quod est causa (impulsiva), cur Deus in tempore nobis salutem conferat, id etiam causa est, cur ad salutem nos elegerit. Atqui meritum Christi est causa (impulsiva), cur Deus in tempore nobis mlutem conferat. Ergo meritum Christi est etiam causa, cur Deus nos ele· gerit.

Cujus major propositio cum a posteriori probari potest, seu quod ita communiter de his, quae ex praeeunte decreto voluntatis aguntur, judicare solemus, neque de causa impulsiva decreti dubitamus, quando de causa impulsiva executionis certi sumus, quippe quod causas impulsi vas utrinque easdem esse agnoscamus, tum a priori, seu ex natura ac ratione formali causae impulsivae, per quam ipsa importat habitudinem ad voluntatem causae efficientis alliciendo aut movendo eam (formaliter aut virtualiter) ad actum volendi seu decernendi, agere id, quod ejus impulsu agere dicitur, ita ut contradictionem incurrere necesse sit, si quis, causam impulsivam executionis admittens, eandem neget esse decreti causam, quando videlicet decretum executioni, et PART. III. CAP. XII.

haec illi, accurate respondet, neque vel ex parte objecti, vel ex parte voluiitatis ejus, qui decernit et exequitur, mutatio aliqua intervenit. Vid. b. Musaei Disp. Inaug. de Aet. Praed. Decr. cap. IV. § 51. sqq. et Dissert. de Aet. Elect. Decr. An. 1668. edita, cap. III. § 82. sqq. p. 59. sqq. et cap. VII. § 166. sqq. p. 123. sqq.

Minor autem propositio argumenti confirmatur per ea Scripturae loca, quae nos propter Christum salvari docent; adeoque sicut meritum Christi esse causam meritoriam salutis actu conferendae, ita idem respectu voluntatis divinae rationem causae impulsivae, habere, docent. Confer, quae ante diximus, et b. Musaei Dissert. de Elect. An. 1668. hab. cap. V. § 102. sqq.

Neque pugnat meriti alieni acceptatio cum eo, quod electio adscribitur gratuito favori Dei. Vid. 2 Timoth. 1, 9. praesertim, si meminerimus, quomodo Deus ipse nobis dederit mediatorem, qui pro nobis praestaret, quod debebamus. Rom. 8, 3. Joh. 3, 16.

Ac potuit meritum Christi, licet in tempore praestitum, tamen in ordine ad aeternum Dei decretum habere rationem causae impulsivae. Sufficit enim, fuisse objective praesens, seu praevisum a Deo, ut suo tempore praestandum. Conf. b. Mus. Dissert. de Aet. Elect. Decr. cap. VII. §§ 177. 178. p. 132. 133.

Calvinianorum, qui ex causis electionis meritum Christi excludunt et ad media executionis in tempore suppeditata referunt, adeoque negant, Christum esse causam meritoriam nostrae electionis. Pontificiorum, qui etiam absolutum praedestinationis decretum defendunt; sic enim Thomas Aquin. Formula consensus Helvetica: ,,In gratioso autem illo electionis divinae decreto ipse quoque Christus includitur, non ut causa

meritoria vel fundamentum, ipsam electionem praecedens, sed ut ipse quoque εκλεκτός, electus (1 Petr. 2, 4. 6.), ante jacta mundi fundamenta praecognitus, adeoque primarium ejus exequendae electus mediator, et primogenitus frater noster, cujus pretioso merito ad conferendam nobis, salva justitia sua, salutem uti voluit. Scriptura enim sacra non tantum testatur, electionem factam esse secundum merum beneplacitum consilii et voluntatis divinae (Matth. 11, 26. Eph. 1, 5. 9.), sed etiam destinationem et dationem Christi, mediatoris Christi, ab enixo Dei Patris erga mundum electorum amore arcessit.“ (§§ 14. 15. A. 1675. Vid. Collectio conf. in eccles. Reform, pubi, ed Niemeyer. 1840. p. 731. sq.) § 15.

Causa a impulsiva externa minus principalis b decreti c electionis est fides d in Christum,e eaque f finalis. Virtualiter causans, seu ratio a priori, uti in prioribus quoque vocem accipiendam esse diximus.

Seu id, quod nostro modo concipiendi prius est decreto electionis atque ad illud sese habet, tanquam id, cujus intuitu simus electi, ita ut quaerenti, cur hi, qui salvantur (praecise, non alii), ah aeterno sint electi ad vitam? adducendo aut exprimendo illud (nempe h. 1. fidem, ut videbimus) convenienter respondeatur: neque tamen ipsum habet meritum proprium, bonitatem, dignitatem ac perfectionem propriam, qua voluntas agentis, sive eligentis, ad agendum, seu eligendum, moveatur, sed alterius, tanquam causae impulsivae principalis, merito, bonitate, aut perfectione elevatum, seu vi alieni meriti, bonitatis, aut dignitatis se habet ut ratio, cujus intuitu voluntas Dei ad decernendam nobis salutem se determinet et ab aeterno se determinaverit. Conf. b. Mus. Diss. de Elect. An. 1668. cap. II. § 18. sq. p. 24. 25. § 63. p. 45. Ad ipsum, inquam, decretum, seu actum electionis, hic respicitur, quod ex ratione formali causae impulsivae patet. Vid. not. c. ad § 14. Intelligitur autem h. 1. causa seu ratio impulsiva non in ordine ad decretum de toto processu seu negotio procurandae salutis, seu de praedestinatione latius accepta, sed strictius, uti jam monuimus § 12.

Nempe meritum Christi, in se absolute spectatum, citra respectum ad homines, qui illud sibi per fidem applicant, universale est et ad reprobos etiam se extendit, movet autem ad decernendam certis hominibus salutem, quatenus ab his fide apprehenditur. Atqui ita fides quoque h. l. consideranda est, non in se, ut est habitus vel actus supernaturalis (qua ratione etsi habeat aliquam dignitatem propriam, non tamen per illam NB. ullatenus movet Deum ad salutem nobis decernendam), verum ex parte meriti Christi, quod apprehendit et per modum objecti includit. Vid. b. Musaeus 1. c. cap. II. § 40. ad 44. Caeterum fidem in Christum alii quidem nostratium causam instrumentalem decreti electionis, alii conditionem ejus, quidam conditionem ex parte objecti eligendi, alii partem ordinis praedestinatorii dixerunt, sed sensu eodem, inter se et cum his, qui causam impulsivam minus principalem appellant. Omnes enim agnoscunt, fidem neque nudam condiPART. HI. CAP. XH.

tionem esse, quae nullam causalitatem exerceat, sed prout ad actum salvandi, sic ad actum decernendi salutem per modum causae (saltem virtualiter causantis) se habere tanquam id, cujus intuitu simus electi, neque tamen ipsam sua dignitate movere potuisse Deum ad nos eligendos, ut esset causa principalis.

Unde, quando fides alias dicitur habere se instar manus aut organi, quo gratia Dei eligentis et meritum Christi ut causa salutis apprehenditur, atque hac ratione etiam hic instrumentum dici consuevit, hic tamen indicandum est, quomodo fides ad ipsum decretum electionis sese habeat; ubi nostrates non dicunt, habere se per modum instrumenti, quo causa efficiens principalis, Deus eligens, utatur ad producendum reali influxu actum electionis. Qui vero camam instrumentalem moralem dixerunt, non possunt aliud quid, quam causam impulsivam minus principalem intelligere.

Porro, quando fides pars ordinis praedestinatorii dicitur, addendum est, qualem respectum (intra ea, quae totus ordo actuum praedestinationis latius dictae continet) habeat ad ipsum actum decernendi certis hominibus, nempe flnaliter credituris, salutem. Itaque superest tandem ea loquendi formula, qua fides caum seu ratio impulsiva, non tamen χατ έξοχψ sive principalis, verum cum addito, vitandae ambiguitatis causa, minus principalis dicatur, in ordine ad ipsum electionis actum. Et qui quondam noluerunt dicere, fidem esse causam impulsivam electionis, respexerunt causam impulsivam principalem, de minus principali causa impulsiva non cogitantes.

Vide omnino b. Musaeum 1. c. § 50. sq. p. 32. sq., quem etiam in hoc toto negotio omnino videndum dicit eique plane accedit b. D. I A. Scherzerus in System. LXVIII. p. 488. sqq., praesertim p. 510., ubi argumentum ab executione decreti electionis petitum eodem prorsus modo proponit atque urget, et meritum Christi esse causam impulsivam externam principalem ac meritoriam decreti electionis, fidem vero esse causam impulsivam externam minus principalem et organimm, in terminis docet. Confer, p. 512. 513. 514.


### On Predestination and Reprobation: Indeed, even the blessed Balthasar Meisner, Anthrop

Indeed, even the blessed Balthasar Meisner, Anthrop. Dec. II. disp. IV. membr. III. § 36, after having said: "When faith is called a cause of election, do not understand it as principal, impelling, or meritorious, but only as instrumental, and indeed not of the whole decree, but rather of a part, namely, the merit of Christ, which faith apprehends. For since it is a cause of a part of the decree, hence in a popular way of speaking it is called a cause of the decree itself," and having added: "It is more convenient, however, to call faith either a condition of election, lest it be imagined to be absolute, or a part of the predestinarian order, which God from eternity regarded no less than the merit of Christ," he finally concludes notably: "It seems most convenient that faith not be considered separately, as a peculiar cause of election distinct from the merit of Christ, but conjunctively together with the merit itself apprehended, so that both joined together constitute one impelling cause of election. For neither merit without application, nor faith by itself moved God to elect, but both joined in the divine foreknowledge, that is, merit apprehended by faith, or faith apprehending merit."

These things certainly agree entirely with the aforementioned opinion of the blessed Musaeus. For thus, in any case, the relation of faith to election is such "as a cause or impulsive reason has to that of which it is said to be the cause; and yet, not insofar as it is considered separately, or in itself absolutely, but insofar as it is considered on the part of the merit of Christ, so that it is not as if..."

the merit of Christ and faith stand in relation to the decree of election not as two associate or partial causes (if one may speak thus in this place), but as subordinate causes and by way of a principal and instrumental cause (which, just as in the genus of efficient cause they produce an effect by a single influx, although they are otherwise distinguished from one another, so in the genus of impulsive cause they move the will of the agent, as if by a single impulse, to will to act or to decree): which is the very opinion explained thus far.

J. Musaeus: "As to what kind of *habitudo* (relation) *fides praevisa* (foreseen faith) imports toward the decree of predestination—whether it is that of a cause, or of a condition required on the part of the subject to be predestined, or something else—those of our side (the pure theologians) have for many years had divergent thoughts, and they have not been able to fully agree even on the terms and phrases by which the same might most fittingly be described and expressed. The excellent theologian D. Aeg. Hunnius, who has deserved well of the Christian Church and who applied great diligence above others in the explanation and clarification of this article, and who also defended the same powerfully against the Calvinists, was of the constant opinion that *fidem esse praedestinationis causam* (faith is the cause of predestination), and he founded his opinion on the fact that faith is the *causa justificationis* (cause of justification); for the phrases of Scripture, 'to justify by faith,' 'through faith,' 'from faith,' import a *vera habitudo causae* (true relation of cause), which is thereby attributed to faith in order to justification and salvation, as to the execution of the decree of predestination. Now, however, the causes of the decree and of the execution are the same. But he was immediately met with the scruple, not only by Calvinists but also by several theologians of our own side, that if faith were the cause of the decree of predestination, it would have to be its meritorious cause. For they saw well that the *vis causandi* (power of causing) of any impulsive cause must consist in merit, or at least in some proper dignity or goodness, by the value of which the cause decreeing or acting is moved to decree or act; and they supposed, therefore, that if faith were the cause of the decree of predestination, it would also have to contain within itself a merit or dignity, perfection and goodness, by the value of which it moved God from eternity to establish the decree of predestination. Whereupon the blessed Hunnius further explained himself, that just as faith is the instrumental cause of justification, not the meritorious—for it makes one righteous not as a quality or habit, by reason of any of its own dignity, perfection, or value, nor as a meritorious act, but only *in quantum* (insofar as) it apprehends the merit of Christ and applies it to us—so also it is the instrumental cause of the decree of predestination, not the meritorious. For it is also the cause of that, not as a quality or habit by reason of any of its own dignity or goodness, or as a meritorious act, but also insofar as it grasps Christ’s merit and appropriates it to us, and God, according to His omniscience, has seen such from eternity; and thus faith, apprehending the merit of Christ, is in God’s eternal foreknowledge the instrumental cause of the decree of predestination, just as it is of justification. But because the phrase 'faith is the instrumental cause of the decree of predestination' sounds somewhat harsh and, according to the words, seems to have this meaning: that it is the instrumental cause on the part of God predestinating to establish the eternal decree concerning our salvation; and also because the blessed Hunnius’s adversaries, especially Samuel Huberus and Daniel Tossanus, interpreted the same still differently, namely, that 'faith is the instrumental cause of the decree of predestination, because it apprehends our predestination,' although against Hunnius’s express protestation that this was not his meaning: therefore, several other theologians of our side have hesitated to use the same and have preferred to say that 'faith is a condition of predestination required on the part of the subject to be predestined, and a part of the order of predestination,' rather than that it is..." 36 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III. PART. III. CAP. XII. the instrumental cause of predestination. Even if one adds the blessed Hunnius’s correct explanation without misinterpretation, that faith is the instrumental cause of the decree of predestination, just as it is of justification, insofar as it is the instrumental cause of the apprehension of the merit of Christ, there still remains for the students the scruple as to what kind of relationship (*habitudinem*) of cause faith holds within itself, both toward the act of justification and toward the decree of predestination itself. For indeed, the apprehension of the merit of Christ is one thing, and the act of justification and the decree of predestination are another. The apprehension of the merit of Christ is an act of faith in us, and because it is an act of faith, there is no doubt that faith is the cause of the same in the genus of efficient cause. However, the act of justification and the decree of predestination are acts of God in God—to speak in our mode of conceiving—and if faith is the cause of these, there still remains the scruple as to in what genus or order of cause it is the cause of them, and in what their causal relationship (*habitudo causalis*) to those acts consists. But the other two phrases do not seem to be subject to this difficulty: that faith is a condition of the decree of predestination, required on the part of the subject to be predestined, or that it is a part of the order of predestination; and it also seems to be enough against the Reformed absolute decree of predestination if one maintains this, that the decree of predestination includes within itself faith foreseen as a condition required on the part of the subject to be predestined, and as a part of the order of predestination. And we would also hold it to be safest that one should remain with this simple way of speaking, were it not that something else stands in our way. But it stands in our way, firstly, that Holy Scripture so consistently attributes to faith the relationship of a cause in relation to justification and salvation, as to the execution of the decree of predestination, and so consistently teaches that we are justified and also become saved πίστει, by faith, δια πίστεως, through faith, εκ πίστεως, from faith, etc. But what is the cause of the execution must also be the cause of the decree. Furthermore, it also stands in our way that in the main controversy with the Calvinists concerning predestination, we must either abandon for ourselves the most important and strongest argument taken from the execution, which we are accustomed to use against the Calvinists’ absolute decree, or at least we cannot urge it with any emphasis as long as we deny, or hesitate to say, that faith is the cause of the decree of predestination, and only remain with the position that it is at least a condition required on the part of the subject and a part of the order of predestination. For if one wanted to conclude thus: "what is the cause of justification and salvation, that is a condition of the decree of predestination required on the part of the subject," the Calvinists would be able to elude the argument with many evasions and instances. Thus, for the emphatic use of this argument, it is not enough to say that faith is the cause of the execution, but one must explain distinctly in what genus or order of causes faith is the cause of the execution, namely of justification and salvation. For this consequence—"what is the cause of the execution is also the cause of the decree"—does not hold true for every genus of causes, and it is therefore necessary, if one wishes to use this argument with emphasis, that one first knows and shows exactly in what genus or order of causes faith is the cause of justification and salvation, and then one can powerfully conclude and explain to the studying youth whether and in what genus or order of causes faith is also the cause of the decree of predestination. Now, to remedy this difficulty, and to explain clearly and thoroughly to the students what kind of relationship faith in Christ holds toward the decree of predestination—whether that of a mere condition, or of a cause, and of what genus of cause—we have first and foremost directed our attention to the matter itself and found that, throughout, all the pure theologians and teachers of our Church, who [taught] the doctrine concerning pre-

Latin:

Imo vero etiam b. Balthas. Meisn. Anthrop. Dec. II. disp. IV. membr. III. § 36., postquam dixisset: Cum fides electionis causa dicitur, non intelligas principalem, impellentem aut meritoriam, sed tantum instrumentalem, et quidem non totius decreti, sed potius partis, nempe meriti Christi, quod fides apprehendit. Cum enim sit causa partis decreti, hinc populari modo loquendi causa dicitur ipsius decreti, et addidisset: Convenientius tamen est, fidem nuncupare vel conditionem electionis, ne fingatur esse absoluta, vel partem ordinis praedestinatorii, quam Deus ab aeterno non minus ut meritum Christi aspexerit, denique notanter concludit: Convenientissimum illud videtur, fidem non considerari seorsim, ut causam electionis peculiarem a Christi merito distinetam, sed conjunctim una cum ipso merito apprehenso, ut sic utrumque copulatum unam electionis causam impellentem constituat. Neque enim meritum sine applicatione, neque fides per se movit Deum ad eligendum, sed utrumque in praescientia divina conjunctum, hoc est, meritum fide apprehensum, vel fides meritum apprehendens.

Quae profecto cum b. Musaei sententia memorata prorsus conveniunt. Sic enim utique fidei habitudo ad electionem talis est, ‘qualem habet causa vel ratio impulsiva ad id, cujus causa esse dicitur; nec tamen, quatenus ipsa seorsim, aut in se absolute, sed quatenus ex parte meriti Christi consideratur, ita ut non velut

duae causae sociae aut partiales (si ita h. 1. loqui licet), sed tanquam causae subordinatae et per modum causae principalis atque instrumentalis (quae sicut in genere causae efficientis uno influxu producunt effectum, licet inter se alias distinguantur, ita in genere causae impulsivae uno velut impulsu moveant voluntatem agentis ad volendum agere seu decernere) sese habeant meritum Christi et fides ad decretum electionis: quae est ipsa sententia hactenus explicata.

J. Musaeus: ,,Was der fides praevisa für eine habitudinem ad decretum praedestinationis importire, an causae, an conditionis ex parte subjecti praedestinandi requisitae, an aliam, darüber haben sie (unseres Theils reine Theologi) von langen Jahren her ungleiche Gedanken gehabt und auch über den terminis und phrasibus, womit dieselbe am füglichsten möchte beschrieben und exprimirt werden, sich nicht allerdings vergleichen können. Der fürtreffliche und um die christliche Kirche wohl verdiente theologus D. Aeg. Hunnius, der in Erklärung und Läuterung dieses Artikels für andern grossen Fleiss angewandt und denselben auch wider die Calvinisten gewaltig vertheidiget hat, ist in der beständigen Meinung gewesen, fidem esse praedestinationis causam, und hat seine Meinung darauf gegründet, dass der Glaub justificationis causa sei; denn die phrases scripturae, justificare fide, per fidem, ex fide importiren eine veram habitudinem causae, welche dem Glauben in ordine ad justificationem et salvationem, velut ad executionem decreti praedestinationis, dadurch zugeeignet werde. Nun aber sein decreti et executionis eaedem pausae. Es wurde ihm aber alsobald nicht allein von Calvinisten, sondern auch von etlichen unsers Theils Theologen der Skrupel gemacht, dass wenn der Glaube causa decreti praedestinationis wäre, so müsste er causa meritoria desselben sein. Denn sie sahen wohl, dass cujusque causae impulsivae vis causandi bestehen müsste in merito, oder doch in propria quadam dignitate vel bonitate, cujus valore causa decernens vel agens ad decernendum vel agendum moveatur, und vermeinten daher, wenn der Glaube causa decreti praedestinationis wäre, so müsste er auch ein meritum oder dignitatem, perfectionem et bonitatem quandam in sich halten, cujus valore Deum ad condendum praedestinationis decretum ab aeterno permoverit. Worauf sich denn der sel. Hunnius weiter erklärte, dass wie der Glaube justificationis causa instrumentalis ist, nicht meritoria, denn er mache gerecht nicht ut qualitas vel habitus, ratione ullius suae dignitatis, perfectionis vel valoris, auch nicht ut actus meritorius, sondern nur in quantum meritum Christi apprehendit et nobis applicat, also sei er auch decreti praedestinationis causa instrumentalis, nicht meritoria. Denn er sei auch illius causa nicht ut qualitas vel habitus ratione suae cujusdam dignitatis vel bonitatis vel ut actus meritorius, sondern auch, aisfern er Christi Verdienst ergreift und uns zueignet, und Gott nach seiner Allwissenheit solches von Ewigkeit her gesehen hat, und sei also fldes Christi meritum apprehendens, in Dei aeterna praevisione, decreti praedestinationis eben, wie justificationis, causa instrumentalis. Weil aber die phrasis, fidem esse decreti praedestinationis causam ins^rumentalem, etw&s hart lautet und den Worten nach diese Meinung zu haben scheint, eam ex parte Dei praedestinantis esse causam instrumentalem condendi de salute nostra decreti aeterni, und auch des sel. Hunnii adversarii, sonderlich Samuel Huberus und Daniel Tossanus, dieselbe noch anders und also deuteten, fidem esse decreti praedestinationis causam instrumentalem, quod praedestinationem nostri apprehendat, wiewohl wider Hunnii ausdrückliche Protestation, dass diese seine Meinung nicht wäre: als haben etliche andere unsers Theils theologi derselben sich zu gebrauchen angestanden und lieber sagen wollen, fidem esse conditionem praedestinationis ex parte subjecti praedestinandi requisitam, et partem ordinis praedestinatorii, ais, eam esse 36 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther. III. PART. III. CAP. XII. causam praedestinationis instrumentalem. Wenn man auch gleich des sel. Hunnii rechte Erklärung ohne Missdeutung hinzu thut, dass der Glaube sei, wie justificationis, also auch decreti praedestinationis causa Instrumentalis, in quantum est causa Instrumentalis apprehensionis meriti Christi, so bleibet doch bei den discentibus noch der Skrupel, was denn der Glaube für eine habitudinem causae cum ad actum justificationis, tum ad ipsum decretum praedestinationis in sich halte. Denn ja ein anders ist die apprehensio meriti Christi, ein anders der actus justificationis und das decretum praedestinationis. Die apprehensio meriti Christi ist ein actus fidei in nobis, und weil sie ein actus fidei ist, so ist kein Zweifel, dass der Glaube derselben causa, sei in genere causae efficientis. Der actus justificationis und das decretum praedestinationis aber sind actus Del in Deo, nostro modo concipiendi so zu reden, deren causa, wenn der Glaube ist, so bleibet noch der Skrupel, in quo genere vel ordine causae er derselben causa sei und worin desselben habitudo causalis ad actus illos bestehe. Dieser Difficultät aber scheinen nicht unterworfen sein die andern beide phrases: quod fides sit conditio decreti praedestinationis, ex parte subjecti praedestinandi requisita, oder quod sit pars ordinis praedestinatorii und scheinet auch wider der Reformirten absolutum praedestinationis decretum gnug sein, wenn man dieses erhält, dass das decretum praedestinationis den fidem praevisam in sich begreife velut conditionem ex parte subjecti praedestinandi requisitam, et ut partem ordinis praedestinatorii, und hielten auch wir fürs sicherste, dass man bei dieser einfältigen Redensart bliebe, wo uns nicht etwas anders im Weg läge. Es liegt uns aber im Wege, erstlich, dass die heilige Schrift den Glauben so beständig habitudinem causae in ordine ad justificationem et salvationem, velut ad executionem decreti praedestinationis, zueignet und so beständig lehret, nos justificari et fieri etiam salvos πίστει, fide, δια πίστεως, per fidem, εκ πίστεως, ex fide etc. Was aber causa executionis ist, das muss auch causa decreti sein. Darnach liegt auch uns im Wege, dass wir in dem Hauptstreit mit den Calvinisten de praedestinatione des allerwichtigsten und allerstärksten argumenti ab executione petiti, dessen wir uns wider der Calvinisten absolutum decretum zu gebrauchen pflegen, uns eiftweder von uns selber begeben müssen oder doch dasselbe mit keinem Nachdruck urgiren können, so lang wir leugnen, oder anstehen zu sagen, fidem esse decreti praedestinationis causam, und nur dabei bleiben, eam esse saltem conditionem ex parte subjecti requisitam et partem ordinis praedestinatorii. Denn wenn man also schliessen wollte: quod est causa justificationis et salvationis, illud est conditio decreti praedestinationis ex parte subjecti requisita, so würden die Calvinisten mit vielen Ausflüchten und instantiis das Argument elidiren können. So will auch zum nachdrücklichen Gebrauch dieses Arguments nicht gnug sein, dass man sagt, fidem esse causam executionis, sondern man muss distincte erklären, in quo causarum genere vel ordine fides executionis, nempe justificationis et salvationis, causa sei. Denn nicht von jedwedem genere causarum diese Consequentia: quod est causa executionis, est etiam causa decreti, richtig angehet, und ist demnach nöthig, wenn man dieses Argument mit Nachdruck gebrauchen will, dass man vorher genau wisse und zeige, in quo genere vel ordfne causarum fides justificationis et salvationis causa sei, und alsdann kann man kräftiglich schliessen und der studirenden Jugend erklären: an et in quo genere vel ordine causarum fides auch decreti praedestinationis causa sei. Dieser Difficultät nun abzuhelfen, und was der Glaub an Christum für eine habitudinem ad decretum praedestinationis in sich halte, an conditionis nudae, an causae, et cujus generis causae, denen discentibus deutlich und gründlich zu erklären, haben wir zum ersten und zuvörderst unser Absehen gerichtet gehabt auf die Sache selbst und befunden, dass durchgehend alle unser'er Kirchen reine theologi und Lehrer, welche die Lehre de prae-


### On Predestination and Reprobation: have explained the decree of predestination and defended it against the…

have explained the decree of predestination and defended it against the Calvinists' *absolutum decretum*, finally arrive in their explanations, as far as the matter itself is concerned, at the point that *fidem praevisam esse decreti praedestinationis causam impulsivam minus principalem* [foreseen faith is a less principal impulsive cause of the decree of predestination]. For as far as the *status quaestionis* [state of the question] is concerned, all agree that the main dispute between us and the Reformed consists in this: *An detur causa aliqua extra Deum, cujus intuitu Deus nos ab aeterno elegerit sive praedestinaverit ad vitam aeternam* [Whether there is any cause outside of God, in view of which God has from eternity chosen or predestined us to eternal life]. Which disputed question can be understood as being about no other cause than the impulsive cause, and *causa, cujus intuitu Deus nos elegit sive praedestinavit ad vitam aeternam* [the cause, in view of which God chose or predestined us to eternal life] is nothing other than *causa, qua praevisa Deus ab aeterno permotus est ad praedestinandum nos ad vitam aeternam* [the cause, by the foreseeing of which God was moved from eternity to predestine us to eternal life]. To this main question, they all answer unanimously: *Deum praedestinasse nos ab aeterno intuitu praevisi meriti Christi fide apprehendendi* [that God predestined us from eternity in view of the foreseen merit of Christ to be apprehended by faith] or that he predestined us in view of our foreseen faith, and thus they all unanimously admit, as far as the matter itself is concerned, that the impulsive cause, by which God was moved from eternity to predestine us to eternal life, is the merit of Christ, foreseen as apprehended by faith, or that the impulsive cause is foreseen faith in Christ. But when it is further asked, *quomodo fides in Christum ab aeterno moverit Deum ad nostri praedestinationem, an ut qualitas, habitus, vel actus, sua propria dignitate, bonitate, merito et valore, an modo alio* [how faith in Christ moved God from eternity to our predestination, whether as a quality, habit, or act, by its own dignity, goodness, merit, and value, or in another way], they all answer unanimously that God, in establishing the decree of predestination, did not look upon faith *ut qualitatem, actum vel habitum* [as a quality, act, or habit], nor for any of its own dignity, worth, or perfection, and thus they confess that faith in Christ is not the principal cause of the decree of predestination, much less a meritorious cause of the same, but that this belongs solely and alone to the merit of Christ. But if one asks further how God then looked upon faith in establishing the decree of predestination, they answer again unanimously that God looked upon it insofar as it grasps and appropriates to us the merit of Christ, and that God was thus moved to ordain us to eternal life, not out of any of faith's own power, dignity, and goodness, but solely and alone through the fully valid merit of Christ, which it grasps and appropriates to us. Which is nothing else than *fidem esse causam decreti praedestinationis impulsivam minus principalem, quae moverit quidem Deum ad nostri praedestinationem, non tamen ulla sua dignitate, valore aut merito, sed solius meriti Christi, quod apprehendit et Deo Patri in sua aeterna praescientia velut λύτρον pro peccatis nostris sufficientissimum exhibuit, dignitate et valore* [that faith is a less principal impulsive cause of the decree of predestination, which indeed moved God to our predestination, yet not by any of its own dignity, value, or merit, but by the dignity and value of the merit of Christ alone, which it apprehends and exhibits to God the Father in His eternal foreknowledge as a most sufficient λύτρον (ransom) for our sins]. Faith, insofar as it grasps and appropriates to us the merit of Christ, can be a cause of predestination in no other *genere causae* [kind of cause] than that in which the merit of Christ is a cause of the same. But according to the confession of all, the merit of Christ is a cause *in genere et ordine causae impulsivae* [in the kind and order of an impulsive cause]; therefore, that which grasps the merit of Christ and holds it before God must also be a cause of the same *in hoc genere vel ordine causae* [in this kind or order of cause].

Thereafter, we have further looked at the reason why the theologians of our church, regarding the matter itself, in which they are thoroughly unanimous, have used such unequal *terminos* and *phrases*, and have not expressed the same with their own *terminis* and said that faith in Christ foreseen is a less principal impulsive cause of the decree of predestination, but have partly said *eam esse decreti praedestinationis causam instrumentalem* [that it is an instrumental cause of the decree of predestination], others that it is a condition required on the part of the subject to be predestined and a part of the predestinatory order, whereby the *discentes* [learners] in their growth in thorough knowledge in this piece have been not a little held back and hindered.

In a closer examination of such causes, we have found that the main causes of this inequality in *terminis* and modes of speech have been that at those times, from the distinction *inter causas impulsivas principales* [between principal impulsive causes... PART III. CHAP. XII. and less principal [causes] in our schools knew nothing, but stood in the delusion that every *impulsiva causa* (impulsive cause) must contain within itself a *meritum* (merit) or a *dignitatem* (dignity), *bonitatem propriam* (proper goodness), by the force and value of which it might move the efficient cause to decree or do something, and that therefore every *causa impulsiva* is a *causa principalis* (principal cause).

And because no *meritum*, no *dignitas*, *bonitas et perfectio propria* (proper goodness and perfection) belongs to faith in Christ in itself, by the value of which God might have been moved to our predestination, some theologians, as mentioned, did not want to call faith in Christ a *causa decreti praedestinationis* (cause of the decree of predestination) at all, because they clearly saw that faith could not be a cause of the decree of predestination in any other *genere causae* (genus of cause) than in the genus or order of impulsive causes; and if it were to be a cause of the same, it would have to be an impulsive cause of it, while at the same time they stood in the firm belief that every impulsive cause includes a merit or some other proper motive force and is a principal cause.

And one should not be surprised at this. For in those times, metaphysics—to which the *doctrina de generibus causarum* (doctrine concerning the genera of causes) and specifically also concerning principal and less principal impulsive causes belongs—was little known, and one will not easily find a Lutheran university where it was ordained in the statutes of the philosophical faculty to profess metaphysics in former times. Furthermore, *causae impulsivae minus principales* (less principal impulsive causes) are not as common in general usage as the *causae minus principales* in the genus of the efficient cause tend to be, and therefore they are rarely or never treated in metaphysical compendia. . .

Thus, the hypothesis that all impulsive causes contain within themselves a proper merit or a proper motive force and are principal causes is false; and after this scruple is removed, nothing further stands in the way or hinders one from expressing in their own words the doctrine unanimously confessed by all our theologians, as far as the matter itself is concerned, that *praevisa fides in Christum* (foreseen faith in Christ) is a *causa impulsiva minus principalis* (less principal impulsive cause) of the decree of predestination, and from saying: *eam praevisam esse decreti praedestinationis causam impulsivam minus principalem* (that it, being foreseen, is a less principal impulsive cause of the decree of predestination).” (*Bedenken vom consensu repetito* [Considerations on the Repeated Consensus], 1680. See Calovius, *Histor. syncretist.*, pp. 1041–1046.)

N. Selneccerus: “Is foreseen faith the cause of election? If justifying faith were our work, our quality and virtue, this question would have a place. But because that faith is the work of God in us, there is therefore no great need for this question, to which, however, it is not difficult to respond. Election is certainly the eternal purpose of God concerning the saving of men. Faith in Christ is subject to this purpose of God, which faith God Himself also gives according to the order instituted by Himself. Foreseen faith, therefore, cannot be the cause of eternal election, of which faith is, as it were, a consequence and effect in us who are born in time and also ceases in us as we die in time. But if foreseen faith were called the cause of election, a false opinion concerning our foreseen dignity and concerning the merits—not only of faith as our quality, but also of our other good works—could easily occupy minds. God knows who are His, and He chose them before the foundations of the world were laid. And there is no other cause of this election except the gratuitous mercy and clemency of God through and on account of Christ the Mediator and His merit, to be apprehended and applied by faith alone. Since this faith is the hand or instrument by which the grace of God and the merit of Christ are apprehended, it cannot be the cause of grace and election, but is that medium and organ by which the application of the grace and merit of Christ to us is effected.” (*In omnes epp. D. Pauli commentar.* [Commentary on all the Epistles of St. Paul], I, 213 sq.)

Hülsemann: "The Epitome of the Book of Concord and the Thorough Declaration of Article XI teach that the impulsive cause of predestination is the merit of Christ, but that the foreseen non-rejection of the offer of this benefit and the admission of it through faith do not pertain to the causes—much less the impulsive causes—of predestination, but rather to the condition without which the execution does not occur. The impulsive"

that the cause of the decree of perdition is the foreseeing of sin and of final perseverance in it, and therefore that sin is the impulsive cause not only of the execution, but of the decree itself.” (Praelect. in lib. Conc., p. 698 sq.)

Hutterus: “We do not reluctantly grant that neither faith nor the foreseeing of faith is the cause of our election. Faith indeed is not, because it, in and of itself, insofar as it is a virtue, habit, or quality, does nothing at all toward our election or our justification; and in this case it obtains exactly the same condition as the works or merits of men. But we do not grant that the foreseeing of faith is, strictly speaking, the cause of our election either; since it has already been shown that foreseeing, like foreknowledge, is not the cause of any thing foreknown or foreseen, but merely comprises the knowledge of all things foreknown.” (Libri Conc. explic., p. 1101.)

Latin:

destinationis decreto erklärt und wider der Calvinisten absolutum decretum vertheidigt haben, in ihren Erklärungen, so viel die Sache selbst betrifft, endlich dahin kommen, fidem praevisam esse decreti präedestinationis causam impulsivam minus principalem. Denn was den statum quaestionis anlanget, kommen alle darin überein, dass der Hauptstreit zwischen uns und den Reformirten darin bestehe: An detur causa aliqua extra Deum, cujus intuitu Deus nos ab aeterno elegerit sive praedestinaverit ad vitam aeternam. Welche streitige Erage von keiner andern causa als de causa impulsiva kann verstanden werden, und ist causa, cujus intuitu Deus nos elegit sive praedestinavit ad vitam aeternam, nichts anders als causa, qua praevisa Deus ab aeterno permotus est ad praedestinandum nos ad vitam aeternam. Auf diese Hauptfrage nun antworten sie alle einmüthig: Deum praedestinasse nos ab aeterno intuitu praevisi meriti Christi fide apprehendendi oder eum praedestinasse nos intuitu praevisae fidei nostrae, und geben also alle einmüthig, so viel die Sache selbst betrifft, zu vernehmen, die causa impulsiva, qua Deus ab aeterno permotus est ad praedestinandum nos ad vitam aeternam, sei das meritum Christi, praevisum ut apprehensum fide, oder die causa impulsiva sei fldes in Christum praevisa. Wenn aberweiter gefragt wird, quomodo fldes in Christum ab aeterno moverit Deum ad nostri praedestinationem, an ut qualitas, habitus, vel actus, sua propria dignitate, bonitate, merito et valore, an modo alio, da antworten sie alle einmüthig, dass Gott den Glauben in condendo praedestinationis decreto nicht angesehen habe ut qualitatem, actum vel habitum, noch einiger seiner eignen Dignität, Würde oder Vollkommenheit, und bekennen also, dass der Glaube an Christum nicht causa decreti praedestinationis principalis, weniger aber causa mentoria desselben sei, sondern dieses komme einig und allein Christi Verdienst zu. Fragt man aber weiter, wie denn Gott den Glauben in condendo praedestinationis decreto angesehen habe, so antworten sie abermal einmüthig, Gott habe ihn angesehen, sofern als er Christi Verdienst ergreift und uns zueignet, und habe sich also Gott bewegen lassen, uns zum ewigen Leben zu verordnen, nicht aus einiger des Glaubens eigner Kraft, Würde und Gütigkeit, sondern einig und allein durch das vollgiltige Verdienst Christi, das er ergreift und uns zueignet. Welches nichts anders ist, als fldem esse causam decreti praedestinationis impulsivam minus principalem, quae moverit quidem Deum ad nostri praedestinationem, non tamen ulla sua dignitate, valore aut merito, sed solius meriti Christi, quod apprehendit et Deo Patri in sua aeterna praescientia velut λντρον pro peccatis nostris sufficientissimum exhibuit, dignitate et valore. Es kann auch der Glaube, sofern er Christi Verdienst ergreift und uns zueignet, in keinem andern genere causae praedestinationis causa sein, als in welchem genere causae Christi Verdienst desselben causa ist. Christi Verdienst aber ist nach aller Bekenntniss desselben causa in genere et ordine causae impulsivae; drum muss auch der Christi Verdienst ergreift und Gott fürhält, in hoc genere vel ordine causae desselben causa sein.

Darnach haben wir weiter gesehen auf die Ursache, warum denn unserer Kirchen theologi von der Sache selbst, worin sie durchaus einstimmig sind, so ungleiche terminos und phrases geführet, und dieselbe nicht mit ihren eigenen terminis exprimirt und gesagt haben, fldem in Christum praevisam esse decreti praedestinationis causam impulsivam minus principalem, sondern theils haben gesagt, eam esse decreti praedestinationis causam instrumentalem, andere, esse conditionem, ex parte subjecti praedestinandi requisitam et partem ordinis prae des tinatorii, wodurch die discentes im Wachsthum in der gründlichen Erkenntniss in diesem Stück nicht wenig zurückgehalten und gehindert worden.

In genauer Untersuchung solcher Ursachen haben wir befunden, dass die Hauptursachen dieser Ungleichheit in terminis und Redensarten diese gewesen, dass man zu selbigen Zeiten von der Distinction inter causas impulsivas principales PART. III. CAP. XII. et minus principales in nostris scholis nichts gewusst hat, sondern in dem Wahn gestanden ist, eine jede impulsiva causa müsse ein meritum oder eine dignitatem, bonitatem propriam in sich begreifen, cujus vi et valore causam efficientem moveat ad decernendum vel agendum aliquid, und sei also eine jede causa impulsiva eine causa principalis.

Und weil dem Glauben an Christum an sich selbst kein meritum, keine dignitas, bonitas et perfectio propria zukommt, cujus valore Deus permotus fuerit ad nostri praedestinationem, haben etliche theologi, wie gedacht, fidem in Christum gar nicht wollen causam decreti praedestinationis nennen, weil sie wohl sahen, dass der Glaub in keinem andern genere causae könne decreti praedestinationis causa sein, als in genere vel ordine causarum impulsivarum, und wenn er sollte desselben causa sein, so müsste er causa impulsiva desselben sein, und darneben in denen festen Gedanken stunden, omnem causam impulsivam includere meritum vel aliam quandam vim motivam propriam et esse causam principalem.

Und hierüber ist sich nicht zu verwundern. Denn zu selbigen Zeiten ist die metaphysika, wohin die doctrina de generibus causarum und in specie auch de causis impulsivis principalibus et minus principalibus gehöret, wenig bekannt gewesen und wird man nicht leicht eine lutherische Universität finden, worauf in statutis facultatis philosophicae metaphysicam zu profltiren vor Alters wäre verordnet gewesen. Zu dem sind die causae impulsivae minus principales in communi usu nicht so gemein, wie etwa die causae minus principales in genere causae efflcientis zu sein pflegen, und wird daher in compendiis metaphysicis de causis impulsivis minus principalibus selten oder gar nicht gehandelt. . .

So ist nun die hypothesis, dass alle causae impulsivae ein meritum proprium oder eine vim motivam propriam in sich halten und causae principales sein, falsch und nachdem dieser Skrupel gehoben ist, liegt nichts mehr im Weg und hindert weiters nicht, dass man die von allen unsern Theologen, so viel die Sache selbst betrifft, einhellig bekannte Lehre, dass praevisa fides in Christum decreti praedestinationis causa impulsiva minus principalis sei, nicht mit ihren eigenen Worten aussprechen und sagen möge, eam praevisam esse decreti praedestinationis causam impulsivam minus principalem.“ (Bedenken vom consensu repetito. •1680. Vid. Calovii Histor. syncretist. p. 1041—1046.)

N. Selneccerus: ,,Estne praevisa fides causa electionis f Si fides justificans esset nostrum opus, nostra qualitas et virtus, haec quaestio locum haberet. Sed quia fides illa est opus Dei in nobis, ideo non admodum opus est hac quaestione, ad quam tamen respondere, non est difficile. Electio certe est aeternum Dei propositum de salvandis hominibus. Huic proposito Dei subjicitur fides in Christum, quam et ipsam Deus dat secundum ordinem a se institutum. Praevisa igitur fides non potest causa esse aeternae electionis, cujus quasi consequens et effectus fides est in nobis in tempore natis et in tempore etiam cessat nobis morientibus. Quod si praevisa fides diceretur causa electionis, facile falsa opinio de praevisa nostra dignitate et de meritis non tantum fidei, tanquam qualitatis nostraef sed etiam aliorum bonorum operum nostrorum, animos occupare posset. Scit Deus, qui sint sui, et eos elegit ante jacta mundi fundamenta. Et hujus electionis causa nulla alia est, nisi misericordia et clementia Dei gratuita per et propter Christum mediatorem ejusque meritum, sola fide apprehendendum et applicandum. Haec fides cum sit manus seu instrumentum, quo apprehenditur gratia Dei et meritum Christi, non potest esse causa gratiae et electionis, sed est illud medium et organum, quo fit applicatio gratiae et meriti Christi ad nos.“ (In omnes epp. D. Pauli commentar. I, 213. sq.)

Huelsemannus: ,,Docet Epitome libri Concord. et Declaratio uberior art. 11., causam impulsivam praedestinationis esse meritum Christi, praevisam autem non rejectionem offerendi hujus beneficii et admissionem ejus per fidem non pertinere ad causas, nedum impulsivas praedestinationis, sed ad conditionem sine qua non executionis. Impulsivam

vero causam decreti perditionis esse peccati et finalis in eo perseverantiae prae visionem, adeoque non solius executionis causam impulsivam esse peccatum, sed ipsius etiam decreti.“ (Praelect. in lib. Cone, p. 698. sq.)

Hutterus: ,,Non inviti largimur, neque fidem, neque praevisionem fidei esse causam electionis nostrae.. Fidem quidem non, quia illa in se et per se, quatenus est virtus, habitus aut qualitas, nihil quicquam facit vel ad electionem vel ad justificationem nostram; et hoc casu eandem plane conditionem ea obtinet, quam opera sive merita hominum. Verum neque praevisionem etiam fidei causam electionis nostrae, proprie loquendo, esse largimur; si quidem jam ostensum fuit, praevisionem, ut et praescientiam, non esse causam ullius rei praecognitae sive praescitae, sed complecti duntaxat notitiam rerum praescitarum omnium.“ (Libri Cone, explic. p. 1101.)


### On Predestination and Reprobation: M. Hannekenius: “Faith is not the principal efficient cause of election, but…

M. Hannekenius: “Faith is not the principal efficient cause of election, but God chose us in the Son apprehended by faith, Eph. 1:4: ‘You did not choose me, but I chose you,’ John 15:16. Whence it is gratuitously opposed to us by Polanus, lib. 4, Synt. c. 11: ‘If faith is the efficient cause of election, it will follow that we chose God first.’ ... Faith is not the instrumental cause of the divine counsel or decree concerning election. ‘He would be a fool,’ writes the blessed Menzerus in resp. ad defens. 2. part. conversat. Pruten. Crocii c. 2, ‘who would say that faith is the cause of the Gospel, but it is far more foolish to call the faith of man the instrument of the divine counsel or decree concerning election. The cause of the divine decree is the most wise and omnipotent will of God; faith, however, is the organ or instrument and, as it were, a certain spiritual hand, apprehending the grace of God offered in the Gospel in Christ the Mediator.’” (Verae th. Synops., p. 54 sq.)

Calovius: "Does faith, insofar as it enters into the decree of election by way of an impulsive cause, also contribute something to the decree by its own power?" The Jena writings (Musaeus) maintain the affirmative... Although such things can be explained conveniently in some way, a phrase of that kind is not easily to be admitted... This assertion cannot be solidly proven by any testimony of Scripture. For we are not said to be elected *propter fidem* (on account of faith), but *per fidem* (through faith) in Christ; the former is significant of an impulsive cause, the latter of an instrumental cause. Hence our theologians reject the term "impulsive cause." "When faith is called the cause of election, do not understand it as impelling," warns the blessed Meisner (l.c.). "For election does not depend on faith as an impulsive or meritorious cause," says the blessed Hutter (Comment. in F. C. art. 11, p. 1103). Gerhard says it is "ἄλογον" (irrational) that "faith is the impulsive cause of election." Regarding which, Dr. Musaeus (dissert. de decr. elect. c. 2. th. 62) says: "Our theologians of old, in the present controversy concerning the relation of faith to the decree of election, rejected the term 'impulsive cause' no less than the term 'meritorious cause,' and feared, indeed refused, to call faith an impulsive cause of election just as much as a meritorious one." He adds a reason, which is not frivolous or vain if you look at the common mode of speaking: "The cause of this matter (as Dr. Musaeus himself teaches in the same place) is that they were persuaded that every impulsive cause imports a certain merit or at least a goodness, dignity, and perfection of its own, by which the will of the efficient cause might be moved to act... Since this does not befit faith, it is a matter of conscience for us to call it, so absolutely and simply, the impulsive cause of election. For the assertion would be most false and contrary to the Holy Scriptures. For just as the Scriptures nowhere say that we are justified *διά την πίστιν* (on account of faith)—which phrase imports an impulsive cause, strictly so called, or a principal one—but rather *διά πίστεως* (through faith), *εκ πίστεως* (out of faith), *πίστει* (by faith), which formulas of speech extend more broadly and are also suitable for a less principal impulsive cause; so neither can we be correctly said to be elected *διά την πίστιν* (on account of faith), but we must be said to be elected *intuitu fidei* (in view of faith), or *ex fide praevisa* (out of foreseen faith), or *fide praevisa* (by foreseen faith)." Menzer, in PART III. CHAP. XII. resp. ad defens. sec. part. conversat. Pruten. D. Joh. Crocii p. 92, says: "It is most foolish to call the faith of man an instrument of the counsel or decree of election." And how could faith be an impelling cause, or impel God to justify and predestine believers, and that by its own virtue, when faith here obtains no virtue or activity, but behaves itself only nakedly and passively, and merely receives the grace of God and the merit of Christ, while God imputes that to us out of grace as if it were our own merit? Therefore, man behaves himself here more passively—receiving Christ and admitting Him through faith, who insinuates Himself into our heart through the Word—than actively, so that it is properly the work of God, and not our own, while it is being produced; and whatever there is of our activity in that reception of Christ or apprehension of the divine grace offered and conferred—after, namely, faith has been produced in our hearts by the Holy Spirit—that certainly does not come into the account when our justification is being dealt with. So much so, that faith itself, insofar as it is an instrument, is rightly said to be opposed not only to all works of obedience and piety, but even to faith itself, insofar as it is our work or act, and to its virtue. Unless this is holily asserted, the Arminian heresy concerning faith as a quality or work and act of ours that justifies us can easily creep in. (System. T. X, 629 sq. 631, 632.)

Gerhard: "We profess with a resounding voice that we maintain that God found nothing good in man when electing him to eternal life, and that He did not look upon good works, nor the use of free will, nor even faith itself, in such a way that He was moved by these things or elected certain people on account of them." (Loc. de elect. § 161.)

The Theological Faculty of Wittenberg: "When faith is introduced into the matter and article of the election of grace, it does not carry the meaning that God would have elected us for the sake of faith, as if it were our merit, or that we would have been elected by God because He had foreseen from eternity that we would believe in Christ and thus show ourselves worthy of the grace and election of God." (Gründliche Widerlegung. 1596. See Consilia th. Witebergensia. I, 569. a.)

The same: "Therefore, it is a shameful fabrication that we Wittenbergers are supposed to teach that God has elected only those who have given Him cause to do so. How this man dares to base the main controversy (p. 18 of his libelous writing) upon this! Accordingly, it is also undoubtedly false that man is elected for the sake of faith, as D. Huber fabricates about us... Furthermore, it is rejected by us as false and godless if it were said or taught by anyone that believers choose God through faith before He chooses them, and give Him cause to elect them afterward. Which D. Huber, with unfathomable groundlessness, does not fear or shame himself to blame us Wittenbergers for, and to set the status or main controversy upon it, and even dares to say that our entire foundation rests upon this, p. 69. Whereas faith itself originates from the eternal election of God, and is not worked by us, but solely through God's power within us." (Bek. von der ewigen Gnadenwahl. See Consil. Witteb. I, 616.)

The same: "Thereafter he blames us, as if we were to interpret the words of St. Paul in such a way that, when the Apostle says: 'God has chosen you in faith,' it must have the meaning that God would have elected us for the sake of faith. Such is once again a fabricated, false accusation, since it is impossible for D. Huber to prove that we should ever have written in our books, or otherwise said, that God has elected us for the sake of faith... If one is only in agreement on the matter, namely, that God does not merely [elect] to that end, but in gracious regard for faith in Christ, [elects] the believers and not also the unbelievers in Christ to eternal"

We] have chosen life, we will not quarrel with anyone over this, whether faith should be called a *causa*, *συναίτιον*, or a necessary piece, *membrum* and *requisitum*, or a property, *proprietas* and *attributum* of the elect and thus also of the election of grace. Only this alone: that faith not be set aside, and that eternal predestination not be sought entirely in the bare will of God and the merit of the Lord Christ—even if the same is not grasped by true faith—without faith in Christ, as Dr. Huber does; but that one should teach with the Christian Book of Concord and thus say, as it stands in the summary: “That God in His eternal divine counsel has decreed that He will save no one outside of those who acknowledge His Son Christ and truly believe in Him.” (Gründliche Widerlegung. 1596. See Consil. Witteb. I, 589 sq.)

The same: “Dr. Huberus writes thus: ‘It is taught in the Visitation Book that every person should appropriate the election of grace to himself, which cannot happen unless a general election and provision from God over all men precedes it.’ Answer: That men should appropriate and apply the election of grace to themselves is nowhere written in the Visitation Book. But the words from the cited page 299 read as follows: ‘Thus faith is required in the election of grace, that we should accept with true, living faith the grace of eternal election, which has been granted to us in Christ and has come to us solely because of His redemption, and that everyone should apply and appropriate it to himself.’ There we hear indeed that we should apply to ourselves the grace of eternal election and appropriate it through true faith; but that we should appropriate to ourselves the election and election of grace itself through faith, as Dr. Huberus speaks, that is nowhere to be found here or elsewhere in the Visitation Book. Now, however, it is a very different thing to speak of the grace or mercy of God, which is included with the election of grace and extends over all men, which we must also grasp with faith and appropriate to ourselves, than it is to speak of the complete election of grace and the election or choosing of God in itself.” (L. c. I, 608.)

The Electorate Theologians: “Your Princely Grace will find in none of our books that any one of us has ever taught that God has chosen us for the sake of foreseen faith. Hunnius would make an open retraction if he had ever made faith a merit for the sake of which we were chosen.” (Gründl. Widerlegung des zu Staffort etc. Wittenberg. 1602. p. 568.)

S. Schmidtius: “Altogether, this predestination of God was made out of mere grace, without any merit of works, whether these are said to arise from natural powers or from supernatural ones; and also without any regard for the same works, or even for faith itself, as a condition impelling God to predestination by its own dignity, whether proper and natural, or imputed.” (Aphorism. th. p. 294.)

Latin:

M. Hannekenius: ״Fides non est causa efficiens principalis electionis, sed Deus nos elegit in Filio fide apprehenso Eph. 1,4.: ,Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos.‘ Joh. 15,16. Unde gratis nobis opponitur a Polano 1. 4. Synt. c. 11.: ,Si fides est causa efficiens electionis, sequetur, quod nos priores elegerimus Deum.‘ . . . Fides non est causa Instrumentalis consilii sive decreti divini de electione. ,Stolidus foret‘, scribit b. Menzerus in resp. ad defens. 2. part. conversat. Pruten. Crocii c. 2., ,qui diceret, fidem esse causam evangelii, at longe stultius est, fidem hominis vocare instrumentum consilii sive decreti divini de electione. Decreti divini causa est sapientissima et omnipotens voluntas Dei, est autem fides organum sive instrumentum et quasi quaedam spiritualis manus, oblatam in evangelio gratiam Dei in Christo mediatore apprehendens.‘“ (Verae th. Synops. p. 54. sq.) '

Calovius: ,,An fides, quatenus ingreditur decretum electionis, per modum causae impulsivae, propria etiam vi aliquid conferat ad decretum? — Affirmativam tuetur Scriptum Jenense (Musaei). . . . Quamquam vero aliqua ratione ista explicari commode possint, non tamen admittenda phrasis ejusmodi facile est.... Nullo testimonio Scripturae solide haec assertio probari potest. Non enim electi dicimur propter fidem, sed per fidem in Christum, quorum illud est causae impulsivae σημαντικόν, hoc causae organicae. Unde aversantur nostrates terminum causae impulsivae. ,Cum fides electionis causa dicitur, non intelligas impellentem‘, monet b. Meisnerus 1. c. ,Neque enim electio pendet a fide tanquam causa impulsiva sive meritoria‘, ait b. Hutterus, Comment. in F. C. art. 11., p. 1103. . . Gerhardus,αλογον‘ hoc esse dicit, ,fidem esse causam electionis impulsivam‘. Quo de Dn. D. Musaeus dissert. de decr. elect. c. 2. th. 62.: ,Causae autem‘, inquit, ,impulsivae terminum in praesenti, quae est de fidei ad electionis decretum habitudine, controversia nostri olim non minus, quam causae meritoriae terminum, aversati sunt et fidem aeque impulsivam ac meritoriam electionis causam dicere formidarunt, imo recusarunt.‘ Addit rationem, quae non frivola vel vana est, si communem loquendi modum spectes. ,Cujus rei causa est (ipsomet Dn. D. Musaeo ibidem docente), quod persuasum habuerunt, causam impulsivam omnem importare meritum quoddam vel certe bonitatem, dignitatem et perfectionem propriam, qua voluntas causae efficientis ad agendum moveatur. . . Quod cum fidei non conveniat, nobis etiam religio sit, eam ita absolute et simpliciter electionis causam impulsivam dicere. Assertio enim foret falsissima, scripturis s. adversa. Sicut enim nuspiam scripturae nos justificari dicunt δια την πίστιν, propter fidem, quae phrasis causam impulsivam absolute dictam sive principalem importat; sed διά πίστεως, per fidem, εκ πίστεως, ex fide, πίστει, fide, quae loquendi formulae patent latius et causae etiam impulsivae minus principali conveniunt, ita nec electi recte dici possumus διά την πίστιν, propter fidem, sed intuitu fidei, vel ex fide praevisa, vel fide praevisa electi dicendi sumus.‘ . . Menzerus in PART. III. CAP. XII. resp. ad defens. sec. part. conversat. Pruten. D. Joh. Crocii p. 92. ait: ,stultissimum esse, fldem hominis vocare instrumentum consilii seu decreti electionis‘. . . Et quomodo fldes causa esset impellens vel impelleret Deum at justificandum et praedestinandum credentes, idque virtute propria, quum fides hic nullam vel virtutem vel activitatem obtineat, sed nude tantum passive sese habeat et gratiam Dei ac meritum Christi solummodo recipiat, Deus autem nobis ex gratia illud imputet, acsi proprium nostrum meritum esset? Magis ergo hic sese passive habet homo, recipiens Christum et admittens per fidem, qui per verbum in cor nostrum sese insinuat, quam active, ut ita opus sit Dei proprie, non vero nostrum, dum procreatur et quicquid est acti vitatis nostrae in illa Christi receptione vel gratiae divinae oblatae et collatae apprehensione, postquam nempe fides per Sp. S. producta est in cordibus nostris, id ipsum certe in censum non venit; cum de justificatione nostra agitur, adeo, ut fides etiam ipsa, quatenus instrumentum est, recte dicatur opponi non tantum operibus omnibus obedientiae et pietatis, sed ipsi fidei, qua opus vel actus noster est, ejusque virtuti. Quod nisi sancte adseratur, facile Arminiana haeresis de fide ceu qualitate vel opere et actu nostro nos justificante subrepere potest.“ (System. T. X, 629. sq. 631. 632.^.)

Gerhardus: ,,Sonora voce profitemur, nos statuere, quod Deus nihil boni in homine ad vitam aeternam eligendo invenerit, quod nec bona opera, nec liberi arbitrii usum, neque adeo ipsam etiam fidem ita respexerit, ut hisce motus vel propter ea.quosdam elegerit.“ (Loc. de elect. § 161.)

Facultas th. Wittebergensis: ״Wenn in dem Handel und Artikel von der Gnadenwahl der Glaube eingeführt wird, hat es nicht die Meinung, dass uns Gott um des Glaubens willen, als wegen unsers Verdienstes, erwählet hätte, oder dass wir von Gott darum erwählet wären, dieweil er zuvor von Ewigkeit gesehen, dass wir an Christum glauben und also der Gnaden und Erwählung Gottes uns würdig erzeigen würden.“ (Gründliche Widerlegung. 1596. Vid. Consilia th. Witebergensia. I, 569. a.)

Eadem: ,,Derwegen es ein unehrbar Gedicht ist, dass wir Wittenberger lehren sollen, Gott habe nur die erwählet, welche ihm Ursach dazu gegeben. Wie dieser Mann den Hauptstreit (p. 18 seiner Lästerschrift) hierauf setzen darf. Demnach ist auch ungezweifelt falsch, dass der Mensch um des Glaubens willen erwählet werde, wie D. Huber von uns fabulirt. . . Demnach wird von uns ferner also falsch und gottlos verworfen, wenn von jemand gesagt oder gelehrt würde, dass die Gläubigen erwählen durch den Glauben Gott, ehe dass er sie erwähle, und geben ihm TJrsach, dass er sie hernach erwähle. Welches D. Huber mit unerfindlichem Ungrund uns Wittenbergern schuld zu geben und den statum oder Hauptstreit darauf zu setzen, sich weder scheuet noch schämet, und noch sprechen darf, hierauf stehe unser ganzer Grund, p. 69. So doch der Glaub selber von der ewigen Wahl Gottes ursprünglich herkommet, auch nicht von uns, sondern allein durch Gottes Kraft in uns gewirket wird.u (Bek. von der ewigen Gnadenwahl. Vid. Consil. Witteb. I, 616.)

Eadem: ״Darnach gibt er uns schuld, gleichsam sollten wir die Worte S. Pauli also deuten, dass, wenn der Apostel sagt: Gott hat euch erwählet im Glauben, solches den Verstand haben müsste, dass uns Gott um des Glaubens willen erwählet hätte. Solches ist abermal eine erdichtete falsche Anklage, sintemal D. Hubero unmöglich ist zu erweisen, dass wir jemals in unsern Büchern sollten geschrieben oder auch sonsten gesagt haben, Gott habe uns um des Glaubens willen erwählet. . . Wenn man nur der Sachen eines ist, dass nämlich Gott nicht blos dahin, sondern in gnädiger Ansehung des Glaubens an Christum die Gläubigen und nicht auch die Glaublosen in Christo zum ewigen

Leben erwählet habe, wollen wir mit niemands hierüber zanken, ob der Glaube eine causa, σνναίτιον, oder nothwendiges Stück, membrum und requisitum oder Eigenschaft, Proprietät und Attributum der Auserwählten und also auch der Gnadenwahl solle genennet werden. Nur alleine, dass der Glaube nicht ausgesetzt und die ewige Prädestination ohne den Glauben an Christum nicht im blossen Willen Gottes und Verdienst des Herrn Christi, ob derselbe schon nicht durch wahren Glauben ergriffen wird, vollkömmlich gesucht werde, wie D. Huber thut; sondern dass man mit dem christlichen Concordienbuch lehre und also sage, wie im summarischen Begriff stehet: ,Dass Gott in seinem ewigen göttlichen Rath beschlossen habe, dass er ausserhalbe denen, so seinen Sohn Christum erkennen und wahrhaftig an ihn glauben, niemand wolle selig machen.‘ “ (Gründliche Widerlegung. 1596. Vid. Consil. Witteb. I, 589. sq.)

Eadem: ,,Dr. Huberus schreibt also: ,Es wird im Visitationbuch gelehret, dass ein jeder Mensch ihm solle die Gnadenwahl zueignen, welches nicht geschehen kann, es sei denn, dass eine allgemeine Election und Versehung aus Gott über alle Menschen vorhergehe.‘ Antwort: Dass ihnen die Menschen die Gnadenwahl sollten zueignen und appliciren, stehet im Visitationbuch nirgend geschrieben. Es lauten aber die Wort vom angezogenen 299. Blatt also: ,Also wird der Glaub in der Gnadenwahl erfordert, dass wir die Gnade der ewigen Wahl, so uns in Christo bescheiden und um seiner Erlösung wegen allein begegnet ist, mit wahrem, lebendigem Glauben annehmen und ein jeglicher ihm appliciren und zueignen solle.‘ Da hören wir zwar, dass wir uns die Gnade der ewigen Wahl appftciren und durch wahren Glauben zueignen sollen; dass wir uns aber die Election und Gnadenwahl selbst, wie Dr. Huberus redet, sollten durch den Glauben zueignen, das ist allhier und sonsten im Visitationbuch nirgend zu finden. Nun ist aber viel ein anders, die Gnade oder Barmherzigkeit Gottes, welche der Gnadenwahl mit eingeschlossen wird und über alle Menschen gehet, welche wir auch mit dem Glauben ergreifen und uns zueignen müssen, dann auch ein anders die vollkömmliehe Gnadenwahl und Election oder Erwählung Gottes an ihr selbst.“ (L. c. I, 608.)

Theologi Electorales: ,,Ew. fürstl. Gnaden wird in keinem unserer Bücher finden, dass je einer von uns gelehrt, Gott habe uns erwählt um des zuvor gesehenen Glaubens willen.
