Hunnius würde einen offenen Widerruf thun, wenn er je so den Glauben zum Verdienst gemacht hätte, um dessen willen wir erwählt seien.“ (Gründl. Widerlegung des zu Staffort etc. Wittenberg. 1602. S. 568.)

S. Schmidtius: ,,Omnino praedestinatio haec Dei facta est ex gratia mera, sine ullo merito operum, sive haec ex viribus naturalibus, sive ex supernaturalibus fleri dicantur; sine etiam ullo respectu ad eadem opera, imo ipsam fidem, tanquam conditionem ex sua dignitate, sive propria atque naturali, sive imputata, Deum ad praedestinationem impellentem.“ (Aphorism. th. p. 294.)


### On Predestination and Reprobation: Formula of Concord: “Therefore, we believe and hold that those who conduct the…

Formula of Concord: “Therefore, we believe and hold that those who conduct the doctrine of the gracious election of God to eternal life in such a way that troubled Christians cannot take comfort in it, but are thereby caused to become faint-hearted or to despair, or that the impenitent are strengthened in their wantonness, that such doctrine is not driven according to the Word and will of God, but according to reason and the instigation of the miserable Satan; because everything that is written, as the Apostle testifies, ‘was written for our instruction, that by patience and comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope’ (Rom. 15:4). Therefore, we reject the following errors: 1. As when it is taught that God does not will that all men should repent and believe the Gospel. 2. Item, when it is said that when God calls us to Himself, it is not His earnest will that all men... PART III. CHAP. XII.

should come to Him. 3. Item, that God did not wish that everyone should be saved, but without regard to their sin, solely out of the mere counsel, purpose, and will of God, ordained them to damnation, so that they cannot be saved.

4. Item, that not only the mercy of God and the most holy merit of Christ, but also something in us is a cause of the election of God, for the sake of which God has chosen us to eternal life.

All of which are blasphemous and horribly erroneous teachings, by which all the comfort that Christians have in the holy Gospel and the use of the holy Sacraments is taken away from them, and therefore they should not be tolerated in the Church of God.” (Concordia, p. 556 sq. § 16—21.)

ANTITHESIS. Hollazius: “If faith in Christ, notwithstanding that it is a gift of God, is a cause why God justifies and saves us in time, why could it not also be a cause why He chose us to salvation from eternity?” (Exam. p. 625.)

However, it is proven that faith is a less principal impulsive cause of the decree of election by an argument drawn from the execution, in this way: That, in view of which as a less principal cause or impulsive reason God saves us in time, in view of that, as a less principal cause or impulsive reason, He decreed from eternity to confer salvation upon us in time. But faith in Christ is that, in view of which as a less principal cause or impulsive reason God saves us in time. Therefore, faith in Christ is that, in view of which as an impulsive cause God decreed from eternity to confer salvation upon us in time.

The major premise rests upon the same proof by which we showed the argument for the principal impulsive cause of election to rest in note c to § 14. For regarding the agreement of the decree and the execution, it is necessary that the reason be the same on both sides, not only for the principal impulsive cause, but also for the less principal cause or reason.

The minor proposition, however, is proven from those passages of Scripture in which we are said to be saved by faith, from faith, through faith, Rom. 3:28; Eph. 2:8, where a certain causality of faith in relation to our salvation is ascribed, and that not of a principal, efficient, or impulsive cause, but of a less principal one—yet not one that is physically efficient, but impulsive, or that God, who saves, is moved to the end that He wills to save through faith, not indeed viewed by reason of its own dignity; for we are not said to be saved because of faith, but insofar as it apprehends the merit of Christ, so that in view of it God wills to save and does save. Compare the blessed Musaeus and Scherzer in the cited places.

Faith has the nature of an impulsive cause in relation to the eternal decree of election, not because it existed from eternity, but because it was foreseen from eternity in the foreknowledge of God. To this pertains that passage in Rom. 8:29: οὓς προέγνω, καὶ προώρισε, whom He foreknew (as being future in Christ Jesus through faith, according to verse 1), them He also predestined. Whence it is said elsewhere that the foreseeing of the merit of Christ to be apprehended by faith, or the foreseeing of faith in Christ, is the reason or impulsive cause of the decree of election. Compare the blessed Musaeus, Disp. Inaug. de Aet. Praedest. Decr. cap. III. § 50.

Selneccerus: “That action has a foundation in God: 1. πρόθεσιν, that is, a certain and immovable purpose and will or eternal and immutable decree concerning the saving of men, ὡρισμένην βουλήν, Acts 2, a defined counsel, βουλήν τοῦ θελήματος τοῦ θεοῦ and εὐδοκίαν, ἣν προέθετο

the good pleasure, which God proposed in Himself, Eph. 1. Next, He has πρόγνωσιν, foreknowledge or prescience, by which God knows those whom He deems worthy of salvation, and has them in His fatherly sight.” (On Rom. 8:28, 29. See *Commentary on all the Epistles of the Apostle Paul*. Leipzig, 1595. I, 178.)

Chr. Cornerus: “The Jews are saved whom God foreknew, that is, according to His gracious will, He chose them as sons and foreknew that they would be saved.” (On Rom. 11: 2. See *Writings on the Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Romans*. Heidelberg, 1583, p. 139.)

L. Osiander: “‘For whom He foreknew’: whom also, before they were born, according to His immense and eternal wisdom, He foresaw, who are pleasing to Him by grace, so that they might become heirs of the heavenly kingdom (whom He has chosen), these ‘He also predestinated’ or ordained (He has ordered them thither and dedicated them to that end), ‘to be conformed to the image of His Son,’ that is, that they might be sanctified and suffer adversities with Him and afterwards become partakers of eternal glory with the same.” (On Rom. 8:29. See *All the Epistles of the Apostle Paul*. Tübingen, 1583. Vol. I, p. 90.)

The same: “‘God has not’ therefore in general ‘cast away’ or rejected ‘His people’ the Jewish people; but I say that that people is not rejected, ‘whom He foreknew,’ that is, those Jews whom He predestinated from eternity to life.” (On Rom. 11:2. Ibid., p. 118.)

P. Lyserus: “He says (Christ, John 10:14): ‘I know My sheep and am known by Mine.’ Where the word ‘to know’ does not signify a bare awareness, but simultaneously comprehends diligent care and custody; it denotes not only an affection, but an effect. Whence He also adds: ‘As the Father knows Me and I know the Father.’ Where certainly the Father knows the Son, because He acknowledges Him as His natural Son, embraces, loves, and intimately cares for and approves all things of His, even when He lays down His life for the sheep, i.e., when, pressed by the cross, He breathes out His soul, etc. Conversely, the Son knows the Father, because He acknowledges that He has and has received all things from Him, and that He is dear to Him and in His care, even if the whole world should persecute Him. This is the knowledge between the Father and the Son; such also is that between Christ and the sheep. Christ so knows His sheep, that He knows they were predestinated by the Father from eternity and given to Him to be redeemed and saved. ‘For the Lord knows those who are His,’ 2 Tim. 2:19; therefore, by loving His own, He solicitously provides for them whatever pertains to their salvation.” (On John 10:14. See *Harmon. ev.* I, 2162 sq.)

Meisnerus: “By the ‘knowing’ of the Lord (2 Tim. 2:19) is not understood a bare knowledge, which in the schools they call theoretical or general, but rather the benefits of God to be conferred upon the elect, which they call practical or special knowledge. For theologians have a rule: Words of science and knowledge often denote not a bare knowledge, but the effects following the knowledge. Thus it is taken in Ps. 1, last verse: ‘The Lord knows the way of the righteous’; where Bede writes that it is to be understood as knowledge of 1. approbation, 2. promotion, 3. remuneration. Thus it is taken in Matt. 7:23: ‘I never knew you.’ Luke 13:27: ‘I do not know where you are from’; which sayings, if explained only of general knowledge, produce a most false sense. Similarly, in this saying 2 Tim. 2, γνώσις πρακηκή is understood, which consists chiefly in three degrees: 1. in special love; 2. in the consolation of the beloved; 3. in the glorification of those preserved. Therefore, the sense here is: the Lord knows those who are His, i.e., the Lord specially loves His own and those chosen by Him, preserves them from all evil and final fall, and will finally glorify them... Matt. 7:22, the Lord says to the hypocrites and temporary believers: ‘I never knew you,’ namely, with the knowledge of election; you were never inscribed in the book of life. Therefore, you can no longer be saved. Many certainly of those will be baptized, and yet it will be said to them: ‘I never knew you,’ namely, with the special knowledge pertaining only to the elect.” (*Anthrop. disp.* XVI. B. 1.) PART III. CHAP. XII.

Thomasius: "The mediation which later dogmaticians attempted, the distinction between a *voluntas antecedens* and *consequens*, I do not consider a happy one; their determination that election occurs *ex praevisa fide* [out of foreseen faith], I consider downright mistaken." (*Das Bekenntniss der ev.luth. Kirche in der Consequenz seines Princips.* 1848. p. 222.)

Frankius: "The theological expedient of a *praevisa fides* in connection with the *voluntas Dei antecedens* and *consequens*, which later became popular, does not, it seems, succeed for the reason that, on the one hand, faith itself is to be regarded as an effect of grace, in such a way that before they existed and had done anything good, before the foundation of the world, the elect were chosen for salvation by God’s purpose out of grace in Christ; and because, on the other hand, the Confession nowhere makes use of that expedient. For Chemnitz answers in the *Enchiridion* to the question of whether such a choice of God happens only in time, when men repent and believe, or whether it happens in consideration of their previously foreseen piety: the choice of God does not follow our faith and righteousness, but precedes them as a cause of all this; the election of grace is a cause of everything that pertains to salvation." (*Th. der Concordienf.* IV. p. 266. sq.)

Just as we are not saved except through final faith. See above, Chapter III, § 19. § 16. The objects of predestination are men, sinners, but finally believing, and these all and only. Others call this the subject of election. And it coincides with the end to which. Indeed, the predestination of angels, just as it was not done in Christ, so it does not pertain to the present. Compare Part I, Chapter III, § 32.

Latin:

Eormula Concordiae: ,,Demnach glauben und halten wir, welche die Lehre von der gnädigen Wahl Gottes zum ewigen Leben also führen, dass sich die betrübten Christen derselben nicht trösten können, sondern dadurch zur Kleinmüthigkeit oder Verzweiflung verursacht, oder die Unbussfertigen in ihrem Muthwillen gestärkt werden, dass solche Lehre nicht nach dem Wort und Willen Gottes, sondern nach der Vernunft und Anstiftung des leidigen Satans getrieben werde; weil alles, was geschrieben ist, wie der Apostel zeuget, ,uns zur Lehre geschrieben (ist), auf dass wir durch Geduld und Trost der Schrift Hoffnung haben‘. (Rom. 15, 4.) Demnach verwerfen wir folgende Irrthümer: 1. Als wenn gelehret wird, dass Gott nicht wolle, dass alle Menschen Busse thun und״dem Evangelio glauben. 2. Item, wann Gott uns zu sich berufe, d’ass es nicht sein Ernst sei, dass alle MenPART. ΙΠ. CAP. ΧΠ.

sehen zu ihm kommen sollen. 3. Item, dass Gott nich wollte, dass jedermann selig werde, sondern unangesehen ihre Sünde allein aus dem blossen Rath, Vorsatz und Willen Gottes zum Verdammniss verordnet, dass sie nicht können selig werden.

4. Item, daSs nicht allein die Barmherzigkeit Gottes und allerheiligste Verdienst Christi, sondern auch in uns eine Ursache sei der Wahl Gottes, um welcher willen Gott uns zum ewigen Leben erwählet habe.

Welches alles lästerliche und erschreckliche irrige Lehren sind, dadurch den Christen aller Trost genommen, den sie im heiligen Evangelio und Gebrauch der heiligen Sacramente haben, und derwegen in der Kirche Gottes nicht sollten geduldet werden.“ (Concordia, p. 556. sq. § 16—21.)

ANTITHESIS. Hollazius: ,,Eides in Christum, non obstante, quod Dei donum sit, causa est, cur in tempore Deus nos justificet et salvet, quidni etiam ab aeterno, cur ad salutem nos elegerit, causa esse potuerit?“ (Exam. p. 625.)

Probatur autem, fidem esse causam impulsivam minus principalem decreti electionis, argumento ab executione petito, hoc modo: Cujus, tanquam causae aut rationis impulsivae minus principalis, intuitu Deus nos in tempore salvat, ejus, tanquam causae aut rationis impulsivae minus principalis, intuitu decrevit ab aeterno, nobis in tempore conferre salutem. Atqui fides in Christum est illud, cujus, tanquam causae aut rationis impulsivae minus principalis, intuitu Deus nos in tempore salvat. Ergo fides in Christum est illud, cujus, tanquam camae aut rationis impul· sivae, intuitu Deus decrevit ah aeterno, nobis in tempore conferre salutem.

Major nititur eadem probatione, qua argumentum pro causa impulsiva principali electionis niti ostendimus nota c. ad § 14. Nam quoad convenientiam decreti et executionis non solum impulsivae principalis, sed et minus principalis causae seu rationis, rationem eandem utrinque esse oportet.

Minor autem propositio probatur ex illis Scripturae locis, quibus dicimur salvari fide, ex fide, perfidem, Rom. 3,28. Ephes. 2, 3., ubi fidei causalitas quaedam in ordine ad salutem nostram adseribitur, eaque non causae principalis, efficientis aut impulsivae, sed minus principalis, nec tamen physice efficientis, sed impulsivae, seu, quod Deus, qui salvat, ad id, ut velit salvare, moveatur per fidem, non quidem ratione suae dignitatis spectatam; non enim dicimur salvari propter fidem, sed quatenus apprehendit meritum Christi, ut sic ejus intuitu Deus salvare velit et salvet. Confer, b. Musaeum et Scherzerum 11. cc.

Habet autem fides rationem causae impulsivae in ordine ad decretum electionis aeternum, non quod ab aeterno extiterit, sed quod in Dei praescientia ab aeterno praevisa fuerit. Quo pertinet illud Rom. 8, 29. 0ος προέγνω, xa\ προώρισε, quos praescivit (futuros in Christo Jesu per fidem, juxta vers. 1.), eos etiam praedestinavit. Unde alias dicitur, praevisionem meriti Christi fide apprehendendi, aut praevisionem fidei in Christum, esse rationem aut causam impulsivam decreti electionis. Confer, b. Mus. Disp. Inaug. de Aet. Praedest. Decr. cap. III. § 50.

Selneccerus: ,,Ea actio habet fundamentum in Deo: 1. πρόΰεσιν, id est, certum et immotum propositum ac voluntatem seu decretum aeternum et immutabile de salvandis hominibus, ωρισμένην βουλήν Act. 2.' definitum consilium, βουλήν του θελήματος του ΰεοΰ καί ευδοκίαν, ήν προέΰετο

beneplacitum, quod proposuit Deus in se ipso, Eph. 1. Deinde habet πρόγνωσιν, praenotionem seu praescientiam, qua Deus novit eos, quos salute dignatur, habetque eosdem in conspectu suo paterno.“ (Ad Rom. 8, 28. 29. Vid. In omnes epp. D. Pauli apost. commentar. Lips. 1595. I, 178.)

Antwortet doch Chemnitz in dem Enchiridion auf die Frage, ob solche Wahl Gottes allererst in der Zeit geschehe, wenn die Menschen Busse thun und glauben, oder ob sie geschehen in Betrachtung ihrer zuvor ersehnen Frömmigkeit: die Wahl Gottes folge nicht nach unserm Glauben und Gerechtigkeit, sondern gehe als eine Ursach dieses alles voran, die Gnadenwahl sei eine Ursache von dem allen, was zur Seligkeit gehöret.“ (Th. der Concordienf. IV. p. 266. sq.)

Prout non salvamur, nisi per fidem finalem. Vide supra cap. III. § 19. § 16. Objectum a praedestinationis sunt homines b peccatores, sed flnaliter credentes, iique omnes c et soli.d Alii subjectum electionis appellant. Et coincidit cum fine cui. Nempe angelorum praedestinatio, sicut non facta est in Christo, ita ad praesens non pertinet. Confer. P. I. cap. III. § 32.


### On Predestination and Reprobation: Gerhardus: "We warn that the word 'predestination' is used *καταχρηστικῶς*…

Gerhardus: "We warn that the word 'predestination' is used *καταχρηστικῶς* [improperly]; for what is said in Romans 1:4, that Christ is predestined as the Son of God, is more correctly translated from the Greek as that He was certainly demonstrated and declared to be the Son of God." (*Loc. de elect.* § 159.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: 1. Of Augustine, who in many places, especially *de praedest. sanctorum* c. 15, says that Christ the man, who was assumed by the Word, was predestined so that He might be the Son of God and the exemplar of all the predestined. 2. Of the Calvinists, who posit that Christ and the angels enter into the number of the elect; as Bucanus, *Loc.* 36, q. 6. ... To this pertains the impudence and blasphemy of certain Contra-Remonstrants in Belgium (Drentanus, Part 2, *Actor. ad a. 3. 4. Remonstrat.* th. 12, p. 342), who posit that 'Christ is a particle of the corrupt Adamic mass, which God out of mere benevolence predestined to grace and glory, and thus separated this particle from the remaining lost mass,' etc. ... 3. Of the Scholastics and Papists, who likewise include Christ and the angels among the objects of predestination; as Thomas, Part 1, *Summa*, q. 23, a. 1. ... 4. Of certain Scholastics and Papists, asserting that the object of election is man before the fall, still constituted in his concreated integrity. ... 5. Of the Supralapsarian Calvinists, who [place] man in the state of nature as instituted or of perfection (just as

On the contrary, the Sublapsarians constitute the object of election in the state of destitute nature, or of the fall; see the *Acta* of the Remonstrants, Part 2, *declarat. sent. circa a. 1. de praedest.*, pp. 11 and 17.

Furthermore, man in his integrity is directly posited as the object of predestination by the founder of this school, Calvin. . .

This opinion is indirectly supported by the Leiden theologians and many others, who contend that the decree of creation is, in the order of divine reason, posterior to the decree of election; that is, that God conceived of man as eligible before He conceived of him as creatable, or that the determination of a rational creature to a salutary or perditive end preceded, in the order of divine reason, the decree to create man and to thrust the created man into sin.

They therefore maintain that God, before He had decreed to create any men or had foreseen men as created or fallen into sin, had determined with Himself to declare His mercy and justice; mercy, indeed, in saving some, but justice in destroying others.

However, in order to attain this end, He willed to create men, so that from them He might elect some and reprobate all the rest, without any regard either to Christ the Mediator and faith in the former, or to any sin in the latter, but that He absolutely reprobated the latter and absolutely elected the former, for this reason only, because it so pleased Him to illustrate His glory. . .

The contrary is defended by a more recent Calvinist, Sam. Maresius, theologian of Groningen, namely: "The object of divine predestination is not man as creatable, but as created and fallen, or as to be created and to fall." (*L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 63. sqq.*)

Just as the cause or impulsive reason for election extends to all these. For because the merit of Christ does not move [God] to save us or to decree salvation for us, except insofar as it is apprehended or to be apprehended by final faith, therefore the decree of predestination does not terminate upon men lacking final faith. §

17. The proximate end of election is salvation itself, to be conferred upon the elect in time; the ultimate end, however, is the glory of divine goodness.

Or that for the sake of which the decree of election was made, in our mode of understanding, from eternity. See Matt. 25:34, where the faithful are bidden to take possession of the kingdom prepared for them, or destined by divine decree, from the foundation of the world, and therefore destined so that they might one day attain it.

Formula of Concord: " 1. Initially, the distinction between *praescientia* and *praedestinatione*, that is, between the foreknowledge and the eternal election of God, is to be noted with diligence. 2. For the foreknowledge of God is nothing else than that God knows all things before they happen, as it is written: 'God in heaven can reveal hidden things; He has shown King Nebuchadnezzar what shall happen in future times.' (Dan. 2:28.) 3. This foreknowledge extends at once over the pious and the wicked, but it is not the cause of evil, neither of sin, that one should do wrong (which originally comes from the devil and the evil, perverted will of man), nor of their destruction, for which they themselves are guilty, but it only orders the same and sets a limit for it, how long it shall last, and [ordains] that everything, notwithstanding that it is evil in itself, shall serve for the salvation of His elect. 4. But predestination or the eternal election of God extends only over the pious, well-pleasing children of God, which is a cause of their salvation, which He also creates, and ordains what belongs to the same, upon which our salvation is so firmly founded that the gates of hell cannot overcome it. (John 10:28; Matt. 16:18.)" (*Concordia*, p. 554.)

The same: "And in this His counsel, purpose, and ordinance, God has not only prepared salvation ('salutem suorum') in general ('in genere'), but has also graciously considered, chosen for salvation, and ordained ('decrevit') all and every person of the elect ('omnes et singulas personas electorum') who are to be saved through Christ, that He wills to bring them—in the manner just mentioned—to participate in eternal salvation ('salutis aeternae participes facere'), and to help, promote, strengthen, and preserve them through His gifts and the working of His grace." (L. c. p. 708.)

Frank: "When it is said in the Latin text concerning the individual elect, 'clementer praescivit, ad salutem elegit et decrevit, quod' etc., it does not follow from this that, according to the later adaptation of the doctrine, the *electio* is thought to be conditioned by the *praevisio*, since that 'praescivit' is only an imprecise expression for the German, God 'has graciously considered' ('habe in Gnaden bedacht'); for the underlying statement by Chemnitz, 'God has considered in His eternal counsel, according to His gracious purpose,' excludes that misinterpretation." (Th. der Concordf. IV. p. 167.)

The same: "And in this respect the mystery of providence is revealed to us in God's Word, and if we abide by it and hold fast to it, it is a very useful, wholesome, and comforting doctrine; for it confirms most powerfully the article that we are justified and saved without any of our works and merit, purely out of grace, solely for Christ's sake; for before the time of the world, before we existed, indeed, before the foundation of the world was laid, when we could not have done any good, we were chosen for salvation in Christ according to God's purpose out of grace, Rom. 9:11; 2 Tim. 1: 9.

Thereby all opinions and erroneous doctrines concerning the powers of our natural will are also laid low, because God in His counsel before the time of the world considered (decreverit) and ordained that He Himself would create and work everything that pertains to our conversion with the power of His Holy Spirit through the Word within us.

This doctrine also gives the beautiful, glorious comfort that God has let the conversion, righteousness, and salvation of every Christian be so highly important to Him, and has meant it so faithfully, that He, before the foundation of the world, held counsel concerning it and in His purpose (in illo arcano suo proposito) ordained how He would bring me to it and preserve me therein; likewise, that He wished to secure my salvation so well and certainly—because it could easily be lost from our hands through the weakness and wickedness of our flesh, or be torn and taken away by the cunning and violence of the devil and the world—that He ordained the same in His eternal purpose, which cannot fail or be overturned, and placed it for safekeeping into the almighty hand of our Savior Jesus Christ, from which no one can tear us, John 10: 28. Therefore Paul also says in Rom. 8:28, 39: 'Because we are called according to the purpose of God, who then shall separate us from the love of God in Christ?' ('Therefore Paul builds the certainty of our blessedness upon the foundation of the divine purpose, when from the fact that we are called according to the purpose of God, he concludes that no one can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus, our Lord, Rom. 8:28, 39.')

This doctrine also gives glorious comfort in cross and tribulations, namely, that God in His counsel before the time of the world considered and resolved that He would stand by us in all distresses, grant patience, give comfort, work hope, and

wishes to provide such an outcome that it may be for our salvation. Likewise, how Paul handles this most comfortingly in Romans 8, that God in His purpose before the time of the world ordained through what cross and suffering He would make each of His elect like unto the image of His Son, and that for everyone his cross should and must serve for the best, because they are called according to His purpose, from which Paul concluded for certain and without doubt that "neither tribulation nor distress, neither death nor life, etc., shall be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus."] (L. c. p. 713—715.)

The same: "That they may know that their salvation does not stand in their own hand; otherwise they would lose it much more easily than happened to Adam and Eve in Paradise, indeed, every hour and moment; but in the gracious election of God, which He has revealed to us in Christ, out of whose hand no one shall snatch us, John 10:28, 2 Tim. 2:19." (Concordia, p. 724.)

Cf. the words of the Formula of Concord cited above in § 2. a. Luther: "Therefore, in no way does predestination cause some of the children of God to become children of the devil, or the temple of the Holy Spirit to become a temple of demons, or the members of Christ to become members of a harlot, 1 Cor. 6; but rather, predestination causes children of the devil to become children of God, and the temple of demons to become a temple of the Holy Spirit, and the members of a harlot to become members of Christ; because He Himself binds the strong man and plunders his vessels, rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them from ignominy into glory. However, those of whom it is said, 'They went out from us,' etc., went out by their own will, fell by their own will. And because they were foreseen as going to fall, they were not predestined. They would have been predestined, however, if they were going to return and remain in holiness and truth. Behold, this predestination of God is for many a cause of standing, for no one a cause of falling." (Briefe etc., ges. von de Wette. VI, 428. sq.)

Latin:

Gerhardus: ,,Monemus, vocem praedestinationis καταχρηστικάς ita usurpari; quod enim Rom. 1, 4. Christus dicitur praedestinatus Dei Filius, id ex graeco rectius vertitur, quod certo demonstratus ac declaratus sit Dei Filius.“ (Locv de elect. § 159.)

ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: ,, Antithesis: 1. Augustini, qui multis locis, inprimis de praedest. sanctorum c. 15., Christum hominem, qui a Verbo assumtus est, praedestinatum dicit, ut esset Filius Dei et exemplar praedestinatorum omnium. 2. Calvinianorum, qui Christum et angelos ingredi electorum numerum statuunt; ut Bucanus Loc. 36. q. 6. . . Huc pertinet ContraRemonstrantium quorundam in Belgio (Drentanorum P. 2. Actor, ad a. 3. 4. Remonstrat. th. 12. p. 342.) impudentia et blasphemia, statuentium, ,Christum esse corruptae massae Adamiticae particulam, quam Deus ex mera benevolentia praedestinaverit ad gratiam et gloriam, adeoque hanc particulam a reliqua perdita massa discreverit‘ etc. . . 3. Scholasticorum et Pontificiorum, qui itidem Christum et angelos inter objecta praedestinationis referunt; ut Thomas P. 1. Summae q. 23. a. 1. . . 4. Quorundam Scholasticorum et Pontificiorum, asserentium, objectum electionis esse hominem ante lapsum, in concreata integritate adhuc constitutum. . . 5. Calvinianorum Supralapsariorumf qui hominem in statu naturae institutae vel perfectionis (sicut

e contrario Sublapsarii in statu naturae destitutae seu defectionis) constituunt electionis objectum; vide Remonstrant. Acta P. 2. declarat, sent. circa a. 1. de praedest. p. 11. et 17.

Caeterum directe homo integer statuitur objectum praedestinationis a conditore hujus gentis, Calvino. . .

Opinioni huic indirecte suffragium impertitur a Leidensibus, aliisque plurimis contendentibus, decretum creationis in sigho rationis divinae posterius esse decreto electionis, h. e. Deum prius concepisse hominem eligibilem, quam creabilem, sive determinationem creaturae rationalis ad finem salutarem vel perditivum in signo rationis divinae praecessisse decretum creandi hominem et creatum in peccatum detrudendi.

Statuunt itaque, Deum, antequam ullos homines creare decrevisset aut homines creatos vel in peccatum prolapsos praevidisset, constituisse secum, misericordiam et justitiam suam declarare; misericordiam quidem in salvandis quibusdam, justitiam vero in perdendis aliis.

Hunc finem autem ut assequeretur, 'creare voluisse homines, ut ex iis quosdam eligeret, reliquos omnes reprobaret, nulla habita ratione, sive Christi mediatoris et fidei in illis, sive peccati ullius in his, sed hos absolute reprobasse, illos absolute elegisse, ideo tantum, quia sic piacuit illi suam gloriam illustrare. . .

Contrarium ex recentioribus Calvinistis defendit Sam. Maresius, theol. Groening., sc.: ,Objectum divinae praedestinationis non esse hominem creabilem, sed creatum et lapsum, sive creandum et lapsurum‘.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 5. f. 63. sqq.)

Prout causa seu ratio impulsiva electionis ad hos omnes se extendit. Quia enim meritum Christi non movet ad nos salvandos aut salutem nobis decernendam, nisi quatenus fide finali apprehensum aut apprehendendum est, ideo ad homines fide finali carentes praedestinationis decretum non terminatur. §

17. Finis electionis proximus est salus ipsa,b electis in tempore conferenda; ultimus autem gloria bonitatis c divinae.

Sive illud, cujus gratia decretum electionis factum est, nostro modo intelligendi, ab aeterno. Vid. Matth. 25, 84·, ubi jubentur fideles occupare regnum sibi paratum, seu divino decreto destinatum, ab exordio mundi, adeoque propterea destinatum, ut aliquando consequerentur.

Formula Concordiae: ,,1. Anfänglich ist der Unterschied zwisehen der praescientia et praedestinatione, das ist, zwischen der Vorsehung und ewigen Wahl Gottes, mit Fleiss zu merken. 2. Denn die Vorsehung Gottes ist anders nichts, denn dass Gott alle Dinge weiss, ehe sie geschehen, wie geschrieben steht: ,Gott im Himmel kann verborgene Dinge offenbaren; der hat dem König Nebucadnezar angezeigt, was in künftigen Zeiten geschehen soll. (Dan. 2, 28.) 3. Diese Vorsehung gehet zugleich über die Frommen und Bösen, ist aber keine Ursache des Bösen, weder der Sünde, dass man unrecht thue (welche ursprünglich aus dem Teufel und des Menschen bösem verkehrtem Willen herkommt), noch ihres Verderbens, daran sie selbst schuldig, sondern ordnet allein dasselbige und steckt ihm ein Ziel, wie lang es PART. III. CAP. XII. währen, und alles, unangesehen, dass es an ihm selbst böse, seinen Auserwählten zu ihrem Heil dienen solle. 4. Die Prädestination aber oder ewige Wahl Gottes gehet allein über die frommen, wohlgefälligen Kinder Gottes, die eine Ursache ist ihrer Seligkeit, welche er auch schaffty und was zur selbigen gehört, verordnet, darauf unsere Seligkeit so steif gegründet [isi], dass sie die Pforten der Hölle nicht überwältigen können. (Joh. 10, 28. Matth. 16, 18.)“ (Concordia, p. 554.)

Eadem: ,,Und hat Gott in solchem seinem Rath, Vorsatz und VerOrdnung nicht allein ingemein (״in genere“) die Seligkeit (,,salutem suorum“) bereitet, sondern hat auch alle und jede Personen der Auserwählten (omnes et singulas personas electorum“), so durch Christum sollen selig werden, in Gnaden bedacht, zur Seligkeit erwählet, auch verordnet (,,decrevit“), dass er sie auf die Weise, wie jetzt gemeldetf durch seine Gnader Gaben und Wirkung darzubringen (,,salutis aeternae participes facere“), helfen, fördern, stärken und erhalten wolle.“ (L. c. p. 708.)

Erankius: ,,Wenn es in dem lateinischen Texte von den einzelnen Erwählten heisst,clementer praescivit, ad salutem elegit et decrevit, quod‘ etc., so folgt daraus nicht, dass hier gemäss der späteren Passung der Lehre die electio von der praevisio bedingt gedacht werde, da jenes,praescivit‘ nur ein ungenauer Ausdruck ist für den deutschen, Gott,habe in Gnaden bedacht‘, wie denn die zu Grunde liegende Aussage bei Chemnitz, ,Gott habe in seinem ewigen Rath, nach seinem gnädigen Vorsatz bedacht‘, jene Missdeutung ausschliesst.“ (Th. der Concordf. IV. p. 167.)

Eadem: ,,Und sofern ist uns das Geheimniss der Vorsehung in Gottes Wort geoffenbaret, und wenn wir dabei bleiben und uns daran halten, so ist es gar eine nützliche, heilsame, tröstliche Lehre; denn sie bestätigt gar gewaltig den Artikel, dass wir ohne alle unsere Werke und Verdienst, lauter aus Gnaden, allein um Christus willen, gerecht und selig werden; denn vor der Zeit der Welt, ehe wir gewesen sind, ja, ehe der Welt Grund gelegt [ward], da wir ja nichts Gutes haben thun können, sind wir nach Gottes Vorsatz aus Gnaden in Christo zur Seligkeit erwählet, Röm. 9, 11. 2 Tim. 1, 9.

Es werden auch dadurch alle opiniones und irrige Lehren von den Kräften unsers natürlichen Willens ernieder gelegt, weil Gott in seinem Rath vor der Zeit der Welt bedacht (decreverit) und verordnet hat, dass er alles, was zu unserer Bekehrung gehört, selbst mit der Kraft seines Heiligen Geistes durchs Wort in uns schaffen und wirken wolle.

Es gibt auch also diese Lehre den schönen herrlichen Trost, dass Gott eines jeden Christen Bekehrung, Gerechtigkeit und Seligkeit so hoch ihm angelegen sein lassen und es so treulich damit gemeinet, dass er, ehe der Welt Grund gelegt, darüber Rath gehalten und in seinem Vorsatz (in illo arcano suo proposito) verordnet hat, wie er mich dazu bringen und darinnen erhalten wolle; item, dass er meine Seligkeit so wohl und gewiss habe verwahren wollen, weil sie durch Schwachheit und Bosheit unsers Fleisches aus unsern Händen leichtlich könnte verloren oder durch List und Gewalt des Teufels und der Welt daraus gerissen und genommen werden, dass er dieselbige in seinem ewigen Vorsatz, welcher nicht fehlen oder umgestossen werden kann, verordnet, und in die allmächtige Hand unsers Heilandes Jesu Christi, daraus uns niemand reissen kann, zu bewahren gelegt haty Joh. 10, 28. Daher auch Paulus sagt Röm. 8, 28. 39.: ,Weil wir nach dem Vorsatz Gottes berufen sind, wer will uns denn scheiden von der Liebe Gottes in Christo?‘ (,,Ideo Paulus certitudinem beatitudinis nostrae super fundamentum propositi divini exstruit, cum ex eoy quod secundum propositum Dei vocati sumus, colligit, neminem nos posse separare a dilectione Dei, quae est in Christo Jesu, Domino nostro, Rom. 8, 28. 39.)

Es giebt auch diese Lehre in Kreuz und Anfechtungen herrlichen Trost, nämlich dass Gott in seinem Rath vor der Zeit der Welt bedacht und beschlossen habe, dass er uns in allen Nöthen beistehen, Geduld verleihen, Trost geben, Hoffnung wirken und

einen solchen Ausgang verschaffen wolle, dass es uns seliglich sein möge. Item, wie Paulus dies gar tröstlich handelt Röm. 8., dass Gott in seinem Vorsatz vor der Zeit der Welt verordnet habe, durch was Kreuz und Leiden er einen jeden seiner Auserwählten gleich wollte machen dem Ebenbilde seines Sohnes, und dass einem Jeden sein Kreüz zum Besten dienen solle und müsse, weil sie nach dem Vorsatz berufen sind, daraus Paulus für gewiss und unzweifelhaft geschlossen, dass,weder Trübsal noch Angst, weder Tod noch Leben u. s. w. uns scheiden könne von der Liebe Gottes in Christo Jesu‘.“ (L. c. p. 713—715.)

Eadem: ,,Dass sie wissen, dass ihre Seligkeit nicht in ihrer Hand stehe; sonst würden sie dieselbige viel leichtlicher, als Adam und Eva im Paradies geschehen, ja, alle Stund und Augenblick verlieren; sondem in der gnädigen Wahl Gottes, die er uns in Christo geoffenbart hat, aus dess Hand uns niemand reissen wird, Joh. 10, 28. 2 Tim. 2, 19.“ (Concordia, p. 724.)

Cf. verba Pormulae Concordiae citata supra § 2. a. Lutherus: ,,Nullo ergo modo praedestinatio facit, ut aliqui ex filiis Dei flant filii diaboli, aut ex templo Spiritus S. fiat daemoniorum, aut ex membris Christi membra meretricis, 1 Cor. 6.; sed potius prae· destinatio facit, ut ex filiis diaboli filii fiant Dei et ex templo daemonum templum fiat Spiritus S. et ex membris meretricis fiant membra Christi; quia ipse alligat fortem et vasa ejus rapit, eruens eos de potestate tenebrarum et transferens de contumelia in gloriam. Hi autem, de quibus dicitur: ,Ex nobis exierunt‘ etc., voluntate exierunt, voluntate ceciderunt. Et quia praesciti sunt casuri, non sunt praedestinati. Essent autem praedestinati, si essent reversuri et in sanctitate et veritate mansuri. Aspice, haec praedestinatio Dei multis est causa standi, nemini causa labendi.“ (Briefe etc., ges. von de Wette. VI, 428. sq.)


### On Predestination and Reprobation: The same: "How false it is, therefore, that the righteous are predestined on…

The same: "How false it is, therefore, that the righteous are predestined on account of future works, just as false it is that they are justified on account of future works of faith. But just as the grace of predestination afterwards effects the works themselves without works, choosing and calling the one to be justified and to work, so faith effects the works themselves, justifying without works and blotting out sins before works." (Briefe etc., gesammelt von de Wette. VI, 433.)

The same: "1 Pet. 1:2: 'According to the foreknowledge of God the Father.' (Peter) means to say: That you are chosen, you have not attained through your own powers, works, or merit, for the treasure is too great, so that the holiness and righteousness of all men is far too small to attain it; furthermore, you were Gentiles, knew nothing of God, had no hope, and served dumb idols; therefore you come without all your own doing, out of pure grace, to such unspeakable glory, namely, in that God the Father has foreknown you for it from eternity. He thus makes the foreknowledge of God very lovely and comforting, as if he were to say: You are chosen and shall indeed remain so, for God, who has foreknown you, is strong and certain enough that His foreknowledge cannot fail Him, provided that you also believe His promise and hold Him to be a faithful God. From this we should briefly take this doctrine, that the foreknowledge is not founded upon our worthiness and merit, as the Sophists pretend, where the devil could make it uncertain and overturn it every moment, but it stands in God's hand and is founded upon His mercy, which is unshakeable and eternal, whence it is also called God's foreknowledge and is therefore certain and cannot fail... '

Through sanctification of the Spirit.' God the Father, he says, has foreknown you, that you should be His chosen children and be sanctified, not through the outward, bodily holiness of the Law, which with all its holiness no one has ever been able to make perfect according to the conscience, Heb. 7, 9, Phil. 3; much less, however, through your heathen ways and idolatrous worship..." PART III. CHAPTER XII.

etc. By what means then? By the sanctification of the Spirit, for your hearts are sanctified and cleansed by faith from the filth of idolatry and superstition.” (Exposition of the 1st Epistle of St. Peter. Erlangen Ed. P. LH. p. 5. sq. 7.)

U. Rhegius: “Whoever is ordained to eternal life believes the Gospel and amends his life, for God calls him in His own time, one in youth, another in old age, according to His will; no elect person remains finally in unbelief and a sinful life; but whoever always does evil and persists in it, he shall be damned, for he has no Christian faith; if he believed, he would live as a Christian and amend his life; therefore, whoever finally does no penance is certainly one of the damned. Therefore it is certain: whoever is ordained does not always do what he wills, but is converted and thereafter does what God wills; whoever does evil can and shall be damned if he persists in evil. Just as God has ordained Peter, Paul, and us other Christians to salvation, so has He also beforehand ordained and provided for their conversion, their Christian conduct, penance, and good works, in which they must walk and testify to their calling and faith.” (Formulae caute loquendi. Ed. Feustking. 1710. p. 37. sq.)

Chemnitius: “Does such an election of God happen only in time, when men do penance and believe? Or did it happen in consideration of their piety foreseen beforehand? St. Paul says in Eph. 1: We are chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world was laid. And 2 Tim. 1: He has saved us and called us not according to our works, but according to His purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the time of the world. Thus, the election of God does not follow our faith and righteousness, but precedes them as a cause of all this; for those whom He has ordained or chosen, them He has also called and justified, Rom. 8. And in Eph. 1, Paul does not say that we are chosen because we were holy or would be holy, but says: We are chosen that we might be holy; for the election of grace is a cause of everything that pertains to salvation, as Paul says: We have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of Him who works all things after the counsel of His own will, that we should be to the praise of His glory, and according to the working we believe, etc. And this same election happened not out of consideration of our present or future works, but out of God’s purpose and grace. Rom. 9. 2 Tim. 1.” (Handbüchlein, etc. 1574. See Frank: Die Th. der Concordienf. IV, 336.)

The same: “Is then God’s eternal ordination directed only to the matter of salvation and not also to the persons of those who are to be saved? In this article, Scripture always includes the persons of the elect; for the meaning is not that God only prepares salvation in general, while the persons who want to be saved must and could strive for it by themselves and through their own powers and abilities, as to how they might attain it; but God has considered each and every person of the elect who are to be saved through Christ in His eternal counsel, according to His gracious purpose, and has ordained and chosen them for salvation, and has also ordained how He will bring, promote, and preserve them thereto through His grace, gifts, and working.” (Handbüchlein der fürnehmsten Hauptstücke, etc. 1574. See Frank: Die Th. der Concordienf. IV, 335. sq.)

The same: “Predestination is spoken of regarding the special action of God in the elect, by which He calls, justifies, and makes them saved.” (Loc. th. Ed. P. Lyser. P. I. f. 148.)

L. Osiander: “In the ninth, tenth, and eleventh chapters” (of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans) “he shows us the true fountain of our salvation, namely, the eternal predestination of God, by which He has predestined us to eternal life...”

He] lived before the foundations of the world were laid; which doctrine we ought to oppose to the most grievous temptations, which seem as though they would shake our faith in Christ; so that we may firmly establish that no creature can separate us from the love of God.” (Epp. S. Pauli apost. omnes. Tübingen, 1583. Vol. I, p. 1, sq.)

P. Lyserus: “True faith is, therefore, an effect of divine predestination, and at the same time a gift of God conferred through the hearing of the Word.” (Harmon. ev. ad Joh. 10, 26. 27. Vol. I, 2187.)

Arcularius: “They are said to have ‘believed’ (Acts 13:48), ‘as many as were ordained to eternal life’; by which is noted the cause of those things which Luke had spoken of a little before, both concerning the joy and the celebration of the divine sermon, namely, faith, flowing forth from the eternal predestination of God as from a fountain.” (Comment. in acta apost. Ed. Menzer, p. 319.)

Gerhardus: “We know that Augustine writes in his book *De praedestinatione Sanctorum*, ch. 17: ‘God chose the faithful, but that they might be so, not because they already were; men do not believe in order that they may be chosen, but rather they are chosen in order that they may believe’; ch. 19: ‘Not because we believed, but that we might believe, He chose us; lest we be said to have chosen Him first,’ etc. But these and similar things were opposed to the Semipelagians or the remnants of the Pelagians; for they maintained that the beginning of faith is from us, and therefore that faith is the meritorious cause of election; that this was their genuine opinion is evident from the letters of Prosper and Hilary to Augustine, which are extant in Vol. 7. To them, therefore, Augustine rightly opposed himself and denied that faith is the cause of election; indeed, he even retracts what he had written in his *Exposition of Certain Propositions of the Epistle to the Romans*: ‘That God chose faith in his foreknowledge, so that He chose the one whom He knew would believe in Him,’ in *Retractationum* lib. 1, ch. 23, and *De praedestinatione Sanctorum*, ch. 3.” (L. c. § 166.)

S. Schmidtius: “The ultimate end of predestination is the glory of God, or, as the apostle speaks in Ephesians 1:6, 12, the glory of His grace and the praise of His glory; the subordinate and intermediate ends are the eternal salvation of the predestined, victory and non-separation from the love of God in Christ, and consolation (Rom. 8:28, 31, 35, 38, 39), as well as the holiness of life (Eph. 1:4). By no means, however, is it the security or despair of men (Rom. 11:20, 23, 24). The distinction of effects into common and proper is excellent. The latter are final perseverance and eternal life (provided they are related among the ends); the former, however, are those which do not flow from predestination alone, nor are they granted only to the predestined, but come about from other causes, even excluding this predestination, and occur even to the reprobate, namely, from universal grace and its means, by virtue of the antecedent will (Matt. 20:16; Heb. 6:4, 5). Where, just as perseverance, although it became the proper possession of the predestined by the consequent will, was nevertheless seriously promised and offered to the reprobate by the antecedent will, so calling, justification, and other common effects, although they are also offered and conferred upon the reprobate, nevertheless proceed for the predestined at the same time from the decree of predestination, both by reason of the reflection of the affection and by reason of the more abundant grace which is sometimes superadded to common grace, not to make this effective, but to make it more illustrious. And thus a man can be said to be predestined to faith itself with the blessed Luther, not only in the general notion of the word, by which whatever God does or gives, He had previously decreed to do or give, but also in this special sense of this passage (Rom. 8:29, 30; Eph. 1:4).” (Aphorism. th. p. 297, sq.)

The same: “We have already judged above that one who is predestined to faith, to justification, to sanctification, etc., can also be called πρόςκαιρος [temporary], and one who does not persevere in faith and holiness, and is therefore finally condemned.” (Articul. E. C. Repetitio, p. 517, sq.)

The same: “That John 15:16 speaks of election to eternal life, the final words prove. For whosoever’s fruit remains, they are saved... He repeats the same election shortly after in verse 19: ‘I have chosen you out of the world.’” (Repet. Artic. E. C. p. 492.) PART III. CHAP. XII.

Idem: ,,1 Pet. 1, 2.: ,Nach der Versehung Gottes, des Vaters.‘ (Petrus) will also sagen: Dass ihr erwählet seid, das habt ihr nicht erlangt durch euer Kräfte, Werk oder Verdienst, denn der Schatz ist zu gross, dass aller Menschen Heiligkeit und Gerechtigkeit viel zu gering ist, ihn zu erlangen; dazu seid ihr Heiden gewesen, von Gott nichts gewusst, keine Hoffnung gehabt und den stummen Götzen gedient; darum kommt ihr ohn all euer Zuthun, aus lauter Gnade zu soleher unaussprechlicher Herrlichkeit, nämlich dadurch, dass euch Gott, der Vater, von Ewigkeit dazu versehen hat, macht also die Versehung Gottes ganz lieblich und tröstlich, als sollt er sagen; Erwählete seid ihr und bleibets auch wohl, denn Gott, der euch versehen hat, ist stark und gewiss gnug, dass ihm sein Versehung nicht feihlen kann, doch so fern ihr auch seiner Verheissung gläubet und ihn für ein treuen Gott haltet. Chemnitius: ״Geschieht solche Wahl Gottes allererst in der Zeit, wenn die Menschen Busse thun und glauben? Oder ist sie geschehen in Betrachtung der zuvor ersehnen ihrer Frömmigkeit? Und ist dieselbige Wahl geschehen nicht aus Betrachtung unserer gegenwärtigen oder künftigen Werk, sondern aus Gottes Fürsatz und Gnade. Röm. 9. 2 Tim. 1.“ (Handbüchlein u. s. w. 1574. Vid. Ebr. 6, 4. 5. ### On Predestination and Reprobation: Aeg. Hunnius: "Neither is this (John 15:19) about election to the apostleship

Aeg. Hunnius: "Neither is this (John 15:19) about election to the apostleship; otherwise Judas, whom Luke reports to have been elected to the apostleship, would be said not to be of the world, i.e., from among the impious, which is absurd and manifestly contrary to the evangelical history. But the discussion here is about election out of the world, by reason of which a man ceases to be of the world, having been selected and segregated from the crowd of unbelievers." (Volum. disputatt. p. 288. b.)

The Theological Faculty of Wittenberg: "The clear context of Romans 8, from which such words ('who are called according to his purpose') are taken, irrefutably testifies that St. Paul is speaking there of the believing and elect children of God alone, and not indiscriminately of all men, whether they be believers or unbelievers, as Huber wishes. For the Apostle's words read thus: 'And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.' Thus, those are called according to the purpose of eternal predestination who are also ordained to salvation according to the purpose of God; as the words immediately following testify clearly. But those who are thus ordained according to the purpose (says the Book of Concord), they hear the Gospel, believe in Christ, pray and give thanks, are sanctified in love, have hope, patience, and comfort in the cross, Rom. 8. If, therefore, because we hold that the purpose of divine ordination and calling to salvation, of which Rom. 8 treats, is directed in the apostolic text notably toward the believers, we were to be considered Calvinists, then the Book of Concord itself would have to be Calvinistic, which clearly, brightly, and plainly directs this purpose, which is mentioned in the aforementioned place, to the elect children of God." (1595. Vid. Consil. Witteberg. I, 627.)

S. Schmidtius: "Nor does the same faith apprehend the benefit of predestination as it apprehends the benefit of justification, sanctification, etc., so as to make predestination its own through faith, in the way that through faith it obtains its justification; but the believer consoles and confirms his faith from predestination, so that he may say with the Apostle: 'If God be for us, who can be against us?'" (Aphorism. th. p. 295.) ANTITHESES.

Racovian Catechism: "Predestination of God in the Scriptures denotes nothing other than God's decree concerning men before the foundation of the world, of such a kind that to those who would believe in Him and obey Him, He would give eternal life, but those who would refuse to believe in Him and obey Him, He would punish with eternal damnation. This appears from the fact that Christ, the perfect interpreter of the divine will, has thus explained to us this counsel and decree of God: that he who would believe in Him would certainly have eternal life, but he who would not believe would certainly be condemned." (Ed. Oederus 1739. Quaest. 440. p. 913. sq.)

Crellius: "Election follows necessarily from predestination, once the condition which it demanded is posited; so that election is, as it were, a conclusion deduced from a major proposition, which predestination posits, and a minor, which the faith and piety of men provide. For the decree of predestination is: Every believer shall be saved. But that Paul, for example, believes, is the assumption. Whence the conclusion follows: Paul shall be saved; which, as long as it consists in the decree, is election, which embraces justification; when it is brought to effect, it is glorification. The major [is] by God alone"

ON PREDESTINATION AND REPROBATION. proposes grace; the minor [premise] is the grace of God and the will and probity of men, excited by the former and subservient to it.”

(Loc. de Deo et attrib. div. c. 32. See Scherzer’s Colleg. antisocin. p. 745.) Ph. J. Spener: “It is impossible that the elect should be persistently led astray, Matt. 24:24. Meanwhile, election is not the cause that such people remain constant in grace, but because they will remain constant, that has caused the Lord to elect them.” (Katechismuspredigten.

1689. p. 355.) The same: “The Calvinists add very many [effects of predestination]: namely, all means to salvation, and the merit of Christ itself; indeed, the supralapsarians also refer the creation of the predestined to the effects of predestination.” (Articul. F. C. Repetit, p. 515.) See Eph. 1:5, 6, where we are said to be elected by God for this reason, or for the sake of this end, that the glory of His grace might be praised.

§ 18. The decree of election, according to what has been said thus far, is established to be (1) particular, and (2) immutable. Namely, that not all men are predestined or elected to salvation; as is manifest from § 16 and the last note. Although the very word election, by which a few are denoted as chosen or segregated from the many, also denotes that particularity.

B. Meisner: “Matt. 20:16, 22:14: ‘Many are called, few are chosen’; by this brief aphorism, as if by some thunderbolt, that indiscriminate Huberite universality is relegated even to the abyss. For if only a few are chosen, then certainly not all will be chosen. Otherwise, calling and election would extend equally wide, so that as many as are called would be chosen. The Savior, however, makes an evident distinction regarding the number between the called and the chosen, while He says that many are indeed called, but few are chosen. What does Huber say to this? He brings forward two little responses, one of which he seeks from grammar, while he distinguishes between ἐκλελεγμένους and ἐκλεκτούς; he confesses that few are ἐκλεκτούς, but all are ἐκλελεγμένους; which little distinction some declare with this analogy: in a school, all boys are ‘taught’ [docti] participially, because all are taught by the teacher, but they are not all ‘learned’ [docti] nominally, because they do not all grasp, nor fix in their memory, those things which they learn from the teacher. The other he takes from the distinction of election into general and special; that the discourse here is about special, not general, election.

Resp. to 1: That distinction between ἐκλεκτούς and ἐκλελεγμένους is nothing. For it is destitute of all authority of the Scriptures. For nowhere is it read that all men indiscriminately are ἐκλελεγμένοι, elected participially, but few are ἐκλεκτοί or elected nominally; but Scripture uses these words without any distinction, so that those who are ἐκλελεγμένοι are also ἐκλεκτοί, and vice versa. Especially, however, let that of the Savior in Matt. 13:30 be referred to here: ‘For the sake of the elect, whom God has chosen,’ etc.; where certainly those whom God has chosen are called the elect, so that no distinction is left between ἐκλεκτούς and ἐκλελεγμένους; which the very sound of the words also argues. For the participle ἐκλελεγμένος is composed with a preposition having the force of segregating or selecting just as much as the verbal noun ἐκλεκτός. Therefore, those who are chosen by God are the elect; and he who is not chosen, him God has not chosen; and therefore, to say that God has chosen all, but that not all are the elect, is an iron-wood [a contradiction in terms].

To 2: It is a begging of the question; for this is the very thing in question.” It is asked whether, besides that particular election of which Scripture makes mention, there is some other universal one. We read everywhere, indeed, that many are called, but few are chosen, and that God has not chosen all men whatsoever, etc. Nowhere, however, is it said that all are chosen without any distinction. Why, therefore, should we not believe Scripture more than the bare assertion of Huber? . . .

The word "election," when it concerns persons, always denotes a separation, in such a way that first some universality is implied, and then the separation of certain ones from it, which is called election. Now, however, if all men are said to be elected to life, that native meaning perishes. For what place does separation have if all are predestined? And how are some chosen from the world, and some from among men, if all are included by the decree of ἐκλογή? . . .

Whoever are the elect are inscribed in the book of life. But, in truth, not all are inscribed. Therefore, not all are elect. The major premise cannot be denied if one wishes to follow the Formula of Concord, which holds those phrases as synonyms. The minor is proven because Scripture proclaims it as a singular benefit that the names of some are written "in heaven" (Luke 10:20), "in the book" (Dan. 12:1), "in the book of life" (Phil. 4:3), "in the book of life of the Lamb" (Rev. 21:27). Whence also all those are said to be about to perish "whose names have not been written in the book of life" (Rev. 13:8; 17:8; 20:15). . .

If many are reprobated from eternity, not all will be elect. But indeed many are reprobated, which, besides the testimonies of Scripture (Rom. 1:28; 2 Tim. 3:8; Tit. 1:16), is argued by the very word "election" itself. For if only certain ones are elected, it must be that the others are reprobated. And we ask here: has God not made a decree from eternity concerning the end of man, as to who are to be saved and who are to be damned? If Huber denies this, he will fashion a God who is idle, who has decreed nothing certain concerning the salvation or damnation of men. If he affirms it, the universality of election will immediately fall. . .

God knows all the elect (2 Tim. 2:19). But He never knows the unbelievers (Matt. 7:23). Therefore, the unbelievers are never the elect. For the confirmation of the major premise, we add the sayings concerning the divine πρόγνωσις, according to which we are elected, which act as follows: Rom. 8:29, "Whom He foreknew, He also predestined"; ch. 11:2, "God has not rejected His people ὃν προέγνω"; 1 Pet. 1:2, "To the elect according to the πρόγνωσιν of God the Father." From these it becomes clear that all the elect were foreknown from eternity and specially known to God. But concerning the impenitent, it is said that they were never known. Who, therefore, are the elect, and indeed by the most proper election made according to πρόγνωσιν? . . .

### On Predestination and Reprobation: The theological rule, which has been chanted in the schools and always used,…

The theological rule, which has been chanted in the schools and always used, holds thus: The elect are not to be sought outside the assembly of the called. The foundation of the rule is taken from the saying of Christ: "Many are called, few are chosen." If, therefore, anyone is excluded from the number of the called, he will be much more excluded from the number of the elect. But Huber completely inverts the matter and utterly destroys that rule, while he posits that the most properly elect—and indeed none but the elect—are to be found no less outside the Church in Turkey and Tartary; whether this is absurd and scandalous, and provides an opportunity for various calumnies, let all who think rightly judge.

(Ἀνθρωπολ. Disp. XVII, B. 1.4. c. 1.2.) Petrus Piscator: "It is clear what is to be thought of the words of Huber, where he writes thus: 'I ask, could all be elected to life?' 'The opposing party concedes this willingly. But if all could be elected, where then is the force of separating in the word "to elect"?' (Modo ineundae Concordiae th. 39.) For we distinguish between a locution that is written and unwritten, proper and improper, broad and strict, exquisite and popular, accepted by the symbolic books and rejected and disapproved by them. But if all were to believe and thus be saved through faith in Christ, and no man had remained in impenitence and unbelief, then the term 'election' would not have been used by the Holy Spirit, but rather 'adoption' or 'acceptance,' or some other term most alien to all disjunction and separation." (Commentar. in F. C. 1610, p. 540 sq.)

J. Olearius: "What is the profit of a catachrestic universal election, whether actual (with Huber), or possible (with Thummius, who says:

"To dispute that 'God willed all to be elect,' after it is sufficiently established from the infallible revelation of Scripture that God indeed willed and wills all to be saved, yet chose only those who believe in Christ (Eph. 1:4), and thus, with respect to the non-believers, by no means all, but few" (See Carpzov, *Isagog.* p. 1681). B. Meisner: "It should be noted that the Apostle speaks of the whole assembly by way of κοινοποίησις (generalization) (Eph. 1:4), even though those epithets apply only to the elect who exist within the assembly of the called." (*Anthropol. Disp.* XVI. D. 4. b.) "The same synecdoche recurs here (1 Tim. 1:9), which others call κοινοποίησις, when the discourse is directed to many, yet that which is said is not applied to all." (*L. c. Disp.* XVII. 1. 3.) Calovius: "Even though (the Apostle) believed that not all among them were elected to eternal life, he nevertheless designated them all the more willingly by the better and superior part, the more ardently he desired that all might be found in the number of the elect; just as today, in public sermons, all hearers are commonly addressed by the most gracious name of the elect in Christ Jesus, because it is hoped that such are among them, and it is desired that all might be such. Augustine rightly says in *De unit. eccl.* c. 12: 'The prophets and apostles are accustomed to rebuke the blameworthy in a people in such a way as if all were being rebuked, and to address the praiseworthy in such a way as if all there were being praised.'" (*Consider. Arminian.* p. 434.) ANTITHESIS. Quenstedtius: "Antithesis: Sebastian Castellio, who in his dialogue on election is the architect of the error concerning universal election, and defended it publicly against Calvin and Beza; he was followed by Samuel Huber, a Swiss, professor of theology at the Academy of Wittenberg toward the end of the previous century (A.D. 1593), who absurdly posited: 'Election is universal; God has chosen all men truly, properly, and univocally to salvation.'" (*L. c. s. 2. q. 6. f. 72. sq.*) Formula of Concord: "But diligent distinction must be made between that which is expressly revealed in God's Word concerning this and that which is not revealed; for beyond what has been said thus far, which is revealed in Christ, God has kept much of this mystery silent and hidden, and reserved it solely for His own wisdom and knowledge, which we should not investigate, nor follow our own thoughts therein, nor draw conclusions or speculate, but should hold to the revealed Word; which reminder is most necessary. For our curiosity always has much more desire to busy itself with this than with that which God has revealed to us in His Word, because we cannot reconcile it, which we are also not commanded to do. Thus, there is no doubt that God knows very well and most certainly, before the foundation of the world, who among those who are called will believe or will not believe; likewise, which of the converted will remain steadfast and which will not remain steadfast; which will return after the fall and which will fall into hardening. So also the number of how many there will be on both sides is without any doubt known and manifest to God. But because God has reserved such a mystery for His own wisdom and has revealed nothing of it to us in the Word, much less commanded us to investigate such things through our own thoughts, but has earnestly restrained us from it, Rom. 11:33 sqq.: we should not infer, conclude, or speculate with our thoughts, but hold to His revealed Word, to which He points us. Thus, God also knows without any doubt and has determined for everyone the time and hour of his calling and conversion; but because this is not revealed to us, we have the command..." PART III. CAP. XII. that we should always hold fast to the Word, but commit the time and hour to God, Acts 1:

7. Likewise, when we see that God gives His Word in one place, but does not give it in another, takes it away from one place, but lets it remain in another; likewise, one is hardened, blinded, given over to a reprobate mind, while another, who is equally guilty, is nevertheless converted, etc.: in these and similar questions, Paul sets for us a certain limit as to how far we should go, namely, that we should recognize God’s judgment in a part; for these are well-deserved punishments for sins when God so punishes the contempt of His Word in a land or people that it even extends to their descendants, as can be seen in the Jews; thereby God shows His severity to His own in certain lands and persons, [showing] what we all have well deserved and would be worthy of, because we behave ourselves wickedly toward God’s Word and often grievously grieve the Holy Spirit; so that we may live in the fear of God, and recognize and praise God’s goodness—which is without and against our merit—in and among us, to whom He gives and leaves His Word, whom He does not harden and reject. For because our nature is corrupted by sin, and is worthy of and guilty of God’s wrath and damnation, God owes us neither Word, Spirit, nor grace; and when He gives it out of grace, we often push it away from us and make ourselves unworthy of eternal life, Acts 13:

46. And such a just and well-deserved judgment of His He lets be seen in certain lands, peoples, and persons, so that we, when we are compared with them and measured against them, may learn all the more diligently to recognize and praise God’s pure, unmerited grace in the vessels of mercy. For no injustice is done to those who are punished and receive the wages of their sins; but in the others, where God gives and preserves His Word and thereby people are enlightened, converted, and preserved, God praises His pure grace and mercy without their merit. If we go thus far in this article, we remain on the right path, as it is written in Hosea 13:9: "Israel, that you perish, the fault is yours; but that you are helped, that is purely My grace." But whatever in this disputation wants to run too high and beyond these bounds, there we should, with Paul, lay a finger on our mouth, reflect, and say: "Who are you, O man, who would contend with God?" For that we cannot and should not search out and fathom everything in this article is testified to by the high Apostle Paul, who, when he has disputed much on this article from the revealed Word of God, as soon as he comes to the point of indicating what God has reserved of this mystery of His hidden wisdom, he suppresses it and cuts it off with the following words: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments and His ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord?" namely, outside of and beyond what He has revealed to us in His Word. (Concordia, pp. 715—717.) Cf. supra citata P. III. c. 1. §7. p. 16 sq. c. 3. §10. p. 153 sq.

154. Luther: "There arises a particular misfortune, that everyone, out of shameful and harmful curiosity, wants to begin first with the predestination of this or that. Since God has known all things: why did He not prevent the fall of man? Why does He still look on in the world and let them promote their own damnation, when He could well prevent it and convert them, so that they would have to be pious? etc. Whoever wants to begin to know God with such questions will actually break his neck, for that is Lucifer’s fall; he also wanted to go above and beyond everything. But it does not work." (Halle Tom. XIII, 332 sq.) The same: "Place three lights before me: the light of nature, the light of grace, the light of glory, as the common and good distinction has it. In the light of nature, it is insoluble that this is just, that the good man is afflicted and the bad man fares well."

have. But this dissolves the light of grace. In the light of grace it is insoluble, how God condemns him who cannot do otherwise by any of his own powers than to sin and be guilty; here both the light of nature and the light of grace dictate that the fault is not of the wretched man, but of the iniquitous God, for they can judge nothing else concerning God, who gratuitously crowns an impious man without merits and does not crown another, but condemns him, perhaps less or at least no more impious. But the light of glory dictates otherwise, and God, whose judgment is now of incomprehensible justice, will then show that it is of most just and most manifest justice, so that in the meantime we believe this, warned and confirmed by the example of the light of grace, which fulfills a similar miracle in the natural light.” (De servo arbitrio. 1525. See Opp. lat. var. argum. Francof. ad M. 1873. Vol. VII, 365. sq.)
