Tom. 1. disp. 10. Marp. th. 88., Gesnerus disp. ult. in Dan. th. 142., Gerlachius disp. de aeterna salvandorum electione th. 11., Bungius disp. 10. in ep. ad Rom. p. 179., Dn. D. Hutterus in Form. Cone. p. 1121. 1163. 1124. 1177. et Dn. D. Menzerus Tom. 1. disp. Giess, disp. 14. th. 10. 40. 78.109.129.131.171. 192. sqq. Hi omnes docent et fatentur: 1. Decretum electiopis, ut aeternum, sic immutabile et certum esse. Quae enim Deus semel decrevit facere, ea certo exequitur, et nisi faceret, fine suo frustraretur, ejusque veritati, sapientiae et omnipotentiae detraheretur. Quem igitur elegit, h. e., salvare decrevit, illum certo salvat et contra. 2. Hinc sequitur, quod electus semper maneat electus, nec unquam fiat reprobus, vel contra, h. e., quod electio nequeat irrita reddi vel evacuari. 3. Licet

igitur electi quidam mortaliter peccent, eo tamen ipso tempore vere sunt et dici possunt electi ob decretum divinum et certum electorum numerum, cui in aeterna praenotione semper manent inclusi. 4. Pari modo, quamvis nonnulli ad tempus vere credant, tamen si ab aeterno viventium libro non sunt inscripti ob praevisam incredulitatem finalem, eo ipso fidei tempore, vi decreti divini, vere sunt et dici possunt in divina praescientia reprobati.5 ׳. Magna proinde differentia est inter renatos et electos, adeo ut pro synonymis haberi nequeant, cum distinguantur tanquam latius et angustius, si quidem omnes electi sunt quidem renati, si non omni, tamen mortis, tempore; sed non contra omnes renati simul sunt electi, nempe ii, qui fidem amittunt et cum finali impoenitentia decedunt.“ ^Αν&ρωπολ. Disp. XVI. A. 2. b. — A. 3. b.) Idem: ,,Matth. 24, 24. Mare. 13, 22.: ,Surgent pseudochristi et pseudoprophetae et dabunt signa magna et prodigia, ita ut in errorem inducantur, el δυνατόν, si possibile esset vel fieri posset, etiam electi.‘ Hinc ita inferimus: si ex electo posset fieri reprobus, tum simul possibile foret, electos seduci finaliter; atqui juxta Christi assertionem possibile non est, electos seduci finaliter; ergo nec possibile erit, ex electo fieri reprobum. Neque valet exceptio, per impossibilitatem esse intelligendam difficultatem, eo, quod impossibile saepe idem sit, quod diffleile. Etenim ut nihil dicam, quod haec explicatio sit principii petitio et ex solis particularibus procedat, vel illud solum studiose considerari velim, Christum non dicere, impossibile est electos seduci, sed ita format stylum: ,Facient signa adeo magna, ut etiam in errorem inducerentur electi, si possibile esset‘, quibus certe verbis non modo difficultatem, sed omnimodam prorsus impossibilitatem seductionis intellectam vult. Nam etiam seducitur, qui difficulter seducitur. Christus autem omnino negat, seductum iri ullum electum, quia hoc non sit possibile. Qualis autem et quam absurda foret paraphrasis: in errorem propter signa et prodigia inducerentur etiam electi, si possibile foret, i. e., nisi difficile foret. Imo inverti posset: Licet sit difficile, tamen induci poterunt, quoniam etiam ea, quae difficulter contingunt, tamen quandoque contingunt et contingere possunt. Nisi ergo verba Christi omnino״ invertere placeat, necesse est, ut fateamur, Christum potius de impossibilitate, quam difficultate seductionis locutum esse. Hic autem exoritur quaestio: annon hoc pacto absolutum statuatur decretum, vel num alia dicta impossibilitatis causa assignari queat? Nos distinguimus inter absolutum et infallibile; statuentes non ex absoluta et fatali necessitate electos conservari et salvari, quasi simpliciter impossibile sit, ut pereant, quicquid etiam agant; sed duntaxat infallibilitatem intellectam volumus. Ipsorum quidem conditio talis est, ut feccare et perire possint; nunquam tamen hoc contingit aut contingere potest, quia, infallibiliter conservantur. Atque sic infallibilitatis istius causam constituimus non fatale decretum Calvinisticum, non perfectionem summam electorum, sed potius: 1. virtutem Dei, custodientis electos in fide ad salutem, 1 Pet. 1, 5.; 2. precationem Christi efficacem pro perseverantia et salute electorum Joh. 17, 11.; 3. potestatem Christi, cui nemo potest oves rapere ex manibus suis Joh. 10, 28.; 4. firmitatem decreti divini 2 Tim. 2, 19.; et denique 5. infallibilitatem praescientiae.“ (Άν&ρωπολ. Disp. XVI. C. ,1. b. sq.) ' Idem: ,,2 Tim. 2, 18. et 19. ,Hymenaeus et Philetus a veritate exciderunt, dicentes, resurrectionem esse jam factam; sed firmum fundamentum Dei stat habens signaculum hoc: Novit Dominus, qui sunt sui.‘ In quo dicto diligentissime observanda est ista άντί&εσίς excidentium et electorum a Domino cognitorum. Quia enim Hymenaeus et Philetus ad tempus quidem crediderant, post autem a fide defecerant, ne quis offenderetur, ac si electi etiam finaliter excidere et perire possent, statim subjungit apostolus: ,Sed firmum stat fundamentum‘, q. d., ne offendamini, quod isti duo, primum fideles, post apostatae facti sint, nec putetis, electos etiam perire posse, quoniam isti, licet PART. m. CAP. ΧΠ. crediderint ad tempus, non tamen fuerunt vere electi, quod eventus docet, cum,firmum sit fundamentum Dei, habens signaculum hoc: Novit Dominus, qui sunt sui‘.“ (Άνΰρωπολ. Disp. XVI. B. 1.) Idem: ,,Statuimus, aliquem minus posse erigi et confirmari de electione, si hujus mutabilitas defendatur. Nam si quis se electum crederet, et tamen dubitaret de sua perseverentia et salute, quia audiret, multos electos excidere et aeternum perire, nescio, an satis posset hic scrupulus ipsi eximi, stante aliorum sententia. Ita enim instaret: non omnis electus perseverat et salvatur, sed multi finaliter excidunt electione et damnantur. Etiamsi igitur jam sim electus, non tamen ex hac electione certitudinem perseverantiae et salutis ob dictam causam firmiter concludere possum. Contra vero si το αμεταμελητον electionis astruatur, invicte quis concludere potest: omnis electus a Deo praeservatur et in errorem finalem induci nequit, sed certo salvabitur et glorificabitur. Atqui ego credo et testimonium praebet Spiritus Sanetus, quod sim electus. Quare certus sum et credo firmiter, Deum me esse conservaturum, ab omni malo praeservaturum et tandem infallibiliter salvaturum atque glorifleaturum. Ita videmus, quanta πληροφορία et certitudo fidei oriatur et deducatur ex immutabilitate electionis; quae si negetur, et istam si non negari, certe tamen magna ex parte labefactari necesse est.“ (,Aν&ρωπολ. Disp. XVI. D. 2. a. b.) Gerhardus: ,,Ex hypothesi et suppositione rectissime dicitur, electorum numerum nec augeri nec minui posse; ibi enim consideratur numerus, ut actu est; omne autem, quod est, eo ipso, quod est, impossibile est non esse vel aliter esse, juxta Boetii regulam.“ (L. de elect. § 213.) Calovius: ,,Si electi perire possent, praevisio Dei falsa foret et electio mutabilis; cum Deus contra falli in praevisione sua non possit. Si incerta ac mutabilis esset electio, ab aeterno facta non esset; quod enim ab aeterno est, mutabile non est. At facta est ab aeterno, Matth. 25, 34. Eph. 1, 4. 2 Tim. 1, 9. Apoc. 17, 8. etc. (Socinism. proflig. p. 744.) B. Menzerus: ,,Sane verum est, electorum fidem finaliter everti non posse. Secus enim non forent electi. Quippe omnes et soli in fide perseverantes ad finem sunt electi, et omnes et soli electi in fide perseverant ad finem.“ (Disp. th. in academ. Giessen, hab. Tom. VII, 499.) S. Schmidtius: ,,Hoc certum nobis esse debet, merae divinae in Christo gratiae esse, quod electi seduci non possunt. Probatur, quia electi, abstracta electionis gratia, possunt seduci, imo certe futurum esset, ut seducerentur, ut textus noster (Matth. 24,24.) clare significat. Posse autem illos seduci, excludit omne eorum meritum, omnes eorum vires hactenus, ut inseducibiles illos facere nequeant. Finge namque, eos saltem tales per merita esse, ut Deus non possit eos seductioni permittere, sed cogatur eos facere inseducibiles, sane in se considerati et extra electionem positi erunt inseducibiles. Atqui noster locus ab electione inseducibilitatem suspendit. Oportet itaque, electionem esse gratuitam et inseducibilitatem inde oriundam merae gratiae.“ (Colleg. bibi, poster. Ed. 3. p. 242.). Scherzerus: ״Objiciunt (Sociniani): 1 Cor. 9, ult.: ,Corpus meum in servitutem redigo, ne, aliis praedicans, ipse reprobus fiam.‘ Ex quo dicto apertissime constat, Paulum, qui ad vitam aeternam electus fuerat, potuisse fleri reprobum. Quod si ipse Paulus reprobus fieri potuit, quanto magis caeteri? Slicht. post Socin. qq. contr. Meisn. f. 40. Resp.: Non agitur de reprobatione electioni, sed improbationi opposita. ’Αδόκιμος est a δοκιμάζω, probo, notatque inutilem, nonnunquam ad tempus tafitum, 2 Cor. 13, 7. At, electum ad tempus inutilem, imo noxium ecclesiae (qualis Paulus ipse ante conversionem fuit) esse posse, concedimus. Inde non sequitur, aeternum reprobari ullum


### On Predestination and Reprobation: of them. If Paul could have become a reprobate or been damned, who, as he was…

of them. If Paul could have become a reprobate or been damned, who, as he was certain that he was not reprobated from eternity (Rom. 8:38; 2 Cor. 13:6), would have been [certain]?" (Colleg. antisocin. p. 769.)

Dannhauer: "It is entirely possible that an elect person is not an actual member of the church, is not 'of this fold' (John 10:16; Rom. 8:9; Gal. 5:24), since he does not yet have the Spirit of Christ, and therefore is not His. 'According to foreknowledge and predestination, how many sheep are outside, how many wolves are inside!' Augustine, Tract. 45 in John." (Hodosoph. p. 62.)

Hollaz: "Some Tübingen theologians use the term 'election' not in a general sense, nor even in the strictest sense, but in a stricter and intermediate sense, so that it denotes the ordination of all believers—whether they believe until the end of life or only for a time—to eternal salvation; in which sense every believer is elect, and by faith extinguished through mortal sins, one becomes a reprobate from being elect. Cf. D. Ad. Osiander, Colleg. th. VI, 110." (Exam. p. 641.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Socinians, who posit that the elect can fall from their election and perish. Thus Socinus in Praelect. c. 12 and 13. ... 2. Of the Arminians, who also make election to glory variable, establishing one election to glory as peremptory and another as non-peremptory. For they assign three orders of believers. The first is of novices, who are recently converted to faith, but when temptations arise, they immediately languish and fail. The second is of those who remain constant for some time in living faith and holy purpose, but eventually, overcome and broken by the allurements of the world, the flesh, or Satan, or by violent tyranny, they fall away and defect from the faith. The third is of those who persevere finally. They assert that the first two orders of believers are elected truly, but not altogether absolutely, nor except for a time; [and that] only the third and last are elected finally and peremptorily, Confess. c. 18, s. 6. 3. Of Huber, who vehemently opposed our thesis. For the universality of election cannot be maintained unless the salvation of many of the elect is impugned." (L. c. s. 2, q. 8, f. 90.)

Kromayer: "The Arminians make one election incomplete, which they ascribe to τοῖς προςκαίροις [those who are temporary], and another complete, which they assign to those persevering in faith who are finally to be saved, Confess. c. 5, s. 7." (Scrutin. relig. p. 194.)

Ad. Osiander: "The elect can utterly fall from the grace of God and be reprobated." (Colleg. th. VI, 110.)

Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of the Anabaptists, regarding whom the Augsburg Confession, Art. 12, condemned grace as being totally losable in these words: '(Our churches) condemn the Anabaptists, who deny that those once justified can lose the Holy Spirit.' 2. Of the Calvinists, who contend that the elect, however they may have fallen, do not lose faith, but, as if having suffered a swoon, retain its habit, seed, and spark, even if they do not perceive it in act, etc. Thus the founder of this sect, Calvin, 1. 3, Instit. c. 2, f. 12: 'Meanwhile, this must be held,' he says, 'however small and weak faith may be in the elect; because the Spirit of God is a certain pledge and seal of their adoption in them, its engraving can never be erased from their hearts; but the reprobate are sprinkled with such a light that afterwards perishes.' Piscator against Schaffm. p. 160 writes: 'Not even David by adultery and homicide, nor Peter by the denial of his Lord, lost the Holy Spirit.' ... Bucanus, loc. 29, q. 27: 'Faith,' he says, 'can receive damage and suffer a kind of swoon, so that it is sometimes varied and shaken by the storms of temptations, obscured, overwhelmed, and becomes languid. Indeed, even in the saints, reason is lulled to sleep and buried no differently than in drunkards and infants. As in David, when he committed adultery, and in Peter, when he denied Christ three times, but yet it is never utterly cast out.'" (L. c. s. 2, q. 7, f. 77 sq.)

PART III. CHAP. XII. Quenstedtius: "Attributes or adjuncts are either of election or of the elect. The attributes of election are: 1. Eternity; Matt. 25:34: 'Inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.' Eph. 1:4: 'He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world.' cf. 2 Tim. 1:9; 2 Thess. 2:13. 2. Particularity; Matt. 20:16: 'Many are called, few are chosen.' 3. Immutability; 2 Tim. 2:19: 'The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are His.' ... The attributes of the elect are: 1. Fewness; Matt. 20:16; 22:14: 'Many are called, few are chosen.' 2. The possibility of temporarily losing the indwelling grace totally. Hence David, Ps. 51:11: 'Do not take Your Holy Spirit from me.' 1 Cor. 10:12: 'Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.' 3. Certainty of election; Luke 10:20: 'Rejoice because your names are written in heaven.' cf. Rom. 8:38 ff.; 2 Tim. 4:8; on the part of man, not absolute, but ordered; Phil. 2:12: 'Beloved, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.' 4. Final persistence in faith; Matt. 10:22: 'He who perseveres to the end will be saved.' cf. Rev. 2:10." (L. c. s. 1. th. 20. sq. f. 29. sq.)

Formula of Concord: "This also belongs to the further explanation and salutary use of the doctrine of the providence of God for salvation: since only the elect are saved, whose names are written in the Book of Life, how one may know, from what, and whereby one may 'recognize who the elect are, who can and should take this doctrine to themselves for comfort. And concerning this, we should not judge according to our reason, nor according to the Law, or from any outward appearance; nor should we presume to search into the secret, hidden abyss of divine providence, but rather pay attention to the revealed will of God. For 'he has made known to us and let us know the mystery of his will, and has brought it forth through Christ, that it should be preached,' Eph. 1:9 f.; 2 Tim. 1:9 f. But the same is revealed to us thus, as Paul says in Rom. 8:29 f.: 'Those whom God foreknew, elected, and ordained, them he also called.' Now God does not call without means, but through the Word, just as he has 'commanded to preach repentance and forgiveness of sins' . . . And such a call of God, which happens through the preaching of the Word, we should not consider to be shadow-boxing, but know that thereby God reveals his will, that he desires to work through the Word in those whom he thus calls, so that they may be enlightened, converted, and saved. For the Word, through which we are called, is a ministry of the Spirit, which gives the Spirit or through which the Spirit is given, 2 Cor. 3:8, and a power of God unto salvation, Rom. 1:16. And because the Holy Spirit desires to be powerful through the Word, to strengthen, and to give power and ability, it is God's will that we should accept the Word, believe, and follow the same. Therefore, the elect are described thus in John 10:27 f.: 'My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life'; and Eph. 1:11, 13: 'Those who are ordained according to the purpose for an inheritance, they hear' the Gospel, believe in Christ, pray and give thanks, are sanctified in love, have hope, patience, and comfort in the cross, Rom. 8:25; and even if all this is very weak in them, they nevertheless have hunger and thirst for righteousness, Matt. 5:6. Thus, 'the Spirit of God bears witness to the elect that they are children of God, and since they do not know what they should pray for as is fitting, he intercedes for them with unspeakable groanings,' Rom. 8:16, 26. So also the Holy Scripture testifies that God, who has called us, is so faithful that, when he has begun the good work in us, he also desires to preserve and complete it until the end, provided we do not turn ourselves away from him, but hold fast to the begun state until the end, for which he has promised his grace, 1 Cor. 1:9; Phil. 1:6; 2 Pet. 3:9; Heb. 3. With this revealed"

We ought to concern ourselves with the revealed will of God, to follow it, and to be diligent in it, because the Holy Spirit, through the Word by which He calls us, grants grace, strength, and ability for this; and we ought not to search into the abyss of the hidden providence of God, as it is written in Luke 13:24, where one asks: "Lord, are there few that be saved?" and Christ answers: "Strive to enter in at the strait gate." ... Therefore, Christ also does not allow the promise of the Gospel to be set forth only in general, but seals the same through the Sacraments, which He has appended as seals of the promise, and thereby confirms it to every believer in particular. Therefore, we also retain, as the Augsburg Confession says in Article 11, private absolution, and we teach that it is God’s command that we believe such absolution and hold it for certain that we are reconciled to God as truly, if we believe the word of absolution, as if we had heard a voice from heaven, as the Apology explains this article; which comfort would be taken from us entirely if we were not to conclude concerning God’s will toward us from the call which occurs through the Word and the Sacraments. (Concordia, pp. 709—712.)

Luther: "In the beginning, God indeed wished to immediately counter this curiosity. For thus He proposed His will and counsel: I will indeed manifest My foreknowledge and predestination to you; but not by this way of reason and carnal wisdom, as you imagine. I will do this: From the unrevealed God I shall become revealed, and yet I shall remain the same God. I will be incarnate or I will send My Son; He will die for your sins and rise again from the dead. And thus I will fulfill your desire, so that you may be able to know whether you are predestined or not? 'Behold, this is My Son, hear Him' (Matt. 17:5), look upon Him lying in the manger, in His mother’s lap, hanging on the cross. See what He does, what He says. There you will surely apprehend Me. 'For he who sees Me,' says Christ (John 14:9), 'sees the Father also.' If you hear Him and are baptized in His name and love His Word, then you are certainly predestined and certain of your salvation. But if you curse or despise the Word, then you are damned, because he who does not believe is condemned. Kill other thoughts and ways of reason or the flesh, because God detests them. Do this one thing: that you receive the Son, that Christ may please you in your heart in His birth, miracles, and cross. For there is the book of life, in which you are written. ...

Latin:

electorum. Si Paulus reprobus fieri sive damnari potuisset, qui, se ab aeterno non reprobatum esse, Rom. 8,38. 2 Cor. 13, 6., certus fuisset?“ (Colleg. antisocin. p. 769.)

Dannhauerus: ,,Pieri omnino potest, ut electus non sit membrum ecclesiae actuale, non sit,de hoc ovili‘ (Joh. 10, 16. Rom. 8, 9. Gal. 5, 24.), cum nondum habeat spiritum Christi, ac ideo non sit ejus. ,Secundum praescientiam et praedestinationem quam multae oves foris, quam multi lupi intus! ‘ Augustin. Tract. 45. in Joh.“ (Hodosoph. p. 62.)

Hollazius: ״Nonnulli theologi Tubingenses vocem,electio‘ adhibent non in sensu generali, neque etiam strictissimo, sed in sensu strictiori et medio, ut notet ordinationem omnium credentium, sive usque ad finem vitae, sive ad tempus credant, ad aeternam salutem; quo sensu omnis credens est electus et extincta per peccata mortifera fide ex electo fit reprobus. Cf. D. Ad. Osiandri Colleg. th. VI, 110.“ (Exam. p. 641.)

ANTITHESES. Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Socinianorum, electos excidere sua electione et perire posse, statuentium. Ita Socinus in Praelect. c. 12. et 13. . . 2. Arminianorum, qui etiam electionem ad gloriam variabilejm faciunt, electionem ad gloriam aliam peremtoriam, aliam non peremtoriam constituentes. Tres enim assignant credentium ordines. Primum növitiorum, qui recens ad fidem convertuntur, sed ortis tentationibus statim languescunt et deficiunt. Alterum eorum, qui in viva fide et proposito sancto aliquanto tempore quidem constantes manent, sed tandem tamen, sive mundi sive carnis sive ‘satanae illecebris aut violenta tyrannide victi fractique, a fide deficiunt ac desciscunt. Tertium eorum, qui flnaliter perseverant. Priores duos ordines credentium eligi vere, at non prorsus absolute, nec nisi ad tempus; tertium ac postremum solum flnaliter ac peremtorie eligi asserunt, Confess. c. 18. s. 6. 3. Huberi, qui acriter sese thesi nostrae opposuit. Electionis enim universalitas obtineri nequit, nisi salus plurimorum electorum impugnetur.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 8. f. 90.)

Kromayerus: ״Arminiani electionem aliam incompletam, quam τοϊς προςκαίροις adscribunt, aliam completam, quam perseverantibus in fide tandem salvandis assignant, faciunt Confess. c. 5. s. 7.“ (Scrutin. relig/p. 194.)

Ad. Osiander: ״Electi gratia Dei penitus excidere atque reprobari possunt.“ (Colleg. th. VI, 110.)

Quenstedtius: ״Antithesis: 1. Anabaptistarum, in quibus gratiam totaliter inamissibilem damnavit Aug. Conf. a. 12. his verbis: ,Damnant (nostrae ecclesiae) Anabaptistas, qui negant, semel justificatos posse amittere Spiritum S.‘ 2. Calvinianorum, qui contendunt, electos, quomodocunque lapsi fuerint, non amittere tamen fidem, sed, quasi deliquium passos, retinere illius habitum, semen, scintillam, etiamsi actu non sentiant etc. Sic conditor hujus gentis, Calvinus, 1.3. Instit. c. 2. f. 12.: ,Hoc interim tenendum est‘, inquit, ,quantumvis exigua sit ac debilis in electis fides; quia tamen spiritus Dei certa in illis arrha est ac sigillum suae adoptionis, nunquam ex illorum cordibus deleri posse ejus sculpturam; reprobos vero tali luce aspergi, quae postea dispereat.‘ Piscator contra Schaffm. p. 160. scribit: ,Ne Davidem quidem adulterio homicidioque nec Petrum Domini sui abnegatione Spiritum S. perdidisse.‘ . . Bucanus loco 29. q. 27.: ,Fides‘, inquit, ,accipere potest detrimentum et veluti deliquium pati, ut nonnunquam varietur et tentationum procellis concutiatur, obscuretur,, obruatur, languida fiat. Imo etiam in sanctis haud aliter, quam in ebriis et infantibus, ratio sopiatur et sepeliatur. Sicut in Davide, cum admisit adulterium, et in Petro, cum ter abnegavit Christum, sed tamen nunquam penitus excutitur.“ (L. c. s. 2. q. 7. f. 77. sq.)

PART. III. CAP. XII. Quenstedtius: ,,Attributa sive adjuncta, alia electionis, alia electorum sunt. Electionis attributa sunt: 1. aeternitas; Matth. 25, 34.: ,Possidete regnum paratum vobis a mundi constitutione.‘ Eph. 1, 4.: ,Elegit nos in ipso ante constitutionem mundi.‘ cf. 2 Tim. 1, 9. 2 Thess. 13. 2. Particularitas; Matth. 20, 16.: ,Multi vocati, pauci electi.‘ Immutabilitas; 2 Tim. 2, 19.: ,Eirmum stat fundamentum Dei, habens signaculum hoc: Novit Dominus, qui sunt sui.‘ . . Attributa electorum sunt: 1. paucitas; Matth. 20, 16. 22, 14.: ,Multi vocati, pauci electi.‘ 2. Possibilitas excutiendi ad tempus totaliter gratiam inhabU tantem. Hinc David Ps. 51,13.: ,Spiritum S. tuum ne auferas a me.‘ 1 Cor. 10,12.: ,Qui sibi videtur stare, videat, ne cadat.‘ 3. Certitudo electionis; Luc. 10, 20.: ,Gaudete, quod nomina vestra scripta sint in coelis.‘ cf. Rom. 8, 38. sq. 2 Tim. 4, 8., ex parte hominis non absoluta, sed ordinata; Phil. 2, 12.: ,Dilecti, cum metu et tremore operamini vestram salutem. 4. Persistentia in fide finalis; Matth. 10, 22.: ,Qui perseverat usque ad finem, salvus erit.‘ cf. Apoc. 11,10.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 20. sq. f. 29. sq.)

Formula Concordiae: ,,Es gehöret auch dies zu fernerer Erklärung und heilsamem Brauch der Lehre von der Vorsehung Gottes zur Seligkeit: weil allein die Auserwählten selig werden, deren Namen geschrieben stehen im Buch des Lebens, wie man das wissen, woraus und wobei 'erkennen köpne, welche die Auserwählten sind, die sich dieser Lehre zum Trost annehmen können und sollen. Und hievon sollen wir nicht urtheilen nach unserer Vernunft, auch nicht nach dem Gesetz, oder aus einigem äusserlichem Schein; auch sollen wir uns nicht unterstehen, den heimlichen verborgenen Abgrund göttlicher Vorsehung zu forschen, sondern auf den geoffenbarten Willen Gottes Acht geben. Denn,er hat uns offenbaret und wissen lassen das Geheimniss seines Willens, und hat dasselbige hervor gebracht durch Christum, d$ss es gepredigt werde‘, Eph. 1, 9. f. 2 Tim. 1, 9. f. Dasselbige aber wird uns also geoffenbaret, wie Paulus spricht Röm. 8, 29. f.: ,Die Gott versehen, erwählet und verordnet hat, die hat er auch berufen.‘ Nun berufet Gott nicht ohne Mittel, sondern durch das Wort, wie er denn,befohlen hat, zu predigen Busse und Vergebung der Sünden‘. . . Und solchen Beruf Gottes, so durch die Predigt des Worts geschieht, sollen wir für kein Spiegelfechten halten, sondern wissen, dass dadurch Gott seinen Willen offenbart, dass er in denen, die er also beruft, durchs Wort wirken wolle, dass sie erleuchtet, bekehrt und selig werden mögen. Denn das Wort, dadurch wir berufen werden, ist ein Amt des Geistes, das den Geist gibt oder dadurch der Geist gegeben wird, 2 Cor. 3, 8., und eine Kraft Gottes selig zu machen, Röm. 1, 16. Und weil der Heilige Geist durchs Wort kräftig sein, stärken, Kraft und Vermögen geben will, so ist Gottes Wille, dass wir das Wort annehmen, glauben und demselben folgen sollen. Daher werden die Auserwählten also beschrieben Joh. 10, 27. f.: ,Meine Schafe hören meine Stimme, und ich kenne sie, und sie folgen mir, und ich gebe ihnen das ewige Leben‘; und Eph. 1, 11. 13.: ,Die nach dem Vorsatz verordnet sind zum Erbtheil, die hören‘ das Evangelium, glauben an Christum, beten und danken, werden geheiligt in der Liebe, haben Hoffnung, Geduld und Trost im Kreuz, Röm. 8, 25.; und ob dies alles gleich sehr schwach in ihnen ist, haben sie doch Hunger und Durst nach der Gerechtigkeit, Matth. 5, 6. Also,gibt der Geist Gottes den Auserwählten Zeugniss, dass sie Kinder Gottes sind, und da sie nicht wissen, was sie beten sollen, wie sichs gebührt, vertritt er sie mit unaussprechlichem Seufzen‘, Röm. 8, 16. 26. So zeugt auch die heilige Schrift, dass Gott, der uns berufen hat, so getreu sei, wenn er das gute Werk in uns angefangen hat, dass ers auch bis ans Ende erhalten und vollführen wolle, wo wir uns nicht selbst von ihm abkehren, sondern das angefangene Wesen bis ans Ende fest behalten, dazu er denn seine Gnade verheissen hat, 1 Cor. 1, 9. Phil. 1, 6. 2 Petr. 3, 9. Ebr. 3. Mit diesem geoffen-

barten Willen Gottes sollen wir uns bekümmern, demselben folgen und uns desselben beiieissigen, weil der Heilige Geist durchs Wort, dadurch er uns beruft, Gnade, Kraft und Vermögen dazu verleihet, und den Abgrund der verborgenen Vorsehung Gottes nicht forschen, wie Luc. 13,24. geschrieben, da einer fraget: ,Herr, meinest du, dass wenig selig werden?‘ antwortet Christus: ,Ringet ihr darnach, dass ihr durch die enge Pforte eingehet.‘ . . Derhalben auch Christus die Verheissung des.Evangelii nicht allein lässt ingemein vortragen, sondern dieselbige durch die Sacramente, die er als Siegel der Verheissung angehänget, versiegelt und damit einem jeden Gläubigen insonderheit bestätigt. Darum behalten wir auch, wie die Augsburgische Confession articulo 11. sagt, dic Privatabsolution, und lehren, dass es Gottes Gebot sei, dass wir solcher Absolution glauben, und für gewiss halten sollen, dass wir so wahrhaftig, wenn wrir dem Wort der Absolution glauben, Gott versöhnt werden, als hätten wir eine Stimme vom Himmel gehört, wie (lie Apologia diesen Artikel erkläret; welcher Trost uns ganz und gar genommen, wenn wir nicht aus dem Beruf, der durchs Wort und durch die Sacramente geschieht, von Gottes Willen gegen uns schliessen sollten.“ (Concordia, p. 709—712.)

Lutherus: ,,Initio quidem statim voluit Deus occurrere huic curiositati. Sic enim suam voluntatem et consilium proposuit: Ego tibi praescientiam et praedestinationem egregie manifestabo; sed non ista via rationis et sapientiae carnalis, sicut tu imaginaris. Sic faciam: Ex Deo non revelato fiam revelatus et tamen idem Deus manebo. Ego incarnabor vel mittam Filium meum; hic morietur pro tuis peccatis et resurget a mortuis. Atque ita implebo desiderium tuum, ut possis scire, an sis praedestinatus, an non? ,Ecce, hic est Filius meus, hunc audito‘ (Matth. 17, 5.), hunc adspice jacentem in praesepio, in matris gremio, pendentem in cruce. Vide, quid is faciat, quid loquatur. Ibi me certo apprehendes. ,Qui enim me videt‘, inquit Christus (Joh. 14, 9.), ,videt et Patrem ipsum.‘ Si hunc audieris et in nomine ejus baptizatus fueris et diliges verbum ejus, tum certo es praedestinatus et certus de tua salute. Si vero maledicis aut contemnis verbum, tum es damnatus, quia, qui non credit, condemnatur. Alias cogitationes et vias rationis aut carnis occidito, quia Deus eas detestatur. Id unum age, ut suscipias Filium, ut placeat in corde tuo Christus in sua nativitate, miraculis et cruce. Ibi enim est liber vitae, in quo scriptus es. . .


### On Predestination and Reprobation: For God did not descend from heaven to make you uncertain about predestination,…

For God did not descend from heaven to make you uncertain about predestination, or to teach you to despise the Sacraments, absolution, and the remaining divine ordinances. Rather, He instituted them to render you most certain, and to take away the disease of doubt from your soul, so that you would not only believe with your heart, but also look with your carnal eyes and touch with your hands. Why, therefore, do you reject these things and complain that you do not know whether you are predestined? You have the Gospel, you are baptized, you have absolution, you are a Christian, and yet you doubt, and say that you do not know whether you believe or not, or whether you hold as true those things which are preached about Christ in the Word and Sacraments. ...

God says to you: Behold, you have My Son, hear and accept Him. If you do this, you are now certain of your faith and your salvation. But I do not know, you will say, whether I shall remain in the faith. Nevertheless, accept the present promise and predestination, and do not inquire more curiously into the hidden counsels of God. If you believe in the revealed God and receive His Word, 'little by little He will also reveal the hidden God,' because 'he who sees Me, sees the Father also' (John 14:9). He who rejects the Son loses the unrevealed God along with the revealed God. But if you adhere to the revealed God with firm faith, so that your heart feels that you will not lose Christ, even if you were stripped of everything, then you are most certainly predestined, and you will understand the hidden God; indeed, you already understand Him in the present." (On Gen. 26:9. See Exegetical Latin Works, Erlangen Ed., Vol. VI, 293—296.)

The same: "Hear the incarnate Son, and predestination will offer itself of its own accord. Staupitz used to console me with these words: 'Why do you torture yourself with these speculations? Look at the wounds of Christ and the blood shed for you; from these, predestination will shine forth.' Therefore, the Son of God must be heard, who was sent into the flesh and appeared for this purpose, that He might destroy this work of the devil and make you certain of predestination. And therefore He says to you: 'You are my sheep, because you hear my voice. No one shall snatch you out of my hands.' (John 10:28-29). ...

I wished to admonish and teach these things studiously and accurately, because after my death many will bring forth my books into the public sphere, and from them will confirm all manner of errors and their own delusions. I wrote, among other things, that all things are absolute and necessary, but at the same time I added that the revealed God must be looked upon, just as we sing in the Psalm: *Er heisst Jesus Christ, der Herr Zebaoth, und ist kein ander Gott* (He is called Jesus Christ, the Lord of Sabaoth, and there is no other God); and very often elsewhere. But they will pass over all these passages and will seize only upon those concerning the hidden God. You, therefore, who now hear me, remember that I have taught this: that one must not inquire into the predestination of the hidden God, but must acquiesce in that which is revealed through the calling and through the ministry of the Word. For there you can be certain of your faith and salvation, and say: 'I believe in the Son of God, who said: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life" (John 3:36).' Therefore, in Him there is no condemnation or wrath, but the good pleasure of God the Father. I have protested these same things elsewhere in my books, and now I also deliver them with my living voice; therefore, I am excused." (L.c. p. 296 sq. 300.)

The same: "Although the calling and election is strong enough in itself, it is nevertheless not strong and firm for you, because you are not yet certain that it concerns you. Therefore, Peter wants us to make such calling and election firm by means of good works. ...

St. Peter means that one should not let faith rest and lie still, because it is so constituted that it becomes more and more powerful through activity and exercise, until it becomes certain of the calling and election and cannot fail. And here a goal is also set as to how one should deal with predestination. There are many frivolous spirits who have not felt much of faith; they fall into this, strike against the top, and concern themselves first with this matter, and want to fathom through reason whether they are predestined, so that they may become certain of where they stand. Desist from that quickly; it is not the way to do it. But if you want to become certain, you must arrive at it through the way that St. Peter proposes to you here. If you take another way, you have already failed; your own experience must teach you this. When faith is well exercised and driven, you will finally become certain of the matter, that you do not fail." (Exposition of the Second Epistle of St. Peter. 1524. IX, 846 sq.)

The same: "If your sin and unworthiness assail you, and it occurs to you on that account that you are not provided for by God, or that the number of the elect is small and the multitude of the ungodly is great, and you are terrified by the dreadful examples of divine wrath and judgment, etc., then do not dispute for long why God does this or that in such a way and not otherwise, when He could well do otherwise, etc. Also, do not presume to fathom the abyss of divine providence with your reason, otherwise you will certainly go astray over it, and either despair or cast yourself into reckless abandon; but hold fast to the promise of the Gospel. It will teach you that Christ, the Son of God, came into the world to bless all nations on earth—that is, to redeem them from sin and death, and to make them righteous and blessed—and that He did this by the command and gracious will of God, the heavenly Father, who so loved the world that He gave His only Son, so that all who believe in Him should not perish but have eternal life, John 3. If you follow this advice—namely, if you first acknowledge that you are by nature a child of wrath, guilty of eternal death and damnation, from which

no creature, neither human nor angelic, can save you, and you then grasp God’s promise, believe that He is a merciful, truthful God who faithfully keeps (out of pure grace, without any of our doing or merit) what He has spoken, and has therefore sent Christ, His only Son, that He should make satisfaction for your sin and bestow upon you His innocence and righteousness, and finally also deliver you from all manner of distress and death, then do not doubt that you belong to the little flock of the elect, etc. When one treats of providence in such a way (as St. Paul is also accustomed to do), it is exceedingly comforting. Whoever undertakes it otherwise, to him it is terrifying.” (Exposition of the 1st Epistle of St. Peter. Erlangen Ed. Vol. LII, p. 6.)

The same: “Here a limit must be set for the insolent and arrogant spirits who first bring their reason to this matter and begin at the top; to search beforehand into the abyss of divine providence and to trouble themselves in vain as to whether they are provided for. Such must needs cast themselves down, so that they either despair or throw themselves into the free-for-all. But you, follow this epistle in its order; occupy yourself first with Christ and the Gospel, that you may recognize your sin and His grace; thereafter, struggle with sin, as the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th chapters have taught here. Thereafter, when you have come to the eighth chapter, under the cross and suffering, that will rightly teach you the providence in the 9th, 10th, and 11th chapters, how comforting it is. For without suffering, the cross, and the agonies of death, one cannot treat of providence without harm and secret wrath against God. Therefore, Adam must first be well dead before he suffers this thing and drinks this strong wine. Therefore, take heed that you do not drink wine when you are still an infant. Every doctrine has its measure, time, and age.” (Preface to the Epistle to the Romans. XIV, 125 sq.)

The same: “In the disputation concerning providence, it is useful and best to begin at the bottom, at Christ; thus one finds and hears the Father; for all who have begun at the top have broken their necks.” (Table Talk. XXII, 1289.)

The same: “And it is not commanded to ask beforehand whether we are elected; rather, it is enough that we know: whoever finally perseveres in his repentance and faith, he is certainly elected and saved, as Christ says: ‘Blessed are those who persevere to the end.’” (Opinion of the year 1536. X, 2001.)

U. Rhegius: “We should not treat of the deep abyss of divine providence with human curiosity, but do what God bids and commands us, namely, to believe the Gospel; whoever believes it is one of the elect, Rom. 8, John 8. Whoever does not yet believe it is either not of the number of the elect, or the hour of his calling has not yet come. Whoever does not wish to fall horribly here, like Lucifer, should remain uninvolved with the secret judgments of God.” (Formulae caute loquendi. Ed. Feustking. p. 38.)

Chemnitius: “I will only add with what various artifices the Papists attempt to mock the passage in Rom. 8. Pighius, following Thomas, says that Paul is speaking there only of the certainty of his own salvation, which he had from a special revelation; and that he does not affirm that every believer in Christ has such certainty; but this is manifestly false. For Paul speaks in the plural in that whole sentence, and lays the foundations of that certainty: Christ died, nay, He sits at the right hand of the Father interceding for us. Andradius, therefore, seeing that these mockeries cannot stand, says that the word πεπεισμαι signifies not a certain confidence, but a probable estimation or persuasion, which nevertheless could be mistaken, because it is so used in certain places of Scripture. But it is also used for a certain, firm, and indubitable persuasion, 2 Tim. 1: ‘I am certain...’” PART III. CAP. XII. am, because He is able to keep that which I have committed unto Him.’ And from this theme, πειθότης [persuasion/certainty] is deduced. The question now is, which meaning fits the passage in Romans 8? The entire context all but cries out: ‘If God be for us, who can be against us? How shall He not with Him also freely give us all things? Who shall lay anything to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died. Who shall separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord? Shall tribulation, or the sword? etc. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him that loved us.’ And after these things, the word πέπεισμαι [I am persuaded]. It is manifest, however, that he is (as they say) raving with reason who would attempt to explain that entire discourse as referring to doubt. And among the Papists themselves, no one has hitherto dared to say that Paul in Romans 8 was uncertain and doubting even of his own salvation, except that the impudence of the Jesuits attempted this, which Andradius strove not only to equal but even to surpass.” (Exam. Trid. concil. Ed. Genev. f. 169. a.)

Latin:

Deus enim non ideo de coelo descendit, ut faceret te incertum de praedestinatione, ut doceret te contemnere sacramenta, absolutionem et reliquas ordinationes divinas. Imo ideo instituit, ut redderet te certissimum, et auferret morbum dubitationis ex animo tuo, ut non solum corde crederes, sed etiam oculis carnalibus adspiceres et manibus palpares. Cur igitur rejicis ista et quereris, te nescire, an sis praedestinatus? Tu habes evangelium, es baptizatus, habes absolutionem, es Christianus, et tamen dubitas, ac dicis, te nescire, utrum credas, an non, num pro veris habeas, quae de Christo in verbo et sacramentis praedicantur. . .

Deus dicit tibi: En, habes Filium meum, hunc audias et acceptes. Id si facis, jam certus es de fide et salute tua. Sed nescio, inquies, an maneam in fide. Attamen praesentem promissionem et praedestinationem suscipe, et non inquiras curiosius de arcanis Dei consiliis. Si credis in Deum revelatum et recipis verbum ejus,paulatim etiam absconditum Deum revelabit, quia, ,qui me videt, videt et Patrem‘, Joh. 14, 9. Qui Filium rejicit, amittit cum revelato Deo etiam non revelatum. Si autem firma fide revelato Deo adhaeseris, ita ut cor tuum sic sentiat, te non amissurum Christum, etiamsi omnibus spoliatus fueris, tum certissime praedestinatus es, et absconditum Deum intelliges, imo jam de praesenti intelligis.“ (Ad Gen. 26, 9. Vid. exeget. opp. lat. Erlang. T. VI, 293—296.)

Idem: ,,Audi Filium incarnatum et sponte se offeret praedestinatio. Staupitius his verbis me consolabatur: Cur istis speculationibus te 38 Baieri Comp. ed. Walther, IU. PART. III. CAP. XII. crucias? Intuere vulnera Christi et sanguinem pro te fusum; ex istis fulgebit praedestinatio. Audiendus igitur est Filius Dei, qui missus est in carnem et ideo apparuit, ut hoc opus diaboli dissolvat et certum te faciat de praedestinatione. Ideoque tibi dicit: Tu es ovis mea, quia audis vocem meam. ,Nemo rapiet te ex manibus meis.‘ (Joh. 10, 29.). .

Haec studiose et accurate sic monere et tradere volui, quia post meam mortem multi meos libros proferent in medium, et inde omnis generis errores et deliria sua confirmabunt. Scripsi autem,inter reliqua, esse omnia absoluta et necessaria, sed simul addidi, quod aspiciendus sit Deus revelatus, sicut in psalmo canimus: Er heisst Jesus Christ, der Herr Zebaoth, und ist kein ander Gott, Jesus Christus est Dominus Zebaoth, nec est alius Deus; et alias saepissime. Sed istos locos omnes transibunt et eos tantum' arripient de Deo abscondito. Vos igitur, qui nunc me auditis, memineritis, me hoc docuisse, non esse inquirendum de praedestinatione Dei absconditi, sed ea acquiescendum esse, quae revelatur per vocationem et per ministerium verbi. Ibi enim potes de fide et salute tua certus esse, ac dicere: Ego credo in Filium Dei, qui dixit: ,Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam/ (Joh. 3, 36.) Ergo in eo non est damnatio aut ira, sed beneplacitum Dei Patris. Haec eadem autem alibi quoque in libris meis protestatus sum, et nunc etiam viva voce trado; ideo sum excusatus.“ (L. c. p. 296. sq. 300.)

Idem: ,,Wiewohl der Beruf und die Erwählung vor sich stark genug ist, so ist sie doch nicht bei dir stark und fest, weil du noch nicht gewiss bist, dass sie dich betreffe. Darum will Petrus, dass wir uns solchen Beruf und Erwählung mit guten Werken fest machen. . .

Das meinet nun St. Petrus, dass man den Glauben nicht soll lassen ruhen und stille liegen, weil er also geschickt ist, dass er von Treiben und Ueben immer mehr und mehr kräftig wird, so lange bis er der Berufung und Erwählung gewiss wird und nicht fehlen kann. Und hier ist auch ein Ziel gesteckt, wie man mit der Versehung handeln soll. Es sind viel leichtfertige Geister, die nicht viel vom Glauben gefühlet haben; die fallen herein, stossen oben an und bekümmern sich zum ersten mit diesem Ding und wollen durch die Vernunft ergründen, ob sie versehen sind, auf dass sie gewiss werden, woran sie seien. Davon stehe nur bald ab, es ist nicht der Griff dazu. Willst du aber gewiss werden, so musst du durch den Weg dazu kommen, den dir hier St. Petrus vorschlägt. Nimmst du einen andern vor dich, so hast du schon gefehlet; es muss dichs‘ deine eigne Erfahrung lehren. Wenn der Glaube wohl geübt und getrieben wird, so wirst du zuletzt der Sache gewiss, dass du nicht fehlest.“ (Ausl, der andern Ep. St. Petri. 1524. IX, 846. sq.)

Idem: ,,Fichtet dich deine Sünde und Unwürdigkeit an und fället dir darüber ein, du seiest von Gott nicht versehen, item, die Zahl der Auserwählten sei klein, der Haufe der Gottlosen gross, und erschrickest über den greulichen Exempeln göttliches Zorens und Gerichts u. s. w., so disputire nicht lange, warum Gott dies oder jenes also mache und nicht anders, so er doch wohl könnte u. s. w. Auch unterstehe dich nicht, den Abgrund göttlicher Versehung mit der Vernunft zu erforsehen, sonst wirst du gewiss drüber irre, verzweifelst entweder, oder schlägest dich gar in die freie Schanz; sondern halt dich an die Verheissung des Evangelii, die wird dich lehren, dass Christus, Gottes Sohn, in die Welt kommen sei, dass er alle Völker auf Erden segnen, das ist, von Sünde und Tod erlösen, gerecht und selig machen sollt, und dass er solches aus Befehl und gnädigem Willen Gottes, des himmlischen Vaters, gethan habe, der die Welt also geliebet hat, dass er seinen einigen Sohn gab, auf dass alle, die an ihn gläuben, nicht verloren werden, sondern das ewige Leben haben, Joh. 3. Folgest du dem Rath, nämlich, erkennest du zuvor, dass du ein Kind des Zorens von Natur bist, des ewigen Todes und Verdammniss schuldig, daraus

dich keine Kreatur, weder menschlich, noch englisch, erretten könne, und ergreifest darnach Gottes Verheissung, gläubest, dass er ein barmherziger, wahrhaftiger Gott sei, der treulich halte (aus lauter Gnade, ohn alle unser Zuthun und Verdienst), was er geredt habe, und habe darum Christum, seinen einigen Sohn, gesandt, dass er für deine Sünde sollt genugthun und dir seine Unschuld und Gerechtigkeit schenken, dich endlich auch von allerlei Noth und Tod erlösen, so zweifei nicht daran, du gehörest unter das Häuflein der Erwählten u. s. w. Wenn man auf solche Weise (wie denn S. Paulus auch pfleget) die Versehung handlet, ist sie über die Massen tröstlich. Wers anders fürnimmt, dem ist sie Schrecklich.“ (Die 1. Ep. S. Petrus ausgel. Ed. Erlang. P. LII. p. 6.)

Idem: ״Hier ist den freveln und hochfahrenden Geistern ein Mal zu stecken, die ihren Verstand am ersten hieher führen und oben anheben; zuvor den Abgrund göttlicher Versehung zu forschen und vergeblich damit sich bekümmern, ob sie versehen sind. Die müssen sich denn selbst stürzen, dass sie entweder verzagen, oder sich in die freie Schanze schlagen. Du aber folge dieser Epistel in ihrer Ordnung, bekümmere dich zuvor mit Christo und dem Evangelio, dass du deine Sünde und seine Gnade erkennest; darnach mit der Sünde streitest, wie hier das 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. Kapitel gelehret haben. Darnach, wenn du in das achte Kapitel kommen bist, unter das Kreuz und Leiden, das wird dich recht lehren die Versehung im 9.10. und 11. Kapitel, wie tröstlich sie sei. Denn ohne Leiden, Kreuz und Todesnöthen kann man die Vorsehung nicht ohne Schaden und heimlichen Zorn wider Gott handeln. Darum muss Adam zuvor wohl todt sein, ehe er dies Ding leide und den starken Wein trinke. Darum siehe dich vor, dass du nicht Wein trinkest, wenn du noch ein Säugling bist. Ein jegliche Lehre hat ihre Masse, Zeit und Alter.“ (Vorr. zum Br. an d. Römer. XIV, 125. sq.)

Idem: ״In der Disputation von der Versehung ists nützlich und das Beste, unten, an Christo, anfahen, so findet und höret man den Vater; denn alle, die oben angefangen haben, die haben den Hals, gestürzt.“ (Tischreden. ,XXII, 1289.)

Idem: ״Und ist nicht befohlen, vorhin zu fragen, ob wir auserwählt sind; sondern es ist genug, dass wir wissen, wer endlich verharret in seiner Busse und Glauben, der ist gewisslich auserwählt und selig, wie Christus spricht: ,Selig sind die, so beharren bis an das Ende.‘ “ (Bedenken vom J. 1536. X, 2001.)

U. Rhegius: ״Wir sollen den tiefen Abgrund göttlicher Versehung nicht mit menschlichem Eürwitz handeln, sondern thun, was uns Gott heisst und befiehlet, nämlich dem Evangelio gläuben; wer ihm gläubt, der ist der Erwählten einer, Röm. 8. Joh. 8. Wer ihm noch nicht gläubt, der ist entweder nicht aus der Zahl der Auserwählten, oder aber es ist die Stunde seines Berufs noch nicht kommen. Wer hie nicht greulich fallen will, wie Lucifer, der soll mit den heimliehen Gerichten Gottes unverworren bleiben.“ (Formulae caute loquendi. Ed. Feustking. p. 38.)

Chemnitius: ״Illud tantum addam, quam variis artificiis locum Rom. 8. ludificare conentur pontificii. Pighius exThoma dicit, Paulum ibi tantum de suae salutis certitudine, quam ex peculiari revelatione habuerit, loqui; non vero affirmare, omnem Christi fidelem ejusmodi certitudinem habere; sed hoc manifeste falsum est. Paulus enim in tota illa sententia in plurali loquitur, et fundamenta illius certitudinis ponit: Christus mortuus est, imo sedet ad dexteram Patris interpellans pro nobis. Andradius igitur videns, has ludificationes non posse consistere, dicit, verbqm πεπεισμαι significare non certam fiduciam, sed verisimilem existimationem seu persuasionem, quae tamen falli possit, quia in quibusdam Scripturae locis ita usurpetur. Atqui usurpatur etiam pro certa, firma et indubitata persuasione, 2 Tim. 1.: ,Certus PART. ΙΠ. CAP. XII. sum, quod potens est depositum meum servare.‘ Et ab hoc themate 7τε7τοί&ησίς deducitur. Quaestio jam est, utra significatio conveniat loco Rom. 8. Illud vero totus contextus tantum non clamat: ,Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Quomodo non omnia cum Eilio nobis donaret? Quis accusabit, quis condemnabit? Deus justificat, Christus mortuus est. Quis separabit nos a caritate Dei, quae est in Christo Jesu, Domino nostro? Num periculum, num gladius? etc. Imo in his omnibus plus quam vincimus per eum, qui dilexit nos.‘ Et post haec verbum πέπεισμαι. Manifestum autem est, eum cum ratione (quod dicitur) insanire, qui totam illam orationem de dubitatione conaretur explicare. Et inter ipsos pontificios nemo hactenus ausus fuit dicere, Paulum Rom. 8. de sua etiam salute incertum dubitare, nisi quod Jesuitarum impudentia hoc tentavit, quam Andradius non aequare tantum, sed et superare contendit.“ (Exam. Trid. concil. Ed. Genev. f. 169. a.)


### On Predestination and Reprobation: The same: “Fourthly, they also object with sentences concerning perseverance

The same: “Fourthly, they also object with sentences concerning perseverance. That even if believers are certain of present grace, yet no one is certain whether he will persevere to the end. And because only those who persevere to the end are saved, therefore there cannot be certain assurance of the salvation of believers. Resp.: That many do not persevere, but fall from grace, both Scripture and experience teach. But this happens not from there and for that reason, as if God were unwilling to preserve to the end those believers whom He once received into grace; but it happens because many, through security, diffidence, and the works of the flesh, cast out the Holy Spirit and shake off faith. Therefore, men are not to be taught that, however they conduct themselves, they cannot fall from the grace of God. For it is written in Romans 11: ‘If thou continue in His goodness.’ Hebrews 3: ‘If we hold the beginning of our confidence steadfast unto the end.’ But they are to be admonished to mortify the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit and to cling firmly to Christ by faith, and to be united to Him more and more through the use of the Word and Sacraments, and to ask of God the gift of perseverance; and let them struggle, lest by the petulance of the flesh they shake off the gift of perseverance. And in this way, they ought not to doubt concerning perseverance, but to conclude, according to the promises of Philippians 1: ‘He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.’ For we have been called to the eternal fellowship of Christ, not so that He might soon cast away again those whom He has joined to Himself, but (as He says) ‘they shall never perish.’ ‘Neither shall any man pluck them out of My hand.’ 1 Corinthians 1: ‘Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.’ Thus David says: ‘I shall never be ashamed.’ And John says: ‘These things have I written unto you that ye may know that ye have eternal life.’ Likewise: ‘We know that, when He shall appear, we shall be like Him.’ Romans 8: ‘Who shall separate us? For I am persuaded that neither things present, nor things to come, shall separate us.’ 2 Timothy 4: ‘There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord shall give me at that day.’ Romans 5: ‘We rejoice in hope of the glory of God.’ These sentences manifestly show that the faithful hope of perseverance is not suspended in ambiguous doubt between heaven and earth.” (Exam. Trid. concil. Ed. Genev. f. 172. b.)

The same: “It is also certain that everything which God has foreseen and knows cannot be otherwise, nor can it fail. But because such a mystery is hidden from God and reserved for His wisdom, and nothing of it has been revealed to us in the Word—much less have we been commanded to investigate such things through our own thoughts, but have been earnestly restrained from doing so, Romans 11—we should not brood over it with our own thoughts, deductions, and conclusions, but hold to His revealed Word, to which He has directed us; as the same is explained above.” (Handb. 1574. Vid. Frank 1. c. p. 343.)

The Theological Faculty of Leipzig: “We teach that believers can be certain of the grace of God and of eternal salvation, and should not doubt it. On the other hand, the Helmstedt theologians teach that a man cannot be certain of eternal salvation, that he must necessarily doubt his final constancy in faith and his eternal salvation. Saint Paul himself would not have been certain of it in this...”

wesen. Laterm. exerc. de praedest. th. 34. — Refutation: Such doctrine strives against God’s Word, Rom. 8, 2 Tim. 1, destroys the confidence of faith and thus faith itself, and is a truly desperate doctrine, by which, as is taught in the Smalcald Articles concerning power, etc., consciences are robbed of true and certain comfort.” (Kurze Verfassung der reinen Lehre. See Thesauri consil. appendix nova. Ed. Gruebel. f. 19.)

B. Menzerus: “Pistorius. . . now proceeds to argue on p. 197: although that papistic doctrine is by far the most certain (false), nevertheless one must perpetually doubt p. 199 concerning salvation, and no man can be certain of his own salvation; understand from other papists: without special revelation. He brings forward these reasons: 1. because that certainty is not had in the Scriptures, p. 199; 2. because no one can be certain of perseverance unto the end. . .

That the certainty of faith and salvation is had in the Scriptures; and likewise of perseverance unto the end, and that every truly pious person can know for certain that he truly believes in Christ, I shall demonstrate clearly and firmly against the most impudent denial of that antichristian man. Let this be the syllogism: If the evangelical promises concerning the remission of sins made to believers through and for the sake of Christ, and concerning perseverance in faith and the attainment of eternal life, are in every way most certain and most firm and established by divine oath, and confirmed by the sacraments as heavenly seals, and sealed by the Holy Spirit in the souls of the pious, and faith apprehending those promises is the basis and foundation of salvation and a most certain demonstration and knowledge, which overcomes all things, so that nothing can separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus, and for that confidence the faithful are commended, whose examples are proposed to us for imitation; it follows that every Christian, endowed with true faith, ought to be and can be certain of the grace and favor of God, of the remission of sins, of perseverance in faith, and of eternal salvation. But Scripture affirms the former. Therefore, it is necessary that the latter also be true.” (Disp. th. et scholast. p. 288, 290.)

B. Meisnerus: “We maintain that two reefs in particular are to be avoided: 1. doubt, 2. presumption. If you strike against the former, you follow the papists, and eventually you are tormented and despair; striking against the latter, you pass over to the Calvinists and fall into carnal security. Therefore, consider first the infallible promises of God, and thus you will be freed from doubt; afterwards the exhortations and threats, and thus you will be freed from security. Let there be here a mixture of hope and fear, not indeed servile, but filial. For thus, between the Scylla of perpetual doubt and the Charybdis of absolute security, the little boat of faith will hold the middle course, following the cynosure of the Word.”

(Άνθρωπολ. Disp. XVIII. C. b.) Gerhardus: “An absolute certainty of election and salvation is not to be asserted, for thus the doors would be opened to carnal security, nor is uncertainty and doubt to be championed, for thus the doors would be opened to despair, but one must insist upon the middle way; God has made us certain of our salvation, but not secure (understand carnal security).”

(L. c. § 175.) The same: “‘Strive, brethren,’ says Peter 1 Ep. 1, 10, ‘to make your calling and election sure’; therefore, it can certainly be made sure for us.” (L. c. § 208.)

The same: “When the ancients deny that predestination can be known, they speak of knowledge a priori, as it is in the divine mind, without revelation, without the Word, outside of Christ, etc.; meanwhile, it can be known from the Word of God generally, and from its effects specifically; concerning ourselves, by the infallible testimony of faith and the Spirit; concerning other believers, by the probable judgment of charity.”

(Conf. cath. f. 1425.) Balduinus: “Does Paul command us to doubt our salvation when he commands us to work it out with fear and trembling? Phil. 2, 12. Resp.: This is a pernicious dogma of the papists, that no one can be certain of his own salvation.” PART III. CHAP. XII. ... can be certain, or, as the Council of Trent speaks in Session 6, Chapter 9, "that no one can know with the certainty of faith, in which there can be no error, that he has obtained the grace of God," and Chapter 12: "that no one, as long as he lives in this mortality, ought to determine with certainty that he is altogether in the number of the predestined."

Therefore, they call the certainty of our salvation a "rash persuasion."

Bellarmine defends this error at length in *De Justificatione*, Book 3, Chapters 2, 3, 4, 5, and 12, and among other things, he also abuses this Pauline saying for his own purpose: because Paul, in the working out of salvation, exhorts all believers to fear and trembling, therefore no one can be certain of his own salvation.

But in truth, the most holy apostle undoubtedly did not contradict himself. In the Epistle to the Romans 8:38, with great πληροφορία (full assurance) of faith, he writes that he is "certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." How, then, could he here command us to doubt our grace and salvation?

Nor is it for you to say that Paul writes this only concerning his own salvation, and that he had that certainty from a special revelation.

For he writes expressly that we cannot be separated from the love of God—that is, all believers. Nor was there any need for Paul to boast of his own certainty to the Romans; rather, he wished to encourage others by his example and to render them certain of their own salvation. For this reason, he writes that the grace shown to him was for the instruction of those who were to believe in eternal life (1 Tim. 1:16).

Hence, Bernard transfers these words of Paul generally to all believers in Sermon 3 on Pentecost: "Be certain," he says, "that neither death, nor life, nor the other things which the apostle enumerates so manifoldly and boldly, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus."

That he had that certainty from revelation, neither does he himself say, nor can it be proven by any letter. He shows another foundation for his certainty, namely, the doctrine of the Gospel concerning the death and resurrection of Christ, His session at the right hand of the Father, and His intercession for us, from which he infers his own certainty and that of all believers concerning the grace of God and salvation.

But as to why he commends fear and trembling to the Philippians, it must be known that Paul does not understand a servile fear, which flees and dreads God and has no trust in His mercy, but a filial fear, which reveres God as a Father, lest one offend Him in any way. Therefore, he places a barrier against our flesh, lest it rule in us and cast off the grace of God.

Menzerus: ,,Pistorius. . . nunc disputare pergit p. 197.: tametsi doctrina illa papistica longe sit certissima (falsum), tamen perpetuo esse dubitandum p. 199. de salute, et neminem hominum posse esse certum de sua salute; subintellige ex aliis papistis: sine speciali revelatione. At prius affirmat Scriptura. Ergo et posterius ess$ verum necesse est.“ (Disp. th. et scholast. p. 288. 290.)

Quare cogites primum promissiones Dei infallibiles, et sic liberaberis a dubitatione; post exhortationes minasque, et sic liberaberis a securitate. Sit hic mixtura spei et timoris, non quidem servilis, sed filialis. Ita enim inter scyllam perpetuae dubitationis et inter charybdin absolutae securitatis medium tenebit navicula fidei, cynosuram verbi secuta.“ (Άνΰρωπολ. Disp. XVIII. C. b.)

XII. certus esse possit seu, ut concilium Trid. loquitur sess. 6. c. 9., ,quod nullus scire valeat certitudine fidei, cui non potest subesse falsum, se gratiam Dei esse consecutum‘, et c. 12.: ,quod nemo, quamdiu in hac mortalitate vivitur, certo statuere debeat, se omnino esse in numero praedestinatorum.‘
