Quem errorem prolixe defendit Bellarminus 1. 3. de justific. c. 2. 3. 4. 5. 12. et inter caetera hoc quoque dicto Paulino abutitur in rem suam, quia Paulus in operatione salutis hortatur omnes fideles ad timorem et tremorem, ideo neminem de salute sua certum esse posse.

Verum enim vero sanctissimus apostolus haud dubie sibiipsi non contradixit. In ep. Rom. 8, 38. magna πληροφορία fidei scribit, se,certum‘ esse, ,quod neque mors, neque vita, neque angeli, neque principatus, neque virtutes, neque instantia, neque futura, neque fortitudo, neque altitudo, neque profundum, neque creatura alia nos separare possit a caritate Dei, quae est in Christo Jesu, Domino nostro‘; quomodo ergo hic nos dubitare jubeat de gratia et salute nostra?

Neque est, ut dicas, Paulum id de sua tantum salute scribere, illamque certitudinem ex peculiari revelatione habuisse.

Expresse enim scribit, nos a caritate Dei separari non posse, h. e., fideles omnes; neque opus erat, ut Paulus suam certitudinem Romanis jactaret, sed alios suo exemplo animare et de salute sua certos reddere voluit; ideo enim gratiam sibi exhibitam scribit ad informationem eorum, qui credituri essent in vitam aeternam 1 Tim. 1, 16.

Hinc Bernhardus ista verba Pauli in genere ad omnes fideles transfert serm. 3. in Pentec.: ,Sitis certi‘, inquit, ,quia neque mors, neque vita, neque caetera alia, quae apostolus tam multipliciter, quam audacter, enumerat, poterunt nos separare a caritate Dei, quae est in Christo Jesu.‘

Quod autem certitudinem illam ex revelatione habuerit, neque ipse dicit, neque ulla litera probari potest; aliud fundamentum suae certitudinis monstrat, nimirum doctrinam evangelii de morte et resurrectione Christi, de sessione ejus ad dexteram Patris, ejusque pro nobis intercessione, ex quibus infert suam et fidelium omnium de gratia Dei ac salute certitudinem.

Quod autem ad Philippenses nobis timorem et tremorem commendat, sciendum est, Paulum non intelligere timorem servilem, qui Deum fugit et horret, nuilamque de misericordia ejus fiduciam habet, sed timorem filialem, qui reveretur Deum ut Patrem, ne quoquo modo offendat; ideo repagulum injicit carni nostrae, ne dominetur in nobis gratiamque Dei excutiat.


### On Predestination and Reprobation: This fear commended to us by Paul is therefore opposed to

This fear commended to us by Paul is therefore opposed to: 1. Epicurean security, by which faith is suffocated, the Holy Spirit is grieved, and the grace of God is lost; 2. Spiritual pride and arrogance, so that we do not become insolent through trust in our gifts, but depend entirely upon the grace and mercy of God, taking care that we do not fall from it.

Against this, Bellarmine says in *De Justificatione*, Book 3, Chapter 12: "All these things have a place in those who are ignorant of their predestination, but not in those who are most certain of it. For those who are certainly persuaded that they are altogether to be saved cannot fear that they might fall from salvation; indeed, they ought not to fear, if they believe this with the certainty of faith, just as they believe Christ to be God; for by that fear of theirs they would do an injury to faith," and he adds: "The Holy Spirit would be exhorting the elect to infidelity when He exhorts them to the fear of losing salvation."

So says he; these things are true regarding servile fear, in which there is no trust in God, and which makes for mere infidelity. We command that this be absent from believers.

For they have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but the spirit of adoption, in which they cry: Abba, Father (Rom. 8:15).

Filial fear, however, does not lack faith, but is its fruit; for the pious fear and revere God for this reason, lest they lose faith and fall from the grace of God, which happens through works against conscience. Therefore, this fear is always joined with the certainty of faith, because as long as the pious flee mortal sins, they have no reason to doubt the grace of God or their own salvation.

For this reason, we are commanded to serve God in fear and to rejoice with trembling (Ps. 2). The rejoicing is of certainty; the service is of the filial fear of which we speak here.

We therefore reject...

ON PREDESTINATION AND REPROBATION. the Papist dogma of doubt, as pernicious and horrendous, to which are opposed the promises and oaths of God. "For this God has said," says Augustine in Ps. 88, "this He has promised; if that is too little, this He has sworn; because, therefore, the promise is firm not according to our merits, but according to His mercy, no one ought to preach with trepidation about that of which he cannot doubt." (Disp. on ch. 2 of the Ep. to the Philippians, Witteb. 1617. Q. VI. c. 2. sqq.) Brochmand: "Can the elect be rendered infallibly certain concerning their election and their perseverance?" The Arminians, or Belgian Remonstrants, stated what they hold regarding the certainty of salvation in these words, in Article 8 of their opinion on the perseverance of the truly faithful: "How a believer can be certain that he will persevere in the actions of faith, piety, and charity, as it behooves believers to do, we do not see." See the synodal acts of the Remonstrants of Dordrecht, pp. 176, 177, et seq. The opinion of the Papists does not differ much from the assertion of the Arminians; for the Papists teach that no one, apart from a special revelation from God, can be certain in this life whether he is among the number of the elect. Let the Council of Trent, Session 6, Chapters 12 and 13, be read. Against this most dangerous dogma of the Arminians and Papists, we oppose various arguments:

1. This doubting of salvation accuses God of lying; for as it is in 1 John 5:10 et seq.: "Whoever does not believe God, makes Him a liar." But God certainly promises eternal salvation to believers (John 3:18; 1 John 5:11, 12; 1 Pet. 1:5), and indeed with an oath interposed (John 5:24; Ezek. 3:11; Heb. 6:17).

2. It fights diametrically against the end of the revealed doctrine concerning eternal predestination to salvation, which is that we might be certain of our salvation. The conclusion of Romans 8:28 to the end of the chapter demonstrates this. These words of Paul in Romans 11:29 also prove this very thing: "The gifts and the calling of God are άμεταμέλητα, that is, those of which God does not repent." The following sayings of the divine Scriptures also contribute to this: 2 Tim. 2:19: "The solid foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are His." John 10:27, 28: "No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands, nor shall they perish forever." Phil. 1:6: "He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ." And ch. 2:13: "It is God who works in you both to will and to perform." 1 Pet. 1:5: "You are kept by the power of God unto salvation." 1 John 3:19, 20: "In this we know that we are of the truth, and we shall πείσομεν τας καρόίας ήμών before Him. For if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things."

3. Doubting of salvation draws its origin from the corruption of nature, and it displeases God in the highest degree, and is a sign of a man who is hastening to eternal destruction. James 1:6, 7: "Let a man ask in faith μηδέν δίακρινόμενος; for he who doubts is like a wave of the sea driven and tossed by the wind. Therefore, let not that man think that he will receive anything from the Lord." 2 Cor. 13:5: "Examine yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless indeed you are reprobates."

4. The pious, who are proposed to us in the sacred code for imitation, are commended for their confidence, which is extremely opposed to the doubting of salvation. The sacred page is a witness to this: Matt. 8:8, 9, 10 et seq., and ch. 15:22, 28; Rom. 4:18; Heb. 11 throughout the whole chapter. Therefore, let the Papist and Arminian doubting of salvation be gone, and let it keep its affairs to itself. But the Papists, just as the Arminians, defend their doubting of salvation in various ways. The sum of the arguments by which the authors cited above fight comes down to this: 1. That the Scriptures warn us everywhere that we should always tremble because of the uncertainty of salvation. Prov. 27:1: "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring forth." And ch. 28:14: "Blessed is the man who is always fearful." Eccles. 9:1: "A man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred." Rom. 11:20: "You stand by faith; do not be haughty, but fear, lest He also not spare you." 1 Cor. 10:12: "Let him who stands take heed lest he fall." Phil. 2:12: "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling." Rev. 3:11: "Hold fast what you have, that no one may take your crown." 2 John 8: "Look to yourselves, that you do not lose those things which you have worked for." 2. Certainty... PART III. CHAPTER XII. [The election and salvation] depend upon the certainty of perseverance in faith in Christ and obedience to the commandments of God, Matt. 10:22; 19:17. But this perseverance in faith and good works is mutable and entirely uncertain, Rom. 10:20; 1 Cor. 10:12; Rev. 3:11; 2 John 8. 3. This certainty, which we urge, is nowhere found to be taught in the Scriptures. 4. Scripture itself deters us from this persuasion of certainty by those passages in which the difficulty of being saved is exaggerated, Matt. 7:13, 14; Acts 14:22; 1 Pet. 4:18. We shall append a solid, yet succinct, solution to these arguments, which are specious at first glance. 1. That the pious ought to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling, I do not unwillingly concede; but that one should infer from this that they must doubt their salvation, I flatly deny. And so that no one may fail to understand that this inference is truly denied, I advise that one remember that Scripture speaks of a twofold fear. One is servile, which is a trepidation arising from the consciousness of unremitted sin and the just divine judgment, joined with flight from and hatred of God. This fear, as it is certainly not that of the elect, so it can by no means consist with the confidence of obtaining salvation, Rom. 8:15. The other fear is merely filial, which is a solicitous dread of offending God and a serious zeal for avoiding falls, joined with humility, religious solicitude, and love and invocation of God. This fear, just as it is proper to the pious, Phil. 2:12; Prov. 1:7; Ps. 128:1, so it has an immovable certainty of salvation joined with it. Hear the Scriptures: "You have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear," Rom. 8:15. "I will give them shepherds who will feed them, and they shall not fear," Jer. 23:4. "Do not fear, little flock," Luke 12:32. Nor is there any weight to the insistence of Bellarmine, who urges that those who are certain of their salvation have no need to fear, and furthermore, that those who are undoubtedly certain of their salvation have no need of the spurs of exhortations to piety and perseverance in faith and holy works. Trifles! Since Scripture teaches both, both must be believed with undoubted faith. Paul was certain of his election, Rom. 8:28 (to the end of the chapter), 2 Tim. 1:12, and yet he worked out his salvation with singular solicitude, 1 Cor. 9:27. Nor is there any reason for Pistorius to object that Paul did not propose his own example to others for imitation. For that this is false is taught in 2 Cor. 1:21; 4:13; 1 Tim. 1:16. 2. The Spirit of God shows in plain words that a man can be certain of his perseverance in faith and obedience. Hear Christ in John 6:37: "All that the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will by no means cast out." Hear Paul in Phil. 1:6: "He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ." And 1 Cor. 1:8, 9: "God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of His Son, who will also confirm you to the end, that you may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ." And Heb. 13:5: "I will never leave you nor forsake you, so that we may boldly say: The Lord is my helper; I will not fear. What can man do to me?" Hear Peter, 1 Pet. 1:5: "We are kept by the power of God through faith for salvation." And it is diligently to be noted that the cited passages testify that the certainty of our salvation is built not upon our own powers, but upon the most certain promise, the efficacious operation, and the faithful guardianship of God. Whence you may also safely conclude that those who are undoubtedly persuaded of their perseverance in faith and the certainty of their salvation rely not upon the foolish judgment of the human mind, but upon the immovable promises of God. 3. We contend that the certainty of salvation, which we urge, is most firmly grounded in the Scriptures. For although the Spirit of God does not say by name that you or I will be saved, yet He affirms in plain speech that all and each who believe in the Son are to be gifted with eternal life, John 3:18, and that God is faithful, by whom we have been called into the fellowship of His Son, who will confirm us to the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 1:8, 9, and that the faithful ought to be certain and most persuaded of this matter, so much so that he who is unwilling to believe God, who certainly promises salvation to those who believe, makes God a liar, 1 John 5:10 ff. 4. That the way which leads to eternal life is obstructed and not so easy to tread, I concede; but to infer from this a vague doubt about salvation is an inference more liberal than is just. For just as the Spirit of God in the cited passages exaggerates the difficulties which [confront] those who...

Latin:

Oppositus ergo est hic timor a Paulo nobis commendatus 1. epicureae securitati, qua fldes suffocatur, Spiritus S. contristatur et gratia Dei deperditur; 2. spirituali superbiae et arrogantiae, ne fiducia donorum insolescamus, sed toti a gratia misericordiaque Dei pendeamus, operam dantes, ne illa excidamus.

Contra haec Bellarminus 1. 3. de justific. c. 12.: ,Haec omnia locum habent in illis, qui praedestinationem suam ignorant, non autem in illis, qui de illa certissimi sunt. Nam qui certo persuasi sunt, se omnino salvandos, non possunt timere, ne excidant salute, imo nec debent timere, si id certo credunt certitudine fidei, quomodo credunt Christum esse Deum; nam isto suo timore injuriam fidei facerent‘, et addit: ,Spiritus S. hortaretur electos ad infidelitatem, cum hortatur ad timorem amittendae salutis.‘

Haec ille; quae vera sunt de timore servili, in quo nulla est fiducia in Deum, quaeque meram facit infidelitatem. Eum a fidelibus abesse jubemus.

Non enim acceperunt spiritum servitutis iterum in timore, sed spiritum adoptionis, in quo clamant: Abba Pater, Rom. 8, 15.

Filialis autem timor non caret fide, sed est fructus ejus; nam ideo timent atque reverentur pii Deum, ne fldem amittant et gratia Dei excidant, quod fit operibus contra conscientiam; semper ergo timor hic conjunctus est cum certitudine fidei, quia, quamdiu pii p.eccata mortalia fugiunt, non habent, cur de gratia Dei aut salute sua dubitent.

Idcirco servire Deo jubemur in timore et exultare cum tremore. Ps. 2. Exultatio est certitudinis, servitus timoris filialis, de quo hic loquimur.

Rejicimus ergo

dogma pontificium de dubitatione, tanquam perniciosum et horrendum, cui opponuntur promissiones et juramenta Dei. ,Hoc enim Deus dixit', inquit Augustinus in Ps. 88., ,hoc promisit; si parum est, hoc juravit; quia ergo non secundum merita nostra, sed secundum illius misericordiam firma est promissio, nemo debet cum trepidatione praedicare, de quo non potest dubitare.'“ (Disp, de cap. 2. ep. ad Philipp. Witteb. 1617. Q. VI. c. 2. sqq.) Brochmandus: ״An de electione et perseverentia sua infallibiliter certi reddi possint electi? Arminiani seu Remonstrantes Belgae, quid statuant de certitudine salutis, his verbis enunciarunt ipsi art. 8. sententiae suae de vere fidelium perseverantia: ,Quomodo vero fidelis', inquiunt, ,certus esse possit, se in fidei, pietatis et caritatis actionibus, ut fideles decet, perseveraturum, non videmus.' Vide acta synodalia Dordr. Remonstr. p. 176.177. sq. Ab Arminianorum assertione non multum abit sententia pontificiorum; pontificii enim docent, neminem citra specialem Dei revelationem posse in hac vita certum esse, utrum ipse sit ex numero electorum. Legatur Concilium Trid. sess. 6. c. 12. 13. Cui Arminianorum et pontificiorum dogmati longe periculosissimo varia opponimus argumenta: 1. Haec dubitatio de salute Deum arguit mendacii; nam ut est 1 Joh. 5, 10. sq.: ,Quicunque non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum.' Deus vero credentibus certo promittit aeternam salutem Joh. 3, 18. 1 Joh. 5, 11. 12. 1 Pet. 1, 5., et quidem juramento interposito Joh. 5, 24. Ezech. 3, 11. Hebr. 6, 17. 2. E diametro pugnat cum fine revelatae doctrinae de praedestinatione aeterna ad salutem, qui est, ut de salute nostra certi simus. Monstrat hoc conclusio Rom. 8, 28. ad finem usque capitis. Hoc ipsum etiam evincunt verba haec Pauli Rom. 11, 29.: ,Dona et vocatio Dei sunt άμεταμέλητα, id est, quorum poenitudine Deus non dudatur. Eodem etiam faciunt haec divinarum litterarum dicta: 2 Tim.2, 19.: ,Solidum stat fundamentum Dei, habens hoc signaculum: novit Dominus, qui sint sui.‘ Joh. 10, 27. 28.: ,Oves meas nemo rapiet e manibus meis, nec peribunt aeternum.‘ Phil. 1,6.: ,Qui coepit in vobis bonum opus, perficiet usque ad diem Jesu Christi.‘ Et c. 2, 13.: ,Deus est, qui efficit in vobis et ut velitis, et ut perficiatis.‘ 1 Petr. 1, 5.: ,Virtute Dei custodiemini ad salutem.‘ 1 Joh. 3, 19. 20.: ,In hoc cognoscimus, quoniam ex veritate sumus et coram ipso πείσομεν τας καρόίας ήμών. Quoniam si reprehenderit nos cor, major est Deus corde nostro, qui novit omnia.‘ 3. Dubitatio de salute ortum trahit e naturae corruptione, et Deo quam maxime displicet, et signum est hominis, qui ad exitium aeternum properat, Jac. 1, 6. 7.: ,Postulet homo in fide μηδέν δίακρινόμενος· 6 γαμ διακρινάμενος similis est fluctui maris a ventis agitato et jactato. Non ergo existimet homo ille, quod accipiat quidquam a Domino.‘ 2 Cor. 13, 15.: ,Vos ipsos tentate, anne sitis in fide, vos ipsos probate. Aniion cognoscitis vosmetipsos, quod sc. Jesus Christus in vobis sit? nisi forte reprobi estis.‘ 4. Pii, qui ad imitandum nobis proponuntur in codice sacro, commendantur a fiducia, dubitationi de salute extreme opposita. Testis est sacra pagina Matth. 8, 8. 9.10. sq. et c. 15, 22. 28. Rom. 4,18. Hebr. 11. per totum caput. Valeat ergo pontificia et Arminiana de salute dubitatio, et res suas sibi habeat. Sed pontificii pariter ac Arminiani variis modis suam de salute dubitationem propugnant. Summa argumentorum, quibus auctores superius citati pugnant, huc redit:

1. Scripturas admonere passim, ut semper trepidemus ob salutis incertitudinem Prov. 27,1.: ,Ne glorieris in crastinum, ignorans, quid superventura pariat dies.‘ Et c. 28, 14.: ,Beatus homo, qui semper est pavidus.‘ Eccles. 9, 1.: ,Nescit homo, an odio, an amore dignus sit/ Rom. 11, 29.: ,Tu per fidem stas, noli altum sapere, sed time, ne et tibi non parcat.' 1 Cor. 10, 12.: ,Qui stat, videat, ne cadat.' Phil. 2, 12.: ,Cum timore et tremore salutem vestram operamini/ Apoc. 3,11.: ,Tene, quod· habes, ne forte alius accipiat coronam tuam/ 2 Joh. 8.: ,Videte, ne perdatis, quae operati estis/ 2. Certitudinem PART.III. CAP. ΧΠ. electionis et salutis pendere a certitudine perseverantiae in fide Christi et obedientia mandatorum Dei, Matth. 10, 22. 19, 17. Hanc autem in fide et operibus bonis perseverantiam mutabilem esse et plane incertam. Rom. 10, 20. 1 Cor. 10, 12. Apoc. 3, 11. 2 Joh. 8.

3. Hanc certitudinem,, quam nos urgemus, in Scripturis nuspiam inveniri tradi,tam.

4. Scripturam ipsam arcere nos ab hac certitudinis persuasione, locis illis, in quibus salvandi difficultas exaggeratur, Matth. 7, 13.

14. Act. 14, 2. 1 Pet. 4, 18. Quorum argumentorum, primo intuitu speciosorum, solidam subjungemus solutionem, sed succinctam. 1. Pios salutem suam cum timore et tremore operari debet, non invitus concedo, sed hinc inferre, dubitandum esse ipsis de salute, plane nego. Et ut nemo non intelligat, vere negari istam illationem, moneo, meminisse Scripturam duplicis timoris, unus est servilis, qui est trepidatio, orta ex conscientia peccati non remissi et justi judicii divini, conjuncta cum fuga et odio Dei. Qui sane timor veluti electorum non est, ita cum fiducia, salutis obtinendae neutiquam consistere potest, Rom. 8, 15. Alter timor est mere filialis, qui est solicitus metus offensae Dei et serium studium vitandi lapsus cum humilitate, religiosa sollicitudine et amore atque invocatione Dei conjunctum. Qui timor quemadmodum piorum proprius est, Phil. 2, 12. Prov. 1, 7. Ps. 128, 1., ita immotam de salute certitudinem conjunctam habet. ' Audi Scripturas. ,Non abcepistis spiritum servitutis ad timorem‘, Rom. 15. ,Dabo eis pastores, qui pascent eas, et non timebunt‘, Jer. 23, 4. ,Noli timere, grex pusille‘, Luc. 12, 23. ,Nec hili est instantia Bellarmini, urgentis, his non timendum esse, qui de salute sua sunt certi, quinimo his non opus esse hortationum stimulis ad pietatem et perseverantiam in fide atque sanetis operibus, qui de salute sua indubie certi sunt. Nugae! Utrurnque cum tradat Scriptura, utrumque indubitata fide credendum est. Paulus de sua electione certus erat, Rom. 8, 28., ad finem capitis, 2 Tim. 1,12., et tamen salutem suam singulari sollicitudine operabatur, 1 Cor. 9, 27. Nec est, quod Pistorius objiciat, Paulum non proposuisse aliis suum exemplum ad imitandum. Nam hoc esse falsum, docetur 2 Cor. 1, 21. 4, 13. 1 Tim. 1, 16. 2. Hominem certum esse posse de sua in fide et obedientia perseverantia, verbis rotundis monstrat Dei Spiritus. Audi Christum Joh. 6, 37.: ,Omne, quod dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet, et venientem ad me non ejiciam foras.‘ Audi Paulum Phil. 1, 6.: ,Qui coepit in vobis bonum opus, perficiet usque ad diem Jesu Christi.‘ Et 1 Cor. 1, 8. 9.: ,Fidelis est Deus, per quem vocati estis in societatem Filii ejus, qui confirmabit vos usque ad finem sine crimine ad diem Domini nostri Jesu Christi.‘ Et Heb. 13, 5.: ,Non te deseram, neque relinquam, ut confidentes dicamus, Dominus mihi adjutor, quid faciat mihi homo?‘ Audi Petrum, 1 Pet. 1, 5.: ,Virtute Dei custodimur per fidem ad salutem.‘ Et diligenter notandum est, testari adducta loca, certitudinem salutis nostrae non nostris viribus, sed certissimae promissioni, efficaci operationi et fideli custodiae Dei superstrui. Unde etiam tuto concluseris, quod, qui de perseverantia in fide et salutis certitudine indubie persuasi sunt, non stolido humanae mentis judicio, sed immotis Dei promissionibus nitantur. 3. Certitudinem salutis, quam urgemus, in Scripturis fundatissimam esse contendimus. Nam, licet Dei Spiritus nominatim non dicat, te aut me salvatum iri, tamen rotunda oratione affirmat, omnes et singulos vita aeterna donandos esse, qui credunt in Filium, Joh. 3,18., et fidelem esse Deum, per quem vocati sumus in societatem Filii ejus, qui confirmabit nos usque ad finem sine crimine ad diem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, 1 Cor. 1, 8. 9., et fideles hac de re certos et persuasissimos esse debere, adeo ut, qui Deo, salutem credentibus certo promittenti, credere nolet, Deum mendacii arguat, 1 Joh. 5, 10. sq. 4. Viam, qua itur ad vitam aeternam, impeditam esse et non adeo facilem calcatu, facilis concedo, at hinc inferre vagam de salute dubitationem, justo liberalior illatio est. Nam veluti Spiritus Dei adductis locis exaggerat difficultates, quae his ob-


### On Predestination and Reprobation: are cast down, who strive straight toward eternal life, [the Scripture] so…

are cast down, who strive straight toward eternal life, [the Scripture] so urgently inculcates the certainty of salvation, and opposes to all these difficulties the power of Christ and the eminent virtue of faith. Hear Christ, Mark 9:23: "All things are possible to him who believes." John 16, last verse: "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world." Hear Paul, Rom. 8:37 sq.: "We are more than conquerors through Him who loved us," etc. Hear John, 1 Ep. 5:4: "This is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith." And thus we have vindicated the certainty of our election and salvation from Popish and Arminian assaults." (Syst. universae th. Tom. I. f. 270. sq.)

ANTITHESES. Council of Trent: "No one, moreover, as long as he lives in this mortality, ought to presume so far regarding the secret mystery of divine predestination as to assert with certainty that he is altogether in the number of the predestined; as if it were true that he who is justified can either sin no more, or, if he has sinned, ought to promise himself certain repentance; for, except by special revelation, no one can know whom God has chosen for Himself." (Sess. VI. c. 12. Ed. Smets. p. 29.)

The same: "If anyone shall say that a man who is reborn and justified is bound by faith to believe that he is certainly in the number of the predestined: let him be anathema." (L. c. can. 15. p. 34.)

Calovius: "We reject those who teach that a man cannot but be doubtful concerning final perseverance in faith and the eternal salvation which depends upon it. Thus teaches Joh. Latermannus in Exercitat. de aeterna Dei praedestinatione et ordinata omnes salvandi voluntate § 43, in these words: 'What? That the matter cannot be otherwise; for since a man is certain of this thing, that he can hereafter fall from the hope of salvation, which for the present can be indubitable, he cannot but be doubtful concerning final perseverance, from which, however, one must judge solely concerning the certainty of salvation. Which ought to seem strange to no one, since God Himself passes judgment concerning this, whether this or that person will certainly arrive at salvation and final perseverance in faith.' Hence the same Latermannus c. 1 adds that Guilielmus Estius well observed from Cajetan and Toledo on the chapter of the Epistle to the Romans 8, that Paul spoke of the keeping of the saints on the part of God. And soon after he adds these things concerning St. Paul: 'Some, induced by the words of the apostle, have thought that Paul’s own perseverance in good was divinely revealed to him, but that is false; for because he clearly stated that he could become a reprobate, he was not certain of his own election.'" (Consens. repetit. Vid. Consil Witteb. I, 965.) §

19. Election or predestination, taken in a broader sense, can be defined as the eternal decree of God, by which God, out of His immense mercy, determined to send a Mediator to all men whom He foresaw would fall into sin, and to offer Him to be embraced through universal preaching; to confer faith also upon all who would not resist, through the Word and Sacraments; to justify all who believe, and to renew those who continue to use the means of grace, and to preserve faith in them until the end of life; and finally to save those who are finally believing, for the glory of His goodness. [

Notes to § 19] a. Regarding the whole business or process of our salvation, according to § 2. b. This is the genus of the definition. c. Who is the efficient cause. d. This is the impulsive cause. e. Thus the acts themselves, to which the decree of predestination is terminated, and at the same time the object, which varies according to the nature of the acts, is indicated. f. Which is the final cause. §

20. Predestination or election, taken in a stricter sense, can be defined as the eternal decree of God, by which God, out of His immense mercy, determined to bestow eternal salvation upon all those and only those men whom He foresaw would finally believe in Christ, on account of the merit of Christ Himself, to be apprehended by final faith and thus foreseen, for the sake of their salvation itself and His own glory. [

Notes to § 20] a. See § 1. b. The common genus returns. c. Wandalinus: "The genus (of predestination) is the eternal act of God; for it is an act by which He chooses, not a bare decree by which He decreed to choose." (Ύποτύπωσ. p. 133.) d. The efficient cause, according to § 12. e. The internal impulsive cause. See § 13. f. The object of election. See § 16. g. The principal external impulsive cause. See § 14. h. The less principal external impulsive cause. See § 15. i. Which is the act itself, in which this decree formally consists. j. The end is indicated, according to § 17.

k. Kirchnerus: "Show briefly what the election of grace is. The eternal election is an order of God, according to which He, out of pure mercy, for the sake of His only-begotten Son, chooses for Himself a congregation or people, to whom He imparts eternal life out of grace, the members of which congregation are all those who believe in Christ and persevere in such faith until the end. Rom. 9: 'I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.' Eph. 1: 'He has chosen us through Christ before the foundation of the world was laid, that we should be holy and without blame.'" (Enchiridion 1583. p. 141.) §

21. Reprobation is similarly a decree of God, and thus acknowledges the triune God as its efficient cause. [Notes to § 21] a. Which is opposed to election or predestination taken in a stricter sense, according to § 11.

Quenstedtius: "Opposite to predestination is reprobation, in Greek ἀποδοκιμασία of those to be damned, which word is not found in the Scriptures *κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν* [literally], in opposition, that is, to the election of the children of God to eternal life; yet the sense of the word is clearly held in the Scriptures. The noun *ἀδόκιμος*, however, exists in 1 Cor. 9:27, 2 Cor. 13:5. It is called otherwise *προγραφή εἰς τὸ κρῖμα*, a prescript or writing beforehand, i.e., made from eternity unto judgment. In the Epistle of Jude 4: 'There have crept in certain men, who were of old prescribed unto this judgment, ungodly men.' ... Mark 16:16, John 3:18, 36.

Observe: 1. He who does not believe, i.e., who pertinaciously perseveres in infidelity until the last breath of life or dies in incredulity, he is actually damned and is already judged, both by reason of the divine decree made from eternity, and by reason of the judgment manifested in the Word and promulgated to the incredulous, the execution of which will follow on the last day. That this sentence of Christ is conceived concerning the eternal decree of reprobation is suggested by the verb of the past tense *κέκριται*, 'he is judged,' to wit, not by himself through *αὐτοκατάκρισιν* [self-condemnation], which indeed does not appear in all the reprobate in this age, but by God, the just Judge, in eternity, i.e., he is judged not here only in his conscience, but also in the forum of the divine decree. 2. The verb *μένει* [abideth] denotes not only the presence of divine wrath, but at the same time the continuous and perpetual act of that presence on account of the contempt of the Gospel of Christ." (L. c. s. 1. th. 22, 23, 27. f. 32, 33, sq.)

The same: "D. Joh. Frid. König wrongly places *θέσιν εἰς ὀργήν* [appointment unto wrath] among the synonyms of reprobation, 1 Thess. 5:9: 'God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation.' For although divine wrath (by which is expressed *ἐπιτομικῶς* [summarily] the whole collection of evils which presses upon the damned) and *περιποίησις* [obtaining] or the assertion of salvation are opposed here; yet it is false that 'He hath not appointed us,' etc., is distinctive of the elect from the reprobate; therefore the consequence which the Calvinists connect here is vicious: the faithful are not appointed to wrath, therefore the others are appointed to wrath. For it is the same as if I were to say: the regenerate are not debtors to walk according to the flesh (Rom. 8:12), therefore the unregenerate are such debtors. Likewise: you are not redeemed with gold and silver, therefore the rest are redeemed in this way. Again, from 1 Thess. 4:7: 'God hath not called us unto uncleanness,' therefore others have been called by God unto uncleanness. Paul simply denies that God has appointed us to wrath, but to salvation through Christ Jesus, which words are general, pertaining not only to the faithful, but to all men." (L. c. th. 23. f. 32.)

Andr. Schmidtius: "The opposite of predestination is reprobation... And in this place, the reason of the opposites will be in some things the same, but in others different. For they agree in genus, efficient cause, and affections; but they differ in the internal impulsive cause (Rom. 9:22 sqq.) and the external (Rom. 11:20), as well as in the end, namely, the vindication of sinners and the manifestation of vindicatory justice in God." (Compend. th. dogm. 1690. p. 205 sq.)

Calovius: "Concerning the word, there is nothing more to say, except that the Reformed distinguish between negative and positive reprobation; the former they call preterition, the latter predamnation; likewise between comparative and simple reprobation and election. They confess that predamnation and reprobation are not absolute, but that election and comparative reprobation—e.g., why this one is rejected from glory or elected to it before another—are ascribed to the absolute constitution by the Bremensians, Berliners, Frankfurtans, and others; yet most, however, also ascribe an absolute, not only a comparative, reprobation to the absolute decree of reprobation." (Syst. Tom. X, 666 sq.)

Scherzerus: "That reprobation was also made from eternity, we prove by a single argument: when God predestinated the elect, He also reprobated the reprobate. But God predestinated the elect from eternity. Therefore, He also reprobated the reprobate from eternity. The reason for the major consists in this, that election and reprobation were made simultaneously, which all other Calvinists confess... Piscator dreams that reprobation was not made from eternity, but only after the fall of the human race. Vol. II. loc. 12. f. 147." (System, p. 537 sq.) PART III. CHAP. XII.

Supposing indeed the universality of divine grace, of the merit of Christ, and of the serious vocation to embrace the Mediator, but nevertheless supposing also on the part of men the contempt of grace foreseen by God, since otherwise, with the universal grace of God and the merit of Christ and the universal vocation standing, no one would have been to be damned, if no one had despised the means of grace and grace itself.

Latin:

jiciuntur, qui ad vitam aeteruam recta contendunt, ita certitudinem salutis urgenter inculcat, omnibusque istis difficultatibus opponit potero tiam Christi et fidei eminentem virtutem. Audi Christum Mare. 9, 23.: ,Omnia credenti possibilia sunt.‘ Joh. 16. ult.: ,Confidite, ego vici mundum.‘ Audi Paulum Rom. 8, 37. sq.: ,Plusquam victores sumus per eum, qui dilexit nos‘ etc. Audi Johannem 1. ep. 5, 4.: ,Haec est victoria, quae vicit mundum, fides nostra.‘ Atque ita electionis salutisque nostrae certitudinem ab impugnationibus pontificiis et Arminianis vindicavimus.“ (Syst. universae th. Tom. I. f. 270. sq.)

ANTITHESES. Concilium Tridentinum: ,,Nemo quoque, quamdiu in hac mortalitate vivitur, de arcano divinae praedestinationis mysterio usque adeo praesumere debet, ut certo statuat, se omnino esse in numero praedestinatorum; quasi verum esset, quod justificatus aut amplius peccare non possit, aut, si peccaverit, certam sibi resipiscentiam promittere debeat; nam, nisi ex speciali revelatione, scire non potest, quos Deus sibi elegerit.“ (Sess. VI. c. 12. Ed. Smets. p. 29.)

Idem: ״Si quis dixerit, hominem renatum et justificatum teneri ex fide ad credendum, se certo esse in numero praedestinatorum: anathema sit.“ (L. c. can. 15. p. 34.)

Calovius: ״Rejicimus eos, qui docent, hominem de finali perverantia in fide et, quae ab ea dependet, salute aeterna, non posse non esse dubium. Ita docet Joh. Latermannus in Exercitat, de aeterna Dei praedestinatione et ordinata omnes salvandi voluntate § 43. hisce verbis: ,Quid? quod res aliter se habere non possit; cum enim homo ea de re cettus sit, quod spe salutis, quae pro praesenti indubitata esse potest, posthac excidere queat, de finali perseverantia non potest non esse dubius, ex qua tamen de certitudine salutis unice judicandum. Id quod nemini mirum videri debet, cum ipse Deus de eo, num ille vel iste ad salutem certo perventurus sit, ac finali in fide perseverantia judicium ferat.‘ Hinc idem Latermannus c. 1. addit, Guilielmum Estium bene ex Cajetano et Toleto ad caput epistolae ad Rom. 8. observasse, Paulum de custodia sanctorum a parte Dei verba fecisse. Et mox de S. Paulo haec addit: ,Nonnulli, verbis apostoli inducti, existimarunt, Paulo suam in bono perseverantiam divinitus revelatam fuisse, sed falsum id est; quia enim se reprobum fieri posse clare statuit, de electione sua certus non fuit.“ (Consens. repetit. Vid. Consil Witteb. I, 965.) §

19. Definiri potest electio seu praedestinatio latius sic dicta, a quod sit decretum Dei b aeternum, quo Deus c ex immensa sua misericordia d hominibus omnibus, quos in peccatum lapsuros praevidit, mediatorem mittere et per praedicationem universalem amplectendum offerre, omnibus etiam, qui non repugnaturi essent, fidem per verbum et sacramenta conferre, credentes omnes justificare ac mediis gratiae porro utentes renovare fidemque usque ad finem vitae in illis conservare, ipsos denique finaliter credentes salvare e constituit ad bonitatis suae f gloriam. 602PART.III. CAP. XII.

Quod totum negotium seu processum nostrae salutis spectat, juxta § 2. Genus hoc est definiti. Qui causa efficiens est. Causa im pulsiva haec est. Sic actus ipsi, ad quos decretum praedestinationis terminatur, ac simul objectum, quod pro ratione actuum variat, indicatur. Quae causa finalis est. §

20. Tom. X, 666. sq.)

### On Predestination and Reprobation: Virtually causing, as we have said concerning the decree of predestination

Virtually causing, as we have said concerning the decree of predestination. As one who decrees, or reprobates. For it is an act of the divine will, and therefore common to the three persons. § 22.

The internal impulsive cause is the vindicatory justice of God. Or the *a priori* reason, through which one rightly answers the question, why God willed not to save certain men, but to damn them.

Or the wrath of God against sins, Rom. 2:5, 8; ch. 9:22, 28. For just as in the cited place, Rom. 2, the damnation of the impenitent is referred to the wrath of God—namely, that God is moved to this, that He wills to punish them, by His wrath against sinners, or the justice by which He is inclined to vindicate the violation of His law—so, since it is certain that God decreed long ago those things which He does in time, it must likewise be acknowledged that, when God decreed to damn certain men, the reason for decreeing was that justice of God: because of the necessary agreement between the decree and the execution. And here also, when in Rom. 9 the reprobate are called vessels of wrath, i.e., objects of divine wrath, from which their destruction and damnation proceed, the same is also rightly referred to the reprobation which is founded in that wrath, or vindicatory justice. § 23. The external impulsive cause is the sins of men, which are and insofar as they are joined with final incredulity.

Namely, God in the ordination to just punishment does not act as a supreme Lord, but according to His ordered power, and as a judge. Compare the blessed Musaeus, *Dissert. de Aet. El. Decr.*, ch. VIII, § 186. Luther: "Human reason imagines an unequal will of God, as if God were a tyrant who has certain fellows whose conduct pleases Him, whether it be good or not good, and on the other hand He hates the others, let them do what they will. Thus one should not think of God's will. This saying is eternally true, Ps. 5:6: 'You are not a God to whom godless conduct or sin is pleasing.' For although He accepts the saints, who yet still have sin in them, He does not accept them without a great payment; Christ had to become a sacrifice, for the sake of which God accepts and spares us as long as we remain in faith and when we are in faith." (*M. Luther's and other theologians at Wittenberg's Opinion on the Sins of the Elect*, Ann. 1536. X, 2001.)

Apology of the Formula of Concord: "Where, indeed, is it written in God’s Word that God does not will that everyone be saved, but that, regardless of their sin, He has, by His own mere counsel, purpose, and will, ordained some to damnation, so that they cannot be saved? Never in all eternity will they be able to prove the aforementioned proposition or statement from God’s revealed Word, no matter how much it may matter to them. Since Holy Scripture nowhere speaks thus, nor dare they, out of sheer audacity, lead such blasphemous doctrine or speech against Scripture and spread it throughout all Christendom. Meanwhile, we do not deny that God does not work equally in all men and enlighten them all, since He does not give His Word to all; and that He nevertheless is and remains both just and merciful, and no one can justly accuse Him of any unfaithfulness, envy, or tyranny, even though He does not (as has been said) give the Word to all and enlighten them. But we say at the same time that when one comes to this mystery, one should lay a finger upon one's mouth and not dispute or ponder, but speak with the Apostle: 'How unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out!' Much less, however, should one rush forth, as our opponents do, and say that God, by free will, and even regardless of sin, has ordained that some should be damned. For what God holds or has concluded in His secret, hidden counsel, of that one can say nothing certain, nor should one involve oneself in such a deeply hidden mystery, but save the same for that life, meanwhile remaining with the revealed Word of God, through which we are called to repentance and faith in Christ, and salvation is faithfully offered to us. Which Word or revealed will of God concerning the refreshing of the weary and heavy-laden is certain, infallible, and indubitable, and in no way contrary to the hidden counsel of God, upon which our opponents alone focus. Just as nothing is to be concluded from it against the will revealed in the Word of God, nor has God Himself pointed us to it in His Word. That now not all accept the same calling, we should not therefore say that God, in His secret counsel, by free purpose and will, even without sin, has ordained those who do not repent to damnation, so that they cannot be converted and saved, for such is not revealed to us in the Word; but we should remain with this: that God’s judgments in these cases are unsearchable and incomprehensible." (Heidelberg Ed., fol. 208b, 209a.)

However, there is no need here to distinguish between a principal and a less-than-principal cause, since sins themselves, by the fact that they violate the law of God, are worthy of punishment not only temporal, but eternal. See Part II, Chapter I, § 15.

For just as in the act of damnation, as the execution of the decree of reprobation, regard is had to the τό non credere [the not believing] in the only-begotten Son of God, as that on account of which, as a meritorious (or demeritorious, as some say) cause, God, who condemns, wills to condemn, John 3:18, 36: so in that very decree, final unbelief acts by way of an impulsive cause, moving the will of God to reprobate, or to decree damnation.

Similarly, just as in Romans 11:20 certain spiritual branches are said to have been broken off in time, or men who had been in a state of grace for some time are said to have been cast away on account of unbelief, or that their unbelief moved God to cast them away: so, that they were once rejected or reprobated by the eternal decree of God, it must be acknowledged that God, in our way of understanding, was moved to decree that, in view of that unbelief, as an impulsive reason. PART III. CHAPTER XII.

Quenstedtius: "The cause of reprobation is not an absolute and simple hatred of God (for God loved the whole world, John 3:16), nor the insufficiency of the merit of Christ (for He is the 'propitiation for the sins of the whole world,' 1 John 2:2), nor a deficiency of the Gospel, which God commanded to be announced to the whole world, Matthew 28:19, but the proper guilt of men, namely, impenitence and final unbelief." (L. c. s. 1. th. 26. f. 33.)

B. Meisnerus: "For the dispelling of calumnies, it should be noted in what sense it was asserted by our side at the Colloquy of Montbéliard that unbelief alone condemns, and not other sins. Our opinion is founded upon that passage in John 3:18: 'He who believes in Him is not condemned; but he who does not believe is condemned already.' And John 16:9: 'The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, because they do not believe in Me.' Here, unbelief alone is established as the λόγος άμεσος (immediate cause) of condemnation. Do other sins, then, not bring about the guilt of damnation? We respond that damnation can be considered in two ways: 1. Formally in itself, insofar as it is the sense of divine wrath and the most grievous punishment; 2. Materially, or by reason of the degrees, which will be unequal in that damnation. For some will suffer more grievous torments than others. We say, therefore, that the cause of damnation, considered formally, is unbelief alone. But the degrees of punishments will be adjudicated according to the quantity of sins, as they were either more grievous or lighter. Furthermore, the cause of damnation can be considered either by reason of merit and guilt, or by reason of the judgment itself and its execution. Regarding merit, all sins condemn and are worthy of eternal death; regarding the judgment itself and its execution, unbelief alone condemns. For men are consigned to the flames of hell for this reason: because they did not apprehend by firm faith the merit of Christ, by which satisfaction was made for all their sins. Thus, Judas will be condemned primarily not because he betrayed Christ, but because he despaired and did not apply to himself the passion of Christ, by which his betrayal was expiated. Meanwhile, we do not deny that Judas will suffer a greater punishment in hell than others on account of the deformity of his crime and the nefarious betrayal of his Master." (Άνθρωπολ. Disp. 20. D. 1.)

For other sins, if faith in Christ intervenes, can be abolished as to their guilt, so that men are not condemned on account of them; whence also they would not be reprobates, unless faith were absent.

Wandalinus: "The cause, on account of which [one is reprobated], is either inadequate or adequate. The inadequate causes are all the sins of the reprobate, both original and actual, which has already been proven and needs no further proof. It is called inadequate because Christ satisfied even for the sins of the reprobate, so that on account of them there would be no condemnation for them, if they were in Christ through faith. And, if God were willing to impute all other sins (except for contumacious άπιστία) or even one of them, 'no one could stand before Him,' Ps. 130: 3. Therefore, the adequate cause of reprobation is contumacious and final impenitence and unbelief. John 3:…18, 36." (Ύποτυπ. p. 138. sq.)

And although they finally come to pass contingently in time, they are nevertheless represented to the divine will through the eternal foreknowledge of God, not by the force of a predetermining decree, but as things that will definitely, though contingently, occur, and are therefore immediately knowable in themselves. §

24. The objects of reprobation are impious men who are finally unbelieving. Or the subject which is reprobated. Namely, such persons in whom that which is the cause or impulsive reason for reprobation has a place. But to men, as men, not

while the will of God, otherwise most benign, is not terminated toward those who are to be damned by sins foreseen—in our mode of understanding—and by final incredulity itself. ANTITHESIS.

Quenstedt: "Antithesis: 1. Of the ancient Predestinarians (whom they also call Predestinates), who lived in the 5th century, and of Godschalk the monk of Rheims, who lived in the 9th century, whose heresy was this, as Gerh. Joh. Vossius reports in his History of Pelagianism, bk. 7, pt. 4, p. 779: 1) That God, just as He predestined some to life, so He predestined some to death. 2) That God does not will all men to be saved, but only those who are actually saved. 3) That Christ did not die for all, but for the elect only, etc. ... 2. Of the Calvinists, who teach that God, out of an absolute and simple good pleasure, without any regard for incredulity or final impenitence, predestined the greatest part of mankind to destruction; thus Calvin, bk. 3, Inst. ch. 23, s. 1, 4, 7. . . The decree of reprobation is defined by the Synodics in the judgment of Gomarus, p. 32, in this manner: 'Peremptory reprobation is a decree of God, by which, according to His most free will, for the declaration of His vindicatory justice, He determined to grant neither grace nor glory to certain men from the human race, but to permit them to fall freely into sin and to leave them in their sins, and finally to condemn them justly on account of their sins.' . . The ancient Calvinists and with them some more recent ones, whom they call Supralapsarians, make the adequate object of reprobation man creatable or yet to be created, as said above; but most moderns posit the object of reprobation as man lying in sin, concerning whom they say it can be asked either absolutely, why God reprobated him, and it is rightly answered, on account of the sin in which the sinner lies; or comparatively, because all lie equally in the same guilt of sin, why does God damn this one rather than that one? Then they appeal to the absolute good pleasure of God, namely, that this one is not condemned because it so pleases Him, but that one is damned because it so pleases Him. . . But however the Calvinists explain themselves, they all agree on the absoluteness of the decree of reprobation; for the adequate object of reprobation for them is 'man abstracted from every sinful quality and constituted in the absolute good pleasure of God,' as the blessed Hulsemann says in E. C. s. 8, § 4. Thus the Synod of Dort, a. 1, th. 15, p. 343 of the Acts, 'place the cause of preterition or reprobation in the sole most free, most just, irreprehensible, and immutable good pleasure of God, by which He decreed to leave others in common misery, and to grant them neither saving faith nor the grace of conversion, but, left in their ways and under just judgment, finally to damn and eternally punish them, not only on account of infidelity, but also all other sins, for the declaration of His justice.' . . And they call this doctrine of theirs 'the heart of the (Reformed) church and the palladium of the absolute grace of God,' as witnessed by the Genevan theologians themselves in the Synod of Dort, sess. 42, p. 212. . . 3. Of certain Scholastics and Pontificians, who posit that there is no cause of reprobation on the part of men; thus Durandus, bk. 1, sent. dist. 40, q. 2; Bellarmine, bk. 2, on grace, ch. 16." (L. c. s. 2, q. 9, f. 97 sqq.) § 25. The end of reprobation is the vindication of sins, and the glory of divine vindicatory justice.

Latin:

Virtualiter causantem, prout de decreto praedestinationis diximus. Tanquam, qui decernit, aut reprobat. Est enim actus voluntatis divinae, adeoque communis tribus personis. § 22.

Causa impulsiva a interna est Dei justitia b vindicativa. Seu ratio a priori, per quam recte respondetur ad quaestionem, cur Deus voluerit homines quosdam non salvare, sed damnare.

Seu ira Dei adversus peccata, Rom. 2, 5. 8. cap. 9, 22. 28. Prout enim 1. c. Rom. 2. damnatio impoenitentium refertur ad iram Dei, scilicet, quod Deum ira sua adversus peccatores, seu justitia, qua inclinatur ad vindicandam legis suae violationem, moveat ad id, ut velit punire eos: ita, cum certum sit, Deum ea, quae in tempore facit, olim decrevisse, similiter agnoscendum est, quod, cum Deus decerneret quosdam homines damnare, ratio decernendi fuerit justitia illa Dei: ob necessariam convenientiam decreti et executionis. Et ic etiam, quando Rom. 9. reprobi dicuntur vasa irae, i. e. objecta irae divinae, ex qua proveniat illorum interitus ac damnatio, idem etiam ad reprobationem, quae in ira illa, seu justitia vindicativa fundetur, recte refertur. § 23. Causa impulsiva externa a sunt peccata b hominum, quae et quatenus cum finali c incredulitate d conjunguntur. e

Nempe Deus in ordinatione ad poenam justam non agit ut Dominus supremus, sed pro potentia sua ordinata, et ut judex. Confer b. Mus. Dissert. de Aet. El. Decr. cap. VIII. § 186. Lutherus: ,,Menschliche Vernunft dichtet einen ungleichen Willen Gottes, als wäre Gott ein Tyrann, der etliche Gesellen hat, deren Wesen er ihm gefallen lässt, es sei gut oder nicht gut, und dagegen hasset er die andern, sie thun, was sie wollen. Also soll man nicht von Gottes Willen gedenken. Dieser Spruch ist ewiglich wahr Ps. 5, 6.: ,Du bist nicht ein Gott, dem gottlos Wesen oder Sünde gefällig ist.‘ Denn ob er gleich die Heiligen annimmt, die doch noch Sünde an ihnen haben, so nimmt er sie doch nicht ohne eine grosse Bezahlung an; Christus hat müssen ein Opfer werden, um welches willen uns Gott annimmt und schonet, so lange wir im Glauben bleiben und wenn wir im Glauben sind.“

Apologie der Concordienformel: ,,Wo stehet es doch in Gottes Wort, dass Gott nicht wolle, dass jedermann selig werde, sondern nnangesehen ihre Sünde habe er allein auf seinem blossen Rath, Fürsatz und Willen etliche zum Verdamniss verordnet, dass sie nicht können selig werden? Nimmermehr in alle Ewigkeit werden sie gemeldte Proposition oder Rede aus Gottes offenbartem Wort erweisen, wann ihnen auch noch so viel dran gelegen. Sintemal die heilige Schrift nirgend also redet, noch dürfen sie aus lauter Dummkühnheit wider die Schrift solche lästerliche Lehre oder Reden führen und in die ganze Christenheit ausbreiten. Unterdess sind wir zwar nicht in Abrede, dass Gott nicht in allen Menschen gleich wirke und sie alle erleuchte, dieweil er auch nicht allen sein Wort gibtf und dass er gleichwohl beides gerecht und barmherzig sei und bleibe und ihn niemand einiger Untreue, Missgunst oder Tyrannei billig beschuldigen könne, ob er wohl nicht allen (wie gesagt) das Wort gibt und sie erleuchtet. Wir sagen aber dabei, dass, wann man an dieses Geheimniss kommt, dass man den Finger auf den Mund legen und nicht disputiren und grübeln solle, sondern mit dem Apostel sprechen: ,Wie gar unbegreiflich sind seine Gerichte und wie unerforschlich seine WegeNoch viel weniger aber soll man herausfahren, wie unser Gegentheil thut, und sagen, dass Gott aus freiem Willen, auch unangesehen die Sünde, verordnet habe, dass etliche sollen verdammt werden. Denn was Gott in seinem heimlichen verborgenen Bathe halte oder geschlossen habe, da kann man nichts Gewisses von sagen, soll sich auch in solch tief verborgen Geheimniss nicht einlassen, sondern dasselbige in jenes Leben sparen, mittlerweile bei dem offenbarten Wort Gottes bleiben, dadurch wir zur Busse und Glauben an Christum berufen und uns die Seligkeit treulich angeboten wird. Welches Wort oder offenbarter Wille Gottes von der Erquickung der Mühseligen und Beladenen gewiss, unfehlbar und unzweifelhaftig ist und dem verborgenen Bath Gottes, darauf unser Gegentheil alleine geht, mit nichten zuwider. Wie denn auch wider den im Worte Gottes geoffenbarten Willen daraus nichts zu schliessen, Gott selbst auch in seinem Wort uns darauf nicht gewiesen hat. Dass nun nicht alle dieselbige Berufung annehmen, sollen wir darum nicht sagen, dass Gott in seinem geheimen Rath aus freiem Vorsatz und Willen auch ohne die Sünde dieselbigen, so nicht Busse thun, zum Verdamniss verordnet, dass sie nicht können bekehrt und selig werden, denn solches ist uns im Wort nicht geoffenbaret; sondern dabei bleiben, dass Gottes Gerichte in diesen Fällen unerforschlich und unbegreiflich sind.“ (Heidelb. Ausg. fol. 208b. 209 a.)

Non autem hic opus est distinguere inter causam principalem et minus principalem, cum peccata ipsa per hoc, quod legem Dei violant, digna sint poena non solum temporali, verum aeterna. Vid. P. II. cap. I. § 15.

Sicut enim in actu damnationis, tamquam executione decreti reprobationis, respectus habetur ad τό non credere in Filium Dei unigenitum, tanquam id, propter quod velut causam meritoriam (aut demeritoriam, ut aliqui loquuntur) damnare velit Deus, qui damnat, Joh. 3, 18. 36.: ita in ipso decreto illo finalis incredulitas habet se per modum causae impulsivae, moventis voluntatem Dei ad reprobandum, sive decernendam damnationem.

Similiter, quemadmodum Rom. 11, 20. rami quidam spirituales in tempore defracti, aut homines, qui in statu gratiae aliquamdiu fuerant, abjecti dicuntur per incredulitatem, seu, quod incredulitas illorum Deum moverit ad abjiciendum illos: ita, quod olim aeterno Dei decreto rejecti aut reprobati fuerunt, agnoscendum est, Deum nostro modo intelligendi motum fuisse ad istud decernendum, intuitu istius incredulitatis, tanquam rationis impulsivae. PART. III. CAP. ΧΠ.

Quenstedtius: ״Causa reprobationis non est odium Dei absolutum et simplex (dilexit enim Deus totum mundum Joh. 3, 16.), aut insufficientia meriti Christi (est enim,propitiatio pro peccatis totius mundi‘ 1 Joh. 2, 2.), aut defectus evangelii, quod Deus jussit annunciari toti mundo Matth. 28, 19., sed propria hominum culpat impoenitentia et incredulitas finalis.“ (L. c. s. 1. th. 26. f. 33.)

B. Meisnerus: ,,Pro dispulsione calumniarum notari debet, quo sensu in Colloq. Mompelg. a nostris assertum fuerit, solam incredulitatem damnare, non caetera peccata. Opinio nostra fundatur in illo Joh. 3, 18.: ,Qui credit in eum, non condemnatur. Qui autem non credit, jam condemnatus est.‘ Et Joh. 16, 9.: ,Spiritus S. arguet mundum de peccato, quia non credunt in me.‘ Hic λόγος άμεσος condemnationis statuitur sola incredulitas. Num E. caetera peccata reatum damnationis non inferunt? Resp., damnationem posse considerari dupliciter: 1. formaliter in se, prout est sensus irae divinae et supplicium gravissimum; 2. materialiter vel ratione graduum, qui in damnatione ista erunt inaequales. Graviora enim tormenta quidam patientur, quam alii. Dicimus ergo causam damnationis formaliter consideratae solam esse incredulitatem. Gradus vero poenarum adjudicabuntur secundum peccatorum quantitatem, prout illa fuerunt: vel graviora vel leviora. Deinde carysa damnationis considerari potest vel ratione meriti et reatus, vel ratione ipsius judicii et executionis. Quoad meritum omnia peccata damnant et digna sunt aeterna morte; quoad ipsum judicium et executionem, sola incredulitas damnat. Ideo enim homines flammis inferni addicentur, quia meritum Christi, quo pro peccatis ipsorum omnibus satisfactum est, firma fide non apprehenderunt. Sic Judas primo damnabitur, non quia Christum prodidit, sed quia desperavit et Christi passionem, qua proditio ejus expiata est, sibi non applicuit. Interim non diflitemur, Judam majorem prae aliis poenam in inferno passurum esse ob deformitatem delicti et nefandam magistri sui proditionem.“ (Άνΰρωπολ. Disp. 20. D. 1.)

Alias enim peccata, si intervenerit fides in Christum, aboleri possunt quoad reatum, ne propterea homines damnentur; unde etiam ni, nisi abfuerit fides, non erunt reprobi.

### On Predestination and Reprobation: For men are destined to punishment by the decree for this reason, that in time…

For men are destined to punishment by the decree for this reason, that in time the punishment may be actually inflicted upon them. For just as it is said in Rom. 9:22 that God, willing to show His wrath or vindicatory justice, and to make known His power, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath, fitted (not indeed by an absolute decree of God; for otherwise there would be no need of much longsuffering to tolerate that which God Himself had made such out of absolute good pleasure, but fitted by themselves or by their own fault) for destruction, which, however, as vessels of wrath, are finally cast away, so that the justice of God may appear, whose executive act was delayed for some time: so, that God, foreseeing how those men would fit themselves for destruction, decreed to reject them, tended toward the glorious manifestation of divine justice as an end. Cf. Rom. 11:22. § 26. The decree of reprobation is also not only particular, but also immutable.

For because some men are elect and only the finally incredulous are reprobate, the particularity of the decree is easily evident. In the same way that we said the decree of predestination is immutable: not by absolute, but by hypothetical necessity.

Quenstedt: "The attributes of reprobation are some that belong to it viewed in the abstract, others that belong to it considered in the concrete. The attributes of reprobation taken abstractly are: 1. Eternity, Matt. 25:41, Ep. Jude 4. 2. Immutability, Num. 23:19, 1 Sam. 15:29, Mal. 3:6. . . He (Christ, Matt. 25:41) does not say that hell-fire is prepared for men, but for the devil and his angels, so that the supreme philanthropy of God may be understood. But hell-fire is prepared for the devils primarily and principally; for the devil sinned and was thrust into hell before the sin of man. He does not say that eternal punishment was prepared 'from the foundation of the world,' as was said of the kingdom in v. 34; lest any occasion be given to anyone to suspect that the punishment was prepared before sin and that the reprobate are damned not so much on account of sin as on account of a certain absolute divine decree. . . The attributes of reprobation taken concretely, or, which is the same thing, of the reprobate, are: 1. Plurality, Matt. 7:13; 2. The possibility of being for a time in the state of the truly regenerate, Heb. 6:4, 5, 6; 10:26; Luke 8:13; 3. Perseverance in final infidelity." (L. c. s. 1, th. 31—32, f. 34 sq.) § 27. Reprobation can be defined as the eternal decree of God, by which God, out of His vindicatory justice, decreed to damn sinful men, finally incredulous, on account of their very sins joined with final incredulity, for the purpose of punishing their sins and for the glory of His divine justice.

The common genus of predestination and reprobation. The efficient cause virtually causing. See § 21. The internal impulsive cause or reason. See § 22.

The object of reprobation is indicated. See § 24. The external impulsive cause, according to § 23. f) The end of reprobation is denoted. See § 25.

APPENDIX

TO THE PRECEDING CHAPTER ON PREDESTINATION, IN WHICH IS TREATED THE INSCRIPTION IN THE BOOK OF LIFE. § 1.

Closely related to the doctrine of predestination or the election of men to eternal life is the doctrine of the inscription of men in the book of life, which the Scriptures, by terms accommodated to human affairs, call otherwise simply a writing in a book, and again, with a double addition, a writing in the book of life of the Lamb, and finally also mention the writing of names in heaven. In a certain sense, this doctrine is indeed the same as that by which election to eternal life is delivered; yet a somewhat broader acceptance is not foreign to the force of the term and the usage of speech, as will be evident from what follows.

Especially in the Johannine Apocalypse, ch. 17:8, ch. 20:15, ch. 22:19, to which Philippians 4:3 corresponds, where to have names in the book of life is to be written in it. Doubtless through a certain άν&ρωποπά&εία (anthropopathy) or συγχατάβασιν (condescension), according to the likeness of a human act by which the names of certain persons are inscribed in a catalog of citizens, families, or soldiers, so that they may obtain the rights, privileges, and benefits of the associates. In the Holy Scriptures, the custom of the kings of the Medes and Persians is mentioned in this regard, for whom it was an accepted practice that the names and deeds of subjects or faithful and well-deserving ministers be written in a book of chronicles. See Esther 6:1 ff.

Daniel 12:1. Exodus 32:32. Apoc. 13:8. ch. 21:27. Luke 10:20. Compare Hebrews 12:23. § 2.

The book of life is the series or multitude of those to whom life is to be granted, insofar as it is present to the divine mind. Life, however, in this place is not understood as natural, but spiritual, which is rightly distinguished into the life of grace and of glory. Baier’s Comp. ed. Walther. III.39 PART III. CAP. XII.

Concerning this, it must first be established so that the inscription into it may be more clearly understood.

The word "book" otherwise denotes materially a Scripture, or a written volume, or a catalog consisting of sensible signs or characters signifying something by convention, just as βίβλος γενέσεως Χρίστου, Matt. 1:1, signifies a genealogy consigned to writing. Thus also סֵפֶר תּוֹלְדֹת, the book of generations, Gen. 5:1, and Neh. 7:5 ff., the book of the census of those who had arrived in Judea under the leadership of Zerubbabel, is mentioned. But just as books or catalogs of this kind are compiled and preserved for the sake of security and against oblivion, by which the minds of men might be occupied and the rights, advantages, and duties of citizens or families might be rendered uncertain or lost: so a certain catalog, as it were, of those to whom life pertains can be conceived with respect to God or the divine intellect, insofar as God, whom forgetfulness of no thing ever seizes, has the series or multitude of those men as if in readiness, or insofar as they are an object of divine knowledge or memory, as those to be endowed with life. Namely, with regard to practical knowledge, or knowledge joined with affection, by which God looks upon men as those to be affected with a certain good, and thus takes account of them; in which sense Nehemiah prays: "Remember me, O my God, for good," ch. 5, last verse. Cf. Ps. 1, last verse.

For although the word "life" otherwise not infrequently denotes that which is called natural, temporal, bodily, animal, and the days of this life are said to be written in a certain book of God, Ps. 139:16, yet that consideration does not pertain to the present matter. Concerning which Paul says, Gal. 2:20: "The life which I now live, I live by the faith of the Son of God." And Rom. 6:11: "Reckon yourselves to be alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord." Finally, he says that the regenerate live by the Spirit, Gal. 5:25.

Of which frequent mention is made in the Scriptures; see Matt. 25:46 concerning the entry of the righteous into eternal life; John 3:16 concerning the eternal life which those believing in Christ are to have. Cf. John 6:47, 51, 54, 68; ch. 10:28. And this life of the faithful, for the present state, is said to be hidden with Christ in God, Col. 3:3. There are those who think the book of life is Christ Himself; which, although it seems it can be admitted in a certain sense, it is nevertheless more correctly taught that, just as the book of life is said to be the Lamb’s, not the Lamb Himself, Rev. 13:8; ch. 21:26, so it is n ot so much Christ Himself as it is the cause and foundation of gracious and glorious life, on account of its relation to Christ. Cf. the blessed Affelmann, Part I, Disp. I, η. VI, p. 11, 12; the blessed Balth. Meisner, Anthropol. Disp. XV, Q. IV, § 1 ff. ad 6; the blessed Joh. Meisner, Disp. de Libro Vitae § 29; J. Cluver, De lucui. Apocal. ad cap. III, 8, p. m. 137. § e.

The inscription into the book of life is an act of the divine will, by which He adds one or more men to the assembly of those living a spiritual life, who may enjoy this life for their own good along with the others.

Or as an insertion into a certain catalog. Or He wills, or decrees, or determines to have regard and care for that man, just as for others, to remember, to be mindful of, etc., as one who is living.

Some, however, also call the actual collation of that life, by which, as by a sign, that divine will is manifested, by the name of inscription into the book of life; just as those who are baptized are inscribed into the book of l…ife through baptism, since they actually arrive at the number of the faithful or citizens in the kingdom of grace, and at the same time as heirs of eternal life.

But the blessed Kromayer judges this to be a catachrestic expression. Theol. Aphorist. L. VI. §. 2. p. 162. § 4.

And thus the inscription into the book of life is twofold, insofar as men are referred by God either precisely to the number of the faithful, or to the number of those certainly to be saved. The former coincides with the decree of God concerning men to be regenerated, justified, and adopted as sons; the latter coincides with the act of election or predestination. Although it must be admitted that by the term "inscription into the book of life," when posited absolutely, not so much the former as the latter act is understood. Just as life itself and the book of life are accustomed to be constituted as twofold, according to the antecedents; although others, while acknowledging one book, acknowledge a twofold mode of writing or inscription. Thus, having regard for the twofold book, some distinguish between inscription into the book of grace and inscription into the book of glory. And thus to be endowed with spiritual life and to be held as heirs of eternal life.

As to the thing itself. Which even the name of election itself declares, insofar as few are chosen out of many for a certain state or office. And although in human affairs it is prior, e.g., to be elected a senator, and posterior to be inscribed in the register of the senate, yet here, where the writing is not material, it is easily evident that the reason is different.

Namely, life κατ’ ἐξοχήν is that which we know to be eternal, and thus the book of life is a catalog of men to whom eternal life pertains. Wherefore also the inscription into the book of life, speaking absolutely, is referred to this, which most of our own also observe. And we, having left behind the former signification, will now further pursue the latter. §

5. The efficient cause of this inscription into the book of life is the triune God. 612 Part. III. cap. XII. Or He who writes or inscribes. However, the cause is understood as virtually causing, according to the nature of internal divine acts. As of election; concerning which see above, cap. XII. § 12. §

6. The impulsive cause is internal, the grace or benevolence of God; external, the merit of Christ to be apprehended by final faith and thus foreseen. Both according to that which was said above concerning election. By reason of which we believe the book of life of the Lamb and the inscription into it are specifically spoken of; just as it is taught by some that Christ is the foundation of the inscription. And the phrase corresponds, by which we are said to be chosen in Christ, Eph. 1:3. For those whom He foreknew would be in Christ Jesus, these He inscribed in the catalog of the elect or those to be saved, according to Rom. 8:29. §

7. The object of the inscription is men who will finally believe, insofar as they are to be saved. Or the persons to be inscribed or inscribed by name. Others call it the subject. For under this formal reason they pertain to that catalog or book and assembly. §

8. The form of the inscription itself consists in the act of the divine will concerning those men, constantly regarding them with divine practical knowledge, in order to confer eternal salvation. Or the formal reason. Compare §§ 3 and 4. See § 2, note b. §

9. The end of it is the very collation of eternal salvation and the glory of God. On the part of the inscribed; just as we are inscribed in a catalog of citizens, so that we may actually possess and enjoy their rights and benefits. Conf. § 1, note c.

Adeoque vita spirituali donandis et pro haeredibus vitae aeternae habendis.

Quoad rem. Quod vel ipsum electionis nomen declarat, quatenus pauci ex pluribus deliguntur ad statum aut munus quoddam peculiare. Et quanquam in humanis prius sit v. g. eligi senatorem, posterius matriculae senatus inscribi, hic tamen, ubi scriptio non est materialis, aliam esse rationem, facile patet.

Scilicet vita χατ9 Ιξοχψ ea est, quam aeternam novimus, et sic liber vitae est catalogus hominum, ad quos vita aeterna spectat. Quamobrem et inscriptio in librum vitae absolute loquendo huc refertur, quod etiam nostrates plerique observant. Ac nos, priore significatione relicta, posteriorem jam porro sectabimur. §

5. Causa efficiens a inscriptionis hujus in librum vitae Deus b trinunus est. 612Part. m. cap. xn. Seu is, qui scribit aut inscribit. Intelligitur autem causa virtualiter causans, juxta indolem actuum divinorum internorum. Uti electionis; de qua supra cap. XII. § 12. §

6. Causa impulsiva a interna est gratia seu benevolentia Dei, externa Christi meritum b fide finali apprehendendum atque ita praevisum.c Utraque juxta id, quod de electione dictum est supra. Cujus ratione peculiariter librum vitae agni et inscriptionem in eum dici credimus; prout fundamentum inscriptionis esse Christum a quibusdam docetur. Et respondet phrasis, qua dicimur electi in Christo, Ephes. 1, 3. Quos enim praecognovit, fore in Christo Jesu, hos catalogo electorum aut salvandorum inscripsit, juxta Rom. 8, 29. §

7. Objectum inscriptionis a sunt homines finaliter credituri,. quatenus sunt salvandi b Seu personae nominatim inscribendae aut inscriptae. Alii subjedum vocant. Sub hac enim ratione formali pertinent ad catalogum seu librum ac coetum illum. §

8. Forma ipsius inscriptionis a consistit in actu b voluntatis divinae de hominibus illis notitia practica divina, in ordine ad salutem aeternam conferendam, constanter c intuendis. Seu ratio formalis. Confer. §§ 3. et 4. Vid. § 2. not. b. §

9. Finis illius a est ipsa salutis aeternae collatio Deique b gloria. Ex parte inscriptorum; prout civium catalogo inscribimur, ut juribus ac beneficiis illorum actu potiamur et fruamur. Conf. § 1. not. c.
